# Patrologia Latina, volume 162 — English translation

*Patrologia Latina*, Vol. 162

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library … of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III … Second Series.*

**Volume CLXII of the Patrology.** St Ivo, Bishop of Chartres; Peter Chrysologus, Archbishop of Milan; Richard, Cardinal; Lambert, Bishop of Arras; Galo, Bishop of Paris; Godefrid, Bishop of Amiens; Anselm, Scholastic and Canon of Laon; Blessed Robert of Arbrissel; Seherus, Abbot of Chaumousey; John, Monk of Saint-Ouen; John, Monk of Bèze; Francis Camenus; Reimbald, Provost of Saint John of Liège.

**Second volume of St Ivo; sole volume of the others.**

Printed and sold by J.-P. Migne, publisher, in the street called d’Amboise, near the gate of Paris commonly called d’Enfer, at Petit-Montrouge. 1854.

## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—entire, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, compared with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscripts.** Very carefully corrected; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works, after the most ample editions completed in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or author of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and with headings at the top margin of each page distinguishing and indicating the subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two comprehensive general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Holy Scripture, through which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon each text of each book of Scripture, and in what places in their works.

A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all the rest if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the thoroughness of the correction, both the variety and number of works reprinted, the highly convenient form of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the course of the whole work, the modest price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and small works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series, in which are published the Latin Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of the *Library of the Universal Clergy*, or *Complete Courses* in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred Greek-Latin volumes for one thousand eight hundred francs. The exclusively Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in a Latin translation.

# Letters of Saint Ivo

## Letter I

Urban [II], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the clergy and people of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0011D]

“We indeed, both because of devotion and reverence for Blessed Mary ever Virgin,” etc. It appears among the letters of Urban II, *Patrologia*, vol. 151.

## Letter II

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richer, Archbishop of Sens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0012D]

“How great were the matters concerning Geoffrey, formerly bishop,” etc. See above.

## 2. Address of Pope Urban to Ivo upon His Consecration as Bishop

[Col. 0013A]

Since, as we believe, at the prompting of God who called you, the clergy and people of the Church of Chartres [Note: Of that city.] unanimously chose you as their ruler, brought you to us, and asked that you be consecrated bishop; and since, by God’s assent, you have been consecrated bishop through the laying-on of our hands: from this point onward, dearest brother, know that you have undertaken the very great burden of labour—the burden, that is, of governing souls. You must serve the interests of many, make yourself the least and servant of all, and render an account on the day of divine judgment for the talent entrusted to you.

For if our Saviour said, “I came not to be served, but to serve” (Mark 10; Matthew 20), and laid down his life for his sheep, [Col. 0013B] how much more ought we, the sluggish servants of the supreme Householder, to labour with the utmost exertion to bring the Lord’s sheep, entrusted to us by the supreme Shepherd, by the aid of divine grace, to the Lord’s fold without sickness or blemish [“and stain”].

We therefore exhort your belovedness to preserve unimpaired and inviolable the faith which we briefly and plainly set forth at the beginning of your consecration, because faith is the foundation of all virtues. We know that from childhood you have been instructed in the sacred writings and taught the ordinances of the canons; nevertheless, we must address a brief word to you. Let no favour exalt you, no adversity crush you; that is, let your heart neither be lifted up in prosperity nor cast down in any way in adversity. Rather, we wish you to act cautiously and with discernment in all things and in every respect, so that you may be proved to live irreproachably before all.

[Col. 0013C] May the Holy Trinity keep your brotherhood safe in its protection, so that, when you have discharged in our Lord with such moderation the burden you have undertaken, you may deserve to hear on the day of eternal recompense him say: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Luke 19; Matthew 25).

## Letter III

[Note: This letter, first published by Juret, was discovered among the old papers of Antoine Loesel, jurist.]

Ivo of Chartres to Urban, supreme pontiff, his father and lord.

If I wished to yield to the impulse of my mind—if, finally, it were considered not punishable as well as intolerable to assail Peter’s successor, placed on the height of the supreme pontificate—then indeed I would not cease to move the camps of hatred against you and pursue you with curses. For I believe, and therefore I speak, that through your actions I have been drawn from the shore of tranquillity and unexpectedly cast into the depths of the sea; and I see that I am to be tossed upon the stormy waves, as it were, of temporal occupations. There, while I am compelled to provide for the interests of many, I despair of being able to suffice for either my own salvation or theirs.

[Col. 0014A] I had chosen to be lowly in the house of God. Neither nobility of birth nor distinction in learning and eloquence gave me ambition; and the devout, charitable fellowship of a few brethren [of Beauvais; cf. letter 17] pleased me more than all riches. Yet, while I was thus hidden and suspected no such thing, the Church of Chartres imposed upon me the burden of the episcopal office (letter 8). Nor would I have yielded to its will, defeated by any consideration, unless it had declared that you willed and commanded this (letter 12)—you, whom it is sinful not to obey.

I commend to your holiness the Bishop of Beauvais [Note: He seems to mean Fulk, in light of what I noted on letter 30 from Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.]. The simplicity of this man has the commendable quality that it can neither please those who act perversely nor displease those who think rightly. Your prudence knows that he has been accused in certain matters, not so much from zeal for justice as from envy of virtue. But it does not seem to me that it can reasonably be done that a matter which deserved to receive its conclusion under the examination of your judgment [Col. 0014B] should be reopened by a person of lesser standing.

But let me return to myself, who am burdened by the bonds of pastoral care; who, having not yet applied correction to my own errors, am compelled to owe correction to the errors of others; whose life, although once deemed culpable in the sight of the supreme Judge, is nevertheless now much closer to accusation of itself than to the excuse of another. Farewell.

## Letter IV

Ivo, by God’s grace humble Bishop of Chartres, to Bernard, most beloved Abbot of Marmoutier, and to the brethren who are with him [variant: “with you”]: greeting in the Lord.

Since the supreme Shepherd wished us to bear the name of shepherd and commanded us to perform the pastoral office, it is fitting that we provide suitable medicine for wandering and sick sheep. Thus we should neither smother any by excessive pressure, nor, through sloth that flatters us, negligently allow any to perish; nor should we prefer our leisure to secular affairs so as to withhold the service owed to the Church in labour.

[Col. 0014C] For although the labour of our calling aims at the embraces of beautiful Rachel, nevertheless, in hope of more numerous offspring, we must endure the embraces of Leah (Genesis 30): for whereas Rachel sees more, Leah bears more fruit; and whereas the vision of the former is most delightful to her, the activity of the latter is necessary to many. To state it more plainly: in the former there is almost solely love of God; in the latter there is manifest also love of neighbour.

The Mediator between God and human beings set forth the pattern by which this love was to be impressed upon his followers. Not only did he come forth for us from his hidden place into our public sphere, but he also gave his assumed flesh over to scourges, blows, spitting, and finally the death of the cross. [Col. 0014D] What does the supreme Shepherd teach us by this deed, except that we who are called shepherds should pursue with unfailing love the straying sheep entrusted to our care, as they flee through every byway and rough place, so that they may be brought back to the flock—even if, in following them, we are torn by brambles (below, letter 272) and bloodied by the repeated pricks of thorns?

Since I know that this does not escape your prudence, I do not know whether, so far as charity permits, I should reproach your patience or your negligence: namely, because you are keeping with yourselves, contrary to the ordinances of the elders, certain brethren whom we had once sent out for the care of souls. In this you permit both our reputation and theirs to be damaged, and you prepare no medical care for the ailments of the sheep entrusted to them.

[Col. 0015A] Therefore, passing over the rest for the present, I admonish you by asking, and ask you by admonishing, that, putting aside every excuse, you send to me by the present beginning of Lent Lord Walter, formerly abbot of the monastery of Bonneval. Having heard from him the reason for his departure, we may approve his release if it deserves approval; or, if it does not deserve approval, we may, with the counsel and help of our fellow-workers, restore him most fully to his office and place. Farewell.

## Letter V

Ivo, by God’s grace humble Bishop of Chartres, to Adela, noble countess: that she may think rightly in Christ.

[Col. 0015B]

The royal blood that descends in your eminence from both lines plainly commends the nobility of your family in everyone’s eyes [variant: “in the eyes of humankind”]. Yet, as I have learned, uprightness of character and a generous hand in giving surpass this nobility greatly in the estimation of devout minds.

I therefore wonder on what grounds you say that you love your cousin Adelaide [variant: *Adalidem*] as yourself, when you labour with such zeal either to defend or to prolong her adulterous embraces with William [variant: Wilelmus]. You provide neither adequately for your salvation nor for theirs, and you take no sufficient precaution concerning the danger and disgrace that threaten me in this matter.

[Col. 0015C] For how will the sword of the Spirit, placed in my mouth, dare to strike people far off who are defiled with a like contagion, if it will not dare—or will pretend not—to touch those near at hand? Will they not say to me those words of the Gospel: “First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see the speck in ours” (Matthew 7)?

The Apostle sternly forbids me to exercise such forbearance toward perpetrators of crimes of this kind, saying: “Those who do such things are worthy of death; and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1). Saint Ambrose calls those who consent people who conceal the matter or defend it.

For this reason I earnestly ask that your highness not be angered with me. He is my witness [Col. 0015D] before whom the abyss of human conscience lies naked: I have undertaken this not from my own ill will or another’s, but solely from the rigour and love of justice. Indeed, if it cannot be otherwise, I would rather incur human ill will than abandon the law of my God.

Yet I shall yield to your request on one condition: that each of them swear to keep himself or herself free from sexual union until the case has been concluded. Otherwise I must strive, by repeated admonition, to call forth from the lowest hell the man already four days dead and stinking far and wide (John 11; Psalm 86). Farewell.

## Letter VI

Ivo, by God’s grace, although unworthy Bishop of Chartres, to Gerard [variants: Girard; Gerald], his beloved in Christ: greeting.

[Col. 0016A]

I recently received, through the bearer of this letter, the written tokens of your charity toward me. In them you carefully asked what peace I enjoy with my neighbours and what favour with princes. You also sent an implement of snowy whiteness for arranging the hair, as a further token of charity. Though it pleases me in its kind as much as things of this sort should please on account of outward beauty, it pleases me even more because of the lofty inward meaning of its beautiful symbolism.

For since disordered conduct or disordered peoples may be understood, by a certain comparison, in hair, [Col. 0016B] I believe that by this small gift, as by a kind of reminder, your prudence awakens my vigilance: I should strive to arrange the disordered conduct of peoples through various modes of exhortation and, by maintaining the moderation of discernment, recall it to due order.

And what do you seem to signify by the beauty of the implement itself, brought to this whiteness by prolonged filing and prolonged polishing, except that I should discipline my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected? (1 Corinthians 9).

I therefore ask you, through the very depths of charity, since your brotherhood has deigned to visit me in whatever way it wished or was able, that as, by the aforesaid tokens of goodwill, you compel us to remember you frequently, so you may frequently remember us in your prayers. [Col. 0016C] Your prayers are healthier in proportion as they are quieter. Ours, though not wounded, are nevertheless often disturbed by pressing necessities [Note: Variant: “needs.” He complains of this in letter 19.] and the tumult of secular business.

Although you do not know the causes of my disturbance by experience, you nevertheless know them by knowledge. For since I was formerly in no way able, on a small river, to steer even a small boat, how shall I now be sufficient to steer so weighty and so shipwreck-prone a vessel, as one led out from the harbour of tranquillity and brought into the deep sea? If I had deserved your presence, as I asked you at Lyons, divine Mercy would, through the prudence of your counsel and through the favour you enjoy in the eyes of our citizens, have accomplished many things [Col. 0016D] which my weakness does not yet dare to attempt.

Accordingly, I persist by knocking and knock by persisting, that, when an opportunity has been sought out, you may gladden us with the consolation of your visit. This will benefit the salvation of many and will not harm the purpose of your holiness.

As for the prosperity and adversity about which you asked, the healing wisdom of God so regulates them that it permits us neither to be broken by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity, so that we may say with the Apostle: “God is faithful, who will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to endure” (1 Corinthians 10). Yet a few lie in wait for my heel; but, by God’s mercy, more desire to be gladdened by the coming forth of morning [Col. 0017A] and evening (Psalm 45).

That “pedagogue” [Note: The name “pedagogue” is taken in a disparaging sense, as in letter 98; Geoffrey is meant, concerning whom see letter 1.]—driven far away from the office and name of shepherd—now has no means of plundering the milk and wool of the lost sheep, except that in Normandy he has usurped and ravaged a certain provostship of our church, with the assistance of the foolish count of that land. Farewell.

## Letter VII

Ivo, by God’s grace humble Bishop of Chartres, to Roscelin: that he may not think more highly than he ought to think, but think soberly.

If you were the hundredth sheep, lost in the wilderness but now restored to the flock (Luke 15; Matthew 18), then, just as my zeal burned against you while I understood you to be turned away and opposed, so my spirit would rest in you if I knew that you had turned and returned to sound teaching.

[Col. 0017B] But since I know that after the Council of Soissons you most diligently defended your former opinion in secret disputations before certain persons whom you know well along with me, and wished to persuade them of the same views you had abjured, and of others no less insane, it cannot enter my heart that you have yet corrected your faith or changed your conduct for the better.

If, therefore, on this account the greedy avarice of certain violent men has afflicted you and stripped you of your possessions, their unjust violence did not accomplish this by itself. Rather, it was done by God’s just wisdom, providing for your correction [variant: “rebuke”], a wisdom which also does its good through evil people, though they do not know it. You had attempted to tear its garment with arguments armed by human reason, [Col. 0017C] though with eloquence that was barren nevertheless (letter 207).

Although the judgment of the ethical writer is demonstrably true from many examples:

> “The jar will long preserve the scent  
> with which, while new, it was once imbued.”

Horace, *Letters*, Book I, Letter 3.

Nevertheless, because of myself I would not fear or dread your presence, hoping better things of you, and things nearer to salvation. But certain citizens of ours, curious to know another’s life though sluggish in correcting their own, would regard you as hateful and me as suspect on your account. Upon hearing your name and of your former way of life, they would, in their accustomed way, rush suddenly to stones and suffocate you beneath a heap of stones. [Note: The same passage occurs in letters 34, 108, and 240, from Saint Augustine, *Confessions*, Book 10.]

[Col. 0017D] Meanwhile, then, I advise you to take up the patience of blessed Job and, although you are far his inferior, nevertheless say with him: “I will endure the wrath of God, because I have deserved it, until he vindicates my cause” (Job 6).

For I assure you: if you turn and groan in repentance, if, wishing to live in simplicity of faith, you swell no longer with the vanity of your carnal understanding, you will not lack the breasts of divine consolation [thus the old manuscripts; formerly: “the words of divine consolation”]. Mother Church, which treated you harshly in your waywardness through paternal severity, will receive you when corrected with maternal tenderness.

It remains, then, for you to write a *palinode*, a recantation; and, having recanted your reproaches, [Col. 0018A] to mend publicly the garment of your Lord which you were publicly tearing. Thus, as you were an example of error to many, you may henceforth become an example of correction [variant: “rebuke”]. [Note: A similar passage occurs in letter 141.] In this way, with a good fragrance going before, consuming the former stench, you will be able to be loved and received by us and by others, and enriched with benefits.

## Letter VIII

Ivo, consecrated and appointed bishop for the Church of Chartres by the hands of Peter [Note: That is, Pope Urban, as above, letter 1.] through the same grace, to Richer, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens: that he should not depart from the peace of the Roman Church and, if he has held otherwise, should very quickly [variant: “speedily”] come to a right mind.

I recently received from certain clerics a letter, insulting and full of bitterness, sealed with your seal and bearing your name [variant: “your own name”], [Col. 0018B] in which I deeply lamented, first, the abasement [one manuscript: “rebuke”] inflicted on me and the false accusations brought against me, and finally the not slight injury done, together with me, to the majesty of the Apostolic See. For when you had been admonished [variant: singular, “when you had been admonished”] by apostolic authority (Letter 2) to make peace and receive me as a son, you neither greeted me in that letter as a brother nor as a fellow bishop—though I have denied you neither any assistance due from a fellow bishop nor any service due from a son [Baronius: “has denied”]. Why, then, do you summon to judgment a foreigner, and bind with the bonds of obedience one whom you acknowledge neither as a suffragan nor as a colleague?

You add a still graver injury to this wrong against me, in that you most improperly call me a mutilator of the metropolitan see. [Col. 0018C] For when a dry branch, which had never grown together with the root of the mother tree and had borne no green fruit of its own, had been cut off by the hand of the great cultivator [Note: Geoffrey, mentioned in Letter 1; he also seems to be called “the enemy man” in Letter 12], that same hand which cut off the branch already dead inserted me into the same tree—not to mutilate it, but, insofar as lay within its power, to fill the place of the deceased [variant: “of the dead man”—i.e. the branch]—because it judged [variant: “considered”] that this could be done both with some hope of fruit and without injury to the mother tree. If, therefore, without your objection, it was lawful for that hand to cut off what was harmful, what reason prevents it from being lawful for it to graft in what it hoped would be beneficial?

You also [variant: “indeed”] say in that letter that I have invaded the see of Geoffrey, your fellow bishop. In this you plainly raise your head against the Apostolic See, while you destroy, so far as lies in you, what it builds, and strive to build what it has destroyed. To oppose its judgments and enactments is plainly to incur the charge of heretical perversity, since Scripture says: “He is evidently a heretic who does not agree with the Roman Church” (canon *Nolite*, Distinction 11).

Moreover, you do not well consult for your reputation when you still call a bishop, and strive to restore as bishop, that scapegoat whose adulteries, fornications, perjuries, and treacheries have been made public throughout almost the whole Latin Church; who for these and similar acts was condemned by the Apostolic See [Col. 0019A], so that, unable to clear himself, he surrendered pastoral staff and ring; and concerning whom you received the apostolic decree in these words (above, Letter 1): “Whoever henceforth assists the deposed Geoffrey in attacking or re-invading the bishopric of Chartres, we judge him to be excommunicated.” What else is it to defend his evil deeds than to call down upon oneself a like sentence of condemnation? For if, according to the Apostle, consent to the sins of others is enough for condemnation, why should it not be even more enough to encourage and defend the same sins? Nor does the shield of ignorance protect you here, since these matters, as I have said, are known not only to the churches of Lyonnais Gaul but to almost all churches of the Latin-speaking world.

There is another matter in that letter in which you have most openly and irreverently set your mouth against heaven, and your tongue has ranged over the earth (Psalm 72), when you called the blessing conferred by the laying on of the pope’s and the cardinals of the Roman Church’s hands not simply a blessing, but “some sort of blessing,” in hostile mockery [Note: He also complains of this in Letter 12]. Yet it belongs to that See chiefly and most universally to confirm or invalidate the consecration [variant: “consecrations”] of metropolitans as well as other bishops; to revise your enactments and judgments; to preserve its own judgments unshaken; and to allow them to be neither revised nor corrected by the judgment of any inferior.

Thus Pope Gelasius writes, in a letter sent to Faustus the master [Note: Gelasius to Faustus, the legate. See the canons under Cause 9, Question 3; they are the same texts.], concerning the rightful deposition of Acacius: [Col. 0019C] “They oppose canons to us, though they do not know what they are saying. By this very fact they show themselves to be opposing them, because they refuse obedience to the First See when it gives sound and upright counsel [variant: “They themselves, however, thereby show that they are opposing them”; the present reading is preferable]. These are the canons which decreed that appeals from the whole Church should be brought to the examination of this See, while decreeing that no appeal whatsoever should be made from it; and thereby they decreed that it should judge the whole Church, but itself proceed to the judgment of no one, nor did they ever command that judgment be passed upon its judgment; and they established that its sentence ought not to be dissolved, whose decrees they instead commanded to be followed.” [Note: The word “not” is superfluous in the old manuscripts, but is found in Gelasius’s letter.]

And a little later: “By what tradition of the fathers do they summon the Apostolic See to judgment?” And again: “Let them see, therefore, whether they have other canons by which to carry out their absurdities. But these canons, which are called sacred, ecclesiastical, and lawful, cannot summon the Apostolic See to judgment.” [Col. 0019D]

Likewise Gregory, in a letter addressed to Gaul concerning Aldric, bishop of Le Mans: “Let no one judge Aldric [variant: “before these words”], or presume to judge him. But if, God forbid, any grave and intolerable charge should be brought against him, our judgment must be awaited, [Col. 0020A] so that nothing may first be decided concerning one who has taken refuge in the bosom of the holy Roman Church and implores its lawful aid, until it has been commanded by the authority of that Church which has so imparted its offices to other churches that they are called to share its solicitude, not the fullness of its power. Therefore let your belovedness, in whose devotion we rejoice, join its care to our arrangements.”

And after much else: “Let it not perhaps trouble or shame you to obey our commands or comply with the precepts of the Apostolic See, because grace is given to the humble, not to the proud [Baronius: “who gives grace to the humble”]. For no one has the right to wish or be able to transgress the precepts of the Apostolic See, nor the ministry of our disposition, which your charity ought to follow. Therefore let anyone [variants: “each person,” or “whoever”] who wishes to oppose apostolic decrees be cast down in grief at his own ruin [Col. 0020B] (chapter 5, *Nulli*, Distinction 19); let him henceforth have no place among priests, but be excluded from the holy ministry; and let no one thereafter concern himself with his judgment, since he is undoubtedly already condemned by the holy and Apostolic Church and authority for his disobedience and presumption.”

Your letter also wrongly accuses me of disobedience. For although the letters of the lord pope commended me to your fatherhood as one who would obey you (above, Letter 2), no paternal admonition of yours was rejected by me, because none was heard. You slanderously allege that I sought a blessing elsewhere. But, truth bearing witness, I shall speak the truth: I sought neither the bishopric nor episcopal blessing from you [variant: “because”], [Col. 0020C] nor from anyone else [variant: “nor from any person”]. Rather, first by the contrivance of clerics and afterward by force, I was presented to the king; then, with a pastoral staff forced upon me by the king, I was brought to the church of Chartres. [Note: He likewise admits that he was raised to the episcopal throne by the hand of King Philip in Letter 22. He discusses the right concerning the staff in Letter 60.] Since, at the request and importunity of the clergy, you were unwilling to appoint any day for my consecration, I resolved meanwhile not to give wholly unqualified assent to their election until I should be certain both of Geoffrey’s deposition and of the will of the supreme pontiff. When I reached him, I was bound by apostolic authority at the petition of the Church of Chartres, and thus was consecrated bishop.

Armed with these and similar reasons and authorities, though summoned more in anger than canonically [Col. 0020D], though I have suffered injury both in myself and in my head—and yours too, if indeed he is yours [Urban]—nevertheless, at a suitable time and in a safe place within the province of Sens, or even at Étampes [Note: Below, in Letter 12, he says that at Étampes he was irregularly accused concerning the ordination received from Urban], if I have a safe-conduct—that is, Count Stephen on behalf of our lord the king, and yours because of the surrounding enemies—I shall be prepared, I say, to meet you and, so far as reverence for the Apostolic See permits, to answer your objections. Perhaps it will at some time be necessary to refer these matters to its hearing. May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your heart and your understanding [variant: “and your soul”], so that the obedience which you render to your superiors may make us obedient and devoutly subject to you.

## LETTER IX. TO PHILIP [Note: Philip I, son of King Henry.], by the grace of God the mighty king of the Franks, his lord, IVO, humble bishop [variant: minister] of the people of Chartres: May he be saved by Him who gives salvation to kings.

When I look round for a witness of my actions in my conscience, I am greatly astonished, because I find nothing in myself [Col. 0021B] for which your gracious gentleness and royal mildness should have turned against me into such bitterness that I hear from your serenity no good message, nothing but harsh words. For whatever small peace I made for the time between the monks of Bec and Molesme [Note: Compare Letter 39], I inflicted no violence upon the monks of Bec in doing so. Rather, the abbot of Bec, recognizing and ashamed of the irregular plundering inflicted upon the Molesme monks by certain newly professed monks of his own, earnestly begged me either to establish peace between them or to decide the matter justly.

But out of reverence for you I postponed judgment for the time being; and, because of the abbot’s charity, I softened the disputes between them by accepting without payment the offer of a portion of his provisions—the portion which the monks of Molesme were demanding back. Your Highness ought not to have been angered with my humility on this account. Even if I had compelled those plunderers themselves to desist from their irregular invasion, I would in no way have offended your royal majesty. For just as it belongs to royal power to uphold civil laws and punish their transgressors with the due penalty, so it belongs to episcopal office to impose ecclesiastical ordinances upon subjects as things to be observed, and to call back those who transgress them to due order by paternal severity.

Therefore let those who disturb your serenity be cut off. If you yield to their persuasions, you will neither walk in the ways of justice nor be able to attain [Col. 0021D] the joys of the heavenly homeland. Whoever they may be, if you send a safe-conduct for me and those who are with me, so that we may be safe in going, returning, and staying with you, I am ready in your presence to answer all the accusations of my rivals and to refute by unanswerable reasoning the calumnies laid upon me by them [variant: “the blind men”]. For you know how many enemies I have, especially for the sake of justice, in this land and at your court. Fare well, and do not hinder your priest from being able to pray for your safety.

## LETTER X. IVO, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Chartres, to the virgins devoted to God in the monastery [variant: cenobium] of Saint Avitus at Châteaudun: May they please the Spouse of virgins in their resolve of virginity.

[Col. 0022A]

The name of virginity is glorious, but its fruit is more glorious. For although every righteous person is commanded to follow the footsteps of his Lord as far as he can, of virgins it is written that “they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Revelation 14:4). And although every rank of married people or continent persons always has something to mourn over from the corruption of the flesh it has committed, undefiled virginity always has in its Creator something in which to rejoice. The higher its rank, the graver its fall. The happier and supreme the glory to be hoped for by one who perseveres [variant: “easier”; Note: the reading in the text is better], [Col. 0022B] the more miserable and final the condemnation to be feared by one who falls.

Virginity is the virtue of the heavenly city and the glory of its citizens, where no one has anything to lose through loss of integrity or to grieve over through corruption. Whoever in this mortal life more zealously strives after it will more familiarly delight in the visitation and love of the Spouse of virgins. But that you may recognize it as a virtue of paradise, remember that the first parents preserved it in paradise before sin; after their fall, when they became exiles upon earth, they lost it. For because they cast down the defenses of their own city, they were easily overcome by the ancient enemy and driven into the miseries of this exile; and deservedly they lost the ornaments of that same city.

Therefore, that you may be able to return from exile to your homeland, arm yourselves with the defenses [Col. 0022C] of that homeland and adorn yourselves with its ornaments, so that you may both strongly repel the cunning temptations of the ancient enemy and be able to please the immortal Spouse to whom you have vowed the integrity of your bodies. You have vowed to marry Christ, not clerics. You have vowed to marry Christ, not to frequent the conversation of secular men. The enclosure of the monastery was made for you so that you might not receive lovers of the world within the stronghold of those fleeing the world; so that you might not go out in public and, by bodily sight of the world, draw foul images inward, allow virginity to be overcome within, and then permit the body also to be subjected to corruption.

How, then, will you be able to preserve chastity, when by daily habit you labour to mix in public or private conversations [Col. 0022D] with shameless men? For you have read: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15). The blessed Virgin Mary, whose life is set before Christ’s virgins as a special [variant formerly: “spiritual”] model, did not sit in public nor delight in the conversation of suitors when she was greeted by the angel, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, and made Mother of the Saviour. So too the other holy women who wished to please God in their purpose of holiness rejected conversation with men, except those to whose needs, prompted by charity, they sometimes ministered from their own resources [Col. 0023A], or from whom they deserved to receive the grace of holy exhortation. Nor did they ever strive to please lovers of the flesh by costly dress, painted face, wanton gesture, or unrestrained gait [Note: “not” is not absent from the old manuscript]. For the immortal Spouse seeks in your inner person incorruptible beauty, not the fair corruption of the outward person [variant: “foul beauty”].

Thus you read in the Psalm concerning Christ’s bride: “All the glory of the King’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44). Therefore a virgin of Christ ought first to have humility of heart; a pale face worn by fasting; skin rough with haircloth, not carefully tended by frequent baths; modesty in speaking; obedience in hearing; frugality in food; sobriety in drink; dignity in walking; and plainness in dress—not extravagance, the nurse and sign of an undisciplined mind. In all these things pleasure must not be served, but necessity. For as a good house is recognized at its very entrance, so the disposition of a religious mind is outwardly recognized by these signs and, by the same signs, is schooled through daily progress toward contempt of self (Ambrose, *On Virgins*, II). The more contemptible anyone is in his own eyes, the more exalted he is in the eyes of his Creator.

You must also always be intent upon prayer, reading, or work, so that the devil may find you occupied (St Jerome, in chapter *Nunquam*, Distinction 5), and not find your minds exposed to harmful and wandering [variants: harmful or wanton] thoughts. For this custom is recorded in the monasteries of the Egyptians: they admitted no one unwilling to devote himself to work (St Jerome, Letter to Rusticus; and Epiphanius, *Panarion*, heresy 80), [Col. 0023C] not from necessity, but to avoid idleness, which is the enemy of the soul.

Perhaps to this you will say what certain people said when departing from the Lord and going after Satan: “This saying is hard” (John 6). “Our age cannot endure such things; our refinement cannot bear them.” To them I reply: Which of you is nobler than blessed Cecilia, who subdued her body with haircloth? Which of you is more tender than most blessed Agnes, who not only despised marriage with nobles but, as she herself says of herself, passed through the filth of the flesh by an undefiled path? The ages are full of examples of religious women and men who, in every condition, every sex, and every age, pleased the Lord by the ways described above. Why, then, will you not be able in the Father of lights to do what these men and women were able to do?

There is another thought which perhaps you will propose even silently: “If we deny our relatives their accustomed conversations, they too will deny us their usual services and withdraw from us the support we need.” To this I promise you in the apostolic voice that the faithful God, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear (1 Corinthians 10), will provide you, in place of one carnal lover, a hundred spiritual lovers, [Col. 0024A] through whom He will furnish your necessities and keep the possessions of your monastery safe and sound.

For if one of you had been joined to someone by a marriage bond [Note: variant, “united”; Augustine on Psalm 83, and canon *Quae Christo*, Cause 27, Question 1] and went over to another, would she not be judged an adulteress? Would she not be punished by judges with a capital sentence? How much greater punishments do you think she deserves who, despising the chaste marriage of the immortal Spouse, bestows her love carnally upon anyone else? Considering these things, dearest ones, cling to the immortal Spouse; devote all your love to him. Henceforth care for your reputation, which you have in part stained, lest I be compelled at some time to come to you with the rod and find you such as I do not wish, and you find me such as you do not wish. [Note: He rebukes the nuns of the monastery of Sainte-Fare similarly in Letter 70.]

Moreover, I will and command, under the highest obedience, that this letter be read once every week [Col. 0024B] in your assembly, so that you may learn carefully to avoid what is dishonourable and may strive eagerly and courageously to observe what is honourable [Note: omitted in the old manuscript] and suited to your salvation. Fare well.

## LETTER XI. IVO, humble bishop of the people of Chartres, to GONTHERIUS (variant: GUNHERIUS), his brother and fellow priest: May he, ascending from the valley of tears, sing the Song of Ascents fervently.

I rejoice that you have, as it were, returned from exile, giving thanks to our Protector, whose mercy preserved you even through the perils of the sea. Now therefore, since you have been restored safe to your brothers, although through your desire for inward quiet you cannot be useful to everyone, do not shrink from being useful at least to a few. [Col. 0024C] Accordingly I exhort your brotherhood to go to the church of the Blessed Ever-Virgin at Gournay, where you will be able both to give yourself to the quiet you desire and to provide for the salvation of some brothers. Henceforth pray for me, dearest brother, lest a storm overwhelm me as I row upon the height of the sea. Farewell.

## LETTER XII. To the most reverend Father of fathers, URBAN, his most faithful son IVO, called bishop of the people of Chartres: May he not fail amid tribulations.

Because by the sacred laying on of your hands [Note: For he was consecrated bishop by Urban at Rome; see above, Letters 2 and 8] divine providence raised me from the dung heap and appointed me a worker in its harvest, in cultivating that field of God [variant: “the cultivation of God’s field”] [Col. 0024D] I exert myself as far as I can. Yet, like one proceeding with an ant’s step, hindered by my weakness, I do not advance as much as I wish [variant: “as I can”]. In scattering the seed of the word I employ such care as divine grace supplies. But because the harvest is plentiful and much darnel was previously sown, or oversown, by an enemy man (Matthew 13; Luke 3) [Note: He seems to mean Geoffrey, mentioned in Letters 1 and 2, whose crimes he indicates in Letter 8], I find that I reap few fruits from my labour.

Fearing therefore to uproot the wheat together with the tares, and flattering myself as if with the discernment of a prudent farmer, I tolerate much and overlook much. But again [variant: “anew”], whether this is the virtue of discernment or the vice [variant: “or a vice”] of laxity [Note: these words are absent from the old manuscript] appearing under the guise of virtue, I do not distinguish clearly enough. In this anxiety of mind, while I more earnestly implore divine help, I ask from your fatherhood the necessary and due aid of your pious prayer for my insufficiency.

For I would never have wished on any account to undertake this burden unless your holiness had forewarned me and your authority had brought it about that I should undertake it. Therefore care for the son of your womb as a father; help him as a father, so that if the divine hand deigns to accomplish anything through me, it may be ascribed not to my littleness but, after God [variant: “the Lord”], to your holiness. For I see many disorders committed [Col. 0025B] in the house of God which torment me, especially this: among us, those who do not serve at the altar live from the altar (1 Corinthians 9). When I seek to deter them from this sacrilege by admonition, rebuke, and excommunication, they wish to redeem the altars from me under the name of a “person,” as they redeemed them from my predecessors [Note: variant, “forebears”; compare the words of the Council of Clermont cited in chapter *Quaesitum*, Canon 1, Question 3] according to a depraved custom. In this matter I particularly need your counsel, if it seems tolerable to you; or your aid, if it is judged intolerable. The other things in our diocese seem to me tolerable or corrigible, if this one matter were compelled by your counsel and aid to be brought into order.

Furthermore, I make known to your Blessedness that the archbishop of Sens [Richerius, from Letters 2 and 8], led astray by the counsel of the bishop of Paris, joined to himself that same bishop of Paris [Col. 0025C] and two others of no less foolishness, the bishops of Meaux and Troyes. This year at Étampes they accused me, quite irregularly, concerning the ordination which I had received from you, saying that I had offended [variant: “sinned against”] royal majesty by presuming to receive consecration from the Apostolic See. Since they were attempting, contrary to your decree, to restore the deposed Geoffrey [Note: He calls him “deposed from the episcopate” in Letter 49] to his former status and pronounce a sentence of deposition against me, I appealed to the Apostolic See and, by apostolic decrees—although they feared these only as regards the future—I recalled them from their presumption. Yet they neither undertook to prosecute the appeal nor wished to have full peace with me.

It therefore seems necessary to me that you send common letters both to the archbishop and to his suffragans, so that they may either have full peace with me or come with me into your presence to render an account of the matter. I also urge upon your fatherhood [Note: omitted in the old manuscript] that you appoint for our region some legate, a man of good repute, who seeks not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2) [Note: Compare Letter 109]. Such a man would be necessary for the Church of God, in which anyone dares anything he wishes, does what he dares, and what he does passes unpunished. [Col. 0026A] [Note: The same statement occurs in Letter 66.]

Whether circumstances concerning you are adverse or prosperous [Note: so the old manuscript, as also in the title of Letter 25], command your special [formerly incorrectly: “spiritual”] son, so that, as God grants, we may endeavour to pray: if they are prosperous, that they may be strengthened; but if adverse, that they may be driven away. If someone comes to you who has been expelled from our church because of disgrace, I ask that nothing be determined concerning him until his case has been heard more fully by you. May your Holiness fare well.

## LETTER XIII. To RAINALD [variants: RAINOLD, or RAMNALD], venerable archbishop of Reims, IVO, humble bishop of the people of Chartres: May he abound in the bowels of consolation.

[Col. 0026B] Having experienced how great is the peril of prelates, as is read in the Psalm: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing work upon great waters, have seen the wonders in the deep. They rise to the heavens and descend to the depths; their soul wasted away in evils. They were troubled and moved like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up” (Psalm 108). In that in which I am less wise by myself, I desire to be instructed or confirmed by your counsel and that of other prudent men.

Recently, when I had been summoned by our lord the king to a conference, he earnestly requested, at the suggestion of certain persons ill-disposed toward me, that I assist him in celebrating the marriage which he intended to contract with Bertrada [variant: Bertrude], called the wife of the count of Anjou [Note: Fulk, his kinsman, as he says in Letter 211; he condemns the same marriage in Letters 14, 15, 19, and 25]. [Col. 0026C] When I replied that this ought not to be done, because the case between him and his wife had not yet been decided, he testified that it had been fully decided by apostolic authority and with your approval and that of your fellow bishops.

On hearing this, I replied that I knew nothing of it and would not wish to take part in such a marriage unless you were its consecrator and author, and your fellow bishops its advocates and fellow-workers, since this belongs to the right of your church by apostolic authority and ancient custom. Therefore, because I trust in your religious integrity—that you will do or say nothing in a matter so perilous and so ruinous to your reputation and to the honour of the whole realm unless it rests upon authority or reason—I most earnestly and devoutly beseech your charity to disclose to me, as I am tossed upon the waves, the truth of this matter as you know it, and to offer sound counsel on it, however difficult and harsh. [Col. 0026D] For I would rather be deprived forever of office and of the name of bishop than scandalize the little flock of my Lord by transgression of the law. There are also concealed reasons which it is fitting for me to keep silent for the present, because of which I cannot [variant: “cannot now”] approve this marriage. Farewell.

## LETTER XIV. To the archbishops and bishops invited to the royal marriage, IVO, humble [Note: omitted in the old manuscript] minister of the Church of Chartres: May they possess, together with the spirit of counsel, the spirit of fortitude.

[Col. 0027A]

I send to your charity a copy of the letter which I sent to our lord the king, so that you may know that I have the same reason as you have for withdrawing yourselves from the marriage to which you have been invited. Therefore, you who have assembled, do not become dumb dogs unable to bark (Isaiah 56) [Note: He makes the same reproach against bishops at the end of Letter 25]; but, like good watchmen who see the sword coming upon the land, sound the trumpet (Ezekiel 33), so that, having done what you ought, you may save with yourselves both your own souls and the souls of those who heed the trumpet’s sound. The copy follows.

## LETTER XV. To his lord PHILIP, mighty king of the Franks, IVO, humble bishop of the people of Chartres: May he so serve as a soldier in the earthly kingdom that he is not deprived of the eternal one.

[Col. 0027B]

As I told your Serenity in person before your oath, so I now write while absent: I neither wish nor am able to take part in this marriage ceremony to which you summon me unless I first know that a general council has decreed and determined that a lawful divorce has taken place between you and your wife, and that you can lawfully enter into marriage with the woman whom you wish to marry. [Note: See Annon the monk, *History*, book VI, chapter 50.]

But if I had been invited to discuss this matter in a place where I could safely deliberate on canonical judgments with my fellow bishops, where I would not fear a reckless multitude, I would most willingly come in order that, with those hearing, I might hear what law and justice dictated; with those speaking, speak; and with those acting, act. Now, however, since I am summoned without qualification to come to Paris [Note: Earlier editions read *Parisium*; the old manuscripts have *Parisius*, as also in Letter 189 and frequently in writers of that age] with your wife—of whom I do not know whether she can be your wife—I would rather, for the sake of my conscience, which I must preserve before God, and for the sake of the reputation which a priest of Christ ought to have among those outside (1 Timothy 3), be drowned in the depths with a donkey-millstone [variant: “be drowned in the depths of the sea”] (Mark 9) than, through me, cause a stumbling block to be laid before the minds of the weak, as before the blind.

Nor do I think that I say this against my loyalty to you, but out of the highest loyalty [Note: Compare Letter 22], since I believe that it will bring great harm to your soul [Col. 0027D] and the utmost danger to the crown of your kingdom. Remember [Note: Letter 28 advises the same king to close his hearing against the serpent’s hiss] that the first parent, whom the Lord had set over all visible creation, was seduced by a woman in paradise, and thus both were exiled from paradise (Genesis 3). Samson also, the strongest of men, deceived by a woman, lost the strength by which he was accustomed to overcome his enemies and was overcome by his enemies (Judges 16). Solomon, wisest of men, through desire for women apostatized from God [Col. 0028A] and thus lost the wisdom in which he excelled (3 Kings 11).

Therefore let your Highness beware lest you fall into their examples and thus, together with the loss of the earthly kingdom, lose the eternal kingdom. Seek counsel from the Angel of Great Counsel (Isaiah 6), so that, having received from him the Spirit of Counsel, you may be able in all your affairs to avoid what is dishonourable and useless and to accomplish what is honourable and useful. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI. IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of the people of Chartres, to WALTER [GALTER], bishop of the people of Meaux: May he stand courageously in the Christian contest.

By your letters, recently sent to me by the bearer of this present communication, your brotherhood consulted my lowliness whether a man may take in marriage the woman whom he previously had as a concubine. This seems unlawful to you because it has hitherto been unfamiliar among you. But you now say that the matter itself has come into doubt because Roger, legate of the Roman Church—previously, incorrectly, called “Roger”; he is called a cardinal in Letter 18—at Rome affirmed this custom at Senlis and confirmed that it might be done on the authority of blessed Augustine.

We reply that on this point we possess differing rulings: some prohibiting it, others relaxing the prohibition. For blessed Gregory says in a letter to Felix, bishop of Sicily: “No Christian either may or shall be permitted to take in marriage a woman whom he has defiled by some unlawful pollution.” We also read in chapter 24 of the Council of Chalon that, according to canonical authority, abductors cannot lawfully claim for themselves in legitimate marriage women whom they have abducted. We have also, in the decree of Pope Hormisdas, that marriages contracted secretly are not legitimate. Pope Evaristus likewise says that the cohabitations, not marriages, are those of women who have not been given by their parents, endowed according to the laws, and solemnly blessed by priests. And in the Council of Aachen (chapter *Placuit*, can. 31, q. 1) it is held: “Whoever has abducted, stolen, or seduced a woman shall never have her as his wife.” Many other passages may be found to this effect.

On the other hand, we read in chapter 5 of the decrees of Pope Eusebius: “Virgins who have not preserved their virginity, if they take as husbands those same men who violated them, because they have violated only the marriage bond, shall be reconciled after one year’s penance.” Blessed Augustine also says in his book *On the Good of Marriage* (chapter *Denique*, causa 31, question 1): “That lawful marriages may indeed arise from persons badly joined together, once an honorable consent subsequently follows, is manifest.”

Therefore, as it seems to me, those Fathers who forbade concubines to become wives, commending the honorableness of marriage and wishing to restrain the foul practice of concubinage, decreed that the strictness of justice should be maintained. But when others wrote differently, I understand this to mean that, moved by mercy and making provision for the weakness of certain persons, they preferred to moderate the rigor of the canons. Between these rulings I see no difference other than that which exists between judgment and mercy. Though these repeatedly meet in one matter, their proper exercise rests in the discernment of rulers, so that, with regard to the salvation of souls, the character of persons, and the circumstances of places and times, the severity of the canons may at one time be enforced and at another time indulgence granted to those who need it (Letter 55).

So much on these matters. Concerning your request that I meet the lord king at the appropriate time to obtain peace for you, I answer in the words of the comic poet, from Terence: “For this client you need the patron whom you are preparing as his defender.” But I advise you this: do not, after the event, rashly approve in word or deed his marriage which, before it took place, you did not commend because reason opposed it (Letter 13). Rather, diligently seek and patiently await the common counsel and judgment of the nine suffragan bishops and the others. And if, for the love of justice, any adversity should befall you, bear it with equanimity, remembering that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). Farewell.

## LETTER XVII

IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of Chartres, to his beloved sons in Christ [God], together with the other brethren—whose proper names are lacking: in one manuscript space was left blank; other ancient books identify them as brethren of the Church of Saint Quentin, namely at Beauvais, as in Letters 31 and 52—that they may so maintain the course of their good purpose as to reach the prize of the heavenly calling [alternatively, “that you may reach it,” one manuscript].

[Col. 0029C] Whatever diverse or adverse reports popular rumor may spread about me among you, the anchor of my hope stands firm, for I have God as faithful, who tempers all my temptations to my weakness and supplies strength to endure them. Thus, if at any time, because of human frailty, I am disturbed by flying rumor or by threats of certain dangers, my reason argues against me—“my” is absent in one manuscript—and, if not in these words, nevertheless in this sense: “Why are you sad, O my soul? Why do you trouble me?” (Ps. 42). Your God, your salvation, who has never failed you, will nowhere—or, alternatively, “will he ever”—fail you. What is the episcopate to you—“to you” in one manuscript—but torment? What else is this honor but a burden? What is this exalted station to you—“to you” in one manuscript—but a storm that brings shipwreck?

[Col. 0029D] Therefore, if, having found an honorable occasion, you withdrew yourself from this burden and devoted yourself to yourself alone, running the course of this life without hindrance, you would reach the prize of the heavenly calling more readily. Take for yourself the wings of a dove; you shall fly away from troubles, rest, and dwell in the solitude of the mind. There you shall await him who—“you” in one manuscript—will save you from faintness of spirit and from the storm (Ps. 54).

In this deliberation of mine, and in a kind of weighing of advantages and disadvantages, I am greatly pleased by the thought that I should earnestly desire some violence to be done to me on account of justice, so that, relieved of the pastoral burden—full of wearisome bitterness [compare the passage in Letter 19], full of clouded care; alternatively, “full of wearisome care”—I might turn to that place to which honorable leisure invites me: full of sweetness that does not weary, full of delightful and radiant security.

But again, in this thought I am in some measure displeased with myself, fearing that I may not follow God’s will but anticipate it by my own desire—alternatively, “but conform to my own desire.” At last reason safely counsels me that, just as I did not anticipate God’s will by aspiring to the episcopate, so neither should I anticipate it by despising it. Rather, subject to his will in all things, I should receive from the Lord’s hand with a tranquil mind both prosperity and hardship—or, alternatively, adversity—according to the Apostle’s saying: “None of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself, but to him who died for them” (Rom. 14).

[Col. 0030B] Therefore I dare not withdraw my hands from the government I have undertaken. I dare not deny the service of my tongue to God’s people, who daily have recourse to it for counsel concerning their souls, lest I be punished with the penalty of the wicked and slothful servant. Accordingly, because of the hope of a numerous offspring, I must endure the companionship of Leah, placed before me by night, though bleary-eyed, until, after completing the sixfold work, I may by God’s grace be able to enter the embraces of beautiful Rachel.

The affection of the clergy, the devotion of the people, and the goodwill of the prince also bind me. This goodwill has been offered to me so freely that even the countess of Chartres, often mentioned by him, though I did not ask, indeed though I refused, pledged herself in my hand, in the most solemn manner, that she and the count would keep every faith toward me and would in no way fail me in any persecution that I might suffer for God’s law.

[Col. 0030C] You know, moreover, that the lord king is hostile to me because I made the reproach which I owed to make, in speech and writing, against his marriage (above, Letter 13). Therefore, until this storm changes into a breeze, I cannot—or, alternatively, “am not able to”—offer you my presence. Though absent, I desire and exhort you to pursue peace and holiness. This you have vowed; this you owe; this you also render—but render it more fully. By this good fragrance, which has hitherto proceeded from you, you shall multiply the resources of your church through frequent increases; and, going from strength to strength as children of peacemaking—or, alternatively, “of peace”—you shall sleep together in peace (Ps. 4).

Nor do I know what else to write to you, except that you must tirelessly hold fast what you have heard, received, and retained from me, and teach all—“to all” in one manuscript—who come to your fellowship—alternatively, “those coming,” one manuscript—to hold it fast. Above all, remember your common life, lest, God forbid, if avarice should take root among you, you forget the apostolic manner of life in which you wish to live and be condemned with Ananias and Sapphira by the apostolic curse (Acts 5). And because every age is inclined toward evil from youth onward, guard your young men with the greatest care, keeping them always engaged in honorable exercises, so that, reared chastely, they may be assigned to sacred ministries.

[Col. 0031A] But if anyone among you walks disorderly, report him to me by letter, so that, when you have assembled and my spirit is with you, we may rebuke him with fitting severity; for my spirit shall not rest upon one by whom the little flock is scandalized. Finally, I repeat the warning I gave (see Letter 32): appoint someone in my place—not because I wish to abandon your brotherhood, but, if the divine order so stands, so that you may at some point serve vigorously under him whom, by my counsel, you have set over yourselves. The following words have been restored with the help of ancient codices: “so that”—absent in one manuscript—and “vigorously”—also absent in one manuscript. Whatever the outcome may be, while I live I would wish to learn by experience from your manner of life what good I may dare hope of you after my death. For the rest, pray for me; write back to me concerning your inward and outward circumstances and concerning the welfare of the brethren. Farewell.

## LETTER XVIII

IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of Chartres, to ROGER, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, that he should not depart from Peter’s footsteps.

That you intend, under the cloak of apostolic authority, to release Simon of Melfa—some codices read *Melphaalius* or *Nihelfa*, which the editor judges more likely; Melfa is a small town in the diocese of Chartres; one manuscript reads *Vita*—while he still continues in his adultery, from the bond of anathema: insofar as lies in you, you greatly diminish apostolic majesty and do not wisely provide for your own reputation. For if he is bound by the just bond of anathema, and if just bonds are dissolved only by a true conversion—or, in one manuscript, “confession”—of heart, then, while he remains in the crime, what is it to destroy this anathema at the persuasion of any splendid personage except to make yourself a transgressor?

[Col. 0031C] But if, having accepted his sworn excuses for his absence—elsewhere in two manuscripts, *absentione*, in another *absentia*—from your council, you conclude that I gave a hasty—or perhaps, the manuscript seems to read, “wrong”—judgment against him (to say nothing for the moment of the fact that by his confession of guilt you conceal his crime), I answer this reasoning as follows. I judged nothing against him from the decision of your council, at which I was not present and whose decrees I neither approved nor heard. Rather, after he had often been summoned and warned, and after extensions of time, which he himself desired, had been granted twice or three times, I investigated his case with much delay and much careful scrutiny. At last, as he evaded every form of justice, I gave judicial sentence against him according to the law and bound him with the bonds of anathema until he should remove the stain of his adultery by the remedy of penance.

[Col. 0031D] Some time later, when the wife to whom he had added the woman whom he now has had died, moved by his prayers and those of certain of his friends, and unable reasonably to close—or, in one manuscript, “open”—against him the door of mercy which he sought, I gave him letters containing the course of his case for the lord pope, so that, once the truth had been learned, he might determine whatever he wished concerning it and send word back to me. I await this reply and shall not otherwise change my judgment unless I hear it either from his mouth or understand it from his letters.

[Col. 0032A] If this appears to you obstinate and unreasonable, I am prepared, in the chapter of Chartres or in the presence of the lord pope, with all my accusers present and with the laws laid before us, to satisfy the demands of justice. Farewell.

## LETTER XIX

IVO, by the grace of God humble servant of the Church of Chartres, to WILLIAM, reverend abbot of the monastery of Fécamp, that he should not be defrauded of the prize of the daily penny.

In your letter, your brotherhood wished to compare me with the great defenders of integrity and opponents of shamefulness, namely John and Elijah. Although we are far unequal to their holiness, nevertheless, insofar as God grants us power, we desire to honor, admire, and imitate their footsteps.

[Col. 0032B] Therefore we suffer grievous losses of ecclesiastical goods not only from the king, whose unlawful marriage we opposed (Letter 13), but also from certain other children of this age, whose perversities we resist as far as we can. We endure their plundering with long-suffering, through God’s grace, in expectation of a greater recompense; and, if necessary, we are prepared to undergo greater things (as above, Letter 16), recalling the Apostle’s saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8), and: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2).

And because those dangerous times are now at hand in which the saying written is fulfilled, “Through the abundance of iniquity the charity of many shall grow cold” (Luke 23), we must say to the rocks of the mountains: “Fall upon us and hide us from the wrath of the Lamb” (Rev. 6). What else is this to say—the following clause is lacking in one manuscript—except to implore men robust in faith and eminent in holiness: “Mercifully stoop down to our misery, and obtain by your prayers that we may not be led into temptation or incur God’s wrath”?

[Col. 0032C] Since we do not doubt that you and many in your holy fellowship are such rocks, we earnestly seek this intercession from you before God, so that we may pass through fire and water in such a way that, under divine guidance, we may be brought into refreshment. For we, occupied with the tumults of public affairs—of which he complains in Letter 6—can scarcely, even by laboring all day to restrain them, suffice for the task; we hardly ever admit the sweetness of inward quiet. We rarely even prevail in performing the canonical office at its appointed hours.

[Col. 0032D] You therefore, and the other servants of God, who sail as it were in harbor, ought to stretch out to us the hands of prayer as far as you can and strive to lead us with you to the desired rest. Moreover, concerning that brother whom you ask me to absolve so that you may freely receive him as a monk, I answer you that, if you knew his conduct by experience as I do, you would not care to have him either bound or loosed—or, alternatively, “would not seek him.”

[Col. 0033A] For he is great in his own eyes, loving the foremost places at feasts, the chief seats in synagogues, and greetings in the marketplace. Though he has renounced the world, he attends to the vanity of clothes and delights in changing places. He is so idle that for ten years he has not completed half a week of the Masses assigned to him in the order of his turn. He has attempted to do so as often as the honor he desired was not bestowed on him by the brethren; and he has ceased as often as he found a place in which to fulfill his vanity. If the brethren of that place absolve him, I shall not hold him bound. Otherwise I cannot do this.

If, then, that brother is so dear or necessary to you, seek this release from his fellow brethren, because, whatever he may say is permitted to him, he is bound without any condition, by the bonds of canonical profession, both to the stability of the place and to the fellowship of the brethren. Farewell.

## LETTER XX

IVO, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to the clergy and laity of Chartres, greetings.

I have heard that the leading men of your city have sworn together that they will make war against the viscount for my release. This is by no means my release, but rather—one manuscript reads “but,” instead of “nor”—not merely an aggravation of my imprisonment, but its endless prolongation. Therefore I prohibit and forbid that it be done. For you cannot please God by burning houses and plundering the poor; you can only greatly provoke him, and without his good pleasure neither you nor anyone can free me.

Therefore I do not wish you to make the ears of God resound against me with the cries of the poor and the lamentations of widows. [Col. 0033C] For it is not fitting that I, who did not come to the episcopate by arms of war, should recover by arms of war (below, Letter 30) what belongs not to a shepherd but to an invader. If the hand of the Lord has touched me and is still stretched out over me, permit me alone to drink my misery to the dregs and bear God’s wrath until he vindicates my cause. Do not heap another’s misery upon my tribulation.

For I am resolved not only to be imprisoned or deprived of ecclesiastical honor, but even rather to die than that slaughter of human beings should occur because of me. I therefore admonish you by the surpassing love of Christ: neither do this nor allow it to be done. Yet if you do it, it is certain that it will profit you nothing, since my detainer has many helpers and possesses nothing that you can take away from him.

[Col. 0033D] Remember what is written: “Peter was kept in prison, but prayer was made without ceasing by the Church to God for him” (Acts 12). Be content, therefore, with prayers and ecclesiastical severity. If you transgress this, I know that you no longer wish to have me as bishop. For in withdrawing once already, as the outcome proves, you did not provide well either for me or for yourselves. Henceforth be content with the boundaries set by your fathers, lest, if you are content with them, I perhaps seek my release [Col. 0034A] in a manner that does not please you. Farewell. May the God of peace and consolation—or, in one manuscript, “of peace and love”—grant you in this affair and in all others to think and act rightly.

## LETTER XXI

To the venerable HOEL, by the grace of God bishop of Le Mans—so in all copies; one manuscript earlier has *Boello*—IVO, by the same grace bishop of Chartres, that he may remain in the affections of Christ.

First I give thanks to God my deliverer, on the day when he rescued me from the hand—or, in one manuscript, “hands”—of all my enemies and from the hand of Saul. He had been thrown into prison by the viscount; see above, Letter 20. Then I give thanks to your most watchful charity, which by intense cries of prayer awakened the Lord sleeping in the ship—or, in several manuscripts, “sleeping amid many”—so that, when he rebuked the winds and the sea, the cloudy storm ceased and calm serenity returned (Mark 4).

[Col. 0034B] Thus you have bound me to yourselves by closer bonds—or, alternatively, “ties”—of charity and have acquired an inexcusable executor of your benefits. Yet amid this cloud of my mind, I have not had full consolation, because I was still confined in prison and did not deserve to be present at that holy rejoicing when the body of blessed Julian was translated. Your brotherhood could quickly turn this cloud of my heart into serenity if you were willing to share with my lowliness some relics of that holy body.

For the patronage of your place would not thereby be diminished; rather, through my occasion, the fame and merit of the blessed confessor would be made known in the Belgic province, where his merit is less well known, and his feast would be celebrated solemnly every year. Therefore tell me, through this brother when he returns to us, whether this can be done, so that I may either send to you or, if it seems good to you, come myself. Farewell.

## LETTER XXII

To PHILIP, most pious king of the Franks, his lord, IVO, humble bishop of Chartres: that he may so govern his temporal kingdom as not to lose the eternal one.

Since, by preceding divine grace, I have been raised from the poor man’s dungheap to the throne of princes through your hand—the reference is to the episcopate; in Letter 8 he says that the pastoral staff was forced upon him by the king—I confess that, after God, I owe you, according to my ability, all things that befit your honor and welfare. But because, angered by the salutary admonitions which, with the utmost fidelity [Col. 0034D] and charity, I addressed to your serenity [see Letter 15], you withdrew your pledged faith from me—he uses the same expression in Letter 173—and exposed the goods of the episcopal household to be plundered by our adversaries, I have suffered from this grave and great losses [compare Letter 19]. At present I can neither safely nor honorably attend the royal court.

I therefore beseech your majesty to bear with me meanwhile in royal gentleness, until I may recover my breath somewhat and repair in part the losses inflicted upon me almost to the point of want of bread. I also expect, through God’s mercy, that you will soon recognize as true Solomon’s proverb: “The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who flatters” (Prov. 27).

[Col. 0035A] Moreover, when it has been made known to me who my accusers are and what they demand, I shall not evade answering those to whom you order me to reply: in church, if the matters are ecclesiastical; or at court, if they are court matters. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIII

IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of Chartres, to WIDO—thus written in seven ancient exemplars, and also in the title of Letter 47, which has the same subject; it was formerly printed *William*. Some parchments bear only the first letter without an expressed name, whence the divergent interpretation arose—steward of the lord king, greetings.

Dearest friend, since I know that you are willing to labor to make peace between me and my lord the king, I give you many thanks. But because this peace could not be stable so long as he wishes to persist in what he has undertaken, my counsel is that we should still wait to see whether perhaps God may give him a good mind, so that he may wish to change—or, alternatively, “turn”—his counsel for the better.

[Col. 0035B] If he should wish to do this, know that everything necessary is prepared to bring about a divorce between him and his new wife—namely Bertrada, his concubine, mentioned above in Letter 13. For I have seen the letters which the apostolic lord Urban sent to all the archbishops and bishops of his kingdom, directing them to bring him to reason and, unless he repented, to compel him by ecclesiastical discipline to come to amendment. Those letters would already have been published, but for love of him I have so far caused them to be withheld, because I do not wish, so far as depends upon me—the alternative reading is corrupt: “in ne est”; the same passage occurs in Letter 28—that his kingdom should be stirred against him on any pretext.

Tell all this to our lord king, and send word back to me according to what you find in him. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV

To HUGH, reverend archbishop of Lyons, humble IVO, bishop of Chartres: that he may abide in the affections of Christ.

I have heard that the apostolic lord Urban has restored to your charity the apostolic legation which you exercised commendably (Letter 109) in the time of his predecessor, Pope Gregory of blessed memory. I heard and rejoiced in the things said to me (Ps. 121:1), both because of the sincere charity with which I embrace you and because of the common benefit of Christ’s Church.

But afterward my joy was disturbed when I was told that, amid so great a disturbance, you were unwilling to put your shoulder—“your” in one manuscript—under this burden, persuaded by some who say that, because the head is sickly, aid cannot suitably be given to the diseased body, nearly exhausted—or, alternatively, “deprived”—of strength.

[Col. 0036A] But such counsel belongs to unskilled physicians, who stroke swellings and, by stroking them, cause corruptions to spread; they love their own tranquility, not the health of the sick, and do not heed what Truth says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician—or, alternatively, ‘doctor’—but those who are ill” (Matt. 9).

Although another Ahab has arisen in the Italian kingdom and another Jezebel in the Frankish kingdom, seeking to undermine altars and kill prophets, nevertheless Elijah must not say, “I alone am left, and they seek my life” (1 Kgs. 19), lest the divine answer say to him: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal” (ibid.). Though Herodias dances at Herod’s pleasure, asks for John’s head, and Herod grants it (Mark 6), John must nevertheless say: “It is not lawful for you to abandon your wife unlawfully and take in marriage the wife or concubine of your fellow countryman.” Though Balaam teaches Balak to eat and fornicate, Phinehas must nevertheless not spare the Israelite who fornicates with the Midianite (Num. 25). Though Nero, at Simon’s persuasion, binds and imprisons Peter—“in prison” in one manuscript—Peter must nonetheless say to Simon: “May your money be with you unto destruction” (Acts 8).

[Col. 0036B] For the more diligently the rashness and audacity of the wicked strive to weaken the settled order of right, the more vigorously their wickedness must be resisted, provision made for the Christian religion, and the lamentable ruins of the Church opposed.
