I write these things not as though you were ignorant of them, but I would have your paternity persuaded to put your hand again to the plow, root up from the Lord’s field such thorns as you can, and not delay to sow over it seeds that will bear a harvest.

So much on this. For the rest, I most devoutly ask your paternity to write to my lowliness whether you intend to lend a hand to the imperiled ship of the Church, even [Col. 0036C] as it is almost suffering shipwreck, and where I may find you around the beginning of Lent. Certain ecclesiastical affairs must be discussed by me with your prudence: burdensome for me, but not burdensome for you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXV

To URBAN, supreme pontiff, IVO, his special son: obedience not of servile fear but of chaste love.

I have often intended to approach your presence, to visit the sweetness of your fatherhood and relieve my daily crosses. But Satan has hindered me, and I have not yet been able to fulfill my vow. For, fighting daily with beasts (1 Cor. 15), I find no rest for my spirit [Col. 0036D]; and I mourn with great contrition of heart the pitiable ruins of the Christian religion, to repair which scarcely anyone, or no one, labors.

Therefore, because I see that I preside but benefit almost no one, I often consider renouncing pastoral care and returning to my former repose [see Letter 17 and the end of Letter 219], where I may await him who will save me from faintness of spirit and from the storm (Ps. 54). But almost the sole thing holding me back is love for your fatherhood, to which I myself cannot adequately measure how much I owe.

[Col. 0037A] Yet, unless I seemed to set my mouth against heaven (Ps. 72), I would bring an action for injuries against him who, when I had served seven years for Rachel, commanded Leah to be placed before me by night (Gen. 29). If she at least bore children and compensated by her fruitfulness for Rachel’s beauty, she could scarcely at last be tolerated on that condition: that after another seven years the opportunity might be granted to attain Rachel’s embraces. But now, because I experience this woman’s barrenness and do not enjoy the other’s delight, I judge myself more miserable than any human being; and I cannot persuade my soul to endure so lamentable a loss for a long time—one manuscript reads “that I should endure.”

If, therefore, it pleases your holiness that I should endure still longer, forge for me an iron rod (Ps. 2), with which earthen vessels may be broken, so that mercy for one may not bring many into danger. I submit this to your holiness because a cleric of our city [compare the end of Letter 12], by false accusations, has now for the second time assailed the ears of your piety, saying that he was accused on conjectures and proscribed on suspicion alone—or, alternatively, *suspectione* for *suspicione*.

[Col. 0037B] But the cause for which he was separated from the clergy has been revealed by such manifest indications, proclaimed by such certain accusation, and demonstrated by such evident result, that no one—not merely among the citizens, but even among the suffragans—doubts that he caused counterfeit coin to be made in his own house. And at the proper time, in your presence, I shall prove, God willing, that this public crime and certain of his dreadful offenses truly occurred in a church of that—or perhaps “a certain”—provostship which Geoffrey sold to him against the will of all the brethren. Geoffrey is the person mentioned in Letter 1.

For this reason, out of regard for charity, I refused to accept the oath that he offered me, knowing that he wished to add the sin of perjury to his earlier sin. Yet, out of reverence for your fatherhood, to which he had fled, though deceitfully, I was willing in the meantime to grant him in full the income—or, alternatively, “revenues”—of one prebend and to allow him food with me at table, until I could deal with this affair in your presence and, by your counsel, mercifully restore whatever appeared to require restoration.

[Col. 0037C] But he, being proud and arrogant, behaved as though by telling lies he had recovered lost innocence. He would assent neither to me nor to his friends unless I restored in full whatever he demanded—things that are not in my power and cannot be taken, against their will, from those who have lawfully received them. Therefore, as may seem good to your discretion, write back to my lowliness something in this matter that will neither add horns to this fool and the others nor exceed my own powers.

[Col. 0037D] I had now intended to come to you, but he most industriously publicized my journey throughout the whole route to Rome. Moreover—the following is absent in one manuscript—this brother will be able to tell you what losses, sufferings, and persecutions I have borne this year, within and without, for God’s law (as above, Letter 19). I have without delay sent your holiness’s letters, secure despite my danger, to the metropolitans and their suffragans—against the king’s adultery, as mentioned above in Letter 23; but they still keep silent like mute dogs unable to bark. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVI

IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of Chartres, to WALTER—alternatively Wulfer or Wulfep—abbot of the monastery of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, that he may stand manfully in his holy purpose.

Since, through the grace divinely granted to you, you faithfully administer to your fellow servants the grain which you can, although you find those same fellow servants ungrateful and insufficiently concerned for their salvation, do not grow weary under the burden and heat of the day, so that, when the day is completed, you may deserve to receive the daily penny from the householder.

For I have heard from your brother Raimbert—or Rambert—a monk of our monastery, namely Saint Quentin at Beauvais, founded by Ivo himself, [Col. 0038B] that, harassed by the frequent onslaught of outward tribulations and worn down by a certain weariness on account of the undisciplined manner of life in the monastery entrusted to you, you intend to lay down the burden imposed on you—an abbot may, with the bishop’s consent, leave his place, chapter *Abbas*, canon 18, question 2—and retire into leisure, choosing rather to be saved in a low place than endangered in a high one.

This perhaps is a good intention, but one to be weighed with the utmost and repeated deliberation, lest the angel of Satan, transforming himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11), under the cloak of this pious intention cast you down from the state of your rectitude and thus gradually, in secret, lead you into committing some disorders.

For if you can benefit some persons there, it is not sound counsel that you should leave in disorder brethren who have been entrusted to you in due order. Rather, spending all your care upon them inwardly and outwardly, you should summon the good to better things by word and [Col. 0038C] example, endure the bad while correcting them, and love all alike. For blessed Pope Gregory says (causa 24, question 4): “The bad must be borne with equanimity where some good persons are found.”

But if all among you are so hostile to their own salvation that your labor is utterly fruitless, I advise your brotherhood to leave the accursed land for a blessed land, where, if not another’s salvation, you may at least provide for your own. For blessed Benedict, your spiritual father, did this when poison had been offered to him: he was unwilling to preside over those whom he could not benefit (St Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 3). If you imitate him, you do not in any way act contrary to monastic profession.

I have taken care to write these few words to you in place of many, at the urging of your said brother Raimbert—Rambert in one manuscript—namely that you should carefully consider the whole matter of this counsel of yours: either bear with long-suffering and some fruit the burden laid upon you, or, if you are to live without any fruit, lay it down. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVII

IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of Chartres, to EUDES—one manuscript has *Eudoni*, another *Reudoni*—steward of Normandy: that he should not grow lukewarm in good zeal …

Your affection has asked me whether, against one who, before his ordination, having been accused by you and other reputable persons before the metropolitan and the bishops of the province of the heresy of simony and certain crimes, evaded the appointed day of examination by bringing it forward, and, having obtained consecration through the violence of a prince, was intruded into an episcopal see, you ought to proceed against him as against a bishop or merely as against a cleric. I answer this question plainly: although through the ignorance of some he may be thought a bishop, he is not so regarded by those in whose consciences he is an invader and a heretic. Hence Pope Leo says in his letter addressed to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Ep. 90, ch. 1; and ch. 1, Distinction 62): “No reason permits those to be reckoned among bishops who have neither been chosen by the clergy nor sought by the people.” And shortly afterwards: “Who can doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred ought not to be attributed to them?” [Col. 0039A–B] These words show that episcopal honour is by no means to be attributed to intruders.

The same Leo proves that they are not even worthy of clerical rank, in a letter addressed to the bishops of Gaul and Germany, saying:

> The faith of the holy Fathers ought thus to be preserved in the Catholic Church: whoever, with blameworthy rashness, has assumed what he did not receive must lose what he had.

[Note: This is attributed to Pope Silverius in ch. *Sic decet*, Causa 25, question 2, Epistle 86.]

Blessed Gregory likewise confirms, in his letter sent to Syagrius and his fellow-bishops, that such persons are not priests:

> Whoever strives to purchase the priesthood by the giving of a price seeks not the office but the name; he desires not to be a priest, but merely to be called one.

[Note: Epistle 110, book VII. See Gratian, under the title *Spirit. emere*, Causa 1, question 1.]

The same writer, in his letter to Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople (Epistle 169, book VI), says:

> As a position of government must be denied to those who desire it, so it must be offered to those who flee from it. And as it is written: “No one takes this honour upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” [Hebrews 5].

And elsewhere:

> Just as one who, when invited, refuses, and, when sought, withdraws, ought to be brought to the sacred altars, so one who voluntarily seeks office or intrudes himself importunately must undoubtedly be repelled.

[Note: Gregory, book VII, Epistle 110 to Syagrius; and in ch. *Sicut*, Causa 1, question 6, book XXX, *On Bishops and Clerics*.]

Hence Pope Paschasius says: “How can we avoid such bishops, abbots, or clerics, when, if we are with them or pray with them, we incur excommunication?” [In one manuscript: “if we even pray together, we are subjected to excommunication”; so manuscript c. 7.] To believe at all that such men are priests is utterly mistaken.

Their rejection is also stated in the canons promulgated at Paris:

> If anyone, through royal ordination, has presumed with excessive rashness to seize the summit of this honour, he must by no means deserve to be received by the bishops of the province, who know him to have been unlawfully ordained.

[Note: Chapter 8 of the First Council of Paris, and ch. 5, Distinction 63. In six old codices the word here written is “at Paris.”]

Blessed Ambrose therefore says in his *Pastoral Book*: “To carnal eyes he appears a bishop as though great, but to the divine gaze he is a leper, who acquired an unlawful rank through money.” Blessed martyr Cyprian also says:

> The people, obedient to the Lord’s commands and fearing God, ought to separate themselves from a sinful priest, since they have the power to choose the worthy and reject the unworthy; for in the Law the Lord shows that priestly ordinations ought to take place only with the knowledge of the people standing by, so that, in the presence of the people, either the crimes of the wicked may be exposed or the merits of the good proclaimed.

[Note: One old codex reads “divine” rather than “the Lord’s”; book I, Epistles 3 and 4. See ch. *Plebs* and following, Distinction 63.]

If, therefore, your grounds are sound, it follows that you must not proceed against him as a bishop [variant: “because”], whom the foregoing authorities do not allow to be a bishop. For, as Pope Boniface says: “It is clear that one confesses a crime who does not make use of the opportunity to clear himself by a granted and delegated judgment.”

Moreover, according to the practice of the Roman Church, procedure against the heresy of simony and that of neophytes differs from that against other crimes (Gratian, Distinction 48). For whereas in other accusations the innocence of accusers and witnesses is investigated, even persons of bad repute are admitted to accuse such men. [Col. 0040A–B]

I could have spoken more fully on these matters and gathered many similar passages from authoritative writings to establish this judgment; but, to avoid making the letter too long, let this suffice for the present. Hereafter I advise your affection not readily to commit yourself in this case to the judgment of those who see their own danger threatening in the deposition of this intruder. For blessed Leo says:

> Bishops who consecrate as priest one who ought not to be such—even if in some way they escape loss of their own rank—shall nevertheless thereafter have no right of ordination, nor shall they take part in that sacrament which, disregarding the divine judgment, they have improperly conferred.

[Note: Epistle 85, to the bishops of Africa; quoted in ch. 24, *Si qui*, Causa 25, question 2. “Thereafter” is absent from manuscript c.]

If therefore judgment is rendered against you otherwise than justice requires, summon the judges themselves to the apostolic hearing, without which affairs of this kind cannot conveniently be concluded. I shall also commend your cause in my letters to the lord pope, if your envoys pass by me. As for the pope concerning whom you asked: I entered Rome peacefully with him in November; I left him there in January. He is still there, and, so far as God grants him strength, struggles against the adversaries of the Roman Church. [Note: Compare the passage at the beginning of Epistle 43.] Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXVIII

To PHILIP, by the grace of God magnificent king of the Franks, IVO, humble cleric of His Exaltedness: that he may so govern himself as to be able to please the King of kings.

[Col. 0040D]

I recently received Your Excellency’s letter, in which I was instructed to meet you, with a troop of soldiers, at Pontoise or Mont Calv, on the day you had appointed, intending to go with you to the conference which is to take place between the king of the English and the count of the Normans. Many great and weighty causes prevent me from doing this at present.

First, because Pope Urban, by apostolic authority, forbids you the bed of the woman whom you have as your wife; and because you forbade the making of the oath concerning the security of the council which he had commanded you. [Note: See Epistles 211 and 46; compare Epistle 35.] Unless you now cease intercourse with her, that same authority separates you from participation in the Lord’s body and blood. It also forbids all bishops to place upon the head of that woman a crown, whom, as is said almost everywhere on earth, you have unlawfully joined to your side.

Therefore, sparing Your Majesty, I refrain from entering your presence, lest, compelled by the command of the apostolic see—to which I must obey in Christ’s stead—I should be forced to proclaim publicly in your hearing and that of many others what I now say in your ear. Yet I do not wish to scandalize you or diminish your royal majesty, so long as I can keep silence on some honourable ground. [Col. 0041A–B]

Furthermore, nearly all the tenants of the church and the other soldiers are either absent or excommunicated for breach of the peace. I cannot reconcile them without satisfaction, and I ought not to send excommunicated men against the enemy. [Note: Thus in six old codices; elsewhere, “I do not dare.”] Finally, Your Serenity knows that I do not enjoy complete security at your court, where that sex is suspicious and hostile to me—which is at times not sufficiently faithful even to its friends. [Note: Because of Bertrada, whose enmity he mentions in Epistle 50.]

I wait, therefore, until at some time divine mercy enlightens your heart, so that you may close your hearing against the serpent’s hiss and open the ears of your heart to counsels of salvation. [Note: See Epistle 13.] This is my desire; for this I pour out prayers daily before God. [Variant: “I pour”; so manuscript c.] Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXIX

IVO, humble bishop of Chartres, to ROGER, his fellow-brother and fellow-presbyter: greeting.

[Col. 0041C]

Since from your childhood you have been nourished and instructed under the discipline and fear of the Lord, and corrected in the failings of regular life by the severity both of words and of blows, you were promoted not only to the dignity of the presbyterate, but your name also rose to such brilliance that your reputation became celebrated not only among the learned but among God’s servants as well. Hence certain persons, seeking good pearls, set aside many others equally or more shining and, in their judgment, found you as a pearl singularly precious; and they set you upon a lampstand as a burning and shining lamp, that you might give light in the house of God.

Who, then, has bewitched you? Who has blinded the eyes of your heart, so that you did not take every possible precaution not only against committing this disgrace imputed to you, but even against its being plausibly fabricated concerning you? [Col. 0041D] I had thought the burning heat of fleshly desire had been cooled to the marrow within you by the river of your tears; and, if that burning fire had at any time left anything cauterized in your conscience, I thought it softened by frequent meditation upon Holy Scripture, as by the application of a tempering poultice, and healed by the divinely infused anointing of the Holy Spirit.

I thought that the angel smiting the firstborn of Egypt had passed over your house among the Hebrews, marked on both doorposts, and had left your firstborn untouched (Exodus 12). But now public rumour declares that you have returned to Egypt, and that this firstborn—namely chastity—has been shattered within you by the hammer of the whole most miserable earth. [Variant: “has perished,” according to some.] At this, weeping presents itself to my eyes almost every day; this now comes back upon me from behind; this is frequently borne in upon my ears from right and left, as though it were new. This is whispered and spread abroad by the inquisitive talkativeness of devout little women. This saddens the dwellings of hermits. This is regarded, as though with pitying wonder, by the communities of monasteries. Certain assemblies of churches seize upon it mockingly as an argument in defence of their own abuses.

Hearing this and therefore groaning deeply, I could no longer endure without pouring out to you the sorrow of my heart, and making you sorrow healthfully through my grief. [Manuscript of Saint-Germain: “pouring in.”] I therefore advise you, whether what is said be true or merely plausible, to descend, on finding an honourable occasion, from the lampstand upon which you have been placed (Matthew 5), lest from now on you emit more smoke than light to those around you. [Note: The same advice is given to Aldebert, Epistle 277.]

For if these things are true, your teaching is discredited among your hearers, and, burdened by the load of your own shameful acts, you will not correct those of others. But if they are only plausible, even so you will make no progress, because you have neglected your reputation, which you ought to have preserved unstained for the benefit of your neighbours. [Col. 0042A–C] If, rejoicing in honour and seeking your own interests, you desire more to preside than to be of use, that community of poor brothers entrusted to you will not merely fail to increase further through your hand, but will be reduced to nothing through daily losses.

But if this counsel now seems unbearable to you, I adjure you by the tribunal of the eternal Judge before whom you shall stand: at least now, suffused with salutary shame, flee henceforth the conversations of suspect persons; dread familiarity with them, lest that prophetic saying be justly cast in your teeth: “The face of a harlot has become yours; you refused to blush” (Jeremiah 3). [Variant in old codices: “be cast in your teeth,” as often elsewhere.] Otherwise, in the future, removed from the face of the Judge, you will be handed over to an officer to be punished without regard for one who pities. [Col. 0042D]

I write this not to shame you, but to admonish you as a most dear son: provide for your salvation, and do not corrupt the morals of the simple by a perverse example. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXX

IVO, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, to FULCO, by the same grace bishop of Beauvais: strength in adversity and humility in prosperity.

[Note: In several old codices the following chapter-heading is prefixed: “He did not approve of a bishop’s overcoming the proud by arms.”]

Since the devil, our adversary, goes about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5), I admonish your brotherhood by this familiar exhortation to strive to guard against all his deceitful circuits with every vigilance, so that, mindful of your purpose and office, you may overcome worldly pride not by the weapons of worldly wickedness but by the weapons of Christian warfare. [Col. 0043A; Note: Epistle 20 is to this effect.]

I also advise by exhorting, and exhort by advising, that you in no way raise your head against the commands of the lord apostolic and of his legate, the archbishop of Lyons, in whom still remains some anchor of our hope, if you intend to reach port after however many storms. [Note: Hugh, concerning whom see Epistle 24.] I send you a copy of the letter that the lord pope sent me concerning the king’s case, after the king’s envoys recently departed from him. [Note: Compare Epistle 28.] Thus you may know that the lord pope, though he does not advance, nevertheless does not retreat. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXI

To FULCO, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais, IVO, by the same grace humble bishop of Chartres: that the anchor of steadfastness may hold him in his holy purpose.

[Note: In several old codices occurs the following chapter-heading: “How he laid down the headship of Saint-Quentin into the bishop’s hand.” This letter should be compared with the following one.]

[Col. 0043B]

Since I have known, both by learning and by experience, that superiors ought to be constantly present among the community entrusted to them, after it pleased Him who had invited me to His banquet to say to me as I reclined in a lowly place, “Go up higher” (Luke 14), I frequently admonished the brothers entrusted to me to choose for themselves, from among their fellow-brothers or elsewhere if they preferred, a superior who could preserve them in the discipline handed down to them and, through daily admonitions, raise them from the valley of tears to the ascents of the heart; lest the invisible wolf, finding an entrance, should enter the Lord’s sheepfold and either snatch away the Lord’s sheep outside it or strangle them within by hidden bites.

Although for their own reasons they have hitherto postponed this, they have at last yielded to my exhortations and intend, as God inspires their minds, to set over themselves someone who will strive, according to the strength granted him, to minister to their needs both spiritual and bodily. Therefore, at the very hour when you receive this letter, by this same letter—though absent in body, yet present in spirit—I lay down into your hand the headship which I have hitherto held in the church of Saint-Quentin. I earnestly entreat that whomever that community unanimously, or the part of sounder judgment regularly, requests to be set over it, you may establish in the place and rank in which I was there, and may, in fulfilment of your office, relieve him in his difficulties with fatherly consolation.

Yet although I lay down the headship, I do not abandon fellowship with that church, in which I may sometimes be useful to you, if God restores peace to His servants. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXII

IVO, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Chartres and faithful brother of your community, to his fellow-brothers: the devoted service of brotherhood.

[Note: Thus the title is worded in the old codices. He addresses the canons of the church of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais; compare Epistles 17 and 31.]

Just as a ship deprived of the presence of its helmsman—even though it has good sailors and other helpers of the vessel, and even favourable wind—nevertheless either drifts, is submerged by waves, or is dashed against rocks, and thus finds lamentation rather than harbour; so the Church of God, bereft of the presence of its ruler [one codex: “its shepherd”], is endangered in many ways in this world as on a shipwrecking sea, and is either long delayed from entry into eternal rest, as from entering harbour, or removed from it forever. [Col. 0044A]

Considering this, as I have often advised before (as above, Epistle 17), so I now advise and grant permission for you regularly to choose yourselves a ruler, whom you should regard with every honour as worthy to be the father of your souls, and whose saving admonitions you should obey in all things with complete humility. For I do not wish, at peril to you and me, to preside over you without benefiting you: to occupy the land and choke, by my shadow, the harvest which cultivated ground would bear. [One codex: “suffocate.”] I would rather see you living under another’s rule than mourn you dead under the covering of my own headship; rather have you ordered as brothers than disordered as sons.

For I do not wish to have laboured among you without cause, you whom with a mother’s affection I begot from the old man into the new through the fear of God; whom I brought up with the milk of my twin breasts until you received solid food; whom I loved so singularly that I rejoiced with those who rejoiced, grieved with those who grieved, became weak with the weak, and bore your burdens with such gentleness as parents can scarcely be found to have endured their own fleshly children. [Col. 0044B]

Since, then, through some dispensation of God which I do not know, you cannot draw milk from your mother’s breasts, seek yourselves an adoptive mother, from whose breasts you may suck milk; lest some of you, weaned before the time, fail to find the mother for whom they wait, and thus fail to attain solid food. [Col. 0044C]

In choosing, therefore, consult all together: let none seek a private opportunity there, none swell with private ambition, none be contentious or refuse humbly to submit to the man whom brotherly concord, having considered the common good, asks to be set over them. Yet he must now be examined by you all the more diligently because afterwards he is not to be criticized but borne with equanimity by all. I do not wish to designate a particular person for you, but to leave you free choice, so that you may bear your chosen man more patiently because you have voluntarily set him over yourselves.

Yet I retain this one right within your fraternity: if I wish to have with me any one of the brothers, send him to me as a son to his father, and permit him without scandal to remain wherever I wish. [Note: “To you” is absent in manuscript c.] In this you need not be afraid, for I shall observe moderation sufficiently. I also wish meanwhile to have this privilege among you: if—God forbid—any dispute should arise between your superior and any brother, and one of them should flare up against the other with some intemperance of zeal, and if this cannot conveniently be calmed among yourselves, this matter must not come to public ears before it is brought to me. I shall endeavour either to moderate that immoderate zeal or at last to give force to canonical severity. [Col. 0044D–0045A]

For an inexperienced charioteer, not knowing how to govern the reins, causes the horse to be exhausted by speed at the very first run. Since therefore the governance of souls is the art of arts and burden of burdens, once your superior has been instructed by practice in that art—what he ought to overlook and what he ought promptly to punish—then, content with his judgment and your own, you will be able suitably to conduct all your affairs.

Whoever he may be, let your fraternity choose such a man as knows how to bring forth from his treasure things new and old; who also knows your dispositions, and whose disposition is not unknown to you. For stones fit together better when, having often been brought into alignment, they have laid aside their unevenness through the repeated exercise of filing. If perhaps he proves less experienced in external affairs (in ch. *Petrus*, Distinction 39), a good conscience and good testimony will assist him in arranging everything entrusted to him. Let him also appoint for himself a provost, who, with his and your counsel, may manage all external matters. But he himself should remain within—[one manuscript: “for the time being”]—devoted, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, to prayer, reading, and the nurturing of brotherly love. [Col. 0045B]

I say much; but, as though only now weaning you, I would have you instructed in everything, that you may know what is right [variant: “good”] and fulfil in action what you rightly understand. But because you are not sufficient for this, consult the Angel of Great Counsel, that He may direct your counsels and bring them to a good end. [Variant, Saint-Victor manuscript: “to the good end.”] May the God of patience and consolation be with you. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXIII

IVO, servant of the Church of Chartres, to LAMBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Arras: the gift of sincere affection.

If our places were as near to one another as our minds are, I should often wish to be delighted by your sweet speech and refreshed by your consolation. I should desire often to pour out my troubles to you, to show you the frequent assaults of my disturbances, that they may be driven away by your prayers, and to bewail with you the lost peace of my spirit—in which I was at times permitted to taste the sweetness of divine love at the table set with the divine word. [Variant in old codices: “to meditate.”]

But since, at God’s command, you too have rowed out into the deep in order to let down nets for a catch, you can now assess my dangers from your own—the dangers which the Psalmist declares that superiors experience in the deep:

> They go up to the heavens and go down to the depths; their soul was wasting away in evils. They were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.  
> —Psalm 106

[Col. 0045D]

In these dangers there is one singular counsel: that with our whole affection we cry to the Lord, to whom sea and winds obey (Matthew 8), that He may turn our storm into a breeze and still its waves. If the Lord, sleeping in the ship in order to test our endurance, delays, let us endure patiently; for He will come, and will not permit us to be tempted beyond our endurance (1 Corinthians 10). For the rest, dearest brother, share your joys and sorrows in their due season with one who is diligent and beloved; for your joys and sorrows are mine, as I do not doubt that mine are yours. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXIV

IVO, humble servant of the Church of Chartres, to ROBERT, a brother now of good hope: ascents in the heart.

Since, as we have learned from the report of certain persons, the world and all its vain hope have now become cheap to you, we believe that favourable divinity has begun in your breast its temple and the holy place of its dwelling. Therefore, to the Giver of all good things, through whom this praiseworthy change from oldness to newness occurs, we render thanks; and we ask that the same Giver of all good things may grant your good beginnings a happy progress and a good end. [Col. 0046B]

You therefore, dearest brother, with divine mercy aiding you, take careful heed lest the unclean spirit, returning to you, find the house he left vacant within and adorned without, bring with him seven other wicked spirits clothed in the appearance of virtues, and thus make your latter state worse than the former (Luke 11). Therefore, since you are to fight against spiritual wickednesses, if you wish to fight safely, join yourself to the camp of Christ’s soldiers who fight in ordered ranks. Otherwise, if you strive, untrained, to fight in single combat against trained opponents, you will be crushed by the innumerable multitude of your adversaries. [Variant: “you strive”; manuscript c.]

But after you have been armed with the Spirit of Counsel and Strength and have learned to avoid the wiles of the ancient enemy, then, more practiced in spiritual combat, you may, if it should happen, enter alone into combat against any enemies whose assaults you have learned to endure in the battle-line. Hence our Lord Jesus Christ warned His disciples, not yet strengthened by the Holy Spirit and still inexperienced in spiritual combat, saying: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24). [Variant: “warns”; old codices and manuscript.]

I could write many things of this kind to your brotherhood; but because you have understanding of your own accord, I especially entreat this: since you have already begun to offer to God from what is yours a sacrifice in His members, strive above all to offer Him a whole burnt offering from yourself. Otherwise—God forbid—it may be said to you: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned, when you bestow what is yours and keep yourself for yourself.” [Note: He cites and explains this in Epistle 47.] Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXV

To RICHER, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy mother Church of Sens, IVO, servant of the Church of Chartres: obedience according to the constitutions of the Fathers; and to his fellow-bishops assembled in the city of Reims, the service of brotherly affection.

[Col. 0047A]

If you had remembered the divine law, of which you ought to be teachers and guardians, you would not have summoned me to a council contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers—especially when you do not know my crime or disgrace. First, because certain bishops who are not my fellow-provincials summoned me: without apostolic authority they ought not to be my judges, since the general decree of both decretals and canons decides that foreign judgments have no force. [Note: Quoted in ch. *Peregrina*, with the following passage, Causa 3, question 6.]

Second, because, at the urging of my metropolitan, you seek to draw my case outside the province. Since this has been prohibited by many enactments of the holy Fathers, I shall bring forward one of the many, that of blessed Pope and martyr Stephen, which, like a two-edged sword, strikes down both designs—that of the summoner and that of the accuser. Blessed Pope Stephen says (Epistle 2):

> The liberty of accusation must not go beyond the boundaries of a province; but every accusation must be heard within the province and concluded by the fellow-provincials, unless appeal has been made solely to the apostolic see.

And: “The liberty of bringing accusations must be denied to accusers before they have rid themselves of the crime under which they are burdened” (ch. *Qui accus. non poss.* and ch. 1, Causa 3, question 11). [Col. 0047B]

Finally, because my accusation proceeds not from the path of truth but from the tinder of hatred, I appeal to the apostolic see. [Note: He says in Epistle 67 that he is harassed by pseudo-bishops.] Apostolic authority grants this to all persons accused of a crime: that it may investigate my case, either itself or through its representatives, in the place and at the time it prescribes for me, and, when the pleadings are complete, order a lawful sentence to be pronounced.

Nor do I, conscious of innocence, do this to avoid judgment; for my clearing of the charge of perjury is plain and brief, since I have never at any time sworn an oath to any person now alive. But I do not wish to become an example to others of departing from due order; nor is it sound counsel to expose myself to certain dangers for an uncertain benefit, or none at all. I sought safe-conduct from my lord the king and could not obtain it. [Note: Compare Epistle 28.] [Col. 0047C]

Indeed, so far as I can gather from threats not yet carried out, I would not be permitted with impunity to speak truth in your assembly. For that truth already stated, and for obedience to the apostolic see, I already suffer such severity that I am accused of having incurred perjury and of having diminished royal majesty. [Note: Absent in the manuscript.] But, with your leave, this charge can more rightly be turned against those who, like kindly physicians, neglect to burn with appropriate cauteries or cut away with the surgeon’s knife a wound made incurable by poultices. [Note: He speaks of King Philip’s marriage with his concubine; on this see Epistle 13.]

Had you stood firmly with me in this judgment, you would already have restored our sick man to health. So long as you delay, consider whether you fully discharge the loyalty you owe and fulfil the duty of your office. Let the lord king, then, do against my smallness whatever, as God permits, he wishes and is able: let him imprison, exclude, or proscribe me. By God’s grace inspiring and sustaining me, I have resolved to suffer for the law of my God; and under no compulsion do I wish to agree with him in fault, since I do not wish to share with him in punishment. [Col. 0047D–0048A] May the Angel of Great Counsel and the Spirit of Strength be with you, that you may understand what is right and do what is right. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXVI

To the reverend fellow-brother PETER, bishop of Poitiers, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: that he may plant good things in such a way as not to strive to uproot good things.

If we could summon your brotherhood before a court, we should, so far as could be done without violating the bond of charity, demand redress from you for many injuries, some common and some personal. Personal injuries: because you compelled, by our admonition and authority, a cleric serving God in our diocese—who, for the beauty and sweetness of contemplative life, was yearning with all his desires for the fountain of life—to go forth into public and interrupt his peace.

When, repeatedly compelled by your letters, we granted him to you for the governance of a certain regular church in your diocese, and sent him after he had been canonically elected by that church itself, he suffered at your hands a rejection far from fitting. In a perverse order, you then began to dispute his headship precisely when, after his election had been made by the brothers and approved by you, you ought to have installed him in the seat of his priory. [Col. 0048B–C] In this you inflicted no small humiliation upon that brother and committed no slight injury against your friend. [Note: The old codices read “your,” that is, Ivo’s; earlier editions wrongly read “our.”] For a friend from whom a gift is requested with such urgency ought not so readily to have been rejected, with a changed judgment, to the injury of both gift and giver.

Nor do the letters of the lord pope protect your brotherhood adequately. We were present at his side while they were being composed; they confirm to the abbot of Saint-Cyprian that right in the aforesaid church which he said he possessed through the lawful grant of certain monks. [Note: This passage has here been restored from the old codices; see the note.] These monks—as we have heard—approve the clerics’ peaceful possession, but altogether disapprove the intrusion of the monks of Saint-Cyprian. For the aforesaid abbot was striving by every means to have the priory of that church granted to him by the lord pope. The lord pope refused to do this, despite our protest and our defence, so far as we were able, of the clerics’ freedom; taking care, as he himself said, lest the abbot under this pretext devise the exclusion of the clerics and the intrusion of his own monks. [Col. 0048C–D]

You inflict a public injury upon the clerical order by raising the monastic order to such ruinous pride that you strive to subject clerics to it. Yet clerics ought to possess such excellence that, according to blessed Augustine: “A good monk scarcely even makes a good cleric.” [Note: Epistle 76 to Aurelius; quoted in ch. *Legi*, Causa 16, question 1.]

But because a cleric has said these things about clerics, let us hear a monk speaking about monks. Jerome says:

> A monk’s office is not to teach, but to mourn.

[Note: *Against Vigilantius* and *On the Institutes of Monks*; and *On the Praise of the Solitary Life*.]

And elsewhere: “Clerics feed sheep; I am fed.” And elsewhere: “If you wish to be what you are called—a monk, that is, one alone—what are you doing in cities?” (Gratian, Causa 16, question 1). Cities, surely, are not dwellings of solitary persons but of many. Every calling has its own leaders. To come to our own case: let bishops and presbyters have as their examples the apostles and apostolic men, whose honour they possess and whose merit they should strive to possess also. But let us have as leaders of our own calling Pauls, Anthonys, Julians, Hilarys, and Macariuses.” [Col. 0049A–B]

And elsewhere: “To me a town is a prison and solitude paradise. Why do we desire the crowd of cities, when we are defined by singleness?” We could gather many passages in this manner concerning the privilege of clerics and the subjection of monks, were we not avoiding the excessive length of a letter. Yet in saying this we do not disparage monastic religion; rather, we desire with our whole mind that they may be true monks—that is, that they may truly pursue a solitary life. We praise them indeed and profess them blessed if they do not transgress the boundaries established by their fathers (Proverbs 22); and we say that they are then more blessed when they strive more to be subject than to preside, since humility and obedience are their highest advancement, whereas ambition and pride are a lamentable downfall. [Col. 0049B–C]

Consider these and similar matters carefully. Honour the clerical order in which you are and over which, by God’s authorisation, you preside, by urging it toward better things; and permit it to be subjected to no other order contrary to ecclesiastical custom. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXVII

IVO, servant of the Church of Chartres, to ROBERT, his brother beloved in Christ: remember Lot’s wife.

Glory to the merciful and wise God, who has subdued your heart—vainly [variant: “emptily”] puffed up and wounded by sharp arrows—to such humility that you now flee to the rocks of the mountains and, desiring to hide from the wrath of the Lamb (Rev. 6), ardently seek from them the life of salvation [col. 49D]. And since you have begun to love the beauty of God’s house and, ascending from the valley of tears, to sing the Song of Ascents, as you yourself know, it remains only that, with the Apostle, forgetting what lies behind, you stretch forward to what lies ahead (Phil. 3), until by an ascent of virtues you reach the mountain of Bethel (Isa. 3), where you may follow with tears of longing the Beloved as he flees, and at last embrace him when he returns in the arms of inward love.

But what manner of life is suitable, or what place ought to be chosen for walking in the way of God by one so disposed as you now are, your brotherhood has not asked, nor can I myself know, unless, when I knock at the door of your heart, you yourself disclose your inner agitations and simply reveal wherein the old man resists you, preventing you from bringing the new man to perfection [col. 50A]. Although, for some reason that hinders it, this cannot presently be done, I shall nevertheless pray to God for your beloved brotherhood that he who has begun his temple in your breast may himself bring it to completion. At the same time I exhort you to choose a settled manner of life, such as God himself has inspired in you [note: “himself” is absent in manuscript c.], in which you may tread the way of humility under the bridle of obedience [variant: “ways”], and learn discipline both through the experience and through the example of your own life.

For thus it is fitting that, beginning from the lowest things, you should be borne upward to the highest, rather than, beginning from the highest, fall away to the lowest. Since in our own times you yourself have seen and heard this happen in certain persons [note: “you yourself have seen” is absent in manuscript c.], you ought to be corrected—or rebuked—by their example, lest you incur a like reproach of backsliding [col. 50B]. Therefore grow feathers in the nest before you fly on high, so that, once the wings of virtue have been strengthened, you may lower them to govern the active life and raise those same wings to the height of contemplation. Farewell. Excuse me to Brother Lambert, because I have not yet been able to write what he wished. I shall write what God grants, when it is opportune for me.

## LETTER XXXVIII. IVO, humble servant of the Church of Chartres, to GUACELIN [variant: GUALCELIN, manuscript c.], venerable bishop of the people of Winchester [printed thus in manuscript c.; formerly “of Wintonia”], greetings.

[col. 50C]

The fame of your generosity, veiled by no cosmetic of pretence, has long been made known to me by many and has pleased me. Trusting in it, through William, provost of Saint-Saturnin, I asked your munificence for a chrism-vessel whose form was unknown to our craftsmen, and I obtained it without delay. The giver’s charity made it more pleasing to me than the petitioner’s desire had done.

Therefore, whenever it is set before my eyes for necessary use, your memory is sweetly recalled to my mind, and fraternal charity is stirred to return the favour should an opportunity arise. Thus I ask your brotherhood also to keep the memory of your fellow brother in your mind, so that you may extend to me, who desire it, the hands of your prayers [note: all the ancient books read “hands”; formerly “gift”; thus manuscript c.], and show me by some sign whether I have obtained this favour from you [col. 50D]. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX. IVO, humble servant of the Church of Chartres, to ANSELM, venerable archbishop of Canterbury: the gift of the prayers of the faithful, according to the measure granted to him.

Although it pleased him who invited you, when you were not seeking high things, to say, “Come up higher” (Luke 14) [variant in seven manuscripts: “that he might say to you, though you were not seeking it”], we do not therefore believe that your fatherhood [variant: “your,” manuscript c.]—a burden to no religious person—is any less mindful of those whom it once loved in Christ, or from whom it received some fraternal service for Christ’s sake [col. 51A]. Yet if this should at some time occur because of the daily pressure of ecclesiastical affairs, we, not unmindful of you [variant: “us,” manuscript c.], bring the remembrance of our lowliness to your exalted mind by such means as we can [variant: “we take care to bring it back”; manuscript c. reads only “to bring it back”], since we desire to be supported by your prayers and, if need be, assisted by your resources.

This year, because of our great goodwill toward you, we stood by the monks of Bec against the monks of Molesme, insofar as reason and authority enabled us [note: Letter 6 appears to relate to this]. And they would already have obtained full justice through us concerning the monastery of Pixiacum [note: elsewhere called Pixicensis, Pixinacensis, Pijacensis; the same variation occurs in the heading of Letter 45], had they not first sought to win the king’s favour [col. 51B].

Furthermore, I commend to your fatherhood Brother Rothard [variants: Rohard or Rotrard], the bearer of this letter, sent into these regions by the obedience of his fellow brothers, that you may strengthen him with counsel and aid in whatever he needs. But if our service can in any respect be useful to your holiness, command one ready to obey. Farewell.

## LETTER XL. IVO, not sufficiently fit minister of the Church of Chartres, to Brother MANEGALD: that he may carry Christ’s cross in such a way as to be able, by its oarage, to cross the sea of this world.

Since, after many wanderings, you have chosen to take up Christ’s light burden and, despising the flower of the world, to live humbly in the house of God [col. 51C], knowing that “a little is better for the righteous than the great riches of sinners” (Ps. 36), we render thanks to divine goodness, which gives grace to the humble. And we pray that same divine goodness more earnestly, that from the talent entrusted to you, like a faithful money-changer, you may return to your creditor a manifold increase.

For the order of reason itself required that you who had instructed very many in the way of life by word should at last shape and strengthen some by example; and that you who, from the seed of the father Jacob, like Zilpah, had borne children through the stale and servile habit of philosophizing, should now, from the seed of that same father, like lovely Rachel, not cease to multiply spiritual offspring from the liberty of inward vision [col. 51D] (Gen. 29). In saying this [so manuscript c.], I do not presume to teach Minerva, from whom I myself have greater need to be taught; rather, rejoicing in my brother’s advancement, I desire better outcomes to be added to good beginnings.

At the same time I beg you to assist with your prayers, from the harbour of your tranquillity, my faint-heartedness as it rows on the high sea and almost sometimes suffers shipwreck; and at times to console it with salutary counsels. For I believe that your prudence knows that, while I was serving for Rachel, Leah was substituted for me by night (Letters 4 and 17). I accepted her unwillingly [variant: “although unwillingly”], and unwillingly endure her: she sees little, bears little, but vexes greatly. Wearied often by these troubles [col. 52A], I groan deeply as I look back upon the beauty of the tranquillity I have lost; and, given the wings of a dove, I desire to fly away (Ps. 54) and again to be at leisure. In this disturbance my only refuge is to pray and to await him who may save me from faintness of spirit and tempest (ibid.). If I did not fear to dissent from his will, being unequal to so great a burden, I would gladly withdraw my shoulder from that same burden.

Therefore, when any persons pass into our regions from you, or return from them, cause me to see your inward person in your letters, as you have in part seen mine in mine. Furthermore, I commend to your brotherhood this brother, bearer of the present letter [some add: “letters”], that you may receive him as a familiar friend [one manuscript: “kindly”] and answer him graciously in your lectures. For, so far as one can judge of a man, he seeks to be built up, not puffed up [col. 52B].

## LETTER XLI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to GAUFRED [variants: GOIFRED, GOIFFRID, GODEFRID], abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, greetings with affection.

So far as I could discern from the tenor of your letter, the chief point of your inquiry was whether a monk who has been blessed only by a monk, and not by his own abbot, ought to be blessed again by his abbot. I judge that this may be done, and may also be omitted, without detriment either to the person blessed or to the person giving the blessing. For a monk’s blessing is neither the laying on of hands nor the celebration of any sacrament handed down from apostolic tradition [col. 52C]. It seems to me to have no more force than absolution pronounced over a penitent, or the prayer of a priest over the people.

For Blessed Jerome says: “The monk does not have the office of teaching [variants: “is not”; or, “the office of a monk is not teaching”], but of mourning: he should mourn for himself and for the world.” Therefore, just as a monk benefits himself alone in this office, so by the grace of the one who calls, he can come to this office alone. Nor does it prejudice his salvation whether he receives the blessing simply from a monk [variant: “from a simple monk,” manuscript c.] or from an abbot, because no outward addition makes a true monk, except contempt for the world and complete love of God.

This is readily apparent in the founders of this order, Paul and Anthony, and many other Egyptian monks. Receiving no blessing from a preceding abbot or monk, they attained the perfect reward of their labour from him who “makes monks dwell in a house” [col. 52D]. But later, when monastic congregations had multiplied, professions were required of them and blessings bestowed upon them. This was done as a precaution, so that the more firmly and solemnly the monastic order was bound in the sight of God and human beings, the more robustly and devoutly it might be observed by them. And if any should wish to withdraw from this purpose, they might be convicted by more witnesses [variant: “conquered,” manuscript c.] and, as recruits sworn to Christ’s service [one manuscript: “perjured”], be compelled to return to their purpose.

From this it is clear that traditions of this sort are nothing but certain bonds of religion, provided for human instability [col. 53A]. For every religious tradition flourishes and blooms in its newness and rarity; but through antiquity and multiplicity, unless it is strictly bound and observed, it grows cold and cheap. Therefore this seems to me to be left to the discretion of abbots: whether they ought to repeat in their presence professions made before others, or blessings given by others. For this is not to violate ecclesiastical sacraments by repeating them, but to place bond upon bond [variant: “bonds upon bonds”] because of the instability of persons.

But if a monk’s blessing were consecration, even among the Cluniacs [note: thus read from the better manuscripts; Letter 78 mentions the monastery of Cluny; formerly printed incorrectly, “among the Gloriacenses”], among whom, as you assert, this custom exists, no repetition of the blessing could—or, variant, should—at all be made. Hence even the consecration of virgins [col. 53B], which by apostolic authority is reserved to bishops as their privilege (canon *Sicut* and canon *Presbyteri*, distinction 68), if it is at any time usurped by priests, is never repeated by bishops because of the sacrament of Christ and the Church contained in it.

I have said what I think on the question proposed; and, so far as appears to me, I have departed in no respect from reason or authority. Farewell; and write to me how you fare in your journey or return, and what you hear concerning the counsel of the lord pope.

## LETTER XLII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to HUGH, by God’s grace bishop of Soissons: be strengthened in the Lord.

Hindered by public affairs, I have not been able to write to your brotherhood the many things I wished. But if I should sometime be granted your sweet conversation, I would say many things safely in your ear which a little sheet could not conceal if, before reaching your hands, it fell into those of enemies [col. 53C].

For the present, therefore, I urge you to occupy your youth with honourable exercises: reading, prayer, and meditation on the sacred law. Thus, if at any time some foul image, bursting through the windows of the senses into the temple of the heart, attempts to imprint itself there, it may either be repelled altogether at its entrance, or, if through some negligence or importunity it has slipped through the door of the heart, be expelled with disgrace while chaste dignity flourishes within.

Thus, by the testimony of a good conscience, you will be able to rejoice in God’s righteousness and confidently [one manuscript: “faithfully”] pour out to your neighbours the taste of inward sweetness. Nor can the discourse of a teacher be unfruitful when the power of divine love kindles and forms him within. But if your brotherhood should thereby incur the hatred and slanders of the wicked, you must endure the blows of words, since you are among those who, walking in the apostolic rank, endured for God’s house not only the plundering of their goods but also bodily tortures and deaths. What they suffered in defence of the faith, we must suffer in rebuking criminal deeds [col. 54A]; otherwise we shall be shepherds feeding ourselves, seeking our own advantage, not healing diseased sheep but devouring the strong and fat ones (Ezek. 24).

Nor should the scarcity of present examples deter you from this courage, since such a reason cannot excuse us before the judge of inward things. Farewell, and for the love of God and of us, help under your protection our brothers serving God at Bistesiacum [variant: Bistisiacum], and sustain them with fatherly care against the attacks of their enemies.

## LETTER XLIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to his lord and father URBAN, supreme pontiff: to fight with Peter and reign with Peter.

Since the Roman Church, after many shipwrecks, has almost reached harbour under your governance [col. 54B], and the kingdom of Italy, long rebellious in your sight [note: above, Letter 24, he says that another Ahab had arisen in the Italian kingdom; at the end of Letter 27, that Urban was struggling with adversaries at Rome], has now almost entirely fallen silent, so that the new king has placed himself in your hands according to the will of God and your own, I rejoice in the Lord; and I am unable to express my joy within any limits of syllables.

I also multiply daily prayers before God for your safety and peace: that through you the word of God may run (2 Thess. 2), advance more and more from day to day, and bring to completion the good things which he has begun through you. I make known, however, to your exaltedness that William [variant: Willelm; concerning him, Letter 5], a brother of good promise, brought up in the Church of Chartres, has been elected bishop by the Church of Paris. He did not wish to presume anything of this kind without our counsel and assent [col. 54C].

Accordingly, we sent with him certain brothers, that they might diligently inquire whether the votes of all concurred in his favour, and whether the election had been extorted from the king through money or some violence. When they reported that all was well, we gave that brother counsel and assent to yield to the election and not withdraw himself from divine appointment. For we feared that another might be introduced by a side entrance and defile the Church with the plague of simony.

We also added to his counsel, because he seemed to us somewhat below the lawful age [note: thirty, called the age of a perfect man in the Council of Agde, cited in the canon *Episcopus*, distinction 77], that he should defer promotion through the ecclesiastical grades for suitable intervals [note: on intervals between orders, Gratian, distinction 77], and meanwhile, either personally or through messengers, seek from your fatherhood a dispensation for such matters as were lacking for the completeness of ordination [col. 54D].

What I write while absent, I would say in person if an opportunity were offered; and for that Church itself and with that Church, I ask your fatherhood, in great confidence toward you [variant: “with great confidence of mind,” manuscript c.], not henceforth to lend an ear to any enemy concerning accusations against it [variant: “give an ear”]. Through the bearer of this letter, determine yourself by your letters for me and for that Church by what order and in what way the undertaking begun may be brought to its end with your favour. May the Lord, I pray, crush Satan beneath your feet (Rom. 16) [col. 55A]. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV. IVO, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to all established within the bishopric of that same Church, greetings in the Lord.

Let it be known to you, beloved, who believe that you belong to the heavenly Jerusalem, that if you desire to deserve the gift of the heavenly King to which you have been called, you must preserve the peace commanded you by God, with every plague of discord removed. For when Christ entered the world, he announced this peace to the world through angelic revelation, as the heavenly host sang together: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). As Christ was soon to depart from the world and shortly return to heaven, he commended this peace, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave with you” (John 14) [col. 55B]. The Apostle warns that it must necessarily be kept: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12).

For since Christ’s coming was intended to reconcile not only heavenly and earthly things with one another but also earthly things themselves with each other, so that in the unity of faith and Christian peace they might become one body of Christ, what benefit will Christ’s coming bring the person found outside peace? You professed this peace when, returning to God, the author and lover of peace, you renounced at the font of life the devil, author and lover of discord, and all his works.

Therefore, brothers, if you do not wish to dissemble, a great necessity of observing peace has been imposed upon you [note: thus the Vatican/Puthean manuscript; others read “enjoined”; manuscript c., Letter 50: “the peace which has been imposed”], since, bound by the sacraments of the eternal King and in expectation of an eternal reward, you have devoted yourselves to the heavenly militia [col. 55C]. For let your brotherhood know with certainty that no place for discord remains in Christ’s kingdom. Only against the author [variant: “agent”] of death and his works is unceasing discord enjoined upon us.

Therefore, since, as has been said, the faith of Christians ought to maintain continual peace [note: thus the Vatican/Puthean manuscript, as he said shortly before: “in the unity of faith and Christian peace.” Others read, “The borders ought to have peace”; manuscript c.], and since not only their minds ought to be free from vices but their hands also from vicious deeds, see how far you still fall short of Christian perfection [variant: “of Christian perfection for yourselves”]. You compel the days which you vowed to heavenly service for the pursuit of salvation to be remitted to you for the practice of malice and the finding of death.

Consider, brothers, if any one of you were to cut his flesh with iron, burn it with fire, or afflict it with any other torment on three days in succession, but on four days merely ceased [variant: “were free”], would he not be bound by his friends? Would he not be taken to a physician as a madman? How much more should one who wounds or kills his own soul be bound with stronger bonds of Christ [note: “of Christ” absent in manuscript c.], that he might cease from the death of his soul and labour unceasingly for life [col. 55D].

But because every age is prone to evil from youth onward (Gen. 6), and wicked people, loving the wages of sin more than righteousness, rise against their correctors [variant: “rebukers,” manuscript c.] as madmen against physicians, we, expecting from you things better and nearer to salvation (Heb. 6), tolerate your imperfection, overlook your impiety, and, since amid abounding iniquity we cannot heal you perfectly, prefer to have you weak and wounded rather than wholly dead.

We therefore ask and entreat, and by the authority of the Lord Jesus—whose embassy we exercise, though unworthy—we command you, mindful of your salvation, at least to keep firmly peaceful these four days [thus the Vatican/Puthean manuscript; variant: “to show yourselves firmly peaceful”], on which both our Lord and Saviour more plainly performed the healing sacraments of our salvation. Restrain your minds, hands, and tongues from every injury [variant: “evil act”], whether against enemies or friends, foreigners or natives [col. 56A–B].

For everyone who is a disciple of the Christian religion knows that on Thursday [variant heading: “observance of Thursday”] the Lord Jesus celebrated his last supper with the disciples (Matt. 26; Luke 22), in which he committed to those same disciples his body and blood—the sacraments of our reconciliation and medicines of our wounds—to be eaten and drunk, and thereafter performed in remembrance of himself. When the mystery of the supper was completed, he washed the feet of those same disciples, as a sacrament of repentance and remission (John 13). By this sacrament he signified [variant: “is signified,” manuscript c.] that even religious hearts are defiled by earthly dust and that there is no mortal who does not need repentance and the forgiveness of sins [col. 56B–C].

At the end of that day, betrayed by a disciple, he was delivered into the hands of the Jews; and he bore this with such patience that he did not resist those mistreating him in any respect, but even graciously restored the severed ear of the servant of the high priest (Luke 22). On Thursday also, after completing the dispensation of his incarnation, he ascended into heaven in glorified flesh in the sight of the disciples (Mark 16), henceforth interceding for us at the right hand of the Father, so that the humility of the flock may follow where the exaltation of the shepherd went before.

What in all these things did our leader show but examples of peace? Namely, that on the day when Christian people received so many medicines unto life, no one, by harming another, may rather harm himself; no one, by killing another, may rather kill himself. For while the injured person perishes outwardly, the one who injures perishes inwardly [variant: “more inwardly”] [col. 56C–D].

On Friday the first Adam was fashioned from clay (Gen. 1), and the second Adam, coming to redeem humanity, was incarnate in the Virgin’s womb at the angel’s announcement (Luke 1). On that same Friday Christ suffered, and ruined humanity was refashioned into God’s image through Christ’s blood (John 19). Therefore, on the day when peace was restored to the world, every person ought to keep peace, lest he return to the death which the first-created human brought upon the whole world.

But on Saturday [col. 57A] God rested from all his work, the Holy Spirit thereby signifying to us that we ought not only to rest from every vicious work, but also to await the rest after the time in which we must keep sabbath from every burdensome work. For it will not be burdensome perfectly to love God and, out of love, to persist without ceasing in his praises. As a figure also of the future and present sabbath-rest [one manuscript: “as a sign also of the present sabbath-rest”], on the aforesaid day Christ’s flesh rested in the tomb, while his soul meanwhile conquered hell and, overcoming the strength of the ancient enemy, brought back the spoils that had been lost.

Therefore, Christian redeemed by Christ’s blood, do not show yourself ungrateful for the benefits of your Redeemer. On this day of your deliverance and rest, do not increase hell by your presence: do not seize your neighbour’s goods, and do not again persecute in his members him who did not seize what belonged to another but gave himself for you [col. 57A–B].

Of the eighth day, which is also the first, no believer doubts that on that day the Lord rose, and by his resurrection gave us a certain pledge and example of our twofold resurrection, in which full peace will be given to the children of adoption, the flesh no longer lusting against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5). For these and other reasons, which would be burdensome to enumerate in a brief discourse, our elders decreed that peace was especially to be preserved on these days, and ordered diverse and severe punishments to be inflicted upon violators of peace according to the rank of the persons and the gravity of the evils.

Following their footsteps as far as we can, we command by exhorting and exhort by commanding that you observe without dispute the peace whose written constitution we send you, and confirm it by your own hand, touching the most holy relics [col. 57C]. For this is good for you, both for the increase of temporal possessions [some: “bodily possessions”] and for the advancement of unchangeable goods. Peace and mercy from God to those who obey; but whoever will not obey this constitution [variant: “these constitutions”], let him be anathema, maranatha. Farewell.

## LETTER XLV. IVO, by God’s grace bishop of Chartres, to the clergy of Mantes and to all within the archdeaconry of Pixiacum [note: several manuscripts read thus; elsewhere Pixecensis; manuscript c.: Pixeiensis, Pixicensis, Pixetensis, as in Letter 39], greetings.

[col. 57D]

It has come to our ears that the count of Mantes wishes to take in marriage the daughter of Hugh, count of Crépieux. The concordant authority of decrees and canons does not permit this [Puthean manuscript: “the authority of the canons contends against its being done”], saying: “We forbid unions of blood relatives.” Their relationship is neither unknown [variant: “unrecognized”] nor remote, as distinguished men descended from the same line testify and are prepared to prove.

They say that Walter [variant: Gautier] the White begot the mother of Count Waleran [variant: Gualeran], who begot the mother of Count Robert. Likewise, the aforesaid Walter [Gautier] begot Ralph, father of another Ralph, who begot the countess of Vermandois. From her was born the wife of Count Hugh, whose daughter the count of Mantes now wishes to marry [col. 58A].

If this genealogy is connected as stated, the marriage cannot be lawful but will be an incestuous union; nor will they be able to have legitimate children, but only illegitimate ones. Therefore, by apostolic and canonical authority, we command you neither yourselves to bless so blameworthy a marriage in the churches of our bishopric nor, insofar as lies in your power, permit it to be blessed by anyone, unless this consanguinity has first been lawfully proved in our presence to extend beyond the seventh degree. Farewell, and transmit this letter to the count of Mantes.

## LETTER XLVI. IVO, son of his holiness, to URBAN, supreme pontiff: the gift of the prayers of the faithful.

[col. 58B]

Envoys will shortly come to you on behalf of the king of the Franks. Through their mouth the lying spirit will speak: men who, led astray by the acquisition or promise of ecclesiastical honours [some: “goods”], will try [variant: “are trying,” Letter 92] to deceive the seat of justice [note: he calls Rome this]. Against their cunning I wish your vigilance to be forewarned and fortified by my lowliness, so that their promises may not soften your firmness nor their threats terrify you.

For whatever they say [variant: “why indeed”], with the axe already laid to the root of the tree (Matt. 13), their aim is only that you may relax the bow or suspend the sword [col. 58C]. Those who are about to come, trusting in the cunning of their petty intelligence and in the charm of their tongue, have promised the king that, for the aforesaid reasons, they will obtain from the apostolic see impunity for his crime. They will employ this argument: that the king and kingdom will withdraw from your obedience [note: see Letters 28 and 211], unless you restore the crown and absolve the king from anathema.

But if pardon is granted to one who is unrepentant, how great a hope of sinning with impunity will henceforth remain to sinners is not for me to instruct your prudence, whose chief concern it is not to foster but to strike the errors of offenders. And if certain deceitful persons [note: “deceitful” is absent in manuscript c.] openly depart from unity with their mother, though they had long ago departed in mind, let the divine answer comfort your holiness: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men” (1 Kgs. 19). And likewise the Apostle’s saying: “Heresies must arise, that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11) [col. 58D].

Furthermore, I wish your vigilance to know that, at the king’s command, the archbishops of Rheims, Sens, and Tours have summoned their suffragan bishops to meet at Troyes, after your replies, on the first Sunday following the feast of All Saints. Though invited, I refrain from going unless fortified by your counsel, fearing that the assembly may devise something against justice and the apostolic see. Therefore, concerning these matters and those around you, let your fatherhood write to me whatever you please, so that I may share your suffering in adversity and congratulate you in prosperity [col. 59A]. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII. IVO, humble bishop of Chartres, to WIDO [note: variant: GUIDO, royal seneschal; Letter 23 to the same person is entirely of the same subject], the king’s seneschal, greetings.

What you communicated to me through Landric the priest I had already heard through your nephew Ebrard: namely, that the king is prepared to abandon many evils and promises to do many good things, if, while retaining peace with the apostolic see and ecclesiastical communion, he may be able to keep for a time the woman [note: Bertrada, concerning whom see Letters 13, 15, 28, and 46] whom he possesses unlawfully.

Therefore I write this to your charity by divine authority: no one can abolish his sin by ransom or exchange so long as he wishes to remain in it, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For those who sin deliberately, no sacrifice for sin remains” (Heb. 10) [col. 59B]. That is to say in other words: no one who wishes to persist in sin can redeem that sin through any almsgiving or offering.

Thus we read that the Lord answered Cain, when he was making his offering yet plotting murder (Gen. 4): “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still” [note: “be still” absent from one Vatican manuscript, as also in Letter 34]. It is as if he said: You sin by dividing wrongly, since you offer your possessions and, while planning murder, withhold from me yourself, who are better than your possessions.

Blessed Pope Gelasius also says (*Legatur*, causa 23, question 2): “Let it be read from the beginning of the Christian religion, or let a certain example be supplied in the Church of God, that pardon was granted by any pontiffs, or by the apostles themselves, or finally by the Saviour himself, except to those correcting themselves. But nowhere under heaven is it either read or said to have been heard from anyone: ‘Grant us pardon, yet let us persist in error.’ Let them show, therefore, on what grounds, by what rules, what reading [variant: “what reasoning”], or what proof—whether from our elders, or from the apostles themselves, who beyond doubt were worthier, or from the Lord Saviour himself, who is believed to judge the living and the dead—it was ever either done, or commanded to be done” [col. 59B–C].

For these reasons and many others like them, I know that the lord king’s plan cannot have a good outcome unless he abandons this sin and submits himself through repentance to Christ’s yoke. For God [variant: “the Lord,” manuscript c.] seeks not our possessions but us, for our salvation. Therefore tell—or, in one Vatican manuscript, “let these things be told”—to the lord king, so that he may seek sounder counsel. If God [variant: “the Lord,” manuscript c.] should provide it to him, he would find me an assistant in every way I could assist [col. 59D]. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVIII. IVO, humble servant of the Church of Chartres, to URBAN, supreme pontiff: the gift of the prayers of the faithful.

Since through experience of daily pressures we know the dangers of the Gallican churches, we earnestly desire to make known to the apostolic see the burdens of those same pressures, that it may relieve them. Therefore we ask that the metropolitan see of Rheims—once your mother, but now your daughter—be refreshed with your consolations with all speed and supported by your aid [col. 60A], lest our adversary, who prowls around seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5), be able through some trick to disturb, or by some disturbance invalidate [variant: “shake”], the election made in favour of Lord Manasses.

For among all her sons that Church could not have found anyone more devoted to the apostolic see or more necessary to her interests, both because of nobility of birth and because of integrity of character. But how necessary it is for the Roman Church to establish in that see a minister devoted to itself is not for me to instruct your prudence. You know that this see possesses the diadem of the kingdom [note: nevertheless, Letter 189 does not approve the view that kings were always crowned at Rheims], and serves as an example of ruin or restoration to nearly all the Gallican churches [col. 60B]. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIX. IVO, unworthy minister of the Church of Chartres, to STEPHEN, count palatine, greetings.

Mildness toward me, embittered as it is, I cannot sufficiently wonder at, since I believe that I have neither injured your person nor in any respect diminished the lawful right of your lordship. Yet if I had done so through some misrepresentation, I ought to have been admonished in private conversation, that I might correct my error; or at least summoned to judgment at suitable places and times—not exasperated by indignant and threatening words. Since, then, none of this has preceded [Note: cf. Epistle 86], let your prowess recognize [Col. 0060C] how suddenly it has risen against a friend, and restrain its indignation. For we are so prepared to comply with your friendship that we nonetheless honor our ministry by satisfying the demands of justice.

For it has long been provided, before the times of your fathers [variant: “our fathers”], by decrees of kings and strengthened in many ways by ecclesiastical enactments, that every secular power be excluded from the cloister of the canons; and this was preserved without any interruption down to the time of Bishop Gaufridus. Do you therefore think that what the Church obtained so freely at first, and possessed peacefully for so many ages, can be taken from the Church’s right through the frivolity or perversity of one man, and transferred into another’s jurisdiction without extensive examination and judicial determination? Let your mildness therefore return [Col. 0060D] to itself and rest in the words of Wisdom: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries, the boundaries which your fathers” [variant: “our fathers,” manuscript C] “set” (Prov. 22).
