Whoever presumes to overstep against the Church entrusted to my lowliness [variant: “our lowliness,” manuscript C] those boundaries, we are ready, according to the power [variant: “ability”] bestowed on us by God, to resist by opposition even to loss of possessions and even to exile; and to strike, pursuing him with the sword of the Holy Spirit, until fitting satisfaction has been made. This sword penetrates [Col. 0061A] towers, casts down fortifications, and every height that raises itself against the humility of Christ and unjustly invades the inheritance which He acquired for Himself by His blood. This sword is stronger in poverty; it is not broken in exile, nor bound in prison, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2).

And if you do not fear us armed with this sword, fear God in us, whose embassy we carry out, though unworthy, and whose sacraments we administer. For the Lord says through the Prophet: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not deal maliciously with my prophets” (Ps. 104). A lawful lordship has the duty to provide for the peace of churches, not to disturb their peace; to give what is its own, not to despoil them of what is theirs, so that the Church, praying to God for princes and authorities [Col. 0061B], may do so not in contention but in piety.

Moreover, concerning the safe-conduct for which you invited me, asking that I provide it for you at Meaux [in one manuscript: *Meldis*, more correctly], it is not my intention to provide it for you elsewhere than in the city for which and from which I owe it to you. Nor does it become a man of such upright reputation to demand from me anything contrary to custom, merely to furnish an occasion for stirring up hatred. For I am not so covetous or fearful that this or that consideration would lead me away from what reason and custom prescribe. Having examined the Church’s records and consulted even its older clergy, I have been unable to find that any of my canonically promoted predecessors provided this safe-conduct to your predecessors except in the city. Farewell, and may the God [Col. 0061C] of peace be with you.

23. EPISTLE L. IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of the Carnotenses, to RICHERIUS, archbishop of the Senonenses: greeting with due obedience.

I was preparing myself, as your fatherhood had instructed me, to come to a conference with you and our fellow-bishops, accompanied by the more learned sons of our Church. But meanwhile certain friends informed me with certainty that snares were being prepared for me by some of your parishioners, relatives of that woman formerly called queen—Bertrada (Epistles 13 and 105)—whose hostility against me has not yet, for any reason, been calmed [Col. 0061D]. I therefore ask your mildness to arrange a safe escort for me from Pithiviers [manuscript C: *Plicuris*] as far as yourselves, if my presence is so necessary to you. For any danger incurred by me on this journey would be as harmful to me as it would be dishonorable to you.

If this cannot at present be done, I write to you in absence what I would say in your presence. Concerning the old dispute which the Church of Lyons has against the Church of Sens, I commend and advise this: if you possess any privileges confirmed by apostolic authority, or authentic documents, which remove from your Church the primacy of the Church of Lyons [Col. 0062A]—a primacy which we infer from lists of cities once existed, and of which Epistle 54 also speaks—and which uphold for that Church the liberty we desire, show them to our fellow-bishops and send them also to our lowliness. Thus, relying on them as firm supports, we may defend, to the extent of our ability, the liberty of our mother Church.

But if you do not presently have such documents at hand, it is not my advice that you stretch out your arms against the torrent. Rather, for the present, acquiesce in the apostolic enactments, without prejudice to privileges or authentic documents which may someday be found, removing this subjection from your Church and defending the liberty of that same Church. Let those who know better give better counsel. Let them only provide [variant: “foresee”] this: since prudence is measured by the outcome of events, let them rescue your head from the threatening sword.

Furthermore, know that the canons of Paris—namely the dean, the cantor, and Rainald the archdeacon—in our presence, in accordance with the command of the lord pope, swore that they had elected Lord William [variant: *Vuillelmum*; as in Epistles 54 and 55] as their bishop, not compelled by any terror from the king or the aforesaid queen [Note: who was the sister of this elect, as he says at the end of Epistle 54], and that they had intended no simoniacal wrongdoing in his election. Therefore I command you on the pope’s behalf that, if the Church of Paris asks that he be ordained and consecrated for itself, you lay hands upon him before the feast of Saint Remigius, according to the authority and custom of your Church; and that, although the use of the honor of the pallium has been temporarily forbidden you [Note: “the dignity of the pallium” is mentioned in Epistle 250], you do not in the least fear to use it [Col. 0062C] in his ordination and consecration.

For the lord pope granted me this at Montpellier, when, at the king’s request, William’s election was being considered; and, after much debate concerning that election, the examination of the matter was entrusted to me by the lord pope. Finally, I ask your fatherhood that, according to the establishment [one manuscript: “constitution”] of peace which the lord pope has imposed upon all the Gallican churches, you administer justice concerning your parishioners of Étampes—namely Ursio son of Theodo and his accomplices—who utterly ravage that part of our bishopric adjoining your bishopric and disturb without cause the peace enjoyed by the remainder of the bishopric. Command, therefore, the archpriest of Étampes [Note: connect Epistle 50] [Col. 0062D] either to bring them to satisfaction, or, having excommunicated them, to forbid divine service in the places where they reside (Epistle 263), in accordance with the custom of the peace. Farewell, and send me word through the bearer of this letter what pleases you [one manuscript: “write back”].

EPISTLE LI. IVO, by the grace of God bishop of the Carnotenses, to his beloved brother and fellow-priest SANCTIO [Note: The bishop’s name has thus been supplied from manuscript S. Germ.; but the Put. manuscript has *Samsoni*. This variation is also noted in the heading of Epistle 53. The first edition had only the initial letter of the name, as do many manuscripts]: right understanding in the Lord.

Let your brotherhood know that letters have been sent to me [Col. 0063A] by the clergy of Orléans who appear to be the leading men of that clergy. They steadfastly accuse you on grave charges: namely, the heresy of simony, the invasion of the Church of Orléans, and other criminal offenses [Note: of which he was later cleared, Epistle 54]. If true, these must be punished with canonical severity. Indeed, in the same letter they bind themselves under the obligation of retaliation [Note: concerning this, Epistle 138], should they fail to prove these things true by the lawful number of witnesses, either in our presence or in the presence of those to whose judgment your case must be referred.

Therefore, by that charity through which we are one body in Christ, I admonish your brotherhood: if your conscience judges you blameworthy in these matters, withdraw your foot from the wrongdoing you have undertaken, lest you waste your own resources in vain and miserably destroy both yourself and those who are yours. Consider that divine mercy has already drawn your age onward into old age [Col. 0063B; Note: Epistle 54 calls this Sanctio advanced in years], and, striking your offenses with measured lashes, has granted you time for repentance. Do not, then, at the very approach of death aspire to that height which your weakness may either be unable to attain or, once attained, fall from and be more grievously crushed; a height which you were unable to attain even when you were younger in age, keener in intellect, and far stronger in bodily powers.

Would it not, dearest brother, have been better for you to be saved in a lowly place than to be endangered in a high one? If at your Lord’s banquet you had chosen the lowest place, and your host had said to you, “Friend, go up higher,” then you would have praise and glory before your fellow-guests (Luke 14). But now, as is said, contrary to ecclesiastical enactments, with an immense sum of money given or promised and with secular power also joined to it, you aspire [Col. 0063C] to the summit of pastoral care—apparently destined to possess the lowest place in shame, after you have disposed of your goods and stripped of its treasures and ornaments the Church you are invading.

For I believe that none of your fellow diocesan bishops [variant: *condiocesanorum*] will dare lay hands upon you unless either the pope commands it or a lawful examination demonstrates that you are innocent of these crimes. Now, though you have idled [one manuscript: “remained”] and lounged until the eleventh hour, you ought to labor in God’s vineyard, so that at least you may work in the evening and receive the daily denarius with those who bore the burden and heat of the day (Matt. 20). I say this not from any bitterness, but from the deepest affection. Farewell.

24. EPISTLE LII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to GAUFRIDUS, dean of the Church of Le Mans: greeting.

[Col. 0063D]

Occupied with many and serious affairs, I have not at present been able to write sufficiently to your brotherhood. Yet concerning Ebrardus [manuscript C: *Eberardus*], I answer you this: because by harshness of character and intolerable presumption alike in his actions and his words he frequently offended his fellow-brethren, he obtained from them permission on this condition [Col. 0064A], and obtained only this: that he should remain a monk of Marmoutier (*Majus Monasterium*).

Therefore, one who, despising clerical life, fled to a monastery, and conversely, despising the monastery, strives once more to aspire to clerical status, does not seem to me readily to be received by those to whom his life, doctrine, and character have not yet become known. If, therefore, you perceive yourself to be burdened by the intrusion of such a person, you are free to reject him. For according to the decree of Pope Celestine (Distinction 61, chapter 12, *Nullus*): “Only then is one to be chosen from another Church, if no worthy person can be found from the clergy of that very city in which a bishop is to be ordained—which we do not believe will occur.”

And because you have understanding of your own accord, it seems superfluous to instruct you concerning the authorities by which you ought [Col. 0064B] to reject persons unknown and arriving from outside. Nevertheless, I advise you to remind the abbot of Marmoutier, whose monk he still is, to restrain the aforesaid Ebrardus from such ambition and, if necessary, curb him with regular severity. For although he consented that he be made abbot, he did not release him from the yoke of monastic discipline. Farewell.

EPISTLE LIII. IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of the Carnotenses, to SANCTIO [Note: The name has thus been supplied from manuscript S. Germ.; the Put. manuscript reads *Samsoni*, and this textual variation is also found in the heading of Epistle 51. In the manuscript of St Victor only *Sal.* is read], bishop of the Orléanais: act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord.

I have heard concerning your brotherhood something that greatly displeases me and all good men: whatever perverse act it commits—for I laid hands upon you—is imputed to me [Col. 0064C], and your rival glories in your offenses not only against you but against me as well. For I have been informed by letter that the cleric whom, on the day of your entry, according to the custom of your city and at our exhortation, you released from prison, you have again cruelly committed to prison custody.

On that very day on which he had served you at Mass and shared your table, you caused him to be beaten, despoiled, and dragged by the hands of servants to prison; and, after delivering him to the secular court, you comforted him in no way and took no care for his release. Was it not better to suffer the plundering of your possessions, or even, as you had promised, to commit your own person to prison, than for your cleric—untried and uncondemned—to be delivered by you to the secular court [variant: “to deliver to the court,” Epistle 66] [Col. 0064D], where he would be tormented like a thief by daily insults and injuries?

This is not the office of a shepherd but of a hireling. The tree which the Lord planted does not bear such fruit; evil beginnings [variant: “these beginnings”] do not promise good outcomes. Therefore, if you wish us to remain your friends and helpers [one manuscript: “coadjutors”], either release the deacon whom you have delivered to the court, or without delay do what pastoral care requires for his release [Col. 0065A]. If you do not, it will undoubtedly be clear that he was seized by your counsel or that of your associates, and that it was fraud rather than good faith that released him at the time of your entry. I had prepared letters to send to the archbishop of Lyons concerning your ordination; I am withholding them until I hear how you have acted in this affair. Farewell.

EPISTLE LIV. To HUGH, by the grace of God archbishop of Lyons and vicar of the Apostolic See: IVO, bishop of Chartres; WILLIAM [variant: GUILELMUS], bishop of Paris; and WALTER [variant: GUALTERUS; Epistle 16], bishop of Meaux—devoted service with due obedience.

Since the acts performed in churches ought to be reported by letter or messenger to the hearing of the Apostolic See or its legates, through those by whom those acts were performed, lest through the slander of rivals or alteration by rumor they be believed to have been done otherwise than they were, we have taken care to report to your knowledge what we have recently done concerning the ordination of the Church of Orléans [Col. 0065B].

After the death of John, bishop of Orléans, the archbishop of Tours—who still arrogated to himself in that Church the offices of provost and archdeacon—and a certain subdean of that Church, surnamed “worse than a wolf,” together with certain confidants of the deceased bishop and of themselves, began by secret machinations to try to have one John, an archdeacon, made bishop with the king’s consent [variant: “having the king’s consent for this, they might elect him bishop”] [Col. 0065C]. His life seemed unworthy of approval, whether because of insufficient years, lack of learning, or immaturity of character. Indeed, because of an indecent intimacy [Note: for he was said to be a *succubus*; see Epistles 66 and 67] which he was said to have had with the deceased bishop and with some of those who wished to obtain him [manuscript C: “wished”], he was in every respect reprehensible.

Hearing this, the remaining clergy, far greater in number and more learned, wishing [variant: “wished”] to avoid the oppression they had suffered at the hands of the aforesaid persons in the time of the deceased bishop, chose, by sounder counsel [variant: “sounder”] suited to time and place, with the king’s consent, as their bishop Sanctio [Note: some manuscripts read *Sancionem*, another *Samsonem*. He writes to Sanctio as fellow bishop in Epistle 62], dean of that Church: a man who, as you know, was advanced in years and mature in character [Note: Epistle 51 indicates that he was then an old man].

When they asked us, at the exhortation of the archbishop of Sens [Col. 0065D], to consecrate him at the castle of Nanton, which is beside [some: “within”; so manuscript C] the diocese of Sens, we wholly refused, on account of the primacy of the Church of Lyons, which that see irrationally rejects, and because of the interdict of the Apostolic See (see Epistle 50). Meanwhile the rivals of the aforesaid elect, having sent letters, asked us not to lay hands upon him, because he was a simoniac and an invader [Note: these two charges were brought against Sanctio, as Epistle 51 confirms], adding at the same time that they would prove this at a suitable place and time, beyond the reach of royal power.

When, therefore, the Church, supported by the king’s urgent requests, insistently demanded that its elect be consecrated for it, alleging that irreparable ruin would befall the Church if this were not done, we sent letters assigning the aforesaid accusers a time and day before the consecration, and the place—namely Chartres—where royal power could not harm them [Col. 0066A]. But they neither came nor sent anyone on their behalf.

25. Since, therefore, the aforesaid accusers withdrew themselves—we do not know by what cunning—from a lawful examination, and since we were overcome by the entreaties of almost the entire Church, after taking counsel among ourselves we received from him and from the better men with him solemn oaths, as many as seven, which cleared him, insofar as he could be cleared before human eyes, of invasion and simony [Note: this is called “the seventh purgation” in Epistle 229].

Thus, after removing the impediments specifically alleged against him, we consecrated him after he had promised obedience to you and sent him to the Church which had requested him. It received him with all devotion and without any objection [Col. 0066B]. If necessary, we shall prove that these things are true, since we handled them with as much diligence as we could.

We therefore ask your fatherhood not readily to lend an ear to those whom, once the truth has been disclosed, you will recognize as seeking their own interests. I, Ivo bishop of Chartres, have also taken care to insert into this letter the oath which, according to the pope’s command, the dean, cantor, and archdeacon of Paris made on behalf of their elect, with the others consenting:

> “We did not elect William [variant: Guillelmus; cf. Epistles 26 and 50] as our bishop because of a gift received or promised by anyone; nor because the king had cohabited with his sister [Note: the aforesaid queen, mentioned also in Epistle 50]; nor because of threats brought against us by the king or his aforesaid sister. So may God help us, and these holy Gospels.”

Thus purified, in accordance with what the pope had commanded at Montpellier at the king’s request, he was consecrated by his metropolitan before the feast of Saint Remigius (as stated in Epistle 50) [Col. 0066C]. Farewell.

EPISTLE LV. To HUGH, by the grace of God archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See: IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres—faithful service with due obedience.

Your fatherhood heard that the case of the elect of Beauvais was recently discussed privately before the lord pope at Nîmes [Col. 0066D], and that you at one time interceded before the lord pope, together with other intercessors, that the election made be confirmed for the Church of Beauvais in accordance with its wishes. But because, for reasons of his own, the lord pope delayed confirming the aforesaid election, the Church did not abandon its purpose. Through various dangers and arduous journeys it sent an embassy after him; with the highest devotion it sought its elect, whom it had foreseen [variant: “provided”] would be useful in recovering its goods, which had been badly scattered [Col. 0067A], and whom it had already found to be useful; and by repeated urgent prayers it obtained him—yet in such a way that your goodwill should be sought in this matter and that the desire of the petitioning Church should be fulfilled by the judgment of your discretion.

Since the outcome of this affair depends upon your decision, we urgently beg your vigilance with repeated prayers: if some pardonable fault has been observed in the person of the aforesaid elect, as befits human frailty, so that complete regular integrity does not appear in him, weigh this by prudent compensation and support him through useful dispensation. This is especially appropriate because the Church cannot presently find another equally useful man to elect bishop with the peace of the realm and the consent of the Church.

For, as it seems to us, canonical rigor is not harmfully relaxed when provision is made for the benefit of many (the same author, Epistle 171) [Col. 0067B]. Thus Pope Pelagius, having long delayed the ordination of an elect of Syracuse because he had a wife and children, subsequently allowed him to be ordained—through the intervention of the patrician Cethegus [Note: most old manuscripts, as also in Distinction 28, chapter 1, *de Syracusan.*; formerly *Metegus*]—when the Church persisted irrevocably in its intended course and he had given the appropriate assurance.

If in like manner we wished to gather examples from past and present times, we would find that rulers of churches have judged some matters more strictly according to canonical rigor, tolerated many owing to the necessities of the times, and overlooked many for the benefit of persons [Note: above, Epistle 16; Gratian under canon 1, question 7; and the heading “Many things [vary] according to circumstances,” etc., Distinction 29]. Since we do not believe these things unknown to your solicitude, we have judged it superfluous to enumerate them. Let your vigilance only take care [Col. 0067C] that, by delaying the elect’s ordination any longer, the Church may not suffer and be endangered [one old manuscript: “that the elect may suffer and be endangered”; cf. Epistle 60]. If you believe that this does not suitably preserve your reputation, it is useful and expedient that you entrust the matter, with your goodwill, to the discretion and foresight of his metropolitan and fellow-provincial bishops. Farewell.

EPISTLE LVI. To PHILIP, by the grace of God most serene king of the Franks: IVO, his humble priest—greeting, and faithful service as to his lord and king.

Concerning the command which your highness gave to my lowliness—that, after two councils held this year by the lord pope, his legate, the archbishop of Lyons, should convene a third general council within the same year and summon to it the bishops of your realm—I reply to your serenity that, when I recently received his letter, I read nothing of the sort in it, nor did I hear it from his messenger [Col. 0067D]. Even if he did so, however, it would not be an apostolic institution or an ecclesiastical custom.

But if anyone is summoned by apostolic legates for his offenses, after a suitable period has been granted him, he cannot evade appearing on the day prescribed for him unless a lawful cause detains him. If anyone should seek to oppress them beyond [variant: “against”] the limits established by the Fathers [Col. 0068A], then, after taking common counsel with them, resist unjust oppressions in your own person, so that they may render to God what is God’s [variant: “so that what is God’s may be rendered to God”] and may not fail to render to Caesar what is Caesar’s (Mark 12). May your highness flourish for a long time.

EPISTLE LVII. IVO, by the grace of God humble bishop of Chartres, to GAUFRIDUS, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme: despise the world together with its flower.

Concerning that brother who fled from you three times and, in accordance with the constitution of the monastic rule, had been received three times (cf. Epistle 160), and who had now turned away and fled a fourth time, but then turned again and returned and mercifully obtained burial with the brethren—I approve very much [Col. 0068B]. For mercy exalts itself over judgment (James 2), and the Lord instructed the prince of the apostles that the repentant sinner is to be forgiven not merely seven times but seventy times seven (Matt. 18).

But because he concealed the sacrilege which he committed [variant: “had committed”], and did not restore to the monastery, by fitting satisfaction, the thing he had stolen, we advise by admonishing and admonish by advising that he lose the burial which he had mercifully received with the brethren. Thus the others may have fear and keep their hands from similar sacrilege; for full remission cannot follow where there has been no true conversion [one manuscript: “confession”]. Farewell.

EPISTLE LVIII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to the congregation of Saint Stephen at Sens: greeting and the assistance due to its necessity [variant: “to their necessity”].

[Col. 0068C]

In your petition, your brotherhood instructed us to ordain your elect to the priesthood at the Purification of blessed [variant: “saint”] Mary, in accordance with our office, and to consecrate him bishop on the following Sunday. But apostolic institution and the canons of the Fathers [Note: Chapter *Nullus*, Distinction 5, and the final chapter, Distinction 75. On the times of ordinations: Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*; and Amalarius, book II, *On Priests and Deacons*: “They are consecrated on Saturday”] prescribe that no Levitical or priestly ordination be made except during the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, or at the beginning of Lent, or on the Saturday in mid-Lent.

Because it is perilous both to the ordainer and to the person ordained to confer or receive holy orders outside [variant: “contrary to”] the order handed down by the Fathers [Col. 0068D], and because Wisdom says, “An inheritance hastily acquired in the beginning will lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20), let your brotherhood meanwhile await the lawful times, until we have conferred with our fellow-bishops and with the elect himself, and have examined carefully among ourselves whatever can or cannot be done.

For certain obstacles appear to stand in the way, concerning which we must deal with the elect himself before confirming his election. With God’s assent, this can presently be done at Sens [variant reading: “at Sens”] [Col. 0069A], when we have assembled together for a conference with the king. Farewell.

EPISTLE LIX. To HUGH, by the grace of God archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See: IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres—offices of devoted service with due obedience.

If your affection once had good hope concerning my lowliness, your gravity ought not so quickly to despair, nor so readily incline its ear to the slanders of ill-wishers who seek not the things of God but their own. You should not, because of the attacks of those who cannot otherwise acquire a reputation for uprightness except by lying in wait for another’s reputation, suspect that I either did not walk [Col. 0069B] in God’s way or deviated from it for human favor.

For the Searcher of hearts and Knower of secrets is my witness that, in the consecration of the bishop of Orléans [Note: Sanctio, or Samso, whose consecration is discussed in Epistle 54], by which I now appear to have angered your mildness, my hand is free from every gift and my mind clear of every expectation of temporal benefit. The evils concerning the aforesaid bishop which were suggested to your solicitude were either unheard of [manuscript C: “reported”] by me, unknown to me, or—if anything reached my ears that seemed worthy of purgation—were, although no lawful accusation had been made [Note: as in the title *Deficientibus accusatoribus*, “who is to be compelled to purge himself,” Cause 2, Question 4], nonetheless so cleared according to canonical institution by public examination upon oaths that any suspicion which might remain because of human frailty seemed to me already [Col. 0069C] reserved not for human but for divine judgment [Note: the aforesaid Epistle 54 testifies that Sanctio was cleared by seven oaths].

Therefore my conscience bears me testimony without any dispute that in this affair I committed nothing contrary to right faith and sound doctrine; nor do I know that I transgressed the general enactments of the Fathers concerning episcopal ordinations. As for your objection that his chastity had not been proven and had not been commended by me in my letters [Note: according to the canons in Gratian, Distinction 81], I considered it superfluous to dispute after the lord pope about his chastity. For I had seen him ordained priest at Rome by the pope’s command—since the same law of continence applies to a priest as to a bishop [Note: the enclosed words are taken from Epistle 90, chapter 3, of Leo I to Rusticus of Narbonne]—and, after the pope’s commendatory letters, I had read that his priesthood had been commended in your letters [Col. 0069D], while you had sharply reproved his bishop, who disparaged that priesthood.

As to your writing that, because of the office of legation entrusted to you, this matter ought first [manuscript C: “afterwards”] to have been referred to your notice [Col. 0070A], so that only then should we consecrate when we knew what pleased you—because Pope Leo so commanded Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica and his legate [Note: Leo I, Epistle 82, chapter 1; cited in chapter 4, *De personis*, Distinction 65]—we understand this to have been a personal privilege, not a general decree. This is especially so because, according to the same Leo, “the office of legation is a part of apostolic solicitude, not the fullness of power.” That part also [Note: cited in chapter *Multum*, Cause 3, Question 6. Saint Gregory says the same above, Epistle 8, of the other churches to which Rome imparts its vicarial authority] now receives more, now less, according to the will of the one entrusting it.

But because I have only now learned through you what I had previously learned from no one by word or writing, it is not my intention to contend against the privilege of your legation or against whatever greatness divine dispensation may have wished to give you. I have always been ready to obey according to my strength [Col. 0070B], and to defend your honor against all your detractors, including those who now attack me before you, to the extent of my power.

I therefore advise your solicitude henceforth to write back what we are to do concerning Daimbert, elect of the Church of Sens. Although elected without consulting us, the clergy of Sens present him to us to be ordained at the beginning of Lent and then consecrated bishop [Note: He is also praised in Epistle 60 for nobility, learning, and good reputation; nevertheless Hugh forbade his consecration for the reason reported in Epistle 65, concerning which the author complains in Epistle 60]. His electors commend him quite emphatically for nobility of birth, integrity of character, and energy in public affairs. If his election seems proper to you, we ask that you attach no delays. If it is unjust, instruct me and my fellow-bishops by your letters concerning the rule by which it ought to be deferred or annulled, so that you impose this burden not upon one or another alone but upon all [Col. 0070C]. Fare well, and carefully guard yourselves against the cunning of the archbishop of Tours [Note: his plots are noted in Epistle 66, and his most shameful conduct attacked in Epistle 67], lest a friend harm you more than an enemy is known capable of harming you.

EPISTLE LX. To HUGH, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See: IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres—greeting and service.

It was done as you commanded: we withheld our hands from the consecration of the elect of Sens [Note: [Col. 0070D] Daimbert, as is clear from Letter 66; this letter is mentioned in Letter 67.], and, in obedience to apostolic authority, sent your letters through the bishops of the province. Therefore, while asking we take counsel, and while taking counsel we ask your discernment henceforth to bind us more sparingly with the bonds of apostolic obedience; lest, by laying unbearable burdens upon our shoulders, you cause us to fall into disobedience, [Col. 0071A] 27 because some impossibility prevents us or some necessity compels us. For it is easy for you to fight from afar by threatening with a bow, but for us it is exceedingly dangerous to strike at an opponent present before us with a sword.

Yet we wish to observe prohibitions or commands promulgated by the Apostolic See for the defence of the faith, the correction of the faithful, the amendment of wrongdoers, and the prevention of impending or future evils, in such a way that, God cooperating, we are ready to endure any adversity in their defence. But when you decree that matters which are indifferent, and in whose non-observance salvation is in no way endangered, nor in whose observance is it in any way helped, are to be kept so insistently; or when you diminish or alter, as you please, matters which antiquity established, custom observed, and the hallowed authority of venerable Fathers [Col. 0071B] confirmed—your prudence ought to consider what benefit you confer upon the salvation of those whom you ought to assist in every respect; whose ordinances should rather be maintained; and to whom obedience should rather be rendered: to those holy Fathers who still speak to us in their writings, or to you, whose purpose is nothing other than to follow and honour the footsteps of your predecessors.

I say this not because new commands may not lawfully be promulgated against new offences. Rather, I say what Pope Zosimus says to the people of Narbonne (canon *Contra*, Cause 25, Question 1): “The authority even of this See cannot grant anything contrary to, or alter, the ordinances of the Fathers; for among us antiquity lives with unshaken roots, to which the decrees of the Fathers [Col. 0071C] have established reverence.”

Likewise, in the book of pontiffs called the *Diurnus*, the profession of the Roman pontiff contains this:

> “Of the tradition which I find handed down and observed by my most approved predecessors, I profess that I will diminish nothing [Note: [Col. 0071D] This is also attested by Letter 73.], alter nothing, nor admit any novelty; but rather, as their disciple and follower, with all the efforts of my mind I profess that I will observe and venerate what I find to have been canonically handed down.”

Blessed Gregory also says to Master Maurentius [one manuscript: “Maurentinus”] in the case of Theodore: “It is altogether grave for priests to arrogate anything to themselves contrary to ancient usage.” Again, the same writer says: “All things which the usage of antiquity has established are to be preserved inviolate.” Hence Leo IV writes to the judge of [Col. 0071D] Sardinia: “Neither custom nor a newly introduced practice of our Church has been for our predecessors to presume novel or unusual things contrary to the statutes of the canons.”

Likewise Gregory, to all the bishops of Numidia (Letter 75, Book I, and in the canon *Nos*, Distinction 12): “We permit a custom which is known to usurp nothing contrary to the faith to remain unmoved, whether concerning the establishment of primates or the other chapters.” Likewise Leo IV to Lothair: “Whatever just and diligent custom [manuscript C: “if this custom and [Col. 0072A] diligence”] has not directed us to imitate, we must guard ourselves against it as though against a great precipice.”

Nicholas also writes, among other things, thus to Hincmar [Note: [Col. 0071D] See canon *Ser. Hingmauro*, alternatively *Hincmaro*; but *Hincmaro* is read in Nicholas’s own first Letter 70, and is also cited in chapter 6, Distinction 12.], archbishop of Reims: “It is ridiculous and a sufficiently abominable disgrace that we should allow the traditions which we received long ago from the Fathers to be broken” [Note: [Col. 0071D] Letter 70 adds: “at the pleasure of those who are always erring.”].

Gelasius likewise writes thus to all bishops throughout Dardania on this same matter (canon *Quia per*, Distinction 64):

> “Because some are not ashamed, through unlawful ambitions, to disturb the rights of Churches and to seize by greedy presumption the privileges which antiquity decreed for metropolitan or provincial bishops, not considering that they will have to render an account to the eternal Judge, not without the ruin of perpetual condemnation, both for injury to Catholic sincerity and for prejudice to paternal traditions [Col. 0072B], if they remain in this obstinacy: we have thought it necessary to instruct your charity, that all of you brothers alike established throughout Dardania or any adjoining province, who remember that you are under your metropolitans, should unanimously endeavour, as ancient custom requires, to have deceased bishops replaced by those same metropolitans; and conversely, if a metropolitan should depart by the lot of human mortality, you should by every means determine that he be consecrated by the provincial bishops, as the ancient form has handed down.” [Several old witnesses: “appoint.”]

Since, then, these and other general ordinances so categorically prescribe the consecration of a metropolitan, we wonder why you strive, by private laws and new traditions, [Col. 0072C] to remove ancient traditions and customs, commanding that the elect of Sens [Note: [Col. 0072D] Daimbert, whose consecration Hugh here hindered for the reason reported in Letter 65.] should appear before you before his consecration and profess submission and obedience by right of your primacy. Hitherto neither antiquity established this in the province of Sens nor custom observed it in other provinces.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas writes, among other things, to Archbishop Ralph of Bourges, who was arrogating to himself certain powers beyond the right of primacy (below, Letter 83):

> “We determine that primates or patriarchs have no privilege above other bishops except insofar as the sacred canons grant [alternatively, “have granted”] it to them and ancient custom has conferred it upon them, so that, according to the Nicene rules, the Churches may preserve their own privileges [Col. 0072D] (chapter 6 of the Council of Nicaea; canon *Mos antiquus*, Distinction 6).”

But if you insist that he must appear before you by the privilege of your legation—though he has been accused by no one either among us or among you—Pope Leo did not so instruct Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica and his vicar. Rather, provincial bishops were to report to him only the name of the elect (canon *De persona*, Distinction 65), while he himself was not to harass rightful elections with any difficulties or delays.

For, as far as we have heard, he is nobly born, suitably educated [Note: [Col. 0072D] Compare the passage at the end of Letter 59.], and of good [Col. 0073A] reputation among those who know him; while serving in his church in the office of deacon, he received an unbought election without any discord. But if he now yielded to these demands, he would be said to have purchased his consecration by the service of tongue or office.

As to what you wrote—that the aforesaid elect had received the investiture of the bishopric from the king’s hand—it has neither been reported to us by anyone who saw it nor become known to us. But even if it had happened, since this act, whether done or omitted, has no sacramental force in appointing a bishop, we do not know what injury it does to faith or holy religion, since after a canonical election we do not find kings forbidden by apostolic authority from granting bishoprics themselves (Letter 104; canon *Cum longe*, Distinction 63).

For we read that supreme pontiffs of holy memory sometimes interceded with kings on behalf of those elected by Churches, that the kings might grant them the bishoprics to which they had been elected (canon *Reatina*, 16, Distinction 63); and that they delayed the consecration of some [Col. 0073B] because they had not yet obtained royal grants (canon *Agatho* and following, Distinction 63). We would have set out their examples, had we not avoided making the letter too long.

Pope Urban also, as far as we understand, excludes kings only from bodily investiture (below, Letter 233), not from election insofar as they are the head of the people, nor from granting; although the Eighth Synod forbids them only to be present at an election, not to grant. Whether that grant is made by hand, [Col. 0073C] nod, speech, or staff, what difference does it make? For kings do not intend to give anything spiritual; rather, they only either assent to the requests of petitioners, 28 or grant to the elect the ecclesiastical estates and other external goods which Churches obtain through royal generosity.

Accordingly Augustine, in the first part of his commentary on John, Tractate 6 (canon *Quo jure*, Distinction 8), says:

> “By what right do you defend the estates of the Church: divine or human? We have divine right in the Scriptures, human right in the laws of kings. By what does anyone possess what he possesses, if not by human right? For by divine right: ‘The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness’ [Psalm 23/24]. By human right one says: ‘This estate is mine; this house is mine; this slave is mine.’ Take away the laws of emperors: who would dare say, ‘This estate is mine; this slave is mine; this house is mine’?” [Col. 0073D]

Again:

> “Do not say, ‘What have I to do with the king?’ What then have you to do with property? Possessions are held through the laws of kings. You said, ‘What have I to do with the king?’ Do not call possessions yours, because you have renounced those human laws by which possessions are held.”

If these matters had been established by eternal law, it would not lie in the power of rulers to judge them strictly in some cases [manuscript C: “vindicate”] and mercifully relax them in others, while those against whom these things are said remain in the honour they have received. [Col. 0074A] But now, because the prohibition of rulers chiefly makes them unlawful, and their remission according to their own judgment likewise makes them lawful [Note: [Col. 0073D] A similar passage occurs in Letters 190 and 236.], we see no one, or almost no one, condemned for a transgression of this sort; but we see very many harassed, very many Churches despoiled, very many scandals arising, and kingdom and priesthood divided—without whose harmony human affairs can be neither sound nor secure [Note: [Col. 0073D] From Leo I, Letter 29, chapter 20: “But affairs,” Cause 23, Question 5. Ivo discusses this in Letters 106 and 214.].

We also see wretched bishops and abbots, neither willing nor able to devote themselves to repairing the ruins of morals or walls, intent only upon making some loud-tongued person their friend, by whose bargaining they may somehow defend themselves. Many elect persons likewise, though they have an unbought and canonical election, [Col. 0074B] are hindered by delays or harassment of this kind; after purchasing mediators and advocates with money, lest they suffer a shameful rejection, they sometimes fall into a simoniacal consecration [Note: [Col. 0073D] Hence he says in Letter 55 that Churches suffer and are endangered; accordingly a primate is warned to bring no delay or difficulty to proper ordinations, chapter 4, *De persona*, Distinction 65.].

Since every institution of ecclesiastical laws must be referred to the salvation of souls, transgressions of these institutions ought either to be corrected more strictly, so that they may benefit salvation, or meanwhile suppressed in silence, lest spiritual or bodily benefits be impeded in the ways stated above. I do not say this as though I wished to raise my head against the Apostolic See, oppose its salutary [alternatively, “health-giving”; so manuscript C] dispositions, or prejudice the judgments of better men, if these rest upon sound reasons and clearer authorities of the ancient Fathers. But this [Col. 0074C] I should wish, together with many who share my pious view: that the ministers of the Roman Church, like experienced physicians, should attend to healing greater diseases, and should not hear from their mockers:

> “You strain out [alternatively, “filter out”] a gnat and swallow a camel; you tithe mint, rue, cumin, and dill, but neglect the weightier commandments of the law” (Matthew 11).

For throughout almost the whole world we see crimes and wicked deeds publicly committed, yet none of them cut away by you with any sickle of justice [Note: [Col. 0074D] Compare Letter 109, where he complains about papal legates.]. Since their examples are either not remote from you or not unknown to you, it is not for me to censure them in particular terms. You must see what you ought to do about these and similar matters.

But now my pen is directed especially to this end: that you permit the elect of the Church of Sens—Daimbert [Col. 0074D], as above—to be consecrated according to the ancient custom, if nothing is found in him contrary to the sacred canons. For we neither wish nor ought to yield the little right possessed by our Churches [Note: [Col. 0074D] For each Church must preserve its own privileges: chapter *Mos*, Distinction 65.]. For the blessed man says (Letter 6, Book I, to Magnus): “Holy Scripture shows how dangerous it is in divine matters for anyone to yield his right and authority, since Esau thereby lost his birthright and could not afterwards receive [Col. 0075A] what he had once yielded.”

If you assent to this petition of ours, we shall earnestly persuade him, once consecrated, to acknowledge the primacy [Note: [Col. 0075D] Mentioned above, and in Letters 50, 54, and 136.] of the Church of Lyons, to show you deference as his primate, and to render every due reverence in accordance with the traditions of the Fathers. If he refuses to yield to our persuasions, nevertheless we shall not depart from what the Apostolic See [in three manuscript witnesses, “the Roman See”] commands. But if you do not assent to our petitions and some schism arises from this against our wish, I shall confidently say: “Neither is it my iniquity nor my sin” (Psalm 58/59); nor will you be able to say that you were not forewarned.

Moreover, I could rightly demand from you restitution for the plunder committed by the people of Puiset against me and the Church of Chartres [Col. 0075B] (Letters 75, 111, 112, and 204), if I could summon your reverence to judgment. For at the instigation of my rivals you restored to communion, without my knowledge, the aforesaid sacrilegious persons whom I and my fellow bishops had deprived of communion, and thereby, by the impunity of their crimes, gave them licence to commit greater sacrileges. Whether this should have been done, or, after the fact, corrected once the truth was known, let your justice judge, since only true repentance dissolves just bonds. If it is not permitted or does not please you to reply to all these matters, let your holiness at least reply to these last two. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. To HUGH, bishop of the first see, legate of the Roman Church, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: greeting and obedience.

[Col. 0075C]

In accordance with your command, we would gladly and devoutly meet you, whenever an occasion and wherever it could suitably be done; but we cannot leave our territory or return to it without great danger, because of certain criminal watchers of our roads, whom for breach of the peace and their other enormities we have handed over to Satan [Note: [Col. 0075D] Compare Letter 211.].

Moreover, according to the custom of our Church, we must hold a synod [Note: [Col. 0075D] On holding synods annually, see Gratian, *Decretum*, Part I, Distinction 18.] on the seventh day before the Kalends of November [26 October]. At it many matters concerning Church business and the peace of the whole country must be discussed by us; without our presence they would either not be discussed or, if discussed, [Col. 0075D] would not be settled.

But concerning your determination to perform at Autun [alternatively, Augustidunum; so manuscript C] the consecration of the elect of Nevers, which belongs to our diocese, I say plainly to your fatherhood that we neither condemn your decision, because we defer to your reverence, nor approve it, because we have neither authority nor custom for the manner of this consecration, and we do not dare to introduce it as a custom without much deliberation, [Col. 0076A] fearing that we may become liable for the pledge we have made to the metropolitan see.

If its rulers do not proceed rightly, it seems to us, according to the Lord’s command, that their enormity should be avoided and their obstinacy rebuked; but the authority of the chair [Note: [Col. 0075D] The same passage occurs in Letter 226.]—granted to persons because of sacred places, not to sacred places because of persons of the present time—must not be overthrown. Therefore, since the metropolitan see is presently suspended from this office, we could, on behalf of the metropolitan see and together with our fellow brothers [manuscript C: “with brothers”], according to our customs, perform this sacrament of consecration within the diocese, once the election of the aforesaid person has been confirmed through the ministry of your legation. If we acted otherwise than with or for that see, or failed to confirm it [Note: [Col. 0075D] *Confirming* is absent from the manuscript.], [Col. 0076B] we should seem in some measure to overthrow the chair set over us.

If it has ever happened, through a shortage of Catholic bishops or some other compelling necessity, that a bishop was not consecrated by his provincial bishops [Note: [Col. 0076D] See Gratian under Distinctions 64 and 65.], such examples ought not to prejudice the common law or general custom. Although your prudence wishes and ought to honour [alternatively, “honourably magnify”; this is the word used in Letters 142 and 146; so manuscript C] its ministry, it should nevertheless remember that although Peter was set over Paul, they yet gave one another the right hands of fellowship (below, Letter 234), so that one might preach the Gospel among the Gentiles and the other among the circumcised (Galatians 2).

Therefore let your discernment consider whether it is lawful for this to be done in this manner, and, if lawful, whether it is expedient; lest those whom you wish to have subject [Col. 0076C] to you perhaps begin to hate and reject your yoke when they understand, from this precedent, that they are being deprived of their rights.

How firmly each Church’s rights must be preserved is shown by Pope Stephen V, writing thus to Patriarch Walbert [Note: [Col. 0076D] Some read “Gualbert”; the fuller passage is found in canon *Nunc vero*, Cause 9, Question 3.]:

> “We wonder that your prudence [alternatively, ‘you’; so manuscript C] denies the Church of Como the right to consecrate a pastor, although you know that you have already [manuscript C: ‘also’] been urged to this by apostolic exhortation. Now we write to you again, unwilling to infringe the privilege of any Church, although by apostolic prerogative we can ordain a cleric from any Church.”

Since, then, the chief virtue of an illustrious man is:

> “To spare the subjected and subdue the proud,” [Col. 0076D]  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI),

your diligence must take care lest, resisting you, they glory over us as though their resistance has profited them more than our obedience has profited us. But we need not labour much in speaking, since we believe that your moderation will claim nothing beyond the bounds of the Fathers. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to SANCTION [alternatively, SANCION; so manuscript C], fellow brother and fellow bishop [perhaps bishop of Orléans, from Letter 53]: greeting and service.

[Col. 0077A]

The peace which I made with Adelecia, lady of the castle of Puiset, and at which you marvel, I did not make in such a way as to usurp any of your right. Rather, I expressly excepted everything belonging to your right. I remitted only my own injury, not yours; and I asked your brotherhood to exercise no vengeance upon the aforesaid woman for my past injuries. Fear of you in large part compelled me to this. For you informed me in your letters that many inconveniences threatened you and your Church [Col. 0077B] if I delayed making peace with her. Therefore, finding an occasion, I wished to provide for both your advantage and mine.

If, then, any injuries remain which belong to your own parish, lest I seem burdensome to you, pursue them as you see fit and reason permits. But regarding the clerics or monks of Puiset, who celebrated Masses against your interdict, buried the dead, and obtained chrism from elsewhere, I answer and advise you thus: if you fully possess the favour of the archbishop of Lyons, by whose consent the said people of Puiset claim that your interdict was annulled, exercise full vengeance according to the rigour of the canons [alternatively, “canonical rigour”] upon such [manuscript C: “this kind of”] transgressors, so that you may restrain both them and others from this [Col. 0077C] [manuscript C: “such”] disobedience, according to the Apostle’s words: “Being ready to punish every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10). Otherwise, it will be more tolerable to endure what it is not lawful fully to punish.

Nor should your brotherhood marvel or be indignant because I admitted Gervasius (Letters 261 and 266) to communion at the Easter court. For I did this in honour of the king, relying on the authority of a law which reads:

> “If royal power receives any of the accused into the favour of its kindness or makes them participants at its table, the assembly of priests and people ought likewise to receive them into ecclesiastical communion, so that what princely mercy receives [or ‘has received’], may not be held alien [alternatively, ‘foreign’] by the priests of God.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0077] In many ancient books: “If anyone”; manuscript C. This law is also cited in Letter 171.]

Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to LEUDON, brother and fellow presbyter: greeting.

[Col. 0077D]

After long forgetfulness I recalled your request and my promise: I had promised [manuscript C: “which”] that I would write something against the absurdities of certain persons—I do not know whether simple or double-minded—who, according to the Apostle, “understand neither what they say nor what they affirm” (1 Timothy 1). They say that any persons whatsoever, even those without sacred order, may utter the words of the Lord, effect the sacraments of the altar and the other ecclesiastical sacraments, [Col. 0078A] and minister them beneficially to their recipients.

Their folly can be disproved in many ways: partly by reason, partly by the testimony of divine works, and finally by the incontrovertible authority of the holy Fathers. First, if divine sacraments could be effected and handled by any persons whatever, the priestly and Levitical order would have been established in the Church superfluously. It is impious for anyone to suppose this, since the old law first established both orders, at the Lord’s command, in figure, and the evangelical and apostolic teaching afterwards consecrated them in truth.

Thus in Exodus the Lord speaks to Moses:

> “Moreover, for Aaron’s sons you shall make linen tunics, belts, and tiaras, for glory and beauty. You shall clothe with all these things Aaron your brother and his sons with him; [Col. 0078B] and you shall consecrate the hands of them all, and consecrate them so that they may exercise the priesthood for me” (Exodus 28).

And later:

> “This anointing oil shall be holy to me, and you shall not make another according to its composition” (Exodus 30).

And again:

> “It shall be most holy in the incense; nevertheless, you shall not make its composition. Whoever makes anything like it shall perish from his people” [alternatively, “from his children”] (ibid.).

Thus we read in Leviticus that Nadab and Abihu, Aaron’s sons, took censers, put fire in them, and offered incense upon it before the Lord—strange fire, which had not been commanded them. Then fire went out from the Lord and devoured them (Leviticus 10). What is it to set strange fire against the sacrifice except to usurp, on one’s own spiritual presumption, the work of the priesthood without legitimate ordination?

We also have in Leviticus that, after Aaron the high priest completed the offerings for sin, the burnt offerings, and the peace offerings, fire went out from the Lord and devoured the burnt offering and the fat which was upon the altar (Leviticus 9). Conversely, in Numbers we read that when Dathan, Korah, and Abiram, wishing to usurp the priesthood, had put fire in their censers and laid incense upon it, divine fire did not consume the incense; rather, after the earth swallowed the leaders, material fire seized the accomplice multitude who likewise offered incense (Numbers 16). [Col. 0078C]

Therefore, just as divine fire visibly consumed and transformed into itself the figurative burnt offerings presented by legitimate priests, but not only rejected the victims of usurpers but also terribly condemned the usurpers themselves, so divine power invisibly consecrates the sacraments of this present age ministered by legitimate priests and transforms them into the reality of Christ’s body and blood. But it not only holds void the offerings of those who presume otherwise; it also condemns the presumptuous persons themselves for the present by inward blindness, and prepares for them irremediable punishments in the future.

For the Lord did not will those sacrifices, which were shadows of things to come, to be performed by words alone. He commanded that all the attendant mysteries and ministries be employed for their completion: namely, altars and vessels consecrated for that work; priests and ministers ordained to offer or administer these things; and, not without mystical vestments, sanctified for this office. Of the consecration of all these things we have the following in Leviticus:

> Moses took the anointing oil with which he anointed the tabernacle and all its furnishings. When, in consecrating, he had sprinkled the altar seven times, he anointed it and all its vessels, and the basin with its base; pouring it upon Aaron’s head, he anointed and consecrated him. He then clothed his sons, who had been presented, in linen tunics, girded them with belts [alternatively, “a belt”], and placed mitres upon them, as the Lord had commanded (Leviticus 8). [Col. 0079A]

And shortly afterwards:

> Taking the ointment and the blood which was upon the altar, he sprinkled Aaron and his garments, and his sons and their garments, and sanctified them in their vesture. But when the consecration had been completed, Moses said to Aaron: “Approach the altar and offer sacrifice for your sin. Offer the burnt offering and make supplication for yourself and for the people.” And immediately Aaron sacrificed a calf for his own sin, whose blood his sons presented to him (Leviticus 9). [Col. 0079B]

In these passages it must be observed that the tabernacle, altar, and vessels, the priests, and the priestly garments are first consecrated. Then they are commanded to approach the altar to sacrifice and make supplication to the Lord for their own sins and those of the people. Thus the Christian people should understand that, if in these sacrifices, which were performed only for purification of the flesh, this ritual of ministers and ministries had to be observed with such reverence, how much more, in the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood—in which the purification of flesh and spirit consists—may no one be admitted at once to the mystical blessings [Col. 0079C] and prayers by which that consecration is effected, unless first consecrated in priestly order and equipped with the full provision of all suitable furnishings and attendant ministries.

That no one other than a priest should approach in order to consecrate is read in Numbers, where the Lord says to Aaron:

> “You and your sons shall guard your priesthood; and all matters which belong to the service of the altar and are within the veil shall be administered through priests. If any outsider [alternatively, “stranger”] approaches, he shall be put to death” (Numbers 18).

What does Aaron signify but high priests, and his sons but lesser priests? Receiving the laying on of hands from high priests, they are advanced to the priestly blessing as by paternal succession. They administer matters within the veil when they consecrate by mystical blessing the Lord’s body and blood—which inwardly are one thing and outwardly appear another—and beneficially administer them to the faithful people.

What, then, is an outsider except one not consecrated to the presbyteral office? Whoever presumes to counterfeit the Lord’s sacraments is rightly put to death, because by his presumption he is cut off from the body of the righteous. [Col. 0079D]

That they ought not minister without sacred garments is read in Exodus. For when the Lord, speaking to Moses, had enumerated priestly vestments, he added:

> “You shall also make linen breeches [alternatively, thigh-coverings], so that they may cover the flesh of their shame from the loins down to the thighs [manuscript C: ‘breeches’]; and Aaron and his sons shall use them when they approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest they die guilty of iniquity” (Exodus 28). [Col. 0080A]

Furthermore, if we turn to the Gospel pages, we read that the Saviour entrusted the sacraments of his body and blood to be celebrated not to lay persons but only to his disciples. When he wished to transfer the old priesthood into the new, he commanded these same disciples to prepare the Passover for him in the upper room. There he plainly exercised the new priesthood and made them successors of this priesthood; after administering the Eucharist, he commanded them: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Mark 14; Luke 22).

Why did the Saviour will that this sacrament first be celebrated in an upper room [*coenaculum*], [Col. 0080B] unless because an upper room is the higher dwelling-place of a house, just as the priesthood is the higher rank in the Church? Since the Lord’s deeds both take place openly and say something else in secret, what did the Lord wish to be signified by this location, except that no one should presume to handle this mystery [some old witnesses, earlier: “ministry”] unless he has first attained the priesthood?

Hence also the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “No one takes this honour for himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5). Jerome testifies in his letter to the monk Heliodorus that this office was left by the apostles to other presbyters by succession:

> “Far be it from me to speak anything unfavourable of those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank [in one witness, ‘priests’], make Christ’s body with their sacred mouth, through [Col. 0080C] whom we too are Christians, and who hold the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

That the divine sacraments are not contained in solemn words alone is testified by the same Jerome, in his exposition on Zephaniah, in these words (chapter 3 on Zephaniah; and canon *Sacerdotes*, Cause 1, Question 1):

> “Priests who serve the Eucharist and distribute the Lord’s blood to his people act impiously against Christ’s law when they suppose that the Eucharist is effected by the words of the one pronouncing the prayer, not by his life; and that only a solemn prayer is necessary, not the merits of priests, of whom it is said: ‘A priest in whomsoever there is a blemish shall not approach to offer offerings to the Lord’” (Leviticus 21).

The Father Augustine agrees with this judgment, that no one can bless unless he has been ordained. Thus he says [Col. 0080D] in the *Questions on the Old Testament* (canon *Dictum* 95, Cause 1, Question 1):

> “The Lord said in Numbers to Aaron: ‘You shall place my name upon the children of Israel; I, the Lord, shall bless them’ (Numbers 6), so that tradition may impart grace to human beings through the ministry of the ordained [manuscript C: “so that the transmission of graces may be imparted to human beings”]. Let us consider from this how great is the dignity of priestly order. For of Caiaphas, the most wicked killer of the Saviour, it was said among other things: ‘He did not say this from himself, but, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied’ (John 11). This shows that the Holy Spirit follows not the person, whether worthy or unworthy, but the order of transmission; or that, even if someone has good merit, [Col. 0081A] he cannot bless unless he is ordained, so that he may exercise the office of ministry. But it belongs to God to confer the effect of the blessing.”

From these things, therefore, it is clear that the fullness of the divine sacraments consists not in mystical prayers [manuscript C: “ordinations”] and solemn words alone, but also requires the supplementary matters listed above [in seven witnesses: “require”]. For he who gave the command that they should be performed in order denied the effect of the reality understood in the sacraments to those who omitted the prescribed order.

Thus the apostles, who had received power over all demons, wished to heal a certain lunatic by word alone but were unable to do so. Returning to the Lord in astonishment, they learned that they had omitted certain necessary things, without which the cure of that lunatic could not be completed. For he said: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17; Mark 9). [Col. 0081B]

If, therefore, those who had received power could not accomplish what they intended when they omitted the order, what mystical or divine thing will those be able to do who have received no authority for handling divine mysteries? Let these things suffice you for the present, dearest brother. Along with what we have said, your diligence will discover much by reading, by which the folly of such empty talkers—supported by neither reason nor authority—will easily be repelled.

May God turn this error away from his Church, which he cleansed for himself “by the washing of water in the word,” that he might have her as a bride without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5). Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV [Note: [Col. 0081D] This letter is numbered 67 in the manuscript codex.]. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to JOHN, elect of Orléans: greeting.

[Col. 0081C]

Of the two clerics, namely Robert and Vulgrin [or William], concerning whom you consulted us, one of whom is said to have usurped the other’s archdeaconry, we cannot give you a definite judgment for two reasons. First, because you set before us a great battering-ram—namely, an enactment of the archbishop of Lyons—against which we neither wish nor ought to advise anyone to proceed. Secondly, because he is not a just mediator who, while one party is litigating and the other absent, wishes to determine a definite judgment concerning an undiscussed matter. But if at any time this controversy is aired before us and the others to whom it pertains, once the arguments of both sides have been heard, we shall gladly pronounce whatever reason persuades and law prescribes. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV

To his lord and father, URBAN, supreme pontiff [some manuscripts: “lord”], IVO, his son [“your son,” manuscript C], greetings and obedience.

After I departed from the presence of Your Blessedness, the many matters arising on every side gave me no opportunity either to return to you or to greet Your Highness through my messenger. For when the bishop of Paris was setting out for you, he had already nearly completed an eight-day journey before I had even heard that he was going to you. Yet, once I heard this, I sent these letters after him through one of his attendants. In them I commend him to your fatherhood, as one reared and educated among us and, so far as appeared during the years of his youth, living innocently and without reproach.

Therefore, because through your indulgence he has undertaken pastoral responsibility, we beseech your fatherhood to receive him with maternal kindness and correct him with paternal gravity, so that, made more upright by your discipline and more weighty by your gravity, he may be returned to us: that is, that he may restrain in himself the pursuit of hunting [Note: [Col. 0081D] Hunting is forbidden to clerics: c. *Esau* with what follows, Distinction 86, and c. 1, *On Clerics Hunting*.] and his other youthful desires, and apply himself more diligently than usual to prayer and reading.

Moreover, we earnestly ask Your Excellency to send him back fortified with apostolic letters against the abbot of Latiniacum and his monks, who, by I know not what novel liberty, defend their misconduct and strive, contrary to canonical ordinance, to shake from their necks the subjection owed and hitherto rendered to the Church of Paris. Such persons need subjection more than liberty, since they misuse liberty as an occasion for the flesh; even if ten thousand guardians in Christ were appointed to keep them, they could scarcely thus be bound by the laws of regular continence. [Note: [Col. 0081D] The monks of Latiniacum lead an incontinent lives.]

As befits the discerning moderation of apostolic governance, temper the matter between the two parties so that the Church of Paris may not be diminished in its right, nor the monastery of Latiniacum suffer any undue burden from the Church of Paris.

Concerning the elect of Sens [Note: [Col. 0082D] Understand Daimbert, by comparison with Letters 59, 60, and 67.], whose consecration is prevented by your legate, the archbishop of Lyons, because before his consecration he does not profess obedience to him by right of his primacy: let your fatherhood write back what we ought to do. Although no other ground had been alleged by any accuser for postponing his consecration, nevertheless, at his command and out of reverence for you, we refrained from consecrating him (see Letter 60). Yet we read nothing established by custom or ordained by law concerning a profession to be made to primates by metropolitans; and Pope Nicholas testifies that nothing has been granted to primates beyond these bounds, writing thus [Col. 0082D] [Note: [Col. 0082D] He cites Letter 83, reported as c. *Conquestus*, Cause 9, Question 3.] among other things to Radulf, archbishop of Bourges:

> “We determine that primates or patriarchs have no privilege above other bishops except insofar as the sacred canons grant it and ancient custom conferred it upon them in former times.” [Variant: *define* / *determine*.]

May the Lord grant us to hear concerning the peace of the holy Roman Church and your prosperity what we desire. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI

To HUGH, bishop of the Church of Lyons, the first see, legate of the Roman Church, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, greetings and service.

[Col. 0083A]

Because we have understood that you have hitherto loved the beauty of God’s house, after the lord pope we have loved you with a special love above all ecclesiastical persons; and we could not bear calmly to have your reputation torn apart by anyone. Therefore, believing that this same zeal in you neither grows cold nor lukewarm, we place before your eyes the misery of the Church of Orléans (Letter 67), which alien sons, seeking their own interests, are strangling and devouring.

After an unfruitful tree had been torn out of it by your hand, a pestilential one is now being grafted in. For the archbishop of Tours, tutor and incubus of the aforesaid Church, placed a crown upon the king at Christmas, contrary to your interdict (Letter 67, at the end). By this device he obtained from the king that John—made archdeacon of that Church through the late bishop John, amid much murmuring and ill-feeling—should be set over the same Church as bishop.

For the king of the Franks himself testified to me publicly, not secretly, that he had been John’s sexual submissive. This report spread so widely throughout the diocese of Orléans and the neighboring cities that he received from his fellow canons the byname of a notorious concubine, Flora. [Note: [Col. 0083D] This Flora is also mentioned in the said Letter 67.] The clergy would attest this, and the people would cry it aloud, were they not suppressed by fear of the king or terrified by the plots of the archbishop of Tours. He has clerics who oppose him delivered to the court by secret denunciations (thus Letter 5), either to be driven into exile or despoiled of their possessions.

Since he cannot hold two bishoprics [Note: [Col. 0083D] In Letter 153 he calls this “bigamy of the Church.”], he wishes to possess the Church of Orléans—which he cannot retain through his own person—through a subordinate person, so that there he may humble whom he wishes and exalt whom he wishes. It does not suffice him that he is tolerated in the Church into which he crept contrary to canonical and apostolic ordinances, unless he is allowed to prostitute the Church of God to whatever suitors he pleases, to darken with the smoke of his vain speeches and the clouds of his promises the eyes of those who see—even physicians, so that they do not hear what they hear about him, do not see what they see, and endure as unknown things which are certain.

For he commonly says of himself that “he has no need of good clerics or canons, since all these things are ready for him in his purse.” Nor is it surprising in one for whom whatever he wishes is permitted, and who does with impunity what is permitted; hence many, scandalized by this, groan more deeply, saying that they can obtain their desires more readily from ecclesiastical judges who are zealous for wickedness than from those who pursue goodness. [Note: [Col. 0083D] The same passage above in Letter 12.]

Truth is my witness that I say these things not because I have some private dispute against these men. Rather, my zeal consumes me when I see briars and thorns choking the good seed in God’s harvest, and no hand—or almost none—uprooting them. Even when there are some who bring about the fall of the evil tree, they do not remain watchful until a fruitful tree has been planted. This is plain in the present affair. The archbishop of Tours did not labor to have Sancio [some older manuscripts and Letter 54: *Sanctio*] deposed so that someone better might be placed over that Church, but so that a man of this sort, who would serve him in everything, might be appointed.

For this youth, intruded into the aforesaid Church at the king’s command and through the coercion of the archbishop of Tours, is subject to the archbishop of Tours as a boy to his tutor. He does not dare sit while standing, nor rise while seated, unless the latter commands or signals him to do so, since he is said to have subjected himself to him for shameful practices.

Finally, although many very wicked and shameful things could truly be said which, through lack of witnesses of the truth and because of human weakness, perhaps could not be proved, this alone is sufficient for rejecting the aforesaid youth: he is a disgraceful person and is shamefully notorious throughout the neighboring Churches.

Accordingly, he has been presented to me by letters from the king and chapter, to be ordained priest at the proper time and subsequently consecrated bishop. But I have neither yet rejected nor approved his election, nor shall I ever approve it unless obedience to the lord pope or to you draws me to do so. For I know that this would be not merely disgraceful but destructive to the Church of God.

I therefore ask your fatherhood most urgently to safeguard your honor and authority in this matter, and to provide for the Church of God, lest another’s salvation be entrusted to the hands of one who has never yet taken thought for his own salvation. Write back to me through the bearer of this letter what you wish me to do in this affair, so that I may answer the people of Orléans by your authority. Yet, presuming too much upon your goodwill, they foolishly say—whatever I may answer—that, at the archbishop of Tours’s request, you will consecrate him or cause him to be consecrated. [Note: [Col. 0083D] Hugh himself had written letters supporting this action, as Ivo indicates in Letter 68.]

Whatever you do, I have delivered my soul. Many people of Orléans would bear witness to what I have said, were they not afraid of prison or exile. And lest you think I have fabricated these things upon some pretext, I have sent you one song, composed in meter and music about him from the viewpoint of his sexual companions, chosen from many such songs. [Note: [Col. 0084D] They are also mentioned in Letter 67.] Young men like him sing it in the crossroads and streets of our cities; he himself has often sung it with those same companions and heard it sung by them.

Furthermore, let your solicitude know [variant: “let your prudence know”] that when the abbot of Bourgueil [older variant: “Gurgueil”] came openly, with outstretched hands and great confidence, to court at Christmas to receive the bishopric, as that aforesaid queen had promised him [Note: [Col. 0084D] Ivo usually suppresses her name; compare Letter 68], they noticed that larger and fuller bags of money lay hidden in the stores of this man’s friends than with the abbot. Thus John was admitted and the abbot excluded. When the abbot complained to—or, in another reading, against—the king that he had deceived him in this way, the king replied:

> “Wait for the present until I make my profit from this man; afterward seek to have him deposed, and then I shall do your will.”

This, then, is the sum of my words: I beg and warn you never to give assent to this election, lest you make God’s house a public brothel and a den of thieves. Finally, since I have once been deceived by the people of Orléans, I ask that if you wish to write anything to me about him, you send it through such a messenger as I can trust. And because obscenity cannot be explained except in its own terms, I ask pardon for having used irreligious words for the sake of religion. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVII

To URBAN, supreme pontiff, IVO, the least son of his holiness: mercy and judgment.

[Col. 0085B]

I have heard that your sweetness has been made bitter toward me, your serenity troubled against me; I heard it, and my inward parts were distressed and my bones shaken (Psalm 6). I carefully consulted my memory [one manuscript: “my soul”] as to what I had said or done, and how I had provoked your gentleness. Nothing occurs to me except what certain persons told me: that I had composed some letters disputing against the Roman Church, which I had sent to your legate, the archbishop of Lyons, concerning the affair of the elect of Sens.

But when I found these letters in my possession and read them carefully [Note: [Col. 0085D] He means Letter 60, to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons], I understood that much had been written there for the Roman Church and nothing against the Roman Church, unless perhaps someone who does not enter into the writer’s intention and does not attend to the single aspect of chaste expressions (thus in the heading of Letter 222) should say—far be it!—that authoritative writings contradict one another and authority attacks authority. For many discordant things are read there unless they are understood in their proper manner and adapted to the writer’s meaning.
