For in these letters, as my conscience and the very tenor of the letters witness for me, I intended nothing other than this: because of the frequent attacks and murmurs [Note: [Col. 0085D] These French complaints are treated in Letters 87, 89, and 109.] against the Roman Church, which daily ring in my ears, I wished, through the lord archbishop of Lyons, to whom you entrust your counsels, to forewarn your solicitude. Thus you might weigh your decrees together with your vicars in such a manner that the Church would not be burdened; the transgressor of these decrees would be punished by his own sentence, providing others an example of correction; and your reputation would remain unblemished. This single intention (thus Letter 189) protects the entire body of those letters.

But because some words there sounded hostile to the lord archbishop of Lyons—more harshly than he wished—especially concerning the primacy of Lyons, he set aside consideration of the writer’s intention [elsewhere: “having set aside the writer’s intention”; thus manuscript C] and, according to his emotion at that time, wished you to share in his bitterness.

Let everyone be permitted to say what he thinks. I think this of myself: there is no person beyond the mountains who has endured so many insults or received so many injuries for loyalty to you and for the defense of your commands. But because those words, on whatever occasion, have embittered your mind, it is not for me to enter into judgment with you. I would rather resign the whole episcopate than endure your anger, whether justly or unjustly. If this satisfaction pleases [variant: “pleases”] your fatherhood, it also pleases my lowliness. Receive it if you please; if more pleases you, add more.

If I cease to be your servant, I shall not cease to be your son; and, as I discovered before becoming bishop, I shall be able to benefit the Church of God more as a private person by example than as a prelate by speech. For it is most pleasing to me to bear Christ’s naked cross naked, that I may be content within that most rich and spacious estate, where love of poverty makes men wealthy and love of riches makes them miserable.

Now, during these seven years past, I have cultivated to the best of my ability the vineyard entrusted to me and have even spread manure around it; yet I have not found the fruit I sought. Therefore let me be granted freedom in the eighth year to undertake this beginning of the true [variant: “truly”] octave, so that I may keep sabbath for myself, pluck the sweet fruits of contemplation, and taste beforehand the joys of that octave.

But if I do not now do this with your permission, necessity will nevertheless compel me to do so because of the king’s renewed hostility to me on the old account (Letters 67 and 141), and because of my parishioners, who despise the word of God. They are inclined to hunger only after earthly things and are never ready to lift their hearts upward. Neither fear of God nor shame at temporal excommunication makes them willing to abandon the sacrileges they commit in churches or to acknowledge God’s justice.

Write back through the bearer of this letter whatever pleases you; and if you accede to my request, keep me in your hand, lest pseudo-bishops [Note: [Col. 0085D] He complains of these in Letter 35.] weary me at their pleasure. Furthermore, whatever may happen to me, I beseech you through Christ’s love: if the archbishop of Tours or any cleric of Orléans comes to you concerning the election of his boy, do not give him a hearing. [Note: [Col. 0086D] Letter 68 mentions this letter.]

To summarize his qualifications briefly: he is a disgraceful person, most shamefully notorious through the cities of France because of his dishonorable intimacy with the archbishop of Tours, his late brother, and many others living dishonorably. Some of his sexual companions, calling him Flora [Note: [Col. 0086D] These are also mentioned in Letter 66. Flora at that time was a notorious concubine, as the said Letter 66 states.], composed many rhythmic songs about him. Foul young men, as you know the misery of that land, sing them in the streets and crossroads of the cities of France. Nor was he ashamed sometimes to sing them himself or to have them sung in his presence. I sent one of them to the lord archbishop of Lyons as evidence; I forcibly took it from someone singing it.

Therefore, for your honor and the Church’s benefit, never allow him to be consecrated, lest you make God’s Church a public brothel and a den of thieves. Know also that the archbishop of Tours, contrary to the interdict (Letter 66) of your legate, placed the crown upon the king at Christmas; and he earned as his reward that this man should become bishop.

And that you may know how childish the election was, one of those who took part in the election jested in this way on the Feast of the Holy Innocents:

> We elect a boy, observing the feast of boys,  
> Not following our custom, but obeying the king’s commands.

## LETTER LXVIII

To HUGH, bishop of the Church of Lyons, the first see, vicar of the Apostolic See, IVO, by God’s grace bishop of Chartres, greetings.

I recently received letters from your fatherhood inviting me, or any others who wished to challenge the election of John, archdeacon of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0087D] Letters 66 and 67 should be read together.], to appear before you on the Kalends of March, to prove the charges which they wished to bring against him, whether of simony [two old manuscripts: “simoniacal conduct”] or other grounds sufficient for his rejection, since you cannot be both accuser and judge.

But your prudence knows that this was said concerning hidden matters. Saint Ambrose, however, testifies that a manifest accusation [Col. 0087C] does not require such a process (c. 5 and c. 17, Canon 2, Question 1). Thus, speaking on the Epistle to the Corinthians about the man who openly had sexual relations with his stepmother, he says:

> “It is not the judge’s role, I say, to condemn without an accuser. But once this man’s act was known, he judged that he should be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For everyone knew his crime; in this matter there was no need of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.”

Pope Nicholas writes something similar to King Charles [Note: [Col. 0087D] Chapter *Quae Lotharius*, Cause 2, Question 1; it appears among the letters of Nicholas I as Letter 55.]:

> “The deeds committed by King Lothair, your nephew, require no accusation.”

For the works of the flesh in him are manifest: fornication and impurity (Galatians 5). Since, therefore, the matters which I wrote in the preceding letters are conspicuous to the knowledge not only of one city but of many cities, many wonder why hidden matters are sought, when manifest matters alone suffice to reject one who has not yet been installed.

Since he lacks many of the things which Paul says are necessary in examining a bishop for consecration, you know well with us that he lacks one thing which the same Apostle, after enumerating the others, commends as especially necessary above the rest:

> “A bishop must have a good testimony from those outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (1 Timothy 2).

But this man has hitherto neglected his reputation; and according to blessed Augustine (Sermon 52; see Letter 240), one who neglects it is cruel, for, so far as lies in him, he kills his neighbor. Episcopal power, however, ought to be for building up, not for destruction.

And although, according to the Apostle, some persons’ sins are manifest and precede them to judgment, while those of others follow afterward, this man’s simoniacal intrusion, though true, does not yet precede him to judgment. For this detestable transaction was carried out through chamberlains and footmen [some manuscripts: “female attendants”; Letter 60, manuscript C: *sequipedam*, “foot-servant”]. Its public disclosure will reach your ears unless you hurry to establish the planting which the Lord did not plant, and by your authority confirm an election extorted by royal entreaties, which according to the common proverb have the same force as threats.

For there are among us certain merchant-creditors of that aforesaid queen [Note: [Col. 0087D] Compare Letter 66; perhaps Bertrada is meant, concerning whom see Letter 13.], who, as they told us, expect a portion of the money promised by John’s parents. Yet that same aforesaid queen reports that, through a certain cautious policy, payment is being deferred until it can be made more safely after his consecration. The action for recovering those exactions, however, will soon be pursued if the consecration is postponed for some time.

What the Seventh Synod says concerning an election made by secular rulers, what the Eighth says, what the other holy Fathers proclaim, and what your own ordinances declare, is not for me to teach your prudence. Moreover, if the initial investigation took place within the province, as the ordinances of the elders require, in a location where an unruly crowd was not feared, there would be no lack of accusers and no lack of witnesses. They do not dare to go to distant places for such affairs or to expose themselves and their possessions to uncertain danger for an uncertain result.

Truth, who is truthful, and love for both parties are my witnesses that I have spoken truth and spoken it for truth and love, providing, insofar as I can, both for the Church’s benefit and your honor. Otherwise—God forbid—if you act other than those who sincerely love you desire, they may afterwards lamentably say that saying of Jeremiah: “The gold has grown dim; the finest color has changed” (Lamentations 4). Know that I have also communicated to the lord pope what I have communicated to you (Letter 67), and that I await his response on these matters.

## LETTER LXIX

IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to WALTER [or GAUTIER], provost of the Church of Stirpes (*Stirpensis*), and to the little flock entrusted to him: greetings and the support of prayers.

[Col. 0088D]

From the letters recently brought to me on your behalf, I understand that your brotherhood is deeply troubled because the bishop of Limoges, acting in synod, forbade all regular clerics both the governance of parishes and the hearing of penitents’ confessions (Letter 213). He would indeed have acted more rightly had he invited all priests to the regular life rather than wholly removing from the care of the Lord’s sheep those living according to rule. For the more far removed they are from their own wickedness, the more greatly they dislike that of others.

Yet, although this prohibition may perhaps appear to have been imposed through some envy of the canonical order, the more wholesome it is, the more welcome it ought to be to your brotherhood. For you proceed along God’s way more freely [manuscript C: “you will proceed more freely along God’s way”] if you do not carry the oppressive bundles of others’ crimes together with the daily falls occasioned by your own transgressions.

For the present I answer your inquiry as follows: regular clerics ought neither to be wholly excluded from this office nor indiscriminately admitted to it. If they are wholly excluded, an unworthy injury is done to the canonical order, to which correction of another’s life may be entrusted all the more safely because it has applied greater diligence to correcting its own life. But if this burden is indiscriminately imposed on regular clerics, ecclesiastical discipline is broken in some cases; and the brethren who in their cloisters, as in military camps, stood firm and conquered against temptations are easily overcome by temptations when they go out alone to battle.

Hence blessed Jerome says:

> “The removal of a man establishes the weapons of chastity [variant: ‘gather them’] and builds the camps of modesty among the better.”

If, therefore, there are in your community prudent and mature men, tested by the fire of temptation, upon whom you wish this burden to be imposed, bring them before the bishop, so that they may receive from him the care [manuscript C: singular, “care”] of souls. Without his judgment, as you remember, according to canonical ordinances, no priest may impose criminal penances, nor, after the penance has been completed, reconcile penitents to the sacred altars.

By doing this, you will render to episcopal reverence what belongs to it, and you will cause no loss to canonical institution. You are called canons because you have vowed to observe canonical rules more strictly than others.

As for your wish that I write something to the bishop of Limoges concerning this matter, I have delayed for the moment because that lord is unknown to me. I await a suitable time when we may discuss these and similar questions among ourselves orally, according to what reason and authority prescribe. Farewell.

## LETTER LXX

IVO, humble servant of the Church of Chartres, to WALTER, bishop of Meaux [or “to Gautier, bishop of the people of Meaux”]: to think holy thoughts and do holy deeds.

[Col. 0089D]

Since zeal for God’s house ought not to grow lukewarm in our hearts, we must love the beauty of that same house and place ourselves as a wall on behalf of it, so that we may either ward off beforehand the assaults which the ancient enemy makes upon it, or, if he has already broken into it at some point, expel him—with God’s grace assisting—by gathering our strength of mind together.

Although it is harder work to restore what has fallen into ruin than to preserve what is whole in its condition, nevertheless we must, through narrow and difficult paths, even amid the bloody wounds of thorns and amid the uncertain paths of mists, seek what has been lost, gather what has been scattered, and cleanse, so far as we can, what has been defiled. We are admonished and instructed by the example of the supreme householder, who left the ninety-nine sheep on the mountains, himself sought the hundredth which had perished (Luke 15; Matthew 18), redeemed it with his blood, and brought it back to the fold from which it had strayed.

Therefore, lest the supreme Shepherd reproach us, as shepherds seeking our own interests, to our shame: “You have not sought what was lost; you have not bound up what was broken” (Ezekiel 34), let no private affection, no favor of any person however exalted, no hope of advantages, and no fear of disadvantages divert us from the purpose of our duty: namely, that we should recall the erring to the way and strive to rescue from the jaws of the invisible wolf those souls deceived by their own frailty or by diabolical illusion.

I urge this upon your love because I have heard, both from the words of the monks of Tours and from letters of Lady Adelaide [or Lady Adela], the venerable countess, a most shameful report concerning the monastery of Saint Fare. It ought now to be called not a place of holy women but a brothel of demonic women, prostituting their bodies for shameful uses to persons of every sort. If they refused correction and merely brought death upon themselves, perhaps they might be tolerated. But because they have become a snare for many souls, I urge and advise your vigilance either to correct the aforesaid women in their place and order, or, if that cannot be done, to endeavor to entrust that place with its possessions to religious monks—having nevertheless received from them a guarantee that they will restrain the aforesaid women under strict discipline and provide them, from the monastery’s resources, with necessities for as long as they live.

In this way you will produce manifold fruit from a good beginning: you will lead those incontinent women back to a purpose of continence; restore to their proper state the possessions of the monastery, assigned by the faithful to the needs of holy persons; suppress the detestable reputation which distresses religious monasteries with its evil odor; and save from eternal destruction the souls of the incestuous who perish through association with those women.

What I write to you I bring forth from the depths of charity, desiring you to do the same to me if you hear that I am negligent in a similar danger. For as we walk in God’s way, we ought to extend to one another the mutual hands of exhortation, so that together at our arrival [some manuscripts: “so that together at the end”] we may rejoice in the sheaves (Psalm 125) of eternal fruits. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI

To WILLIAM [or WILLELM; Note: [Col. 0089D] This was William II, and a most wicked man, as Matthew Paris says], glorious king of the English, IVO, humble minister of the Church, greetings and service.

In the letters recently sent to me by Your Sublimity [variant: “recently sent to me”], I observed the disposition of a gentle and prudent man: Your Dignity preferred first to seek an explanation from my lowliness rather than rashly judge anything about me, according to the saying of the wise man: “Do not judge before you have understood” (Ecclesiastes 1).

For Your Excellency asked my humility on what ground I released [variant: “absolved”] Nivard of Septeuil from the pledges and oaths by which he had bound himself to Your Greatness, since Christians ought to observe toward Christians the pledges and oaths which they give one another. We grant this indeed, provided the oaths were lawful or at least not unlawful.

But the aforesaid Nivard testified to me that the pledges and oaths which he had made to Your Sublimity were contrary to prior oaths which he had made to his natural and lawful lords, from whose hands [most older manuscripts: singular, “hand”] he had received his hereditary benefices. He could not keep the later oaths unless he chose to violate the earlier [manuscript C: “first”] ones.

Supported by reason and authority, I therefore advised him to perform penance for the later oaths and to prefer just obligations to unjust ones, lawful to unlawful ones, and earlier oaths to later ones. Though this can be confirmed by many reasons and authorities, I have taken care to append a few out of many.

For we have in the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 4 (canon *Duo mala*, and following, Distinction 13):

> “Although two evils should altogether be avoided with the utmost caution, nevertheless, if necessity compels us to mitigate one of them, we ought to release that by which we are known to be bound with a lesser bond.”

Hence Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage* (c. 4 and 20, Cause 22, Question 4):

> “If faith is invoked for committing sin, it is remarkable if it is called faith at all. Yet, whatever its character, it is worse to act against it, unless it is abandoned for this reason: that one may return to true and lawful faith.”

Likewise Tarasius the patriarch (c. 18, Cause 22, Question 4):

> “Herod kept an unlawful oath and perished. But Peter denied with an oath, then was converted, wept, and was saved.”

Likewise Jerome, on Jeremiah, book I (*Commentary*, c. 4 and c. 2, Cause 22, Question 2):

> “It must be observed that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment, and justice. If these are lacking, it will in no way be an oath, but perjury.”

On this account Pope Honorius severely rebuked certain bishops beyond the Po who urged Peter, a distinguished man, to break the oaths he had made to King Aconius, father of King Adulbald, and to agree with Ariobald [thus the older manuscripts; formerly “Arlobald”]. He carefully commends that distinguished Peter because he did not acquiesce in the corrupt persuasions of priests, but firmly kept the oaths he had made to Aconius.

From these and other such authorities it can be understood that lawful or permitted oaths must be firmly observed, while unlawful ones must either be avoided or, if made, dissolved with penance. Had I given other advice to the parishioner entrusted to me, I would not have recalled the straying sheep or rendered the care I ought to have rendered to a sick sheep. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII

[Note: [Col. 0091D] This letter is mentioned in Letter 80.]

IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to G., abbot of the monastery of Saint Wandrille [variants: *Guandregesili*, *Wandregisili*, *Guandregesili*], greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0092A]

Your affection consulted my insignificance as to whether altar-slabs once consecrated, when they have been moved and placed upon a new structure of stones, ought to be consecrated anew. This seems to us necessary both by authority and by reason, since the canon says: “If an altar has been moved, the church is to be consecrated anew.” If a church must be consecrated anew because of a movement, how much more the altar itself which has been moved?

Moreover, since signs bear a likeness to those things of which they are signs, just as faith, which is the head and foundation of sacred religion, ought to remain immovable [or: enduring] in the believer, so the visible altar, which bears the figure of faith, ought to remain immovable. And just as, if anyone has been moved away from the foundation of faith, he must be reconciled by the laying on of hands to the Body of Christ, which is the Church, so the altar-table, bearing the type of faith, if it has been moved, must again be imbued with the sacred mysteries.

Nor is the argument sufficiently similar which certain brethren raise against you: that portable [or: moveable] altars, though they are moved from place to place, are nevertheless not consecrated anew. For we do not consecrate these altars otherwise than when they are set into such wooden structures, or into some suitable underlying support, and firmly fastened there. Hence, although they are carried [or: conveyed] from place to place, they are nevertheless not moved from the place in which they were consecrated. If they have been torn away from that place, they must be consecrated anew, like other altars.

I have briefly written back to you on the question proposed, being prepared to set out the same reasons and authorities more fully, if that were appropriate. But I judged that these things would suffice for your prudence. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIII

IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to BERNARD, abbot of Marmoutier, may you deserve to hear: “Well done, good servant.”

The report which was in the mouths of many brought no joy to my ears, since from it I perceived a general injury to monastic religion and a particular trouble arising from your disturbance. For it was reported to me that certain brethren had risen against your community, saying that the charge committed to you had not had a lawful beginning, for these reasons: that you received a blessing from one said to be excommunicated, and that before the blessing you promised the due submission to the metropolitan see.

Perhaps these brethren have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10), thinking that an abbot’s promotion is effected by episcopal blessing rather than by the common election of the brethren [variant: “whether an abbot’s promotion is effected rather by episcopal blessing than by the brethren’s election”]. Yet the Lord confers that blessing not according to the merit of the one giving it, but according to the faith and purity of the one receiving the blessing.

Thus blessed Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Old Testament*: “The Lord said to Aaron in Numbers: ‘You shall place my name upon the children of Israel, and I, God, shall bless them’ (Num. 6), so that grace may be conveyed to human beings through the ministry of the ordained person; and the will of the priest [variant: “of the giver”] can neither harm nor benefit, but rather the merit of the person seeking the blessing.”

Therefore the same Augustine says in the third book *On the One Baptism*: “It is one thing not to have something, and another not to have it by right, or to usurp it unlawfully. Therefore the sacraments of Christ and of the Church are not absent because they are used unlawfully, not only by heretics but also by all wicked and impious persons; rather, those persons must be corrected or punished, while the sacraments themselves must be acknowledged and revered.”  
[Note: The sacraments have equal validity in the good and the bad; Letter 236, at the end.]

Again, the same author, in the book *Against the Letter of Parmenian*: “Just as that which he possessed outside is not bestowed again upon one who returns, so that which he received outside ought not to be repeated for one who comes.”

It follows, therefore, that the perversity of human beings must be corrected, but the holiness of the sacraments must not be violated in any perverse person. For it is clear that it remains unpolluted and inviolable among perverse and criminal persons, whether among those within or among those outside; but in the good it is for reward, and in the wicked for judgment.

Accordingly Pope Anastasius confirms as valid the sacraments celebrated by the condemned Acacius, writing thus to the Emperor Anastasius: “According to the custom of the Catholic Church, may the most sincere heart of your Serenity recognize that no share of injury, on Acacius’s account, touches any of those whom Acacius baptized, or whom he ordained as priests or Levites according to the canons, lest perhaps sacraments administered through an unrighteous man should seem less firm.” And below: “Therefore this man also, whose name we say should be kept silent, by administering good things badly harmed himself alone. For the inviolable sacrament given through him to others retained the power of its perfection.”  
[Note: This is reported more fully in c. 8, distinction 19.]

Again Augustine, *Against the Writings of Petilian*: “For anyone to be a true priest, he must be clothed not only with the sacrament [variant: “with the sacrament alone”] but also with righteousness, as it is written: ‘Let your priests be clothed with righteousness’ (Ps. 131). But one who is a priest by the sacrament alone, as was Caiaphas, the high priest, persecutor of the one and most true Priest, although he himself is not truthful, nevertheless what he gives is true, provided that he gives not his own thing but God’s.”

Those who have once received the order of priesthood, as the same Augustine says in the book *On the Good of Marriage*, are not deprived of it, although some are removed from office for certain faults. Finally, the divine sacraments are such for each person as is the heart with which that person approaches them, as Augustine says in the *Dialogue against Petilian*.

These things, indeed, have been said concerning ecclesiastical sacraments, without which Christian life cannot be called Christian, nor can the reward of eternal salvation be obtained from the Lord. What then is there to dispute concerning the blessing of an abbot, from whatever bishop he may have received it? In it neither the laying on of hands nor consecration takes place (the same author above, Letter 88), but only a simple prayer; and whether that prayer is received or not received, the salvation of those subject to him is neither diminished nor increased.

For your brotherhood knows how many servants of God in Egypt, Palestine, and other provinces were fathers of monasteries, yet received no such blessing from a human mouth. Nevertheless their subjects rendered them every obedience and did not for that reason fear for their salvation.

As for the further accusation that you did not act rightly in promising obedience to the metropolitan see before the blessing—  
[Note: That the situation of an elected bishop toward his primate is different, he writes in Letters 60 and 66 above.]  
—it is an empty accusation, or none at all. For how can the members of Christ’s body be joined together with one another unless the stewards of canonical or monastic communities render to their prelates the obedience which they wish rendered to themselves by their own subjects?

Further, what fault is there if that which is owed is demanded and that which is owed is rendered? Hence Augustine, in the first book *To Simplicianus*: “Who does not see that no one can be charged with wrongdoing for demanding what is owed to him, nor indeed can one who refuses to remit what is owed to him? This, however, lies not in the choice of those who are debtors, but of the one to whom the debt is owed.”

That those promoted to ecclesiastical dignities are debtors bound to promise obedience is attested by the Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 2: “Everyone who is about to enter ecclesiastical ranks shall not receive the consecration of his office until, by the bond of his pledge, he promises that, preserving the Catholic faith with the devotion of a sincere heart, he will live justly and piously, will contradict the canonical rules in none of his actions, and will render in all things the honor due and the reverence of obedience to every person set above him.”

The supreme pontiff himself—  
[Note: He says the same in Letter 60, from the book entitled *Diurnus*.]  
—before receiving the grace of consecration, professes that he will inviolably observe the customs of the Roman Church and the decrees of his predecessors. Thus other pontiffs are examined before consecration and promise their ordainers that they will display every uprightness of ancient conduct [Note: *morum*, “of conduct,” is absent in manuscript C.] and the obedience due.

Since humility alone, which is obedience’s companion, is worthy to be exalted, just as pride is worthy to be cast down, an abbot does not sin if he professes with his mouth what he ought always to have in his heart and, when appropriate, display in deed.

Therefore let such disturbers, themselves disturbed, acting idly and inquisitively, understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm (1 Tim. 1), not drive your community from the sabbath-rest of the heart by their useless investigations and empty whisperings [as the old manuscripts read], nor remove you from the obedience you have undertaken, whatever storm may arise. And let not that hostile mockery fall upon you: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14).

For your diligence knows that the ancient enemy watches chiefly for this: to interrupt the peace of God’s servants; and, once he has interrupted it, to restore to himself the vessels taken away from him and, having regained them, to infect them still more fiercely with ancient and new filth. Therefore observe his manifold snares with the shrewdness of the serpent; bear the vexations of murmurers with the simplicity of the dove; and yet, so far as lies within your power, remove from them any just cause for murmuring, lest, as they say, the property of the monastery fall into ruin through your negligence and the customary assistance for the brethren be diminished.

But if perhaps, through some bodily weakness [variant: “inconvenience”] or devotion to heavenly contemplation, you are less able to suffice for this, there are prudent men with you, walking with you in one spirit, upon whom you may place part of your burden. You yourself may then more freely, and therefore more abundantly, taste the sweetness of heavenly contemplation and in due season dispense the provision of the word to your fellow servants.

I do not write to one ignorant of these things [variant: “I write these things not to one ignorant”], but I wish your charity to be warned, lest a storm arising among you become [variant: “cause”] a stumbling block or scandal to the weak, who, seeking an occasion, encounter that proverb of Solomon: “He who fears the wind will never sow, and he who watches the clouds will never reap” (Eccles. 11).

Therefore remove from all the weak or envious an occasion for blaspheming the holy purpose or for not entering upon the narrow way of life, lest the Lord say to you in rebuke through the prophet: “What had perished you did not seek; what was weak [variant: “was”] you did not strengthen; what was broken you did not bind up” (Ezek. 34). May he avert this from your holiness: he who laid down his soul for us, and both admonished us by word and showed us by example that we should lay down our souls for the brethren. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIV

IVO, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans: patience in tribulation, perseverance in patience.

So far as I gathered from the tenor of your letter—  
[Note: Hildebert’s Letter 19 survives, in which he complains of the cruelty of the king of the English.]  
—the fearsome severity of the king of the English is attempting, at the suggestion of your rivals, to accuse you of the recently committed betrayal of the city of Le Mans. No lawful accusation has been brought against you; rather, there is a report of malicious conjectures veiled in the guise of divinations. And although you are ready to perform a lawful purgation, he is unwilling to believe you free of this betrayal unless, by the trial of red-hot iron, you prove your innocence.

You therefore ask my humility whether, being conscious of no wrongdoing, you ought, for the preservation of your reputation and the recovery of the king’s favor, to yield to his will, or rather suffer whatever adversities may come so as not to depart from due order. I answer you briefly: do not transgress the ancient boundaries, the boundaries set by your fathers. For to defend innocence in another manner [variant: “what if in such a manner?”] is to lose innocence.  
[Note: Compare Letter 205.]

For neither ecclesiastical custom admits judicial combat or the trial of hot iron in the examination of ecclesiastical causes, nor has canonical authority instituted them. Therefore Nicholas, in the case of King Lothair and Theutberga—  
[Note: Below, Theutberga; in Letter 205, alternatively Tecberga or Tieberga; quoted by Gratian in the chapter *Monomachiam*, causa 2, question 5.]  
—who was accused of false crimes, says: “We do not receive judicial combat into law, since we do not find it commanded; for those who follow this and similar practices seem merely to tempt God.”

Augustine says in the book *Questions on Genesis*: “When a person has something to do, he ought not to tempt his God.”

Pope Alexander II likewise wrote to Ramuld [variants: Rimald or Raymald], bishop of Como—  
[Note: Quoted in causa 2, distinction 4.]  
—thus: “Concerning the case of your priest Gisland, accused of the death of his bishop, your predecessor, we have taken counsel in the presence of all the brethren standing around. Therefore, with their unanimous assent, we write to your belovedness that the said Gisland is to be brought before you. There, if definite accusers are lacking, then, justice so directing, the priest shall without all dispute receive back both his priesthood and the full benefices which he has unjustly lost on this account. Yet, before this, if an accuser should fail to appear, we commit to your judgment that he should offer his own purgation in the presence of two priests joined to him.

“Finally, we do not wish either that he himself should undergo, or that you should in any way demand, the popular law unsupported by any canonical sanction—namely, contact with boiling or cold water, red-hot iron, or any other popular invention—because these things are wholly fabricated by envy; indeed, by apostolic authority we most firmly [variant: “most severely”] prohibit them.”

[Note: In c. *Mennam*, causa 2, question 4, and Gregory, book II, Letter 8.]

Pope Stephen V [variant: Sylvester II, manuscript C] likewise says to Lambert [variant: Luitbert, manuscript C], bishop of Mainz:  
[Note: Chapter *Consuluisti*, causa 2, question 4.]  
“The sacred canons have not judged that a confession should be extorted from anyone by the trial of burning iron or boiling water; and what has not been sanctioned by the teaching of the holy Fathers must not be presumed upon through superstitious invention. Crimes made public by voluntary confession or by the proof of witnesses must be judged by those entrusted with governance, with the fear of God before their eyes; but secret and unknown matters must be left to the judgment of him alone who knows the hearts of the children of men.”

I would have written more to you on these matters, had it been possible. You, then, fortified on every side by these and other authorities of the Fathers, act manfully, and do not provide in your own case an example harmful to others, present or future. For if you suffer anything contrary to justice, you shall be purified by tribulation and proved; and from that proof you shall obtain mercy. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXV

IVO, by God’s grace bishop of Chartres, to JOHN, by the same grace bishop of Orléans, greeting.  
[Note: In several old manuscripts the following heading is prefixed: “Whether, by permission of the Apostolic See, one may excommunicate a person of another diocese”; compare the end of Letter 60.]

That I sought permission from the lord pope to excommunicate the lady of Puteaux [Adelicia in Letter 76] and her knights was compelled by great and manifest necessity, because of the unremitting injuries frequently inflicted by them upon the Church of Chartres and not yet redressed by the Church of Orléans.

Even now those who wrote on your behalf seem to be laboring toward this end: interpreting the lord pope’s letters according to their own liking, not conforming their meaning to his will, but laying snares from a grammatical construction—as though those who wrote the apostolic letters had themselves not been grammarians. For when he said that you should confirm our sentence, canonically pronounced against the aforesaid lady, he had already said that she was your parishioner; and nevertheless he gave the Church of Chartres permission to excommunicate her for injuries done to it.

It is therefore canonical, after warning her and summoning her often, to excommunicate her and, if she does not repent, to deliver her to Satan, since that power has granted this whose office it is to judge every person and every Church (Letter 78). I therefore ask and admonish you to fulfill the command you have received, because I too shall not for the present be deprived of the apostolic authority which I received.

What you offer me—namely, that she should be brought before justice in the chapter of Orléans—you yourselves [variant: “yourself”] know is not canonical. For the benefice which she unlawfully occupies contrary to the canons belongs to the Church of Chartres, where I have offered her every form of justice and still offer it. But she wholly refuses, because she knows that her claim is unjust.

Your brotherhood ought to know that every case must first be examined in the places where it arose (Letter 184; Gratian, causa 3, question 6). Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVI

To DAIMBERT, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens, from IVO, humble priest: greeting and due reverence.

Since, according to ancient institution, your solicitude has resolved to celebrate a provincial synod, in which apostolic and canonical enactments must be promulgated for the correction of wrongdoers, I neither wish nor ought to withdraw my insignificance, though of little use, from the assembly to which you invite me, provided that divine mercy preserves my liberty and health.

By whatever route that same divine mercy permits me to come, I ask you to send me, some days beforehand, as safe a conduct as you can to a suitable place. Concerning the election at Nevers, in which the efforts [variant: “votes”] of parties have divided themselves, I believe that your prudence has been instructed by the ordinance of the Fathers to prefer by every means the man who is supported by the greater number of efforts and by merits.  
[Note: Council of Nicaea, canon 6; Antioch, canon 19; Pope Leo, Letter 82; see Gratian, distinctions 61 and 65.]

But because no one is to have hands laid upon him hastily, if you cannot at present discover this fully, it seems to me that the matter should be deferred until the next synod, so that then both the support of the electors and the merits of those elected may be examined more clearly.

Furthermore, regarding Adelicia, lady of Puteaux (Letter 75), and her son Hugh (Letters 111 and 112), with their other helpers: because of the tyranny which they exercise against us, we earnestly request—and in requesting continue to press—that you too excommunicate those whom we have excommunicated by apostolic authority, or cause what has been wrongfully seized to be restored to us.

For it was established in ancient times, and recently confirmed by the unanimous consent of all the bishops present at the Council of Auvergne [in Puteaux manuscript alone: “at the Council of Nevers”], that neighboring bishops should also excommunicate anyone excommunicated by one bishop for injuries to the Church (below, Letters 111 and 120). If she alleges that she has been unjustly excommunicated, let her come to the Church against which she brings her false accusation and from which she has suffered no injury; with God’s help [Puteaux manuscript: “God consenting”], she will hear that the sentence imposed upon her was just.

The copy of the apostolic letters which I sent you will show that she has been excommunicated by us under apostolic authority. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII

IVO, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to HUGH, dean of the Church of Beauvais, and to the other brethren of the same Church: greeting in the Lord.

Concerning the mill which was granted to your Church [manuscript C: “our Church”] by the bishop who constructed that same mill, and which has been peacefully possessed not merely through thirty years’ prescription [variant: *usucaption*, “acquisitive prescription”; in some copies the word *usus*, “use,” is absent] but has also been confirmed by the authority of your privileges: it has now lost its function of grinding because it is obstructed by the impediments of bridges and the refuse of dyers. You seem to have a just cause, supported by every reason, especially against the bishop, who ought not only to commit no unlawful acts in his own time, but also to correct those unlawfully committed by his predecessors.

For Pope Gelasius writes thus to the bishops Cresconius and Mesalia [variant: Massala, manuscript C] (chapter *Decessorum*, causa 25, question 2): “As a successor ought to preserve the enactments of his predecessors when they are lawful and just, so he must also correct their wrongdoings.”

Therefore what the bishop now says is not an adequate reason: that by his command no obstruction was placed in the way of the mill which prevented it from performing its work. This is no excuse unless he removes, by the power of his office, those who obstruct it. For Pope John VIII writes to Emperor Louis (Letter 100): “He shares the fault of the one acting, who neglects to correct what he can correct.”

But if the bishop tries to remove this matter from his authority, let him read the decree of Pope Gelasius’s council. It says (chapter *Placuit*, causa 16, question 3): “It has pleased this holy and great synod that properties or privileges belonging to the Churches of God by long custom, whether bestowed in writing by emperors of blessed memory or by other worshippers of God, and possessed by those Churches for thirty years, shall in no way be removed—  
[Note: The words are absent in manuscript C, as also in the Decree.]  
—from the authority of their prelates by any secular person who withdraws them by force or takes them away by any contrivance [variant: “by any contrivance whatsoever”]. Rather, all things known to have been possessed by Churches within the period of thirty years shall remain under the authority and command of the Church’s prelate. Whoever, cleric [variant: “therefore, cleric”] or layperson, acts against the present definition shall be judged sacrilegious; and until he corrects himself and restores the Church’s own privileges or property, let him be anathema.”

Again Pope Nicholas, concerning the same matter, writes to Ado, archbishop of Vienne:  
[Note: Chapter *De rebus*, causa 12, question 2; it survives among the letters of Pope Nicholas I to Archbishop Odo, Letter 59, vol. III, *Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*.]  
“Concerning property once contributed and dedicated to God, and afterwards invaded and plundered by certain persons under pretext of a grant from princes, we decree that the prince first be consulted [variant: “consult the prince”] in order to cut off so presumptuous an enterprise, to take cognizance of so presumptuous an enterprise, and to ascertain whether it is his grant or the presumption of the invader. If the prince’s grant has been disorderly, then the prince himself must be reproved for correction. But if the invader’s presumption is established, he must be restrained by the punishment of excommunication until he makes amends.”

Objection based on a year’s possession according to the custom of his city, or an obligation of the bishop by which he promised to observe that city’s customs, or a turbulent conspiracy of a concluded agreement, does nothing to prejudice ecclesiastical laws. For agreements and enactments [variant: “customs”], and even oaths, which are contrary to canonical laws and the authorities of the holy Fathers, are of no force, as you yourselves well know.

For Pope Zosimus writes to the people of Narbonne [manuscript C: “to Narbonne”]: “Not even the authority of this see can grant [variant in c. *Contra*, causa 25, question 1: “make”] or alter anything contrary to the enactments of the Fathers. But if anything has been adjudged against you contrary to the forms of the canons, then, if it seems right to you, you shall appeal to the hearing and judgment of those who appear to have greater authority among you, whether to your metropolitan or to the Roman legate.”

After lodging an appeal, within five days you shall request letters from the person from whom the appeal was made (Letter 220; chapter *Si quis*, with the following chapter, causa 2, question 6), addressed to the person to whom the appeal was made, so that he may appoint a day for both parties on which he commands that your case be concluded by judicial sentence. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVIII

IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to the monks of the monastery of Dol: may you dwell together in unity in the house.

Certain persons from your monastery, holding different opinions, came to us and informed us of the dissension that had arisen among you concerning the election of your brother Bernerius, formerly a monk of Bonneval [variant: Bonneval, manuscript C]. Having heard their report, we were deeply grieved, knowing without doubt that Satan had demanded you, and fearing lest upon this occasion you bite and devour one another and be consumed by one another [variant: “consume one another”].

We therefore summoned to us the abbot of the monastery of Bonneval [variant: Bonneval, manuscript C], and, having assembled some of the better brethren of our Church, carefully investigated whether the aforesaid brother had appeared under any notable disgrace either in clerical or in monastic order. We found good testimony concerning him [variant: “his good testimony”] at every stage of life and in every order.

The abbot and monks objected only that he had left the monastery without the brethren’s permission. But the cause of this departure we knew ourselves, and, investigating more carefully through others, we discovered that at the time when he departed there was great disturbance in that monastery. The abbot of that place, unable to bear it, was compelled by necessity to return to the larger monastery in which he had come to conversion.

It is better to keep silent than to reveal, out of reverence for the monastic order, the cause for which the abbot departed. Therefore that departure—which seemed to that brother and to many others of pious judgment to be a change for the better—seems to us to cause him no prejudice [variant: “seems to create no impediment for him”], if the votes of all, or of the better part, among you agree upon him and if modes of conduct incompatible with monastic governance hinder his election. This is especially so since the supreme pontiff (Letter 75), whose office it is to judge every person and every Church, has absolved him from this bond, has even heard Mass from him, and has often communicated with him before religious persons in all ecclesiastical sacraments.

Therefore, if no other things contrary to canonical institutions are found in him, we ask and admonish you to confirm charity toward him and strive to return quickly to the bond of peace. We have at hand examples of religious men who, leaving their monasteries for a probable cause, withdrew to the monastery of Cluny (Letter 41), or to other monasteries, or even advanced without any rejection [variant: “repulse”] to ecclesiastical dignities or the care of monasteries.

[Note: Thus the old manuscripts; see the note of manuscript C.]

Of these, two men from the monastery of Holy Cross, learned and religious men—Guimundus and Robertus—were, by apostolic authority, appointed, the one to the bishopric of Avranches and the other to the governance of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Avranches.  
[Note: Thus in several ancient books.]

Arnulf [variant: Ernulfus], monk of the monastery of Saint Symphorian at Beauvais, a prudent and religious man, left his monastery for a similar cause and now governs the monastery of Canterbury. So too did many others. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIX

IVO, by God’s grace bishop of Chartres, to WILLIAM [variant: Vilelmus] of Paris, JOHN of Orléans, WALTER [variant: Gautier] of Meaux, HUMBALD of Auxerre, and PHILIP, bishop of Troyes: greeting.

When we were assembled at the council of Étampes, many things concerning your brotherhood, though unpleasant for us to hear, were reported, and we were greatly astonished at them. If true, they are burdensome even to the ears of good [variant: “upright”] persons and perilous to your order. Since your envoys reported them, or will be able to report them, we have for the present resolved to remain silent.

But because you were summoned [variant: “invited”] to the council and did not come, nor sent on your behalf either an envoy or a lawful excuse, in writing or orally [variant: “sent beforehand”], we could have pronounced canonical sentence against you. For, according to the laws (law IX, distinction *Quod me*, causa ...), we accept as a lawful excuse only an actual fear of death or apprehension of bodily harm, where no difficulty prevents the journey from being made earlier or by a circuitous route.

Moreover, a certain contempt could be noted in your letters: you neither inserted the name of the metropolitan, as is customary in letters of excuse—  
[Note: One manuscript has “of excuse”; similarly, he called exculpatory oaths *excusatoria sacramenta* in Letter 18.]  
—nor addressed to him any words of excuse.

We, however, more intent upon mercy than judgment, obtained from the lord metropolitan a delay for you until the Sunday next before the Nativity of the Lord, when the consecration of the bishop of Nevers is to take place. Therefore, admonishing, we command, and commanding, we admonish, that then, putting aside every excuse, you present yourself before the lord metropolitan to answer concerning the allegations.

If you neglect to be present, it will no longer be our fault if you receive judgment in place of mercy. Nor need you fear the viscount, who promised you complete security concerning himself, his son, and all his people, in the presence of the whole council. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXX

IVO, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to WILLIAM [variant: Guilelmus], abbot of the monastery of Fécamp: the mutual gift of prayers and devoted service.

I find nothing written in the ancient rules concerning the moving of an altar or of the walls of a church—whether consecration must be repeated or not. But in the collections [MS Put.: “collations”] of Burchard, bishop of Worms, I find the following written from the fifth chapter of the Council of Meaux:

> [Note: [Col. 0101D] It appears in Burchard’s *Decree*, book III, ch. 11, from the decrees of Pope Hyginus, ch. 4. Others call him Brocardus, as in book IV, title 4, of the Decretals.]
>
> “If an altar has been moved, the church is to be consecrated anew; but if the walls have been moved and not the altar, they are only to be exorcised with salt.”

If this chapter is considered carefully, it answers all your inquiries. Since I have at times given the monks of Saint Wandrille [variant: Guandregisili] such reasons as I could concerning the moving of an altar, I have taken care to write the same to your religious community. To them I wrote as follows (Letter 71):

Your affection consulted my lowliness as to whether altar-slabs once consecrated, when transferred and set upon a new structure of stones, must be consecrated anew. Both authority and reason seem to us to require this, since the canon says:

> [Note: [Col. 0102D] Canon “If moved,” 18, *On Consecration*, distinction 1; add title XL, “On the Consecration of a Church or Altar,” book III of the *Decretals*.]
>
> “If an altar has been moved, the church is to be consecrated anew.”

Now, if the Church is to be consecrated anew because the altar alone has been moved, how much more the altar itself which has been moved? Moreover, since signs bear a likeness to the things of which they are signs, just as faith—the head and foundation of sacred religion—ought to remain immovable in the believer, so the visible altar, which bears the image of faith, ought to remain unmoved. And just as someone who has been moved away from the foundation of faith must be reconciled by the laying on of hands to the body of Christ, which is the Church, so the altar-table, bearing the type of faith, if it has been moved, must again be imbued with the sacred mysteries.

Nor is the argument satisfactory which certain brethren raise against you: that portable altars, although moved from place to place, are nevertheless not consecrated anew [variant: “nor do we need to remind you that they are consecrated anew”]. For we consecrate such altars only when they are fitted into wooden slabs or some suitable supporting base and firmly [variant: “steadfastly”; thus MS C] fixed. Therefore, though they are carried from place to place, they are not moved from the place in which they were consecrated. But if they are torn away [variant: “pulled out,” MS C] from it, they must be consecrated anew like other altars.

So much concerning the moving of an altar. But concerning walls: if they are restored, why must they be exorcised only with salt and not consecrated? We must investigate the reason. For this purpose it seems necessary [repeated “it seems necessary,” MS C] first to consider the form of the invisible temple, so that afterwards we may compare with it the figure of the visible temple.

For the Apostle says: “You are God’s field; you are God’s building. I, as a wise architect, laid a foundation” (1 Cor. 3). We understand this foundation, as we said above [MS C: “as”], to be faith. Good works are built upon it, by which love of God and neighbor is demonstrated, as though they were the walls of a spiritual building. Over all these is added, in place of a roof, the loftiness of hope, which advances by penetrating even to that which is within the veil.

The same Apostle writes: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Therefore, if faith is uprooted, the whole spiritual building is without doubt destroyed. But if the remaining building is worn down by age or diminished by some injury, the sacraments of faith are by no means repeated; rather, whatever is stained is cleansed only by the harshness of penitence and the tears of compunction.

Accordingly, following this analogy, when the altar is moved—which, as has been said, bears the image of faith—the whole church must be consecrated, since, when faith is corrupted, it is wholly destroyed. But when the walls are moved, it is to be restored only with water and salt, as with sacraments of penitence. For your prudence knows that the Church prays in this manner: that what is performed in temples made by hands may be spiritually fulfilled in us [Col. 0103A], so that through the worship of visible sacraments we may be drawn to the knowledge [variant: “recognition,” MS C] and love of invisible buildings.

More could be said about these observances in addition to what has been stated; but I think this sufficient for your prudence, which knows how to infer the greatest things from the smallest and more things from few. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: due obedience together with the faithful service of prayers.

My lowliness rejoices that your fatherhood has ascended to the rank of the apostolic summit and succeeded Pope Urban of blessed [MS C: “good”] memory. Giving thanks for this to supreme Providence, it prays God daily, according to its measure, that better outcomes may proceed from good beginnings [Col. 0103B].

For we believe that your religious devotion has hitherto possessed zeal for God and has loved without pretense the beauty of God’s house. Therefore, after we learned that your fatherhood had assumed the office of the apostolic rank, it was our highest desire to approach your presence in person—had we not been held back by the danger of bodily infirmity, which, if we set out, we might easily incur by speaking truthfully about ourselves, or by the danger of a fall of the soul that would threaten us if we denied the truth. For Peter is said to have denied Christ, not because he denied that Christ was Christ, but because he denied that he was Christ’s disciple.

Therefore, for the present I send you this brother, the bearer of this letter [Col. 0103C]. I ask you to receive him kindly in my place and to hear, as though hearing me myself, whatever he beneficially and usefully suggests to your reverence. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXII. IVO, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to GAUFFREY, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme: greetings.

A certain brother of your monastery, named Daniel, came to us and gravely complained that he has repeatedly been treated by your brotherhood in a disorderly and miserable manner, both by insults of speech and injuries of blows. He declares that, as he has experienced you toward himself, so you are toward all, or nearly all.

Therefore I urge your brotherhood to moderate your zeal in such a way that you neither spare what is swollen nor apply the iron to healthy parts; that you correct those whom you correct with charity, and spare those whom you spare with charity. For you know that when one of the prophets was cutting wood and struck excessively hard [41], the iron flew from the handle [Note: [Col. 0103D] “From the hands” is absent in MS C. The same passage occurs in Letter 164, from Deuteronomy, ch. 19.] and killed one of the sons of the prophets.

Thus, dearest brother, the immoderate rigor of discipline does not correct those whom it rebukes; rather, it recklessly drives them into the devil’s snare. I therefore ask and urge your brotherhood, since the aforesaid monk is failing under the weight of your rebuke [MS C: “correction”], to allow him to recover in some cell of your monastery; or, if keeping him seems altogether unbearable to you [Col. 0104A], grant him leave to save his soul in another monastery. Write back to me about this at once. In this way the brother may improve through renewed conduct, and his soul will not be required from your hand. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to the bishops of the diocese of Reims, reverend brethren in Christ: greetings in the Lord.

We have seen and read the letter sent to you by your metropolitan (Letter 85), and I believe your prudence remembers the harsh and threatening terms employed by its author. Yet, whatever threats or insults that letter may contain, it is your duty, both for yourselves and for your fellow bishop of Soissons [Col. 0104B], to take its weight seriously and diligently to avert your own danger in his danger.

For if a metropolitan is permitted to command whatever he wishes in the churches of his province (Gratian, causa 9, question 3), without the consent [MS C: “concession”] of the bishops who preside over them, to judge their clerics, or to suspend them from office, then an unworthy violence will be done to the dignity of bishops and a destructive injury to the authority of the holy Fathers [MS Put. alone: “a calumnious injury”].

At the request of your fellow bishop of Soissons [variant: “the bishop of Soissons”], therefore, we exhort your reverence, by the common obligation of charity, to put forth opposing hands against undertakings of this kind and repel such assaults with the battering-ram of canonical authority.

For you have in the Heptateuch that, in a quarrel between two men, one who lays a hand upon the other’s genitals is to be stoned (Deut. 25; see notes) [Col. 0104C]. What else does this mean but that one who, in some dispute, utters abusive words against another should be sternly reproved by all?

So long as the people of Soissons are prepared to render canonical satisfaction in their chapter through their own bishop, no one ought to charge them with heresy or sacrilege. Nor ought those clerics or their bishop, if canonical authority is observed, to answer the accusations based on the written infamy imputed to them until canonical satisfaction has been rendered [one MS reverses the word order: *debent objectis* for *ad objecta respondere*].

Although what I have written could be fortified by many authorities, I have taken care to append a few out of many [Col. 0104D], not to instruct you, but to remind you. For blessed Augustine says:

> “Whoever has injured another by a curse or an accusation of crime should endeavor from the same mouth to bring forth the remedies from which he brought forth the wounds.”

Otherwise, according to Pope Fabian, one who does not prove what he alleged is himself to suffer the penalty which he imposed (*What Penalty*, etc., in Gratian, causa 2, question 3). Unless perhaps the objection is that the trifles of one’s betters are commonly called “business.”

Concerning the prohibition against judging another Church, Pope Callixtus, agreeing among others with the opinions of many, says (*Letter* 2, and in chapter *Just as*, causa 7, question 1):

> “Just as another man’s wife is not permitted to be adulterated by anyone, nor judged or disposed of except by her own husband while he lives, so neither is the wife of a bishop—by which his church or parish is unquestionably understood—allowed, while he lives, to be judged or disposed of by another without his judgment and will.” [Col. 0105A]

Pope Nicholas likewise writes to Ralph, archbishop of Bourges (reported in Letter 236):

> “Our brother Sigegodus, archbishop of Narbonne, has complained to our apostolic office that you compel his clerics, against his will, to come before your tribunal; and that concerning matters belonging to his Church you make dispositions, without consulting him, as though by a right of your patriarchate. Yet neither antiquity—to which the Fathers decreed reverence—possesses this right, nor does the authority of the sacred canons permit it at all, unless, perhaps, they have appealed to you as their patriarch in cases which they cannot decide among themselves; or unless, when their bishop has died, they have wished the affairs of their Church to be administered under your judgment. For we determine that primates or patriarchs have no privilege above other bishops except insofar as the sacred canons grant it and ancient custom has from old conferred it upon them; thus, according to the Nicene rules, churches are to retain their own privileges” (chapters 1, 2, 8, 10, 17, 21, causa 25, question 2). [Col. 0105B]

I could add much in this manner, but it seems superfluous, since these materials are available among you as among us. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to JOHN, cardinal priest and legate of the Roman Church: may you exercise your legation in Christ.

I recently received letters showing your goodwill, in which you informed my lowliness [Col. 0105C] of certain acts of your constancy. Among these I recognized as notably praiseworthy your abstention from communion with the king.

> [Note: [Col. 0105D] Philip, concerning whom see Letter 211.]

In this you wisely provided both for your reputation and for the legation entrusted to you, although certain bishops of the Belgic province placed a crown upon that king at Pentecost, contrary to the interdict of Pope Urban of good memory, as though they thought that, when the herald of justice had died, justice itself [MS C: “of justice”] had died.

I entirely approve your intention to hold a council at Poitiers or within the province of Aquitaine. For if a council were held within Belgic or Celtic province, many matters which, if discussed, would generate scandal and choke nearly the entire fruit of the council in a certain ferment would have to be suppressed in silence. Yet, if suppressed in silence, as though the word of God were bound, they would greatly detract from the authority of your legation [Col. 0105D; MS Put. alone: “as though the word of God were choked, from Roman authority”].

As for the date for holding the council, which you have fixed as the fourth day before the Kalends of August, the bishops of our regions will readily seek an excuse, saying that there is not adequate time for making the journey and preparing provisions. Many bishops cannot reach the place of the council except by many detours and by hired conveyances procured from every direction.

If it seems good to your prudence, a more suitable date would seem to me to be the beginning of autumn, when [variant: “because”] the year will be more fruitful and every person invited, being granted sufficient [Col. 0106A] time, will be better prepared for it.

But if, contrary to expectation, all these things occur, when God permits us to speak together, I shall discuss with your prudence both the date and place for holding the council, and many other matters. For I pass over many things which, not without reason, I presently refrain from committing to paper.

Accordingly, I send you [42] this messenger with your letter-bearer [one MS: “with this bearer”], through whom you may reply to me concerning the time and place of our meeting and the arrangements for holding the council. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to MANASSES, reverend archbishop of Reims: may you abound in the bowels of charity.

Letters were recently brought to us (Letter 83) which you had sent [Col. 0106B] through your provincial bishops. On reading them, we understood that a grave scandal had recently arisen from a slight cause between the Church of Reims and the Church of Soissons.

Although our judgment is foreign in your province, we do not consider our counsel foreign. Persuaded by charity, we should wish, if we had the ability, to make provision for the good of your reverence and of all religious persons. Yet those letters seemed, if you will permit me to say so, to contain more invective than correction [MS C: “rebuke”], more disturbance than reconciliation; to strike more at the strength of the healthy than to bind the wounds of the weak; and to rely upon authorities that are honorable and firm, but not sufficiently aptly [Note: [Col. 0106D] “Aptly” is absent in MS C.] suited to the matter at issue.

I say this not in biting criticism [Col. 0106C], but in sorrow, desiring in brotherly love that you quiet the scandal by prudent moderation; that you remove as swiftly as you can from those curious to know another’s life (Letters 7 and 118), but idle in correcting their own, the occasion for disputing about you; and that you not place a stumbling-block before the blind.

For it is read in Exodus that, if two men fight and strike a pregnant woman, and an unformed child comes forth, the offender shall suffer loss according to what her husband requires, and he shall pay for his life (Exod. 21). What is this pregnant woman but a weak soul, not yet perfected in the love of God? When religious men contend among themselves and generate scandal by their contention, this soul is struck and scandalized, so that it casts away and loses the love of God which it had conceived only faintly.

But one who causes such a miscarriage in this weaker, womanly soul will suffer loss, because he will be deprived of the reward with which a faithful servant ought to be rewarded for a multiplied talent [Col. 0106D]. The husband of this woman is Christ, who imposes the penalty due for this offense, saying (Mark 9): “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone were placed around his neck and he were cast into the sea.”

That you may be able to avoid such losses, recall your daughter, the Church of Soissons, to a mother’s bosom in a fatherly manner. You call her sacrilegious, although she is prepared to obey canonically, as you have pleased [MS C: “as you have called her”] [Col. 0107A]. Moderate these bitter words—which can become a memorial of eternal enmities—by changing your mind for the better. Otherwise, if you stubbornly bite and devour one another, you will be consumed by one another.

For, as far as I understand, unless you moderate your zeal, she will not without canonical reason guard herself against submitting to your judgment, since you seem to move an army against her as against an enemy and to prepare as it were for battle. Let your prudence therefore employ the counsel, not of angry men, but [one MS: “the counsel of ripe men, but”] of those able to be discerning mediators between both parties, lest after many vexations you be compelled to undergo a foreign judgment. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to STEPHEN, count palatine: affection and peace in Christ [variant: “greetings and affection,” Letter 49].

I cannot send clerics frightened by threats and subjected to insults to you. I therefore send a sheet of writing that neither fears nor blushes, demanding justice and promising justice.

I now urge your excellency for the third time to make your men, who have offended against the peace, come to the justice of the peace which you yourself dictated and promised. When this has been corrected, we are prepared to make amends if we have committed any offense against you. For I have never sent you anything else concerning this affair [Col. 0107C], whatever your envoys may have told you.

Whatever, whether more or less or otherwise, has hitherto been said in your hearing, I now demand justice and offer justice, according to the circumstances of the acts done and the order of the admonitions, as those will jointly decide who have sworn that they will render just judgments concerning the peace. And this is to be done next Tuesday.

But if you refuse, we know that your power and principality have no need of ecclesiastical peace. We, however, shall be content with our own boundaries. We shall relinquish this peace—which is very burdensome and costly to the Church [some MSS: “unfruitful”]—since we cannot maintain it against you; but in other matters we shall serve you [variant: “serving you”] as a great and powerful man. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to JOHN and BENEDICT, cardinal priests and vicars of the Roman Church: may you exercise the legation entrusted to you in such a manner as to please the Angel of Great Counsel.

[Col. 0107D]

Since I formerly informed you by letter, in part, of the downfall of the Church of Beauvais, I cannot now keep silent from your concern about the depth of evils [Note: [Col. 0107D] “Evils” is absent in MS C.] into which it has descended. Otherwise my silence may be imputed to me as a fault, and may provide no remedy for the lethargic disease of that Church.

For that Church has now so long been unaccustomed to having good shepherds [Col. 0108A] that having bad ones seems almost lawful to it, and choosing good ones almost criminal. This is sufficiently clear from the fact that, in defiance of letters from the lord pope (Letter 89, to Paschal) and from you prohibiting an unlawful election or installation of a bishop, they uttered mocking and contemptuous words against you, to the contempt of the Apostolic See. Setting aside all canonical obedience, they elevated as bishop, at the king’s pleasure and that of his concubine [variant: “female cohabitant,” MS C; Letter 13], a certain unlettered cleric, a gambler, devoted to women and other such enticements [variant: “things of this world”], found to be far even from holy orders, and formerly expelled from the Church for public adultery by the archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Roman Church.

The aforesaid intruder is called Stephen of Garland [some MSS: “of Gallanda” or “of Valanda”]. If at any time a way should be opened for him to episcopal ministry [other MSS, including MS C: “consecration”; MS Put.: “If episcopal consecration…”] by apostolic authority, it is evident [some: “if, through you, apostolic authority should permit it, it is evident”] that in our time a ruinous silence has been imposed upon the canonical laws [Col. 0108B]. For how shall we reach the fountain of knowledge [43] if we are not allowed to enter by those who hold the key? [variant: “if entry is not allowed”]

I wish your concern to be forewarned and fortified against these and similar matters, so that you may guard yourselves and make the lord pope cautious concerning them, lest one who stands against you find an occasion to slander you as seeking your own interests and not those of Jesus Christ [Col. 0108C].

For the aforesaid intruder is hastening either to go to Rome or to send someone there, to bend the palace officials to his side by whatever gifts or promises he can, and to deceive the lord pope by whatever stratagem he can. We therefore make the truth of the matter known to you, so that you may protect apostolic authority, provide well for your reputation, support with consolation the Church wasting away amid evils, lift it up with a strong hand, and break the teeth of those who gnaw at it with the stone of sincerity [one MS: “crush”].

If in this matter too our expectation is disappointed, we shall no longer know what to say against those who speak ill of the Roman Church.

> [Note: [Col. 0108D] See what he writes on this subject in Letter 109.]

Nor shall we any longer dare [variant: “be able”] to set ourselves as a wall for God’s house, trusting in the Roman Church. Therefore take counsel quickly concerning God’s worldly house and the vindication of the contempt shown to you [Col. 0108D], and write back through the bearer of this letter what you wish to do concerning this and your other dispositions. When, by God’s gift, we can speak with you, we shall explain these matters and others more carefully and fully. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. IVO, his humble son, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, lord most worthy of every reverence: the affection and fulfillment of all obedience.

I have heard that, through the report of certain liars, word has reached the ears of your holiness that Lord Hilgot [variant: Hilgod], formerly bishop of Soissons [Col. 0109A], took refuge in a monastery after being deposed for certain crimes. May your holiness be far from believing this!

For, marked by no infamy and charged by no criminal accusation, he renounced the episcopate because of the dangers of prelacy [variant: “of precedence”], which experience had already taught him he could not safely bear. Taking refuge in the harbor of a monastery, he escaped naked from the shipwreck of this world.

At that time I was a priest at Beauvais in a certain regular church. He was familiar with me because he perceived [variant: “supposed”] in me some appearance of piety. He came by way of me, poured out his whole heart before God in my hearing, and at last disclosed his purpose. Although I offered him a mild [variant: “slight”] resistance and used many arguments to persuade him to remain in the government entrusted to him [Col. 0109B], after many words exchanged on both sides, the conclusion of his resolve was that he preferred to be saved in a lowly place rather than be endangered on high [some MSS: “at the summit”].

Seeing the constancy of his soul—that a man of such nobility and prosperity thus trampled the world beneath his feet and fled beneath Christ’s light yoke—I approved his intention. He who had made me judge of his conscience thereafter had me as the one who praised his purpose.

How he subsequently conducted himself in the monastery, let those tell you who know, who, after testing and approving his manner of life, chose him as their father. The only charge raised by those to whom an unfamiliar good is more displeasing than an accustomed evil is this: that an unworthy injury would be done to episcopal dignity if one who had been bishop became an archimandrite [Col. 0109C].

For they say that one cannot be an abbot without a blessing [variant: “unless he is blessed,” MS C]. But if he is blessed, they say that a grave injury is done to episcopal blessing. In all this, your judgment must be awaited and your decision upheld. Whatever the prerogative of the apostolic summit chooses to determine, we shall not think that any injury is done to the episcopal sacrament, since an abbot’s blessing is no repetition of a sacrament, nor does abstention from this blessing hinder a man chosen for this office from administering spiritual or temporal goods (see Letter 73).

Your prudence knows by how many examples of modern and ancient Fathers this can be demonstrated. I wished to lay these matters before your holiness, so that you may not believe every spirit nor readily lend an ear to those murmuring dishonorably against an honorable person [Col. 0109D]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIX. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: all that a son owes a father.

Since, as my conscience testifies, I know myself to be a child of the Roman Church’s womb—

> [Note: [Col. 0109D] Elsewhere in MS Put.: “an intimate son.” Thus, already in Letter 12, writing to Pope Urban concerning himself, he says: “Take thought for the child of your womb.”]

—when she is scandalized, I cannot help burning; when she is troubled, I am troubled; when she is torn by the envious tooth of detractors, I am torn apart [Col. 0110A].

Therefore I urge your sweetest fatherhood that, if any cases from our regions concerning bishops or other persons to be accused or defended are brought to your ears, you should not immediately comply with the petitions of those who seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ. Rather, allow fitting and ample time, seek the testimony of religious persons who can clearly know the facts in the neighboring region, and then, once the truth is known, settle every matter justly or mercifully as God inspires you.

For by preserving your good reputation—which is very necessary to the Apostolic See—you will provide for the salvation of many and restrain hostile tongues from slander.
