Otherwise, if the shameful parts of the father should be exposed—may God avert it!—we shall not mock them as sons of aversion; nevertheless, we shall restrain pen and tongue from admonitions of this kind which we see are fruitless [Col. 0110B].

Nor should your holiness be displeased that I, as a son, offer such counsel to your fatherhood. For I have already seen many lovers of justice [variant: “many shepherds”; compare Letters 109 and 110] impose silence upon their mouths because of offenses left unpunished or the crimes of many left unaddressed [variants: “the crimes of many left unaddressed, or offenses,” MS C], and lose much hope of correcting evils.

So much for this. Furthermore, I make known to your excellency that the clerics of Beauvais, contrary to your interdict and that of your legates, have elevated a certain cleric named Stephen (concerning whom see Letters 87, 95, and 104) as bishop [Col. 0110C]. He was far from holy orders, being not yet even a subdeacon; an unlettered man, gambler, pursuer of women, formerly publicly defamed for public adultery.

> [Note: [Col. 0110D] The accusation was made by Lisiard, archdeacon, as he says in Letter 45.]

On this account he was deprived of communion with the Church by the lord archbishop of Lyons, then legate of the Apostolic See. Many other dishonorable things could be said about him, but these true and manifest facts suffice for his rejection if apostolic and canonical enactments have not lost their force.

I wish your holiness [variant: “fatherhood”] to be forewarned and fortified by my lowliness concerning this, lest someone deceive your innocence by deception and attain the episcopate [44] through your permission [Col. 0110D]. If this happens, then, if you do not believe my words, experience itself will eventually teach you how greatly the authority of the Apostolic See will fall in this case.

Therefore, lest that schoolmaster occupy the ground for long, remove him from God’s Church—

> [Note: [Col. 0110D] Used in a bad sense, as in Letters 6 and 98.]

—so that other uncircumcised clerics, seeing this, may desist from similar ambition, and so that God’s word may run and prosper in your days.

Your holiness should know that this Stephen had first been rejected by the people of Beauvais for the reasons stated above. But when the sounder party, with the king’s approval, wished to elect a certain religious man, Stephen was received by certain malicious, excommunicated clerics and laymen [Col. 0111A]. For that Church had long been accustomed [one MS: “had become accustomed”] to have such bishops—

> [Note: [Col. 0111D] Similar passages in Letters 87 and 92 should be connected.]

—as would condemn her, not direct her to the way of life.

It belongs to you, however, to seek wandering and scattered sheep through the mists and trackless wilderness, to lead them back to pasture, and to provide them with a shepherd who will care for the flock. Even if the sheep themselves wish to perish, to wander (see the passage in Letter 102), or to offer themselves to be choked by the savagery of wolves, your holiness must nevertheless say to them: “I do not want you to wander; I do not want you to perish.”

That you may know it is true that he was expelled from the Church for adultery, I have taken care to send you a copy of the archbishop of Lyons’s letter. Farewell.

## LETTER XC. IVO, minister of the Church of Chartres, to DAIMBERT, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens: greetings and service.

[Col. 0111B]

The bearer of your letter was hastening to return, while I was somewhat weakened, for reasons of health, by drink and bloodletting [variant: “reduction”]. Nevertheless, I answer these questions as occasion permits.

For the Truce of God (*trevia*, variant *treuvia*) has not been established by a universal law; yet, as you know, for the common benefit of humanity it has been confirmed by the authority of the agreement and covenant of city and country, bishops and churches. Therefore, judgments concerning the violation of peace must be regulated according to the agreements and definitions established by each Church with the consent of its parishioners and committed to memory by writing or by the testimony of good men.

It is therefore clear that your stepfather and brother, with regard to the man whom they excepted from observance of the peace when swearing to observe the peace, did not violate the compact of peace, even though they incurred the guilt of homicide. But since that exception did not extend beyond the person of the offender, and since his nephew had not previously been charged with aiding him or sharing communion with him, if that nephew had sworn to the peace, then, so far as appears to us, he was unjustly slain contrary to the institutions of peace—unless perhaps you have other reasons, not at all contained in your letter, by which you defend his killer from the charge of violating the peace [Col. 0111C].

Indeed, we hold that even violators of the peace are not to be handed over to enemies for punishment, nor even excommunicated, unless they have first been accused and convicted and have refused to amend their evil deeds [variant: “evil words”]. Thus Augustine says in his book *On Penance*:

> “We cannot exclude [some MSS: ‘deprive’] anyone from communion—even though this exclusion is not deadly but medicinal—unless he has either confessed voluntarily or has been accused and convicted by some secular or ecclesiastical judgment.”

Much could be said in this manner [Col. 0112A], but I do not suppose you are ignorant of these things. Farewell.

## LETTER XCI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to ADELA, noble countess: service together with faithful prayer.

We give thanks to God, who turned the storm of your illness into the calm of restored health. For just as the cloud of approaching illness grieved us, so the brightness of returning health has made us glad.

We therefore entreat divine mercy to make the present scourges of the flesh a medicine for the inner person, so that you may wash away past offenses with tears and take care henceforth not to commit deeds needing tears, lest the divine hand which now mercifully chastises later crush you miserably [Col. 0112B].

For the remedy of your soul I ask you to love the church of blessed John the Baptist, in which, by God’s gift, we have established a regular life; to defend, to the best of your ability, its possessions against those who lie in wait and make incursions; and especially to permit the *regulae* (small holdings) of a certain Haimeric, formerly a servant of Saint Mary’s monastery at Jouarre and now professed in that church, to be possessed there undisturbed by the attacks of your people.

For the abbess of the aforesaid monastery manumitted that servant together with his possessions to that church (according to the canons, under distinction 54), as Lady Hilescendis [variants: Hilesendis, MS C; or Hilensis], the viceregent, will tell you. In return, you will receive from the brothers of that church the gift of their prayers, and from us faithful service. Farewell.

## LETTER XCII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: due obedience with every devotion.

[Col. 0112C]

My mother, the Church of Beauvais, which begot me in Christ and nourished me with her milk, has been greatly harassed and grievously worn down by the frequent succession of harmful or [alternatively, and; see Letters 87 and 89] useless bishops. With tearful cries she calls after me, as though the consecration of her elect [Note: [Col. 0111D] He was Stephen of Garland, as is clear from Letters 87 and 89.] were hindered through me, or as though my intercession might obtain it from Your Holiness. And because a mother’s pains, though not always wholly reasonable, penetrate compassionate hearts with special force, I cannot but be moved by her complaints [Col. 0112D] and pierced by her groans.

That Church asks, in the person of its elect, that one defect alone be remitted: namely, that he has not been found in sacred orders [Note: [Col. 0111D] For he was not yet a subdeacon, as the said Letter 89 states.], although in all else it proclaims his integrity and commends his usefulness. But if anything criminal, or anything contrary to the sacred canons, should be found in him, it is not for us to intercede in such a matter before the seat of justice [Note: [Col. 0112D] Thus he also calls Rome in chapter 46, and the “throne of justice” in Letter 250.], nor for you to lend an ear to disorderly prayers.

We know, however, that it has been reported to Your hearing, and through the testimony of certain of your legates [Col. 0113A], that the aforesaid elect was at one time accused by Lisiard, archdeacon of the said Church, before the Archbishop of Lyons, then legate of the Apostolic See, and was charged with a certain crime [Note: [Col. 0113D] Namely adultery, as Letter 89 writes.]; yet he neither confessed voluntarily nor was convicted by any ecclesiastical or secular judgment.

The aforesaid Church therefore declares that he is ready canonically to answer every charge, if anyone is able canonically to accuse him. That same Lisiard, who then accused him as an enemy, has now changed and loves [alternatively, chooses] him especially, seeks him above others, and defends him with every excuse he can. In cases in which accusers become defenders, it is not for me to remind Your Solicitude [Col. 0113B] what a judge ought to do, or to instruct Your Prudence.

Whatever men may praise or blame in this affair, the elect himself, secure in the knowledge of his own conscience—which is for him an undoubted witness either for or against him—presents himself before your tribunals, ready either to receive mercy or undergo judgment. Therefore we ask with those who ask, and knock with those who knock [Note: [Col. 0113D] He wrote under compulsion from the importunity of the said Stephen, as at the beginning of Letter 95.], that you may so temper judgment with mercy that, so far as may be done without prejudice to your honor, you may mercifully come to the aid of the Church’s pitiable ruins. For we wish to help our friends in such a way as never to wish to harm in any respect the authority and honor of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0113D] As at the end of Letter 133.]. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIII. To DAIMBERT, by the grace of God Patriarch of Jerusalem, IVO, humble servant of the Church of Chartres: the gift of the prayers of the faithful.

[Col. 0113C]

Because divine mercy has willed that your care should preside over that Church from which the word of God went forth, we rejoice both because of the intimate affection with which we embrace you and because of the benefit which we hope your solicitude will confer upon God’s people. Therefore, let those whom bodily sight does not unite be joined by the affection of indissoluble charity; and let daily prayer set us mutually before the eyes of the mind, whose bodily presence the wide expanses of lands exclude.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] Thus some old manuscripts read. In others: “the intervening distance or interval of lands excludes,” manuscript c.]

We pray, therefore, that Amalek may be overcome by hands stretched out to heaven and prayers poured forth on the mountain (Exod. 17), so that, after the many [Col. 0113D] scourges of the children of Israel, in the time of your priesthood the ark of God may return, freed, to Shiloh (1 Sam. 4), where the people may offer peace-offerings and appease God for their offenses by the sacrifice of a contrite heart.

May our Savior and defender also send David the faithful [Note: [Col. 0114D] Thus from the old manuscripts; in one of them it is written “D. D.” The earlier reading “the faithful lord” is wrong.] to your aid, that he may circumcise the numerous foreskins of the Philistines and bring them into the lot of the Israelite people. Thus may this earthly Jerusalem not serve as a slave woman with her children, but imitate the heavenly Jerusalem, which is free [alternatively, “with the free”]; [Col. 0114A] its citizens are [alternatively, become] not only those who make pilgrimage in this earthly Jerusalem, but all who merit to belong to the peace of the heavenly vision [one manuscript: “strive to belong”].

Furthermore, we commend to your care our parishioners who carry this letter, and all others whom you learn have come to Jerusalem: cherish them with fatherly consolations; and, if they have departed from the way of justice, exhort, rebuke, and correct them, warning them to return to the path of heavenly purpose. We ask from you nothing transitory, nothing belonging to the present life; but if you could send us something pious, something holy, which might impress the memory of you more firmly upon our minds and awaken in us a greater grace of devotion, this we would desire and humbly request.

If you should wish to write anything to our littleness [Col. 0114B] concerning your condition and that of our mother, the Eastern Church, you may safely do so through these men. May the Lord, through the ministry of your tongue, increase the faithful people who serve Him worthily and in number. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIV. To PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: the service of obedience and dutiful service owed to his holiness [one manuscript: “himself, as a most obedient son”].

Since, with divine assistance, the Count of Chartres has renounced the evil customs which his predecessors—and he himself—had exercised upon the houses and possessions of the deceased [Col. 0114C] or deposed Bishop of Chartres, at great labor and expense to me and to the Church; and since my insignificance has obtained from Your Holiness a privilege for completing the confirmation of this same liberty, I ask Your Excellency to send letters to the clergy of Chartres containing the following decree: if at any time some Counts of Chartres, or their officials, through greedy rashness and rash greed, should violate the liberty granted by the count, let them be excommunicated by that clergy, under apostolic authority, as sacrilegious invaders of ecclesiastical right; and let the churches, both those within the city and those in the suburbs (Letter 121), be closed until satisfaction has been made.

For a people accustomed to plunder [some manuscripts, “made accustomed”] cannot otherwise be restrained from its wickedness unless it is checked by the utmost rigor of justice [Col. 0114D] and punished by terrible excommunication. Add also that, if a succeeding bishop absolves the perpetrators of that sacrilege without satisfaction, or tolerates them through ambition to acquire the bishopric or fear of losing it, he shall be judged a participant in sacrilege and stripped of the episcopate. By such a barrier the torrent of wickedness may be held back from its habitual plunge and confined within due bounds. Nor is it improper that unusual remedies should be discovered and applied against new kinds of disease. Farewell.

## LETTER XCV. To PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, himself as a most obedient son [manuscript c: “bishop, servant of his holiness, the dutiful service of obedience and service owed”].

[Col. 0115A]

I rejoiced beyond expression both at the rejection of Stephen, suitor of the Church of Beauvais, and at the fatherly rebuke directed against me on his account (see Letters 87, 44, and 97). Yet in my later letters I wrote nothing contrary to the earlier ones, nor did I appeal to Your Holiness for his person’s sake, but for the Church’s ruins. For by his importunity he extorted from me letters which (Letter 92) I believed would by no means [alternatively, in no way, manuscript c] benefit him—indeed, would greatly harm him [one old manuscript, “offend him”]—if they had an intelligent [Col. 0115B] reader [manuscript c, “readers”] and a suitable interpreter.

Your letters made plain to me how steadfast in you are the love of justice and zeal for God’s house; and, as I made them public, this became known to almost all the churches of our kingdom, to the praise of the divine Name. Nothing therefore remains in this business except that a good outcome be set upon good beginnings and good progress.

Furthermore, we make known to Your Prudence [alternatively, “I make known to your wisdom”] that our venerable brother, the Bishop of Châlons, ever a lover of the Roman Church, has through us—who attended the Council of Poitiers—approached and appealed to Your Clemency. He asks that you mitigate or [Col. 0115C] alter for the better your judgment concerning the treasurership of the Church of Châlons, extorted from your innocence by Drogo’s importunity and the clouds [Note: [Col. 0115D] Thus he called “clouds of promises” in Letter 66.] of his words; and that, as becomes apostolic moderation, you command our brother what is just and possible.

And although no one may externally reopen an apostolic judgment (Letter 159), consider it yourself; judge it yourself: ought a synodal decision, fortified by apostolic decrees and canonical sanctions, to have been dissolved without hearing both parties? For it is not unfitting, as we are taught by apostolic examples and writings, that the Apostolic See itself should at times alter a judgment for the better (chapter *Sententiam*, Cause 35, Question 9), when something has been obtained from the Apostolic See by fraud or false petitions.

So that you may recognize that the letters sent by Your Holiness to the Bishop of Châlons were extorted by fraudulent concealment, we shall briefly set forth for Your Prudence the course of the case which we handled. The aforesaid Drogo, burdening the ears of all who sat at the Council of Poitiers with importunate cries, declared that he had been canonically invested by Philip, Bishop of Châlons, with the aforesaid treasurership and had therefore been unjustly dispossessed.

When the truth of this matter had been carefully examined, the clergy of the Church of Châlons testifying, it was objected to the aforesaid Drogo that, according to ecclesiastical order, he could not possess the aforesaid dignity unless he were a canon of that Church. He neither had been nor could be such, since he had already been made canon and archdeacon in another Church [Col. 0116A] and another province. It was also added that the aforesaid bishop, already dying and anointed, overcome by Drogo’s importunity, had not [manuscript c, “nor had”] invested him with the said office, but had granted it only under the condition that, while the bishop lived, he should never concern himself with it nor usurp its usufruct.

Invited to judgment by your venerable cardinals [one copy: “bishops or cardinals”], since no one could oppose the aforesaid arguments, and the same cardinals confirmed our judgment [one manuscript, “the judgment of the brethren”], we judged on grounds of reason and authority that there had been no canonical investiture—against which apostolic decrees, canonical institutions, and almost all councils cry out.

For the laws call “investiture” not a grant but possession, which the aforesaid Drogo did not have during the deceased bishop’s lifetime; after his death, however, he shamelessly intruded himself. Nor does canonical order permit anyone, by a premature leap, to become superior in a Church in which he has never merited to be subordinate. That the aforesaid cleric cannot hold titular office in the churches of two cities [Note: [Col. 0115D] In the Seventh Synod and the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 10; see Gratian, Cause 21 [lacuna] 2.] we establish from the judgments both of you and of your predecessors.

We also understand from Pope Gelasius’s words that, if anything has manifestly been presumed contrary to apostolic decrees, there is no need for it to be summoned to judgment as though it were doubtful, when it has so often been cut off by the apostolic sickle and decided by the judgments of general councils. Nor do you convene councils for any other reason than to recall despisers of your decrees [Col. 0116C] [manuscript c, “commands”] to their observance.

Therefore, if observers of apostolic commands are harassed by your authority, or allowed to be harassed, see for yourselves [alternatively, “you yourselves”] what peace remains for the Church and what vigor [variant, “rigor”] remains to discipline. For thus they will grow negligent in obedience [Codex Putaneus, “obedience”] to the commands of the saints: not only those who observe them under compulsion [alternatively, “who are compelled to observe it”], but also those who wish to keep them diligently. What use, moreover, will councils henceforth have, if judgments supported by however great an authority are made void through one person’s accusation?

We therefore ask Your Holiness, after weighing the advantages and disadvantages [Col. 0116D] which may arise from such disturbance [alternatively, “from its wretched disturbance”], to incline your mind toward the sounder judgment, so that synodal judgments may be annulled only for the strongest reason and apostolic commands may be observed more carefully. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PETER, teacher of the little flock; to L., provost of the Church of Soissons; to H., dean of the same Church; and to the rest of the clergy of that Church: greeting in the Lord.

Peter, archdeacon of your Church, came to us and asked my insignificance to write to your brotherhood, which had requested my counsel, concerning what I thought [Col. 0117A] about the burial of his father. Ecclesiastical communion had been denied to the man after his death, although—as Peter himself said—the deceased had lost it during his lifetime neither through ecclesiastical judgment nor for any offense in which he had been caught.

If this is so, this judgment appears valid to us: we ought not to forbid communion to the dead whom we did not forbid communion while alive; just as we ought not to communicate with those dead with whom we did not communicate while they lived. For the Church has been given no power to bind or loose anything except what is upon earth. It follows that matters not resolved among the living by human judgment must be reserved for divine judgment (Letters 59 and 212).

I therefore entreat and advise your brotherhood that, insofar as it can be done while preserving [Col. 0117B] due reverence for your bishop, you relieve your fellow brother’s distress and arrange for ecclesiastical burial to be restored to his father’s remains, if it was indeed unjustly taken away, as the aforesaid brother asserts. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVII. To the reverend brethren and fellow bishops LAMBERT of Arras and JOHN of Thérouanne [alternatively, Tarvenna], IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: greeting in the Lord.

I believe that you have received, through our fellow brethren the canons of Saint-Quentin, the lord pope’s letters sent also to you. In them we were rebuked for whatever [Col. 0117C] assent we gave to Stephen, suitor of the Church of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0117D] He says the same at the beginning of Letter 95: compelled by prayers, he had written to Paschal, as Letter 92 indicates.], and warned to take every precaution lest a person less suitable for sacred [manuscript c, “sacred orders”] orders creep into the Church of Beauvais.

Since it has always been your custom to reject with perfect hatred wolves entering the sheepfolds of God and, where possible, to assail them as faithful dogs in God’s house, we urgently and seasonably ask and admonish your religious zeal to do in this matter, from the duty of obedience, more earnestly what you have hitherto done from love of justice.

You, therefore, as suffragans of the Church of Reims, should admonish your metropolitan that, according to the tenor of the letters which the lord pope sent to the people of Beauvais (Letter 98), he should urge the clergy of the Church of Beauvais, in fulfillment [Col. 0117D] of his office, to make a canonical election. Thus, under the protection of his authority, the weak may have the means to be healed [alternatively, saved], and the strong the means to be strengthened.

But if he delays or neglects to do this through flattering [alternatively, “if he himself flatters”] indolence, you must admonish him so to honor his ministry that what ought to be done through him is not carried out by the hands of others. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVIII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to his beloved brethren in Christ, the sons of the Church of Beauvais: stand firm, act courageously, and be strengthened in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] After Stephen’s rejection, Paschal ordered another to be elected, as is clear from comparison of Letters 95 and 97. Accordingly they elected Galon, concerning whom see Letter 104.]

[Col. 0118A]

According to our measure, we give thanks to divine mercy that in the body of your Church there are still more sensitive members than we had believed—members who grieve over its pain and labor for its health. Blessed be God, because there remains among you some hope of life, although there are certain alien children among you who, assuming the face of a harlot and not knowing how to blush, for food for the belly which God will destroy (1 Cor. 6), and for worthless little bundles [Codex Putaneus, “and bundles of lust”], disembowel their mother. Sparing neither their lives nor their reputations, like rotten limbs they do not perceive their own stench, and they endeavor to contaminate by their decay and foulness those others who might be healed.

[Col. 0118B]

Therefore you, who still wish to avert [manuscript c, “avoid”] death and fear becoming foul through the aforesaid stench, see to it that, so far as lies in you, you obey apostolic commands and admonitions and promptly endeavor to make an election of another person—not, I say, this one or that one, but simply a Catholic and canonical person—according to the tenor of the apostolic letters. In this way you will free your Church from the multiple invasion of pedagogues [Note: [Col. 0118D] He takes the word in an unfavorable sense, as in Letter 6.], avoid the many vexations now occurring while the affair remains pending, and wisely provide for your reputation.

Nor do I say this in order to recommend any particular person, as has already been stated; for every person will please me who shines in life and doctrine [Note: [Col. 0118D] “Even the lowliest bishop, unless he excels in learning and holiness,” in chapter 45, Cause 1, Question 1.]. I seek nothing of my own in this cause; rather, I place both myself and what is mine without distinction at the disposal of all of you who resolve to stand courageously for God’s house, ready according to my strength to benefit you with counsel and assistance. May the Angel of Great Counsel and the Spirit of Strength work with you. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIX. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to his beloved brother in Christ and fellow presbyter GUALON: greeting in the Lord.

Your affection has asked me whether boys six years old, or younger, can contract between themselves the sacraments of betrothal [alternatively, of betrothals; manuscript c] or marriage; and, once betrothals have been celebrated, whether, if one dies, the survivor may enter into marriage with the sister or brother of the deceased person, with whom he had previously [Col. 0118D] entered the bond of betrothal (Letter 246).

As to marriage, if we consult natural law and attend carefully to the Lord’s words where He says, “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother, shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh” (Gen. 2), we can answer without hesitation that a lawful marriage is first entered into when spouses are able, through the union of the flesh, mutually to render the marital debt to one another.

But if before the years of puberty such sacraments are celebrated for the purpose of extending or preserving [Col. 0119A] peace between persons, we do not condemn it, provided that it occurs between persons between whom the law does not forbid it and with the consent of both. For, as Pope Nicholas says (Letter 243, Book VII and XI, *On Betrothals*), “Consent makes marriage, not intercourse.”

Hence the Book of the Pandects, Book 23, Title 1, also states: “In betrothals the consent of those persons is required whose consent is desired in marriages. Therefore, just as in marriage, so in betrothals a daughter under paternal authority must consent.” And later (law 13, *ibid.*, and Letter 134): “If a son under paternal authority dissents, betrothal cannot be made in his name.”

At what age these things ought to be done has not been fully determined either by ecclesiastical or by human laws.

[Note: [Col. 0119] Law 14, *On Betrothals*. Leo the Philosopher, Novella 109, decreed that betrothals should not be contracted before the seventh year. See Letter 243.]

Thus the aforesaid book says [Col. 0119B]: “In contracting betrothals, the age of the contracting parties is not fixed, as it is in marriages.” Therefore betrothals may be made from the beginning of age, provided it is understood by both persons [manuscript c, “provided it be understood”], that is, provided they are not less than seven years old.

But once betrothals have been contracted by the consent of both persons, they have received the name of marriage. Hence Ambrose says in Book One, *Exhortation to Virginity* (Letters 148 and 246): “A woman betrothed to a man receives the name of wife. When marriage is initiated, then the name of marriage is assumed; for it is not the defloration of virginity that makes marriage, but the marital agreement.”

Likewise Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book 9: “They are rightly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, although [Col. 0119C] marital intercourse is not yet known.” Likewise Augustine, in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: “Nor was it falsely said by the angel to Joseph: ‘Do not fear to take Mary your wife’ (Matt. 1). She is called wife from the first pledge of betrothal, though he had neither known her through intercourse nor was going to know her.”

These authorities therefore make clear that, once marriage has for the most part been established between two persons through the covenant of betrothal and the will of both, a brother can no longer marry his brother’s wife [alternatively, “can”; manuscript c], nor may a sister marry her sister’s husband (Gratian, Cause 27, Question 2). Hence we read in chapter 10 of the Council of Tribur: “It has been decreed that, although a woman may not have been married to a lawful husband, nevertheless one brother may not have a woman betrothed to another brother.”

For the present, dearest one, let this suffice for your questions. From these, as from sparks of arguments [Codex Putaneus, “little sparks”], you will be able to gather greater matters and satisfy those who need it concerning the questions proposed. Farewell.

## LETTER C. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to JOHN, by the same grace Bishop of the Church of Orléans: greeting.

“I waited and waited, and you did not attend to me,” because you have not restored to me, in accordance with the judgment of the synod, the altar among the basilicas which was adjudged to me at the Council of Poitiers [Col. 0120A] [thus the old manuscripts; formerly, “Pictaviensis”]. For Paganus (Letters 112 and 114), the sacrilegious invader of the aforesaid altar, still lays hands upon sacrilege and, both by your consent and under the patronage of the Archbishop of Tours—to whom your brotherhood is subject beyond what is just—usurps my right for himself.

But if you say that you do not consent to this, you cannot be believed, since, though you are able, in fulfillment of your office, to enforce justice, you do not do so. “For he undoubtedly shares the guilt of the doer (chapter 3, Distinction 86, and Letter 77) who does not endeavor to correct what he is able to correct; nor is he free from the stain of hidden consent who ceases to oppose an open crime.” Therefore let your brotherhood know that, if you do not render me full justice concerning the aforesaid invader [Col. 0120B], I shall henceforth seek from one who consents by whatever means I can seek from one who acts. Let your brotherhood write back to me, through the bearer of this letter, what you intend to do in this matter. Farewell.

## LETTER CI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to ADELA, illustrious countess: greeting and the gift of prayers.

I have heard that you are claiming from our archpriest Ralph [some manuscripts, Gradulf] the ban of the league [*bannum*; as in Letter 134], because of a certain false nun, whose small possessions he seized after finding them with a certain burgess of Blois. Therefore we ask and admonish [Col. 0120C] Your Excellency not to inflict [one manuscript, “not to do”] this wrong upon us (thus Letter 121).

For all false preachers, false monks, and false clerics—whether fornicators, adulterers, usurers, or others who offend against Christianity (except those who must be punished by capital penalty)—are to be restrained and corrected by us; both they and their possessions are under our jurisdiction. This is an ancient and unshaken custom not only of the Church of Chartres but of all churches throughout the whole kingdom of Gaul. We are prepared to establish this, whether in our Church or in every Church which can render canonical [alternatively, canonically valid] judgment over us.

Therefore let Your Prudence desist from such an undertaking; and, as you wish your own principality to remain [Col. 0120D] unshaken, so permit the Church to possess its right. Nor let it harm us in Your Excellency’s eyes that we love you and yours and, reluctantly, undertake anything against you even when reason moves [alternatively, advises; manuscript c] us to do so. Let Your Prudence know, moreover, that we take very seriously what your officials have done to the aforesaid archpriest, but overlook it because of our affection for you. If, however—may it not be so—the matter turns for the worse, we shall still exact strict account from them in fulfillment of our office. Farewell.

## LETTER CII. To MANASSES, reverend [alternatively, venerable] Archbishop of Reims, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 0121A]

It is unnecessary to inform Your Prudence how grievously the Church of Beauvais has been burdened by the frequent incursions [one manuscript, “bites”] of wolves and the manifold deceptions of alien children; these matters have not escaped your knowledge [Codex Putaneus, “into whose knowledge these matters have crept”]. But because that Church begot me in Christ and laid in me the foundation of religion, though others, as God granted, have built upon it, I cannot but be weak when it is weak, nor fail to burn when it is scandalized.

Therefore let not Your Vigilance wonder if I intercede with your fatherhood [alternatively, brotherhood] for my mother and nurse: that you, who learn from frequent reports of her daily [Col. 0121B] [“ordinary,” old manuscript c, more correctly] ruins, may endeavor, in fulfillment of your office, to meet her lamentable falls. For it is yours to seek out the scattered sheep on pathless ground in the day of cloud and darkness, and, as far as lies in you, bring them back to the fold—even if they wish to wander, even if they wish to perish (Letter 89, at the end; St Augustine, in chapter *Displicet*, Cause 23, Question 4).

It is yours also, in seeking lost sheep, to constrain yourselves through steep and rough places [variant: “and, if necessary, to bloody your sides amid thorns”], so that you may render to the eternal Judge a good account of the solicitude entrusted to you, joyfully and not with groaning. It is yours to remove for the time being from the fold sick sheep which destroy very many by their contagion [variant: “which destroy many; sometimes remove them from the fold”], and not count them among [Col. 0121C] those who hear the shepherd’s voice; to provide pasture for the healthy and those who do not stray; and to entrust the fold to the shepherd whom the sheep know and desire.

And since through yourselves you well know the integrity of the person elected [Note: [Col. 0121D] Galon, by comparison with Letter 104.], and have heard the will and counsel of the Supreme Pontiff in this matter, it would seem to me [alternatively, “seems”; manuscript c] sound counsel that, after taking and confirming counsel with your fellow bishops, you should hasten [alternatively, “hasten”; variant reading] the consecration of the elect of the aforesaid Church, lest by delaying or failing to do what belongs to you, you give your honor to another.

For, as the Eighth Synod—commended and venerated by the Roman Church—decreed, kings may not involve themselves in episcopal elections or impede [Col. 0121D] [alternatively, obstruct] them for any reason. The Frankish kings Charles and Louis likewise granted episcopal elections to the churches, leaving this written in their capitularies (Book 1, chapter 84) and permitting it to be sanctioned in provincial councils of bishops.

Let God therefore have principally in His Church what is His. Let the king have, in the second place after God, what God has granted him. Nor should it hinder this that it has been maliciously suggested to the king concerning the dependent status of the elect’s parents: he is, according to his station, descended from honorable parents, and their dependent status cannot lawfully be proved by anyone now living.

But if God wishes, according to His custom, to choose the lowly and weak things of the world in order to confound the strong, who can or ought to resist His ordering? Thus David was taken from following the nursing ewes to the kingdom. Thus Peter was called from fishing to the highest apostleship. Thus many needy persons were raised from the dust and exalted [alternatively, raised up] to the highest governments by God’s providence, to show that worldly wisdom and secular power have no weight with Him.

But since all these things are not unknown [alternatively, not unheard] to you, I shall conclude by repeating the substance of our intercession to you: namely, that you should endeavor quickly to assist the falling Church. Farewell.

## LETTER CIII. To PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: to serve with Peter and receive a gift with Peter.

[Col. 0122B]

Your son and our fellow brother, the Bishop of Senlis (Letters 244 and 258), was driven from his own see, and suffered losses to his possessions, on behalf of the Roman Church and against the Roman Church, without hearing or judgment. Although he returned this year fortified with apostolic letters from the Apostolic See, he has nevertheless found no remedy for his affliction with the king, no fatherly support with his metropolitan, and no brotherly solace with his fellow provincials.

Nor has he received any revenues [alternatively, returns] from his prebend at Paris, regarding which you had given special orders out of mercy. Indeed, as is said, the dean of Paris, having handed his own prebend to another, has appropriated the bishop’s prebend for himself. [Col. 0122C]

Therefore, grieving not so much at his misery as groaning over the injury to the Apostolic See, I kept him with me this summer and, according to my means, supplied him with support. I therefore admonish by supplication and supplicate by admonition that, for the wrong done both to yourselves and to your abandoned son, you no longer cease to bend the bow; rather, strive boldly to set the sword [that is, excommunication] upon the necks of those who have proved despisers of apostolic commands.

For if your son, your own creation, finds no protection beneath maternal wings, what may a stranger hope for? Therefore, just as the Roman Church is mother and teacher of all churches (chapter *Non decet*, Distinction 12), so it befits her to repel injuries done to her children and punish the disobedience of despisers, so that the son may rejoice that he has been subject [Col. 0122D] and the disobedient despisers may repent that they have been disobedient [alternatively, “may repent”]. Farewell.

## LETTER CIV. To PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: the dutiful service of owed attendance, with the devoted affection of a son.

The clerics of Beauvais, of better repute and sounder judgment, following your counsel, with the counsel of the leading men of their diocese and the approval of the people, chose for themselves as bishop Lord Galo (Letter 105), a man honourable in life and adorned with literary [or liberal] studies and ecclesiastical learning. Yet a few clerics, accomplices of that rejected Stephen (Letter 95), whom he had baited to his side with the skins of foreign mice and other snares of such vanities, did not assent to this election; nevertheless, they could bring no objection against it that was contrary to the sacred canons. Since they could not obstruct the matter by themselves, they approached the king and dropped certain words into his ears which readily trickled into his heart: namely, that the aforesaid elect had been my pupil, brought up and instructed by me [one manuscript: “educated and instructed”]; adding that he had been chosen by Your Holiness, and that he would become a great adversary to him if he should ever become bishop in his kingdom. The king, therefore, inflamed by these venomous words and turned away from every good intention, is unwilling to give his consent to the election or to release the episcopal revenues to the elect. [Note: [Col. 0123D] The king had also sworn, as Letter 105 says, that this Galo would never become bishop.]

For this reason his electors would already have fled to your fatherhood, had not their metropolitan detained them for an appointed day [one manuscript: “a fixed day”] between the opponents and the electors, supposedly wishing to make peace—or perhaps cunningly to obstruct the matter in accordance with the king’s will. It remains, therefore, most beloved Father, that by your power and authority, as you have begun, you aid the Church in accordance with the reasonable petition of its clergy, and render your counsel incapable of being confounded; lest your plotters and detractors begin mockingly to say of you: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14).

Moreover, I make known to Your Holiness that the king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0123D] The word “of the Franks” seems to have intruded from a gloss, since earlier he speaks only of “the king.”] says that he will shortly come to Rome; this, however, we do not believe. But whether he comes or sends, take care both for yourselves and for us that he may always be held fast by the keys and chains of Peter. And if perhaps he should be absolved and return, as has already happened, to his vomit [Note: [Col. 0123D] That is, to the unlawful union with Bertrada, concerning whom see Letters 13 and 105.], let him immediately be shut up again with those same keys and bound with those same chains. Let this be made known by your letters to all churches. Thus you will break the teeth of the gnawers and satisfy justice. But if perhaps God should enlighten his heart to repentance, remember us, who have borne the burden and heat of the day [Note: [Col. 0124D] He had lost the king’s favour for the justice of this cause, as Letter 141 says.], so that, as we have shared in tribulation, we may likewise share in consolation. Farewell.

## LETTER CV. TO PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: May you abound in the spirit of fortitude.

[Col. 0123D]

Concerning the distress in which the Church of Beauvais is harassed by alien sons, and concerning the French king’s persistence in his disgrace, harmful and shameful to sacred religion (Letters 13 and 104), I can write or say nothing clearer, more useful, or more honourable for your authority than what I have written (Letter 104), except that, at the instigation of Drogo the chanter—who, so far as he can, opposes every form of religion—the king caused, through one of his servants, an oath contrary to the sacred canons and to all religion to be given: that Galo should never become bishop of Beauvais during his lifetime (Letter 104).

In this matter Your Prudence must be armed with the spirit of fortitude. For if a canonical election can be nullified by such an oath, thereafter there will be no election in the kingdom of the Franks except a simoniacal or violent intrusion. If it is objected to Your Holiness that the king ought not to be compelled to perjury, you may recall what blessed Ambrose says in the first book *On Duties*. For he says (*Gratian*, Cause 22, Question 4): “Sometimes keeping an oath promised is contrary to duty, as with Herod, who swore that he would give the daughter of Herodias whatever she should ask, and granted the death of John lest he deny his promise.”

Augustine also says in the sermon which he delivered on the beheading of John the Baptist: “I see David, a devout and holy man, fallen into a rash oath [variant: ‘having fallen into,’ manuscript C]; and he preferred not to do what he had sworn rather than fulfil his oath by the shedding of a man’s blood.” Again: “David swore rashly, but in greater piety did not fulfil his oath. Of two sins he chose the lesser.”

Likewise Ambrose, in the third book *On Duties*: “Many often bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath, and, although they themselves recognize that they ought not to have promised, nevertheless, out of regard for the oath, they do what they have pledged, as we wrote above concerning Herod. How much more tolerable would such perjury have been than the oath—if indeed it could be called perjury—by which he promised amid the dancing choruses?”

Likewise Jerome, Book I on Jeremiah: “It must be observed that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment, and justice” (Letter 16; and chapter 2, Cause 22, Question 2). “If these are lacking, it is not an oath at all, but perjury.” And in the proceedings of the Seventh Synod one reads (chapter *Actione*, Cause 22, Question 4): “Herod kept his oath and perished. Peter denied with an oath, and, having turned back, wept and was saved.”

But since I speak these things to those who know them, I consider myself to be speaking not by teaching, but by recalling and reminding. I come to the point. If the king receives penance from Your Holiness, whether directly or through others [thus manuscript C; earlier: “performs”], and—as we firmly believe—returns to his vomit (Letter 104), instruct me by letter how I ought to conduct myself, and provide me beforehand with written directions. Farewell.

## 50. LETTER CVI. TO HENRY [Note: [Col. 0124D] The First, son of William the Second.], illustrious king of the English, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: May you live and reign in Him through whom kings reign.

Since divine providence [one manuscript: “mercy”; Letter 93] has caused you to ascend the throne of your paternal kingdom, we entreat divine clemency for the grace bestowed upon us [variant: “upon you”], that it may make you imitate your father’s character and your father’s generosity; so that your Highness may in no respect fall below their nobility, nor in any respect decline from their moderation. And because no affairs are rightly administered unless kingdom and priesthood unite in a single purpose (Letters 60, 214, and 239), we beseechingly urge Your Excellency to permit the word of God to run freely in the kingdom entrusted to you, and always to consider that the earthly kingdom ought to be subject to the heavenly kingdom entrusted to the Church.

For as the animal faculty ought to be subject to reason, so earthly power ought to be subject to ecclesiastical governance. And the earthly power has no more worth if it is not formed and governed by ecclesiastical discipline than the body has if it is not governed by the soul. And just as the kingdom of the body is at peace when the flesh no longer resists the spirit, so the kingdom of the world is possessed in peace when it no longer attempts to resist the kingdom of God.

Thinking on these things, understand yourselves to be the servant of the servants of God, not their lord; their protector, not their possessor. Understand that you ought to be one of the cedars of Lebanon which the Lord planted, in which sparrows nest (Psalm 103): that is, under whose protection Christ’s poor may quietly flourish and dwell [variant: “be preserved”]. The more undisturbed their prayers for the stability of your kingdom and your own welfare, the sounder they are; and the sounder they are, the more effective they are known to be. By doing this, with God’s help you will possess your earthly kingdom in peace, and by His mercy attain the eternal kingdom.

Moreover, I commend to you these canons of ours, bearers of this letter, whom our Church sends to Your Excellency because of its need. Having heard them, may you meet that need as seems fit to you and as God inspires you; and strive also to have the love for this Church which your parents had (Letter 118). For this same Church holds your parents in particularly special remembrance among all its benefactors [variant: “holds them in remembrance”], both because of their eminence and because of their generosity. Farewell.

## LETTER CVII. TO THE Venerable MATILDA, Queen of the English, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: May you hear Solomon’s wisdom at the ends of the earth.

[Col. 0125D]

Since report has made known to us that you are one of the prudent women, though distant in body, the fragrance of your good repute has made you present to us and has stirred us to love the charity which the bridegroom of chaste minds has ordained in you. Therefore we desire to deserve from Your Excellency a reciprocal affection—the affection which, before your time, queens of the English showed to the Church which, by God’s authorship, though unworthy, we serve, for the sake of the glorious memory of Mary, Queen of Angels.

Nor is it unfitting for your religion and reputation that one whom you ought, by the common lot, to love as a human being, you should love by a certain privilege as a priest of Christ and, according to his measure, as a lover of the Christian religion. With this confidence, we have sent to your generosity two of our canons, that they may relate to you the need of our Church and receive, as a blessing, the blessing which God shall have put into your heart (Letter 142).

I also ask that, in order more firmly to impress upon my mind the memory of Your Excellency, you send my littleness a long robe (poderis), or some other priestly vestment, such as befits a queen to give and a bishop to wear in the celebration of the divine sacraments. Farewell.

## LETTER CVIII. TO PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: Due obedience with all devotion.

[Col. 0126B]

[Note: [Col. 0125D] The argument in manuscript C is that a monk must not be accused for acts committed before his conversion.]

How lovingly the solicitude of the Roman pontiffs has hitherto watched over the peace of monks; with what zeal it has laboured to keep far from the harassing of monasteries those attacks which burden monasteries; and with what care for caution it has ordered the persons and causes of accusers and witnesses to be examined—this is not for us to teach our teachers, from whom we expect only a pattern for carrying out commands, just as we have received from them a rule for commanding. If Your Holiness wishes to observe all these things in the case of the lord abbot of Marmoutier, we believe that neither the accusers should be admitted to accuse nor the witnesses to testify.

For first, if we consider the person of the accuser—namely, the archbishop of Tours [Note: [Col. 0126D] He frequently blames and rebukes him; see, for example, Letter 59 at the end, and Letters 66 and 67.]—almost everything done in his ordination was usurped contrary to order. Moreover, the crimes committed against him or admitted by him—namely, perjury and treachery—which he alleges against the aforesaid abbot, ought not, so far as appears, readily to be heard by ecclesiastical judges; for either they were never perpetrated, or, by the prescribed cure, they have been brought to healing. As the Apostle says: “Those who seemed to be pillars—what they formerly were is no concern of mine. God does not accept the person of a man” (Galatians 2).

If these charges were true, they should have been made then, when he saw him judging ecclesiastical affairs with bishops in public assemblies and handling pontifical sacraments—things which no hand stained by crime, nor any conscience lacking the witness of innocence, ought to handle. If he could rightly have been challenged on these matters, he ought rather to have been accused of usurping the priesthood than of undertaking the care of a monastery, in which we know there is no kind of ecclesiastical sacrament. For Jerome, the chief institutor of monks, says (above, Letter 36): “A monk does not have the office of a teacher, but of one who mourns: one who mourns for himself and for the world.”

But someone will say that he rightly kept silent then, because the man did him no injury while he was a bishop. Therefore this curious inspector of another’s life, and negligent corrector of his own, is all the less to be heard [one manuscript: “regarded”], now that he strives to encrust a clean vessel—not from love of justice but from the rancour of vengeance (Horace, *Satires*, Book I, Satire 3, line 56)—rather than cleanse an encrusted vessel from filth.

For I believe, and rightly believe, that when, about to put off the old man and bring forth the new, he tore open in the sight of God the sack of his old nature, in my presence, and poured out through confession of the mouth every harmful thing hidden within, he would by no means have concealed these disgraces if he had recognized them in himself. Finally, if you consider the cause of this accusation, you clearly know that this malice has blazed up from no other source than this: the archbishop of Tours cannot, under a decree of the Apostolic See, celebrate public masses in Marmoutier (chapter *Abbatem* and chapter *Luminoso*, Cause 18, Question 2), act imperiously toward the monks, or seize the goods of the monastery as he pleases.

Accordingly, in the synod this very year, as those present say, he renewed [manuscript C: “revoked”; “renewed” is better, as in the text] to the extent that he could the decree of Julian: namely, “that no one renouncing the world should enter the principal monastery of his parish.” Finally, if the persons and causes of those giving testimony are examined, he has suborned [variant: “subordinated”] for himself such men as are notoriously either stained by disgrace, related to him by blood, hired for payment, or drawn from his household. As you know, such persons can readily be commanded to bear witness alike to falsehood and truth.

Since, therefore, the matters stated are thus, although it is not necessary, we nevertheless exhort Your Holiness by supplication to follow in this cause the path of paternal traditions, so that innocence may not be endangered and a perverse will—deserving punishment by a just retaliation—may fall through its own attempts and be entangled in its own snares. Farewell.

## LETTER CIX. TO PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: May you excel in virtue as in authority.

Since daily among us we see the Church collapsing, and no one, or scarcely anyone, raising it up and setting a wall for the house of Israel, the love of Christ compels us to reveal to your fatherhood the grief of our heart, by which we are tormented over the death and diseases of Christ’s sheep. It is the concern of the head to provide for the weaknesses of the members, and to procure fitting remedies according to the quantity or quality of their ailments.

For when you send to us from your side your cardinals, as though sons from the same womb (Letters 60 and 87), because they are merely passing through among us, they can not only not care for the things requiring care, but cannot even inspect them. Thus many people, wishing to strike the deeds of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, say that the Apostolic See seeks not the health of its subjects [manuscript C: perhaps “not the health of clerics”] [Note: [Col. 0127D] On this matter see John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, Book VI, chapter 24.], but its own advantage or that of those at its side [variant: “its associates”].

Therefore I and certain of our fellow-countrymen, unable to receive this murmuring calmly, as united sons of the Roman Church, have resolved to write to Your Holiness, asking you to entrust the legation of the Apostolic See to some transalpine person (Letter 12), who may more closely recognize creeping evils and more promptly be able to remedy them, either personally or by report to the Apostolic See. We have known no one more suited to this charge than the lord archbishop of Lyons, who has long served in the same office and, as we have learned by experience, has been of marvellous [in many copies: “venerable”] benefit both to the Roman Church and to the transalpine churches. [Note: [Col. 0128D] He speaks of Hugh, as in Letter 24.]

For many persons are hindered from visiting the Apostolic See by impending dangers, lack of household resources, difficulty of travel, or bodily weakness. Therefore, if you wished to assent to the suggestion of our humble estate, it would seem fitting that you appoint to this charge an intermediary person, especially one proved in the same responsibility by custom and usefulness, who would recognize emerging evils all the more frequently because he was nearer, and apply such relief as he could more effectively.

I write these things with the boldness of familiarity and filial love, because I believe that in this way the Church of God may better be served together with many others, and that the detractions [variant: “slanders”] of enemies may be avoided. Indeed, although the Lord was ignorant of nothing [variant: “although the Lord was not ignorant”], His disciples suggested to Him many necessary things; and, in order to instruct the posterity of prelates, He not only heard them patiently but also fulfilled them with equanimity. Farewell.

## LETTER CX. TO PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, from IVO, humble son of His Holiness: Whatever may be happier.

Since, because of the grace bestowed upon us, we love the beauty of the Church of God [variant: “house of God”], we grieve deeply that many things are done disorderly within it. When, among certain subjects, we strive either to correct some unlawful practices or to advance some persons to better things, those who wish to rot in their own filth bring us letters from the Apostolic See, obtained, I know not by what deceptions, in order to cloak their malice or defend their disobedience. Thus there arises in the Church a remarkable contempt for God’s commands and an unspeakable corruption of morals, when the perversity of certain persons finds there an unrebuked refuge where innocence alone ought to have protection.

And what is more astonishing and more pitiable: these inquisitive corrupters of their own lives are gladly heard by the very pillars [some manuscripts: “by all the pillars”] when they endeavour to splash the lives of religious persons with certain stains. They are not to be believed concerning another’s injustice so long as they have not departed [variant: “do not depart”] from their own.

Therefore, since these circumstances compel us almost to despair of the fruit of our labour, both because of our insufficiency and because of the hardness of our subjects, we often deliberate to lay down the burden which we bear almost fruitlessly. Begging that the wings of a dove be given us (Letters 17 and 25), we prefer to fly away from useless troubles and rest in the solitude of the mind [variant: “mountain”].

Warned by this necessity, desiring to approach the presence of Your Holiness and to discuss with you the matters mentioned [variant: “the aforesaid matters”], together with many others, we came almost as far as the Alps. In their narrow passes, however, since we heard that ambushes had been prepared for us, we followed the counsel of great men and refrained from undertaking the journey [variant: “having begun the journey”].

We have therefore sent to your fatherhood Lord Gualo, our fellow-brother and fellow-bishop, who is better able to conceal himself in dangerous places. We have placed our words in his mouth, so that you may hear him with paternal care both concerning his own need and ours; correct what must be corrected; and firmly establish what ought usefully to be established. For although what reason advises, what practice approves, or what episcopal moderation orders seems adequately strong in itself, it becomes dearer [Note: [Col. 0129D] Variant: “clearer,” which seems more fitting to the text.] and is, as it were, illumined by a certain light when that which must be prohibited or commanded is strengthened by apostolic decree. Farewell.

## 52. LETTER CXI. TO DAIMBERT, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: Greeting and service.

Having for a long time desired conversation with you, I hoped that I might speak to your fatherhood at the assembly to which we had been invited in the city of the Vellavi [variant: Vellans], and address you face to face concerning the injuries inflicted upon me and upon the Church entrusted to me by Hugh of Puiset, who, in the manner of his family, always repays good with evil (Letters 76, 112, and 211). Neither human shame nor the faith which he owes me as his lord restrains him from plundering, though no injury on our part has preceded it and no justice has been denied him by us.

What we then postponed for a definite reason, we now ask in these letters, with the knees of our heart bent: excommunicate him, whom we have excommunicated (Letter 76); interdict the divine office at Méraiville and its dependencies; and command the bishop of Orléans to do the same at Puiset. [Note: [Col. 0129D] Because one excommunicated by his own bishop ought also to be excommunicated by neighbouring bishops; Letter 76.] Otherwise, if we fear the princes of the world more than God, the gates of hell will plainly prevail; and we, who ought to set a wall for the house of Israel (Ezekiel 13), shall, in the prophet’s mockery, be accounted mute dogs unable to bark (Isaiah 56).

For ecclesiastical property, as even secular laws testify, belongs to divine right, is contained in no one’s goods, and therefore anyone is wholly mistaken who, for his own purposes or at the commands of princes—by whom it especially ought to be preserved—usurps and misuses it (Letter 143). Hence Pope Symmachus says in the Sixth Synod (chapter *Quicunque* and chapter *Praedia*, Cause 12, Question 2): “Whoever seeks, receives, possesses, or retains the estates of the Church, unless he quickly corrects himself, shall be struck with anathema; and let anathema be upon giver and receiver alike, or possessor.” In saying these things we do not instruct Your Prudence, but exhort you to bear firmly the burden of your office, so that your consolation may sustain our faintheartedness and your strength may fortify our patience. Farewell.

## LETTER CXII. From IVO, humble minister of Chartres, to FULCO [Note: [Col. 0130D] He was afterwards elected bishop of Paris; see Letters 138 and 164.], dean of the Church of Paris, and to the clergy entrusted to him: Affection and greeting.

Since every ecclesiastical wrong which is not corrected by admonition must be punished with anathema, if you have excommunicated a maidservant of your Church who kicks against her masters, you have done what was within your right—especially since the law establishes that the authority of masters over their slaves must remain unimpaired (Law II, *On Those Who Are Their Own Persons*, or, alternatively, *On Law*), and permits no person to be deprived of his own right.

As for your assertion that you may do this, by the custom of your Church, without appeal to another person: this is not the custom of the Church of Paris alone, but also of Chartres and of other churches, to which the right of excommunication has been granted by episcopal authority. We can therefore give you no sounder advice than that you hold firmly to this custom; for if you abandon it even once [variant: “withdraw from it”], you will not be able to recover it at your discretion.

Moreover, I blame your affection because you receive into communion Pagan (Letter 114), ecclesiastically excommunicated by us and struck with infamy by apostolic authority on account of his crimes, and likewise Hugh of Puiset (Letters 76, 24, and 60). Yet you would plainly blame us if we did this with persons excommunicated by you. I therefore urge [manuscript C: “we urge”] that hereafter you render us in our need the same justice which you would wish rendered to yourselves by us in your need, lest, if we find you negligent in our affairs, we ourselves be found similar in yours. And so that you may know this ought to be done by apostolic authority, I meanwhile send you the lord pope’s letters which he sent to the Churches of Sens, Orléans, and Paris; the metropolitan has already received them sealed with the bull.

## LETTER CXIII. TO DAIMBERT, by God’s grace Reverend Archbishop of Sens, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: Filial submission and brotherly affection.

[Col. 0130D]

We rejoice with devout exultation over the election of Lord Manasses, made by the Church of Meaux (Letter 115). We have found him to be a youth of good natural disposition and a young man of better promise, clearly marked by gentleness of character; in part we have learned this from the reports of others. Therefore, both because of your paternal summons and because of our welcome affection for him, we would gladly attend his consecration even if we were invited on this account to remote places.

But Your Fatherhood knows no less well than our humble estate what difficulties and dangers hedge in our roads. Therefore, if you wish us to attend this consecration with such urgency, either choose a place to which we can safely come, or provide us with safe conduct. Otherwise, in your paternal discretion grant pardon to one who fears manifest dangers, rather than grant it to one who undergoes the same dangers not without injury to your own reputation.

But if fear of the king, or of others who rage unjustly against us, compels us to remain absent, we shall confirm by letter and in heart, though bodily absent, the consecration which you will perform with voice and hands while bodily present. [Note: [Col. 0131D] As in Letter 115: for it is no more valid to pronounce the sacraments in the election of a bishop than to write them, as Sidonius Apollinaris says, Book VII, Letter 9.] For, all other reasons aside, I grieve deeply that I am not worthy to be comforted by conversation with you and relieved by your consolation. Nevertheless, I offer such thanks as I can to Your Excellency because you sympathize with our tribulations, share sorrow for our griefs, and extend your hand, so far as you can, to assist us. If our other fellow-bishops acted in the same way, the gates of hell would not prevail so greatly (Matthew 16). Farewell.

## LETTER CXIV. TO JOHN, by God’s grace Bishop of Orléans, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: Greeting.

For the sympathy which your brotherhood shows to our tribulations, we offer you all the thanks that we can. But concerning the peace which you wish to restore between us and Lord Louis (Letter 124), we answer you thus: so far as our conscience bears witness to us, we have inflicted no injury upon him. If he should demand anything from us, we would gladly satisfy him before your judgment and that of our fellow-bishops. And if he has done anything against our humble estate unworthy of him, we would bear it patiently.

But we cannot receive Hugh of Puiset (Letter 112), and Pagan the fugitive (Letters 100 and 112) and deserter, without due satisfaction; for this has been agreed between us with the greatest obligation and confirmed by apostolic authority. If, however, Pagan wishes to make himself greater than himself because he has made himself worse than himself, then a grave injury will be done to episcopal dignity and a way more inclined to deviation will be opened to the order [one manuscript: “ordination”] of clerics.

Therefore, in this affair take precaution for your own danger as well as ours. For, to confess the truth to you, we prefer to suffer whatever adversities God permits than, by sparing the children of discord, to bring very many into peril. As for a place in which we may safely confer, I have no settled plan, because within either your bishopric or ours there is no safe way out for me—unless brotherly affection moved you, something I do not presume to ask, to come as far as us and discuss with us, when you wished, the matters upon which it would be good to deliberate. Farewell.

## LETTER CXV. TO DAIMBERT, Metropolitan of the Church of Sens, and to the suffragan fellow-bishops of that Church, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: Greeting and service.

[Col. 0132A]

Because the apostolic saying has been fulfilled in me, “fightings without, fears within” (2 Corinthians 7), I deeply grieve that I cannot attend your holy and desirable assembly (Letters 113 and 119). And because I do not doubt that you are gathered in the name of the Saviour, whatever you have beneficially enacted [manuscript C: “enact”], I enact with you. In particular, I choose with those choosing Lord Manasses, sprung from illustrious birth and adorned with modest manners, whom the Church of Meaux has elected; and the laying on of hands which you, bodily present, are about to perform upon him, I confirm and perform, so far as lies in me, while present in heart. [Note: [Col. 0132D] According to chapters 8, 2, and 6, Distinction 64, and chapters 2 and 3, Distinction 65; Letter 113 also concerns this.] For I believe you to be of such judgment and such strength that you presume nothing unlawful and evade nothing lawful. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVI. FROM IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, TO ADELA, illustrious countess: Greeting and service.

The charity through which I have loved your nobility from the beginning has by no means grown cold in me; rather, through your benefits toward me, both past and subsequent, it grows more and more ardent. Therefore I beseechingly urge Your Excellency, and urgently beseech you, that if any evil report is made to you that I have done or said anything against you or yours (Letter 121), you should not believe it in any way, nor presently decree anything which your servants, speaking at anger’s prompting, may demand.

For when the land is disturbed outwardly, if internal wars also arose, danger might suddenly threaten the people and the city. But when, with God’s favour, you come to us, then you will learn everything more truly and, from what you hear, take sounder counsel. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVII. TO PASCHAL, Supreme Pontiff, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: With the obedience owed, happiness in both lives.

When recently I had received certain commands (Letter 133) or interdicts of your fatherhood for cutting away the Church’s evil customs, and had announced them to the brethren entrusted to me, some [manuscript C: “some things”] received them so gladly [manuscript C: “gravely”] that they not only approved them in words but, adding certain provisions which seemed conducive to the honour or liberty of the Church, strengthened them by oath.

Because these and similar measures seem for a time displeasing to certain persons who seek their own interests, whose reputation or advantage they appear to oppose, the brethren ask, through the intercession of our humble estate, that they be observed in such a way that they may remain unshaken under Peter’s key through succeeding ages, and that no lesser key may henceforth be permitted to loosen them (Letter 126) or remove them from their stability.

We have therefore sent two brethren from our company to set forth to the ears of Your Fatherhood the order and reason of the matter. When you have understood for how great a freedom and honour—or for the avoidance of which harms—they have done what they did, confirm it by letters sent to the Church, through the authority in which you excel. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVIII. TO HENRY, illustrious king of the English, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: May you serve the King of kings happily [in one manuscript: faithfully].

Since the eminence of kings is often bent by persistent prayers, although we blush to seem importunate, nevertheless we now for the third time, through the bearer of this letter, namely Lord William [manuscript C: *Guillelmus*], a canon of our Church, knock at the ears of Your Highness. May we at least now find the door of your goodwill open, so that you may revive the love which your parents had in affection for the aforesaid Church (Letter 106) and proved in deed.

Since in kings piety, gentleness, and justice ought especially to flourish, we consider it to belong to piety that we ask some small branches of your resources to be extended even to us for divine worship. It belongs to gentleness that you bear with equanimity the importunity of petitioners; to justice, that you recognize yourself as debtor for what you have promised.

For we ask nothing from Your Excellency for private or human uses; rather, where we are insufficient for adorning or maintaining the house of God, we mercifully seek your aid. Nor do we believe that your generosity will be fruitless. For what we cannot accomplish by our own strength, we confidently trust may be obtained through the merits of the blessed and perpetual Virgin, whom, by God’s authorship, we serve. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIX. TO DAIMBERT, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens, from IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: Greeting and service.

Because we have heard that opposition has arisen against the election of Lord Manasses (Letters 113 and 115), we grieve, with the compassion owed both to the distress of that Church and to the injury done to the elect himself. For it is said that the accuser who came forward against the aforesaid Manasses [Col. 0133D] is supported by no assistance of witnesses, has produced in the accusation nothing that he himself saw or heard while present, but only what he persuaded himself from suspicions or conjectured from flying rumours. If this is so, since the accuser himself was long ago marked by infamy, his accusation is by no means to be admitted, nor ought a lawful election to be harassed by any delays. For, as you know, the ordinances of the elders provide “that those cases which are not contained in the laws are not to be heard at all by ecclesiastical judges” (Letters 220 and 241). Yet, if it should seem good to your prudence, it accords with the reputation of the elect and with your own that you summon, for his purgation, such brethren of the clergy of Meaux as you find to be of better testimony (according to chapter *Illud*, distinction [Col. 0134A] 23), and, once his purgation has been received, ordain him publicly. For if I were present, provided the matter stands as I have stated above, I should advise your reverence of nothing else. Farewell.

## LETTER CXX. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Robert, Count of Ponthieu, greeting.

If the divine office has unjustly been forbidden you by the bishop of Séez, this displeases me both on account of the one acting and of the one suffering. But because I ought not to do to my neighbour what I would not wish to suffer from him, do not be surprised if for the present you do not receive the chrism which you request from us. For it is an ecclesiastical law that those interdicted or excommunicated by one Church are not to be received by another [Col. 0134B] (Letters 76 and 111). Nor is it mine to judge one who is absent, even if I were to consider [so v. c.; S. G. reads *praeessem*, “were in charge”] whether your pastor has bound you justly or unjustly, since I ought only to observe that I do not put my sickle into another’s harvest. I would gladly seek a remedy for such great evils, if God gave me the opportunity [and, MS c., the ability] to accomplish it. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Adela, illustrious countess: may you abound in the dispositions of patience and peace.

Because of the great affection with which I love your principality, I have already once and twice warned your highness (Letters 116 and 136) not immediately to accept what your servants, prompted by anger, [Col. 0134C] suggested to you, but to await your return to us, so that the truth of what was done might be heard and known; for all the canons of Blessed Mary were ready, and still are, to carry out through my hand whatever reason dictates and justice requires.

Yet, although they showed themselves ready to execute every justice toward you and yours, your servants, as they say, at your command violently took the Church’s grain-rent at Châteaudun and at Bonneval, and seized Lord Hilduin the cantor’s wine in the street of the tanners (Letter 101); they also inflicted many indignities upon clerics and their men. Therefore the clerics urgently demand [Col. 0134D] that I interdict the divine office in the city and throughout the whole diocese (Letters 94 and 120), until they recover what they declare was unjustly and precipitately taken from them.

And because I cannot fail justice, I requested a truce from them, which I scarcely obtained, until I could now send to you for the third time and remind your excellency to correct what has wrongly been done. I therefore admonish and advise you to have the clerics’ property restored, lest so distinguished a Church be deprived of the divine office on such holy days, and lest an opinion of you, unworthy of your station, be spread abroad by passers-by. In a matter capable of restoration, a sentence ought not to be given so hastily, nor ought the unregulated cruelty of ill-wishers to be satisfied.

Thus I have warned, and again warn you, prompted by the affection with which I love you from my heart, [Col. 0135A] to correct what requires correction and to defer whatever harsh measures you intend until a lawful examination, lest, when your anger has subsided, you repent of doing what, reason teaching you, you will see ought not to have been done. But if you are unwilling to yield to my admonitions and petitions, so often repeated, and reject a just satisfaction, do not be surprised if I grieve with those who grieve and mourn with those who mourn; for I was wholly ready both to rejoice in your joys and to share your sorrows. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Vulgrin, archdeacon of Paris: may you not grow lukewarm in zeal for justice.

Because the bearer of your letter was hastening to return [Col. 0135B] and I was hindered by public and domestic business, I could not write at greater length.
