Briefly, then, concerning the Jewish woman who was baptized and married to a Christian, but afterwards returned to Judaism, I reply to your fraternity that hers was a true marriage, since it was lawfully celebrated between persons under the same law, with no intervening cause that dissolves marriage.

Although, therefore, the woman committed fornication in two respects—because she returned to Judaism and married another man, namely one following the Jewish rite—the Christian husband who took another woman while she was alive undoubtedly committed adultery. For the canon plainly says, as you yourself know well (Letter 225): “For incestuous unions we reserve no pardon, unless they cure their adultery by separation.”

For blessed Augustine says in the book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (last chapter, cause 32, question 7, and Letter 125): “There remains between living persons a certain marital bond which neither separation nor union with another can take away.” Jerome also, in his letter to Oceanus [in two v. c. copies, “at the end”] on the death of Fabiola, says: “The Lord commanded that a wife ought not to be dismissed except for the cause of fornication, and that, if she is dismissed, she should remain unmarried. What is commanded to men applies consequently to women also. For an adulterous wife ought not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained.” Much more might be found in this manner, but I do not doubt that you know these matters well. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIII. IVO, minister of the Church of Chartres, to brother Gualter [otherwise Gauter], librarian of the Church of Beauvais, greeting.

[Col. 0135D]

Asked by you what penance should be imposed upon a priest who mockingly altered the divine words of the sacrament and the signs of the priestly office in the nuptial blessing of a certain virgin, substituting one thing for another, I reply for the present that I have found no special ruling on this matter. For neither have I further heard that such an adulteration—or rather sacrilege—of the divine sacraments has been committed anywhere by anyone [otherwise: “that such a sacrilege of sacred things was anywhere committed”].

It seems to me, therefore, that just as this is [55] a new kind of crime, so a new trial of a remedy must be devised—yet without judging anything too severe in such a sacrilege without the support of divine authority. Where special rulings are unavailable (*Laws*, XII), the general rulings promulgated against violators of divine sacraments seem to me sufficient. For the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 11, contains the following:

> “Let nothing contrary to order be presumed by an audacious act of rashness; nor let those things held in the highest veneration be violated by even the slightest act of presumption.”

And shortly afterward:

> “If anyone presumes to violate these things, he shall undergo the sentence of excommunication.”

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Julius sent to the bishops throughout Egypt:

> “A priest who acts otherwise than commanded shall cease from offering sacrifice until, corrected by lawful satisfaction of penance, he returns to the rank of his office [Col. 0136B] which he lost.”

And these provisions concern those who erred simply and in ignorance. How much more do they concern those who fraudulently perverted sacred words and thus, so far as lay in their power, consigned a woman who came in simplicity to fornication? Let these remarks suffice concerning them. Farewell.

> **Note:** [Col. 0135D] This is given more fully in chapter *Nihil*, cause 7, question 1.

## LETTER CXXIV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Daimbert, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens: devoted service in all things.

Let your fatherhood know that Hugh of Puiset, touched by the fear of God and compunction of heart (Letters 111 and 112), restored completely, so far as his own share was concerned, the things he had taken from our Church. He confirmed to me, under a pledge of faith and after giving hostages, that he would restore all that belonged to me and mine. But because I had been warned by your fatherhood to exercise discretion, I deferred accepting these things until he should abstain from the exactions and forced services which he was accustomed to impose in the territory of Fréteval.

Therefore we render to your fatherhood the greatest thanks [MS c.: “as great as we can”], because you extended your hand to us in this necessity and compassionately shared our suffering, as was fitting. We also ask that, on our account, you no longer hold him or his men interdicted or excommunicated, so long as he remains faithful to his undertaking and does not impose the aforesaid exactions.

But Lord Louis refuses to make peace with us (Letter 114), because I am unwilling to elevate to ecclesiastical honours that pagan, fallen into infamy, who disembowelled his own mother and tore her, with whatever claws he could, by schism. I therefore offer him through your hand every justice; or, if he comes to make satisfaction, such mercy as I can show him without the law forbidding it. And because he rejects both alternatives, one course remains to me: to await God’s mercy until He vindicates my cause. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Daimbert [other copies wrongly read Umbert], by God’s grace archbishop of Sens: service with humble devotion.

[Col. 0137A]

Concerning the Jerusalemites whose wives committed fornication (Letter 188), your holiness seems to me to judge rightly: according to evangelical and apostolic teaching, they must either return to their own wives or, while those wives live, remain without any carnal intercourse. Otherwise, those who do not now shrink from adulterous women will be accounted adulterers and judged by God with the punishment of adulterers, according to the Apostle’s saying: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Hebrews XIII).

Hence Augustine, in the book *On the Ten Commandments*, says: “You shall not commit adultery—that is, you shall not go to another woman besides your wife.” The same author, in *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (chapter 20, in chapter 28, [Col. 0137B] cause 32, question 7), says: “So strongly do the rights of marriage once entered into remain between living persons that they are more truly spouses to one another even when separated than to those others to whom they have attached themselves.” And a little later: “There remains between living persons a certain marital bond which neither separation nor union with another can take away.”

Jerome likewise, to Oceanus (on Matthew XIX, cause 32, question 5), says: “The Lord commands that a wife is not to be dismissed except for the cause of fornication, and that, if she has been dismissed, she is to remain unmarried (Matthew XVI). Whatever is commanded to men applies consequently to women. For an adulterous wife is not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained.”

Relying upon these and similar authorities, if a case of fornication should ever arise among us and such a divorce take place [otherwise: “take place”], we compel the separated parties by ecclesiastical censure either to be reconciled to one another or to remain without hope of marriage. But if those who ought to surpass their wives in virtue wish their wives to be victors over lust, while they themselves are conquered by lust because they desire to attach themselves to other women (Letter 148), we admonish them to consider the frailty of the female vessel and allow to the weaker sex what they desire should be allowed to the stronger.

For blessed Augustine says in *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount* (in chapter *Nihil*, cause 32, question 6): “Nothing is more unjust than to dismiss one’s wife on account of fornication, if the husband himself is convicted of wishing to commit fornication. For the Apostle’s saying applies: ‘In judging another you condemn yourself, for you do the same things that you judge.’ Therefore, whoever wishes to cast away his wife on account of fornication must himself be free from fornication.” The same author, in *On the Words of the Lord*, tractate 47, says: “You seek an untouched woman: be untouched yourself. You seek a pure woman: do not be impure.”

But if they fear that they will be blameworthy for receiving adulterous women, let them hear what Jerome says in his exposition of Hosea (Book I on chapter 1; Letter 148): “The prophet Hosea is not to be blamed if he converted the prostitute whom he had married to chastity; rather, he is to be praised because he made a good woman out of a bad one. For the person who remains good is not defiled if joined to an evil person; rather, an evil person is converted to good if he follows the examples of the good.”

And because I speak to one not ignorant of the law, I judge that these few points which have been said are sufficient for the questions asked. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Daimbert, by God’s grace archbishop of the Church of Sens, greeting and service.

We give thanks [otherwise, “render thanks”] to your excellency because you watch over us with fatherly diligence and warn us to take precautions lest a greater tumult be stirred up between the Church of Chartres and the countess’s following. This we too have endeavoured to do, although provoked by many injuries and insults (Letter 121).

Nevertheless, let your most loving fatherhood know certainly that the oath made by the clerics—not to receive into the body of canons persons born [56] of common people, nor any others born from an alien household [Col. 0138B] [so v. c.; formerly, “of an alien race”]—was made without consulting me. Yet, since it is not mine to cast into infamy the sons entrusted to me, I allowed what they had done, lest they incur perjury; indeed, I even interceded for them with the lord pope, asking him to approve what they had done and confirm it by the text of his decree, lest anyone might be permitted to loose with a lesser key (Letter 117) what he knew had been locked with the chief key.

I have therefore sent the form of this decree to your holiness, so that, if it happens that you hold a conference with the countess, you may persuade her either to bear patiently this injury—which, so far as she is concerned, is no injury at all—or to accept what justice and law dictate. Otherwise the clerics are ready to be driven into perpetual exile rather than in any way be drawn into perjury. Farewell.

> **Note:** [Col. 0137D] See also Letter 133 on freed persons, and Letter 147 on persons of servile condition.

## LETTER CXXVII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Louis, by God’s grace king-elect of the Franks, greeting and service.

When your letter came to us, I was wholly unprepared to come safely and honourably to your conference on such short notice. Moreover, a truce stands between the countess and me until the arrival of the bishop of Albano, through whose counsel or judgment she promises to make satisfaction to God and to our Church. During this truce, therefore, it is neither lawful nor honourable for me to seek any evil or injury against her, or even to render myself suspect in this matter.

After the truce has elapsed, I shall be able to meet your highness wherever it pleases you, under your safe-conduct, and freely and openly discuss and decide, as reason and the outcome of events may require, the matters to be considered. Therefore let not your sublimity be angered against me if my humility fears to incur suspicion of deceit and perfidy. Once those suspicions are removed, I desire to have a conference with you and to offer my service to the extent of my power. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Odo, fellow-brother and fellow-priest, greeting.

The envoy whom your fraternity sent to me did not await [Col. 0139A] our answer or reply. I therefore now answer your fraternity concerning that person whom you intended to send to our conference: I recall Virgil’s words,

> “… I fear the Danaans, even when bearing gifts.”  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid*, II.49

For he has always regarded me with suspicion and, before high authorities [otherwise, “persons”], accused me as much as he could. Hence, if the matter turned out otherwise than he wished, he would make me, already suspected, still more suspect, and would stir up greater enmities against me.

But if he should come of his own accord, at his own prompting, to our conference—or if anyone from that party were to communicate to me a means of making peace—I would, with such power as God grants, humbly wash and wipe the dust from the feet of those bringing peace. For our purpose is, as far as we can, to labour for the peace of the Church and to use the authority given us by God for building up and not for destruction.

And however much either my own weakness hinders me from fulfilling this, or the obstinacy of my hearers resists it (Letters 12, 25, 67, 204), or the detraction of rivals tears at me, this intention nevertheless chiefly flourishes in my heart. For the sun, although it does not emit the rays of its brightness when covered by a cloud, is not deprived of the power of its heat. In these matters, therefore, I appeal to the Judge of inward things; and when I desire good but lack the power to accomplish it, I say to my Judge: “Your eyes saw my imperfection” (Psalm CXXXVIII). Let your fraternity therefore pray with my other fellow-servants that He who gave the will may also add the power [Col. 0139C] to accomplish it for the sake of good will. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIX. IVO, by God’s grace humble bishop of the Church of Chartres, to Geoffrey, Count of Vendôme, greeting.

Since we ought to provide with pastoral diligence for all the sheep committed to us by God, lest they abandon the pastures of life or expose themselves to the bites of invisible wolves, we owe this especially to your nobility, because you are both our parishioner and a *cataneus* of our Church [a noteworthy word; a rare adjective]. I write this to your affection because I have heard that you wish to marry the viscountess of Blois, whose deceased husband was your blood relative, as noble men related both to you and to the late Viscount Robert have written to me and are prepared to prove.

Therefore I command you, and by Christian law forbid you, those deadly and incestuous nuptials, which you will be able neither to defend by law nor to obtain lawful heirs from. If, therefore, you accept our salutary admonitions, when you have sent to us, we shall appoint you a fixed day and place at which you may come for a lawful examination and receive the judgment which Christian law dictates concerning such a betrothal [otherwise, “accept”]. But if you presume otherwise to carry out what you have begun, you will incur excommunication and will not escape the mark of infamy.

The relationship between you and the husband of the aforesaid woman is as follows. Landricus Sorus [Col. 0140A] had a son and a daughter. The son, named Lancelin, begot a son, Lancelin, from whom came Agnes; she bore Robert, and this Robert married the daughter of Hugh of Dunois. The daughter of Landricus Sorus was married by Burchard [otherwise Burcardus] Rata-pilata. From them was born Burchard the Bald, from whom Fulk Aser [otherwise Anser] was born; from him descended Nifrana [otherwise Vifrana or Infrana], who bore Geoffrey Grey-Tunic, and he wishes to marry her. Farewell.

> **Note:** [Col. 0139D] Such marriages are forbidden in Letters 45 and 221. See also Gratian, cause 35, question 1 and following.

## LETTER CXXX. IVO, by God’s grace humble bishop of the Church of Chartres, to Matilda, Viscountess of Blois, greeting.

> **Note:** [Col. 0140D] Compare the preceding letter.

Since we owe salutary admonitions and commands to you and to all whom we love in God or for God’s sake, we admonish and command you by Christian law to defer the marriage which you have agreed to contract with the Count of Vendôme until a lawful examination, and not to lose the good reputation which you have hitherto possessed [otherwise, “forfeit”].

But if you presume otherwise, you will be subject to excommunication, and you will lose the property [57] which you have alienated for this marriage. For the common blood relatives of the Count of Vendôme and of Robert the viscount, your deceased husband, say that the Count of Vendôme and Robert your husband were relatives in the degree shown by the letter sent to the count, and they are prepared to prove it. When you and the count send your envoys to me concerning this matter, I shall appoint you a day and place. [Col. 0140C] The order of relationship is written above (Letter 129).

> **Note:** [Col. 0140D] These words are not part of the body of the letter.

Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Wlgrin, archdeacon of Paris, greeting.

Concerning the priest who, under no compulsion of necessity, renounced into your hand the church which he governed, and who now endeavours through the agency of laymen to ascend to the bed of the bride—whom, by renouncing her, he judged either himself unworthy of or her unworthy of himself—I reply to your fraternity that it is just that he remain subject to the judgment which he pronounced against himself, and that he not presume to violate the bride whom he repudiated while the brother who was lawfully incardinated to her remains alive.

If he seeks to intrude himself by lay violence, your fraternity knows that the ancient rules provide that no authority has been assigned to laymen to ordain priests in a church or expel them from a church (canon under cause 16, question 7). If a priest attacks a church against this rule, it is your office to wield the sword of anathema against that presumptuous priest [otherwise, “exercise”], and to exclude from the thresholds of the Church the lay collaborators in this usurpation until they desist. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Daimbert, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens, greeting and service.

[Col. 0141A]

Since the importunity of those who knock often obtains what it seeks, we ask and ask again your fatherhood to have justice, hitherto delayed by the archpriest of Étampes (Letter 50, at the end), now expedited concerning Haimo, parishioner both of yours and ours at Étampes. He unjustly compels my man and another man of this archpriest of mine to ransom themselves through the hardships of imprisonment and hunger. He also compelled that same archpriest, when he was carrying your and our embassy to him, to pledge on faith that he would make no further complaint against him either to you or to us.

Take fitting notice, therefore, of this shameful injury [Col. 0141B] and render the justice required, both to yourselves and to me, in these matters. Moreover, I want you to know the dispute between the parties in our Church, which I shall briefly set down for you. When the cloister of Chartres was violated last summer (Letter 133), the greater part of the clergy, both in persons and in number, unable to endure the countess’s injuries and threats, left the city and sent some of their number to you. Others approached the king and the king’s son to protest the injury done to them. From the brothers’ common funds they expended what was necessary.

The opposing minority says it suffered injury because common property was spent without common counsel. The other party replies: “What we spent, we spent for both your benefit and ours; and the reason why we did not discuss this with you beforehand was that we feared obstruction from some among you and were not permitted to return to our Church.” Many whom I assembled for this agree that what was spent for a common necessity by the consent of the greater and more numerous party must be paid from the common resources. I wish, therefore, that through the bearer of this letter you have your own judgment and that of your Church written back to me on this matter. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Richard [otherwise Richard], by God’s grace bishop of Albano and legate of the holy Roman Church: may you fare well and not believe every spirit.

Knowing that “the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who flatters” [Col. 0141D] (Proverbs XXVII), and the Psalmist’s saying, “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me” (Psalm CXL), I have accepted your caustic words (Letter 277) with equanimity, insofar as your intention is straightforward. But I have taken serious notice of the duplicity of false brethren, who, as by certain robberies of the night (Letter 219), suggest falsehoods as truths to your solicitude. Their falsehood will soon be disclosed when it is struck by the light of truth and will not dare to come into the light.

Some of these believe that they can cover their own infamy only by injuring the reputation of good men and contriving to encrust pure vessels [Col. 0142A] (Horace, *Satires* I.3). They condemn simony for no other reason than that they themselves cannot be simoniacs, while others in the Church obtain what these men, impeded by certain hostile attacks, do not deserve to obtain. If they turned the eyes of their minds upon themselves, apart from simony they would rightly reprove in themselves many crimes and disgraceful acts, so that the Apostle’s words could openly be said to them: “In judging another you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge” (Romans II).

I do not say this because I understand my conscience ever to have been contaminated by such a crime; rather, I wonder why this alone, or why it in the Church of Chartres alone, is reproved, when this and many other equally condemnable things prevail in almost every Gallican Church. What has been suggested to you—that, with my permission, the Simoniac heresy publicly rules in the Church of Chartres—is wholly without truth. From the beginning of my clerical life I have always abhorred this evil, and since coming to the episcopate I have, with such power as God has granted, cut it away at the surface.

This would be manifest if it could be done without offending our fellow-brethren and fellow-bishops, in whose Churches many evil customs still raise their heads—customs which, by God’s help, have been put to sleep in the Church of Chartres during the time of our priesthood (Letters 94 and 117). But if the dean, cantor, and other ministers still publicly exact certain things, by ancient custom, from those made canons, they defend themselves, despite my opposition and prosecution, by the custom of the Roman Church. There, they say, chamberlains and ministers of the sacred palace exact much from consecrated bishops or abbots, disguising it under the name of offering or blessing; there, as they say, neither pen nor paper is had freely. With this they dash my forehead against a stone [58] [Col. 0142C], and I have nothing to answer except the Gospel saying: “Observe and do what they say; but if they do it, do not act according to their works” (Matthew XXIII).

If I cannot uproot this pestilence altogether, this must not be attributed solely to my weakness. From the beginning of the rising Roman Church, the Roman Church has laboured on this matter and has not been able completely to eliminate from even her own bosom those who seek their own advantage. Nor will greed cease to reign in evil days until, the end of the world completed, charity receives the kingdom of peace.

Meanwhile, to use Augustine’s words (Letter 137 to the people of Hippo, in chapter 6, distinction 47): “However much the discipline of my household watches, I am a human being and live among human beings. I do not dare arrogate to myself that my household is better than Noah’s ark, where among eight persons one reprobate, a mocker of his father, was found (Genesis IX); or better than Abraham’s household, where it was said: ‘Cast out the handmaid and her son’ (Genesis XXI); or better than Isaac’s household, concerning whose two twins it was said: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’ (Malachi I).”

And, to come to Christian times: Christ always suffers in His members Judas the betrayer; the Church suffers Nicholas, the praiser of fornication; Simon, the pursuer of sacrilegious gain. And, to speak universally, chaff will always abound until the threshing-floor is winnowed. Yet, whenever things of this kind are publicly reported to our hearing in judicial order and established by certain evidence, we do not permit them to pass unpunished, while preserving the course of the laws. But uncertain matters we reserve for judgment by the tribunal of the eternal Judge, knowing that one who has no authority to condemn an accused person, or cannot prove the accusation, is free from blame.

Therefore let your fellow-servants understand that, living in evil days like ourselves, they have not yet had revealed to them the hidden things of darkness and the manifest [otherwise, “manifested”] counsels of hearts, just as neither have we. Let them not judge our imperfection from their own imperfection, [Col. 0143B] nor hasten to judge what is uncertain. But if perhaps they proceed simply to cut wood, let them beware lest, through an excessive blow, the iron fly from the handle and kill one of the sons of the prophets (Deuteronomy XIX; Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book X, chapter 9; Peter of Blois, *Letters*).

Moreover, I make known to your solicitude that the clerics of the Church of Chartres suspect you because you invited them to Blois to receive judgment concerning the immunity of the cloister of Chartres (Letter 127). There, they say, they fear the violence of a rash multitude [otherwise, read: “an opposing multitude”], since the countess’s following has chief power there. She complains that the ordinance of the Church of Chartres forbidding the admission of freed persons to the clergy was made against her honour.

Therefore the freedom of your religious office ought to stand so impartially in the middle [Col. 0143C] that you may not appear, in judgment, to disregard the person of the poor and honour the countenance of the powerful. I say this not because I suspect anything evil on the countess’s part, but because I am bound, so far as my smallness permits, to provide for the honour of the Roman Church (Letter 92). If I do not honour its envoy, I do not seem to honour the one who sent him.

> **Note:** [Col. 0141] On this matter see Gregory the Great, Letter 44, reported in chapter *Sicut*, cause 1, question 2.

> **Note:** [Col. 0143] Thus most old manuscripts; the Ser. copy reads *libertinis*, “freed persons.” Letters 126 and 147 should be joined with this passage.

## LETTER CXXXIV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Daimbert, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens, greeting and service.

Concerning the marital agreement made between two nobles (*Titia*, *On the Meaning of Obligations*), whereby the father who had a daughter swore that he would give her to whichever of the other noble’s sons he wished when the girl reached marriageable age [Col. 0143D], I reply to your fatherhood that nature has ordained, and both ecclesiastical and secular law have established, that those whose bodies ought to become one through conjugal union must likewise have a mutual consent of minds.

Therefore, whatever the father may have sworn [otherwise, “swears”] without the girl’s knowledge, once she has been brought to years of reason [or, “has reached them”], is invalid according to the laws, even while her father lives, unless the girl herself consents. Hence Pope Nicholas writes to Archbishop Hincmar: “According to the laws, the consent alone of those whose union is in question is sufficient” [otherwise, “under the laws”; so MS c., as in chapter 2, cause 26, question 2].

If that consent alone should be lacking in marriage, all other things—even sexual intercourse itself—are frustrated, as John Chrysostom, the great teacher, attests when he says: “Marriage is made not by intercourse but by will.” Likewise, in the Roman laws [otherwise, “of the Romans”; Letter 99] of Emperor Justinian it is stated: “Betrothals, like marriages, are made by the consent of those contracting them. And therefore, as in marriages, so in betrothals daughters under paternal authority must consent.” And elsewhere: “Betrothals may be made from the beginning of age, provided it is understood that both persons do so—that is, if they are not younger than twelve years.”

This is my judgment concerning the question proposed [otherwise, “inquiry”; so MS c.], and if such a controversy reaches my hearing, I decide it on this reasoning. Moreover, I make known to your fatherhood [Col. 0144B] that, although no injury had been inflicted by me and no justice denied, and although a truce stood between the countess and me (Letter 127), with an apostolic representative mediating, William, the countess’s son, conspired before the altar [otherwise, “at the altar”; so MS c.] of Blessed Mary for the death of the clerics of Chartres (Letter 136), for my destruction, and for the destruction of all who belong to us. He compelled all citizens subject to the ban to join the same conspiracy, unless we yield to the will of his servants and he usurps by violence what he ought to obtain [or retain] by grace alone.

Having heard this Herodian oath, I thereafter refused to administer the divine sacraments in the presence of such conspirators or to give them the episcopal blessing in the customary manner. Yet I delayed pronouncing upon them the anathema they had deserved, until I should receive the counsel of your fatherhood and of our colleagues, and, strengthened by the counsel and aid of many, recall them by the due censure from their deadly conspiracy.

When, therefore, I send again to you, I wish you to be forewarned, so that you may have ready at hand such counsel and assistance as will be honourable to you and useful to us, and may hasten to extend your hand to those shipwrecked before they sink. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXV. IVO, humble minister of Chartres, to Paschal, supreme pontiff: the obedience due, with devotion.

This knight, the bearer of the present letter, named Raimbald, fought bravely in the siege of Jerusalem. On returning home, however, overthrown by diabolical prompting and an outburst of anger, he had a certain monk and priest of the monastery of Bonneval castrated because that priest had caused some of his servants, who were stealing grass, to be beaten. Since this was unheard of among us, we assembled an ecclesiastical tribunal, deprived him of his arms, and imposed upon him a penance of fourteen years: on prescribed days he was to abstain from richer foods and expiate so monstrous a crime by almsgiving and fasting. He accepted this obediently; but afterwards, having enlisted many great intercessors, he wearied us with urgent and repeated entreaties that, because of the attacks of his enemies, we might permit him to use arms. But we were unwilling to consent to such requests, fearing that by so easy an indulgence we should expose both him and many others to danger (Letter 161). Therefore, reserving this dispensation for apostolic moderation, we have sent him to the thresholds of the Apostles, so that he may both cleanse his sin by the hardship of the journey and find, in the depths of your compassion, that mercy which God may inspire you to grant him. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to ADELA, Countess Palatine: may you abound in the affections of peace and charity.

Many things are reported to you concerning me which you ought not to believe are true. For I have had, and still have, many powerful advisers urging disturbance (Letters 116 and 124), who even promised that they would be helpers in every way and in all things. This I have hitherto diligently avoided and have avoided in the past, although many attribute this not to religion but to timidity.

And I thought that I had found a means by which peace could be made, consistently with your honour and the wishes of the clergy, had not your son, on the counsel of foolish and malicious men, taken that Herodian oath (Letter 134) and compelled his burgesses to do the same.

> [Note: He calls them citizens in the said Letter 134.]

Having taken the counsel of honourable men after this was done, I refused thereafter to give them a blessing. Yet for love of you I deferred the curse; for those who have deserved a curse are not worthy of a blessing, since they have rashly conspired for the death of undeserving persons—formerly printed, “for the death of enemies”—until they repent and seek pardon for their unlawful oath.

Therefore, before matters turn for the worse, we ought, either through you or through suitable mediators, to hold a conference and endeavour, as God may best grant, to bring so dangerous and useless a mob back to peace. For I shall no longer be able justly to dissemble for long without striking with a just anathema the instigators of such evils and their accomplices, unless a remedy be prepared for such great and unlawful audacities, by which the impious undertaking and useless mob may be transformed into the calm of peace. Farewell; and send back through the bearer of this letter whatever seems better to you.

## LETTER CXXXVII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to the congregation of the Church of Beauvais: divine consolation in tribulations.

[Col. 0145D]

Let your brotherhood know that I am afflicted in your afflictions and sympathize with your sufferings (Letters 263 and 264). But because your affair is placed in a difficult position, we cannot give you definite counsel as we ought; for unless God mercifully provide in this matter, you must either offend the law or the king. For if you allow your fellow-canon, criminally accused, to be examined elsewhere than in the Church, you offend canonical law; if you reject the hearing of the royal court, you offend the king.

In this dispute, although you yourselves know, both by reason and authority, what is truer and what is more honourable—

> [In one old manuscript: “what is more becoming, or what is more honourable.”]

—yet, according to the exigencies of the times, you will have to follow what is more tolerable for your weakness (Letter 171).

But if we knew that you were prepared to endure with joy the destruction of your houses, the banishment of your persons, and the plundering of your goods, we could exhort you to follow the counsel of Susanna, who chose rather to fall into the hands of men than to abandon God’s law (Daniel 13). Yet because counsel and fortitude are joined together among spiritual gifts, we do not dare give counsel other than that which your endurance can bear, since we do not know the measure of your strength.

As to avoiding the secular court in cases involving clerics (Gratian, cause 11, question 1), and as to accusations or testimony of clerics against laymen or of laymen against clerics—what the decrees, the canons, and even secular laws proclaim—you have these matters among you, and we should in part have written them to you, except that the bearer of your letter came to us on Friday afternoon and hastened back. For the present we can offer your brotherhood no other help except that we shall entreat the Angel of Great Counsel to direct your counsels and actions and bring them to a good conclusion. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to his beloved brethren in Christ, the archdeacons Wulgrin and Stephen of Paris: love the beauty of God’s house and seek the things that are Jesus Christ’s.

[The recipients are Parisian archdeacons, from Letters 122 and 131.]

[Col. 0146C]

When the election of a bishop was being considered among you, and your lord dean Fulk was chosen by certain among you—

> [Note: Of the Church of Paris, as is clear from the heading of Letter 112. See also Letter 139.]

—we have heard that an ugly contention arose among you, offending the ears of many and spreading far and wide from your Church no good savour. We grieved with fraternal compassion at the darkening of your peaceful serenity, since we have learned by experience what injuries are wont to arise for Churches from fraternal schism.

Yet to your petition we reply that we shall not give our assent to the election of Lord Fulk or of another, unless he has been chosen either by the agreement of clergy and people, or approved by the judgement of the metropolitan, with the concurrence—elsewhere, “agreement,” in manuscript C—of the suffragans, after lawful investigation has taken place (Gratian, distinction 61).

Therefore, in offering counsel, we admonish your brotherhood that no one among you should exercise private hatreds in so great a crisis; that none should seek private honour or private advantage; that none should assail his brother with public infamy unless he can prove judicially what he alleges. Otherwise, while rashly alleging what cannot be proved, he may himself receive retaliation—

> [Note: Letter 51 calls it “the bond of retaliation.”]

—and bring both himself and his possessions into danger.

We are also surprised at your prudence: why have you arranged for this cause to be examined before the king, against the king?

> [Note: Ivo was later invited by the king to the discussion of this election, as the following letter testifies.]

There the king’s will will have more power than the justice of the law, and truth will neither be able to be investigated in peace nor, once found, preserved. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXIX. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to DAIMBERT, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens: the service due from a son.

The appeal made by the Parisians should have been referred to you, so that you might appoint for them a day and place at your discretion and invite the suffragan bishops to this inquiry, allowing a suitable interval. Since this was not done, the election of Lord Fulk (Letter 238), and the inquiry into that election which is to follow, seem to me to have been made too hastily.

And since nothing is ever done quickly enough for a soul that desires, what Wisdom says may come to pass:

> “An inheritance hastily acquired at the beginning will lack a blessing at the end”  
> (Proverbs 29).

I had been invited by Lord King Philip to this inquiry, but this displeased me, because no such summons from you had preceded it according to ecclesiastical custom and canonical institution. Now, however, having heard your summons, I shall, God granting, take care to come if the king gives me the safe-conduct he promised.

But if some impediment prevents me from coming, and if not enough of our colleagues assemble to suffice for the determination of so great a matter, permit the affair either to be deferred to another time or both parties to go to the Apostolic See, to which Lord Fulk intends to go whether his election is confirmed or annulled. Farewell.

## LETTER CXL. IVO, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to his beloved brother and fellow-priest GUNHER: peace of mind together with bodily repose.

[Col. 0147C]

If the ecclesiastical sacraments, said by rumour to have been forbidden by the Apostolic See and in which you fear to participate dangerously, had been prohibited to your brotherhood by apostolic letters or by the spoken word of the person to whom authority to impose such a prohibition had been entrusted, I should advise you not merely to fear participation in them but wholly to abhor them. This would not be because what is celebrated is not a sacrament, but because, for those who communicate, what has been usurped through disobedience becomes harmful.

Therefore let a clean conscience make you secure in such matters, for according to the Apostle:

> “All things are clean to the clean”  
> (Romans 14);

but to those who are defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, because their mind and conscience are defiled (Titus 1).

If, therefore, you present yourself at the divine sacraments either by custom or at the invitation of the brethren, receive with the hand of your heart whatever you find celebrated among any persons; marvel at it, and lay up its signified realities in the belly of memory, sweetly to be chewed over as nourishment of life.

> [Note: From Eusebius of Emesa, cited at the end of Letter 287.]

Do not greatly heed what opinion or rumour may cast upon the matter, but what an embassy of superior authority, duly reaching you, prohibits or commands. For just as ecclesiastical judges are not to believe matters other than those which are publicly brought forward in judicial order and confirmed by manifest testimony, even if they are true (chapter *Quamvis*, 73, cause 11, question 3), so neither are all reports to be entrusted to faith unless they are confirmed by authentic letters or publicly announced by the oral statement of their bearers.

For the present, I make this reply to your brotherhood concerning your doubt, without prejudging the opinion of wiser men. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to RICHARD—elsewhere RICHARDUS—by God’s grace Bishop of Albano and vicar of the Apostolic See: greeting and service.

As we were deeply grieved by the king’s excommunication because of the harm done to Christian religion, so we should rejoice greatly at his absolution, if it could be effected for the honour of God and of the holy Apostolic See, because of the increase of that same holy religion.

> [Note: On the absolution of the excommunicated King Philip. Compare Letter 144.]

But we do not dare advise that anything be done otherwise than as has been entrusted to your care by the lord pope, because, like you, we are uncertain of the outcome. If, however, divine grace has humbled his heart to repentance, it seems to us advisable that, in the presence of very many bishops, you publicly and solemnly absolve him, so that, just as his estrangement was widely known, so his desired return may be everywhere proclaimed by the testimony of many religious persons.

In this matter your diligence must take care that those who lost his friendship for love of justice and obedience to the Apostolic See may be restored to favour upon his reconciliation (Letter 104). Yet I should have thought it better for your reputation if this absolution were performed somewhere other than Sens, where every person could freely state his opinion.

Furthermore, I greatly desire to go to the appointed council; but I cannot discover by what road, safe-conduct, or detour I can reach Troyes against the will of the king, whose hostility I have endured now for a decade.

> [Note: The king’s hostility toward Ivo: Letter 67; his threats: Letter 35; Ivo’s fear of him: Letter 113.]

Therefore, if you can obtain some security for me either through the king himself or through the countess, I earnestly beg you to endeavour to do so.

## LETTER CXLII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to MATILDA, Queen of the English (Letter 107): may you reign in heaven with the Queen of Angels.

[Col. 0148D]

Since every gift must be valued not so much according to its quantity as according to the affection of the giver, we have gratefully received the bells which you gave to the blessed and everlasting Virgin, both because of your devotion and because of their delightful sound, as though from that everlasting Virgin herself; and we have caused them to be placed in a conspicuous location where they may be heard by crowds of people.

Whenever they are rung to mark the stated hours, they so delight the minds of their hearers—elsewhere, “the minds of the hearers are delighted”—that your memory is renewed in every heart. Nor is such remembrance to be lightly esteemed: it flourishes anew at the time when that unique victim, offered upon the altar of the Cross for our redemption, is daily consecrated on the Lord’s table by ministers of the new priesthood; when God is honoured—elsewhere, “is glorified”—by the faithful with heavenly hymns, as with calves of the lips; when God, offended by sinners striking their guilty breasts, is inclined to mercy by the sacrifice of a contrite spirit.

Without doubt, those who provide God’s ministers, for his honour and love, with the goods in which they abound and which the ministers lack, share in these benefits. Thus your abundance has already graciously begun to supply what our poverty lacked, and has most generously promised that it will make provision for repairing—or elsewhere, restoring—the roofs of our Church.

So the ancient people of God, at the Lord’s command through Moses, offered gold, silver, and bronze for the use of the tabernacle, together with fine linen, scarlet, purple, and blue; women also offered jewels and earrings (Exodus 35). By these things the vestment of the high priest and the tabernacle were then visibly adorned, and the holy character of the ministers of the New Testament was signified. Those who lacked these precious things offered goats’ hair, from which hair-cloth coverings might be made to preserve the brilliance of the interior ornaments, lest they be defiled by dust or decay from rain.

Your Excellency will follow this pattern of piety when, for the repair of the furnishings or roofs of God’s house, you supply necessities wherever and in whatever measure you wish. For all these things, await without doubt that rewarder whom you have learned to be the teacher of such deeds. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLIII. IVO, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to ROBERT, Count of Meulan: greeting and the aid of prayers.

We give thanks for your generosity—manuscript C, “liberality”—and prudence, because you honourably treat Lord Richard, abbot of the monastery of Préaux, a religious and prudent man, as he deserves—manuscript C, “may you treat”—and faithfully and devotedly assist him in his affairs as is necessary—manuscript C, “may you assist.” We further ask that you bring what you have well begun to a better conclusion.

For he labours to recover the possessions of the monastery entrusted to him because he is compelled by the obligation of his profession. From every abbot, when he is to receive blessing from a bishop, this is required: that he profess himself bound to gather again the property of his monastery which has hitherto been wrongly scattered, and faithfully administer it for the use of the brethren and the poor.

And the decrees of Pope Symmachus and of the other holy Fathers concerning alienated goods of the Church provide (Letter 111) that both giver, receiver, and possessor are subject to anathema; nor may one who dissipates what religious souls have left for the support of the poor protect himself by any obstacle before Christ’s tribunal.

Likewise, the Council of Agde provides that the following rule be observed in sales made by abbots:

> “Whatever has been sold without the bishop’s permission shall be recalled to the bishop’s authority.”

> [Note: The same passage is in the second book of the Decretum, title *On the Alienation and Exchange of Ecclesiastical Property*; and in Gratian, chapter 12, question 2, “Whether the Property of the Church…”]

The same may be said of your own valour, because divine providence has prepared you as defender of that place. For whatever has been alienated from the aforesaid monastery without your assent ought all to be restored to that monastery and most fully returned to the uses of the brethren for which these things were given.

So much for this matter. Henceforth, however, we blame your nobility because you so lightly esteem a benefice of the Church of Chartres—which seems great even to other great men—that you make no effort either to recover what was dispersed by your predecessor or to perform for us any part of the service owed. For those who have occupied that benefice swim between the two sides: they serve neither us because of you nor you because of us.

We therefore admonish you to take counsel on this point and send us word, because it brings no advantage to your greatness but brings us great disadvantage. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLIV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: with due obedience, the service of the prayers of the faithful.

We inform your fatherhood that on the third—elsewhere, fourth—day before the Kalends of August, many bishops of both the province of Reims and that of Sens, summoned by Lord Richard—elsewhere, Richardus—Bishop of Albano, your legate, assembled at a town in the diocese of Orléans called Beaugency, to effect the king’s absolution (Letter 141), according to the tenor of the letters which your moderation had sent on this matter.

The king also came, with his companion at his side (Letters 13 and 28), and, according to your command, they were ready, with their hands upon the most holy Gospels, to abjure absolutely every practice of carnal intercourse and also every private conversation with one another, except in the presence of witnesses entirely beyond suspicion, until your dispensation.

But because your letters contained the instruction that the Bishop of Albano should employ the counsel of prudent men in this absolution, he wished the entire burden of counsel to depend upon the judgement of the bishops. The bishops, however, apparently suspecting something—we do not know what—continually repeated that they ought to be companions in this counsel, not its leaders. Although some of us thought that the aforesaid absolution could honourably be carried out as stated above, and that it was being obstructed, not altogether reasonably, because of certain persons’ animosities.

When the matter thus remained undecided, the king loudly complained that he had been badly treated. Nevertheless, both personally and through us he still knocks at the ears of your fatherhood, asking you to moderate his cause according to the tenor of your letters and the instructions given to our fellow-bishop Lord Galo, lest Solomon’s saying be fulfilled in his case:

> “He who presses—elsewhere, ‘is pressed’—too hard draws blood”  
> (Proverbs 30).

No wise person has ever disapproved the method of dispensation. Thus blessed Cyril, writing to the presbyter Gennadius (Letter 171), says:

> “Just as those who sail the sea, when a storm presses and the ship is in danger, throw out certain things so that the rest may be saved, so we too, when we have no certainty of saving all affairs, disregard some of them, lest we suffer the loss of everything.”

And because we say these things by way of suggestion, not instruction, the sum of our suggestion is that henceforth you should accommodate yourself, so far as you can without harm to his salvation, to the weakness of the man, and rescue from this danger the land endangered by his anathema.

Furthermore, we humbly suggest to your holy fatherhood that you command our fellow-bishop Lord Galo (Letters 145 and 146), who cannot possess the bishopric of Beauvais because of the oath of Lord Louis, to be transferred by the hand of the Archbishop of Sens to the bishopric of Paris, which the king and the king’s son gladly and devoutly grant him for love of you. The bearer of this letter, a canon and cleric of the Church of Paris, will tell you how the wishes of clergy and people concur in his favour, so that you may know that he can rightly be transferred, since for no reason can he obtain his own see. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Lord MANASSES, Archbishop of Reims: greeting and service.

[Col. 0151C]

Because I embrace your fatherhood as the true son of your daughter, the Church of Beauvais, with a love as though inborn, I exhort you with all the sincerity I can command, according to evangelical and apostolic institution, that all your affairs may be done in charity.

Therefore, in giving counsel we suggest, and in suggesting we give counsel, that you relax with wiser moderation the rigor of justice which you have at last, I know not at whose urging, directed against the Church of Beauvais, now that the matter has almost—elsewhere, “entirely”—reached harbour. Do so until the peace between the lord king and Lord Galo, consecrated to the Church of Beauvais (Letter 144), is either fully secured or altogether broken.

Otherwise your office will seem that of a pilot preventing a ship tossed by storms from being able to reach either its desired harbour or another. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLVI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to DAIMBERT, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens: service with due reverence.

We inform your fatherhood that the clergy and people of the Church of Paris have by wish and voice chosen as bishop Lord Galo, consecrated to the Church of Beauvais (Letters 144, 145, and 260). Having sent suitable persons from among the clergy, they humbly and devoutly asked him in person—manuscript C, “presenting [the election]”—to receive the pastoral care of the aforesaid Church, confirming the election by letters.

But because transfers of bishops (Letter 288) ought, when necessity urges, to be effected by metropolitan authority and the dispensation of the supreme pontiff, we, so far as lies in us, give our assent to that election and urge your fatherhood to support it by asking the lord pope to command that the aforesaid bishop be transferred through your hand, since he cannot obtain his own see.

Thus you will honour—elsewhere, “will glorify”—your own ministry, and, by giving consolation to a desolate Church, will bind the devotion—elsewhere, “love,” and so manuscript C—of those electing and of the one elected more closely to yourselves. We also offer you this counsel lest, if the affair should have another outcome, the dignity of your Church be diminished in any respect and mutual charity be joined by a less firm bond. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLVII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: due obedience with sincerity.

Because our fathers, your predecessors, have in many cases relaxed something of severity (Letters 214 and 231), where salvation was in no danger, in order to apply themselves to removing greater evils, we therefore, with the knees of our hearts bent, humbly entreat the apostolic majesty in that confidence: pour forth the depths of mercy toward the Church of Chartres (Letter 126), and endeavour to restore peace long disturbed, which shakes and scatters the sweet-smelling flower of the Church together with the growth of good fruits.

This matter depends so entirely upon your judgement that we may confidently say to your holiness in the words of the evangelical centurion:

> “Only say the word, and my servant shall be healed”  
> (Luke 7).

At last, through frequent persuasions and public and private prayers, with much delay and much polishing, God granting, we have bent the hearts of the clergy of Chartres to this: that they may faithfully intercede with your fatherhood to except from the privilege you granted that Church—not to admit persons of servile condition—the *conditionarii*, that is, persons bound to another—

> [Note: Persons obliged to someone else, who were forbidden admission to sacred orders: chapter 7, distinction 34; chapter 15, distinction 54.]

—born from the lawful marriage of the household of the Count of Chartres, and the royal fiscal dependants, for whom a similar disturbance might arise; and that you command—elsewhere, “permit”—them to return to the same status in which they were before the privilege.

> [Note: Also those born in common wedlock; Letter 126.]

For the oath which the clergy previously took in this matter does not prevent this, because both the greater and lesser clergy know and publicly acknowledge that they made that oath on the condition that they might add what was beneficial to their institution and except what was harmful. Otherwise the losses, scandals, disturbances within and without, disputes, angers, and quarrels, all arising from this cause and arising daily (Letter 132), cannot be calmed.

But all these things will cease by God’s working if your vigilance, while maintaining in their stability those included in the privilege, dispenses with paternal foresight only those things for which the Church requests dispensation and restrains by apostolic censure those things which should be restrained.

I thought that I could say all this to your holiness in person. But from the beginning of autumn a serious illness has so afflicted and weakened me that I am still unable to undertake not only a long journey but even a short one. I have therefore sent in my stead Lord Bernerius, abbot of the monastery of Bonneval, a man of good reputation and well known to the Roman Church, who may explain our necessities to you and bring us back from your holiness the answers entrusted to him.

The canons also sent in their stead their fellow-canon, Lord Goselin—elsewhere Guaslin or Gauslin, and so manuscript C—a priest, who may declare to you with sincere truth the common wish of his fellow-canons and report to them what your holiness shall decide upon it. We also wish the dean and chanter, whom you invited, to be excused before your holiness, since age and the importunity of disturbances—elsewhere, “of disturbers”—now weigh heavily upon them. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLVIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to HILDEBERT, by God’s grace Bishop of Le Mans: greeting.

Concerning the man who first clung to a certain woman in concubinage, but afterwards, when that same woman was afflicted by illness, entered into a marriage compact with her by giving a ring (Letters 16 and 155), we reply to your prudence as follows: he fulfilled the sacrament of marriage in its greater part, and thereafter it could not be dissolved, unless adultery intervened, since divine and human law forbid this.

Thus Augustine, in the book *On the Good of Marriage*, says:

> “That marriage may indeed arise from persons wrongly joined, when an honourable agreement subsequently follows, is evident.”

The same writer, in the same work:

> “It is customary to ask whether, when a man and woman, neither he the husband nor she the wife of another, unite with one another not for the begetting of children but for intercourse alone because of incontinence, on the intervening pledge that he will not do this with another woman nor she with another man, they should be called married. Perhaps it may not unreasonably be called marriage, if this arrangement pleases them until the death of one of them and if they do not avoid the generation of offspring, although they did not unite for that purpose, so as either to wish that children not be born to them or even to do some evil deed to prevent their birth.”

Ambrose, in his exhortation to virginity:

> “A woman betrothed to a man receives the name of spouse. For marriage begins when the marriage is initiated; then the name of marriage is assumed. It is not the deflowering of virginity which makes marriage, but the marriage compact. Finally, marriage exists when the girl is joined, not when she is known by union with a man.”

> [Note: Consent alone completes marriage; see Letter 46.]

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 9, chapter 7:

> “They are more truly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, although marital intercourse is not yet known between them.”

Likewise Nicholas (Letter 243), to Bishop Hincmar—elsewhere Hicmar or Igmar:

> “According to the laws, the consent alone of those whose union is in question is sufficient.”

If this consent alone happens to be absent in marriage, every other ceremony, even with intercourse itself, is performed in vain. John Chrysostom, the great doctor, testifies to this when he says (*Homily 16 on Matthew*):

> “Intercourse does not make marriage, but will.”

Hence the book of the Constitutions also provides (final law, chapter *On Divorce*):

> “If anyone, without dotal instruments, has taken a wife with marital affection, let him not dare send her away without a cause recognized by the laws.”

Likewise, in the Novels (Novel 22, *On Marriage*, sections “Marriages” and “Thus”):

> “If anyone, touching the divine Scriptures, has sworn to a woman that he will have her as his lawful wife, or has made such an oath in an oratory, she shall be his lawful wife, although no dowry, no written instrument, or other formal act has intervened.”

If it is said that, because adulteries were committed by both parties, they can no longer be joined, consult Jerome writing to Oceanus (above, Letter 23):

> “Among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men, and the same servitude is judged under equal conditions.”

Likewise:

> “Husbands are indignant if they hear that adulterous men suffer penalties similar to adulterous women, although they ought to be punished all the more severely because it belongs more to them both to prevail by virtue and to govern women by example.”

Likewise (above, Letter 125):

> “Even after adulteries committed and purged, reconciliation of spouses will not be shameful or difficult, where remission of sins is not doubted to occur through the keys of the kingdom of heaven; the adulteress is to be called back after separation from her husband, not so that the adulteress should not be called back after union with Christ.”

The same author, on Hosea:

> “The prophet Hosea is not to be blamed if he turned to chastity the prostitute whom he married—elsewhere, ‘may have turned’; below, Letter 188—but rather praised because he made a good woman out of a bad one. For one who remains good is not himself defiled if joined to an evil person; rather, one who is evil is changed into good if she follows the examples of the good.”

From this we understand that the prophet did not lose chastity by being joined to a prostitute, but that the prostitute assumed the chastity which she had not previously possessed.

From these and similar authorities, therefore, your prudence may infer that true marriage existed between the aforesaid persons; that if the man marries another woman, or the woman marries another man, adultery is manifest; but that if they are reconciled by mutual consent, there is no disgrace. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLIX. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to WILLIAM—elsewhere VILLELMUS—by God’s grace Archbishop of Rouen, and to the other bishops of the diocese of Rouen: greeting and the service of due charity.

We give thanks to the just and merciful God, who chastises his offending Church with paternal severity and mercifully visits her when worn down by scourges (Letters 153 and 154), so that, like a loving mother, he may give the bread of consolation to one who mourns, after having justly inflicted scourges upon one who sinned. We have learned that this has now come to pass in the Church of Lisieux, God being propitious and your diligence cooperating.

By your counsel and assistance, the filth—

> [Note: Letter 153 calls it “dung.” On the prohibition against neophytes becoming bishops, see the canon under distinction 48.]

—of boys was removed from that Church: a new and unheard-of heresy of neophytes usurping in the same Church the episcopal chair. Although you endured this for a time through some rational consideration or through some weakness of spirit, it has now, as it seems to us, been changed for the better. For you have caused those flame-bearing boys to be expelled from the aforesaid Church—

> [Note: See Letter 157, which concerns Ranulf Flambard.]

—and chosen as pastor of that Church a vigorous and honourable man, namely Lord William, Archdeacon of Évreux.

We warmly rejoice, therefore, at your generosity and promise our charity that, if the help or counsel of our smallness should be useful in this business, it is ready according to its strength. Farewell.

## LETTER CL. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to his Lord and Father PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: every obedience within his power.

After the Ides of January I received letters from your fatherhood, admonishing me to come to a council to be held by your holiness on the Nones of March. From that date only seven weeks remained until the day appointed for the council.

Comparing my strength with the brevity of so short a term, I perceived that I could by no means accomplish this undertaking in so brief a time. I had neither sufficient money at hand to prepare so quickly what was necessary for so great a journey, nor such health of body or free agility of limbs as could complete so long a journey, by difficult and ruined roads, with such speed.

My truth and my conscience are witnesses that what I say is true; and these two witnesses are not to be brought forward with impunity for false testimony. By their testimony I also profess that I most earnestly desire to see your face—not in a crowd, nor in passing, but in that tranquillity in which I might for some while familiarly enjoy your sweet speech, pour out the heat of my heart before your eyes, and draw into my heart from the spring of your sacred breast some health-giving draught for the refreshment of my languishing soul.

Therefore bear my absence with paternal discernment until God grants that, in his own time, I may present myself before your sight. Farewell.

64. LETTER CLI. To Geoffrey, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, wishes that he may provide beneficially for himself and the flock entrusted to him.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] In the margin of one manuscript of St Victor there is added here, in the hand of an early copyist, “TO PEJOR LUPO.” Now, however, in letter 54 [Col. 0156D] mention is made of a subdeacon whose surname was PEJOR LUPO.]

I know how far I have fallen short of the hope raised by your promises; and those who heard your promises with me know it as well. Contrary to my request and your promise, contrary to canonical and apostolic ordinance, despite the opposition of the elder and more prudent brethren of the Church of Saint Quentin [Note: that is, of Beauvais, as is noted in an old codex], you have confirmed as abbot in the aforesaid Church Odo—formerly a brother, but now an enemy—though this could not have been done without me. May God, who did not plant it, uproot this planting of yours. For, so far as lies in your power, you have taken from me the fruit of my firstfruits in this matter, and perhaps have not provided very advantageously for yourselves. Those who gave you this counsel craftily wished to bring about a rupture between you and me. With what intention this was done, if you do not now perceive it [Col. 0156B], perhaps you will perceive it some day.

But if you do not wish, or are unable, to correct this deed of yours at present, at least cause to be restored to me what you promised me among other things: the ornaments which I entrusted [lent, manuscript c] to the aforesaid Church. Let them be kept in the cell of Brother Gunherius [Note: alternatively Gonherius; perhaps he is the person to whom letter 228 is addressed], until I decide in due course what I wish to do with them. Meanwhile, wherever there are persons who do not receive the aforesaid usurper, do nothing harsh or intolerable [alternatively “not to be tolerated”] against them, nor permit anything of the sort to be done. For, feeling themselves grievously oppressed, they appeal both through me and on their own behalf to the Apostolic See; and its injury will be involved if anyone henceforth inflicts violence upon them. Farewell.

## LETTER CLII. To Leodegarius, venerable archbishop of Bourges, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting and service.

[Col. 0156C]

Since we have been appointed watchmen for the house of Israel (Ezekiel 3), those placed on high are more closely observed and examined by those around them and by those at a distance than if, placed in a lowly position, we strove to devote our care only to our own salvation and private interests. Therefore, in all our administrations we must proceed straightforwardly and make particular effort to avoid giving scandal to our brethren. For if, as the Apostle admonishes, we must have a good testimony from those who are outside (1 Timothy 3), how much more must we do so before those who know our domestic manner of life [Col. 0156D], and who, if offended by us in any respect, are ready to reveal our shameful things rather than conceal them, should they wish?

I mention this to your love so that you may attend, with the zeal of paternal affection, to the injuries of Lord Hugh of Maidun, hitherto neglected, as he himself says; and that what cannot be corrected by word or tongue you may strike with the staff of severity. For it does not become your honourable position to forget how, as he recalls, he stood by you as helper and defender in all your necessities [Col. 0157A], and how he grieved over your troubles as over his own—lest perhaps your having proved ungrateful for his benefits should bring harm upon you and furnish an example to others.

Accordingly, charity urging me, I admonish your excellence that what you have hitherto done with insufficient care toward this noble man, you should henceforth endeavour to fulfil more diligently; lest, if his cry reaches a higher hearing, you incur both a loss of reputation and a diminution of your resources, not without vexation to your person. Farewell.

## LETTER CLIII. To William [alternatively Wuillelmus], by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, and Gilbert [alternatively Gislebertus, thus manuscript c], bishop of Évreux, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, wishes abundance of the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

[Col. 0157B]

Since you have begun to stand for the house of God and to set a wall for the house of Israel, your concern must take the greatest care that the pan which has begun to boil may not yield to any fires, but that the zeal for God’s house and love for its beauty may kindle ever more vehemently in your minds day by day. I remind your holiness of this so that what you have well begun concerning the Church of Lisieux, you may strive to bring to a better conclusion, offering the tail of the victim together with its head (Leviticus 3).

For we have heard, and we grieve, that the filth which had been cleansed from the aforesaid house of God by your labour has been carried back into it, with the number of wicked spirits increased, and that this very house has been infected by an error more serious than before [Col. 0157C]. Unless you take notice of this injury to God’s house as is fitting, unless you correct it in accordance with the office you bear, we are certain that, when this foul and fetid report reaches apostolic ears through our report or that of others, former neglects will not be forgiven, and these matters will be sternly exacted.

Therefore, while there is time, we warn your love so that in due time we may be able openly to defend your reputation and to knock upon apostolic ears on your behalf, both opportunely and importunately. For if, in the very infancy of the world, Lamech’s carnal bigamy was condemned, how can that be praised in the bride of Christ, which is the Church, which both sacramentally and in the reality of the sacrament must be betrothed to one husband alone? Let Ranulf [alternatively Rannulfus; see letter 154], bishop of Durham, therefore be removed [Col. 0157D] from the Church of Lisieux, so that bigamy may not be admitted; let his children be removed, so that the heresy of novices may be uprooted. We are not speaking to persons ignorant of the law, but we charitably admonish you to have regard for your own honour and for the Church’s welfare. Farewell.

## LETTER CLIV. Ivo, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to Robert, count of Meulan: May you walk in the way of life and not depart from it.

Since we believe that you belong to the fold entrusted to us, although you abound in pleasant pastures, it is nevertheless ours to minister to you some food of holy admonition and to fortify your love against invisible wolves. For although you have found favour in the sight of the king of the English, many ecclesiastical persons testify that you strive to please him more than the King of angels. Yet we do not blame you for pleasing him in matters that do not displease God. But if royal power undertakes anything against the Lord and His Christ, and against His Church [Col. 0158A], you must remember that you have been redeemed by Christ’s blood, initiated into Christ’s laws, and regenerated [reborn, manuscript c] through the sacraments of the Church. You belong to Him who made Himself a servant for your sake, so that your freedom may understand itself to owe nothing to anyone whereby it offends the divine majesty and diminishes the Church’s liberty.

We offer this counsel to your nobility so that you may guide the aforesaid king by sound counsels and in no respect disturb the ecclesiastical laws handed down by the holy Fathers and confirmed by catholic kings. For what reason, what law permits Ranulf, bishop of Durham, to pass from the Church of one realm to another Church (letters 153, 157, and 185), and, as though by a kind of adultery through his own presence [“your presence,” manuscript c], or by the occupation of his sons, violently to invade the Church of Lisieux through the English king? To do or tolerate this is against law and against the king, because it is not to provide government for the people, but to increase danger. Therefore, insofar as his counsel depends upon your judgment, persuade him to free the Church of God as far as he is able, and not multiply his own sins by those of others.

Thus those who thought and foretold good things concerning his coming into these regions [Col. 0158C] must, whether they wish it or not, change the brightness of their praise into the cloud of reproach. For kings are not established in order to break laws, but to strike down with the sword those who pervert laws, if they cannot otherwise be corrected. Farewell.

## LETTER CLV. Ivo, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to Odo, archdeacon of Orléans, greeting.

In your letter, your brotherhood asked whether a woman pregnant by fornication may lawfully marry (letters 107 and 147). No easy answer can be given to this question from a direct ruling; but what must be observed in such cases may be gathered by reasoning from analogous cases by those who do not claim wisdom beyond what is proper [Col. 0158D]. In this matter, you ought, from the reason with which you are endowed, to consider that one medicine is appropriate to the healthy for preserving health, another is owed to the sick for recovering soundness; and to distinguish what is commanded to the healthy by precept from what is allowed to the infirm by indulgence.

According to the natural command and institution, no woman, whether pregnant through disgraceful conduct or through marriage, ought to have carnal intercourse with a man before her child is weaned; otherwise [“unless,” manuscript c] the requirements of marriage are not fulfilled. But if we consider the apostolic moderation which says, “Let each man have his own wife because of fornication, and each woman her own husband” (1 Corinthians 7), we shall not except a widow, a pregnant woman [Col. 0159A], a fornicator, or an incestuous person—provided only that it be “in the Lord,” that is, that the marriage itself is not in itself disgraceful or criminal.

Nor is a man to be blamed because he has married a fornicator; rather, he is to be praised because he has made an immodest woman chaste. Hence Jerome, on Hosea, book 1 [Note: Reported in chapter 14, cause 32, question 1]:

> “The prophet Hosea is not to be blamed if he converted the prostitute whom he married to chastity; rather, he is to be praised because he made a good woman out of a bad one. For a person who remains good is not defiled if joined to one who is bad; but one who is bad is turned toward good if that person follows the examples of the good.”

From this we understand not that the prophet lost his chastity by being joined to a fornicator, but that the fornicator received the chastity which she had not previously possessed. And if husbands complain that their wives had been fornicators before marriage [Col. 0159B], let them also consider whether they themselves may perhaps have fallen into the crime of fornication or adultery. Why, then, should a man not grant indulgence to his wife if he wishes her to grant it to him?

Hence Jerome, to Oceanus on the death of Fabiola (in chapter 20, cause 22, question 5):

> “Among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men; for the same servitude binds both under equal condition.”

Likewise Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages* (chapter 8, cause 22, question 1):

> “The remission of sins, even after adulteries have been arranged and cleansed, will not be shameful or difficult: not that, after divorce from her husband, the adulteress should be recalled, but that, after union with Christ, she should no longer be called an adulteress.”

If this may be done in the case of one who violated the marriage bond, why should it not be allowed all the more in the case of one who committed no offense against a marriage bond which she had not yet entered [Col. 0159C]?

Let men who bring accusations of this sort also heed what Augustine says in the book *On the Words of the Lord* (sermon 46; and in chapter 2, cause 32, question 6):

> “If you are going to take wives, preserve yourselves for your wives. Such as you wish them to come to you, such ought you yourselves to be found by them. What young man does not wish to marry a chaste wife? And if he is going to marry a virgin, who does not desire her untouched? You seek one untouched? Be untouched yourself. You seek one pure? Do not be impure. For she cannot do it while you cannot.”

From these and similar authorities it can therefore be understood and proved that, if you were not bound to a wife, you could deliberate; but after you have been bound to a wife by mutual consent, you ought not seek release. Thus the natural [alternatively “original”; thus manuscript c, or “condition”] and inviolable sacrament of marriage has remained from the very creation of the world [Col. 0159D], so that neither the transgression of the first parents took it away nor the sentence of the Flood, washing away crimes, altered it.

What divine judgment established and willed to be unchangeable must not be separated by human prohibition, unless it was made without the consent of the contracting parties, or is in itself criminal—that is, adulterous or incestuous. When this occurs, delay is improper: it must be remedied by separation. But where these conditions are absent, whether the spouses are abductors, excommunicated persons, or tainted by any other vice, all such things must nevertheless be endured for the preservation of the fidelity of marriage [Col. 0160A].

For who was compelled by the preachers of the New Testament, whether in circumcision or uncircumcision, to dismiss after baptism the wife whom he had before baptism? Yet I do not say that marriages ought to be contracted contrary to prohibitions; but, if they have been contracted, they ought not to be dissolved for these reasons. Those who have contracted such marriages contrary to prohibitions, or the priests who have solemnized them, should be corrected for their disobedience by an appropriate satisfaction, at the discretion of their judge, so that others may be restrained from such rashness.
