But marriages themselves should by no means be dissolved unless the cause has been established by law.

For just as the sacrament of ordination, even when once received from ordainers who have unlawfully usurped the right to ordain, remains in those ordained, so the sacrament of marriage, even when imposed by disobedient priests, remains in those married [Col. 0160B], because the evil merits of usurpers cannot nullify the power of the sacraments. Therefore their holiness must always be honoured, but the perversity of those who usurp must be punished. Thus the censers of Korah, because service had been rendered before God with them, were placed upon the altar by God’s command; but their makers were consumed by fire (Numbers 16).

Avoiding excessive length in this letter, I have not dared to put more upon the page, because I did not wish to burden your brotherhood with a multitude of matters well known to you. From these few points, however, you can understand what I think concerning the matters stated above and what I answer others who ask about them. Farewell.

## LETTER CLVI. Ivo, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to his beloved brother in Christ Olric [alternatively Alric], greeting.

[Col. 0160C]

Your letter states that a certain criminal man set fire to the house of one of his neighbours and, because he refused to make satisfaction, was excommunicated by his priest. Later, when he wished to be absolved, he confessed his crime [alternatively “his deed in secret”] privately to his priest, although he was unwilling to restore anything from the property lost to his neighbour. Your brotherhood therefore asks what you think his priest, who excommunicated him, ought to do when the excommunicated man enters the church: whether he should be publicly repelled from communion, or tolerated by some form of dissimulation.

In this matter certain rulings seem to conflict with one another [Col. 0160D] unless they are weighed by a careful balancing of discernment. First, a priest cannot absolve a sinner unless he repents, according to what blessed Augustine writes to Armentarius and Paulina (letter 54, to Macedonius; and in chapter *Si res*, cause 14, question 6):

> “If the thing for which the sin was committed, when it can be restored, is not restored, repentance is not performed but feigned. If, however, it is truly performed, the sin is not forgiven unless what was taken away is restored—provided, as I said, that restoration is possible.”

There are also other canonical rulings (chapter *Excommunicatos*, cause 11, question 3), as you yourself know, which sternly forbid praying with excommunicated persons (2 Corinthians 6), taking food with them, or saying “Hail” to them (2 John 1). There are also other rulings which do not permit the secrets of confessants to be made public. Thus, in the Council of Agde, chapter 8, it is stated:

> “If a bishop alone knows himself to be privy to another’s crime [alternatively, “to someone’s crime”], so long as he cannot prove it he should disclose nothing; rather, with the accused person he should labour by secret corrections toward compunction of heart. If, when corrected, that person becomes more obstinate and intrudes himself into public communion, he shall remain in the communion of all, save only that of the one who judges him guilty [alternatively, “in the communion both of all and of the one who judges him guilty”], so long as nothing can be proved.”

In the conclusion of this ruling, the excommunicator alone is not commanded to be excepted from the communion of the person whom he excommunicated; rather, by permitting an exception, he is allowed to abstain, because exceptions are not usually rules, but permissions [Col. 0161B].

There is another ruling which not only forbids the publication of a secret confession but also imposes a penalty upon the person who makes it public [alternatively, “a public penalty”]. It is contained in the Council of Carthage, chapter 7, attended by Faustinus [alternatively Fautinus], legate of the Roman Church (in chapter 3, cause 6, question 2):

> “It has been decided that, whenever a bishop says that someone has confessed a particular crime to him alone and that person denies it, the bishop should not think it an injury to himself that he is not believed when he stands alone. And if, because of the scruple of his own conscience, he says that he is unwilling to communicate with that person, so long as that bishop does not communicate with the excommunicated person, other bishops shall not communicate with that bishop, so that a bishop may take greater care not to allege against anyone what he cannot prove by other evidences [Col. 0161C].”

Hence Augustine, to Vincentius (letter 48; in chapter 10, *Quam magnum*, cause 23, question 4):

> “The deeds of wrongdoers which cannot be shown to innocent persons, or believed by innocent persons, do not defile anyone, if, for the sake of the innocent, known offenders too are endured. For the good are not to be abandoned because of the bad; rather, the bad are to be endured because of the good. Thus the prophets endured those against whom they spoke such things, yet did not abandon the communion of the sacraments of that people; thus the Lord Himself endured the guilty Judas until his deserved end and permitted him to share the sacred supper with the innocent; thus the apostles endured those who proclaimed Christ through envy—which is the vice [alternatively, “the very essence”] of the devil.”

Therefore, lest these rulings appear discordant, they must be qualified so that those which speak of avoiding communion with evil persons are understood only of those wrongdoers whose crimes are either so notorious as to need no proof, or are manifest through an evident confession, publicly disclosed by judicial process, or established by sufficient testimony. Thus Augustine also says in book 2 of *On the One Baptism*:

> “Certainly, if you are a judge, if you have received the power of judging from ecclesiastical rule [alternatively, from evangelical rule; alternatively, from apostolic rule], if an accused person is brought before you, if he is convicted by true documents and witnesses—restrain him, rebuke him, excommunicate him.”

The same author, in a sermon *On the Words of the Gospel* (chapter 8, cause 23, question 4):

> “Always be separated from the wicked in heart; for a time, join with them cautiously in body.”

Again, on the same subject (*On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 18):

> “Withdraw; go out from among them, and touch no unclean thing—but by the contact of the heart, not of the body. If what someone [“everyone,” manuscript c] has sinned displeases you, you have not touched the unclean thing: you have reproved, rebuked, admonished, and, if the matter required it, you have also applied suitable discipline that does not violate unity; you have gone out from among them.”

We could collect much more of this kind, but from these and similar passages your love can understand that we ought not physically separate from our communion a sinner who secretly confesses his sins, nor communicate by inward consent with that person’s perversity [Col. 0162B]. By this approach we shall preserve both rulings: the one commanding us not to communicate with excommunicated persons, and the one ordering us not to disclose the crimes of confessants.

Priests ought, however, without naming persons, to preach to the people that persons excommunicated in this manner stand condemned before the tribunal of the Judge who sees all things: namely, those who, against God’s command, have injured their neighbour and transferred that neighbour’s goods by insatiable greed to their own use, or removed them from the midst through devilish malice. Thus the Lord, saying to His disciples, “One of you is a devil” (John 6), without naming the individual, pronounced Judas excommunicated, and yet did not exclude him from His own communion or that of His followers. Since, therefore, the life of the Lord Jesus is a discipline of conduct, everyone will be perfect, as the Lord says, if he is like his master (Luke 6) [Col. 0162C]. This is my view on the question proposed; thus I answer those who ask such things, from reason and authority. Farewell.

## LETTER CLVII. To Paschal, supreme pontiff, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, his due service in all submission.

Since the state of the Church suffers lamentable ruin almost everywhere on earth, every lover of God’s house mourns its dishonouring all the more abundantly the more nearly he feels it; for fire burns what is nearer. I have said this beforehand to Your Majesty because, while in other places every prostitute of God’s house attempts to cover his wickedness with some veil, in the land of the Normans the Church has been so openly prostituted that the prophetic saying may be applied to it: “They have proclaimed their sin like Sodom and have not hidden it” (Isaiah 3).

Your fatherhood may recognize this in the Church of Lisieux, which for several years has been occupied by Ranulf [alternatively, byname] Flambard, bishop of Durham, through an unheard-of kind of invasion [Note: [Col. 0161D] He is mentioned in letters 153 and 154, in the latter of which Ivo calls these children “fire-bearing”], for he caused his two sons, scarcely twelve years old, to be installed in the aforesaid Church by the count of the Normans after receiving the pastoral staff, on the condition that, if the firstborn died, the other should succeed him in the bishopric after the manner of the Jews [Gratian, cause 8, question 1] [Col. 0163A].

After the Church had long endured this, while many partly grieved and partly mocked, I sharply rebuked the archbishop of Rouen, solely from charity, at the urging of certain religious persons. The aforesaid Church belongs to his diocese (letters 149 and 153), yet he did not stand against this abuse or oppose a wall for the house of Israel. I did the same to the other bishops who were suffragans of that metropolitan. At length, when the count of that land was pressed by the danger of losing his principality, he was apparently moved by repentance; and, at the exhortation of the bishop of Évreux together with his metropolitan, he ordered that the aforesaid bishop of Durham be expelled from the Church along with his offspring and that a bishop be canonically elected there.

The aforesaid Church was therefore offered the opportunity [Col. 0163B] to elect a bishop for itself according to ecclesiastical custom. Having consulted the bishops, they elected William, archdeacon of Évreux, a vigorous man, and requested that their metropolitan ordain him bishop. But when it was heard that the metropolitan had been suspended from episcopal office, the aforesaid archdeacon—because he was a close acquaintance of mine and wished knowingly to presume nothing against the canons—came to me and deliberated with me whether, notwithstanding this scruple, he might receive sacred ordination from his metropolitan or from the suffragans, to whom metropolitan authority customarily directs such matters.

In this deliberation, there occurred to me the Apostle’s saying: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14), and Augustine’s statement: “For consecration depends more upon the faith and devotion of the person requesting the blessing than upon the merit of the person granting the blessing.” I therefore advised the aforesaid brother (letter 73) not to receive so great a sacrament while any dispute remained, but to consult the Apostolic See either in person or through its legates, and to bring to completion by apostolic authority the matter which, as it seemed to us, had been well begun [Col. 0163C].

Seeing that the consecration was delayed, the bishop of Durham adopted another kind of evasion and asserted that the aforesaid bishopric had been granted by the count of the Normans to one of his clerics. That cleric was therefore summoned before the metropolitan see to produce whatever claim of right he trusted that he had in the bishopric. He could establish by no reasoning that he had the election of the clergy, the consent of the people, or even received the count’s gift—which should have harmed rather than benefited him. Accordingly, acting on our advice and that of certain of his fellow provincials, he came before Your Majesty, to receive either a just judgment according to law or necessary counsel by dispensation. Therefore, in the boldness of filial familiarity, I submit to your holiness that the Church may rejoice to have found paternal assistance in Your Majesty, who is accustomed to deny medicinal remedy to none who flee to you. Farewell.

## LETTER CLVIII. To Hugh, by the grace of God bishop of the foremost see, the Church of Lyons, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting and service.

[Col. 0164A]

Because, God permitting, we are working with the king of the Franks and his son, the designated king, so that the incestuous marriage between Constance, daughter of the aforesaid king, and the count of Troyes may now displease them, they, supported by the authority of the laws and the assistance of good men, wish to hasten the divorce of this marriage. Since this desire is so fervent [some codices: “so recent”], at their urging I admonish and request your fatherhood to send letters of admonition to the archbishops and bishops for the court to be held at Soissons on the Nativity of the Lord, so that they may hear from the king himself the calculation of the genealogy [Note: Thus in the old codex, and also shortly afterward; previously, incorrectly, “the union of the genealogy”], which he says he is prepared to establish by oath and confirm by suitable witnesses [Col. 0164B].

And because this genealogy has frequently been calculated for you by the men of Auvergne, they earnestly request that you send the same calculation, openly authenticated by letter through the bearer of this present letter, to the bishops at the court, and make the truth of the matter clearer through the testimony of documents. For it is not fitting that blood of such nobility should for longer be defiled by so public an incest [alternatively, “incestuous union”], and that carnal desire should be encouraged by its deadly example to perpetrate similar incest. Therefore, as a son and familiar dependent, I advise you—as one who ought [alternatively, “oughts”] to insist importunately—that now, when the occasion is fitting, you should not delay, insofar as you can, to apply a healing poultice to the wound. Farewell.

## LETTER CLIX. To Paschal, supreme pontiff, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: May you sail prosperously over the sea of this world and, after overcoming shipwrecks, bring your ship into safety.

[Col. 0164C]

Since we have learned, upon the teaching of the Roman Church itself, that judgments of the Roman Church cannot be reconsidered externally by anyone (chapters *Patet*, *Nemo*, *Ipsi*, *Cuncta*, cause 9, question 3), if any persons at times complain that they have been grievously burdened by that Church’s authority, we give them this counsel: that they should not go down into Egypt for help, but flee from that Church to itself; and seek relief from the very source from which they complain that they received the burden. For she who sometimes corrects with paternal severity frequently gathers together with maternal mercy.

We have said this beforehand to Your Blessedness so that you may patiently hear the case of the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés and, insofar as this can be done without compromising apostolic reverence, mercifully relieve their anxiety. They complain that they were grievously burdened at the Council of Tours because, at the instigation of the count of Anjou, Pope Urban was induced by deception to remove the monastery of Saint-Maur, situated in the territory of Anjou—which for three hundred years or more had previously been under the jurisdiction of the monastery of Fossés—from that monastery’s jurisdiction, and, after appointing an abbot there, to establish it as free [Col. 0164D].

This was done despite the monks of Fossés asserting their right and many of those attending the council holding another opinion, when they saw that the privilege upon which the Fossés monks relied had been snatched from their hands by the men of Anjou and torn into many pieces [Col. 0165A]. Having therefore enlisted the intercessions of many persons, the aforesaid monks ask that their case be reconsidered by Your Majesty through lawful examination and concluded either by mercy inclining you or by justice dictating the result. Farewell.

## LETTER CLX. Ivo, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to O. [Odo], abbot of the monastery of Jumièges [in some old codices, Gemeticum], may you abound in the inward affections of paternal love.

This sheep from the flock entrusted to you, having abandoned its flock and exposed to the bites of wolves, wanders miserably through the deserts of this world [Col. 0165B], and endures many wars from its commerce with that world, so that it is almost compelled to fall into contempt for its order and monastic habit. Now longing for the bread of sons, it says, in both intention and speech: “I will arise and go to my Father” (Luke 15). Yet it says that it has found paternal affection closed, so that it can be received neither among sons nor among hired servants.

Your brotherhood knows, however, that whoever bears the name of shepherd must, by imitating the supreme Shepherd, fulfil the office of shepherd: He sought wandering sheep, found lost sheep, cared for weak sheep, healed sick sheep, rejoices over those who return, and admonishes us to grieve over those who turn away. I do not say this as though teaching you, but, reminding you through those very affections of charity by which we ought to love one another [Col. 0165C], I admonish and ask you to receive this returning brother (letter 57) with fatherly care from the far country of dissimilarity, and, with the satisfaction due for his transgressions, gather him within the fold from which he had strayed. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXI. Ivo, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to Radulf, provost of the Church of Rheims, and to Odolric, brother of good hope, greeting.

Concerning a man who entered into a marital pact with a woman whose marriage was not forbidden, but afterwards proceeded to marriage with another woman (letter 167), this is my judgment: the sacrament of marriage, undertaken with perjury and violation of a marital agreement, either is void [Col. 0165D] or remains for judgment. If it is void, it is clear that he must return to the earlier agreement; but if it remains for judgment, the acts of marriage must cease. If he does neither, he will always be a violator of another’s right.

For one who confirmed a marital agreement by oath has, for the greater part, fulfilled the sacrament of marriage. Thus the angel calls the blessed mother of the Lord, who had entered into a marital agreement with Saint Joseph, Joseph’s wife: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matthew 1). Yet he had not brought her home, nor was he ever to know her by carnal intercourse. On this matter we have provided many testimonies of the Fathers in the letter sent to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans (letter 148) [Col. 0166A].

There is also the canonical ruling: “What is presumed contrary to the laws deserves to be dissolved by the laws.” For example, if someone presumes to usurp for himself the sacrament of priestly orders contrary to decrees, he must either be entirely deposed by the laws or suspended from ministry at the altar. From these authorities and arguments it is clear that what has been unlawfully presumed with injury to one’s neighbour ought not prevail over what was earlier lawfully and honourably contracted by the consent of the parties. Even if the former did prevail, since there is wrongdoing on both sides, the compensation which defends one crime by another is nevertheless, according to the Scriptures, dangerously admitted (St Augustine, in chapter *Quod ait*, distinction 14).

For Holy Scripture does not praise Lot’s wish to prostitute his daughters to the Sodomites (Genesis 19), in order to restrain them from their depravity by that exchange [Col. 0166B]. Therefore, if some compensation is to be admitted in such matters, that must be preferred which, with just severity, provides for the welfare of neighbours, not that which, under a feigned indulgence, opens a broader path to slippery persons for committing perjuries and crimes. [Note: Letter 135 and letter 170. Also chapter *Disciplina* and chapter *Sunt namque*, distinction 45.]

For it is safer not to spare the will of a single violator of another’s right than, by an example of false mercy, to bring many into danger. Moreover, one ought not pass from lesser sacraments to greater except in orderly fashion: a woman betrothed to one man must not marry another; just as a married man, unless released from marriage, cannot be ordained a priest or enrolled as a monk; and there are many other instances of this kind. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXII. Ivo, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to Joanna, by the same grace bishop of Orléans, greeting.

Dealing briefly with the priest who profaned the sacraments of the Church upon a female statue: he must be judged a sacrilegious person and an idolater. If you wish to proceed against him according to canonical censure, you must, having associated with yourselves five other bishops, publicly strip him of his priestly vestments and depose him through each of the grades; then condemn him, once deposed, to perpetual imprisonment or drive him into everlasting exile. [Note: [Col. 0165D] See chapter 27, *Novimus*, *Extra*, “On the Meaning of Words.”] But if this should be difficult for you to do, nevertheless suspend him from every clerical honour, and carry out in his person the other measures stated above [Col. 0166D] for the correction [variant: correction] of others. That he ought to be deposed on account of the deservingness of his sacrilege is attested by the decretal ruling which says: [Note: [Col. 0166D] Variant: which says; cause *Posteaquam*, C. 25, question 2, and chapter where this occurs, distinction 74.] “He deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power granted to him.” That he ought to be removed from the sight of those who have learned of his crime, lest the foul memory of the deed disturb the minds of the simple, may be proved from this: according to the Law, an innocent beast mounted by bestial men was commanded to be killed (Lev. XIX; Augustine, question 74 on Leviticus, chapter XX), not because of any guilt in the subjected animal, but in order to erase [Col. 0167A] the memory of so execrable a foulness. How much more, then, must he be removed from the eyes of those aware of the matter, when no innocence defends him and no ignorance excuses him. Therefore, to conclude, let your prudence restrain this unheard-of sacrilege with such severity that all who hear of it may be turned away from so execrable an abuse. For as the crime is unheard-of, so, if necessary, it must be corrected by an unheard-of punishment; because, according to blessed Augustine, new kinds of diseases compel us to discover new kinds of cures (Letter 288). Farewell.

## LETTER CLXIII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, TO GEOFFREY, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme: that he may hold the balance of justice in all things.

[Col. 0167B] Concerning that monk whom you bound by oath never again to administer that obedience which he had for some time usurped for himself through disobedience, my counsel is that he should have it no longer; for this would be criminal in him and ruinous to the other brethren. For since an oath has justice and truth as its companions (Jer. IV), if what he swore—although presumptuously and against order—was just (from St Jerome, Letter 105), it must also be true. For the Apostle testifies that an oath is an unchangeable thing (Heb. VI), by which, he says, God declared to the heirs of the New Testament the immovability of His counsel. Moreover, it would redound to your own disgrace if, under the cover of obedience, you lent your connivance to one committing perjury. We could say more on these matters, [Col. 0167C] but we pass them over in silence because we do not believe they are unknown to you. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXIV. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, TO GEOFFREY, cultivator of holy solitude: that with unturned eyes he may stretch forward to the things before him.

How delightful and how necessary for servants of God is repose of mind together with repose of body, your holy brotherhood has learned, I believe, both by knowledge and by experience. For a mind exposed to the rumours of those running about and to the slanders of dissenters has prayers that are disturbed or wounded; nor can it, by however great an effort of its own, gather itself into unity, until the Lord sleeping in the boat, tossed by such great waves, is awakened by loud crying, and at His rebuke the desired tranquillity returns (Mark IV). Therefore your holy brotherhood ought to repel from both the hearing of the ear and the hearing of the heart the words of those who, under the appearance of affection and counsel, pour in the poison of deceivers and destroyers.

I have said this beforehand to your brotherhood because certain letters addressed by you to Abbot Maurice were lately brought to me by some monks of Blois. I can scarcely believe that they were dictated by you, since they seem to have been dictated not in a tranquil spirit but in a disturbed one, like a sword drawn from its hilt and, with indiscriminate blows, striking not wood but a brother (Deut. XV). They seem also to have [Col. 0168A] no small odour of vanity and ambition, as though you had retained the abbey with affection and lost it with grief (Letter 208). For in those letters—if indeed they are yours—you say that the aforesaid Maurice, though in some fashion placed in your office, expelled you through the prompting of evil men, made you the most contemptible of all, and was imposed upon you by the wicked. You also speak threateningly against him, should you perceive him to oppose your will in anything.

If these are your words, you have gone far outside yourself. They do not accord with your purpose; they do not accord with your deeds. For, when acting through the hand of the legate of the Roman Church, with no one compelling you [variant: with no one then compelling you]—indeed, with the legate himself dissuading you—you relinquished the abbey and gave the first voice in the election of Maurice himself. Return then, dearest brother, to your heart; and do not believe your flatterer—indeed, your disturber—more concerning yourself than yourself, because at times enemies reproving us correct us more than friends falsely flattering us assist us. You know that the apostolic saying declares: “Pursue peace, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. XII). Let no recollection of past injuries, therefore, take peace from you. Nor think that you ought to grieve or be grieved for because you escaped naked from shipwreck; rather, grieve for those whom you still see endangered on the deep.

Thus we have understood you until now, and thus we still judge you, unless the duplicity of disturbers moves your simplicity and drives you from tranquillity of mind. Henceforth, therefore, if you learn that anything in the abbot or in those subject to him requires correction, admonish fraternally in gentler words, so that you may seem to strive for edification, [Col. 0168C] not vengeance. But if they do not listen to you, strive, before any dissension arises, to bring the wrong done to our attention, so that by such admonitions we may endeavour to establish the peace necessary for monasteries. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXV. TO SANSON, by the grace of God bishop of Worcester [variant: Worcester, manuscript C], IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: good health and dwelling in the uttermost parts of the sea.

Although at present you were hidden from my eyes, you were not hidden from my soul, because from regions beyond the sea I caught the good fragrance of your name and loved what I had thus perceived [two old manuscripts: “smelled”] deeply. [Col. 0168D] At last the eye announced, and the hand experienced, what the heart’s sense of smell had first perceived through hearing. Thus, as my inward senses brought good tidings, I learned that your charity toward me had not grown lukewarm, although we had not yet enjoyed full personal conversation with one another.

Your generosity therefore anticipated my delay [variant: your delay] by sending evangelical shoes, [Note: [Col. 0167D] Letter 207 calls them sandals worthy of apostolic feet.] a gift by which you showed your affection toward me and urged me to carry out more diligently the office entrusted to me. Therefore, as you yourself have urged, while we row across this broad and stormy sea, let us extend to one another the mutual hands of prayer, so that we may sail prosperously and be able to bring the ships entrusted to our governance into the desired harbour of salvation. [Col. 0169A] This, according to our small measure, we promise your affection; and in return we ask it of your devotion. Let no local distance separate hearts that love one another, whom the affection of fraternal love binds together. I would write more, but I do not wish to burden the ears of a wise man with unnecessary words. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXVI. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, TO HUMBALD, by the same grace bishop of the Church of Auxerre, greeting.

Let your affection know that last summer, when Lord Bruno, bishop of Segni (Letter 167), was exercising the apostolic legation, Hugh the White came into his presence and informed him how Pons, nephew of the bishop of Troyes, had seized for himself in marriage his daughter Matilda, previously given by her parents to Galeran, the king’s chamberlain, although she resisted and wept. [Note: [Col. 0169D] On this matter, chapter *Desponsatas* and chapter *Atho*, cause 27, question 2.] Since both parties were absent, the aforesaid legate charged the bishop of Paris to summon each party to the case on a suitable day and, after hearing both sides’ arguments, to settle, by the counsel and judgment of prudent men, the controversy between Pons and the said Matilda.

The bishop of Paris, having returned, appointed a day and place for Pons and Matilda and charitably invited me and certain of his fellow bishops to examine and settle this case. Accordingly, on the appointed day the accusers and the accused, [Col. 0169C] witnesses and judges, assembled at Paris for the case. The said Matilda was asked why she rejected marriage with Pons. She answered briefly that she was not lawfully joined to him, since she had previously been given by her parents to Galeran (Letter 247), and, resisting this to the utmost of her power and weeping, had been joined to Pons without her mother’s consent. When Pons was invited to answer the allegations, he sought certain evasions, answered nothing to the allegations, and departed rather inappropriately from the assembly before which he had appeared. He was therefore commanded once and again either to answer the allegations or not to delay hearing judgment.

Since he thus declined judgment, it was adjudged concerning him, in accordance with an apostolic decree, that he ought not to gain a delay of sentence through absence. [Col. 0169D] Then rulings were produced from the authority of laws and canons (chapter *Decernimus*, cause 39, question 9): if the witnesses of the woman proceeding against Pons could, after giving oaths, prove what the woman had alleged, she would be free from marriage with Pons and could marry whom she wished in Christ. Pons was again commanded to come to hear these oaths, or, if he could lawfully object to the persons testifying or to their statements, to make his objections. As he evaded this, like the rest, through either his simplicity or duplicity [variant: or cunning], oaths were given and received from ten men or more; by these it was proved both that the woman had first been given by her parents to another [Col. 0170A] and that she had been joined to Pons against her will.

The matter having therefore been carefully examined and concluded in judicial order, we judged that the woman was free from Pons’s—not, I would say, marriage, but cohabitation—and that she could marry whom she wished in the Lord. We have written this to your holiness because a parishioner of yours wishes to have the said woman in marriage, lest any scandal concerning the former marriage arise among you or any stumbling-block be placed in the present matter. Farewell, and in mutual affection remember my [variant: our] smallness.

## LETTER CLXVII. TO HILDEBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Le Mans, IVO, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting.

[Col. 0170B] A certain parishioner of yours, commonly called Petitus of Les Roches [thus all the old manuscripts; formerly: Peter], recently came to our Church for prayer and requested an interview with us. Among other things, he related to us that he had given his daughter in a marital bond to another parishioner of yours, from the settlement called Pontiac; and that this man had sworn unconditionally that he would take her as his wife at the time appointed for him. [Note: [Col. 0170D] Compare Letter 161 and the canons *Quicunque*, *Conjugali*, and *Duobus modis*, cause 27, question 2.] But now he has taken another wife contrary to the marital pact which he had previously entered lawfully with the other woman.

For nuptial compacts are lawful between persons whose marriage is not forbidden, when a daughter under paternal authority does not dissent from her father’s will. Both divine and human laws forbid these compacts to be dissolved. And if the woman wishes to pass to another man, the canonical [Col. 0170C] ruling says that it is not lawful for a woman betrothed to one man [variant: another] to be possessed in marriage by another. Conversely, if the man wishes to enter another marriage, we read in the law of the Novels (Novel 22, *On Marriage*, and chapter 9, cause 30, question 5): “If anyone, having touched the divine Scriptures, swears to a woman that he will have her as his lawful wife, or gives such an oath in an oratory, she shall be his lawful wife, even though no dowry and no written instrument has intervened.”

Whoever acts otherwise acts contrary to the laws; and according to the apostolic decree (chapter *Vides*, distinction 10): “What is presumed against the laws deserves to be dissolved by the laws.” Thus, when last summer the bishop of Segni (Letter 166), legate of the Apostolic See, was among us and a similar case had been brought to our ears, after the laws had been produced we judged it just [Col. 0170D] and lawful. I have written these things to your affection at the request of the aforesaid knight, that I might intercede [variant: forbid] with you for him, although I strove to persuade him that this was unnecessary. For we think well of your religious character: whenever the true and just judgment shines forth to you, you will not turn aside from the royal road. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXVIII. TO DAIMBERT, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, IVO, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres: greeting and service.

Because in certain affairs doubtful or [Col. 0171A] difficult questions arise (Letters 169 and 170), we ought to extend to one another hands of assistance or the gift of counsel. I have thought it fitting to make known to your fatherhood the course of a case which arose among us last summer and still continues; by apostolic letters this case is chiefly entrusted to you for settlement, and secondarily to us, so that you and we may provide carefully, neither despising apostolic obedience nor burdening anyone unjustly.

There was a certain estate in our parish. One knight held a part of it, with his house separately upon it; another held another part, likewise with his house separately upon it. For the protection of this estate, both rendered service to the viscount of Chartres. The viscount gave this protection together with its service [Col. 0171B] as a benefice to one of his knights, namely the lord of Courville. Not long afterwards Count Rotrou bought that part of the estate which was an allod, raised an embankment there, and constructed a fortification.

When the viscount, who was about to go to Jerusalem, and the lord of Courville heard of this, they raised an outcry before the Church, asking that justice be done them which was due to those going to Jerusalem and to the peace [Letters 169 and 173]. A day was appointed for both parties to prosecute the case. When they met, the viscount alleged against Count Rotrou that he was unjustly and contrary to the peace building a fortification on land under his protection. In answer for Rotrou it was said that the land did not belong in the least to the viscount’s protection, but rather to the protection of [Col. 0171C] Count Rotrou.

When this dispute had continued for some time, we ordered judgment to be made. It was adjudged that the case could not be settled without trial by combat, and that we were not permitted to handle a judgment of blood (Letter 247); therefore both parties were to go [variant: one was to go] to the court of the countess, to whom such judgments belonged and from whose fief [variant: “foedo”] they held these things. As had been adjudged, both came to the countess’s court; and, after the actions had been debated on both sides, the viscount, for reasons unknown to me, lost his case.

Afterwards Ivo, lord of Courville, who asserted that he held this benefice from the viscount, and Count Rotrou began to wage war against one another (Letter 20) and to plunder each other’s goods. As the outcome of war is variable, one day, when the said Ivo was proceeding [Col. 0171D] with an armed band to carry out certain affairs of his own, he was captured by Rotrou’s knights and imprisoned. Therefore, from the complaint of Hugh the viscount, the Apostolic See commands you and us that, as our office requires, we render justice to Guy, guardian of the property of the brethren, and to the captive Ivo.

Having read the apostolic letters, therefore, examine their words carefully, and, according to the course of events and the tenor of the apostolic letters, determine for yourselves in what order the case ought to proceed: whether Rotrou should immediately be excommunicated, or summoned to judgment. For in whatever order your exalted rank proceeds [variant: commands] both in the prosecution of the case and in the execution [Col. 0172A] of justice, our subject humility will follow to the extent of its power. And if at present a certain judgment does not become clear to you, appoint a suitable place and day for those named in the letters, and invite the accusers and the accused to the same place, so that, after truth has been fully heard and ascertained in their presence, you may more completely satisfy justice. Write back to my smallness what seems better to you from these alternatives. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXIX. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, TO GALON [variant: WALON], by the same grace bishop of Paris, greeting.

When Count Rotrou was building [variant: making] a fortification on a certain estate in our parish, which he maintains [Col. 0172B] to be within his right and protection (Letters 168 and 170), while the viscount of Chartres and Ivo, lord of Courville, contend that it belongs to their right, it was represented to the lord pope—as you perhaps heard from Hugh the viscount, travelling to Jerusalem—that he should do justice regarding this wrong and defend the cause of the Jerusalem-bound man according to his enactments (Letter 173). Ignorant of the truth of the matter, the pope wrote to the four of us—the archbishop of Sens and the bishops of Chartres, Paris, and Orléans—that, as our office requires, we should do justice both concerning the invasion of the estate and concerning Ivo’s capture.

Having received these letters, Guy, guardian of the property of the brethren, and the lord of Courville importunately demand of me that I excommunicate the said Rotrou [variant: Retrochus, also in what follows] without a hearing and without judgment, though Rotrou himself says that he is ready to come at a suitable time and place before the hearing of the lord metropolitan, or ourselves, or the bishops of the province, and to satisfy the allegations according to just judgment. I, therefore, keeping to the path of the laws, do not wish to punish anyone without a hearing in the manner of assassins; I do not wish to hand him over to Satan until he either evades a hearing or contumaciously refuses judgment. Let the Gospel be consulted on this point; let divine and human laws be consulted. [Note: [Col. 0171D] See the canons, cause 3, question 9.] If any law commands otherwise concerning a matter under dispute, I shall gladly set aside my own judgment and yield to another’s.

Nor do I think the lord pope understood otherwise when he commanded [Col. 0172D] us to render justice, as our office requires, to the aforesaid petitioners. Though this thunderclap [variant: thunder] was sounding around me, I wrote nevertheless, although I was not doubtful of the truth, to the metropolitan, to whom the apostolic letters had already come, asking him, after carefully examining the apostolic letters and understanding the truth of the events which I had set down for him, to give me counsel whether I ought to excommunicate Rotrou without a hearing or summon him to judgment. He, however, by I know not what prompting or understanding, wrote back that I should obey the apostolic letters and excommunicate Rotrou. Yet he did not determine, in accordance with my inquiry, whether I ought to do this with a hearing.

[Col. 0173A] By your letter, therefore, we ask that our judgment be confirmed if it is just, or removed if it is not just. We add also to our request, if it proves necessary, that if you are fraternally invited, you will come into our presence and do with us what ought to be done. Farewell. So that you may understand them better, I have sent you a copy of the apostolic letters.

## LETTER CLXX. TO DAIMBERT, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: the full service of due submission.

Concerning your parishioner who killed a certain woman’s husband and afterwards took the murdered man’s wife as his own wife, we answer your excellency thus. If the woman can clear her conscience of the death of her husband, and if the man, as you say, can lawfully clear himself of having committed adultery with that woman while her husband lived, and of having killed that woman’s husband in hope of this marriage, then, according to the law of nature and the ancient condition of marriage, the indulgence which the apostolic key opens to widows may be opened to her: namely, that they may marry whom they wish in Christ. [Note: [Col. 0173D] As in Letter 166; some manuscripts read “in the Lord,” as also in Letter 155.] Thus David—of whom it is said, “None is holier than David”—after committing adultery and homicide, when it was said to him, after penance had been performed, “Your sin is forgiven you,” retained Bathsheba, Uriah’s wife, in marriage (II Kings XII).

But later diligence, having experienced the human race’s proneness to falling, and recognizing that in cases of this sort sparing one person would be nothing other than exposing many to danger, enacted most strictly that no such marriage between such persons should be permitted unless the man and woman first proved by a rigorous examination that they were innocent of adultery and homicide. We, however, who are appointed physicians of souls and ought to provide for the salvation of our subjects, have determined in our deliberation to maintain either the rigour of discipline or the moderation of indulgence according to urgent necessities, so that indulgence may not soften the strong nor excessive severity break the weak.

Furthermore, if it is reported to you that we have not yet excommunicated Rotrou, know that we have not acted disobediently (Letter 169), but have deferred for a reasonable and lawful cause. For while a matter is pending, I do not dare, the law forbidding it, to excommunicate even the lowliest person. Nor did the pope, when he was being strongly urged in our presence by many arguments toward this excommunication, wish it done otherwise; in his letters he warned us, who were neighbours, to investigate the truth of the matter and, when the truth was known, not to precipitate a sentence, but, as our office requires, keeping to the path of the laws, to punish the disobedience of rebels.

Rotrou’s accusers, moreover, neglect to come to a hearing and prove their case—either because they lack confidence in their cause, [Col. 0173D] or because they are attempting to extort from us a hasty sentence—although Rotrou promises that he will come before your hearing or ours and do what law and justice prescribe. I do not say these things as though I wished to defend Rotrou or to confirm by my judgment the fortification which he is making (Letters 168, 169, and 173), a fortification that will harm no one so much as myself and the Church entrusted to me. Yet I wish to pronounce such a judgment against him as I may be able to approve, by morals and laws, in every assembly of good men. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXI. TO DAIMBERT, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: delightful goings forth of morning and evening.

[Note: [Col. 0174D] In old manuscripts this subject-heading is prefixed: “Concerning an impenitent person whom fear of the king compels one to absolve.”] As we have learned from your letters, you are hard pressed on every side: if you receive into communion without satisfaction plunderers and violators of holy days whom you have justly separated from communion, you offend the law; if you persist, as is fitting, in their separation from the Church, you offend the king. In this matter, if the spirit of fortitude were present to us as the spirit of counsel is present, we would judge that the severity of discipline ought to be maintained (Letter 137). But because you perceive the danger of serious dissensions threatening in this rigour, we understand that the matter requires dispensation. Therefore we set before your eyes not our own counsel but that of the holy Fathers.

For Bishop Cyril says to Gennadius, priest and archimandrite (Letters 214 and 144): “Dispensations in affairs sometimes compel some persons to depart a little from what is due, so that they may gain some greater advantage. For just as those who sail the sea, when a storm presses and their ship is endangered, throw out some things so that the rest may remain safe, so we too, when we do not have complete certainty of saving all concerns, disregard some of them lest we suffer the loss of all.” Hence Augustine, in his letter to Marcellinus (Letter 158), says: “I am accustomed to hear that it is within a judge’s power to soften a sentence and punish [variant: judge, thus manuscript C] more mildly than the laws require” (Letter 236). The same writer, in the third book *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, says: “Whenever one of the brethren and Christians established in the fellowship of the Church is discovered in some such sin as to deserve anathema, let this be done where there is no danger of schism.” Again: “When anyone’s crime is known and appears detestable to all, so that he has either no defenders at all, or no defenders of such a kind that schism might occur through them, let the severity of discipline not sleep.”

Since dispensations in temporal affairs are assigned to kings, and kings (*basilei*), that is, the foundation and head of the people, if they sometimes abuse the power granted them, they must not be harshly provoked by us; but where they do not comply with priests’ admonitions, they are to be reserved for divine judgment, where they are to be punished all the more strictly because they were less subject to divine admonitions. Hence in the book of Royal Capitularies established by episcopal authority [Col. 0175A] it is written: [Note: [Col. 0175D] This has already been cited in Letter 62 and occurs in the Twelfth Council of Toledo, chapter 3.] “If royal power either receives any offenders into the favour of its kindness or makes them partakers of its table, assemblies of priests and peoples ought to receive them into ecclesiastical communion also; so that what princely piety receives may not be regarded as foreign [variant, Letter 62: alien] by the priests of God.”

I therefore confess to your fatherhood, from my own weakness, that if some dispensation compelled me to admit an impenitent person to reconciliation, I would plainly say to him: “I do not wish to deceive you. I permit you to possess an entrance into this visible Church at your own peril, but I cannot open to you by such a reconciliation the gate of the heavenly kingdom. Accordingly, I absolve you only so far as your accusation requires and forgiveness belongs to us.” Perhaps stronger men will say stronger things, better men better things. Therefore, according to my modest capacity, this is my view: not prescribing a law in such cases, but understanding that, in order to avoid greater dangers to the Church, one must yield to the necessity of the times if it cannot conveniently be done otherwise. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, TO ALL SONS OF THE CHURCH, both present and future.

What we have considered fitting to come to the knowledge of many, we have decreed by prudent deliberation to commit to the memorials of writing. Let the present age, therefore, and all succeeding posterity know that Maurice, abbot of the monastery of Saint Laumer at Blois, within the bounds of a parish belonging to him called Ulcha [Note: [Col. 0175D] He calls it this again at the end of this letter.], strengthened by our authority, began [Col. 0175C] [variant: “had begun,” manuscript C] to build a chapel, to which certain parishioners remote from the mother church might come at the due times to render their offerings.

When the abbot of Vendôme heard this, he sent a petition challenging it canonically and asked that a day be granted him against the monks of Blois. He received one by agreement of both parties. When they came on the appointed day for the case, the abbot of Vendôme said that for almost twenty years he had held the offerings of the parishioners who dwell in the settlement called Mont Faun, had denied justice to no one, and that therefore the monks of Blois had unjustly taken them. He therefore said that he must first be reinvested before proceeding to the litigation of the other causes.

When he was asked whether he had held these offerings by grant of the bishop of Chartres, by the right of a parishioner, or by the gift of some lawful possessor, he could allege nothing except the obstinacy of retention. To this the monks of Blois answered that they had received all parochial dues from those parishioners, and that the portion of the offerings which the monks of Vendôme had usurped, Lancelin of Beaugency had occupied by force. [Note: [Col. 0175D] If several old manuscripts are followed, another reads “of Balgiac,” thus manuscript C; formerly “Balgeracensis.” Abbot Suger mentions Zancelin of Beaugency [Col. 0176D] in the *Life of Louis the Fat*.] Nor, they said, had the Vendôme monks held them during those twenty years on which they relied without synodal protest. Indeed, the monks of Vendôme who occupied the aforesaid Mont Faun had been expelled from it by the judgment of the Church of Chartres and had sought refuge in a certain wood.

When this was confirmed by the testimony of many and was in no way refuted by the abbot of Vendôme, it was judged that the abbot ought not to be reinvested, since nothing is taken away from ecclesiastical uses if each person receives what is his own. When this judgment displeased the abbot of Vendôme, he appealed to the Apostolic See, not from confidence in justice but in order to occasion delay. Out of reverence for the lord pope, we patiently endured that appeal, although, under the safeguards of the laws, he had neither sought from us a written statement for the person who was to hear the appeal (Letter 220), nor observed the time, [Col. 0176B] manner, or order for prosecuting an appeal. Understanding, therefore, that he had forfeited the case, we henceforth confirm the chapel which we permitted the men of Blois to build and decree that they shall hold undisturbed all the offerings of the chapels adjoining the parish called Ulcha.

## LETTER CLXXIII. TO PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: due obedience with every devotion.

In accordance with the tenor of your letters which you gave to Hugh, viscount of Chartres, when he was going to Jerusalem, we summoned Count Rotrou to justice, [Note: [Col. 0176D] This matter of Rotrou has already been addressed in Letters 168, 169, and 170.] because he was accused of having begun to build a fortification, after Hugh had taken the cross, on land belonging to the right of the said [Col. 0176C] Hugh; and of having unjustly captured and ransomed Ivo, Hugh’s knight, who held the aforesaid land from Hugh in fief. At this summons Count Rotrou was asked, until the outcome of the case, neither to build anything on the fortification begun nor to receive anything from Ivo’s ransom (Letter 168).

On the appointed day the parties came to the case. Rotrou submitted himself to judgment. According to the order of events, the petitioners, who spoke for Hugh, said that they did not wish to enter into this case unless he first satisfied them concerning the uninterrupted construction of the fortification and the ransom of Ivo which had been taken. It was answered on Rotrou’s behalf that neither was required, because that fortification had been adjudged to him in the court of the countess, from whose fief it was held, when this case had been transferred by the judgment of the Church to the aforesaid court. [Note: [Col. 0176D] Because it was a case of blood, as Letter 168 says.] And the said Ivo was by no means to be restored on account of Hugh’s pilgrimage, since Ivo had renounced faith toward Rotrou, his lord, had first taken Rotrou’s spoil, was holding his men in chains on the day when he was captured, and on that day was proceeding with an armed band of knights to commit violence against him.

It was said by the other side that they could disprove all these defences by true assertions in their proper places and times, [Col. 0177A] but that they ought not to proceed to those matters until satisfaction had been made concerning what had first been alleged, unless they were compelled by judgment. The clerics who were surety for the matter were therefore ordered to settle the dispute by a just judgment. After debating it for a long time, they could not agree upon one judgment, saying that the institution of ecclesiastical protection (Letter 169) to be given to the goods of knights departing for Jerusalem was new, and that they did not know whether this protection extended only to their properties or also to their holdings which powerful men, defending themselves and their possessions by their own strength, hold.

They therefore asked for a postponement until your judgment on this matter could be sought. Count Rotrou wished to grant this postponement on condition that construction of the fortification should not be interrupted [Col. 0177B] and Ivo’s ransom should not be suspended. The other party wholly refused to grant this and again asked for judgment on this point. Since Count Rotrou feared that this judgment would weigh against him, he appealed to an apostolic hearing, whose authority we were invoking against him. We therefore send them to your fatherhood with our letters containing the course of the case, so that by the wisdom and power divinely granted to you you may settle this dispute; for these men are great among us and cannot, as is fitting, be compelled to peace by our smallness. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXIV. TO MATILDA, illustrious queen of the English, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: the gift of devout prayers.

[Col. 0177C] The reputation of your devout piety has deeply moved the minds of many very religious persons and sweetened them with a certain sweetness of holy love. Therefore, for the grace divinely bestowed upon us, we give thanks to the supreme Giver of all good things, who has placed manly strength in a woman’s breast, not only for avoiding shameful deeds and crimes, but also for providing necessary assistance to those in need. We, therefore, not unmindful of both your public and private benefits, have devoutly received the petitions of your excellence; and for the soul of your brother, the religious king, we pour out devout prayers to God—though this is little, as our sins deserve—although we confidently and without doubt trust that his soul has been placed in Abraham’s bosom, if his life was as it is said to have been. [Col. 0177D] But since the condition of souls after *animal* is uncertain [Note: [Col. 0177] Thus written out in full in most old manuscripts; in others abbreviated, *post animal*; in two, *post corvora*. The passage is suspect as corrupt.], it does not seem useless for us to intercede for those who already enjoy rest, that their rest may be increased, and for those assigned to purgatorial places, that through the prayers of the faithful they may obtain forgiveness. Your Excellence may lay these and other matters upon our shoulders, provided they do not exceed our strength. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: due service with every devotion.

I was preparing, to the extent of my ability, for the journey to the council proclaimed by your fatherhood; [Col. 0178A] but because, at the season when I was accustomed to take a purge, the press of your court did not permit me to do so, the entire confluence of humours suddenly rose into my head, and thus the middle part of my head, as phlegm congealed, hardened into a certain rigid swelling. Since, moreover, because of the proposed journey I still delayed purging myself, waiting for the swelling of the head to subside of itself as the phlegm dissolved, it not only did not subside, but became still more seriously and dangerously swollen [hardened]. Compelled by this necessity, therefore, I took a purgative; yet I recovered well neither from the purgative’s laxative effect nor from the hardness of the swelling, so that I cannot undertake even a short journey without danger to my body. For although the swelling has been dispersed externally, the pain within has not yet been soothed.

I have therefore sent three archdeacons [Col. 0178B] of the Church entrusted to us with our letters, that they may bear witness to the letters themselves and have me excused before your fatherhood. Nevertheless, it remains my intention to see your face before the council is dissolved, if God restores me fully to health and grants me an opportunity to come to you. But if any more private matters must be spoken of, these brothers will tell you. Farewell.

## 74. LETTER CLXXVI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: due obedience with every submission.

Having returned from the Council of Troyes, our son [your son, manuscript C] Wlgrin, chancellor of our Church, complained anxiously that the Church of Dol, having sent certain of its envoys [Col. 0178C] to your Excellence, had elected him bishop in your presence, and that at their request your fatherhood had granted assent to this election (Letter 178), nor had yet been willing to listen to his excuses, however suitable. Although he is well educated and adorned with good morals, nevertheless, humbly alleging his own insufficiency for many reasons, he says that he would rather endure many grave hardships than undertake the burden of a bishopric at this time.

Your fatherhood knows that secular laws (law XII, chapter *On Marriages*) do not permit a betrothal to be made in the name of a son under paternal authority when he dissents. How much more ought this to be observed in the betrothal of the Church, in which, unless sincere [Col. 0178D] charity comes to aid, what good can human weakness accomplish by compulsion—whether by distributing its possessions or exposing itself to martyrdom? For no one does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good (*Present*, Cause 20, Question 3). Hence the Holy Spirit admonishes us in the Song of Songs: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken the beloved or rouse her until she herself desires it” (Song 2).

Therefore do not, for our Jacob who loves Rachel, put Leah in his place by night (Genesis 29), unless perhaps Rachel desires Leah’s firstborn’s mandrakes and, for this payment, permits Jacob, hired thereby, to sleep with Leah (Genesis 30). For in such an order, the reward of a good work might arise from such a union, [Col. 0179A] and strength—which is most necessary to every government for enduring the labours of that government—might abound.

And, lest we burden your holiness too long with words, with the knees of our heart bent we implore your clemency, fittingly and insistently, that you bind the aforesaid brother with no bonds of obedience [Note: [Col. 0179D] For the pope can compel an unwilling man to a bishopric; Letter 178.]. We ought, so far as we can, to provide for his welfare, because we received him from the sacred font; and he himself has chosen rather to be saved in a lowly place than to be endangered in a high one. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXVII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to GAUFRID, by the same grace bishop of Beauvais: fear in prosperity, courage in adversity.

Before I had read the letters of your affection, I learned [Col. 0179B] the extent of your affliction; I heard and grieved. For I should be a degenerate son if I bore with an unmerciful spirit the miseries of my mother, the Church of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0179D] He likewise calls himself her true son in Letters 92 and 145. He also calls himself a Beauvaisian in Letter 181.].

In this crisis the highest and sole remedy is to cry to the Lord, that he may turn the cloud of so great a storm into a breath of serenity and make the waves of so great an evil be still—he who commands winds and sea according to his will. Further, concerning the cleric who communicated with the excommunicated Drogo both at Mass and at table, I advise your affection to impose upon him a suitable penance, which may frighten the rest from a similar act, provided that he does not wish arrogantly to defend what perhaps he committed through fear. Otherwise, sentence should be pronounced against the contumacious man, depriving him both of office and benefice.

The measure of penance, however, is placed in the discretion of the bishop, to whom the power of binding and loosing has been granted by the Lord. Hence Augustine says in his book *On Penance* (chapter 85, Distinction 1): [Col. 0179C]

> “Let a man judge himself while he can do so voluntarily, lest, when he can no longer judge himself voluntarily, he be judged by the Lord against his will. Let him come to the bishops, through whom the keys are administered to him in the Church; and, as one now beginning to be a good son, with the order of his mother’s members established [variant: preserved], let him receive from the stewards of the sacraments the measure of his satisfaction, and in offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart let him remain devout and humble. Yet let him do what benefits not only himself for recovering salvation, but also others by way of example; so that, if [if it happens that] his sin consists not only in his own grave [Col. 0179D] harm but also in so great a scandal to others, and if the bishop sees this as expedient for the Church’s welfare, he may not refuse, nor resist, doing penance in the knowledge of many or even of the whole people, lest through shame he add a swelling to a deadly wound.”

But if the aforesaid brother, after he had been charged with the fault of excommunication, intruded himself into communion before a hearing, then, according to the decree of Pope Martin (*If Any Bishop*, Cause 11, Question 3), and the Council of Carthage (*It Has Been Decreed*, Cause 11, Question 3), he is judged to have pronounced upon himself a sentence of condemnation.

Concerning the other cleric, who denies that he communicated with Drogo and denies that, [Col. 0180A] knowingly, he prayed in church while Drogo was present—though he does not deny [variant: it is denied] that he prayed in the church of the profane—it seems to me sufficient if, under two suitable witnesses, he can prove the innocence of his conscience. We could confirm these matters by many testimonies, if we were not avoiding the lengthiness of a letter. On the matters proposed [variant: proposition], this is my view, without forestalling the decisions of my elders by any prejudice of my own. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXVIII. IVO, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to the clergy of the Church of Dol and to Count STEPHEN: greeting.

We praise the intention of your good purpose, in that you have chosen our son Wlgrin, honourable in life and distinguished in learning, as your archbishop (Letter 176). But, as it seems to us, [Col. 0180B] your effort is undertaken in vain, because neither is it the will of our aforesaid son to assent to your election, nor is it within our power to compel him unwillingly to do so. For imperial laws provide that, when a son under paternal authority dissents, betrothal cannot at all be contracted in his name (law XII, Code *On Marriages*, and law XI, *On the Rite of Marriage*). Much less, then, should the mind of a spiritual bridegroom be drawn by compulsion into union with a spiritual bride.

The aforesaid brother has already, through our letters and his own representations, communicated this matter to the lord pope and, as far as he could, rejected the burden of a bishopric. If therefore you do not wish to alter your purpose, and do not wish to transfer your deliberation [your deliberation, manuscript C] to another person, you must seek recourse not to us but to the supreme pontiff, to whom it has been granted [Col. 0180C] to compel unwilling persons to these offices and to ordain bishops of the Church of God from those both willing and unwilling. Therefore, to the extent that the lord pope compels me in this matter, I shall compel the aforesaid brother. Farewell.

## 75. LETTER CLXXIX. IVO, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to ADELA, illustrious countess: sound judgment and good action.

As we have heard (Letters 121 and 136), by your order bread and water, and all necessities of life under your power, have been forbidden to our sons, the canons of Blessed Mary of Exitus Viarum. What else is this than to condemn innocent and unarmed men to [Col. 0180D] death without a hearing and without judgment? For hunger and thirst kill just as the sword does. What more cruel decree could savage Turks, persecutors of the Christian name, proclaim against God’s servants than to take from them the necessities of life?

Therefore, by advising I exhort and by exhorting I advise your nobility: moderate the unconsidered severity of your sentence for the better until a hearing is held, and do not condemn to death by so severe a sentence persons who have neither been convicted nor judged. For, out of love for you, we have moderated our own sentence, though it was just and fixed by judgment; and we have denied neither the sacrament of baptism, nor confession, nor penance—[Col. 0181A] things sufficient for the salvation of souls in necessity—even to the persecutors themselves.

Conduct yourselves, therefore, so that the praise of the strong woman commended by Wisdom (Proverbs 31) may be proclaimed concerning you, rather than the cruelty of the perverse woman, whom Chrysostom condemns in Herodias, being published throughout all our provinces. But if you are unwilling to heed my sound and pious admonitions, I remind you by the peace which, in the present year, you promised in the hand of the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0181D] Paschal II, who may be inferred from this to have been in Gaul at that time.], and three years earlier in my hand, that you appoint for us, through the bearer of this letter, a suitable day for carrying out justice; and, in the meantime, permit the sons of the Church freely to enjoy their possessions according to the institution of peace.

But if you despise all these things, know beyond doubt [Col. 0181B] that the Church, with contrite and humbled heart, calling to itself all its subject churches, will daily, before the body and blood of the Lord and the intercessions of the saints, cry out against all perpetrators and accomplices of this evil; and for this very purpose it will summon, as a duty, all neighbouring bishops with their subject churches. I say this in sorrow, yet in doing so I have regard for your honour and reputation, seeking nothing else than that you administer justice according to custom and law, and that, if there is any claim against the Church, you may obtain justice. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXX. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to LEODEGAR, by the grace of God archbishop of Bourges: greeting and service.

[Col. 0181C] It greatly pleases our lowliness that we have heard that you wish to preserve the strictness of justice by an unbending [variant: unbent, manuscript C] course. But since the priest’s breast ought to have the rational breastpiece fastened upon it and joined to the ephod (Exodus 28), it is fitting that a ruler should so maintain moderation in justice that neither excessive severity should cast those to be corrected into the depths of evils through despair of mercy, nor indiscriminate mercy increase arrogance.

I suggest this to your holiness because I have heard certain of your parishioners murmuring that you are so bound to certain of your parishioners that, without their consent, you cannot either enforce or relax justice. Thus it recently happened, as we heard, that through their harsh obstinacy Arnulf of Virson’s case was so embittered [Col. 0181D] in your court that, after judgment had been given in that case, appeal was made to the Apostolic See, and the final sentence in the same case was delayed until the apostolic hearing. How great an inconvenience this is, how great an expense of resources, and how uncertain the outcome of proceedings, you have learned both by experience in your own affairs and by hearing of others’ cases.

I therefore considered it necessary to write to you the advice which I learned from certain lovers of peace: namely, that through Ralph of Belgeiacum [variant: Balgiacum or Belgiacum, manuscript C] you grant somewhat lengthy respite to the aforesaid Arnulf—not for diminishing ecclesiastical justice, but only for not bringing [Col. 0182A] the common [*communia*, thus manuscript C] [measures] against him. Meanwhile [variant: “however,” manuscript C], as the aforesaid Ralph said, through his mediation peace will be restored between Arnulf and his adversaries; justice will be endangered in no respect; and the appeal made in your court will be reduced to nothing without inconvenience to you or yours.

You, therefore, weigh what I say with prudent deliberation; and if what is said is true, and no better course occurs to you, test it yourselves [variant: yourselves, manuscript C], because, with charity as my counsellor, your peace, justice preserved, would please me. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to RICHARD, by the grace of God bishop of Albano: greeting and due service to the Roman Church.

[Col. 0182B]

Understanding that, through grace divinely bestowed, zeal for justice burns in you, I have taken care to communicate to your concern the truth as I know it concerning the case of the monastery of Vézelay and the Beauvaisian monastery of Saint Lucian [one manuscript: Vézelay]. The church of Buglensis, now under dispute, was formerly, between the aforesaid monasteries, under the jurisdiction of the monastery of Saint Lucian. But when the Norman persecution had devastated the monasteries of the territory [variant: monastery, manuscript C] of Beauvais and reduced them to solitude, the goods of the monasteries were largely transferred to lay uses for the defence of the land.

Before that devastation could be fully repaired, certain canons were appointed in the church of Buglensis. Thus, by succession, [Col. 0182C] canons succeeded canons down to the time of Guy [variant: Wido, manuscript C], bishop of Beauvais, and of Hugh, count of Buglensis. Having taken counsel with Bishop Guy [Wido], Count Hugh restored the aforesaid church to Saint Lucian, asking pardon for himself and his predecessors, who had unjustly held it.

But the abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Lucian, because the clerics of the aforesaid church objected, in his simplicity deferred for some time installing his monks there, waiting until he could settle everything peacefully with the clerics. And because the aforesaid count, disregarding the moderation of discretion, hastened by whatever means to introduce monks, he caused the monks of Vézelay [variant: Vizelay], who had a cell nearby, to be summoned; [Col. 0182D] and, despite the objections of the clerics and the monks of Saint Lucian, he granted them, without the bishop’s consent, the church—which was no longer his—to them. 76. Afterwards, however, moved by repentance when many reproved him, he restored the same church to blessed Lucian.

But because the monks of Saint Lucian received their own property from invaders without judges (Letter 268), at the Council of Issoudun possession alone was adjudged to the Vézelay monks [variant: Vizelay, as also shortly below], pending the time of lawful examination. Nor was any final sentence given there which deprived the monks of Saint Lucian of their right, or adjudged that the Vézelay monks should hold the aforesaid church permanently. I knew this to have been the course of the affair, as a Beauvaisian [Ivo of Beauvais], and, having been present at this hearing in the Council of Issoudun, I could prove these things true if I were present. [Col. 0183A] I have therefore written them to you so that, once you know the truth, you may better know to which party you may safely [variant: are able to] incline your ear. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to DAIMBERT, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens: greeting and service.

Recently, while in our chapter I was dispensing certain offices according to the custom of the Church and, with the book presented, wished to confer the subdeanery upon Fulk, a cleric [Col. 0183B] of vigour and greatly necessary in conducting ecclesiastical cases, Hugh, the dean’s nephew, and the dean himself rose against me, inflamed by old hatred (Letter 227), together with two elderly men, the chanter and his brother. They had gathered certain young men who had come forth from their households, and they began tumultuously to object to my action, alleging nothing definite except that I was not doing this with their counsel.

But I, knowing that I found no such custom in the Church, and that I had not observed it in those very objectors when they received their own offices, did not desist from what I had begun, lest I diminish my authority. Although they were my men, bound both by hand and by oath, they furiously and noisily surrounded my seat, snatching [Col. 0183C] the book [Note: [Col. 0183D] The book by which the investiture was performed, as he says at the beginning of the letter.] from my hands and uttering against me shameful, false, disgraceful words utterly contrary to sacred order. Fearing death in so great a crowd, I became silent and did not open my mouth; and only with difficulty, through the protection of the others [variant: through their protection] who had sounder judgment and had not conspired with these men, did I escape their hands.

Thinking that there would be some remedy for their fury, they first warned me to render them justice concerning myself. I replied that I was ready both to receive justice from them and to render justice, either before elected judges or according to the judgment of the metropolitan see, in the order prescribed by canonical authority. Since they chose the judgment of the Church of Sens, we have jointly sent to you, that you may appoint for us a day and place for conducting the case around the middle [Col. 0183D] of Lent, as may be convenient to you. We also humbly ask your fatherhood to appoint us such a place that we may go there safely and return safely. We further request that you summon some of your suffragans to this judgment. For the injury inflicted upon the episcopal order is not slight, but unheard of.

If I dared add to my petition, I would ask, with the knees of my heart bent, that you visit the Church of Chartres and, in your own person, hear more fully from clergy and laity the injuries inflicted upon me—or rather, upon the entire episcopal order—in my person. For it is fitting that a mother should console her daughter even in tranquillity, [Col. 0184A] and how much more in disturbance? But, lest I prolong my words further, may your fatherhood send us word through the bearer of this letter of the day, place, security for the journey, or whether your highness will deign to visit our lowliness. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXIII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to WILLIAM [GUILELMO, manuscript C], archdeacon of Paris: greeting.

Concerning the knight who made an agreement with another knight regarding his daughter [variant: betrothal, manuscript C], this is my reply to your affection according to my understanding. If the claimant produces against him witnesses who were present at the betrothal itself, or others who testify that the girl’s father himself admitted in their presence that he had made this betrothal, [Col. 0184B] and if they are willing to confirm this by oath, it will be necessary to hold the betrothal valid [variant: “because the betrothal,” manuscript C], since according to the laws [Note: [Col. 0183D] Law XXIII, chapter *On Proofs*; chapter *In Cases of Default*; Cause 2, Question 4; Gregory, Letter 25, or chapter 125, book V.] the burden of proof rests upon the person who affirms, not upon the one who denies.
