I believe that you agree with me that, just as in Christ there is neither slave nor free, neither male nor female (Galatians 3), so in the contracts shared in common by the Christian people—free persons with slaves, and all persons of whatever condition—if a controversy arises concerning them, persons of whatever status may reasonably be admitted as witnesses, provided that they are of honourable life and good reputation [variant: persons nevertheless of honourable life and good reputation]; and that in civil or criminal cases this distinction of persons alone [Col. 0184C] ought to be observed.

In cases of this kind trial by combat (Letter 205) must by no means be admitted, because, according to blessed Augustine: “So long as a man has something [variant: that which] he can do, he ought not to tempt his God” [Note: [Col. 0184D] Cited from the book *Questions on Genesis*, Letter 74.]. The keeping or breach of a monetary pledge, however, ought not to impede marriage, if the betrothal was made by the consent of those contracting it.

I have written these matters briefly for your prudence, asking that you do what we wish to obtain from your fraternity through Lord Walter [variant: Lord Gauter or Gualter, manuscript C], the monk. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXIV. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to WALTER [variants: GAUTER, GALTER, manuscript C], librarian of the Church of Beauvais: greeting.

[Col. 0184D] Your fraternity has informed me that a claim has arisen from certain laymen against the Church of Beauvais. They reject the judgment of the clerics of that Church because those clerics possess the things concerning which the laymen themselves are claimants before them. But those who attempt in this manner to overthrow the standing of the Churches are not sufficiently skilled in either ecclesiastical or secular laws. Both decretal writings, imperial laws, and ecclesiastical customs plainly oppose them; without these, divine and human affairs cannot remain secure if they abandon their own documents, by which [Col. 0185A] our forebears decreed that they should remain safe and unimpaired.

For first, in many decretal decisions one reads that all lawsuits and disputes are first to be heard and decided in the churches in which they arose (Letters 75 and 168), unless either both parties choose judges by agreement or one party appeals to a higher hearing. Numerous decrees of pontiffs declare that judgment must be decided by the sons of the very Church in which the dispute arose, and not by others; they contain these words (*Foreign Judgments*, with the following canons, Cause 3, Question 7): “By a general enactment we prohibit foreign judgments.”

Imperial ordinances agree well with this, declaring that ecclesiastical goods are not subject to human but to divine law. Hence Justinian, in Book Two [Col. 0185B] of the *Institutes*, chapter 1:

> “Sacred, religious, and holy things belong to no one; for what is under divine law belongs to no one’s property. Sacred things are [variant: for sacred things are, manuscript C] those which have duly been consecrated to God by pontiffs—for example, sacred buildings and gifts duly consecrated to [variant: for] the service of God—which we also prohibit by our constitution from being alienated or pledged.”

Since reason and truth wholly agree with the ordinance of a religious prince, it seems that nothing prevents clerics, who are of the Lord’s portion, from determining a just judgment concerning sacred things over which they plainly have no ownership. Furthermore, the Church’s universal custom is such that, unless it were maintained immovably, the Church would be deprived of all or nearly all [Col. 0185C] its goods.

There is abundant authority from the holy Fathers concerning the observance of a custom which does not conflict with law. Augustine says in his letter to the presbyter Casulanus [Note: [Col. 0185D] Thus in the old manuscripts; formerly “bishop.” Cited in chapter 7, Distinction 11.]:

> “In those matters concerning which divine Scripture has laid down nothing certain, the custom of God’s people and the institutions of the ancestors are to be held as law.”

And, just as transgressors of divine laws are to be restrained, so are despisers of ecclesiastical customs. Gregory also writes to all the bishops of Numidia (Letter 75, Book I): “We permit the custom, which is known [variant: recognized] to assume nothing contrary to the Catholic faith, to remain unchanged.” Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book Five, chapter 3: “Custom is a practice approved by antiquity, or [Col. 0185D] unwritten law.” Likewise: “Custom is a kind of law instituted by the ancestors, which is accepted as law when written law is lacking. Nor does it differ whether it rests upon writing or reason.” And in Book Eight of the Code, title 53 [Note: [Col. 0186D] In the Codes, Book VI, title 11, manuscript C, law II, *What Constitutes Long-standing Custom*.]: “The authority of long-standing custom and usage is not slight; yet it does not prevail so far by its own force as to overcome either reason or law.”

In this manner your prudence may select many passages from authoritative writings, by which it may stop the barking of laymen against the Church. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to WILLIAM [variant: GUILLELM], by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen: greeting and service.

[Col. 0186A]

“Concerning the cleric who bears this letter, who, by an irregular and over-hasty leap, though he had not been blessed as a cleric, had himself ordained subdeacon, I reply to your highness that, if you wish to maintain the strictness of justice, you should neither permit him to minister in orders irregularly received nor promote him to higher ranks [variant: advance him]. For it is read in pontifical decrees (*You See*, Distinction 1) that ‘what is rashly undertaken contrary to the laws deserves to be dissolved by the laws.’

“But if his honourable life or the Church’s benefit so requires, you may, by way of dispensation, after granting him clerical status and requiring due satisfaction, extend to him such mercy that, when it happens that you celebrate sacred ordination, [Col. 0186B] he may be present, with heart and body humbled, at the sacred blessings—not to be reordained, but to be confirmed, in suitable words, in the orders he has received. Concerning such irregularities, I do not have at hand an independent decision favouring the extension of mercy; but, for a similar case, I transmit to your discretion the dispensatory judgment of Pope Alexander II. Fortified by its example, if it seems worthy to you, after due consideration you may both confirm what has been received and grant what has not [variant: what has not yet, manuscript C] been received.

“The judgment is as follows: Alexander II to Rumald [variants: Rumand or Grimald; in chapter *Solicitude*, Distinction 52], bishop of Constance:

> ‘The concern of your affection [Col. 0186C] has sought our advice whether the bearer of this letter is fit to perform the office of deacon and priest, or not, since he is known to have ascended to it by an over-hasty leap or [the words “leap or” are absent in manuscript C] course—namely, without the order of subdeacon—through negligence rather than pride. Therefore, in advising your charity, we direct you to forbid him the priestly office until, at the next fast of the Four Seasons, you duly confer upon him the ministry of the subdiaconate [variant: duly upon yourself], and thereafter permit him to proceed to higher offices.’”

Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXVI. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to LAURENCE, monk of the monastery of Charity: greeting.

Your numerous inquiries require a varied and lengthy answer, [Col. 0186D] which cannot conveniently be unfolded within the brevity of a letter; indeed, they would require the copious discussion of books and support from the authority of many writings that might be cited. Moreover, if in some matters we wished to employ the moderation of the canons, we would seem to certain simple-minded zealots for the law [formerly “accumulators”] to act contrary to the canons, while to others we would seem to have prepared arguments for the defense of ambition. Therefore such discussions [variant: dispensations, thus manuscript C] do not seem fit to be committed to writing, lest, if they come into many hands, they harm the undiscerning more than they benefit the discerning. Yet there is a paternal rule [Col. 0187A] which, carefully considered, may suffice for many of your questions: namely, “the communion of evil persons defiles no one, but consent to their deeds does.” And elsewhere: “No one’s crime defiles one who does not know of it.” [Note: [Col. 0187D] From St Augustine, Letter 48, in the chapter *Nimium*, Cause 13, Question 4.] And elsewhere: “He who has no power to condemn the guilty person, or cannot prove him guilty, is innocent.”

Accordingly Augustine says in the second book *On the One Baptism* (Book I, in the chapter *Forte*, Cause 23, Question 4):

> Perhaps among the people of God there stands beside you a greedy man, a robber, coveting another’s possessions; you know him to be such, and he is a believer, or is called a believer. You cannot drive him out of the Church; you have no means of doing so. Correct him by rebuking and reproving him. He will approach the altar with you: do not be afraid. For each person shall bear his own burden (Gal. 6). “How,” you ask, “am I to bear [Col. 0187B] one whom I know to be evil?” Would you not bear him better than carry yourself outside? See how you would bear him, if [“if” absent from two old editions] you attended to the Apostle saying, “Each person shall bear his own burden”: that saying would set you free. For you would not share his greed, but you would share Christ’s table with him; and what harm would there be to you if you shared Christ’s table with him? The Apostle will say: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11)—to himself, certainly, not to you, provided that you are a judge, that you have received the power of punishment [Note: [Col. 0188D] Thus most old editions, including Letter 288; others have “of judging”; thus manuscript C.], by ecclesiastical rule; if he is accused before you and convicted by true proofs and witnesses, restrain him, rebuke him, excommunicate him, depose him.

The same writer, in his letter against Parmenian, says:

> Truly, [Col. 0187C] when the contagion of sin [variant: “of sinning”] has invaded a multitude (Letter 288), the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary. For schemes of separation are both vain and pernicious and sacrilegious, since they are impious and proud, and they disturb weak good people more than they correct resolute evil people.

The same writer, in his letter to Vincentius (Letter 48), says:

> Good persons are not to be abandoned on account of evil persons; rather, evil persons are to be tolerated on account of good persons. Thus the prophets endured those against whom they spoke such things, yet did not abandon communion in the sacraments of that people; thus the Lord himself endured the guilty Judas until his fitting end, and allowed him to share the sacred supper with the innocent; and likewise [“also,” manuscript C] the apostles endured those who proclaimed Christ out of envy, [Col. 0187D] which is the devil’s own vice.

Let these sayings of the blessed man concerning the need not to avoid communion with evil persons suffice. But if someone persisting in his impiety has been named by the Church and deprived of communion by the Church’s judgment, communion with that person alone must be avoided by those to whose ears that excommunication has come. Hence the Apostle says: “If one called a brother is a fornicator [“is,” manuscript C], or greedy, or a worshipper of idols [variant: “or one serving idols”], do not even take food with such a person” (1 Cor. 5).

With regard to giving gifts to, or receiving gifts from, such persons, this principle seems to me to be observed: nothing should be given to them except in consideration of and compassion for human need, [Col. 0188A] and nothing should be received from them unless unavoidable necessity compels it. This should by no means be done for the increase of one’s household property, but only to meet necessity. Thus the Israelites received goods in the land of the Egyptians (Num. 22); thus in the land of Midian they received the possessions of the Midianites for necessary uses (Exod. 12).

When consulted on this matter, Pope Gregory VII wrote as follows (chapter 101, *Quoniam*, Cause 11, Question 3):

> Since, through the demands of our sins, we see many people daily perish because of excommunication—some through ignorance, some through excessive simplicity, some overcome by fear, and some even by necessity—we temper the sentence of anathema with mercy, as far as [one old edition: “for a time, as far as”] we can. By apostolic authority, therefore, we release from the bond of anathema the following: wives, [Col. 0188B] sons, male and female servants, or slaves; likewise peasants and retainers; and all those who are not so much courtiers that crimes are perpetrated by their counsel; also those who unknowingly communicate with excommunicated persons, and those who communicate with persons who communicate with the excommunicated. But if any ploughman, pilgrim, or traveller comes into the land of excommunicated persons, where he cannot buy, or has nothing from which to buy, we grant permission to receive from excommunicated persons. And if anyone wishes to give to excommunicated persons, not to sustain pride but from motives of humanity, we do not forbid it.

Concerning purchases of ecclesiastical property made by monks from laypeople, we answer your [Col. 0188C] brotherhood as follows: if they redeemed ecclesiastical property from lay control by paying a price and restored it to ecclesiastical right and episcopal governance, we would not merely refrain from disapproving but would praise them strongly. For this would not seem to be a purchase, but a redemption deserving praise from all rightly devout persons. Thus captives are redeemed through the piety of the faithful, when those who redeem them do not reduce the redeemed to their own servitude but restore them to their former freedom. But because rare indeed, or perhaps no one, buys such things except for his own use or that of his people, this should not be called a pious redemption, but a greedy and dangerous transaction between buyers and sellers.

Concerning the offerings of evil persons whom we still tolerate within the Church, we hold that, so long as we communicate with them in the Church’s administration, [Col. 0188D] it would seem vain and superstitious to reject their offerings. For Zacchaeus the publican invited into his house even the Lord Jesus Christ, whose life was a discipline of morals, and ministered to him from his own resources (Luke 19). Christian religion proceeds rightly when it either does what Christ did or avoids [variant: “avoids those things,” manuscript C] what Christ is known to have avoided.

But we advise that gifts and grants from excommunicated persons—persons to whom one must not even say “greeting” (2 John 1)—be avoided on account of the weak. For although the Apostle says, “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1), he nevertheless adds accordingly: “But it is evil for the person who eats through causing offense” [Col. 0189A] (Rom. 1:4). Thus he says also in the Letter to the Corinthians:

> If an unbeliever invites you and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no question on account of conscience. Therefore, whether you eat or drink, do all things for the glory of God. Give no offense to Jews, to Gentiles, or to the Church of God, just as I please all persons in all things, seeking not what is useful to myself, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved (1 Cor. 10).

This is apostolic and sound doctrine. Therefore gifts and grants from such persons must be avoided, not because God’s creation becomes unclean through them—the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord (Ps. 23)—but lest the conscience of the simple be weakened by this, when, by such conjectures, they suppose that their misdeeds are done for the sake of their benefits [Col. 0189B] [variant: “please”], or that the evils they formerly abhorred are not evils.

For a similar reason divine and human laws alike reject and avoid their testimonies and judgments [one old edition: “command their testimonies and judgments to be rejected”; thus manuscript C], not because they do not sometimes bear true witness and issue just decisions, but so that, confuted by such rejection, they may desist from their error.

Concerning those who confess criminal sins secretly, I can give no better answer than what blessed Augustine writes in a certain letter (Letter 206): “We suspend no one from communion unless he has been publicly accused [variant: ‘we cannot suspend anyone’; variant: ‘we can suspend no one unless publicly accused,’ manuscript C] and convicted, or has voluntarily confessed likewise in public.”

[Col. 0189C] But concerning manifest sins, the judgment is manifest: those who have sinned openly must be openly rebuked and corrected by public penance. Yet it should be said to them, not by commanding but by advising, that they should suspend themselves from ecclesiastical offices or abstain from communion in the sacraments; for by such humility and penance the case is more truly handled and restored salvation is more safely fortified. Yet divine sacraments administered by such persons are not made worse by their unworthiness, just as they are not made better by the worthiness of better persons (Letters 73 and 236), but, according to blessed Augustine, they are themselves the same wherever they are found.

Concerning persons excommunicated by a general judgment but not named individually—whether that excommunication was made in a chapter or in a council, whether they are simoniacs [Col. 0189D] or married priests—the same counsel applies as in the case of other criminals: they are not to be suspended from communion unless publicly convicted or publicly confessing. For the Lord knew Judas to be a thief, and so excommunicated that he even called him a devil; nevertheless, because Judas was not accused until he revealed himself by betraying the Lord, the Lord did not reject him at all.

We think the same also concerning subjects: they ought not to abandon their prelates unless they first see them publicly condemned or individually excommunicated. Concerning mutual confession, of which the apostle James says, “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5), I reply that this suffices for [Col. 0190A] daily and light sins, provided suitable satisfaction follows. But if the faults are grave, absolution must be sought from him to whom the power of binding and loosing has been given.

Concerning an excommunicated person received as a guest, it seems sufficient if the host who received him refrains from the excommunicated person’s table and kiss. [Note: [Col. 0189D] Ivo reports this from Pope Calixtus, Book V of the *Panormia*, “On the Judgment of Excommunication,” and Gratian, in the canon *Excommunicatos*, [Col. 0190D] Cause 11, Question 3.]

I think that I have answered briefly almost all your questions—and, if not all, at least the weightier ones—leaving it to your discretion to apply the general judgments, set out here and there under individual headings, to each case. When carefully considered, I would not say that each judgment can meet every individual question, but almost every judgment can address several headings. When, however, by God’s providence we can speak together [Note: [Col. 0190D] “Together” is absent in manuscript C.], we shall gladly answer whatever remains, whether from what we have now written or from other matters which the Lord may be pleased to inspire. [Col. 0190B] Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXVII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to ADELA, noble countess: greeting and service.

The abbot of the monastery of Bonneval and the community entrusted to him strike upon the ears of God and men with tearful and pitiable cries, complaining that, because of the killing of Hugh the Black, you unjustly harass them and the men subject to their jurisdiction, and impose upon them forced services contrary to the privileges and institutions of your predecessors [variant: “you impose”], to such an extent that you leave them no place with you either for mercy or for judgment [variant: “you leave”]. Hearing this, I cannot but groan with their groans; for I ought both to rejoice with them in prosperity [Col. 0190C] and to suffer with them in tribulation.

Therefore, in advising I ask, and in asking I advise, that you temper your threatened severity by prudent and discerning counsel, lest the Lord’s flock be scattered by the storm of an unfamiliar tribulation and religion, which has flourished anew in these times, be diminished or utterly reduced to nothing. Moreover, you ought to take counsel for your salvation and your reputation, lest it seem pointless that you support with your gifts, and enlarge in every way you can, monasteries that are not under your jurisdiction, while you diminish those that are under your jurisdiction and subject them, as it were, to servile oppression.

Therefore, lest these matters reach the ears of many and greatly detract both from your reputation and from your salvation, as I have advised, so I advise again: act more mildly, lest unfamiliar and intolerable severity become an example to [Col. 0190D] your descendants and an eternal [variant: everlasting, thus manuscript C] sin to you. For you ought to fear lest the groans of God’s servants reach his ears, and those who find no mercy with you close to you the gate of mercy. For, as those oppressed by you themselves say, they will continually fill God’s ears with groaning and, by daily complaint, the ears of God’s people in places near and far, until the Lord commands the winds and the sea and its waves are stilled. Since this is dangerous and disgraceful to you, may the Lord grant you a spirit of counsel, that you may choose better things and flee what is dangerous. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXVIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to RALPH, venerable archbishop of Reims: enduring patience in tribulation.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] The cause and explanation of this title must be sought from what he writes in Letter 190.]

[Col. 0191A]

Your prudence knows better than I do that I was asked whether a woman who, after the sacraments and ceremonies of marriage have been completed, is known to have given birth within two or three months, ought to remain in marriage because of the marriage bond, or to lose the dignity of marriage because of the disgrace committed before marriage, since the law of Moses [Note: [Col. 0191D] Thus all old editions have it; formerly, “Mosis.”] commands such a woman to be stoned.

On this matter I do not remember having found a canonical judgment. Yet, without prejudice to a better judgment, I say that if the woman’s disgrace had been known before the celebration of the sacrament of marriage, she ought not, according to the severity of the laws, to have been honored with marriage, but severe correction should have been applied to her through harsh rebukes, like the casting [variant: striking] of stones. [Col. 0191B] But after the marriage bond has been contracted with a straightforward preceding consent, after the marriage documents have been delivered and the remaining sacraments of marriage completed, the man and woman have become one body through the union of flesh. I do not understand that the marriage can be dissolved unless adultery occurs as cause for divorce. For although [Note: [Col. 0192D] “Although” is absent in manuscript C.] a woman may, according to the teaching of the Gospel, be reconciled to her husband after adultery, how much more after simple fornication committed when she was not yet bound by marital law?

It is contained in the Book of Constitutions [Book XXIII, Code, *On Marriages*] that prostitutes may choose a more honorable life [Col. 0191C] and enter into the rights of marriage; how much more may women who have sinned secretly and have not made their bodies a source of profit? Hence Augustine writes in the book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices*:

> Permission to marry is granted to certain persons—that is, to those who [variant: “who,” thus manuscript C] have by no means professed virginity or widowly chastity [variant: masculine plural, thus manuscript C]. But fornication is granted with impunity to no one.

This judgment did not except the fornicating woman, nor the fornicating man, from the law of marriage. Likewise Paul, meeting the falls of human weakness, writes to the Corinthians: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have [Note: [Col. 0192D] “Have” is absent in manuscript C.] her own husband” (1 Cor. 2). By these words a healing provision was made: carnal union, which would be condemnable by the baseness of vice, became pardonable [Col. 0191D] through the honorability of marriage. Women who had previously been dishonorable are no longer counted as fornicators, nor may men dismiss them because of their earlier fall, as the Apostle says: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7).

Since fornication is regarded as equally disgraceful and condemnable in both the Old and the New Testament, the Lord commanded Hosea, in order to make a dishonorable woman honorable, to take a fornicating woman as his wife. Hence blessed Jerome writes in his exposition on Hosea (Book I, chapter 1, and Letter 148):

> The prophet Hosea is not to be blamed if [Col. 0192A] he converted the prostitute whom he took to modesty; rather, he is to be praised because he made a good woman from a bad one. A person who remains good is not himself polluted if joined with one who is evil; rather, one who is evil is turned toward good if that person follows good examples. From this we understand that the prophet did not lose his modesty by being joined [variant: “through union”] to a fornicating woman, but that the fornicating woman acquired the modesty which she had not previously possessed.

From these words of blessed Jerome one may infer that, if through union with a chaste husband a woman is made chaste, then conversely through divorce from him she is made unchaste. Therefore, since laws ought to provide for honorability and salvation, it seems safer to me that a husband retain as wife the woman whom he has taken, even though unknowingly unchaste, rather than by divorcing her make both her a fornicating woman and himself a fornicator.

[Col. 0192B] Our blessed teachers Ambrose and Augustine likewise advise that the falls of women of this kind should rather be forgiven by their husbands than strictly and mercilessly judged, since the husbands themselves can scarcely be seen [variant: “found”] free from similar unchastities (Letter 125). Hence Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, Homily 47:

> If you are going to take wives, preserve yourselves for your wives. As you wish them to come to you, so they too ought to find you. Do you seek an untouched woman? Be untouched yourself. Do you seek a pure woman? Do not be impure.

And Ambrose, in the sermon *On the Accused Lord*, says:

> No man ought to accuse a case of chastity unless he himself is chaste. For chastity deserves such an arbiter, before whom modesty is not endangered. What can you think more divine or more just than that the person who is free of sin should strike at sin? [One old edition: “should judge sins, who”; thus manuscript C.] How can you endure one who avenges another’s crime while defending his own?

Hence Augustine also says in *On the Words of the Lord*, Homily 47:

> The Lord says what the gentle and just man ought to say: “Let him who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at the adulteress” (John 8). This is the voice of justice: let the sinful woman be punished, but not by a sinful man. Let the law be fulfilled, but not by transgressors of the law.

Again Augustine, *On the Ten Strings*:

> Since chastity is a virtue, you fall under a single assault of lust, and yet you want your wife [“your,” manuscript C] to be victorious while you lie defeated? If the husband is the head, he ought to live better and precede his wife in every good deed.

From these and similar judgments of the holy Fathers [Col. 0192D] it may be inferred by reasoning that unlawful intercourse committed before marriage or betrothal cannot subsequently dissolve a marriage once entered into—how much less can childbirth, which is not the fruit of vice but of nature?

If, looking more deeply into this matter, someone objects from the words of Pope Leo that there is no marriage in which the sacrament of Christ and the Church is not contained—and Paul says concerning this sacrament, “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 2)—let him hear Jerome speaking in his exposition of the eighty-sixth Psalm:

> I tell you a marvelous thing, yet a true one. Our Zion, in which there are at times foreigners, and Tyre, and the Ethiopians, [Col. 0193A] that watchtower, that prostitute Rahab, that Babylon, she who spread [variant: “spread out”] her feet with every passer-by according to Ezekiel [variant: “Ezechiel”]—that prostitute, if she wishes, suddenly becomes a virgin.

If, therefore, Rahab is not rejected from the spiritual marriage of Christ, why is a fallen woman not admitted to marriage with an honorable man? For the sacrament of Christ and the Church does not differ from the bond of marriages of this kind. Therefore it does not accord with Christian piety, nor should such an injury be inflicted upon ecclesiastical sacraments, that, although they have been celebrated sooner or later than the transmitted order requires, we should nevertheless by undiscerning severity compel those whom they have transferred from disgrace to honor, from the city of the devil to the city of God, to return from honor to disgrace, from the city of God [Col. 0193B] to the city of the devil.

But if a different ruling is found in certain chapters, it must be attributed to the severity of discipline. Where salvation is endangered, however, we understand that the moderation of laws must provide for salvation. Moreover, let your affection know that, for the peace both of the Church of Reims and of yourself, we have humbly and faithfully petitioned the king (Letter 190), and will not cease to petition him at the proper time. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXIX. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] In one old edition the title is: “On the ordination of the king of the Franks.” In another: “On the consecration of King Louis.” See the passage of Abbot Suger in the *Life of Louis [Col. 0194D] the Fat*.]

Let the holy Roman Church know, and let all Churches to which the complaint of the clergy of Reims has reached know, that in the consecration of Louis, king of the Franks, we sought nothing for ourselves, but watched prudently for the common good of kingdom and priesthood. For there were [Col. 0193C] certain disturbers of the realm who strove with all zeal [variant: “who strove for this,” thus manuscript C] either to transfer the kingdom to another person or seriously to diminish it. Lest this happen, with God’s help, we endeavored to take such precautions as we could for the integrity of the kingdom and the tranquillity of the Churches.

Therefore it seems attributable to envy or arrogance if anyone disparages an action that is useful and honorable, one which that person can neither refute by reason, weaken by custom, nor condemn by law. For if we consult reason, he was consecrated king by right to whom the kingdom belonged by hereditary right and whom the common consent of bishops and nobles had long before chosen. Moreover, the reason that the people of Belgica may create and consecrate their own king, [Col. 0193D] although he is to rule in other provinces too, if the will of the kings themselves and the opportunity of times and places so present themselves, is equally the reason of the Celts and Aquitanians, who owe nothing to the province of Belgica, to choose their own king, although he too is to rule in Belgica, and to render him every service owed to a king.

But if we appeal to custom, which is especially demonstrated by examples, we answer from Augustine’s words that reason must be preferred to examples—though examples too agree with it. Behold, we have given a reason, and we do not believe that an equally valid one can be found among them regarding this matter. [Col. 0194A] Let us add examples agreeing with reason. For, as is read in the *Deeds of the Franks*:

> When the kingdom was divided among the sons of Lothair, grandsons of Clovis, Charibert and Guntram received the provinces of the Celts and Aquitanians into their kingdom. One of them, Charibert, established Paris [variant: “at Paris,” thus manuscript C, as in Letter 5] as his royal seat and extended his kingdom to the river [variant: “stream”] Garonne; but Guntram established his royal seat at Orléans [variant: “Orléans”] and received Burgundy, which is part of Celtica, into his kingdom.

These kings received neither blessing nor crown from the archbishop [variant: bishop] of Reims; rather, they were raised up and consecrated [variant: “consecrated”] by the priests of the provinces which they ruled.

[Col. 0194B] But after the kingdom of the Gauls had been brought back under one monarchy, with the line [variant: offspring] of Clovis extinguished, Pippin and his sons Charles and Carloman [variant: Charlemagne or Carloman] were neither raised to kingship at Reims nor by the archbishop of Reims, nor were they anointed there. Louis, grandson of Louis the Elder, and his wife were likewise consecrated and crowned as rulers at Ferrières, a place in the district of Sens, by certain bishops, with no metropolitan present. Hence the *Deeds of the Franks* reads:

> Hearing that Louis the grandson, with his wife, was coming into these regions, Abbot Hugh and the other chief men who were acting with the sons of their former lord Louis [Note: [Col. 0194D] The word is used in the same sense in Letter 194.] sent certain bishops to the monastery of Ferrières and had them consecrated and crowned [Col. 0194C] kings there.

Likewise in the *Deeds of the Franks*:

> There remained two sons of Count Robert of Anjou, a man of Saxon race. Of these the elder was called Odo, the other Robert. The Franks, Burgundians, and Aquitanian nobles assembled together and chose the elder, Odo, although reluctant, as guardian of the boy Charles and governor of the kingdom; Walter [variant: Galter, Gualter, or Gauter] archbishop of Sens anointed him.

Again:

> Charles the Simple having been placed in prison, Rodulf, the noble son of Richard, duke of the Burgundians, whom Charles had received from the sacred font, was raised to the kingdom with [Note: [Col. 0194D] “With” is absent from three old editions.] the counsel of Hugh the Great, son of the aforesaid Robert, and of the Frankish nobles. Rodulf himself was anointed [Col. 0194D] king in the city of Soissons on the third Ides of July. After the death of King Rodulf, Louis, son of Charles the Simple, was brought back from England into France through Archbishop William [variant: Guillelmus], and was anointed king at Laon on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [variant: read “and on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July”; or, in manuscript C, “the twelfth day before the Kalends of July”]. But after the kingdom of the Franks had been transferred to the line of Hugh the Great, Duke, the most pious King Robert, son of King Hugh, was consecrated and crowned king at Orléans, and his son Hugh the Younger was anointed and raised to kingship at Compiègne.

From these and similar examples [Col. 0195A] it is evident that not all kings of the Franks were consecrated in the Church of Reims or by the archbishops of Reims; rather, many were consecrated in many other places and by many other persons. To recount all these matters would make the discourse lengthy and the argument superfluous, since no writings or examples can prove that the archbishop of Reims [variant: “of the people of Reims”] anointed or crowned a king of the Franks outside Belgica.

Since the same authority belongs to every metropolitan in his own metropolitan province, it is surprising why [variant: “I do not see why”] one man should ambitiously claim for his private right what is known to be common to many—unless perhaps someone dares to say that the sacraments possess greater force with some persons than with others, which would be schismatic and would divide the unity of the Church.

[Col. 0195B] In saying this we do not criticize the ecclesiastical institution by which the peace of the Church is more firmly bound together, when inferior persons receive the administration of sacraments from superior persons and do not presume to usurp more than has been granted them. But where the authority of persons is equal, and one owes the other nothing beyond charity, if one seeks to take the other’s right away and arrogate it exclusively to himself while pursuing his own interests, he is deceived by worldly ambition.

We do not envy the Church of Reims; and if the kings of the Franks have such devotion toward it that they prefer to be consecrated by its metropolitan rather than by another, we do not oppose it, nor do we resent it. Indeed, if we happen to be present at their blessing, we will gladly answer “Amen” in the place of an ordinary layman. The foregoing [Col. 0195C] sequence of words has shown that we did nothing contrary to custom in the anointing of King Louis. It remains to show that we did nothing contrary to law.

For law is a written command or prohibition, directing whatever it commands or forbids to the common good. We did nothing contrary to this, since, prohibited by no objection, we provided in this action for the common good at charity’s prompting. But if the Church of Reims relies on privileges, those privileges are nonexistent for us, because they have neither been read aloud in general councils in our hearing, nor sent to our Churches by letters [old editions: “by letter”] duly prepared, nor, to put it more plainly, made public to us by any private or public means. Therefore we are not transgressors of a law of which we have never been hearers.

[Col. 0195D] Yet even if it had been heard, it ought not to have harmed us. For a law must be just and practicable, suited to place and time. Whether it is just, God knows. For the moment, we neither approve it as just nor condemn it as unjust, since we do not yet know it. But it was not practicable, because the consecration of a king at Reims by an archbishop not yet enthroned [Note: [Col. 0195D] Gervasius and Ralph contended with one another over the archbishopric of Reims, as Letter 190 indicates.] could not have been celebrated without the utmost disturbance and shedding of blood. It was unsuitable to the place because the city lay under anathema. It was not timely because, if the king’s consecration were delayed, the stability of the kingdom and the peace of the Church would be gravely endangered.

What [Col. 0196A] we did, therefore, we did with sound deliberation and prudent dispensation, envying no one and seeking to arrogate no one’s authority to ourselves, but keeping ourselves within our own bounds with a single eye (Letter 67). Let those who wish think otherwise. We do not fear the tribunal of an earthly judge, because our conscience makes us secure before the tribunal of the inward knower [“Creator,” manuscript C]. For we know that the measure of necessary dispensation has never displeased any wise person (Letter 214). Not only private laws, which provide neither for the truth of faith nor for moral integrity, but even general laws promulgated against heretics or criminals admit it, when, in healing greater diseases or removing greater evils, the moderation of sincere charity provides help more effectively than [Col. 0196B] the rigor of undiscerning severity.

This [“that,” manuscript C] could readily be proved first from evangelical authority, then from the Acts of the Apostles, thirdly from the Letters [“examples,” manuscript C] of the Apostle, and lastly from the decrees of Roman pontiffs and the judgments of other orthodox Fathers, were it not that the length of the letter would seem to exceed its proper limit.

## LETTER CXC. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: the love of a son and obedience in all things of one subject.

We wish Your Excellency to know that I and Lord Theobald, prior of the Parisian monastery of Blessed Martin, having heard of the pitiable and astonishing desolation of the Church of Reims, petitioned the king of the Franks, opportunely [Col. 0196C] and importunately, with the boldness of familiarity, that he should restore peace to that Church by expelling the intruder Gervasius, and permit Lord Ralph, metropolitan of the same Church, restored to his favor [Note: [Col. 0196D] On this depends the interpretation of the words at the end of Letter 188.], to preside over that Church.

At length he yielded to our prayers and granted that we might bring Ralph safely to his court, which was to assemble at Orléans at the Nativity of the Lord, and there discuss this matter with him and with the princes of the realm, as far as possible without injury to the kingdom’s integrity. It happened as had been arranged; and, coming to court with many intercessors, we repeated our petition once [Col. 0196D] and again. But because the court objected, we could not obtain full peace unless the aforesaid metropolitan, by hand and oath, rendered to the king the fidelity which all archbishops of Reims had previously rendered to their predecessors, the kings of the Franks, as had all other bishops of the Frankish kingdom, however religious and holy.

At the persuasion and urging of the leading men of the entire court, this was done, although the strictness of the commands made it less permissible, because the peace of the Church and fraternal love so required. Since charity is the fulfillment of the law (Rom. 13), we believe that the laws were obeyed in that in which we recognized the work of charity to have been fulfilled.

Therefore we ask on bended knees of the heart that paternal moderation, with the same regard for charity and [Col. 0197A] peace, may regard as pardonable what is made unlawful not by eternal law but solely by a prohibition imposed by rulers with the intention of acquiring liberty (Letters 60 and 236). Thus, where the transgressions of children have been incurred through useful dispensation and balancing considerations, let a word suffice the father in place of a blow, and let the devout supplication of his children be counted as the highest punishment.

For if apostolic authority wishes strictly to judge all things that are arranged through healing condescension, almost all ministers will have to renounce their administrations or leave the world; nor will they have where to sow spiritual things unless they are permitted to tolerate certain carnal things (Letter 214). Therefore apostolic sublimity teaches that one must yield to the necessity of the times, and the authority of the orthodox counsels, saying that where the slaughter of peoples lies widespread, [Col. 0197B] something must be relaxed from the severity of the canons so that sincere charity may aid in healing greater diseases (chapter *Necessaria*, and following chapters, Cause 1, Question 7; and Letter 236).

Yet in saying this, we do not teach your learned fatherhood; rather, in advising and begging, we urge it to strive to abound in the bowels of counsel and compassion where it is not permitted to exercise the fortitude that is due. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCI. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to HUGH, reverend abbot of the monastery of Cluny: greeting and service.

In a certain monastery within your jurisdiction there is a brother who, while he was a cleric living in the world, assaulted a pregnant woman with whom he had intercourse. A few days afterwards the woman miscarried. But whether she miscarried because of this assault or for some other reason was uncertain both to the assailant and to the woman assaulted. Nevertheless, on this account he has been suspended from receiving holy orders and removed from the administration of the sacraments.

This judgment appears excessively harsh to many: that so severe a sentence should be confirmed for an uncertain fault, when the canonical ruling consonant with the Gospel says (Pope Sixtus, in c. *Si quis*, causa 30, question 5): “Let none of the pontiffs presume to judge uncertain matters.” Yet, if the fault had been certain, it could, according to the examples of the ancients, have been punished more mildly—provided, however, that this did not harm weak minds.

For holy David, after performing penance for adultery and homicide, did not lose the spirit of prophecy (1 Kings 11). Peter, after denying Christ with an oath, washing away his fault with tears (Matt. 26), remained not only an apostle but also prince of the apostles (Ambrose, Sermon 47, *On Peter’s Faith*; canon *Hi qui*, distinction 50). Paul, after persecuting and slaughtering the disciples of the Lord, attained the apostolic summit. That murderer whom blessed John had entrusted to the bishop of Ephesus to be fed and instructed, after murders and robberies, was brought to repentance and obtained not only pardon, but, by the ordination of blessed John, was also made head of the Ephesian Church. [Note: Abdias of Babylon, book; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 17; and Nicephorus Callistus, book II, chapter 42.]

Because these memorable persons performed true repentance, they deserved full pardon—not merely as a remedy for their fault, but even for attaining the eminence of pastoral care. Nevertheless, these examples do not make a law. For, as blessed Augustine says:

> “The diligence of later generations has most strictly decreed that, after penance has been performed for a crime, no one is to remain in the clergy and no one is to enter the clergy. This is believed to have been said not by the dispensation of mercy, but by the rigor of discipline, because some, out of an ambition for the powers of offices, performed feigned repentance.”  
> [Note: St Augustine, Letter 10 to Boniface. See Gratian, *Decretum*, book I, distinction 50; and Ivo, *Decret*, book III, title *On Those Fallen after Ordination*.]

It therefore seems to me that, just as feigned repentance excludes falsely repentant persons from the clergy, so true repentance admits genuinely repentant persons to the clergy. In saying this, we do not oppose the sacred rules of the Fathers, but understand, from reason and from the recollection of examples, that the matter has been placed in the discretion of those who preside: they may promote to ecclesiastical service those whom they see have performed true repentance, provided that they have not performed public penance. [Note: Chapters 49, 50, 52, 53, distinction 50; and chapters 1, 2, 3, distinction 55; unless necessity or custom requires otherwise, chapter 62, distinction 50.] For clerical status is denied to such persons because, on their account, hostile persons disparage the divine sacraments, and the minds of the simple are either scandalized or weakened.

But in this case none of these conditions applies: the fault is not certain; the penance was not public; and the person is honourable, so far as human conscience can judge another’s life. He therefore seems to us able to offer sacrifice to God, because he has made himself a whole burnt offering to God. The brothers carrying this letter will tell you who the brother is of whom we speak. For him we beseech your reverence, that, relaxing the rigor of your custom, you may permit him to be promoted to holy orders. We speak to one who is prudent, teaching you nothing and saying nothing which your prudence does not know and your skill has not often considered. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to the monks of Coulombs [some manuscripts: “of Coulombes”], that they may think the same thing in the Lord.

To use the Lord’s words: “Behold, Satan has demanded you, that he may sift you like wheat” (Luke 22), because you have been disturbed from your proper understanding by the persuasions of certain persons. Inflated with Pharisaic leaven, rather than made rich with the Lord’s wheat, they glory in the cheapness of their food and in not sparing the body; although, according to the Apostle, bodily exercise is useful for a little while (1 Tim. 8), and the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. 14).

For such persons, not having their faculties trained in the understanding of the Scriptures, do not think soberly (Rom. 12), nor do they understand with due discernment the matters about which they make assertions (1 Tim. 1). [Col. 0199A] They do not think that good persons can live piously in the company [variant: “collection”] of evil persons. They attend to Ezekiel’s words: “Depart; go out from there” (Ezek. 14; Isa. 52), but do not attend to what follows: “And do not touch what is unclean” (ibid.; 2 Cor. 6)—which must be understood of contact of the heart, not of the body.

Accordingly Augustine says in Sermon 18, *On the Words of the Gospel* (reported in chapter *Ecce* and chapter *Recedite*, causa 23, question 4):

> “What is ‘go out from there’ except to do what belongs to the correction of evil persons, so far as can be done, without breaking peace, according to each person’s rank and position? You have been displeased by another’s sin: you have not touched the unclean thing. You have reproved, corrected, admonished; you have also applied fitting discipline that does not violate unity: you have gone out from there. Moses cried this out (Num. 16); Isaiah cried it out (Isa. 52); Jeremiah cried it out (Lam. 4); Ezekiel cried it out (Ezek. 14). Let us see whether they abandoned the people of God and transferred themselves to other nations. How much and how vehemently Jeremiah rebuked the sinners and criminals among the people! Yet he was among them: he entered one temple with them, celebrated the same sacraments, lived in the same congregation of criminal persons, but by crying out he went out from there. This is not to touch the unclean thing: to go out from there, not to consent in will and not to spare with one’s mouth.”

The same author, in the same work (chapter 8, *A malis*, causa 23, question 4), says:

> “Always separate yourselves from evil persons in heart; at times, cautiously, be united to them bodily. An evil person does not defile you in two cases: if you do not consent and if you rebuke him. This is not to communicate: not to consent. For communication takes place when the fellowship of one’s will or approval is joined to another’s deed. Therefore neither consent to evil persons so as to approve them, nor be negligent so as not to rebuke them, nor be proud so as to rebuke them insultingly.”

The same author, in the conciliar letter to the Donatists (chapter *Si quis*, causa 23, question 4), says:

> “Whoever lives well in this Church is not prejudiced by the sins of others, because in it each person shall bear his own burden. Therefore the communion of evil persons does not defile anyone through communion in the sacraments, but through consent [variant: “the agreement”] to their deeds.”

The same author, in book III, chapter 3 of *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, and in chapter *Non potest*, causa 23, question 4, says:

> “When the same disease has seized many, nothing remains for good persons but grief and groaning, so that through the sign shown to holy Ezekiel they may deserve to escape unharmed from their devastation. For counsels of separation are both vain and pernicious and sacrilegious, because they are impious and proud, and disturb weak good persons more than they correct strong evil persons.”

These and similar arguments are used by preachers of this kind—who do not understand or do not read [manuscript C: “do not read or do not understand”]—to persuade monks to abandon their monasteries on account of their abbots and the stewards of their monasteries, who have acquired for their monasteries certain tithes that by right belong to the administration of bishops.

Let these exceedingly subtle investigators of divine judgments tell me what is more beneficial for monks: whether to remain cenobites under obedience to their superiors—which is better than sacrifice—and there to live on tithes and offerings of the faithful, which the Church can, by the law [manuscript C: “in the ecclesiastical law”] of charity, share not only with monasteries but also with hospitals, the sick, and pilgrims; or to become Sarabaites, so that they may live in private places by their own authority and receive their food from the property of the poor through the hands of plunderers, and from the usury of merchants. [Note: These persons are also mentioned a little later.]

For although tithes and offerings are owed principally to the clerical ministry, the Church may hold all that it possesses in common with all the poor. How much more with those poor persons who, having left their own possessions, follow the poor Christ—not carrying Christ’s cross under forced service [*angaria*]?

Yet there is one respect in which I do not consider abbots and monastery superiors deserving of indulgence: if they receive tithes and offerings from persons to whom these do not belong, namely laymen (Letter 289); if they acquire them disorderly from whatever persons; if they overstep ancient boundaries—that is, if they diminish and usurp for themselves the stipends of priests established from antiquity. Yet monks who do not know of these things, or who do not approve them, should not for that reason abandon their community [variant: “collection”] or become less obedient to their abbots. For the Lord says of the superiors of churches and monasteries under the name of the scribes and Pharisees: “Do what they say, but do not do according to their works” (Matt. 23).

Nor should the use of these very things be forbidden to persons whose conscience is innocent. For the Apostle says, “All things are clean to the clean” (Tit. 1); and, “Each person shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “What enters the mouth does not defile a person; rather, evil desire proceeding from the heart and approval of an evil deed proceeding from the mouth—these defile a person” (Matt. 15).

The aforementioned propagators of the divine word, and insufficiently discerning interpreters of it, pay too little heed to this. While they go out, as it were, to cut wood (Deut. 19), with indiscreet and unsalted words they strike the consciences of the weak as with immoderate blows, while despising the Church throughout the world and seeming to say: “Behold, Christ is here; and behold, there; behold, in the inner rooms; and behold, in the wilderness” (Mark 13). Thus thinking, before the time they arrogate to themselves the winnowing-fan by which the Lord’s threshing-floor is to be winnowed at the end—as though only chaff remained among the universal Church, while the wheat passed over to them to be stored in the Lord’s granary. In this presumption there is great danger lest the person who judges himself wheat separated from chaff should, swollen with Pharisaic leaven, become chaff.

Furthermore, those who are unable to provide themselves with necessities from the labour of their hands do not reflect properly that they often do themselves what they blame in others. Conquered by want of food, they preach their innocence to the people—which is to sell sheep; they preach in order to eat—which is to sell oxen. But the Lord drove such sellers out of the Temple together with the sellers of doves (Matt. 21), and prefigured that persons like them should be expelled from the fellowship of Catholics (John 2).

Nor does it seem to excuse them that they do not receive money with their own hands; for they either keep their own Gehazi-like agents [cf. 4 Kings 4] with them or send them after themselves to take the collections and spend them for whatever uses they choose. If they considered these things in themselves, they would not attack clerics, monks, and rulers of churches and monasteries with such zeal.

I have written these things to you, brothers, so that you may not be frightened by the thunder of empty threats, nor be moved away from your own understanding, but may order your life according to the statutes of the preceding Fathers, and may firmly maintain the obedience you owe your prelates and the stability you have professed to your monastery, lest you incur the condemnation of those who make their vows void.

In saying this, I do not condemn the life of anchorites (Letter 256): namely, of those who, trained in the disciplines of regular cenobitic communities, withdraw in an orderly manner into the wilderness. To them solitude is paradise and the city a prison; living by the labour of their hands, they practise the active life, or refresh their minds by the sweetness of the contemplative life; they thirst for the fountain of life with the mouth of the heart, and, forgetting the things behind, look back upon them no more.

But some of this profession wander about through villages, castles, and cities in their sheepskins, displaying to the people, by the humility of their clothing and the meanness of their food [variant: “the humility of their clothing, the meanness of their food”], their own merits. [Note: See John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, book VII, chapter 21, where he treats of the hypocrites of his own time who sought to conceal ambition beneath the false appearance of religion.] They aspire to be teachers though they have never been disciples, disparaging the life of all other persons because they are not what [variant: “what or who”] they themselves are.

I understand that such persons are to be counted neither as hermits nor cenobites, but as wanderers [*gyrovagi*] [Note: They were never stable, serving pleasures and gluttony, and were worse than Sarabaites, as is said in the Rule of St Benedict, chapter 1.] or Sarabaites, who reduce Christ’s body, which is the Church, as though it were a single member. They do not heed that each person has his own gift from God; that in God’s house one walks in one way, another in another; that not all members have the same activity; and that, in the same body of Christ, the lowest member does not say, “I am not of the body because I am the lowest,” nor does the highest member boast against the lower because it is the highest.

Those who contend that the Church of God belongs only to a few solitaries thus destroy, so far as lies in them, the universality of Christ’s body. If they truly recognized themselves, they would wisely forgive the imperfection of others, since they would understand that they themselves are not immune from mixture with evil persons. For the Lord, speaking of every rank of Christian profession, says of individuals: “One will be taken into the number of the elect, while another will be left in the mass of the condemned” (Mark 13; Matt. 24).

For the secrecy of forests and mountain summits do not make a person blessed if he does not possess inward solitude, the Sabbath of the heart, tranquility of conscience, and ascents in the heart. Without these, every solitude is accompanied by sloth of mind, curiosity, vainglory, and dangerous storms of temptations; nor is fitting tranquility granted to the imperiled soul unless God, by rebuking it, drives away the importunate storm of temptations. But if you possess these things, wherever you may be and in whatever order or habit you may serve God, you will not lack the prize of eternal reward.

But because Satan sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light, I fear that, as the ancient serpent seduced Eve by his cunning, so the crafty tempter may seduce the minds of some through his hidden operations and make their consciences, corrupted by his deceits, dwellings of seven wicked spirits—dwellings which, covered with the veil of vain religion, he falsely represents as homes of the Holy Spirit—and may, through the deceived, spread more widely the snares of his deception.

That this may not happen, according to the Apostle, “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” (1 John 3). For discernment of spirits, together with the counsel of the Scriptures, will be able to calm these impulses in you and preserve you in stability of mind, so that you may say against your tempters with the Psalmist: “Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am moved” (Ps. 12).

“I could write many things in this manner for your edification, but for those who daily hear the sacred Scriptures or hear saving admonitions, I think these things can suffice. Farewell.”

## LETTER CXCIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to GAUFRID, venerable bishop of Beauvais, greeting and service.

We have often appealed to your affection on behalf of the Church of Saint Quentin (Letter 31), and from your sweet speech we have brought back good hope and a good promise. Therefore, still with humble devotion, we implore that same affection of yours through pious prayers, asking and knocking, that you both preserve the peace of the aforesaid Church and strive to have it preserved by others—setting aside every grant of advantage, pretext, and accusation of rivals.

For we have never wished to come into judgment against you, and we have never lent the ear of our heart to your rivals and detractors. But if any unfitting report concerning you was heard, we have sought piously to overlook it and to cover it with brotherly compassion. [Note: Ivo complains of this Gaufrid, bishop of Beauvais, in Letter 151.]

This, however, is what we have requested from your affection, and still request: that you preserve inviolate the privileges which the said Church of Saint Quentin obtained from your predecessors, which the apostolic authority confirmed, and which royal majesty also established by pragmatic sanction—just as you would wish them preserved unimpaired if they were your own. We do not wish to appeal to the ears of exalted persons against you until we find the bowels of your mercy persistently closed to us; for swellings must be lanced with iron only when they refuse to feel soothing applications.

Let your prudence know that whatever good your predecessors did for the aforesaid Church is yours, and will benefit you as much as it benefited them if you rejoice with it; but it will harm you both temporally and eternally if you permit the Lord’s little flock to be troubled and disturbed from that tranquility of mind necessary to the servants of God for the sake of some temporal gain. It belongs to you to water and nourish what others planted, so that the second grace may yield the same fruit to the nourisher which the first grace will bring to the planter.

For your solicitude should know that the founder of the aforesaid Church, Lord Guy, bishop of Beauvais of blessed memory, retained for himself, his successors, or any authority whatsoever no monetary fine, no exaction, and no customary due in the aforesaid Church or the village adjoining it. He granted all these things through the royal hand, then through the agreement [in certain copies: “connivance”] of the bishops of the province, and finally through apostolic authority; by the aforesaid sanctions he assigned them all permanently to the aforesaid Church.

The Church has possessed this liberty without disturbance from the time of my priesthood and during the time of Lord Galo [Note: He was first elected bishop of Beauvais; Letters 104 and 105.], later bishop of Paris. Yet, as I have heard, your intention now seeks, through the persuasion of ill-wishers, to annul it, saying that the matter stood otherwise than we have stated—although it is agreed that what is plainly undertaken against privileges must not be treated as law.

But if anyone of the Church’s dependents or parishioners acts against peace or Christian law, compel him through your office to make satisfaction. As for the Church, allow it, with its abbot, peacefully to serve God. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCIV. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to HUGH, dean of the Church of Orléans, to VULGRIN, archdeacon of the same Church, and to the common chapter of the said Church, greeting.

[Note: In manuscript C this letter is placed after the following one.]

You informed me by your letters that Reginald Canard denies that he is my parishioner. If there were a conference between us, and we proved the matter by law and custom, he would deny it unjustly. But because this cannot conveniently be done at present, we meanwhile notify and request that he, having been excommunicated by us, be treated as excommunicated in your churches (Letters 76 and 111).

If you are unwilling to comply with me in this, at least obey the authority of the Fathers, which declares that parishioners of another Church, excommunicated by another Church while they reside in its parish, ought not to be received by their own Church. For we read in chapter 2 of the Council of Meaux:

> “Concerning those who have a benefice or inheritance within a parish but are parishioners of another bishop, and who travel from place to place committing robberies and plunder: it has been decided that they are to be excommunicated and are not to depart from the parish before they have worthily amended what they have done. Their excommunication is to be notified to their senior [Letter 189] and proper bishop (chapter 20, *Curae*, causa 11, question 3), so that they may not receive them before they return to the place where they committed the robbery and fully make amends for everything.”

If anyone attempts to stand against this judgment, so clear and so firm, and still wishes to conceal the wickedness of an unrepentant man, I appeal to the hearing of the metropolitan see.

## LETTER CXCV. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to GAUFRID, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme: do not think lofty thoughts, but agree with the lowly.

I have received your letters, which stroke and sting: in some places breathing the sweetness of honey, in others sprinkling the bitterness of gall. They charge me with having exposed you and those entrusted to you to robbers and evildoers, and with having inflicted many evils upon you in deeds and words. I say utterly, with Truth—which is God—and my conscience as witness, that I exposed neither you nor your possessions to anyone, nor have I planned with anyone that the affairs of the monastery entrusted to you should be mishandled.

But because I frequently drink bitter things from you, it is not surprising that I cannot offer you sweet things or present myself as a father when I do not find you a son. Therefore it is not unjust if I withhold a mother’s milk from you, since you do not render me the honour due to a father.

Know that the excuses you put forward are empty: namely, that you rejected the profession owed to the Church of Chartres out of obedience to the Roman Church. For the Roman Church has received from God no unjust power—no power, that is, to violate faith or fail to render to each person his due—but only the power to bind what ought to be bound and loose what ought to be loosed. Therefore, in brief answer to all your objections or previous allegations, omitting every superfluous word: Do what is yours, and I shall do what is mine. So long as you postpone doing this, do not wonder if I postpone doing those things which are yours.

## LETTER CXCVI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the Franks, his sweetest [manuscript C: “and most beloved”] lord: greeting and service owed to the extent of his ability.

I have been told that, at the suggestion of enemies, you gravely accuse the abbot of Saint-Denis and seek to defame him by the testimony of a certain pseudo-monk concerning a falsehood alleged against him. Neither the laws nor the institutions of your royal predecessors permit that anyone who has confessed concerning himself should be believed regarding another’s crime (Letters 229 and 249; *Codex*, final title, chapter *On Accusations*).

I therefore beseech your excellence first to take thought for royal majesty and for the noble monastery, which with all its dependencies is subject to your will: do not diminish its rights in any respect; rather, defend and assert the benefactions which your predecessors conferred upon that venerable place as though upon your own alms. [One copy: “turn”; others, including manuscript C: “fear.”]

And because it is dangerous to disturb holy places and trouble those serving in holy places, it would seem to me [variant: “seems”] sound counsel that, putting aside the accusations [variant: “insinuations”] of rivals, you should summon or await for this investigation persons who would give you counsel without any disguise of malice and would beneficially provide both for your interest and for the monastery’s peace. In these matters and in all things may the Lord give you a spirit of counsel, strength, and piety. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCVII. IVO, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to WILLIAM [variant: Wuillelm], by the same grace abbot of Marmoutier: may you please the supreme Shepherd in a holy purpose.

Your letter states that a priest set fire to his own house, as though to frighten enemies; and that, when the fire gained strength, a certain boy following his mother died in the blaze. Your brotherhood therefore asks whether this priest, having become a monk, can thereafter handle Christ’s sacraments, or whether he must remain excluded from priestly office for all time.

I answer you from the words of Pope Nicholas, writing in a similar case to a certain Bishop Hosbard [variant: Hosbald]:

> “Although the priest did not have the intention to kill, nevertheless rage and indignation, from which that deadly disturbance arose, are forbidden in all persons and especially in God’s ministers, and are everywhere condemned. …”  
> [Note: The passage appears more fully in chapter *Studeat*, distinction 50.]

From these words it may be inferred that, if the priest had done something lawful and orderly, and an unexpected death had resulted from it apart from his intention, he would have been innocent. But now, because, at the devil’s prompting, he first did what was unlawful and contrary to the priestly calling, and because a worse outcome followed from an evil beginning, we must not—and cannot—judge the priest innocent or worthy of priestly office, unless a long trial of monastic life proves him and pastoral obedience restores him to the interrupted ministry by prerogative of his merits.

## LETTER CXCVIII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to GISLEBERT, brother of good hope and raised to manifold honour.

Let your affection know that letters have been sent by the lord pope to me and to our fellow bishops of Paris and Soissons, commanding us to summon you and Gaufrid, your fellow canon, before our tribunal in a suitable place by the Ides of July, and reasonably decide the case which the said Gaufrid has against you concerning the provostship of Suobrium [variant: Sodobrium, as in the following letter].

We have therefore appointed Étampes as the place, where each of you may bring persons necessary for his case and conduct his claims without fear. We designate the Ides of July as the day [variants: “we name”; manuscript C: “we designated”]; and by the authority entrusted to us, we summon you to that place and day. [Note: What follows is missing.] We request that you inform us at once whether you will come when summoned. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCIX. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to GISLEBERT, nephew of the lord archbishop of Tours, greeting.

By command of the lord pope, we summoned you to a case against Gaufrid, your fellow canon, concerning the provostship of Suobrium [in two copies, Sodobrium, as in the preceding letter], on a specified day and at a specified place. Because we were uncertain of your obedience, we explicitly warned you to inform us of your arrival, lest we and the others who were to come [variant: “were summoned”] for this case should be wearied in vain.

But you disregarded our warning—or rather, the lord pope’s—and gave no response to our delegation. Without our knowledge, you came, seeking by our absence to gain the removal or postponement of judgment; and because you had not arranged the case with the judges, you did not find the judges. In this matter innocent and simple truth could assist you better in absence than a duplicity, searched out with much scrutiny and concealed, could benefit you in your presence for harm.

For just as deceitful absence cannot benefit, so deceitful presence cannot rightly benefit; since, as blessed Augustine says, “Simulated equity is not equity, but simulation and iniquity.” Therefore we again give the warning which we and our colleagues gave by apostolic command: return to judgment. We prescribe for you, without changing the place, the Kalends of September as the day. If you intend to come, do not neglect to notify us before the Assumption of blessed Mary, because we ought not otherwise to assemble for this hearing unless we know beforehand that you will come.

Otherwise, you will avoid (Letter 201) an iron bow and incur a bronze bow (Job 20). Farewell.

## LETTER CC. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to DAIMBERT, by the grace of God reverend archbishop of Sens [variant: “of the Senones”], his metropolitan: due obedience with every devotion.

Since we have been appointed guardians and attendants of Christ’s bride, we ought to be zealous for that same bride with chaste love, so that we may present her immaculate to her Bridegroom. If, therefore, a stain or wrinkle darkens her beauty, we ought to make every effort either to restore the wrinkle of duplicity to simplicity or to wash away the stain of disgrace with the nitre and soap of due rebuke [variant: “correction”].

We have said these preliminary things to your eminence because we have learned that a serious scandal has arisen in the Church of Sens committed to you by God: partly because the cantor of that Church, contrary to the pledges [*sacramenta*] he made, has occupied for himself by rash ambition a seat in the Church which was not due to him; partly because a certain one of the Church’s prelates has publicly taken to himself two prostitutes [variant: “associated with himself”] and has already prepared a third concubine for whom he is to draw up marriage documents (Letter 218).

How disgraceful these things are and how contrary to apostolic commands, it is not for me to teach your prudence; I only remind you with filial affection not to suppress such transgressions lukewarmly or timidly [manuscript C: “nor timidly”]. It befits your greatness to cut away these wounds with a healing cautery, lest the gangrene spread more widely, and by the example of these persons restrain others from similar infection.

If you cannot accomplish this through your own means, bring with you two or three of your suffragan bishops, by whose counsel and assistance you may strive to calm this scandal; lest so great a stench, spreading farther and more widely, reach the nose of the Roman Church and, along with bodily exhaustion, inflict serious losses of property as well. Farewell.

## LETTER CCI. IVO, son of his exalted holiness, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: with due obedience, whatever may be more blessed.

By command of your majesty, we summoned Gislebert, nephew of the archbishop of Tours, to decide the case between him and Gaufrid, his fellow canon. We assigned him a day and place; and because we were uncertain whether he would come to this hearing, we warned him to announce [variant: “give notice of”] his arrival, lest we should be wearied in vain. He gave no response to this warning.

Without our knowledge, he came to the assigned place, as though by our absence he would gain the removal or delay of the judgment; but he did not find the judges from whom he had deceitfully concealed his arrival. Thus deceived, we set him another day and sent him a messenger with letters repeatedly. But he, in his customary manner, sought hiding places and avoided hearing the letters as though it were poison.

We therefore send the said Gaufrid back to your fatherhood, that, according to the order of the events, you may decide concerning him what God inspires in you, and may relieve his weariness and misery with paternal compassion. For it befits apostolic majesty to catch such evaders in their own cunning and shoot from afar, with a strongly drawn bronze bow, those who avoid an iron bow (Letter 199). Farewell.

## LETTER CCII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to LOUIS, by the grace of God sweetest king of the Franks, his lord: greeting and service owed to the extent of his ability.

It does not befit royal majesty to seek trivialities or any enticements of vanity from a priest; nor does it belong to the priestly office to comply with royal majesty in such matters. I give this answer to certain little letters [variant: “letters”] which, on your behalf, requested from me two pairs of cat skins. [Note: Letter 104 calls them “the little skins of foreign mice,” or “an abundance of frivolities.”]

When I read them, I blushed greatly for your honour and could not believe they had been sent to me on your behalf. Yet, as though they had been sent by you, I wrote the foregoing reply, so that you may never again ask such things from me or from any other bishop if you care to preserve the honour due to royal majesty. Farewell.

## LETTER CCIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to LESIARD [variant: LISIARD], by the grace of God bishop of Soissons, greeting.

Of the portions of churches belonging to the bishop which your archdeacons appropriated to themselves before and after your election [Col. 0208B], your belovedness asked whether I possessed a canonical ruling opposed to such audacities and restraining their rapacity by canonical rigor. These are new kinds of diseases and therefore require new kinds of remedies. Yet, if we examine Isidore’s letter addressed to Leufred, bishop of Cordova [Note: [Col. 0207D] Alternatively, Leofred; thus manuscript C; Leufrid, Ludifrid. It is cited by Ivo, *On the Offices of Orders*, book III, and by Gratian [Col. 0208D] in canon *Perlectis*, distinction 15.], it may plainly be understood that an archdeacon has no right, beyond his own portion, to retain for himself anything from the revenues [alternatively, incomes] of parishes, or to appropriate anything beyond the boundaries established by the Fathers. For the aforesaid letter says:
