> “The archdeacon inspects the parishes by the bishop’s command, and reports to the bishop the ornaments and property of the basilicas or parishes, and the records of ecclesiastical freedoms [Col. 0208C]; he himself receives the money collected from the communion and brings it to the bishop.”

These words make clear that he ought to retain nothing for himself beyond his own portion. But if he appropriates anything, let him incur the decretal judgment of Pope John, who says:

> “He who seizes another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore not merely what he seized, but fourfold, according to the Gospel sentence: ‘If I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold’” (Luke 19).

Concerning exactions which must by no means be imposed upon priests, the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 20, reads:

> “Let neither priests nor deacons be burdened with compulsory services or with any imposts.”

If, however, these things were done during your absence, it belongs to your discretion either to pardon them or to punish them with canonical severity. For the law [Col. 0208D] so pardons what is past that it prohibits it for the future (*Law* VII, chapter *On Laws and Imperial Constitutions*). I write little, because I am answering one who is not ignorant of the law. Farewell.

## LETTER CCIV. To his lord and father PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: whatever obedience and whatever service his humility can render.

Let your fatherhood know that I have cut off Guy of Puiset, a fugitive [Note: [Col. 0208D] Compare Letter 76, where he also complains of Hugh of Puiset.], and deserter from the clerical militia, as a rotten limb from the body of the Church, on account of his sacrileges; on account of the lamentation and [Col. 0209A] oppression [alternatively, lamentable oppression] of orphans and widows; on account of unlawful compulsory services; and on account of the intolerable exactions which he practices upon the possessions of the Church of Chartres. I have delivered him, together with his followers [thus manuscript C; earlier editions: “those following”], to Satan, whom in almost every respect he serves.

Therefore, bending the knees of my heart, I beseech your fatherhood to confirm by apostolic authority the sentence of anathema justly pronounced against him; and by your apostolic authority command the archbishop of Sens, the bishop of Orléans, and likewise the bishop of Paris, to pronounce [alternatively, cast] the same anathema against him. For unless you strike the perversity of rebellious sons with paternal severity; unless you cherish the afflicted with maternal consolation [alternatively, [Col. 0209B] compassion]; unless you extend a helping hand to those who labor and are almost falling, the Church will rightly cry out in lament:

> “My head is full of dew, and my locks full of the drops of the night” (Song of Songs 3),

because the briars of vices occupy almost the whole body of the Church, and scarcely any hand is found to root them out. For among us iniquity has so abounded in the leading men of the people that they obey neither paternal admonitions (Letter 128), nor fear God when he threatens, although through the barrenness of the land he afflicts their poor with famine, and by the disease called the holy fire brings the limbs of many to amputation and the bodies of many to death. Their malice must therefore be rebuked both in season and out of season [printed: *increpanda*; earlier edition: *inculpanda*], so that in this way at least God’s severe mercy may be recognized by them.

Moreover, there is a certain disagreement [Col. 0209C] between two prelates of our church, namely the dean and the subdean. In ecclesiastical matters they have certain customs in common and certain customs separately; likewise, certain revenues in common and certain separately. The dean therefore says that some of those things which the subdean has held separately by long possession ought to be common to the dean. Since in this matter the judges are unwilling to agree upon one judgment, in order to say upon whom the burden of proof rests—upon the party affirming or the party denying—we ask that this dispute be settled by your judgment and the dissenting brethren [alternatively: “I wish the matter to be wholly settled and the disagreeing brethren …”] recalled to concord.

For the subdean [alternatively, dean] is prepared, in peace, to relinquish whatever the claimant can prove to be his right, [Col. 0209D] according to the course of the law, which commands judgment against the claimant and possession to remain in its place when the claimant cannot prove that the thing he claims is his (*Institutes* 2, title *On Legacies*, §4). Certain lovers [alternatively, authors] of litigation disturb this matter, pouring out the poison of their envy and hatred by such importunity; they refuse to acquiesce in the institutions of their elders unless bound by irrefutable authority.

Let your fatherhood therefore write to the Church of Chartres whatever it judges concerning this disagreement. Write also to the above-mentioned bishops concerning the restraint of the lamentable malice of sacrilegious persons. The bearer of this letter will report to your holiness [Col. 0210A] the remaining matters necessary to these cases, which it would have taken too long to write; and he will convey to the aforesaid persons whatever pleases your prudence [alternatively, providence]. Farewell.

## LETTER CCV. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to WILLIAM, noble and valiant [alternatively, most valiant] knight, greeting.

The cleric sent by you anxiously and carefully asked my insignificance on your behalf (Letters 252 and 280) what I thought of the dishonorable suspicion which you have cast upon your wife. You allege against her that the child she bore while you were staying in England was not begotten by you, because, after calculating the days between conception and birth, there were found to be seven fewer days than was believed to be the customary duration [Col. 0210B] of pregnancy [Note: [Col. 0209D] See Aulus Gellius, book III, chapter 16, and Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chapter 5.]. You further increase your suspicion because the knight whom you suspected of intercourse with your wife, having undergone the ordeal of hot iron to clear himself, was burned; and no accuser or witness is produced who provides any evidence for your suspicion other than conjectures. Neither the custom of the ancients nor any authority of the laws permits anyone to be condemned on such grounds.

First, concerning the calculation of the days which are said to be lacking, I reply that they provide you with no certain proof; for respectable and experienced women, when questioned by us in order to ascertain the truth, have plainly answered [alternatively, answer] that childbirth does not always occur within the same term [alternatively, number] of days. According to the vigor or [Col. 0210C] weakness of nature, births normally occur a little earlier at one time, a little later at another, after conception. This may easily be inferred from the nature of seeds, since according to the temperateness or intemperateness of the air, crops ripen earlier for harvest in some years and later in others.

Likewise, the branding of the knight offers you no certain proof; for in trials by hot iron, through the hidden judgment of God, we see many guilty persons released and many innocent persons frequently condemned. Moreover, since such an examination is a testing of God, it is not surprising that divine assistance is withheld when someone undertakes it rashly and without judicial sentence. Thus blessed Augustine, defending Abraham for pretending that his wife [Col. 0210D] was his sister, says:

> “When a person has something that he can do, he ought not to test his God.”

Thus Pope Stephen writes to Leubert, bishop of Mainz [manuscript C: “bishop of Mainz”]:

> “The sacred canons do not judge that a confession may be extorted from anyone by an ordeal of hot iron or boiling water (Letters 74 and 280); and what has not been established by the teaching of the holy Fathers must not be presumed upon through superstitious invention. Public offenses, established by voluntary confession or by the testimony of witnesses, are to be judged by those entrusted with governance, with the fear of God before their eyes; but secret and unknown matters must be left to the judgment of him who alone knows the hearts of the children of men” [thus manuscript C; earlier editions: [Col. 0211A] “the hearts of the faithful”].

Likewise, when King Lothair wished to compel his wife Teutberga [Note: [Col. 0211D] Alternatively, Theberga, as in Letter 74; Nicholas the Pope regularly writes Theutberga.] to engage in single combat because of similar suspicions, Pope Nicholas wrote against him:

> “We do not admit trial by combat as law (Letter 280), for we do not find that it has been commanded. Although we read that some have undertaken it—as Sacred History relates concerning holy David and Goliath (1 Samuel 16)—divine authority has nowhere decreed that it should be held as law; since those who follow this and similar practices seem only to be testing God.”

Corrected by these and similar judgments, moderate your zeal, lest by excessive severity you drive yourself, your wife, and your offspring into an infamy which you will not be able to quell, even though you may later, moved by repentance, strive with much toil to quell it. [Col. 0211B] Let the sworn testimony of your wife and of persons of proven character suffice you [manuscript C: “the testimony with an oath”], as the Apostle says: “An oath is the end of every controversy among them” (Hebrews 6). Farewell.

## LETTER CCVI. To HILDEBERT [one copy: LAMBERT], by the grace of God bishop of Le Mans, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting.

Concerning the subdeacon torn by the stain of infamy, we can give your belovedness [manuscript C: “your”] no answer which your prudence does not already know. But because it is pleasing to every right-minded person, when he has learned that many agree in one judgment, it is not unwelcome to our insignificance to write what we have gathered from the authority [Col. 0211C] of the Fathers and what we ourselves are accustomed to observe in such affairs.

For blessed Augustine says (*Homily* 50; canon *Multi*, cause 2, question 1):

> “We cannot remove anyone from communion unless he has either confessed voluntarily, or has been accused and convicted in some ecclesiastical or secular court.”

Likewise Pope Stephen V writes concerning a certain deacon accused from public report [alternatively, “through rumor”; thus manuscript copy] to Leo, bishop of Tiano [alternatively, Theano], canon *De crimine*, cause 5, question 5:

> “If suspicion rests upon a deacon, and suitable accusers are found, and witnesses such as the sacred canons prescribe, then, when he has been proved guilty by lawful witnesses, let him be struck by canonical sentence. But if he neither confesses voluntarily nor are lawful accusers or witnesses found, [Col. 0211D] and evil report becomes widespread, let him clear himself by a secret oath, not in a public examination but before you and the most reverend priests and deacons, and let him remain of good repute.”

On a similar matter Pope Nicholas writes to Solomon [Note: [Col. 0212D] Alternatively, Salon, as in Gratian, canon *Presbyt.*, cause 15, question 5.] bishop of Constance:

> “If, when the bishop investigates the case of a priest or deacon, that priest or deacon has perhaps not been convicted by proof from witnesses, the crime is not lawfully manifest to the bishop, unless perhaps the priest or deacon voluntarily confesses the crime himself. For voluntary confession alone, and the lawful number [alternatively, canonical number] or quality of witnesses—when the bishops have decided and the accuser has proved what he alleged [Col. 0212A]—deprive a cleric of his rank.”

Hence blessed Gregory writes to John, bishop of Palermo, canon *Si quid*, cause 15, question 7:

> “If anything concerning any cleric should come to your ears which can justly give offense, do not readily believe it, lest [alternatively, “and not”] an unknown matter inflame you to vengeance.”

Thus the same writer says in a certain letter (chapter *Presbyter quilibet*, cause 2, question 4):

> “If a priest or any cleric has been accused by the people, and there are no reliable witnesses to establish the truth of the charge brought, an oath shall be administered, so that he may present as witness to the purity of his innocence him to whom all things are naked and open; and thus let him remain in his own rank.”

The authority of the Fathers cited above appears to establish that any cleric assailed by evil report can clear himself by his own hand alone [Col. 0212B] and remain in his rank. Yet the diligence of later [alternatively, subsequent; thus manuscript copy] generations, having learned by experience that human rash cupidity would easily add perjury to wickedness, prescribed a stricter purification to allay the infamy of a priest. It added something to the severity in order to provide more carefully for the honor of priests, since in their mouths the word of God is not precious among the simple unless they also possess a good testimony from those outside (1 Timothy 3).

They placed these matters in the discretion of bishops, so that according as they hear evil report against priests becoming widespread and grave, they may require purgatory oaths from priests under suspicion, with three, five, or seven fellow-priests. Thus the Council of Lleida, chapter 10 (Ivo, book V; and Gratian, canon *Presbyter si*, cause 2, question 4), contains:

> “If any priest has been defamed by the people entrusted to him, and the bishop cannot establish the charge by lawful witnesses, let him be suspended until he has made suitable satisfaction, lest the people suffer scandal on his account. But whether according to the canons or at the bishop’s discretion, let him associate with himself five or seven fellow-priests, with whom, the sacred Gospel having been placed before them, he shall swear that he is free from the crime alleged.”

Some of the earlier Fathers adopted this satisfaction as a custom, following the example of Pope Leo, who was cleared by oaths (Letter 229). From these and similar statements and examples, we believe that it lies within the power of bishops to make the purification of priests more stringent or more lenient, according as [Col. 0212D] they judge necessary both for the protection of their reputation and for the welfare of the peoples entrusted to them. We would have written you more, but we do not think even these things necessary for your prudence. Farewell.

## 89. LETTER CCVII. To SAMSON, by the grace of God bishop of Worcester [alternatively, Wigorniensis], IVO, by the same grace humble minister of the Church, greeting and service.

Although dangers of the sea separate bodily presence by local distance, no spaces of place, however remote, separate the fellowship of minds. Your care has nevertheless shown this in my own lowly person by a manifest proof of affection, [Col. 0213A] when you sent me sandals worthy of apostolic feet (Letter 165). If I have not rendered to your grace the thanks due to it, I did not omit this because [manuscript C: “that”] I am ungrateful, but because I am slow, of unfruitful eloquence, and of manners insufficiently urbane (Letter 7). Therefore, with a request for indulgence, I reproach my own slowness. Yet I would not be found slow if an opportunity presented itself to my longing soul to serve you or yours.

Meanwhile, let us love one another with brotherly affection; and, sailing over this billowy and shipwreck-strewn sea, let us extend to one another the mutual hands of prayer, so that after these perils of the sea we may be able to rest safely in the harbor of salvation. Farewell.

## LETTER CCVIII. IVO, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to GEOFFREY, his beloved brother in Christ [Note: [Col. 0213D] He is called a cultivator of solitude in the heading of Letter 164.]: to behold the Jerusalem of Zion.

[Col. 0213B]

Dearest brother, you know concerning yourself—and know better than I—with how great a confidence of hope and how great a commendation from men, after trampling down the flower of the world, you chose the solitary life; and how, after preserving that solitary way of life commendably for some time, you were called to govern a monastery. You know that you could not endure, in preference to your love of inward quiet, the popular disturbances without which not even a modest management of household property can be administered. Therefore you strove by every means to return to the quiet you had interrupted. You yourself chose in your place as abbot [Note: [Col. 0213D] Maurice, as is clear from comparison with Letter 164.] the man whom the community entrusted to you desired; and, like a dove flying away from troubles, [Col. 0213C] you withdrew [alternatively, flew away], in order to remain in solitude and wait for him who would save you from faintheartedness and restlessness.

Now, however, as some say, contrary to your purpose you gladly receive within your cell gossiping monks wandering from place to place, disparaging their abbot, and double-tongued; you willingly open your ear to their murmurings; and you spend not merely a great part of the day but also of the night, not merely in superfluous (Letter 240) but even in harmful conversations. You make your secluded place public, while through an undue curiosity, enticed by I know not what vanity, you allow the silence of monks to be interrupted by flattering and disparaging speech.

It is also said that you do not permit those knights who hold benefices of the monastery (Letters 153 and 168), as though reserving them for yourself, to render homage [some books: *hominatum*, “homage-service”] to the abbot. Many things are said in this fashion, all of which your religious profession ought most carefully to guard against, so that they either do not exist at all or cannot plausibly be invented. God knows why I wrote this to you: I wrote it because, even if not everything is as reported, but has perhaps been fabricated by enemies, I nevertheless know that slandering enemies sometimes benefit us more than flattering friends; and Solomon says that “the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses [Col. 0214A] of one who flatters” (Proverbs 27). I could write much in this manner to your prudence, but these things suffice for a wise man. Farewell.

## LETTER CCIX. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to HUGH, illustrious count of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0213D] One manuscript wrongly has “of Utrecht”; Letter 245 [Col. 0214D] is addressed to Hugh, count of the people of Troyes.], greeting and service.

I wish to make known to your highness that the inquiry due to be heard at Sens on the octave of Pentecost, concerning the marriage of the king and your cousin, the daughter of Marquis Boniface, is neither honorable nor useful to the maiden whose marriage is to be considered. It is useless because the agreement entered into regarding that marriage will be wholly annulled by the counsel of bishops and nobles [alternatively, magnates]. Nor will it be honorable, because the dishonor of the maiden—who was not born of a lawful marriage—will be spread far and wide.

For no one who has sworn fealty to the king will presume to give counsel contrary to his fealty and diminishing the majesty of the kingdom. Among the duties contained in fealty, what is useful and honorable must above all be observed. Those who decreed that a woman born from an incestuous marriage should be joined to the royal person would by no means observe these principles. Already there is heard the murmur of dukes and marquises [Note: [Col. 0214D] Thus manuscript C; alternatively, *marcionum*; one manuscript wrongly has “nations.”], who are already deliberating whether they should withdraw from the king [alternatively, “from the kingdom”] if they can find so manifest an occasion.

You therefore, who are the intermediary in this marriage, can provide for both parties: so that the king may not incur perjury, [Col. 0214C] nor your cousin a shameful repudiation—especially since the king says that he was ignorant of this stain and swore simply upon your word. For this reason I write to you while absent what I would say in your presence, taking counsel in this matter both for my own fidelity and for the honor of your nobility: namely, that you may regulate this matter so discreetly and prudently that you meet by sound counsel all that may arise from this contract [earlier: *contactu*, “contact”]. It seems to me more advisable, therefore, that the convoked assembly not be held, lest the matter, further debated, turn out worse. Farewell.

## LETTER CCX. To PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: for faithful stewardship, may you enjoy the eternal vision.

[Col. 0214D] Because consideration of apostolic dispensation does not please everyone equally, nor is equally known to everyone, men sometimes murmur against a good steward who would not dare murmur against a just judge. Your dispensations, therefore, ought to be so weighed that, if they grant mercy to the undeserving, they do not inflict violence upon those who have deserved well.

I have prefaced this to your fatherhood out of filial affection because Lord Odo, bishop of Cambrai, laments anxiously, together with many who lament with him, that you have deprived Ralph, archdeacon of Brabant [alternatively, Bribant or Bribat], of his archdeaconry without a hearing and without judgment, though he has always stood with the Roman Church; while you have invested Geoffrey [alternatively, Gaucher, Gaulcher, or Galcher], an opponent of the Apostolic See, with the same archdeaconry. Therefore, for the sake both of justice and of the honor of the Apostolic See, we beseech your holiness that, if a severe judgment against one who has deserved well was wrung from your mouth by someone’s importunity, it may be so moderated by your discretion that the anxiety of the religious bishop may be relieved and the deserving brother not burdened. Thus in this action those who have deserved ill may not glory in their presumption, nor those who have deserved well, falling from their hope, be compelled to grieve. For the ancient praise of strong men is:

> “To spare the conquered and subdue the proud.”  
> [Col. 0215B] (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI)

Farewell.

## LETTER CCXI. To RALPH, by the grace of God [manuscript C: “reverend”] archbishop of Reims, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting and service.

I learned of the consanguinity said to exist between the son of the count of Flanders and the daughter of the count of Rennes when I was at the court of Pope Urban. This was not because of these children, who perhaps were not yet born, but because of their grandfathers or paternal or maternal great-grandfathers, whose consanguinity was then being discussed under pressure of necessity. At the suggestion of the lord pope, in my hearing, a certain monk of Auvergne named Castus calculated it [Col. 0215C]—a man mature in age, born of the nobles of that land, honorable in life and reputation.

At another time, the legates of Fulk, count of Anjou, calculated the same consanguinity in the aforesaid court and established it when King Philip of the Franks was accused of having taken from the said count his kinsman’s wife [Note: [Col. 0215D] Letter 13 calls her Bertrada.], whom he was also unlawfully retaining. Because of that accusation and the proof of the incest committed, the king [manuscript C: Philip] was excommunicated by Pope Urban at the Council of Clermont [Note: [Col. 0215D] Urban II presided over this in the year 1095.]. When, after the divorce had been made, the said king returned to the company [manuscript C: unlawful] of the aforesaid woman, he was excommunicated at the Council of Poitiers by Cardinals John and Benedict.

I write these things while absent, though I would say nothing else relevant if I were present. I would gladly meet with you for conversation, dear to me though it is, were I not hindered by the serpent in the road, the horned viper in the path—namely the lord of Puiset [Note: [Col. 0216D] Alternatively, *domnus*, “lord.” See Letters 76 and 111, concerning Hugh of Puiset.]—whom we have excommunicated because of the intolerable injuries he inflicts on our church. The genealogists whom you instructed to come with me, and whom I have mentioned above, are not my parishioners; nor do I even know whether they are alive, so that I can invite them to this inquiry.

The genealogy is as follows:

Geoffrey Greycloak [two manuscript copies and manuscript C: “brothers”]; Fulk, count of Anjou. [Col. 0216A] Countess of Vexin [alternatively, Vastinensis or Vassenensis]; Fulk Rechin; countess of Rennes; her daughter N.; Blanche, countess of Arles; Queen Constance; Adera, countess of Flanders; Albert Friso [manuscript C: Robert]; Robert, son of Friso; in the sixth degree, N., son of this Robert.

## LETTER CCXII. Ivo, minister of the Church of Chartres, to GEOFFREY, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais, greeting.

Concerning the man who many years ago devoted his goods to the monastery [Col. 0216B] of Saint Symphorian and, at the time of his death, entrusted himself and his goods to it, no one contesting this: I reply to your belovedness what accords with laws, customs, and reason. Namely, if no action was brought against the aforesaid monk while he lived in the monastery, what he conveyed to the monastery cannot be alienated from it by any claim of right, provided that this challenger knew of the conversion of the aforesaid monk.

For just as the law and reason teach concerning accusations (*final law*, chapter *On the Julian Law*)—so also concerning agreements (*Law* IV, Digest *On Leasing*, and *Law* L, Digest *On Things Adjudged*)—that one who is already subject solely to divine judgment is not to be summoned further before human judgment. Moreover, even if the things which that challenger alleges are true, namely that he was named heir by the aforesaid monk, the book of the *Institutes* concerning heirs nevertheless provides [Col. 0216C] that an earlier will is dissolved by a later one. And in the Theodosian laws (Anianus, scholium to Paul’s *Sentences*, book V, title 11):

> “If anyone gives one thing by lawful documents to two persons, to one earlier and to the other later, it is not to be asked in these gifts who is first and who later; but whoever, when the donor delivers it, has possessed the thing, shall possess that which has been delivered to him.”

Unless other matters of which we have not heard prevent it, the proposed controversy may be decided reasonably and lawfully in this way. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXIII. To JOHN, by the grace of God bishop of Orléans, Ivo, by the same grace minister of Chartres, greeting and love in the Lord.

[Col. 0216D] Certain brethren living in common in your bishopric came to us, carefully asking whether clerics living according to a rule can govern parishes and have the care of souls (Letter 69). I answered them that in the primitive Church no one was appointed a ruler of souls unless he had been chosen from the common life, because no one is more rightly set over the guardianship of another’s life than he who has first been made guardian of his own life. This is better demonstrated nowhere than among those in whom regular life seems to flourish, since another’s wickedness displeases them only as much as their own first displeased them.

Thus Clement says in his fourth letter (Letter 5; and canon *Dilectissimis*, [Col. 0217A] cause 12, question 1):

> “The common life, brothers, is necessary for all, and especially for those who desire to live irreproachably and wish to imitate the life of the apostles and their disciples.”

And in what follows:

> “Therefore, giving counsel, we exhort your prudence not to depart from the apostolic rules, but, living the common life and understanding the sacred Scriptures, to strive to fulfill what you have vowed to God.”

Likewise Pope Urban says in his first decretal (the first [letter] in canon *Scimus*, cause 12, question 1):

> “We know, brothers, that you are not ignorant that common life has hitherto flourished among good Christians and still flourishes by the grace of God, especially among those chosen for the Lord’s portion—that is, among clerics.”

These apostolic judgments exclude no cleric from the common life, neither a priest of a city church [Col. 0217B] nor one of a suburban church. That the common life has almost failed in all churches, both metropolitan and diocesan, must be attributed not to authority but to disuse and decay: love has grown cold, though it wishes all things to be held in common, while cupidity reigns, seeking not the things of God and neighbor but only its own.

Relying upon these reasons and authorities, we firmly maintain that those are not to be heard who judge clerics living according to a rule to be excluded from the governance of souls (Letter 69) because they have renounced the world. Rather, they ought for that very reason to be chosen for it, because they have despised the pleasures and pomp of the world. For it is not the business of worldly trade to call souls away from vices and summon them to the heights of virtues. Therefore those who fulfill in action what they say teach these things more suitably than those who are teachers of the law but not doers of the law. Nevertheless, none should be chosen for this office except those whom life and teaching commend, and whom episcopal authority finds fit for its exercise.

I have written this fraternally to your belovedness, so that you may restrain the rapacity of those who seek their own advantage against the little flock of God and enable them to live quietly in the clerical militia. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXIV. To BRUNO, by the grace of God bishop of the first see of the Belgians, Ivo, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Chartres: may you arrive, across this broad and stormy sea, at the harbor of eternal blessedness.

Although your bodily presence is hidden from the eyes of my body, [Col. 0217D] the divine grace that shines in you is not hidden from the eyes of my mind. By it there still remain in the world certain lights which, shining in word and example, can illuminate the darkness of vices and make bright the splendor of virtues. For just as, when vapors of this lower air intervene, the lights of heaven sometimes cannot cast their light upon the earth, yet do not cease to illuminate the calm spaces of the upper air, so the lights of the Church, although they sometimes refrain from setting what is holy before dogs and pearls before swine (Matthew 7), lest the word of God, because of barking and trampling, run and bear fruit less fully among weak hearers, nevertheless, if they find anyone devout, humble, and quiet in this vale of weeping, they form him by examples and do not cease to enlighten him with the rays of spiritual teaching.

And the more we see the world lying in evil—which Isaiah laments in saying, “The whole head is sick and the whole heart faint; from the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isaiah 1)—the more those in whom God has placed the light of his grace ought to oppose the lamentable ruins of the Church and, to the extent of their powers, restore Christ’s bride, darkened by stains and wrinkles, to the beauty of her virginity.

For we see kingdom and priesthood torn apart [Note: [Col. 0217D] On account of the controversy over investitures; see Letter 236.], though the stability of God’s tabernacle was firmly fastened by them as its chief and strongest pegs, so that it might not be overthrown by any force of storms and whirlwinds. [Col. 0218B] In so great a rupture, in so great a tempest, Mother Church cannot flourish and bear fruit—she of whom it is said, “My dove, my bride, is one” (Song of Songs 6).

The members of Christ ought to labor to repair this unity, cutting away these corruptions medicinally with the knife, or endeavoring to heal so great a rupture with the fitting poultice of dispensation. For amid such great danger to salvation, the rigor of medicine alone must not be observed; the method of dispensation also, which displeases no wise person, must in some cases be admitted in order to calm such disturbances. For Cyril of Alexandria teaches [Note: [Col. 0218D] Chapter *Dispensationes*, cause 1, question 7; also cited in Letter 171.] that, just as sailors endangered at sea, when they have no hope of saving all their cargo, throw some things overboard so as to save others, so in ecclesiastical dispensations, where the truth of faith and uprightness of morals are not endangered, [Col. 0218C] we ought to moderate certain enactments in order to aid such great ruins of the Church.

Thus the haircloth curtains in God’s tabernacle, laid beneath fine linen and purple, scarlet and hyacinth (Exodus 35), received rain and dust upon themselves, so that they might preserve the beauty of the inner ornaments from wetting by rain and darkening by dust. This is the work of love, which “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4), which is weak with the weak, burns with those who are scandalized (2 Corinthians 11), and becomes all things to all (1 Corinthians 9), so that it may deserve to benefit all.

Therefore the dispensation of prelates ought not to be reproved by subjects if, with the foundation of faith preserved (Letters 190, 250) and the common rule of morals recognized, they do or tolerate certain imperfect things in order to be able to preserve the life of their subjects in the purpose of holiness. Thus blessed Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule*:

> “If inwardly you shine red like scarlet, why do you accuse the haircloth by which you are protected?”

Thus we sing both mercy and judgment to the Lord (Psalm 100). Judgment, when we resist vices with all severity; mercy, when we temper the rigor of discipline by beneficial compensation. In saying these things I do not instruct the prudence of my elders and fellow bishops, but desire, as it were, to awaken them by the prompting of love from a long sleep, so that at last each may, according to the office he bears, oppose such great ruins, lest through his [Col. 0219A] silence he perish like a dumb dog.

Out of the boldness of love, I have written these few things from remote regions to your excellency, whose good renown, reaching even us, I have sweetly perceived. And because in the Belgian province you excel in religious devotion and authority, I beseech your holiness to remember my insignificance from time to time and endeavor, on this journey of pilgrimage, to refresh with a consoling word my faintheartedness, which murmurs and sometimes almost fails [Note: [Col. 0219D] Thus several manuscript copies; others, “to comfort.” Letter 150 speaks of “the refreshing of the soul.”]. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXV. To THOMAS [alternatively, TUSTAN], archbishop of York, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: for faithful dispensation, may you merit the joy of the good servant.

Blessed be God, who makes your manner of life shine [Col. 0219B] amid the darkness of a barbarous people, so that you may benefit those set under your charge by word and example, and may send even to us the fragrance of your good repute. Desiring therefore to bind more closely between us the bond of love, I have sent these present little letters [variant: letters] to your kindness, so that by this reminder we may learn mutually to refresh one another with reciprocal consolations and to support one another with the devoted assistance of prayers. For, since those placed in governance are often threatened by the perils which the Psalmist mentions, saying: “They go up to the heavens and go down to the depths; they were troubled and reeled like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up” (Ps. 106), this is the one remedy we must seek which follows: “They cried to the Lord in their distress, [Col. 0219C] 92 and he brought them out of their tribulations” (ibid.).

Love makes this cry worthy of hearing; neither the inequality of times hinders it nor the distance of places cuts it off, since the One who hears is present everywhere, who both supplies pious vows [variant: who, together with pious vows] and does not delay to fulfill petitions. Hence it is that, as a figure of those who love one another in the tabernacle of God, the two cherubim look at one another and turn their faces toward the mercy-seat (Exod. 25): so that they may display mutual love among themselves and may confidently trust, with God’s favor, that they can obtain what love prompting them has requested.

Let us in this manner look upon one another with the gaze of love, extend to one another the hands of prayer, and humbly ascribe to divine propitiation whatever is necessary for our salvation, whether already obtained or yet to be obtained [Col. 0219D]. It will so moderate the dangers of this stormy sea, in which are creeping things without number (Ps. 103), that it will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can endure, but will provide with the temptation a way of escape (1 Cor. 10)—he who commands winds and sea (Matt. 8)—so that we may overcome the swellings of the waters.

Moreover, let your Excellency know that our smallness is ready not only to offer the aid of prayers, [Col. 0220A] but also every office of charity which the resources or learning divinely bestowed upon us can provide. Farewell.

## LETTER 216. IVO, HUMBLE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO RICHARD, BY GOD’S GRACE BISHOP OF ALBANO AND VICAR OF THE HOLY APOSTOLIC SEE: OBEDIENCE AND GREETING.

[Note: [Col. 0219D] In several ancient codices this heading occurs: “Concerning the dispute of the abbot of Bonneval and the abbot of Blois over the Church of Ver.” This seemed worth noting [Col. 0220D], because throughout this letter, as also throughout the following one, no mention is made of the Church of Ver.]

The abbot of Bonneval frequently assails the ears of your concern, avoiding in his accounts of his affairs what harms him and exaggerating by rhetorical declamation what benefits him, as though I were diminishing something granted by me to him and conceding it to the abbot of Blois. But I wish to defend inviolate for each man what I have granted. For I granted the abbot of Bonneval nothing other than what he could acquire from the possessors—or rather, the holders without right—of a certain parish belonging to us. [Col. 0220B] Yet he wishes, through our grant, to extort even things which he cannot obtain from them.

The abbot of Blois, however, obtained from the holders the remaining portions of the same church, which no one had granted to the abbot of Bonneval. Had he wished to share these with the abbot of Bonneval, peace between them would already have been restored. Since justice did not permit me to inflict violence upon the abbot of Blois in this matter, I wished to end this dispute so that each should be content with the portion granted him and neither should occupy the other’s boundaries. But the limitless greed of monks causes their discord to remain limitless.

[Note: Elsewhere he calls the envy of monks “demonic,” Letter 266.]

Therefore let not your discernment be angry with me if I cannot accomplish in this business what I wish. Furthermore, the abbot of Bonneval complained quite unjustly that, concerning his monastery, [Col. 0220C] the judgment promulgated at the Council of Fleury concerning the cemetery—over which there was a dispute between the abbot of the monastery of Chartres and the abbot of the monastery of Bonneval—had not been observed. Yet Truth knows that the oaths adjudged at the aforesaid council were taken with every diligence. But the abbot of Bonneval disdained to hear them, because he saw that they harmed him; for his own will is chiefly his reason and authority. Farewell.

## LETTER 217. IVO, HUMBLE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO RICHARD, BY GOD’S GRACE BISHOP OF ALBANO AND VICAR OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE: DUE AND DEVOTED OBEDIENCE.

In accordance with your counsel and admonition (Letter 216), I summoned the abbot of Blois and the abbot of Bonneval [Col. 0220D] before us, so that in discharge of my office I might either restore peace between them or settle their dispute by judicial procedure. At the first hearing [variant: approach, MS C], I directed my efforts toward securing for him peacefully from the possessors the fourth part of the church concerning which the litigation had arisen, although he did not yet hold it, even though it had been granted by me. Then I sought to acquire another fourth part, granted to him neither by me nor by anyone else, so that solely through goodwill [Col. 0221A] he might thus enter into the labors of others, gather where he had not scattered, and reap where he had not sown—on this condition, however: that if thereafter any disputes concerning it should be raised by laymen, both abbots should work together to obtain peace; if any expense were necessary, they should bear it together; and they should divide benefits and burdens in equal measure.

When the abbot of Blois had given his assent to this arrangement, if not willingly, yet obediently, the abbot of Bonneval would acquiesce neither in my counsel nor in my judgment. In this affair he can allege no adequate reason, unless perhaps the poetic saying: “Every power is impatient of a partner in rule” (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, I.92–93). He relies upon some novel and hitherto unheard-of injunction which attacks charity rather than follows authority [Col. 0221B].

[Note: Perhaps an injunction of the Roman pontiff, such as that which he refutes in Letter 195.]

Yet, if it remains inviolate, it will benefit the abbot of Blois more than the abbot of Bonneval. For the monastery of Blois had for many preceding years possessed a share of the tithes and offerings belonging to the church from which this dispute arose, as the evidence itself proves and as the abbot himself will be able to disclose when necessary. I have written this meanwhile to your concern, lest you attribute it to idleness or contempt if you should hear that I had taken no action in the matter. Farewell.

## LETTER 218. IVO, HUMBLE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO GUALO, BY GOD’S GRACE BISHOP OF PARIS: GREETING.

Concerning the canon of your church who, contrary to your prohibition, drew up for himself marriage contracts [Col. 0221C] (Letter 200), I have no ruling ready to hand of which your charity would be unaware, if it carefully searches the writings preserved with it. Nevertheless, I judge that the counsel which I myself would give, if I found one of the brethren entrusted to me bound in the marital fetter (*uxoria compede*) (canons 16, 17, 18, distinction 81), is safe: namely, that the sacrament of marriage should remain, but that the cleric who, abandoning clerical continence, has descended from a higher order to a lower should lose the pay of clerical service.

For your charity knows that, when someone is taken from lay life into the clergy [variant: from lay conduct into the clergy], he is dedicated not to marital activity but solely to the service of God. Hence [Col. 0221D] 93 at the ordination of clerics their ordainers say of them: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord” (Ps. 23); it is not said, “of those who seek marriage,” but “of those who seek the Lord alone.” For, as apostolic teaching testifies: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved [variant: proved himself] acceptable” (2 Tim. 2).

After, therefore, someone has received the higher rank from the lower rank of laypeople—that is, clerical service—and has then hurled himself down into marital pleasure, no reasoning permits him, while in that condition, to enjoy the dignity and benefit of that order which he seems to have exchanged for miserable pleasure. For clerical service was instituted [Col. 0222A] in order that it might offer God the daily sacrifice of psalmody and hymnody. Rightly he cannot offer this sacrifice who, in order to please his wife more than God, must devote himself to her, through his wife’s enticement and the deceiving pleasure of the flesh.

For if, according to the Apostle, laypeople are not permitted to pray except during the period in which they practice continence (1 Cor. 7, cited in ch. 1, distinction 31), how much more ought those always to remain continent who are commanded to pray both for their own sins and for those of others. Indeed, the offerings of the faithful were assigned as the pay of clerics [Note: [Col. 0222D] Thus in several old codices; previously, incorrectly, “prayers.”], so that they might both live continently and be able, through the intercession of holiness, to cleanse the sins of their benefactors; thus those on whose alms they live may attain through the clerics’ merits what they do not deserve to attain through their own.

So long as they are engaged in this contest [Col. 0222B] and abstain from all things from which they ought to abstain, they are deservedly held worthy of the pay of their service. But when they have disdained to observe these things [variant: when they have disdained to approve these things], they are judged unworthy of it. For their deposition, this alone seems sufficient: that they both presume what is unlawful and disdain to obey the salutary commands of bishops, according to the Apostle’s words: “Having in readiness to avenge all disobedience” (2 Cor. 10).

Furthermore, one who stubbornly and proudly despises an honorable and useful custom of the Church—which authority judges must be held as law—plainly proves to be a violator of canonical institution. Whoever spares such contempt exposes many to danger. Thus the canons of Nicaea (Nicaea, canons 3 and 16, distinction 32) and the Council of Agde [Col. 0222C] forbid a cleric not only to enter into carnal union with women, but even to have a household association with them, excepting persons who afford no ground for suspicion (law XIX, ch. *De episcopis et clericis*, and chs. 25 and 29, distinction 8). The judgments of the holy Fathers—Augustine, Jerome, and the other doctors who wrote on the life of clerics—also agree with this ruling. I mention all this briefly because I know that none of it is unknown to you. Farewell.

## LETTER 219. IVO, HUMBLE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO HIS LORD AND FATHER PASCHAL, SUPREME PONTIFF: TO A FATHER HONOR, TO A LORD FEAR.

[Col. 0222D]

To use Cyprian’s words: “If some falsehood concerning me has preceded me to the Apostolic See, truth ought to follow,” so that it may uncover the robberies of the night (Letter 133) and clearly disclose the sequence of events. Recently I received letters, sealed with an apostolic seal, from a certain young man, a canon of our church. When I had opened and read them, I considered them suspect for many reasons, thinking that they were either surreptitious or fraudulently obtained by some suggestion.

First, because the aforesaid young man is hostile to me because I do not permit him, contrary to the canons and decrees of councils, to usurp the priesthood in a certain [Col. 0223A] church through lay investiture (canon *Sub caus.*, 16, question 7), and to appropriate to his own uses the offerings taken from the priest. The other cleric who was with the young man is likewise hostile to me. In this matter he is a nobody, since he is not a canon and ought not to be heard in an assembly of honorable men; I have suspended him from the office of deacon because of incest committed with the wife of his kinsman. Let this suffice for the moment concerning the persons involved.

Moreover, we have neither read nor heard that it has hitherto been the custom of the Apostolic See to render judgment against an absent person upon the accusation of one person, however eminent—especially one who had neither been heard nor summoned. Although I could complain and argue extensively concerning such lawlessness, I preferred to preserve the humility of one who obeys [Col. 0223B] rather than arrogate to myself the cleverness of one who disputes.

It remains, therefore, that I should defend my innocence, which has God and my conscience as witnesses. For those letters, whoever their authors may be, allege against me that I bestowed half of a certain provostship upon the community of canons, and that I took the same from those canons, contrary to the canons, under the threat of royal power. To this calumny I reply from the testimony of my conscience: it is wrongly said that what could canonically have been bestowed upon them, whether by me or by anyone else, was taken away; nor should that be restored which cannot be proved ever to have been established.

I shall therefore tell your Fatherhood what I gave and what I did not give, why I gave it, and why I refused to give anything further.

[Note: [Col. 0223D] “These things and some others made those letters suspect to me. Yet, whoever their authors may be, they accuse my innocence: namely, that I bestowed half the provostship upon the community of brethren and took the same from the brethren, contrary to the canons, under the threat of royal power. To this calumny: If anything against me has been carried to the Apostolic See, truth, not deceitful, ought to follow on my behalf with the legate’s document, so that it may answer the charges and defend [Col. 0224D] my innocence. Recently I received letters from a certain young man, a canon of our church, sealed with an apostolic seal. When I had opened and read them, I was astonished that, at the suggestion of a certain young man and contrary to the custom of the Apostolic See, those letters rendered judgment against an absent man—namely, one who had not been heard or summoned.” Thus MS codex.]

Since observance of regular discipline had fallen into disuse among very many of the canons [Col. 0223C] of Chartres [variant: clerics, MS C], I deliberated with myself, in order to make the negligent diligent, the sleepy watchful [variant: vigilant], and the tardy assiduous [thus several old codices; formerly “accustomed”], in attending the canonical hours, that I should give them half the provostship. From it there would be made a daily bread: the assiduous would receive it, the tardy would lose it. Thus, although their annual prebend ought to have been sufficient for this purpose, the nourishment of bodily bread might incite them to attend the canonical hours, when the sweetness of inward bread did not move them.

Yet, certain of their past negligence and anxious concerning the future, I ordered them to send me two men from that clergy. When they were sent, I entrusted to them the produce currently available for that year, [Col. 0223D] that they might prepare daily bread from it and, according to the arrangement delivered to them, distribute it among their fellow brethren [variant: with the brethren]. Truth knows that I gave nothing else, giving or promising them nothing further, except that, if I found them faithful and assiduous in this small matter, I might be pleased to grant them possession of the property and confirm it by lawful stipulation.

Within three months this arrangement [Col. 0224A] had been so perverted that no desire or reason persuaded me, and no counsel of fellow bishops or religious men approved, that I should diminish episcopal dignity for the unfruitful enlargement of canonical resources. For some of the older men sold those loaves; some of the younger gave them for dice-playing; and he who presented himself to be seen [variant: one presented himself to be seen, MS C] at the night hours withdrew himself from the daytime ones; and he who heard the Mass of the Catechumens slipped away from the Mass of the Sacraments. Such was the outcome that it recalled me from my purpose 94: I did not take from them what I had not given, but neither did I undertake what I had proposed.

By these words it is clear that, of the things I bestowed upon them, I took away absolutely nothing under the threat of royal power [Col. 0224B]; nor did I invite or admit the king into ecclesiastical dispensations or cases. By great labor, sweat, and many expenses, I kept him far from molesting the Church, from burnings and plundering of ecclesiastical goods. In this matter the greater and sounder part of the Church was with me. But some, less experienced in such proceedings, understood the affair to have been otherwise than it was. When their calumny had been brought before the metropolitan and finally referred to him, a definite decision was issued in this matter; every controversy was put to rest, confirmed by the kiss of peace, and praised in a full chapter by all except those who had not been present [variant: had not attended].

When these matters had been settled in their order, [Col. 0224C] I wished, out of my goodwill—which brought me many burdens—to grant the aforesaid part of the said provostship to twelve priests, if such persons could be found who might be chosen for this office and in due time advanced to the priesthood. Although I diligently sought them through the dean of the church, through myself, and through letters of Lord Richard, bishop of Albano and your legate, not one was found who either wished or was able to be advanced or chosen for that office.

Therefore, on the counsel of that same legate of yours and of almost the entire Church—with no one resisting or contradicting—I made a personal appointment as best I could, so that the Church might not be disturbed by this matter repeatedly; and I bestowed it upon an honorable cleric, useful both for administering and defending that same property [variant: granted; thus MS C]. [Col. 0224D] For this appointment I would have sought no one other than the man who held the other half, except that he was suspect to the Church, as though this disturbance in the Church had arisen through him. Once this man had been appointed there, the murmuring was quieted and the Church rested.

Therefore, lest the Church should henceforth be disturbed on this empty pretext, with the knees of our hearts bent, we beseech your fatherly mercy [Col. 0225A] not to reopen a case once decided because of the accusations of greedy and malicious persons; not merely not to shake the peace which the Church now has, but to approve it with the affection due to your fatherhood; and henceforth not to permit my old age to be harassed by the excessive and unpunished license of appellants. For while adversity inflicted by a superior authority presses upon us, our authority to govern is weakened within us, since we dare not exercise ecclesiastical discipline against those who appeal against it—not through confidence in justice, but to delay judgment.

If, however, we still possessed enough youthful vigor to travel on foot over the ruined [variant: “noisy,” MS C] paths of the Alps, to ride across the precipitous waters of rushing torrents, and to precede or follow our accusers to the Apostolic [Col. 0225B] See, without doubt the tongue of the murmurers would restrain itself; it knows as yet too little how great the difference is between the serenity of charity and the darkness of greed. If, then, you do not provide some remedy against these troubles, and expose me to harassment by men hardened by long evil days and by undisciplined young men—who scarcely deserve to possess what they have, much less to seek what they do not have—one safe and complete counsel remains to me: to take up the wings of a dove (Ps. 54), fly away from useless vexations, and rest in the solitude of a mountain, where I may await him who saves me from faintness of spirit and unrest.

Both before becoming bishop and during my episcopate, my will has always been [Col. 0225C] to be saved rather in a lowly place than endangered in a high one, and to be lowly in the house of God rather than preside over those to whom I could not be of benefit. But because we do not wish to burden the ears of such high dignity with words unto weariness, these brethren will supply whatever has been said less fully than necessary, and, if needed, prove it. Farewell.

## LETTER 220. IVO, BY THE SAME GRACE HUMBLE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO HILDEBERT, BY GOD’S GRACE BISHOP OF LE MANS: GREETING.

Concerning the procedure of appeal, so far as I judge, nothing is found with us which is not likewise found with you. Yet, lest it seem wearisome to reply to a friend, I briefly write back to your charity [Col. 0225D] what I think on this matter. First, then, I understand this: because of an appellant’s plea, you must never go from church to church or province to province unless the appellant first brings letters of summons from the judge to whom the appeal has been made; in these letters that judge sets the day and place for hearing the case.

Thus Pope Felix says (canon 15, cause 3, question 6, and Letter 172): “No one ought to be brought from province to province except upon a communication from the judge to whom appeal has been made.” The appellant himself must, within five days, receive from the judge from whom he appealed letters to be sent to the judge to whom he appealed. Whoever neglects to receive or request these [Col. 0226A] is, according to the statutes of the laws, to be barred from proceeding. And if he has perhaps appealed unjustly, he must be compelled to pay the expenses which his opponent incurred in pursuing the appeal.

Furthermore, the abbot’s demand that, through your stipulation, he may hold undisturbed the common property of the brethren seems quite absurd. It is absurd to demand from you what is manifestly proved not to be within your legal power, since canonical authority prohibits it (ch. *Sine*, cause 12, question 2): namely, that no bishop may alienate, exchange, or give away the property of the Church without the assent [variant: agreement] of the clergy. Hence one reads in the pontifical Decrees: “Cases not governed by laws are not to be heard at all by ecclesiastical judges” (same, Letters 119 and 241). I write only a little in reply to your questions, because I do not doubt [Col. 0226B] that you know these matters and better ones. Farewell.

## LETTER 221. IVO, BY THE SAME GRACE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO JOHN, BY GOD’S GRACE BISHOP OF ORLÉANS: GREETING.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] This subject is also treated in Letter 242.]

Concerning a free man who unknowingly took a slave woman as his wife, afterwards dismissed her when he learned the truth, and now, with permission received from you, intends to marry another: I state to your charity what I think. If we wish to consult the decrees of the Fathers and the laws of the world on this matter, we shall find that lawful marriages are held to exist only between freeborn persons and equals, and that where another result has occurred through ignorance, divorces are lawful.

But if we consult the divine institution and the law of nature, in which there is neither slave nor free, I cannot easily be persuaded that a human law enacted later can annul the sacrament of marriage because of a social condition which nature did not possess [Col. 0226C] and which divine 95 law did not exempt from the law of marriage—although the sacrament is known to have been confirmed by the old law and by the Gospel. If the husband, because of marital affection, does not wish to undergo slavery, and does not wish to procure freedom for the woman, I think the matter should be arranged thus: if by some dispensation we permit marital relations to cease, we should not therefore permit the sacrament of marriage to be annulled.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] *Ideo* (“therefore”) is absent in MS C.]

Thus we shall be neither outright violators of the Gospel nor despisers of human laws. This is my view of the proposed question; yet I do not dissent from those who say better and more firmly, if they think in accordance with the Gospel and the Apostle. Farewell.

## LETTER 222. IVO, BY GOD’S GRACE HUMBLE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO THE CLERGY OF AUTUN [variant: Edulensian, MS C]: TO GIVE HEED TO THE SINGLE FACE OF PURE UTTERANCES.

[Col. 0226D]

Since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24), we do not understand the divine Scriptures to disagree with one another when one passage upholds the rigor of justice and another follows the dispensation of indulgence. Leaving aside for the moment the allegorical meaning, I think that this must be considered in relation to the Gospel judgment, which absolutely advises an adulteress either to be reconciled to her former husband (Matt. 19) or to remain unmarried (1 Cor. 7), and to the Old Testament ruling which says that an adulteress dismissed by her former husband and joined in marriage to another may by no means be reconciled to the former husband if she is repudiated by the latter.

This ruling, which forbids reconciliation of the adulteress, seems to me to follow the rigor of justice, lest, while one person is spared, many be put at risk, and liberty allowed to a few cause the crimes of very many to flourish. This is notably found in the very wording of the law, where this is added to the prohibition: “Do not cause the land which the Lord your God gave you to possess to sin” (Deut. 24). The Gospel ruling, however, adapted to human weakness, wills mercy rather than judgment. It moderates the severity of the law, advising without any exception that reconciliation be effected for an adulterous woman. Our Fathers after the Gospel [Col. 0227B] followed it, understanding mercy to be more useful than judgment in such a situation.

But blessed Jerome, honoring the legal sanctity of the sacraments in his customary manner, follows in this ruling the severity of the law, understanding that salvation can thus be safeguarded more securely. In this ambiguity evangelical authority puts an end to the matter, against which neither personal nor epistolary opinion should prevail. Hence Leo IV writes thus to the bishops of Britain:

[Note: [Col. 0227D] It appears more fully in Ivo’s *Decretum*, book II, and in ch. *De libellis*, distinction 20.]

> “It is not fitting for anyone to judge from the writings and commentaries of any persons whatsoever, and to abandon the rules of canons and decrees.”

Blessed Augustine likewise testifies in many of his works that his own writings and those of persons like himself are not to be counted among the canonical Scriptures.

[Note: Prologue to book III of *On the Trinity*, and book IV, chapter 1, *On the Soul*.]

If you press me with the authority of the Old Testament [Col. 0227C], I reply briefly: these and other precepts of the Old Testament which were set down there figuratively have been fulfilled spiritually in the Church. For when any soul has been joined to Christ by faith, if, withdrawing from Christ through heretical perversity, it has cleaved to another husband—that is, the devil—then, if it should perhaps wish to return to its former husband, that is, Christ, according to the determination of the ancient canons it is not to be joined to his fellowship until the end of life; that is, it is not to be admitted to communion in the sacraments of Christ and the Church. This is not because a truly penitent person should despair of forgiveness, but so that in this separation he may humbly bewail his fall. I could confirm what I have said with numerous judgments, but I think these suffice [Col. 0227D] for understanding my view. Farewell.

## LETTER 223. IVO, BY GOD’S GRACE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO AUDOENUS, BISHOP-ELECT OF THE CHURCH OF ÉVREUX: MAY YOU ATTAIN A PRIESTHOOD PLEASING TO GOD.

Since divine speech compares us to vinedressers and farmers (Matt. 20; Luke 10), we ought to rejoice in the Lord when divine grace supplies such laborers to our husbandry [variant: cultivation], through whom the vine of the Lord of Hosts may spread its branches [Col. 0228A] more widely and the field of God may become more fruitful. Although this was necessary from the beginning of the nascent Church, as the Lord said, we see it to be especially necessary in these days, when before our eyes we have manifest signs of the last days, as it was foretold: people loving themselves (2 Tim. 3), seeking their own interests and casting behind their backs the things of God; men and women alike adulterating, through every member of their bodies, the order of nature; and in this manner doing many things which it is shameful not only to do but even to mention.

Since we have heard through Lord William [variant: Vuilelmus], abbot of the monastery of St Peter [variant: Blessed Peter] at Chartres, that these things displease your brotherhood, we have rejoiced in the Lord because we believe [variant: believed] that you will be a useful vessel in God’s house. [Col. 0228B] At the same time, we desire that we should confirm familiar love between us and expect from one another, as neighbors, consolations and support according to the needs arising from ecclesiastical affairs and actions.

Therefore, by these letters we have decided to visit the beginning of your episcopate, so that from now on we may feel brotherly love for one another and bear one another’s burdens. Thus, in accordance with canonical institution, we may unanimously pursue with the sword of the Spirit those who oppress the poor of the Church, and have them barred from communion while living and from burial when dead. For among our parishioners, persons deprived by us of communion have certain priests and monks at Musivum [Note: [Col. 0228D] Thus the old codices have it; the earlier printed text had *Musuvim*.], from whom they seek and receive communion. These men also cross the river from which that village of Musivus [Note: [Col. 0228D] Thus also the old codices; formerly *Musuvis*.] takes its name [Col. 0228C], and consign the bodies of excommunicated persons to burial in a certain false cemetery [variant: cemetery].

May your charity forbid this from happening henceforth, lest, if this evil practice remains, detestable perversity result: the authority of excommunication may be cheapened and the impunity of criminals become insolent. Against these and similar evils may the Lord give you a spirit of counsel and courage, so that, like a lamp placed upon a lampstand, you may shine in God’s house and provide necessary light to ignorant ministers. Farewell.

## 96 LETTER 224. IVO, BY GOD’S GRACE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO GUIDO, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF MOLÈSME: GREETING IN THE LORD.

[Col. 0228D] This brother, the bearer of the present letters, came to us with your letters and tearfully disclosed how disorderly it was that, concealing truths and asserting falsehoods, he had aspired to the summit of priesthood when examined for ordination. He judged it more prudent to cease altogether from an office received irregularly than to minister dangerously in it. After careful inquiry into the anxiety of his heart, I write to your brotherhood what I think and what I have gathered from the canonical Scriptures.

Although he approached sacred order irregularly, he nevertheless received the holiness of the sacrament. Yet [Col. 0229A], so long as he persisted in the perverse intention of temporal gain, he was a fictitious priest and a priest by sacrament alone, to his own destruction, though to the salvation of others. If the rigor of the canons were observed in his case, he would be suspended for all time from the office irregularly received.

But once, with a changed intention, divine grace bestowed upon him what his priestly integrity lacked, added newness of life to the holiness of the sacrament, and fulfilled in him the saying, “May your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131), he was no longer a fictitious priest nor a priest by sacrament alone. By priestly ministry he could effect not only others’ salvation but his own as well.

Hence Augustine says in his book *Against the Letter of Parmenian*:

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Cited in ch. *Per Isaiam*, cause 1, question 1.]

> “We warn that in almost all such questions this must be understood: namely, that [Col. 0229B] although all sacraments harm those who handle them unworthily, they nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such persons.”

Likewise:

> “The Holy Spirit is present in the purpose or minister of the Church in such a way that, if he is not feigned, he works through him and makes his reward serve for everlasting salvation and for the regeneration or edification of those who are either consecrated or evangelized through him. But if he is feigned, the Spirit is indeed absent from his salvation and withdraws from his thoughts, which are without understanding; nevertheless, he does not abandon the ministry which works salvation for others through him.”

From these and similar authorities it is plain that the present brother may mercifully be admitted to the ministry of sacred order, unless something else is concealed which appears contrary to the sacred canons. Yet, that his conscience may be safeguarded more securely, paternal obedience must be awaited in this matter [Col. 0229C], so that true humility may heal what ambitious greed has damaged. Farewell.

## LETTER 225. IVO, BY THE SAME GRACE MINISTER OF THE CHURCH OF CHARTRES, TO DAIMBERT, BY GOD’S GRACE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS: WITH DUE OBEDIENCE, GREETING AND LOVE.

Concerning the knight who, before contracting a lawful marriage, had intercourse with his wife’s sister, and publicly confessed his fault, I answer Your Paternity what you know well: he has brought public disgrace upon himself, and henceforth he can neither accuse nor give testimony against an honorable person. Yet since no criminal can make a confession except concerning either a shameful act or a crime, we cannot refuse to receive the confessions which penitents make against themselves out of fear of God and for their own salvation, nor can we refuse to impose lawful penances upon them; for if we denied them these, we would expose them to be devoured by the jaws of invisible wolves. But if we allow such self-accusers to pass lightly and with impunity, we dangerously expose the good of marriage—established from the beginning by nature and law—to violation. Therefore, since, according to the Apostle, the end of every ecclesiastical controversy is an oath (Heb. XVI), that confession must be approved [another reading: “established”] by solemn oaths and by six reliable persons, whether persons present who knew of this shameful act, or persons able, on the evidence of their faith, to establish the truth of the matter. [Col. 0229D–0230A] For new kinds of diseases compel us to seek new tests of remedies.

When that confession has thus been established, it will be evident that the marriage was incestuous: “For incestuous unions, according to the canons (canon *De incestis*, causa 35, question 2), we reserve no pardon, unless they remedy the shameful marriage by separation.” The violator of the marriage and accuser himself (canon *Concubuisti*, causa 32, question 7) must remain unmarried at all times, as though a widower, until the period of his penance has been completed; another reading has, “or at least until then.” The woman, however, must not lose the price of her chastity, namely her dowry. In this way we shall satisfy both the confession and provide beneficially for the good of marriage in the future.

Meanwhile, Your Discretion may do this without any detriment to our order, until in due time we come to a general council or general assembly, where we may deliberate concerning these and similar matters with the concurrence [some manuscripts: “assembly”] of the bishops. [Col. 0230B] For this is what I do whenever anything of this kind comes before me; and so I did in this present Lent in the case of a certain knight, always reserving for a general hearing the decision as to what is to be decreed concerning one who violates such a marital good. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXVI. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to BERNERIUS, abbot of the monastery of Bonneval, and to the brethren entrusted to him: an abundance of merciful compassion.

The monk who bears this letter has tearfully confessed to us the flight by which he escaped from your monastery, and has earnestly begged me to obtain for him pardon from your brotherhood. Moved therefore by compassion for this unhappy man, I ask and urge you, in season and out of season, to receive with fitting satisfaction the sheep that had strayed from the flock and anxiously desires to return. Be instructed by the example and word of the supreme Shepherd, who not only receives the lost sheep when it returns, but also sought it when fleeing and wandering, and brought it back to the fold (Luke 15). [Col. 0230C]

Therefore, after the example of him, temper judgment with mercy; and extend in brotherly charity the mercy which each of you would wish shown to himself if he were in the same condition. I could write more to you on this subject, but I think this is enough for those who devote themselves daily to the reading of Scripture. [Col. 0230D] Farewell.

## 97. LETTER CCXXVII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: may you always rejoice in him who can make delightful the goings forth of morning and evening.

Since we heard that Your Paternity had been forcibly pressed into service by the citizens of Babylon for more than a thousand paces, we groaned with deepest sorrow; and, since we were unequal to anything else, we entreated, with all the earnest prayer we could, the maker of good things and disposer of evils to turn the waves of so great a storm into the breeze of serenity—he who raised Peter, walking on the waves, lest he should sink (Matt. 14), and delivered his fellow apostle Paul from the depths of the sea in his third shipwreck (1 Cor. 11).

> **Note [Col. 0229D]:** This appears to refer to the time when Paschal was seized in Rome by armed force by Emperor Henry; see Letter 237.

Therefore may Your Sublimity not disdain to make our humility a participant in your consolation, so that she who has compassionately shared your adversity from the heart may be able to rejoice more abundantly in your prosperity. For we have not forgotten the apostolic teaching which exhorts us: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member rejoices, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Cor. 12). How much more should all the members grieve with the suffering head, or rejoice with the rejoicing head? [Col. 0231A]

Moreover, if through any person any complaint or representation should come to your ears concerning a certain prebend which I had intended to give to a priest named Guarin, I wish Your Paternity to know that, as I intended, so, insofar as lay in my power, I was prepared to carry it out—and another reading has, “I did carry it out”—on this condition: that the Church should suffer no scandal on this account. For, as you know, she ought rather to be joined together by the bond of peace and brotherly love than wounded by the disagreement of any schism. In this matter nearly the whole Church, together with the dean, openly opposed me (Letter 182), and does not permit the priest seeking the prebend to be enrolled among the canons according to the custom of the Church. [Col. 0231B]

For this reason I delayed doing what I had proposed, since I did not promise to give that priest anything otherwise, whatever he himself may say, unless it could be done in peace with the Church. Therefore let Your Paternity firmly believe these things, and by the wisdom divinely bestowed upon it make provision that the Church may not be disturbed on that account. [Col. 0231C] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXVIII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to GONHERIUS, priest of good hope: knock at the door of truth, that Truth itself may deign to open itself to you.

> **Note [Col. 0231D]:** Gonherius is also mentioned in Letter 151.

Your brotherhood asks how the prophetic saying, “At whatever hour the sinner, having turned, groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18), can agree with the synodal judgment which suspends for a time from communion in the body and blood of Christ those who confess their crimes. For it seems to you that the judgment of the head and of the body contradict one another: that those whom the head—that is, Christ—quickly frees from sin, the body of Christ—that is, the Church—keeps bound for a long time under the penalty of sin. Another reading has: “The judgment seems to you to be at variance”; the earlier printed text is corrupt.

This question is easily resolved if one considers more carefully the punishment imposed by the inward Judge and the condition of human frailty. Since a criminal fault separates the offender from the head and from the body, the order of reason requires that the inward Judge remit it the more quickly because he alone sees more deeply within; whereas the judge who sees only what is outward must keep offenders under sin’s penalty until, by the manifest fruit of penance, he understands what the penitent’s disposition is. [Col. 0231D–0232A] For inward groaning gives satisfaction to the inward Judge; and therefore he grants remission of sin without delay, because the inward conversion is manifest to him.

But the Church, because she does not know the secrets of the heart, does not loose one who is bound, even though restored to life, unless he has been brought out from the tomb—that is, cleansed by public satisfaction. Hence the Church suspends those confessing their crimes from communion in the sacraments, and excludes for a prescribed time from the entrance of churches those placed in ashes and haircloth, so that by this she may test whether they have already been made alive within, after they have been proved by the prolonged mortification of penance. If Your Brotherhood attends to these things, you will see that the prophetic and synodal judgments do not disagree: the former assigns what belongs to the head, and the latter grants what belongs to the body.

Yet it lies within the discretion of bishops to shorten or prolong the time according to the penitent’s disposition, as blessed Augustine says (*Enchiridion*, chapter 65; and canon 83, *On Penance*, distinction 1): “In the work of penance, for which the guilty person must be separated from the altar, the measure of time is not to be considered so much as that of sorrow; for to the extent that you acknowledge it, God acknowledges it, according to the Psalmist’s words: ‘According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul’” (Ps. 93). [Col. 0232B] Let this satisfy [another reading: “suffice”] concerning the question proposed. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXIX. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to LISIARD, by the same grace bishop of Soissons: greeting and service.

Concerning the marriage of the woman about whom Lord Stephen consulted me on your behalf—a woman said to have had an affair before marriage with a kinsman of the man whom she now has as her husband—I reply, relying on the authority of the laws, that her seducer cannot accuse her, even if what he says is true.
