For an apostolic decree says (chapter *Nemini*, causa 15, question 3; and Letter 196): “No one who has confessed concerning himself ought to be believed concerning another’s crime”; and elsewhere (chapter *Incerta*, causa 30, question 5): “No one is to be judged guilty unless convicted in judicial order,” that is, unless the person against whom the accusation is brought either freely confesses himself guilty, or is proved guilty by unimpeachable witnesses in some secular or ecclesiastical court.

But when, because of his own wickedness, the accuser produces witnesses who did not see the act, they are not to be heard, even if they speak the truth; for the laws provide that witnesses against an accused person are not to be admitted except concerning acts known to have been done in their presence. [Col. 0232C–D] If, however, the woman, taking thought for her reputation, wishes to clear herself of this disgrace, then, instructed by the example of the Roman pontiffs Sixtus and Leo, we advise Your Prudence (Letter 206) to accept her purgation by an oath with five supporters, or with seven, according as the rumor has spread. Thus you will neither do violence to the laws nor fail to provide for your conscience and for the quieting of rumor.

> **Note [Col. 0232D]:** In Letter 54 he called this being cleared “by seven sacraments,” that is, by seven oaths.

Furthermore, I wish to be considered excused in your regard for the separation made at Chartres in my absence between a certain Guy, your parishioner, and a certain Matilda, our parishioner, who had previously been betrothed to his brother. Yet, whatever the state of the matter, I neither rendered judgment concerning your parishioner nor caused one to be rendered. They themselves of their own accord sought a divorce from one another on the advice of certain clerics; they themselves, without my knowledge, proved the causes of divorce by oath. If this was done wrongly, you know better than I; and if any claim arises from it concerning our parishioner [another reading: “our parish”], I shall judge, insofar as lies in my power, as reason and law advise. [Col. 0233A] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXX. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to HILDEBERT, by the same grace bishop of Le Mans: greeting and service.

> Another reading adds: “and love in Christ.”

Since marriage is evidently sanctioned from the beginning of the human condition by natural ordinance, I believe that no divorce can take place unless a cause intervenes which the law or the Gospel permits. For the marriages of Jews and gentiles, contracted according to natural law, were still in force, and Christian marriages were nonexistent or exceedingly rare, when, in answer to the apostles’ question, “Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatsoever?”, the Lord replied that no divorce among married persons could take place except for the cause of fornication (Matt. 5; 32).

But because, according to apostolic teaching, the marriage-bed must be undefiled and marriage honorable in all things (Heb. 13), as the Christian religion increased, incest was added to the causes of divorce. If incest is found in any union, the marriage-bed cannot be proved undefiled and honorable. Therefore this, it seems to me, must be considered concerning the woman who, leaving Judaism, hastened to baptism: whether she was related by blood to her former husband or not. If this is found to be so, I believe that under the Christian law which she has professed she may be separated from her former husband and marry whom she wishes in the Lord. Otherwise, the man whom she marries will be an adulterer, and she an adulteress; for, according to Pope Innocent (chapter *Gaudemus*, title 19, *On Divorce*, book IV of the *Decretals*; and chapter 10, *Si quis*, distinction 34), “baptism forgives sins; it does not dissolve marriages.” [Col. 0233B–D] This is my opinion on the question proposed, without prejudice to a better judgment. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXI. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to PONTIUS, venerable abbot of Cluny: may you please the supreme Ruler in the governance entrusted to you.

Your prudent diligence and diligent prudence asked my insignificance what the elevation of the chalice and its subsequent setting down signify; what those signs of the cross signify which are made over, within, and outside the chalice; and why these seem to have been omitted in the little book which I composed, *On the Harmony of the Old and New Priesthood*.

> **Note [Col. 0233D]:** It survives today as an addition among Ivo’s sermons.

I omitted them because they seemed to bear little or no relation to the harmony discussed in that work. Yet considered in themselves, they seem to contain some mystical meaning, apart from [one old manuscript: “because of”] those signs of the cross which are repeatedly made before these, distinctly, in three places. In these latter signs particular attention is directed to the transformation of the gifts, now called sacrifices, into Christ’s body and blood, or to their becoming, once transformed, salutary for us.

When the bread and chalice are elevated with the deacon assisting, the exaltation of Christ’s body upon the cross is commemorated. When, with the host already consecrated, the sign of the cross is made within or above the chalice, from the eastern side of the chalice to the western and from the northern to the southern, we understand this to signify what the Lord foretold to his disciples before his Passion, in commemoration of that Passion: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). [Col. 0234A–B]

The host also, which is signed beside the chalice, ought to be placed so that, by its own position and that of the chalice, it represents Christ’s right side, from which flowed the blood of redemption and the water of baptism; Your Prudence does not fail to know that both are contained in the chalice. But when, with the deacon cooperating, the chalice is set down, the host is restored to its place, and covered with the corporal pall, this commemorates how Joseph and Nicodemus, having obtained Pilate’s permission, took Christ’s body down from the cross and reverently committed it to burial.

> **Note [Col. 0233D–0234D]:** In an old manuscript there survives a question by Waleran, bishop of Neufburg, concerning the rationale of this covering, together with the response of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

This is my understanding of these matters, without rejecting the interpretation of anyone able to say higher and more hidden [another reading: “more sacred”] things concerning them on authority or divine inspiration.

Concerning the monk who was the cause, not by intention but by accident, of a young man’s falling into a fire: what he did does not appear to me criminal. Blessed Augustine testifies and says: “Sin is so voluntary that, if it is not voluntary, it is certainly not sin.” Therefore, if that monk is suspended for a time from his office or postponed from some promotion, it would seem fitting to me that neither his carelessness should go unpunished nor his companions lack an example warning them against like carelessness. It depends, then, solely on Your Prudence whether, according to the quality of his life and knowledge [another reading: “and conscience”], you suspend him altogether or permit him to minister in sacred orders. [Col. 0234C–D]

Furthermore, if you wish to punish according to the rigor of the canons the transgression of that monk who castrated himself in order to cure epilepsy, he can neither be promoted to a higher grade nor minister in the order which he held. As you know well, this would not be forbidden him if he had been cut by physicians. For if, according to the Nicene canons, those who cut themselves on the pretext of preserving chastity are removed from ecclesiastical offices, much more must those be removed who castrate themselves to cure bodily illness.

Yet just as rigor has been entrusted to rulers to be maintained according to the needs of places and times, or in view of advantages to be sought or disadvantages to be avoided, so dispensations have been permitted to them, provided that they do not generate scandal in the Church of God because of the standing of persons or the benefit of public affairs.

> **Note [Col. 0235D]:** The manner of dispensations is also approved in Letters 250 and 260.

In all these cases rulers must exercise diligence, so that they neither permit what would harm nor prohibit what would benefit. For just as sick persons are sometimes not cured by strict observance of the rules of medicine, though they would be healed by an appropriate relaxation of those rules, so in curing diseases of souls one must consider whom the rigor of discipline benefits and whom the moderation of indulgence benefits. In all these matters the highest counsel is that which we have from Father Augustine, who says in his treatise *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*: “Have charity, and do whatever you will; if you spare, spare with charity; if you correct, correct with charity.” [Col. 0235A–B]

I have briefly answered your questions according to my understanding, because when the bearer of your letter came to us I was somewhat ill, and he was hurrying to return. Farewell.

## 99. LETTER CCXXXII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to HILDEBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Le Mans, and to F., precentor of the Church of Le Mans: greeting.

> **Note [Col. 0235D]:** The address has thus been restored and completed from two old manuscripts: “precentor of the Church of Le Mans.”

Concerning the man who, before taking a wife, defiled her mother in the region of the sexual parts by external pollution, I can give no sounder answer than that which Pope Urban gave to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, when he consulted him about a similar matter.

> **Note [Col. 0235D]:** This is cited in chapter *Extraordinaria pollutio*, causa 35, questions 2 and 3.

After consultation, he answered that a lawful marriage was not to be dissolved because of such a shameful act. Yet he advised that the most careful and strict investigations be made to determine whether, in that act of shamefulness, there had occurred any mingling of flesh, by which, in the mingling of seed, they became one flesh, and because of which a marriage wrongly entered into or violated ought to be dissolved. [Col. 0235C]

I have heard that the man in question cleared himself of the accusation made against him by the ordeal of red-hot iron (Letters 74, 205, 252, and 280), and was found unharmed by the fire’s injury. If this is so, and if in the sacrament of his purgation he declared that he had never become one flesh with his wife’s mother, I understand that no further judgment is to be sought against divine testimony. [Col. 0235D] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXIII. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to HENRY, abbot of the monastery of Angély: greeting and the mutual gift of prayers.

Concerning the investitures of churches made by laymen, I praise and confirm, insofar as lies in my power, the judgment of the earlier Fathers Gregory and Urban (chapters *Si quis* and *Quoniam*, causa 16, question 7; Letter 60). Whatever name such an invasion may properly bear, I judge the position of those who wish to defend lay investitures to be schismatic.

I do not say this against the lord pope, for in certain letters he wrote me that he had done what he did under compulsion, and that he still forbids what he forbade, although he permitted certain abominable things to be written by certain abominable persons.

> **Note [Col. 0236D]:** One old manuscript reads *propter dominum* (“because of the lord”); he speaks of Paschal II. On this matter see Letter 236.

And because we ought rather to cover than uncover a father’s shame (Gen. 9), I think he should be admonished in private letters redolent of charity, so that he may judge himself or retract his action. If he does so, let us give thanks to God and let the whole Church rejoice with us, she who is grievously sick while her head labors, weakened by so great an affliction. [Col. 0236A–B]

But if in this sickness he should be incurably ill, it is not ours to judge the supreme pontiff (Letter 236). For we have the Gospel sentence which makes us secure: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat: observe and do what they say, but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23). This saying means that the commands of those presiding which belong to the chair must be obeyed—even if they are such as the Pharisees were—but that such persons must not be removed from their seats by factional conspiracy.

But if they command things contrary to Gospel or apostolic teaching, we are taught by the example of the apostle Paul that they are not to be obeyed in that respect.

> **Note [Col. 0236D]:** Then, he says in Letter 236, the keys are to be deprived of their power.

Paul resisted Peter, his superior, openly when Peter was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel; nevertheless, he did not reject him. Where human judgments fail, divine mercy must be sought, so that, with peace preserved among the grafted branches, those who have been cut off may themselves strive to be restored to the unity of the Church and rejoice in communion with the grafted branches.

> **Note [Col. 0236D]:** He alludes to words of St Augustine which he also cites in Letter 288.

Otherwise, neither will the cut-off branches be grafted in, nor will the grafted branches be permitted to bear fruit or blossom amid so great a shaking of storms. [Col. 0236C] This is my answer to the question proposed, without prejudice to the judgments of my elders, which may provide for the Church’s peace and edification. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXIV. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to WILLIAM, abbot of Marmoutier, and to the brethren entrusted to him: love in the Lord.

“That small things grow through concord, whereas the greatest things fall apart through discord” (Sallust, *Jugurthine War* 10): I believe that your brotherhood has learned this by experience. Therefore, although Noah’s ark, prefiguring the Church, was extended through its several dimensions by many cubits, it was nevertheless completed in one cubit (Gen. 6), so that by this prefiguration the Church’s form would then be understood to be perfect when its lower members offered full obedience to their prelates. [Col. 0236D–0237A]

Since you have not rendered this obedience as you ought for a long time (Letter 235), your love should not be surprised if what is owed is demanded of you—one old manuscript reads, “what is not owed”—namely, that you promise your metropolitan the obedience due to him with your mouth and confirm it by giving your hand. Thus a threefold confession was required of Peter when the Lord questioned him (John 21), because his threefold denial had preceded it when he was afraid (Matt. 26). Thus Peter received from Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that they should not usurp the apostleship entrusted to him: Paul was to preach the Gospel among the gentiles, Peter among the circumcised (Gal. 2).

In this manner, if it pleases you, you may lawfully enough promise with your mouth and confirm with your hand what you owe and hold in your heart [concerning an oath given by the hand], since an obligation of the hand seems to me no greater than an obligation of the mouth. The Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). Yet new intensifications of diseases sometimes compel us to devise new kinds of remedies. [Col. 0237B]

And even if—far be it!—what has been said is demanded on some empty pretext, nevertheless, since it harms neither faith nor good morals, you ought to comply out of due humility for the sake of restoring peace. Thus Paul, contrary to his own purpose, allowed Timothy to be circumcised at Lystra because of the scandal of the Jews (Acts 16), although he knew and preached that the sacrament of circumcision was not necessary to the Christian religion. By his own example, therefore, he taught us that dispensation is to be admitted where rigor is dangerous. I could write more in this vein, but since I speak to prudent men, let these few words suffice. [Col. 0237C] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXV. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to RADULF, by the grace of God archbishop of Tours: greeting and service.

I have heard, and rejoiced, that the neighboring bishops of Le Mans and Angers are endeavoring to restore peace between your metropolitan see and the brethren of Marmoutier, and that only one thing remains: the abbot does not wish to confirm by giving his hand what he professes with his mouth. But Your Prudence knows better than I how costly this disagreement has been to that monastery and how burdensome to you. Therefore Your Excellency should take counsel to pursue peace and unanimity [another reading: “unity”], so that the monastery may render you due submission and the gravity of your age may spend its remaining days of life in peace and quiet. [Col. 0237C–D]

For if the abbot has professed due submission with his mouth—since confession with the mouth and faith in the heart suffice for obtaining salvation—I believe that, once he has testified to this in the hearing of the Church, he will not make his promise void, for that would cast him into disgrace and make him liable to condemnation. For, as human simplicity tends to be, the abbot shrinks more from doing this because it is unusual than because it is unlawful. And since the Apostle says, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10), what suffices for salvation may, it seems to me, suffice for promising submission. I would have written more, but enough has been said to the wise. [Col. 0238A] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXVI. DAIMBERT, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens; IVO, bishop of Chartres; WALO, bishop of Paris; JOHN, bishop of Orléans; and the other fellow bishops of the province of Sens, to JOHN, by the grace of God archbishop of Lyons, the first see: the reverence established by the Fathers.

> **Note [Col. 0237]:** The superscription of this letter has thus been restored and completed with the help of two ancient manuscripts.

[Col. 0238B] By the right of your primacy you invited us to a council to be held at Anse, at which you proposed to deal with faith and lay investitures (Letter 233). We do not at all disdain to come to it; but we fear to transgress the boundaries established by our fathers, the ancient boundaries. For nowhere has the venerable authority of the Fathers decreed, nowhere has antiquity been accustomed to observe, that the bishop of a primatial see should invite bishops situated outside his own province to a council, unless either the apostolic see commanded it, or one of the provincial Churches, on matters which it could not settle within the province, appealed to the hearing of the primatial see. This is not something that we prophesy from our own hearts, but, fortified by apostolic authority, [Col. 0238C] we demonstrate it by unanswerable judgments.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas writes in these terms to Ralph, primate of the Aquitanias [or: Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges], who was arrogating to himself powers beyond the right of primacy (chapter *Conquestus est*, Cause 9, Question 3): “Our brother Sigebod, archbishop of Narbonne, has complained to our apostolate that, against his will, you compel his clerics to come to judgment, and that, without consulting him, you dispose, as though by right of your patriarchate, of matters belonging to his Church. Yet neither does antiquity, to which the Fathers decreed reverence should be shown, admit this, nor do the authority of the saints and the canons permit it at all—unless perhaps, in matters which cannot be settled locally, they have appealed to you as to their patriarch; or, if their bishop has died, they have wished the affairs of their Church to be administered by [Col. 0238D] your judgment. For we determine that primates or patriarchs possess no privilege above other bishops except insofar as the sacred canons grant it and ancient custom formerly conferred it upon them, so that, according to the Nicene rules, the Churches may retain their privileges.”

Clement and Anacletus concur with this judgment. After the apostles, they ordained in which cities the primatial sees and metropolitan sees should be located (*Urbes* and *In illis*, Distinction 80), determining that the judgment of bishops is to be referred to primates only if an appeal has been made to their hearing. Fortified by these authorities, we do not wish to introduce into your Churches [“our Churches,” manuscript C] an unheard-of novelty [Col. 0239A] or alter rights established for them in antiquity.

Moreover, because in this council you propose to discuss lay investitures, which some count among heresies [Note: Improperly, in Letter 233], you will rather uncover your father’s [or: our father’s] shameful parts (Genesis 9)—which ought not to be published in Gath or proclaimed in the streets of Ashkelon (2 Kings 1)—and expose them to mockery, than, by covering them behind your back, obtain for yourselves a father’s blessing (Genesis 9). What the supreme pontiff [Note: Paschal II, of whom Letter 233 speaks] accepted upon himself for the avoidance of slaughter among the people, necessity compelled; his will did not approve. This is clear because, after he escaped the danger, as he himself wrote to some of us, he commanded what he had commanded and prohibited what he had prohibited, although, under pressure of danger, he allowed certain impious [Col. 0239B] writings concerning certain impious matters.

Thus Peter cleansed his threefold denial (Matthew 26) by a threefold confession (John 21), and remained an apostle. Thus Pope Marcellinus, deceived by pagans (*Nunc autem*, Distinction 21), burned incense before a temple [one manuscript: “before a pagan”]; yet, though in no way judged by his brethren, after a few days he deserved to be crowned with martyrdom. Thus Aaron in the wilderness, while Moses delayed on the mountain, because of the unbearable tumult of the people, allowed a molten calf to be made, which the foolish people worshipped (Exodus 32). Yet he was not led astray by the people into believing it to be God or offering it the reverence due to divine worship. Nevertheless, so great an offence obtained pardon, and at the Lord’s command he was raised by the hand of Moses to the high priesthood (Leviticus 8).

Thus Moses himself, [Col. 0239C] who spoke with the Lord as friend with friend (Numbers 12), nevertheless offended God when, because of the murmur of the people saying, “Can he bring forth water for us from this rock?” (Numbers 20), he was compelled to doubt and to ask the Lord for water with disputation (ibid.). Thus the teacher of the nations, who publicly cried in the synagogues, “Circumcision is nothing, and Christ will profit you nothing if you are circumcised” (Galatians 5), allowed Timothy to be circumcised because of the scandal of the Jews, so that by this accommodation he might win the Jews (Acts 16).

The greatest and holiest men suffered these infirmities through plausible necessity or prudent dispensation. God made good use of our evils in order thereby to teach them to know themselves, so that they might learn to attribute their weaknesses to themselves and refer the good gifts bestowed upon them to God’s grace. Nor were these things written in order that they might be taken as examples for living, but so that the lesser may learn from the fall of the greater to fear lest they incur similar falls, and, if they should fall, may rise again with the utmost speed.

But if the pope does not yet exercise due severity against the German king, Henry IV, we believe that he prudently delays it in accordance with the judgment [or: counsel] of certain teachers, who advise that some dangers should be admitted in order that greater ones may be avoided. Hence Augustine says in the third book against Parmenian the Donatist (Book III, [Col. 0240A] chapter 2):

> “The Church’s soundness observes this: whenever any brother—that is, any Christian established within the communion of the Church—is discovered in such a sin as to deserve an anathema, let this be done where there is no danger of schism; and let it be done toward him with that love concerning which the Apostle elsewhere commands, saying: ‘Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother’ (2 Thessalonians 3). Here he sufficiently shows that, when this fear is absent and there remains complete security grounded in the certain stability of the wheat—that is, when the crime of any person is so well known and appears so detestable to all that he has either no defenders at all or none such as can bring about a schism—then the severity of discipline must not sleep. In this [Col. 0240B] correction of depravity is more effective in proportion as the preservation of charity is more diligent.
>
> “This, however, can then be done without injury to peace and unity and without damage to the wheat, when the multitude of the Church’s congregation is alien from the crime which is anathematized. Nor can correction by many be salutary except when the person corrected has no associated multitude. But when the same disease has seized many, nothing remains for the good except grief and groaning, so that by that sign revealed [manuscript C: ‘is revealed’] to the holy Ezekiel they may deserve to escape unharmed from the devastation of those persons (Ezekiel 9). For if some brother is named in a crime unlike that of the others—and indeed, if the contagion of sinning has invaded the multitude—the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary. But counsels of separation are both vain and destructive and sacrilegious, because they are made impiously and proudly, and disturb [manuscript C: ‘trouble’] weak good persons more than they correct [variant: ‘do correct’] resolute wicked ones.”

For this [or: these] reasons it does not seem to us a useful counsel to attend those [manuscript C: “these”] councils [Note: He speaks of a provincial council] in which we cannot condemn or judge those persons against whom proceedings are brought, because they are shown to be subject neither to our judgment nor to that of any [or: any other] human beings (Letter 233). Hence it is clear that we are exempt from blame if we fear to strike their deeds with the sword of speech, since the Mediator himself commands us to obey them—even if they are such as the Pharisees were—provided they rightly command those things which pertain to the chair, though they themselves do not do them (Letters 61 and 233).

From all this it seems clear that we should place priestly breeches over the shameful parts, lest we expose what is shameful [variant: venerable] in ourselves to our enemies for mockery and, where we seek to restore the Church’s strength, fall into greater weakness. In saying these things, we do not instruct your prudence but excuse our innocence; for we do not wish to deprive the principal keys of the Church of their authority, whatever person holds the place of Peter, unless he manifestly departs from evangelical truth. [Note: Boniface the martyr establishes the same in chapter *Si papa*, Distinction 40; and Ivo says in Letter 233 that one must not obey him when he commands against evangelical teaching.]

In saying these things, we do not deny [Col. 0241A] that any metropolitan may, according to ancient law, summon bishops and celebrate a provincial synod, while preserving reverence for the Roman Church (*Nec licuit* and *Multis*, Distinction 17). If it cannot at present crush Satan beneath its feet, it will nevertheless not oppose your salutary measures, in which, as is read in the aforesaid book [Note: From St Augustine, Book III against the letter of Parmenian, chapter 1, and reported in canon *Quisquis*, Cause 3, Question 4], whoever either corrects by rebuke what he can, or excludes—without breaking the bond of peace—what he cannot correct, or condemns in equity and bears with firmness what he cannot exclude without breaking the bond of peace, is peaceable; and he is altogether free, wholly secure, entirely removed from that curse which Scripture pronounces: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil; who put darkness for light and light for darkness; who [Col. 0241B] put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!” (Isaiah 5).

Content with these boundaries of the Catholic Fathers, we wish to correct, according to the decrees of the Fathers and without breaking the bond of peace, what we can correct; but what we cannot correct, we have resolved, if necessary, to endure until the harvest, as the Lord teaches. By these words we believe ourselves excused for restraining our tongues from tearing at the lord pope; and if he seems to have done anything, contrary to his own judgment and that of his predecessors, Gregory VII and Urban II, regarding investitures remitted to the German king [manuscript C: “the German kings”], we excuse it with filial charity.

For he is not a transgressor of the law who fails in a law through deceptive misrepresentation or compelling necessity, [Col. 0241C] but one who deliberately attacks the law and does not care to acknowledge his offence. Therefore we not only do not accuse this transgression of his, but, reason so dictating, approve it (Letter 233), if, with slaughter of the people imminent, in fatherly charity and at some cost to himself he chose to expose himself to such dangers, in order that with sincere charity he might assist in greater maladies (Letter 190).

Nor was he the first or the only dispenser of the Lord’s commands. For the Mediator of God and men, whose life on earth was a discipline of conduct, first commanded his disciples not to carry purse or bag (Matthew 10), because then no necessity pressed them. But when the time of his passion was at hand, knowing that they would suffer want of bread as they travelled from place to place, he moderated the command, [Col. 0241D] giving them permission to carry bag and purse (Luke 22), no longer issuing orders at greed’s prompting [Note: So all manuscripts. Baronius, however, adds in the margin: “No longer complying with greed.”] but yielding to necessity.

Likewise, when heresies of different kinds were springing up in diverse parts of the world, it was very strictly decreed, so that Catholics, frightened by the severity of the judgment, might avoid the seductions of heretics, that those returning from heresy either should not become clerics or should not remain clerics. Yet when the Church suffered very great losses from the rigor of this decree, the prudent discernment of religious persons wished and taught that the judgment should be changed, and [Col. 0242A] fraternally received those returning from heresy and professing Catholic unity, permitting them to remain in their offices. They judged it better that some wound should be made in the bark of the mother tree, which charity might heal, than that the Church should fail to gather as her own members all whom she could.

Finally, some call investiture heresy (Letter 237), although heresy is nothing but error in faith. For just as faith of the heart leads to righteousness and confession of the mouth to salvation, so heresy is error leading to impiety, while profession of that same error leads to destruction. Both faith and error proceed from the heart; but that investiture about which there is such agitation exists only in the hands of giver and receiver (Letter 60), which may do good and evil but cannot believe or err in faith.

Moreover, if this investiture were heresy, one who renounced it could not return to it without a wound. Yet we see, in the regions of Germany and Gaul, many honourable persons, after removing this blemish by whatever satisfaction, restoring pastoral staffs and receiving investitures disavowed by the apostolic hand. The supreme pontiffs would by no means have done this if they had known heresy and sin against the Holy Spirit to lie hidden in such investiture. Therefore, when things not sanctioned by eternal law (Letter 60), but established or prohibited for the Church’s propriety and advantage, are temporarily remitted for the same occasion for which they were instituted, this is not a harmful violation of ordinances but praiseworthy and most salutary dispensation.

Since many who are less zealous [Col. 0242C] do not understand this at all, they judge before the time the movable spirit and the immovable spirit [some manuscripts: “stable”; thus manuscript C; Letter 288], not understanding the difference. But if any layman bursts into such madness as to think that, in the giving and receiving of the staff, he can confer a sacrament or the reality of an ecclesiastical sacrament, [Note: Letter 60 says that kings maintain that they intend to give nothing spiritual in the investiture of bishops, etc.] we judge him altogether a heretic—not because of manual investiture, but because of his diabolical presumption.

If, however, we wish to give things appropriate names, we may say that that manual investiture performed by laymen is an encroachment upon another’s right and a sacrilegious presumption. For the liberty and propriety of the Church, it must, if possible and without breaking the bond of peace, be cut off utterly [Col. 0242D] [old manuscripts: “cut off”]. Therefore, where it can be removed without schism, let it be removed; where it cannot be removed without schism, let it be deferred with a discriminating protest. For by such an encroachment nothing is taken away from ecclesiastical sacraments to prevent them from being holy (Letter 73), because, wherever they may be [manuscript C: “they themselves are”], whether among those inside or those outside, they remain the same.

We have written this to your affection, prepared to be refuted without obstinacy if your prudence, fortified by canonical Scripture, teaches us something better than what we have written. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXVII. JOHN [or: JOSCEMNOS], archbishop of the primatial see of Lyons, to DAIMBERT, archbishop of Sens: greeting.

[Col. 0243A]

[Note: This answers the preceding Letter 236.] Because few words suffice for the wise, we have resolved to address your brotherhood briefly; and because “in much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Proverbs 10), avoiding a multitude of words, we have taken care to answer your prolixity with such brevity as we could.

You have therefore advanced certain points in which you seem partly to mark our person as guilty of presumptuous [thus the old edition; variant: “assumed”] arrogance, partly to detract from the dignity of the Church of Lyons, and partly to wish to introduce an incurable blemish into the body of the whole Church. First, then, let us clear ourselves, so that [Col. 0243B] we may approach the remaining matters more freely and readily.

For your discretion saw fit to charge us with inviting you beyond your province to a council to be held at Anse (Letter 236), to deal with faith and lay investitures, and to judge those persons [Note: He means the pope, as in Letters 233 and 236] whom it is not lawful for us to judge. We call God and our conscience as witnesses that we did not wish to draw your brotherhood either beyond your province or to the judgment of those persons. Rather, we simply sought to invite your beloved presence to converse and take counsel concerning the various disturbances that have arisen in the Church of God, so that we might share with you and with other religious men the labour, the merit, and the reward of labour and merit.

For just as there is a first Lyonnaise province, so there are nonetheless a second and a third Lyonnaise provinces. Therefore, when the prelate of the primatial see of Lyons summons the prelates of the second or third province because of his own necessities or theirs, he does not draw them into a foreign province. Rather, preserving a reasonable and just order, he recalls the lower members to the head, that they may either grieve with it in adversity or rejoice with it in prosperity.

Nor do we believe that your prudence [variant: “your,” plural] is unaware that all metropolitans have the right to summon provincial councils within their own boundaries. But metropolitans are known to stand in the same relation to their primates as suffragans do to their metropolitans, so that cases which cannot be settled by inferiors may be decided by superiors, [Col. 0243D] unless an appeal has been made to the Roman hearing, with the privileges of each Church nonetheless preserved.

Would that, dearest brother, you had seriously said that you did not wish, or did not dare, to transgress the ancient boundaries established by the Fathers. Nearly all Latin Christendom knows the boundaries of the Church of Lyons and of Sens, established by the ancient Fathers. Yet we cannot sufficiently wonder why you have asserted that several persons are exempt from ecclesiastical judgment, unless perhaps you have wished to include all bishops in that same immunity.

But if you attempt to exempt kings or emperors from pontifical judgment, turn to the great emperor [Col. 0244A] Constantine, who is read to have spoken such words at the Council of Nicaea, Pope Sylvester being present (appendix to Canon 4, Cause 11, Question 1): “You bishops,” he says, “are to be judged by the Lord alone.” He did not say, “I and you are to be judged by the Lord alone.” For by excluding bishops alone, he undoubtedly subjects himself and all kings to ecclesiastical judgment.

Do you find fault with the act of the most distinguished teacher Ambrose, who excommunicated the emperor Theodosius for his offence? Do you accuse Gregory VII, who condemned King Henry for his crimes? You added that you feared lest perhaps the shameful parts of our father should be revealed in our conference. You were afraid where there was certainly no fear. For we would undoubtedly rather be blessed with the piety of modest sons than cursed by the immodesty of an irreverent son. And would that the father himself would permit these shameful parts, as you call them, to be covered according to our wish!

Moreover, you pleaded dangerous times; you pleaded the strength and multitude of the opposing party; you pleaded the weakness and small number of our own party. Yet surely, the more dangerous the times, the more vigorously servants of God must strive (Letter 18), lest, when iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold, the charity of the few also grow cold. Do you not remember what Christ said to his few disciples? “Take courage,” he said, “for I have overcome the world” (John 16). If, then, you teach distrust, you proclaim the world’s victory and cast down Christ’s victory.

It is a new and unheard-of kind [Col. 0244C] of philosophizing: to urge the timid against the brave, the slothful against the importunate; to become fugitives in war, bold in peace, secure in danger, provident in security. An accursed master of a ship is one who, in calm serenity, displays the height of his skill, but in a storm lets go the helm and all the other gear. Do not be afraid, brother: Christ has sown good seed in his field. Do not sow weeds over it, for they grow of themselves and strive to choke the good seed (Matthew 13). The number of evildoers increases; the children of distrust abound. But Christ is able to strengthen his own and to overthrow adversaries. For what does the Apostle say? “I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me” (Philippians 4). Was Christ in Paul alone? Could he do all things in Paul alone? We believe and confess that he can do all things in every individual believer. “Behold,” he says, “I am with you all days” (Matthew 28).

As to your rebuke of those who count among heresies lay investitures of ecclesiastical dignities, you do not seem to do so very effectively. Although, just as Catholic faith remains in the heart, so heretical error remains in the heart, nevertheless, just as we recognize a Catholic by Catholic works, so we recognize a heretic by heretical works. “By their fruits,” the Lord says, “you shall know them” (Matthew 7), and every tree is known by its fruit. Although we do not [Col. 0245A] classify external investitures performed by laymen very properly under the name of heresy [Note: It is called schismatic in Letter 233, and counted among heresies if one thinks it confers a sacrament, in Letter 236], nevertheless to hold and defend that they ought to be done is undoubted heresy.

As to your saying that permission was granted to some persons to receive investitures from lay hands, you seem to know that this was written, as though to soothe and diminish the offence, because what the law permits in the present, it forbids in the future (Letter 203). Hence it is clear that every remission of past offences is a warning and prohibition regarding future ones.

Perhaps, too, you fear that we intend to annul the rights of your episcopal see. We do not wish to usurp anything pertaining to your right or that of your Church; we seek from you in charity only that obedience which a metropolitan owes his primate. We are prepared to comply with you as with a dearest brother and in turn to receive your compliance. You may remember [Col. 0245B] that, since you recovered the friendship and familiar association of the Church of Lyons, it saw you gladly, received you joyfully, and honoured you with as much affection as it could. Do not, brother, believe every spirit. We once felt this storm, but by God’s favour it subsided for a time [variant: “somewhat”], and by his action it was calmed.

We did not wish, nor do we wish, to draw you beyond your province. For we believed, and believe, that it is more fitting for the prelates of the second provinces to be invited to the first province when the need of cases requires it than for pontiffs of primatial sees to be drawn to the provinces of the second rank on account of whatever cases. Otherwise, how will that stand which the sacred canons prescribe: that greater causes are to be referred to their primates? For this would not be referring causes to primates, [Col. 0245C] but bringing primates down to the cause of each individual province.

Finally, if a bishop of a primatial see, proceeding to a second, third, or perhaps fourth province, does not go beyond his province, then surely a metropolitan of the second, third, or fourth rank summoned to the first is not drawn into a foreign province. For no court for cases is more suitable to the prelates of the second provinces than their own first province. We have written these few words to your affection. If you wish to prepare anything in reply, whether face to face or from afar, we are ready to hear and answer. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXVIII. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to his lord and father PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: the service of filial obedience.

[Col. 0245D]

Your fatherhood knows that the kingdom of the Franks, above other kingdoms, has always been subject to the apostolic see; and therefore, insofar as the royal persons themselves were concerned, there was no division between kingdom and priesthood [one old edition: “and the supreme priesthood”; thus manuscript C]. What has hitherto been observed with the peace and advantage of the Church, we humbly ask may henceforth be observed, and that no deception dissolve the peace of the kingdom of the Franks and of the supreme priesthood.

We say this beforehand because we have heard that the clerics of Tournai have come to the apostolic see to request an apostolic command whereby they may have a bishop of their own and render void the privilege of the Church of Noyon. As sons and faithful servants, we ask and advise that this not be done: allow the established condition of the Churches, which has endured for nearly four hundred years, to remain unshaken, lest on this occasion [Note: Arising from the question of investitures, of which Letter 236 speaks] you raise in the kingdom of Gaul the schism which exists in the German kingdom against the apostolic see.

Nor do we in this resist the apostolic see’s power to diminish the extent [two old editions: “the multitude”] of dioceses or enlarge their narrowness, if the advantage of God’s people so requires and no schism results. Since the king of the Franks, Louis the Fat, is a man of simple disposition, devoted to the Church of God and well-disposed towards the apostolic see, we ask and advise that no deception [Col. 0246B] withdraw you from his goodwill and no persuasion estrange you from it.

For your fatherhood knows that, when kingdom and priesthood agree with one another, the world is well governed and the Church flourishes and bears fruit. But when they disagree, not only do small things fail to grow, but even great things miserably collapse. What we request with our fellow bishops is neither against the majesty of the apostolic see nor against the advantage—indeed, I would not say the dignity—of the Church of Tournai: namely, that the ancient boundaries which their Fathers established and which long antiquity observed should be preserved.

Moreover, since episcopal dignity cannot honourably bear poverty in these times, provision must be made lest, through this division, each bishop become poor. The people of Noyon, who have experienced the resources of both Churches, bear witness to this. Further, if the case of Milo and the daughter of Count Stephen should reach your ears, let your fatherhood know that Milo did not canonically put away his first wife, and that he did not canonically marry the daughter of Count Stephen, as has been proved by the judgment of bishops. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXIX. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres by the grace of God, to LOUIS, king of the Franks by the grace of God: may you live and reign in him for whom to serve is to reign.

What we heard by common report, we have learned more certainly from the letters of your Excellency: namely, that you propose to take as wife the niece of the countess of Flanders, a girl of marriageable age, noble in birth, and—so it is said—commendable in honourable conduct. We believe this to be pleasing to God, honourable to your reputation among men, and welcome to those who sincerely love the stability of your kingdom.

For, taught by the Lord, we have learned that there are three callings of those who live well: namely, those who are married, the continent, and rulers of the Church. Whoever is found in none of these callings will, before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, be proscribed and deprived of the eternal inheritance. For when the Lord spoke of the distinction between the elect and the reprobate, he said: “If Noah, Daniel, [Col. 0247A] and Job should be in their midst, they themselves indeed will be saved, but their sons will not deliver their own souls” (Ezekiel 15). In Job he understands the rank of faithful married persons; in Daniel, the life of the continent; in Noah, the calling of prelates.

Instructed by these examples, we implore God’s mercy in daily prayers for your honour and salvation, that he may guide the kingdom of the Franks in your hand and enroll you among the elect. Moreover, what we have urgently advised, we urgently advise: strive, so far as lies within you [variant: “as much as”], to bring your purpose to completion, lest the ancient enemy hinder you by some fraudulent deception, even through friends, and thus exclude you from your good purpose and from the number of the elect.

Furthermore, if the Spirit of God is in you, you ought to provide both for your own advantage and [Col. 0247B] for the stability of the kingdom and the peace of the Churches. [Note: To this effect, Aimoin’s continuator, *History of the Franks*, Book V, chapter 52.] If you depart this life without an heir, all these things will be divided into many fissures, and what the Lord says will come about: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house” (Matthew 12). No tongue can tell, nor can the human mind adequately conceive, how great and how miserable that ruin will be.

Therefore, that all these evils may be avoided, do not weave delays into entering the order of married life, lest that hostile mockery [variant: derision] fall upon you concerning what you have so often purposed and so often deferred: “This man began to build and could not finish” (Luke 14). Hasten, therefore, that from your loins may come one who destroys the vain hope of so many ambitious men and brings them back to the uncertainty of hoping in one [Col. 0247C] man. This will both restrain unlawful motions of the flesh and make your detractors and mockers fall silent in your presence. May your Highness prosper, and do not abandon your good purpose.

## LETTER CCXL. IVO, minister of the Church of Chartres by the grace of God, to GEOFFREY, anchorite: may you enjoy tranquillity of mind.

Since every professor of chaste religion ought to abound in the inward affections of charity, so that he strives to provide both for his neighbours’ salvation and his own, he must chiefly seek these two things: a pure conscience and a good reputation—conscience for his own sake, reputation for his neighbour’s. Whoever neglects his reputation is cruel, for, as far as lies in him, he kills his neighbour (Augustine, Sermon 52; and canon *Nolo*, Cause 12, Question 2).

Therefore, whoever wishes to preserve his reputation [manuscript C: “whoever neglects to preserve his reputation”] ought not only to do good things but also to avoid those things which can plausibly be made to appear evil. Paul, considering this in himself, confidently said: “It is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself, for I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Corinthians 4).

We, therefore, though far unequal to Paul’s holiness, nevertheless strive, insofar as we can by God’s granting grace, to preserve our reputation with a good conscience, lest we set a stumbling-block or scandal before a blind and weak brother and, as the Apostle says, the weak brother perish through our conscience [Col. 0248A] (1 Corinthians 8). This sometimes occurs when inquisitive neighbours, corrosive critics of our life but idle correctors [variant: reprovers] of their own, observe our simple actions—which can be turned in either direction—and add conjectures that sometimes ought to be believed and sometimes ought not.

Therefore, in consideration of a brother’s weakness, we ought not to do before the eyes of the weak things which they may use as a pretext for veiling their own perversity or darkening the serene simplicity of our mind. Since this is dangerous, every occasion of evil-speaking must be avoided by us, so that one who stands opposed, seeking an occasion, may find none, but, instructed by a good example and corrected, may return to himself.

I have sent this to you, most beloved, out of brotherly love, not to teach your prudence but to remind it that, as you are guardian of your life, so you should be guardian of your reputation. For you have weak brethren whom you scandalize by your frequent and familiar conversation with a certain devout woman, who often comes into their sight at unsuitable times and places (Letter 208) and with whom she wishes to exchange words curiously and idly. This gives your rivals occasion to speak ill both of you and them, and it interrupts your Sabbath.

Moreover, even if within yourself you have built the camp of chastity for yourself, your security should not become a cause of ruin to those who are outside that camp. For the holy living creatures are described as having eyes before and behind (Ezekiel 1; Revelation 4), which, as [Col. 0248C] you know, means that the life of the saints ought to be circumspect: each should so love himself that he does not postpone the love of the one above him; and so love the one above [manuscript C: “himself”] that he does not despise the one beside him.

This is true and ordered charity. Without it, however great bodily exercise may be, it is not true religion but vain superstition under the veil of religion (Letter 192). May the almighty mercy and merciful omnipotence avert this from us. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXLI. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres by the grace of God, to HUMBALD [or: GUMBALD; thus manuscript C], bishop of Auxerre: greeting and affection.

[Col. 0248D] We could dutifully burden the ears of our hearers with a multitude of opinions, which you have asked to have sent to you, if we had at hand such opinions as were necessary for your case. We do not have them at hand precisely because we are wholly ignorant of the allegations of your accusers and of the arguments by which they support them. To draw the bow and shoot arrows that do not strike the enemy [variant: enemies] is a cause of laughter for spectators, not a defence for combatants. Moreover, battle is not necessary for you, because your case has already been cut off by the apostolic sickle. If you reopen it before clergy and laity without consulting the supreme pontiff, [Col. 0249A] you will offend apostolic majesty and will rightly forfeit your case, which is now secure.

But if the count, by reason of his homage, compels you to reopen an ecclesiastical case, he acts against the fidelity which he owes you, since he drives you into danger to your rank. You will find fully in the canons and decrees that you ought not to conduct an ecclesiastical cause before a secular judge (canon under the title *Whether a cleric may plead a case before a civil judge*, cause 11, question 1). For it is contained in the decrees (Pope Fabian, chapter 3, cause 3, question 6): “Let the person who is accused state his case before his own judge; before a judge who is not his own, if he wishes, let him remain silent.” Pope Julius confirms this in these words: “No bishop (chapter 1, cause 5, question 4), when accused of certain charges, is to be heard, judged, or condemned except in a lawful synod, convened at the proper time by apostolic authority. If certain persons presume otherwise, what they have done shall be brought to nothing [variant: shall be brought to nothing; thus manuscript c], and shall in no way be accounted [variant: be accounted] among ecclesiastical proceedings.”

The canons also plainly prohibit (letter 200) causes not contained in the laws from being heard by ecclesiastical judges. But the laws do not permit—indeed, they forbid—that a bishop be summoned by a secular judge for an ecclesiastical cause or subjected to the sentence of a girded [variant: lay] judge. If it is forbidden in the Council of Chalcedon for a cleric to be enrolled in the churches of two cities (chapter 10; Gratian, cause 21, question 1), how much more is it forbidden for a bishop of one city to be set over a church in another [Col. 0249C] province?

Although these few points seem sufficient to extinguish the present controversy, nevertheless, if your accusers persist obstinately, appeal to the judgment of your metropolitan and fellow bishops, so that, according to the proper order of proceedings, and as far as can be done without prejudice to apostolic reverence, your case may there receive final judgment. Farewell.

## Letter 242. To Audoenus, by God’s grace bishop of Évreux, from Ivo, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres: greeting and service.

Your affection wrote to me that you had heard from some persons that I dissolve marriages between free persons and female slaves, [Col. 0249D] and conversely (letter 221; Gratian, cause 29, question 2; Gregory, book IV, title 9); and that this seemed to you contrary to the evangelical sentence which says: “It is not lawful for a man to dismiss his wife except on account of fornication” (Mark 10; Matthew 19).

To this we reply to your affection that we knowingly do nothing, nor wish to do anything, contrary to that sentence. For if we effect a separation between a free man and a female slave, we do not dissolve a marriage, but dissolve and separate the cohabitation of persons improperly joined. Hence Pope Leo writes to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (letter 9; and chapter 12, cause 32, question 2): “Not every woman joined to a man is a wife; for the bonds of marriage are lawful among the freeborn [Col. 0250A] and among equals.” Therefore, when we separate those who are not joined by this law, we do not call that a marriage which does not contain the sacrament of Christ and the Church.

That union of man and woman seems least to contain that sacrament in which the commandment of love is not observed. For it is not true that genuine love exists between persons one of whom reduces the other to slavery through cohabitation. Since, therefore, the principal evangelical commandment is that we love one another, and that one should not do to another what one does not wish done to oneself (Matthew 17), it is clear that those whom we see bodily joined contrary to the evangelical commandment are not joined by God; nor is that a true marriage which is plainly undertaken against God’s law.

This is also provided for in secular laws, which Catholic kings enacted and, by the authority of the Roman Church, handed down for observance by Catholic peoples. Thus Justinian in the Code of Novels (Novel 12, *On Marriages*, chapter 2, § *But if*, and chapter 2, *Extra*, *On the Marriage of Slaves*): “If someone through error takes a slave woman as wife, believing her free, or conversely, if a free woman is through error joined to a slave, then, once the truth has been discovered, it must be said that no marriage has existed. For marriages cannot be contracted between a free person and a female slave, or between a slave and a free woman.” In such a contract, therefore, what the law condemns is separated not by a human being but by justice. For what is presumed contrary to the laws (chapter *You See*, distinction 10, and following letter) deserves to be dissolved by the laws.

But if a free man has taken a slave woman in marriage, he shall not have permission to dismiss her if, knowing her condition beforehand and consenting to it, they contracted marriage; for consent makes marriage, not intercourse. Where marriages have therefore been contracted in good faith, there is force in the saying, “What God has joined, let not man separate” (Genesis 2); and, “It is not lawful for a man to dismiss his wife except on account of fornication” (Matthew 19). But where human deception has corrupted the marriage bond, God does not make such marriages, but man; and God, not man, makes their separation.

We could discuss these matters at length and bring forward authoritative judgments concerning them, but I believe these points suffice for your prudence. Furthermore, you wrote that certain clerics had come [Col. 0250D] to you with our letters, seeking by the authority of those letters to be promoted from acolyte as far as the diaconate. But I knew nothing whatever of this, because I have ordained no cleric, nor sent anyone to be ordained, by such a leap. Farewell.

## Letter 243. From Ivo, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to Gualo, by the same grace bishop of Paris: greeting and affection.

Recently, when we were at the castle of Meulan, Lord Stephen the chancellor told me [Note: [Col. 0249D] He writes to him in letter 260] that certain marriages had been celebrated in your bishopric against your decree, between a certain [Col. 0251A] little boy and a certain little girl, while they were still almost in their cradles [Note: [Col. 0251D] He treats of the betrothals of children in letter 96 and in Gratian, canon *Betrothals* and chapter *Where*, cause 30, question 2.].

Since these marriages are without faith, without offspring, without consent, and without every marital good, he carefully asked whether they could lawfully be dissolved. Following the course of the laws, I replied briefly: what is presumed contrary to the laws (chapter *You See*, distinction 10) deserves to be dissolved by the laws. Hence Pope Nicholas writes [Note: [Col. 0251D] This occurs in Pope Nicholas I’s book of Responses to the Questions of the Bulgarians, chapter 3, and is cited in letter 148.]: “Consent makes marriage, not intercourse. If this consent alone is lacking in marriage, all the rest, even when intercourse has taken place, is void.”

Having heard this, he asked me to write to you, that you might either not permit such marriages to be made or order those already made to be dissolved. For what we write is not unknown to you; therefore, both for observance of the laws and out of affection for him, we urge you to do what pertains to your office, [Col. 0251B] so that others may be taught by this example not henceforth to be joined in imaginary—indeed, false—marriages. The aforesaid chancellor will inform you who the persons in question are. Farewell.

## Letter 244. To Paschal, supreme pontiff, his lord and father, from Ivo, humble minister of the Church: may he so serve the supreme King as to deserve to receive the prize of eternal blessedness.

Lord Hubert, bishop of Senlis, your creation, complains tearfully that he has been unjustly accused before his metropolitan by certain of his clerics, persons, as he says, of ill repute, of selling sacred orders (canon under cause 2, question 1); [Col. 0251C] and that certain fellow bishops have caused him prejudice. Feeling himself aggrieved, he appealed to the apostolic see, at which and through which such burdens are customarily relieved with maternal compassion and restored, in the balance [variant: “stateram,” perhaps “the balance”] of rectitude, by the scales of justice.

We therefore beseech your blessedness, once the case of the accusers and witnesses has been heard and examined, so to temper judgment with mercy that justice may not be endangered and the judicial order of cases may not be disturbed. For no place will remain for innocence if persons of any sort, pursuing their own interests, are allowed to stain the life of any innocent person contrary to the sanctions of the laws. What manner of life and reputation he has, and on what grounds the aforesaid adversaries accuse [Col. 0251D] him, the bishop himself, when present before your fatherhood, will report; and he will expose their public ill repute by a truthful statement. Farewell.

## Letter 245. From Ivo, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to Hugh, magnificent and distinguished count of Troyes: may he so serve in the way as to be able to reign in the homeland.

We have heard and learned that, intending to set out for Jerusalem, you have devoted yourself to Christ’s warfare—undertaking that evangelical warfare in which one safely fights with [Col. 0252A] ten thousand against one who comes to fight against us with twenty thousand (Luke 14). For ten, the second unit, signifies integrity and firmness of virtues because of the Decalogue; but twenty, being double ten, signifies the duplicity and weakness of vices.

For vices are more numerous than virtues, because vices are not only openly opposed to virtues, but some vices are also concealed beneath the appearance of virtues. Thus, according to the Apostle, Satan’s angel transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11); when he goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5), he strives to deceive some through vices resembling virtues whom he could not induce to open shameful deeds or crimes.

At times he seems to recommend justice [Col. 0252B] so that, under the appearance of justice, he may introduce [variant: introduce] cruelty. He urges some to give away their own goods, so that, stripped of their own possessions, he may drive them to plunder those of others; although it is better not to have something to give than to acquire wrongly something that one gives. He urges some to fast, not that they may love continence, but that they may hunt vain glory. He urges some not to render the marital due to their wives, so that beneath the veil of chastity he may send them into unlawful fornications, or their wives into committing adultery.

In this manner many vices present themselves as virtues, and the simple soul is deceived by them as by hidden snares. Its life may indeed seem honourable, yet it is not sufficiently watchful. Dearest friend, I have written these things with the boldness of affection, so that you may examine your intention in such a way that, just as it appears praiseworthy in human eyes, [Col. 0252C] so it may appear acceptable in God’s eyes; and that you may fulfil voluntary vows without omitting lawful obligations.

You have taken a wife: nature’s law initiated this, and evangelical and apostolic law subsequently confirmed it. [Note: [Col. 0252D] These words show that Hugh, after dissolving the marriage which he had previously contracted with Constance, daughter of King Philip, married another woman when he set out for Jerusalem. For Ivo had disapproved of the earlier marriage, as is evident from comparison with letter 158.] For the old law says: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2). And the Gospel: “What God has joined, let not man separate” (Matthew 19). And the Apostle: “Let each man have his own wife because of fornication; and let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband—unless perhaps by consent, for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (1 Corinthians 7).

But this consent must be so voluntary [Col. 0252D] that it is neither extorted by force nor concealed by any pretence. Otherwise, if you practise chastity without your wife’s consent, even if it is done for God, you do not preserve the marital union, nor do you offer a sacrifice from what is yours but from what belongs to another. For, according to the Apostle, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife; nor does the wife have authority over her own body, but the husband (ibid.). Things vowed from another’s property are not pleasing to the Most High (title *On the Conversion of Spouses*; and canon *Agathosa*, with what follows, cause 27, question 2). Therefore, in this [Col. 0253A] undertaking you must provide for yourself in such a way that you fulfil these latter vows without breaking established natural and lawful obligations. Farewell.

## Letter 246. To Lisiard, by God’s grace bishop of Soissons, from Ivo, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres: greeting and affection.

Let your affection know that I have never approved the marriage of Peter, son of Gervasius, and the daughter of Waleran of Britueil [variant: Galeran of Britueil, or Brutalensis]; nor did I give counsel or consent that it should take place. Indeed, through the cleric Drogo, when Waleran [variant: Galeran] sought my counsel, I advised against it, because such a marriage could not stand if someone challenged it.

I also added the judgment of the law: one husband could not have two sisters in marriage, just as one woman could not enter into lawful marriage with two brothers. [Note: [Col. 0253D] Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, takes this view in letters 7 and 17 concerning the marriage of the son of Walter of Clincamp; there he cites the following passages from authorities. Compare also Ivo’s letter 99, [Col. 0254D].] For Sinegundis, sister of the young woman whom the aforesaid Peter now has as wife, was Peter’s wife—not only lawfully betrothed to him but also joined to him by priestly blessing.

If you object that there was no marriage where carnal intercourse demonstrably did not follow, I answer on the authority of the Fathers that marriage is indissoluble from the point at which the marital agreement has been ratified. Hence the angel says to blessed Joseph: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matthew 1). He called her Joseph’s wife, though Joseph had not known her by physical union and never would know her.

[Col. 0253C] Hence Ambrose, in book two of his *Exhortation to Virginity*: “When she has been betrothed to a man, she receives the name of wife; for when marriage is begun, then the name of marriage is assumed. It is not the defloration of virginity that makes marriage, but the marital agreement. In short, when a girl is joined in betrothal, there is marriage; not when she is known through union with a man.” Likewise Isidore, book nine of the *Etymologies*: “They are more truly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, although marital intercourse is as yet unknown between them.”

That a man cannot have in marriage the sister of a woman to whom he was previously betrothed, just as a brother cannot have as wife the betrothed woman of his brother—since the judgment is the same in like cases—is contained in chapter 5 of the Council of Tribur (canon *A Certain Man*, cause 27, question 8; book V, chapter *On Incestuous Marriages*): “A certain man betrothed [Col. 0253D] and endowed a wife. He could not have intercourse with her; his brother secretly violated her and made her pregnant. It was therefore decreed that, although she could not be married to her lawful husband, nevertheless the brother could not have her, since she had been betrothed to his brother.”

In order that marriage might be honourable and the marriage-bed undefiled, our Fathers took the greatest care to prevent a woman betrothed to one brother from marrying another brother, or a man allied to one sister from taking the other as wife. For through such licence, with the devil deceiving, many shameful and incestuous marriages could arise; these are prevented when the lawful prohibition is observed. [Col. 0254A] I have written a few things to your affection which your prudence knows with me and your diligence is accustomed to observe.

Furthermore, I commend to your fatherhood [variant: brotherhood] our brothers, the clerics of Saint Quentin [Note: [Col. 0254D] Namely, of Beauvais, as in letters 31 and 151.], who are staying with you, that you may extend your protection to them and expect recompense from God. Farewell.

## Letter 247. To John, by God’s grace bishop of Orléans, from Ivo, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres: the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

Our clerics, recently returning to us (letter 248), who had been present at Orléans in the case of Count Theobald, reported that a knight of Lord Ralph [variant: Lord Radulf] had challenged one of the count’s knights to single combat, [Col. 0254B] and that your church had ratified this challenge by judicial decision and appointed the day for the duel.

Hearing this, we were greatly astonished, since single combat can scarcely, if ever, be conducted without the shedding of blood; yet the authority of the Fathers, which must be observed, forbids clerics to administer a judgment of blood, and the Roman Church does not admit it as law. Pope Nicholas says in the case of Lothair against Queen Theutberga: “We do not admit single combat as law, since we know that our predecessors did not accept it.” How can the Church judge that another’s blood ought to be shed when from her first beginning she was commanded to shed her own blood? (chapter *Those by Whom*, cause 23, question 8; and title *That Clerics or Monks May Not Engage in Secular Business*, book III of the Decretals.)

[Col. 0254C] Let girded [variant: all; manuscript c] judges do these things—those who bear the material sword for the punishment of evildoers—not those who fight against spiritual wickedness with the sword of the Spirit. Thus, when no member of the Church usurps another’s office, it may deserve the praises sung of Christ’s bride in the Song of Songs: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle order” (Song of Songs 1).

Otherwise, if we are usurpers of another order, we shall obtain the merit neither of our own office, which we have set aside, nor of the other office, which we have usurped; but, as though our head were placed downward and our feet raised up, we shall imitate the gait of stage-performers [uncertain reading: *thymelicorum*; variant reading: “drunkards”]. Moreover, if through your judgment someone should perhaps incur danger of death, you may incur lasting [Col. 0254D] enmities and danger to your own order. I say these things out of affection to your brotherhood, so that by sound counsel you may reconsider this judgment and, by prudent dispensation, if it cannot be otherwise, undergo lesser dangers in order to avoid greater ones. Farewell.

## Letter 248. From Ivo, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to Ralph of Baugency: greeting and affection.

Your serenity instructed me that you wished to have conversation with us, or sound counsel by letter in the present emergency. Concerning your present affair [Col. 0255A] I have written to the bishop of Orléans (letter 247) what seemed useful to him and to you. From him you will be able to hear what I think of this conflict between you and the count, Theobald, and what counsel I give for the present time.

Meanwhile, however, I answer your request: whatever agreement there may be between you and the count, always render him honour and do not cast upon him the mark of infamy. For the Apostle says: “To whom honour, honour; to whom fear, fear” (Romans 13). And elsewhere: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” (ibid.). Thus David, although destined to be king, rendered honour to Saul, a faithless king; and when at one time he had an opportunity to kill him [thus three old codices; in others: “when he had an opportunity to kill him”], he cut off only the hem of Saul’s cloak [Note: [Col. 0255D] The passage is 1 Kings 24, on which see chapter *The Lord*, distinction 86, cause 1, question 1, and Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*.], and was moved to repentance such that his heart smote him for this small act. Though Saul persecuted him, David always honoured him while alive and mourned him when dead.

Take your example, therefore, from such persons, and imitate what belongs to peace and fidelity toward your lord. But if you complain of any injury from him, use arguments; abandon abusive and insulting words, lest proud words generate endless hatred. For pride humbles, while humility exalts. Farewell.

## Letter 249. From Ivo, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to Gilbert, archdeacon of Paris: greeting.

Since the Apostle condemns deed and consent with equal punishment (chapter *All*, cause 17, question 4; Romans 1), and crimes must be proved through innocent witnesses, these witnesses [Col. 0255C] do not seem to me sufficient to convict an adulteress: while the adulterer lived, out of fear or affection they refused to reveal or accuse her. Some of them also facilitated the shameful adultery as procurers; and thus, as they themselves now testify, they were undoubtedly consenting parties. Therefore, as you know, the self-confessed are not to be believed concerning another person’s crime (letter 229).

Nevertheless, if they are honourable in other respects, and if their accusation makes the report widespread and the foul rumour wounds weak consciences, the woman must be compelled to clear herself, at the discretion of the presiding authorities, of the alleged crime by the testimony of persons of proven standing. Or, if she cannot do this, she should prove her innocence by the ordeal of red-hot iron. [Note: [Col. 0255D] He also approves this in a case of necessity, letter 252.]

If this case were being debated before [Col. 0255D] me, I would wish it treated thus and the truth of the matter investigated thus—without prejudging the opinion of others, who perhaps think otherwise and consider such affairs more often. Farewell.

## Letter 250. To Paschal, supreme pontiff, from Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: devoted obedience as to a father, due reverence as to a lord.

Since I presume that I have some favour in the eyes of apostolic majesty, [Col. 0256A] I sometimes make requests, with that presumption and some hope, even for things which seem to be contrary to apostolic strictness but not contrary to apostolic honour. For it is not unfitting for the apostolic see to sing to God of mercy and judgment. Therefore, when it is appropriate, I confidently knock at the throne of justice (letter 46); when reason requires, I knock with pious confidence at the throne of mercy.

Every judge ought to administer judgment without any dispute; but concerning mercy one must deliberate whether it is expedient or not. I write this not to those ignorant of it, but I preface these matters so that, whichever of these two directions my request takes, either justice may not be denied to one who asks, or the door of mercy may not be closed to one who knocks piously. [Col. 0256B] Your fatherhood will be able to discern this well when you have heard the substance of our petition and learned through the present envoys the reason for their coming.

For your fatherhood knows how long the Church of Canterbury languished, bereft of a pastor after the death of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, of good memory. [Note: [Col. 0255D] He died in the year of the Lord 1109, in the thirteenth year of his pontificate, at the age of seventy-six; see Eadmer the Englishman in his Life.] It knows how the king of the English appropriated episcopal goods for secular uses, and how zealously he prevented an episcopal election there. But now, after your rebukes and after many admonitions from the diocesan bishops, the aforesaid Church, with the consent of the bishops and finally with the king’s acquiescence, elected as its archbishop Ralph, bishop of Rochester, a religious and honourable man, distinguished in learning and character.

He resolved, according to the institutions of the ancients, to visit the apostolic see in person. [Note: [Col. 0256D] Bishops-elect were accustomed to go to Rome, as letter 254 also indicates.] But bodily infirmity partly impeded him and the danger of the Roman journey partly deterred him. Therefore the aforesaid Church sends religious persons in place of its elect, earnestly requesting in speech and writing that you confirm the aforesaid elect in the bishopric of Canterbury and grant him the dignity of the pallium. [Note: [Col. 0256D] The honour of the pallium is mentioned in letter 50.]

I too, by the affection of brotherly charity and the boldness of filial love, ask by advising and advise by asking, that, even if it cannot be done otherwise, you nevertheless come to the aid of the languishing Church by some dispensation; and that, because of the Church’s necessity and then because of the usefulness and worthiness of the person, you mercifully [Col. 0256D] incline your ear to the petitioners’ supplications. Unless a healing hand quickly comes to aid, the aforesaid Church will relapse into its former ruins, and the delaying voice of the powerful will be extended without limit beyond all measure.
