For when our Lord, the institutor of the Sabbath, performed works of mercy on the Sabbath and was reproved by the Pharisees because he was breaking the Sabbath while his disciples plucked ears of grain, he answered their murmuring: “If you had understood, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’” (1 Samuel [Col. 0257A] 15), “you would never have condemned the innocent” (Matthew 12); and elsewhere: “Do you not know that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath?” (Mark 2). By this he instructs teachers that they may temper the rigour of laws because of ecclesiastical necessities (letter 214), when the relaxation of the laws itself contains nothing contrary to the truth of faith or the honesty of morals.

Instructed by these examples, we confidently knock at the door [variant: throne, letter 258] of mercy, believing that it is not unworthy if the apostolic man follows either the command or the example of the One who sends him. Finally, insofar as the human mind can judge another’s heart, it seems to us sound counsel that you receive him paternally, so that you may rejoice that you have adopted a generous son and one faithful to you. Farewell.

## Letter 251. To Manasses, by God’s grace bishop of Meaux, from Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: greeting and service.

[Col. 0257B]

It was recently asked of my lowliness on behalf of the abbess of the monastery of Jouarre whether priests had done wrong in not daring, according to custom, to give the viaticum to a certain sick man who had vomited after a meal; for the sick man himself advised them to delay until the following day, so that he might receive this sacrament while fasting (chapter *We Read*, *On Consecration*, distinction 2) and, so far as he could, show the sacrament the reverence due to it [variant: exercise it].

On hearing this, I praised the sick man’s devotion, and I found nothing for which to censure the priests’ careful hesitation. The sick man’s fear was devout; the delay of the remedy was devout [thus the old codex; earlier edition: “praise”]. In neither case, therefore, was there blameworthy negligence, but salutary and cautious diligence; neither does the physician seem to have failed in his duty, nor the dying man to have lacked divine assistance.

Hence Augustine writes concerning reception of the Eucharist (book *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 53; and chapter *Daily*, *On Consecration*, distinction 2): “Let each person do what he devoutly believes, according to his faith, ought to be done. For Zacchaeus and the centurion did not dispute with each other, nor did either prefer himself to the other, when one of them gladly received the Lord in his house (Luke 19), while the other said, ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof’ (Matthew 8). Both honoured the Saviour, though not in one manner; both were miserable because of sins; both [Col. 0257D] obtained mercy.”

I therefore urge your affection to investigate the truth of the matter; and if the truth is so, create no scandal in the Church over it, lest it be imputed either to excessive simplicity or to some hidden greed. Farewell.

## Letter 252. To Ralph, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, from Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: greeting and service.

With the boldness of charity, I send to your fatherhood the bearer of this letter, a canon of Saint Quentin, a brother of good promise, that for the love of God and of us you may carefully attend to the business for which he has visited your fatherhood; direct it fatherly, and, so far as can be done without prejudice to [Col. 0258A] justice, support it with aid and counsel.

For the brother now present has a married sister whom her husband suspects of adultery on conjectural grounds: she has not been caught in adultery, convicted by witnesses, or accused by anyone. Yet although matters stand thus, this woman’s husband has deserted the marriage and withheld the marital due. Hearing of it, the father met his son-in-law and carefully asked why he did this. Having heard the reason, he wished his daughter to clear herself of the alleged crime by oath; and then, in rash resolve and without counsel, he added that the woman was prepared to prove by the ordeal of red-hot iron (letter 280) that she had never been one flesh with the aforesaid man, from whom so shameful [Col. 0258B] a suspicion had arisen.

A little later this case was argued before ecclesiastical judges. Some said that in such a case an ordeal should not be admitted, since no accusation made in judicial order had preceded it. Others, disagreeing with the others, judged that this ordeal, which the woman had offered on her own initiative, was just. They did not consider that no one ought to put God to the test so long as he has something to do himself (cf. letter 74). For a person then puts God to the test when, setting aside judicial procedure, he seeks divine testimony by the ordeal of red-hot iron or boiling water.

Hence Pope Stephen writes to Litbert, bishop of Mainz: “The sacred canons do not judge that a confession should be extracted from anyone by the ordeal of red-hot iron or boiling water; [Col. 0258C] and what has not been sanctioned by the teaching of the holy Fathers ought not to be presumed upon through superstitious invention. Offences made public through spontaneous confession or the proof of witnesses are to be judged by those entrusted with governance, with the fear of God before their eyes; but matters hidden and unknown must be left to the judgment of Him who alone knows the hearts of human beings.”

Yet we do not deny that recourse must sometimes be had to divine testimonies when, after an ordinary accusation has preceded (cf. letter 249), human testimony is altogether lacking. This is not because divine law instituted it, but because human unbelief requires it; just as we have concerning oaths in the Gospel: “Do not swear at all. But let your speech be ‘yes, yes,’ ‘no, no’; what is beyond this is from evil”—not from the one who swears, but from the one who compels him to swear [Col. 0258D] (Matthew 5).

Therefore, though the evangelical commandment thus forbids every oath, Paul nevertheless permits ecclesiastical matters to be settled in the Church in such a way that, because of the weakness of litigants, an oath is the end of every dispute (Hebrews 6). I do not write these things to one ignorant of them, but remind you so that your prudence may accomplish in this litigation, and in every matter brought before it, what it knows. Farewell.

## Letter 253. To Louis, by God’s grace most serene king of the Franks, his lord, from Ivo, humble minister of Chartres: to obey the commands of Him whom to serve is to reign.

Lord Geoffrey, bishop of Amiens, a religious and honourable man, recently lodging at Beauvais, came to [Col. 0259A] speak with us in his humility. He tearfully disclosed to us his unbearable miseries and distresses, by which he is harassed by violators of the peace, and anxiously sought from me counsel on how he might mitigate such great evils. Since this exceeded my powers—for counsel without strength is usually useless—one course above all others occurred to me: that I should urge him to approach royal majesty, where counsel may be found and the strength of aid may be joined to it.

By the right of fidelity and affection, therefore, we admonish and beseech your royal majesty to weigh his tearful complaints with attentive ear and, at the prompting of compassion, let the barbs of his grief pierce your heart. For it befits your royal majesty not to permit the pact of peace, which by God’s inspiration you caused to be confirmed in your kingdom, to be violated through any flattering friendship or deceptive negligence. If at this very beginning you should choose to spare one person, you would expose many to danger. On the contrary Scripture says: “When the pestilent person is scourged, the wise man will become wiser” (Proverbs 19); and, “The discerning will possess governments” [uncertain reading: “tabernacles”] (Proverbs 1).

If the punishment of the wicked is useful to the wise, much more will the impunity of the wicked harm the foolish. Let the royal sword therefore fulfil its office in punishing evildoers, so that, as it gathers the devout by gentleness, so it may restrain the impious by just severity. Thus the devotion of the poor will pray to the Lord [variant: God] for your welfare, and will obtain what it asks from the Saviour. Farewell.

## Letter 254. To Paschal, supreme pontiff, from Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres: with due obedience, devoted service.

[Col. 0259C]

More than one cause compels me frequently to knock at the ears of your fatherhood, so that my admonition or petition may benefit those who are little known to the Apostolic See but well known to us. Therefore, let not your paternal serenity be burdened by this frequent visitation through letters alone, which I would more gladly offer in bodily presence, were the difficulty of the mountains not an obstacle to the weakness of my old age. We have prefaced these words in order to excuse our importunity and obtain the occasion of a fatherly hearing.

For we ask your paternal discretion on behalf of Lord Geoffrey, Archbishop of Rouen, who only then obtained permission from his lord, the king of the English, to visit the Apostolic See in person; yet in his own time he did not delay to visit it through another person. We therefore do not think that what necessity commanded, not sluggishness discouraged, nor neglect held back, should be imputed to contempt of the Apostolic See. For we confidently intercede for him, because from his youth we have learned from others—and have ourselves experienced—that he is a useful and honourable man. Since, therefore, he has been called to a higher place at the table of his Lord [Col. 0260A] (Luke IV), we both give thanks to God and earnestly desire that he be established as an immovable pillar in the house of God; and we request that apostolic discretion respond to our desires, not without reason. Farewell.

## LETTER 255. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to RALPH, abbot of the monastery of Saint Fuscian: the patience of blessed Job.

For a long time now we have heard of your illness, and we have grieved both from human fellow-feeling and from an affection of piety. If we could suitably apply remedies of medicine, according to the fitness of places and the opportunity of times [Note: [Col. 0259D] “Opportunity” is lacking in manuscript c.], and if we knew the illness to be curable, we would gladly endeavour to procure some remedies. [Col. 0260B] But since the distance between places and the burdens of countless affairs [Note: [Col. 0259D] Of these he often complains, as in Letter 19.] do not permit us leisure for this—and since bodily presence itself scarcely suffices to cure chronic conditions—it seems safer to us not to administer medicine than to administer it uselessly or harmfully.

Therefore we advise that you patiently endure bodily afflictions, which the stern mercy of God has bestowed upon you as a purgatorial fire for the cleansing of vices and the preservation of virtues. Nor do we believe that you need fear another purgatorial fire if you patiently endure this one and remain in thanksgiving. Moreover, if you see that you cannot suffice for the governance of the monastery, I do not advise you, like an unfruitful tree, to occupy the ground; rather, make way for one of the brethren whom the community has regularly elected, so that he may [Col. 0260C] govern the monastery and, in a quiet place, serve you with filial affection as long as you live.

But I do not think that the anointing which you received once should be repeated [Note: [Col. 0259D] Chapter *Nihil*, *On Penance*, distinction 3; yet that it may be repeated was defined today by the Council of Trent, session 14, chapter 3.], because, according to the institution of the Apostolic See, it is a kind of sacrament. Whoever repeats the sacraments of Christ and of the Church does injury to the sacraments themselves. For the anointing of the sick is a sacrament of public penance, and Augustine and Ambrose testify that it is not to be repeated, just as baptism is not repeated [Note: [Col. 0260D] These statements seem distorted and not to concern the anointing mentioned in James v.].

Augustine, in his letter to Macedonius: “It has been cautiously and beneficially provided that the place of that most humble penance be granted once in the Church, lest the medicine, being cheapened, appear less useful to the sick—a medicine which is the more salutary the less contemptible it has been.”

Ambrose, in the second book *On Penance* (chapter *Quamvis*, distinction 50, and the same, *On Penance*, distinction 3): “As there is one baptism, so also there is one penance, which is performed publicly. For we ought to repent daily of sin; but this latter repentance concerns lighter offences, whereas that former one concerns graver offences.”

## LETTER 256. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to brother RAINALD: greeting and affection.

Your affection knows that, desiring to follow the pattern of the primitive Church, you professed holiness in the church of blessed John the Baptist as a prudent Nazarite (Judges XVI) [Col. 0261A]; you professed fellowship in common life; and, like some other lamp [variant: “another”] in the house of God, you began, for the advancement of your purpose, to minister the light of the word to those less learned. But now, as I hear, bewitched by I know not what spirit, you are resolved—having abandoned communal life, not without scandal to the weak—to fly to the wilderness, where you would offer only the sacrifice of turtle-doves, putting aside the offering of pigeons.

In this matter your prudence ought to consider that Christ your head, whom the joined members ought to follow—for as he walked, he commanded us to walk (1 John II)—came forth from his hidden place into our public sphere, in order to commend his love to us and, forming us by his example, lead us by the paths of life back to lost blessedness. Yet you, setting aside this example, desire to flee the common life to which you have devoted yourself. In that life, with no wind of vanity obstructing you, you can preserve solid glory; you can order ascents in your heart in the solitude of the heart [variant: “solitude of mind,” Letter 219]; you can benefit many by word and example. But in secret places you would make your life more conspicuous than useful—which is to bring your glory down into the dust (Psalm VII).

If you do this, you will in part have fallen away from your vow and profession. You who had begun, as if on two feet—namely holiness and fellowship in common life—to make your return toward the homeland by the twofold way of love, will, after one foot has been cut off and one way of love closed, seek, as though lame, [Col. 0261C] the growth of religious life; and I fear that you will incur grievous loss. In saying this, I do not condemn the life of anchorites (Letter 192), but I prefer the life of those living in common. They have not only left their possessions, but have also renounced their own wills, and thus denied themselves in accordance with the evangelical admonition (Matthew XVI; Luke IX).

Even if they are troubled by certain temptations arising from visible objects, they are easily freed from such suggestions, either because an opportunity for solitude is unavailable or because they are occupied with ecclesiastical studies. Solitary life, however, is inferior because it is voluntary and full of importunate thoughts. Like tiny flies rising from mud, these fly into the eyes of the heart [Col. 0261D] and interrupt the sabbath of the mind. Thus the wretched mind, wounded and bloodied by their stings, loses that beauty of which the Psalmist says: “All the glory of the King’s daughter is within” (Psalm XLIV). Running through its fantasies and vain imaginings [variant: “images,” as in Letter 10], it is at times so overcome that, should an opportunity present itself, it would readily fall into the snare of its temptation.

We say this not from conjectures, but because we have learned it to be true from those who have experienced it. We have sometimes seen such people live commendably in the common intercourse of human beings; yet, when they transferred themselves to solitary life, we have known them—by their own confession—to have fallen grievously. [Col. 0262A]

If you condemn the eating of meat, which is sometimes used [variant: “mixed in”] at the tables of those living in common, you should consider that it is more praiseworthy to use more sumptuous foods without the foul flame of desire and not be filled, than to gorge oneself on cheap foods with the foul flame of gluttony (St Augustine, chapter 1, distinction 41). Thus John the Baptist, enjoying agreeable food—locusts and wild honey—was praised by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0261D] “By the Lord” is absent in the other witnesses c.], for abstinence (Matthew III; Mark I). Esau, on the other hand, stuffing himself with a cheap food, namely lentils, was blamed for the desire of gluttony (Genesis XXV).

In saying this, I do not teach you, but remind you to distribute your good in such a way that, while you strive for perfection, you do not become a scandal to the weak. For it is better sometimes to bear weaknesses [Col. 0262B] than to do the highest things with schism [variant: “than to do what is firm with schism”]. I could write much to you in this manner; but your prudence knows sufficiently these matters and other things fitting for love. Farewell.

## LETTER 257. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to PHILIP, by the same grace bishop of Troyes: greeting and service.

We give thanks to your generosity because, mindful of your beneficence, you wished regularly to settle through the Church of Saint Quentin the dispute that had arisen between Lord Odo, prior of the church of Saint George, and certain brethren entrusted to him; and you sent those dissenting brethren to the aforesaid church. For it has been established by your fatherhood [variant: “formerly, by my lowliness”] and by the church entrusted to you that the church of Saint George should acknowledge from you ecclesiastical and temporal benefices with due humility, but receive regular institutions from the Church of Saint Quentin.

Accordingly, what you commanded was done. Some of the dissenting brethren came to dispute against their prelate and to receive the sentence due to their merits. But, knowing that “through concord small things grow, while through discord even the greatest things fall apart” (Sallust, *Jugurtha* 10), we devoted ourselves to peace and unanimity. Since such great discord could not have arisen without their fault, we persuaded them to seek pardon from their prelate for what they had done and to ask forgiveness.

This having been done, peace was made between Lord Odo and the brethren present, and an agreement was made [Note: [Col. 0261D] Thus two witnesses c.; elsewhere “and established.” Letter 114: “thus it was agreed between us”; and Letter 289: “according to the preceding agreement.”] between those present and absent: whoever wished to remain with him should remain in due submission; whoever did not wish to remain should, with brotherly love preserved, pass to the Church of Saint Quentin or to a church adjacent to it, with the consent of Lord Odo and by the dispensation of Lord Ralph, abbot.

Peace having thus been restored, we did not wish to allow another to enter into Lord Odo’s labours. For there he had long [variant: “formerly”] gathered, with much labour and sweat, whatever he could, and had faithfully administered it according to his understanding. But if zeal for the house of God had stirred him to excessive jealousy, we also admonished him [Col. 0263A] to moderate his zeal and, according to the Apostle, become weak to the weak and all things to all people, that he might gain many (1 Corinthians IX).

We have therefore sent him back under your protection and that of your church, that he may serve you humbly and obediently, and that in ecclesiastical necessities he may confidently seek paternal help from you. I request this from your fatherhood, and from your sons—Rainald the provost and your archdeacons Peter, Drogo, Joscelin, Simon, and Odo the chamberlain—that they console the poor church by word and defend it by aid. Farewell.

## LETTER 258. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: a son’s love and a subject’s obedience.

[Col. 0263B]

Since mercy and justice flourish at the Apostolic See, all who are oppressed ought humbly to have recourse to it, so that there each may receive either a just judgment according to the truth of the facts, or a merciful consolation according to apostolic moderation. Therefore, with the knees of our hearts bent, we beseech your excellency to reserve for your own hearing the case of Lord Hubert, bishop of Senlis (Letters 244 and 103), where no rash multitude may terrify him and no violence of princes compel him, but truth alone—stated and proved in accordance with the testimony of his conscience—may defend him.

For we know that in past years, when Lord Richard, bishop of Albano, was exercising an apostolic legation, a council was held at Troyes by that legate. At it, malicious and hostile persons accused the same bishop of the crime of selling holy orders; but, with the bishops agreeing in this, the accusation was by no means proved because the accusers were inadequate persons. Yet the aforesaid bishop, desiring to avoid the disgrace of so grave an accusation, voluntarily cleared himself of the charge at the discretion of your legate, as those who were present testify, and proved his innocence by oath.

By this act we understand that the case was decided in judicial order and that, according to the tenor of the laws, it should not be reopened. But because final judgments of bishops are to be referred to the Apostolic See, he humbly knocks at the throne of mercy (Letter 250), through us and through others favourably disposed toward him, intending to secure the conclusion of his case and to confirm through honourable persons what he has said. He asks that justice be so observed toward him that innocence is not endangered—something we hope the Apostolic See would do even without our intercession. Yet we desire that the free offerings of our mouth (Psalm CXIX) be approved by it. Farewell.

## LETTER 259. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to RALPH, venerable Archbishop of Rheims by the same grace: greeting and service.

Your sublimity commanded Ralph, abbot of Saint Quentin of Beauvais, under the force of obedience, that on seeing [Col. 0264A] your letters he should within fifteen days execute the judgment made by the bishop of Amiens [thus the witnesses c.; earlier, “of Albi”] concerning the mill of Saint Quentin. The abbot replies that he has heard of no judgment in this affair and has not evaded one. Even if such a judgment had been made, it would not be consistent with law, since a law ought to be just, possible, and suited to place and time (Letter 189); reason plainly proves that all these conditions are lacking in this affair.

For it is not just that another should repair the harm which the abbot’s negligence or obstinacy brings upon himself, when the abbot studiously evades strengthening the banks of the stream running beside the meadows in dispute. If they had been fortified as we saw them and often passed by them, there would be no dispute concerning the water that overflows into the meadows. Likewise, it is not just that all the water discharged from every mill within the Beauvais league [variant: “leuga”] should be diverted into the mill of Saint Quentin. If these were restored to their former condition, the entire dispute would be settled.

For the abbot and certain monks of Saint Lucian pursue old hostilities against the Church of Saint Quentin, which, as long as it had a guardian and defender, was free from these disturbances and possessed its property peacefully for forty-five years. Further, every obedience must be possible and, as has been said, suitable to time and place. But this obedience of yours, imposed upon the aforesaid abbot with such severity, cannot at present be carried out in any way because of the severity of winter [Col. 0264C] and the marshy ground—even if it ought justly to be performed by him. For at this time no labourer can work in marshy and watery places.

If, then, something has been extorted from you through importunity or misrepresentation, we ask your fatherhood, having considered the circumstances of things and times, to moderate the sentence with discretion: so that the Church of Saint Quentin may not be compelled to weaken its mill to such an extent that it loses the function of grinding, and so that the monastery of Saint Lucian may not lose its right before those judges who are handling the case in judicial order. Farewell.

## LETTER 260. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to STEPHEN, the king’s chancellor (Letter 243): may you abound in the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

[Col. 0264D]

Recently, on returning from Orléans, Lord Walter, archdeacon of Chartres, informed me of the fluctuations of your heart and how your soul wastes away amid evils, as you ask what above all you should choose or avoid among the matters set before you. He also asked that, in accordance with what I had heard, I answer your affection and write back to your prudence the counsel which, God inspiring, I judged to be sounder.

Having heard this, I can give you no more useful counsel than that you cast your care upon the Lord (Psalm LIV), for he will free you from every fluctuation and restore tranquillity of heart within you. Yet I give you this one counsel especially: never set your own will before God’s will, but humbly assent to him who calls you to his husbandry; and do not resist when he says to you, though placed in a humble station: “Come up higher” (Luke XIV).

For what do you know whether that almighty physician wishes by this honourable path to draw you out of the mire of the dregs and establish you upon the rock of his love [Note: [Col. 0265D] The king’s chancellor may at the same time be a bishop.]? Nor should it terrify you or turn you away from a good purpose that the lord pope did not give an unqualified answer to your petitions—whether concerning the retention of your dignities together with the bishopric of Paris, or concerning the Church of Beauvais: namely, that Lord Walo [variant: “Vualo,” as manuscript c and Letter 144] should not otherwise be transferred to it unless that same church recalled him.

For I know the custom of the Roman Church: it neither customarily nor willingly openly contradicts its own decrees. Yet, once they have occurred, it customarily tolerates many weaknesses by dispensation [variant: “dispensatorily”], both because of the necessities of places [Col. 0265B] and because of the usefulness and honourableness of persons (*Sententiam*, canon 35, question 9; Letter 231). Nor ought the supreme pontiff otherwise to be compelled to write or do what is contrary to himself, lest he be forced to say that apostolic saying: “If I rebuild what I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor” (Galatians II).

Considering this, confidently come up higher. For when you have ascended, you will obtain, we believe, what you seek—so far as the matter can be moderated without prejudice to the honour of the Roman Church—the tolerance which you do not now obtain unconditionally, both because of your own energy and through the intercession [variant: “meditation”; Letter 180, “through his mediation”] of many who love you. Farewell.

## LETTER 261. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to HENRY, by the grace of God illustrious king of the English: may you so flourish in the earthly kingdom as to enjoy the eternal.

[Col. 0265C]

Since, as report proclaims, your glory has spread far and wide, it is fitting that the truth of facts should embody what report declares concerning your generosity. For you will truly possess a kingdom if you govern it well and call your subjects back from wickedness by the rod of justice. This is the true glory of kings: to follow the pattern of the supreme King, of whom the Psalmist says: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom; you have loved justice and hated iniquity” (Psalm XLIV).

I have prefaced this to your excellency because I have heard that you have betrothed one of your daughters to one of our [the witnesses thus; earlier incorrectly, “your”] parishioners, namely Hugh, son of Gervase. Their parents are said to have been born within such a degree of consanguinity that they cannot contract marriage with one another except incestuous—and therefore unlawful—marriage. It is wholly unfitting for royal majesty to admit in itself a fault which it ought to punish in others by the severity of laws.

Therefore, from true reverence and affection, we desire that your greatness be forewarned and forearmed, so that, while it can still be done honourably, you do not permit such a marriage to take place, lest a union presumptuously made contrary to the laws deserve to be dissolved by the laws. What we say is not based on conjecture, for we have before us a written genealogy, which noble men born of the same lineage caused to be written. They are ready to reckon out this same genealogy in a safe place before ecclesiastical judges and to prove it according to the institutions of the laws.

Accordingly, I have sent you the same genealogy, beginning from its stock and set down by reckoning as far as the persons named above, so that, after examining it, you may investigate the truth of the matter and by prudent counsel cause the said persons to desist from an unlawful union. For we cannot depart from the course of the laws if we see our parishioner committing some abomination, especially in the marriage compact; as the apostolic judgment says: “We reserve no pardon for incestuous unions, unless they have cured the incest by separation” (Letter 225).

Although we revere the power of temporal kings, we ought still more to revere the power of the almighty eternal King, so that we may render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s (Matthew XXII). The genealogy, then, is said to stand as follows:

Gonnor and Seufria were sisters. From Gonnor came Richard; from Richard, Robert; from Robert, King William [variant: *Vuilelmus*]; from William, King Henry; and from this king came the girl given to the son of Gervase.

Likewise, from Seufria came Joscelina; from Joscelina, Roger of Montgomery [Note: [Col. 0265D] See William of Jumièges, book VIII, *On the Dukes of the Normans*, chapters 35 and 36.]; from Roger, Mabel, sister of Robert of Bellême; from Mabel, Mabel, wife of Gervase; and from this Mabel, Hugh, son of Gervase, to whom this girl is given.

## LETTER 262. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to PONTIUS, venerable abbot of the monastery of Cluny: greeting and affection in the Lord.

[Col. 0266C]

Your diligent affection asked me, as one who diligently investigates divine mysteries, why the words “mystery of faith” are placed among the sacramental words at the consecration of the Lord’s chalice, when the Lord, in the mystical words of the supper, did not use these words in giving his body and blood to the disciples, nor did any Evangelist insert them among the Gospel words dictated by him.

Let us now consider why these words are placed in the canon; then we shall be able clearly to determine whether they were omitted by the Evangelists or admitted somewhere in an equivalent sense. For many weak persons were scandalized, and are still scandalized [Col. 0266D] [Note: [Col. 0266D] In Ivo’s time the sect of Berengar was still flourishing.], by how the body and blood of Christ can be received under the appearance of the elements, when the human senses report nothing except the colour and taste of bread and wine. Because of their doubt, I believe that “mystery of faith” was placed in the canon, as though it said: “The sacraments which you see on the altar must be judged not by appearance but by faith.”

For the eyes of the outward person report one thing, while the eyes of the mind affirm another to you. Thus, when the Lord had said to his disciples some time before he celebrated the Last Supper with the apostles: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI), many of the disciples withdrew, saying: “This saying is hard” (ibid.). They thought that they were commanded to eat his flesh either boiled in pots or roasted on spits, and to drink bloody blood from cups.

Therefore, lest this error offend all the others who remained, the Lord instructed them by these words how what he had said should be understood: “The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (ibid.); as though he said: “You ought to understand spiritually the words I have spoken to you” [manuscript: “are to be understood”]. The food of which I speak to you is not food for the belly, but food for the mind.

If we attend carefully to these words of the Lord, we shall see that the “mystery of faith” placed in the consecration [Col. 0267B] of the Lord’s chalice contains the same sense; and we shall recognize that it was inserted into the canon from no other source than the words of the Lord. I have answered the first of your questions as I think, without prejudice to a better opinion.

Furthermore, concerning Melchizedek commemorated among the sacred mysteries, I understand none other than the king of Salem himself, whose priesthood the Apostle commends (Hebrews VII). Before the Levitical priesthood had been instituted, he foreshadowed for us in the offering of bread and wine the form of the new priesthood. Likewise, in Abel’s sacrifice we see innocence prefigured, and in Abraham’s offering obedience commended. The commemoration of all these is shown to have this force: that, as the aforesaid Fathers pleased God through faith in things to come, [Col. 0267C] so we may strive to please him through faith in things already bestowed. Thus it is proved that the faith of the Law and of the Gospel, of shadow and truth, is one, although, while future, these were foreshadowed by different figures, and, when past, confirmed by manifest proofs.

These things could be explained in fuller words, but these few points seem sufficient for a wise man. I have sent you, as a memorial of affection, through Lord Ernald—now your monk, formerly our cleric—the collections of canons [Note: [Col. 0267D] He means the *Decretum*, whose prologue appears among these letters as no. 288.] which you requested from me, together with my small works which you wished added to them. Farewell.

## LETTER 263. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to the brethren of the Church of Beauvais: stand firm in adversity and resist the perverse.

[Col. 0267D]

When the letter recounting your calamity [Note: [Col. 0267D] Now first published; it is also found at the end of an old Saint-Victor manuscript. Its subject is plainly the same as that of the following Letter 26; compare Letter 137, written to the people of Beauvais.] was read aloud among us, the substance of the letter gave rise in us to material for tears. With dry eyes we could not read of your exile, the attacks of the townsmen, the plundering of houses, and the invasion of lands. In all these things there was force, not reason; and lay presumption, hostile to clerics, prevailed.

We do not see what it has to do with the king whether you cease from divine offices, justly or unjustly [Note: [Col. 0268D] The Church of Beauvais had in fact been suspended from divine service; see Letter 264.]. If clerics commit an offence, it is not to be avenged by secular power, but must be punished by canonical judgment and episcopal censure. Yet in such an interdict no offence has occurred, nothing has been done rashly, and nothing appears to have been presumed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since it is written, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake” (Matthew V), do not be troubled; do not be afraid. God, into whose presence enters the groaning of those in bonds (Psalm LXXVIII), permits his Church to be afflicted, but does not abandon it. See, then, beloved friends—see that you do not fail because of the loss of your possessions, which we greatly fear. For love of money produces failure, and failure disgrace; and you cannot escape this at all if you place your necks beneath the feet of laymen.

If the honour of the Church is endangered through you, if the rigour of justice is destroyed through you, the example will be shameful for you all and dangerous for some. Far be it that the Church of Beauvais, which has flourished among other churches, should be stained by the mark of so great a disgrace! Far be it that the liberty of the Church should through you be reduced to slavery!

We, indeed—most dear brothers—are with you in all things and through all things, according to our ability and according to your will. We offer ourselves and what is ours to you; and, if you wish, we shall fulfil in deeds what we promise in words. Farewell. May the angel of peace be with you.

## LETTER 264. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to LOUIS, by the grace of God most serene and most sweet king of the French, his lord: may you reign in him whose kingdom has no end.

[Col. 0268C]

Since royal sublimity [variant: “power”] ought to hold the balance of mercy and justice, justice must be so tempered by mercy that neither indiscreet mercy nourishes insolence in subjects nor excessive rigour of justice [variant: “rigour of justice raised too high”] oppresses innocence. For the power of ancient kings is known to have flourished and prevailed in this way: at times they overlooked the sins of humble subjects; at times they corrected them with the rod as sons; but they punished stubborn and proud persons by strict chastisement [variant: “struck them”], so that punishment might render subject those whom impunity and forbearance had made proud.

Having said this, I beseech your excellency with the knees of my heart: let it be apparent in this matter that I have found favour in the eyes of royal majesty, namely, that for the love of God and of us you endeavour to deal with both clergy and people of Beauvais (Letter 263), concerning the rash killing of a man, in such a way that innocence is not burdened, and rashness—incautiously stirred by diabolical instigation—is not struck by the vengeance of men who are proud, but corrected by the rod of those who repent.

For, as has been said, it does not befit royal moderation to treat the subject [manuscript: “subjects and the proud”] alike, lest under the appearance of correction the fury of cruelty steal in, and excessive terror scatter to every wind a people hitherto beloved [Col. 0269A], from whom royal majesty [variant: “royal power”] can receive honourable service above that of the other cities of Gaul.

But if your sublimity does not assent in this to my counsel and prayers, my humility at least earnestly seeks to obtain this from your majesty: that you consult ecclesiastical and honourable persons, who without ill will or love of vengeance wish and are able to give you sound counsel—not counsel for dispersing and crushing the people, which would be attributed to cruelty and afterward make repentance accompany your deed.

If you have any controversy against the dean or clergy, I urge and advise that you cause each person to be examined according to his rank and settle the case of each under ecclesiastical judges. Thus royal majesty will not be diminished in anything, and each person’s own right will be preserved. But concerning the divine service from which the Church of Beauvais has been suspended [the supplied reading adds “mother” (Letter 266), of uncertain syntax], such a counsel does not seem sound to me; for this severity should nowhere be applied except where the fault of sacrilege or a violated peace cannot otherwise be punished (Letter 50). Farewell.

## LETTER 265. IVO, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to LOUIS, by the grace of God most sweet and serene king of the French, his temporal lord: may you live and reign in him through whom kings reign.

It has been represented to your excellency that the clerics of the Church of Chartres are diminishing the right of their provosts and taking away from them what they have possessed through long usage. [Col. 0269C] Therefore I advise your serenity not to believe every spirit, especially one seeking its own interests and not those of Jesus Christ.

For nothing is diminished or taken away from the right of the provosts; rather, unlawful forced services (Letter 271) and oppressions of the poor are forbidden them by apostolic authority—practices which they are permitted neither to exercise nor to exact, not merely from clerics but not even from laypeople. When this had come to apostolic ears through the report of clerics according to ecclesiastical custom, the pope, Paschal, forbade under the bond of anathema that unlawful forced services should any longer be imposed upon poor ecclesiastics (Letter 271), and confirmed in writing what he forbade.

Therefore an apostolic decree cannot, without consulting the Apostolic See, be annulled, altered, or diminished by me or by anyone else without danger to his office. Accordingly, with the knees of my heart bent, I beseech your excellency to grant suitable delay to me and the Church in response to your admonition, until the heat of the dog days has passed and delegates of the Church of Chartres can be sent to the Apostolic See. Then, with the Apostolic See’s permission, your will may be carried out without danger to the Church, while justice is preserved and oppression of the poor removed.

Meanwhile, I ask and admonish your royal majesty to remain at peace with the Church and not add your own sin to another’s sin. Royal majesty ought to keep the royal road and not incline ear or tongue to the ambitions of the greedy [Note: [Col. 0269] They said that this privilege of the Church had been made against royal rights, and had therefore deceived the king, as Letter 271 states.]. For know that [Col. 0270A] I desire no diminution of the provosts’ right where justice and peaceful possession can lawfully support them. May your strength and glory be well and live for long ages.

## LETTER 266. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to CONO, by the grace of God bishop of Palestrina and legate of the holy Apostolic See: obedience and greeting.

As I visit your presence through a messenger and letters, so I would visit in person, were I not still held back by weakness contracted through a long illness. First, therefore, I simply urge upon your vigilant care that you should not believe every spirit. For Hugh, son of Gervase (Letter 261), has alleged that, because he violated the peace, he was unjustly excommunicated and that the divine office was unjustly forbidden in his father’s land ([Col. 0270B] Letter 264), since he says that, on the day when he had been summoned to justice, he was detained by his lord the king. This excuse carries no weight with us in respect of a violated peace, because the king and prince granted their knights this leave: that within seven days after being warned to appear for justice, they should swear unrestricted fidelity to the peace and to the demands of peace, unless prevented either by bodily illness or by forcible detention of their own persons—without exception for king or lord.

Therefore, if I were to absolve the aforesaid Hugh without satisfaction, my parishioners would regard me as a heathen and a tax collector; and the man whose goods he plundered would demand from me, to the last farthing, everything that he had lost, and would exact from me and mine the severest retaliation he could. Moreover, I beseech your holy care that, for deciding the case which you fixed for the third day before the Kalends of September between myself and the abbot of Marmoutier (Letters 267 and 268), you surround yourself with prudent and religious persons, who seek neither to be deceived nor to deceive, and who can be overcome neither by money nor by entreaties. For the monks place their confidence in this: that they promise many things, great things, to many persons.

So that you may know the truth of this matter, I shall briefly disclose it to you, intending to speak or write more fully, if God grants opportunity. This church, situated in the township called Curvavilla, was assigned by its founder to an order of canons in honour of St Nicholas; and this devotion of the said founder was strengthened by episcopal authority and by the severity of an anathema. After the founder’s death, his successor, named Jerogius, enlisted certain mason-monks, to whose monastery he promised to give the aforesaid church if they would fortify the said township with a wall. When the monks of Marmoutier, who were living in a neighbouring cell, heard this, they did not wish to have monks of another monastery as neighbours. Without consulting the Church of Chartres, to which the aforesaid church belongs by right—not merely by canonical right [“amonicali,” MS C], but also by parochial right—they accepted from Jerogius two prebends and seized that church, despite the opposition of the clerics of that place ([Col. 0271A]). Nor could they obtain even communion with the canons, except with certain flatterers.

Accordingly, one of those canons, a religious and learned man named Robert, together with several others, approached Lord Hugh, bishop of Die, who was then legate of the apostolic see, that is, of Pope Gregory VII (Letter 274), and privately and publicly raised before him an outcry concerning this seizure. Robert returned home with letters from the legate; by these letters the legate prohibited the aforesaid monks from their seizure of the aforesaid church. They therefore surrendered the church within the prescribed term and thereafter left it undisturbed for thirty-two years or more, without synodal complaint.

But now, while I was endeavouring, with the consent of the clerics, not to destroy the canonical order but to advance it to a better state in that church ([Col. 0271B]), the monks, stirred by devilish envy, wished to put their sickle into another’s harvest and to deprive me of episcopal right.

> [Note: Col. 0271D] Their violence is complained of in Letter 268, and their calumnious objections in Letter 274.

As for their assertion that this church was granted to them by my predecessor (Letters 1 and 2), whatever they may say, the Church of Chartres, of which it is a member, knew nothing of it; and they lost what they had seized there, he neither protesting nor assisting. I have written this briefly so that you may gird yourselves more closely for the defence of truth and, as far as you can, repair the ruins of the clerical order to which you belong (Letter 36). Farewell.

## LETTER 267. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to CONO, by the grace of God bishop of Palestrina, devoted and due obedience to apostolic legates.

[Col. 0271C]

Your care invited me to prosecute, either personally or through my representatives, the case concerning the church of St Nicholas against the monks of Marmoutier. It is situated in the township called Curvavilla, and they once presumed to occupy it contrary to ecclesiastical law. But, according to the course prescribed by the laws [canon *Vides*, Distinction 11], what they had unlawfully presumed was, at the command of the apostolic legate Lord Hugh, bishop of Die,

> [Note: Col. 0271D] He had been legate in Gaul under Pope Gregory VII, as appears from Letter 274.

dissolved by legal means. I undertook to pursue this case because I thought that I could conduct it in person. But now, because I am still unable to ride or endure any conveyance, I beseech your holiness to ensure that this case is handled so impartially that my absence may suffer no prejudice because of the inadequacy of my representatives ([Col. 0271D]); rather, if necessary, my presence should be awaited in a suitable place or at a suitable time, according to the tenor of the canons.

For whatever the monks may say, if I were present I would prove beyond contradiction that those monks possessed nothing in the aforesaid church except by seizure or fraud: in part after the clerics had been expelled from their place, in part after they had been intimidated by threats, and in part after they had been severely beaten (Letters 268 and 274). Nor do they possess documentary warrants, whether from apostolic or episcopal authority, except such as they extorted by deceit.

> [Note: Col. 0272D] What follows was added from an old manuscript.

Therefore, exercise such care in this case that, since the report of this matter has spread far and wide, it may redound to the honour of God and of the holy Roman Church. Farewell.

## LETTER 268. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to the bishops WALON of Beauvais, WILLIAM of Châlons [or VUILELM of Châlons], GAUDFREY of Amiens, and CLAREBALD of Senlis: may you abound in the spirit of knowledge and piety and in zeal for justice.

Since, according to the decretal writings and the enactments of the canons, all ecclesiastical controversies must first be examined in the places where they arose and, unless an appeal has been made, brought to an end there, the abbot of Marmoutier, setting aside judicial procedure (Letters 267 and 274), disregarding brotherly charity, brought to the apostolic see an unjust and disorderly complaint against me ([Col. 0272B]). Yet I had done him no injury; indeed, before Walter [or Gauter] the archdeacon, Hugh the subdean,

> [Note: Col. 0272D] Thus the old manuscript; formerly “subdeacon.” The subdean is mentioned also in Letters 54 and 204, and the subdeanery in Letter 182.

and many others, I had offered him every justice before the tribunal of the church entrusted to me. I therefore first protest this injury in the hearing of the lord cardinal, of you, and of this whole assembly. If justice is delayed or denied me in this matter, so that it is not brought into due order, I shall cry out far and wide, in speech and writing, that violence is inflicted upon one who is ill and unable to bear the assault of the monks.

For this case was settled, by the command of Lord Hugh, bishop of Die, formerly legate of the apostolic see, in the council of Issoudun (Letter 181), while I was present and heard it, together with certain other clerics of Chartres ([Col. 0272C]). Therefore, if we were not parties to the case, we should judge canonically with the other bishops that it is not to be reopened. What I say can be demonstrated by the testimony of honourable persons, who heard the complaint of the canons of the church in question at several councils and knew with complete certainty the judgment requiring the removal of the monks from the church.

A further witness to that removal is peaceful possession for thirty years: throughout all that time canons succeeded canons in the aforesaid church, and neither those departing nor those arriving heard any canonical claim from the monks. During all those thirty years I likewise knew of no canonical complaint concerning this matter before my predecessor, Geoffrey (Letter 266), on whose grant they rely ([Col. 0272D]); nor, during the twenty-five years in which I have held the episcopate, have I heard that a canonical complaint was ever made, either before me, before provincial synods, or before general councils. Whatever the monks may say, these things will be proved as I state them, if necessary [variant: “if it should be necessary,” thus P and MS C]. I could add much, but I believe this sufficient for your prudence to defend my right.

A fuller account of the events is contained in the letters sent to the cardinal, a copy of which I have sent to your care ([Col. 0273A]), so that the truth may be known from them more certainly. Farewell.

## LETTER 269. IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres, to BERNER [or BERNERIUS], abbot of the monastery of Bonneval, and to the brethren entrusted to him: may you abound in the affections of brotherly love.

Since divine grace has gone before the brother who bears this letter with blessings of sweetness, so that, advancing from strength to strength, he strives to follow the arduous paths of the Fathers; since, after long experience of cenobitic life, he desires to enjoy the sweetness of solitary quiet; and since in solitude of mind (Letter 219) and [Col. 0273B] heart (Letter 256) he desires to contemplate in Zion the Lord of lords, he ought not, in our judgment, to be deprived of his desire, but supported and advanced, lest so devout a devotion of divine love grow cold or lukewarm in him.

We therefore urge that no envy prick our minds regarding this purpose of our good brother, and that his great advancement should not appear a diminution of fraternal reputation, as though he were striving to win favour and set himself above others in human eyes—he who in this purpose contends to please only the Father of lights. Therefore, even though it is not granted to all to imitate him, nevertheless do not oppose him, nor extinguish in him the spirit that burns and gives light and inspires such desires. Farewell.

## LETTER 270. IVO, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to TURGED, by the grace of God bishop of Avranches [variants: Ambricensium; Abricensium]: may you be refreshed by the consolation of the Paraclete.

[Col. 0273C]

Since, when one member suffers, all members ought to suffer with it, I have felt compassion and grief on hearing of the afflictions of your tribulations. Yet I do not dare to give you definite advice, because I do not see how you can follow it without offending some authority. For, on one side, the legation of the apostolic see compels you to obey its commands; on the other, royal power presses you to resist. Since apostolic and royal commands thus oppose each other ([Col. 0273D]), no one can give you sounder advice than that which Susanna, prompted by the Holy Spirit, gave herself: “It is better for me to fall into the hands of men than to forsake the law of my God” (Daniel 13).

That is: either obey the apostolic see fully through its legates, or send your representatives directly to the apostolic see, where they may make satisfaction for you and restore to you the favour of the apostolic see. Otherwise, you can break the bond of anathema; you cannot loose it [variant: “but you cannot loose it,” thus MS C]. In all these uncertainties may the Lord give you the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, so that you may think soundly and carry out the same things courageously ([Col. 0274A]). Farewell.

## LETTER 271. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, by the grace of God supreme pontiff [to his father and lord].

> [Note: Col. 0273D] The enclosed words are absent in certain old manuscripts; they are present in MS C.

Entire and devoted obedience according to my ability.

We give thanks to your supreme fatherhood

> [Note: Col. 0273D] “Supreme” is absent in MS C.

because, after examining our letter through its bearer, you confirmed the desired privilege for the common clergy of the Church of Chartres against the rapacity of the provosts (Letter 265), in order to restrain the oppression of ecclesiastical poor persons ([Col. 0274B]; Book II, chapter *On Bishops and Clergy*). Two of the provosts, whose names the bearer of this letter will give to Your Highness, have stubbornly risen against it; they represented to royal authority that this privilege had been made to diminish the king’s realm.

> [Note: Col. 0274D] The plunder of the provosts was concealed under the name of royal right. Letter 265 warns the king not to lend them his ears.

Thus they have sinned grievously against the apostolic see, if it chooses to take notice, to their perpetual disgrace. Therefore, on behalf of the clergy and together with the clergy, I beseech Your Highness with knees bent in my heart: by renewed writings, strengthen your decree, and send to the Church of Chartres, in clear language without ambiguity, a fearsome sword striking disobedience from both sides, declaring what penalty these present contemners of the apostolic decree ought to suffer.

For they have misled the king (Louis, [Col. 0274C] Letter 265), as they wished and were able, so that he sent me threatening letters against the clergy, declaring under threat that he would take the property of the clerics wherever he could, unless your privilege were destroyed and the rapacity of the provosts permitted in peace. I have therefore sent these letters to Your Highness; when you have seen them, pronounce a severe sentence upon their instigators, so that they may always lie under disgrace unless those who have lost their property on this pretext receive it back in full. In this way you will both relieve the oppression of the poor and restrain others from similar transgression.

Concerning the *precariae*—benefices granted on request (canons 4, 5, and 6; Cause 10, question 2)—which you have already forbidden twice in the Church of Chartres, we similarly pray most earnestly that your judgment may never be changed but rather strengthened ([Col. 0274D]). For, when these were received personally, unlawful buying and selling arose among those receiving and not receiving them, together with shameful contention, anger, quarrels, jealous rivalries, enmities, and many unlawful things, which Your Highness ought to decree must be uprooted from the Church.

Moreover, both the clergy and I beseech Your Highness on behalf of this bearer: if he suffers any adversity because of this affair, may he experience the apostolic hand as avenger and helper. Before this matter he was at peace; now, under the pretext of other grounds, he is surrounded by threats and hatred from both the king and the count of Chartres ([Col. 0275A]). Yet he does not cease to devote himself and his possessions faithfully and mercifully to the Church and to the poor. We also ask that, if he requests anything concerning this matter which is not contained in the present little letter, you may hear him in this affair as though he were ourselves. Farewell.

## LETTER 272. IVO, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to REGINALD [RAGINALD, MS C], by the grace of God bishop of Angers [“of the people of Angers,” MS C]: may you so govern the flock entrusted to you that you are not compelled to render account for it to the eternal Judge sorrowfully and groaning.

Since the care of the Lord’s sheepfold has been entrusted to us priests in order that we may strive to lead the sheep committed to us through the pastures of life, we ought not to separate an erring sheep from the unity of the flock so irrevocably (Letter 279) as to expose it to be devoured by the jaws of wolves. The charge entrusted to us demands rather that we pursue the wandering sheep through byways and, if necessary, force our way through thickets and briars with the scratching and bleeding of our sides,

> [Note: Col. 0275D] Thus in two old manuscripts; formerly, incorrectly, “with sacrifice and clarification,” or even “with rubbing.”

so that we may be able to restore it to its sheepfold.

I have offered these words beforehand to Your Love because, at the request of Lord Geoffrey, dear to us and her kinsman, we have been asked to entreat your care on behalf of one of your parishioners, named Matilda: may you consider her errors and lapses so mercifully and discerningly that, putting aside every hostility and erasing every resentment, you do not reject her while she seeks counsel for life; rather, after the example of the supreme Shepherd, who received the weeping sinful woman ([Col. 0275C] Luke 7), strive to heal her wounds and restore her to the way of salvation and honour.

For since the life of the Lord Jesus was moral instruction upon earth (Letter 279), we rightly walk in the paths of life when we avoid what we know that he avoided, or do [variant: “imitate”] what we have learned that he did. We would say more, but fear to burden your prudence with the weariness of excessive speech.

## LETTER 273. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to CONO, by the grace of God bishop of Palestrina and legate of the holy apostolic see: greeting and obedience.

Your care knows that the cows which bore the ark, leaving their calves at home, went toward Beth-shemesh; and, though lowing for their calves and looking back ([Col. 0275D]), nevertheless they did not stray from the way (1 Samuel 6). Your care ought to consider this: although we do not wish for any reason to dissent from obedience to the apostolic see, yet sometimes, in the affection of brotherly compassion, we are compelled to appeal to the apostolic see or its representatives for brothers placed in tribulation, so that, with the rigour of justice moderated, we may obtain some remedy of consolation for our friends and associates.

Therefore, on behalf of the bishop of Bayeux, who for good reasons is a close friend to us, we beseech your care (Letter 270): for the love of God, of ourselves, and of the others who petition for him, temper in his case the excommunication threatened against the bishops of Normandy, so that, if you cannot permit him to exercise episcopal office, you may at least not deny him entrance into the church for a time. For, placed under another’s authority as under a press,

> [Note: Col. 0275D] Namely, the king’s. For in three old manuscripts this letter has the following heading: “Concerning a bishop who grieved and lamented that he could do no more than the king allowed.”

he grieves and laments that he can do no more than he is permitted ([Col. 0276A]). We therefore beseech you again and again that our intercession for him may avail before you—an intercession which nothing compels us to make except the affection of brotherly love. Farewell.

## LETTER 274. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: with full obedience, full joys of salvation.

[Col. 0276B]

Because bodily illness prevented me from attending the case which you commanded to be heard before the bishop of Palestrina, legate of the apostolic see, between myself and the abbot of Marmoutier (Letters 267 and 268), I nevertheless sent my representatives and my letters to counter the calumnious objections of the monks

> [Note: Col. 0276D] Letter 266 calls their envy devilish.

before that your legate and the bishops whom he had summoned to hear this case. Since the monks were unable by any judicial procedure to disprove the truth of those letters, and although no judgment had yet burdened them nor any sentence been pronounced against them, they summoned me, absent and ill, to the apostolic see (Letter 219), not because they trusted in justice but to cause delay. Yet through my representatives I was willing ([Col. 0276C]) to bind myself to refute the matters which they had alleged against me and to prove judicially the matters by which I had answered their unjust objections in my letters, if a suitable place and time were allowed for my illness.

To state the whole truth briefly, let Your Holiness [variant: “holy fatherhood,” MS] know that they have never possessed any investiture of the church in dispute, either wholly or in part, except by seizure or fraud. When this seizure was brought to the hearing of Lord Hugh, bishop of Die, who at that time was legate of Pope Gregory VII (*Register*, book IX, Letter 15 and following), he sent letters, freed the aforesaid church from the monks’ seizure ([Col. 0276D]), and, by apostolic authority, left it in peace to the canons serving there.

From that time, therefore, the same church endured no disturbance and no lawful claim, whether in the chapter of Chartres, in a provincial synod, or in a general council. Instead, under its bishop, with clerics succeeding one another [variant: *viritim*, “man by man”] for thirty years or more, it served in clerical order. But now, when I wished to raise the life and order of those clerics to a better condition, the monks rose against me and obstructed my purpose ([Col. 0277A]) by unjust accusations [old manuscripts: “by many accusations”]. Although I had denied them no justice, they made an injurious complaint before the apostolic see by a disorderly leap and with judicial procedure set aside.

I therefore beseech Your Holiness with knees bent in my heart: consider this injury done to me as your own, and command that this case be heard and concluded within our province, before judges appointed by your fatherhood, in a nearby place where I can appear in person; or, once the course of events has been examined, compel the monks to cease their unjust accusation. I have accordingly sent Your Fatherhood the letters which I wrote to your legate, Cono, as appears from Letter 267, and to the bishops whom that legate summoned to this case, so that from them you may clearly know the truth which I was ready to prove in a suitable place ([Col. 0277B]) and may better provide for repelling injustice and defending justice.

For I am ready to prove canonically whatever is contained there concerning this case, if a suitable place and time are granted to my weakness. May Your Blessedness therefore take thought for its reputation, lest it allow prejudice to be done before it to my old age and weakness, or to the dismemberment of the church entrusted to me. Moreover, I beg you through the bowels of fatherly mercy: if any cleric of Chartres should seek to obtain from you through any deceit a doubling of ecclesiastical honour for himself, do not consent, lest it be charged as transgression and the harmful custom which had been abolished be restored.

Under the same prayers I commend to Your Fatherhood the Church of Blessed John the Baptist and the abbot of that church, the bearer of this letter ([Col. 0277C]), so that he may obtain what he requests for the necessity of the little flock entrusted to him, whereby the religious life of the place committed to him may grow and flourish. Farewell.

## LETTER 275. IVO, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to CONO, by the grace of God bishop of Palestrina and legate of the apostolic see: greeting and obedience.

I recently received your letters, containing the excommunication of those who captured the count of Nevers, who were present at his capture, who received any share of his spoils, or who gave assistance in this matter ([Col. 0277D]), except only the person of Count Theobald [or Tebald], to whom you granted a truce until the octave of All Saints. Yet unless he restores the count of Nevers in the meantime, from that point you have subjected him to the same excommunication.

I therefore had these letters read and explained to Count Theobald [or Tebald], so that, on hearing the severity of ecclesiastical discipline, he might perhaps reflect, or God might inspire him, to restore the aforesaid count and to restore peace to a land already disturbed and likely to be disturbed still more grievously. Having heard and understood these things, he was greatly surprised that the king had lodged a complaint against him before ecclesiastical judges,

> [Note: Col. 0277D] Violators of the peace were customarily excommunicated, as in Letter 61.

although, as the king’s vassal, he had denied him no justice. He therefore offers himself for every justice before the judges of peace, in the order required by the sequence of events, in every place to which he can safely bring his actions and where he can safely pursue [variant: *exerere*] them ([Col. 0278A]). Yet he demands beforehand redress for the injury done him in that his knights were excommunicated precipitately and without due procedure, although they either committed no offence against the peace agreement or denied no justice concerning it.

Having heard his answers, I thought it best to send reverend persons to Your Religiousness, who might report to you these and other words of the count, so that you may discuss them with the lord king and strive to establish peace between him and the count. For the count defends his innocence so plausibly in words, and so magnifies the injury done by the king and the count of Nevers, that he seems to have a just case unless he is convicted by judicial procedure and irresistible reason ([Col. 0278B]). Your prudence should know, however, that I would have appeared in person in these proceedings if bodily weakness allowed me to ride and bear the labour of travel.

Therefore, after consulting with the bishops and the judges of peace, strive to settle this controversy in such a way that the opposing party may have nothing to criticize and that the peace of the churches and the tranquillity of the poor may remain firmly established. For the count says that he will willingly restore, or release upon surety, the count of Nevers if, having heard his arguments, the judges of peace agree to this and decide it at the dictate of justice. Farewell.

## LETTER 276. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, his father and lord: due and devoted service of obedience.

[Col. 0278C]

Because the apostolic see comes to meet the needs of all who piously appeal to it, all its children who suffer tribulation run to it as to a mother’s bosom for consolation, so that from it milk may be supplied to infants and solid food to adults, according to each one’s need. Therefore, the Church of York, situated in the western regions and long bereft of a shepherd, piously appeals to the hearing of its mother, both through its sons and through its dependants, so that, placed in tribulation, it may find the bowels of maternal mercy.

For the aforesaid church has chosen as archbishop a venerable man named Tustinus [perhaps Turstinus or Turstanus], who, so far as his person is concerned, is of continent life and honourable reputation and is useful to the holy Church of God, insofar as human conscience can judge another person’s life. His consecration has been deliberately delayed because of an improper custom, contrary to the privileges of the same church, which the Church of Canterbury demands from him. But since it belongs to fatherly discernment to settle the disputes of churches and restore peace among them, although we appear to act beyond what is required, we nevertheless beseech Your Fatherhood to defend the right of the aforesaid church and, while apostolic privileges remain firmly established, to confirm its elect in the dignity to which he has been called, as he deserves ([Col. 0279A]). Farewell.

## LETTER 277. IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to ALDEBERT, elect of the Church of Le Mans: the gift of sincere affection.

> [Note: Col. 0279D] Thus two ancient manuscripts read, not “Hildebert,” as MS 6 does.

Since, in the words of Wisdom, “the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who flatters” (Proverbs 27), I admonish your brotherhood not to take my words harshly, though they are somewhat caustic and biting, because they aim at correction, not accusation; cleansing, not attack [variant: “not assault”]. Your temporal advancement indeed pleases me, if it is not an eternal downfall; if the Psalmist’s saying is not fulfilled in you: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” ([Col. 0279B] Psalm 72).

For I have heard concerning you things that cause me grief and horror. If they are true, you will not be able to provide governance for the people but will increase their danger. Certain leading men of the Church of Le Mans, who testify that they know your past life, say that you loosened the reins of chastity beyond measure, so much so that, after you received the archdeaconry, with a crowd of little women lying at your side, you begot a great crowd of boys and girls. Yet you know that one who is raised to the summit of pastoral responsibility ought to be of proven chastity. Otherwise, a man who falls after sacred ordination ought not only not ascend to a higher rank but ought not even to minister in the order in which he fell.

Accordingly, blessed Gregory writes to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (*Pervenit*, Distinction 50): “Whoever has fallen into the sin of the flesh after receiving sacred orders must so lose sacred order that he may no longer approach the ministry of the altar.” You also know that he who is assumed to the pastoral office,

> [Note: Col. 0279D] Peter of Blois very eloquently expresses a similar opinion in Letter 15, to a count elected bishop of Chartres.

since he is to make supplication for the sins of God’s people, becomes a mediator between God and men. But blessed Gregory says in the *Moralia*: “A man placed in grave sins, while oppressed by his own sins, does not wash away those of others.” The same author says in the *Pastoral Rule*: “It is clear to all that, when one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angered person is without doubt provoked to worse things.”

The aforesaid persons also add to this accusation that you were elected neither by their counsel nor with their consent. If all this is so, it is dangerous for you, dearest brother ([Col. 0279D]), and, in my judgment, will produce endless trouble. Therefore take counsel for yourself according to the testimony of your conscience: either complete what you have begun honourably and cautiously, or, providing for your salvation, voluntarily withdraw yourself.

> [Note: Col. 0280D] He gives the same advice to Roger in Letter 29.

For a withdrawal is joyful when an outcome of salvation is hoped for in it. Farewell; and trust me in all just and honourable matters as you would a friend.

## LETTER 278. IVO, by the same grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to ROBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Lincoln: may you, having taken the wings of a dove, dwell in the farthest parts of the sea.

[Col. 0280A]

The more distant the province from which your generosity remembered our lowliness, the greater the thanks we ought to return to that same affection. With no merit of ours preceding it, your affection conceived a pure-minded remembrance of our humility and proved it by the performance of a deed. Therefore, if any grace has been divinely bestowed on us which may be useful either to you or to yours, the effect, God granting it, will prove in performance what affection promises in speech.

If, then, any service of ours pleases your goodwill, write to us through your pupils residing among us, whom we love both for their own honourableness and for your affection, so that through their mediation we may satisfy your wish according to our ability and bind more closely your affectionate regard for us ([Col. 0280B]). Meanwhile, let us extend to one another the reciprocal hands of prayer, so that, having crossed the stormy sea of this life, we may deserve to establish our dwelling in the secure harbour of eternity. Farewell.

## LETTER 279. IVO, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to LISIARD, by the grace of God bishop of Soissons: may you abound in the bowels of discernment and mercy.

The bearer of this letter came to us and exposed his wound as to a physician, but did not receive the remedy of medicine, as though he were in no way to be healed through us. Nevertheless, we gave him counsel concerning what remedy would be useful to him and from whom it ought beneficially to be sought ([Col. 0280C]). He replied to my words that he had done all this and had sought from Your Fatherhood, according to regular discipline, a measure of penance; but, because of the hostility of certain persons, he had found not a remedy of healing but the severity of cutting.

I therefore beseech Your Love either to command that he be received into the Church with the satisfaction required by regular discipline, or to obtain for him permission to serve God in another regular church. For it is not fitting that a sheep expelled from its sheepfold should be exposed to the jaws of wolves (Letter 272), and, afflicted by excessive severity, be swallowed up by more abundant sorrow. We must remember that good Shepherd who, when reviled, did not revile; when struck, did not threaten, but set before us his patience as an example ([Col. 0280D]), whose life has been set before us for moral instruction (Letter 272). He will in no way belong to that Shepherd’s fold who scorns to be stamped with the pattern of his life.

But if you judge that he must be cast away as a diseased sheep which would infect the whole flock, you must carefully examine his life and conduct, lest you put to death one who is alive or deem one who is dead to be alive (Ezekiel 13). Yet since it is not my part either to instruct Minerva in wisdom or to embellish Mercury in eloquence, the sum of my request is that you temper judgment with mercy in such a way ([Col. 0281A]) that judgment does not crush him and mercy does not breed insolence.

## LETTER 280. IVO, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to LISIARD, by the grace of God bishop of Soissons: may you keep pastoral watch over the sheep entrusted to you.

Your archdeacon, the son of Lord Nivelo of Péronne, came to us with certain honorable brethren and carefully sought the advice of our lowliness as to how, in accordance with the laws, he might free his sister from the dishonor which the Count of Soissons, her husband, maliciously imputes to her. Having heard them, it seemed to me that he does not proceed against her by judicial process, nor summons her to lawful purgation. For the ordinances of the Novels of the laws say [Col. 0281B] (JUSTINIAN, Novel 117, “That it may be lawful for a mother and grandmother,” ch. 15)—ordinances which the Roman Church commends and observes—that a person suspected by a husband of wishing to violate the chastity of his wife is not first to be handed over to punishment or held convicted unless the husband has warned him three times through suitable witnesses not to have any familiar conversation with his wife, either in his own house or another’s. Once this has been done, if thereafter he finds them conversing in a private place with three suitable witnesses, then, and only then, may he either summon them to judgment or inflict the punishment due.

Otherwise, neither secular nor divine laws allow anyone to be made guilty on conjectures; and your prudence well knows that the disposition of accusers [Col. 0281C] and witnesses ought to be free from offence, so that nothing may be done through enmity, and that the accuser himself may not be blameworthy in the very respect for which he accuses another. As for the fact that the count summons her to the ordeal of red-hot iron (ep. 252), because he testifies that she offered this voluntarily, or to trial by single combat, ecclesiastical laws prohibit this rather than command it. Hence Stephen to Liutbert, bishop of Mainz:

> “The sacred canons do not judge that a confession should be extorted from anyone by the ordeal of red-hot iron or boiling water; and what has not been established by the teaching of the holy Fathers must not be presumed upon through superstitious invention.
