Offences made public by voluntary confession or the testimony of witnesses are to be committed to the judgment of rulers, with the fear of God before their eyes; [Col. 0281D] but hidden and unknown matters are to be reserved for the judgment of Him who alone knows the hearts of the children of men.”

Likewise Pope Nicholas I says (ep. 50 to Charles, king, vol. III of the Epistles of the Supreme Pontiffs):

> “We do not admit single combat into the law, for we do not find it to have been commanded. Although we read that some persons undertook it—as Sacred History relates concerning holy David and Goliath—divine authority has nowhere established that it is to be held as law, since those who pursue this and things of the same kind appear merely to put God to the test.”

From these and similar pronouncements it is clear that the aforesaid [Col. 0282A] count cannot convict his wife of adultery except by the lawful number of witnesses, especially since he has shown her neither the affection of marriage nor scarcely rendered the marital due. I could write much more to this effect; but, since I write to one learned in the law, I think this sufficient. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXXI. IVO, humble bishop of Chartres, to ANSELM, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais: greetings.

We have heard that the canons of St. Peter of Beauvais bring a claim against the canons of St. Quentin, who possessed that land without any objection in the time of Lord Wido, bishop and your predecessor, and of the succeeding bishops down to your own time. Know that, if a fixed and suitable time [Col. 0282B] is appointed at which I may appear before you in your chapter, I am prepared, through someone acting in my stead, to prove that I was present at the chapter of your canons and saw and heard that they granted to the canons of the aforesaid church the land of which I have spoken, to be held peacefully in perpetual right, no one objecting.

Take care, therefore, lest in your time the poor church be diminished in its possessions, since justice is not done by him to whom, through God’s providence, the government of ecclesiastical property has come; lest we and other lovers of that church be compelled to bring its wrongs before a higher tribunal. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXXII.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] This letter is without an address in manuscript C, in which it is numbered 213.]

IVO, minister of the Church of Chartres.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] This is the form of the title in the old manuscripts; but it is not properly a letter, any more than the four that follow. Therefore they are relegated [Col. 0282D] to the end of the book.]

[Col. 0282C]

Since what the devotion of the faithful has customarily given to hospitals, poorhouses, or other religious houses [Note: [Col. 0282D] These are mentioned in Laws 19 and 20, *On Holy Churches*, Code; formerly, *procot.*] for the redemption of their souls, for the support of those who dwell there (ep. 183), ought no longer to be reckoned among human possessions, because they belong to God, it is fitting that the rulers of churches should undertake their defence as divine patrimonies and, drawing the sword of the Spirit, should not delay to strike their invaders and despoilers with canonical severity as despisers of God.

Accordingly, I, IVO, minister of the Church of Chartres, considering this with devout concern, receive under the paternal protection of the holy Church of Chartres and of ourselves all things that have been bestowed by the faithful upon the Poorhouse [*Ptocotrophium*; variant: *procot.*] situated at Châteaudun [two old manuscripts: *Castrodumo*], near the church of Blessed Mary Magdalene, or that, God granting, shall be bestowed in the future. [Col. 0282D] We declare that their invaders and despoilers are to be dreadfully condemned before the tribunal of the eternal Judge; and in this temporal Church, without communion with which no one can attain the eternal Church, we exclude them from the body and blood of the Lord and from the communion of that Church, until they repent and strive by humble satisfaction to restore Christ’s patrimony.

But upon those who preserve and enlarge that same patrimony of Christ, may there be blessing [Col. 0283A] and peace from the Lord Jesus Christ, who, though rich, became poor and weak for us, that he might enrich us by his poverty and heal us by his weakness.

## LETTER CCLXXXIII. IVO, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Chartres.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] In manuscript C there is no title; but in the margin appears: “Privilege of the abbot of Tours,” and it stands among letter 230. Compare letter 282.]

Since what the devotion of the faithful customarily gives to religious places for the redemption of their souls, for the support of those who dwell there, ought no longer to be counted among human possessions, because they belong to God, it is fitting that the rulers of churches should undertake their defence as divine patrimonies and, drawing the sword of the Spirit, should not delay to strike their invaders and despoilers, as despisers of God, with canonical severity. [Col. 0283B]

Accordingly, I, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, considering this with devout concern, make known by the record of this present writing to all orthodox sons of the Church, present and future, that Rotrou, noble and valiant count of Mortagne, came before our lowliness, requesting that we consecrate the cemetery of a certain monastery situated on the river called Thirone, for the use of certain religious monks who had chosen to lead an eremitic life in that place and had built there a monastery as place and time permitted.

We, therefore, assenting to the devout petition of so great a man, consecrated the aforesaid place for use as a cemetery, solely on this condition: that henceforth no secular power should receive there any secular customary dues or exact any exactions. [Col. 0283C] The aforesaid count graciously consenting to this condition, granted more abundantly than had been requested, adding to the aforesaid freedom that whatever might be granted to that place from his fief should enjoy the same immunity.

Therefore, to preserve the tranquillity of the servants of God, at the petition of the aforesaid count we receive the aforesaid place, with its appurtenances, under the paternal protection of the holy Church of Chartres and of ourselves; and we declare its invaders and despoilers to be dreadfully condemned before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. In this temporal Church, without communion with which no one can attain the eternal Church, we exclude them from the body and [Col. 0283D] blood of Christ and from communion with the same Church, until they repent and strive by humble satisfaction to restore Christ’s patrimony.

But upon those who preserve and enlarge that same patrimony of Christ, may there be blessing and peace from the Lord Jesus Christ, who, though rich, became poor and weak for us (2 Cor. 8), that he might enrich us by his poverty and heal us by his weakness.

## LETTER CCLXXXIV.

[Note: [Col. 0284D] Now first published from three old manuscripts.]

IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres.

Since the pages of decrees and canons entrust the administration of ecclesiastical affairs to episcopal care, [Col. 0284A] bishops themselves must carefully attend to this: whatever dispute there may be among men, that a faithful man may be found, they, being conscious of their own integrity, should devoutly and sincerely order what must be ordered, extending their hands especially to those who have renounced worldly occupations and, stripped bare, have followed the naked cross of Christ. For if, as the Rule of the Fathers says, “under the compulsion of charity a bishop is the servant of the people, not their lord,” then much more must he be minister and servant of those for whom the world has been crucified.

Accordingly, I, IVO, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, make known to all the faithful of the Church, future and present, that the religious man Bernerius, abbot of the monastery of Bonneval (ep. 226 and 269), came humbly before us, petitioning, [Col. 0284B] through Gauslin, archdeacon of the same place, that we should grant to the monastery of Bonneval the church of Blessed Peter situated at Châteaudun, which certain uncircumcised clerics had occupied from the hand of a layman by means of money.

Because his petition seemed to me conducive to the salvation of souls, I assented, and, with the said layman, named Odo, who had occupied it hitherto, present and consenting, granted the aforesaid church to the monastery of Bonneval on these terms: that the clerics should retain their prebends for life, if they lived chastely and served God in that church as is fitting. But after their death the monks shall retain them for their own uses, for the benefit of those who serve God in the same church under monastic observance. If, however, the aforementioned [Col. 0284C] clerics commit a criminal offence or refuse to serve the church, they shall be removed from the church by episcopal judgment, and their prebends shall be assigned to the monks’ use.

We have further added that whatever they have hitherto peacefully possessed for a year and a day from the estate of the Church of Chartres by grant of those possessing and presiding, they shall henceforth possess peacefully by our grant, saving the course of the laws and in all things preserving the right of the Church of Chartres. We also confirm for them the chapel of St. Innocent [one old manuscript: Vincent] situated at Chartres near the Ashen Gate, which Hugh the viscount gave to him.

## LETTER CCLXXXV.

[Note: [Col. 0284D] Now first published from old papers.]

IVO, by the grace of God minister of the Church of Chartres.

Since it is fitting that matters to be transmitted to the knowledge and memory of posterity should be committed to writing, [Col. 0284D] I, IVO, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Chartres, though unworthy, with the consent and assent of our brother Odo, archdeacon, have commanded that this little page record what I wish to be held in perpetual remembrance concerning the church of St. Nicaise situated at Mantes.

This church of St. Nicaise had been inhabited and possessed by secular clerics who entered it through the hand of a layman, namely the count of Mantes, until it pleased Lord Robert, count of Mantes, with the goodwill of the clerics instituted in the aforesaid church, to convert that church to better uses [Col. 0285A] and to labour that God might be served there according to rule. Therefore Count Robert himself, with the consent and goodwill of the aforesaid clerics, transferred that church to St. Mary of the monastery of Bec, so that monks might be appointed in the aforesaid church of St. Nicaise from that monastery as should be expedient, and might serve God according to rule.

Brother William, abbot of Bec, together with certain brethren of his monastery, brought before us this transfer made by the aforesaid Count Robert, humbly requesting that our consent should strengthen the aforesaid gift. Since their request appeared worthy, while preserving the right and honour of the Church of Chartres, we granted them the often-mentioned church of St. Nicaise, that they might appoint there monks who [Col. 0285B] serve God according to rule. And by the book [Note: [Col. 0285D] Investiture was made by the presentation of a book, as in letter 182.] we gave that church itself to Brother William, abbot of Bec, with our brother Odo, archdeacon, present and assenting; and also Hilduin, cantor, Ansellus, chancellor, Ernold, archdeacon, Guaslin, provost, and Gerald, chaplain, present.

## LETTER CCLXXXVI.

This is not a letter, but the instrument of foundation of the monastery of St. John in the valley of Chartres. See below among Ivo’s diplomas.

## LETTER CCLXXXVII.

IVO, least priest of Blessed Quentin of Beauvais, to HAIMERIC, brother of good hope: may that which he devoutly knocks for be openly opened to him.

I recently received your brotherhood’s letter; for [Col. 0285C] I was not at home when it was brought to our church, having gone to Lyons on business relating to a certain ecclesiastical matter. In that letter your brotherhood asks whether our Lord Jesus Christ, at the supper which he held with his disciples before his Passion, gave them his passible body, whereas we receive it from the table of the altar as impassible.

If in answer to this question one says that Christ’s disciples received his body such as it then was, whereas we receive it such as it now is, I see no authority that opposes this, nor any force of reasoning that compels me otherwise. Indeed, if I said otherwise, I should see reason and authority in opposition to me. For no one denies that the body which the Lord then commended to his disciples was still to suffer, [Col. 0285D] as you yourself cited from the Lord’s authority in your letter: “This is the body which shall be given up for you.” Who can deny that what was to suffer was passible? You yourself have also well established by apostolic [variant: “the Apostle’s”] authority that what we receive is now impassible, since Christ, rising from the dead, “dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

For if a potter gave me an earthen vessel before the kiln, raw and fragile, and after the kiln returned the same vessel baked, sound, and fit for human use—a use it could not have had unless it had first been baked—so Christ’s body before the Passion, being what it was, was given passible to the disciples, and through the Passion it was to pass into impassibility. [Col. 0286A] Nor could that passible weakness of the body have profited anyone unto salvation unless the glorification of an impassible and immortal body had followed.

Just as a potter could say to me: “The vessel which I give you before the fire is useless and fragile; after the fire I shall immediately return it to you useful and sound [variant: “and robust”],” so our Lord Jesus Christ expressly said: “Take this body which shall be given up for you”; and subsequently added: “Do this” (Luke 22). He said this, not something else; yet he did not deny that it would become something else, so that he might leave it to our understanding that the body which we receive from the Lord’s table is of the same substance [variant: “essence”], although, by the example of his transfiguration and the teaching of his authority, he had foreshadowed to his disciples that it would possess another glory.

Nor should this be passed over in examining the matter: when he had said, “Do this,” he added, “in remembrance of me.” What that remembrance is, the blessed Apostle explains, saying: “For as often as we receive the bread of the Lord and drink his cup, we proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes.” Therefore, just as reception of the impassible body is a remembrance of the Lord’s death now past, so reception of that passible body was a foretelling of that same Lord’s death still future. It does not matter what kind of body was received then or is received [Col. 0286C] now, but with what benefit it was or is received. Since one end is found for both receptions, all doubt about the quality of the thing received should be set aside.

For when I am hungry, I do not ask what my bread is like—whether soft or hard, cold or warm. Nor, when I thirst, do I care whether my wine is *sapa* (boiled must) or *carenum* (reduced must) [Note: [Col. 0285D] In one old manuscript: “whether it is savoury or sour,” which has the appearance of a gloss.]; rather, I attend to whether it may restore the collapse of my stomach and satisfy my need. So it is of no concern to me what kind of body of Christ was received by the disciples or is now received by Christians; let it only fulfil the benefit for which the Lord established that the faithful people should receive it.

You further said that you were perplexed by certain words of blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 0286D] Letter to Irenaeus, and in chapter “Not this,” distinction 2, *On Consecration*.] endeavouring to explain the words of the Lord instructing the twelve apostles who remained, [Col. 0286D] when almost seventy had withdrawn. These are the words:

> “You will not eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will shed.”

This may suitably be understood as meaning that it is the same body and not the same body: the same in material essence, but not in visible form. Hence he adds: “Although it must be celebrated visibly, it must nevertheless be understood invisibly.”

For those who withdrew thought that they would tear the flesh of the living Lord into pieces in the manner of beasts and eat it either boiled [Col. 0287A] or roasted on spits. Unless they were willing to do so, they could not be his disciples. But we eat and drink Christ as sacrificed in such a manner that we believe him to remain whole at the right hand of the Father. And although he once offered himself as a living sacrifice, passible and mortal, in the distinction of his members and the manifestation of his body, nevertheless every day, under the veil of bread and wine, he is sacrificed by the holy Church; and his body is received by the mouths of the faithful neither torn into parts nor bloody. This is what is meant by the words, “You will not eat this body which you see.”

For blessed Augustine would not deny that what we receive from the altar is the true body, since he expressly affirms this in many passages of his treatises. Thus he says in a sermon on the words of the Gospel:

> “What you see on the altar is bread and a cup, as your eyes themselves report; but what faith, which must be instructed, requires is this: the bread is the body, the cup is the blood.”

And after inserting certain remarks:

> “How is bread the body, or how is that which the cup contains blood? These things, brethren, are called sacraments [Col. 0288A] because one thing is seen, another understood.”

The same author says in a sermon to the newly baptized:

> “Receive in the bread what hung upon the cross; receive in the cup what flowed from Christ’s side.”

Eusebius of Emesa also says concerning this invisible reception of Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 0287B] Homily 5, and in chapter “Because the body,” *On Consecration*, distinction 2.]:

> “When you ascend to the venerable altar to be fed with spiritual food, look upon the sacred body and blood of your God with faith; honour it, marvel at it, touch it with the mind, receive it with the hand of the heart, and above all receive the whole of it by the draught of the inner man.”

I could indeed gather more [variant: “very much more”] from the Scriptures in support of this view, but for the present let these things suffice for your brotherhood. Farewell.

## CCLXXXVIII. H. of Pontigny

[Note: [Col. 0287B] This is Hugh of Pontigny, to whom St. Bernard’s letter 33 is addressed.]

and B. of Clairvaux,

[Note: [Col. 0288B] Bernard, who together with the said Hugh writes to Pope Honorius in letters 46 and 49.]

to the most reverend Father and Lord O., by the grace of God abbot of Marmoutier, and to the holy community united in the charity of Christ: may they walk in the Spirit and never grow weary of seeking the face of the God of Jacob.

[Col. 0288B]

Charity, brethren, etc.

(Printed among the letters of St. Bernard, no. 397, otherwise 387.)

[Col. 0287]

# ADDITIONS: LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF ST. IVO WHICH WERE LACKING IN EDITIONS OF HIS WORKS

## I. LETTERS

### I. To Pope Paschal II, on behalf of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres

[Col. 0287C]

To PASCHAL, supreme pontiff: Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, with due obedience, wishes whatever the human mind can desire and hope for in earthly and heavenly things.

Warned and strengthened by apostolic authority, we ought to devote ourselves to ecclesiastical peace and monastic tranquillity. Where our own efforts are insufficient to accomplish this, we are compelled to seek the counsel of the Apostolic See, that we may experience as our helper the authority which we have had as our commander, so that we may fittingly say to your Apostolic Eminence: “Give what you command, and command what you will.”

We have said this beforehand to your Highness because we wish your solicitude to know that in the suburb of Chartres there is a monastery in honour of Blessed Peter, founded by my predecessors and enlarged, as resources permitted, from the goods of the Church of Chartres. Religious observance there sometimes flourished and sometimes grew lukewarm, because, as commonly happens, when the integrity of prelates failed, the soundness of their subjects could not follow. But since, by God’s prevenient grace and with some cooperation of our own effort, the vigour of religious observance has flourished anew in the aforesaid monastery, we wish to provide for that monastery the tranquillity necessary to monasteries [Col. 0288C] and to free it entirely from the forced services and burdens which archdeacons seeking their own advantage attempt to impose there. Certain of our predecessors thought they had also done this; but that liberty did not retain its full force because it was not fortified by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, the whole congregation of the aforesaid monastery asks that, through the mediation of our humble office, the monastery with its appurtenances be received under the protection of the holy Roman Church, and that the freedom which our predecessors granted to the monastery and its possessions—while preserving the right of the bishop of Chartres—be strengthened by apostolic authority. For what the principal key has itself shut, the lesser key cannot open; and what it has opened, the lesser key cannot shut.

We have therefore sent a certain brother of the aforesaid monastery, bearer of this letter, who may identify by name more fully and specifically the matters which should fittingly be freed and defended by apostolic authority, and may bring back to us the instruments of liberty confirmed [perhaps: “of confirmed liberty”].

### II. To Adela, countess of Blois

(Published from an autograph of Marmoutier, engraved by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 385.)

I[VO], humble minister of the Church of Chartres, to the noble countess A[DELA]: greetings.

[Col. 0289A] Setting aside every worldly desire, I praise your devout purpose in desiring to restore to its former condition the church of St. Martin of the Valley, which was formerly a monastery. At the same time I advise you to strive carefully to bring what you devoutly desire to a speedy fulfilment, lest the ancient enemy impede your purpose and prevent you from reaching the desired end. For my part, to fulfil this, insofar as reason and ability allow, I promise both counsel and help. Farewell.

### III. To Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme—On not repeating the anointing of the sick

(It is the twentieth letter in Book II of the Letters of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLVII.)

### IV. To William, archbishop of Rouen

(*Works of Guibert of Nogent*, edition of d’Achery, appendix, p. 689.)

To GUILLELMUS, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen: Ivo, humble minister of the Church, greetings and service.

Concerning the cleric who bears this letter, who, in irregular fashion and by an over-hasty leap, caused himself to be ordained subdeacon although he had not been blessed as a cleric, I reply to your Highness that, if you wish to observe the rigour of justice, you should neither permit him to minister in the orders irregularly received nor promote him to higher grades. For it is read in the pontifical decrees that what is rashly undertaken contrary to laws deserves to be dissolved by laws.

If, however, his upright life or ecclesiastical usefulness so requires, you may mercifully grant him a dispensation, after he has been made a cleric and has rendered due satisfaction. Thus, when it happens that you celebrate sacred ordinations, he may be present, humble in heart and body, at the sacred ordinations—not in order to be reordained, but in order that, by appropriate words, he may be confirmed in the orders already received. I do not have at hand a personal ruling concerning the mercy to be granted in such transgressions; but concerning a similar case I send to your discretion the dispensatory ruling of Pope Alexander II. Strengthened by its example, if it appears fitting to you, after due consideration you may both confirm what has been received [Col. 0290B] and grant what has not yet been received.

The ruling is as follows:

> “Alexander II to Rumald, bishop of Constance: The solicitude of your charity has sought our advice whether the bearer of this letter is fit to perform the office of deacon and priest, or not, since he is known to have advanced to this by an over-hasty course, namely without the order of subdiaconate, through negligence rather than pride. Therefore, in answer to your consultation, we command your charity to prohibit him from the priestly office until, at the next fast of the Four Seasons, you duly impose upon him the ministry of subdiaconate, and thus afterwards permit him to return to the higher offices. Farewell.”

## II. DIPLOMAS

### I. Charter for the church of St. Mary and Bourg-Moyen

(BERNIER, *History of Blois*, p. 8, from the archive of the monastery of Bourg-Moyen.)

[Col. 0289C]

I, Ivo, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, wish all the faithful of the Church, present and future, to know that Countess Adela, wife of Count Stephen, inflamed by the fire of divine love and kindled with the desire of increasing religious observance, humbly approached our lowliness, asking that by the authority of our excommunication we should confirm the liberty of the church of St. Mary of Bourg-Moyen, of its canons and other clerics serving that church, and also of their servants—a liberty formerly granted by Count Odo and his wife Bertha, somewhat diminished over time, but most carefully restored by her.

We, therefore, assenting to the just petition and just desires, together with the flock entrusted to us, excommunicate the violators of that liberty and exclude from the thresholds of the said holy church both them and those who support them in infringing the aforesaid liberty. Let them not be visited by priests in sickness; at the hour of death let them not receive the body and blood of Christ; let them not be buried in the cemetery of Christians; let them incur the eternal flames of Gehenna, unless, repenting, they seek amendment and satisfaction. [Col. 0290C] And, so that this may remain confirmed and stable in succeeding times, we have ratified this charter with our own hand and delivered it to be ratified by the hands of the prelates of our Church.

Sign of Ivo, bishop. Sign of Arnald, dean. Sign of Helduin, cantor. Sign of William, archdeacon. Sign of Seran, subdean. Sign of Warin, subcantor. Sign of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury. Sign of Fulk, archdeacon. Sign of Arlon, archdeacon. Sign of Odo, archdeacon. Sign of Andrew, archdeacon. [Col. 0290D] Sign of Hugh, provost. Sign of Gerosius, chamberlain.

Given at Chartres, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 1105 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction XIII, in the forty-sixth year of the reign of Philip, king of the Franks.

### II. Charter of the Church of Chartres for Bernard, abbot of Thiron

(MABILLON, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 680, from the archive of Thiron.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. The Church of Chartres, to all Christ’s faithful, present [Col. 0291A] and future: greetings and peace.

Since it is not lawful to pass over in silence the wonderful signs and manifestations of our Saviour Jesus Christ and of his mother Mary, our own loving mother, that have occurred in our time, we wish to bring them into the light of public knowledge and make known to all posterity that, when for three continuous days certain visions appeared to several of us—as we now understand—to some, a most sweet swarm of bees approaching our dwelling; to others, a man clothed in monastic habit, surrounded by marvellous brightness, awakening them from sleep; and the visions themselves being accompanied by a wondrous and most sweet fragrance of every kind of spice: after we had repeatedly considered these things for two days, at length diligently examining, each one of us, day by day, moment by moment, hour by hour, what these visions were and what matter they concerned, and after the Mass of the Holy Spirit had been celebrated and his grace sought, news shortly afterward came that Lord Bernard, the reverend father of the Thironian monks, was present and requested leave to speak with our assembly.

Admitted into our chapter while we were assembled there, he stated that he and his community preferred to dwell in the territory of Blessed Mary rather than in that of an earthly prince, and asked from us a ploughland of land upon which his community might build a monastery. Recognizing the visions that had occurred two days earlier, we willingly granted to them and their successors the said ploughland with every jurisdiction, right, legal power, and every other spiritual and temporal liberty, to be held by them as freely and peacefully [Col. 0291C] as we had previously held it.

Rejoicing at their arrival, we grant them the following liberties, if they build a monastery for themselves upon the ploughland which we gave them in our territory of Garzay. For we wish to cherish them in peace and tranquillity, lest, as the wickedness of the world increases, they should be disturbed in the peace we desire for them. We will and grant in perpetuity to that monastery that the monastery itself, its cells, houses, and administrations, present and future, and those dwelling in them, present and future, shall be subject to the bishop of Chartres alone. They shall not be subject to us as dean and chapter, nor to any of our archdeacons, dignities, offices, or prebends; they shall answer to none of them in any matter; and no spiritual or civil jurisdiction shall be exercised over them by anyone except the bishop of Chartres.

Yet we remove and withdraw them from the chapter, archdeacons, dignities, offices, and prebends, and assign them to the bishop, under the following condition previously established: the bishop shall not compel the abbot of Thiron to come to or attend his synod, unless he has been or is to be summoned, by a written notice expressly communicated to him, to seek his counsel and consent concerning some new ordinance affecting the entire ecclesiastical condition of the diocese. For we wish him more freely to devote himself to the solicitude and care entrusted to him.

Moreover, wishing that they should be raised in honour above others because they preferred to live in our territory, [Col. 0292A] we will and grant that the abbot of Thiron shall rank first, in every honour whatsoever, after the bishop. Further, so that it may grow more abundantly in temporal goods, inasmuch as we hope and desire that they will bring forth abundant fruit in the house of the Lord, we will, grant, and concede to them in perpetuity that, in whatever lordships and territories belonging to us or subject to us, they may freely acquire property and may freely hold and possess in perpetuity what they acquire in mortmain; nor may any claim concerning this be brought against them by us or any person of ours. They and their people shall be free and immune from every secular custom and exaction in all our lordships and jurisdictions.

And so that these our grants may remain firm and valid for them in succeeding times, we will and grant that no lapse, no contrary use or possession, may hinder them from enjoying these liberties and grants inviolably in perpetuity and using them in the future. Indeed, from this moment we invalidate and annul all such acts, uses, possessions or quasi-possessions, and prescriptions that may have followed, and decree them invalid and void.

Wishing these provisions to be confirmed in perpetuity by decree of the legate and of any of our superiors, and all uses, acts, possessions or quasi-possessions, and prescriptions whatsoever that may follow contrary to the grants made by us above to be invalidated and annulled by him and by them [Col. 0292C] in perpetuity, and all things by which they might contravene them to be decreed void and invalid: therefore, under the subscriptions and signs of the names of us who constitute the Church of Chartres, made by our hands, we have judged that these things should be granted to the said religious men under the devices of our seals, by the unanimous will and consent of all, to bring perpetual validity.

I, Ivo, bishop of Chartres. Arnald, dean. Gerogius, cantor of Chartres. Hugh, subdean of Chartres. Warin, precentor of Chartres. Ansgerius, archdeacon of Chartres. Walter, archdeacon at Châteaudun. [Col. 0292D] Goslenus, archdeacon at Pacy. Rambaud, archdeacon at Dreux. Odo, archdeacon at Blois. Landricus, archdeacon at Vendôme. Geoffrey, provost in Normandy. Henry, provost at Mazerolles. Jeraudus, provost in Eure-et-Loir. Hugh, provost at Ingré. Rodulfus, chamberlain of Chartres. Stephen, abbot of St. John.

Given at Chartres by the hand of Wlgrin, chancellor, on the third day before the Nones of February, in the year 1110 from the Incarnate Word, in the reign in France of Louis, son of Philip.

### III. At the request of Abbot Bernerius, he grants to the monastery of Bonneval the church of St. Peter of Châteaudun.

(Edited by D. d’Achery in his notes on Abbot Guibert, p. 664.)

[Col. 0293A]

Since the pages of decrees and canons entrust to episcopal care the administration of ecclesiastical affairs, bishops themselves ought diligently to take heed that, whatever dispute may arise among men, a faithful man may be found; conscious of their own good intent, they should with devout affection and sincere purpose order what must be ordered, extending a hand especially to those who have renounced the affairs of the world and, naked, have followed the naked cross of Christ. For if, as the Rule of the Fathers says, under the compulsion of charity a bishop is the servant of the [Col. 0293B] people, not their master, then much more ought he to be minister and servant to those for whom the world has been crucified.

Accordingly, I, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, make known to all the faithful of the Church, present and future, that the religious man Bernerius, abbot of the monastery of Bonneval, approached our humility, through Gauslin, archdeacon of that same place, petitioning that we grant to the monastery of Bonneval the church of Blessed Peter situated at Châteaudun, which certain uncircumcised clerics had seized by money from the hand of a layman. Since his petition seemed to me conducive to the salvation of souls, I gave my assent, in the presence and with the consent of the layman himself, named Odo, who had occupied it hitherto; and we granted the aforesaid church to the monastery of Bonneval [Col. 0293C] on the following condition: that the clerics retain their prebends during their lifetimes, if they live chastely and serve God in that church as is fitting. But if the said clerics commit a criminal offence, or refuse to serve the church, they are to be expelled from it by episcopal judgment, and their prebends are to be assigned to the uses of the monks.

We have also added that whatever, from the casamentum [estate or holdings] of the Church of Chartres, they have hitherto held peacefully for a year and a day by the grant of those possessing and presiding, they shall henceforth hold peacefully by our grant, without prejudice to the course of law and in every respect without prejudice to the right of the Church of Chartres. We likewise confirm for them the chapel of St. Vincent, situated at Chartres beside the Ashen Gate, which Hugh the viscount gave them.

### IV. Charter of the foundation of the monastery of St. John in the valley of Chartres

(From an old charter of the church of St. John of Vallières.—This instrument, like the following one, occurs among Ivo’s letters; edition of Fronteau.)

[Col. 0293D]

Since, by the ineffable mercy of the supreme Father disposing all things, we—though unworthy and sinners—have undertaken pastoral care, we ought by continual vigilance of heart diligently to provide for the common good and the salvation of souls; and, since we are to receive the penny in the evening, to extend on every side the branches of the Lord’s vineyard. Therefore, with heavenly grace enlightening our [mind], and with our true [Col. 0294A] beloved, as it were through the opening made by compunction, extending toward us the hand of advancement and assistance (Song of Songs 5), we have often reflected and, in reflecting, sought how we might have in this city or its suburb some church in which a devout assembly of the faithful might lead a devout life worthy of God and ordered according to the canonical rule.

Now at last the great and inexplicable goodness of our Savior Jesus Christ, who knows how to answer those who cry rightly and to open to those who knock worthily, no longer deferring the fulfilment of our desires, has offered us the church of Blessed John of Vallières—a place indeed well suited, and most fitting for such sacred institutions, since it is set somewhat apart from the popular noise of the city. [Note: [Col. 0293D] See Letter 91.] And by enlightening and preparing the hearts of certain brethren who held the benefices [Col. 0294B] of that place in a manner not sufficiently ecclesiastical, it has brought them, beside themselves in mind, in accordance with the Apostle, to wish to live no longer for themselves but for God, and to become some beginning of God’s creation.

I therefore, Ivo, by God’s grace bishop of the holy Church of the Mother of God at Chartres, by the common counsel and consent of the whole chapter and of our leading men, have decreed that the canons in the aforesaid church of St. John shall be such as, setting aside private property, live the canonical life according to the institution of Blessed Augustine. Since they cannot devote themselves to divine service without the support of temporal goods, we have added to the provisions they formerly possessed, for their sustenance, the entire revenues for one complete year of the prebend of each deceased brother of our congregation, or of any brother who assumes a monastic or canonical habit [Col. 0294C] [Note: [Col. 0294D] Thus the old slip.], or who, if he relinquishes his prebend, sets out for Jerusalem or the wilderness, renounces the world, or gives up his prebend through fear of death, illness, or an improper entrance. These revenues are to be used so that, on every day of one complete year, masses may be celebrated for the soul of the brother when he has died.

We also grant that the church of St. John shall hold in perpetuity in the church of Blessed Mary the prebend which Abbot Albert held when he adopted the canonical rule. We have given also the church of St. Stephen and all that pertains to it: namely, the altar of Morentia with the portion of synod dues pertaining to that altar; likewise the church of the village of Mundonis, free from synod dues, circada, and every exaction; together with male and female serfs, and lands both cultivated and uncultivated. We grant also the church of St. Faith, the church of Luciacum, and the field portion of that land which we formerly possessed; all the customary dues of the land of St. John—that is, of that village—and the land with offerings of Osanivilla, both episcopal and canonical. We also grant the land of Aucherivilla.

In addition, we have given the junioratus [junior officialship] of the church of Pontegodon, together with all our houses, all the mixed fodder of oats, all our land beyond the water then uncultivated, and the oven of that village; likewise the tithe of the mills and vineyards. We also confirm the gift of the altar of the church of Serni, made by Gauslin, canon and provost of St. Mary; and [Col. 0295A] the gift of Vigeria of Valeia, and of all the land of Moncellis with all its customary dues, made by Hugh, vicedominus of this city. We likewise confirm the gift of the whole land of Eddevilla with all its customary dues and fiefs; also the gift of the church of Ardueluth with all its tenants and with land for two ploughs.

So that this work of charity of ours may remain firm and stable through succeeding times, we have caused it to be committed to written record and confirmed by the impression of our seal and by the authority and presence of John [Note: [Col. 0295D] Ivo writes to him in Letter 87.] and Benedict, cardinals of the apostolic see by God’s grace; and we have given it to be confirmed by the hands of our canons and of the other faithful. If anyone should attempt to bring any challenge against this canonical institution or to invalidate [Col. 0295B] anything, struck by our anathema he shall find God angry with him; and unless he corrects his fault by worthy satisfaction, let him be assigned to the punishments of hell [perhaps: “he shall be assigned,” *deputabitur*].

Furthermore, we have decreed that if the abbot of the aforesaid church should die or should depart for some canonical reason, the brethren shall elect as their abbot someone from the same congregation or from another regular community, if no suitable man can be found there; and for this election they shall associate with themselves persons of sound counsel. The abbot elected shall be presented in the common chapter of Blessed Mary, receive the abbey from the bishop, and, like the other canons in the church of Blessed Mary, perform his week of service.

I, John, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed. [Col. 0295C] I, Benedict, by God’s grace cardinal of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed. I, Ivo, by God’s grace bishop of Chartres, have subscribed. Α + Ω. Mark of Ernauld, dean; of Hildun, cantor; of William, archdeacon; of Serannus, subdean; of Garin, succentor; of Ragibald, canon; etc.

### V. Charter by which the church of Hanches is granted to Marmoutier

(From an old slip of Petavius.)

I, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Walter, archdeacon, [Col. 0295D] wish it to be known to posterity and to the present generation that William, abbot of St. Martin of Marmoutier, with certain of his monks, came before us, humbly imploring that we grant to the church of Blessed Martin the church of Hanches, which Paganus, canon of Blessed Mary of Chartres, held. The said Paganus, appearing there, freely surrendered the aforesaid church into our hand. We, attentively heeding the prayers of Lord Abbot William and his monks, without prejudice to the right of our Church, graciously consented to their petition and granted them to have and possess the aforesaid church [Col. 0296A] as Paganus held it, with the intercession and consent of Paganus himself and with the consent of his brothers Raherius, Goscelin, Guarin, and Amary.

The same Raherius, brother of Paganus, who held the tithe of the church by lay usurpation, by presently surrendering to the monks the small tithes, granted them these tithes; and he granted them the tithe from the monks’ cultivated lands, to be held after his departure. In this gift he also granted them to possess in perpetuity the chapel of Hidulf’s Bridge, together with that part of the land and water which he then surrendered to them.

And just as we consented to what was presently being bestowed upon the monks by name, so too we charitably granted to them by name all that was promised for future possession from the aforesaid brothers and from others holding anything there. These things promised [Col. 0296B] were: land for two oxen and dwellings with arpents of land. The grant of this gift was made in the year from the Incarnation 1114, in the presence of those whose names we have subscribed below.

On the part of the bishop and archdeacon were Raimbaud, archdeacon of Vendôme; Ausger, archdeacon of Blois; Gualeran, canon; Rainald, his cleric; Bernerius, regular canon; Radulf, regular canon and chamberlain of the bishop.

On the part of the abbot: William, prior; Peter Laidet; Gilo and his son; Gilduin; Hugh, hospitaler.

Of the servants: Anald, chamberlain; Paganus, chamberlain; Landric, servant of the prior; Gaucelin; Peter Burdo; Hubert Mainbodus.

### VI. Charter concerning the obedience and subjection which the monks of Belle-Lieu owe to Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and to his successors; on this condition alone Ivo permitted them to construct and consecrate their monastery

(Petit, *The Penitential of Theodore*, vol. II, p. 597, from a manuscript codex of the privileges of the Church of Chartres.)

[Col. 0296C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

I, Ivo, though unworthy, bishop of the Church of Chartres, wish it to be known to all present and future that Lord Hugh, venerable abbot of the monastery of Cluny, together with the flock entrusted to him, and especially the Brethren of Charity, humbly approached us, asking that I grant them permission [Col. 0296D] to establish and consecrate a monastery outside the city of Chartres, in the place which William had chosen for building a monastery. Since their petition seemed worthy to be granted and beneficial to many, with the consent of our brethren of Blessed Mary we granted that a monastery be established and consecrated in the aforesaid place, on the condition that they render to me, to the Church entrusted to me, and to my successors all the obedience and subjection rendered by the monks situated round about; and that without my consent and that of the chapter of Blessed Mary and of our successors, they shall not presume to invade the rights of our Church or of the churches granted to it.

[Col. 0297]

## 125. FRANÇOIS JURETUS GREETS THE KIND READER

Twenty-four years ago, the letters of Ivo of Chartres, drawn from darkness into light, appeared under the auspices of Pierre Pithou, the distinguished jurist—a man of the greatest merit and of the most devoted disposition toward the republic of letters—through whose singular generosity I had obtained most of them in a more complete form. But since copies of the first edition had long been sought after and the printer pressed for their reprinting, it came about that, after several older manuscripts had been sought out and carefully collated with one another, the book was rendered better and enlarged.

The earlier edition indeed suffered from lacunae, and the order of many letters was confused and inverted, since several later letters addressed to Paschal were placed before some sent to Urban, although the succession of times clearly proves that Paschal succeeded Urban. It is unnecessary to mention individually other matters of the same kind, which will become readily clear by mutual collation, although in this respect I have not yet fully satisfied myself. That disordered sequence, however, has been altered and restored, not without guidance from ancient codices; and likewise, on their authority, lines and words have been inserted throughout the work.

It must nevertheless be regretted that, among so many ancient manuscripts, none has yet been discovered that seemed complete in every number and respect. Some contained more letters, some fewer, and these often swarmed with errors. Moreover, they disagreed in their order, so that one may infer from this that they were not originally arranged by the author himself, but were collected here and there by enthusiasts after his death. Only the copy in the Royal Library was divided into ten books, a division which the other codices by no means recognize and which is not greatly necessary.

The most renowned men of the robe—Jacques-Auguste de Thou, president; Louis Servin, the king’s advocate in the supreme court; and Nicolas Faber—assisted this work by communicating manuscripts and by their manifold and recondite learning. My very meager discourse adds nothing to their distinction. Nor were the manuscripts of the monasteries of St. Victor and St. Germain lacking, nor those of the most learned and accomplished Puteani and of Charles Labbé. Whatever has been achieved, however—and I perceive that it is very little—if it meets with approval among upright and candid men, I shall be less displeased to have put my hand to the restoration of the work of this Gallican bishop. From reading him, many remarkable facts are learned which contemporary writers have not recorded.

For this reason the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius speaks deservedly and honorably of Ivo, calling him now “the lamp of the western world,” now “the glory, ornament, and splendor of the Gallican Church.” He inserted various letters of Ivo into the later volumes of his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, from whose springs he drew many things worthy of observation and knowledge.

Why should we linger over unfair judges of writings, who, because of a few expressions less Latin or less elegant, rashly think that ancient writers must be rejected and their reading wholly avoided? As though a person who delights in knowledge of things, and prefers to cultivate the mind rather than the tongue, ought not to examine every class of authors. Yet I have not been able to include in this book of observations all that I had conceived in my mind, because intervening business hostile to literary study compelled me to direct my attention elsewhere. It will therefore be better to leave the more important matters to another’s diligence. Far be it from me to envy or malign anyone who makes better these and similar matters which I once touched upon.

I have intentionally omitted here the summaries attached at the head of the letters in the earlier edition. They are absent from some handwritten codices; in others they vary, since they were formerly composed according to each person’s judgment; and they seem superfluous, since they may more readily be recovered from the index of subjects and words. Fare well, and enjoy these things.

[Col. 0297]

## 126. OBSERVATIONS ON THE LETTERS OF IVO OF CHARTRES

### ON LETTER I

[Col. 0297A]

**By Geoffrey, former bishop.** The same Urban, in Letter 2 to Richer, says that the Church of Chartres had endured many troubles on Geoffrey’s account and that many complaints concerning him had been brought to the apostolic see. This is also proved by the words of Gregory VII, where he is called Gotfredus, though in other codices Galfridus. It is worth setting down the words for the sake of clarifying the history, from Book V, Letter 17 of the Register:

> “Gotfredus, bishop of Chartres, because he had been judged while neither summoned nor present, was restored by us to the episcopal office, on this condition: that his case must be reconsidered and decided before our legate.”

He is mentioned also in Book IX, Letter 15, to H., bishop of Die. That letter denotes Hugh, as other passages of Gregory himself indicate; so too Ivo, Letter 274, and Lisiard in the *Life of St. Arnulf, Bishop of Soissons*, chapter 26, who mention [Col. 0297B] Hugh, bishop of Die and legate of Gregory VII. That Letter 15 therefore says that the bishop of Paris came to Rome with the bishop of Chartres and complained that Hugh had prejudiced the case against the bishop of Chartres and had subjected one not canonically accused to sentence of excommunication and deposition. Finally, Gregory orders that, after the two have been instructed to await matters at Rome in the meantime, Hugh himself should either come or send a messenger.

The same writer, in Letter 16 to the clergy and people of Chartres, says that Bishop Gotfredus cleared himself at Rome of the suspicion of Simonian depravity by taking an oath upon the body of St. Peter. He then exhorts them to obey their own pastor.

But after Gregory’s death, when Geoffrey’s crimes subsequently became fully known to the apostolic see, and the man—unable to clear himself—had surrendered his pastoral staff and ring, Urban, Gregory’s successor, deposed him, since there was no longer any room for dissimulation. This is proved by Ivo’s writings: in Letter 8 to Richer, he calls him a scapegoat and affirms that he had been condemned for adulteries, perjuries, and treacheries publicized throughout almost the entire Latin Church. Ivo also means the same man when, at the end of Letter 6, [Col. 0298B] he says that a schoolmaster had been driven far from the office and title of shepherd and now had no means of plundering the milk and wool of lost sheep—except that, with the count’s aid, he was usurping for himself a certain provostship of the Church of Chartres in Normandy.

[Col. 0299A] **“Anticipating the wish of your hearts,” etc.; “you have canonically elected according to our admonitions.”** The same Urban, below, in Letter 21 to Richer, says that he gave the people of Chartres leave to elect this Ivo. Likewise Ivo himself, writing to Pope Paschal in Letter 104, testifies that Galon was elected bishop by the clergy of Beauvais, following the counsel of the same pope. From this it is inferred that in that period, when bishops of Gaul were to be elected, the Roman pontiffs customarily intervened and commended to the clergy those whom they judged well-disposed toward themselves and likely to be useful.

### ON LETTER III

The heading varies in the manuscripts. Some have: “Admonition of Pope Urban to Ivo, a priest consecrated bishop of the Church of Chartres.” In others it is “edict” or “address” which the pontiff gives to the bishop whom he blesses. In Baronius, volume XI of the *Annals*, it is “the speech or address of Pope Urban to Ivo.”

**“People of the Church of Chartres.”** Thus it is better in some old slips than the earlier reading, “people of that city.”

**“Without sickness or stain.”** This is the expressed reading of all our codices. Baronius likewise prints “without sickness and *mancha*,” and at the margin adds the variant *macula* (“stain”); it is uncertain whether *mancha* derives from some ancient exemplar.

### ON LETTER IV

**“Out of an affection of charity.”** Thus the constant spelling in old codices, except that in a few it is *Karitatis*. Incorrectly, in commonly printed editions of other authors, through an inveterate but erroneous practice, it is everywhere printed with an aspirate. It is enough to have noted this once, lest anyone think it done here without reason.

**“Lord Walter.”** One codex has *donnum*. This is a medieval word frequent among ecclesiastical writers. From it some maintain that the name *domnionis* was corrupted in St. Jerome, and *domnulae* in Salvian of Marseilles, in his letter. See the notes below on Letter 28.

### ON LETTER V

**“Descending from both lines, nobility of birth.”** The ancients called this nobility *aequa prosapia* (“equal lineage”), as Cyprian does in the *Life of St. Caesarius*:

> “St. Caesarius, the most holy and blessed bishop of Arles, is said to have been a native of the territory of Chalon. His parents, of equal lineage—which is an illustrious and exceptional example of nobility—flourished above all their fellow citizens in faith and morals.”

Here the editor is mistaken in thinking the passage corrupt and noting that *egregia* (“distinguished”) should be read in place of *aequa* (“equal”).

### ON LETTER VI

**“As at Lyons.”** There is an old copy in which *Lucduni* is written. Some approve this spelling as derived from the name of Lucius Plancus, who restored that city, after it had been consumed by fire, in better form. But other ancient authors held that the name derived from light. Of this opinion was Hericus, Benedictine monk, in Book VI of *The Life of St. Germanus of Auxerre*:

> “With even courses the Saône raises itself toward the heights of Lyons,  
> Hiding itself beneath the walls in the Rhône.  
> The Gauls proclaim that the name Lucdunum was once imposed,  
> Since it is likewise a shining mountain.”

On the other hand, Sidonius Apollinaris reproaches the Lyonnese mists and days obstructed by morning fog, scarcely opened even by the heat of noon. His friend congratulates him in Book I, Letter 8, that he sees at last the sun which the drinker of the Saône had seldom seen.

### ON LETTER VII

**“Roscelin.”** Thus it is written in our old codices; by certain modern writers he is called Rozelinus or Rucelinus. An old anonymous historian, in the *Historical Fragment on the Franks from Robert to the Death of Philip I*, states:

> “In dialectic there were also these powerful sophists: John, who argued that the same sophistical art was vocal; Robert of Paris; Roscelin of Compiègne; and Arnulf of Laon.”

Aventinus, Book VI of the *Annals of Bavaria*:

> “I find that in these same times there was also Rucelinus the Breton, master of Peter Abelard, founder of the new Lyceum, who first established the science of words or terms and discovered a new way of philosophizing. Under his influence, two kinds of Aristotelians, or Peripatetics, began to exist: the one old, rich in producing things, which claims for itself the knowledge of things and is therefore called Realist; the other new, which disperses that knowledge and is therefore called Nominalist, because, miserly in things but lavish in names and notions, they appear to be defenders of words. Between these two kinds there is division and civil war. Thomas Aquinas, an Italian, and John Duns Scotus are leaders of the former; William of Ockham, an Englishman, of the latter,” etc.

Ivo indeed indicates that this Roscelin defended his insane opinions concerning certain articles [Col. 0300B] of the Christian faith, but he does not state what they were. This may, however, be clarified by the words of Anselm, abbot of Bec, then flourishing. For he writes to Fulk, bishop of Beauvais—whose words I cite from a manuscript copy because they had not yet been published:

> “I hear—though I cannot believe it without doubt—that the cleric Roscelin says that in God there are three persons, three things separate from one another, as there are three angels, though there is one will and power; or that the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate, and that three Gods may truly be said, if usage admitted it. He asserts that Archbishop Lanfranc, of venerable memory, held this opinion, and that I do. For this reason, it has been said that a council is soon to be assembled by the venerable Rainald, archbishop of Reims. Since I think that Your Reverence will be present there, I wish you to be instructed as to what you ought to answer on my behalf if reason requires it.”

And a little later he adds:

> “Whoever, whether human or angel, asserts as true the blasphemy which I have stated above that I heard Roscelin utter, is anathema. And I shall declare in confirmation: so long as he persists in this obstinacy, let him be anathema; for he is altogether not a Christian,” etc.

These words serve to interpret another passage of the same Anselm, later made archbishop of Canterbury. Writing to Pope Urban, he reports that while he was abbot in the monastery of Bec, a certain cleric in France had advanced this assertion: if in God there are three persons, there is only one thing and not three things; therefore the Father and the Holy Spirit, together with the Son, were incarnate. A little later he adds that, in the council assembled by the venerable Rainald, archbishop of Reims, that man abjured his error; but that he later heard the author of the aforesaid novelty, persisting in his opinion, say that he had abjured what he said for no reason other [Col. 0300C] than fear of being killed by the people. For this reason, then, Anselm wrote his book *On the Incarnation of the Word*. He does not specify the place of the council, but from this letter of Ivo it is plainly evident that Soissons must be understood.

**“Of an ethical writer.”** The earlier edition has *ethnici* (“pagan”), as a few codices have, with the variant *ethici* (“ethical”) noted at the margin. The latter reading must be followed, since the more numerous and better handwritten books report it. But for *tractatoris*, one old copy incorrectly has *tractatoris* [as printed, apparently an unmarked variant]. Here he understands *tractatorem* as “author,” as ancient writers sometimes do. St. Jerome, against Helvidius:

> “Which almost all the writers of Greece have left in their volumes.”

St. Augustine, in the book *On the Mirror*:

> “The Catholic expositors of the divine books, old and new, have aimed at this.”

Cassiodorus, in the preface to Book I of *On Divine Reading*:

> “It is enough to have indicated to you the most learned expositors.”

Sidonius Apollinaris, Book II, Letter IX, speaking of Origen:

> “We discussed why he was judged by certain chief initiates to be an ill-omened and dangerous [Col. 0301A] writer.”

Alcimus Avitus, in the book *On Virginity*, addressed to his sister:

> “And all the many mysteries which truthful expositors  
> Have expounded in their worthy little books,  
> You have drunk in, holding them all in your thirsty mind.”

Pope Nicholas I, Letter 42:

> “For if by their decree the works of other expositors are approved or rejected.”

**“You will write a palinode.”** An old codex of St. Germain incorrectly has *palidoniam*, and another *psalmodiam*.

**“To be loved and gathered in.”** The first edition had intruded *et coli* (“and cultivated”), but all the manuscripts more correctly have *et colligi* (“and gathered in”). The word is used in a similar sense in Letter 65: “that you may gather him in with maternal affection”; Letter 159: “she frequently gathers in with maternal affection”; and Letter 160: “that you may gather [him] into the fold from which he had strayed.” Likewise Letter 253: “he gathers the pious in by gentleness.” Anselm, abbot of Bec, in a letter to Henry: “He earnestly desires to be wholly gathered back into the flock in which he was suckled and nourished.”

Moreover, after transcribing this letter, Baronius, volume XII of the *Annals*, adds: “Thus far Ivo’s letter, without a salutation prefixed or the customary wish for well-being appended at its end,” because Ivo was writing to a heretic. But in fact, in some manuscripts, several of Ivo’s letters to others, including non-heretics, lack a similar prayer at their close. Thus this seems more likely to have resulted from the negligence of a copyist than from the author’s intention.

### ON LETTER VIII

**“To Richer, by God’s grace archbishop of Sens.”** Baronius, volume XI of the *Annals*, says that Richer was rebuked by Ivo with constancy of mind and that Ivo wrote this letter full of wisdom—a letter from whose title and salutation alone Richer could have been instructed and restored to sound judgment, had he been wise.

**“Let whoever wishes to oppose apostolic decrees be cast down.”** In three old copies it is written in abbreviation [Col. 0301C] *quisque*, which has the value of *quisquis* (“whoever”), as in the codices of Reims, St. Victor, and St. Germain. The Royal codex has *quisquis*; in Servin’s book, *quicunque*. Older writers used *quisque* for *quisquis*, a fact which many, failing to observe, have often altered and corrupted in authors contrary to the authority of ancient manuscripts.

An old inscription states:

> “Whoever shall either sell this monument or give it away as a donation shall incur …”

A manuscript Aesop, in the *Life of Alexander*:

> “Whoever consults you does not oppose your truthfulness.”

St. Hilary, in the fragment *On Synods*:

> “But whoever does not condemn these things when reported must necessarily declare himself a partner in their designs.”

Tertullian, in the poem on Jonah:

> “You also, whatever god is yours, utter vows and prayers.”

An old anonymous poet, in an epitaph:

> “Whoever reads, grieve; avoid such fates.”

[Col. 0301D] Rutilius, Book I of the *Itinerary*:

> “Whoever wishes to be good will be eloquent.”

Paulinus also, in Book I of *The Life of St. Martin*:

> “. . . You, whoever you are, reading and despising these so worthless  
> Poems, while mocking the words, will marvel at the deeds.”

**“When clerics were petitioning and knocking, you would set no day for my consecration.”** Urban above, in Letter 2, likewise reproaches this Richer because, although the pope himself was demanding it, he nevertheless refused to lay hands upon Ivo. In a general synod held at Rome under Innocent II, chapter 28—reported in the chapter *Obeuntibus*, Distinction 63—it had been forbidden for a church to remain vacant more than three months. Pope Leo also, in Letter 82 to Bishop Anastasius, had ordered that no delay or difficulty be introduced into the proper celebration of a bishop’s ordination, lest the Lord’s flocks be deprived too long of pastoral care. This is likewise reported in the chapter *De persona*, Distinction 65.

Pope Stephen had also once written to Gualbert, patriarch, that he should cease, through zeal for anyone, to delay Lintuard, bishop-elect of the Church of Como, who had been elected by the clergy and requested by the people. He threatened that, if Gualbert delayed and the elect meanwhile came to Rome, the pope himself would consecrate him. Stephen adds that he would do so because, by apostolic prerogative, he could ordain a cleric from any church, though he did not wish to infringe any church’s privilege. The passage in full is reported by Ivo in Part V of the *Decree*, chapter 13; shortened by the same author in Letter 61; and by Gratian in the chapter *Nunc vero*, Cause 9, Question 3.

Gregory VII likewise, in a similar case involving the bishop of Chartres, had previously admonished this Richer to beware of introducing delays in ordaining the man canonically elected bishop, threatening deprivation of office. For the letter survives in the Register, Book IV, Letter 15. Thus there is an easy excuse if Ivo, with Richer hostile and evasive and unwilling to perform his office, went to Rome and was consecrated by the pope.

[Col. 0302B] For Richer favored Geoffrey, whom the same Urban had deprived and stripped of office because of his crimes. He had evidently been misled by the counsel of the bishop of Paris and of two bishops of like folly—if what Ivo writes to Urban in Letter 12 is true; and I do not think Ivo lied. Nor can it be denied that, if anyone in that age, he was highly skilled in canonical learning, and that he would have undertaken or suffered nothing of the kind if the ancient canons had opposed it.

These things have been noted in passing because some recently criticized Ivo’s act and wrote that he had offended against the rights of the Gallican Church by attempting to transfer them into the hands of the Roman pontiff. They say that, at the same time, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, entirely devoted to the pope, was striving with all his might to strip the king of England of the right of regalian privileges. But the cases are very different. Anselm, leaving England or living in exile and residing for the most part at Rome, finally succeeded through obstinate effort in making the king of England—from whom he had received the archbishopric—abandon the inveterate custom of investing the bishops of his kingdom. Nothing of this sort is ever read of Ivo. He showed the greatest deference to his king and preferred to endure the investitures of churches performed by princes for the sake of public concord rather than furnish a cause for schism and rise against the king, as Letter 60 shows.

Nor is there even slight ground to suspect that he wished to deprive his metropolitan of Sens of the right due to him to consecrate. For he repeatedly insists that the rights of individual churches must remain inviolate and that the boundaries established by the Fathers must not be transgressed. This is clear from his dispute against the archbishop of Lyons, papal legate, in Letters 60 and 61. There he says that examples of bishops not consecrated by their fellow-provincials because some necessity compelled it ought nevertheless to cause no prejudice to the common law and custom. Indeed, in Letter 12 he declares that he does not wish to attend the marriage of King Philip and Bertrada unless the archbishop of Reims is its consecrator and author, because this belongs to the right of the Church of Reims by ancient custom of the kingdom and apostolic authority.

Finally, in Letter 83 to the bishops of the diocese of Reims, he writes that the attacks of the metropolitan must be repelled with the battering ram of canonical authority when, in churches of the same province and without the consent of the bishops presiding over them, he judged clerics, suspended them from office, or commanded whatever he pleased. Had Ivo’s critics carefully observed these matters, they could have complained less.

There is also no reason why anyone should suspect that he was moved by ambition, so that, consecrated by Urban, he might enjoy the bishopric more freely. For he repeatedly complains that this dignity had been conferred upon him by the people of Chartres and the pope against his will and resistance, when he had entertained no such thought—Letters 25 and 289. In the latter he says that he is little short of pursuing Urban with curses on that account. Everywhere he laments that he is overwhelmed by the burdens of that dignity, and in Letter 17 desires to return, as by right of postliminy, to his former tranquillity of mind.

[Col. 0303A] “And thence, with the pastoral staff forced upon me by the king, I was brought to the Church of Chartres.” He mentions this staff in Letter 60, where he says that churches were customarily granted in various ways: by hand, gesture, speech, or staff. And in Letter 236 he says that many had returned their pastoral staffs; shortly afterward he says that a layman does not confer a sacramental thing in the giving and receiving of the staff. Elsewhere, namely in Letter 157, he calls it the pastoral crozier.

Osbern, in a manuscript letter to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: “What could be sweeter to affection, or more excellent for innocence, than that you should be violently dragged before the bed of a sick man; that your right hand should shamelessly be drawn from your bosom by the hands of others; that your left hand, lest it should aid its sister, should be firmly held back; that the staff should be cruelly thrust between thumb and forefinger, while your other fingers stubbornly remained closed; that after this you should be lifted bodily from the ground in episcopal arms and carried to the church; and that there, though you were still protesting and resisting with vehement threats, *Te Deum laudamus* should be sung over you?”

Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick I*, book II, chapter 6, writes that a bishopric is conferred by the emperor through the sceptre; and in chapter 5, kingdoms through the sword and provinces through the banner. By this staff, moreover, the authority granted to the bishop was signified. To these, because of the similarity of the matter, may be added what Abbot Suger says in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, and after him the continuator of Aimoin, *History*, book V, chapter 50: that, when King Louis the Fat was consecrated, a sceptre and staff were given him, and through these, the defence of the churches.

It was also a mark of honour. Hence, in the palace of the Gothic king, the superintendent of the palace—he was the architect—used to walk with a golden staff, as is indicated by Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book VII, formula 5. Paul the Deacon likewise, *Deeds of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 3, reports that Felix the grammarian was so dear to King Heribert that the king gave him a staff adorned with gold and silver. To these should be joined the matters noted on Letters 1 and 7 concerning the pastoral staff.

## ON LETTER XII

“Take thought for the son of your womb.” Thus I have restored the text, following several more accurate manuscripts; formerly it read, “Take thought for your son.” Below in this same letter, and again in the superscription of Letter 19, he calls himself the special son of Pope Urban, just as at the beginning of Letter 44 he calls himself the uterine son of the Roman Church. In the same sense he calls the cardinals the uterine sons of the pope, Letter 53.

Emperor Frederick I, in his letter to Pope Adrian, in Radevicus, book II, chapter 16: “It is most fitting that the holy Roman Church, as mother of all churches, should gather together the sons who are the fruit of her womb, and distribute those whom she has gathered through houses and families for the adornment of God’s house; upon whom our empire also ought and wishes to bestow suitable honour, as upon those proceeding from the womb and bosom of our mother.”

“They wish to redeem altars from me under the name of a *persona*.” This reading varies in no manuscript. In Ivo’s age this matter was frequently dealt with in Gallican synods. For in canon 7 of the Council of Clermont, held in December 1094, in Baronius, volume X:

> “That altars given to communities of canons or monks through *personae*, upon the death of the *personae*, should return free into the hands of the bishops, unless they have been confirmed to those communities by their documents or privileges.”

And in the canon *Quaesitum*, Causa I, question 3, are reported the words of the Council of Auvergne under Pope Urban: that it had become customary in Gaul for churches or tithes—commonly called “altars”—given to monasteries to be sold by bishops and redeemed by monks upon the death or replacement of the clerics called *personae*. This was prohibited there, while preserving the bishops’ annual due.

Pope Urban, in a letter to Ingelian, bishop of Laon:

> “The more familiarly you are loved by the Roman Church, the more dearly you ought to have cherished and embraced those whom she herself loves. Therefore let your fraternity cease harassing the brothers of Saint Remigius, and restore to them the altar in the estate called Corbiniac, which those brothers are known to have possessed. For although we have removed the *personae*, we have not taken from monasteries the right of ancient possession. In that very change of *personae*, there arose a renewal of avarice and a dissipation of ecclesiastical property. Moreover, we wish altars which monasteries have possessed for forty or thirty years, as has been decreed in synod, to remain undisturbed in their hands. Therefore henceforth inflict no annoyance upon those brothers concerning the aforesaid altar, while preserving your episcopal rights.”

This letter exists in the manuscript codex of Antoine Loisel and, so far as I know, had not previously been published by others.

John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, book VII, chapter 17:

> “Indeed, it is remarkable prudence if someone acquires altars by whatever means, so that, as though according to the Memphitic rite, he may be able daily to immolate victims upon new altars. Yet those who live from the altar do not wish either to rule the priesthood or to serve the altar—lest, as the people complain, I should say that they live luxuriously—but they have introduced certain *personati*, under whose right the burdens may be assigned to one person and the profits to another.”

Relevant also is what Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, writes in Letter 12 of book III to the bishop of Angers. He testifies that he attended the said Council of Clermont and explains the meaning of the redemption of altars (*Patrologia*, vol. CLVII, col. 118). The same author, in a letter to G., legate of the Apostolic See (see there, book I, Letter 27), complains of the bishop of Angers:

> “He is contriving to annul that decree which the same Lord Pope Urban established at the Council of Auvergne against simony, which bishops were accustomed to practise under the name of vicars of God. He is also attempting to extort from our simplicity, under the name of an annual payment, the redemption of churches—which, in that great council, was called heretical perversity and condemned by the Apostolic See—although it had been performed through vicars no more than once in many years. And because I and our brethren judge this to be a crime and therefore reject it, he has forbidden the divine office in our churches.”

From these passages depends the interpretation of the words of Gregory VII, book IV, Letter 7, to Hugh, bishop of Die:

> “Forbid both him and all others henceforth to commit that common evil of almost the whole land—namely, that altars are sold—which this man too does not deny having done in the exercise of his archdeaconry.”

He is speaking of Gerard of Cambrai and of the summoning of a synod of the bishops of France.

## ON LETTER XIII

“Concerning the marriage which he was arranging with Bertrada, called the wife of the count of Anjou.” The old manuscripts of Ivo give the spelling *Bertreda*, but in other authors she is usually called Bertrada. The author indicates in Letter 15 that she married Philip; in various places, suppressing her name, he calls her queen—namely, Letters 66 and 68. She is also discussed in the notes on Letters 28 and 144.

“Because this belongs to the right of your Church.” After the author’s time, because the matter depended on the will of kings, practice in this respect often varied. The wives of kings were not always blessed and consecrated at Rheims or by the archbishop of Rheims.

The chronicler of Auxerre, under the year of the Lord 1154:

> “In this year Louis, king of the Franks, took in marriage at the city of Orléans the daughter of the emperor of Spain, a woman distinguished by honourable character; and there, when the wedding had been solemnly celebrated, she was anointed queen by Hugh, archbishop of Sens. This Samson, archbishop of Rheims, took badly, saying that it belonged to his right that wherever the kings and queens of the Franks might be, they ought to be consecrated by him. Yet neither reason approves this nor precedent supports it. For Ivo of Chartres, most learned in decrees and laws, establishes in his letters by arguments and examples that no writing or example can ever prove that the archbishop of Rheims anointed or crowned a king of the Franks outside the province of Belgica. And therefore, since every metropolitan possesses the same authority within his own metropolis, it seems unjust for one man to seek to claim as his private right what is evidently common to many.”

The same author, under the year 1160:

> “In that same year died the queen of France, daughter of the emperor of Spain, a woman praiseworthy in life, renowned in deeds, and richly endowed in character. King Louis, by counsel of his magnates, took in marriage the daughter of Theobald, count of blessed memory; afterward the aforesaid Hugh, archbishop of Sens, anointed her queen at Paris and, on the same day, in the presence of three cardinals—namely Otto, William of Pavia, and Henry of Pisa—crowned her with her lord Louis in the church of Blessed Mary. In the same church, with those cardinals and many others present, he solemnly celebrated the office of the Mass. This action greatly displeased the archbishop of Rheims and his bishops.”

An ancient writer, in the *Life of King Louis VIII*, speaking of Margaret, daughter of the count of Provence, under the year 1224:

> “The king took her as his lawful wife at the city of Sens, and caused her to be anointed as lady and queen of the Franks by Walter, archbishop of the city of Sens, and solemnly crowned with the royal diadem.”

William of Nangis, in the *Deeds of Philip III*, whom some call the Bold, speaking of Mary, daughter of Henry duke of Brabant by a daughter of Hugh duke of Burgundy:
