> “In the year of the Lord 1275, when the barons and prelates of almost the whole kingdom of France had assembled at Paris, Mary, queen of France, was there solemnly crowned and anointed by the hand of Peter, then archbishop of Rheims, as is the custom in crowning the queens of France.”

And shortly afterward:

> “There also Giles, archbishop of Sens, brought a complaint before the legate of the Roman Curia, Lord Simon, cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia, who was present. He said that the queen had been crowned there by the archbishop of Rheims to the prejudice of his church, because, as is read in a certain letter of Ivo, formerly bishop of Chartres, to the bishop of the Belgic see which is Rheims, the anointing of kings and even queens does not belong to him outside his province. But on the king’s side it was argued that the archbishop of Sens had no ground for complaint, because the king’s chapel at Paris was exempt and therefore, by reason of the place, the anointing did not pertain to him.”

The letter of Ivo which those writers mention is the one printed in this edition as Letter 189.

## ON LETTER XV

“And that a divorce has intervened between you and your lawful wife.” The continuator of Aimoin, *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 50, calls her Bertha:

> “King Philip, at the suggestion of the devil, repudiated Queen Bertha and, withdrawing his presence from her, sent her to the castle called Montreuil, situated above the sea, with which he had endowed her.”

An old anonymous author, in a fragment of history from Robert to the death of Philip:

> “King Philip, having repudiated Bertha, the mother of Louis, took another wife, Bertrada,” etc.

Accordingly, it should be considered whether there is an error in the received edition of Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, who was Ivo’s contemporary, where she is called Bertrada rather than Bertha. His words deserve to be quoted because they are worthy of notice. Thus, in chapter 18 of his *Life of Saint Arnulf, Bishop of Soissons*, he records that Arnulf had foretold that she would at last be expelled by her husband Philip:

> “As soon as the abbot had been appointed, there suddenly rushed up the aforesaid Pontius, a mad violator of monastic order, bringing with him Queen Bertrada, in order that by royal authority she might expel Gerald and unlawfully install Pontius in the administration of the holy place. When Christ’s servant Arnulf learned this, he came out of his cell, gently addressed the raging queen, and humbly begged her that, although she was queen, she should nevertheless remember the condition of womanhood, remember the divine judgments, fear to act against ecclesiastical laws, and modestly refrain from doing injury to so great a man. But when, because of royal haughtiness and arrogance, she would not accept the holy man’s warning, he said to her by a prophetic spirit: ‘Believe, if you please, O queen, Brother Arnulf—or rather believe the Holy Spirit. For if you expel Brother Gerald from here, you too, by God’s vengeance, will before your death be expelled from the kingdom, and, despised and miserable, will die.’ It is clearer than daylight that the prophecy of the man of God was fulfilled, since all know that after some years that queen offended the king’s mind so greatly that he wholly refused reconciliation; removed from partnership in the kingdom and transferred to the region of Ponthieu, after prolonged misery she died and was buried there in common fashion.”

The same writer, chapter 27, again calls her Bertrada and relates that the same Arnulf foretold to her that a Louis would be born from her who would succeed Philip, king of the Franks.

“That I may come to Paris with your wife.” Thus the earlier edition, and this reading also appears in certain manuscripts, such as those of Thuanus, Loisel, and others; I have retained it elsewhere. But many old books unanimously have *Parisius* here. Although this may seem less consistent with the grammarians’ rule, in the author’s age it was common for that name to be used absolutely, as can be proved by almost innumerable examples from Vincent of Beauvais, Peter of Blois, chronicles, and so forth.

An old writer in chapter 9 of the *Life of Saint Philibert, Abbot of Jumièges*: “A certain discord had arisen, on account of which he quickly betook himself to Paris.” Thus the old codex of Nicolas Faber has it, where the editor changed it to: “he betook himself to Lutetia.”

## ON LETTER XVI

“He needs this patron.” For the king was hostile to Ivo because he would not approve the king’s union with his concubine Bertrada, as Letter 17 indicates.

“So that you did not approve his marriage, which had formerly been contracted against the dictates of reason.” From this some wish to infer that, although the lawful marriage with his wife Bertha had not been dissolved, the king nevertheless took Bertrada, his concubine, as wife. This occurred, that is, after he had been emboldened by the reply of Cardinal Roger, the papal legate, who, when consulted at Senlis, answered that a concubine could lawfully marry her adulterer. This is probable, for in Letter 13 Ivo warns the other bishops, when summoned to the royal wedding, to absent themselves. Nor is it a frivolous conjecture that this legate was corrupted by gifts, as such men are everywhere noted in the histories of that time. The author also freely rebukes him because he released Simon of Niel from the bond of anathema, although Simon, while his wife was still living, had brought in an adulteress, as Letter 18 proves.

“And the judgment of the bishops of the same province.” Berthold, *Deeds of Pope Urban II*, under the year 1094:

> “In a city of Gaul commonly called Autun, a general council was assembled by the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, with archbishops, bishops, and abbots of diverse provinces, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November [16 October]. At that council Philip, king of the Gauls, was excommunicated because, while his wife was living, he had brought in another woman.”

## ON LETTER XVII

“Love.” Formerly printed *charitas*, with the mark of aspiration; but in ancient copies that mark is entirely absent. I have retained this spelling throughout the work, although the other has become commonly established.

“Because, by word and writing, I made against his marriage the objection which I ought.” The Puthean codex alone has “because against its beginnings,” but wrongly. For here he says that he made the due objection against the marriage; elsewhere he says that he opposed the unlawful union, Letter 19, which indeed deals with the same marriage of King Philip and Bertrada. He therefore takes *calumnia* in a favourable sense, as he calls it a canonical objection in Letter 268. Conversely, in a worse sense, he calls a marriage litigious in Letter 45. Yet he often uses the word for a dispute or lawsuit, as in Letter 76: “Let him come to the church against which he brings suit”; and Letter 179: “If there is any claim against the church, obtain justice.” Likewise Letter 184: “That a claim has arisen among laymen against the Church of Beauvais”; Letter 219: “Their claim was brought before the metropolitan”; and again Letter 229: “If any claim should arise thence in our parish.”

Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, Letter 32: “We are indeed informed that in England you conduct nothing but lawsuits and claims.” In old ecclesiastical instruments or charters, examples of this usage are innumerable. Thus Ivo understands *calumniator* as the author or claimant in Letters 212 and 241.

## ON LETTER XVIII

“But absent—excepted.” Some manuscripts have “but as though present”; another has “but I desire to be present in spirit.”

## ON LETTER XIX

“We can rarely fulfil the canonical obligation at the appointed hours.” What he here calls *pensum* (“task” or “obligation”), some ancient writers called the *cursus* (“course”). Ignorance of this word has caused certain passages to be corrupted and interpolated, which it will not be unwelcome to note in passing.

Baudonivia, *Life of Queen Radegund*, book II, chapter 18: “At times she stood by night before her cell, chanting the course with heart and voice.” Thus the old codex of Nicolas Faber reads. But the editor of that author, following his own judgment, substituted: “chanting canonical prayers with heart and voice.”

He did the same in the deacon Wandelbert, author of the *Life of Saint Goar*. Where the same old codex reads: “Seeing that every day, after sunrise, when he had completed his course, he celebrated Masses, and afterward showed charity to the pilgrims and poor who had come to him,” that editor inserted: “From sunrise paying Christ the praises of psalmody and then celebrating Masses”; and shortly afterward, instead of “showed charity,” he substituted “took his meal.”

Then where the text continues: “Passing the night in God’s praises, when first light had risen, having completed his course—as he did by day—he began and fulfilled the solemnities of the Masses,” the same editor coined a longer circumlocution: “He began to render to God the vows of psalmody and prayers which he performed by day; then, when he had completed this, [he began] the Masses,” etc.

Certainly, when that man—who deserved very well of ecclesiastical history—published the lives of saints from ancient manuscripts, he would have acted more wisely had he changed nothing. But, as he himself admits, he often polished and refined words and expressions, without any mention of the old reading. The result was that many expressions of the ancient age became unknown, though they would not have been unwelcome to antiquarians, had some editors been more conscientious in their publications.

An old author likewise, in the *Life of Saint Eligius, Bishop of Noyon*, book I, chapter 10: “Day and night, in his chamber, they diligently strove solemnly to fulfil the canonical course.” In the edition of this passage, the annotator rightly notes in the margin that by “canonical course” are meant the hourly or canonical prayers. Therefore it is undoubtedly a gloss which he inserted into the text in book II, chapter 21, where one reads: “For some reason he forbade the course—that is, canonical prayers—and the sacrifice to be celebrated in a certain basilica.” The author did not write it that way.

Moreover, what Ivo complains of—that because of the countless occupations of public affairs he was scarcely able to complete the canonical obligation at the prescribed hours—is likewise said by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, in a certain letter: “Business hostile to my spirit comes upon me, claims me entirely for itself, steals away the privacy of prayers, and deprives ecclesiastical offices of their proper times,” etc.

Relevant to this is what others recount from Peter the Venerable, in a letter to Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, concerning Saint Severinus, bishop of Cologne, famous for his reputation: namely, that after death he appeared burning to a cleric and said that nothing in him deserved punishment by vengeance except this: that while he was entangled at court in imperial counsels, he had not performed the offices of the canonical synaxis at the separate intervals of the hours. For, gathering everything together in the morning, he thereafter enjoyed unrestricted leisure throughout the day as business pressed upon him.

For this negligence concerning the hours he suffered the punishment of burning. This story seems a fable to many. Roger, bishop of Salisbury, who had been chancellor and confidential secretary to Henry I, king of England, and afterward bishop—a prudent man of most unimpeachable reputation—may have feared the same thing. For though occupied with many secular affairs, he nevertheless did not neglect the ecclesiastical offices; every day he honourably performed them all in the morning, so that he might thereafter attend to other matters more readily and safely, as William of Malmesbury, monk, writes in *Deeds of the Kings of England*, book V.

An ancient author, in the *Life of Saint Hubert, Bishop of Liège*: “He steadfastly persisted in the customary work of prayer [or: *consueto*, ‘customary’], and before daylight appeared rendered to the Lord the sacred office dedicated to the number seven.”

Pope Innocent III, in a diploma concerning Saint Homobonus of Cremona:

> “Frequently attending the office of Mass and the other hours with the utmost devotion, he so persevered in continual prayers that at the appointed hours he either prayed without ceasing or sometimes anticipated the hours themselves—unless some just cause detained him in other works of mercy.”

[Col. 0308B] “He attempted to do this as often as…” This is the reading of the old codex. Formerly: “so often, and as often as.” Yet that too is correct. In ancient monuments, however, the same spelling is common, for, as others have observed, the ancients often placed *n* between *e* and *s* in order to pronounce it more softly.

## ON LETTER XX

“They would make war.” The codices vary here. The Puthean book has “they would make a conflagration”; one manuscript of Nicolas Faber has “they would make *werra*,” a spelling which occurs elsewhere in authors.

Abbot of Ursperg, under the emperor:

> “If a freeborn man, ministerial, or man of any condition, commits arson for his own *werra*, for a friend, or for a relative…”

Where another manuscript has “for *guerra*”; and in Matthew Paris’s English history, *Life of William II*: “He provoked his neighbours by continual *werrae* and exactions.” The same author, *Life of Henry I*: “He steadfastly carried on the laws of *werra* against him with sword and fire alike.”

The word is less Latin, but exceedingly common in the author’s age; below, in Letter 168: “to make war against oneself.”

## ON LETTER XXIV

“Which you laudably exercised in the time of your predecessor, Pope Gregory of blessed memory.” Gregory VII is meant, as is clear from his Letters 30 and 32, book IX. Sigebert likewise, under the year of the Lord 1080, mentions Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate under the same pope; and under the year 1098 notes that he performed the same legation under Urban II, whom Ivo also means in Letters 30 and 109, although in those places he does not state the name.

William of Malmesbury, book I of *Deeds of the Bishops of England*: “Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, apostolic legate in Gaul, was a man of great name and power, and not lacking in religion.” Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, book I of *Miracles*, chapter 22, writes that Pope Urban appointed this Hugh legate over almost all Gaul because of his great integrity of conduct and religious manner of life.

Yet, when summoned to the council convened at Piacenza in 1095, he did not come and did not send a legate there in his place with a canonical excuse; consequently, he was suspended from the office of archbishop by Urban, as Berthold reports in his chronicle. The same author, under the year 1083, notes that this Hugh, bishop of Lyons, was indispensable to Gregory VII. It is therefore no wonder that Gregory, when near death, urged the bishops to choose him as Roman pontiff, as Leo of Marsi writes in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book III, chapter 64; but this was futile.

Victor, who succeeded Gregory, rebuked him sharply because, out of pride and ambition for the Apostolic See which he coveted, he acted against Victor with deceit and injuries, though he had sought and received from Victor the legation in the regions of Gaul. Victor therefore ordered people to abstain from communion with him, as is recorded in the said *Chronicle*, book IV, chapter 71.

Indeed Ivo rebukes in this Hugh the arrogance of the apostolic legation, Letter 60; yet in Letter 109 he writes to Paschal that the legation in Gaul should be entrusted to him.

“Because of the feeble head.” He means Urban, who was then struggling with Guibert, or Wibert, the antipope. The faction of each was powerful, and they maintained their cause by armed force, not without dreadful and public slaughter among Roman citizens, while fortune inclined now to one side and now to the other. This is clearly apparent from the chronicle of Berthold, an adherent of Urban, who arranged Urban’s history year by year.

“Another Ahab in the Italian kingdom.” In Letter 43, he says that the kingdom of Italy, long rebellious, finally fell silent in Urban’s sight.

“And another Jezebel in the French kingdom.” He means Bertrada, the concubine most hostile to Ivo, because he would not applaud her incestuous adultery or marriage with the king. Hence in Letter 28 he says that he did not enjoy complete security at Philip’s court because of the unfaithful sex, and in Letter 50 that the hostility of the said queen toward him had by no means been appeased.

## ON LETTER XXV

“His special son.” This has been restored on the authority of the old codices; formerly *spiritualis* (“spiritual”) had crept in, through an error arising from an abbreviation in the handwriting. The same blemish appears in Baronius. But above, in Letter 12, it has likewise been corrected: “Give orders to your special son.” In this sense he calls himself the son of Pope Urban’s womb in Letter 12.

John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, book VII, chapter 21, speaking of the hypocritically religious of his age:

> “That more things may be permitted them with impunity, they exempt themselves from the jurisdiction of all churches and become special sons of the Roman Church; yet they are so situated that, in matters where they are defendants, they may be summoned everywhere, but cannot themselves be summoned except at Rome or Jerusalem.”

For this is the entirely correct reading in the earliest editions; in others, “spiritual sons” is wrongly printed.

Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, Letter 12:

> “When I heard of the disturbance of the holy Roman Church, I grieved, because, as a special son, I could not hear of my mother’s grief without compassion. For that grief rested more especially upon me, whom she has always hitherto loved with such charity, honoured with such familiarity, and distinguished with so many benefits and honours.”

Nevertheless, it is clear that there are several letters of Pope John VIII addressed to kings in which he calls them spiritual sons, for example in the headings of Letters 172, 186, 187, 192, 197, and 199; but in another sense.

“I would bring charges of injuries against him.” Thus corrected on the authority of the old codex. Previously the singular “injury” had wrongly crept in; the same error is also present in Baronius’s edition, which assigns this letter to the seventh year of Urban’s pontificate.

“Outlawed on suspicion alone.” Most books have *suspicione* (“suspicion”). I preferred, however, to follow the reading of Servin’s best manuscripts, *suspectione*, because it is less commonplace and obvious. The same word has been altered in many authors’ passages, as in Aquilinus Gaius Vettius Juvencus, *Gospel History*, book I: “Does such a suspicion touch Judas?” Thus some editions read; others have *suspicio*.

Likewise in a verse of Paulinus of Nola to Ausonius:

> “Lest any false suspicion should draw upon the holy parent  
> A cloud contracted from a silent breast.”

Others changed it to *suspicio*. Terence, *Andria*, act III, scene I:

> “What suspicion has entered your mind?”

Ennius, in Nonius:

> “To entertain a false suspicion severely is characteristic of fools.”

## ON LETTER XXVIII

“When I should meet you with a body of soldiers on the day you had appointed.” Even in time of war, the bishops of the kingdom of France did the same. A notable passage on this matter occurs in Rigord’s history, in the deeds of the twenty-ninth year of Philip Augustus:

> “When all the barons and bishops summoned to this army had assembled at Meudon and had sent, at the king’s command, their men as they owed for that expedition, the bishops of Orléans and Auxerre returned with their knights to their own lands, saying that they were not bound to go or send to the army unless the king himself personally set out. And since they could protect themselves in this matter by no privilege, general custom standing against them, the king demanded that they make amends. Since they refused to make amends, the king confiscated their regalian rights—that is, only those temporal possessions which they held from him as fiefs—leaving their tithes and other spiritual possessions in peace. For that most Christian king always feared to offend the Church of God and its ministers. Therefore, when they placed the king’s land and men under interdict, sent to the Roman curia, and went there in person, Pope Innocent III was unwilling to infringe or alter in any respect the customs and rights of the kingdom. At length, after amends had been made and paid to the king, they recovered after two years all that the king had confiscated.”

“Lord Pope Urban.” One old codex has *dominus*. It may be observed that in these manuscripts *domnus* is almost always written when ecclesiastics are concerned, while *dominus* is used for secular persons. Though slight, this should not have gone unmentioned. In later ages the word *dominus* seemed proper to God alone, which Tertullian did not wish to be bestowed upon emperors; and among the pagan Caesars there were some who rejected such a title, as others have long observed. Therefore certain modern editors acted wrongly in rejecting *domni* as though it were barbarous, so that no trace of it remained.

An example occurs in the edition of the deacon Wandelbert’s *Life of Saint Goar*: “That the envoys of Lord Bishop may show charity with us; for they are on the road.” Thus the old manuscripts read. But in the said volume IV another editor substituted on his own authority: “that the envoys of our bishop may dine with us.”

And in book II of Baudonivia’s *Life of Queen Radegund*, chapter 5: “Lord Germanus obeys the king, comes to Poitiers, enters the monastery, [and enters] the oratory of Lady Mary.” The editor substituted: “The apostolic man Germanus obeys the king,” and shortly afterward “the oratory of Blessed Mary.” And in chapter 14: “She went to the oratory of Lady Mary.” The same editor printed: “She went to the oratory of the most blessed Virgin Mary.”

“The bed of the woman whom you regard as your wife.” The passage in Letter 15 should be added. On this matter, an old anonymous author in a fragment of Frankish history from Robert to the death of King Philip says:

> “King Philip, having repudiated Bertha, mother of Louis, took another wife, Bertrada, daughter of Simon of Montfort, who had married Fulk, count of Anjou. The king took her from him; and although Pope Urban of blessed memory repeatedly warned him, he did not consent.”

Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum*, book XXVI, chapter 88:

> “This Fulk had a wife who, leaving him, married Philip, king of France. The king was so captivated by love of her that she ruled him in all things, though he wished to rule all men. Finally, for her lust he endured for several years being pointed at by every finger and excommunicated by the whole Christian world.”

Abbot Suger, *Life of King Louis*:

> “Thereafter, as the son advanced day by day, his father King Philip declined day by day. For after bringing in the countess of Anjou, he did nothing worthy of royal majesty; but, seized by desire for the wife he had seized, he devoted himself to gratifying his pleasure. Hence he neither provided for the commonwealth nor, excessively self-indulgent, spared the health of his noble and handsome body. One thing alone remained: through fear and love of his heir, his son, the condition of the kingdom continued to flourish.”

Thus, incidentally, that passage must be restored to its integrity on the authority of the old codex, because the reading has been foully corrupted in the recently printed book, together with Glaber, Helgaud, and several others. He later repudiated this Bertrada. Add the notes on Letter 144.

“From participation in the Lord’s body and blood.” From this they wish to infer that in Ivo’s time laymen still communicated under both kinds. To this also belong the words of Letter 63, where he says that the body and blood of the Lord are beneficially administered to the faithful people.

Suger, on Louis the Fat: “When, to the amazement of all, he had first made confession of sins, he communicated most devoutly in the body and blood of Jesus Christ.”

Certainly, in Baronius, *Annals*, volume X, is reported a diploma of Pope Urban II to the canons of Saint Martin of Tours:

> “If any ecclesiastical or secular person should rashly attempt to act against this, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Redeemer.”

Under the year of Christ 1095, Baronius likewise reports canon 28 of the Council of Clermont under Urban:

> “Let no one communicate from the altar unless he receives the body separately and likewise the blood, except in necessity and with caution.”

After these words Baronius adds that this was decreed because of the recently condemned Berengarian heresy, which held that the figure was sufficiently fulfilled under one species only.

Moreover, the casati of the Church. This is the consistent reading in the better archetypes; for the Put. codex alone, corrupting the ancient wording, offers *praeterea et causa Ecclesiae* (“moreover, and the cause of the Church”); another has *quassati*, which comes closer to the truth. Here he understands the *casati* of the Church as a class of vassals. Mention is made of them in an ancient inscription from Orléans, still to be seen, broken and inserted into the wall of the church of Holy Cross:

> BY THE BENEFICE OF ST. +, THROUGH JOHN THE BISHOP, AND THROUGH ALBERT, THE *CASATUS* OF ST. +, THE BOOK “LEMTBERTUS” WAS MADE, THIS HOLY CHURCH BEING WITNESS.

In the Frankish laws formerly collected by Abbot Ansegisus and published at Basel in 1557 (these are called the capitularies in the later editions), book I, chapter 68: “Let them cause to be recorded how many *mansi* each man holds as a benefice, or how many *casati* men are on that benefice”; and book IV, chapter 75: “Concerning the lord’s vassals who still serve within the household and are known to hold benefices for so long: it has been decreed that whoever among them remains at home with the lord emperor shall not keep his *casati* vassals with him, but shall allow them to go with the count in whose district he is.” They seem to have taken their name from cottages (*casae*). Paulinus of Nola, Letter 2 to Amandus: “That he may receive in a Church cottage a little plot of land from which to procure his sustenance.” In Ivo himself, *casamenta* of powerful men are mentioned in Letter 173; *casales* are also mentioned elsewhere.

They have been excommunicated for violating the peace. Examples of this matter are found below in Letter 61, concerning wicked violators of the highways; such was the lord of Puteaux, Letter 211; and concerning the knights of Count Theobald, Letter 235; and Gervase, Letter 266.

To send into the *host*. That is, into a military army; examples of this sense are varied among French writers. Suger, in the *Life of Louis*: “An astonishing *host* of thirty thousand soldiers having been assembled.” And in the same book: “When requested, he entered their territory not with an army, but with the military force of his household.” Add passages from the history of the monk Aimoin, book V, chapters 22 and 27. There is an old French vernacular proverb: “If the army knew what the army was doing, the army would often undo itself.” Elsewhere Suger calls it *hostium*: “With these and such circumstances, the king was nowhere secure; conspicuous for the vigor of his native greatness of spirit, provident in straits, he even girded himself with a sword in the army.”

## 135. ON LETTER XXX

To Fulk, by the grace of God Bishop of Beauvais: fortitude amid adversities. Writing to the same man in the immediately following letter, Ivo admonishes or wishes in the title that he may hold himself fast to his holy purpose by the anchor of gravity. Since authors of that age—something Ivo himself often does—were accustomed to prefix to their letters titles suited and appropriate to their subjects, an argument may be drawn from this that Fulk was agitated by various disturbances in the bishopric of Beauvais. To illustrate this, passages from the letters of Anselm, Abbot of Bec, should be added.

He had asked advice whether he should undertake the dignity offered him. Anselm replied that it was safer for a man always fearful of his own weakness to flee a great burden than readily to submit his shoulders in confidence in his strength. The burden, therefore, should be refused; but if he could not avoid it without sin, he should undertake it obediently and carry it diligently. That letter indeed does not state [Col. 0312A] what the burden was. But from the subsequent letters it is inferred that both were speaking of episcopal dignity. For Pope Urban II, in a letter to Abbot Anselm, says that he had granted the Bishop of Beauvais what seemed unjust in his ordination, and had imposed upon him the care of the bishopric against his will and resistance. Finally, he admonishes Anselm to stand by the bishop, as by his own son, as helper, corrector, and counsellor.

Anselm replies to Urban that he had previously advised his friend to undertake the charge and satisfy the wishes of those requesting it; but that now the man was compelling him to approach the pope, so that by his authority he might resist his opponents. These are the words: “Concerning our most beloved Bishop of Beauvais, etc.” It is Letter 34 of Book II among the letters of Saint Anselm. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLVIII. But later, after the passage of several months, when the same bishop, attacked by many plots, saw that he was making no progress and was in danger of his life, he made great efforts to resign the bishopric and travelled to Rome for that purpose, as is attested by the said Anselm’s letter to Urban (see above).

[Col. 0312B] But the Roman pontiff did not assent to Fulk’s request, because he did not wish one useful to himself to leave the bishopric. An indication of this is that in the body of Anselm’s manuscript letters are found several letters of Anselm himself to Fulk, 136 Bishop of Beauvais, in which he relates that he had been dragged, unwilling and resisting, from the monastery of Bec to the archbishopric of Canterbury. From comparing the foregoing passages, it may be inferred that the following, written in the ancient Chronicle of Bec, is to be understood of the same Fulk; and it seems worth noting:

> A certain monk of Bec was sought for the bishopric of the Church of Beauvais. When Saint Anselm, the abbot, refused to give his assent to this election and would not yield his monk to those requesting him, the petitioners said: “Lord, we choose him; he does not thrust himself forward. Why will you not grant the one whom we seek?”  
>   
> But he answered: “Even if God Himself chose me, I should still be afraid; for through the prophet He chose Saul, and through Himself Judas the traitor, [Col. 0312C] and both were rejected.”

Moreover, the foregoing may serve in interpreting Ivo’s ninth letter (which you will find at the end of these letters, no. 289) to Pope Urban. In it he says that the Bishop of Beauvais, a man of upright and commendable simplicity, had been accused by envious persons but nevertheless acquitted by Urban.

“Mindful of your office: worldly pride not with the weapons of worldly malice.” Elsewhere he likewise rebukes bishops who, forgetful of their rank, were accustomed to usurp the use of the material sword, although the Church forbids the shedding of another’s blood, as he shows in Letter 247. Even when he himself was a captive, he refused to be freed by weapons of war and restored to his bishopric, as appears from Letter 20. Well known is what Saint Bernard says in *On Consideration*, Book IV, chapter 3, to Pope Eugenius: there are two swords, but the material one is to be wielded by the hand of the soldier, at the priest’s nod and the emperor’s command.

To this should be referred the words of an early historian in the book *On the Life, Character, and Deeds of All the Princes*, which survives in manuscript in the Royal Library. Speaking of the army of Pope Leo IX against the Normans who were in Apulia, he notes under the year 1053:

> This was the first of the Roman pontiffs from blessed Peter down to his own time who went forth to war with an armed hand. Although he was holy and acted with this pious intention, nevertheless, because this was not his office, nor had it been permitted to him by the Lord who had come to suffer and had forewarned His followers that they should rather suffer from others than persecute others, the multitude of his army was slaughtered while he looked on. For the Lord did not command His disciples, nor did those apostles command their successors, to protect God’s people, like princes of this world, by worldly concerns and the material sword; rather, they were to admonish by the word of teaching and instruct by the example of a devout life.

## ON LETTER XXXIII

“The proximity of places to us.” In other books, “our proximity [Col. 0313A] of places.” But since in the Put. manuscript I found written, though corruptly, *nobiscum vicinitas* (“proximity with us”), it was not difficult to restore the true reading.

## ON LETTER XXXV

“See whether you fully render the fidelity which you owe, whether you discharge the duty of your office.” Below, in Letter 190, he likewise mentions the fidelity which all bishops of Gaul promised the king by hand and oath. In Letter 15 he declares that from the highest fidelity he cannot and ought not to attend the king’s unlawful marriage. In Letter 253 he says that by the right of fidelity he asks King Louis to aid the distressed Bishop of Amiens against violators of the peace. Likewise, in Letter 209, he says that in the fidelity pledged to the king, what is useful and honorable must above all be observed, and that one must not presume to give the king counsel contrary to fidelity and diminishing the majesty of the realm.

He had already warned the bishops of France, in the affair of King Philip concerning his incestuous union, that they should possess the spirit of fortitude along with the spirit of counsel, Letter 14. But [Col. 0313B] because they were lukewarm and timid, he charged them with silence and rebuked them because, like mute dogs, they could not bark, at the end of Letter 25. Pope Gregory VII had shortly before imputed a similar fault to the same men, in Register, Book II, Letter 5, to Manasses of Reims, Richer of Sens, Richard of Bourges, archbishops, and Adraldus, Bishop of Chartres, and the other bishops of France; there he recounts the various wicked and abominable crimes of the same King Philip.

## 137. ON LETTER XXXVI

“The letters of the lord pope, at the dictating of which we were present at his side.” This passage had been corrupted in most books. The earlier edition read *alacri interfuimus* (“we were present eagerly”). In the Putean manuscripts: *alacres interfuimus* (“we were present eagerly”), with the variant added above: *vel alacri mente interf.* (“or, we were present with an eager mind”). In the St-Germain manuscript and another of Thou: *alatri interf.* In the Royal manuscript: *alati*. But from the manuscripts of Faber and Servin I restored *a latere* (“at his side”), than which no reading is better or truer.

For Ivo had stayed in Rome more than once, as Letters 27 and 65 also indicate, and was familiar with Pope Urban, whom he meant here to be understood; he had moved about in Urban’s court, as he says in Letter 211. In a similar expression he says that cardinals are sent “from the pope’s side,” Letter 109, where he also calls them “the attendants at the side of the Apostolic See.”

Hilary. Thus most manuscripts. Earlier editions had *Hilariones*; but the former suits and agrees better with the other names.

## ON LETTER XXXVIII

Guacelin. The manuscripts vary: “Guatcelin, Gualcelcin, Laucelin, Gualcherin.” The earlier edition has Guacelm. William of Malmesbury, Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, chapter on the Bishops of Winchester: “After Stigand’s deposition, Walkelm, appointed by King William, succeeded; his good works, surpassing fame, will repel the decay of old age for as long as the episcopal see endures there,” etc. The same words occur in Book III of the said historian’s *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, where, however, *Walkelin* is read. In the first part of Roger of Howden’s *Annals*, he is called Walcelm: “In the year 1098,” he says, “Walcelm of Winchester died on the third day before the Nones of January, a Sunday.” But there *Walcellin* should have been printed. For Matthew Paris, under the year 1093: “When, before the examination of the bishop about to be consecrated, Walkelin, Bishop of Winchester, was reading the election document in the ecclesiastical manner, Thomas, Archbishop of York, complained that the document had not been properly drawn up.” The same author, under Christmas Day 1098: “At the same time Walkelin, Bishop of Winchester, died.”

“Bishop of the Wentonenses.” Some read “of the Wintorienses”; elsewhere, “of the Guittorienses.”

“That you may extend to me, who desire it, the hands of prayers.” Thus plainly the ancient manuscripts. Earlier, *munus* (“gift”) was printed; this too may be defended, as he says in Letter 168, “to extend hands of help” or “the gift of counsel.” But it seemed right to retain [Col. 0314A] the other reading, confirmed by so many manuscripts. Thus in Letter 19 he speaks of “extending hands of prayer,” and in Letters 207 and 215, of “extending mutually the hands of prayers.” Likewise, in Letter 70, of extending mutually to one another the hands of exhortations. Pope Paschal II, in a letter to Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury: “That, as you approach God more nearly by the steps of virtues, you may extend to us the hands of your prayers.” Paulinus of Nola, Letter to Sebastian: “Pray for us; join strong hands of prayer, that you may overcome the multitude of our sins.”

Saint Augustine used this figure at the beginning of Book V of the *Confessions*: “Receive the sacrifice of my confessions from the hand of my tongue, which You have formed and stirred.” This is taken from the ancient translator’s rendering of Proverbs, chapter 18: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue.” There Saint Salonius the Bishop says that “the hand of the tongue” is said metaphorically, like “the wings of the wind”; for the hands of the tongue are the words themselves.

## ON LETTER XXXIX

[Col. 0314B]

“Because of the great goodwill which you have toward the monks of Bec.” On the Abbey of Bec, its first abbot Herluin, and his successor Anselm, see William of Jumièges, Book V, *On the Dukes of the Normans*, chapter 9. For Anselm embraced the monastic rule at the monastery of Bec in Normandy in the twenty-seventh year of his age. Lanfranc then held the office of prior there, and Anselm succeeded him in the same headship, as the Englishman Eadmer relates in his *Life*.

## ON LETTER XL

Manegald. In the old papers of Antoine Loisel this letter is addressed to “Master Manegald.” Ivo indicates that he had been devoted to the study of philosophy before entering the clerical order. I think him to be the same person who elsewhere is called Manigaud the German. An ancient anonymous author, in a fragment of a history of the Franks from Robert to the death of Philip, says:

> At this time there flourished, both in divine and human philosophy, Lanfranc, Bishop of Canterbury; Guido the Lombard; Manigaud the German; and Bruno of Reims, who later led the life of a hermit.

Some think him the same man whom Berthold, a contemporary writer of Ivo, mentions in his chronicle under the year of the Lord 1095, where he says that in Alsace Master Manegold of Lautenbach wonderfully rekindled ecclesiastical religion, long since extinguished in those regions. Under the year 1093 he says: “Manegold, the venerable provost of the canons dwelling at Marbach, was long held captive by King Henry because he favored Urban and would not obey the schismatics.” Finally, under the year 1100, he reports in Germany that the venerable Abbot Manegold of the monastery of Saint George was killed by his monk.

“And again and again to be at leisure.” In two ancient manuscripts these words are not repeated, contrary to the agreement of the other codices. Other passages certainly support the repetition: Letter 132, “Again and again we ask”; and Letter 273, “Therefore again and again we beseech.” Pedo, in his elegy on the death of Drusus Nero:

> With their final cry they call upon you again and again.

Paulinus of Nola, in his poem to Licentius:

> Yet I shall repeat this and admonish you again and again.

“So that you may flee the slippery paths of harsh military service.” Virgil, *Aeneid* III:

> And, repeating it, again and again I shall admonish you.

The same author, Book VIII:

> Again and again a great crash thunders.

## ON LETTER XLII

“I would say very many things into a safe ear.” In the Servin manuscript, 138, “into your ear”; the Put. codex likewise has that reading, in which there remains a trace of an erased letter, showing that *tuta* (“safe”) had originally been written there. This is the better reading, confirmed by the agreement of the others. Horace, Book I, Ode 28:

> Whatever you have to do, do it; entrust it to safe ears.

## ON LETTER XLIII

[Col. 0315A]

“As a new king.” Baronius, *Annals*, volume XI, understands this of Conrad, son of Emperor Henry III, who came to Pope Urban and was released by him from excommunication; he refers the passage to the sixth year of Urban’s pontificate. William of Malmesbury writes:

> But the malice of Matilda favored the more equitable cause, as it seemed. Forgetful of her sex and not unlike the ancient Amazons, she, a woman, led armored ranks of men into war. By her support Urban obtained the apostolic throne and enjoyed secure leisure for eleven years.

“May the Lord, I pray, crush Satan beneath your feet.” The St-Germain codex alone reads: “May the Lord convert [him].” But the former reading is more suitable and is supported by the passage of Saint Paul in the final chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, and likewise by Ivo’s words in Letter 236: “Saving,” he says, “due reverence for the Roman Church, to celebrate: which, if at present it cannot cast Satan down beneath its feet…” Arnulf of Lisieux, Letter 19 to Pope Alexander:

> Moreover, paintings in the Lateran palace show that such schisms have occurred frequently in the Roman Church. There schismatic pretenders are represented under the feet of the Catholic Fathers as a footstool, where wisdom by its own power crushes and tramples the necks of the proud and exalted. This was certainly done so that the inscription of the witness of victory might redound to the glory of the holy Fathers: in it those pretenders either suffer the penalty of being crushed or beg pardon for their presumption. Therefore the chair of your holy Apostolate ought not to be without a footstool, but should be adorned by a nobler footstool.

Abbot Suger, Book *On the Life of King Louis the Fat*, speaking of Burdinus, the schismatic antipope, who at Rome by Pope Calixtus’s command was placed backward on a camel, clad in goatskins, and led through the forum: “To preserve the memory,” he says, “of so great a punishment, they depicted him being trampled beneath the feet of the lord pope in the chamber of the palace.”

## ON LETTER XLIV

[Col. 0315C]

“Though wounded outwardly, he may perish while wounding inwardly.” An excellent correction made with the help of the ancient manuscripts, in place of the earlier intruded reading: “though Jesus [is] outwardly, Jesus may perish inwardly.”

“Let him be anathema, maranatha.” This latter word was absent from some books, perhaps through the error of a scribe to whom it seemed new and unfamiliar. It has been added on the authority of the other codices. It occurs in Saint Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 16, and in chapter *Gulisarius*, Cause 23, question 4. In an ancient poem of Theodoric, Abbot of Saint-Trond:

> Say: “God, let these be maranatha”; say: “let these be anathema.”

In the Council of Toledo, reported in the ancient Synod of Reims held at Durocortorum: “Those who presume against this your definition, let them be anathema maranatha—that is, perdition at the coming of the Lord—and let them have a portion with Judas Iscariot.” On this word, see Saint Jerome, Letter 137 to Marcella. Baronius also, *Annals*, volume I, under the year of Christ 57, explains why it was added to anathema.

## ON LETTER XLVI

[Col. 0315D]

Baronius, *Annals*, volume II, refers this to the synod convoked at Clermont among the Arvernians in the seventh year of Urban II’s pontificate.

“Trusting.” The word has been added from a manuscript codex.

“By the cunning of their little talent.” The St-Germain codex alone reads “talent.”

“And by the charm of his tongue”: the Put. codex has this reading; the other copies read “and by fluency,” and the latter reading is preferable. For although the author’s age was less polished, many men of eloquent speech still remained in Gaul, a distinction of which Gaul has never been deprived, even according to the testimony of foreign nations. Cato, cited by Sosipater Charisius, says that Gaul always pursued two things most zealously: military affairs and witty speech. Saint Jerome, in *Against Vigilantius*, says that Gaul always abounded in very brave and very eloquent men. Fortunatianus also noted in his books of school rhetoric that, in the native speech of the Gauls, *faceti* [Col. 0316A] was customarily said in the sense of “eloquent.” In this sense also Abbot Suger, in the *Life of King Louis the Fat*: “Especially and alone the Archbishop of Trier, an elegant and pleasant man, rich in eloquence and wisdom, trained in the Gallic buskin, delivered an eloquent speech.”

“That the king with his kingdom will withdraw from obedience to you.” Hence it is clear that the Franks favored Pope Urban, not Guibert the antipope. To this belong Berthold’s words in his Chronicle under the year of the Lord 1089: the pope received letters from King Philip of France promising him due submission. Again, under 1091, he says that the pope, dwelling in the region of Champagne, was honored with due reverence by all Catholics and by Philip, King of the Franks. Finally, under 1094, he reports that at Autun, a city of Gaul, at a general council held by Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, excommunication was renewed against King Henry IV, Guibert, invader of the Apostolic See, and all their accomplices.

“Unless you restore the crown, unless you release the king from anathema.” This passage supports the view of those who maintain that, when Philip was excommunicated by Pope Urban II, the kingdom of France was also placed under interdict. Other passages may confirm this. In Letter 66 to Hugh, legate of the Roman Church, Ivo says that the Archbishop of Tours placed the crown upon the king against the legate’s interdict, and by this device obtained from the king the appointment of a certain ill-reputed man as Bishop of Orléans. He repeats this at the end of Letter 67 to Urban. In Letter 84 he praises John, the cardinal legate, who had abstained from communion with the king, although certain bishops of the Belgian province, against Pope Urban’s interdict, had placed the crown upon the king, as though, with the herald of justice dead, justice itself had died.

Likewise, writing to Pope Paschal in Letter 144, where he treats of reconciling Philip to the Church, he says that the land endangered by Philip’s anathema [Col. 0316C] must be rescued from danger. Certainly, writing previously to Philip himself in Letter 15, he openly declares that there will be the greatest danger to the crown of his kingdom if he takes the concubine before the case is considered in a general council. Shortly afterward he adds that Philip should beware lest, along with the diminution of his earthly kingdom, he lose the eternal one. Moreover, in Letter 23, sent to the king’s steward, he says that he had withheld Urban’s letters because he did not wish the kingdom to be stirred in any way against 139 the king himself.

The words of the continuator of the monk Aimoin, *History*, Book V, chapter 1, support this: he writes that the king and all his land had been bound by the bond of anathema by the lord pope, because the king led his life in a most wicked manner and would not cease from it at anyone’s warning. William of Malmesbury, Book IV, chapter 2 of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, speaking of the Council of Clermont under Urban II, says:

> At that council the lord pope excommunicated Philip, King of France, and all who should call him either king or lord, obey him, or speak with him, except insofar as concerned correcting him; likewise, that cursed wife of his, and all who should call her queen or lady, until they should come to amendment, so that each should separate from the other.

The same author, Book V, in the *Life of Henry I*, says that the same Philip, “with advancing old age weighed down by lust and enslaved by unlawful passions for the beauty of the Countess of Anjou, was therefore excommunicated by the apostolic see; in the town where he stayed, no divine service was performed. But as he departed, the ringing of bells burst forth everywhere, and he expressed his foolish folly with laughter: ‘Do you hear,’ he said, ‘how beautifully they drive one away?’ So much was he a laughing-stock to all the bishops of his province that none would marry them except William, Archbishop of Rouen; for the rashness of that deed he paid by many years under interdict and was scarcely at last restored to apostolic communion through Archbishop Anselm.”

An ancient author of the fragmentary *History of the Franks from Robert to the Death of Philip*, after saying that Philip, repeatedly admonished by Pope Urban, never consented, adds that Urban’s successor Paschal sent two cardinals into Gaul. Meeting the king and finding him obstinate, they assembled a council at Poitiers and subjected all France to anathema on this account. An author of the ancient Chronicle of the monastery of Saint-Denis is also cited, noting that throughout the period of this excommunication it was customary in public ecclesiastical acts to subscribe “Christ reigning,” rather than “Philip reigning.” Yet this now seems to some to be a monastic invention. They support their opinion from the fact that subjects willingly obeyed their king and Ivo himself, in letters sent to the same man, although excommunicated, calls him the magnificent King of the Franks and his own lord. In the title of Letter 22 he wishes that he may govern his temporal kingdom in such a way as not to lose the eternal one. From these titles, they say, Ivo would have abstained altogether if the Roman pontiff had forbidden obedience to Philip and had caused him to cease governing the kingdom.

[Col. 0317B] But it should not seem at all new or unheard-of if Urban, and afterwards Paschal, are said to have interdicted the kingdom after excommunicating Philip. For shortly before this, Pope Gregory VII, whom Urban succeeded, had already openly and repeatedly threatened to deprive the same king of the kingdom because of various other crimes. It seemed proper to append his words from Register, Book I, Letter 35 to Roderic, Bishop of Chalon, in which he attacks Philip as a seller and destroyer of churches:

> Let him know that we shall restrain his hard obstinacy in disobedience with canonical severity. For either the king himself, having repudiated the shameful commerce of the Simoniacal heresy, will permit suitable persons to be promoted to sacred government; or the Franks, struck by the sword of a general anathema, will certainly refuse further obedience to him, unless they prefer to cast off the Christian faith.

The same pope, Book II, Letter 5, writing to Manasses, Archbishop of Reims, Richer of Sens, [Col. 0317C] Richard of Bourges, and the other bishops of France, concerning the crimes of the said Philip:

> Admonished and bound by apostolic authority, imitate your mother, the holy Roman and Apostolic Church, with due faith and obedience; completely separating yourselves from his service and communion, publicly forbid throughout all France the celebration of every divine office. And if he is unwilling to repent even under such a penalty, we wish it to be hidden from no one or doubtful to no one that, with God’s help, we shall attempt by every means to wrest the kingdom of France from his occupation.

The same pope, Letter 18 to William, Count of Poitiers:

> If he persists in the perversity of his designs and, according to the hardness of his impenitent heart, stores up for himself the wrath of God and Saint Peter, then, with God helping and his wickedness deserving it, in the Roman synod we shall without doubt separate from the body and communion of the holy Church both him and whoever shall render him royal honor or obedience; and his excommunication shall be confirmed daily above the altar of Saint Peter.

These are Gregory’s words. From them it seems clear that, when Philip was excommunicated by Urban and Paschal, the kingdom was simultaneously interdicted. For what else do Ivo’s foregoing words in Letters 66 and 67 concerning the crown placed upon the king against the interdict, and in this Letter 46 concerning restoration of the crown, as well as Letter 144 concerning the land endangered by anathema, signify?

It is also probable that when the prince was excommunicated, some of his subjects refused him honor and obedience, while others continued to honor and obey him—as we have seen happen, in the recent civil war, when French loyalties were divided between Henry III and Henry IV. In this way the diversity of views may be reconciled. Certainly, before Philip’s excommunication, other kings of France had been subjected together with the entire kingdom to papal censure, as was Robert, son of Hugh. The above-mentioned author in the fragmentary *History of the Franks from Robert to the Death of Philip* says:

> The same king took as his wife the mother of Count Odo, Bertha by name, who at that time was a little boy; moreover, she was the same king’s co-godmother. For the king had received her son from the sacred font. When Pope Gregory learned this, he struck all France with anathema. But the king, held beyond measure by love for the same woman, would not consent to put her away, until the Almighty undertook to correct the king Himself. For when the woman conceived by the king, believing that she would bear a son, she bore a monster. This event terrified the king and compelled him to give the woman a letter of repudiation. Having done this, he deserved to be absolved together with his whole kingdom.

Aimoin, too, in *The Life of Saint Abbo, Abbot of Fleury*, chapter 11, relates that Abbo went to Rome at King Robert’s request, because Gregory had threatened to lay anathema upon the entire kingdom of the Franks because Arnulf, Archbishop of Reims, had been deprived of his see without a just hearing and consigned to custody.

Whether the Roman pontiff ought or was able to excommunicate the kings of France and simultaneously interdict the kingdom has been debated by more learned men. Let only this be added: Rigord relates in *The Deeds of Philip Augustus* that, when in the year of the Lord 1199 Cardinal Peter, having convened a council at Dijon, placed the French king’s realm under interdict and did not defer to the appeal of the king’s messengers to the Roman See, the king was greatly angered because the bishops of his realm who had attended that council had consented to the interdict. Therefore, he expelled those bishops from their sees and stripped them of their goods.

## 140. “Let it be left alone; it is not mine.”

One codex punctuates it thus: “Will it be left? It is not mine.”

“From the unity of his mother.” In some copies “Church” is added, but apparently from a gloss. A similar passage occurs in Letters 98 and 124.

## ON LETTER XLVII

“To Guy, steward of the king.” The word “king” is now added for the first time on the authority of the ancient codices; some of these also have “royal.” It was wrongly absent from the first edition. The reference seems to be to the steward of the King of France, because this letter concerns the case of Philip and his concubine. There was another steward of Normandy, as the title of Letter 27 indicates. Bishop Hildebert alluded to this office of dignity when he said in a certain letter that a king’s steward had become the devil’s feast.

Saint Bernard of Clairvaux’s rebuke, in Letter 78 to Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, is elegant. It concerns a cleric, a deacon, so elevated by ecclesiastical honors that he seemed inferior to no bishops, and so involved in military offices that he was preferred to dukes. Since the nature of this courtly dignity may be gathered from his words, it is pleasant to pluck a few:

> An equal abuse exists on both sides: whether a deacon is assigned to the service of the royal table, or the king’s steward serves the mysteries of the altar. Who, indeed, would not marvel—or rather detest—that one and the same person should lead an armed army and, clothed in alb and stole, proclaim the Gospel in the midst of the church; sound the trumpet to summon soldiers to battle, and make known to peoples the commands of the bishop?

And shortly afterward:

> Although he is archdeacon, dean, and provost in different churches, none of these titles delights him as much as being called the king’s steward.

Then he adds:

> Certainly, the emblem which he wears upon his head befits royal pride more than service; likewise royal eminence rests more upon arms than psalms,

etc.

## ON LETTER XLVII

“Be at rest.” It is absent from one ancient codex.

“It is read from the time when…” The reading varies in Gratian, chapter *Legatur*, Cause 23, question 2. In some manuscripts it is: “Nor is it read, from the time when the Christian religion existed, nor is a certain example given”; in others: “Nowhere is it read, from the time when the Christian religion existed,” etc.

## ON LETTER XLVII

“To annul by disturbance.” Thus four ancient codices, a reading approached by the corrupt reading of the St-Germain codex, *cessare* (“to cease”); the received edition has *quassare* (“to shake”), as do certain handwritten books. But *cassare* (“to annul”) is more correct and frequent in this author: Letters 39, 62, 87, 155, and 209. Nonius Marcellus notes the distinction.

## ON LETTER XLIX

“Geoffrey, former bishop.” Earlier, “bishop” was printed, as it is read in some manuscripts. In others it appears in abbreviated form as “bishop.” The Royal codex wrongly offers “example.” But the manuscript of Nicolas Faber and another from Saint-Victor have “former bishop.” He calls him former bishop because he had been deposed by Pope Urban, as Letters 1 and 2 indicate. Besides, the former terms *ex-consuls*, *ex-praetors*, and *ex-quaestors*, and many similar expressions, are too well known to require proof by examples.

“I would make honey.” Thus three manuscripts; in two others, “at Meaux.” The Put. codex alone wrongly reads: “I would make better.”

## ON LETTER L

“Aplicueris.” The readings vary. Earlier editions printed *a Picueris*, as some written codices have. Others have *a Pitueris*; in the margin of another, *a Jemeris*; some, *a Plicueris*. The following gloss is also added: “A town in Boeotia which in French is called Puviers, or Bluviers.”

“Concerning the old complaint which the Church of Lyons has against the Church of Sens.” Below, in Letter 54, he says that the primacy of the Church of Lyons is irrationally contested by the See of Sens. There are testimonies showing that the Archbishop of Sens was formerly primate of Gaul. The Chronology of Auxerre, under the year 1002: “In these days Lord Sevinus, Archbishop of Sens, died. At Rome he received from the hand of Pope John the archiepiscopal pallium with which his predecessors had been invested, and the primacy of Gaul.”

But Pope Gregory VII confirmed the primacy of the Church of Lyons in Book VI, Letter 34. 141 To that letter is appended another of the same Gregory, addressed to his fellow bishops of Rouen, Tours, and Sens, to the same effect: that they should render obedience to the Archbishop of Lyons as primate, confirmed by him on the authority of the ancient Fathers. There he also explains the rationale and origin of the different ranks in the Church. But it is unnecessary to copy it out. It should be consulted in volume III of the *Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*, Book VI of the Register of Pope Gregory VII, Letter 35.

William the Breton of Armorica, *Philippid*, Book XII, treats of this primacy in these verses:

> And the Archbishop of Lyons, by whose primacy all Gaul was accustomed,  
> as report has it, to be governed and to refer difficult causes,  
> so that there the final dispute of litigations might be settled.  
> No case was sent to Rome unless  
> the tribunal of Lyons could not itself bring it to an end.  
> An epigram on the seal still recalls that honor,  
> as does the coinage issued for commercial exchange,  
> and the holy fathers whom the rank of suffragans  
> subjected by law to that metropolitan.

Therefore Saint Bernard of Clairvaux rightly says, in Letter 174 to the canons of Lyons, that among the churches of Gaul it is agreed that Lyons has hitherto held pre-eminence, both in the dignity of its see and in honorable pursuits and praiseworthy institutions.

Let him forbid the divine office in the places where they reside. Here one should note the custom of that age, by which the divine office was commonly prohibited in the places of those who violated the public peace. Evidence of this likewise appears in Letter 263: when a disturbance of clerics arose at Beauvais against the ministers of King Louis, the divine services were suspended. And in Letter 264 he says that this severity ought by no means to be observed except where the crime of sacrilege and the violation of peace cannot otherwise be punished. Likewise, in Letter 94, he asks Pope Paschal to order both the city churches and those of the suburbs to be closed if anyone should infringe the privilege and liberty granted to the Church of Chartres. Again, in Letter 121 he says that the clerics of Chartres urgently requested that the divine office be forbidden in the city of Chartres and throughout the entire bishopric until the goods taken from them were restored. But to many the atrocity of the act seemed all the more astonishing because, throughout an entire kingdom, [Col. 0320A] the rites of public religion were everywhere prohibited by the supreme pontiffs on account of one man’s offense.

Gregory VII, Book III, Letter 5, to the bishops of France, where he treats of the crimes of King Philip I: “Separating yourselves wholly from his communion, publicly forbid throughout all France the celebration of every divine office.” William of Malmesbury indeed testifies in *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, Book IV, that after the same Philip had been excommunicated, divine service ceased in the town where he lived with his concubine Bertrada; his words are quoted at greater length under Letter 46. Aimoin, in the book *Life of Saint Abbo, Abbot of Fleury*, chapter 12: “In that privilege, among other provisions, it is contained that the bishop of Orléans shall never enter the monastery of Fleury unless invited, and that none of the pontiffs shall ever prohibit the divine office in that monastery, even if all Gaul should be struck by the vengeance of an anathema because of the sins of the people.”

The author of the *Chronology of Auxerre*: “In the year of the Lord [Col. 0320B] 1200, the appearance of the Church throughout the whole kingdom was mournful, because no sacraments or divine offices were celebrated in the churches except viaticum and baptism. Nor did services cease only in churches: they ceased in monasteries as well. Burial was denied to the dead. Thus mourning was spread everywhere throughout the kingdom, since here the instruments of the Church were silent and the mouths of those singing to the Lord were closed. Octavian, bishop of Ostia, legate of the lord pope in France, absolved the kingdom from the interdict and induced the king to bring back into the kingdom the queen whom he had expelled; yet she was neither received with due honor nor restored to the marriage bed.” He means Philip Augustus, who had repudiated his wife Queen Ingeborg and taken the concubine Mary. The same author, shortly afterwards: “All England is subjected to a most severe interdict; and, with every privilege suspended both in monasteries and churches, the instruments of joy are silenced in divine stillness.”

## ON LETTER LIII

“That cleric whom, on the day of your entry [Col. 0320C], according to the custom of your city, at our exhortation you released from prison.” For *your*, as the old manuscripts have it, *our* had formerly crept in incorrectly. This passage deserves notice. For even today the bishops of the city of Orléans retain that custom, which is said to have been confirmed by a decree of the court of Bordeaux in 1522. Yet the source from which it sprang is somewhat obscure. It seems to have arisen from the very ancient custom by which bishops often interceded with secular judges for accused persons and prisoners, so that they might either be punished more mildly or released; this has been discussed elsewhere at length.

Priscus, the author of the *Life of Saint Anianus, Bishop of Orléans*, writes as follows, in Surius, vol. VI, under 17 November: “When he had already been elected bishop by the common votes of all, he asked Agrippinus, a distinguished man and commander of the soldiers, to allow all those whom the prisons held bound to depart free. Agrippinus refused, alleging some pretext or other; but when he wished to enter the church [Col. 0320D] to pray, a stone fell from above upon his head and, inflicting a dreadful wound, drew much blood from him. He immediately perceived that this had happened because he had rejected the prayers of the holy bishop. Therefore, after he had been carried home by his servants, he sent men to summon the bishop; for death appeared imminent because of the excessive loss of blood. The bishop came, made the sign of the cross upon the wound with his hand, and the blood stopped; strength returned to one whose condition had almost been despaired of. The prisons were opened, and the wretched captives went out, restored to freedom through the intercession of the blessed Bishop Anianus.”

It is also recorded that the king of England wished those bound in chains to be released in honor of Anselm after he had been elected archbishop of Canterbury. Concerning this, Osbern writes in a certain letter to the same Anselm; I quote a portion from an old copy because it has not hitherto been published:

“For what more conspicuous sign could God show for your election than that, when you were promoted, the king—renowned for victories [Col. 0321A] and feared by all for his severity—had taken to his bed and fallen sick even unto death; whereas, once you had been promoted, he immediately recovered his breath and health, and from being fierce was rendered at once most gentle and mild? What, I ask, could be more magnificent for divine praises or more joyful as a human spectacle than that, at your election, all the afflictions of the past storm being excluded, everything returned, as it were at the limit of a jubilee, to the possession of its own right: the bound to release, the imprisoned to light, the captives to liberty, and those oppressed by the most cruel fury of tax-collectors to relief? All these things speak of you, serve you, and are ascribed to your merits.”

Priscus, author of the *Life of Saint Eligius, Bishop of Noyon*, Book II, chapter 15, relates that Eligius came to the city of Bourges, where many persons were held in chains for killing a fiscal judge. As the holy man approached, the doors of the prison were broken by divine will, the bolts shattered, and all the bonds of the fettered prisoners loosed. Then [Col. 0321B] he advised the accused to flee to the basilica of Saint Sulpicius. [Col. 0321C] When they found every door barred against them, a door was suddenly opened. And when soldiers pursued the fugitives and, laying hands on them, chained them again with iron before the altar, the chains were broken by the prayers of Eligius and fell to the ground, while the soldiers were struck by great fear and begged forgiveness for what they had done.

Similar examples may be gathered from the histories of the saints. It is probable that devout and lenient rulers sometimes granted to the honor and sanctity of ancient bishops the privilege of releasing accused persons, though guilty of lighter offenses. But since all things tend to become corrupted over a very long period, it is to be feared that some later invented stories pleasing to an unlearned and excessively credulous populace, relying upon which they extended a personal favor more broadly and abused grace more freely, granting impunity to three-gallows rogues. Of this sort many today consider to be the privilege, or *pravilegium*, commonly called that of Saint Romanus of Rouen, concerning which a most serious controversy arose and was debated in the king’s council. For no trace of the popular tale concerning the dragon and the criminal is found in the *Life* of that holy bishop, written by an ancient and trustworthy author and most recently published by the most learned and polished jurist Rigault, whom love of truth and justice moved to do so.

“Handed over to the court.” Below, in Letter 66, he reproaches the archbishop of Tours for having clerics opposed to him handed over to the court through secret accusations. In these passages he seems to use *court* for a secular tribunal, so that clerics might undergo punishment there by the judgment of laymen. Thus he distinguishes the court from the Church in Letter 23, where he says that he will answer in the Church for ecclesiastical matters and in court for court matters. Likewise, in Letter 137 he says that the court must be avoided in the cases of clerics. So too Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, says in one letter that subjecting accused persons to torture is the discipline of the court, not of the Church. In the same sense canonists in the following [Col. 0321D] century distorted the term in chapter *Novimus*, *Extra*, “On the Meaning of Words,” which is commonly said to mean “handed over to the secular arm.”

But since, in Ivo’s age, the form of the commonwealth had long since changed in Gaul and the ancient orders of municipal councillors had ceased to exist, he could not say that clerics were handed over to the *curia* in the sense in which earlier Roman pontiffs used the phrase, at a time when the orders of *curiales* were still in use. Thus Pope Fabian, in chapter 28, Cause 11, question 1: “Removed from the clergy, let him be handed over to the *curia*, which he shall serve all the days of his life.” And Pope Stephen, in chapter 8, Cause 3, question 4: “Because a cleric has become infamous, he ought to withdraw from his rank and be handed over to the *curia* to serve.”

For formerly clerics unworthy of their office and separated from the ministry of the Church were customarily enrolled among the *curiales*, as the words of Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius indicate in law 39, “On Bishops, Churches, and Clerics,” in the Theodosian Code. Epiphanius likewise relates, *Tripartite History*, Book I, chapter 9, that persecutors assigned many Christians to the municipal councils, although [Col. 0322A] they had not been *curiales* by birth; this was eventually forbidden by Emperor Constantine the Great. Later Julian, from hatred of orthodox religion, withdrew the privileges of clerics and again handed them over to the *curia*, as the same Epiphanius relates, *Tripartite History*, Book VI, chapter 7. He likewise records that many bishops under Valens were handed over to the *curia*. For, in place of punishment, they were assigned to municipal councils, since it was forbidden by the enactment of Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius in law 108, “On Decurions,” Theodosian Code, where they declare that dignity ought not to accompany criminals, but punishment ought to do so.

Such *curiales*, however, were liable to many heavy public duties, by whose burden they were overwhelmed; hence many declined such burdens. As a result, it became necessary to protect decurions with certain privileges, lest the municipal councils be left empty, to the great harm of the cities, as is clear from various constitutions under the title “On Decurions” in the Theodosian and Justinianic Codes.

## ON LETTER LIV

[Col. 0322B] “By the surname ‘Worse than a wolf.’” Thus all our manuscripts. Cujas had added in the margin of his book, “a wolf worse than a wolf,” perhaps on the authority of some old codex. A similar surname occurs in the notes to the title of Letter 151.

“Strict oaths, up to seven.” Formerly printed *distinct*, but less correctly, as the better manuscripts prove, as do similar passages by the author: Letter 170, “unless they were proved by a prior strict examination”; Letter 225, “by strict oaths and through six approved persons”; and Letter 232, “he nevertheless advised that the matter be investigated by most diligent and strict examinations.” Constantius, *Life of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*, Book I, chapter 13: “when he examined him by a strict inquiry.” Pope Saint Gregory, in chapter *Habet*, Cause 2, question 5: “at the most sacred body of blessed Peter, we caused them to take strict oaths in abundance.” Ivo says in Letter 206 that oaths of purgation were demanded from defamed priests together with three, five, or seven colleagues.

[Col. 0322C] These were called *sacramentales* (“oath-assistants”), as in the ancient law of the Alemanni, titles 6, 7, 37, 90, and 91, and in the law of the Bavarians, titles 1 and 5. They are also called *coniuratores* (“co-swearers”) in the said Alemannic law, title 6, and *compurgatores* (“compurgators”) in chapter *Quoties* and canon *Accepimus*, title “On Canonical Purgation.” Thus, in one old copy of this Letter 54, the words “up to seven” were altogether absent, though they occur in the rest. For the same sort of expression appears in Ivo’s Letter 229: “you shall accept her purgation by the fifth hand of a woman, or by the seventh.” Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, Letter 69 to Honorius: “It was adjudged concerning the dean that, since he sought a delay of judgment on behalf of Nicholas for certain delaying reasons, he nevertheless ought to be purified for the Church, which held him suspect, and in the seventh hand of his order to declare his innocence by oath according to law.” Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, Letter 95 to Pope Adrian IV: “We adjudged to the abbot a purgation by the seventh hand: namely, of three abbots and three priest-monks of known reputation and standing, by whose oaths he might procure the necessary remedy for his injured reputation.”

In the law of the Alemanni, title 6, one reads, “to swear by the sixth hand”; and in the Ripuarian law, title 35, “to establish faith by the seventh hand.” In the law of the Frisians, title 14: “to purify oneself from the accusation of a crime by an oath with one’s own twelfth hand”; and shortly afterwards: “to excuse oneself by a conclusive oath with the twelfth hand.” There are also many examples of this form of speech in canon law. Thus in the title “On Canonical Purgation,” chapter 5, one reads “to be purified by the fourth and fifth hand.” Likewise, in chapter *Quoties*, Cause 2, question 5: “to clear himself by the third hand of his own order, and by the fourth [Col. 0322D] hand of abbots and religious priests.” Some copies so read; in others it is “and four abbots.” And in canon *Requisisti*, Cause 23, question 1: “to declare by oath with the seventh hand of kinsmen, touching the most holy relics”; likewise in chapter *Laudabilem* and chapter *Litterae*, “On Frigidity and Sorcery.” Elsewhere one reads that a cleric accused by evil report “can purify himself by his hand alone,” in Ivo, Letter 206.

There is an outstanding passage on this custom of swearing in the ancient law of the Alemanni, title 6, “On Jurors,” [Col. 0323A] where the procedure is prescribed:

“But oaths ought to be made in this manner: the oath-assistants shall place their hands upon the casket, and he alone for whom the case is brought shall speak the words, and shall place his hand over the hands of all, so that God, or those relics, and the hands which he holds joined together may so help him that he is not guilty in the matter concerning which he has been accused.”

That the hand was for the ancients a symbol of pledged faith is evident. Therefore, in the Council of Tribur, whose words are reported in chapter *Si quis*, Canon 2, question 5, where the oath of priests is discussed, it is said: “Can the hand through which the body and blood of Christ are made be defiled by an oath? Far be it!” Accordingly, in the Capitularies of Charlemagne, Book III, chapters 4 and 10, and Book V, chapter 125, a perjurer is ordered to lose his hand.

[Col. 0323B] Helmold, *History of the Slavs*, Book I, chapter 29: “Rudolf, wounded in the right hand, fled to Merseburg; and, being already near death, he said to his attendants: ‘You see my right hand wounded by this blow. With it I swore to Lord Henry that I would not harm him or plot against his glory. But the command of the Apostolic See and the entreaty of the pontiffs brought me to the point of violating my oath and usurping an honor not due to me. Therefore you see what end has overtaken us: in the hand by which I violated my oaths I have received this mortal wound.’” With these words must be joined what the ancient author writes, etc.

An ancient and anonymous author, speaking in the *Life of Emperor Henry IV* of Rudolf, usurper of the kingdom: “A great lesson was given to the world: let no one rise against his lord. For the severed right hand of Rudolf displayed a most fitting punishment for perjury, since he did not fear to violate the fealty sworn to his lord the king. And, as though other wounds were insufficient [Col. 0323C] to bring about death, the punishment of this member was added, so that guilt might be recognized through punishment.”

## ON LETTER LV

“Hugh.” Baronius, *Annals*, vol. XI, reproves this Hugh because he exercised authority too importunately against the bishop-elect of Beauvais, and for this purpose adduces Letter 30 to Fulk.

“Had judged more strictly.” One manuscript has *vindicasse*, “had punished,” and Letter 60 has: “that they should judge strictly in certain matters.”

## ON LETTER LVI

“Philip.” Baronius, *Annals*, vol. XI, assigns this letter to the eighth year of the pontificate of Urban II. After transcribing the letter, he adds that indiscreet ministers greatly harm the Church when they sometimes command harsh measures without counsel, measures which can scarcely be carried out.

## ON LETTER LX

“Hugh, archbishop of Lyons.” Baronius, *Annals*, vol.
