XI, under the year of Christ 1099, the twelfth of Urban’s pontificate, notes that this apostolic legate was at fault in pressing the matter too boldly, importunately, and imperiously. He adds that the imprudent minister had thrown the state of the Gallican Church into great dangers. Finally, he freely acknowledges that Pope Urban, stirred by the words of this legate, was violently angered against Ivo, because deeds wrongly done by ministers are commonly defended by the prudence of the flesh rather than of the spirit.

“But if he yielded to these exactions.” Thus corrected from an old codex. It had previously been printed incorrectly, *actions*. Moreover, the same Baronius, offended by the statement here that investiture in a bishopric received from the king of Gaul did nothing to harm religion, writes that the remaining words of this letter are plainly rather rough, since Ivo speaks too submissively—indeed, contemptuously—of forbidden investitures, and introduces many remarks which, unless corrected by other letters of the same author, would have brought his reputation [Col. 0324A] and glorious name into the greatest danger—the name he had most worthily acquired by defending apostolic truth.

“To have received investiture from the king’s hand.” There is a chapter of Sylvester, pontiff of the Roman Church, from his letter to Nicholas, bishop of the Church of Santa Rufina: “Let none of the clergy receive prebends or ecclesiastical offices in the holy Church except from the hand of a bishop, the hand of an abbot, or the royal hand. If they act otherwise, let them know that such a reception cannot stand.” But later pontiffs were unwilling that even kings themselves should be permitted this, as noted under Letter 233. To this purpose also belong the words of Pope Paschal in a letter to Anselm, speaking of the envoys of the king of England:

“We have heard them say that, if the king behaved properly in other matters, we would not forbid investitures of churches nor excommunicate those already made; and that we were unwilling to commit this to writing lest, under that pretext, other princes too should cry out against us. Therefore we call Jesus, who searches the reins and hearts, as witness upon our soul: since we began to bear the care of this holy [Col. 0324B] see, this monstrous crime has not even entered our mind.”

And shortly afterwards:

“But if by our silence we allowed the Church to be polluted with the gall of bitterness and the root of impiety, on what ground could we be excused before the inward Judge? It does not belong to laymen to hand over the Church, nor to sons to defile their mother by adultery. Rightly, therefore, should he who defiles his mother by adultery be deprived of his inheritance; nor does he deserve fellowship in ecclesiastical blessing who persecutes her with impious assault. It belongs to laymen to protect the Church, not to hand her over.”

And shortly afterwards: “The sacred canons forbid princes and secular men not merely to give investitures, but even to dare to insert themselves violently into the election of bishops.” Join to these the remarks under Letter 190.

“What the Churches obtain through the munificence of kings.” From this arose the complaints of many, who branded the clergy with the charge of ingratitude. Walthram, bishop of Naumburg, in his treatise *On the Investitures of Bishops*: [Col. 0324C] “The Roman pontiffs and other prelates built and adorned churches from property and estates acquired through devout laymen, men and women, and confirmed by secular authority. They ought not to inflict insult upon those from whom they received favor. And if they have sinned concerning investitures, let them be treated after the example of the first Gregory, as Paul says: ‘Reprove, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and doctrine’ [2 Tim. 4].”

Otto, bishop of Freising, in the preface to Book VII of his *Chronicle*: “There are, nevertheless, some who say that God willed the kingdom to be diminished in this way in order that the Church might be exalted. For no one doubts that the Church was exalted and enriched by the resources of the kingdom and the beneficence of kings. And it is clear that she could not previously have humbled so great a kingdom unless it had first been disembowelled and exhausted of its strength for love of the priests, and destroyed when struck not only by its own—that is, spiritual—sword, but by its proper material sword. To judge or investigate this is beyond our powers. Yet the priests seem blameworthy in every respect, since [Col. 0324D] they seek to strike the kingdom with its own sword, which they themselves possess through the favor of kings.”

The people of Liège, in their letter against Pope Paschal II: “Therefore, from the words of these men and of the holy Fathers, bishops beholden to kings and emperors through what they have received from their royal grants should take counsel for themselves, lest they kill them with their own sword—that is, with their benefits.” To the same effect are the words of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, who, after much discussion of the investitures of churches customarily made by kings, concludes that the Church ought to beware, in asserting her liberty, lest, by squeezing too hard, she draw blood and break the vessel itself while trying to remove rust from the vessel. The passage is quoted below under Letter 190.

“In the hands of the presiding authorities, so that they might judge strictly in certain matters.” The Puthean manuscript alone has *in manu possidentium*, “in the hands of possessors,” but with a corrupted sense. For immediately afterwards he calls them *presidentes* (“presiding authorities”), as in Letters 190, 191, and 233; by this name he understands the Roman pontiffs. [Col. 0325A] To the same purpose belongs what is said in Letter 236: that in the regions of Germany and Gaul many had surrendered the pastoral staffs and received investitures rejected through the apostolic hand. The supreme pontiffs would by no means have done this if they had recognized that such investiture contained heresy and a sin against the Holy Spirit.

For elucidating this passage, it will be useful to collect several examples from writers of that age. An ancient author, in the *Life of Saint Otto*, relates that in the year 1102, after the death of Rupert, when the insignia of the bishopric had been brought to the court of Emperor Henry IV, the bishopric of Bamberg was conferred on Otto. Although invested by the emperor, troubled by scruple he vowed to travel to Rome in order to be invested anew and consecrated by the pope. The author’s words deserve transcription:

“Having been compelled to ascend the episcopal throne by this arrangement and in this order, he consented only with difficulty and much hesitation, on account of the dispute then existing between the kingdom and the priesthood over investitures and the elections [Col. 0325B] of churches, which imperial authority strove beyond measure to nullify and claim for itself. Yet he feared in turn that it was not without divine direction that a bishopric was now offered to him for the third time, and that, if he rejected it for the third time, the sentence might apply to him: ‘He would not have blessing, and it shall be far from him’ [Ps. 108]. Placed amid these anxieties, he resolved to seek refuge in what he regarded as the one saving course: the help of the holy and apostolic see and Catholic mother. At that very moment, while still at the emperor’s court, he made a vow to the Lord that he would never remain in the bishopric unless, with the consent and petition of his own Church, he should deserve both to be consecrated and to receive investiture from the hand of the supreme pontiff himself.”

And shortly afterward:

“Mindful of his vow, a few days after entering the town, before they settled anything concerning other matters, he sent envoys with letters to Rome to the lord pontiff Paschal II. Summoned by letter from him, [Col. 0325C] he set out for Rome. When he arrived during the feast-days of Christ’s Ascension and did not find the pontiff there, he went into Campania and found him at Anagni. The honorable men who had come with him, after greetings had been given and received, greeted the pontiff also in the name of the Church of Bamberg and added their prayers and vows on behalf of their bishop-elect. Otto, without delay, explained the order and manner of his elevation to the bishopric, concealing nothing in silence. He laid the staff and ring at the pontiff’s feet, sought pardon for his rashness and error, adding nevertheless that it had been done not by his own will but through another’s power; and he asked that canonical discipline be exercised against himself. Pope Paschal, astonished at the man’s great prudence and constancy, ordered him to take up the insignia. But he refused and declared himself unworthy.”

Then:

“Immediately, bidding farewell to the pontiff and his court, he began to return home. But what could he do? He was called back by a command of obedience and urged on by his companions. [Col. 0325D] Thus he returned to the pontiff with fear and reverence; and on that most holy Pentecost, at the petition of the envoys of the Church of Bamberg, he received investiture from the Roman pontiff himself and, with great splendor and the exultation of the whole court, invoking the Holy Spirit, was consecrated bishop during the solemnities of Mass.”

These are the author’s words as they are expressed in Surius’s edition.

Matthew Paris says: “Anselm of Canterbury explained to the king in plain terms the decrees concerning investitures of churches which he had received at Rome in a general council: namely, that no prelate of churches—bishop, abbot, or cleric—should receive investiture in any ecclesiastical dignity from the hand of laymen. Accordingly, the same archbishop deposed certain abbots who had obtained abbeys from the hands of laymen and by payment of money. And because, at the king’s command, he refused to consecrate certain bishops who had received appointments from the king, or to communicate with them, the king became violently angry and ordered Gerard, [Col. 0326A] archbishop of York, to consecrate them. But William Giffard, bishop-elect of Winchester, who was to be consecrated, spurned Gerard’s consecration; for which reason he was expelled from the kingdom by the king’s judgment. Rainelm, bishop of Hereford, because he had received appointment from the king, surrendered his prelacy to him.” Yet in the narrative that follows, he does not conceal that pardon was granted to the deposed prelates, through the mediation of monetary offerings.

“In the year of the Lord 1103, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, after many tribulations and injuries which he had suffered from the king, went to Rome as had been agreed between himself and the king, taking with him the deposed abbots and William, bishop-elect of Winchester. On coming to Rome, William was reverently received by Pope Paschal. Then, on the day appointed for the king’s business, William de Warenne, a cleric and agent of the king of England, set forth the king’s case; and among other things he firmly maintained that [Col. 0326B] the king would not surrender the investitures of churches even at the loss of his kingdom, and he affirmed this in threatening language. To this the pope replied: ‘If your king, as you say, would not permit himself to lose the grants of churches even at the loss of his kingdom, know certainly that, before God, I say that not even for the redemption of my own head would I permit him to retain them with impunity.’ Thus the king’s business being concluded, Archbishop Anselm began to entreat the lord pope with many urgent prayers on behalf of the deposed bishops and abbots, that he would mercifully make provision for them so that they might recover their lost dignities. Then that most merciful see, which is accustomed to fail no one—provided that some white or red intervenes—restored the aforesaid bishops and abbots to their former dignities and sent them back to their sees with joy.” Thus writes the monk of St Albans.

William of Malmesbury likewise, speaking in the *Life of William II* of Herbert, who had been a great source of simony in England and had obtained an abbey and bishopric from the king by money, says: “Nevertheless, penitence in maturer years wiped out the misguided [Col. 0326C] impulse of youth. Having gone to Rome, he laid down there the simoniacal staff and ring, and deserved to receive them again by the indulgence of the most merciful see. For the Romans judge it more holy and orderly that the revenues of all churches should serve their own purses rather than be employed for the uses of any kings whatsoever.” From the letters of Anselm and Pope Paschal II it is also clear that many bishops, because of investitures and acts of homage rendered to the king of England, were released from the bonds of papal censure.

The same historian, *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*, Book II: “The king therefore came, splendid in the lofty trophy of victory and borne along in triumphal glory into England, and permanently resigned the investitures of churches into Anselm’s hand; Anselm in turn granting that none should be excluded from blessing on account of homage rendered to the king. Five bishops were therefore consecrated at Canterbury by Anselm.” Moreover, although Anselm himself had formerly been consecrated archbishop [Col. 0326D] of Canterbury and had rendered homage to the king of England, Pope Urban either forgave or overlooked the offense, as is clear from Anselm’s own letter to Walter, bishop of Albano and cardinal, in which he refutes the calumnies brought against him concerning that deed.

“I do not say these things as though I wished to raise my head against the Apostolic See.” Baronius notes here that the author supplied the following antidote because the preceding remarks on investitures might seem, if taken in the worse sense, to contain poison. But impartial judges of matters can scarcely censure the author’s position. For elsewhere too he declares that he adheres to the decree of the Roman pontiff, provided that investitures customarily made by laymen can be abolished without harm to the concord of the Christian commonwealth. Clearly that ancient maxim must always remain fixed: “Let the safety of the people be the supreme law.”

“You restored them to communion without my knowledge.” On this matter he likewise reproves Fulk, deacon of Paris, in Letter 112. For, by Canon 6 of the Council of Antioch, [Col. 0327A] one excommunicated by his own bishop ought not to be received by others before being restored by his own bishop; this is reported in chapter 2, *Si quis*, Cause 11, question 3. Indeed, one excommunicated by a single bishop was also to be excommunicated by neighboring bishops, as the author writes in Letters 165 and 194.

A similar complaint is made by Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, in a letter to Ralph, archbishop of Tours: “We have complained to you very often concerning Herveus of Malliaco; and, because of many injuries which he had unjustly and violently inflicted upon our monastery, we learned that you had justly and reasonably excommunicated him. But we heard that he was absolved without prior satisfaction and while still unrepentant. If he is believed to have been able to be absolved in this way, it is not apparent what sin harms or what repentance benefits. For if true misery is denied to the unrepentant, then surely false blessedness is promised to those who repent of their sins.”

The same author, in a letter to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans: “An excommunicated or interdicted person ought not to obtain the remedy [Col. 0327B] of absolution while the person who suffered his injury objects. Since this is so, we are greatly astonished on what ground H. is said to have been absolved, when our injuries against him still cry out and still complain.” Finally, he clears his monks of the suspicion of such conduct in a letter to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres: “You alleged that persons excommunicated by you were received by our brethren. We believe this was invented not by you but by another, who, like one accusing Susanna, offered false testimony. Far be such great injury to Christ and such detestable burial of ecclesiastical justice from the integrity of our brethren. For they do not know how to bury God’s justice; but wherever they recognize it as dead, they endeavor by their prayers to restore it to life.”

“At least these two matters.” Thus the Puthean old codex; others have *saltem* (“at least”). In the old Saint-Germain codex one reads only: “these two matters.” Let it be noted once for all that, wherever I found *saltim* in ancient manuscripts, I have retained it, and have not altered it elsewhere. There is no need to repeat what has formerly been noted about this word.

## ON LETTER LXI

[Col. 0327C]

“Hugh.” Baronius, *Annals*, vol. XII, calls this letter altogether excellent for restraining the arrogance of an apostolic legation.

“Augustidunum.” Some books have *Augustudunum*, but in five manuscripts it is clearly *Augustidunum*, a spelling also found in most manuscripts of other authors. Hericus the Benedictine, Book I of the *Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*, in his description of the city of the Aedui: “The city likewise received its advancement in merit and name. Finally it began to be called Augustidunum, a name which in the Celtic tongue conveys that of Augustus.” William the Breton, *Philippid*, Book I, notes that it was taken from the Romans by Arthur and later destroyed by Rollo the Norwegian, reduced utterly to nothing, so that scarcely any traces remain.

“The pledge to perform the matter which [was made] to the metropolitan.” See the remarks under Letter 237.

## ON LETTER LXII

[Col. 0327D]

“According to canonical rigor.” Thus most old codices; formerly, “according to the canons.” In the same manner he calls them “canonical judgments” in Letter 15, “canonical severity” in Letter 51, and “canonical judgment” in Letter 101, as also “canonical censure” in Letter 162 and “canonical accusation” and “canonical complaint” in Letter 268.

Of the law in which it is read: “If any of those charged with offences [are restored by] royal authority.” He repeats this same passage in the same words below, in Epistle 171, to Daimbert. He also adduces it in his Decree, part XVI, chapter 344, from book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 383; yet I do not think it is found today in the printed copies, an indication that Ivo used more extensive manuscripts. It is, however, found in the Twelfth Council of Toledo, chapter 3, held under King Erwig. It is worth setting down the words:

> “We have seen some men, and have lamented that, though belonging to the number of offenders received again into the favour of princes, they nevertheless remained excluded from the fellowship of priests. This practice produces a blameworthy evil: for princely licence, at the very point where it takes greatest care to free itself more freely [variant: *volvi*, ‘to turn itself’], binds others; and those whom it seems to receive into its own communion it chooses to separate from the communion and peace of the Church. Thus those who dine with the prince are deprived merely of communion with the priests. Therefore, since the remission of those who act against the king, the nation, or the fatherland is, by the definitions of the ancient canons, placed solely in royal power—the power against which they are known to have sinned—henceforth no communion of priests shall abstain from such persons. Rather, those whom royal authority has either received into the favour of its kindness or made participants at its table, assemblies of priests and people also ought to receive into ecclesiastical communion, so that what princely mercy has already accepted may not be regarded as alien by the priests of God.”

Here, by the term *culpatores* (“offenders”), excommunicated persons are rightly understood. It should be observed that the ancients thought that nothing harmed the security of one’s conscience if someone communicated with an excommunicate with whom the king communicated.

To the same effect one should note the words of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. When he stubbornly resisted Henry, King of the English, over the rights of investiture, and Pope Paschal forbade him to communicate with those who had received investitures of churches from the king’s hand, he nevertheless admitted that others could without penalty communicate with those with whom the king communicated. The passage is in his letter to Prior Ernulf.

## ON EPISTLE LXIV

The ordinance of the Archbishop of Lyons. He too is mentioned, though unnamed, in Epistle 30. He is perhaps Hugh, frequently mentioned in these letters, concerning whose legation, repeatedly exercised in Gaul under Gregory VII, Urban II, and Paschal II, remarks have been made on Epistle 24.

## ON EPISTLE LXV

“And other youthful desires.” The manuscript of Saint-Victor alone has *juvenialia*, perhaps for *juvenalia*; the latter spelling is frequent in manuscripts of ancient authors. [Col. 0328C]

“The subjection owed to the Church of Paris.” In that century monks left no stone unturned in order to be entirely free of the jurisdiction and censure of bishops; and the Roman pontiffs were inclined and ready to assist this purpose. This seemed neither acceptable nor lawful to Ivo, as this passage shows, and likewise Epistle 195, where he refutes the exceptions of the Abbot of Vendôme, who, under the pretext of obedience to Rome, refused to make the profession owed to the Bishop of Chartres.

Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, writing to Pope Innocent concerning the Archbishop of Trier, who wished to restore the monastery of Saint Maximin to the episcopal see despite the monks’ resistance, says that they sought not so much liberty, as they pretended, as the escape from discipline (Epistles 179 and 180). The same Bernard, in Epistle 42 to Henry, Archbishop of Sens, marvels that certain abbots, beneath a humble habit and tonsure, were so proud-minded that, while they would not permit their subjects to pass beyond even one little word of their commands, they themselves despised obedience to their own bishops, despoiled churches in order to emancipate themselves, and bought their own freedom in order not to obey. Shortly afterward he adds that the liberty of the Church which they continually claimed to seek was a liberty more slavish than every servitude, since it consigned them to the service of the worst pride.

There survives a notable and memorable history concerning the dispute of the monks of Saint Valery. They fabricated counterfeit privileges of a certain Roman pontiff, which they were not ashamed publicly to produce and boast of at a celebrated assembly at Rheims, in order to prove that they were subject to no one but the Roman pontiff. Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens, exposed their fraud when he rubbed away the ink of the recent writing with his garment. Yet the monks went to Rome and, by a lavish distribution of gifts, obtained from Paschal II what they wanted, as Nicholas, a monk of Soissons, relates in his *Life of the said Godfrey*, book II, chapters 11, 14, and 15. He nevertheless testifies that Paschal afterward reversed his judgment (chapter 21), from which time the abbey of Saint Valery obeyed the Bishop of Amiens, as he says in chapter 24. Compare the notes on Epistle 108.

“Concerning the peace of the holy Roman Church and your prosperity.” He says this because of the faction of the antipope, still powerful at Rome at that time, as has been noted above on Epistle 24.

## ON EPISTLE LXVI

“They say it while indulging in vanity.” Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, in Epistle 42 to Henry, Archbishop of Sens:

> “Whatever is added to your vanities is taken away from our necessities. In short, two evils proceed from one root of covetousness: while you perish by indulging in vanity, you destroy us by despoiling us.”

Thus, I think, the commonly printed *vanitando* ought to be corrected to *vanizando*.

Abbot of Bourgueil. Some copies read *Burgoilensis*, or: “that the Abbot of Bourgueil had come to court at Christmas.” Some books read *in Natali*, “at Christmas.” Here *curia* means the royal court, as in Epistle 28 and Epistle 158: “to the court which is to be held at Christmas at Soissons”; and Epistle 190: “to his court, which was to be assembled at Orléans at Christmas.” Elsewhere he mentions a court held at Easter, Epistle 62. Such were the solemn assemblies customarily summoned by the kings of the Franks.

Turpin, Archbishop of Rheims, in book *On the Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 20:

> “At four solemnities throughout the year, especially in Spain, he held his court wearing the royal crown and bearing the sceptre: namely, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, on Easter Day, on Pentecost, and on the day of Saint James.”

Many passages from historians concerning royal assemblies or courts of this kind among the ancient Gauls have been collected by Hotman, book I, *On the Ancient Law of the French Kingdom*, chapters 13 and 14. The practice was also used by other kings. An ancient author in the *Life of Emperor Henry IV* says that the king “proclaimed a court at Mainz for the Nativity of the Lord, invited the nobles, and summoned many.” Shortly afterward: “that you may arrange your father’s Easter court elsewhere.” And then: “Where our Easter court was to have been held.” Matthew Paris likewise mentions this in the *Life of William, King of the English*.

“More and fuller bags of coins.” Ralph Glaber, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 6, severely laments the simoniacal stain of that age, concerning ecclesiastical offices seized for shameful profit:

> “For a long time now this plague has raged far and wide among the prelates of all churches throughout the whole world, since almost all princes have been blinded by unsuitable gifts. At last they have turned the free and venerable gift of Christ the almighty Lord into a profit of avarice, adding to their own condemnation. Accordingly, such prelates are so much the less fit to perform the work of God, since it is clear that they did not enter upon it through the entrance of the chief door. And although the canon of the sacred Scriptures cries out in many ways against the insolence of such persons, it is nevertheless now found to occur more frequently than usual among the various orders of the Churches. For kings themselves, who ought to have been discerning appointors of persons fit for holy religion, corrupted by the lavish giving of gifts, judge that man more suitable for the governance of churches or souls from whom they hope to receive larger gifts. Hence those who are especially insolent and swollen with the arrogance of pride thrust themselves forward of their own accord into every office of preeminence. They fear less to incur ruin through neglect of pastoral care because their whole confidence depends only on the purses of amassed money, not on the gifts of acquired wisdom. Having obtained office, they apply themselves all the more to avarice, insofar as they have fulfilled their own ambition by it. And, setting it up for themselves as an idol in place of God, they serve that by which, having been fashioned for such a title, they rushed into it without merit or work. This becomes for the less cautious a deceitful model to imitate, and likewise in turn a stubborn envy.”

Shortly afterward he says:

> “From this also proceed the continual tumults of lawsuits; frequent scandals arise; and, by transgressions of various kinds, the order of ranks is overturned”—for thus it must be read.

The same historian, book V, final chapter, praises King Henry, who by a proposed edict forbade ecclesiastical office to be acquired at any price, threatening both giver and recipient, with loss of honour, with anathema. He then reports that Henry said to the Gallican bishops corrupted by the wickedness of simoniacal love of money:

> “As the Lord freely gave me the crown of empire solely by His mercy, so I too shall freely bestow what pertains to His worship. I wish, if it pleases you, that you likewise do the same.”

“Bear with it meanwhile, until I make my profit from this.” So all the copies read, lest anyone suspect an error. Writers of that age used the same word. Thus Gregory VII, book VI, Epistle 2, to Manasses:

> “He ought not to take it badly if, for a time, we endeavour for the sake of the common honour and advantage to refuse requests that are contrary to utility.”

Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his letter to the monks of Bec:

> “Do not lose the king’s favour, which is necessary for you, without any profit—indeed, with the greatest loss.”

From this may be perceived King Philip’s insatiable hunger for gold. He was accustomed to sell churches; nor did he allow free elections, or permit men elected by the votes of clergy and people to obtain a bishopric or abbey unless they supplied money. Lisiard, Bishop of Soissons, in the *Life of Saint Arnulf*, chapter 9:

> “Urged by the spirit of ambition, a certain Pons, a pseudo-monk, in the comparative degree—not according to grammar, but according to simony—obtains from Philip, King of the Franks, the name and seat of abbot.”

Thus Matthew Paris rightly said of this Philip in his account of William II that he was blinded by the darkness of money. Gregory likewise severely censures this sordid avarice in various places. See the *Register*, book I, Epistle 35, to Roderic, Bishop of Chalon; book II, Epistle 5, to Manasses of Rheims, Richer of Sens, Richard, Archbishop of Bourges, Adrald, Bishop of Chartres, and the other bishops of France.

In the same book, Epistle 32, to Manasses, Archbishop of Rheims, he says among other things:

> “Now therefore, as you ought, receive carefully and diligently the unheard-of evil, the detestable crime, which Philip, King of France—indeed, a ravening wolf, an unjust tyrant, an enemy of God and of the religion of the holy Church—has committed against God and the honour of his kingdom toward merchants of Italy and other provinces, and other things concerning which cries have very frequently reached our ears,”

and so forth.

Finally, in book VIII, Epistle 20, writing to Philip himself, he exhorts him to be a lover of justice, to defend the Churches, to reject the counsels of wicked men, and not to impede the canonical election which the clergy and people of the Church of Rheims were then to make after the deposition of Archbishop Manasses. He concludes:

> “Act, then; and now that age has made you a man, take care in this matter that we may not seem to have spared you in vain for the faults of your youth, nor to have waited for your amendment to no purpose.”

## ON EPISTLE LXVII

“Certain adverse words there sounded otherwise than he would have wished.” The old books also read: “certain words seemed harsher to him than …,” omitting the word *adversa* (“adverse”). Here the expression *secus* seems to have degenerated, and the other word, *durius* (“more harshly”), to have entered from a marginal note; perhaps the author wrote *secius quam vellet*, “more unfavourably than he wished.” For it has been noted in its proper place, with examples, that this word was more than once corrupted in other authors.

To this should be referred what Geoffrey writes to Ivo concerning the case of Daimbert, the same elected Archbishop of Sens, addressed to Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons (book II, Epistle 18). From this it may be inferred that Daimbert did not return Ivo’s favour in equal measure, and that Pope Urban was offended because Ivo had spoken freely. [Col. 0331A]

“Do not lend him an ear.” Perhaps Ivo feared that Urban, bribed by an offering of gifts together with his courtiers, would turn aside from what was right. For most men who were forced upon churches in Gaul through influence or money used to go to Rome to win favour by the same arts, as the words of Ivo himself indicate in Epistle 87, written to the cardinals. That Urban was not at all free of the reproach of avarice, indeed that he was venal, may be confirmed by the words of William of Malmesbury, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, book I, where he treats of the envoy of the King of the English sent to Rome against Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury:

> “He burned to accomplish something by which he might secure a greater place in the king’s favour. Therefore, carrying through the affair by the art in which he was skilled, courting each man individually with gifts and promises, he obtained for the king a postponement until the feast of Saint Michael. Urban hesitated greatly before granting this, because Anselm’s religious character and the offer of gifts struggled within his mind; but money finally prevailed. Does money thus conquer all things, crush all things? It was an unworthy act that concern for reputation should become cheap to the heart of so great a man—I mean Urban—that regard for God should yield, and money should overturn justice. Anselm therefore thought it useless to waste expectation on so venal a man and resolved to return to Lyons. Yet he could not obtain permission, because the pope detained him in order to lessen the odium of the act by some consolation. He therefore made him remain with him until the council in the Patriarchate, and gave him a house there by a perpetual right of hospitality.”

“And concerning the dishonourable intimacy of the Archbishop of Tours.” Ivo is accustomed to reproach and defame this man, as in Epistle 66, though he does not state his name. One may suspect him to have been Ralph, whom Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, also mentions and of whom he complains that many shameful and perverse acts were done, in a letter written to Richard (book I, Epistle 17). There the words “the aforesaid Archbishop of Tours” suit well Ivo’s words, for in Epistle 66 he says that this man had crept into the Church against canonical and apostolic ordinances and was tolerated in it.

“That you may know that the election was childish.” Shortly before this he calls him a boy, and in Epistle 66, a young man. Of the same sort is what he censures in Epistle 157: the Bishop of Durham had caused his two sons, scarcely twelve years old, to be forced into the bishopric of Luxeuil. Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, Epistle 42 to Henry, Archbishop of Sens:

> “Schoolboys and boys not yet of age are promoted to ecclesiastical dignities on account of nobility of blood, and are transferred from beneath the rod to rule over boys.”

The same Bernard, in Epistle 290 to the Lord of Ostia, speaking of Cardinal Jordan, who had left foul and horrible traces among the Gauls:

> “He is reported everywhere to have committed shameful deeds, carried away the spoils of churches, and promoted handsome little boys, where he could, to ecclesiastical honours; where he could not, to have wished to do so.”

Ralph Glaber, *History*, book IV, chapter 5, laments similar abuses:

> “At that time persons holding every office of government, both in secular power and in ecclesiastical religion, were of childish age. For because of the sins of the people, that saying of Solomon came to pass: ‘Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child’ (Ecclesiastes 10). For the universal Roman pope himself, nephew of the two men, Benedict and John, who had preceded him, was almost a boy of ten when, through money from treasuries being interposed, he was elected by the Romans. Thereafter they often expelled and disgracefully restored him; he exercised no authority. And, as we have already censured the other prelates of the Churches of that time, gold or silver rather than merit raised them up. Shame!”

He repeats the same at the end of book V, chapter 5.

## ON EPISTLE LXIX

“He forbade all secular clerics.” Berthold, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1095, says that a general council was assembled in the Gallican city of Autun by Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, in which monks were forbidden to usurp in parishes the offices of parochial priests. In the ancient manuscript of President Auguste de Thou, however, I find the following written:

> “In churches where monks dwell, the people are not to be governed by a monk; rather, a chaplain to govern the people is to be appointed by the bishop, so that both his ordination and his administration, and the whole conduct of his life, may depend upon the bishop’s sole discretion.”

This is from the synod of Septimania held at Clermont.

## ON EPISTLE LXX

“Of possessed women.” These two words have been added on the authority of the old manuscripts; they were lacking in the first edition.

“May you endeavour to entrust that place with its possessions to religious monks.” In Ivo’s age there were many examples of this kind in Gaul. For similar moral depravity, in the year of the Lord 1107 Philip I, King of the Franks, expelled the nuns from the monastery of Saint Eligius at Paris and introduced monks from Saint-Maur-des-Fossés. Letters were issued in these terms:

> “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Philip, by the grace of God King of the Franks. We wish it to be known to all worshippers of God’s holy Church, both future and present, that by the clemency of divine providence and the assent of Lord Pope Paschal, as also by the admonition and counsel of the canons of the holy Church of Paris, and likewise by our consent and that of Louis our son, Gualo, Bishop of Paris, drove out from the church of blessed Eligius—a member of his bishopric—the nuns who, because of the unrestrained fornication which they practised imprudently, openly violated the temple of the Lord by wicked custom, though they had been canonically rebuked very often, and wholly neglected the correction of their pastor. Having therefore received the letters of the lord pope, who was then coming to Paris, and having been granted permission to establish an order of religious life there, by our permission and ordinance, at the entreaty of our son Louis, we granted and assigned the aforesaid church of Saint Eligius to blessed Peter of Fossés and to Theobald, abbot of the same place, as a cell of twelve monks with its prior, to possess and hold in perpetuity—while preserving the right of his authority and of the Church of Paris, as is determined in the charter itself. And in order that this charter may remain firm and inviolate, we command that this record be made, signed and confirmed by the character of our name and the sign of Philip, in the presence of those of our palace whose names and signs are appended.”

The sign of Hugh of Crécy, then our seneschal.

The sign of Waston of Pissy, then our constable.

The sign of Pagan of Orléans, then our butler.

[Col. 0332D] The sign of Guy, then our chamberlain.

> “Done at Paris, in the chapter-house of Saint Mary, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, the forty-seventh year of our reign. Stephen the chancellor subscribed after reading it aloud.”

William of Nangis likewise writes in his *Chronology*, about the year of the Lord 1129, concerning the nuns of Argenteuil:

> “Certain infamous nuns, who had long occupied the church of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil through the power of a sister of Charles the Great, King of the Franks, were expelled from it through the agency of Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis in France, and it was restored to the monks of the same place, to whom it had formerly belonged.”

Suger treats the matter more fully in his *Life of King Louis*, where he reports that it was restored by the judgment of Pope Honorius.

The continuator of Sigebert, Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel, records the same occurrence in the same year concerning the nuns of Saint John at Laon:

> “At Laon, in the church of Saint John, by counsel of the king and princes, the nuns, who were notoriously disreputable, having been expelled and monks appointed in their place, Drogo, venerable for religious devotion and eloquence, was ordained by Bishop Bartholomew as the first abbot.”

A fuller account of this matter occurs in an ancient manuscript, a copy of which Marcus Scarbot, advocate, kindly provided. His narrative shows that at that time there were some men of absurd judgment who reproached Bartholomew for expelling the utterly unchaste nuns. It will not be useless to set down the passage:

> “After these things, the aforesaid Bishop Bartholomew also endeavoured to reform the monasteries, including that of Saint John the Baptist. This abbey is said to have been older, more eminent, and more noble than all the other above-mentioned monasteries of the diocese of Laon. For, as is read in her *Life*, blessed Salaberga built it, placed nuns there, and herself was their first abbess.”
>
> And shortly afterward:
>
> “That abbey possessed such dignity that whenever the King of the Franks was to be crowned at Laon on solemn days, he especially wore the golden crown there. No four-footed animal could enter within the wall or gate of the abbey without immediately being turned to rabies and madness. Thus, whenever the king, bishop, or other princes came to the abbey, all their horses had to be left outside the gate, while they themselves proceeded on foot to the church. Upon blessed Salaberga’s death, her daughter, namely Saint Anstrudis, succeeded as abbess; and so, for nearly three hundred years and more, nuns were there and long possessed many properties from the gifts of kings and princes.
>
> “But in the days of the aforesaid lord Bishop Bartholomew, the ancient religious observance in that monastery had greatly cooled; its external possessions too had gradually diminished; and unfavourable reports were made about some of the virgins there. The same pontiff was greatly saddened, for he saw that, frequently admonished by him, they promised amendment in word but did not fulfil it in deed. By the counsel and authority of Lord Pope Innocent, Lord Renaud, Archbishop of Rheims, and Louis, King of the Franks—to whom that church was said properly to belong—he expelled all those nuns from it.
>
> “He also took the religious man Lord Drogo, prior of the monastery of Saint Nicaise at Rheims, ordained him there as its first abbot, and established there a sufficient number of monks drawn from various monasteries.”
>
> And some time afterward he adds:
>
> “But because I have heard certain insufficiently informed persons finding fault with these things and saying that so great a change ought not to have been made, nor even innocent persons expelled because of the sins of certain nuns, nor the entire church handed over to monks—especially since the aforesaid noble matron Saint Salaberga, together with her daughter Saint Anstrudis, built it from the possessions of her own patrimony, placed nuns in it, and adorned it through manifestations of many signs—it pleases me, in order to restrain and correct their folly or simplicity, to recall a few examples from Holy Scripture concerning a similar or even greater change.
>
> “Is God’s planting not greater than a human planting? Yet of the Jews it is said through David, king and prophet: ‘You transplanted a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You were a guide on its way before it; you planted its roots, and it filled the land’ (Psalm 79), along with the rest added concerning its establishment. Although the Law had been given them through Moses, they received the land of promise, produced kings and prophets who performed many miracles, and the Lord promised them a perpetual dwelling in that land, nevertheless, because they cast the son of the householder out of the vineyard and killed him, saying, ‘This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours,’ they at once received the judgment which they themselves had proposed against themselves: that, when he came, he would miserably destroy the wicked men and lease his vineyard to other husbandmen. Immediately thereafter they heard him add: ‘The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits’ (Matthew 21).
>
> “Elsewhere also the Lord sets forth the parable of the fig tree. Coming to it for three successive years and finding no fruit, he ordered it cut down. But when the cultivator of the vineyard intervened, he granted a delay even for a fourth year (Luke 13). In the same way, Lord Bishop Bartholomew admonished those nuns concerning correction, both personally and through religious men, in the first and second years, in the third and fourth, and likewise in the fifth and sixth. Seeing that he made no progress, he undoubtedly ought, according to the Lord’s command, to cut down the unfruitful tree and entrust the Lord’s vineyard to other husbandmen who would render its fruit in its proper seasons. Since he did this not by his judgment alone but by the counsel of the pope and religious men, he was surely worthy not of blame but of praise.
>
> “Nor need it be feared that by this he incurred the anger of the holy women Salaberga and Anstrudis, who built the same church and assigned it to the order of nuns. On the contrary, it should rather be believed that through their prayers such a purpose came to him by divine prompting, and that such abbots are to be appointed by God as strive continually both for His service and for the restoration of that church. Indeed, in no monastery of the kingdom of the Franks, founded exclusively according to that institution, do we see greater religious devotion or charitable hospitality flourishing today than in this one—except that Abbot Baldwin himself, being greatly occupied in seeking out and recovering the Church’s possessions which the nuns had negligently allowed to be alienated, and wearied by daily labour, complains of nothing more than that he cannot continually be present with the community of brothers or perform for the guests themselves, as he would wish, the office of hospitality.
>
> “Therefore, when those holy women themselves, whose bodies are kept in that church, see there continually, day and night, the divine office performed so devoutly, silence and religious observance zealously kept, the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood celebrated not as before but a hundredfold more devoutly and frequently, and religious guests arriving each day received with the sweetness of charity, should it not be believed that they delight in so sweet a service of God? And, when they see the monks passing before the altar and humbly inclining their heads in supplication before their shrines, do they not often say to them: ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’ (Psalm 128), and: ‘Blessed are you by the Lord, who made heaven and earth’ (Psalm 113)?
>
> “What others think, I do not know. I believe—and, believing, confidently declare—that these holy women take greater delight in the divine offices of such monks than of the nuns who remained there in the time of Lord Bartholomew, and pray for the mercy of the Lord as much for those monks’ salvation as for that bishop’s. And just as King David, composing the psalms, said: ‘Let these things be written for another generation, and the people who shall be created shall praise the Lord’ (Psalm 101), thereby plainly showing that he composed them not for the Jews but for Christians, so I believe that those holy women rejoice that the church which they built has come into the hands of monks such as these and that the Lord has permitted their possessions to come to support them.
>
> “Now, although it was said above that nine abbeys were founded by Lord Bishop Bartholomew, and that he found none of them, whoever carefully considers the matter will declare this truly to be a tenth: it had been built more than three hundred years before his time, but had grown lukewarm in religious fervour in his time, and through himself—by divine grace—was known to have been rebuilt and renewed by the introduction of monks. [Col. 0335A] This renewal took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1127.”

Thus far the ancient manuscript.

Moreover, Nicholas of Cusa, *On Catholic Concord*, book III, chapter 8:

> “Care ought to be taken concerning nuns and their custody. For that holy Boniface writes to Ethelbald, King of the English, that among Greeks and Romans one who were guilty in this respect—of having lain with a nun—would have brought upon himself something like blasphemy against God.”

This passage, incidentally, is taken from Ivo’s *Decree*, part VII, chapter 129, where he gives the words of Boniface the martyr to Hyleribald, or Hiltribald, King of the English:

> “Among Greeks and Romans, he would have brought upon himself something like blasphemy against God if, when questioned before ordination concerning this sin in particular, he were found guilty of having lain with a veiled and consecrated nun; he would be excluded from every rank of the priests of God.”

## ON EPISTLE LXXI

[Col. 0335B] “Their natural and lawful lords, from whose hands he had received his hereditary benefices.” This passage is worthy of notice and bears upon a feudal question, as does another, Epistle 248, where he advises a knight always to render honour to his superior lord by right of the fidelity he has promised, even though a grave dispute has arisen between them. For the bond of faith and honour cannot be dissolved. Anselm speaks finely to the same effect in his letter to the Bishop of Winchester (book III, Epistle 98; *Patrologia*, vol. 159).

“May he compel one of these to moderate himself.” All the old manuscripts here indeed read *unum temperare*. But in Ivo’s *Decree*, part XII, chapter 15, where the same passage is cited, it is noted that other manuscripts vary, reading *unum temerare* or *unum tentare*. Perhaps *unum temnere*, “to despise one,” should be read, for contempt follows there:

> “But when we fulfil harmful promises, proudly despise God’s commands, injure our neighbours with impious cruelty, and slay ourselves with the crueller sword of death.”

In all Ivo’s manuscripts, however, this passage is cited from the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 4. But in the margin of the printed *Decree* it is noted otherwise, namely as from the Eighth Council, chapter 2.

Tharasius, Patriarch. Ivo there cites from the fourth session of the Seventh Synod.

Ariobald. In the aforesaid Ivo, part XII, chapter 25, it is printed differently, namely *Ariopaltus*. But it is preferable to transcribe the entire passage, since it is very uncommon and throws more light upon the matter:

> “Pope Honorius to Hysiacus, patrician and exarch of Italy. From the writings of certain persons we have learned that certain bishops in the regions beyond the Po declared to Peter, son of Paul, certain words hostile to episcopal office, and by the prompting of impious persuasion suggested that he would incur the guilt of perjury unless he consented, not to King Adulubald, but rather to the tyrant Ariopalt. And since the aforesaid glorious Peter refused to be bent by the wicked persuasions of those priests—if it is permissible to call them so—but rather firmly kept the oaths which he had made to King Aco, father of the aforesaid Adulubald; and since so great a crime is hateful to God and to pious minds, namely, that those who ought to have forbidden others from committing it themselves exhorted its commission: now that, by the nod of heavenly power and through your labours, the aforesaid Adulubald has been restored to his kingdom, deign, with God’s help, to send the aforesaid bishops to these Roman regions. For we shall permit no such crime to go unpunished for any reason.”

These words, preserved in Ivo alone, Charles Sigonius inserted also in book II of his *History of the Kingdom of Italy*, but he does not state in what place or book Ivo reported them. There too he varies the names. Yet I did not wish to depart from the spelling which I found in the ancient copies.

It is preferable to add Sigonius’s own words, so that the history may be clearer. Thus, under the year of the Lord 623:

> “Eusebius came as ambassador from Heraclius to King Adavald concerning important affairs. While he dealt familiarly with the king, whether following the emperor’s command or his own counsel, he gave Adavald, as he came out of the bath, a cup apparently health-giving; after drinking it, the king began to lose his senses and became wholly bereft of mind. Others wrote that he had been anointed with ointments. When Eusebius perceived this, he urged the king, young and deranged as he was, to remove the Lombard princes for the sake of his own safety.
>
> “After the slaughter had begun and twelve of the leading men had already been killed, the Lombards, fearing that the evil might spread further and, like the contagion of a slow wasting disease, gradually reach each individual, accused him of acting as a tyrant rather than a king. In the following year, after a tumult had been raised, they drove him from the kingdom together with his mother, Queen Theodelinda, and appointed in his place Arioald, Duke of Turin, to whom Gundeberga, sister of King Adavald, was joined in marriage.
>
> “By this act a great civil conflict suddenly arose in the kingdom, all the leading men, sacred and secular alike, being divided into two parties and attached to one side or the other. The bishops beyond the Po embraced Arioald and strove to draw others also to their party. Pope Honorius, however, and, at his urging, Exarch Isaac—whether moved by affection for Theodelinda or hostile to Arioald as infected by the Arian taint—undertook the defence of Adavald. Isaac attempted to restore him to the kingdom with an army.
>
> “When Honorius heard that the bishops beyond the Po were vigorously persuading the nobles to desert Adavald contrary to their oath and to join Arioald, he wrote in the following year to Isaac that, after Adavald’s restoration, he should send the bishops of the opposing party to Rome to answer their case. These letters are still preserved in Ivo.”

Thus far Sigonius.

## ON EPISTLE LXXIII
To Bernard, abbot of Marmoutier. An old writer, in a little book *On the Tribulations Unjustly Inflicted upon Marmoutier by the Archbishop and Clerics of Saint Maurice of Tours* [Col. 0336C], mentions this Bernard:

> “At Brioude,” he says, “when a certain council was sitting, our brethren having been sent there—Lord Bernard the prior, Hilgod, bishop of Soissons, his brother Andrew, and James the physician—our cause was debated according to the foregoing proceedings.”

This passage appears more fully in the notes on Epistle 108, where shortly afterwards he is called abbot. The same is expressly confirmed by another ancient writer in a manuscript tract, which treats of the restoration of Marmoutier after the devastations of Astignus and Rollo:

> “After ninety years had subsequently elapsed, namely in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1095, the thirty-seventh year of Philip, king of the French, and the thirteenth year from the appointment of Bernard as abbot of this monastery, the glorious Pope Urban II came from the city of Rome and visited Gaul solely out of charity. At the Council of Clermont, in the presence of nearly five hundred fathers—that is, archbishops, bishops, and abbots—all of whom, together with Ralph [variant: Rodolph; Col. 0336D, as in the notes on Epistle 108], archbishop of Tours, acclaimed and authorized the drawing up of privileges of liberty and immunity. The pope himself had sent these to us and our monastery from Rome through the hands of our venerable brethren Lord Bernard of Rheims, surnamed Pontius, then our prior, and Lord Rainer, who afterwards became a priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and subsequently archbishop of Reggio, and who sat at the aforesaid council as an archbishop-cardinal. This had been done in the eighth year of his pontificate, in the octave of the winter feast of Saint Martin, finally to establish peace and concord between ourselves and the canons of Blessed Maurice of Tours, who had then for ten years not ceased persecuting us.”

And, after much intervening matter, the same book states in its catalogue of abbots, no. 153:

> “Bernard, the sixth abbot, rests here in the right-hand portico of the church, in its lower part. He laboured greatly for the liberty of this Church, and, by apostolic authority, with the help of God and blessed Martin, freed it from every subjection to the archbishop.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “He governed this Church until the year 1136, namely for thirteen years, and died on the eighth day before the Ides of May [8 May].”

“You received a blessing from one who was said to be excommunicated.” He seems to mean Rodolph, archbishop of Tours, who had been excommunicated by Amatus, the pope’s legate; on this matter see below, in the notes on Epistle 108.

“And you promised the due subjection to the metropolitan see before the blessing.” He means the archbishop of Tours; the words of Epistles 134 and 135 also concern him. Pope Gregory, however, had forbidden bishops to exact any profession from the abbots of Marmoutier. He had permitted only that ordinations and consecrations be received from the archbishop of Tours, provided that he was Catholic, as is indicated by the words of the ancient author quoted below in the notes on Epistle 108. Here, however, it should be observed that Ivo considered futile and empty the opinions of those who maintained that abbots to be consecrated [Col. 0337B] ought not to swear any obedience to bishops. On this question he disputed with the abbot of Vendôme, as is discussed at length in the observations on Epistle 195.

“By their inquisitions and empty whisperings.” Owing to the omission of a letter, the printer in the first edition had given *susurris* (“whisperings”). But all the old manuscripts have *susurriis*, a word used by contemporary writers. Peter of Blois, Epistle 56, to Richard, archbishop of Canterbury:

> “And the almost universal common endeavour is to loosen insolent tongues against you into detestable whispering.”

The same writer, Epistle 40, to a prelate who slandered the king: “You unlawfully loosen your uncircumcised lips into whispering and detraction.” St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, *Sermons on the Song of Songs*, Sermon 24: “You may see them walking apart, and presently loosening their insolent tongues into detestable whispering.” The same, Epistle 78, to Suger: “They will mutter fraternal whispering only against your person, not against the abbey.” Thus the old editions read; in more recent editions they changed it to *susurrum*. They falsely thought the word corrupt. Finally, in Ivo himself, *Decretum* X, part XI, chapter 26, some books read:

> “Let sorcerers be condemned to death, who kill men by hateful arts, poisons, or magical whisperings.”

## ON EPISTLE LXXIV

“Upon the allegation of your rivals concerning the recent betrayal of the city of Le Mans.” Hildebert himself, in a certain letter in which he complains of the tyranny of the consuls of Le Mans and of the burning and plundering of the city, reports that he was summoned to undergo judgment in England because he had refused, at the king’s command, to pull down the towers of the Church:

> “It would take long,” he says, “to relate with what relentless tyranny the king of England has raged against us. Casting aside a king’s moderation, he determined that he would not obey the bishop before he had compelled the bishop into sacrilege. Since we refuse to pull down the towers of our church, we have been compelled to submit to transmarine judgments and to endure the injuries of the sea: namely, the singular hardship of the journey and the unique dissolution of the whole human frame. Therefore, tossed here by such storms, we have determined to set out for the thresholds of the Apostles, judging it a great remedy for this new tribulation if the Roman pontiff assists us both with counsel and with aid.”

But, in order that the whole affair may be explained more clearly, it is necessary to append the narrative of the event from an old sheet communicated by a learned man; for it serves to elucidate this letter. Speaking, then, of Bishop Hildebert, it says:

> “A most serious war arose between Henry I, king of the English, and Elias, count of Le Mans, because the king was challenging the bishopric and was therefore attempting to prevent the bishop’s appointment. When he heard that the appointment had been made, he made this clear by open military incursions; and Count Elias began to resist his undertakings. When this became known, Fulk, count of Anjou, came to the city and, with the consent of the citizens, placed guards in the city’s fortifications; leaving his son there, he hastened elsewhere. Meanwhile the king of the English, seeing that the city was deprived of the protection of its lord, came there. He approached the suburbs, encamped against the city with a great army, and afterwards burned the suburb. But the king, seeing that he had been deceived, withdrew with his army. When they had prepared themselves for battle, they learned of the king’s flight and returned to the city.
>
> “On hearing this, Count Elias, fearing that Fulk, count of Anjou, might seek his proscription, summoned Bishop Hildebert and certain leading men of the city to himself, and began with them to devise ways by which they might surrender the city to the king and free him from his bonds. For Count Elias himself was in the bonds of the king of the English. He feared that Count Fulk, deceived by royal gifts, would make peace with the king and, once the city had been handed over, would condemn him to perpetual exile. The bishop, taking pity on his distress, discussed with him his release. The king himself, however, shortly afterwards allowed him to depart free and unharmed.
>
> “After taking the city and placing garrisons in its fortifications, the king crossed the sea into England. But certain clerics, envying the bishop’s advancement and plotting deceitfully against him, accused him before the king of England, saying that he had been privy to the betrayal when Count Elias occupied the city with everyone’s consent. Therefore, holding Hildebert under suspicion, the king urgently required him to order the destruction of the towers of the church—which, he said, had caused him damage—before he crossed into England. In order that he might destroy the towers, he offered the bishop a very great weight of gold and silver for building the shrine of Saint Julian, as he said. Seeing that this was being done to his disgrace, the bishop, having taken counsel, returned to his Church. First, he openly brought forward two precious cymbals, an excellent cloak of cloth, and two silver basins, together with many other ornaments.
>
> “Meanwhile, exceedingly anxious at the king’s command, most sorrowful over the burning of the city, the destruction of his houses, the expulsion of citizens, and the dispersal of clerics, he continually prayed to the mercy of almighty God that He might deign to turn away the wrath of His indignation from the Church and its people. But the Lord, pitying that affliction, mitigated His anger beyond what could have been hoped, and filled the faces of Hildebert’s enemies with confusion and disgrace, so that their song was turned into mourning, and their organ into the voice of weeping. For one day, when the king had gone into a forest to hunt, he was struck by an arrow from one of his own knights who were with him and died.
>
> [Note: Col. 0337D. He speaks of William, king of the English, who died on the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August], 1100.]
>
> “Once the city was pacified and its enemies put to flight, Hildebert set out for Rome. Pope Paschal II received him with great attention; then, as Hildebert proceeded into Apulia and Sicily, all showed him honour and reverence as though he were an angel of God. Roger, duke of Sicily, having heard of the bishop’s reputation and learning, received him with the highest honour and reverence. The same Roger gave him one hundred ounces of gold for work on Saint Julian’s church, and ten pounds of money for the sustenance of the canons [Col. 0338D]. Afterwards the same bishop returned to the province of Le Mans.”

“And although you are ready to undergo the lawful purgation, he does not wish it otherwise.” On this, see Epistles 54 and 229.

“So that you do not depart from your order.” He frequently gives this counsel to ecclesiastical men, as to Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, Epistle 241, and to John, bishop of Orléans, Epistle 247. He himself also says that he does not wish to provide others an example of departing from their order, Epistle 35.

“Advising that you should not transgress.” He likewise censures this voluntary ordeal by red-hot iron in the case of a wife whose chastity was under suspicion, in Epistles 205, 252, and 280. Yet he appears to have approved it if it were undertaken not rashly, but after a lawful accusation and judicial sentence, in the said Epistles 205 and 252—namely, because of human unbelief, if all other testimony were wholly lacking, Epistle 252. He therefore calls it “divine testimony,” Epistle 232. Thus Arnulf, accused at the Council of Rheims, chapter 30, says:

> “I shall hand over my serf to the bishops, who, walking over glowing ploughshares, will by manifest signs declare that God judges concerning you.”

The number of tests was often fixed. For nine glowing ploughshares are mentioned in the ancient law of the English and of the Warni or Thuringians, title 15, *On Sorceries*, and in the Capitularies of Emperor Charles, in Ansegisus’s *Frankish Law*, book IV, title 3. Moreover, Franciscus Hotomanus, in his *Disputations on Fiefs*, chapter 41, collected many examples from authors who mention this ordeal or proof by red-hot iron; the diligent reader may consult them there. A formula for consecrating the iron, much fuller than those of other authors, was most recently published by François Pithou, most learned in ancient learning, in his *Glossary to the Capitularies of Charlemagne*, second edition, from the manuscript *Order* of Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury.

“Namely, of boiling or cold water.” This ordeal is mentioned in the laws of the Visigoths, book VI, title 1, chapter 3, on how a judge should investigate a case by the ordeal of a boiling cauldron; and in the laws of the Frisians, title 3, *On Thiubda*, §§6 and 8, and again title 14, *On a Man Killed in a Crowd*, §3. In these places it is called the judgment of God, as likewise in the Frankish laws, book IV, chapter *On the Honour of the Church*, a passage cited by Ivo in the sixteenth part of his *Decretum*, chapter 238, from book IV, chapter 13 of the Capitularies. In the same fourth book of the Frankish laws, among the secular chapters of the same Charles, another chapter, 33, records that a slave is declared fit for the boiling-water ordeal. Adalger, at the Council of Rheims, chapter 11:

> “If any of you thinks otherwise and considers me unworthy of belief, let him believe fire, boiling water, glowing iron. Let the tortures furnish proof where my words do not suffice.”

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, in the book he wrote against his nephew Hincmar, bishop of Laon, chapter 43, discusses Nivinus, who had seduced a nun in his diocese and removed her by night from her monastery:

> “As to what you say—that I asked him how he might clear his reputation—I did not ask because I did not know that he could not do this, but so that I might at least compel him by this means to confession and penance, and afterwards to forgiveness, since I could not induce him voluntarily to these things. And I brought him so far that, if the aforesaid men of his—for they were not of free condition—should come forth to God’s judgment by either hot or cold water, what God should reveal in that matter would suffice for me. But when he saw that he was convicted and constrained by reason, he burst out into obstinacy and insults.”

Thus writes one who lived under Charles the Bald, king of the Franks; his words have been drawn from an ancient manuscript written by hand. From them one may also infer that scarcely any but persons of servile condition were customarily subjected to such an ordeal; this is confirmed by the words of a certain Council of Trier, quoted by Gratian in chapter *Nobilis*, Cause 2, Question 5.

There is also a manuscript book by the same Hincmar of Rheims concerning the case of King Lothar—namely, the son of Emperor Lothar I, about the year of Christ 855—and his wife Queen Theutberga. When she had presented her substitute for the ordeal of boiling water and he came out unscalded, she was restored to the royal bed by the same decree by which she had been suspended. There Hincmar treats most fully of this form of purgation. But because the whole discussion is set forth in a long circuit of words, nothing could easily or conveniently be excerpted. Anyone more curious may read the recently published book *On the Antiquities of the British Church*, under Robert, thirty-first archbishop of Canterbury, where the author writes that the ancient English and Saxons called proof by boiling or cold water, or by glowing and ignited iron, *ordal*; he recounts its various forms and collects much material on this subject which it is not my intention to transcribe.

The ancient Salic Law also mentions it, title 56, *On Redeeming the Hand from the Cauldron*, and title 76, *On the Antrustion*, §1, where there is mention of a heated cauldron and of a hand put into the cauldron, in the peace agreement of Kings Childebert and Chlothar:

> “If a free man accused of theft, challenged to the cauldron, burns his hand, he shall pay compensation for the theft of which he is accused.”

Although such ordeals were in use, ecclesiastical canons objected to them, as Pope Stephen V argues in chapter *Consuluisti*, Cause 2, Question 5. At the Lateran Council, chapter 10, under Innocent III, it was expressly forbidden for any cleric to provide the rite of any blessing or consecration for an ordeal by boiling or cold water, or by glowing iron; its words are also quoted in chapter *Sententiam*, title *That Clerics or Monks Should Not Involve Themselves in Secular Affairs*. In the fourth addition to the ancient laws of Charles, chapter 81, the ordeal by cold water is likewise prohibited from being performed any longer.

In an old manuscript from Laon an example is related of a certain religious Anselm, who had stolen the treasure of the Church of Laon but nevertheless wished to undergo the water ordeal in order to prove himself innocent. Since this history has not yet, so far as I know, been published, and was written by a canon of Laon contemporary with Ivo, it does not seem useless to append the words relevant to the matter:

> “A general assembly of the canons and citizens,” he says, “was summoned; they debated what had to be done; and, above all, Master Anselm, then the lamp of the entire city, was consulted. Being most skilled in divine law, he immediately recounted the story of Joshua: how the Lord commanded that the theft committed at Jericho, though no one knew of it, should be investigated by lot—first by tribes, then by families and households, and lastly one by one by individual men [Joshua 7].
>
> “Following the model of this most subtle investigation, Master Anselm advised that the author of so great a crime should be sought by the ordeal of water, and that one innocent child from each parish of the city should be placed in a vessel filled with blessed water. If any parish were found culpable, one child from each house of that parish should be placed in the water; and if any house were detected, all men and women belonging to it should be compelled to clear themselves by the ordeal of water.
>
> “When the citizens learned this counsel of Master Anselm and his brother Master Ralph, they were terrified, though conscious of their own innocence. They rushed to the bishop and loudly declared that those who were not far away, but rather the guardians of the church and those living near the temple [Col. 0340C], ought first to be called to judgment. The bishop agreed and summoned six men upon whom the greater suspicion rested to undergo the ordeal. Among them he singled out the aforesaid Anselm by name, declaring that he was moved by suspicion against him in this affair.”

A little later he adds:

> “While he was being kept under guard, one night he had a very large vessel filled with water and caused himself to be lowered into it bound, wishing to test whether he would sink completely in the water or float. But when he saw himself taken into the water without any delay and reaching the bottom of the vessel [Col. 0340D], he rejoiced and said that he feared nothing further, but would enter the water voluntarily. Why delay longer? The appointed day came. An innumerable crowd of clerics, knights, and country people of different sex and age gathered at the church; young men and virgins, old persons with the younger, invoked the name of the Lord and of His most glorious Mother. The first man placed in the water emerged safe and rejoicing; the second sank; the third was safe; the fourth was found guilty; the fifth was freed; the sixth, Anselm himself, was found guilty. Thus he learned that it had availed him nothing previously to test God, but that this water differed greatly from the water into which, while under guard, he had earlier caused himself to be lowered.
>
> “Immediately, therefore, bound in chains and warned by the bishop to restore the stolen treasure, he at once publicly cursed himself, saying that he deserved to be hanged like Judas, who betrayed God, if he possessed or had stolen any part of it. When the bishop saw that he could achieve nothing by exhortation, he handed him over to Nicholas the castellan, ordering him to compel restitution of the treasure by torture. Nicholas had him stripped, thrown down upon the ground, bound, and drenched with hot bacon-fat, but could extract nothing,” etc.

The ordeal mentioned in this story appears to have been that of cold water. But from a fragment of a letter by some ancient bishop—for the name is missing there—it may be inferred that this ordeal was considered less weighty. Speaking of the cases of simoniacs, he says:

> “We do not accept the judgment of cold water, nor the testimony of those who share the same disease, but that of religious brethren who resist the same crime in purpose and will. Yet these witnesses are to be obtained not by cold water, but by glowing iron or boiling water [perhaps: ‘sought out,’ *conquirendi*]. Simoniacs are not admitted to judgment if credible persons, even laymen or women, testify that they received payment from them. For to come to judgment in matters that are manifest is nothing other than to test the Lord. Hence we are very often deceived in such cases, because God is far from those who test Him.”

Moreover, I thought it worthwhile to append again here the formula for consecrating hot or cold water, which I discovered long ago in an old codex of Saint Benignus of Dijon and published in print, in order to satisfy those who delight in curiosity about such matters. For these practices, according to the different times, have been attributed now to piety, now to error.

### Blessing, or exorcism, of hot water into which the hand is put for judgment

> “I exorcize you, creature water, in the name of God the almighty Father, and in the name of Jesus Christ His Son, our Lord, that you may become exorcized water for driving away every power of the enemy and every phantom of the devil; so that, if this man who is about to put his hand into you is innocent of the charge brought against him, the mercy of almighty God may free him; and if—God forbid—he is guilty and has dared presumptuously to put his hand into you [Col. 0341C], may the power of that same Almighty deign to make this clear concerning him, so that every person may fear and tremble at the holy name of the glory of our Lord, who lives and reigns as God through,” etc.
>
> “Lord Jesus Christ, who are a just, mighty, and patient judge, and most merciful; through whom all things were made; God of gods and Lord of lords; who for us human beings and for our salvation descended from the bosom of the Father, deigned to take flesh from the Virgin Mary, redeemed the world upon the cross through Your Passion, descended into hell, bound the devil in outer darkness, and by Your great power freed thence all the righteous who were held there by original sin: Lord, we ask You to deign to send Your Holy Spirit from the highest height of heaven upon this creature water, which appears to boil and grow hot by fire, so that through it You may prove and make manifest a just judgment concerning this man in question.
>
> “We humbly beseech You, Lord God, who in Cana of Galilee by the wonderful sign of Your power made wine from water, brought the three boys Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego unharmed out of the burning furnace, freed Susanna from a false accusation, opened the eyes of the man born blind, raised Lazarus, four days dead, from the tomb, and stretched out Your hand to Peter when he was sinking. Do not look upon our sins in this prayer, but deign to make Your true and holy judgment manifest before men in this matter: so that, if this man now puts his hand into this water boiling by fire because of this charge—namely theft, homicide, adultery, sexual immorality, or any other culpable cause—and is not guilty in this matter, You may grant him that no injury or mark appear upon that hand, through which he may undergo accusation though guiltless.
>
> “Again, almighty God, we Your unworthy and sinful servants humbly beseech You to deign also to make Your holy, true, and righteous judgment manifest to us in this matter. Thus, if this man accused in this cause is guilty by some evil deed, prompted by the devil, by greed, or by pride, whether in act or consent, and, relying upon wicked cunning, has dared presumptuously to put his hand into this water in order to subvert or violate this ordeal of proof, may Your mercy deign to make this so evident that it can be recognized in his hand that he acted unjustly; so that henceforth he may, through true confession and penitence, attain amendment, and Your holy and true judgment may be made manifest among all nations, through You, Redeemer of the world, who are to come.”

### Judgment by cold water

> “When you wish to send men to the judgment of cold water for proof, you must proceed thus. Take those men whom you wish to send into the water, lead them into the church, and let the priest sing Mass before them all [Col. 0342B]; make them offer at that Mass. When they come to Communion, before they communicate, the priest shall question them under adjuration and say: ‘I adjure you, men, by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; by your Christianity which you received; by the only-begotten Son of God; by the holy Trinity; by the holy Gospel; and by these holy relics which are in this church: do not dare in any way to communicate or approach the altar if you did this, consented to it, or know [variant: *scitis*, “you know”] who did it.’
>
> “But if they all remain silent and no one has confessed [variant: ‘and no one has said this’], the priest shall approach the altar and communicate, after those who are to be examined have been separated. Afterwards he shall communicate those whom he wishes to send into the water. As each communicates, the priest shall say before the altar: ‘May this body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be to you today for proof, for the praise and glory of His name [Col. 0342C], and for the benefit of His Church.’
>
