> “When Mass is finished, the priest shall make blessed water and carry it to the place of the ordeal [variants: ‘and go to that place where all are tested’; ‘and proceed to the place’; these readings have been restored from other sheets]. When he comes to that place, while he performs the litany and all pray to the Lord concerning the same cause, he shall give those to be examined some of that blessed water to drink. As he gives it to each, he shall say: ‘May this water of the Lord be to you today for proof, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true and just judge.’ Then he shall adjure the water into which they are to be put.
>
> “After the adjuration of the water, he shall strip them of their garments and make each kiss the holy Gospel and the cross of Christ. After this, he shall sprinkle each man with that same blessed water and immediately cast them one by one into the water. He must do all these things fasting; nor may those who put them into the water eat beforehand.”

[Col. 0342D]

### Adjuration of the water

> “I adjure you, water, in the name of God the almighty Father, who created you in the beginning, separated you from the upper waters, and commanded you to serve human needs. I adjure you also by the invisible and ineffable name of Christ Jesus, Son of the living almighty God, beneath whose feet you offered yourself to be trodden, who also deigned to be baptized in you and consecrated you by His baptism. I adjure you also by the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the Lord baptized in you and made you, consecrated by invisible sanctification, an ineffable sacrament for the cleansing of souls. Through you the people of Israel once passed with dry feet, and Elisha, by divine power, made the iron which had accidentally fallen into the water float contrary to nature and return to its handle. Therefore, do not in any way receive this man if he is guilty in any respect of that which is charged against him—whether by act, consent, knowledge, or any contrivance [Col. 0343A]—but by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ reject him from yourself and make him float upon you, so that Christ’s faithful may know that no evil deed and no trickery can resist divine power without being detected and made manifest to all.
>
> “I adjure you also by the power of the same our Lord Jesus Christ, that, to the praise of Him whom every creature serves and whom the heavenly host attends, crying, ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,’ you may obey us who adjure you and beseech His mercy—He who reigns and rules through endless ages of ages. Amen.”

### Adjuration of the man

> “I adjure you, man, and call you to witness by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; by the holy and undivided Trinity; by all angels and archangels; by all principalities and powers, dominions and virtues; by the seats of God, cherubim and seraphim; by the dreadful day of God’s judgment; by the twenty-four elders who daily praise God [Col. 0343B]; by the four Evangelists; by the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors; by holy Mary, Mother of God; by all virgins; by the entire holy people of God; and by the holy baptism in which you were reborn: if you committed this evil of which you are accused, gave your assent to it, carried it, received it into your house, knew of it, or were an accomplice in it, say so before everyone.
>
> “But if, at the devil’s urging, you determine to conceal it and are guilty in this matter, may your fattened and hardened heart melt away; and may the water not receive you, unbelieving and deceived as you are, so that the people may say: ‘Our God is judge, whose power endures for ages of ages.’ Amen.”
>
> “After the adjuration of the water, he shall strip them of their garments, make them kiss the holy Gospel and the holy cross, and, after all have been sanctified with blessed water, let the Son of God, in His mercy and with fear and reverence, cast them into the water.
>
> “At the request of Lord Emperor Louis, blessed Eugenius established this judgment, commanding that all bishops, counts, abbots, and the whole Christian people within his empire should uphold this judgment: that the innocent may be defended and the guilty examined; and that perjurers, consenting to evil, may not lose their souls upon the relics of the saints.”

Thus far the old exemplar.

But because manuscript copy “v. c. Pet.” differs in some points from the preceding text, it has seemed proper to append its reading so that comparison may be made.

### Adjuration of the water

> “I adjure you, water, in the name of God the almighty Father, who created you in the beginning and commanded you to serve human needs, and who also commanded you to be separated from the upper waters. I adjure you also by the ineffable name of Christ Jesus, Son of the living almighty God, beneath whose feet the sea—the element of waters—offered itself to be trodden; who also chose to be baptized in the element of waters.
>
> “I adjure you also by the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the Lord when He was baptized; I adjure you also by the name and holy undivided Trinity, by whose will the element of waters was divided and the people of Israel passed over it with dry feet. At the invocation of whose footstep [reading uncertain], Elisha made the iron which had come off its handle float upon the water. Therefore, do not in any way receive this man, N., if he is guilty in any respect of that which is charged against him—whether by act, consent, knowledge, or any contrivance [Col. 0343D]. Instead make him float upon you; and let there be no deed or trickery that can prevail against you without being able to reveal this.
>
> “Having been adjured through the name of Christ, we command you to obey us through His name, whom every creature serves, whom cherubim and seraphim praise together, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,’ who also reigns and rules through endless ages of ages. Amen.”

[Col. 0344A]

### Adjuration of the man

> “I adjure you, this man, by the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the judgment of cold water. I adjure you by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; by Jesus Christ; by all angels and archangels; by all saints of God; by the dreadful day of judgment; by the twenty-four elders who daily praise God; by the four Evangelists Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; by the twelve apostles; by the twelve prophets; by all saints of God; by martyrs, confessors, and virgins; by principalities and powers, thrones, dominions, and virtues, cherubim and seraphim; by all heavenly mysteries; by the three boys who daily praise God, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; by the 147,000 who suffered for Christ’s name; by Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ; by the whole holy people of God; and by that baptism by which the priest regenerated you [Col. 0344B].
>
> “I adjure you: if you knew of this matter, saw it, carried it, received it into your house, consented to it, were an accomplice in it, possess a fattened and hardened heart, or are guilty in it, may your heart melt away and may the water not receive you; nor may any evil art prevail against this. Therefore we earnestly beseech You, Lord: make such a sign that, if this man is guilty, he may by no means be received by the water. Lord Jesus Christ, do this for the praise, glory, and invocation of Your name, so that all may know that You are our blessed God, who live,” etc.
>
> “Almighty God created this judgment because it is true; and blessed Pope Eugenius and Lord Emperor Louis established that all men—bishops, abbots, and counts—in every region should perform it. It has been tested among us, and it is certainly true; it was instituted so that men might not be permitted to commit perjury upon the Holy of Holies. Amen.”

Thus far that ancient codex. Aventinus had previously produced another formula for the consecration of hot water in book IV of his *Annals of Bavaria*. François Pithou likewise, a most distinguished man, in his *Glossary to the Capitularies of Charlemagne*, second edition of 1603, published another and different formula of the same kind, much fuller than the others, from the *Order* of Dunstan, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury. From comparison of them all it may readily be inferred that no fixed formula for this practice was formerly prescribed; rather, the bishops of the individual Churches composed them as they pleased.

Contact with red-hot iron. Only the manuscripts of Loisel read *contractum* (“contracted”), but wrongly. Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, in Letter 17: “It was therefore superfluous to bring the aforesaid girl to the touch of hot iron, as though she were to prove by such a test that she had had no sexual intercourse with her own husband. For a law is invoked in vain when it affords no assistance whatever toward deciding an urgent case.” Ivo, however, in Letter 205 says that the cautery of red-hot iron provides no certain proof, since, by God’s hidden judgment, many guilty persons appeared to be delivered and innocent persons condemned. Such a proof was therefore rightly forbidden at last: by Pope Stephen V, in the chapter *Consuluisti*, Cause 2, Question 2; by Innocent III, in the chapter *Ex litteris*, *De excessibus praelatorum*; and by Honorius III, in the chapter *Dilecti*, *De purgatione vulgari*. And why could there not have been room here for trickery, when Strabo relates, *Geography*, Book V, that on Mount Soracte the pagans formerly worshipped the goddess Feronia by a marvelous form of rite: those inspired by her divine power walked barefoot upon coals and yet suffered no injury?

Or of any popular invention. A little later he calls them “superstitious inventions.” Under that designation may be included the tests then customary in hidden and uncertain matters: namely, judgment by the cross, concerning which see the laws of the Frisians, the Capitularies [Col. 0345A] of Charlemagne, and the Formulae of Marculf; likewise judgment by the body and blood of Christ. To examples of this practice collected long ago by others may be added a passage of Glaber, *History*, Book V, chapter 1, and Helgaud’s account that Archbishop Leotheric of Sens was severely reproved by King Robert for this reason, when such a perverse doctrine had already begun to spread.

Indeed Theodorus Balsamon, on Canon 61 of the Sixth Synod in Trullo, testifies that in his own time a priest was accused and deposed because, on Maundy Thursday, he had given bread to many persons so that the guilty in a theft might be convicted by this test. Similarly Acron, on this passage of Horace, Book I, Epistle 10:

> “And, like a runaway slave of a priest, I reject sacrificial cakes,”

writes that persons under suspicion of theft were brought to pagan priests, who gave each of them a crust of bread enchanted by a spell. Of the same madness are the formulas found in monastic codices, in which, for detecting thefts, the Lord’s Prayer was ordered to be written on bread and cheese; then crosses were to be made of aspen, one of which was placed beneath the right foot and another above the head of the suspected man; [Col. 0345B] afterward, following various invocations of the deity, it was to be prayed that the culprit’s tongue and throat might be bound so that he could not swallow, but that all his limbs might tremble and he might find no rest. Related to this is the formula of Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, recently published by Pithou in the Glossary to the Capitularies.

Because these things are altogether fabricated by envy as their contriver. Thus all the manuscripts read, as does Gratian in the chapter following Cause 2, Question 4. The first edition wrongly printed *facta*, “made.”

Pope Stephen V. The earlier edition had “Pope Sylvester II,” as do some old books; but Ivo attributes it to Stephen in Letters 205 and 252. This Stephen V lived before Sylvester II; moreover, in the corrected text of Gratian’s *Decree*, the same words are attributed to Stephen V. The error arose from the initials “S. V.”

Lambert. The codices vary: *Luitbertus*, *Libertus*, *Liutbertus*, *Vimpartus*.

## ON LETTER LXXVI

[Col. 0345C]

Because of the tyranny which they exercise against us. “Against us” is added on the authority of an old codex; it was absent from the first edition, leaving the sense incomplete. In Letter 75 he says that he had requested from the pope permission to excommunicate the lady of Puiset and her knights for their unceasing injuries inflicted upon the Church of Chartres. What he says in this letter concerning her son Hugh, whose tyranny he censures, must be joined with the passage in Letter 111, where he says that Hugh, after the manner of his family, always repaid good with evil and was restrained from plunder neither by shame nor by faith. He is also called “a horned viper in the path” and “a serpent in the way,” Letter 211.

Aimoin, Book IV, *On the Miracles of St Benedict*, chapter 24, mentions this Hugh while speaking of Louis, king and son of Philip: “Certain magnates of France rebelled against him, trusting in the wealth and power of William, king of the English. Among them Hugh of Puiset took up arms against him, [Col. 0345D] gathering many helpers to his side. The king, wishing to curb his audacity, drew together from every quarter a force of soldiers.” Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis, in his *Life of King Louis the Fat*, describes this same man’s criminal deeds and testifies that he grievously afflicted the people of Chartres. I shall set forth the words, corrected in several places with the help of two manuscript codices kindly supplied by the distinguished men Paul Pétau and Antoine Loisel, because they greatly illuminate this letter and at the same time mention Ivo, whom Hugh had confined in prison:

> “Just as the most welcome fruit of a well-bearing tree restores its fragrant flavor either through transplantation of the stock or grafting of the branches, so the propagation of iniquity and wickedness, which must be uprooted, drawn from the stock of many wicked men and congealed in one man—like a serpent stinging a serpent among eels—drinks its native bitterness as though it were wormwood. Of this sort was Hugh of Puiset, a wicked man, enriched only by the tyranny both of himself and of his ancestors. When he succeeded his uncle Guy in the lordship of Puiset—for his father, in extraordinary pride, had taken up arms in the 158th year at the beginning of the Jerusalem expedition—he did not cease to prove himself in every evil a seed of wickedness inherited from his father. Those whom his father had scourged with whips, he, worse than his father, scourged with scorpions.
>
> “Swelling with pride because he had cruelly oppressed poor churches and monasteries with impunity, he went so far as to set foot where ‘the workers of iniquity have fallen; they have been cast down and could not stand.’ Since he held neither the King of all nor the king of the French in esteem, he attacked the most noble Countess of Chartres and her son Theobald, a most handsome young man and valiant in arms; and, laying waste their land as far as Chartres, he exposed it to plunder and fire. The noble countess and her son did sometimes—though late and inadequately—endeavor, as they could, to take vengeance. Yet they never, or scarcely ever, approached within eight or ten miles of Puiset. Such was Hugh’s audacity, and such the power available to his domineering pride, that few loved him, [Col. 0346A] many served him; many longed to defend him, but even more to destroy him. For he was feared more than loved.
>
> “When the aforesaid Count Theobald perceived that he could accomplish little against Hugh by himself but much through the king, he hastened with his most noble mother—who had always been accustomed to serve the king nobly—to him. He besieged him with many prayers, represented that he had earned his help by much service, and recounted certain affronts of Hugh, his father, grandfather, and great-grandfathers. ‘Remember, lord king,’ he said, ‘as befits royal majesty, the insult and disgrace which Hugh’s grandfather foully inflicted by perjury upon your father Philip, when he shamefully repelled him from Puiset as he endeavored to avenge the many injuries done to him. Through the insolence of a most wicked kinship and factious conspiracy he drove his army in flight as far as Orléans; he dishonored in his prison the captured Count of Nevers, Lancelin of Beaugency, nearly a hundred knights—of this Ivo speaks in Letter 172—and, what had hitherto been unheard of, certain bishops.
>
> “‘She added also, by way of reproach, what cause, what origin there was for a castle, built in the midst of the land of the saints by the venerable Queen Constance for its protection, not to have existed from ancient times; and how, after making everything his own, he had left the king nothing but injuries. Now, if it pleased him, because the force of the armies of Chartres, Blois, and Dunois—on which Hugh had been accustomed to rely in resisting—would not only fail him but even work against him, he could easily avenge both his father’s injuries and his own by destroying the castle and disinheriting Hugh. If he did not wish to punish injuries done either to himself or to those who had deserved well of him, then he should either make his own or remove the oppressions of churches, the plundering of the poor, and the utterly impious vexations of widows and orphans by which Hugh despoiled both the land of the saints and its inhabitants.’
>
> “When the king, pressed by these and many other pleas, had appointed a day for considering them, we assembled at Melun. There many archbishops, bishops, clerics, and monks gathered, crying out because he devoured their [Col. 0346B] lands more greedily than a wolf. They even lay at his feet against his will, begging him to restrain the most rapacious robber, Hugh; to rescue from the dragon’s jaws the prebends established by the generosity of kings in the fertile grain-bearing Beauce for the servants of God; to strive to set free the lands of priests, which alone had been freed even under Pharaoh’s cruelty; and to restore free to God, whose image the king bears for giving life, that portion of God over which he was vicar. Having received their prayer in a good spirit, undertaking nothing improperly, when the prelates of the Church had departed—the Archbishop of Sens, the Bishop of Orléans, and the venerable Ivo of Chartres, who had been imprisoned and whom Hugh had compelled to be depicted in that same castle—he sent me, with the agreement of Abbot Adam of blessed memory, our predecessor, to Toury, which I governed in Beauce, a useful and grain-rich estate of Saint-Denis, yet wholly unfortified. He ordered me, while he himself was still summoning Hugh to answer concerning these matters, to see to the village and to use every effort to support it by the military force of his men and ours, lest Hugh destroy it by fire. For Hugh was fortifying it and, as his father had done, intended from there to attack the castle.”
>
> There follows there a long account of the siege of the castle, at the end of which he added: “The king not only disinherited Hugh of Puiset, but also overthrew and leveled the castle of Puiset, its walls destroyed and its wells filled in, as a place laid open to God’s curse. Yet another time, long afterward, when Hugh had been restored to the king’s favor through many hostages and many oaths, he again rebelled through repeated treachery and showed himself an apt pupil who had surpassed Sulla, his master, in crimes. Besieged again by the king and again disinherited, after he had pierced with his own lance Anselm of Garland, the king’s steward and a valiant baron, he could not unlearn his innate and habitual treachery; until the Jerusalem journey, as it did for many other wicked men, extinguished by taking his life his wickedness, inflamed with every poison.” [Col. 0347A]

Thus Suger. Furthermore, the continuator of Aimoin, Book V, chapter 52, also reports that Hugh of Puiset, who had risen against Louis, was defeated by him, and that Puiset was demolished so that in the course of time neither Hugh nor his heirs might be able to resist the lord.

## ON LETTER LXXVII

To John of Marseille. Thus also it is printed in the corrected edition of Gratian, in the heading of the canon *Decessorum*, Cause 25, Question 2. But the name varies in other codices, which have *Massaliae*, *Massiliae*, or *Massalae*.

Or by emperors of divine memory. In one old codex, with the words truncated, there is only “or by emperors.” But in other copies the alternative reading is consistently preserved, and is confirmed by the corrected edition of Gratian in the canon *Placuit*, Cause 24, Question 4. For this reason the reading here has now been changed from that supplied by the earlier edition, “or by emperors of divine memory”; not because that wording contains any fault, but because “of divine memory” has the support of more books and better reflects the language of ancient [Col. 0347C] times. Thus, in the heading of Letter 87 of Pope John VIII: “To Louis, glorious king, son of Charles II Augustus, emperor of divine memory.” Likewise, in the heading of Letter 91: “To the beloved daughter Angelberga, empress, widow of the lord Louis, most pious emperor of divine memory.”

Many examples of this kind occur in books of imperial constitutions: “under Constantius of divine memory,” in Law I, *De collatione Donatorum vel relevatione possessionis*, Theodosian Code; and “from the beginning of the reign of my father of divine memory,” in the final law under the same title. Likewise, “according to the law of Gratian of divine memory,” in Law XXXV, *De episcopis, ecclesiis et clericis*, in the same Theodosian Code. Pope Alexander III, in a rescript to Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux: “Of the divine and venerable memory of Pope Innocent.”

Nor did they call the memory “divine” only when speaking of Christian rulers, but also when speaking of deserters and enemies of the orthodox faith. Thus Julian the emperor is called “of blessed memory” by Valentinian and Valens in Law II, *De numerariis et actuariis*, Theodosian Code; likewise by Arcadius and Honorius in Law VII, *De proximis comitum dispositionibus*, of the same Code; and by Leo in Law LXI, *De decurionibus*, Code of Justinian. Brisson, in his *Formulae*, says that this last instance cannot be tolerated. But if it is true, as Minucius Felix wrote in the *Octavius*, that kings were consecrated by pagans not because they believed them divine, but in honor of authority meritoriously exercised, such language ought not to seem so strange.

John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, Book III, chapter 10, reproves princes distinguished by the light of faith because they dare—and delight—to be called “divine,” a custom, he says, prevailing through inveterate fault and contrary to Catholic belief. Georg Cassander, in the preface to his *Ecclesiastical Hymns*, likewise disapproves the recent practice of calling those “divine” whom the ancients called saints or blessed, since there is no difference between “divine ones” (*divi*) and gods (*dei*).

“We decree that, after first consulting the prince, the question be examined whether this presumptuous faction ought to be cut off.” Previously printed: “We decree that first,” etc. In Gratian, chapter *De rebus*, Cause 12, Question 2: “We decree that you shall first consult the prince concerning the cutting off of so presumptuous a faction, and ascertain whether…”

## ON LETTER LXXVIII

To the monastery of Cluny. Ralph Glaber, *History*, Book III, chapter 5, speaking of the Rule of Saint Benedict, says that the institution, now almost exhausted, chose for itself a seat of wisdom and was to bear fruit with manifold growth in the monastery of Cluny, so named from the site’s slope and low position, or rather from *cluere*, since *cluere*, he says, means “to grow”; for from its beginning it received a remarkable increase of diverse gifts. Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, in a letter to Hugh, calls it a second paradise.

They ascended without any refusal. Previously “without any” had crept in. But comparison of several old codices, agreeing well with one another, now restores [Col. 0348B] “without all.” The same expression occurs in many other places in Ivo himself, namely Letters 74, 196, and 281, and also in other authors: for example, Pope Urban II, Letter 1, to the clergy and people of Chartres, above at the beginning of these letters. The same pope, in a privilege for the abbey of Cava: “It shall be lawful for it to receive the goods thus devolved upon it without any opposition from himself, his heirs, or successors.” Elsewhere: “That they themselves should confirm for you all grants and exceptions through their privileges without any payment and delay of tardiness.” Similar are Gregory VII, Book II, Letter 5, “without any danger to yourselves”; Book VII, Letter 12, “without any fear”; Peter of Blois, Letter 6, “without any envy and detraction”; and Henry the emperor, to the king of the Celts, “without all Christian communion.” Other examples occur in Letters 21, 23, 62, and 63 of Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux.

Guimundus. Otherwise, *Guitmundus*.

To the bishopric of Aversa. Thus most manuscripts; [Col. 0348C] others have “of Auvergne,” as did the earlier edition. But the former reading is sounder, for Guimundus is meant here, bishop of Aversa, who wrote three books against Berengar and flourished under Urban II. William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, Book III, in the life of William I, speaking of Berengar: “Lanfranc the archbishop answered him in books; but especially and vigorously Guimundus, formerly a monk of Saint-Leufroy in Normandy, afterward bishop of Aversa in Apulia, the most eloquent man of our age.”

Of Saint Lawrence of Aversa. Thus many codices have it, supported by the Putean book: *Adversensis*, “of Aversa.” In others, *Avernensis*, “of Auvergne,” as in the earlier edition.

## ON LETTER LXXIX

Humbald of Auxerre. The name of the city is written in that form in most of the better manuscripts. Some also have *Altissiodorensis*, others *Antisiodorensis*, [Col. 0348D] which became the common form. Long ago the name was pronounced in various ways, as the verses of Heiric’s *Life of Saint Germanus*, Book I, attest:

> Celtic Gaul, which wakes the regions lying at its center,  
> and that Gaul which is gentler either to its lands or to its settlers—  
> the earlier Gauls set there a city by no means obscure,  
> rich in fertile fields, in the gift of excellent Bacchus,  
> and in the agreeable use of an abundant year,  
> able to compare itself with many great cities.  
> The ancients report that it was once called Autricus.  
> A later age set wings and lofty roofs  
> upon its ancestral walls, defenses for harsh war.  
> From the enlarged walls its name was changed:  
> whether, following usage, you call it Antissiodorum,  
> or, if you wish to shorten it, Altiodorum,  
> the same city is richer under a different name.

So wrote that poet seven hundred years ago. In the Itinerary of Antoninus Augustus it is also written *Autesiodorum*; while in the edition of Ralph Glaber, Book II, chapter 8, it is *Antisioderum*, where, speaking of King Robert, he records this remarkable fact: “He surrounded it with a siege; and, after remaining there long wearied by repeated assaults, he did not prevail against it, which is said never to have been deceived either by treachery or by an enemy.” [Col. 0349A]

## ON LETTER LXXXI

Succeeded Pope Urban. Berthold, in his Chronicle under the year 1099: “At Rome the venerable Pope Urban, the second of that name, after governing the Roman see for eleven years and five months, at last departed this life on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, after many tribulations. After his death, Lord Paschal, also called Rainerius, was ordained the 162nd pope in succession, and it was everywhere proclaimed that this had occurred by divine revelation. He was ordained by the clergy and people on the sixteenth day after the departure of his predecessor.” What he adds concerning divine revelation should be elucidated by the words of Abbot Dodechin, who recounts the tale of a slip of paper partly hairy and partly clean, signifying that the period of that papacy would be peaceful in part and turbulent in part.

That we might easily incur danger in going. Baronius, volume XII of the *Annals*, interprets this passage thus: “Clearly, if he said, as was the case, that he was going to Rome to Paschal, he would be detained by those favoring Paschal’s enemy, the emperor and antipope. But if he denied, as was the case, that he adhered to Paschal, he would incur no slight sin.” A little later he adds: “Certainly, as regards dangers, Domnizo writes, concerning Henry the emperor, a public enemy of the Roman Church, that at this time the roads were so occupied by hostile forces, and that this enemy had the road of Saint Peter guarded, ordering pilgrims to be despoiled.” Thus Baronius.

Abbot of Ursberg writes in his Chronicle under the year 1102 that Emperor Henry publicly announced that he was going to Rome so that, with both his own cause and that of the apostolic see canonically argued, Catholic unity between kingdom and priesthood, which had remained divided for so many years, might be confirmed. [Col. 0349C] Yet he did not come, did not send messages professing submission to the apostolic dignity, and was said to have attempted, if possible, to set up another pope in opposition to Paschal, but without success. Shortly afterward he writes:

> “Meanwhile a certain Wernher, one of the order of the king’s ministerials, who governed the March, which was in the region of Aquino, as though intending to revive that same heresy, gathered forces from every part of Italy and also corrupted certain Romans with much money. While the lord pope was staying in the territory of Benevento, Wernher—shameful deed!—placed upon the chair of Saint Peter a certain false abbot of Farfa and wished him to be called the pope of Caesar under the name Sylvester. Shortly afterward, however, he was shamefully expelled by the Catholics, as he deserved; and he received as the reward for his madness the loss of money wickedly acquired and still more wickedly squandered, besides the loss to his faith, which his blind heart did not grieve over.”

Dodechin’s words have the same bearing: “Meanwhile Wibert, invader of the Roman and apostolic [Col. 0349D] see, dies; and because he had no successor of his party, the whole people flocked to Pope Paschal. Thus his heresy, which had flourished until then, was annihilated.” He says this under the year of the Lord 1098.

Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in a manuscript letter to Henry, king of the English: “I say only this: the apostolic Paschal has been ecclesiastically elected according to God, and has now been received and confirmed throughout the whole Catholic Church. But that invader whose report is abroad has no election or reception except from the sons of the devil, enemies of the Church of God. Therefore we await the fulfillment upon him—if it has not already happened—of what the Lord said: ‘Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up.’”

## ON LETTER LXXXIII

For you have it in the Heptateuch. Most old codices do not prefix the sign of aspiration to this word; and in books of other authors one finds *heptateuchus* and *heptaticus* written. Here he means the passage in Deuteronomy, chapter XXV, the words of which are commonly transmitted in this form: “If two men have a dispute between themselves and one begins to quarrel against the other, and the wife of one, wishing to rescue her husband from the hand of the stronger, puts out her hand and seizes his genitals, you shall cut off her hand; you shall not bend toward him with any mercy.”

Ivo therefore misremembers when he says that one who puts a hand upon the genital member is to be stoned—an organ which Lactantius Firmianus calls “the divine and marvelous work of God,” *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 13, and Cassiodorus calls “beautiful and precious,” *On the Soul*, chapter 16. For the words must be understood only of a wife; she is ordered not to be struck with stones, but to have her hand cut off.

The reason for this designation is that ancient ecclesiastical writers used to unite and bind together the five books of Moses and, along with them, the following two books, Joshua and Judges; thus the *heptaticus* comprised the Pentateuch. If they cited a passage from those [Col. 0350B] books, they cited it under the name *heptaticus* or *heptateuchus*. Ignorance of this fact caused certain passages in authors to be corrupted and altered. Marianus, bishop of Rieti, observed this long ago from the reading of an old codex in Saint Jerome’s Letter 7 to Laeta, where some had substituted *pentateuchum* for *heptateuchum*; and in Letter 28 to Lucinius, *octateucho* for *heptateucho*. Similarly, in Gratian, canon *Sancta*, Distinction 15, *heptateuchum* was corrected in the Roman edition from *pentateuchum*, on the authority of Ivo’s *Decree*.

I have also observed that a verse of Arator, *Apostolic History*, Book I, canto 17, suffers from the same fault, commonly printed thus:

> “The Almighty approves that Moses joined the Ethiopian woman to himself by the bond of marriage.”

This error occurs in many manuscript codices, so that no one should think it originated in our age. But in an ancient exemplar of the highest authority one plainly reads:

> “The Heptateuch approves…”

Only Aldus retained this word. Mention of the Heptateuch occurs in Eusebius of Emesa, homily for the seventh Sunday after Pentecost and homily on Luke, chapter 15; in Sidonius Apollinaris, Book V, Letter 15; in Pope Gregory I, Book VII, Letter 49, and Book XII, Letter 30; and in chapter *Qualiter*, Cause 7, Question 1. Hincmar of Reims: “Both of these acts, committed separately, are punished with death in the Heptateuch by the Lord’s command.” Elsewhere the same author: “But what is written in the Heptateuch concerning jealousy…” Henry of Ghent, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 8, says that Peter Riga, cleric of the Church of Reims, wrote the Heptateuch in verse. [Col. 0350C]

## ON LETTER LXXXIV

Because, contrary to the interdict of Pope Urban of blessed memory, they placed the crown upon the king himself. Philip had previously been excommunicated by Pope Urban at the Council of Clermont, as Ivo says in Letter 211. Later he repented and was absolved; but when he learned that Urban had died, he returned to association with his concubine Bertrada. For this reason Paschal, Urban’s successor, sent two cardinals to France; having convened a council at Poitiers, they excommunicated the king anew, as the author indicates in the aforesaid Letter 211. [Col. 0350D]

## ON LETTER LXXXV

And when this has been corrected. Thus corrected from an old codex; previously, wrongly: “And this which shall have been right.”

Whatever your legates shall say to you. Thus I have restored it from most old codices; previously: “Rather than what our legates shall say to you,” as one manuscript has it.

## ON LETTER LXXXVII

And with the lethargic illness of that Church. The reading of the earlier edition is supported by the agreement of various manuscripts. But in other copies the word has been altered: instead of *veterno*, “lethargy,” there is *veteri*, “old,” as in Servin’s old codex. There is also the Putean book, which reads “and in the [lacuna] third.”

[Col. 0351A]

With every canonical obedience. In one codex: “With every canonical election.”

Illiterate, a gambler, and devoted to other enticements of this kind. Thus from the better old codices. The earlier edition had: “Devoted only to the game of dice and to the other enticements of this world.”

At the king’s will. That is, Philip’s, who, as Pope Gregory VII testifies, had already inflicted various injuries upon the Church of Beauvais; Gregory writes to him in Book I, Letter 75.

Stephen is called “of Garland.” I have preferred the reading of the more numerous and better codices, since writers of that age mention a similar surname. Suger, in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, mentions another Anselm of Garland, steward and valiant knight; shortly thereafter, Anselm of Garland, a valiant baron; and elsewhere William of Garland. William of Tyre, *History of the Holy War*, Book I, chapter 17, has Guy of Garland, steward of the king of the Franks.

## ON LETTER LXXXVIII

[Col. 0351B]

Hilgod, formerly bishop of Soissons. It ought to have been printed thus, as the better old codices have it, not “Hilgot.” For in an ancient catalogue of the abbots from the time when Marmoutier was restored—not, that is, founded—he is called Hilgod. Its words assist the interpretation of this letter, in which Ivo says that he had been elected in a monastery but does not state the name of the place:

> “Hilgod, seventh abbot. He brought privileges concerning the liberty of this church, for which Lord Bernard had long labored, granted by blessed Pope Urban. He also went to England and obtained thirty marks of silver which we receive annually from the king and queen of the English, together with several pluralities. He was first bishop of the Church of Soissons and afterwards abbot of the aforesaid monastery. He rests at the entrance, on the right-hand side, near the altar of Saint Anthony. He governed this church from the year 1136 to the year 1148 and died on the Ides of October.”

Another ancient writer, in the little book *On the Tribulations of Marmoutier*: “At that time, therefore, while a certain council was sitting at Brioude, our brethren having been sent there—Lord Bernard the prior, Hilgod bishop of Soissons, his brother Andrew, and James the physician—our cause was discussed according to the foregoing proceedings.” A little later in the same book he again mentions him. [Col. 0351C]

## ON LETTER XC

Because the Truce of God has not been established by common law. In some books the word has a doubled letter, *treuvia*. Elsewhere it is *tregua* or *treua*. William of Tyre, *History of the Holy War*, Book I, chapter 15: “That the peace which in common speech is called a truce (*treuga*) should be kept inviolate by all.” Ralph Glaber, *History*, Book V, chapter 1: “Moreover, it pleased all, as it is commonly called, that it should be named the Truce of the Lord; it was supported not only by human proclamations but also by the divine terrors of many.”

## ON LETTER XCI

And especially little properties. Thus I have corrected it on the authority of the better codices. For it was first wrongly printed *regulas*, “rules,” a blemish that also affects many old manuscripts. In Servin’s manuscript I found *regulares*. But the author used *reculas*, as in Letter 101: “whose little properties he seized,” where one old codex intrudes *regulas*, “rules.” Donatus, in the *Life of Virgil*: “Coemundus increased his little estate through the management of woods and bees.” Salvian, *On the True Judgment of God*, Book V: “Because they cannot transfer there their little properties, their humble dwellings, and their families”; and shortly afterward: “stripped of their little properties.” Thus the Paris edition of 1575 reads. But Pithou’s edition has *resculas* and *resculis*, not without support from an ancient exemplar. The same Salvian, Book I, *To the Catholic Church*: “Why do we not use in good faith the small goods given by God?” Other authors use *reiculas*. Agobard, in a letter to the emperor: “He who is commanded to love as himself the man whom he desires to kill or overcome is to regard as dung those little possessions for which he contends.” I observed this reading in an old codex of Papire Masson; the common edition corruptly intrudes *recusias illas*. In the Capitularies of Charles and Louis, Book VII, chapter 192: “those who seek a small possession of the Church from kings.” [Col. 0352A]

## ON LETTER XCIII

To Daimbert, by the grace of God, of Jerusalem. In one exemplar, “Lambert,” a name spelled variously in other authors. William of Tyre, *History of the Holy War*, regularly calls him Dagobert, for example Book IX, chapters 14 and 15; Book X, chapters 7, 25, and 26; and Book XI, chapter 14. Dagobert also appears in the ancient anonymous author of the fragmentary *History of the Franks from Robert to the Death of King Philip*, where Pope Urban is said to have sent to the people of Jerusalem Dagobert, bishop of Pisa, a man adorned with every excellence.

Matthew Paris, in his *English History* under the year of the Lord 1100, reports that Arnulf, a certain priest’s son, notorious among the pilgrims for licentiousness and excessive frivolity, was intruded into the patriarchal see through the favor of Robert, duke of Normandy, and of a certain bishop of Maturana in Calabria. But he adds [Col. 0352B] that Arnulf was compelled, because death soon intervened, to lay down the dignity rashly assumed. After him, when the see had been vacant for five months, the princes then present placed the venerable Daibert on the patriarchal throne. “He had previously,” he says, “been bishop of the Church of Pisa, a man fully learned and trained from youth in ecclesiastical affairs.”

William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, Book IV, chapter 2, says that he does not doubt that Pope Urban’s consent was secured in appointing him, because he was venerable in age, powerful in speech, and strong in purse. Fulcher of Chartres calls him a pious shepherd and outstanding teacher, harassed by the hatred of ill-wishers and driven from his Church through the envy of Cardinal Robert and Arnulf, archdeacon of the Holy Sepulchre; a certain unlearned Evermarus was appointed in his place. But after Daibert had gone to Rome and complained about Robert, Arnulf, and his clergy, Pope Paschal restored him to his former place and dignity. William of Tyre calls him “a learned and prudent man, very religious and a friend of integrity,” Book IX, chapter 14.

His ambition, however, was noted. For, after Jerusalem had been captured through the great labor of the princes, he had it surrendered to himself with all its appurtenances, ostensibly under the fair pretext of religion, thereby dispossessing Duke Godfrey. The princes who were responsible had never transferred the kingdom to Godfrey on the condition that he should bind himself to any person by an obligation of any service, as the same [Col. 0352C] Tyrian says, Book IX, chapter 16. For this reason he is not undeservedly censured by François de Belleforest in his *Cosmography*.

Our mother, the Eastern Church. Pope Urban II, in the sermon delivered at the Council of Clermont: “Hasten to defend the Eastern Church. For she is that Church from which the joys of all your salvation have flowed; she who poured into your mouths the breasts of divine milk; she who offered us the most holy teachings of the Gospels.” Daimbert the patriarch calls Jerusalem “the singular mother of all Churches and mistress of the nations,” in William of Tyre, *History of the Holy War*, Book X, chapter 4. [Col. 0352D]

## ON LETTER XCIV

And he shall be adjudged the despoiler of the bishopric. The passage has been restored with the aid of the old Putean codex, which alone retained the true and uncorrupted reading. Previously it had been printed “the buyer of the bishopric,” a corrupt reading also found in other manuscripts. In the book of Saint-Germain both words are entirely absent.

Here it should be observed that in the author’s time, when a bishop had been deposed, died, or was near death, both laymen and clerics were accustomed to plunder his goods. Traces of this evil custom remain in canon *Illud*, Cause 12, Question 2. It was later forbidden by the Council of Lleida, cited in canon *Haec hujus*, and by the Council of Clermont in canon *De laicis*, cited under Cause 12, Question 2. William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, Book IV, reports that in England under King William I, after the death of a bishop or abbot, all revenues were customarily kept intact [Col. 0353A] to be surrendered afterward to the pastor appointed in his place; but that, immediately upon the king’s death, everything was altered, and the revenues were carried into the royal treasury through the rapacity of Ranulf the administrator, concerning whom see below in the notes on Letter 153.

## ON LETTER XCV

Against me because of him. Thus the old codex; previously, “continually.”

From predecessors. In two old manuscripts, “from forebears” (*de praecessorum*). There is some difference between the two expressions, for the term *praedecessores* (“predecessors”) has a wider application. Cassiodorus, *Variae*, IV, epistle 44: “He complained that a house belonging to his right had been possessed for a long period before the time of our deceased predecessor and predecessor.” The same, VIII, epistle 16: “For what long-standing custom gave you through our deceased predecessors and predecessors in the days of the lord our grandfather.” Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, in his letter to Pope Nicholas: “I asked for nothing except that I might use it, as my deceased predecessors and predecessors had been accustomed to use it in the ordination of a bishop.” Let Anthony Contius therefore consider this, for in his preface to the Code of Justinian he counts the word *praedecessor* among the expressions which, he says, the barbarous age wrongly inflected [Col. 0353B], and adds that, without giving any reason for his correction, he everywhere substituted *decessor* for *praedecessor*.

## ON LETTER C

“And it is not without the blemish of agreement.” Thus in all manuscripts. But for *naevo* (“blemish”), *scrupulo* (“scruple”) has been substituted in canon 3, distinction 86, where these words are attributed to Pope John VIII; likewise in canon 8, causa 23, question 3, where they are ascribed not to John but to Anastasius and Damasus.

## ON LETTER CI

“Whose goods he seized”: only the Put[ean] manuscript has *regulus*; a similar error is noted above on Letter 91. Most parchment manuscripts have *saisivit* (“he seized”), for which certain codices read *sasivit* or *saivit*. The same word is used in Letter 121: “They seized [*saisierunt*] in the street of the tanners.” William of Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, I: “The king therefore seized the archbishopric.” Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, in a letter to Henry, king of the English: “You received me into your peace in Normandy, and restored me to possession [*resaisistis*] of my archbishopric.” [Col. 0353C] The same, in a letter to Ernulf: “The king restored me to possession of the whole archbishopric.” William of Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, I: “That you should order Anselm to be restored to possession [*resaisiri*].”

## ON LETTER CII

“In his capitularies.” The Basel edition of 1557 had given the book the title *Laws of the Franks*. There these enactments appear in book I, chapter 78. But the latest Pithou edition of 1603 more correctly entitled them *Capitularies*, as they are called by ancient authors. They are also called “royal chapters” by Ivo, Letter 171, and “chapters of the emperors” by Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims. The passage meant here by Ivo occurs in the same capitularies of that edition, chapter 84; for this ruling consult Gratian, chapter *Sacrorum*, distinction 63.

“Concerning the servile status of parents.” For those subject to servile status were forbidden to become bishops, chapter 1, distinction 34; likewise persons bound to the soil, chapters 9 and 15 of the same distinction; and indeed all dependants, chapter 7, distinction 34, and chapter 15, distinction 54.

## ON LETTER CIV

“Lord Galon, a man of honourable life.” There is a letter of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, mentioning this election (see Anselm’s Letters, III.69, *Patrologia*, vol. CLIX). 163 Other matters concerning Galon are also noted on Letter 110.

“And in literary studies.” Thus most old manuscripts; formerly, “and in liberal studies.” Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, in *Against Hincmar, Bishop of Laon*: “For the present I permitted you only to apply yourself to literary study, boasting of the judgment, until at a more mature age I might also restrain you from that fault.” Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, Letter 36: “You ask to become a canon, and that your nephew be substituted for you—a man distinguished in character and trained, along with his contemporaries, in the disciplines of literary learning.” Gregory VII, IX.2, to the king of Spain: “Concerning the person to be elected archbishop, we say that, although he appears sufficiently prudent and cultivated, he nevertheless lacks the foundation of discipline, namely competence in literary learning. You yourself fully understand how necessary this quality is, not only for bishops but even for priests, since without it no one can either teach others or defend himself.” [Col. 0354A]

“They melted into his heart”: incorrectly, only the Put[ean] manuscript has *eloquerentur* (“they might speak out”), perhaps for *eliquarentur* (“they might melt”).

“That the aforesaid elect was my pupil.” For this reason he was suspected by Ivo’s rivals, since when he wrote this he had not yet been reconciled with his king Philip, as the words at the end of this letter clearly indicate.

“If he should at any time become bishop in his kingdom.” Of the same kind is the matter for which Pope Nicholas reproves King Lothair: he would permit no one in his Lotharingian kingdom to be elected or promoted to a bishopric [Col. 0354B] unless he favoured him; chapter *Porro*, distinction 63.

“He does not wish to give his consent to the election.” By ancient law the consent of the king of the Franks was required in the elections of bishops and abbots within his realm, as may be gathered from several passages in Ivo himself, Letters 54 and 89. Indeed, although at times the election of clergy and people was free, the king nevertheless had to be consulted. A few examples will sufficiently show this. Nicholas, a monk contemporary with Ivo, writes in the *Life of St Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens*, I.18, that Henry, abbot of Nogent, permitted free authority to choose a pastor in his place. Then, by the counsel of bishops and of Ingelram, count of the castle of Coucy, it was decided that this burden should be laid upon the monk Godfrey. The matter was referred to Philip, king of the Franks, who rejoiced at the election of so great a man and ordered it expedited. In chapter 29 he reports that the same Godfrey was later elected bishop of Amiens, and that an embassy was sent to the same Philip, to whom he was most dear and familiar. He adds: “Accordingly, in the royal manner, he ordered his promotion to be expedited.” [Col. 0354C]

Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, in his *Life of Louis the Fat*, testifies that the monks of that monastery were subjected to insults and confined in prison because they had dared to elect Suger himself as their abbot without first seeking the permission of the said king, though Suger afterwards obtained his favour. “He announces,” he says, “the death of Abbot Adam and the election, made by the whole community in full assembly, of our person; but because it had been done without consulting the king, when the better and more religious brethren, and even the more noble knights, had offered the election to the lord king so that he might grant his assent, he reports that they were assailed with many insults and shut up in the castle at Orléans.” And a little later: “I was distressed by a threefold loss: whether, by accepting the election against the will of the lord king, I should endure the Roman Church’s severity and the authority of Pope Calixtus, who loved me, despoiling and draining Mother Church—which had never ceased most sweetly to cherish me from the breast of the most welcome lap of her generosity—while, because of me, both despoilers had occasion to dissipate her, though they had never sought anything of the kind; whether I should allow brethren and friends, for love of us, to be disgraced and dishonoured in a royal prison; or whether, abandoning her on account of these and similar matters, I should incur the reproach of so great a rejection.” [Col. 0354D]

Robert of Torigni, in the appendix to Sigebert’s *Chronicle* for the year 1141, notes that, when a dispute arose between the Roman pope and Louis, king of the Franks, the Gallican Church was disturbed. For after the death of Alberic, archbishop of Bourges, Pope Innocent sent a consecrated pastor to that Church; but King Louis rejected him because he had been ordained without his assent and therefore was not admitted to the city. On this matter see also below on Letter 105. Moreover, St Bernard of Clairvaux’s Letter 282 to Louis, king of the Franks, says that it was neither reasonable nor customary to seek the king’s favour as often as the clergy disagreed in electing a bishop. It was enough, he says, that they had once obtained the prince’s assent. [Col. 0355A]

“Nor to leave the episcopal goods to the elect.” An excellent passage on this occurs in the testament of King Philip Augustus. As he was setting out for Jerusalem, he entrusted the guardianship of the kingdom to his mother Adela and to William, archbishop of Rheims, his uncle: “If it should happen that an episcopal see or a royal abbey becomes vacant, we wish the canons of the church, or the monks of the vacant monastery, to come to the queen and the archbishop as they would have come to us, and ask them for free election. And we wish them to grant it without objection. We moreover admonish both canons and monks to choose such a pastor as may please God and be useful to the kingdom. But the queen and archbishop shall hold the regalian rights in their hands until the elect has been consecrated or blessed; and then the regalian rights shall be restored to them without objection.” This passage appears in Rigord, book I, *De gestis Philippi Augusti*.

[Col. 0355B] “The king of the Franks says that he will come to Rome shortly.” For while the schism between Paschal II and Guibert, the antipope, was still burning, Philip and his whole kingdom adhered to Paschal’s party, just as he had favoured Urban, as noted on Letter 46.

“And shall have returned to his vomit, as has already happened.” See Letter 84.

## ON LETTER CV

“Besides that oath”: thus more correctly from the old manuscript than the earlier reading, “because of which.” The author of Letter 144 says that the same Galon, though elected, could not peacefully possess the bishopric of Beauvais because of Louis’s oath. There were therefore two oaths in this affair: those of King Philip the father and of his son Louis the Fat. Each prince clung stubbornly to his oath. A comparable act of King Louis may be referred here. When the pope, without the prince’s knowledge, had ordained Peter archbishop of Bourges after Alberic’s death, the king—as Matthew Paris says—was violently indignant that this had been done to the injury of his dignity. Having publicly displayed the most sacred relics before many persons, he swore that the aforesaid archbishop should not enter the city of Bourges as long as he lived. St Bernard, Letter 221, calls this an unlawful and accursed oath, most rashly assumed against the Church of Bourges; and in Letter 223 to Stephen, bishop of Palestrina, he calls it a Herodian oath. Likewise, in Letter 219 to the four bishops of the curia, he says that he does not excuse the king, because he had sworn unlawfully and persisted unjustly; yet this arose not from will but from shame: “For among the French it was deemed disgraceful to break an oath publicly sworn, however wrongly; although no wise man doubts that unlawful oaths are not to be kept,” etc. [Col. 0355C]

“Through a certain one of his servants.” Thus the old manuscript, as in Letters 65, 116, 121, and 135.

[Col. 0355D]

## ON LETTER CVII

“At the ends of the earth.” As in Letter 278, “at the furthest parts of the sea,” because the Britons were utterly separated from the whole world; so Virgil, *Eclogues* 1. Heric, book III of the *Life of St Germanus of Auxerre*, describing Britain:

> The records of earlier fathers report  
> That Ocean has encircled the earth’s farthest edge  
> With its everlasting boundary.  
> Here indeed it had made an end of the squared world,  
> Where swift waves lash the Gallic shores,  
> Had not that island, vast in its expanse of lands,  
> Almost given its name to another world—  
> Britain, as the decree of the ancients calls it.  
> [lacuna]

“Mary, Queen of Angels.” These words have been added from an old manuscript; they were formerly lacking.

## ON LETTER CVIII

“That this ill will had arisen from no other source.” The name [Col. 0356A] of the archbishop of Tours, suppressed here, can be supplied from the heading of Letter 235, where he is called Rodulf; from reading that letter and Letter 234 it is likewise clear that at this time grave and bitter disputes had arisen between that archbishop and the abbot and monks of Marmoutier. Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, incidentally mentions this matter in his letter to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, found among the letters of Geoffrey of Vendôme (*Patrologia*, vol. CLIX). There he emphasizes the monks’ pride and reproves them for disparaging their own bishop.

I found a fuller account of this controversy in a manuscript tract by an old anonymous monk of the aforesaid monastery, preserved in the library of Laurent Bouchel, advocate of Paris. Its words are these:

> “These enemies who had hitherto afflicted us were none other than those who should have guarded and defended us as sons and brethren: namely, Rodulf [Note: [Col. 0355D] He calls him thus in what follows; elsewhere Radulf or Radulph.] archbishop of Tours [Col. 0356B] with his clergy.”
>
> And he immediately adds:
>
> “What they intended was most difficult and intolerable even to hear—something their predecessors had not dared—to reduce, after the fashion of the other monasteries of their diocese, in which they are accustomed to riot in unbecoming wantonness and, in secular fashion [old manuscript: *secculari*], shameful to relate, the monastery from which religion had taken its beginning and increase throughout many lands, to this greater disgrace. Yet we had never hitherto denied them, whether from a custom whose origin or date we do not know, unless perhaps because of the ancient veneration and affection due to the place, that the archbishop should solemnly celebrate the Paschal station in our monastery; although we lamented that many evils, even homicides, had resulted from it. This continued until, under the cover of permission granted, they began to demand unlawful things, and modern abuse turned into mockery and buffoonery that which ancient religion had customarily done in devotion.
>
> “Therefore, although we offered justice and a peaceful settlement, in whatever court they wished, concerning all the complaints they had against us, they were angered and took it ill because every matter did not proceed at their nod. The archbishop acted impatiently against us and, without any regard for God or men, rashly launched excommunication against us and our house. Everywhere he defamed us before kings and princes, marked us out to be avoided as heathens and publicans, and incited bishops of various provinces to inflict the same sentence upon us as rebels and profane persons. Thus their indignation and our humiliation grew so great that their retainers arrogantly despised our elders, who had formerly been revered even by kings, when they saw them cast down from their horses, robbed of their goods, subjected to injuries and insults, and crying as they were driven through marshes.” [Col. 0356C]
>
> Then follows:
>
> “In this danger we sought counsel and aid from Lord Amatus, legate of the Apostolic See and archbishop of the Church of Bordeaux. Greatly pitying our affliction, he declared void the excommunication which the archbishop of Tours and his accomplices had attempted against us. [Col. 0356D] For he himself had previously excommunicated that same Archbishop Rodulf for certain offences (compare the note on Letter 73); and he firmly declared that we were more guilty in having in any way obeyed one who was disobedient to him and communicated with one excommunicated by him than in having reasonably resisted his rashness and obstinacy. Having forgiven that offence and imposed penance, he strictly commanded us thereafter neither to communicate with him nor in any manner to observe his binding sentence, but everywhere to put forward the legate as our defender and advocate in this matter.”
>
> And below:
>
> “Accordingly, at that time, while a certain council was sitting at Brioude, our brethren were sent there as delegates. Our cause was discussed according to the foregoing account and carefully examined; it was found sound and irreproachable and was approved by all, in the presence of that Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, of whom we have often complained, and his agents. Shame itself marked their faces, because, whereas they had thought to bind us, they themselves were judged more bound and more blameworthy.” [Col. 0357A]
>
> A little later he adds:
>
> “Lord Hugh, vicar of the Roman See and primate of the Gauls, the metropolitan of Lyons, presided over this synodal decision. The archbishops of Auch and Narbonne sat with him, together with many bishops and abbots from various provinces. But the stubborn, inveterate obduracy of those cruel men who lay in wait for us could not be softened by the counsel of so many wise charmers, nor could the affection of their perverse mind, once glued and confederated with hatred, be torn from it.
>
> “Not long afterward another council was held at Autun by the aforesaid venerable primate and archbishop, Lord Hugh. Present there were our tireless antagonist Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, and Lord Hoel, bishop of Le Mans, his suffragan and supporter; many administrators of ecclesiastical offices gathered from every quarter; and those same brethren of ours, whom we noted at the earlier council [Col. 0357B], together with some others. The causes of both parties were rehearsed. The more carefully ours was investigated, the more surely and honourably it was found; the more theirs was examined, the more blameworthy it appeared.”
>
> A little later, speaking of those there reconciled, he says:
>
> “But, as the event afterward proved, they consented to this peace not so much out of true charity as because of synodal rebuke and the inexcusable shame of a just denunciation. What they did not have in their hearts they feigned in their faces. For as soon as they had departed, they destroyed whatever had been decreed and, as though provoked after receiving a blow, rose more bitterly against us with unprecedented slanders and plots.”
>
> After a few intervening words he adds:
>
> “Finally, at the conference of Dol, [Col. 0357C] held at that time before the primates and legates of the holy Roman Church, namely Lord Hugh and Lord Amatus, of whom we have spoken, and in the presence also of the bishops of Le Mans and Poitiers, many other bishops and abbots, our lord Abbot Bernard, and a very great number of brethren from our community, after the causes had been rehearsed on both sides, it was found and publicly proclaimed before the assembly that Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, who was present in person with his clergy, had been excommunicated by Lord Amatus before the sentence which he had wrongly inflicted upon us. His offences were made clear and set forth; though he wished to excuse himself, he could not. In many further gatherings of priests and courts of princes, wherever they had defamed us, we resisted their shamelessness and obstinacy with fitting reason. Very many who had erred against us at their instigation offered us satisfaction by way of amendment; but they themselves remained in their error and drew with them into error and hatred against us all whom they could.” [Col. 0357D]
>
> He then adds:
>
> “Archbishop Rodulf, persisting in his cruel sentence, sought to strip us from our foundation; but, being himself rather stripped by the judgment of God and driven from his see, he could not halve his days. He had [Col. 0358A] Rodulf of Orléans as successor. This man, taking on his image and power, supplemented to the full, by the reproaches and injuries which he inflicted upon us by that authority, whatever had been lacking in the former’s judgment. Yet at the beginning of his entry he began, under an appearance of kindness, to seek our favour. He strongly condemned the persecution which his predecessor had exercised against us and, with certain of our elders as witnesses to his pledge, promised that he would indissolubly maintain peace and affection toward us and our house, demand nothing from us concerning the aforesaid disputes, and, if we could obtain from the Roman See a privilege of protection, would in every respect be our supporter and helper. Why he promised this to us, when he kept none of it, we do not know—unless perhaps he believed that we intended, though we did not, to injure his appointment. But after he had been enthroned and rendered more secure, he publicly revealed what he bore in his heart.
>
> “This new archbishop therefore undertook to renew his father’s works: to revive the old spirit of persecution against us; publicly to proclaim us excommunicated by the authority of his predecessor and his own; and everywhere to denounce us as rebels against bishops.
>
> “We, therefore, who had hoped to escape the face of the bear, when we perceived that we had fallen more dangerously upon the lion and his cubs [Col. 0358B], and found that neither the patronage of primates nor councils of bishops helped us, were at last compelled by so long and intolerable a persecution to flee to the bosom and wings of the holy Roman Church. There we were received and refreshed. We consequently received a privilege of liberty against the attacks of inferior dignitaries, first from the Apostolic lord who had formerly been abbot of the venerable religious community of the monastery of Monte Cassino; then from his most pious and ever-to-be-embraced successor, Pope Urban.
>
> “Nor do we wish to pass over in silence that this same Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, who had changed his countenance toward us and broken the treaty made with us, when he sought his pallium from blessed Pope Urban, could not obtain it until he had ceased persecuting us and promised Pope Urban, in the presence of certain brethren whom we had sent there, that he would obey him in assenting to our protection and liberty, etc.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0357D] Pope Victor, successor of Gregory VII, previously abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, renowned for its religious life.]
>
> [Col. 0358C]
>
> “When we thought that we held by his pledge a man who could not be held, and rejoiced as if, our labour completed, we had reached rest, we were again compelled, as the flood rose, to return to the Apostolic bosom. Thus both sides were summoned to the council of Clermont. There Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, when, at our complaint, he had been summoned by the lord pope, denied, so far as he could remember, that he had called us excommunicated before the whole council on account of the mark of excommunication which his predecessor had unjustly placed upon us and which he himself had publicly confirmed, although the Apostolic See was in communion with and protecting us. Yet, if such words had ever escaped his mouth, they had proceeded more from agitation or indignation of mind than from deliberation. Although we could establish by the testimony of lawful persons what he had proclaimed in his councils and thundered throughout almost all Gaul, we considered ourselves sufficiently satisfied, with the assent of all present. All declared that it was more advantageous for us and more honourable than any amendment—and more disgraceful for him—to retract with his own mouth in a public council what we could prove he had publicly said.”
>
> He then adds:
>
> “After this the lord pope ordered the privilege which he had granted us to be read before all. He allowed Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, and his clergy, and all others who wished to be his supporters—indeed also those who, inclining to neither side, attended solely to justice—to oppose, if they could do so canonically, the privilege and Roman authority. While those burdened by the case barked obstinately, those of sound judgment responded in peaceful acclamation, assenting to justice. The lord pope imposed silence and, etc., confirmed our privilege: namely, that no bishop, as blessed Gregory forbids, should dare to celebrate a public station in the house of Marmoutier because of the disturbance of God’s servants; that no bishop should demand a profession from the abbot of Marmoutier; and that no bishop should dare to impose excommunication upon the house of Marmoutier or upon any of its monks, whoever he might be, except the Roman pontiff, who had received them into the bosom of his fatherly care to protect and sustain them because of the aforesaid necessities. The brethren of the monastery, however, should receive the other sacraments of ecclesiastical discipline from the archbishop of Tours, provided only that he was catholic and established in apostolic favour. Otherwise, they should have the right, without any impediment, to receive their ordinations and consecrations from the Roman supreme pontiff [Col. 0359A], or wherever else they pleased.”
>
> After a few intervening words follows:
>
> “This determination, or settlement, of Marmoutier’s liberty was made at the council of Clermont by Pope Urban, in the octave of St Martin, archbishop of the city of Tours, in the year 1093 from the Lord’s Incarnation, while King Philip reigned in Gaul. Present was the aforementioned Rodulf, archbishop, with whom we had our dispute, and his clergy. They wished indeed to object; but because they could not give a reason, they fell silent before the inviolable reasoning of the Apostolic See. Present likewise were our lord Abbot Bernard and, among our monks, Lord Rangerius, cardinal, who was archbishop of Reggio,” etc. [Col. 0359B]

[Col. 0359C] In the same old copy follows the testimony of Arnulf, archbishop of the see of Tours. From it one may infer that, even after the foregoing decrees of councils, the evil practices at Marmoutier had not ceased—practices which this bishop expresses somewhat more clearly and was compelled again to forbid:

> “When, according to the aforesaid custom, once a year—namely on the fourth day of the Paschal solemnity—I was going to that place to perform what was my official duty, the place called Marmoutier because St Martin is believed first to have served God there and instituted monastic life, I discovered that certain practices attended my arrival which made our visitation hateful rather than welcome to the inhabitants of that place. For very many who pretended to come with me for the sake of the holy celebration, both lay and clerical, had so forgotten all propriety that, despising the things of God and abandoning the celebration of Masses, they violently broke into the cloisters of the monastery, irreverently violated the monks’ seclusion, and, with shameless brow, demanded that feasts be provided for them in places appointed for divine worship, as though by customary payment. I learned that these evils had grown so great that, through the occasion of this disgraceful demand, certain sacrileges and almost homicides were committed.
>
> “Desiring to put an end to these miseries, I decree [Col. 0359D] that no one whatsoever shall thereafter demand or commit the things we have mentioned, but that all things, as the Apostle says, be done with charity. Thus our coming to holy places may more properly be called a fatherly visitation than tyrannical plundering or a hostile incursion. Whoever therefore wishes to come there with me must come with a pious and God-devoted purpose: that is, to hear what belongs to God’s praise, to seek what concerns the soul’s salvation, choosing to refresh the mind with spiritual food rather than burden the body with shameful banqueting; demanding no due in that place, presuming through no rashness to violate the monks’ inner retreats, and disturbing their tranquillity with no vexation. Let him endeavour so to return to his own home that he expects the recompense of his visitation from God alone, so that God’s servants may not be troubled by any importunity of those who come with us and our visitation may be more welcome than hateful to them. Therefore, desiring in no way that their peace be disturbed, by the authority of this present command we forbid any of our successors, when holding a station at the aforesaid monastery, to cause any disturbance to God’s servants or to consent to those wishing to cause it. That this command may remain irrevocable and may be more certainly believed to have been issued by us, we and many of our faithful persons then standing with us have marked it below with our own signs,” etc. [Col. 0360A]

Moreover, relevant to the same issue is what a certain John, monk of Marmoutier, writes in the *History of Geoffrey, Duke of the Normans and Count of Anjou*. I cite his words from an old manuscript:

> “Frequent and extensive controversy arose between the count himself and the archbishop of Tours. It happened on one occasion that they openly disputed. The archbishop, stirred by bile, said to the count: ‘Because you inflict such and such injuries upon the property of the Church over which, by God’s authority, I preside, know for certain that I shall excommunicate you.’ The count, unmoved, with a calm voice and expression, said: ‘My lord bishop, I do not refuse either to clear myself of the charge of injuries which you make against me or to amend it if convicted. But I do not at all fear the threats of your excommunication which you add.’
>
> “When he heard this, the bishop, grieving more over the contempt than the injuries, said: ‘You do not fear my sentence? You increase the injuries inflicted by insolence, and by contempt of us you offend the divine majesty. Are you not my parishioner? Ought I not, as your pastor, to have care for your soul?’
>
> “To this the count replied with a smile: ‘Good pastor, attend to those for whom you ought to provide, and have care for those entrusted to you. Do you, then, exercise lordship over the canons of St Martin and the monks of Marmoutier? But I am both a canon of St Martin and a monk of Marmoutier. Therefore restrain your jurisdiction, limit your power, and exercise upon your own people the sentence with which you threatened me.’ Thus the wise man escaped the bishop’s unjust sentence and demonstrated how highly he valued the privileges of churches.” [Col. 0360B]

[Col. 0360C] “And every harmful thing.” These words, together with the seven words connected with them, have been added on the authority of old parchment manuscripts; they were previously missing.

“To celebrate public Masses at Marmoutier, to act imperiously toward the monks, to usurp the monastery’s goods at will.” In a similar sense Anselm, abbot of Bec, writing to Urban that the monastery of Bec be honoured with some privilege, says: “For I think it is not unknown to Your Excellency that many bishops delight not so much in nourishing monasteries with fatherly affection and instructing them with episcopal care as in burdening them with a certain harsh domination and their own will.” Ivo too, Letter 193, reproves Geoffrey, bishop of Beauvais, for violating the privileges of the monks of St Quentin and wearying them with exactions. Gregory VII, II.69, reproves Cunibert, bishop of Turin, for afflicting the monks of St Michael with vexations.

Nevertheless, because of various abuses connected with these exemptions of abbots from episcopal jurisdiction—whether granted by apostolic authority or by forged bulls—Peter of Blois, archdeacon, discusses the matter at length in Letter 68 to Pope Alexander III. St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, in *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius, III.4, complains that there were no churches, or few, which did not suffer or fear this plague. He adds that the supreme pontiff, by withdrawing abbots from bishops, archbishops from bishops, and so forth, proves that he possesses fullness of power, though perhaps not likewise fullness of justice; he does this because he can, but whether he ought to do it is a question. To these should be added the passages in John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus*, VII.21. [Col. 0360D]

## ON LETTER CX

“Galon, our brother and fellow bishop.” Eadmer, II of the *Life of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury*, testifies that he saw at Rome this Galon, whom he calls Walon: “Meanwhile,” he says, “Walo, bishop of Paris, came to us—a man of good religious character, imbued from his earliest age with the institutions of ecclesiastical observance; known at Rome and employed in the service of the apostolic legation, he enjoyed the friendship of Father Anselm.” Although Ivo does not designate the episcopal see in this letter, comparison with other passages makes it clear that Beauvais is intended; see the notes on Letter 104. Baronius therefore rightly observes, *Annals*, XII, under the year of Christ 1104, that this Galon is called sometimes bishop of Beauvais and sometimes bishop of Paris, yet is by no means a different man because of the different bishoprics. He was first consecrated bishop of Beauvais and then, through the king’s persecution, transferred to Paris. Ivo testifies in Letters 104 and 105 that he was elected by the people of Beauvais. But Ivo indicates at the end of Letter 144 that he was transferred from Beauvais to Paris with the king’s consent. He therefore addresses several letters to Galon, bishop of Paris—Letters 169, 218, and 243—and Letter 193 also concerns him. The passage in Letter 144 concerns this Galon, where Ivo says that Pope Paschal imposed certain words on Bishop Galon concerning the absolution of King Philip. He subsequently took part in the coronation of King Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, as the continuator of Aimoin, *History*, V.50, reports. Suger, in his *Life of the said Louis*, writes that, when Pope Urban II was in Gaul, he stoutly answered before him the many complaints with which this Galon assailed the church of St Denis, by open reasoning and canonical judgment. [Col. 0361B]

## ON LETTER CXIII

“We rejoice with pious exultation.” This is the sounder reading than “with trembling” in one ancient manuscript. A similar error lies at the beginning of book V of Robert the Monk’s *History of Jerusalem*: “When the Babylonian envoys approached and saw so many people trembling with such great joy, they wondered.” It should be corrected to: “leaping for joy with such great gladness.” For he says in the same way in book IV: “How great was the joy and exultation of leaping on that day in the camp.” The abbot of Ursberg in his *Chronicle*: “Received with the incredible exultation of the whole city and of many peoples, he was most honourably enthroned.” Sigebert in his *Chronicle*: “With great exultation of both clergy and people they went out to meet the king of the Franks.” Berthold in his *Chronicle*: “At last the pope returned to the apostolic see with great glory and exultation.” Examples of this usage are countless. [Col. 0361C]

## ON LETTER CXVII
