“They received [it] so gratefully.” Thus the better manuscripts, as in Letters 110, 141, and 144; one old manuscript has *gnaviter* (“vigorously, diligently”). In the formerly published text, *graviter* (“seriously, heavily”).

## ON LETTER CXX
Even if I should consider whether [it is] justly or unjustly. The first edition had *etiamsi praeessem* (“even if I were in charge”), as do some manuscripts; in others, *etiam si possem* (“even if I could”). But the reading of the Saint-Germain manuscript, *etiamsi pensem* (“even if I should weigh/consider”), seemed truer. [Col. 0361D] *Pensare* in the sense of “to consider” is frequent, as in Letters 25, 33, 180, and 250, and in Pope Saint Gregory I.

## ON LETTER CXXI

“And throughout the whole bishopric I shall forbid the divine office.” Here one should note the custom of that age, in which the celebration of the divine office was customarily prohibited publicly when someone seized and invaded property belonging to another’s right. It is not easy to conjecture at what time that custom began. Examples may be produced from Pope Gregory VII: in Book VII, Letter 16 of the *Register*, to Hubert, bishop of Thérouanne, where he forbids every divine office to all the canons of the castle of Saint-Pol—Hubert alone being for the present excepted until a hearing—and to them and their places, until they have canonically restored the town, with its church and other appurtenances, to the church of Saint Mary and Saint Omer, and have made satisfaction before Hugh, bishop of Die, for their disobedience and excommunication.

The same pope, in the same Book VII, Letter 18, commands William, archbishop of Auch, [Col. 0362A] to compel the abbot of Pézenas to restore to the monastery of Aurillac the church concerning which there was litigation. If perchance he should, hardened in a spirit of pride, refuse to comply, he orders the divine office to be forbidden to that monastery which has been invaded, and every entrance into the church to the invader.

## ON LETTER CXXV

Daimbert. Some manuscripts wrongly read Humbert. Many letters of the author to this man survive. The Auxerre chronology, under the year 1096: “After Richer, Daimbert, vice-lord of that church, presided over the church of Sens.” The same work, under the year 1120: “After Daimbert, Henry surnamed Aper presided over the church of Sens.”

## ON LETTER CXXVII

“There is a truce between me and the countess until the arrival of the bishop of Albano.” Thus all copies read, as also a little later: “Therefore, during this truce it is neither lawful nor honourable for me to seek [Col. 0362B] any harm against her.” The same author, Letter 134: “Since there was also a truce between me and the countess through the apostolic see.” This was a term of that age, also used by Rigord in Book I, *On the Deeds of Philip Augustus, King of the French*, in the chapter on the establishment of tithes: “They shall have a reprieve from the next feast of All Saints after the day of the lord king’s departure, for two years.” And shortly afterwards: “He shall have a reprieve concerning his debt according to the arrangement made.” And immediately: “He shall have a reprieve concerning that debt until the next feast of All Saints, provided that good security is given for making peace on that matter then.”

Likewise: “For all debts for which a reprieve is granted, the debtor must give equally good surety, or better, than he had previously given.” [168] Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, Letter 75 to Abbot Gauslin: “But I, not without experience of your correction, granted him a reprieve on 29 September.” Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres: “In your kindness you instructed me that you had accepted, between me and her, [Col. 0362C] a reprieve either for pleading or for making an agreement until the feast of the blessed saint.”

## ON LETTER CXXIX

“And the *cataneus* of our Church.” This is indeed the reading of the first edition, and it occurs in many manuscripts, except one, which has *capitaneus*. Some think the wording has been shortened: that from *capitaneus* ancient scribes made *captaneus*, whence later *cataneus*. Certainly the ancient author Romuald II, archbishop of Salerno, continuator of the as-yet-unpublished book *On the Life and Character of All Princes*, now kept in the library of the king of France, used this word near the end of the book: “And the countess of Berthenora, with William of Markysella, a noble Ferrarese *cataneus*, was coming with a great multitude of knights and foot-soldiers to relieve that city.”

Who were designated by the name *capitanei* may be learned from the books of fiefs. In Ivo’s time, moreover, churches endowed by royal munificence already had many military [Col. 0362D] vassals, as the author’s words in Letter 28 to King Philip indicate: Philip had ordered Ivo to come forth attended by an armed force. In Letter 153, too, he reproaches the count of Meulan because he held cheap the benefice of the Church of Chartres, which seemed great to other great men. Here *beneficium* must be understood as a military fief; this is a conjecture. Others, more acute, may interpret the matter better.

## ON LETTER CXXXI

“To adulterate one who is lawfully incardinated to him.” This is an excellent emendation drawn from three manuscripts: one in the Royal Library, another of Saint-Victor, and a third of Saint-Germain. Other copies, as also the first edition, read *incarnatus* (“incarnated”). Cardinal priests existed not only in the city of Rome but also elsewhere, where *tituli*, that is, parishes, were customarily entrusted to them. In Canon 15 of the Council of Neocaesarea: “That neither baptisteries be built in the same place in future times, nor a cardinal priest appointed.”

This title is frequently mentioned in the letters of Pope Saint Gregory I, in whom a cardinal priest or bishop occurs in Book I, Letters 78 and 79; likewise a cardinal priest appointed by a bishop in Book II, chapter 9; Book VII, Letter 71; Book VIII, Letter 3; and Book X, Letter 34. A priest is also called *incardinatus* when he has been ordained, Book II, Letter 25. The same author mentions incardination in Book I, Letter 81: “If he has not been made a cardinal priest by your predecessor, one must refrain from his incardination.”

The received editions of Gratian had corrupted that word in the chapter *Fraternitatem*, Distinction 71, where the words are reported of Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, Book V, Letter 111: “We recall that you requested us to grant Gratian, deacon of the Church of Venafro, to your Church to be incardinated.” Others substituted: “to be ordained for the Church.” Likewise in the canon *Pastoralis*, Cause 7, Question 1: “If the aforesaid city is oppressed by the continuous calamity of captivity, you ought to remain in this Church in which you have been incardinated by us.” There he treats of John, a bishop whom he had made a cardinal priest from the captive [Col. 0363B] city of Lisbon.

Priests and deacons were formerly called cardinals because they were first in rank and of chief authority. For whatever was principal was designated by the name *cardinalis*. Hence Servius Honoratus, in two places in Book I of the *Aeneid*, calls four winds cardinal; Saint Augustine calls the chief men of Donatus’ party cardinals, Book I, *On Baptism against the Donatists*; Aurelius Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book VII, chapter 31, in the formula for the prefecture of the city of Rome, mentions a cardinal prince in the service of the Gothic king; and Marianus Scotus in his *Chronicle* calls the praetorian prefect of the East a most illustrious and cardinal man. In the ancient *Notitia of the Two Empires* it is also said that the office of the mastership of the present power is held as cardinal; and elsewhere, that the office of the mastership of the power throughout the East is held as cardinal.

Moreover, the functions of these cardinals were distinct, and it was not lawful for them, because of the dignity of their place, to put a sickle into another’s harvest. This is indicated by these words of Pope Paschal II in a letter to Diego, bishop of Compostela, in Baronius, Volume XII of the *Annals*: “The Church which, by God’s ordering, you have undertaken to govern has long lacked the assistance of a pastor, even though it might appear to have one.” And shortly afterwards: “Appoint in your Church such cardinal priests or deacons as can worthily bear the burdens of ecclesiastical government committed to them. Further, let those matters which concern priests be entrusted to priests, and those which concern deacons to deacons; but let no one intrude to another’s detriment.” [Col. 0363C] Read Onuphrius’ treatise on cardinals.

“To draw the sword of anathema.” Thus the better books, while others have “to exercise.” Although the latter can be defended, the former reading is preferable. In other authors these two words are often interchanged: in Law IV, *On the Collation of the Founders’ Patrimony*, “in which vengeance is to be exercised,” for “drawn forth”; in Law XXII, *On the Public Post*, in the Theodosian Code: “The fitting vengeance must be drawn”; and in Law XII, *On Bakers*, in the same Code: “The fitting penalty shall be exacted.” Victor of Cartenna, *On Penance*, chapter 7: “By right, a sevenfold punishment was brought to bear against him.”

## ON LETTER CXXXIII

“Your caustic words.” This is the reading of the first edition, which I later found confirmed by the authority and agreement of many ancient manuscripts. But it varies in other old copies: they have “your austere words,” as may be seen in the Saint-Germain manuscript and that of Nicolas Faber. In the margin of Cujas’s book another reading is noted: “your chastising words,” which appears to have flowed into later texts from glosses. Since *caustica verba* (“caustic words”) was a rarer or more obscure expression, pedantic scribes long ago interpolated the passage. The author has a similar expression in Letter 277 to Aldebert: “Do not take my words harshly, although they are somewhat caustic and biting.”

“I took severe notice.” Two old manuscripts have *gravati*, perhaps for *gravate*.

[Col. 0364A] “When it shall be struck back by the light of truth.” Thus the better books. Others read: “when, having soon been struck back by the light of truth.”

“[It] holds sway in almost every Gallican Church.” An ancient author in the *Life of Saint Eligius, Bishop of Noyon*, Book II, chapter 1, says: “The Simoniac heresy was sprouting monstrously in the cities and throughout all the territories of the kingdom of the Franks, especially from the time of Queen Brunhild. Therefore Pope Saint Gregory, in a letter written to the kings of the Franks, had admonished them to endeavour to prohibit from the borders of the realm the detestable evil of the Simoniac heresy and of neophytes.”

The author of the historical fragment from Robert to the death of Philip, around the year of the Lord 1037: “Pope Leo came into France and assembled at Rheims a council of many bishops [169] and abbots, in which he smote with the sword of anathema the Simoniac heresy that had spread over almost the whole of Gaul, humbling many whom that plague had exalted, and restoring the enactments of the holy Fathers, which had been almost abolished among the Gauls.”

Glaber, *History*, Book V, chapter 5, “On the Extirpation of Simony”: “Therefore, when this same Henry perceived that the covetous desire of Simoniac avarice was raging throughout Gaul and Germany, he caused both the chief archbishops and the other bishops to be assembled from all his empire, and addressed them in the following manner,” etc. There it is said that, when the bishops had been severely rebuked by the king for this spiritual robbery, they had no answer, because they feared that on account of this fault they would lose their own sees. He then adds: “The bishops too, seeing that they were entangled in a grave accusation, implored the aid of mercy. But the prince, moved by mercy, offered this word of consolation: ‘Go,’ he said, ‘and strive to dispose rightly of what you have received unlawfully; and remember to intercede more earnestly for the soul of my father, who is held guilty with you in this offence, so that you may obtain from God forgiveness for him for this crime,’” etc.

“The Roman Church suffered, nor from the bosom…” Not Ivo alone, but many other contemporary writers testified to the same thing. Rodulfus Glaber, *History*, Book V, final chapter, in the address of King Henry on simony: “It is therefore most manifest that because of this offence diverse calamities have come upon the children of men—namely famine and mortality, and also the sword. For all ecclesiastical ranks, from the highest bishop to the doorkeeper, are oppressed by the price of their own condemnation; and, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, spiritual robbery rages everywhere.” And shortly afterwards: “And because this most wicked depravity had sprung up not only among Gallican bishops, but had occupied all Italy much more extensively, all ecclesiastical ministries at that time were for sale, like secular merchandise in a marketplace.”

At the end of the chapter he adds: “At that same time the Roman see also, which is rightly held to be universal throughout the world, had suffered most miserably from the aforesaid pestilential disease for a period of twenty-five years. For a certain boy, about [Col. 0364D] twelve years old, had been appointed to that see against law and right; money in gold and silver alone commended him more than age or holiness. And because he had an unhappy entrance, he experienced a more unhappy end.”

“The Church endures Judas the traitor among her members; it praises Nicholas, the defender of a fornicator.” Thus read all the old copies which I have used. Yet the writer of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, when citing this passage, adds an asterisk and a lacuna, in this form: “It endures Judas the traitor among its members, [lacuna] the Church [praises] Nicholas, [defender] of a fornicator”; and “Antiochene” is added in the margin. But the author’s statement is general, and writers contemporary with Ivo indicate that it does not pertain to Antioch alone, testifying that several other churches were polluted with the Nicolaitan stain.

At the Roman synod under Gregory VII in 1088: “A sentence of anathema was pronounced against all Simoniacs and Nicolaitan heretics hardened in the sect of their error.” Peter Damian, in a letter to Rodulf, Vitalis, and others: “The heresy of the Nicolaitans, which seemed rooted out through your and our labours, is springing up again. God wishes to test the constancy of his own. Behold: those who were formerly held by the snares of the Nicolaitan and Simoniac heresy are now, to crown their destruction, perjurers after violating an oath. Yet this is not new in the Church of Milan, which has always had men of diverse doctrine, from the beginning established by Auxentius and Ambrose.”

Bertold, under the year of the Lord 1095, speaking of the Council of Piacenza under Urban II: “There too the heresy of the Nicolaitans—that is, of incontinent subdeacons, deacons, and especially priests—was condemned without qualification, so that henceforth those who do not fear to remain in that heresy may not concern themselves with ecclesiastical office, nor may the people in any way receive their ministrations if those Nicolaitans presume to minister contrary to these prohibitions.” Abbot Urspergensis, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1105, treating of the general council held in the royal town called Northusum: “The fornicating intercourse of the Nicolaitans [Col. 0365B] was there also renounced by all.”

## ON LETTER CXXXV

“With ecclesiastical rigour having been brought to bear.” Thus in all the old manuscripts, as also in the first edition; there is no need for anyone to alter it and read “of the assembled [rigour].”

“We took away his arms.” For by pontifical law a penitent soldier was forbidden to gird himself with arms, chapter *Admonere*, Cause 33, Question 2; nor was it thereafter lawful for him to bear them except by the counsel of bishops, in defence of justice, chapter *Falsas poenitentias*, *On Penance*, Distinction 5. At the synod near Worms in the time of Emperor Louis, as Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, reports: “Whoever, having abandoned his lawful wife or killed her without cause, takes another wife, shall lay down his arms and perform public penance; and if he is obstinate, he shall be seized by the count and bound in irons.” Sigebert in his *Chronicle*: “Emperor Louis, abandoned and betrayed by his followers [Col. 0365C] and reduced to the power of his sons, laid down his arms by the judgment of bishops and was confined to perform penance.”

## ON LETTER CXXXVI

“Helpers in all things.” In one old manuscript, after these words, a blank space of several lines has been left.

## ON LETTER CXXXVIII

“With the connivance of the suffragans.” Thus several manuscripts; the Saint-Germain book has *convenientia* (“agreement”), a variation frequent in other places. See the notes on Letter 220.

## ON LETTER CXLI

“Whose hatred I have now endured for ten years.” From this Baronius, Volume XII of the *Annals*, notes that this letter was written by Ivo in the year of Christ 1104, the fifth year of Pope Paschal’s pontificate.

“Or to come to Troyes by a circuitous route.” The author of Letter 258 mentions this council, held by Richard of Albano.

## ON LETTER CXLIV

[Col. 0365D]

“The king’s absolution.” Concerning this, above in Letter 141, the continuator of Aimoin, *History of the Franks*, Book V, chapter 50, reports that Philip, after being bound by the pope with the bond of anathema, at length feared the sentence after several years; as the end of his life approached, he came to his senses, sought pardon, and dismissed his concubine Bertrada, by whom he had begotten Philip and Florus, and the countess of Tripoli.

This absolution was solemnly performed at Paris, as is recorded in the fragment of an ancient author’s history of the Franks from Robert to the death of King Philip. For after saying that Philip had been excommunicated by Cardinals John and Benedict, whom Pope Paschal had sent into Gaul, he adds: “Not long afterwards, the same king, pierced in heart, sent certain of his men to Rome, promising that he would obey the pope in whatever he commanded, provided only that he might deserve to be absolved. The pope sent to him [170] two men of honourable life from his own side, to release him from the bond of anathema. Coming to the king at Paris in the presence of a great assembly of nobles, they did as had been ordered: namely, they received him into the communion of the faithful, but on this condition, that he should not thereafter have intercourse with Bertrada, nor speak with her except in the presence of two men of good testimony. He had, however, already had by her Philip and the woman whom Tancred afterwards took in marriage.”

Moreover, after Philip had been released from anathema, some say that near the end of his life he adopted the monastic habit, intending by that outward form to erase the offences of his former life; Bertrada, his concubine, did the same. The words of William of Malmesbury, *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*, Book V, plainly state this: “Meanwhile Philip’s insane drunkenness had no respite until, stricken by a final illness, he took the monastic habit at Fleury. More nobly and more fortunately did she”—whom a little earlier he calls the countess of Anjou—“seek the veil among the nuns at Fontevraud while age and health were intact and her beauty not yet wrinkled. Nor long afterward did she bid farewell to the present life: perhaps God providing that the body of a delicate woman could not serve the labours of religion.” [Col. 0366B]

“The king, crying out, insisted.” This has been supplied on the authority of old manuscripts. In a similar case may be mentioned the action of King Philip Augustus. When, in 1201, he had received his wife Ingeborg again into some degree of favour and had temporarily separated from himself Mary, whom he had brought in: “A council was summoned at Soissons by Octavian and John of Saint-Paul, cardinal priest and legates of the apostolic see. The king attended with archbishops, bishops, and the princes of the whole realm; and for fifteen days there was discussion concerning the confirmation or dissolution of Queen Ingeborg’s marriage. But after various and many disputations by legal experts, the king, wearied by the long delay, left the cardinals and bishops there and departed very early in the morning with his wife Ingeborg, without saluting them. Through his messengers he instructed them that he was taking his wife with him as his own, and did not then wish to be separated from her. When this was heard, the council was dissolved, the cardinals and bishops being astonished, since they had assembled to effect a divorce. John of Saint-Paul then departed altogether in great embarrassment. Octavian, however, remained in France; and thus King Philip on this occasion escaped the hands of the Romans.” So Rigord, in the deeds of Philip’s nineteenth year.

## ON LETTER CXLVI

“But because translations of bishops [may be made] when necessity presses.” Above, at the end of Letter 144, he asks Pope Paschal to order Galon, bishop of Beauvais, transferred from the bishopric of Beauvais to that of Paris. Under canon law, however, translations of bishops are disapproved unless necessity and clear common utility require them, so that the see, not the mind, may be changed. This matter is treated in the canon *Mutationes*, chapter *Temporis qualitas*, Cause 7, Question 1, and in Book I, Title 7, “On the Translation of Bishops,” of Gregory’s Decretals.

Innocent III severely rebukes a cardinal, legate of the apostolic see, because on his own initiative he had presumed to transfer the bishop of Troia from the Church of Troia to that of Palermo; this is in chapter 3, *Nisi*, “On the Office of a Legate.” Zonaras, Volume III, reports that Agapetus, Roman pontiff, disapproved a bishop’s translation made by Justinian without cause. Likewise Eugenius III refused to confirm the transfer of Bishop Guicmar of Sice, whom Frederick had elected to preside over the Church of Magdeburg, as Otto of Freising relates, Book II, chapter 8. There it is said that such translations ought to be preceded by far greater agreement of clergy and people than other elections, and certain bishops of Germany are criticized for attending to what pleased an earthly prince.

But after Eugenius’ death, the emperor obtained from his successor Anastasius ratification of his act, with a [Col. 0367A] pallium, not without scandal to some who had heard the Romans declare from their own lips that they held it immovably fixed that this should never happen. Thus the authority of the prince grew greatly in arranging not only secular but also ecclesiastical affairs, as Otto writes in the said Book II, chapter 10. Paschal II also granted Jordan to the Milanese and restored Grossolanus to the place from which he had been transferred, because the translation seemed to have turned to the harm of souls and bodies. The author, the Abbot of Ursperg, records this in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1116.

Examples of bishops translated long before are nevertheless found in Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 36; Theodore Balsamon, in his interpretation of Canon 15 of the Council of Nicaea; Burchard, *Decrees*, Book I, final chapter; and Ivo himself in the preface to his *Decree*, or below in Letter 188. To this belong the words of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury:

“To his dearest lord Henry, by God’s grace king of the English and duke of the Normans, Anselm archbishop [Col. 0367B] offers faithful service with prayers. Your graciousness instructed me through the bishop-elect of Winchester to write to you whether Lord Hervé, bishop of Bangor, could be made bishop in the Church of Lisieux. I do not understand how this could readily be done. For just as no bishop ought to be consecrated for any church without the assent and counsel of the archbishop and the other bishops of the whole province, so one who has been consecrated bishop cannot canonically be made bishop in another province without the counsel and assent of the archbishop and bishops of that province, together with apostolic authority; nor without release by the archbishop and bishops of the province in which he was consecrated. Such a release cannot be made without the serious and common consideration and counsel of those without whom, as I have said, he could not be consecrated. May almighty God direct you in this and in your other actions. Amen.”

I have copied this in full from ancient parchments because it had not yet been published in print.

## ON LETTER CXLIX

[Col. 0367C] “In the Church of Lisieux.” This spelling is consistently found in Ivo’s ancient parchments, including Letters 153, 154, and 157, lest anyone perhaps think that it was a printer’s error: already in the first edition *Luxoviensis* is everywhere read, whereas today *Lexoviensis* is commonly written, to distinguish it from the monastery of Luxeuil. Some think that monastery was formerly called *Lussedium*, on the basis of two passages in an ancient author, Book I, chapter 21, of the *Life of Saint Eligius, Bishop of Noyon*, in Surius. Incidentally, Surius attributes that work to Audoenus, archbishop of Rouen, surnamed Dado; yet from chapters 8 and 12 it may be inferred that it had a different author. The old spelling also remains in other writers, as in Anselm of Canterbury’s letter to Henry: “whether he could be made bishop in the Church of Lisieux.” Peter the Venerable likewise calls him bishop of Lisieux.

## ON LETTER CLI

[Col. 0367D] “Odo, once a brother, but now an enemy.” This complaint against Odo, confirmed by Geoffrey, bishop of Beauvais, gives grounds for the conjecture that he is the man whom Anselm of Canterbury, in an unpublished letter to Gonherius, says the canons [171] of the said Saint-Quentin of Beauvais wished to remove from his prelacy—not rashly, but for many reasons—and to replace with this Gonherius, although unwilling. For that reason Anselm exhorts him not to withdraw from the honour because of devotion to contemplation. Ivo mentions Gonherius elsewhere, as he does likewise Geoffrey of Beauvais, concerning whom he complains in Letter 193 because he was violating the privileges of the said monastery of Saint-Quentin.

## ON LETTER CLIII

Ranulf, bishop of Durham. Some books read *Ranulfus*. English historians unanimously condemn the wicked character of this most depraved robber, so that Ivo, who knew him, had very just cause to write in Letter 154 that those who had predicted good things of Ranulf ought to change their praise into blame.

William of Malmesbury, shortly after the beginning of Book IV of *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*, speaking of William II: “When he lacked what he might give, poor and exhausted, he turned his mind to plunder. Ranulf the clerk, a man of the lowest birth who by eloquence and cunning had risen to the highest rank, added fuel to his avaricious mind. Whenever a royal edict went forth requiring England to pay a specified tax, he added a double amount: despoiler of the rich, destroyer of the poor, confiscator of other men’s inheritances; an invincible pleader, excessive both in words and deeds, raging alike against the simple and the rebellious, [Note: [Col. 0367] Elsewhere the same author reads, in Book I of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*: “while the king repeatedly laughed and said that he alone was a man who knew how to exert his talent in this way.”] while some repeatedly laughed and said that he alone was a man who knew how to exert his talent in this way, and cared nothing for others’ hatred provided that he pleased his lord, the sacred honours of churches whose pastors had died were, at this man’s instigation, put up for sale. For as soon as the death of any bishop or abbot was heard, the king’s clerk was immediately sent in, to record in writing everything found there and to bring all future revenues into the royal treasury. Meanwhile inquiry was made who might suitably be placed in the deceased man’s position—not by trial of character, but of money—and at last the honour, so to speak, was bestowed naked, though purchased at a high price.

“These things appeared all the more shameful because, in his father’s time, after the death of a bishop or abbot, all revenues were kept whole to be handed over to the incoming pastor, and persons commendable for the merit of their religious life were chosen. But after a few years all had been changed. No one was rich unless he was a money-changer; no cleric unless a pleader; no priest unless, to use a word that is scarcely Latin, a *firmarius* [revenue-farmer]. Any little man of any condition, guilty of any crime, was heard as soon as he appealed to the king’s profit; the noose was loosened from the very jaws of that robber if he promised a royal advantage,” etc. [Col. 0368C]

The same author, at the beginning of Book V, writes: “After William was killed, Henry, elected king, immediately sent an edict throughout England forbidding the injustices established by his brother and Ranulf; and, lest anything be lacking to the joy, Ranulf—the dregs of wickedness—was shut up in the darkness of prison.” The same author, Book III of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*, writes among other things: “This is Ranulf, once chaplain of King William, who, of uncertain birth, rose by eloquence and cunning to the highest rank and became administrator of the entire kingdom.” And shortly after: “By relying on these arts he obtained the bishopric of Durham. He came therefore to Durham and at first acted rather timidly, fearing to offend the saint, who is said to be an especially severe corrector of sinners. But after one and then another offence was committed without punishment, he proceeded so far that, whenever an accused person fled to the church of the saint, he did not hesitate to drag him away—daring a crime unheard of in all previous years.”

Roger of Howden, *Annals*, first part, under William the Younger: “William Rufus, king of the English, returned from Normandy to England and held his court in London at Pentecost; and he gave the bishopric of Durham to Ranulf, whom he had appointed exacter of the affairs of the entire kingdom. Thomas, archbishop of York, promptly consecrated him there.” Shortly afterwards he adds: “The devil, appearing frequently in a dreadful form to many Normans in the woods, spoke much with them concerning the king, Ranulf, and certain others; nor is this surprising. For in their time almost all justice of the laws was silent; with the causes of justice suppressed, money alone held sway among the great.

“Finally, in the same period, Ranulf—contrary to ecclesiastical law and the order of his rank, for he was a priest—first obtained from the king at rent abbeys and then bishoprics whose fathers had departed this life, and every year paid him no small sum of money for each. His power was so great and in a short time grew so much that the king made him the royal pleader and exacter of the whole kingdom. Having obtained such power, he everywhere in England punished certain richer and more prosperous men by taking away their goods and lands, while he continually oppressed poorer men with a heavy and unjust tax. In many ways, both before obtaining the bishopric and while he held it, he afflicted alike greater and lesser men. And this continued until the death of that king. For on the day when the king was killed and perished, he held in his own hand the archbishopric of Canterbury and the bishoprics of Winchester and Salisbury.” [Col. 0369A]

The same historian shortly afterwards, in the *Life of Henry I*: “In the year 1101, Ranulf, bishop of Durham, on 1 February escaped from custody by the greatest cunning, crossed the sea, went to Robert, count of the Normans, and persuaded him to invade England as an enemy,” etc.

Matthew Paris, in his history of Henry I: “At that time the king held in custody Ranulf, bishop of Durham, a perverse man ready for every crime, whom his brother King William had made bishop of Durham and subverter of the realm of the English. Since he was excessively familiar with the said king, the king had appointed him his administrator in the realm, so that he might root up and destroy, seize and squander, and carry together all men’s goods for the benefit of the treasury. But when the wicked king died and Henry was crowned, the king, by the common counsel of the English people, put him in chains. After he escaped from them by bribing his guards with money, he secretly crossed the sea to Normandy and by his exhortation stirred Duke Robert against his brother the king.” The same historian says that he died in the year of the Lord 1133.

Moreover, in the letters of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, mention is made of Bishop Ranulf restored by the king of England to his bishopric and later accused before Pope Paschal II of various crimes; this is thought to refer to this Ranulf. These are the words from Anselm’s interrogatories:

“Anselm: Ranulf, concerning whom I formerly sought your counsel, has been restored to the bishopric by the king. Therefore, if it please you, inquire into his life from our bishops who have now come to you; and concerning him consult his archbishop and me, his primate.

“Paschal: Since Bishop Ranulf has been restored to his own see in accordance with our command, we do not permit his case to pass without examination. For reports of his most grave crimes have been brought to the apostolic see by many people. We therefore wish that, in your presence and in an assembly of bishops, the matters written to us concerning him be fully examined. Once the inquiry has been held, unless he can clear himself with the seventh hand of his order, let him immediately be sent to us with the attestation of our letters. But if, trembling in his conscience, he should refuse to come before our tribunal, let him be expelled through your agency from the Church which he occupies, and let a bishop be appointed in it according to canonical enactments.” [Col. 0369D]

172

## ON LETTER CLIX
…that you may guide the aforesaid king by sound counsels and ecclesiastical laws. William of Malmesbury mentions this Count of Meulan, who enjoyed great favor with Henry I, king of the English, in Book V of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*. His words are these:

> “The king of England compelled the Romans to admire and praise the prudence of the Normans. And, lest anything be lacking to the accumulated splendor of the display, he produced young men of most illustrious birth, the sons of the count of Meulan, to dispute with the cardinals concerning dialectic. When their intricate sophistries could not be resisted because of the quickness of their arguments, the cardinals were not ashamed to confess that the western regions flourished in literary learning more greatly than they had heard or thought possible in their own country.  
>   
> [Col. 0370A] Thus this conference obtained the result that the Apostolic Lord declared that nothing was more just than the cause of the king of the English, more eminent than his wisdom, or more abundant than his eloquence. The father of these boys was Count Robert of Meulan—as I have said—the son of Roger of Beaumont, who founded the monastery of Préaux in Normandy: a man of ancient simplicity and faith. Though William I repeatedly invited him to come to England, where he would be rewarded with possessions lavishly suited to his wishes, he declined, declaring that he wished to cherish the inheritance of his fathers, not to seek or seize overseas and undeserved possessions. He had two sons, this Robert and Henry. Henry, Count of Warwick, a man of gentle and peaceable disposition, led and ended his life in pursuits befitting his character.  
>   
> The other, more astute and, in accordance with his character, inclined to craftiness of heart, acquired by purchase from the king of France, besides his paternal inheritance in Normandy and vast estates in England, the castle called Meulan, which his maternal uncle Hugh, son of Cualerannus, had held. As, in the time of the preceding kings, he advanced gradually into distinction as hope little by little sprang up, so in this king’s age he blossomed into the highest eminence. The king relied on his counsel as though he had consulted a divine sanctuary. He was already—and deservedly—considered to have attained the maturity of judgment: a promoter of concord, a dissuader from discord, and, in whatever he undertook, a most rapid persuader through the force of his eloquence.”

A little later he adds:

> “In judicial assemblies, a champion of justice; in wars, a provider of victory; urging that the lord king and the severity of the laws be upheld—though he himself did not follow those laws, but set them forward; free from treachery toward kings, and its persecutor in others.”

Much later in the same book he reports that the count of Meulan was responsible for Henry I, king of the English, disputing for a long time with Pope Paschal over the practice of investitures, “because he alleged that royal majesty would be greatly diminished if, abandoning the custom of his predecessors, he did not invest the person elected by staff and ring.”

There survives in an ancient manuscript of the library of St. Victor at Paris an epistle of Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, to Ernulf on the same matter:

> “The lord pope”—he speaks of Paschal II—“recently sent the count of Meulan his greeting and blessing, on this condition: that he should favor the liberty of the Church, which hitherto he seemed to resist. Otherwise, he merely barred him from entering church, as he had formerly done in the case of him and the other advisers of the king who shared his designs, in those letters of which I sent you a copy. But because the same count promised me that he would endeavor to make the king obey the pope’s commands, he permitted him entry into the church from which he had been excluded.”

The same William of Malmesbury, in Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, speaking of the same King Henry, says:

> “Having now in all things been refined and matured by his own prudence and the counsel of Robert, count of Meulan, he graciously accepted salutary counsels.”

Ivo mentions Robert, count of Meulan, in Epistle 45, and [calls him] “of Meulan” in Epistle 285.

### “Let him pass to another Church, and as though by a kind of adultery.”

This is quite correctly the reading in the better manuscripts; in others appears “by a certain contrivance” (*quadam machinatione*), less fittingly. By “adultery” he intended to signify bigamy in the case of this bishop Ranulf, who was endeavoring by wicked arts to become bishop of two Churches.

The Church or parish is called the wife of a bishop or priest by the compilers of the ancient canons: by Pope Callixtus in the chapter *Sicut*, Cause 7, Question 1; and the bride of a priest in the Council of Reims, reported in the chapter *Sicut unaquaeque*, Cause 21, Question 3. There it is written that the Church cannot be divided between two men, because she is the wife and bride of Christ, not a prostitute.

Ivo too, in Epistle 131, speaks of “adulterating the bride” and “ascending the bride’s bed,” concerning a priest who had repudiated his Church and wished to recover it while another man still lived who had been lawfully incardinated in it—or, as some manuscripts have it, “incarnated” in it. The same Callixtus says that one enjoys intercourse with the Church, in the aforesaid chapter *Sicut*, Cause 7, Question 1.

Ivo, treating of the same Ranulf in Epistle 153, says: “Let him be removed from the Church of Luxeuil, [Col. 0371A] so that digamy may not be admitted.” He also affirms, in Epistle 66, that no one may become bishop of two Churches. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 15; Rufinus, *History*, Book I, chapter 6; and Epiphanius, *Heresy* 68, write that several Churches cannot be entrusted to one bishop.

In Liutprand of Cremona, Book IV, chapter 3, there is a notable passage about Manasses, bishop of Arles, who, abusing the authority and example of the Apostle Peter and Mark the Evangelist, received from Hugh, then king of Italy, the bishoprics of the Churches of Trent, Verona, and Mantua. Yet for a just cause one and the same bishop may hold two bishoprics, as is reported from Gregory in the chapters *Relatio* and *Illud*, Cause 21, Question 1.

### “They sowed good things.”

This reading in some manuscripts is preferable to the alternative, “they perceived good things,” although the latter can be defended. For he used “to sow good things” in the sense in which others say “to disseminate speech.”

### “That they may break the laws, but [are] perverters of laws.”

The first edition had foisted upon the text “but doctors of laws.” When Baronius perceived that reading to be corrupt, he substituted “breakers” for “perverters,” as may be seen in volume XII of the *Annals*, where he adduces this passage. I have restored “perverters,” following the authority and agreement of the ancient manuscripts, since this plainly is the genuine reading.

## ON EPISTLE CLVII

### “Having received the pastoral staff.”

The whole sequence of the epistle shows that an episcopal staff is meant. The staff is counted among the symbols of pontifical dignity. St Bernard of Clairvaux, in his sermon on baptism, says:

> “As outward signs differ, so investitures differ according to the things with which we are invested. For example, a canon is invested by a book, an abbot by a staff, and a bishop simultaneously by staff and ring. As it is in such matters, so too the divisions of graces are conveyed by diverse sacraments.”

In chapter 3 of the *Book of Sentences*, he says that a bishop holds a rod in his hand in order to correct the gentle more gently, a staff in order to rebuke the hard and wicked more sharply, and, when necessary, to strike with the sentence of anathema.

The ancient and anonymous author of the Life of St Romanus, bishop of Rouen, writes:

> “Accordingly, among the palatine nobles a common agreement was reached concerning the holy man. All unanimously advised the king that Christ’s flock should not be deprived of what it desired, but that the divine election should immediately be brought to effect. Delighted by this counsel, the king summoned both bishops and abbots and bestowed the pastoral staff upon him. Thus he was enthroned in the pinnacle of pontifical office,” etc.

This passage plainly proves the use of the most ancient right by which the kings of Gaul invested the bishops of their kingdom. Romanus flourished under Louis and Clotilde, about the year 623.

There is a memorable story in Rodulfus Glaber, Book V, chapter 1, about Robert, king of the Franks. The abbot of a certain monastery had given the king an excellent horse in order to win his favor. When the aforesaid abbot was summoned, the king said to him:

> “Lay down the staff of pastoral rule, which you think ought to be borne because of the gift of a mortal man.”

When he had cast it from himself, the king took it and placed it upon the right hand of the image of the Savior, saying:

> “Go, abbot, and receive it from the hand of the almighty King. No longer be indebted to any mortal for it, but use it freely, as becomes the eminence of so great a name.”

The abbot gladly received it, gave very many people joy by this act, and thereafter flourished in complete liberty.

An ancient fragment of a history from Robert to the death of Philip says of Hildebrand and the Emperor Henry:

> “The same pope also demanded that he relinquish dominion over all the churches of his empire, so that he might not give the pastoral staff to anyone, according to what is contained in the decrees of the ancient Fathers. He refused to do this; and this was the more just cause of his excommunication.”

Waltram, bishop, in his treatise *On Investitures*, says:

> “The ancient constitution must be maintained purely and wholly, lest Christ’s little ones be scandalized. For it makes no difference whether king and emperor invest or enthrone a bishop by word, command, staff, or any other object which he holds in his hand. On the day of consecration, coming forward, he places ring and staff upon the altar and receives each into pastoral care from the stole and authority of St Peter. But it is more fitting that, through the staff—which is temporal and spiritual—the prior investiture by the king render all things quiet and peaceable in the lands and possessions of the Church against tyrants and plunderers.”

There is an extraordinary story in Matthew Paris, in the *Life of William II*, about Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester. Attacked by his opponents, he refused to surrender his episcopal staff or rod except to the tomb of King Edward, from whom he had received it during the king’s life. When it had been fastened there, no hand afterward could tear it away, except Wulfstan’s own. By this miracle God demonstrated that the episcopal staff had most justly been granted to him earlier by the king.

Pope Innocent III allows the patriarch of Constantinople to use a staff, after the manner of other pontiffs, in the chapter *Cum venisset*, *On Sacred Unction*. In that passage he adds that the Roman pope does not use a staff, both for a historical and a mystical reason. That reason must be sought in Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, Book III, chapter 15; Durandus, *Rationale*; and Jordan, *On Empire and Election*.

Although, to note this in passing, it may be doubted whether Innocent’s assertion that the Roman pontiff does not use a staff is altogether true. For Liutprand of Cremona, at the end of Book VI of *The Affairs Accomplished throughout Europe*, relates that a certain Pope Benedict was deprived of office; his pallium and pontifical *ferula* were taken from him and restored to Leo, who broke it. Regino, *Chronicle*, Book II, confirms this in these exact words:

> “Pope Leo, having assembled a synod of many bishops, by the judgment of all deposed the same Benedict, the invader of the Roman see, from the rank he had invaded; he cut off the pontifical pallium which Benedict had put upon himself, seized the pastoral *ferula* from his hand, broke it into pieces before all, and, at the emperor’s request, allowed him to retain only the rank of deacon.”

In these passages it is beyond doubt that *ferula* means the same as staff or rod. Elsewhere it is called a *pedum*, as by the ancient anonymous author of the *Life of St Otto, Bishop of Bamberg and Apostle of the Pomeranians*, chapter 3:

> “At that time emperors conferred investitures of churches; and whenever any bishop died, the Church over which he had presided sent the *pedum* and ring to the emperor, requesting from his court that a bishop be given to it. Many noble and distinguished men, relatives and sons of princes, therefore attended the imperial court, performing the service of chaplains in hope of obtaining some bishopric.”

A little later, speaking of Emperor Otto:

> “He placed the bishop’s ring upon his finger, gave him the *pedum*, and thus invested him and committed him to the envoys.”

To these should be joined what was noted concerning the pastoral rod under Epistle 8.

### “By the count of the Normans.”

They interpret this passage as referring to Robert, who was defeated and thrown into chains by his brother Henry, king of the English, and with whom all Normandy was at the same time subdued. Eadmer, in the *Life of Anselm of Canterbury*, and William of Malmesbury, Book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, speak of him. The latter writes that Robert had sought his brother’s kingdom and falsely alleged that he was less fit to govern the commonwealth because of gentleness of disposition.

## ON EPISTLE CLVIII

### “Which is between Constance, daughter of the aforesaid king, and the count of Troyes.”

After this marriage had been dissolved, Hugh, count of Troyes, had taken another wife, as may be inferred from the words of Ivo, Epistle 245. On this matter Andrew, an ancient unpublished author, writes in Book III of his *History of the Franks*:

> “After the death of his guardian Count Baldwin, Philip, on the advice of Robert the Frisian, took as wife Bertha, daughter of Florent, duke of Frisia. By her he begot Louis and a daughter, Constance. When she was grown and had reached marriageable age, she married Hugh, count of Troyes; afterward, separated from him because of consanguinity, [Col. 0373A] she married Bohemond, prince of Bari, a great-hearted and valiant man,” etc.

Suger also mentions her in the *Life of Louis the Fat*. Since the words are corrupted in the common edition, they will here be corrected incidentally from an ancient manuscript:

> “The reason for Bohemond’s coming into these regions was that he sought by every means to have joined to him in marriage the most noble Constance, sister of the lord Louis-designate, refined in manners, elegant in person, and most beautiful in face. For the valor of both the kingdom of the Franks and Lord Louis was so widely proclaimed that even the Saracens were terrified by fear of this alliance. The lady was free, having rejected Count Hugh of Troyes as a suitor, nor did she seek a suitable husband in a second union. The prince of Antioch, skilled and lavish alike in gifts and promises, devoutly succeeded in joining that lady to himself in a most celebrated marriage at Chartres, in the presence of the king and Lord Louis, with many archbishops, bishops, and magnates of the realm standing by.”

### “I admonish [you] at their prompting.”

Thus the ancient manuscript reads better than the earlier text: “Therefore, since this desire of theirs is so ardent, I admonish [you].”

## ON EPISTLE CLIX

### “At the Council of Tours.”

Berthold notes in his chronicle that Urban II celebrated this synod in the year 1096.

### “Fraudulently obtained from Lord Pope Urban.”

St Bernard of Clairvaux aptly writes to Pope Eugenius, Epistle 247:

> “It matters who is deceived, and in what matter. The greater your power and dignity, the more dangerous—and also the more shameful—is any fraud perhaps imposed upon you, especially in ecclesiastical causes.”

The same author writes to Pope Innocent, Epistle 178:

> “This is especially characteristic of the Apostolic See: it does not hesitate to revoke what it discovers was perhaps extracted from it by fraud rather than deserved by truth. This is a deed full of equity and worthy of praise: that no one should profit from falsehood, especially before the holy and highest See.”

### “To Urban, that the monastery of Saint Maur.”

Peter the Deacon, in Book IV, chapter 18 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, writes of this matter:

> “The same pontiff, moreover, having entered Gaul for ecclesiastical business, as we have said above, at the Council of Tours over which he himself presided, restored the monastery of Saint Maur at Glanfeuil—[Note: [Col. 0373D] It is in the diocese of Angers]—which had been withdrawn from the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés by tyranny, to its former dignity and liberty, to remain perpetually under the authority of the monastery of Monte Cassino alone.”

So writes this monk of Monte Cassino. But the ancient author of the miracles of Blessed Maurus, deacon and abbot, chapter 3, recalls an edict of Emperor Louis which had decreed that the rulers of the monastery at Fossés should always administer the monastery at Glanfeuil. His words are:

> “Finally the venerable Count Rorigo, lest in succeeding times the place itself, perhaps through the negligence of its inhabitants, should depart from the rectitude of the regular path, obtained by sacred writ an imperial edict from the most serene Emperor Louis. By it the rulers of the monastery of Fossés, always having charge of that place, were to apply the diligence of their solicitude to both place and community in every respect with vigilant care, appointing from their own community such brothers as masters and priors that, by their direction and governance, all things needing to be done there, within and without, might be diligently ordered. How this was taken away and burned by fire in the time of Ingelbert, we consider better left unspoken than set forth.”

## ON EPISTLE CLX

### “Of the monastery of Jumièges.”

Other manuscripts vary, reading *Gemetensis*, which appears less suitably written. An ancient author in the *Life of St Philibert, Abbot*, calls it *Gemmeticum*, says that it lies in the district of Rouen, and says that it was built under Clovis, king of the Franks. It was so named, he says, because it is conspicuous, like gems, for the varied beauty of its flowers and trees.

Thomas Walsingham, in the *Hypodigma Neustriae*, similarly explains that, like gems in a ring, it gleams by reason of the site and abundance of its produce. William of Jumièges, monk, *On the Dukes of the Normans*, Book I, chapter 6, gives another explanation: those who groan there for their offenses will not groan in avenging flames.

That the monastery was most celebrated is shown by Thomas’s statement that it grew to the number of nine hundred monks. William also says that many bishops and noble laymen, despising worldly display, bent their necks beneath the yoke there. But he adds that, after a pagan incursion, its buildings were destroyed and it became for thirty years a den of wild beasts.

## ON EPISTLE CLXIII

### “He might administer that obedience.”

Anselm of Canterbury, in his Epistle to Ernulf, says: “For the purpose of holding some authority which we call an obedience.” Gregory VII, Book VI, Epistle 21, to the canons of Lyons, says: “He freely resigned into our hands the obediences of the Church and the other benefices which he had acquired without the common consent of the brethren.”

## ON EPISTLE CLXIV

### “Into the hands of the legate of the Roman Church, with no one compelling him.”

He means Bruno, bishop of Segni, concerning whom see Epistle 166. This matter is mentioned by Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, an eyewitness, in this epistle to Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and the chapter of St Mary:

> “We have learned that this is the virtue of true justice: that one ought not to aid a friend by falsehood, nor fail an enemy where truth is concerned. Concerning the deposition of Lord Abbot Geoffrey and the promotion of Lord Maurice—who, while unjustly exercising hostility against us, advanced complaints of little profit to himself—we bear witness to the truth, as we saw and heard.  
>   
> We saw Lord Geoffrey, in the presence of Lord Bruno, then legate of the Roman Church, relinquish his abbey and elect Lord Maurice as abbot by his own voice; and we saw him lead the elected man with his own hands and establish him in the place which he himself had formerly held. We saw this and testify openly before God and men that it was so done. But if anything was done otherwise in secret, we confess that we know nothing whatever of it; for it could have happened that Lord Geoffrey declared one thing with his tongue and concealed another in his heart. Yet whatever was done at Blois in our presence concerning this case, so far as we could perceive, would not, we believe, harm Lord Maurice, if no other obstacle intervened.”

### “To put an end to such disturbances.”

Thus the better ancient manuscripts; earlier editions had “admonitions,” an error found in most manuscripts. Some also read “our admonitions.” He uses *motiones* (“disturbances”) as in Epistle 197, “a deadly commotion arose,” and Epistle 336, “concerning which there is so great a disturbance.”

## ON EPISTLE CLXV

### “To Samson, bishop of the Church of Worcester.”

William of Malmesbury, Book IV of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, in the chapter on the bishops of Worcester, says:

> “Samson succeeded Wulfstan, a canon of Bayeux, a man of no small learning and not contemptible eloquence, of ancient manners. He ate generously himself and gave lavishly to others. He was harmless toward the monks, except that he took from them Westbury, where Wulfstan had placed monks and had fortified them with the privilege of his sanctity. Samson plundered it and, not many years later, died in the same village where he had committed the offense.”

Matthew Paris, in the *History of the English*, under William II, about the year of Christ 1097, says: “In the same year Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated Samson bishop of Worcester at London, in the church of St Paul, on Sunday, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June].”

## ON EPISTLE CLXVI

### “To Humbald, by the same grace bishop of Auxerre.”

He writes to the same man in Epistle 241, though in that passage one manuscript varies and calls him Cumbald. An ancient chronology by a monk of Auxerre, under the year of the Lord 1096, states:

> “After Robert, Humbald governed the Church of Auxerre. He richly benefited that Church and adorned it inwardly and outwardly, multiplied its buildings, and distinguished it with honors. He established the churches of St Peter and St Eusebius as churches of Regular Canons. His life was so honorable and sober that, from the time he became bishop, he abstained from meat; a meal of legumes sufficed him, and he drank only a little wine. At last he set out for Jerusalem and, while returning, perished in the waves when his ship was endangered.”

Under the year 1114 it notes that the monastery of Pontigny was founded under the venerable bishop Humbald, then presiding at Auxerre.

### “Bruno, bishop of Segni, by apostolic legation.”

The epistle immediately following confirms that he was likewise the pope’s legate in Gaul. Suger mentions him in the book *On the Life of King Louis the Fat*, where the name is corrupted because *Brusoniganus* was mistakenly printed. But on the authority of ancient manuscripts the passage must be restored thus:

> “There also stood the lord Bruno, bishop of Segni, apostolic legate of the Roman See, who, sent by Pope Paschal, had accompanied Lord Bohemond to urge and encourage the way to the Holy Sepulchre. From there he held at Poitiers a full and celebrated council, at which we too were present.”

The abbot of Ursperg, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1116, says: “But Bruno, bishop of Segni, began from a higher point.” Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, mentions the same man in his epistle to Ivo, bishop of Chartres, cited above under Epistle 164.

### “He might evade [it] by his simplicity or duplicity.”

The earlier edition printed “or by his cunning,” a reading likewise found in most manuscripts. I would not have altered it had not the ancient manuscript of Nicolas Faber warned me otherwise. It reads “duplicity,” a term which he commonly uses elsewhere with the same meaning; there can therefore be no doubt that “cunning” crept into the other books from a gloss.

Other ancient books, however, omit both “cunning” and “duplicity,” leaving the sense incomplete. The following examples confirm and elucidate the correction: in Epistle 63 he calls them “the follies of double-minded persons”; in Epistle 133, “the duplicity of false brethren”; and in Epistle 164, “the duplicity of disturbers.” In Epistle 199 he contrasts cloaked duplicity with simple truth. In Epistle 200 he desires that the wrinkle of the Church’s duplicity be restored to simplicity. Finally, in Epistle 245, he calls duplicity and softness vices.

Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, in Epistle 7 to Leotherius, archbishop of Sens, writes:

> “We must strive toward the harbor of the heavenly fatherland. Therefore do not yourself mix in your heart a double sea—*bithalassum*—of doubt and duplicity. For the way of the Lord is simple, and one who walks simply walks confidently.”

Pope Urban II, chapter 46, *Excommunicatorum*, Cause 23, Question 5:

> “Impose upon them a fitting penance, by which they may appease the eyes of divine simplicity toward themselves, if perhaps, through human frailty, they have incurred some duplicity in that offense.”

St Bernard, Sermon 82 on the *Song of Songs*:

> “Nevertheless, in every soul general simplicity remains along with original duplicity, so that confusion may be increased by the comparison.”

John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, or *On the Trifles of Courtiers*, Book VI, chapter 24:

> “For he asserts that in the Roman Church there is a certain root of duplicity, and a nourishment of avarice, which is the head of all evils.”

An ancient author, in the book *On Preserving the Unity of the Church*, writes:

> “Christ presented to himself a glorious Church having neither stain nor wrinkle through duplicity; for by justice she is clean, and by simple intention she is spotless.”

## ON EPISTLE CLXVIII

### “To a knight as a benefice.”

He uses this expression in the same sense in Epistles 71, 143, 168, and 208.

### “Because it was an allod.”

This is a feudal term, used frequently among others by Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, as in his epistle to Pope Paschal:

> “The predecessors founded the monastery and offered it to Blessed Peter as a patrimony and proper allod, together with the possessions pertaining to it.”

Thus he calls himself an *allodiary* of the Roman Church in his epistle to Girard:

> “To Lord Girard, bishop of praiseworthy life, legate of the holy Roman See: Brother Geoffrey, allodiary and servant of the same See.”

Likewise in his epistle to Conon:

> “To Conon, bishop of praiseworthy life, legate of the holy Apostolic See: Brother Geoffrey, allodiary and servant of the same See, [sends] affection and the service of all affection. What liberty, immunity, and dignity the monastery of Vendôme, the allod and patrimony of Blessed Peter, has possessed until now, and will possess until the end of the age with God’s protection…”

### “And it was judged that this case could not be settled without single combat.”

Observe that the bishops’ judgment held that the dispute of knights ought to be settled by single combat. Yet ecclesiastical laws at that time are said in Epistle 280 to prohibit it rather than command it. Therefore, in Epistle 247, he rebukes the Church of Orléans, which by its own judgment had appointed a day for the performance of single combat between two disputing knights.

Formerly this was called the judgment of God, as in the Bavarian law, title 2, *On Dukes*, and the Lombard law, title 2, *On Scandal*. King Liutprand, in his edict, title *On Single Combat*, said that he could not prohibit this impious law because of the custom of his people. No more may be said of it here, since many others have labored on this subject.

Let only two testimonies be added, from unpublished authors of Ivo’s age, from which it may be inferred that such single combat was customary even among clerics and monks. Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, writes to Peter, bishop of Saintes:

> “We have heard, most beloved Father, that your cleric Rainald Chesnell and our monk Lord William have undertaken a duel, though neither he nor the monk had any witness on his side. Since the laws of the world permit this in no way and the sacred canons utterly forbid its taking place, we humbly ask that what is known to have been undertaken in your bishopric by ecclesiastical persons against ecclesiastical rules be rendered void and corrected by your authority. Otherwise, perhaps, through a perverse custom human iniquity will prevail over canonical equity and, God forbid, truth will thus be subjected to falsehood.  
>   
> But if your Rainald attempts to wield the keys of the holy Church and annul the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, which utterly prohibit single combat between ecclesiastical persons, we appeal against his inflated attempts to the humility of the Roman Church, which knows how to burst the inflated and crush the proud.”

An ancient history by a canon of Laon says of a certain religious man, Anselm Beesso, to whom the custody of the treasury of the Church of Laon had been entrusted:

> “Secretly taking no small part of it, he handed it over to a certain goldsmith to sell, having first received from him a pledge of faith that he would reveal to no one that Anselm had been responsible for this matter. But when the same craftsman sold the gold or gems at Soissons, the canons of Laon, arriving by God’s will, recognized the engraved works of gold. They immediately brought a complaint and had the aforesaid goldsmith seized by the judge. Having been seized and terrified, he confessed that they had been handed over to him by Anselm. He was therefore brought back to Laon and, in a contest of single combat against Anselm, who denied these things, he was promptly overcome and defeated—perhaps, as many thought, because of the guilt of his violated pledge, since he had promised Anselm that he would not expose him.  
>   
> Anselm, exceedingly elated by this victory, because he knew that he had committed the theft and nevertheless had defeated his adversary, and had gained much praise from men who declared him innocent, was emboldened to commit greater crimes and enriched with many lands and vineyards.”

[Col. 0377A] See the treatise of Agobard, the ancient archbishop of Lyons, addressed to Emperor Louis, in which he inveighs against single combat and says that many perverse outcomes of judgments resulted from it.

## ON EPISTLE CLXXI

### “And *basileis*, that is, the foundation of the people.”

He took this from Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book IX, chapter 3. Pope Nicholas I writes to King Charles:

> “For unless you who are placed in royal eminence bore the world, as the bases of a vast structure, by your labor, you would by no means receive in Greek the title *basileōn* [βασιλέων].”

Nicholas of Cusa likewise follows this common opinion in *On Catholic Concord*, Book III, chapter 4.

### “They are not to be harshly exasperated by us; but [only] where they have not acquiesced in the admonitions of priests.”

This passage is especially worthy of notice. In the same sense the people of Liège wrote beautifully in an epistle composed about the year of the Lord 1107 against Pope Paschal II:

> “Therefore, from the words of these men and of the holy Fathers, let bishops who are beholden to kings and emperors for what they have received from their royal benefices take care not to kill them with their own sword—that is, with those benefices. If anyone, in reverence for the Holy Spirit, reviews the Old and New Testaments and the deeds [of the past], he will plainly find that kings and emperors can either not at all or only with difficulty be excommunicated, according to the etymology of those names and the definition of excommunication; and the dispute is still before the judge. They may indeed be admonished, rebuked, and reproved by God-fearing and discerning men, because Christ left to his own judgment those whom he established on earth in the place of the King of kings, to condemn and to save.”

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, writes in an epistle:

> “But with the most serene king there is need rather of exhortation than rebuke, counsel than command, teaching than rod. By these means he had to be approached; by these he had reverently to be instructed, lest he expend his arrows upon an aged priest; lest he nullify canonical enactments; lest he persecute the ashes of the Church now buried—ashes among which I eat the bread of sorrow [Col. 0377C] and drink the cup of mourning, from which to be delivered and escape is to pass from death to life.  
>   
> Yet amid these straits, anger never so triumphs over me that I would wish to raise an outcry against anyone over the Lord’s anointed, or to obtain his peace by a strong hand and the arm of the Church. Peace is suspect when exalted powers come to it not through love but by force; it is easily broken, and sometimes its latter state becomes worse than its former. There is another way by which, with Christ as guide, I may reach it more quickly: I shall cast my thought upon the Lord, and he will grant the petitions of my heart. He is the one in whose hand the hearts of kings are like wax. He alone bends them wherever he pleases and changes them into whatever form he wills. If I find favor in his eyes, I shall either easily obtain the king’s favor or profitably lose it.”

## ON EPISTLE CLXXII
He said that he ought first to be reinstated. It is probable that, under the reference to the abbot of Vendôme, Geoffrey is meant, who, though in a different factual setting, is accustomed to press such complaints in the manuscript copy. For in a letter to this same Ivo, complaining of the clergy of Chartres, he adds: “When, concerning our property, long and justly possessed by us and unjustly taken away, we have been reinstated according to the sacred canons, if thereafter they complain of us, we do not refuse to do what the just judge and the divine law shall decide ought to be done.” Likewise, in a letter to Ranulf, bishop of Saintes, he says that he will not accept a deadline fixed for judicial proceedings unless he has first been fully reinstated. He repeats this in fuller terms in a letter to Bishop G.: “If anyone says that a person despoiled may or ought to be summoned, not to the trial of the cause but to the trial concerning reinstatement, he is shaking the keys of holy Church and attempting to violate the laws of the Catholic and Apostolic See, by which it is forbidden that any despoiled person be summoned to judgment or be judged in any matter, since it would be vain and empty to summon to judgment one who is permitted to be judged in nothing.” [Col. 0378A]

And shortly afterwards he attests that Pope Urban, in the Council of Auvergne, issued on this matter a ruling, approved by all the bishops and abbots present: that whoever had been despoiled without summons and judgment should likewise be reinstated without summons and judgment. In the following letter he refutes the same bishop, who by his interpretation furnished more occasion for despoiling those in possession than for reinstating the despoiled.

Gregory VII, Book VI, Letter 25, to Abbot Arnald: “For we judge it unworthy, and altogether too far removed from canonical institutions, that a cause requiring examination should be brought to trial unless he who suffers violence has first been reinstated with regard to the matters in dispute.”

St Bernard, Letter 45, to King Louis, speaking of the bishop of Paris: “The same bishop, through the hand of all religious persons, offers himself for justice—provided, however, that his property which has been taken away is first restored to him, since justice itself seems to demand this.” [Col. 0378B]

In the fourth part of Ivo’s *Decree* are reported the decrees of Zephyrinus, Felix, and Eusebius to the same effect. To these should be added the canons collected by Gratian under Cause 3, Question 1, and the chapters in Gregory’s Decretals under the title *On the Restoration of Those Despoiled*.

In this connection, what an ancient author writes in the book *On Preserving the Unity of the Church* is noteworthy. Treating the case of Emperor Henry IV, whom the bishops of Saxony and the defenders of Pope Hildebrand had expelled from the Saxon kingdom, and of a subsequent assembly held so that the dispute might be settled by books rather than swords, he reports that it was demanded that the emperor at least be allowed to use the right allowed even to the lowest person in the Church. Then a chapter from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs was publicly read: no despoiled person may be accused, judged, or excommunicated before everything taken from him has been fully restored. He adds that all the bishops of the opposing party were so confounded that they had nothing to answer, while victory remained with the Church of God.

## ON LETTER CLXXIII

[Col. 0378C]

“After he had taken the cross.” The word *crucem* (“the cross”) has been added on the authority of the old manuscripts; it was previously absent, leaving the sense of the words mutilated. In the Jerusalem expedition of that century it had been prescribed that the saving sign of the life-giving cross should be sewn upon their garments, and that they should carry on their shoulders the memorial of him whose rule was made upon his shoulder as he hastened for our redemption. Concerning this too is that saying of Isaiah: “The Lord will raise a standard among the nations,” etc., as William of Tyre says, *On the Holy War*, Book I, chapter 16.

Peter the Deacon, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 11, says that they impressed the sign of the holy cross upon their garments above the right shoulder. They also impressed it upon the flesh—that is, upon the forehead. Berthold, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1096, speaking of Urban II: “He also caused all who vowed themselves to this journey to mark themselves upon their garments with the sign of the cross; and that sign even appeared marked in the very [Col. 0378D] flesh. Hence very many believed that the journey itself had been begun by God’s ordinance and inspiration.”

Robert the Monk, Book II: “And when he asked what sign they wore for the pilgrimage, he learned that they bore the sign of the holy cross either upon their foreheads or upon their right shoulders.” The historian of Newburgh, *History of the English*, Book III, chapter 22, calls it receiving the Lord’s mark, the Lord’s sign, and the sign of the King of kings. Hence the army is called cross-bearing in the chronicle of the abbot of Ursberg.

“Redemption pledged anew” (*recredita redemptio*). Thus all the manuscripts read; compare Letter 275: “which he will willingly restore or pledge anew concerning the count of Auvergne.” Geoffrey of Vendôme, in a letter: “If they were captured, he caused [them] to be restored or pledged anew.”

“He had renounced allegiance to his lord” (*dominum suum diffiduciasset*). This is precisely the reading of the old copies, whereas the printer had previously published *diffiduasset*. Other authors use *diffidare*. Yet the other expression is also correct, and Ivo himself had already used it in Letter 22, to King Philip: *me diffiduciastis*, “you have renounced allegiance to me.” [Col. 0379A] Matthew Paris, in the prologue to the *History of the English*: “He drove him from the royal throne, having repudiated him.” The abbot of Ursberg, in the constitution of Frederick I: “We also decree that whoever else intends to injure or harm him must, at least three days beforehand, through a definite messenger, renounce allegiance to him. But if the injured man wishes to deny that he has been so renounced….”

Elsewhere Ivo speaks of giving pledges of faith to the king and of releasing persons from pledges and an oath made to the king, Letter 71. Robert the Monk, *On the Jerusalem War*, Book II: “He swore this pledge of faith to him, and the emperor agreed.” There is, however, someone who writes that *diffiduciare* is a barbarous expression compared with *diffidare*. But if *diffidare* could be formed from *fides* (“faith”), by the same reasoning *diffiduciare* ought to be permitted from *fiducia* (“trust,” “pledge of faith”).

“He had renounced allegiance, and had first seized his prey.” Relevant here is the complaint of Cusanus, *On Catholic Concord*, chapter 31: “Today,” he says, “we see either the greatest confusion in judicial order, or no justice at all. Honour is distinguished from law by honour. And nobles say that they can lawfully occupy even the greatest lordships where they admit that the possessor had and has no right at all. By the most worthless method of declarations of defiance, they think that honour is preserved; and after such a declaration of defiance has been announced, they believe that things violently seized, openly or secretly, in whatever manner, from any invented cause or from no cause, may lawfully be possessed—even if they were the goods of churches or clergy. O presumptuous audacity against all laws and rights! O most unjust judgment, distinguishing the honourable from the just and affirming that what is unjust may be possessed with honour!” [Col. 0379B]

And in chapter 34 he advises that a law be established forbidding anyone, for any cause whatever, to seize another’s goods or inflict harm through declarations of defiance; rather, everything should be done by judicial authority, and judges should also be able to grant reprisals against the contumacious.

“And for committing an offence” (*ad forisfaciendum*). This is the consistent manuscript reading. Pope Urban II, in the diploma of privilege granted to Peter, abbot of the monastery of Cava: “That you may possess, concerning these same men, a free court and all *forisfacturae* [judicial fines or forfeitures], without any bailiff or official.” The same pope: “If anyone commits an offence whereby those things might by right be applied to a public due.” Matthew Paris, under Henry I: “If any of my barons or men commits an offence, he shall not give a pledge in the misery of his money, as he did in the time of my father or brother, but according to the measure of the offence.” Anselm of Canterbury, in a letter to King Henry: “I hear that Your Excellency is exercising punishment upon the priests of England and exacting a forfeiture from them because they did not observe the decree of the council.”

Elsewhere it is written *forifacere*, as in Abbot Dodechin, in the appendix to the *Chronicle of Marianus Scotus*: “Estates proscribed by the king’s judgment, if they have rightly been adjudged away from offenders.” Elsewhere also one finds *forefacere* and *forefactor*. Rigord, Book III, *Deeds of Philip Augustus*: “And the offences which are properly ours shall be recorded there.” The same author shortly afterwards: “That they may hear the offences of our bailiffs.” William of Nangis, *Deeds of Philip*: “And whatever they had previously committed as offences against the clergy, he caused them promptly to make amends for to those burgesses.” [Col. 0379D]

“By truthful assertions.” Thus the old manuscript; previously, incorrectly, “by assents.”

“To falsify.” Thus all the old manuscripts, instead of “to show false.”

“Maintaining that the institution whereby ecclesiastical protection is extended to the property of soldiers departing for Jerusalem is new.” He calls it new because it had begun to come into use in that century, through Pope Urban II. These are Urban’s words in the address delivered at the Council of Clermont, in William of Tyre, *On the Holy War*, Book I, chapter 15: “Meanwhile, those who, through the ardour of faith, have undertaken this labour in order to overthrow them, we receive under the defence of the Church and the protection of the blessed Peter and Paul as sons of true obedience; and we decree that they remain secure from all disturbances, both in the property of others and in their own. But if anyone should presumptuously venture to molest them, let him be struck with excommunication by the bishop of the place, and let the sentence be observed by all until both what has been taken is restored and fitting satisfaction is made for the injuries inflicted. Bishops and priests who perhaps do not resist such persons shall be punished by suspension from office until they obtain the mercy of the Apostolic See.” [Col. 0380A]
