There is also this canon of the same Urban at the same council: “It has been decreed that all the goods of those who go to Jerusalem shall everywhere and always remain safe under peace and truce until they return.” The same was afterwards done by Pope Gregory, according to William of Newburgh, *History of the English*, Book III, chapter 20: “From the time when they have taken the cross, their goods, together with their servants, shall stand under the protection of the holy Roman Church and likewise of archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of the Church; and, until it is known with complete certainty whether the man himself has returned or died, they shall suffer no legal challenge concerning those things which they possessed peacefully when they took the cross. Rather, in the meantime their goods shall remain whole and undisturbed.”

William of Tyre, however, testifies in Book I, chapter 16 of the work mentioned that at that time many sought Jerusalem in order to evade and outwit their creditors, to whom they were bound under the burden of many debts. [Col. 0380B]

“To their *casamenta*.” This word also occurs below, in Letter 284. St Bernard, Letter 39, to Prince Theobald: “Receive likewise our bishop and yours, namely the bishop of Langres, with the more abundant honour fitting to him; and concerning the *casamentum* which you hold, reverently and humbly offer him the homage which you owe.” A passage of Bishop Fulbert’s letter on the form of fidelity, in Ivo, Part XII of the *Decrees*, chapter 76, indicates that it means a benefice or fief. After he has explained the six things which one who swears fidelity to his lord must always bear in mind, he adds: “It is right that the faithful man avoid these injuries, but he does not thereby deserve the *casamentum*. For it is not enough to refrain from evil unless what is good is done. It remains, therefore, that in the same six matters mentioned above he faithfully provide counsel and assistance to his lord, if he wishes to seem worthy of the benefice and to remain secure in the fidelity which he swears. The lord also ought to render the same in return to his faithful man in all these matters.” [Col. 0380C]

Here I wrote *casamentum*, whereas the common edition has *cassamentum*, and the margin adds *causamentum*; but both terms are corrupt. Some points about *casati* are noted on Letter 28.

## ON LETTER CLXXVI

“From the Council of Troyes.” Baronius, *Annals*, vol. XII, under the year of Christ 1107, the eighth year of Paschal II’s pontificate, distinguishes this council from the one mentioned by Ivo in Letter 258, since the latter had earlier been held in Gaul by Cardinal Richard, legate. He holds that the council mentioned in this Letter 176 was held three years after the preceding one by Paschal himself. Suger, in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, testifies that Paschal came to Troyes and held a general council. The chronology of the monk of Auxerre, under 1107: “Pope Paschal held a council [Col. 0380D] at Troyes.” The abbot of Ursberg, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1107, mentions it and says that Paschal held a considerable council at Troyes around Ascension; there, among many things which he corrected according to the circumstances and necessity of the time, he promulgated a decree in accordance with his predecessors’ rulings concerning the free election of pastors and the restraint of lay presumption in ecclesiastical dignities. He adds that Emperor Henry sent envoys to the pope regarding the matter of investitures.

“What a burden of the episcopate he would be undertaking at this time.” Namely, because of the gravest disturbance of public affairs. Accordingly Ivo himself, having experienced how great at that time was the danger of holding prelacy—as he says in Letters 13 and 33—often wished to be relieved of the pastoral burden, full of wearisome bitterness, as the words of Letters 17 and 25 indicate. For this reason Bishop Hilgot of Soissons is said to have resigned his episcopate in Letter 88. At the same time Fulk, bishop of Beauvais, [Col. 0381A] went to Rome so that he might be stripped of his episcopal mitre; see the note to Letter 30.

## ON LETTER CLXXX

“You [singular] to be so bound.” Thus all the old manuscripts; previously, “you [plural] bound.” But this author has many examples of that construction: Letters 8, 30, 75, 86, 95, 134, 124, and 209.

## ON LETTER CLXXXVI

“As far as we can, we moderate [it].” It ought to have been printed: “For the time being, as far as we can, we moderate [it],” as the old manuscripts Th. and Lois. have, as also does Ivo’s edition in the *Decree*.

“They communicate with excommunicated persons, or those who communicate with them.” These nine words have now for the first time been inserted on the authority and agreement of several manuscripts, and are confirmed by Ivo’s reading in the passage cited above. Berthold, however, in his *Chronicle* under 1089, notes that Pope Urban confirmed this ruling promulgated by his predecessor Gregory against the antipope Guibert, Emperor Henry, and the rest of that party. The same writer, under 1094, records that there was great difficulty in avoiding excommunicated persons, unless, he says, Pope Urban had in some manner moderated the sentence and, after the manner of his predecessor Gregory, had excluded many from excommunication. Finally, under 1100: “By now, almost everywhere, the sentence of excommunication had begun greatly to grow lukewarm, so that even certain religious persons, who up to that time had been most fervent in that cause, withdrew from Catholics and did not fear to be promoted among the excommunicated.” [Col. 0381B]

Therefore Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, moved by this abuse of reciprocal excommunications that had become widespread in that century between Gregory, Urban, and Guibert and their respective supporters, wrote thus under 1088: “Hence scandals in the Church and dissensions in the kingdom increase, while one differs from another, while kingdom and priesthood disagree, while one excommunicates another and the other despises the excommunication of the one, either because of prejudice concerning the cause [or] the person; and while one abuses the authority of excommunicating against the other more according to his own will than with regard for justice, the authority of him who gave the power of binding and loosing is utterly despised.” [Col. 0381C]

Therefore, when in this letter Laurence, a monk of the monastery of Charity, seeks Ivo’s advice on how excommunication should be avoided, it is probable that this should be referred to the case of Philip, king of the Franks, who was still bound by the censure of the Roman pontiff mentioned above. For many Frenchmen of both orders had suspended themselves from communion with him and with those who communicated with him. This may readily be inferred from the words of the ancient author of the books *On Preserving the Unity of the Church* against the said Gregory VII. Although he does not state the king’s name, no one other than Philip can be meant: “For it is known to those who have experienced it, especially to those who grieved over the division of the Church, how many—not only laymen, but bishops, clerics, and monks—having indeed zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, as the Apostle says, suspended and separated themselves from communion with all the churches of the world which communicate with the king of the Franks and the emperor of the Romans in our time. And these persons, demanding this of us rather than we of them, are afraid to communicate with us, whether in conversation, in the kiss of peace, or in devotion to prayer.” [Col. 0381D]

That the matters asked by that monk are believed to concern the king’s excommunication is also supported by Ivo’s words, who says that such disputes ought not be committed to writing, lest, if published and falling into many hands, they harm the undiscerning more than they benefit the discerning.

## ON LETTER CLXXXIX

“The murmur of the clergy of Reims.” Suger, Book I of the *Life of Louis the Fat*, and from him the continuator of the monk Aimoin, Book V, chapter 50, after saying that Louis was crowned at Orléans, adds: “He had not yet, after the celebration of the divine rites, laid aside his festal garments, when suddenly bearers of evil tidings from the Church of Reims appeared, bringing letters of protest and, had they arrived in time, threatening by apostolic authority that the royal anointing should not take place. For they said that the first-fruits of the king’s first crown belonged by right to the Church of Reims—so it should be read in Suger—and that from the first king of the Franks, Clovis, baptized by St Remigius, this prerogative had remained unimpaired and inviolate; whoever should violate it with rash boldness would be subject to perpetual anathema.

“On this occasion they hoped either to obtain peace for their archbishop, the venerable and distinguished man Ralph the Green, who had incurred the lord king’s gravest and most dangerous hostility because he had been elected and enthroned in the see of Reims without his consent, [Col. 0382A] or that the king would not be crowned. But because they arrived too late, they returned home speechless there but talkative at home; or, if they said anything, they nevertheless achieved nothing useful.”

“For the common benefit of kingdom and priesthood.” Observe the order of the words. Since in this royal consecration the matter of the whole kingdom was especially at stake, he names the kingdom first and the Church second. So that you may not think this was done without judgment by a prudent bishop, he maintained the same order in two other passages of this letter: “For the integrity of the kingdom and the tranquility of the churches, we have endeavoured, insofar as we could, to prevail.” And much later: “For if the king’s consecration were delayed, the condition of the kingdom and the peace of the Church would be gravely endangered.”

Likewise, Letter 55: “Whom he should choose as bishop for the peace of the kingdom and the consent of the Church.” Of the same kind are the words in Letter 214: “For we see kingdom and priesthood divided.” Also Letter 238: “There was no division between kingdom and priesthood.” And shortly afterwards: “May the peace of the kingdom of the Franks and of the supreme priesthood not be dissolved by any underhanded act.” Then: “When kingdom and priesthood agree with one another, the world is well governed.” But in Letter 239, writing to King Louis about his forthcoming marriage: “As you ought to provide for your own advantage, so you ought to provide for the stability of the kingdom and the peace of the churches.” Finally, elsewhere he names secular judgment first and ecclesiastical judgment second, as in Letter 229. Famous is that saying of Optatus, bishop of Milevis, Book III: “For the commonwealth is not in the Church, but the Church is in the commonwealth—that is, in the Roman empire.” [Col. 0382C]

“For there were certain disturbers of the kingdom.” Among them was Wido or Guido of Rochefort, whom Suger mentions shortly before the words cited concerning the king’s consecration, and gives the reason: “Accordingly, the aforesaid Count Wido of Rochefort, whose marriage being contracted between the designated lord—he means Louis the Fat—and his own daughter had, through the plotting of rivals, been challenged on grounds of consanguinity and dissolved by divorce in the presence of the lord pope—he is speaking of Paschal II, who was then in Gaul—having conceived resentment on this account, fed a small spark into blazing fires.

“No less did the designated lord burn with indignation against him. Suddenly the Garlande family interposed themselves: they broke friendship, dishonoured the alliance, and intensified hostilities. The designated lord therefore found an occasion for war because Hugh of Pomponne, a valiant knight and castellan of Gournay, a castle situated on the River Marne, unexpectedly seized the horses of merchants on the royal road and brought them to Gournay. Louis, almost beside himself at this affront of presumption, gathered an army and very swiftly surrounded the castle with a sudden siege, so that it might lack abundance of provisions. Attached to the castle is an island delightful for the beauty of its pasturelands,” etc.

This passage has been quoted at somewhat greater length because it is corrected from the authority of manuscript copies; for it is corrupt in the common edition. The same historian, shortly after recounting the consecration, mentions Guido the disturber: “Accordingly, the aforesaid Guido [Col. 0383A] the Red, and his son Hugh Cruciatensis [Creciacensis, ‘of Crécy’], a capable young man,” vigorous in arms, suited alike to robbery and arson, and a most swift disturber of the whole kingdom, their resentment growing because of the disgrace of their allied castle of Gournay, did not cease to disparage the royal majesty,” etc.

## ON LETTER CXC

“Lord Ralph.” Thus in all Ivo’s manuscripts. In Suger, Book I of the *Life of Louis the Fat*, and in the continuator of Aimoin, *History*, Book V, chapter 50, he is written Rodulfus, and is said to have incurred the gravest hostility of King Louis because he was elected and enthroned in the see of Reims without the king’s consent. Robert of the Mount, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1114: “In the metropolitan church of Reims, after the distinguished man Manasses, Gervase having been expelled, Ralph succeeded; he bore the surname the Green.” Lisiard, in the *Life of St Arnulf of Soissons*, chapter 36, mentions this Ralph the Green, archbishop of Reims, as does also the monk Nicholas in the *Life of Godfrey, Bishop of Soissons*, Book III, chapter 24. Peter the Venerable likewise says that he had been treasurer of the Church of Reims before becoming bishop. [Col. 0383B]

“That through hand and oath he should render that fidelity to the king.” He joins both together in Letter 182: “They, therefore, although they were my men and [bound] by oath….” Adalger, priest, in chapter 11 of the synod of the Gallican Church held at Durocortorum (Reims) under Hugh and Robert, kings of the Franks: “That this deed might be covered under the appearance of honour, I gave Charles both hand and oath.” In a diploma of Louis the Fat, dated 1137, granted to Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux, and his suffragans: “In the elections of their bishops and abbots we grant complete canonical liberty, without the obligation of homage, oath, or fidelity given by hand.”

The hand, of course, was a symbol and testimony of more important and stricter fidelity. For this reason, when the metropolitan archbishop of Tours required the abbot of Marmoutier to confirm by giving his right hand the complete obedience which he had promised orally, and the abbot resisted, Ivo replied that an obligation of the hand was no greater than one of the mouth, Letter 234. Yet scholars should observe at this point that in the author’s age a most grave dispute had arisen among emperors, kings, and other laymen concerning the fidelity to be rendered by ministers of the Church through the hand, and concerning homage itself, although this had been received by very long usage. [Col. 0383C]

For, in order that ancient rights of princes might fall into disuse, certain more subtle persons began to cry out that it was a sacrilegious crime for priests to promise fidelity in the hands of laymen; and they invented arguments whose validity and irrefutability—or colouring and deceitfulness—others shall judge.

At the Council of Clermont under Urban II, canon 17: “No bishop or priest shall render liege fidelity to a king or any layman into his hands.” Thus Baronius reports it from an old manuscript in volume XI of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 1095. Roger of Howden, Part I of the *Annals*, under 1099: “Pope Urban, in the third week of Easter, held a great council at Rome, in which he excommunicated all laymen who confer investitures of churches, all who receive those same investitures from lay hands, and also all who consecrate those appointed to office in such a manner. He likewise excommunicated those who become the men of laymen for ecclesiastical dignities, saying that it seemed exceedingly execrable that hands which have risen to such an eminence that, by their sacramental sign, they create God, the creator of all things—something granted to no angel—and offer that same God before the eyes of God the Father for the salvation of the whole world, should be reduced to such baseness or folly as to become the servants of hands defiled day and night by obscene contacts or stained by devotion to robbery and unjust shedding of blood. And all cried out: ‘So be it! So be it!’ And in this the council was concluded.” [Col. 0383D]

Suger, Book I of the *Life of King Louis*, treating the dispute over investitures between Pope Paschal and the emperor, says that the archbishop of Trier, on behalf of Emperor Henry, alleged to the pope that by ancient right the prelates of churches, after election, were invested with ring and staff by the emperor and rendered him fidelity and homage. He then adds: “Concerning these things the lord pope replied, through the carefully considered voice of the bishop of Piacenza, that the Church, redeemed by the precious blood of Jesus Christ and established free, ought in no way to be enslaved. If the Church cannot elect a prelate without the emperor’s approval, then Christ’s death is nullified and she is subjected to him as a slave. If she is invested with staff and ring, since such things belong to her altars, he usurps them against God himself. If she places hands consecrated to the Lord’s body and blood beneath lay hands by binding them with hands stained by the sword and blood, she detracts from her order and sacred anointing.” These words, incidentally, have been corrected from the authority of old manuscripts because they circulate corruptly in the common [Col. 0384B] edition.

“They therefore wished that no homage or oath of fidelity should be rendered to a secular prince or layman in the investiture of a benefice.” Gregory is said to have been the first author of this measure, and it seems that the following, found in an old manuscript belonging to Auguste de Thou, should be attributed to him: “Let no cleric ever submit to judgment by a layman, either concerning land or other property which he holds from him, nor render homage to him; but let him altogether relinquish what he holds from him before suffering any injury. Otherwise, let him lose his rank.” The bare name Gregory is prefixed to this chapter. Yet it is probable that Gregory VII is meant, since he openly set forth what others had left unused, as William of Malmesbury says, by excommunicating elect persons who received investitures of churches from a lay hand.

His successor Urban decreed the same, and afterwards Paschal II, whose words are these: “Paschal, bishop of the holy see of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop Anselm of Canterbury. Recently, in a synod held at the Lateran council chamber, we renewed the decrees of our fathers, ordaining and forbidding that no cleric whatsoever render homage to a layman or receive churches or ecclesiastical gifts from a lay hand. For this is the root of Simonian depravity: foolish men, while desiring to obtain honours in the Church, seek to please secular persons,” etc. [Col. 0384C]

For that reason a serious controversy arose between Paschal and the king of England. William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, Book I, speaking of King Henry and that same Anselm: “Nevertheless, when the king, according to the custom of his predecessors, demanded homage from the archbishop, and he deferred because of the excommunication enacted at Rome, envoys having been sent to Rome by both sides, he was ordered in the meantime either to render homage to the king or, the bonds of delay being loosed, to leave the kingdom. ‘Rather,’ he replied, ‘let the apostolic letters be examined, and let what their tenor contains be done.’ For the envoys had already returned from Rome and had worn out the road in vain, because Pope Paschal upheld his predecessor’s ruling with invincible firmness. ‘What are apostolic letters to me?’ said the king. ‘I do not wish to lose the rights of my kingdom.’”

Very similar is what Radevicus, *History*, Book II, chapter 30, reports of Emperor Frederick I. When cardinals acting as Pope Adrian’s envoys declared—as the same historian counts it among the harshest demands—that Italian bishops ought to render only an oath of fidelity, without homage, to the lord emperor, Frederick replied: “I indeed do not desire the homage of the bishops of Italy, provided that they too take no pleasure in possessing anything from our regalian rights. If they are pleased to hear from the Roman pontiff, ‘What have you to do with the king?’, then they should not be displeased to hear in turn from the emperor, ‘What have you to do with property?’” These last words are St Augustine’s and are cited by Ivo in Letter 60 to prove that bishops may lawfully be invested by a prince with temporal goods. [Col. 0385A]

Frequent mention of this homage occurs in the manuscript letters of Anselm mentioned above. Their testimonies should be brought forward so that this whole dispute may be better understood. When Paschal had ordered Anselm to have no communion with those who had received investitures of churches from the hand of King Henry, Anselm wrote back to the king: “But I cannot act toward you as my predecessor did toward your father, because I dare neither to render homage to you nor, in view of the aforementioned prohibition made in my hearing, to communicate with those receiving investitures of churches from your hand.”

The same, in a letter to Prior Ernulf: “Know this, however: it is my will, with God’s help, to become the man of no mortal, nor to promise faith to anyone by oath.” And shortly afterwards he adds: “If anyone requires from any monk of our church an oath, a bond of fidelity, or any agreement contrary to his order, in order to hold some authority which we call obedience, consider carefully and, insofar as possible and as you know how, avert the evil.”

In another letter of the same Anselm to Paschal are certain questions relating to this matter:

“ANSELM. If no cleric ought to become a layman’s man, and he ought to hold certain benefices or non-ecclesiastical possessions from a layman, but the layman refuses to give them unless he becomes his man, what is to be done?

“PASCHAL. Paul says that the Church is free. Therefore it is unworthy that a cleric, already received into God’s portion and even raised above the rank of laymen, should render homage to a layman for earthly gain, lest the Church perhaps be left idle or burdened while he is claimed as subject to secular service. For it is written: ‘No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs.’” [Col. 0385B]

To insert this incidentally: David Scot, bishop of Bangor and supporter of Henry IV, formerly said that the Apostle’s words did not oppose the ambitions of pontiffs invested by laymen, because it is not a secular affair if a cleric renders homage to a layman. William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, Book V, calls this frivolous.

That same Anselm, in a letter to Bishop Gundulf: “The advice you seek concerning what you ought to do if my lord the king and I are not reconciled I set down briefly in the prior’s letter. For the present I say only this: let no threats, no promise, no cunning draw from your religious profession either homage, oath, or a bond of fidelity. If anyone demands any of these, let this be your answer: ‘I am a Christian, I am a monk, I am a bishop, and therefore I wish to keep faith with all men according to what I owe to each.’ Whatever else may be said to you, add nothing to these words and subtract nothing that departs from this position. I say the same of myself, and, with God’s help, I do not wish to add anything to this or diminish anything from it.”

Finally, writing to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons: “The whole difficulty of the case between the king and me,” he says, “now seems principally to rest in this: although the king will, as I hope, permit himself to be overcome by apostolic decrees concerning investitures of churches, he nevertheless does not yet wish to abandon the homages of prelates, but says—may I say it?—that he seeks from her permission for this according to his will. If he obtains it, I doubt what I ought to do if some religious man, elected to a bishopric or abbey, refuses to become the king’s man. For it seems hard to me to command this of him by obedience; and if I do not, I shall seem to grant to irreligious men wishing to do it the boldness to approach dignities unworthily. I also think that the king will demand that those who have already received prohibited investitures, and those who consecrated them, remain in what they have unlawfully presumed.” [Col. 0385D]

So far he. After long disputes Paschal accepted that the prince should retain homages. Thus William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, Book II: “Envoys sent to Rome settled with singular skill the controversy debated for so many years. The pope granted that the king should receive homages from the elect, but should invest no one by staff and ring.” Elsewhere the same historian writes that Anselm’s many journeys to and from the city obtained the result that the king yielded to the pontiff the investiture of ring and staff, while retaining the privilege of election and regalian rights.

There are, however, writers of the preceding century who maintained that investitures may lawfully be made by princes, and that the homages of bishops may be required by them; among these was Theodoric of Niem. Waltram, bishop of Naumburg, likewise argued about the year of the Lord 1109 that, after churches had been endowed with fiefs by kings and emperors, and their rights transferred into the lordship of bishops, it was fitting and necessary that homages, oaths, and hostages should be demanded from them, so that, in an enemy incursion, kings might know to whom they had entrusted their cities. Finally, he concludes that in every kingdom the ancient rights and customs concerning the investiture of bishops ought to be observed. Nicholas of Cusa also, *On Catholic Concord*, book III, chapter 29, boldly asserts that not only were outright investitures wrested from the emperor by the Roman pontiff, but so much money was extorted that throughout Germany all complained that they were burdened and ruined. He adds that ambitious bishops are possessed by so rabid an appetite that all their concern is for temporal affairs and none for spiritual matters. “This,” he says, “was not the emperors’ intention: they did not wish spiritual things to be swallowed up by temporal things.”

He should render the king the same fidelity that he rendered to his predecessors. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, formerly wrote a letter on the form of fidelity which a person swore to his lord; part of it is quoted by Ivo in the twelfth part of the *Decree*, chapter 76, and by Gratian in the chapter *On the Form*, Cause XXII, question 5. In a synod of the Gallican Church held at Reims, there survives a document of Bishop Arnulf composed in these words:

> “I, Arnulf, by the prevenient grace of God archbishop of Reims, promise Kings Hugh and Robert of the Franks that I shall preserve for them the purest fidelity [Col. 0386C], shall supply counsel and aid according to my knowledge and ability in all affairs, and shall not knowingly assist their enemies by counsel or aid in disloyalty to them. Standing before the sight of the divine majesty, of the blessed spirits, and of the whole Church, I promise this, to receive the rewards of eternal blessing if I keep it well. But if—which I do not wish, and may it be far from me!—I depart from these things, let all my blessing be turned into a curse; let my days be few, and let another take my bishopric. Let my friends withdraw from me and become my enemies forever,” etc.

This was his formal written profession when he was endowed with the metropolitan see of Reims, as Archbishop Gerbert of Reims writes in his apology to Bishop Wilderod. The continuator of the monk Aimoin, *History*, book V, chapter 24, reports another, less comprehensive oath of the tonsured bishop of Laon:

> “Hincmar, bishop of Laon, from this time forth shall be faithful and [Col. 0386D] obedient to my lord and senior, King Charles, according to my office, as a man ought to be to his lord and a bishop, by right, ought to be to his king.”

This oath is also found in the book of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, against that same Hincmar of Laon. Philip Augustus, in a diploma of Arras issued in 1203, says:

> “The canons of the aforesaid church may freely elect, without requesting from us or our successors leave to elect; but they shall present to us their confirmed elect, so that he may render us fidelity, as other bishops are accustomed to render it to us.”

Moreover, there can be no doubt that the kings of France did what Cusanus writes of the emperors in *On Catholic Concord*, book III, chapter 28:

> “It was,” he says, “the custom of emperors readily to admit accusations of broken faith and perjury, so that fidelity, by which alone the empire endures, might never through negligence be held of little account. The punishment for one who did not keep faith was deprivation.”

[Col. 0387A] Because of the affinity of this argument, it may be added that Hildebrand’s action was long ago censured by many: after excommunicating Emperor Henry, he released the people, by the same hand, from the bond of fidelity due to him. For the ancient and distinguished writer who composed the life of that Henry in an elegant style says on this subject:

> “He even added this: he absolved all who had sworn fidelity to the king from their oath, so that this absolution might drive them against him whom the obligation of fidelity held bound. This action displeased many—if, indeed, one may be permitted to dislike what the apostolic pontiff did.”

Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, criticizes this more openly in his *Chronicle*:

> “Indeed, if I may say so with the leave of all good men, this novelty alone—not to call it heresy—had not yet arisen in the world: that priests of Him who ‘calls the king apostate’ [Note: [Col. 0387D] He alludes to Job, chapter XXIV.] and who ‘makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people’ should teach the people that they owe no subjection to wicked kings; that, although they have sworn an oath of fidelity, [Col. 0387B] they nevertheless owe no fidelity, nor are those called perjurers who take a position against the king; indeed, that whoever obeys the king is to be regarded as excommunicated, while whoever acts against the king is absolved from the guilt of injustice and perjury.”

The ancient author of the books *On the Unity of the Church* argues at greater length to the same effect. His words are:

> “It is evident that the aforesaid Pope Hildebrand unjustly and unworthily fastened this stain upon either Zachary or Stephen—religious pontiffs, certainly, of the Roman Church—in order that, by the example of one of them or by the testimony of that sacred Scripture, he might absolve from the oath by which either princes or soldiers of the commonwealth had sworn fidelity to their king. For ‘he who breaks an agreement, shall he escape?’”

Far later, while accusing the pontiff of falsehood in his narration of history, he writes as follows:

> “Neither of them, as we know for certain, absolved the Franks from the oath of fidelity which they had promised to any king, as Pope Hildebrand wrote and preached, so that the princes of the kingdom might be deceived [Col. 0387C] by such an example: as though he himself could absolve them from the oath of fidelity that they had sworn to their king in the name of the Lord, intending that he should thereby be deprived of the kingdom and deposed. Although this was repeatedly attempted throughout these fourteen years, or more, it nevertheless could not be brought to effect,” etc.

The passage in which Gregory wrote this is found in Ivo, fifth part of the *Decree*, drawn from his letter to Hermann, bishop of Metz. There too is reported a chapter of Gregory VI absolving from the oath of fidelity those who adhere to excommunicated persons; likewise, one of Urban II absolving from their oaths knights who had sworn to Count Wigo, an excommunicate. Guibert, the antipope, is also said in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book III, chapter 69, to have absolved Emperor Henry from observance of the oath which he had formerly rendered to Pope Gregory.

But solely with the intention of acquiring liberty. It may seem doubtful whether he means the general liberty of the churches or that of the Roman pontiff alone. Certainly, in the then much-troubled controversy over investiture between popes and kings, they wished it to be believed that they were moved solely by love for the Church’s liberty, and were not seeking private advantage. For Paschal II, in his letter to Henry I, king of England, says:

> “It grieves us that you appear to demand from us what we absolutely cannot grant. For if we consent to, or permit, investitures to be made by Your Highness, immense danger will without doubt be yours and ours. In this matter we desire you to consider what you lose by not doing it, or gain by doing it. For in this prohibition we acquire nothing further, for the churches, either of obedience or of liberty [the edition reads ‘generosity’]; nor do we strive to take anything from your due power or right, except in order that God’s wrath against you may be lessened and all things may thus prosper for you.”

This letter is found [Col. 0388A] in William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of England*, book V. Paschal himself likewise objected to Emperor Henry that the Church, redeemed by Christ’s blood and constituted free, would again be reduced to servitude if the prince retained investitures, as was related shortly before from Suger.

Geoffrey of Vendôme, in a letter to Paschal, writes:

> “The Church lives and flourishes by faith, chastity, and liberty; if it does not have these, it languishes and is separated from life. For it is founded upon faith, adorned with chastity, and protected by liberty. But when it does not oppose but commands lay investiture, which according to the traditions of the holy Fathers is proved to be heresy; when it is itself corrupted by gifts; when it is subjected to secular power—then faith, chastity, and liberty are simultaneously taken from it; and that which has no life is, not without reason, believed dead.”

The same writer, speaking to Cardinal Leo of this same investiture, says:

> “For when king and Roman pontiff are raised against one another—the former for the custom of the kingdom, the latter for the liberty of the Church—the kingdom neither can nor will be able to retain that custom, and the Church loses very much of its liberty.” [Col. 0388B]

Ivo likewise, at the end of letter 236, says that this practice must be cut off for the liberty and honour of the Church; but he adds: while preserving the bond of peace and without danger of schism, if this can be done. Geoffrey himself says in the preceding letter:

> “Let the Church have its liberty; but let it take the greatest care lest, while squeezing too hard, it draw blood, and while trying to scrape rust from a vessel, it break the vessel itself. This is the chief part of discernment: that no one be ensnared by Satan through any action of the Church. For a person is ensnared by Satan when, under the appearance of justice, one whom indulgence could have saved happens to perish through excessive sorrow.”

“We therefore beseech you with knees bent in the heart.” An entirely similar passage occurs in Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, in a letter which he wrote to Pope Alexander. There he treats the case of the archbishop of Canterbury, to whom, after various disputes, the king of England had restored his possessions [Col. 0388C] for the honour of God and the Church—while, of course, preserving the dignity of his kingdom. He adds that Alexander’s envoys were offended by this clause, and finally wisely counsels that the pope should not, under this pretext, allow his followers to disturb the public order:

> “Afterwards, having withdrawn their consent, they refused to admit the phrase concerning the preservation hereafter of royal dignity, and declined to carry out what had been arranged, although the archbishops, bishops, abbots, religious persons, and magnates of the kingdom who were present had earnestly urged it by many prayers for the sake of so great a peace; because, in preserving royal dignity, it did not in any way seem to us that ecclesiastical liberty or dignity was weighed down. Indeed, ecclesiastical dignity promotes rather than removes royal dignity [the common reading here incorrectly has *casum*, ‘fall,’ in place of *quam adjuvat*, ‘than assists’]; and royal dignity is accustomed rather to preserve than to take away ecclesiastical liberty. For ecclesiastical and royal dignity meet, as it were, in mutual embraces: since kings do not preserve salvation without the Church, nor does [Col. 0388D] the Church preserve peace without royal protection. Therefore, falling at the knees of your holiness with all the devotion we can, we humbly and urgently entreat that your wisdom may not judge the points of letters and verbal formulations more worthy of embrace than the matter itself; but, according to the spirit of discernment given you by God, act so that the cause of one man may not be turned into the ruin of many—indeed, of almost countless persons—because for the good of peace the gentleness of grace sometimes advances matters more than the severity of discipline.”

Thus Arnulf. Moreover, Baronius, in volume XII of the *Annals*, after transcribing the preceding letter of Ivo, adds that Pope Paschal assented after the event to what had been requested, though he had utterly opposed its being done; and in support of his view he cites the argument of letter 260.

“Let a word suffice the father in place of a lash.” The ancient anonymous author in the *Life of Emperor Henry IV* says:

> “Why say more? He forgave his son both punishment and fault; [Col. 0389A] and this was the father’s avenging of his son’s injury: his correction of his son by paternal gentleness, in accordance with the saying of the Comic poet: ‘For a son’s great fault, a little punishment is enough.’”

## ON LETTER 192

“Whether Sarabaites may be made.” Thus he calls them also a little later, and the ancient manuscripts do not vary here in that spelling. They are likewise called thus by John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, book VII, chapter 23, and in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 1. Elsewhere the form is written *Sarabattae* or *Sarabatae*, as in two passages in the ancient author of the books *On Preserving the Unity of the Church against Hildebrand*.

## ON LETTER 195

“I received your letters, caressing and pricking.” In an ancient manuscript there are several letters of this Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, in which he complains of Ivo (see *Patrologia*, vol. CLVII).

## ON LETTER 200

“Daimbert.” Thus most manuscripts; previously, incorrectly, “Lambert.” [Col. 0389B] For many letters of the author survive addressed to this Daimbert, archbishop of Sens.

“That we may present her to her Bridegroom immaculate.” In one manuscript the fuller wording is: “that we may present her to her Bridegroom, having no stain of disgrace or wrinkle of duplicity.” But what follows sufficiently shows that these words are superfluous, and therefore I have not wished to repeat them.

“Nitre and soap.” This is the reading of the better books; others incorrectly read *intro sapore*. A not dissimilar passage occurs in Saint Cyprian, letter 76 to Magnus:

> “For in the saving sacrament the contagions of sins are not washed away as, in a bodily and secular bath, the stains of skin and body are washed away, so that soap and nitre, and other aids besides, and a leaf and a pool are needed.”

Pamelius warns that all the books should be read thus; nevertheless he is not satisfied with this reading and, by conjecture, emends *nitris et sapone* (“nitre and soap”) to *aphronitris*.

## ON LETTER 203

[Col. 0389C] “And the property of basilicas.” Thus most manuscripts; others read “and the property of churches,” which seems to have arisen from a gloss. That *basilicas* is used for churches is proved by so many examples from ancient writers that those who wrote that these words differ, and that the term *basilicas* signifies temples not yet consecrated, ought not to be heard.

“If I have defrauded anyone.” One manuscript reads *defrudavi*.

## ON LETTER 204

“And the disease called holy fire.” Thus the better ancient books; some others incorrectly read “and the disease called sacrilege.” Sigebert notes in the *Chronicle* that, in the year of the Lord 1095, many were seized by holy fire, their limbs becoming black like coals. The abbot of Ursberg recounts this more fully, calls it invisible fire, and adds that for this reason many Frenchmen enlisted in the Jerusalem expedition:

> “The western Franks could easily be persuaded to leave their fields. For Gaul had for several years been grievously afflicted now by civil conflict, now by famine, now by pestilence. Finally, the plague which arose around the church of Saint Gertrude at Nivelles had terrified men unto despair of life. Its nature was as follows. Anyone touched by invisible fire in any part of the body burned with a perceptible—indeed incomparable—and irremediable torment, until he lost either his life amid the agony, or the agony together with the limb that had been touched. Some, mutilated in hands or feet by the punishment, bear witness to this even now.” [Col. 0389D]

Glaber, *History*, book V, chapter 1, under the year 1041, understood this as a fire of deadly burning:

> “Then also, by God’s hidden judgment, divine vengeance began to rage among the people themselves: for a certain deadly burning consumed many, both of the great and of persons of middle and low rank. Yet it preserved some, after cutting off parts of their limbs, as an example for those to come.”

Holy fire is mentioned by Pliny [Col. 0390A], book XXVI, chapter 11; Columella, book VII, chapter 5; and Cornelius Celsus, book V.

## ON LETTER 206

“Hildebert, by God’s grace bishop of Le Mans.” This reading is established by the agreement of so many ancient books that it should deservedly be preferred and the alternative, “Lambert,” rejected. There are various letters of Ivo to this Hildebert, whose memory it is pleasing to recall through testimonies gathered from various places.

An ancient sheet says:

> “The venerable Hildebert, born at the castle of Lavardin to parents of modest but honourable station, was made master of the schools by Lord Hoel, bishop of Le Mans; then archdeacon; and after Lord Hoel’s death was appointed in his place. Mild and modest in character, at the beginning of his episcopate he devoted himself tirelessly to restoring what through his predecessors’ negligence had either been destroyed or lost.”

An anonymous monk of Saint Marianus at Auxerre, in his *Chronology* under the year of the Lord 1007, says:

> “At this time flourished [Col. 0390B] Hildebert, first bishop of Le Mans and afterwards archbishop of Tours, a man distinguished for learning and endowed with a peculiar grace both in versifying and in prose composition. This is shown by his various little works composed in verse and by his letters addressed to different persons; all of these are remarkably commended both by the elegance of their thought and by the charm and brevity of their language. Hence someone said of him:
>
> > Illustrious in prose and in verse, in every way foremost,  
> > Hildebert everywhere breathes nothing but the rose.”

So he says. William of Jumièges, *On the Dukes of Normandy*, book V, chapter 9, speaking of Anselm, says:

> “For he had refuted the Greeks at the Council of Bari, who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. From material drawn thence, at the request of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, he composed this book.”

For the name must be restored thus there, because in the standard edition it is incorrectly printed *Idebertus*. William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of England*, book III, calls him the praiseworthy bishop, whose teaching, he says, serves posterity as an example of how one ought to live. Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, calls him a religious man and, after he became metropolitan, the foremost in the province; Geoffrey also wrote many letters to him. Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, calls him a man of all reverence in letter 123; in the heading of letter 124, “a great and exalted priest in the word of glory”; and in the text of the same letter, “a great pillar of the Church.” [Col. 0390C]

There is, however, a recent historian who writes that this Hildebert, because he had most freely rebuked the tyranny of the supreme pontiff and the utterly corrupt morals of the Roman curia, was imprisoned and badly treated at Rome, citing Ranulf’s *Polychronicon* on the matter. I have not yet had occasion to read Ranulf. But the same historian’s further suggestion—that there were two contemporary bishops of the same name (whom the ancients called namesakes), one bishop of Le Mans and the other archbishop of Tours—need not be accepted. It is refuted by the testimony of the Auxerre *Chronology* just quoted, and by Platina, who writes that Pope Honorius II greatly praised Hildebert’s talent and subsequently made him archbishop of Tours because of his exceptional power in heroic and elegiac verse. It is further confirmed, for greater certainty, by the words of the ancient sheet that follow:

> “Guillebert, archbishop of Tours, died, and Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, obtained his rank and place, with the consent of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord 1129. At last, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January—that is, 18 December—in the year of the Lord 1136, he fell asleep in the Lord in a good old age and was buried at Tours in the church of Saint Maurice. He governed the Church of Tours for seven years and six months, and the Church of Le Mans for twenty-two years; his life was about eighty years long.” [Col. 0390D]

This bishop will also be discussed below under letter 277.

“To clear oneself by one’s hand alone.” Comparable is the phrase “to swear by one’s hand” in *Fiefs*, book II, title 27, § *If a Rustic*. So too: “to establish oneself as qualified in each particular by one’s own hand together with an oath,” in the *Capitularies* of Charlemagne, book I, final chapter. Arnulf, in the synod held at Reims, chapter 30, says: “After I have spoken, I shall confirm by oath with my right hand that this is so.” Saint Bernard, letter 235, says: “Unless the dean repelled by an oath of his own hand what had been objected against him.”

This custom is mentioned in papal decrees, from which it may also be inferred that it had a place in lighter cases but not in criminal ones. An ancient compiler, under the title *On the Purging of Subjects against Prelates*, adduces the following three testimonies. Pope Sylvester:

> “A person accused on testimony shall clear himself by an oath of his hand alone, if the matter is not a crime.”

Pope Felix:

> “If any bishop or archdeacon accuses a priest on any ground, the priest must clear himself by his hand alone in the accuser’s presence. If someone accuses him in a criminal matter, he must defend himself against his superior with a seventh hand, always in the accuser’s presence.” [Col. 0391B]

Augustine:

> “If anyone casts any stain upon one subject to him, that subordinate ought to clear himself, without any other assertion, by his hand alone, unless it is a criminal matter, in which even a subject must clear himself with a third hand.”

“With three, or five, or seven colleagues.” This was a very ancient custom: accused persons swore together with many others, who for that reason are noted under letter 57 as being called *conjuratores*, “co-swearers.” The ancient author, in the *Life of Saint Eligius, Bishop of Noyon*, book III, chapter 51, says:

> “A certain man, through greedy desire, wished to claim for himself a field of the Church of the holy bishop situated near Chaumont, but Sparnus, abbot of that church, resisted him. The matter was brought before the king’s court, and the king pronounced that, if the abbot were willing to swear in a sacred place that the field belonged to the Church, he himself should retain it. But the abbot preferred that the obstinate man should swear that the field was his and not the Church’s. Therefore judgment was given that the man should swear with many [Col. 0391C] others; for such was the established custom among the Franks. But the abbot released all the others from the oath, lest they be implicated in another’s wrongdoing. By judgment of the nobles, the usurper of the field alone was ordered to swear.”

Some, however, abused that custom of swearing when the swearers colluded with one another, as though by agreement. This is evident from letter 186 of Hincmar, bishop of Reims, to his fellow bishop John:

> “We instruct your charity how, by the authority of our elders, we hold that an ill-reputed priest is to be dealt with; and as Saint Gregory decreed: if an evil report concerning a priest has arisen throughout the parish from circumstances giving it likeness of truth, and lawful accusers and witnesses are lacking, then, lest—contrary to the Apostle—the hearts of the weak be wounded by the bad report concerning the priest, lest our ministry be reviled, and lest priests, being too secure, slip more freely into sin, let him clear his reputation by an oath with seven designated neighbouring priests, whom we know do not wish to commit perjury. But if he cannot have the priests designated by us to clear his reputation, and brings others with him to swear, then, because we have found that some have conspired with one another so that, being mutually accepted, they swear in each other’s purgation, just as the priests, full of wicked intent, conspired against Susanna: let the priests who offer themselves with the accused priest to swear in his purgation undergo judicial examination through the advocate of the accused priest, so that they may not destroy themselves before God in the oath, as we have learned that some already have done in this matter. The invocation over one who comes forth for judgment is as follows: that this priest has not had such access, association, cohabitation, and conduct contrary to the sacred canons as could justly give rise to evil suspicion and a report unworthy of a priest.” [Col. 0391D]

So he says, as the words are composed in the ancient Codex Thuanus; for only a portion of this chapter is quoted by Ivo, sixth part of the *Decree*, chapter 420, and by Gratian in the chapter *If an Evil Report*, Cause 2, question 4. Smaragdus also, in *On Ecclesiastical Oppressions* (*Patrologia*, vol. CII), part I, rejects this practice of co-swearing and says that it was invented so that malicious persons might more freely mistreat God’s priests, when they compel an accused person to employ a defence which he is utterly unable to carry out, or which wholly hinders him by the law of his office.

## ON LETTER 208

“To render homage to the abbot.” Thus the ancient parchments; in only one manuscript, *hominatum*, as the first edition also had it. Pope Gregory too used that expression: “A cleric is never to be brought to justice by a layman, neither concerning land nor concerning other property which he holds from him; nor is he to render him *hominatum*,” etc. These words occur in an ancient handwritten book, but it does not specify which Gregory is meant.

They also said *hominiscum*, as in an ancient instrument recording an acknowledgment made by Rostagnus of Montpezat to Lord P., archbishop [Col. 0392B] of the castle of Saint-Nazaire, in June 1226, during the reign of King Louis:

> “By my hands I swear you fidelity and render *hominiscum*.”

The author himself, in letter 241 to Humbald, said “to compel by *hominium*,” an expression used by many in that century. Most also said *homagium*, “homage.”

## ON LETTER 209

“You are the *paranymphus* of this marriage.” This is the reading of many manuscripts. So too in letter 200. There is frequent mention of *paranymphs*—marriage-attendants formerly employed in weddings—in Saint Ambrose, book IX, letter 70; Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XIV; Pope Evaristus in the chapter *Otherwise*, Cause 30, question 5; the Fourth Council of Carthage, quoted in the chapter *Bridegroom*, the same Cause 30, question 5; the Lombard laws, title *On Public Force*; and Saint Bernard, book III, *On Consideration*, final chapter.

## ON LETTER 211

“The king was excommunicated by Pope Urban at the Council of Clermont.” Bertold, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1094, relates that at a council held by Hugh of Lyons in the Gallic city of Autun, this Philip was excommunicated; his words were quoted above under letter 16. Under the following year he says that Pope Urban held a synod at Piacenza, to which King Philip of France sent his embassy and announced that he had begun his journey to it but had been hindered by legitimate impediments (*soniis*—thus I correct in passing the common printing *sociis*, “companions”); and that, through the intercession of the synod, he obtained from the pope a truce until Pentecost.

Bertold adds under 1095:

> “In Gaul, at Clermont, a general synod was assembled by the lord pope on the octave of Saint Martin, at which thirteen archbishops with their suffragans were present, and 205 pastoral staffs were counted. In this synod the lord pope confirmed the same statutes as at the preceding Synod of Piacenza. Moreover, he excommunicated Philip, king of France, because, having dismissed his own wife, he joined to himself in marriage the wife of one of his knights. There he also announced another synod, to be held at Tours in the third week of the following Lent.” [Col. 0392C]

William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of England*, book IV, under the year 1095, speaking of the same pope, says:

> “At that time, after putting away their lawful wives, many contracted divorce, attacking another’s marriage; and therefore in both sorts of conduct there was a confused forest of crimes, for the punishment of some of the more powerful persons whose names were specified. This matter was dealt with at the Council of Clermont, where King Philip of the Franks was excommunicated with his concubine Bertrada.”

Bertold himself, under 1096, says:

> “Philip, king of France, long since excommunicated for adultery, at last came quite humbly to make satisfaction to the lord pope while he was still staying in Gaul; having renounced the adulteress, he was received into favour and showed himself very ready for the lord pope’s service. After setting affairs in Gaul in good order, reconciling the king of France, and holding many councils, the lord pope finally returned to Lombardy with great triumph and glory.” [Col. 0393A]

## ON LETTER 212

“And in the Theodosian laws, if anyone [has] one thing.” No ancient exemplars vary here. It should nevertheless be noted that the words cited are those of Anianus, the ancient interpreter of the Theodosian Code, on Paulus, *Sentences*, book V, title 2. In the same manner Gratian, leaving aside the words of Paulus himself, cites Anianus’s words in the chapter *On Account of*, Cause 2, question 6, though suppressing Anianus’s name. The reason is that ancient copyists were accustomed very often to transcribe only the interpretations; several manuscripts of the Theodosian Code show this, for in them the fuller text of the laws has been omitted and only Anianus’s scholia remain. Subscriptions bearing consuls’ names were also added to these scholia, thus misleading an incautious reader. It is likely that Ivo had such a manuscript when he wrote these words.

## ON LETTER 214

[Col. 0393B]

“In so great a rending, in so great a storm.” Gregory VII caused it, and it was a great scandal to the whole world, as Sigebert says in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1111. How justly and urgently Ivo laments such discord will become clearer from the words of the ancient author, book II of *On Preserving the Unity of the Church*:

> “Pope Hildebrand divided the priesthoods, just as he divided the Church of God and the commonwealth of the empire; for he separated parties from it for himself. Grave and irreconcilable discords arose between him and King Henry, the pope striving mightily that the king be deprived both of royal power and dignity, while the king strove in opposition to defend himself from the attack of his enemies, who, fighting on the pope’s side, sought to crush him. From this the Church was divided, and the Church’s priesthoods were divided, and every kind of scandal arose. From this grew a grievous and long-lasting war—not merely civil war, but more than civil war—and, with no regard alike for God and humanity, there followed devastations of churches and slaughter of men. From this the divine and human laws alike were corrupted, laws without which neither the Church of God nor the commonwealth of the empire endures. From this public and catholic faith was violated. From this too grew that injustice whereby false testimonies were produced for truth, and perjuries abounded in place of catholic faith, so that, after laws had been forced into silence by war,” etc. [Col. 0393C]

The same author says shortly afterwards:

> “But once the empire and priesthood had been divided together, king rose against king, nation against nation, bishop against bishop, people against people. How many slaughterings of men then occurred, how many destructions of churches, and how great a confusion of affairs thereby arose throughout the whole Church—this seems to require tragedy rather than history.”

Emperor Henry IV, in a letter to the archbishop of Cologne, says:

> “Take care that you do not withdraw yourself from the oppressed Church, but grieve together with the kingdom and the priesthood; for just as through both the Church has hitherto been exalted, so now—alas!—it is humbled and bereaved. For one man, while claiming both for himself, destroyed both; nor did he benefit in one who was unwilling and unable to benefit in either.”

And shortly afterward:

> “You yourself know, if you have wished to know, how Hildebrand’s madness has thrown this ordinance of God into confusion. By his judgment no one may be a priest unless he has begged this from his arrogance.” [Col. 0393D]

William of Malmesbury, book V of the *Deeds of the Kings of England*, testifies that this schism disturbed the state of the Church for more than fifty years.

But the method of dispensation also met with no disapproval from any wise person. Relevant here is a fragment of an ancient but unidentified Roman pontiff:

> “For many years now the broad extent of the German kingdom has been divided from the unity of the apostolic see. In that schism so great a danger has arisen that, to say it with grief, scarcely a few Catholic priests or clerics can be found throughout so wide a region. Since therefore so many children lie slain in this devastation, the necessity of Christian peace requires that the maternal bowels of the Church be opened toward them. Instructed accordingly by the examples and writings of our Fathers, who at different times received Novatians, Donatists, and other heretics in their respective orders, we have received into the episcopal office the bishops of the aforesaid kingdom who were ordained in schism, unless they are proved to be intruders, simoniacs, or guilty of crimes. We have decreed the same concerning clerics of every rank whom their life and learning commend.”

To the same purpose belong the words of Pope Paschal II in answer to the questions of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury:

> “Anselm. It is often necessary, for compensatory reasons, to relax something of the apostolic and canonical enactments, especially in a kingdom in which almost everything is so corrupt and disordered that scarcely anything at all can be done there in accordance with ecclesiastical statutes. I ask that, with your permission, I may moderate in some way, according to the discretion which God may give me, what I asked of Lord Pope Urban, and which he left to my judgment.
>
> “Paschal. The method of dispensation, as blessed Cyril says in his letter to the Synod of Ephesus, has never displeased any of the wise. For we know that our holy Fathers, and the Apostles themselves, employed dispensations according to the exigencies of times and the circumstances of persons. Therefore, entertaining no doubt whatsoever concerning your long and widely proven religious devotion and wisdom, we entrust the matter to your judgment, so that, according to the understanding divinely given to you, when so great a necessity of the Church over which you preside demands it, you may be able, by timely and reasonable prudence, to moderate the strictness of the holy canons and decrees.” [Col. 0394A–B]

To these should also be joined the words of Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, to Pope Calixtus:

> “Dispensations must sometimes be made in the Church, not indeed from love of money or from any human favour, but with a devout and merciful intention. For a dispensation is then believed to be made devoutly and mercifully by a pastor of the Church when something is done less perfectly for a time by him, or is permitted to be done, not through his own will but through the necessity of others, lest the Christian faith itself be endangered in them. Thus a dispensation must be made by the Church in such a manner that the truth of our faith is always safeguarded, and that, if anything has been done or promised otherwise for the moment, it may be corrected at a suitable time.” [Col. 0394C]

And somewhat later:

> “Dispensations can and ought also to be made by which the customs of churches and monasteries are changed, but only where a lesser good is set aside in order that what is better may be established,” etc.

These words occur in the manuscript copy. One should consult what St Augustine argues most excellently in Letter 5 to Marcellinus, where he says that, when the reason of the times changes, what was rightly done before is rightly not done afterward unless it too is changed.

## On Letter CCXV

**To Thomas, Archbishop of York.** The superscription varies in ancient copies: some read *Tustannus*, others *Thomas*. The latter is found in the first edition, and perhaps this is the origin of the variation, since in some ancient manuscripts only the first letter, “T.,” is written; later readers interpreted it in various ways. Moreover, below, in Letter 276, Ivo mentions Tustannus, or Tustinus, Archbishop-elect of York.

In the author’s lifetime two Thomases governed the Church of York: namely, that Thomas by whom Henry I, king of the English, was crowned. When he died shortly thereafter, Gerard succeeded him; and when Gerard soon died, Thomas, chancellor of the said Henry, was appointed in 1108. It is also recorded that this Thomas, Archbishop of York, died in 1113, and that Turstan succeeded him. A letter of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, to him survives (Book II, Letter 149). There is also another letter of Anselm to the same Thomas [Col. 0394D–0395A], which plainly confirms what was just said: that there were two bishops of York called Thomas at nearly the same time (Book III, Letter 155).

**“Amid the darkness of a barbarous nation.”** Pope Paschal II calls the same English people barbarous in a letter to Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury:

> “But thanks be to God, because episcopal authority always endures in you, and, placed among barbarians, you do not cease from proclaiming the truth, whether through the violence of tyrants, the favour of the powerful, the kindling of fire, or the shedding of blood.”

In another letter to Anselm himself he says:

> “What you must therefore arrange in these matters in barbarous regions, you will be able to determine by comparing the command itself.”

## On Letter CCXVIII

**“He drew up marriage contracts for himself.”** What is said here of a canon of Paris is likewise written in Letter 200 concerning a certain prelate of the Church of Sens, who, besides two prostitutes, had drawn up marriage contracts with a concubine. From this it may be inferred that at that time it was difficult to persuade clerics in the Gallican Church to live continently, and that many were bound to wives.

Nicholas the monk, Book II, chapter 8, of the *Life of St Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens*—to whom Ivo’s letters are addressed—writes:

> “He was everywhere so distinguished and zealous a guardian of holiness and chastity that he steadfastly excluded notorious clerics, or those joined in an impure marriage, not only from his own fellowship but also from entry into the choir. For this reason he was assailed by them with many insults and many plots.”

And in Book III, chapter 15:

> “There was present among the others a certain man of the clergy, of the class of those whom we have mentioned above as defiled by an impure marriage; the blessed bishop had much trouble with such men before they could be corrected.” [Col. 0395B]

The *Chronology of Auxerre*, under the year of the Lord 1119:

> “Guy, Archbishop of Vienne, brother of Stephen, Count of Burgundy, is elected pope; and the council previously summoned by his predecessor is held by him at Rheims. There all simoniacs were excommunicated, as were those who demand payment for burial, chrism, or baptism; and the cohabitation of wives and concubines with priests, deacons, and subdeacons was there entirely forbidden.” [Col. 0395C]

**“And they disdain to obey the salutary commands of bishops.”** An example occurs in the unpublished letters of Anselm of Canterbury to Ernulf. Although the king of England had ordered that priests should have churches and women as they had in the time of his father and of Archbishop Lanfranc, Anselm, on the contrary, commanded throughout England that all priests keeping women should be deprived of their churches and every ecclesiastical benefice. In another letter to the said Ernulf and to the Archdeacon of Canterbury, he excommunicated those same priests who had proudly despised the order concerning forbidden women. Matthew Paris treats this matter in his *English History*. [Col. 0395C–D]

**“Which authority judges should be regarded as law, stubbornly and proudly.”** These nine words are now added for the first time on the authority of ancient manuscripts, from which they had hitherto been absent.

## On Letter CCXIX

**“To use Cyprian’s words.”** In the Royal manuscript the beginning of this letter is as follows:

> “If anything concerning me against me has been reported to the apostolic see, it is proper that a truthful document should follow me with the legate, answering the charges and defending my innocence. For I have recently received letters,” etc.

**“Who had neither been heard nor summoned.”** At this point there is a disgraceful blemish in the manuscripts, which also disfigured the first edition. They contain several words vainly repeated and reiterated from what precedes through the carelessness of ancient copyists; these therefore had to be removed.

**“Who was hearing the Mass of the catechumens.”** Many old copies read *cathicuminorum*. The use of this Mass is most ancient; it is mentioned in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 84, cited in the chapter *Episcopus*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1; and in the Council of Lleida, cited in the chapter *De his qui*, cause 35, questions 2 and 3. St Augustine, Sermon 38 *On Time*, says:

> “Behold: after the sermon, the catechumens are dismissed. The faithful remain; we proceed to the place of prayer.”

Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, in his manuscript work against Hincmar, Bishop of Laon, chapter 24:

> “It would have been useful for you to inquire into those things which you ought to have borne in mind for the salvation of yourself and of those entrusted to you: namely, how you should understand from the sacred rules that some are commanded to remain in church until the dismissal of the catechumens, while others are to be joined only within the church to the prayer of the faithful and to the celebration of the sacred mysteries, but are to be separated from the banquet of the Lord’s table.” [Col. 0396A]

**“That you may not rehear a case once decided because of the accusation of the greedy and malicious.”** These words are now added for the first time from several ancient books.

[Col. 0396B] **“They appeal, not from confidence in justice, but in order to delay the judgment.”** This is more correctly read from old copies than the former reading, “but for the pronouncement of judgment.” Letter 172 says similarly that the Abbot of Vendôme appealed to the apostolic see, not from confidence in justice, but in order to introduce delay. In Letter 180 the author complains of the excessive freedom of appeals to the apostolic see, because of harassment, expense, and the uncertain outcome of cases.

St Bernard also discusses this matter in Book III of *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius, chapter 2, where he teaches what procedure ought to be followed in appeals to the Roman see. This was an old and frequent complaint of the bishops of the Gallican Church. Of this sort is a letter of Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours, to Pope Honorius, in which he says among other things that by such delaying and superfluous appeals the poison of death is planted in the Lord’s garden: relief for the afflicted dies, episcopal vigour languishes, the economy of justice comes to nothing, while the abundance of offences receives increase. [Col. 0396B–C]

## On Letter CCXX

**“Let him alienate nothing without the connivance of the clergy.”** The reading varies in the copies. Some have *sine convenientia*, “without agreement,” as in Gratian, chapter *Sine*, cause 12, question 2. Printed books give: “without the connivance and subscription of all the clerics”; Contius, the jurist, notes in his Code that *convenientia* is read there, approving the latter reading and rejecting the former. But in Ivo’s *Panormia*, title *On the Alienation of Ecclesiastical Property*—where that canon is cited—one reads *sine collaudatione*, “without approval,” as in Burchard’s *Decretum*, Book III, chapter 170.

Yet *conniventia* is found in so many places in the sense of “consent” that it ought not rashly to be changed. In the canon *Obeuntibus*, distinction 64: “What has been done without their consent and connivance shall be held invalid.” Hincmar of Rheims, in the work against Hincmar of Laon: “to subscribe with the connivance of the clerics.” St Bernard, Letter 163: “Those men in whose connivance the matter rests.” Arnulf of Lisieux, Letter 21: “Until he might confirm by the connivance of your assent what he had conceived in his mind.” William of Tyre, *On the Holy War*, Book X, chapter 7: “Whom the same Church had set over itself by the common connivance of all.” The word occurs in the same sense in Ivo himself, Letters 138, 163, 195, 220, and 250. [Col. 0396C–D]

## On Letter CCXXIII

**“They commit the bodies of excommunicated persons to burial in a certain false cemetery.”** Because episcopal censures were exceedingly frequent, and often imposed for comparatively minor causes, it is not surprising that excommunications were then despised and that the prohibition of burial was treated as an additional burden. On this matter there are various complaints by Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, in a manuscript copy, from which I shall transcribe the words.

Thus, in a letter to this Ivo, who had prohibited the divine office in the castle and throughout the league of the Count of Vendôme:

> “You have permitted the bodies of the poor to be buried; this we can neither refuse nor dare to refuse. But, with your peace and reverence preserved, we say that, if they remained unburied for the sake of the Church’s justice, their souls would not therefore have less glory. And since burial is granted to the poor by your Holiness, under the name of the poor no one is now excluded from burial.” [Col. 0397A]

Another letter of the same author to Ivo follows:

> “Let your belovedness know, dearest Father, that in the castle of Vendôme those so-called Regular Canons of St George celebrated the feast solemnly in the Church of St Peter with the doors open, contrary to your interdict; and that other clerics of the same castle committed a certain deceased burgess to burial with public processions—burying with the dead man justice itself, as though it were dead. Concerning this burial of ecclesiastical justice, which is known to have been performed in a spirit of contumacy, and concerning the punishment of such burial, our humility would have written something to your eminence, if a single monk sufficed to accuse a multitude of clerics of disobedience, and if it did not seem presumptuous to instruct a bishop of such discernment. Yet let your belovedness consider this: if so great an injury to justice is borne patiently, it is to be feared that the holy Church will lose very much of her standing on this occasion and suffer an intolerable loss of her honour and order.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For which rich man wishes to be buried contrary to your interdict and is not buried? But burial is denied to poor people, who bear no guilt. Churches are opened to the powerful; the powerless—by whom what has been badly done cannot be corrected—are excluded from the churches,” etc. [Col. 0397A–B]

The same author, in a letter to Rannulf, Bishop of Saintes:

> “We likewise do not pass over in silence what you did concerning Aimeric of Rancon. Aimeric, indeed, because of the many evils which he had done to us, had been excommunicated by the lord pope and by you; and, while under that excommunication, he was struck down by the just judgment of God, and was therefore excluded from the cemetery. Yet afterward, corrupted by the prayers of his wife and, as some say, by money, you communicated with that excommunicated man by absolving him without satisfaction; and, in the presence of our brethren, through whom our injuries sounded in your ears and have not ceased to sound, you yourself committed his body to burial. Nevertheless, on the authority of the holy canons we firmly maintain and in no way doubt that we ought not to communicate with the dead when we do not communicate with them while alive. Whoever does otherwise, if he is a layman, ought himself to be excommunicated; if a cleric, of whatever dignity or order, he ought to be utterly deposed. Farewell, and consider wisely what has been said.” [Col. 0397B–C]

These matters have been set down at greater length because they also concern Letter 62, in which Sanctius, Bishop of Orléans, seeks advice as to what he ought to do in the case of clerics or monks who had celebrated Masses and buried the dead contrary to an interdict. This he understands concerning excommunicated persons.

## On Letter CCXXIX

**“By the example of Sixtus and Leo.”** Pope Nicholas mentions the vindication of Pope Sixtus III in the chapter *Nunc autem*, distinction 21; Anastasius the Librarian also mentions it in the *Lives of the Popes*. Sixtus’s own words are cited by Gratian in chapter *Mandastis*, cause 2, question 4.

Evidence for the vindication of Pope Leo is found in Gratian himself, chapter *Omnibus*, cause 2, question 5, where Leo is said to have had twelve bishops in his vindication. The Monk of St Gall, in the *Life of Charlemagne*, says:

> “Leo, taking up the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, placed it upon his head and, in the presence of Charles and his soldiers, with his persecutors also standing by, swore in these words: ‘So may I be a sharer in the Gospel on the day of the great judgment as I am free from the crime falsely charged against me by these men.’”

Another monk of St Cybard of Angoulême, in his account of the life of the same Charles, and likewise another anonymous writer of the *Annals of Pippin, Charlemagne, and Louis*, under the year 1300, relate that this occurred at Rome before all the people in the Basilica of St Peter, when Leo, carrying the Gospel, ascended the ambo. The oath of the said Leo is recorded by Burchard, *Decretum*, Book I, chapter 198. Join to these the note on the letter. [Col. 0397D–0398A]

## On Letter CCXXXI

**“Who made himself a eunuch in order to cure epilepsy.”** The reading of this passage varied in manuscript codices, which have *epileusiam*, *epilesiam*, *epylensiam*, or *epilemsiam*. The better reading is *epilepsiam*, “epilepsy.” Relevant here is the statement of Innocent III in the chapter *Ex parte*, title *On Those Defective in Body and Ordination*, that a priest who, on a physician’s advice, had his genitals cut off lest he fall into leprosy retains full liberty to exercise his ministry. Aetius also writes, Book XIII, chapter 125, that castrated persons do not suffer from this disease of leprosy.

Theodore Balsamon, on Apostolic Canon 23, reports that many somewhat more prudent men who intended to castrate themselves were accustomed to come to the Church and disclose both the illness and the excision of their testicles. On chapter 1 he likewise says:

> “The Nicene Synod testifies that in its time it had seen no one admitted to holy orders who had been permitted to castrate himself because of illness, although many had requested this by synodal authority.” [Col. 0398A–B]

## On Letter CCXXXII

**“Concerning marital relations.”** These three words were absent from the first edition; they have been added on the authority and agreement of several manuscripts.

**To Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble.** Formerly printed *Gratiopolitano* [rather than *Gratianopolitano*]. In some editions of Gratian, where this rescript of Urban appears, the superscription is: “Urban II to Gratian, Bishop of Naples”; but this is erroneous, and has rightly been corrected in the latest edition.

The Monk of Auxerre, in his Chronicle under the year 1078, says:

> “In this year St Hugh becomes Bishop of Grenoble, where for fifty-two years he flourished incomparably in examples of virtue,” etc.

Sigebert of Gembloux mentions that Hugh and likewise calls him Bishop of Grenoble. Speaking of Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, around 1084, he says:

> “The collaborator and emulator in this holy purpose was Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, of blessed memory. He received the monastic habit from Bruno himself and furnished a notable example to all who lived there.” [Col. 0398B–C]

Robert of Torigni, in his Chronicle under 1132:

> “The holy man Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, died. Guigo, Prior of the Charterhouse, which is not far from Grenoble, wrote an account of his religious life.”

## On Letter CCXXXIII

**“Of the Fathers Gregory and Urban.”** The word “Fathers” is added from several old copies. He means Gregory VII, also called Hildebrand, whose canon at a Roman synod is this:
