> “Since we have learned that in many places investitures of churches are made by lay persons contrary to the enactments of the holy Fathers, and that from this many disturbances arise in the Church by which the Christian religion is trampled underfoot, we decree that no one shall receive an investiture of a bishopric, abbey, or church from the hand of an emperor, king, or any lay person, male or female. If anyone presumes to do so, let him acknowledge that such investiture is null by apostolic authority and that he is subject to excommunication until he makes fitting satisfaction.” [Col. 0398C–D]

The words of William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, Book II, speaking of Urban’s council, indicate that Urban decreed the same:

> “At this council the pope, together with all, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against lay investitors of churches, against those invested by laymen, against those consecrating persons thus invested, and against those who become the men of laymen for ecclesiastical dignities.”

This council was held at Rome about 1098, as Thomas of Walsingham, among others, notes in the *Ypodigma Neustriae*. These canons are also cited from the Council of Clermont, at which Urban himself was present:

> “Let no ecclesiastic receive any honour from the hand of laymen.”
>
> “It is forbidden that kings or other princes make any investiture of ecclesiastical honours.” [Col. 0399A]

Above, in Letter 60, Ivo says that he had heard that Urban excluded kings only from corporal investiture. Here, however, one should not pass over the remarkably frank testimony of Onuphrius, the most learned of Italians, in the book he wrote on the life of Gregory VII:

> “By that earlier decree he attacked not only Emperor Henry IV but also all Latin and Western kings; then the bishops and the entire clergy of Gaul, Germany, and Italy. The majesty and dignity of the Roman Empire were overthrown, and, what was far worse, foundations were laid by which its power was altogether shaken.”

**“I judge it schismatic.”** In the conclusion of Letter 236 he likewise says that the layman who believes that he can confer a sacrament through the giving and receiving of a staff is a heretic. John, Archbishop of Lyons, says below, in Letter 237, that external investitures made by laymen are not quite properly designated by the name of heresy, but that to defend them must be heresy. In the manuscript codices of Jacques Sirmond there is a treatise by Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, to Cardinal Peter Leo, *On the Ordination of Bishops and Lay Investiture*, in which he argues that it is heretical (see *Patrologia*, vol. CLVII, col. 214). [Col. 0399A–B]

**“In certain letters he wrote to me that he had been compelled.”** Below, in Letter 236, he says that Paschal wrote the same thing to other bishops. Relevant here are the words of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in a letter to Paschal:

> “This year after Pentecost I sent letters to your Holiness through Bernard, servant of your chamberlain Lord Peter, reporting that the king of England complains that you allow the German king to grant investitures of churches without excommunication; and therefore he threatens that he will undoubtedly resume his own investitures, since that king retains his in peace. Let your prudence therefore consider without delay what you ought to do about this, lest what you have so well built be irrecoverably destroyed. For our king diligently asks what you are doing with that king.”

The pope answered Anselm in these words:

> “Furthermore, because in those letters you signified that some are scandalized because we tolerate the German king’s granting investitures of churches, know that we have never tolerated it, nor do we tolerate it, nor shall we tolerate it. We waited indeed for the fierceness of that people to be subdued. But if the king persists in the path of his father’s wickedness, he will without doubt experience the sword of blessed Peter, which we have already begun to draw.” [Col. 0399B–C]

These passages are taken from a manuscript copy, since they have hitherto been unpublished.

## On Letter CCXXXV

**To Radulf, by the grace of God Archbishop of Tours.** Gregory VII mentions Rodulf, Archbishop of Tours, in Book II, Letters 19 and 20, and in Book IV, Letter 5. Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, likewise mentions in his letters Radulf, Archbishop of Tours, who lived in his own age; a passage concerning him has also been cited above on Letter 67.

An ancient author, a monk of Marmoutier, expressly testifies that in Ivo’s lifetime there were two men of this name, one the immediate successor of the other; his narrative is found in the observations on Letter 108. In those manuscripts the name is sometimes written *Radulfus* and sometimes *Rodulfus*, and must be understood as the same name. Thus he whom some call Rodulf the Green, Archbishop of Rheims, is called Radulf by others, as noted above on Letter 190. [Col. 0399C–D]

## On Letter CCXXXVI

The title of this letter was different and simpler in the earlier edition: “To John, Archbishop of the First See of Lyons: Ivo, minister of the Church of Chartres, greeting.” For this is how I had found it in the ancient manuscripts which I then used. It is now restored in the form in which it is written in the codex of St Victor and another Royal codex, in which the names of the bishops are expressly given. It is probable that it was composed by Ivo, as the style sufficiently indicates.

Thus above, in Letter 79, he wrote a letter in his own name and in that of four other bishops to Philip of Troyes; similarly, in Letter 189, he wrote the defence of King Louis’s coronation in his own name and in that of the other bishops. [Col. 0400A]

**“To be held at Anse.”** Only the St-Germain codex has *Ausam*, incorrectly; for John, Archbishop of Lyons, also calls it Anse below in Letter 237.

**“If they command rightly those matters which pertain to the see, but do not do those matters at all.”** The earlier edition has: “but do not at all do those things which act against the see.” In the old Ser. copy, differently: “but do not at all do those things which pertain to the right of the see”; there is a superfluous repetition of words.

**“We wish to correct [them] while preserving the bond of peace.”** Formerly it was printed, “we wish to correct while preserving the bond,” which made the sentence incomplete. Baronius, who transcribed this letter in volume XII of the *Annals*, therefore added “the bond of charity.” A little earlier Ivo calls it the “bond of peace” twice. [Col. 0400A–B]

**“He seems to have made concessions concerning investitures remitted to the German king.”** In only one copy was the reading “concerning investitures remitted to the king.” But in other codices the word *Germanico*, “German,” occurs; without it the sense is somewhat obscure. A little earlier in this same letter he calls him the German king: “For if,” he says, “the pope has not yet exercised due severity against the German king.” He means the same king when, in Letter 233, he says that the pope permitted certain wicked things in writing; there too he deals with investitures made by laymen.

This is the controversy which in that century stirred up the most sorrowful and terrible tragedies in the Christian world. If anyone perhaps wishes to know its origin and course, it will not be useless to draw from pure sources by bringing forward and comparing the testimonies of contemporary historians, so that what Ivo writes throughout this remarkable letter may be understood more clearly.

William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, Book III, under William I:

> “Henry, Emperor of the Germans [Note: This was Henry IV.], son of Henry, of whom we have spoken above, angry with the pope because he had pronounced excommunication against him on account of investitures of churches, came with an army, besieged Rome, expelled Hildebrand, and introduced Guibert of Ravenna [Note: Abbot of Ursperg in his Chronicle, and likewise Dodechin in his continuation of Marianus Scotus, call him Wigebert.].” [Col. 0400B–D]

And shortly afterward he states who was the first author and instigator of the conflict:

> “Alexander having died, Hildebrand succeeded him, called Gregory VII. What others had left unused, he openly advanced—so the editions read, though someone changes *inusitaverant* (‘had left unused’) into *mussitaverant* (‘had muttered’)—by excommunicating elect persons who received investitures of churches from the hand of a layman through ring and staff. Hence Henry, Emperor of the Germans, furious that he should presume such things without his knowledge, drove him from Rome after eleven years, as I said, having introduced Guibert; and not long afterward the pope was struck by a fatal illness.” [Col. 0400D]

Sigebert, in his Chronicle under the year of the Lord 1111:

> “King Henry goes to Rome to settle the discord between kingdom and priesthood. It had been begun by Pope Gregory VII, who was called Hildebrand, and pursued by his successors Victor and Urban, and above all by Paschal; it was a great scandal to the whole world.”

William of Tyre, *The Holy War*, Book I, chapter 13, speaking of the same Gregory:

> “A custom had arisen, especially in the Empire, that when prelates of churches died, the ring and pastoral staff were sent to the lord emperor. He then invested one of his household servants and chaplains [Note: These were sons of princes; see the note on the letter.] and sent him to the vacant church to exercise there the office of pastor, without awaiting the election of the clergy. The lord pope, judging that this was done contrary to every propriety and perceiving that ecclesiastical rights were trampled underfoot by this practice, warned the same emperor once, twice, and three times; when he could not bring him back, he bound him with the bond of anathema. Taking this action most indignantly, the emperor began to persecute the Roman Church and raised up against the lord pope Guibert, Archbishop of Ravenna, a very learned and very wealthy man, as an adversary,” etc. [Col. 0400D–0401A]

Gregory VII was succeeded by Victor, pope for a few days, who likewise prohibited lay investiture of churches, as an ancient writer of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* relates. After Victor’s death, his successor Urban II, having held a council at Rome about 1098, likewise forbade them, as noted above on Letter 233.

But after Urban’s death the conflict flared up far more fiercely. Matthew Paris, *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, under Henry I:

> “In the year of the Lord 1112 a conflict arose at Rome between Pope Paschal and Emperor Henry for this reason: the emperor wished to make use of the privilege held by his predecessors for three hundred years under sixty Roman pontiffs, who had lawfully conferred bishoprics and abbeys by ring and pastoral staff. On the other hand, the Roman pontiffs judged that they neither could nor ought to,” etc. [Col. 0401A–B]

The same words also occur in Sigebert’s Chronicle under the year of the Lord 1111. William of Malmesbury, Book V of the *Deeds of the Kings of the English*:

> “When Paschal had succeeded Pope Urban, the question of investitures of churches was again debated; wars and disputes again arose, neither side yielding ground. The emperor had on his side all the bishops and abbots of his kingdom on this side of the mountains, because Charlemagne, in order to curb the fierceness of those peoples, had bestowed almost all lands upon churches. He had most prudently considered that men of sacred order would not as readily as laymen renounce fidelity to their lord. Moreover, if laymen rebelled, he could restrain them by the authority of excommunication and the severity of power. The pope had subjected the churches beyond the mountains to his own policy, and the cities of Italy paid little heed to Henry’s rule, believing themselves freed from servitude after the death of his brother Conrad. Left by his father as king in Lombardy, Conrad died at Arezzo. But Henry, in no respect inferior in courage to the ancient Caesars, after pacifying the German kingdom, ambitiously aspired to the Italian one, intending to subdue the rebellion of the cities and settle the question of investiture according to his own will.”

Sugerius, however, testifies that Pope Paschal came to the western regions “to consult with the king of the Franks, and the king’s designated son, and the Gallican Church concerning certain troubles and the new disputes over ecclesiastical investiture, by which the Emperor Henry was both harassing him and threatening to harass him still more.” And a little later: “Indeed it was resolved at Rome, because of the mercenary treachery of the Romans, that it was safer to debate the aforesaid—indeed, all—questions concerning the king, his son, and the Gallican Church in France than to suffer shipwreck in the city.”

Thus those words should incidentally be corrected on the authority of the old manuscripts, since they have been miserably corrupted in the common edition. Hence, taking the opportunity, I shall set forth the remaining words bearing upon this controversy, corrected in many places, so that meanwhile the passage of the Vulgate edition may be restored to its proper brilliance, until a more complete edition of Suger’s *History* is printed. Speaking, then, of the pope’s arrival at the monastery of St Dionysius, he says:

> “There the king Philip and his son Lord Louis met him, gratefully and devoutly bending their royal majesty at his feet out of love for God, as kings customarily bow with lowered diadem at the tomb of Peter the fisherman. The lord pope raised them with his hand and made them sit before him as most devoted sons of the apostles. With them, wisely acting as a wise man, he conferred familiarly concerning the state of the Church; and, gently persuading them, he begged them to bring aid to blessed Peter and to himself, Peter’s vicar, to uphold the Church, and—as the custom introduced by the predecessor-kings of the Franks, Charlemagne and others, had become established—to resist boldly tyrants and enemies of the Church, especially the Emperor Henry.
>
> “[Col. 0402A] They gave their hands in pledge of friendship, aid, and counsel; they placed the realm at his disposal; and, hastening to meet the emperor’s envoys at Châlons, they joined with him archbishops, bishops, and Adam, abbot of St Dionysius, with whom we too were present. While the lord pope remained there for some time, the envoys of the Emperor Henry, appointed by agreement, not humble but stern and obstinate, took up lodgings at St Memmius. Leaving there Chancellor Albert, through whose unanimity of speech and heart the emperor himself acted, the rest came to the court in a great company, with great pomp, splendidly adorned [variant: *falerati*].
>
> “These were the archbishop of Trier, the bishop of A[?]lvertat, the bishop of Münster, several counts, and Duke Welf, before whom the sword was borne everywhere: a corpulent man, remarkable and vociferous in the whole expanse of his great height and breadth. They appeared to have been sent to make a tumult for intimidation rather than for negotiation. The archbishop of Trier alone in particular [Col. 0402B]—a polished and agreeable [variant: *jocundus*, ‘pleasant’] man, rich in eloquence and wisdom, trained in the French manner of elevated speech—delivered an elegant address. He conveyed to the lord pope and the court the emperor’s greeting and service, saving the right of the kingdom. Proceeding to his instructions, he said:
>
> “‘This is the business of our lord the emperor for which we have been sent. In the times of your predecessors, holy and apostolic men—Gregory the Great and others—it is known that the following order belonged to the right of the Empire: in every election, before the election is publicly announced, it is to be reported to the ears of the lord emperor; and, if the person be suitable, his assent is to be obtained before the election is made. Then, in an assembly, it is to be published according to the canons: by petition of the people, election of the clergy, and assent of the dignitary. Once consecrated, he is freely and without simony to return to the lord emperor, that he may be invested with ring and staff for the regalia, and render fealty and homage. Nor is this surprising: for cities, castles, marches, tolls [variant: *thelonea*], and every dignity of the Empire [Col. 0402C] ought by no other means to be acquired. If the lord pope will permit these things, kingdom and Church will cleave together in prosperity and good peace, to the honour of God.’
>
> “To this the lord pope, prudently, replied through the bishop of Piacenza, his spokesman: ‘The Church, redeemed by the precious blood of Jesus Christ and made free, must in no way be made a slave again. If the Church cannot elect a prelate without his consultation, then Christ’s death is annulled and she is subjected to him as a servant. If he invests with staff and ring, since these pertain to the altars, he usurps authority against God himself. If hands consecrated to the Lord’s body and blood are subjected by bonds to lay hands stained with the sword’s blood, this diminishes their order and sacred anointing.’
>
> “When the stiff-necked envoys heard this and similar statements, they ground their teeth and raised a tumult with Teutonic fury; and, if they had dared safely, they would have spewed insults and inflicted injuries. ‘Not here,’ they said, ‘but at Rome shall the dispute be settled by swords.’ [Col. 0402D]
>
> “But the pope sent many tested and experienced men to the chancellor, that they might approach him about these matters in an orderly and peaceful fashion, hear him, and earnestly beseech him to labour for the peace of the realm. After they departed, the lord pope came to Troyes, honourably held the long-announced universal council, and returned successfully to the see of St Peter, aided by the love of the Franks, who had served him greatly, and by fear and hatred of the Teutons.
>
> “About the second year after his departure, the emperor, having collected the astonishing host of thirty thousand soldiers, who rejoice in having no roads except those opened by spilled blood, marched toward Rome. Very cunningly he pretended peace, laid aside the dispute over investitures, promised much good—this and other things—and, since he could not otherwise enter the City, he flattered. Nor did he fear to deceive the supreme pontiff and the whole Church—indeed, the very King of kings. Since they heard that so great and so destructive a question troubling God’s Church had been lulled to sleep, the Roman Quirites rejoiced beyond measure, the clergy exulted exceedingly, and with glad rivalry strove to receive him with the greatest honour and elegance.
>
> “[Col. 0403A] As the lord pope hastened to meet him, surrounded by a company of bishops and cardinals in ceremonial dress, mounted on horses covered with white trappings, and followed by the Roman people, men were sent ahead to receive from the emperor, upon the holy Gospels which they touched, an oath of peace and a renunciation of investitures. This was repeated at the place called Mount Joy. [Note: [Col. 0403D] See Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 39 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*.] There, as they first approached the thresholds where the visible shrines of the blessed apostles meet those arriving, the same was again done. In the portico, before the marvellous and universal spectacle of the Romans, the oath was given three times by the emperor’s own hand and by those of the magnates.
>
> “Then, more splendidly than if a triumphal arch smiled upon him after an African victory, he was crowned with the diadem, in the manner of the Augusti, by the most sacred hand of the lord pope, amid hymns and the manifold triumph of praises. He was led to the most sacred altar of the apostles in a most celebrated and solemn act of devotion: the clerics sang their chants, while the dreadful cry of the singing Germans pierced the heavens. When the lord pope, celebrating masses of thanksgiving, had consecrated the body and blood of Jesus Christ, the emperor communicated, receiving the divided Eucharist [variant: *Euccaristiam*] as a wondrous pledge of the Church in a covenant of indivisible love and preservation of the agreement.
>
> “Before the lord pope had yet laid aside his episcopal vestments after Mass, Teutonic fury, raging with unforeseen wickedness under the pretext of a feigned dispute, broke forth. With swords drawn, they ran about like men mad with insanity and attacked the Romans, who in such a place were rightly unarmed. They cried out under oath that all the Roman clergy, bishops and cardinals alike, must be seized or slaughtered; and, beyond what any insanity can further attain, they did not hesitate to lay impious hands upon the lord pope.
>
> “[Col. 0403C] With inexpressible grief and heartfelt anguish, both the Roman nobility and the people mourned, though they perceived the *faucionem*—perhaps “plot” or “contrivance”—only too late. [Note: [Col. 0403D] One old manuscript has *faucionem*; another, *fauctionem*. The edition of Suger has *sanctionem*. All are corrupt; perhaps one should read *factionem* (‘faction’) or *fictionem* (‘contrivance’), since a little earlier he said: ‘under the pretext of a feigned [Col. 0404D] dispute.’] Some ran to arms; others fled as though stunned. They could not escape the unexpected war of their enemies except by pulling down beams from the portico and making their fall a defence against them.
>
> “But the aforesaid emperor, terrified by the torment of his evil conscience and criminal deed, left the city as swiftly as possible, carrying off as booty—unheard-of among Christians taken from Christians—the lord pope himself and all the cardinals and bishops whom he could seize. He withdrew to the town of Castellana, a place fortified in the highest degree by nature and art. There, after shamefully stripping the cardinals, he treated them disgracefully; and, what is dreadful even to say, he did not fear proudly to lay hands upon the Anointed of the Lord, stripping even the lord pope himself of his cope, mitre, and every insignia of the apostolic office which he wore. He inflicted many injuries and did not release him or his followers, afflicted with much disgrace, until he compelled him to grant the aforesaid agreement and thereafter to issue the resulting privilege.
>
> “He also extorted from the lord pope’s hand another surreptitious privilege, allowing him henceforth to invest [bishops]. This same privilege the lord pope, in a great council of three hundred bishops and more, while we heard, shattered [better: ‘annulled’], and reduced to nothing under a perpetual anathema. [Col. 0403D]
>
> “But if anyone asks why the lord pope acted so weakly, let him know that, when the shepherd and the pillars standing beside him had been struck down, the Church languished; and the tyrant, enslaving her, almost occupied her as his own because there was no one to resist. He gave sure proof of this in fact: when he had somehow caused the brethren—the pillars of the Church—to be released for her defence and restoration, and had restored whatever peace to the Church he could, he fled to the wilderness of the desert. He would have remained there permanently had not the universal Church and the violence of the Romans compelled his return. [Col. 0404A]
>
> “But the Lord Jesus Christ, redeemer and defender of his Church, neither endured her to be trampled longer nor allowed the emperor to go unpunished. Those who had neither been taken captive nor bound by an oath, taking up the cause of the afflicted Church, gathered the Church in a celebrated Gallican council by the support and counsel of the designated Lord Louis. There they bound the tyrant emperor with an anathema and pierced him with the sword of blessed Peter,” etc.

Thus far Suger.

But the settlement extorted during Paschal’s violent imprisonment of three weeks was later invalidated by a council held in 1112, the twelfth year of Pope Paschal’s pontificate, as William of Malmesbury writes in book V of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*. For the privilege of investiture was condemned—indeed, on account of its perversity they called it a “perverse privilege” (*pravilegium*) rather than a privilege. Thus the word should be read in the passage of [Col. 0404B] the said William; this reading is confirmed by Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 14. At this council held in Rome, the decrees of Gregory VII and Urban III against lay investitures were renewed and confirmed.

Accordingly Emperor Henry, stirred by this, in the seventeenth year of Paschal’s pontificate, again made for Rome, intending to exact sharper vengeance upon him. But in the meantime Paschal died; and, after his successor Gelasius had soon been expelled and had died, Guido was chosen pope—he was called Calixtus. He immediately held a council at Rheims, at which lay investitures were again forbidden and the emperor, unless he repented, was placed under anathema.

At length, when the Empire had been weakened in many ways and the emperor saw the kingdom gradually slipping from him, he reflected upon his father’s example and was pressed by fear of anathema, as Godfrey of Viterbo says in part XVII of his *Chronicle*, and Otto of Freising in book VII, chapter 16 of his *Chronicle*. Therefore, his spirit softened, he was restored to communion with [Col. 0404C] the Roman see and surrendered to Calixtus ecclesiastical investitures by ring and staff. In return, Calixtus granted that he might give his assent to the elections of bishops and abbots in the Teutonic kingdom, and that the person elected should receive the regalia from him by the sceptre, as the same William of Malmesbury in book V and the abbot of Ursperg under the year of the Lord 1125 write.

These statements contribute to the interpretation of the passage in Otto of Freising, *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick I*, book II, chapter 6. Otto also reports, in book VII, chapter 16 of his *Chronicle*, the quibble of the Romans, who said that the privilege granted to the emperor—that the elect were not to be ordained before receiving the regalia from his hand by sceptre—had been given to Henry alone for the sake of peace, not to his successors. Thus at last was calmed the inveterate disease which had disturbed the condition of the Church for more than fifty years.

There are also other ancient writers who mention this controversy between Paschal and Henry: Abbot Dodechinus, in the appendix to the *Chronicle* [Col. 0404D] of Marianus Scotus, and Martin of Poland, in the *Life of Paschal*. Long ago I also published evidence of the matter discovered in ancient parchments, on whose authority others have drawn. Since these documents pertain to the interpretation and elucidation of this Ivorian Letter 236, I have thought it fitting to append them again.

### Letter of John, bishop of Tusculum, on the capture of Pope Paschal, sent to Richard, bishop of Albano

[Note: [Col. 0404D] This bishop, as Peter the Deacon says in book IV, chapter 41 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, never ceased to stir up the minds of the faithful by letters to bring help to the Church.]

> “JOHN, by the grace of God bishop of Tusculum, acting on behalf of Lord Paschal, pope and prisoner of Jesus Christ, to his venerable brother RICHARD, bishop of Albano: greeting in the Lord.
>
> “Since, as the Apostle says, we are one body [Col. 0405A] in Christ, and if one member suffers, the other members suffer with it, we inform your brotherhood of what has been done to our head and almost the whole Church. When Henry, king of the Teutons, arrived at Sutri [variants: *Sutriam* or *Sutrium*], he sent certain envoys to Rome. By oath they guaranteed that the envoys of Lord Pope Paschal would be conducted there and back safely, and that the king himself would confirm by oath that he would entirely renounce every investiture of churches. He was also to give hostages that he would not return to this outrage, and that he would leave wholly free and undisturbed the ecclesiastical properties, regalia, and patrimonies of blessed Peter. He was also to give hostages for security when [the pope] went out to crown him at the basilica of blessed Peter.
>
> “Afterward, on the Church’s side, it was confirmed by laymen that, if the said king observed what had been promised, our lord would receive him graciously, place the royal diadem upon him, and, once crowned, permit him to enter the city if he wished. He also received hostages for the crossing [Col. 0405B] of the bridge, for whom he gave an oath that, if he crossed the bridge on that Sunday, he would restore them into the free power of our people.
>
> “When, therefore, all these oaths had been performed by both sides and hostages given, and the pope went out to St Peter’s church to crown him, the king disregarded the oaths and released the hostages; in that very church he violently seized him together with the bishops, cardinals, and many Romans, and holds them in the strictest captivity. But on the following day the Romans assembled, attacked the enemies of the Church, and compelled them to flee from the portico, after killing many of their men and causing them to lose their horses, tents, money, and countless furnishings. Thereafter all unanimously swore, with one mind and one will, to fight against him.
>
> “Therefore be watchful with prudence; and, the greater the necessity you perceive, the more earnestly labour, and do not cease to aid the mother of all Churches. Cause prayers for the liberation of our lord—indeed, for the Church itself—to be offered wherever you can. Farewell. This [Col. 0405C] occurred in the year of the Lord 1111, in the fourth indiction, on the day before the Ides of February, in the basilica of St Peter, prince of the apostles, on the Sunday before the beginning of the fast.”

### In this manner the reconciliation between Pope Paschal and Emperor Henry was made

#### Oath of the emperor

> “I, Henry, shall release unharmed on the next Wednesday or Thursday Lord Pope Paschal, the bishops and cardinals, and all prisoners and hostages who have been captured for him and with him; and I shall cause them to be brought forth free outside the gate of the Transtiberine city. Nor shall I hereafter seize, or cause to be seized, those who remain faithful to Lord Pope Paschal. I shall preserve peace and security, both through myself and through my men, for the Roman people and the city of the Transtiberine island, in their persons and property, provided that they keep peace with me.
>
> “I shall restore the patrimonies and possessions of the Holy Roman Church which I have taken away; and, in good faith, I shall help it recover and hold all that it ought to have according to the custom of my predecessors. I shall obey Lord Pope Paschal, [Col. 0405D] while preserving the honour of kingdom and Empire, as Catholic emperors [obey] Catholic Roman pontiffs. I shall observe all these things in good faith, without fraud or evil intent.”

These are the oath-takers on the side of Emperor Henry: Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; Gebehard, bishop of Trent; Bruno, bishop of Speyer; Burchard, bishop of Münster; Albert the chancellor; Count Hermann; Count Berengar; Frederick, Count Palatine. Also Count Frederick; Boniface, margrave; Albert, count of Blandraco; Count Godfrey; Warner, margrave.

#### Grant of the pope concerning the investitures of bishoprics

> “Lord Pope Paschal grants to Lord Emperor Henry and his kingdom, and shall confirm and strengthen by his privilege under anathema, that, with the emperor’s assent, a bishop or abbot freely elected without simony shall be invested by the lord emperor with ring and staff. A bishop or abbot invested by the emperor shall freely receive consecration from the bishop to whom it belongs. But if anyone is elected by clergy and people and is not invested by the emperor, he is not to be consecrated by anyone; and archbishops and bishops shall have freedom to consecrate those invested by the emperor. Moreover, concerning these matters Lord Pope Paschal shall not trouble King Henry, nor his kingdom and Empire.”

195

#### Oath on the pope’s side

> “Lord Pope Paschal shall not trouble Lord Emperor Henry or his kingdom concerning the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys, nor concerning the injury done to himself and his followers in their persons and goods; nor shall he inflict any harm upon him or upon any person on this account. He shall never at all lay an anathema upon the person of Emperor Henry; nor shall anything remain undone by the lord pope to prevent his crowning him as the order provides. He shall assist kingdom and Empire, by the help of his office, according to his ability. And Lord Pope Paschal shall fulfil these things [Col. 0406B] without fraud or evil intent.”

These are the names of the bishops and cardinals who, at the command of Lord Pope Paschal, confirmed by oath the privilege and friendship to Lord Emperor Henry: Peter, bishop of Porto; Centinus, bishop of Sabina; Robert, cardinal of St Eusebius; Boniface, cardinal of St Martin; Anastasius, cardinal of St Clement; Gregory, cardinal of the Apostles Peter and Paul; Gregory, cardinal of St Chrysogonus; John, cardinal of St Pudentiana; Risus, cardinal of St Lawrence; Ramerus, cardinal of Saints Marcellinus and Peter; Vitalis, cardinal of St Balbina; Dinzo, cardinal of St Martin; Theobald, cardinal of John and Paul; John, deacon of St Mary in the Greek School; Leo, deacon of St Vitalis the Martyr; Abbo, deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

### Privilege of Pope Paschal which he made for Emperor Henry concerning the investitures of bishoprics and abbeys

[Col. 0406C]

> “Paschal, bishop,” etc. See under Paschal II, at the year 1118.

### Letter of Pope Paschal condemning the privilege which Henry had extorted from him by force, sent to Guido, archbishop of Vienne

> “Paschal, bishop,” etc. See there.

### Excommunication issued against Emperor Henry by the council held at Vienne under Archbishop Guido

> “Following the authority of the holy Roman Church, we judge investiture of bishoprics, abbeys, and all ecclesiastical offices from a lay hand to be heresy. In the power of the Holy Spirit, we condemn as void and declare to have no blessed memory that document, or privilege, which King Henry violently extorted from Lord Pope Paschal concerning investitures and an anathema upon his own person, rather than obtaining it freely.
>
> “We excommunicate, anathematize, and exclude from the bosom of holy mother Church Henry, king of the Teutons, who came to Rome feigning peace and, after giving oaths [Col. 0406D] to Lord Pope Paschal regarding his life, limbs, freedom from evil captivity, and renunciation of investitures, betrayed and seized that same lord pope in the apostolic see before the body of blessed Peter—after kissing his foot, mouth, and face—by treachery, perjury, and sacrilege, like another Judas, together with cardinals, bishops, archbishops, and many Roman nobles. Having carried him off to the camp, he stripped him of the apostolic insignia, treated him with unworthy and disgraceful mockery, and violently extorted from him the above-mentioned most wicked and detestable document. He shall remain excluded until, renouncing all these things, he gives full satisfaction to that same Church.”

### Rescript of Archbishop Guido to Lord Pope Paschal concerning confirmation of the council held at Vienne

> “To Lord Paschal, holy and most sweet father, Guido, archbishop of Vienne and legate of the Apostolic See, and all the other bishops and abbots who were present at the council of Vienne: due submission and obedience. Following the commands of your holy piety,” etc. See under Paschal II.

“We excuse [him] with filial charity: for he is not a transgressor of the law.” A little earlier he had already said that this action was undertaken by the pope from necessity, not choice, in order to avoid the slaughter of the people. The words of the abbot of Ursperg in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1116 are especially relevant to elucidating this passage. There he discusses the council held at Rome under Paschal, for retracting what Paschal had shortly before conceded to Emperor Henry concerning investitures:

> “Then the apostolic pope set forth the cause of the council and the intention of his mind in these words: ‘After the Lord had done with his servant what he willed, and had delivered me and the Roman people into the king’s hands, I saw robberies, burnings, murders, and adulteries occurring everywhere day by day. These and evils of this kind I desired to turn away [Col. 0407B] from the Church and people of God; and what I did, I did for the liberation of God’s people. Yet I acted as a man, for I am dust and ashes. I confess that I acted wrongly; but I ask you all, pray to God for me, that he may forgive me. But that evil document made in the tents, which because of its perversity is called a privilege, I condemn under perpetual anathema, so that no one may ever regard it with favourable memory; and I ask you all to do the same.’
>
> “Then all cried out together: ‘Let it be done! Let it be done!’ But Bruno, bishop of Segni, began in a louder voice: ‘Let us give thanks to almighty God, because we have heard Lord Pope Paschal, who presides over the present council, condemn with his own mouth that privilege which contained perversity and heresy.’
>
> “To this he added, with a quibbling intent: ‘If that privilege contained heresy, then he who made it was a heretic.’ John Caetani, moved by this, answered the bishop of Segni: ‘Do you then here, in the council and in our hearing, call the Roman pontiff a heretic? The document made by the lord pope was indeed evil, but it was not heresy.’ Another added: ‘Indeed, it ought not even to be called evil. For if it is good to liberate God’s people, what the lord pope did was good. But it is good to liberate God’s people by the authority of the Gospel, which commands us even to lay down our lives for our brethren.’
>
> “At this, the patience of the lord pope, assailed by the dreadful name of heresy, was aroused. Signalling silence with his hand, he checked the shouts and murmurs of the disputants with this argument: ‘Brothers and my lords, this Church has never had heresy; rather, all heresies have been shattered here,’” etc. See the notes to Letter 233.

You now have, reader, a compendium of the whole history of the controversy over investitures between the Roman pontiffs and the emperors, which gave rise to the dreadful schism. The interpretation depends upon this history in several passages of Ivo: in Letter 214 to Bruno he laments the division [Col. 0407D] between Church and kingdom which had occurred in his age; and he also mentions it in Letter 238 to Pope Paschal, in which he warns him to take care not to stir up in the kingdom of France the schism that existed in Germany against the Roman see.

“Therefore, where it can be removed without schism, let it be removed; where it cannot be removed without schism …” Thus the defect has been supplied from the old manuscripts. This was sound counsel on Ivo’s part. To the same effect are the words of Godfrey, abbot of Vendôme, in his letter to Peter Leo, cardinal of the Roman Church. After arguing at length against investitures made by laymen—arguments reported below in the notes to Letter 233—he finally concludes that certain investitures should be permitted to laymen in order to avoid public schisms.

“Or among those who are outside, the same things are present.” Thus one old manuscript reads, and the words are not said by Ivo without reason. For while the schism of Gregory VII, Urban, and Paschal on the one side, and Emperor Henry on the other, was raging, there were some especially devoted to the pope who maintained that the sacraments of the opposing party were utterly ineffective. Bertold testifies to this in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1091. Opposed to the Guibertists and Henricians, he reports that Bernard of Constance, master of the schools, wrote in support of the judgment of the said Gregory against sacraments administered by schismatics outside the Church. But, led by excessive zeal, Bernard exceeded due bounds in some respects. For he absolutely denied that sacraments could be performed by them or by those in communion with them, holding that persons ordained by them, if they repented, ought to be ordained again. Yet this opinion conflicts with the Council of Nicaea and the African Council, and likewise with the opinions of Augustine, Pope Anastasius, and Gregory I.

Finally Bertold concludes:

> “This same venerable Bernard, in this matter, just as blessed Cyprian was in his opinion on rebaptism, did not act stubbornly against the Church; but, zealously opposing schismatics beyond measure, they somewhat exceeded the ecclesiastical rule.” [Col. 0408B]

That Bernard’s letter to Adalbert has recently been brought to light.

## On Letter CCXXXVII

“John of the First Lyonnaise,” etc. The heading has thus been restored on the authority and agreement of several old manuscripts. The earlier edition read: “John, archbishop of the First Lyonnaise see, to Ivo, bishop of the Church of Chartres.” The letter was less correctly addressed to Ivo alone. For John here answers the preceding Letter 236, which had been issued in the name of Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, and other fellow bishops.

Moreover, in one old manuscript I found it written twice through the carelessness of an early copyist. For after he had first written, “John of the First Lyonnaise,” etc., a few pages later, forgetting himself, he wrote, “Hugh of the First Lyonnaise.” But both cannot stand; Hugh the archbishop seems already to have been dead. In another ancient book only the first letter of the name is given: “I., of the First Lyonnaise,” etc.

“Since the First Lyonnaise province, though a Lyonnaise province, is nevertheless …” This passage too has been restored with the help of two manuscripts. The repetition of the words gives clearer light to the sense, which in the first edition and other old manuscripts had otherwise been obscurely expressed in this form: “Since the First Lyonnaise is a province, nevertheless the Second.” In an old manuscript from the Thuanus collection: “Since the First Lyonnaise province is Lyonnaise providence.” But an ancient hand corrected *providentia* to *provincia* in the margin. Three Lyonnaise provinces are mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary.

“Unless perhaps you wish all the bishops also to be included in the same *emunitas*.” Thus all our old manuscripts read. Cujas had noted in the margin of his book, “in the same *enormitas*,” I think rather from an old book than as a conjecture. But I find that word in no copy, for they agree alike in reading *emunitate*. Yet in one manuscript its scribe had long ago noted in the margin that the word *emunitas* signifies violence; but that note is plainly foolish and absurd.

The author therefore wrote *emunitate*. For the archbishop refers here to these words of Letter 236: “They are acknowledged to be subject neither to our judgment nor to that of any human beings; hence it is clear that we are exempt, if we fear to strike down their deeds with the sword of speech.” Thus he used *emunitas* for *immunitas*, “immunity.” Most writers of the older age used the term in this way. Ivo, Letter 133: “for the immunity of the cloister.” St Gregory, in the canon *Cum devotissimam*, Cause 12, Question 2: “they did not wish to amend that for violated immunity.” In the Ripuarian Laws, title 67: “unless the king’s immunity should oppose this.” In the Council of Orléans, chapter 10, in Burchard, book III, chapter 90: “because these things are held for immunity.” In the council at the royal estate of Theodon, chapter 2, in the same Burchard, book III, chapter 94: “Because these things are held in the ancient canons for immunity, [Col. 0409A] let no one dare to remove [them].” In the Council of Tribur, chapter 20—also reported by Gratian in the chapter *Si quis*, Cause 17, Question 4—“for immunity he shall pay nine hundred solidi”; and chapter 30: “whatever must be made good for violated immunity shall be paid to the altar.” Likewise, in the Council of Metz, chapter 2: “for immunity he shall pay the bishop 1,400 solidi.” Finally, in Charlemagne’s *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 24: “Let robbers for a breached immunity be presented by the judge of that immunity at the count’s assembly.” This word, therefore, is groundlessly suspect to some.

“[Do you accuse] Ambrose, who excommunicated Emperor Theodosius for his fault? Do you accuse Gregory VII, who [excommunicated] King Henry?” Otto, bishop of Freising, speaking of the same Henry IV in book VI, chapter 35 of his *Chronicle*, states that nowhere is anyone found among kings and emperors before this man to have been excommunicated or deprived of his kingdom by a Roman pontiff:

> “Unless perhaps,” he says, “someone considers as an anathema the fact that Philip was placed for a short time among the penitents by the Roman bishop, or that Theodosius was excluded from the thresholds of the Church by blessed Ambrose because of a bloody massacre.” [Col. 0409B]

The ancient author of book I, *On Preserving the Unity of the Church*, reproves the same Gregory, or Hildebrand, more openly. In order to establish and confirm the schisms of his party, Gregory adduced that history; but the author replies that Gregory abused the example and departed very far from the deed of that holy bishop. Theodosius, he says, was indeed restrained mildly by ecclesiastical discipline; yet Ambrose did not divide the Church, nor did he release princes and soldiers of the commonwealth from their oath of fidelity and separate them from association with and obedience to their emperor. Gregory had done this in a novel manner; he had set aside decrees, confirmed under anathema by many Roman pontiffs, concerning the investiture of bishops by kings and emperors.

Nor had Ambrose attempted anything of this kind when he was being assailed with threats and blows because of the zeal for heretics of Emperor Valentinian and his mother Justina. That author pursues these and many other matters. Some think that he was Venericus of Vercelli; others, Sigebert, monk of Gembloux; others, someone else.

“Would that it might be permitted to be concealed according to our wish.” This is said because Pope Paschal, troubled by a certain scruple of religion, feared to retract his action. For, as is read in the privilege of investiture that he granted, when he crowned Emperor Henry he testified that he gave him the body of the Lord as confirmation of true peace and concord between the two sides. Indeed, as Suger says, he had given the divided Eucharist as a pledge of a covenant of indivisible love and preservation of the agreement.

Peter the Deacon also reports in book IV, chapter 42 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* that Paschal used an imprecation:

> “When he came to the breaking of the host, he took one part himself and handed the rest to the emperor, saying: ‘As this portion [Col. 0409D] of the life-giving body is divided, so may he be divided from the kingdom of Christ who attempts to break and violate this agreement.’”

Afterward, when captive in the tents he granted that privilege, he withdrew in weariness to the solitude of the wilderness. He would have remained there permanently had not the Romans, by force, brought him back, as Suger says. William of Malmesbury too, in book V of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*, says that Paschal endured many injuries from the ministers of the Roman Church because they reproached him with having elevated the tyrant Henry by the imperial blessing and bestowed upon him a sacrilegious privilege.

William adds that the chief instigators were Guido or Wido, archbishop of Vienne—who afterward attained the papacy—and Gerard of Angoulême, legate in Aquitaine. The two mocked their fellow bishops in order to bring to nothing what Paschal had granted. Accordingly, not so much at Paschal’s command as with his connivance, a council was afterward held at Rome to retract the privilege. Thus Ivo did not without reason oppose the wish of this archbishop of Lyons, who was labouring to have Paschal’s action dissolved by a provincial Gallican council. For he feared, as he says in Letter 237, to expose the pope’s shameful acts to ridicule.

Nevertheless, the same Suger indicates that a synod was held in Gaul when he writes that, by the support of the lord-designate Louis, in a celebrated council of the Gallican Church the tyrant emperor was bound under an anathema and pierced by the sword of blessed Peter; and that the Gauls, joining themselves to the German kingdom, stirred up against him the greater part of the realm. William of Malmesbury likewise, *De Gestis Regum Anglorum*, book V, says that all Gaul directed the vigor of its ecclesiastical zeal against Henry and did not conceal its abhorrence of him. But they do not state whether the privileges of investiture granted by Paschal to Henry were condemned, or only the violence inflicted upon the pope.

**“An unspeakable master of the ship.”** This is the reading of all our manuscripts [Col. 0410B]. Yet in the ecclesiastical annals into which this letter is inserted, the old and genuine wording has been displaced and *detestabilis* (“detestable”) substituted. Nothing ought to have been changed. Sallust, in the *Jugurthine War*, writes: “he seems wicked and accursed”; Lepidus the consul, in the same author’s *Histories*: “if he should be worse and more accursed”; Tacitus, *Annals*, book XV: “he in turn charges him with being accursed and criminal.” Some have also corrupted at this point a verse of Marius Victorinus, book III on Genesis. For where the first edition reads:

> Not to mention the unspeakable crime of the magical monster,

as it is likewise found in the manuscript, they have instead inserted: “the execrable crime of the magical monster.”

**“But perhaps you fear that we wish to annul the rights of your prelacy.”** These ten words are now restored for the first time on the authority of ancient manuscripts, since they had accidentally been omitted from the first edition. The Council of Nicaea had decreed that the several churches ought to retain their own privileges; many canons to this effect are collected by Gratian under *Causa* 25, question 2 [Col. 0410C]. Ivo likewise wished this principle to be maintained steadfastly, as is evident from Letter 69, in which he declares that he neither wishes nor ought to yield even the smallest right of his church. In Letter 61 he says that the rights of the metropolitan see and of its fellow bishops must not be usurped. The same writer, in Letter 83, says that a metropolitan ought not, without the consent of each of the 199 fellow bishops, to undertake anything that would be an injury or violence to episcopal dignity.

Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, in a letter to Ranulf, bishop of Saintes, says:

> Again, against the archbishop who, in your diocese and without consulting you, already does much and still attempts to do more, an arrow is directed from the quiver of blessed Pope Julius in this fashion: “If any metropolitan bishop, except in matters belonging solely to his own proper diocese, attempts to do anything in the province without the counsel and will of all the bishops of the province, he shall be liable to the peril of his rank; and what he has done shall be held void and without effect.”

The chronologist of Auxerre also reports [Col. 0410D] under the year of the Lord 1081 that, after the death of the bishop of Meaux, a council was held in that city by Hugh, bishop of Die and legate of the Apostolic See, and that Robert, abbot of the church of Rebais, was ordained bishop. Richard, archbishop of Sens, indignantly protesting that this had been done without his consent and presence, excommunicated Robert and ordained and installed another bishop in his place.

Likewise Rodulfus Glaber, monk of Cluny, *History*, book II, chapter 4, in speaking of the monastery of Lucca built by Fulk, count of Anjou, says that Hugh, archbishop of Tours, in whose diocese it lay, delayed consecrating it unless Fulk first restored the estates and serfs which he had unjustly plundered from the mother church of the see entrusted to him. When Fulk, travelling to Rome, had obtained from Pope John, by a great quantity of gold, that Peter the cardinal should be sent and Fulk’s demands fearlessly carried out, he adds:

> On hearing this [Col. 0411A], all the prelates of Gaul recognized that a sacrilegious presumption had proceeded from blind greed: namely, that one man was seizing and another receiving what was seized, and that they had newly created a schism in the Roman Church. All likewise abhorred it together, because it seemed altogether unseemly that he who governed the Apostolic See should be the first to transgress the apostolic and canonical rule. Moreover, it has from ancient times been confirmed by manifold authority that no bishop may presume to perform this in another’s diocese unless compelled or permitted by the bishop to whom it belongs.

A little later he concludes the chapter thus:

> Although the pontiff of the Roman Church, on account of the dignity of the Apostolic See, is held in greater reverence than the others established throughout the world, he is nevertheless not permitted to transgress in anything the rule of canonical restraint. For just as every bishop and bridegroom of the orthodox Church alike bears the image of the Savior in his own see, so no one at all is permitted wantonly to perform anything in the diocese of another bishopric. [Col. 0411B]

**“Since you have recovered friendship and familiarity with the church of Lyons.”** This passage may serve as evidence that this letter was rightly considered to have been written to Daimbert, archbishop of Sens. For there had been discord between him and Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, because before his consecration Daimbert did not wish to profess obedience to Hugh; Hugh therefore obstructed his consecration, as the words of Ivo’s Letters 60 and 65 indicate. There had also been another dispute over primacy between the two archbishops, as Ivo himself notes in Letter 50.

But Baronius, after transcribing and inserting this letter of the archbishop of Lyons in his annals, adds:

> No reply from Ivo himself is found; indeed, unwilling that his opponent’s letter should perish—as he had not done in other cases—he stitched it together with his own letters, so that it might be preserved with them forever, thereby indicating that it was worthy of everlasting remembrance.

So he says [Col. 0411C]; but others think that some diligent person collected these letters after Ivo’s death.

## On Letter CCXXXVIII

**“It has always been subject.”** What *obnoxius* means in Latin is noted by Aulus Gellius, book VII, chapter 17; and Ivo, in Letter 102, uses *obnoxietas* for a kind of servile condition. Here, however, *obnoxium* means nothing other than the willing and ready disposition of the Gauls toward friendship with and favor for the Roman pontiff. Without tracing the truth of this matter further back, it will suffice to offer several examples from Ivo’s age.

Guibert, speaking of Urban II, says: “He arranged to travel into France. For it had from ancient times been customary for the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, if they had suffered any injury from a neighboring people, always to seek assistance from the Franks.” Abbot Suger confirms this in three passages of his *Life of Louis the Fat*. He reports that Paschal II [Col. 0411D], because of the hired treachery of the Romans, came into Gaul to seek aid from King Philip and his son Louis against Henry IV; the relevant words have been quoted in the notes to Letter 236. Speaking likewise of Pope Gelasius, he says: “He fled, as they had been accustomed to do in antiquity, to the guardianship and protection of the most serene King Louis and to the compassion of the Gallican Church.” Finally, speaking of Innocent, he says: “As a safe and tried refuge of defense for his person and his Church, he chose the most noble kingdom of the Franks.”

Indeed, Suger himself says that the Franks, though neither bound nor obligated by faith, undertook the cause of the Roman Church and Pope Paschal against Emperor Henry; his words are quoted in the notes to Letter 236. Pope Gregory VII, writing to Philip, king of the Franks, book VIII, Letter 20, says:

> In this you show yourself a friend solicitous for your salvation, if, as befits a Christian king, you desire to seek and obtain apostolic favor. [Col. 0412A]

And at the end of the letter:

> Strive especially to make blessed Peter, in whose power are your kingdom and your soul, and who can bind and loose you in heaven and on earth, your debtor.

**“The clergy of Tournai had come to the Apostolic See to make their request.”** Robert of Torigni, in the appendix to Sigebert’s *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1147, writes: “The church of Tournai, which for approximately six hundred years, from the time of blessed Medard, had been under the bishop of Noyon without a priest of its own, began in this year to have its own bishop.” This is how the printed editions have it, but elsewhere the number of six hundred years is varied, as follows in a work written by an ancient and uncertain author who lived in Ivo’s time and was a cloistered canon of Laon:

> When this same Anselm had presided over the monastery of Saint-Vincent for nearly seventeen years, and had travelled to Rome for the benefit of the monastery with his brother, Lord Walter, a monk of that house, he was there found, by a remarkable event ordained by God, by the clergy of Tournai, who had now lacked their own bishop for four hundred years [Col. 0412B]. He was elected bishop and, unwilling and resisting, was consecrated pontiff by Lord Pope Eugenius, bound by the bond of obedience. Thus through him the ancient dignity was restored to the church of Tournai in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1145, on the Sunday *Laetare Jerusalem*. Returning, therefore, from Rome and received at Laon with a great procession, he was unwilling to leave the monks, his former sons of Saint-Vincent, orphaned; he accordingly appointed in his own place one of them, Baldwin, young in years but grave in character, as their abbot, and had him ordained by Lord Bartholomew, the bishop. Thus he proceeded to Tournai to govern the flock entrusted to him.

Robert’s statement cited above, that the people of Tournai had lacked their own bishop from the time of blessed Medard, is made clearer by the words of the ancient writer Fortunatus the priest in the *Life of St Medard, Bishop of Noyon*, chapter 18:

> While Medard was most happily governing the church which he had built at Noyon [Col. 0412C], and, as we have said, strengthening all his people for eternal reward, it happened that holy Eleutherius, pontiff of the church of Tournai—whom Medard himself had foretold in his childhood would become bishop—put off the human condition. After his mournful funeral rites, when they were deliberating together on the election of a bishop, they completed a three-day fast and devoutly offered to God the solemn sacrificial offerings. Then, set aflame by a sudden inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they unanimously chose this holy pontiff Medard. At last, overcome by the authority of the metropolitan and his fellow provincials, by the assent of the king and nobles, and by the people’s unceasing acclamation, he scarcely consented. Then, in the time of Pope Hormisdas, under holy Remigius, then archbishop of Rheims, he finally accepted, by the unanimous episcopal and royal authority of the bishops of the province, with the assent of the king and court officials and the acclamation of both peoples; and, so that the cathedral honor might always remain to each church [Col. 0412D], he graciously granted it.

**“That the Apostolic See may diminish the extent of dioceses or enlarge their narrowness.”** In two old manuscripts: “diminish the multitude of dioceses.” Relevant here is what St Innocent says in his decretal letter to Alexander, bishop of Antioch: although provinces may be divided by imperial judgment so that two metropolitan sees are made and two metropolitan bishops must be named, nevertheless the Church of God is not to be altered according to the changing necessities of worldly affairs, nor to undergo those honors or divisions which the emperor may deem appropriate for his own purposes. This passage occurs in chapter *Lege*, distinction 10.

Likewise, in the Second Council of Carthage—reported in chapter *Felix*, *Causa* 16, question 1—it was decreed: “Dioceses which have never had bishops shall not have them; and one which has at some time had one shall have its own bishop.” Gratian, in the argument to chapter *Et temporis*, *Causa* 16, question 1, observes that the pope may unite two bishoprics into one and divide one into two [Col. 0413A]; chapter *Quod translationem*, *De officio legati*, bears on this matter.

An old unpublished author, in a manuscript tract *On the Tribulations and Distresses of Marmoutier*, composed in Ivo’s time, speaks of the privilege granted to that monastery by Urban II at the Council of Clermont in 1093, exempting it from the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Tours:

> The lord pope, after silence had been imposed, rose to his feet and addressed the whole council on the authority of the Apostolic See and the papal decrees. He declared that he was permitted to make two bishoprics out of one and likewise one out of two; and that, as the principle of equity required, he could unite or divide abbeys and other communities in whatever way seemed better to him, and that no one could oppose his authority in receiving into the lordship and patrimony of the holy Roman Church whatever he wished. He showed that such things had been done by his predecessors, and he himself did them at that present council without anyone dissenting. Therefore, when the most wise pope had truly stopped every mouth by such reasoning, he confirmed and authorized our privilege with an indissoluble bond by the authority of God, blessed Peter the apostle, all the apostolic pontiffs, and his own. He satisfied all except those whom the fury of envy and wrath agitated, because he possessed the power, such as we have described, to do what he wished. [Col. 0413B]

Theodore Balsamon, at the end of canon 16 of the Council of Carthage, maintains that it was within the emperor’s power to raise bishoprics to metropolitan sees, to remove them from their metropolitans, and to establish bishops and metropolitans anew, because he was subject neither to canons nor to laws. He says the same in his interpretation of canon 38 of the Sixth Synod in Trullo, which declares that ecclesiastical order follows civil and public forms; by “forms” he understands imperial commands, as he likewise writes on canon 12 of the Council of Chalcedon.

To these should be joined Justinian’s Novel concerning the privileges of the archbishop of Justiniana Prima; the material collected by Burchard in chapters 33 and 34 of his *Decree* from the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, chapter 4; and Ivo himself, *Decree*, part V, chapter 144. By the authority of that council, the act of Wamba, king of the Spaniards—or, as some read, of the Gauls—was declared void: he had, contrary to the canons, established a new episcopal see in small settlements. Bishops ought not, indeed, be established in castles, small cities, or villages, lest the name of bishop be cheapened; see canon *Episcopi* and those following, distinction 80 [Col. 0413C].

## On Letter CCXLI

**“The count compels you by his homage.”** Earlier editions printed: “by his lord.” The reading differs in other manuscripts, which have “by his man,” as does the manuscript of Saint-Germain. Both are erroneous. I have therefore restored “by his homage,” as the parchments of the Royal Library give it; and the sense indeed shows that it must be read thus. Above, in Letter 208, he has already used the term *hominium*, concerning which Hotman writes in his commentaries on fiefs.

The more ancient writers called it *homagium*, as Albert Krantz’s words in *Wandalia*, book III, chapter 39, indicate: “Having paid Caesar an immense sum of gold in satisfaction and rendered *homin(i)um*, which they now call homage, he obtained immunity.” It appears to be taken by Robert the Monk, *History*, book II, in a sense other than its usual feudal meaning:

> He asked our men that the leaders of the army should render him *hominium*, that is, a guarantee of peace, and that he should lead them through the deserted regions which they were about to enter.

And shortly afterward:

> They therefore rendered him *hominium* with an oath, on the condition that it should last as long as he persisted in his oath and promise. [Col. 0413D]

**“This too [is affirmed by] Pope Julius.”** Thus, from old manuscripts; earlier editions printed *Julianus* (“Julian”).

**“Or let him be subjected to the judgment of a girded judge.”** This passage is now for the first time restored to its proper clarity. It was formerly printed, “of a lay judge”; although that could be approved and retained, especially since certain other ancient manuscripts support that reading, it is beyond doubt that it has hitherto crept in through the hand of a glossator. For he wished [Col. 0414A] to explain what the word *cincti* (“girded”) meant; because the word was less familiar and common, it could easily degenerate and be altered.

But *cincti* is plainly read in the ancient parchments of the Royal Library, and likewise in the Thuanus, Servin, and Fabri manuscripts. This reading is confirmed by the summaries of letters prefixed at the beginning of old books: “What has been decided by apostolic judgment is not to be reconsidered; nor are ecclesiastical causes to be judged by a girded judge.” In the Servin manuscript, *accincto* (“girded”) is read.

A passage of Ivo himself, Letter 247, had been marred by a similar blemish, where I restored on ancient authority: “Let girded judges do these things, who carry the material sword for the punishment of evildoers.” For *cincti*, the earlier edition there read *cuncti* (“all”).

Pope Sylvester, in his decrees, says:

> No cleric, deacon, or priest shall enter a court for any cause, nor presume to plead a cause before a girded judge, because every court is so called from bloodshed and the sacrifice of idols. [Col. 0414B]

Thus that passage is cited by the ancient author of the book *On Preserving the Unity of the Church*, and by Ivo himself, *Decree*, part VI, chapter 334. But in Gratian, canon *Nullus clericus*, *Causa* 11, question 2, where part of those words is cited, the old and more elegant reading was commonly changed: for *cinctum* they wrongly substituted *civilem* (“civil”).

By “girded persons” were understood laymen who had attained authority. Sidonius Apollinaris therefore plays upon the word in book V, Letter 7, to Thaumastus:

> These are the men who begrudge reverence to clerics, lineage to nobles, a seat in council to their betters, association to their equals, rights to the girded, and privileges to the ungirded.

These words, along with several further consecutive passages from the same letter, were wrongly ascribed by modern authors of the *Catalogue of the Witnesses of Truth* to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, or even archbishop of Tours. They published that fragment as new and not previously brought to light; indeed, under the falsely attributed name “Romans,” [Col. 0414C] they prefixed at its beginning: “The Romans are those whom they fear and who are feared.” This deceived a recent historian, otherwise very diligent and learned, who, having drawn it from muddy streams, failed to notice that it was part of a letter of Sidonius, who was much earlier than Hildebert. Nor does Hildebert’s style agree. In the same catalogues, by an equal error, *cunctis iura* (“rights to all”) is still printed for *cinctis iura* (“rights to the girded”).

The same Sidonius, book I, Letter 7: “Earlier girded with custody than ungirded with authority.” In the imperial constitutions frequent mention is made of the belt of officials. Cassiodorus, on Psalm XXIX, “You have girded me with gladness,” says:

> Consider the word “You have girded.” The belt signifies what belongs to a judge’s dignity. For all authority is known to be comprised in this very word. Thus we call a judge “girded” when we declare his fasces and honors.

St Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, tractate 19—reported in chapter *Militare*, *Causa* 23, question 1—says:

> Scripture does not speak only of those soldiers who are engaged in armed service; rather, whoever wears the belt of his office is enrolled as a soldier of his rank. Accordingly, this saying may be addressed, for example, to soldiers, protectors, and all rulers. [Col. 0414D]

Pope Marcellus, in chapter *Nullus*, *Causa* 11, question 1: “Any magistrate who has dared to command this shall be punished by loss of property and belt.” Following their example, clerics claimed for themselves the belt of honor and of heavenly service, which is irrelevant to this correction.

## On Letter CCXLII

**“Whom rather against …”** The following words have been added from old manuscripts, where they were previously lacking.

**“Has violated the covenant of marriage.”** In one old Pithoean manuscript: *initiaverit* (“has initiated”). Perhaps this is not a bad reading, for below, in Letter 245, he also says: “You have taken a wife, which the law of nature has initiated.”

## On Letter CCXLIV

**“And to restore [it] into a state of uprightness by the balance of justice.”** This is the vulgate reading, supported by most ancient manuscripts. The author of Letter 24 says: “The rashness and audacity of the perverse seek to undermine the state of uprightness”; and in Letter 26: “Lest he cast you down from the state of your uprightness.” In one ancient copy, however—the royal manuscript—the text reads differently: “and in the balance of uprightness.” Perhaps it refers to these words of St Gregory, *Morals*, book XX, part IV, chapter 6, also reported in canon 10, distinction 45:

> Everyone who judges rightly holds a balance in his hand. In each scale he bears justice and mercy, so that by a just weighing he may correct some things by equity and pardon others through mercy. [Col. 0415A]

## On Letter CCXLVII

**“Let girded judges do these things, who carry the material sword for the punishment of evildoers.”** Here lay an error which could not easily have been detected without the aid of ancient parchments. The received reading was: “Let all judges do these things,” as certain ancient manuscripts also have it [Col. 0415B]. But since three manuscripts plainly read “girded judges,” there is no further doubt that this is much more correct. Variant readings support this text: one manuscript has *accincti*, another *succincti*, and a third *xcinti*. The last is found in an old book of Saint-Victor. The correction is plainly confirmed by the passage in Letter 241: “Or let him be subjected to the judgment of a girded judge,” where “lay” had hitherto been read for “girded.”

**“Of the office which we have set aside.”** Thus restored with the aid of old manuscripts. It was earlier printed: “which we have proposed.” One old manuscript has: “which we have set.”

**“With head placed downward and feet raised, we shall imitate the gait of theatrical performers.”** Other old manuscripts have *temilicorum*; but the Servin copy reads differently, *temulentorum* (“drunkards”), which may seem to have come from the hand of an ancient glossator unfamiliar with the word *thymelicorum*, theatrical performers. From the somewhat later traces of ink it is clear that the Servin copy originally read *thymelicorum*, and that the text was subsequently interpolated. In a similar sense St Augustine says, chapter 3, *Causa* 32, question 6: “Where a woman lives better than a man, the household hangs with its head downward.” [Col. 0415C]

## On Letter CCL

**“In the eyes of apostolic majesty.”** Only the Servin manuscript has: “in the eyes of divine majesty,” but this is less fitting. The author is accustomed to speak of apostolic majesty, or the pope’s majesty, as in Letters 8, 147, 157, 159, 201, and 238; so do other contemporary writers. John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, book VII, chapter 21, says: “Nor do I think that apostolic or royal majesty should be resisted.” St Bernard, Letter 268 to Pope Eugenius, says: “Let others fear the majesty in you and, with trembling lips and fingers, scarcely arrive at the point after long detours and winding circumlocutions.” Thus Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, writing to Pope Adrian, attributes majesty to him in Letter 8, and likewise to Pope Alexander in Letters 26, 27, 45, and 64; in Letter 21 he calls it “the summit of apostolic majesty.” The same Arnulf calls an archbishop’s status “majesty” in Letter 15, and a cardinal’s in Letter 65 [Col. 0415D].

**“But they are not.”** Elsewhere: “if they are not.”

**“When appeal is made to the throne of justice; when reason requires, I appeal to it with pious confidence.”** All these words have been added on the authority and agreement of the manuscripts, from which they had previously been absent.

**“After the death of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, of blessed memory, the Church was bereft of a pastor.”** This passage is illuminated by the words of William of Malmesbury, book I of *De Gestis Pontificum Anglorum*:

> After Anselm of venerable memory, escaping the bonds of his earthly body, took leave of this life, the archbishopric was vacant for a full five years. Throughout that period, when the king—Henry I is meant—was urged to provide for the widowhood of the Church, his mother, he delayed his answer, saying: “The best archbishops had been appointed by my father and brother; I do not wish to fall short of my parents’ good fortune. Therefore the choice must be weighed with great scrutiny, so that I may appoint among the archbishops one who either follows his predecessors in virtue with equal steps or rivals them closely.” [Col. 0416A]

A little later, concerning Ralph of Rochester, mentioned in this letter of Ivo, he reports that the electors said:

> Let such a man be named as wounds no one’s conscience. There have been more than enough archbishops from a foreign people; the country abounds in men of its own tongue, who may equal Lanfranc in learning and display Anselm in religion, in both garb and character. There is Ralph, bishop of Rochester, whose reputation equals that of the ancients and whose humble affability surpasses both old and new. If you examine his birth, he is sprung from a distinguished Norman lineage; if you examine his life, it has not been touched even by a stain of infamy. He alone has a religious life which even envy cannot criticize as lacking discretion. If you search his knowledge of letters, he has drained Athens dry; if you require eloquence, speech flows from his mouth in a kind of honeyed stream. Added to this is the polished and, as it were, carefully combed speech of his native soil, that is, of Maine.

These merits gained such support that the king immediately changed his view and adopted their wish. This was done on the fifth day after the completion of the fifth year from Anselm’s death. Ralph, at Sées, an abbey of Normandy, had devoted himself as a monk in the first flower of youth; as his virtues grew, he became first subprior, then prior, and finally abbot, and so forth [Col. 0416B].

The same author shortly afterward adds concerning Ralph’s death from paralysis:

> He died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the ninth year of his patriarchate, in the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation. Thus ended Ralph, inferior to no one in religious devotion, splendidly powerful in literary learning, and certainly foremost of all in affability. He gained nothing more from greatness of fortune than the ability to do greater good to whom he wished. Although, in the public estimation, as much was taken from his glory as was added to his fortune. Yet he was not marked by even a slight suspicion of any fault, except that he was more inclined to laughter and jokes than seemed fitting for his dignity or rank. But whatever he did, that man did with a good intention; to entertain any unfavorable suspicion concerning him is to strive against religion. [Col. 0416C]

So he writes.

**“Earnestly requesting.”** This is the reading of the better manuscripts, as in Letter 141, “I earnestly ask,” and Letter 271, “we earnestly beseech.” Some have *obnoxie post* (“submissively request”), which is not fitting: it was not customary for this pallium to be granted to bishops unless it was sought from the supreme pontiff with the most urgent prayers. Thus what this author calls “earnestly request,” others call “ask strongly and insistently.” St Gregory the Great, book VII, Letter 5, says:

> Ancient custom has maintained that the honor of the pallium ought not to be given unless the merits of the case demand it and it is strongly requested.

An old author on ecclesiastical rites, or the sacred ceremonies of the holy Roman Church, book I, section 10, chapter 5, testifies that the person to whom the pallium was granted used these words:

> I, N., elected [bishop] of the church of N., urgently, more urgently, and most urgently request that the pallium taken from the body of blessed Peter, in which is the fullness of the pontifical office, be delivered and assigned to me. [Col. 0416D]

There he records much concerning the use of the pallium; among other things, he says that in the law of grace the ancient ephod—that is, the pallium—was instituted by Linus, the second Roman pontiff after Peter, and granted to our prelates as a privilege of exceptional authority. Rupert of Deutz, *On the Divine Offices*, book I, chapter 27, writes that Maternus, sent by the blessed apostle Peter, left to the church of Trier the inheritance of the pallium for his successors.

Some think, however, that this custom was received rather from the Caesars; for this they cite the words of Agnellus, bishop of Ravenna, who reports that Emperor Valentinian subjected to the bishop of Ravenna the bishops of fourteen cities and adorned him with a pallium made of white wool, which at that time only emperors used.

**“That you grant him the dignity of the pallium.”** Pope Gregory VII, *Register*, book I, Letter 24, to Bruno, bishop of Verona, says that by a decree of his predecessors the pallium should be granted only to a person present. He therefore tells him to come to Rome to receive it. Pope Urban II, in Platina, writing to the archbishop of Milan, says:

> Moved by your letters, with the blessing of the Apostolic See we send a pallium to your fraternity; this distinction of dignity was granted to no one before you except when present. [Col. 0417A]

Yet the words of Pope Gregory the Great, book VII, Letter 5, to Queen Brunhild, show that long before this the pallium had also been given to someone absent and not requesting it:
