> Moreover, because he who wishes to use it had not sent us a special petition asking us to grant it to him, and because before the case arose we ought in no way to give it without his request—especially since ancient custom has maintained that the honor of the pallium ought not to be given unless the merits of the case demand it and it is strongly requested—nevertheless, we …

Rodulfus Glaber, *History*, book V, chapter 4, in dealing with the dispute over the see of Lyons, likewise reports that the Roman pontiff sent a pallium and ring to Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and commanded that he become archbishop of Lyons. But that religious man, observing the commitment of his humility, refused altogether, reserving the pallium and ring for the future bishop.

Paschal II, however, sent the pallium to this Ralph of Rochester, archbishop of Canterbury, through the legate Anselm, nephew through a sister of Saint Anselm, the preceding archbishop, as William of Malmesbury reports in book I of *De Gestis Pontificum Anglorum*. It should be noted that the ancients held the dignity of this matter in such high esteem that St Bernard of Clairvaux wrote in Letter 246 to Pope Eugenius that he found it more tolerable to be forbidden to celebrate Mass than for the archbishop of Bourges to be forbidden the use of the pallium [Col. 0417B].

## On Letter CCLIII

**“His miseries and distresses, by which he is harassed by violators of the peace.”** [Col. 0417C] What Ivo writes here receives illumination and interpretation from the words of Nicholas the monk, in the *Life of Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens*, book II, chapters 30, 31, and 34, and book III, chapters 2–5. I reduce his more extensive account to a summary.

When this bishop was returning to Amiens from a journey, he had with him Adam, lord of that city, then destitute of military protection. When Adam advised taking another road because he feared the very fierce enemy Guermond, viscount of Picquigny, the bishop answered that the count should be safe, because Guermond had recently sworn solemnly that he would faithfully preserve the peace and respect his bishop as his temporal lord. It happened soon afterward that Guermond, attended by a large force of cavalry, met the travellers; immediately, on seeing Adam, he attacked him with drawn swords and threw him from his horse. Seeing this, the bishop leapt from his horse, threw his whole body over Adam, offered his neck, and cried out: what madness drove Guermond to dare such a deed in his presence? He even exposed his own neck, begging him to devise nothing against Adam [Col. 0417D].

The bishop’s companions, terrified, fled. Adam was put in chains and carried to Picquigny, while the bishop followed alone, weeping, wailing, and tearing his hair, crying out that he was Adam’s betrayer and the cause of such calamity. When they arrived at Picquigny, the others were admitted, but the bishop was compelled to remain outside. He therefore returned to the city and reported the matter to the clergy and people, lamenting the captivity of his lord Adam and the injury done to the bishop. He accordingly struck Guermond with an anathema and ordered the churches in the territory of that faithless lord to be closed.

There followed repeated ravaging of fields, devastation of villages, and burning of churches. Deeply afflicted by these things, the bishop said that he was wretched to have fallen upon such times. Guermond could not be induced to release his captive Adam, even though the king and the princes of the realm intervened. At length the bishop, thinking to soften the hardness of his mad subject’s heart by a new act of humility, came again to Picquigny during winter, clothed in haircloth and barefoot [Col. 0418A]. Prostrate upon the ground in the middle of the market square, he embraced the tyrant’s feet and tearfully begged him to restore his Adam. But Guermond disgracefully repelled the bishop, insulting and mocking him.

This, then, is why Ivo earnestly asks King Louis to hear Godfrey’s tearful complaints, so that afterward he may draw the sword for the punishment of the evildoers who had violated the peace with impunity.

**“Let the royal sword therefore perform its office for the punishment of evildoers.”** Suger, in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, speaking of Louis’s coronation, says: “Having set aside the sword of secular knighthood, he girded him with the ecclesiastical sword for the punishment of evildoers and gladly crowned him with the diadem of the kingdom.”

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, writes elegantly to H., bishop of Sées, concerning the twofold sword:

> Both swords were fittingly found among Christ’s disciples, because both are still shown in the members of Christ’s body. For the king is a member of Christ; the priest is a member of Christ. I speak to one who knows: you know the king’s sword; you know the priest’s sword. The king’s sword is the jurisdiction of the court; the priest’s sword is the strictness of ecclesiastical discipline. You have read that the Evangelist prefigured this when he said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords.” If there were one who freed me by the sword of royal power, the sword of priesthood would not be asked to be drawn on my account. But you see that authority now bears the sword without cause: it lies sheathed, covered with the skins of dead animals. Malchus stretches out his hands against Christ, Belshazzar against the vessels of the Temple, with impunity. There is no one consumed by zeal for the house of the Lord; no one who threatens with Moses and says: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh,” and so forth. [Col. 0418B]

## On Letter CCLIV
Who has at last obtained permission from his lord, the king of the English, to do so in person. At that time English bishops were not permitted to travel to the city of Romulus unless they had first sought the king’s permission. Some give the reason for this: [Col. 0418C] rulers feared that, if subjects could freely leave the realm, they might change their dispositions under a foreign sky and, corrupted by outsiders, introduce many innovations contrary to the established laws of their homeland. William of Malmesbury, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, book I, speaking of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, says:

> “Wishing to discuss these matters with the pope, he requested leave to go to Rome—twice, three times, and in vain. ‘I understand,’ said the king, ‘that permission must be refused him, since I know that he is burdened by no grave sin for which he should seek absolution from Rome, nor does he need the counsel of that place, since he lacks no abundance of learning. Indeed, I would sooner say that Urban should yield to Anselm’s wisdom than that Anselm needs Urban. But if he persists more obstinately in what he has undertaken, I shall reduce the whole archbishopric to my fisc. For he transgresses the promises by which he bound his faith to observe all the customs of my kingdom. For it is unfamiliar to me that any one of my nobles should go to Rome unless above all at my command.’”

Among the articles or heads [Col. 0418D] of the constitution proposed by the king of the English to Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, Edward, in his *Life*, chapter 6, records this:

> “That it shall not be lawful for an archbishop or bishop to leave the kingdom and come at the summons of the lord pope without the king’s permission.”

Certainly, that the same practice was formerly observed in the kingdom of the Franks may readily be inferred from the letter of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, to Pope Adrian II:

> “Concerning the matter in which Your Sublimity wrote to my littleness, that I should send the same Hincmar”—he means the bishop of Laon, his nephew—“and three other bishops representing all the bishops of the kingdom of Lord Charles to the synod at Rome: let your authority know that I have no power to send to Rome, or to any place, under my recommendation, either the aforesaid Hincmar or any bishop at all of the diocese of Rheims—still less bishops of other provinces—unless the lord king commands it. Nor can I myself proceed beyond the boundaries of his kingdom [Col. 0419A] without his knowledge, as I told the envoys of Your Holiness in the presence of the venerable Bishop Odo and the devout priest and abbot Ansegisus, who are acquainted with our affairs.”

Gregory VII, however, rebukes the king of the English who forbade the bishops of the churches of his realm to travel to Rome. Thus in book VII, letter 1, to Hubert, subdeacon of the Roman Church:

> “There are many grounds upon which the holy Roman Church can complain against him. For among all kings, even pagan ones, no one presumes to attempt against the Apostolic See what he was not ashamed to do: namely, that anyone of such irreverent and shameless spirit should prevent bishops and archbishops from the thresholds of the Apostles. We therefore wish your prudence, acting in our stead, diligently to admonish him that he should not labor so greatly to diminish the honor of the holy Roman Church—the withholding of which from his own subjects he would take most grievously—and that, by rendering the gratitude due, he may seek to acquire the favor of blessed Peter.”

To visit the Apostolic See in person. [Col. 0419B] Gregory VII was a firm adherent of this practice. For in book VI, letter 30, to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, he says that he is astonished and wonders why Lanfranc had taken so little care to come to him from the time when he became pope. He ought not to have been kept from the pope’s presence through fear of the English king or through superstitious regard for any person:

> “So that,” he says, “we may confer in person concerning these and other affairs, and, with God’s favor, the welfare of the Church may be able to receive increase from our conversation.”

And in book IX, letter 20, to the same Lanfranc—for thus the gap in the common edition may be supplied—he rebukes him because, although he had often been invited by apostolic legation to come to Rome, even for the confirmation of Christian faith and religion, he had nevertheless either proudly or negligently abused Gregory’s patience by delaying, and had not even pleaded a canonical excuse.

> “For labor or difficulty of travel,” he says, “does not sufficiently excuse you, since it is well known that many living far away, though physically weak [Col. 0419C] and infirm and scarcely able to rise from their beds, nevertheless, burning with love for blessed Peter, hasten in vehicles to his thresholds.”

Finally, he threatens that Lanfranc will be suspended from every episcopal function unless, laying aside excuse or empty fear, he ceases any longer to neglect, within four months, to amend the offence of disobedience. Likewise, in book IX, letter 1, he is angry with W . . . [Note: [Col. 0419D] Perhaps “William” should be read.] archbishop of Rouen, because he had for so long made light of visiting the thresholds of the Apostles, although peoples newly converted to the faith came there every year from the very ends of the earth. Indeed, he did not take much care to approach even the pope’s legates who were nearer at hand; and he postponed acquiring, according to custom, from the Apostolic See the most splendid badge of dignity, the pallium. Gregory concludes that, unless he corrects his fault, he will lose the right of ordination and consecration.

## TO LETTER 255

“But I do not think that the anointing which you have once received should be repeated.” Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, held the same opinion. His letter appears in a manuscript copy:

> “Brother Geoffrey to Ivo, bishop of Chartres: greeting from the Lord, and from himself the service due to you. Just as we praise monastic customs that accord with the Rule of blessed Benedict, so we cannot praise those which Saint Benedict neither teaches nor commands, and which appear wholly contrary to reason. For among monks there are certain institutions which reason in no way admits, which none of the holy Fathers has found, but which the custom of foolish men has instituted. Some monks claim these for themselves in monasteries as law; and, although Christ said, ‘I am the truth,’ and did not say, ‘I am custom,’ they nevertheless alter the law of truth for the sake of their own custom. And, to pass over other matters, they err, as it seems to us, not a little in holding that the anointing of the sick ought to be repeated, although it is called a sacrament by the holy catholic and apostolic [Col. 0420A] See, and although no sacrament ought to be repeated. Blessed Pope Innocent calls the sacrament of anointing so great that it is thought for no reason capable of being granted to penitents, to whom the other sacraments are denied. Yet we desire to know what Your Great Discretion thinks on this matter and teaches should be maintained. For although we do not doubt that these points are true in both reason and authority, we nevertheless wish and ask that they be confirmed by the decree of your authority.”

In the same copy the concluding part of this letter of Ivo is appended. Elsewhere the same Geoffrey writes concerning repetition of a sacrament:

> “A sacrament is repeated where the same thing is given again, as though what was given before were believed able to be given afterward. For example, if someone already baptized were again immersed in the waters of baptism with the intention of being freed from original and other sins. Otherwise he is not rebaptized, even if someone is immersed many times in baptismal [Col. 0420B] waters. But where it is given for one purpose and then for another, the sacrament is not repeated; rather, it is bestowed as a manifestation of power. For although a person is first anointed with chrism on the crown of the head and afterward on the forehead, the sacrament of chrism is not repeated, because, as we said above, this is done for one purpose and then another. So baptism is by no means repeated, even if after baptism we are sprinkled many times with baptismal water. The anointing of the sick is a great sacrament, and therefore it is on no account to be repeated. For just as Christian religion is believed to have received the other sacraments through the Apostles, so there is no doubt that it received this too from apostolic tradition. But every sacrament is forbidden to be repeated by the Holy Spirit through the holy teachers in whom he speaks; and this is plainly so that the holy remedy may not become cheapened and less useful—for it is more health-giving in proportion as it is found less contemptible.”

## TO LETTER 258

A council was held at Troyes by the same legate. [Col. 0420C] The author of letter 141 mentions it, as does Nicholas, monk of Soissons, in book I, chapter 30 of the *Life of Saint Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens*:

> “At that time Richard, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, held at Troyes a most celebrated assembly of bishops, abbots, and the magnates of Gaul.”

This is different from the council held at the same Troyes by Pope Paschal, mentioned above under letter 176.

## TO LETTER 263

“If you place your necks beneath the feet of laymen.” Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, writing to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, on the dispute between his church and the countess of Vendôme:

> “For it is altogether just, and seems wholly contrary to the sacred canons—as you yourself know better—that an ecclesiastical cause should be decided by a secular and alien tribunal, and that what it is fitting for you and your own people to do should be entrusted to other ecclesiastical persons as well. If this could occur, your Church would suffer loss and forfeit much of its right and honor. [Col. 0420D] For to give the glory of your Church to another belongs neither to one born of holiness nor to a member of religious life. You know well, dearest friend, that secular men endeavor by their custom to nullify the authority of holy Church; and when, in even a small matter, an occasion from any custom is granted them against ecclesiastical rights, thereafter they strive to claim it for themselves for all time. Whoever does this against his own Church stirs up a worldly quarrel; and when he later wishes to act otherwise, the secular storm does not permit it.”

The same writer, to Pope Calixtus:

> “When the Church is subjected to secular power, she who was formerly mistress becomes a handmaid, and she loses the charter of freedom which Christ the Lord dictated on the cross and, as it were, wrote with his own hands from his blood.”

## TO LETTER 266

“To Cono, by God’s grace bishop of Palestrina.” [Col. 0421A] Thus the better manuscripts have it; three other letters are written to the same man. His name has more than once been corrupted, as in the common text of the chronicle of Robert of Torigni, continuator of Sigebert:

> “In the city of Beauvais,” it says, “a council is held by Cono, legate of the Apostolic See.”

Instead of *Conone*, the printed text has *canonice* (“canonically”). The passage in Nicholas the monk, *Life of Saint Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens*, book III, chapter 9, confirms it:

> “Meanwhile Cardinal Conon, legate of the supreme pontiff, and Ralph, archbishop of Rheims, hold a synod at Beauvais.”

Suger also mentions him in his *Life of Louis the Fat*. Since the words of that passage are corrupt in the common edition, they are given here in a more corrected form. Speaking of Thomas of Marle, a most abandoned man, who, with the devil prospering him—as Suger puts it—had ravaged the districts of Laon, Rheims, and Amiens, he adds:

> “Wearied by his intolerable harassment, the Gallican Church sat in general assembly at Beauvais, [Col. 0421B] in order that it might begin here too to pronounce the first acts of judgment and a condemnatory sentence against the enemies of the true spouse, Jesus Christ. The venerable Cono, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the holy Roman Church, assailed by countless complaints concerning the tyranny exercised against churches, poor persons, and orphans, cut down that tyranny with the sword of blessed Peter—that is, with a general anathema—and, although he was absent, stripped him of his knightly belt; he deprived him, by the judgment of all, of every honor, denouncing him as a criminal, dishonored man, enemy of the Christian name.”

There *Beliaci* has been printed instead of *Belvaci*; and *Cenoprestinus* instead of *Cono Praenestinus*. In the chronicle of the abbot of Ursperg for the years of the Lord 1116 and 1119, he is called Cuno; there it is added that he pronounced his sentence of excommunication against Emperor Henry at Jerusalem, and afterwards confirmed it in five councils—in Greece, Hungary, Saxony, Lorraine, and France. An old chronicler of Auxerre writes:

> “In the year of the Lord 1115, three councils were held in Gaul by Cono, legate of the Apostolic See: the first at Rheims, the second at Beauvais, the third at Châlons.”

[Col. 0421C] These words also bear upon the elucidation of the passage from the letter of Guy, archbishop of Vienne, cited below in the notes to letter 236. There survive letters of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, addressed to Cono, bishop of praiseworthy life and legate of the holy Apostolic See. William of Malmesbury, however, in book I of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, writes that this Cono, while he was discharging a legation in Gaul, was not easily swayed; his words are quoted under letter 273.

“And that the divine office has been unjustly forbidden in the land of his father.” Examples of this penalty occur in Geoffrey’s letters. Writing to Ivo, bishop of Chartres:

> “We give thanks because you caused the count of Vendôme to be summoned to account on our behalf; and because he neglected to correct what he had done unjustly, you removed the divine office from his castle and from the banleuga [league, or surrounding jurisdiction, of the castle].”  
> [Note: [Col. 0421D] Thus the best manuscript copy has it.]

A little later he explains the rationale of this punishment:

> “One thing would nevertheless be useful to us—indeed, most necessary—for which we humbly beseech you as sons beseech a father: [Col. 0421D] that the kind of piety by which a pastor of the Church, when necessity requires, ought to become impious for the Lord’s sake—for, as blessed Jerome says, it is a kind of piety to become impious for the Lord’s sake—might be extended by the zeal of your uprightness against the count and all his land. That is, you should separate his entire county from the divine offices and bind him himself with the bonds of stricter justice, so that all the people, who know both our injury and his wickedness, who are greatly displeased by his injustice and would not be displeased by greater justice, might take this occasion to cry out against him. Thus, since for love of God he does not voluntarily wish to desist from unjust action, he might desist through the combined outcry and fear of men.”

Yet the same Geoffrey rebukes Ivo himself for having ventured this against the monastery of Vendôme, which he calls an allod of the Roman Church; and he openly declares that he did not comply [Col. 0422A] with the command:

> “Since you cannot and dare not lay hands on our greater church, you have removed the divine office from our other churches situated in your bishopric—not, indeed, with sufficient justice. And because this is known to have been unjustly done by your authority, by Roman authority, which stands opposed to every perverse authority, it shall be sung both privately and publicly in those churches by our brethren. By the holy and irrevocable permission of the Roman pontiffs it is granted us that, if an interdict has unjustly been imposed upon our churches by any bishop, it is in no way to be observed by us.”

These should be connected with the remarks on letter 50.

“He receives certain monk-masons, *cementarii*, or *coementarii*.” Geoffrey of Vendôme, in a letter to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans:

> “You know most certainly that John the mason is a monk of our church, and that he has often departed from that church through disobedience.”

And in another letter to the same man:

> “[Col. 0422B] John the mason, indeed a monk, but possessing no cement of charity, because he has abandoned the obedience of his proper place and rendered void the pledge of his profession.”

## TO LETTER 268

“At the council of Issoudun.” Since at this point he says that Hugh, bishop of Die and apostolic legate, attended the council, it is evident that the council held in 1081 must be meant. For the author of the Chronology of Auxerre writes:

> “In the year of the Lord 1080, a great earthquake, with a grave roar of the earth, occurred on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, at the first hour of the night. In the following year a council was held at the castle of Issoudun, situated in Berry. In the year after that, upon the death of the bishop of Meaux, the venerable Hugh, bishop of Die and legate of the Apostolic See, held a council in the same city and ordained Robert, abbot of the Church of Rébais, bishop.”

## TO LETTER 271

[Col. 0422C]

“To his Father and Lord.” These four words are absent from several manuscripts, but are confirmed by examples in the titles of letters 250, 244, and 238. John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, book VI, chapter 24, addressing Pope Adrian:

> “All applaud you; you are called Father of all and Lord, and all the oil of the sinner is poured upon your head. If, therefore, you are a father, why do you expect gifts and payments from your sons? If a lord, why do you not strike fear into your Romans and, repressing their audacity, recall them to fidelity?”

“When they were received personally.” The martyrology of the Church of Chartres, speaking of Ivo himself:

> “He converted all the *minoratae* [minor benefices] and *precariae* of this Church to common uses, and by both his own privilege and an apostolic privilege forbade their future distribution to persons.”

On “persons,” see the remarks on letter 12.

## TO LETTER 273

“That you may so moderate the excommunication threatened against the bishops of Normandy.” [Col. 0422D] Perhaps this passage should be interpreted by the words of William of Malmesbury, book I of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*:

> “At the beginning of Henry’s reign, Guy, archbishop of Vienne, who later became pope, had come to England to exercise a legation; then there came Anselm’s [legate], and not much later a certain Peter. All returned without accomplishing their business, carrying off great booty—Peter especially, because all were wary of angering him, since he was the son of Peter Leo, supreme prince of the Romans. Roman legates therefore frequently came to England, plotting against Ralph’s weakness; but all were driven away by Henry’s caution. For he did not wish, contrary to ancient custom, to receive in England any legate other than the archbishop of Canterbury; and they readily checked their efforts because of the force of money. Cono the legate in Gaul, however, was not so easily bent: he involved all the bishops and abbots of Normandy [Col. 0423A] in the mark of suspension because, though summoned to his councils three times, they had not come. After deliberation on this matter, Archbishop Ralph and Herbert of Norwich were sent to Rome to settle, through their efforts, so great a confusion caused by the legates.”

## TO LETTER 274

“My *responsales*, nevertheless.” Thus in the manuscript copy, as also a little later. In letter 267, which is plainly of precisely the same subject, he calls them vicars. Ancient writers frequently mention these *responsales*, especially Pope Gregory I, who sufficiently indicates their office when he speaks of deacons sent to the emperor to make ecclesiastical replies: book II, indiction 11, letters 91 and 92; likewise book VII, letters 5 and 6.

“He served in the clerical order”: the words are corrected thus on the authority of the old codices. Previously *judiciali ordine*, “in the judicial order,” had wrongly been printed.

[Col. 0423B] “Of all who devoutly knock.” Thus the manuscript copy has it better than the previous printed reading, *o. pene puls.* [reading uncertain because abbreviated or corrupt].

“By all the sons.” These words, with the nine immediately following, have been added on the authority of the same manuscript copies; they were missing from the printed text, leaving the sentence incomplete.

“Turstin as archbishop.” The first edition has *Turstinum*. But afterwards I found his name variously written in other copies. Roger of Howden, in the first part of his *Annals*, under Henry I, calls him Turstin:

> “Turstin, the king’s chaplain, is elected to the archbishopric of York at Winchester on the day of the Assumption of Saint Mary.”

The edition notes that *Torstanus* is read elsewhere. Others call him Turstanus or Turstannus. Matthew Paris, in his *Life of Henry I, King of the English*:

> “In the year of the Lord 1113, King Henry gave the archbishopric of Canterbury to Ralph, bishop of London, and invested him with ring and pastoral staff. In the same year Thomas, archbishop of York, died, and Thurstan succeeded him.”

In the old parchment manuscripts of Antoine Oisel, jurist, [Col. 0423C] containing several letters of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, he is called Rustin, through a copyist’s error for Turstin. Hildebert declares himself Turstin’s friend and asks him not to believe the false rumor that he intended to travel to Rome in the name of the archbishop of Canterbury against Turstin:

> “To Turstin, by God’s grace venerable elect of York, his dearest friend: Hildebert, humble priest of the people of Le Mans, [wishes him] not readily to distrust a friend. As Seneca testifies,” etc.

See Hildebert below, under the year 1134.

“What the Church of Canterbury demands of him.” Thus the manuscript copy; the first edition has *Cantuariensis*. The reason for this dispute is that York refused to be subject to Canterbury, a grievance often renewed, as English historians indicate. Matthew Paris, under William the Conqueror:

> “In the year of the Lord 1072, at Windsor, by command of Pope Alexander and with the assent of King William, [Col. 0423D] in the presence of Hubert, legate of the Roman Church, the question of the primacy of the Church of Canterbury over the Church of York was debated. At last, by the authority of ancient writings, it was proved and shown that the Church of York ought to be subject to the Church of Canterbury and to its archbishop, faithfully obeying, in all matters pertaining to the Christian religion, the ordinances of the primate of all Britain. Thus, if the archbishop of Canterbury wishes to hold a council, wherever he judges it useful, the archbishop of York, [Col. 0424A] with all his suffragans and subject clergy, must appear before him and obey his canonical ordinances. He must also receive episcopal blessing from him and make to him a canonical profession confirmed by oath. To this constitution the aforesaid king and Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and Thomas, archbishop of York, consented, together with the aforesaid cardinal and all the bishops and abbots of the realm.”

The same writer, under the said year 1113:

> “A great disagreement arose between Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, and Thurstan, archbishop of York, because the archbishop of York refused, according to custom, to be subject to the archbishop of Canterbury, as his predecessors had been accustomed to do. The case was often debated before the king and lord pope, but it has not yet been settled as it should be.”

A little later he adds:

> “In the year of the Lord 1113 Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, was consecrated at Canterbury by Anselm, legate of the lord pope, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, and received the pallium from him. On the same day that archbishop consecrated Theophilus, bishop of Worcester, and Bernard, bishop of St Davids. Then, after a few days, when Thurstan, elect of York, was summoned by the archbishop of Canterbury to receive blessing from him according to custom and render obedience to him and to the Church of Canterbury, [Col. 0424B] he replied that he would gladly receive blessing from him, but would by no means make the profession which he demanded. When King Henry heard this, he publicly declared that, unless Thurstan rendered to the Church of Canterbury what he owed according to the custom of his predecessors, he would entirely lose the bishopric of York together with its blessing. And so, after an appeal was entered by the archbishop of Canterbury that he should not receive consecration from any other than himself, they parted from one another.”

The same writer, after a few intervening words, speaking under the year 1119 of Pope Calixtus:

> “He held a council at Rheims, to which King Henry sent certain bishops of England and Normandy. Thurstan also, elect of York, obtained from the king leave to go there, having pledged that he would not receive blessing from him. Coming to the council, he won the Romans to his side, as is customary, by the benefit of generosity, and through them obtained consecration by the pope. When this became known to the king of the English, he forbade him every place within his dominion. [Col. 0424C]”

The same author shortly afterward, under the year 1125:

> “In that year William of Canterbury and Thurstan of York, the archbishops, disputed concerning the primacy—which of them seemed more worthy.”

He immediately adds:

> “In the year of the Lord 1127, King Henry held his court at Christmas at Windsor. There Thurstan, archbishop of York, wished, to the prejudice of William, archbishop of Canterbury, to crown the king; but by the judgment of all he was repulsed, and the bearer of the cross which he had caused to be carried before him into the king’s chapel was expelled from the chapel with the cross.”

He says that this Thurstan died in the year of the Lord 1139.

But what William of Malmesbury wrote about this controversy is wholly worthy of quotation, so that the history of the matter may become clearer. Thus in book III of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*:

> “Thurstan succeeded, a cleric of commendable steadfastness. When, after some years, he refused to make to Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, the profession required by his election, [Col. 0424D] he voluntarily resigned the archbishopric at the king’s wish. But later, at the urging of his clergy, he went to Rome and obtained this letter:
>
> ‘Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Henry, illustrious king of the English, greeting and apostolic blessing. We have heard that the elect of York, a wise and vigorous man, has been removed from the Church of York without judgment—something plainly contrary to divine justice and the institutions of the holy Fathers. We wish neither that the Church of Canterbury should be diminished nor that the Church of York should suffer prejudice; but we judge that the arrangement established between those churches by blessed Gregory, apostle of the English people, should remain firm and inviolate. Therefore let the same elect be restored by every means, as justice requires, to his church. But if any question should arise between those churches, let it be examined in our presence, [Col. 0425A] with both parties present.’”

Supported by this letter, Thurstan gladly reclaimed his see. The disagreement between him and Archbishop Ralph grew daily, because Ralph could be brought by neither blandishments nor threats to lay hands upon him unless he made the profession, while Thurstan declared that he would not do so even at the risk of his life. Therefore, when Gelasius, successor to Pope Paschal, came this side of the Alps, both determined to meet him and present their cases. But the pope’s death, not long delayed, checked their efforts, until Calixtus, his successor, came to Rheims to hold a council. Thurstan hastened there energetically, having promised the king that he would undertake nothing against the honor of the Church of Canterbury. As soon as he saw an opportunity, he broke that promise and, contrary to all the customs of his forefathers, received episcopal blessing from the pope.

To the pope there had previously gone an envoy of the king—also Ralph’s brother, Seffrid, later bishop of Chichester—to notify the pope that he must in no way consecrate Thurstan himself, [Col. 0425B] or allow him to be consecrated by anyone other than the bishop of Canterbury, according to ancient custom. If the pope wished to assert the authority of his apostolic office against this, he should be certain that the king would not change his resolution in this matter even at the loss of his crown. The pope replied:

> “Let the king not suppose that I shall act otherwise in the matter under discussion than he wishes. For my will has never inclined me to diminish in any way the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, over which so many illustrious Fathers have presided, as is known to almost the whole world.”

Persuaded by these assurances, the envoy hastened his return. After his departure, the pope, obliged by the demands of the Romans, who had passed into Thurstan’s friendship, consecrated him. When John, archdeacon of Canterbury, openly forbade this, the pope replied:

> “We wish to do no injustice to the Church of Canterbury. But, preserving its right and dignity, we carry out what we have proposed.”

Those who heard this judged it frivolous, [Col. 0425C] since the deed differed from the statement. When he heard of it, the king prohibited Thurstan from every land of his dominion. Nor would he relax this severity even when the pope personally appealed to him at Gisors, declaring that, by the authority of blessed Peter, he would release him from the pledge by which the king said he was bound. Since this proved fruitless, the king then remained unreconciled. But in the following year, when the aforesaid pope was now established more firmly on the apostolic throne and could dispose more freely as he wished, he sent a letter commanding that either Thurstan should enjoy his bishopric, or the king should be punished with anathema and the bishop of Canterbury with suspension from priestly office. This fear compelled the king to abandon his undertaking, and Thurstan was restored to his see. Thus, although Ralph and his successor William made many efforts and advanced many arguments, Thurstan by his persistence refuted and rendered void all their allegations.”

So William of Malmesbury. Elsewhere he also clearly indicates [Col. 0425D] that the Romans had formerly fostered such disputes by crafty methods. For, near the end of book I of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, in the chapter “On the Archbishops of Canterbury,” he quotes words of a letter written by Pope Paschal himself to the bishops of England and King Henry regarding Ralph’s case, where among other things the pope concludes:

> “The dignity which the Church received through blessed Augustine, and which our brother Anselm of holy memory is known to have held by lawful right and possession, we certainly in no way diminish; rather, we wish the Church of Canterbury to remain in the same condition, so that its authentic privileges, in accordance with canonical enactments, may be disturbed by no agitations.”

The historian adds:

> “If here the pope had expressly said: ‘The Church of Canterbury has had these and these dignities, and I confirm those same dignities to it,’ he would have settled the dispute [Col. 0426A] and imposed an end upon the controversies. But when he said, ‘Whatever authentic privileges it has, we in no way diminish,’ he left the matter, as it was, undefined and unresolved.”

With these final words agrees what Saint Bernard says in letter 42 to Henry, archbishop of Sens: that the Romans of his age cared little by what outcome matters were resolved, because they greatly loved gifts and pursued recompense. Moreover, anyone desiring further material on the controversy of those churches should read what the same William of Malmesbury wrote in book III of *On the Deeds of the Kings of the English*, under William I.

“As he deserves.” These words have been added from the manuscript copy.

## TO LETTER 275

“He magnifies the injury done by both the king and the count of Nevers.” These seven words, absent from the first edition, have now been added on the authority of the manuscripts. Here belongs what John, monk [Col. 0426B] of Marmoutier, writes in his ancient history of Geoffrey, duke of Normandy and count of Anjou:

> “Count Theobald was an illustrious man; in his time no one in the kingdom of the Franks surpassed him in wealth, fidelity, or just judgment. Under his lordship the count of Nevers and Hugh, surnamed the Manceau, were at enmity. Count Theobald repeatedly summoned them, as his men, to justice in his court. But the count of Nevers, as the stronger party, wishing rather to overcome his enemy by force than submit to law, evaded Count Theobald’s court. While the struggle was thus carried on by both sides through slow and continual hostilities, the count of Nevers, wishing to crush his enemy completely, brought against him the king of the Franks and the bishop of Autun, each with a large army. Hugh, no less, advanced against the enemy with as great a body of knights and foot-soldiers as he could muster. Thus, the three armies having assembled, king, bishop, and count besieged Hugh in the castle called Cona.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0425] “A town called Cona in the territory of Auxerre,” says Geoffrey in *Life of Saint Bernard*, book IV, chapter 4.]

> “[Col. 0426C] There was absolutely no hope of escape: with the castle surrounded on every side by enemies, no one could enter and no one go out. Therefore the Manceau, brought into straits, sent envoys to Count Theobald, reporting his danger and begging aid. Without delay, because delay would mean danger to his own man, he assembled his own followers by command, relatives by entreaty, and friends as well. Among these, and above all others, he earnestly entreated and confidently requested Count Geoffrey of Anjou, in whose assistance he had especially confident hope. Geoffrey, as ever most ready to aid friends, did not hesitate: he promised help and pledged his faith. He therefore joined to himself 140 selected and battle-tested knights, with 300 retainers, and hastened with these alone. Count Theobald and our count of Anjou, now united, hurried to relieve the besieged Manceau. When news of their arrival flew ahead, the king of the Franks—certainly by sound counsel—broke camp and abandoned the siege; hatred of his enemy made the count of Nevers somewhat slower to flee. [Col. 0426D] Count Geoffrey charged after him, while Count Theobald was occupied with the rest. Then the illustrious man, surpassing his companions in valor as in rank, bore painted lions on his shield, yet in courage was no inferior to real lions. Having overtaken the fugitives, he raged against the enemy without restraint. Like a thunderbolt of war, he was the first to break into their ranks; his companions followed. Some he cut down with the sword; others he overthrew by his charge. No one escaped unharmed from his pursuit. Why say more? Having killed very many and put the rest to flight, the count captured the count of Nevers himself and delivered his captive to Count Theobald. Our Count Geoffrey, distinguished by such outstanding courage and renowned for such great excellence, was, as he was humane and graciously merciful, so too bravely good, strong, and spirited; [Col. 0427A] whence it follows that what was truly his was:

> ‘To spare the conquered and subdue the proud.’”

VIRGIL, *Aeneid* VI.853.

## TO LETTER 277
Aldebert, appointed to the Church of Le Mans. Previously it was given as “to Hildebert”; I do not know whether through a printer’s error, or because whoever arranged for this letter to be added to the first edition found it so written in his old manuscript. For it was lacking in those old books which I had used at that time. More recently, when I came upon an ancient manuscript of Saint-Victor, I found the same letter at the end of Ivo’s letters, but with a different name for the person elected. For it has not “Hildebert,” but “Aldebert”; another handwritten copy confirms this reading. In the variation and discrepancy of the writing, it has now seemed preferable to follow this reading, so that due honour may be restored to the memory of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans. For the author of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume XII, from the words of this letter [Col. 0427B] censures Hildebert’s conduct, also because he had written a poetic epitaph in praise of his master Berengar, who was tainted with heresy. This epitaph, elegant and complete, survives in William of Malmesbury, *De gestis regum Anglorum*, book III. Following, no doubt, the reading of the edition hitherto commonly printed, he was able to accuse Hildebert of unchastity. So important a matter it is to come upon books of reliable authority.

Yet there is a double reason for revising that judgment. First, in those old archetypes, as I have said, Aldebert is expressly named, not Hildebert. Second, there are preceding letters addressed to Hildebert already as bishop of Le Mans, which, restored to their proper order on the evidence of several ancient manuscripts, indicate that this later letter can scarcely be correctly addressed to him. Hildebert, moreover, is numbered among the best and most praiseworthy bishops of his age; see further the notes on Letter 206. Who this Aldebert was remains unknown to me.

[Col. 0427C] “Although somewhat caustic and biting.” The same writer of the *Annals*, in the cited place, transcribes this whole letter and presents a gap marked with an asterisk thus: “although somewhat * . . . . and biting”; and in the margin he adds, “perhaps it should be read: ‘although these things themselves are somewhat biting.’” But the reading of our manuscripts is entirely sound and contains no defect; for a similar expression occurs in Letter 133 to Richard.

### On Letter CCLXXVIII

To Robert, bishop of the Church of Lincoln. Henry of Huntingdon mentions him in *History*, book VII:

> “In the sixth year of his reign the younger William gave the bishopric of Lincoln to Robert, surnamed Bloet, his chancellor. No other was more handsome in appearance, more serene in mind, or sweeter in speech. The king also promised that he would amend bad laws and establish peace in the house of God. But once he had recovered, he regretted it and became worse than usual. Therefore, grieving that he had not sold the bishopric of Lincoln, [Col. 0427D] he joined with the archbishop of York in accusing Bishop Robert, alleging that the city of Lincoln and the province of Lindsey ought to have been subject to that archbishop. Nor could the case be settled until Robert had agreed to pay the king five hundred pounds for the liberty of his Church. This was reckoned simony for the king, but justice for the bishop.”

Matthew Paris has this also under William II, in the year of the Lord 1092, except that the final words differ slightly: “But this,” he says, “was at first reckoned simony for the king, but afterwards justice.”

Roger of Hoveden, in the first part of his *Annals*, records that this bishop died suddenly of illness while in the company of Henry I, king of England, on 10 January 1112. William of Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, book IV, in the chapter on the bishops of Lincoln, relates that it happened while he was riding beside the king, and adds that he had lived as bishop for slightly fewer than thirty years; that he was a cheerful man and not very serious, second to none in knowledge of secular business, but not similarly versed in ecclesiastical matters.

### On Letter CCLXXX

Of Peterborough, otherwise Petraefungensis, Petraefingensis, Petraefuntensis.

### On Letter CCLXXXV

[Col. 0428B] “Through the hand of a layman,” which Letter 131 and Letter 219 say is done contrary to the canons.

“And through the book, the Church itself.” Compare Letter 182, where he says that he had wished to perform the investiture of a subdeanery by presenting a book. Saint Bernard, in his sermon on baptism: “A canon is invested through a book.” In an old copy, under the heading *On reinvestiture in a prebend*, there survives a formula of Pope Gelasius in these words:

> “Brother, in the name of the Lord, I reinvest you through this book and through this bread in this prebend, by command of our prelate and by command of the canons of this Church,” etc.

### On Letter CCLXXXVII

Since this letter was written by its author before he became bishop of Chartres, it might, on chronological grounds, have seemed suitable to place it at the beginning of the work, though not on account of episcopal rank. For in the commonly printed copies the heading states that it was written by Ivo, priest of Blessed Quintin of Beauvais. Yet in [Col. 0428C] no ancient manuscripts is this heading placed at the beginning of these letters; indeed, in most it is entirely absent. The title also varies.

For in an old copy from the College of Navarre it is given as: “Of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, to Haimaric, abbot of Anchin, concerning the body and blood of the Lord.” In an old sheet belonging to Antoine Loisel there is a double heading. The first: “Letter of Ivo, provost of Saint-Quintin of Beauvais, to Aimeric, a monk then at Arras and afterwards abbot of Anchin, concerning the body and blood of the Lord.” The second: “Ivo, the least priest of the Church of Blessed Quintin of Beauvais, to Haimaric, brother of good hope,” etc. Elsewhere it is written *Aquiscincti*, as in Letter 65 of Saint Bernard to Alvisus, abbot. Sigebert mentions the Church of Anchin in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 1100. Robert the monk, *History of Jerusalem*, book VII, calls it Aquiscingense, if the reading there is correct: “He was an indefatigable helper in all things of the monastery of Aquiscingum.”

[Col. 0428D] “Whether it be *sapa* (boiled must) or *carenum*.” This ancient reading is supported by the words of Bernard, abbot of Bonneval, *Life of Saint Bernard*, book II, chapter 1:

> “There coarse bread was provided instead of fine flour, boiled must (*sapa*) instead of *carenum*, blera instead of turbot, and vegetables instead of every sort of delicacy.”

[Col. 0427]

## New Observations of Jean-Baptiste Souchet, Doctor of Theology and Canon of the Church of Chartres, on Ivo’s Letters

When Juretus, a man most devoted to ancient practice, in his observations on the letters of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, either deliberately passed over, neglected, or—being a man from another land and lacking knowledge of local history—did not know certain matters which might perhaps not be unwelcome to the reader, I decided to add them, so that, if possible, little might be wanting to the letters’ full elucidation.

For that most learned man deliberately omitted and neglected, as he himself confesses, summaries of all the letters. Although many requested them, I would have satisfied their wishes, had not the authority of the manuscript codices, and of Pierre Pithou, a man highly deserving in literary affairs, who had prefixed such summaries to Ivo’s letters, delayed me—either because it was rejected or not sufficiently approved. For what would a hoarse goose accomplish by squawking among melodious swans? Moreover, Ivo’s style is easy, his text so plain and lucid that it needs no Oedipus, nor a torch to illuminate the author’s mind.

I therefore sought only to determine, insofar as it could be done, to which persons or in what years those letters were written; and I would have arranged them in the order in which they were drafted or sent, had I not yielded to the manuscripts, which opposed this and required another order. I neither wished nor ought to overturn that order, so that antiquity might retain its due honour and the arrangement of our forebears remain unimpaired. For everywhere the memory of predecessors is to be revered, and I judge it wrong to depart from it.

Nor was it ever my intention, by adding to Juretus’s learned labours, to detract anything from his glory; my sole aim was that the little notes I had conceived in my mind while reading might serve as appendices to his, and might shed some light upon the tablets needed for elucidating Ivo. Therefore, lest I incur the odium of trespassing upon his labours, I have abstained from citations of the Fathers and other authors which Juretus himself had excerpted or noted either in the margin of the text or in the body of his observations. I have added only what was omitted.

I undertook this labour not at the prompting of my own judgment—which has always seemed suspect to me—but at the urging, indeed command, of friends, to whom I could scarcely refuse my small assistance or diligence. Whatever these *anagraphai* [supplementary notes] may be, they appear rough. While the press was running, illness assailed me and daily occupations distracted me; I was unable to apply the file and polish them. Let the reader therefore judge kindly and fairly: if he finds in them anything pleasing to the mind, let him be grateful; if anything too lowly and humble, let him pardon it generously. Such is the human condition—or rather, infirmity—that people are ignorant of more than they can learn, and it is granted to few, or to none, to please everyone.

### On Letter III

[Col. 0429A] In the preceding edition Juretus had relegated this letter to the end, since it had been sent to him too late and the greater part of the letters had already been printed, as he himself noted in the margin. But because it truly belongs in this place, we have inserted it here in the place of the third “letter,” which is certainly not a letter but an address or papal admonition to a bishop whom he consecrated, as Baronius observes in volume XI of the *Annals*, and as may be seen in the Roman Ordinal, which bears the title, “How a bishop ought to be ordained.” There it is fuller than in Ivo.

The admonitions there concerning how a bishop ought to conduct himself are excellent and highly worthy of reading; but because they are very extensive and do not belong here, we refer the reader to the Roman Ordinal. Since, however, this address occurs in all the manuscripts and printed codices under the name of an address, admonition, or discourse of Pope Urban to Ivo, etc., we deliberately retained it, changing only its designation from “letter” to “address.” Thus we disturbed in no way either [Col. 0429B] the number and sequence of Ivo’s letters or the order of Juretus’s notes.

### On Letter IV

To Bernard, abbot of Marmoutier. That he was elected abbot of that monastery after Bartholomew is established for the year 1083, reckoning from Easter according to the French custom, from the text concerning the dedication of the church of Marmoutier—for so the printed codex reads—at whose beginning are found these words:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1095, on 10 March, the eleventh lunar day, epact 23, concurrent 11, which was the thirty-seventh year of Philip, king of the Franks, and the thirteenth year from the ordination of Bernard, abbot of this our Marmoutier, the glorious Pope Urban II, etc., in the eighth year of his apostolate—that is, in the octave of the winter feast of Blessed Martin—having at last visited our monastery in order to make peace and concord between us and the canons of Blessed Maurice of Tours, who had then for ten years not ceased to persecute us; having been received by our poverty for the time being sufficiently and fittingly, as was proper; and having rested or refreshed himself among us for seven days, not without much expense—on the eighth day of his arrival, which is the date noted at the head of the page, dedicated to God, in honour of the Holy Cross, the most blessed Mother of God and perpetual Virgin Mary, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and Blessed Martin, the greater basilica of this our Marmoutier.”

This is confirmed by an instrument copied on folio 180 of the cartulary of that monastery, entitled: “Record concerning the goods which Michael and his father Almarus gave and sold at Château-Fracteval.” There it is stated:

> “Let all know that in the year in which Pope Urban dedicated the basilica of Marmoutier, etc., the two brothers Robert Michael and Almarus themselves came to Marmoutier, [Col. 0430A] and in our chapter received the benefit of our fellowship, in the time of Lord Abbot Bernard, in the thirteenth year of his ordination,” etc.

Since that letter is first in the order, I think it was the first or second of those which Ivo wrote to different persons, around 1090.

“Lord Gautier, formerly abbot of Bonneval monastery.” He was Bernerius’s predecessor. Ivo rightly considers that he should be recalled to his monastery, since he was not permitted to abandon it without the permission of his bishop. For severe penalties are threatened against clerics and monks who wander without letters of recommendation or authorization from their bishop by the Councils of Agde, canon 52; Paris VI, canon 34; Meaux, canon 50; and Vannes in Armorica, canon 5:

> “The canon states: Clerics or monks are not to have permission to travel or wander without letters of recommendation from their bishop; and wherever they come without their bishop’s letters, as stated, they are to be considered excluded from communion.”

Likewise the First Council of Orléans, canon 19:

> “Abbots, on account of the humility of religion, are to remain subject to the authority of bishops. And if they do anything outside the Rule, they are to be corrected by bishops.”

Ansegisus repeats this in precisely the same words, *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 137. Something similar is read in Orléans II, canon 21, where it is said that “abbots who despise the commands of bishops are not to be admitted at all to communion, unless, having embraced humility, they abandon their obstinacy.”

This was the form of letters of authorization or recommendation, as I find in ancient manuscripts:

> “To the most reverend and beloved N., bishop of the Church of N., N., bishop, sends manifold greetings in the Lord. Let the zeal of your holiness, most religious Father, know that the present N. by name—here his rank is to be written, namely deacon, subdeacon, etc.—has been retained in our diocese, instructed there in sacred letters, and of good reputation in his conduct. Now he has asked us to order letters of recommendation to be made for him. Assenting to his requests and desires, according to the promulgated authority of canonical institution, we have granted him these letters of our humility. We therefore humbly beseech your magnificence to deign mercifully, for the increase of eternal reward, to promote the aforesaid N. in that Church to the sacred order of N. And so that no one may demand him back from you by canonical authority, and so that no fraud of falsity may appear in this letter, which Latin custom calls a *formata*, we have marked, according to the Council of Nicaea, in the first reckoning the Greek letters of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, π, υ, α—which letters signify the number four hundred and eighty-one. We have also added the first letter of the Apostle Peter, Π, which signifies eighty; likewise the first letter of our own name; the second of yours; the third of the recipient’s; the fourth of your city; and, in addition, the number of the present indiction. We have also added the number ninety-nine, which in the idiom of its own language signifies ἀμήν, ‘Amen.’”

Pope Zosimus, in Letter 5, which is Letter 1, decreed to the bishops of Gaul that anyone from any part of Gaul who sought to go to Rome in any ecclesiastical rank, or intended to go to another land, must receive *formatae* from the metropolitan of Arles, by which he would demonstrate, through the metropolitan’s written attestation, his priesthood or ecclesiastical position; otherwise, he should know himself separated from the communion of the Church. He confirms this in Letters 5 and 9—or also 6, elsewhere 11—to Patroclus, bishop of Arles; as does Pope Vigilius in Letter 2 to Auxanius, bishop of Arles. Many formulas of these *formatae* may be seen in Sirmond, *Councils*, vol. II, p. 663 and following.

The transfer of monks from one monastery to another is assigned exclusively to bishops by the Second Council of Vern [Vernum], canon 10:

> “That monks who truly live according to the Rule, the text of the council provides, are not to be permitted to wander to the Roman See or elsewhere unless they perform obedience to their abbot. And if such a case should occur—which God forbid—that the abbot is found so lax or negligent that the monastery itself falls into the hands of laymen, and the bishop cannot correct this; and if there are monks there who, for God’s sake, wish to move from that monastery to another for the salvation of their souls, then, with the bishop’s consent, they may have permission in whatever way their souls may be saved.”

### On Letter V

To the noble countess Adela, wife of Henry Stephen, count of Chartres.

“Royal blood in Your Excellency.” Adela herself traced her descent from William I, king of England, and Matilda, his wife, daughter of Baldwin, count of Flanders, who was the niece, through a sister, of Henry I, king of the Franks. Orderic Vitalis explains this in *Ecclesiastical History*, book III:

> “In these times William, duke of Normandy, was greatly increasing in virtue and power, and surpassed all his neighbours in liberality and magnificence. He took as wife the noble Matilda, daughter of Baldwin, duke of Flanders, namely the niece through the sister of Henry, king of the Franks.”

And in book IV, speaking of the same Matilda, he writes:

> “She was a kinswoman of Philip, king of the Franks, and drew her origin from the kings of Gaul and emperors of Germany; she was distinguished by exceptional nobility of both birth and character. To her excellent husband she bore the desired offspring of both sexes: Robert and Richard, William Rufus and Henry, Agatha and Constance, Adelaiza, Adela, and Cecilia,” etc.

That Adela married Henry Stephen, count of Chartres, is attested by the same author in book V:

> “Stephen, count palatine of Blois, wishing to strengthen friendship with King William, asked him for his daughter Adela in marriage; and, on the counsel of prudent men, she was granted to him by her father,” etc.

William of Jumièges, a monk, has the same in *History of Normandy*, book VIII, chapter 34. In what year this letter was written is not sufficiently clear; nevertheless, I think it was published in 1090.

### On Letter VI

“To Gerard, beloved by him.” It is exceedingly difficult to know who this Gerard was, since we have only the bare name. Yet, if conjecture is permitted, I would suppose him to have been a regular canon of Saint-Quintin, an intimate of Ivo, who later became abbot of Saint-Loup at Troyes, and to whom Ivo wrote this letter at the beginning of his episcopate.

“Also an implement of snowy whiteness for arranging the hair,” etc. He means an ivory comb suited to parting the hair, not merely for domestic and common use but also for sacred use. For, as Durandus observes, *Rationale of Divine Offices*, book IV, chapter 3, it was ancient custom for bishops, after putting on stockings and sandals, to comb their heads:

> “Third, the head is combed. For by the hair are signified superfluous thoughts and the cares of earthly concern; by the head, the mind and intention, which rise above all the soul’s acts as the head above the other members. Fittingly, therefore, the hairs are smoothed and arranged by the comb, and plucked out and set apart, to signify that at that time especially he ought to compose his conduct and cast away superfluous thoughts from himself, according to that prophetic saying: ‘Put away the evil of your thoughts’; and that his mind ought, by antecedent discernment, to be separated, calmed, and cleansed of earthly cares, and ordered by virtues. For the comb, on account of its ordered division in its teeth, signifies discernment, by which the intention of the soul is adorned, just as the hair of the head is by the comb.”

Ivo’s meaning in this letter is the same when he writes: “I believe that by this little gift, as by a certain reminder, your prudence is awakening my vigilance, so that I may endeavour by different modes of exhortation to compose the disordered manners of peoples and, through the moderation of discernment, restore them to due order.”

Artemidorus, however, in *Interpretation of Dreams*, book VI, compares the comb to time, which dissolves and corrects all harsh things—as though by this gift Gerard wished to incline Ivo’s mind to endure equally all evils arising either from his opponent Geoffrey, deprived of the bishopric, or from Geoffrey’s uncle, the bishop of Paris and chancellor of the realm, from the king himself, and from the metropolitan of Sens, who defended the cause of the deposed bishop.

“In Normandy, a certain provostship.” Richard, duke of Normandy, had granted this provostship to the Church of Chartres around the year 1017, as is clear from the instrument of donation. The portion relevant to the matter is as follows:

> “In the reign of the Lord Jesus Christ for ever, in the seventeenth year after one thousand from His Incarnation, in the fifteenth indiction, and in the twenty-sixth year of Robert, king of the Franks, I, Richard, margrave of Normandy, etc. I wish all to know how I have not suffered the Church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at Chartres to lack an experience of my generosity, both because of the help which it possesses before God above all others, and because of the considerable wrong which I had gravely committed in its neighbourhood, etc. I therefore give, with equal purpose and the common favour of my sons and also of my kinsmen, and from my own right; by direct donation we transfer into the proper dominion of God, to whom all things belong, and of Saint Mary of Chartres, to possess perpetually: namely, in the county of Évreux, the entire village of Ébrard with its church, and the tithe of hunting from the wood called Bortis; and in the same district, the church alone of Hauville; and in Lisieux, the church alone of Bonneville, and in the same territory the entire English village with its church; and the church of Saint Julian with two dependencies. These gifts, therefore, etc., we have bestowed, abandoning entirely every customary claim or disturbance of ours,” etc.

[Col. 0432D] “With the aid of the foolish count of that land, he usurps and devastates it.” After being expelled from the Church of Chartres, Geoffrey, bishop of that name the First, withdrew to Normandy. There, relying on the protection of William, count of Évreux, he was wasting the revenues of the provostship. On this William, see Orderic Vitalis, *Norman History*, book II, under 1108. From these facts I judge that the letter was written immediately after Ivo’s episcopate began, since Geoffrey, former bishop of Chartres—whom Ivo calls the scapegoat—retired to Normandy after his deposition, as is clear from this letter.

### On Letter X

“To the virgins consecrated to God in the monastery of Saint Avitus at Châteaudun.” This monastery was founded for nuns not far from Châteaudun before 1045, when Wanelus, treasurer of Saint Martin of Tours, granted certain goods of his possession, held as a benefice from the bishop of Chartres, to the church of Saint Avitus for the use of the nuns serving God there, as he himself acknowledges in the charter of cession made by him. What rule they originally followed is not clear, since at that time abbots and abbesses laid down whatever rule they wished for themselves, or at least received whichever rule was observed from the bishop. Some embraced the rule of Saint Caesarius, archbishop of Arles, and his sister Saint Caesaria; others that of Saint Columbanus, Saint Benedict, or another which pleased them more. They now profess the Benedictine rule, having laid aside their old habit and put on a new one. I think this was sent about 1092.

### On Letter XII

“To the most reverend Father of Fathers, Urban II.” He was a Frenchman by birth, according to Onuphrius, from the town of Châtillon in the diocese of Reims; he was called Lord Odo. From a regular canon of the Lateran he became a monk of Cluny; then Gregory VII made him bishop of Ostia. Finally, after Victor III, Roman pontiff, had died, he was elected and consecrated at Terracina in Campania on 12 March 1088. He sat for eleven years, four months, and eighteen days. He died at Rome, in the house of Peter Leo, on 29 July 1099, and was buried at Saint Peter’s.

Baronius contends that Ivo sent this letter to Urban in 1093, no. 8; I do not accept this. It seems to have been written immediately after Ivo returned from Rome. Richer, metropolitan of Sens, and his suffragans were unwilling to admit him into their body and, after convening a council at Étampes, attempted to strip him of his rank. But by appeal to the pope he broke the force of their attack. Charter 170 of the cartulary of the monastery of Vendôme, which names Ivo as witness in 1091, indiction 14, on Friday of Easter week, proves that he had returned from Rome at least in that year, in which that synod of Étampes was assembled; and the letter was written immediately afterwards.

“They wish to redeem altars from me,” or tithes, Juretus adds in the Notes, “which they commonly called altars.” I delete this. For not tithes, but the churches to which tithes were given, were called “altars.” Since in Ivo’s age many people offered to congregations and monasteries, or even sold to them, churches which they themselves had founded or which belonged to their jurisdiction, to be freely possessed, they cloaked that sale under the name of redemption. Thus the *Chronicle of Maurigny* says:

> “The conscience of the abbot and certain other brothers was troubled because our predecessors had acquired some churches and tithes not only by gifts but also by money. For at that early beginning of the foundation of this church the question of simony was not debated as vigorously as it was by the diligence of later generations. But if anything ecclesiastical was bought from laymen, it was called not a purchase but a redemption,” etc.

Wishing to restrain this evil lest it spread further, bishops—to whom, by common law, belonged the ordering and authority of all churches in their dioceses, according to the First Council of Orléans, canon 19, the Council of Chalon, canon 10, and many others—sometimes granted these churches to monks on the condition that, whenever their vicars, whom they called *personae*, were changed, they should pay a fixed sum of money distinct from the synodal and cathedral dues owed to prelates. This too was called the redemption of an altar.

The Council of Clermont abolished this exaction, which had the flavour of simony, as found in 16, question 7, canon 2, *Congregato*. Yet after the synod prelates demanded payment of an annual rent in place of that redemption, called *tallia*. Paschal II, Urban’s successor, wishing wholly to prohibit that abuse, sharply rebuked Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Ranulf, bishop of Saintes, because they did not refrain from this exaction. This is clear from his letter addressed to them, preserved in the cartulary of the monastery of Vendôme. Since it is highly relevant to the subject, it will not be out of place to report it; it begins:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishops Ivo of Chartres and Ranulf of Saintes, greeting and apostolic blessing. According to the ordinances of the holy canons,” etc.

See Paschal II under the year 1118. I find this all the more surprising in Ivo: in this letter he censures this custom as evil among his predecessors and consults the supreme pontiff about its exaction; yet he “sees and approves the better course, but follows the worse,” as Seneca says in the *Medea*. The decree was renewed besides at the Council of Poitiers, by John and Benedict, cardinals of the Holy Roman Church and legates of Paschal, canon 6; see *Councils*, vol. VII, part I, p. 533; and at another council there under the same legates, canon 9, p. 540. Letter 12, book III, of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, to Ulger, bishop of Angers, concerns the same matter.

Since the resources and revenues of churches were scant, and since, according to the Council of Nicaea, chapter 41, bishops were obliged every year to assist the patriarch with some subsidy called a charitable gift, so that he might be supported in keeping with his rank, priests likewise assisted the bishop. Therefore Justinian, *Code*, *On Bishops and Clerics*, book XVI, mentions a certain capitation payment owed by some clerics to churches under the bishop’s authority.

Because offense in this matter had more than once been committed, either by bishops or by those reluctant to support their bishop, it was agreed, for the sake of concord and mutual goodwill, that in certain dioceses bishops should claim for themselves the fruits and offerings of one, or the first, year of vacant parish churches, called *deportus*, with some part granted to archdeacons, since responsibility for parishes and their ordering belonged to their care, as Isidore states in his letter to Ludifred, bishop of Córdoba. In this way the churches of the whole diocese were released from that ancient redemption of altars.

For, as Chopin says, *De sacra politia*, book III, title 3, no. 3, just as military and secular benefices granted to soldiers for fidelity and service revert on the death of the final tenant, and in that event the lord takes the fruits of the first year for renewal and restoration of the fief; so they say that the lapse-year of a sacred benefice ought to go to the benefit of the giver of the benefice, so that after the incumbent is removed by death, the bishop or archdeacon receives the lapsed revenues of that year. This is strictly observed throughout Neustria; elsewhere it is not, but varies according to the custom of different churches. Perhaps this letter was written in 1092.

### On Letter XIII

“To Rainald, reverend archbishop of Reims.” He means Rainald the Cripple, formerly treasurer of Saint Martin of Tours, who succeeded Manasses and was consecrated by Hugh, bishop of Die and legate of Gregory VII, at the synod of Lyons in 1080. Baronius considers that Ivo wrote this letter to Rainald in 1093, no. 13. I place it in the following year [Col. 0434D], since only in that year did Philip, king of the Franks, take Bertrada—of whom the text speaks—as his wife, and have the royal crown placed upon her, as Juretus correctly observed at the end of his note on Letter 16. Rainald did not survive long thereafter, for he died at Arras on 24 January 1095, as Robert writes in his work on the archbishops of Reims, no. 45.

### On Letter XVI

“To Walter or Gualter, bishop of Meaux.” This is Walter II, who was promoted by Richer, archbishop of Sens, against Robert, who had formerly been ordained by Hugh of Die, then primate of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, as Odorannus, monk of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens, records.

“Roger, legate of the Roman Church.” At that time I find no legate of the Apostolic See of that name. Hugh of Lyons, mentioned above, at Ivo’s request in Letter 12, exercised the legation in Gaul; after him came Richard, cardinal-bishop of Albano, then Cono. Who then was this Roger? Ivo calls him only a cardinal in Letter 18.

“This I advise you.” From this it may be affirmed that the letter was written after King Philip had entered into marriage—or rather concubinage—with Bertrada, and thus in 1094 or 1095.

### On Letter XVII

“What I have advised, I advise again: appoint someone in my place.” Although Ivo had obtained the bishopric of Chartres, he did not therefore lay aside responsibility for the monastery of Saint-Quintin of Beauvais, because the canons of that church resisted; he writes this letter to them so that they may appoint another over themselves. He finally obtained this, as is clear from Letters 31 and 32. This letter was written about 1092, since in 1093 he entirely renounced the office, with Odo appointed in his place.

### On Letter XVIII

“That Simon of Melfa.” “Of Melfa” is erroneous because of faulty punctuation; it must be read “of Nielfa,” a town not far from Montfort, ruled by Almeric, as he was called. Simon, discussed here, was its lord, as Orderic Vitalis states in *Ecclesiastical History*, book XII:

> “There Simon of Parona, Simon of Nealpha, Guy surnamed Malusvicinus, and Peter of Maule, his nephew; likewise William Aculeus—who were all nobles of the diocese of Chartres—and nearly two hundred other warriors from France, served Count Waleran,” etc.

The *Chronicle of the monastery of Maurigny*, book I, also mentions him when it writes:

> “King Philip gave us the churches of Old Étampes—that is, Saint Martin, Saint Alban, and Saint Medard—and confirmed this gift by royal letters. He ordered his son Louis, king-designate, to grant the same; and Louis, having brought with him Amaury, lord of Montfort, and Simon of Nealpha, came into our chapter, humbly sought and received a share in our benefices.”

This letter was written about 1093.

### On Letter XIX

“Whom you ask me to absolve.” Ivo does not here speak of sacramental absolution, but of permission or leave to depart from a monastery or place, as may be seen in the following Letter 78. Thus, when the superior of an order deprives his subordinate of office, he uses the word “I absolve,” as though saying: “I release you from the bond by which you were bound to your office and restore you to your former liberty.” In what year the letter was written is uncertain; but if conjecture has any value, I think it was published in 1094 or 1095, from what is read in it.

### On Letter XX

Against the viscount, namely Hugh, lord of Puiset and viscount of Chartres. To gratify Philip, king of the Franks—because Ivo condemned in speech and writing the king’s adultery with Bertrada, wife of Fulk, count of Anjou—he kept Ivo imprisoned for a long time. There Ivo suffered many hardships, even to want of bread, as Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, says in Letter 100. Baronius assigns this letter to 1095, no. 21, and I readily agree, since in that same year Urban II, at the Synod of Clermont, prohibited Philip from water and fire because of his adultery with the aforesaid Bertrada.

### On Letter XXI
Hoel, bishop of Le Mans, Hildebert’s predecessor. Of his remarkable elevation to the bishopric of Le Mans, Orderic Vitalis writes thus in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*:

“After Ernaud, bishop of Le Mans, had died, King William [of England] said to Samson, his chaplain and bishop of Bayeux: ‘The see of the bishopric of Le Mans has been bereft of its bishop; and there, God willing, I now wish to install you in his place. Le Mans, so called from canine madness, is an ancient city; its people are insolent and bloodthirsty toward their neighbours [Col. 0436A], ever rebellious against their lords, and eager for insurrection. Therefore I have resolved to entrust you with the episcopal reins: you whom I have nurtured from childhood and diligently loved, and whom I now desire to raise among the greatest magnates of my realm.’

“Samson replied: ‘According to apostolic tradition, a bishop must be blameless. But throughout my whole life I have been highly blameworthy; before the sight of the Godhead I am defiled with every vice of mind and body. Wretched and contemptible on account of my crimes, I cannot attain to so great an honour.’

“The king said: ‘You are shrewd, and clearly perceive that you ought rightly to confess yourself a sinner. Yet I have made a fixed determination concerning you, and I shall not withdraw what I have ordained: either you must accept the bishopric, or present another to become bishop in your stead.’

“Delighted on hearing this, Samson said: ‘Now, my lord king, you have spoken excellently, and, with God’s help, you will find me ready to undertake this business. In your chapel there is a poor cleric, but noble-born and well-conducted [Col. 0436B]: entrust the episcopate to him in the fear of God, for he is worthy, I think, of such honour.’

“When the king asked who he was, Samson replied: ‘He is called Hoel, and is a Breton by birth; but he is humble and truly a good man.’

“At once, by the king’s command, Hoel was summoned, still unaware why he had been called. When the king saw the young man, lean and clothed humbly, he despised him; turning to Samson, he said: ‘Is this the man whom you recommend so highly?’

“Samson replied: ‘Indeed, lord. Without hesitation I faithfully commend this man; I rightly prefer him to myself and to men like myself. He is gentle and kindly, and therefore the more worthy of the episcopate. Let not the leanness of his body make him contemptible. His humble dress makes him more pleasing to the wise. God does not look only upon outward things, but beholds what lies hidden within.’

“The prudent king listened attentively to the wise man’s words and began to examine them shrewdly. Recalling his scattered thoughts to himself, he gradually restrained them by the bond of reason; he immediately summoned the cleric who had been named and entrusted to him the care and temporal jurisdiction [Col. 0436C] of the bishopric of Le Mans.
