The king’s decree was made known to the clergy, and the testimony to the good life of the aforesaid cleric was discussed by those who knew him. For so pure and straightforward an election, the faithful rendered devout praise to God; and the bishop-elect was honourably conducted to the folds of his sheep by bishops and the other faithful, to whom this had been commanded by the king.

“But he was no less astonished at so sudden an elevation to the episcopate than David was when, after his first-born brothers had been rejected by Samuel, he was raised to the kingship. Thus Hoel became bishop of Le Mans, and for fifteen years he discharged the episcopal office holily. He began to build the episcopal basilica in which rests the body of Saint Julian the Confessor, first bishop of Le Mans, and other good works necessary for the Church of God; and, as opportunity allowed, he diligently sought to complete what he had begun.”

Baronius maintains that this letter was written to Hoel in 1095, no. 23—the year in which Hoel himself celebrated the elevation of the sacred relics of Saint Julian—and that he died late that year, or in the course of the next [Col. 0436D], as may be inferred from Orderic in the passage cited above.

## ON LETTER XXIII

To Guy, the king’s steward. Baronius, under the year 1095, no. 13, calls him William; Juretus likewise acknowledges this, while writing that it had previously been printed as “William.” The error may have arisen from manuscripts which, without giving the name in full, present only its first letter, W: some interpreted it as Wido [Guy], others as Willelmus [William]. Thus each has played with the letters according to his own opinion.

I would support this opinion, since William of Garland succeeded his brother Anselm in this office. Thus the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Morigny*, Book II: “King Louis of the Franks also, and his wife Adelaïs, and William the steward, who is called seneschal.” Orderic, in Book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, calls this man “commander of the French soldiery” [Col. 0437A]. Yet the chronology of Ivo’s episcopate opposes this view. From 1090, when he began, until 1115, when Ivo died, I find no William placed over the royal household. For that William of Garland mentioned above succeeded to the dignity of his brother Anselm only in 1118, the third year after Ivo’s death; after him came Stephen, likewise their brother, as we shall say on Letter 87.

I therefore judge that “Guy” should more correctly be read. Guy called the Red, lord of Rochefort-en-Yvelines, held that dignity under Philip I and Louis the Fat, kings of the Franks, until 1110. In the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, fol. 76, I then first find Anselm of Garland, in a charter of that same King Louis concerning the serfs of Saint Martin, called steward. No one who has read even a little of the deeds of Louis the Fat written by Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, can deny that Guy was steward at that time:

“He adds,” says Suger, “that Guy of Rochefort, an experienced man and veteran knight, uncle of the aforesaid Guy of Trussel, having returned from the expedition to Jerusalem in renown and abundance, attached himself gladly to King Philip. Because through an old familiarity he had already on a previous occasion been his steward, both the king himself and his son Lord Louis placed him as steward over the conduct of public affairs.” And shortly afterwards: “For in the same tower was the wife of the aforesaid Guy, betrothed to his son Lord Louis; when this had reached the ears of Guy the steward,” etc. [Col. 0437B]

Since, then, we see Guy—or Wido—as steward, and Baronius agrees in the passage cited, no. 17, and the time fits, it is clear that Ivo wrote to this Guy. But the year is more uncertain, unless, with Baronius, we consider it written in 1095, near the end of the year, after the Council of Clermont and before Guy undertook the journey to Jerusalem.

## ON LETTER XXIV

I have nothing to say in illustration of this letter except that Baronius has informed me that it was written in 1094 [Col. 0437C]. See his no. 5.

## ON LETTER XXV

Baronius maintains that it was written in 1094, nos. 23 and 24. I would date it 1095. For if, as he himself relates, Letter 20 was written in the same year, no. 21, and in this letter Ivo says that he had resolved to go to Pope Urban II in order to relieve his daily crosses, and that he fought daily with beasts—words which sufficiently indicate the injuries inflicted upon him by Hugh of Puteaux, both upon himself and upon the property of the Church which Hugh plundered—who does not see that this letter was written only after those harassments had been received?

## ON LETTER XXVI

To Welfer, abbot of the monastery of Fossatus. “Welfer” is more correct, as certain manuscripts at the monastery of Fossatus have it, and as he is called in the series of the abbots of Fossatus. The monastery of Fossatus was founded in the castle of the Bagaudae on the River Marne [Col. 0437D], around A.D. 650, formerly by Saint Baubolenus, disciple of Saint Columbanus, through the agency of Bledegisilus, deacon of the Church of Paris, with King Clovis II supplying the expenses. It has now been secularized and united to the bishopric of Paris. The year in which this letter was written is not clear.

## ON LETTER XXVII

To Eudo, steward of Normandy. According to Orderic Vitalis, Book III, he was the son of Toustain, surnamed Halduc, and was eminent among the magnates of Normandy in wealth and power in the district of the Cotentin.

The heresy of the neophytes. It is the same as that of the Nicolaitans, which flourished especially in that century, as is plain from Ivo’s Letter 149. The doctrine of the Nicolaitans was that clerics of every rank might be united in marriage, as appears from Letter 6 of Book I of Saint Peter Damian, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Ostia, addressed to Pope Nicholas II. But the same author expresses it better in Baronius, vol. XI, under the year 1059, no. 46:

“Nicolaitans are clerics who have intercourse with women contrary to the rule of ecclesiastical chastity. They become fornicators when they enter into the unions of shameful commerce; they are rightly called Nicolaitans when they disseminate this deadly plague as though by authority. For vice is turned into heresy when it is established by the assertion of a perverse doctrine.” [Col. 0438A]

That the Nicolaitans and the neophytes are the same, I prove from Orderic Vitalis, who speaks of them thus in Book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*:

“For after the arrival of the Northmen, the chastity of the clergy in Neustria was so utterly dissolved that not only priests but even bishops freely used the beds of concubines and openly boasted of the numerous offspring of sons and daughters. This practice became established in the time of the neophytes who were baptized with Rollo and violently occupied the desolated country, equipped not with letters but with arms. Thereafter priests descended from the Danish stock, only slightly instructed in letters, held parishes; bearing arms, they defended a lay fief through military service. At last Bruno of Lorraine, bishop of Toul, was summoned to Rome and, by God’s dispensation, became Pope Leo, etc. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1049, he came into Gaul and dedicated the church of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, on the Kalends of October, etc. There he held a general council and, among the other beneficial ordinances he established for the Church, forbade priests to bear arms and to have wives. Thereupon the deadly custom gradually began to be emptied out. Priests gladly ceased to bear arms, indeed, but they still refuse to abstain from concubines.” [Col. 0438B]

Vitalis was writing in Ivo’s time. They were called Nicolaitans—though improperly—from Nicholas, one of the seven deacons, whom the book of Revelation mentions; and Neophytes because their heresy had begun with those newly baptized and still unformed in the faith.

I conjecture that this letter was written in 1094, or not long afterwards, from what it contains near its conclusion: namely, that in November he was with Pope Urban, whom he certainly means by the words, “the pope himself concerning whom you asked,” and that in January he left the same pope there, where Urban was still staying and, so far as God granted him strength, struggling against the adversaries of the Roman Church. From what Baronius reports from Berthold, an eyewitness, under no. 1, it may be inferred that this occurred in that year. [Col. 0438C]

## ON LETTER XXVIII

“That I might meet you at Pont-Saint-Maxence or Montchauvet, with a force of soldiers, on the day which you had appointed.” The whole cause of this military levy is read in Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, under the year 1094:

“Then a great war arose between William of Breteuil and Ascelin Goel, on the following occasion. William, the knightly brother of the young Goel, committed an outrage against a woman near Pacy. When she complained, William of Breteuil, as befitted a just ruler, exacted lawful justice from the contumacious young man. Ascelin therefore became angry with his lord because he compelled his brother to answer publicly at law. Not long afterward, by ingenious fraud, he stole from him the castle of Ivry and delivered it to Robert, duke of the Normans; Robert redeemed it from him for a great weight of silver. Afterwards a savage feud burned between them over this theft, and each desired to harm the other.

“In February, Ascelin enlisted Richard of Montfort and the household of King Philip; he boldly received, defeated, and captured his lord William as William came against him to battle, and routed his army, taking certain knights captive, etc. In the following year, William, driven by unrest, renewed the war and placed his soldiers in a fortification at the monastery of monks which Roger of Ivry had built in honour of Saint Mary. Goel, who held the castle, gathered a force of soldiers and approached the monastery, which had then, alas, become a den of robbers. In the heat of summer, around Pentecost, he attacked it fiercely, set fire to it, and consumed with devouring flames the basilica and the monks’ buildings with their furnishings, etc. [Col. 0439A]

“William of Breteuil barely escaped by flight and strove with all his might for vengeance for such injuries. The wealthy lord, inwardly pierced by excessive grief, was angered that his own man should rage against him with such force; and Goel’s strength was increased beyond measure for three years by ransoms from captives and the plundering of peasants. At last William contracted with Philip, king of the Franks, for seven hundred pounds, and promised great sums to Robert, duke of the Normans, and many others, if they would faithfully assist him and subdue the hostile forces. Therefore, during Lent, the king of France and the duke of the Normans besieged Bréval, and laboured there for nearly two months. Priests brought banners with their parishioners, and abbots were compelled to assemble with their men,” etc. [Col. 0439B]

Ivo, though summoned there, did not attend, for the reasons he gives. At that time, and long afterwards, bishops and abbots were bound to follow the king to war with an armed company of soldiers, as is clear from the authorities cited by Juretus in his notes on this letter and from what Sirmond has in the *Councils of Gaul*. From this I think that Ivo sent this letter to Philip at the turn of the year 1096.

## ON LETTER XXX

To Fulk, bishop of Beauvais. He was the son of Lancelin of Beauvais, raised from being a monk of Bec to episcopal mitres, although Anselm, his abbot, opposed him. In the ninth of his letters, Anselm writes to him in 1094, when Anselm himself had been summoned to the primacy of Canterbury in Great Britain and was near consecration. This occurred in the same year on the Sunday on which the Church sings *Populus Sion*, that is, the Second Sunday of Advent, as appears from Anselm’s letter to Geoffrey, bishop of Paris. Ivo sent his own letter to Fulk at the same time.

Since Fulk was accused of various crimes before Pope Urban, as appears from a letter addressed to him by Urban himself, which may be read in Louvet, Book IV of the *History of Beauvais*, chapter 21, he considered renouncing his benefice; with the pope’s support, at Anselm’s request, he resigned it to Roger, his successor.

## ON LETTER XXXIII

To Lambert, bishop of Arras. The Churches of Cambrai and Arras had long been united; under this bishop they were separated in 1094, according to George Colvenier in the list of bishops of Cambrai prefixed to the *Chronicle of Cambrai and Arras*; or in 1095, according to James de Meyer, *Annals of Flanders*, Book IV, at its very beginning, where he writes:

“1095. Urban II, hostile to the people of Cambrai because they had supported Emperor Henry, the rebel against the Church, and had stirred up a party against the godly, removed Arras from their city and set over it a bishop of its own, Lambert, archdeacon of Thérouanne.” [Col. 0439D]

Ferreolus Locrius, in the *Belgian Chronicle* under the same year, 1094, explains the separation of these Churches more fully:

“In the year 1094, while the people of Cambrai were disputing in various ways about the appointment of a bishop after the death of Gerard II, Pope Urban II, hostile to them because they favoured Henry IV, emperor and proscribed enemy of the Roman Church, granted the people of Arras a bishop of their own, sending them this decree:

“Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“‘The Church of Arras,’” etc. See Urban II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLI.

Molanus, *On the Feasts of the Saints*, 5 February; Sigebert; Iperius; the records of the Church of Arras; etc. Locrius immediately adds:

“In the year 1095, Lambert, a native of Guînes, cantor at Saint Peter’s in Lille and archdeacon of Thérouanne, a man of distinguished learning and virtue, was appointed—though unwillingly—as first bishop of the Church of Arras since its separation from Cambrai; summoned to Rome by the supreme pontiff, he was consecrated with very solemn pomp and made legate of the entire province of Rheims. Then, having received various privileges from that same pontiff, he proceeded to govern the flock committed to him; dividing the parishes of his city, he most abundantly satisfied the wishes of all,” etc. [Col. 0440A]

He continues these matters at greater length, not unworthy of being seen or known. From the foregoing, however, it follows that this letter was written after the year 1095.

## ON LETTER XXXV

I observe nothing concerning this letter except that Baronius, under the year 1095, no. 14, says it was written then. I do not deny it, since in that year I find in Locrius that a council of Rheims, mentioned by Ivo in the heading of the letter, was held on the Sunday on which *Oculi mei* is sung—that is, the Fourth Sunday of Lent—with Archbishop Renaud presiding with his suffragans. [Col. 0440B]

## ON LETTER XXXVI

To Peter, bishop of Poitiers. He was Peter II of that name, elected in 1086. During his episcopate at Poitiers, numerous complaints arose against the Cluniac monks, who coveted almost every benefice and strove to claim for themselves every rich priestly office. The monks of Saint Peter of Chartres brought a case against them concerning Saint-Denis of Nogent, recently founded by Rotrou, count of the Perche, at the Council of Autun—which Berthold says was held in 1094 by Hugh of Lyons, Urban’s legate—but did not prevail, as appears in the cartulary of that monastery.

Geoffrey the Fat, in the *Life of Blessed Bernard, First Abbot of Tiron*, sections 24 and 28, a contemporary of this Peter of Poitiers, writes that Bernard was sued by the Cluniacs over the Church of Saint Cyprian at Poitiers, over which he presided with Peter’s approval; they claimed that it ought to be subject to their authority. Since this author has not yet appeared in print complete, I shall set down what he reported concerning that dispute:

“Bernard therefore,” he says, “resuming his labour anew, lest he succumb to blows of graver fortune, feared that he would sin if through his own sloth or negligence the monastery of Saint Cyprian should lose its liberty. Coming again to Rome, he asked the aforesaid pope, Paschal II, to examine attentively the cases of both sides and render a just judgment. Avoiding this, Paschal commanded him either to subject the church to the Cluniacs or never again to exercise the office of abbot there. [Col. 0440C]

“After the man of God had certainly learned that he would make no progress in the Roman court and would not turn the apostolic pontiff from his decision, he was compelled to appeal to the hearing of a higher court. Although this cannot be found in mortal tribunals, Bernard was not ignorant from whom it ought to be sought. Thus, inflamed by zeal for justice and following Solomon’s saying, ‘The righteous man shall be as bold as a lion, without terror,’ he firmly declared to the lord pope and all his accomplices in this matter—not with presumptuous audacity but with free magnanimity—that at the judgment of the last day they would stand before the Judge of judges, who is deceived by no darkness of ignorance and knows no corruption by gifts.

“Having heard such freedom of speech, the pope in indignation ordered the man of God to leave him. Then he consulted his advisers about what ought to be done in the matter. They unanimously replied that it was unsafe to dispute with a man of such holiness concerning the controversy of this cause before the Judge of all; nor would they in any way consent to take part in any dispute against him. Indeed, by common judgment they declared it just that his dignity should be restored to him and that forgiveness should be sought from him for the labour and injury inflicted.

“John and Benedict, two cardinals present there, publicly proclaimed before the pope magnificent testimonies to Bernard’s virtues, which they had known in Aquitaine. They declared to the Romans that he was now such a man as they themselves had seen at the Council of Poitiers, where he had been ready to suffer martyrdom for justice. [Col. 0441A]

“When the apostolic pontiff learned the perfection of so great a man, he restrained his anger and ordered Bernard to return to the council. Once he had entered, he gave him leave to speak for himself and imposed silence so that he might be heard more freely by all. The man of God began thus:

“‘Most reverend pope, I beg the excellence of your high office to endure for a little while the few words which I am about to speak, words not departing from the truth. Your fatherhood, and very many men who sit in this sacred assembly—men highly honourable by reason of their life and wisdom—know, as they have known in previous years, that the Church of Saint Cyprian, committed to the governance of our littleness, flourished in great religious observance, enjoying its liberty through the course of many years, before the monastery of Cluny even began to exist. But now the abbot of Cluny, in accordance with Isaiah’s prophecy, does not cease to neigh after my wife; and over me, an abbot however insignificant, he seeks to exercise mastery like an arch-abbot with proud tyranny. He strives to make our Church serve him as a handmaid, while his own reigns and rules. This new and unheard-of form of ambition—for it takes its beginning from him—unless cut off at the root of its stock, will send forth a large progeny of poisonous offspring; and, if permitted to arise, a seed-bed of immense corruption will grow up,’ etc.” [Col. 0441B]

Having eloquently delivered these things, the holy man fell silent. The apostolic pontiff then commanded the advocates of the Cluniac monks’ cause to speak. But since they could discover no arguments, having no solid foundation of truth, by which they could show that the Church of Saint Cyprian ought to be subject to their laws, they began, through veiled detours full of ambitious circumlocutions, to fabricate certain assertions. When the assembly present understood that these wholly contradicted the rules of justice, it declared the monastery of Saint Cyprian free from them. Confirming this judgment, the apostolic pontiff restored to the holy man the office of abbot which he had forbidden him to exercise, and earnestly sought from him acceptance of the dignity of cardinal-priest and permanent residence at Rome, where he might securely handle ecclesiastical cases. [Col. 0441C]

Orderic Vitalis, Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, agrees with this account in these words:

“About this time Bernard, abbot of Quinciacum—that is, Saint Cyprian—left the territory of Poitiers, because he refused to subject the aforesaid monastery, which until then had been free, to Cluny. And because, as it is written, ‘the righteous is bold as a lion,’ he pleaded before Paschal the pope in the Roman synod for liberty; and because Paschal had not given him full justice, he summoned him to the divine judgment. The pope feared his formidable resolve and begged him to remain with him under the protection of the Roman Church.”

As for Peter, I find this eulogy of him in the aforesaid Geoffrey:

“While these things were taking place, the bishopric of the city of Poitiers was governed by the venerable Bishop Peter, who afterwards endured exile for justice until death. The holiness of his life was remarkable, as became evident after his death through the testimony of miracles.” [Col. 0441D]

I judge that the letter was written in 1094, when Peter was alive.

## ON LETTER XXXVIII

To Gauscelin. According to Roger of Howden, he died on Sunday, the Nones of January, in the year 1098. Therefore this letter may be asserted to have been written before that year.

## ON LETTER XXXIX

To Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of England, to whom Ivo wrote this letter immediately after his installation.

To the monks of Bec against the Molesme monks. I am wholly ignorant what this dispute was, unless perhaps it concerned certain *parceries* situated in the archdeaconry of Pacy, belonging to the monastery of Bec, about which a controversy may have arisen between them. It cannot easily be inferred from this letter, any more than from the preceding one.

At that time the monasteries of Bec and Molesme flourished in renown: Molesme, in Champagne and the diocese of Langres, had been founded by Robert, monk of the Cell in the island of Germany, in the diocese of Troyes; Bec, in the diocese of Rouen, was founded in 1034 by Herluin, whose name it bore and was therefore called Herluin’s Bec. On these, see William of Jumièges, Book VI of the *History of the Normans*, chapter 9, and Orderic Vitalis, Books III, V, and VIII, pp. 460, 549, and 711. [Col. 0442A]

## ON LETTER XL

To Brother Manegold. Saint Juretus’s conjecture is correct. This letter could have been written in 1096 to Manegold of Lautenbach, provost of the congregation of Marbach. Münster writes of him thus in Book III of his *Germany*:

“At a distance of half a mile from Murbach is situated the community of Lautenbach, which was once a Benedictine monastery founded by a certain count of Lenzburg, who also founded the monastery of Erstein around the year of Christ 998. Then, in 1090, the monastery of Marbach was founded by Lord Burkhard of Gebweiler and Master Manegold of Lautenbach.”

This monastery of Marbach is situated in Lower Alsace. [Col. 0442B]

## ON LETTER XLI

To Geoffrey, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme. Sirmond made him known in his notes on Geoffrey’s letters. Geoffrey sent several letters to Ivo, which are read in Book II, but I find none relevant to the present purpose. The monastery of Vendôme lies in the diocese of Chartres. It was founded in 1040 by Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou, and his wife Agnes; its abbots are distinguished by the purple and the title of Saint Prisca. On this matter we have written elsewhere. The year in which this letter was written can scarcely be known.

## ON LETTER XLII

To Hugh, bishop by the grace of God. From the records of the Church of Soissons, Hugh began to hold the see in 1090 and ceased in 1103, when, returning from Jerusalem at Aquileia, he departed this life. From this I cannot conjecture the time when the letter was written, although I can affirm that it appeared before 1100. [Col. 0442C]

## ON LETTER XLIII

William. Baronius and C. Robert, in his list of the archbishops of Paris, contradict themselves: Baronius says that the letter was written in 1093, no. 7; Robert says only in 1097, and I follow him. For if this William was elected in the latter year, how could the letter have been written in 1093?

He was a canon of Chartres, son of Amalric, count of Montfort, and brother of Bertrada, concubine of Philip I, king of the Franks, as is clear from the following Letter 54. Robert, however, maintains that he was a child of Humbert, count of Maurienne, and brother of Adelaïde, wife of Louis the Fat. This certainly cannot agree with what Ivo says in that letter, since the canons of Paris expressly state that they did not elect William “because his sister had cohabitation with the king,” etc. This cannot be understood of Adelaïde, wife of Louis the Fat, since *contubernium* denotes not lawful marriage but concubinage only.

I add that William was elected only in 1096, as may be inferred from the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, fol. 37, charter 79, and fol. 87, charter “On the Altars of Montmartre.” For there the year 1098 is stated in the dating clause to be the third year of William’s episcopate. Finally, Louis married Adelaïde only in 1114, as the same cartulary proves: at fol. 78, the year 1116 is called the second year of Queen Adelaïde, and William was no longer alive in that year. For, dying in 1102 or thereabouts, he had left his dignity to Fulk, dean of Paris. [Col. 0442D]

## ON LETTER XLIV

This may be called not so much a letter as a pontifical edict, by which Ivo exhorts his diocesan flock to peace. At the Council of Clermont, to which our bishop subscribed, it had been decreed in canon 1:

“That monks, clerics, women, and those who were with them should remain in peace every day; but that on three days—namely, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday—an injury inflicted by anyone upon another should not be reckoned a breach of the peace; whereas on the four remaining days, if anyone inflicted injury upon another, he should be held guilty of breaking the holy peace and should be punished as prescribed.”

This decree was made for the benefit of those who either set out for the Holy Land to free it from the yoke of the unbelievers, or at least contributed something of their resources to that cause. Tyre writes of that peace in Book I, chapter 15, of his *History*, speaking of Pope Urban II:

“Having said this, he ended his address, commanding the prelates of the Churches who were present that, once returned home, they should with every earnestness and due diligence exhort and invite their peoples to the same undertaking.” And shortly afterwards: “Before all else, labouring faithfully according to the statutes of the synod, that the peace commonly called the Truce might be observed inviolate by all, lest any obstacle be placed in the way of those wishing to go, or to travel about for necessities.” [Col. 0443A–B]

This agrees with the decree of Pope Alexander III found in the *Extravagants*, “On Truce and Peace,” chapter *Treugas et innovamus*, and canons *Si quis Romipetas* and *Illi qui peregrinos*, 24, question 3, which accord with Ivo’s words. According to Ralph Glaber, Book V of his *History*, this statute or pact was first issued in Aquitaine in the year of the Lord 1041, and afterwards confirmed throughout Gaul, as we shall say below on Letter 168. I therefore judge that this decree was published in 1095 or 1096, after the Council of Clermont.

## ON LETTER XLV

To the count of Meulan: namely Robert, son of Roger, lord of Beaumont, and Adeline, daughter of Waleran, count of Meulan, who obtained the county of Meulan after his uncle Hugh. I learn this from the *Book of the Deeds of William, Duke of Normandy* and from William of Jumièges, Book VII of the *History of the Normans*, chapter 4. One of them mentions him in these words:

“A certain young Norman, Robert, son of Roger of Beaumont, nephew and heir of Hugh, count of Meulan,” etc.

The other, writing of Roger, says:

“He took as wife Adeline, daughter of Waleran, count of Meulan, by whom he begot two sons, Robert and Henry, counts afterwards of great power. Robert indeed flourished as count of Meulan for more than twenty-seven years after his uncle Hugh.”

Orderic Vitalis has the same in Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 709:

“Robert possessed by hereditary right the county of Meulan in the Vexin after Hugh, brother of his mother Adeline; and in England he happily obtained, by the gift of King Henry, the county of Leicester, with many others and great treasures.”

This Robert took as wife Elizabeth, daughter of Hugh the Great, third son of Henry I, king of the Franks, and of Adelaïs, countess of Vermandois, despite Ivo’s opposition. Orderic, in Books IX and XI of his *History*, the latter at p. 805, speaks of their marriage thus:

“He also had as wife the beautiful Isabel, niece of the king of France; she bore him twin offspring, Waleran and Robert, and Hugh surnamed the Poor, and five daughters.” [Col. 0444B]

William of Jumièges agrees, Book VIII, chapter 40:

“In the same year”—that is, 1096, when this letter was written—“Hugh, count of Crépy, entrusted his land to his sons Ralph and Henry, and gave his daughter Isabel to Robert, count of Meulan; setting out abroad, that is, for Jerusalem, he led with him a noble company of Frenchmen.”

Their consanguinity. Ivo omitted one degree in the enumeration of this genealogy, carrying the betrothed pair’s relationship from the fourth to the fifth degree, whereas both stood at the same degree—namely, the fifth—from the common stock. Their kinship should be set out thus:

Walter, called the White, by Adelaïde, lady of Crépy, begot:

Ralph, count of Crépy, who by the daughter of Gilbert, count of Breteuil, had another

Ralph, count of Crépy, by whom and by Eleanor, his first wife, was born

Alicia, wife of Herbert, count of Vermandois, who bore another

Alicia, who married Hugh the Great and by him, among other children, bore

Elizabeth, betrothed to Robert of Meulan.

N., wife of Robert, count of Meulan, who bore her husband Adeline or Helen.

Adeline or Helen, wife of Hugh, lord of Montfort in Neustria, who bore him:

Robert, who died without issue;

Hugh, who died childless;

Waleran, who by his wife Oda begot

Adeline, wife of Roger of Beaumont, and Hugh; Adeline bore

Robert and Henry, of whom the former married Elizabeth.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] He is called Waleran in the Cartulary of Colombs.]

[Col. 0443C] This is their true genealogy, as may be seen in Nicholas d’Avanne, *Life of Saint Nicasius*, chapters 54 and 55; Adrian Morlerius, in the genealogical tables placed after the *Antiquities of Amiens*; and others who have written on the counts of Vermandois.

“Having exceeded the seventh degree.” Ivo speaks according to the ancient canons: 35, question 2, *On Affinity*, *Nullum*, *Progeniem*, *Nulli*; question 4, *Consanguinitas*; and question 5, *Ad sedem apostolicam*, and those following.

## ON LETTER XLVI

According to Baronius, the letter was written in 1095, no. 9. I think rather that it was sent in the following year. From the matters Ivo alleges, it is more than sufficiently clear that it was written only after the pope had forbidden Philip’s intercourse with Bertrada at the Council of Clermont—which Baronius himself acknowledges was held on the eighteenth day of November that year—unless it was published immediately after the synod had been held.

## ON LETTER XLVII
Ebrard, your nephew. He means Ebrard, son of Hugh of Le Puiset [Col. 0444C], nephew through his sister of Guy of Rochefort, to [Col. 0444D] whom Ivo writes. Thus Aimoin’s continuator, *De gestis Francorum*, book V, ch. 46, speaks of them:

> “Theobald, surnamed *filans stupa* (‘spinner of tow’), forester of King Robert, fortified Mont-Lhéry. He had one son, named Guy, who took as wife the lady of La Ferté and of Gometz. By her this Guy begot Miles of Bray and Guy the Red; also the countess of Rochefort, Bonnevoisine of Ponts, Elizabeth likewise, wife of Joscelin of Courtenay, and moreover the lady of Le Puiset,” etc.

The cartulary of Saint-Martin of the Fields, fol. 109v, however, states that Ebrard was the son of Hugh of Le Puiset and his wife Agnes. From this it follows that he was also Guy’s nephew. Among those who set out for Jerusalem in 1096, Ebrard of Le Puiset is listed by William of Tyre, book I of the *History of the Holy War*, ch. 17; and after the beginning of book II of the chronicle of the monastery of Maurigny occur these words:

> “He bought it—namely Philip I, king of the Franks [Col. 0445A]—from Ebrard, upon whose fief it depended, who was accounted lord of Le Puiset and was setting out for Jerusalem.”

The letter, moreover, was written in the same year as the preceding one.

## ON LETTER XLVIII

“Your former mother, the metropolitan church of Reims.” For Urban II, before being raised to the supreme dignity of the Church, had been a canon of Reims, according to the Life of St Bruno in the Reims breviary.

Manasses. This was Manasses II, whom Robert, in his list of the bishops of Reims, states to have been a kinsman of Urban, being descended from the family of Châtillon. According to that same Robert, he was elected in 1096, the year in which this letter may also have been written, since Ivo requests confirmation of that election.

## ON LETTER XLIX

“To Count Stephen Palatine.” He also possessed the counties of Chartres and Blois. He was called count palatine, or of the palace, because in the king’s palace [Col. 0445B] he held precedence over the king’s table-companions, or was distinguished among them. In this letter Ivo treats of the immunity of the cloister of the church of Chartres. On that account many disputes and quarrels arose between the bishop and the clergy of the principal church on the one hand, and the counts of Chartres on the other. This letter was written before the count first undertook his journey to Jerusalem, which occurred in September 1096, according to Fulcher of Chartres, chaplain to Baldwin, brother of Godfrey of Lorraine, who was present in the count’s company, in his book *On the Deeds of the Frankish Pilgrims*, etc., and according to other writers of the period.

“Concerning the assurance for which you have summoned me.” By “assurance” he means the oath or sworn undertaking which the bishops of Chartres customarily make to the counts of that city at the altar of St Candidus, in the tower or palace of the counts, upon their first arrival or entrance into the city. By it new bishops declare that they will do nothing whereby the county may be lost.

## ON LETTER L

[Col. 0445C]

Picueris. More correctly, *Pitiveris*: a town of the Wastine district, or rather of Upper Beauce, commonly called Pluviers, Piviers, and Pitiviers.

“That they elected William bishop there.” He was discussed above in the commentary on Letter 43, from which it is clear that he had formerly been a member of the church of Chartres. This letter was written about 1097 or 1098.

## ON LETTER LI

Sanctio. From dean of Orléans he became bishop about 1099. With the permission of the metropolitan of Sens, he was consecrated at the castle of Nanton by Ivo of Chartres, William of Paris, and Walter of Meaux, notwithstanding the opposition of the party which favoured John the archdeacon, who was seeking the bishopric of Orléans. Yet he scarcely occupied the see for a full year before, through the contrivance of that John, he was overthrown and expelled by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See. So write Senertius in his list of the bishops of Orléans; Sausseius, *Annals of Orléans*, book IX, no. 9 ff.; and Symphorianus Guy, *Chronological History of the Bishops of Orléans*, no. 63, under “Following.” Letter 54, which is wholly concerned with Sanctio’s promotion to the episcopate, follows. No one can doubt that this letter was written in 1099, since his episcopate both began and ended in that year.

## ON LETTER LV

“The bishop-elect of Beauvais.” That is, Anselm, who, according to Louvet, *History of Beauvais*, book IV, ch. 2, and Robert in his list of the bishops of Beauvais, no. 49, was elected in this year, 1099. Baronius also attests that this letter was written in that year, and I do not dispute him.

## ON LETTER LVI

“Two councils.” Namely, those of Clermont, or Auvergne, and Tours, held in Gaul in the same year; the council of Piacenza is irrelevant. This is according to Baronius himself, under the year 1095, no. 53, who assigns this letter to that year.

## ON LETTER LVII

“Concerning that brother who, fleeing from you three times, had three times been received according to the constitution of the monastic rule.” Not only in the Rule of St Benedict, ch. 29, but also in those of other holy Fathers—such as Pachomius, article 9; Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, ch. 20; the Master, ch. 64; and similar rules—it is said that monks who flee and return are to be received. Yet they disagree over the number. St Benedict, together with the Master, judges that they are to be received only up to the third time. St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, supports them in the letter he writes to Peter, abbot of Cluny:

> “If a brother frequently goes out from the monastery, when he returns, up to the third time, let him be received again; thereafter let him no longer be received. For such is a man’s fidelity in divine service, as God recognizes it, as is the steadfastness of his feet among men.”

Peter the Venerable, book I, letter 18, agrees with our Ivo, considering that a fugitive monk should be admitted to the monastery as often as he returns repentant, in accordance with the sentence of Christ the Lord, who commands that enemies be forgiven seventy times seven—that is, whenever they ask pardon. Our Peter of Blois asserts the same, letter 88, which he wrote in the name of Richard, primate of Canterbury, to the abbot of Thérouanne:

> “He asks mercy devoutly and humbly; he offers himself for every satisfaction in accordance with the Rule of St Benedict; he does not exclude judgment from mercy. The mercy which the founder of the monastic order restricted to the number three, the gentleness of evangelical grace has extended to seventy times seven.”

The members of the Society of Jesus do not readmit anyone who has departed or been dismissed from their congregation and is afterwards brought back or returns voluntarily, as is clear from the rules of the Provincial, ch. 5, no. 46, and the final rule, because such persons are rarely found fit for the discipline of their institute.

[Col. 0446C]

“But because of the sacrilege which he had committed.” Perhaps he had retained certain goods of the monastery and made them his own. This is especially forbidden to a monk because of the vice of private ownership, prohibited to all ascetics. Thus St Benedict says in Rule, ch. 33:

> “Above all, this vice must be cut out by the roots from the monastery: no one is to presume to give or receive anything without the abbot’s permission, nor to possess anything as his own—absolutely no thing,” etc. “If anyone is found to delight in this most wicked vice and, after being admonished once and twice, does not amend, he is to undergo correction.”

In the Rule of St Fructuosus, ch. 8, private ownership is also called an abomination:

> “Private ownership, whether in utensils, clothing, or even any very cheap and contemptible things whatsoever, must by every means be avoided; for it is an abomination to monks to possess any superfluous thing of disreputable kind, or to reserve as one’s own, or secretly, anything which is not far removed from the example of Ananias and Sapphira.”

This is the view of St Augustine, Sermon 27, *On the Words of the Apostle*, where, speaking of Ananias, he says:

> “When he withheld part of what he had promised, he was condemned for sacrilege and fraud: for sacrilege, because he had deceived God in his promise; for fraud, because he thought that some portion might be withheld from gifts which ought to have been entire.”

Chrysostom follows him in Homily 12 on Acts:

> “Why did you do this?”—he addresses Ananias. “Did you wish to possess it? You ought to have possessed it from the beginning and not promised it; but now, after you have consecrated it, you have committed a greater sacrilege.”

Oecumenius takes the same view when he calls the sin of Ananias sacrilege. So do Arator, book I on Acts; Bede, Hugh, and Lyra on Acts ch. 5; indeed Theodore Beza too, commenting on this chapter, no. 2:

> “When Ananias and Sapphira had consecrated this estate to the Lord, they afterwards, by sacrilege, set aside part of the price so that it might not come before the Church; [Col. 0447A] yet they concealed this, so that distrust and hypocrisy were added to sacrilege.”

Therefore monks who suffer from the vice of private ownership are truly guilty of sacrilege: both because they appropriate the resources of the monastery, which belong to God, who left to their superiors only the use in fact, not in law, and a beneficial, not absolute, ownership; and because, having vowed poverty, they become deserters from their vow through private possession. The penalty awaiting monks or cenobites devoted to private ownership is stated both by Ivo in this letter and by the chapter *Cum ad monasterium*, *On the State of Monks*: they are to be separated from the others at death and are not to share a common burial-place with the other brethren.

This was provided by the English council held at London in 1075 under Lanfranc, archbishop of the church of Dorobernia, or Canterbury:

> “From the Rule of Blessed Benedict, the Dialogue of Gregory, and the ancient custom of regular houses, that monks may maintain their proper order,” etc. “But if anyone is found at death to possess anything of his own without the aforesaid permission, and before death has not restored it, confessing his sin with penitence and sorrow, no bells shall be rung for him, no saving sacrifice shall be offered for his absolution, nor shall he be buried in the cemetery.”

Indeed, if he has already been granted burial, the canons command that he be dug up and thrown upon the dung-heap. Thus the previously cited chapter *Cum ad monasterium*, §2:

> “If private property is found with anyone at death, it is buried with him outside the monastery in a dung-heap as a sign of perdition, according to what Blessed Gregory relates that he did in the *Dialogue,”*

namely book IV, ch. 56. And this is to be done provided it can be done without scandal, as appears from the chapter *Super quodam* under the same title. Therefore, according to the counsel of Blessed Leander, *On the Instruction of Virgins*, ch. 18, a monk should avoid the evil of such great wickedness as a precipice into Gehenna and a path leading, as it were, to hell. See John of Torquemada on the Rule of St Benedict, ch. 97. In what year this letter [Col. 0447C] was written is unknown.

## ON LETTER LVIII

“To the congregation of St Stephen at Sens”: that is, to the college of canons of the mother church, or, as people commonly say, the chapter of the principal church, dedicated in the name of St Stephen. On the dignity of the city of Sens, read Claude Robert in his *Catalogue of Its Archbishops*.

222. “Your elect.” He means Daimbert, who, upon the death of Richer on 27 December 1096, was elected archbishop by the clergy of the church of Sens, having been archdeacon and vicedominus. Ivo consults Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, concerning his consecration in the following Letter 59; and in Letter 60 he yields to Hugh’s prohibition, so that, as he himself says, he withheld his hands from Daimbert’s consecration. Since Daimbert was elected in 1096, no one can doubt in what year this letter was written.

## ON LETTER LIX

[Col. 0447D]

“Against the craftiness of the archbishop of Tours.” This was Ralph II, who, while holding the provostship in the church of Orléans, was attempting to impose a certain John, archdeacon of that church and utterly discredited by popular report, and left no stone unturned in order to cast down Bishop Sanctio, already consecrated, from the height of the dignity he had obtained, as Letters 66 and 67 show. Since Sanctio was deposed by the fraud of the said Ralph in 1099, I suppose that this letter was written in the same year.

## ON LETTER LX

“By the men of Le Puiset.” Namely Hugh the father; Ebrard; and the other Hugh, Guy, and Waleran, sons of the same first Hugh. They had inflicted many injuries upon Ivo and upon the church of Chartres, which has many towns and possessions subject to it in Beauce: they had destroyed country buildings, consumed their crops by fire and sword, and had attempted to divert and claim for themselves the rights of the bishopric. On account of the injuries done to him and his church, Ivo himself and other bishops had barred them from the sacred rites. Ivo is angry with Hugh the legate because, without consulting him, he had restored them to communion with the Church without any satisfaction having been made for the losses he had suffered.

At the Council of Verneuil I, canon 9, one reads:

> “If anyone complains that he has been unjustly excommunicated, he shall have permission to come to the metropolitan bishop and there be judged according to canonical institution; meanwhile, he shall observe his excommunication. If anyone despises all these things and the bishop is wholly unable to correct him, he shall be condemned to exile by the king’s judgment.”

There is not a word there to the effect that he may be absolved by the metropolitan or primate; rather, it says that he must observe his excommunication. Therefore Ivo had just grounds for complaint against Hugh the legate. Baronius maintains that this letter was written in 1099, no. 4. I place it in 1096, since Hugh and Ebrard of Le Puiset undertook the journey to Jerusalem in that year and are numbered among the nobles by William of Tyre, book I, ch. 7; book II, ch. 1; and book VI, ch. 17; by Orderic Vitalis, book IX; and by Suger in his *Life of Louis the Fat*. Speaking of Hugh, son of the other Hugh, Suger says: “His father, in extraordinary pride, took up arms at the beginning of the Jerusalem journey.” We have seen concerning Ebrard above, on Letter 47; see also the following Letters 75 and 76.

## ON LETTER LXI

“According to the custom of our Church, we ought to hold a synod on 26 October.” It was decreed that synods should be held twice a year by Nicaea I, ch. 8; Antioch I, canon 18; Riez, canon 4; Orange I, canon 29; and many others, as appears in Gratian, Distinction 18, *Habeatur* and *Propter*: namely, on the calends of March and October. Although this was repealed by the Eighth Synod, in the same Distinction 18, *Quoniam quidem*, the custom was nonetheless observed in the church of Chartres of holding synods twice a year: on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday within the octave of Pentecost, by the archdeacons and chapter of Chartres; and on the Wednesday after the feast of St Luke the Evangelist. Therefore I conclude that this letter was written in 1099, because in that year the seventh day before the calends of October fell on a Wednesday, since the Dominical letter of that year was B.

“The bishop-elect of Nevers.” Namely Guy, not Hervé, nor even, as Sausseius writes, Hugh. The latter, formerly a canon of Auxerre and elected bishop of Nevers in 1103, was to be consecrated at Autun by Hugh, primate of Lyons, within his province; but Ivo opposed this, because no bishop ought to be consecrated outside his province, Distinctions 64 and 65. The former, according to Severtius in his list of the bishops of Nevers, was elected in 1097. The chronological table must therefore be understood as referring to Guy’s election, since Guy was bishop-elect in 1099; Baronius assigns this letter to him, no. 22, and I do not deny it.

## ON LETTER LXII

[Col. 0448D]

“Adelicia, lady of the castle of Le Puiset.” Wife of Hugh of Le Puiset and mother of the other Hugh, Ebrard, Guy, and Humberga, as I gather from the register of St Peter in the Valley at Chartres, fols. 103 and 109.

“Parish.” Here *parochia* is used for an entire diocese, as it often is among authors.

“Concerning the clerics or monks of Le Puiset.” Ivo means the monks of Marmoutier, to whom the cell or priory of Le Puiset belonged. Since they were exempt from episcopal correction, they made use of their privilege and refused to observe the interdict imposed by Sanctio, bishop of Orléans, in whose diocese Le Puiset was situated.

“Concerning Gervase.” He was lord of Châteauneuf-en-Thymerais in the diocese of Chartres, as appears from the following Letter 261. It is clear that Ivo wrote this in 1099, since Sanctio, to whom he sends it, obtained the bishopric of Orléans in that same year and was deprived of it in the same year.

## ON LETTER LXIII

[Col. 0449A]

I can say nothing concerning this letter except that it is certainly worthy of notice and should be read by priests and innovators, so that the former may recognize their office and the latter may learn not to usurp, to another’s prejudice, a ministry which does not concern them.

## ON LETTER LXIV

“To John, bishop-elect of Orléans.” By the contrivance of Ralph, archbishop of Tours, and of Sanctio’s rivals, he was intruded into the see of Orléans after the expulsion of his predecessor, as the year 1099 was ending. The letter too was written in that year, although an unfavourable report was circulating that he practised unnatural sexual vice. That John was another brother of Ralph is sufficiently established by what has been said, and will become clearer from Ivo’s Letters 66, 67, and 68.

## ON LETTER LXV

“The abbot of Lagny.” Lagny, in the diocese of Paris, in the archdeaconry of Brie, of the Order of St Benedict, lies between Paris and Jaigny of Meaux, on the river Marne. It had St Fursa [Col. 0449B] the Scot as its founder; Herbert, count of Champagne or Troyes, who awaits the resurrection of the dead there, as its restorer about the year 993.

## ON LETTER LXVI

“The abbot of Bourgueil.” Namely Baldric, a native of Orléans. Having entered among the monks of Bourgueil, he was elected abbot of that monastery in 1083. When he sought but did not obtain a prelacy at Bercosol [reading uncertain], he finally obtained that of Dol in 1108, as he himself acknowledges in the preface to his *History of Jerusalem*. Argentré, however, *History of Armorica*, book III, ch. 44, reports that this occurred after the death of Rodland, bishop of Dol, in 1111. Yet it is certain that immediately after Wlgrin, chancellor of the church of Chartres, who had refused to accept the election made of him, Baldric was elected.

Compare what is said on the following Letter 176. Orderic Vitalis mentions him near the end of book IX of his *Ecclesiastical History* [Col. 0449C] in these words:

> “Thus far I have followed the footsteps of the venerable Baldric,” etc. “I resolved reverently to honour this aforementioned elder, whom I knew well. He was a citizen of Orléans, monk and abbot of Bourgueil, trained in the liberal studies and venerable for the merits of his religious life. From there, on account of his religious devotion and wisdom, he was raised by ecclesiastical election to the rank of the archbishopric of Dol. In the episcopate he retained the monastic life and generally lived with monks as circumstances permitted. For he ruled the untamed Bretons, whose perversity he could not endure; hence he frequently left those lawless and insolent men and fled into Normandy, where the church of Dol had possessed, peacefully and quietly, estates on the river Risle from the time of St Samson, during the reign of Hildebert, king of the Franks. There by his writings and teaching he stirred his hearers to the worship of God; and he visited the neighbouring monasteries—namely Fécamp, Fontenelle, Jumièges, and many others—and strengthened them by sacred sermons in the fear [Col. 0449D] of God. At last he died in a good old age and was buried at Préaux, in the basilica of St Peter the Apostle, before the crucifix.”

This occurred on 7 January 1129, or perhaps 1131, according to Severtius in his list of bishops of Dol. Peter, abbot of Maillezais, also speaks thus in a letter sent to him:

> “Truly happy and beloved of God is the land of Brittany, illumined by the flashing radiance of so great a star. The East rejoices, adorned like a most glorious palm by the teaching of the apostolic Fathers; let the West likewise rejoice, marked by the titles of so great a primate. Let that fierce people lay aside, in some measure, its native savagery, hastening to the honeyed graciousness of its watchman. Let no natural foolishness be further imputed to it, now instructed by the teaching of so wise a bishop.”

He left certain writings to posterity: namely, a *History of Jerusalem*; the Life and Deeds of Robert of Arbrissel, often mentioned in these observations [Col. 0450A]; the acts of St Samson, his predecessor; and certain other works which have either perished through the injury of time or the negligence of later generations, or still lie hidden in decay and dust, feeding moths.

As for the letter, it is easy to understand from its contents that it appeared late in 1099, or at least at the beginning of 1100. Bourgueil is a Benedictine monastery in the diocese of Angers, three French leagues from Saumur, founded and richly endowed about the year of the Lord 992 by Emma, daughter of Theobald I, called count of Chartres, and wife of William, count of Poitou, as I have read in the very instrument of foundation.

## ON LETTER LXVII

“Behold, now that this seven-year period has passed.” From this I conclude that the letter was written in 1098, not 1099, as Baronius has it under that year, no. 15; for Ivo was consecrated bishop of Chartres at the end of 1090, as I prove elsewhere, and not in 1092, as Baronius and others maintain.

## ON LETTER LXIX

“To the provost of the church of Stirps.” Stirps, or St Peter of Stirps, commonly l’Estreppe, is a monastery of regular canons in the diocese of Limoges.

“The bishop of Limoges.” Perhaps William, successor to Humbald, whom Urban had removed from office; he died in the third year of his pontificate, at Genevo [reading uncertain], about 1099, perhaps the year in which this letter was written.

## ON LETTER LXX

“To the monastery of St Fara.” The monastery of Fara is commonly called Faremoutiers. It is Benedictine, in the diocese of Meaux, founded about 660 by St Fara, sister of St Faro, bishop of Meaux. I think this letter was written in the year mentioned above, while Adela’s husband was absent on account of the Holy War.

## ON LETTER LXXI

[Col. 0450C]

“To William, glorious king of the English,” called Rufus, third duke of the Normans of that name and second king of the English after his father William. Since he was inaugurated in 1088, it cannot be denied that this letter was written at least after that year and before 1100; I therefore judge that it was sent in 1099. In a manuscript codex in my possession I find the following letter sent to him by the chapter of Chartres; lest it perish, I shall set it down here:

> “G., by the grace of God king of the English: A., dean, and the canons of the church of Chartres, wish you to please him through whom kings reign. No small necessity of excellence rests upon you, if you remember the courage of your glorious and magnificent father, the king, and the wisdom of your most holy and eminent mother. Their death, as it was unbelievably harmful to humankind, so brought incredible common grief to all. Yet, by God’s grace, it is well that we have you surviving, in whom the image of paternal fortitude is represented so fully that scarcely any difference remains: not so much a likeness as the very identity of your father is expressed. We have written this to you not as beggars, but because we desire it to come to your knowledge, beseeching you to return to us love in return. Your love will not be fruitless if you bestow it upon the Church, the mother of God; for, as she deserved special love with her author and son, so she possesses exceptional power to intercede for whomever she wills. Farewell.”

This letter may indeed have been sent in 1088, immediately after his inauguration.

“Nivard of Septueil.” Orderic Vitalis, book X of the *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 767, under the year 1099, speaks of him in these words:

> “King William, together with William duke of Poitou, under the leadership of the young Amaury of Montfort and Nivard of Septueil,” etc.

Septueil is a town in the diocese of Chartres and the archdeaconry [Col. 0451A] of Poissy, commonly called Septueil. Therefore Ivo calls Nivard his parishioner because he lived in his diocese.

## ON LETTER LXXII

“To G., abbot of St Wandrille.” This was Gerard, who succeeded Lanfranc in 1091 and governed this monastery until 1125, according to Claude Robert, under Fontenelle in his *Abbeys of Gaul*. From this the year in which this letter was sent can scarcely be determined. What Ivo writes here concerning the reconsecration of altars has now become obsolete and is no longer observed, whether through custom or ignorance.

## ON LETTER LXXIII

“To Bernard, abbot of Marmoutier.” In the book *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Tours and the Abbots of Marmoutier*, he is placed too early among the abbots of Marmoutier. For it says there:

> “He governed this church until the year 1036, namely for thirteen years, and died on 8 May.”

But this cannot stand [Col. 0451B], for that Bernard was elected abbot only after Bartholomew, who ceased office on 24 February 1083 or thereabouts, as we noted in P. on Letter 4. This appears from charter 180 of the cartulary of that monastery, “On the benefices situated in the province or archdeaconry of Vendôme,” for it says that the year in which Pope Urban II consecrated the church of Marmoutier—1096—was the thirteenth year of Bernard’s administration. I think this letter was written about that year, or a little later, because it mentions his blessing as a recent event.

“Episcopal benediction effects an abbot’s promotion.” See the gloss on Clementine *Attendentes*, *On the State of Regulars*; John Andrew; and Henry of Susa on chapter *Tuam* 10, *On the Age and Qualifications of Those to Be Ordained*.

## ON LETTER LXXIV

[Col. 0451C]

“To Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans.” Orderic Vitalis, book X of the *Ecclesiastical History*, pp. 770–71, writes of him under the year of Christ’s birth 1098:

> “In these times Hoel, bishop of Le Mans, a Breton by birth and of venerable life, died. Count Elias elected Geoffrey the Breton, dean of the same church, to the episcopate; but the clergy, acting first, compelled Hildebert of Lavardin, archdeacon, to sit in the episcopal chair.”

And a little below:

> “After the death of Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, Hildebert was elected by clergy and people, and by God’s will passed from the height of Le Mans to the metropolitan see. He was gentle and devout, zealous in both sacred and secular literature, and in our times flourished as an incomparable writer of verse; he composed many poems equal or superior to ancient poetry,” etc. “For he speaks elegantly and wisely of Christ and the Church, of body and soul, of the deeds of the saints and their virtues, of the praise of virtues and the condemnation [Col. 0451D] of vices,” etc. “This holy hero exercised the office of bishop for nearly thirty-five years and applied himself especially to good studies, in teaching and in conduct. He adorned in many praiseworthy ways the church of St Gervase, where the body of the outstanding confessor of Christ, Julian, rests,” etc.

Baronius also speaks honourably enough of Hildebert under 1107, no. 14; consult him. This letter must have been written at the beginning of 1100, since on the same day—5 August—William Rufus, whom Ivo here mentions without naming and who accused Hildebert of treason, died in the New Forest in England from an arrow-shot, as Orderic Vitalis, book X, p. 783, relates.

## ON LETTERS LXXV AND LXXVI

“To John, bishop of Orléans.” He was John I, not John II. What I said above on Letter 60 prevents any other conclusion. For the family of Le Puiset—father, mother, and sons—whom Ivo had devoted to curses, were restored to ecclesiastical communion by Hugh of Lyons in 1096, before they joined the Holy War; indeed Ivo himself writes to Sanctio, bishop of Orléans, in Letter 6 that he had made peace with Adelicia, lady of the castle of Le Puiset, and forgiven her offence against him. But Sanctio succeeded that first John only in 1099. Therefore he could not complain, in that year, of injuries done to him by Hugh of Le Puiset, Adelicia’s husband, who was then in Syria, because Jerusalem had been captured in that year by Godfrey of Bouillon and the Franks—especially while the Truce of God was in force, by which a truce was granted to those marked with the cross and bound for the overseas expedition, as appears in the following Letter 168—unless one says that those lords of Le Puiset, namely Hugh and Ebrard, having returned home in 1099, returned to their vomit and inflicted fresh injuries upon Ivo. This I certainly do not deny, since in that same year Daimbert occupied the see of Sens, John II that of Orléans [Col. 0452B], and Guy of Nevers was called bishop-elect because he had not yet been confirmed.

“At the council of Clermont.” Several canons of this council are certainly missing. Among those published by Baronius, whether from Lambert, bishop of Arras, or from François de Belleforest, who copied them from the library of Saint-Denis, and others, nothing is found concerning the matters Ivo treats here. For canon 32 of Lambert’s edition says only:

> “If anyone seizes and imprisons a bishop, let him be subject to perpetual infamy and never again bear arms.”

And canon 9 of the later edition reads:

> “Whoever lays hands upon a bishop, or carries him into chains or prison, shall be declared impious and, as one devoid of law and knowledge of God, shall be struck with anathema and cast out from the communion of the Church.”

There is not a word about the excommunication of other bishops. Nevertheless, the canons of this council may have been more extensive, since writers cite others which are not found among those published; indeed, those that have been published do not agree with one another. Nor should one suppose that Ivo, who was present at the council, intended to impose upon the truth.

## ON LETTER LXXVII

“To Hugh, dean of the church of Beauvais.” He was surnamed de Gerberoy, according to Claude Robert in his list of the bishops of Beauvais, no. 49, and Louvet, *History of Beauvais*, book IV, ch. 23.

“Against the bishop.” Against Anselm, bishop of Beauvais, who entered the see in 1099 and held it until 20 November, when he died.

## ON LETTER LXXVIII

“To the monks of the monastery of Déols.” That monastery of Déols, in the province of Bourges, was founded by Ebbo, a local lord, in the time of Charles the Simple, king of the Franks, about 913, on the little river Augerim or Indre [Col. 0452D], commonly the Indre. It is contemptible in appearance, but is difficult to cross in many places because its channel is frequently divided into multiple courses and because of marshes, says Aimoin of Fleury; it rises in the territory of Bourges above Châtre, between the castle of Raoul and that same ascetic house of Déols.

The church of Déols was dedicated by Pope Urban II while he was in Gaul in 1095. After it had been destroyed by the savage Huguenots, the monks of that celebrated abbey and of neighbouring St Gildas were secularized in 1623 by Pope Gregory XV, at the request of Henry of Bourbon, prince of Condé, who died on the very day on which I was writing this, and with the consent of Louis XIII, king of the Franks. The king permitted the establishment of a community of canons in the church of St Martin at Châteauroux; its patronage, or right of nomination, he granted to the same prince. See Robert, *Abbeys of Gaul*, L. D. V., “Déols.”

“Bernerius, formerly a monk of Bonneval.” He was the future abbot of Bonneval [Col. 0453A], who had then been elected abbot of Déols; see note 1 on Letter 147.

“Concerning the monastery of the Cross.” It is otherwise called the Cross of Helton, the monastery of La Croix-Saint-Leufroy, or the monastery of the Cross of St Leufred, in the diocese of Évreux, of the Order of St Benedict. There, according to Orderic Vitalis, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 524 ff., the glorious confessor of Christ Leufred is recorded to have served the Lord happily for forty-eight years in the time of the young kings Hildebert and Chilperic.

Guimond. Concerning him the same Orderic, in the place cited above, writes as follows:

> “Guitmond, a venerable monk of the monastery called the Cross of Helton, where the glorious confessor of Christ, Leudfred, when summoned by royal command, crossed the Channel, and wholly refused the burden of ecclesiastical government offered him by the king and the magnates of the realm. For he was of mature age, devout, and most learned in letters; a brilliant proof of his genius is plainly evident in his book on the Body and Blood of the Lord against Berengar, [Col. 0453B] and in his other shorter works. Therefore, when the king asked him to remain with him in England and await a suitable time for his promotion, he deliberated carefully with himself and, showing that the vow of his purpose was otherwise, answered the king: ‘Many causes repel me from ecclesiastical government,’ etc. The king and his magnates, admiring the constancy of the distinguished monk, humbly and devoutly paid him fitting reverence and, having honorably provided for him, ordered him to return to Neustria and there await his presence wherever he wished, etc. Not long afterwards, when John, archbishop of Rouen, had died, the king and many others elected Guitmond to the archbishopric; but his rivals, whom he had rebuked, prevented his becoming archbishop as far as they could. They found nothing to object against so great a man except that he was a priest’s son. But he, wishing to be cleansed of all avarice, and preferring to distinguish himself among strangers by poverty rather than foster dissensions among his own people, reverently approached Odilo, [Col. 0453C] abbot of his monastery, and humbly sought and received from him permission to go on pilgrimage. The unlettered abbot, however, did not know how great a treasure of wisdom lay hidden in the aforesaid doctor; therefore he readily dismissed from his monastery the desirable philosopher, whom Pope Gregory VII joyfully received on his arrival, made cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and whom Pope Urban, already proven in many things, solemnly ordained metropolitan of the city of Aversa. This city was built in the time of Pope Leo IX by the Normans who first settled Apulia; and it was called Aversa by the Romans because it was built by hostile bands.”

It did not stand long, since it was razed to the ground by Roger, prince of Sicily, in 1135, according to the Chronicle of Benevento. I have certain things concerning Robert in manuscripts, but they are not at hand. What has been said of one is enough for credit to be given to what is said of the other.

## ON EPISTLE LXXIX

To Philip, bishop of Troyes. He held office from 1080, [Col. 0453D] or 1082, according to Camusat’s *Promptuary of the Antiquities of Troyes*, until 1114 and afterwards. The synod of which Ivo speaks here was held about 1099; toward the end of that year Guy, bishop-elect of Nevers, was consecrated, and this letter was written.

“But because, though summoned to the council, you did not come,” etc. On the penalty to be imposed upon bishops who do not attend a synod, see Distinction 18, *Cum pervenit* and other chapters, in Ivo, book IV, title 2, chapters 3 and 6; Panormitanus, part V of the Decretals, chapter 114; and Antonio Agustín, *Epitome of Ancient Pontifical Law*, book VI, title 65.

## ON EPISTLE LXXX

To William, abbot of the monastery of Fécamp. Of him Orderic Vitalis writes thus, book III, p. 495:

> “William of Ros, a cleric of Bayeux, who in that Church possessed a threefold dignity—for he was cantor, dean, and archdeacon, etc.—not long afterwards voluntarily abandoning the pomps of the world, became a monk at Caen; [Col. 0454A] and thence, before he had made progress for a single year in monastic life, he was appointed to govern the monastery of Fécamp.”

And in book XI, p. 832, speaking of him:

> “This venerable man, he says, endowed with good morals, lived praiseworthily; enriched from boyhood with the nectar of many virtues, he flourished, and in clerical and monastic life shone upon the world as a model of good works. While still a novice in the monastic habit, he undertook the aforesaid monastery, governed it for nearly twenty years, and reformed it in many respects within and without.”

For his beauty he was also called “the Maiden,” as Orderic himself writes. Orderic says that William died as he was returning from Lisieux, where Henry I, king of the English, had summoned an assembly, or council, of the Norman magnates, in March 1107; and that he was buried before the altar of the glorious Virgin Mary in the church of Fécamp newly built by him. Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, composed an epitaph for him, still to be read fixed upon his tomb:

> [Col. 0454B]  
> Rich toward the poor, William, abbot of the sacred name,  
> Yet, in body only, a tiller of the soil, lies here.  
> Freed from Egypt, returning, he left the deserts behind,  
> And now, victorious and rejoicing, possesses Jerusalem.  
> With vices he made war; with good conduct he made an everlasting  
> Friendship; steadfast in both, he remained firm.  
> On the grievous day that came six days before April,  
> His spirit returned to its homeland, his bones to the earth.

“Concerning the moving of an altar or of church walls, whether consecration must be repeated.” To the first part of the question Pope Innocent III replies in a letter to the archbishop of Nidaros: “An altar on which a consecration blessing has been conferred by pontifical ministry, if moved or severely broken, ought quite properly to be consecrated again.”” This is the opinion of Sylvester, *Summa*, under “Altar,” nos. 6 and 7, and “Consecration,” II, no. or § 7 and 8, and of the Doctors on chapter *Proposuit*, *On Consecration*. To the second part Durand answers in book I of the *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, under the rubric “On the [Col. 0454C] Dedication of a Church,” about the middle; the reader may consult him.

I think this letter was written before the new basilica at Fécamp, built by the William mentioned above, was consecrated and dedicated by William, archbishop of Rouen, and four other bishops on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, as Orderic states in the place last cited. The year is uncertain, unless it was 1100 or 1101, in one of which years, from what Orderic has in book V, p. 568, and Dadreus in his chronological history of the archbishops of Rouen, William of Rouen died—although the Chronicle of Saint Stephen at Caen writes that he lived until 1110. For if, as Dadreus says, William began in 1079 and ruled twenty-two years according to Orderic, it is true that he died in 1101; and thus this letter may be conjectured to have been written in one or the other of those years.

## ON EPISTLE LXXXI

To Paschal, supreme pontiff: the successor of Urban II, [Col. 0454D] who, Urban having died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August 1099, as Onuphrius and Baronius state under the year 1100, no. 1, was proclaimed supreme pontiff at Rome by the cardinals of the Gregorian party on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September of that same year, and was crowned on the following day. He was a Tuscan by nationality, from the town of Blera in the county of Galliate, called Lord Rainerius; by profession a regular canon of the Lateran, then a monk of Cluny, abbot of Saints Stephen and Lawrence outside the walls of the city, and cardinal-priest of Saint Clement, created by Pope Gregory VII. He reigned against the antipope [pseudo-]Clement III for eighteen years, five months, and eight days. Baronius maintains that this letter was written in 1100, no. 14, with whom I readily agree. For it congratulates Paschal on his recent elevation to the highest summit of the Church.

## ON EPISTLE LXXXII

Daniel. Perhaps the man who was afterwards abbot of Évron (commonly [Col. 0455A] Euron) in 1123. Évron is a Benedictine monastery in Lower Maine, dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary by Hadoind, twelfth bishop of Le Mans, about 650, during the reign of Clovis III, king of the Franks. See Geoffrey of Vendôme, book I, letter 3, and Sirmond there and on letter 20, book V.

## ON EPISTLE LXXXIII

“To your metropolitan A.” Manasses d’Affray, or of Châtillon, recently archbishop of Reims, a kinsman of Pope Urban II, concerning whom see above on letter 48.

“To the bishop of Soissons.” He was called Hugh, brother of Nivelon of Pierrefonds. Having undertaken the journey to Jerusalem, he died at Aquileia in 1103. We have spoken of him on letter 42.

## ON EPISTLE LXXXIV

“But because you intend to hold a council at Poitiers, or within the province of Aquitaine.” Much light is thrown upon this passage by what Geoffrey the Fat writes in his *Life of Bernard, First Abbot of Tiron*. Since that book has not yet appeared in print, I shall not hesitate to set down his testimony here:

> “At that time,” says Geoffrey, “two cardinals, John and Benedict, acting as legates of the Apostolic See, called a council at the city of Poitiers, at which one hundred and forty Fathers were present. They struck Philip, king of the Franks, with the punishment of anathema because he kept in adultery the wife of Fulk, count of Anjou. When this excommunication became known, William, duke of the Aquitanians, who was present, an enemy of all chastity and holiness, fearing that he might suffer a like punishment for like offenses, was inflamed with excessive fury and ordered all of them to be plundered, whipped, and killed. As his servants began to do this, the bishops and abbots fled here and there and struggled to find safe hiding places in order to preserve their temporal lives. But Bernard and Robert of Arbrissel, who were present at the council, most valiant champions of justice and assailants of all wickedness and injustice, [Col. 0455C] remained so unmoved and steadfast that they did not desist from the begun excommunication, but considered it most glorious to suffer death or disgrace for Christ. Although their persecutors did not inflict death upon them, they nevertheless endured martyrdom, so far as lay in them.”

A fragment of an old Fleury manuscript mentions this John, to whom Ivo writes, his companion or colleague Benedict, and the Council of Poitiers; so do Vincent of Beauvais, *Mirror of History*, book XXVI, chapter 68; Gaguin, book VI, immediately after the beginning; Suger, *On Louis the Fat*; and others. This council was held in 1100, according to Bouchet, part III of the *Annals of Aquitaine*, chapter 2, and the Chronicle of Tours under that year. Therefore Baronius rightly asserts that this letter was written in the same year, no. 20.

## ON EPISTLE LXXXVI

To Stephen, count palatine. I suspect [Col. 0455D] that this letter was written by Ivo to Stephen, count of Chartres, in 1110, after his return from Palestine. For he twice girded himself for the journey to Jerusalem, in 1096 and 1101. On the first expedition see Fulcher of Chartres, *Deeds of the Pilgrims of the Franks*, chapter 1, and Robert, monk of Saint-Remi at Reims, *History of Jerusalem*, book VI. On the second, Albert of Aachen, *History of Jerusalem*, book VIII, chapter 6, and book IX, chapters 5 and 6; also William of Tyre, book X, chapters 12 and 19; and Matthew Paris, under Henry I, p. 40. Orderic Vitalis, book X, p. 789, writes in those passages that Stephen, moved by repentance because he had not brought aid to the Christians besieged at Antioch—and indeed had fled to the utmost disgrace of his reputation—returned to Jerusalem in 1101 and was captured in the siege of Ramla by Azopart, governor of the Babylonians, and paid with his head at Joppa.

## ON EPISTLE LXXXVII

Stephen of Garlande. Brother of Anseau, leader of the French soldiery, [Col. 0456A] and himself chancellor and seneschal of the king after his brothers Anseau and William. From the Chronicle of the monastery of Morigny I learn the following. Writing in book II about the community of canons at Étampes, it says:

> “A certain Algrin, count palatine and royal clerk, supported their party, as did Stephen the chancellor, brother of Anseau the seneschal and the king’s most intimate counsellor, by whose judgment the kingdom of France was then governed; both were canons of Étampes.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “William the seneschal, called the steward, and Stephen the chancellor, his brother, by whose counsel all France was governed.”

About three pages later it adds:

> “Meanwhile, when William, brother of Anseau the seneschal, had died, Stephen the chancellor, the brother of both men whom we mentioned while he was still alive, became Major of the royal household. In past generations it had been unheard of for a man exercising the office of deacon to hold at the same time, after the king, the chief position in military affairs. This industrious man, endowed with worldly [Col. 0456B] wisdom, flourishing through the revenues of many ecclesiastical dignities and through such familiarity with the king that some said he ruled rather than served him, surpassed all mortals of our age in temporal prosperity,” etc.

That Stephen of Garlande was elected bishop of Beauvais after Anselm’s death. Yet he lost the election through Ivo’s opposition; Walo, elected at Ivo’s urging by clerics of better reputation and sounder judgment, was substituted by the supreme pontiff. But, since Philip king of the Franks and his son Louis the Fat opposed it, Walo did not obtain the dignity; rather, he was shortly transferred to the Church of Paris. I therefore judge that this letter was written in the same year in which these events occurred, namely 1103, although Baronius disagrees under 1101, no. 8. See the following letters, 89, 92, 95, 97, and 98.

## ON EPISTLE LXXXVIII

[Col. 0456C] “Lord Hilgot, formerly bishop of Soissons.” I do not even find his name among the bishops of Soissons. Perhaps he merely refused the bishopric to which he had been elected and embraced monastic life, while Ivo had not yet been raised to the see of Chartres, as he himself seems to indicate here.

## ON EPISTLE XCI

To the noble countess Adela: countess of Chartres, of whom we have already spoken above. Ivo consoles her as she lay ill from grief over the loss of her husband, slain overseas, as is clear from what was said concerning letter 86; and he asks her to protect the monastery of Saint John in the Valley near Chartres, recently founded by him.
