For he had laid its first foundations in 1099 and assigned it to regular canons, as the familiar verse says:

> When one year was lacking from one hundred and a thousand years,  
> This place first flourished under the canonical order.

She possesses in that church, as Ivo says in this letter, an office of prayers—that is, an anniversary commemoration on the eighth day before the Ides of March—as is clear from the necrology of Saint John in the Valley, in these words: “Adela, countess of Blois, died.”

“To Lady Helisendis, vicomtesse.” The necrology of the Church of Saint John in the Valley at Chartres says of her:

> “On the sixth day before the Ides of July. Helisendis, vicomtesse, died, through whose counsel and aid our church possesses the share of the vicariate belonging to the viscount; also the village called Moncelle and Ermantarville.”

And in the cartulary of the same abbey, part I, chapter 26, one reads of the gift of Ermanterville, with the assent of Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Elizabeth, daughter of that vicomtesse and sister of Hugh the viscount. Helisendis was the wife of Guérin the viscount and mother of Stephen, also viscount, who renounced worldly affairs, became abbot of Saint John in the Valley, and afterwards [Col. 0457A] patriarch of Jerusalem; see William of Tyre, book XIII, chapter 25. The same Helisendis is mentioned in the foundation of the abbey of Josaphat in 1120 and in the Cartulary of Saint Peter in the Valley at Chartres. There was another Helisendis, vicomtesse of Chartres, wife of Geoffrey de Melle, viscount; but she was a full century later, as is stated in the same Josaphat Cartulary. I note this lest anyone be deceived by the name. I think this letter was written in 1101 or 1102, after the death of Henry Stephen, count of Chartres, became known. On this see Matthew Paris, under Henry I, p. 41.

## ON EPISTLE XCIII

To Daimbert, by the grace of God patriarch of Jerusalem. He was substituted for Arnulf when Arnulf was deposed, according to Guibert the abbot, *History of Jerusalem*, book VII, chapter 13. He had been archbishop of Pisa and was sent there as legate by the supreme pontiff; William of Tyre also asserts this, book IX of his *History of Jerusalem*, chapters 14 and 15. Baronius assigns this letter to 1100, no. 34; I assign it to 1101, since in that year Stephen, count of Chartres and Blois, returned from Jerusalem with many soldiers of the diocese of Chartres—whom Ivo calls his parishioners—up to sixty thousand cavalry, [Col. 0457B] and a greater number of infantry.

## ON EPISTLE XCIV

“The count of Chartres [concerning] the evil customs which his predecessors and he himself exercised over the houses and possessions of the bishop of Chartres.” When bishops died, the counts of Chartres, or their officials, claimed as their own right whatever remained in the bishops’ houses and other buildings. To redeem himself from this harassment, Ivo obtained the renunciation of that right from Henry Stephen when he was returning to Syria, and transmitted it to his successors. The following charter confirms the grant and shows what those evil customs were:

> “I, Henry, count surnamed Stephen, and Adela my wife, together with our sons, wish it to be known to all faithful members of the holy Church of God, both lay and clerical, present and future, that Ivo, humble servant of God and venerable bishop of the Church of Chartres, came into our presence and earnestly requested that we grant freedom from that evil custom, which our predecessors and we ourselves have hitherto exercised over it, to the episcopal house—that house, namely, which he transformed from a wooden into a stone building, and from mean into splendid—so that, when bishops depart this life or leave for any reason, the aforesaid house may not be despoiled; that no iron, lead, glass, wood, or stone may be carried away or torn down; and that it may not be stripped of any of its furnishings. Likewise, that grain, [Col. 0457C] wine, hay, sheep and oxen, other animals, and all movable goods assembled or gathered in the city or outside it before the death or departure of bishops shall be left untouched by us and ours, for the benefit of those for whom the bishop has decreed to reserve or give them, either personally or through his *oeconomus* [steward]; or whom the chief persons of the Church may designate if, because of some circumstance preventing the bishop, he has been unable to do so.
>
> “He also added to his request that the exaction commonly called *tallia* [tallage], customarily levied upon the bishop’s servants or peasants when bishops die or depart, should be remitted for the same reason. Therefore, judging it unworthy to frustrate the request of so great a man, and considering that ecclesiastical property ought rather to be increased than diminished, for the salvation of the soul of my father, myself, my wife, and my sons, we free the aforesaid property from the evil custom: namely, the house, and its iron, lead, glass, wood, stones, and other furnishings—tables, benches, stools, wine-vessels, beds, kitchens and barns, granaries, cellars, wine-presses, ovens and oven-houses—whether in the city or outside it; and woods, so that they may neither be sold, cut down, nor given away. We likewise leave untouched by ourselves and our sons William all grain, wine, hay, oxen, sheep, other animals, and every other movable good [Col. 0458A] assembled or gathered, either in the city or outside it, before the death or departure of any bishop, for the benefit of those for whom the bishop has decreed to reserve or give them, either personally or through his *oeconomus* [steward], or whom the chief persons of the Church may designate if, because of a circumstance preventing the bishop, he has been unable to do so. We further grant that the aforesaid exaction, customarily levied upon the bishop’s servants or peasants when bishops die or depart, shall henceforth never be made.
>
> “And because we have made these concessions so graciously, the bishop and the whole community of canons of Blessed Mary have granted to me and my wife Adela that, every year, our anniversaries shall be celebrated at their proper times in the Church of Blessed Mary. If anyone attempts to annul or weaken the aforesaid agreement, we grant, so far as lies in us, that the divine office shall be prohibited both in the city and in the suburbs, and that the perpetrators of so great a sacrilege, after warning, if they do not repent, shall be punished most severely by the sword of anathema until satisfaction has been made. But if any future bishop builds a tower or fortifications in the aforesaid house, only the tower and fortifications shall be destroyed; the house and its appurtenances shall remain untouched.
>
> “And so that this agreement may remain firm and unshaken through succeeding times, it has pleased us to commit it to writing, to strengthen it by the attestation of magnates both clerical and lay, and to confirm it by the testimony of our seals. + Seal of Count Stephen. + Seal of Countess Adela. + Seal of William. + Seal of Stephen. + Seal of Odo [otherwise Hugh]. + Seal of Theobald. Witnesses on the part of the count and countess: Stephen, viscount of Meaux; Galcher of Montmirail; Ralph of Balgenci; Guicher of Château-Renard; Guermond of Châtillon; Garner Mangot; Count Rotrou of Perche; Stephen the vicomte; Herbert of Châtillon; Pagan of Verzy; Hervé Bel; Hugh Berbel; [Col. 0458C] Ansold Berbel; Robert Bellin; Bernard Forester; Renaud the chaplain; Alexander the chaplain.”

On the prohibition against plundering the goods of a deceased bishop, see Antonio Agustín, book IV, title 83, and book XV, title 34, throughout those titles.

## ON EPISTLE XCV

“The bishop of Châlons.” Hugh, who succeeded Philip, son of Theobald, count of Chartres, and Adelaide. For this letter makes clear that Philip had yielded enough. A council was held at Poitiers in 1100, according to the Chronicle of Tours, in the forty-fourth year of Emperor Henry and the fortieth of King Philip.

“But that the aforesaid cleric cannot hold titular churches in two cities.” Matthew Paris, *History of England*, under William II, p. 15, col. 2, reports that this was forbidden to clerics by statute at the Council of Clermont, or Auvergne. But Pope Vitalian had provided for it much earlier in letter 3 to Paul, bishop of Crete. The decree was also renewed at the Council of Poitiers in 1100, as appears from the same source, volume VII of the Councils, part I, canon 2, p. 533.

## ON EPISTLE XCVII

“To Lambert of Arras and John of Thérouanne.” Concerning Lambert, see what was said on letter 33. Concerning John of Thérouanne, or bishop of the Morini, I have nothing except that he was enrolled among the saints and occupied his see from 1099 to 1127; see Meyer, book VI of the *Annals of Flanders*, under 1101. Thérouanne, or Tarvanna, was completely destroyed by order of Emperor Charles V in 1552, during the wars then raging between him and Henry II, king of the French. Its episcopal see was divided three ways and transferred partly to Boulogne—where the ancient port of Gesoriacum stood—partly to Saint-Omer, and partly to Ypres. As to the letter, I think it was written in or about 1101.

## ON EPISTLE XCIX

[Col. 0459A]

To Walo: abbot of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais; Ivo’s disciple, as appears in the following letters 104 and 105, reared and educated by him. On the marriage matter which he asks about, consult authors who write concerning the impediment of public decency. Compare letters 144 and 145. These documents were sent to Walo in 1102, when he was elected bishop of Beauvais, according to Baronius under that year, no. 8, or at least in the following year.

## ON EPISTLE C

To John, bishop of the Church of Orléans. He is the second bishop of that name, appointed in 1099 after the expulsion of Sanction. See Sausseius, *Annals of Orléans*, book IX. The letter to him was written about 1101 or 1102.

“The altar of Basilicas.” Perhaps more correctly, “of Bazoches,” which lies in the diocese of Orléans and belongs to the right of patronage of the bishop of Chartres by reason of the temporal lordship of that place and of Balneoles. Thus Sausseius is less correct in attributing the presentation to the church of Bazoches-le-Haut to the archdeacon of Beauce in the Church of Orléans, when the charters of the bishops of Chartres state that it belongs to their presentation.

## ON EPISTLE CII

Baronius maintains that this was written in 1101, no. 12; I do not disagree.

## ON EPISTLE CIII

“The bishop of Senlis.” Hugh, or Letold, [229] who lived in Ivo’s time.

## ON EPISTLES CIV AND CV

Baronius judges that they were written in 1101, no. 8. But I place them in 1103, since only then was the Walo mentioned above elected bishop of Beauvais.

Walo, namely abbot of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais, had been elected by the greater and sounder part of the clergy after the rejection of Stephen of Garlande. Yet, although the opposing party was smaller, it prevailed; Walo was not admitted by King Philip and his son Louis the Fat, because he was a disciple of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and had been reared and educated by him, as this letter says. At that time the prince was especially hostile to Ivo because Ivo opposed his incestuous marriage with Bertrada. Further, by the fraud of his rivals, the king had bound himself by oath that Walo should not become bishop of Beauvais for as long as he lived. Therefore Ivo writes to the supreme pontiff, asking him not to permit so great an injury to be done to the elect, unless he wished all future episcopal elections to become void or almost infected with the stain of simony, if they were left to the king’s discretion and depended upon him.

## ON EPISTLE CVI

“To Henry, most excellent king of the English.” Henry I, son of William the Conqueror, who, when his brother William Rufus, king of the English, died, took possession of the kingdom against his elder brother Robert Curthose; [Col. 0459D] as William of Jumièges teaches in book VIII of his *History of the Normans*, chapter 10. Concerning him see also below, letter 118. Baronius assigns this letter to 1100, no. 29, which may be correct, since Henry received the royal diadem in that year, according to the same William of Jumièges.

## ON EPISTLE CVII

“To Matilda, queen of the English, surnamed the Good”: elder daughter of Malcolm, or Malcolm III, king of the Scots, and Margaret, sister of Edgar prince of the English, as Buchanan states in book VII of his *Scottish History*, and as appears in the genealogy of the dukes of Normandy, p. 213 of the *History of the Normans*. Of her and her husband Henry, William of Jumièges writes in the place last cited:

> “That the same king might live lawfully, he married in that same year the venerable Matilda, daughter of King Malcolm of Scotland and Margaret, etc. Nor should it be passed over that the same Matilda was betrothed to the most noble King Henry by Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury of holy memory, at Westminster on the feast of Saint Martin, [Col. 0460A] and on that same day was adorned with the royal diadem.”

On them see Matthew Paris, under Henry I, king of the English, for 1101, p. 40, col. 1. It may be asserted that this letter was written to the queen in the same year in which she married the king. Compare letter 142.

## ON EPISTLE CIX

Baronius judges that this letter was written in 1100, no. 15. His conjecture is supported by the appointment of Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, as legate, which occurred only in 1094.

## ON EPISTLE CX

Baronius assigns this letter to 1103, no. 12; I assign it to 1104, since Walo was transferred by the supreme pontiff to the bishopric of Paris in that year. Indeed, in the Cartulary of Saint Martin-des-Champs at Paris, fol. 37, the year 1107 is called the third year of Walo’s episcopate, and at fol. 70 the year 1108 is called the fourth.

## ON EPISTLE CXI

This letter was written to Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, against Hugh, lord of Puiset, [Col. 0460B] asking him to exclude Hugh far from communion with the faithful, lay under interdict the land that he possessed in his diocese, and exhort John, bishop of Orléans, to do the same. For Hugh, like one returned to his vomit, had appropriated to himself the revenues both of the bishopric and of the Church of Chartres; this was also the subject of many complaints against him, as may be read in several places in the cartularies of the Church of Chartres, fol. 1; of Bonneval, fol. 1; and of Saint Peter in the Valley.

Merarivilla. I suspect this is Mervilla in the diocese of Sens, not far from Étampes, which then belonged to the lords of Puiset. Yet in a confirmation of Louis the Fat, king of France, issued to the monks of Bonneval in 1110 regarding privileges which former kings of France had granted them, I read Guy of Mereville as a witness; he may have been lord of that village.

## ON EPISTLE CXII

“But it is [a matter] of the Church of Chartres and of other Churches.” Of the other Churches there is nothing for me to say. It is enough to speak of the Church of Chartres, which, by grant of the supreme pontiffs, possesses the right to punish those who injure it by exclusion from the sacraments and to restrain their obstinacy by ecclesiastical censure. So that this may be clear to all, I shall append here a bull of the supreme pontiff.

## ON EPISTLE CXIII

Manasses. He was elected bishop of Meaux from the archdeaconry in 1103; perhaps this letter was written in that year.

## ON EPISTLE CXVI

The disagreement or controversy that arose between Ivo and his canons on the one hand, and Adela, countess of Chartres, on the other, was this: Ivo and the chapter of Chartres complained that the immunity of their cloister was being violated. They had issued a statute that freedmen, co-freedmen, and other persons of low condition, especially bankrupts, bastards, and those born out of wedlock, were not to be admitted into their sacred body. This statute prevailed so greatly that, the laws of servitude and freedom having disappeared, its final provision still remains. For no one has access to a canonry and prebend at Chartres unless he swears that he was born of lawful marriage, as will be said below on letter 147. This letter may have been written in 1103.

## ON EPISTLE CXX

“To Robert, count of Ponthieu.” He means Robert Talvas, [230] lord of Bellême, to whom the county of Ponthieu had come, by way of dower, with his wife Agnes, daughter of Guy, count of Ponthieu. See William of Jumièges, book VIII, chapter 35, and Orderic Vitalis, book VIII, pp. 675 and 708.

## ON EPISTLE CXXVII

“To Louis, by the grace of God king-designate of the Franks.” Philip was nearing his end, and his earlier age, given over to lust, had surrendered his exhausted body to old age. Therefore, since he was of benefit neither to himself nor to the commonwealth, some years before he died he placed all care of his kingdom in his son Louis. Thus the Cartulary of Saint Martin-des-Champs, fol. 82, says at the end of a charter of Geoffrey, bishop of Amiens, concerning the Church of Lignières:

> “Done in the Church of Amiens in the year 1104 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction 12, Philip being king of the Franks and his son Louis commander of the army,” etc.

But it says this in plainer words at fol. 66 verso, in a charter of Hubert, bishop of Senlis. With the consent of his lord Louis, now king-designate, he confirms the gift of the church of Saint Nicholas of Acy, made by Robert the viscount with the consent of Bishop Letard, from whose fief the church belonged to Saint Martin-des-Champs in the city of Paris, in 1106. Suger also expressly writes the same in *On Louis the Fat*, where he calls him king-designate when Bohemond married the sister of Louis the Fat. The Chronicle of Morigny, book II, is clearer still:

> “The noble King Philip gave [it], confirmed this donation by royal letters, and ordered his son Louis, king-designate, to grant the same,” etc.

From these sources and from Gilles, historian of French affairs, I think this letter was written in or about 1105.

“Respite” (*respectus*). This is what we call in the vernacular a *respit* [a delay or reprieve]. Thus Geoffrey of Vendôme, letter 24, book II: “You have received a respite until the feast of Saint Beatus”; and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, uses it frequently.

## ON EPISTLE CXXVIII
Od[o], his fellow brother and fellow priest—namely, a canon of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais. Unless I am mistaken, the following often-recurring letter to Ivo is his; I publish it from old manuscripts:

> “To his most excellent father and lord Ivo, by God’s grace bishop of the Church of Chartres, Brother Odo—unworthy to be counted among the servants of God—greetings, due prayers, and to be joined pontifically in the body of the supreme pontiff.
>
> “My dearest father and lord: even if my small measure of Minerva [learning] were more eloquent than the philosophy of Socrates, more subtle than the skill of Aristotle, or more fluent than Cicero’s eloquence, I should never think myself sufficient, whether daring or able, to write to a person so reverend as you, instructed alike in divine and philosophical learning. Yet, lest I perhaps seem to have sewn my lips shut through indignation or through a great lack of philosophical—or rather divine—eloquence, I shall attempt to write, not presumptuously indeed, but in lamenting the necessities of my soul.
>
> “Nevertheless, I shall do so not as the measure of your eloquence, the degree of your great learning, or the supreme integrity of your religion would require, but as the smallness of my knowledge, the clarity of my understanding, or the necessity of writing to you may suggest. May it therefore please your fatherhood to learn the pattern of continence observed by your pupils. For we have a good place, a suitable church, an excellent bishop, many books, food and clothing: in short, everything very necessary for the present business—thanks be to God—and hence we perceive God to be most gracious toward us. Yet, notwithstanding the aforesaid outward prosperity, know, Father, how severe is my inward languor.
>
> “For behold: shattered by many wounds, by the stain of my fallen sins, I have more than enough cause for grief—and would that I grieved; but wounded, I do not grieve. Indeed, forgetful of myself, I rejoice. Therefore, I beg you, do not, do not allow me to perish without your remedies; rather, pray to the supreme physician, that through the merits of your intercession he may soothe me, cleanse me, and make me whole, after pouring in the oil of mercy. But if the strength of the divine Spirit were increased in my soul as it ought to be, it would unceasingly share the burden of our labour. For whatever we are, and whatever we may become, we owe wholly to you. We are bound to love you greatly for all the benefits which, while we were with you, it pleased your pious charity to bestow upon us. For these benefits, therefore, we offer boundless praise and thanks to supreme God and to your gracious fatherhood. Would that the pious and gracious Lord might send me kindly and useful companions.” [Col. 0461C–0462A]

Later, however, a small flame of hostility or disagreement arose between Ivo and this Odo, as may be inferred from Letter 151. For after Odo had become abbot of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais, Ivo opposed his election as far as he was able.

## ON LETTERS CXXIX AND CXXX

To Geoffrey, count of Vendôme, called Grisagonella (“Grey Little Cloak”), who married Matilda, Robert’s widow, about the year 1105, notwithstanding the impediments raised by Ivo. For in charter 277 of the cartulary of Vendôme I read the following:

> “We wish all men to know that Geoffrey, son of Count Geoffrey, who was called Grisagonella, brought a claim against us concerning a certain plot of land, in which there had formerly been a wood near the town of Dieu, which his father Count Geoffrey had given us at the request of Countess Matilda, mother of that Geoffrey who brought the claim,” etc.

It is therefore beyond doubt that Grisagonella married that Matilda. But what Ivo alleges concerning consanguinity between Grisagonella and Matilda’s former husband is less certain. For from the cartulary of the monastery of Vendôme itself I learn that their genealogy was otherwise. Thus, on folio 13 of the second part, I find that the elder Burchard, count of Vendôme and Corbeil, begot Reginald, bishop of Paris, and an unnamed daughter, wife of Fulk Nerra, count of Anjou. By her Fulk had Adela, whom her uncle Reginald gave in marriage to a certain powerful Burchard who lived farther away. She bore him four sons. The eldest, Burchard, upon his uncle’s death obtained the dignity of Vendôme and the Vendômois.

But because he was still too young to administer them, Fulk, his mother’s father, assumed his guardianship and the dignity, which he surrendered when the boy had grown up. By his second wife Fulk had begotten Geoffrey, called Martel. With the assent of Henry I, king of the French, Burchard and his mother entrusted to him the preservation of the counties of the Vendômois and Vendôme, retaining only the usufruct for themselves. [Col. 0462B–C] When Burchard died without issue, that double dignity passed to Fulk the Goose, or Little Goose, brother of Eufronia—whom Ivo calls Nifrana. By Petronilla, his wife and daughter of Lancelin of Baugency, he begot the younger Burchard, so called in charter 222, part 1; the printed text then has the feminine relative *quae* (“who”), saying that this person married Geoffrey, called Jordan of Preuilly.

When Burchard died, the county of Vendôme passed to Eufronia and her husband Geoffrey of Preuilly. From their union was born Geoffrey Grisagonella, who, after the death of Robert or Ralph of Baugency, married Matilda, daughter of Hugh, viscount of Châteaudun, as we said above and as will appear from what follows. This Ralph is called the son of Landry of Baugency; he traced his descent from another Lancelin, otherwise called Landry, himself son of yet another Landry. Those more penetrating in these matters may decide which account they prefer.

This letter was written about 1103, the year in which, or the preceding year, Grisagonella entered upon the county of Vendôme after the death at Jerusalem in 1104 of his father Geoffrey of Preuilly. [Col. 0462C–D]

## ON LETTER CXXXII

“Allowing the heresy of simony publicly to prevail in the Church of Chartres.” At that time the crime of simony was particularly notorious among churchmen—and scarcely anyone could be found who was not infected by that pestilence. Ivo laboured, as far as he could, to expel it from his church, but his effort was futile. His successor Geoffrey of Leves, however, at the urging of Robert of Arbrissel, wholly drove it out. I learn this from Andrew, the writer of Robert’s Life and his companion. For he reports the matter thus:

> “Because the simoniacal heresy, which had for a very long time defiled the basilica of the canons of Chartres, was, with the consent of Bishop Geoffrey—whose life even in our own age breathes forth the sweetest fragrance—and with the consent of the canons of that same community from the greatest down to the least, extinguished in perpetual condemnation through our Robert. And so that this execrable pest might be condemned forever in that church, they confirmed by oath the vow which they had made.” [Col. 0462D–0463A]

That oath is as follows, and is still taken by one awaiting investiture with a prebend:

> “I, N., who am to be made a canon in the church of Chartres, swear upon these holy relics that for this prebend, investiture in which I await, I have neither given nor promised, nor has anyone, to my knowledge, given or promised on my behalf, gold, silver, any money, or anything else which ought or can be acquired for money; and, if anything has been promised, it shall not be paid through me,” etc.

“But if there are still things which, according to ancient custom, the dean, the cantor, and other ministers publicly demand from those who become canons.” Usage—indeed, rather abuse—prevailed so greatly that this exaction could never be removed from the Church of Chartres. It is covered by the designation of right or of laudable custom and is demanded, on the pretext of examination, from those enrolled in the holy fellowship of the cathedral church by the four senior dignitaries of that church. Yet an abuse is not confirmed by time; for, as the rule of law has it: “What was invalid from the beginning cannot become valid through the passage of time” (*On Rules of Law*, in the Sixth Book).

No one may receive anything, however small, in return for a benefice, especially since the following bull provides against it:

> “Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing. Things established in God’s Church in view of the honourableness of religion ought to be preserved with unshaken firmness. Since, dearest brother in Christ, desiring to expel every simoniacal perversity from the church committed to you, you established, with the consent of the dean, precentor, subdean, succentor, and other prelates of the church—and with the approval and unanimous request of the assembly of brethren—that neither dean, precentor, subdean, succentor, nor any other ecclesiastical person, nor any canon, should demand or receive anything from the dignities or prebends of the church, either personally or through an intermediary.
>
> “None of those who become canons is to give or promise anything for a prebend, either personally or likewise through an intermediary. And after the death of the prelates now living in your church, no dean, precentor, subdean, or succentor is to be appointed to such an office until, in the common chapter, he has plainly sworn that he has given or promised nothing for his office; and likewise until he has sworn that he will demand or receive nothing for prebends, either personally or through an intermediary.
>
> “Likewise, after the death of the ordinary canons now living in the Church of Chartres, no one is to be appointed canon in their place unless he has first sworn in the common chapter—or his guardian has sworn for him, if he is under age—that he has given or promised nothing for the prebend, either personally or through an intermediary.
>
> “Therefore, this constitution, prudently devised by your fraternity for the honour of God and the salvation of souls, we, God granting, confirm by the authority of the apostolic see and decree that it shall remain valid hereafter,” etc.
>
> “Given at Rheims by the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of November [2 November], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Incarnation of the Lord, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Calixtus II,” etc. [Col. 0463B–D]

Let those whom it concerns, therefore, consider whether after this bull they can demand anything from persons “to be made canons,” as they call them.

“Statute of the Church of Chartres concerning the exclusion of freed persons from the clergy,” etc. The canons of Chartres confirmed this statute by oath. Before serfdom was expelled from our Gaul by the will of Louis XI, king of the French, no one was admitted to the greater fellowship of the cathedral unless he declared that he was of free condition: not granted freedom or manumitted; not a *collibertus*, that is, not born of a free father or mother and a slave, or conversely.

For the cantor, or another acting in his place—for the installation of canons and all other clerics of the church, excepting the dean alone, belonged to him—asked the person about to enrol himself in the community in these words:

> “You swear upon these sacred relics that you were begotten in lawful marriage; likewise, that you are of free condition, that you are not a *collibertus*, nor the son of a *collibertus*,” etc. [Col. 0464A]

The person to be made a canon answered that he had been born in and of lawful marriage and was a free man. He repeated this when the chapter was sitting, adding the following oath:

> “I also swear in good faith that, with the assistance of the chapter, I shall observe the custom of this church concerning the exclusion from the canons or clergy of persons born from the bed of manumitted persons or sons of manumitted persons—except those whom the Church of Chartres knowingly customarily receives—and concerning the exclusion from the canons or choir-clergy of sons of concubines.”

And because at that time disputes and conflicts were active between Countess Adela and the chapter of Chartres concerning the defence of the church’s liberties and privileges, they added to this oath:

> “Likewise, I swear that I shall faithfully defend, including by contributing expenses if necessary, with the counsel of the chapter, the liberties of the church, its statutes, lawful and approved customs, especially its privileged customs, and privileges which have not been derogated from and which the church employs in its business and lawsuits.
>
> “Likewise, I swear that, in the affairs which we have and shall have against the count of Chartres and Blois and his bailiffs, officials, and servants, and against any other persons whatever, I shall give faithful counsel and assistance in good faith, according to my conscience, for the Church of Chartres; and that I shall never knowingly act against the church, its customs, statutes, privileges, and liberties—whether I am present in chapter or, if absent, when I am summoned.
>
> “Likewise, I swear that, if any canon or person of Chartres suffers loss or injury, without manifest fault on his own part, at the hands of the count or his men on the occasion of litigation brought against him, his men, and us, I shall give counsel and assistance and shall contribute to the aforesaid matters if necessary.” [Col. 0464B–C]

So reads the old book of oaths of the Church of Chartres. I have not hesitated to report these matters to elucidate this letter, which Baronius, no. 9, dates to 1104.

## ON LETTERS XXXIV AND XXXVI

“William, the countess’s son.” That is, the firstborn, concerning whom Orderic Vitalis writes as follows in Book V of his *History*, p. 574, speaking of Stephen, count of Chartres, and his wife Adela:

> “Stephen begot by the aforesaid wife four sons: William, Theobald, Stephen, and Henry. The first three are powerful counts and are reckoned among the greatest nobles of France and England. The firstborn, William, son-in-law and heir of Gilo of Sully, is a good and peaceable man, abundant in offspring and wealth.”

And in Book II, p. 110, speaking of Adela:

> “After her husband’s pilgrimage, that praiseworthy lady honourably governed his county and diligently raised her young sons for the protection of holy Church. William, who was eldest by birth, took as wife the daughter of Gilo of Sully; possessing his father-in-law’s inheritance, he lived long in peace and begot worthy offspring, Odo and Rainer,” etc. [Col. 0464C–D]

We have mentioned him above in the notes on Letter 94. The present letter may have been written about 1105.

## ON LETTERS CXXXVIII AND CXXXIX

“That your dean Fulk should be elected.” The year in which Fulk was elected bishop of Paris is wholly uncertain, although it is known that he succeeded William. Yet, if conjecture has any value, I agree with Severtius that he was elected about 1100, since I find that in 1099 William occupied the see of Paris in charter 58, folio 26, of the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. But I say that this letter was sent before 1104, because of the subsequent Walo, or Galo, who obtained the bishopric of Paris at the end of that year. On him see Severtius, *Series of the Bishops of Paris*, no. 65. [Col. 0464D–0465A]

## ON LETTER CXLI

To Richard, bishop of Albano, who was then acting as legate in Gaul, so that in the place of Paschal, the supreme pontiff, he might first release Philip, king of the French, from the excommunication which he had incurred because of the shameful liaison he had maintained with Bertrada, an adulteress, and restore him to the sacraments, whether his penitence was genuine or feigned.

The bishops of the provinces of Rheims and Sens had indeed assembled at Baugency with their metropolitan at the legate’s command. But as they disagreed among themselves, and the king also complained that he was being badly treated, the whole affair was referred to Paris, where the king’s absolution was solemnly performed, as is evident from Ivo himself and from the fragment of the *History of France from Robert to the Death of King Philip*.

“That I may be able to come to Troyes.” Two councils were held at Troyes under Pope Paschal: one in 1104 under his legate Richard, the other in 1107 with Paschal himself presiding. From what has been said, I judge that this letter was written at the time of the former. [Col. 0465A–B]

## ON LETTER CXLIII

Richard, abbot of Préaux. Orderic Vitalis speaks of him thus in Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 709:

> “Richard of Fourneaux governed the same monastery in modern times. Robert of Tombelaine—Robert of Monte, continuator of Sigebert—received him as a monk at Bayeux, in the church of Saint-Vigor. But while Odo, bishop of Bayeux and founder of the new monastery of Saint-Vigor, languished in King William’s prison, and Robert the scholar returned to Mont-Saint-Michel-in-Peril-of-the-Sea, where he was a monk—or rather migrated to Italy, as I have related above—the new and unfinished foundation was swiftly destroyed; and the congregation of faithful people that had flocked there from diverse places, lacking a ruler, was quickly dispersed.
>
> “Richard, one of their number, was very learned in sacred letters. Amid so great a devastation of the tender flock he sought religious scholars, among whom, cleaving to wholesome teachings, he lived reverently. For at that time Anselm of Bec, Gerbert of Fontenelle, Guntard of Jumièges, and many others shone in Normandy as lamps in the temple of God. Greatly enlightened by them, he drew from them an abundance of saving teaching.
>
> “After the death of Abbot Goisfred, Richard was elected to govern the abbey of Préaux. He held it for nearly twenty-four years in the time of Duke Robert and King Henry, and died there. He was most devoted to the study of sacred books; from youth he ran in God’s way, following the footprints of the ancient Fathers while singing psalms; he graciously broke the enigmatic bread in the house of God for hungry boys; and he cheerfully and generously distributed it to those stretching out their hands, while compelling the sluggish and unwilling to partake.
>
> “He produced a commentary on Genesis for Maurice, the very learned abbot of Saint-Laumer at Blois; and he composed another work for Lord Adelelm, a very learned priest, a monk of Flavigny, who grew old while reverently serving the Holy Trinity together with the monks of Fécamp. For Pons, the eminent abbot of Cluny, he composed an outstanding exposition of Solomon’s Proverbs. For other venerable persons he lucidly expounded Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, and Deuteronomy; and he composed many treatises, allegorical or tropological, upon the obscure problems of the prophets.” [Col. 0465B–D]

The monastery of Préaux, as Orderic himself writes in the last-cited passage, is situated in a very favourable place in Neustria, near the harbour of the sea and the bridge of Adémar, where the swift Risle seeks the sea and flows into it. It was built by Robert and Henry, brothers and counts of Meulan. It is therefore no wonder that Ivo commends it to Count Robert of Meulan. This letter may have been written about 1104.

## ON LETTER CXLIV

Baugency: a town washed by the Loire, ten miles from Orléans, furnished with an excellent bridge which our kings formerly caused to be built. The bishops of Gaul assembled there to absolve King Philip and Bertrada, his introduced concubine, as we noted above on Letter 141. There too the long-contracted and offspring-confirmed marriage of Louis the Younger, king of the French, and his wife Eleanor, or Alienor, was dissolved by mutual consent—a dissolution that was the beginning of the long, disastrous, and ruinous wars against the English. The town was further distinguished at other times by the frequent assemblies of bishops and princes held there. [Col. 0466A]

## ON LETTER CXLVI

“The clergy and people of the Church of Paris, by unanimous wish and voice, had elected Lord Galo, consecrated bishop of the Church of Beauvais, as bishop.” Because Philip, king of the French, and his son Louis the Fat opposed him, he could not obtain the bishopric of Beauvais. He therefore went to Rome to Pope Paschal II. While they were laying aside their indignation and digesting the resentment they had conceived against him, Paschal sent Galo into Poland. Returning thence about the end of 1104, he was elected bishop of Paris through Ivo’s agency and with the supreme pontiff’s approval. Compare the preceding Letters 144 and 145, and Letter 260 following, with this letter, which, for the reasons stated above, can be doubted by no one to have been written in 1104. [Col. 0466A–B]

## ON LETTER CXLVII

“Persons under condition” (*conditionarii*). Besides what we said above on Letter CXXXII concerning slaves not being admitted to the clergy, a few matters may here be added for greater clarity. Papal rescripts require those subject to servile condition also to be counted among slaves, throughout Distinction 54. For, as is said there in the canon *Si quis propter obligationem servilem*, the clergy rejected them and did not permit their ordination unless they had first obtained freedom from their masters.

This is expressly stated in the canon *Nulli* of the same Distinction:

> “Let no one of servile condition be promoted to sacred orders unless he first obtains lawful freedom from his own master. The charter of that freedom shall be read publicly from the ambo before ordination; and if no one objects, they shall be consecrated lawfully. But a slave not canonically consecrated, after he has fallen from his rank, shall be of the condition in which he was before receiving that rank.” [Col. 0466B–C]

They were called *conditionarii* because they were bound to some servile tax, condition, or the patronage of some household, as the same canon *Si quis* states. Under this designation were also included the *adscripticii*, persons who had remained upon the soil for thirty years; see *Code*, *On Agriculturists and Census-Payers*, Book II, chapter *Cum satis*. The *colonus*, tenant, and similar persons are defined under the same title, in the laws *Originarii vel servus* and *Si coloni*. Like a runaway slave, they do not acquire freedom by prescription through the passage of time; see *On Fugitive Slaves*, Book L.

All *originarii* likewise—who traced their origin from *adscripticii* and had been born on that very soil—as well as agents, managers, executors, or guardians of wards, were excluded from receiving orders by the canon *Magnus* of the same Distinction, because they were subject not to their own right but to another’s. [Col. 0466C–D]

Therefore, when the countess of Chartres wished to force her slaves and freed persons into the Church of Chartres, the canons resisted, maintaining that no one should be admitted to their fellowship unless he was of free, not servile, condition. For although they were called manumitted, they were not thereby free: since their service was retained, they remained liable to servitude and could, whenever she wished, be returned to their former slavery. This tended to the disgrace of the clergy. If clerics became slaves—that is, were restored to their former state—it was disgraceful for the clergy to see the members of their order relapse into servitude and be impeded by base duties.

Accordingly, lest so great an injury be inflicted upon the clerical order, the members of the greater church or mother church enacted a statute excluding freed persons and *colliberti* from the clergy, as we reported above on Letters 32 and 116, in order wholly to exclude those *conditionarii* from orders and ecclesiastical benefices. The countess took the decree badly and left no stone unturned to procure its revocation as far as she could. In her way stood the confirmation of the supreme pontiff, in a charter or bull still read among the church’s privileges.

The countess’s *conditionarii* pressed their case. Born in lawful marriage, they were also royal *fiscalini*: that is, members of the lord’s household—as in Marculf’s *Formulas*—or slaves assigned to the fisc. Marculf says of each fiscal estate that three persons among the male and female servants should be released from service. See also *Capitularies*, Book III, chapter 16. These *fiscalini*, I say, persons attached to the fisc, pressed for an exception from the privilege granted to the Church of Chartres excluding *conditionarii*, and asked that the supreme pontiff order them restored to the condition in which they had been before the privilege. [Col. 0467A–B]

Ivo intervened with Paschal. Certain canons of Chartres did not oppose the dissolution of the statute or of the oath taken by them, although others resisted, since they admitted that they had made it upon this condition: that they might both add to their institution what was advantageous for the future and exclude what was harmful, as Ivo says here. The countess added threats; embittered by each fresh refusal, she stirred up losses, scandals, anger, quarrels, and disturbances.

At length Adela’s importunity and the obstinacy of her followers prevailed. From Paschal II, the supreme pontiff, they extorted rather than obtained this charter:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clerics of the Church of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing. We have learned from the unquestionable testimony of truthful brethren,” etc.

See Paschal II, under no. 403. [Col. 0467B]

Yet neither that charter nor the decree of papal judgment calmed the disturbances which had arisen from it, since certain members of the highest collegiate body of the diocese would not depart even a nail’s breadth from the statute they had made concerning *conditionarii* and persons of common birth. This is clear from the oaths cited above on Letter 132. It is certain that even afterwards the canons of Chartres made a solemn oath against the count of Chartres and Blois and his officials.

The oath concerning the admission into the Church of Chartres of legitimate offspring from marriage still remains. But there is now no mention of freed persons or *colliberti*, since ecclesiastical decrees and the enactments of kings and princes have loosed and cast off the yoke of servitude from their heads.

Bernerius, abbot of Bonneval. See above on Letter 78 concerning him. He was summoned from the abbacy of Déols in Berry to the prelacy of Bonneval. He had been a monk, and finally abbot, of this Benedictine monastery in the Dunois, built by Emperor Charles the Bald in the year of the Lord 840. At his request, and at the request of Theobald, count of Chartres and Blois, and Hugh, viscount of the Dunois, Louis the Fat, king of the French, confirmed at Étampes, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October [14 September] 1110, all that his predecessors had granted to the monastery, as the letters show.

Certain disputes arose between Ivo and Bernerius. Robert of Arbrissel and Bernard of Tiron laboured greatly to settle them in 1115. To Bernerius there survive Letters 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 19 of Book IV of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme. The year in which this letter was written does not appear clearly; but I should judge it to have been sent in 1105. [Col. 0467C–D]

## ON LETTER CXLIX

To William, archbishop of Rouen. William of Jumièges says of him in Book VII, chapter 26, of his *History of Normandy*:

> “After him”—that is, Lanfranc, abbot of Caen and afterwards archbishop of Canterbury—“William, a monk and son of Radbod, bishop of Sées, held the government of the church of Caen; and after John, metropolitan of Rouen, he himself received the archbishopric.”

He was the first professed monk and second abbot of the monastery of Caen, recently founded by William I, duke of the Normans and king of the English, and finally metropolitan of Rouen. Orderic Vitalis expressly writes in Book V of his *History*, p. 551:

> “At the church of Caen, William, son of Radbod bishop of Sées, succeeded Lanfranc. About nine years later, as I think, King William promoted him from there to govern the metropolitan church of Rouen. He was a cousin of William, bishop of Évreux, son of Gerard Flaitel, whose power in Neustria was especially great in the time of the Richards.
>
> “As canon and archdeacon of Rouen, he served Bishop Maurilius. Burning more ardently with the love of God, he travelled abroad with Theodoric, abbot of Jumièges, and reverently visited the glorious tomb of the Saviour at Jerusalem. On his return, lest he lose the fruits of his earlier labours, he wholly withdrew from worldly enticements and gladly devoted himself to God’s service at the monastery of Bec. Then, with Lanfranc, he was brought to instruct the novices flocking to the castle of Caen for Christ’s service; shortly afterward he became their praiseworthy father and master.” [Col. 0468A–B]

And in Book V, p. 568, after speaking of John, he adds:

> After him William, noble and gracious man,  
> Governed the people of Rouen in catholic faith.

He adds these words:

> “He was the second abbot of Caen and, having been brought thence, flourished for twenty-two years in the archbishopric during the pontificates of Popes Gregory, Victor, Urban, and Paschal. He buried King William and Queen Matilda at Caen.”

According to the chronicle of Caen, he died in 1110, in January or February, as is also shown by his epitaph. From what he relates below concerning the Flammards, it is evident that this letter was written in 1107.

“Flame-bearing boys.” This alludes to their surname. They were sons of Ralph Flambard—called in English *Flamme*—bishop of Durham. With a new and unheard-of presumption he had thrust them into the church of Lisieux while it lacked a pastor, although they were twelve-year-old boys, striving to have one succeed the other, should the first fail, as though by hereditary right.

Orderic Vitalis discusses the matter at greater length in Books VIII and X. From them I have excerpted only what bears upon the elucidation of this letter and explains why William, whom Ivo calls bishop-elect of Lisieux, did not obtain the episcopate:

> “Not long afterwards, the aged bishop of Lisieux, Gislebert surnamed Maminot, died in August. Fulcher, brother of Flambard, was consecrated bishop of that see by Archbishop William in June. Almost illiterate, he was snatched from court into the episcopate through his brother’s influence. After possessing it with praiseworthy generosity for seven months, he died in January.
>
> “Then Ranulf Flambard, living in exile in Normandy and deprived of the bishopric of Durham because of the hostility of the king whom he had opposed, procured the bishopric of Lisieux for his boy son Thomas and governed it for three years, not as bishop but as administrator. Meanwhile William of Pacé strove to seize the episcopate after giving a huge price to the count; but, condemned first at Rouen and afterwards at Rome for simoniacal corruption, he paid bitterly for his rashness.
>
> “Thus Lisieux lacked a ruler for nearly five years, and the Lord’s flock, lacking its appointed pastor, lay exposed to wolves’ teeth, until by God’s grace John was designated bishop for the consolation of his people.” [Col. 0468B–D]

## ON LETTER CL

“A council to be held by your Holiness … at the Lateran or at Troyes.” The latter was held about the feast of the Lord’s Ascension in 1107, according to Abbot Ursperg in his chronicle. I therefore conclude that this letter was written in that year.

## ON LETTER CLI

To Geoffrey, bishop of Beauvais: successor to Walo, or Galo, after his translation to the see of Paris, he was elected in 1105. This letter may have been sent to him in that year or the following. [Col. 0469A]

## ON LETTER CLII

To Leodegar, venerable archbishop of Bourges. He entered upon the see in 1097 and held it until 31 March 1120. He is mentioned in the Life of Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the Order and monastery of Fontevraud. He attended Robert’s funeral both at Orsan in his diocese, where Robert died, and at Fontevraud, where he received his grave. For Brother Andrew, writer of Robert’s deeds, records:

> “At that same time Leodegar, a man flourishing in life and age, held the archbishopric of the diocese of Bourges. As I think, an inseparable affection joined him to Master Robert. They were united, I believe, by so great a mutual love that what one wished the other would scarcely refuse.” [Col. 0469A]

To this we may add what is contained in charter 159, folio 49, of the cartulary of Fontevraud:

> “The authority of the ancient Fathers ordained that whatever was bestowed upon churches should be entrusted to the memory of writings, lest it be erased by the darkness of forgetfulness. Let all men, future as well as present, know that on the same day when the body of Master Robert of Arbrissel, by God’s grace brought from far away, had been buried in the place of Fontevraud which he founded with God’s help, no small multitude of religious persons had gathered there to perform the funeral rites of so great a man. One of them was Leodegar, archbishop of the Church of Bourges.” [Col. 0469B]

Such affection existed between Leodegar and Robert that Leodegar wished, in accordance with the desire of his beloved Robert, to make his testamentary disposition at Orsan, a nunnery in the diocese of Bourges belonging to the same Order of Fontevraud. Thus Leodegar wished to be buried at Orsan in accordance with the desire of his beloved Robert, so that those who had been one heart while alive might sleep in harmony after death, and those who had loved each other in life might not be separated even in death. This letter was sent by Ivo about the year 1105. [Col. 0469B–C]

## ON LETTER CLIII
Gilbert, bishop of Évreux. Orderic Vitalis says of him as follows, in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 520: “When William, bishop of Évreux, had died, Baldwin, the duke’s chaplain, succeeded him and governed the bishopric canonically for almost seven years. When he died, Gilbert, son of Osbern, canon and archdeacon of Lisieux, succeeded; he held the bishopric beneficially for more than thirty years, increased the Church’s resources in many ways, and improved them by his prudence.” And in Book XII, p. 840: “In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1112, Gilbert, the aged bishop of Évreux, having lived thirty-four years in the episcopate, died in a good old age on the fourth day before the Kalends of September [29 August], and was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which he himself completed, caused to be dedicated, enriched with possessions and ornaments, enlarged its clergy, and devoted night and day to ecclesiastical worship,” etc.

I possess in manuscript a letter written to Ivo on behalf of this Gilbert by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons. Since it has not yet been published, I shall set out its text here: “H., bishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, to his reverend brother J., bishop of Chartres, greeting. Let your brotherhood know,” etc. See under Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, *Patrologia*, vol. CLVII.

Who this Ursio was, however, I do not sufficiently know—unless perhaps he was a son of Nivelon of Fractavalle, concerning whom Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, frequently complained, and who were ordered by Paschal II to abstain from sacred offices. See his letters II.8, 9, 13, 24, and 30. That this letter was written by Ivo in 1096 is clear, because in that same year the Church of Sens was vacant through the death of Richer.

## ON LETTER CLIV

Ranulf of Durham. Although we have said something above concerning him in the note on Letter 149, since almost all writers of that age mention him, I have thought it proper to add the following, so that he may become better known in all respects and be depicted in his own colours.

Accordingly, from Orderic Vitalis, Books VIII and X: he was the son of a certain Thurstan, a commoner and priest of Bayeux. His mother, given over to divinations, often spoke with a demon, and had lost an eye as a result of that impious intercourse. From childhood he grew up among court retainers and low parasites, devoting himself more to crafty evasions and ingenious verbal contrivances than to the art of letters. Hence Robert, the royal steward, surnamed him Flambard; and that name was bestowed upon him, as it were prophetically, in accordance with his character and deeds.

When he had grown older, he won the favour of King William of England in his youth, and incited him to make a new survey and division of the whole of England, and to take away from inhabitants—whether natives or newcomers—whatever they possessed beyond the prescribed assessment. Hence arose the stain of evil.

For the youthful king, when prelates of churches died, appropriated their revenues and granted a portion, though sparingly, to each of his retainers, keeping the remainder for himself; so that churches remained bereft of pastors for one, two, or indeed five years or more. Anselm, abbot of Bec, having been raised to the metropolitan see of the people of Dorobernia or Canterbury, endeavoured to remedy so great an evil. He repeatedly admonished the king and nobles to abstain from the resources of the churches, but achieved nothing; indeed, he endured exile and harsh treatment, and was ordered to remain away from the kingdom for a long time.

Meanwhile Flambard obtained the bishopric of Durham. Together with the king’s agents, he ravaged everything in England; coveting churches deprived of their prelates, he amassed the treasures of the dead and assigned them to the fisc. Consequently, having become chief administrator of the royal wealth and justiciar, he despised all the nobles, including Henry himself, the future heir of the English realm; and, gathering resources from every side and increasing his honours, he rose above all to universal astonishment.

This man, raised from the dregs of the people to the highest dignities of the kingdom, offended many; hated by all, several devised how to cast him down from so great a height of prosperity and restrain his arrogance. William Rufus’s death conveniently occurred. Deprived of his protector, he was thrown down from the lofty summit of power and committed by Henry to the custody of William de Mandeville in the Tower of London.

But, enclosed in a cask and lowered by a rope sent in by his followers, he escaped from the tower. Carried swiftly on a riding horse into Normandy, he met Robert, Henry’s adversary, by whom he was kindly received and made governor of Neustria. He did not remain long in that dignity: when Robert’s fortunes fell, his own fell likewise. Yet, sharp in intellect and cunning by skill or deceit, he ingratiated himself with Henry, formerly his enemy. Peace having been restored to him by the prince, he abandoned the bishopric of Lisieux, upon which he had laid claim and which he had tried to preserve for his sons, and returned to Durham.

Nicholas Harpsfield adds certain details which are not altogether unworthy of notice and should therefore be reported here. In chapter 28 of his account of the eleventh century, he writes:

> “When he was attacked before the king by many accusations, to which the king gave no hearing, a certain Gerald conspired with others to kill him. Employing a crafty plan, he came to him, pretending that he had been sent by Maurice, bishop of London, who was dangerously ill and greatly desired to speak with him; and that, lest there be any delay in coming, Maurice, who was staying on the bank of the Thames, had sent his boat. Ranulf embarked; Gerald took him out into the open sea and placed him aboard a ship crowded with armed men. Deliberation was already being held concerning his death. The task was assigned to two sailors, who were to receive as the reward of their crime the costly garments which he wore. But, since by chance they could not agree about dividing them, the killing was deferred until the following day. Meanwhile a violent storm arose, and all were in danger of their lives. When the storm had subsided, with the help of a certain man who was the principal figure after Gerald, Ranulf was at last put ashore and returned to land. Gerald went into voluntary exile.
>
> “The king thereafter held Ranulf in greater favour than before, praised his abilities as so suited to his own purposes—although they brought the greatest harm to the commonwealth and the utmost envy and hatred upon Ranulf—and finally advanced him to the bishopric of Durham. After Rufus died and Henry succeeded, Henry threw him into the Tower of London. From there he later escaped by night and, through letters, stirred up Robert, Henry’s brother, who granted him the bishopric of Lisieux and afterwards invaded England with an army. But when peace was subsequently made between the king and Robert, he remained in the bishopric until the year of Christ 1128. In order to secure more firmly the king’s favour and that of those most intimate with the king, he spent lavishly, and oppressed his church with heavy exactions; yet he was never able fully to recover it,” etc.

Three years after his return, he began that castle on the bank of the River Tweed. He also built a notable bridge on the banks of the River Wear,” etc.

Matthew Paris also writes about him under Henry I; so do Polydore Vergil in his *English History* and others. The letter was written in 1107.

## ON LETTER CLVII

Baronius maintains that this was written by Ivo to Paschal in 1107. As to his statement that the church in Normandy had been prostituted, compare this letter with our notes on Letter 27 and on the preceding Letters 149 and 156.

## ON LETTER CLVIII

The count of Troyes: namely Hugh, as Juretus correctly observes on this letter. This Hugh was the son of Theobald, count of Chartres, and Adela of Crépy, and brother of Stephen Henry, likewise count of Chartres and Meaux. By parental succession he acquired the counties of Troyes and Bar-sur-Aube, and thus sometimes assumed for himself the title Count of Champagne.

In 1097 he first betrothed Constance, daughter of Philip I, king of the Franks; by her he had Odo and Philip, as appears from the cartulary of the monastery of Avenières. But after a divorce on grounds of consanguinity in 1104, Constance married Bohemond, prince of Antioch, at Chartres in 1106, according to Suger in his account of Louis the Fat, Orderic Vitalis, Book XI, p. 817, and others.

Hugh, however, married a Lombard woman. Leaving her pregnant, he sold the county to his nephew Theobald the Great, count of Chartres, son of his brother, and went to Syria. There, while his wife was still living, he professed the military order of the Brothers of the Temple, as Bernard states in Letter 31 and Ivo in the following Letter 245. He lived long, even to extreme old age.

**Genealogy.** It is not easy to say in what degree of kinship Hugh and Constance were connected through a common ancestor on their parents’ side. Since authorities differ in their explanations, I shall not do the same; I leave the matter to more learned persons for examination. The letter was written in 1104, after the Council of Troyes.

## ON LETTER CLIX

Baronius maintains that this was written in 1096, no. 10. But I do not see how he can say this, since Paschal was elected only on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [29 July] 1099, according to Onuphrius; and from what is said in this letter it is clear that it was sent not in that year but later.

As for the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés: “Blessed Father Benedict,” writes Orderic Vitalis in Book VIII of his history, p. 712, “as is plainly clear to us all, sent blessed Maurus, prior of his monastery, whom he had raised from childhood, into Gaul; and through him he sent to the Franks the book of the Rule, which the man of God himself had written in his own hand, together with a pound of bread and a measure of wine. Received by King Theudebert, he remained in Gaul until his death and, aided by Florus, counsellor of the king, built a monastery there and trained 140 monks according to the Rule in the place called Glanfeuil,” etc.

“But after the death of blessed Maurus,” as Rodulfus Glaber says in Book III, chapter 5 of his history, “in the course of time the monks were driven out by hostile attacks from the monastery surnamed Glanfeuil, which he himself had built, as is recorded in his deeds, in the territory of Anjou.” Not far from Saumur, on the bank of the Loire, they carried the holy man’s body, or sacred relics, to the monastery of Fossés, to be kept there.

Odo, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Maur, attests in the preface to his book on the Life of that saint that this happened in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 868, under Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, and Arura [reading uncertain], bishop of Paris. For in 845, when Count Rorico had restored Glanfeuil after its destruction by barbarians, he subjected it to Ingelbert, abbot of Fossés. The latter took brethren from his own congregation and sent them there; under Gauslin, governor of the monastery, in the time of Ursmar, archbishop of Tours, Ebroin, bishop of Poitiers, and Dodo, bishop of Angers, they remained there until the Northmen ravaged Gaul.

Then, around 861, they removed the holy remains of blessed Maurus from the monastery lest they be defiled by impious persons. Carrying that pious burden about in wandering for six years, they finally laid it down in the monastery of Fossés on the Ides of November [13 November] 868. From the saint’s name it was called the Abbey of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, and it is still so called.

Pope Urban II, at the Council of Tours in 1096, dissolved the union of Glanfeuil with the monastery of Fossés and assigned Glanfeuil to Monte Cassino, as Peter of Monte Cassino writes in Book IV, chapter 18 of his chronicle. We have not quoted his words because they are given by Juretus. The monks of Fossés, who took this grievously and with resentment, employed Ivo as their advocate before Pope Paschal II, asking that Glanfeuil be restored to them, as appears from this letter, which may have been written to Paschal while he was in Gaul in 1106 or 1107.

## ON LETTER CLX

O., abbot of the monastery of Jumièges. He was called Orsus or Ursus. Thus Orderic Vitalis calls him in Book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 765: “Guntard, the energetic abbot of Jumièges, died at Clermont on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [26 November], while the famous synod was being celebrated there. The king put in his place Tancard, provost of Fécamp. After several years, however, a shameful disturbance having arisen between him and the monks, he departed in disgrace; Ursus of Rouen, a monk of that same church from childhood, succeeded him for twenty years.”

He likewise calls him so in Book XII, p. 846, and he is designated by this name in Robert’s succession-list of the abbots of Jumièges. As for the letter, I conjecture that it was written about 1107.

The monastery of Jumièges belonged to the Benedictine order in the diocese of Rouen. William of Jumièges, a monk, says of it in Book II, chapter 6:

> “The place is rightly called Jumièges [Gemeticum], because those who groan there for their offences will not groan amid avenging flames. Some, however, think that it is called from a jewel [gemma], because, like a jewel in a ring, it shines in its situation and abundance of fruits. In the time of Clovis, king of the Franks, it was built by Saint Philibert, with the aid of Queen Bathildis, and it grew to such greatness that its community amounted to nine hundred monks. There a very great multitude of bishops, clerics, and noble laymen, despising worldly splendour, assembled to serve Christ the King and bowed their own necks beneath the most salutary yoke,” etc.

But when, in the first invasion, the Northmen levelled the monastery with sword and fire, William II, duke of the Normans, restored it and granted the monks rich estates for their support. The same author discusses these matters in Book I, chapter 6; Book II, chapter 9; and Book III, chapters 7 and 8.

## ON LETTER CLXI

**Obedience.** The ancient monks called an *obedientia* the administration of a particular place, to which certain persons were assigned from the monastery in order to gather its crops and other revenues and convey them to the monastery. Such places are now called priories or chapels, though they were formerly also called cells.

Thus Geoffrey of Vendôme, Book I, Letter 9: “The obedience which I afterwards had to redeem for twenty-five thousand solidi.” And Book II, Letter 32: “They so plundered and devastated our obedience that the monks who inhabit and cultivate it must leave, and it must be reduced to solitude.” Also Book V, Letter 18: “You asked, therefore, that we should restore Rainald Quartald to the obedience from which we removed him,” etc.

Fulbert, in our Letter 1, uses the word in the same sense, as do papal letters throughout. Hence those monks who are sent to outlying cells or priories are called *obedientiarii*, “obedience-holders.”

A cell is a small monastery subject to another monastery and is commonly called a priory or provostship. Lupus of Ferrières says of it in Letter 2: “The cell of Saint Josse, which the great Charles formerly entrusted to Alcuin for the giving of alms to pilgrims,” etc. And in Addition I to the Capitularies of Emperor Louis, title 44, it is written: “that abbots may be permitted to have cells in which there are either monks or canons, and that the abbot shall ensure that he permits no fewer than six monks to live there.”

The name is derived from the Greek **ἀπὸ τοῦ κελλίου**, “from *kellion*, a little house.” Hence Moschopulus, in his notes: **Κέλλιον κοινῶς παρὰ Ἀττικοῖς δωμάτιον**, that is, “*kellion*: among the Attic writers, commonly a little dwelling.”

## ON LETTER CLXIV

Maurice, abbot of Saint-Laumer at Blois, was appointed in place of Geoffrey when the latter renounced his rank, as may be seen in Geoffrey of Vendôme, Book II, Letter 14, quoted by Juretus. We mentioned him above from Orderic Vitalis in the note on Letter 143. He died on the sixth day before the Ides of July [10 July], according to the necrology of Saint-Pierre-en-Vallée at Chartres. In what year I do not know. He was nevertheless alive in 1106 and 1107, in one of which years this letter may have been written.

## ON LETTER CCLXV

Samson, bishop of Worcester. He was advanced from a canonry at Bayeux to the episcopal mitre of Worcester. Nicholas Harpsfield thus writes of him in his *Ecclesiastical History of England in the Eleventh Century*: “When Wulfstan died, Samson, canon of Bayeux, was appointed his successor by King Rufus. He was not lacking in learning, eloquence, or distinction in other respects. Yet some held it against him that, where Wulfstan had established monks at Westbury, he deprived them of it.”

Orderic Vitalis also speaks of him thus, in Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 665: “Among the disciples whom Hugh, bishop of Bayeux, thus raised were Thomas, archbishop of York, and his brother Samson, bishop of Worcester.”

## ON LETTER CLXVI

Baronius judges that this letter was written in 1104, no. 17. I judge it to be from 1105, since Bruno, bishop of Segni, was sent as legate into Gaul by the supreme pontiff only in 1104. This is clear from Ivo himself, when he writes that in the preceding summer Hugh the White had appeared before the legate—unless he reckons years in the French manner.

Indeed, Sirmond observes in his note on Book II, Letter 14 of Geoffrey of Vendôme that this legation of Bruno, bishop of Segni in the Italian Campania, fell only in 1106. He attempts to prove this from the fact that Peter the Deacon and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, write that Bohemond, prince of Antioch, came into Gaul in that year.

More correctly, however, others say that Bohemond came into Gaul in 1105, in which year, as we noted above on Letter 158, he married at Chartres Constance, daughter of King Philip and sister of Louis the Fat. Orderic Vitalis, Book II, p. 817, likewise affirms this when he says that in March of that year Bohemond went to the shrine of Saint Leonard, famous in the Limousin, and, after fulfilling his vow, married the aforesaid Constance after Easter.

Suger mentions Hugh the White in his account of Louis the Fat in these words: “Seeing this, the most noble men Enguerrand of Boves, Ebalus, count of Roucy, Andrew of Ramerupt, Hugh the White of La Ferté …”

Waleran, the king’s chamberlain. He is mentioned in title 18 of the *Great Campbel* in the act or instrument of a grant made to the monastery of Saints Bartholomew and Magloire at Paris by Simon, lord of Montfort, in 1072, concerning the churches of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Lawrence, archdeacon and martyr, in the town of Montfort (Judith 10). There Waleran the chamberlain is listed among the witnesses. He is likewise named as witness in the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, fol. 75, in King Philip’s charter concerning a mill at Grand-Pont, dated at Orléans in 1075. Tilliet calls him Guy Waleran, in *On the Kings of France, Their Court and Household*.

## ON LETTER CLXVIII

Baronius writes that this letter was written in 1104; I say 1106, since Hugh of Pithiviers, of whom the letter treats, went to Jerusalem in that year or the following. For he undertook the journey to Jerusalem with Bohemond in 1106, as may easily be inferred from the fragment of a history of the Franks published by Robert at the death of King Philip.

For there one reads:

> “Bohemond, etc., crossed the sea and came into Gaul. He led out from it an innumerable multitude both of horsemen and soldiers and, drawing them not only from Gaul but from the whole West, attempted to disturb the empire of the Greeks, on the ground that the emperor always opposed all those travelling to Jerusalem, etc. Bohemond therefore married the daughter of King Philip and, having prepared supplies necessary for so great an army, crossed the narrow sea at the port of Bari in springtime and brought his fleet safely to the opposite shore. Then, passing through the Greek empire and devastating cities, towns, villages, and fields, he came to Dyrrhachium, which he surrounded with a siege and attacked for a long time, etc. The duke, hearing that imperial legions were coming against him, likewise sent a strong force from his own men to meet them, six days’ journey away. On Holy Saturday they reached the foot of the mountain upon which the castle of Corbianum is situated, etc.; but in the morning, since it was Holy Easter, they all received communion. Finally the enemy, drawn up for battle, awaited them. The Franks, therefore, exhorting one another cheerfully, attacked them. Their leaders were Hugh of Pithiviers, Rainerius Brunus, Philip of Mont-Aureol, Robert of Vieux-Pont, and others.”

From this I infer that, if Bohemond betrothed Constance at Chartres after Easter in 1105 or 1106, he besieged Dyrrhachium only in the following year, 1106 or 1107, and fought the Greek emperor’s forces on Easter Day after a full year had passed. Accordingly I maintain that Hugh of Pithiviers was in the army in that same year.

The events here related concerning that Hugh and Ivo, lord of Courville, must have occurred within the same year in which Bohemond came into and departed from France, since Hugh and the others named above travelled east with him. Therefore it is clear that this letter was written in 1106 or 1107, not 1104, when Hugh and the others were already preparing to depart.

Ivo himself settled the dispute between Ivo of Courville, the viscount Hugh, and Rotrou, count of the Perche. Seeing that he was being pressed by a powerful adversary, Ivo of Courville conceived the plan of setting a more powerful man against him—namely Theobald, count of Chartres. He sold to Theobald the disputed possessions, as appears from the following instrument copied from the cartulary of the monastery of Tiron:

> “Ivo of Courville, renouncing the world, left Courville to Count Theobald, together with everything he held from the fief of that count or of the viscount. For these things Count Theobald gave him two hundred marks of silver and swore that, with his own knowledge, he would maintain the alms-gifts. He also swore that he would hold the land with the customs under which Ivo held it; that he would impose no customs upon the lands of the saints, nor knowingly permit his servants to impose them through the castle of Courville; and that he would restore the land to Robert of Vieux-Pont when Robert himself repaid him the aforesaid money.
>
> “He swore the aforesaid oaths and that, from the first Christmas after this agreement until a year had elapsed, he would restore it to no one else. If Robert did not come by that term, he would restore it to the son of William of Tortaquerque, whom William had by Robert’s sister, under the aforesaid arrangements concerning Robert. If there were no son, he would marry one of William’s daughters, whom William had by Robert’s sister, to one of his own men, together with all that land, under the aforesaid arrangements concerning Robert.
>
> “As sureties for these agreements, Count Theobald gave upon his faith Geoffrey, viscount of Châteaudun; William Gohiet the younger; Guy of Gallardon; Andrew of Bâliment; Gohier of Aulnay; Gerard Boel; Gauslin of Leuges; Hugh of Château-Thierry; and the men of Évrardville. The count gave these as sureties upon his faith, so that, if he departed from the aforesaid agreements, they would adhere to the rightful heir.”

“That justice might be done him which was owed to those travelling to Jerusalem and to the Peace.” Rodulfus Glaber, Book IV of his *History*, chapter 5, writes thus of that Peace in the year one thousand from the Passion of the Lord, etc.:

> “Then for the first time, in the regions of Aquitaine, gatherings of councils began to be assembled by bishops, abbots, and other devout men of sacred religion, drawn from the whole populace, etc. It was proclaimed throughout all bishoprics that councils should be held in appointed places by bishops and the magnates of the entire country, for restoring peace and establishing the sacred faith. When the entire multitude of the people heard this, great, middling, and small alike went eagerly, all ready to obey whatever the shepherds of the Church commanded—not less than if a voice sent from heaven spoke to men on earth.
>
> “For all were terrified by the calamities of the preceding time and were troubled by fear lest they fail to obtain the prosperity of future abundance. A detailed written statement had been drawn up, containing both the acts forbidden and those which they had resolved to offer to almighty God by a devout promise. Chief among these was the preservation of an inviolable peace: that men of either rank, whatever offence they had formerly incurred, might proceed unarmed without fear.
>
> “A robber or invader of another’s property was to be severely punished under the strictness of the laws, either by forfeiture of goods or by bodily penalties. Likewise, such honour and reverence were to be shown to the sacred places of all churches that anyone guilty of whatever crime who took refuge there should depart unharmed—except only one who had violated the agreement of the aforesaid Peace; yet even he, if seized, was to suffer the prescribed penalty at the altar. Likewise, no one travelling through the country with clerics, monks, or nuns was to suffer any violence from another.”

And below:

> “This indeed gave assurance concerning other matters that might be doubtful. All were inflamed with such zeal that they raised their staffs to heaven by the hands of the bishops, while they themselves, with hands stretched out to God, cried unanimously, ‘Peace, peace, peace!’ Thus there might be a sign of the perpetual covenant concerning what they had promised between themselves and God.”

This is what he says concerning that Peace. Whatever Sigebert may say under the year 1032; Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, in the *Chronicle of Cambrai and Arras*, Book III, chapters 52, 53, and 54, in almost the same words; and Baronius under 1034, nos. 2, 3, and 4—the Peace was at last publicly established by Pope Urban II in the Synod of Clermont, as may be seen in his Canon I and in Baronius himself under 1095, no. 50, who records the following canon, which I quote here as a corollary to the foregoing:

> “Likewise it has been decreed that all goods of those travelling to Jerusalem shall always and everywhere remain safe under peace and truce until they return.”

Indeed, Urban said in the address delivered at the Council of Clermont, as reported by Tyre, Book I, chapter 15:

> “Trusting in the mercy of God and in the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we remit immense penances for their sins to the faithful and Christians who take up arms against them and undertake for themselves the burden of this pilgrimage. Those who die in true repentance should not doubt that they will obtain forgiveness of sins and the reward of eternal recompense.
>
