> “Meanwhile, we receive under the Church’s defence and under the protection of blessed Peter and Paul, as sons of true obedience, those who undertake this labour in the fervour of faith in order to overcome them; and we decree that they remain secure from every disturbance, both in other persons’ property and in their own. If anyone should rashly presume to molest them, let him be struck with excommunication by the bishop of the place, and let the sentence be observed by all until what has been taken is restored and fitting satisfaction is made for the injuries inflicted. Bishops and priests who perhaps fail to oppose such persons shall be punished by suspension from office until they obtain the mercy of the Apostolic See.”

A little later he adds:

> “Before all things, labouring faithfully in accordance with the decrees of the synod, let the peace which in the common tongue is called the Truce be observed inviolate by all, so that no impediment may be placed in the way of those wishing to go or to travel for necessities.”

Ivo therefore rightly calls this Peace “justice,” since it had passed into law. Hugh and Ivo of Courville rightly complain that Rotrou, count of the Perche—not count of Maine, as Baronius writes—was disturbing the Peace and appropriating for himself resources protected by the Church from those preparing for the holy war. Compare Letter 90, where that Truce is discussed.

Count Rotrou. He was the son-in-law of Henry I of England, having married his natural daughter Matilda, who perished by shipwreck in 1120 with her brother William Atheling: see William of Jumièges, Book VIII, chapter 29; Orderic Vitalis, Book II, p. 810, and Book XII, p. 870. He had undertaken the journey to Jerusalem with many others in 1096, and therefore returned in 1100, as Orderic records in Book XIII, p. 890:

> “In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, when the leading men had accomplished the business for which they had gone to Jerusalem, they returned and recovered what was theirs, as was just. Then Robert, duke of the Normans, Robert of Flanders, Rotrou of Mortagne, and many others happily returned, and each possessed his own property, while his kinsfolk rejoiced as was fitting.”

In the cartulary of the monastery of Saint-Denis at Nogent, founded by Geoffrey, Rotrou’s father, the following is found at the end of a charter of Theobald of Molesmes: “Witnesses: Rotrou, count of Mortagne, who came from Jerusalem; Hugh, viscount of Châteaudun,” etc.

“This case could not be settled without single combat, and he said that an ordeal of blood ought not to be brought against us.” In Ivo’s age, litigants who could not prove the grounds of their suit—or, as they say, the points at issue—settled matters by single combat, duel, or, as they called it, war; by the test of red-hot iron; or by the proof of cold or boiling water.

All these practices were forbidden by the Lateran Council under Innocent III, canon 18, and by the decretal *Ne clerici vel monachi*, chapter *Sententiam*. Since the ensuing text bears on our subject, we shall quote it:

> “Nor shall any cleric be placed over crossbowmen, archers, or men of blood of this sort; nor shall a subdeacon, deacon, or priest practise that part of surgery which entails cautery or incision. Above all, let no one impart any rite of blessing or consecration to the ordeal of boiling or cold water or of red-hot iron, without prejudice, nevertheless, to the prohibitions concerning single combat or duels promulgated earlier.”

On these matters see *Monomachia*, 2, question 4; and concerning the ordeal of blood, Ivo, *Decretum*, Part V, chapter 315, and Part VI, chapter 222. But since Juretus treats these matters more fully in his notes on Ivo, we add nothing further.

Ivo, lord of Courville. There were several lords of Courville of this name. Courville is a town in the territory of Chartres, four French leagues away from that city. The Ivo of whom our author speaks was the second son of George and Philippa, as appears from the records of Saint-Pierre-en-Vallée at Chartres under the year 1094.

That he was a pious and generous man may be inferred from his granting the church of Saint Nicholas at Courville to the regular canons of Saint John in the Valley of Chartres; from his giving to the monks of Tiron the land of Orgeville, not far from Prunay-le-Gillon; and from his bequeathing many other things to religious houses. On these matters see the cartularies of those abbeys and the note on Letter 267 and later letters.

## ON LETTER CLXIX

Galo, bishop of Paris. He began his episcopate at Paris in 1104, near the end of the year, as appears in the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs at Paris, fols. 37r and 70v.

For in a charter recording the donation of Annet made by Waleran of Villeperat, otherwise Villepreux, with the consent of his brother Guy of Pithiviers and of Hugh, son of Évrard of Pithiviers, it is written that the gift was made publicly in the chapter of Blessed Mary at Paris in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1108, indiction 15, epact 17, concurrent 3, in the first regnal year of King Louis, and the fourth year of the episcopate of Galo.

In the cartulary of the monastery of Coulombs there is another charter of the same Galo, given at Paris in the chapter of Blessed Mary in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, indiction 14, epact 14, concurrent 7, in the forty-eighth regnal year of King Philip and the second year of the episcopate of the said Galo, in the presence of Bernerius, dean, Adam, precentor, etc.

Guy, keeper of the brothers’ possessions. This Guy was brother of Hugh of Pithiviers and viscount of Chartres, and of Évrard, lord of Villeperat, as we said above concerning this letter. I learn this from Book II of the chronicle of the monastery of Morigny, where the following is written: “Guy, viscount of Étampes, etc., was the son of that great Hugh, lord of Pithiviers, in whose fief this church was founded.”

The same is confirmed by the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, fol. 28, charter 60, where it is written: “The witnesses of this grant were Hugh of Pithiviers and his brother Guy.” And at fol. 14v, charter 31:

> “Let all know that Waleran of Villeperat gave to the church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, for the repose of his soul and the salvation of his deceased parents, the land called Aulnay, situated near Saint-Cloud, etc. This gift was granted by Guy, who then held the castle of Pithiviers and was Waleran’s brother, etc.
>
> “After these things had occurred and some time had passed, Hugh, son of Évrard, to whom by paternal right the aforesaid castle of Pithiviers belonged, came one day to Saint-Martin. At the request of Lord Theobald the prior and Lord Gildwin, brother of the aforesaid Waleran, he granted the gift which his uncle had made. Going to the altar, he placed it upon it before the following witnesses: Walter the shield-bearer, etc.
>
> “So that this gift might stand more firmly and the church of Saint Martin might possess the aforesaid land peacefully and without claim in times to come, Count Robert of Meulan granted the gift made by Waleran and confirmed it by his authority. For the land was held from his fief. When he granted it to them, the following witnesses heard it: the advocates William of Bourg-Neuf, Odo of Morainvilliers, and Waleran. This was done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1108, indiction I, in the first year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, while Galo was bishop of the city of Paris.”

From this anyone may understand that Hugh, Waleran, Guy, and Gildwin were brothers and sons of Hugh of Pithiviers.

## ON LETTER CLXXII

Ulcha, commonly Oucques, in the archdeaconry of Dunois and the deanery of the Belsia district, diocese of Chartres.

In the settlement called Montfauni. An instrument preserved in the archive of the monastery of Vendôme contributes much to elucidating this letter; its text is as follows:

> “Whoever, with provident mind, observes the changing frailty of this age ought above all to long for the happiness that endures for ever. Since the manifold grace of God has established many paths by which that happiness is to be sought with the utmost devotion and with all the effort of our mind, each person frequents them in his own way according to the measure of his faith: one enters upon the road to the heavenly kingdom by teaching good things, another by doing what is right, another by some other kind of virtue.
>
> “Among these, I, Ralph of Baugency, though a sluggish traveller, yet, through the capacity for doing good given me by God and borne along by the vehicle of almsgiving, have resolved to pursue the path of life. Therefore, for the salvation of myself and of my predecessors, from my goods and possessions [Col. 0478B] I give and grant to blessed Launomar and his monks land within my stronghold called Montfauni, for building a church and establishing a borough, where until now there has been no parish church.
>
> “The chapel there is dependent upon the mother church founded in the place called Ulcha, in honour of Saint John; to that church are conveyed, from the aforesaid borough and from the whole stronghold, all parochial dues and all the solemn offerings, according to ecclesiastical custom. By the right of that church—which is known to belong to blessed Launomar and his monks—the said chapel, situated in my stronghold, together with the possessions held by the aforesaid monks through the hand of my late father Lancelin, after the monks of Blois had been despoiled of them, was entered upon by the monks of Vendôme, not without usurpation. Thereupon a dispute arose between the said monks in the court of the church of Chartres, with Bishop Ivo presiding. After judicial examination, the monks of Vendôme were expelled, and the chapel itself was restored by that bishop, with the assent of the clergy and by canonical judgment, to the monks of Blois. [Col. 0478C]
>
> “Accordingly, understanding the judgment to be right and acknowledging the right of Saint Launomar, by the command of the same bishop I grant in perpetuity to the aforesaid saint and his monks, without any reservation, whatever I possess in the aforesaid chapel. But because divine service cannot be performed there, and the other greater sacraments and offices of holy Church cannot be celebrated there under the law governing a chapel, while the parish church of Saint John is far removed from it, I have obtained from the aforesaid monks of Blois, with the approval of the aforesaid bishop, permission to build, within the bounds of that same parish and near the aforesaid stronghold, another and more convenient church. I grant them land for building this church and their borough, as stated above, according to the boundaries marked out.
>
> “Let them retain all the settlers whom they can retain there, apart from the inhabitants of my stronghold; and let those settlers be altogether free and exempt from every customary exaction, except that, if necessary, they shall follow me to Campale when I go forth to battle. If the wood called Long Wood should abound in acorns and pasture for swine, all the pigs of the monks, of their men, of those dwelling there, and of others wherever they may live, shall have free use of that wood without any charge for pannage. [Col. 0478D]
>
> “I grant all these things in the terms here set out, so that in the aforesaid new church all sacraments and offices belonging to a parish may henceforth be celebrated.
>
> “These are the names of the witnesses present: on my side, Arraldus Malaterra, Gajuldus, Garnerus Bisol, the bailiff-provost, Thomas the chaplain, Geoffrey the chancellor. On the monks’ side: Bartholomew, Gerard of Doraco, Peter the chamberlain, John of Luco, Leoderic Major. The mark of Ralph; the mark of Macheldis, his wife.”

## ON LETTER CLXXIII

[Col. 0479A]

It is of the same subject matter as the preceding Letters 168 and 169.

## ON LETTER CLXXIV

“For the soul of your brother, the religious king.” That is, Edgar, prince of the Scots, who died without children in 1107, as is clear from Book VII of Buchanan’s Scottish History. I therefore judge this letter to have been written in that or the following year.

## ON LETTER CLXXV

“Of the council summoned by your fatherhood.” He understands the council of Troyes from the following letter, which Baronius asserts, no. 3, was written by Ivo in 1107 to Paschal, who presided over the council.

## ON LETTER CLXXVI

“Wlgrin, chancellor of our church.” That is, of the church of Chartres. When he had been elected bishop by the chapter of Dol in 1107, he did not acquiesce; rejecting the election, he remained, through Ivo’s intervention, in his original position, while Baldwin, abbot of Bourgueil, accepted the dignity which Wlgrin had declined. See volume VII of the *Councils*, part I, p. 540, Morel’s Paris edition of 1636. [Col. 0479B]

## ON LETTERS CLXXVII AND CLXXVIII

“To Geoffrey, bishop of Beauvais.” Claude Robert incorrectly places him before Walo in his series of the bishops of Beauvais, since this Geoffrey began only in 1105, by which time Walo had already been transferred from the bishopric of Beauvais to that of Paris. Baronius, under the year 1107, no. 4, considers Letter 178 to have been written in that same year; and I think the preceding one was written then as well.

## ON LETTER CLXXIX

“The cruel Turks.” *Turcus* and *Turca* are used interchangeably by writers of that age. Thus Albert of Aachen, *History of Jerusalem*, I.22: “Folker, a man of the greatest renown in his land, from Chartres, fell near Nicaea in an encounter with the Turks.” And likewise in V.22: “Baldwin establishes in the city of Sororgia one hundred worthy and battle-seasoned knights against the Turks”; also Book IV, chapter 10, of the *Deeds of the Franks* and other writers on Jerusalem. Soliman, son of the elder Soliman, is called leader of the Turks. Further, in Book VI of the history of Robert, monk of Saint-Remi of Rheims: “He beheld innumerable squadrons of Turks.” William of Tyre also, in Book VI, chapter 22, of his *History of Jerusalem*: “The Turks, having learned of the Christians’ arrival, had thrown themselves down”; and this usage is common. [Col. 0479C]

## ON LETTER CLXXX

“Ralph of Baugency.” Son of Lancelin, lord of that place; see above on Letter 172 and below. Concerning Lancelin I find the following in charter 227 of the cartulary of the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme:

> “Lancelin, lord of the castle of Baugency, was, as regards birth, most distinguished by nobility of lineage and of parents; [Col. 0479D] But as regards the praise of his own virtue, he was especially celebrated for the power of his military courage and for his industrious concern in managing his household affairs. He completed a church in the suburb of his castle which certain faithful persons had begun, caused it to be dedicated by Rainier, bishop of Orléans, in memory of the Holy Sepulchre, and gave it to the Holy Trinity. The canons of Saint Lifard of Baugency contested this, claiming that it stood within their cemetery. Lancelin settled the dispute at Meung in the presence of the same bishop; he then went to Rome, and, on his return, obtained from those same canons the grant to the Holy Trinity of that portion of the cemetery. Ancelin of Beaumont, son of Saint Ralph, son of Lancelin of Baugency, subscribed; he was Lancelin of Baugency’s brother, according to charter 288. Done at Baugency in the year 1081, indiction IV; confirmed by the canons on the fourth Ides of June near the church of Saint Firmin, in the public square.”

Near the end of the same cartulary one reads:

> “Grant of Ralph of Baugency at the city of Poitiers, 1098. [Grant] of Simon, lord of Baugency; of Adenordis, his wife; of Lancelin, Simon’s brother; concerning the fairs of Saint Beatus; and [grant] of Lancelin at Baugency, in the presence of Lord Robert the abbot, seated on his palfrey, in the year 1150.” [Col. 0480A]

Ralph is numbered among the nobles who set out for the holy war in 1096 by William of Tyre, Book I, chapter 17 of his *History*; and among those who supported Theobald, count of Champagne and Chartres, against Louis the Fat, as is stated by Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. Among other things he writes:

> “This same cause enticed Ralph of Baugency, since he had as wife a full-blooded kinswoman of the king, daughter of Hugh the Great.”

And, after a few intervening words:

> “The men of Chartres, Châteaudun, and Brie were kept back, with no one opposing them, by the support of Ralph of Baugency.”

From this one may infer the man’s distinction and noble birth. I think the document was written in 1108, or thereabouts.

## ON LETTER CLXXXI

“Of Vézelay.” Elsewhere, *Vezeliacensis*. Vézelay, or Videliacum, is a place in the diocese of Autun, where stands the church sacred to the Blessed Mary Magdalene, famous for the ashes of that holy penitent. Pope John VIII dedicated it while travelling to the council of Troyes. Gerard, lord of Roussillon, had formerly founded there a convent of nuns; it later passed to ascetics of the Benedictine order, and finally to canons, after the former had been granted secular dress. [Col. 0480B]

“The monastery of Saint Lucian of Beauvais.” Also of the Benedictine order. Childebert, king of the Franks, raised it from its foundations, but his successor Chilperic put the finishing touch to it.

“The church of Buglensis.” More correctly, Bullensis, or the church of Bulles, in the diocese of Beauvais and deanery of Breteuil. Its priory depends upon the church, or collegiate body, of Vézelay. A document restoring the churches and castle of Bulles to Saint Lucian’s abbey, printed by Louvet in Book III, chapter 17 of his *History of Beauvais*, contributes greatly to elucidating this letter. Its text is as follows:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Guy, by the grace of God bishop of the city of Beauvais, have taken care to make known to the faithful the acts performed in our times, for the encouragement of all good persons. Therefore, when Lord Hugh, count of Dammartin, came before us concerning the churches of Bulles—which he admitted that he had held unjustly—we believe that we have given the best possible counsel for his soul. For Saint Lucian the martyr had formerly possessed the same churches with the entire integrity of the castle itself, through the gift of King Childebert and of Constantine, bishop of Beauvais; but afterwards, through incursions of barbarians and the invasion of the impious—that is, the Northmen—he had lost everything. [Col. 0480C]
>
> “Considering this, I immediately advised and persuaded Hugh to restore to the holy martyr what had been unjustly taken away and wrongfully retained. Obeying the commands of our counsel, he went to Lord Theobald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Lucian; acknowledged his own injustice and that of his predecessors; and, with the approval of the canons whom he had placed there, by our command and with the consent of our clergy, restored to the holy martyr those churches with all their appurtenances.
>
> “When the same abbot had gone, by order of our admonition and with certain of his monks, to the named castle, and had received the churches—as stated—by our command and by the count’s restitution, he asked that a document should be made for him concerning this and confirmed by the seal of our authority, since he wished to hold the churches as Saint Lucian had held them. Gladly acceding to his request, we confirmed this charter for him by the impression of our seal. I, Guy, bishop of Beauvais, ordered this charter to be made and subscribed it with my own hand. I, Theobald, abbot, subscribed. I, Hugh, count, subscribed. Done in the city of Beauvais in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1075, in the reign of King Philip, indiction XIII, epact I.” [Col. 0480D]

Ivo wrote this letter in 1108, or approximately then.

“Council of Exoudun.” In French, Issoudun. I have not found in authors the year in which that council was held, unless perhaps it is the one mentioned in the cartulary of Saint-Denis of Nogent-le-Rotrou. In a notice concerning the council of Autun it is so entitled, and is called the Council of Seldun in place of Exoldun. Thus the document reads: “He proceeded to another council which was held at Seldun”—not *Seldulium*, as Brice reads it in his *History of the Counts of Alençon and Perche*, III.4. The cartulary of that same monastery, which is in my possession, reads it thus.

Since the council was summoned between the councils of Sens and Meaux, held in 1080, it must have been celebrated in that year. This appears from the records themselves, which establish that the council of Autun was convened fifteen years later; and it is certain from Berthold and others that the latter was assembled in 1094. As for the letter, I judge it to have been written about 1105 or 1106, since in those years Richard, bishop of Albano, to whom Ivo addresses it, was acting as legate in Gaul. [Col. 0481A]

## ON LETTER CLXXXII

[Col. 0481B]

“I should wish, by presenting the book, to make the investiture of the subdeanery.” At that period the investiture, and likewise the resignation, of lesser benefices was usually made by means of a little book, as that of greater benefices was by a staff or rod. Just as recipients took up a book when receiving benefices, so, when relinquishing them, they laid it down or returned it. See below on this note, where this is discussed. Ivo mentions the ceremony in the instrument granting the priory of Saint Nicasius of Meulan, numbered among the letters by Juretus as no. 285; and Geoffrey of Vendôme, Book I, Letter 6, also mentions it. Writing there about Pagan, formerly abbot of Saint Albinus of Angers, he says:

> “In my presence, in his chapter, he had entirely resigned the abbey into the hands of the bishop of Angers together with the Rule of Saint Benedict.”

Sirmond sheds light upon this in his notes, where he produces testimony from the cartulary of the same monastery of Saint Albinus:

> “Therefore, concerning this alms, I myself, Samson, with the Rule of Saint Benedict by which, as I recall, I had received the Church’s benefice from the abbot and brethren, invested the aforesaid abbot and convent; and I laid that same Rule upon the altar of Blessed Albinus, as a memorial of perpetual validity.” [Col. 0481C]

At times benefices were also surrendered to patrons merely by bending or inclining the body. It was likewise a custom of that age, when persons conferred even secular property upon churches, to lay upon the altar of the church a clod of that land, a knife, a staff, or some other object as a token of investiture. This was called *scotulium* by the authors. Pope Innocent IV teaches this in his letter to the archbishop and chapter of Lyons, and in the *guberno*, *Extra*, chapter *Exsultatis*, “On Custom.”

Various examples of this ceremony occur in ecclesiastical records; and in the archive of the church of Chartres many knives may still be seen to which instruments of donation are attached. In charter 186 of the cartulary in the Chamber of Accounts of the aforesaid church one reads:

> “I, Robert of Chartres, knight, make known that I, a devoted son of the church of Chartres, have granted and given as alms to the canons of the same church revenues of twenty shillings at Rouas and ten shillings at Notre-Dame, etc. Therefore, that fuller notice of this matter may be given hereafter, I humbly approached the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the aforesaid church, acknowledged the aforesaid gift previously made in the Chapter, and, having placed and offered upon that altar a knife with my own hand, confirmed it in the sight and hearing of many,” etc. [Col. 0481D]

The same is found in several charters of the cartulary of the monastery of Vendôme, for example folios 195, 209, 222, and 282, and elsewhere. The same cartulary also shows that investiture was made by placing a piece of wood upon an altar: in Rainald of Burgundy’s confirmation concerning the church of Credon; and in Simon of Baugency’s grant to Robert, abbot of Vendôme, of the fair of Saint Beatus. In the cartulary of Saint Peter in the Valley at Chartres, folio 59, one reads:

> “Concerning the winnowing-fan of Bermaerville, Odo, count palatine and of Chartres, granted that winnowing-fan to the same monastery by placing a branch of savin upon the altar of Saint Peter the Apostle.”

At Saint-Martin-des-Champs there is an instrument in which Henry, son of King Louis the Fat and abbot of Blessed Mary of Étampes, assigns a prebend in the same church of Étampes to the monks of that place, according to the tenure in which Master Albert the Cantor had held it:

> “Which,” he says, “he surrendered into my hands by bread and book; and I in turn likewise entrusted it, by bread and book, into the hands of the venerable Theobald, prior of the Fields.”

The ceremony of investing canons of Chartres by the delivery of a little book still continues in that church. [Col. 0482A]

“Hugh, the dean’s nephew.” Richard of Albano, legate in Gaul, wrote the following letter to him and to his uncle Ernald, a letter which I find in manuscripts in my possession:

> “R., a sinner and an unworthy servant and legate of the Apostolic See, such as he is, minister of the church of Albano, to his dearest friends E., dean of the church of Chartres, and Hu., his nephew: greeting. Since we place great confidence in you, and are willing gladly to assist you, if necessary, in your affairs, we direct our requests to you frankly and confidently; and we are assured of your counsel and assistance, as of those of our friends. Trusting in that assurance, we ask your brotherhood to assist our dearest friend Lord Robert in such a manner concerning his prebend that he may thereby recognize how great the ardour of charity is between us and you. You will find us ready for a like act of service whenever you need us.” [Col. 0482B]

## ON LETTER CLXXXVI

“The monastery of Charity.” It belongs to the Cluniac order and the diocese of Auxerre. Ivo the bishop granted it a church, or cell, in the diocese of Chartres, at the place called Little Bellua, one or two miles from the city. On this monastery see Coquille, *History of the Counts of Nevers*.

## ON LETTER CLXXXVIII

“To Ralph, venerable archbishop of Rheims.” If this is so, the letter was certainly written in 1108 or later, since Ralph obtained the see of Rheims only in that year.

## ON LETTER CLXXXIX

“At the consecration of Louis, king of the Franks.” Baronius maintains, no. 44, that this letter was written in 1106. I place it in 1108, after the inauguration of Louis the Fat. How could Ivo speak of the king’s consecration before he had been anointed? But from better authorities it appears that Louis the Fat began his reign in 1108; hence this letter may be presumed to have been written in that year, not the preceding one. [Col. 0482D]

## ON LETTER CXC

“Lord Theobald, prior of Blessed Martin at Paris.” Paschal II, supreme pontiff, wrote to him on the second day before the Kalends of May, indiction XV, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1108. The bull, issued at Saint-Denis in France, is preserved in the collection of charters of the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs.

“That, after expelling the intruder Gervasius, he should restore peace and permit Lord Ralph, metropolitan of that church, once restored to his favour, to preside over that church.” Ralph, called the Green, archbishop of Rheims, had incurred the very grave and dangerous enmity of Louis the Fat because, without Louis’s consent, he had been elected and enthroned archbishop of Rheims in 1108. In order to reconcile them, the clergy of that church sent envoys to oppose, on behalf of that church, the king’s intended inauguration at Orléans. They were to declare that the first fruits of the king’s crown belonged by right to the church of Rheims, as Suger says in his *Life of Louis the Fat*, and as the continuator of Aimoin, Book V, chapter 45, states:

> “And from the first king of the Franks whom he baptized, Clovis, [the church of Rheims] has possessed this prerogative unimpaired and inviolable.”

They were to subject to perpetual anathema anyone who rashly attempted to violate it. At that time Ralph was in exile, while Gervasius, son of Count Hugh of Rethel and Melisendis of Montlhéry, occupied his see in the meantime. Ivo and Theobald, prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, wrote to Pope Paschal on Ralph’s behalf; they finally secured his restoration to his own see. Robert of Torigni’s continuation of Sigebert, under the year 1114, teaches this:

> “In the metropolitan church of Rheims also, after Manasses, a distinguished man, Gervasius the intruder having been expelled, Ralph succeeded, who bore the surname Green.” [Col. 0483A]

See also Orderic Vitalis, Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 699. He says that Ralph succeeded not Manasses but Renaud. Robert’s statement is nevertheless more certain, since Letter 185 of Ivo is extant to that same Manasses, who immediately succeeded Renaud. From what is stated in the letter itself, I presume that it was written only in 1114.

## ON LETTER CXCII

“To the monks of Coulombs.” Coulombs, or Columba, is a monastery of the Benedictine order in the district of Chartres, situated at the first mile from Nogent-le-Roi. It was begun by Roger, son of Odo II, count of Chartres, by his first or second wife, and himself chancellor of France and bishop of Beauvais; and was completed by Odelric, bishop of Orléans, Roger’s nephew through his sister, in 1028, during the reign of Robert II, king of the Franks, as is certain from the foundation records of this monastery, which we have published elsewhere. The year in which the letter was written is not sufficiently clear. [Col. 0483B]

## ON LETTER CXCIII

[Col. 0483C]

“The church of Saint Quentin.” Namely, that at Beauvais.

“Guy, bishop of Beauvais.” See Louvet, *History of Beauvais*, Book IV, chapter 14.

## ON LETTER CXCIV

“Renaud Canard.” Lord of Loupéville, from whom that district received its name; it is called in the vernacular *Louville-la-Chenard*. Since it lies in the diocese of Chartres, that Renaud is called Ivo of Chartres’ parishioner.

## ON LETTER CXCV

“Had rejected the profession to the church of Chartres.” All abbots residing in the diocese of Chartres gave the bishops and church of Chartres a profession, or oath, of obedience, as may be read in old codices of the bishopric of Chartres and in records of the church. Vendôme alone was exempted from this rule by a special privilege of the Roman Church, and remains exempt. The privilege troubled Ivo, who bore it most ill; this will become known to everyone from the cartulary of the monastery of Vendôme, from which I produce the following:

> “Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and Agnes, countess, his wife: greeting and apostolic blessing. Whenever, sons,” etc.

See Clement II, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLII. This letter of Ivo seems to answer the letter which Geoffrey of Vendôme wrote to him, the second in Book II of Geoffrey’s letters, as is clear from its reading. [Col. 0483D]

## ON LETTER CXCVII

“To William, abbot of Marmoutier.” No William is counted among the abbots of that monastery; in his place is listed Geoffrey of Conan. More concerning him may be found in the little work *On the Deeds of the Archbishops of Tours and the Abbots of Marmoutier*, p. 112 and following.

## ON LETTERS CXCVIII, CXCIX, AND CCII

“Concerning the provostship of Sodobrium.” It belongs to the collegiate church of Saint Martin of Tours, in the territory of Blois, and is called the *Prévôté de Syeure*. [Col. 0484A]

## ON LETTER CCIII

“Of basilicas.” The larger churches were called basilicas, either because they were built by kings or princes, or because sacrifices are offered there to God, king of kings and of all. On this matter see Stephen Durant, *On the Rites of the Church*, Book I, chapter 1, no. 9 and following.

“To Lisiard of Soissons.” He was called of Crépy, and was elected bishop of the church of Soissons from its provostship in 1108. This is evident from folio 82 of the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, in which is copied a charter of the same bishop concerning the church of Lerniaco, given by him to the monks of the Fields with the consent of the countess of Crépy and her son Ralph, in 1123, indiction I, in the sixteenth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and the fifteenth year of the episcopate of the said Lisiard. If 1123 was Lisiard’s fifteenth year, 1108 necessarily was his first; this letter was therefore written in that year or the following one. [Col. 0484B]

## ON LETTER CCIV

“Against two prelates of our church.” Namely Ernald the dean and Fulk the subdean. King Louis ultimately favoured Fulk, as is clear from the following document addressed to Ivo, which I found among my manuscripts:

> “L., by the grace of God king of the Franks, to I., bishop of Chartres, and to the whole chapter of the holy church of Chartres, greeting. Having heard that Arnald the dean and F., the subdean, our clerk and familiar friend, are in conflict with one another, let your affection believe without doubt that this greatly displeases us and causes us more distress than you may suppose. For, when we have learned in due order how and in what manner the matter stands, it seems clear to us and to all the most prudent persons whom we ourselves have consulted that F. is being dealt with prejudicially and unjustly.
>
> “Therefore we request your affection—indeed, we earnestly entreat it—to settle diligently, for our sake, the dispute between them to the honour and advantage of Lord Fulk, insofar as you care for our friendship and honour. If you do so, you will find us ready, according to your will, for whatever may please you. But if you neglect to heed us in this small matter, let your discretion be certain that, by provoking us to anger, you will in some manner endure the judgment of our vengeance. We wish you therefore to be diligent in this matter, so that, if it please you, we may hear no further complaint about it. Should that happen, we would see to it that his loss was redeemed fourfold. Farewell. Otherwise, we present to you the aforesaid Fulk, our clerk, as one who will seek justice in your court.” [Col. 0484C]

Being able to repel from himself the odium of the judgment, Ivo consults the supreme pontiff by this letter, requesting a reply as to what he ought to do. Fulk does not tolerate a delay of judgment and therefore sends the following to the king against Ivo:

> “F., provost, to L., king of the Franks, his unconquered and most dear lord: greeting. Know, my most dear lord, that whatever you ordered our bishop on our behalf is not on our behalf but against us; and because of your command he has become worse toward us than he was before. Although he had set us a day for proceeding at law, before the appointed day he sought and obtained by his letters from a cardinal that the cardinal should admonish him and, in admonishing him, command him not to proceed in the case with us. He accused us before the cardinal, saying that we had gone to the king and had caused the king to intervene in the affairs of our church; and that, having therefore appealed to you and fled to your assistance and counsel, we now harm him.
>
> “Now he has both refused and refuses us justice, and he draws us unwillingly to Rome and summons us there. Know also this: there are many privileges in our church which were made and confirmed with the assent and authority of the king and queen of the Franks. But in this most recent privilege no mention at all has been made of you. In this may be understood an injury and dishonour to your kingdom and crown. Farewell. Whatever he may tell you, know in truth that he seeks nothing but evil and prefers every worse course to amendment and peace.” [Col. 0485A]

From these manuscripts it is abundantly clear that this subdean held a poor opinion of Ivo, though Ivo was greatly praised by others, and was ill-disposed toward him. I think this letter was written about 1109 or 1110.

## ON LETTER CCX

“Odo, bishop of Cambrai.” Elsewhere he is called Odoard, born at Orléans; he was raised from abbot of Tournai to this see. See Molanus, *Natals of the Saints of Belgium*, 9 October.

## ON LETTER CCXI

[Col. 0485B]

“But the genealogy is thus.” Jacob Meyer reports it differently in Book IV of his *Annals of Flanders*, under the year 1110:

> “Baldwin, son of Robert, count of Flanders, took as wife the daughter of Alan, count of Brittany. Conon, bishop of Palestrina, in the presence of Pope Paschal, set forth the consanguinity between Count Baldwin and his wife, the daughter of Alan, count of Nantes or Brittany, in this manner. Constance, queen of the French and wife of King Robert, and Ermengard, countess of Auvergne, were sisters. From Constance came Adela, countess of Flanders; from Ermengard, another Ermengard, countess. From Adela came Robert the Frisian, count of Flanders; from Ermengard, Bertha, countess. From Robert the Frisian came another Robert the Frisian; from Bertha, Hawise, countess of Nantes. From Robert II came Baldwin; from Hawise, Count Alan; from Alan, this maiden, Baldwin’s wife.”

Peter d’Oudegherst has the same account in chapter 59 of his *Annals of Flanders*, as does James Marchantius concerning the Flemish line. I, however, find by another reckoning that they were related in the sixth degree. For Fulk the Good, count of Anjou, by his wife Eheberga, had Geoffrey “Grey-tunic,” or, as they say, “Grey-gonelle”—a kind of garment whose name is still retained by the Occitans—and Blanche, wife of William, prince of Arles and Provence. Geoffrey, by his wife Adela, had Fulk Nerra, likewise count of Anjou, and Ermengard, wife of Conan, duke of the Armoricani. Blanche bore Constance, wife of King Robert. Fulk Nerra, by his first wife Adela, had Adela, wife of Geoffrey, lord of Château-Landon, or count of the Gâtinais, as Bourdigné maintains in Part II, chapter 38 of his *Annals of Anjou*; or, as the monk Odo writes in the *Life of Burchard, Count of Corbeil*, he fathered her by that Burchard. From King Robert and Constance came Adela, first wife of Renaud, count of Nevers, and afterwards wife of Baldwin of Flanders. [Col. 0485C]

From Adela of the Gâtinais, or of Corbeil and lady of Vendôme, came Fulk le Réchin, otherwise called Auser or Auserulus, just as Robert the Frisian came from Adela and Baldwin of Flanders. Fulk le Réchin was not born of Petronilla, his wife, who was the daughter of Lancelin, lord of Baugency, as Bourdigné held in Part II, chapter 39 of his *Annals of Anjou*, and Argentré in Book III, chapter 43 of his *History of Brittany*. Rather, by Ermengard, daughter of the lord of Bourbon, he had another Ermengard, countess of Rennes, second wife of Alan Fergent. Robert the Frisian, by Gertrude of Saxony, had another Robert the Frisian, called the younger. Ermengard, countess of Rennes, bore Agnes to Fergent, count of Armorican Brittany. Robert the Frisian, by the sister or niece of Pope Clement, later Calixtus II, had Baldwin the Axe-bearer, or “little axe,” ruler of Flanders. He married that Agnes, although they touched one another in the sixth degree of kinship from the original stock through their respective lines, as no one can doubt from the descent set out above. [Col. 0485D]

In Ivo’s lifetime marriages between relatives descended from a common ancestor were forbidden as far as the seventh degree. From Meyer I infer that this letter was written after 1110. Baldwin left no children by Agnes, since by Pope Paschal’s command he separated from her on account of the bond of kinship. Compare Letter 128.

## ON LETTER CCXIV

[Col. 0486A]

“To Bruno, bishop of the first see of the Belgic peoples.” This was Bruno, successor to Engelbert, who occupied the see of Trier from 1101 to 1123. Ivo calls him bishop of the first see of the Belgic peoples because Augusta Treverorum, lying on the Moselle, is the chief metropolis of Belgica; indeed, as Saint Athanasius writes in his work *To the Solitaries*, or as Theofrid, abbot of Épte, writes in the preface to his *Flower of the Saints*, it is the first metropolis of the threefold Gaul. Ammianus, Book XV, also calls it “the renowned residence of princes”; the *Notitia of the Empire*, “the most powerful city of Gaul”; and Salvian, Book VI, *On Providence*, “the most eminent and wealthy city of Gaul, more ancient than the others,” because it was built by Trebeta of Babylon in Abraham’s time, nearly two thousand years before Christ’s birth. [Col. 0486B]

The metropolitan himself is an elector of the Holy Roman Empire and archchancellor in Gaul for the kingdom of Arles. Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, calls this Bruno, in his *Life of Louis the Fat*, “an elegant and agreeable man, richly endowed with eloquence and wisdom, practised in Gallic dignity.” In 1106 he pleaded before Paschal II, supreme pontiff, on behalf of Emperor Henry III, as Baronius records for that year, no. 10; he is also named there by the abbot of Ursperg.

## ON LETTER CCCXV

“To Thomas of York.” York is a city of Great Britain, called *York* by the English. Thomas, of whom this passage speaks, was placed over its church by William Rufus, king of the English, in 1070, according to Orderic Vitalis, Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 516, and Book V, p. 548. Nicholas Harpsfield, Century II, p. 271, says of him:

> “After Aelred, Thomas, a Norman and canon of Bayeux, was designated bishop of York by King William,”

etc.; see the passage there. Thomas died in the same year in which Henry I was inaugurated, as is stated in the same source. I therefore suspect that this letter was written not to him but to his successor. There was another Thomas, bishop of the same see, mentioned by Harpsfield, p. 394, and by Juretus in his note on this letter. He died in 1114 and was succeeded by Thurstan, a cleric of Bayeux who was the king’s chaplain, as Orderic Vitalis writes, Book XII, p. 858. It is more likely that Ivo wrote to this Thomas. [Col. 0486C]

## ON LETTERS CCXVI AND CCXVII

“The abbot of Blois and the abbot of Bonneval.” The former was named Maurice, the latter Bernerius. See above on Letters 78 and 174. In the title or summary of the letter, however, the dispute between those abbots is said to have concerned the church of Verd, although there is no mention of that church in the body of the letter; moreover, that church belongs to the archdeacon of Châteaudun, not to the said abbots. [Col. 0486D]

## ON LETTERS CCXIX AND CCXX
### On the procedure for appeals

The ancient practice was that an appellant should request *apostoli* within five, or at least ten, days. I shall briefly explain what these *apostoli* are. They are letters, or a letter of dismissal, granted to those lodging an appeal by the judge from whom the appeal is made, so that the losing party may have recourse to a superior judge on account of the grievance received. They are especially required in the interlocutory judgments so called, in which the judge has wished to repair the injury and is able to reform the judgment. See chapter *Cum cessante*, *De appellationibus*, in the *Extra*. Therefore these letters, or *apostoli*, are called “restorative,” or, if one prefers, “reparative,” because the judge, acknowledging that he has injured the appellant, repairs the injury set forth in the notice of appeal, restores that appellant to the condition in which he stood before the lawsuit, and pronounces upon the appeal, in the prescribed form, [Col. 0487A] by which words he indicated that the judgment was to be reformed by him, perhaps when reduced to a form establishing the matter.

In definitive judgments the matter does not proceed in the same way; in such cases the loss is repaired only through an appeal: law *Quod jussit*, *Digest*, *De re judicata*. Therefore *apostoli* are requested in vain after final judgment, as was provided by royal edict of 1539, article 117. Nevertheless, this practice was observed in ecclesiastical courts: in all appellate cases, the *apostolus*, or letter of dismissal, was required from the judge *a quo*. In it the judge declared whether or not he deferred to the appeal; in the former case he extended the day for appeal to the superior court according to the distance of the places, as in chapters 1 and 7, *De appellationibus*, in the *Sext*; in the latter case he declared that he would proceed further notwithstanding the appeal and without prejudice to it.

247 **ON LETTER CCXXIII**

To Audoin, bishop-designate of the Church of Évreux. Orderic Vitalis writes of him as follows, book II of his *History*, p. 840:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1112, Gilbert, the aged [Col. 0487B] bishop of Évreux, after living thirty-four years in the episcopate, died in a good old age on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, etc. In the following year Audoin, the king’s chaplain from Bayeux, succeeded him. Endowed with literary learning, he regularly showed the way of God to those committed to him.”

And in book XIII, p. 919:

> “Audoin, bishop of Évreux, went to England in Easter week and there died and was buried at Melton, in the canonical monastery, on the sixth day before the Nones of July [1139]. Born in the district of Bayeux, he pursued literary studies and, trained in the liberal arts, came to rank among the most learned. Becoming intimate with King Henry, he found favor among the chief royal scribes. At length, raised from the king’s chapel, he held the diocese of Évreux for twenty-six years; he instructed the clergy and the subject people in keeping God’s law, diligently maintained the worship of the church, and restored from its foundations the basilica of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, which at that time [Col. 0487C] had been burned. Rotrou, son of Henry, count of Warwick, archdeacon of Rouen, was then raised to the bishopric of Évreux. In the same year, as I think, Thurstan, archbishop of York and brother of the aforesaid Audoin, died.”

From this it is readily inferred that this letter was written only after 1113, or at least in that year.

To William, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres: successor of Eustace and predecessor of Vernis, or Guy, whose life during Ivo’s pontificate is confirmed by several records of that monastery.

**Musivus Vicus** (*Mussy*). This place lies not far from Dreux, on the bank of the Avre, in the diocese of Évreux, and is now popularly called Mussy. The Avre is a stream separating France from Normandy. Hence the verse:

> “The Avre, though small, divides the fields of the French.”

Its nearer bank belongs to the bishopric of Chartres; [Col. 0487D] its farther bank to those of Sées and Évreux.

**ON LETTER CCXXIV**

To Guy, abbot of the monastery of Molesme—the third abbot, that is. Robert, founder of that ascetic community, was its first abbot; after him came Annas, whom this Guy succeeded about 1114, when perhaps this letter was written. On the monastery of Molesme and its founder Robert, see Orderic Vitalis, book VIII of the *History*, pp. 711 ff.

**ON LETTER CCXXVII**

To the citizens of Babylon. This letter seems to have been written when Paschal II, supreme pontiff, was permitted to depart free from the chains of the Romans in 1112. Matthew Paris indeed writes that Paschal II was imprisoned by Emperor Henry IV. This is confirmed by a letter written in the same year by John of Tusculum and Richard of Albano, legates in Gaul, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, indiction IV. For when Henry IV had received the crown of the realm from the pope’s hand at Rome, [Col. 0488A], he cast into chains the pope himself—who feared no evil from him—and the cardinals accompanying him, and extorted a privilege concerning the investiture of bishops and abbots. But once liberty had been recovered, the pope immediately revoked the privilege, or, as Otto of Freising says in book VII, chapter 14, “unprivileged the privilege,” and cursed the emperor with anathemas.

Paschal’s imprisonment occurred at Rome in the church of Saint Peter, on the Sunday before the beginning of the fast. On these matters see Pithou’s notes on Ivo’s letter 238—136 in our reckoning—and Baronius, under the year 1112, no. 6. Rome is called Babylon by Saint Peter, First Epistle, chapter 5, because of confusion, in an entirely different sense from that in which the Innovators interpret it. See Cornelius a Lapide on this passage, and on Revelation chapters XIII and XVII.

**ON LETTER CCXXVIII**

He excludes from entry into the church, for a fixed period, those placed in ashes and haircloth. This ceremony is still observed [Col. 0488B] in the Church of Chartres: on Ash Wednesday penitents are expelled from the church, and on Maundy Thursday they are readmitted. There can be no doubt that this custom derives from the ancient rite of public penitents, upon whom, on that very day and at the beginning of the fast, satisfactions for their committed sins were imposed.

The canon beginning *In capite*, which is canon 62, distinction 50—though a learned man wrongly writes that it is a novel canon of the Council of Agde, held in 566, whereas it is nowhere found in that council—fully explains the ceremony:

> “At the beginning of Lent, all penitents who undertake or have undertaken public penance are to present themselves before the doors of the church to the bishop of the city, clothed in sackcloth, barefoot, with faces cast down to the earth, declaring themselves guilty by their very clothing and appearance. There should be present the deans, that is, the archpriests, the parish priests, and the priests of the penitents, who ought diligently to examine their penitence and conduct, [Col. 0488C] and impose penance according to the measure of the fault through the aforesaid ranks. After this, they are to bring them into the church; and, with all the clergy, the bishop, prostrate upon the ground, is to chant with tears the seven penitential psalms for their absolution. Then, rising from prayer, he is to lay hands upon them as the canons command, sprinkle blessed water over them, and first place ashes upon them. Next he is to cover their heads with haircloth and, with groaning and frequent sighs, declare to them that, just as Adam was cast out of Paradise, so they are expelled from the church for their sins. Afterwards he is to command the ministers to drive them outside the church doors. The clergy are to accompany them with the responsory: ‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,’ so that, seeing Holy Church shaken and troubled because of their crimes, they may not make light of penance. But at the Lord’s sacred supper they are again to be presented at the thresholds of the church by their deans and priests.”

[Col. 0488D] The condition of the penitent is represented by ashes and sackcloth, or haircloth, as may be seen in Esther chapter IV, Lamentations chapters III and IV, Isaiah LVIII, Jonah chapter III, Psalm XXXV, the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 10, and Agde, chapter 15.

It will also, I think, not be unpleasant to report what John Bohemus writes in book III, 248 of *Europe*, after Aeneas Sylvius—who became Pope Pius II—in chapter 31 of *Europe*, and Raphael Volaterranus in book VII: namely, that at Halberstadt, a Saxon town, this is done every year.

> “On Ash Wednesday,” he says, “some one person from the people, judged in public opinion to be the most wicked of men, is selected. With veiled head and black clothing, they bring him to the sacred rites; when these have been duly performed, he is expelled from the church. Having been expelled, he wanders barefoot through the city throughout the whole fast, visiting the shrines of the saints. The priests provide him with food. Then, on Maundy Thursday, he is again brought into the church and, after the consecration of the oil, is absolved by the whole clergy and dismissed, having first received an alms which he devoutly offers to the church. [Col. 0489A] They commonly call him Adam, because, as that first-created man is free from every crime, the city too is believed to be expiated through him.”

That penitents did not enter the church throughout that period, but lay prostrate upon the ground before its doors, is attested by Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 11, speaking of Ecebolius, the sophist of Constantinople. Adapting himself to the dispositions of emperors, under Constantius he pretended to be a most fervent Christian; under Julian he became a pagan; afterwards he again pretended to be a Christian. For, Socrates says, “throwing himself face-down before the church door, he cried out: ‘Trample me underfoot like tasteless salt.’” For more, see Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 16.

**ON LETTER CCXXXI**

To Pons, venerable [Col. 0489B] abbot of Cluny. He was the son of the count of Melgueil in the province of Provence. In 1109 he was elected father of those monks, and on the seventh day before the Ides of May of that year was blessed by Guy, archbishop of Vienne, later Pope Callixtus II. Robert, in his series of the abbots of Cluny, reports that Pons was also admitted by him to the company of the purple-clad—that is, made a cardinal—at Callixtus’s first creation in 1119. I do not know on what basis this rests, since Onuphrius omits him and Orderic Vitalis, book XII, p. 871; Baronius under 1109, 1114, and 1126; Peter of Cluny; and Peter of Poitiers judge him very differently.

He died in 1123, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, and was buried at Cluny in the principal basilica, beside the altar of Saint Martin. From this I infer that the letter was written after 1109.

**On the concordance of the sacraments.** I do not recognize this book, unless it is the work joined in this volume under the title *Sermons*. For these are *On the Sacraments*.

**ON LETTER CCXXXIII**

To Henry, abbot of the monastery of Angériac—more correctly, Augériac. [Col. 0489C] It is called Augériac in the *Life of Saint John the Baptist*, to whom the principal church of the ascetic house is dedicated; from him the monastery took its name and is commonly called Saint-Jean-d’Angély. It is a Benedictine monastery situated among the Santones, founded long ago in 761 by Pepin, king of the Franks, and utterly destroyed by the Normans. Baronius, under 1111, no. 34, states that Ivo wrote this letter to him. Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, also writes to the same man in book IV, letters 3, 4, and 5; the first calls him “a man of venerable life.”

**ON LETTERS CCXXXVI AND CCXXXVII**

A council to be held at Anse. This place is distinguished by the holding of two councils: the first in 1025, the second in 1111, of which Ivo speaks here and Baronius under this year, no. 36. Anse is a town situated on the boundary of the Lyonnais and Beaujolais, four leagues from the metropolis. It took its name from the little river which waters it; see Papire Masson, *Description of France by Rivers*, p. 13.

The council discussed here, like the preceding one, was only provincial. [Col. 0489D] The acts of both councils have perished, or at least lie hidden somewhere, since, as far as I know, they have not yet come to light. On them see Severtius, in his accounts of the archbishops of Lyons, Burchard and John, pp. 200 and 231, and of the bishops of Mâcon, pp. 87, 89, and 91; the rest is found in Juretus.

“We judge him altogether a heretic.” For at the Council of Vienne, held in the year of the Lord 1112, canon 1, every investiture of an ecclesiastical thing from a lay hand had been judged heresy. From what is read in this letter, and from what we have said above, I judge it to have been written in 1113.

**ON LETTER CCXXXVIII**

The people of Tournai, otherwise called Nervii, situated on the Scheldt under the bishop of Noyon, remained so from the time of Saint Medard until 1146. In that year Pope Eugenius III, at the persuasion of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, restored their own bishop to them; so Meyerus records under that year.

[Col. 0490A]

**The case of Milo and the daughter of Count Stephen.** Suger gives another reason for the divorce; read it there. In what year this letter was written is scarcely known, unless it was in 1111.

**ON LETTER CCXXXIX**

Niece of the countess of Flanders: namely, Clementia, widow of Robert the Younger, called the Frisian, count of Flanders, and sister of Pope Callixtus II and Stephen, count of Burgundy. That niece was Adela, wife of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, daughter of Humbert II, count of Maurienne, and of a sister of Callixtus and Clementia; or, as Papire Masson has it in his account of the dukes of Savoy, daughter of Lawrence, or Argidia, or Gilla, daughter of the count of Vienne and wife of that Humbert. See Suger on Louis the Fat and Paul Arvil, p. 98.

I think this letter was written shortly before Ivo’s death. [Col. 0490B] For in the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, fol. 77, 1117 is called the third year of Queen Adelaide, and on the reverse of the same folio 1116 is written as her first year. From this it is plain that Louis married Adela in 1115; and this letter must necessarily have preceded the marriage.

**ON LETTER CCXLIII**

Lord Stephen the chancellor: Stephen of Garlande, namely, as Ivo explains once in letter 260, and as is evident from several charters of that period and from what was said on letter 87.

**ON LETTER CCXLV**

To Hugh, the great and distinguished count of Troyes. We have already spoken of him above on letter 158. We shall add that Hugh went twice to Jerusalem, as is clear from an instrument reported by Camuzat in the *Promptuary of the Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*, p. 286.

The first journey was in 1114, as I read in the cartulary of the monastery of Celle, in a charter beginning:

> “In the name of the Holy and undivided [Col. 0490C] Trinity. Since [the examples] of our Fathers…”

There it is said:

> “Therefore I, Count of Troyes, following the customs of my fathers, have taken care to mark by the notices of these letters the benefactions and liberties which I have bestowed upon the Church of Blessed Peter of Île-Germanique for the redemption of my soul and those of my predecessors. Therefore I make known to all who wish to know that, when I wished to set out for Jerusalem, etc. These things were publicly enacted at Troyes in the year 1144 from the Incarnation of the Word, while King Louis vigorously guided the helm of the kingdom of the Franks.”

It is clear that this letter too was written in that year.

He undertook his second journey to Jerusalem about 1122, as is plain from the cited instrument, which reads:

> “In the name, etc. We wish it to be known that Lord Hugh, most excellent count of Troyes, when for the second time he was proceeding to Jerusalem, at the city of Auxerre, etc. This was publicly enacted in the city of Troyes, in the cloister of Saint John the Baptist—now called Saint Blaise—of the castle, on the seventh day before the Ides of October, etc., in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1122.”

He undertook the first journey while his second wife was still living, as is clear from this letter—indeed, while she was pregnant and near childbirth, as Pithou says—though perhaps with her approval of the vow. He had returned by 1119, since in that year Orderic Vitalis, book XII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 857, says that he attended the Council of Rheims and was sent by Callixtus II with troops of soldiers to meet the archbishop of Mainz.

**ON LETTER CCLXVI**

Waleran of Breteuil. He was descended from the viscounts of Chartres, or lords of Puiset, and lived in the time of William II, king of England; see Orderic Vitalis, book III, p. 485. He was the son of Hilduin, or Gelduin, viscount of Chartres, founder of the monastery of Breteuil in the diocese of Beauvais around 1040, according to Louvet, *History of Beauvais*, book IV, chapter 3.

**ON LETTERS CCXLVII AND CCXLVIII**

[Col. 0491A]

Ralph: of Balgentiac, as is clear from the following letter.

**ON LETTER CCL**

Baronius contends that this letter was committed to writing in 1114, no. 9. I do not dissent; for I agree with him from what will be said below.

Ralph, bishop of Rochester. Besides what Juretus has from Harpsfield, I shall add the following, which Harpsfield writes concerning him in the twelfth century, chapter 15, p. 325:

> “When Henry [that is, Henry I, king of England] had already begun to be notorious for great infamy and feared that he would incur everlasting marks of his most shameful lust, and could no longer use the remarkable artifice of dissimulation of which we have spoken in order to evade them, he began seriously to consider appointing a pontiff of Canterbury in Anselm’s place. Although his inclination [Col. 0491B] was especially toward Faricius, abbot of Abingdon, he nevertheless referred the entire deliberation to the bishops, declaring that they would render an exact account to God of their election. Some wished an individual from the secular clergy, one not initiated into monastic life, to be chosen; but the others resisted and exclaimed that this was an unprecedented example, supported only by Stigand, who had stained his wicked entrance into that office by a still fouler and more shameful exit. Yet Faricius was not acceptable, either because they feared his excessive severity or because he was a foreigner. Although two most excellent men from that class had occurred to them, they said that their country was not so barren that it did not have at home men equal to sustaining that dignity on account of their highest gifts, worthy of the supreme pontiff. Among them was Ralph, bishop of Rochester, whose devout and holy [Col. 0491C] life had always escaped every trace of even the slightest infamy. Because of the greatness of his learning, he could judge all matters soundly and truly; and because of his eloquence, he could speak of them elegantly and ornately. Thus, by the most ready votes of all, Ralph was declared bishop of Canterbury, five years after Anselm’s death.

> “He was Norman by birth, a monk of Sées in Normandy, and then abbot of that place. By his industry he greatly enriched and enlarged a place which had previously been poor and slight. He had at one time stood high in the favor of Robert of Bellême, prince of that province, but afterwards completely fell from it and was expelled from Normandy because he refused, contrary to the pope’s decree, to swear faith and an oath of feudal service. He fled therefore to England, where he lived for some time among others, and then went to Anselm, with whom he had enjoyed familiar intercourse from youth. After Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, died, Anselm appointed him as his successor.

> “When he was about to be consecrated bishop, they say that Anselm [Col. 0491D] earnestly prayed to God that a prophecy of this kind might be set before Ralph, by which it would appear that divine judgment also had responded to his decision. When the Gospel book was opened again, this passage first presented itself: ‘They shall be like the angels of God.’ The pallium was brought to Ralph by a legate of the Roman pontiff, who was a nephew through the sister of Anselm of Canterbury. Guido had earlier come to England as legate, and Peter came after Anselm; but Henry wished to recognize no legate other than the archbishop of Canterbury. For this reason Ralph was sent to Rome with Herbert, bishop of Norwich. They brought letters from Paschal to the bishops and king concerning the prerogative of the see of Canterbury, which he wished to remain wholly intact, unimpaired, and exempt.

> “After Paschal died—whom Ralph could meet only through messengers [Col. 0492A] because of the war which the emperor waged against him—and then Gelasius also died, both of whom he had planned to petition in person in defense of his dignity against the intruder Thurstan of York, he returned to England. He sent messengers to Callixtus, who was convening a council at Rheims in Gaul, on the same matter, etc. Thurstan of York attended it with certain other bishops of England. Although Ralph’s legates were graciously heard and had good hope of an excellent outcome for their cause, they were nevertheless disappointed of their hope. For Callixtus, contrary to all examples of antiquity, consecrated Thurstan, etc.

> “Paralysis severely afflicted Ralph after his return. Though he was a prudent, grave, and highly judicious man, he was so provoked by the great force of that illness that anger was accustomed to boil over in him, particularly if anything was attempted against the dignity of himself or his church. Thus, [Col. 0492B] when Henry was to marry at Windsor, after the death of Matilda, Adeliza, daughter of the duke of Lorraine, and Roger, bishop of Salisbury, had attempted to celebrate the sacred mysteries—because Ralph seemed unfit to celebrate them on account of his hesitant and impaired speech—as though this office belonged to Roger by prerogative before others, especially in his own diocese, Ralph stripped Roger, already clothed in the sacred vestments, and assigned the duty to William of Winchester. On the following day, when the king stood present to hear the sacred rites wearing his crown, Ralph attempted to remove the diadem from the royal head, because it had been placed there without his knowledge; and he would have removed it, had he not been overcome partly by the great murmur and uproar of the people, partly by intervening entreaties, and refrained from that purpose. He afterwards died in the year of Christ 1122, the ninth year of his pontificate.”

From this I infer that Ralph took possession of the see of Canterbury in 1114 [Col. 0492C], and therefore that this letter was sent to him in the same year while he was still governing Rochester. On him see Orderic Vitalis, book XI of his *History*, p. 812, and Matthew Paris, *English History*, under Henry I. The latter writes that he was elected archbishop of Canterbury, or Dorobernia—which is the same—on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, 1114. Lists of the archbishops of Canterbury written at the time report that he died in 1123. They say:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1123, Archbishop Ralph died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November. William of Corbeil, a regular canon, succeeded him after some years.”

**ON LETTER CCLI**

Of the monastery of Jouarre. Jouarre is a monastery of Benedictine nuns in the diocese of Meaux, on the Marne. It was founded by Ado, brother of Saint Ouen, bishop of Rouen, according to Aimoin, book IV, chapter 41, and Vincent of Beauvais, book XXIII, chapter 91.

**ON LETTER CCLIV**

To Lord Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen. He was elected or nominated [Col. 0492D] by Henry I, duke of the Normans and king of England, in 1111, according to Orderic Vitalis, book XI, p. 840:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1111, indiction IV, Geoffrey the Breton, dean of Le Mans, was summoned into England by King Henry and made bishop for the people of Rouen. Distinguished by eloquence and learning, he taught clergy and people in the Catholic faith and profitably governed God’s Church for seventeen years.”

According to the same Vitalis, book XII, p. 888, he died in indiction VII, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December. The year in which this letter was written is not clear; but it may be stated that it was sent after 1111, perhaps in 1113 or 1114.

**ON LETTER CCLV**

Saint-Fuscien. Saint-Fuscien is a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Amiens, established and founded by Fredegund, queen of the Franks, and restored by Ingelram, count of Amiens, about 1080.

**ON LETTER CCLVII**

[Col. 0493A]

To Odo, prior of Saint George. This church of Saint George of Gameyo, in the diocese of Troyes, was assigned to the monastery of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais by Philip, bishop of Troyes, in Ivo’s time. Louvet, *History of Beauvais*, book IV, chapter 15, and Camuzat, *Promptuary of the Antiquities of Troyes*, fol. 117, report the documents of that grant, as well as those of the grant of a prebend in the Church of Troyes, fol. 118. This letter may have been sent in 1114.

**ON LETTER CCLVIII**

Baronius, under the year 1107, no. 6, maintains that this letter was written then. I do not disagree, since in that same year Paschal, to whom Ivo writes on behalf of Hubert, bishop of Senlis, held a synod at Troyes.

**ON LETTER CCLIX**

[Col. 0493B]

To Ralph, abbot of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais: namely, the fourth abbot after Ivo, who undertook a serious lawsuit against Gerlo, or Serlo, abbot of Saint-Lucien, over the mill of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais. Ralph lived and presided over the community of regular canons of Saint-Quentin from 1105 to 1136, according to Louvet, *History of Beauvais*, book IV, chapter 15. Perhaps in the ninth year of that abbacy this letter was sent by Ivo to Ralph the Green, bishop of Rheims.

**ON LETTER CCLX**

As some write, Galo, or Walo, bishop of Paris, was raised to the cardinalitial dignity. Stephen of Garlande, the king’s chancellor, who coveted the episcopal chair of the Church of Paris, devised a plan to have Galo transferred to Beauvais, so that he himself might obtain the episcopate which Galo relinquished. Stephen disclosed the matter to Pope Paschal, whose opinion of him was unfavorable [Col. 0493C]; when the pope did not answer according to his wish, Stephen consulted Ivo on what he should do, entrusting the entire business to Walter, archdeacon of the Church of Chartres.

They assert that Galo was at last transferred to the see of Beauvais and Stephen promoted to Paris. Yet, with their leave, I should say that this was not so. I confidently assert that Galo was never admitted among the Fathers of the supreme senate of the Church. Ivo, who wrote several letters to him, and Aimoin, or his continuator, who mentions him in book V, chapter 50, nowhere call him anything but bishop of Paris. Further, Ivo, who outlived Galo—for Galo died in 1114, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, and Ivo on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, 1115—would not have suppressed a dignity which greatly added to Galo’s splendor.

The statutes which Margarin de la Vigne, in volume VI of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, and Severinus Binius, part I, volume VII of the *General Councils*, p. 539, attribute to Galo, cardinal and legate in Gaul, whom they wish to be bishop of Paris, are not even his statutes; indeed, they are those of another cardinal of the same name. This can be proved from the fact that Ughelli and some others maintain that Galo, bishop of Paris, was created cardinal priest by Paschal II. But the Galo whose statutes are handled by men is described not as a cardinal priest but only as deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, as is apparent at first sight to readers; and, what is more, he is called not Galo by Onuphrius, but James Gualla.

[Col. 0493D] Whatever the case, I read of a legate named Galo sent into Gaul, but in 1216, when Innocent III sent him to Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, and John, king of England, to restrain them and make peace between them, as may be seen in Matthew Paris, p. 194. But this is not Galo of Paris.

You say that he was a legate *a latere*, a dignity belonging only to cardinals. I deny that Galo of Paris was a legate, and I deny that in this period legation *de latere* belonged only to the purple-clad Fathers. Longinus indeed, in Baronius, writes only that he was sent [Col. 0494A] among the Poles as an envoy to Boleslaus, with the authority of a legate *de latere*; no one says this among the French. For if Galo had been legate in Gaul and had obtained the bishopric of Paris upon returning from Poland, he lived contentedly among his own people and never, in public acts—which I have read in number—styled himself legate or cardinal. He certainly would not have omitted these titles, which contributed greatly to the dignity of his person.

Again, those are called legates *a latere* who are delegated by the pope’s living oral pronouncement, whether they are bishops, chaplains, as they call them, or officials; so teaches the *Speculator*, William Durand, formerly dean of Chartres, under the title *De legato*, “How many kinds of legates there are,” § *Lateran*, and Hostiensis in the *Summa* after the beginning. They are so called because of the reverence due to the supreme pontiff, whose garment’s fringe they have touched. Nor, before Galo’s time, were all legates even *a latere* cardinals: 2, question 6, chapter *Decretor*, and *Si quis episcopus*, and the gloss on chapter *Excommunicatis*, *Extra*, *De officio legati*, and chapter *Ad eminentiam*, *De sententia excommunicationis*.

As Platus observed [Col. 0494B] in book *On the Dignity and Office of Cardinals*, chapter 32, under Pope Callixtus II—that is, about 1120—the great and shameful controversy between emperors and popes, which had continually disturbed the whole Church for nearly fifty years, was at last entirely removed through the distinguished work of three cardinal legates, and indeed with great benefit to the Church, since its right of conferring benefices, which the emperors had usurped, was restored. These eminent cardinals were Saxo, a count and priest; Lambert, bishop of Ostia; and Gregory Papareschi, a deacon. The latter two afterwards became popes: one Honorius II, the other Innocent II, each of that name. Such legations began to be employed still more frequently not long afterwards by Alexander III.

Yet even if Galo had performed a legation, he could not therefore be declared a cardinal. From the style and practice of the Roman Curia of that period, cardinals alone are called legates *a latere* [Col. 0494C], since they constitute part of the pope’s body; compare canon *Si quis cum militibus*, 6, question 1, § *Verum*. More subtle than the old glossator Vincentius’s distinction is this: legates who are not cardinals are called *a latere*; cardinals, however, *de latere*, because of a certain union and proximity which they have with the pope. But that distinction is destroyed by chapter 20, *Ad eminentiam*, *De sententia excommunicationis*, where the text, speaking of a cardinal, calls him without qualification “a latere,” as though legation *a latere* were proper to the cardinalate. Yet this does nothing for our subject, since it occurred after the age of Ivo and Galo.

[Col. 0494D] Therefore Galo was neither legate nor cardinal nor bishop of Beauvais. Not only does the series of bishops of Beauvais, in which he is not found, oppose this claim, but so does his death in 1114. Stephen of Garlande, who according to the Chronicle of Morigny could do everything with the king, may perhaps have attempted Galo’s transfer to Beauvais; but Galo’s death intervened and frustrated all Stephen’s efforts. Granted neither the bishopric of Beauvais nor that of Paris—for Gilbert obtained the former and Geoffrey the latter—he remained unsuccessful; only after Gilbert died in 1123 was Stephen raised from archdeacon to the see of Paris. I believe this letter was written in the same year, 1114.

**ON LETTER CCLXI**

To Hugh, namely the son of Gervase. This Gervase was lord of Châteauneuf in Thimerais, in the diocese of Chartres and archdeaconry of Dreux; on that account Ivo calls him his parishioner.

The genealogy, as it is called, runs thus. It is recited almost in the same form by Du Chesne at the end of his *History of Normandy*, and he proves it from the cited passages. But because he differs in some particulars, I shall set it down here as it should truly be understood.

[Col. 0495] 252

Gunnor was first the concubine and then the wife of Richard I, duke of the Normans, according to Gemeticensis, book VIII, chapter 36. By her he had:

Richard II, as Du Chesne, *History of Normandy*, pp. 2 and 213, records. Richard married Judith, daughter of Geoffrey, count of Brittany, as Gemeticensis writes, book V, chapter 13. She bore him:

Robert, duke of Normandy after his brother Richard III, according to the same Gemeticensis, ibid., chapter 17, and book VI, chapter 3. By his concubine Harleva, called Herletta by others, he begot:

William the Bastard, according to the same Gemeticensis, book VI, chapter 12, and book VII, chapter 1. By his wife Matilda, daughter of Baldwin, count of Flanders, he had, as Orderic Vitalis reports, book IV, p. 512, and book VII, p. 638:

Henry I, king of England after his brothers Robert and William Rufus, and duke of the Normans [lacuna], who was born, perhaps, of a concubine, Elizabeth, sister of Waleran, count of Meulan, as Gemeticensis writes, book VIII, chapter 29, and book VII, p. 638.

N., who married Hugh of Châteauneuf. I do not know whether she is Mary, who was swallowed by the waves in that famous shipwreck in which the whole flower of French nobility perished, as Polydore Vergil reports at the end of book II of his *English History*, and others do; since I see Henry’s other daughters named and married elsewhere. I read of this woman nowhere except in the aforesaid Polydore Vergil.

[Col. 0496]

1. Samfria, sister of Gunnor, according to Gemeticensis, book VIII, chapter 36, was the wife of a certain forester; from them descended:

2. Josceline, wife of Hugh of Montgomery, according to the same Gemeticensis, book VIII, chapter 38, whom he makes mother of:

3. Roger of Montgomery, father of Robert of Bellême. By Mabel, daughter of William Talvas, lord of Bellême, that Roger had sons and daughters, among whom, according to the same Gemeticensis, book VII, chapter 16:

4. Mabel, wife of Hugh of Châteauneuf, as is found in Orderic Vitalis, book IV, p. 546. From her was born:

5. Mabel, who married Gervase and brought him the honor of Châteauneuf, as appears in the cartulary of the abbey of Colombs, concerning the land of Barlet and two churches. They were succeeded by:

6. Hugh, their firstborn son, of whom this letter treats.

In Ivo’s time, moreover, kinship among those descended from a common stock was calculated to the seventh degree, as we observed above on letter 45.

**ON LETTER CCLXII**

[Col. 0495A]

This letter deserves to be read and seems to have been written in 1114.

“Ernald, now your monk, formerly our cleric.” That he was dean of Chartres is inferred from Geoffrey of Vendôme, book II, letter 7, and from Sirmond’s notes on that letter.

**ON LETTER CCLXIII**
[... ] of the provosts. The provosts burdened the Chapter and harassed its lesser ecclesiastics with forced services. The leading members of the sacred college complained to Ivo of their oppression and accused them of misconduct. He wrote on their behalf to the supreme pontiff, who sent them the following bull invalidating the provosts’ rights: “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the canons of the Church of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing. From our venerable brother Ivo, etc.” See Paschal under the year 1118, no. 396.

[Col. 0495B] When this Bull came to the provosts’ notice, they attempted to stir King Louis against Ivo and obtained from him letters, or an epistle, addressed to Ivo himself, to which he replies here. At that time there were four provosts in the Church of Chartres, namely of Belsia, Nougent-le-Roi, Amilly, and Fontenay.
