At their own discretion they administered and squandered the canons’ property; the canons, bitterly resenting this, procured their removal from office and had the revenues and resources of their college restored to common ownership. Yet, lest the church should suffer loss in its dignities, four precarial benefices or lordships were allotted them, from which those who retained the title of provost, after the former holders had been removed, received their designation. For, changing the old appellation, they now call them the provosts of Vuogradu or Jugreyo, of Northmannia, of Masengeio, and of Awersio. From the aforesaid bull and epistle I judge that this letter was written in the spring now declining and the year 1115 already turning toward summer heat.

### ON LETTERS CCLXVI, CCLXVII, CCLXVIII, AND CCLXIX

To Cono, bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See. Robert of Monte, Sigibert’s continuator, writes of him as follows:

[Col. 0496A] “A council was held in the city of Beauvais by Cono, legate of the Apostolic See. This is Cono, one of those religious men who first led the eremitical life at Tronc-Bérenger and became founders of the Order of Arrouaise, an order which flourishes and increases to this day.”

Indeed, Ferreolus Locrius, in his Belgian Chronicle under the year 1090, writes that the monastery of Arrouaise, called in French *Erouaige*, in the territory of Artois at Tronc-Bérenger, was built in 1090 by Cono the German, legate of the Apostolic See and cardinal-bishop of Palestrina—who is the same man as this Cono—together with Haldemar, hermit-priest of Tournai, according to these verses:

> In the thousandth year of the Lord, and the nineteenth thereafter,  
> A new rule began to be observed at Berengar’s Trunk.

Anyone wishing to know more about this monastery, which became the head of twenty-six monasteries—or, rather, houses—of the Order of Regular Canons, should read Ferreolus Locrius himself in the place cited above; Molanus, 4 May; Gazaeus in his catalogue of the bishops of Arras; Massaeus, book XVI of the *Chronicle*; James of Vitry, chapter 23 of his *Western History*; and the others cited there by Locrius.

Concerning the church of St Nicholas of Courville. After our Ivo had obtained it from Ivo, lord of that town, he granted it to the regular canons of St John in the Valley of Chartres, whom he had founded. This is clear from the letters, or instrument of donation, which I publish from the cartulary of the same abbey, part 2, chapter 39. They are of the following tenor:

> “I, Ivo, minister of the Church of Chartres, etc., make known that Lord Ivo of Courville came before us, moved by the power of the Holy Spirit, and humbly acknowledged that both he and his predecessors had held the church of St Nicholas of Courville unjustly and contrary to the law of God. After so salutary an acknowledgment, which the grace of the Holy Spirit had infused into his heart, kindled by that same Spirit, he placed the said church in our hand, so that henceforth neither he nor any of his heirs should make any claim whatever to it. For the remission of his sins and the deliverance of the souls of his predecessors, he left it to be disposed of at our discretion.

> [Col. 0496C] “We, therefore, in our chapter, with all the prelates of our church present, as well as the other brethren, both greater and lesser, with the assent of all—and also with the assent of the canons of the aforesaid church of St Nicholas, who devoutly requested this of the brethren—granted the said church to the brethren of St John, living under rule, for their use and maintenance, to hold in perpetuity, etc.

> [Col. 0497A] “And so that this grant may be held most firmly by our successors and believed wholly true, we confirmed it with the double seal, namely that of Blessed Mary and our own, strengthened it with the subscription of our name, and delivered it into the hands of worthy men to be ratified and sealed. The sign of Ivo, bishop of Chartres; the sign of Arnaud, dean; the sign of Gerogius, cantor; the sign of Hugh, subdean; the sign of Gaucherius, archdeacon; the sign of Guarin, succentor; the sign of Gaflenus, archdeacon; the sign of Odo, archdeacon; the sign of Landric, archdeacon; the sign of Aulgerius, archdeacon; the sign of Wigrin, chancellor; the sign of Ralph, chamberlain; the sign of Hugh, provost; the sign of Geoffrey, provost; the sign of Fécamp, provost; the sign of Henry, provost; the sign of Ebrard,

> [Col. 0497B] capicerius [keeper of the choir-cloak]; the sign of Garin, provost; the sign of Caracen; the sign of Haimo, priest, etc.; the sign of Hugh; the sign of Andrew, dean; the sign of Hubert, deacon, etc. Given by the hand of Wlgrin, chancellor. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1115, indiction VIII.”

But the monks of Marmoutier, out of hostility to that donation, brought suit against the canons of St John in the Valley, alleging that the church had previously been granted to themselves. Ivo undertook the protection of the canons to whom he had conveyed the church, and wrote this letter on their behalf to the supreme pontiff against the monks of Tours—namely, in the same year in which the preceding instrument of donation was drawn up, since that suit is later than it. The dispute was at last settled, through the agency of William, bishop of Châlons, and the count of Perche, on 29 November 1119, indiction 12, as appears from the same cartulary of St John.

Gerogius, lord of Courville. This is certain from the cartulary of St Peter in the Valley of Chartres, where the following is read:

> “In the name of the Lord, Amen. I, Philippa of Courville, and Ivo my son, etc., commit to memory [record] that the *ban* [seigneurial right] which we had from our predecessors, namely Ivo and Gerogius, in the town called Pomeriaca, etc., with the consent of our lord and patron Nivelo, we gave to Lord Eustace, abbot of the monastery of Chartres, free from every disturbance, etc. These things were done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1094, in March, indiction II, while King Philip reigned and Ivo presided as bishop of Chartres.”

Orderic Vitalis also mentions him in book IV of his *History*, p. 489, while writing of Ernald of Échauffour, son of William Geroianus. Mabel, daughter of Talvas and wife of Roger of Montgomery—of whom we spoke above on Letter 261—attempted to poison him; had an immediate antidote not been at hand, he would have exchanged life for death:

> “Then,” he says, “this woman prepared the deadly draughts. But she gave them to Ernald, her lord, and to Gerogius of Corbeville,

> [Col. 0497D] and to William, surnamed Gouet, of Montmirail—whence the Perche Gouet. Thus three nobles were simultaneously infected with one poison at Corbeville. But Gerogius and William, who were carried to their own homes and there were able to arrange their own treatment as they wished, recovered, God making the physicians’ remedies effective,” etc.

In that place mention is made of an apparition of St Nicholas to the above-mentioned Ernald as he lay ill from poison. Perhaps from this Gerogius acquired the devotion which later led him to build, found, and procure the consecration in his town of the church of that saint now in question.

The monks of Marmoutier, who lived in a certain neighboring cell—namely, at the cell of Chuisua, founded in the time of Ivo, the first lord of Courville, as appears from the following instrument:

> “We wish it to be known to the sons of God’s holy Church, present and future, that when William the priest, moved by salutary concern for his soul, had built in the district of Chartres, in the place called Chouina, a church in memory of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius,

> [Col. 0498A] and had arranged around it dwellings suitable for monks living in community, he granted that church and the cells which he had built, with all that he had bestowed upon that church, to the Lord and to St Martin of Marmoutier. He placed them in the hands of Lord Albert, abbot set over the monastery called Marmoutier, so that, made a participant in their prayers and benefactions, he might acquire for himself the reward of eternal recompense.

> “The same William, surnamed the Preacher, made the following agreement with the said abbot and the brethren of Marmoutier: that the abbot himself or his successors should, at their own will, send to that cell, for God’s service, such chosen monks from among their own as they thought fit, according to their judgment and the resources of the place; and that they should there serve the Lord by living under rule. Nor should that cell or church ever have abbots of its own, but it should always be subject to the abbot of Marmoutier, who should cause such monks of his own, as many as he wished and for as long as he wished,

> [Col. 0498B] to dwell there. There are many witnesses to all these things, some of whom have subscribed this notice as witnesses, should need arise: Ivo of Courville; Letherius Bursardus,” etc.

That the priory of Chuisua was founded in the lifetime of Ivo, lord of Courville, appears from the confirmation of his gift to the monks of Marmoutier by Gelduin of Breteuil and his son Harduin, viscount of Chartres, who were living in the year of the Lord 1049, as is clear from Louvet’s *History of Beauvais*, book IV, chapter 8; there Ivo himself, who is named as witness in the charters of the grant, is also mentioned.

“In the twenty-five years during which I remained in the episcopate.” Therefore Ivo’s see at Chartres lasted twenty-five years. Therefore, since he departed this life on 23 December 1115, it follows that he must have begun his see in the year 1090. This is clear from an instrument in my possession concerning the church of St Nicholas, situated in the cloister of the principal church of Chartres, in whose date the following words occur:

> “This charter was made in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1114, in the sixteenth year of the ordination of Lord Pope Paschal and the fifteenth year of the ordination of Lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres, while Louis, son of King Philip, reigned as king of France.”

From this and from the matters reported above in the second annotation, it is plain that this letter was written before the feast of Easter in the year 1115 according to Roman reckoning, and according to our now common computation. Baronius nevertheless assigns it to the year 1114, no. 11; he might, however, be excused if he reckoned his years according to the French computation, in which the year began with the Resurrection of the Lord.

### ON LETTER CCLXX

To Turgis, bishop of Avranches. From Orderic Vitalis, book IV of his *History*, p. 507: Turgis succeeded Michael, successor of John, who had been promoted to the see of Rouen, in the bishopric of Avranches; and he held the episcopal office for nearly thirty years. And in book XII, p. 889, under the year 1129, indiction VII:

> “In the same year,” he says, “King Henry [Henry I of England] gave his daughter Matilda to Geoffrey, count of Anjou; Turgis, the aged bishop of Avranches, united them with the pontifical blessing.”

Therefore I do not judge this letter, as Baronius writes under the year 1094, no. 15, to have been written then, since from the facts reported he was not yet bishop of Avranches. For if he held the see of Avranches for nearly thirty years and was alive in 1129, it is surely true that this letter could not have been written to him as bishop of Avranches in 1094, but only in the following year, in which Ivo died.

### ON LETTER CCLXXI

This letter should be compared with 265 and with what we have said concerning that letter. It may have been written in the same year as the preceding one.

### ON LETTER CCLXXII

To Renaud, by the grace of God bishop of Angers. He was called “of Mayenne” or “of Martigné,” son of the lord of Brient’s Castle, so named from him; later, in or about 1124, he transferred to Reims.

[Col. 0499A] He had been elected bishop of Angers after Geoffrey of Mayenne, who, having renounced the episcopate, entered the Cluniacs in 1102. Thus the *Chronicle of St Albinus of Angers*:

> “In the year 1093 Geoffrey, son of Hugh of Mayenne, was ordained on the Kalends of December. He remained scarcely seven years in the episcopate. For, because very many persons accused and complained before the pope that he had been ordained by the pope’s command while a novice and almost unlettered, at the advice of Pope Urban himself he left the see and became a monk at Cluny. After his departure Renaud was ordained bishop at Angers on the day before the Ides of January, in the year 1102.”

Yet in another old chronicle of the same monastery of St Albinus, of which I possess a manuscript extract, I read: “1096: Geoffrey of Mayenne was ordained bishop.” Hence I suspect an error has entered the earlier date. For this latter statement accords better with the facts just given. Therefore Robert, in his series of the bishops of Angers, wrongly, in my judgment, writes that Renaud consecrated in 1099 the church of the abbey of La Roë, founded by the lords of Craon.

[Col. 0499B] In what year this letter was written is not sufficiently clear.

### ON LETTER CCLXXIII

For the bishop of Bayeux: Richard, son of Samson, who succeeded Turold about 1109, according to Orderic Vitalis, book X, p. 765, and held the bishopric for twenty-six years. According to the same Orderic, book XIII, p. 897, he died in 1133, in Easter week itself.

### ON LETTER CCLXXV

The count of Nevers: namely William, who was kept in chains by Theobald, count of Chartres. Brother Andrew mentions him in these words in the *Life of Robert of Arbrissel*, founder of the monastery and order of Fontevraud:

> “When peace had thus been made with the people of Chartres, the faithful dispenser of the word of the Lord left the city of Chartres, never to return there again. He joined to himself the venerable Bernard, abbot of Tiron, whose companionship had always been most pleasing to him; and the two came together to the castle popularly called Blois. In that castle the religious Count William of Nevers was kept imprisoned because, in support of peace, he had upheld the cause of Louis, king of France, against the count of Chartres. This William too, by the merits of his life, was dearly esteemed by both men.”

Orderic Vitalis, book XII of his *History*, p. 859, also writes as follows concerning the same count of Nevers, making Louis the Fat address Pope Calixtus II at the Council of Reims:

> “Count Theobald is my man, but at the instigation of his uncle, namely Henry I, king of England, he has wickedly risen against me. Puffing himself up with his uncle’s wealth and power, he has rebelled against me, has waged cruel war against me in faithless fashion, and has thrown my kingdom into disorder, to the injury of many. The lawful and worthy man Count William of Nevers, whom you know well, was returning from the siege of a certain castle belonging to an excommunicated robber

> [Col. 0499D] [Thomas of Marle], where there truly was a robbers’ den and a pit of the devil. Theobald seized him and has committed him to prison until this very day.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “Accordingly, the aforesaid hero, returning peaceably with my permission, was captured and has been held by Count Theobald until this day, although a multitude of nobles on my side have often humbly petitioned for the count’s liberation, and all his land has been anathematized by the bishops.”

I judge this letter to have been written shortly before Ivo put off his mortal body, since Robert of Arbrissel and Bernard of Tiron visited that Count William of Nevers on the third or fourth day after Ivo’s funeral.

### ON LETTER CCLXXVI

To Thurstan, archbishop of York. The following may be added to Juret’s notes concerning him. Orderic Vitalis, book XII, p. 857, writing of the council gathered at Reims in October 1119, says:

> [Col. 0500A] “A synod was held in the metropolitan church. There, on Sunday, 19 October, the pope sang Mass and consecrated Thurstan of Bayeux archbishop of York; and he granted him the privilege that he should be subject to the metropolitan of Canterbury not as to a master, but as to a fellow bishop.”

Nicholas Harpsfeld gives a more extended account of the controversy between the archbishops of Canterbury and York, in words that may cast some light upon this letter:

> “When Thurstan obtained the bishopric, that old dispute between him and Ralph of Canterbury broke out anew. He was so resolute in it that, when pressed by the king either to resign his office or to obey Canterbury, he preferred to resign his dignity rather than be subject to the see of Canterbury. Afterwards, however, the canons of York secretly sent messengers to Rome; concealing the truth of the matter, they complained vehemently to Pope Paschal as though Thurstan had unjustly been driven from his see. They achieved so much that he wrote to the king that Thurstan should be restored to his see, but without prejudice to the Church of Canterbury, whose dignity he had no wish to diminish; and that, if any controversy remained between the Churches of Canterbury and York, he would examine it.

> [Col. 0500B] “Thus, two years after he had crossed with the king into Normandy, Thurstan returned to England. A synod was then summoned at Reims in France. Thurstan hastened through Normandy to the synod, in order to settle his affairs there. When he came to the king at Rouen, the king was greatly angered against him because he had left England without his knowledge and consent. He then ordered him not to go to the synod until something more certain was known about the Roman pontiff—for two men were claiming that see through a wicked schism. All Gaul and England adhered to Calixtus, who was the true and legitimate pontiff; the emperor and others adhered to a certain Gregory. Numerous bishops were already gathering for Calixtus’ synod at Reims, to which Henry sent some men from Normandy. There were also present from England William of Exeter, Ranulf of Durham, Bernard of St Davids, and Urban of London.

> [Col. 0500C] “The king sent letters to Calixtus asking him not to take ill the absence from the synod of William of Canterbury, whom he had retained with him in Normandy because of illness; but, above all, asking that he should neither consecrate Thurstan himself nor allow him to be consecrated by another unless he first followed the example of his predecessors in rendering obedience to the Church of Canterbury. If Thurstan did not observe that condition strictly, he was to know that England and Normandy would thereafter be barred to him for return. The king steadfastly declared that no argument would subsequently induce him to depart from that decision, even though he must imperil his kingdom and incur the anathema of seven whole years.

> “The pontiff replied to Sifred, monk of Canterbury and the king’s messenger—whom the pope had long known and with whom Sifred had formerly been intimate—that both the king’s will and the dignity of the Church of Canterbury were matters of great concern to him. After this Thurstan asked the king to allow him, with the king’s favour, to go to the synod. At length he was allowed, though reluctantly, and only after he had promised on his pledged faith that he would admit nothing contrary to the dignity of the Church of Canterbury or prejudicial to it.

> [Col. 0500D] “But he promptly deceived and broke the pledge he had given; through those who had influence with the pontiff, he obtained from him consecration, although John, archdeacon of Canterbury, openly resisted and cried out that an injury was being done to the Church of Canterbury. The pontiff answered him that what he did would preserve that church’s dignity and inflict no injury upon it. The bishops of England had not yet arrived at the synod, for Thurstan had hastened his journey with the utmost speed and had left nothing undone for the rapid completion of the journey and indeed of the entire affair. Accordingly, other foreign bishops who had assembled for the synod assisted the supreme pontiff in consecrating Thurstan. Hubald, archbishop of Lyons, though requested by the pope, refused to be present because of the exceptional reverence he had for the said Church [of Canterbury].

> [Col. 0501A] “When the king received certain report of these events as they had occurred, he forbade Thurstan access to all his dominions. Nor could he be softened into receiving him into favour, even when Calixtus consented, at the conference he held with him at Gisors, to many of the king’s requests—including the request that he should thereafter not send his legate into England without the king’s consent, except in matters so arduous and difficult that they could not suitably be settled by bishops. But when Calixtus later forbade the archbishop of Canterbury to exercise priestly office and threatened the king himself with anathema unless Thurstan were restored to his see, the king at length yielded his own position and Thurstan returned to York, after consultation with the princes and bishops and by their counsel, etc. He prolonged his life into the reign of King Stephen, to the fifth year of that reign, etc.; and before his death, laying aside the pastoral burden, he withdrew into quiet and solitude, in order to devote himself undisturbedly to God, and professed himself a monk at the Cluniac monastery of Pontefract.”

From these facts I infer that this letter was sent to Pope Paschal in 1115, when Thurstan had only been elected.

### ON LETTER CCLXXVIII

To Robert, by the grace of God bishop of Lincoln. Orderic Vitalis, book X, p. 765, calls this Robert Bloet:

> “Robert, surnamed Bloet, who had been chaplain to William the Elder and, after his death, had crossed the sea from the port of Tolochae with William the Younger and carried the king’s letter concerning the coronation of his offspring to Archbishop Lanfranc, received the bishopric of Lincoln after the death of Remigius, and held it for more than twenty years.”

Harpsfeld, in his *Eleventh Century*, p. 258, among the bishops of Lincoln, writes that he was chancellor of King William Rufus, held episcopal dignity for nearly thirty years, and died in 1123 after being struck by apoplexy. I cannot see in what year this present letter was issued, and it is absent from my manuscript.

### ON LETTER CCLXXX

[Col. 0501C] Lord Nivelo of Pierrefonds. He is mentioned in the Cartulary of St Martin of the Fields at Paris, fols. 73 and 109, where Nivelo of Pierrefonds is called the father of Drogo of Pierrefonds.

The count of Soissons. Who he was, I am wholly ignorant, unless he was Cono, count of Soissons, husband of Agatha of Pierrefonds, after Ivo of Noyon, who died without children, and who himself also died without issue.

### ON LETTER CCLXXXI

The canons of St Peter of Beauvais bring a complaint against the canons of St Quentin. When Ivo complained to Pope Paschal of the various suits which the members of the principal church of Beauvais, known by the name of St Peter, were bringing against the canons of St Quentin of Beauvais, Paschal wrote the following letter in reply to Anselm, bishop of Beauvais. Since it greatly contributes to the elucidation of this matter, I reproduce it here from Louvet’s *History of Beauvais*, book IV, chapter 15:

> [Col. 0501D] “Paschal, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Beauvais, greeting and apostolic blessing. The duty of the priestly office,” etc.

See Paschal II. Since mention is made in this reply of the supreme pontiff of Galon or Gilbert, bishop of Paris, who are individually denoted by “Clement,” and since, as we said above, the former exchanged life for death on 23 February 1114, I judge this letter to have been written in that year or the preceding one. Compare Letter 259.

### ON LETTER CCLXXXII

This is not a letter, as Juret rightly observed; he therefore ought not to have listed it among the letters, but rather to have expunged it altogether. It is a privilege granted to the hospital of Châteaudun, situated there below the church of St Mary Magdalene.

### ON LETTER CCLXXXIII

It is incorrectly counted among Ivo’s letters, since it is an instrument for the blessing of the cemetery of Tiron,

[Col. 0502A] which I judge occurred in or about 1111. The year is lacking. Yet I believe this must be understood not of the first settlement of Bernard, first abbot of Tiron, but of the second. For Geoffrey Grossus, ascetic of Tiron, writes in the *Life* of that Bernard:

> “At the same time, lest Christ’s soldier Bernard should lack the struggle of labour and tribulation, the monks [of St Denis of Nogent-le-Rotrou], whom we have already mentioned, claimed that the tithes and the dead bodies of that land which the aforesaid count [Rotrou] had given him belonged to their jurisdiction. Compelled by this claim, Bernard abandoned the buildings which his disciples had constructed with the greatest labour and set about seeking another piece of ground where he might be permitted to live. He therefore approached the venerable bishop Ivo and the canons of that most celebrated Church of Chartres, dedicated in honour of the ever-virgin Mary, and requested that they give him some small portion of the estate which they possessed adjoining his own small holding, for the foundation of his monastery.

> [Col. 0502B] “There was a certain little tract belonging to the aforesaid canons, adjoining the land which the count had given to the man of God, called Gardeya. They received God’s servant with due reverence, heard him with merciful kindness, and, in the magnificence of their generosity, granted more land than he had asked for. When the grant had been made, they drew up a charter and sent Lord Geoffrey, canon of that church and provost of that territory, with certain persons to point out the land. Having arrived at the aforesaid estate, they granted him, by decree of the chapter, beside the stream called Tiron, the land he had requested for building the workshops of his monastery—free in the same manner as they themselves had held it.

> [Col. 0502C] “Moreover, a certain matron of royal lineage, namely Adela, countess of Blois, was at that time offering St Bernard broader expanses of land, and land much more suitable for the construction of his monastery. He nevertheless declined them, preferring to establish his monastery under the protection of the Blessed Virgin Mary rather than under the advocacy of any secular person whatever,” etc.

### ON LETTER CCLXXXIV

It is an instrument granting the church of St Peter of Châteaudun to Bonneval monastery, not a letter.

“We also confirm to them the chapel of St Innocent.” This is a very bad reading; the better and correct reading is “St Vincent,” whose dedication still exists at Chartres. It is mentioned in the charter granted to Bonneval monastery by Louis the Fat, king of the French, at Paris in 1122, the fifteenth year of his reign. Speaking of Hugh, lord of Le Puiset and viscount of Chartres, it says:

> “The said viscount, gratefully accepting this and promising upon his faith to defend the monks’ land according to his ability, in order that they might lovingly forgive the wrongs he had done them because of that gift which he had long before devoutly bestowed upon the monastery of Bonneval, through the hand of the venerable Ivo, bishop of Chartres—namely, the chapel of St Vincent and his houses at Chartres,” etc.

[Col. 0502D] Near the Ashen Gate. In the act restoring St Peter of Chartres, by Agavo, bishop of Chartres, I read:

> “We therefore restore to them a certain piece of land possessed by their predecessors in ancient times, but afterwards wrongly taken away, so that they may possess it fully, as it is proved by the testimony of many that their predecessors held it. This land lies within and without the walls of the city of Chartres, near the Ashen Gate. It is bounded on one side by the road which is the exit from the city; on the other by the land of St Peter of Poitiers and St Amand,” etc.

That gate was called the Ashen Gate because, in the public procession customarily held on Ash Wednesday, the people passing through it were marked with ashes.

### ON LETTER CCLXXXV

Nor is this a letter, but rather a charter of the donation to the Bec monks of the cell or priory of St Nicasius of Meulan,

[Col. 0503A] founded in 1062 or about that date by Waleran, count of that place, and given by Robert, count of Meulan, with the assent of Odo, archdeacon of Pontoise, and of the clerics living there, as appears here from Ivo. Accordingly Nicholas d’Avanne must be corrected in his little work *On the Life and Martyrdom of St Nicasius*, chapters 56 and 57, where he writes that, after the monastery of that saint had been built, Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, consecrated the church in 1067 and appointed Brother Robert of Beaufort, monk of Bec, its first prior. For no Geoffrey had yet received the mitre of the Church of Chartres in that year, as I prove elsewhere; nor had Robert, count of Meulan, yet granted that church to the monks of Bec. If some bishop of Chartres named Geoffrey appointed a prior there, this must be attributed to Geoffrey of Lèves, Ivo’s successor, not to the other Geoffrey, who was driven out and banished from the see of Chartres in the year 1090.

### ON LETTER CCLXXXVI

[Col. 0503B] This act is not to be counted among Ivo’s letters. It is a charter, or instrument, for the foundation of the abbey of St John in the Valley, in the suburb of Chartres, made by Ivo in 1099, as we said above on Letter 91.

Minoratus. Incorrectly; rather, *Junioratus*, as at the end of Ivo’s Life. These were benefices, or prebends, granted to junior clerics for assistance in their office. They are mentioned in Book V, chapter 21 of the Capitularies:

> “Whoever is there called a judge, or a layman, who presumes, without a hearing before the bishop, archdeacon, or archpriest, to inflict an injury upon a priest, deacon, any member of the clergy, or any of the juniors, is to be held under anathema, cut off from the communion of all Christians.”

This capitulary is in fact taken, though with certain words changed, from the first Synod of Auxerre, canon 43. Hence they may be seen to have been counted among the clergy. What their office was appears from what follows: namely, to read the lessons in church and to perform other duties pertaining to divine worship [Col. 0503C]. Therefore, at the Second Council of Tours, canons 12 and 19, their care is entrusted to archpriests; indeed, to parish priests or curates as well, in canon 1 of the Second Council of Vaison, where the following is read:

> “It has therefore been decreed that all priests established in parishes, according to the custom which we have learned is most beneficially observed throughout all Italy, shall receive into the house in which they themselves appear to reside as many unmarried junior readers as they have, and, nourishing them spiritually as good fathers, shall strive to have them learn the psalms, apply themselves to the sacred readings, and be instructed in the law of the Lord; so that they may provide worthy successors for themselves and receive eternal rewards from the Lord. But when they have attained mature age, if any one of them, because of the weakness of the flesh, should wish to have a wife, he is not to be denied permission to contract marriage.”

In agreement with this is the decree of the First Council of Mâcon, canon 8, found in *11, question 1*, *Nullus clericus*, and [Col. 0503D] chapter 3, *Ut quisque*, in the Extravagants, *On the Life and Honesty of Clerics*—though it is wrongly cited as from the same or from the other Council of Mâcon, since it occurs in neither. For the last of those texts says:

> “Let every priest who governs a people have a cleric to sing with him, to read the epistle and the lesson, and to maintain schools, and to admonish his parishioners to send their sons to church to learn the faith, so that he himself may instruct them in all chastity.”

For this reason a church’s endowment ought, at the least, to provide for two persons, according to the Gloss on the chapter *Cum sicut*, Extravagants, *On the Consecration of a Church or Altar*. Thus in many churches an income was assigned to junior clerics, that is, to those established in the minor orders, so that they might minister there more conveniently and have at least food and clothing; for he who serves at the altar ought to live by the altar.

Some, however, sought these prebends or benefices for members of their own household, just as persons in colleges assign their own household, or persons of a specified income, to places intended for the bursars or collegiates, as they call them, thereby excluding outsiders. Of the many examples I could produce, I shall offer only these.

In the Cartulary of Marmoutier concerning benefices situated in the district of Vendôme, notice 4, the following is read:

> “Let it be known to our successors, etc., that after the agreement which we made with Theobald, son of Letherius of Vendôme, concerning the juniorate of the church of Naveil, Hamelin of Langes had challenged our possession of that same juniorate, saying that we could not hold it without his authorization, since that church belonged to his estate. Theobald likewise claimed that whatever right he could assert in it was held by him from Hamelin. But our documents stated that we had formerly made such an agreement with his parents concerning that church and the property belonging to it, that henceforth no one of their stock ought to make any claim concerning all these properties or the church. But when the recital of the documents did not suffice for him, we proved by the oath of one of our men that nothing there of the aforesaid properties belonged to him or to anyone of his family, according to the agreement formerly made with his parents concerning these matters. Thus at last he abandoned his claim at Vendôme,” etc.

This is repeated there in notice 7. Likewise, in the cartulary of Saint Peter in the Valley of Chartres, folio 83, Albert, son of Hugh, viscount of the Holy Church of Chartres, gives to Saint Peter and the monks serving him, with the consent of his brother Guéric, then Viscount, the juniorate of the church of Saint Leobinus, founded in the castle of Brou over the river Ozanne, for the souls of his parents, while Arrard was bishop of Chartres [Col. 0504C].

But Gregory of Tours, Book V, chapter 26 of his history, explains the matter more plainly when he writes:

> “After this, King Chilperic ordered fines to be exacted from the poor and the juniors of the church or basilica because they had not marched with the army. For it was not customary for these persons to pay any public tax.”

Since the term *junioratus* has become antiquated and fallen out of use, I have treated it at greater length, lest the memory of the thing itself should be entirely lost.

## ON EPISTLE CCLXXXVII

This letter is surely worthy to be read by the curious and by those who inquire into the reasons for our sacraments, although faith alone suffices for the Christian; and it explains why, or in what manner, it sounds ill in a believer’s mouth, as Cyprian writes.

## ON EPISTLE CCLXXXIX

[Col. 0504D]

The following charter is not a letter, but an instrument granting the church of Hanches and the chapel, or chaplaincy, of Gidulphe’s Bridge, in the same parish and diocese of Chartres, to the abbot and monastery of Marmoutier, or to their priory of Saint Thomas of Sparnon.

## [SERMONS]

[Col. 0505]

**SERMONS OF SAINT IVO, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, ON ECCLESIASTICAL SACRAMENTS AND OFFICES, AND ON THE PRINCIPAL FESTIVALS OF THE YEAR.** (C)

**259 LIST OF SERMONS**

[Col. 0505A]

**SERMON I.** A sermon on the sacraments of the newly baptized, delivered in a synod.  
**II.** A sermon on the excellence of holy orders and the life of those to be ordained, delivered in a synod.  
**III.** On the meanings of priestly vestments.  
**IV.** On the sacraments of dedication.  
**V.** A short work on the correspondence of the old and new sacrifice, as the author himself entitled it.  
**VI.** Why God was born and suffered.  
**VII.** On the Advent of the Lord.  
**VIII.** On the Nativity of the Lord.  
**IX.** On the Circumcision of the Lord.  
**X.** On the Epiphany of the Lord.  
[Col. 0505B] **XI.** On the Purification of Saint Mary.  
**XII.** On Septuagesima.  
**XIII.** On the beginning of the fast.  
**XIV.** On Lent.  
**XV.** On the Annunciation of Blessed Mary.  
**XVI.** On Palm Sunday.  
**XVII.** On the Lord’s Supper.  
**XVIII.** On Easter.  
**XIX.** On the Ascension of the Lord.  
**XX.** On the holy day of Pentecost.  
**XXI.** On the chair of Saint Peter.  
**XXII.** On the Lord’s Prayer.  
**XXIII.** On the Apostles’ Creed.  
**XXIV.** On adulterated dress.

## SERMON I  
### On the Sacraments of the Newly Baptized, Delivered in a Synod

[Col. 0505C]

Since the people called to faith must be instructed by visible sacraments, so that through the presentation of visible things they may attain the understanding of invisible things, it is fitting, lords and priests who handle these sacraments, that you know the manner and order of the sacraments and the truth of the things signified. Otherwise, the stewards of such great mysteries are like blind guides of the blind, deriving from them no more benefit than beasts of burden derive when they carry bread for the use of others—although divine grace does not abandon the sacrament through which it works the salvation of peoples.

Let, therefore, the ministers of the Lord’s sacraments consider that Christ’s Church is daily gathered from among the nations through the operation of those same sacraments. The people of God’s possession, whose head is Christ, is brought to birth through faith; it is nourished through charity unto a perfect man; it is strengthened in that same faith and charity through the hope of eternity. Let them refer the administration of all sacraments to this end: that they may understand the Church of God to be founded in faith as the house of God; that love of God and neighbour may be built upon it as walls well joined together; and that its height may be raised by hope of the most glorious eternity.

Although this body of Christ followed the birth of its Head according to the customary order of birth, certain members preceded the birth of this Head in the unity of the body that was to follow him: namely, the patriarchs, prophets, and many righteous persons, who by many wonders and proclamations foreshadowed the birth of the Head of the body that was to come after them.

This was well shown in Jacob, who bore the type of the inward people. Hurrying to birth, he first put forth his hand, holding with it the heel of his elder brother [Col. 0506B] (Gen. XXXVI). By this act he signified that, once the former people, represented by Esau, had been rejected, the younger people—the Christians—would be born, and would possess the blessing of God the Father in an eternal inheritance.

For the sacraments of that former people are our lessons: by them that people, like a little child, was fed, and was occupied with worship of the one true God, lest it wander after gods either false or foreign. Hence, from the beginning of the world, in every age the sacraments of Christ and the Church were celebrated, by which both that people might be nourished and the manner of our redemption might be set forth.

For in the first age Adam, a human being, was fashioned by God on the sixth day from earth his mother, without an earthly father, in the same image [as God] (Gen. I); and in the last age of the world, through Christ, born from an earthly mother without an earthly father, humanity was re-formed into that same image of God. In correspondence with this, in the same age Eve was formed from the side of Adam, who was the figure of Christ to come (Gen. II); and through the blood flowing from Christ’s side, together with the water of sanctification, the Church was built.

In the second age of the world, through eight souls delivered from the engulfing flood by the ark, the same Church was prefigured: in the hope of the eighth, that is, the resurrection, it is delivered through the waters of baptism, not without the aid of the saving wood, from the overwhelming flood of temptations [Col. 0507A].

Finally, in the third age, the people of God, freed from Egyptian slavery, crossed the Red Sea. The sea gave way when struck by Moses’ rod; it provided a path for the people of God; the enemies followed from behind and were drowned. Here baptismal sanctification, obtained [or: consecrated] through the saving wood, was again represented. For the Red Sea is red, and baptism too is red, consecrated by Christ’s blood. The enemies following from behind die, because past sins are erased by baptism.

Then, in the fourth age, the kingdom of David shone forth in the earthly Jerusalem, prefiguring the kingdom of Christ and the Church. From David’s seed Christ himself was born; he reigns spiritually in his Church and, after the times are completed, gloriously crowns her in obedience to him.

Hence those who are to be baptized on Holy Saturday are brought to church in the fourth week of Lenten observance—which supplies us with the weapons of self-restraint—and on the fourth day of that week, to be catechized and exorcized. There they are to hear and be instructed how they must fight against spiritual evils. Yet their baptism is postponed until the Saturday of Easter, the Church observing in this that those called to the contest in this present life are baptized in hope of future rest. Thus those who are to fight against visible enemies are not chosen for military service before the age of life, that is, youth, so that, as those about to fight at that age are stronger for repelling visible enemies, so those chosen for the Christian warfare under the figure of this number may manfully wage the Christian contest and, in order to deserve a crown, not withdraw from the battle line [Col. 0507C].

After the period of the kings of Israel, when the fifth age began, because of the perversity of the aforesaid people, part of that people was carried away into Babylon by the king of Babylon. Having voluntarily served confusion, it served unwillingly the king of Babylon, whose name means “confusion.” After seventy years, Cyrus bringing this about, the same people returned to Jerusalem, as Isaiah and then Jeremiah had foretold.

This fittingly concerns the condition of the Church, which, after the many afflictions it has suffered or will suffer under the kings of this spiritual Babylon during the times of this age—times which revolve in the sevenfold number of days [Col. 0507D]—will return to the heavenly Jerusalem, where it will enjoy the vision of peace and will serve confusion no more. Hence the Apostle says:

> “The creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope; because the creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of this corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII).

Throughout all these ages there did not fail to be righteous men, members of the future Church; nor did sacraments suited to each age fail, as nourishment for the people. Many could be recounted concerning them, were we not aiming at brevity.

At last, in the sixth age, Christ was born of a Virgin, just as on the sixth day the first-created man was fashioned from virgin earth [Col. 0508A]. This Christ is the end of the Law and the truth, fulfilling everything that had preceded in the shadow of sacraments. In the fullness of time, as has been said, Christ was born, grew, and reached manhood. In the thirtieth year of his life [variant: “in the year of his age”], as the Evangelists relate, he was baptized by John—not because he needed it, but because his life was a discipline of conduct for Christians.

Thereafter he chose apostles, preached the Gospel, and was crucified, giving us an example of humility and patience. On the third day he rose again, strengthening his members by the hope of his resurrection. Shortly before ascending to heaven, he instructed his disciples what they ought to do, saying:

> “Go, teach all nations; preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Matt. XXVIII; Mark XVI).

In these few words the Lord’s priests, successors and vicars of the apostles—of whom it is said, “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. XLIV)—are taught how they must catechize untaught peoples who still bear the image of the earthly human being, and how, through the washing of water in the word, they must transform them in newness of life into conformity with Christ [Col. 0508B].

This was done in the times of the apostles and martyrs, who proclaimed Christ’s Gospel among Jews and Gentiles to intelligent persons and to all persons capable of receiving God’s word. But after the Church had been extended and gathered [*aggregata*: “assembled”] among the nations, and no unbelieving person of mature understanding was found among the faithful, provision was made also for the salvation of their little children, lest they should leave this life before the years of reason and remain strangers to Christ’s fellowship. They were baptized in the sacrament of faith and reconciled to God through another’s faith, just as they had been alienated from God through another’s sin.

Accordingly, this new form of sacramental practice was instituted: little children were to be catechized, exorcized, initiated, and finally baptized. In their case the Church hears on behalf of the child and answers the questions, until the child reaches the age of understanding and himself understands the sacraments of faith, charity, and hope imposed upon him. Concerning the meaning of these sacraments, insofar as the Lord may choose to inspire us, we have proposed to say something to your charity, so that you yourselves may understand the power of the sacraments [Col. 0508D] and strive to teach your hearers.

It must first be noted how the child to be baptized is conceived in the womb of Mother Church, and by what nourishment he is fed within that womb until the birth of the new person. For there are three things through which the one to be baptized is conceived, nourished, and brought forward unto the integrity of newness, until he is clothed with it: catechisms, exorcisms, and prayers.

The person called to faith is catechized so that he may be moved by the free choice of his own will toward that to which he is called. He is exorcized so that the wicked power of the devil may be driven away from him. Prayer is added for him so that grace may go before and follow him, supplying strength to free choice and causing every deception of the malignant spirit to be put far away.

Thus the person to be baptized is first marked with the sign of the cross on forehead, breast, eyes, ears, nostrils, and mouth. By its power the devil was conquered and Christ exalted. Hence Habakkuk said:

> “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Hab. III).

By this sign the senses of the whole body are fortified; through its power all our sacraments are fulfilled and all the devil’s contrivances are frustrated. Thus, when the firstborn of Egypt were being destroyed, the Hebrew people, having marked the doorposts of their houses with the blood of the Paschal lamb [Col. 0509A] (Exod. XII), a type of the Lord’s Passion, were saved; while the Egyptian people, because they lacked this sign, were grievously struck in their firstborn.

Thus in Ezekiel Jerusalem is promised deliverance from impending destruction, if *Tau*, which represents the form of the cross, should be marked on the foreheads of those who groan and mourn—that is, of those who repent (Ezek. IX).

Afterward blessed salt is given into the child’s mouth, so that, seasoned with salt under the figure of wisdom, he may be free from the stench of iniquity. Let him no longer decay through the worms of vices, but be preserved incorrupt for receiving the full grace of Christ; let him no longer lose his savour from the seasoning of wisdom, nor look backward like Lot’s wife (Gen. XIX).

Then the malignant spirit is blown out; this is what the sacred mysteries signify when the child is breathed upon and exorcized. For it is not God’s creature in infants that is exorcized and expelled, but he under whose power those are born who are born under sin. They have not yet been reborn through holy baptism, but by the sign of the cross they have already been conceived in the womb of Mother Church [Col. 0509B].

All the anointings of priestly ministry are performed in the form of the cross. All the sacraments performed by exorcisms, prayers, and breathings upon are like foods refreshing little children in the womb, so that Mother Church may joyfully present them to Christ when they have been reborn through the water of salvation.

Afterward the child’s ears and nostrils are touched with saliva. Saliva descends from the head into the mouth, signifying heavenly wisdom. By its touch the ears of the heart are opened to understand God’s word, and the nostrils to repel the stench of harmful pleasures. Hence Blessed Ambrose says in the book *On the Sacraments*:

> “What did we do on Saturday? Namely, the opening; for the sacraments of opening were celebrated, because he touched your ears and nostrils.”

This the Lord Jesus Christ signifies in the Gospel, when a deaf and mute man was brought to him. He touched the man’s mouth because he was mute, and his ears because he was deaf, and said:

> “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened” (Mark VII).

Then the priest comes to the font. The font is consecrated in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If the water of salvation is consecrated by these words, baptism is received neither better from a good person nor worse from an evil person. Hence Augustine, in Book III *On the One Baptism*:

> “Water over which God’s name is invoked is neither profane nor adulterated, even if it is invoked by profane and adulterous persons; for neither the creature itself nor the name itself is adulterated.”

The Creed of faith, composed by the twelve apostles and contained in an equal number of propositions, is also delivered to those being instructed in the new life [Col. 0510A].

Finally, the child is asked by the priest at baptism: “Do you renounce Satan and all his works and his pomps?” Thus he may first reject error and then draw near to truth, so that, according to the Apostle, he may put off the old man with his deeds (Eph. IV), renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires according to his former manner of life (Tit. II). The child answers through the mouths of those who carry him: “I renounce.”

Hence Augustine, against Julian, Book IV:

> “Whoever denies that little children renounce and believe through the mouths of those who carry them must deny that they receive baptism, which they accept while struggling in the hands of those who carry them.”

The same writer, in the book *On Penance*:

> “For little children, for the consecration and remission of original sin, the faith of those who offer them is beneficial, so that whatever stains of sins they have contracted through others, from whom they were born, may also be cleansed through the questioning of others.”

After the renunciation, the catechumen is anointed on the breast with holy oil, as though fortified against the invisible enemy, lest he persuade him to impure and harmful desires. He is also anointed between the shoulders, where there is strength for carrying a burden, so that he may receive strength to bear the burden of the day and heat, like a good athlete.

Then he is asked whether he believes in God the almighty Father; in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord; and in the Holy Spirit—one God in Trinity and in unity; whether he confesses that there is one holy catholic Church; and whether he believes in forgiveness of sins and eternal life. If he professes that he believes all these things, the old man already begins to die in him, and through faith the new man begins to live, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth [Col. 0510C] (Eph. IV).

In renouncing the former possessor, prompted by charity, he already desires to enter the house of the lawful possessor, in whom he now professes belief and from whom he awaits eternal rewards. The old leaven has now been purged out (1 Cor. V), but he is not yet a new dough unless the washing of the sacred font follows.

Therefore, in response to the threefold interrogation, the catechumen is washed from the defilements of oldness by three immersions; clothed with the new man, he is buried with Christ in the Lord’s three-day burial. Hence the Apostle says:

> “All we who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been made one with the likeness of his death, we shall also be one with his resurrection” (Rom. VI).

Hence Blessed Ambrose also says in the book *On the Sacraments*:

> “You were asked: ‘Do you believe in God the almighty Father?’ You said, ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed—that is, you were buried. You were asked again: ‘Do you believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, born and suffering?’ You said, ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed—that is, you were buried with Christ. But whoever is buried with Christ will rise with Christ. You were asked a third time: ‘Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?’ You said, ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed a third time, so that the third confession might remove the manifold fall of thought, speech, and action.”

This cleansing of holy baptism, celebrated in likeness of Christ’s death, was prefigured by the water of sprinkling in the old Law (Num. XIX), by which one who had touched a corpse was cleansed so that he might return to the camp. Into it were mixed the ashes of a red heifer burned outside the camp, hyssop, scarlet, and cedar [Col. 0511A].

The heifer, because it is of the female sex, signifies the frailty—that is, the passibility—of Christ’s flesh. It was red because of the shedding of blood and was cast out outside the camp; by this it was figured that the Lord too, when about to suffer, was led outside the city. The fact that the tabernacle and all its vessels were sprinkled seven times with the heifer’s blood signifies the complete cleansing which Christ’s blood conferred within and without [*extra*; variant *foris*: “outside”].

For the soul consists of a threefold power, while the body is constituted by a fourfold combination of elements; both were cleansed by the sprinkling of Christ’s blood. That the flesh, hide, and dung of the heifer were burned signifies that the whole humiliation and ignominy of the Passion was transformed into the glory of the resurrection. This is aptly signified by fire, which always tends upward and transforms into itself whatever it takes up.

The hyssop mingled with this sprinkling signifies that sins are cleansed by faith in Christ’s death. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV).

Hyssop signifies faith because, although it is a lowly herb, it clings firmly to the rock. Scarlet is employed for this cleansing because, by its flaming colour, it signifies charity [Col. 0511B], without which whatever faith performs is dead. Cedar also assists this cleansing. It is called an incorruptible tree and takes root upon high mountains; therefore it signifies hope of incorruption and heavenly glory.

The union of all these things consecrates the water of sprinkling, because, as stated, one who had touched a corpse is cleansed. Thus one freed from dead works, that is, original sins, is baptized in holy baptism in faith in Christ’s death and resurrection, with a pledge of charity and hope. Hence the Apostle says to the Hebrews:

> “If the blood of a heifer, sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more shall Christ’s blood, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself to God, cleanse our consciences to serve the living God?” (Heb. IX).

It should be noted that the text says that, if he dies before purification, he remains in uncleanness and that soul perishes from Israel—that is, from the fellowship of God’s people. What else does this mean than that punishment remains for that soul even after death if, while living, it has not been cleansed by this sacrament, by which Christ’s baptism is prefigured?

But it says that this purification is performed by a clean man, whereby are signified ministers bearing the person of their Lord, who is the clean man. Hence in what follows, concerning one who sprinkles the water of sprinkling, it commands him to wash his garments—that is, to be clean in mind and body.

When the sacraments of baptism have been completed and the baptized person has come up from the font, he is anointed with holy chrism upon the crown of his head, so that he may know that he has been promoted to the royal and priestly race [Col. 0512A]: that is, so that he may be called a Christian from fellowship with Christ and be a co-heir of the eternal kingdom. Through this sacrament, perfection follows the water [variant *postquam*: “afterward”], when at the priest’s invocation the Holy Spirit is poured out.

Then a white garment is given to the Christian, so that one who had darkened the beauty of his first birth with the rags of oldness may display in the dress of regeneration the garment of glory. After the sacred anointing, his head is also covered with a holy veil, so that he may understand that he possesses the diadem of royalty and, as said above, priestly dignity.

Finally, a lighted candle is placed in the hands of the baptized, “so that they may be taught to fulfil that saying of the Gospel: ‘Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven’” (Matt. V). If he does this steadfastly, he will not be driven from the bridegroom’s door with the foolish virgins, his lamp extinguished, but will be gathered with the prudent to be glorified (Matt. XXV).

Through all the sacraments above mentioned, the new man is begun, advanced, completed in the womb of the Church, and joined to the unity of the Church. Therefore, if his health permits, he is also strengthened by the sacraments of unity, that is, Christ’s body and blood.

When he has reached the years of understanding, he must be admonished by priests and by those through whose voice he renounced and received the Creed of faith, so that what he promised through the mouths of others he may now strive to believe in his heart, confess with his own mouth, and imitate in deed.

Hence Augustine, in a sermon delivered on the first Sunday after Easter:

> “Before all else I admonish you, both men and women who have received children at baptism, that you should recognize yourselves to have become sureties before God for those whom you received from the sacred font. Therefore always admonish them to preserve chastity, love justice, and maintain charity; to do to all what they wish to be done to themselves; not to observe omens; not to pay vows to trees and branches [*frondes*; variant *fontes*, “springs”]; to flee incantations, charms, sacrileges, and amulets as though they were the devil’s poisons; not to commit theft or bear false witness. Above all, you yourselves must know the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer and show them to those whom you have received.”

Moreover, every Christian must be taught to love him who received him from the sacred font as a father [Col. 0512C]. A son must not contract marriage with the daughter, nor a daughter with the son, of his spiritual father; such a union should not be called marriage but rather an incestuous cohabitation. Hence Pope Nicholas, in his response to the Bulgarians:

> “Among spiritual brothers and children there is a gratuitous and holy communion. It ought not to be called consanguinity, but rather spiritual brotherhood. Therefore we judge that no lawful marriage can take place between them.”

The Lord’s priests must know these and other similar necessary and honourable matters, and teach their hearers, so that those who hear may live rightly under their guidance, while the priests themselves receive a reward for good administration and render their account not groaning but with joy.

## SERMON II  
### On the Excellence of Holy Orders and the Life of Those to Be Ordained, Delivered in a Synod

[Col. 0513A]

Since in baptism you professed the Christian warfare and received spiritual weapons against invisible enemies through the laying on of hands, you have served for a time in the Lord’s camp as common soldiers—provided that you rejected what is hostile to the Christian name and strove to do what is fitting.

From the Christian warfare that was common to you with the other faithful, you have chosen the clerical state: that is, to renounce the world and, together with the garb of humility, to promise the disposition of humility, so that you may deservedly say with the Psalmist:

> “I have chosen to be abject in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. XXIII).

It is not for you to seek the first place at your Lord’s table, unless he who invited you says to one of you:

> “Friend, go up higher” (Luke XIV),

so that honour may be given him in the presence of those reclining with him.

For no one ought to become a cleric in order to serve pleasure, pursue curiosity, or thirst after ambition. Nor ought he to seek anything but to possess as his inheritance God, whom he has chosen and by whom he has been chosen when he was admitted to the clergy. For this is what the Greek name *cleric* signifies: that he belongs to the Lord’s lot, because both God has chosen him as his lot and he has chosen God as his lot.

That the cleric has chosen God as his lot is aptly said in the psalm, in the person of the cleric himself when he is marked with the badge of the clerical state. For he says to God:

> “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV).

And in another psalm:

> “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. XXIII).

But that the Lord has chosen the cleric himself as his lot is said, in the Lord’s person, at the cleric’s tonsure, from the preceding psalm:

> “The measuring-lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is glorious to me” (Ps. XV).

Therefore, whoever seeks through the clerical office something other than God has neither been chosen by God nor chosen God, since in his lot he has either preferred a creature to the Creator or placed it on equal terms with him.

In saying this, we do not forbid you the necessities of this life, whether acquired from offerings, from the work of your hands, or from other innocent trades; but they must not be gathered from usury, shameful gains, commerce [Col. 0513C], or other unlawful occupations. For thus the tribe of Levi, which went before as a figure of the clerical order, had no portion among the remaining tribes, but lived from the first-fruits, tithes, and offerings which the other tribes offered.

If, then, you intend to live from the alms of the temple, and seek nothing apart from God—who, if you are content with him, will be for you a most ample and rich estate—you have approached the clerical state healthfully, because your life accords with your name and your profession appears in your works.

But if you do not possess in your heart the poverty and humility displayed by your bodily dress and the form of your head, I fear that your portion may be with the hypocrites and your hope empty of eternal reward. For you seek only temporal gain in the clerical warfare, not as clerics but as *acephali*, “headless men.”

For this reason you shave the hair on the crown of your head in the form of a crown: both to show by this figure the spiritual kingdom in which you surpass others, and to cut from your heart the repeatedly returning enticements of mortal care, just as you shave from your head the repeatedly growing hair [Col. 0514A].

You ought to cut the remaining hair in such a manner that it leaves the ears, eyes, and other senses of the head free, and recognize that care for outward things should be exercised not in superfluous desires of the flesh, but only in necessities. If, therefore, you are disposed to walk in God’s way as stated above, you are worthy to be called clerics and to be promoted to the greater offices of clerical warfare.

These offices are distinguished in seven grades, because Holy Church is adorned by the gift of sevenfold grace. Our Lord displayed these offices in his own person and left them to be performed by his Church, so that the pattern which had gone before in the Head might be represented in the body.

In these seven offices the first rank is that of the doorkeepers, who are able to distinguish between good and bad, worthy and unworthy persons; to admit into the Church those whom they know to be worthy, and to repel those whom they know to be unworthy. Their charge is both to guard the entrance of the church and to watch over the Church’s goods with vigilant care. Therefore, when they are ordained, the bishop hands them the keys of the church and says to them: “Act thus, as men who must render an account to God for the things that are unlocked by these keys.” Our Lord himself instituted this office for us when, having made a whip of cords, he “drove from the temple those who were selling and buying, and overturned the tables of the money-changers” (John 2). By this act he signified that every form of trade in ecclesiastical goods ought to be expelled from the Church. Therefore he, the aforesaid doorkeeper, says: “I am the door” (John 10): “if anyone enters through me, he will enter and go out”; that is, whoever has canonically received the administration of the ecclesiastical kingdom shall enter—that is, shall be received by me—and shall go out, because, after completing the stewardship entrusted to him, he shall be freed from the bondage of this corruption.

From there one is promoted to the office of readers, so that he may now, by commission of the Church, read in church the prophetic and apostolic lessons. Therefore, in the presence of the people, the book of the divine Scriptures is handed to them, and it is said: “Receive it, and be proclaimers of the word of God; if you faithfully and profitably fulfil your office, you shall have a share with those who have ministered well.” He who is advanced to this rank must be instructed in letters, so that he may understand the meaning of the words, know the force of the accents, and read distinctly, lest by confused pronunciation he deprive the hearers of understanding. He must attend to what should be read indicatively, what interrogatively, where there is a lesser pause in the sentence and where a medial pause; for the incorrect observance of these matters disturbs the meaning and exposes the reader’s grammatical manner to ridicule. For the reader must serve both ears and heart. Our Lord showed this office in his own person when, in the midst of the elders, he opened the book of Isaiah the prophet and read distinctly for understanding: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Luke 4; Isaiah 61), together with the rest that follows in the same chapter. By this example the reader may know that he ought to shine with spiritual grace and thus proclaim the word of God to his hearers.

Third follows the order of exorcists, who perform over catechumens the rites of opening and have spiritual authority over unclean spirits, in order to cast them out of possessed bodies. He who commands unclean spirits ought, however, to possess a clean spirit, so that his life may accord with his office; and so that the evil being whom, through the office received, he expels from another’s body, he may expel from his own heart by purity of life. Otherwise the remedy which he administers to another will not benefit himself, and it may be said to him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4), if through impurity of conscience he retains an unclean spirit. When they are ordained, they receive from the bishop’s hand the book of exorcisms, and are told: “Receive it, and have authority to lay your hand upon one possessed, or upon a catechumen.” The Lord exercised this office when he touched with his saliva the ears of the deaf and mute man and said: “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened” (Mark 7). By this example [variant: “by this same example”] he taught us that, by such a sacrament, we ought to open the ears of the inner heart for understanding and the mouth for confession. This occurs [variant: “what occurs”] when, the demon having been expelled, the true possessor receives back his vessel.

In the fourth place come the acolytes, called in Latin *ceroferarii*, “candle-bearers,” because they carry lighted candles while the Gospel is read or the sacrifice offered. This is not in order to illuminate the darkness of the air, but so that, as they bear visible light in their hands, they may display works of light to their neighbours and, after the manner of light, guide those who wander and grope in darkness along the way. The Lord testifies in the Gospel that he holds this office, saying: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8). When they are ordained, after they have been taught by the bishop how they ought to act in their office, they receive from the archdeacon a candlestick with a candle, so that they may know that they are appointed to light lamps. They receive an empty cruet for pouring water into the chalice in which the blood of Christ is to be consecrated. Here commemoration is made of the blood flowing from Christ’s side and of the water issuing from it. These two are mixed in the chalice because we have been redeemed by Christ’s blood and washed from sins by the water of baptism (John 19).

In the fifth place subdeacons are ordained. They already approach the ministry of the altar, because they carry the vessels of the body and blood of Christ. Therefore the law of continence is imposed upon them, that they may fulfil the Prophet’s words: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52); that is, that they may present themselves as vessels unto honour, not unto dishonour, and may carry to the altar, and bring back from the altar to God’s glory, those vessels by which the Lord’s body is ministered [variant: “to the Lord’s body”—*corpori*]—namely, so that they may flee every impurity of the flesh. They minister in the offices of the Levites and receive in the temple of the Lord the offerings of the people. It belongs to their provision to place upon the altar only as much of the offerings as may suffice for the people. It is their office to wash the corporals, altar-cloths, and coverings, and to bring water into the baptistery [variant: “to force water in”—*urgere*]. When they are ordained, they receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice. From the hand of the archdeacon they receive a cruet with water, a towel, and a hand-cloth [variant: “water, a hand-basin, and a hand-cloth”], with which priest and Levite ought to cleanse their hands when they are about to handle the Lord’s sacraments. The Lord exercised this office when, after supper with his disciples, he girded himself with a linen cloth, poured water into a basin, washed the disciples’ feet, and dried them with the linen cloth (John 13).

The linen cloth and the hand-cloth have one significance, since both are made of flax and attain whiteness through much beating and washing. With the linen cloth feet stained with dust are first washed with water and then dried. Thus with the Psalmist we say: “Every night”—that is, at every offence—“I will wash my bed” (Psalm 6), that is, my conscience, in which I rest when healthy and suffer when ill; and with the Apostle: “I discipline my body and bring it into bondage” (1 Corinthians 9). In the same way ministers wash and wipe their hands three times when they shake from their works every earthly desire.

The order of deacons is in the sixth place, not without some mystery of the number six, by which, because of its perfection, perfection of works is signified. This order has its beginning in the Old Testament from the tribe of Levi. For the Lord commands Moses (Numbers 2, 3, and 4), after the ordination of Aaron and his sons, that the tribe of Levi should in turn be appointed to the ministries of divine worship, consecrated to the Lord, and serve for Israel before Aaron and his sons in the tabernacle of God; that they themselves should carry the ark, the tabernacle, and all its vessels; that they should pitch their camp around the tabernacle; and that, when the tabernacle was transported, they should take it down and set it up again. From twenty years of age and above they were commanded to serve in the tabernacle. The holy Fathers established this rule also in the New Testament, because this age is strong enough to bear burdens. What was instituted for that order by Moses is also represented in the New Testament when the stole is placed over the deacon’s left shoulder and, on fast days, the chasuble is folded over that same shoulder. For whatever labour and endurance we bear in this life, we carry, as it were, on the left, until we have rest on the right—that is, in eternity.

This order took its beginning in the New Testament from the apostles, when, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, they chose seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit, for this office and, after prayer, laid hands upon them (Acts 6). Thereafter the apostles and their successors decreed that in every *matrice* [variant: *matre*, “mother”] church seven deacons should stand around Christ’s altar in a higher rank, like pillars of the altar—not without some mystery of the number seven. It signifies that, shining with the Spirit of sevenfold grace, they should be holy in body and spirit. For this number consists of four and three: four refers to the body, because of the harmonious combination of the four elements in the body; while three refers to the soul, because of the soul’s threefold power, through which we are commanded to love God threefoldly: with all the heart, which refers to understanding; with all the soul, which refers to will; and with all the mind, which refers to memory.

These are the seven angels whom we read of in the Apocalypse as sounding trumpets (Revelation 8): angels, because they are messengers; sounding trumpets, that is, outwardly resounding high mysteries from inward inspiration. These are the seven golden lampstands: that is, bearing the light of the Gospel in their hands, namely in their works, and proved under every testing of fire, that is, of tribulation. They are also the seven thunders, shaking bestial minds by terrible threats as with a dreadful thunderclap. John the Baptist uttered such thunder when he said: “Brood of vipers, who will give you escape from the wrath to come?” (Matthew 3). And the Lord in the Gospel: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matthew 7), and many sayings of this kind.

Like a herald, they openly exhort all to pray and to bend the knee. They proclaim the Gospel; they dispense the sacraments. Priests are not permitted to lift the Lord’s chalice at the table [reading *mensa*; variant *missa*, “Mass”] unless it has been handed to them by the deacon. Levites place the offerings upon the altar; they prepare the Lord’s table; they veil the lofty mysteries [variant: “the altar of mysteries”]; clothed in white vestments, they stand at the altar. In this is signified how great a purity of brightness they ought to have in their minds, corresponding to that which they display in their bodies. For it is fitting that God should have such ministers—men defiled by no contagion of the flesh but radiant in complete chastity of mind and body.

The Apostle teaches most fully, in writing to Timothy, what kind of deacons ought to be ordained. For after speaking first of priests, he adds: “Deacons likewise must be blameless” (1 Timothy 3)—that is, free from accusation, like bishops; chaste, that is, restraining themselves from lust; not double-tongued, namely lest they disturb peace among those who possess it; not given to much wine, because where drunkenness is, there lust and madness rule; not pursuing shameful gain, lest they seek earthly profit from spiritual ministry. After this he adds: “Let these first be tested, and then let them minister, having no charge against them.” Thus they, like bishops, ought to be examined before ordination; and, if found worthy, are to be admitted to sacred ministry.

The Lord exercised this office (John 13) when, after supper, he himself consecrated and distributed the sacraments by his own mouth and hands, and when he invited [variant: “urged”] the sleeping apostles to pray, saying: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26). When they are ordained, the bishop alone lays hands upon them, because they are admitted to ministry [variant: “to sacrifice”], not to priesthood. The bishop places the *orarium* or stole over their left shoulder, so that by this they may recognize that they have received the Lord’s yoke, by which they must both bear down and subject to the Lord’s yoke all things belonging to the left—that is, to the present life. They also receive the book of the Gospels from the bishop’s hand, that they may understand that they ought to be heralds of the Gospel.

The order of presbyters took its beginning from the sons of Aaron. They share much in common with bishops in their office: those now called presbyters were then called priests, and those now called pontiffs were then called chiefs of the priests. The sole difference between pontiffs and priests of the present time is that the ordination of clerics, the dedication of basilicas, the consecration of chrism, the laying on of hands, and the general blessing over the people have been added to pontiffs alone; whereas in the other sacraments—in catechizing, celebrating Mass, and preaching in church to the people—the ministry is common to both. But the matters mentioned above are reserved to the highest priests lest the same authority of power, claimed by all, should make them insolent and, when the bond of obedience had been loosened, generate scandal.

Those who are called *presbyteri* in Greek are called *seniores*, “elders,” in Latin—not so much on account of age as of prudence and maturity of character. Hence it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “Grey hair is the understanding of men, and a blameless life is old age for a human being” (Wisdom 4). Presbyters are indeed successors and vicars of the seventy disciples who went before the Lord Jesus into every city and place where he was about to come (Luke 10). Thus presbyters, because they are the bishops’ assistants, initiate untaught peoples, incorporate them into the unity of the Church through baptism, and minister to God’s people in all sacraments up to the laying on of hands. Bishops, however, are successors of the apostles; because of necessity, they seek for themselves the assistance of priests and the reinforcement of their office, so that they may more easily govern innumerable peoples.
