So Moses in the wilderness chose seventy prudent men (Numbers 11), by whose counsel and assistance he might readily govern the immense multitude of the people of Israel.

Whether they are priests of lower rank or of the highest rank, they bear the office of Christ the high priest when they call sinful people to repentance and heal them by the medicine of their prayers. Therefore the Apostle says: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore, I beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5). They exercise, as has been said, the office of mediator when they intercede with God for the people and reconcile penitents by absolving them. Therefore, just as the mediator between God and human beings reconciled the world by sharing in our mortality and absolved it by sharing in divinity, so priests of both orders ought, as good mediators, both to have compassion on sinners through consciousness of their own weakness and to have God’s peace [variant: “peace with God”] through the eminence of holiness. “For a mediator,” as the Apostle says, “is not of one” (Galatians 3), because he is a friend to both parties whom he wishes to reconcile.

The same Apostle, writing to Titus, describes what presbyters should be like: “For this reason I left you in Crete: that you might appoint presbyters in the cities, as I directed you” (Titus 1): if anyone is without accusation, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of debauchery or insubordination. “For a bishop must be without accusation.” By this statement he shows that presbyters too are designated under the name of bishops. Thus, in writing to Timothy about the ordination of bishop and deacon (1 Timothy 3), he is silent concerning presbyters, understanding them under the name of bishops. Therefore the Apostle also speaks to Titus (Titus 1), and the canons themselves testify, that such persons ought to be appointed presbyters in the Church as bishops.

When they are ordained, while the bishop blesses them and holds his hand over their heads, all the presbyters present raise their hands beside the bishop’s hand over their heads and invoke the Holy Spirit upon those being ordained. After the invocation of the Holy Spirit, they receive the stole over both shoulders. It protects the right side and the left like supports, so that they may understand that they are armed with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left: neither adversity may break them nor prosperity exalt them. They also receive from the bishop’s hand a chalice with wine and a paten with a host, that by these instruments they may receive the power to offer pleasing sacrifices to God.

The Lord Jesus Christ exercised this office (Matthew 16; Mark 14) when, after supper, he changed bread and wine into his body and blood and ordained his disciples to do the same in remembrance of his passion. He fulfilled this office still more manifestly and excellently when he, both priest and victim, offered himself upon the altar of the cross for the sins of humankind and, entering the eternal holy places through his own blood, reconciled heavenly and earthly things. This shows how great is the excellence of the priestly office, through which Christ’s passion is daily celebrated at the altar and every guilty person who turns from sins is reconciled to God. Having briefly treated all these matters concerning the priestly order, Christ’s priests ought to be admonished that, as they excel in the dignity of their order, so they may excel in holiness of life, so that the people entrusted to them, instructed by their discipline, may gladly obey them and advance day by day through imitation of them.

## SERMON III. Delivered in a synod: On the meanings of priestly vestments

Since the holiness of the ministry demands holiness in its ministers, we briefly recalled in the preceding sermon, from apostolic institution, what sort of persons ought to be promoted to the priesthood. But we did not add to that sermon what dress they should wear when ordained or when approaching the altar. We must therefore carefully consider priestly and pontifical vestments: what the variety of garments signifies in priests’ morals; what the gleam of gold signifies; what the brilliance of gems signifies. For nothing there should lack a rationale; rather, everything should be a form of holiness and an image of every virtue. As a good house is known from its very entrance, so Christ’s priest shows outwardly, through the adornment of sacred vestments, what he ought inwardly to be in himself.

This rite of sacred vestments began through Moses, although Christian religion, more intent upon realities than figures, does not clothe its priests in all those ancient ornaments. Let us first examine the ornaments of the ancient high priests: in what order they used them, whether when ordained or when they entered the Holy of Holies to offer incense. Then, comparing our vestments with theirs, let us consider what they have alike, what unlike, and how they agree even in the things signified. For the two Cherubim look upon the mercy-seat (Exodus 23), because the sacraments of both Testaments are directed toward faith in divine propitiation, which in the old priesthood is shadowed under the manifold covering of sacrifices, but in the New Testament is fulfilled through the one true and perfect sacrifice. Thus in the adornments of priests of both covenants both the sublimity of the priesthood is commended and the chaste dignity of priests is signified, so that through their outer dress those who bear the office of that true and highest pontiff may learn what they ought inwardly to be. In him was every fullness of the virtues which the outward ornaments of the members profess.

But let us now come to our subject, and first see how Moses, at the Lord’s command, adorned and then clothed Aaron and his sons. For thus we read in Leviticus: “And Moses did as the Lord commanded him. He assembled the congregation at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony; and Moses brought forward Aaron his brother and his sons and washed them with water. He clothed him in a tunic, girded him with a belt, clothed him with an inner tunic, placed the shoulder-garment upon him, girded him according to the workmanship of the shoulder-garment, placed upon him the breastpiece, and upon the breastpiece manifestation and truth; he placed a mitre upon his head, and before his face upon the mitre he set a golden plate on which the name of the Lord was written” (Leviticus 8).

The order of the words should be noted. Although the Lord had commanded and chosen the high priest to be appointed, the congregation is nevertheless summoned. The people’s presence is required in the election of a priest so that all may know that he who is the most learned of the whole people, who excels in every virtue, ought to be chosen for the priesthood—and this with the Church’s consent—lest later there be any reconsideration or lingering doubt. Rather, he is commended by everyone’s testimony, according to the Apostle: “A bishop must have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Timothy 3). Thus Moses first washes those approved by the people’s testimony and afterward clothes them.

In this action Moses bears the type of the law, which first washes the priests to be ordained before clothing them. For unless a man has first been approved through observance of the law, he is not to be promoted to the priesthood. Once thus approved, he is clothed in a tunic, which among them is of *byssus* and among us is linen. *Byssus* is a kind of very white flax, brought to the highest brightness through much beating and washing. It signifies perfect purity of the flesh, according to what is read in the Apocalypse: “Fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints” (Revelation 19). The priest’s flesh does not possess this purity from itself, just as flax is not white of itself; rather, as has been said, it is made white through many disciplines and washings, so that it may become fit for the high priest’s garments.

The pattern of priestly purity is that, according to the Apostle, priests should discipline their flesh and bring it into servitude (1 Corinthians 9), and, grace going before, obtain through diligence what they could not possess by nature. This garment is called in Greek ποδήρης (*podērēs*), that is, “reaching to the feet,” because it extends from the neck to the ankles. It is so close-fitting and proportioned to the limbs of the body that its very form testifies that the priest has nothing loose or slack, but is prepared for every good work. This same garment is more firmly tightened about the loins by a belt, so that the priest’s chastity may not be loosened by any heat of incitements.

This is aptly signified by the four colours with which that belt was varied: fine linen, purple, hyacinth-blue, and scarlet. By these colours the four elements are signified, from whose mixture human nature is composed; their imbalance generates the flux of the flesh unless it is restrained by the medicinal remedy of continence. Those who speculate about such matters wished the earth to be signified by fine linen, because it grows from the earth; water by purple, because it is dyed with the blood of sea-shellfish; air by hyacinth-blue, because it imitates the colour of the clear sky; and fire by scarlet, which gleams with a flaming hue. Their excess, as has been said, produces especially in the loins superfluous and corrupt humours, unlawful impulses; unless these are checked by the bridle of moderation, the dignity of chastity is easily endangered by their assault. Where the conflict is greater, a greater guard must be employed. Hence, among the pontifical vestments, linen breeches are also applied about the loins, not so much to cover the shamefulness of the flesh, already concealed by the customary garments, as for a sign that chastity must be preserved.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Our honourable members have no need; but those which are dishonourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour” (1 Corinthians 12). The high priests of the new priesthood do not use breeches, upon whom the daily necessity of preserving chastity is laid, just as the authority to offer daily is granted to them. By contrast, the high priests serving the shadow, having completed their term, took off their breeches, though they wore them during the time of their service. The remaining two garments, the foot-length tunic and the belt, are common vestments to old and new priests. Although our priests’ belt is not woven with four colours—whether through lack of materials or absence of craftsmen, whatever the cause—both that belt and this bear one type of temperance.

The fourth garment follows: the inner, or hyacinth-blue, tunic. In both Old and New Testament only high priests use it. The high priest is fittingly clothed with two tunics because he ought to bring forth from his treasury things new and old: that is, to understand the law according to the letter, as it was observed before Christ’s coming, and according to the Spirit, as it is understood after his coming. Thus the second tunic is called inner, or hyacinth-blue; its colour imitates the serenity of heaven, so that it may be understood that the high priest ought to think more of heavenly than of earthly things. For the proper order is that we should first strive for purity of flesh, through which we may come to purity of heart, which advances us to understanding of divinity, according to: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

The fifth garment is the shoulder-piece, called in Hebrew *ephot* [variant: *ephod*]. Among us it is both a priestly and a pontifical garment; among the Hebrews, however, it was only pontifical. Among them it was varied with the same colours as the pontifical belt. Of it the ordination of the high priest says: “And he girded him”—speaking of Moses—“according to the workmanship of the shoulder-piece.” The shoulders are strong for doing works and carrying burdens. They are bound by the encircling shoulder-piece and its fastenings because the high priest ought to be bound both by innocence and by works of righteousness, so that nothing loose or lax may be found in him. The varied colours in the belt signify the same thing in the shoulder-piece: whatever we do in earthly matters, whether in giving generously or restricting temporal things, we derive wholly from the balanced mixture of the four elements.

Thus four multiplied by ten rises to forty, because the due administration of the abundance of the four elements—signified by ten—leads to the true jubilee, obtained by the performance of good works. For the number forty, when its constituent parts are counted, makes fifty. In the law this number denotes the aforementioned jubilee, that is, the year of remission (Leviticus 25), prefiguring true liberty. Whoever has attained it will henceforth fear no slavery.

It accords with this signification of good works that the names of the twelve patriarchs were carved upon two precious stones of the shoulder-piece, six on one and six on the other. One was placed upon the right shoulder, the other upon the left. None of this lacks mystery. The number six, because of its perfection, signifies works of righteousness; the patriarchs’ names signify the memory of the saints, which we ought always to hold as an example of good works, on the right and on the left—that is, in prosperity and adversity. Therefore these names are written on stones, because what is carved in stone is scarcely, if ever, effaced. Nor is it without mystery that the high priest is girded according to the workmanship of the shoulder-piece, because each person will be repaid according to his works (Matthew 16). That the shoulder-piece of our high priests is not woven with so many colours or adorned with such precious gems makes no difference, since Christian religion, serving truth, makes the same thing understood through concise figures as ancient observance did through costly ones.

After the high priest’s private parts have been covered with their vestments, after he has begun to meditate upon heavenly things, after he has been adorned with works of righteousness, and after he has been strengthened by both girdles so as to stand firmly and perseveringly in all things, the breastpiece is placed upon the high priest’s breast. In Greek it is called *logion*, and by it wisdom, which consists in reason, is signified. Upon the breastpiece are placed “manifestation” and “truth.” Manifestation, because it does not suffice for the high priest to possess wisdom unless he can also make known what he knows and give an account of the faith and hope that are in us. Truth, because the high priest ought not to prophesy from his own heart, but to disclose only what truth possesses.

The breastpiece and shoulder-piece are joined to one another because reason and works ought mutually to adhere: what we conceive by the reason of the mind we should fulfil in deed. The order of these things should be noted: the breastpiece does not come before the shoulder-piece, because wisdom does not come before works; rather, works come first, then wisdom. Thus the Psalm says: “From your commandments I have understood” (Psalm 118). And of the Lord Jesus it is said: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). Then manifestation does not come before the breastpiece, because no one ought to teach what he does not know. The prophet agrees with this order when he says: “Sow for yourselves righteousness, reap the fruit of life, and enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hosea 10).

In this breast ornament twelve stones were set, bearing carved upon them the names of the twelve patriarchs, because the high priest ought always to hold the examples of the holy Fathers in memory and regulate his actions accordingly. In the twelvefold number of stones apostolic teaching may be signified [variant: “be figured”], because the stones were distributed in four rows, three placed in each corner of the breastpiece. This fittingly corresponds to apostolic teaching, which preached the faith of the Trinity through the four Gospels in every region of the world. This adornment belonged only to the high priest, as even now it belongs to those who are permitted to use it, because of the distinction between greater and lesser priests.

When the high priest has thus been adorned, a mitre is placed upon his head, also called a *cidaris* or tiara. By it is understood the sovereignty over the five senses, in which the high priest ought to excel. For in the head lies the use of all the bodily senses; when this is well governed, the head of the man—that is, Christ—is fittingly adorned. And because the head of Christ is God (2 Corinthians 11), a golden plate is laid upon it, inscribed with the name of God, which the Hebrews call the Ineffable Name. By this it is understood that God, as he is the maker of all things, is also their ruler, and that whatever is well administered by the Lord’s priests ought to be referred to his honour and glory.

Moses ordained in Exodus that these vestments should be eight in number; but in Leviticus, while treating of the same garments, he was silent concerning the eighth, namely the breeches. Jerome therefore writes in his letter to Fabiola:

> “Where it is related how Moses clothed his brother Aaron in pontifical vestments, nothing at all is said of the breeches. I think this is for the reason that the law did not lay its hand upon our genitals and private parts, because we ourselves ought by confession to conceal our more secret monstrosities, and ought to govern and veil what is worthy of shame [variant: “and to be able [*valere*]”], and preserve before God the judge the consciousness of purity. But others can judge the remaining virtues—courage, justice, humility, gentleness, generosity. Chastity is known to conscience alone, and human eyes cannot be certain judges of this matter, except those who everywhere rush into lust after the fashion of brute animals. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 7). And in the Gospel, when the Lord spoke of voluntary and involuntary eunuchs, he added at the end: ‘He who is able to receive it, let him receive it’ (Matthew 19). It is as though he said: I do not clothe you with breeches, nor do I impose necessity upon anyone. Whoever wishes to be a priest, let him clothe himself; let him fortify himself with chastity. Therefore let us ourselves take up the breeches; let us ourselves cover our shameful parts [variant: “private parts”]; let us not seek the eyes of others. Let the genitals be so covered that, when we enter the Holy of Holies, no shamefulness may appear, lest we die.”

It should further be noted that lesser priests are given neither a double tunic, nor a shoulder-piece, nor a breastpiece, nor a golden plate, but only a foot-length tunic, mitre, and belt with which the linen tunic is girded. They nevertheless exercise the priesthood, but not with that sublimity exercised by those adorned with all eight vestments. Priests of the New Testament likewise do not use all those garments, since they do not use two tunics or a breastpiece except the high priests alone; and no one uses the golden plate. For, as blessed Jerome says in the above-mentioned letter, “what was once shown on the plate is now displayed in the sign of the cross. For the blood of the Gospel is more precious than the gold of the law.”

They use a linen tunic, called the *poderis* [long robe], [Col. 0524D] or talar garment, which symbolizes the chastening of all the members; and a girdle which binds the tunic close, restraining chastity from becoming loose and lax. They also use a shoulder-garment, by which works of righteousness are required of the priest: for temperance and abstinence from evil, signified by the two preceding vestments, are insufficient unless works of justice and mercy follow. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXI; 1 Pet. III). Therefore it is fastened to the *poderis* by the shoulder-piece [variant: “is afflicted”].

They also use a stole, called by another name an *orarium*, which the ancient priesthood did not use. This is laid upon the neck near the shoulders, like a yoke upon oxen ploughing or threshing, [Col. 0525A] so that they may fulfil that evangelical saying: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI). Descending from the neck along the front, it adorns both the right and the left side, teaching the priest that he must be armed with the weapons of righteousness 268 on the right and on the left—that is, in prosperity and adversity. This belongs to fortitude, without which the other virtues are easily overcome and by no means crowned. Hence the Apostle says: “You have need of patience, that you may receive the promises” (Heb. X). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. X, XXIV). Thus the stole is tied to the girdle of the *poderis* by certain fastenings, because [Col. 0525B] virtues aid virtues, lest they be moved by some onset of temptation.

Over all these vestments is placed the chasuble, also called the *planeta*. Because it is a common outer garment, it signifies charity, which is placed over all virtues, since the other virtues accomplish nothing useful without it. Hence the Apostle says: “And I will show you a still more excellent way: strive after charity” (1 Cor. XII). He subsequently proves how useless the other virtues are without it, affirming that even the chief virtues—namely, knowledge of languages, the distribution of one’s possessions, and martyrdom itself—are nothing, or have no value, without it. It is therefore assigned the place of prudence, because love is the fulfilment of the law (Rom. XIII); and because *acedia* often stealthily enters minds well ordered and devoted to [Col. 0525C] divine worship, diligent watchfulness must be employed frequently to wipe it away, so that this rising rheum may often be cleansed from the eyes of the heart. Hence a small cloth is placed in the left hand, to wipe away the often-flowing rheum of the eyes and remove their bleary inflammation.

These ornaments, as has been said, are not the virtues themselves but the insignia of virtues. Those who use them are reminded by them, as though by writings, what they ought to seek, what to avoid, and to what end they should direct their deeds. It should be added that levites also use, in their own fashion, the above-mentioned vestments, with the same meanings that they have for presbyters. Levites use the dalmatic, which, because of its breadth, signifies care for neighbours [Col. 0525D] and has the same meaning for them as the chasuble has for presbyters; for both kinds of ministers must exercise the same vigilance in fulfilling love.

Bishops and cardinal-presbyters also use sandals, which are the footwear of preachers. They have an unbroken sole away from the ground [variant: “to the ground”], so that the foot does not touch the earth. Above, however, it is made of leather pierced with certain straps, because the Gospel ought not to rest upon earthly advantages; nor should all evangelical [variant: “ecclesiastical”] mysteries be revealed to everyone, nor concealed from everyone. Hence the Lord said to the disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Matt. III). [Col. 0526A] The prophet understood this meaning of the sandals when he said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who proclaim good things!” (Isa. LII; Rom. X).

Before they are clothed in sandals, they are vested in fine linen or linen leggings, extending to the knees and tightly fastened there. By these it is signified that they must make straight steps with their feet, strengthen weak knees—that is, knees made lax by negligence—and thus hasten to preach the Gospel. Moreover, the hands of presbyters and bishops are anointed, so that they may know that through this sacrament they receive, in the power of the Holy Spirit, the grace of consecrating, and that they ought, according to their strength, to exercise works of mercy toward all. The bishop’s head, however, is specially anointed, so that he may understand [Col. 0526B] himself to be the vicar of him of whom it is said in the Psalm: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

By this anointing they receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that whatever they bind on earth may be bound in heaven, and whatever they loose on earth may be loosed in heaven (Matt. XVIII); and whose sins they retain may be retained, and whose sins they remit may be remitted (John XX). Having thus briefly set forth these matters concerning priestly and pontifical adornment, you must be admonished that, just as you have heard profound sacraments, so you should strive both to understand them in your heart and to fulfil them in deed. “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers” (Rom. I).

For each one of you can possess within himself a royal priesthood and priestly ornaments, if observance of the law has washed and made him clean; if the grace of baptism and the anointing of chrism remain unblemished; if he is clothed in the double vestments—namely, letter and spirit—and girded strongly in them, so as to be chaste in mind and body; if he is justified by the shoulder-garment of works; if he is guarded on the right and left by the stole of fortitude; and if he is filled with the fullness of knowledge, signified by the *planeta*. Thus adorned, I say, he can possess true priesthood within the temple of God, which he himself is. But those who presume to approach God’s altar neither clothed in sacred vestments nor adorned with honourable morals shall, like Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu, who were consumed by the strange fire they offered before the Lord (Lev. X), be tormented in eternal fires with those who entered the royal wedding without a wedding garment (Matt. XXII), since they seize the priesthood for themselves not by divine appointment but by their own presumption. [Col. 0526C–D]

Therefore it is said in Leviticus: “And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to Aaron your brother, that he may not enter at every hour into the inner holy places, lest he die” (Lev. XVI). This shows that if he entered the Holy of Holies disorderly—unprepared, not clothed in priestly vestments, and without first making God propitious to himself—he would die, and deservedly, as one who had not done the things that ought to be done before approaching God’s altar. For this concerns all of us; the law of God instructs us all, so that we may know how we ought to approach God’s altar and offer: namely, that we should put off filthy garments, [Col. 0527A] that is, the uncleanness of the flesh, perversity of morals, and defilements of lust.

Thus in Exodus, after the Lord had enumerated the garments in which Aaron and his sons were to be clothed, he added: “You shall clothe your brother and his sons with all these things; you shall consecrate the hands of them all and sanctify them, that they may exercise the priesthood for me” (Exod. XXVIII). It follows: “Aaron and his sons shall use them when they enter the tabernacle of testimony, when they approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest, guilty of iniquity, they die” (ibid.). From all this is gathered how great is the dignity of the priestly ministry, and how great the holiness ought to be of its ministers. Whoever possesses that holiness will not lack the merit of priesthood. But whoever does not possess it and usurps the office of priesthood will deservedly perish with the above-mentioned presumptuous persons. We have passed over much concerning the dignity of priesthood and the mystical beauty of priestly vestments, avoiding undue length, because these matters suffice for the building up of morals and the benefit of the hearers.

269

## SERMON IV. On the Sacraments of Dedication

Since you have devoutly assembled today for the dedication of this present basilica, you must recognize that everything which you see done in these holy things made by human hands has been fulfilled in you. First, you were brought to the Church in the hands of godparents and presented to priests or exorcists to be catechized. While they catechized you, [Col. 0527C] while they initiated you into Christ’s laws, they cut away the old mass corrupted by transgression. The profession of faith itself, and the renunciation of wicked conduct required from you, brought forth within you an inner newness, by which you might bear the image of Christ from heaven—reborn by grace—as formerly you had borne the image of the earthly parent from whom you were begotten by nature.

Instructed by these teachings, you approached the water and were washed in the fountain of salvation. There, according to the Apostle, through triple immersion you were buried with Christ, so that, just as he died once in the flesh and, rising from the dead, dies no more, so you, washed from sins and regenerated by the first resurrection, should not be subject to the death of the soul—that is, sin (Rom. VI). [Col. 0527D] Then you were anointed on the head with holy oil, so that charity, given through the Holy Spirit, might always abound in the heart, according to that saying of Wisdom: “Let oil never fail from your head” (Eccl. IX). Hence also the Apostle: “The love of God has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

The same Spirit was indeed given when you were washed with the saving waters, but there for the remission of past crimes, and here for building in your hearts love of God and neighbour. This love, in Christ’s body, does not prefer the native-born to the foreigner, the noble to the low-born, or man to woman; rather, by the Spirit of adoption it makes all children who through the same Spirit cry: “Our Father, forgive [Col. 0528A] us our debts” (Matt. VI). Therefore, in this body of Christ, that person alone is deemed higher who is stronger in the love of God.

You also received holy oil upon the breast, so that wisdom might flourish in your heart. You received it also upon the right shoulder, so that patience might be preserved unfailing in the exercises of good works, and so that your left hand might never know what your right hand does [variant: “has done”]. Because the shoulders possess the strength for bearing a burden, by the anointing of this part you were dedicated as athletes of Christ, that you might know yourselves called to contest and destined, throughout the whole course of your lives, to fight against the ancient enemy in public and private encounters. Finally, a white garment was given to you, covering head and limbs. By its whiteness it bore the image of the newness you had received [Col. 0528B] and the hope of future immortality, to which you shall come from hope to sight if you enter the king’s wedding wearing a white garment—that is, with the innocence of life.

Initiated and confirmed by these sacraments, you were made the temple of the living God: founded in faith, built up in charity, and filled with hope in the promised eternity.

Having thus briefly set forth these matters concerning God’s spiritual temple, let us now come to the sacraments performed in these visible temples; and, explaining them more fully as the Lord grants, let us compare them with the foregoing. First, the stones brought together to build this structure are either cut from mountains, dug from underground places, or gathered from fields. Then the hand of the masons is applied, frequently striking with iron and laying a rule upon them, to plane down the roughness and irregularity of the stones and, by the discipline of its craft, bring them to the required squareness, by which greater stones could be joined evenly with smaller ones. [Col. 0528C]

We see these things spiritually fulfilled in God’s holy temple when you, from every class of humankind—high, low, and middling—assemble to hear the word of life and willingly lay aside the strength of your former life under the adze of heavenly discipline, so that you may be arranged in God’s building as polished stones. There the noble person no longer despises the low-born, nor the rich the poor, when he knows that they share the same Father in heaven. A binding, adhesive strength of mortar is also added to the levelled stones when they are arranged in the walls according to the order of a single line, as ours are. It binds the stones together and does not permit them to be separated from the order imposed upon them, though in one place a greater stone seems placed beneath a smaller and elsewhere a smaller pressed beneath a greater. [Col. 0528D]

We see this also done in the temple not made by hands, when those whom unity of faith has gathered are bound by indissoluble charity: lest the greater resent the precedence of the lesser, or the lesser complain of the rebuke [variant: “correction”] of the greater, since the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. VI). When the temple has thus been built and, as it were, brought into the form of one stone through the binding mortar, so as to deserve the name and honour of God’s temple, we first baptize the temple itself, each in its own manner and order, to commend the sacrament of baptism by which a new people are to be created in that same temple; afterward we dedicate it with the manifold holiness of the sacraments.

First, therefore, we bless water, to which salt is added. Water bears the figure of repentance, which, like water, washes away the stains of sins. We bless it when we preach to peoples coming to the faith the power of repentance. Hence Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles to certain persons pierced in heart: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (Acts II). Salt is added to it—that is, evangelical doctrine—which binds the unstable hearts of hearers with pleasant sharpness [variant: “moderation”] and wisely orders them to preserve newness of life. [Col. 0529A] We sprinkle the outside of the church with this water by going around it, as a certain image of baptism; for where the threefold immersion customary for the baptized cannot be performed, it is necessary that a threefold sprinkling take place by whatever likeness of the sacrament we can achieve.

For triple immersion and triple sprinkling have one meaning: whatever is committed in thought, speech, and deed is wholly washed away by the saving fountain. Meanwhile twelve lights are kindled around the church to be dedicated, signifying that the bright and burning doctrine of the apostles is to be commended. Thus, when the temple constructed by Solomon had been dedicated at the Lord’s command, twelve leaders brought the same gifts, but each offered them on a separate day. By this the Holy Spirit signified that, in building the Church, [Col. 0529B–C] apostolic doctrine, unanimous and harmonious, should be preached, and yet each nation should receive its own preacher. 270

At each circuit the pontiff comes to the door of the basilica, followed by clergy and people, and strikes the threshold with the pastoral staff while singing the antiphon: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates” (Ps. XXIII; Matt. X; Mark VI). The pastoral staff signifies priestly authority, which the Lord bestowed upon his disciples when, sending them to preach, he allowed them to carry nothing on the way except a staff alone. With this staff holy priests console the humble, terrify the proud, and strike the unrepentant.

The Son received this power from the Father when, through the humility of his assumed humanity, he received dominion over heavenly, earthly, and infernal things. The Lord granted the same power to his bishops when, to Peter and in him to the rulers of the Church, he gave authority, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVI). It is evident that he over whom the gates of hell shall not prevail, and to whom the privilege of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth is entrusted, rules over heaven, earth, and hell. Therefore, when the pontiff strikes the threshold of the future church three times with the pastoral staff, he shows that the authority of heaven, earth, and hell yields to him. [Col. 0529D–0530A]

Hence, after the triple striking, the door is opened, because the opposing party cannot resist a priest who unworthily preserves his authority. For the church itself, before the pontiff enters it, represents the ignorant people enclosed in the darkness of unbelief. He who stands within, as though marvelling at the pontiff’s command, bears the type of this ignorant people and asks: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. XXIII). The pontiff commands demons or vices, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes” (ibid.), that they may lift up their gates, so that the heavenly gates—that is, virtues—may be raised, through which the King of glory enters. Conversely, sins are the gates of death. Hence the Prophet glories in the Lord: “You who raise me from the gates of death” (Ps. IX).

There are chiefly three gates raised in the Church: the preaching of the sacred word, the grace of baptism, and the honour [variant: “anointing”] of chrism. Through them the King of glory enters the hearts of those who come to faith. When the door has been opened, the pontiff enters with clergy and people, saying three times, “Peace to this house” (Matt. X), because Christ, entering the world by the assumption of our flesh, destroyed the wall of enmity raised by our sins and, by the mediation of his coming, restored peace between God and humankind, between earthly and heavenly things. [Col. 0530B]

Thus, as the pontiff enters the church, he cries, “Peace to this house,” because holy teachers intend that the people who had been estranged from God through sins should be reconciled to him through the practice of good works. When, at the entrance of the pontiff into the church, clergy, priest, and levites prostrate themselves on the ground and cry to the Lord for the sanctification of the house, this is what the Lord did before his Passion when he prayed for his disciples and other believers: “Father, sanctify those whom you have given me” (John XVII). Thus Paul too, as though entering a church, exhorts all to prayer, saying: “I urge, first of all, that prayers and petitions be made for all people,” and so forth (1 Tim. II). [Col. 0530C]

Therefore, when the pontiff enters a new church to sanctify it and immediately gives himself to prayer, he fulfils the voice of the Apostle, who commands that prayer first of all be made for all people. He still represents those who begin to teach an unformed people. Thus, rising from prayer, he does not yet greet the people by saying, “The Lord be with you,” but only exhorts all to prayer, because a newly formed people does not yet seem worthy of the priest’s greeting. Such persons, therefore, who have not yet been initiated ought to be prayed for, but not greeted, because one must not agree with or applaud them. Hence the Lord tells the preachers themselves “to greet no one on the way” (Luke X): that is, they should not soothe with vain hope anyone who desires transient things. [Col. 0530D]

When these things have been completed, the pontiff begins from the left eastern corner and writes the alphabet across the pavement as far as the right western corner; then again, from the right eastern corner to the left western corner of the basilica. What is to be understood by the alphabet except the beginnings and rudiments of sacred doctrine? Hence Paul says to the Hebrews: “When by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught what are the elements of the words of God” (Heb. V). The pontiff also writes in the order of the alphabet when he teaches the simplicity of faith. For just as it belongs to the education of little children first to know the elements of letters, then to reach syllables and gradually, through words, attain knowledge of sentences, so there are certain stages of understanding in the instruction of holy Church. [Col. 0531A]

That the first line ends from the left eastern corner at the right western corner, and then returns from the right eastern corner to the left western corner, suits a double figure. The first is that in this form a cross is shaped, so that the death of Christ may be chiefly set forth in evangelical doctrine by which the simple are to be instructed. Hence Paul said to the Corinthians, still unformed: “I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. II). The left eastern corner, from which the first line begins, signifies the Jewish people, from whom the Lord arose. It reaches to the western corner because, although our Lord arose from the Jews, faith in his incarnation and death was received by the nations. But when the same line returns from the right eastern corner to the left western corner, this seems to signify: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. XI). [Col. 0531B–C]

Thus the two lines signify the gathering of both peoples into the single framework of the cross. “Hence Jacob, blessing Joseph’s sons and making with crossed hands the image of the cross, placed his right hand upon the head of Ephraim the younger, and his left upon the head of Manasseh the elder” (Gen. XLVIII), signifying that the people formerly on the right would turn to the left, and the people on the left to the right.

That this writing is performed with the pastoral staff signifies that this passage from the Jews to the nations, and the conversion to be completed again at the end of the world, will be accomplished through the office of priests. Then the pontiff ascends to higher ground and, standing before the altar, invokes God’s assistance as one now beginning to work; for the preceding acts were, as it were, certain preliminaries. He says: “O God, make haste to help me,” and the rest without *Alleluia* [variant: “up to *Alleluia*”]. [Col. 0531D] For this is the cry of those who labour in this life and struggle against visible and invisible enemies, and therefore invoke God to help them. Yet they do not add *Alleluia* to God’s praises, because they see that they are still amid labours and sweat. 271 *Alleluia* signifies not the praise of this present time but the glory of eternal life. Hence the custom has arisen that *Alleluia* is not sung during the days of Septuagesima before Easter, because they are days of mourning and repentance.

Therefore, the pontiff who still contends with the ignorance and opposition of his subjects asks God’s help, but does not yet sing *Alleluia* fully with those whose salvation he does not yet fully hope for. Afterwards water is blessed with salt and ashes mixed into it. The Apocalypse testifies that water signifies a people, saying: “Many waters, many peoples” (Apoc. XVII). Salt signifies the doctrine of the divine word. Hence the law commands: “You shall offer salt in every sacrifice” (Lev. II), and “you shall not remove the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God from his sacrifice.” That is to say: works not seasoned with divine wisdom are not pleasing to God. Ashes signify the remains—that is, the remembrance—of the Lord’s Passion, as the ashes of the heifer sprinkled for the people’s expiation signified it. Thus water is blessed so that it may be sanctified; salt is mixed with ashes when the people, so that they may be sanctified, are instructed in divine wisdom [variant: “knowledge”] and faith in the Lord’s Passion. [Col. 0532A–B] A cross is made three times over the water, salt, and ashes when faith in the Trinity is added to faith in divinity and Passion.

Wine is then added to this mixture together with water. These two signify the twofold nature in one person: namely, divinity and humanity. The sequence is to be observed. First, the pontiff enters [variant: “opens”] the door; then he prays for the people; after this, he writes the alphabet; next, he blesses water with salt and ashes and mixes wine into it. For each person first opens for himself the gate of salvation by confession; then it is the priest’s task to pray for him; afterward to give him the first principles of faith and, as it were, make him a catechumen; then to teach him through sacred doctrine how he may be joined to the body of his Saviour, and also to teach that Jesus Christ is God and man; finally, to cleanse him in the sacred font. The same thing was signified by the outer sprinkling of the walls. But it must not therefore seem superfluous to perform the inner sprinkling of the walls here, because whatever is done in outward sanctification is superstitious unless it is fulfilled in the inner person. [Col. 0532B–C]

After this the priest dips his finger in the water and makes a cross upon the four horns of the altar. The altar bears the figure of the Church, extended through its four horns because it is spread through the four quarters of the world. As its type Abraham was told: “You shall be extended to east and west, north and south” (Gen. XXVIII). Thus it is fitting that a cross be made from water on the four horns of the altar, to show that the whole Church must be cleansed from the filth of sins through the washing of water and faith in the Passion.

Then he comes before the altar and sprinkles it seven times. This number signifies the fullness of the Holy Spirit: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI). The same water is sprinkled with hyssop, a lowly herb that cleanses the inner breast and penetrates the hardness of rocks with its roots; under the law cleansings were performed by its sprinkling. It signified the humility of Christ, who healed the swellings of our pride by the sprinkling of his blood. Thus water is sprinkled with hyssop when the baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood is given to the Church. [Col. 0532D–0533A]

He goes around the altar sprinkling this same water, to show that a teacher ought not to be idle but must labour for the cleansing of those whom he has initiated, and must always pray that the Lord may send an angel around them to instruct [variant: “deliver”] them. Then he goes around the whole church and sprinkles its walls, showing that he expends every care upon every age and sex. He does this a second and a third time, showing that those who are baptized must be cleansed not only from sins of thought but also of speech and deed.

Meanwhile the Psalm “Let God arise” (Ps. LXVII) is sung with an antiphon, so that those who oppose the sacraments of faith may be deprived of strength. They also sing the antiphon, “He who dwells in the help of the Most High” (Ps. XC), affirming that no one is protected by God except the one who, presuming nothing upon his own powers, continually implores God’s aid. Nevertheless, the pontiff himself must not rest, but, conspicuous as it were, proceed through the midst of the Church, instruct all by his example, make known to all the sacraments of the cross and the Lord’s death, and sing: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Isa. LVI; Matt. XXV). That is, he must prepare such a Church as is not a den of thieves but a house of prayer—not thieves and robbers, but those who bless the Lord at all times—so that he may freely sing the following verse: “I will declare your name to my brethren; in the midst of the church I will praise you” (Ps. XXI). [Col. 0533A–B] The pontiff does these things well when, for every good work he begins, he asks that it be completed by God’s counsel.

Therefore, after these acts, the pontiff gives himself to prayer, that all who enter the same house to pray may rejoice that they have been heard. Thus he shows that he bears, with Paul, concern for all his subjects and frequently remembers them in his prayers (2 Tim. I). When the expiation has been completed, the pontiff turns to the altar, beginning the antiphon, “I will enter unto the altar of God” (Ps. XLII), with the psalm, and pours what remains of the water of purification at the base of the altar. For he humbly entrusts to the Lord what he himself cannot do: namely, the cleansing of his subjects. As a human being, he can cooperate and labour toward it; but inward and perfect cleansing belongs to God alone.

Thus, in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, the blood of victims was either put upon the horns of the altar, or, from certain victims, sprinkled by the priest’s finger before the Lord; and what remained was poured out at the base of the altar. For it belongs to priests to do whatever they can for the benefit of the flock committed to them, but to commend most devoutly to the Lord what exceeds their powers. [Col. 0533C–D] The first Shepherd left this example to shepherds when, approaching his Passion, he said to the Father: “Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me” (John XVII). So also Paul, at the crisis of this present life, as though pouring water at the base of the altar, commended his disciples to the Lord, saying: “And now I commend you to the Lord and to the word of his grace.”

The antiphon also suggests this, for it says that he will enter the altar of God: that is, the altar signified by this visible altar, which the eye of flesh cannot penetrate but the pure intention of the mind can; and this is what follows: “to God who gladdens my youth” (Ps. XLII). Afterwards the altar is wiped with a linen cloth. Flax, springing from the earth, is brought to whiteness through great labour. So Christ’s flesh, sprung from earth—that is, from the Blessed Virgin Mary—came through the sufferings of the Passion to the honour of the Resurrection. Therefore the teacher wipes the altar, as it were, with linen when he impresses upon the minds of hearers the imitation of the Lord’s 272 Passion, saying with the Apostle: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example that you should follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. III). [Col. 0534A]

Therefore, when the teacher does such things, he wipes, as it were, the altar wet with the labour of humanity by the linen of imitation of the Lord. Then incense is made [variant: “incense is offered”], signifying the prayers of the saints, according to what John said concerning the angel: “Much incense was given to him, that he might offer it with the prayers of the saints upon the altar” (Apoc. VIII), which is before the Lord. Therefore, after pouring the water at the base of the altar, the altar is wiped with linen and incense is offered, because the priest who commends to the Lord the salvation of the people entrusted to him must accomplish this pious intercession both through bodily affliction and through intention.

Hence also the Lord, after commending his disciples to the Father, immediately prayed for them as he was about to undergo the Passion (John XVII). [Col. 0534B–C] Meanwhile the pontiff pours oil upon the altar, making a cross from it in the middle of the altar and upon its four corners. The order is suitably observed: after cleansing with water and the other things mentioned, the altar is poured over with oil, because holy Church too is first cleansed with water in the font of baptism and then marked by anointing through the pontiff’s hands, so that it may merit the coming of the Holy Spirit. For oil signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit (Rom. V), by which love is poured into the hearts of the elect for loving God and neighbour.

Then the altar is marked by the anointing of most holy chrism, while the antiphon is sung: “God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV), [Col. 0534D] so that by this anointing we may understand the fullness of grace which first went before in the Head and afterward shone forth in the body. When the Spirit was sent from above, the manifest grace of chrism was given to the apostles, of which the Apostle says: “We all received from his fullness grace for grace” [variant: “grace upon grace”] (Acts II; John I), that is, through the grace of faith, diverse chrismata.

Hence, from the consecrated altar, those twelve crosses are anointed upon the walls which bear the apostolic type: the apostles both received the firstfruits of the Spirit and strove to reveal to peoples and nations the mystery of the cross. Finally, once the consecration has been performed, the altar is covered with white veils, by which both the sacrament of newness is understood and, as was said when we spoke of the baptized, the glory of future incorruption is foretold. For the true and full consecration of this temple not made by hands will occur when this passible body puts on impassibility, and this mortal body receives immortality, and what has already gone before in the Head is fulfilled in the body.

Whence in the psalm already entitled “At the Dedication of the House,” these words are spoken in the voice of the Mediator, both for himself and for his members: “You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness” (Ps. 29). By “mourning,” he means our mortality, which must be bewailed so long as we are pilgrims away from God and the vision of peace is deferred from us—a vision enjoyed by those for whom it is sweet to grieve amid the sorrows and hardships of this life and to sigh after the joys of eternal life. This mourning, this sorrow [Col. 0535B] is turned into joy (ibid.) when, our pilgrimage completed, we reach the homeland from which we are now exiled. Hence he continues: “You tore my sackcloth” (Matt. 25). Sackcloth is woven from the wool of goats and kids. Kids, because they are wanton animals, stand in Scripture for sinners. Therefore our sackcloth is torn when the passibility and mortality of human nature, arising from sin, are changed into immortality, and are changed into unchangeable joy through restored immortality. This is what follows: “That my glory may sing to you” (Ps. 29)—you for whom my misery sighed and wept—“and that I may not be pierced” (ibid.), because, sin having been abolished in the flesh, the thorn of sin will not prick the conscience: that thorn would be the sadder in recollection in proportion as it had been more pleasant [Col. 0535C] in its commission. “O Lord my God, I shall confess you for ever” (ibid.); that is, I shall render you eternal praises for everlasting glory. “For blessed are they who dwell in your house; for ages upon ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83).

He shall take part joyfully and festively in this most pleasant and solemn dedication who, in this material temple, having received the wedding garment, has kept the temple of God—which he himself is—holy and inviolate until this eternal and inviolable dedication. Having briefly explained these matters, therefore, we exhort your brotherhood: what you have heard with the ear, believe with the heart and strive to fulfil in deed, through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honour and glory for ages upon ages. [Col. 0535D] Amen.

## SERMON V, OR A TREATISE ON THE HARMONY OF THE OLD AND NEW SACRIFICE

I have proposed to recall in part the benefits which the Saviour bestowed on earth for the reconciliation of those to be saved—benefits long beforehand foreshadowed in the enigmas of the patriarchs and foretold in the visions and oracles of the prophets. Although the Church of God recalls them at their proper seasons in an annual celebration, she nevertheless commemorates the same things with devout devotion in the daily sacraments of the Mass, so that, through confidence in what has been performed, she may faithfully [variant: “assiduously”] intercede with the Mediator, whether to obtain pardon for sins committed or to attain the rewards of merits. I say that I have proposed to recall these things in [Col. 0536A] part, because to collect them all exceeds my powers and is not profitable for the fastidious minds of hearers.

What I am about to say has this purpose: that through ecclesiastical [variant: “evangelical”] truth it may become plain how the old sacraments agree with the new, since the Church, by such imitation as she can make, honours these same sacraments in a sacred rite derived from evangelical tradition, and testifies that what the old sacraments foretold as future has now passed. Let us therefore gather some necessary passages from the ancient books which speak beforehand of Christ and the Church, so that, when we see them fulfilled in Christ’s Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit, we may then more easily understand the harmony of both sets of sacraments: [Col. 0536B] what the former confess to be future, the latter imitate as the Lord instituted.

Let us demonstrate what we have said by adducing testimonies, so that we may first see the shadow harmonizing with the truth. “First, let Moses come forward, speaking with God in the bush that was kindled and not consumed” (Exod. 3). By this event it is figured that from the Jewish people, beset with the thorns of sins, he would come forth who, in the fire of divinity, would take upon himself the sins of our flesh as though the thorn of a bush, yet would preserve unconsumed the substance of our humanity even amid the flame of divinity.

Likewise, in the same writer, Aaron’s rod, which after its dryness [273] flowered and bore nuts (Num. 17), is Christ. Born from the flesh of a virgin without moisture being poured in from outside, he endured in the flesh the bitterness of the Passion as in a shell, [Col. 0536C] and feeds the minds of the saints with the sweetness of his inward delight, as with the sweetness of a kernel.

Then, in the book of Judges, what is understood by Gideon’s fleece drenched with dew (Judg. 7), except what the psalm foretold concerning Christ’s birth: “He shall descend as rain upon the fleece” (Ps. 71)? This signifies that Christ poured himself from heaven into the virginal womb without sound and without corruption of flesh. For he did not wound his mother’s womb, but consecrated it by cleansing it. We have inserted these few points into this little work as though oracles concerning the manifold future birth of Christ.

Let us now come, passing over the signs, to the proclamations of the prophets that accord with evangelical truth, by which it was foretold that Christ would be born of a virgin and would bring a new covenant and a new priesthood to Jews and Gentiles. Moses first says: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren; him you shall hear as me” (Deut. 18). That Christ himself is from the beginning the Word and God with God is attested by the psalm which says: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king” (Ps. 44). And another psalm says: “By the Word of God the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32).

That this same Christ, the Son of God, is the wisdom of God—and concerning the mystery of his Incarnation, Passion, chalice, altar, and the apostles who were sent to preach—one reads in Solomon’s Proverbs: “Wisdom has built herself a house and set beneath it seven pillars; [Col. 0537A] she has slain her victim, mixed her wine in the bowl, and prepared her table. She sent her servants, crying aloud from the heights to the bowl and saying: Whoever is foolish, turn aside to me. And to those lacking understanding she says: Come, eat of my breads and drink the wine which I have mixed for you. Forsake foolishness and seek prudence, and amend yourselves unto the understanding of knowledge” (Prov. 9).

That God would come as the illuminator and Saviour of humankind is said in Isaiah: “Take comfort, faint-hearted ones; do not fear. God will render judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear [variant: ‘shall be opened’]” (Isa. 35).

And that, though he was from the beginning the Son of God, he would have a new generation according to the flesh, is found thus in the psalm: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). Likewise, that he would be born of a virgin, Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7).

Likewise, that Christ, God and man, is compounded from both kinds [Note: [Col. 0537D] These words are not to be understood as a confusion or mixture of natures, which is the impious doctrine of Eutyches, but, against Nestorius, as referring to the unity of person: he intended to say that Christ is one person in divinity and humanity, compounded from both kinds—that is, consisting of divinity and humanity, that is, God and man—while the substance of God and man remains unconfused.], so that he might be a mediator between us and the Father, Jeremiah says: “And he is a man; and who shall know him?” (Jer. 17). Likewise, in Numbers: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24). Likewise there: “A man shall proceed from his seed, and shall rule many nations; and his kingdom shall be exalted and increased.” Likewise Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Isa. 61).

Likewise [Col. 0537C] Isaiah: “And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and godliness; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Luke 24; Isa. 11). Likewise in Psalm 131: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him: From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne.” That he would be born in Bethlehem is said by Micah: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are you perhaps small among the thousands of Judah? From you shall proceed for me one who is to be ruler in Israel; and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5; Matt. 2).

In this manner many things may be collected from the ancient Scriptures which speak beforehand of Christ’s temporal birth [Col. 0537D] and bear witness in confirmation of evangelical truth. But that, at Christ’s coming, carnal circumcision was to be abolished and spiritual circumcision to succeed, Moses says: “In the last days God shall circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed, that you may love the Lord your God” (Deut. 30). Likewise in Joshua: “And the Lord said to Joshua: Make for yourself very sharp stone knives, and circumcise the children of Israel a second time” (Josh. 2). Likewise Jeremiah: “Thus says the Lord: Men of Judah and inhabitants of [Col. 0538A] Jerusalem, renew a renewal among yourselves, and do not sow among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to your God, and circumcise the foreskins of your hearts, lest my wrath go forth like fire and there be none to quench it” (Jer. 4).

That the earlier law given through Moses would cease, Isaiah says: “Then those who seal the law shall become manifest, lest they learn; and you shall say: I await the Lord, who has turned his face away from the house of Jacob; I shall be confident [variant: ‘trusting’] in him” (Isa. 8). That a new law would be given, Micah says: “The law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he shall judge many peoples” (Mic. 4). Likewise Isaiah: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he shall judge among the nations” (Isa. 1). Likewise Jeremiah: “Behold, days shall come, says the Lord, and I shall establish over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. 31).

That the old sacrifice would be cast out [variant: “abolished”] and the new celebrated is said by Isaiah: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of the burnt offering of rams and the fat of lambs, and I have not desired the blood of bulls and goats” (Isa. 1). Likewise Malachi: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I do not accept sacrifice from your hands; for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place fragrant incense [Col. 0538C] is offered to my name, and a clean sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations” (Mal. XLI). Likewise in Psalm 111 [109]: “Before Lucifer [the morning star] I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.” In the book of Kings, the Lord God says to Eli the priest: “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest who shall do all that is in my heart; and I shall build him a faithful house, and he shall pass before my anointed ones all days. And whoever remains in the house shall come to worship for an obol of money, and for bread and wine” (1 Sam. 2).

Having set forth these prophetic utterances concerning Christ’s birth, [Col. 0538D] preaching, the mission of the apostles, and the change of the priesthood, let us add some statements of the same authors which speak beforehand of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. Let us also include the principal ancient sacrifices offered in the outer tabernacle, which agree with the same end, so that afterwards we may more conveniently relate our sacraments to the old priesthood and evangelical truth.

First, then, in Genesis, the death of Abel (Gen. 4) prefigures Christ’s death: for just as Abel was killed in a field by his elder brother, so Christ, the head of the younger people by birth, was killed at Calvary by the [Col. 0539A] Jewish people, elder by birth. Likewise in Genesis, who was signified by Abraham in the sacrifice of his son except the high Father? Who in Isaac except Christ? (Gen. 22). For as Abraham offered to God his only and beloved son as a victim, so God the Father did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us (Rom. 1). And as Isaac carried upon himself the wood on which he was to be laid, so Christ carried on his shoulders the wood of his cross, on which he was to be crucified (Matt. 27).

But the ass that carried these things is the senseless folly of the Jews, which carried all our sacraments and did not know it. Yet what does the ram caught by its horns in the thicket signify except Christ, who is also called a sheep, whose flesh, while his divinity remained untouched, is fastened to the [Col. 0539B] cross? For he was suspended among the thorns of Jewish sins.

Samson prefigured him in the book of Judges: shut up in Gaza, city of the Philistines, and surrounded by a careful guard, he carried away the gates at midnight; and he not only went out free, but also ascended the summit of the mountain (Gen. 22). Whom does this deed signify except Christ, who, rising before dawn, not only came forth free from hell but also destroyed hell’s very gates and penetrated the heights of heaven?

That he would come humble in his first advent, Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 51). “We announced before him as little children, as a root in a thirsty land. He has neither form nor splendour; and we saw him, and he had neither form [Col. 0539C] nor comeliness, but his form was dishonoured and failing beyond other men: a man set in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness, because his face was turned away; he was dishonoured and was not reckoned.

“He bears our sins, and suffers for us; yet we considered him to be in pain, affliction, and distress. But he was wounded because of our crimes and weakened because of our sins; the discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed. All we like sheep went astray. Each man wandered from his way, and the Lord delivered him up for our sins; and because he was afflicted, he did not open his mouth.” Likewise the same prophet says: “I am [Col. 0539D] not rebellious, nor do I resist; I gave my back to the lashes and my cheeks to the palms. I did not turn my face away from the shame of spittings, and God was my helper.”

That he is the righteous man whom the Jews would kill is said in the Wisdom of Solomon: “Let us beset the just man, because he is unpleasant to us and opposed to our works; he reproaches us for sins against the law, promises that he has knowledge of God, and calls himself the Son of God. He has become to us a rebuke [variant: ‘a contradiction’] of our thoughts. He is burdensome for us even to see, because his life is unlike that of others and his ways have been changed. We have been regarded by him as trifles; he keeps himself from our ways as from impurities, and prefers [Col. 0540A] the latter end of the righteous, and boasts that God is his Father. Let us see, therefore, whether his words are true, and test what shall happen to him. Let us question him with insult and torment, that we may know his reverence and test his patience. Let us condemn him to a most shameful death.” These things they thought, and they erred. For their own malice blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God” (Wis. 2).

That he is called the sheep and lamb which was to be slain, and concerning the mystery of the Passion, Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he was led to the sacrifice [variant: ‘slaughter’], and as a lamb before its shearer is voiceless, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). “In his humility his judgment was taken away. But who shall recount his generation? For his life shall be taken away from the earth. Because of the crimes of my people he was brought to death; and I shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich themselves for his death, because he did no crime, nor was deceit in his mouth. Therefore he shall gain many and shall divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was delivered to death and he was reckoned among criminals; and he bore [variant: ‘endured’] the sins of many, and was because of their crimes.”

Likewise Jeremiah: “Lord, make known to me, and I shall know. Then I saw their designs. I, like a lamb without malice, was led to the sacrifice; against me they devised a design, saying: Come, let us put wood into his bread, and erase his life from the earth, [Col. 0540C] and let his name no longer be remembered” (Jer. 11).

Likewise, in Exodus, the Lord says to Moses: “Let each take for himself a sheep according to the households of the tribes: a sheep without blemish, perfect, male, one year old; you shall take it from the lambs and from the kids. And the whole multitude of the assembly of the children of Israel shall kill it in the evening. They shall take of its blood and put it upon the two doorposts and upon the lintel in the houses in which they shall eat the flesh that same night, roasted with fire; and they shall eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs [OCR: *pigidiis/pigridiis*]. You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted with fire. You shall devour the head with the feet and entrails. You shall leave nothing of it until morning, and you shall not break a bone of it; whatever remains of it until morning shall be burned with fire. Thus shall you eat it: [Col. 0540D] your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste. For it is the Passover of the Lord” (Exod. 12).

That the Jews would fasten him to the cross, Isaiah says: “I stretched out my hands all day to a disobedient people, who contradict me, who walk in ways not good, but after their own sins” (Isa. 65). Likewise Jeremiah: “Come, let us put wood into his bread, and erase his life from the earth” (Jer. 11). Likewise Deuteronomy: “And your life shall hang before your eyes; and you shall fear day and night, and shall not believe in your life” (Deut. 28). Likewise in Psalm 21: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones.”

[Col. 0541A] That in the Passion of the cross and its sign there is all power and authority, Habakkuk says: “His power covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise; and his splendour shall be as light. Horns shall be in his hands, and there the power of his glory was made firm; and he shall establish mighty love. Before his face the Word shall go, and shall go before into the fields according to his steps” (Hab. 3). Likewise Isaiah: “Behold, a child has been born to you and a son has been given to you, whose rule is upon his shoulders, and his name has been called Messenger of Great Counsel” (Isa. 9). By this sign of the cross Amalek was defeated by Joshua through Moses (Exod. 17).

That in this sign of the cross salvation is for all who are marked upon their foreheads, the Lord says through Ezekiel: “Pass through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark with the sign *tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and mourn over the iniquities done in their midst” (Ezek. 9). Likewise there: “Go and strike; do not spare with your eyes, do not have pity. Kill old men and young men, virgins and little children and women, so that they may perish. But do not touch anyone upon whom the written sign is found” (ibid.). Likewise in Exodus God says to Moses: “The blood shall be for you as a sign upon the houses where you shall be; and I shall see the blood and protect you, and there shall be no plague of destruction among you when I strike the land of Egypt” (Exod. 12).

That darkness would come at midday during his Passion, Amos says: “And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, that the sun shall set at noon, and the day of light shall be darkened; [Col. 0541C] and I shall turn your feast days into mourning and all your songs into lamentation” (Amos 8). Likewise Jeremiah: “She who bears children is terrified, and her soul has grown weary. The sun has set while it was still midday; she has been confounded and accursed. I shall give the rest of them to the sword in the sight of their enemies” (Jer. 15). Likewise in the Gospel: “From the sixth hour darkness came over all the earth until the ninth hour” (Matt. 27).

That he would not be conquered by death or remain among the dead, Psalm 29 says: “Lord, you brought my soul up from hell.” Likewise Psalm 3: “I slept and took sleep, and I rose, because you helped me.” Likewise in the Gospel of Saint John: [Col. 0541D] “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself; and I have power to lay it down and I have power to take it up again. For this command I received from my Father” (John 10).

That he would rise from the dead on the third day, Hosea says: “He shall revive us after two days; on the third day we shall rise” (Hos. 6). Likewise Exodus: “And the Lord said to Moses: Go down and charge the people, and sanctify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments and be ready for the day after tomorrow. For on the third day the Lord shall descend upon Mount Sinai” (Exod. 19). Likewise in the Gospel: “A wicked and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall [Col. 0542A] the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12; John 2).

The same thing was figured in Jacob’s words when he blessed the patriarch Judah, as follows: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have ascended. Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49). In a typological sense he calls the Lord Saviour a lion’s cub, as born from a leonine stock—that is, descended from royal lineage. He is aptly called a lion’s cub because it is said to be the nature of the lion that, when born, it sleeps for three days and then rises, awakened by its father’s roar. This figure most beautifully accords with the Lord’s sleep: sleeping for three days, he cries to the Father, “But you, O Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up” (Ps. 40). But, raised up, he ascends to the prey, because in despoiling hell [Col. 0542B] he triumphantly led all the righteous upward as excellent spoil. He lay down as a lion and as a lioness because he who chose to sleep in the flesh in the tomb triumphed like a lion, victorious over his enemies. But where it adds, “Who shall rouse him?” it is understood: Who, except the Father? (Gen. 49).

That when he had risen he would receive from the Father all authority, and that his authority is eternal, Daniel says: “I watched in a vision by night, and behold, one like a Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven came to the Ancient of Days and stood before him; and those standing by presented him, and kingship was given him, and all the kings of the earth, and every race [variant: ‘nation’] of glory serving him; and his authority is eternal and shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. [Col. 0542C] 7). Likewise Isaiah: “Now I shall arise, says the Lord; now I shall be glorified; now I shall be exalted. Now you shall see; now you shall understand; now you shall be confounded. The strength of your spirit shall be vain; fire shall consume [variant: ‘confound’] you” (Isa. 33). Likewise in Psalm 109: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet. The Lord shall send out from Zion the rod of your power, and you shall rule in the midst of your enemies.”

That he is King of kings and will reign for ever, Zechariah says: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, just and saving the meek, and seated upon an untamed ass” (Zech. 9). Likewise Isaiah: [Col. 0542D] “Who told you that a fire burns? Who told you of the eternal place? He who walks in justice and withholds his hands from gifts, who stops his ear lest he hear a judgment of blood, and closes his eyes lest he see injustice—this man shall dwell in the lofty cavern of the rock; strong bread shall be given him, and his water shall be sure: you shall see the King in glory” (Isa. 33). Likewise Malachi: “I am a great King, says the Lord, and my name is illustrious among the nations” (Mal. 2). Likewise in Psalm 2: “But I have been established king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his decree.” Likewise in Psalm 21: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him, [Col. 0543A] for kingship belongs to the Lord, and he shall rule over all nations.”

Further, what do those Levitical sacrifices signify except Christ suffering, rising, ascending to heaven, and sanctifying the peoples of the New Testament by the sprinkling of his blood in the water of baptism? In order that this may be clearer, let us now set forth the chief sacrifices themselves, which were burned upon the altar of the outer tabernacle, together with their interpretations. We shall reserve for their proper place those things performed at the altar of incense in the inner tabernacle, because we judge that order suitable to the work proposed.

The varieties of victims prefigured an image of Christ’s Passion.
