For after he himself was offered, all those victims ceased which had gone before in his type or shadow, prefiguring [Col. 0543B] the sacrifice offered by the one true priest, the mediator between God and human beings. The preliminary figures of this sacrifice had to be celebrated in animal victims for the cleansing of flesh and blood, through which one victim forgiveness might be effected of the sins contracted from flesh and blood—flesh and blood which shall not possess the kingdom of God, because that same bodily substance will be changed into a heavenly quality.

For he himself was offered in the calf because of the power of the cross; in the lamb because of innocence; in the ram because of sovereignty; in the goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh, so that through sin he might condemn sin; in the turtledove and dove because of God and man, since the mediator of God and human beings was shown in the union of two [Col. 0543C] substances. Moreover, in fine flour he plainly showed the Church, the body of Christ, gathered by the water of baptism from the mingling of believers. But morally we offer God a calf as a gift when we overcome the pride of the flesh; a lamb, when we correct irrational and foolish impulses; a kid, when we overcome wantonness; a dove, when we show simplicity of mind; a turtledove, when we preserve chastity of flesh; unleavened breads, when we walk not in the leaven of malice but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Fire in the sacrifice signified victory, as it were swallowing up death. These things were rightly celebrated among that people whose kingdom and priesthood were prophecies of the coming King and Priest, who would rule [Col. 0543D] and gather believers among all nations and introduce them into the kingdom of heaven, into the sanctuary of angels, into eternal life.

As the Hebrews celebrated the true sacraments of this true sacrifice, so pagans imitate them sacrilegiously. “What the nations sacrifice,” says the Apostle, “they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Cor. 10). For the sacrifice of blood is an ancient and predictive matter, testifying from the beginning of the human race to the future Passion of the Mediator. Abel is found in the sacred Scriptures to have offered it first (Gen. 4). At the beginning of Leviticus four kinds of principal offerings are described, commanded to be offered to the Lord as an odour of sweetness (Lev. 5): first, a calf [Col. 0544A] without blemish from the herd; second, a lamb from the sheep; third, a turtledove and a dove; fourth, fine flour mixed, unleavened, anointed with oil, and baked in an oven. The remaining sacrifices, however, were offered in the person of the Lord according to the character of the cases.

The first sacrifice, then—the calf from the herd—showed Christ descending from the lineage of the patriarchs. With the plough of his cross he subdued the soil of our flesh and enriched it with the fruitful seed of the Holy Spirit’s virtues. This calf is without blemish because he is led to the Passion without sin. “But it is offered not in the tabernacle, but at its entrance, because Christ suffered outside the camp” (Heb. 13). His blood is offered through the sons of Aaron the priest, which may be understood of Annas and Caiaphas, who, [Col. 0544B] plotting against him, shed Christ’s blood.

“The second victim offered from the sheep is the lamb” (Isa. 53); that is, Christ is figured because of innocence. This is the lamb who is led to sacrifice in Isaiah and was pointed out to all by John: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). The lamb, therefore, was fittingly offered in sacrifice, so that the figure of Christ’s innocence and Passion might be shown. And likewise the kid, because through his death the author of sin, the devil, is known to be slain.

The third sacrifice is called the turtledove and the dove. That the turtledove is Christ’s flesh is clear, Solomon saying: “Your cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove” (Song 1). John the Baptist declares that the dove figures the Holy Spirit, saying: “He upon [Col. 0544C] whom you see the Holy Spirit descending as a dove, this is my Son” (John 1). Thus the turtledove and the dove—that is, Christ’s flesh united with the Holy Spirit—are, through the mystery of the Passion, a sacrifice to God as an odour of sweetness. These three sacrifices are offered by a man, that is, by Christ Jesus.

But the fourth is offered by the soul; that is, the Church offers a sacrifice of fine flour, foretelling the figure of the Catholic Church, which has been gathered from concordant members, as fine flour from many grains of believers, and separates, by the millstone of Law and Gospels, letter from spirit. Joined with the water of baptism, anointed with the oil of chrism, made firm by the fire of the Holy Spirit, and made through the spirit of humility into a pleasing victim to God. [Col. 0544D] These are the four offerings, showing the fourfold condition of Christ and the Church.

We shall attempt to say something about the red heifer, whose ashes the Law commanded to be efficacious in the water of sprinkling and for cleansing those who had touched a dead body.

For in it a most evident sign of the New Testament is prefigured, and in our haste we cannot speak worthily enough of so great a mystery. First, who would not be moved and made most attentive to the depth of the mystery by the way Scripture begins to speak of this matter: “And the Lord spoke,” it says, “to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the distinction of the law, whatsoever the Lord has established” (Num. 19). Surely there is no distinction except between two [Col. 0545A] or more things. Singularity does not require distinction. Nor did it mention the distinction of just any matter, but added “of the law”; nor of merely any law, for Scripture constantly says concerning every particular matter that is lawfully commanded, “This is the law of this or that thing,” rather than of the universal law which contains everything that is lawfully commanded.

But here, after saying, “This is the distinction of the law,” it immediately adds: “Whatsoever the Lord has established”—that is, by commanding, not by creating. For some interpreters have even translated: “Whatsoever the Lord commanded.” Therefore, if this is the distinction of the law, whatsoever the Lord commanded, it is beyond doubt a great distinction; and it is rightly understood to mean the two Testaments. For the same things are in the old and in the new: there they are shadowed, here [Col. 0545B] revealed; there prefigured, here manifested. For not only are the sacraments different, but the promises as well. There temporal things seem to be proposed, by which a spiritual reward is signified secretly; here spiritual and eternal things are promised most plainly. But what distinction is clearer and more certain than that between temporal and carnal goods and spiritual and eternal goods than the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ? In his death it became sufficiently clear that this earthly and transitory happiness is not to be hoped for and desired from the Lord God as a great gift; rather, because he willed his only-begotten Son to suffer such great things, it ought to be sought and expected that something far different should be asked of him. This he made plain by the clearest distinction.

Therefore, the account of the slaughter of the red heifer fittingly prefigures this Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ as the distinction [Col. 0545C] of the two Testaments. “For the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the distinction of the law, whatsoever the Lord has established” (Num. 19); and then he begins to command, adding and saying: “Speak to the children of Israel.” It may also be construed thus: “And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the distinction of the law, whatsoever the Lord has established by saying”—not whatsoever the Lord has established by creating, such as heaven and earth and all things in them, but whatsoever the Lord has established by saying, namely in the two Testaments—so that there then follows: “Speak to the children of Israel, and let them receive from you a red heifer without blemish.”

The red heifer signifies Christ’s flesh: it is female because of the [Col. 0545D] weakness of the flesh; it is red because of the bloody Passion itself. But when he says, “Let them receive from you,” he shows in Moses himself a figure of the Law, because they thought that they killed Christ according to the Law, since in their view he violated the Sabbath and, as they supposed, profaned lawful observances. Therefore it is not surprising that this heifer is called without blemish. That flesh was also figured by the other animals, where similarly unblemished cattle are commanded to be sacrificed. For that flesh was in the likeness of sinful flesh, but was not sinful flesh.

Nevertheless, here, where God wished to commend the distinction of the law more expressly, it was not enough to say “without blemish,” unless it were added, “which has no blemish in itself.” [Col. 0546A] If this was said for the sake of repetition, perhaps it is not without purpose, since the repetition itself commended the matter more firmly. Yet this also does not depart from the truth: that the addition, “which has no blemish in itself,” is to be understood, although “a heifer without blemish” had already been said, because the flesh of Christ had no blemish in itself, whereas it had blemish in others, who are his members. For what flesh in this life is without sin, except that flesh alone which had no blemish in itself? “And no yoke has been laid upon her”: for she was not subjected to the iniquity from which, finding men subjected, he set them free, and [“whom he found subjected, and”] broke their bonds, so that it might be said to him: “You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115). For no yoke was laid upon the flesh of him who had power to lay down [Col. 0546B] his life and to take it up again.

“And you shall apply her [give her] to Eleazar the priest.” Why not to Aaron, unless perhaps this was thus prefigured: that the Lord’s Passion would come not to the priesthood of that time, but to the successors of this priesthood? “And they shall cast her outside the camp,” just as the Lord was cast out (Heb. 13), to suffer outside the city. But when it says, “into a clean place,” this signifies that he had no evil cause. “And they shall kill her in his sight,” just as Christ’s flesh was killed in the sight of those who were to become priests in the Lord’s New Testament. “And Eleazar shall take her blood and sprinkle seven times from her blood toward the front of the tabernacle of testimony.” Here is the testimony that Christ shed [Col. 0546C] blood for the remission of sins according to the Scriptures. Therefore it is toward the front of the tabernacle of testimony, because it was not declared otherwise than divine testimony had foretold it. And it is seven times because that number belongs to spiritual restoration.

“And they shall burn her in his sight.” I think that the burning pertains to the sign of the resurrection. For it is the nature of fire to move upward, and what is burned is converted into it. Indeed, the Latin verb *cremare*, “to burn,” is derived from Greek from the notion of being raised up. But the added phrase, “in his sight,” that is, in the priest’s sight, seems to me to indicate that Christ’s resurrection appeared to those who were to be a royal priesthood. Then follows: “Her skin and flesh [Col. 0546D] and blood, with her dung, shall be burned.” This explains how she is to be burned; and it signifies that not only the mortal substance of Christ’s body, intimated by the mention of skin, flesh, and blood, but also the insult and rejection by the people—signified, I think, under the name “dung”—will be transformed into glory, which the flame of burning signifies.

“And the priest shall take cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet, and shall cast them into the midst of the heifer’s burning.” Cedar wood is hope, which must dwell steadfastly in things above; hyssop is faith, which, though a lowly herb, clings by its roots to the rock; scarlet is charity, whose fiery color bears witness to the fervor of the Spirit. We ought to cast these three into Christ’s resurrection [Col. 0547A] as into the midst of that burning, so that our life may be hidden with him, as the Apostle says: “And our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3).

“And the priest shall wash his garments, and shall wash his body with water; and afterward he shall enter into the camp, and the priest shall be unclean until evening.” What are the washing of garments and body except the cleansing of outward and inward things? This concerns the priest.

Then follows: “And he who burns her shall wash his garments and his body with water, and shall be unclean until evening.” In the one who burns her, I believe those are figured who buried Christ’s flesh, committing it, as it were, to the conflagration of resurrection. “And a clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer and shall place them outside the camp in a clean place.” What are we to say [Col. 0547B] that the ashes of the heifer are—the remains, plainly, of the slaughter and burning—except the report that followed Christ’s Passion and resurrection? For “there are remnants for the peaceable man” (Ps. 36). For it was ash, because he was despised by unbelievers as though dead; and yet it cleansed, because believers believed that he had risen. And because this report shone forth especially among those who were in the other nations and were not of the fellowship of the Jews, I think that this is why it was said, “A clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer”: clean, certainly, from Christ’s killing, which had made the Jews guilty. “And he shall place them in a clean place,” that is, he shall treat them honorably, yet outside the camp, because evangelical honor shone forth apart from the observance of Jewish custom. “And it shall be for the synagogue of the children of Israel [Col. 0547C] as an ordinance: water of sprinkling for purification.”

Afterward it explains more fully how water of sprinkling was made from this ash, by which they were cleansed from contact with the dead; and this plainly signifies cleansing from the iniquity of a dying or death-dealing life. Yet what follows is remarkable: “And he who gathers,” it says, “the ashes of the heifer shall wash his garments and shall be unclean until evening.” How shall one who approached clean become unclean by this, unless because even those who seem clean to themselves acknowledge in the faith of Christ that “all have sinned and need the glory of God, being justified freely through his blood” (Rom. 3)? Yet it says that he washes his garments, not also his body. I believe that, through gathering that ash and [Col. 0547D] placing it in this clean place—if these things are understood spiritually—he is now to be understood as inwardly cleansed, just as Cornelius, hearing and believing what Peter preached, was cleansed (Acts 10), so that, before visible baptism, he and those present with him received the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, the visible sacrament could not be despised: so that, having been washed inwardly, he might also in some manner wash his garments inwardly [variant: outwardly].

“And it shall be,” he says, “an eternal statute for the children of Israel and for the proselytes who are joined to them.” What else does this show except that Christ’s baptism, signified by the water of sprinkling, would benefit both Jews and Gentiles—that is, the children of Israel and proselytes—as natural branches and the wild olive grafted into the richness of the root? But who would not attend closely to what is said after [Col. 0548A] the washing of each person: “and he shall be unclean until evening”? This is said not only here but in all, or nearly all, such purifications. I do not know whether anything else can be understood here except that every person, after the fullest remission of sins, while remaining in this life contracts something by which he is unclean until the end of this same life, when this day is in some manner closed for him, signified by evening.

Then Scripture begins to say, and sets out, how persons made unclean are purified by that water of sprinkling. “Whoever touches a corpse, any human soul, shall be unclean seven days. He shall be purified on the third day and on the seventh day, and he shall be unclean.” Here too I see nothing else to be understood [Col. 0548B] except that contact with the dead is a person’s iniquity. I think the uncleanness of seven days is said on account of soul and body: the soul in the number three, the body in the number four. Why this is so would take long to discuss. In accordance with this, I think it was said through the prophet: “For three and for four impieties I will not turn away” (Amos 1–2).

He adds and says: “But if he has not been purified on the third day and on the seventh day, he shall not be clean. Everyone who has touched a dead person, the dead body of any human soul, and has died without being purified”—that is, has died after touching the dead before he was purified—“has defiled the tabernacle of the Lord; that soul shall be cut off from Israel.” It should be noted that in these books one finds with great difficulty anything written more explicitly concerning the life of the soul after [Col. 0548C] death. Therefore, when it says here that, if one has died before purification, uncleanness remains in him and that soul is cut off from Israel—that is, from fellowship with God’s people—what else does it intend us to understand except that the soul’s punishment remains even after death, if while living it has not been cleansed by this sacrament, by which Christ’s baptism is figured? “For the water of sprinkling,” it says, “has not been sprinkled over him who is unclean; his uncleanness is still in him”—that is, still after death.

But when it said above, “He has defiled the tabernacle of the Lord,” it surely said this as far as he himself is concerned, just as the Apostle says, “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5), although the Spirit cannot be quenched. For if it had intended that the tabernacle itself was thereby made unclean, it would surely have commanded it to be cleansed. But afterwards it commands all to be cleansed from dead works, which are iniquities.

“And they shall take for the unclean person from the ashes of the burnt purification, and shall pour living water over [Col. 0548D] it into a vessel. And a clean man, taking hyssop and dipping it in the water, shall sprinkle the house, the vessels, and all the persons who are there, and the one who has touched a human bone, or one wounded, or one dead, or a tomb. And the clean man shall sprinkle the unclean person on the third day and on the seventh day; and he shall be purified on the seventh day, and shall wash his garments and be washed with water.” I think this water is to be understood spiritually by signification, not by its inherent nature. For without doubt it was visible, [Col. 0549A] like all those shadows of things to come. Accordingly, one rightly washed by the sacrament of baptism, which that water of sprinkling prefigured, is cleansed spiritually—that is, invisibly—in both flesh and soul, so that he may be clean in body and spirit.

But that it says the hyssop is used to sprinkle the water of sprinkling—and we said above that this herb signifies faith—what else comes to mind except what is written: “cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15)? For baptism does not benefit if faith is absent. It says that this is done by a clean man, signifying ministers who bear the person of their Lord, who is truly the clean man. For concerning these ministers it says later: “And he who sprinkles the water of sprinkling shall wash his garments,” that is, he shall also guard his body. “And whoever touches the water of sprinkling shall be unclean [Col. 0549B] until evening; and everyone who touches that unclean thing shall be unclean; and the soul that touches it shall be unclean until evening.” I have already said above what “until evening” seems to signify to me.

These things which we have mentioned, and others which the law commands to be offered for various occasions, prefiguring Christ’s priesthood and the events which those figures foretold, the Church represents by a concise imitation when it frequently celebrates the mysteries of the Mass daily throughout the world.

First, the Introit of the Mass, drawn from the Psalms and [or] other prophetic Scriptures, is sung together with the glorification of the Holy Trinity; and the following litany represents the devout expectation of those who desired Christ’s coming [Col. 0549C] with all their heart, and who sighed because their desire was delayed in this faithful expectation. Such were Simeon, Anna, and many others whom God knows, though Scripture does not commemorate them all. Under this desire of the saints, as had been foretold by the prophets, Christ was born of a Virgin, according to that which the Psalmist says in his person, speaking to the Father: “You did not require holocaust and sacrifice for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 39).

This is fittingly represented when the priest, imitating the person of Christ, while the choir sings the aforesaid Introit, proceeds to the right side of the altar. By this he signifies the mediator between God and men, who says of himself: [Col. 0549D] “I am not sent except to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). That people, being as it were the right side, alone maintained the worship of the one God and had not wandered after foreign gods, which the Gentile people worshipped, as though to the left side.

After the Introit follows the angelic hymn, bearing witness to Christ’s temporal birth, since the heavenly citizens proclaimed that they had thereby glorified God and that the wall of hostility had fallen when peace was restored to humankind. Then follows the prayer, while the priest still remains on the same side of the altar. The Lord commanded that prayer should be offered at the beginning of his preaching, when, gathering the apostles on the mountain, he established a form of prayer by handing down the Lord’s Prayer (Matt. 6). This prayer briefly comprehends, in certain general expressions, other kinds of prayer [Col. 0550A] by which we seek things to be loved, avoid things to be fled, or heal the wrongs we have committed.

There then follows a prophetic or apostolic reading, representing the preaching of Christ’s disciples, whom the Lord sent two by two before himself into every city and place where he himself was to come (Luke 10). After the reading the choir responds in song, showing that it has given the sacred reading hearing and affection [or “effect”]. And because these things are understood to be the gift of God, Alleluia follows, which means “Praise God,” so that the apostolic command may be fulfilled: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1).

When these things have thus been performed in their order, the deacon or priest crosses to the left side of the church to read the Gospel. By this [Col. 0550B] is signified what the apostles said when the Jews refused to believe: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you have rejected it and shown yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). Therefore the Gospel is still preached toward the Gentile world, in which the coldness of unbelief long reigned, as it were in the northern region, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters and, at last, under Elijah and Enoch, the remnant of the Jews comes to faith. This too is signified when the priest returns to the right side to complete the mysteries of the Mass.

After the Gospel, the Church professes her faith by singing the Apostles’ Creed, to show how much it has advanced through the Gospel. Finally, after greeting the people, while the priest receives the host [or “the host receives”] from the ministers [Col. 0550C] and offerings of various kinds from the people, the clerics sing the offertory. The Church received this custom from what is read in the Book of Chronicles: when the temple was dedicated by Solomon, the people, with Levites sounding trumpets, pipes, and cymbals, with voices and every kind of musical instrument, offered many sacrifices (2 Chron. 6).

We are admonished by the Psalmist to offer such sacrifices spiritually: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28)—that is, ourselves, whom the apostles, leaders of the Lord’s flock, have begotten. And elsewhere: “Take sacrifices and enter into his courts” (Ps. 95). Bread and wine are offered principally by the ministers, to be changed by priestly blessing into Christ’s body; [Col. 0550D] and Melchizedek was the first to offer these to Abraham (Gen. 14), as he returned from the slaughter of the five kings. By this the Holy Spirit signified that the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood are not to be shared with any except those who have overcome the kingdom of the five senses—that is, those who have crucified themselves to vices and desires. This is well signified by the number of household servants with which Abraham defeated the aforesaid kings, a number expressed, according to the calculation of letters, by the letter tau, T, representing the form of the cross.

In likeness of such offerings, the Lord willed that, being made under the law, he should be offered in the temple by his parents, and that a sacrifice of doves and turtledoves should be offered for him, although he had no need of such things. By this he signified that his Church is to be cleansed either by [Col. 0551A] common prayers, signified by doves, or by private prayers, signified by turtledoves. The gifts of the three Magi (Matt. 2), who offered three gifts to Christ newly born—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—foretold something similar: gold, by which spiritual understanding is morally indicated; frankincense, by which the purity of devout prayer is understood; myrrh, by which the mortification of fleshly corruption is figured [signified].

It should be observed that all these things mentioned from the Introit of the Mass onward are suitably compared with the sacrifices which priests offered in the outer tabernacle. For just as the people were not excluded from seeing those sacrifices, so all these things are celebrated within everyone’s hearing. Yet someone may wonder what comparison there is between these sacraments, since the old ones were performed with [Col. 0551B] bodies, whereas these new ones are performed in words. But they agree well in the things signified: for the utterances of figurative words commemorate as accomplished the same dispensation of the incarnate Word which the riddling figures of things, as said above, prefigured.

Therefore, whether we pray, sing a psalm, or recite a reading from prophetic, apostolic, or evangelical words that establishes the truth of faith or commends moral uprightness, we offer, as it were, a calf of our lips at the altar, because we disclose the mystery of God’s Word to minds that savor lofty wisdom, in which the fire of divine love burns and the flesh is consumed. Therefore the hide is, as it were, stripped from this calf when, the veil of the letter having been removed, spiritual understanding is revealed. The flesh of this calf is also cut into pieces when milk is given to infants in Christ (1 Cor. 2), vegetables to the weak, and solid food to the perfect [Col. 0551C] (Heb. 5), according to apostolic tradition.

And note that this calf is offered at the door of the tabernacle of testimony when what the Law and Prophets foretold is believed to have been fulfilled and revealed in Christ’s coming. He says of himself: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10). For he is the key of David, who “opens and no one shuts” (Rev. 3), and shuts and no one opens. The sons of Aaron lay their hands upon the head of this calf when Christ’s priests attribute all their good works to Christ, who is the head of the Church. Of him it is said: “He sent his word and healed them” (Ps. 106); and he says of himself to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

The entrails of this calf are washed when nothing contrary is mixed with sound doctrine, which those sacraments celebrated; and its feet are washed when the preaching of that same Word is not defiled by the dust of fleshly desire. Thus the prophet says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, who preach good things” (Isa. 52). But the dung of this calf is burned outside the camp when spittings, blows, and every insult inflicted on God’s Word—even the disgrace of the cross itself—are transformed into the glory of the resurrection, with every fleshly observance removed [Col. 0551D] (Rom. 1 [citation uncertain]). This is well signified by fire, which converts into itself what it takes up and always strives upward.

[Col. 0552A] As we said above that the Word of the Lord is designated by the calf, ploughing up our hearts with the plough of the cross, so we may understand him also through the ram when we preach Christ as our leader, or commend his innocence, according to the prophet’s words: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). We likewise signify the same Word through the goat when we commemorate that Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh and was offered for the sin of the human race. We signify the same through the turtledove and dove when we attest that human nature is joined in Christ to the Holy Spirit. For Christ’s flesh is fittingly figured by the turtledove, because it assumed the groaning of our capacity for suffering, humanity, and mortality.

Therefore the Psalmist says: “The turtledove found herself a nest,” that is, the dispensation of his incarnation, in which he produced young (Ps. 83), that is, begot believers. But by the dove the Holy Spirit is understood, who appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove. Hence it was said to John: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining is he who baptizes” (John 1).

In the same Word of God we offer fine flour when, having purged out the leaven of malice and wickedness, we summon peoples to ecclesiastical unity. While they are catechized, they are as if ground; when they are baptized, they are united in one body so as to become one bread; when they are trained for the contest, they are strengthened as if by the baking of an oven, according to: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, but the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” [Col. 0552C] (Sir. 27:5; citation printed as Ecclus. 7). And: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2). Then these same peoples are anointed like bread of offering with oil, when through laying on of hands and sacred chrism they are strengthened to endure that same contest bravely against spiritual wickedness.

We too, if we strive to please God, are commanded morally to offer all these things to God. We offer a calf when we overcome pride by humility. We immolate a sheep or ram when we preserve true innocence. We offer a goat when we cleanse the stench of lust by chastisement of the flesh and compunction of a contrite heart. We offer a turtledove when we bewail the afflictions of this exile in the solitude [Col. 0552D] of the mind, saying with the Psalmist: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Ps. 119). We offer a dove when we admire the dove’s simplicity, so that we devise deceit against no one. We offer loaves baked in an oven when no tribulations divide us from the unity of the Church. We offer unleavened loaves from a frying pan to God when we moderate zeal for justice with bowels of mercy. We also offer bread baked on a griddle when, through zeal for abstinence, we wear down our flesh with fasts and labors.

Our readings, delivered from whatever books in historical or allegorical style, commend these sacrifices of Christ and the Church; the melodies of singers, stirring the minds of the people to an affection of piety through sweet song, resound these; hymns [Col. 0553A] and psalms resound them; and whatever is regularly performed in ecclesiastical offices, whether nocturnal or diurnal, whether in the silence of private rites or before the hearing of the people, is not done idly. Rather, all is directed toward either the building up of faith or the ordering of morals by those who serve not the killing letter but the life-giving Spirit.

There are also many other sacrifices offered for various occasions: for thanksgiving, for the ordination of a bishop, for cleansing from leprosy, or for a nocturnal emission. These likewise prefigured the one sacrifice of which we have spoken and build up faith and morals. They were many and were often repeated because, according to the Apostle, they could not make perfect the worshipper (Heb. 9); but this sacrifice, offered once, cleansed original and actual sins and reconciled heavenly and earthly things.

We have shown above, as briefly as we could, how the sacraments of the old and new priesthood, celebrated openly, correspond. It remains now to show, as the Lord grants, how especially those things which our priests do in mystical prayers or actions correspond to those which the high priests did within the Holy of Holies.

First, let us consider what likeness to the Gospel belongs to the secret prayers which the priest says after the offertory, in which the bread and wine that are to be changed by the Lord’s words into Christ’s body and blood are called victims, offerings, or sacrifices. For in the Gospel we read that, [Col. 0553C] after supper, the Lord went with his disciples into a garden; and there, before those who were to seize him reached him, withdrawing from his disciples, he prayed the same prayer three times in silence, pitying the wretched Jews and saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26; printed “19”). But because the world was to be redeemed from its original transgression through his obedience, he chose rather to leave Judea in its blindness [variant: “to sin”] than to leave God’s children in eternal death, according to the saying: “Nineveh would not have been saved unless the gourd had withered” (Jonah 4).

The high priests in the Old Testament imitated this threefold prayer, in which the Son devoted himself to the Father’s will as a ram for a whole burnt offering, when they were about to enter the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement. Then a calf was offered for the high priest, a ram for a whole burnt offering, and the goat upon which the Lord’s lot had fallen for the sins of the people; their blood—that is, the blood of the calf and goat—was to be brought into the holy place, while their bodies were burned outside the camp. In all these kinds of sacrifice Christ was prefigured, presenting himself in that threefold prayer as one to be offered to the Father: as a calf for the sins of the high priests, as a ram for a whole burnt offering, and as a goat for every transgression of the people.

After the secret prayers have been completed, the priest first admonishes the people by greeting them; then he exhorts them to set their minds on things above and not to be ungrateful to their redeemer; and he counsels them to ascribe all these things to the grace of the mediator. [Col. 0554A] This may fittingly be understood to have been done by the Lord Jesus during the intervals of the threefold prayer, when he came to the disciples three times and said: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26). What is it to watch except not to presume upon one’s own merits, but in all things to have recourse to the mediator’s grace? Thus we are healthfully taught that it is fitting for this to be done by human frailty, when we know that angels, archangels, and all the heavenly hosts praise and worship God because they acknowledge that they obtain their blessedness through the mediator’s beneficence.

This is why the two cherubim covered the mercy seat with their wings: angelic powers honor God for the virtues bestowed upon them, and look upon the mercy seat, trusting that they possess the excellence they have from the merciful goodness of God. Therefore the priest prays that, in confession of the Holy Trinity, our praises may be joined to those of the angels, since “at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings” (Phil. 2).

Therefore, because to our mediator, as he himself says, “all power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28), the priest continues and asks God the Father that through him the offered mysteries may be blessed—that is, transformed into the truth which those sacrifices offered on the Day of Atonement had borne in the foretold shadow. Since there are those three things—the calf, the ram, and the two goats—they are commemorated by three names, being called gifts, offerings, and sacrifices, although they represent one sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, through which [Col. 0554C] divine and human things have been reconciled.

For the two goats signify Christ’s two natures: the human nature in which he suffered for our reconciliation, signified by the goat slain for sin; and the divine nature, signified by the goat which is sent alive into the desert by the prepared man—that is, by Christ himself—into the desert where, leaving the ninety-nine sheep, the good shepherd came to seek the one that had been lost (Luke 15). With the blood of these animals, namely the calf and goat, the high priest entered the Holy of Holies; and the Lord Jesus entered the Holy of Holies through his own blood, which was figured by the blood of the aforesaid animals, having obtained eternal redemption (Heb. 9). Likewise our priest, with Christ’s blood—that is, with remembrance of the Lord’s Passion—enters to celebrate the holy mysteries.

The Levitical priest, entering the tabernacle of testimony, prays for himself and for his household (Lev. 16). Christ, about to ascend into heaven, prays for himself, saying: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17; printed “12”). He also prays for his household, saying: “Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me” (John 17). And our priest, beginning to handle the sacred mysteries, prays for the supreme pontiff, the holy Church of God, and those in high positions, according to the Apostle, so that “we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and holiness” (1 Tim. 2).

The Levitical priest carries coals from the altar, on which the flesh of animals is burned, with him [Col. 0555A] into the holy place, filling the censer from them (Lev. 16). Our supreme priest ascended into the tabernacle not made with hands, carrying with him a body filled [the text reads *refectum*, “refreshed”] with every sweet odor of virtues. These virtues humanity received as living coals from the fire of the Holy Spirit, as from an altar that burns the flesh of evil desire.

Our priest also carries with him coals received from the same altar when he commemorates the apostles and certain martyrs, who, brought from death to life through the love of the Spirit, themselves burn inwardly with divine love and labor by their example to make others, who are dead, alive. We have this commemoration of saints during the secret prayers from the Old Testament, where Moses commands (Exod. 28) that Aaron, entering the sanctuary, should have on his breast the breastpiece, upon which were written the names of the twelve patriarchs, engraved upon twelve stones distributed in three rows at the heads of the four corners. This signifies that, together with faith in the Trinity and evangelical doctrine, the priest’s mind must always retain the memory of earlier Fathers, so that he may be formed for good living by their examples and protected by their intercessions.

When spices had been placed upon them, smoke proceeded from the censer to overshadow the oracle, lest the high priest be seen while he was in the sanctuary.

We also read in the Apocalypse concerning our supreme priest, who was the Angel of Great Counsel, that, when the censer had been filled from the fire of the altar—that is, when omnipotent divinity dwelt in Christ’s body—such fullness and ascent [Col. 0555C] of virtues proceeded from him as exceeded all human understanding (Rev. 8; Col. 2), as John says: “For he does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3; printed “10”). Likewise, when our priest prays while celebrating the sacraments of the New Testament, such purity of prayer, like the smoke of burning spices, is directed to God as surpasses both human reason and every understanding.

For the priest prays that the Lord may deign to make the offering placed upon the altar blessed: that is, to transform it into that uniquely blessed offering, immune from every sin; enrolled, that is, not newly instituted but assigned by ancient figures and Scriptures; ratified, that is, not transitory, because the old victim was made void after Christ, the true victim, had been offered on the cross; reasonable, that is, not animal, since the blood of bulls could not make perfect the worshipper (Heb. 9). But this our victim is rational because it is both the one sacrificing and the sacrifice itself. For when the Apostle gave the reason why Christ offered himself, he added: “If he were on earth, he would not even be a priest” (Heb. 8), as though saying: He became the victim because there was not upon earth another victim equally worthy and sufficient to exhaust the world’s crimes. He became the offerer because there was no priest equally worthy, since the law appoints sinful priests, who first offer for their own sins and then for those of the people. Therefore a sinful priest, unable to suffice for himself, could not offer so holy a victim; but that holy and innocent one offered herself because she willed it. Hence he says in the Gospel: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down” (John 10).

After those words, the priest explains spiritually what he asks: namely, that those bodily materials may become for us Christ’s body and blood. This prayer, like the smoke of the most subtle spices, overshadows the mercy seat: it asks that earthly and corruptible matter be incorporated into the heavenly and incorruptible body. But to this depth of divine counsel faith alone must be applied, for faith reaches even within the veil. It would have no beginning if it strove to prove by the persuasive words of human wisdom the sacraments which it contains.

The priest serving the shadow sprinkles the mercy seat, the sanctuary, and the tabernacle with the blood of the calf and, in the same rite, with the blood of the slain goat, facing eastward. For the same Christ who was figured by the calf was also signified by the goat offered for sin; and Christ, ascending eastward—that is, to the Father from whom he sprang—sprinkles the Father himself, whom he made propitious toward us by the sprinkling of his blood. He also sprinkles the sanctuary and tabernacle because, entering the holy places through his own blood, he reconciled divine and human things; for, as the Apostle says, “it pleased the Father through him to restore all things that are in heaven and things that are on earth” (Col. 1): that is, the Church, which on earth had been lost through the disobedience of the first parent, and in heaven diminished through the fall of the apostate angel.

Our priest imitates this sprinkling of Christ’s blood within the holy mysteries, as though within the veil, whenever, facing eastward—whence the Savior came to us—he names the mysteries themselves by their typical or proper names and seals them with the sign of the cross.

What does it mean, then, to make the sign of the cross over the sacred things, or things to be consecrated, within the mysteries, except to commemorate the Lord’s death? Hence the Lord also, when he handed down the form for consecrating his body and blood, said among other things: “Do this in remembrance of me. As often as you do this, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11). After the sprinkling of Christ’s blood has thus been commemorated by the Lord’s words, there follow the words of the sacraments, likewise commemorating that sprinkling of blood [Col. 0556D], as the priest directs his prayer to the Father: “Therefore, O Lord, we your servants, mindful of the passion, resurrection, and ascension of your Son, offer to your majesty”—that is, through these visible gifts of yours we commemorate as offered to you—“a pure victim,” that is, without the leaven of malice; “a holy victim,” that is, consecrated to you; “an immaculate victim,” that is, such as were signified by the animals sought out without blemish for sacrifice. And the priest asks that this commemoration of the true sacrifice may be made acceptable to God the Father, just as the gifts of Abel, Abraham, and Melchizedek were acceptable—offerings in which the sacraments of the new priesthood were initiated, before the priesthood of the Levitical order had yet been established.

What is figured by Abel, except Christ, who [Col. 0557A] was innocent and slain by the guilty? What by Abraham, except the obedience by which he was obedient to the Father unto death? And what again by Melchizedek, except that same Christ, changing bread and wine into his body and commending this rite of the new priesthood to his disciples? It is neither surprising nor to be attributed to superfluity if, in our sacraments, that is frequently commemorated which was not idly and frequently prefigured in the ancient shadows.

After the offering of incense, after the sanctuary, tabernacle, and altar had been sprinkled with the blood of the bull and the goat, the sons of Aaron lay their hands upon the head of the goat, the scapegoat, and, pronouncing imprecations over it, send it alive into the wilderness, bearing the sins of the children of Israel. Then the high priest returns to the camp, praying for his house [Col. 0557B] and for the entire assembly of the children of Israel. Thus the Jews, serving the ancient shadow, laid their hands upon Christ—that is, upon his divinity, which was the head of his humanity, according to the Apostle, saying: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). Resisting him, they pronounced an imprecation upon themselves while imprecating against Christ: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). They sent him alive into the wilderness, since they could not harm his divinity; for they allowed him, free from the death of the flesh, to ascend to that solitary glory which he has with the Father, through a man prepared—that is, through himself—bearing the sins of the children of Israel, that is, taking away the sins of the world, not possessing them.

Our priest commemorates this when he says to God the Father: “Command these things to be borne by the hands of your angel [Col. 0557C] to your sublime altar.” Who is that angel, unless the Angel of Great Counsel, who by his own hands—that is, by works endowed with singular worthiness—merited to ascend into heaven and to lift up himself to the sublime altar, that is, to the Father’s right hand, interceding for us (Rom. 8)? Thereupon the high priest is sent back to the camp; and the Lord, instructing his disciples concerning his assumption, says: “I am with you [all days] until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

Let our priest imitate both these things. First, by his prayers lifting Christ’s body above every heavenly height; then, as though returning to the camp, saying: “That as many of us as shall receive the most holy body and blood of your beloved [Col. 0557D] Son from this participation at the altar may be filled with every heavenly blessing.” Behold, there come to mind the words of the blessed apostle Andrew, by which he maintains both that the Lord’s body is in heaven and that the Lord’s body can be received from the altar. “Although,” he says, “his flesh is eaten on earth by the people and his blood is drunk, nevertheless he himself remains whole and living in the heavenly places at the Father’s right hand until the time of the restoration [resurrection] of all things. If you ask how this can be, I shall answer briefly: because it is a sacrament of faith, it may be investigated profitably; otherwise it cannot be investigated without danger.”

This is why certain carnal disciples withdrew from him when he had said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life” (John 6). For they thought that [Col. 0558A] he would distribute his body to them either boiled in pots or roasted on spits. Therefore the Lord instructs those who remained, saying: “If you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before” (ibid.). It is as though he said: Then you will understand that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose, and that the grace of God is not consumed by bites.

Thus Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm 54: “Until the world is ended, the Lord is above; yet here too the Lord is with us as truth.” Behold, we have Christ whole in heaven, through the manifestation of his flesh, interceding with the Father for us; and we have his body whole in the sacrament of the altar. In the heights, the prayer of his Son is: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John 17). This [Col. 0558B] is a prayer for his household, for his members.

And this is what is read concerning the high priest: returning to the camp, he washes his garments. For Christ in the camp—that is, in the Church—washes his garments when he cleanses our sins through baptism or confession, for we are his garment, as it is said through the prophet: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with a garment” (Isa. 45). The priest also washes his garments when, after descending from the height of the mysteries to the care of lower things, he mourns the sins of the peoples joined to him and labours to reconcile them to God through the aid of prayers, saying with the prophet: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may mourn for the slain of my people?” (Jer. 9).

The following [frequent] prayers contain these things, making mention both of the dead and [Col. 0558C] of the living. But it should be noted that among these prayers the intercession of the saints is invoked—namely, of the apostles and martyrs—by whose examples the present Church asks to be instructed and by whose merits to be defended. This commemoration of the fathers who preceded harmonizes with the ancient priesthood. For the high priest, as he entered the holy place, bore the names of the patriarchs on two garments, on the breastpiece and the shoulder-piece, which were bound to one another; the Holy Spirit thereby signifying that the priest of Christ should strive to have in action the justice and truth which he possesses in his heart. For the breast is the place of the heart, while the shoulder is the place for bearing a burden.

In correspondence with this, within our sacraments there is a twofold commemoration of the saints: so that our priest [Col. 0558D] may meditate upon the deeds of the saints in his heart and imitate them in his deeds. After the deeds of the saints have been commemorated, the priest, not presuming upon his own merits, prays that through the merits of the saints we may attain what we are unable to attain through our own merits—and this only through the Mediator who was made for us propitiation, redemption, and sanctification (1 John 11; 1 Cor. 1). Through him these sacraments were instituted for us as medicine for our wounds.

This is what follows: “Through whom you create all these things”—that is, you change them into another essence and efficacy than their first condition possesses or appearance displays. “You sanctify, you give life”: that is, you make them sacraments of holiness and life. It follows: “Through him is all honour and glory to you,” that is, because you work all things through him, you are rightly honoured above all things by all through him, who is also from you [Col. 0559A], and glorified by the praise of all. “And with him” there is glory to you, because the Son too, as co-equal with you, is honoured and glorified together with you in the works which you do through him. “And in him” there is spiritual glory to you, as you yourself said by the voice of your dove: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3, 17).

In these words we openly commemorate the Lord’s Ascension, in which we confess that the Son is honoured with the Father in equal glory. As though proceeding by these praises from inward things to outward, the priest seeks the assent of the Church, saying in a resonant voice: “Through all ages of ages.” The people supply the place of the unlearned person in his prayer and answer, “Amen” (1 Cor. 14). By making itself a participant through this one word [Col. 0559B] in all the charisms which the priest has sought to obtain through the manifold diversity of the sacraments, the priest, now as though changing the vesture he wore while handling the sacred mysteries, changes his voice. Thereafter, as though in the outer court, he completes the remaining sacraments of the Mass, urging the people with him to say the Lord’s Prayer, by which both the consecration of the sacraments is completed and the people are prepared by prayer to complete those same sacraments.

Then follows the breaking of the sacrament, which we received from the tradition of our Lord, who broke his body, consecrated by his own hands, and distributed it to his disciples. In this breaking he indicated his possession which was soon to come, and opened the seal of the ancient Scriptures, beneath which the spiritual understanding—the supersubstantial bread of the soul—was enclosed. But in distributing that same body to his disciples he prefigured the Church, to be incorporated into himself, living upon heavenly bread. This too was prefigured in the offering of the high priest, who was commanded to offer in the morning and after midday portions of fine flour mixed with oil, that [Col. 0559C] the sweetness of inward bread, which in the morning—that is, at first—lay hidden in the letter, might after midday—that is, when the light of truth appeared—be mercifully presented for believers to taste.

We too do not without purpose divide the sacrament of Christ’s body into three parts. For through this we commemorate Christ’s passion as past, which that offering signified as future; and in this number we understand three things by which we commend the unity of the Head—that is, Christ—and of the Church. By the first portion we signify Christ’s substantial body, which rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, concerning which the Lord himself says in the psalm: “My flesh shall rest in hope” (Ps. 15). And in the following words he promises his resurrection and his session at the Father’s right hand: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with joy before your face, delights at your right hand unto the end” (ibid.).

The second portion, which we place on the paten with the first, signifies that part of Christ’s body—that is, of the Church—which already rests, as it were, in the Sabbath with its Head and already possesses one robe of immortality. We believe that the thief is in this portion, to whom the Lord said as he confessed upon the cross: “Today you shall be with me [Col. 0560A] in paradise” (Luke 33); and concerning which the Church sings: “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven.” The third portion, which we place in the blood, signifies that part of the Church which drinks the Lord’s cup—that is, imitates Christ’s passion—of which the Lord said to the apostles: “In me you shall have peace, but in the world you shall have tribulation” (John 16).

When the breaking of the sacrament has been performed and the prayer joined to the Lord’s Prayer has been completed, the priest and ministers, and on certain [all] days the faithful people, receive communion. In this matter the unity of the Head—that is, Christ—and the Church—that is, Christ’s body—is again signified, as he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6).

In view of the three portions mentioned above, while the sacraments are received, the choir sings *Agnus Dei* three times. First the Church prays to the Lamb—not the lamb that figures this Lamb, but the true one who takes away the sins of the world—that she may be numbered among his members, whose body and blood she receives; that is, that she may cleave to him as to her Head. Second, she prays to the same Lamb that she may be joined to that part of Christ’s body which already rests in peace with the Head. The priest prayed this above when, after naming the apostles and martyrs, he added: “Into whose fellowship, we beseech you, admit us, not as an assessor of merit, but as a giver of pardon.” Third, she prays to the same Lamb that she may not be overcome by the pressures of the world and by wickedness, which the Lord’s Prayer had expressed above: “And do not [Col. 0560C] lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen” (Matt. 6). The prayer connected with the Lord’s Prayer contains this same petition.

Nothing of the Lamb’s flesh remains which this prayer does not consume. It consumes the head when it makes itself his body; it consumes the entrails when it wishes to be counted and incorporated among his inward members; it consumes the feet when it strives to incorporate into itself those who are to labour with the Head on earth. Therefore, in this third prayer the Church asks that peace be granted to her. After this the priest returns to the right side of the altar and there completes the office of the Mass, signifying that “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11).

It should be noted that after handling and receiving [Col. 0560D] the sacraments, before the priest turns toward the assembly of the Church—which ought to have been cleansed through participation in so great a holiness—he washes his hands as though from the touch of an unclean and dying thing; and that very water is poured into a sacred place assigned to this rite. None of these things appears to be done without the sacrament of a great reality. Here I am reminded of what accords with this act: namely, that on the day of propitiation, after the flesh of the bull and goat had been burned outside the camp, the priest did not return to the camp until his garments and body—signifying outer and inner things—had been washed. Yet, though washed according to the Law, he was regarded as unclean until evening.

Those who burned the flesh of the victims outside the camp prefigured Christ’s passion, which occurred outside the city. But our priests commemorate in the celebrations of the Mass that passion which they, as has been said, prefigured; yet they judge themselves unclean until evening—that is, as long as they live—and unworthy to carry out such great mysteries [Col. 0561A].

Hence blessed John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “When you have done what I command you, say that we are unprofitable servants: we have done what we ought to do” (Luke 17). For this reason they wash their hands and reverently handle the water of washing, thereby honouring the height of the sacrament and commemorating their own unworthiness by such washing.

So too the priest washes his hands before approaching to handle the sacraments, just as the high priest, upon entering the Holy of Holies, washed his hands at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony and so came to burn the spices. This cleanliness is outwardly displayed, but is commanded to be accomplished inwardly, because “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44). For it is not the dirt on our hands that contaminates the most sacred sacraments. Rather, if we approach to handle and receive them without corrected morals and disciplined actions, we receive from them not the medicine of life but incur the judgment of death. The Apostle bears witness, saying: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11) [Col. 0561C]. Therefore we must labour so that, just as the outward defilements of the hands are washed away, so the enticing desires within our minds may be purified.

Then follow prayers in which the benefits received are commemorated and thanks are given. These two things are like the ashes of the heifer burned outside the camp, which a clean man sets aside after Christ’s slaying in a clean place—that is, he keeps them in a clean heart—outside the camp, that is, outside Jewish observance, beyond which Christian faith shone forth. When all these things have been completed, the priest or Levite says: “Go, it is the dismissal,” that is, the meditation and intercession which he had performed [expended] has been completed [Col. 0561D].

What we have written could be unfolded through many figures of the ancients, expanded through many differing interpretations, and adorned with many ornaments of rhetorical figures. But it was not our purpose in this little work to pursue the matter in this fashion and plant a grove in the house of the Lord. Our sole purpose was to seek the correspondence between the old and the new priesthood, so that it might be shown that what was prefigured there by the manifold rite of sacrifices has been fulfilled in the new priesthood by the very few, very easy to perform, and most august observances of the sacraments.

Nor do we trust that we have dealt with these matters sufficiently, concerning him who said through a certain wise man: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12). For our contemporaries or successors, stirred by our pious presumption, will, insofar as God grants them, say greater things more greatly, and better things more well; and if they find in this little work anything unpolished or less than perfect, so far as my purpose is concerned, may they spare the charity which perhaps could not state with exactness what it wished to say [Col. 0562A].

## SERMON VI. Why God Was Born and Suffered

When the world had been corrupted by original and actual sins, the Creator of the world, by a hidden and wondrous counsel, willed through the mystery of the incarnate Word to restore the fall of that same world. By that Word through whom he was able to create all things from nothing, he was able to refashion what had been lost: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32) [Col. 0562B]. We do not believe that this power of his was diminished; we do not believe that it was changed—“with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration” (James 1)—so that he might be less powerful or wise in restoring than he had been in forming (Luke 1).

For the hand of the almighty potter, whose “all ways are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24), which had raised clay from the earth to the dignity of a rational nature, willed to restore the ruin of the fragile vessel in such a way that it would neither leave human sin unpunished, because it is just, nor leave it incurable, because it is merciful. If he were only just, whose wisdom “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8), he could by his strength have contended against the deceiver of the human race and restored the lost sheep, brought back to the flock, to its Lord. But in that way he would seem merely to have displayed the eminence of his power, not to have bestowed healing mercy upon those redeemed. Nor would it appear with how great a love the Creator loved the creature, from whom he sought to be loved through many benefits; so that wretched man, grace going before, might obtain also by merit what was being repaid to him, though not owed to him, through evil merit.

Therefore, what God’s wisdom could do wisely and powerfully, it willed to do sweetly: uniting to itself the weakness of our flesh, which it would first heal in itself and through this, as through a healing remedy, restore health to the human race [Col. 0562D]. This was not because it could not have been done otherwise, with regard to the skill and power of the physician, but because no more suitable antidote could be provided with regard to the constitution of the sick person. “For what is weak in God is stronger than men, and what is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1).

This course [or “cause”; the text is uncertain] seems to us to be the particular reason why the Son of God willed to put on humanity and dwell among human beings: that by dying he might overcome the mortality which he had received from us, and might call our nature, restored above the dignity of its first origin, back with himself to immortality; so that the humility of the flock might follow where the exaltation of the shepherd had gone before. Thus the sunbeam dries up the moisture which it draws to itself, yet neither diminishes nor changes the power of its heat and brightness. Thus fire converts into itself the material it takes up, yet for this reason neither changes nor diminishes its own nature.

Much more powerfully, that fire of which it is said, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12), took our mortality and passibility into itself; and thereby reassumed the whole body with the grace of healing [or “healing itself”; variant: *sanitatis / sanitatem*] [Col. 0563A]. A wonderful and incomparable kind of medicine, for which the physician willed to become ill; and he decreed to heal by his own weakness the sick for whom he was procuring a remedy of salvation.

In this it appears how incomparably he loved us: because, in seeking his deserters, he took hold of Abraham’s seed, brought back those wandering, and healed the wounded, he added nothing to himself. He was not thereby made higher; he was not thereby made more blessed. This whole dispensation provided for our benefit, served our salvation, and contributed nothing to divine power. For even when we were vessels of dishonour, we could not escape the hand of the almighty potter. He used vessels of wrath as he willed, for the manifestation of his glory. Thus it was said to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exod. 9; Rom. 9) [Col. 0563B]. Did not the demons also, when they were cast out by the Lord from possessed bodies, glorify the Lord when they said: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of the living God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Mark 1)

It is therefore clear from these and other such things that divine power had no need of our restoration. Yet by that goodness by which it created us, it willed also to reform us; and for this purpose it applied not such medicine as it could perhaps have made, but that which it saw would suit more gently the constitution of the sick person. Skilled physicians are accustomed sometimes to cure the diseases they undertake to treat by contraries, sometimes by like things. This is what our Lord Jesus Christ did: enriching us by his poverty, raising us by his humility, healing us by his weakness, and giving us life by his death.

Thus, according to the method of medicine, dry remedies are applied to moist conditions, moist remedies to dry, hot remedies to cold; and weaker contraries are overcome by the intervention of stronger contraries. By a similar method, like things are applied to like when the length or breadth of plasters is measured according to [Col. 0563D] the size of wounds or swellings. Thus the flesh of a scorpion cooked in oil heals the stings of scorpions. Thus theriac, prepared from serpent flesh, counters a serpent’s bites and, taken as a drink, expels drinks infected with poison.

In accordance with this likeness, our physician healed by the death of his flesh the death that came to our flesh from the serpent, and refashioned it into the form of his immortality, to be completed at the time of restoration. Here it must be considered more carefully that death which came through wood was overcome through wood. And the very form of the wood was conformed to the length, breadth, and height of the human body, so that, just as the whole body had been moved to stretch out its hands toward what was forbidden, so the body might be stretched out through all its members upon the cross, and all that had been shattered by the guilt of the ancestral transgression might be strengthened by the kneading of this plaster [Col. 0564A].

But a medicine composed by means of like things was mixed with medicine made through the opposite. For here obedience healed what disobedience had corrupted there; and what the delight of gluttony had defiled there, the torment of the cross restored here. A deeper sacrament is contained in this figure of the cross; and the deeper it is, the more carefully it must be considered. In the breadth of the cross is understood love of neighbour, which must be extended not only to friends but also to enemies who are to be loved. In its length likewise is understood the long and persevering endurance of labours and persecutions, which our pilgrimage, longing for the homeland, must bear patiently both for love of neighbours and for the performance of all good works.

Similarly, in its height is figured the eminence of hope, penetrating even to the inner side of the veil, where those who are here manifoldly afflicted by the citizens of Babylon shall enjoy the vision of peace, until they are liberated from the bondage of this corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God [Col. 0564B].

The Lord Jesus signified this breadth of charity upon the cross: raising his head toward the east, lowering his feet toward the west, and stretching out his hands toward north and south, so as to fulfil what he had foretold of himself before his passion: “When I have been lifted up from the earth”—that is, when I have been crucified—“I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12), that is, I shall summon the whole world to myself.

By this sacrament of the cross, holy Elisha raised the son of the Shunammite, placing mouth to mouth and his hands upon the child’s hands, and restored him alive to his mother (4 Kings 4). By the power of the same sacrament, Moses in the wilderness struck the rock twice with his rod and brought water from the rock for the thirsty people. For the twofold striking of the two pieces of wood is figuratively understood as the joining effected in the cross. Thus the rock is struck twice when Christ—of whom the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10)—stretched out on the two beams of the cross, is pierced with a lance. Water flowed from this rock when the blood of redemption and the water of baptism, by which we are transformed into a new human being, flowed from Christ’s side [Col. 0564D].

Moreover, among these dimensions of the cross, the depth of the cross must be carefully considered, because the mystery of the cross is deep. In it the minds of many who appeared wise failed, since they dared to criticize what they could not comprehend by human reason: namely, why the Word, coeternal with God the Father, containing all things and filling all things, enclosed his whole self within the humanity he assumed and yet did not cease to govern, fill, and contain the whole world. They do not sufficiently consider that what has power in the lesser can much more have power in the greater, since one whole voice proceeds from the speaker’s mouth and comes whole to the ears of many.

Those who dispute too anxiously about this question and, as though a door were closed, grope along the wall, should first hear the Apostle saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9) [Col. 0565A]. Then let them become gentle and knock with devotion, that it may be opened to them; and they will understand that the Creator was just in condemning and merciful in redeeming, and that what the justice of the Almighty had justly condemned could not be healed without mercy.

From this they will further discern, when divine omnipotence has humbled itself even to the poverty of captive humanity and the disgrace of the cross (Phil. 2), how the just sentence condemned guilty humanity in paradise. For when he was accused by the Lord of the disobedience he had committed, he did not humbly accuse himself as his fault required; rather, he proudly accused his author, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as companion gave me of the fruit, and I ate” (Gen. 3). By saying this he thought himself excused and the Creator—the maker of the woman who had drawn the man into sin—made blameworthy [Col. 0565B]. Had he humbly accused himself and not thrown the blame back upon his maker, he would not have been exiled from paradise.

But it was contrary to divine justice to restore an unrepentant offender to his former rank, rather than by whatever means it willed compelling him to attain the fruit worthy of repentance. Therefore, by divine sentence he was condemned to death, and with all his posterity that was to proceed from his loins he was cast out of paradise and condemned to a wretched exile. And he who could not return to his former state without repentance had to be stirred and admonished to repentance, so that voluntary and subject humility might reform him whom wickedness, wrongly raised up, had corrupted [variant: *voluntary and subject humility*].

For it was not fitting that he who had voluntarily fallen into punishment should be dragged unwillingly to repentance, lest he prove as ungrateful for his restoration as he had been for his first creation. A remedy suited to the sick person was therefore provided, which might soften the hardness of his swelling in such a way that, once softened, he would voluntarily pour out the deadly poison, as the Psalmist says: “Pour out your hearts before him” (Ps. 61), that is, cast out through confession from your consciences all uncleanness. As long as the world delayed doing this, it remained unclean.

Therefore, that this might take place, our physician sent before himself his heralds and witnesses, legislators and prophets, to prepare the hearts of hearers for repentance and bear witness to him in the time of grace [Col. 0565D]. The physician himself came in the time of fullness, publicly preached the purpose of his coming, and became a teacher of medicine, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4). And again: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 6). Many received this counsel of healing. To those who despised it, the hiss of the serpent that destroys was still more pleasing than the persuasion of the physician who redeems [or “Redeemer”; variant: *redimentis / redemptoris*]. But the son of adoption heard and obeyed the voice that promised, whereas in paradise he had not obeyed the command that threatened death.

When the dispensation of his teaching had been completed, and blindness had persisted in Israel in part, he finally presented himself as physician and made himself the medicine [Col. 0566A]; he presented himself as priest and made himself the sacrifice, that he might accomplish the purpose for which he had come and prove how great was the love with which he loved those for whom he offered his body upon the altar of the cross. Thus he had foretold in his Gospel: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 1). Hence the Apostle says: “God commends his love toward us, because when we were enemies he reconciled us to himself through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5).

And because it is natural that people who love should be loved, by this humility and love the hardness of the world was humbled and melted, so that it might recognize the benefit of its restoration, though it had not recognized the excellence of its creation. Hence the Psalmist says: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he has been compared with senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48) [Col. 0566B]. But after he returned to himself and, through love for the Redeemer and instruction from the one who admonished him, learned from how great a glory he had fallen and in how great a misery he lay, he discovered that he needed great mercy; and what the Psalmist says was fulfilled: “Their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened” (Ps. 15).

From then on the power of the cross was preached throughout the whole world. Its parts are extended through the four regions of the world, and it embraced and filled the whole world with its kneading. The world could no longer be wholly ungrateful, since it had been healed by so great a love. Our Crucified One rose from death, ascended into heaven, and left us the cross in remembrance of his passion. He left the cross for healing; he left the cross for sanctification. By this sign demons are put to flight; by this antidote healings are accomplished. This sign is protection for friends and an obstacle to enemies.

By the mystery of this cross, the unlearned are catechized; by the same mystery, the font of regeneration is consecrated. Through the laying on of hands marked with the sign of the same cross, the baptized receive gifts of graces. When basilicas are dedicated, altars consecrated, and [Col. 0566C] the sacraments of the altar performed with the insertion [variant: laying on] of the Lord’s words, this sign of the cross is used. Priests and Levites are advanced through it to holy orders; and, universally, all ecclesiastical sacraments are performed by means of it.

Whoever desires to cross without shipwreck this great and wide sea, in which are creeping things without number, should follow the cross, hold fast to the cross, and not abandon it until he reaches the desired harbour of salvation. It directs our course; it trains us for the contest; it helps us in the struggle; it advances us to victory; it destroys evil deeds and reduces to nothing all the devices of demons. What Christ’s bodily presence did on earth, that the memory of the victorious cross, marked by the faithful invocation of Christ’s name, does. It would take long to set forth the power of the cross in every particular. But one who bears Christ’s cross under compulsory service can learn by experience more of its power than speech can recount or human thought comprehend [Col. 0566D].

## SERMON VII. On the Coming of the Lord

[Col. 0567A]

Because in the observance of these present days we celebrate both advents of Christ, it must be distinguished for your brotherhood what you ought to believe as past in this observance and what you ought to await as future; so that expectation of the things to come may, through fear, restrain you anxiously from evils, while faith in things past may, through charity, strengthen you—without growing lukewarm—in good works. For none of you doubts that the Lord has already come in the form of a servant in order to be judged; none of you denies that he will come in the same form in order to judge.
