His first advent, therefore, was hidden; his second will be manifest. Of the first advent it is thus read: “And he is a man—who shall recognize him?” [Col. 0567B] (Ps. LXXXVI). And in the Gospel: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not recognize it” (John 1), with many passages to the same effect. But of the second the Psalm says: “Our God will come manifestly, and will not keep silence” (Ps. XLIX).

At his first advent indeed he kept silence—not in regard to commandment, but in regard to judgment. “For when he was cursed, he did not curse in return; when he was struck, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. II; Isa. LIII); and, like a lamb before its shearer, he did not open his mouth. At the second he will not keep silence, when he renders to each according to his works. Thus he will say to those at his left hand: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). But to those at his right: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation [Col. 0567C] of the world” (ibid.).

His first advent was in humility and gentleness; his second will be with terror and majesty. Of the first the prophet says to the Church: “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle and humble” (Zech. IX; Matt. XXI). Of the terror of the second the Psalm says: “Fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. XLIX), so that the tempest may drive the reprobate far away from the glory of his vision, and thereafter fire may burn them up. Of this tempest it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI). But concerning the fire to which the reprobate are to be delivered, the Lord says through Moses: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. XXXII). [Col. 0567D] He himself likewise says that he will come to judgment in majesty: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, all nations shall be gathered before him” (Matt. XXV).

At his first advent he came to justify the ungodly; at his second he will come to condemn the ungodly. At his first he came to call back those who had turned away; at his second, to glorify those who have been converted. At his first advent Christ was delivered to an undeserved death for the ungodly; at his second he will deliver the ungodly to their deserved death. At his first advent he came to reform us inwardly into the image of God. At the second he “will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. III).

For as through the first, earthly man sin entered into the world, and through sin death (Rom. V), so it was fitting that through the second, heavenly man, humanity should first be justified from [Col. 0568A] sin and afterwards restored through that same one to immortality (1 Cor. XV). For it had to be repaired in the order in which it had perished. The first death is transgression; from it was generated the second death, the corruption of the flesh through the withdrawal of the soul. Thus the first resurrection is justification; the second is the restoration of corrupt flesh to immortality.

Since both advents were necessary for our restoration, the holy Church has customarily venerated both under the observance of one season: that it may recall with thanksgiving the benefits begun in the former advent, and await with devout trembling the completed blessings of the advent to come. Therefore, during these four weeks, those things written concerning both advents of the Lord in the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the Gospel are recited in church with particular frequency by reading and singing, so that by these four kinds [Col. 0568B] of testimonies we may be fortified—or, perhaps, “admonished” (*moneamur*, for printed *muniamur*)—to give thanks for benefits received, and may prepare ourselves with an un-sluggish concern for what is to come.

Let us therefore preserve the first robe of innocence which we receive in the first advent, so that, when we go to meet the master of the household for the wedding feast clothed in it, we may also deserve to receive the second robe, that of immortality. Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, so that we may see in safety as judge the one whom we gladly receive as redeemer. “The day of the Lord,” as the Apostle says, “will disclose what sort of work each person’s work is, because it will be revealed in fire” (1 Cor. III).

For on the day of the Lord this air near the earth, as far as the waters of the Flood rose, will be filled with fire; [Col. 0568C] through it every person who rises again and is presented before Christ’s tribunal will pass. And just as fire either tests or refines gold and silver, so this fire will test the perfected works of those raised again and cleanse their imperfect works. Thus the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work remains, it will be tested by fire; if anyone’s work is burned up, he himself will be saved, yet only as through fire” (ibid.).

Knowing these things, dearest brethren, let us prepare ourselves for [or: “at”] the advent of the Judge, so that he may find in us not what he condemns but what he crowns. “Let us go before his presence with confession” (Ps. XCIV); let us mourn the evils that we have committed. Let us appoint our consciences judges against ourselves, because, as the Apostle says, “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged” [Col. 0568D] (1 Cor. XI). For the supreme High Priest, who offered himself to God the Father for us, still intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand (Heb. IX; Rom. VIII). He still reserves a place of pardon for sinners, whereas for those who turn away and do not return he afterwards reserves only a place of vengeance. Therefore, while we have time, let us avoid the vengeance due to our former life by the correction of life [printed: *per correctionem*; variant: *vitae correptione*]; let us seek mercy through the observance of righteousness, lest at last the strict Judge sit in judgment against us—he who now, as the merciful High Priest, intercedes for us: Jesus Christ our Lord (ibid.).

287  
## SERMON VIII. On the Nativity of the Lord

It pleases me to direct the mind’s gaze toward the greatness of divine mercy [printed *mertis*, evidently *mentis*, “mind”], and, from recollection of his benefits, to gather how much the rational creature owes to its Redeemer. First, because he wonderfully fashioned man from the earth when he did not yet exist; then, when man had been ruined through the serpent’s cunning and the woman’s deception, he restored him yet more wonderfully. In creating, marvelous power appeared; in restoring, the still more marvelous humility of power appeared.

For human weakness does not marvel so greatly if some powerful person powerfully acquires for his dominion countless servants who will serve him, as it does if he apprehends those same servants when they have fled, having recalled them by the enticements of undeserved humility—meanwhile concealing his power and setting threats aside. In the first state of his creation, man acted foolishly: because he feared power, he did not love majesty; he sought freedom and fell into slavery; and he who could have been made divine through obedience deserved, by aspiring to this, to be subjected to vanity. [Col. 0569B]

Therefore the kindly Creator, unwilling that what he had created should perish, appeared to his fellow servants in the guise of a servant, so that by familiar intercourse he might make his majesty known and stir them to charity. Thus, by making eye-salve from earth and saliva, he opened the eyes of the man blind from birth; for the wisdom of God, united in the unity of person with our nature, restored in the human race—blinded from its first origin—the understanding by which it might know God and the love by which it might love him once known. Thus, bound by so many benefits, it could not fail to love him whose many benefits it knew had already been bestowed upon it.

For in the benefit of the first creation the Creator’s wisdom and power shone forth; but in the benefit of reconciliation, by which he recalled to himself those who had turned away and deserved ill, remitted their punishments, and promised rewards, he clearly showed how greatly he loved what he had created. Thus he kindled the fire of his love in those whom he had first loved. [Col. 0569C]

The sick man recognized that the physician of his salvation was both affectionate and skilled; marveling both at his humility and at his wisdom, he loved health. He recognized how precious was the remedy which his physician had made in order to escape a disease so acute and so long-established. Nor could one who had received so many benefits from his Redeemer remain ungrateful.

For he recognized humility because this our physician reclined, as it were, upon the bed of the sick in the weakness of our flesh, so that he might experience what was necessary to heal his sick. The sick man also recognized the wisdom of this physician because, according to the method of medicine, in some cases he bestowed health upon the sick through like things, and in others removed disease through opposites. Through like things, indeed: because he was born so that we might be reborn; he became weak by enduring the passible conditions of our mortality, so that we might be saved from every passibility; he was crucified so that we might not be subjected to eternal torments; he died temporally so that we might not die eternally; he rose again so that we might rise with him; he ascended so that, by his sitting at the Father’s right hand, he might draw with himself the humility of his devoted flock. [Col. 0569D]

But if we consider by what opposites he removed contrary diseases, we see that through the person of a servant he restored our freedom; through his humility he cast down the pride of the ancient enemy; through his obedience [Col. 0570A] he healed our disobedience. He taught all these things in word and proved them by example, so that we might obediently fulfill what he set forth for imitation, and hope without hesitation for what he promised as objects of hope.

Let us hear from the mountains what price this physician paid for our redemption. For from the deep cries out that lofty mountain to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted by the mountain of mountains: “You were redeemed, not with corruptible gold and silver, from your vain manner of life, but with the precious blood of an immaculate lamb” (Matt. XVI; 1 Pet. I). Another mountain agrees with him, the teacher of the nations illumined by the sun of righteousness: “You were bought at a great price; glorify God and bear him in your body” (1 Cor. VI).

This spotless lamb is not that one which, in the old sacrifice, was required from the flocks without any diversity of blemish; rather, he is the true and innocent one, begotten from the spotless womb of the Virgin. He is not the one by whose blood doorposts were stained, but the one in whose faith the foreheads of believers are marked by the imprint of the cross; not the one whose blood was poured out by priests’ hands, but the one who, as true priest, was prefigured as to be offered by himself for our salvation. [Col. 0570B] For neither a victim equally worthy and equally pure could be found to be offered for our cleansing, nor a priest equally worthy and equally pure by whom so worthy a victim might worthily be offered. For he himself says of himself: “No one takes my life from me; rather, I lay it down, and I take it up again” (John X).

This lamb without blemish and wrinkle united to himself a virgin as bride, just as he had previously sanctified his virgin mother. Hence the nativity in which Christ was born in time is not unlike the nativity by which the Christian is born spiritually. For as Christ’s mother conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin, so the mother Church, Christ’s bride, daily brings forth Christian peoples by the washing of water in the word, in order that she may remain a virgin. In the former, integrity of flesh is present; in the latter, purity of faith is commended.

Let us hear Paul, the bridegroom’s friend, zealously loving the bride with chaste love—not for himself but for the bridegroom—saying thus to the Church of Corinth: “For I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy, because I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. X). [Col. 0570C] Here, having received the pledge of the Spirit, she is a virgin in integrity of faith and moral uprightness, to be led from hope to hope, so that there she may rejoice with full delight in full love for the bridegroom, whose arts [printed *arces*, evidently *artes*] she preserves, despising every seduction of the serpent.

Let us next hear how he sanctified the mother of his flesh, so that from this the catholic may rejoice and the unclean heretic be confuted. For he erased in her every stain of both original and actual guilt; and so, taking her flesh, transformed that same flesh into divine purity. Scripture indeed says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV; Heb. XII). Therefore, as material fire cleanses every material thing that it takes up and converts it into itself, so the material element of our flesh which the divine fire assumed could not remain devoid of divinity, so that what God is by nature it might begin to possess by grace. [Col. 0571A]

For the first parent of the human race, because she received the force of the serpent’s persuasion, succumbed to a twofold curse: both that she should incur death with her husband and that she should bear with pain the children whom she conceived through the pleasure of the flesh. All Eve’s daughters succeeded as heirs of this curse, and all bore their children under the condemnation of necessary death. This mother alone, who believed not the serpent’s hiss but the words of the announcing angel, deserved to hear a blessing that excluded both curses: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke XIV), because you will neither conceive through fleshly desire 288 nor bear your son in pain; “and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (ibid.), namely, that Son who, born neither of bloods nor of the will of a man, underwent temporal death not by necessity but by will, and delivered us from eternal death.

In this Nativity of Christ, God was born a human being so that human beings might be reborn as gods. In it divinity is bent down so that humanity may be lifted up. God, bending down as a humble and mighty helper, as it were places his shoulder beneath us in order to raise us. Between the profound dissimilarity of corruptible nature and immutable substance, he set forth his own person, sharing in both natures, as mediator; through what it has equal with us, that person lifted us up. And as from the lantern of flesh, for bleary eyes and for those unwilling to see the sun except beneath a cloud, he poured forth the radiance of tempered light and illumined the darkness of our ignorance. [Col. 0571B]

For wretched man, created in God’s image, “when he was in honor, did not understand; and therefore he became like the senseless beasts” (Ps. XLVIII). These beasts had no grass by which they might be nourished; they had forgotten to eat their bread, as the Psalmist says in lament: “My heart has withered, because I have forgotten to eat my bread” (Ps. CI). Therefore the bread of angels became grass for animals—that is, nourishment for the simple—so that the little child might suck milk from the same source by which the angel is fed with strong food. Thus, having been brought up into manly strength through the nourishment of milk, he may at last attain the inward and eternal taste of the divine majesty: that is, that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). Let him contemplate with angels the Word of the Lord, who was in the beginning with God: for the present through a mirror in an enigma, but afterwards by open vision. [Col. 0571C]

Here it is as on the way; there it is as in the homeland. Here let us rejoice that the benefits of the physician of our salvation have been bestowed upon us wisely, powerfully, wonderfully, and mercifully. By remembrance of these benefits, let us lighten the labors of our pilgrimage, so that we may serve long-sufferingly on the way and receive the reward in our homeland.

## SERMON IX. On the Circumcision of the Lord

Today we celebrate the eighth day of the Lord’s Nativity, on which the child Jesus received from the parents of his flesh the carnal sacrament of circumcision. “For, as he himself says, he came not to destroy the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V). He fulfilled the Law, indeed, because he drew out the spiritual meaning from the dregs of carnal observances; and he added in the Gospel certain lofty moral precepts to those commands which had been relaxed for the Jews because of their weakness. He also observed those carnal observances carnally until the time of correction.

Hence the child was circumcised by his parents on the eighth day, and on the fortieth day was presented by them in the temple with the legal offerings (Luke II). As a young man he also frequently went up to Jerusalem for the feast of Dedication and the other feast days, as we read in the Gospel (ibid.); and in no respect did he reject those legal sacraments, until, on the holy day of the Supper, after the old Passover had been sacrificed, he transformed the old priesthood into the new, when he presented himself to his disciples as both guest and meal. [Col. 0572A] “Therefore, when the priesthood was transferred, as the Apostle says, it was necessary that a transfer of the Law should also take place” (Heb. VII).

And this was the time of correction, when the carnal shadows under which Christ had been born and brought up to manhood were to be renewed. Hence the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the Law, in order that he might redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. IV). If an outsider to the observance of the Law were to expound its sacraments to persons who knew the Law, who would give him a hearing? Therefore, according to the proper order of teaching, he wished first to be a hearer of the Law before becoming its teacher; first to observe it before reserving its sacraments, so that through his life and teaching he might be recognized as the one to whom the Law and the Prophets bore witness.

Now then, since we have given some reasons why the Lord was born under the Law, let us discuss, as the Lord grants, the sacrament of circumcision which is at hand. The eighth day and circumcision accord in a single sacrament. In Scripture the eighth is customarily set for eternity. For just as the revolving course of the number seven signifies the mutability of temporal things, so eternity is fittingly signified by the eighth, which follows seven. [Col. 0572B]

Hence it may not unfittingly be inferred that, just as in the preceding span of seven days we represented Christ’s temporal Nativity, by which he came among men to endure the evils of this exile and to bestow his benefits on a sick world, so in the present eighth day we celebrate figuratively Christ’s Nativity by which, in the humanity he assumed, he passed from this world to the Father, by which his flesh was transformed from corruption to incorruption and from mortality to immortality. In his flesh death has already been swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. XV). As we already believe with certain faith that this was completed in him, so we do not doubt with certain hope that it will take place in our flesh. For the Apostle says: “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be of his resurrection” (Rom. VI).

But let us hear from him what that likeness of death is: “For we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (ibid.). This likeness of death is the complete abolition of sin, newness of life, and the observance of righteousness. This itself is the first resurrection in the soul, of which John says: “Blessed are those who have a part in the first resurrection; over them the second [Col. 0573A] death—that is, eternal death—will have no power” (Rev. XX).

This is likewise the true circumcision, by which we do not strip the skin of the flesh with stone knives, but, conformed to Christ, put off the old man—that is, the likeness of the old man—with his deeds. Elsewhere the Apostle says of it: “For circumcision is not that which is performed outwardly, that is, in the flesh; rather, the true circumcision is circumcision of the heart, not in the letter but in the Spirit” (Rom. II). That exterior circumcision, therefore, is a figure of this interior one, just as the same Apostle says of Abraham, already justified by faith, that “he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. IV).

It appropriately accords with our eighth day that circumcision of the flesh takes place in that part of the body through which human mortality is propagated. For true circumcision will be completed in our eighth day—that is, in the general resurrection—when this corruptible body shall put on incorruption and this mortal body immortality. And just as it was commanded to be performed carnally in this part of the flesh in order to signify that it must be performed spiritually, so it must be performed spiritually in the remaining limbs of the body, although it is not displayed bodily; so that, according to the Apostle, “we may not offer our members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but as instruments of righteousness to God” (Rom. VI). [Col. 0573B]

Let us therefore circumcise our ears from unlawful hearing, our eyes from unlawful sight, our nostrils from unlawful smell, 289 our mouth from unlawful taste, our heart from unlawful thought, our tongue from unlawful speech, our hands from unlawful touch, and our feet from unlawful walking; lest, according to the prophet, “Death enter into our souls through our windows” (Jer. IX). Thus the chief of the martyrs says to the Jews, who do not keep the senses of their body from what is unlawful: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts VII).

Therefore, whenever we observe this feast in its yearly recurrence, let us honor according to faith the deeds read concerning Christ, so that, applying the same things to justification and edification of character, we may retain firm faith, unfeigned charity, and certain hope until, when that which is partial has been done away, we deserve to attain the perfection promised to us. For if these remain unshaken, when the house of this dwelling is dissolved, we shall have [printed *habeamus*; variant: *habebimus*] a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. [Col. 0573C]

## SERMON X. On the Epiphany of the Lord

[Col. 0573D]

Our forefathers ordained this day of the Epiphanies to be held solemn for three reasons. Every faithful person knows these reasons who is accustomed to read or hear the Gospel history. A few things should be said concerning them: how they serve the honor of God and what they contribute to our edification.

The first reason occurred as today’s Gospel relates (Matt. II): when a new star arose, indicating the rising of the true light, the Magi were stirred up in eastern regions, came to Jerusalem, and inquired about the place of Christ’s birth. Then, led by the aforesaid star, which stood over the house where the child was, they found the child and [Col. 0574A] offered him mystical gifts: gold, incense, and myrrh.

First, it advances the edification of our faith that the arising of a new star announced that the rising of divine light had appeared on earth, lest the rational creature be able to excuse itself from recognizing him when it saw even the elements serving him. In this respect Judaea was less excusable: though it did not believe in him whose birth it had learned from the Scriptures, it saw the Magi—like the first fruits of the nations—moved by present signs to worship and honor him with mystical gifts.

These Magi were not necromancers, as some suppose, but philosophers among the nations, who had learned by practice to weigh the things signified from signs and to recognize related events from the circumstances of things. Hence, by fitting symbolism, they represented through gold, which is customarily given to kings as tribute, the royal power of the infant who was born; through incense, which is burned in sacrifice to God, the divine essence of that same infant; and through myrrh, by which dead bodies are embalmed, his mortal nature.

That these three things were in the person of Christ, the catholic mother—the Church—both believes and proclaims. She honors and worships him reigning in heaven, not with mystical gifts, but with gold, incense, and myrrh drawn forth from the treasury of her heart. [Col. 0574B] For we offer gold to God when, tested through patience, we do not fail in tribulations. Gold is extended when struck by hammers; likewise, when a devout soul is afflicted, it advances through patience to better things. Tribulation is its hammering; perseverance its extension. Thus the Apostle says: “Tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; and testing, hope” (Rom. V; Jas. I).

We also burn incense for him on the altar of the heart when, burning with inward love for him, we strive to please him through the practice of contrite and tearful prayer. We likewise draw myrrh from the chest of our heart when, for love of him, we tame the wantonness of the flesh by attending to vigils, prayer, fasting, and other honorable exercises. Thus the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My fingers distilled the first myrrh” (Song V). There is indeed a “first myrrh”: chastisement of the flesh undertaken with discretion, which does not pursue the praises of people but aims at the flourishing of souls. Paul’s hands distilled this myrrh when he said: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate” (1 Cor. IX). [Col. 0574C]

For the brevity of this sermon, these remarks on the first Epiphany of Christ, whether for edification in faith or in morals, are sufficient.

Another reason for this feast is that Jesus, having completed the thirtieth year of his age, came to John in the Jordan; when he was baptized by him, the heavens were opened, and by the Holy Spirit appearing in the form of a dove and the Father’s voice, he was declared the Son of God (Luke III). These events both confirm for our faith the truth of Christ’s birth and instruct the simplicity of those coming to faith concerning the desirability of baptism and the benefit of that baptism. For Christ’s life established the life of the Christian.

Therefore, when you believe that Christ, not only pure in himself but also the cleanser of the world’s sins, received the sacrament of baptism from a servant, how can any person, however pure or holy, excuse himself from receiving that same sacrament from a fellow servant? Regeneration is necessary for all whose generation has been preceded by defect. Since this was not the case in him of whom it is read, “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. XXIII), he received this sacrament solely in order to leave his descendants an example of righteousness to be fulfilled. [Col. 0575A]

But the fact that, when he descended into the waters, the heavens were opened above him and, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him, he was called the Son of God (Matt. III), greatly commends the sublimity of Christian grace. For in the waters of baptism the flaming sword which barred us from paradise is extinguished, the entrance to paradise is opened, and every baptized person, receiving the pledge of the Spirit, becomes through adoption a child of God.

The third reason for this feast is that the Lord, on the anniversary of his baptism, in the presence of his disciples, approved marital good by his presence and by the beginning of his signs. By changing water into wine at the wedding (John II), he commended to us a great mystery. First, by displaying the miracle, he made known his divinity to disciples still unformed. Mystically, the water changed into wine at the wedding signifies that, when God was united with human nature and the two became one flesh—Christ and the Church—then the Law, which had until then been observed carnally, came to be understood spiritually through the dispensation of Christ’s humanity. We too, transferred through this union of Christ and the Church from the foul and flavorless life of the old man, have been brought into the adoption of the children of God. [Col. 0575B]

More and lengthier things could certainly be said about these matters and proved by testimonies of Scripture; but lest hearers be burdened by the length of the sermon, these things are enough for now. For a moderate person receives food more beneficially the more eagerly he does so; and he becomes the more fastidious the more abundantly he is supplied. Therefore, beloved, from the recollection of the events above mentioned let us confirm our faith concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity. Let us conform our character and conduct to these solemnities which we celebrate in time, so that through the temporal feasts we observe we may deserve to attain eternal joys. [Col. 0575C]

## SERMON XI. On the Purification of Saint Mary

[Col. 0575D]

Ecclesiastical custom retains many representations drawn from events, by which it both presents the truth of what occurred and moves simple hearts to devotion, so that through the things they venerate outwardly they may be drawn to love of inward things. Thus, in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, we raise crosses in church; at the season of the Ascension, we elevate banners signifying Christ’s triumph in the more prominent place of the church, as if upon a triumphal arch; and we recall the miracles or martyrdoms of saints by pictorial representations.

From such a custom it has become established that, on today’s feast, faithful people proceed to church carrying lighted candles [Col. 0576A] and offer them, once blessed, to the priests during the solemnities of the Masses. For your brotherhood knows that, according to the Gospel history, the Lord Jesus was brought to the temple by his parents on the fortieth day after his birth—that is, today—and there received by holy Simeon and presented blessed in the temple (Luke II). The holy Church represents this on today’s feast.

For just as Saint Simeon received weakness in his hands but inwardly recognized majesty, illuminating the interior darkness of our unbelief, so each believer representing this sacrament carries wax in his hands, as if the fragile flesh, while seeing light borne above it, illuminating the outward darkness of this air (John IV). For just as Christ’s flesh proceeded from flesh most pure and full of the good fragrance of virtues, and violated his mother’s integrity neither in conception nor in coming forth, so the wax carried today in believers’ hands, gathered from pure and fragrant flowers, is the fruit of the bee, a creature that is, that is to say, virginal, whose sex—as it is said—is violated neither by males nor damaged by offspring. [Col. 0576B]

Therefore, when we carry it under this signification, let us carry Christ in our mouth, Christ in our heart, Christ in our hands, so that, dismissed in peace, we may deserve with holy Simeon to see the salvation of God. Do you wish to know how to carry Christ in your mouth? He says of himself: “I am the truth” (John XIV). Let truth therefore be in your mouth; let falsehood, idle talk, and foul talk be absent; and Christ will be in your mouth. Let charity be in your heart, and Christ will be there. For John says in his Epistle: “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John IV).

Let innocence be in your works, so that you take from no one anything belonging to that person. Let justice be present, so that you render to each what is his own, and you will have Christ in your hands. For he became for us from God both justification and righteousness (1 Cor. I). Bring him, therefore, with you to church; bring him back with you; and you will have Christ with you. Thus Saint Paul the Apostle exhorts: “You were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. VI). [Col. 0576C]

What is it to bear God? To represent God’s image; to imitate Christ. Innocence bears this image; justice bears it; truth bears it; chastity bears it; sobriety and every form of uprightness bear it. For as we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us also bear the image of the heavenly (1 Cor. XV). Therefore, laying aside the muddy affairs of the old man, let us cast off the works of darkness and exercise ourselves in works of light, so that, seeing our good works, they may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).

Let us adorn the house of our heart with these ornaments of virtues, so that we may be able to have God dwelling within it. For today the holy Church is admonished under the figure of the bride: “Adorn your bridal chamber, Zion, and receive Christ, the King of kings.” This admonition requires ornaments of character, not draped garments for walls, so that the Lord, the lover of the chaste mind, may rest in holy character as a bridegroom rests delightfully [Col. 0577A] in an adorned bridal chamber.

Thus in the Gospel also (Luke XII) we are commanded to gird our loins—that is, to restrain the loose impulses of the flesh—and to hold lamps in our hands—that is, to show our neighbors examples of light—so that we may be found ready to take part in the banquet of the heavenly bridegroom and rejoice with him without end. May Jesus Christ our Lord mercifully deign to grant this to us: he who deigned to be born in time for us, so that through him we might be reborn into eternity.

## SERMON XII. On Septuagesima
Knowing, most beloved, that as long as we are in the world we are away from the Lord (II Cor. V), we ought with daily tears to mourn the evils of this exile [Col. 0577B] and to pant with our whole desire for the eternal homeland. But because the Church, honored with many sacraments, cannot observe this daily in public assemblies, these seventy days, as a figure of the whole period of time, have been specially commended to us: during them, by the recitation of readings and chants, we recall the fall of the human race and, attending to the sorrows of our mortality, mourn each day.

Therefore, in the introit of today’s Mass, holy Church laments that death was brought upon her through the fall of the first parent; and, cast down amid the sorrows of this life into these lower regions, she cries that she grieves: “The groans of death surrounded me; the pains of hell surrounded me” (Ps. XVII). To signify this also, from this day until Easter we omit the word most customary in the Church, namely “Alleluia”; and in place of this Hebrew word we frequently use the Latin: “Praise to thee, O Lord, King of eternal glory.”

For just as earthly Jerusalem bears the image of the heavenly homeland, so this word—once commonly used in the praises of God in the aforesaid city—signifies the praises of the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, of whom it is sung in the psalm: “Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise thee” (Ps. LXXXIII). Therefore, while we praise God with a Latin word during our pilgrimage in Jerusalem, we signify the pilgrimage of our exile.

The meaning of these seventy days agrees with the meaning of the seventy years during which the citizens of this earthly Jerusalem [Col. 0577D] were led captive under the king of the Assyrians and held in servitude in Babylon. At that time they could not celebrate the praises of God according to their ancestral custom, but mourned the evils of their exile. Foreseeing prophetically that this would happen, the Psalmist sang of it as though it had already passed, saying: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Ps. CXXXVI).

For *Assur* is interpreted “exalted”; Babylon, “confusion”; Jerusalem, “vision of peace.” Therefore the king of the Assyrians, the king of the proud, is the same as the king of the Babylonians—that is, the devil, king of those who live without order. He oppresses under the harsh yoke of servitude the children of peace, the people who long for the heavenly vision; and, so far as he can, delays them from returning to and entering the heavenly city [Col. 0578A]. Of this servitude Scripture says: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of their return to the mother of all” (Ecclus. XL).

Therefore, held in this servitude, we sit, as it were, by the rivers of Babylon when we do not immerse our minds in the passing desires of this world; yet we weep, because we are wretched, and with constant longing sigh for the vision that is heavenly and eternal. Hence the Apostle says: “Every creature groans and labors in childbirth until now” (Rom. VIII). “And we ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan, awaiting the adoption as sons, the redemption of our body.” This creature is the soul, recreated from the corruption of sin in the image of God: groaning within itself because of the vanity to which [Col. 0578B] it is subject, it becomes anxious, like a woman in labor, through its excessive longing because it is delayed so long from its homeland.

Thus the Psalmist labored in childbirth when he said: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX). And the Apostle himself, who had received the Holy Spirit among the first members of the Church, longing to possess in reality the adoption as sons which he already possessed in hope, thus labored in childbirth when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I).

Thus, wearied by disgust at the evils of Babylon and stirred by longing for the heavenly city, we hang our instruments, as it were, upon willows: that is, before the oppressors of our age, rooted in the world’s desires—or rather, before those who despise divine grace—we refrain from proclaiming the joys of the heavenly kingdom, lest we seem to scatter pearls before swine [Col. 0578C] and give what is holy to dogs. Therefore the captives say to their captors: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI).

The foreign land is the multitude of the reprobate, who do not belong to the heavenly city. Like swine, they trample underfoot through neglect the pearls—that is, God’s luminous word—or, like dogs, argue wickedly against what is holy, God’s word, through erroneous belief.

Now that we have touched upon our captivity through its ancient and present meaning, let us briefly hear why the number seventy is set forth as a figure of the whole of time. For the entire time of this present life runs its course in a cycle of seven days, during which we are commanded to keep the commandments of the Decalogue. Therefore, while we observe the ten precepts of the law within this span of our life, we multiply, as it were, ten by seven and complete the sum of seventy.

During these days, then, let us devote ourselves more specially and earnestly to groaning and weeping in doing what must be done at all times, so that we may return by bitterness of heart and lamentations to our homeland, from which we fell through deadly delight. There we shall recover the “Alleluia” now omitted and shall praise God without end with the heavenly citizens. This we signify during the fifty days of the Lord’s resurrection, when we repeat “Alleluia” in every chant.

Meanwhile, then, let us mourn on the way, so that afterward we may rejoice in our homeland. Let whatever is sweet in worldly things become bitter to us in comparison with the sweetness [Col. 0579A] of God and the beauty of God’s house. Let each person understand that, the more he loves God above all things, the more he belongs to the heavenly homeland. Let us thus run the course of this present life with our gaze turned back, that we may be able to attain the prize of the heavenly calling.

At whatever hour we have been hired into the Lord’s vineyard, let us unfailingly bear the burden and heat of the day, that at evening we may not be deprived of the day’s denarius. For the Lord says: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. X and XXIV). Let us not be foolish travelers, so that, forgetting our homeland, we love exile instead of our homeland and remain upon the road. Let us not be insensible, so that we fail to grieve amid the sufferings of our passible and mortal condition, and fail to seek, in those very sufferings, the remedy of healing.

For people are ordinarily despaired of when, though sick, they do not perceive that they are ill. Let us therefore run to the physician of eternal salvation. Let us show him our wounds through confession; let each cry to him with inward cry: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled” (Ps. VI). Thus our physician will be merciful to our iniquities, will heal all our sickness, and will fill our desire with good things.

## SERMON XIII. On the Beginning of the Fast

Today Mother Church corrects with paternal severity her children, in whom she recognizes that she has suffered loss, so that she may gather them with maternal affection once they have been reformed by healing restraint. She invites the wounded to show [Col. 0579C] their wounds, lest, if not shown, they fester without treatment; she appoints for those who show them different kinds of correction, so that remedies suitable to their cure may be applied according to the extent of their wounds.

Hear, therefore, children, your mother, again laboring to give you birth and desiring again to restore the image of God, erased in you through sin. Hear her crying to you with an angelic voice: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. XXIII and XXIV). But how you ought to repent, the Lord warns you in the prophetic voice, saying: “Return to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; and rend your hearts, and not your garments” (Joel II).

Those turned away [perhaps: “those who have turned away”] are commanded to renounce all their iniquities and not suppose that their conversion can otherwise please God, since it cannot be that one part of your heart is cleansed for God while another, unclean, is reserved for the devil. How you ought to return is then added in the words, “in fasting and weeping and mourning”: externally you are to chastise the flesh by fasting, but inwardly to afflict the mind by groans and lamentations.

It is added, “And rend your hearts,” so that nothing may remain closed within which the compunction of heart does not expel and confession of the mouth does not disclose. This is what is sung in the psalm: “Pour out your hearts before him” (Ps. LXII); that is, vomit out through confession every impurity of your hearts, lest, like vessels containing foul liquid, you merely remove the lid and emit a stench [Col. 0580A] while retaining the impurity within.

For the person does not pour out his heart before God who opens his mouth in confession but does not remove evil desire from his heart. Hence the Lord complains of such persons: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX; Matt. XV). Likewise, the person does not pour out his heart before God who defends his fault in confession, who does not humble himself with the Psalmist saying: “I shall confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and thou hast forgiven the impiety of my sin” (Ps. XXXI). For one confesses against oneself when one accuses oneself and does not ascribe one’s sin to the seasons, fate, or stars.

Whatever you have committed, whether by hidden suggestion or another’s persuasion, let it be disclosed in confession in such a way that it is also driven from the heart, for all things are washed by such confession. Therefore let murders be far from your hands, so that hatreds may likewise be far from your hearts; for, according to apostolic teaching, whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and no murderer has a share in the kingdom of Christ and God (I John III).

Let him who committed fornication no longer commit fornication; let him who committed adultery no longer commit adultery. For, as the Apostle says, “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. XIII). Nor should any of us seek an opportunity to see a woman whom he desires; for according to Scripture, “Whoever looks upon a woman so as to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). Fornication, however, is the general name for every voluntary defilement of the flesh, contracted in whatever manner, except within lawful marriage.

“Let him who stole steal no more” (Eph. IV); let one who was a plunderer cease to be a plunderer, lest he incur the curse which says: “Woe to you who plunder, for you shall be plundered” (Isa. XXXIII). Let false testimony, shameful and jesting words, be removed from your mouths, for according to Scripture, “A false witness shall not go unpunished” (Prov. XIX). And for every idle word that people speak they shall render account on the day of judgment (Matt. XII).

Let envy be far from you, because “through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. II). Let covetousness not even be named among you; it is compared to the service of idols. For as, in the worship of idols, a creature is loved in place of the Creator, so the covetous person neglects God in order to retain or acquire the money he loves [Col. 0580D].

Let not the foot of pride come upon you, by which you withdraw from God; for there those who work iniquity have fallen: they were cast out and could not stand (Ps. XXXV). Do not sow discord among brothers; for just as the Lord has commanded blessing for brothers living in concord, so he threatens eternal curse to lovers of discord. Remove unnecessary oaths from your habitual speech, lest by swearing often you fall into perjuries and, to your condemnation, invoke Truth as witness to your falsehood.

Most beloved brothers, put away all these things together with every malice; and redeem the time you have hitherto spent in them by watching, praying, weeping [Col. 0581A], fasting, and generously giving alms, so that by these outlays you may be able to obtain the kingdom of God, which is promised to be near you. For this is why times of repentance have been granted you: that, considering God’s patience, which leads you to repentance, you may by no means store up wrath for yourselves on the day when the just judgment of God is revealed (Rom. II), when he will render to each according to his works (Matt. XVI).

Let each consider how wretched he is and how blessed he will be, and not fear in this time to suffer, for God’s love, whatever is lowly and hard, so that through this temporal purgatory he may attain an eternal remedy. “For,” as the Apostle says, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. III).

Therefore, you who, entangled in grave sins, have fled to the remedy of repentance, should not think it unfitting that Mother Church casts you from her bosom. For just as she ought to grieve over the loss she has suffered in you, so she ought to be appeased by your satisfaction, so that after satisfaction you may be reconciled, through her to whom God has given in your pastors the power of binding and loosing (Matt. XVI), to your head, and through him and with him may glory.

For just as a sick person patiently endures it when a physician burns or cuts away putrid flesh, so you should bear these sacraments of repentance with equanimity: that you are placed outside the Church in ashes and sackcloth, that you seem as though handed over to Satan. For this shame of separation brings about the destruction of the flesh for you, so that the spirit may be saved [Col. 0581C] on the day of your resurrection (I Cor. V).

## SERMON XIV. On Lent

Your brotherhood has heard from the apostolic preaching that whoever says that he remains in Christ ought also himself to walk as Christ walked (I John II). Let the Christian, therefore, learn how Christ walked, so that the Christian’s life may be shaped by Christ’s life. Let the newly baptized learn what Christ did after departing from baptism. Let the advanced hear what examples of light Christ showed his disciples from the beginning of his preaching. Let the perfect person attend to the fact that Christ was brought to completion through the bitterness of his Passion. For in his head each will find every stage by which he may be instructed, advanced, and brought to perfection.

Let the newly baptized learn, then, that Jesus, returning from the Jordan, was led by the Holy Spirit into the desert; there he fasted forty days and, after the fast, being hungry, permitted himself to be tempted (Luke IV). He went into the desert to show the newly baptized an example: they should not emerge into public immediately after their conversion, immediately seize the office of preaching, or again plunge themselves into the tumultuous affairs of this world; rather, fleeing as it were into the solitude of the mind, they should attend only to the correction of their own life and there await him who saves those who are fainthearted and troubled.

Thus the Lord suspended his disciples, still untrained and not yet tested in tribulation, from the duty of preaching, saying: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” [Col. 0582A] (Luke XXIV). And it is said through Moses: “You shall not plow with the firstborn of your ox” (Deut. XV); that is, you shall not preach at the beginning of good conduct.

He fasted in order to teach us to restrain the appetite of gluttony and to warn us to abstain from the enticements of temporal life. For just as he did not need baptism to cleanse original sin within himself, so he did not need fasting to restrain within himself the incentives of the flesh which he did not possess. He willed to be tempted, showing in himself that temptation will not be lacking to anyone who begins to live devoutly. But just as he repelled his tempter in every respect, so let us not go after our desires, but restrain ourselves from our own will.

Let the pleasure of the flesh not weaken the strength of our mind; let curiosity not delay us from a good purpose; let worldly ambition not turn us toward the left-hand side. For in every temptation in which Christ conquered, the Christian ought to conquer.

The mystical number forty also accords with this mystical fast, being formed by multiplying four by ten; by it we are to understand that we ought to fast not only from bodily foods but also abstain from every temporal pleasure. For we multiply four, as it were, by ten when we forcefully bend our frailty—contracted from the conjunction of the four elements or the changing character of the four seasons—to the laborious discipline of the Decalogue.

Therefore this Lenten observance is commended to us as a figure of the whole time [Col. 0582C], so that what we have performed less fully during the rest of the year owing to manifold occasions, we may now render without excuse: not only in sparingness of food, but also in uprooting vices and practicing virtues.

For fasting without almsgiving and other works of mercy is of as much value as a piece of unshrunk cloth sewn into an old garment, as the Lord testifies: “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth into an old garment, lest a greater tear be made” (Matt. IX; Mark II). For just as a new patch does not make the whole old garment new, but either makes a tear or disfigures its oldness merely by its newness, so abstinence from food alone does not make a person perfect, but makes the rest of that person’s ugliness more conspicuous.

Therefore let your fast be felt by the weakness of the sick, the hunger of beggars, and the weariness of travelers, so that what you withdraw from your own body you may supply to those in need. Be like diligent harvesters, so that in this season you may both repair the losses of the past year and prepare for the future that by which your soul may live.

Restrain the appetite of gluttony in such a way that you yourselves neither utter slanderous, buffoonish, idle, or malicious words nor willingly listen to those who utter them. During this time, by mutual consent let the wife withhold the marital due from her husband, and let the husband show honor to the womanly vessel, so that, according to the prince of the Apostles, your prayers may not be hindered (II Pet. III). For one ought not devote oneself to pleasure at the time when one desires through repentance to be cleansed from pleasures previously committed.

Although Christ, immediately after returning from the Jordan, as has already been said, consecrated this fast by his example, nevertheless the times near the Paschal feast have been assigned to this observance, so that the Christian people might endeavor, according to their ability, to imitate their head also in this fast, and so that, purified by this fast, we might receive the holy days. It was very fitting that the joy of the Lord’s resurrection should follow the time of affliction, so that after enduring the tribulations and overcoming the temptations of the present life, we too may hope to receive the joys of our resurrection, when we shall be delivered from the bondage of this corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God (Rom. VIII).

For just as by genuflections and the affliction of this time we signify that we are weighed down by the burden of sins and bent beneath harsh servitude, so by the ending of the fast during the fifty days after the Resurrection, and by the fact that we pray standing, we prefigure, as far as we can, the liberty of our incorruption.

Therefore, brothers, let us meanwhile hold this image in such a way that we now possess its reality in hope and may finally receive it in actuality. For these things are fitting for pilgrims on the way; but those things will be rendered in the homeland to those whose military service has been completed and who have received their discharge.

## SERMON XV. On the Annunciation of Blessed Mary

Let us rejoice in the Lord, most beloved, and, though not such great thanks as we ought, yet such as we can, by his gift, let us return thanks to our Creator, lest we be found ungrateful for his grace [Col. 0583C], which abounds in us.

For today’s feast sets before us the new conception of the Virgin, celebrated as the beginning of our restoration, and offers a sure proof of divine mercy and power. For if the Lord of all things, seeking his fugitive servants, were coming to exercise judgment rather than show mercy, he would by no means put on the frailty of this clay vessel, by which he might suffer with us and suffer for us.

And although this very thing seems foolish and weak, according to Paul’s saying (I Cor. I), to the Gentiles, who rely on the reasoning of empty philosophy and judge the Creator according to the laws of the creature, yet what is more powerful than to grant conception to a Virgin contrary to the laws of nature, and through the death of assumed flesh to restore mortal substance to the glory of immortality? Hence the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (ibid.).

Indeed, we judge wise those physicians of bodily illnesses who know, according to the kind of diseases, how to apply like things to like. How much wiser is this physician, who came, preserving the proper proportion of medicine, to free the human race from every bondage of this corruption, not only in body but also in soul? For he came in the likeness of sinful flesh, that he might be tempted in every respect according to likeness, yet without sin, in order that in that wherein he was tempted and conquered, he might minister from heaven the grace of victory to those who are tempted.

He also opposed his newness to our oldness, his justice to our injustice, his obedience [Col. 0584A] to our disobedience, and his humility to our pride, so that we who had fallen from the flower-bearing seat of the blessed through pride and disobedience might, re-formed through his humility and obedience, at some time return to the joys of paradise. And this is what the Apostle says: “What is foolish in God is wiser than men.”

For it seemed foolish to the wise of this age that he who was in the form of God should will to be humbled in the form of a servant; that the Lord should be rejected by servants, spat upon, struck, and killed. But this foolishness has become for us a great and incomprehensible wisdom from God, because it has been the healing medicine that restores lost life.

Divine power could indeed have come to the aid of human falls in another way. But, like a good orator, by these means he wished both to win the goodwill of his hearers toward himself and to demonstrate his favor among them; that favor would have appeared less clearly if, remaining wholly invisible, he had refused to be seen by all and to live among human beings.

Let us ask ourselves, most beloved, whether, if we had been deprived of an eternal inheritance and placed in a most dark prison, a king or some person of corresponding rank, laying aside royal splendor, so condescended to us as to endure the miseries of our captivity as though one of us, in order that, when an opportunity was found, he might free us from that captivity: by what means could he better make his love toward us known and stir up ours toward him? Hence Truth itself says: “No one has greater love than this: that one lays down his life for his friends” (John XV).

Therefore, for a similar reason our Lord, our physician, our liberator, came down to his servants, his captives, humble and exalted: humble in suffering with them, exalted in powerfully freeing them from the slavery of the devil [Col. 0584C]. Therefore all of us who have been called in Christ should consider with the entire gaze of our minds, love with the entire affection of our minds, and honor with due service the wondrous beginnings of this liberation, so joyous and so necessary, recalled to us on the present feast; so that we may deserve to await wondrous and joyous endings from beginnings that are joyous and wondrous.

Today the womb of the Virgin becomes the gate of heaven, through which God descends to human beings in order to grant them ascent to heaven. For the most blessed Virgin hears and marvels that she will bear a son, although she knew herself to be wholly unacquainted with a man’s embrace; but she is strengthened and instructed by the angel as to by what power and merit that might be fulfilled in her which nature does not permit to occur in other women: “Do not fear,” he says, “Mary; you have found grace with the Lord” (Luke I)—as though he said: What I announce to you has no claim upon nature, but is the gift of incomparable grace.

Then follows: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (ibid.). For, as some foolish and erring persons imagine, the Holy Spirit did not take the place of seed in her; rather, such great power of divine love was granted to her that it kept her inviolate in mind and body, so that no heat of fleshly desire [Col. 0585A] could prevail over her. She alone deserved to be chosen, from whose immaculate body he might fit to himself an immaculate body—he who before the ages was predestined Son of God in power.

Therefore it is said to that most blessed Virgin: “For that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (ibid.). Certainly that which was to be offered for the sanctification of sinners had to be holy. It was fitting also that his generation should be free from defect, through whom the defective generation of Eve’s children was to be cleansed.

For Eve brought three evils upon her followers: that they should be subject to men; that they should conceive in the offense of fleshly desire; and that they should bear children in pain (Gen. III). But in this conception no pleasure of fleshly desire was mingled, when the Virgin conceived the Word through hearing, the Word acting outwardly as bridegroom; and, with the Holy Spirit making her fruitful, the divine sublimity joined itself in unity of person to our humility in the bridal chamber of that same Virgin’s heart.

With this splendor the Son of God is conceived; with this purity he is born. No sorrow could occur for her in conceiving, no difficulty in bearing; for he who had come to make a sorrowful world glad ought not to make the lodging of the womb sorrowful. Therefore, just as this conception lacked every corruption, so, whatever heretics may chatter, the Virgin’s womb remained uninjured in conceiving and in bearing.

Christian gentleness can certainly know this and reasonably demonstrate it to others by drawing an inference from lesser matters to greater, from earlier things to later [Col. 0585C]. For if a ray of the sun penetrates crystal without piercing it as it enters or shattering it as it exits, how much more does the virginal womb remain closed and whole at the entry and exit of the true and eternal Sun?

Thus the burning bush that was not consumed is read to have been shown to holy Moses as a type of inviolate virginity (Exod. III). Thus Aaron’s rod, the rod of the high priest, foreshadowing the same thing, though neither animated by sap nor made fruitful by seed, produced flowers and fruit which nature had not given it (Num. VIII). What reason, then, is there for disbelieving that God can make a human being from a woman without a man, when he made the first human being neither from a man nor from a woman? (Gen. I.)

The conception and human birth plainly testify to true humanity, while the inviolate womb proves true divinity. There is contained in this conception, most beloved brothers, a great and marvelous sacrament: the bond-document of transgression being canceled, divine and human things are joined in covenant, and the two become one flesh—namely, Christ and the Church.

The virginal womb became, as it were, the bridal chamber of this union. From it, after nine months had passed in accordance with the law of women giving birth, he came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber with his wife—that is, with our flesh—and “set his tabernacle,” that is, the assumed flesh, “in the sun” (Ps. XVIII), because he exhibited to all his flesh, through which he was to overcome the enemy.

Thus, through condescension to our humanity, he became like milk for little children, who in the sublimity of his divinity is the bread of angels. For through the flesh we have drawn in majesty. Thus loving mothers administer through their breasts solid food made milk within themselves to meet the need of infants; and through the breasts it comes about in them that the infants no longer need breasts, when, strengthened by the nourishment of milk, they become capable of chewing the solid food of bread [Col. 0586A].

So too our restorer and nourisher willed to feed, with the milk of his incarnation, those far removed from him in the region of unlikeness, so that he might make us grow into the most sweet and ineffable taste of his divinity. Yet, as long as we walk by hope and not by sight (II Cor. V), this is not fully granted to anyone, however pure in heart; its perfect satisfaction is reserved for the eternal recompense of the righteous, when the glory of the Lord shall be revealed. For it is impossible for a traveler to possess during pilgrimage what is promised to him upon arrival.

Let us therefore, most beloved brothers, weigh these things by diligent meditation; let us taste this inestimable sweetness of God with the entire eagerness of our minds, considering what and how great are the things promised in heaven, lest those things which seem desirable to blind and covetous minds on earth call us back from the prize of the heavenly calling.

Let us love the mercy through which we were redeemed when we had been lost. Let us preserve chastity, whose lover he showed himself to be when from the womb of a chaste woman he fitted an immaculate body to himself. Let us be conformed to him who set before us his life on earth as the rule of Christian conduct; who at his first coming willed inwardly to reform us into his own image, and at his second coming will also refashion the body of our humiliation [Col. 0586C] to be conformed to the body of his glory: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. On Palm Branches
Whoever wishes to see a human being made perfect will find in Christ every lesson in virtue. Among these, he girded himself with humility and patience as with more powerful weapons: with these he entered the world, with these he departed from the world, and through these he subdued the world. By them, indeed, he overthrew the devil and freed us from his power. With them he bound the strong man armed, and he, being stronger, snatched away the vessels which that man possessed in power and peace, and, once cleansed, kept them for himself (Matt. 12).

It was humility that, living among human beings, he ate with tax collectors and sinners (John 4); that, weary from the journey, he asked the Samaritan woman for a drink (Matt. 9); that he did not refuse the touch of the sinful woman (Luke 8); that he washed his disciples’ feet (John 13). It was humility and patience together that he gave his body to those striking him; that he did not turn his face from those spitting upon him; that he did not curse those who cursed him; and that at last he bowed himself even to an ignominious death—namely, death on a cross, which was due only to criminals (John 19). Hence it is said through the prophet: “And he was reckoned with criminals” (Isa. 53). And in the Psalm: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16).

These weapons [Col. 0587A] that ancient serpent did not recognize. He scorned these weapons through pride, and, unwary, was overcome by them. He sensed the bait and bit it, but the hook of divinity caught him fast, pierced his jaw, and bound him away from his customary power. At his Father’s voice, the lion’s cub lay down, to rise again in strength and, because of his humility, to receive the name above every name (Phil. 2).

The proud superstition of the Scribes and Pharisees did not believe this manner of exaltation. It despised the Lord as he came to it in humility; it blasphemed him as though he cast out demons and worked miracles by Beelzebub, although he rebuked their pride (Matt. 12). The crowd of the poor alone follows him; the innocence of children accompanies him, because innocence embraces innocence, humility humility, and thus deserves illumination, so as inwardly to recognize majesty. For Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4; 1 Pet. 5).

Such persons meet the Lord today as he comes to the place of his Passion. They saw a humble man seated upon an ass, yet rendered him triumphal glory by carrying branches of trees and spreading them along the way; they sang him imperial praises (Matt. 21), because by a prophetic spirit they recognized him as conqueror of the devil and death, and giver of life.

Dearest brothers, you represent the image of this crowd when you carry in your hands green branches of trees behind the banner of the holy cross. [Col. 0587C] And you represent it well if that which greenness signifies in your hands is always maintained in your conduct; if it does not fall in winter or wither in summer, so that you may say with the Psalmist: “I will bless the Lord at every time; his praise is always in my mouth” (Ps. 33).

But remember that only children are invited to these praises: “Praise the Lord, children,” says the Psalmist (Ps. 119). The Apostle explains who these children are: “Be little children in malice, but perfect in understanding” (1 Cor. 14). And the Lord says to his disciples: “Unless anyone humbles himself like this little child, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (Matt. 18). He calls himself the little child whose imitation he urges us to adopt in humility, that we may deserve to enter the kingdom of God. For those are not members which do not follow the head.

Therefore, by the weapons with which Christ conquered the devil, the Christian too must conquer. As Christ was exalted through humility, so the Christian must be exalted. For the Lord says: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18); and Peter says: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation” (1 Pet. 5). Christ humbled himself for us; let us humble ourselves for our own sake. He bent down like a camel, took upon himself the burdens of our sins, and passed through the eye of the needle, because he passed through the straits of his Passion in order to lead us out into the breadth of joys.

Let us too humble ourselves to bear the burdens of our neighbors. Let none of us think lofty thoughts or hope in the uncertainty of riches; rather, having cast off the craving for pride as though it were a goiter, let him enter through the eye of the needle—therefore let him undertake the narrow and arduous way. For the reason why, on these days, the Passion of the Lord is read in the Church and the signs of the Lord’s Passion are displayed in the Church is that the Lord’s Passion may thereby be recalled to memory and the devotion of the faithful stirred to suffer with him, so that the blood may worthily be received by the mouths of the faithful which was unworthily shed by the hands of unbelievers.

Let both doorposts be marked with this blood of the spotless Lamb—that is, minds and foreheads—so that belief may be in the heart unto righteousness, but confession made by the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10); and let the remembrance of the cross adhere sweetly to the mind, while its sign is impressed upon the forehead. Therefore, brothers, let us worthily suffer with Christ in this commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, so that we may deserve to be raised with Christ rising again. [Col. 0588B] Let us forgive our debtors their debts, because Christ himself, set before us for imitation, prayed for his persecutors when he suffered. For the Lord himself commands: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Luke 6).—“But if children, then heirs: indeed heirs of God, and co-heirs of Jesus Christ” (Rom. 8).

## SERMON XVII. On the Lord’s Supper

The longed-for day of release has come to us, most beloved: Mother Church receives back into the fellowship of her members those members whom she had hitherto cast away as though putrid. She admits her sinning children—corrected by the laws of penitence and disciplined by the shame of exclusion—to the sacrament of reconciliation. And this day is rightly assigned to this sacrament, because on it our Lord Jesus Christ gave his disciples for eating the body which he was shortly to hand over for us, and gave them to drink the blood which he was to pour out for us.

Therefore, on this day no faithful person ought to remain estranged from Christ’s body, which is the Church, on the day when the Church receives the medicine of its reconciliation: namely, the body and blood of Christ. Today the rite of the old priesthood—by which the blood of calves was poured out and the ashes of a heifer burned outside the camp were sprinkled (Num. 19) for the cleansing of the flesh alone—has been removed. In its place has been established the rite of the new priesthood, by which the flesh of Christ suffered outside the gate and Christ’s blood was poured out for us, sanctifying those cleansed in flesh and spirit. [Col. 0588D]

For the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation” (2 Cor. 5). On what day, then, ought ministers of the new priesthood more fittingly to celebrate this sacrament of reconciliation than on the day when it was first instituted by the author of the new priesthood?

The washing of the disciples’ feet today also accords with this sacrament of reconciliation, as does his command that his disciples preserve this practice. It was not because they needed washing, as he himself says (John 13), for they had been washed in saving water; rather, it was because human affections—by which, as by feet, one approaches God or withdraws from God—cannot avoid being defiled by earthly dust. They must move amid the whirlwinds of the world, among and dwelling with people who have unclean lips, and amid the muddy affairs of the world.

This washing of feet, therefore, is the cleansing of the affections: if we have drawn inward any foul images from earthly intercourse, we wash them away by this sacrament. And it fittingly accords with this sacrament of reconciliation that the head—that is, Christ—washes the feet of the body: that is, through the ministry of pastors he reconciles to himself his lowest members. For we who are called pastors, and are as it were members nearer to the head, when we pray for your sins and shed tears for your transgressions, what else do we do than wash for you the feet by which you may return to God? [Col. 0589B]

And when, terrified by the recollection of our [your] sins, we shed tears from the head in our prayer, do we not cleanse our consciences, like unclean feet, from the filth of earthly contact? Therefore, brothers, since on this day we admit you to so desirable a sacrament of reconciliation, labor under God’s mercy, so far as lies in you, that what is ministered to you outwardly through our office may be fulfilled in your minds in actual reality.

Do not be that house swept clean with brooms—that is, covered over with the sacraments of penitence—to which the unclean spirit returns, after having gone out from it through confession. Finding it empty, that is, devoted to no true virtue, he enters it with seven other spirits more wicked than himself, that is, with every kind of superstition; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first (Matt. 12). For their last state becomes worse than the first because they secretly commit the sins which they renounced in confession, and strive to cover them over with various colors of superstition.

The Lord compares hypocrites of this kind to whitewashed tombs and to vessels cleansed outside, which within are full of stench and filth (Matt. 23). Therefore cleanse your consciences, brothers, so that you may be honorable vessels fit to receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ: through whom you were redeemed when you were lost; through whom you are reconciled when you had again turned away; through whom you will be saved if you are found within the fellowship of Christ’s members, to whom you have been reconciled.

For whoever eats unworthily is guilty of the Lord’s death (1 Cor. 11). Who is it that eats unworthily? The one who receives with the mouth but does not receive with the heart; the one who is not a member of the head nor a part of Christ’s body. Such a person, receiving the Lord’s body, will pay the penalties of the Lord’s death, because he will be punished with the punishment inflicted upon those who unworthily handed the Lord’s body over to death. Remain therefore in Christ, that Christ may remain in you, and that you may worthily approach participation in the Lord’s body and blood.

## SERMON XVIII. On the Day of Easter

Whereas the other feasts affect the minds of the faithful with spiritual joy in remembrance of events accomplished, at Christ’s resurrection both hearts and bodies alike rejoice, for when Christ rose our inward person was raised with him from the death of sin, and our outward person has had the hope of its resurrection confirmed by the most convincing proof. Rightly, therefore, both rejoice: for both are raised with Christ, the inward person in reality, but the outward in hope.

For this reason this solemnity does not return to its anniversary day as the other solemnities do, in which there is only remembrance of past events. Rather, it is assigned to the Lord’s Day and to the course of the moon after the full moon nearest the vernal equinox. The Lord’s Day, which is the eighth day, fittingly represents the Lord’s resurrection, which occurred on that day, and prefigures ours, which will occur after the sevenfold cycle of this time. [Col. 0590B]

The moon’s course is assigned to this observance because of a definite mystery. According to the investigation of astronomers, the globe of the moon is always half illuminated and half unilluminated. When the moon is waxing, its lower part is illuminated; when it is waning, its upper part is illuminated. In Holy Scripture the moon bears the type of the Church, which endures the failing of its mortality by the necessity of its origin, yet in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation illumines, according to the measure of its understanding, the night of human ignorance.

To this Church, renewed and raised with Christ, the Apostle says: “Seek the things above; set your minds on the things above, not on things upon the earth” (Col. 3). This is impressed upon us by the Paschal mystery; this is commended by the figure of the Paschal moon, waning below and waxing above: from the time of our renewal, our love should always diminish in the desire for earthly things and increase by daily progress in longing for heavenly things.

Then we celebrate the true Passover if we always preserve in life and conduct what we signify through the mysteries of things and times. For this reason we celebrate holy Easter for seven days in white garments, that we may be reminded always to retain purity of body and the joy of resurrection. Hence Wisdom says: “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil never be lacking from your head” (Eccl. 9). That is to say: let purity never be absent from the body, nor spiritual joy from the heart. [Col. 0590D]

The same thing was signified when the Jewish people, after eating the lamb, ate unleavened bread for seven days (Exod. 23). The Apostle interprets the thing signified as follows: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). It is as though he said: In order that you may be fit to celebrate the true Passover and eat the flesh of the true and spotless Lamb, purge out the old leaven—that is, remove the old sin—so that you may be a new lump, that is, recover the newness of the new life which you received in the holy washing.

For when a people coming to faith is catechized, it is, as it were, ground: for as the diversity of grains is forced through the mill into unity, so the diversity of peoples is united through instruction in faith into a certain unanimity. But it is not yet dough. Water is added, and bread is made. Thus the Apostle says elsewhere: “One bread, we are one body in Christ, all of us who eat his bread and drink his cup” (1 Cor. 10).—“Therefore let us feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5).
