It is as though he said: Because the Lamb whom we feast upon is true, let us approach the eating of his flesh in such a way as to preserve a heart clean from malice and a tongue free from deceit. Thus we shall pass, as pleasant bread, into Christ’s body and incorporate Christ into ourselves, so that we may always have Christ abiding in us; and thus we may celebrate the true Passover not merely for seven days, but at every time: that is, that we may pass with all longing from the depths to the highest joys of heaven.

## SERMON XIX. On the Ascension of the Lord

Today, brothers, Christ’s victory is completed; today his triumphal banners are raised. Hell, together with its prince, grieves at its spoliation; the heavenly host rejoices at the restoration of its loss. Today that flesh which was lifted up from the earth has been placed at the Father’s right hand, because it has been set above every creature, and every principality and power has bowed before it.

Today the new way of which the Apostle speaks (Heb. 10) has been inaugurated for us, because through Christ’s flesh the entrance of heaven—through which no flesh had previously passed—has been opened. The same Apostle calls it still living (ibid.), because it has been prepared for Christ’s members, who in their own time are to enter by that same way. Today the opening of the book has been completed, which no one could open except the Lamb who was slain (Rev. 5), because its mysteries have been revealed, when, with the dispensation of his humanity accomplished, those things found in the Law and Prophets concerning Christ were fulfilled today.

Christ first descended, that he might share in our nature; at last he ascended, that he might make us sharers in his glory. Descending, he nursed infants, as it were, through temporal intercourse and visible miracles; ascending, he gave gifts to human beings. Taught by these gifts and brought up, as it were, to manly strength, they would no longer desire his temporal vision, but would strive with all longing to follow where he had gone before them. [Col. 0591D]

Therefore, since we have been deprived of his temporal presence, let us hasten with whole-hearted intent toward his eternal vision. Let us say to him in the Psalmist’s voice: “My heart has said to you: I have sought your face; Lord, I will seek it; do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. 26). For the entire dispensation of Christ’s humanity intended and accomplished nothing else but to direct our attention upward and, when the time of our mortality has been fulfilled, to bring us to the manifest vision of himself; and, once brought there, to satisfy us with the eternal glory of his countenance. For, as the Apostle testifies, “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16).

These are the good things of Jerusalem [Col. 0592A] which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2). The Psalmist beheld these good things in an enigma, so far as he could, when he said: “For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. 72). He spoke in wonder: “What have I in heaven?” because he was unable either to explain in speech or to comprehend in thought the greatness of heavenly glory.

Let us hunger and thirst for these things, because for this purpose the high priest ascended as our forerunner into the true Holy of Holies—for us, that is, to the Father’s right hand—that he might confirm the hope of his members: namely, that the humility of the flock would follow where it believes its shepherd has gone before. For the Lord himself promises his disciples: “Where the body is, there the eagles also shall be gathered” (Luke 17; Matt. 24). He calls the saints eagles, who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 3).

For eagles are said by nature to detect carrion beyond the sea by their sense of smell and to hasten there in swift flight to satisfy their hunger. This hunger of the eagles therefore signifies the longing of holy souls, which, sensing with the nostrils of faith that their head is placed outside the world’s whirlwinds in highest repose, would wish by the flight of hope to stand in the Creator’s presence and rejoice without end in the satisfaction of his countenance.

This, indeed, is the meaning of this solemnity: that we should believe Christ now reigns at the Father’s right hand and meanwhile follow him, as it were, with the twin wings of virtues—namely, charity and hope—so that, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, we may reign with him without end. Therefore, as the Psalmist exhorts, “Because the Lord has reigned, let the earth rejoice” (Ps. 96)—that is, let the Church rejoice in faith, because “you, Lord, are most high over all the earth; you are exceedingly exalted above all gods” (ibid.); let it rejoice in hope, because “we shall be filled with the good things of your house” (Ps. 64).

Let us cry out from the marrow of our hearts with the Apostle: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or the sword?” (Rom. 8). For when he has brought us from hope to sight, God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15): he himself will be food and drink, clothing and everything which can be honorably conceived and desired by all. Let Christ’s soldiers desire this reward, and let them not abandon their military service until, their contest completed, they receive from their emperor the unfading inheritance.

## SERMON XX. On the Holy Day of Pentecost

The day of Pentecost is hallowed in the Law and in the Gospel. In the Law, because on the fiftieth day from the day when Egypt was despoiled, the Law, written upon stone tablets by the finger of God, was given to God’s people on Mount Sinai (Exod. 19). In the Gospel, because on the fiftieth day from the day when hell was despoiled, the law of charity was written by the Spirit of God on tablets of fleshly hearts for the Nazarene people (Acts 2). Hence the Apostle says: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

But that law was given into slavery, whereas this one was given into freedom. Of that law the Apostle says: “One covenant indeed, which is from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery” (Gal. 4). But of this one: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3). And elsewhere: “For you have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear, but the Spirit of adoption as children, in whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom. 8).

Under this signification the ancient people of the Hebrews, in the fiftieth year, which was called the jubilee, abstained from every servile work and customarily granted freedom to those who had served under the yoke of slavery in the preceding years. For seven multiplied seven times makes forty-nine; and, that there may be fifty, unity is added to the forty-nine. Because the revolving course of times does not depart from the number seven, eternity, which succeeds time, is signified in the unity that follows, in which true freedom will be given. [Col. 0593B]

We fittingly received the Holy Spirit, therefore, on the fiftieth day: for as, after the course of this age, we are to be freed from the bondage of this corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, so on this day we received the Holy Spirit himself as the pledge of eternal inheritance and true freedom (Rom. 8). This is also why the same Holy Spirit was sent on the tenth day after the Lord’s Ascension: for a denarius is promised as a wage to laborers who persevere in working in the Lord’s vineyard.

Therefore, because it is rash to define anything concerning his ineffable essence, let us say some things which the Spirit himself has given concerning his wondrous and lovable operation. The Holy Spirit is the distributor of graces; he is the discerner of the heart’s thoughts and intentions; he is the revealer of divine secrets. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God; and as no one knows what is in a human being except the human spirit which is within that person, so no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2).

To those who ask for worthy things, he gives a devout disposition for prayer and grants them swift effect in obtaining their requests from him who regards devout vows. He inspires penitence in sinners; he retains the sins of the unrepentant; he wipes away the sins of the penitent. Thus the Lord says to his disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 10).

He makes those converted to the path of righteousness humble through fear, gentle through piety, mourning through knowledge, strong through the love of righteousness, merciful through counsel, pure in heart through understanding, contemplative through wisdom, and patient in enduring persecutions. To such persons the Lord promises the kingdom of heaven, because those whom fear begins, wisdom completes in the seventh degree, and patience frees and crowns in the eighth, as in the true jubilee.

On this day the Holy Spirit advanced the prince of the Apostles to this summit of perfection, so that he who had trembled at the voice of a single maidservant during the Lord’s Passion (Matt. 16) might no longer fear openly to refute the faithless multitude of the Jews with prophetic testimony (Acts 2). He made Thomas such a man that he who, in doubt, had asked to touch the scars of the risen Savior (John 20), after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been bestowed, might be sent confidently to preach the Gospel to the nations when the Apostles had divided their fields of mission.

By the same grace Christ’s disciples were made such persons that they who, having abandoned the Lord at the time of his Passion, had hidden through fear (Mark 14), thereafter went rejoicing from the presence of the council because they were judged worthy to suffer insult for Jesus’ name (Acts 5). Today the Holy Spirit showed himself so swift and effective a teacher that in a single moment he instructed the hearts of unlearned people in knowledge and formed their tongues for eloquence in every language (Acts 2).

That we may also consider how great an artisan this Holy Spirit is, let us hear the Apostle saying: “To each is given the manifest grace of the Spirit for usefulness: to one indeed, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another the grace of languages; to another interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). [Col. 0594B]

This Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of Father and Son, proceeds from the Father and from the Son, and is sent alike to believers’ hearts by the Father and by the Son. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “When the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father, he will teach you all truth. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 15).

Didymus, renowned by the title of “illustrious man,” interprets these words thus: “The Spirit is inseparable from the will of myself and the Father”; and further: “Because he is not from himself, but from the Father and from me. For the very fact that he subsists and speaks is from the Father and from me.” What, then, is it for the Holy Spirit to subsist from the Father and the Son, except for that same Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son? Hence he says in what follows: “The Holy Spirit is the expression of agreement, who is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom. You cannot hear the Son speaking things he does not know, since he himself is what is uttered by the Son: that is, God proceeding from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding from Truth, the Comforter flowing from the Comforter.”

We have produced these statements, on the authority of a Greek author, against the heresy of certain Greeks who say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, lest any Latin suppose that all Greeks are made foolish by this error and, relying on their authority, deserve to become salt that has lost its savor.

The same point is plainly affirmed in the creed of the Council of Ephesus, which is known to have been Greek, in these words: “Although in his substance he is the Spirit of the Son, and in person is understood as a property, insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, he is nevertheless not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is truth (John 14). Hence he proceeds from him likewise as from God the Father.”

Finally, this same Spirit glorified the Lord Jesus Christ, after he ascended into heaven, by performing glorious miracles through the hands of the holy Apostles. Moreover, just as the Son was called the hand of God the Father—not because there is any inequality between him and the Father’s majesty, but because of identity of substance and the manifest display of works—so the Holy Spirit was called the finger of God because of the unity of substance which he has with the Father and the Son, and because of the manifest distribution of charisms. For operation is customarily effected through the hand, which exists in the unity of the body; and distinction is customarily indicated through the finger, which remains in the unity of the hand while nevertheless distinguished by its own joints. [Col. 0595A]

But when any person in the Godhead is named by words transferred from elsewhere, the whole nature of the things from which those words have been transferred must not be ascribed to the Godhead. Rather, attention must be given only to those causes for which bodily things can be compared with incorporeal things. For every human word can speak of nothing but bodily things, while the Trinity, of which we are now speaking, surpasses all material substances. Therefore no word can be properly fitted to it, or properly and worthily express its substance.

And because the Spirit himself is the distributor of charisms, let us invoke that Paraclete whose solemnity we celebrate today, whose gifts bestowed on the faithful we marvel at today, that he may increase faith in us, enlarge charity, strengthen hope, and bestow the other charisms of virtues necessary to us in this pilgrimage, with the Father and the Son working together; with them the same Paraclete lives and reigns through eternal ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. On the Chair of St Peter

[Col. 0595C]

Not unfittingly, brethren, this verse of the Psalm, once sung forth by divine foreknowledge, is introduced into the rejoicing of today’s celebration, on which the blessed man is established in the episcopal chair. For it seems fittingly applicable to blessed Peter, whom the Church’s observances of this day proclaim exalted in the judicial seat. For holy David, also inspired beforehand by the Holy Spirit, says: “Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders” (Ps. 106). For today Peter is exalted in the assembly of the people, 299 and praised in the seat of the elders, since in the Church where the people of God’s possession gather he is appointed chief after God, [Col. 0595D] and in the chair of the elders he is praised as bishop. This, indeed, is the sacred ordinance of today’s feast, when he was honoured with the office of an episcopal see.

Today, brethren, blessed Peter is ordained bishop of the Church of Antioch; today he is set over as shepherd of the people whom he himself acquired for God. Today also, in the ordination of blessed Peter, holy Church has been exalted, because he himself is promoted to whom it was specially entrusted by the Lord in these words: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16). Blessed declaration of the name: that Peter should be named from the Rock concerning which it is written, “And the Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), and should be adorned by participation in Christ’s name—Christ himself imposing the name upon him, that he should be and be called Peter.

[Col. 0596A] Upon this rock also the Lord ordained that his Church should be built, so that he whose confession of faith, because of its firmness, was to be compared with a rock, might also answer to the designation of his own name. Peter therefore does not today obtain the episcopal chair through human ambition, as often happens in such matters; he does not occupy the foremost places by gifts, nor thrust himself upon splendid cushions. Peter is instructed by God himself, the Son of God testifying; teaching derived from flesh and blood is removed from him; the most effectual revelation of the Father who is in heaven is granted him. At that truthful prompting Peter thundered forth: “You are,” he says, “the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16).

O delightful converse of king and soldier, in which the soldier confesses his king to be the Son of the eternal King; while the King, in reciprocal return, [Col. 0596B] declares that his soldier, set apart from fleshly instruction, is the disciple of his Father alone, and judges him worthy of suitable rewards, adding these words: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). O truly blessed gatekeeper of heaven, to whom not only the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted, but also the counsels of heavenly mysteries were confided! He exercises by authoritative privilege the power of binding and loosing, and the care of the Lord’s sheepfold is committed to his discretion. For the Lord says to him in special familiarity: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (ibid.).

[Col. 0596C] Therefore Peter was assigned to the watches of the Churches, not by the sudden applause of supporters but by God’s provident dispensation and universal decree; and today he is assumed at Antioch in a particular intimacy. Him whom God had set over his sheep as universal shepherd, the people of Antioch today establish for themselves as universal bishop. Yet the Antiochene people do not strive to oppose God’s will, but with timely insistence endeavour to honour God’s vicar. Peter had long since been ordained by the Bishop of bishops; he had received the task of pouring out, by the effusion [reading perhaps *derivationem*, “outpouring”] of the Holy Spirit, the oil of Christ’s gladness; he had long exercised the ministry entrusted to him, yet had not until then been assigned particularly to any one place.

Today, therefore, he is selected from the breadth of the whole world, to preside over and benefit those who are properly his; today he is allotted to a people. Yet the extent of his care is not thereby diminished; rather, the solicitude of his apostleship is enlarged twofold. For there are the bleatings of the sheep now present, to occupy him with their daily advancement; nor are there lacking to him the affections of brotherly love, reaching even to the ends of the earth, to weary him.

[Col. 0596D] But it will happen to you—it will happen, I say—city of Antioch, that Peter will yet be transferred from see to see, that, as the need and advantage of peoples demand, he will be moved elsewhere [the text has *alias*, perhaps *alios*]. You cannot keep as your own one whom holy Church has received for a common ministry. Therefore share him lovingly for the dispersion of the brethren, and relax somewhat your hold upon him whom you have bound to yourself in dear embraces. “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 5), and you will bear calmly that Peter is sent to another bishopric.

Meanwhile, blessed city, rejoice in Peter’s presence; soothe him with pious services; bind him inwardly to yourself by the most devoted responses of obedience; win for yourself, by whatever acts of devotion you can, this intimate friend of God. Share in his banquets and his discourses, and watch more carefully over your future lack of instruction. Abundant security has ruined many: because they trust in present prosperity, they are not sufficiently concerned about tomorrow’s want. Those who have fixed their whole hope upon the present time do not know how to provide for tomorrow.

[Col. 0597A] But you, Antioch, rejoice in the present graciousness of blessed Peter; enjoy his conversation as though amid every abundance of riches, and provide for yourself against his future absence. While there is opportunity, suck the maternal breasts; “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elder, and he will speak to you” (Deut. 23). Today you have chosen for yourself the prince of the apostles as priest; today you have enthroned the gatekeeper of heaven as bishop.

O admirable dispensation of God in every particular! O wonderful discernment of divine providence! What shall I say, brethren? Shall I go where the impulse of the Spirit leads me? Shall I speak, or be silent? Yet we judge it better to speak than to be silent, since silence would be, as it were, to withhold something from the praises of blessed Peter. The Lord says of himself in one place: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10). If the Lord indeed declares that he is the door and promises salvation to those entering through himself, nevertheless he begins thus with Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

[Col. 0597B] You can now see, most dear brethren—and you see what your own affection longs to express—but through the abundance of the Spirit I cannot bring out all that I turn over in my mind. For it often happens that, beneath the weight of overflowing joy or grief, the spirit lacks sufficient words, when the spirit itself has not yet decided to which side it should yield; and in this abundance of spirit the greatest confusion arises, as when varied riches are placed before some greedy person. In excessive eagerness he hesitates what he should seize first; and while he gasps after each thing, he stretches his hand toward all. So it is with us: [Col. 0597C] the multitude of thoughts hinders us concerning so great and such a mystery; yet, with God’s favour, your diligent prayers will free us.

You know, most dear brethren, that a bolt and keys are applied to a door, by whose operation [the text perhaps reads *juvantibus*, “assisting”] the leaves of that door are opened and shut. Gatekeepers too are assigned to doors; at their suggestion they speak beforehand concerning access to the Lord’s inner chambers, according to the convenience of the doors. Therefore, since Christ, as he says, is the door, while Peter is the keeper of the keys, what else follows but that Peter is the doorkeeper of this door, so that, in some manner, through Peter’s service as vicar we may have entrance into him who is the door?

From the apostolic number he is joined to the priestly college, 300 so that you may admire something higher in Peter’s priesthood than—even if it may be said—in the title “apostle.” Of Christ it is said: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

[Col. 0598A] He is not said to be an apostle—although he was made lower than the angels—but is proclaimed by authoritative speech to be a priest. Peter, therefore, was made an apostle, which Christ was not made; he was also adopted as priest, which the Lord already was. He was made Christ’s fellow-priest and co-heir, but was not made his fellow-apostle. Perhaps Christ too could be called an apostle, but he was the Apostle of the Father, while Peter was the Apostle of Christ (Heb. 3).

The proclamation of the Wise Man also seems consonant with today’s feast: “Behold a great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous” (Ecclus. 50). This man, indeed, after Christ the most renowned [perhaps *most desired*, *optatissimus*] of priests, a priest most acceptable to God in his days, marked by the distinguished title of righteousness, dedicated the whole course of his life to Christ’s service. He willingly sacrificed to God; he watched fittingly over the sheepfold entrusted to him; little by little he bound to the citizens of heaven those whom he could; he distributed his Lord’s wheat most cautiously for profit.

[Col. 0598B] Most fervent in the love of God, most steadfast in asserting the faith, most ready in love of neighbour, he lived a celibate life on earth. Finally, he abounded in miracles, so that the sick were laid in beds in the streets, in order that, when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow some one of them and they might be delivered from their infirmities (Acts 3). The grace of the Holy Spirit supplied his tongue with such eloquence that before kings and governors he neither considered what he should say nor ever lacked what he might say with the greatest eloquence. Transferred from the catching of fish to the catching of human beings, he spread the nets of faith for the wandering fish of this storm-tossed world.

Today also, made priest of the highest God, through the burning of fragrant incense and *thymiama* [incense], he was received gladly and joyfully by the highest Priest of priests. He offered himself as a living sacrifice, an odour of sweetness, and paid his vows most diligently to the Most High. Therefore the Lord gave him the blessing of all nations and confirmed his covenant upon his head.

[Col. 0598C] Therefore also his good things have been established in the Lord, and the whole Church of the saints shall recount his almsgivings. “Blessed,” therefore, is he “whom you have chosen and taken to yourself, O Lord”; behold, rejoicing, “he shall dwell in your courts” (Ps. 64). I believe, then, that blessed Peter is second to none among the saints, since the Holy of holies placed him in the foundation of his Churches and raised him to the loftiest watchtower over his sheep. No fellow-apostle was more ardent in love for his Jesus; none was more courageous even at the very despair of the betrayal.

Peter has been promoted from his little boat; today he is established in a chair—not a chair of pestilence (Ps. 1), nor that of those selling doves (Matt. 21), but an episcopal chair—that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory (1 Sam. 2). The Lord established with him a covenant of peace, that he might perform the priesthood and offer him incense worthy of the sweetest fragrance.

[Col. 0599A] Therefore act, bishops, who sit in the place of blessed Peter, whom episcopal pre-eminence has raised up: consider whom you imitate, and in whose dignity you glory, lest you seem to misuse the care entrusted to you. Let being called bishops not be for you an arrogant boast; rather, be willing and desire truly to be bishops. “For he who desires the episcopate desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3). Therefore do what is fitting, what will nourish and cherish the flock of the Lord entrusted to you, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, you yourselves become reprobate (1 Cor. 9).

You also, the remaining priests, the lesser dwelling-places of the house of the Lord, whose lips preserve knowledge—for you are angels of the Lord of hosts, and the law is required from your mouth (Mal. 2)—you who eat the sins of the Lord’s people (Hos. 4), awaken at last. Although you are not bishops according to the distinctions of rank, remember that you are Peter’s fellow-priests. Stand therefore in your station, girding your loins manfully, and follow Peter, the great priest, effectively.

[Col. 0599B] For the fact that today, adorned with the priestly mitre, he is placed in the chair raises up the humility of your teaching office, strengthens the deliberative discernment of your judicial authority, and adorns the dignity of your whole ministry. You too, according to your capacity, are God’s fellow-workers and helpers; after Peter’s example you have received the priesthood. “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). If your hands have touched any corpse, [Col. 0599C] wash your hands and cleanse your consciences, lest through the defilements of wicked impurities the vessels of the Lord be made unclean, and lest through your negligence those vessels themselves become displeasing along with their portions.

You have blessed Peter as an example of holiness, a pattern of purity, a rule of all zeal. May he render acceptable to our God the blessings and vows of your prayers, and through his offerings commend us all to him who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. On the Lord’s Prayer

There are two things, beloved, to which human vigilance ought principally to attend: the dignity of its creation and the excellence of its restoration. To the dignity of its creation, that it may fear to sin; to the excellence of its redemption, that it may not prove ungrateful for redeeming grace. For by the Creator’s will alone humankind was raised from the lowliness of the earth and exalted to God’s likeness by the privilege of reason. Miserable man lost this when, deceived by diabolical persuasion, he proudly departed from the ordinance of his Creator. Considering that fall, the Psalmist said almost in compassion: “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48).

[Col. 0599D] Falling from the highest elevation through his own choice, he was deservedly condemned to the lowest abasement. He could fall by himself, but could not rise again by himself. Human frailty must lament this fall with daily lamentations, so that by daily lamentations it may return to the place from which it fell through vain pleasures; and, having fallen by the foot of pride, it may strive to rise by the foot of obedience. Considering this, the Psalmist said: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me. There have fallen those who work iniquity; they have been cast out and could not stand” (Ps. 35). They were cast out from inward rest, and could not stand—that is, they could not return by themselves. As it is said of the same persons through the same Psalmist: “For they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77).

[Col. 0600A] For this return or resurrection, therefore, the healing grace of the Redeemer was necessary, that by humility it might heal what had been corrupted by pride’s exaltation. The Word of God therefore took the form of a servant (Phil. 2), in which he could instruct his fellow-servants by word, 301 and shape their conduct by the discipline of his life as an example. For he taught humility and obedience by word and example when, exhorting his disciples, he said: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11). His yoke of obedience is deservedly sweet, because to serve him is to reign; and the burden of his commandments is light, because it does not weigh down by pressing, but helps by grace toward fulfilment.

He also taught sobriety by word when he said: “Let not your hearts be weighed down by carousing and drunkenness” (Luke 21); he taught it by example, for he did not refresh the crowd following him with costly luxuries but with barley loaves (John 6).

[Col. 0600B] Directing our intention toward inward goods, he taught how fasting ought to be done when he said: “When you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites” (Matt. 6), thereby censuring those who affect the strictness of abstinence in mournful and unkempt appearance in order to appear to people to be fasting. Nor did he wish to pass over in silence how almsgiving ought to be done, when he said: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (ibid.). By this teaching he instructs us that almsgiving and every work of mercy which we do should be performed, not in pursuit of human praise, but with the intention of eternal life, signified by the right hand.

He also taught how prayer ought to be made, when he said: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber” (ibid.), that is, have a tranquil heart, free from every tumult of occupations; and, with the door shut—that is, after excluding the crowd of imaginings—pray to your Father.

[Col. 0600C] Behold, it has been said how one should pray; he also adds what should be prayed, continuing thus: “Thus, then, shall you pray: Our Father” (ibid.), and so forth. This prayer, in concise words—that is, in seven petitions—embraces every kind of prayer by which we address God, whether to seek good things, avoid evils, or blot out sins committed. Of these seven petitions, the first three concern eternity; the following four, the necessity of the present life. For the sanctification of God’s name, his coming in glory, and the fulfilment of his will “as in heaven, so on earth”—whether we understand this as concerning the righteous and sinners, soul and body, or Christ and the Church—[Col. 0601A] although they take their beginning from Christ’s humble coming, will nevertheless be fulfilled only at the end of the age, and all three will remain eternally.

The remaining four, however, appear to concern this temporal life. Even daily bread—that is, spiritual bread—although it is everlasting, nevertheless belongs to this time insofar as it is ministered to the soul by certain signs, namely spoken or written words. It is called bread because it is learned through labour and exposition, and thus swallowed, as it were, by chewing. [Col. 0601B] Now too sins are forgiven us and we forgive others; this is the second portion [the Petavian manuscript has *petition*] among the four. Now too temptations assail our life; and deliverance itself from evil belongs to this life, because through God’s justice we incur death and must therefore be delivered by his mercy.

Since these things are so, the words of the petitions themselves ought to be examined more carefully, so that when understood they may produce a greater affection of heart, and what is sought may be brought more swiftly to effect. Let us therefore say, “Our Father,” whom we serve not through fear but through love. It was not said to the former people that they should pray to a father; rather, the Lord was made known to them, whom they obeyed not with filial love but obeyed submissively with servile fear.

[Col. 0601C] By this word the rich and noble, once they have become Christians, are admonished not to exalt themselves against the poor and lowly, since together they say “Our Father.” They cannot say this truly and piously unless they recognize themselves as brethren. Thus by this name charity is stirred up, because nothing ought to be dearer to children than their father; humble affection is stirred up when human beings say, “Our Father”; and there arises a certain confidence of obtaining what is asked, since even before the petition we have received so great a gift that we may say “Our Father.” For what will a father now fail to give to children who ask, when he has already given them this very thing, that they should be children? Finally, how great a care touches the mind of one who says “Our Father,” that he may not be unworthy of so great a Father. Let the people of the New Testament therefore use this utterance—the new people called to eternity—“Our Father.”

[Col. 0601D] The prayer is fraternal. It does not say “My Father,” as though one were praying only for oneself, but “Our Father,” embracing in one prayer all who know themselves to be brothers in Christ: “who dwell in heaven,” that is, in those whose citizenship is in heaven. This comparison is most fitting: the distance believed to exist spiritually between a righteous person and a sinner is as great as the bodily distance between heaven and earth. For to the sinner it was said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” To signify this matter, when we stand for prayer we turn toward the East, whence heaven rises—not because God is there as though he had abandoned the other regions of the world, but so that the mind may be admonished to rise toward the more excellent nature, that is, toward God.

[Col. 0602A] Let us now consider what ought to be sought. “Hallowed be your name”: this is not asked as though the name of God were not holy, but that it may be regarded as holy by human beings, and that God may thus become known to them, so that they judge that there is nothing holier and therefore fear more greatly to offend him. For to sanctify the name of God is to fear God, of whom it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110); and elsewhere: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Matt. 18).

It follows: “Your kingdom come,” that is, be made manifest to the world. Just as present light is absent to the blind, so the kingdom of God, although it is everywhere, is absent from those who do not know it. Or: may you reign in us and we in you, through your gift. This petition concerns piety, which stands at the second degree among the beatitudes. For if piety is that by which the meek are blessed (Matt. 5), let us ask that the kingdom of God may come into us—that is, that we may become gentle and not resist.

[Col. 0602B] It follows: “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth,” that is, as in the angels, so also in human beings; or as in the righteous, so also in sinners; or let the flesh consent to your will as the spirit consents.

This petition concerns knowledge, which is third among the beatitudes. For if knowledge is that by which those who mourn are blessed, let us pray that God’s will may be done as in heaven so on earth—that is, that the flesh may consent to the spirit. For human misery has no greater cause for grief than that the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that with the Apostle we are compelled to cry: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7).

[Col. 0602C] The fourth petition follows: “Give us this day our daily bread.” It may be understood simply of bodily food and spiritually of the bread of the divine word. If it concerns bodily food, this speaker does not extend his petition far into the future; he follows the Gospel commandment: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow itself will be anxious for itself” (Matt. 6). So the blessed Apostle also instructs us: having food and covering, let us be content with these.

[Col. 0602D] But if he understands this bread spiritually, understand either Christ himself, who is the supersubstantial bread of the soul, because he surpasses every substance, who says of himself: “I am the living bread 302 which came down from heaven” (John 6); or understand the knowledge of the divine word itself, which is necessary to us to repair the ruins of the soul so long as it is called “today.” This petition concerns fortitude, which is placed fourth among those ascending to the height of blessedness. For if fortitude is that by which those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are made blessed, we ought to pray that this daily bread may be given to us, strengthened by which we may be able to attain that perfect satisfaction.

It follows: “And forgive us our debts.” Perhaps someone has sinned against you: forgive one who asks you for pardon, lest, while you deny mercy to your brother, you shut against yourself the Father’s forgiveness. For the Apostle James says: “God’s judgment is without mercy to one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. 1). This petition is referred to counsel, which is placed fifth among the degrees of the beatitudes. For if counsel is that by which the merciful are blessed, let us forgive our debtors their debts, and so pray that our debts—that is, our sins—may be forgiven us. Because of them we are delayed from obtaining pardon unless forgiveness bestowed upon our brethren hastens it.

[Col. 0603A] It follows: “And lead us not into temptation,” that is, do not allow us to be led into it—that is, deceived by the tempter. This, then, is what we pray: that God may not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but may make, with the temptation, a way of escape so that we may endure it. This petition concerns understanding, which is sixth in the number of beatitudes. For if understanding is that by which the pure in heart are blessed—that is, those who have cleansed the eye of the mind from earthly dust—let us pray not to be led into temptation, that is, not to have a double heart, but to desire one simple good.

It follows: “But deliver us from evil,” namely, the evil into which we may be led, and from that into which we have been led; in this manner nothing will remain to be mourned. To this petition corresponds wisdom, which holds the seventh place among the beatitudes. For if wisdom is that by which the peacemakers are blessed—that is, those who, having ordered their impulses, make all things serve the spirit—we must pray to be delivered from evil. For this deliverance makes us free, that is, children of God, so that in the Spirit of adoption we may cry: “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8).

[Col. 0603B] “Amen” in all these petitions signifies that what is asked is undoubtedly granted by the Lord, if the agreement of the final condition is held firmly.

The heavenly physician specially commended to us these three kinds of remedy: almsgiving, fasting, and prayer. By these, as by healing antidotes, we may cure long-standing evils, drive away present ones, and, by preserving health, guard against those to come. Appropriately, there are three kinds of treatment, just as three kinds of corruption precede them. [Col. 0603C] For every sin either takes place in the soul through consent to a perverse suggestion, thereby violating God’s temple; or it takes place through the wrongful use of the body to harm one’s neighbour, which is criminal wrongdoing (*facinus*); or it takes place through wrongful use of the body to corrupt oneself, which is shameful vice (*flagitium*).

[Col. 0603D] For although criminal wrongs are committed through the body, such as murders, robberies, and thefts, they do not affect or corrupt the body of the perpetrator. Of these the Apostle says: “Every sin whatever a person commits is outside the body” (1 Cor. 6). Shameful vices, however, are both committed through the body and affect and defile the body. Of these the Apostle says: “But he who commits fornication sins against his own body” (ibid.). Therefore criminal wrongs, which occur outside the body, are rightly cleansed by almsgiving as by an outward medicine. For just as the wrongdoing injured one’s neighbour, so almsgiving—which is outside us, though given through the body—ought to benefit one’s neighbour. Shameful vices, however, are fittingly cleansed by the medicinal discipline of frugality, because, just as the flesh in its pleasure drew one into fault, so, afflicted, it ought to lead one back to pardon.

If there are any for whom these remedies are unsuitable—because they cannot give alms owing to extreme poverty, or cannot fast owing to weakness of stomach—they have the third kind of medicine, from which none can excuse himself [Col. 0604A] unless he has scorned to heal the diseases of his soul. Let us therefore practise this remedy diligently and devoutly, a remedy which no sound mind can lack, fulfilling the apostolic command: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5). For this antidote meets every disease in such a way that, used continually, it drives away all diseases and restores everything corrupted to wholeness, through the favour of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. [Note: [Col. 0603] This sermon too is here first published from a manuscript of the Royal Library and the Petavian manuscript, and from an old parchment of Souchet.] On the Apostles’ Creed

Your love knows that soldiers of this world, before receiving temporal benefits from temporal lords, are first bound by military oaths and profess that they will keep faith with their lords. [Col. 0604B] How much more ought those who are to serve the eternal King and receive eternal rewards to be bound by heavenly sacraments and publicly profess the faith by which they will please him. For the Apostle says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 2).

He who searches minds and hearts recognizes this faith in our hearts; but, for preserving the unity of the Church, under the dispensation of this time confession by the mouth is necessary together with faith of the heart, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10)—not only for preachers but also for hearers. For a brother could not otherwise think well of a brother, nor could the peace of the Church be preserved, nor could it be necessary for salvation to teach another or learn from another, unless one transmitted to the hearts of others what one holds in the heart by signs of speech, as though by its own vehicles.

[Col. 0604C] Faith, therefore, must be kept in the heart and uttered with the mouth. Faith is the foundation of all good things and the beginning of human salvation. Without it no one can attain the number of God’s children, because without it no one obtains the grace of justification in this world or possesses eternal life in the world to come. And if anyone does not walk by faith, he will not attain the vision.

Considering this, the holy apostles handed down a certain rule of faith. They called it the *symbolum* [creed], because it was comprised in twelve propositions according to the number of the apostles, so that through it believers might maintain catholic unity and refute heretical perversity. For members of an association commonly give a *symbolum* when they admit someone to their fellowship, and thus confirm the covenant of faith entered upon. Following this analogy, the holy apostles joined together a spiritual fellowship and composed this creed, so that those wishing to enter their fellowship might be joined to them by the exchange of faith and thus be made participants with them at the heavenly table.

[Col. 0604D] Let everyone, therefore, who has professed the apostolic faith through the mouths of those bearing him at baptism, when he has reached the years of understanding, say: “I believe in God”; and let him meditate in his heart what he professes with his mouth. He does not say *credo Deum* (“I believe that God exists”) or *credo Deo* (“I believe God”), though these also are necessary for salvation.

For it is one thing to believe that God is, and another to believe God, because he is truthful. As the Apostle James testifies, “even the demons [Col. 0605A] believe and tremble” (Jas. 2); but they do not believe *in* God, because by believing they are not moved to go into his will. Therefore the spirit of fear does them no good, because the spirit of love is not in them.

But we, who by the adoption of grace are children of God, should say: “I believe in God the Father almighty,” that is, let us believe in him in such a manner as to cling to him through love. He says “Father,” who before all times begot the Son coeternal with himself: “almighty Creator of heaven and earth,” that is, who through his omnipotence is Creator both of heavenly and earthly things—that is, of visible and invisible things—so that no one may doubt that God is able to do so, when he hears that he is able to do all things.

These words were stated against the Gentiles, who through unbelief thought that the images which they had made were gods, while abandoning the true God by whom they themselves had been made.

[Col. 0605B] “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” As one believes in the Father, so one must believe in the Son. And because he is equal in majesty with the Father, we owe him as much honour as we owe the Father. Jesus is interpreted “Saviour.” “Christ” is named from *chrism* [anointing], because, just as ancient kings were anointed with sacred oil, so our Lord Jesus Christ was filled with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. These titles show that he is rightly to be believed in: beyond being equal to the Father, he is our Saviour, redeeming us; and he is Christ—that is, king—ruling us; and our only Lord, who, having despoiled the ancient enemy, claims us for his own singular lordship.

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit,” that is, the Holy Spirit alone was the author of whose conception. For just as a worm is formed from pure mud when the sun warms it, so, when the Holy Spirit illuminated and sanctified the Virgin’s heart, Christ’s flesh was conceived from the Virgin’s flesh alone, with no seminal origin of flesh at work. Hence, comparing himself to a worm, he says through the Psalmist: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI); that is, not conceived in the human manner. “Born of the Virgin Mary”; that is, just as conception did not open his mother’s womb, so neither did birth open it. We do not, as certain utterly wicked persons suppose, call the Holy Spirit “seed,” but say that this was wrought by the power and virtue of the Creator. “The Word was made flesh” (John I); that is, he was made man, conceived from the Virgin and born of the Virgin through the cooperation of the Father and the Holy Spirit, so that, by the ineffable proof of his generation, he who made himself to be created through the Holy Spirit was himself the Creator within the Virgin.

“Suffered under Pontius Pilate.” Pilate is mentioned to indicate the time, not to confer dignity on the person. “Crucified, dead, and buried.” The weaknesses of the incarnate Word are recalled, concerning which the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. I). For this reason he suffered: that he might restore us to impassibility. For this reason he was crucified: that he might free us from everlasting torments. For this reason he truly died a death—as he was truly born by birth—that he might free us from everlasting death. For this reason he was buried: that he might bury us with himself as regards vices and desires. Hence the Apostle says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI); that is, having put away all oldness, we may be conformed to Christ’s likeness. This weakness of Christ, therefore, overcame all the strength of the world.

“On the third day he rose from the dead.” Death in a three-day burial clearly shows that, while the body lay in the tomb, that soul triumphed over the lower world. “He ascended into heaven.” Therefore he placed above the heavens at the right hand of the Father the condition of our nature, which, born from a human mother, he had assumed. “He sits.” His being said to sit does not signify a posture of the limbs, but judicial power. “At the right hand of God the Father Almighty.” “At the right hand” must be understood as said of the highest blessedness, just as the goats will be placed at the left hand, that is, in the utmost misery. “From thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead.” He will judge the living and the dead: that is, those whom his coming will find before our death, and those already dead whom he will raise; or “living and dead” means the righteous and sinners.

Let those who profess this faith attend to the fact that, in this Creed, Christ’s humanity—through which they were reconciled—is recalled, lest they prove ungrateful for the benefits of their Redeemer, who reconciled them through his humanity and absolved them through his divinity, lest through ingratitude they be deprived by divine right of the paternal goods allotted to them.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit,” equal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, proceeding equally from both. Therefore he must be believed in as the Father and the Son are believed in. “The holy catholic Church,” that is, the Church of the whole world—not that of which it is said, “Behold, here; behold, there” (Matt. XXIV), that is, which is said to be in inner rooms or in the wilderness, but that which is spread throughout the whole world and established in unity of faith. “The communion of saints,” that is, the reality of the Church’s sacraments, in which the saints shared who departed this life in the unity of faith. “The forgiveness of sins”: not only of those remitted through baptism, but also of those cleansed by humble confession and worthy satisfaction. “The resurrection of the flesh,” which will be common at the Lord’s coming, but different for good and evil persons, according as the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. XV)—understood: for the better. “Life everlasting,” that is, what the same Apostle says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (ibid.).

These twelve articles, which most firmly belong to the rule of the true faith, must be faithfully believed, steadfastly held, and truthfully and patiently defended. If we know anyone to teach doctrines contrary to them, let us flee from him as from a plague and reject him as a heretic. For these propositions, set forth and compressed into brief words, so accord with the catholic faith and so confront heretical perversity that those firmly adhering to this rule are not permitted to err or stray from the path of right faith. But if anyone should choose to think otherwise, let us pray that God may deign to reveal this to him. As for us, let us walk in what we have received and persevere firmly in what is certain to us.

Teach this Creed to your spiritual children, for whom you made a promise in baptism, whom you received from the sacred font. Teach it to your children whom you have received from your own flesh. Teach it to those whom you have admitted under your patronage, so that through your instruction they may avoid every error, flee what is hostile to the Christian faith, and accomplish with all their strength what is fitting. Through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV

[Note: This sermon, already published by Juret at the end of the letters from a manuscript of St Victor, Paris, is issued again, revised according to the manuscript copies of the Royal and Petau libraries.]

On the adulterated attire of men or women.

We have heard from the Gospel parable that a certain householder made a wedding for his son and invited very many persons to it. Among them, when one person entered without a wedding garment, he was seen by the householder and ordered not only to be excluded from the wedding, but also to be thrust into the outer darkness. This parable plainly rebukes the senseless people of our age, although through a deeper investigation something more hidden and sacred may be understood. Let us first ask, therefore, who this householder is, who this son is, and what this wedding is. Once these have been examined, we shall more easily understand why the man who came to this wedding in an adulterated garment was excluded from it.

We understand, then, that this householder is God the Father Almighty, whom all the households of the nations serve; who begot a Son coeternal and coequal with himself, in heaven without a mother, on earth without a father. He made a wedding for him when he joined to him the Church from every class of humankind. To this union of Christ and the Church are summoned noble and ignoble, rich and poor, every social condition, every sex, every age. Among them came one who alone deserved exclusion, because he lacked attire suited to the holiness of such a wedding. Attend, brothers. This one person is many persons, and yet this whole multitude is embraced under the name of unity. They are many in number through the distinction of persons, but they are one through agreement in a single perversity. For just as there is one Church by faith under Christ its head, so the entire multitude of the reprobate, whether manifest or hidden, is one body under the devil as its prince.

Whoever openly departs from God through unbelief does not come to this wedding. But the unbeliever who comes departs in mind: bodily he enters the Church with us and shares Christ’s table with us. Good and bad fish are still hidden within the nets until they are separated on the shore. Chaff is still tolerated until the threshing floor is winnowed. Then it will plainly appear that “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII). Then this adulterator of the wedding garment will plainly be excluded at the householder’s command and thrust into prison.

Meanwhile the friends of the bridegroom are not ignorant of such a pretender, because the indecent attire of the body is a messenger of the adulterated heart. Indecent bodily attire in men consists in excessive and disordered growth of hair; affected imitation of women’s clothing; and feigned length of footwear exceeding the bounds of necessity. In women it consists in a painted face, imitation of male clothing, and alteration of the hair’s natural colour. Such attire is adulterated in either sex, unworthy of fellowship in the holy wedding, and altogether to be removed from the sight of so great a bridegroom and so great a bride.

Nor should the bridegroom’s friends, who love the beauty of God’s house, pass over this in silence. They ought publicly to bark at such adulterations, lest it be said of them: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI.10). For whoever strives to transform into another form the size or shape fashioned by the almighty and most wise Maker, does he not plainly seem to say to him who made him, “Why did you make me thus?” It is shameful audacity to despise the Creator’s creature so greatly as to transform, so far as lies in one’s power, one’s own size and shape into something else—something which, if one possessed it by nature, one would grieve to possess beyond comparison.

Nor do we say this of ourselves, as though from ourselves. We have our fathers, distinguished teachers, who wrote against these things before us and condemned them with irrefutable authority. Let us hear Paul, teacher of the nations, saying to the Corinthians concerning excessive hair: “If a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him” (1 Cor. I). Since by God’s ordinance man has precedence over woman, he who, contrary to the honour of his sex, covers his head with an excess of hair strips himself of his precedence; so that it may deservedly be said of him: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared”—to speak truthfully—not merely with women, but also “with senseless beasts” (Ps. XLIX). For by the judgment of the laws, one is rightly cast down from an attained dignity if one abuses the privilege entrusted to oneself.

Let us hear also blessed Cyprian, distinguished martyr and most gracious teacher, discussing adulterated attire. In the letter he writes *On the Dress of Virgins*, he says:

> “God’s work, his handiwork, his creature, ought by no means to be adulterated by applying yellow colouring or blackness, or any cosmetic whatever [or black powder, rouge, or anything else] that corrupts the natural features. For God says: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’ (Gen. I). And does anyone dare to alter and transform what God has made? They lay hands upon God when they strive to refashion and transform what he formed, knowing [or: unaware] that everything born is God’s work, while whatever is changed is the devil’s work.
>
> If an artist in painting had marked someone’s face, appearance, and bodily quality with emulous colour, and another person were then to bring [or: lay] hands upon the image already finished and completed, and, as though more skilled, reshape what was already formed and painted, this would seem a serious injury and a just ground for indignation to the first artist.”

And later:

> “Do you not fear that, when the day of resurrection comes, your Maker may fail to recognize you; that he may remove and exclude you as you come toward his rewards and promises, rebuking you with the authority of censor and judge, and saying: ‘This is not my work; this is not our image. You defiled yourself with a false cosmetic; by a deceit you disfigured the form I gave you. Your face is corrupted; your limbs are alien. You will be unable to see God, since you have not the eyes God made, but those which the devil infected.’”

[Note: “But falsely.” The remainder is somewhat differently worded in Cyprian.]

[Note: The following also is drawn from Cyprian.]

Hear me, therefore, as a parent; hear me, I beg you, as one teaching and at the same time admonishing you; hear one who faithfully seeks your benefit and advantage. Be such as the Lord, the craftsman, made you. Be such as your Father’s hand established you. Let your face remain uncorrupted, your neck pure, your form unfeigned; let your feet be free from superfluous footwear, your hair dyed with no colour, and your eyes worthy to behold God.

[Note: In Cyprian: “Let the feet be free from golden fetters.”]

It is the voice of the Apostle, whom the Lord called the vessel of election. For he says: “The first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven. As we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. XV). Virginity bears this image; integrity bears it; holiness and truth bear it; those mindful of God’s ordinances bear it, retaining righteousness with religion, steadfast in faith, humble in fear, strong for every endurance, gentle in bearing injury, ready in showing mercy, united [variant reading: *uniames*] and harmonious in brotherly peace. All these things we ought to observe, love, and fulfil, so that we may fulfil the Apostle’s command: “For you were bought at a great price: glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. VI). We bear God in our body when we do not disfigure his image by unclean and profane inventions, and when we strive by every service of obedience to obey the command of the Redeemer. For thus he will recognize his image in us and will not exclude us, adorned in wedding attire, from his own fellowship and that of the saints. May he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages mercifully deign to grant this to us. Amen.

CLI, col. 974, is attributed to Ivo by Henry Wharton in the Supplement to Ussher’s *On Sacred and Vernacular Scriptures*, p. 359: “From a manuscript codex of the Lambeth Library,” he says, “I discovered that Ivo is the author of the *Micrologus*—a fact that has hitherto escaped scholars. ## [CHRONICLE]

### TO THE READER

I had intended to publish a rather extensive Chronicle, from Ninus to Louis the Pious. Its middle portion had already been published in the collection of French history under the name of Ivo, bishop of Chartres; and we had also recovered from the monastery of Saint-Evroult a complete manuscript under the same name of Ivo, bishop of Chartres. But, comparing it with several manuscript Chronicles of Hugh of Fleury—two especially notable copies being in the library of St Victor, Paris—we discovered that it was identical with them in every respect, and was therefore falsely ascribed to our Ivo.

Several persons were deceived in this matter because the Chronicle has at its head a certain letter of Hugh to our Ivo, in which he asks him to inspect and correct his Chronicle, which he sends him to read, if he should find anything in it requiring correction. This error, however, was learnedly recognized by André Duchesne, royal historiographer, in vol. III of the *Writers of French History*, p. 347, where he speaks of Hugh of Fleury’s various Chronicles. Add to this that none of those who have written on Ivo has ever mentioned this Chronicle, as can be seen in the eulogies of Ivo which we placed at the beginning of this book. Therefore we wished to warn the reader here, lest he should think that anything among the works of so great a man has been withheld from him.

## CHRONICLE OF ST IVO, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, ON THE KINGS OF THE FRANKS

[Note: Others prefer to attribute this very brief history of the Franks to Hugh of Sainte-Marie, monk of Fleury. But it contains nothing that indicates his intellect or style. Georg Waitz, Prolegomena to Hugh of Fleury, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IX; *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII.]

The emperor Valentinian wished the Franks to be called in the Attic language from their ferocity, hardness, and boldness. Shortly afterward, when they refused tribute to the Romans and could not withstand the Roman attack, they departed from Sicambria and reached the farthest borders of the River Rhine, in German towns. There they settled for several years with their leaders Marcomir and Sunno. There they first set Pharamund over themselves as king and subjected themselves to laws which their leading men Wisogastus, Arbogastus, and Salegastus devised.

Pharamund, first king of the Franks. Nicetas, bishop of Vienne. Justus, bishop of Lyons, leaving his bishopric, died as an anchorite in Egypt; his bones and the bones of Viator, his attendant, were brought back to Lyons. Martin, bishop of Tours, shone with the glory of miracles.

Didio, son of Pharamund, second king of the Franks. From this time the Franks began to have long-haired kings. At the same time the Romans held Gaul, while the Goths held the territory south of the Loire.

Clodio, after Didio, third king of the Franks. Departing from the territory of the Thuringians, he crossed the Rhine, defeated the Roman army, occupied the Carbonarian Forest, and established his seat there.

Merovech, after Clodio, fourth king of the Franks. Metz having been burned by the Franks, they advanced as far as Orléans.

Childeric, after Merovech, reigned twenty-four years.

Clovis, after Childeric, sixth king of the Franks, reigned thirty years. He was the first of the Frankish kings to be baptized by blessed Remigius together with his people. Syagrius, son of the patrician Aegidius, joining battle with Clovis at Soissons, was defeated and killed; and thus Roman power in Gaul fell. King Clovis subjugated Burgundy. Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, was renowned. Ten miles from Poitiers, Clovis engaged King Alaric in battle, defeated and killed him, and subjected to himself Toulouse, Saintes, and all Aquitaine. Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, and Avitus of Vienne were renowned.

After Clovis died, his wife Clotild held the kingdom of the Franks with her four sons: Theuderic, Clodomir, Childebert, and Clothar. Clodomir, Childebert, and Clothar marched an army against Sigismund and against Godomar. When the Burgundians fled, Sigismund fled to the monastery of the martyrs of Agaunum, was captured there by Clodomir, and there killed with his wife and sons. Consequently Clodomir, fighting later with the Burgundians, was killed by them. The Franks, taking this grievously, pursued and killed Godomar. Childebert and Clothar killed the sons of Clodomir, their nephews, so that they would not reign in their father’s place. One, however, Clodoald, escaped; he became a cleric and, full of virtues, departed to Christ. Blessed Medard departed to Christ and was buried in the city of Soissons by King Clothar, who himself died not long afterward and was buried in the same church. He had reigned fifty-two years.

The four sons of Clothar divided the kingdom among themselves. Charibert received Clodomir’s kingdom and established his seat in Paris. Guntram received Childebert’s kingdom and established his seat in Orléans. Chilperic received the kingdom of his father Clothar at Soissons, and Sigebert received Theuderic’s kingdom at Rheims. King Charibert died and was buried in the church of St Romanus in the fortress of Blaye. Blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, flourished. Chilperic buried his brother Sigebert, who had been killed through the treachery of Queen Fredegund, on the road at Lambani; he was then transferred to the basilica of St Medard. King Guntram was buried in the church of St Marcellus at Chalon. He reigned thirty-one years.

Chilperic, killed through the treachery of Landric and of Queen Fredegund, his own wife, was buried in Paris in the church of St Vincent.

Theudebert and Theuderic, sons of Childebert, together with their grandmother Brunhild, were installed in Burgundy, the kingdom of the glorious King Guntram. Then Theuderic began a war with his brother Theudebert and killed him. At last Brunhild, because of her many crimes, was bound by the legs and arms to unbroken horses in the presence of King Clothar and torn limb from limb; her bones were burned with fire.

Clothar, son of Chilperic, eighth king of the Franks. He devastated the land of the Saxons so thoroughly that no man there remained taller than his own sword. Not long afterward he died, in the forty-fourth year of his reign.

Dagobert, son of Clothar, ninth king of the Franks, was an energetic man; he had two sons, Sigebert and Clovis. In the forty-fourth year of his reign, he was struck by a severe fever and died, and was buried at Bindion.

Clovis, son of Dagobert, tenth king of the Franks, whose wife Bathildis, of Saxon stock, bore him three sons—Clothar, Childeric, and Theuderic. Clovis died in the sixteenth year of his reign.

Clothar, son of Clovis, eleventh king of the Franks. He reigned four years and died.

Theuderic, son of Clovis and brother of Clothar, twelfth king of the Franks. Ebroin, mayor of the palace, subjected Bishop Leodegar and his full brother to many punishments and struck them with the sword. Theuderic died in the eighteenth year of his reign.

Clothar, son of Theuderic, thirteenth king of the Franks, reigned three years.

Childebert, son of Theuderic and brother of Clothar, fourteenth king of the Franks. He died in the thirteenth year of his reign.

Dagobert, son of Childebert, fifteenth king of the Franks, was still a boy; Theudebald, son of Pippin, duke of the Austrasians, was mayor of the palace. Dagobert died after reigning five years.

After Dagobert, the Franks set over themselves a certain cleric named Daniel, after he had discarded his tonsure, calling him Chilperic; they advanced an army against Charles as far as the River Meuse. From another side Duke Radbod rose against the same Charles with the Frisians. A fierce battle took place, and Charles, suffering great loss, withdrew. Chilperic and Raganfrid entered the Ardennes Forest and advanced as far as Cologne; but when Charles suddenly fell upon them and battle was joined, Chilperic and Raganfrid were put to flight. Chilperic fled to Duke Eudo and was delivered by that duke to Charles; five years afterward he died in the city of Noyon.

Theuderic, son of the younger Dagobert, seventeenth king of the Franks. Charles, mayor of the palace and prince of the Austrasians, devastating everything and plundering the fields of the Saxons, made war upon them, in which there was a most grievous slaughter of men dying on both sides. After several years he set out for Bavaria and with the greatest labour forced it to submit; when they resisted afterward, he subdued them on a second expedition. He went again into Saxony, then against the Swabians and Lantfrid, restraining them from attacks and injuries. From there he went against Eudo, duke of the Aquitanians, and drove him into Gascony. Moreover Charles severely routed the Saracens, who came in long ships and were ravaging many cities of Septimania and of the Viennois, and drove them back into Spain. After several years he went as far as Gascony and devastated Aquitaine; he also subdued the Saracens who were ravaging Aquitaine and other provinces.

Childeric, after Theuderic, eighteenth king of the Franks. The mayors of the palace were Carloman and his brother Pippin. But Carloman, putting aside secular dress, went to Rome and then proceeded to St Benedict on Monte Cassino. Grifo, fleeing from Duke Pippin, fled into Saxony and Bavaria and subdued Pippin’s duchy. Grifo then fled to Waiofar, duke of the Aquitanians; together they prepared war against Pippin. Meanwhile Pippin, seeing that the kingdom of the Franks had failed, was raised to kingship by command of Pope Zachary.

Pippin, nineteenth king of the Franks, reigned eighteen years. Immediately after his anointing he made war upon Saxony and defeated it. Stephen succeeded Pope Zachary. King Pippin gave Pope Zachary assistance against Aistulf, king of the Lombards, who had seized the possessions of the Roman Church within his kingdom, and forced him to restore what he had taken. Again Pippin entered Saxony and compelled it to pay the Franks horses each year as tribute. He then died in the year 868 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

Charles, glorious twentieth king of the Franks, son of Pippin and Queen Bertrada. He subdued the Saxon people. When his army was suffering from severe thirst, in the middle of the day water suddenly flowed in the greatest abundance from a certain stream, enough for the entire army. Pope Adrian summoned Charles into Italy against Desiderius, king of the Lombards. He captured Pavia, killed Desiderius, and subjugated all Lombardy. Again he defeated the Saxons when they rebelled, secured matters on both sides, stationed guards, received hostages, and returned. Again the Saxons attacked the fortress of Heresburg. While preparing engines to capture it, they saw two flaming globes, in the form of a shield, above the church which stood within the fortress. Terrified by this vision and abandoning their preparations, they escaped in such flight that they pierced one another with their own swords. Hearing this, King Charles entered Saxony, gained control of all their strongholds, and joined all the Saxons to himself in the faith after they, their wives, and their children had been baptized.

The same Charles celebrated Easter at the Aquitanian fortress of Cassinogil.

[Note: Cassignol, in the diocese of Agen.]

He entered Spain, destroyed Pamplona, and subdued the Saracens. He returned through Narbonne and Gascony. Then, for prayer, he entered Rome, captured Benevento, and received the duke’s sons as hostages together with very great gifts. He also subdued the fierce people of the Avars, whose leader came to him, believed, and was baptized. Charles also entered Rome and was the first among the Frankish people there to assume the title of Emperor and Augustus; those who had dishonoured Pope Leo he deposed and sent into exile. At that time a great earthquake occurred.

At the same time the king of Persia sent Charles a pavilion and tents, many precious silk cloths, and also a clock of brass marvellously fashioned by mechanical art. In it the course of the twelve hours was regulated by a water-clock, with the same number of bronze balls, which fell at the completion of the hours and, by their fall, made a cymbal beneath them ring. There were also the same number of horsemen, who emerged through twelve windows when the hours were completed and, by the movement of their departure, shut the same number of windows which had previously been open. There were also many other marvels in this clock. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 814, Emperor Charles died at Aachen, in the forty-fifth year of his reign.

Louis, son of Charles the Great, twenty-first king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans, reigned twenty-eight years, a lover of piety and religion. At the beginning of his empire he enjoyed favourable and tranquil peace, but his end was troubled by many calamities.

Charles the Bald, son of Louis, twenty-second king of the Franks, reigned thirty-seven years, also emperor of the Romans. He conducted the beginning and end of his reign prosperously, built churches of God, loved the poor, and bestowed many benefactions upon God’s churches in crosses and other ornaments.

Louis, son of Charles, twenty-second king of the Franks, reigned two years.

Charles, son of Louis, twenty-fourth king of the Franks, reigned thirty-eight years. He was called Tutudi—Martel—by his people. Because in his reign he scarcely, or rarely, had peace, he granted Church property for the most part to his soldiers as pay. After his death, while buried in the church of the blessed martyr Dionysius at the left side of the high altar, he was seen at night, in the form of a dragon, to break open his tomb and depart through a church window amid great terror.

Rudolf, twenty-fifth king of the Franks, son of Conrad, duke of Burgundy, reigned nineteen years: a cultivator of justice, a restorer of churches, he successfully defeated those who resisted him.

Louis, son of Rudolf, twenty-sixth king of the Franks, reigned eighteen years.

Lothar, son of Louis, twenty-seventh king of the Franks, reigned thirty years. At that time William was duke of the Normans.

Louis, son of Lothar, a cleric, twenty-eighth king of the Franks, reigned two years. Captured by the Franks at Laon, he died, and thus the line of Charlemagne failed.

Hugh, son of Hugh Capet, twenty-ninth king of the Franks, reigned ten years.

Robert, son of Hugh, thirtieth king of the Franks, reigned thirty-five years; his wife was Constance. Ruling his kingdom justly and religiously, he rested in a holy end. Pope Gilbert.

Henry, son of Robert, thirty-first king of the Franks, reigned thirty-two years. William, most noble duke of the Normans, fought at Val-ès-Dunes. King Henry, strong in war, died at Vitry.

Philip, son of Henry, thirty-second king of the Franks, reigned forty-nine years. In the seventh year of his reign, William, the glorious duke of the Normans, subdued the English and, made king there, reigned twenty-two years. He was succeeded by his son William Longaspata (“Longsword”), who reigned fourteen years and died by an arrow in the New Forest. He was succeeded by his brother Henry, a noble, wise, justice-loving, amiable man, comparable to no one of modern times in governing a kingdom; he reigned thirty years.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1119, LAMBERT, BISHOP OF ARRAS

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, III, 322)

Lambert, a native of Guînes, of distinguished family, was archdeacon of Thérouanne, canon and precentor of St Peter’s at Lille, a man endowed with great holiness.

[Note: Writing to him, Count Guy of Ponthieu asks that he deign to come to Abbeville on the Saturday before Pentecost, because on the following Sunday he was to equip Louis, the king’s son, with military arms and admit him to knighthood: “Therefore,” he says, “even if you decline to come for Louis himself, I nevertheless entreat you to deign to come for my sake and because of the kinship between you and me.” Vol. V of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, p. 310.]

He was chosen bishop by the clergy of Arras and consecrated at Rome by Pope Urban II, at Santa Maria Nuova, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, on Laetare Jerusalem Sunday, in the year 1093. In that same year he assumed the governance of the bishopric, according to a charter of Rheims; certainly, in an instrument of the abbey of Molesme, Lambert’s second year is connected with the year of Christ 1095. He was invited by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, to the Council of Autun in 1094, where Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, was discussed. In the same year he promised obedience to the Church of Rheims. Urban names him among the bishops whose counsel he used when he decreed that the Church of Dol should be subject to Tours as to its mother church.
