In 1095, as he was travelling to the Council of Clermont, he was captured with his companions by Guarnerius, knight of the Castle of Pont; but through the intervention of Philip, bishop of Troyes and Guarnerius’s brother, he was released shortly afterward. Being present at the synod, he took care to collect its acts and canons. Thus at the end of an old codex, after the canons, one reads: “These things were found in the book of Lambert, bishop of Arras, written four hundred years ago.” Returning from the council and appointed legate of the province of Rheims, he devoted himself to the care of the flock entrusted to him and fulfilled all the duties of a most watchful bishop. He held a synod in the church of St Mary and established a division of parishes.

In 1096 he subscribed the charter of Philip, bishop of Châlons, by which the right of advocacy was remitted to the monastery of St Basolus. He showed himself generous toward the monastery of St Amand at Elnone, to which he granted many altars in 1097. He attended the synod held at Rome by Urban II in the third week after Easter, 1099. In the same year he is also found subscribed at the Council of Saint-Omer, over which Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, presided.

In 1104 Pope Paschal II entrusted him with apostolic authority for the absolution of Philip, king of the Franks, excommunicated because of his incestuous marriage to Bertrada of Anjou. Knowledge of this matter is drawn from a manuscript codex of the abbey of Igny; and we have included among the documents Lambert’s letter on this matter to the same supreme pontiff. Finally, after discharging the pastoral office with the highest praise, the pious bishop departed to Christ on 16 May 1115. He is buried in the cathedral church, where this epitaph may be seen on marble affixed to the wall at the left of the choir:

> In the year of the Lord 1115, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, Lambert, cardinal bishop of this see of Arras, of blessed memory, died. Through him the dignity of this bishopric, which for many years had been entrusted to the bishop of Cambrai, was restored. To this bishop and to two minstrels, Itherius and Norman, blessed Mary appeared in this church, giving them a candle through which those burning with the fiery sickness are healed.

The chronicler of St Bertin gives another account in these verses:

> Vedastus was the proper bishop of this city;  
> after his death, this see, long without its own bishop,  
> wept while subject to Cambrai.  
> Until Urban II, pope at Rome, consecrated Lambert—  
> whom this tomb encloses—  
> outstanding in character, wise, and devout,  
> and restored to this see its own shepherd.  
> He departed from the world when May was passing beyond the Ides.

May the Lord grant him rest abiding without end [probably *sine fine manentem*].

He was intimate with Ivo of Chartres, as is shown by Ivo’s Letter 33, which begins in these words: “Moreover, dearest one, share your joys with your devoted and beloved friend in due season, because your joys and sorrows are mine, just as I do not doubt that mine are yours.” He also wrote to him another letter, [Col. 0618C] no. 97. For more on Lambert, consult the Belgian authors. Some have supposed him to have been a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, because in the letters of Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, and elsewhere he is repeatedly called a *cardinal bishop*; but we think that by this title is meant a bishop proper, attached to a particular Church under such a title—much as the expression “cardinal bishops” frequently occurs in the letters of Gregory the Great.

[Col. 0617]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, vol. X, p. 44.)

[Col. 0617D] Casimir Oudin (*Writers*, vol. II, p. 280) prides himself on being the first to have raised Bishop Lambert to the rank of an ecclesiastical writer. But in saying this he had forgotten that William Cave (p. 543), whom he nevertheless often copies, had already bestowed the same honor upon him. Lambert deserves it on more than one count, since he had the principal part in compilations of great interest for literature, though until now no care has been taken to make known what they truly are. We shall endeavor to supply this omission.

[Col. 0618D] 1. One of these compilations was published by Baluze (*Miscellanies*, vol. V, pp. 237 and 300; Lucca folio edition, vol. II, pp. 127–156). Grignon, doctor of the Sorbonne and canon of Arras cathedral, had supplied him with a copy made from the manuscript bearing the name of Bishop Lambert and preserved in the library of that same church. From this title and from the nature of the documents it contains, there can be no doubt that Lambert himself directed it, or at least took care to have it made. [Col. 0619A] Three parts may be distinguished in it. Several items had already been published in other compilations, such as the Belgian Chronicle of Ferréolus Locrius, Dom Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, Father Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts*, and his *General Collection of Councils*. Likewise, Aubert le Mire and some others had already published several documents included in the third part of the collection; and, since it appeared publicly, other writers have drawn from it several pieces which they inserted into their works, as may be seen especially in the proofs of the third volume of the *Gallia Christiana* (*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., vol. III, appendix, pp. 77–79).

The first part of this important collection contains the documents concerning the re-establishment of the bishopric of Artois: namely, the bulls issued for that purpose by Urban II; those of Paschal, his successor, confirming it; and the letters written concerning this affair by the Church of Arras, Lambert [Col. 0619B] bishop-elect, Renaud, archbishop of Reims and metropolitan of the province, and others. One of the most substantial pieces in this first part is the discussion of the rights of the Churches of Cambrai and Arras, held in the provincial council assembled on the third Sunday in Lent, 1093, and forming its acts. All these documents, arranged in their proper places, are connected by short accounts of events which occurred both in connection with the restoration of this episcopal see itself and in relation to the election and ordination of the new bishop. To make his work more complete, the author took care to carry his narrative through to the end of the Council of Clermont in 1095, in which this great matter was fully brought to completion. This purpose led him to include the adventures which befell Lambert on his journey there.

Whoever took the care of arranging this [Col. 0619C] part of the collection, one cannot deny him the credit of possessing taste and skill. Although Bishop Lambert may have conceived its plan and had some further share in it, one passage nevertheless makes it likely that it was carried out by one of the clerics who accompanied him to Rome rather than by Lambert himself. He was accompanied there by Odo, cantor of his church; Achard, scholasticus; and Drogo, provost of Aubigny. From the detail into which the author enters concerning the dispute over the rights of the parties—that is, the Churches of Arras and Cambrai—it is evident that the former defended its cause very well. Among the ancient authorities which it cited were the Second Council of Africa, the Council of Sardica, the False Decretals, the letters of Pope St. Gregory, the Life of St. Remigius, the historian Orosius, and chronicles dealing with the founders of cities. One read there that Romulus and Remus had founded Rome and Reims, and Pompey Arras and Soissons.

[Col. 0619D] The second part of the collection comprises 144 letters written by a large number of persons of the highest rank: popes, cardinals, legates, archbishops, bishops, kings, princes, princesses, and other persons established in dignity. It displays not only many particulars concerning the discipline of the ecclesiastical province of Reims over more than twenty years, but also several events memorable for its history, and even for the general history of France. It further contains various curious details concerning the manners and customs of that age. Among these letters, forty-nine belong to our bishop, and it is important to give a brief account of them, at least of the more interesting ones.

The ninth, in the order of the collection, was written to the Church of Reims in reply to the preceding letter, by which that Church had informed Lambert of the death of Renaud, its archbishop, on 21 [Col. 0620A] January 1096, and of the election of Manasses to replace him. Lambert assures the canons of Reims that, having learned of this death before they had announced it to him, he had already caused the customary prayers for the repose of the deceased prelate’s soul to be offered in his cathedral and in the abbey of Saint-Vaast, and had ordered them throughout the rest of his diocese. For the rest, he approves their new election and congratulates them on having chosen so worthy a man, whose praises he gives in a few words. His letter is dated the second day of February in that same year.

If the other letters of our bishop are later in date than the preceding one, it is evident that none of those he wrote during the first three years of his episcopate, reckoning from his election, was included. Of all these, only two survive, and they occur in the first part of the collection: one to Archbishop Renaud, the other to the canons of his [Col. 0620B] church. Lambert wrote them some time after his ordination and return from Rome, complaining that, despite his diligence in having delivered to them the papal letters which he had brought, and despite the legitimate excuses which he had conveyed for not having yet been able to go in person to render the obedience due to his metropolitan—though he had sent him a written profession of it—he had still received no token of goodwill, nor even the slightest consolation, from his metropolitan Church. On the contrary, if public reports were to be believed, it regarded him as a usurper of his see. At the end of these two letters is Lambert’s profession of obedience to Archbishop Renaud. From this one must conclude that the collection in question does not contain all the letters of our prelate, and that many others have been lost.

One of those which remain to us and deserves to be known is the twenty-ninth letter of the second part of the collection, addressed to Gerard, bishop of Thérouanne. Achard, canon and provost of Arras, after offending his bishop, had left his Church and taken refuge in that of Thérouanne, where he was retained contrary to the rules, although his bishop had gone himself to reclaim him and had more than once asked Gerard to send him back. Lambert complains of this violation of the canons and cites in this connection the authority of the Councils of Carthage and of Pope St. Leo the Great, copying a rather lengthy passage from the latter. The author thereby shows himself very learned in ecclesiastical discipline. This also appears from the twenty-fifth letter of the same collection, addressed to the regular canons of Guastines, where the same Achard had previously withdrawn without the bishop’s permission.

Lambert addressed two other letters of his, the thirty-fourth and thirty-sixth in the collection, to Pope Urban II, with the title “Father of fathers,” [Col. 0620D] which is equivalent to “bishop of bishops.” He also gives this title to Paschal II, Urban’s successor, though not always consistently. The first letter to Urban concerns the affair of Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi of Reims. To avoid repetition, however, we defer reporting it to the article on Robert, one of our historians of the First Crusade (*see Patrology*, vol. CLIII, in the appendix to King Godfrey). The other letter to the same pope is a simple recommendation on behalf of Gerard, bishop of Thérouanne; it was written after the council which that pontiff held at Nîmes in July 1096, on his return from France to Italy.

As many as twelve letters of Bishop Lambert to Pope Paschal are counted. The collection contains at least as many letters from Paschal to Lambert, several among both sets attesting the dignity of legate in Belgica Secunda with which our bishop was invested. In one of these letters he asks the Roman pontiff [Col. 0621A] to confirm the judgment which he had delivered in this capacity between John, bishop of Thérouanne, and the clerics of the Church of Ypres—a judgment from which the latter, having been condemned, wished to appeal to the Apostolic See.

In another, he entreats the same pope to uphold what he had already begun so successfully. The matter concerned a small abbey which Lambert had established under the Rule of St. Benedict, by authority of the Apostolic See and in dependence upon the Church of Arras, at a place called Saint-Préjet de Ferchères. The abbot of Saint-Préjet in the diocese of Noyon sought to claim it as dependent on his own monastery.

The last three letters to Paschal, the most prolix of all, concern disputes between the canons of Arras cathedral and the monks of Saint-Vaast on one side, and the canons of Tournai cathedral and the monks of Saint-Martin [Col. 0621B] on the other. These disputes, although over trifling interests, caused great disturbances in these Churches and more than once tested our bishop’s patience. At last he succeeded in settling them; and the 144th letter, the final one of the entire collection, reports to the pope how he had succeeded in reconciling, in particular, the interests of the canons and monks of Tournai. Lambert concludes this letter by earnestly entreating the pope, with profound faith and piety, to pray the Lord to show him mercy by forgiving his sins and removing him from the prison and darkness of this life. He makes the same request at the end of another of these letters, from which it is evident that this devout bishop felt the full weight of the episcopate and had the future blessings deeply at heart. Nearly all his other letters to the same pope are merely recommendations on behalf of persons who appealed to Lambert’s influence with this supreme pontiff. The last of all is preceded by the agreement or settlement he made between the canons of Tournai and the monks of Saint-Martin.

Lambert also addressed several letters to Archbishop Manasses II, his metropolitan. One of the most notable is the one he wrote in reply to the latter’s demand that a general interdict be observed in the diocese of Arras, just as he was enforcing it in that of Reims, because of the outrageous injury done to Hugh, bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne, who had been arrested and held prisoner in his own diocese. Lambert, surprised by such a proposal, first alleges the reasons he had for refusing to believe that it came from his archbishop. He then shows him, by several examples and by what had happened to Lambert himself on the way to the Council of Clermont, that this was neither the spirit nor the practice of the Church, and that only those who commit faults [Col. 0621D] ought to bear the penalty for them. An interdict is among the gravest penalties and would extend to an infinite number of innocent persons.

The collection presents only a single letter from Lambert to St. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, although there are two from Anselm to Lambert. It is the ninety-second, and is not otherwise especially interesting, except that it is written in fine terms and with great courtesy. Concerned about the holy archbishop’s health, Lambert asks him for news of it and for the help of his prayers, especially at the holy altar.

He makes the same request in the same terms to Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, to whom he addresses another of his letters, the ninety-ninth in the collection. This too is a letter of pure courtesy, well written, in which he tells Daimbert that he is sending him a pair of gloves embroidered with gold, together with a towel for the hands (*manuterge*).

[Col. 0622A] The 105th, 106th, and 109th letters, which likewise belong to Lambert, are also merely letters of courtesy and recommendation. The first of the three was written to King Louis the Fat, asking him to honor with an audience the bearer charged with communicating orally to this prince certain matters from our bishop. In this letter, as in several others, the author takes in the address only the title of priest, and most often adds, as another expression of humility, the description “unprofitable servant.” The other two letters named are addressed: one to Ralph the Green, archbishop of Reims, from whom there is one letter to Lambert; and the other to the legate Richard, bishop of Albano, who addresses one of his own to Lambert in the same collection and for whom there is another letter, in his favor, to Robert the Younger, count of Flanders.

One of Bishop Lambert’s fine and most instructive letters is the 110th of the collection, written to one of his uterine brothers, whose name is indicated only by an F. It concerns lying entirely, and seeks to inspire him with horror of it by copying for him several apt passages of Holy Scripture. The author wished to spare his brother the embarrassment of having posterity learn wherein he was guilty on this point. He leaves to the bearer of the letter the task of declaring it to him orally. Lambert mentions his sister-in-law, using the term *fratrissa* instead of *fratria*, which shows that his brother was married.

The letter addressed to one named Pomon, superior of a community of canons near Pavia, as appears from what follows, is curious. Two acquaintances of Lambert had told him that a canon of that house, who had subsequently become a monk, had seen and heard—apparently in sleep—St. Augustine celebrating [Col. 0622C] Mass at the altar standing at his tomb. Our prelate earnestly asks Pomon to send him an account of it, including the words which the saint had used in celebrating the holy mysteries. But in order to obtain something authentic, Lambert, as a man of judgment, asks Pomon to take care to state the year, indiction, day, and hour at which this event had occurred, and to specify under what pope and what bishop of Pavia it happened. It is otherwise unknown whether Pomon took care to satisfy Bishop Lambert’s laudable curiosity.

Almost all his other letters, which we pass over in silence, concern the ordinary affairs of his diocese or of those dioceses of the metropolitan province within which his legation extended. Some others are simple letters of recommendation, courtesy, or friendship; and all show the extensive connections of their author, not only in France but also in foreign lands.

[Col. 0622D] This is shown still better by nearly a hundred other letters in the collection which belong to him only because they are addressed to him or concern him in some manner. We have already given an account of a great number of them in treating those who wrote some of them: Pope Urban II; the legate Hugh, archbishop of Lyons; the archbishops of Reims, Renaud and Manasses II; William Good-Soul, archbishop of Rouen; St. Anselm of Canterbury; the bishops of Noyon, Rabod and Baudri; Poppo of Metz; and Odo of Cambrai. We shall proceed in the same way when we later speak of the other persons who wrote another part of the letters in the collection: Ralph the Green, archbishop of Reims; the bishops Ivo of Chartres, Galon of Paris, Walter of Maguelone, Lisiard or Lietard of Soissons; Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi of Reims; and perhaps some others as well. As to the authors of certain of these same letters, [Col. 0623A] to whom we shall give no separate articles, we shall now say a few words by identifying the letters which they wrote, although few of them are of interest.

Four belong to Hugh of Pierrefonds, bishop of Soissons, and a fifth is jointly his and Anselm’s, Anselm having recently been elected bishop of Beauvais. All are written to Lambert and contain nothing remarkable except the great confidence Hugh had in our prelate’s judgment and the close friendship which they had formed with one another; moreover, they were close relatives. Three of these letters concern in particular the injury which Hugh complained of receiving from the abbot of Saint-Médard and the satisfaction subsequently made to him. This bishop, to whom Ivo of Chartres addressed the forty-second of his letters, was brother of Nivelon II, lord of Pierrefonds, where he founded the monastery of Saint-Sulpice, dependent on the abbey of Marmoutier. Hugh held the see of Soissons [Col. 0623B] from 1092 to 1103. Having then undertaken the pilgrimage to Jerusalem, he died at Aquileia in Italy, where he had gone to embark from one of the ports of that country.

Four other letters in the same collection—the second, twenty-eighth, ninety-sixth, and 120th—all addressed to Lambert, belong to two bishops of Amiens: the first two to Gervin, who governed that Church from 1071 to 1102; and the other two to the celebrated St. Godfrey, his immediate successor. The latter, previously abbot of Nogent, was elected or confirmed bishop of Amiens at the Council of Troyes at the end of March 1104. He spent only ten years and some months in the episcopate, and even interrupted its functions for a time because of his strong attraction to solitude. He died at the abbey of Saint-Crespin at Soissons on 8 November 1115 and was buried there. Nicholas, [Col. 0623C] a monk of that place, of whom mention will be made later, took care to write his life. The four letters of these two bishops otherwise concern only ordinations, except the first, which invites Lambert to the ceremony for the translation of the relics of St. Fuscian. The two of St. Godfrey in particular are, one merely a simple *exeat*, and the other letters of orders. Elsewhere, however, there is another letter of this holy prelate, written to Baudri, bishop of Noyon, urging him to compose the history of the Church of Amiens, because he believed him to be the author of those of Cambrai and Thérouanne. This letter is dated from the abbey of Mont-Saint-Quentin, where Godfrey had first been a monk, in May 1108, and was translated into French by Jacques le Vasseur in his *Annals of the Church of Noyon*.

The twenty-fourth and fifty-second letters of the collection which we continue to describe concern the current affairs of the condition in which their author then found himself. This was Manasses, bishop of Cambrai and formerly archdeacon of the metropolitan church of Reims. His election, though legitimate and approved by the Apostolic See and the bishops of the province, caused in the Church of Cambrai a schism lasting about ten years. Gaucher, elected by the clergy, did not please the people, who in turn elected Manasses. Later, Gaucher was deposed and excommunicated at the Council of Clermont in 1095, and Manasses was ordained to govern this Church. But Gaucher, supported by Emperor Henry IV, succeeded in maintaining himself there. Manasses had undoubtedly died when, in 1105, Blessed Odo was elected to fill this see.

The twenty-sixth letter of the collection is merely a brief note from Gerard, bishop of Thérouanne from 1084 until about 1098, when he was deposed, asking the bishop of Arras to ordain as priest a deacon whom he was sending to him.

The forty-second is a request by the Church [Col. 0624A] of Noyon, headed by its dean, asking Lambert to consent to its recent election of Baudri as bishop and kindly to attend the ceremony of his consecration. It contains a fine eulogy of the bishop-elect; and what is said there of him, compared with what the author of the Chronicle of Cambrai says of himself, clearly shows that they were two very different persons.

In the forty-fourth letter, Guy, count of Ponthieu, a close relative of Lambert, urges him to be at Abbeville on the Saturday in the octave of Pentecost. The motive for so pressing an invitation was to attend the ceremony on the following Sunday, at which he was to make Prince Louis, son of King Philip—who later reigned as Louis the Fat—a knight.

The forty-fifth letter belongs to Clementia, countess of Flanders and mother of Count Baldwin [Col. 0624B] VII. Our prelate addressed to her the thirty-first and thirty-ninth of his own letters. In it she asks him to induce the archbishop of Reims to render her justice in her dispute with the clerics of Thérouanne cathedral.

There are two letters, the forty-seventh and fifty-fourth, from Philip of Champagne, bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne from 1093 until the end of that century. By the first he asks Lambert to confer sacred orders on clerics whom Poppo, bishop of Metz, had sent to him for that purpose, but whom he could not ordain. By the other he invites him to the dedication of his cathedral church. This last letter shows that there was an intimate union between the two bishops.

The sixty-first is a production of the pens of the cardinal-legates John and Benedict, whom Pope [Col. 0624C] Paschal II had sent into France to hold councils. In terms honorable to Lambert, they invite him, with the abbots of his diocese, to the council which they had summoned at Poitiers for November 1100. A postscript follows in the hand of Cardinal John alone, asking Lambert to continue his friendship and assuring him of John’s own friendship and of the confidence he placed in Lambert’s judgment.

One of the most interesting letters in the whole collection is the sixty-third, written to Lambert by Roger and Lisiard, archdeacons of Beauvais, in the name of all the clergy and all the people of that Church. It informs us of an event not found in the other records of our history. It is known in what deplorable condition the diocese of Beauvais stood at the beginning of the twelfth century, deprived of a bishop for two or three years. King Philip and Bertrade wished to install there Stephen of Garlande, who was himself very willing to put himself forward. But the pope and the wisest prelates of France, especially Ivo of Chartres, opposed them, and the intended plan could not succeed. Galon was then elected and consecrated to fill the vacant see; but the king in turn opposed this, and another bishop had to be sought. It cannot be said precisely in which of these three circumstances the event mentioned in the letter occurred: whether before Stephen of Garlande was proposed, after he had been rejected, or after Galon’s misfortune.

In any event, the clergy and people of Beauvais, grieving to find themselves without a shepherd, agreed to elect as their bishop Stephen, archdeacon of the Church of Paris, a worthy man suited to fill the office. But he steadfastly refused to consent, despite the delegation of the leading persons of the clergy sent to him for that purpose. A second deputation was sent; and, after his Church had consented to grant him, he finally accepted his election. It is clear [Col. 0625A] that Stephen of Garlande is not meant here: he was a layman and, far from refusing the office, openly coveted it. After giving Lambert this account, the archdeacons of Beauvais ask him to use his good offices with the pope in order to secure the success of their election, and accordingly to write him letters in due form. They add that they had obtained similar letters for this purpose from Archbishop Manasses and the other bishops of the province, who had recently held at Soissons an assembly otherwise unknown. Finally, they entreat him to enlist in this affair his good friend Cardinal-Legate John, already mentioned. Despite all these prudent precautions, the election of Archdeacon Stephen failed, like the other two; and Geoffrey succeeded Galon in the episcopal see of Beauvais.

The seventy-third letter is merely a recommendation to Bishop Lambert from the treasurer of Saint-Quentin, whose name is designated only by a J, in favor of the person who was to deliver it to him. But, since the author had no seal with which to affix his seal, he gives Lambert a sign by which to recognize the hand that writes to him.

The seventy-sixth is from Robert the Younger, count of Flanders, to announce to Lambert that he had been obliged to render the homage owed to the emperor, but that he had discharged this obligation without derogating in any respect from his Christian standing, his duties toward the Roman Church and that of Reims, or his regard for the dignity of the bishop of Arras. For the emperor—then Henry IV—was regarded in those regions as a schismatic and excommunicate.

The letter immediately following in the collection belongs to Ebremar, then patriarch of Jerusalem. [Col. 0625C] It is dated 3 April 1104, apparently as soon as he had been made patriarch, but did not arrive at Arras until the following 19 November. On it one sees the author’s lead seal, with a Greek inscription reading, “The Holy Sepulchre of Our Lord Jesus Christ,” and another Latin inscription declaring, “The seal of Ebremar, patriarch of Jerusalem.” The content of this letter consists of courtesies and an announcement to Lambert that he was sending him a gold ring and two crystal flasks filled with balm. Lambert replied in the seventy-eighth letter, which immediately follows the patriarch’s letter in the collection and was sent to him through an archdeacon of Thérouanne.

There are two letters from Richard, bishop of Albano. Sent as legate of the Apostolic See to France in 1104, he presided over the councils of Troyes and Beaugency held in that year; six years later he convened three more, one at Clermont, another at Toulouse, and the third at Fleury, or Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire. Of these there remain, as the sole record, two very brief letters from the legate. The two letters in the collection belonging to him are the eighty-fourth and 111th. The first is written to Robert, count of Flanders, to ask for his protection on behalf of Bishop Lambert, whom it praises highly in a few words. The other is addressed to Lambert himself, urging him to abolish the bad custom introduced into the diocese of Arras, where there were sometimes three holders of one and the same church office: when one of the three died, the other two continued to enjoy, dividing between them, what had belonged to the deceased. The collection presents no reply by our bishop to Richard’s letter. But it contains another which Lambert wrote to him on a different occasion, using lofty titles of honor and the description “friend,” on behalf of the person who was to deliver it. Richard had first been [Col. 0626A] a canon of Metz cathedral; his attachment to the Apostolic See raised him from there to the highest dignities of the Church.

The 112th is from Gildouin, or Geldouin, who, after having been abbot of Anchin and then deposed amid the divisions which agitated that monastery at the end of the preceding century, was again sought to fill the same office. Bishop Lambert had some part in this latter design because of the esteem in which he held the former abbot. Gildouin wrote this letter to thank him and to declare his aversion to every dignity. He was then in his retreat at Saint-Bertin, from which he went shortly thereafter to England, where he ended his days around 1112.

After his refusal, the monks of Anchin elected as abbot Alvise, then prior of Saint-Vaast at Arras. But because he was professed from the abbey of Saint-Bertin, and they needed the consent of Lambert, [Col. 0626B] its abbot, they addressed themselves to the bishop of Arras, asking him to obtain it. This is the subject of their letter, the 114th in the collection. Moved by their request, Lambert wrote to the abbot of Saint-Bertin, and his letter is the 116th.

The 119th is an expression of thanks from Walter II, abbot of Mont-Sainte-Catherine, otherwise called the Trinity at the gate of Rouen, to our bishop for giving his monastery a church in the diocese of Arras. In recognition, he promises in his own name and that of the community that after Lambert’s death prayers shall be offered for him equal to those customarily offered for each abbot of that house, and, for each canon of his cathedral, equal to those offered for each monk.

The 130th makes known to us a bishop of Nantes named Robert, who is absent from the lists or catalogues of that Church and must be placed between Benedict of Brittany and Briccius. It is a formal [Col. 0626C] letter addressed to our prelate on behalf of one named Thiesbold. Having left the diocese of Nantes in order to attend the schools of other regions, he was then at Arras, where malicious persons accused him of various crimes. Robert attests his innocence in recommending him to Bishop Lambert, and testifies that there is nothing in his birth or conduct which could hinder his advancement to sacred orders and ecclesiastical dignities.

Of all the letters in the second part of the collection, there remain only the hundredth and the hundred and first to be made known. They are very short, together with several others of which we defer speaking until the articles on the men of letters to whom they belong, which will appear later. The hundredth is a note from Henry I, king of England and duke of Normandy, thanking Lambert for certain counsels he had received from him and assuring him of his goodwill. The following letter is another note from a cardinal-priest [Col. 0626D] of the holy Roman Church, whose name is indicated only by an O, but who may be the same man who bore the pallium to Thomas II, archbishop of York. Indeed, on that other occasion his name too is not otherwise specified. Some call him Odeleric. Be that as it may, he appoints Lambert to meet him at Corbie, where he was to communicate the pope’s orders to him.

In the third part of the collection there are fourteen charters, or “privileges,” as they are styled, arranged in chronological order. They are so many monuments to the beneficent and generous piety of Bishop Lambert toward as many abbeys and other churches, both in his own diocese and in neighbouring places. Besides distinctive evidences of their author’s piety, they contain many others that may greatly assist in illustrating the history of the country, especially the ecclesiastical history of the metropolitan see of Reims. There is no privilege which is not [Col. 0627A] subscribed by several abbots, canons, and other persons holding office, from which light may be drawn for correcting the catalogues of the abbots of the region. It may be added that these privileges are well written in every respect.

This part of the collection is followed by a fourth, containing forty-six further documents. But since these are later than our prelate, we defer reporting on them to another occasion.

**2.** We are also indebted to Bishop Lambert for another highly interesting collection. It is the principal collection of the canons—thirty-two in number—promulgated at the great council of Clermont in Auvergne, held in 1095 and attended by him, as has been said. We call it the principal collection because there are three others: one containing nine, another twenty-four, and the third ten further canons, all said to belong [Col. 0627B] to the same council. It would in any event be very difficult to give a decisive reason why Lambert, who took care to collect the thirty-two of the first recension, did not add the forty-three of the three other collections. On this point only mere conjectures present themselves, and it is better to suppress them [Col. 0628A] than to weary the reader, who would not thereby become better informed.

That the first recension is due to our prelate’s care is attested by a manuscript more than four hundred years old, from the end of the sixteenth century, which bears at its head the following title: “Book of Lambert, Bishop of Arras,” and in which the thirty-two canons are read consecutively. It was from this same manuscript that George Couvenier, doctor of theology and scholasticus of Saint-Pierre at Douai, made a copy of the same canons, which he sent to Binius; by means of it Binius recorded the variants of these canons in his general collection of councils. Apart from these variants, the text was found to be the same as in the edition already published by Antonio Augustinus. At the end of his recension Lambert took care to indicate the number of archbishops, bishops, and abbots present at this council. But, as [Col. 0628B] we have already observed in accounting for its acts in the article on Pope Urban II, among all the writers who have undertaken to inform us of this number, perhaps not two agree exactly on this point.

[Col. 0627]

## I. HERE BEGIN THE ACTS BY WHICH THE CITY OF ARRAS, UNDER URBAN, BISHOP OF THE ROMAN AND APOSTOLIC SEE, HAVING CAST OFF THE YOKE OF SUBJECTION TO CAMBRAI, WAS RESTORED TO ITS ANCIENT DIGNITY.

[Col. 0627C] Therefore, in the year of Christ 1092, on the third Ides of August [11 August], when Lord Gerard the Younger, bishop of Cambrai, who had also presided over the see of Arras, had died, the Church of Arras, long deprived of the comfort of its own shepherd, poured out with groaning into the ears of Pope Urban II its long travail, calamity, and spoliation of its possessions. The pope, exercising care for all churches and mindful of the dignity of the Church of Arras—indeed, wishing to restore twelve bishoprics to the metropolitan see of Reims—wrote to Lord Raynold, venerable archbishop of Reims, on behalf of the aforesaid Church of Arras, in these words:

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Raynold, venerable archbishop of Reims: greeting and [Col. 0627D] apostolic blessing.
>
> “Let your brotherhood know,” etc. See under Urban II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLI.

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “The Church of Arras,” etc. See above.

### Letter of the Church of Arras to Lord Rainold, Archbishop of Reims

To the most reverend father Raynold, archbishop of Reims, the clergy and people of the Church of Arras: constancy in prayer and faithful obedience in all things. Our Lord Jesus Christ, seeing—indeed, seeing—the affliction of our Church, long and disgracefully oppressed by the tyrannical yoke of the people of Cambrai through many revolutions of years, and pitying the peril of its children, who through lack of pastoral teaching were falling into diverse vices, has in these days resolved, by the command of the apostolic lord Urban, by the assent also of our prince Robert and of the rejoicing whole clergy and people, to restore a proper ruler to that Church. We therefore implore God’s mercy not to abandon us in this undertaking. We also seek the consolation of your fatherhood: do not delay to send from your side to the election itself, sought from the Holy Spirit by prayer and fasting, a discerning and noble cleric or abbot, who may take part in this sacred ministry as your representative. For we [Col. 0628D] are not seeking any pretext for delay, but are prepared to obey at once the reasonable command of the apostolic lord.

### Letter Sent by Rainold, Archbishop of Reims, to the Church of Arras

Raynold, archbishop of Reims, to the Church of Arras: greeting and blessing in the Lord Jesus.

Let your brotherhood know that we have instructed the clerics of Cambrai to come to Reims for the council which we are to hold on the Sunday on which is sung *My eyes are ever toward the Lord* [the third Sunday of Lent], and to bring with them their privileges, by whose authority they wish to subject your Church to the dominion of their bishop. We therefore command you [Col. 0629A] to come to that same council, supported by the authorities and judgments of the Fathers which you moreover possess from blessed Remigius, your founder, and not timidly to produce them before the council. If your arguments gain the place of victory, we shall not permit you, by command of the lord pope and counsel of the whole council, to be defrauded of your desire.

Thus invited to the council, the Church of Arras poured forth before the entire council this complaint of its long calamity:

May the provident care of the lord archbishop hear, and may the devout assembly of this holy synod also hear, the complaints which their sister, the Church of Arras, makes in her need. This city, formerly entrusted and supported by its own proper shepherd and subject only to the holy Church of Reims, one of the ancient and nobler cities of the entire metropolitan see of Reims, flourished in every form of ecclesiastical discipline. That it possessed both the name and the dignity of a city is testified by the priest Orosius in his book *Against the Pagans*, where he makes frequent mention of it in his treatise. The chronicle books, moreover, which treat most certainly of the founders of cities, report that Rome and Reims were founded by Romulus and Remus, Soissons and Arras by Gnaeus Pompey, and the remaining neighbouring cities by certain Gauls. That this is a city and had its own bishop is gathered from the summary of the holy canons in the Churches of Arles, Vienne, Lyons, and indeed in this holy Church of Reims, where the Gallican metropolitan sees and their suffragans are enumerated. Among them this city of Arras is found as the fourth under Reims and placed before Cambrai. Thus one reads in the *Life of Saint Remigius*: “At the same time King Clovis received from the emperor Anastasius the codicils for the consulship. Hormisdas also, pontiff of the Roman See, committed his vicariate in the kingdom of Clovis to Saint Remigius, bishop of the ancient metropolis, which at that time had under it twelve cities and the same number of bishops presiding over them.” Likewise, in the *Life of Blessed Vedast*: “Saint Remigius, therefore, by divine dispensation and the salutary counsel of priests, ordained blessed Vedast bishop and sent him to the city of Arras to preach the word of life,” etc. Likewise, the testament issued by blessed Remigius himself confirms that the city of Arras had its own principal bishop, in this manner:

> [Col. 0629D] “I, Remigius, have assigned to the Church of Arras, for which, the Lord consenting, I consecrated my dearest brother Vedast as bishop, two estates from the gift of King Clovis—namely Orcos and Sabucetum—for the support of the clerics; and I command that twenty solidi also be given for the remembrance of my name. I, Remigius, have reread, signed, and subscribed my testament and, with God’s help, have completed it in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

After the excommunication against the violator of this testament had been pronounced, Bishop Vedast was first to respond:

> “Whom my father Remigius cursed, I curse; and whom he blessed, I bless.”

Bishop Genebold was also present and subscribed. Bishops Lupus, Medard, Benedict, and Eulogius said the same. Since, therefore, it is evident that the Church of Arras, supported by such numerous and great authorities, had its own principal bishop, that same city being more populous than before, and its clergy and people being unable longer to bear the absence of their native shepherd, demands that the shepherd whom it formerly lost be restored as its own. In the year of Christ 1092, on the third Ides of August [11 August], when Lord Gerard the Younger, bishop of Cambrai, died—who, if only he had endeavoured to benefit the see of Arras as it happened that he presided over it—the aforesaid Church, miserably afflicted inwardly and outwardly, poured into the ears of Urban, lord pontiff of Rome, its long travail and grief. This most prudent father, understanding that the time had come to have mercy upon it and possessing the authority to restore ill-ordered things to their former dignity, [Col. 0630B] granted the Church of Arras free power to choose for itself its own bishop according to the ordinances of the holy canons. He also commissioned you, venerable Father Raynold, not to delay consecrating the man elected.

That a shepherd ought to be restored to the same Church, which desires to have one, because it is both a city and very populous and formerly had one, can be gathered from the following judgments of the holy Fathers. For in one of the letters of blessed Pope Clement one reads:

> “Peter, my master, commanded us to send prudent and simple bishops to each city to which he had not sent them. But you are to consecrate and send bishops through your dioceses: one in each city, not two or three; nor in villages, castles, or small cities, lest their name be made cheap.”

This is finely continued in the Council of Sardica: a bishop is to be ordained in those cities which have had bishops, or in a city that is of such a kind or so populous that it deserves to have a bishop. Felix, bishop of Selemsela, likewise said at the Second Council of Africa:

> “Also, if it pleases your holiness, I submit that dioceses which have never received bishops should not have them; but a diocese which once had one should have its own bishop; and if, as time passes and the faith increases, the people of God has multiplied and wishes to have its own ruler, then, by the will of him in whose authority the diocese has been established, it should have its own bishop.”

All said: “It pleases us.”

That the aforesaid pope laudably determined this matter, and that it lies within his discretion to separate those joined together and unite several bishoprics, may be gathered from the *Life* or *Register* of blessed Gregory, who often united three or four and often separated those that had been united. Thus he writes also to Felix, bishop of Acropolis:

> “Since Velina, Buxentum, and Blandana, situated near you, are known to lack episcopal governance, we therefore solemnly impose upon your brotherhood the task of visitation over them.”

Likewise, to Januarius, bishop of Caralis in Sardinia:

> “It has come to us that in a place situated within the province of Sardinia and called Phausiana, it was customary for a bishop to be ordained; but this custom, because of the necessities of circumstances, has been abolished for a long time. Since we have learned that, because of a lack of priests, certain pagans remain there and, living in a brutish fashion, are wholly ignorant of God’s worship, we exhort your brotherhood to hasten to ordain a bishop there according to the ancient custom—one, namely, who is suited to this task in character and speech and who may zealously endeavour, with pastoral concern, to lead the erring to the Lord’s flock—so that, while this benefit for souls lies unprovided there, neither may you be found to have asked for something superfluous nor may we repent of having restored in vain what was formerly destroyed.”

Therefore, holy Fathers and lords, under the protection of the Holy Spirit, in whose name you have been assembled, look upon your sister, the Church of Arras. Deliver her from the yoke of servitude under which she has long been unjustly held captive, lest, worn out at last by weariness, she begin to wander after the tracks of the flocks, bereft of a shepherd.

When the people of Arras had, as they had been instructed, read aloud in full council this proclamation and also the deliberation of their Church, while the clerics of Cambrai, on the contrary, neither produced the privileges by which they claimed the Church of Arras as their possession nor were able by any reasoning to invalidate the authorities read there, the lord archbishop, like a pious father concerned for the restoration of that Church, ordered that the apostolic letters addressed to him be brought forth and read. They contained the following:

> [Col. 0631B] “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Raynold, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing. Let your brotherhood know that the Church of Arras,” etc., as above.

Finally, at the archbishop’s command, the book of the holy canons was brought forward. Having taken it, the notary read this judgment before all:

> Hosius, bishop, said at the Council of Sardica: “Permission to ordain a bishop should not be granted indiscriminately. For if suddenly some village or small city, for which one priest is sufficient, should wish to ordain a bishop for itself, so that the name of bishop and the authority of the highest honour may be debased, persons invited from another province ought not to make a bishop there, except in cities which have had bishops, or in a city or place so populous that it deserves to have a bishop.”

The synod replied: “It pleases us.”

Lord Burchard, abbot of [Col. 0631D] Saint-Basle, and Dudo, chaplain, who had recently returned from the presence of the apostolic lord, also rose and testified that the same pope had instructed and commanded the archbishop through them to ordain a bishop in the Church of Arras without delay. Upon all these matters the archbishop sought advice from the bishops present there—namely Lord Hugh of Soissons, Lord Elinand of Laon, Lord Rabbo of Vermand, Lord Fulk of Beauvais, Lord Gerwin of Amiens, and Lord Gerard of Thérouanne—and from the entire council. But when the bishops, together with the archdeacons, the higher-ranking persons of the clergy present, and certain abbots, had returned from consultation, they requested from the archbishop a postponement for deciding so great a matter.

When Galcherus, archdeacon of Cambrai, with other clerics of that Church, saw that the lord archbishop was unwilling to comply with the request for a postponement but was instead insisting on obedience to the apostolic decision, he sprang into the midst and attempted to disturb the cause of the Church of Arras. He declared that the Church of Arras ought by no right to have its own bishop, and that he himself or the clerics of Cambrai were prepared to prove this before the lord pope. On hearing this, the archbishop advised Lord Galbert, provost, and the other men of Arras not to hesitate, for the confirmation of their cause and satisfaction of those protesting, to seek again the presence of the apostolic lord. The whole council consenting, eight days were appointed, namely from the Sunday before the Ascension of the Lord until the following Sunday, within which each party should present itself before the apostolic lord, and the party arriving first should wait for the other.

When silence had been made, the lord archbishop at last settled the matter in this way. So that they might know this with certainty, he publicly declared it to the entire synod: if the party of Arras neglected to go, he would hear them no further in this matter; but if the people of Cambrai refused to go, he would ordain a bishop in the Church of Arras without delay, according to the command of the lord pope. How the clerics of Arras, John and Drogo, remained nine days in the apostolic lord’s presence, and how the lord pope then confirmed for a second time what he had first decreed, is evident from his letter, which spoke thus to the archbishop:

> [Col. 0632C] “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop in Christ, Raynold of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “The clerics of Arras,” etc. See above.

When these letters had been reverently received and read by the archbishop, he privately asked the aforesaid bearers of the letters whom the Church of Arras proposed to choose as bishop. They informed the archbishop of the names of three persons, as they supposed their Church desired. He particularly praised and commended one of them, Lord Lambert of Guînes, and advised that he be chosen. When the aforesaid clerics, accepting the archbishop’s advice, pressed him to send his own letters together with those of the apostolic lord, he replied that it was neither necessary nor fitting for him to add his own letters further to the pope’s letters, which for the second time commanded the Church of Arras concerning the ordination of a bishop and had decided the matter. “For it is yours,” he said, “to elect; ours to consecrate.”

Thus these clerics, instructed by their archbishop’s counsel, came to Arras and brought the apostolic lord’s letters to the clergy and people of that Church. Their form is as follows:

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> [Col. 0633A] “Two clerics of your Church,” etc. See above.

The clergy and people of Arras, therefore, recognizing that the will and authority of the lord pope directing them to choose a bishop had now been sent to them again, appointed by common agreement the sixth Ides of July [10 July] as the day for holding the election, after proclaiming a three-day fast and litanies. For this day they took pains to invite by sealed letter not only clerics of their own see but certain men of the neighbouring diocese, especially the canons of the community of Lille, as friends of their fraternity and association, and especially because they knew that the treasure they desired resided in that Church. The letter sent to them was as follows:

> “Gualbert, provost of the Church of Arras, together with the dean and all the children of the Church, to Lord Gualter, provost of Lille, the dean, and the other brethren: greeting and love in Christ Jesus.
>
> “As is not unknown to you, most beloved brethren, our Church, formerly deprived by the oppression of the people of Cambrai of its estates, ornaments, and every earthly adornment, in these days, when after Lord Gerard’s death it lacked a shepherd, approached the mercy of the apostolic lord Urban and anxiously laid before him its calamity. This most prudent father, understanding that the time had come to have mercy upon it, declared that it should choose a bishop of its own. Therefore, dearest brethren, by the love of God, love of neighbour, and love of holy mother Church, we earnestly entreat and beseech you to deign to send to this election, which we have appointed to be held next Sunday, three or four of your brethren who, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, may provide us counsel and assistance in so great a work. Among them, setting every excuse aside, take particular care to send Lord Clarembald, Lord Lambert the Cantor, and another Lambert of Comines. Farewell.”

Accordingly, on the sixth Ides of July [10 July], which was then a Sunday, when a very great multitude of clergy and people had assembled in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, after the solemnities of Mass had ended, the Holy Spirit had been invoked, and the pope’s letters commanding that a bishop be ordained in the present see had also been recapitulated from the pulpit, Lord Lambert, a native of Guînes, but a canon and precentor by title of the community of Lille, called by God and long desired by the whole aforesaid Church, was first unanimously nominated by name in the chapter of Blessed Mary by Lord Gualbert the provost, Guibert the dean, and the other canons, and was then presented before the sight of the whole Church. Thus, with the Lord’s consent, elected by the clergy and acclaimed and praised for the third time by the people, though unwilling and resisting strongly, he was chosen, taken, and enthroned in the episcopal seat.

While he wept and in no way consented to become bishop, and while his dean Ingelran and the other canons of Lille wept bitterly and grievously endured what seemed like the seizure of their fellow canon and precentor, the judgment of the apostolic lord was read, containing this form:

> [Col. 0634A] “By apostolic authority we forbid anyone elected by the canonical consent of clergy and people to evade the election imposed upon him through any pretext in this new ordination.”

The canons of Lille, considering the apostolic prohibition, acquiesced, although unwillingly, on the condition that the Church of Arras should canonically request from the community of Lille that he be lawfully given to it as bishop. The Church of Arras took diligent care to fulfil this. The entire city rejoicing at the successful canonical election of the shepherd so long desired, they sent letters to the archbishop asking him to consecrate the aforesaid elect. The archbishop’s reply was as follows:

> “Raynold, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to Lord Gualbert and the whole community of the Church of Arras: greeting and blessing in the Lord Jesus.
>
> “You have written to us asking us to state the time at which we would wish to consecrate your elect. But since that consecration appears, according to the sanction of the canons, to belong not only to our authority but also to that of our fellow bishops, we have judged that it would by no means be fitting to state a day for this consecration to you without their counsel. Yet, since at the feast of Saint Mary in the middle of August we shall hold a great assembly of bishops and clerics at Reims, we shall not delay to inform you what counsel we have received from them concerning this matter, and the time at which we ought to consecrate your elect. Farewell.”

On that day the Church of Arras again presented itself before the lord archbishop at Reims through these persons: Lords Abo, Heribert, John, and another John. From them he again requested a second postponement of this consecration until the feast of All Saints. But the oft-mentioned Church, worn down by the long weariness of desolation and unable to consent to such uncanonical delays, took steps to seek for the third time the gentleness of the lord pope. Therefore two clerics were sent, namely Odo, cantor of the Church, and John the deacon, who presented this letter to the lord pope:

> [Col. 0634D] “To the venerable and magnificent Urban, pope of the entire holy Church, the devoted clergy and people of Arras: unceasing prayer and complete submission of a mind humbly bowed.
>
> “With full hearts we render immeasurable thanks to our Creator and Restorer, who, inspiring and moving your heart, has deigned to visit and free us, hitherto oppressed and groaning through many revolutions of years, from the yoke of our stepmother, namely the Church of Cambrai. You have strengthened by canonical writing and apostolic authority our return to ancient liberty, testifying that the Church of Arras was one of the nobler cities of the metropolitan see of Reims and a principal episcopal see, possessing its own diocese and other pontifical rights; and you commanded us, in accordance with the sacred canons, to choose a shepherd worthy before God and men. This we have done, following the example of the holy Fathers, by a three-day fast, tearful prayers, and certain alms: namely Lambert of Guînes, a religious man, who waters the hearts of the faithful with an abundant fountain of preaching, so that many thousands of the devout people cry out: ‘A great prophet has arisen among us,’ and, ‘God has visited his people.’ We therefore hold him bound by the chain of your obedience, awaiting through you the fulfilment for us of the mercy of God, from whom all blessings proceed.

> “For we, holy ruler, obeying you in all things as your clemency commanded, have already twice sent an embassy to the archbishop of Reims concerning his consecration, that he might either consecrate him or send him to you with his letters to be consecrated. But he, delaying to obey your holy and canonical command, has found a postponement perilous to the souls of the faithful and supported by no reason, as your dignity will be able to discern from the report of these brethren. Now therefore, pious Father, compelled by this most serious necessity, we are constrained to return to you as our sole refuge under God, so that you may not delay, for love of him by whose blood we have been washed, to fulfil what you have holily and worthily begun for God. We humbly ask that, in complete obedience, within a period pleasing to your determination, you command the archbishop to consecrate him, or order him brought to your dignity for consecration, lest, through evasion, your command now imposed on the archbishop for the third time and proclaimed throughout almost every region of Gaul should appear to be rendered void.”

The lord pope, therefore, pitying the distress of the Church of Arras—and indeed wondering at the archbishop’s delay in bringing so sacred a business to an end—sent a sealed letter to the same archbishop in these words:

> [Col. 0635C] “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother and fellow bishop Raynold of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “What we have decreed concerning the Church of Arras,” etc. See above.

### Letter Sent by the Lord Pope to the Elect of Arras

[Col. 0635D]

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow priest Lambert, elect of the Church of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “We rejoice concerning you in the Lord, dearest brother,” etc. See above.

Therefore, after receiving and reading the lord pope’s letters, the archbishop wrote to the elect of Arras in these words:

> “Raynold, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to his most beloved brother and fellow priest Lambert: greeting and blessing in the Lord Jesus.
>
> “We have received the letters which the lord pope sent us concerning your consecration, and we have also seen a copy of those sent to you. After reading them, we transmitted them to our fellow bishop of Soissons and directed him to transmit them to the other suffragans, so that, after taking counsel from them, we might respond to your brotherhood. Therefore we command you to send one of your envoys to us by the octave of Saint Andrew, through whom we may write to your belovedness what we intend to do concerning all those matters which the lord pope has enjoined upon us concerning you. Farewell.”

But we—that is, the clerics of Arras—sent our envoys to him on the appointed day. Yet we received neither a definite date for the consecration nor his letters. Nevertheless, we refused to desist from the work begun. We sent our elect to him with the following attached letter:

> [Col. 0636B] “To the beloved father and lord Raynold, archbishop of Reims by God’s appointment, whom we truly love and honour, the clergy and people of the Church of Arras, together with Lambert, though an unworthy servant of his holiness: true affection, with prayers and obedience.
>
> “We render many thanks to the dignity of your excellency because hitherto, like a pious father, you have gladly provided us assistance and have promised to be kindly disposed toward us in every part of our cause. But we greatly wonder that your fatherhood has become lukewarm at the conclusion of our affair, since, within the time appointed by the apostolic lord to your magnificence for the consecration of our elect, you have neither solemnly summoned our elect to consecration by your letters, as we expected, nor set a definite day within the prescribed time. But now, since the consecration can no longer take place within the thirty-day limit, we ask you most peacefully at least to be willing to give us letters under your authority, to be carried to the apostolic lord, as he has commanded, concerning the consecration of our elect. Farewell.”

Accordingly, the bishop-elect of Arras, in obedience to the lord pope, though summoned to consecration by his metropolitan, Lord Raynold, on grounds not altogether reasonable, nevertheless—lest arrogance or injustice be imputed to him—presented himself to the archbishop at Reims on 17 December, then a Sunday, in accordance with the tenor and deadline fixed for him by the lord pope. The archbishop, however, having adopted counsel more shrewd than prudent, sent the bishop-elect of Arras to Rome to the lord pope, supported by the attestations of letters both of his own and of the Church of Arras.

Therefore the bishop-elect of Arras, Lord Odo the cantor, Achard master of the schools, and Drogo provost of Aubigny, with their attendants, left the city of Reims on 24 December, then the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. At the city of Châlons, in the monastery of All Saints, they were honourably received by Lord Odo, the venerable abbot of the canons living there in common; and on the feast of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, they were escorted as far as the city of Troyes by Brother Nevelon, priest and canon of the said monastery. Although at Troyes he stayed amid danger and fear because of the hostility of Philip, king of the Franks, and Robert, count of Flanders, yet, through God’s mercy, he reached Molesme in the territory of Duke Odo in peace. There he waited for Lord Walter of Douai, formerly castellan, a religious man though a layman.

At last, rejoicing and comforted by the arrival of Lord Walter of Douai, he undertook the labour and difficulties of the roads. At Dijon, the notable castle of the duke of Burgundy, he lodged for two days in order to refresh both his horses and riders. While he remained there, there arrived that burning and shining lamp in the house of God, praiseworthily honourable and honourably praiseworthy, Lord Hugh, primate of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See. When the cause of the bishop-elect of Arras became known, the venerable aforesaid primate and legate of the Apostolic See, Lord Hugh, conducted the bishop-elect himself and all his company with him, through the lord abbot of Cluny, a man of great name and religion, his friend and namesake. At Lyons he detained them for six days because of the excessive flooding of the waters and the severity of winter, and abundantly supplied every necessity.

Having at last received the blessing of so great a pontiff, the bishop-elect of Arras and his travelling companions set out more securely. After many perils of road and winter, they entered the portico of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, on the Friday before the Sunday *Esto mihi in Deum protectorem* (“Be to me a protecting God”). Lest any injury be inflicted on them by the Guibertines, early on the following Saturday they sent their bishop-elect ahead to Lord Pope Urban, who was then staying in Rome at Santa Maria Nuova.

The bishop-elect, prostrating himself at the feet of Lord Pope Urban, tearfully asked the lord pope to release him from that election. He said that he was unsuitable and ought not to be called to so unbearable a burden: both because of the harassment of Henry, the excommunicated emperor, to whose empire Cambrai had hitherto belonged; because of the persecution by the clergy and laity of Cambrai, wealthy, powerful, and very worldly-wise; and also because of the extreme devastation and poverty of the temporal resources and religious estate of the Church of Arras.

But the most blessed pope, having granted absolution and given his blessing, received him with the holy kiss, as is the custom of the Apostolic See, and, making light of all these things, said to him: “Brother, the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us,” and other words of encouragement which do not now fully occur to memory. At last he added: “Brother, have you found lodging?” And: “Where are your fellow pilgrims?” He answered: “I have not yet found lodging, but I left my companions at blessed Peter’s in the portico.” Hearing this, the pope at once ordered Lord Daibert, archbishop of Pisa, to be summoned, and said to him: “Receive this brother of ours, Lambert, bishop-elect of Arras, into lodging; and you and Peter Leonis must see as quickly as possible that he, his people, and his goods are brought safely to us from the portico of Saint Peter.”” And this was done.

When the lord pope gave him an opportunity and place to speak, he again, as before, prostrated himself at his feet, begging that for God’s sake he be released from the election imposed upon him. But the lord pope did not assent even to this request. Moreover, the aforesaid canons and those who had come with him to Rome earnestly implored the lord pope to have pity on them and on their Church, and not delay consecrating their bishop-elect. Having taken counsel, the lord pope, on an appointed day and in the absence of the bishop-elect, caused the entire case of the Church of Arras to be recited before his bishops, cardinals, and the Romans. When the Romans heard it, they requested that the bishop of Ostia be appointed for them. But the lord pope, acting prudently lest the new plantation of the Church of Arras be uprooted, did not grant the Romans’ request in this matter. After some days, however, he privately addressed the frequently mentioned bishop-elect and, in the name of the Lord and on behalf of blessed Peter, commanded him to undertake this obedience for the remission of his sins.

At length, yielding to divine appointment and apostolic obedience, he was consecrated bishop at Rome, at Santa Maria Nuova, by the often-mentioned Lord Apostolic Urban, in the year of Christ 1093, on 19 March, then the Sunday *Laetare Jerusalem* (“Rejoice, Jerusalem”), in the presence of the venerable bishops John of Tusculum, Humbald of Sabina, John of Porto, Bruno of Segni, Lord Daibert archbishop of the Pisans, the cardinal-priests, and a very great multitude of Romans.

Having been confirmed bishop of Arras, as is canonical, by the privilege and authority of letters from the Apostolic See, he sent Drogo ahead with certain companions, and afterwards Odo the cantor and Achard master of the schools. He himself, accompanied by Lord Ralph, archbishop of Tours, and retaining Walter of Douai with him, left Rome on the Friday after the Sunday *Quasi modo geniti* (“As newborn babes”), entered the sea at Ostia, and, after some stormy dangers, reached the much-desired port of Pisa. From there they sent Odo the cantor and Walter of Douai ahead to Chiusa.

There they found Peter, archbishop of Aix.

> [Note: [Col. 0637] Read “Aix,” that is, Aix-en-Provence. The clerics of Arras did not know how to render in Latin the name of this archbishop, who is commonly called *l’archevêque d’Aix* (“the archbishop of Aix”).]

The archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Arras again entered the sea and anchored at Genoa. Leaving the archbishop of Aix there, the fellow pilgrims from Tours and Arras, joined at Chiusa in Lombardy by their travelling companions Odo the cantor and Walter of Douai, prosperously reached Lyons; there they parted. Thus, through God’s mercy, Lord Lambert was devoutly received by the clerics and citizens of Arras on Pentecost Day, and before the third hour was enthroned in the episcopal seat by the authority of blessed Peter and obedience to the Roman Church.

But since we have made a brief digression, let us return our pen to the order of events.

> “To Lord Urban, most reverend pope of the holy and Apostolic See: Raynold, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, though unworthy, sends in the Lord the most abundant offering of salvation, service, and due submission.
>
> “After the letters first sent to us by your fatherhood, it pleased your apostolic majesty, most serene Father, to send us others again, commanding by precept that, within thirty days after seeing your letters, we should not delay to consecrate the bishop-elect of the Church of Arras as bishop. Your prudence also added that, if any cause should arise on account of which we feared to undertake that office, we should send him to you to be consecrated, with the attestation of our letters.
>
> “Therefore, having received the written commands of this injunction of yours, lest we presume anything without consulting our fellow bishops and fellow priests—for it is certainly established that this consecration depends upon both their authority and ours—we sent the schedule of your commands to every one whom we could reach, and asked the opinion of each, that they might provide us with such advice in this matter as would neither conflict with obedience to you nor diminish the dignity of the Church of Reims.
>
> “Accordingly, this was the unanimous voice and judgment of all our bishops and clerics: that we should indeed withhold our hand from consecrating that bishop-elect, but should send him to you, since your letters commanded this, and should leave to your decision whatever your exalted prudence might decree ought to be done. For they feared, and still fear, lest the people of Cambrai, taking occasion from this act, should sever themselves from the Church of Reims; both because their city is regarded as belonging to another kingdom, and because the king of that kingdom has long been hostile both to us and to the Roman Church.
>
> “They further added that it would be a very damaging exchange if the Church of Reims, while consenting that Arras should have a bishop, should lose Cambrai, which is six times more compact and wealthier than Arras. We therefore beseech your excellence, most holy Father—and our bishops and clerics beseech you—that you, who preside in the citadel and watchtower of all the Churches, may so moderate this affair that no one, God forbid, may on that account condemn the disposition of your decrees, and that the Church of Reims may suffer no loss of its dignity in your times.
>
> “Nevertheless, we who have resolved always to comply with your decisions, whatever form the consecration may take, shall, once your dignity has consecrated him, kindly receive the consecrated man and thereafter honour him as our bishop and suffragan. We further wish your exaltedness to know that we have by no means delayed this affair so long in order either to strive at any time against your commands or to detract in any respect from that lord. We judge him worthy not merely of this honour, but worthy by right to receive the summit of any other promotion whatsoever. May your blessedness remain unharmed in the Lord.”

> “To Urban, pope by the grace of God, most fervent in zeal for good and most excellent restorer of the Churches: the Church of Arras, breathing again in some measure, the yoke of undue servitude cast off, wishes to live and flourish for ever in Christ, with the offering of prayers and obedience.
>
> “We render many thanks to the praiseworthy fatherhood of your holiness. And though we have been wearied by a fourfold journey, nevertheless we both extol and embrace in you the virtue of perseverance; for in the restoration of our Church there is found in you no ‘yes and no.’ Rather, visited by you at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, we are granted our ancient liberty and receive the rights of our own diocese.
>
> “Therefore, let the whole fellowship of the perfected rejoice, because health recovered by one member becomes joy to the whole body of Christ. As your sublimity commanded, we delivered your letters concerning the consecration of our bishop-elect to the archbishop, and presented the same bishop-elect within the thirty-day term appointed by your authority. That he delayed to consecrate him we attribute not to his negligence, but to the ordinance of God, from whom is all power. You shall learn in due order, from the brothers reporting them, what grounds for delay he advanced.
>
> “Now therefore, because of the pressure of time, the imminence of dangers, and the poverty of a Church long afflicted in its resources, we send him to your excellence with a few brothers for consecration, earnestly beseeching you through Christ and in Christ that our bishop-elect, raised to the episcopal mitre, may be returned to us without delay; for he is greatly needed by us, being a most skilled physician of our souls.
>
> “We also beseech your holiness, rich in mercy, to grant this privilege to your servants: that thereafter, should any persons perhaps raise a challenge, we need not answer concerning this canonical incorporation; for what has once been rightly determined ought to remain unshaken for ever. And may your authority likewise command that the division between the two kingdoms, namely those of the Franks and the Germans, be the boundary of our bishopric, as we have learned it was in ancient times from the report of predecessors and other sure indications, lest a dispute ever arise from this, or the wickedness of discord be produced. For it becomes your holiness to bring to a good end what it is clear that you have laudably begun.”

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop Raynold of Reims, greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “The prudence of your brotherhood ought to have laboured more diligently to restore the dignity of the Church committed to you,” etc. See under Urban II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLI.

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers and fellow bishops Raynold of Reims and his suffragans, greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Since the clerics of Arras,” etc. See above.

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Alard, archdeacon of Arras; Bernard, archdeacon of Ostrevent; and all provosts and deans, with all clerics in the aforesaid archdeaconries, greetings and apostolic blessing.

> “The authority of the Apostolic See compels us,” etc. See above.

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Alold, abbot of Saint-Vaast; Richard, abbot of Marchiennes; Albert, abbot of Hasnon; Hameric, abbot of Anchin; likewise to the abbess of Saint-Ragenfred and the abbess of Strem, greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “The Apostolic See,” etc. See above.

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Robert, count of the Flemings, greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “You should be congratulated with great rejoicing,” etc. See above.

> “Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Lambert, bishop of Arras consecrated by our own hands, and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.
>
> “It is evident from the enactments of the holy canons,” etc. See above.

This privilege was recited at the Council of Clermont by command of Lord Pope Urban II, who himself presided, together with the Roman cardinals, thirteen archbishops, two hundred and twenty-five bishops, and ninety or more abbots, apart from the honourable and religious clerics and laymen of various regions and provinces. It was heard attentively and in great silence by the entire assembly of the council, praised, and confirmed on 28 November, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

> “To the reverend fathers, Lord Manasses the provost, L. the dean, and the entire chapter of the holy Church of Reims: Lambert, unworthy servant of the see of Arras, sends himself and eternal salvation in the Lord.
>
> “Since we know that your diligence is not unaware that, as soon as we could, we sent to the lord archbishop, through Lord Lambert the monk, a religious man, the letters of Lord Pope Urban sent to him and his suffragans on my behalf; and since we did not omit letters setting out the impediment to my coming to the holy see of Reims, and afterwards sent canonical excuses through Lord Hugh, abbot of Saint-Denis, I am greatly surprised that I have not yet deserved to receive any consolation or mercy either from him or from you. Rather, through the abbot of Anchin and the monks of Marchiennes, it has pleased you to call us an intruder upon the see of Arras and, as it were, a contemner of the holy Church of Reims.
>
> “But the Lord knows, before whose eyes all things are naked and open—and likewise the Apostolic See—how much I was asked, compelled, indeed bound by the authority of apostolic obedience, and forced to serve the aforesaid see of Arras. As to the alleged contempt in failing to come to the holy see of Reims, on which the lord archbishop has chosen to accuse us, I am prepared to satisfy you through these present brothers of ours.
