I, LAMBERT, humble priest of the holy Church of Arras, having been asked by my beloved sons and brothers in Christ, the brethren of the holy Church of Tournai, to make them a written record concerning the complaint [Col. 0698B] between them and the monks of Saint Martin, established in the suburb, so that, their case having been decided, they might be protected in the future, have willingly undertaken to bring it to a conclusion. For we considered their request honourable, and that they were prudently providing and taking counsel for themselves and for the peace of the churches.

We do not refuse, out of love, to explain to readers of good will—not to fastidious hearers—how the handling of this matter was imposed upon us. Lord Paschal II therefore sent letters from the apostolic see to me and to John, venerable bishop of the Morini. In them he commanded us to appoint for the canons of the holy Church of Tournai and the monks of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tournai a suitable place where we should endeavour, after careful examination, finally to decide their complaint, which had long and bitterly been disputed [Col. 0698C], and, appeals being removed, impose its proper conclusion, so that through God’s grace no occasion for this complaint might thereafter remain.

Accordingly, bound and instructed by so great an authority, we at last, by the Lord’s favour, met on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August in the district of Vermandois and the bishopric of Noyon, at the castle of Capi, in the church of Saint Medard, glorious confessor of Christ. There, in the presence of bishops, archdeacons, abbots, and religious clerics, we first of all earnestly and commendably urged the canons of Tournai and the monks, and gave them the choice that, as children of love, whose manner of life ought to be in heaven [Col. 0698D], if either party had reprehensibly usurped anything belonging to the other contrary to the sacred canons and the decrees of the Fathers, they should utterly relinquish it for fear of God and for their own salvation.

When we achieved nothing by this, after hearing the complaint of the canons and the monks’ reply, we again warned them not to persist any longer in a contention so ruinous to souls, but rather to strive to establish between themselves the peace of brotherhood and Christian perfection. But when they were unwilling to listen to us fully, we withdrew apart and, having taken counsel with venerable brethren, with before us also the chapter of blessed Peter which he delivered in the sight of the whole holy Roman Church on the day of Saint Clement’s ordination:

> If any of the brethren have disputes among themselves [Col. 0699A], let them not be judged before secular judges, but let whatever the matter may be be settled before the priests of the Church; and let them altogether obey their decisions;

and that of the blessed apostle Paul:

> We are ready to punish every disobedience;

then, sitting again in assembly and fortified by the authorities of the aforesaid apostles, and instructed by the command of Lord Pope Paschal, we imposed upon this most pernicious and bitter dispute the following settlement, suited to peace, concord, and mutual remission:

The monks shall possess without objection and without rendering any lordship-dues their garden and whatever they cultivate in it; except that, if the vegetables of the garden, the fruits of the trees, or other garden produce are sold, they shall then give the canons a tenth of the sale proceeds. They shall also peaceably and without any dispute give the canons the tithe of beans, legumes, grain, sheep, pigs, and livestock from the parish of the holy Church of Tournai. [Col. 0699B]

The canons granted free burial to the monks and their converts, subject to the condition that the monks should presume in no way to bury in their cemetery any person from the parish of Tournai, any of the canons’ own parishioners, any of the bishop’s peers or tenants, or any of the peers or tenants belonging either to the city or to the castle, unless with the permission and licence of the canons.

By the authority of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of Lord Pope Paschal, and of our assembly, we decree that this arrangement of peace be firmly observed by both parties. If anyone thereafter disturbed it for any reason, he should incur the wrath of almighty God, lose the favour of the apostles Peter and Paul, and lie under the severity of the canons as one guilty and infamous, until he brought forth fitting fruits of penance for so great an offence. [Col. 0699C] That this decree of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we have caused suitable and trustworthy witnesses, in whose presence it was issued, to be recorded.

Lord John, bishop of the Morini, was present and consented to this settlement. Lord Baldric, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, was present and consented to this settlement. Lord Odo, bishop of Cambrai [Col. 0699D], was present and consented to this settlement. Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras; Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevent; Henry, abbot of Saint-Vaast of Arras; Albert of Hasnon; Fulcard of Marchiennes; Richard of Mont-Saint-Éloi; Cono, priest of Arida Gamantia, of the title of the Holy Trinity; likewise Odo, religious hermit and priest of Arida Gamantia, of the title of Saint Mary ever-virgin, our Lady.

Canons and priests of the episcopal see: Odo, provost and priest; Anastasius, cantor and priest; Rotger, priest; Baldwin, priest; Drogo, steward; Walter of Douai; Hugh, son of Baldwin; Gerard, dean of the castle of Saint-Vaast; [Col. 0700A] Adso, priest of Béthune; Hugh, provost of Béthune; Baldwin, dean of Saint-Albin; Adam, priest of the same title; Honoratus, priest of Lord Medard.

I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, was present and consented to the aforesaid settlement; and, that it may be held in remembrance, I caused it to be set down in writing and sealed with the seal of my humility.

Done at Capi, in the church of Saint Medard, glorious confessor and bishop, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the first indiction, in the year 1108 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

## LETTER CXLIV. OF LAMBERT TO POPE PASCHAL

[Col. 0700B] To the most reverend lord and Father of Fathers, Pope PASCHAL, LAMBERT, unprofitable servant of the holy Church of Arras, due reverence with prayers.

The bearer of this letter, G., provost of the Church of Tournai, brought to me and to John, venerable bishop of the Morini, letters from Your Apostleship during the past summer. In these you commanded us to appoint for the canons of Tournai and the monks of Saint Martin in their suburb a suitable place where, after carefully examining the complaint of both parties, we should endeavour to decide it completely and, appeals being set aside, impose its proper conclusion, so that through God’s grace no occasion for complaint might remain thereafter. [Col. 0700C]

Although oppressed and hindered by grave illness, nevertheless, with God’s help and the counsel of the venerable bishop of the Morini and of our clerics, we provided a suitable place for accomplishing what you commanded. There the canons of Tournai, the monks, and their advocates wearied us much and long; but at last, by the favour of divine mercy and in obedience to your authority, having mutually forgiven both losses of property and resentments of heart, we allowed the aforesaid canons and monks to depart in peace, in the kiss of peace and Christian love, in the presence of the bishops of Tournai and Cambrai and also of abbots and religious clerics and laymen.

Before [Col. 0700D] our assembly was dissolved, the clerics of Tournai asked us to confirm in our writing the agreement and concord made between them and the monks, lest the malice of some evil person should in future impair or corrupt it. This we did. We made no document for the monks, because we were not asked to do so.

We urge upon the justice of Your Most Serene and Most Beloved Holiness that you conduct this case in such a manner that you may receive from almighty God a good reward for justice and may not incur a loss of reputation for your dignity and religious discernment among the clergy and people of Tournai, who are very numerous. Fare well, most holy and sweetest Father, in the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour; and assist by your holy prayers [Col. 0701A], that the ineffable mercy of almighty God may deign to bring me, a sinner absolved from sins, out of [Col. 0702A] the prison and darkness of this life, and out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth.

[Col. 0701]

## III. PRIVILEGES GRANTED BY LAMBERT

BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, edition of Luc[a], II, 158.

### I. For the Monastery of Saint Denis of Reims (1097)

[Col. 0701B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras.

In granting the sweetest requests of you and of the church which you are known to govern, most beloved brother and son Hugh, abbot of the venerable community of the unconquered martyr Saint Denis of Reims, for the redemption of our sins we grant to you and to your successors, who serve in the place and order in which you are under the Rule of Saint Augustine, the altar of Aix, without any exaction of shameful profit; indeed, by the authority over which we preside, we freely confirm it to you in perpetuity. The right and revenues of the bishop of Arras, and of his archdeacon and ministers, are reserved in every respect.

If anyone after this decree of ours should attempt sacrilegiously to take it away from the church to which, by God’s ordering, we have granted it, or should presume to act against these provisions by artful contrivances, let him be anathema with Simon Magus. The aforesaid Lord Abbot Hugh, and every abbot who succeeds him in that place, shall attend if invited to the synod of the bishop of Arras. If detained and occupied by such affairs that he cannot attend, unless he remains with the bishop’s consent, he shall send through one of his canons the grounds of his synodal [Col. 0701D] excuse.

We also grant, with unshaken permanence, the following bond between the Church of Arras and the Church of Reims of the most glorious martyr Saint Denis: upon hearing of the bishop’s death, the people of Reims shall not delay to celebrate his obsequies fraternally, and shall keep his anniversary in perpetuity; and the people of Arras shall do the same upon the death of the abbot of Saint Denis. Desiring that the authority of this charter remain valid and unshaken, we have authenticated it in the presence of the undersigned witnesses.

Witness: Lord John, archdeacon of Arras. Witness: Lord Clarebold, archdeacon of Ostrevent. Witness: Lord Alold, abbot of Saint-Vaast. Witness: Lord John, abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi. Witness: Lord Odo, provost of Saint Mary. Witness: Lord Guibert, dean. Witness: Anastasius, cantor. [Col. 0702B] Witness: Robert, master. Witness: Walter, keeper. Witnesses: the canons of Blessed Mary—Herbert, Baldwin, Algis, Hugh, another Hugh, Robert, another Robert, another Baldwin, Gerard, Arnold, Ralph, Bertulf, Algis, Andrew, Peter. Witness: Lord Cono of the Holy Trinity. Witness: Mascelin, archpriest. Witness: Drogo, provost of Albiniac.

I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, have reread and subscribed this gift of liberty and, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, + have confirmed it with my own hand.

Done at Arras in synod, in the year of Christ 1037, in the fifth indiction, on the Nones of February, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

### II. For the Monastery of Elnone (1097)

[Col. 0702C]

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, earnestly desiring to uproot every Simoniacal heresy from our diocese and satisfying the requests of Lord Hugh, venerable abbot of the monastery of Elnone, dedicated to Blessed Stephen the protomartyr and glorious Saint Amand, and of the other brethren of the same church, freely confirm in perpetuity to the aforesaid community, for the remission of our sins and of the sins of our successor bishops, and with every simoniacal exaction removed, the following altars which they had hitherto held in person: Scaldin, Lurcy, Ruoth, Bulciniol, and Dierac. Yet this is on the condition [Col. 0702D] that, when the priests of those places die, suitable men be brought by the abbot to the bishop, and that the care of souls be granted to them freely by the bishop. In all respects, the right and revenues of the bishop of Arras, and the customary dues of his archdeacon and ministers, are reserved.

If anyone after this decree of ours should presume to replant the aforesaid uprooted heresy, or should demand money in such a matter, let giver and receiver alike be anathema with Simon the heretic. The aforesaid Lord Abbot Hugh, and every abbot succeeding him in the monastery of Elnone, shall attend if invited by the bishop of Arras to a synod. If detained and occupied by such matters that he cannot attend, unless he remains with the bishop’s consent, he shall send through one of his monks the grounds of canonical and synodal excuse. The monk who is administrator of the aforesaid altars shall always attend synods.

We also grant, with unshaken permanence, this bond between the Church of Arras and the Church of Elnone: upon hearing of the bishop’s death, the people of Elnone shall not delay to celebrate his obsequies fraternally; and the people of Arras shall do likewise upon the death of the abbot of Saint Amand. Desiring that the authority of this charter remain valid and unshaken, we have authenticated it in the presence of the undersigned witnesses.

Witness: Lord Clarembold, archdeacon of Ostrevent. Witness: Lord John, archdeacon of Arras. Witness: Lord Odo, provost of Saint Mary. Witness: Lord Gasbert, dean. Witness: Lord Anastasius, cantor. Witness: Lord [Col. 0703B] Walter, keeper. Witness: Lord Robert, master. Witness: Mascelin, archpriest of Arras. Witness: Amalric, dean of Masten. Witness: John, dean of Douai. Witness: Lord Alold, venerable abbot of Saint-Vaast. Witness: Lord John, abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi. Witness: Lord Albert, abbot of Hasnon. Witness: Lord Richard, abbot of Marchiennes. Witness: Lord Hameric, abbot of Anchin. Witness: Lord Rainer, abbot at Cambrai of the Holy Sepulchre. Witness: Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Saint Andrew of the New Castle of Cambrai. Witness: Lord Gerold, abbot of Ham in the territory of Thérouanne.

I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, have reread and subscribed [Col. 0703C] this gift of liberty + and, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, have confirmed it.

Done at Arras in synod, in the basilica of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, our Lady, in the year of Christ 1097, in the fifth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

### III. For the Church of the Apostles Peter and Paul on Mont-Saint-Éloi (1097)

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one true and supreme God. Amen.

Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, to his successors: the joy of the present life [Col. 0703D] and the glory of the future.

We read in the deeds of the bishops of the Churches of Arras and Cambrai that Lord Fulbert, bishop of those cities, raised the body of Saint Vindician from the earth and, at the place called Mont-Saint-Éloi, rebuilt a church dedicated to the apostles Peter and Paul after the former church had been destroyed. There he established eight clerics and the stipends from which they might live, and gave them this liberty: that they should be subject to no authority except that of the bishop alone.

After his death, however, they began day by day to grow lukewarm in God’s service, and the church declined until the time of Lord Lietbert, bishop. Grieved by that ruin, that man of mercy—another Samaritan, as I may say—had compassion on its wretchedness and began to consider with himself how it might be restored to a better state. [Col. 0704A] The one who instils such a desire into the heart supplied him with counsel fitting for this undertaking. For, with the advice of his faithful men, he established there regular clerics living from a common fund, and set over them an abbot of their profession. Accordingly, having made a privilege, he asked his successors to advance them and become their helpers.

He also confirmed anew the liberty of the church and its possessions, and gave it the altar of Hucin on condition that it should pay twelve denarii each year at the feast of Saint Remigius, and thereafter be free of every redemption-payment. He likewise gave the altar of Hodricourt in such a way that it should remain without a *persona* [a beneficed incumbent]. Lord Gerard, my predecessor and his successor, likewise gave, without *personae*, the altars at Novilla and Mediana Villa, with the bishop’s right [Col. 0704B] and revenues and the customary dues of his archdeacon reserved.

I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, grant to you, most reverend brother and son John, abbot, and to all your successors who, for the sake of your religious life, shall live devoutly and communally in the place and order in which you are, that all these things, as determined above, shall remain firm and unshaken. We also grant that, when need arises, the regular canons living there devoutly and without private property may, with the counsel and authority of the bishop of Arras, freely choose in accordance with the fear of God and the sacred canons a superior and abbot.

But if no person suited to such office is found there, with their bishop’s approval and consent they shall choose from another monastery a religious man of their own order and profession, to be appointed over them as superior and abbot. He shall afterwards be brought before the bishop and receive from his hand the temporal benefice of the place, the care of souls, and the abbatial blessing. At the request of Lord Clarebold, knight, I add to these benefices the altar of Rebroniis, on condition that it pay only two solidi to the bishop’s service at the Lord’s Supper; thereafter, all of it shall be placed under the abbot’s lordship. [Col. 0704C]

Witnesses to this act: Lord John, archdeacon; Lord Clarebold, archdeacon; Odo, provost; Wibert, dean; and the other brethren of the entire community of Saint Mary ever-virgin. Lord Clarebold, therefore, the promoter of this act, wishing to make no heir whatsoever other than the Church of Rebroniis, gave there all the inheritance which he held in the vicinity, so that the aforesaid abbot might hold that place through his clerics, to the honour of God and Saint Mary ever-virgin, and that, as its outward resources increased, the service of God within might grow.

That is, he gave at Baraflo an entire mill, the land of one plough, and five householders; and at Dahellicurt a fourth part and the woodland pertaining to it. Witnesses to this act are again the two archdeacons, namely John and Clarebold, and the whole assembly of the Church of Arras; likewise Lord Alold, abbot of Saint-Vaast; Philip, brother of Count Robert; Clementia, countess of Flanders; Robert, advocate; Baldwin of Colhem; Frumold of Jusula. [Col. 0705A]

Therefore, whoever should presume to usurp this gift, or any other gift lawfully made, and attempt to divert it to wrongful uses, shall be subject to canonical excommunication.

I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, have reread and subscribed this gift of liberty and, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, have confirmed it with my own hand.

Done at Arras in synod, in the basilica of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, our Lady, in the year of Christ 1097, in the fifth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

### IV. Privilege Granted to Cono, Priest (1097)

[Col. 0705B]

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one true and supreme God. Amen.

I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, rejoicing in your religious manner of life, most reverend brother and fellow-priest Cono, earnestly desire to provide for your peace and tranquillity both now and in times to come. At your arrival, you and Lord Heldemar, your master and fellow priest of good memory, chose at Arida Gamantia, in our parish called Rochennias, a place for serving God. Once a place to be shunned, like a den of robbers, it has now, through God’s visitation and through you and the brethren dwelling with you, become a refuge and solace for those who pass by. [Col. 0705C]

Therefore we grant you, in the place and order in which you are, and your successors who shall live there religiously and canonically, this liberty: that you shall answer only to the bishop and remain in his hand in the freedom of the Spirit. We also convey to you, and through you to your lawful successors together with the brethren who live and shall live there religiously and without private property, for the increase of the peace and tranquillity of your place, the aforesaid parish of Rochennias, subject to a payment of twelve denarii at the Lord’s Supper for the bishop’s service.

If at any time—may it never occur—through the instigation of the ancient enemy, anything should happen to the aforesaid place or parish for which reconciliation were necessary, we grant to you and your lawful successors, in our stead, upon receiving the water of consecration and reconciliation, authority to reconcile it for your religious community. If, by the Lord’s favour, the aforesaid place should grow to such abundance of goods and servants of God residing there that they ought to elect a superior, they shall freely have power, with the counsel and authority of the bishop of Arras, to choose a superior and lord for themselves according to the fear of God and the ordinances of the holy canons. [Col. 0705D] He shall afterwards be brought before the bishop and receive the temporal benefice of the place, the care of souls, and the blessing of his office.

Accordingly, we ask in the Lord both our present brethren and our successor bishops, and by the authority of the holy canons and our own authority forbid, that no one presume to violate or corrupt this gift of liberty. If anyone knowingly infringes the privilege of this ordinance of ours, let him lie under excommunication until he comes to his senses and makes satisfaction to God’s Church. So be it, so be it. That this decree may remain firm and stable for all time, we have caused trustworthy witnesses to be recorded.

Witness: Lord John, archdeacon of Arras. Witness: Lord Clarebald, archdeacon of Ostrevent. Witness: Lord Alold, abbot of Saint-Vaast. Witness: Lord Hameric, abbot of Anchin. Witness: Lord Albert, abbot of Hasnon. Witness: Lord Richard, abbot of Marchiennes. Witness: Lord John, abbot of Saint Vindician. Witness: Odo, provost of Saint Mary ever-virgin. Witness: Lord Wibert, dean. Witness: Robert, master. Witness: Anastasius, cantor. Witness: Lord Walter, keeper. Witness: Mascelin, archpriest. Witness: John [Col. 0706B] dean of Douai. Witness: Baldwin, dean. Witness: Adso, dean of Béthune. Witness: John, dean of the Castle. Witness: John, dean of Dangeville.

I, Lambert, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, have reread + and subscribed this gift of liberty and, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, have confirmed it with my own hand.

Done at Arras in synod, in the basilica of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, our Lady, in the year of Christ 1097, in the fifth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

### V. For the Monastery of Saint-Vaast (1097)

[Col. 0706C]

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one true and supreme God. Amen.

Since among the other precepts of the Christian religion the twofold branch of charity—namely, love of God and of neighbour—is most strongly commended, unless we raise up our neighbour and carry him on the beast of salvation, after the example of that Samaritan, we shall not merit the grace of this holy love. Rightly indeed should we embrace the charity which divine providence has taken such pains to commend. For this was first made known to the world through the Law and through the prophets, before the Son of God should commend it more deeply, appearing visibly in the time of grace and setting his tabernacle in the sun. And since charity says, “Give to everyone who asks of you,” and [Col. 0706D] the bowels of charity never lack abundance, we ought to labour to minister cheerfully to those who ask, according as reason and equity shall dictate.

Wherefore I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, often and earnestly entreated, have wished to satisfy the most sweet prayers of Lord Alold, venerable abbot of the monastery of Arras, bearing the title of the glorious confessor of Christ Vedastus, and of the other brethren of that same church: namely, that we should confirm to the aforesaid community for free possession the altars which they had held personally. Therefore, after taking counsel with our faithful men, to you, most reverend brother and son Abbot Alold, and to your lawful successors, for the redemption of our sins, without any exaction of shameful gain, we not only grant those altars, but also by the authority with which [Col. 0707A] we preside freely confirm them to you in perpetuity; on this condition, however, that, when the priests of those places die, other suitable men shall be brought by the abbot to the bishop, and the cure of souls shall be bestowed upon them freely by the bishop. Saving in all things the right of the bishop of Arras, and his revenues, and those of the archdeacon and his officials.

Moreover, the abbot, promising and professing to us as our first-born son, shall serve faithfully and obediently in the private and public affairs of our Church, both in chapter and outside it, if summoned by the Church.

These are the altars by name: Salgi, Florbacs, Laventies, Felcy, Vi, Contehan, Remchendencourt, Afceel, Hadas, Mons, Novilelle, Pabule, Basiliere, Bomvillers, Guarluse, Fiscau, Bairy, Fontenellis, Ateias, [Col. 0707B] Gaurerle, Fuscariis, Bertricurt, Bigartu, Hambleng, Frasne, Noveville, Iser, Tenluz, Moflanes, Ymercurt.

But if anyone, after this our decree, with sacrilegious hand should presume to take away what, by God’s ordering, we have granted, or to exact money, let giver and receiver alike be anathema with Simon the heretic.

For this reason, we desire that this pledge of charity, to be repaid to us, be recalled to memory, so that, when news of our death is heard, both the brethren then present and their abbots may take care to celebrate perpetually our obsequies, our thirtieth-day commemoration, and our anniversary. And because it is a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead, that they may be released from sins, we ask you, most beloved son and venerable abbot, and all your successors who shall be abbots in the place and rank which you now hold, that [Col. 0707C] in the charity of the Holy Spirit, in whom is remission of all sins, what we have ordained to be done for us may likewise be done for our successors who shall be bishops in the see of Arras.

And since times decline for the worse, and human acts cannot be remembered except through writings, we have thought fit that this grant of freedom be recorded in the present charter. And that it may remain unshaken and without opposition, we have subscribed the names of witnesses for greater confirmation.

The sign of Lord Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras.  
The sign of Lord John, abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi.  
The sign of Lord Albert, abbot of Hasnon.  
The sign of Lord Aemeric, abbot of Anchin.  
The sign of Lord Rayner, abbot of Cambrai.  
The sign of Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Neufchâtel.  
The sign of Lord Adam, abbot of Saint-Aubert.  
The sign of Lord [Col. 0707D] Odo, provost of Saint Mary.  
The sign of Lord Guibert, dean.  
The sign of Anastasius, cantor.  
The sign of Robert, master.  
The sign of Gualter, custos.  
The sign of Mascelin, archpriest.  
The sign of John, dean of Aginville.  
The sign of Ralph, dean.  
The sign of Ascon, dean of Béthune.  
The sign of Guarner, dean.  
The sign of Baldwin, dean of Bapaume.  
The sign of Guagon, dean.  
The sign of John of Douai.  
The signs of Gualter, dean, and Arnulf of Lens, provosts.  
The sign of Bernard.  
The sign of Lord Conon of Arida Gamantia, of the title of the Holy Trinity.  
The sign of Lord Achard.  
The sign of Lord Drogo.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, have read again and subscribed this grant of freedom +, and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit have confirmed it with my own hand.

[Col. 0708A] Done at Arras in synod, in the basilica of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, our Lady, in the year of Christ our God 1097, in the sixth indiction, on the third Ides of October, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

## VI. He confirms the church of Aiulcurtis to the priest Odo and Dean Baldwin. (Year 1101.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, rejoicing in your religious manner of life and eremitical life, most reverend brother and fellow-priest Odo, desire earnestly to provide for your peace and quiet both [Col. 0708B] in the present time and in the future. Therefore, favourably pursuing your just petitions and those of our dean Baldwin, we grant to you and to your successors, who shall live there religiously and canonically, this freedom: that you shall answer only to the bishop and remain in his hand in the freedom of the Spirit.

Accordingly, the church which your devotion has built in the solitary place called Aiulcurtis we entrust to you and to your successors persevering in the purpose of religion, to be freely possessed; we commit to you the cure of souls of your fellow hermits; and we grant to the same church the tithe of the surrounding field which your hermit brethren cultivate.

Therefore, in the Lord we ask both our brethren now present and our successors as bishops, [Col. 0708C] and by the authority of the holy canons and our own we forbid, that no one presume to violate or corrupt this grant of freedom. If anyone knowingly infringes the privilege of this our institution, let him be subject to excommunication until he comes to his senses and makes satisfaction to the Church of God. So be it, so be it.

And that this decree may remain firm and stable for all time, we have taken care to record faithful witnesses.

The sign of Lord Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras.  
The sign of Lord Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevant.  
The sign of Lord Alold, abbot of Saint-Vaast.  
The sign of Lord Albert, abbot of Hasnon.  
The sign of Lord Hameric, abbot of Anchin.  
The sign of Lord Richard, abbot of Marchiennes.  
The sign of Lord Robert, abbot of Molesme.  
The sign of Lord Siger, abbot of Saint Peter of Ghent.  
The sign of Lord John, abbot of Mont-[Col. 0708D]Saint-Éloi.  
The sign of Lord Adam of Saint-Aubert, abbot of Cambrai.  
The sign of Lord Rainer, abbot of the Holy Sepulchre.  
The sign of Lord Conon of Arida Gamantia.  
The sign of Lord Odo, provost.  
The sign of Anastasius, cantor.  
The signs of the canons Gualter, Algis, Robert, Baldwin, Roger, Gerard, Andrew, Guimar, Peter, Ansellus.  
The signs of the deans Mascelin, Arson, John, Gerard, Guarner, Guagon, Baldwin, Ralph, and another John.  
The signs of Arnulf, provost of Lens, and of Lictard and Guagon, canons.  
The signs of Herbert, dean, and Durand, Amand, Gualter, and Odechin, canons of Douai.  
The sign of Flotbert, priest and holder of the altar of Flers.

Done at Arras in synod, in the church of Blessed Mary [Col. 0709A] ever Virgin, in the year of Christ our God 1101, in the ninth indiction, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

I, Lambert, bishop of Arras, have read again, marked, and subscribed this grant of freedom +, and have completed it in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

## VII. Privilege for the church of Lens. (Year 1106.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, of the one true and highest God. Amen.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, assenting to the just and honourable petitions of the honourable Count Eustace and his noble wife, Countess Mary, as well as of Ida, the religious countess, mother of the said count, wish it to be known to our sons and brethren both present and future that, at the request of the aforesaid persons, we have confirmed by the privilege of our authority, as valid and stable for all time, the freedom of the Church of Lens and of the canons of that Church.

Accordingly, all those things which have come into the possession of the aforesaid Church—whether from princes, as is contained in their precepts and charters, or from other faithful of God—things which have already been justly granted and canonically possessed by the said Church, known to have been founded from the beginning under the title of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, our Lady, and Blessed Wlganius the Confessor; [Col. 0709C] and likewise things to be granted hereafter, we authorize to be administered by the canons and their prelates under the weight of our authority.

Furthermore, the churches of Saints Leodegarius and Lawrence, martyrs, and their episcopal revenues, just as our predecessor, the venerable and religious Bishop Lietbert, gave and granted them for the use of the canons, we also accordingly approve and grant; provided, however, that the priests who are to be placed over those churches among the people shall always be presented through the hand of the canons or their prelates to the bishop of Arras; that, as is canonical, they shall make a profession to their bishop concerning the honourableness of their life and promise obedience; and that thus they shall receive and exercise the cure of the people.

Concerning the dean [Col. 0709D] to be chosen according to the fear of God and the authority of the holy canons, we grant the canons free power of election. Likewise, concerning an advocate in their causes, as we have learned by the count’s request and permission, the canons may have as advocate such a man as they wish, for as long as they wish, and no longer.

And lest any doubt or ignorance should arise concerning the possessions of the oft-mentioned church, we order the gifts of movable and immovable property to be written below. The toll in the same town shall be free and may be granted or removed only by the canons themselves; nor may the count receive from it anything more than one cartload of wine, of eighteen modii only. The brewery and oven, the mill at Becherel, the *bodium* at Guerchin, and likewise the churches of Béthay and Dourges, the canons of Lens shall hold with the benefice-holder; [Col. 0710A] and they shall pay to the bishop and his officials what pertains to episcopal rights. When the benefice-holder dies, one of the canons of Lens shall be restored by the bishop in his place without any redemption-payment.

In the town of Guendin: land for two ploughs, six tenants, a brewery, and an oven; at Guistregumgles, one ploughland and the other things contained in the count’s charter.

But if anyone, knowing this charter of our constitution, should hereafter presume by any wrongful practice to infringe, diminish, or violate the dignity of this privilege, we exclude him from the thresholds and bosom of holy mother Church; and if, rationally admonished a second or third time, he neglects to amend what he has wrongly done, we subject such a presumptuous person and despiser of Christian discipline to the bond of canonical excommunication.

Done at Arras in the year of Christ our God 1106, in the fourteenth indiction, on the seventh Ides of June, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras, while King Philip reigned in France, Robert the Younger in Flanders, and Eustace was count of Boulogne and Lens.

On the feast of Saint Dionysius the aforesaid canons shall pay the bishop five solidi from Béthay and Dourges. Since we desire the authority of this charter to remain valid and unshaken, we have authenticated it in the presence of the undersigned witnesses.

The sign of Lord Clarembold, archdeacon.  
The sign of Lord Robert, archdeacon.  
The sign of Lord Odo, provost.  
The sign of Lord Anastasius, cantor; of Baldwin among the priests; of Arnold, Peter, and Roger, deacons; of Drogo, Gerard, [Col. 0710C] and Ansellus, subdeacons.  
The sign of Lord Gualter and Sasgualon.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, have read again and subscribed this grant of freedom +, and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit have confirmed it with my own hand.

## VIII. Privilege granted to Abbess Guisendis of Melbodius. (Year 1106.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, of the one true and highest God. Amen.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, relying on the petition and counsel of our venerable brethren, grant to you, honourable sister in Christ, Abbess Guisendis of Melbodius, and through you to abbesses succeeding in the place and rank which you now hold, regularly elected and canonically advanced, the altar of Herem, subject to this condition: that you attend the synod of Arras, and likewise the abbesses succeeding you, unless you remain away by permission of the bishop or through a canonical and synodal excuse.

We further provide for your peace and freedom that the abbess of Melbodius shall bring a suitable priest before the bishop of Arras, who shall make profession of the honourableness of his life and promise canonical obedience, and thus shall receive freely from the hand of the bishop the cure to be exercised among the people of God.

And that the written text of our charter may remain unshaken and stable for all time, we order faithful witnesses, [Col. 0711A] in whose presence the aforesaid altar of Herem has been granted by us without a benefice-holder, saving in all things the right of the bishop of Arras, and his revenues and customs, as well as those of the archdeacon and his officials, to be recorded below.

The sign of Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras.  
The sign of Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevant.  
The sign of John, abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi.  
The sign of Lord Gerard.  
The sign of Conon of Arida Gamantia.  
The sign of Richard of Rebroniis.  
The sign of Gualter, canon of Arras, formerly castellan of Douai.  
The signs of John, Mascelin, and Robert, deans.  
The signs of Everard, Roger, and Guarimund of Douai.  
The sign of Henry, abbot of Saint-Vaast.  
The sign of Rainer of the Holy Sepulchre, of the city of Cambrai.

But if anyone, knowing the writing of this our charter and constitution, [Col. 0711B] should presume to act against it, violate it, diminish it, or infringe it by any device of ingenuity, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not come to his senses and make satisfaction to the Church of God, we subject such a presumptuous person and despiser of the sacred canons, bound by the severity of canonical excommunication.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, have read again and subscribed this grant of freedom +, and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit have confirmed it with my own hand.

Done in the year of Christ our God 1106, in the fourteenth indiction, on the eighth Ides of November, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert.

## IX. Privilege for the monastery of Corbie. (Year 1108.)

In the name of the one true and highest God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, for love of your kindness and of the venerable brethren of the monastery of Corbie, honourable Abbot Nicholas in Christ, saving in all things the right of the bishop of Arras and his officials, grant to you, for you, and through you to all abbots who, by God’s ordination, shall be deemed worthy to preside in the place and rank which you now hold, the altar of Monciacum without a benefice-holder and its dependent chapel of Berla, to be possessed in the freedom of the Spirit, without any sale or exaction of any shameful gain.

We further provide that, by the care of you and of your successor abbots, a suitable priest shall be presented to the bishop of Arras, to make to him a profession concerning the honourableness of his life and his chastity, as is canonical, and to promise obedience; and thereafter he shall freely receive from the bishop’s hand the cure to be exercised among God’s people in the church of Monciacum. This priest shall always attend the synod of Arras and endeavour kindly and cheerfully to pay the synodal revenues and customary cathedral dues.

And that the writing of this our constitution may remain stable and unshaken, we have taken care to record as faithful witnesses our brethren:

Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras; Odo, provost; Anastasius, cantor; Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevant; Roger, priest; Wido, subdeacon; [Col. 0712A] Drogo, steward of the bishop; Lavulf, dean; Mauring; Robert son of Ermenfrid; Baldwin; Peter, acolyte.

Witnesses of Corbie: Lambert, priest of Saint Peter; Robert, priest of Saint John; Lambert, deacon of Corbie; Robert, acolyte.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, have read again and subscribed this grant of freedom +, and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit have confirmed it with my own hand.

Given at Corbie, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the first indiction, in the year of Christ our God 1108.

It was read aloud at Arras, in the secretarium of the greater church of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, our Lady, [Col. 0712B] on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

## X. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter of Balinghem. (Year 1110.)

In the name of the one true and highest God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, at your humble petition and for love of the brethren of the monastery of Balinghem, honourable Abbot Ansbold in Christ, saving in all things the right of the bishop of Arras and his revenues, grant to you, through you, and for you, and to all abbots who, by God’s ordination, shall be deemed worthy to preside in the place and rank which you now hold, [Col. 0712C] the altar of Harnes and its dependent chapel named Alnay, henceforth to be possessed in the freedom of the Spirit without any sale or exaction of any shameful gain.

We further provide that, by the care of you and of your successor abbots, a suitable priest shall be presented to the bishop of Arras, who shall make to him a profession concerning the honourableness of his life and chastity, as is canonical, and promise obedience; and thereafter shall freely receive from the bishop’s hand the cure to be exercised among God’s people in the aforesaid church of Harnes.

And the abbot of Saint Peter’s monastery of Balinghem—you, namely, reverend brother Ansbold in Christ, and your successor abbots—shall not neglect to attend the synod of Arras, unless excused with the bishop’s permission or with that of his archdeacon, should he hold the synod while exercising the bishop’s office.

And that the writing of this our constitution may remain stable and unshaken, we have taken care to record our brethren as faithful witnesses:

Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras; Herbert, archdeacon of Mory; Albold, abbot of Formoselle; Odo, provost; Robert, provost of Lille; Roger, deacon; Lambert, deacon of Tournai; Guido, subdeacon; Robert, master; Robert son of Ermenfrid; Peter, acolyte; Hubard, reader; Baldwin, dean of Bapaume; Simon, his brother.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, have read again and subscribed this grant of freedom + [Col. 0713A] and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit have confirmed it with my own hand.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, on the eighth Ides of April, in the third indiction, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop.

## XI. Privilege granted to Guarin, prior of Abbatisvilla. (Year 1110.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, of the one true and highest God. Amen.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, for the discipline and religion of the monastery of Cluny, in which you were educated and are known to be a monk, reverend my brother Guarin, prior of Abbatisvilla, [Col. 0713B] grant to you and to your successors, the priors of Abbatisvilla, our place situated in the territory of Béthune, under the title of Saint Praejectus the martyr, to be governed in the fear of God and under the Rule of blessed Benedict, and to be nurtured bodily and spiritually.

We further add to the aforesaid place our parish named Fuscherias, saving in all things the right of the bishop of Arras, his revenues, and the customs of his officials. We likewise confirm by our writing that you and your successor priors of Abbatisvilla shall show due obedience to me and my successors, as was renewed and established at the Council of Clermont.

You shall bring to the bishop of Arras a suitable priest for the parish of Fuscherias, who shall make a profession and promise obedience, [Col. 0713C] and thus shall freely receive from the bishop’s hand the cure of God’s people.

And that the charter of this our constitution may remain stable and unshaken, we have taken care to record our faithful and suitable brethren as witnesses.

The sign of Lord Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras.  
The sign of Lord Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevant.  
The sign of Lord Odo, provost.  
The sign of Lord Anastasius, cantor.  
The sign of Baldwin, priest.  
The sign of Roger, priest.  
The sign of Roger, deacon.  
The sign of Peter, deacon.  
The sign of Drogo, Ansellus, and M. Rennus, subdeacons.  
The sign of Sasgualon and Lambert, acolytes, and of Hubard, reader.  
The sign of Azo and Mascelin, deans.  
The signs of the parish priests of Arras: Albert, Roger, Ebrulf, Isembard.

Done at Arras in the year of Christ our God 1110, in the [Col. 0713D] third indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

## XII. Privilege for the church of Saint Peter of Lille. (Year 1111.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, of the one true and highest God. Amen.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, for the love ever to be revered by me of the Church of Blessed Peter the Apostle of Lille, for the urgent renewal and confirmation also of brotherly love and mutual fellowship in petitions and prayers, and at your intervention, beloved brother Lambert of Comines in Christ, as well as that of certain of our brethren, [Col. 0714A] grant to the church of Blessed Peter of Lille the altar of Moncels, saving in all things the right of the bishop of Arras, ecclesiastical customs, and those of his officials, free from every exaction of shameful gain; on this condition, that for the church of Blessed Peter you, beloved brother Lambert, now obedientiarius of Moncels, and your future successors as benefice-holders, shall receive freely from the bishop’s hand, without any buying or selling; that in synodal time you shall gladly prepare and pay the cathedral and synodal revenues to the archdeacon, dean, and official of the bishop; and that you shall not neglect to come to the synod.

We further provide that the church of Blessed Peter shall, through you, present to the bishop of Arras a suitable priest, who shall promise him obedience [Col. 0714B] and make, as is canonical, a profession concerning the honourableness of his life, and thereafter freely receive the cure to be exercised among the people of Moncels.

Therefore, that the writing of this our charter may remain unshaken and stable, we have taken care to record below faithful and suitable witnesses to confirm it.

The sign of Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras.  
The sign of Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevant.  
The sign of Odo, provost.  
The sign of Drogo, dean.  
The sign of Anastasius, cantor.  
The sign of Robert, scholasticus.  
The signs of the canons Roger and Alulf.  
The signs of the deans Warner and Gerard.  
The signs of Hilvin and Arnulf of Lens.  
The signs of Peter and Robert, acolytes.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, have read again and subscribed the writing of this our charter, and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0714C] have confirmed it with my own hand. +

Done at Arras in the year of Christ our God 1111, in the fourth indiction, in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

## XIII. He grants the church of Ambrisne to Abbot Gualter. (Year 1111.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, of the one true and highest God.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, honourable Abbot Gualter in Christ, grant to you the church of our diocese called Ambrisne, saving in all things the right and revenues of the bishop of Arras, and the customs of the archdeacon [Col. 0714D] and his officials. For we are moved by the honourable manner of life of you and of your community, and also by the intervention of certain of our brethren, to give you the altar and aforesaid church; and we grant it to you and, through you, to all who are known to preside in the place and rank which you now hold, and to your successor abbots to be ordained and established by the grace of God.

And because both you and your monastery belong to the metropolitan jurisdiction of another province, namely Rouen, we establish by this establishment, as we read confirmed in the Council of Chalcedon and renewed in the Council of Clermont by Pope Urban II, venerable and of worthy memory, that the monk whom you choose to be prior at Ambrisne shall both promise and render canonical obedience to me and to the future bishops of the Church of Arras, insofar as our diocese is concerned. [Col. 0715A]

We further provide that you and the prior of Ambrisne shall present to the bishop of Arras a suitable priest to be placed among the people of Ambrisne; he shall make to the aforesaid bishop a profession concerning the honourableness of his life and his chastity, promise obedience as is canonical, and thus freely receive from the bishop’s hand the cure to be exercised among God’s people.

Furthermore, because attendance at our synod would burden your person, the prior of Ambrisne shall not neglect to attend the synod of Arras and shall endeavour cheerfully to pay to the bishop and his officials the cathedral and synodal revenues, as from a mother church.

And that the writing of this our charter may remain unshaken and stable, we have taken care to record below our brethren, faithful and suitable witnesses, to confirm it.

The sign of Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras.  
The sign of Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevant.  
The sign of Drogo, dean.  
The sign of Odo, provost.  
The sign of Anastasius, cantor.  
The sign of Robert, master.  
The signs of the canons Roger and Baldwin, priests; Roger and Peter, deacons; Hilvin, subdeacon; Sasgualon and Lambert, acolytes.  
The signs of the rural deans Mascelin, Ralph, and Gerard; and of the priests Albert, Ebrulf, Guenemar, John, and Tetbold.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, have read again and subscribed the writing of this our charter, and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit have confirmed it with my own hand.

[Col. 0715C] Done at Arras in the year of Christ our God 1111, in the fourth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

## XIV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Amand. (Year 1112.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, of the one true and highest God. Amen.

[Col. 0716A] I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, at your humble and long-standing petition, and also for love of the community of brethren of Saint Amand committed to you, grant to you, reverend Abbot Bovo, the altars and churches with their endowments, namely those of Bulceng, Masteng, and Helemiis, saving in all things the cathedral revenues of the bishop and the customs of the archdeacon and his officials.

Upon the death or lawful removal of the priest of each of the aforesaid places, the abbot of Saint Amand shall provide for and arrange for another suitable priest to be presented to the bishop of Arras. He shall make a profession to him and promise obedience, and thus freely receive from the bishop’s hand the cure to be exercised among God’s people.

But you, reverend brother and Abbot Bovo, and all abbots who by the grace of God shall in future [Col. 0716B] be known to preside in the place and rank which you now hold, shall not neglect to attend the synod of Arras, unless perhaps one of you has been excused with the bishop’s goodwill.

And that the writing of our charter may remain unshaken and stable, we have taken care to record below our faithful and suitable brethren as witnesses.

The sign of Lord Clarembold, archdeacon of Arras.  
The sign of Lord Robert, archdeacon of Ostrevant.  
The sign of Lord Odo, provost of our Church.  
The sign of the canons Evrard, priest; Roger, deacon; and Guido, subdeacon.  
The sign of Lord Richard, abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi.  
The signs of the deans Amalric, Mascelin, and Gerard.  
The signs of the priests Ebroin, Baldwin, and Helgot.  
The signs of Sasgualon and Peter, canons of Arras.  
The sign of Roger, priest, and Guibert, [Col. 0716C] deacon.

I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, have read again and subscribed the writing of this our charter, and in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit have confirmed it with my own hand. +

Done at Arras in the year of Christ our God 1112, on the third Ides of April, in the fifth indiction, in the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras.

[Col. 0715]

# Canons of the Council of Clermont, in the Year of the Incarnation 1095, in the Time of Pope Urban II, His Eighth Year, and the Thirty-Sixth of Philip, King of the Franks, Collected by Lambert, Bishop of Arras

[Note: “I have added variants,” says Severinus Binius, “from a manuscript sent to me by the reverend Lord George Colvenerius, doctor and professor of theology at Douai, canon and scholasticus of the collegiate church of Saint Peter there, who has deserved exceedingly well of the Church.”]

(Labbe, *Concilia*, vol. X, p. 506.) In the year of the Lord Christ 1094 [Note: 1095.], in the month of December [Note: the fourth day before the Kalends of December, or the sixth.], the decrees [Note: apostolic decrees.] of Pope Urban II, lord, issued at the Council of Clermont [Note: of Auvergne.].

## I. On Peace Not to Be Broken

[Col. 0715D]

It was decreed [Note: “We compared [this] with the most ancient parchments in our possession and with other manuscripts.”] that on every day monks, [Col. 0716D] clerics, women, and those who are with them shall remain in peace. But during three days, namely Monday, [Col. 0717A] Tuesday, and Wednesday [Note: “injury.”], an injury inflicted by one person upon another shall not be reckoned a breach of peace [Note: “infringement.”]; but on the remaining four days, if anyone inflicts injury on another, he shall be held guilty of breaking the holy peace and shall be punished according to the judgment rendered.

## II. On the Journey to Jerusalem

Whoever sets out to liberate the Church of God at Jerusalem solely from devotion, not for the acquisition of honour or money, let that journey be reckoned to him in place of all penance. [Note: Perhaps *ei*, “to him,” is missing.]

## III. That a Dean Shall Be a Priest and an Archdeacon a Deacon

[Note: Distinction 6, chapter “Nullus.”] Let no one be made dean in the Church unless he is a priest; no one archdeacon unless he is a Levite—that is, a deacon. [Note: “We have found in manuscripts in which the order of the following canons is not always the same.”] Let no cleric hold an archdeaconry unless he has the grade [Col. 0717B] of that dignity. Let no one be an archpriest—what in some places is called a dean—unless he is an ordained priest.

But in Gratian, *Decretum*, Distinction XL, chapter 1: “No bishop shall presume to establish in his church an archdeacon unless he be a deacon, nor to ordain an archpriest or dean unless they be priests.” That this may be observed more strictly, we prohibit and forbid it by apostolic authority.

## IV. That Clerics Shall Not Bear Arms

Let no cleric carry weapons.

## V. That One Not Yet a Deacon Shall Not Be Chosen Bishop

Let no layman, cleric, or merely [Note: at least.] subdeacon be elected bishop.

## VI. On Purchased Altars or Churches

Let no one buy a prebend for himself. If anyone [Col. 0717C] has bought one, or if his parents have bought one for him, let him place himself under the hand and disposition of the bishop. [Note: “let them place themselves under the hand and disposition of their bishop.”] The same shall be done concerning an altar and every ecclesiastical benefice.

## VII. On Altars Given to Monasteries through Benefice-Holders

Let altars given to communities of canons or monks through benefice-holders revert freely, upon the death of the benefice-holders, into the hands of the bishops, unless they have been confirmed to those communities by written privileges.

## VIII. That No One Shall Demand Payment for Burial

Let no one henceforth demand payment for burial.

## IX. On Clerics Taking Wives

Let no priest, deacon, or subdeacon, nor indeed anyone who holds a canonry, join to himself a union of fornication. Whoever does so shall be entirely barred from the canonry. [Col. 0717D]

## X. That Clerics Shall Not Keep Women in Their Houses

Let it not be permitted for any women to live in the houses of clerics, except those whom the holy canons permit.

## XI. That Sons of Concubines Shall Not Become Clerics

Let no sons of concubines be promoted to orders or to any [Col. 0718A] ecclesiastical honours unless they have lived monastically or canonically in the Church.

## XII. That No One Shall Have a Prebend in Two Cities

Let no cleric henceforth be permitted to hold two prebends in two cities, since he cannot hold two titles.

## XIII. That Clerics Shall Always Be Ordained to Their First Title

Let every cleric always be ordained to the title to which he was first ordained.

## XIV. That No One Shall Hold Double Offices in the Same Church

Let no one henceforth hold double offices in one church.

## XV. That No One Shall Receive an Ecclesiastical Office from the Hand of a Layman

[Col. 0718B]

Let no member of the clergy [Note: “ecclesiastical.”] receive any office from the hand of laymen. Let a cleric receive no office of the Church from a lay hand.

## XVI. That Rulers Shall Not Make Investitures

It is forbidden that kings or other [Note: any.] rulers make any investiture concerning ecclesiastical offices.

XVII.—That a bishop or priest shall not swear fealty to laymen.

No bishop or priest shall perform liege fealty to a king or to any layman by placing his hands in his.

XVIII.—No one shall become the chaplain of a layman without the bishop’s permission.

[Col. 0718C] No priest may be the chaplain of any layman without the authorization [Note: [Col. 0717] perhaps: “without permission.”] of his bishop. No prince shall have a chaplain except [Note: [Col. 0717] “except, with the bishop’s consent.”] one whom his bishop or archdeacon has appointed for him as a chosen guardian of his soul; from another manuscript codex.

XIX.—That laymen shall neither retain nor receive tithes.

Laymen shall not retain a tenth part of the proceeds of their labor; just as they ought not to retain it, so neither ought they to receive it [Note: [Col. 0717] “receive.”].

XX.—That laymen shall no longer retain altars or churches.

Accordingly, all laymen are forbidden henceforth to retain altars or churches for themselves.

XXI.—That no one shall usurp another’s inheritance.

[Col. 0718D] No layman shall usurp another person’s inheritances for himself. If anyone does so and does not make satisfaction to the injured party [Note: [Col. 0717] “to justice.”], no priest shall meanwhile admit him to penance.

XXII.—No one shall be admitted to penance unless he has made a complete confession.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0717] “also.”], it has been decreed that no other person is to be admitted to complete penance unless he has made a complete [Col. 0719A] confession—for example, if, having committed homicide, he remains in adultery [Note: [Col. 0719] Alternatively: “if, after confessing a homicide he has committed, he remains in adultery.”], or in something of that kind. Yet we advise [Note: [Col. 0719] “let only this counsel be given to him.”] that he fast and give alms, so that he may be able to return to the way of truth.

XXIII.—That meat shall not be eaten throughout the whole of Lent.

No Christian shall eat meat from the beginning of the fast until Easter.

XXIV.—At what times ordinations are to be performed.

Ordinations [Note: [Col. 0719] “ordinations.”] shall not be performed except at four fixed times, and on the Saturday in the middle of Lent [Note: [Col. 0719] “of mid-Lent.”]. Then the fast shall be prolonged until evening and, if possible, until [Note: [Col. 0719] “on.”] the following day, so that it may appear more clearly that the ordinations [Col. 0719B] are performed on Sunday [Note: [Col. 0719] “ordinations.”].

XXV.—That the sons of priests shall not become clerics unless they are monks or regulars.

The sons of priests, deacons, or canonical subdeacons shall not be promoted to orders or to other ecclesiastical dignities unless they have become monks or canons [Note: [Col. 0719] “regulars.”]. Unless they become either monks or regular canons.

XXVI.—Concerning the fast of Holy Saturday.

On Holy Saturday the fast shall be prolonged toward nightfall.

XXVII.—Concerning the fasts of spring and summer.

The spring fast shall always be observed in the first week of Lent; the summer fast, within the week of Pentecost.

XXVIII.—That all shall receive the body and blood separately from the altar.

[Col. 0719C]

No one shall communicate from the altar unless he receives the body separately and likewise the blood, except in necessity and as a precaution [Note: [Col. 0719C] This was because of the recently condemned Berengarian heresy, which maintained that the figure was sufficiently fulfilled under one species alone. [Col. 0720C]].

XXIX.—That those who flee to a cross are free.

If anyone, while enemies are pursuing him, flees to any cross on the road, he shall be free as though he remained in the church itself.

XXX.—Concerning those who flee to a cross or church.

If anyone has committed some crime against the security of the church or of the aforesaid [Col. 0720A] cross, and has fled to a church or cross, having received security of life and limb, he shall be handed over to justice.

XXXI.—That no cleric shall plunder property.

No cleric shall plunder the property of bishops or clerics, whether during their lives or after their deaths, or divert it to his own uses. If anyone does so, let him be anathematized. And it was said by all: “So be it, so be it.”

In Gratian it reads thus [Note: [Col. 0720C] 12, question 2, chapter 46.]: A question was raised concerning laymen who, when bishops or other clerics die, seize the property of the deceased and steal it from the Church and the poor. Against them the common anathema of the whole council was pronounced, the pope himself promulgating such a sentence.

If anyone, after learning of the present prohibition, seizes the property of bishops [Col. 0720B] or priests or other clerics, he shall be excommunicated until he makes satisfaction. The property of deceased bishops shall be distributed in alms for their salvation through the hands of archpriests or archdeacons, or according to the determination made by the deceased; alternatively, it shall be reserved for the successor who is to come. The same shall be done concerning the property of priests or clerics, through the bishop or the aforesaid persons, or through whomever the deceased have entrusted with the matter. But if anyone presumes to act against these provisions, let him be anathematized.

XXXII.—Concerning those who imprison bishops.

If anyone seizes and imprisons a bishop, let him be subject to perpetual infamy and never again bear arms. And all cried out: “So be it.”

[Col. 0720C] Thus far the canons. But he who copied them added the following: “These were found in a book of Lambert, bishop of Arras, written four hundred years ago; and, because they were readily at hand, I thought they should be sent.

“In the same book of Lambert, who attended the council, as we have shown above, the following occurs and ought not to be omitted: At the Council of Clermont, over which Lord Pope Urban II presided, there were with him Roman cardinals . . . . . thirteen archbishops, two hundred and twenty-five bishops, and more than ninety abbots, apart from the honorable and religious clerics and laymen of diverse regions and provinces.”

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1115: FRANCISCUS CAMENUS

[Col. 0719]

NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, II, 194)

Franciscus Camenus of Perugia, whose Sapphic hymn on Saint Nicholas the Pilgrim, an Apulian of Trani [Col. 0721A], who died in 1094 and was enrolled among the saints in 1098, is extant in the *Acts of the Saints*, June, vol. I, p. 253. Papebroch noted that it was composed not long after the canonization, certainly before 1117.

[Col. 0721]

HYMN TO SAINT NICHOLAS THE PILGRIM

[Col. 0721A] O Nicholas, shining star of heaven,  
Great protector of the people of Trani,  
Grant, I pray, strength to one singing  
Your renowned wonders.

Born in Greece of a Greek father,  
You called the Lord the shepherd of the flock,  
Ever crying, in the manner of the initiates,  
“Kyrie, have mercy!”

Breathing more deeply of higher things, leaving your sheep,  
You choose the cave of a sleeping bear;  
You drive her away by a sign, and by the Lord’s command—  
He at whose word the world trembles.

Here an old man, a monk of venerable appearance,  
Stood naked before you, his face gray-haired;  
He strengthened you with wholesome counsel  
[Col. 0721B] and then withdrew.

At last, at your mother’s command, you are anxiously seized,  
Struck and confined in a stronghold;  
but a thunderbolt is made from heaven, and you emerge,  
The barrier broken.

Again they vainly restrain you with chains;  
You are ever loosed by the hands of the Thunderer,  
And above the rays of the sun you are lifted  
By your melodious voice.

A wicked crowd secretly plunges you, returned to earth,  
Bound, into the deep sea.  
A dolphin receives you after your bonds are loosed  
And bears you back.

Soon returning to the saving wilderness,  
You raise the gracious sign of the cross upon a cedar;  
[Col. 0721C] you lead your brother, and he sees  
A wondrous pillar of fire.

A radiant angel conveys you both;  
yet steadfastly you endure in the cave  
Whatever the holy teachings  
Of exalted Christ enjoin.

Hence you deserve so often to be caught up alive.  
And now, suppliant, you behold in a radiant grove  
The shining images of the saints  
By a threefold lamp.

Here the messenger of heaven shows you Trani,  
Soon to be yours: a lasting title  
Unto the final generation of this world  
In a consecrated church.

[Col. 0722A] How many punishments do you undergo for heaven’s rewards?  
How often did you bear blows though undeserving?  
At last the heavenly powers heal your wounds  
By their supreme power.

While sailors plot to bring you death  
Amid the waves, the kindly Virgin bears you safely  
To Otranto; and at once you drive away  
Various plagues.

Walking toward the people of Taranto, holy one,  
You shed blood when harshly restrained;  
thence you passed on to renowned Trani,  
Welcomed as a cherished guest.

Here, safe, you cry: “Kyrie, have mercy!”  
And a boyish breeze follows you;  
for you asked for a like refrain  
[Col. 0722B] in return for an apple.

With bread and water you sustain  
Your small body, clothed in a wretched tunic;  
and always you went barefoot,  
Your tongue in supplication.

Still breathing, thirsty, you ask for a cup  
Of water and drink; but the water left behind  
Becomes nectar, as once  
Christ Jesus did.

Who could fully tell your praises, Nicholas?  
Who could number your great wonders?  
By the sign of the cross, holy one, you restore speech  
To your sister.

How many lame walk by your aid,  
How many blind see? A great multitude, formerly crippled,  
Readily moves its limbs  
[Col. 0722C] everywhere in supplication.

You drive demons from wretched bodies,  
You loosen fetters and manacles for many,  
Shipwrecked vessels enduring winter storms,  
And hostile arms.

Holy one, calm the sea for sailors;  
holy one, watch over our salvation,  
That we may enjoy the eternal rest of heaven  
When our course has safely ended.

Let there be glory to God the Father and to the Son;  
let us equally worship the Holy Spirit:  
God is Three and One everywhere  
Through everlasting ages. Amen.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1125: GALO, BISHOP OF PARIS

[Col. 0721]

NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VII, p. 54)

[Col. 0721D] Galo, also called Walo and Gualo, was a disciple and successor of Ivo of Chartres in the abbey of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais. When, after being elected bishop of Beauvais, he could not obtain the king’s approval because of the powerful faction of his rival Stephen [Col. 0722D], he went to Rome to establish before the supreme pontiff the validity of his ordination, which his adversaries had attacked. Paschal II ratified it; but since it did not lie within his power to secure Galo possession of the see of Beauvais, he sent him as legate into Poland to reform abuses. There Galo deposed two bishops.

That legation is mentioned by Longinus, historian of Polish affairs, by Eadmer in the *Life of Saint Anselm*, and by Baronius in volume XII of the *Annals*. On his return to Gaul, Galo was solemnly and canonically elected bishop of Paris by the clergy in place of Fulk [Note: [Col. 0723D] Ivo of Chartres, letter 146.], who had died on 8 April; delegates were sent to request humbly that he not refuse the care of this Church. Yet two things opposed his election: the king’s hostility toward him and the rigor of the canons, which did not permit transfer from see to see [Note: [Col. 0723D] The same, letter 144.]. But King Philip, who by oath had prevented Galo from obtaining the see of Beauvais, gladly allowed him the bishopric of Paris.

Indeed, Galo had already attended, under this title, the assembly at Baugency on 29 July 1104 for the reconciliation of the same king with other bishops. He attended the translation of the body of Saint Lifard, abbot of Micy, and the dedication of the church of Meung in October. He was also present at the synod of Paris on 2 December of the same year [Note: [Col. 0723D] Bollandists, June, vol. I, p. 302; *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 130; Hardouin, *Councils*, vol. VI, col. 1799.], at which Lambert, bishop of Arras, by the pope’s command absolved King Philip from the bond imposed for his unlawful marriage.

Later he returned to Rome. Received there most kindly by the supreme pontiff, he not only obtained authorization for his transfer, but the pope also commended him on 6 April in letters addressed to the clergy of the Church of Paris [Note: [Col. 0723D] Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 182.]. Rejoicing with them over so great a pontiff granted to them, he delegated to Galo his own authority against invaders of ecclesiastical property. There is still extant the reply of the clergy of Paris to Paschal II [Note: [Col. 0723D] *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 128.], in which they thank him for granting them Bishop Galo, whom the canons should endeavor to imitate and by whose instruction they should be formed in virtue [Col. 0723C] and good conduct.

Meanwhile, returning from Rome, Galo passed through Lyons, where he saw Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, bound to him by friendship, then living there in exile, and Eadmer, to whom he gave a portion of the relics of Saint Prisca the martyr [Note: [Col. 0723D] *Life of Saint Anselm*, book II.]. He had formerly received these from the cardinal of that title when the body of the martyr was discovered and raised at Rome after Galo’s return from the Polish legation.

Finally, when Galo arrived in Paris, he was received by the Parisian clergy, installed in the episcopal chair, and began to administer the Church of Paris early in 1105. In that year, at the feast of the dedication, he attended the election of Ralph as abbot of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais; and in the first year of his episcopate he confirmed the church of Saint Eligius, granted by Guy of Tournai with the consent of Bishop Geoffrey to the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés. In the following year, 1106, the second of his episcopate [Col. 0723D], he confirmed the church of Marly, granted by Hervé of Marly with the consent of Geoffrey to the church of Coulombs [Note: [Col. 0724D] Proofs for the *History of Montmorency*, p. 68.].

In 1107 he approached the supreme pontiff at La Charité to complain about the monks of Saint-Denis; Suger, then a monk, says that he satisfied him by open reasoning and canonical judgment. This complaint is understood from a letter of Pope Paschal to the abbot of Saint-Denis, in which Bishop Galo is called good and Catholic, and is said to administer the sacraments freely and without corruption; the abbot was forbidden to approach other bishops for receiving the sacraments. The letter survives in an old Victorine codex.

By command of the supreme pontiff he expelled nuns from the church of Saint Eligius because of their shameless conduct, and granted it to Theobald, abbot of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, as a cell for twelve monks [Col. 0724A]. King Philip confirmed by his charter the letters issued by Galo on this matter in 1107, the third year of his episcopate. The highly devout clerics of Saint Paul, called Barnabites, now serve in the monastery of Saint Eligius in Paris.

In the same year he granted four altars to the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, at Érinniacum, Ermenonville, Duigniacum, and Louvres [Note: [Col. 0724D] *History of Saint-Martin-des-Champs*, p. 497.]. He also subjected the servants of the dean and canons of Sainte-Geneviève to their authority. He attended the funeral of King Philip, who died on Wednesday, 24 July 1108, with certain prelates who carried the body from the church of Blessed Mary at Melun to the monastery of Fleury for burial. He later attended the coronation of King Louis the Fat on the Sunday that was the second day of August, in the church of Holy Cross at Orléans, and subscribed the charter granted by the same king to the men of Fleury at Bourges in that year.

In 1108, the fourth year of his episcopate, he gave the land of Aulnay to the monks of Saint-Martin [Col. 0724B]. In the same year he confirmed the free authority granted by Imbert to the canons of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, enabling them to confer the prebends of Saint Opportuna upon whatever suitable persons they wished, without consulting the bishop [Note: [Col. 0724D] *History of Paris*, vol. III, p. 17.]. He subscribed the charter of Louis VI which, in 1109, empowered servants of the Church of Paris to bear testimony in judicial and civil cases and in pleas against all persons, and even granted them permission to wage war. Paschal II confirmed this privilege by letters addressed to Galo on 24 January 1114 [Note: [Col. 0724D] Hardouin, *Councils*, vol. VI, col. 1819.].

Together with the canons he went to Noyon on 30 July 1109 to meet the Holy Cross, which Ansellus, once a cleric of Paris and then cantor of the church of the Holy Sepulchre, sent to the Church of Paris with the letter found among the documents. On Friday it was placed in the church of Saint-Cloud; on the following Sunday the cross was carried into the greater basilica, where it is still held in honor [Col. 0724C].

Galo blessed William, abbot of Saint-Germain, in 1110. In the fifth year of his episcopate he approved the gift made by Burchard of Montmorency to the monks of Saint-Florent of Saumur. He affixed his seal to King Louis’s charter for the canons of Sainte-Geneviève on 12 March 1111, the third year of the king’s consecration. Gerard du Bois considers that Galo attended the assembly at Melun convened by King Louis in the same year [Note: [Col. 0724D] *History of the Church of Paris*, vol. II, p. 7.].

In the same year, if I am not mistaken, a council was held at Sens by Archbishop Daimbert against the privilege concerning investitures granted by Paschal to Emperor Henry. Galo attended it and subscribed, with the bishops of his province, the letter to John, bishop of Lyons, who had called them to the Council of Anse to be held in the following year, but which they declined to attend. About that time Gualo was delegated by the supreme pontiff together with Ivo of Chartres in the case of Gilbert, canon of Tours, concerning the provostship [Col. 0724D] of Sodobrium.

He is recorded as a subscriber to the charter of Louis the Fat, issued at Châlons for the foundation of the monastery of Saint-Victor at Paris in 1113. When Geoffrey, bishop of Beauvais, died about that time, Stephen of Garlande wrote to Paschal requesting that, if Galo were transferred to Beauvais, he himself might take Galo’s place [Note: [Col. 0724D] Ivo of Chartres, letter 260.]. But this transfer did not take effect, the supreme pontiff refusing it. In a bull of the same pope in the cartulary of Monte Cassino we read that Galo, bishop of Paris, was staying with Pope Paschal at Benevento in 1113.

In 1115 [Col. 0725A] he subscribed the charter of Matilda, lady of Caunac, acknowledging herself guilty of injuries inflicted upon tenants of the Church of Paris. His name is still found in the synodal letters of the Council of Châlons concerning the dispute between the monks of Saint-Vaast and Saint-Quentin, issued in the same year. Therefore he did not die in 1114, as the Sammarthani maintain, but at the latest in February 1116. He is said to have been buried in the Victorine chapel of Saint-Denis, on the left. The necrology of the Church of Saint-Quentin, under 23 February, says: “Died, Lord Galo of holy memory, second abbot of this church, afterwards bishop of Paris.”

The close relationship between him, Anselm of Canterbury, and Ivo of Chartres proves the esteem in which he was held. Several of Ivo’s letters to Galo survive. In book II of the *Life of Saint Anselm*, Eadmer calls him “a man thoroughly religious and steeped from early youth in the institutions of ecclesiastical customs.” [Col. 0725B] This is indeed demonstrated by his letter to Lambert, bishop of Arras [Note: [Col. 0725B] Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol.
