V, p. 360.], who had written to him that the whole Church ought to agree with the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church in faith, in the celebration of the sacraments, and, in accordance with the teaching of the orthodox Fathers, in frequenting the canonical hours. Accordingly Galo instructs him about the Roman rites for performing the divine office, which he himself had learned while living in Rome.

It seems appropriate here to insert the epitaph which Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, composed for Galo and addressed in the name of another Galo—perhaps a nephew—to his successor [Note: [Col. 0726B] *Works of Hildebert*, p. 1325.]:

Father and shepherd, a son and flock wish you well;  
Father, receive the vows of your son; shepherd, those of your flock.

[Col. 0726A] Be also a father to me, since that good father—indeed,  
The best of fathers—has ceased to be my father.

What that father, as I recall, said to me about you,  
Gualo, is effective above others; this man prevails among them.

To you I entrust the father whose possessions I share,  
To whom I am burdensome in this one respect: that I spare his goods.

“I am going to Rome; farewell.” He pretended he was going to Rome,  
But could have said more truly: “I am going to die.”

Death, falsely gentle to the man and diminishing his labor by rest,  
Broke off light by night and the road by delay.

“I do not wish the man to sweat among the cold Alps;  
Rather let him stand, let him remain, let him die,” it said.

A vessel of faith, a vessel of justice, a vessel of simplicity  
Has fallen; those virtues fall with their vessel.

But I hear that you have been placed as a vessel of justice beneath the fallen vessel;  
And if this is not so, may it nevertheless be so.

But the assertion of Ciaconius, Franciscus Quercetanus, and the necrology of Saint-Victor at Paris that Galo was created cardinal by Paschal II is erroneous. [Col. 0726B] For Galo, bishop of Paris, is different from Gallo, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico, whom Innocent III sent into Gaul in 1208 to visit churches and act against the Albigensians, as Rigord, Spondanus, and other authors wrote. His synodal statutes, promulgated by him, survive in volume VI of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*; they are wrongly attributed to Galo of Paris, together with certain constitutions found in volume XXVI of the Royal Printing-House edition of the Councils. Gabriel Cossart, S.J., had already noticed this error in his notes on the constitutions of Cardinal Gallo, volume XI of the *Councils*, part I, col. 35.

[Col. 0725]

LETTER OF GALO TO LAMBERT, BISHOP OF ARRAS

(It is the one hundred and twenty-ninth among Lambert’s letters and letters to him. See *Patrology*, vol. CLXII, col. 694.)

[Col. 0725]

CHARTER OF GALO, by which, after expelling the nuns, he grants the church of Saint Eligius to the monks of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés. (Year 1107.)

*Gallia Christiana nova*, VII, documents, 42.

[Col. 0725C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Reason indeed, and the authority of the Holy Scriptures, admonish those who preside pastorally over churches to examine and inspect the lives of their subjects with watchful care and pastoral concern. Thus, if they see in the churches entrusted to them persons who are dishonorable and incorrigible, they should endeavor either to restore them to the state of religious life or entirely to replace them with other persons, lest those who live well be corrupted by the example of those who live badly, and lest the shepherds, if they conceal the matter or keep silent, be condemned forever through the consent implied by their silence.

Therefore we wish all to know that the monastery of Saint Eligius at Paris had indeed formerly been assigned to an order of nuns. But at last, through diabolical instigation, that frail sex sank into such wretched degradation that, publicly and shamelessly adhering to secular life [Col. 0726C], breaking its vow of chastity and wholly casting aside the purpose of religious life, it made the temple of God a den of fornication and would not at all heed the voice of our admonition.

I therefore, Galo, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, and William the archdeacon, unable to endure so great a scandal and such a plague, have, by command of Lord Pope Paschal, by the counsel of our king Philip and his son Louis, and also at the urging of our canons, removed and wholly excluded from the aforesaid monastery those notorious and incorrigible persons because of the baseness of their lives, and, with God’s help, have adorned the holy place with a more exalted order of religious life.

Let all, both present and future, therefore know that we grant to the Church of Blessed Peter at Saint-Maur-des-Fossés the monastery of Saint Eligius with all its appurtenances, to hold forever, saving the right of the Church of Paris [Col. 0727A]. That is: the abbot of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés shall possess the said monastery as his cell and exercise full and perfect abbatial authority over the monks serving God there. It has been established that at least twelve monks, with their prior, shall be placed there to serve God, who appear sufficient to maintain the order according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

It should further be known that we retain wholly and forever, in relation to the abbot of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, the same authority which our predecessors formerly had over the monastery of Saint Eligius and the abbess of that place, insofar as it appears to pertain to the monastery of Saint Eligius and its possessions.

But, in order that every cause of dispute may hereafter be excluded [Col. 0727B], we have distinctly and openly specified what authority, right, and custom the bishop and the canons of Saint Mary formerly possessed, and now possess, over both the abbess and that monastery. It must therefore be understood that whenever the bishop of Paris summoned the abbess to justice, she without doubt appeared before the bishop to perform whatever justice was required. But if any servant, maidservant, or guest of that monastery committed an offence against the person of the bishop or against his own property, the abbess, having first heard the bishop’s order, brought them before the bishop to render justice; and, after the bishop’s justice, the abbess received her own jurisdiction, if she wished.

If the abbess wished to grant freedom to servants or maidservants [Col. 0727C] of that monastery, alienate land, or make a *manufirma* (a legally binding conveyance), she had no power or permission to do so without the bishop’s consent and without a charter sealed by his seal and confirmed by his chancellor. Our predecessors are known to have possessed this authority over the abbess and monastery of Saint Eligius, and we likewise hold the same dignity of authority over the abbot of the Church of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, as determined above. We relinquish or relax none of our right, but merely change the abbey into a cell.

By customary obligation, the monastery of Saint Eligius pays the canons of Blessed Mary two meals each year: one at the feast of Saint Paul and the other at the feast of Saint Eligius; both meals are received in the canons’ refectory [Col. 0727D]. It is also customary that the community of the said monastery make one procession with the canons of Blessed Mary, on Rogation Days, on Ascension Day, and at the funerals of the canons. In any other processions which the canons decide to make, whether for clear weather, against some storm, or because of some necessity, the said community must follow the ordinances of the canons and always accompany them in those processions if commanded.

We have not wished to pass over in silence the fact that whenever the mother church ceases from the divine office, the monastery of Saint Eligius must of necessity also cease and remain silent [Col. 0728A]. Under this distinction, therefore, we have briefly included the powers, rights, and customs of both bishop and canons, so that no controversy may henceforth arise and that the right and custom of both churches may be defended by this present privilege.

Saving, therefore, as stated, the right of the Church of Paris, and with the assent of our king Philip and his son Louis and the common consent of our canons, we grant to the Church of Blessed Peter at Saint-Maur-des-Fossés the monastery of Saint Eligius to possess as a cell. The condition is that, whenever the abbot of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés makes the required profession in the Church of Paris, he shall there, in the bishop’s presence, profess that he holds and possesses the monastery of Saint Eligius by the gift of the bishop and the benefaction of the Church of Paris.

We also wish to determine that the men of the said monastery shall in no way go into the king’s army without consulting the bishop; rather, the abbot or prior, by the bishop’s counsel and command, must warn them and send them into the army [Col. 0728B]. It is also determined that, on the feast of Saint Eligius, the canons of Saint Mary shall occupy the right choir, while the monks occupy the left, so that the prior or cantor of the monks may be received to hold the choir with the canon who holds it; and no other person shall be admitted to do this. The abbot or prior shall sing the Mass; if neither is present, one of our clergy shall celebrate it.

It should be known that on that day the aforesaid meal is supplied: six live pigs of sound flesh, two muids of wine and half a sextary, and two sextaries and half of well-winnowed wheat [Col. 0728C]. The meal supplied on the feast of Saint Paul consists of eight rams, two muids of wine measured according to our cloister’s measure, three sextaries of well-winnowed wheat, and six denarii and an obol.

That this grant and ordinance may remain unshaken, we have ordered this present charter to be made and, as a sign of complete validity, have sealed it with our seal and handed it over to be confirmed by the hands of our canons.

Sign of Galo, bishop. Sign of Berner, dean. Sign of Adam, precentor. Sign of William, archdeacon. [Col. 0728D] Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Rainald, archdeacon. Sign of Roger, priest. Sign of Landon, priest. Sign of Durand, priest. Sign of Anscher, deacon. Sign of John, deacon. Sign of Guineran, deacon. Sign of Theobald, subdeacon. Sign of William, subdeacon. Sign of Guilbert, subdeacon.

Publicly enacted in the chapter of Saint Mary, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1107, the fifteenth indiction, epact 25, concurrent 1; in the forty-seventh year of King Philip’s reign and the third year of Galo’s episcopate.

Gilbert, chancellor, wrote this.

APPENDIX TO GALO

[Col. 0729]

LETTER OF ANSELLUS, CANTOR OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE, TO THE CHURCH OF PARIS. He sends a portion of the wood of the Holy Cross. (Year 1108.)

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, VII, documents, 44.)

I.

To GALO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris; to STEPHEN, archdeacon, whose greatness in renown and power is celebrated even among us in many parts of the world; to B., dean; R., archdeacon; N., precentor; and to the whole community of Saint Mary of Paris: ANSELLUS, cantor and priest, though unworthy, of the most glorious Sepulchre—submission, reverence, and love; and may you so live in this world that through your prayers I may deserve to rejoice with you without end in the world to come.

Though I have now been bodily separated for twenty-four years from your church and from you, in which and among whom I was nourished and educated, yet, ardent in my affection for you, I dwell with you in mind and spirit in your Church [Col. 0729B]. For with those who have come from you to us each year, who knew you and were known by you, I have always spoken and diligently inquired about the condition of your Church, what you are doing, and how you fare—especially concerning those of you whom I saw and knew. So long as I live, although absent, I shall always love you. Often, too, in dreams, I seem to take part in your solemnities and processions and also in your weekday matins and offices, and to sing psalms with you.

Therefore, concerned for you because of this affection, I asked the venerable lord patriarch and our canons that you might be joined as brothers and participants in the prayers and benefactions of our community. Granting this petition, they in turn ask and request the same from you [Col. 0729C].

Moreover, from the gifts which God has given me for the honor, glory, and exaltation of your Church, of yourselves, and of your city, I have devoutly sent you, through your faithful servant Anselm—from whom I also received the letter you sent us—a great and incomparable gift: a cross made from the wood of the Holy Cross.

As we have learned from Greek and Syriac writings, the instrument of Christ’s cross consisted of four pieces of wood: one on which Pilate wrote the title [Col. 0730A]; another on which his outstretched arms and palms were fastened; a third on which his body hung; and a fourth on which the cross was fixed, which was also moistened and sanctified by the sprinkling of the blood from his side and feet. This cross which I sent you is made from two woods, because one cross is inserted into another. The inserted portion is from that on which he hung; the cross into which it is inserted is from the foot-support on which the cross was fixed. Both are worthy; both are holy.

Further, David, king of the Georgians, who with his predecessors held and guarded the Caspian Gates, where Gog and Magog are shut in—and whose son does the same even now—whose land and kingdom lie against the Medes and Persians and are to us like a defensive wall, held this cross in the highest veneration and affection while he lived. When he died and his son succeeded to the kingdom [Col. 0730B], his wife, venerable more for holiness than for nobility of birth, cut off her hair and assumed the religious habit. Taking this cross and much gold, she came to Jerusalem, with a few companions, not intending to return but to end her life there in tranquil silence and prayer. From the gold she had brought she distributed shares to the religious communities of the holy city and gave alms to the poor and pilgrims. Afterwards, under the authority of Lord Gibbelin, patriarch, she established the community of Georgian nuns which is in Jerusalem.

Not long afterward, at the request of the sisters and the patriarch, she assumed the government of the community. Finally, after distributing and giving away all that she had brought, and spending it for the necessities of the community entrusted to her, when famine had oppressed our region [Col. 0730C], she herself began to suffer want with those subject to her. And since she had already received much as gifts and much as loans, she was compelled by pious concern to do for the needs of the community entrusted to her what she would by no means have done for the needs of her own body.

Thus this wood, not to be purchased at any price, was purchased for a price in this manner. Behold, I have sent it to you; I beseech you, keep it honorably, as you ought. Yet, so that it may be a memorial to posterity and to our successors of whence [Col. 0731A] and how you received it, write in your books: “Our cleric Ansellus sent this cross, made from the wood of the Holy Cross, from Jerusalem to our Church and to us.”

I ask you therefore to love me who loves you, and after my death to keep remembrance of me in your prayers. Inform me by your letters what befell the bearer of so great a treasure, and whether he arrived safely among you.

II.

You asked by what means and under what necessity this portion was taken from the Lord’s Cross. I shall make known to you what I heard and learned concerning it from letters and from the report of Syrian elders. It is read in the Gospel: “Jesus indeed performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book” [Col. 0731B]; and you have read many things, though not everything. For the Greeks possess many things which the Latins do not possess. You have nevertheless read that Saint Helena caused the Lord’s Cross to be cut in half, carried one cross to Constantinople to her son, and left the other at Jerusalem. After Jerusalem had been ravaged, Chosroes seized the portion left there and carried it into Persia; after Chosroes had been killed, the Emperor Heraclius brought it back to Jerusalem and placed it at Calvary, to be venerated by the Christian people.

After Heraclius’s death, however, the people of the unbelievers so oppressed the Christians that they attempted to extinguish Christ’s name and to obliterate the memorial of the Cross and the Sepulchre. Accordingly, having piled up wood beneath it, they burned part of the Sepulchre [Col. 0731C] and wished likewise to burn the Cross; but the Christians hid it [Col. 0732A], and for that reason many of them were killed. Finally, after taking counsel, the Christians divided it, once cut, into many portions and distributed these among the churches of the faithful, so that, if one portion were taken from them to be burned, the other portions might thereby be preserved.

Thus, in the city of Constantinople, besides the emperor’s cross, there are three crosses from it; in Cyprus, two; in Crete, one; in Antioch, three; in Edessa, one; in Alexandria, one; in Ascalon, one; in Damascus, one; in Jerusalem, four. The Syrians have one; the Greeks of Saint Sabas have one; the monks of the valley of Jehoshaphat have one; we Latins at the Holy Sepulchre have one, which is one palm and a half in length, one inch in width, and one inch in thickness, square in section. The patriarch of the Georgians [Col. 0732B] also has one; and the king of the Georgians likewise had one, which now, thanks be to God, you possess.

Now, further to complete your joy, and for the glory and honour of your church, your royal dignity, your city, and yourselves, I have devotedly sent you, through Bernard, precentor of Sainte-Geneviève, a man honourable by your own testimony, a most great gift and incomparable treasure, not inferior to the former: namely, a cross made from the stone of the Lord’s Sepulchre. I earnestly beg you to keep it honourably, as is fitting. I therefore ask that after my death you remember me in your prayers. Inform me by your letters what befell the bearer of so great a treasure, and whether he arrived safely among you [Col. 0732C]. Farewell.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1115: SAINT GODFREY, BISHOP OF AMIENS**

[Col. 0731]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT GODFREY

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. X, col. 1168)*

[Col. 0731D] Two authors of the twelfth century wrote contrary accounts of Saint Godfrey: Guibert, his immediate successor in the abbacy of Nogent [Note: [Col. 0731D] See *Patrologia*, vol. CLVI, cols. 898, 1126.], and Nicholas, monk of Saint-Crépin of Soissons. The former was a man of gravity and mature age; the latter a youth who had scarcely passed the years of puberty when he undertook to write the saint’s Life. One was his contemporary and, as it were, his equal; the first was distinguished in learning and rank, the second a simple monk, known only through his *Life of Saint Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens*, which he composed from the report [Col. 0732D] of certain persons.

Nicholas continually exalts Godfrey with praise. Guibert has seemed to some rather unfair toward the holy bishop and somewhat suspect in his case; nevertheless, he extols the holy man’s virtues and upright deeds, and for that reason his testimony should carry still greater weight. Let us examine them both.

The see of Amiens had been vacant for some time, namely two years, when, after fasts and prayers had first been offered, proceedings were undertaken to elect a successor. According to Nicholas, Godfrey, abbot of Nogent in the diocese of Laon, was elected; or, as Guibert prefers, a certain archdeacon of Amiens, whose representative Godfrey acted as at the Council of Troyes. His election, approved by King Philip, according to Nicholas, was confirmed at the council held at Troyes in April 1104.

Godfrey was certainly present there, whether as abbot of Nogent, bishop-elect of Amiens, or representative of the archdeacon. Having seen and heard the envoys of the people of Amiens concerning the election, he contemplated flight; but he was intercepted by Cardinal Richard and the bishops, and was proclaimed bishop of Amiens by all. He was consecrated at Reims by Archbishop Manasses, with Lambert, bishop of Arras, and John, bishop of Thérouanne, standing beside him. Coming then to Amiens, he entered barefoot the church of Saint Firmin the martyr.

[Col. 0733B] In the first year of his episcopate, on 26 February 1104 [1105], he confirmed to the monks of Lihons the gifts made by Robert the Younger, count of Flanders, etc.; and two days later, on the day before the Kalends of March, he granted to the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs the church of Lignières. In the same year he gave the church of Saint Remigius in the wood to the monastery of Saint-Fuscien, whose foundation or restoration he confirmed in a synod of his clergy at Amiens in 1105.

The following year he confirmed the priory of Saint Peter near Abbeville; and, after Manasses, archbishop of Reims, had given the altar of Condé, Godfrey subscribed at Reims to the grant for the monks of Reims. He was then there to complain about the monks of Saint-Valery, if the account of the Valery controversy is authentic—a matter which we shall discuss later. Immediately afterwards [Col. 0733C] he travelled to Italy to the supreme pontiff. On his return, at Lambert of Arras’s request, he solemnly consecrated the church of Arrouaise with John of Thérouanne on 23 September 1106.

He attended the Council of Troyes, presided over by Pope Paschal II, in May 1107, and there procured confirmation of the church of Saint Remigius which he had previously granted to Saint-Fuscien. In that same year, Guibert’s words are: “When, as he supposed, the body of the martyr Firmin was being transferred from one shrine to another, he found there no little writing—not even a testimony of a single letter—showing who lay there. I report what I heard from the bishop of Arras and from the bishop of Amiens himself.” On this account the bishop of the city immediately inscribed on a lead tablet that Firmin, martyr and bishop of the Amiens people, was buried there [Col. 0733D].

Without delay, the same thing occurred at the monastery of Saint-Denis. When the body was being raised from the more ornate chest prepared by the abbot, and when the head was being unwrapped together with the limbs, a little parchment was found in the martyr’s nostrils, declaring that he was Firmin, martyr of Amiens. These are Guibert’s statements, which agree excellently with the dates already assigned by us for the discovery of Saint Firmin the martyr, for the episcopate of Saint Salvius, and for King Dagobert I’s gift of Saint Firmin’s relics to the monastery of Saint-Denis—a gift published by Luc d’Achery from an old manuscript codex of the library of Saint-Victor at Paris, in his notes on Guibert, p. 567.

It should incidentally be observed [Col. 0734A] that nearly the whole city of Amiens was consumed by fire on 16 October 1107. In May 1108, from Saint-Quentin-du-Mont, where Godfrey was staying, he wrote to Balderic, bishop of Noyon, asking him, just as he had written the chronicles of the churches of Cambrai and Arras, to commit to writing also the deeds performed in the diocese of Amiens, lest the very ancient foundations of churches and most cloisters, already ruined through human injury, should be handed over to everlasting oblivion. From these letters, say the Sammarthani, it is sufficiently clear that the investigation of ecclesiastical origins and records, and the restoration, as it were, of life to those whom death and the calamity of time had condemned to oblivion, are matters worthy of episcopal care.

[Col. 0734B] In the same year Godfrey was summoned by Balderic, bishop of Noyon, his familiar friend, when Odo, lord of the castle of Ham, granted him lordship over the church of Ham and, with Godfrey’s consent, regular canons were installed. Still in 1108, Godfrey granted certain altars to the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Crépy by an instrument issued in the church of Amiens on 8 November.

In 1109 he confirmed the agreement by which the chapter of Amiens yielded to the monks of Lihons the church of Fortincourt for an annual rent of five modii of grain. In the same year, while journeying to the thresholds of the holy Apostles, at Pavia in Italy he learned in a dream of the departure from this life of Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, which occurred at Cluny on 29 April, as related by the other Hugh, author of the Life of the holy abbot. This Hugh wrote the letter to Godfrey concerning the estate of Grandvilliers given by Roric and his mother to Saint Lucian of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0733D] *Annales Benedictini*, vol. V, p. 676.].

During this journey Godfrey was splendidly received by Paschal II and obtained from him, on 11 May, a bull for the regular canons whom he had established in the church of Saint Martin of Gemelles. He visited Saint Nicholas’s tomb at Bari, redeemed the ring of Saint Honoratus, bishop, which Gervin, his predecessor, had sold, and brought it back to Amiens. The Valery case cannot, however, be referred to this journey, because it had already been argued before Archbishop Manasses, who died in 1106.

In 1110 Godfrey, invited by Ancher, abbot of Centula, to be a witness of Saint Angilbert’s miracles, first sent the priest Ingutio [Col. 0734D], and then attended in person. In 1111, the eighth year of his episcopate, he confirmed to the monks of Lihons the church of Mérincourt and half the altar of Herbonnières. In the same year, on 11 June, in the third year of King Louis, he transferred the body of Saint Salvius at Montreuil from its old chest to a new one.

In 1112 he not only attended the Council of Vienne but presided over it in place of Guy, archbishop of Vienne and legate of the Apostolic See, who was impeded by a speech defect, according to Nicholas. In the same year he appears in the instrument of settlement made by Adela, countess of Vermandois and advocate of the town of Fécamp, with Nicholas, abbot of Corbie.

In 1113, the tenth year of his episcopate, he confirmed to the monks of Marmoutier [Col. 0735A] the cell of Saint-Denis, formerly built and given to them by the priest Ingutio, on condition that they should yearly celebrate the anniversary of Drogo, bishop of Thérouanne. This cell was then situated in a suburban meadow; it is now enclosed within the walls and has been given to the Fathers of the Society of Jesus. In the same year Godfrey subscribed the charter of foundation of Saint-Victor at Paris.

On 17 April 1114, in a synod, he confirmed to the monks of Lihons the altars of Herbonnières and Hangest, previously granted them by Otger, provost of the church of Amiens, who had there assumed the monastic habit. In the same year, on 4 July, he confirmed the acts of his predecessor Gervin in favour of the monks of Marmoutier, who lived in the cell of Bodincourt in Ponthieu, within his diocese. He attended the Council of Reims held on 2 September, as also the dedication of the church of Laon, performed on 6 September.

Two months later, fleeing the disturbances aroused in his city by the commune established by the citizens, by Enguerrand, count of Amiens, and by others, he took with him a certain monk of Nogent and, without consulting anyone, resigned his bishopric [Note: [Col. 0735] Pressed by these evils, he had gone to Ivo, bishop of Chartres, at Beauvais, from whom he obtained Letter 255 to King Louis.]. Having sent his ring and sandals back to the archbishop of Reims, he went to Cluny, where, Guibert says, “as a former bishop, he consecrated an altar.” From there he went to the Grande Chartreuse, where he remained outside the community in a cell from the Ember days of Saint Nicholas in December until the beginning of Lent. Recalled by the synods of Beauvais and Soissons, he obeyed their commands and presented himself at Reims. There, severely rebuked by the legate Cono [Col. 0735C] and Archbishop Ralph for rashly abandoning his see, he was ordered to return to his church.

There, on Ash Wednesday, he vigorously opposed and endeavoured to abolish the practice, contrary to custom, of eating meat during Lent; and on Maundy Thursday he excluded the intemperate from the holy table on Easter Day, postponing them until the following day. Guibert, p. 516, tells the withdrawal and return of Godfrey somewhat differently, adding that Godfrey returned from the Charterhouse on Palm Sunday and, together with the king, attacked the tower of the rebels; on that occasion the king himself was wounded in the breast by a javelin.

In the same year Godfrey ratified the restoration of certain altars to the church of Compiègne, made on 16 June 1115, the twelfth year of his episcopate; and he subscribed the synodal letters of the Council of Châlons, issued in the octave of the Apostles, in the dispute between the monks of Saint-Vaast and Saint-Quentin-du-Mont. Finally, late in 1115, while travelling with Archbishop Ralph to Reims to transact certain business, he died on the road on 8 November, in the fiftieth year of his age. He was buried in the chapter-house of the greater monastery of Saint-Crépin near Soissons.

Bernard, dean of Soissons, wrote certain poems concerning Saint Godfrey; and Joscelin, bishop of Soissons—formerly archdeacon of Bourges and a celebrated master at Paris—composed his short epitaph. This Joscelin transferred Saint Godfrey’s body in 1138 from the chapter-house [Col. 0736B] into the church of Saint-Crépin and honourably placed it beneath a vault before the high altar; but though carefully sought by our people, it could not be found. Joscelin’s verses are these:

> Glory of bishops, honour of clergy and monks,  
> Beauty, leader of the flock, example of morals—Godfrey  
> Lies here, ascending to the stars on the eighth day of November.

The feast of Saint Godfrey is observed on the same day in the monastery of Saint-Crépin and in the church of Amiens. He is praised as illustrious in holiness in the *Life of Saint Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*, and in the letter of Hugh, likewise a monk, to Abbot Pons: “the honour of bishops, outstanding in learning, conspicuous in holiness.” Nicholas, monk of Saint-Crépin, wrote Saint Godfrey’s Life in two books and dedicated it to Rothad, dean of Soissons. Surius abridged it in his usual manner; thus Nicholas’s original perished, and nothing remains of it except the abridgment found in an old codex of Rouge-Cloître near Brussels. Some chapters are lacking in it, and these create difficulties in the earlier account.

A great example of his piety and of the veneration in which the people held him while alive was displayed when, as he celebrated the sacred rites at Christmas, he refused the offerings of those who wore their hair long in the manner of women. In order not to be deprived of the bishop’s favour and blessing, they immediately seized knives and cut off their hair.

[Col. 0735]

# LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF SAINT GODFREY, BISHOP OF AMIENS

## I. Letter of Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens, to All the Faithful—Confirmation of Gifts Made to the Monastery of Lihons by Robert the Younger, Count of Flanders, and by Robert of Péronne. (1104)

*[Dom d’Achery, Spicilegium, vol. VIII, p. 163.]*

[Col. 0735D] GODFREY, by the grace of God bishop of Amiens, [Col. 0736D] to all who believe in Christ and have been reborn through the sacred font of baptism: greeting and salvation.

The monks of the church of Lihons, our most beloved brothers, came to us bearing charters sealed by Robert the Younger, count of Flanders, by his wife Clementia, by their son Baldwin, by Robert of Péronne, brother of our count Enguerrand, and by Robert’s wife Adela. The charters recorded that these persons had, with joyful devotion, granted to the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in which the aforesaid brothers served the Lord, the whole allod of Harbonnières and everything belonging to it, except the altar. Their purpose was that, by taking these goods from their own temporal needs and giving them for the sustenance of Christ’s poor, this might become for the souls of themselves and their ancestors a reward of recompense.

After these documents had been presented and read, the brothers asked us, since the aforesaid allod lay within our bishopric, to attest and confirm by our charter what had been done. Willingly receiving this petition and satisfying their prayers, we testify that it was so done and, so far as concerns us, grant and establish it—desiring above all increase, not diminution, for their possessions [Col. 0737B].

We found the following witnesses recorded in the aforesaid charters.

In the Flemish charter:

The abbot of Molesme; Robert of Béthune; Onulf, seneschal; Baldric of Colham; Amalric of Neura; Osto Bostelarius; William, castellan of Saint-Omer; Hacetus of Bruges; Baldwin, chamberlain; Siger of Lillers; Theobald of Ypres.

[Col. 0737C] In the charter of Péronne were:

Mainerus of Péronne; Odo, son of Enguerrand; Peter, son of Hilisendis; Acard, son of Gerard; Gerard Frotetus; Gerald of Capi; Gonzo and Rabellus; Drogo; Lupus; Waldric of Vermandvillers; Sibod, son of Roger; Rainer of Lihons; Herbert, mayor of Herbonnières; Herbert, his maternal uncle; [Col. 0737D] Walbert and Gilbert.

If any persons violate this, they shall, as sacrilegious persons condemned by episcopal judgment, be separated from the body of Christ, which is the Church.

Given at Amiens on 26 February, in the first year of Bishop Godfrey.

## II. Grant by Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens, of the Priory of Saints Vitus and Modestus of Ligniac, on the River Conchie, in the Territory of Arras. (1104)

*[Marrier, History of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, p. 349.]*

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0738A] Brother GAUDFREY, by God’s grace bishop of Amiens, to all present and future children of the holy mother Church, in faith and works: continual prosperity of present well-being and peace, and, after the departure from this passing life, unending joy.

The traditions of the orthodox Fathers and canonical ordinances impose upon me, while I exercise the episcopal office, the duty that the affairs of the Church which, by God’s authorship, I serve should be administered with reasonable care, and that they should be apportioned to each of its ministers according to their merits. When these things have been distributed with diligent care, we must also, as far as possible, provide for what makes for their peace, fortifying with authoritative enactments and firm privileges those things against the storms and tempests of the world which arise from the snares of the faithless.

Therefore, stirred with all vigilance by these obligations incumbent upon my office and rank, I took care that the possessions of my Church which, in my time and by God’s gracious gift, had been recovered by religious men and reclaimed from unjust lay seizure should be granted to persons of good repute and religious leaders, to be possessed continually by them from our Church, from ourselves, and from our successors; and that, to repel the weapons of those who seize them, they should be confirmed with privileges as with a shield of protection and an impregnable wall.

Accordingly, I, our archdeacon Enguerrand, and the other dignitaries of the church of Amiens grant to the church of Saint Martin, the eminent confessor, situated in the Parisian suburb in the place called “the Fields,” the church of Lignières with its appurtenances, to possess in perpetuity, for supplying the necessities of the monks who serve the Lord there and at the monastery of Cluny [Col. 0738C].

Nevertheless, we diminish none of our right or ancient authority in it for ourselves, our successors, or our ministers. Rather, just as the proper see of my predecessors had from ancient times existed for conducting ordinations and preparing chrism and whatever other ecclesiastical sacraments, so may this continue forever, with the monks giving their due consent. It shall pay synodal dues, rents, *circadae*, and all other things canonically exacted from the churches of our bishopric—not for the property, but for the church of Vi and Villereia, and for what is canonically acquired.

We also grant to the brothers whatever they and the Church of Cluny may unquestionably acquire within our bishopric, while preserving the rights and advantages of our aforesaid church and its ministers. We reserve to our own jurisdiction unjust occupations and the investigation of criminal cases involving clergy and people, matters which canonical constitutions leave undetermined for the monastic order. That this confirmation of the grant may remain valid and inviolable, I affix the sign of the subscription below, so that this instrument of privilege may suffice as a testament for the witness of posterity and the proof of truth.

Sign of Bishop Godfrey. Sign of Archdeacon Enguerrand. Sign of Archdeacon Fulk. Sign of Dean Roger. [Col. 0739A] Sign of Provost Otbert. Sign of Treasurer Rainer. Sign of Cantor Roger. Sign of the priest Gislebert. Sign of the priest Clarus. Sign of the priest Hugh. Sign of the priest Ralph. Sign of the priest Baldwin. Sign of the deacon Nantald. Sign of the deacon Girald. Sign of the deacons William and Tetselin.

Signs of the subdeacons Warin, Hugh, and Solomon.

Done in the church of Amiens, in the year 1104 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction 12, in the reign of Philip, king of the Franks, with his son Louis as commander of the army, and with Enguerrand as count of Amiens; happily, in the first year of Godfrey’s episcopate. Amen.

Girald, subdeacon of the church of Amiens, acting in the place of the chancellor, subscribed.

Given at Amiens, 28 February.

## III. Foundation of Saint-Fuscien-in-the-Wood (1105)

*[Gallia Christiana, vol. X, instruments, p. 299.]*

Brother GODFREY, by God’s grace bishop of the people of Amiens, to all children of holy mother Church: by the authority of the holy Scriptures, may we walk in faith through this vale of weeping in such a way that we deserve to ascend the mountain of true and everlasting exultation to behold the face of God [Col. 0739C].

If we say, my brothers, that from ancient times certain holy persons, recognizing the exile of their pilgrimage and longing with all their hearts for the blessed foundations of the heavenly city, have, by a fitting act of self-denial, trampled under the foot of reason the flowing current of transitory pleasure; and that, poor themselves, they imitated poor Christ, so that they might be made rich with rich Christ, and most devoutly enslaved themselves to his service—which alone makes free—then, as this saving example has by God’s grace been handed down to our own times, we see some die to the world through monastic contemplation, others live according to the regular order, and still others exercise themselves in God’s work in eremitical solitude.

But because not all receive this saying, and because one who cannot adhere to so great a perfection is not therefore commanded to despair of God’s mercy, let such a person, by comforting holy persons in need and sharing material goods with them for their spiritual goods, aspire with the sure confidence of fixed hope toward the blessed foundations of which we speak. For when Truth itself spoke of the manifold building-up of souls, in order to stir human minds to works of mercy and set before them the fruit of such works, among other things it uttered in few words a great saying: “Give, and it shall be given to you.”

Therefore Enguerrand the count, hearing with the ear of his heart the voice of this divine exhortation and promise, when he first began to build the monastery of the martyr of Christ, Blessed Fuscien, devoutly granted the whole territory of that mountain to the venerable Odolric, first abbot and builder of that place, and to the monks who would follow his direction. The purpose was that, after the house of God had been built there, the place formerly uncultivated might become a dwelling of people, free and exempt from every secular power, custom, or exaction [Col. 0740A].

This was likewise approved and expressly granted by Enguerrand of Mondidier, under whose hereditary lordship part of that territory fell by right, subject to Count Enguerrand. To this benefaction Count Enguerrand added male and female serfs on his estates, four tenants with half the enclosure of Amélie, half the village of Saints and more, all granted in equal freedom and exemption, together with serfs and maidservants, woods and cultivators, and the usages exacted from and rendered by them.

He also granted that, if any of his dependants wished, for the salvation of his soul, to bestow some benefit from his means or possessions on the house of God being built and enlarged, he might do this freely and without challenge. This was especially appropriate since Enguerrand himself would retain no right or exaction, either for himself or for his heir, in matters belonging to the monastery, reserving only for the honour of God the protection of the monastery for himself and his heir.

Having heard of this freedom, Herlebold of Trucivilla gave one tenant on his estate and, at the place called Pulemont, arable land sufficient for half a ploughland. Peter of Glissy, son of Gualcedus, offered to the monastery one tenant in his village, one hundred eels annually from his fishery, and the whole of Fraisnet adjoining the castle of Picquigny. The monks purchased half the vicariate of that estate from Drogo of Gissencourt and Gudard of Picquigny [Col. 0740C].

When Gilo of Golencourt assumed the monastic habit, he granted, with the consent of his son Sevin, half of the whole field of all his estate, except the newly cleared lands belonging directly to the lord of the village; and, from the circuit of the bridge called Pratense, the ground on both sides divided by the ditch named Rivery, where a settlement was also made of cultivators belonging directly to the aforesaid church.

Hugh of the village of Saint-Martin, for the soul of his brother William when the monks had buried him, gave one tenant and land at Alodiis. Hato, canon of Boves, became a monk at the end of his life and gave at Boves two tenants, the allod which he held at Costeney, and three tenants with land, meadow, and wood.

Four men held in equal portions the allodial land adjoining the place called Cambagnaldios, though they paid a small rent from it—namely two solidi—to Ancher Dernuretel. They offered the whole of it to the monks as an allod: Harricus of Salou, with the consent of his son Hugh; Gerold of Bossincourt, with the consent of his brothers Fulbert, Hugh, and Fulk; Ralph of Salcosis, with the consent of his nephew Ralph Richard; and Guy of Fontaines, with the consent of his cleric brother Hugh. When Ancher learned of this free alms, he remitted the aforesaid rent to the church.

[Col. 0741A] On his deathbed, Hibert of Gemelles, having asked to be buried by the monks, ceded half the village of Moreuil, with the consent of Peter and Ancher, his brother, sons of Hato, to whom the inheritance of that land belonged most directly. Hervé, son of Hermenric, gave two tenants at Desclemviller and the fief of three knights: Ursellus, Goeselin, and Gieselin.

Adam, brother of Adelmus, having become a monk, gave what he possessed at Amiens: namely, two half-ovens and eight sextarii of wheat each month at the count’s mill. The same church holds the mill of Til from Hugh of Salou, Archdeacon Enguerrand, and Hugh of Caniet, paying them the following rent: to Hugh of Salou, three modii of wheat, and at Christmas two *rasiales* of wheat, twelve coins, and two domestic fowls; to Archdeacon Enguerrand, two modii of wheat, and at Christmas two *rasiales* of wheat, six coins, and two domestic fowls; to Hugh of Caniet, the same amount at the same time [Col. 0741B].

Albert, priest of Boves, gave a vineyard and three fields; Hermenric the knight gave the tithe of the vineyard and fields. Amundus of Mondidier, beyond the bridge at Boves, gave three tenants; the lord of the castle gave three in the same place, together with the place of Saint Marcellus and the adjoining land. Gualbert of Sessolicio gave two tenants and a holding adjoining the church. Hibert of Dommedard gave one tenant at the place called Gurgetum. Peter of Glissy gave two small enclosures, and Richard of Gemelles three. Gerold of Gutincourt gave one tenant in his village. Hersendis of Amélie and her son Drogo gave one tenant, half the field in the valley of Hairard, and land to be cultivated. Tainfrid of Espany granted, on the estate of Caisnetel, one-third of three tenants and of three measures of arable land. Guerus of Picquigny, father of Stephen, gave at Curcelles the fief of one knight.

A certain woman, daughter of Dimon of Cuncty, gave the allod that she possessed at Espany. Joined to it is the allodial land which Avelina, wife of Hilo of Hisnu, possesses; she granted that after her death it should be possessed by the monks, with her husband’s consent.

After a long dispute over a certain piece of land, an agreement was also made between the monks of the aforesaid church and one Gualdric of Saints: the monks were to hold three parts of Campiparte in that land, Gualdric the fourth, the land itself being given and granted to them in common for ploughing, sowing, and harvesting [Col. 0741D].

When the pastor of the same monastery dies, the brothers elect an abbot for themselves and, according to God, confer the pastoral staff upon him. He is presented to the bishop of this see for consecration and becomes subject and obedient to him.

I, Godfrey, bishop of this see by God’s ordinance, grant these possessions of the aforesaid monastery and confirm them by the attestation of the persons present and the impression of our seal. But if anyone maliciously contrives anything against this decree, in order to alienate the goods of the church, let him be anathema; and unless he duly repents, let him be deprived of passing goods and unable to cleave to those that endure.

[Col. 0742A] I, Godfrey, bishop of the see of Amiens, first subscribed to this privilege and gave my most willing consent, when it was unanimously confirmed in the synod of Amiens in the church of Saint Mary.

Sign of Bishop Godfrey. Sign of Archdeacon Fulk. Sign of Archdeacon Enguerrand. Sign of Dean Roger. Sign of Provost Obert. Sign of Cantor Roger. Sign of Treasurer Rainer. Sign of Walter, abbot of Saint-Josse. Sign of Robert, abbot of the monastery of Forest. Sign of John, abbot of Saint-Germer. [Col. 0742B] Sign of William, abbot of Saint Mary of Breteuil. Sign of Ancher, abbot of the church of Vertus.

Done in the year 1105 of the Incarnate Word, indiction 13, while Paschal II presided in the chair of the Roman Church, Manasses in the archiepiscopal see of Reims, Godfrey in the bishopric of Amiens, Philip as king of the Franks, his son Louis as commander of his army, and Enguerrand as count of Amiens. Happily, amen.

Geraud, subdeacon of the church of Amiens, acting in the place of the chancellor, subscribed.

## IV. Letter of Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens, to Balderic, Bishop of Noyon (1108)

*[Gallia Christiana, vol. X, p. 301.]*

[Col. 0742C]

To his beloved fellow bishop BALDERIC, bishop of Noyon, GODFREY, bishop of Amiens: greeting in the Lord.

God raised me, though unworthy, to this pastoral charge, that I might do what is fitting for the devotion of the flock. Since there are in this diocese exceedingly ancient ecclesiastical foundations, and most monasteries have now been ruined through human neglect, I earnestly pray in the Lord that, lest they be consigned to everlasting oblivion, and so that the memory of pious places may lift the minds of the faithful toward devotion to the propagation of divine worship, and so that God may be rendered propitious toward our wickedness through many intercessors and bestow mercy, you may gird yourself for this pious labour—or rather persevere in it—and become the copyist and historian of our diocese [Col. 0742D] and church, as you were in the churches of Cambrai and Thérouanne, a faithful pen of a swiftly writing scribe.

Do not hide your talent in the earth, and do not fail in doing good. Peter the archdeacon greets you, as do I, your fellow servant in Christ’s sheepfold, in which may you prosper.

Written at Saint-Quentin, my delight, near the town of Péronne, in May 1108.

## V. Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens, Benefits the Church of Crépy (1108)

*[Gallia Christiana, vol. X, p. 208.]*

In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0743A] Brother GODFREY, by God’s grace bishop of Amiens, to all present and future children of the holy Church: greeting and good peace.

To the beloved brothers of the monastery of Cluny serving the Lord in the church of Saint Arnulf at the monastery of Crespy, who, by perfectly fulfilling the ready command of the Gospel, have renounced earthly resources and buried within themselves the desires of the world: we have judged it fitting to assist from the resources of our Church, sharing our substance with them and, by the counsel of our clergy, introducing them into our church as adopted sons. Therefore we make known to all, present and future, now and for ever, that we have granted them, and by this present privilege confirmed, the altar of Garmeni and the altar of Villers, [Col. 0743B] and half the altar of the village—excepting the right of the clergy of Mondidier, namely the *personatus* [parochial benefice] and the lordship of the priest and the appointment of that same priest [lacuna]—and excepting the offerings of the whole year, apart from those of the Nativity, the Purification of Saint Mary, Easter, and the feast-day offerings of the saint of that place; in these both clergy and monks share equally. The rents and the lordship over the guests of the precinct are also excepted; for in all the tithes of those same guests they are equal sharers. Also excepted is a certain portion of the land belonging to the said altar, on which five minas of grain may be sown, which belongs by right to the clergy, except that they themselves and the monks divide the tithe of that land equally between them.

Let all know that we have granted these things to them in order that, joined to us by this benefit of our affection, [Col. 0743C] they may not cease through the devoted practice of their prayers, in fraternal union, to reconcile us to God—believing that they are helped more before God by common and reciprocal prayers than by individual and private ones. But let them pay in full and by perpetual right to us, our successors, and their ministers, the synod dues, the visitations (*circatae*), and all canonical customary payments which the aforesaid altars have from ancient times paid to our predecessors.

Seal of Bishop Godefrid. Seal of Fulco, archdeacon. Seal of Ingelram, archdeacon.

Witnesses: Roger, dean; Otbert, provost; Roger, cantor; Clarus, priest; Anscher, priest; Rodolf, priest; Acard, priest; William, [Col. 0743D] deacon; Tethelin, deacon; Adso, deacon; Girald, subdeacon; Hugh, subdeacon; Rohard, subdeacon.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1108, in the first indiction, on the eighth day of November, in the church of Amiens, under Bishop Godefrid, with Ingelram and Fulco as archdeacons, Louis reigning, and Ingelram happily serving as consul of Amiens. Amen.

The seal of Bishop Godefrid.

## VI. Saint Godefrid, bishop of Amiens, confirms to Marmoutier the church of Saint Dionysius. (A.D. 1113)

[MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictines*, V, 692.]

[Col. 0744A]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

GODEFRID, by the grace of God bishop of Amiens, to all brothers and sons of the Catholic Church, present and future: unending joy of health and peace.

We consider it necessary, most beloved brothers in the Lord, that we, who by God’s gratuitous kindness discharge in the Church the office of pastoral care, should attend most diligently, with zealous concern and a mind unceasingly watchful, to the fold of the Lord’s flock entrusted to us by the Lord; and that, according to the strength bestowed on us by God the Father, we should imitate the actions of that Watchman Himself, who, standing continually upon His watchtower by day and night, does not slumber and never shall slumber, guarding and protecting the people whom He chose for Himself out of all the family of Israel as His own peculiar possession.

For we are appointed as guardians upon the walls of this earthly Jerusalem, which, placed through the fault of our first parent in the valley of tears, is in bondage with her children; by reason of our office we profess her cultivation, government, protection, and the unceasing observance of our order. We must therefore at all times provide for her against hostile attack and, with unwearied vigilance, [Col. 0744C] take precautions lest, overwhelmed by sudden injuries from wicked persons, she lose in the time of our negligence the small possessions assigned to her by the faithful for necessary uses.

For from the covetousness of faithless people—who love plunder rather than generosity—there are wont to spring up disturbances and disruptions of peace that do not serve its interests; losses and destructions too are multiplied. Unless all these are prevented by vigilant foresight, they are not cut away; and the ecclesiastical portion, set apart for very many useful purposes, is dissipated. From such dissipation, as we have said, very many disadvantages follow; very many dangers arise for stewards and administrators; and the memory among us of those who, either by a vow of perfection or for the redemption of sin, [Col. 0744D] bestowed their possessions upon churches is abandoned. Those who could faithfully distribute such goods to needy persons are deprived of the office and crown of faithful stewards.

For ecclesiastical resources include the patrimonies of the poor, the due support of those serving Christ, lodging for pilgrims and guests, the repair of collapsing churches, the redemption of captives, and the freeing of those in fetters. If these things are destroyed, great comforts are withdrawn from those suffering need. It follows, therefore, beloved brethren, that, in order to avert the misery of the needy, suppress the groaning of the poor, defend religion, and fulfil the vocation of our place, we should rise up and [Col. 0745A] draw against the wicked invaders of ecclesiastical possessions the sword that reaches even to the soul. For it will be pleasing to God and welcome to all lovers of what is good when they perceive that we are zealously taking precautions lest the Church be deprived of her right.

Therefore come, brothers, summoned with us today to the battle-line of God’s camp: let us arm ourselves with the shield of faith, by which we may quench all the fiery darts of the most wicked one; guarded by the helmet of salvation, let us gird on the spiritual sword; and by a unanimous written decree let us establish a lasting defence in perpetuity for all the possessions of the monastery of the blessed martyr Dionysius, built in the meadow of the suburb of Amiens by Ingutio, a priest full of divine love and grace, and granted by our predecessors to the religious brethren of Marmoutier.

Therefore, in confirming today the privilege of the said monastery, we excommunicate and strike with an indissoluble anathema all who presume to invade, despoil, separate, or assign to their own right the estates, possessions, tenants, livestock, gold, silver, gems, or any other movable or immovable things belonging to the sustenance or adornment of the aforesaid monastery; and, universally, all gifts which have already come to it through the devotion of the faithful and which are to be added in the future—namely the altar which has already come to them, all its offerings, the whole church of the aforesaid martyr, all burial rights, and whatever they have planted or built. Let the tithe of their livestock and wool likewise remain, under the confirmation of this privilege, undisturbed, free, and released for ever from every payment, [Col. 0745C] except that each year, on its feast, they shall pay to the church of the eminent confessor Nicholas two candles worth twelve denarii and as much incense as will suffice for the feast-day.

Let them also be joined by the bond of charity to the brethren dwelling in the church of the aforesaid confessor, so that at funeral offices clergy shall attend with monks bearing candles, and monks with clergy. Let them mutually commend to God the souls of departed brethren, and for thirty days chant Masses for one another. Let them also observe the anniversary of Lord Drogo, bishop of Thérouanne.

Likewise: the altar of Dury, its precinct, and seven small holdings, with all their revenues and customs; the altar of Sarton and its precinct; the altar of Saint Gratian and its precinct; one third of the altar of Curcelles; one third of the altar of Casseincourt, together with the appointment of the priest; the altar of Wulpi and its precinct; half the allodial lands, fields, woodland, and advocatial rights; the altar of Septemville and its precinct, with every tithe; the altar of Contay and its precinct; the altar of Chédrisc; one third of two thirds of the altar of Placy; three and a half tenants; half the tithe of the church-house of Roboredi; the whole tithe of the church-house of Ulinastri; one small holding and an orchard; three fields and three tenants at Senercourt; the land of Magnocamp; half of Albert’s lands adjoining the city [Col. 0746A] of Amiens on the side of the aforesaid church; and five solidi and ten capons from the tenants of that same Albert; five solidi, six denarii, and twelve capons from the alms of Wermund, vice-lord; and every week three cartloads of wood from the alms of Haimo of Chiedriu, in the wood of Fragailet; and one four-horse cartload in the wood of Douxville, from the alms of Ermecinis and her daughter Emmelina; and, in that same village, two small holdings; likewise the tenants whom he had in our city and outside the city. Also the *allagisterium* of the second mill [lacuna] together with these things belonging to the episcopal court. Also the altar of Douxville, its precinct, and half the tithe of the church-house. Also the *gavulum* of that same village, which [lacuna] belongs by right to Bishop Rurico and his successors.

[Col. 0746B]

Seal of Bishop Godefrid. Seal of Fulco, archdeacon. Seal of Ingelram, archdeacon. Seal of Roger, dean. Seal of Warin, treasurer. Seal of Radulf, chancellor. Seal of Baldwin, priest. Seal of Radulf, priest. Seal of William, deacon. Seal of Adso, deacon. Seal of Robert, subdeacon. Seal of Simon, canon. Seal of Baldwin, canon.

Seal of the canons of the church of Saint Nicholas: Milo, priest; Waller, deacon; Roger, subdeacon; [Col. 0746C] Robert and Arnulf, acolytes.

Α + Ω  
Alpha and Omega.

This charter was confirmed in the year 1113 of the Incarnate Word, in the seventh indiction, in the chapter-house of Saint Mary, in the sixth year of the reign of King Louis, and in the tenth year of the episcopate of Lord Bishop Godefrid. Happily, amen.

## VII. Charter of Godefrid, bishop of Amiens, by which the restoration of certain altars to the church of Compiègne is ratified. (A.D. 1115)

[MABILLON, *On Diplomatics*, p. 617, from the cartulary of Compiègne.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. GODEFRID, by God’s grace most humble minister of the Church of Amiens. [Col. 0746D]

Because the institutions of the holy canons everywhere condemn laymen who possess altars, we see many already, by God’s mercy, abandoning this usurpation; and, so that they may abandon it ever more fully, we do not cease to preach due admonition with solicitude to the Lord’s flock entrusted to us. Accordingly, one of our parishioners, Elinand, knight of Montdidier, moved by divine inspiration and admonished by our persuasion, resolved to surrender to the holy church of Compiègne—which he especially loved as one of its confreres—the altars of Méteville and Pronast, which he had long held at peril to his soul, with their appurtenances.

But since he could accomplish this only through the countess of Vermandois, from whose hand he held the said altars, as though in fief, he finally obtained her assent as well, after many earnest prayers, because she too was a sister of that church. Nevertheless, since the matter could not proceed without the consent of the bishop of Amiens, within whose diocese the altars stand, and from whom the countess herself said that she held them in fief: Elinand came to us, and the countess came with her sons. At the general synod which we were solemnly holding at Montdidier, they jointly effected the surrender to us, as equity required, of the altars, so that we might restore them to the said church of Compiègne.

I therefore, Godefrid, bishop of the church of Amiens, at the request of the illustrious Countess Adela of Vermandois, at the request also [Col. 0747B] of her sons—namely Count Radulf, Henry, and Simon the cleric—and further at the wish, indeed the devout entreaty, of the knight Elinand, give and grant to the holy church of Compiègne the altars of Méteville and Pronast with their appurtenances. So that it may possess them peacefully in perpetuity, I confirm by these memorial letters, under the authority of our seal, what has been given and granted. I also confirm by the same authority the gift of the altar of Herces, which the same persons had previously made to the often-mentioned church of Compiègne at the prayers of Louis, most serene king of the Franks, just as they did in the case of these altars.

Our lord Fulco, our archdeacon, in whose archdeaconry the said altars lie, also grants all these things and confirms them by his approval insofar as lies in his power. We reserve, however, this dignity to the Church of Amiens: for all the aforesaid altars, one of the brethren of the church of Compiègne shall appear at the synod of Amiens, and we in no way relax the remaining synodal and episcopal rights. But if anyone presumes to weaken or erase this confirmation of our donation, let him be struck for ever by the sword of anathema.

This was done, confirmed, and read aloud at Amiens, at the episcopal see, in a full synod, in the year 1115 from the Incarnation of the Lord, [Col. 0748B] the twelfth year of our episcopate, in the eighth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June].

Radulf, chancellor, wrote, subscribed, and read it aloud.

Seal of Bishop Godefrid. Seal of Roger, dean. Seal of Simon, provost. Seal of Fulco, archdeacon. Seal of Ingelram, archdeacon. Seal of Warin, treasurer.

[Col. 0747]

## ORIGINAL ARTICLES OF THE COMMUNAL CHARTER OF AMIENS, apparently granted by Saint Godefrid in A.D. 1106

(Augustin THIERRY, *Essay on the History of the Third Estate*, vol. I.)

[Col. 0747C]

1. Every person shall faithfully observe, in all things and according to justice, faith, aid, and counsel toward his fellow sworn member.

2. Whoever is caught committing theft within the boundaries of the commune, or is found to have committed it, shall be handed over to our provost; and whatever the judgment of the commune decides must be done to him shall be done. The provost shall restore to the claimant what was stolen, if he can recover it; the remainder shall be applied to our uses.

3. Let no one presume to molest within the banlieue of the city any person dwelling within the commune itself, or merchants coming to the city with their goods. If anyone does so, the commune, if it can seize him or anything belonging to him, shall exact justice from him as from a violator of the commune.

[Col. 0747D]

4. If any member of the commune takes the goods of a fellow sworn member, when summoned by our provost he shall appear before the commune and there perform, saving our right, whatever the aldermen shall adjudge concerning it.

5. But if one who is not a member of the commune takes another’s goods and refuses to render him justice within the banlieue, after the commune has made this known to the men of the castle where he resides, should it be able to seize him or anything belonging to him, our provost shall retain it until that person has rendered justice, until we have our redress and the commune likewise has its own.

6. Whoever strikes by fist or open hand any member of the commune—except a habitual disturber of the peace or a *lecator* [uncertain term]—shall, unless he can justify himself before our provost against the person struck by two or three witnesses on the ground of self-defence, pay twenty solidi: fifteen to the commune and five for the lords’ justice.

7. But whoever wounds his fellow sworn member with weapons, [Col. 0748D] unless he can similarly justify himself against the wounded man by lawful testimony and an oath sworn in self-defence, shall lose his fist; or, for redemption of the fist, shall pay nine pounds—six, that is, to the fortification of the city and the commune, and three for the lords’ justice. [Col. 0749A] If he cannot pay, he shall, at the mercy of the commune but with the lords’ chattels reserved, surrender his fist. [lacuna]

9. But if one who is not a member of the commune strikes or wounds a member of the commune, unless he is willing to render justice according to the judgment of the commune before our provost, the commune, if able, shall pull down his house, and the principal goods shall be ours. And if it can seize him, before the provost [lacuna] the mayor and aldermen shall exact justice from him, and his chattels shall be ours.

10. Whoever assails his fellow sworn member with foul and dishonourable insults, if two or three persons hear him, shall be convicted upon their testimony, and shall pay five solidi—two to the person insulted and three to the commune.

11. Whoever says anything dishonourable about the commune in the hearing of some persons, if it is made known to the commune and he refuses to clear himself before the judgment of the commune by proving that he did not say it, the commune, if able, shall pull down his house and shall not allow him to remain in the commune until he has made amends. If he refuses to make amends, his chattels shall be in the hand of the Lord [lacuna] and of the commune. [lacuna]

14. Whoever, after a complaint against his adversary has been made, cannot pursue justice through the provost, mayor, and judges of the commune, but afterwards does something against him, shall be lawfully summoned by the commune; and, when his case has been heard, it shall decide what is thereafter to be done.

[Col. 0750A]

15. Whoever, summoned by the mayor, judges, and deans—that is, the officers of the commune—evades the justice and judgment of the commune, they shall, if able, pull down his house. They shall not permit him to remain among them until he has made satisfaction, and his chattels shall be at the mercy of the provost [lacuna] and the mayor.

16. Whoever knowingly receives an enemy of the commune in his house and associates with him by selling, buying, eating, drinking, or furnishing any comfort; or gives him counsel or aid against the commune, shall become liable to the commune. Unless he promptly makes satisfaction according to the judgment of the commune, the commune, if able, shall pull down his house, and his chattels [lacuna] shall be [lacuna].

20. Whoever wishes to convict the judges of the commune of a false judgment, unless he can prove it as justice requires, shall be at the mercy [lacuna] of the mayor and aldermen, with respect to everything he possesses. [lacuna]

44. If any agreement has been made before two or more aldermen, no judicial field or duel shall subsequently arise from that agreement, if the aldermen who were present at the agreement give testimony to it.

45. All these rights and ordinances of the mayor and the commune which we have set forth apply only among sworn members; there is no equitable judgment between a sworn member and a non-sworn person.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1115: REIMBALD, PROVOST OF SAINT JOHN OF LIÈGE

[Col. 0749]

## NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. VI, p. 63.)

Reimbald, whom Mabillon calls a canon of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert at Liège, was more correctly provost of Saint John at Liège; for thus he is styled in the heading of the letter of Wazo to be mentioned below. He lived about A.D. 1115, at which time he was compelled to flee from Liège and to hide for eight months with an Abbot Richerius, of whom I know nothing further. At this host’s urging he composed a book *On the Canonical Life*, which Jean Mabillon examined in the manuscript of the monastery of Aulne, as he testifies in his *Analecta*, p. 473.

Reimbald sent this same book to Wazo, prior of Saint James at Liège, asking him to give it the finishing touch and correct what required correction. Wazo modestly replied that he had nothing to add or amend, but rather congratulated him; Reimbald answered him in a second letter. Martène and Durand published these three letters—Mabillon had noticed only two of them—from the same manuscript of Aulne in the *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. I, p. 338 ff. His *Stromata* occur twice in the Vatican Library. Bernard de Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum Manuscriptorum*, pp. 101, 138. Verses on the Life of Saint Majolus are found in *Acts of the Saints*, vol. II for May, p. 668.

[Col. 0751]

## LETTERS OF REIMBALD

(D. MARTÈNE, *Anecdota*, I, 338–340.)

### I. Friendly letter of Reimbald of Liège to Wazelin, prior of Saint James

—He asks him to put the final touch to his little works and to correct what needs correction.

[Col. 0751A]

REIMBALD, by the grace of God what he is, to WAZELIN, prior: abundant greeting in the Lord.

In the Gospel the Lord permits one, when necessity so requires, to flee from city to city. Necessity pressed upon me; leaving my own seat and church under this command—or permission—of the Lord, I fled to another place, though not far from our diocese. Here I lay concealed for nearly eight months. Meanwhile the man who had received me as his guest, Abbot Richerius, a very religious and honourable man, thinking perhaps more highly of me than I did myself, urged me with a kindly persistence to collect certain materials concerning the canonical life and, as it was more recent, perhaps to fashion something from them that might be more useful, in my judgment.

I could not resist more obstinately. But what was this? At last both the service and zeal of my host prevailed over me. I do not confess that, presuming beyond my powers, I set forth for canons a form and rule of life which I myself did not know. Rather, as the Lord granted it, I explained in this modest writing what correction of life and morals may be, and what progress toward perfection there may be in it—both for canons themselves and for all other professed adherents of holy religion.

Now, dear friend, you will do well if, before this work is published, you review it with a certain judicial severity, as they say. Correct what is faulty; remove what is superfluous; [Col. 0751C] supply what is lacking; and carry this out with such diligence that afterwards no one here may be able to speak against it except through ignorance or, God forbid, malevolence—the cure for these maladies is either slow or nonexistent. Therefore, you need not labour greatly over such matters, provided that by a fitting and adequate correction of this little work you shall, as I hope, render a service both to me and to those who piously endeavour to attain this end. Farewell.

### II. Reply of Wazelin

To his lord and friend REIMBALD, provost of Saint John, WAZELIN, his own servant: greeting and the service of good will.

Having read and reread your book on the canonical life, I have pronounced your soul blessed, since it has received the good gift and perfect donation from above, from the Father of lights, and has produced this holy, worthy work, full of blessing. For truly, I believe, you have found the treasure hidden [Col. 0752A] in the field, and you have not hidden it from friends who seek it with you, so that what God’s grace has given you individually you may make common to His faithful people.

As to your command that I should revise the book itself, amend it, supply what had been insufficiently said, and remove what was excessive, I confess that you yourself have done this more diligently, saying everything sufficiently, briefly, and clearly; and all these things will be useful to all persons of goodwill. Therefore, in the edifice built upon the apostolic foundation, where others have built upon it gold, silver, and precious stones, you too have fashioned this precious four-sided pearl, which corresponds in equal measure to the fourfold order of the canonical life and joins together its sides.

Blessed be God, who has taught you from His law and has given a right word into your mouth, so that from the good treasure of your heart you have brought forth things new and old. For I hope that whoever reads these things with a good mind will find in them advancement toward his own edification in the canonical life. Farewell.

### III. Another reply of Reimbald

REIMBALD, by the grace of God what he is, to his beloved in Christ, WAZELIN, distinguished prior of his community and order: greeting in the Lord.

Most beloved, with whatever zeal and diligence I could, I lately sent to you, in friendly confidence, the little work on the canonical life which I had produced, as though to a whetstone and file for examination. You returned it to me entirely in the same form, as they say, as though it were blessed and complete in every respect; indeed, you adorned and illustrated it with such praise that, unless I had known the simplicity and sincerity of your friendship toward me, I should have believed it was done with some colouring and mist of flattery.

But now, as is fitting, having good hope and good thoughts in every respect concerning my friend and intimate, I answer you in words not my own, but those of Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni. Writing to a certain friend of his, Namatius, he said this about a certain Flavius Nicetius, when that man, as he reported, had extravagantly praised some of his little works:

> “So far as it can be done without boasting, I rejoice in the authority of a most excellent man, if he is certain; in his affection, if he is mistaken.”

In the same words, dearest friend—I do not know whether with the same feeling, but I do know that it is with a simple and pious one—I answer you here in almost the same words: namely, so far as it can be done without boasting, I rejoice in your most excellent authority, if you are certain; in your affection, if you are mistaken. Farewell.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1115: THE CHRONICLE OF JOHN, MONK OF BÈZE, PRECEDES THE CHRONICLE OF SAINT BENIGNUS OF DIJON, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

(Dom D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, de la Barre edition, vol. II, p. 356.)

[Col. 0753]

## NOTICE

About ten years ago, when the most distinguished Pierre Pithou had lent me the Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon from the royal library, I conceived the intention of bringing the work into public light. Nor did it lack an elegance of handwriting inviting one to read; but when I turned it over and inspected it more closely, I encountered such roughness in so extensive a writing—some words transposed, some mutilated, some wholly lost—that I came to believe that the copyist’s first concern had been painting, his last writing. Hence it became necessary to abandon my earlier purpose.

Later, after the monastery of Saint Benignus had adopted the discipline of the Congregation of Saint Maur, several learned men approached me, asking that I arrange for the autograph manuscript possessed by that abbey to be sent to Paris and made public. For it had been buried in oblivion for so many years, unknown to scholars, but was now eagerly sought by those who expend effort and labour in illuminating French affairs, contending, as it were, for altar and hearth. Nor were they alone: those diviners with mercenary pens and curled style, who dared, by a rash effort, to call this Chronicle, as also that of Bèze, to their aid in attempting to remove from the way the darkness surrounding the hereditary right of the kingdom—what they call the Salic law. A reader will see how little either work supports them.

Thus spurred on, I immediately wrote once, twice, and a third time to Dijon requesting that the autograph manuscript be sent to me. Meanwhile the delay which I had foreseen intervened: for the most illustrious Lord de Castille, commendatory abbot of Saint Benignus, who kept this monument of antiquity hidden away like treasure, was reluctant that it should be removed from his little museum or carried outside the region. Nevertheless, endowed with singular courtesy and unwilling to begrudge the literary enterprise, or the public good, he readily permitted Dom Claude Bertaigne, monk of Saint Benignus, a priest and theologian of our congregation, to return the work to Paris as soon as possible. With the greatest care and utmost diligence Bertaigne had, as I asked, collated with the archetype the copy taken from the faulty manuscript in the royal library and restored it to its proper condition. Without delay, after first adding variant readings and conjectures in the margin, I sent it to the printing-house.

It will not be irrelevant, reader, for you to observe from the very preface that the authors of the Chronicles of Saint Benignus and Bèze have woven their history of French affairs in exactly the same words and syllables. Such chronicles seem to me like buskins, each fitting either foot; thus you may discern, were it only from the shadow of conjecture, the original author. From the material appended to the Chronicle of Bèze, therefore, it is plainly evident that the monk John—called secretary a little above—was the author of the account of the affairs of Bèze: this is clear from the epitaph and from the catalogue of books copied by John. The epitaph says:

> “The pious care of the monk John made known to all,” etc.

And at the end of the catalogue:

> “He also composed this book from various matters and charters.”

Do you see that he is described as the compiler not merely of charters, but also of various matters? Do not those “various matters” imply history both local and French? John’s own words certainly support this.

Nevertheless, the Chronicle of Saint Benignus raises a difficulty, for it shows clearly enough that it preceded John in time: it brought its narrative only to the death of Halinard, archbishop of Lyons and formerly abbot—that is, to the year 1052. John, however, records the grants made to the monastery of Bèze by Guillen, bishop of Langres, and by Geoffrey, abbot of Bèze, in about 1129 and 1135. For the items following the epitaph and the charter have been added in indiscriminate mixture; and he places the colophon at this abbot. But enough and more than enough on these matters. There is no need to prolong such a dispute, since I would by no means deny that, as regards secular history, the authors of the chronicles have very frequently reproduced word for word the histories of Gregory of Tours and Fredegar.
