I used the autograph of the Chronicle of Bèze, preserved, unless I am mistaken, in the Royal Library; and I considered it a matter of conscience to depart from its text by even a nail’s breadth. To prevent the repetitions in the Bèze chronicle from repeatedly provoking bile or nausea in the reader, I omitted them and referred the reader to the Chronicle of Saint Benignus. Nevertheless, I judged it worthwhile to reprint those passages which contributed greatly to the fuller illustration of French history, vigorously contested the glory or right of the king, or otherwise interrupted the thread of the narrative.

I did not think that the appendix to the Chronicle of Saint Benignus, written by its author in the following century, would be unwelcome if I added it. I had also intended to include more monuments of antiquity to elucidate both chronicles, but I laid this burden upon the shoulders of my fellow members, who are to devote their labour to composing the histories of those same monasteries.

[Col. 0755]

## CHRONICLES OF THE VENERABLE ABBOTS AND ILLUSTRIOUS BENEFACTORS AND FOUNDERS OF THIS MONASTERY OF THE MOST BLESSED ATHLETE OF CHRIST, BENIGNUS OF DIJON

To this has been added, with great labour and many nocturnal studies, what you will find after Halinard, the venerable father of this aforesaid monastery.

### HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF COLLECTED MEMORABLE MATTERS

## PREFACE

[Col. 0755A]

It was a praiseworthy—and indeed imitable—endeavour of the wise men of ancient times not only to transmit to the memory of posterity, through written records, the things that happened in their own days, but also the brave deeds of heroes of old. This undertaking brought them great human praise and furnished those who should later read or hear these accounts with an example and an incentive to emulation.

Considering these things, we who from childhood have been inhabitants and lovers of the sacred monastery of Dijon, lest perhaps our successors should rightly be angry with us—as we ourselves deservedly blame our predecessors for their negligence—will undertake, with God’s help, to describe, though in a rustic and wholly unpolished narrative, what has been handed down concerning the antiquity of the aforesaid place, and what has been bestowed upon the same flock of God’s faithful by the generosity of devout persons: namely, by kings, bishops, dukes, counts, and illustrious men, insofar as we have been able to learn it through truthful report.

Thus there may be added, both to the honour and to the monastery itself, an account of the possessions bestowed upon it and of memorable events performed in it; and, together with the duty of divine praise, may there come to its benefactors the desired reward of heavenly glory. Yet first it must be said at what time Saint Benignus, our advocate and special Christian protector, came into Gaul; how many years he preached the holy Gospel of Christ to that most fierce people; on what day and under what persecutor he completed the martyrdom of his contest; and also when, after many years, [Col. 0755C] his sacred body was revealed and translated.

### Saint Irenaeus is crowned with martyrdom. Saint Benignus is sent into Gaul by Saint Polycarp.

Therefore, in the 195th year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the third indiction, while Severus was emperor, this witness of Christ was sent with his companions to the people of Gaul under the terrible storm of Severus’s persecution. At that time this people was enslaved to the worship of demons.

This sending of the servants of God was divinely commanded and urged upon Polycarp, bishop and metropolitan of Asia, by blessed Irenaeus, archbishop of Lyons, on the seventh day after the passion of that saint, which was accomplished in the thirteenth year of Severus’s reign.

[Note: [Col. 0755] “Servants of God.” Thus I have emended it by conjecture. Acherius had printed “of the age of God.”]

For after Claudius Albinus—who had made himself Caesar at Lyons—was killed, Severus gave the whole city to the sword. There Saint Irenaeus was martyred with the entire people of Christians, numbering eighteen thousand. So great was the slaughter of the slain that, as blood flowed down from the summit of the mountain on which the city was situated, the Rhône and Saône, which join there, were seen to run red for many miles.

When this martyrdom had been completed, Saint Irenaeus appeared with the multitude of martyrs to blessed Polycarp and instructed him to send the holy priests Benignus and Andochius, Thyrsus the deacon, and Andeolus the subdeacon into Gaul to preach. These saints of God, sent by Saint Polycarp and led by an angel of the Lord, came to Lyons, the metropolitan city of Gaul. There they found the holy priest Zacharias, who, because of the storm of persecution, was hiding secretly in a crypt among the tombs of the martyrs and was praying that divine help might come to the Church tossed by the waves. This man, finally, governed the aforesaid Church after Saint Irenaeus.

Therefore, meditating on the word of God with him and rejoicing in the Holy Spirit, they prayed the Lord to direct their steps. And while they remained there, prompted by an angel of the Lord, they resolved to send Saint Andeolus to the city of Carpentras for the sake of preaching. As Saint Andeolus set out for the aforesaid place, preaching the word of God everywhere among the nations, not long afterward he was afflicted with many torments by the emperor Severus and was crowned with martyrdom. But these witnesses of Christ, strengthened by many exhortations from blessed Zacharias to proclaim fearlessly to all the word of God and the name of Christ, and having also received from him a blessing and authority to perform every ecclesiastical and divine rite, hastened to the city of Autun, accompanied by Christ’s power and the grace of miracles. Upon reaching this city on their journey, they found Faustus, a most noble man of prefectural rank and a most genuine lover of Christianity; they came to him at an angel’s prompting. Receiving them with every joy, when he learned that they were priests, he humbly asked them to consecrate by the grace of baptism his son Symphocianus, then three or five years old, together with his friends and household. When they heard this, Saint Benignus baptized him, while Saint Andochius received him from the sacred font.

The illustrious Faustus also had a full sister, Leonilla by name, a Christian matron of the city of Langres. She had three little grandsons through her son, twins, men most beautiful in appearance but more beautiful in spirit. He earnestly begged that Saint Benignus might deign to come to her. Leonilla received him as heavenly manna. At length these three twin brothers, instructed in faith in the Holy Trinity, were consecrated by Saint Benignus through the grace of baptism, together with their whole household and a multitude of people; and not long afterward they were crowned with martyrdom. Saint Benignus, meanwhile, traversing the whole region far and wide in preaching and converting many to Christ, came to the fortress of Dijon.

In the eighteenth year of Severus’s reign, he died in Britain; his son Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla, succeeded to the empire and held it for seven years. Upon his death Macrinus ruled for one year. After him Marcus Aurelius Antoninus held the empire for four years. This man, full of every vice and in the persecution of Christians inferior to none of the earlier emperors, while ranging through Gaul and persecuting the people who believed in God, came from the city of Sens to the estate of the aforesaid Faustus, called Sede-locus. There, after Saints Andochius and Thyrsus had been brought to their end by martyrdom, he himself made for Dijon and sent Heraclius, a persecutor of the saints like himself, to the city of Autun. Heraclius therefore ordered Saint Symphorianus—first beaten with dreadful scourges and wasted under prison custody—to be put to the sword. Saint Symphorianus was twenty-five years old when he suffered martyrdom, as is found in his Passion and in the acts of the above-mentioned holy martyrs. From this it may be known that the period of Saint Benignus’s preaching was about twenty years, during which he converted many in this Gaul by preaching, sanctified them with the water of baptism, consecrated churches in certain places, and appointed priests and ministers for divine worship.

### Saint Benignus suffers martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian

The emperor Aurelius, who was commonly called Aurelian—

> [Note: “Who was also called Aurelian.” There can be no doubt that he is speaking of Elagabalus, whom we know to have been called Marcus Aurelius Antoninus on his coins, sharing the common name of that illustrious emperor in whom, they say, nothing could be criticized except that he was Commodus’s father; and also sharing it with the other son of Septimius Severus, commonly called Caracalla. Anyone not wholly unfamiliar with ancient history knows that the same man was called Varius and Elagabalus; no one called him Aurelian. To this is added the fact that Elagabalus can scarcely be believed ever to have come into Gaul.]

—entered the fortress of Dijon. Having learned of the holy martyr’s preaching and virtues, which divine mercy performed through him, and with Terentius the count, minister of his cruelty, standing by, he ordered Saint Benignus to be sought out and brought before him bound and beaten. He had him stretched upon the rack and scourged with thongs for a very long time, so that the inward parts of his body lay exposed; then he threw him again into prison. There the attendants and executioners fastened his feet in a stone with molten lead—

> [Note: “With molten lead.” Perhaps “lowered lead,” says Acherius; to me it seems an incurable textual blemish.]

—and drove ten very sharp, red-hot awls into the fingers of his hands. They shut up with him for six days twelve most savage dogs. But an angel of the Lord came, gave him heavenly bread, removed the awls, and rescued him from the lead. Finally, he ordered his neck to be struck with an iron bar and his body pierced with a spear. When this had been done, a snow-white dove ascended from the prison to heaven in the sight of Christians, and a most sweet fragrance, as it were of paradise, followed.

### Gregory, bishop of Langres, discovers the tomb of Saint Benignus

Blessed Leonilla came and buried his body, embalmed with spices, not far from that very prison in a great sarcophagus. In that place Christians built a crypt. But, because of fear of the pagans, honor worthy of so great a martyr was not paid to him: the savagery of the persecution which the rulers of the state inflicted upon Christians deterred the faithful who believed in Christ.

Thus, after many courses of years had passed—for from the time of that emperor himself to the end of Diocletian and the reign of Constantine are counted eighty-one years, and from Constantine to the emperor Zeno and the reign of King Clovis about one hundred and eighty years, making in all two hundred and sixty-one—in this interval of years, as the Christians of that age were taken from this light, the place of the holy martyr’s tomb was so neglected and consigned to oblivion that it was believed that the body resting there was no longer that of a martyr, but rather of some very powerful pagan. Only the simple learning of the country people, shrewd in seeking knowledge of ancient things through the reports of old men, led the rustics to pay their vows there; and what they asked, they obtained quickly. This ignorance, increasing daily, endured through many courses of years until the time of Saint Gregory, bishop, who stands sixteenth in the catalogue of the bishops of Langres. This bishop, believing—as do other men—that some pagan had been laid there, by no means believed in the miracles performed there; rather, he detested the place lest people should worship there.

At last God’s martyr revealed himself to the blessed confessor and said:

> “What are you doing? It is not enough that you despise me yourself; you also spurn those who honor me. Do not do so, I beg you, but prepare a covering over me more swiftly.”

Shaken by this vision, he went to the blessed tomb and there, weeping, begged forgiveness; and then followed the other things recorded in the words and deeds of blessed Gregory, bishop of Tours. Since he fully described the translation of this body and of the others resting in this place, it is not necessary for us to repeat it. Therefore, setting these matters aside, we shall relate what was done thereafter.

Below are named the holy men and women resting in this sacred place, and the places in which they lay.

### Discovery and translation of the body of Saint Benignus

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 485, in the eighth indiction, while Pope Symmachus presided over the holy Roman Church, Zeno Caesar ruled in the commonwealth, Clovis first reigned in Francia, and Gaudebald in Burgundy, the body of Benignus, the life-giving martyr, was discovered and translated on the eighth day before the Kalends of December [24 November] by blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Langres, through the revelation of divine providence. This is related by Gregory, bishop of Tours, in the *Book of Miracles* (Book I, ch. 51). When it had been worthily transferred with the help of heavenly power, lest Christ’s witness thereafter be deprived of due services, this same venerable bishop built a church for him and gathered there many persons from various regions who were prepared to serve God.

### Men outstanding for holiness in Gaul

At that time many men conspicuous for holiness of life shone throughout Gaul. Among them were Saint John, abbot of the monastery called Reomaus, and also Eustadius and Saint Sequanus, natives of this province. Of these, we know with certainty that Eustadius presided over this place for some years and lived by training those subject to him in religious observance. Thus, when he died, he deserved worthy burial beside the body of the oft-mentioned holy martyr Benignus. Tranquillus succeeded him. How great his holiness was is attested by the frequent healings granted to the sick from his tomb, as Gregory of Tours relates in *On the Glory of the Confessors* (ch. 44), having himself experienced them. He was buried on the right-hand side of the tomb of the holy martyr Benignus, beside Saint Paschasia; Saint Florida was laid beside him. On the other side, beside Saint Eustadius, was the tomb of Saint Hilary the senator and of his wife, Saint Quitta. These were the ancestors of the above-mentioned John. Since the aforesaid Gregory of Tours has fully recalled in his book *On Illustrious Men* (ch. 42) who and what kind of man this Hilary was, it is enough to have said only this much.

Since, therefore, we have briefly touched on the burial of the saints, we must explain, because of the presumptuous slander of certain persons, how the cemetery of the inhabitants of this town was established in ancient times.

### The cemetery of Dijon; a community of holy women there; several bishops of Langres buried in that cemetery

From the very beginnings of Christianity a church was built there. This church, they say, was consecrated by Saint Benignus in honor of Saint John the Baptist and John the Evangelist. We know that others who had been disciples of this same apostle did likewise in the other cities in which they preached. The church was dedicated to God for this purpose: that there, through the regeneration of holy baptism, the people of believers might pass into adoption as children of God; and that it might receive into its bosom the bodies of those whose souls it brought to God.

Accordingly it was so highly honored that a congregation of holy women was established there, and very many bishops of the city of Langres ordered their bodies to be buried here, namely from devotion to the holy martyr Benignus: they wished to be buried in the same soil as he in whose priestly order they followed. Hence Saint Urban, one of their earliest bishops, is known to have lain there. Saint Gregory also, the bishop to whom Saint Benignus first deigned to reveal himself, following the example of his predecessors, asked to be buried in this church; and beside him, right and left, lie two bishops. Saint Tetricus, his successor, was placed on the right side of this basilica.

Thus that place flourished for many years, so that it was a noble abbey, subject to no lordship except that of the bishop of Langres. The burial-ground of all who lived within and outside the fortress of Dijon extended in ancient times from the bed of the stream flowing through the middle of the town to the place where the monastery now stands. This is attested by the multitude of vessels set very frequently throughout that plain, far and wide. At the westernmost boundary of this burial-ground, the body of Saint Benignus was placed after his martyrdom by Blessed Leonilla, a humble crypt having been built over him, as the straitness of the time permitted. Beside that crypt lay Saint Paschasia, who likewise completed martyrdom through fire.

### Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres, builds the monastery

Therefore, after Saint Gregory had transferred the holy martyr’s body, as divinely revealed to him, and had ordered a worthy basilica of elegant construction to be built for it, he gave all this land of which we have spoken to Saint Benignus. He decreed that this alone should be the general cemetery, belonging henceforth and forever to the right of this monastery. Hormisdas confirmed this ordinance by apostolic authority; then John, nineteenth to preside over the Roman Church after Saint Gregory, strengthened it in writing. Sergius, third after him, prohibited under the bond of anathema anyone who should presume to violate it. We shall not be reluctant to insert a copy of his letter in its proper place in this book.

Other popes, their successors, and likewise the bishops of Langres bound with the bond of excommunication those who violated this institution, and all who should inflict any violence or vexatious claim upon the above-described land, or upon the enclosure which lies around this place, or should oppress the holy household and servants. Among them, especially Bishops Isaac and Geilo struck all wrongdoers in this place with a terrible imprecation: unless they repent and come to amendment, may they have God, all his saints, and Saint Benignus—against whose possessions they act wickedly—hostile and opposed to them.

We must now proceed to the account of the matter for which this book was principally begun.

### Saint Gregory enriches the monastery

After Saint Gregory, as we have said, had built the church in honor of God and his holy martyr Benignus and gathered here a community of monks, he endeavored to enrich this place with generous benefactions of lands and possessions, so that they should not lack temporal support. He therefore gave very much from his own property and from the bishop’s property. Among other things, he gave the estate called Saciacus, with its church and all appurtenances: namely thirteen villages, Corlenis, Isiadus, Rumiliacus, Frascinus, Camberia, Linerolus, Brucialis, Bruciacus, Cernadus Vallis, Bonacurtis, Juvenadus, and Longus-Campus. These villages, with all adjoining lands and everything situated upon them—fields, meadows, woods, orchards, pastures, approaches, waters and watercourses, and all revenues—he gave entire, together with slaves, freed persons with all their peculium, and resident dependants, for the service of the monks, to be possessed by perpetual right.

> [Note: Here some material concerning Count Hilary, which cannot be read in the autograph manuscript, is lacking.]

Accordingly, since at the beginning of this book we mentioned the kings who ruled at that time in Francia and Burgundy, we must continue their chronicles down to King Guntram, who greatly exalted this place, and then to the emperor Charles, son of Caesar Louis, who restored this monastery when it had almost collapsed. For the purpose of knowing the succession of abbots who presided here at different times, the gifts bestowed upon this place under the rule of each one by the generosity of the faithful, and also the bishops of the Church of Langres who showed themselves generous toward this place, we shall take care to identify each by name and show separately what each contributed to the increase of this house of God.

> [Note: Acherius printed “were placed” (*collocata sunt*) for “were bestowed” (*collata sunt*).]

### Clovis frees Gaul from Roman imperial rule; marries Clotild; defeats Gundebald and also Alaric, king of the Goths; enters friendship with the emperor Anastasius; dies

When Childeric, king of the Franks, died, his son Clovis succeeded to the kingdom, a warlike man and vigorous in arms. In the fifth year of his reign, Syagrius, son of Aegidius, a Roman patrician who lived in Gaul, resided in the city of Soissons, which his father had held. Clovis came against him with an army and defeated him. Syagrius fled to Alaric, king of the Goths, and lived for some time at Toulouse. Clovis sent envoys to Alaric, ordering him to surrender Syagrius, or else know that war would be brought against him. Alaric, afraid, handed Syagrius over bound to the envoys. Clovis consigned him to custody, took over his kingdom, subjected everything that had been his to his own power, and ordered him to be killed with the sword. From that day Gaul was removed from the dominion of the empire.

In the tenth year of his reign, Clovis raised an army and subjected the province of Thuringia. Then, through the intervention of Aurelian, his adviser and envoy, he took as wife Clotild, a very beautiful and truly Christian girl, the niece of Gundebald, king of the Burgundians—namely, the daughter of his brother Chilperic, whom Gundebald had killed with the sword. The wedding was prepared at Chalon. The Franks came swiftly, took Clotild from Gundebald, placed her in a covered carriage with many treasures, and conveyed her to Clovis. Afterwards Gundebald, repenting and remembering that he had killed Clotild’s father, mother, and brothers, immediately sent an army after her. They caught up with her, seized back the treasures and the carriage and retained everything; but Clotild, mounted on a horse by the Franks, escaped to Clovis. Receiving her with royal honor, he loved her in marriage with perfect affection.

Clovis already had a son by a concubine, named Theodoric. Meanwhile Godegisil, brother of King Gundebald, plotting treachery against his own brother, sought help from Clovis through envoys, having learned that he was most valiant in battle. He promised that, if through Clovis’s aid he could drive Gundebald from the kingdom, he would be ready to pay him tribute. Gundebald, ignorant of the plot but urged on by that same brother, prepared a great army for battle. Clovis came with the Franks against the two kings, surrounded by a vast multitude. Battle was joined on the river Oscara, beside the fortress called Dijon. Godegisil joined Clovis; the two armies crushed Gundebald’s people. Perceiving his brother’s treachery, Gundebald turned his back and, following the bank of the Rhône, entered the city of Avignon. Afterwards he sought peace from Clovis through his adviser Aridius.

Clovis returned home with great plunder and the Frankish army, leaving five thousand Franks with Godegisil. Having obtained victory, Godegisil partially fulfilled what he had promised Clovis and pursued Gundebald to Vienne. Gundebald came out of Avignon, renewed his strength, and besieged Godegisil in Vienne. Entering the city through an aqueduct, he killed Godegisil and slaughtered with the sword the assembled Franks in one tower, intending thereafter to pay Clovis nothing.

Afterward Clovis sent an envoy, an able man named Paterius, to Alaric, king of the Goths, with a message concerning terms of friendship between them.

> [Note: “Named Paterius.” In the other manuscript, *Paternus*.]

But Alaric wished to deceive Clovis through Paternus; Paternus investigated Alaric’s circumstances and, by ingenuity, carried off his treasures, and so Alaric was deceived. Clovis therefore took up arms against Alaric. In the plain of Vouillé, ten miles from the city of Poitiers, he killed Alaric, slaughtering a great host of Goths. Clovis occupied his kingdom from the Tyrrhenian Sea and the river Loire, and from the Pyrenees to the Ocean Sea. Carrying away Alaric’s treasures from Toulouse, he brought them with him to Paris.

At the same time King Clovis received from the emperor Anastasius documents conferring the consulship. Along with these documents Anastasius also sent him a gold crown adorned with jewels and a purple tunic. From that day he was called consul and Augustus. After this King Clovis died in peace and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, which he and his queen had built in Paris; today it is called the church of Saint Geneviève. He died in the fifth year after he fought with Alaric, king of the Goths. He reigned thirty years. From the death of Saint Martin to the death of Clovis there were one hundred and twelve years.

### The sons divide the kingdom

When King Clovis died (514), his four sons—Theodoric, Clodomir, Childebert, and Chlothar—divided his kingdom equally among themselves. Theodoric received Metz as his seat; Clodomir, Orléans; Childebert, Paris; and Chlothar, Soissons. Theodoric already had a son, Theodebert, capable and vigorous. Amalric, son of Alaric, married their sister; he was killed at Barcelona by Childebert and the Franks. The Danes attacked Gaul by naval expedition and invaded Theodoric’s kingdom; they were defeated by Theodoric’s son Theodebert and lost all their plunder and their lives.

### Sigismund builds the monastery of Agaune

Sigismund, son of Gundebald, was elevated to the kingdom at the command of his father, at the estate of Quadrunium near the city of Geneva. He had as wife a daughter of Theodoric, king of Italy, by whom he had a son named Sigiric. After she died, he took another wife. At his stepmother’s intrigues he ordered his son, whom he had had by his first wife, to be killed. Afterwards, doing penance for this, he built the monastery of the saints of Agaune, a work of marvelous construction. While he continued there in prayers, devoted to fasts and almsgiving, an angel revealed to him that he should establish choirs of psalmody after the pattern of the heavenly host. Having received this counsel from God, he consulted bishops and other religious men as to whether he was considering the matter beneficially. After the holy bishops had discussed this question among themselves, although the undertaking was unprecedented, they unanimously confirmed it with the Lord’s assent. This holy work of God’s service was perfectly established and confirmed by the common agreement of all. From that time praises are offered to God at every hour; and the aforesaid Sigismund built many other monasteries.

### Chrotild continually urges her sons to avenge the death of her father, mother, and brothers

For this reason they attack Burgundy and defeat Sigismund and Gaudemar, Gundebald’s brother, in battle. Clodomir captured Sigismund as he fled to the monastery of the saints and brought him, with his wife and children, to Orléans. Godemar turned his back and hid; later, having recovered his strength, he held the kingdom of Burgundy. Clodomir again moved an army against Godemar. He killed Sigismund together with his wife and children. Abbot Avitus foretold to Clodomir that he himself would suffer in like manner what he had done to Sigismund. When the Franks and Burgundians went to war at Vézeronce, Clodomir was beheaded, deceived by the auxiliaries of Theodoric, who had Sigismund’s daughter as his wife. But the Franks, recovering strength in that same battle, defeated and annihilated the Burgundians and devastated their country.

Chlothar took Clodomir’s wife, Gundioca, as his wife. Crothechildis reared her three sons, Idoald, Guntarius, and Clodoald. Chlothar and Childebert, after driving out Godemar, occupied Burgundy. Theodoric betrothed his son Theodebert to the daughter of a certain king, named Wisigarda. Theodoric died in the twenty-third year of his reign. Theodebert took his kingdom and showed himself great in all respects and especially eminent in goodness.

### Childebert and Chlothar ravage Spain

After this Childebert and Chlothar, as we have said, attacked Spain and ravaged the greater part of it. They killed King Amalric at Barcelona and carried off their sister. The city of Saragossa was delivered by prayers and fasts. Theodoric, king of Italy, had married a sister of Clovis, who left him one daughter together with her mother. When the mother was arranging a union for her with the king’s son, she was taken by a servant named Traquilla.

> [Note: “She is taken.” Read “she is deceived.” That is, the same thing happened to Theodoric’s daughter as had happened earlier to Honoria, sister of Valentinian; nor did she preserve her chastity more carefully than Honoria.]

Traquilla was captured with an army by the girl’s mother and beheaded. The mother took her daughter away with her, after administering punishment to her. The daughter killed her mother with poison. Theodatus, having gained Theodoric’s kingdom, ordered the daughter, who had proved a parricide toward her mother, to be shut in a bath heated intensely; there she was burned. On account of this affair, fifty thousand solidi were sent as compensation to Childebert, Chlothar, and Theodebert. Childebert and Theodebert divided this money between themselves and gave none of it to Chlothar. When Theodatus died, Totila succeeded to the kingdom; the patrician Narses killed him, and the Gothic kingdom in Italy was destroyed.

Narses was maliciously accused by the Romans before Justin and his wife Sophia of oppressing Italy by servitude. Afraid, he withdrew to Naples in Campania and wrote to the people of the Lombards, asking them to come and possess Italy. King Theodebert entered Italy with an army and ravaged it along its maritime borders, while the patrician Narses was put to flight. Afterwards Bucellinus, duke under Theodebert’s command, occupied Sicily and gained dominion over all Italy. Great good fortune attended all these events.

### Childebert dies

Chlothar had by Ingund Gunthar, Childeric, Aribert, Guntram, Sigibert, and a daughter Clodesind; by Arigund, Ingund’s sister, Chilperic; and by Unxina he had Chrann. Bucellinus fought bravely and repeatedly in Italy against the patricians Belisarius and Narses, put them to flight, and crushed their army. At last, weakened by flux of the belly, while his army too was worn down by this sickness, and after Belisarius had already been killed, he was defeated and slain by Narses.

Theodebald, son of Theodebert, took Walderada as wife. He was very unjust to his subjects. In the second year of his reign Theodebald died, and Chlothar took over his kingdom, taking Walderada as his own wife. In that year, when the Saxons rebelled, Chlothar raised an army and detained a very great part of them, ravaging Thuringia because its people had presumed to assist the Saxons. Not long afterward the Saxons rebelled again, and Chlothar moved an army against them. The Saxons offered to make good all that they had done wrong and promised as compensation to give half of all their possessions except their wives and children. The Franks rejected this offer, wishing instead to kill them all. Battle was joined, and the Saxons inflicted such slaughter upon the Franks that it would have been astonishing.

King Childebert died at Paris and was buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent, which he himself had built. Chlothar took his treasures and kingdom. On account of the sins he had committed or performed negligently, Chlothar hastened to the shrine of blessed Martin the confessor. Thence, coming to the estate of Compiègne, he died, afflicted by fever, in the fifty-first year of his reign (561). Chilperic seized his father Chlothar’s treasures at the estate of Brennac and occupied Childebert’s seat at Paris, but was soon driven out. Aribert, Guntram, Chilperic, and Sigibert divided their father’s kingdom. The lot gave Aribert Childebert’s kingdom, with Paris as his seat; Guntram received Clodomir’s kingdom, with Orléans as his seat; Chilperic, Chlothar’s kingdom, with Soissons as his throne; and Sigibert, Theodoric’s kingdom, with Metz as his seat. At the same time the Huns attacked Gaul. Sigibert moved an army against them, defeated and drove them off, and afterwards made peace with them.

Guntram, reigning in Burgundy, was a good king who feared God and gave alms generously to the poor. He held his kingdom in such prosperity that all even the neighboring peoples sang his praises to the full. First he took a concubine, Veneranda by name, by whom he had a son named Gundebald. Afterwards he married Marcatrude, daughter of Magnacharius. After she had borne a son to Guntram, she poisoned Gundebald, the son of his earlier consort. By God’s judgment, she herself lost the son she had, and by her gluttony incurred the king’s hatred. Having put her away, Guntram took as wife Austrechild, surnamed Bochilane. By her he had two sons, Clotair and Clodomir.

Guntram appointed Celsus patrician in the place of Auricolanus, a man ready in speech and most prompt in every matter. The Lombard people, accompanied by famine and pestilence, invaded all Italy and, devastating it, besieged the city of Rome itself. At that time their king was Alboin. He had as wife Clodesind, daughter of King Chlothar. When Alboin died, the Lombards chose as their king a man named Cleph. King Charibert, Guntram’s brother, married a wife named Ingoberg. Leaving her, he married Merofled, daughter of a wool-worker, and took another wife, Theudechild, daughter of a shepherd of sheep. By her he had a son, but Charibert himself died immediately.

Sigibert, seeing that his brothers were taking low-born wives, sent Drogo, mayor of the palace, on an embassy to King Athanagild, asking that he give his daughter, named Bruna, to him in marriage. Athanagild sent her to Sigibert for marriage with many treasures. To embellish her name, it was enlarged so that she should be called Brunhild. Sigibert received her as his wife with great rejoicing and delight. She immediately made Drogo hated in Sigibert’s eyes, and afterwards Sigibert had him killed at her instigation. So many evils and outpourings of blood were brought about in Francia through Brunhild’s counsel that the prophecy of the Sibyl was fulfilled:

> “Bruna comes from the regions of Spain; before her face nations shall perish. She shall be torn asunder by the hooves of horses.”

Chilperic married her sister Galswintha, leaving Fredegund and the other wives whom he had had. Later he broke the oath he had given to the envoys of the Goths, that he would never remove her from the height of royal dignity, and had her strangled. After her death, he again took Fredegund as wife. Chilperic had by his former queen Audovera three sons: Theodebert, Merovech, and Clovis. Sigibert ordered the citizens of Auvergne to occupy Arles. At Guntram’s command the Auvergnats were slaughtered by the patrician Celsus. When King Athanagild of Spain died, Lenna and his brother Levidus assumed the kingdom. Lenna died. Levidus held the entire kingdom of Spain, having as his wife Gadunda, mother of Brunhild.

At the same time, when the emperor Justinian died at Constantinople (566), Justin sought the empire, a wicked and greedy man. Sigibert sent to him the envoys Warnacharius the Frank and Count Firminus to make peace with the emperor. They returned in the second year. When Aribert died, Sigibert obtained his kingdom. When the Lombards broke into Gaul, Amatus the patrician was killed by them, and much slaughter of Burgundians was carried out there. After Amatus, Mummolus assumed the patriciate. When the Lombards again invaded Gaul, Mummolus fought stoutly against them and crushed them to annihilation. Few of them returned to Italy.

The Saxons whom Theodebert had sent into Italy broke into Gaul and pitched camp at Stuplon. They perpetrated much slaughter throughout neighboring districts, but were defeated by Mummolus and fled back to Italy, losing everything they had plundered. Again the Saxons hastened into Gaul with wives and children, so that, once received by King Sigibert, they might return to the place from which they had departed. When they came into the territory of Avignon, Mummolus immediately met them and would not permit them to cross the Rhône. Afterwards, having accepted gifts, he allowed them to cross. They went on to Sigibert and were settled in the place from which they had formerly departed.

After Clip’s death, the Lombard dukes Chamo, Zabau, and Rhodanus invaded Gaul. Mummolus came against them with an army and destroyed these three dukes and their forces to annihilation. In another year Mummolus, with an army of Tours and Poitiers, at Guntram’s command took those cities from Chilperic’s control and restored them to Sigibert’s portion. Many from Chilperic’s army and the Poitevins themselves were slaughtered with the sword there.

The Lombard dukes Taloardus and Uncio entered the territory of Sion with an army by way of Hoscola and came as far as the monastery of the saints of Agaune. At Baccis-villa, not far from that monastery, their army was killed with immense slaughter by Violicus and Theodoric, dukes of Guntram. Only forty of them fled back to Italy.

Afterward Chilperic and Sigibert, having formed a plan, both raised an army, wishing to kill Guntram and seize his kingdom. But, by God’s will, their plan was changed: Sigibert attacked Chilperic, whose army, hurrying home, was already far away. When Chilperic learned this, he turned his back and reached Tournai. Sigibert came behind him to Paris; and there, when Sigibert saw the holy and most blessed Germanus, bishop of the city of Paris, he heard from him these prophetic words [Col. 0767C]:

“If you intend so to pursue your brother as to plan his death and take away his kingdom, it is written: ‘Into the pit which you prepare for your brother, you shall fall yourself.’”

Unwilling to heed this rebuke, he planned to carry out what he had begun. When he came to Vitry, all the Neustrians [Note: [Col. 0767] *Nephrasii*. In another manuscript, *Rutrasii*.] submitted themselves to his power. Ansoald alone remained with Chilperic. Fredegund sent two boys by treachery; they killed Sigibert and were themselves killed. Chilperic, having recovered his strength, regained his kingdom. Brunhild, with her son Childebert, was held under guard at Paris. But through the contrivance of Duke Gundoald, Childebert was placed in a bag, lowered from a window by a boy, and brought alone to Metz; there he was raised to his father’s kingdom by Gundoald or the Austrasians [Col. 0767D]. By Chilperic’s order Brunhild was sent into exile at Rouen. Sigibert was buried in the church of Saint Medard, aged forty, in the fourteenth year of his reign.

**The death of St Germanus.** At that time St Germanus, bishop of Paris, died. Mummolus, Guntram’s patrician, made war against Clovis and Desiderius, Chilperic’s duke, and defeated them. For Chilperic had sent his son Clovis to invade Childebert’s cities beyond the Loire. Fifty thousand men of the army were slain by Mummolus, and twenty thousand by Desiderius. In one year Chilperic lost three already grown sons, whom he had by Fredegund, to the illness of dysentery [Col. 0768A]. There still remained his son Clovis; later, at Fredegund’s instigation, Chilperic shut him up in custody in chains, and there, through Fredegund’s plotting, he died after being struck with a knife. Chilperic again ordered that all prisoners be released, so that a son might be born to him.

King Guntram put to the sword the two sons of Magnacharius, at Queen Austrechild’s instigation, and brought their property into the fisc. Guntram’s two sons immediately died. Guntram adopted Childebert as his son. Moreover, in the third year of King Childebert—which was the sixteenth year of Chilperic and Guntram—a bright star was seen in the middle of the moon. King Childebert gave his sister Ingund to Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Visigoths; by the exhortation of Leander, bishop of Seville, and of his own wife, Hermenegild was converted to the Catholic faith [Col. 0768B]. In the fifth year of King Childebert such great pestilences occurred throughout all regions that everyone found them astonishing; and all rivers passed boundaries which they had never before exceeded. King Childebert entered Italy, and the Lombards committed themselves to his authority. Childebert returned thence gloriously. He had previously received fifty thousand gold solidi from Emperor Maurice in order to drive the Lombards from Italy. Yet he not only did them no harm, but entered into friendship with them.

**King Guntram makes many gifts to churches.**—When Guntram, king of the Franks, had already ruled the kingdom of Burgundy prosperously for twenty-three years (587), seeing that he had no surviving children, he began to distribute his treasures in alms to the poor and to enrich monasteries [Col. 0768C] and holy places from those treasures. Among these he exalted with excellent gifts the church of our patron, namely the holy martyr Benignus. The most distinguished lord King Guntram himself gave to Saint Benignus the estate, then of great extent, called Élariacum, situated in view of the monastery, with all its appurtenances, upon the river Ouche (*Oscara*). And the said prince granted to the holy martyr Benignus all that even now belongs to the possession of this place, from the bridge of Dijon to the estate of Floriacum: namely, at Biciso [Note: [Col. 0767] *In Biciso*. In another manuscript: *Bisico . . . Colonicas . . . siliniaco*. Likewise below: *vestita et hapsa*.], in the estate called Colanias, at Plombières, Seliniacum, Sconsium, Villars, Campiniacum, Lanterinacum, Giron, Corcelles, Flaviniacum, Prunidum [Col. 0768D], Jussiacum, Matriniacum, and Barbiriacum: farms, cultivated lands and holdings (*mansa, vestita et absa*) in these and other places, with many enslaved persons of both sexes, cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, woods, meadows and pastures, waters and watercourses, rights of access, exit, and egress, and all things acquired or to be acquired. In their entirety the memorable King Guntram granted them to God and Saint Benignus for the sustenance of the monks serving God in this place, so that the monks dwelling there might implore the divine mercy for his own salvation and that of succeeding kings, for the remission of sins, and for the preservation of the whole kingdom.

Moreover, he ordained that, after the model of the monastery of the saints of Agaunum, the divine office should be performed in this church by day and night without interruption [Col. 0769A]. And lest this institution should grow lax in succeeding times or the monastic order perish, he decreed that the abbots of that place should be governors and overseers in this house, so that there might be one community and one order observed in both places. He made a similar arrangement for the place of Saint Marcellus, where the king himself rests in body; he enriched it with treasures, money, and many possessions, and adorned it with remarkable works and buildings.

**On the monastery of St Benignus.**—We find that Apollinaris, among others, was abbot of Saint Maurice, of this place, and of Saint Aper at Toul, as they themselves report having discovered in ancient writings. His successors also took charge of this place for many generations [Col. 0769B]. Accordingly, in those regions our patron St Benignus acquired many landed estates at that time, so that abbots and those faithful to them might have places belonging to their own possessions in which to lodge on their journeys to and fro. For beside the village called Urba is a church consecrated in the name of St Benignus, which the inhabitants of that place say once belonged by right to this church. At the settlement called Pont-de-Roide, situated on the river Doubs, half of that settlement, together with a church dedicated in honour of St Benignus, and an estate near the settlement called *ad Stabulos*, formerly belonged to this abbey. These were lost through their being granted in precarial tenure, through the violence of their possessors, the injustice of princes, and the various chances of time [Col. 0769C]. On the swift-flowing river Loue, at the place called Petregium, through which there was formerly a route for those travelling to Rome, and which lies near the settlement called Salins, the free men dwelling there committed themselves and their property to the protection of St Benignus; every year they paid at his altar the rent which they had imposed upon themselves.

**Many gifts are conferred upon the monastery of St Benignus.**—Finally, since at that time the holy martyr Benignus shone forth through frequent signs of miraculous power, and evidences of miracles and gifts of healing were displayed to all who came to his tomb, and since the most lavish goodness of the Lord was in such things venerated, worshipped, adored, and magnified, kings and princes began, because of the holy martyr’s merit [Col. 0769D], to cherish the place and exalt it with gifts and goods; nobles began to bestow possessions and estates; the devout people to contribute very much; and many also to commit themselves to his protection. Then certain distinguished men from the district of Besançon, from the estate called Cussiacum, came to the threshold of this saint and commended themselves devoutly to his protection. For many years they remained in the service of St Benignus and of the monks serving him, until that same estate was lately granted in precarial tenure to Count Alberic; he unjustly conveyed it to St Stephen, patron of the aforesaid city, as the site of his burial. Nevertheless, even today the people of that possession declare themselves to be servants of St Benignus [Col. 0770A].

**The death of Chilperic.**—Chilperic’s envoys Ansoald and Domegiselus, who had been sent to Spain to inspect the dowry, returned. In those days King Leovigild was encamped with an army against his son Hermenegild, whom shortly afterwards he killed. Hermenegild’s wife, wishing to return to Francia, was captured with her son and taken to Sicily, where she lived in exile until her death. Chilperic sent his daughter Fredegund to Spain, into her service, with great treasures and a large household; Leovigild’s son took her as his wife. Not long afterwards Chilperic came to the estate of Chelles, nearly one hundred stadia from the city of Paris [Col. 0770B], and hunted there. One day, after he had returned from the hunt in the darkness of night, while he was being lifted down from his horse and had one hand upon a boy’s shoulder, a man named Falco arrived, sent by Brunhild, and struck him under the arm with a knife; with a second blow he pierced his belly. Immediately, as a great quantity of blood flowed from both his mouth and the wound, he gave up his spirit.

When it had been reported to Guntram that his brother Chilperic had been killed (589), he went to Paris and ordered Fredegund to come to him with Clotaire, Chilperic’s son. He ordered the boy to be baptized at Rueil, and, receiving him from the holy font, confirmed him in his father’s kingdom. In the twenty-fifth year of his reign Guntram’s army entered Spain [Col. 0770C]. But burdened by the difficulty of the terrain, it immediately returned home. In the twenty-sixth year of the same reign Leudiscus was appointed by Guntram as patrician over the provinces. The birth of Theudebert, son of King Childebert, was announced. That year there was an excessive flooding of rivers in Burgundy, so that they greatly exceeded their usual bounds. In that same year King Leovigild of Spain died, and his son Reccared obtained the kingdom. In the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Lord Guntram, the birth of another son of Childebert, named Theuderic, was announced.

**The Lombards pay tribute to the Franks.**—I shall relate how the Lombard people paid twelve thousand solidi in annual tribute to the authority of the Franks [Col. 0770D], and in what manner they had relinquished to the Franks the two cities of Aosta and Susa with their territories. [Note: [Col. 0769D] *Cassaverant*: a meaningless word; perhaps *cesserant*, “had ceded”?] After the death of Prince *Clip*, the Lombard dukes spent twelve years without kings. During that time, as is written above, they broke through at various places into the Frankish kingdom. In compensation for this presumption, they delivered Aosta and Susa, together with their whole territory and population, to Guntram’s dominion. After this they sent an embassy to Emperor Maurice. These twelve dukes each sent envoys, seeking the peace and protection of the Empire. They also sent twelve other envoys to Guntram and Childebert [Col. 0771A], seeking the patronage and protection of the Franks, undertaking to pay twelve thousand solidi annually in tribute to the two kings, and relinquishing to Guntram’s dominion the valley called Ametegis. By these embassies they were to secure protection wherever it was more advantageous for them. Afterwards, with complete devotion, they chose Frankish protection. Soon afterwards, with the consent of Guntram and Childebert, the Lombards raised a duke over themselves to the kingship. Another duke, Antharius, together with his entire duchy, submitted himself to imperial authority and remained there. King Antharius paid yearly the tribute which he had promised to the Franks. After his death his son Ago, raised to the kingship, is known to have fulfilled it in the same manner.

[Col. 0771B] **Guntram dies (597).** In the thirty-second year of Guntram’s reign, from morning until midday the sun was so diminished that scarcely a third part of it appeared. In the thirty-third year of Guntram’s reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the king himself died and was buried in the church of Saint Marcellus, in the monastery which he had built. Childebert took over his kingdom and held it for four years. In the third year of Childebert’s reign in Burgundy, many signs were displayed in heaven and a comet appeared. In the fourth year after Childebert received Guntram’s kingdom, he died, and his sons Theudebert and Theuderic took over his kingdom. Theudebert received Austrasia, with his seat at Metz. Theuderic received Guntram’s kingdom in Burgundy, with his seat [Col. 0771C] at Orléans. In the fourth year of Theuderic’s reign, a glandular plague grievously devastated Marseilles and the other cities of the province. That year, in Lake Dunense, into which the river Arola flows, the water boiled so violently that it cooked a multitude of fish. In the fifth year of Theuderic’s reign, the signs seen in the previous year appeared again: fiery globes running through the sky, and something like a multitude of fiery spears appearing toward the west. In that same year Kings Theudebert and Theuderic raised an army against Clotaire and joined battle with him upon the river Aroanna, not far from the village of Dormelles. There Clotaire’s army was slaughtered most grievously; he himself turned in flight with those who remained, while they ravaged and devastated the districts and cities of the Seine that had submitted to Clotaire [Col. 0771D]. Very many captives were carried away by the army of Theudebert and Theuderic. Oppressed, whether willing or unwilling, Clotaire confirmed by a binding agreement that Theuderic should possess the territory between the Seine and the Loire as far as the Ocean and the frontier of the Bretons, while Theudebert received the entire duchy of Dentelin, between the Seine and the Oise, as far as the sea. Twelve districts, however, between the Oise and the Seine and the Ocean, remained to Clotaire.

[Col. 0772A] In the sixth year of Theuderic’s reign (602), a son by a concubine, named Sigibert, was born to him. That year Theudebert and Theuderic sent an army against the Basques; with God’s help they conquered them, reduced them to their rule, and made them tributary. In the same year the body of St Victor, who had suffered at Solothurn with St Ursus, was discovered by the blessed Bishop Econius of Maurienne. For he had seen in a vision that, rising immediately, he should go to the church which Queen Sedeleuba had built in the outskirts of Geneva, and that the place in the middle of the church where the holy body lay had been marked out. When he had gone to Geneva with the blessed bishops Rusticus and Patricius, after they had fasted for three days, a brilliant light appeared by night where that glorious body was. The three bishops, in silence, with tears and prayers, lifted the stone and found it buried in a silver shrine [Col. 0772B]. They found its face ruddy, as though it were alive. King Theuderic was present there; he enriched that church with many gifts and bestowed there the greater part of Warnacarius’s resources. In the same year Eucherius [Note: [Col. 0771D] Eucherius: he is the man commonly called Aetherius.] bishop of Lyons died, and Secundinus was ordained bishop in his place. In the same year Phocas, duke and patrician of the commonwealth, returned victorious from the Persians, killed Emperor Maurice, and assumed the empire in his place. In the seventh year of Theuderic’s reign a son by a concubine, named Childebert, was born to him. That year the sun was darkened. In the eighth year of Theuderic’s reign another son by a concubine, named Corbus, was born [Col. 0772C].

At the same time Berthoald, a Frank by birth, was mayor of the palace of Theuderic: a man of measured character, wise and cautious, strong in battle, and faithful to all. After the death of Duke Wandalmar in the district of Ultramran [Note: [Col. 0771D] *Ultramrano*. Acherius conjectures *ultrajurano*, “beyond the Jura”; but was the same duke both beyond the Jura mountains and in the district of Saintes? I certainly think not. Below, there is no doubt that one should read “and so that Berthoald …” [Col. 0772D].], and in the district of the Santones, Protadius was appointed patrician at Brunhild’s instigation. In order that Berthoald might perish, they sent him from the bank of the Seine as far as the Ocean Sea through districts and cities to investigate the fisc. Berthoald, sent by Theuderic with only three hundred men, hurried to those regions. When Clotaire learned this, he sent his son Merovech and Landeric, mayor of the palace, with an army to attack Berthoald. Contrary to the agreement, he seized the greater part of the districts and cities between the Seine and the Loire from Theuderic’s kingdom.

[Col. 0772D] When Theuderic learned that a part of his kingdom had been unlawfully taken by Clotaire, he immediately came with an army to Étampes, upon the river Loa. There Merovech, son of King Clotaire, came against him with Landeric and a great army. Since the crossing where the river Loa was crossed was difficult, scarcely a third part of Theuderic’s army had crossed when battle began. Merovech, son of Clotaire, was captured there; Landeric was turned to flight; and an immense multitude of Clotaire’s army was slaughtered in that battle. King Theuderic entered Paris victorious [Col. 0773A]. Afterwards Theuderic made peace with Clotaire at the estate of Compiègne. Both armies returned home.

In the tenth year of Theuderic’s reign, Brunhild his grandmother and Protadius, mayor of the palace, continually urged him to move an army against his brother Theudebert. At last, when by Theuderic’s command the army had assembled and pitched camp at a place called Carisiacum, his leudes urged him to make peace with Theudebert. Protadius urged each man to begin battle. Theudebert was encamped not far away with his army. Then the whole army, finding an opportunity, fell upon Protadius, saying that it was better for one man to die than for the entire army to be put in danger [Col. 0773B]. Protadius having been killed, Theuderic, dismayed and compelled, made peace with Theudebert; both armies withdrew home unharmed. In the twelfth year of his reign Theuderic sent Aridius, bishop of Lyons, Recco, and Eboric, count of the stable, to King Betheric of Spain, to bring back his daughter Hermoberga to be joined to him in marriage. After receiving oaths that she would never be degraded from royal rank, they brought her and presented her to Theuderic at Chalon. He received her joyfully. But through the machinations of his grandmother Brunhild he did not consummate the marriage; she was made so hated that, after a year, stripped of her treasures, she was sent back to Spain. That year Theuderic, acting upon the persuasion of his grandmother Brunhild and the counsel of Aridius, bishop of Lyons [Col. 0773C], ordered the holy Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, who had returned from exile, to be stoned. Wonderful miracles still take place at his tomb.

At the same time Mitius was bishop of the church of Langres, while the venerable abbot Gudinus governed the abbey of Dijon, where the holy martyr Benignus rests. In his days, namely in the fourteenth year of King Theuderic’s reign, a noblewoman called Goyla, with the consent and approval of her husband Bonevassus, gave to the aforesaid holy martyr Benignus, in the estate called Longus-vicus and throughout all its bounds, whatever she appeared to possess, together with all its adjoining lands and appurtenances: namely Fedenniacum, Postomniacum, Monasteriolum [Col. 0773D], Attegias, half of Glemponum, Curce-buntiana, Ficiacum, Chevenas, and Marcenniacum. Of all these things she made Saint Benignus heir after her own death and that of her aforesaid husband.

**The bishops of Langres, abbots of St Benignus.**—After Bishop Micetius died, Dodoald succeeded to the episcopate. He exchanged the estate called Massiacum from his own property with the man by whom it was possessed, and gave it to Saint Benignus. At that time Bobolenus exercised the office of abbot in this place. Abbot Richimarus succeeded him, when Betroald already held the episcopate. Although we have not found in writing what they added, we know that they carefully administered and firmly retained what had been granted—especially the estate of Élariacum, which King Guntram had assigned here to St Benignus with all its appurtenances [Col. 0774A], and which was harassed by the frequent encroachments of neighbouring inhabitants. Their successors do not cease to contend with this even today. Indeed, their fathers and predecessors killed God’s martyr himself; this man, however, does not cease to persecute those who serve him. In those times there were also other abbots in this place: Etherius, Vidradus, Hugo, Odeleus, and Maurinus. Of their deeds nothing has come down to us; we find only the anniversary days of their deaths recorded in ancient martyrologies.

In the twelfth year of Theuderic’s reign, a son by a concubine, named Merovech, was born to him; Clotaire received him from the holy font. That year, after Betheric’s death, Sisebut succeeded to the kingdom of Spain [Col. 0774B], a wise man, highly praiseworthy throughout all Spain, and full of piety. He fought bravely against the commonwealth, brought the province of Cantabria under Gothic rule, and subdued it. A duke named Francio, who had been king over Cantabria in the time of the Frankish kings, had paid tribute to the Frankish kings for a long time. But when Cantabria had been recalled to the Empire’s side, it was seized by the Goths; Sisebut took several cities from the Roman Empire along the seacoast and destroyed them to their foundations. At that time Isidore, the teacher, was bishop of Seville.

In the thirteenth year of Theuderic’s reign (609), King Theudebert had a wife named Belichild, whom Brunhild had purchased from merchants. Since Belichild was capable and was greatly loved by all the Austrasians [Col. 0774C], bearing honourably with Theudebert’s simplicity, and since she saw herself to be in no way inferior to Brunhild and frequently disparaged Brunhild through envoys—while Brunhild reproached her for having been her slave—at length, as the envoys went back and forth with these and other words, the two women vexed one another. A meeting was arranged between Colerence and Suentense, in order that these two queens might meet to discuss peace between Theuderic and Theudebert. But Belichild, by the counsel of the Austrasians, delayed coming there.

**Blessed Columbanus suffers much from Brunhild.**—At that time Blessed Columbanus, whose fame for holiness had by then spread everywhere throughout all the provinces of Gaul and Germany [Col. 0774D], was praised by everyone’s report and revered in every form of religious observance. King Theuderic therefore often came to him at Luxeuil and with all humility sought the aid of his prayers. Since he came to him very frequently, the man of God began to rebuke him because he involved himself in the adulteries of concubines rather than enjoying the comfort of a lawful wife, so that a royal offspring might proceed from an honourable queen rather than appear to emerge from brothels. And when the king was already obeying the man of God’s command and promised to abstain from everything unlawful, the ancient serpent approached the mind of Brunhild the grandmother—another Jezebel, as she was—and stirred her with the goads of pride against the man of God, because she saw Theuderic obeying him [Col. 0775A]. For she feared that, if the concubines were dismissed and he made a queen mistress of the court, he would curtail the extent of her own rank and honour.

It happened, therefore, that one day Blessed Columbanus came to Brunhild, who was then at the estate of Brucariacum. When she saw him entering the court, she brought to the man of God the sons whom Theuderic had by adulterous unions. When he saw them, he asked what they wanted of him. Brunhild said: “They are the king’s sons; strengthen them with your blessings.” But he said: “By no means. Know that these men will not receive royal sceptres, because they have emerged from brothels.” She angrily ordered the little boys to go away. As the man of God left the royal court and crossed the threshold, a sudden crash arose, shaking the whole house and striking terror into everyone; yet it did not restrain the fury of that wretched woman [Col. 0775B]. She then began to plot snares and urged the nobles of the court and all the leading men to disturb the king’s mind against the man of God. She also undertook to solicit the bishops, so that, by criticizing his religious observance, they might defile the standing of the rule which he had imposed upon his monks to observe.

Accordingly, yielding to the persuasions of Auligerius and the wretched queen, they disturbed the king’s mind and compelled him to visit the place and inspect its religious practice. The king, thus driven on, came to the man of God at Luxeuil and complained to him that he departed from the customs of his fellow provincials, and that all Christians were not allowed access within the more secluded enclosure. Having heard these and other words, Blessed Columbanus, bold in spirit as he was, replied reproachfully to the king [Col. 0775C]: “If you have come to this place for the purpose of destroying the monasteries of God’s servants and defiling regular discipline, know that your kingdom will utterly collapse and will be submerged together with your whole royal offspring.” Subsequent events proved this true; for the king had already, in a rash attempt, entered the refectory. Terrified by these words, he hastened back outside.

After this the king was pressed by the stern rebukes of the man of God, and Theuderic replied: “Do you expect me to inflict upon you the crown of martyrdom?” He then said that he was not so mad as to commit so great a crime, but that, if he adopted the wiser course, he would make suitable arrangements, so that the man who departed from every custom should strive to return by the road on which he had come. But since it would take too long to recount all the deeds—the queen’s plots, the exiles and afflictions he suffered—let us briefly set out the end of the matter [Col. 0775D]. The man of God, with guards appointed by Theuderic not to leave him until he had been expelled from the territory of his kingdom, proceeded as far as Nantes. Having stayed there a little while, and knowing that it did not please the divine majesty that he should return to his homeland, he then went to Clotaire, son of King Chilperic, who ruled over the Austrasians and the Franks in the furthest parts of Gaul lying upon the Ocean.

**St Columbanus approaches King Clotaire.**—Clotaire had heard what great and manifold injuries Brunhild and Theuderic had inflicted upon the man of God [Col. 0776A]. When he saw him, he received him as a heavenly gift; Clotaire kept him with himself as many days as he could. For Clotaire was strong in love of wisdom.

**His prophecy.**—While Blessed Columbanus was staying with Clotaire, a dispute arose between the two brothers Theudebert and Theuderic as both contended over the boundaries of their kingdoms. Therefore, in the fifteenth year of their reign, each sent envoys to Clotaire; each requested help against the other. Clotaire took care to lay this matter before the blessed man, asking his advice whether he ought to agree with one and fight against the other. Filled with the spirit of prophecy, Columbanus said to him: “Know that it is not fitting for you to comply with either man’s counsels; within three years the kingdoms of both will come under your power [Col. 0776B].” Seeing that such things had been prophetically spoken to him by the man of God, Clotaire was unwilling to support either side; faithfully awaiting the time promised to him, he obtained the triumph of victory.

In the sixteenth year of his reign (612), Theuderic raised an army, and in May an army was assembled at Langres from all the provinces of his kingdom. Marching through Audelange, he captured Nasium, situated upon the river Orne, and then proceeded to the city of Toul. There Theudebert came against him with the army of the Austrasians; they fought in the plain of Toul. Theuderic defeated Theudebert and routed his army. In that battle an immense multitude of brave men was killed. Theudebert turned his back [Col. 0776C] and, coming through the territory of Metz and crossing the Vosges, fled swiftly to Cologne. Theuderic pursued with his army behind him, crossed the Ardennes, and reached Zülpich (*Tulbiacum*) [Note: [Col. 0775] “He reached Tulliacum.” Acherius observes both here and below that one ought to read *Tulbiacum*; he also restores “could assemble.”]. Theudebert summoned at Zülpich the Saxons, Thuringians, and other peoples from beyond the Rhine, and all whom he could enlist against Theuderic. There battle was again joined by the Franks and other peoples. Such slaughter was wrought there by both armies, where the battle-lines fought in close engagement, that the bodies of the slain had nowhere to fall, but stood dead, as though alive, tightly wedged among the others. With God’s help Theuderic again defeated Theudebert; from Zülpich [Col. 0776D] as far as Cologne, Theudebert’s army was slaughtered by the sword and covered the face of the land.

At that time the man of God Columbanus was dwelling in the wilderness, content with the company of only one attendant. At the very hour when battle was joined at Zülpich, he was sitting upon the trunk of a decayed oak, reading a book, when sudden sleep overcame him and he saw what was taking place between the two kings. Immediately awakened, he called his attendant, described the whole battle of the kings, and sighed greatly that human blood was being shed. Theuderic then pursued Theudebert and, through the treachery of his own men, captured him and sent him to his grandmother Brunhild at Chalon. When she received him, because she favoured Theuderic’s cause more greatly [Col. 0777A], she furiously ordered Theudebert to be made a cleric and, not long afterward, impiously ordered him killed.

**Theuderic, king of Austrasia and Burgundy, dies (617); Brunhild is killed.**—In the seventeenth year of his reign (617), Theuderic ordered an army to be raised from Austrasia and Burgundy, wishing to attack Clotaire. The army was already setting out when Theuderic died at Metz from dysentery amid the blazing fires of the city. The army immediately returned to its homes. Brunhild established his son Sigibert in his father’s kingdom. Clotaire, having gathered an army, attempted to recover the boundaries of the kingdom which ought to have been under his dominion. Sigibert came against him, about to fight with battle formations; Clotaire captured him through the treachery of his followers and killed him [Col. 0777B]. In fury he also captured Brunhild, the boys’ great-grandmother, together with five other sons of Theuderic, his brothers. He killed the boys separately; Brunhild, however, he first placed disgracefully upon a camel and displayed while being led around before the enemy. Then he tied her to the tails of unbroken horses and put her miserably to death. Thus, with Theuderic’s line wholly and utterly uprooted, Clotaire alone gained the monarchy of the three kingdoms.

**Clotaire obtains both kingdoms of Theuderic.**—In the thirtieth year of his reign (614), Clotaire obtained the kingdoms of Burgundy and Austrasia. In the thirty-fourth year of Clotaire’s reign, he ordered Walnarius, whom he had appointed mayor of the palace in Burgundy, to come to him at Bonneuil with all the bishops of Burgundy and Burgundio, son of Faro [Col. 0777C]. There, assenting to all their just requests, he confirmed them by royal precepts.

**Dagobert, king of Austrasia.**—In the thirty-eighth year of Clotaire’s reign, he made his son Dagobert his partner in the kingdom and appointed him king over the Austrasians, retaining for himself what the Ardennes and the Vosges cut off toward Neustria and Burgundy.

**Contention between Clotaire and his son, settled by St Arnulf.**—In the forty-second year of Clotaire’s reign, Dagobert came in royal splendour, by his father’s command, with his leudes to Clichy, not far from Paris, and there married Gomatrude, sister of Queen Sichild [Col. 0777D]. On the third day after the wedding a serious dispute arose between Clotaire and his son Dagobert, because Dagobert wished to receive under his own authority everything belonging to the kingdom of Austrasia; Clotaire strongly refused, wishing to concede nothing of this to him. Twelve judges from among the Franks were chosen by the two kings, in order that their decision might settle the dispute. Among them was Lord Arnulf, bishop of Metz, who spoke between father and son for the concord of peace. At last, through the bishops and most wise noblemen, the father was reconciled with his son, giving him the whole territory assigned to the kingdom of Austrasia; he retained under his own authority only what lay on this side of the Loire [Col. 0778A], or in the provinces.

### Clotaire dies (628). He is buried in the church of St Vincent, now St-Germain-des-Prés.

In the forty-fifth year of his reign, Clotaire died and was buried in the suburb of Paris, in the church of St Vincent. Seeing that his father had died, Dagobert ordered all the leudes whom he ruled in Austrasia to muster an army; he sent envoys into Burgundy and the other parts of the kingdom, that they might choose his rule. When he had come to Rheims and was proceeding to Soissons, all the bishops and leudes of the kingdom of Burgundy are known to have submitted themselves to Dagobert there; moreover, the Neustrian bishops and the greater part of the nobles seem to have sought Dagobert’s rule.

His brother Aribert [Col. 0778B] strove, if possible, to take the kingdom; but, because of his simplicity, his wish achieved little effect. When the whole kingdom had been occupied by Dagobert and its treasures brought under his control, he was at last moved by mercy and followed the counsel of wise men. He granted to his brother Aribert the districts and cities lying on this side of the Loire and the frontier of Spain and Gascony, and of the Pyrenees: namely Toulouse, Cahors, Agen, Périgueux, and Saintes, together with whatever territory extends from these places toward the Pyrenees. He confirmed this by a binding compact. Choosing Toulouse as his seat, Aribert ruled in the regions of the province and Aquitaine. Three years after he had begun to reign, he conquered all Gascony and considerably enlarged the extent of his kingdom.

[Col. 0778C] At almost the same time (633), that is, in the fifth year of Dagobert’s reign, a certain distinguished man named Ermembert, with his wife Hermeneara, gave to St Benignus certain estates from their possessions, called Posciacum and Fontem Lagnis, in the district of Latiscense; and Masiacum in the district of Langres. This latter estate had formerly been assigned to this place by Edouald, bishop of Langres, but had been seized through the violence of evil men.

### Dagobert is commended for his justice.

In the sixth year of his reign Dagobert entered Burgundy. The arrival of Dagobert had indeed struck such fear into the bishops, nobles, and all those dwelling in the kingdom of Burgundy that he was an object of wonder to all because of their fear [Col. 0778D] of the justice which he administered to the poor. Accordingly, coming to the city of Langres, then leaving Dijon and staying for several days at Latona, he applied himself so earnestly to administering justice to the people of his kingdom that, from his desire for this benevolence, he could neither take sleep with his eyes nor be satisfied with food, thinking with the utmost concentration that all might return from his presence having received justice.

One day, while hastening from Latona to Chalon, deliberating, and entering the bath before daybreak, he ordered Brunulf, the uncle of his brother Aribert, to be killed. Brunulf was killed by the dukes Amalgar and Aribert and by Wilbald the patrician. Thereafter King Dagobert went on to Chalon, in his love for completing the work of justice which he had begun. He then proceeded to Autun, thence to Auxerre, then to the city of Sens, [Col. 0779A] and from there came to Paris. Leaving Queen Gomatrude at the estate of Romiliacum, where he had contracted his marriage, he took Nantild, one of her serving-girls, and raised her to the rank of queen.

In the seventh year of his reign, while he was making a royal progress through Austrasia, he took a certain girl named Ragnitrude to his bed; by her he had in that year a son named Sigibert. Aribert came to Orléans and received Sigibert from the holy font. In Dagobert’s eighth year King Aribert died, leaving a little son named Chilperic, who also died shortly afterward. It is reported that he was killed through Dagobert’s contrivance.

### King Dagobert enters into an alliance with the Emperor Heraclius.

In the tenth year of Dagobert’s reign (638), when he had been informed [Col. 0779B] that an army of the Wends had entered Thuringia, he set out from the city of Metz with an army from the kingdom of Austrasia. Having crossed the Ardennes, he approached Mainz, intending to cross the Rhine. He had with him a picked force of brave men from Neustria and Burgundy, together with dukes and counts.

The Saxons sent envoys to Dagobert, asking him to remit the tribute which they paid from the domains of the fisc; they promised to resist the Wends and pledged themselves to guard the Frankish frontier in those regions. Dagobert granted this at the counsel of the Neustrians. The Saxons who had served as ambassadors for this request ratified the agreement on behalf of all Saxons by oaths sworn upon weapons, according to their custom. Yet afterward they proved false, as in other matters. Nevertheless, by Dagobert’s decree the Saxons were granted remission of the tribute which, having been assessed by the elder Clotaire, they had customarily paid every year—five hundred cows due as an impost. At that time Dagobert’s envoys, whom he had sent to the Emperor Heraclius, named Servatus and Paternus, returned and announced that they had confirmed a perpetual peace with Heraclius.

### He grants to his sons Sigibert and Clovis the kingdoms of Austrasia and Burgundy.

In the eleventh year of Dagobert’s reign, when the Wends were fiercely ravaging the land and repeatedly crossing their frontier to lay waste Thuringia and attack the other districts of the Frankish kingdom, Dagobert came to Metz. With the counsel of bishops and nobles, and with the consent of all the leading men of his kingdom, he elevated his son Sigibert to royal power [Col. 0779D] and allowed him to have his seat in the city of Metz. He appointed Cunibert, bishop of Cologne, and Duke Agalgisus to govern the palace and kingdom. He gave his son sufficient treasure and, as was fitting, raised him worthily to the height of kingship. He decreed that every grant he had made to him should be confirmed separately by royal charters. Thereafter the kingdom of the Austrasians and the frontiers of the Frankish kingdom against the Wends are known to have been effectively defended.

When, in the twelfth year of Dagobert’s reign, a son named Clodomer was born to him by Queen Nantild—

> **Note:** [Col. 0779] *Clodomeris*. From what follows it is clear that *Chlodoveus* must be read. Not much later, *Neustria et Burgundia* must be restored.

—it is known that, by the counsel of the Neustrians and the urging of his leading men, he confirmed by a binding compact [Col. 0780A] that Neustria and Burgundy should belong to the kingdom of Clovis after Dagobert’s death; while Austrasia, being equal both in population and territorial extent, ought to belong to the kingdom of Sigibert. Whatever had from ancient times belonged to the kingdom of Austrasia was to be subject to King Sigibert’s authority and remain under his perpetual rule, except for the duchy of Dentelin, which had been separated from Austrasia, lest it should again be joined to Neustria and subjected to Clovis’s government. But the Austrasians appear to have confirmed these agreements under Dagobert’s compulsion and terror, whether willing or unwilling. It is clear that after his death, while his sons administered the kingdom, they were dissolved.

### He marches into Spain.

At the same time [Col. 0780B] it must be related what happened in the regions of Spain under their kings. After the death of the most merciful King Sisebut, Sentilla succeeded to the kingdom for one year. Since Sentilla was exceedingly unjust toward his subjects, he incurred the hatred of all the leading men of his kingdom. Therefore a certain Sisenand, one of the nobles, with the counsel of the others, sought Dagobert’s help, asking that he assist him with an army in order to drive Sentilla from the kingdom. As recompense for this service he promised to give Dagobert a golden serving-dish from the treasures, weighing fifty pounds of gold.

When he heard this, Dagobert, being greedy, ordered the entire kingdom of Burgundy to be summoned for an army to assist Sisenand. When it had been announced in Spain that the Frankish army was entering Spain to aid Sisenand, the whole army of the Goths submitted to his authority.
