Abundantius and Venerandus, with only the army of Toulouse, advanced with Sisenand as far as the city of Saragossa. There all the Goths of the kingdom of Spain raised Sisenand to the throne. The aforesaid dukes returned with their army to their own seats, honored with gifts.

Dagobert sent Duke Amalgar and Venerandus as envoys to King Sisenand, that he might send him the serving-dish he had promised. Although Sisenand handed over that dish to the envoys, the Goths took it away from them on the road and did not permit it to be carried off. Later, after negotiations by envoys, Dagobert received from Sisenand two hundred thousand solidi, the assessed value of the dish. [Col. 0780D]

### He sends an army against the treacherous Gascons.

In the thirteenth year of Dagobert’s reign, when the Gascons were fiercely rebelling and making many raids in the Frankish kingdom formerly held by Aribert, Dagobert ordered an army to be raised from the whole kingdom of Burgundy. He placed at its head Adoind, the referendary, a man formerly proved valiant in many battles in the days of King Theuderic; to him he attached ten dukes and their forces.

These were Arembert, Amalgar, Leudebert, Vandalmar, Walderic, Hermendric, Baront, and Airard, of Frankish stock; Ramelenus, of Roman stock; Willibad, a patrician of Burgundian stock; and Aichin, of Saxon stock, besides many counts who had no duke set over them. When they had marched with the army into Gascony, and the whole province of Gascony had been filled by the Burgundian army, the Gascons came out from their mountain hiding places and hastened to battle. When battle began, they did as was their custom: seeing that they were about to be overcome, they turned their backs and withdrew into the narrow valleys of the Pyrenees. They posted themselves in the safest places among the crags of that mountain. The pursuing army killed many of them, carried off a multitude of captives, committed all their houses to the flames, and stripped them of livestock and goods.

At last the Gascons, crushed and subdued, sought pardon [Col. 0781B] and peace, promising that they would present themselves before the glory and presence of King Dagobert; that, having submitted to his authority, they would fulfill all that he commanded. The army returned home unharmed, its victory accomplished. But Duke Arembert, while guarding the rear of the army, was killed by the Gascons in the valley of Subola, together with the leaders and nobler men of his force.

### Judicael, king of the Bretons.

While staying at Clichy, Dagobert sent messengers into Brittany, ordering the Bretons swiftly to make amends for the wrongs which they had committed within the borders of the Frankish kingdom and to submit themselves to his authority. Otherwise, the Burgundian army which had been in Gascony would immediately invade Brittany. On hearing this, Judicael, king of the Bretons, came to Dagobert at Clichy with many gifts, promising to make amends for all the unlawful acts committed there by his people against Frankish leudes. He also promised that he and the kingdom of Brittany would always be subject to the authority of Dagobert and the Frankish kings. Then King Judicael, taking leave of Dagobert, returned to Brittany, though he was fittingly honored by the king with gifts.

In the fifteenth year of Dagobert’s reign all the Gascon elders of that land came with Duke Amand to Dagobert at Clichy. There, terrified by royal fear, they fled into the church of St Denis; through Dagobert’s mercy their lives were spared. There the Gascons firmly promised by oaths to King Dagobert, his sons, and the Frankish kingdom that they would be faithful at all times; but, according to their accustomed manner, they lied. With Dagobert’s permission they returned to their own homes.

### Dagobert’s death (643). His praises.

That same year King Dagobert came to the estate of Spinogellum, on the river Seine, not far from Paris, and there began to suffer from a flux of the bowels. From there his attendants carried him to the basilica of St Denis. After a few days Dagobert gave up his spirit and was buried in the church of that holy martyr, which he had worthily built and adorned with gold, gems, and many most precious ornaments. He had bestowed there such wealth, estates, and numerous possessions in many places that it inspired great wonder.

He had ordered singers to be established there after the model of the monastery of the holy Agaunensians [Col. 0782A]; this was accomplished through the zeal and diligence of Abbot Aigulf. He despoiled many churches in order to enrich this one. For he devoted himself with all his piety to the service of his special patron. Therefore, after his death, he was not disappointed in his hope. How his soul was rescued from the power of demons through this martyr, with Saints Maurice and Martin assisting, was divinely revealed to a certain hermit. For while he lived, he especially honored the basilicas of these saints. Although he was devoted to greed and to the love of women, he was nevertheless generous in almsgiving to the poor.

### The Saracens ravage the Empire.

After Dagobert’s death his son Clovis, still of tender age, was raised to the throne. All the leudes of Neustria and Burgundy elevated him as king at the estate of Mosollacum. Ega, whom Dagobert had left as guardian of the boy and protector of the kingdom, governed the palace and kingdom fittingly with Queen Nantild.

In the second year of Clovis’s reign Constantine, son of Constantine, was elevated to the imperial throne at Constantinople. In his time the empire was devastated most severely by the Saracens. For during the reign of the Emperor Heraclius, the Saracen people left their own territories and invaded kingdoms subject to imperial rule in order to lay them waste. Heraclius sent an army against them to resist them. The Saracens overcame the soldiers and slaughtered them grievously by the sword. It is reported that one hundred and fifty thousand soldiers were killed by the Saracens in that battle. [Col. 0782C]

Again Heraclius gathered a great army; again he was defeated. Finally, the unhappy man, following the heresy of Eutyches and abandoning the worship of Christ, ended his life cruelly. He was succeeded in the Empire by his son Constantine, in whose time the commonwealth was excessively ravaged by the Saracens. This devastation lasted forty-seven years, until the times of the Constantine mentioned above. Then Jerusalem was captured and the other cities overthrown. Lower and Upper Egypt were overrun; Alexandria was captured and plundered; all Africa was devastated and occupied by the Saracens; Asia and Europe were shaken; and they ranged through all kingdoms bordering the sea.

At last the Emperor Constantine himself, constrained and compelled, became tributary to the Saracens, so that Constantinople with a few provinces and islands, and the city of Rome with its surrounding territory, might be retained under his authority. For about three years, and indeed nearly longer, he supplied the Saracen treasuries each day with one thousand gold solidi. At last Constans, having recovered his strength and regained the Empire to some extent, refused to continue paying tribute to the Saracens.

### Ega dies. Erchinoald becomes mayor of the palace. Pippin is mayor of the palace of Sigibert, king of the Austrasians.

In the third year of Clovis’s reign, Ega, to whom Dagobert had entrusted care of the kingdom, died, and Erchinoald was appointed mayor of the palace in his place. At that time Sentilla, king of Spain, whom Sisenand had overthrown, died, and his son Tolga was put in his father’s place at his father’s request.

[Col. 0783A] Seeing the state of the kingdom declining because its ruler was weak and insufficiently knowledgeable, being a mere youth, the Gothic leaders and chief men finally chose one of their foremost men, named Chintasind. Having gathered many Gothic senators along with the rest of the people of Spain, they elevated him to the throne, deposed Tolga, and had him tonsured for the clerical state. Chintasind brought the whole of Spain under his authority. He killed many Goths whom he knew had been accomplices with him in the deposition of the preceding kings. When he was full of days, he elevated his son, named Richisind, to rule over the whole kingdom of Spain.

After the death of his father Anchis, Pippin became mayor of the palace of King Sigibert in the kingdom of the Austrasians. Pippin was God-fearing, a lover of justice, prudent in counsel, full of faith, cautious in every pursuit of wisdom, diligent in arms, energetic, and bold in spirit. As long as he lived, he governed the kingdom with great moderation, and no gift could ever turn him away from justice.

### Flaucatus, mayor of the palace. Queen Nantild dies. Wibald is killed. Flaucatus dies of fever.

In the fourth year of Clovis’s reign (648), Queen Nantild came with her son, the king himself, to the city of Orléans in the kingdom of Burgundy. There she ordered all the elders—namely bishops, dukes, and chief men of the whole kingdom—to come before her. Drawing each of them to herself by flattery, Nantild established Flaucatus, a man of Frankish stock, in the dignity of mayor of the palace in the kingdom of Burgundy, with the approval of bishops and princes. [Col. 0783C] She betrothed to him her niece, named Ragnebert.

Flaucatus traveled through the kingdom of Burgundy and, binding himself in friendship with Erchinoald, mayor of the palace, planned to kill Wibald the patrician. In that year Queen Nantild died. That same year Flaucatus, King Clovis, Erchinoald the mayor of the palace, and some Neustrian nobles set out from Paris and came by way of Sens and Auxerre to Autun. There Clovis ordered Wilbald to come before him.

Wilbald the patrician, perceiving that Flaucatus and the other dukes had formed a plan for his death, gathered with him a very large force of soldiers, together with such bishops, nobles, and strong men as he could assemble, and set out for Autun. Hermenric, the royal chamberlain, was sent to meet him by King Clovis and his dukes, because Wilbald was afraid to approach more closely. But after receiving a guarantee of safety from the king, he came to Autun, having first honored the king’s envoy with fitting gifts.

On the following day Flaucatus and the other dukes who had conspired for his death left the city early with an army. Erchinoald, with the Neustrians whom he had with him, began the battle. On the other side Wilbald took up arms and met them with whatever battle-lines he could assemble. The dukes Flaucatus, Amalgar, Ermanlenus, and Walbert fought against Wilbald. There Wilbald was killed, and very many of his men were slaughtered with the sword.

After these events, Flaucatus left Autun on the next day [Col. 0784A] and went to Chalon. Having entered the city, on the following day that city was consumed by fire. Struck by the judgment of God and afflicted with fever, Flaucatus was placed in a boat. Traveling by water along the river Arar, called the Saône, and hurrying toward Latona, he gave up his spirit on the eleventh day after Wilbald’s death. He was buried in the basilica of St Benignus in the suburb of Dijon.

### Gundeberga, queen of the Lombards, is thrust into prison.

At this time the following were kings of the Lombards. After Authari reigned his son Ago. He sent envoys to Clotaire, offering thirty-five thousand solidi if he would cancel the twelve thousand solidi of tribute which the Lombards paid to the Frankish kings. Clotaire granted this and confirmed a perpetual peace with the Lombards by oaths and treaties.

After him reigned his son Adoald. When he had been killed by a cup of poison because of his excessive cruelty, Charoald, duke of Turin, who had as his wife Gundeberga of Frankish stock, was elevated to the throne. Believing false accusations, Charoald thrust Queen Gundeberga into exile in a single tower in the fortress of Caumellum. King Clotaire sent envoys to Charoald asking why he had humiliated a queen who was a kinswoman of the Franks. Out of reverence for the Frankish king, Charoald restored Gundeberga from exile after three years and raised her again to royal rank.

Afterward King Charoald died. Queen Gundeberga took in marriage one of the dukes, named Chrotarius, from the district of Brescia. Having received his oath that he would never remove her from royal dignity, she established him on the throne. But after several years Chrotarius forgot the oath which he had made. He cast Gundeberga down from the royal throne and confined her in a single chamber at Ticinum, in the palace court, [Col. 0784C] and made her live in private dress. Five years passed under this confinement. Since she was a Christian, she blessed God while placed in this tribulation.

At last it pleased God that Aubedo should be sent as an envoy from King Clovis to Chrotarius, king of the Lombards. Arriving at the city of Pavia, called Ticinum, and seeing that the queen—by whom he had been kindly received upon his arrival on the embassy—was confined, he represented to King Chrotarius, among other matters, that he ought not so to humiliate a queen who was a kinswoman of the Franks and through whom he had also obtained the kingdom; for this reason the Frankish kings and all the Franks would be hostile to him.

Immediately, out of reverence for the Franks, Chrotarius ordered Gundeberga released from custody and allowed her to go throughout the whole city and beyond it in royal state, visiting holy places for prayer. He ordered that everything she had lost from the estates and wealth of the fisc be restored to her. She thereafter held these possessions in royal state happily until the day of her death. Aubedo, richly rewarded by Queen Gundeberga, returned to the king.

### Sigibert, king of Austrasia, dies.

After the death of Sigibert, king of the Austrasian Franks, his son Dagobert succeeded to the kingdom. Pippin, as we have said, administered the care of the whole kingdom after the king. His son, named Grimoald, governed the palace under his father’s authority. Seeing Dagobert to be incompetent and ill-suited to the care of the kingdom, he had him tonsured into the clerical order.

### Concerning Abbot Wlfechrannus.

King Clovis, then, who was also called Clotaire, died in the first bloom of youth after completing eighteen years in the administration of the kingdom. He left three sons, Clotaire, Childeric, and Theuderic, together with their mother Queen Baldechild. Of these, Clotaire, the eldest by birth, obtained the kingdom of his father Clovis—Neustria and Burgundy. Childeric received the seat of Austrasia and Germany.

In the eighth year of his reign, King Clotaire was residing at his palace of Mosollacum when Wlfechrannus, abbot of this place, came before him, complaining of the violence of certain soldiers. King Guntram had given to St Benignus the martyr, patron of the place of Dijon, the estate of Clariacum with all its appurtenances. From the lands of this possession the aforesaid claimants inflicted many troubles on the said abbot and the monks of this place. King Clotaire therefore granted his requests, issued a charter to St Benignus concerning the aforesaid estate, and ordered it authenticated with his ring, so that none of the aforesaid claimants, their heirs or successors, or any other person whatsoever, of whatever rank and dignity, should dare to inflict any violence upon the designated property. The mayor of the palace at that time was the aforementioned Aubedo, whom the text of that charter calls Audebellus.

### Eronus, bishop of Langres.

[Col. 0785C] In the time of the aforesaid Abbot Wlfechrannus of venerable memory, the venerable Bishop Eronus presided over the church of Langres. Among the other benefits which he conferred upon this place, he sought a decree for this place from the supreme pontiff—or, more accurately, from the Roman pontiffs John and Sergius of the Roman Church. It provides that no one except the person belonging to this church of St Benignus may presume to establish or consecrate a cemetery; and that no one may dare to inflict any violence within the cloister or borough belonging to this place.

It pleased the compiler to include a copy of this decree in this book, so that those who see it might learn how great a danger threatens those who do not fear to be bound by the bond of anathema through the vicar of the apostle Peter. In the year 696 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, Sergius was presiding as pope over the holy Roman Church. These are his words.

### Letter of Sergius I obtained by Wlfechrannus.

> “Sergius, by the grace of God bishop of Rome, to Eronus, bishop of Langres: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “My dearest brother, we must be vigilant above all things lest the malignant enemy disturb Christ’s flock by any occasion. A complaint has reached us from the monks of Dijon, devotedly serving the martyr Benignus under the rule of Abbot Wlfechrannus, that the clerics of the aforesaid fortress are attempting to transfer their cemetery to themselves. Since this conflicts with the decrees of my predecessor John, successor, indeed, of Benedict, it is forbidden by the authority of blessed Peter and our own, under the penalty [Col. 0786A] of anathema.
>
> “For just as Gregory, your predecessor of old, at the urging of the aforesaid martyr, founder of that monastery, ordained one common cemetery, in harmonious agreement, for both communities of the living, where the saint lies; so the letters of our authority have decreed that this be confirmed. Whoever also presumes to remove anything from the same borough or cloister on the side of the stream which divides the two boroughs, except the abbot or monks, is to know that he will condemn himself by a like sentence. Fare well.
>
> “Given through the hand of John, librarian of the then holy Apostolic See, in the tenth year of the pontificate of the lord Sergius, universal pope, in the most holy see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the eleventh indiction (679).”

### Abbots Agilbertus and Bobolenus.

After the death of Abbot Wlfechrannus, Agilbertus succeeded to the office of rule [Col. 0786B]; after him Bobolenus presided.

### Clotaire dies. Childeric, king of Austrasia, succeeds him.

King Clotaire, after holding the kingdom for some years, was overtaken by untimely death and left it without an heir. Mourning his death, the Frankish princes elevated to rule over the entire Frankish kingdom his brother Childeric, king of the Austrasians, whom they had heard to govern his kingdom wisely and prudently. Having attained sovereignty, he most wisely restored to its former condition whatever he found unsuitable and contrary to the laws of earlier kings and great princes, whose lives had once been praiseworthy.

At that time a certain Godinus, one of the leading men of Burgundy, together with his wife named Lantrude, gave St Benignus [Col. 0786C] an allod of his own right, called Albiniacum, situated in the district of Decolatunse, now generally called Portuensis.

### Theuderic succeeds him. St Leodegar and St Lambert. The praises of Pippin. St Willibrord is sent into Frisia.

Childeric, after holding the Frankish kingdom for a few years and governing it with fair moderation and just laws, died. His brother Theuderic was elevated to the kingdom in his brother’s place. He held it for sixteen years. In his days St Leodegar was killed by Ebroin, mayor of the palace, and St Lambert, bishop of Tongeren, by Count Dodo. Innocently killed at one time, these men obtained the crown of martyrdom.

At that time, when the kings had already declined from their former strength, care of the whole kingdom was administered by the dukes and princes of the palace. Among all of them Pippin, whom we mentioned above, pre-eminent, a man adorned with every wisdom; and the greater part of that kingdom was in his hands. Having conquered Frisia and put to flight its king, named Rathod, he sent there to preach servants of God who had come from Britain: Willibrord and his companions. They converted no small multitude of people to Christ. When King Theuderic died, his son Childebert succeeded to the kingdom.

In the year 709 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Pippin went into Swabia against Willarius. In the following year he again raised an army against the aforesaid tyrant. In the third year the waters flooded violently. King Childebert died, and the Frankish army went into Swabia. In the fourth year the Frankish army again went into Swabia against Willarius, and Eribert, king of the Lombards, died.

### Pippin dies.

In the year 714 Pippin died in the month of December, and his son Grimoald likewise died; Charles succeeded in his father’s place.

At that time Astoricus was bishop of Langres, and Babolenus ruled this monastery. Then Ermenoara, consecrated to the Lord, gave to St Benignus everything she possessed in the estate of Ruffiacum: namely, *mansi* with the buildings erected upon them and all their appurtenances.

### Dagobert II dies. Charles Martel.

[Col. 0787B] In the year 715 King Dagobert died, and the Saxons devastated the land of the Bavarians. In the year 717 there was a battle at Vinciacum between Charles and Ragofred, mayor of the palace. Ragofred fled, and his army was struck down in a great slaughter as far as the river Wisera. In the following year Charles entered Saxony and ravaged it. In the year 721 Eudo expelled the Saracens from his land. Four years after this Charles subdued the people of Anjou because they were rebelling against him.

Theuderic, son of the younger Dagobert, had then been raised to the royal throne. He was succeeded by Clotaire; Clotaire by Childebert; Childebert by Childeric. In him the line [Col. 0787C] of King Clovis, which had reigned until then, failed.

### Charles performs many deeds vigorously. He defeats the Saracens. Why he was called “the Hammer.” Carloman and Pippin. Carloman becomes a monk.

In the year 725 Charles subjected the Bavarians to himself, and the Saracens invaded Gaul. Six years afterward Charles went into Swabia against Laufred. In the following year Charles was in Gascony against Eudo, and the tyrant Ragofred died. In the next year Charles fought the Saracens in the month of October, on a Saturday, near the city of Poitiers.

Again, in the year 737, an innumerable multitude of Saracens gathered together. They had twelve kings over them, the first and greatest of whom was Abdirama, king of the city of Córdoba. They occupied Gothia and besieged the city of Narbonne. When Charles heard this, he assembled a large army and also summoned Liutprand, king of the Lombards, to aid him. Engaging the Saracens in battle, he crushed them so completely that scarcely anyone could escape from so great a multitude. Even to this day that savage people fears Frankish arms.

In the year 739 Charles entered Provence as far as Marseille; he invaded Gascony, devastated Frisia, subdued Saxony, and crushed Alemannia and Bavaria. In the year 741 Charles Tudites died. He was called *Tudites*, that is, “the smith’s hammer,” because, just as every implement of iron is beaten with a hammer, [Col. 0788A] so Charles crushed all the kingdoms neighboring his own. After Charles’s death, his sons Carloman and Pippin took up the care of the kingdom.

In the year 742 Charles went into Gascony. In the following year he devastated Alemannia. In the fourth year Carloman and Pippin invaded Saxony. In the seventh year Carloman, leaving care of the kingdom to his brother Pippin, went to Rome and established a monastic dwelling on Mount Soracte. Later, unable to endure the inconvenience caused by the frequent visits of those who traveled from Francia to the thresholds of the apostles, he moved to St Benedict on Mount Cassino.

### Pippin is inaugurated king. St Boniface the martyr dies.

In the year 752 Lord King Pippin was consecrated by the hands [Col. 0788B] of Pope Stephen, as were his two sons Carloman and Charles, who was called the Great. In the fourth year King Pippin entered Lombardy, and Pope Stephen returned to Rome. At the same time St Boniface, preaching to the Frisian people, received martyrdom. In the sixth year King Pippin again went into Lombardy, and King Haistulf died. In the following year organs sent from Greece by the emperor were brought to Lord King Pippin with certain gifts.

In the year 760 King Pippin went into Gascony against Waffarius. Again, in the next year, he went with his sons Charles and Carloman into Aquitaine and acquired the city of Bourges. In the ninth year of King Pippin, a certain man named Rocolenus gave St Benignus his allod, called Villare, situated [Col. 0788C] in the district of Beaune, in the territory of Milliacum, with all its appurtenances. At the same time a certain cleric named Bago gave St Benignus all his inheritance which he possessed at Asiriacum, Istodorum, and Salas: whatever he appeared to possess in the aforesaid estates, both *mansi* and the lands elsewhere belonging to those same *mansi*.

### Pippin marches into Aquitaine. He departs this life.

In the year 762 King Pippin again went with an army into Aquitaine together with Carloman. Having captured the whole district of Auvergne, he burned the city of Clermont and the fortress of Bourbon with fire. In the year 764 King Pippin held a great assembly with the Franks at the estate of Quierzy. In the same year there was an extremely severe winter: frost lasted from the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January [14 December] until the sixth day before the Kalends of April [27 March].

In the year 767 King Pippin again entered Aquitaine and conquered the city of Limoges. His wife, Queen Bertha, wintered at Bourges. In the following year, namely 768, King Pippin died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September], at the city of Paris, of dropsy; and Waffarius was killed.

Charles and Carloman are crowned. Carloman dies. — In the same year Lord King Charles and Carloman were anointed kings on the seventh day before the Ides of October. For the Franks, having solemnly held a general assembly, [Col. 0789A] appointed both as their kings, on the stated condition that they should divide the whole body of the kingdom equally, and that Charles should undertake, for purposes of government, that portion which their father Pippin had held, while Carloman should undertake that portion over which their uncle Carloman had presided. The conditions were accepted on both sides, and each received the share of the divided kingdom allotted to him.

This concord, although with the greatest difficulty, endured, many on Carloman’s side attempting to dissolve the association, so that some of them were contemplating beginning wars. But the outcome itself proved that there was more suspicion than danger in this. After Carloman’s death, his wife fled to Italy with her sons and certain men who had been foremost among his magnates; and, [Col. 0789B] without any cause, rejecting her husband’s brother, she placed herself and her children under the protection of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. Carloman, then, died after jointly administering the kingdom for four years. Charles, however, upon his brother’s death, was established as sole king of all the Franks.

Charles the Great defeats the duke of Aquitaine. — In the year 769, the second of his reign, Charles undertook the Aquitanian war—the first of all the wars he waged—which his father had begun but had not yet completed. Since it seemed capable of being swiftly concluded, he undertook it while his brother was still alive, having also requested his assistance. Although his brother disappointed him in the aid he had promised, Charles nevertheless carried out the expedition he had undertaken with the utmost energy, and refused to desist from what he had begun until he had brought to a completed end that which [Col. 0789C] he had intended to accomplish.

For he compelled Hunald, who after Waiofar’s death had occupied Aquitaine and had attempted to renew a war already almost finished, to leave Aquitaine and seek Gascony. Not allowing him to remain there either, Charles crossed the river Garonne and ordered Lupus, duke of the Gascons, to surrender the fugitive; unless he did so without delay, Charles declared that he would overcome him by war. Lupus adopted the wiser course: he not only surrendered the fugitive, but also committed himself and the province over which he ruled to Charles’s authority.

At Pope Adrian’s request, he undertakes war against the Lombards. — Having thus settled affairs in Aquitaine and finished that war, and his partner in the kingdom having now been removed from human affairs, Charles, prevailed upon by the prayers of Adrian, bishop of the city of Rome, undertook war against the Lombards.

In the year 772 King Charles entered Italy and, having stirred up war—the same war which had earlier been undertaken by his father, at the entreaty of Pope Stephen, with great difficulty, because certain leading Franks with whom he used to deliberate had resisted his intention so strongly that they openly declared they would desert the king and return home—he now commenced it against King Aistulf and completed it very swiftly. Yet although the cause underlying the undertaking of the war seemed similar, indeed identical, for him and for his father, it is clear that it was not fought with similar exertion or completed with a similar result. [Col. 0790A]

Pippin, indeed, by a siege of a few days at Ticinum, compelled King Aistulf to give hostages, to restore what he had taken from the Romans, and to pledge by oath that the restored possessions would not be reclaimed. Charles, however, once he had begun the war, did not desist until he had received into surrender King Desiderius, whom he had worn down by a long siege; had compelled Desiderius’s son Adalgis, in whom the hopes of all seemed to rest, to leave not only the kingdom but Italy itself; had restored to the Romans everything taken from them; had crushed Chrodogausus, prefect of the duchy of Forum Julii, while he was plotting revolution; had captured his father-in-law Habilinus, besieged in the city of Tarvisium; had subdued all Italy; and had set his son Pippin as king over the subdued land.

The end of this war was the subjugation of Italy; the assignment of King [Col. 0790B] Desiderius to perpetual exile in Francia; the expulsion of his son Adalgis from Italy; and the restoration to Adrian, ruler of the Roman Church, of the possessions taken by Lombard kings. It would take long to recount how difficult was the Alpine passage when he entered Italy, and with what exertion the pathless mountain ridges, sky-soaring crags, and rugged rocks were overcome by the Franks.

War against the Saxons. The city of Charles. — In the year 776, when King Charles heard that the Saxons had again rebelled against the Franks, he moved an army against them, and the war which had seemed, as it were, interrupted was resumed. The Saxons, indeed, like almost all the peoples inhabiting Germany, were naturally fierce, devoted to the worship of demons, and hostile to our religion; nor did they fear to transgress either divine or human laws. [Col. 0790C] There were also causes capable of disturbing peace daily: namely, the boundaries of the two peoples lay in open country, and killings, plundering, and burnings on both sides never ceased.

For this reason the Franks built a city on the Saxon frontier, which they called Charles’s City. The war undertaken against them was waged for thirty-three continuous years with great spirit on both sides, yet with greater loss to the Saxons than to the Franks. Seeing that they could not resist the Franks, the Saxon elders came to Lord King Charles and asked for peace; and a multitude of their people was baptized.

Saxons defeated by King Charles. — In the year 777 the glorious King Charles came into Saxony, to the place called Paderborn; there he held a great assembly, and there the Saxons gathered for catholic baptism. The Franks built a church there, and many thousands of people were baptized, upon the condition proposed by the king and accepted by them: that, casting aside the worship of demons and abandoning ancestral ceremonies, they should receive the sacraments of the Christian faith and, united with the Franks, become one people with them.

Although this war was prolonged over a considerable period, Charles himself engaged the enemy in battle no more than twice: once near the mountain called Osning, at the place named Theotmelli; and again by the river Aisne, the two engagements occurring within one month and only a few days apart. [Col. 0791A] In these two battles he so utterly routed and defeated the enemy that thereafter they did not dare to resist the king when he came. Yet many men of the nobility of both Franks and Saxons, including men who had held the highest offices, perished in that war.

Thus the king, greatest in prudence and most outstanding in greatness of spirit among all who ruled nations in his age, declined nothing that had to be undertaken or carried out because of toil, nor shrank from it because of danger.

He proceeds into Spain. The Gascons attack the Franks and kill many. — In the year 778, while King Charles was contending in incessant and almost continuous war with the Saxons, he placed garrisons at suitable points along their frontiers [Col. 0791B] and attacked Spain with the largest military preparation he could command. Having crossed the Pyrenees and received into surrender every town and fortress that he approached—namely Pamplona, Huesca, Barcelona, and Girona—he then returned with his army safe and unharmed, having taken hostages.

Except that, on his return, he experienced for a short time the treachery of the Gascons on the Pyrenean ridge itself. For while the army advanced stretched out in a long column, as the terrain and narrow passes permitted, the Gascons, having set an ambush on the mountain summit—for the place, because of the thick shade of its forests, which are especially abundant there, is well suited for laying ambushes—rushed down upon the rearmost baggage-train and upon those marching last, who protected the troops ahead as a rear guard, and cast them into the valley below. [Col. 0791C] Joining battle with them, they killed every man to the last; then, having plundered the baggage, and protected by the onset of night, they scattered with the utmost speed in different directions.

The lightness of the Gascons’ arms and the character of the place where the action occurred aided them in this deed; conversely, the heaviness of the Franks’ arms and the unfavorable terrain rendered the Franks in every respect unequal to the Gascons. In this battle were killed Eggihard, steward of the royal table; Anselm, count of the palace; and Roland, prefect of the Breton march, together with many others. Nor could the deed be avenged at the time, because after perpetrating it the enemy dispersed so completely that not even a report remained as to where in the world they might be sought.

He also subdued the Bretons, who lived westward, in an extreme part of Gaul along the shore of Ocean, and were not obedient to commands. He sent an expedition against them and compelled them to give hostages and promise to do what was required of them. [Col. 0791D]

Charles goes to Italy. — King Charles again entered Italy with an army and, travelling by way of Rome, came to Capua, a city of Campania. There he pitched camp and threatened the Beneventans with war unless they surrendered. Arichis, duke of that people, forestalled this by sending his sons Romuald and Grimoald, with a large sum of money, to meet the king. He asked the king to receive his sons as hostages and promised that he himself and his people would do what was commanded, [Col. 0792A] provided only that he himself should not be compelled to appear before the king.

The king, considering the advantage to the people more than the duke’s obstinacy, received the hostages offered to him and granted what was requested. Retaining one of the sons as a hostage, he sent envoys with Arichis to exact and receive oaths from the Beneventans; he then returned to Rome and thence went back to Gaul.

Again into Bavaria. Queen Hildegard and Bertha his mother die. — In the year 787 the Bavarian war, suddenly arising, was rapidly brought to an end; it had been provoked by the pride of Duke Tassilo. At the urging of his wife, daughter of King Desiderius, who believed that she could avenge her father’s exile through her husband, he made an alliance with the Huns, eastern neighbors of the Bavarians, and attempted not only to refuse obedience to commands but even to challenge the king to war.

The king’s spirit could not endure his contumacy. Accordingly, gathering forces from every quarter and intending to march into Bavaria, Charles came with a very great army to the river Lech, which separates the Bavarians from the Alemanni. Having stationed his camp on its bank, he decided to test the duke’s intentions through envoys. Tassilo, judging obstinacy to be advantageous neither to himself nor to his people, submitted humbly to the king and gave hostages, including his son Theodo. He further gave his pledge under oath that he would not consent to any person urging him to defect from the king’s authority. Thus the war, which had seemed likely to be very great, was brought to the swiftest conclusion. [Col. 0792C]

In the following year Duke Tassilo was summoned before the king because he had attempted to violate the agreement. He was not permitted to return, nor was the province which he had held thereafter entrusted to a duke; it was committed to counts for administration. In the fifteenth year of King Charles’s reign, Queen Hildegard, wife of the aforesaid ruler, died, and Bertrada, his mother, died in the same year.

War against the Wends. — In the year 789 war was made upon the Slavs who in our usage are called Wends (*Wilei*, that is, *Winidi*), but in their own speech Welitabi. In this war the Saxons too served, as though more eager than the other nations, who were more responsive to the standards when commanded, though with feigned and less devoted obedience.

[Note: [Col. 0791] “More eager” (*avidiores*): read “auxiliaries” (*auxiliares*) . . . “which, when ordered, followed the royal standards.” Below I restore: “he so crushed and subdued [them].”]

The cause of the war was that they continually harassed the Abodrites, who had long been allied with the Franks, and could not be restrained by command. [Col. 0792D] A certain gulf stretches eastward from the western Ocean, of unknown length, but of a breadth nowhere exceeding one hundred Roman miles, although in many places it is narrower. Many nations live around it. The Danes and the Suebi, whom we call Northmen, hold the northern shore and all the islands in it. Slavs, Aesti, and various other peoples inhabit the southern shore.

Among these, the principal people, against whom the king was then making war, were the Wentelabi. In one expedition only, and one which he conducted personally, he so crushed and subdued them that thereafter they did not at all refuse to obey commands. [Col. 0793A]

He makes war upon the Huns. — In the year 791 King Charles, having assembled a great army, made war upon the Huns. Apart from the Saxon war, this was the greatest of all the wars conducted by him, and he pursued it more vigorously than the others and with far greater preparation. He himself made only one expedition into Pannonia, the province inhabited by that people; he entrusted the rest to his son Pippin, to provincial prefects and counts, and to envoys for completion.

Though these men administered it most vigorously, it was only completed in the eighth year. How many battles were fought in it and how much blood was shed is attested by Pannonia, emptied of every inhabitant, [Col. 0793B] and by the place where the royal residence of the Khagan stood, so deserted that not even a trace of human habitation appears there. In this war all Hun nobility perished, all their glory fell, all their money and treasures accumulated over a long time were plundered. No war against the Franks can be recalled within human memory by which they were more enriched and increased in wealth: so much gold and silver was found in the royal residence, so many precious spoils were taken in battle, that one may reasonably believe that the Franks justly took from the Huns what the latter had unjustly taken from other nations.

Only two Frankish nobles died in that war: Eric, duke of Forum Julii, and Gerold, prefect of Bavaria. Otherwise this war was almost bloodless for the Franks and had a successful outcome, although its magnitude prolonged it considerably. After it, the Saxon war too received an end proportionate to its length. The Bohemian and Linonian wars which subsequently arose likewise could not last long. Both were swiftly completed under the command of Charles’s son, whom he had placed over the kingdom of Burgundy. [Col. 0793C]

Waldric, abbot of Saint Benignus. — Called bishop. — At the time when the aforesaid great King Charles assumed the care of the kingdom, an abbot named Waldric governed this abbey. During his time, a man named Ansegald bestowed upon the church of the martyr Saint Benignus part of his inheritance which he possessed in the estate called Salins, as well as another estate called Barges.

Likewise, a man named Leotad [Col. 0793D] gave a not insignificant portion of his property in the aforesaid estates to the aforesaid martyr, protector of the place at Dijon. He made the donation by drawing up a charter, in which the same Waldric is called bishop. Its text reads:

> “To the lord of the most holy basilica of Saint Benignus the martyr, constructed beneath the fortress of Dijon, where the venerable man Lord Waldric is seen to preside as bishop, and David the priest,”

and the rest which follows. David himself performed the office of provost. For he [verb missing] from a certain relative of his, named Aldebert, one *mansus* with all the land belonging to it, in the estate of Asiriac. At the same time a man named Egremar and his wife Eva gave, in the estate called Norvia, [Col. 0794A] a certain portion of their possessions to the aforesaid place of Saint Benignus.

Aridius, abbot. — After the death of Abbot Waldric, Aridius succeeded to the administration of the pastoral office. In his time, a young man of noble birth, named Dodo, came to conversion in this monastery of Dijon, wishing to serve God and Saint Benignus. He gave to the aforesaid Abbot Aridius and to the monks of this place everything that he appeared to possess in the estate of Salins and in Barges, wholly and in its entirety; and, in the estate called Monfarulf, the half belonging to him, with all appurtenances and the resident serfs thereon.

He ordained that these servants should each year, on one day, provide for the brothers’ table one *modius* of grain in bread, one *modius* of wine, two *modii* of ale, [Col. 0794B] and the price by which two cooked dishes might be prepared, according to what the monastic Rule prescribes.

Hildebrand, abbot. Hildebrand’s death. Herlegaud succeeds. — When the aforesaid Abbot Aridius had died, Hildebrand assumed the charge of government. In his days, a man named Frodo gave to the aforesaid church of Saint Benignus a certain parcel of land belonging to him, situated in the district of Beaune, in the territory of Cosimac, at the place called Varnay. This donation was made in the first year of the empire of the great King Charles.

After some years had passed, Hildebrand died while holding pastoral charge. Herlegaud succeeded him as abbot, born of noble stock in this province. He gave wholly to this church which he governed all the patrimony that he possessed as left to him by his ancestors, [Col. 0794C] and whatever he had been able to purchase from his relatives.

During his time, a man named Winiter gave to the holy martyr Benignus two fields from land of his own property in the estate of Asiriac. Already at that time the fervor of monastic religion had grown lukewarm; already each man sought to become heir to his parents’ goods. Consequently, some publicly transferred what they had acquired to the service of the brothers and the common benefit of the place.

Thus Dodo, Amalbald, and Heraclius gave the possessions which they held in the estate of Salins and at Barges. Similarly, the priest Witger gave to Saint Benignus whatever he had been able to acquire in the aforesaid estates from his parents. A cleric named Lebranld, a priest by order and related to the aforesaid Abbot Herlegaud, bestowed upon the holy martyr, patron of this place, one *mansus* within the fortress of Dijon and, outside the walls, lands belonging to that aforesaid *mansus*. He had bought these from one Adalrao, brother of Farulf, who were relatives of both himself and the aforesaid abbot. [Col. 0794D]

The aforesaid abbot lived and continued in the governance of the monastery until the times of Louis, son of the oft-mentioned Charlemagne.

Charlemagne’s last war. On the Northmen or Danes. The acquisitions of Charlemagne’s Frankish kingdom enumerated. — The aforesaid King Charles waged his final war against the Northmen, who are called Danes. At first they practiced piracy; then, after gathering a larger fleet, they ravaged the coasts of Gaul and Germany. [Col. 0795A] Their king Godfrey was so puffed up with vain hope that he promised himself power over all Germany, and regarded Frisia and Saxony no differently than his own provinces. He had already reduced his neighboring Abodrites to his rule; he had already made them tributary.

He even boasted that he would soon come with very great forces to Aachen, where the king’s court was. Nor was credit denied his words; rather, the event seemed likely to follow the utterance, had he not been forestalled by a sudden death. For, killed by one of his own retainers, he brought the war he had begun to a swift end.

These are the wars which the most powerful king waged over forty-seven years—for so many years he reigned—in different regions of the earth with supreme prudence and success. Through them he enlarged the Frankish kingdom, which [Col. 0795B] he had inherited from his father Pippin already great and powerful, so nobly that he added to it almost its equal again.

For previously no more than the portion of Gaul lying between the Rhine and Loire, the Ocean and the Balearic Sea; and the portion of Germany lying between Saxony, the Danube, the Rhine, and the river Saale, which divides the Thuringians and Sorbs, inhabited by the Franks called Eastern Franks; besides the Alemanni and Bavarians—belonged to the Frankish kingdom. By the wars mentioned above Charles first added Aquitaine and Gascony, the whole ridge of the Pyrenees, and the land as far as the river Ebro, which rises among the Navarrese, cuts through Spain’s most fertile fields, and joins the Balearic Sea below the walls of the city of Tortosa.

Then he added all Italy, extending from Augusta Praetoria to Lower Calabria, where the boundaries of the Greeks and Beneventans are said to be; it stretches for more than one thousand Roman miles. [Col. 0795C] He added Saxony, a substantial part of Germany, thought to be twice as broad as the Germany inhabited by the Franks, though perhaps equal to it in length. He added both Pannonias; Dacia lying on the other side of the Danube; Istria, Liburnia, and Dalmatia—excepting the coastal cities, which, because of friendship and the alliance joined with him, he allowed the emperor of Constantinople to retain.

He also completely subdued all the barbarous and fierce nations which inhabit Germany between the rivers Rhine and Vistula, and the Ocean and Danube—nearly alike in language but very different in customs [Col. 0795D] and dress—and made them tributary. Among them the principal were the Weletabi, Sorbs, Abodrites, and Bohemians. He fought against these; the others, much more numerous, he received into surrender.

He also increased the glory of his kingdom by securing the friendship of certain kings and peoples. Thus he bound Alfonso, king of Galicia and Asturias, to himself in such alliance that, when Alfonso sent letters or envoys to him, he ordered Charles to be called nothing other than his own lord. By generosity he so bent the kings of the Scots to his will that they never called him other than lord, and declared themselves his subjects and servants. [Col. 0796A] With Aaron, king of the Persians—who held almost the whole East, except India—he enjoyed such harmonious friendship that Aaron preferred Charles’s favor to the friendship of all kings and rulers in the entire world, and judged him alone worthy of being honored and enriched by him.

The emperors of Constantinople also—Nicephorus, Michael, and Leo—of their own accord sought his friendship and alliance and sent him numerous envoys. Yet, because he had assumed the title of emperor, and because it seemed that he wished thereby to take the empire from them, they regarded him with great suspicion. He nevertheless established a most firm treaty, so that no opportunity for any scandal might remain between the parties; the power of the Franks was always an object of suspicion to the Romans and Greeks. [Col. 0796B]

Wives and offspring of Charlemagne. Concubines. Conspiracies against him. — He had a wife named Hildegard, a woman of most eminent nobility from the people of the Suebi. By her he begot three sons—Charles, Pippin, and Louis—and as many daughters: Hernodrid, Berrit, and Gisela. After Hildegard’s death, he took Fastrada as his wife; by her he had two daughters, Theoderada and Hiltrud. She was from the people of the Eastern Franks, that is, the Germans. After her death, he took the Alemannic woman Liutgard. After her death, he had only three concubines: Gerswinda, Adalind, and Regina, who bore him Drogo and Hugh.

Of all these children, before he died he lost only two sons and one daughter: Charles; Pippin, whom he had made king of Italy; and Ruodrude, his eldest daughter, who had been betrothed to Constantine, emperor of the Greeks. He had a son named Pippin, born of a concubine; he was handsome in appearance but deformed by a hunchback. [Col. 0796C] While his father was wintering in Bavaria during the war against the Huns, he feigned illness and conspired against his father with certain Frankish magnates, who had enticed him with an empty promise of kingship.

After the fraud had been uncovered and the conspirators condemned, Charles allowed him to remain confined in the monastery of Prüm, living religiously and now willing to devote himself to that life. An earlier serious conspiracy was also formed against Charles in Germany. Its authors were partly blinded, partly left physically whole, but all were sent into exile. None was killed except three, who, in order not to be captured, defended themselves with drawn swords and had even killed some men; since they could not otherwise be restrained, they were killed.

The cruelty of Queen Fastrada is nevertheless believed to have been the cause and origin of these conspiracies. In both cases, indeed, the conspiracy against the king arose because, by assenting to his wife’s cruelty, he appeared to have departed monstrously from his native kindness and customary gentleness. [Col. 0796D]

Why he went to Rome a fourth time. — Above all other sacred and venerable places, he revered at Rome the church of the blessed apostle Peter. Into its offerings he amassed a great quantity of money in gold, silver, [Col. 0797A] and gems. He sent many and innumerable gifts to the popes. Throughout his reign he considered nothing more important than that the city of Rome, flourishing through its ancient authority, should through his exertions be maintained, and that the church of Saint Peter should not only be safe and protected through him, but should also be adorned and enriched by his works above all churches.

Although he valued it so highly, during the forty-seven years of his reign he went there only four times, to fulfill vows and to pray. The causes of his last visit were not only these, but also the fact that the Romans had inflicted many injuries upon Pope Leo—namely, they had gouged out his eyes and cut off his tongue—and compelled him to seek the king’s protection. Charles therefore came to Rome and, in order to restore the condition of the Church, [Col. 0797B] which had been excessively disturbed, spent the entire winter there. At that time he received the name of Emperor and Augustus.

Louis is proclaimed king and emperor by his father. Emperor Charles dies and is buried at Aachen. — At the end of his life, when he was now burdened by illness and old age, he summoned to himself his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, the only surviving son of Hildegard. Having solemnly assembled the leading men from the whole Frankish kingdom, he made Louis, with the counsel of all, his associate in the whole kingdom and heir to the imperial title. Placing a diadem on his head, he ordered him to be called Emperor and Augustus.

This decision was received with great favor by all present, for it seemed divinely inspired in him for the welfare of the kingdom. [Col. 0797C] The deed increased his majesty and struck no small terror into the other nations. He died in the year 815 (i.e. 814) from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the seventy-second year of his age and the forty-fifth from the beginning of his reign, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February [26 January].

Many prodigies marked his approaching end, so that not only others but he himself perceived that they portended it. For during the three continuous years nearest the end of his life, eclipses of both sun and moon occurred very frequently; and a spot of black color was visible in the sun for seven days. He himself, during his final expedition in Saxony against Godfrey, king of the Danes, set out one day from camp before sunrise. [Col. 0797D] Suddenly he saw a blazing meteor descend from heaven and cross the clear sky with great brilliance from right to left. While everyone wondered what this sign might portend, the horse he was riding suddenly plunged its head downward and fell, throwing him so violently to the ground that the clasp of his cloak broke, his sword-belt came apart, and the attendants who hastened to him had to disarm him and raise him without assistance. Even the spear which he happened to be holding slipped from his hand and fell more than twenty feet away.

He was buried in the basilica which he had built in his palace at Aachen, out of love for God and our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0798A] and in honor of Mary, his holy and perpetual Virgin Mother. He was buried there on the very day he died. Above the tomb was constructed a gilded arch with an image and an inscription written as follows:

> Beneath this tomb lies the body of Charles the Great, orthodox emperor, who nobly enlarged the kingdom of the Franks and happily ruled for forty-seven years.

Louis administers the empire prudently. He divides it among his sons. — After his death Louis, surnamed the Pious, succeeded to the imperial throne and governed the Frankish kingdom with great moderation for twenty-five years. The frontiers which his father had extended far and wide by fighting, Louis wisely [Col. 0798B] guarded everywhere against enemies. He avoided by prudent counsel the tricks and quibbles of the Greeks; forcefully checked the treachery of the Saracens, who wished to break forth from Spain; and terrified the boldness of the Danes by military strength.

He had three sons: Lothar, Louis, and Pippin. After his first wife died, he took another named Judith, by whom he had Charles. He divided the kingdom among his children as follows. Lothar, the eldest, to whom he also granted the imperial insignia, was to possess after him the kingdom of Italy, the part of Francia enclosed between the rivers Meuse and Rhine, and part of Burgundy. Louis was to possess Germany—that is, Bavaria and Saxony—and the remaining kingdoms which his father Charlemagne had subdued by war: Pannonia, Dacia, Istria, Liburnia, and Dalmatia; [Col. 0798C] likewise the barbarian peoples whom he had made tributary—the Weletabi, Sorbs, Abodrites, Bohemians, and the rest, too numerous to enumerate. All these peoples the aforesaid Emperor Louis kept subject throughout his life. To Pippin he also granted the kingdom of Aquitaine with Gascony, and all the land as far as Spain which Charles had subdued.

Herlegaud, abbot of Saint Benignus. Diploma of Louis the Pious for restoring the church of Saint Benignus. — Charles, the youngest, received Francia, Burgundy, and Neustria. His brothers were angered by this, either because they did not wish one born of another mother to be made their equal, or because the principal and [Col. 0798D] better portion of the kingdom had been assigned to him by their father. Hence, after the emperor’s death, a serious war arose among them. But although in this struggle they brought together the strength of Frankish armies

[Note: [Col. 0797D] “Brought together” (*contulerint*). Rather, “crushed” (*contuderint*).]

and gave outsiders an opportunity to rebel, they could not alter what their father had done. Eventually Charles obtained the kingdom of Aquitaine as well. For Pippin had died before his father and left a son, also called Pippin. Seeing him to be less fit to govern the kingdom, his magnates and leaders attached themselves to Charles.

Herlegaud—whom, as stated above, [Col. 0799A] we have reported to have been abbot of this place—came before this ruler and represented to his serene majesty that the basilica of the martyr Saint Benignus had fallen into ruin and that he had no means by which to restore it. Moved by pious concern, the emperor accordingly wrote to his princes and magnates as follows:

> “In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ: by the ordering of divine providence, the Emperor Augustus, to Count Amadeus, Elias and Waldo, Isembard and Barbert, our vassals. Let it be known to you that we will that you render assistance to Herlegaud the deacon for restoring and re-roofing the church of Christ’s martyr Saint Benignus. The reason is that we have learned that you hold benefices from the property of the same church; therefore cause ninths and tithes to be given in all things, as is just. [Col. 0799B] We therefore direct you to give assistance for the restoration and roofing of that church. See that you fulfill this in every respect. We expressly command you to show no negligence in this matter, if you wish to retain our favor. And, that you may know with certainty that this is our command, we have ordered it sealed with our ring.”

Alberic, bishop of Langres, restores monastic discipline while the co-bishop Helebert governs the abbey. — At that time Lord Alberic, bishop, presided over the church of Langres. After the death of the aforesaid Abbot Herlegaud, when the monastic order had almost fallen apart, the aforesaid Bishop Alberic assumed the charge of governing this place, appointing as pastor for the community living there his co-bishop Helebert. [Col. 0799C]

At this time very many exchanges or purchases of lands were made, both by the bishop himself and by the administrators of this place. Among them was an exchange between Seraphim, abbot of the place of Bèze, and that same co-bishop Helebert. Helebert gave, in the estates of Lux and Varois, whatever belonged by right to Saint Benignus; in return Seraphim transferred the lands of Saint Peter which lay at Dijon, in the territory of Saint-Pierre, at Longvic, Canavilles, Arzillières, Tremolois, Fontaines, Prouvis, and Disto.

Likewise, Bishop Alberic and Fulcher exchanged lands. Fulcher gave three fields in the territory of Sacier; and Bishop Alberic gave him one field and one meadow at Is-sur-Tille. Likewise, the aforesaid bishop exchanged with Alderan. Adalran gave one *mansus* within the fortress of Dijon and three fields outside the walls at the place called Petraficta. In return Bishop Alberic gave a small piece of land in the district of Dijon and one field in the territory of Tremolois. [Col. 0799D]

Likewise Baldo the provost and the other clerics with him exchanged land with the priest Leotad. Leotad gave two small parcels of land: one beside the fortress of Dijon, the other at the place called Petraficta. The brothers gave the priest Leotad land in the territory of Tremolois.

### Louis the Pious Dies; His Sons Quarrel

When Louis the Pious exchanged the insignia of his earthly kingdom for eternal blessedness, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 840, his sons, disastrously divided against one another, tore apart by an ugly partition the kingdom of the Franks, formerly united in a most beautiful structure composed of diverse nations. Consequently, while the leading men of the court of each royal son pretended to seek one another’s favor, they did not hesitate to demand whatever they thought would be advantageous to themselves. And the young kings, each looking after himself and guarding against another being preferred to him, were sometimes compelled to grant unjust requests, though often unwillingly. Thus this place suffered the serious loss of possessions which it appears to have held until that time: namely, Masciacum in the district of Langres; Posciacum and Fons-Laguis in the district of Latice; Visernacum in the district of Tonnerre; and Vulnonem in the district of Sens, which it lost.

[Note: Col. 0799D: “Fontem Laguis.” Above, it is written “Fons Lagnis.”]

When, as we have said, discord had arisen between the brothers, terrible wars, as it were civil wars, then gathered among the chief men of the realm. Guarding of the shores of the Ocean Sea was abandoned. The number of enemies increased; the countless multitude of Northmen, Danes, and Britons grew. Everywhere there were massacres of Christians, plundering, devastation, and burnings. Whatever cities they approached were taken, with no one resisting. Bordeaux, Périgueux, Saintes, Limoges, Angoulême, and Toulouse were captured; the cities of Angers, Tours, and likewise Orléans were destroyed. At last the kings, seeing that their discord added strength to foreigners and that their citizens’ losses were the enemies’ gains, first made peace among themselves; then they made a treaty with the enemies, whom they had been unable to drive from the kingdom, and redeemed with money what they ought to have defended by arms.

### Emperor Lothar

Lothar, therefore, having obtained the imperial scepter, was content with a portion of the kingdom together with Italy and the city of Rome. At that time the Saracens, invading Rome, plundered the tombs of the Apostles and the other holy places. In the year 844 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Lothar had a son named Louis. Wishing him to become his successor and to receive the imperial crown, he sent him to Rome, together with Drogo, archbishop of Metz—his own maternal uncle—and the other princes of his realm. On arriving at Rome, they behaved toward the Romans with excessive harshness, and thereby provoked their minds to resentment. Having received the empire, he returned home and died not long afterward, as is written in the deeds of the Roman pontiffs.

### Ingelrannus Takes Charge of the Monastery of Dijon

At the same time, after the death of the co-bishop Herlebert, who had held the pastor’s office in this place, Ingelrannus succeeded to the governance of souls, holding the same ecclesiastical office. He made an exchange of land at Marcenniacum with a certain Madalgerius: he gave a field belonging to Saint Benignus, measuring twenty-five perches in length, and received double that amount from him.

Likewise, when Alberic, bishop of Langres, died, Bishop Theutbald obtained the see. Like his predecessor, a zealous benefactor of this place, he made exchanges of lands in several places with certain men. He exchanged land with Adalsavus at Lower Fontanas, with Albert at Plomberias, and with Wldegerius in the territory of Domiso.

In his days the priest Leotaldus, one of the clerics residing here, gave part of his inheritance in this borough and in the territory of Tremoles. Another cleric, named Olisius, sold to the residents there portions of his inheritance at Longus Vicus and Ficiacum. Geraldus the priest also exchanged land at Longus Vicus with Usuardus, receiving in exchange land at Ilariacum; both properties belonged to Saint Benignus.

At the same time a certain Balduin gave this place land from his inheritance in the village of Fontanas. Likewise Odolberga and her sons gave one mansus at Dijon. Warnerius, with his wife, gave four *journales* of land at Merneolum. In the district of Chalon, at the village of Rubiliacum, a certain Constantinus gave one mansus. The priest Hainardus sold to the administrators of this place his property situated in the village of Norvia. Another priest, named Hirsonnus, conveyed his vineyard in the village of Fontanas. A certain Adalranus likewise sold, for a price, one field in the same village. Ebbo, with his wife and son, gave in the district of Alsace, at Sermatia and Vitriacum, a mansus with everything belonging to it. The aforementioned Bishop Theutbald exchanged land at the village of Alberic, called Curtis, with Samson. Wherever he could, he took care to improve the property of this place.

### Isaac, Bishop of Langres, Restores the Abbey of Dijon

[Col. 0801C] After his death, Lord Isaac assumed the episcopate. Following the good example of his predecessors, and allowing himself to be inferior to none of them, he not only cultivated this place but increased its condition to twice what it had previously been. He restored the basilica of Saint Benignus, already nearly ruined, to its former state; he re-established the monastic order and added possessions for the sustenance of the same monks. He accomplished all this with the joint encouragement and assistance of the eminent King Charles.

### Emperor Charles the Bald; Second Invasion of Gaul by the Northmen

The same illustrious King Charles, ruling the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 871, was most zealous for the worship of God’s Church. Accordingly he overcame many dangers, and the glory of his kingdom continually increased.

After the death, as has already been said, of his brother Pippin, king of Aquitaine, Pippin’s son was placed in the kingdom; but, failing to govern it vigorously, he was abandoned and deposed by his own people and made a monk in the monastery of Saint Medard. Charles, sought by all the princes, obtained the kingdom of Aquitaine. A few years later, after the death of his brother Emperor Lothar, Charles received the empire.

But Louis, his other brother, wishing to unite the monarchy of the kingdom, again stirred up war against Charles and summoned the Northmen and other peoples into Charles’s realm. With the Lord’s help Charles drove his brother from his territories and confined the Northmen within Neustria. This was the second invasion of France by the Northmen. Some years later Louis died, leaving three sons: Louis, Carloman, and Charles.

### Charles’s Piety; His Many Gifts to Saint Benignus

Having obtained the empire, Charles, the devout patron of God’s churches, strove with all the energy he could command to correct what was corrupted in religious observance, rebuild what had been destroyed, and raise up what had fallen. Learning, among other things, that this place had been reduced almost to nothing, he urged the venerable Bishop Isaac to restore it to its former condition, promising that he would assist in every way.

Accordingly, the same illustrious King Charles gave, for the restoration of this place and for the use and maintenance of the monks serving God here:

- In the suburb of the castle of Dijon, demesne land on which 150 *modii* of seed could be sown;
- Vineyards yielding 500 *modii* of wine;
- Meadows producing fifty cartloads of hay;
- Woodland sufficient to fatten 600 pigs;
- A fishery extending from the bridge of Dijon to the village of Floriacum;
- Six mills;
- Ten *colonicae*;
- A market, together with the borough and jurisdiction;
- Six *colonicae*, and five at Lariacum;
- Ten *colonicae* at Bisicum;
- Six and a half *colonicae* in the village called Colonicae;
- One *colonica* at Siliniacum;
- Half a *colonica* at Dicmensis;
- Six *colonicae* at Sconsius;
- Three *colonicae* and two mills at Villare;
- One and a half *colonicae* at Lentennacum;
- Two *colonicae* at Giron;
- One *colonica* between Corcellas and Flaviniacum;
- Half a *colonica* at Provisum;
- Half a *colonica* at Camboium;
- One *colonica* between Patriniacum and Marcenniacum;
- Two *colonicae* at Quitiniacum;
- One *colonica* at Sacuninum;
- Two *colonicae* at Cromacum;
- At Aguliacum, a chapel possessing one and a half mansi;
- Half a *colonica* at Ruffiacum, and half of the village of Scoriacum;
- Half a *colonica* at Casnedum;
- One *colonica* at Bargis;
- Three *colonicae* at Missiniacum;
- One *colonica* at Norgia.

Likewise, at other Corcellas he gave half a *colonica*; and in the village of Aziriacum, everything which Saint Benignus appears to possess—namely, a chapel with one *colonica*, six and a half other *colonicae*, a mill, and demesne land on which 100 *modii* could be sown, together with meadows from which 150 cartloads of hay could be gathered.

In the village of Carle he gave a demesne mansus with a chapel and everything that appears to belong to it. At Prunidum he gave a demesne mansus and everything belonging to that mansus, with all its appurtenances, property, and dependants. At Jusiacum he gave two *colonicae*; at Campaniacum one *colonica*; and at Ateis two *colonicae*.

The aforementioned Charles gave all these properties, with the male and female dependants living upon them, to the servants of God, the monks serving the Lord in this place and remaining there in future times, so that they might implore the Lord’s mercy for him, his wife, his children, and the condition of the whole realm. He confirmed this by the authority of his charter, so that none of his successors might dare to alienate, diminish, or divert to other uses anything from these same properties.

### Berthilo, Co-Bishop and Abbot of Saint Benignus; Isaac Grants the Right to Elect an Abbot

The venerable Bishop Isaac therefore assembled monks in this place under the co-bishop and abbot Berthilo, that they might live according to the Rule and serve God forever. Concerning all that the illustrious prince had bestowed through the generosity of his charter, episcopal authority issued a corresponding privilege. In this privilege, first of all, it granted to the monks of this place the right, in succeeding generations, to elect an abbot from among themselves according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

He pronounced that anyone who should dare to oppose the brothers’ election; inflict any violence upon that congregation; oppress its household; remove anything from the monastery; or grant any of the aforesaid properties as a benefice to anyone, should, by his and his fellow bishops’ authority, be excommunicated, punished with the curse of eternal damnation, condemned by the vengeance of Saint Benignus, whom he had sought to injure, and further subjected to the anathema *maranatha*. Five archbishops and ten bishops subscribed to this excommunication, and afterward all the bishops of the church of Langres who succeeded him.

### Many Things Taken from Saint Benignus Are Restored

In the twenty-sixth year of Lord King Charles, that is, the year 866 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Bishop Isaac, Count Odo, and the other royal envoys were sitting in public court at the village of Luco to hear and judge cases. Alcaudius, advocate of Saint Mammet, Saint Benignus, Saint Stephen, and of Lord Bishop Isaac himself, brought suit against a certain Hildebrannus, alleging that he, his Franks, and his servants had felled one oak in the territory of Saciacum, Bruciacum, and Gonliacum, on land or in woodland belonging to Saint Benignus.

Because the matter was not then settled, in the following year, in the same court and place, the same advocate again summoned the same man, lodging the same complaint. In the third year, at the court of Arnon, while Lord Bishop Isaac, Count Odo, Abbot Hildebert, Bertran, and the other royal envoys were holding court, Alcaudius again summoned the aforesaid Hildebrannus, alleging that he unjustly retained property of Saint Benignus: namely, the aforesaid village of Saciacum with its appurtenances.

The aforesaid *scabini* then judged that he should either undergo the legal penalty and provide sureties for his wrongful acts, or lawfully restore what he held unjustly. He did so and restored to Saint Benignus what had been violently taken away.

We have inserted this record into this work in order to show that the above-mentioned estate of Saciacum had belonged to this place from ancient times, although it was taken away many times both before these times and afterward. The most excellent Emperor Charles, surnamed the Bald, likewise restored to us the village called Longus Vicus, which had similarly been taken from the lordship of this place, together with its churches and all the property belonging to that village. Likewise he restored Albiniacum in the district of Portus—that is, the estate itself with its churches and lands. Furthermore, by a charter of royal authority, he decreed that no one henceforth should dare to seize or remove the aforementioned properties from the jurisdiction of this basilica dedicated to God.

Berthilo, co-bishop and abbot, established in this place, began to devote himself earnestly to the care of the office entrusted to him and endeavored to increase its possessions by gifts, purchases, and exchanges of land. He purchased from Fulcardus, provost of the church of Langres, for the price of seven pounds, one mansus at the village of Aziriacum and arable land divided into nine fields. Fulcardus the priest also gave, in the same place, one field to God and Saint Benignus. Eldejarnus sold in the same village land on which six *modii* could be sown. Another man, named Eleardus, sold four mansi with buildings and superstructures in the same village. Another, called Mummius, on entering religious conversion in this monastery, gave four mansi with their appurtenances in the same village. The aforementioned Abbot Berthilo exchanged one mansus in that same village of Aziriacum with the above-named Fulcardus. With another man, named Bernoart, he exchanged land in the territory of Longus Vicus, at the village of Corcellas, receiving from him an exchange-property in that village at the place called Cassanias.

### Abbot Saro

[Col. 0804C] Seeing that co-bishop and abbot Berthilo could not suffice for both offices, because at that time ecclesiastical and public affairs alike were in grave danger owing to pagan attacks and the disturbed condition of the kingdom, Lord Bishop Isaac appointed Abbot Saro as his associate in governance and in the care of souls. Thus, while Saro, joined by the community of brothers, devoted himself to divine contemplation, Berthilo might more freely attend to ecclesiastical ministries.

At the same time certain persons gave from their property to increase the maintenance of the brothers, as divine mercy inspired each of them. A certain priest Louis gave at Aziriacum one field, a meadow, and a dependent peasant. Vindricus gave one vineyard at Patriniacum; and Moses gave at Cangiacum, in Arsis, one small holding, one vineyard, and fourteen *journales* of arable land.

Countess Bertha, for the remedy of the soul of her husband Count Unfred, gave in the district of Dusmensis, at the village called Colonicae, three mansi with the male and female dependants residing upon them. A nobleman named Richard gave his inheritance in the district of Beaune, at Santiliacum, Mammiacum, and Cussiniacum, and in the district of Magnimontensis, at the village called Alba Terra. The priest Teudfred, entering religious conversion, gave one mansus at Bargis with the lands attached to it, and at Dijon one and a half mansi with arable lands. Gislebert gave the church situated at Saviniacum, together with a mansus, courtyard, burial ground, garden with buildings around it, lands, dependants, and woodland sufficient to fatten forty pigs.

Moreover, Bishop Isaac and Berthilo, co-bishop and abbot, then reclaimed lands at Bargis, Escoriacum, and Siliciacum which had recently been taken from the lordship of this place, from those who had seized them. The same Lord Bishop Isaac exchanged lands with a certain Epplenus, one of the nobles living in the castle of Dijon, at that knight’s request. Epplenus gave from his own freehold to Bishop Isaac and the monks of this place properties at Corcellas, Caviniacum, Quintiniacum, Criciacum, Brisco, and Tremoledum. In return, Lord Isaac gave Epplenus one mansus at Casnedum with all its appurtenances.

### Bishop Isaac’s Book of Canons; His Death and Burial; Gello Succeeds Him. King Charles Dies; Louis the Stammerer Is King; the Danes Invade Gaul for a Third Time but Are Driven Out by Abbot Hugh; King Charles

[Col. 0805B] The same venerable Bishop Isaac did many other useful things in his episcopate, reforming monasteries and supporting churches. He also compiled the book called the *Canons of Isaac*, because, selecting the more useful material from books of canons, he condensed it into one volume. After completing twenty-five years in the episcopate, he died at Châlons and was buried at Rheims. Some years later, through the efforts of Bishop Argrinus and King Charles called the Simple, his body was translated as a gift and now lies honorably entombed in this basilica. Gello succeeded him in the episcopate, himself outstanding among the foremost.

Emperor Charles, intending for a second time to go to Rome, entered Italy. Carloman, son of King Louis, Charles’s brother, entered the same land by another route and confronted him with an immense army. Charles returned to Gaul and, on reaching the territory of Lyons, died there. He was buried in the monastery of the Apostles Peter and Paul, in the place called Nantoide because of the multitude of waters flowing together there. Later, by angelic admonition, he was translated from there and royally buried at Paris in the church of Saint Denis.

Louis succeeded his father on the throne, scarcely bearing the royal title for two years. In his days Pope John of Rome came to France and spoke with the same king at the city of Troyes; after staying there for a short time, he returned to Rome.

In these days the savage nation of the Danes came to inflict a third disaster upon Neustria. They would have inflicted a greater disaster than the earlier ones, had not Hugh—honored with the dignity of abbot throughout Gaul—restrained their reckless assaults. With God’s aid, he routed such great enemy battalions with a small force that scarcely anyone survived to report it. Humbled by this defeat, the Danes left Gaul undisturbed for some time. King Louis commanded this war.

When Hugh was closing the last days of his life, and Prince Louis died after ruling, as we have said, for two years, Charles, afterward called the Simple, remained fatherless while still in the cradle. There survived two sons of Robert, count of Angers, brothers of Abbot Hugh. The elder was named Odo; the other, Robert, bore his father’s name.
