[Note: Col. 0805D: “Brothers of Abbot Hugh.” Learned men dispute whether *fratres* (“brothers”) or *fratris* (“brother’s”) should be read here. To me nothing seems to require alteration; I shall set forth the reasoning of this opinion at an appropriate time and place. Col. 0806D.]

The Franks chose the elder, Odo, as guardian of the boy and governor of the realm, because renewed Norman raids threatened. In the parts of the kingdom held by Lothar and Louis, the sons of that same Louis ruled; for Lothar had died childless. Of these three brothers, one was called by his father’s name, another Carloman, and the third Charles. But when two died within five years, supreme power came to the younger Charles, who subsequently obtained the monarchy of the empire.

The reverend prelate Lord Gello approached him and asked that a charter of royal authority be issued concerning certain properties taken from this place and restored by Gello. Charles willingly assented and decreed by charter that no one thereafter should presume to alienate from this house or take from the same ministry twelve mansi at the village of Homberias assigned for the lights of the church of Saint Benignus. This document was made in the year 885 from the Lord’s Incarnation; in the fifth year of this Charles’s empire in Italy, the fourth in eastern Francia, the first in Gaul, and the tenth after the death of Charles the Bald.

### Charles Dies; the Northmen Ravage Gaul; Odo Is Made King

A certain writer relates in the work which he composed in metrical style concerning the destruction of the city of Paris—besieged and ravaged by the Northmen for seven years—that this Charles wished to attack the Northmen after assembling an immense army. On hearing this, they sent envoys to Charles, promising to submit to him and to do all that he commanded, declaring themselves ready for whatever he wished, provided only that they might remain within the kingdom and live peacefully with the Franks. Deceived by these promises, the king, believing what was said to be true, abandoned the war.

Not long afterward Charles died. The Northmen, however, recovering their boldness, invaded the cities of Beauvais and Meaux and devastated the fortress of Melun. Chartres and the other neighboring cities everywhere were captured; for on their first arrival they had already ravaged Rouen, Évreux, Bayeux, and the other cities of Neustria. They ranged through Gaul, went into Spain, entered the river Rhône, devastated Italy, and brought the entire kingdom of Christians to ruin.

Meanwhile the princes of France assembled and took counsel on matters of great importance. They made Odo king, although he resisted. Kind in disposition, he governed vigorously by repelling the enemies of the commonwealth, and after Charles had grown up and demanded back his kingdoms, he patiently restored them to him. Charles rewarded him with a portion of the kingdom; and for as long as he lived Odo remained terrible to the enemies. At this time the year 891 of Christ’s Incarnation was passing.

### Theobald, Bishop of Langres; The Abbots of Saint Benignus Enumerated

At that time, after the death of Bishop Gello, Theutbald governed the church of Langres. The sequence of the abbots of this place, interrupted for a little while, must now be resumed. After Abbots Berthilo and Saro had passed to eternal life, Hingo succeeded. Saro was buried in the place entrusted to him at Pultariensis. Berthilo, however, when he died, deserved burial here among the tombs of the saints. At his tomb, whenever the faith of those who seek asks it, frequent cures of those suffering from fever occur.

Finally, in the year 1045 of the Lord’s Incarnation, during the fifteenth year of Abbot Halinard’s governance of this place, Berthilo’s body was translated because his tomb impeded the entrance to the crypt of Saint Benignus. The tomb was opened from the south side, and another pit was prepared at his feet, into which he was to be moved. While the monks stood present with crosses, censers, and lights, and many set their hands to move the sarcophagus because it was immense, suddenly all fell to the ground. Rising, they found the sarcophagus properly placed in the prepared spot. Approaching to see how it had been set in the tomb, they opened the lid; and all who were present perceived the fragrance of a wonderful odor. Behold: his body was clothed in monastic dress and adorned with a priestly stole woven with gold. His head, which had been cut off, was joined to the body, and the blood around it had clotted in the tomb.

Hingo, therefore, having been ordained abbot, was a devout cultivator of the Lord’s field, though only for a short time, that is, three years. For so far as he could, he increased temporal and external resources, while allowing divine worship to grow slack in nothing. It will not be tiresome to record the landed properties which in his days were either purchased or acquired by exchange.

A certain priest Waltemus gave part of his inheritance at Ruffiacum, Patriniacum, and Gironnum; Salamannus gave at Aziriacum; Flothbertus at Marcenniacum; Attila at Patriniacum; and Richulfus at the village of Asinariae. A certain nobleman, Deodatus, entering religious conversion, gave at the village of Attegiae a mansus with its superstructure and the dependants living there. Bivinus gave at the village of Norvia a chapel dedicated in honor of Saint Valerius, together with a demesne mansus, lands, and all its appurtenances. Warnerius gave, in the district of Beaune, at the village called Bononicurtis, one field. A certain Hugh gave in the castle of Dijon one small plot or building site, and outside it, land belonging there in the same territory, as well as a vineyard. The priest Bettho, provost of the canons of Saint Stephen, gave one mansus with its superstructure and buildings at the village of Curte Mulnisa in the district of Dijon. Fulchradus sold the same abbot one field at Aziriacum, and Teudegerius another.

The abbot received by exchange from a certain Hubert land and an adjoining vineyard at Canavis, giving him one field at Salonis Villa. He did likewise with Euvrard, giving at Aguliacum a small holding with a vineyard and two fields of arable land, and receiving from him at the village of Burgis one mansus with its superstructure and everything belonging to that mansus in the village itself or at Norvia.

After Hingo’s death, Hildebrannus succeeded in the governance, and after a few years he too departed for the heavenly kingdom. Both presided over this monastery under Bishop Gello. After Hildebrannus, Godefridus assumed the office of abbot in the time of Bishop Theutbald. But after some years, when he too had departed, Walo undertook the responsibility of government. Both governed in the time of King Odo.

At that time Duke Richard of Burgundy restored to Saint Benignus one mansus with vineyards and other lands adjoining it and belonging to it, situated in the neighboring district of Beaune and in the village of Giuriacum. Bishop Theutbald, Counts Girbald, Wido, and Radulf, Madelgaudus, viscount of the Oscarienses, and Guntrardus, witness and advocate of Saint Benignus in this matter, were present at this transaction. Done at Longus Vicus in the public court.

### The Empire Is Taken from the Franks; the Kingdom of Gaul Is in Extreme Danger

In the year 893 of the incarnate Word, while Odo ruled in France and Arnulf in Italy and Saxony, Charles, now a young man, reclaimed the scepter of the kingdom, and the aforesaid Arnulf seized the monarchy of the empire. Then for the first time the empire was transferred from the kings of the Franks to foreigners, because the princes of the kingdom despised Charles for his slow intellect. King Odo died in the twelfth year of his reign; while he lived, he had vigorously repressed the enemies.

Renewed waves of Northmen and Danes rose up. Hungarians from the north and Saracens breaking forth from the south and from the borders of Spain converged for the destruction of Gaul. Everywhere the sword raged, everything was given to fire, and holy places were handed over to devastation.

### Burgundy Ravaged; the Sons of Duke Richard

While these evils raged on every side, it happened that the body of Saint Benignus was carried to the city of Langres. Lord Argrinus then presided over that church, a pastor exceedingly attentive to the care of this place. The abbot of the monks living in this place was named Lauterius, very zealous for his office.

Burgundy was then ravaged by the Northmen. Duke Richard, mentioned above, met them at a place called Argentoilum; battle was joined, a very great multitude of them was slain, and the humbled Danes were compelled to withdraw. Again at Chartres, Richard fought the Northmen, with Duke Robert, brother of King Odo, as his ally, and killed an innumerable multitude of them.

The same Richard had a son named Rodulf, who became king of the Franks. Another son was called Boso, who received the kingdom of Upper Burgundy, called Gallia Comata. The third son was named Hugh, surnamed Capito, who was duke of Lower Burgundy. Discord arose between Charles and the princes of the realm; lawsuits, wars, robberies, and burnings, with innumerable evils, raged everywhere. At last the king, repentant of what had occurred, urged the princes toward concord and concluded the desired peace with them.

### The Abbey of Saint John Is Given to the Monks of Saint Benignus

[Col. 0809A] At the request of Duke Richard and Count Manasses, this King Charles made us a charter concerning the abbey of Saint John and all the property belonging to it.

At that time there was a certain illustrious man, Ademarus, one of the senators, possessing many estates both in the district of Dijon and in other regions, namely the districts of Tours, Orléans, Sens, Auxerre, and Tonnerre. Ademarus and his wife, named Lampaia, gave Saint Benignus one demesne mansus with its superstructure, the lands belonging to it, and woodland. This mansus lay in the village of Ruffiacum. Subject to it, apart from the demesne lands, were seven occupied *coloniae* and mansi, and five unoccupied ones. They also gave forty-eight male and female dependants.

They gave the church consecrated in the name of Saint Gregory, situated in the village of Escoriacum, with everything belonging to it and everything they possessed in that village of Escoriacum. They also gave their portable private chapel, with relics of saints—namely, of the Holy Savior, Saint Mary, and other saints—together with crosses of gold and silver, reliquaries, vestments, and all the ornaments of those relics.

After Ademarus’s death, his wife Lampaia gave to the altar of Saint Mary established in this place, which was anciently called the “head of the church,” Stolivicum in the county of Tonnerre, and a demesne mansus near Stolivicum in the place called Sairocurte, with all its appurtenances and the male and female dependants residing upon it.

### Very Many Things Are Granted to Saint Benignus

The praiseworthy Bishop Argrinus, most fervent in increasing the property of this place, gave for the common benefit of the brothers the abbey of Saint John, which a certain monk Fulbert held by benefice. He also granted, for buying the brothers’ clothing, the half of the annual market belonging to him.

At the request of Abbot Lanterius, he remitted for the use of those monks at the village of Aziriacum the tithes, the customary dues (*parata*), and all revenues of that church, then a cell of the monks of this place. He did likewise with the church at Longovicus and the chapel at Prunidum, which he assigned to the service of the sick; and he assigned the above-mentioned church of Saint John to the service of guests.

He further restored nineteen mansi in various places which had been taken away in the time of his predecessor Bishop Theutbald and granted as a benefice to a certain Wido. Regarding all these matters previously stated, he made privileges under episcopal authority, solemnly enjoining and exhorting subsequent bishops to preserve intact, with paternal affection, the almsgiving which he had made, so that the prayers and vows of God’s servants dwelling in this house might benefit both them and all other faithful persons, living and dead, before God. Whoever should try to take away, grant as a benefice, or remove any of these things in whatever manner, he struck with the sword of anathema, unless he repented.

The same Lord Bishop Argrinus made an exchange of land with Abbot Lanterius inside the castle of Dijon. The bishop gave, beside the castle wall, a plot measuring nine *perticae ancingales* in length and eight perches in width. In return Abbot Lanterius and the monks gave two plots, each six perches long; one was four perches wide and the other five. Land of Saint Stephen lay on every side.

At that time Count Manasses gave Saint Benignus a demesne mansus at Longus Vicus, with the male and female dependants residing upon it and the lands belonging to it, both in that territory and in other villages, on condition that, while retaining the income for himself during his lifetime, he should provide the monks each year, on the feast of Saint Maurice, with a suitable meal. After his death, a similarly proper meal for the brothers was to be supplied from that mansus on the anniversary of his death; what remained was to benefit their needs. The approvers and witnesses of this gift were his son Walo and the younger Count Manasses.

The aforementioned Duke Richard also gave to the church of Saint Anthony situated at Ficiatum, which belonged to Saint Benignus, one mansus called Rovira, with the male and female dependants living upon it. This was approved by his wife Adeleia, his son Rodulf, and Counts Hugh, Boso, Manasses, and Gillebertus.

Milo gave at Saviniacum sixty *journales* of land and woodland sufficient to fatten forty pigs. His father Gislebert had given the same amount in the time of Bishop Isaac: namely, sixty *journales* of arable land and woodland to fatten forty pigs, together with a chapel dedicated in the name of Saint Gervasius.

Countess Atila, for the repose of the soul of her husband Count Milo, gave Saint Benignus at Dumisovilla a demesne mansus with small holdings constructed upon it and other lands belonging to it. Done in the year 902 of the Lord’s Incarnation—that is, 901—in the fourth year of King Charles. The approvers were Count Girbardus and his wife Reintrudis, daughter of Atila herself.

A certain nobleman, Winebaldus, also gave in his villages—namely Marcenniacum and Dumiso—and in their territories, everything which he appeared to possess: that is, lands with the male and female dependants residing upon them.

[Col. 0810D] Lanterius, Fulbert, and Godrad, abbots.—While Abbot Lanterius governed this monastery, an honourable man named Berengarius came to conversion and gave from his possessions, in the estate called Longopratum, one demesne holding, with a spring rising upon it and a mill situated beside it; half of the church at Missiniacum; vineyards; and other holdings belonging to that estate, “which are occupied seven, without thirteen” [reading uncertain], together with fifty male and female serfs. He also gave, in the district of Beaune, at the estate of Sentenacum, one tenant-farm. Likewise the canon Hildemodus and the priest Arico, entering upon the monastic life, gave all their inheritance at the estate of Siliciacum. Adalreus also, seeking this place with like devotion, gave whatever he possessed at the estate of Barges.

Gotzelinus, canon and abbot of the church of Saint Mammes of Langres within the walls of that city, gave one holding beside the church of Saint Desiderius. Abbot Lanterius made an exchange at the estate of Carli with a certain Rohard, and at Upper Corcelles with Isoard.

When Abbot Lanterius, after long labours, hastened toward the heavenly prize, Fulbert succeeded him—himself likewise a veteran soldier of many days. After one year, laying down the burden of the obedience he had undertaken, he entrusted the care of government to Godrad, in the seventeenth year of King Charles. This Godrad bought at Aziriacum from Heldierius and his wife Natalia one meadow, measuring sixty-five Angical perches in length and [Col. 0811B] thirty-two perches in breadth. Lord Argrinus, therefore, having relinquished the honour of the episcopate, became a monk in this monastery; and, dying after two years, was honourably committed to burial within the enclosure of this church.

### Warnerius, bishop of Langres, and Godrad, abbot of Saint Benignus

At last Lord Warnerius, bishop, succeeded him in pastoral care; he too was a devoted augmenter of the goods of this place. In the first year of his ordination, namely the year 912 of the Incarnate Word, the fifteenth indiction, while he was sitting in synod in the bosom of the mother church of Saint Mammes before the archdeacons, abbots, and all the clergy, he was petitioned by Abbot Godrad and the monks of our patron Saint Benignus concerning a certain church within the [Col. 0811C] walls of the fortress of Dijon, consecrated in honour and under the name of Saint Vincent. Lord Bishop Geilo had granted it to them to possess in perpetuity as a place of refuge and for the protection of the body of the oft-mentioned Saint Benignus.

Although they had used it for a long time, they had been dispossessed by Ratherius, archdeacon and canonical abbot of Saint Mammes and provost of the abbey of Saint Stephen. The aforesaid bishop, therefore, considering the dangers which then frequently threatened through the incursions of the Northmen, with the counsel and approval of Ratherius himself and of the whole synod, restored to Abbot Godrad and the monks the aforesaid church of Saint Vincent, with the dwellings belonging to that church in place of an atrium, which the monks themselves had formerly built there as a refuge. [Col. 0811D] Concerning this church he made them a privilege by episcopal authority, so that none of his successors thereafter should inflict any violence or legal molestation upon Saint Benignus and the monks serving him.

### Gozuinus, Panto, and Suavus, abbots of Saint Benignus

After happily completing seven years in pastoral government, Abbot Godrad departed to Christ. After him an abbot named Gozuinus was ordained. When he died after two years, an abbot named Panto succeeded in his place. He too died after completing four years of government. An abbot named Suavus succeeded him.

As the day of his death approached, Bishop Warnerius asked to be buried in the church of his patron [Col. 0812A] Saint Benignus. Having summoned Abbot Suavus to himself, he gave him, in the capacity of Saint Benignus, one meadow at Aziriacum, where one hundred and fifty cartloads of hay could be cut. Apart from the other things which he had bestowed with generous intention, he gave this meadow so that the anniversary of his death might be solemnly observed by the brethren and an appropriate meal prepared for them by the abbot, or by him to whom the abbot had entrusted the duty of making that provision. On dying, he was buried in this basilica before the altar of Saint Benignus.

Lord Gotzelinus succeeded him in the honour of the episcopate, in the tenth year of Robert’s reign. Since mention has been made of him, it is necessary to say how Robert obtained the kingdom.

### Robert seizes the kingdom. Charles is consigned to prison by Herbert. Rudolph, ruler of Francia, expels the Northmen

After King Odo died, his brother Robert hoped and desired to obtain that part of the kingdom which Odo himself had held; and because it was not restored to him by Charles, lord of the whole kingdom, he openly seized tyrannical power. This was after the death of Duke Richard, who received his surname from the execution of justice. For as long as he lived, Richard remained ever faithful to King Charles.

Robert, therefore, wishing openly to wield the power of the tyranny at which he aimed, compelled certain bishops, partly by flatteries and partly by threats, to crown him with the royal diadem and invest him with the sceptre of the kingdom. But he by no means had a happy outcome from this presumption. For after reigning one year, he was met in battle on the fields of Soissons by Charles’s commanders and deprived of life. Although his army won the victory, he himself paid the price of his wicked audacity.

Yet the associates in his revolt, not frightened by his death, did not abandon the obstinacy of their treachery. Rather, Count Herbert of Vermandois, by an unspeakable crime, treacherously seized Charles, his lord and king of all Francia, bound him in chains, and sent him to be confined in a dark dwelling at Péronne. Since the condition of the kingdom was uncertain without a prince—especially because the boyish age of Hugh, Robert’s son, who later earned the name “the Great” by his noble deeds, prevented him from assuming the royal insignia, while Herbert incurred the hatred of all, particularly those whom compassion for the prince’s misery moved to mercy—at last Rudolph, a Burgundian by birth, son of Duke Richard, [Col. 0812D] was set over the governance of the land of the Franks.

Having attained the royal throne, he was severe in punishing evildoers and most shrewd in restraining enemies and defending the kingdom. In his days the companies of Danes and Northmen again arrived and ranged not only through Francia but throughout all Burgundy. Taking up arms against them, Rudolph so checked their insolent attacks that even to the present he has kept Gaul quiet from their invasion. At that time the body of our patron Saint Benignus happened to be carried within the walls of Dijon fortress and kept there in the church of Saint Vincent.

> **Note:** [Col. 0811D] Note the author’s chronological error.

### King Rudolph favours the monks of Saint Benignus

Gotzelinus [Col. 0813A] was then bishop governing the church of Langres. Going to King Rudolph’s palace, he petitioned the king’s clemency together with Count Manasses, asking that by royal precept he should determine the status of certain properties taken from this place but recently restored to Saint Benignus by his predecessors, namely Argrinus and Warnerius. The king assented and, by his royal munificence, restored the properties themselves to Saint Benignus: namely the estate of Saciacum with its church, the other estates belonging there, and everything which episcopal authority had possessed there; also the little abbey of Saint John; likewise the market held every Saturday in the borough, and half of the yearly fair held at the feast of Saint Benignus; also the meadow at the estate of Aziriacum, which Bishop Warnerius had granted there at the end of his life; eight holdings in the county of Alsace, at the estate of Nermedis, with male and female serfs; and one holding at the estate of Gibriacum in the district of Beaune, through the favour and petition of Count Manasses. The aforesaid King Rudolph granted all these things to God and Saint Benignus in the year 925 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the thirteenth indiction, and the fourth year of his reign.

### Rudolph resides at Dijon

The same King Rudolph, after the death of his brother Duke Hugh, went to Burgundy. While residing in the fortress of Dijon in April, and while Count Robert of the palace, Count Gislebert of Burgundy, and many others, both counts and noblemen, were conducting his cases, Viscount Robert was summoned by Vizo, advocate of Saint Benignus, concerning certain serfs. Though born of Robert’s male serf, they were born of a female slave of Saint Benignus and from the jurisdiction and fisc of Longvic; they ought therefore to serve Saint Benignus rather than Robert himself. Then, in that very judicial assembly and in the presence of the princes, Robert renounced those serfs and restored them to Saint Benignus, promising that if any of his relatives or heirs thereafter should seek or lay claim to them, he himself would be Saint Benignus’s witness and defender against them.

### Abbot Alberic. Letricus, Ericus, Achardus, and Widricus, bishops of Langres

At that time a certain Boso and his wife Plectrudis gave Saint Benignus, at the estate of Aziriacum in the place called Wora, a share in one jointly held estate; Abbot Suavus bought the other share from them for one hundred solidi. After ten years of government, [Col. 0813D] Abbot Suavus died. Alberic was ordained abbot in his place by Lord Bishop Gotzelinus.

The bishop himself continued in the episcopate for some years and died. As long as he lived, he endeavoured to benefit this place according to his ability. Would that his successors had done the same! Bishop Letericus succeeded him in the episcopate; Ericus followed him, then Achardus, and after him Widricus. Nearly forty years and more passed under these bishops, during which the condition of this place steadily worsened, since bishops and abbots cared more for other things than for it.

### Rudolph dies childless. Charles dies in prison. Louis Overseas. Fulcherius and Manasses, abbots

When King Rudolph died without children—for his son Louis, whom he had had by his wife Queen Emma, died before his father—and when Charles, confined in prison, was released by captivity in soul, not body (while he lived he was called “the Simple” because of his kindness of spirit), he may now rightly be called holy, since, unjustly afflicted by his faithless and perjured men with long imprisonment, he passed to the higher life. He left a son, Louis, born of Eadgifu, daughter of the king of the English. Fearing to be entangled in the storms of his father’s misfortune, Louis withdrew to the English and Saxons, invited by the bond of his maternal kinship.

After King Rudolph’s death, recalled by Hugh the Great, he was restored, in appearance at least, to his ancestral kingdom, in the year 938 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the eleventh indiction. The administration of this kingdom proved burdensome to one wishing to exercise the right of dominion, both because he was captured by Count Theobald of Chartres and because, after the recovery of the kingdom, fortune’s unstable events varied.

In the second year of his reign Fulcherius was ordained abbot. He held that office for fifteen years and did nothing good in this house. When he departed, an abbot named Manasses succeeded him, himself worse than his predecessor.

### On Louis’s death, two sons survive. King Lothair

When King Louis died, he left two surviving children, Lothair and Charles, whom Gerberga, sister of Otto, later emperor of the Romans, had borne him. [Col. 0814C] Charles, the younger in age, grew old in private circumstances; Lothair succeeded to the whole inheritance. He exercised royal power for more than thirty years.

At the time when Manasses was acting as abbot, Count Hugh of Dijon, nearing death, asked to be buried in the atrium of Saint Benignus. For the repose of his soul and for the place of burial, his wife Countess Adalburgis, with the approval of her sons—namely Gibuinus, bishop of Châlons; Richard, who held this county after him; and Hugh, count of the Attoarii—gave one holding at the estate of Patriniacum and everything belonging to that holding.

At the same time a certain Erimarus gave, at the estate called Curte Arnono, six holdings with a church built there and nineteen male and female serfs dwelling upon them. Moreover, he gave to God and Saint Benignus whatever he possessed between the two rivers Tille and Bèze. Evrard also, on behalf of his brother Restantius, a monk of this place, gave at the estate of Corcelles one demesne holding and everything belonging to it.

Ado, a priest who became a monk, gave in the district of Beaune, at the estate of Cussiniacum, one holding, arable land, and meadow. Likewise, at Flaviniacum, he gave one holding and handed over to Saint Benignus everything he possessed there or anywhere else in lands and serfs.

The above-mentioned Bishop Gibuinus and his brothers Richard and Hugh, after their mother’s death, gave, for the repose of her soul and that of their father, the inheritance which they had at the estate of Missiniacum. Abbot Manasses granted that land in precarial tenure to a certain noblewoman, Retrudis, and her sons Gotescalcus and Willerius. Likewise, at the estate called Barges, he granted Retrudis twenty-seven *journaux* of land in precarial tenure. Another Retrudis gave Saint Benignus, near Dijon on the river Ouche, one mill and eight *journaux* of arable land in the same place.

### Bruno, bishop of Langres, seeks to restore the disordered diocese to its former splendour. Abbot Azo

In the year 980 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the eighth indiction, and the twenty-fifth year of King Lothair’s reign, the same king gave the bishopric of the city of Langres to Bruno, a cleric of the church of Rheims and his close kinsman by blood. This Bruno was ordained bishop by the hands of Burchard, archbishop of Lyons, in the church of Saint Stephen, at the age of twenty-four; and in the same year, namely 981 from Christ’s Incarnation, he was received by the clergy of the city of Langres.

Having acquired the episcopate, he strove with every effort he could to follow the example of the Good Shepherd. Seeing that the monasteries belonging to his diocese had been almost reduced to nothing both in religious observance in spiritual matters and in the administration necessary for temporal affairs, he began to seek a means, by God’s disposing will, of restoring them to their proper condition. He therefore removed Abbot Manasses of this place from an authority which he was not exercising well, and installed in his place an abbot from the monastery of Der, named Azo. He was Aquitanian by birth, adorned with good morals and religious conduct. After two years of government, he returned to his own monastery, relinquishing the governance of this place, and Abbot Manasses again received his office.

### With Saint Maiolus’s help he restores monastic observance at the monastery of Dijon. Saint William, abbot of Saint Benignus

Bishop Bruno, therefore, seeing the condition of the place in jeopardy, humbly approached Lord Maiolus, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and urgently begged him to enable its restoration through his assistance—for inward religious observance and outward possessions alike. Moved by his prayers, the reverend Abbot Maiolus gave him twelve monks selected from the whole congregation, trained in the disciplines of holy religious life, taught in divine and human wisdom, and distinguished by noble birth.

When they arrived, Bishop Bruno arranged that, on the feast of the translation of Saint Benignus, while the monks already there, with the clerics subject to them, celebrated the night office before the tomb of the oft-mentioned martyr in the crypt, the newcomers should begin the morning synaxis in the upper choir before the principal altar of Saint Maurice. This was fittingly done, so that those who came to display the light of religious observance might enter as daylight drew near.

Accordingly, as those men went hither and thither, those dwelling in the place began to shine in holy conduct; and the place which had previously seemed disgraced in everyone’s eyes by evil deeds and unspeakable negligence now appeared to flourish through the happy exercise of every virtue. Yet because the industry of the aforesaid Father was directed to other places, and this place could not be without an abbot, Maiolus, again pressed by the prayers of Bishop Bruno, appointed over the flock of this monastery a brother named William: a most fervent practitioner of his Order, shining with the splendour of every nobility, laudably rooted and grounded in true humility, the charity of brotherly love, and the supreme virtue of discretion—recognized as the mother of all virtues. Thus he established a spiritual father for the sons who sought one.

William was Italian by origin, born of a very exalted stock and noble lineage. When the aforesaid Lord Maiolus was returning from Rome, he found him in the monastery called Luccio, where he had been brought up from childhood. At William’s own request he took him and brought him with himself to Cluny, while he was in the flower of youth.

### Saint William is ordained in 990. The deeds of his holy life are described

William was therefore ordained abbot by Bishop Bruno in the year 990 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the third indiction. Having received the office of abbot, he began to exercise himself in divine virtues. He was chaste in body, devout in mind, gracious in speech, endowed with prudence, renowned for temperance, firm in inward courage, steadfast in the rule of justice, constant in long-suffering, strong in patience, gentle in humility, full of the grace of good works, and indeed overflowing with the affections of charity.

He was always solicitous for the poor. Loving Christ with all his heart, since he could not serve him bodily as Martha did, he daily fed him in the needy. He offered to all a most generous use of hospitality: no one was excluded, and no one suffered refusal. He delighted in the sayings of the divine commandments, because through them he was taught both to order his own conduct and to instruct and correct those entrusted to him. He presented himself to all as an example of good living. As he was first in rank, so he strove to be first in work, according to the evangelist’s saying: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

Those who sinned he rebuked publicly from the zeal of loving devotion, so that the others might be afraid. The words which he spoke in rebuke and correction seemed hard and sharp like goads, so that they were almost feared more than blows, according to the saying: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed” (Eccli. XII, 11). Some he addressed with gentleness, others with admonitions, others with terrors; and thus, in accordance with the Apostle, “he proclaimed the word, being urgent in season and out of season, reproving, entreating, rebuking, in all patience and teaching.”

He was afflicted by the calamities of the wretched as though he himself suffered them. His mouth was so filled from the abundance of his heart that almost nothing but the divine law resounded from it; and because Scripture says, “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22:17), he persuaded as many as he could to withdraw from the wickedness of the world. And as he himself yearned with all his strength for the heavenly kingdom, so he desired, if possible, that all people should go there with him.

Nor was he in any way defrauded of the desire conceived within him by true love. For he who is Charity, who fulfils the will of those who fear him, brought the fervent desire of the man of God to fulfilment. At his exhortations, many abandoned what they possessed, submitted themselves to regular discipline, followed the footsteps of blessed Benedict, denied themselves, and served the true King with all their strength. An innumerable multitude flowed to his monastery from diverse regions. Though different in nationality, they were united in mind, so that the words written in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the beginning of the growing Church appeared to be literally fulfilled in them: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

### Bishop Bruno provides temporal necessities for monks living religiously

As zeal for religious observance grew inwardly, the supply of outward resources began to abound no little, as the Lord promised his own in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matthew VI, 23). Bishop Bruno, greatly rejoicing in heart at their good manner of life, took every care to provide what was necessary for their use.

He restored to Saint Benignus and his monks the church situated at Saciacum, together with the entire jurisdiction and estates belonging to it, whole and intact, just as it had been possessed in ancient times, but afterwards many times alienated and plundered by wicked men. Count Otto, surnamed William, successor and heir of Duke Henry, restored to Saint Benignus, for the remedy of his soul, the protection-right of that estate, after paying a debt of no small sum of money to Geoffrey, lord of the fortress of Mailly.

Lord Bishop Bruno also restored the church of Saint Apollinaris and granted land beside this monastery for planting an orchard; he likewise granted, in every direction for work on the vineyards, many acres at Lariacum, Bèze, Surdiliacum, Patriniacum, Foedeniacum, the field of Solomon, and Marcenniacum. Though these works were built through the monks’ zeal and labour, they were undertaken at Bishop Bruno’s encouragement. Everywhere he investigated and restored what had been taken away; and from his own right he willingly granted them whatever was necessary and useful. While both men—Lord Bishop Bruno and the venerable Abbot William—strove zealously in restoring this place, it began to grow and, as it were, to bloom anew.

### Hugh and Robert, kings of the Franks. Sons of Hugh the Great

At the time these things were being done, King Hugh, son of Hugh the Great, ruled the kingdom of the Franks together with his son Robert. For after King Lothair exchanged, as we believe, his earthly kingdom for a heavenly one (987), his son Louis succeeded him. But Louis was overtaken by premature death in adolescence and left the kingdom of the Franks destitute of its proper heir.

Certainly his uncle Charles tried, if possible, to claim for himself the kingdom long held by the founders of his family, but his intention attained that result. For the leading men of the Franks, abandoning Charles, went over to Hugh, son of the great Hugh already mentioned, who was then vigorously administering the duchy of Francia, and raised him to the royal throne in the city of Noyon. In the same year he chose his son Robert as his partner in the kingdom. He began to reign in the year 991 from Christ’s Incarnation and reigned ten years. After his death Robert alone held the kingdom.

King Hugh had two brothers, Otto and Henry, sons of Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks. After their father’s death Hugh received the duchy of Francia and Otto that of Burgundy. Otto had as wife the daughter of Gislebert, who held the duchy of Burgundy after Hugh, brother of King Rudolph. But when Otto died young and childless, his brother Henry succeeded him. He was adorned with good morals, especially gentleness, and was a man devoted to the Church.

### Abbot William restores Vézelay and many other monasteries

Duke Henry, having heard of the religious fame of the outstanding Father William, entrusted to him the abbey of Vézelay, which had been reduced almost to nothing, so that he might restore it to its former condition; and with God’s help he did so. Bishop Bruno, seeing Father William so fervent in religious observance and monastic discipline, and seeing the places entrusted to him prosper day by day, committed to his care all the monasteries in his bishopric: namely, the abbey of Bèze, dedicated in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul; the monastery of Saint John called Réome; the place of Saint Michael the Archangel near the fortress of Tonnerre; and the abbey of Moutiers-Saint-Jean, where Saint Valerius, archdeacon and martyr, rests. He governed all these so vigorously that, after him, when each was assigned to its own abbot, they could not equal the condition in which they had been while governed by him.

### Concerning the deeds of the same saint

In the sixth year of his ordination, Abbot William went to Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles, seeking their patronage with devout prayer; from there he made for the holy mountain of the Angel, Gargano. But on arriving at Benevento, he was bound by the fetter of a most grievous illness. Afflicted for a long time by the weakness of this illness, and now despaired of by his companions as unable to recover, one night he was caught up in spirit and set before the tribunal of the fearful Judge. There, being reproved for certain offences, especially for indiscreet severity, he feared, as it seemed to him, that he would be condemned for these faults to the eternal punishments of Gehenna.

Saint Pope Gregory received him under his protection, on the assurance that thereafter he would live with more careful concern and would amend his former errors by works of piety and mercy. After the vision he returned to himself, began from that day to recover from the illness, and changed his former harshness into the greatest compassion. Thereafter throughout his life he honoured Saint Gregory with special love.

Then many began to come to him from his own country, Italy: some well trained in letters, others skilled in the mastery of various crafts, and others endowed with agricultural knowledge. Their skill and ingenuity greatly profited this place. Thus the number of monks living under his instruction grew daily, so that—apart from those who were in other monasteries—there were daily seventy or eighty brethren in this community.

### How many benefits Bishop Bruno conferred

Among the other good deeds performed by Lord Bishop Bruno in this place—it would take too long to enumerate all his acts—we may say this briefly: everything bestowed on this place in ancient times, then plundered by wicked men or divided up by bad rulers, was restored by Bishop Bruno. Though the earlier donors do not lose the reward of their almsgiving, Bruno is nevertheless no less worthy of thanksgiving; for through him this place was raised from dead ashes to a condition more excellent than it had ever been before.

### A brief enumeration of the founder and benefactors

This abbey was founded by Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres; established and enriched by King Guntram; restored by Emperor Charles surnamed the Bald and Lord Bishop Isaac; and renewed by the venerable Bishop Bruno and Abbot William, not only in other matters but also through a new construction of the church. In building this basilica, the bishop expended resources and brought marble and stone columns from every side; the reverend abbot hired master craftsmen and directed the work itself. Labouring together, they built a church worthy of divine worship. The design and refinement of this skilfully wrought work are not pointlessly displayed in writing to those less instructed, because many things in it appear to have been made with mystical meaning and ought to be attributed more to divine inspiration than to the skill of any master.

### The plan of the ancient church of this monastery of Saint Benignus follows

This church was founded in the year 1001 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the fourteenth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March [14 February]. Its length was nearly two hundred cubits and its width fifty-three. Its height will suitably be described below.

The lower house of prayer, in which the most sacred body of Saint Benignus the martyr is venerated, having almost the same dimensions, is supported by one hundred and four columns. Made in the form of the letter T, with four rows of twelve columns each, it extends equally in length and breadth; it rises ten cubits in height and has concealed vestibules on either side. It contains five altars: the first is consecrated in honour of Saint Benignus himself; the second in memory of Saint Nicholas and all confessors; the third in veneration of Saint Pascasia the virgin, who rests there, and of all virgins; the fourth in honour of Saint Irenaeus and all martyrs; and the fifth under the names of the holy confessors and abbots Saints John and Sequanus, and Saint Eustadius the priest, who rests there.

In it are the bodies of the saints whose blessed members surround the body of the oft-mentioned witness of Christ; their names are recorded at the beginning of this book. The bodies of the holy confessors and bishops Urban and Gregory were originally buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist, but after a long time were raised from there. One half of Saint Gregory’s body was placed in the church of Saint Benignus when, out of fear of the pagans, the exhumed body of that holy martyr was carried to the city of Langres; the other half of the aforesaid confessor’s body was then retained there.

When Saint Urban’s body was raised and placed in a shrine, the Lord, through him, gladdened the hearts of his servants dwelling in this place with many miraculous signs. When the body of the venerable Bishop Isaac was transferred elsewhere by certain priests because the construction of the church required it, it is said to have been found for the most part whole, together with its head, still wearing clerical dress. Similarly, the priestly garments of Lord Argrinus, bishop and monk, together with his cowl and inner hair-shirt, were found incorrupt, as testimony to his holiness.

Not far from this place Saint Radegund was found, with a plaque bearing her name at her head, on a sheet of lead. Her bones, wrapped in waxed linen, were found in a wooden chest buried in the earth. Moreover, Saint Gregory, bishop of Tours, mentions the other saints whose bodies are known to be buried here, describing certain miracles of theirs (*Book of Miracles*, I, chs. 51–52; *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chs. 42–44): namely, Benignus the martyr, our special patron; Tranquillus the confessor; Hilary the senator and his wife Saint Florida, a holy woman; and Pascasia, virgin and martyr.

Pascasia, taught and baptized by Saint Benignus, was seized after his martyrdom by the cruelty of the pagans and led to punishment. Since she remained immovable in faith in Christ, she was first afflicted by the foulness of prison and afterward sentenced to capital punishment for confessing the Godhead, as an ancient glass painting, surviving to our times, elegantly represented. Therefore this church, of which we are speaking, is honourably enriched with the venerable bodies of so many saints, apart from the relics of other saints whom it would seem superfluous to enumerate.

Connected on the eastern side to the lower crypt described somewhat above is an oratory built in a circular form, illuminated by the light of six windows, thirty-seven cubits in diameter and ten in height. This oratory is encircled by three rows of columns, forty-eight in all, arranged geometrically. Its elevated summit, raised to a lofty peak, is covered by an elegant construction of twenty-four columns and thirty-two arches, divided in three sections of equal number.

This oratory is consecrated in honour of Saint John the Baptist; its altar is illuminated by the light of three windows. From this church, on the right and left, there are thirty-seven spiral steps, sufficiently lighted by numerous windows, by which one ascends safely to the basilica of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God. This church itself is supported by sixty-eight columns, having almost the same dimensions and form in diameter and height as the lower church, and is illuminated by eleven glass windows.

One ascends to the marble altar of the perpetual Virgin by four triple steps. Beside these, on either side, are altars: on the right, those of John the Evangelist, James his brother, and Saint Thomas the Apostle; [Col. 0821B] on the left, those of Saints Matthew, James, and Philip the Apostles.

Again corresponding to it and sufficiently well lit, thirty steps on either side, by a spiral stairway, provide a continuous ascent to the church of the holy and undivided Trinity. Built in the form of a crown and likewise supported on thirty-six columns, it gleams with extraordinary brightness, light being admitted on every side by windows and from above through the open sky. It is similar in extent to the lower church, but is twenty cubits high. The altar of the Holy Trinity is so placed that it is visible from every direction to those entering and to all standing anywhere in the church.

From there ascent to the upper levels is open by four stairways, made on either side. Two of these, arranged alike, extend by fifteen [Col. 0821C] steps to the oratory of Saint Michael, which is thirty-three cubits long and ten high, built on a modest plan; it has seven windows. The other two direct one’s steps upward by fifty stairs. At the foot of the stairways there are two walkways constructed upon the wall. Extending at an equal distance from the eastern side to the western, both beneath the church through arched passages and above the roof of the building upon a wall approximately three cubits high running all around, they protect those walking there from falling. Beginning, however, at the right and left sides of the church, these lead the way inward on a level path, as stated, beneath and within its wings, by certain concealed approaches directing one’s steps to the upper roof, until, reaching the lintel of the western doors, they descend by matching stairways of twenty steps into the porticoes of the greater church.

This church, built in the form of a cross, is one hundred and twenty-eight cubits long; it is fifty-three cubits wide, as specified above; its height is thirty-one cubits in every direction at the outer portions, and forty in the middle. It is lit by seventy glazed windows and supported by one hundred and twenty-one columns. Some of these seem, near the heads of the very strong forty square-set piers, to be crowned together, as it were, by one crown, although the form of them all is not of one size. On either side it has double porticoes, elaborated in two tiers, in which there are four altars, two and two.

On the north side, one is in honour of the holy apostles Peter and Andrew; the other in honour of the apostles Saint Bartholomew, Simon, and Thaddaeus. The altar of Saint Paul is in the upper church, before the altar of the Holy Trinity, because he was caught up to the third heaven and saw the mysteries of God. On the south are altars: one in honour of the holy apostles Matthew and Barnabas, and Luke the Evangelist; the other in honour of the holy martyrs Stephen, Lawrence, and Vincent. There is another altar on the western side of the church, on the same southern side, in honour of the holy martyrs Mammēs, Desiderius, Leodegar, Sebastian, and Gengulph. On the other side it is in honour of the holy martyrs Polycarp, Andochius, Thyrsus, [Col. 0822B] Andeolus, Symphorian, George, and Christopher, and of the holy confessors Urban and Gregory, whose bodies adorn the present church.

The principal altar is consecrated in honour of Saints Maurice and Benignus; and at its right is an altar in honour of all the saints, Saint Raphael the archangel, and all blessed spirits. At the left is one in honour of Saint Mark the Evangelist; and in the middle of the church itself is the altar of the Holy Cross and of all the saints. Before this altar is a triple entrance to the crypt; from it one ascends fifteen steps to the upper church.

The tomb of the holy and glorious martyr is constructed as follows. There is a tomb built of squared stones, eight cubits long and five [Col. 0822C] wide; its stone summit is supported by four columns. Above it, four marble columns were formerly set. Long ago, upon the stone arches enclosing the apse, they bore a wooden structure six cubits long, three broad, and seven and a half high, which, clad everywhere in gold and silver, displayed in excellent, projecting carved and painted work the history of the Lord’s Nativity and Passion.

But this most fitting ornament of which we speak was dismantled by Lord Abbot William in time of famine for the relief of the poor; together with a golden casket wonderfully adorned with gems, three panels, two silver censers, and crosses, every ornament in gold and silver [Col. 0822D] was sold. Before these times, moreover, distinguished ornaments—gems, precious cloths, caskets, panels, crowns, ecclesiastical vessels, and candlesticks made of gold and silver—as well as an image of our Lord and Saviour made of gold in cast work, were carried away by thieves through deceit, after the guards had been killed, on the feast-day of that saint. These ornaments had formerly been bestowed upon this place by Guntram and other kings in reverence and honour of God and of Saint Benignus the martyr; but, having been sacrilegiously removed in ancient times by the wicked hands of evil men, no ruler afterwards arose who could recover so great a treasure.

These few remarks have been made to make known the antiquity and glory of the place of Dijon. It should be stated finally [Col. 0823A] that the building of this church contains three hundred and seventy-one columns, excluding those in the towers and at the altars; one hundred and twenty windows glazed, or to be glazed; eight towers; three gates; and twenty-four doors.

### Again concerning Saint William the Abbot

**He restores observance of Saint Benedict’s Rule in various monasteries.**—Let us now turn our pen to explain the deeds of Father William that we had omitted. Whenever he visited the palaces of emperors or kings, he sought there not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ, so that by familiar conversation with them he might, through his intervention, aid the oppressed, or might gain persons for God from either secular or clerical life; that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, they might abandon what was their own and, putting aside worldly cares, [Col. 0823B] strive to serve God in peace.

Very many therefore came to him, as we have said; and though diverse in nations, they were united in mind. The shepherd rejoiced in the increase of his flock, and rejoiced the more because all stood firm in the work undertaken. But because he watched with diligent care over the flock entrusted to him, he deserved through divine grace to rejoice in this life in the fruit of their labours. For he restored to its former condition, by correction, the discipline of the regular life which had almost fallen away through the negligence of earlier generations, as blessed Benedict had established it. Through many monasteries in various parts of the world which had strayed from the regular path, both in person and through those whom he had appointed abbots, he brought them under the monastic order. Rejoicing in this, he gave thanks to God because he saw that many of those [Col. 0823C] whom he had trained under his care would be fit to govern the monastic order. We have judged it proper to include some of these in this book, so that posterity may know what vigorous monks came forth from this congregation and their memory may endure in praise.

### Distinguished disciples of Saint William

When the venerable William first assumed the office of abbot, there was among the monks living in this place a young man called Hunaldus. Seeing him to be of diligent ability, the aforesaid Father kept him with himself when the others departed. Having especially imbued him with every kind of learning, he established him in God’s house as a chosen vessel. Indeed, in everything necessary to him, he was aided by the ingenuity of the aforesaid brother. Finally, he entrusted to him the care of this sacred enclosure, which Hunaldus discharged with such concern that almost every ornament in this basilica was acquired through his efforts. At last, after the death of the aforesaid Father, he obtained the abbacy of Tournus and there died, having spent twenty-seven years in government.

Another citizen of this fortress-town of Dijon, Rudolph, surnamed the White, born of noble stock, came to conversion at the very beginning of this new reformation. By his money the poverty of the aforesaid Father was relieved, and by his counsel and assistance the burden of governing this place and the monastery of Bèze was lightened—for William still had only a small number of monks. This brother aided him so greatly in external affairs that [Col. 0824A] he alone seemed to supply the assistance of many. But, contrary to his wish, the shortness of his days took this aid away from him.

Another man attached to the aforesaid Father was Theoderic, a citizen of this region. After long training, William made him prior of the abbey of Fécamp; at last he appointed him abbot of Jumièges. Another, a knight from the fortress called Beaune, named Ledbaldus and surnamed “the Wise” on account of his learning, joined Father William. Having been imbued with his spiritual teaching, he was for some time appointed archimandrite at Tournus.

### Abbeys entrusted to Saint William for reform: Saint Arnulf at Metz and Fruttuaria

A cleric of Metz, named Benedict, born of noble family, was stirred by the fame of the outstanding Father William’s holy life and joined himself to his discipleship. In a short time, by striving to imitate him, he attained perfection in monastic life in learning and conduct. Through his report, therefore, Lord Adalbero, bishop of Metz, learned of Father William’s religious way of life. Summoned by him with earnest entreaty and granted the abbey of Saint Arnulf, William appointed Benedict father there. There he devoted himself to sacred works for many years, died, and shone with many virtues.

So that the reverend Abbot William should not return empty-handed from so great a bishop, he received from that prelate a stole woven with gold and two purple copes adorned with a golden border. Benedict also, once appointed abbot, offered William for his blessing a chasuble suitably ornamented with gold and other ornaments [Col. 0824C]. These the aforesaid Father distributed as he pleased, both in this place and at Fruttuaria, which he had newly founded. He governed the aforesaid abbey of Saint Arnulf for many years after the death of the abbot just mentioned.

There also came to him from the clergy of Toul one named Arnulf, excellently educated in letters and learned in every kind of worldly wisdom. Having quickly attained the discipline of a more perfect life, he was entrusted by Lord Father William with the care not only of this place but of all the places under William’s supervision. How many good things he accomplished here we shall recount later; for those deeds which shine through his industrious works ought not to be hidden in silence.

### Saint Aper of Toul

[Col. 0824D] Meanwhile, let us continue to recount the memory of distinguished men. Although we, their followers, waste away in sluggishness far from the fervour of their religious life, and, assailed on every side by inward and outward evils, are benumbed in every good endeavour and bound by idleness and sloth, perhaps there will nevertheless be some after us who, reading their deeds, will strive to imitate their examples.

Lord Berthold, bishop of the Leuci—whose city is called Toul—sought an interview with the often-mentioned Abbot William after receiving a complaint from one of his clerics. Observing in William’s words the unshaken and unflattering constancy of his mind, and admiring the other notable virtues shining in his deeds and character, he urged him with pressing entreaty to assume the abbey of Saint Aper and reform it in accordance with Saint Benignus’s institution. Yielding to his prayers, William transformed that monastery within a few years into a regular state. He found there vigorous monks, one of whom, named Widricus, he appointed after not many years as father of the monks in the same monastery. A teachable disciple of an outstanding master, he strove so to imitate him in all things that Father William seemed in some manner to be represented in all his words and deeds. Training many, finally, in holy conduct, he produced from his own congregation several fathers of monks for other monasteries.

### Many bishops and abbots submit themselves to William’s teaching

Many priests and abbots, leaving the care of places or churches entrusted to them, accordingly flocked to Father William’s teaching. A bishop of the city of Albenga, situated near Genoa on the sea in Italy, abandoned his bishopric and submitted himself to the authority of the aforesaid Father. Another bishop, called Barnabas and Greek by birth, lived in this monastery under his instruction for many years. Yet another bishop, named Benignus, came here from Rome and for several years lived with him in submission and obedience. Very many abbots also, coming from different regions, voluntarily submitted themselves, ready to obey. Among them were Abbot John called “the Capuan”; another Abbot John of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris in the city of Ravenna; Benedict, [Col. 0825C] abbot of the monastery of Saint Severus in the city of Classe; Anastasius and Marcus; and many other abbots whom it would be tedious to enumerate. The monks who came from those regions were beyond number.

A certain archdeacon of Milan, named Gotefred, came in a manner befitting a nobleman, nobly and with many treasures. Among them he brought an onyx altar suitably ornamented with gold and silver and everything belonging to a chapel, that is, ecclesiastical ornaments. He remained a monk in this monastery for many years; later, recalled to his homeland with Abbot William’s consent, he was made abbot near Milan.

Finally, those holy men themselves, fathers and teachers of hermits, renowned far and wide for holiness—Romuald, William, and Martin, whom the city of Ravenna held in great veneration—and the others whom Italy contained, sought Father William’s fellowship. For the union of holy persons is pleasing and delightful, and most necessary to the Church; conversely, the association of the wicked hinders the good. These cultivators of the wilderness abandoned the tranquillity of solitude and rejoiced to join cenobites under his instruction. Two of their number, John and Paul, both learned men, accordingly joined him; their wisdom advanced the salvation of many souls. Both were most fervent in monastic religion; in cenobitic life they were examples for the others to imitate, while in the contemplative life they devoted themselves constantly to reading and prayer, becoming equally an example and an object of admiration to those who saw them.

Paul, of reverend memory, died peacefully among us. John, however, a man of God so called on account of his holy conduct, was appointed abbot of the monastery of Fruttuaria by Lord Father William. Since occasion has arisen, it seems fitting to say briefly how that place was founded.

### Origin of the monastery of Fruttuaria

The often-mentioned Abbot William had two brothers, Nitardus and Gotefred. The first was distinguished by the dignity of count; the other was content with the pay of military service. By frequent admonitions the aforesaid Father drew them away from the enticements of the world and converted them to Christ. Both came, therefore, to this monastery of Dijon and, besides other things, gave to our holy protector Benignus a certain estate belonging to them, called Vulpianum, through a certain foreknowledge of the future. In that place Lord William founded a church in honour of Saint Benignus, so that knowledge and honour of that saint might increase in that land, and so that he might build something acceptable to God upon the inheritance of his parents. Further, he did so that their offering might profit their souls, and that the fruit of the good works performed there might be for himself and for them the blotting out of sins and a worthy recompense of the rewards of eternal life. Hence that place was called Fruttuaria.

Within a short time, therefore, it became a notable monastery. From this place spiritual and temporal resources were brought there: many relics with bodies of saints, volumes of books, every ecclesiastical ornament, and many monks likewise went there. From other places subject to his authority, and from supplies offered from every quarter, the place was enriched in possessions and wealth, so that during William’s lifetime its community numbered one hundred monks, excluding the dependent sites of cells, which numbered nearly thirty. Having therefore summoned the bishops of the country, King Arduin also—who afterwards was buried there with his wife—and many nobles of that kingdom, he caused that place to be consecrated in honour of the holy Mother of God Mary, Saint Benignus, and all the saints.

### He founded several monasteries

He also established other monasteries in the same country, in which, monks having been assigned and abbots appointed, the monastic order still flourishes. He also founded a monastery of nuns.

### At Count Richard’s request, he undertakes the government of Fécamp; many flock to him for instruction in monastic discipline

The most noble Count Richard of the Normans, having heard of the fame of the man of God, sent to him, reverently begging him to come. At length William went willingly as he had been asked and came to him; Richard received him with the honour fitting for him. By Richard’s many entreaties William was persuaded to take charge of the church dedicated in name and honour to the holy and undivided Trinity, at the place called Fécamp, long ago built and suitably enlarged by Richard, and to adorn it with a community of monks. Yielding to his prayers, William furnished the aforesaid place with every religious observance and all other resources for good works, so that it might ever flourish in blessed growth beyond all places in that province.

Many noble men, clerics as well as laymen, gathered in this place, desiring to be trained by his teaching. Among them Bishop Osmund [Note: [Col. 0827] **Osmund.** Baluze conjectured that this passage concerns Osmund, bishop of Salisbury.] was a monk of holy and religious life. Two clerics, exceptionally educated in the liberal arts, setting aside the royal court, sought Father William with devout purpose. One was called Locelinus, the other Beringerius. The former later became an abbot; the latter ended his life in that same place. From regions beyond the sea, that is, the land of the English, there also came to the same monastery a noble man distinguished by royal descent, named Clement. Having abandoned the pomps of the world, he wished to serve as God’s soldier there. But as visitors coming from his native land frequently saw him, he preferred to serve God in quiet rather than often hear worldly vanities, and sought the monastery of Dijon, where he completed the course of a praiseworthy life. In accordance with the etymology of his name, he was gentle (*clemens*) in spirit, adorned with every virtue, particularly humility. He declared himself so lowly and worthless that, though holding priestly rank, he presumed to approach this ministry only once during his entire life.

### Saint William appoints a successor as abbot of Fécamp; the age of the author of this chronicle

After Abbot William had governed the monastery of Fécamp for nearly thirty years, when he was now burdened by old age and illness and had chosen Fruttuaria as his dwelling-place, wishing to rest in the soil of his homeland, Robert, ruler of the realm of the Normans after the death of his father and brother, considered that the condition of the place could not otherwise remain without loss. He therefore asked the same Father through envoys to appoint a successor as abbot. In response to this request, William appointed as abbot a monk greatly beloved by him, John, prior of that same place—though he would have preferred to set him over another place.

John was born in Italy, in the region of Ravenna, learned in letters, and instructed in medical art at the Father’s own command. More diligently than all others, he imitated William’s religious life, learning, and every virtue. Because of his small body he was called by the diminutive name Joannelinus; yet such grace of humility, wisdom, discernment, and other virtues shone in him that, as Saint Gregory relates in the *Dialogues* (book I, chapter 5) concerning the priest Constantius, it was a marvel to beholders that such great gifts of God’s grace should abound in so small a body. But because he still inhabits a house of clay, it is enough to have said only this; for Scripture says: “Do not praise a man during his life.”

### Saint William administers the monasteries of Jumièges, Saint-Ouen, and Mont-Saint-Michel, as well as Saint-Germain, Saint-Faron, and Gorze

[Col. 0828A] Count Richard also entrusted other places to the often-mentioned Abbot William: the monastery of Jumièges, as we have already said; Saint-Ouen; and the Mount of Saint Michael the Archangel. In the latter place, after the death of the aforesaid Father, the above-mentioned Abbot John appointed as father a monk of the aforementioned Father William. This brother was called Subpo, born in the land of the Romans and trained by the instruction of the aforesaid master in every holiness. Later, after certain conflicts arose, he left that place and governed the abbey of Fruttuaria for many years.

King Robert also asked the aforesaid Father to undertake the abbey of Saint-Germain at Paris and order it according to regular observance; and he did so. Count Odo likewise, with equal devotion, entrusted the place of Saint Faron in the city of Meaux to the same venerable Father. The honourable Theoderic, bishop of the church of Metz, also, prompted by the same zeal for God, committed the abbey of Gorze to him after the death of that place’s abbot. While he governed the aforesaid place, he drew from the clergy of Metz a certain cleric named Sigifridus, well taught in letters, into the monastic order; after William’s death Sigifridus governed the same community.

But Lord Arnulf, prior of this place, as we have already said, was urged by the prayers of Father William and the aforesaid bishop to accept the care [Col. 0828C] and office of abbot of the place just mentioned. A lover of humility, he did not consent in any way; he preferred to be subject rather than to rule. He asked only for the care and lordship of a certain small place from the aforesaid Father William. This place lies on the boundary of the dioceses of Toul and Langres, at the place called the estate of Brienne (*Brittiniaca curtis*). We shall now relate how it was granted to Saint Benignus, patron of this place.

Jacob, bishop of the city of Toul, was returning from Rome when, stirred by the fame of miracles which God’s mercy worked in this place through the merits of this saint, he came to the tomb of this martyr of Christ, wishing through the intercession of this glorious martyr to obtain from God forgiveness for his sins. After remaining for some days at his tomb and penetrating the inner mysteries of heaven, he was called by the Lord to the heavenly kingdom. Assisted by Saint Benignus’s prayers, he received glory with him in heaven and worthy burial on earth beside his tomb. His sister Liliosa came to the thresholds of Saint Benignus and gave her aforesaid estate to Saint Benignus the martyr for her brother’s burial. In that place the monks inhabiting it built a church in honour of Saint Benignus, where God glorified this holy martyr by many miracles.

But the neighbouring inhabitants impeded those serving him with many vexations. Yet, seeing the miracles performed there, they were broken from their obstinacy. For Saint Benignus bears with those who oppose him for a long time, but afterwards sternly punishes the impenitent. A noblewoman named Natalia gave to that place land from her own possession at the boundary of the estate of Brantica, and a meadow at the boundary of Businiaca. Both lie on the boundary of the aforementioned estate. The aforesaid woman made this donation in the time of King and Emperor Charles. The aforementioned Lord Arnulf, choosing this place for himself, laboured with every care to enlarge it. First he built there a large basilica, workshops, and the remaining dwellings useful for monks; he established a notable monastery and made provision to increase it with possessions and lands.

A knight named Evrard gave to Saint Benignus, at the same place, his estate called Mannisis, having received from Lord Arnulf a substantial price for it. The land of that allod extends as far as the gate of the fortress called Rifnellus. When the lord of that fortress, Count Odulricus, wished to claim that allod for himself, Bishop Bruno pursued him with excommunication and the force of hostility until he abandoned and formally surrendered (*wirpiret*) the allod; moreover, he swore that neither he nor any of his heirs would inflict violence there.

Beraldus, called archdeacon of Langres, gave to Saint Benignus a church dedicated in honour of Saint Desiderius in the estate of Algisy, together with the estate itself; also land in the estate of Brualdus and mills on the river Marne, at the place called Mortuellus. Gerard, count of Metz, gave half of the estate called Godonis curtis. A nobleman named Gotbert gave his allod at the place called Solinimons. When one of his relatives disputed this and, though often admonished by the aforesaid Prior Arnulf, would not comply, he was at last captured in battle by his enemies and pierced with many wounds. This knight, named Rudolph, from the fortress of Bar, recognizing that these and other evils had befallen him because of his injury to Saint Benignus, summoned the aforementioned administrator of the place and abandoned the entire claim he had been making. His son Rainardus, when he did likewise, received similar punishment.

The aforesaid provost bought in the estate of Lineroles a church and part of that estate; likewise in Montigny, [Col. 0829D] Calmillas, Latona, the field of Clini, Conches, Salcido, and Salsuris. In these and other places he bought many holdings of land, which are still possessed by the monks of that place. Nor should it be passed over in silence how much he accomplished in this monastery. He restored to Saint Benignus the estate called Wlnonis in the district of Troyes, repeatedly approaching Counts Stephen and Odo and paying much money. To prevent its being taken away thereafter, he established a cell of monks there, built their necessary workshops, and constructed a spacious and handsome basilica in honour of Saint Benignus.

In the district of Port, he caused the estate of Albiniacum, granted in *precaria* tenure and lost through lapse of time, to be taken from its usurpers and restored to Saint Benignus, repeatedly petitioning Bishop Bruno [Col. 0830A] and Count William. In that place he built a large monastery in honour of Saint Benignus and established a cell of monks. An ancient church dedicated in honour of Saint Marcellus the martyr already stood there and remains to this day. Two other churches were later added there, at Cimbinno and the hamlet of Duellari, together with a very extensive landed estate.

It would be tedious to report every item, since almost everything acquired by this place in Father William’s time was achieved through the counsel and labour of Lord Prior Arnulf. Beyond the other things he accomplished, he himself adorned this church of Saint Benignus with the ornament of books, supplying the expense, while Lord Girbertus did the writing. Girbertus was among the first whom Lord Abbot William trained [Col. 0830B] and was called “the scribe” from his office.

### Girbertus the scribe

Count Odo, surnamed William, whom we mentioned earlier, at the request of Lord Abbot William, to whom he was related, gave Saint Benignus at the borough of Salins the site of one salt-boiling pan. Subsequently, Lord Arnulf and the monks of Dijon bought another boiling pan from the wife of the same count, with the approval of her son Rainaldus.

William and his above-mentioned son Rainaldus also gave Saint Benignus adjacent lands in these places: in the estate of Cerny and in Dornon, namely arable lands and meadows from which fifty cartloads of hay can be cut. At Dordone there is one meadow from which one hundred scythefuls may be cut; and it owes as rent eight shillings, three wethers, and one hundred shingles. In another place called Callis there is another meadow with woodland intermixed.

The same Count Odo gave Saint Benignus authority over the estate of Vivarais for the soul of Duke Henry, who had adopted him as a son; for the soul of his mother Gerberga, wife of the aforesaid duke; of his own son Guy; and of Hermitrudis, his wife. For the salvation of his own soul he gave the aforesaid authority with its appurtenances, just as he had lawfully held it complete for thirty years by the grant of the aforesaid Duke Henry and his wife, his own mother Gerberga: together with the churches situated there, one in honour of Saint Mary and another beside it dedicated in the name of Saint Peter the Apostle; and with many estates and lands, namely at Chrocherco, Grugiaco, Frigida villa, Colombario, Lusiniaco, Romanisca curtis, Destagno, Cadiniaco, Milleponto, Turiaco, Albania, Cariaco, the estate of the Count, and whatsoever other places; with many male and female serfs, and all revenues and customary dues owed by those serfs, male and female, and also by those who call themselves Franks, residing wherever they may be within that authority. This donation was made in the year 1004 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the second indiction.

### Various churches are bestowed upon Saint Benignus

At the same time Odo, viscount and son of Duke Henry, gave Saint Benignus a certain church situated by the walls of the fortress called Beaune, formerly consecrated in honour of Saint Stephen but already ruined for many courses of years. He and his wife, named Hingala, rebuilt it from its foundations on a larger scale and gave it in perpetuity to the oversight of Abbot William and the abbots of Dijon. So that the monks living there should not lack provisions, he gave to that place, in the county of Duesmois, the estate called Dry Époisses (*Empiliacus siccus*), with all appurtenances, customary dues, and legal claims, including dues lawfully to be exacted from those assessed under the name of Franks. In the estate of Millepont he gave arable lands and vineyards; at Polmarco and Vallilias, a dwelling-holding, vineyards, and meadows.

So that this gift might remain perpetual, he requested that it be confirmed by a royal charter of Robert, king of the Franks, through the intervention of Lord Walter, bishop in whose diocese the aforementioned place lay, and Count Odo, to whose benefice it belonged, to be possessed in perpetual right in Saint Benignus’s name. This charter was made in the year 1005 of the Incarnate Word.

Another knight of the aforesaid Count Odo, named Letbaldus, gave Saint Benignus a certain church dedicated in honour of Saint Peter at the place called Puteolis, which he held from the count by benefice tenure. He enriched it with his own property and, so that this gift might be secured, requested of the aforesaid King Robert, the aforementioned envoys intervening, that it be confirmed by royal munificence, so that the monks serving God there might strive to pray to the Lord for the king himself, his offspring, the donors of this gift and their descendants, and all the Christian people. Done in the year 1006.

Humbert, lord of the fortress called Salmacia [Note: [Col. 0831] **Salmacia.** This fortress is elsewhere called Sarmacia.], gave Saint Benignus for perpetual possession the church of Saint Mary situated in that fortress, under the supervision of Abbot William and his successors, so that monks might be sent there to serve God and his Mother and to pray for him and for all the living and the dead. For their sustenance he gave two other churches: one at the estate called Buxo, with holdings and other lands, a granary, male and female serfs; the other at the estate of Mermedis.
