This donation was made in the twenty-sixth year of King Robert, in the year 1013 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

In the year 1012 from the Incarnation of the Lord, William, abbot of Dijon, and Amadeus, abbot of Flavigny, made between themselves an exchange of lands. The aforesaid Abbot Amadeus gave, from the abbey of Saint Peter, everything known to belong to it in the estate of Dienay, the estate of the Count, another estate called Salice, the estate of Carli, the estate of Icio, Marciaco, the estate of Tarsu, and the estate of Meleis, with the entire population of both sexes and every appurtenance. In return, Lord Abbot William gave everything he possessed from the abbey of Saint Benignus and the place [Col. 0832A] of Saint Stephen in the estate called Dry Époisses—formerly transferred to the aforesaid place of Saint Benignus by Odo, viscount of Beaune, with the consent of his wife Inge and of his sons, Abbot Aquio and John—which was adjacent to the abbey of Saint Peter of Flavigny. The exchange was made with male and female serfs, all appurtenances, and revenues, by the approval and consent of Lord Bruno of Langres and Lord Walter, bishop of the Aedui, to whose dioceses the aforesaid churches belonged.

Afterwards a certain Hugh, knight of Parvi and inhabitant of the fortress of Dijon, gave to Saint Benignus a portion of his inheritance which he held in the aforesaid village of Dienat, with the consent and approval of his wife Hildegard and his son Humbert, [Col. 0832B] before Bishop Lord Bruno, with many clerics and noble laymen standing by. Later, in the presence of his successor, Bishop Lord Lambert, when he laid aside the hair of his head, he repeated the gift at the altar of Saint Benignus before a multitude of people, giving his estate in the aforesaid village of Dienat, or wherever it was situated, with male and female slaves and with all customary dues to be collected. Done in the year 1017.

From this land there are, in the village of Karli, ten mansi with other lands belonging to those mansi, and many male and female slaves living thereon. In Dienat there are fifteen tenant-farms, twenty small enclosures, and land beyond valuation; more than [Col. 0832C] seventy male and female slaves. There is a wood called Mount Rigon at Largo Fonte; fifteen mansi there, with male and female slaves and much land. In Scalurco, one mansus with its appurtenances. In Hodesca, six tenant-farms with slaves and their appurtenances. In Carco there was an estate called Britonia; there are two small forests there, one called Basescoth, the other Petra. In Fontanis there are two mansi with lands and vineyards. In Marcenniac there are three *journales* of vineyard-land.

Lord Abbot William gave the church of Saint Anthony, situated at Ficiac, to the monks of the cell of Bèze, in exchange for the above-mentioned Empiliac-le-Sec and Dienat. He gave to the monks of the cell of Sarmoise, for cultivation and safeguarding, the land of Saint Benignus, [Col. 0832D] situated in the village of Sarmoise and at Viriac.

At the same time Countess Addita, wife of Richard, count of Dijon, restored to Saint Benignus whatever the said Count Richard, her husband, had held as a benefice from Abbot Manasses out of the lands of Saint Benignus, for the salvation of the soul of that same husband and of her son Count Letald—whose bodies she had buried in this monastery of Dijon—in the presence of envoys sent for this purpose by Lord Bishop Bruno. She delivered upon the altar of Saint Benignus that wine-rent, so that neither she thereafter nor any of her knights should retain anything from that benefice, except during her lifetime. After the death of each holder, what he held was to return to the right of Saint [Col. 0833A] Benignus. This restoration was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1007.

At that time a young man named Achedeus, canon of the church of Langres, in the presence of Lord Bishop Bruno and Count Otto, gave the church of Saint Albin to the altar of Saint Benignus, patron of Dijon. He transferred the aforesaid church with its appurtenances to the said place, for himself and for his father Letbald, who, as we have said, became a monk in this place, on this condition: that every year for as long as he lived he should pay as rent for the aforesaid church ten solidi and two sextaries of oil. Afterwards a certain knight Henry, husband of his mother, although the rent was being paid, came into the presence of Lord Abbot William and sought to have [Col. 0833B] the aforesaid rent commuted. He obtained this, and the rent was reduced to four denarii; and, in compensation for this and for the salvation of his soul, he gave the estate of Molens with all things belonging to that inheritance. This estate lay in the county of Oscheret, upon the rivers Saône, Ouche, and Tille; and it had extensive boundaries, as is written in the charter. This gift was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1003.

There then arose a dispute between the monks of this place and the monks of the monastery of Saint Leodegar concerning a certain woodland called Alta Silva, belonging to the village of Sasiac, whose boundaries are marked by two streams approaching from opposite sides. One is called Tramant, the other Scitilaria. When the prior of that place, [Col. 0833C] named Fulcher, brought the matter before Duke Henry, advocate of the aforesaid place, and Count Otto—also called William—who was then advocate of this place, and in the presence of Lord Bishop Bruno, it was finally decided that both sides should accept a postponement concerning the wood. Count Richard, with many citizens of Dijon, namely Walter, Remigius, Humbert, and other nobles, is known to have been present to determine the matter according to justice. They therefore decreed that a judicial combat should be held, fixing the day on which it was to take place. Why say more? The prior of this place, Dominic, was present with his men and prepared. But he who made the claim withdrew and refused to come to the appointed hearing. Thereafter, for many years and without anyone’s complaint, the house of Saint Benignus retained its possession. [Col. 0833D]

Later Arnulf, successor of the aforesaid Fulcher, again began to press a claim concerning the same wood before the aforesaid Count William against the said Prior Dominic of this place. When they came jointly to the hearing, they decreed that a new judicial combat should be arranged. Many noble men were present, as were the said prior of the monks of this place, Arnulf, his successor, Waldo the sacristan, and Henry; and the hearing was appointed there. On the Tuesday of the following week the aforesaid claimant again approached Lord Bishop Bruno and began to offer reasons why he could not come to the hearing for the judicial combat, asking that it be deferred to another time. When [Col. 0834A] Lord Bishop Bruno heard this, he summoned the monks of Saint Benignus and said: “What you began to adjudicate, and the wood which you have held, continue to hold, for these claimants can show no right.”

A certain knight Higelbert, from the village called Millepont, coming to death and made a monk in this monastery, gave Saint Benignus, in the county of Autun, the estate called Bruerias with all its appurtenances lying round about: namely, in the village of Adeunt, a demesne mansus with its appurtenances, a slave and his sons; and in the villages of Mardelco, Barbarisco, Poliac, and Vinsiac. This gift was made in the year of the Incarnation 1007. He also gave, in the village of Valongias, one mansus with its appurtenances, before Bishop Bruno, [Col. 0834B] Count William, Count Rainald his son, Count Otto, son of his son Guy.

A certain knight Garnerius gave Saint Benignus, in the village of Discac, one mansus and a slave with one son; and at Viriac, one mansus with its appurtenances, male and female slaves, and two vineyards. This same Garnerius and his brother Aldo gave their allod lying in the place called Mortariis, in the county of Dijon. The allod consisted of cultivated and uncultivated lands, separately divided in its own right. In the woods, however, it was partly held separately and nearby, and partly shared with other heirs.

The private allod is bounded on one side by the land of Saint Mammes, from the place called Niger Solium, in the upper part as far as the village of Vadarn; and in the lower [Col. 0834C] part from the said Niger Solium as far as William’s *exactum* [a due or levy], and as far as the wood belonging to Savignac. Likewise, on one side is the land of Odo belonging to Spaignac. Likewise, on another side, from the place called Nerlange as far as the field called Peduliosus, and as far as the lake, and as far as the land of Saint Peter of Villacomitis, shared with other heirs. Likewise, on the other side is land belonging to Vadarnod. The common allod begins at the oak called Perduliosus [reading uncertain] and extends as far as Spaignac, Cangegium, Casnedum, and the count’s estate.

Therefore, in order that they might transfer both the private and common holdings together to the aforesaid house of Saint Benignus, they received from Lord Abbot William and the monks of that place eight pounds of denarii. Thus, with the consent of the wife and [Col. 0834D] children of Varnerius [Garnerius], they transferred and granted the aforesaid private and common allod to the named monastery, in the presence of Lord Bishop Bruno and other illustrious men, with Count Walo and his brother Walter consenting and bearing witness.

Another Warnerius, likewise a nobleman, gave Saint Benignus, in the county of Dijon and the village of Spaignac, thirteen occupied mansi, one unoccupied mansus, eight tenant-farms, sixty-three male and female slaves, and all the rents, customary dues, and exactions owed by that property; likewise all land belonging to the aforesaid inheritance, except the wood. This was on the condition that the slaves should continue, for as long as he held them, to observe in full the same customary practice [Col. 0835A] which they had observed in regard to the aforesaid wood. Warnerius made this gift with the approval and consent of his wife Alda, before Count Richard and his brothers Hugh and Odo, and other noble men of the fortress of Dijon: Walter, Hugh, Remigius, and Humbert. On the anniversary of his mother, a meal for the brethren was to be prepared from that property; the remainder was to be assigned to their wardrobe for the clothing of the same brethren.

### On the character of Bruno, bishop of Langres. His death.

Because it would take long to recount everything bestowed upon this monastery during the time of Lord Bishop Bruno, and the goods by which it was enriched through him or on his account by others, let us come to the end of his life—an end forever to be mourned and lamented by the inhabitants [Col. 0835B] of this house of God. But first we shall take care to describe briefly what manner of life he lived.

He was generous in almsgiving, diligent in vigils, devout in prayer, perfect in charity, lavish in kindness, ready in speech, and most holy in conduct. To the irreverent he was terrible in appearance, formidable in severity, reverend in bearing, and venerable in benevolence. He tempered the strictness of authority with the gentleness of humility. In each person he regarded not the power of rank but excellence of character; and he honoured each man more highly in proportion as he had learned to live more holy a life.

He was a father to clerics and monks, to nuns also, and to widows and orphans; and he stood so midway between rich and [Col. 0835C] poor that the poor looked upon him as a father, while the rich feared him as a richer superior. As long as he lived, he protected and defended Burgundy through his patronage—not with shield and spear, but with the wisdom of counsel, by which he had bound to himself all the princes of the country. Thus, when Robert, king of the Franks, repeatedly entered this land with a very great army and laid waste many places by fires and pillaging, he could retain nothing in it while Bishop Bruno lived. Since he could not injure Bruno, because of this hostility he took from Lord Abbot William the abbey of Saint John at the monastery of Reôme, because William, as was right, favoured the cause of his bishop.

Finally, at one time the said king came with a large army to the fortress of Dijon, devastating and depopulating the surrounding region. [Col. 0835D] Fearing his wrath, the aforesaid Abbot William ordered all the monks to withdraw from this place to other monasteries. He caused some of them, with the books and all the ornaments of the church, to remain within the fortress of Dijon, in the church of Saint Vincent, which at that time the monks of this place possessed by undisputed right. Only a few brethren were left in this place with Lord Abbot Odilo, for the protection of the place and the service of Saint Benignus. William had summoned him for this purpose: that, if perhaps the king should devise any evil against this place, he might, moved by Odilo’s prayers, refrain.

But the king, being kindly disposed, was greatly grieved when he learned that the monks had been dispersed because of him. A few days later he returned to Francia, having accomplished nothing. [Col. 0836A] In that same year, namely 1016 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Lord Bishop Bruno died on the second day before the Kalends of February [31 January], having completed thirty-five years in the episcopate. He was the thirty-first in succession among the bishops from Saint Gregory, bishop and founder of this place, and the eleventh after the venerable Bishop Isaac.

### Lambert succeeds.

Bishop Lambert succeeded him. In his days a certain archdeacon of the church of Langres, afterwards bishop of Paris, named Imbert, offered Saint Benignus the abbey of Saint Amator, situated before the walls of that city, which he held by benefice from the bishop of that see. This was done by gift and approval of the aforesaid Bishop Lambert, so that monks might be established there to serve God with hymns and praises day and night. [Col. 0836B]

Likewise, a certain canon of the same church, called Gozelin, gave in the suburb of that city one half of a church; but the entire altar, whole and undivided, which he held by gift of the bishop, was transferred by that bishop to Saint Benignus for the sustenance of the monks dwelling in the aforesaid place.

With the same devotion Count Aymo gave the abbey consecrated in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God, situated before his fortress called Saxonis Fons. With the approval of the aforesaid Bishop Lambert, he offered it to Saint Benignus and Abbot William to possess forever, so that the monastic order once established there might be restored through William’s care.

Moreover Richard, count of the Normans, gave Saint [Col. 0836C] Benignus the church of Saint Adelbert, with the estate and all lands belonging to it, situated in the district of Oximin. His son Richard, Richard’s son Robert, and Robert’s son William afterwards, in successive times, approved and confirmed the gift. They were, and still are, advocates and defenders of these possessions for the protection of this house of God.

A certain knight of the same count, named Gotbert, gave, in the place called Longus Campus, a church dedicated in honour of Saint Martin, with the land belonging to it. In order that this gift might remain firm and not be challenged by any of his relatives, the aforesaid Abbot William gave him sixty pounds of denarii. Richard, duke of the Normans, and Robert, his brother and archbishop, [Col. 0836D] approved the gift and subscribed the charter, in the year 1003.

A certain cleric Henry, one of the nobles, gave Saint Benignus his estate of Prisceia, with the church situated there, in the presence of Bishop Lambert and his archdeacons Berald, Humbert, Gerald, and Odo, with very many other clerics and laymen standing by, and Abbot William with his monks. Done in the year of Christ’s Incarnation 1020.

A certain noblewoman, called Aremburgis, mother of Letbald, bishop of Mâcon, together with that son gave Saint Benignus, in the village of Luvocata, seven [Col. 0837A] mansi with the adjoining wood and the slaves who held tenant-farms from those seven mansi.

Another noblewoman, named Tetiardis, gave her dower-property to Saint Benignus with the approval of her son Guy. It lies in these villages: Quintignac, Albignac, Sulliac, Attegias, and the court of Arno, with a third part of the church situated there, dedicated in honour of Saint Germanus. There are twenty-one mansi, with the lands belonging to them.

A certain knight called Robert, coming to conversion, gave Saint Benignus all his inheritance lying in the counties of Bèze and Chalon, and in the following villages: Seviciac, Ruelod, Mossiac, Ambassac, Monticellis in the estate of Gislus, and Scodingiis in the estate of Sesilliis, with the male and female slaves [Col. 0837B] dwelling in the aforesaid places and all the land in the named places belonging to his share. He gave it before his lords, Count William and his son Rainald. Done in the year 1007.

Another knight, called Alberic, gave at Curte Curonis one mansus with the lands belonging to it, and in the village of Assiriac a third part of his inheritance. Done in the aforesaid year.

Likewise another knight, named William, with his wife Theudgarda and his son Romestannius, placed a portion of his inheritance in the village of Attegias in pledge for twenty-four years, under this agreement: after the said years had elapsed, if it had not been redeemed by him or by his sons or daughters, it could never thereafter be redeemed; rather, the monks of Saint Benignus, whose [Col. 0837C] money had been advanced there, were to possess it in perpetual right. Similarly, another knight, called Calado, with his wife Theodrada, granted his inheritance in Attegia and Pontificiac to the aforesaid monks of this place under the same agreement.

### Saint William, before departing this life, visits the monasteries and exhorts the brethren. He dies and is buried at Fécamp. On the death of Lambert, bishop of Langres, Richard is appointed in his place; shortly afterwards he is killed by poison. Hugh succeeds him immediately and is condemned for corrupt morals.

There are still very many matters which could be described; but since we are approaching the end of the book, omitting these we take care to report the death of Father William. After he had for forty-two years, as a diligent cultivator of the Lord’s vineyard, continually laboured to extend and [Col. 0837D] enlarge it, he was now weighed down by old age and many infirmities. Desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ, and wishing to bring the good completion of his labours to fulfilment, he went around all the monasteries under his direction, beginning from Italy, exhorting the brethren to retain in their minds what they had learned from him and strive to fulfil it in deed.

For his teaching was that, as the Rule of Saint Benedict commands (chapter 7, degree 12, and chapter 72), they should always display humility to those who saw them—in speech, in every action, and in the character of their dress—and that, outdoing one another in honour, they should show love without pretence. He instructed them, while devoted to these and other works of virtue, also in the art of distinct reading [Col. 0838A] and chanting.

Having travelled through the other monasteries while teaching these things, he came to the monastery called Fécamp. There, more burdened than usual by illness and sensing that the final day of his calling was near, he summoned the brethren. For eight days he exhorted them, entrusted them to God through absolution and prayer, and on the eighth day—Christmas Day—after receiving the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, rendered his spirit to God. His body, embalmed with spices by the physicians present, was honourably committed to burial in that monastery, before the altar of Saint Taurinus the confessor.

After his death, Lord Halinard took up the care of governing souls. The aforesaid Father had chosen him as his successor with the counsel and approval of the brethren, and had transmitted to him the pastoral staff. [Col. 0838B] Our aforesaid Father William died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1031. In that same year Lord Lambert, bishop of Langres, died on the tenth day before the Kalends of September [23 August].

Before Father William died, King Robert had appointed in Lambert’s place a bishop called Richard, a cleric excellently educated in letters and adorned with good morals, but contrary to the will of the entire clergy and people. Therefore, after he had held the episcopate for five months, he was seized and expelled from the city; not many days later, he ended his life by poison.

The king, stirred to anger by the counsels of the queen, again gave the bishopric to a certain cleric of the church of Chartres. This man was called Hugh, and he would have been a useful vessel [Col. 0838C] in the house of God had he taken care to avoid youthful desires and trample pride. But, adding cruelty and proceeding by right and wrong alike, after he had afflicted the clergy and people of Langres for eighteen years, he was finally driven from his see by the judgment of Pope Leo IX and the archbishops: Halinard of Lyons, Hugh of Besançon, Guy of Reims, Eberhard of Trier, and many others present at the council held in the city of Reims in the presence of the said Pope Leo. There were present nearly all the archbishops and bishops of Gaul, with an innumerable multitude of clergy and people.

### Death of King Robert. His notable gift to Saint Benignus.

While Hugh’s installation was imminent, as he had been conducted by the young King Henry to the city of Langres with great [Col. 0838D] pomp, news was brought to that king of the death of his father, King Robert. Robert had reigned for forty-one years, while Henry himself was already in the sixth year of his reign.

King Robert, through the intervention of Lord Bishop Lambert and Hugh, bishop of Auxerre and administrator of this place, remitted the *salvamentum*—the protection-due—of the villages belonging by right to Saint Benignus. These are their names: Lariac, Bicisus, Quintiniar, Cromanius, Sulliac, Aguliac, Ruffiac, Aschiriac, Bargas, Provisum, Colonias, Plomberias, Escuncias, Gironus, Corcellas, Tremolendum, Villarium, Pruneius, Lenteniac, Dissum, Congus Vicus, Saciac, and all the hamlets belonging to it: Siliac, Asverias, Upper Corcellas, Norgias, Aziriac, Dinat, Mercenniac, Pamerras, Fedeniac, Spaignac, Villakarli, the Count’s Estate, and Ontearum. [Col. 0839A]

> [Note: Col. 0839D: “Ontearum.” Elsewhere, *Curte-Amon*.]

In these and other villages, wherever the land of Saint Benignus paid the protection-due, King Robert ordered it abolished, so that it should no longer be exacted by anyone. He restored it to God and Saint Benignus for the benefit of the monks, placing the gift upon the saint’s altar, with the approval of his wife Queen Constance and of his sons Henry, then duke, and Robert his brother, who succeeded him. He confirmed this gift by royal decree, ordered it to be marked with his ring, and ordered the bishops, counts, and other leading men present to ratify it.

Those present were Lambert, bishop of Langres; Hugh, bishop of Auxerre; Azelinus, bishop of Laon; [Col. 0839B] Geoffrey, bishop of Chalon; and Berald, bishop of Soissons. The counts were William of Nevers and Otto of Mâcon.

> [Note: Col. 0840D: “Azelinus.” Acherius proposes that it should be read *Adelbero*.]

Done in the year 1015, the twenty-eighth year of the king himself. He did likewise concerning places belonging to this house, namely the cell of Bèze and Puteolis, as we have said above. For these things it is fitting that his anniversary be observed by us.

### On the golden chalice of eight pounds.

At that time Count Otto, also called William, died, namely in the year 1027, and was buried in this monastery of Saint Benignus; there too his son Count Guy had lain buried some years previously. For the many benefactions which he bestowed upon this place, some of which we have described, he deserved [Col. 0839C] that his memory should always be observed by the monks of this place.

The above-mentioned Hugh, bishop of Auxerre and count of Chalon, protector and advocate of this place, gave Saint Benignus a golden cup weighing five pounds, that a golden chalice might be made from it for the expiation of his sins. To this alms Richard, duke of the Normans, added a sixth pound of gold, so that for this and many other benefits granted to us he might receive from God the reward of eternal inheritance. Empress Cunigund, wife of Emperor Henry, also gave two pounds of gold for the repose of the soul of the aforesaid ruler; in addition, she supplied all the gems for the same chalice with its paten and took care that a most elegant vessel should be made, so that she might thereby be remembered for ever.

For these and our other benefactors [Col. 0839D] we must persist in prayer with the most urgent supplication, lest, enjoying at no cost the good obtained by others and adding their sins to our own, we pile a heavy burden upon our heads.

### The deeds of Halinard, bishop of Lyons, are described. He becomes a canon.

At the time when these things occurred, Lord Halinard held the office of prior in this place. In the following period he also attained the title and merit of abbot and shepherd. It is fitting that we commit to writing the memory of one who instructed us with affectionate and fatherly ordinances.

He was a native of Burgundy, sprung from a family of noble men. His father was a citizen of Langres, [Col. 0840A] his mother a citizen of Autun. From the earliest beginnings of childhood he was committed to literary studies, and by heavenly providence shone very effectively in a twofold knowledge. He was loved with fatherly affection by the venerable bishop of the city of Autun, named Walter, whose godson he was; and for that reason Walter brought him up with greater diligence, so that he might later be made a lamp in the house of God.

As time passed and childhood was over, when adolescence had already claimed him, his father entrusted him to Lord Bruno, bishop of Langres. Seeing that he possessed a talent for the liberal arts, Bruno took care to join him to the college of canons. In that city, while he listened to philosophers and ecclesiastical men, by the inspiration of divine grace he was inferior to none of his companions in wisdom. The abundance of his eloquence was ordered by the gravity of wisdom. From the material of this union he began to be a vessel of [Col. 0840B] election.

Since his mind was capable of everything, he left nothing unattempted and, indeed, nothing unmastered. When he had begun to be clothed with the flourishing blossoms of youth, he so equipped his adolescence with good morals that even then he seemed already a monk. He preserved himself whole and uncorrupted, with every vigilance, from those vices by which people of that age are accustomed to be defiled. For he feared to be imbued with them, lest, infected by them in tender age, he should later be unable to be free of them. This accords with what is written: “Train up a young man according to his way; even when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Proverbs 22:6). Enjoying the companionship of good men, and especially prudent ones, he hated the followers [Col. 0840C] of shamefulness.

### He then becomes a monk; for this reason he suffers many indignities from his relatives.

Accordingly, although he was loved by Lord Lambert, bishop of Langres, because of his benevolence, which made him dear to all, and although that bishop wished to raise him through the conferral of ecclesiastical grades, Halinard rejected the unstable and passing glory of the world. He took care to fulfil in deed what the Lord commands in word: “Whoever wishes to come after me,” he says, “let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Mark 16:24; Luke 9:23).

Therefore, despising all the revenues of earthly possessions because of hope in the promise to come, he assumed the habit of holy religious life. But here too the trial of tribulation did not fail. His relatives pursued him and, with the bishop’s consent, forcibly removed him from this monastery. [Col. 0840D] Stripped of the monk’s habit, they led him publicly about in such a manner that, through shame, he might hate that which he had embraced so ardently.

But the cunning art of the evil one avails nothing against the teaching of the Holy Spirit. They were wholly unable to recall him from his purpose. Rather, after a short time had passed, he fled, so that outside his native land he might accomplish what he was not permitted to fulfil on his native soil. But he was pursued again, captured, and brought back to the bishop, who caressed him with many promises and blandishments, seeking somehow to recall his mind from this purpose. When he saw [Col. 0841A] that Halinard persisted in his resolve, he at last, and only with difficulty, allowed him to do what he wished.

Thus, having attained what he had desired, he thereafter lived under another’s authority, so that, as far as he could, he might not deviate in any respect from the purpose of holy observance. For, having put far from himself dullness and murmuring, he pre-eminent above the rest in the singular virtue of obedience, fulfilling among the brethren what Saint Benedict says (Rule, ch. 71): “The good of obedience is to be shown not only to the abbot, but the brethren also should obey one another.”

Indeed, as an imitator of blessed Benedict, to whose discipleship he was subject, he embraced God’s wise folly, as the Apostle commands: “If anyone among you wishes to be wise in this world, let him become foolish, that he may become wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18). For just as philosophers [Col. 0841B] devote all the effort of their minds to the arguments of syllogisms, so he devoted himself to learning those things which must be performed in the monastery through daily practice. When he had diligently made himself acquainted with all these matters and entrusted them to memory through experience, he began already to seem more learned than all.

### He becomes prior and abbot of Saint Benignus.

When Father William recognized that he was so wise in the monastic order, he set him over the community of brethren and entrusted him with the care of souls. He fulfilled this ministry with such authority and such solicitude that he was both an example and a terror to all who lived with him. Content with the regular observance, he cultivated frugality in such a way that he appeared in no respect to differ from the fellowship [Col. 0841C] of the common table.

When he saw faults in some that required rebuke, he first proclaimed what was praiseworthy in each person, and then, as one who understood, corrected what required rebuke. Yet he frequently warned all to present themselves to God inwardly such as public opinion, on account of their religious habit, considered them outwardly to be.

### He excels in learning and eloquence. The spirit in which he read philosophers.

Having been tested in every office of the monastery and having diligently fulfilled the services of every ministry, he first exercised for four years the office of provost under the authority of the abbot himself. Finally, after the death of the aforesaid Father, he was compelled by the entire community of brethren to take up pastoral care, since the teaching of justice required it.

Although he accepted the office reluctantly and against his will, when he was devoted to the cultivation of the divine vineyard as its appointed [Col. 0841D] worker, he sought the common benefit of the many rather than his own private advantage. Kind to all and fair to everyone, he harmed no one and strove to benefit all whom he could. Sound teaching was indeed within him, because he diligently did what suited his calling, following the Apostle’s words: “Giving no offence to anyone, so that our ministry may not be blamed; but in all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God” (2 Corinthians 6:3–4).

Endowed also with holy and modest speech, he utterly barred his ears against obscene and shameful words, following what is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclesiasticus 28:28). He was so devoted to reading that, when travelling, he often carried a small book in his hands; thus while riding, his mind was refreshed by reading.

When he read philosophers and books of secular wisdom, he pursued with discerning industry what the divine voice commands through the lawgiver concerning the captive [Col. 0842A] woman. Whatever useful things he found in the books of philosophers he deemed worthy to retain in memory; but whatever was superfluous—namely, matters concerning love and the care of worldly things—he shaved away as poisonous and deadly. In this he made her bald; these things he cut off with a very sharp blade, as though they were her nails. Thus, through constant reading, he was formed by the authority of the Scriptures. He was so strong in canonical and monastic institutions that no one seemed his equal in the decrees of law and philosophical arguments.

Then, endowed with virtue and wisdom and enriched with a most honourable abundance of speech, he adapted himself [Col. 0842B] to each person in such a way that he was loved by all, fulfilling the Apostle’s saying: “I have become all things to all, that I might save all” (1 Corinthians 9:22). Whatever he said was ordered by the gravity of wisdom. His speech was seasoned with salt; being brief and infrequent through the weight of virtue, it was judged precious for its prudent sweetness. Therefore, whenever he delivered a discourse for moral edification, he was considered as welcome as he was eloquent.

Governing the flock entrusted to him with provident kindness, he warned them to fight in united and holy contest against the worst enemy of all saints; and that each should not cease to do whatever good he was able, lest he wish to do so when he was no longer permitted. He often also brought before them the admonition of blessed John, who says in his Epistle: “Pursue peace with [Col. 0842C] all people, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Hebrews 12:14).

### Offered the archbishopric of Lyons, he persuades the emperor to choose Odelric.

He was greatly loved by the kings of the Franks, Robert and Henry. Emperor Conrad and his son Henry Caesar also revered him with extraordinary affection. Therefore, when the see of Lyons was vacant, Emperor Henry himself offered him the honour of that bishopric, because he had long known him and loved him greatly for his religious life and reputation for holiness.

But Halinard, through the safeguard of humility, declined the heavy burden of that storm-tossed eminence, maintaining that a monk was in no way suited to so great a charge. There was then in the clergy of Langres a cleric [Col. 0842D] named Odelric, advanced alike in age and holy conduct and exceptionally learned in letters. He was then present at the king’s court, though not fully known to the ruler.

Our Father Lord Halinard urged that Odelric should be sought out, since both his abundance of wisdom and the dignity of old age commended him. When these words were reported to the king, he marvelled both that Halinard thought so lightly of the offered honour of the priesthood and that he sought so earnestly for another what he refused for himself. He agreed and granted the dignity of the episcopate to Lord Odelric. Father Halinard himself escorted him to the see and provided everything appropriate to his service, as though he were one of Odelric’s household.

Odelric governed the church of Lyons for five years, [Col. 0843A], instructing the minds of his subjects by word and the example of good works. Afterwards, having suffered plots from certain malicious and envious persons, those who could not kill him by the sword did not shrink from killing him by poison. Thus slain, he was joined to the other holy bishops resting there.

### Halynard, unwillingly made Archbishop of Lyons after Odelric’s death. His humility and prudence.

At last the voice of all the clergy, with the agreement of the people, urged him to bow his neck to assume this high office, and begged him to undertake among them the care of a shepherd. They sent an embassy to the emperor, requesting that Lord Bishop Halynard be given to them. An imperial command was issued, ordering that Lord Halynard be enthroned. But his spirit, strengthened by divine power, was not at all bent to this until he was summoned by letters of the apostolic pope. John, surnamed Gratian, then occupied the Apostolic See. When he learned that Halynard would not yield to the wishes of those who entreated him, he sent him an order, by pontifical authority, to obey the prayers of clergy and people.

Thus made a participant in, and equal to, the Apostle’s honour, he led an apostolic life in deed as well as name. The same virtue of humility remained in him, while charity’s works multiplied. Whatever he did he seasoned with the savour of virtue. As one is accustomed to do by looking into a mirror, so inwardly he examined himself through divine reading, and from this his mind’s adornment was ordered; but whatever deformity was detected was corrected by the moderation of justice. Whenever he was joined by learned men and something from the Scriptures was proposed, as commonly happens, he listened gladly and answered wisely and modestly. If anything unsound was proposed, he refuted it not sharply but with natural reserve—not by overcoming one who disputed against him through crafty argument, but by kindly teaching through the examples of venerable doctors. Then he would bring forward the sayings of the orthodox together with evangelical authorities; and in this way he showed himself most learned, while seeming to flee both pride and the display of learning. He altogether avoided swearing, lest perhaps he should commit perjury. Therefore it must not be passed over in silence what he did in the emperor’s palace.

### Why the emperor possessed the kingdom of Burgundy. Halynard refuses to swear an oath to the emperor. Bishops who flatter.

The Emperor Henry III governed the kingdom of Burgundy. For King Rudolf of Burgundy, having no children, made Emperor Henry II heir to his kingdom; after him the empire passed to Conrad. He had as wife the sister of the aforesaid king, named Gisela, by whom he begot Henry III. To him the kingdom of Burgundy came by right through paternal succession. Within the bounds of that kingdom lies the city of Lyons, which Lothair, king of the Franks, gave as a dowry to his sister Queen Matilda, whom he betrothed to Conrad, king of Burgundy, father of the above-mentioned King Rudolf.

Therefore Lord Halynard, elected because of the gift of the bishopric, went to the court of Emperor Henry, together with the suffragan bishops, the delegates of the archdeacons, and the clergy of Lyons seeking their own shepherd. The emperor, as was customary, demanded from him the oath of fidelity owed to himself because of the episcopal honour granted. Lord Hugh, Archbishop of Chrysopolis, was intermediary and mediator for these words. On hearing them, Halynard replied:

> “If I set aside the commands of the eternal King and of the Rule which I promised by oath, what trustworthiness will there be in me to keep an oath to the emperor? For the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Do not swear at all’; and the Rule of Father Benedict commands a monk not to swear and to make himself a stranger to secular affairs.”

When these words were reported to the king, he marvelled at and inwardly embraced the firmness of his spirit. Yet, wishing to test his constancy, he said that he would by no means give him the bishopric if he did not obey his commands. But Halynard said: “It is better for me never to receive the priesthood than to transgress God’s command.”

At this the bishops of those regions—and especially Sigebaud, bishop of Speyer, where these events occurred—pressed the matter, saying: “Who is this man who has presumed, in the prince’s palace, not to obey his commands, something none of us has ever dared to do? Let him either swear fidelity to the king or be cast out.”

But Theoderic, bishop of Metz, Bruno, bishop of the Leuci, and Richard, bishop of Verdun, being his friends, urged the prince not to inflict distress upon a religious man on this account, since they knew his mind to be steadfast in faith and in the other virtues. The emperor replied: “Persuade him, if he will not take the oath, at least to present himself for it, so that he may seem to have done so, lest the custom of our country be annulled.” He answered: “It is the same if I pretend as if I had done it. Far be this from me.”

Seeing him so firm, the emperor was unwilling to trouble him further. Relying solely on Halynard’s word and promises as a pledge of faith, he granted what was requested. In his own presence he had him ordained, providing whatever was necessary for priestly consecration. And he made provision in this way not only for Halynard and the other bishops, but also for levites and ministers of the altar—vestments, books, linens, and every necessity—as though he were not a prince but a servant. For he was indeed a devout king, very ecclesiastical and most devoted to divine worship.

### Halynard is ordained archbishop in the emperor’s presence.

The venerable Father Halynard was ordained by the hands of Lord Hugh, Archbishop of Chrysopolis, at a place called in the German tongue *Herbrestinc*, which in our language signifies “good lodging-places,” in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1046.

In the same year the said prince went to Rome and there received the imperial crown on Christmas Day from the hands of Pope Clement, whom the emperor himself had ordered to be ordained. He also caused John, then presiding in the papal chair, Benedict, and Sylvester to be deposed; at the council then held, after their guilt had been examined, they were found not only to be simoniacs but also usurpers of Christ’s Church. This council was attended by the Lord Archbishop of Lyons himself, by the above-mentioned Archbishop Hugh, and by many other bishops assembled from various regions.

Halynard had been accustomed frequently to go to Rome for prayer, that he might implore the patronage of the holy apostles and martyrs who protect that city. For it was his wish, if possible, to render his soul to God there. Accordingly, he was not disappointed in his desire: as he wished, so the Lord granted to him.

After the death of the aforesaid Pope Clement, the Romans requested Halynard from the emperor. For the emperor had exacted from the Romans a considerable payment, on the condition that no pope should be elected without his permission. Knowing the wish of both prince and people, Halynard avoided going to the court, until, as the matter was delayed, another should be elected. For the Romans loved him greatly because of his eloquence and graciousness of speech: he pronounced the native sound of the language of every people as far as the Latin language reaches, as though he had been born in that same country.

### Concerning St Leo IX, pope. Death of Halynard.

When Lord Bruno, bishop of the Leuci, who was called Pope Leo, had been ordained, Lord Archbishop Halynard was summoned by him to a council at Rome, together with all the bishops of Gaul, to deliberate there on the condition and reform of the holy Church. In that same year the pope himself went to France and held a council of bishops at Reims, as we have already said; there our aforesaid Father was with him. Then the body of St Remigius was translated by the apostolic lord and the bishops who were present, and the church itself was consecrated.

For a third time the aforesaid pope held a council in the city of Rome, at which the said prelate was present; and, when Leo again hastened to Gaul, Halynard was his inseparable companion. Coming to the city of Langres, Halynard ordained there, in the pope’s presence, Lord Arduin as bishop in place of the man who had been expelled.

Again, in the following year, journeying to Rome, he hastened with the apostolic lord to Benevento and Capua, Monte Cassino, and Monte Gargano to St Michael the Archangel. The aforesaid pope went into those regions in order, if possible, to relieve their inhabitants from the oppression by which they were excessively burdened by the Normans. But because Lord Archbishop Halynard was exceedingly powerful in speech, and his tongue sufficed to persuade in any matter, the apostolic lord took him with him so that he might serve as mediator and ambassador of peace between himself and the aforesaid Normans.

On returning from there, since the pope was hastening to a meeting with the emperor, who was then perhaps in the regions of Hungary, he ordered Halynard to remain in Rome until he himself returned. In Halynard’s company was the aforementioned bishop of Langres, Hugh. Repentant for the things which he had done no otherwise, he asked the pope to prescribe a measure of penance for his offences and to grant absolution of his sins.

> **[Note: Col. 0845, “which he had done otherwise than he ought.”]** Acherius reads “which he, blind, had done”; but the text should be restored as “which he had done otherwise,” with the negation removed.

The apostolic lord, being merciful and kind in spirit, saw that Hugh was truly repentant and afflicted; moved with compassion, he immediately granted him pardon, saying that what he had suffered was sufficient penance. As Hugh departed after absolution of his offences, Leo rewarded him very generously and moreover granted him permission to resume his bishopric.

When Lord Archbishop Halynard came to Rome, intending to take leave of the pope and his other companions, he reclined with them at table. There a fish infected with poison was offered him by a certain false friend. Of those who partook, all—both Halynard himself and the others—either died within eight days or wasted away and died after a long illness. Two monks from this place who were with him were killed by this food. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [29 July], in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1052, having completed seven years in the pontificate and twenty years in the governance of this place.

### He is buried at Rome in the church of St Paul. The great benefits he bestowed on St Benignus.

He ordered that he be laid to rest at St Gregory’s at the Clivus Scauri, for the pope had granted him that place as a residence. But Roman nobles who had visited him during his life ordered his body to be carried to St Paul’s. There he was honourably committed to burial on the left side of the church, and an arch was built over his tomb.

All the ornaments that he used in the sacred ministry he sent to St Benignus, his holy protector, together with a considerable quantity of gold and silver vessels belonging to his service. He greatly increased the ornaments of this church; among them, he caused a gold cross adorned with gems to be made. He also ordered many books to be copied and renewed the workshops of this monastery. Although learned in every art, he applied himself especially to geometry and natural philosophy. Nor should it be passed over in silence what was increased in this place in lands and possessions during his days.

Hugh, Archbishop of the See of Chrysopolis, his very intimate friend, gave a church situated in the borough called Salins, which his parents had built from the foundations. It was consecrated in honour of the martyrs Saints Symphorianus and Agatha, and St Anatolius the Confessor rests there. On the feast day of that martyr, when he was to celebrate Mass there, Hugh placed the charter of donation of that place upon the altar of St Benignus. Before all the people assembled, he bound by the bond of excommunication anyone who should remove that place from the lordship of the abbot and monks of Dijon.

This donation was made in the year from the Incarnation 1037, in the fifth indiction, the sixth year of his episcopate. By episcopal privilege he granted another church in the same borough, dedicated in honour of St Mary. Count Rainald gave this church to St Benignus for the repose of the soul of his father Otto, called William; and for this gift he received from Lord Halynard a considerable sum of money, while Halynard was still holding the office of prior.

### [Col. 0847A] The author speaks of himself.

The aforesaid Count Rainald gave in the above-mentioned borough a site for the construction of a church. On it a chapel was built in honour of St Andrew the Apostle. Made of timber, it was later reduced to nothing through neglect. He gave at Évirey land which had belonged to Theudebert. The monks possessed it for some time, but because of the opposition which a certain Odilo made against them, they relinquished it, until the said count, after they had acquired possession of the place of St Anatolius, restored it to them again. This took place in the year from the Incarnation 1026, after the death of Count William, who died in that same year.

Several clerics and laypeople among the inhabitants of that town, coming to monastic conversion in this monastery, gave their property to St Benignus, our holy protector. Several who offered their sons likewise made gifts from their possessions. Among them, my own father, offering me, gave, besides other things, a house beside the well and the site of one boiling-vat. This was later granted in return for the payment of a rent, on the condition that whoever held it should pay forty-six solidi every year.

After some time had passed, the same Count Rainald gave, near the castle called Vesoul, a church consecrated in honour of St George, so that a monastery might be built there and four monks established there, who, serving God at all times, might pray for the repose of the souls of his father, mother, and brother, and for himself and all his kindred. He gave for their support vineyards and lands, and whatever was necessary; moreover, fishing rights together with the men who served him in that occupation.

The aforementioned Archbishop Hugh was present at this donation. By the staff which he customarily carried in his hand, he gave the altar of the aforesaid church to Abbot Halynard; and, in remembrance of this act, they exchanged their staffs. Count Burchard also gave the place called the estate of Offo, formerly a noble abbey consecrated in honour of St Leodegar, earnestly asking the aforesaid Abbot Halynard that monastic observance might be restored there.

Likewise Rotger, lord of the castle called Wangion’s Stream, gave the church which his father Wido had built in honour of St Stephen, intending that, after the canons had been expelled, monks should be placed there to serve God day and night. Rainald also, lord of the castle called Châtillon, when approaching death and taking the monastic habit, gave the estate of St Julian, with all the lands, serfs, and appurtenances belonging to it, together with the church dedicated to that saint’s name. There he asked that monks be established to pray to God for his soul and those of the other faithful.

In the same way Albert, count of Metz, gave the estate called Wulfhere’s Court, with male and female serfs. He had indeed intended to give it during his lifetime, but after his death his son Duke Gerard carried out the gift. Likewise, a certain noblewoman, named Letgard, sister of Bishop Lambert, gave a church situated in the village called Isle, upon the river Meuse, in the county of Bassigny.

### [Col. 0847] End of the present history.

### [Col. 0847] Continuation of the Chronicle of the Abbey of St Benignus

We, the modern cultivators of the monastery of this ancient and sacred St Benignus, must not pass over or consign to oblivion what the most illustrious successors of the above-mentioned abbots and benefactors did or granted for the honour and adornment of this church and the benefit of the whole community. For who could worthily recount the benefactions of the venerable Fathers Jarento, Odo, Hugh, Robert, and Alexander, or of that greatest benefactor of ours, Lord Claude de Charmes? Or who would not rather desire with all zeal to learn of them? Therefore, since, as someone says, examples move more than words, and so that by their example we may strive to live well and conduct ourselves holily in this congregation, we shall dare, God granting it, to take up the pen in order to set forth—even if stammeringly—their most noble and illustrious deeds, and we shall endeavour to do so.

### Concerning Jarento, the most vigilant shepherd

Jarento, then, the venerable third abbot of this monastery after Halynard—for John and Adalbero had presided before him, but we have been able to discover absolutely nothing concerning their deeds—came to this monastery and found it almost abandoned. Its possessions outside had nearly been destroyed through the machinations of wicked princes, while within, regular observance and the fervour of religion seemed altogether to have grown cold.

But in the days of this venerable Father, God appeared to look upon this church sufficiently kindly, gently, and graciously, whereas in some preceding times he had seemed miserably to despise it, if I may speak in this fashion. For this venerable shepherd, supported by divine aid, restored religious observance to its former state, recovered no small number of lost possessions, and by his prudence deserved to acquire others never possessed before. Since he was profound in learning and eloquence and prudent in counsel, he was greatly pleasing to princes both ecclesiastical and secular. Whenever he approached them, he held a high place in their courts and returned magnificently rewarded by them.

Nor was it enough for him to seek advantages for the church committed to him in neighbouring places. Traveling to foreign and remote regions, namely Spain and England, he brought back from every quarter gold, silver, cloths, and some ecclesiastical ornaments. As a faithful steward, he faithfully devoted to the needs of his house what the faithful had entrusted to him. Thus, by divine mercy’s favour, it came to pass in his days that this church raised its head above all its neighbouring churches, both in the esteem of religious observance and in the abundance of foreign goods.

Let us, however, mention some possessions recovered or acquired by him. This venerable Father recovered by his industry the cell of St Mary of Chalon, as well as the cell of the Sarcophagi. Tuntard, bishop of Valence, at the urging of the aforesaid Father Jarento, gave us the churches which we possess in the territory of Valence.

> **[Note: Col. 0849D, Tuntard.]** Acherius emends the name to “Gontard.”

Hugh, Archbishop of Besançon, also bestowed upon us, through the favour of Father Jarento, the chapel of Logia Novella. Agano, bishop of Autun, likewise gave us the church of St James of Arnet. Through Jarento’s intervention, moreover, two noblemen who had become converts under him gave their freehold estate of Hischin and St Benignus of the Wood. By the labour of Jarento and his monks, these villages began to be inhabited and rebuilt: Greater and Lesser Casnedus, Marcennarius, Varescis, and Misiniacus. Of these, he assigned two—Casnedus and Marcennarius—for the celebration of his anniversary.

In the time of this aforesaid Father, the venerable bishop of the Church of Bayeux, called Odo, did not in the least depart from the salutary path of his ancestors, the counts of Normandy, who had loved this church of Dijon with singular affection and greatly advanced it in goods and possessions. Rather, being their perfect imitator, he laboured to renew their affection in his own time, so that the memory of both him and them ought deservedly to endure among us ever fresh.

To touch upon some evidence of his devotion: on one occasion, when he was seeking Pope Urban, then in Gaul, he came to Dijon and was received by the said Father Jarento and the brethren of this place with such honour that he considered himself entirely unworthy if he did not repay such service with a corresponding return and establish by an enduring memorial his affection toward them. Therefore, at the urging of William, dean of the Church of Bayeux, and likewise of Richard, archdeacon of Rouen, he gave to St Benignus, protector of this Church of Dijon, through the hand of the above-mentioned Abbot Jarento, the monastery or priory of St Vigor, situated outside the city of Bayeux on Mont Chrismate, together with all its appurtenances: namely, the full tithe of the whole village in which the monastery stood, both from its people and territory and from everything else.

He also gave four burgesses: two at Champ Fleuri and the others by Albert’s bridge, with their land and customary dues. He also gave the full tithe from the village of Tur, with the priest’s land; likewise the church of Olferes, the church of Cruceyo, and the church of Colgrino, with their full tithes, the lands belonging to them, and the priests’ lands. He gave also the full tithe of all Crecavilla, with the priest’s land—that is, the land belonging to the church.

Moreover, the above-named bishop established that his own burial place, and that of all future bishops and canons of Bayeux, should be made there. Yet, because he had given all these things, and those mentioned above, to the church of Dijon while in Gaul, afterward at Bayeux he delivered the same donation into the hand of the aforesaid abbot, with the approval and testimony of his clergy. By a charter he confirmed not only what he had given, but also added much more: namely, a large sum of money, houses filled with various crops, and herds of animals of mixed kinds numbering more than a hundred.

### Robert, bishop of Langres, grants many things to St Benignus. Jarento dies. Abbot Ademarus.

Lord Robert, bishop of the Church of Langres, descended from the exalted lineage of the kings of France and dukes of Burgundy, after he had assumed the governance of the episcopate by divine favour, laboured to form himself after the example of his predecessor bishops. They had always cherished this church with paternal affection; Robert accordingly transferred their spirit into himself, so that as long as he lived he loved this place with remarkable affection and sought to enrich it, in its freedom, by munificent and immense gifts.

Inflamed with love of God and St Benignus, and repeatedly exhorted by the aforesaid Abbot Jarento, he gave us the church of Noant, with the chapel or sanctuary of the same castle and all churches and altars belonging to them. He also gave the church of Clermont, the church of Magnomont, the church of Icio, the church of Casnedus, the church of Spaniac, the church of Vareso, the church of St Lupus, the church of Germani Villare, the church of Riviac, the church of Occeio, and the church in the district of Adeleni Curtis.

He further added a great proof of his goodwill toward this place. The chapel of Wangion’s Stream belonged by right to the Church of Dijon; but while clerics held it, no benefit came from it. Therefore, frequently pressed on this matter by the prayers of the aforesaid Father Jarento and repeatedly exhorted by Guydo, the most noble lord of the same castle, Robert removed the clerics and delivered that chapel to the monks, together with all its dependencies: namely, the church of Sariscac with all belonging to it; half of the chapel of Roecourt and half of its tithes; the entire tithe of the church of Masnili; the altar of the church of Hericourt; the land of Grincourt; and half of the tithes of Columbeiac, where there are two churches.

The aforesaid Bishop Robert also ordained that we should possess more freely and peacefully the churches of St John and St Philibert, situated within Dijon; that priests should celebrate in them, or be appointed or removed, at the will of the abbot or monks of this place; and that those priests should be free from every exaction of priesthood, bishop, or archdeacon. The bishop further ordered that all the bread customarily offered in those churches should be set before the brethren in the refectory, so that, when their bodies were more often refreshed by it, they too might refresh the giver’s soul by their prayers.

Our aforesaid Father Jarento ended his final days in the Lord, departing to the Lord in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1105. Ademarus succeeded him in the governance of the pastoral office. He deserved to be counted among the benefactors of this church.

### Abbots of St Benignus: Hugh, Peter, Peter, Philip.

After Ademarus’s death, Henry presided in the governance of this congregation; after him, Hugh, Peter, and another Peter succeeded as abbots. When these had died, Lord Abbot Philip presided over this church. He is counted among the principal abbots, and on the day of his death he left an outstanding provision; for his anniversary we possess many benefactions.

### John, Aymo, Peter.

Around this time, a knight named Richard Bigot gave this house four acres of vineyard, situated in the field of Bertrand, with three measures of grain. Odo, a knight and son of the same Richard, gave us three *journals* of vineyard in the territory of Descolonges for his anniversary to be celebrated every year. Both of these obtained burial in this place.

A noblewoman, Aglantina, wife of Bartholomew, knight of Ville-Comte, also gave forty solidi of annual income. She was buried in this church with her aforesaid husband and also with her son. John and Aymo were then abbots over this monastery; while governing, they did few things. Peter, succeeding them in pastoral care, is said to have done much for the adornment and benefit of his church.

### Nivaldus, Walter, Adam, Gilebert, Stephen, Peter, Richard, Aymo, Hugh.

The following Fathers succeeded him: Nivaldus, Walter, Adam, Gilebert—one of the principal benefactors of this abbey—and his successor Rainald.

> **[Note: Col. 0851D, Rainald.]** Elsewhere: Raymund.

Rainald established a provision for his anniversary. Stephen Raymund Loys bestowed very many benefits upon us and therefore deserved to be listed among the principal benefactors. In his time, as is believed, Otto, lord of Grandson, granted this monastery thirty-three pounds of annual revenue for one Mass to be celebrated daily at the altar of St Stephen, and sixty solidi for his anniversary to be celebrated every year.

When the aforesaid venerable Father Stephen departed to Christ, the venerable Peter was chosen shepherd. He is reported to have conferred very many benefits upon us, although we have found nothing concerning them in writing. For that reason he too was listed among the principal benefactors, and he has twelve portions in the refectory. After him Richard and Aymo presided over this abbey; they too have twelve portions.

In their days a certain man named James gave the monks of this place one hundred Dijon solidi of annual revenue or rent. When Aymo, mentioned above, hastened to Christ, there arose from their midst Hugh of Arcu, a Father venerable above all, of most honourable conduct and adorned with good morals.

In his time a dreadful and remarkable event occurred in this monastery. A stone tower in the middle of the old church, firmly set upon stone bases and of great length, breadth, and height, built with noble workmanship, collapsed horribly. But—O wondrous thing!—the wooden shrine, which held most precious relics in the lower part of the church and rested upon two small stone columns, bore the greater weight of the ruin. The shrine itself remained wholly uninjured. Though its two small columns were broken and no other visible support was beneath it, it stood by itself in a miraculous manner. The lamps continually burning at the site of the said shrine in veneration of the holy relics were not extinguished, either by so great a collapse, so dreadful a blast and sound, or the unimaginable whirling of dust.

### Abbot Hugh builds the church of St Benignus.

What, then, did these events foretell, unless they signified God’s disposition for the future rebuilding of this temple and the future arrangement for elevating the holy relics? For just as holy David was forbidden by God to build the house of God in Jerusalem because he was a man of blood, while it was permitted to his son Solomon, so also, by some special counsel of the Holy Spirit, the holy Fathers living in this monastery had not been permitted to rebuild the Lord’s house or elevate the holy relics. This work was reserved by the grace of a special privilege for this peaceful Solomon: namely, the aforesaid Father Hugh.

And because obedience is better than sacrifices, the venerable Father, not resisting divine inspiration but obeying most devoutly, quickly set his hand to the work of constructing this church, as it now stands. The building itself speaks and sufficiently shows with what careful planning and laborious expense it was conceived and erected.

When the front part of the aforesaid building, which in the common tongue is called the presbytery, had been completed, the oft-mentioned Father undertook a work long conceived in purpose, most sweet and beloved: to construct a silver shrine of most fitting workmanship, composed of gold, silver, and gems, in which the holy relics, long hidden below, might be honourably enclosed. When it had been completed, trusting in the aid of him who perfects and makes all things firm, the aforesaid Father summoned barons, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other prelates, serving the one Lord in differing orders and ranks, together with a great multitude of clergy and people.

When so noble an assembly had gathered, they removed the most precious relics of our patron, Benignus, athlete of Christ, from the place where they had rested for many years. Blessing the Lord in hymns and confessions, they placed them, amid the greatest joy of clergy and people, within the said shrine or chest, suitably and magnificently set high behind the high altar, in the year from Christ’s Nativity 1288, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October].

In the time of this venerable Father, many of his kin and many other outsiders bestowed many benefits upon this church and its inhabitants. Among them, foremost were Hugh, knight and lord of Arcu, and his wife Margaret. This Hugh gave us sixty Viennese solidi, situated and assigned upon the men of Disier, to be received by the monks of this place on the day of his anniversary, celebrated every year. Humbert of Arcu also gave three measures of grain for a provision. A noble lady called Isabella of Pesinis also gave us, for her anniversary, forty Tours solidi to be received yearly on the day of her death; when dying, she chose burial within this church.

### Abbots Gerard, Henry, Millo, John, Otto, Peter.

After the oft-mentioned Hugh, venerable and lamented Father, had happily departed to eternal joys following many years spent in pastoral care, Abbot Gerard succeeded him. After Gerard, Henry presided over this church, then Millo. Few benefactions are found to have been made in their time. But when they were called to the heavenly kingdom, the venerable abbot named John succeeded. He established a provision for the day of his anniversary.

Around this time, a priest named Walter of Boux, moved by devotion toward our blessed patron Benignus, gave us six *modii* of wine every year for his anniversary. He also freely gave us an image of our aforesaid protector Benignus. After the said John, Otto presided in this place; he is found to have done nothing for the adornment of his church. Peter succeeded him and proved similar to his predecessor.

### Another Peter, John, William, Peter.

After these men there arose another named Peter, who deserved to be enrolled among our principal benefactors. As I heard from certain trustworthy persons, because of the holiness in which he shone and the nobility of his conduct, he was earnestly asked by Lord Hugh, then count of Burgundy, and by the brethren of this place, to deign to visit with him the church of Blessed James in Galicia. With the consent of all the monks, he happily accomplished this. At length, commending his spirit to the Lord, he had as successors John, William, and Peter, abbots of this place.

### [Col. 0854A] Vladislaus, duke of Poland, a monk.

In their days, although few persons are found to have benefited this church, one John, a monk of this place, who caused the dormitory warming-room to be made and endowed the timber necessary for it, is nevertheless numbered among the others. Hugh de Ray, prior of St Apollinaris, together with his father Huot and his mother Margaret, gave us twenty francs, besides the house of La Tannarie.

Likewise, the most illustrious and noble man named Vladislaus, formerly the White Duke of Poland, afterward became a monk in this place. But, since he lacked offspring, he was dispensed by the pope to leave the habit until he should have an heir to succeed him in the kingdom. At length, dying and choosing burial here, he gave this monastery two thousand five hundred florins for two anniversaries.

Alexander of Montaigu, Abbot.—But, that we may relate something in praise of the venerable Alexander of Montaigu, successor of the aforesaid Peter, the pen must by no means be laid aside. For when he had been made abbot of this distinguished Church, he continuously strove greatly to adorn it both within and without. He bestowed upon us silver vessels, golden cloths, many silken ornaments, and whatever was then suitable for adorning that church. He endowed the warming-room of the refectory, likewise his anniversary commemoration, and an alms to be given on that day to thirteen poor persons, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April]. This venerable Father further most wisely reformed religious observance [Col. 0854C] in this place, maintained it, and suffered it in no respect to grow lax for as long as he lived. He also governed the whole monastery energetically, restored it, and adorned it in many ways. Meanwhile, the aforesaid Father Alexander left to his successor John about six thousand gold pieces, apart from his other goods. And, to sum him up briefly, we do not believe that anyone his equal presided over this place until Abbot Hugh, who, as we have mentioned above, made the church and the silver shrine. This Alexander also caused the church of this monastery to be dedicated; and, on the morrow of that dedication, a solemn annual anniversary was freely granted to him by the convent of this place. He twice caused the great [Col. 0854D] bell called Benigna to be recast. He recovered the rights of our aforesaid monastery, which we were nearly losing, and obtained formal decrees of the Parliament of Paris concerning them.

John, Abbot.—In the time of this our reverend shepherd, a certain man called John, who was a lay brother in this house, gave us eighty francs for his anniversary, to be celebrated yearly by the brethren of this place, and did many other things for us. Moreover, he caused the crucifix painted in the corner of the cloister to be made. The aforementioned venerable Father Alexander, after having most devotedly governed for many years the abbey of Flavigny—for he had formerly been abbot there—as well as the present monastery, was called by Christ [Col. 0855A] in the year of our Lord 1417, on the fifth day of September, leaving us as successor the aforesaid John de la Marche, abbot.

Stephen.—When he died, a man named Stephen was abbot of this place. In his days a certain Renaudot, chamberlain to the Duke of Burgundy and staff-bearer in this place, permanently endowed a Mass at the altar of Saint Paul, which he had newly built, by assigning it forty pounds. Of these, twenty-four are given to the cantor and the refectorian, who celebrate it, while the remainder belongs to the convent. The said Renaudot also gave, at the end of his life, two hundred gold pieces to endow two [Col. 0855B] anniversary commemorations.

Peter; Hugh of Mont-Cuniculus.—After the aforesaid Stephen, Peter was administering the government of this Church. John, surnamed de Laon, gave us, for the alms of this monastery, an annual rent of twenty solidi, charged upon a certain house situated in the castle of Jussey. John de Vison, counsellor of the Duke of Burgundy, and his wife Joan also gave us a silver vessel in which is kept a bone from the arm of Saint Lawrence the martyr. At last, when the aforesaid Father Peter passed to the Lord, he was succeeded by the venerable Hugh of Mont-Cuniculus. In his time Brother John Broissandi, chamberlain of this monastery, caused the convent hall, situated [Col. 0855C] beside the Chamberlain’s house, and the house of Albanus, with the press-house situated before the church of Saint Philibert, to be rebuilt. He also endowed a distribution of meat, which is given to the brethren in the refectory three times weekly from Easter until the Ascension of the Lord. He likewise endowed a meat meal to be provided on the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene. He also endowed a lamp, continually burning with oil before the altar of blessed Mary in the nave of the church. He further endowed illumination on the feasts of the same blessed Virgin, as is done on the feasts of the apostles; and illumination for his two anniversary commemorations, as is customary for other principal commemorations. Andrew of Montmoret, infirmarian in this place, then gave us a silver image of Saint Blaise, [Col. 0855D] very richly adorned with gold, together with a most sumptuous golden cope. For his anniversary, James, brother of the aforesaid Andrew and subprior of Larrey, personally handed over to the convent one hundred Tours pounds, together with a cope of the colour commonly called crimson, for his own anniversary. A woman called Agnes of Citerney also gave us thirty solidi, charged and assigned upon a certain house situated in the Cemetery.

Humbert of Saulbiez.—The aforesaid Father Hugh gave us two hundred gold pieces together with four Tours pounds to endow one anniversary commemoration. He also caused bells, or drums, to be made in this church. Furthermore, he gave 120 francs for providing hospitality at the translation of the holy [Col. 0856A] Father Benedict. He passed to the Lord in the year of the Incarnation 1467. After him, Dom Humbert of Saulbiez presided over the pastoral care of this Church; at his own expense he ordered the great window at the entrance to the church to be made. In his days the prior of Arnet, named William d’Aguilly, gave the inhabitants of this monastery an annual rent of twenty Tours pounds, redeemable for three hundred pounds.

Walter of Falerenc; Louis of Tintaville.—Humbert was succeeded by Walter, surnamed de Falerenc. He distributed, as they say, seven hundred gold pieces to the convent. Indeed, in accordance with his intention, in the Mass of blessed Mary the collect *Inclina* (“Incline”) is to be said; and after the aforesaid Mass—that is, the Mass said in the old church—the antiphon of the aforesaid blessed Virgin is to be said daily, together with her collect; and *Deus cui proprium* (“O God, whose property it is”), for that Father. The venerable Father Louis, called de Tintaville, succeeded him in the administration when he died; but he is found to have done little.

About this time, a certain religious, named Benignus de Chemilly, chamberlain in this house, endowed a Mass of the blessed Mother of God to be celebrated every Saturday, and ordained that the same Mass should also be said on all solemnities of the same blessed Virgin. William Regnandieu, cloistral prior of this house, personally gave us one hundred Tours pounds for one anniversary commemoration. [Col. 0856C] Godfrey, surnamed Domboys, chamberlain of this place, also granted this monastery three *heminae* of wheat, to be received by us every year.

Claude de Charmes: the integrity of his character.—After all the aforesaid venerable shepherds, God willed to raise up in His Church a true lamp for us: namely, a most watchful shepherd of His flock, the venerable Father and lord, Lord Claude de Charmes, most worthy abbot of this sacred monastery. Descended from the noblest stock of the leading men of Dijon, and clothed from childhood in this sacred place with the habit of our most blessed Father Benedict, as soon as he had come to years [Col. 0856D] of discretion, he began first to flourish, and increasingly to put forth shoots, in the vineyard of the Lord. For, on account of the eminent moderation of wisdom in which he excelled, his pious kindness toward all, and his uprightness of conduct, he was made sub-cellarer and also almoner in this house. By a certain presage of his future eminence, he also merited at certain times to hold the office of sacristan. And, to state it briefly, as was said above of the venerable Father Halinard, he seems to have carried out almost all the offices of this Church diligently, assiduously, and wisely.

At last, when the reverend Father Louis de Tintaville, abbot of this place, of whom we have spoken above, had died, Claude was elected to the pastoral office of this house of the Lord—not by force of arms or by the clatter of horses, nor on account of the exalted nobility in which he stood pre-eminent, but rather because his virtuous character demanded it, because of the good repute of his life already known in every respect, and, as is devoutly believed, by the granting will of God. [Col. 0857A] In the Lord’s field, as a diligent cultivator and faithful steward, he resolved not to dig into the earth or hide the talent entrusted to him, but to employ it with all his strength for the splendour, honour, advantage, and adornment of his Lord and of His bride, holy mother Church.

The benefits he bestowed are described.—Beginning, then, at the top, the aforesaid Father ordered that in this house the bell-tower, or belfry, should be erected in a marvellous work, surpassing others in workmanship [Col. 0857B], and covered with carefully installed sheets of lead, as can very easily be seen by all who come to this place. He also caused the church itself to be whitewashed at his own expense and adorned more splendidly than it had formerly been. The aforesaid abbot also caused the great bell, drum, or cymbal to be recast; at its blessing he wished it to receive the name Benedict, and he added many pounds of metal to it. He likewise had the cross standing before the high altar gilded.

In the past year, 151, on the fourth day of January, the aforesaid venerable Father, prompted by fervent devotion, gave and personally delivered to the prior and convent of this above-named monastery the sum of three thousand Tours pounds for purchasing rents and revenues. [Col. 0857C] His intention was that two Masses should be celebrated and said daily, in perpetuity, by the brethren of the monastery for himself and all his relatives, household, and benefactors, living and dead, for the hope of his salvation and preservation. The first was to be sung aloud, with deacon and subdeacon, at the high altar of the aforesaid monastery, in the form and manner in which other conventual Masses were accustomed to be celebrated in that church.
