The second was to be celebrated in a low voice by one brother of the aforesaid monastery, in the place, manner, and time more fully set forth in the letters drawn up concerning the foundation [Col. 0857D] of the same.

Moreover, the aforesaid venerable Father Claude, not at all content with the above-written benefits freely bestowed upon us by him, but moved by a still greater fervour of devotion, with the acceptance of the aforementioned prior and convent, gave and personally delivered to the prior and convent the sum of two thousand four hundred Tours pounds, with the aforesaid intention, to purchase rents and revenues for payment of the divine services which he desired and intended to be performed. In addition to the above-described suffrages, the aforesaid abbot ordained that at each Ember season, on Wednesday, three high Masses should be celebrated by three priors of the aforesaid monastery at the said high altar, [Col. 0858A] and one hundred low Masses, which are to be said nowhere except in the aforesaid church of Saint Benignus, by brethren of the monastery or by other religious or secular clergy, as is set out in the aforesaid letters. On the Tuesday preceding the Ember Wednesday, after dinner, the aforesaid brethren must also say aloud and solemnly the Office of the Dead with nine psalms and nine lessons.

Likewise, the frequently mentioned Father intended that, on every day of Advent and Lent, at the second hour after noon, the aforesaid brethren of the monastery should likewise say in full, solemnly, and aloud the Office of the Dead with nine psalms and nine lessons, except on Sundays, on which it is not said. Those who say or attend these suffrages or divine services are to receive from the pittancer of this monastery the sums specified for this purpose in the aforesaid letters. [Col. 0858B] The aforesaid Abbot Claude gave us not only the monies mentioned, but also many golden and silken ornaments for the church. For the adornment of his church and the exaltation of divine worship, he gave one most precious and richly endowed chasuble, with dalmatic and tunicle. These vestments are abundantly interwoven and composed with the most brilliant gold. He further gave a silver cup, richly adorned with much gold, in which the body of the Lord is kept. He then caused small cupboards to be made on the left side of the high altar in the new church. Their inner portions are made of iron in the form of latticework or small windows, magnificently gilded with gold, so that the sacred and precious relics of the church might be stored there more fittingly and reverently—especially the necks or heads of the saints, namely of our Father Benignus, Gregory, our founder and bishop of Langres, and Radegund, queen of the Franks. [Col. 0858C] The heads of Gregory and Radegund, as they now stand, this Lord Father Claude very lavishly adorned, strengthened, and decorated with much silver and gold. He also had six bases, columns, or, if you prefer, pillars cast in bronze, made before the aforesaid altar and for its adornment. Above, they support images of six angels representing the emblems of Christ’s Passion; richly decorated and emblazoned with gold, they may readily be seen by all.

The city of Dijon is besieged.—About the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1513, while the most Christian King Louis XII was triumphant in France and the aforementioned reverend Father presided in this house, the people of the Swabians—or, as some call them, the Swiss—a fierce and greedy people, emerging from the regions of Germany, pursuing not the things of their lord but their own interests, besieged Dijon at the command, as they said, of Maximilian, then emperor. It would have been laid waste and plundered [Col. 0859A] had it not been delivered through the prayers and merits of our most holy protector Benignus, to whom they fled for refuge, and of the holy saints resting in this town of Dijon. For, by divine providence, after an agreement had been made between us and them concerning a very great sum of money to be given them, they returned to their own country—but not without grave misfortune to the aforesaid Father and the whole congregation. At that time the suburbs of Saint Nicholas, Saint Peter, and the Holy Spirit were burned. From these we received many rents and revenues each year. At Saint Apollinaris they devastated everything, and the priory of that place suffered most grievous loss. The inhabitants of other neighbouring places likewise lost much; for the aforesaid enemies numbered more than forty-five [Col. 0859B] thousand men. To save our monastery from the hands of those enemies, the aforesaid abbot and the convent gave two thousand pounds of silver, in addition to the already mentioned grievous losses.

Then, because of the devotion which the aforesaid venerable abbot had for blessed Urban, bishop of the Church of Langres, formerly buried here and now resting here, he caused a silver shrine, richly decorated with much gold, to be made, so that the holy and precious relics of the bishop might be honourably deposited there. In these times a woman named Guillemette, mother of Stephen—the wife of a former merchant who, beneath the shrine or chest of the most blessed patron Benignus, recovered his senses through that saint’s prayers—passed in peace to the Lord and, for her anniversary, gave us the sum of one hundred pounds, personally handing it over to the convent. John Callot, master of the chamber, also gave us the sum of one hundred Tours pounds, for his anniversary to be celebrated yearly by us. John Moreaul, infirmarian of this monastery, gave, for the adornment of our church and for the more reverent performance of the divine office, one very large golden cope, marvellously made. [Col. 0859C] In these days, too, Theobald, surnamed Demipont, of noble descent and a monk in this place, moved by devotion, founded and established lighting on the solemn feast of the Body of Christ and throughout its octave. For this purpose two candles must burn continuously day and night before the stone cupboards [Col. 0859D] in which the aforesaid sacrament is kept. The treasurer receives one franc in coin annually for this. Brother John, a lay brother residing at Larrey, personally handed us forty francs for his anniversary.

Finally, together with the above-written ornaments granted by him to this place, the aforesaid venerable Father gave us two most beautiful and richly endowed golden copes, made with exceptionally fine craftsmanship. [Col. 0860A] He also gave us green ornaments for the high altar, of silk workmanship, together with two green copes, a chasuble, and a dalmatic.

This most reverend Father, beloved by all and loved by all, and powerfully defending his own, was therefore sought by all. For he was elected guardian of the Lord’s flock at Saint-Germain of Auxerre, and for many years most wisely carried its burden. But in the end, setting aside that honour and transferring the burden to the most religious man Lord Francis de Beljeu, his kinsman—who excelled in letters, learning, and upright conduct, and had for many years been chamberlain of this place—he appointed him abbot. He also refused other abbeys, namely Saint-Jean de Réôme [Col. 0860B] and Saint-Seine, both of which their religious inhabitants, having learned of his good conduct, offered him with humble entreaty. A certain man called Abbot succeeded through resignation.

Let us therefore all pray, who live under their protection, that He who sees all things beneath His feet, governs and directs them by His own will, may permit both to live long among us, sound and unharmed; may grant and inspire them to instruct and teach the flock entrusted to them by conduct and word; so that, after the long labours of this vale of miseries, the Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto everlasting ages, may deign to receive them, with the household committed to them, into His eternal dwelling-places and perpetual inheritance.

[Col. 0860C] Many benefits were also bestowed upon this sacred monastery, which ought now to be inserted upon this page. But since it would be too long to recount them all, we pray that these may satisfy the reader, and we set an end to the work.

A brief poem composed in praise of the distinguished and illustrious Father and lord, Lord Claude de Charmes, most worthy abbot of the sacred monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, follows.

Claude, bright in name, led a bright life in this monastery;  
He was its abbot.

Illustrious Dijon brought him forth from lofty stock,  
Yet God chose him to be our father.

What Aeneas did for the Trojans, Samson for the Hebrews,  
[Col. 0860D] What Solomon did for Jerusalem, he bestowed upon his own.

This church has been exalted by many benefactions,  
And made splendid through this Father’s aid.

He always safely protected his own, and with every effort  
Increased the sheep entrusted to his care.

May God Himself grant him life through Nestor’s years,  
And may he complete the days of the Phoenix.

And when the harsh Fate has cut the tender thread,  
May his spirit, I pray, seek the heavenly homes.

Amen.

[Col. 0861]

**CHRONICLE OF JOHN THE MONK OF BÈZE. Here begins the book of memorable events, or charters, of the monastery of Bèze**

[Col. 0861A] It was the laudable, and therefore imitable, practice of the wise men of former ages [Note: [Col. 0861C] These are the exact words of the Chronicle of Saint Benignus.] to commit to written records for the memory of posterity not only the things that happened in their own days, but also the brave deeds of heroes of old. This useful practice furnished them with material for human praise, and gave to those who would later read or hear these things an example and incentive to emulation. Considering such matters, we, the humble inhabitants and lovers of the sacred monastery of Bèze, lest perhaps our successors should justly be angry with us, as we deservedly blame our predecessors for their neglect, shall undertake, with God’s help, to write in a rustic and wholly unpolished narrative what we have been able to learn concerning the antiquity of the aforesaid place, and the gifts bestowed upon it by the generosity of kings, bishops, dukes, counts, and illustrious men devoted to God. [Col. 0861B] Thus the account of the possessions bestowed upon our monastery and of memorable deeds done there may redound to its honour, and the heavenly glory to be hoped for may be rendered, in accordance with the obligation of divine praise, to its benefactors.

First, therefore, we must trace the chronicles of those who reigned in France and Burgundy down to Chlotar, son of Chilperic, in whose time this monastery of Bèze was built by the excellent Duke Amalgarius and his wife Aquilina, and very richly endowed from their own possessions, in the year 600 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the third indiction, while Saint Gregory was pope and head of the holy Roman Church, Mauricius Caesar ruled the commonwealth, and blessed Columbanus was living in Burgundy. Since we intend to make known in succession the abbots who presided here at different times, and the things bestowed upon this place under the rule of each through the generosity of the faithful; and also the bishops of the Church of Langres, who showed themselves generous toward this place, we shall take care to name each individually and to show, one by one, what each gave toward the increase of this house of God. [Col. 0861C]

Thus, under King Childeric, etc. What followed in this Chronicle of Bèze, down to the account of the foundation of the monastery, you will find in the Chronicle of Saint Benignus.

**On the construction of this place in the time of Chlotar II, in the year 600. On Amalgarius. Description of the Bèze.**

[Col. 0862A]

Since we have already stated that this monastery of Bèze was founded by Duke Amalgarius in the time of King Chlotar, we have thought it proper to explain somewhat more fully how and where it was built by him, with what possessions he first enriched it, and how it was afterward enlarged through the very liberal resources of other God-fearing—indeed, God-loving—persons. At that time there were two dukes in Burgundy. One, named Waldelenus, governed the peoples inhabiting the country within the barriers of the Alps and the Jura forests. His wife was named Flavia. Since they had no joy of any heir to whom they might leave after themselves the abundant support of their wealth and honours, through the God-worthy prayers of blessed Columbanus, who presided at Luxeuil, they received a son; and, as Columbanus himself had requested, they offered the child to him to be lifted from the sacred font. Thus the holy man baptized him and gave him the name Donatus. He was afterward trained in wisdom in the same monastery and most illustriously governed the archbishopric of Besançon.

The other duke, most extensive lord of these two regions round about, was named Amalgarius. His wife was called Aquilina, and by her he had sons. To one, named Audalric, he left after himself the government of his duchy. He had another son, named Waldalenus, whom, wishing to offer to God, from whom he had received him, he entrusted through the hands of blessed Columbanus to be educated in the aforesaid monastery of Luxeuil, [Col. 0862C] which then flourished above the other monasteries of Gaul and Burgundy in religious observance. He also had a daughter named Adalsinda, whom he determined should be offered to God and devoted to divine worship.

While these two, Waldalenus and Adalsinda, were being instructed in Christ’s school, their father Amalgarius considered where he might build places suitable to their religious life, and from what resources those who afterward wished to serve God with them might have sufficient food and clothing. Since he wished to establish two folds of Christ in his duchy, and to set over the sheep of both sexes whom God would gather there, from among the children whom God had given him, shepherds—Waldalenus over the men and Adalsinda over the women—he found among the other places in his duchy [Col. 0863A] two that were most beautiful and quite suitable for this purpose.

There is a place between the rivers Saône and Ognon, and beside the river called Tille, where a considerable spring rises, called Bèze; the place itself is also called Bèze. This spring is most clear, fit for drinking, and exceedingly rich in fish of many kinds. Unlike many other springs which, flowing on and increasing, take the name of a river, it is called a river at the very place where it rises, because of its size. Various kinds of herbs grow there, which provide poor people with sustenance if the supply of grain should be insufficient. Thus this spring, watering all the region around it, makes it suitable for nurturing everything sown or cultivated there. The land is quite good and, if there is someone to work it, extremely fertile in crops. [Col. 0863B] There are abundant meadows nearby, by which livestock can be fed and all other domestic needs supplied. The place has woods close at hand and adjoining it, sufficient for constructing buildings and for everything necessary to humankind.

Amalgarius builds the monastery.—Duke Amalgarius therefore judged such a place worthy to offer to God and to His holy apostles Peter and Paul; and, under the authority of his son Waldalenus, he endeavoured to gather monks there who would serve God and His saints under the rule of blessed Columbanus. What more need be said? He appointed Waldalenus abbot there, freely offered the place, as we have said, to God and Saint Peter and Paul with all its appurtenances—lands and buildings, woods and every access, slaves, tenant-farmers, and servants. In short, all that he appeared to possess there he gave most freely and wholly, retaining nothing whatever from it for himself or anyone else. Since he wished by every effort to exalt and enlarge the place, he resolved to enrich it with other properties and appurtenances.

Accordingly, he gave Vieux-Vignes with its appurtenances, and the woods of Tileries, Bèria, Trégias, Cipet, Buxatellum, and Vendovera. He also gave Auxiliacum with its appurtenances, adjoining lands, woods, and tenant holdings; Blaniacum, Bertariacum, Baima, Viriacum, Attiviacum, Noviliacum, the estate of Collatunna, the mill estate, and Marcenniacum, with twelve vineyards, vine-growers, and tenant-farmers who seem to cultivate them. At Cocheiacum he gave vineyards of no small extent. [Col. 0863D] In the district of Beaune he gave eight vineyards with vine-growers and tenant-farmers. In the village called Vaona he gave vineyards and lands, with the male and female slaves cultivating them. With the other possessions, he also transferred to Saint Peter the lands he held at Dijon, at the boundary of Saint Peter, at Longovicum, Canavis, Arsilirias, Tremoldus, Provisus, and Distus. At Gibriacum he gave a considerable quantity of vineyards, with vine-growers and tenant-farmers, woods, meadows, and other adjoining lands, with male and female slaves: everything entirely freely and wholly exempt from every customary claim. Likewise, in the village and at Caciacum, whatever he possessed; and, in the village called Patriniacum, one excellent *mansus* [holding] with its appurtenances. With all these things, he gave the village [Col. 0864A] of Maiescum and its adjoining lands to the aforesaid monastery. Having granted these things and made a charter sealed with his own hand, he delivered them to it for perpetual possession.

Foundation of another monastery by Amalgarius.—These matters having been arranged, and the construction of the monastery of Bèze having been described, since we have mentioned above another place which Amalgarius built in his duchy, where he placed his daughter Adalsinda as abbess over nuns, we think it right to say where that place is, what it is called, and with what appurtenances it was enriched, so that food and clothing would not be lacking to those serving God there. There is a place not far from the city of Besançon, on the river called Doubs, separated from the city only by the course of that river. On the other side it has a mountain called Waldalenus, from the name of the Vandals, who, according to the old inhabitants, had a fortress there. It is called Dornatiacum, also Virzilias, and has a church dedicated in honour of Saint Martin. Duke Amalgarius gave it to his daughter Adalsinda; and, establishing a congregation of nuns so that they might live there regularly under her government, he made a grant from his own possessions: namely, the village called Assona, the village of Parnatiacum, the village of Pontentiacum, and the half which he seemed to possess at Balatunna; likewise from the village of Montaniacum. How, with all these possessions, the aforesaid place of Dornatiacum was later given and joined to the church of Bèze, we shall insert below, where appropriate.

In the thirty-fourth year of Chlotar’s reign, he ordered Warnarius, whom he had made mayor of the palace in Burgundy, to come to him at the estate of Bonogellus with all the bishops of Burgundy and Burgundia, [Col. 0864C] etc., as in the Chronicle of Saint Benignus.

In the sixth year of his reign Dagobert entered Burgundy; and the arrival of Dagobert had struck such fear into the bishops, nobles, and all those dwelling in the kingdom of Burgundy, that all marvelled at the fear inspired by the justice which he administered to the poor. Coming therefore to the city of Langres, and then proceeding to Dijon, and staying several days at Latona, he was so intent upon administering justice to all the people of his kingdom that, from his desire for this benevolence, he could neither bring sleep to his eyes [Col. 0864D] nor take satisfaction in food, as he pondered most earnestly how all might depart from his presence having received justice.

(About the year 634.)—Since, therefore, we have carried our narrative through the succession of kings down to the time of King Dagobert, we have thought it worthy to insert here what benefit Dagobert himself bestowed upon our monastery of Bèze, with what appurtenances he enlarged this place, and how he confirmed it by the authority of his decree, so that what he offered to God and His holy apostles Peter and Paul might remain perpetually inviolate. For, hearing the good report of Abbot Waldalenus, of whom we have spoken above, who then presided over this sacred monastery, he made a gift through Waldalenus’s hand to God and the Church of Bèze from the village called Artasia, with its lands and appurtenances. This village lies within the territory of Campolimis. [Col. 0865A] He also gave the village called Monasteriolus, not far from the aforesaid Artasia and within the same boundaries.

As religious observance increased in this place, Duke Amalgarius, founder of this holy monastery, granted to this church the lands which he had received in benefice from King Dagobert himself: namely, the village of Alteriacum with its adjoining lands, and the village called Boensis with all its appurtenances. He gave all these entire, with the consent and decree of King Dagobert himself. He likewise gave the village of Ginceniacum and the village of Talamara, with all things everywhere belonging to them.

One day King Dagobert, intending to hasten from Latona to Chalon before daylight, entered a bath and ordered Brunulf, the uncle of his brother Aribert, to be killed. Brunulf was killed by the dukes Amalgarius and Arnbert, and by Wilbad. After this King Dagobert proceeded to Chalon, to complete, out of love for justice, what he had begun. Then he went to Autun, thence to Auxerre, afterwards to the city of Sens, and thence came to Paris. Leaving Queen Gomatrude at the estate of Romiliacum, where he had contracted marriage, he took Nantild, one of the girls in her service, and elevated her to queenship, etc., as in the Chronicle of Saint Benignus.

(Year 660.)—King Clovis, therefore, who was also called Chlotar, died in the first bloom of youth after completing eighteen years in the administration of the kingdom, leaving three sons, Chlotar, Childeric, and Theuderic, together with their mother, Queen Balthild. Of these, Chlotar, the eldest by birth, obtained the kingdom of his father Clovis—Neustria and Burgundy—while Childeric acquired the realm of Austrasia and Germany.

Now it seems fitting to insert into our narrative what we promised above to tell: namely, how the place called Dornatiacum, or Birgilias, was given and joined, together with its appurtenances, to this place of Bèze. At roughly the same time, while Donatus, of whom we spoke above, was archbishop of the see of Besançon, Abbess Adalsinda, who presided over that place, afflicted by the wrongs of evil men and by many adversities, and no longer able to endure them, gave that place, with all its appurtenances, into the hand of her brother Abbot Waldalenus, to God and His holy apostles Peter and Paul, with the consent of Donatus, archbishop of Besançon, as the following subscribed letter will show:

To the holy lord and brother beloved in Christ, Waldalenus, Adalsinda, abbess.

> “Since, harassed by the injuries of evil men and by various adversities, I could not remain there, my brother Adalric and I petitioned you and your brethren that I might dwell, in God’s name, at the monastery of Saint Peter under a rule and order; and you granted this out of the zeal of charity. Therefore you ought, in God’s name, to receive the monastery of Dornatiacum, consecrated in honour of St Martin [Col. 0866A], which my father Amalgarius and my mother Aquilina built and endowed with the greater part of their property, together with the estates belonging to that place and all its appurtenances universally: namely, the estate of Assona, the estate of Parniacum, Potentiacum, and the half-share which our parents held in Balatonna. Receive likewise, from this day forward in God’s name, all the remaining property which our parents assigned to that monastery of Dornatiacum. And, from the estate of Montaniacum, which our father Amalgarius and Amoloaldus jointly acquired from the fisc, reclaim our share from this day forward into your lordship, so that neither I nor anyone on our side, nor any opposing person, may presume to raise against [Col. 0866B] you a claim or dispute concerning the aforesaid things. But if anyone does so, let him pay to the most sacred fisc twenty pounds of gold and fifty pounds of silver. Executed publicly at the monastery of Fons Besuus. In God’s name, I, Adalsinda, subscribed this our conveyance. I, the nun Hermena, subscribed at the command of my lady Adalsinda. I, the nun Aga, subscribed at the command of my lady Adalsinda. Daginus subscribed this donation. Mark of Manaulfus, priest. Mark of Victor. Mark of Proculus. Mark of Walibertus. Mark of Landebertus. Mark of Trasgarius. Mark of Rogitus. I, Allo, wrote and dictated this conveyance, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 652, indiction 10, epact 6, while King Clotaire was reigning in Francia, in the first year of his reign, and while the venerable man Donatus held the see of Besançon. [Col. 0866C] On the Wednesday immediately before the middle of February.”

### The monastery of Bèze devastated, and its charters plundered

Accordingly, in the time of King Clotaire, when this place had been most richly endowed and flourished in the pursuit of religion, the devil, the enemy of every good, strove by every effort to ensure that the goods which the faithful had bestowed there should be taken away, and, if possible, consigned to perpetual oblivion. For after the death of Duke Amalgarius, while the Franks were at discord among themselves, fighting one another in civil fury and ravaging the lands under their authority in a war more than civil, it happened that this monastery suffered the violence of such men and sustained the loss of all its possessions—to such a degree that even the documentary instruments [Col. 0866D] of charters and donations which the aforesaid Amalgarius and other God-fearing and God-honouring persons had bestowed upon that monastery were carried off and given over to destruction.

But the aforesaid Abbot Waldalenus, seeking to repair this loss, dealt with Duke Sichelm, then exercising ducal authority in Burgundy, so that he might receive a record concerning the property of the monastery, confirmed by the agreement and subscriptions of many worthy men. Armed with such authority, he therefore approached King Clotaire, made everything known to him, and requested that he might obtain the king’s command for its perpetual protection. The aforesaid king granted his assent and graciously issued his precept. We shall make this clearer from the documents themselves.

### Letter of Duke Sichelm sent to the chief officers of the palace

[Col. 0867A]

To our own lords, REIDEBERT, CHRODEBERT, and EMERULF, chief officers of the household of the sacred palace: SICHELM, with your other faithful men and servants, whose subscriptions or marks are appended below to this petition.

We believe that our most glorious lord has heard how the illustrious man Amalgarius, during his time as duke, constructed a monastery in a place called Fons Besuus, in the district of Attoariensis, in honour of the holy apostles Peter and Paul; that he also gathered there a community of monks to dwell there; and that he assigned to the aforesaid monastery the greater part of his property. We believe also that it has come to your [Col. 0867B] knowledge how, some days ago, that monastery was broken into and laid waste by evil men; how all the property which the monks possessed, together with their charters, was carried away; and how their entire dwelling-place was given over to plunder and devastation. We therefore humbly presume to petition your compassion, that you may bring this to the notice of our most glorious lord, so that in his clemency he may order such an authorization to be drawn up for that place that no one may presume to seize, violate, or disturb the aforesaid goods which worthy men assigned there; but that the monks may be able, in your times and those to come, to possess and hold without disturbance, by your command, the things which they appear at present to have or possess. Thus may they delight more earnestly to pray for God’s mercy for your life, for the stability [Col. 0867C] of your highness, and for your kingdom. Dominicus heard the petition. Farulfus subscribed. Abbo subscribed. Ermerbertus subscribed. Frodoaldus subscribed. Warato subscribed. Fulgoaldus subscribed. Eurcharius subscribed. Given on the day before the Kalends of October, while our lord King Clotaire was reigning.”

They made this petition known to the king; and his precept will declare what he decreed concerning it.

### Precept of King Clotaire — He confirms all that was bestowed upon Bèze

> “Clotaire, king of the Franks, to the illustrious man Duke Sichelm. We believe that the King of heaven—who rules over all kings by limitless power and is ruled by no sovereignty, and who by his mercy and power holds primacy over all angelic thrones—will favour the throne of our kingdom, which he himself entrusted to us to govern, if with devout mind we grant suitable benefits to the places of the saints or confirm them by our decrees.  
>
> Therefore the venerable man Abbot Waldalenus, coming into our presence, represented to the glory of our kingdom that his father Amalgarius and his mother Aquilina had formerly, for the love of God, built by their own labour a monastery called Fons Besuus in the district of the Attoarii, in honour of St Peter and St Paul; that they had gathered monks there under the rule of blessed Columbanus [Col. 0868A] or of blessed Benedict.  
>
> [Note: [Col. 0867] “Or of blessed Benedict.” I have no doubt whatever that these words were transferred from the margin into the text.]  
>
> They had also assigned to that monastery the greater part of their property. But afterward, through hostile plotting, that monastery was broken into and stripped by evil men, and all the charters which the said Amalgarius or his wife had granted there concerning the aforesaid place or other places were carried away along with many other things. Hence the said Waldalenus, supported by your report and seeking security, petitioned our highness that we should confirm by the authority of our precept, in God’s name, whatever property belonged to that monastery and aforesaid place. Desiring by granting his petition to acquire for ourselves eternal and divine reward in all things, know that we have granted and confirmed this.
>
> We therefore command that whatever is established to have been bestowed upon that monastery by the aforesaid Amalgarius and his wife Aquilina, or by other God-fearing men, shall be held, retained, and possessed by it in its entirety, in our own times and in those to come, God helping: namely, Bèze itself with all its appurtenances, lands and buildings, woods and every right of access, slaves, tenant-farmers, and dependants—everything most freely and wholly; Vetusvineas with all its appurtenances and woods; Tilerias, Beria, Tregias, Cypetum, Buxatellum, Vendovera, Auxiliacum with its appurtenances, woods, and tenant holdings; Blaniacum, Berlaria, Bayma, Variacum, Attiniacum, Noviliacum; the estate of Calatunna, the court of Molinensis, Marcennacum with twelve vineyards, vine-dressers [Col. 0868C], and tenant-farmers who appear to cultivate them; at Cocheiacum, vineyards of no small extent; in the district of Beaune, eight vineyards with vine-dressers and tenant-farmers; in the estate called Vaona, vineyards and lands, with the male and female slaves cultivating them; the lands which he possessed at Dijon, in the territory of St Peter, at Longovicus, Canavis, Arzilias, Tremoldus, Provisus, and Distus; at Gibriacum, a considerable quantity of vineyards, with vine-dressers, tenant-farmers, woods, meadows, and all their appurtenances, together with male and female slaves—all without exception most freely held; and in the estate and at Chaciacum, whatever the same Amalgarius possessed. In the estate called Patriniacum, one excellent holding with all its appurtenances; [Col. 0868D] the estate of Majescum with its appurtenances; likewise the estate of Alteriacum and the estate of Boensem, with all their appurtenances; the estate of Talamara and the estate of Ginceniacum. All these things, wholly and freely, with everything belonging to them.
>
> And so that this writing may remain firm and stable forever and may not be altered by any of our successors, we have ordered it to be marked with our name and sealed by the impression of our ring.
>
> Mark of King Clotaire.
>
> Given in the month of August, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 658, first indiction, in the eighth year of Clotaire’s reign. Executed happily at Nîmes.”

[Col. 0869A] He not only confirmed these things, but also appointed as defender and advocate of the aforesaid monastery Gengulfus, a most illustrious man, as his letter will show.

### How Clotaire appointed the blessed Gengulfus advocate of this place

> “The venerable man Abbot Waldalenus, of the monastery of St Peter at Fons Besuus, which his father Amalgarius and his wife Aquilina had formerly been seen to build by their own labour, represented to the clemency of our kingdom that this monastery had been laid waste by evil men and that the instruments of its charters, together with very many other things, had been carried away from it. For this reason he petitioned us that the illustrious man [Col. 0869B] Gengulfus should undertake all the lawsuits of that monastery, in order to pursue and restore them. Know that we have granted him this benefit. Therefore by this present precept we order that, with our permission, he shall have authority to pursue all the aforesaid claims of that monastery and to restore each thing as is just, provided, however, that this shall continue only so long as both parties so wish.
>
> Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth year of the reign of our lord King Clotaire.”

Supported, therefore, by these royal and princely authorizations and aids, the aforesaid Abbot Waldalenus lawfully and peacefully held the property belonging to that monastery, and, as many evidences make clear, observed the monastic order regularly [Col. 0869C] and devoutly with his monks. By his example many embraced the monastic life, granting some of their possessions to the poor and some to that same holy place, in accordance with the Lord’s command. We still retain their donations with their charter instruments.

(Year 664 or 674.) King Clotaire, after holding the kingdom for some years, was overtaken by untimely death and left it without an heir. The princes of the Franks, grieving over his death, raised his brother Childeric, king of the Austrasians—whom they had heard governed his kingdom wisely and prudently—to rule over the whole kingdom of the Franks. Having obtained sovereignty, he very wisely restored to its former condition everything which he found improper and contrary to the laws of earlier kings and of the greatest princes whose life had once been praiseworthy.

(Year 677 or 679.) King Childeric, therefore, after governing the kingdom of the Franks for the few years during which he held it with fair moderation and just laws, died. His brother Theoderic was then elevated in his place to the kingdom, which he held for sixteen years. In his days St Leodegar was killed by Ebroin, mayor of the palace, and St Lambert, bishop of Tongeren, by Count Dodo. These two innocents, slain at one time, obtained the crown of martyrdom. King Theoderic deigned to bestow the bounty of his generosity upon this place, [Col. 0870A] and we have judged it necessary to append a copy of his precept.

### Here begins the precept of King Theoderic — The property of Duke Adalric, adjudged to the royal fisc, is granted by the king to the monastery of Bèze

> “Those who possess benefits seem deservedly to forfeit them when they prove not only ungrateful to the donors of those benefits, but also unfaithful to them. Accordingly, after it had become manifest to all how Duke Adalric, with God opposed to him, had shown himself unfaithful to us and allied himself with the Austrasians, so that he might, if the Lord God permitted, carry out his crimes against us and our faithful men, we ordered all his possessions to be restored to our fisc because of that offence.
>
> Let your eminent dignity therefore know that we have granted wholly, by full and complete favour, to the monastery called Fons Besuus—which is built in honour of St Peter and Paul and the other saints, and over which the venerable man Waldalenus is known to preside—the named property of Fiscafelinis, together with its appurtenances, dependencies, tenant holding, *trevarium* [meaning uncertain], and whatever the aforesaid Adalric held or possessed there from any acquisition. [Col. 0870B] Accordingly, by this our precept we decree and ordain, and we wish it to remain forever, that the said Abbot Waldalenus shall receive and possess in perpetuity, for the aforesaid monastery of Fons Besuus, the aforementioned property together with its buildings, slaves, resident dependants, lands and meadows, woods, pastures, waters, watercourses, every right of access [Col. 0870C], and any other benefits whatsoever, with every usufruct, as a gift of our bounty. And in order that this precept may be held more firmly and observed inviolate in future times, we have decreed that it be strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand.
>
> Mark of King Theoderic.
>
> Given on the fourth day of September, in the fourth year of King Theoderic’s reign.
>
> Glybertus, notary.”

### The first abbots of Bèze

Accordingly, in the time of the aforesaid Waldalenus the monastic order flourished in regular observance. His successors as abbots followed him in monastic governance, like good sons imitating their father’s conduct in regular discipline: namely Bercangus, who succeeded him in office, and Ferreolus, who assumed the governance of the monastery after Bercangus. Syrannus also, a religious man, nobly exercised pastoral care. Thus, with such founders, planters, and waterers, while God gave the increase, monastic observance vigorously flourished in the said cenobium and endured until the time of Pepin, father of Charles the Great. At that time, since the kings had fallen from their former vigour, the administration of the whole kingdom was conducted by dukes and princes of the palace. Foremost among them all was Pepin, whom we mentioned above, a man endowed with every wisdom; and the greater part of that kingdom was in his hands. Having conquered Frisia and driven out the king of that realm, named Radbod, he sent there to preach [Col. 0871A] servants of God who had come from Britain—Willibrord and his companions—who converted no small multitude of people to Christ. After King Theoderic’s death, his son Childebert succeeded to the kingdom.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 709, Pepin went into Suvania, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

### The property of the Church of Langres given to a layman, and the monastery of Bèze to a woman, by the king

In the year 752, Lord Pepin was consecrated king by the hands of Pope Stephen, as were his two sons Carloman and Charles, who was called the Great.

King Pepin had a brother named Remigius, to whom he granted many places in Burgundy. Among these were possessions belonging to the bishopric of the Church of [Col. 0871B] Langres, which he distributed among his followers as he saw fit. But—O wickedness!—he gave this monastery to Angla, wife of a certain Theodard, because he had enjoyed her sexually; he gave it to her not for preservation but for plunder. The monks, justly affronted by this outrage, left the monastery, except for a few weakened by age and infirmity. The rest sought the cenobium of Luxeuil and other monasteries in which they knew that monastic observance endured.

The aforesaid Angla administered the monastery’s property in the manner suited to such a woman. Prevented by those old men who remained from entering the most sacred basilica of the apostles, she restrained herself for a time. But after she had profaned the other sacred places with impunity, she even presumed boldly to enter [Col. 0871C] the oratory itself, and immediately experienced the consequence of raving against God. For, as we learned from trustworthy men who had learned it from those who were present, saw, and heard:

> [Note: [Col. 0871D] A note concerning the author’s period.]

as soon as she entered the aforesaid oratory, she began to burn with an invisible fire. Crying out loudly that she was being consumed, she demanded to be carried to the river Bèze, which flows nearby. This was done immediately, but such water could not extinguish such a fire. Then, admonished and instructed by the aforesaid old men, she ran to the fountain of mercy and thus deserved to be saved; first, however, she confessed her rashness and promised amendment, henceforth renouncing such presumption. She also honoured the aforesaid place with such gifts as she could, some of which are preserved among us [Col. 0871D] as testimony to so great a daring act.

### The monks expelled and canons substituted

But after Remigius had been removed and the bishopric of Langres had passed to lawful bishops, this monastery was recovered by the bishop. Yet he did not exercise the care worthy of a shepherd, to recall the scattered sheep to their own fold; instead he rejoiced that the possessions granted to the monks should accrue to his own use and that of his household. Thus the monastic order was utterly erased from this place, and none of the succeeding bishops cared to restore its former religious life. Some established abbots of the canonical order; others decreed that it should serve themselves, [Col. 0872A] until the reign of Louis of most pious and august memory was reached.

Pepin is inaugurated king. In the fourth year, King Pepin entered Lombardy, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

In the days of Emperor Louis, Betto, bishop of Langres, made certain divisions of the land of St Peter, as we shall show here.

### Property taken from the monks of Bèze is restored

> “Let it be made known to posterity and commended to memory that, before the illustrious man Count Hildegarn, the judges called *scabini*, and many other persons who were present with him at Montaniacum in a public judicial assembly, convened to hear many cases and determine just judgments, Bishop Betto came, together with his advocate Burgoardus, and presented nine lawful witnesses. Their names were Simeon, Agano, Bertramus, Gono, Marchirius, Adalardus, Gervio, Gerento, and Sirannus. They testified and swore concerning the boundaries of the monastery of Bèze that, from the boundary of Pontense, from the boundary of Vendobrinse or Vilense, Vetus-vendobrinse, Vaurinse, Tillense, Vetus-Viniense, Bustellense, Bustense, Lucense, Burbureninse, and the hamlet of Berechelpo, through these boundary-marks, the immunity of St Peter belongs wholly to it; likewise at the place called Wood of the Monks; and at another place called Long Wood, the immunity of St Peter belongs wholly to it. And in another Long Wood, there is common land. And within the very boundary of Bustellense, the immunity belongs wholly to it; and from that boundary of Bustellense as far as the Stony Way; then [Col. 0872C] as far as the Broken Road; and then as far as the boundary of Burburenense and Vilarum, the immunity of St Peter belongs wholly to it.
>
> Traversing these boundary-marks, the nine witnesses named above, with Balacterius, an illustrious man, sent with them by Count Hildegarn and his *scabini*, declared and testified judicially that from the time of King Pepin onward, through the time of the lord Emperor Charles the Great, they had seen lawful investitures there held on behalf of St Peter; so that neither Aldo nor his heirs had ever held any lawful investiture from it, but the investiture of St Peter of Fons Besuus belonged to it by law and justice. Then the *scabini* unanimously judged that these properties, within those boundary-marks, had at all times been vindicated and acquired by legal process for the benefit of St Peter. These witnesses were present: Balacterius, Madalbertus, Beatus, Epplenus, Baldricus, Aiso, Vormerius, Milo, Albricus the notary, Ferlagius, Leuduinus, Arbertus, and Servius. Walterius was present and subscribed. This record was given on the Wednesday immediately following in the month of May, in the second year of the reign of our lord Louis, king and emperor.”

(815.) Record of how, before Bishop Betto and Viscount Balactarius, acting in place of Count Hildegarn, and before the *scabini* present there, Bernard, advocate of the monastery of St Peter of Fons Besuus, and Bishop Betto came to the boundaries of the estate of Bodingis [Col. 0873A] and the estate of Alteriacum. There he produced thirteen witnesses, called by these names: Ursnaldus, Aglardus, Guirindus, Marcherius, Aggo, Symeon, Garinus, Adalardus, Syrannus, Winierius, Ulgerius, Amalerius, Flauminus. They testified that, between those old estates, one of which runs from the estate of Alteriacum to the estate of Colonias, and the other from the estate of Furtum to Vilarum, between these two roads as far as the place called Vaccaria and the spring called Springus, the land belongs to St Peter, in fields as well as woods; and that this house of God—the monastery of St Peter of Bèze—had always been invested in it by law and right. Executed in the presence of Madalbertus, Adalelmus, Viscount Balatterius, Ursnadus, Gunduinus, [Col. 0873B] Flaumirus, Syrannus, Aglardus, Marcherius, Aggo, Girvius, Adalardus, Winerius, Ulgerius, Betto, deputy and envoy of Count Hildegarn, Zizo, Unibaldus, Hugbertus, Aribastus, Vebaltus, and Laipno. I, Aldoerius, reader, wrote this record in the fourth year of the reign and empire of our lord King and Emperor Louis (817).

### How long the monks were exiled from the cenobium of Bèze; why they were recalled; Albericus, bishop of Langres, restores the monastery of Bèze

When the devil, enemy of every good, perceived that this monastery of Bèze flourished in religion, he was grieved that earthly persons should ascend there by humility and obedience, from which he himself had fallen by pride and disobedience. He therefore brought it about that the monastic order was utterly removed from this place. This did not last merely for a short interval, but endured from the time [Col. 0873C] of King Pepin and the time of Charles until the time of Lord Emperor Louis.

For, after Bishop Betto’s death, Louis appointed Albericus, a man worthy of the episcopate, to the Church of Langres. This man is known to have restored the place for the following reason. The aforesaid bishop was at Bèze, healthy and cheerful, when he was suddenly seized by a most severe pain in his intestines; he could obtain no remedy for such agony. While the physicians laboured greatly without effect, he began to despair and to think only of death. As all his people groaned and wept and expected his death, he fell asleep and saw in a dream a venerable man coming to him, distinguished by venerable grey hair. When that man asked [Col. 0873D] how he was, he answered truthfully that excessive pains were pressing him toward death. The other then asked what reward he would render to one who obtained for him from the Lord not only life, but also health and long duration. He replied that, although no recompense could be worthy of such promises, he would nevertheless repay as much as he could and as that man required. Then the old man said:

> “This monastery was consecrated to the Lord under my name and that of my brother Paul, and was inhabited by good brethren and God-fearing monks; but now, as you yourself see, it lies desolate. Promise me, therefore, that you will restore this place and reinstate the monastic order in it, and I shall obtain health for you from the Lord.”

He promised upon oath and awoke from sleep. Immediately [Col. 0874A] every pain left him, as though he had experienced no torment during those days; he rose healthy, and the mourning of all was turned into joy. He recounted what he had seen, what he himself had promised, and on what condition he had deserved health. He begged all to assist in fulfilling the promise. But the works themselves testify better than words with what zeal and care, mindful of his oath and promise, he repaired this monastery. He gathered monks drawn from monasteries, placed an abbot over them, restored not only the possessions belonging to the monastery itself, but also subjected to it other property from the bishopric of his own church, with the counsel of the provincial synod and the consent of his church.

This Bishop Albericus, fearing—because he had learned it by experience regarding the same [Col. 0874B] monastery of Bèze—that the possessions he had given it might again be plundered through the wrongful seizure of successors, took care to confirm by not merely his own but royal authority whatever it then possessed, whether through his own liberality or, in future, that of other faithful persons. He therefore approached Emperor Louis and requested a royal precept on this matter. The emperor consented and confirmed it by his authority, as is written below.

### Precept of Emperor Louis

> “In the name of the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ: Louis and Lothair, august emperors by the ordering of divine providence. If, from love of divine worship, we favour the just and reasonable petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that we shall be strengthened by heavenly grace.
>
> Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable man Albericus, bishop of the Church of Langres, represented to our mildness how he had rebuilt from the foundations a certain abbey called Fons Besuus, from the property of his bishopric: a place where monks had formerly lived in regular observance but which in modern times had been utterly destroyed. He built suitable buildings, gathered monks, and appointed an abbot named Seraphim. In order that the monks gathered there, with God’s help, might serve God better and more freely under the norm of the holy rule, he not only restored there the property that lawfully belonged to the aforesaid abbey [Col. 0874D], but also subjected to it other property from the aforesaid bishopric. He further showed us the charter of foundation by which, with the consent of his metropolitan Archbishop Agobard and his suffragans, as well as the clergy subject to him and certain noble laymen, he had confirmed these arrangements. In it was written more fully that he had not only restored to the said abbey the property lawfully belonging to it, but had also subjected to it certain property from his aforesaid bishopric. These are their names:
>
> Pauliacum with its appurtenances; the village of Bellenavum with its appurtenances; Arcon with its appurtenances. He gave these estates, with all their dependencies and everything situated upon them—fields, meadows, woods, orchards, pastures, rights of access, waters and watercourses [Col. 0875A], and all revenues—wholly and in their entirety, together with slaves, freedmen, all their personal property, and resident dependants, for the monks’ service and for perpetual possession. He made the church located in the estate of Bellenavum, in honour of St Stephen, entirely free from every customary exaction. He also gave the church of the estate called Danbrum, with its appurtenances; the estate of Danblim, with its church and all its appurtenances; the estate of Trescasas, with its church and all its appurtenances; likewise the church of the estate called St-Seine, with its appurtenances; and the church of the estate of Morniacum, with all that belongs to it; also the church in the valley of Verona, in honour of St Maurice; and the church of the estate of Beria, in honour of St Lawrence, [Col. 0875B] with all its appurtenances.
>
> Moreover, in the territory of Dijon, he gave the tithes of those vineyards which Lord Duke Amalgarius, founder of this sacred cenobium, had bestowed upon this church. At the estate called Fiscinis, he gave a considerable quantity of vineyards, with meadows and fields and male and female slaves for their cultivation; likewise vineyards in the estate of Fisciacum and likewise at Marcennacum.
>
> Having made this donation of all these things, he petitioned our clemency as earnestly as he could that they might deserve to have the authority of our confirmation over the same foundation, so that the aforesaid place—which he restored for divine love and for our alms, and in which he gathered monks to pray continually for the Lord’s mercy for us and all the people subject to us—might be confirmed by our authority. That is, if it should please any of his successors to add further possessions there, that authority to do so should remain in his own right and power, with due regard for prudent judgment. Otherwise, his act of devotion, made and confirmed by the counsel of so many worthy men, should remain firm and stable by our precept of liberality.
>
> Judging his petition worthy and reasonable, we ordered these our imperial letters to be issued. By them we decree and command that the aforesaid arrangement which the venerable Bishop Albericus established at the said place shall remain inviolate; that no superior succeeding there shall have authority to alter the prescribed order or in any way take away the property which he restored or subjected there [Col. 0875D]; but that his foundation shall remain firm and stable through this our confirmation. And in order that this authority of our confirmation may possess inviolable and unshaken force in future times, we have ordered it to be marked below with our ring.
>
> Mark of Emperor Louis.
>
> Mark of Lothair, his son.
>
> Executed in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 830, indiction 8, epact 15.”

Having then received the royal authorization, Bishop Albericus returned home. After confirming the properties, as we have said, he drew up his own document so that the matter might be known to those present and those to come. In it, recording everything he had given to this cenobium and what he hoped would thereafter be given through the generosity of future faithful persons, he spoke as follows [Col. 0876A]:

### Charter of Lord Bishop Albericus
> “In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Let it be known to all faithful members of God’s holy Church that I, Alberic, by God’s gift bishop of Langres, found a place now ruined, called Fons-Besuus, built in honour of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of others besides, where monks had formerly served God according to the Rule under Duke Amalgar, with King Clothar’s permission. Therefore, out of love for God and for the forgiveness of my sins, inspired by God, I resolved to rebuild the aforesaid place, with the permission of the most glorious Emperor Louis and the consent of [Col. 0876B] his most devout son, Emperor Lothair. I gathered monks there under an abbot named Seraphim, that they might live according to the Rule and faithfully serve God there for ever.
>
> “For I granted them whatever the aforesaid place had acquired through donations made by charters; and whatever our predecessors had taken away from this place, I willingly restored for the alms of the aforesaid prince and his sons. Therefore, by the counsel of our archbishop Agobard, with the consent of our fellow bishops and also of our most devout princes, of all the clergy, and of all the faithful of our church, we added from our bishopric the following estates: Pauliacum with its appurtenances; the estate of Bellenavum with its appurtenances; and Arcion with its appurtenances.
>
> “These estates, [Col. 0876C] with all adjoining lands and all property situated upon them—fields, meadows, woods, orchards, pastures, rights of access, waters and watercourses, and all revenues—entirely and without exception, together with slaves, freed persons, all their peculium, and resident tenants, I gave for the service of the monks, to be possessed by perpetual right. I also gave the church situated in the estate of Bellenavum, dedicated to Saint Stephen, wholly free from every customary exaction; likewise the church of the estate called Dambrun, with its appurtenances; the estate of Trescasas, with its church and all its appurtenances; likewise the church of the estate called Saint-Seine, with its appurtenances; the church of the estate of Morniac, with everything belonging to it; also the church in the valley of Verona, [Col. 0876D] dedicated to Saint Maurice; and the church of the estate of Beria, dedicated to Saint Lawrence, with all their appurtenances.
>
> “Moreover, in the territory of Dijon, I gave the tithes of those vineyards which Lord Duke Amalgar, founder of this sacred monastery, had bestowed upon this church. At the estate called Fiscinis, I gave a considerable quantity of vineyards, with meadows, fields, male and female slaves for their cultivation; likewise vineyards at the estate of Fisciac; and likewise at Marcennac, for the monks’ sustenance and the feeding of the poor, so that God’s servant may there delight in serving the Lord and continually imploring the Lord’s mercy for the king, his consort, his children, and the stability of his whole empire.
>
> “On this condition, namely, [Col. 0877A] that the aforesaid place should always be subject to the church of Saint Mammes, and that neither I myself nor any of my successors should presume to violate this document, I requested that the lord emperor’s confirmation be made upon it.
>
> “Done publicly in the city of Langres.
>
> “In Christ’s name, I, Agobard, archbishop of the church of Lyons, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Angeric, bishop, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Alberic, bishop, have subscribed to what was made by me.
>
> “In Christ’s name, I, Faova of Chalon, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Modoin of Autun, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Winitarius, unworthy abbot of Calticum, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Audinus, unworthy chorepiscopus, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Motuinus, unworthy priest, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Hiltibald, bishop of Mâcon, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Ragenard, priest, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Jacob, though unworthy chorepiscopus, have subscribed in God’s name. [Col. 0877B]
>
> “I, Sigoald, priest, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Woanilo, priest, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Adalbert, priest, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Simeon, priest, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Unric, deacon, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Bajus, deacon, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Beatus, deacon, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Frideric, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Teuthmar, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Rogenald, have subscribed.
>
> “The mark of Humbert.
>
> “The mark of Hiltann.
>
> “The mark of Bertard.
>
> “The mark of Fulcrin.
>
> “The mark of Eruic.
>
> “The mark of Radald.
>
> “I, Betto, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Bernorogitus, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Ragnoard, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Bavo, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Ragenard, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Hilperic, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Hildigis, priest, have subscribed.
>
> “In Christ’s name, I, Bernard, archbishop, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Godelsad, abbot, have subscribed.
>
> “I, Birico, though unworthy levite, have subscribed.
>
> “Done in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0877C] 830, in the eighth indiction, the fifteenth epact, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [20 November], in the fourteenth year, by Christ’s favour, of the reign of Lord Emperor Louis, and in the sixth year of his son, Emperor Lothair.”
>
> In the time of Lord Bishop Alberic, very many exchanges and purchases of lands were made, both by the bishop himself and by the heads of this place. Among these was an exchange made by our abbot Seraphim and Herlebert, abbot of Dijon. Herlebert gave, in the estates of Lucus and Verona, whatever belonged by right to Saint Benignus; and in return Seraphim transferred lands of Saint Peter situated at Dijon, in the district of Lord Peter and Longovico, and at Canavis, Arzilerias, Tremoldo, Fontanis, Proviso, and Disto.
>
> Nor was it enough for Bishop Alberic, this place’s lover, most generously to enlarge it during his own lifetime; having heard that Bishop Betto, his predecessor, had legally defined the boundaries of Besua’s territory by nine lawful witnesses, he confirmed the same by his authority. At that time a certain man named Hligarius gave this place land from his inheritance at Aquatovilla, for the remission of his sins: namely, one demesne holding, together with a house and granary. This land measures forty-three arpent-rods and ten feet in length, and at its upper end nine rods and four feet in width. He gave it all entire, with lands, enclosed homestead-plots, buildings standing upon it, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters, and watercourses. [Col. 0878A]
>
> Likewise, a certain man named Widald sold to Lord Bishop Alberic one holding of land in the estate of Casoto, and seven dayworks of land. Lord Alberic gave it to Saint Peter. Likewise another man, named Aylard, sold to Lord Bishop Alberic, through the hands of Abbot Seraphim, property belonging to him situated in the county of Atuyer, in the place called Bustellus and in the district of Bustellus and its vicinity: whatever his mother was seen to possess there, in holdings, fields, meadows, woods, orchards, pastures, and every right of access. There were twelve witnesses, including Radulf and Amalric. This was done on the Kalends of February [1 February], in the sixteenth year of Louis’s reign.

### Charter of Abbot Theuto

Likewise an exchange was made between Seraphim, abbot [Col. 0878B] of Besua, and Abbot Theuto of the monastery of Saint Leodegar, called Capellense. Its text is as follows:

> With the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, it pleased and was agreed before Lord Alberic, bishop of Langres, between Abbot Seraphim and Abbot Theuto of the monastery of Saint Leodegar, that they should exchange certain lands of Saint Peter of Besua and Saint Leodegar for their common advantage. This they did.
>
> Abbot Theuto gave from his portion to that of Seraphim, before Bishop Alberic in the monastery of Saint Peter of Besua, one enclosed homestead-plot situated in the estate of Besua. This plot measures forty-eight arpent-rods in length and three arpent-rods and seven feet in breadth. On both sides lies land of Saint Peter.
>
> [Col. 0878C] Bishop Alberic and Abbot Seraphim, from the land of Saint Peter of Besua, gave to Abbot Theuto of Saint Leodegar one enclosed homestead-plot situated in the estate of Baciac. On one side it is bounded by land of the monastery of Flavigny, and it measures sixteen arpent-rods, and five arpent-rods in breadth. Likewise, in another place within the same district of Baciac, they gave one small parcel of land measuring eight arpent-rods in length and four arpent-rods in breadth.
>
> If anyone—something we do not believe will happen—whether one of our heirs or any other person, should attempt to act against this exchange, let him pay to the person against whom he brings suit two ounces of gold.
>
> Done publicly at the monastery of Fons-Besuus, on the third day before the Kalends of April [30 March], in the thirteenth year of the reign of Lord Emperor Louis.

### Charter concerning Bustellus

In the fifteenth year of Louis’s reign, Lord Alberic, bishop of Langres, purchased from a woman named Adda, and from Laburdus, Albuin, and Laibulf, land situated in the place called Bustellus, in the district of Vetus-vineae: everything which they appeared to possess at Bustellus and Blaniac, including lands, enclosed homestead-plots, buildings standing upon them, fields, meadows, woods, cultivated lands, orchards, pastures, waters, watercourses, and every right of access. [Col. 0878D] They sold everything entire and received fifty solidi as the price.

### Another [charter]

In the eighteenth year of Louis’s reign, Lord [Col. 0879A] Alberic, bishop of Langres, again bought the slaves Arlebard and Hayco, together with a female slave named Humeldi and her daughters Adalberga and Eldeardis, from a certain Nerduin, who received fifteen solidi as the price.

Louis the Pious, exchanging the earthly insignia of kingship for everlasting blessedness in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 840, etc., as in the Chronicle of Saint Benignus.

### On the death of Bishop Alberic

It is not within our power to show in words how great was Lord Bishop Alberic’s devotion toward this place, or how much he loved it. Yet, if our words do not suffice for this, his works and benefactions cry aloud and demonstrate it. For it is clear that he loved this monastery above all things because he omitted nothing that he could obtain for this place from any source.
>
> We have recorded some of his gifts, insofar as the weakness of our memory could recall them. Some we still retain and possess; others we have lost, partly through our own weakness and partly through the faithlessness of those who seized them. We possess a pallium very beautiful to behold, in which doves are woven in orderly sequence and with great beauty, from which he wore a mitre for many days. We have books which he offered to the holy apostles Peter and Paul: one Gospel-book; Augustine *On the Literal Meaning*; the Book of Kings with the Acts of the Apostles in the same volume; and Bede on Luke.
>
> For not without reason did he hope to obtain from the Lord Jesus Christ salvation and life for his soul through those by whom he had received bodily health and well-being. [Col. 0879B–C] Trusting in the constancy of this hope and faith, after he had sent many things before him to this place, and when he drew near the end of his life, he wished to be buried in this monastery; and this was done. His blessed body lies at the right side of the altar of Saint Mary; may his soul rest in peace with the elect and the saints. Amen.

### Charter concerning Auxiliacum

Walcaud, abbot of Besua.—At the same time, after the death of Abbot Seraphim, who had held the office of shepherd in this place, Abbot Walcaud succeeded to the governance of souls, performing the same ecclesiastical office. Likewise, when Alberic, bishop of Langres, died, Bishop Teutbald obtained the see. Like his predecessor, he was a diligent patron of this place and made exchanges of land with certain persons in several places.
>
> For a certain man named Eurulf, for the remedy of his soul and by Bishop Teutbald’s counsel, gave Saint Peter of Besua monastery one field situated in the estate called Auxiliacum. It is bounded on one side by land of Saint Leodegar; on the other by the donors’ own heirs; on one end by a running stream; and on the other by the public road. Within these boundaries he conveyed the whole without exception to Saint Peter.
>
> In another place he also gave one field in the same estate, bounded on one side by common woodland and on the other by the public road; on one end by Godefrid’s land, and on the other by the heirs’ own land. [Col. 0879D–0880A] Likewise, in another place he gave one meadow bounded at one end by a running stream, while the heirs hold the other end and one side.
>
> The mark of Adalmar. The mark of Odolgar.

### Charter concerning Maiascus

Lord Bishop Teutbald and Abbot Walcaud made an exchange of lands with a certain man named Wlfric. Wlfric gave from his portion to that of Saint Peter one field situated in the county of Atuyer, in the estate called Maiascus, or in the same district. It is bounded on one side by land of Saint Peter, on the other by the donor’s own land, on one end by land of Saint Mammes, and on the other by the public road. It measures twenty-five rods and ten feet in length, eleven rods in width, and on the two ends eleven rods and four feet. In return Abbot Walcaud gave, from Saint Peter’s portion to Wlfric’s, one field situated in the county of Atuyer, in the estate called Maiascus. [Col. 0880B]
>
> Wherever he could, Bishop Teutbald took care to improve our place. After his death Lord Isaac received the episcopate. Following the good example of his predecessors, he bestowed many benefits upon this monastery.
>
> Charles, therefore, surnamed the Bald, having obtained the empire, was a devout cultivator of God’s churches. With every effort in his power he strove to correct what had been corrupted in religious observance, rebuild what had been destroyed, and raise up what had fallen. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 871, while ruling [Col. 0880C] the kingdom of the Franks, he was most zealous for the worship of the Church; consequently he overcame many dangers, and the glory of his kingdom continually increased.
>
> When his brother Pippin, king of Aquitaine, had died and Pippin’s son had succeeded to the kingdom, the latter failed to govern the realm energetically; he was abandoned and deposed by his own men, became a monk in the monastery of Saint Medard, and Charles, sought by all the princes, obtained the kingdom of Aquitaine. A few years later, when his brother Emperor Lothair died, Charles received the empire. But Louis, another brother, wishing to seize the monarchy of the kingdom, again stirred up war against Charles and summoned the Northmen and other peoples into Charles’s realm. With the Lord’s help Charles expelled his brother from his territories [Col. 0880D] and contained the Northmen within Neustria. This was the second invasion of the Northmen into Francia. Some years later Louis died, leaving three sons: Louis, Carloman, and Charles.

### Charter concerning Lucus

Warino and Teutbert, abbots.—When Abbot Walcaud died, Warino succeeded him. In his days a man named Baldric, for the remedy of his own soul, that of his father Romanus, and those of his other ancestors, gave Saint Peter one holding situated in Upper Lucus, or in the estate of Lucus itself, with all its appurtenances. It is bounded on one side and at one end by land of Saint Marcellinus, and on the other side and the other end by the fisc.
>
> Of his own property situated in the same county and in the district of Lucus, or in the estate of Lucus itself, he likewise transferred to that monastery in perpetual right one holding with the aforementioned appurtenances—fields, meadows, enclosed homestead-plots, woods, pastures, orchards, and one mill at Busceria—together with waters, watercourses, rights of egress and regress, and every right of access: whatever he had from his parents’ portion or had acquired by documentary charters. [Col. 0881A]
>
> Some years later a certain man named Utlaius, before his lady Eva in the field called Limito, asserted that he ought to have a share in the mill which the cleric Josmund and his brother Baldric had given to Saint Peter at Lucus without anyone’s objection. Eva therefore ordered her faithful men to go with the aforesaid Utlaius to the monastery of Besua to investigate the case. Aldric then came on Utlaius’s behalf with many others, bringing suit concerning the aforesaid mill against the abbot and monks. The monks had many witnesses, whereas Utlaius had none, for everyone knew that he was a liar. Thus frustrated in his hope, he relinquished to the monks and formally renounced everything he had claimed.
>
> Afterwards Abbot Teutbert, who had succeeded the aforesaid Warino, granted the mill back to Utlaius on the condition that, should it fall into a worse state, he should pay thirty solidi. This mill is bounded on both sides by linden trees; Isaac and his wife hold one end; and at the other are a right of egress and regress and the path leading to this mill. [Col. 0881B–C]

### Charter concerning Vetus-vineae

A certain knight of the fortress of Dijon, named Epplenus, for the remedy of himself and his parents, gave this church of Besua, in the estate called Veteres-vineae, or within its boundaries, so much arable land as could be sown with one hundred modii of grain.

### Charter concerning Auxiliacum

Another man, named Roger, gave the same church one field, situated in the county of the Atuyers, in the estate of Auxiliacum. It is bounded [Col. 0881D] on one side by land of Saint Peter, on the other by fiscal land, on one end by the public road, and on the other by the running river Vincenna.

### Charter concerning Lucus

While the venerable Bishop Isaac sat in his episcopal chair at the estate of Basiac, and all his clergy eagerly assembled from every direction, along with a considerable company of noble abbots, archdeacons, priests, and the whole assembly in general synod to settle ecclesiastical cases, a dispute arose, among the other holy deliberations which they held together, between Ansuin, priest of Saint Martin at Lucus, and Adalard, priest of Saint Marcellinus in the same small estate, concerning the tithes of those churches.
>
> Ansuin asserted [Col. 0882A] that every tithe in its entirety had from ancient times belonged to his church. Adalard, on the contrary, maintained and vigorously contended that it ought rather to belong wholly to his own church. Thereupon in that synod highly distinguished and competent witnesses for the aforesaid priest Ansuin arose. By true proofs they refuted Adalard and established and determined that the ancient arrangement should stand: namely, Abbot and Archdeacon Magenard; Otbert, who held the same office of archdeacon; Arnold, distinguished by the same rank; Isaac; Fredrad; Adalmann; Evorin; and almost the whole synod. Priest Ansuin was amply confirmed and strengthened by the testimony of these truth-speaking witnesses; and thus each of them received an end to this complaint.
>
> These things were done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 870, in the third indiction, while King Charles was reigning and the venerable Bishop Isaac governed the church of Langres. [Col. 0882B]

### Death of Lord Bishop Isaac

Bishop Geilo succeeds Bishop Isaac; the body of Saint Prudentius is bestowed on Besua.

When Bishop Isaac ended the day of this life, Geilo was appointed bishop in his place. He was most friendly to this monastery of Besua, and, of almost all those better than ourselves, the best to us. Others had provided us with earthly aid; he secured for us before God the patronage of souls.
>
> Returning from Aquitaine, he brought to this place the body of the most blessed martyr Prudentius and, as was fitting, placed it with many other pledges of saints, to implore God for himself and for [Col. 0882C] us. In their honour and reverence he offered certain property from his episcopal estate to provide lights, and, having legally and publicly made a donation of what he offered, issued this document as follows.

### Concerning what Bishop Geilo bestowed upon this place

> We wish all persons of every dignity, high and low, of either sex and every rank, to know how I, Geilo, humble bishop of the church of Langres, moved by the inspiration of almighty God, have placed with worthy honour the most blessed Prudentius, martyr of Christ, in the monastery of Besua, built in honour of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.
>
> This blessed martyr shone by miracles before the entrance to the atrium, at the entrance of the church, and thereafter, as has been made clear to all Christ’s faithful round about. Therefore, moved by the will of the divine majesty, I bestowed upon him, for the provision of lights, some revenue of Saint Mammes in Upper Lucus: namely, the chapel of Saint Marcellinus, with its appurtenances and slaves of both sexes, which I had recently recovered from the bishop of Verdun by a fitting exchange. I also bestowed upon the most holy martyr Prudentius Pontiliacum with its adjoining lands, and the church consecrated in the same place in honour of Saint Hippolytus. [Col. 0882D] I likewise assigned to that saint in its entirety the church of Chasuit with all its appurtenances, so that from this day onward he may have, hold, and possess these gifts for ever, without opposition.
>
> “From my successors, for God’s sake and on account of God, I earnestly ask only this: if they wish to add something, let them do so; but if not, let them not take away or remove these small gifts bestowed by us. And if any, tempted by the devil, should attempt to seize these gifts, let no place in the Church be granted them among other Christians; and, unless they quickly come to their senses, let them be subjected to curses with Dathan and Abiram, with Judas the betrayer of the Lord, and to the punishments of Gehenna. Moreover, let them pay five pounds of gold in compensation to the refectorers of the church of Besua.
>
> “I, Geilo, humble bishop, performed this conveyance in a synodal assembly and asked that it be confirmed. In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 883, in the first indiction, the ninth epact, while Charles the Great was reigning [Note: [Col. 0883D] ‘Caroto Magno.’ Or ‘Carloman.’]. The mark of Lord Bishop Geilo, donor of these [Col. 0883B] goods. The mark of Elias. The mark of Obert. The mark of Galcaud. The mark of Helgaud. The mark of Arnald. The mark of Guntard. The mark of Odo and of all the others who were present at that synod, on Sunday, the eighth day before the Ides of October [8 October].”

### Charter concerning the church of Saint Martin at Lucus

Synod of Chalon.—In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 886, and in the second year of the reign in Gaul of Lord and most serene Emperor Augustus Charles, in the fifth indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June [18 May], a sacred assembly of bishops met in Christ’s name at the church of Saint Marcellus the martyr, in the suburb of Chalon, to establish the peace and tranquillity of God’s holy Church and settle ecclesiastical business. Present were the lords and most holy archbishops Aurelian and Bernuin, together with the most reverend bishops [Col. 0883C] Adalgarius, Geilo, Stephen, Gyrald, Adalbald, Isaac, and Leboin.
>
> Geilo, the aforesaid most reverend bishop of the church of Langres, seated in this most sacred assembly with the fathers named above, informed them of the notice written above: namely, that Lord Isaac, his predecessor, in his holy synod had justly and legally recovered for the church of Saint Martin at Upper Lucus, from Saint Marcellinus’s chapel, against Adalard, priest of that chapel, the property and tithes of the church at Lucus.
>
> On hearing this, all the aforesaid bishops agreed with Bishop Geilo’s common report and with the record of Lord Isaac’s recovery, and by agreeing confirmed it: if anyone, convicted of rash and sacrilegious presumption and blinded by blind greed, should presume in any respect to violate what we confirm by the authority of God, Lord Isaac, and ourselves, let him know that he will be punished with eternal damnation, burned in everlasting fire with the devil and his angels, tortured with Judas the betrayer of the Lord and with Dathan and Abiram in perpetual punishment; and further, let him be held an exile from the thresholds of God’s holy Church and from the fellowship of all faithful Christians [Col. 0883D], until, repenting of his unlawful presumption, he is restored by fitting penance.

### Charter concerning Middle Lucus

In those days a man named Isaac gave to the monastery of Besua one holding situated in the county of Atuyer, in the estate called Middle Lucus. It is bounded on one end by the running river Phila and on the other by the public road.
