The aforesaid Isaac also gave the same place, in the district called Mount Mainbert, at the place called Spinido, two dayworks of land; in another place called Cabrario, two dayworks; and in another place called Fontinella, three dayworks. He conveyed this gift to Walcaud, then abbot of that place, and to his successors in perpetuity. [Col. 0884A]

### Charter concerning Vetus-vineae

Another man named Ingelger and his wife Amalild sold the brothers of the monastery of Besua one garden in the estate called Veteres-vineae. It is bounded on one side by land of their own inheritance, on the other by land of Saint Leodegar, on one end by land of Saint Peter, and on the other by the public road. The garden measures, on the end adjoining Saint Peter’s vineyard, two arpent-rods and six feet; on the other end, one rod; and in length eleven rods and nine feet. Within these measurements and boundaries, the aforesaid Ingelger sold the whole without exception to the monks of Besua. Having received from them two solidi and eight denarii as the price, he granted it to them for perpetual possession. [Col. 0884B]

### Another [charter]

A man named Otger, for the remedy of the souls of his father Isaac and his brother Waldric, gave Saint Peter of Besua monastery a slave named Amalerius, because Waldric, the donor’s brother, had put out the eyes of a slave of Saint Peter called Lanfred. [Col. 0884C]

### Charter concerning Novus Vicus

Likewise, a certain Bernard and his wife Miltrudis gave to Teutbert, abbot of Besua, and to the monks living under him, a share in a vineyard situated in the county of the Atuyers, in the estate of Novus Vicus, so that they might have power to do with it whatever they preferred.

### Charter concerning Villare

A knight from the county of Portus, named Aigard, and his wife Rotlind, granted to the servants of the most blessed Peter in the monastery of Besua all property belonging to them by right situated in the county of Portus, in the estate called Villare: everything that they possessed in the estate or within its boundaries—fields, meadows, pastures, tithes, streams, springs, waters, watercourses with their appurtenances, and whatever could be spoken or named, and whatever the monks could claim there in their name. [Col. 0884D] Having received from the monks a price amounting to four pounds of silver, they confirmed so great a gift by testament and decreed that the monastery should possess it perpetually.

### Another charter

A certain man named Guttin gave the same monastery of Besua one holding in the county of Atuyer, and everything belonging to that holding: fields, meadows, woods, waters, and slaves of both sexes dwelling there. [Col. 0885A]

### Charter concerning Pontus

A certain Aurailus and his wife Ermengard sold the monks of Besua one holding with its appurtenances—fields, meadows, woods, pastures, fruit trees, waters, and watercourses—situated in the county of the Atuyers, in the estate called Pontus. It is bounded on one side by land of Saint Leodegar, on the other by fiscal land, on one end by the public road, and on the other by meadows.
>
> They also sold their other property situated in the district of Vendour, in the district of Pontus, and in the district of Lulus. Having received sixty solidi from the monks for this grant, they transferred it to their authority for perpetual possession. [Col. 0885B]

### Another [charter]

A knight named Waldrann, for the repose of his own soul and those of his parents, gave the aforesaid monastery a female slave named Lampas, to serve there with all offspring descended from her. Every year on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul she was to pay two denarii and perform every service required of the other tenant women.

### Charter concerning Lujat

A woman named Landrada likewise gave the monastery of Besua a holding belonging to her by right, situated in the estate called Lujat. The holding is bounded on one side by Flammeria’s land, on the other by land of Saint Leodegar, on one end by the public road, and on the other by the running river Thila. [Col. 0885C]

### Another charter

A tenant of Saint Peter named Vautsonius and his wife Manuheldis gave the often-mentioned place a slave belonging to them by right, named Gunduin, on the condition that he should remain a tenant, as Vautsonius himself was.

### Another [charter]

A knight named Hugh, for the repose of his own soul and those of his ancestors, gave to the place of Besua a slave named Wlfing, together with his wife Ayma and their children Ermenasia, Suffucia, Susanna, Adalsina, Supplicia, and Godolberga. [Col. 0885D]

### Charter concerning Picangiae and Mercennacum

A noblewoman named Wandalmodis, for the repose of the soul of her husband Humbert and of her other ancestors, gave to the place of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Prudentius the martyr, in the estate of Fractomons, a slave named Gundulf with his sons Wlferius, Waringaud, and Rambald, and half a holding which they themselves held, subject to this service: every year they were to render for the monks’ corvée one daywork of wheat and another of oats, eulogiae, and two denarii in wax.
>
> [Col. 0886A] The same Wandalmodis also gave the aforesaid place, in the estate of Picangiae, a slave named Humbert with his mother Plectrud, one holding there, and everything belonging to it. Likewise, in the county of Dijon, in the estate of Mercennac, she gave the same place one daywork of vineyard.

### Charter concerning Vivarius

A noblewoman named Eva gave the church of Besua property belonging to her by right situated in the county of the Atuyers, in the place called Vivarius: namely, the estate itself called Vivers. She granted the aforesaid place the whole without exception, together with everything adjoining it: holdings, male and female slaves, enclosed homestead lands, woods, waters, watercourses, and slaves of both sexes. By the hand of a slave named Ajembald, she invested the aforesaid church of Besua with these goods. [Col. 0886B]

### Charter concerning Brescon

A levite named Elias gave, in the county of Dijon, in the estate of Brescon, one well-cultivated vineyard to provide lights for the same church of Besua, that it might possess it perpetually without any opposition.

### Charter concerning Fissiacum

A certain Adoerius, converted from a layman in the same monastery, gave one vineyard in the estate called Fissiacum in the county of Dijon. It is bounded on one side by land of Saint Benignus of Longovico, on the other by the public road, on one end by the vineyard of Saint Mary of Balma, and on the other by land of Saint Eusebius of Escubili. [Col. 0886C]
>
> This vineyard measures twenty-four arpent-rods in length on one side; on the other, twenty rods and two feet; on one end, twenty rods; and on the other, fifteen rods and seven feet.

Emperor Charles, preparing to go to Rome for a second time, entered Italy. Karloman, son of King Louis, his brother, entered the same land by another route with an immense army and confronted him. Charles returned to Gaul and, on reaching the territory of Lyons, died there. He was buried in the monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul, at the place called Nantoade, from the multitude of waters flowing together there. Afterwards, by angelic warning, he was transferred from there and interred at Paris with royal burial in the church of Saint Denis. Louis succeeded his father on the throne, scarcely bearing the royal title for two years. In his days Pope John of Rome came to Francia, conferred with that king at the city of Troyes, remained there a short time, and thus returned to Rome. [Col. 0886D]

In these days the savage nation of the Danes arrived to inflict a third calamity upon Neustria, and would have inflicted one greater than the preceding ones had not Hugh, distinguished with the office of abbot throughout Gaul, restrained their reckless ventures. With God’s help, with a small band he routed such great formations of the enemy that scarcely anyone survived who could have reported it. Humbled by this defeat, the Danes left Gaul undisturbed for a certain period. King Louis commanded this war.
>
> But when Hugh was closing the last days of his life, and Prince Louis, after administering the kingdom for the two years mentioned above, died, Charles—later called the Simple—was left fatherless while still an infant in the cradle. There remained two sons of Robert, count of Anjou, brothers of Abbot Hugh: the elder was named Odo, the other Robert, bearing his father’s name. Because renewed incursions of the Northmen threatened, the Franks chose the elder, Odo, as guardian of the boy and governor of the kingdom. [Col. 0887A]
>
> In those parts of the kingdom which Lothair and Louis had held, the sons of the same Louis reigned, for Lothair had died without children. Of these three brothers, one was called by his father’s name, another Carloman, and the third Charles. But when two died within five years, supreme power passed to the younger Charles, who afterwards acquired the monarchy of the empire. [Col. 0887B]
>
> A certain writer relates, etc., as in the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus*.
>
> In these times the year 891 of Christ’s Incarnation was passing.
>
> ### On the destruction of this place
The aforesaid and venerable Bishop Geylo, as he approached death, recognizing that he too had much within himself to leave behind or to purge before he should meet, with us all, at the general resurrection, commended in death to Him in whose sight not even the heavens themselves are clean—the One whom he had served in life—not only his soul but also [Col. 0887C] his body. He therefore ordered that his body be conveyed to this monastery of Bèze; and, entrusting his whole self to God and to His holy apostles, to whom it has been given to shut heaven or to open it to whom they will, and likewise to the patronage of the most glorious other saints whose relics are kept here, he was buried with his predecessor Alberic, likewise bishop of Langres.

At approximately the same time, as it is written, sorrow was mingled with our laughter, and mourning seized the end of our joy. For when the Northmen came through Francia into Burgundy, this monastery of Bèze came to be utterly laid waste. And since we find that this place was violated and destroyed seven times by faithless Christians or by pagans, [Col. 0887D] this final destruction is not without reason called by us, emphatically, “the desolation of desolations.” Let us therefore say, insofar as we have scarcely been able to recover it from our ancient little parchments, how and by whom it was devastated six times, so that we may then proceed to discuss somewhat more fully this final and most terrible desolation.

The first time it was devastated by Christians in civil wars: invading this place, they carried off, along with other things, all the documentary titles. We have already made some mention of this above. Another time it was devastated by the Vandals, faithless pagans. The third time was by the Saracens, when they destroyed the city of Autun in the year 831 from the Incarnation of the Lord. It is also reported that on one occasion this place was abandoned by the monks [Col. 0888A] because of fear of a certain disease that was ravaging this region. The fourth time was in the days of Remigius, brother of King Pippin and son of Charlemagne, through a woman named Angla, to whom the aforesaid Remigius had given this place; we have likewise mentioned this above. Whoever wishes to know the sequence of that affair more fully should turn to that brief narrative in the description. But this too must be known: from that time until Lord Alberic, who restored this place, monastic observance ceased there entirely.

We must now speak of that final desolation, which harmed not merely this place but all Francia, while the Northmen laid it waste and the Franks found nowhere a secure strength from which to resist. [Col. 0888B] Many bodies of saints were brought into the fortress of Dijon because it seemed most strong and impregnable. Some were later carried back, while others remained there; still others were transferred elsewhere.

The body of blessed Medard, bishop, was brought from Soissons. The body of most blessed Silvinus, their bishop, was brought by the people of Thérouanne. The body of our own patron, most blessed Prudentius, was likewise brought there and placed in the basilica of St Stephen, where it remained for many years. At length, with God propitious to us and peace restored, the body of most blessed Prudentius was carried back from there; and the body of blessed Silvinus, together with blessed Angla, his most intimate companion, was given to us by God. Thus it came about that, as the chief protection of this place belongs to Peter, prince of the apostles, together with Paul, [Col. 0888C] most blessed martyr Prudentius adorns one side of it, and blessed Bishop Silvinus, with venerable Angla, the other.

We have delayed our account of our desolation for a little while, unwilling that it should be covered in silence how, after we seemed bereft of our patron, God afterwards provided two for us in place of one. Now let us return to the matters we omitted.

When the monks who were here heard of the Northmen’s arrival, some hid themselves through fear of punishment and death, while others migrated to other monasteries. Nor is this surprising, since those who remained here were slain by the sword. Their names are these: the monk Ayrmannus; the monk Genesus; the monk Beraldus; [Col. 0888D] the monk Sifardus; the monk Rodco; Ansuinus, priest; and Adalricus, a little boy. All these were piously slaughtered for Christ, rendering vengeance to God; having become a sacrifice to God, in the year 838 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

### Duke Richard attacks the Northmen

Nevertheless, since no one was found who could or dared resist them, there was in those same days a certain duke in our region, named Richard, who, on account of his zeal for justice, was himself called the Justifier. Partly inflamed by zeal for his country’s liberty, but much more for the defense of God’s churches, and having God as his helper, he undertook to fight them. Although the hostile attack advanced as far as this Bèze, [Col. 0889A] and the madness of their frenzy raged here so violently that, as we said above, they killed our monks with swords and devastated everything—to such an extent that, for the entire four days, they dried up by the drinking of innumerable quadrupeds even the spring itself, which pours forth from itself the stream of a great river—yet neither the strength of the place nor the fearsome martial prowess of the renowned duke permitted them to press on to Dijon. Rather, the aforesaid Duke Richard met them at a place called Argenteuil; battle being joined, a very great multitude of them was slain. Thus the Danes together with the Northmen were forced to turn back.

In the year 893 from the Incarnation of the Word, while Odo was reigning, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

In the year 911 from the Incarnation of the Word, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August [21 July], [Col. 0889B] a Saturday, while the Northmen were besieging the city of Chartres and it was already on the point of being taken, Richard and Robert arrived with their men, strengthened by God’s aid and the patronage of Blessed Mary. They made a very great slaughter of the pagans, taking hostages from the few who remained. This same Richard had a son named Rodulf, who became king of the Franks. Another son was called Boso, who received the kingdom of Upper Burgundy, called Gallia Comata. A third son was named Hugh, surnamed Capet, who was duke of Lower Burgundy. Discord having arisen between Charles and the princes of the realm, disputes and wars, plunder and conflagrations, innumerable evils raged everywhere. At length the king, repenting of what had happened, moved the princes toward concord and established with them the desired peace.

### [Col. 0889C] Exchange made between Abbot Walcaud and Teuthard

At that time an exchange was made between a certain Teuthard and Abbot Walcaud concerning lands that appeared to be under their respective jurisdiction. Thus Teuthard gave, from his portion, to Abbot Walcaud’s portion one field situated in the district of Atois, in the territory of Pauliacum; and, in return, Abbot Walcaud gave from his portion to Teuthard one field situated in that same territory of Pauliacum.

### Death of Geylo

Teuthbald and Agrinus, or Algrinus, succeeded Geylo, bishop of Langres. After Bishop Geylo died, Teuthbald succeeded him. When he too had died, Bishop Agrinus succeeded him, very diligent in pastoral care. [Col. 0889D] He restored to us Pontiliacum and the church of St Hippolytus, which a certain Waltarius had unjustly taken away, as we shall show here.

### Charter and confirmation of Bishop Agrinus concerning the gifts made by Bishop Geylo to this place

> “Agrinus, humble bishop by the disposing mercy of God, to all the faithful of God’s Church, of either sex and every rank, dwelling wherever they may be. It has become known to many how Bishop Geylo, of pious memory, my predecessor, transferred St Prudentius from Aquitaine, brought him into our bishopric of Langres, and solemnly placed him in the monastery of Bèze to the praise and glory of God’s name. There, for love of God and [Col. 0890A] reverence for that same St Prudentius, he bestowed upon the same monastery certain possessions of his church—namely, Pontiliacum with its appurtenances and a church consecrated in honour of St Hippolytus—so that they might in future times contribute to the increase of the monks and servants of God serving the Lord there.
>
> “After he was taken from this life, just as the remaining possessions of our church were, without reason, dispersed at the will of plunderers, so Pontiliacum also was sacrilegiously seized and improperly alienated by Waltarius, as is most certain, from the place to which it had been granted by the aforesaid bishop. Therefore Gaulcaud, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Bèze, came with his brother monks before our humility and made known, with tearful complaints, the injury unjustly inflicted upon the place; and he humbly begged that, through our generosity, [Col. 0890B] what had been improperly taken away should be restored, for love of God and reverence for Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and for holy Prudentius.
>
> “We therefore received his petition in a fatherly way. Having discussed it with the faithful clerics and laymen of our church, and having found it just, reasonable, and right, by the counsel and consent of our entire church, as the aforesaid possessions were granted to the oft-mentioned place by our predecessor, so we also now grant them, and by this our authority, under the reign of our Lord, consecrate them in perpetuity.
>
> “And so that this present restoration of ours may retain inviolable force in future times and may suffer thereafter no improper and unjust loss, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it to be confirmed by the subscriptions of [Col. 0890C] our faithful men, humbly and earnestly urging our successors, through the holy and inseparable Trinity, to preserve inviolate what has been piously established by us. I, Agrinus, humble bishop of the holy church of Langres, have strengthened and signed this in Christ’s name. I, Otbert, provost and archdeacon, have signed. Bernard, archdeacon, signed. Madalgaud, deacon, signed. Isaac, archdeacon, signed. Emmarricus, archdeacon, signed. I, Ewardus, deacon, have signed. I, Helgaudus, priest, have signed. Arnaldus, archdeacon, signed. Fuculsus, deacon, signed. Albericus, deacon, signed. Aclevertus, subdeacon, signed. Wlleus, subdeacon, signed. Siquinus, subdeacon, signed. I, Josselmus, acolyte, have signed. I, Gislerius, acolyte, have signed. I, Brantio, an unworthy priest, wrote and dictated this restoration [Col. 0890D] on 12 April, the eighth indiction, in the second year of the reign of King Odo [A.D. 889].”

### Charter concerning Taxnatellum

A certain man named Alard gave his own property in the village called Taxnatellum, within that territory: namely, one enclosed homestead, bounded on one side by the land of St Leodegarius, on the other by Willeri’s land; on one end by the public road, on the other by the fisc. Within those boundaries, and everything pertaining to that holding—lands, meadows, woods, pastures, waters, watercourses, rights of egress and return—he gave wholly and in full to God and the church of Bèze.

### [Col. 0891A] Charter concerning Lucus

At the same time a certain man named Karlus and his wife Retrudis gave to the church of Bèze and to Abbot Walcaud their own property situated in the village called Lucus, bounded on one side by the land of St Vincent, on the other by the public road; on one end by the fisc, and on the other by the neighbouring tenants’ enclosure. Likewise, in that same territory, he gave one *journal* and a small piece of land; and in another territory, called Campania, he gave two *journals*. In another territory called Mount Mainbert, he gave one *journal* and a small piece of land. In another place he gave land capable of being sown with eight modii of wheat, and a female slave named Mainberga, in the time of King Odo.

When Bishop Agrinus died, Bishop Warnerius [Col. 0891B] succeeded him. At the request of the monks of this monastery, he brought back the blessed martyr Prudentius from Dijon. He was received with a festal demonstration of honour by innumerable clerics of different ranks and by an innumerable people of both sexes. Finally, when monks of the aforesaid monastery, with an uncountable multitude of people, came out from afar from the monastery to meet him, he was received with immense praises, in the year 921 from the Incarnation of the divine Word, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October [23 September].

### Abbots of the monastery of Bèze. Bishops Warnerius and Gotselmus of Langres. King Robert

After Abbot Walcaud died, Walcadus succeeded him; and when he died, Galcaudus became his successor. After his death an abbot named Milo succeeded, later bishop of Mâcon, who did nothing good in this house. When Warnerius, bishop of Langres, died, Gotselmus succeeded to episcopal rank in the first year of King Robert’s reign. Since he has been mentioned, it is necessary to say how Robert obtained the kingdom.

After King Odo died, his brother Robert, hoping, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

After Bishop Gotselmus died, Bishop Letericus succeeded him in episcopal rank; after him, Ericus; then Achardus; and after him Widricus. Under these bishops nearly forty years and more passed, during which the condition of this place always went from bad to worse, because the bishops and abbots cared more for other things than for it.

After King Rodulf died without children, etc., as [Col. 0891D] in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

### Concerning Bishop Bruno

In the year 980 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eighth indiction and the twenty-fifth year of King Lothair’s reign, that king gave the bishopric of the city of Langres to Bruno, cleric of the church of Reims and his kinsman by blood. This Bruno was ordained bishop by the hands of Burchard, archbishop of Lyons, in the church of St Stephen, being twenty-four years of age; and in that same year—namely, 981 from the Incarnation of Christ—he was received by the clergy of the city of Langres. Having obtained the bishopric, he endeavoured with every effort in his power to follow the example of the good Shepherd.

Observing that the monasteries belonging to his diocese [Col. 0892A] had been almost wholly deprived, spiritually, of religious observance and, temporally, of the necessary administration, he began to seek how, by God’s disposing will, he might restore them to their proper condition.

When we discussed the many kinds of desolation suffered by this monastery of Bèze, we said, insofar as memory permitted, according to what we found in old slips of writing, that it had been abandoned and almost reduced to nothing six times. Yet, searching the remaining material more carefully afterwards, we found that this same place had been burned five times by the Hungarians, since it had neither defense from an earthly prince nor a fortification capable of resisting enemies. We know when two of these burnings occurred. In the year 936 from the Incarnation [Col. 0892B] of the Word, the Hungarians came into Burgundy in July. Again, in the year 937 from the Incarnation of the Word, when Louis son of Charles had been anointed king and before that year had ended, the Hungarians came through Francia, Burgundy, and Aquitaine and devastated everything. This devastation so harmed this place that for fifty-one years, until the year 981 from the Incarnation of the Word, when Lord Bruno was placed over the church of Langres as bishop, it could not recover its former condition.

Seeing the state of this place and of the abbey of St Benignus at Dijon in a precarious condition, Lord Bishop Bruno humbly approached Lord Majolus, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and with much entreaty asked that, by Majolus’s help, he might be able to restore them for the better, both inwardly in religious observance and outwardly in possessions. Moved by his prayers, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

At the time when these things were done, King Hugh, son of Hugh the Great, ruled the kingdom of the Franks with his son Robert, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

Lord Bishop Bruno, observing that Father William was so fervent in religious devotion and monastic discipline and that the places entrusted to him were improving daily, entrusted all the monasteries in his bishopric to William’s prudence. Seeing, however, that this abbey of Bèze, dedicated in honour and in the name of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, [Col. 0892D] had been almost reduced to nothing, he urged William with insistent prayer to undertake its reform according to regular discipline. Assenting to his prayers, William restored this monastery in a few years to a regular condition, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

At last, many began to come to him from his homeland, that is, Italy: some well educated in letters, others trained in the mastery of various crafts, and others skilled in agriculture. Their art and ingenuity greatly benefited this place. When Abbot William visited the palaces of emperors or kings, he sought there not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ: that through familiar conversation with them he might, by his intervention, aid the oppressed; or that he might win persons for God from the secular or clerical estate, [Col. 0893A] so that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, they might leave their own possessions and, putting aside secular cares, serve God in tranquility, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

### Concerning Rodulf, who acted as the abbot’s deputy under St William

As soon as the venerable William undertook the office of abbot, a citizen of the fortress of Dijon, nobly born, named Rodulf Albus (“the White”), came to conversion at the very beginning of his new ordering. By this man’s money the poverty of the aforesaid father was relieved, and by his counsel and aid the burden of governing this monastery of Bèze was lightened; for William still had only a few monks. The aforesaid brother helped him so greatly in external concerns that he alone seemed to supply [Col. 0893B] the assistance of many. But, contrary to his desire, the briefness of his days took this support away from him.

If, in mentioning this man, we depart a little from the order of our account, let it not weary anyone; for we have taken care especially to record those who proved more devoted or generous toward this place. Rodulf, since this church, because of its small size, did not seem worthy of such great patrons—Peter, that is, and Paul—began from the foundations, carried the work through to completion, and completed it in the condition in which it now stands. Under Abbot William he governed this place as grand prior, most vigorous both in providing and administering external and internal matters, since he had learned this very thing through constant care and practice. Before coming to conversion, [Col. 0893C] he had been viscount of Dijon. Thus, turning secular zeal toward ecclesiastical purposes, he obtained better ends from good beginnings. He died on the Ides of November [13 November]. May his soul rest in peace. Amen.

Another monk, named Hunaldus, etc., as in the Chronicle of St Benignus.

It would take long to enumerate every good thing that Lord Bishop Bruno did in this place; nevertheless, we shall set forth what we have been able to find in our charters.

> “In the name of the Lord God and Saviour Jesus Christ. Bruno, humble bishop of the holy church of Langres by the disposing mercy of God. If, in all places—and especially in sacred places and for their rulers divinely entrusted to our unworthiness—we give, according to our ability, pious and timely assistance in what they need, and with solicitous care come to the aid of their difficulties, [Col. 0893D] we not only follow the practice and custom of venerable, God-devoted bishops and pious shepherds in this matter, but also provide for the salvation of our own soul.
>
> “Therefore let all know, both our contemporaries and those after us, that Lord Abbot William—whom, because of his holiness and venerable religious observance, we have lovingly placed over the houses in our diocese, at Dijon and Bèze—came to us and represented that certain properties of those abbeys needed to be transferred between them for the purpose of rendering a rent, and that we ought to approve and consent to this in every respect. We not only approved his prudence and praiseworthy discernment, but also earnestly urged him to carry it out promptly in accordance with his own judgment and the need of the places.
>
> “Accordingly, all that the abbey of St Peter at Bèze is known to possess in the village of Bruciacum was taken from it and joined to the abbey of St Benignus at Dijon, on this condition: that every year eight modii of wine shall be rendered as rent before the feast of St Prudentius; and that the monks of St Benignus shall possess in perpetuity all that we have stated above. If, through negligence or forgetfulness, this rent is not paid by the prescribed date, they shall restore the rent double, and the agreement shall remain unshaken. If anyone after our death attempts to infringe this decree, approved by the voice of many nobles, [Col. 0894B] unless he quickly comes to his senses and performs fitting penance, let him beware the “throat” (*jugulum*) of anathema, with which we have decreed to strike all who desire to uproot the ordinances of our decrees. And so that this may remain unshaken through the ages, we have confirmed it with our hand below and have requested that it be confirmed by many. Sign of Bishop Bruno. Sign of Lambert, provost. Sign of Teudric, archdeacon. Sign of Berald, archdeacon. Sign of Wido, priest. Sign of Teudo, archiclavius. Sign of Wido, archdeacon. Sign of Berald, subdeacon. Sign of Odo. Sign of Amelius. Sign of Bruno the boy. Sign of Humbert the boy. Sign of Nivard. Sign of Gozelm.”

### Gifts made to this place by Bishop Bruno

[Col. 0894C] As zeal for religious observance increased in this place, Lord Bishop Bruno, exceedingly delighted by their good manner of life, gladly granted from his own rights whatever was necessary and useful for them. Among the other things that he bestowed on this place, he ordered that during Rogationtide all men and women from churches within six leagues of Bèze should come with offerings to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

### In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity

### Offerings to be made to the church of Bèze. The monks’ authority to hear confessions

> “I, Bruno, bishop of Langres, considering that negligence in my office would tend toward the condemnation of my soul, have laboured, according to the measure of my understanding, to provide God’s churches [Col. 0894D] with guardians who, scattering within them the talent of God’s word and, together with me, bringing to the Lord Jesus Christ the profit gained from it, might be enriched with the reward of eternal life.
>
> “I therefore wished that Lord William, a most religious man, should preside as abbot over the church of Bèze. While he arranged everything there according to rule and religiously, realizing that his own resources were insufficient in certain respects, he requested that the church of Langres contribute something to the church of Bèze for the provision of lights. Recognizing that the petition of the man of God ought not to be refused, with the counsel of the entire chapter of Langres I ordered that during Rogationtide all men and women from churches within six leagues of Bèze [Col. 0895A] should come with offerings to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.
>
> “Also considering seriously that, since they ought at the same time to come to Langres, some were prevented by the length of the road, others by bodily weakness, and others by certain other hindrances, and were deprived of the nourishment of the divine word and the remission of sins which they ought to receive there: let them therefore come at the appointed time; and, asking forgiveness for their sins from those whose tongues have been made the keys of heaven, let them be admonished by those monks serving God concerning the salvation of their souls; and, absolution having been pronounced and a blessing given, let them return rejoicing in peace. Whoever presumes to oppose this institution of ours, by the authority of almighty God and of those whose acts of binding on [Col. 0895B] earth shall be bound also in heaven, and of all the saints, let him be anathematized and excommunicated. Amen.
>
> “And so that this may remain unshaken through the ages, we have confirmed it with our hand below and have requested that it be confirmed by many. Sign of Bishop Bruno. Sign of Abbot William. Sign of Lambert, provost. Sign of Berald, archdeacon. Sign of Teudric, archdeacon. Sign of Bruno, archdeacon. Sign of Teudo, archiclavius. Sign of Wido, archdeacon. Sign of Amelius. Sign of Wido, priest. Sign of Berald, subdeacon. Sign of Nivard. Sign of Gocelm, and many others. I, Airard, chancellor, wrote this and, with the others, was an approver and confirmer. These things were enacted in the year 1008 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the sixth indiction, epact 11, concurrent 4, in the reign of King Robert, [Col. 0895C] while Lord Bruno held the see of Langres.”

We wish to commend to the knowledge of future generations the goodwill and devotion of Lord Bishop Bruno toward this place, which will benefit us today and our posterity as long as the world endures.

There is a church not far from this place of Bèze, dedicated in honour of St Leodegarius, endowed by kings, dukes, and counts with very extensive estates and broad lands. The monks of that place inflicted no small injuries and vexations upon this house, occupying our lands and imposing unjust customary dues upon them. Because our possessions lay contiguous within theirs, they extended their hands beyond what was just, and, relying upon the assistance—even if unjust—of earthly [Col. 0895D] princes, enlarged their place from our property by every means they could.

There is a village called Cusiriacum in the parish of the village called Belenava. When the monks of St Leodegarius wished to build a church and establish a new parish there, Lord Bishop Bruno, hearing this, excommunicated and anathematized those who should build a church there and those who should celebrate the divine office there. Yet, considering that the parish church—namely Belenava—was too far away, and, as a good shepherd, providing for the care of souls lest through the distance of the road, a priest’s negligence, or the people’s ignorance, souls should be deprived of the nourishment of the divine word, he ordained that they should gather in the village [Col. 0896A] called Besuuncula, which was nearby, for Mass and the offices of Christian worship, on the condition that, because the labourer is worthy of his wage, they should give to that church one half of whatever pertained to the priestly office.

Likewise, in the village called Anblins, because they held a share of the water with us, they began to bring claims against us; and if we wished to build anything, they hindered it as much as they could. Father Bishop Bruno came and himself drove a sharpened stake into the middle of the water, which remains there even today, so that the monks of St Leodegarius should possess one half of the water as far as the stake, while the other half as far as the stake should remain to us in peace.

In our village called Trecasas, they once wished customarily to exact a *corvée* [compulsory labour service]. [Col. 0896B] Since there was no one else to resist, a certain peasant, inflamed with zeal for justice and faith, went to where the oxen had been yoked and cut through all the yokes over their heads, which peasants call *convincula*. Yet, fearing that evil might be done to him on account of this deed, even though unjustly, he fled. Again our Bishop Bruno, Bruno both in name and in fact, when he heard this, did not hesitate to come to the place. Before beginning to discuss the matter, he sent for that peasant, who had hidden himself in fear and did not dare return: “Where,” he said, “is my son who did this and acted so manfully in my stead?” When the man came before him, he said: “You are the son of St Peter and my son. Do not be afraid, being certain that whoever hates you hates me.” [Col. 0896C] “Be secure: for whoever injures you will share that matter with me as well.” When these things had been said, and when it had been proved through the local inhabitants and elders, who possessed knowledge and memory of former times, that those monks had in no way the customary right they claimed in our village, the lord bishop returned to his own affairs.

### Charter concerning the tithes of Nova Villa

### Restoration of tithes

At the same time when Lord Abbot William governed the monastery of Bèze, a certain knight named Gyrard recognized that he was receiving, by no rightful custom, the tithes of a certain church belonging to that monastery. The church was consecrated in honour of St Prudentius in the county of Atois, at the place called Nova Villa. [Col. 0896D] Its tithes were being transferred to another church, as though to a mother church, established in the village called Frasnetum. Therefore, while he was residing in his castle called Fons-venti, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April [26 March], he restored, for the remedy of his soul and those of his wife and son Humbert, those tithes to the aforesaid monastery, to which the chapel was subject by hereditary right. This was done in the presence and with the consent of his wife Gertrudis and his aforesaid son Humbert. So that none of their heirs or successors might thereafter have permission to reclaim those tithes, they ordered this record to be made. Whoever should challenge it is to be struck by the anathema of perpetual excommunication. [Col. 0897A] The names of the witnesses who confirmed this record are these: Theoderic; Humbert; Aymo; Joffred; another Humbert; Arembert; Gybuin; Mainfred; another Haymo; Wido, priest; Deodatus; and very many other distinguished men. All gave testimony, on sound grounds, that it was better and more proper for the aforesaid church to stand independently with its tithes in the domain and possession of the monastery of Bèze than to be subject to any other church.

### Another charter

> “When, at our see of Langres, I, Bishop Bruno in God’s name, together with our archdeacons and a gathered multitude of the children of our diocese, was holding a general synod, a certain monk of the monastery of Bèze, named Benedict, came before us. He presented a charter previously made by a certain knight named Girard, with the consent of his wife Gertrudis and his son Humbert, restoring to the aforesaid place the tithes of a certain church in the county of Atois—namely Nova Villa—consecrated in honour of St Prudentius. [Col. 0897B] All of us, hearing this charter together, confirmed and approved it. Since the same church had been built upon the estate of the aforesaid monastery, we decreed and ordained that its tithes should belong by hereditary right at all times to that same monastery, with none of our successors nor any of the heirs of the aforesaid Girard disputing this or bringing a claim. If anyone should challenge this testament, all his sins shall be exacted from him, down to the last farthing. Done publicly at Langres. Names of the witnesses who confirmed this testament: Lambert, provost; Teudo, abbot and archdeacon; Berald, archdeacon; another Berald, archdeacon; Bruno, archdeacon, nephew of Lord Bishop Bruno.”

### Charter concerning Bustellum

> “We wish it to be known to those present and future that Fulbert and Berengerius, brothers, departing from Bustellum because of hostilities which their neighbours inflicted upon them, gave the allod of that village of Bustellum to St Peter; and they commended themselves and all their posterity to that same saint in perpetuity, each man and [Col. 0897D] woman owing one denarius’ worth of wax each year. This was on the agreement that, if they themselves or anyone from their descendants should return to the region, they should hold from the abbot of the place and the monks the inheritance which they had given to the saint.
>
> “Thus, leaving the bishopric of Langres in the time of Bishop Bruno and Duke Henry, they came into the diocese of the archbishopric of Besançon in the time of Archbishop Hector and Count William. They reached the place called Rollens and remained there upon the land of Teduin and his brother Beroard; Teduin was the father of Bernard. They remained on their land on this agreement: that they should pay to them the revenues and customary dues of the land, but should bring annually to St Peter at Bèze the rent which they owed. [Col. 0898A] The monks, however, fearing that in later times the heirs of Teduin and of his brother Beroard might inflict some violence upon these people or wish to reduce them to servitude, went with their abbot William to a council at which Archbishop Hector and Bishop Bruno sat with other bishops. They requested that they jointly confirm by ecclesiastical authority this charter and the liberty of these people. Willingly granting this, with the consent of the other bishops and of the entire holy council, they decreed that these people were free people of St Peter and excommunicated by perpetual anathema anyone who should dare in any way to impose upon them the yoke of servitude. Sign of Hector, archbishop. Sign of Bruno, bishop. [Col. 0898B] Sign of Walter, bishop. Sign of Burchard, bishop. Sign of Goslen, bishop.”

### Charter concerning Buxiacum and Lama

A certain man named Gybuin gave to God and to the church of Bèze one male serf named Walcaud, with his wife and all who should descend from them; and one holding divided into two parts. One part lies in the village called Buxiacum, bounded on two sides by the land of the knight Girard, on the third by the land of St Peter at Bèze, and on the fourth by the water called the Tille, and contains thirty-two *journals*. The other part lies in the village called Lama, bounded on every side by the land of St Peter, and contains twenty-eight *journals*. Later, on the day of his burial, when his body had been brought [Col. 0898C] for interment, all his relatives gave one female serf named Abdiarda and confirmed this charter anew. Whoever removes anything from the aforesaid property, may his soul be cut off from fellowship with God.

### Another charter
In these same days Oggerius, bringing a claim against two maidservants—one named Susanna and the other Hildegard—together with their own children, whom the monks of St Peter had lawfully possessed for a very long course of time, stubbornly tried to reduce them to his own servitude. Therefore, at the command of Bruno, most eminent of bishops, an assembly of his faithful men was convened, and a day was also appointed for trial by combat.

[Note: [Col. 0897D] *Campiendi*, that is, for entering into a duel in the field.]

But lest Oggerius himself incur the guilt of homicide or perjury, the monks dwelling there offered him fifty solidi. Having accepted these, he at last voluntarily desisted from this complaint. And although he had unjustly attempted to bend them to his own service, having received the price, so to speak, of their redemption, he restored them before witnesses to St Peter, to whom they more truly belonged; so that neither he himself, nor his co-heir, nor any suspect person may ever dare to bring any claim concerning them or their offspring. These are the witnesses: Count Girard, Walter, Nerduin, Aldo, Odo, Count Hugh, Odilo.

### Charter concerning Gibriac

At the same time, a certain man named Jozald, [Col. 0899A] for the remedy of his soul, on the advice of his sons and friends, conveyed as a gift to the place of St Peter of Bèze a certain vineyard in the village of Gibriac, in the place called Casal, together with its adjoining land. It measures twenty-six perches in length and seventeen perches in width; it is bounded on one side by the land of St Mary, on the other by that estate itself; on one end by the public road, and on the other by fiscal land. This estate had been given to him by his two predecessors, Wicherannus and Archirannus, together with his wife Tetsana and his two children Ostrad and Vucherannus. Therefore, just as it had been given by those two predecessors to him, so he too conveyed it to God, St Peter, and the monastery of Bèze, to be held and possessed in perpetuity.

### Charter concerning Sètes

[Col. 0899B] Let the faithful in succeeding ages know that a certain man named Lambert, though free-born, living at Sètes with his wife Eremburg and their children Framuer and Dominic, who were of the same condition, freely gave himself to St Peter to serve at the place called the Fountain of Bèze, and the monks living there in God’s service, so that freedom might accrue to their souls.

But he did this under this tenure, condition, and obligation: that he and his successors should faithfully guard the alms which Count Rainald of the region, together with his wife, bestowed upon the aforesaid St Peter. For whatever profit they may be able to gain from it, whether by revenue or business, they are to render it for the clothing of the brethren in the treasury of the aforesaid place. And in order that this written record might remain firm, [Col. 0899C] at that time they gave to this community as a memorial: the man two asses, and the man’s wife ten solidi for repairing the cauldron. They likewise gave one boat.

Moreover, let the monks of that place know that he has no advocate other than themselves, and that therefore they are always to provide for him in clothing, footwear, and food. And so that they might remain beyond suspicion, the elders of the place anathematized with perpetual anathema anyone who should in any way molest him or his children, by the authority of God and St Peter, for whose love Lambert gave himself to service, unless satisfaction has been made and forgiveness obtained. The witnesses to this subscription are all the inhabitants of the holy place itself: Aldo the provost, Humbert, Wido the dean, Orbert, Necteus, Rainerius. These things [Col. 0899D] were done in the time of Abbot William and Benedict, provost of the place.

### Charter concerning Talamaro

The cunning of perverse men, who devise deceits in their hearts, requires that decreed matters be committed to a written document, for the sake of caution and the security of those who follow. Such men are so often swept about by fickle instability that, even when confirmed by testimonial signature, they nevertheless strive craftily to oppose matters by malicious guile. Guarding against the wiles of such men, we, the brethren of the place of Bèze, serving under the rule of Lord Abbot William, have recorded the agreement which we made with the parishioners of the village of Talananc concerning the churchyard of St Valerius.

For, fearing hostile attacks, they came to us unanimously, asking [Col. 0900A] that this churchyard be given to them as an aid for building dwellings and establishing their own homes. Overcome by their importunity, we granted the churchyard for common use, subject to payment of rent, under the following arrangement: whoever occupied seven feet or one measure within the lordship should pay a rent of two denarii; but whoever occupied twelve or thirteen should pay four denarii on the feast-day of St Benignus. Whoever exceeded the prescribed boundary should know that he must make restitution with interest according to the law.

### Charter concerning Luco Ibuxiaco

A certain woman named Hildegard, for the remedy of her soul and those of her husband and sons—namely Norgaud and Hildebert—conveyed to the monastery of the holy apostles Peter [Col. 0900B] and Paul, situated in the place called the Fountain of Bèze, this land with its appurtenances, which she seemed to possess by hereditary right. And, so that it might benefit posterity and be believed more firmly, she requested that it be set down in writing.

Accordingly, in the village of Bussiac there are four crofts: two on one side of the river called Tila, and two on the other side of the same river. On one side is the land of St Saviour; on the other, the land of Gibuinus. At one end runs the aforesaid river, namely the Tila; at the other is the public road. Beside the other two crofts, which lie on the other side of the same river, on one side is the land of Girard, on the other the land of Gibuinus; at one end is the land of the aforesaid Girard, and at the other runs the often-mentioned river.

In the village of Luco, beside the bridge, there is one croft; on every side is land of the aforesaid monastery. In the same village there is another croft: on one side [Col. 0900C] the land of St Peter; on the other, the land of Willer; at one end the public road; at the other the often-mentioned river.

Likewise, in another village called Luco at St Martin, there are two crofts: on one side is a certain passage for going to the water; on the other is the land of St Leodegarius; at one end runs the Tila, and at the other the aforesaid road. Likewise, in the already mentioned village of Luco at the bridge there are three small crofts; on every side lies the land of the same monastery. Likewise, in the same village there is one croft: on one side is the land of Girald, on the other the land of St Saviour; at one end the monastery itself holds it, and at the other is the river already and repeatedly named. Likewise, in the same village there is one croft: on two sides the land of St Leodegarius; at one end the land of Gibuinus; at the other the often [Col. 0900D] mentioned river.

Therefore the aforesaid Hildegard, together with her aforesaid sons, bestowed these things upon the said monastery and strengthened the grant by her faithful subscription and lawful witnesses, in the reign of Robert, king of the Franks. She also bestowed, together with all the aforesaid crofts, everything belonging to them: namely four meadows, arable lands, pastures, and all that she possessed by hereditary right in the aforesaid three villages.

### Charter concerning Lu and Fractus Mons

Likewise, another woman, called Heremburg, for her own soul and the souls of her lords and children, gave to God and to the most holy church, at the place called Bèze and dedicated in honour of the blessed apostle Peter, certain property belonging to her by right: namely four holdings situated [Col. 0901A] in the district of Langres. Three of these are in the village called Lu at St Martin.

She gave these three, together with the serfs dwelling upon them, to the aforesaid church, on the condition that during her lifetime she should possess them by usufructuary right; after her death they should pass to the governors of that church. Another holding is situated in the same district, in the village called Fractus Mons. This she delivered into possession to the aforesaid church, so that the governors of that place might hold and possess it.

The names of the male and female serfs living on these lands are: Stephen and his wife Deodata, and their children Mainard, Leotasius, Danucia, Ermengarius, Rainard, Ernincia, Mainard, Bernard, Fulgerius, Rotrudis, and Olosma.

Thus she granted these holdings, with the serfs and all appurtenances, to the aforesaid holy [Col. 0901B] church, over which Lord Abbot William presided, and to the said community, for those whose remembrance I have made above, and also for the soul of Leudo, who conveyed them to her. Mark of Heremburg, who ordered this to be made and confirmed. Mark of Bishop Lebald. Mark of Adalard, priest. Mark of John, deacon. Mark of Haymo, deacon. Mark of Constantine. Given through the hand of Ranulf, deacon, on Friday, the first day of January. In the reign of King Robert.

### Another charter

A certain knight, Hirmuinus by name, visiting the monastery of Bèze with the consent of his wife Bertila, gave to that place, for love of St Peter and St Prudentius and for the remedy of the soul of a certain son of his, named Hirmuinus, [Col. 0901C] recently deceased, a certain serf named Eward, with his wife Stephana and their children. This was done on the condition that both they and all their posterity should from that day belong by hereditary right to the service and lordship of the monks of the aforesaid monastery, with no one contradicting or bringing a claim.

### Charter concerning Flaciac

Another knight, named Hugh, gave to St Peter, for the burial of his wife Wandelmodis and for the remedy of her soul, one holding in the village called Flaciac, with all its appurtenances: namely arable land, woods, and meadows. And so that this gift might never be exposed to any claim but might remain continually unshaken, he placed this charter upon the altar [Col. 0901D] of St Peter, confirmed it with his own hand, and delivered it to be strengthened by faithful witnesses.

### Charter concerning Beria

“We wish all the faithful, future as well as present, to know that a certain knight named Milo, of the village called Beria, approached the clemency of Lord Abbot William, known to preside over this monastery of Bèze, and of Lord Benedict, who after him exercised the office of prior, asking that property of the same monastery be bestowed upon him as a benefice. He promised that he would submit himself in all things to the services of the aforesaid monastery and would assist its interests by every means within his power.

Since he persisted constantly in his petitions, [Col. 0902A] both personally and through his messengers—

[Note: [Col. 0901D] *perstaret*; the printed text had *prestaret*.]

—the aforesaid Lord Prior Benedict, compelled by his requests and with the consent of the aforesaid Lord Abbot William, gave him a third part of the church of the said village, namely Beria, retaining the other part. For the priest held one third in return for service. He also gave him one holding in the village called Alta Villa, one quarter-holding in the village called Juvenalis, and one juger of vineyard in the village called Curtis Adonis.

This arrangement was made, however, on the condition that he should hold this benefice during his lifetime. After his death, neither his son nor his daughter nor anyone of his kindred might presume to take possession of it or lay claim to it, unless it were granted to them by the good will or voluntary gift of the abbot or [Col. 0902B] his monks. He confirmed this agreement under oath in his own person and that of his son Aduin, the son himself being present and willingly consenting. He also produced faithful witnesses to this matter, whose names are: Odo, Rotbert, Wido the dean, Luitprannus, Aldo the provost, Albert the monk, Rotbert the monk.”

### On the death of Bishop Bruno

Since it would take too long to recount everything bestowed upon this place in the time of Bishop Bruno, let us come to the end of his life. But first we shall take care briefly to describe what manner of life he led.

He was generous in almsgiving, etc., as in the *Chronicle of St Benignus*.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1016, Lord Bishop [Col. 0902C] Bruno died on the second day before the Kalends of February [31 January], having completed thirty-five years in the episcopate. Bishop Lambert succeeded him, himself a devout enlarger of the possessions of this place.

### Charter concerning Nova Villa

In his days, a certain Henry, his son Vilgerius, and his wife named Aduldis obtained burial in the monastery of St Peter of Bèze. On this account, they restored to St Peter, for the remedy of their souls, the village of Nova Villa, which Henry’s father had held as a benefice. But lest this restoration should be rendered futile, Lord Prior Benedict gave him one holding in the village called Corcellis for his lifetime, to return to St Peter after his death.

And lest this be forgotten, [Col. 0902D] when the monks then known to him had died, he asked that it be made known to posterity by these letters, under the testimony of the priors, and appended thereto. He further provided that, just as the anniversary day of the deceased brethren is celebrated, so his own should likewise be celebrated. Humbert, cleric of Tilecastrum, witness. Wido the dean, witness, and many others.

### Another charter

In the name of the highest and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Henry, wish all to know that whatever St Peter appears to possess in Nova Villa I once held as a benefice; but, having been taken from me by Bishop Bruno, it was restored [Col. 0903A] to the monks. Yet after Bruno’s death I renewed my claim; therefore Abbot William, angered, and the monks, bringing their complaints before Bishop Lambert, compelled me to relinquish Nova Villa.

Afterward, however, presumption having been turned into humility, I secured Bishop Lambert himself as my helper. Through his intercession the monks restored to me the same land, divided into three and a half holdings, on this condition: that, retaining the corvée for their own uses, they should have David, his son, and Rainald, together with the land which they hold, additional day-works, cart-service, and rent together with *eulogiae* [customary dues or gifts]. The monks, however, should receive the *receptum* and the court-payment from the men, together with whatever is found in that village beyond the three and a half holdings. They should also receive whatever is included in crofts and arable land, the demesne meadow, woodland, and mills.

This was also confirmed by my promise: that I would demand from the men, beyond the lawful land-rent, nothing either on the pretext of lodging or because of any new necessity. If I should presume to do so, I would again lose the land unless I appeased the monks by satisfaction.

[Col. 0903B] In return for the military service granted with this land, nothing else is required of me except continual defence against the plunderers and defrauders of the same church. But, lest I should seem burdened in this matter, this defence is not required against men more powerful than I, but against those equal to me in birth and power and against those inferior to me in both. If I am proved negligent in this defence, I am again bound by the condition of losing the land.

[Col. 0903C] Therefore I restore to the right and property of the monks’ provision this land of Nova Villa, received upon this condition, together with all other property which I held from St Peter: namely, the small monastery with its church situated on the same allod; one holding in Fractus Mons; half a holding in Wainart; and one quarter-holding in Manneium, for the remedy of my soul. I alienate and disinherit all my descendants from every property which I held as a benefice from St Peter, lest they claim a hereditary right; and, to preclude an occasion for seeking such inheritance, I restore before the witnesses present, by this chartered record, everything which I possessed.

I too, Lambert, bishop of the see of Langres, stand as witness to this restoration. And because it was done by my arrangement [Col. 0903D] that Nova Villa and all other land which Henry held as a benefice should return to the provision of the monks, I willingly confirm it. And lest after Henry’s death it should hereafter be withdrawn from the monks’ use in the manner of a benefice, I prohibit this; and by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, invoking St Peter, prince of the apostles, I excommunicate those who consent to or effect such withdrawal. Mark of Bishop Lambert. Mark of Berald. Mark of Rotger. Mark of Wido. I, Henry, confirm this with my own hand and produce witnesses. Mark of Count Girard. Mark of Milo. Mark of Oldebrand. These things were done publicly at Tilecastrum, in the presence of Lord Bishop Lambert, in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0904A] 1017, indiction 15, in the reign of Robert, king of the Franks, in the month of February.

### Charter of Fons Vennae

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, to all worshippers of the orthodox faith. It is clearer than light that the human race daily offends its Creator both through diabolical seduction and the frailty of its own nature, and continually provokes His anger, according to that apostolic saying: “In many things we all offend.” And if he says that all, which is true, offend, excluding neither the cautious nor the perfect from the generality of offenders, how much more ought we, who are wholly secular, scarcely remembering the Lord’s commandments, and in whose acts almost nothing can be recognized except sin, to believe that we offend?

[Col. 0904B] For we knowingly commit many evils and unknowingly fall into many others. From these there is a pressing necessity that, before we are compelled to be brought before the tribunal of strict judgment, we should strive somehow to be absolved. And because by the Lord’s and the Gospel’s words we are taught that one who receives a prophet and a righteous man receives a prophet’s and a righteous man’s reward, if we receive a servant of God—something which appears to be denoted by the name “righteous”—we judge that we may somewhat lighten the burden of our offences. But lest we delay too long in speaking, let us now bring the purpose we have begun to its subject.

“I, Lambert, by God’s grace bishop of the church of Langres, wish it to be known to all children of holy Christianity, present and future, that Girard, lord of the [Col. 0904C] castle of Fons Vennae, wishing to build before the said castle a monastery in honour and memory of the Holy Sepulchre and St Mary ever Virgin, proposes to establish there monks who may always serve God.

For the cloister and workshops, garden and granaries, and for arranging all things necessary to that place, he gives them land from the farther bank of the water of the Vennae—which lies on the left for those coming from Langres to the castle—as far as the wood which lies on their right; and on the other side, from the cross fixed in the middle of the heath as far as the castle itself, along the road leading to the wood. Since the castle itself, with the adjoining land, is known to be of the estate of our diocese, by our approval he grants to St Mammes, in exchange for the aforesaid land, land at the village of Arcionis Curtis, which fell to him from the inheritance of Geretrudis, his wife. I too approve this exchange of land for the remedy of my soul, to the aforesaid church, so that I may share in the almsgiving.

The aforesaid Girard wishes to establish this place under such an agreement that it shall remain for all time under the subjection and discipline of St Peter of Bèze and the abbot of that church. Likewise, whatever he gives to the place at present, whatever he may give in the future during his life, and whatever other faithful persons may wish to bestow for the remedy of their souls, shall always remain under the jurisdiction of the aforesaid abbey of Bèze.

[Col. 0905A] “He also earnestly asks me to confirm by episcopal authority that the bodies of all deceased knights who cannot, according to their custom, be brought from this castle of Fons Vennae to Bèze, may customarily be buried in the cemetery of this place consecrated by me. All likewise who die within the castle district, or in the settlement and refuge of the castle district itself, shall be buried in the aforesaid cemetery of St Mary by perpetual observance.

Understanding the faithful and devout purpose of his request, I willingly grant and confirm what he asks, with the consent of all the archdeacons and other faithful persons, approving that place to St Peter of Bèze. Moreover, I order this written record to be made, and I confirm it with my own hand. If anyone, deceived by a perverse mind, should undertake to alter otherwise or wholly destroy this confirmation of the request, [Col. 0905B] agreement, and written instrument, let him be struck by the bond of eternal anathema and perpetual curse, and, having been convicted by the justice of the law, pay one hundred pounds of gold; and let the matters contained in this charter remain inviolate.

I, Lambert, bishop of the see of Langres, ordered this charter to be made and signed it, so that it may be remembered through the ages. I, Berald, bishop of the city of Soissons, signed. Berald the elder, archdeacon and abbot, signed. Girard, count of Fons Vennae, signed. Bruno, archdeacon, signed. Another Girard, signed. Count Hugh, signed. Odo, archdeacon and abbot, signed. Wido, signed. Rotgerius, signed. Hugh, chaplain, signed. Another Hugh, signed. Rainold, signed. Done publicly at Langres in the year from the Incarnation [Col. 0905C] 1019, indiction 2, epact 12, concurrent 3, in the month of May, in the reign of Robert, king of the Franks. I, Odolricus, dictated in place of Chancellor Berald; on Thursday I wrote and subscribed.”

### Another charter

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Girard, wish all faithful persons still living in the flesh, and those yet to come, to know that I, with my wife Gertrude, gave a certain part of my inheritance to Bishop Lambert in exchange, by one agreement.

“There was a field beneath my castle, called Fons Venti, in which I wished to build a monastery. Seeing that I could not [Col. 0905D] accomplish this without the bishop’s permission, I gave the same amount of land to my lord in exchange for that place, in the village called Arcuncurtis. The land in question is bounded in front by the land of the church of St Peter at Geneva, and my inheritance is known to adjoin it on all sides. I conveyed it under this condition: that the place in which the monastery has been built, in honour of the Holy Sepulchre and St Mary ever Virgin, shall always be subject to the abbey of St Peter of Bèze and remain under the abbot’s authority.

“If any of our heirs should attempt to bring any claim against this transaction—which, by God’s grace, I do not expect to happen—let him be compelled by the laws to pay one pound of gold into the royal treasury. [Col. 0906A] Let this conveyance remain firm and stable for all time. I confirmed it with my own hand and delivered it to be confirmed by the undersigned witnesses. Mark of Girard. Mark of Gertrude. Mark of Girard, cleric. Mark of Humbert, their son. Mark of Haimo. Mark of Otbert. Mark of Nocher. Mark of Aymo. Mark of Arluin. Mark of Nerduin. Mark of William. Mark of Lentilli. Mark of Arulf. Mark of Otbert the Norman. Mark of Teubald. These things were done at Langres on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May [16 April], indiction 2, in the thirty-second year of King Robert’s reign and the third year of his son Hugh. I, Odolricus, dictated in place of Chancellor Berald; on Thursday I wrote and subscribed.”

### Charter concerning Arcionis Curtis

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. We wish it to be made known [Col. 0906B] to present and future persons alike that I, Lambert, by God’s grace bishop of the church of Langres, gave to God and the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre and St Mary—which had been built before the castle of Fons Vennae by Girard and his wife Gertrude, with my approval, upon land belonging to our estate—the land of Arcionis Curtis. Girard himself and his wife restored it to me in exchange for the land of our estate upon which they had built the monastery.

Therefore, at their request, I gave it freely to God, the Holy Sepulchre, St Mary, and St Peter, for the monastery of Fons Vennae, on the condition that I should be a participant in their almsgiving. And because this land had belonged to the jurisdiction of Lovuncurtis, they separated it from that jurisdiction and made it wholly free, [Col. 0906C] so that none of the officials of that jurisdiction might henceforth presume to exact or take anything from that land.

The people dwelling on that land are to use the forest of that jurisdiction, as before, for building houses and making their fires, and likewise, according to custom, for pasturage for their pigs and other animals which they possess. Whoever should presume to make any demand concerning that forest or jurisdiction shall be struck with perpetual curse and excommunication. Mark of Bishop Lambert. Mark of Girard. Mark of Geretrudis. Mark of Humbert, father of Theoderic. Mark of Haymo, father of Wido of the Burgundian village. Mark of Haymo, father of Manasses.”

[Col. 0906D]

### Charter of Helpricus Curtis

“In the name of the highest and undivided Trinity, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Lambert, by God’s grace bishop of Langres, desire it to be known to all who truly believe in Christ God that, when on a certain day I was at Langres and, according to my capacity, was discussing with my clerics and Catholic laymen alike the strengthening of the state of holy Mother Church and the restoration of vigour to corrupted religious life, behold, certain brethren of the monastery of Bèze presented themselves before me. In humble and urgent entreaty they begged that, compassionating their need in brotherly charity, I would grant them the altar of the church [Col. 0907A] of Helpricus Curtis, for the support of the brethren, present and future.

I hastened without delay to fulfil their petition in practical effect, because it was supported by the aid of a future reward. Therefore, with the consent of the clerics of the church of Langres and the faithful laity alike—namely B., provost, and also L., archdeacon, in whose ministry the aforesaid altar was—I gave the aforesaid altar to the church of Bèze, for the sake of eternal recompense and the relief of the brethren’s need, on condition that the services owed to our see should be rendered at suitable times.

Among the others present was a certain knight named Humbert, in whose benefice the aforesaid altar appeared to be situated. [Col. 0907B] Desiring to obtain God’s grace, he granted that benefice to the brethren of the same place, saying: ‘I, Humbert, for love of almighty God and the salvation of my soul, give to St Peter and the brethren of the monastery of Bèze the benefice of the church of Helpricus Curtis, with the consent of my wife, named Histiburg, and my son Siguin, to be possessed in perpetuity. From this day they may assign it to their own uses, derive support from it, and have permission to do whatever they please with it. But if any of my heirs—God forbid—should attempt to bring a claim against this donation, let him be compelled by the laws to pay ten pounds of gold, and let this donation possess lasting force and stability for ever.’

Done publicly at Langres, on the sixth day before the Ides of January [8 January], indiction 5, [Col. 0907C] in the year 1022 from the Incarnation of the Word, in the reign of Robert. Mark of Bishop Lambert. Mark of Bruno, archiclave. Mark of Girard, archdeacon. Mark of Humbert, archdeacon. Mark of Odo, dean. Mark of Ansculf, priest. Mark of Hugh, priest. Mark of Constantius, priest. Mark of Maurice, priest. Mark of Wido, layman. Mark of Gotzelm, layman. Mark of Odolricus, layman. Mark of Wido, layman. Mark of Rotger, layman. Mark of another Rotger. Mark of Humbert. Mark of his son Siguin.”

### Charter concerning Vetus Vineae

“Let faithful Christians, present and future, know that after the monastery of Bèze had been founded by Duke Amalgar in honour of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, estates of no small extent were bestowed there by him, [Col. 0907D] including the allod called Vetus Vineae. Gathering in that place a multitude of servants of God prepared to live under the Rule, he set his son, named Wandalenus, over them.

But after the passage of many years, partly through hostile invasion, partly through the irruption of the Huns—by whom that place is reported to have been burned five times—and no less through the negligence of bishops, it began to suffer loss rather than, as formerly, increase, until it was granted to obtain Betto for the see of Langres. So long as he remained in this life, he presided as a capable shepherd. After his death Albericus was chosen as successor. Through an apostolic visitation, divine mercy helping him, he restored the place to its former state and enlarged it with his own gifts. For a long time it remained steadfast in honour and religious life.

Afterwards a certain Hugh held Vetus Vineae, whether through favour of a benefice or through usurpation. On his death the place recovered it again and possessed it peacefully and securely in the time of Bruno, bishop of Langres. After Bruno’s death, however, like other holy places, Bèze fell to plunder. Those who had seemed peaceable then became robbers. Among them were a certain Gerard and his brother Lambert, descended from the family of the above-mentioned Hugh, who invaded Vetus Vineae as though by hereditary right. But as they gained nothing by this invasion, they were at length convicted by justice and voluntarily restored the place. In this restoration they voluntarily relinquished any right which might have seemed to belong to them from their predecessors, [Col. 0908B] both for the remedy of their own souls and those of their parents, and to obtain forgiveness for the seizure of pigs and the burning of the village of Fielinx which they had unjustly committed. Witnesses were present who saw the restoration and satisfaction.

And, so that this restoration and satisfaction might endure in memory, they requested that this record be made and confirmed by their own hands and those of these witnesses. Mark of Girard. Mark of Lambert, who requested this charter to be made. Mark of Helvidis, their mother. Mark of Wido and his wife. Mark of Walter, cleric. Mark of Wido, dean. Mark of Odo. Mark of Rotbert. Mark of Erlebald. Mark of Aldo. Done publicly at the castle of Dijon, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March [17 February], in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1023, in the reign of King Robert.”

[Col. 0908C]

### Another charter, concerning Tusleium

A certain woman named Ezelina, wife of the knight Nerduin, conveyed one holding to St Peter of Bèze in the village called Vetus Vineae, with one serf and everything belonging to that holding, for the redemption of the soul of her aforesaid husband. She also gave at Tusleium one holding containing four jugera, twenty-nine of arable land, and meadow sufficient for one cartload. In order that this gift might remain firm and stable in perpetuity, she confirmed it and requested its confirmation by the undersigned witnesses. These are Gibuinus, brother of the aforesaid knight, Bernard, and Aldo. She also restored the protection-right from the village called Septem Fontes, which had already belonged to St Peter. Done publicly [Col. 0908D] at Bèze in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1027, indiction 10, epact 11, concurrent 6, in the month of October, in the reign of Robert, king of the Franks.

### Charter concerning Flaciac

A certain man named Haymo also gave to the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and St Prudentius the martyr, situated in the place called the Fountain of Bèze, one holding in the village called Flaciac, together with all its appurtenances, namely arable lands, woods, and meadows. And so that this might benefit posterity and be more firmly believed, he requested that it be recorded in writing under lawful witnesses, in the aforesaid year from the Incarnation of the Lord. These are the witnesses: Mark of Bernard. Mark of Odo. Mark of Rotbert. Mark of Aldo. Mark of Hugh.

[Col. 0909A]

### On the death of Abbot William

There are still many matters which could be recorded, but omitting these, we take care to report the death of Father William, etc., as in the *Chronicle of St Benignus*.

At the very time when King Robert held the monarchy of the kingdom, he heard that in these regions certain persons, violently plundering the property of others on every side, had built strongholds and new castles for themselves in order to retain their spoils more freely and with impunity. Accordingly, with a large army befitting a king, he came to besiege and destroy Miribel, for it was one of the haunts of the plunderers. By God’s favour he accomplished this quickly. But while he was besieging it, a messenger arrived, saying that our father Abbot William had departed this life.

[Col. 0909B] Therefore King Robert, unwilling that this place should remain long without a shepherd, lest ravening wolves should invade the flock, appointed as abbot of this place Lord Ulgerius, who at that time held the place of prior under Abbot William. Our aforesaid father William died in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1031, etc., as in the *Chronicle of St Benignus*.

### On Abbot Ulgerius

**The monks of Bèze are expelled by force.**—When the appointment of this Hugh was imminent, he was brought by King Henry, then a young man, to the city of Langres with great pomp. News was brought to the king of the death of his father, King Robert, who had reigned forty-one years, while Henry himself was already in the sixth year of his reign.

The aforesaid [Col. 0909C] bishop, once he had received the episcopate, was not, as he ought to have been, a diligent benefactor of God’s churches, but on the contrary negligent and dissipating. Accordingly, when he imposed many vexations and unwonted exactions on this place, and Lord Abbot Ulgerius would by no means assent to him, he appointed Halinard, abbot of Dijon, as abbot of this place.

Halinard came with his monks and, through the violence of Bishop Hugh, took our Lord Abbot Ulgerius captive along with certain of our monks and led them to Dijon. Leaving his own monks here, he handed this place over to them—not to preserve and build it up, but to destroy and plunder what was within. This afterwards became evident. For once, pretending that they were going [Col. 0909D] to carry wine, they placed a wine-vessel, called a *tunna* [tun], upon a cart and put into that vessel the ornaments, together with books and the greater part of the treasure.
