But the people of this village realized this, especially because the tun was excessively heavy. They opened it, discovered our possessions inside, and retained them. Some of our men report that at that time those monks carried away to Dijon seventeen copes, besides no small quantity of other ornaments, together with a Gospel-book and a most precious cross.

While the lord abbot Ulgerius was thus held at Dijon, those monks of his who had been dispersed from this place informed him that he should prepare himself [Col. 0910A] to leave the monastery. They sent him horses on which to flee and stationed them in a suitable place. When he learned this, he left the monastery, mounted the horses, and in uninterrupted flight made for the castle near us called Bellimont. From there, with his monks, he attacked the men of Dijon who had wickedly seized this place and, whether willing or unwilling, compelled them to return to their own homes. He himself governed both the revenues of his church and this place well and according to the Rule for a long time.

### Charter concerning Mornad

“Through the fault of the first parent it befell his race after him that, as he himself had been, so he left those born after him. Therefore, as he himself was not without misery [Col. 0910B], so he begot all men miserable; and as he himself forgot the blessedness bestowed upon him by God, so he made all human beings forgetful. Since, therefore, the living creature is forgetful, and the grounds of transactions may often slip from the human mind unless they are written in ink and entered in the written characters of charters—so that future people may be instructed by these examples concerning matters which they have not learned either by sight or hearing—we accordingly make known what has been done in our times and what the old age of our elders remembers.

“We wish it to be known to all, present and future, how three brothers named Wido, Odilo, and Ansericus confirmed a certain piece of land situated in the village of Mornad, which was owed by right to Saint Peter. For in the time of Bishop Bruno there was a knight named Lezelinus who wished to hold this land contrary to the right of that bishop and of the lords of the aforesaid place, as indeed he claimed it. After him there was another, surnamed Humbert, who likewise seized the land. As he came to death, he restored at the thresholds of Saints Peter and Paul, to the aforesaid place, whatever he seemed to hold in that land, whether belonging to him by right or unjustly taken: he restored everything by means of his little shoe, commonly called an *osa*, which he filled with earth from that land; and he took a twig from the orchard as testimony. He sent these, indeed, through his messengers, but through negligence they were not received by the holy place.

[Col. 0910D] “Accordingly, the aforesaid brothers, desiring to possess it hereditarily, seized the land as though it had been left to them by their forefathers. Acting as they pleased and pressing their claim with much force, they attempted—and did accomplish—what was contrary to the will of the lords dwelling in the place of Saint Peter. Yet those men did not abandon their purpose, but continually protested, both personally and through the princes of the realm, exposing their unjust claim. At last, by God’s will and after the brothers had come to their senses, they went with the counsel of their lords to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, did penance, and there granted to that place everything which they appeared to hold in the aforesaid land, whether rightfully or wrongfully. This was on the condition that, after their deaths, the land should serve as testimony [Col. 0911A] of their burial and association there, for which reason they restored it. Moreover, the lords of the aforesaid place restored to them another piece of land situated in the village called Osiliac, which had been held in pledge against them.

“Done publicly at the monastery of Bèze, on the feast-day of Saint Benedict the abbot, namely 12 days before the Kalends of April [21 March], in the first year of the ordination of Lord Abbot Ulgerius. Sign of Count Hugh of Bellimont, who ordered this restoration to be made. Sign of his nephew Odo. Of Wido the dean. Of Willerius; of Odo the knight. Of Leutprannus; of Aldo the provost. And these are the names of the brothers: sign of Wido, Odilo, Ansericus.”

### Charter concerning Fractum-Montem

“Let the charity of present and future persons know for certain that a certain Milo of Tilcastle gave to Saint [Col. 0911B] Peter and Saint Prudentius, at Fractum-Montem, for the remedy of his soul, one *mansus*, to which belong nine *jugera* of arable land and one mowing of meadow. And so that this might benefit posterity and be more firmly believed, he requested that it be recorded in writing under lawful witnesses. In the year from the Incarnation 1026; indiction VIII; epact zero; concurrent 4; in the month of July; in the reign of Robert, king of the Franks. These are the witnesses: sign of Wido; sign of Odo and of his brother Robert; sign of Aldo and of his son Milo; sign of Otbert.”

### Charter concerning Beria

In the same year Milo of Beria gave to Saint Peter, in the monastery called the Fountain of Bèze, for the remedy of his soul, one *mansus* in that village, to which belong [Col. 0911C] nine *jugera* of arable land and one mowing of meadow, together with a serf named Lambert, his wife, and children. Witnesses: Wido, Bernard, Aldo, Lambert, Grimejus, Romarus, Hugh son of Aldo.

### Charter concerning Icium

Elinandus also gave one *mansus* at Icium to Saint Peter of the monastery of Bèze, for the remedy of his soul, with a serf named Teduin, his wife, and children; nine *jugera* of arable land and one mowing of meadow belong to it. Witnesses: Wido, Hugh, Aldo, Stephen.

### Another charter

Odilo likewise gave, in the same village, one *mansus* to Saint Peter of the monastery of Bèze, with a serf named [Col. 0911D] Ansald, his wife, and children. Witnesses: Wido, Aldo, Berarmannus, Robert.

### Charter concerning Besueta

The distinguished gift of Odo the knight.—“In the name of God almighty. We wish it to be known to all who desire to know how, for the remedy of the soul of Odo, an excellent knight, son of Nerduin, a youth of the highest distinction, who was killed by a sudden blow, his maternal uncle, namely Count Hugh of Bellimont, Odo’s wife Gertrude, and Hugh’s brother gave, in memory of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Prudentius the martyr, at the place of the monastery of Bèze, a serf named Theoderic; likewise another named Stephen; and one maidservant [Col. 0912A] named Leutgarda, with the entire succession of the sons and daughters of them all.

“They also gave one *mansus* of a very extensive free allod, or a very large holding, in the village of Besueta, with all appurtenances belonging to that *mansus*: namely cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, watercourses and outlets, rights of water, and rights of use in the surrounding woods, both about the rivers Bèze and Vincenne; in the manner in which the aforesaid Odo, or his father or grandfather, held them during life, without objection from anyone of their family or from any outsider. This land owes annually four modii of grain and three and a half modii of *tremissis*; and six denarii in the month of May; then a wether and a pig; at vintage-time [Col. 0912B] a cart-service and a sextary of wine; and at Christmas two sextaries of wine. From this day forward it shall belong to the lordship of the aforesaid saints of the monastery of Bèze, so that the monks serving God there may do with it whatever they judge and choose to be most useful.

“And so that this alms or gift may remain firm and stable for all time, with the will of our relatives and the consent of all our faithful men, we publicly confirm it by touching with our own hands and have our names and those of our principal men written down. But if anyone—God forbid—should arise as an adverse claimant against this our act, which we have made for love of God and for the redemption of the soul of our dear kinsman, he shall feel the wrath of the eternal Judge and of Peter [Col. 0912C] his key-bearer, unless he makes amends with satisfaction.

“The names of the confirmers who confirmed this charter: sign of Count Hugh; sign of Countess Letgarda; sign of Gertrude, wife of Odo the knight; sign of Gybuin; sign of Richard; sign of Nerduin, his son; sign of Wido the archdeacon; sign of Hugh; sign of Wido, Odilo, and Joffrey; sign of Bernard; sign of another Bernard; sign of Willerius; sign of Richard; sign of Ulric; sign of Olgerius; sign of Willencus; sign of Humbert. Done publicly at Bèze, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1034, indiction II, epact XXVIII, in the eighth year of the reign of King Henry, in the month of November. I, Heldemannus, monk, wrote and subscribed.”

### Charter concerning Fontanelles

[Col. 0912D] A certain knight named Richard, reflecting not inappropriately and fearing greatly, relying upon the counsel of sacred speech, confidently undertook this: “Give alms, and it will pray for you, and all things are clean for you”; and, “Give, and it shall be given to you”; and similar sayings. Therefore, for the remedy of his soul, he gave to the heavenly Gatekeeper and prince of the apostles, Saint Peter of the Fountain of Bèze, one *mansus* in the place called Fontanelles. His wife, named Radmodis, and his son Hugh willingly approved this; indeed, they also promised that they would give more to the holy place. This was done publicly in the monastery of the aforesaid saint and upon his altar. Our Lord Jesus Christ reigning with the Holy Spirit at the right hand [Col. 0913A] of the paternal majesty, in the year of his Incarnation 1036, indiction IV, epact XX, on the day before the Kalends of July [30 June], Wednesday, the third day of the moon, on which the Passion of Blessed Paul is solemnly commemorated; after the feast of his fellow apostle Peter had on the preceding day been observed with due honour; while King Henry ruled with the sceptres of the Franks and Hugh, in the honour of the episcopate, governed the Church of the holy see of Langres.

### Charter concerning Caviniac, Priniac, and Blaniac

A certain cleric Gybuin, touched by fear of God, for the remission of his sins and those of his brother Nerduin, and of the latter’s sons, his nephews—namely Odo and Hugh—gave half a *mansus* in the village called Primiac, and one small enclosure with the serf who lived on that land, named Humbert, together with his two sons Odo and [Col. 0913B] Humbert. He also restored a piece of land situated in the village of Caviniac, which his above-named brother Nerduin had at one time appeared to hold unjustly. He restored the protection-right (*salvamentum*) of the villages of Auxiliac and Blaniac. He also restored Oldierius with his brother Hugh and their sister Fratburga, whom his aforesaid brother and his nephews held under protection-right. He also gave the serf Guntarius and Ingerranus with Stephen his son. For Ingerranus had formerly been given for Odo, and his son for Hugh. Gybuin himself, who made the donation, confirmed the charter.

### Charter concerning Vetus-vineae

A certain man named Otbert restored to Saint Peter of the Fountain of Bèze whatever he claimed in the village [Col. 0913C] called Vetus-vineae, on the Lord’s Day when, in mid-Lent, “Rejoice, Jerusalem” is raised in joyful chant at Mass. There he received from Lord Abbot Olgerius of the same place and from the monks, as he was setting out for Rome, both the pilgrim’s bag and absolution. This was done publicly upon the altar of the aforesaid prince of the apostles, five days before the Kalends of April [28 March], on the twenty-sixth day of the moon, while Henry vigorously wielded the sceptres of the Franks and Hugh happily presided in the episcopal chair and piously governed the Church of the see of Langres, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1036, indiction IV, epact XX.

### Charter concerning Blaniac

[Col. 0913D] “It is clearer than light that anyone wishing to crush the devices of the crafty enemy must, with unwearied effort, follow the footsteps of Christ’s followers. For one who bears a pure heart devoted to righteous works longs to obtain the blessed joys of heaven. Without doubt, this is attained by transferring earthly possessions to heavenly treasures and relieving the miseries of the poor through the generous bounty of liberality. Holy Scripture exhorts us to this, declaring a man’s own riches to be the redemption of his soul. For sins are redeemed by mercies to the poor; and as water extinguishes fire, so by almsgiving the flame of the everlasting pyre is quenched. For this reason I, Gybuin the cleric, brother of Hugh of the castle of Bellimont, having regard to divine mercy and brought to the end of my days, grant and give to God almighty [Col. 0914A] and Saint Peter all my inheritance in the village called Blaniac: namely all arable land, with fields, meadows, woods, pastures, and fisheries, from which the greater part of that village consists. Moreover, I add the serfs Rotgerius and Alcherius, Utbaldus, Warnerius, Sendradus, and Archimbaldus, with their wives, children, and entire households; and all male and female serfs belonging to that inheritance of mine, wherever they may dwell, so that henceforth they may serve Saint Peter and the monks serving him, as they have hitherto served me, and may render their customary dues with devout intention.

“Lest after my death anyone should, through unjust presumption, appear as a violator or falsifier of this alms-gift, I entrust to my nephew Ulric, before all the people at the altar of Saint Peter, the duty of setting it forth by his own legal title, handing it over in my stead to the saint and the monks, and strengthening the charter as witness of truth by a binding stipulation and by witnesses and signatories. The document subsequently sets forth the names of the signatories: sign of Ulric, his nephew; sign of Ansericus the knight; sign of Willencus the knight; sign of Walterius the knight; sign of all the monks present; sign of Wido the archpriest; sign of Constantius the priest; sign of Rotbert the priest; sign of Haimo the cleric; sign of Hugh the provost and of the entire household. Done publicly at the monastery of Bèze, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1044, indiction XII, epact XVIII, on the third Ides of June [11 June], the feast-day of Saint Barnabas the Apostle, while Henry held the kingdom of France, his brother Robert ruled Burgundy, and Hugh—who afterward deserved rejection—presided, now in name a shepherd, in the episcopate of the holy mother Church of Langres.”

### Another charter

After the death of the aforesaid Gybuin, Fulco, who had his niece in marriage, began to demand customary dues in that land and from the serfs who inhabited it, whom Gybuin had left to Saint Peter and the monks; so too did two knights, Hugh, brother of Odo of Mont Saligon, and Willencus of the village of Saint-Seine, to whom he had granted those dues as a benefice. But, frequently admonished and compelled by the claim of justice, Fulco came to the monastery and, before the altar, forgave those same dues to God, the saints, the monks themselves, and the male and female serfs. He compelled those who held them as a benefice from him to do likewise, and declared those male and female serfs free from himself and from all men. Sign of Fulco. Sign of Ulric. Sign of Walter. Sign of Wido.

### Charter concerning Luc, Genciniac, and Cinciac

[Col. 0914D] “In the name of God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Since the human mind is unstable and deeds quickly fall from memory unless they are entered in the written characters of charters, we, though least, judge it fitting to commit to posterity what is now done in our times, lest, as we have said, it perish through oblivion.

“We wish it to be known to all, both present and future, how Erembert, formerly a knight, restored the benefice which he appeared to have held in former times, namely in the days of Lord Abbot William and of Provost Rodulf. This Erembert was of noble lineage according to worldly rank, but because of the internal wars waged among false Christians he had been brought almost to nothing, so that he wished to sell the benefice of which we speak and transfer it to other hands. Recognizing this, we, the brothers of Saint Peter of Bèze, considered it a loss if the saint’s land should be sold into alien hands. We summoned him to our council and admonished him that he was not acting rightly toward the fidelity due to Saint Peter; yet we ourselves paid him the price which he wished others to give him. And this was done. For the knight came to the monastery of Saint Peter of Bèze, in the presence of Lord Abbot Olgerius and the other brothers of the same [Col. 0915A] community, with many other God-fearing clerics and laymen assembled. In their gathering, before the altar of Peter the apostle, prince of the apostles, he and his son named Wido, having received a price of one hundred solidi in exchange for the land, restored it, neither he nor any of his heirs retaining any ground for reclaiming it. If anyone should presume to reclaim it, let him know that by the authority of the apostle Peter he is excluded by the bond of anathema.

“The benefice in question is situated in several places: in the village called Luc, half a *mansus*; likewise another half in the village of Vendovera; one *mansus* in Tasnat; one *mansus* in Genciniac; and one *mansus* in Cinciac. These are the witnesses whom we record: sign [Col. 0915C] of Wido the dean; sign of Hugh the provost; sign of Odolric of Bellimont, son of Count Hugh; sign of Walter; sign of Odilo; sign of Haimo; sign of Aleric; sign of Bruno of Cambon; sign of Rainald; sign of Rotmar; sign of Hervé; sign of Rainer; sign of Otbert; sign of Humbert. Done publicly at Bèze, in the monastery, in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1043, while King Henry reigned in Francia and Robert, his brother, ruled Burgundy.”

### Charter concerning Gibriac

“I, Higmarus, called in the name of God, wish all faithful members of the holy Church of God, and all my relatives and kinsmen, present and future, to know that Olgerius, abbot and outstanding cultivator of holy religion, of the monastery called Bèze, dedicated in the name and honour of Peter, the gracious key-bearer, came with several monks subject to his authority to the estate called Gibriac, situated in the county of Oscheret, in order to hold a plea with me concerning certain complaints which I intended there to bring against him.

[Col. 0915D] “Considering, therefore, the purity of innocence of the aforesaid abbot and his fellow monks in God’s service, and considering that through them I might appease God for myself, by the counsel of the good men present—and especially of the monk Robert, the knight Otbert, and my brother-in-law Henry—for God and for the blessed repose of my own soul and those of my father, mother, and all my relatives, I forgive every complaint which I had against the aforesaid abbot and his monks. I give to God and Saint Peter, for the monastery of Bèze and the monks dwelling there, my serfs Fulcherius and Albert, on whose account the dispute had arisen, without any contradiction on my part: they shall serve there while they live, together with their sons whom they have or will have, and all who shall descend from them forever.

[Col. 0916A] “I shall have this charter of donation confirmed by my brother Bernard, my sister Eva, and her son Odilo. But if anyone attempts to challenge this gift, he shall not prevail; moreover, having incurred the wrath of the heavenly Judge, he shall be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold to the aforesaid place. Done publicly at Gibriac. Sign of Higmarus, who requested that this be made and confirmed. Sign of Bernard, his brother. Sign of Henry, their brother-in-law. Sign of Eva, his wife. Sign of Odilo, their son. Sign of Otbert. Sign of Gislebert. Sign likewise of Gislebert. Sign of Waldric. Sign of Humbert. Sign of Arnulf. Sign of Wido. Sign of Walter. Sign of Otrannus.”

### Charter concerning Renaves

“I, Helgerius, with my brother Guntard, in consideration of the benefices of Lord Benedict, prior of the monastery of Bèze, and of the monks of that place, given to us in the village called Colonica, gave to Saint Peter, in the village called Renaves, one *mansus* of our allod, having appurtenances of eighteen *jugera*, meadow for three cartloads of hay, and a right of use in the wood belonging to that village. This land enters the village on one side; on the other it is bounded by the public road leading toward [Col. 0916C] Champagne; and on the third side it is enclosed by our allod. We also gave another *mansus* in the aforesaid village of Colonica, having appurtenances of six *jugera*, meadow for one cartload of hay, and a right of use in the wood belonging to that village. This land enters the village on one side; on another it is divided by Saint Peter’s land; on a third it is bounded by Erembert’s land; and on the fourth it is enclosed by the neighbouring stream.

“We made this donation on the condition that during our lifetime we should hold this land together with the aforesaid benefice, paying for it an annual rent of two solidi at the feast of Saint Peter. But if one of us dies first, his portion shall immediately revert to them, unless perhaps, by their free will, it should again be granted to the other. And that this donation might remain more secure, we confirmed this charter with our hands and placed it upon the altar of Saint Peter, and we called in faithful witnesses: sign of Guntard; sign of Helgerius; sign of Odo; sign of Rainard; sign of Salecon; sign of Bernard. Given on the second Nones of June [4 June].”

### Charter concerning Fontenelles

[Col. 0916D] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Hildeberga, make known to present and future persons that my son Odilo, overtaken by untimely death, ended his last day and was buried in the cemetery of Saint Peter’s monastery of Bèze. For his soul, and mine together with it, I gave to that place one *mansus* at Fontenelles, which I held by right of dower and on which a serf named Hamedeus lived, on this condition: that as long as I live I shall hold it in usufruct, and each year, on the feast of Saint Peter, shall pay twelve denarii at investiture; and after my death it shall belong, without any contradiction, to the lordship of Saint Peter of the same place. And that this donation may remain firm, I ordered this charter to be made for the information of posterity, and with my son Joffrey I confirmed it by my hand before witnesses, whose names are these: sign of Landric, my son; sign of Hagan the Long; sign of Girard of Deujustrui; sign of Humbert of Campanis; sign of Robert of Baleneva; sign of Odo; sign of Aldo the provost.”

### Charter concerning Gentiniac

[Col. 0917B] A certain knight named Arembert of Longchamp, holding a benefice of Saint Peter of Bèze in several places, came to the aforesaid place and restored to it a certain portion—namely the benefice situated in the village called Ginciniac—in its entirety, so that neither he nor any of his heirs might be able to reclaim it. He made this restoration in the presence of Lord Abbot Olgerius and others from his monastery standing before the altar of Saint Peter.

### Charter concerning Caviniac

A certain woman named Alburga, married to a knight named Pons, gave—or, as some think, restored—the land situated in the village called Caviniac, which a predecessor of no small nobility named Gibuin [Col. 0917C] had granted to Saint Peter, but which she had apparently set apart and retained by hereditary right. Sign of Abbot Olgerius. Sign of Moron the provost. Sign of John the prior, and of many others.

### Charter concerning Calmontis-villa

“In the name of the highest and undivided Trinity. We wish it to be known to present and future persons that I, surnamed Moron, touched by fear of God and fear of my sins, came to the monastery of Bèze, where the protections of many saints are preserved, especially of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, with his companion the apostle Paul, and where Lord Abbot Olgerius was known to preside. There, in the presence of certain monks of that monastery and faithful God-fearing Christians [Col. 0917D], whose names are appended below, I had myself tonsured and vowed to remain a monk under the rule of Saint Benedict the confessor.

“I therefore gave to the aforesaid monastery half of everything which I appeared to possess by hereditary right in Calmontis-villa and in the other surrounding estates—in meadows, watercourses, woods, and mills; that is, as I have said, the entire half—by means of a serf named Arnald, whom I gave to Saint Peter; and through him I conveyed all male and female serfs to the holy place, under a binding stipulation. Done publicly at the monastery of Bèze, with Benedict the provost, the monk Heldelmannus, the monk Adelmus, the monk Odo, [Col. 0918A] Countess Girberga of Fontis-Vennae, and many others present.”

### Charter concerning Altrisiac, Maxiac, Bodenac, and Lentiliac

“In the name of the highest and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Let it be known to all faithful persons, living and future, that I, Gibuin, and my niece Eraungardis, convey to Saint Peter four holdings in the village called Altrisiac, for the remedy of the soul of my brother Hugh, who while still alive had assigned the said holdings to Blessed Peter, together with the male and female serfs whose names are these: Rodulf with his wife and children; the brothers Abraham and Danninus, with their wives and children; Orrannus and Laibo with their wives [Col. 0918B] and children; Lambert with his wife and children; and Erbert, who was still a boy. We grant these freely to Blessed Peter with all their appurtenances, so that, as they have stood in our power from the days of my great-grandfather Gibuin, of his son Hugh, and of Hugh my father, so from this day forward they may remain in Saint Peter’s power, for the remedy of the soul of my brother Hugh. They shall have the customs which they formerly had, both in woods, meadows, waters, fields, and all boundary lands. Let no *maior*, forester, or dean of the authority of Altrisiac henceforth presume to impose any burden upon the men aforesaid, their children, or those descended from their stock in succeeding times.

“And if through negligence it happens that the animals of these men, without a keeper, enter the lord’s meadow or the *corvata*, they shall not be compelled by law to pay a penalty, but only to make good the assessed damage. We grant to Saint Peter the same custom in respect of two small enclosures which he had formerly held in that village. Likewise, we give Saint Peter one *mansus* in the village called Maxiac, with its appurtenances.

[Col. 0918C] “Moreover, for the remedy of their souls and ours, we relinquish and renounce all the customary dues which my father and my brothers Hugh and Wido received in the village called Bodens and in Lentiliac, except the *corvata* which they perform for the wood. And if any of my heirs—which I believe will by no means happen—attempts to challenge these things, he shall be unable to reclaim them, and by the right hand of God almighty and the authority of Peter, prince of the apostles, let him be anathema maranatha. And that this charter may remain firm and stable, I confirmed it with my own hand, and ordered my niece, her husband Fulco, and the other faithful persons to confirm it. Sign of Gibuin. Sign of Fulco. Sign of Ermingardis. Sign of Bernard. Sign of Wido the archdeacon. Sign of Richard. Sign of Goffrey. Sign of Wido. Sign of Odilo. Sign of Odolric. Sign of Willencus. Sign of Leubrannus. Sign of Milo, Gosbert, Humbert, Lambert, and Ulgerius.”

### Charter concerning Luc

At the same time a certain woman named Adilina, with her sons Nocherius and Pons, gave one *mansus* [Col. 0919A] in the village called Luc, with all its appurtenances and rent-payments, the house standing upon it, and a serf named Alberic.

### Charter concerning Buxiac

Likewise Ezilinia gave an allod in the village called Buxiac, in its entirety, with its appurtenances, tenant-farmers, fields, woods, and waters, with the approval of her son Kalon.

### Another charter

Another man named Bernard gave whatever appeared to be his right within the bounds of Vetusvineae.

### Charter concerning Longa Boella

Likewise Bernard, called Francus, gave Saint [Col. 0919B] Peter two *journals* of land in the boundary called Longa Boella.

### Another charter

Ewardus of Pons also gave two small portions of meadow at the place called Molonga Prata, and two fields: one at Montannos and the other at Pontem-villam.

### Another charter

A woman named Anna gave Saint Peter one small enclosure at Pons for her burial.

### Charter concerning Mariac

With kindly purpose for posterity, we wish to imprint upon these pages that Milo, called Bicellus, brother of Majolus, whose surname was Mazilinus, gave Saint Peter in the village of Mariac one *mansus* [Col. 0919C] with its appurtenances and a serf named Gerard, with his wife and children.

### Charter concerning Vachiriac

We believe it should be recorded for future persons that Teto, a knight of Mont Salion, conveyed to Saint Peter one *mansus* in the former village of Vachiriac, now deserted, together with a serf named Ewrinus, his brother.

### Charter concerning Luc

We judge it right to commit to memory that Hugh, cleric of Launna, assigned Saint Peter one *mansus* on the saint’s feast-day, while the lords were celebrating the general Mass of that feast. Publicly approaching the altar, he conveyed the gift before the watching people, affirming that his father Gibuin had given him that *mansus* [Col. 0919D] on the day when the crown of his head was blessed for him. This *mansus* is in the village of Luc; the land belonging to it lies in the valley called Vernevalley, after the little river Vernela which flows through it. Sign of Abbot Olgerius. Sign of Hugh. Sign of John. Sign of Wido the dean. Sign of Robert the priest. Sign of Girard the cleric.

At the same time Emperor Henry III governed the kingdom of Burgundy, etc., as in the Chronicle of Saint Bénigne.

The same pope, therefore, coming to the city of Langres, ordained there Lord Arduin as bishop in place of him who had been expelled. While he remained there, various disputes and mutual claims of various churches were brought forward, as matters properly and canonically to be decided before the universal and apostolic father. It happened that a case concerning us and the canons of Langres was also heard. They wished to have the tithe from our vineyard below Gibriac. When Lord Pope Leo had heard the case, he cried out and showed what he had seen concerning it in the archives of the holy Roman Church, saying: “By the authority of the holy Fathers who presided before me over the holy Roman See, it has been decreed that no church founded in honour of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, shall pay rent or tithes to another church.” Overwhelmed by the weight of this argument and authority, the canons fell silent.

The same venerable Bishop Arduin, among the other benefits which he conferred upon this place, at the request [Col. 0920B] of Abbot Olgerius obtained from the supreme pontiff of the Roman Church the issuing of a decree providing that no one should presume to inflict force upon this monastery or reduce it to the subjection of any monastery; and that no one should dare to inflict any violence within one league of the monastery. It seemed good to insert a copy of this decree in this book, so that those who hear may learn how great a danger threatens those who do not fear to be bound by the bond of anathema through the vicar of the apostle Peter. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1052, Lord Pope Leo presided over the holy Roman Church. These are his words:

### Privilege of Lord Pope Leo

“Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Olgerius, abbot of the monastery of Bèze, and to your successors, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

“It accords with apostolic governance …” See Leo IX, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIII, no. 110.

### On the death of Abbot Olgerius

When Abbot Olgerius died, Abbot Odo succeeded him in the administration of the pastoral office. What was given or purchased in landed possessions during his days must not be passed over in silence.

### Charter concerning Vetus-vineae

A certain knight of our religious community, named Olgerius, born of noble lineage, set out with many others for the places of Jerusalem; but on his return, after enduring many dangers for Christ, he left the light of this present life in a blessed death, as we believe.

[Col. 0920D] In the presence of his fellow travellers and hearers, he assigned to Saint Peter of Bèze and its monks, at Vetusvineae, one stocked *mansus*, with a serf dwelling upon it named Arnald, just as Arnald’s father, named Adhemar, had held it until the day of his death and left it to his son Arnald. He ordered that Arnald’s wife, named Tedinda, with sons and daughters, be given with him; and likewise requested that the palm branches which he had brought from Jericho as witnesses of his pilgrimage be placed upon the altar. His wife, called Tetburgis, and his sons willingly approved this donation and compelled their men to approve it. This *mansus* owes a pig and a ram, six loaves and three sextaries of wine, cart-service [Col. 0921A] and all customary dues which serfs ought to render to their lords. We mark in writing all the witnesses whom they produced: sign of Tetburgis, his wife; sign of his sons Henry and Ulric; sign of Tetbald; sign of Aldo, Formald, Nerduin, Humbert, the younger Nerduin, and Wido the dean; sign of Hugh the provost; sign of Robert the priest; sign of John; sign of Arengerius; and of all his serfs dwelling at the holdings.

### Charter concerning Altrisiac, Villare, and Cinciac
Another knight, named Humbert, deprived of all hope of offspring, while sound and well gave to God and to Saint Peter at the place of Bèze the whole inheritance of his freehold estate that had come to him by paternal [Col. 0921B] right, without objection from any person. For he had already divided from his brothers, Hugh and Ulric, and each had separately set apart his share from that of his brother. When brought to death, he confirmed this gift again and, at the very hour of death, bound any challengers under eternal malediction. He gave his entire portion of the freehold in the village of Altrisiacum, with all appurtenances throughout the whole jurisdiction of Altrejaca—in woods, fields, meadows. Likewise, at Villare, his whole share of the inheritance, as he himself had held it in his lifetime. At Nova Casa, all his freehold, as he had possessed it. At Cinciacum likewise his freehold, with every appurtenance—in waters, fields, meadows, woods; at Calmetis, likewise all his freehold, as he had possessed it. [Col. 0921C] At Romaniaca and at Ponto also, the entire freehold with every appurtenance—in waters, meadows, fields, woods. There is also there one mill, a third part of which he gave to Saint Peter. At Beria likewise, every portion of his freehold—in waters, fields, meadows, woods. In the county of Alesia, in the village called Velinniacum and in Villare Corcellis. At Bretoneria, all his freehold, with all appurtenances in fields, meadows, waters, and woods. Sign of lord Abbot Odo. Sign of the monk Moron. Sign of the monk Hugh. Sign of the monk Theoderic. Sign of Count William. Sign of Fulk, lord of Belmonte. Sign of Gilbert, lord of Rescia. Sign of Walo, lord of Beria. Sign of Odilo. Sign of Willencus. Sign of Landric. Sign of Widric. Sign of Ralph and of his brother Olger. [Col. 0921D] Sign of Guy. Sign of Tetzilin. Sign of Robert. Sign of Berno. Sign of Heriald. Sign of Gerard. Sign of Isambert. Sign of Hugh. Humbert’s brother Hugh approved this gift before all the people, and granted to Saint Peter his entire share from this same freehold, because after his death he likewise possesses as much.

### Charter concerning Mornado

Let all present and future persons know that a certain knight, named Robert, out of fear and love of God, conveyed to the place of Saint Peter of the monastery of Bèze a certain holding which a certain matron named Ermengard and her son Odric, a cleric, had assigned. That holding lies in [Col. 0922A] the village of Mornado, and has attached to it cultivated and uncultivated lands, serfs and free persons dwelling upon them, meadows, fruit-bearing trees, and watercourses and return flows; all of which he assigned and restored to the aforesaid place of Saint Peter. And so that this might be done from a better will, he received from the monks of that place one horse and participation in all their good works; thereafter he caused this charter to be made, confirmed it with his own hand, and handed it to his friends and kinsmen to be confirmed and approved. Done publicly at the monastery of Bèze, on the sixth day before the Ides of February. Sign of Robert, who ordered this charter to be made. Sign of Odo. Sign of Geoffrey. Sign of Achard, and of many others.

### Charter concerning Genevrerias

[Col. 0922B] A certain woman named Sufisia, for the remedy of the soul of her son Guy, whom she had borne by Gilbert, gave one holding to Saint Peter in the village of Bellifons, with all its appurtenances and with every right in field, water, and wood; also the serf dwelling there, named Martin. She gave another holding at Genevrerias, with all its appurtenances and rights in field, water, and wood, on the condition that she should add to the same holding, to make up what it lacked, fifteen *journals* of arable land from her freehold at the boundary of that village. She also gave the serf dwelling there, named Alberic, with his wife called Fratburga and their children. And so that this alms might endure in perpetual support, she requested that the names of these witnesses be written below: Sign of Sufisia. Sign of Aeduin, her stepfather. Sign of Warner, husband of her sister. Sign of lord Abbot Odo. Sign of the monk Moron, and of many others.

### Charter concerning Mariacum

We also wish it to be clear to persons now living and to their successors that a certain knight named Sewald, from Mont Saligon, gave to Saint Peter, for the redemption of the soul of his brother Elirannus, one holding at the village of Mariacum near Tilcastrum, with all its appurtenances, together with one serf named Odilard. Sign of Sewald. Sign of lord Abbot Odo. Sign of Moron. Sign of Peter. Sign of the knight Pons.

### Charter concerning Flaciacum

[Col. 0922D] We wish all who come after us to know that a certain knight, named Sigefred, when brought to his last extremity, gave Saint Peter two holdings at the village of Flaciacum. In one lived his serf Erbert, and he owes, on the feast of All Saints, half a sextary of wine; at the Nativity of the Lord, one sextary of wine, two loaves, and two hens. The other holding in the same village lies abandoned. He also gave ten day-measures of land within the boundaries of that village, belonging to the same holdings, with meadows, woods, and all their appurtenances. Sign of Ruzindis, wife of Robert, brother of the said Sigefred, who placed this gift upon the altar in Sigefred’s stead. Sign of [Col. 0923A] Odo, brother of Mazilin. Sign of Willer. Sign of Amalric. Sign of Peter, cleric.

### Charter concerning Bodens and Lentileium

Inspired by divine authority, the noble matron Ermengard made Saint Peter her heir and admitted for their use all the brethren of the monastery of Bèze who serve God and that supreme prince of the apostles, granting them the protection-right (*salvamentum*) of Bodens and Lentileium, and of all things belonging to that protection-right, for the remedy of her own soul, of her lord Hugh, and of her son Guy, who had then died and who, after his father’s death, had possessed that protection-right by hereditary right. Her sons, namely Hugh and Nerduin, together with Gibuin, who were still alive, cooperated in this act. And so that this conveyance might be known to future persons as it is to present persons, she caused it to be committed to writing, so that what she could not attest after death might be attested by a charter preserved in the treasury of that monastery. Therefore, that it might remain unshaken, she subscribed it with her own hand in the presence of witnesses. Ermengard subscribed; Hugh, Nerduin, Gibuin. These are the witnesses.

### Charter concerning Buxiacum

Let all persons, present as well as future, know that Gertrude, wife of Gerard, knight of the castle of Fontis-Vennae, with her sons Gerard and Humbert, gave, after her aforesaid husband had already made a gift, to Saint Peter of Bèze, for the redemption of the soul of that husband and of her sons, one whole holding in the village [Col. 0923C] called Buxiacum, as Robert Major appeared to hold it, together with Robert himself, his wife, and children, and with everything belonging to that holding, in lands, woods, meadows, pastures, and waters. And so that this gift might remain firm and stable forever, she confirmed it and asked that it be confirmed by the following subscribing witnesses: Aymo, Olger, Geoffrey, Librand, Odo, Arlebald, Guy, Aldo. She also restored one holding in the village of Patriniacum, which had formerly been Saint Peter’s freehold, receiving as its price two pieces of a warrior’s equipment, commonly called a helmet (*helmum*) and a hauberk (*osbergum*).

### Charter concerning Moringas and Mornado

[Col. 0923D] Let present and future persons know that Richard of Belmonte had long contested, on behalf of his wife, certain land situated between the villages of Moringas and Mornadas, belonging to the abbey of Saint Peter’s monastery of Bèze, and had taken much from it to its detriment. The monks of Saint Peter often wished, for the sake of settlement, to determine this claim by oath or by whatever legal process; but the aforesaid Richard, moved by God’s prompting, gave that very claim to Saint Peter, whether it was just or unjust, in the presence of the lords of the place, a stipulation having been placed upon the altar. I, Richard, with my wife Wandelmod, confirmed this and handed it over to be ratified by witnesses. Sign of Guy the dean. Sign of Aldo. Sign of the monk Benedict. Sign of Heldemn. Sign of Albert.

### Charter concerning Saint Maurice

[Col. 0924A] We make known to the charity of the faithful that a certain knight named Herenbert, long afflicted by the troubles of illness, at last, when he perceived that the end of life was drawing near, requested to be buried at Bèze, in remembrance of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul; and this was done. For the absolution of his soul, his father, named Odo, gave to the same place half a holding with half a dwelling, since Herenbert’s brother held the other half together with a holding in the village called Saint-Maurice, with adjacent lands, meadows, and woodland. He gave this in that village and in another village named Romania, with lawful conveyance, and caused it to be confirmed by the hands of witnesses; their names are these: Hugh, Theoderic, Alelmus, John, another Hugh, Teudin, Hemma. [Col. 0924B] He himself followed him after a short time; he was not only buried at the same place, but, as he had requested, clothed in the monastic habit, he ended the day of this life in a good end. After his death, we gave one small fief which we held to his son, received three *jugera* in exchange, joined them to our lands, and assigned them to two men to dwell under service, one of whom was his serf and gave himself to the place.

### Charter concerning Tasnatum and Germaniacum

We wish it to be evident to present and future persons that a certain knight named Walo, for the redemption of the soul of his wife, called Addila, gave Saint Peter one freehold holding at Tasnatum [Col. 0924C] and another at Germaniacum. The latter pays in due rent half a hemina of wheat, half a hemina of oats, one sextary of wine, one pig worth six denarii, five denarii as meadow-rent, one wheel, and one ox at vintage time. He also gave the serfs Hunald, with his wife and children, and Mainerd with half his children, without any claim. And so that this gift might retain perpetual force, he requested that it be made known in writing and confirmed by witnesses. Sign of Walo. Sign of Fulk. Sign of Odilo. Sign of Milo. Sign of Warner. Sign of Guy. Sign of Henry. Sign of Widric. Sign of Warner.

### Charter concerning the village of Colonica

We wish all faithful persons, future [Col. 0924D] as well as present, to know that a certain knight named Gontard, with his brother Helger, approached us, asking that we grant them something from Saint Peter’s land as a benefice, promising that in every respect they would remain faithful in the service of Saint Peter and of us. As they sought this for a long time, overcome by their prayers, we gave them everything Saint Peter possessed in the village called Colonica, which their brother Henry had formerly held, together with the church situated in that village. We imposed upon them annually, on the feast of Saint Peter, a rent of two solidi, on this condition: that they should hold during their lifetimes what we had given; but after their death it should return to the right of Saint Peter and his monks, so that none of their descendants might in any way lay claim to it, unless through the free will or friendly grant of the abbot or monks of the same place. If one of them should die first, his part shall immediately return to us, unless perhaps it is again granted to him by our own free will. And so that these agreements might endure more firmly, they confirmed this charter with their own hands and produced faithful witnesses. Sign of Gontard. Sign of Helger. Sign of Rainard. Sign of Salecon. Sign of Bernard. Given on the second day before the Nones of June.

### Charter concerning Lu

Record of the grant which Bernard of Belmonte and his deceased nephew Richard made to Saint Peter of Bèze concerning certain land lying at the boundary of the hamlet called Lu of Saint Martin: within [Col. 0925B] those boundaries he gave one holding, containing nine *journals* of arable land, with two serfs.

### Charter concerning Villa Curtis

A certain knight named Stephen, falling into grave illness, came to the monastery consecrated in honour of the prince of the apostles, called Bèze; and there, for the remedy of his soul, he gave to that place one holding in the village called Curtis, and four *journals* of land in the field called Fistilliacum, together with a serf named Gaudius. It lies between, on both sides, the land of Gislerius. His sons Guy, Walter, and Hugh, and his wife named Fera, in whose dower the land that he restored to her lay, cooperated in this act. And so that this gift might be known to posterity, he ordered this little charter to be made, placed it upon [Col. 0925C] Saint Peter’s altar, and handed it over to be confirmed by witnesses. I, Stephen, subscribed. Sign of my son Guy. Sign of my son Walter. Sign of my son Hugh. Sign of Aymo. Sign of Guy. Sign of Milo.

### Another item

Two other knights, Adunus and his brother Milo, and their sister Teburgis, gave to God and Saint Peter Giberga with her children. And so that their gift might be exposed to no claim, they decreed in a public assembly that none of their heirs should inflict any violence upon any part of it by hereditary right. Whoever does so shall incur the penalty of excommunication. Aduinus and his brother confirmed this little charter. Sign of Sophia. Sign of Teburgis. Sign of [Col. 0925D] Guy, archpriest. Sign of Lezelin. Sign of Hugh the provost and of the entire household. Done publicly at the monastery of Bèze, in the presence of lord Abbot Odo.

### Another item

Likewise Humbert, his wife, and his sons, who were unjustly attempting to retain Saint Peter’s serf Fuldrad, namely, and his wife Richeldis and their children, released them as free, so that they might return to their own lord, the heavenly key-bearer.

### Charter concerning a certain vineyard

Likewise Samson of Vadona and his wife gave to God and Saint Peter one *jugerum* of vineyard in the place [Col. 0926A] called Adalechassana; likewise, in another place called Austivacca, two *jugera*. The witnesses of the gift are these: Sylvester, monk, received it; Grimald, reeve; Harbert.

### Charter concerning Mariacum

Doda of Mariacum also, with the consent of her husband Jocer, gave Saint Peter and the monks serving God there one meadow extending as far as the upper mill-dam of the same village. For this gift, which she made orally, she produced living witnesses; their names are: Folrad, Nero, Grimald, Lambert.

### Charter concerning Icio

We notify persons now living and their successors that Hildeberga, sister of Aerleius, the learned cleric, gave Saint [Col. 0926B] Peter one holding in the village called Icio, and one day’s ploughing in the bounds of the same village belonging to it, on the condition that the man dwelling and cultivating it, named Jordanius—who is nevertheless free—shall pay the monks the rent he was accustomed to render her. Moreover, she gave one female slave called Raimburgis, who is to render each year the customary due of two denarii for her head. The witnesses of this gift are: Robert, Widric, John, Hugh.

### Another item

Hildesendis, a religious woman, gave Saint Peter a girl named Osanna, daughter of Humbert and Retrudis.

### Another item

[Col. 0926C] Altrudis also, a most noble woman, mother of Aduin and Milo, gave Saint Peter the wife of Ulric, priest of Granantis-villa, named Girburga, with her children.

### Charter concerning Buxiacum

Let all, present as well as future, know that Betta, wife of the knight Hermuin, with her sons, gave to Saint Peter of Bèze, for the redemption of the soul of her aforesaid husband, one whole holding in the village called Buxiacum, as Lambert Major held it, with everything belonging to that holding, in lands, woods, meadows, pastures, and waters. And so that this gift might remain firm and stable forever, she confirmed it by the following subscribing witnesses. These are: Guy, Aldo, Gonterius, Otbert.

### Charter concerning Pruncethel

Likewise Sejuvold and his wife Ida gave Saint Peter of the monastery of Bèze one holding, adjoining which are nine *jugera* of arable land and one meadow from which two cartloads of hay can be gathered each year, in the place called Pruncethel. This was on the condition that whatever the monks of that place might wish to do with it, they should have free discretion in all matters to do so. The witnesses of this gift, written below, are: Albert, monk; Odo; Robert, priest; Dares; John, cook.

### Charter concerning Vetus-vineae

Aymo, likewise, born at Vetus-vineae, brother of Guy [Col. 0927A] and of the monk Waro, gave Saint Peter his freehold situated in that village, and with his son Guy placed it upon Saint Peter’s altar; and he caused his daughter Gertrude to approve it. Sign of lord Abbot Odo. Sign of Gerard. Sign of Ulric.

### Charter concerning Flaciacum

A certain archdeacon named Aerleius, canon of Saint Mammetus, gave Saint Peter one holding in the village called Flaciacum, with its appurtenances, for the remedy of the soul of his brother Milo. He also added one serf and two hangings of marvellous workmanship and enormous size. Lest this gift should in subsequent times be frustrated by any opposing person, he asked his kinsmen and those present to confirm the charter of this gift with their own hands and testimony. Sign of Aerleius. Sign of Odo. Sign of John, prior. Sign of Guy, dean.

### Charter concerning Dalaima

We make known to present and future persons that Hugh, a canon of the highest probity and builder of the monastery of Saint Mary of Lagoniacum, gave Saint Peter his share of all his father’s freehold situated at the village of Dalaima, with the approval of his brothers and nephews. Sign of Hugh. Sign of Otto. Sign of Radald. Sign of Peter.

### Charter concerning Luco

We notify all persons now living and their successors that a certain woman named Helisabeth, daughter of Willer [Col. 0927C] of the village of Campanis, newly bereaved by the death of her husband Ozilin, came to the monastery of Bèze and gave Saint Peter one holding in the village called Luco, very suitable and advantageous, with its appurtenances. Sign of Helizabeth. Sign of Ezilina, her mother. Sign of her brothers Hugh and Radalon, monks.

### Charter concerning Blaniacum

We wish it to be made known that a certain man named Rainard, born in the village of Varona, granted Saint Peter the freehold which he had formerly purchased in the village of Blaniacum, for the remission of his sins. His brothers, Sewin the cleric and Alberic, kindly assenting to this alms-gift, while conveying his body, laid upon a bier, to the monastery, firmly established it and, in his stead, gave it to the saint and the brethren at the altar, strengthening it before all by supporting testimony. Sign of Sewin. Sign of Alberic. Sign of Vilric, knight.

### Charter concerning Busciacum, Lujatum, and Luco

We also wish to set forth in writing that Helizabet, also surnamed Liezilina, mother of the monk Hugh, gave Saint Peter, in the village called Busciacum, one holding with its dependent farmstead, and the other holdings belonging to it, with their dependent farmsteads and all their appurtenances—in fields, woods, meadows, waters, watercourses, and fisheries—whether in the same village or in the other villages adjoining it, namely Lujatum, Luco, Dalaima, or wherever [Col. 0928A] that land lies; she gave all of it in its entirety to God and Saint Peter, with the consent of her sons and brothers, in the presence of all the monks. Sign of Hugh, her son, a monk; of Richard, her son; of Bernard, her brother.

### Charter concerning the two prebends of Saint Gengulf

When Henry, king of the Franks, was already burdened with illness and old age, he assembled the leading men of the Franks and, with the counsel of all, made his son Philip his associate in the whole kingdom; placing the diadem upon his head, he ordered him to be called king.

In the first year of his reign (1060), lord Arduin, bishop of Langres, solely for the reward of prayers, gave to Saint Peter and the community of Bèze, [Col. 0928B] with the approval of all the canons, two prebends—that is, as much as is received by two canons—as we shall show here.

The fortunate prudence of the ancients strove to provide this salutary remedy for their successors: what passing times could not transmit to posterity, they should set forth in letters supported by the authority of that prince in whose presence confirmation would be made by written charters or the impression of a seal. Foreseeing that this would benefit the sons of our church and the sacred congregation of Saint Mammetus, we likewise record in writing, according to the tenor of both parties, how they came to agreement.

By the grant of the renowned Hugh, bishop of Langres, the church of Saint [Col. 0928C] Gengulf was bestowed upon the church of Bèze, together with the stipend received by the person who served there at the holy thresholds.

The venerable bishop not only granted what we have mentioned above, but also conceded in perpetual right the village called Bannus. Afterwards, certain persons, resenting this unworthily, after he had departed from human affairs but before the venerable Arduin was honoured with the episcopal see, strengthened by the support of Provost Gerard and pursuing their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, brought it back under their own control, as it had formerly been possessed by them. When the venerable Arduin, now invested with the episcopal mitre, learned this, he began to feel compassion and, overflowing with piety, to urge the whole congregation that those who had taken away the village bestowed by his predecessor should at least have pity on those serving God there and provide something from which the dependants of the church might be supported. Finally, in the presence of Albero, abbot of Dijon, with the approval of all the canons, he obtained from them that, when the aforesaid canons ate twice, the monks should likewise receive as much as two of them received—namely morning and evening; and if they ate only once, then likewise the same quantity of bread and wine should be given as two canons receive.

Since at that time money was lacking, by which food ought under customary law to have been supplied to all the children of the church, they adopted this arrangement, and it seemed good to all that they should receive the confraternity offered [Col. 0929A] to them in exchange for food, on this condition: if anyone should be reported to have died, the day of burial should be observed by the monks in the same way as they customarily observe it for all congregations joined to them; moreover, their names should be written with the names of the brethren, so that the day of their anniversary might be known and celebrated by all. And so that what we have said might be held more firmly, our men and they likewise approved that they should do the same for our people.

Therefore, lest what we have written be effaced in succeeding records, in the presence of the venerable man Arduin, bishop of this holy see, we record below, by order of the same bishop, the names of the living persons who were present, on these conditions. Sign of the same Bishop Arduin. Sign of Willencus, archdeacon. Sign of [Col. 0929B] Rainard, who was surnamed Hugh. Sign of Roger, treasurer. Sign of Eward, dean. Sign of Aerleius, archdeacon. Sign of Gerard, archdeacon. Sign of Warner. Sign of Gibuin. Sign of Hildegard. Sign of Milo of Saint-Lupus. Sign of Emmaric. Moreover, the sign of all the canons, who unanimously approved this in chapter. Done at Langres, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1059, Indiction XII, Epact IV. But whoever shall presume to violate this, or shall take anything from Saint Peter, or shall attempt to oppose the rulers of the monastery of Bèze, by the authority of almighty God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—of blessed Peter, of all the saints, and of ourselves, let them be excommunicated, anathematized, driven from the lot of the just, and eternally damned unless they make amends by worthy satisfaction. Sign of [Col. 0929C] Abbot Odo and of all the monks of that monastery.

### Charter concerning the village of Coriaut

Let all present and future persons know that Berno, reeve of the village of Janlint, gave to Saint Peter, under this condition, a certain freehold belonging to him and lying in the village called Coriaut; and with his own hand placed it upon the altar, retaining the usufruct of that freehold during his lifetime. But after his departure from life, it shall return in its entirety to the place of Saint Peter. For this gift, which he made orally, he produced living witnesses; their names are: Odilo, provost; Rodulf; Bado; Aldo; Eward.

### Charter concerning the vineyard at Briscona

[Col. 0929D] The matron Albordis, for the remedy of the soul of her late lord Erembert, with the consent of his brother named Ozelin, gave to Saint Peter of the monastery of Bèze the vineyard called Clausmors, in the village called Briscona.

### Charter concerning Vetus-vineae

Likewise Alburgis, daughter of Willencus, brother of Hugh, lord of the castle of Belmonte, gave Saint Peter to possess in perpetuity everything she had in the village of Vetus-vineae—in meadows, fields, and woods—together with the serfs Guy and Theoderic, their sister Bilina, and three other female slaves, Heldegard, Evizaida, and Teodrada. Sign of her lord Pons. Of the knight Guy. Of the knight Walter.

### Charter concerning Moringas

[Col. 0930A] We think it should be recorded for future persons that Willencus gave to God and Saint Peter two holdings in the settlement of Moringas with all their appurtenances, and the serf named Ulric with his wife and children. And so that this gift might obtain perpetual validity, this document sets forth below the names of those who signed: Sign of his son Pons; of Fulk; of Odilo; of Berno, cleric.

### Charter concerning Condiliacum

We notify all persons now living and future persons that a certain matron Helvindis gave Saint Peter, for her husband Walter, who was called Albus, one holding at Condiliacum and one serf named Erimbert. Sign of Gilbert, Hugh, Willer, and Maurice, sons of the same lady.

### Charter concerning Vaunna

[Col. 0930B] The same Helvidis, after the first gift, gave Saint Peter one holding at Vaunna for her son Maurice, whom she had had by the aforesaid Walter. This holding is so free from every customary claim of any person that neither the duke nor his officials may demand anything from it; it is wholly exempt from exactions by other princes or persons. She also gave a serf named Richard. Sign of her son Haymo; of Gilbert.

### Charter concerning the village of Crepon

We wish all present and future persons to know that Rainald of Autriacum gave Saint Peter one holding at the settlement of Crepon, with all [Col. 0930C] its appurtenances. It owes the official of the lordship of Fontana one denarius each year, if the man dwelling upon it should use the woodland of that lordship. Sign of Rainald, Odilo, Odo.

### Charter concerning Fontanellae

Prompted by the counsel and example of the same Rainald, his nephew Odo, called Gibbosus, likewise gave Saint Peter all the freehold he possessed in the settlement called Fontanellae. Sign of Odo, Odilo, Rainald.

### Charter concerning the settlement of Buciacum

We wish it to be clear to all that the brothers Arlebald and Odo granted Saint Peter one field of fifteen *jugera* in the settlement of Buciacum. Sign of lord Abbot Odo, Moron, Benedict.

### Charter concerning Flaciacum

[Col. 0930D] We wish it to be known to present and future persons that Odilina, mother of Pons of Besoeta, bestowed upon Saint Peter one holding at Flaciacum. Sign of Pons, Hugh the provost, John.

### Charter concerning Lisciacum

We wish all present and future persons to understand that Guy of Lisciacum gave Saint Peter, at the same settlement of Lisciacum, one holding with all its appurtenances. He also gave the site of a mill, where that mill was to be built, with one serf named Drogo; moreover, he restored the serf whom he had earlier given for his brother Anseric, named Odo. Sign of Odilo, Anseric, Hugh the provost.

### Charter concerning Moringas

[Col. 0931A] Record that Aduin gave Saint Peter, for his brother Milo, called Albus, a certain portion of the freehold he had in the settlement named Moringas, on the condition that after his death the other portion should pass into the monks’ demesne. He also gave a serf named Aerbert. Moreover, he had previously given, for his mother Altrudis, the wife of Ulric, priest of Granantis-villa, with all her children. Sign of Aduin, his son Henry, Aerembert.

### Charter concerning Domnus Aper

We wish all to know that Hugh of Lanfred’s court granted Saint Peter one holding in the village called Saint Aper, because of the church constructed in that village in honour of Saint [Col. 0931B] Aper. He also gave the serf living there with his wife and children. Sign of his son Landric. Sign of his son Hugh. Sign of Odo.

### Charter concerning the village of Arciacum

We commit to writing for the remembrance of posterity that Odo, a cleric of Gimelles, granted Saint Peter one estate in the village of Arciacum, for his brother Dodo. Sign of Odo, Bernard, Berald.

### Charter concerning Beria

We desire that it be clear to all successors that Aduin of Beria gave Saint Peter one holding at that same village of Beria with all its appurtenances, and one serf named Algrin. Sign of Walo, Warner, Milo.

### Another item

[Col. 0931C] We wish all persons, both present and future, to know that Walo granted Saint Peter one holding at Beria with its appurtenances, and one serf named Hugh of Vado, with his wife and children. Sign of Aldo, whose byname is Rusticellus; of Milo; of Maiolus, surnamed Mazilinus.

### Charter concerning the village of Nogdant

We wish it to become known to all that Hildelerius gave Saint Peter, for his son Guy, slain by a crossbowman at Saint Julian, one holding in the village of Nogdant with appurtenances and customary rights, together with two female slaves who were sisters. Sign of Odo, Walter, Bernard, Berald.

### Charter concerning the village of Albiniacum

[Col. 0931D] The same Hildelerius also granted Saint Peter, in the village of Albiniacum, which lies in the county of Dijon, for his wife, two holdings with their appurtenances—in lands, fields, meadows, woods, and pastures. Sign of Odo, Walter.

### Charter concerning Pinriacum

We wish all to know that Milo of Bellomonte granted Saint Peter, for his wife, one holding in the settlement of Pinriacum with its appurtenances, and one serf named Eward with his sister. Sign of Milo, Fulk, Odilo.

### Charter concerning the village of Campanis

We also wish to set forth [Col. 0932A] for the memorial of future persons that Gilbert of Rescia granted Saint Peter, for his wife, one holding in the village of Campanis with all its appurtenances, together with one serf named Lotzelm. Sign of Frodo, Widric.

### Another item

We wish it to be made known to all that Odo, lord of Mont-Salion, gave Saint Peter, for his brother Hugh, one holding in the same village of Campanis with its appurtenances, together with one serf named Lozuin. Sign of Pons, Hugh, Arlebald.

### Charter concerning Genciniacum

We have judged it right to declare that Walo of Scuviliacum gave Saint Peter, to his predecessors, one holding with its appurtenances in the village of Gencinniacum [Col. 0932B] and a serf named Isembard, with his sister. Sign of lord Abbot Odo. Moron, Benedict.

### Charter concerning Nogdant

We have judged it worthwhile to commit to writing that Hilderius, mentioned above, gave Saint Peter, for his daughter—the wife, namely, of Odo called Vetulus—one holding in the aforesaid village of Nogdant, with one female slave. Sign of Odo, Bernard, Berald, Walter.

### Charter concerning Vaura

We wish to make known to present and future persons that Hugh Rufus gave Saint Peter, for his father Humbert, son of Hildebrand, two holdings with their appurtenances in the village called Vaura, together with a serf. Sign of Formald, [Col. 0932C] Theoderic, Bernard, Berald.

### Another item

We also wish to insert into this ink-written charter that, for the knight Vislerius, his wife gave Saint Peter, in the aforesaid settlement of Vaura, one holding with its appurtenances. Sign of Milo, Robert, priest, Hugh the provost.

### Charter concerning Curtis Salionis

We judge it fitting to notify present and future persons in writing that Robert, knight of Mont-Salion and brother of Guy the Great, when approaching death and receiving the monastic habit, granted Saint Peter one very large holding in the settlement of Curtis Salionis, in the parish of the village of Ruciacum, with one serf named [Col. 0932D] Alberic. Sign of his brother Guy. Of Odo, lord of Mont-Salion. Of his brother Hugh. Likewise of Hugh of Lanfred’s court.

### Charter concerning the village of Verona

We wish all to know that Milo Balbus, knight of the castle of Tilensis, gave Saint Peter one holding in the village of Verona for his wife, with its appurtenances. Sign of Formald; of Aldo, Milo’s stepson.

### Charter concerning Luco

The same Milo, with Odo, provost of Dijon, who had married his niece, when about to fight a single combat, gave Saint Peter the land he had at Luco near the churchyard, [Col. 0933A] so that Saint Peter might be his helper in the appointed battle. Sign of Lambert, Odo, Formald.

### Another item

We wish all to know clearly that Pons of Besoeta, for the violence he committed against Saint Peter’s sanctuaries by violating them, when he dragged a certain Harduin out from there, gave that saint one very large holding with its appurtenances at Luco. Sign of lord Abbot Odo, Moron, Benedict.

### Another item
This also we have thought fit to record concerning him: that, in some measure repentant for the many wrongs, crimes, and depredations committed by him against the holy place or the poor of that place, he granted Saint Peter another mansus in the same village with its appurtenances, and one serf named Josbert, who was also called Babilinus. Sign of lord Abbot Odo, Moron, Benedict.

### Charter concerning the village of Villars

[Col. 0933B] We deem it fitting to make known to all by letters that Hugh the provost, for the sake of his wife, granted Saint Peter one mansus in the village called Villars, near the castle of Gradiac; and one serf named Lambert. Sign of lord Abbot Odo. Signs of Benedict and Tetbald.

### Charter concerning Auxiliacum

[Col. 0933C] We judge it necessary, for the benefit of posterity, to commit to writing that Willerius of Criciacum gave Saint Peter one mansus in the village of Auxiliacum with its appurtenances, and a serf named Humbert. Sign of lord Abbot Odo, Benedict, Gerard his brother-in-law, Humbert, collector of tavern-dues.

### Charter concerning Bettonis-Curtis

We wish it to be known to those present and future that Hagano of Vissiacum, approaching death, gave Saint Peter, for the redemption of his soul, one mansus at the village of Bettonis-Curtis and one serf named Dominic, with his wife and daughters. And so that this charter might obtain perpetual validity, he requested that the names of the witnesses be written below. Signs of Gislebert, Hugh, Willerius, Robert.

### Charter concerning Rainald’s Court

[Col. 0933D] A certain knight, Humbert, being at the end of his life, gave Saint Peter at Marceacum-villa half a mansus for the remission of his sins; the other half had already long before been given by his brother Gerard to Saint Peter. He also transferred a serf named Constantius, with his wife and children; likewise one mansus at Rainald’s Court, in which David lived, with all its appurtenances, in fields, meadows, woods, and watercourses. He also assigned to the monks of the place the fishery of the aforesaid Constantius, just as he had held it during his lifetime. And, in order that this gift might retain the strength of perpetual validity, he solemnly recorded it in writing. Signs of Gerard his brother, Odo, Hugh, and Adelaide, wife of Humbert himself.

### Charter concerning Saint-Seine

[Col. 0934A] We wish all future persons to know that a certain distinguished matron, Raimodis, coming to her end and leaving Saint Peter a great quantity of money of various kinds, gave half a tenancy at Saint-Seine, at Helpricurtis, together with one female slave. And lest any forgetfulness in succeeding times should be able to erase this alms, she requested that it be committed to parchment for confirmation. Signs of Hugh her son; Gertrude her daughter; Regina her daughter; Landric, her son-in-law.

### Charter concerning Picangiae

We wish all present and future persons to know that Hugh, encouraged by this hope—he was called the protector of Crilliacum-villa for the security of that village—gave Saint Peter, for his own soul and that of his son Wido, who had long ago been killed, seven mansi at the village of Picangiae, and a serf named Halinard, his steward, and a female slave named Addeta, with her son named Girald and his sister. Signs of Hugh, Formald, Halinard, Odo, son of Hugh himself.

### Charter concerning Ewald’s Court

[Col. 0934B] We wish it to be known to those present and future that Rismodis, wife of Otbert, coming to her end and touched by divine inspiration, gave Saint Peter at Ewald’s Court one mansus, with the serf living there named Haimo, his wife, and children; and, in the village called Fontaines, near Vilecastle, one mansus with one dependent, called Christian. Signs of Otbert, Humbert his son, Aldo his son.

### Charter concerning Old Vines

We wish it to be known to both present and future persons that Henry, for his brother Ulric, gave Saint Peter half a mansus at Old Vines, and his serf Girald with his wife, on the condition that whatever children they should henceforth beget should pass into the service of the monks. Signs of Henry, Humbert Rufus.

### Charter concerning Icium

[Col. 0934C] We wish present and succeeding persons to understand that Odo, called the Elder, when brought to his last extremity transferred to Saint Peter in the village of Icium one mansus and three jugera of land within the bounds of that village, with one serf named Erbert and his son with him. Signs of Formald, Walter, Bernard.

### Charter concerning Icium and Verona

[Col. 0934D] We desire all to know that Wido of Fossatum granted Saint Peter, for his brother Aldo the cupbearer, two mansi: one in the village of Icium and the other in the village of Verona, with one serf named Aldo. Signs of Wido, Amalric, Aldo.

### Charter concerning Saint-Seine

Record of how a certain knight named Wido, for the remission of his sins, assigned to Saint Peter at Saint-Seine, Helpricurtis, one mansus and one curtilage in the same village, and one fourth of the wood of Tachiriacum, and one female slave named Anna with her two daughters. Signs of Pontius, Widric, Belin.

### Charter concerning Pauliacum

[Col. 0935A] We wish it to be manifest to all who flourish in the present life and in the future age that Formald of Icium gave Saint Peter, for the soul of his wife, who was Willenc’s sister, one mansus at Pauliacum, under the testimony of both families. Signs of Formald, Bernard, Berald.

### Another charter

Because the condition of this life is unstable, we wish mortals to know that a certain matron, Emma by name, wife of Hildemod, transferred to Saint Peter one mansus at Pauliacum, with one enclosure, under the testimony of the brethren then present. Signs of Wido, Aerembert, Anselm.

### Charter concerning Lalandi Court

[Col. 0935B] A certain knight, Lambert by name, stepfather of Willenc, granted Saint Peter one mansus at Lalandi Court for the remedy of his soul. Signs of Willenc his stepson, Formald, Pontius.

### Charter concerning Saviniacum

We wish all to know that Wido of Porta, coming to his end, granted Saint Peter two mansi: one in Saviniacum, the other in Granciacum in the district of Dijon; and one serf named Tedo, dwelling in the village of Verona. Signs of Tetbald, Wido, Humbert.

### Charter concerning Arciacum

We wish it to be manifest to all that Tetbald, son of that Wido, transferred to Saint Peter one mansus in the village of Arciacum, and one serf named Maurice, together with his sister, whom Edward, reeve of the village of Acetis, had taken in marriage. Signs of Wido his brother, Humbert, Guxzo.

### Charter concerning Auxiliacum

[Col. 0935C] We wish it to be disclosed to all that, for Morannus, his wife and son gave Saint Peter one mansus at Auxiliacum, together with a serf named Waldric. Signs of his wife, Joffrey his son, Henry.

### Charter concerning Pontus

Record that Wido, brother of Morannus, granted Saint Peter one mansus in Auxiliacum and another in the village called Pontus, and restored and surrendered the benefice which he held from the monks. Signs of Wido, lord Abbot Odo, Moron, Benedict.

### Charter concerning Calmis

[Col. 0935D] We wish it to be manifest to all present and future persons that Mainfred, for his son Maurice, gave Saint Peter two mansi at Auxiliacum; and he granted all the freehold that he possessed in the village of Calmis, which is near the castle of Miribel. Signs of Mainfred, Leutbrann his son, Arlebald.

### Charter concerning Pontus

The same Mainfred likewise gave Saint Peter one mansus in the village of Pontus for his first wife, who was the sister of Abbot Tetbald. Signs of Mainfred, Maurice, Leutbrann.

### Another charter

[Col. 0936A] At Crusciacum also he gave, for his second wife, all the freehold which he held in the same village from her share, with the assent of that lady’s brothers. Signs of Mainfred, Theoderic, Wido.

### Charter concerning the village of Chimiscum

We wish all to know that Odo and Hugh transferred to Saint Peter, for their brother Wdo, who had been killed, one mansus with its appurtenances in the village of Chimiscum, with one female slave named Helgard. Signs of Odo, Hugh, Milo.

### Charter concerning Wandaleni Court

We desire it to be known to all that Hildemod granted Saint Peter all the freehold which he possessed in the village of Wandaleni Court, which is under the authority of Hortesis, together with one serf named Theoderic, subject to a rent of two denarii of wax. Signs of Odo, Pontius, Hugh.

### Charter concerning the village of Nogdant

[Col. 0936B] The swiftness of life’s limit compels memorable matters to be impressed upon the characters of charters, lest, as the length of time intervenes, they be erased from human memory. Therefore we desire to make known to all that Arlebald, knight of Mont-Salins, transferred to Saint Peter one mansus in the village of Nogdant, with one serf. Signs of Odo, Hugh, Pontius.

### Charter concerning the village of Villars

Let all diligence know that Aymo, who was a *glabrio*—an uncertain term, perhaps an official or servant—granted Saint Peter one mansus in the village called Villars, with one serf named Raimbald. Sign of Henry, Odo, Wido.

### Charter concerning Auxiliacum

[Col. 0936C] We have also taken care to announce in the same manner that Joffrey gave Saint Peter ten jugera of land in the village of Auxiliacum. Signs of Odo, Henry, Willerius.

### On the death of Bishop Arduin

Rainard succeeded Bishop Arduin. Abbot Odo was succeeded by Wido, and Wido by Gausbert.

After the death of the venerable Bishop Arduin, Rainard obtained the episcopal see. Likewise, when Abbot Odo died, Wido, a monk from the monastery of Areomarus, succeeded to his place. After spending a few years in office, he returned to his own monastery, relinquishing the governance of this place; Gausbert succeeded him in the rule of souls, holding the office of prior in the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon.

### Charter concerning the church of Saint Remigius

[Col. 0936D] In the name of the Holy Trinity and the one Godhead. Let every succession of ages, both present and future, know that lord Rainard, bishop of Langres, at the request of Abbot Gausbert and the monks of that place, made the church of Saint Remigius free from all the customary dues contained in the polyptych—namely, provisions and the payment which the priest owed at the synod—remitting them; provided, however, that the priest should indeed customarily attend the synod with the others, but should pay no other rent. In order that this might remain unaltered, the aforesaid bishop ordered this record and confirmation to be made, lest any of his successors should presume to invalidate this gift; and he imposed the threat of eternal condemnation from almighty God upon anyone who should attempt to inflict a violation upon this record. Done at Langres in full synod, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1080, indiction III. Sign of Bishop Rainard, who ordered this record to be made; and of the entire synodal assembly, his archdeacons and deans.
