Sign of Gerard, archdeacon; Aerleius, archdeacon; Walter, dean; Hugh of Butgiacum, canon.

### Another charter

The same bishop claimed a certain man named Robert of Gurziacum, with his wife and only daughter, and likewise the children of that daughter, whom she had by Lambert, serf of Saint Peter. But, having received one hundred solidi, he granted the brethren whatever right he seemed to possess in them, and transferred them from his own jurisdiction into their lordship. Signs of Walter, Rainer, Richard, Gislebert, Aymo.

### Charter concerning the church and village of Saint Valerian

[Col. 0937A] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. All who wish to attain the summit of perfection are known to set before the eyes of their mind the rule of the Lord’s command, by which He commands each person to dispose of his own possessions for His sake and devoutly distribute them to the poor. For the righteousness of such persons shall endure throughout all the ages, and their horn—that is, the reward of their struggle—shall be exalted in heavenly glory, since earthly patrimonies transferred into heavenly treasures shall profit their givers in everlasting life.

[Col. 0937B] “Strengthened, therefore, by this confidence of hope, I, Pontius, lord of the castle of Bellijocus, desire to give to the Redeemer of all some of my possessions which were left to me by hereditary right from my parents. I therefore give to God and Saint Peter of Bèze the chapel built in honour of Saint Valerian, with its honour and freely, just as I have hitherto appeared to possess it, with the assent of my brother Eromuin; together with a vineyard; and a field as far as the stony ground and as far as the spring; and whatever the monks or their men can bring under cultivation from the wood which lies beside the vineyard. I likewise grant from the wood situated between the church and the river Saône whatever they and their men may wish to acquire for the use of meadowland.

[Col. 0937C] “I also grant the market with all freedom, and all the customs which my brother and I appeared to possess; and the other custom of pasture which we and our men have in all the woods surrounding the castle of Bellijocus shall likewise belong to the monks and their men. Thus the men on our side who use pasture shall pay the pasture-dues to the monks themselves; and we grant, free of charge from our woods, building timber for houses to the monks and to their men who may wish to remain there. We grant to the monks the finding of game or of bees which belongs to our share and which their men may discover; and the monks shall have the tithes and third-parts of all the land under cultivation which we give them, so that, wherever their plough works the land of any person within the parish, we give them the tithes.

[Col. 0937D] “Concerning theft or any complaint arising from an offence committed in that territory, we grant the monks jurisdiction; they shall lawfully possess the stray and the prohibited matter, and no person apprehended shall be judged under anyone’s authority except by the judgment of the monk.

[Col. 0938A] “If, however, a man of the monks commits an offence, he shall not be constrained by anyone’s violence before a complaint has been made to the monks; and, if the monks have not executed justice, that complaint shall first be referred to the abbot. Done publicly at Bellijocus, on the vigil of the Ascension of the Lord, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1083, while Hugh, formerly notary, governed the archbishopric of the church of Besançon; Philip was king of the Franks; Odo ruled the duchy of Burgundy; Robert, his brother, administered the episcopal office of the church of Langres; Count William prospered in his affairs; and Gausbert directed the government of the abbey of Bèze. Signs of Pontius, Hermuin, Herluin, Walter the viscount, Heurelmus, and another Pontius.”

### Charter concerning the protection of Nerontis-villa

[Col. 0938B] We wish it to be known to present and future persons that Fulco and his son Joffrey relinquished to Saint Peter and the monks the *salvamentum*, or protection and commendation, which they received at Nerontis-villa, after a complaint was made by the brethren before Duke Hugh and Count William in a general court, with those men present at Bèze and with all the other noblemen urging the matter; on the condition that all that the monks could justly have taken from them in a case of violence and wrong in past times, apart from the landholding and the person himself, should be entirely remitted, and that the inhabitants of the aforesaid village should remain forever free from the above-mentioned claim and from every injury or wrong. And in order that this remission might obtain the force of perpetual validity, and that none of their heirs should ever be able to reclaim the aforesaid violence, they requested that it be recorded in letters and, for more firmly preserving the memory of future generations, confirmed by the names of those who sealed or witnessed it. Signs of Duke Hugh; Count William; Count Wido of Mâcon; Gerard of Fontvenne; Wido of Wangion’s River; Pontius of Glana; Aldo of Tilcastle; Sewin; Wldenaius; Gislebert. Done publicly at Bèze in a public assembly, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1076, indiction XIV, while Philip was king of the Franks, Duke Hugh was present, and William was count of Burgundy, on Tuesday, 31 May.

[Col. 0938C] Therefore, after Bishop Rainard had closed his eyes to the light of day and made an end of this present life, according to what is written: “They became priests in greater numbers because they were prevented by death from remaining” (Hebrews 7:23), it was necessary to appoint another in his place. And because Rainard himself had ruled the see of Langres very splendidly and gloriously, he had kindled in the hearts of all who had had him as pastor a longing and emulation such that, by God’s favour—indeed, by God’s gift—they might be granted a pastor who would be Rainard’s successor and likewise his imitator. What more need be said?

Lord Robert was elected, himself also illustrious in every respect, born of the stock of the kings of the Franks and brother of Duke Odo, surnamed Borel. He was not excessively tall in stature, nor short, but of moderate height. Although he flourished in the eloquence of twofold learning, his speech was most sparing unless circumstances required it. Therefore, as was fitting, Robert was elected by the common vote of both clergy and people; adorned with the pontifical mitre, he was appointed bishop over the church of Langres.

[Col. 0939A] We should appear ungrateful if, forgetful of the benefits which he conferred upon this church, we allowed them to be covered in silence. Let us therefore first tell how he himself transferred to God and Saint Peter of the church of Bèze the chapel of the castle called Fontvenne.

### Charter concerning the chapel of Fontvenne

Because the human race, preoccupied with the corruptible mass of flesh, has contracted the defect of frail and failing memory, our predecessors wisely decided that whatever they wished to be held firm and inviolable should be entrusted to the faithful custody of letters. We likewise, using the same reasoning, have endeavoured to preserve by the transmission of writing the matters set down below, lest they should ever be erased by forgetfulness.

[Col. 0939B] I, Robert, bishop of Langres, grant to the church of Bèze, to be held in perpetuity, the chapel of the aforesaid castle, for Humbert of Fontvenne, a vassal of the church of Langres, who was slain in the service of that church; his wife, his brothers, and all the vassals of the same castle approving and advising this act. He was buried in the cemetery of that church, so that through the intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the prayers of the monks serving God there, he may obtain pardon for his sins.

[Col. 0939C] We also judge that this gift must be maintained at Langres in full synod, such that if any cleric or layman presume, against the will of the monks of Bèze, to do anything concerning the benefices belonging to the aforesaid chapel, he shall be subject, if a cleric, to the peril of his order; if a layman, to excommunication, until he comes to his senses. Witnesses to this gift are Count William of Burgundy, his son Rainald, Humbert Rufus and his brother Wido, Wido Rufus, and the other vassals. These things were done while Philip reigned, Robert was bishop, and Stephen the chancellor dictated the document.

### Josbert, abbot of Bèze

[Col. 0939D] At that time lord Abbot Josbert, a man of complete simplicity and religious devotion, presided over this monastery. Yet, because in the Church of God some are walls built with battlements and others are a door fashioned with cedar planks, this man—because he could not, like a wall, repel the enemies of God’s house, while countless robbers were outside and dangers from false brethren within—was nevertheless like a door made of cedar planks for opening and closing: for he had a mouth for speaking and for silence, enriched with the sayings of various lofty and incorruptible Fathers.

[Col. 0940A] Seeing, therefore, that it was good for his soul to dwell with himself under the gaze of the heavenly Inspector, he chose the better part, which would not be taken from him. For he sought Cluny and spent there the remainder of his life, seeking peace and finding peace, joined to Christ, who is the peace of angels and of men. Amen.

### Concerning the cell of Saint Eugendus

Meanwhile the aforesaid lord Robert, bishop of Langres, earnestly considered whom he should appoint as abbot of this church in Lord Josbert’s place. He turned the eye of his heart in every direction, seeking one to whom he might entrust the staff of this church. God did not allow him to be disappointed in his desire, nor to be wearied long in his search.

[Col. 0940B] For there is a cell of Saint Eugendus, not far distant from the city of Langres, in the same diocese but in the county of Troyes: a church dedicated in honour of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, most fittingly established on a certain high hill called Bar. It thus came about that what had had to be sought long and far was found there. Lord Stephen presided over that place. Though not greatly mature in age, he was nevertheless fortified by piety and religion, rooted and grounded in the fear and love of God and, according to the Apostle, in charity.

### Concerning Lord Abbot Stephen

#### Abbot Stephen, born of noble lineage. A survey of his deeds.

[Col. 0940C] It seems not unfitting to touch briefly upon the line of his descent, since nobility often greatly helps both a person in preserving humility and the churches of God in resisting plunderers. He was thus born of a most noble father named Joffrey, who himself was not only a count but also derived his descent from a father and grandfather who were counts. What should I say of the mother of the aforesaid Lord Stephen, except that on both sides—namely, paternal and maternal—she was born from the line of counts, indeed from counts themselves? For she was daughter of the most noble and courageous Count Arnulf of Risnel, and had as her mother a daughter of the most illustrious Count Gerard of Fontvenne.

[Col. 0940D] That this lion’s whelp, first changed into a lamb and afterwards appointed as a ram to defend the church with his horns and beget in her spiritual lambs, was the grace of God: this was the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. I wish, if I can, though not with elegant speech yet with truthful speech, to recount how he abandoned the roaring lion and followed the Lion of the tribe of Judah; and how, through the spotless Lamb, he was made a lamb in order to follow Him wherever He goes.

In those days the Bridegroom, namely Christ, called his bride, the Church, to come from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards by way of the mountain of myrrh and the hills of Lebanon. For the princes who had formerly resembled lions because of cruelty and terror, and leopards because of the variety of their iniquities, having been cleansed by hyssop—that is, humble confession—were made whiter than snow through the mortification of myrrh and the brightness of Lebanon.

### Concerning Simon, Count of Crépy. He becomes a monk with many other nobles at the monastery of Saint Eugendus, or Saint Claude.

[Col. 0941A] The head and leader of these was a most noble count of the Franks, Simon, son of Count Rudolph. Looked upon by divine mercy, he fled the fleeing world and followed Christ who called him. He sought the monastery of Saint Eugendus in the Jura, there to sacrifice himself to Christ. Before him he sent two most distinguished men, Lord Rudolph and Lord Franco; with him he brought Lord Robert, Lord Arnulf, and Lord Warner. All these, most illustrious according to worldly lineage and most noble according to God, afterwards offered themselves as a holocaust to God.

### Stephen among them

[Col. 0941B] Lord Stephen, of whom we speak, was still young, though already adorned with military arms. But, following wiser counsel—indeed, by God’s inspiration—he followed the aforesaid Fathers; renouncing the secular belt and taking up Christ’s yoke, he embraced the monastic life in the aforesaid monastery. There, under Lord Abbot Hunaud, he devoted himself to God’s service for ten years.

He then sought Cluny, where he stayed for a year with his uncle Lord Wido, the great prior. When that Wido was later made abbot because of his religious devotion and holiness of life, Stephen followed him to Poitiers and was continually becoming better than himself. Finally, returning to his own monastery, he was sent to the cell of Saint Eugendus at Bar. All this occurred by God’s ordering, without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the earth.

[Col. 0941C] Thus Lord Stephen was found there and, by the venerable aforesaid Robert, bishop of Langres, and by his own abbot, was granted to this place. Although reluctant, he was made abbot in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1088, indiction XI, epact XXV.

### Made abbot of Bèze, he restores everything

[Col. 0941D] How greatly he then endeavoured, with what care and zeal, to reform and enlarge this place, the works themselves bear witness even if words are silent. For although this monastery had first been built five hundred years or more before, it seems to have taken its beginning from the time of Lord Abbot Stephen: everything was renewed; everything was changed for the better.

Wherever he went, this was his desire and the longing of his mind: if he saw anywhere anything honourable or necessary for his church, he either brought it back himself or constructed something similar in his own church. In religion this place flourished anew so greatly in his days that Bèze had a renowned name as far as Rome, mistress of the world, and throughout all Gaul to the shores of the sea. Thus it happened that, when he first came here, there were scarcely twenty monks, whereas in his days there were fifty or sixty serving God and receiving the necessities of food and clothing.

### Distinguished monks who lived under Stephen’s discipline

[Col. 0942A] If we count those dwelling in our cells outside Bèze, the number will rise to one hundred. God also granted him this: that in his days some men converted to the Lord and received the monastic habit from him in this place, afterwards becoming lights of churches themselves. Lord Abbot Wido was placed over the church of Saint Michael at Tournus. Lord Abbot Henry was placed over the church of Saint-Seine. Lord Eustace was placed over the church of Saint Eligius at Noyon. Lord Godefrey was placed over the church of Saint John. Although he had not himself been our monk, he was nevertheless taken from our monastery. Very many others besides, led by paternal emulation under Stephen, imitated their father in building and acquiring, and enlarged, adorned, and fortified this church as their mother.

### Churches dependent upon Bèze

[Col. 0942B] Concerning the buildings and acquisitions both within Bèze and outside it; the restoration of the body of the monastery itself and of its workshops; the library, of both the Old and New Testaments; ecclesiastical ornament in tablets, reliquaries, chalices, crosses, censers, and garments belonging to the divine office; cloaks and curtains, hangings and banners acquired by him and by the other brethren and sons of this church in his time and bestowed upon this place—we shall speak somewhat more fully below.

For the present, let us speak of the churches bestowed upon this place in his days, both in this diocese and in others: the church of Saint Symphorian at Albiniacum; the church of Saint Benignus; the church of Saint Christopher at Camlintum; and, in the diocese of Toul, the church of Saint Willegaud at the castle of Romon. The charters inserted in this little book show how and by whom these were bestowed.

### Charter concerning Albiniacum and the church of Saint Benignus

[Col. 0942C] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Because our predecessors entrusted to the custody of letters whatever they wished to be held firm and indissoluble, so that the representation of letters might reveal what negligent forgetfulness erased, we have deemed it fitting to commit to writing those matters which we wish to remain forever.

[Col. 0942D] “I therefore, Robert, bishop of Langres, grant to the church of Bèze, to be held by it, the church of Albiniacum and its atrium; also the provisions and *eulogiae* belonging to the bishop; and the church of Saint Benignus and its atrium. With the consent and counsel of the brethren of Langres, I transfer them hand to hand in a full synod held at Langres to Stephen, abbot of the aforesaid church, and establish them to be held perpetually by him and his successors.

“We judge that this gift must be so held and maintained that, if any cleric or layman presume to take these things from them or unjustly disturb them concerning them, he shall be subject, if a cleric, to the peril of his order; if a layman, to anathema, until he comes to his senses. Signs of Gozelm, archdeacon; Hugh, archdeacon; Guarnerius, archdeacon; Norgaud, archdeacon; Gerard, archpriest; Guidric, archpriest. These things were done while Philip reigned, Robert was bishop, and Stephen the chancellor dictated the document.”

### Charter concerning Sivoio

[Col. 0943A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let all faithful Christians know how one half of the church of Sivoio came to be attached to the church of Bèze. Abbot Stephen, a religious man, was returning by boat on the Segunna to the church of Bèze when Hermuin, born of noble lineage in that village, received him as a guest. He welcomed him with most kindly affection and showed him every courtesy of hospitality. On the following day, exchanging perishable things for eternal, he transferred at the port of Prantenum, by the hands of the aforesaid abbot, one half of the church of Sivoio and the church of Saint Dionysius in the same village—as he possessed them in patrimony—for his own soul and those of his ancestors, by lawful testimony, to the apostles Peter and Paul and to the church of Bèze.

[Col. 0943B] These things were done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1093, indiction I, epact XX, lunar day VIII, in the thirty-fourth year of the reign of Emperor Henry, while Count Stephen ruled and Archbishop Hugh held the archiepiscopal see. If anyone violates this charter, let him be separated from the choirs of angels and joined with Dathan and Abiram, here and eternally in the lowest hell. Signs of our witnesses: Hermuin, Aimo, Lavencha, Girald, Albric, Tebert, Stigand. I, Godefrey, chancellor of the abbot, dictated and duly subscribed this document.

### Charter concerning the church of Camlintum and Majas

[Col. 0943C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Since it is customary, and derived from the prudence of our predecessors, that matters which seem worthy to be commended to memory should be consigned to the custody of writing, we have deemed it fitting faithfully to preserve within the bosom of this charter the matters set forth below, lest they perish through forgetfulness or lest anything that was done concerning them should ever be altered by some fraud.

[Col. 0943D] I therefore, Robert, bishop of the holy church of Langres, repeatedly urged by the requests of Stephen, abbot of the church of Bèze, at last acceding to his wish, when we were celebrating a synod in the church of Langres and diligently treating ecclesiastical affairs to the best of our ability, with the counsel and assent of the archdeacons sitting with us, grant to blessed Peter of the monastery of Bèze and to the brethren serving God there the two priestly benefices, namely, of the church of Camlintum and of the church of Majas, to be held henceforth. The parish priests who sing the office in them shall receive through the hands of the abbot of Bèze one half of all that pertains to those priestly benefices; they shall render the services due to the archdeacons and other ministers, and shall jointly pay the provisions and *eulogiae* at the proper time.

These things were done at Langres in full synod, while Pope Urban held office and Philip reigned in Gaul. Signs of Willenc, archdeacon; Gocelm, archdeacon; Garnerius, archdeacon; Norgaud, archdeacon; Gosbert, archpriest. Stephen the chancellor dictated; Durannus the notary wrote.

### Charter concerning Albiniacum

[Col. 0944A] In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Let it be made known to those desiring knowledge in the present age and to persons hereafter that Odo, lord of Mont-Salins, desiring to escape the punishment of eternal torment and receive the rewards of paradise, on the day of the burial of his brother Hugh, of his own free will summoned to the chapter at Bèze a considerable portion of the knights of Mont-Salins, dependants, friends, and neighbours, before the body of the deceased was carried to the tomb. There he confirmed in this manner the gifts which he had earlier made of the churches—namely, of Albiniacum, Saint Benignus, the chapel of Mont-Salins, and Icioma.

[Col. 0944B] In the presence of Lord Abbot Stephen and the monks, and of those whom he himself had summoned, the aforesaid Odo and Lord Peter, his uncle, made anew and confirmed in full the donation of the aforesaid churches to God and Saint Peter of the church of Bèze, to be possessed forever.

They also placed upon the altar, to confirm the gift, a Gospel book covered in silver, for the soul of the aforesaid Hugh, for the souls of all their deceased ancestors, and for themselves. They further added to this alms one mansus in Albiniacum, one serf, and one female slave.

At their request, Lord Abbot Stephen procured from Bishop Robert in synod absolution for the aforesaid Hugh, his father, and his deceased ancestors, in confirmation of this matter. And in order that this gift may remain unshaken, we set down the witnesses. Signs of Abbot Stephen; Wido the prior; Willenc; Odo and Peter, who made this gift.

[Col. 0944C] These things were done at the time when Paschal held the supreme pontificate in Rome, Philip exercised rule in Francia, Robert held the episcopal see at Langres, and Abbot Stephen held pastoral care at Bèze: in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1101, indiction VIII, epact XVIII. Signs of Tebold, Theoderic, Landric, Lanfricurtis, Lambert of Domarim, Widric the provost, Richard of Vircillis, Rudolph, Odo of Bellomonte, Haimo of Fontaines, Odo, Walo of Calmis; and, among the clerics, Humbert the archpriest, Willenc the priest, and John the priest.

### Charter concerning the churches which Humbert and Wido gave to us

[Col. 0944D] Let the life of believers acknowledge this: among human deeds nothing renders God more propitious than almsgiving performed with a good intention, as Scripture says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving destroys sin.” Therefore two brothers, Humbert Rufus and Wido, sons of Humbert of Fontvenne, were not deaf but faithful hearers of this saying. In the flower of their youth, for the salvation of their souls and of their faithful ancestors, they granted to God, Saint Peter, and the monastery of Bèze the churches which they held by their own right on this side of the water called Asmantia. So that charity might be more firmly established, at the city of Besançon, beside the basilica of Saint Vincent, in the presence of Archbishop Hugh, they delivered the aforesaid [Col. 0945A] churches in perpetuity to Abbot Stephen and the church of Bèze.

Namely, the fourth part of the basilica of Saint Martin of the monastery; whatever the church of Saint Christopher of Camlin possessed; the fourth part of the church of Saint Maurice of Sivoie; half of the church of the village of Fontvenne; likewise the chapel of the Castle; and, in the same manner, the church of Livocourt, under this testimony: the sign of Archbishop Hugh; of Mainier, archdeacon; of Bernard, master; of Ermuin; of Sewin.

On that same day the aforesaid bishop granted to Abbot Stephen liberty to possess all churches which he might be able to acquire in his diocese.

These things were done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1098, indiction VI, epact XV, Urban presiding as pope at Rome, [Col. 0945B] Henry ruling in the Roman Empire.

### Charter concerning Albiniac

Let every order of the faithful know most firmly that Odo, son of Hugh, lord of Mont-Salion, after receiving his honour from Robert, bishop of Langres, at Calma of Perciac, restored to the aforesaid Robert the church of Albiniac, on the condition that, at his request and with his consent, Robert should deliver it to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze for perpetual possession.

When the bishop heard this, he joyfully accepted the gift, which, as the aforesaid Odo had requested, he firmly granted to Abbot Stephen and the church of Bèze, under these witnesses: the sign of Robert, bishop; of Stephen, abbot; of Alberic, monk; of Warner, archdeacon; of Humbert, archpriest; of William of Fontvenne; [Col. 0945C] of Wido of Raiac; of Sewin, his son; of Odo, who made the gift; of Widric, provost; of Theobald; of Landric; of Walo; of Alelm and his brother; of Pagan of Icioma.

These things were done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1098, indiction VI, epact XXVI, Philip reigning as king of the Franks, Odo holding the duchy, and Robert, his brother, governing the episcopal see. If anyone violates this charter, let him be separated from the choirs of angels and joined with Dathan and Abiram here and eternally in hell.

### Charter concerning Lisseiac

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Let it be known to all present and future persons that Odilo, knight of Lisseiac, [Col. 0945D] most freely gave to God and Saint Peter whatever he possessed at the same village of Lisseiac, with serfs and handmaids. When he too was near death, appointing his nephew Anxiric as his heir, he commanded him that, unless he preserved the aforesaid gift, he should in no way retain his inheritance.

The sign of Geoffrey of Belmont; the sign of Hugh the Great; the sign of Gibuin; the sign of Hugh Columba.

### Likewise, another [charter]

A certain very noble woman, commonly called Facies, cousin of Alberic, monk of Arcione, granted to the monks of Bèze whatever she possessed in the aforesaid village, together with two serfs, Gerard and William, with their wives and children, on this condition: that she should be given the monastery’s sustenance by those same monks [Col. 0946A] as long as she lived. This small possession was afterwards assigned to the sacristan for the church lights, through the prayers and pious insistence of the aforementioned Ansiric.

The sign of Anseric; the sign of Odilo, his brother; the sign of Alberic, monk; the sign of Ulric, monk.

### Charter concerning Cypet

It seemed worthwhile and necessary to commend to the memory of posterity the fact that Odo Chaterius of Cypet, though he had unjustly contested the alms given by his mother-in-law Elizabeth, also called Charity—namely, her share of the wood adjoining the village called Old Vines—afterwards came to his senses and most freely granted to Saint [Col. 0946B] Peter and the church of Bèze the earlier gift exactly as it had been made.

He further added that the monk who resides at Cypet should have the freest right of use in the woods, fields, and meadows, and fishing in all waters, except the fishpond given to Lord Dato; but also in that fishpond, if the abbot should come to the village of Cypet.

Witnesses to this matter: the sign of Odo, who made this gift; the sign of Odo Viridis; the sign of Abbot Stephen; the sign of Wilenc. And of the household of Saint Peter: the sign of Otbert Coccus; the sign of Hugh; and of many others.

### Charter concerning Fontanis

Let it be made clear to all living persons and those yet to come that Hugh the young knight of Fontanis, as he approached his death, sought and devoutly received the habit of a monk. Having become a monk, for the salvation of his soul [Col. 0946C] and of his faithful ancestors, he gave to God and Saint Peter and to the church of Bèze, at the aforesaid Fontanis, one free mansus with all liberty, seven jugera of land, and three scythe-cuttings of meadow.

That this gift may remain unshaken, we designate trustworthy witnesses: the sign of Bertrand, knight of Fontanis; the sign of Theodoric, his son; the sign of Hugh Carruca; the sign of Widric, his son; the sign of Wilenc, knight; the sign of Walo Columba of Bellomont; the sign of Rudolph, knight of Aquis; the sign of Rudolph, peasant of Fontanis. Of the monks: the sign of Wilenc; the sign of Warner; the sign of Odilo; and of many others.

### Charter concerning Lixiac

Among the other alms given to the church [Col. 0946D] of Bèze, let all faithful persons know that Wido, knight of the island of Bollin, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze whatever he possessed or believed himself to possess at Lixiac from his ancestors, for the salvation of his soul and of his faithful ancestors. And this was done before he set out for Jerusalem.

After he began this journey and recognized that he was approaching death, through his companions Hugh, knight of Excuviliac, and Constantius of Diniac, he remitted to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze six ounces of gold, and confirmed for their perpetual possession his alms which he had made from Lixiac and the alms of his mother from Flexus.

The sign of Wido the knight, who made this gift; the sign of Hugh, knight; the sign of Constantius; the sign of [Col. 0947A] Stephen, abbot; the sign of Wilenc, prior; the sign of Alberic Captivus; and of many others.

### Charter concerning the Chapel of Mont-Salion

In the name of the supreme and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Since it is customary, and sanctioned by the diligence of our predecessors, that matters which seem worthy of perpetual remembrance should be committed to the custody of written records, we have judged it fitting faithfully to deposit in the bosom of this charter the matters set forth below, lest they perish through forgetfulness or what has been lawfully done concerning them should at some time be altered by fraud.

Therefore I, Robert, by God’s providence bishop of the venerable see of Langres, while we were dwelling in the bosom of the mother basilica entrusted to us by Christ, and were unanimously deliberating with the faithful of that church, by their counsel and will, concerning its condition and advancement, there appeared among them our friend, Lord Stephen, abbot of the church of Bèze. He humbly sought our favour, asking that we might not disdain, by a written instrument, to grant and mercifully bestow upon Saint Peter of the church of Bèze the chapel situated in the castle of Mont-Salion, belonging to the church of Albiniac and dedicated in honour of the holy Mother of God.

[Col. 0947B] Willingly accepting his just and reasonable petition, we took care, by the counsel of our faithful men, to bring into effect in due order what he had piously and reasonably requested: giving and granting the aforesaid chapel, while preserving all customs of the church of Langres, on the condition, however, that a chaplain serve the chapel and receive and possess his benefice from that abbot of Bèze.

That the testament of this our grant may be preserved in future times and kept without any diminution or alteration, we confirm it with our own hand and entrust it for confirmation to our archdeacons.

The sign of Goscelm, archdeacon; Wilenc, archdeacon; Hugh, archdeacon; Amalric, archdeacon; Warner, archdeacon.

These things were done at Langres in a full synod, Paschal, apostolic ruler of the Roman see, governing; Philip reigning; Robert ruling the church of Langres as bishop; Stephen serving as chancellor and Duran as notary, each discharging his office.

### Likewise, concerning the same chapel

[Col. 0947D] Let all who read or hear these letters know that Lord Stephen, abbot of Bèze, gave the chapel of Mont-Salion for the term of his life to Widric, cleric of Orgis, nephew, that is, of Widric the provost, upon this agreement and condition: that he should perform the service thereof wholly and faithfully toward Saint Peter, the church of Bèze, and the aforesaid abbot.

If he himself, or the priest-chaplain who is his deputy there, should wrongfully take or withhold anything from our division, then, after admonition, he shall present himself and the priest at Bèze before the abbot for justice to be done, as a man subject to him. Likewise, if the lord abbot wishes to go on a distant journey, the aforesaid cleric shall be ready, with his horse, [Col. 0948A] to serve him. As stated above, he shall do this during his lifetime; after his death it shall revert into the hand and power of the abbot.

We appoint witnesses to this subscription: the sign of Stephen, abbot; of Wido, prior; of Wilenc; John; Warner; Landric; Alberic; Geoffrey. Of the laymen: Widric, provost of Mont-Salion; Gilbert of Miribel; Otbert, cook; Hugh, servant.

### Charter concerning the holding of Germanus the priest

Let the faithful assembly of both present and future persons fully acknowledge that Lord Odo the younger, lord of Mont-Salion, came to Bèze on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. There, for his soul and the souls of his faithful ancestors, by the Gospel book placed upon the holy altar of the aforesaid apostles, he made an offering to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze: the holding of Germanus the priest, belonging and adjacent to the altar of Saint Symphorian of Albiniac—namely, the tithe from the lord of Mont-Salion’s own vineyard, a third part of the tithes belonging to the bishop’s demesne, from vineyards, corvées, and thirds, and every tithe from the land of Saint Peter.

Moreover, he abandoned and granted to the church and monks of Bèze, to hold by perpetual right and with all liberty, the claim which he had unjustly advanced concerning the cemetery of Albiniac, the cellars, and all things. This was all done at the request of Germanus the priest and his sons; Germanus subsequently became our monk.

We designate witnesses to this arrangement: the sign of [Col. 0948C] Odo, who granted this; Theobald, knight; Richard of Vircillis; Widric, provost; Lambert, knight of Domarim; Calo of Silviniac; Gerard Crispus, knight; Humbert, knight of Bigorna; Hugh, knight of Torciniac; Theodoric of Dijon, knight; and many others.

### Charter concerning Peter, lord of Miribel

Let every faithful person, layman as well as cleric, plainly know and acknowledge that Lord Peter of Mont-Salion, lord of Miribel, because of a certain misfortune which befell him, came one day to the monastery of Bèze. In the presence of Lord Stephen, abbot, the monks, and many laymen, the aforesaid Peter and his nephew Lord Odo, lord of Mont-Salion, wholly abandoned every claim to the fishing which they held upon our water, extending from the mill beyond our little village of Néron to Bèze. Whatever right they or their ancestors had ever possessed there, they on that day remitted eternally to God and the church of Bèze.

Concerning this matter, the aforesaid Peter made satisfaction in the presence of Lord Stephen, abbot, for his misdeeds which he had previously wickedly committed against the church, and put an end to every claim. That peace might be more firmly maintained and the good settlement endure throughout all the days of his life, he swore with his own hand, before everyone and over the holy relics, to observe the settlement and peace. So likewise did his provost Rainald of Miribel, [Col. 0949A] Hugh the cleric, and Lambert of Jergeiac, who swore that it should be kept in perpetuity.

Moreover, by the authority of the knights through whom he did this, he gave as sureties Lord Geoffrey with his sons Hugh and Fulk; Hugh Columba with his son Walo; Milo with his son Ewin; his nephew Lord Odo; Theodoric of Dijon, son of Stephen; Aymon of Dijon, surnamed Chag; and Odilo of Lisiac.

The sign of Lord Stephen, abbot; Wido, prior; Wilenc; Alberic; Landric; and many others.

### Charter concerning Burburena

Let all men know how the native inhabitants of the village called Burburena, living at Bèze after the burning of the houses which [Col. 0949B] they had formerly possessed on our land, desired to rebuild others and came to the abbot of this place, named Stephen, requesting permission to rebuild.

He said to them: “Far be it that henceforth you should have dwellings on our estate as you have had them until now, unless you render the customary services, as our own men and others do who are under our authority. But if you are unwilling, you will not obtain from me further permission to build.”

When they heard these words of the abbot, they took counsel among themselves and firmly concluded an agreement with him: henceforth each should pay only twelve pennies from the general plea, and should perform the other customary dues, except the carrying of wine from Gibriac, unless any one of them chose to perform it of his own goodwill.

The same Abbot Stephen also established for them that neither he nor anyone thereafter should levy a tallage upon them, but should exact the other customary dues from them. They likewise established that if any of them suffered injury from the monks or the servants of Saint Peter, he should seek neither complaint nor outside justice until the justice of the abbot and the provost of the monastery had failed him.

The sign of Stephen, abbot; Landric, provost. Many of the household of Saint Peter were then present there: the sign of Aydulf; Gerald; Alberic; the reeve of the village of Burburena; and many others.

### Charter concerning Majas

Let every order of the faithful firmly acknowledge that Wido, knight of the village called La Ferté, falling [Col. 0949D] ill, became our monk, together with his brother Theodoric, Theodoric’s wife, and his sons and daughters. They devoutly offered in alms to God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and the church of Bèze, for the salvation of themselves and their ancestors, living and dead, the entire allod which they possessed in the village called Majas, in houses, fields, meadows, and woods, both from their own kindred and from Gibuin of Bellomont and his wife.

That this gift might be held more firmly, Theodoric’s wife received as a token one gold ring, and Richard, her son, one cup from the refectory. Afterwards the aforesaid Wido gave every share belonging to himself in the property which he possessed beyond the River Saône: namely, at the village called Valerius, at another deserted village called Arcensis, and at another village called Luvinensis, in houses, fields, woods, serfs, and handmaids.

The sign of Hugh of the castle of Cunvulens; Henry; Ramald; Wido; Berno; Lord Stephen, abbot; Gerard, monk; Warner; Wilenc; Alberic; Aymon.

These things were done at the time when King Philip reigned in France, Robert was bishop at Langres, Stephen was abbot at Bèze, and Duke Odo held the duchy.

### Charter concerning Balenava

Let all faithful persons, laymen, clerics, and monks alike know that the officials of Duke [Col. 0950B] Odo—the provost and others—were demanding evil customary dues upon our land which Saint Peter and the church of Bèze possess at Balenava, namely a tallage for the duke’s food; for this they took five shillings from the inhabitants.

Because of this wrong, Lord Abbot Stephen lodged a complaint with the aforesaid duke and his wife, the duchess. Both parties then settled the case at Dijon. Going there, Lord Abbot Stephen, armed with his charters and testimonies, freely set forth that the aforesaid land owed no customary due whatsoever to the duke, his officials, or any living person, but only to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze.

On hearing this, the duke and his wife immediately caused the aforesaid abbot to be repaid the above-mentioned five shillings through Erveius, provost. Since he did not have the money ready, the latter took the pelts from around his own neck and handed them over to the surety, namely Joscelm. Joscelm then gave them to Abbot Stephen, who carried them away and kept those pelts until Erveius the provost, willing or unwilling, repaid the five shillings.

### Charter concerning Picangiae

A certain noble lady, Alburgis by name, a countrywoman, the most honourable wife of Walter of Minoio, being about to depart from this world, assigned to Blessed Peter, Abbot Stephen, and the other brethren persisting in God’s service at the monastery of Bèze, land at the village called Picantiae, meadows, woodland with water, just as she had possessed them during her life. Her sons Walter [Col. 0950D] and Raymond, in the presence of her brother Sevald and before very many witnesses, willingly consented.

The sign of Landric, monk; Theodoric; and Alberic, monk; Peter, canon of Granceiac; Odo, knight of Iciac.

In the year 1100 from the Incarnation of the Lord, King Philip reigning in Gaul, Robert being bishop at Langres, and Wilenc and Goscelm, archdeacons, governing the church of Langres with him.

### Charter concerning Villarium

Let all who read or hear these letters know that Richard, son and successor of Milo and son-in-law of Hugh the Great, who became our monk, unjustly seized the land of Hugh surnamed Barbe, which Hugh had given to Saint Peter in the deserted village called Villarium. For two years he held it in defiance of the claim of Abbot Stephen and his monks; thereafter he came to his senses and restored the land and all its produce wholly to Saint Peter and Lord Abbot Stephen, making satisfaction.

The abbot likewise absolved Richard from his past offence on this condition: if he or any successor should wish to reclaim it, he should remain under the curse of anathema.

The sign of this matter: Stephen, abbot; Wilenc; Geoffrey; Aymon; Richard. Likewise the sign of Milo, his father; Hugh, reeve; Otbert; Gerard of Verdun; Hugh, servant; Gislebert, servant; Gerald’s son; Gunter; and many others.

### Charter concerning Bellojoc

[Col. 0951B] We make known to all persons now living and to those to come that the noble lady Aludis of Bellojoc, sister of Ermuin and wife of Ulric of the castle of Trevia, at her death, for the salvation of her soul and those of her ancestors, faithfully gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze one mansus at Bellojoc with a serf named Robert dwelling on that mansus, his wife, one son named Theobald, and one daughter called Grimoeldis. She also gave one new vineyard, that is, one recently planted.

All this—the mansus, vineyard, male and female serfs—just as she possessed it by her own right, she and all her sons honourably and with all liberty gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, as stated above.

Lest any unbeliever should judge this false, we designate witnesses: the sign of Theodoric, her son; of Pontius, likewise her son; of Theodoric the boy; of Odo of Bellomont and his wife; of Hugh Columba; of Odo of Scia; of Milo of Bellojoc; of Fulk; of Hugh; of Herbert, reeve; of Gerald, tanner. Of the clerics: Acilin, priest; Ramald, deacon; Theobald of Agiliac. Of our monks: Wido, prior; Wilenc; Warner; Landric; and many others.

### Charter concerning Old Vines

Let all now living, and those to come after us, know that Oltrudis, daughter of Wido of Old Vines and niece of Waro the monk, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze all her inheritance which she possessed at the aforesaid Old Vines, [Col. 0951D] in houses, lands, meadows, and woods. Lord Odilo, our monk, who then governed there, gave her as a token of obedience half an emina of wheat and another measure of millet.

That this gift may remain firm, we designate witnesses: the sign of Wido, prior; Wilenc; John; Geoffrey; Pontius; Odilo. Of the laymen: Robert, reeve of Old Vines; Bernard; Rotger; Peter; Hugh, servant; Rainald.

### Charter concerning Lucus

Let all present and future persons hear that Raymond, knight of Granceiac, who was wounded at Salina, before he died, in the presence of many witnesses, gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze, for his soul and those of his ancestors, [Col. 0952A] two manses: one at Lusum with its appurtenances, and another at Rariac; two serfs, Waldric and Humbert; and two handmaids, Aluvidis and Ermessendis.

We designate witnesses to this matter: the sign of his wife, his son, and his brother Walter; Artald, knight; Pontius, knight; Henry of Icius; and many others.

### Charter concerning Secuniac

Let it be clear to all who see or hear these letters that Odo, knight of the village called Icius, as he approached his death, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, for his soul and those of his ancestors, one mansus in the village called Secuniac with its appurtenances, so free and so good that it retains a share in pasture-rights and thirds, and liberty throughout all the bounds of that village.

We subscribe as witnesses to this gift: the sign of Odo, his wife, and their son Pontius, knight, who made the alms; the sign of Sevald Balbus; Raymond; Aymon, knight; Pagan, provost; Martin Barbat; and many others.

### Charter concerning Gaviniac and Auxiliac

Let all present and future persons know that Wido, knight of Auxiliac, as he approached death, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze one mansus at Caviniac, with all its appurtenances and all liberty. He also gave the orchard of Pontus with its appurtenances, with all [Col. 0952C] liberty, and likewise a third part of the mill of Auxiliac, together with any fish caught there.

That this alms may remain unshaken, we subscribe witnesses: the sign of Wido, son of the aforesaid deceased man, who placed the alms in his father’s stead upon the altar of the holy apostles Peter and Paul; the sign of his brother Rainald; Hugh, knight of Bellomont; Geoffrey, knight; Walo, knight, surnamed Columba; Gislebert; Warner; Hugh, his brother; and many others. Of the monks: Warner, Wilenc, Landric.

### Charter concerning Romanisca

We have deemed it worthy to commit to memory that Hugh surnamed Rufus and his wife surnamed Regina, through the hand of Abbot Stephen, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze the land called Romanisca in its entirety, with its appurtenances wherever it lay, with serfs and handmaids, and also the church of Verona.

On this agreement: if the aforesaid noblewoman, after her husband’s death, while living wished to go to Bèze, the monks should receive her, together with the land, and provide for her. But if she did not wish this, after her death it should pass with all liberty and with serfs and handmaids, as specified above.

For this alms Lord Abbot Stephen gave both the man and the woman fellowship and every good thing that should be done in the church of Bèze until the end of the world, for the salvation of their souls and those of their faithful ancestors.

[Col. 0953A] That this conveyance may remain firm, we designate witnesses: Ulric, knight, who was Hugh’s brother; Wido, knight, his son; Richard, knight of Vircillis; Wido, his brother; Wido, chaplain; Peter, priest; Roger, who was Hugh’s son; Duran of Majas; Fanuël; and many others. Of the monks: Stephen, abbot; Warner, prior; Wilenc; Wido, chaplain; Alberic.

### Likewise, another [charter]

We wish it to be known to present and future persons that Virberga, wife of Marcellus the shoemaker, gave herself to Saint Peter the Apostle together with her children: Martin, Ermengard, Mary, Richildis, and Ada.

Present were Godfrey, prior; Gerard; Walter; Robert; Drogo, provost; Theobald; Ingelran; Stephen; [Col. 0953B] Lambert, provost; John, son of John the Elder; William, shoemaker; Marcellus, shoemaker.

### Charter concerning Cusiac and Chimissin

Holy Scripture testifies that almsgiving frees the soul from eternal death and leads it to everlasting life. Mindful of this, Hugh, knight surnamed of Chimissins, as he approached his death, for his soul and those of his faithful ancestors, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze four manses: two at Ruvriac, a deserted village, with all their appurtenances; another at Cusiac with its appurtenances; and another at Chimissin, with four jugera of land and one scythe-cutting of meadow. The aforesaid Hugh gave these manses free, with every liberty.

[Col. 0953C] That this alms may remain unshaken, we designate witnesses: the sign of Hugh; of Wido, his son; of Walo; Aymon; Hugh, his nephew; Awin of Beria; Nerduin, knight; Andrew, priest; Richard; Constantine; and many others.

### Charter concerning Nogdant-le-Ferreux

Let all living persons, and those to come after us, know that Hugh the boy, son of Wilenc of the village called Roseius, and his uncles Walo the monk and Wido the knight, brothers of the aforesaid Wilenc, for the soul of Wilenc himself, for the souls of his brothers, and for all their ancestors, living as well as dead, gave to God and the church of Bèze two manses: one at Nogdant [Col. 0953D] le Ferreux, namely the mansus of Arnulf with its appurtenances; and another in the village called Néron, beside the castle of Gradiac, with two serfs, Letbald and Wido his brother, and with its appurtenances.

That this charter may remain unshaken, we designate witnesses: the sign of Wido; Walo; Wido; William, his son; Hugh; Raimo of Longchamp; Hugh of Néron.

### Charter concerning Burgundion

Let it be clear to all now living and those yet to come that Henry, knight of La Ferté, lying in bed and approaching death, with the consent and counsel of his wife, sons, and all his household, gave to God, Saint [Col. 0954A] Peter, and the church of Bèze, for his soul and those of his faithful ancestors, one mansus at the village called Burgundion, with all its appurtenances, free with every liberty; three serfs living on that mansus, namely Arnulf, Henry, and Gislebert; half of the sons or daughters of the aforesaid Arnulf; and, on the other side, one handmaid.

We designate witnesses to this charter: the sign of Leodegard, who made the gift; Hugh of the castle of Comulens; Richard of Vircillis; Wido, his brother. Of the dependants: Henry; Ulric; Julo, his son; Robert, reeve; Bernard; Arnold, cleric; Wido, priest; and many others.

### Charter concerning Saint Sequanus

[Col. 0954B] In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Let all faithful persons know that Alwidis, wife of Wilenc of the village called Altason, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze two free manses with every liberty, for the soul of her husband Wilenc; also for the soul of her son Rainald, who died young; and for her own soul and those of her faithful ancestors. One was in the village called Saint Sequanus, with its appurtenances, and the other at Viriniac, with its appurtenances.

That this charter may remain firm and unshaken, we designate witnesses: the sign of Alwidis, who made the gift; Humbert of Bellomont; Wido; Eldebert; Hugh. Of the monks: Stephen, abbot; Warner, prior; Wilenc; and other monks. If anyone, instigated by the devil, should wish to oppose or diminish [Col. 0954C] this gift, let him be anathematized with Dathan and Abiram.

### Charter concerning Viriac

Saint Peter and the church of Bèze also possess another mansus at Viriniac, which Falco, knight of Riveria, and his brother Wicard gave for their souls, with all its appurtenances. It has right of use and common pasture throughout the entire jurisdiction of Montiniac, in woods, meadows, pastures, and everywhere. The aforesaid knights also handed over Peter, who holds the mansus, insofar as this belonged to them.

There is another mansus in the aforesaid village, namely Viriniac, which Peter the reeve and his brother Tebert, reeve of Montiniac, gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze for the salvation of their souls, with its appurtenances. And in the aforesaid village there are four other manses with appurtenances, which other benefactors gave, for their souls, to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze with every liberty, such as Ishmael of Granceiac and other faithful persons, under the testimony of Christ.

### Charter concerning Cusiac

Let all now living and those to come after us know that a certain knight, Rainer of the village called Cusiac, when approaching death, devoutly gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze, for the salvation of his soul and those of his parents, three manses, exactly as he possessed them in [Col. 0955A] the aforesaid village of Cusiac. Two of these owe two sextaries of wine, bread, and meat; the third, because it is smaller, half a sextary, bread, and meat. He also gave a handmaid dwelling there, named Rolendis, with her three sons, under this testimony: the sign of Odo, lord of Mont-Salion; of Theobald; and of Odilo, his deceased brother, with his sons.

### Charter concerning Fontanis

Let all who cherish these things know that a certain knight of Mont-Salion, Pontius of Bigorna by name, on the day of his death, for his soul and those of his faithful ancestors, granted to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze two manses to possess in perpetuity: one in the village [Col. 0955B] called Fontinelles, with its appurtenances; and another in the village called Curcelles, near Fontvenne; and one serf, with his sons and daughters, in the village of Campania.

The sign of Humbert, his son, together with his mother; Walo of Calmis; Alelm of Icioma.

### Likewise, another [charter]

Let all who hear or read these letters faithfully retain that a certain knight of Bellomont, Milo by name, for the salvation of the soul of his deceased son Hugh, adding his own soul and those of his ancestors, conveyed to the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the monastery of Bèze two manses in the village called Fontinelles, with their appurtenances, wholly and freely, [Col. 0955C] and one serf equal in status to the land, named Wido, with his son Albert and daughter Alix.

The sign of Milo, who made the gift; Richard, his son; Aewin; Walo; Aymon of Fontana; Wido, his son; Stephen, abbot; Wilenc; Geoffrey; Alberic.

These things were done in the time of King Philip.

### Charter concerning Vachiriac

Let all present and future persons know that Hugh surnamed Troaudus and his younger brother Waldin gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church half of the village called Vachiriac, for the souls of their father Rainald, their mother, and all their faithful ancestors, as they and their ancestors had held it: wholly, with every liberty, in cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, woods, and rights in waters. As a token, Wido the monk, who held Pauliac, gave these two brothers eleven shillings in coin.

That this charter may remain unshaken, we designate witnesses: the sign of Odo, knight of Bellomont; the sign of his wife, called Ailadis; Wido, knight, surnamed Margot; Rudolph, knight, his brother; Hugh, reeve of Pauliac; Wido, monk; and many others.

### Likewise, another [charter]

In the same way, at another time, two brothers who were knights, namely Achard and Pagan of Saint Julian, granted to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, for the salvation of their souls, whatever they possessed from their own estate in the deserted village called Vachiriac: [Col. 0956A] lands, meadows, woods, and watercourses.

The sign of Warner; Ulger; Wido; Walter; Humbert; and many others.

### Charter concerning Wascum Curtis
Let it be known to all, present as well as future, that Sewinus, knight of Raico, for the soul of his father Wido, and for his own soul and those of his faithful forebears, gave to God, to Saint Peter, and to the church of Bèze, in the presence of Lord Stephen the abbot and the monks, one holding from his own estate, with all its appurtenances, in the village called Wascum Curtis: fields, woods, and meadows, with every liberty, under this testimony: [Col. 0956B] the mark of Sewinus and of his wife; of Wido, lord of Fontis Vennae; of Odo of Bellomonte; of Hugh of the village called Geniperias; of Berald, his brother; of Kalon of Silviniac; and of many others.

### Charter concerning Firdriacus

Let it remain ratified and known to those now living and to those who will come after us that Sewinus, knight, and his wife, of the place called Villesons, granted to Saint Peter and to the church of Bèze, as alms for the salvation of his soul and of his parents’ souls, two holdings: one in the village called Firdriacus, with a serf dwelling there named Bisonticus; and another in the village called Wascum Curtis, with a serf [Col. 0956C] belonging to that same holding. The mark of Wido of Raiacus; Sewinus; Hermuin; Theoderic of Trevia; Fulco; Odo; and Morannus, archpriest.

### Charter concerning Morengis

All to whom God has granted the happy enjoyment of this present life must take the greatest care always to be solicitous concerning the everlasting life. Of this there was mindful during his lifetime a certain knight, Pontius, of the village called Saint-Seine near Palliacum. For the salvation of the soul of his son, namely Wido, adding his own soul and those of his parents, he handed over to the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, and to the church of Bèze, one serf, Tewinus; the land of Morengis; and the wood called Noaino, wholly, just as he possessed it. [Col. 0956D] The mark of Pontius, who gave this; of Nerduin, his brother; of Widric of Arcus; of Odo of Bellomonte; of Aimo; of Hugh Columba; of Hugh, steward of Palliacum; of Lambert, his son; and of John, his son.

### Charter concerning Vetus-Vineae

Let it be made known through these letters that Gertrude, wife of Henry of Novavilla; Warnerius, her son-in-law; and her daughter, Warnerius’s wife, surnamed Cara, for the salvation of the soul of the aforesaid Henry and of their own souls and those of their forebears, offered to God and Saint Peter of the church of Bèze, upon the altar in the village of Vetus-Vineae, one half of a holding, with six jugera of land, from their own estate; and together with it one serf, named Tetbert, and one female slave, his sister, named Oltrude. Both the serf and the female slave [Col. 0957A] were born of Peter Rusticus of Vetus-Vineae. The mark of those who made the gift: Odo; Richard, his brother; Hugh of the castle of Conulensis; and Rainald, his serf of Vetus-Vineae. The mark of Lord Stephen the abbot; Wilencus the monk; John the cantor; and the other monks.

### Charter concerning Picangiae

Let all, future as well as present, know for certain that Alburgis, surnamed Pagana, wife of Walter of Mignoio, when approaching her death, gave for her soul to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze her share—namely, everything that she had or possessed during her life—in the village called Picangiae: lands, meadows, woods, altogether the whole. This alms was confirmed by the sons of the aforesaid [Col. 0957B] lady, namely Raymond and Walter, and likewise by their maternal uncle Sewaldus, surnamed Balbus. That this charter may remain unshaken, we assign to it witnesses: the mark of Odo, knight of Icio, and Pontius his son; of Aimo, knight; of Henry, who was the lady’s steward; of Wido, priest; of Peter, canon of Granciacum. Among the monks: the mark of Lord Stephen the abbot, Wilencus, John, and Alberic; and of the household of Saint Peter, many were present: Otbert, Hugh, Gislebert, John, and Aidulf.

### Charter concerning a plot for a house situated at Bèze

Let all, present as well as future, know that Lord Peter, lord of Mont-Salion, and his wife Eva, moved in heart for the salvation of his soul and those of his forebears, restored to Saint Peter, the church of Bèze, and the monks, wholly free, a certain vacant house-site called the *Plastrum*, which he and his forebears [Col. 0957C] had held from the abbots and monks of Bèze. On this condition: if any of his heirs thereafter should wish to raise any claim concerning this, let him be anathematized, *maranatha*, for ever. That this restoration may remain unshaken, let us subscribe witnesses to it: the mark of Peter; Hugh of Varva; Rudolf, knight of Aquae; Hugh, cleric of Miribellum; of the household of Saint Peter, Robert the provost, Otbert the cook, Hugh, William, Lambert, Theobald, John the cook, and many others; among the monks, the mark of Lord Stephen the abbot, Warnerius the prior, Wilencus, John, Philip, [Col. 0957D] Widric, Roffred, and others.

### Charter concerning the wood called Vallis Victoris

Let this be recalled to memory: there were two brothers, Henry and Bernard of Fractomons. They said that they possessed a certain allod within our land in the Valley of Victory. The aforesaid Henry, moreover, having fallen into poverty, gave all his inheritance to Lord Hugh of Beria, and Hugh supported him until his death. Hugh gave the part of Henry’s aforesaid allod to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze for the soul of his deceased son, the boy Warnerius. Euvinus, Bernard’s son, gave Bernard’s share of that allod; and his mother Poncia, his brother-in-law Milo, and Richard, brother of Euvidus, gave and confirmed [Col. 0958A] both donations, for the soul of their father Bernard and for their own souls and those of their forebears. Our monk Lord Odilo gave them five solidi in coin as a token. That this charter may remain unshaken, we record witnesses: the mark of Stephen the abbot, Wido the prior, Alberic, and Odilo. Among the laymen: Euvinus, Milo, Hugh the servant, Gislebert, Robert of Vetus-Vineae, Bernard, and Rainald. And on that same day the aforesaid Euvinus, by joined hands, became the man of Lord Stephen the abbot, because of certain claims which the abbot had against him.

### Charter concerning persons given to Saint Peter by Pontius

Let it be made clear to all now living and to those who will come after us that Pontius, knight, son of Henry of Firmitas, [Col. 0958B] which is called Anrosiacus, for the soul of his father and of his forebears, and for his own soul, by the counsel of his men, freely and perpetually gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze five persons, three males and two females: namely Gandrada with her three sons, whose names are these: first, Peter; second, Alberic; third, Theoderic. The other woman is called Elizabeth, wife of the above-named Peter. The aforesaid Pontius made this gift on the feast of Saint Peter and, before many witnesses, confirmed the gift with his own hand upon the altar by the book called the Rule of Saint Benedict, on this condition: if ever any of his relatives, or anyone prompted by the devil, should wish to oppose or challenge this charter, let him be anathematized. [Col. 0958C] We assign witnesses to this charter: the mark of Pontius himself, who made this gift; the mark of Richard and Wido, his brother, of Vircillis; Julon of Granandum; Wido, son of Rainald of Conulensis; William of Fossatum; Odilo of Lissiacum; Hugh of Torcennacum; and other nobles who were present. Among the monks: the mark of Stephen the abbot; Wilencus; Alberic Captivus; Anthony, his brother; Pontius; and many others.

### Charter concerning Gerald of Lucus’s fief

Let all now living and those who will come after us know that Gerald, our steward of Lucus, had often been at odds with our service because of certain wrongs which he committed concerning our lands, [Col. 0958D] which did not belong to his fief. Therefore Lord Abbot Stephen, by the counsel of the brothers, wishing to establish peace and concord on both sides, at his command and at Gerald’s command caused monks and laymen to make a precise inquiry into Gerald’s fief from the stewardship. When the inquiry had been made, fifty-two jugera of land and four scythe-measures of meadow were found. Lord Abbot Stephen and our monks granted these jugera of land and these scythe-measures of meadow to the aforesaid Gerald: a tenth [lacuna] to his fief; likewise, one half of the grain called *Ungranus*, concerning which there had been contention between him and the monks and which he there wholly relinquished. That is, at the aforesaid settlement the lord abbot and monks granted him that aforesaid half of the *Ungranus* for the term of his life and no longer, [Col. 0959A] out of mercy and for a good settlement; and each year a measure from the monks’ granary, or one *becharium*, that is, half a hemina of wheat or rye. Lord Abbot Stephen, by counsel of the brothers, granted this to Gerald so that he might remain faithful to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze, better than he and his brother Olardus had been before. We assign witnesses to this matter: the mark of Stephen the abbot, Wido the prior, Wilencus, Alberic, Landric, and Theoderic. Among the laymen: Gerald; Olardus of Lucus; Hugh the steward; Euvrard; Gerald, son of Gunter; Gerald; Hugh the servant; and many others.

### Charter concerning the mill at Fontanae

We judged it worthwhile to record in writing that Alisendis, wife of Aymon of Fontanae, when approaching [Col. 0959B] death, gave for her soul to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, with every honour and every liberty, one half of the mill in Hairard’s meadow, with the approval and consent of Aymon her husband and Wido her son. That this donation may remain firm and unshaken, we assign witnesses: the mark of Aymon of Fontanae, who made this gift; of Wido his son; Hugh Carruca; Wilencus, knight; Hugh of Porta; Bertran, knight of Fontanae; Herbert the steward and Odo his brother; Hildemar, priest; and many others. And among our monks: the mark of Lord Stephen the abbot, Wilencus, Gerald, John, and Alberic.

### Charter concerning Lucus

Let the remembrance and acknowledgement be known to all now living [Col. 0959C] and to those who will come after us: Gerald of Lucus, our steward, and Humbert, surnamed Ingelricus, of Cipetus, restored to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze, in the presence of Lord Stephen the abbot and the monks, a certain part of the tithe from the land called Saint Vincent of Lucus, which for some years they had wickedly appropriated and retained under anathema and as theft. Acknowledging their guilt and confessing their fault, they promised never, either personally or through any of their successors, to reclaim so execrable a robbery.

### Charter concerning the appurtenances of Arcio

Since we daily see the ordinances of the fathers who went before being undone by their successors, and see that those things which appeared more firmly established in the world have either already fallen or [Col. 0959D] threaten to fall, we have taken care to commit to the tenacious memory of writing—for words, as soon as they begin to be formed, already no longer exist—the manner in which peace and concord were established between the monks of Saint Leodegarius after long contention.

This contention concerned the tithes of two churches of Saint Peter, namely Danblin and Danbrun, a wood called Ferrariae, and one field.

It therefore pleased Robert, venerable bishop of the see of Langres, to summon Stephen, abbot of Bèze; Hugh of Auxerre, abbot of that place, namely Saint Leodegarius; and also Jerenton of Dijon. At last the aforesaid dispute was settled in this manner. It was approved and ordained [Col. 0960A] by Stephen, abbot of Bèze, the aforesaid Hugh, abbot of Auxerre, Robert, then prior of Saint Leodegarius, and the men of both parties, that the parishioners of Saint Leodegarius, from what they cultivate in those parishes, namely Danblin and Danbrun, shall take half the tithes with them and leave half to the churches. In the aforesaid wood which we have said is called Ferrariae, our men and theirs shall have common rights. From the three woods of Saint Leodegarius, whose names are these—Granzuvaure, Chalmes, and Droul—the monk who is at Arcio shall make his house and, as it is commonly called, the *aasimentum* of his house. If cultivation is carried out in the aforesaid wood called Ferrariae, the person to whom the land itself belongs shall have [Col. 0960B] one third. They shall have pasture in common in our lands and theirs, each without causing damage to the other. If damage is caused and restitution is made without complaint, there shall be peace. But if a complaint reaches the lord, whoever caused the damage shall make good the loss and pay the prescribed penalty to the lord. Lord Stephen, abbot of Bèze, relinquished to Saint Leodegarius and to Lord Hugh, abbot of Auxerre, that field within the territory of the village called Trescasas, as it had been pointed out and ploughed.

This agreement was made in a field above Cyriacum by Stephen, abbot of Bèze, and Hugh, abbot of Auxerre. Among the monks of Bèze there were present Warnerius the prior, Lebaldus, Alberic, who lived at Arcio, and Landric, brother of Hugh surnamed [Col. 0960C] Columba. Among the monks of Auxerre there were present Robert, prior of Saint Leodegarius; Itherius, secretary; Emelbertus; and Artaldus, prior of Saint Marcellus. Among the knights: Humbert of Lissei and his brother Odilo; Hugh Columba; Wido of Agullini; Wido of Danbrun and his brother Humbert; Hugh, provost of Saint Leodegarius; and Emelbertus, provost of Auxerre. Of the household of Saint Peter: Arlebaldus of Belenava, provost; Otbert the cook; and Gislebert the servant. Of the household of Saint Leodegarius: Hugh, steward of Ballenava; Odilo; Paganus, provost of Magnei; Humbert and Hugh, his brothers; and Peter of Mosteriolum. These acts were done in the year from the Incarnation 1109, in the second indiction, epact 17, concurrent 4, in the reign of King Louis, son of Philip, [Col. 0960D] in the second year of his reign, while Lord Robert presided over the episcopal see of Langres. He held this assembly and approved this agreement. On 28 October.

Moreover, seeing that charity was growing cold, truth diminishing among the children of men, and not only that gifts once made to the churches of God were for the most part ceasing, but even that gifts already bestowed were being taken away, Lord Abbot Stephen went to Rome and approached the pope then seated on the apostolic throne, namely Lord Paschal. By the authority of Blessed Peter, and also by the privilege of the aforesaid pope, who at that time in Peter’s place had the care of the universal and Catholic Church, he had inviolably confirmed whatever [Col. 0961A] this monastery of Bèze possessed, or might thereafter justly and canonically acquire through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful. Having obtained what he sought, forgetting the things behind and stretching forward toward those before him, he made light of the dangers and labours of the journey—for it was winter—and did not remember his hardship because of the joy which followed. We have taken care to transcribe below an example of that privilege.

### Privilege of Lord Pope Paschal

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Stephen, abbot of Bèze, and to his successors to be regularly promoted, for ever.
>
> “It is fitting readily to grant consent to religious desires, etc.”

See Paschal in volume 163 of the *Patrologia*. [Col. 0961B]

### Pope Paschal visits the monastery of Bèze. He delivers an address to the monks (1108).

Accordingly, after two years had elapsed, it happened that Pope Paschal himself visited the regions of Gaul. When he came as far as us, he was devoutly received in this monastery of Bèze by Lord Abbot Stephen and by us others, with a numerous retinue of his cardinals—bishops, priests, and clerics alike—as well as other bishops, abbots, and persons of various ranks in ecclesiastical order. He remained there until the third day. Greatly pleased by the situation of this place and especially by the community and discipline of the brethren, praising everything and blessing everything, he finally came into the chapter-house [Col. 0961C] and sat down. There, delivering an address, he began with the place where it is said: “Brothers, whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope” (Romans 15:4). Since he was speaking to monks, for whom patience is especially necessary, he set it down as a foundation. Then, showing that patience produces hope, he discoursed upon hope and came to faith. Teaching us, moreover, to hold a faith without pretence, and instructing us much concerning it, he finally ascended to charity, which is God. He spoke of it—or rather, of Him—as time and reason required. When he had ended his sermon, asked by the lord abbot and the other brethren, as one who held the place of him to whom the power of binding and [Col. 0961D] loosing in heaven and on earth was given, he consented to grant us and our brethren, both living and dead, absolution and blessing. Beginning Psalm 50, together with the Lord’s Prayer and the collect as he had been asked, he absolved and blessed us.

Nor should this be omitted: he himself consecrated the altar of Saints Peter and Paul in their honour, celebrated Mass there solemnly, and commanded that that day be celebrated every year as the Nativity of the Lord is celebrated.

We have written below the names, insofar as memory could supply them, of the cardinals, bishops, abbots, priests, and clerics who were present with him. Richard, cardinal bishop of Albano; Divizo, [Col. 0962A] cardinal of Saint Martin; Risus, cardinal of Saint Lawrence; Gregory, cardinal of the Holy Apostles; John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church; Robert, bishop of Langres, at whose request these acts were done; the bishop of Piacenza; the bishop of Viviers; the bishop of Cambrai; Henry, abbot of Angeriacum; Lambert, abbot of Pultaria; Henry, abbot of Saint-Seine; Wido, abbot of Saint Michael; and many others. Of clerics and laymen of lower rank, there was an almost innumerable multitude.

Since all things follow God’s eternal disposition, and since He has mercy freely upon His own when and how He wills, in His gratuitous mercy He willed that we should be strengthened by apostolic blessing. These things were done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1107, indiction 15, epact 25, on the twelfth day before the Kalends [Col. 0962B] of March [18 February].

### Charter concerning the sacristan’s vineyard at Bèze — The name and period of the author of this Chronicle

From the example of evangelical authority we have learned that the faithful and prudent servant in a small matter will be set by the Lord Jesus over much. Therefore I, John, have endeavoured to recover for the church of Saints Peter and Paul the land lying around the basilica of Saint Mary, which had long ago in some manner been alienated, as we shall explain below.

For Lord Abbot Odo had given it to Warnerius, father of Ulgerius, to cultivate and plant as a vineyard, so that he might hold it during his life; but after his death it was to be restored to the church. Yet when he died, this did not happen. Since the church owed money to his aforesaid son Ulgerius, [Col. 0962C] Lord Abbot Stephen granted him that land on the terms on which his father had held it. But I, desiring to increase the talent entrusted to me, gave Ulgerius 120 solidi, that is, six pounds; and he and his sons restored, into the hand of Lord Abbot Stephen, whatever they claimed in the land to God and Saint Peter. Lord Abbot Stephen then gave and granted it to the monastery’s secretary, through my hand, to be held freely in perpetuity, without rent and without any customary due paid from other vineyards. He also granted the customary right which Warnerius and Ulgerius had enjoyed: namely, that from the wood called Castanetum it should be permitted to make for the vineyard stakes, forks, pegs, and whatever might be [Col. 0962D] needed in it. And that this charter may remain unshaken, we also assign witnesses: the mark of Lord Stephen the abbot; Warnerius the prior; John the secretary; Theoderic the provost; Landric; and Gerald. Among the laymen: Otbert the cook; Martin the cleric; Ulgerius; Amalbert; Gerald; Stephen of Beria; Formatus; Peter; Humbert and Warnerius, sons of Ulgerius.

### Charter concerning Mercennacum

Fixing the eye of pious consideration upon the examples of the holy Fathers for imitation, we who have undertaken the governance of the holy Church recognize it to be necessary—indeed, equitable and salutary—to order it faithfully, and wisely to provide that whatever good we arrange in it may not quickly be destroyed or perish.

[Col. 0963A] Therefore we, Stephen, abbot of the church of Bèze, and the other guardians of the same monastery who are with me, make known to all present and future successors that we have assigned a certain vineyard, which Brother John had bought at Gibriacum, among the vineyards from which wine is brought to the common cellar; and that we have granted to him and to all who shall come after him whatever lands, vineyards, and customary rights we possessed at Mercennarium, so that from their revenues things suitable for the ministry of our church may be procured, and moreover that the altar of Saint Martin, situated on the left side of the monastery, may be continually illuminated from them. Having embodied this ordinance in writing, we command by the authority which we possess that it remain inviolate. [Col. 0963B] The mark of Lord Stephen the abbot; Warnerius the prior; Wilencus; John; and the other monks.

### Another charter

Let all present and future know that Theobald, now called of Saint Prudentius, restored to Blessed Peter, Abbot Stephen, and Secretary John, to possess in perpetuity, whatever building-work he had upon the field adjoining the chapel of Saint Mary, namely the vineyard. In exchange Secretary John gave him twenty-five solidi and one *comba* which he had planted; he shared it with him on these terms: he shall cultivate one half and take one half of the fruit. On this condition, if he proves a faithful cultivator, he shall hold it honourably for his lifetime without rent. After his [Col. 0963C] death, if any lawful heir of his should wish to possess the aforesaid vineyard, he shall first offer it to the secretary, who is its lord and partner. If the secretary retains it for himself, well; but if he does not wish to do so, the heir shall, by counsel of the abbot and monks, sell it to one of Saint Peter’s serfs who will faithfully cultivate it and render to the secretary the rent and customary dues.
