We assign witnesses to this charter: the mark of Stephen the abbot; Wilencus; John the secretary, who made this arrangement; Gerald; Alberic; Theobald; Hugh the steward; Haidulf; Hugh the servant; Berengar; Baldus; and many others of the church’s household.

### On the death of Bishop Robert

After Lord Robert had governed the church of Langres through the course of many years, he was seized by a most severe illness and, drawing near to his end, at the castle called Châtillon sent for his abbots: Stephen of Bèze, Wido of Molesme, and likewise Wido of Ternodurum. Humbly accusing himself in God’s sight and asking forgiveness of his sins, he received the monastic habit from Lord Wido, abbot of Molesme. Then, not long after, receiving the Viaticum, the very Body of Christ, he ended his life. He was buried fittingly, as was proper, in the chapter-house of the monastery of Molesme. Lord Jocerannus was appointed in his place to govern the see of Langres. [Col. 0963D]

### Charter of Duke Hugh concerning carts at Dijon

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. The divine testimonies of the holy Scriptures show how great [Col. 0964A] a devotion of mind we ought to have toward the holy Church of God; indeed, they command that she be enriched with gifts and declare and commend that she be made glorious with every manner of veneration. Moved by this consideration and spiritually inspired by the Holy Spirit, I, Hugh, duke of Burgundy, make known to all faithful persons, present and future, that I have given to God, Saint Peter, Abbot Stephen, and all the monks of the church of Bèze the toll on carts which I was accustomed to exact at the gate of Dijon. Henceforth, in whatever years or times monks of the said church, whether cloistered or residing in dependent houses, come to Dijon, they shall obtain this liberty from me and my successors: that they may pass with their carts freely, without any hindrance or exaction of any toll. Inflamed with zeal for God, I have bestowed this gift upon the church of Bèze for the salvation of my father’s soul, so that each year he may be remembered in that church by all, and, according to Catholic custom, that his anniversary may be celebrated by the children of the Church, so that through the prayers of God’s faithful servants forgiveness of all sins may be granted to him and all my forebears. Therefore, because I see many and very great institutions of our ancestors passing into silence and oblivion among those now living, it has pleased me to commit this gift to an authentic privilege [Col. 0964C] and to strengthen it by the subscribed testimony of approved men. The mark of Duke Hugh; Henry, the duke’s brother; Walo, abbot; Hugh, dapifer; Waleran, knight; Hugh, provost; Ewrard, provost; Dominic the younger. The mark of Stephen, abbot of Bèze; Warnerius the prior; Alberic. Among the laymen: Otbert; Ewrard; Gerald; Arnold, steward of Langres. These acts were done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1113, indiction 6, epact 1, during the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and the episcopate of Jocerannus in the city of Langres.

### Charter concerning the tithe of Casotus

We judged it worthwhile to record in writing that Richard, who was the nephew of Esembert of Casotus, abandoned and wholly relinquished, in the presence of Abbot Stephen, the monks, and laymen, every claim which he had concerning the tithe from the [Col. 0964D] above-mentioned village. Accordingly, so that firm peace might be maintained in this matter on both sides, the aforesaid Abbot Stephen gave him annually at the aforesaid Casotus four heminae of grain: two of wheat and two of barley, whatever kind should be there, as a fief, on this condition and for this reason: if the aforesaid village should come to the aforesaid destruction, so that he could not receive there the aforesaid measure, namely the four heminae, he shall wait patiently until the village improves and he can again receive what is due to him. His brother Sewinus and his sister approved this. We assign witnesses to this matter: the mark of Richard, who did this; Theobald, knight of Casotus; Paganus, provost of [Col. 0965A] Tilecastrum. Of the household of Saint Peter: Otbert, Amalbert, Gislebert, Hugh, and Gerald.

### Another charter

Let all, present as well as future, know that the daughter of Pontius, surnamed Besueta, and her son Odo, knight, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze for ever, for the salvation of their forebears, whatever right or claim they possessed concerning the children of Gerald, surnamed Aligrinus, before the altar of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and in the presence of Abbot Stephen and the monks. That this charter may remain unshaken, we assign witnesses to it: the mark of Odo, knight, and of his mother, who made this gift; Benzon, priest of Tilecastrum; Humbert, surnamed Angelricus; Vivian; [Col. 0965B] Hugh the steward; John; and many others.

### Charter concerning churches given by the lords of Mont-Salion

In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We notify all faithful persons to whose ears this little charter may come that Lord Peter, after succeeding his nephew Lord Odo in the honour and lordship of Mont-Salion, began to challenge the gifts which Odo himself and his uncle Rainald had made to God and to the church of Saint Peter at Bèze—namely, gifts of churches. Meanwhile Archbishop Jocerannus of Lyons, the bishop of Chalon, and the bishop of Autun came to Dijon. There Lord Peter himself, admonished by their counsel—or rather by their reasonable counsel—restored into the hand of Lord Jocerannus, archbishop of Lyons, everything [Col. 0965C] which he had challenged concerning the aforesaid possessions. The archbishop then placed that gift in the hand of Lord Abbot Stephen and thereby reinvested the church of Bèze. We assign witnesses: the mark of Jocerannus, archbishop; Stephen, bishop of Autun; Walter, bishop of Chalon; Wilencus, archdeacon; Lord Jocerannus, archdeacon; Stephen, abbot; Verento, abbot; Stephen, abbot of the New Monastery; Warnerius, prior; John; Alberic. Among the knights: William of Fontis-Vennae; Hugh, dapifer; Peter, who made this gift; Wibric; Otbert the cook; and Hugh the servant.

### Charter concerning Arcio

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. We considered it fitting [Col. 0965D] to record in writing that Arlebaldus, provost of Saint Peter at Belenava, restored to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze every fief which he held from the abbot and monks concerning the holdings of Arcio, as stated above; he, his wife, and his sons placed upon the altar as a gift every customary right and every claim or right which he had concerning the aforesaid holdings, for his soul and those of his forebears, for ever. In order that this gift might remain unshaken, Alberic, the monk then administering Arcio, gave him two heminae of wheat and one cow, and redeemed for him from Rainald of Miribellum, for forty solidi, five heminae of grain which he had lost at Cusiriacum. [Col. 0966A] We assign witnesses to this matter: the mark of Stephen, abbot; Wilencus; John; and Joffred. Of the household of Saint Peter: Otbert, Hugh, Gislebert, Nerduin, John, and many others.

### Charter concerning Caviniacum

Let it be plain to all now living and to those who will come after us that Suffisia, wife of Pontius of the village called Saint-Seine, and her son-in-law Humbert of Lissiacum, for the soul of the aforesaid Pontius, who died on the Jerusalem journey, for his repose and for the souls of their faithful forebears, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze one holding, with its lands and appurtenances, in our village called Caviniacum, and one serf, Ulric by name, with one half of his children, in the aforesaid village of Saint- [Col. 0966B] Seine. Lest such a memorial be erased, we assign witnesses: Humbert, knight of Lissiacum, who made the gift, with his mother-in-law; Widric of Saint-Seine; Theoderic of Campus Curtus. Among the clerics: Wilencus, archdeacon; Humbert, canon; John, priest. Among the monks: Wido, prior; Wilencus; Henry; John; Joffred; and others. Of our household: Hugh the servant; Aidulf; Arnulf, steward of Caviniacum; and Robert, his son.

### Charter concerning the people of Novavilla

Let all who now live and who will come after us know that Deodatus of Novavilla and his wife rendered to Saint Peter, the church of Bèze, and Abbot Stephen a head-payment for themselves, as other male and female serfs of Saint Peter do: the man four pennies and the woman [Col. 0966C] two. We record this in writing so that their sons and daughters, or their descendants, if they should wish to deny it, may never be able to deny it. For letters written concerning this will always possess the testimony of truth.

### Charter concerning Fontinellae

Let it be made clear to all now living and to those after us that Wido, knight of Fontanae, son of Haymo, lying sick and approaching his death, together with his comrades and his brother Robert, the young man, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the monastery of Bèze one holding in the village called Fontinellae, with its appurtenances, called the holding of Hugh the provost, and four serfs: Constantius, called “the knight,” with his sons, under this testimony: the mark of Richard of Vircillis; Hugh [Col. 0966D] Carruca; Wilencus, knight of Fontanae; Herbert the steward; Hugh of the castle of Convulensis; Lord Robert the young man, who made and approved the gift; and many others.

### Charter concerning Beria

Let the faithful community, of the present as well as of the future, fully acknowledge and retain in memory that Humbert, surnamed Solitarius, son of Arlebaldus, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, for his soul and those of his faithful forebears, one holding in the village of Beria, with all its appurtenances—meadows and cultivated and uncultivated land—endowed with every liberty. The aforesaid Humbert also gave one serf and one female slave, brother [Col. 0967A] and sister, Humbert and Rotrude, belonging in perpetual right to the aforesaid holding. We assign witnesses to this matter: the mark of Hugh, knight of Chimissiacum; Leterius and his sons, Stephen, Richard, John the priest, Andrew the priest, and many others of Beria. If any perverse person should wish to oppose this alms or take anything away from it, let him be anathematized.

### Another charter

In the same village of Beria there is a holding which Milo, knight of Bellomonte, and his wife Adilina honourably gave to God and Saint Peter with every liberty, on the day when their son Joffred first celebrated Mass, under this testimony: the mark of Milo; the mark of Joffred, monk, who received the gift [Col. 0967B] through his knife; of Odo; Stephen; Robert; and many others.

### Charter concerning Majasco
Every faithful person should fully recognize that almsgiving guides the faithful living to life and frees the souls of the dead from death. Accordingly, Odo, a knight of Cipeto surnamed Caterius, mindful of this, faithfully gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, for the soul of his mother, called Besueta, of his father, and of his faithful forebears, as alms, a *corvata* at Majas, with all the customary rights belonging to it, freely from his own right, and five jugera of land, as well as his share of the field lying above the castle, called Vinea. We monks of Bèze, in return for this token, granted him and his faithful people the prayers and benefactions of the church, for both living and dead, forever.

We assign as witnesses to this charter: the mark of Odo, who made the alms-gift; William of Fontis Vennae; Humbert of Cipeto; Benzo, priest of Til-Châtel; Pagan, provost; William of Fossato; and very many of our household.

Likewise, another.

Let all present and future persons know that Odo, knight of Bellomonte, granted and wholly gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze whatever claim, whether just or unjust, he or his forebears had ever possessed against the children of Lambert, who was called “the Large Penny.” We assign as witnesses to this notice: the mark of Odo, who performed this act on behalf of himself and all his forebears; the mark of Sewin of Rejac; of Odilo, knight of Lisiac; of Hugh Columba of Bellomonte; of Lambert; of Otbert his son; and of Widric. Among the monks: Warner, prior; Landric; Theoderic; and many others.

### Charter concerning the people of Burbureno

Let all know from the notice of these letters that the native men of Burbureno who received Saint Peter’s land from the hand of Abbot Stephen in order to plant vines—namely Albric, Warner, and Nerduin, with their brothers—received the aforesaid land on this condition: if any one of their sons takes a maidservant of Saint Peter as wife and wishes to remain in the service of the church, he shall possess the building and the land named above. Whoever does not do this, after his death the church shall recover both the building and the land in its own right.

### Charter concerning the churches given for Humbert Bruno

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Let it be known to all who read or hear these brief records that, on the day when the body of Humbert Bruno, lord of Fontis Vennae, was committed to burial at the monastery of Bèze, with the counsel and approval of Robert, bishop of Langres, and of the brothers, knights, and retainers of the aforesaid Humbert, his wife on that day gave, for his soul, to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, the chapel of the castle of Fontis Vennae and the share which she held in the church of Saint Valentine of Lurocurte, to hold and possess in perpetual right; and also two silver cups. This was given on the condition that every year, on his anniversary, his memory and that of his forebears should be faithfully celebrated in the assembly of the monks.

That this charter may remain inviolate, let us subscribe and name suitable witnesses: the mark of Robert, bishop; of William, count of Burgundy; of Rainald his son; of Guy of Raiac; of Guy of Burgundione-villa; of Hugh of Bellomonte; of Lebald of Petro; of Henry of Nova-villa; of Henry of Firmitate; of Robert, chaplain; and of many others. Among the monks: the mark of Gausbert, abbot; Warner, provost; Benedict, prior of Fontis Vennae; and Constantius. These things were done while Philip reigned and Robert held the episcopate.

Likewise, another.

Let all present and future persons know that Odo, son of Hugh, who was brother of Abbot Odo, because Lord Abbot Stephen had granted him a certain vineyard after the death of his father, namely the aforesaid Hugh, pledged himself to remain in the service and fidelity of Saint Peter and the monks as a free man. On these terms: if he dies without an heir of his own who is not born of a maidservant of Saint Peter, the aforesaid vineyard and whatever shall have been built there shall come, for his soul, into the right and ownership of Saint Peter and the monks. But if he takes a maidservant of Saint Peter, his children shall possess the vineyard for as long as they serve; and by this agreement, if he is overtaken by death while under our charge, we shall hold him as one entrusted to us.

### Charter concerning Veona

Let it be brought to the remembrance of those now living and of those who will live after us that Theobald, chaplain of Verziac, made and confirmed an agreement with Stephen, abbot of Bèze, concerning two jugera of Saint Peter’s land at Veona, which he sought in order to plant it, on condition that annually, during his lifetime, he should pay twelve coins to the church of Bèze as a token. After his death, the aforesaid church shall receive its land, free and built upon, with every building. We subscribe as witnesses to this arrangement: the mark of Stephen, abbot; of Guilenc; of Albric; of Geoffrey, prior of Dijon; of Robert, priest of Gibriac; of Humbert, cleric of Dijon; and also of many others.

### Charter concerning Lambert’s land at Nova-villa

Description of the land of Lambert of Poliac, situated near Nova-villa, above the spring: one and a half days’ ploughland in the *villenae*; two in Campanolas; four in the whole tract of the village of Marcellus, on the side where the chapel of Saint Langis stood; four by the field beside the meadow called Campus Natoriae. And, in the *milliarium*, two in the field of Elchallo, and three in the field of Delfinum. Meadow for four and a half scythe-cuts.

### Charter concerning Ewrard’s wife

Let it be made clear to all now living and to those who shall come after them that Humbert the younger, son of Humbert of Cipeto, for the soul of his father and his forebears, gave to God and the church of Bèze Elizabeth, daughter of Warner of Burburano, betrothed to Ewrard, son of Gislebert of Fonte. Lest any unbeliever should regard this as falsehood, we assign witnesses: the mark of Humbert, who made the gift; of Pagan, provost of Til-Châtel; of Walter; of Hugh, his brother, of Til-Châtel; of Otbert of Picangis; of Theobald of Casato; of Humbert; of Engelric; and of Albric of Burburano. Of Saint Peter’s household: Ewrard, Gunter, Gerald, Albuin, Gerald, Otbert, and Hugh the servant.

### Charter concerning Majas

The faith and devotion of religious men have always been especially praiseworthy in this respect: they have not only kept what had been acquired for the churches of God but have also diligently sought to acquire other things from every quarter. Following their example as far as I could, I, Stephen, though unworthy abbot of the church of Bèze, wishing to build a church beside the castle called Confluentum, asked Iterius, then lord of that castle, to grant to God and the church of Saint Peter of Bèze whatever rights of use he possessed in meadows, woods, waters, or fields. Understanding that our petition proceeded from the fountain of piety, he granted what I requested, together with his mother and his brothers and sisters. Warner of Fulcheroles likewise granted this, insofar as it concerned him. Likewise Pontius of the castle called Firmitas granted to the church of Bèze, in the same manner, whatever belonged to him.

### Charter concerning Lentiliac

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The religious diligence of the faithful, watchful over the affairs of the holy Church, ought so to provide for its possessions that whatever it holds may be held without disturbance, and that it may rejoice in possessing forever in the future all that it acquires through its own labours or through devout offerings. For very many men of this age, cruel and most savage, not only do not care to increase the bride of Christ—that is, the Church—but even strive by every means to destroy what is her own.

Therefore let it be known to all faithful people of the present and future age that Lord Geoffrey, lord of Bellomonte, with Gertrude his wife and Hugh his son, for the salvation of the soul of his son Fulk and of his forebears, granted unanimously, as alms, to God, Saint Peter, and the brothers of the monastery of Bèze, whatever he possessed at Lentiliac in lands, waters, and woods—that is, absolutely everything which he held there by his own right in revenues or in any appurtenances. Since this gift has been approved by him and his heirs, it has been judged proper to secure it by a charter, lest in the passage of time it be dissolved through some loss of memory, and to strengthen it by the testimony of the men who were present.

The mark of Geoffrey, who made the gift; of Hugh his son; of Guy, lord of Fontis Vennae; of William, his uncle; of Hugh of Poliac; of Seuvin of Raiac; of Odilo of Lixiac; of Humbert of Faberniac; of Mainfred of Arco; and of Audo of Fontinelles. Of Lord Geoffrey’s household were present Guy the provost; Warner, surnamed Pirdix; and Hugh his brother; Gislebert, provost of Alteriac; Rodulf of Alteriac; Gislebert of Poliac; Warner of Solarium; and many others. These things were done in the year 1114 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction VII, epact XII, while Louis reigned in France, Jocerannus was bishop at Langres, and Stephen was abbot at Bèze.

### Another charter concerning the same matter, made afterward because of the dispute arising over that first gift

Taught by the counsel of the Almighty, and likewise considering that every person is either punished or rewarded by Christ for all that is done in this life, I, Geoffrey, with my wife Gertrude and my son Hugh, resolved to redeem the time of my life, since the days are evil.

Accordingly, with my wife and son, I grant to the church of Saint Peter of Bèze whatever I have at Lentiliac—in the village itself, in the fields, the meadows, and the other appurtenances—wholly free, as freely as it was ever possessed by my forebears or by me. Of the wood called Brouls, it shall possess the half on the side of the village of Lentiliac altogether free from every customary due. In my other half, the monks and the men and women who shall dwell at Lentiliac shall have free and customary passage for themselves and their beasts. Access to that portion of the wood which is mine shall be from the side called the “lined angle”; and on this condition: if, in passing, damage is unknowingly done, it shall simply be made good; but if knowingly or deliberately, the damage shall be repaired with the legal penalty.

> [Note, Col. 0969: “With the law,” that is, with a monetary fine, and indeed a light one.]

But if war comes upon me or my heirs from the castle of Fontis Vennae, Aquato, or Chargeiac, access to my part of the wood shall be available to me and mine by the ancient and original roads. Again, on this condition: if damage is unknowingly done in passing, it shall simply be made good; but if knowingly, the damage shall be repaired with the legal penalty.

We assign as witnesses to this gift: Jocerannus, bishop of Langres; Stephen, abbot of Bèze; Warner, prior; Lebald; Theoderic, provost; Albric. Of the clerics: Josbert, dean; Lambert. Of the knights: Geoffrey with Gertrude his wife and Hugh his son; Humbert of Lissey with Odilo his brother; Guy, reeve of Gradei; Rocelin; Robert of Furt; Richard of Poiens; Virric of Altrei; Guy his brother; and Hugh of Pauliac.

### Charter concerning the church of Saint Martin

Let it be made clear to persons of the present age and to those of future time that Lord Gerard, archdeacon of the church of Langres, gave to the church of Bèze, for the peace of his soul and those of his forebears, whatever he held in the church of Saint Martin of the castle called Bellimons, namely half of the church and the priesthood, with the approval of Lord Robert, bishop, and the whole chapter of Langres. Since we see that almost all things slip from human memory, it pleased us to insert this in a charter, so that if anyone should hereafter wish to oppose this gift, he may be restrained by the authority of these letters.

There were very many witnesses to this matter, of whom it pleased us to set down certain ones here by name: Lord Robert, bishop; Abbot Stephen; Warner; Constantius; and, among the knights, Rainald of Mont-Salions and Peter his brother.

Lord Abbot Stephen, with Gibuin the priest and his brother, sons of Berengar, confirmed the following agreement concerning this same matter. He retained for himself one third of the tithe of all grain, except hemp; and, from the offerings of the four feasts—Christmas, the Purification of Saint Mary, Easter, and All Saints—one fourth part, together with the candle offering and the offerings for the dead.

For peace to be maintained on both sides, Gibuin the priest gave as sureties Warner Perdic and Warner of Solarium, so that if these should fail, others should be supplied by him. It was also established that if Lord Abbot or any monk of Bèze comes into the house of the priesthood, the priest shall receive and serve him willingly. The following was also added: if the priest withholds anything from our share, he shall be at peace if he restores it to the lord abbot, monk, or official demanding it; otherwise, after being admonished once and twice through the sureties, if he does not restore it, he shall thereafter pay both the principal sum and the legal penalty.

### Charter concerning Vactis

We wish it to be known to all that Alefrid, knight of Vactis, approaching death, gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze all the inheritance which he possessed from his own estate: namely, his own *mansus* with its house, the site of a mill with meadow, and every possession of his allod, as stated above, in fields, woods, and meadows, wherever situated. That this charter may remain inviolate, we assign witnesses: the mark of Andrew, priest of Beria; of Walter, priest of the church; of Stephen, provost of Beria; of Hugh of Chimissiac; of Humbert, who was his nephew; of Walter of Vactis, son of Laifin. Of our monks: the marks of Warner, Aymon, and Odilo, and many others.

### Charter concerning Beria

Let it be evident to all now living and to those who shall live afterward that Lord Hugh, knight and lord of Beria, on the day when he took up the pilgrim’s wallet in order to make the journey to Jerusalem—namely Palm Sunday—came into the chapter house at Bèze, threw himself at the feet of the monks, and prayed and asked that they would have mercy on him and deign to remember him in their prayers. On that day, in that present chapter, before witnesses, he gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze two excellent *mansi*, for himself and his soul and for the souls of his faithful forebears: one in the village called Beria, with all its appurtenances, namely the *mansus* of Ogerius, held by Walter his elderly son, brother of Stephen the provost, who is called Albus; the other in the village called Luecurtis, with all its appurtenances, which he named the *mansus* of Otbert of Arbore.

Lest any malicious person deem this void, we assign witnesses: the mark of Hugh, who made the gift; of Nerduin, who has his daughter; of Hugh Columba of Bellomonte; of Milo of the same castle; and of all the monks who were present there.

Likewise, another.

By these letters, therefore, let all present and future persons know that Nerduin, knight of the village called Pinus, and his wife Hermengard, daughter of Hugh of Beria, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze one *mansus* in the village of Beria, namely the *mansus* of Gunter, with all its appurtenances in meadows and lands; one male servant named Stephen, whom the aforesaid Hugh had previously granted; one maidservant called Osana; and her sister. Nerduin and his wife delivered all this to God and Saint Peter, as stated above, for the soul of the boy Walo, for the soul of her father, the aforesaid Hugh, and for the salvation of the souls of all their forebears, both living and dead.

We assign as witnesses: the mark of Nerduin, who made the alms-gift; of Milo of Bellomonte; of Richard his son; of Hilbert, knight of Salix; of Walo his brother; of Hugh, knight of Chimissiac; of Andrew, priest; and very many of our household. This gift and alms were delivered by the hands of Nerduin and his wife, by means of a piece of stone, upon the altar of the Apostles Peter and Paul, to be possessed forever with every honour and freedom.

### Charter of Lord Peter

Gifts bestowed upon the Church of God by the faithful are, without doubt, committed to written records lest, in the long course of succeeding ages, they be erased from human memory. Therefore we judge that it will be useful for posterity if we commend to enduring written characters what has lately been granted to our church. The matter is as follows.

Peter, lord of the castle of Mont-Salions, surnamed Malus Respectus, granted to God, the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and the church of Bèze, with the approval of his wife and sons, the allod which he had formerly given at Lentiliac, to be possessed freely thereafter. Moreover, in the chapter, while the abbot sat with the monks, he added a male servant named Walter and a maidservant called Alvide, dwelling in the village called Trescase. To prevent any controversy from arising concerning these things in future times, we assign suitable witnesses: the mark of Peter himself and his wife; of Otho and Rainald, his sons; of Rodulf, knight; of Gaudin, knight; of Walter, provost; of Humbert, son of Olger; of Gerard, abbot; of Wilenc, prior; and of the entire convent.

### Charter of Hugh Herlus

In the name of the Lord. Let all present and future persons know that Hugh, knight of Renavis, surnamed Herlus, willingly and with great affection gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze his entire allod, with every liberty, which he held and possessed in the village called Ausiliac, for his soul and the souls of his forebears: in fields, meadows, *mansi*, woods, and waters. That this alms-gift and donation may stand firm, we assign suitable witnesses: the marks of Hugh of Bellomonte; Walo and Haimon Columba; Richard; Milo of Poiens; Urric of Renavis; Rodulf his brother; Rodulf, son of Urric; Guy, surnamed Chiminal. Among the monks: Gerard, abbot; Theoderic; Guy of Renavis; Lebald; Remigius, priest; and many others.

At that time Rodulf, son of Urric, granted from the aforesaid allod to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze one *mansus* which his grandmother was to convey to him after her death, wherever she should die.

### Charter concerning Secuniac

Let all present and future persons know that Walter, knight of Chortoson, approaching his death, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, for his soul and those of his forebears, one free *mansus*, with every liberty, at the village called Secuniac, with woodland, lands, and all appurtenances belonging to that *mansus*. Everything which Walter himself and his nephew Walter seemed to possess there, in lands and woods, they gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze in perpetual right; and also one maidservant called Doda.

That no falsifier may oppose this alms-gift, we assign witnesses: the mark of Milo, knight; of Walo and Hilbert, his sons, who made the gift with their mother; of Walter his nephew, who likewise made the gift. And among the knights of Beria: the marks of Walo; Hilbert; Pagan, their brother; Mainfred of Archo; and Andrew, priest of Beria.

### Charter concerning Lisseiac

Let the faithful know that Odilo of Lisseiac bestowed upon the Church of God, Saint Peter, and Bèze, as alms, whatever he possessed everywhere at Lisseiac, in land, water, meadows, pasture, and woods, as honourably as he himself held them. The monks of Bèze likewise granted to Odilo what they themselves possessed at Brucciac, on condition that, when he departed this life, it should remain to the church of Bèze with everything that he had built there.

He offered upon the altar of Saint Peter, by means of a gilded Gospel-book, both this gift and, as we have said, the property at Brucciac, before witnesses, monks and laymen alike. Some of their names are: the mark of Odilo, who made this gift; of Maurice, knight of Probato; of Otbert; of Hugh; of Gislebert; of Euvard; of Lord Stephen, abbot; of Wilenc; Lebald; and Albric.

Hugh the elder, Odilo’s brother, made a similar gift from the island of Bollina, of his share of Lisseiac: he himself, his young son Guy, his wife, and his daughter Aia, gave the whole of it, with freedom, to be held and possessed forever by Blessed Peter and the church of Bèze, for his soul and the souls of his faithful forebears. The mark of Hugh and Guy his son; of Humbert of Lisseiac; of Odilo his brother; of Gislebert, priest of Malliac; of Humbert, overseer or steward; and of many others.

### Charter concerning Majas

We recognize it as the practice of wise men to preserve forever for future times, by committing them to writing, things of the present. We have therefore judged it worthy to write that Robert of Rinei brought to an end and peaceful settlement the claim which he made concerning the land situated at Majas, in exchange for two horses which he received from Abbot Stephen and the brothers of the church of Bèze. Therefore, whatever right, just or unjust, he claimed to have in the aforesaid land, he freely granted to God, Saint Peter, and the aforesaid brothers to possess forever.

That this may be more securely established, the following writing identifies the witnesses who were present: the mark of Robert, knight of Fontanis, and of his wife Avilina; of Richard, knight of Vircillis; of Odo Viridis; of Haimon of Mont-Salions; of Bertran, knight of Fontanis; of Wilenc, knight of Fontanis. Of Saint Peter’s household: the mark of Otbert; of Hugh; of another Hugh; of Aygulf; and of many others.

### Charter concerning Luat

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.” A certain knight, Otbert of Til-Châtel, lord of Cipeto, was not a deaf hearer of this. In order to make alms more freely from his own possessions, he first made himself an alms-gift. Coming to conversion at the monastery of Bèze, he gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze one *mansus* in the hamlet called Luat, with its appurtenances, lands, and meadows, freely and honourably, so that this *mansus*, called the *mansus* of Letald, should have passage and customary rights through all the woods belonging to Cipeto on this side of and beyond the Tille; one male servant, Bricio, with all his household goods, who was a steward of his lands; one excellent mule which he possessed; and he relinquished whatever claim he had against the land of Saint Peter and its people.

That this charter may remain inviolate, let us set down suitable witnesses: the mark of Humbert of Cipeto, his son; of Aimon, his son; of Guy, his clerical son; of Injulric; of Humbert, his son, of Til-Châtel; of Aldo the Elder; of Odiler, knight; of Guy, knight of Fossato; and of many others. Among the monks: the mark of Josbert, abbot; Benedict; Constantius; Robert, provost. Of Saint Peter’s household: the mark of John, reeve; Humbert Coccus; and Gerald, cleric.

Saint Peter and our church of Bèze possess much land in that hamlet called Luat, both within it and throughout its boundaries: namely, the land of Isembert of Casoto, with its appurtenances; the land of Walter, cupbearer of Bellomonte, with its appurtenances; and the land of Landric, with its appurtenances.

### Epitaph

The pious care of the monk John shows to all  
What he was in the Church from his childhood years,  
Striving to imitate the devotion of Abbot Stephen.  
More than others he laboured to do what is good.

The abbot honourably renewed the Church  
And, as is evident, built its deserted houses.  
Desiring to have a share in this labour,  
John devoted every hour to writing books.

Stephen doubled the possessions of his Church  
As he multiplied its revenues, estates, and lands.  
While this keeper guarded well the things entrusted to him,  
With manifold zeal, studious himself, he amassed books.

Stephen enlarged the treasures of the Church  
And improved nearly all its enclosed precincts by alteration.  
While this keeper watched attentively over its affairs,  
He built more within it than its other keepers.

Stephen made the Church rich from poverty,  
Rejecting every superfluity as he ordered it more fittingly.  
And this follower did not fall short of his work,  
As he adorned the Church’s possessions to the extent of his power.

Stephen extended the head of the Church above the river;  
We know that John likewise gave his aid.  
And since each now gives much by his service,  
May both be worthy, at the end of their course, of the prize.

Each loved the beauty of the Lord’s Church,  
As his service, according to his means, rendered honour.  
Each, a faithful servant of the Lord, would not  
Bury his talent, but sought to render a hundredfold from one.

The life of Father Stephen should be imitated by pastors;  
The life of John will deservedly be remembered.  
The former shall be an example to prelates, the latter one to follow;  
Each is to be regarded as a successor in his office.

Therefore we who possess so many goods of so great a father,  
And who see so many flourishing writings, the work of John,  
Let us pray, with hands outstretched to the King who reigns everywhere,  
That he may grant to each the reward of piety;  
So that he who justifies great and small alike  
May number them among the citizens of the heavenly homeland.

Here are the books named above which John caused to be copied: namely, a great part of Josephus; Augustine also on the last fifty Psalms, from *Domine exaudi* (“Lord, hear”) to *Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum* (“Let every spirit praise the Lord”); Ambrose’s *Hexameron*; Ambrose *On Duties*, *On the Sacraments*, and *On the Death of His Brother Satyrus*; Ambrose *On Virginity*; the *History of the Vandals*; the history of Orosius; the history of Justinian; the history of Jerusalem; a homily of Origen; Augustine’s *Confessions*; a new collection; Guido’s *Music*; two excellent antiphonaries of music; a gradual and a nocturnal; the Life of Saint Faith; Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*; Gregory, *On Miracles*; the Life of Saint Gall and many other lives and passions of saints; the Life of Saint Leo; Jerome on Zephaniah, Haggai, Joel, and Malachi; ten Conferences of the Fathers and another seven; Jerome’s *Lives of the Fathers*; the *Book of Sparks*; Bede’s Questions on the Books of Kings. He also compiled this book itself from diverse materials and charters.

### Charter concerning Preopapa

Let all present and future persons know that a certain Milo, knight of Mont-Salions, surnamed Pagan, approaching death and receiving the monastic habit with great devotion, for the salvation of his soul, he and Ascherius, knight and his nephew, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, in the village called Preopapa, three scythe-cuts of meadow; a fourth at the village called Praeciac; one *mansus* with six jugera of land; and, from the wood belonging to the village above named Preopapa, they gave the monks of Albiniac passage and customary rights of pasture. If they send their pigs there, they may take from that wood everything necessary for making houses, for all their dwellings, and for all their implements that can be made of wood. They gave these things to them in perpetual right with every honour.

Likewise, the peasant who should dwell in the aforesaid *mansus* shall have, honourably, all customary rights of the aforesaid village in woods, waters, meadows, and pastures, and shall never serve anyone except Saint Peter and the monks. They also gave in this alms-gift one *plastrum* beside the chapel of Mont-Salions. If any falsifier should wish to oppose this alms-gift, let him be anathema.

That this charter may remain inviolate, let us set down witnesses: the mark of Archerius, who makes this gift; of Lambert of Domarim; of Hugh, knight of Cortiniac; of Odo Viridis; of Aymon, knight; of Robert, priest; of Dominic. Among the monks: the marks of Constantius, John, and Ulgerius.

### Charter concerning the wood of Vetus Vinearum and the small holding called Domos

Just as death entered the world through the devil’s envy, he striving thereby that no one might return to life, scarcely is there one who does good—scarcely even one. We judge it necessary that, if anyone confers anything upon the Church, it should be transmitted in a written memorial to the knowledge of future faithful people.

A certain woman, distinguished enough in the world both by birth and conduct, daughter of Henry of Nova-villa, named Elizabeth and surnamed Caritas, when she was approaching death, bestowed as alms upon the church of Saints Peter and Paul, for the remission of her sins and those of her forebears, whatever she possessed in the wood of Vetus Vinearum and in its small holding, which she called Domos. She also gave a male servant named John and a maidservant named Emma, to be held wholly freely and honourably, as fully as she knew and could. Her sons Guy and Philip approved. The witnesses were Alinard, cleric; Odo of Bellomonte; Seuvin of Raiac; Cerard Crispus; Hugh of Voslun; Theoderic, official; Pagan, chaplain. Among the monks: Gerard, prior; Ulgerius Calvus; Albuc the captive; Gerard, son of the same woman.

### Charter concerning Lixiac

Considering the changes and vicissitudes of this age, we have judged it worthwhile to commit to lasting memory what has been bestowed upon the church of Bèze in our time. Therefore let it be known that Humbert of Lissey gave to God and Saint Peter of Bèze, entirely and most freely, whatever he or his forebears had or had held in that village, so that henceforth neither in the cemetery nor in the village itself may it be permitted to him, his heirs, or any person acting in his place to inflict injury, molestation, or exaction upon any person, whether his own man or another’s; and, as we have stated, that within the whole village he may not violently seize not merely a man but anything whatever.

This was given by the aforesaid Humbert, with his wife and sons, before the witnesses recorded below: Albric his brother; Theoderic, monk; Baldwin; Lencelin; Pontius, knights; on the day when the church was consecrated by Lord Jocerannus, bishop of Langres, in the year 1119 from the Incarnation of the Word of God, indiction XII, epact VIII, concurrent II, on the second day before the Kalends of June, a Sunday.

At the same time, and in the same week, on Wednesday, a certain knight, Humbert of Cynciac, gave to Saint Peter, for the soul of his son Guy and of his forebears, twelve denarii from the church of a certain village called Mentusca, and one *mansus* at the village of Cynciac, at the harbour, with bridge-toll and fishery. He offered all these things at the altar, placing a book upon it, before witnesses: Letbald, Wilenc, and very many other monks; and Guy his brother, Walter of Beria, and many others.

### Charter concerning the churches of Cipeto and Tasneto

We believe that it will benefit our successors considerably if, according to the custom of our elders, we too leave to posterity a memorial, if not eloquent yet true in expression, concerning the things bestowed upon this church. Therefore let it be known that Lord Jocerannus, bishop of Langres, gave the church of Cipeto to the church of Saint Peter of Bèze through the hand of Lord Abbot Stephen, in the chapter of Saint Mary of the castle of Fontis Vennae, before his archdeacons and with their approval: Wilenc, archdeacon, and Ayrard, archdeacon; Humbert, canon; the mark of Abbot Stephen; and Ulgerius and Rodulf, monks.

He also gave the church of Tasneto to the aforesaid church of Bèze, in the wood called Volort, before Warner, archdeacon, who approved it and gave whatever he possessed in it; Robert, provost, and others being present.

### Charter of Bishop Jocerannus concerning Mentusca
I, Jocerannus, by God’s will bishop of Langres, while, according to my ability, together with our faithful men and sons, we were making faithful provision concerning the affairs and revenues of the Church of Langres, was approached by the venerable lord Abbot Stephen. He humbly and devoutly requested that we should give to God and to the brothers of the monastery of Bèze the wastelands of a certain wilderness situated in the territory of the Attoarii beside the river Saône, which belong properly to our episcopal lordship alone, and should establish them as heirs of the aforesaid possession. Speedily consenting to his just and reasonable request, with the approval and counsel of our faithful archdeacons of the Church of Langres, we freely give to the aforesaid abbot and to his successors henceforth, saving the customs of the Church of Langres, whatever we ought to possess by episcopal right in the village called [Col. 0978C] Mentusca; likewise the church itself with all its appurtenances. And by episcopal authority we confirm the things given.

Sign of Wilencus, archdeacon. Sign of Garnerius, archdeacon. Sign of Ayrardus, archdeacon. Sign of Wido, archdeacon. Witnesses to this act are the lord Gualo, regular canon; Jozaudus, dean of Chalon; Guilencus, monk; Albericus, monk; Rodulfus. These things were done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1119, indiction XII, epact VII, concurrent II; in the first year of the pontificate of Calixtus, ruler of the Apostolic See; while Louis was king of the Franks, Jocerannus governed the bishopric of the Church of Langres, and Durannus dictated as notary.

[Col. 0978D] Likewise, concerning Mentusca.

Let every man hear that Gualo of the castle of Ruphiacum, son of Ulgerius of Colongiae, and his brother-in-law Gualo, together with his brother Haimo, gave to God and to Saint Peter of the church of Bèze whatever they had or held in the church of the village of Mentusca: namely, the cemetery and the priesthood of that church, with everything pertaining to that priesthood in holdings, meadows, and lands; also the third part of the tithe of that village; and customary rights of use in all the lands, meadows, woods, and waters of that jurisdiction.

Sign of Abbot Stephen. Sign of Wilencus. Sign of John, monk. Sign of Gualo [Col. 0979A] who made this gift. Sign of Gualo. Sign of Haimo, his brother. Likewise, sign of Gualo of Vilar. Sign of Henry. Sign of Robert, provost. And of our household: sign of Theobald, hospitaller; sign of Humbert, baker; and of very many others.

### Concerning the market of Bellimont, falsely claimed

From the pages of the divine Testament we have learned that he who strives to persecute the Church of God and to contend against its ministers ought to be subjected to the curse of eternal condemnation. For it is impious to disturb the peace which the angel sang at the Nativity of the Redeemer for people of good will.

Therefore I, Hugh, lord of Bellimont, led by repentance because in my ignorance I have so often harassed the brothers of the monastery of Bèze, resolved henceforth to cease from wronging them and to live with them from now on in perpetual and sweet concord. Accordingly, to settle the claim concerning the market which I had taken from them, I came before the bishop of Langres, to whom a complaint concerning this had been made by the abbot of the aforesaid place; and, because I had refused to render justice and give account to him who indeed ought to protect and defend the abbeys of his bishopric, I made amends and promised that I would correct myself hereafter.

Thus, on a certain solemn day, when the church of Blessed Remigius was dedicated at Bèze, and countless people had flocked together from every quarter out of devotion to so great a celebration, I promised, in the monastery of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, before the brothers, the aforesaid bishop, very many nobles, clerics, and knights, that I would no longer take their market from them, either in my castle [Col. 0979C] or throughout my land and power; that I would establish no market for sale; and that I would not prevent the people of my land from attending the market of Bèze. I caused my son Hugh also to promise and swear this. I myself, Hugh, confirmed it by an oath of my right hand; and moreover, lest any future claim of my successors should arise, I placed upon the altar, for God, Saint Peter, and the brothers of the church of Bèze, everything which my right, justly or unjustly, possessed or had possessed from this market; and I gave the market itself as a gift.

And lest this be lost through the forgetfulness of long time, it pleased us to strengthen this charter by the testimony of the men subscribed below. Sign of Bishop Guillencus. [Col. 0979D] Sign of Gocelinus, archdeacon. Sign of Fulco, archdeacon. Sign of Garnerius Rufus, archdeacon. Sign of Pontius of Rivel. Sign of Abbot Gerard. Sign of Wilencus, prior. Sign of Rodulfus, sacristan. Sign of Josbertus, provost. Sign of Albricus of Arcione. Sign of Theobald of Ganibreres. Sign of Rainald of Granceio. Sign of Milo of Poiens. Sign of Odelricus of Renavis. Sign of Guido Ranivel. Sign of Obertus. Sign of Hugh the Steward. Sign of Constantius, Giroardus, and his son.

### Charter concerning the annual revenues of the cantor

All the faithful ought to support one another either by prayers or by gifts: so that those who lead a quiet life may aid by their prayers those occupied with many matters, and those latter may charitably supply what is necessary for their benefit. For they must conduct temporal affairs in such a manner that they may thereby attain eternal rewards.

Accordingly, the lord Abbot Gerard, hearing that since the venerable John, cantor, had departed this life no one had established a memorial of books (*monimentum librorum*), established that every year a hemine of wheat should be given to the cantor from each obedience. Though he wished to give more, he did not wish to burden anyone, so that both richer and poorer men might more willingly consent, and the arrangement might not be burdensome to those to come. All the heads of the obediences assented to this decree, which was imposed upon them for the remission of sins, and willingly promised to do this. This was decreed by the aforesaid abbot with the approval of all, on the feast day of the Apostles Peter and Paul; and it was established that each should have paid this gift to the cantor from the Kalends [1 October; Col. 0980B] of October until the Kalends of November.

Sign of Wilencus, prior. Sign of Warnerius, precentor. Sign of Rodulfus, sacristan. Sign of Albricus of Arcione. Sign of Josbertus, provost. Sign of Bartholomew, sub-cantor, and of all the monks.

### Concerning Haimo and his sons

Let it be made known to our present and future brothers that the lord Abbot Gerard and the entire convent appointed Haimo, and, after his death, his sons, to be toll-collectors of the market, so long as they faithfully and without fraud perform that office. But if any one of them is found to be fraudulent in this, let him be deprived of the aforesaid office forever.

Sign of Wilencus [Col. 0980C], prior. Sign of Rodulfus, sacristan. Sign of Warnorius, precentor. Sign of Tigerius, cellarer. Sign of Josbertus, provost. Sign of Otbertus, servant. Sign of William. Sign of Hugh of Ulmis.

### Charter of Beria

We wish it to be clear to all that Ewinus, lord of Beria, on the anniversary of his mother’s death, together with his wife Annilina, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze one holding in the village of Beria and five jugera of allodial land; likewise one female servant called Gocia, with her three sons, whose names are Ogdierius, Girardus, and Hugh; also another female servant, named Hodierna; and half of a certain meadow, since the other part has been known to be ours from ancient times.

That the present charter may possess unbreakable force, we appoint these witnesses to it: sign of Haimo; sign of Hebertus; sign of Wido; sign of Robert; sign of Humbert; sign of Lambert; sign of Gunterius; sign of Warnerius, cleric, and Bartholomew, his brother. Of the monks: sign of Abbot Gerard; sign of Wilencus, Warnerius, and Josbertus. Wido, brother of Ewinus, approved this alms at the market of Bèze before Mainfredus of Arco.

### Likewise, concerning a certain plot situated in this village of Bèze

Let it be known to the children of the Church that Ayvinus, knight and lord of Beria, gave perpetually to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze a certain plot which he possessed in the village of Bèze, whether by right or wrong; and so did his wife and the boy Willermus.

That this alms may remain firm, we appoint these witnesses: sign of Abbot Girard; Wilenchus; Rodulfus. Of the laity: sign of Ayvinus; Wido of Chimisi; Robert; Ilbertus, knight of Salice; Lambert and his son Rainard; Humbert and his son; Gunterius; Richard; Henry and his son; Heinricus; and very many others.

### Charter of the lord Galon called Columba

Everything that is born tends toward destruction, according to Solomon—not merely words, which, once uttered, already no longer exist. Therefore we record here that Galon of Bellimont, surnamed Columba, upon receiving the religious habit, gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze, in the village of Lentiliacum, half of the tithes belonging to him, namely from the monks’ own oxen; and, in the village of Saint Benignus of Dijon, at Casnetum, a holding with the land and meadows belonging to it; likewise half of a mill near the village of Percejum; together with half of a plot situated in this village of Bèze.

He also added a holding at Lisseium, with the land called Montis Salionis belonging to it; and there, in meadows called *paniciariae*, whatever can be cleared from woodland into meadow. This was approved and granted by Odo, lord of Montis Salionis, and by the lord Abbot Girard, with Albert of Toul and Guido of Vircillis standing as witnesses. Hugh, his son; Haimo, his brother; and his wife, laying the book upon the altar with their own hands, approved this gift made by the aforesaid Galon. We strengthen it by the testimony [Col. 0981C] of worthy men: the lord Abbot Girard; Guilencus, prior; Albert of Toul; Bartholomew; and the remaining monks; and, of the laity, Milo of Poiens, Hugh of Roife, Humbert Salomon, Humbert the Rich, Robert, provost, and very many others.

### Charter of Hugh of Torcennacum

We impress upon the written memory of posterity that Hugh, knight of Torcennacum, on receiving the religious habit, gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze a certain holding at Rosecium and his share of the wood of Montanicum, with the approval of his sons; Robert, chaplain of Montis Salionis, and Wido, knight of Ortis, together with his brother Hugh Rufus and many others, being witnesses.

[Col. 0981D] Let all who read these letters know that Odo, knight of Picangiae, surnamed Saxo, having become a monk at the end of his life, yielded to Saint Peter whatever he claimed in the mill near the village of Lucus; and, with the approval of his brothers, he devoutly handed over that mill to the church of Bèze to possess forever. And lest anyone hereafter presume to invalidate this, we append the signs of the witnesses who were present: sign of Abbot Gerard; Rodulfus, sacristan; Hugh of Bellojocum; Lebald of Genevreres. Of the laity: sign of Hugh, Walter, Milo, and Humbert, brothers of the aforesaid Odo; sign of Robert, provost; Humbert the Rich; Otbertus Coccus; Giraldus, reeve.

[Col. 0982A] Charter of the lord Ascherius of Montis Salionis

The alms of the faithful are therefore recorded in writing so that those who will come after, reading what they have not seen, may know it; and, should any claim by wicked men arise concerning it, may be able to resist by the authority of their predecessors. We therefore judge that it should be made known to posterity that a certain knight, Ascherius of Montis Salionis, when approaching death, gave to God and Saint Peter of Bèze, in the land called Craias, a certain holding as freely as he himself held it, with its people, meadows, and other appurtenances; also two brothers, inhabitants of the village of Albiniacum, Albricus and Stephen, and their niece Avilina.

Witnesses of this alms are Gerard, prior; Rodulfus, sacristan; Heinricus; Garnerius, precentor; and Gunterius. [Col. 0982B] Of the knights: Hugh and Odo, brothers of the aforesaid Ascherius; Paganus of Buiris; and very many others.

### Charter of the lord William of Fontis Vennae

Because the present life inclines toward evil, each person ought by alms or works to conceal from the sight of the Lord the evils he has committed, since the Apostle commands us to redeem the time because the days are evil. William of Fontis Vennae, fulfilling this by God’s grace, gave to the church of Bèze, while still engaged in secular knighthood, a fishery in the village of Calintensis, with a holding belonging to it and a fisherman named Albricus, together with his wife and children.

But after he had become a monk by divine regard, he granted in the village called Cortesours to God and Saint Peter of Bèze two holdings [Col. 0982C] with their appurtenances, and two men, Stephen and Theodericus, their inhabitants, with their wives, children, and everything belonging to them; likewise all the customary produce, called “thirds,” of the two villages of Cortesours and Lare. Excepted were sixty jugera which the two brothers Verduinus and Amalricus, reeves of the lord Girard and sons of the same William, retained for the mayoral holding.

As stated above, William and his son Girard granted these things to the church of Bèze, with the approval of Guido, lord of Fontis Vennae, with his son Theodericus, and Guido, lord of Jovis Villa.

Furthermore, on the day of the burial of the aforesaid William, Girard and Guido, lords of Montaniacum, abandoned the unjust custom which they had exercised against our men of Pauliacum, and decreed that if either of them should seek justice from any man of Saint Peter for any offence, the other should in no manner demand the same from that man. Previously each of them had exacted double payment from one person for a single offence. For all these matters we adduce as witnesses the lord Abbot Girard, Guilencus, prior, Rodulfus, sacristan, Garnerius, precentor, Widricus, prior of Fontis Vennae, Albert of Toul; likewise Hugh of Tilecastrum, lord of Bellimont, and his son Hugh; Haimo of Tilecastrum; Hugh of Bellojocum; Milo of Poiens; Odo of Domna Petra; Widricus of Monz; Ulgerius of Burgus; Walter; Odilo, provost of Calintensis; Otbertus Coccus; [Col. 0983A] Hugh the steward; and the aforementioned brothers Nerduinus and Amalridus.

### Charter of Milo, surnamed Pautenerius

In accordance with the prophet’s exhortation, “Break the bonds of wickedness; loosen the bundles that oppress,” Milo, knight of Tilecastrum, called by the additional name Gyrovagus, freed Oddilina—daughter of Humbert Vetula, wife of Odo Maleth, son of Evrard of Dijon—from his own servitude and service and that of his forebears; and, declaring her free, placed her upon the altar of Saint Peter, while his brothers Humbert and William Desfosses, and his sons, heard, saw, and approved this.

We confirm this gift by the following witnesses: Gerard, abbot of Bèze; Guilencus, prior; Robert, provost; Otbertus Coccus; [Col. 0983B] Girard, son of Aidulf; Drogo, son of Gerbert; Hugh of Ulons; Lambert Falsart; Aldo and Odo, brothers of Fontanis; and many others.

### Concerning Dominicus Malner

We record in these letters, as a matter worthy of remembrance, that Rodulfus, knight of Saint Michael, gave to Saint Peter of Bèze and placed upon the altar whatever he had held and possessed, justly or unjustly, from his predecessors over Dominicus Malegrinus, whom he had treated as a serf. Many witnesses were present: Abbot Girard; the monks Henry, Lebald, Richard, and Hugh. Of the laity, there were present the knights Wido Ravines, husband of the donor’s sister; Ewinus of Excelsus; Walterius Malsualez of Granceium; Odo of Furnus; and of our household, Humbert Salomon, William, Peter of [Col. 0983C] Pauliacum, and also Peter and Robert of Montis Salionis.

### Concerning Orcevalis

[... ] let all, both present and future, know that Nerduinus, lord of Asperimont, and his son Hugh, knight, and Galo of Willer and his son Haimo, for their souls and those of their forebears, handed over to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, in the place called Orcevalis, forty jugera of land. To this gift we appoint these witnesses: sign of Hugh Francigena; sign of Rodulfus of Renavis; Hugh of Conitensis; Ewinus Spinellus.

### Concerning the wife of Theodericus the Carpenter

Let whoever reads these letters firmly retain [Col. 0983D] that Mainfredus of Arco granted to God and Saint Peter of Bèze the wife of Theodericus, together with her children, for his soul; and for this cause—or rather from friendship—the lord Abbot Stephen gave Mainfredus twenty solidi. But because the human mind often departs from good, after the death of Theodericus, when the children complained before the lord Abbot of Bèze as though Mainfredus had not granted them freely or willingly, the same Mainfredus, moved by reason, acknowledged that he had granted them freely. Confirming the same alms, he gave it anew, most freely and forever, to this church; and he caused it to be approved by his wife and children.

For the peace or commemoration of this agreement, Abbot Girard gave him ten solidi, and two solidi to Humbert of Baleneva. We append suitable witnesses who were present to this charter: sign of Abbot Girard; Guilencus, prior; Heinricus; Albricus; Lebald. Sign of Hugh of Bellimont and Hugh, his son; Guido, provost of Saint Julian; Humbert, reeve of Baleneva; Valeth; Obertus Coccus; Girardus, reeve.

### Concerning the village called Trescase

Let it be clear to the memory of present and future people that Hugh, reeve of Baleneva, and his sons Humbert, John, and Peter restored in peace to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze the land of Saint Peter at Trescase, which they had claimed for many years. Acknowledging that they had sinned by seizing it, they sought and received, in chapter, absolution for their offence from the lord Abbot Girard and all the brothers.

For this deed we appoint as witnesses Abbot Girard, Guilenchus, prior, Albricus, and the rest of the chapter; likewise Mainfredus of Arco, Guido, provost of Saint Julian, Valeth of Baleneva, and Otbertus.

### Concerning the village of Saint Sequanus

Since we have learned of preceding deeds through written record, it pleased us also to leave this in writing to posterity, that it might remain inviolate forever: Joffredus, lord of Bellimont, with his wife Gertrude, for the salvation of their souls, granted to Saint Peter and to the abbot and monks of Bèze a certain village called Saint Sequanus in Baascha, just as they themselves held it freely; with the approval of their son Hugh, their grandson Joffredus, surnamed [Col. 0984C] Martellus, and all who appeared likely thereafter to disturb this gift.

But it happened, at the Devil’s instigation, that Martellus, their successor, after the death of the aforesaid predecessors, was not ashamed to violate what he had previously approved: namely, by claiming justice and jurisdiction over theft (*latrocinium*) in the aforesaid village. Yet afterwards, through the prompting of the Lord, who does not permit His Church to be deprived of alms, and when the lord Abbot Girard had admonished him, he returned to himself. Devoutly he came to the chapter of the brothers, received fraternity, and for the repose of his own soul and of his forebears freely granted everything which he claimed or possessed in the village, except the holding of Odilo and his brother Galo, his serfs.

Sign of Abbot Girard. Sign of Lebald. Sign of Richard, monk. Of the knights: Martellus, Welfo, Elvinus, Haimo, Savarinus, Odilo, Wibertus. Of the household of Saint Peter: sign of Otbertus Coccus; sign of Wido, Humbert the Rich, and Humbert Salomon.

We judge it right to commit the rents of the church to the memory of the faithful, lest through our neglect they should at any time be diminished by wicked men. Therefore we record here a certain knight named Haimo, son of Galo of Viler, claiming justice and jurisdiction over theft (*latrocinium*) in the precinct of Saint Martin of Montusca. For this reason he carried off plunder and inflicted many other injuries upon the church of Bèze. Since he persisted for a long time in this obstinacy, Abbot Girard set a hearing in the same village. Both parties therefore met on the appointed [Col. 0985A] day. Having taken counsel from his mother, who had come to plead with him, and from his other friends, he peacefully relinquished to the abbot the complaint which he had made concerning the household of our monks living there; likewise his claim concerning two men whom the monk caused to live outside the precinct.

This was on the condition that, if any crime should be committed there by his own men or by others, he should make his complaint to the abbot of Bèze; and for any crime committed—even homicide or adultery, whose penalty is recognized as greater than that of other offences—he should receive nothing beyond five solidi by the law of right.

### In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity

All members of the Christian faith ought, with devout minds and with gifts as generous as they can offer, to make the holy Church of God glorious and rich. Moved by this consideration and spiritually inspired by the Holy Spirit, I, Hugh of Bellomont, with my sons Hugh and Joffredus, for the remedy of my soul and of my forebears, have granted as a gift to God, Saint Peter of Bèze, Abbot Gerard, and the monks of Bèze wishing to serve God in the parish of Saint Martin, whatever the lord Remigius, priest of that place, held in churches, fields, meadows, woods, houses, and all the uses of human life; and, further, whatever pledges he possessed which he has either already given to the aforesaid monks or may wish to give in the future.

It also pleased us to annex to this gift the provision that the men [Col. 0985C] who shall lodge at Saint Martin and dwell near the monks, in the lands of the castle of Bellomont, shall freely have every right of use in woods, meadows, pastures, and all the resources by which people live. That is, if the men should unknowingly cause damage, they shall restore the damage without penalty; but if the monks themselves or their servants in any way cause damage knowingly or unknowingly, they shall wholly restore the damage without penalty. I also gave them fishing rights above Bellomont, to fish where, when, and how they please; below Bellomont, however, I granted them fishing only as far as wading depth.

Lest any cloud of forgetfulness should cover this gift, it pleased us to commit it to writing and to strengthen it by the testimony of approved men who were present. [Col. 0985D] Sign of Abbot Girard. Sign of Richard of Vircillis. Sign of Lebald of Genevreres; Josbertus, provost; Henry, chaplain; Humbert, merchant; Peter Rufus; John, servant; Christianus; Hugh, lord of Bellimont; Hugh, his son; Remigius, priest; Milo of Poiens; Hugh of Aces; Ewrardus of Rolens; Fredericus of Campaneium; Wido of Renavis; Rodulfus, son of Odolricus; Erbertus Capicium. These things were done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1134, indiction XII, epact XXIII, concurrent VII.

### Concerning the precinct of Saint Martin

It belongs to all people who are called by the name Christian continually to meditate day and night on the law of the Lord. For the law of the Lord is without reproach; it converts souls, and, being a faithful testimony, gives wisdom to the little ones.

Therefore I, Haimo of Tiricastro, little in knowledge and burdened by the folly of many evils which I had done, when before my death I had been oppressed by a long illness, returned to myself. Reflecting further that before God I bore no sheaf of righteousness, for the remedy of my soul and of my parents’ souls I granted to God, Saint Peter, and the monks of the monastery of Bèze the precinct of Saint Martin of Lucus; and I relinquished to them everything which I had possessed there, justly or unjustly.

The witnesses present were Richard, chaplain; Peter, chaplain of the same Richard; Hugh of Conulent; John, cleric; Theobald of Casoto; and Wido Talanat.

[Col. 0986B] I, Agnes, wife of the lord Haimo of Tiricastro, after my husband Haimo had been buried in the cemetery of Saint Florentius, and while clerics, kinsmen, and friends were present, when we had returned together to the cloister and were discussing his alms, considered it good, together with my children, to make and confirm before them and the many worthy men present the gift which the lord Haimo had made to the church of Bèze concerning the precinct of Saint Martin of Lucus.

Therefore I gave and confirmed the gift which he had made: namely, the precinct of Saint Martin of Lucus, to be possessed forever by the monks of Bèze in peace, with every liberty, for the soul of my husband. Lest this be erased or surrendered to oblivion through the passage of time, we strengthen it by the testimony of the men subscribed below: Peter, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon; Theobald, dean; Richard, priest; Dominicus, prior of Saint Florentius; Bonet of Mare; John, cleric; Peter, chaplain; Haimo of Nimie; Wido of Saut; Nocherus; Wido Talanat; Theobald of Casoto; Wallerus; Rollanus; Wido; Marescallus; Malveslot; Theobald Excotex; Robert, his son.

This was done and acknowledged: that the gift which they made of the precinct was not made because the precinct was theirs, but because in the precinct belonging to Saint Peter they committed seizures and exactions, and wrongfully and violently took those things which by right or justice they had no claim to in that precinct.

[Col. 0986D] Concerning Montigniacum

Since all things pass away, and those things which are in this world never long remain in the same condition, we record in writing that Rodulfus and his brother Milo, who were called Bigornenses by their surname, for the souls of their brothers Guido and Roger, and for the remedy of the souls of their father, mother, and forebears, gave to God, Saint Peter, and the monks of the church of Bèze two holdings at Montigniacum: one holding called the holding of Odo Eurvinus, and the other called the holding of Wido Malaefilia.

They made this gift at Bèze on Parasceve, that is, the day of the Passion of the Lord, both holding the book by which, in the presence of the lord Abbot [Col. 0987A] Giraldus, they placed this donation upon the altar.

Sign of Abbot Girard himself. Sign of Widricus, prior of Fontis Vennae. Sign of Albricus of Arcio. Sign of Albert of Toul. Sign of Girbertus of Algeriacum. Sign of John, priest of Bèze.

### Concerning Domna Petra

It is clear that the human race ever declines toward its end, since indeed human honour and power fail, and the beauty of youth, quickly withering, vanishes. Therefore it is necessary for a person to seek the remedies of alms, because almsgiving appeases the face of the Lord and obtains mercy. And lest the gifts of the faithful be surrendered to oblivion, we ought to make them known in writing.

Accordingly, at the time when the church of Saint Martin was given to Saint Peter of Bèze by the lord Wilencus, bishop of Langres, that same bishop granted us the priesthood of the church of [Col. 0987B] Domna Petra. But Humbert of Lissey and his sons, in whose lordship it then lay, claimed it and held it by force. When Theodericus, son of the aforesaid Humbert, died, the brothers of that Theodericus—namely Wido, together with three others, with the approval of their father—freely handed over that priesthood and the church precinct to Saint Peter of Bèze, retaining only the judicial rights of the precinct.

This was on the condition that, if a man of Saint Peter should commit any offence in that precinct, the complaint should be made to the abbot of Bèze, and, after making satisfaction, he should pay no more than what the law would have required of him in his lifetime.

They also gave four scythe-cuts of meadow in their enclosed wood of Saint Sequanus, and a man named Abbricus with his wife, children, and holdings; likewise his sister, the wife of a certain Elluinus. They added a third part of the “thirds” from Blaniacum, and the allod and everything which they held there, except a certain Walter’s holding with its appurtenances.

The aforesaid brothers of the deceased—Wido and Humbert—for the remedy of his soul confirmed this alms to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze by placing the book upon the altar, before the witnesses whom we shall record here. Sign of Abbot Gerard. Sign of Rodulfus, prior; Heinricus; Albertus; Richardus; Ansiricus; Bartholomew; Richardus. Of the knights: sign of Hugh of Bellimont and his sons Hugh and Joffredus; Otto of Miribel; Hugh of Asperimont; Euvinus of Aces; Milo of Poiens; Haimo Columba; Ulricus [Col. 0987D] of Renavis; and his son Milo.

### Concerning Mentusca

It is certain that the affairs of the world pass by in manifold variety; therefore it is necessary that matters worthy of remembrance be recorded in writing. We make known to posterity that Galo of Rofei, for the soul of his wife Annilina and the souls of his forebears, gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze the small tithes of the village called Mentusca and all the tithes from the village of Cincei, as freely as he possessed them.

But it happened that later, prompted by avarice, he challenged the gift which he had made. A monk who was in charge of Mentusca spoke with him about this matter; and the same Galo, acknowledging that he had erred, devoutly granted that the aforesaid alms should be held in peace by the church of Bèze.

[Col. 0988A] Sign of Richard, monk of Mentusca, and Anselm, his companion. Sign of Ulgerius, monk and son of Galo who made the gift. Sign of Richard, provost. Likewise, sign of Hugh and William, sons of the aforesaid Galo. Sign of Notbert, chaplain. Richard, conversus of Molesme. Sign of Wido and Lemenfredus, and many others.

### Concerning Cusiacum

It is fitting to recount the alms of the faithful, who, as the Lord commands, strive to lay up treasure for themselves in heaven. Therefore let it be clear to all who desire to know that, after the death of his brother Haimo, Milo of Fontanis, together with his mother Petronilla, gave for Haimo’s soul to Saint Peter of the Church of Bèze one holding at Cusiacum with its appurtenances, and a man named Benignus with his wife and household.

We already had from them at Fontanellae three jugera of land; together with these, they freely gave us three additional jugera, as they possessed them. The administrator of that land also relinquished his administration to the church of Bèze. They likewise gave, at Fontanae, five solidi each year on the vigil of All Saints for the brothers’ refectory.

The aforesaid Milo, with his mother Petronilla, devoutly bestowed these things on Saint Peter of Bèze, with the approval of Euvinus and his other brothers, and of his brother-in-law Gibuinus and his wife. Sign of Abbot Gerard; Rodulfus, prior; Widricus, prior of Fontis Vennae; Richard, provost; Bartholomew; Richard; Pontius; Widricus, priest. Of the laity: sign of Theodericus, Widricius, and Humbert, brothers; [Col. 0988C] Lebald and Hugh.

### Concerning Colongiae

In the name of the supreme and undivided Trinity. I, Gothefredus, humble bishop of the people of Langres by God’s grace, address all sons of holy mother Church forever. We make known to both the present generation and future posterity that the lord Gerard of Bèze and the monks of that place gave and granted, through our hand, to the nuns of Colongiae the tenth part of the allod which they held at Colongiae, and the entire parish with its appurtenances.

This was on the condition that every year the abbot of the church of Bèze should receive from the nuns six pounds of wax, by the octave of the Nativity of the Lord, for the allod and parish. With the consent of his chapter, he also granted the nuns of Colongiae the tithe of that place, which certain men had appropriated to themselves. For this tithe, the women devoted to God there shall give them eight measures of grain annually, in two instalments.

### Concerning Lisseiacum

We judge it fitting to commit to written memory that Robert of Billeiacum, intending to go to Jerusalem, gave to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze all the allodial land which he held at Lisseiacum, and a man named Bernard with his wife and children. This was on the condition that, if by God’s grace he returned from Jerusalem and wished to make a monk either of himself, his brother, or any of his sons or grandsons, that person should willingly be received.

He also caused this to be approved by his brother Peter before Count William and many knights at Malleiacum. Therefore the lord Abbot Gerard gave him seventy solidi. We appoint suitable witnesses to this charter: Count William, Martellus of Malleiacum, Wido Trosellus, Haimo Columba. Sign of Abbot Gerard; Richard, provost; Albert; Pontius; Girbertus.

### Concerning Greater Perciacum

Touched by the grace of the sacred Spirit, Guido of Perciacum sought to sow in blessing, so that he might reap blessing. During his life he gave to God and Saint Peter of Bèze all his allods which he held at Greater and Lesser Perciacum, at Noidant, and wherever else he had them, in holdings, meadows, fields, lands, and woods, with a certain intervening mill.

He also asked that, if he should ever wish to become a monk, he might be received into the same monastery; and by God’s ordering he deserved to attain this at last. We subscribe suitable witnesses to this charter, who by their approval confirmed the aforesaid alms before the altar of Saint Peter: Eguinus of Beria; Guido Talevar, with their wives, sisters of the aforesaid Wido of Perciacum; Paganus Busun; Erluinus; John, cleric; Hugh Falsarius. Sign of Abbot Gerard; Rodulfus, sacristan; Richard, provost.

### Charter of Brutino the priest
To all sons of the Church let it be known that Lord Abbot Gerard granted the priestly office of the church of Saint Remigius to the priest Theodoric, surnamed Brutinus, on this condition: that, so long as he faithfully administered the property of the church for the benefit of the monks, he should hold that church with the consent of the brethren. But if he should be found to be taking away the goods of the brethren or dishonouring them, then, unless he made amends to their satisfaction, he should lose the church itself. We designate as witnesses of this matter: Humbert the Rich and his brother Garnerius; Gerand and Berno; Simon and Walter, brothers-in-law of the same priest; and also his brother John, who on that very day relinquished the matricular church. All these, in chapter, with an oath of fidelity placed in the hand of Lord Abbot Gerard, promised concerning the aforesaid matter that they would be faithful toward the monks, making restitution for their losses.

[Col. 0989D] Concerning Saint Benignus.

By these letters we make known that Haymo, priest of the village of Saint Benignus, when he wished to receive from the tithes of that village more than was right, or than his predecessors had received, came with Garnerius, who then presided over that place, before Lord Abbot Gerard. It was decreed that he should receive only a fourth part of the tithes of wheat and oats. Moreover, half of the baptismal dues and half of the *sperae* were granted to the same priest, so that he might remain faithful to the monk.

> [Note: [Col. 0989] *Sperarum*. Acherius suggests that this perhaps means an accidental or contingent due, French *le casuel*.]

The same priest approved this and promised to receive nothing beyond what was his due, in the presence of Lord Abbot Gerard, Garnerius prior of Saint Benignus, Richard the provost, Pontius, and several others.

Concerning Furt.

It is plainly necessary that what is given by the faithful to the Church of Christ be committed to writing, lest what devotion prepares for God be taken away by avaricious desire. Let it therefore be known that Robert, of the village called Furt, upon entering monastic life, gave to Saint Peter of Bèze the meadow which he had possessed in that village, on the condition that it should be redeemed from the ten solidi for which it was held in pledge. He also gave a fourth part of the mill, half the common pasture of the same village, and two holdings with their appurtenances beside the spring of the village of Lentilliac.
