His wife approved this gift, together with her son Hugh and her daughter called Boillot, Matthew the monk of Lentilliac, Richard, and Robert being witnesses. Of the laymen: Berno, Humbert the Rich, Ralph, and William the servant.

It happened, however, that Hugh of Furt, the aforesaid Robert’s son, challenged this alms, although he had approved it. When he was reproved on this account by the monk who presided at Lentilliac, at length compelled by reason, he offered this same gift upon the altar of Saint Peter by the placing of a book, and promised never thereafter to challenge it. Mark of Matthew of Lentilliac. Mark of Richard, Pontius, Bartholomew, and Gerard. Of the laymen: mark of Humbert the Rich, Berno, Peter of Pauliac, and John Coccus.

Concerning freed serfs.

We wish it to be manifest to all the faithful in Christ that Severinus of Faverney and his brother Guiard manumitted as free and released persons, to Lord Gerard, abbot of the church of Bèze, Peter of Saint-Apollinaire and his brother, all their heirs, and likewise the sons of the priest of Bellenave and that priest’s grandsons—all of whom they had long claimed as their own. Excepted from the sons of the aforesaid priest was one who served them, whom they retained in their own service.

They decreed to make this aforesaid manumission both for their own salvation and for the remedy of the souls of their parents, and also because their brother, named Peter, had already become a monk in the aforesaid church. Witnesses of this matter are, on their side: Humbert of Vuchey, Stephen, provost of Fonnei, and Meifrid of Arc. On the abbot’s side: Narduin of Aspermont and Pontius of Silveneiac, monks; Humbert of Gillens, who at that time lived at Arc; Humbert, steward of Bellenave; and Vaslo of the same village.

This was done in the fields of the village called Arc, before the canons’ granary, at the place popularly called Corbiton, on a Sunday upon which the feast of the Holy Cross is celebrated.

Concerning the village of Calent.

In the name of the Lord, amen. The name of our forebears and the authority of other saints have taught us to keep, for recalling the past, written charters of our ecclesiastical benefices and the privileges of revenues established for our use; and they have left us very many examples of their own ordinances. We are accustomed to entrust to the holy record of writing all benefices conferred upon us in Christ’s name by our noble faithful persons, or by humble clerics or laymen, so that, when the records of our benefactions are frequently displayed, the souls of our benefactors may frequently be remembered in prayers; and so that these benefices may be kept in memory, lest troublesome error follow from the erasure of their memory.

Therefore, among our many other benefices, we did not judge it proper to conceal in silence one special and great benefaction bestowed upon us by Count Renald of Burgundy, both because so great a matter deserves to be recorded and because it was performed by so eminent and worthy a person.

Accordingly, by this present writing we strive to make known to all Catholics that the most powerful Count Renald, under divine inspiration, compelled by no injury but of pious and good will, freely and absolutely gave to God, to Saint Peter His apostle, patron of the basilica of Bèze, and to the holy martyr of God Christopher, protector of our cell of Calent, whatever each person, noble or humble, cleric or layman, of the same village had given or might give to the brethren of our aforesaid cell from his fief, for himself or for the repose of the souls of his predecessors—provided only that he himself did not thereby relinquish his whole fief.

The occasion for this act was that his provost Odo had, through his tyranny, taken seven marks of silver from the men of Neuville; and the count firmly declared that he would restore them to Lord Abbot Gerard as soon as he learned of the injury. He gave to the aforesaid abbot as sureties for this restitution Lord Hugh of Beaujeu, Lord Gerard of Strabona, Otto of Durnay, and Humbert of Trimolay.

When this whole benefaction had been concluded, he entered swiftly, accompanied by many persons, the church of the holy martyr of God Christopher; there, before the altar, with bent knee and before all standing present, laying his hand upon the altar itself, he made satisfaction to God, Saint Christopher, and Abbot Gerard for the aforesaid injury. In doing this, he acknowledged that he had no right and no claim regarding the infliction of that aforesaid injury upon the men mentioned above.

This was done early on a Sunday, while the divine Mass was being celebrated in the aforesaid church. On that day he was also setting out for a conference against the bishop of Langres. Witnesses of this matter are the four above-named sureties for the silver: namely Hugh of Beaujeu, Gerard of Strabona, Otto of Durnay, and Humbert of Trimolay; together with his provost Odo, William Sylvestris, Odo the White, and his brother Hugh. These are on the count’s side. On the abbot’s side: Guirric, prior of Fontenay; Godfrey, prior of Calent; and Pontius of Silveneiac. In Christ Jesus our Lord.

## Epitaph of Hugh of Beaumont

[Col. 0992A]

Those who enacted decrees  
Established this by their decrees:  
that whatever had been determined  
should be recorded in writing,  
or whatever all had confirmed  
should be marked with seals,  
lest it perish through age  
or the passage of days.  

Our forebears established this  
and left behind the ordinance.  
The care of men today preserves  
such usages of the ancients;  
for through writings or figures  
they are accustomed always  
to mark out their institutions,  
or to display them by sealing.  

But since such a flourishing custom  
is widespread among all,

[Col. 0992B]

we, following customary practice,  
should diligently strive  
to record in writing and confirm  
a certain special gift—  
a gift, I say, so great  
or worthy of remembrance  
[lacuna] sufficiently  
that we may describe it perfectly.  

Therefore let it be known to all,  
and let it vanish from no one’s knowledge;  
let every learned and unlearned person alike know  
that Hugh of Beaumont  
gave of his own free will,  
with a heart of good will  
and an affection of piety,  
to God and to the brethren,  
his fellow believers in Christ,  
of the church of Bèze,  
for the repose of the dead,

[Col. 0992C]

for himself and his son Geoffrey,  
for the remedy of his parents,  
both for all the faithful  
and for his own heirs,  
a chief holding—or, if you prefer,  
a coeval holding—  
together with a small parcel of land,  
commonly called Rupecula,  
enlarged by four great meadow-mowings.  

He gave these to the aforesaid brethren of Bèze,  
who diligently served  
the cell of Saint Martin.  
These lie in the territory  
of Beaumont, beneath the estate.  

Moreover, after wrongfully making a claim  
and through his own violence,  
he had wickedly driven from his homeland

[Col. 0992D]

a certain man called Carbon,  
who had built a small dwelling  
near the said cell  
in order to serve the brethren  
ministering there.  
Hugh at once declared him free  
and restored him to freedom.  

In addition, by grace he gave  
his whole right of justice  
in Boens, in all things  
both named and done.  
Thereafter it pleased him  
to grant a safeguard-right  
over the estate of Cavennei,  
which he held as his own.  

Finally he renounced  
the complaint or claim  
concerning Blegne,

[Col. 0993A]

whether rightful or not,  
so that he retained nothing.  

Again, he had a little daughter,  
whom he was rearing in his home,  
born of a concubine—  
something forbidden by holy law.  
A certain Garcio sought always  
to join her to himself  
in lawful marriage,  
on the covenantal condition  
that, under Hugh’s protection,  
there should be rendered to him  
from the aforesaid Bèze  
a return from the provostship,  
or an account of it—  
concerning which he had made  
a claim, though not a just complaint.  
But Garcio did not obtain  
what he had thus arranged.  

For Hugh, despite the urgent entreaties

[Col. 0993B]

of the monks,  
refused to give his daughter  
and was unwilling to provide assistance.  

These aforesaid gifts  
were made in the church  
of the monastery of Bèze,  
upon the steps of the altar,  
by means of the Gospel-book.  
The matter is publicly known.  
What the father did,  
his son Hugh performed more willingly.

Concerning Bellenave.

The Catholic mother Church rejoices in the advancement of her children and mourns for the failings which she suffers from rebellious stepchildren. In the place of children she cries out in the words of David, saying: “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. 34:12). And through Isaiah: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they, despising me, have rejected me” (Isa. 1:2).

Such a one indeed was Robert, born of the male and female serfs of this church of Bèze and raised by it to the office of provost. Again and again he devastated the church that had raised him by violence, lawsuits, plundering, and burnings. Afterwards, repenting through regard for God’s mercy of so many evils, and believing that he could be saved in no other way, he relinquished to the church of Bèze the office itself—that is, the provostship—with everything belonging to it, and granted it in the presence of Lord Abbot Stephen and many others, whose names are these: Ralph and Vigerius, monks; Obert Coccus; Hugh the seneschal; and Berno.

On the day of his wife’s burial,

[Col. 0993D]

he confirmed the same gift anew in our chapter. The church held this donation for many days in peace, quiet, and without challenge, until one day Humbert of Bellenave came to Abbot Gerard and asserted that Robert had established him and his brothers as heirs of that same provostship.

Robert, greatly angered and vigorously denying this, declared that he had once been put into captivity, and that if he should die in that captivity, he had given them the right to his provostship. Why say more? They confirmed a judicial duel on the matter; but on the appointed day of combat, while Robert was duly present, Humbert and his men neither came nor sent a counter-message.

Thus this claim having been stilled, after some days the aforesaid Robert sought and received monastic life, and, repeating the grant and gift which he had made and repeated before, caused it to be strengthened by the testimony of our whole chapter. But after he had entered the way of all flesh, the brothers of Bellenave—Humbert, Peter, and John—rose against us, asserting claims to that provostship; likewise the provost of Saint-Julian, with his nephews. Their case was settled in the court of Duke Hugh, through the intervention of the duke himself, his wife, and the magnates of the court.

For, overcome by legal argument and by the giving of gifts, they renounced and forswore everything which they claimed in the provostship, whether by right, wrong, kinship, or anyone’s gift; and, having given their faith, they promised to provide warranty against all their kindred and against all persons. We attest that Hugh, duke of Burgundy, and his wife, Widric, abbot of Bèze, Peter, abbot of Dijon, Guy the prior, Narduin of Aspermont, Pontius of Silveneiac, and Humbert of Virzeyac, monks of Bèze, saw and heard this.

Urric of Renaves and his sons, taking occasion from the fact that Haymo, brother of the deceased Robert, had married Urric’s daughter, rose against us, claiming that same provostship. But, coming to their senses, they renounced it with all its appurtenances and swore off their claim. Urric himself and his sons Ralph, Milo, Guy, and Hugh, together with the daughter on whose behalf they were claiming, consented and approved that the church of Bèze should possess it peacefully and with complete freedom forever.

We strengthen this by the testimony of worthy men: Lord Abbot Guidric, Prior Ralph, Albert of Toul, Narduin of Aspermont, Pontius of Silveneiac, and the rest; and, among the knights, Euvin Daleelz, Haymo Columba, Milo of Poiens, and Mainfred.

Charter of Geoffrey of Beaumont the Younger.

Let all the faithful joined together in the body of holy Church, who recognize themselves as members of Christ, the true Head, consider how they ought to cherish their infirm members, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26). For holy Church, after the manner of a net cast into the sea, gathers all who come into the bosom of her mercy, refreshing some with solid food, pouring upon others the milk-drink of sweetness,

[Col. 0994D]

and saving some from the shipwreck of death.

Thus Geoffrey, knight and son of Lord Hugh of Beaumont, incurred this shipwreck through the instigation of the devil. Having been overtaken by death in military service, he sought to escape to the shore of the prayers of the faithful and strove to redeem his deeds by alms. How worthy of remembrance this alms is we shall show in what follows.

Because of the execration of so great a crime, his dead body remained without burial for more than a year, until, by God’s disposal—who wills that none should perish—the venerable Godfrey, then bishop governing the Church of Langres, went to Rome.

When he had successfully completed all for which he had gone, he returned with apostolic authority and permission,

[Col. 0995A]

absolved Geoffrey from the bond of his excommunication, and, offering the saving sacrifice for him, honourably buried his unburied remains.

At that time Count Renald of Burgundy was at Bèze with the bishop, accompanied by a great company of knights. On that day he swore before all to maintain the peace of the Church and to attack with armed force all who plundered it. Before them the devout Hugh, father of the deceased Geoffrey, came with his son Hugh and promised Lord Abbot Widric and the church of Bèze that he would maintain peace and bring aid against all who usurped anything belonging to the monastery as though they were devastating his own land.

After this, both Hughs—the father and his son Hugh—confirmed before many witnesses, through the hand of Bishop Godfrey, the alms which he had earlier made for Geoffrey.

Accordingly, for the soul of his son and for the souls of his forebears, he gave to God, Saint Peter, and the church of Bèze, with his son Hugh present and approving, his own corvée-service, which the priest Remigius held from them in pledge; a certain piece of land called Rupecula, extending from the road leading to Luillae as far as the village that goes toward Fleix; four meadow-mowings beside our cell of Saint Martin; and a man named Carbon, whom he had driven from his homeland because of many injuries.

Moreover, he freely granted, without customary reservation, the right of justice and the corvée-services which he claimed in our village called Boens. He also gave the safeguard-right over our village of Caveney,

[Col. 0995C]

and freely relinquished the claim he made upon our land near the village called Blaineis, whether the claim was rightful or wrongful.

We wish this donation to be strengthened by the testimony of worthy men, whose names are these: mark of Hugh, who made this alms, and of his son Hugh; mark of Euvin of Acels and his son Hugh. On the day of Geoffrey’s burial, when this alms was again confirmed through the hand of the bishop, many others were present, whose names are these: mark of Bishop Godfrey; of Count Renald; mark of Abbot Guy; mark of Haymo Columba; mark of Mainfred d’Arc; mark of Richard of Fretis; mark of Milo of Poiens; mark of Hugh Chaine; mark of Urric of Renaves and his sons. Of the monks: mark of Abbot Widric; mark of Pontius; mark of Narduin of Aspermont; mark of Warnerius; mark of Albert; mark of Matthew; mark of Ralph, bearer of this charter; and many others.

Concerning half the tithes at Majas.

Since certain institutions of our fathers seem to have been consigned to perpetual oblivion through the errors of their successors, we judge that great care must be taken concerning present institutions, so that they may always be kept in memory through the succession of written records.

Accordingly, so far as lies in our power, we commit to the service of the pen that Bartholomew, son of Ralph the steward of Majas, became a monk of the church of Bèze, with the approval of the convent, through Lord Abbot Gerard, without the knowledge of his father and mother. At that time the father of the aforesaid Bartholomew held in pledge from Guy the chaplain, for fifteen solidi, half of the minor tithes in the village called Majas, on this condition: unless he redeemed it during Guy’s lifetime, after Guy’s death Ralph and his sons should inherit it.

That half of the tithes of which we have spoken above Ralph gave, for his son Bartholomew, to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and to the holy church of Bèze, in the presence of Lord Abbot Gerard, with his wife and sons approving. This done, his wife asked Lord Abbot Gerard to permit her, for her lifetime, to retain whatever share in Canabo those tithes brought her; Lord Abbot Gerard granted her petition before all who were present.

Charter concerning the two brothers of Beria, namely Robert and Walter.

By these present letters we make known that Lord Hugh of Beria gave Stephen, with his heirs, to Saint Peter and the church of Bèze. After his death, Hugh of Magne and his brother Aldo, born from the daughter of that same Hugh of Beria, began to claim the sons of the aforesaid Stephen, refusing to acquiesce in or approve their grandfather Hugh’s having given them.

Therefore they underwent the judicial proof imposed upon them, establishing that their grandfather Lord Hugh had given to God and Saint Peter everything that he had in their father and his heirs. The aforesaid Hugh, who had challenged them, seeing his claim annulled, admitted that he had claimed them unjustly and yielded them to God and Saint Peter by placing a book upon the altar in the church of Bèze.

The worthy witnesses who were present are Haymo, Odo Malenutritus, and Haymo Strabus; and of ours, Abbot Widric, Narduin of Aspermont, Pontius of Silveneiac, and Ulric of Renaves; among the laymen, Berno, Peter, and Humbert.

When the aforesaid Hugh and his brother Aldo had approved this at Bèze, they fixed a day on which they would cause their mother and wife to approve it. On that day Pontius the monk was present at Magne, and before him Hugh’s mother, his wife, and his only son approved it beside the wooden chapel, Hugh and Aldo being present, together with Haymo, Odo Malenutritus, Hugh, and Ulric of Angele.

Concerning the wood called Rotardus.

Let all know that Pontius of Saint-Seine and his brother Humbert, for the peace and settlement which they made with Gislebert of Avenne concerning the death of their brother William, who was killed at the village of Saint-Seine, and with their maternal uncles Guy and Renald, gave to God and Saint Peter whatever they possessed in the wood called Rotardus.

Likewise, for this same peace and settlement, Hugh, lord of Beaumont, ordained that five solidi of annual rent from the holding of Siligne at Montignac should be given to Saint Mary of Fontenay, where the body of the deceased lay, on the third day after the feast of Saint Bartholomew, on which his anniversary is observed.

We also wish this to be strengthened by the testimony of worthy living persons. Mark of the abbot of Tusey. Mark of the abbot of La Charité; of Roger of Abens, monk of Bellevallée; and of Odo of Furno. Of our monks: mark of Richard the provost, Pontius, and Narduin. Of the knights: Haymo and Hugh Channe.

Concerning Saint Martin and Lissiac.

Our merciful Creator, the father of the household, not only does not deprive of reward those who have faithfully laboured from childhood in His vineyard, that is, holy Church, but also rewards with the denarius of eternal blessedness those who, arriving late—that is, already weighed down by old age—endeavour to live devoutly in it.

Accordingly, by divine regard, Humbert of Bigorna, renouncing the world in old age, came with a devout mind to the monastery of Bèze and granted that monastery four meadow-mowings: three at Saint Martin of Beaumont and one at Lissiac. He also gave a holding at the village of Casotum and a field of three *jugera* between Albiniac and the castle of Mont-Salions.

Humbert himself, his brothers Ralph and Milo, and their nephew Pontius gave this alms to Saint Peter of Bèze, placing the book upon the altar. Mark of Abbot Widric; of Gunterius the chaplain; Richard the provost; William the servant; Peter of Pauliac; Guy; and Peter Coccus.

Concerning Genciniac.

We commit to the memory of the faithful that Urric of Renaves, for the soul of his son Hugh, gave Saint Peter of Bèze a holding at Ossiliac, which was bound by right to pay each year twelve denarii and two portions, or two hens, at Christmas. He also added the half which he possessed of our corvée at Genciniac, so that this corvée might remain with the church of Bèze. Mark of Ralph, Milo, and Guy, sons of the aforesaid Urric. Mark of Guy Rufus, nephew of the same Urric.

Concerning Podiens.

“The present life,” as blessed Pope Gregory says, “is the road by which we travel to our homeland.” Therefore, whoever desires to reach the homeland of life should, while still on the road and before death, strive to send before him to the Lord an embassy of good works or alms.

Accordingly, we record that Odo was taken from this life by untimely death; for his soul, his father Milo of Podiens gave the church of Bèze a field of ten *jugera*, with his wife, children, and kinsmen approving. Mark of Abbot Widric; mark of Matthew; of Albert; mark of the brothers Bartholomew and Richard. Among the knights: mark of Hugh, lord of Beaumont.

Concerning Boilliac.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, amen. The Church of God, which rejoices to be enlarged by the gifts of the pious and delights in acquiring them, ought always to remember them in order to avoid the harm of forgetfulness. For because no shepherd can remain forever, being prevented by death, whatever he does or knows to be advantageous to his Church, he ought to show by letters and writing to his successors.

Therefore I, Abbot Stephen, make known to all faithful people of the present and future age that Lord Simon of Beaujeu and his brother Lord Hugh, before they had married, freely granted and, by authentic grant before many persons, without any reservation, conceded to Saint Peter, to me who appeared to preside, and to the monks of the church of Bèze, as Saint Peter’s woman, the daughter of Gerald the Rich. Her parents and friends had intended to give her in marriage to Peter, son of Lambert of Pauliac.

Lest this could be revived as a challenge through the envy or malice of any ill-disposed person, it seemed right to me that this charter should be strengthened by the testimony of the men present whose names are subscribed. Mark of Simon. Mark of his brother Hugh. Mark of Pontius of Silveneiac. Mark of Fulk of Vore. Mark of Rainald the priest. Mark of his brother Bernard. Mark of Gerald the Rich. Mark of his son Walter. Mark of Abbot Stephen. Mark of Gerard, prior of Fonsvens. Mark of Guillenc. Mark of Albert of Toul, prior of Saint-Valerian. Mark of Lambert of Pauliac. Mark of his brother John. Mark of Gislebert the servant.

Concerning the same matter.

It should further be known that after the death of Lambert of Pauliac, Audo sought from his brother Peter a share of the house which stood in the marketplace. Peter answered that he would in no way answer him concerning this matter, because their father Lambert, without any share for his other sons and daughters, had given it to him when he married. Audo answered that he did not know this.

They both therefore came to judgment, and it was decided in the court of Abbot Gerard that, if Peter had lawful witnesses concerning this matter, he should remain in peace. When the day of the hearing came, Peter appeared with his witnesses, namely Robert the provost and Hugh the seneschal, together with his mother, affirming this. Thus, the house was declared free and restored to Peter in peace; Audo gave the aforesaid men as sureties for maintaining the peace.

Those present at the judgment were Josbert the provost, Lebald, Albric, and Albert. This house brought Peter *domnum*, namely thirty pounds [the reading and sense of *domnum* are uncertain].

Concerning Saint Martin.

Since, through the changeability of things, many matters which seemed more firmly established are destroyed and appear to have been abolished as though they had never existed, we judge it proper to commit to writing those things by which the Church of Christ is increased in temporal goods, so that by the authority of the records they may be defended or made known to the future.

Accordingly, we record that a certain knight of Beaumont, named Richard and surnamed Truta, had a son named Haymo, whom he resolved should become a monk in the church of Bèze. He came to Lord Gerard, then governing the church of Bèze, and to the brethren of that monastery; before many witnesses he handed over this son to the abbot and brethren, and for him endeavoured to enrich that church from his own possessions.

He therefore gave that church, at Saint Martin in the district of Beaumont, half of the corvée-service which he possessed by hereditary right, and the meadow Roseros, which he likewise possessed. He also granted the customary dues which he had from our men living at Artasia, namely corvée-service and all else that he held there.

Not long afterwards, he chose to sell the half of the corvée of Saint Martin which he had retained. Having first approached the aforesaid Abbot Gerard about it, the same abbot bought that half from him, with Richard’s wife and son approving in the chapter of Bèze.

Later, however, a brother of Richard’s, named Theodoric, about to go to Jerusalem, began to challenge everything which his brother had given or sold to us, with Richard’s consent, as subsequently became known. Abbot Gerard gave them thirty solidi, and both of them placed [an object not specified in the surviving text] upon the holy altar in the chapel of Saint Bartholomew before many witnesses, with Richard’s wife and sons present and approving.

After several years had passed, and Gerard of good memory had been taken from their midst and the venerable Widric had succeeded him, Richard, of whom we speak, repudiated and opposed the whole matter before Abbot Widric—whom he treated as inexperienced and ignorant—and the monks living at Saint Martin. But Abbot Widric, like a good shepherd resisting a ravaging wolf, opposed him and brought the suit to settlement.

When both came on the appointed day, the aforesaid abbot, supported by prudent counsel, brought with him suitable witnesses who had heard and seen these things. Since Richard could not oppose them, he admitted that he had made this challenge unjustly and under compulsion of necessity. He also promised never again to cause trouble, but to be faithful in this matter and in all others in which he could be of service.

Lest this matter be disturbed again, we strengthen it by the testimony of worthy men. Mark of Hugh, lord of Beaumont; Guy of Sauz; mark of Nocherius; mark of Euvin Daces and his son Hugh; Milo of Poiens and his brother Hugh; mark of Pontius Crassus; Guy Ravinel, Guy Rufus, and Wiard; and, among the retainers, Humbert of Soleri and his brother Warnerius, Albert Christianus, Warnerius Crassus, and Dominic the official.

Charter of Hugh, lord of Beaumont.

Foreseeing the praise of almighty God and the advantage of future generations, we commit these matters to written records, lest they be obscured by any cloud of forgetfulness or someday disturbed by the audacity of wicked persons.

Therefore we make known to all faithful persons present that Lord Hugh, lord of Beaumont, inflamed by divine fire and concerned for the salvation of his soul, gave to God, Saint Peter, and this church of Bèze the mill, situated before the church of Saint Martin, which Peter Rufus held, together with the miller, his house, the meadow, and all its appurtenances. His son Hugh, then lord of the aforesaid castle, and his wife Matilda approved this, through the hand of Godfrey, bishop of the Church of Langres, on the day when he consecrated the aforesaid church.

We designate as suitable witnesses of this donation: mark of Bishop Godfrey; mark of Euvin Dacels and his sons Hugh, Hugh surnamed Werra, and Milo; mark of Milo of Poiens and his brother Hugh; mark of his son Hugh; and, among the retainers, Humbert of Soleri and his brother Warnerius, Christianus and Albert, and many others.

[Col. 1000A]

Not long afterwards, when divine Providence had stirred the faithful to oppose the faithlessness of the pagans, Hugh, son of the aforesaid Hugh, was moved with compunction. Since he was about to depart on the expedition to Jerusalem, uncertain what outcome his affair might have, he came devoutly to the chapter of the brethren to bid them farewell. He asked forgiveness for the wrongs he had inflicted upon the church of Bèze and, commending himself to the brethren’s prayers, made an alms.

For in the village of Saint Peter called Pauliac he possessed half the rights of justice, land, and the men holding it. He granted all these things to them, his father Hugh being present and approving. Witnesses of this matter are nearly the entire multitude of the men and monks of Bèze who were present with him in chapter; and among the knights, his father Hugh, Josbert, Gloseius, Guy of Dessartinis, Wiard of Renaves, Guy Rufus, Hugh Chaine, Guy Ravinellus, and many others.

We add also that another knight, Frederick of Champagny, setting out for Jerusalem, granted in the same chapter to Saint Peter and the brethren of the monastery of Bèze a mill with its appurtenances at Blainiset, together with the land and everything he possessed in that village. Hugh, lord of Beaumont, and his brother Hugh Chaine were present and approved this, together with the rest named above.

Charter by which the lord bishop of Langres gave us certain churches and chapels at Saint Martin above Vingeanne and Beaumont.

[Col. 1000C]

The variability of worldly affairs, attended by manifold decay, leads a wise person to deliberate, so that, as a precaution of foresight, he may cast the eye of his mind into the future lest anything good that he has done should perish. For whatever is done among human beings is quickly effaced either by the passage of time or by the cloud of forgetfulness, unless—as we know from the examples of the Fathers and the practice of holy Church—we endeavour to record in writing, for remembrance, the alms and good works performed by holy men.

Therefore I, Godfrey, by God’s grace bishop of Langres, make known to all faithful people of the present and future age that our venerable brother Widric, abbot of Bèze, came before us and humbly requested that I should again grant and confirm by our authority the churches held by Lord Remigius, priest of the castle of Beaumont. These churches had previously been given to Lord Gerard, abbot of Bèze, by our predecessor of blessed memory, Lord Wilencus, bishop of the Church of Langres. He further requested that, in order to make the donation more secure and to avoid the claims of wicked persons—which ecclesiastical prudence always strives to avoid—I should seal it with our seal.

Therefore, saving the rights of the Church of Langres, I give to God, Saint Peter, our venerable brother Abbot Widric, and the monks of the monastery of Bèze the churches which, as has been said, the priest Remigius held: namely, the church of Saint Martin with the chapel of Saint Bartholomew; the church of Auxiliac; the churches of Champagny, namely Saint Julian and Saint Hilary; and the church of Dompierre. I confirm this by pontifical authority, so that no one may henceforth expel or dare to trouble the abbot or the brethren of the monastery of Bèze in their possession of these churches, or usurp them by fraudulent means in any controversy. If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that, as his own guilt requires, he lies under sentence of anathema.

Concerning Néron.

Although the children of the Church of God are commanded to maintain simplicity by divine authority, they are nevertheless known to be required by the same precept to employ serpent-like shrewdness, so that we may neither hasten innocently toward evil nor fail to undertake what appears useful. For when, according to the Prophet, the world sets a boiling pot—that is, the human conscience—toward the face of the North, and in these times very many, through their desire for evil, are engulfed in the storms of vices, it is right that ecclesiastical prudence should both hold its own possessions innocently and wisely avoid losing in the future what it has held.

Therefore, to awaken the memory of those to come and to shut out the mist of forgetfulness, we commit to writing that Lord Wido of Lyscio, when he approached death, for the remedy of his soul and those of his ancestors, gave to God and to the monks of Bèze as alms everything that he possessed at Néron, and everything that he claimed ought to be his there by hereditary right or in any other way. This alms was placed upon the altar of St. Peter through the hand of his wife Charteia and his son Wilencus, with his brothers Pontius and William present; they too made this gift, in the hearing and sight of very many approved men—monks, clerics, and laymen—whose names are subscribed, who were present. He also relinquished his claim concerning the meadow held by Albricus. Mark of Wido; of Albert, subprior; of Albert of Toul; of Richard, monk.

### Charter concerning Wido the Miller

The blessedness which the universal Church understands from the Lord’s Prayer—“May thy kingdom come”—we ought to pursue with every effort of mind and body, so that afterward we may be able to rejoice with the saints who shall reign with him. Moved by this consideration, I, Cecilia, wife of Ewrard of Rollens, together with my son William, have given a certain servant of mine, Wido, to God, St. Peter, and the monks of the church of Bèze, for the remedy of my husband’s soul and the salvation of my ancestors. Holding the book of the Gospels with my aforesaid son, I placed this gift upon the altar, and caused my daughter Elizabeth to approve this donation.

That it may not become void or perish in the mist of forgetfulness, I have graciously permitted the witnesses who were present to be recorded. Mark of Wido the Prior. Mark of Albert of Toul. Mark of Wido. Mark of Lambert of Racio. Mark of Bartholomew of Arcu. Mark of Peter, cellarer of the kitchen. Mark of Humbert the Rich. Mark of Gerald. Mark of Chalucoth, smith. Mark of Stephen, nephew of Abbot Widricus. Mark of Peter, minister of Bassey.

### Concerning Aldric the Serf

The Church of God is struck by varied and frequent storms of tribulation, like an island in the sea repeatedly battered while a whirling wind blows—that is, while the pestilential persuasion of the enemy disturbs the peace of the faithful who appear to be devoted night and day to the service of God. Therefore they must watch diligently, that they may peacefully retain what they have and possess, lest by the craftiness of evil persons they lose what they ought to preserve.

We therefore wish it to remain an everlasting record, committing to writing how the claim which Lord William of Tricastel brought against Aldric, a man of St. Peter, was settled. This William said that the aforesaid Aldric had resided at Verona and had possessed the money of his brother who had died. Aldric, on the contrary, said that he had never received a holding in Lord William’s land, nor had possessed the money of his deceased brother. Therefore, through the mediation of worthy men who were present, Aldric gave Lord William four pounds and ten solidi; and William relinquished everything that he claimed against him. Thus he abandoned both his claim and the man in peace.

That this may remain unshaken and not be erased by the mist of forgetfulness, it must be confirmed by the testimony of the men who were present, and their names must be set down individually. Mark of Abbot Widricus; of Albert of Toul. Mark of Wido the chaplain. Mark of Humbert the Rich. Mark of Warnerius. Mark of Peter of Pauliac. Mark of Audo. Mark of John. Mark of Haimo. These things were done at Bèze.

Afterward, at Tricastel, the wife of Lord William herself approved and graciously granted the peace which her husband had made concerning Aldric. The witnesses present were William himself; Ulric, chaplain of Clermont; Richard, priest; Warnerius, his nephew; John, clerk; Nocherius, knight; William of Casoto; Bardulf; Walter; Wido Checevath; Pagan; William, son of Miribel; Warnad; Hugh; Wido; and the reeves of Luco. Mark of Bardulf; Walter of Pichangi; Wasler Malvasloth; Lambert of Marcelliac; Serianth; Milo Falsart; Warnerius of Verona; Warnerius of Solunge.

### Charter concerning the Wood of Rothart

Although the providence of ecclesiastical governance ought, by the Lord’s command, to be strengthened with serpent-like shrewdness, it is nevertheless ordered to be tempered by dove-like simplicity, so that what is thus held by us may not, through imprudence, be relaxed beyond proper measure. Attentive to this consideration, I, Abbot Widricus, make known to all my successors forever how the church of Bèze, over which I appear to preside, was at last freed from the vexations and pains which it had long endured because of the claim concerning the Wood of Rothart.

For certain men of Belmont, called provosts’ men, asserted a hereditary share in the aforesaid wood, and rose against us with no slight harassment, inflicting very many evils. Since the severity of this suffering had continued for a long time, it happened, as we believe by God’s will, that one of them, named Brutinus, while one day sharpening a knife in a smith’s workshop and carelessly setting it upon the ground, fell wounded by that very knife and died most quickly without viaticum and confession.

When his relatives and friends mourned one who had died such a death and learned that he had been excommunicated, they began to inquire how he might be buried in consecrated ground with the rites of Christianity. This seemed impossible unless he were absolved from the wrongs which he had done to the Church because of the claim to the wood, for which he appeared to have been excommunicated. Accordingly, through the action of his brother Clarinus, who was the wiser, an agreement was made with another brother, Widricus: the wife of Brutinus, called Baldulfa, and his children Peter and William, together with the entire household, relinquished their claim to the aforesaid wood. Receiving from us a measure of millet, then expensive because of the season, they granted it to God, St. Peter, and the monks of the church of Bèze for his absolution. Witnesses were Haimo the monk, Clarinus, Widricus, Christian, and Humbert Loir, who were present as witnesses and hearers.

Thereupon the brothers and kinsmen, taking his perilous death as an example to themselves, through the action of Clarinus, who, as has been said, had better understanding, all agreed to make peace with the aforesaid church. Lest they should appear guilty before God because of the claim to the wood, they all unanimously relinquished that wood to God and St. Peter. Moreover, they received a temporal blessing from the monks: Widricus, forty solidi and a measure of millet; Clarinus and his brother William, forty solidi. Hugh the provost, because he relinquished that wood to God and St. Peter, obtained that his son should become a monk in our church.

Thus the claim to the wood having been relinquished, all made good peace and concord. Upon the altar of St. Peter they gave and relinquished to God and St. Peter everything which they claimed, rightly or wrongly, in the aforesaid wood and its appurtenances; moreover, they swore that they would never reclaim it. And if any claim should thereafter arise, they would, by faithful declaration and providing lawful warranty, defend us against all claimants.

That this peace may not perish through the passage of time or the harm of forgetfulness, it must be confirmed by the testimony of the lawful persons who were present: Haimo Columba; William of Saint-Seine; Peter; his brother Aldo of Pauliac; Malet; Humbert; Warnerius; Christian; Humbert of Solio; Clarinus; Widricus; William. Sibyl, wife of Hugh, approved the peace and gift of the wood made by her husband Hugh and their children Milo and the others. When Malvaslet was dying, he relinquished the aforesaid wood in the presence of the abbot, Pontius, chaplain of Fisneta, his son Gislebert, and Christian. Again, when Hugh of Aquato was dying, he relinquished this wood in the presence of his wife. Witnesses were Christian, Malvaslet, Amalric, and Garnerius Silvestris.

### Charter concerning Saint-Seine at Bèze

How ardently we ought to desire eternal things is shown by the decay of the passing world, which seems to be reduced to nothing by daily failures. For the present life, which appears wretched in its circumstances, whatever it confers is weak and fragile; and it is clearly proved that it finally makes its lover utterly miserable. Amid its losses, because through the weakness of the flesh we suffer manifold harm, death itself, by which all flesh is forsaken, is for us a cause of pain and fear.

For this consideration, I, Martellus of Mallei, no longer wishing to obey flesh and blood, but desiring to win the favor of the Majesty of heaven and to do penance for the sins which I committed through the licentiousness of my youth, resolved to visit the Lord’s tomb at Jerusalem. By the counsel of charity I also determined to enrich, by a more generous bestowal of my goods, the church of Bèze, which is my parish, as the burial-place of my father and ancestors testifies.

Therefore, in the presence of Lord Abbot Gerard, with the consent and approval of Count William, to whose custody and protection I entrusted my land, I gave to God, St. Peter, and the brethren of the monastery of Bèze two fisheries in the Saône: one which I had given before, and another which I gave when I undertook this journey. I gave them on this condition: if necessary, the fisherman shall have an assistant to help him steer the boat and to supply him, in service, with the things necessary to the art or office of fishing. A man who strives to work alone, since he accomplishes little or nothing, must be helped.

I also gave one meadow called Lambert’s Arm. Finally, I gave to the monks dwelling there the wood near the Saône called Wevra, and all the woods which I possess around the village called Bèze—[lacuna]—from these, whatever may be necessary for the food of the monks and their men.

I also gave the tithes of Flagey, its parochial rights, and every use and custom in the woods and forests of that village, with complete freedom. To this donation I added the tithe of a fourth part of the port. I also gave the paagium (pannage-right) of Saint-Seine, which was mine, and granted and gave to the monks of Bèze that they may send their demesne swine into my woods wherever I have them, and that they may range freely everywhere without pannage. Likewise, the monks who dwell at Bèze may send their demesne swine through all my woods without pannage, and, if they wish to bring swine in, one hundred in addition.

Because those monks of Bèze are devoted there for the remedy of my ancestors, I do not wish them to be afflicted by any evil vexation from my men. Therefore I granted and established for myself as an alms that the monks themselves may inhabit with complete freedom that village, namely Bèze, in which they dwell. I ordered that my men who hold lands in the village should enclose them and put up suitable hedges, lest the animals of the village be able to devastate what lies within. If they refuse to enclose them and any loss results, the villager shall not be brought into suit, shall answer to no one, and shall pay neither damages nor legal penalty on that account. But if a man of the aforesaid village suffers loss through a badly made enclosure, he shall bring his complaint before Count William, and the count himself shall render full justice in the matter.

And that this donation may be strengthened by an authentic privilege, we confirm it by the testimony of the men subscribed. Mark of Martellus, who made this gift. Mark of Count William. Mark of Abbot Gerard. Mark of Abbot Constantius. Mark of Pontius. Mark of Gislebert, prior of Bèze. Mark of Paris, canon of Masey. Mark of Robert, knight of Bille; Wido Trosellus; Walo of the land of Dijon. [Lacuna] for his own salvation and that of his kin [lacuna] of his son William, recently deceased and buried at Bèze, freely gave to God and the church of Bèze, to be possessed in perpetual right, the things written below, with the consent and approval of his wife and sons, and also of his brothers Richard and Gerard.

Namely, one holding at Balenava, on the condition that its occupant shall have the customary rights as before in the waters, lands, pastures, and woods of the same Humbert and his successors. He also remitted the four denarii which the monk of Arcenant owed him annually for the bank of his mill at the feast of St. Martin. He also gave four jugera of land near the elm-tree called “of Mulms.” To these he added a meadow-mowing near Arcenant.

We have also taken care that suitable witnesses to this donation should subscribe. Their names are these. Of the monks: Abbot Joffredus, Pontius the prior, and Guido the sacristan. Bartholomew, brother of the same Humbert; Robert Verna. Knights: Hugh of Aspermont; Aymo Columba; Aymo of Minure; Aymo Bornus. Townsmen: Peter of Pauliac; Maletus; John the cook; and very many others.

### Charter concerning Fontenelles

It ought to be impressed in enduring letters that Hugh, knight of Fontaines, for the soul of his brother Haimo, recently slain and honorably buried at Bèze, with the approval of his sister, nephews, and the others to whom the property seemed to pertain, gave to God and the church of Bèze at Fontenelles one holding with a meadow-mowing and a third part of half the small tithe.

This was caused to be done by Milo, knight and lord of Fossato, together with his brother Robert—to whom it chiefly pertained—on the day of Haimo’s burial at Bèze, with many present, whose names are partly noted below: Abbot Joffredus; Hautio, prior; Wido, sacristan; Bartholomew; Gybuinus, monks; Milo of Fossato and his brother Robert, knights.

## In the Year of the Lord 1117: Peter Chrysolanus, Archbishop of Milan

## Historical Notice concerning Peter Chrysolanus

*(Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Late Latin Literature, I, 436)*

Chrysolanus is called “Crisolanus” by Trithemius, chapter 397 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; “Chrysolanus” by Baronius and Du Cange; by Ughelli, vol. III, p. 126; and by Allatius, Peter Grosolanus. Others call him Arisolanus, Grysolanus, or even Proculanus. From bishop of Savona he became archbishop of Milan in 1102, but was deposed in 1112 on the accusation of simony.

Pope Paschal II sent him, while in exile, to Constantinople to Alexius Comnenus, in order that he might bring the Greeks back to the embrace of Roman worship. There he wrote *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* to Emperor Alexius. When John Phurnus, head of Mount Ganos, Nicholas of Methone, and Eustratius, metropolitan of Nicaea, replied to him from among the Greeks, he in turn set against John Phurnus a disputation on the same subject.

It is uncertain whether he himself wrote in Greek or rather in Latin; but Greek manuscripts, apparently translated from Latin, survive in the library of the Most Christian King. See Allatius, *On the Agreement of the Two Churches*, II.10, p. 626 ff., and Baronius under the year 1116, no. 7 ff., where he gives the *Disputation to Emperor Alexius*, or a compendium and argument of it, from the Latin translation of Federicus Metius, bishop of Thermulae. Trithemius also notes that Chrysolanus wrote a book *On the Holy Trinity*, letters and sermons, and other various treatises, though they were not seen by Trithemius. Chrysolanus died at Rome in 1117.

## Oration of Peter Chrysolanus, Archbishop of Milan, concerning the Holy Spirit, addressed to Emperor Alexius Comnenus

*(Published in Greek from manuscripts and in Latin from the translation of Federicus Metius, bishop of Thermulae, by Leo Allatius, **Greek Orthodoxy**, vol. I, p. 379.)*

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**A discourse of Peter, bishop of Milan, addressed to the lord Emperor Alexius Comnenus, establishing that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and likewise from the Son.**

### 1.

Hear and understand what I say to you, by God’s inspiration, most wise and forbearing, mighty and gentle Emperor Alexius. Do not look to me, who am the least of all God’s servants; rather, look to him whose cause is at issue—to the Lord Jesus Christ, King of kings and greater than all rulers. Through him kings reign and makers of laws judge what is right.

For him and concerning him I, his servant—though unworthy and useless—speak to you, so that you may not endure insult being done to him in your empire, lest he himself receive from you a grievous and imperial retribution in his own kingdom.

Does not the person who says, “The Son is not equal to the Father,” inflict insult upon the Son of God? For the Apostle says of him: “Though he existed in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” [Phil. 2:6]. Behold: the Son is reckoned equal to the Father. But one who says that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son does not suppose the Son to be equal to the Father. For how shall the Son be equal to the Father unless he possesses glory equally with the Father? It is the Father’s glory that the Spirit of the Father should proceed also from the Son. If this glory is not in the Son, so that the Spirit of the Father may proceed also from the Son, it is evident that the Father’s glory is greater than the Son’s. If the one is greater and the other lesser, it is clear that the Father’s and the Son’s glory are not equal. And if the Father’s and Son’s glory are not equal, neither is their authority equal, nor their Godhead one, nor their majesty.

### 2.

But why is it not granted to the Son of God that his Spirit should proceed from him, when it is confessed that the Spirit is sent and given by him? The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son, the sending of the Son, and the gift of the Son, just as he is the Spirit of the Father, the sending of the Father, and the gift of the Father.

It belongs, then, to the perfection of faith that whoever believes that the Spirit of the Father and Son is sent and given equally by both should also believe that the Spirit of the Father and Son proceeds equally from both. Whoever believes the former and does not believe the latter is less than fully faithful.

### 3.

But perhaps such a person will say: “I fear that the glory of the Father and of the Holy Spirit may suffer diminishment if the Paraclete Spirit is shown to proceed from the Son just as from the Father.” Far be it! For the glory of the Son is the glory of the Father, just as the glory of the Father is the glory of the Son.

The Father never seeks a glory exclusively his own apart from the Son, nor does the Son seek glory apart from the Father, except that by which the one is Father and the other Son; for otherwise it is common, not individual. Thus the Father has an individual glory by which he is Father; indeed, even this is in some manner the Son’s glory, since the Father is more glorified in this: that the latter is his Son.

What we say about the glory of the Father and Son, we also faithfully understand about the glory of the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the glory of the Spirit is the glory of the Son. They have no intervening individual glory between them, except that the one is such that the Spirit proceeds from him, and the other such as proceeds from the Son. Similarly, we speak and think about the glory of the Father and the Holy Spirit. The Father’s glory is the Spirit’s glory, and the Spirit’s glory is the Father’s glory. Yet they have this distinctive relation to one another: the Father is such as the one from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Spirit is such as the one proceeding from the Father.

### 4.

That the purpose of these statements may be seen more fully, let us briefly gather and examine what was said above. It has been shown that the Father has, so to speak, two individual glories—one in relation to the Son and one in relation to the Holy Spirit; and that the Son likewise has two—one toward the Father and one toward the Holy Spirit. The Spirit likewise has two—one toward the Father and one toward the Son.

Therefore whoever says, “The Spirit proceeds from the Father and does not also proceed from the Son,” leaves two glories to the Father, but takes one away from the Son and one from the Holy Spirit. Against such a person the catholic faith plainly stands and contends, affirming that the glory of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is equal.

For equal glory belongs to the Trinity in the Trinity and in the Unity, and to the Trinity in all other things, while in every respect the property of the Father remains intact in the Father, that of the Son in the Son, and that of the Holy Spirit in the Holy Spirit. No one could say anything of the Father by which he might be shown to be begotten or proceeding; nor anything of the Son by which he might be shown to be proceeding or a begetter; nor anything of the Holy Spirit by which he might be shown to be a begetter or begotten.

### 5.

Behold, therefore, most wise and most gentle Emperor: by the things written above, through God’s guidance, we have shown that there is equal glory in the three and individual glory in each, without confusion of generation and procession. More particularly, we have shown that one who says that the Spirit proceeds from the Son does not diminish the Spirit’s glory at all; rather, the one who says that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son takes something away from the glory of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Such a person sins against the Son and the Holy Spirit, and it shall not be forgiven him in the present age or in the age to come, unless, repenting, he believes and confesses that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son.

For it is known that, just as nothing in this Trinity is greater or lesser, so nothing in it must be thought earlier or later. The whole Trinity is equal in honor and coeternal. The Father was not before the Son, nor was the Father or Son before the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the Father is not greater than the Son, nor is the Father or Son greater than the Holy Spirit, since in the Trinity the Father is in every way of equal glory with the Son and Holy Spirit, and the Spirit and Son are in every way of equal glory with the Father. Therefore it cannot be understood otherwise than that the Spirit proceeds from the Father together with the Son.

### 6.

But someone says: “The Gospel states that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, but does not state that he proceeds also from the Son.” I do not wish to pass over this in silence; rather, I wish to investigate it carefully, as one seeking to learn, so that perhaps, with God teaching, I may find beyond dispute what a faithful person ought to think about it.

Truth says, “The Spirit proceeds from the Father.” But the Greek adds, saying, “The Spirit proceeds from the Father alone.” The Latin likewise adds, saying, “The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.” Thus the Greek adds, and the Latin adds, because in the aforesaid Gospel words neither “alone” nor “from the Son” is found. If, then, what the Greek says is true, what the Latin says would be false.

Neither Greek nor Latin differs from the words found in the Gospel; rather, the Greek differs because of the addition which the Latin makes. Therefore, most wise sovereign, ascend gently to the tribunal of your heart. Sitting as judge upon the throne of your mind, judge righteous judgment; and do not, as often happens, favor the Greek as though he were your own possession. Familiarity frequently causes judges to turn aside from truth. Set forth the arguments of both sides, and let there not be with you one weight and another weight, or one measure and another measure; for both are an abomination before God.

Hear then with an unprejudiced heart why the Greek adds “alone,” and why the Latin adds “and from the Son.” Wherever you see an addition supported by reason, rest in reason and join yourself to that addition; but wherever you see an addition lacking reason, follow reason and separate yourself from that addition. I wish to set out the Greek’s argument and the Latin’s argument, so that, when you have examined both, you may be able to judge the truth concerning both additions.

### 7.

The Greek says: “I rightly believe that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and not from another. Since ‘from the Son’ or ‘from another’ was not added there, I do not wish to add ‘from another’; rather, I understand ‘from the Father alone.’ For if Truth understood that he proceeds also from another, she would certainly have said that he is from another.”

In defense of the Latin, I answer: “It is not necessary in this passage to understand that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone merely because the Father’s name alone is placed there. For in many sayings and propositions of Holy Scripture the Father’s name alone is placed, yet the Father is not thereby understood alone, so that the Son is not also appropriately understood there. Thus the Gospel says: ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you’ [Matt. 10:20].

“Behold: Truth, with the Father’s name alone placed, says these two things: ‘the Spirit proceeds from the Father,’ and ‘the Spirit of your Father speaks in you.’ 

“Must we then understand ‘the Spirit of your Father’ and not of the Son, just as the Greek understands the Spirit to proceed from the Father and not from the Son? But if the Spirit of the Father is not the Spirit of the Son, what then is the meaning of the Apostle’s words: ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ [Gal. 4:6], and again, ‘If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him’ [Rom. 8:9]? Does Truth say ‘Spirit of the Father,’ while the Apostle of Truth is not telling the truth when he says ‘Spirit of the Son’ and ‘Spirit of Christ’?

“If both are true in this passage—what Truth says, ‘Spirit of the Father,’ and what Truth does not say, ‘Spirit of the Son’—why should both not likewise be true in the other passage, where Truth says that the Spirit proceeds from the Father?

“I offer two other examples from the Gospel in which the Father’s name alone is placed, though the Father is not understood alone apart from the Son. So that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses, the Lord Jesus said to his disciples in the Gospel: ‘If you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your trespasses’ [Matt. 6:14]. Again, elsewhere he says: ‘Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my brother’ [Matt. 12:50].

“Behold: in these two passages the name of the Father alone is placed. Yet the catholic faith does not allow the Father to be understood alone, apart from the Son, in them. In the matter of the will, the Father’s name alone is placed, yet the Father is never understood alone. The will of the Father is also the will of the Son; and the forgiveness of sins which is from the Father is likewise from the Son. Similarly, when the Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, even if the Father’s name alone is perhaps placed, the faith of Christians does not endure or permit the Father to be understood alone apart from the Son.”

### 8.

This, however, must be understood: sometimes the Father’s name alone is placed and the Father alone is understood, as in the Gospel: “The voice of the Father was heard: ‘This is my Son.’” In this passage the Greek may say that it is the voice of the Father, but not also of the Son; for the voice was heard from the Father, not from the Son.

Nevertheless, he cannot say this merely from the fact that the Father’s name alone is placed there; he can say it from the nature of the voice itself, which pertains to the Father alone: “This is my Son.” Therefore, in every proposition and statement in which the Father’s name alone is placed, one must carefully consider what sort of thing is being proposed. If it is such that it pertains to the Father alone, Greek, Latin, and every Christian ought to understand it of the Father alone. But if what is proposed is such that it pertains simultaneously to the Father and the Son, no Christian ought there to separate the Father from the Son or the Son from the Father; rather, he should understand Father and Son together.

In this proposition and statement that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, both Greek and Latin must consider whether the procession of the Spirit pertains to the Father alone, or simultaneously to the Father and the Son. From the simple statement itself no one can certainly infer whether he ought to understand the Spirit’s procession as from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son. If, then, the Greek wishes us to understand it there as from the Father alone, he must produce some authority or demonstrate some probable argument by which we ought to believe this. If he is unable to provide any authority or testimony about it, it must be conceded that it should not there be understood as from the Father alone. Therefore the reason which we gave above on behalf of the Greek is not reasonable, unless perhaps another reason can be stated.

## Oration of Peter, Bishop of Milan, to the Lord Emperor Alexius Comnenus, Proving That the Holy Spirit Proceeds from the Father and the Son

### 1.

Hear and understand what I say to you, by God’s inspiration, most wise and most merciful, mighty and most gentle Emperor Alexius. Do not look upon me, although I am the last of all God’s servants; rather look upon him whose cause is at issue, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who is Emperor of emperors and greater than all emperors, through whom kings reign and lawgivers decree what is just.

For him and concerning him I, his servant, although unworthy and useless, speak with you, lest you in any way permit any insult to be done to him in your empire, lest he himself exact from you grievous penalties, worthy of emperors, in his own kingdom. How does not one who says that Christ the Lord is not equal to the Father bring insult upon the Son of God? For the Apostle affirms of him: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” [Phil. 2:6]. See how the Son considers himself equal to God the Father.

But whoever says that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son supposes that the Son is not equal to the Father. How, indeed, shall the Son be equal to the Father unless he obtains glory equal with the Father? For it is the Father’s glory that the Spirit of the Father proceed from the Father and the Son. If this is not likewise found in the Son, that the Spirit of the Father should proceed also from the Son, it is plainly evident that the Father’s glory is far greater than the Son’s glory. If, therefore, the Father’s glory is greater and the Son’s glory lesser, it is clear that the Father’s and Son’s glory are not equal. But if the Father and Son do not have equal glory, neither will they have equal power, nor one Godhead, nor one majesty.

### 2.

But for what reason is it not granted to the Son of God that his own Spirit proceed from him, when we confess that the Holy Spirit is sent and given by him? The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son, the Son’s sending, and the Son’s gift, just as that same Spirit is the Father’s sending and the Father’s gift.

It pertains to the perfection of faith that whoever believes that the Holy Spirit is sent and given equally by the Father and Son—by each of the two—should also believe that the Holy Spirit of Father and Son proceeds equally from each of the two. Whoever believes the former but does not believe this is not perfectly faithful.

### 3.

But perhaps he will say: “I fear lest the glory of the Father and the Holy Spirit suffer some loss and diminishment if the Holy Spirit is shown to proceed from the Son just as from the Father.” Far be this! For the glory of the Son is the glory of the Father, just as, conversely, the Father’s glory is the Son’s glory.

The Father never seeks an individual glory separated from the Son, nor does the Son seek for himself a glory separated from the Father, except that sole glory by which he is Father and by which he is Son; otherwise it is common and not individual. Therefore the Father’s individual glory is that by which he is Father. Indeed, even that is in a certain way the Son’s glory, because the Father is more glorified in this respect: that the Son is his Father’s Son.

What we say concerning the glory of the Father and Son, we faithfully hold also concerning the glory of the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit’s glory is also the Son’s glory. They have no individual and private glory between themselves, except that the one is such that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, and the other such that he proceeds from the Son. Similarly, we speak and think concerning the glory of the Father and the Holy Spirit. The Father’s glory is the Holy Spirit’s glory, and the Holy Spirit’s glory is the Father’s glory. Yet they possess this individual distinction between themselves: the Father is such as the one from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, and the Holy Spirit such as the one who proceeds from the Father.

### 4.

That it may be most plainly apparent toward what end we say these things, let us briefly collect and consider what has been said above. We have shown, therefore, that just as the Father has, so to speak, two individual glories, one with respect to the Son and the other with respect to the Holy Spirit, so the Son also has two glories, one with respect to the Father and the other with respect to the Holy Spirit. Likewise the Holy Spirit has two glories, one with respect to the Father and the other with respect to the Son.

Therefore whoever says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and not from the Son leaves two glories to the Father, but takes one away from the Son and likewise from the Holy Spirit. The catholic faith opposes and resists this, as does the common consent of all. For the catholic faith affirms that the glory of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is equal.

For the Trinity has equal glory in Trinity and Unity, and in all other respects, with the property of the Father remaining wholly intact in the Father, the property of the Son in the Son, and the property of the Holy Spirit in the Holy Spirit. Thus no one could affirm anything of the Father by which he might be known to be begotten or proceeding; nor anything of the Son by which he might be shown to be proceeding or begetter; nor anything of the Holy Spirit by which the Holy Spirit might appear to be begotten or begetter.

### 5.

See then, most wise and most merciful Emperor, how by the things said above, with divine aid favoring us, we have shown that the three divine persons have equal glory, and each an individual glory, without any confusion of generation and procession. We have further shown that whoever says the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son brings no loss to the glory of the Holy Spirit; rather, the one who says that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son takes something away from the glory of the Son and Holy Spirit, sins alike against the Son and the Holy Spirit, and shall not be forgiven, either in the present age or the future age [Matt. 12:32], unless, moved by repentance, he believes and confesses that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Let this be manifest to you: just as in this Trinity there is nothing greater or lesser, so in it nothing ought to be understood as earlier or later. The whole Trinity is to be venerated with equal honor and is coeternal. The Father did not precede the Son, nor did the Father or Son precede the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the Father is not greater than the Son, nor is the Father or Son greater than the Holy Spirit. For in the Trinity the Father is altogether equal in glory with the Son and Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit and Son are altogether equal in glory with the Father. Therefore they cannot be understood otherwise than by understanding that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father together with the Son.

### 6.

But someone says: “In the Gospel it is found that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father [John 15:26], yet it is not found that he proceeds from the Son.” I do not wish to pass this over in silence; rather, I wish carefully to investigate, that I may learn whether, with God teaching, I can find without doubt what a faithful person ought to think on this matter.

Truth says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. But the Greek adds further, saying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. The Latin also adds, saying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore the Greek adds, and the Latin adds, since in the aforementioned Gospel words neither “from the Father alone” nor “from the Son” is found. If, therefore, what the Greek says is true, then what the Latin says would undoubtedly be false.

But neither Greek nor Latin differs from the words found in the Gospel; the Greek differs from the Latin because of the addition which the Latin makes. Therefore, most wise king, ascend graciously to the tribunal of your heart. Sitting as judge on the throne of your mind, judge righteous judgment [John 7:24], and do not, as is commonly done, favor the Greeks as your own possession. Familiarity often causes judges to depart from truth. Set before yourself the arguments of both sides; do not have one weight and another weight, or one measure and another measure, for God abominates both [Deut. 25:13–16].

Hear, then, with an unbiased heart why the Greek adds “from the Father alone,” and why the Latin adds that the Holy Spirit proceeds “also from the Son.” Wherever you see an addition placed with reason, there let your mind rest and attach yourself to that addition. But wherever you see an addition alien to reason, adhere to reason and separate yourself from that addition. I wish to bring forward the argument of Greek and Latin, so that after you have weighed both arguments, you may discern the truth concerning both additions.

### 7.

The Greek says: “I rightly believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and not from another; and because ‘from the Son’ or ‘from another’ was not added there—that is, in the Gospel—I do not wish to say ‘from another,’ but understand ‘from the Father alone.’ For if Truth had understood that he also proceeds from another, she would surely have said that he is from another.”

To this I reply in defense of the Latins: “It is not necessary in this passage, for the reason that only the Father’s name is placed in the Gospel, to understand that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. In many places and statements of Holy Scripture only the Father’s name is placed, yet the Father is not understood alone for that reason, so that the Son might not also be fittingly understood there. Thus the Gospel says: ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ [Matt. 10:20].

“See: Truth, with the Father’s name alone placed, says these two things: namely, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, and that it is ‘the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.’ [Yet the same Truth, the Son, says to those same disciples: ‘For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict’ (Luke 21:15). The same Evangelist makes plain in the Acts of the Apostles that by ‘mouth and wisdom’ he understood nothing other than the Spirit which believers would receive, when he says concerning Stephen: ‘They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke’ (Acts 6:10). Therefore the same Spirit of Father and Son is said to be given by the Father and by the Son, and not by the Father alone, although he said, ‘the Spirit of your Father.’]

“Must we then understand the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of your Father and not of the Son, as the Greek understands the Spirit to proceed from the Father and not from the Son? But if the Spirit of the Father is not the Spirit of the Son, what does the Apostle mean when he says, ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ [Gal. 4:6], and again, ‘Unless anyone has the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him’ [Rom. 8:9]? Does Truth say ‘Spirit of the Father,’ and is it not true that the Apostle of Truth says the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son and of Christ?

“But if both are true in this passage—what Truth says, ‘Spirit of the Father,’ and what Truth does not expressly say, ‘Spirit of the Son’—why are not both likewise true in that other passage where Truth says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father?

“Further, I shall offer two other examples from the Gospel in which the Father’s name alone is placed, yet the Father is not understood alone without the Son. So that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses [Deut. 19:15], the Lord Jesus said to his disciples in the Gospel: ‘If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your trespasses’ [Matt. 6:14]. In another place he said: ‘Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother’ [Matt. 12:50].

“See: in these two passages the name of the Father alone is placed. Yet the catholic faith does not allow the Father alone to be understood in them apart from the Son. Although only the Father’s name is placed in connection with the will, the Father is never understood alone: the Father’s will is the Son’s will, and the forgiveness of sins which is from the Father is likewise from the Son. Similarly, when the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, even if the Father’s name alone is perhaps placed, the faith of Christians does not tolerate or permit the Father to be understood alone without the Son.”

[Col. 1016A] **8.** This, however, must be understood: sometimes the Father’s name alone is used, and the Father alone is meant, as in the Gospel: “The voice of the Father was heard: This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3). Here the Greek may say that the voice of the Father, not the voice of the Son, is meant; for the voice was heard from the Father, not from the Son. Yet he cannot say this merely because the Father’s name alone speaks those words, but rather because the voice itself is one that refers to the Father alone: “This is my Son.” Therefore, in every proposition and expression in which the Father’s name alone occurs, careful attention must be paid to the character of what is asserted. For if it is such that it refers to the Father alone, then Greek, Latin, and every Christian alike ought to understand it of the Father alone. But if what is asserted is such that it refers jointly to the Father and the Son, then at that point a Christian ought not to separate the Father from the Son or the Son from the Father, [Col. 1016B] but understand both Father and Son together.

But in the proposition and expression that says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, both Greek and Latin must consider whether the procession of the Holy Spirit is attributed to the Father alone, or jointly to the Father and the Son. From the bare expression itself, no one can plainly determine whether he ought to understand the procession of the Holy Spirit as from the Father alone, or from the Father and the Son. Therefore, if the Greek wishes us to understand it there as from the Father alone, he must bring forward some authority or show some fitting reason by which we ought to believe this. But if he can demonstrate no authority or testimony for this, it is plainly evident that one ought not in that place understand the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father alone. Therefore, the reason which we stated above on the Greek side is not fitting, unless perhaps some other fitting reason is brought forward.

## A.D. 1117. BLESSED ROBERT OF ARBRISSEL, FOUNDER OF THE ORDER OF FONTEVRAULT.

# TWOFOLD LIFE

*(Acta Sanctorum of the Bollandists, February, vol. III, p. 593)*

[Col. 1017]

# PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY

## § I. The principal monastery of the Order of Fontevrault, instituted by Blessed Robert: its name and holiness

[Col. 1017A]

**1.** Fontevrault is a noble monastery of women in France, from which the very celebrated order derived both its origin and its name. The order is divided into monks and nuns, who dwell in separate monasteries; yet it is governed by the abbess of Fontevrault as its general superior. Its name has been variously written by authors. More commonly it is called *Fons Ebraldi* or *Euraldi*, in French *Font Evrauld*. Others call it the Fountain of Everard. William of Newburgh, book I, chapter 15, calls it *Ebraudi*. King John of England, in a charter dated 30 August in the first year of his reign—that is, A.D. 1199—preserved in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 193, calls it now Fontevrault, now Font-Ebrard. Roger Hoveden, in the latter part of his *Annals* under the year 1177, writes *Frunt Everoit*; John Bromton, abbot of Jervaulx, in his *Chronicle* under the same year, writes *Ebrardi* and *Embraldi*; others use other forms.

**2.** The monastery took its name from the spring at the site where it stands. Baronius, vol. XII of the *Annals*, under the year 1117, gives this account from popular report:

> “They relate that Ebrald, once a young man of noble birth but corrupt morals, attended by a great band of cutthroats, formerly infested the neighbouring royal roads with robberies and lay in wait in the woods, of which considerable remnants survive even today. Afterwards a certain Parisian theologian, a man of outstanding learning and a distinguished preacher of the divine word, Robert of Abrissel by name, came there. By his holy exhortations he not only induced that young man to change his conduct and life, but also persuaded many people of every class to despise the vanity of the world and embrace the rules of a stricter life. For their habitation he founded separate monasteries within the same enclosure, building distinct establishments for men, virgins, the sick, and other women; and he set an abbess over the whole congregation,” etc.

These are Baronius’s words, copied word for word, though without citing him, by Miraeus, [Col. 1018A] book II of *The Origins of Monasticism*, chapter 10. Guerrois narrates the same matter at much greater length in his commentary on the holiness of the people of Troyes, under the year 1106, no. 8 and following, and affirms it to be true history.

But who can accept it when Baldric, bishop of Dol—formerly abbot of the monastery of Bourgueil, only a few leagues from Fontevrault, and moreover a contemporary of Blessed Robert—testifies to the contrary? In no. 16 he writes:
