> “The place was uncultivated and desolate, overgrown with thorns and brambles, and from ancient times called the Fountain of Eurald; it was remote from human habitation, and lay about two miles from the cell of Candes, adjoining the diocese of Poitiers.”

When Blessed Robert came there, the place had already from ancient times been called the Fountain of Eurald. It therefore did not take its name from Eurald, whom Robert supposedly converted there while he was still a young man.

**3.** I would not, nevertheless, deny that in former times there may perhaps have been dens of robbers there amid thick woods. For local tradition commonly reports that when St Martin, bishop of Tours, came to Candes, a village in his diocese, he asked what was that place thick with trees which he saw in the distance. When he heard that it was a wooded tract notorious for plundering and robbery, he replied that one day it would be made illustrious by holy prayers and the religious worship of God; and that this finally came to pass seven hundred years later. Yet that very account is confirmed by no ancient testimony.

**4.** The village of Candes—now a town, which the French call *Candes*—lies at the farthest boundary of the diocese of Tours, on the river Vienne, which not far from there joins the Loire. Fontevrault is two miles from it, as Baldric writes, or a short French league; it is three leagues from the town of Saumur on the Loire. Francis Ranchin writes that Bourgueil and Fontevrault are the principal abbeys of the province of Anjou. But, when speaking of Poitou, he says that Fontevrault lies on the borders of Touraine and Anjou, but belongs to the diocese of Poitiers. Gervase, monk of Canterbury, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1177, calls Fontevrault a monastery of [Col. 1019A] Anjou. John Bromton likewise, under the same year, says: “The king sent into Anjou, to Fontebrard, for a community of holy nuns.” But later, under the year 1189, he says: “Richard, count of Poitiers, proceeded with the body of his father Henry II, king of England, as far as Font-Embrald in Normandy.” Whether he located that monastery in Normandy because Normandy was the principal region among the French dominions possessed by the kings of England, or through a lapse of memory, it is needless to ask.

Miraeus writes in the passage already cited:

> “At Fontevrault, within the compass of what is as it were a single town, there are four monasteries: three of nuns, numbering about two hundred, and one of monks, numbering about forty, who have their own prior.”

And a little later:

> “The high altar of the monks’ monastery of Fontevrault is situated on the boundary of the dioceses of Poitiers, Tours, and Angers.”

He testifies that he received these and other facts “in the year 1017 from the Reverend Father William Richer, abbot of St Vincent at Le Mans, formerly visitor of Fontevrault.”

**5.** This is the head of that most religious order; this is the seat of the abbess who presides over it all. For the founder wished—as Baronius notes in the passage cited above, and as will appear more clearly below—that the abbess “should possess supreme authority over both men and women, ordaining that men should obey virgins or women after the example of St John the Evangelist, and that these in turn, following the example of the Blessed Virgin, should embrace religious men as sons. Finally, he prescribed separate statutes and constitutions for each sex.” A little later Baronius says that the order was approved by authentic bulls of many popes, who teach “that it derived the origin and rationale of its institution from those words of Christ, ‘Behold your son; behold your mother.’”

Various charters of supreme pontiffs have recently been published, in which they either praised the holiness of the founder or fortified the congregation established by him with the privilege of apostolic authority. Thus Paschal II, in a charter dated the seventh day before the Kalends of May, indiction XIII, A.D. 1106, and likewise in another dated on the Nones of April, A.D. 1113, addressed “To the beloved sisters in Christ, the holy nuns serving almighty God in the monastery of Fontevrault,” declares that he is “stirred to greater fervour by their religious pursuits,” etc.

**6.** Calixtus II, in a charter issued at Tours, at Marmoutier, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, indiction XIII, A.D. 1119, says:

> “To our beloved daughter Petronilla, abbess of the monastery of St Mary of Fontevrault, and to those who shall regularly succeed her in the same government for ever. As we were passing through the diocese of Poitiers in the service of the Church, at the request of our venerable brother William, bishop of Poitiers, we turned aside to the monastery of Blessed Mary of Fontevrault. There, recognizing through the mercy of almighty God that the discipline of the monastic order flourished, we decreed to foster under the protection of Blessed Peter the place itself and all that belongs to it. Accordingly, with our own hands, as though they were the hands of Blessed Peter, we dedicated an oratory in honour [Col. 1020A] of the most blessed and most glorious Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary.”

The same pope says in another bull:

> “At the monastery of Blessed Mary of Fontevrault, the discipline of monastic religion, as we ourselves have seen while present, endures through the grace of almighty God; therefore religious men who fear the Lord and are near it love the place itself.”

Calixtus’s predecessor Gelasius II likewise says: “There, through the grace of almighty God, the greatest observance of religion has now been maintained for a long time.” Later Innocent II says: “How tested and renowned is the religious life of the monastery of Fontevrault, and how much good proceeds from it through the cooperation of God’s grace,” etc. Lucius II, who held the see in 1144, says, addressing Abbess Petronilla: “Indeed, because of the ampler distinction of religious life which by God’s grace is spread far and wide from your place,” etc. Addressing the nuns themselves, the same pontiff says: “Because we have great confidence in you, we beseech your charity through almighty God to offer special prayers to the Lord for me, and to take care that they be offered throughout all the communities of your order.”

**7.** Suger, abbot of St Denis, in a letter to Pope Eugenius III, published from manuscripts by our own Jacques Sirmond in the notes on the letters of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, writes among other things in praise of the nuns of Fontevrault:

> “May it please Your Excellency to rescue them from these troubles”—which, I suppose, Gilbert of La Porrée, bishop of Poitiers, was causing them—“and, that they may serve God in peace, in the abundance of your mercy provide for them, cherish and protect them under the protection of the God of heaven and by your apostolic authority. For this is a place of such great religious life that, when we were studying in the schools in those regions, we saw it newly begun; and by God’s will we have heard, and rejoice, that it has now increased to almost four or five thousand nuns.”

Suger died early in A.D. 1152, in the seventy-ninth year of his life, as Claude Robert relates.

**8.** Nearly two years before Suger, the aforementioned abbot of St Denis near Paris—namely in 1150—“on the eighth day before the Kalends of May,” as the necrology of Fontevrault says, “departed from the world Lady Petronilla, of pious memory, a venerable nun, our incomparable and irreparable mother, first appointed abbess by our lord Master Robert.”

Blessed Robert himself, as Baronius writes in the passage cited, and Miraeus after him, “had ordained that, when the abbess whom he had appointed should close her days, the woman whom the religious sisters themselves chose by their votes should succeed her. This was always observed by them as long as the practice of election remained in monasteries. Moreover, both while the power of election remained and after abbesses began to be appointed by pontifical authority, they always obtained excellent and memorable abbesses, more distinguished by integrity and holiness of life than by birth, although most were daughters of kings and princes, or at least of very noble knights.” I wonder whence Baronius derived this; why should Miraeus not dare to follow so weighty an authority? We had no evidence by which either to confirm or refute the opinion of both. Afterwards, when these pages had already been sent to press, I learned that the right of electing the abbess still belongs to the nuns of the Greater Monastery—which alone has an abbess, the other monasteries having prioresses—but not to the monks.

**9.** From that time the holiness of this congregation was widely celebrated. Nuns were summoned thence even into Spain and England, to restore relaxed discipline in certain old monasteries of other orders or to found new ones. Certainly, in 1177, they were called into England and given the monastery of Amesbury in Wiltshire, formerly founded by Ælfthryth, stepmother and murderer of St Edward, king and martyr; this is related in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 191, from Roger Hoveden. These are Hoveden’s words under that year in the latter part of his *Annals*:

> “In the same year King Henry II, having expelled the nuns from the abbey of Amesbury because of their incontinence, and distributed them among other religious houses under stricter custody, gave the abbey of Amesbury itself to the abbess and house of Frunt Everoit”—read Fontevrault—“to possess in perpetuity. And when a community of nuns had been sent from Frunt Everoit, Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, introduced them into the abbey of Amesbury on the second day before the Kalends of June, a Sunday,” etc.

The same is narrated in the *Chronicle* of John Bromton, and it is said that the abbess was “deposed by order of Pope Alexander III; and all the nuns there who would not abandon their error and the shamefulness of their life, and would not observe the order of Fontebrard, were scattered from that house. After they had been thus scattered, the king sent into Anjou to Fontebrard for a community of holy nuns,” etc. Here you see the nuns of Fontevrault called “holy nuns.” Gervase of Canterbury also treats of this Amesbury colony in his *Chronicle*.

**10.** The same Bromton calls it “the famous and noble monastery of Fontebrard.” William of Newburgh, book I, chapter 15, calls it “that most famous monastery of women at Fontevrault”; and in book III, chapter 25, “a famous and noble monastery,” and later “a monastery illustrious under the title of most celebrated religious life.” William of Tyre, book XIV, chapter 1, speaking of Matilda—whom he himself calls Mahald—the second abbess of Fontevrault after Petronilla, writes:

> “She had been betrothed to the son of Henry, king of the English, the first of that name. But before they came together, her bridegroom, sailing to England, suffered shipwreck and was drowned in the sea. His betrothed, however, having vowed perpetual celibacy, spent her life permanently as a nun in a highly religious convent of young women at Fontevrault.”

James of Vitry, a suffragan of William of Tyre and afterwards cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, writes in chapter 20 of his *Western History*, concerning Black Monks:

> “We have said these things, however, with due peace and reverence toward certain holy and venerable communities of this order, which still persevere in the purpose of honourable and praiseworthy conduct and in the strictness of religion. Such are the Cluniacs at their head and in certain members not differing from the head; likewise those at St Martin of the Fields in the city of Paris; moreover, the religious monks of Canterbury in England; those of Affligem in Brabant; the Black Nuns of Fontevrault; and certain other communities of Black Monks devoted to God. He who supplies them patience and perseverance knows their charity and humility, their constant labours and almost unbearable burdens, so that, while others fail on the way, they may hasten to the prize set before them and attain their desired end.”

**11.** William of Malmesbury, somewhat older than both, in book V of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, both describes the origin of Fontevrault and extols its holiness:

> “Contemporaries and companions in religion of this Peter [bishop of Poitiers] were Robert of Arbrissel and Bernard, abbot of Tiron. The former was the most famous and most copious of all preachers of his age. His eloquence flourished not with froth but with honey to such a degree that, as men zealously heaped up wealth, he built that excellent monastery of nuns at Fontevrault, in which, after the whole pleasure of the world has been cut off, a multitude of women devoted to God—greater than anywhere else—burns with zeal in God’s service. For, besides renouncing every other enticement, how small a matter is this: that, under a rule of perpetual silence established by their master, they speak nowhere except in chapter, since, once silence has been relaxed, women are prone to mutter trivialities?”

**12.** Yet John Picard of Beauvais, a canon regular of St Victor at Paris, observes in his notes on chapter 15 of book I of Newburgh’s *History* that “these regular observances, otherwise rather severe, were mitigated by the authority of the supreme pontiff about the year 1450. For Mary of Brittany, at once a most devout and a most noble virgin, superior of Fontevrault, had arranged, with the help and counsel of prudent men, that certain chapters should be selected from the Rule of St Benedict and the ordinances of Robert the founder and observed more carefully in all the nunneries of her order; and that matters which seemed somewhat obscure should be described more plainly. Of the things thought harsher, however—namely silence, which prohibited conversation everywhere except in chapter—it was moderated so that speaking might be permitted after the prayers called Prime, and then after the signal for work had been given.”

## § II. The homeland and life-history of Blessed Robert; the annual commemoration and the designation of him as Blessed and Saint

**13.** Blessed Robert was therefore founder of this most celebrated monastery and order. Authors differ over his surname, as André Duchesne notes in letter 17 of book II of Peter the Venerable; as our Honoré Nicquet does in book II, chapter 3, of the *History of Fontevrault*; and as Jean-Baptiste Souchet does in his notes on chapter 11 of the *Life of Blessed Bernard of Tiron*. Thus Geoffrey, in the said *Life of Blessed Bernard*, calls him *de Arbrissello*, *Arbrissellensis*, and, in chapter 23—if the text is not corrupt—*Orbreselensis*. He is called *de Abrezello* in an inscription cited by Souchet, and *de Abrincello* in a manuscript from Ronceray cited by the same author; *de Herbressello* by Peter, bishop of Poitiers, in a charter issued in 1106; *de Arbusculo* by Newburgh; *de Arbrussello* in a manuscript codex from Le Mans containing works of Geoffrey of Vendôme; *de Brussello* by Peter the Venerable; *de Bruxelles* by Jean Bouchet; *de Bruxello* by John Hirsau, cited by Souchet; *de Arborecello* in certain public records cited by Guillaume Catel; *de Arbricellis* in the Chronicle of St Albin of Angers; *de Arbricel* and *Arbrisel* in charters of Ronceray; *de Arbeisel* by Malmesbury; *d’Abruissel* by Nicquet. Souchet judges *de Abrissello* more correct; we retain *de Arbrissello*, the most widespread form among writers.

**14.** The name was derived from his birthplace, a small village seven leagues from the city of Rennes in Armorican Brittany, then called Arbrissel, as Baldric, bishop of Dol in the same Brittany, testifies; it is now commonly called Arbesec. But Guerrois, in his *Commentaries on the Holiness of Troyes*, under the year 1106, no. 7, affirms that Robert was born in the territory of Troyes, two miles from Troyes, in a village called l’Aubrussel. He cites no author attributing that homeland to him and offers no argument to establish it beyond the sole similarity of the name. Baldric, who both knew Robert, governed the monastery of Bourgueil near Fontevrault, and later became bishop of Dol in Brittany, says in chapter 1, no. 7, of the *Life* that Robert “was a native of Lesser Brittany, originating from the district of Rennes, an inhabitant and resident of the village commonly called Arbrissel.” In no. 8, Sylvester, bishop of Rennes, addresses the same Robert, summoned to him from Paris:

> “You see, dearest brother, how the holy Church of Rennes, your mother, wavers without governance.”

For how could the Church of Rennes have been called his mother if he had been born in the diocese of Troyes and had hitherto lived only in his homeland and at Paris?

**15.** Guerrois had not seen the twofold *Life* of Blessed Robert which we here provide: one, as stated, written by Baldric; the other by a religious of Fontevrault and disciple of the same holy man, generally thought to have been Andrew, mentioned in chapter 6, no. 36, of that very *Life*. He seems to be mentioned thus in an old necrology: “On the third day before the Ides of August died Andrew, priest and chaplain of Master Robert.” Both lives were first published from Fontevrault manuscripts by Michel Cosnier, parish priest of that town. Having afterwards investigated other records of the chief monastery, he sent us quite a few materials lacking from his first edition. After Cosnier’s death, both lives were more elegantly published at La Flèche in 1647, with a lucid French paraphrase printed opposite, prepared by Father Jean-Baptiste Chevalier, priest of our Society.

Our Honoré Nicquet wrote the history of Fontevrault in French with the greatest care, in four books. In the first he recounted the deeds of Blessed Robert; in the second, his holiness; in the third, the institutions of the order; and in the fourth, he briefly narrated the acts of all the abbesses. The same writer has ready for the press a second volume, treating of all the priories of the order: those that existed or still exist in Spain, including wealthy ones, in Great Britain, and in France, flourishing in religious discipline and in great number. In this volume, divided into three books, he describes the lives of virgins distinguished by learning, birth, and virtue. Perhaps he will add a third volume if life and strength do not fail him in his seventies, already burdened with extensive and other work.

[Col. 1024B]

**16.** The woman who now governs that most holy order with equal renown for devotion and prudence, the thirty-first after Petronilla, Blessed Robert’s disciple, is Jeanne-Baptiste de Bourbon, daughter of Henry IV the Great, king of France. While she applies herself with the greatest zeal to preserving the spirit of religious observance and the dignity of religious exercise still flourishing in the order, she especially endeavours by every means possible to increase the honour of its most holy founder Robert. For this reason she arranged that the two *Lives* I have mentioned, published at La Flèche in 1641 and 1647, should be sent to us together with other small books, composed especially by our Honoré Nicquet. One of these contains “Testimonies of supreme pontiffs, cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, bishops, princes, and illustrious writers concerning the holiness of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel”; the other is entitled *The Glory of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, Founder of the Order of Fontevrault; or, a Summary of His Life, Virtues, and Eulogies*.

Finally, because of the great kindness with which she regards our very small Society, she deigned to commend to us by letter that, in our vast work on the Acts of the Saints, we should give a place also to the *Life* of Blessed Robert. We had already freely decided to do this, as may be seen from what was said on 7 January concerning Blessed Vitalis of Savigny, although at that time we had not yet obtained any *Life* of Blessed Robert, but only certain praises of him from various writers. We have excerpted not a few matters from these two books and from Nicquet’s history to illustrate the memory of the holy man.

**17.** Robert has not yet been entered among the heavenly citizens by a ruling of the supreme pontiff in such a way that an ecclesiastical Office may be recited or the sacrifice of the Mass offered for him. Yet the same Abbess Jeanne-Baptiste is striving with all her resources to obtain this. For several years the Most Serene Queen of Great Britain has also pressed for public ecclesiastical veneration to be granted to Blessed Robert. She wrote frequently to the pope about the matter and, through her ambassador, presented a petition in 1645. From it the following is quoted in the cited *Glory of Blessed Robert*, so that anyone may understand what finally moved her to seek for Robert the honour due to the saints:

> “In the great tumult of Great Britain, by which nearly the entire kingdom is now being turned upside down [lacuna], it will be to me both a remedy and the most immediate relief of evils if I gain for myself the grace and favour of some eminent servant of God by securing honour for him on earth, so that he may be an advocate in heaven before God for the happy outcome of English affairs. Therefore I humbly beg Your Holiness to permit the Order of Fontevrault to recite the Office and celebrate Mass for the Venerable Father Robert, founder of that order. He was formerly especially dear to, and indeed counsellor of, Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou, Tours, and Le Mans, afterwards king of Jerusalem, one of the ancestors of my most serene husband, the king of Great Britain. Other ancestors of his also—Henry II and Richard I, kings of England—as well as certain English queens, Eleanor and Elizabeth, and many princesses, most devoutly desired to be buried in the same church in which the relics of the venerable servant of God lie; and they propagated the order founded by him through various provinces of the English realm.”

**18.** Thus far from the petition of the Most Serene Queen. The Most Christian King also, as we have learned, wrote to Pope Innocent X on the same matter and instructed his ambassador to press the case. “The most excellent and most reverend Lady Jeanne-Baptiste de Bourbon, abbess of the Greater Monastery and head of the entire Order of Fontevrault, also presses it—as we have already indicated, and as is reported in the same words in the cited *Glory*. The whole order presses it, together with the chapter of canons at Candes of St Martin and other neighbouring chapters: namely, that it may be permitted, by the assent and authority of the Apostolic See, to venerate as a saint that same Robert, who has consistently been distinguished by the title of Saint up to the present; who is most renowned for holiness of life and great merits toward the holy Church; eminent in apostolic eloquence and constancy; most devoted to the Holy Roman See and a staunch defender of apostolic authority; a perpetual hammer of heretics; most eager for martyrdom; one who suffered very much at the hands of the impious for the cause of piety; noble through the commendation of supreme pontiffs, bishops, and illustrious writers; an unconquered champion of every justice and holiness; father of so many saints; one who gained for God so many thousands of people of both sexes; the surest refuge of the wretched of every kind; [Col. 1023D] whose holiness heaven proclaims by frequent miracles, and earth attests by daily prayers, vows, and offerings.”

**19.** These praises, here heaped together, will be established partly by evidence already given, partly in their respective places in the *Life*, and partly here from the same booklet on his *Glory*. Certainly, some five hundred and thirty-seven years ago, Bishop Baldric, a writer endowed with remarkable wisdom, already called him Blessed. Thus in chapter 1, no. 7: “Blessed Robert, of whom we have decided to speak, was an heir and son of the Christian profession.” And in no. 24: “The miracles which Blessed Robert performed are evident.” Finally, in no. 25: “As years passed and passed, Blessed Robert perceived by certain signs that his end was approaching.”

**20.** The frequently cited *Glory*, p. 33, shows that from all remembered time Robert has customarily received not only the title Blessed but also Saint:

> “In the ancient litany-supplications of the ecclesiastical order there is, after the invocation of St Benedict, this invocation of Blessed Father Robert: ‘St Robert, good master, pray for us.’ Moreover, the spring which formerly was called Fontevrault is now called simply the Fountain of St Robert, in honour of Blessed Robert, who drank from that spring and founded in the valley in which it rises the monastery that is the head of the order. So firmly has the designation ‘saint’ adhered to the servant of God that it is celebrated by the common speech of peoples.”

**21.** Earlier, on p. 13, the following had been reported:

> “Leodegar, archbishop of Bourges, accompanied the body, carried with great ceremony to the monastery of Fontevrault. Fulk, count of Anjou, Ralph, archbishop of Tours, Reginald, bishop of Angers, many abbots, innumerable priests, and an infinite multitude of people went out to meet the sacred relics. His heart was retained at Orsan and honourably enclosed in a pyramid-shaped monument. The nearest altar is called the Altar of the Holy Heart.”

And on p. 29 it is said that Leodegar, archbishop of Bourges, wished to be buried “at Orsan, where the holy heart of Blessed Father Robert is venerated with great reverence by the people.” Therefore we do not fear that anyone will censure us for freely adorning him with the title Blessed, since it was bestowed on him more than five hundred years ago by so weighty a bishop, and since from time immemorial he has been called Saint in the united devotion of the people, even in sacred litanies.

**22.** Saussay records the annual commemoration of Blessed Robert in the supplement to the *Gallican Martyrology*, p. 1216; and our own Jacques Rinaldi, in *The Lilies of Holy France*, says it ought to be entered on 30 August. Both celebrate him with a distinguished eulogy. Our Jacques Sirmond, in his notes on the letters of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, p. 84, identifies Robert’s true heavenly birthday from the Chronicle of St Albin, where these words occur:

> “In the year 1116 Robert of Arbrissel died, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March. He was the founder of the monastery of Fontevrault.”

Charles Saussay asserts the same in book IX, no. 12, of his *History of Orléans*. Nicquet likewise informed us of it by letter. For whereas he had previously thought that Robert died on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, he undertook to correct this in book I, chapter 35, of his *History*. It is sufficiently certain, from the agreement of the whole order, that he died in the year of Christ 1117, which under the French reckoning of that age was called 1116, since the year began with the celebration of Easter—a practice only corrected under King Charles IX. But on the feast of St Matthias, the following is read the next day in the martyrology of the Order of Fontevrault:

> “On the same day, in the territory of Bourges, at Orsan, occurred the glorious falling asleep of the reverend Lord Robert of Arbrissel, doctor of theology, venerable priest, and our most beloved Father. He was a most Christian man, a splendid morning-star of the holy Church, and in holy preaching in some manner another Paul. He was born in the diocese of Rennes, in the province of Brittany; thoroughly filled from the fountain of heavenly doctrine and commendably grounded in religion. From its first foundation he was the author of Fontevrault; he founded, built, and multiplied its church and very many cells belonging to that church; and in those places, by God’s inspiration, he faithfully gathered men and women together to serve almighty God. While still living, he fully instructed them, by the examples and rules of the holy Fathers and by all sound doctrine, in word and example. This strong athlete and most faithful steward of the word of the Lord, while according to his custom he was travelling among foreign peoples for the sake of holy preaching, at the aforesaid place—called Orsan—which he himself had built with God’s favour and which is eighteen miles, that is twelve leagues, from the city of Bourges, was summoned by God. An old man and full of days, he entered upon the way of all flesh; while heaven rejoiced and earth mourned, resting in a glorious end, he returned his body to the earth and his spirit to heaven, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1117.”

## § III. The holiness of Blessed Robert celebrated by the testimonies of eminent men; his tomb

**23.** I think it will be worthwhile here to collect briefly from both booklets already cited the praises by which outstanding writers and other illustrious men, especially pontiffs, have adorned Robert’s virtues and holiness. Pope Urban II appointed him an apostolic preacher: “For he understood,” as Baldric relates in the *Life*, “that the Holy Spirit had opened his mouth.” Paschal II called him, while still living, “a man of great religious devotion” and “a venerable man.” Calixtus II, after his death, called him “of good memory” and “of venerable memory”; Honorius II, “of happy remembrance”; Lucius II, “a priest of good memory and proven religious life”; and delegates of Sixtus IV, “a Father worthy of remembrance.”

24. Bishop Baldric, who, as we said in the preceding section, several times called Blessed Robert simply “blessed,” elsewhere names him “a holy and righteous man.” Elsewhere he writes: “May the Holy Spirit, therefore, assist my obedience, and may the holiness of Lord Robert support me.” Then: “Indeed, I would call him the dwelling-place [Col. 1027D] of Jesus Christ and the instrument of the Holy Spirit, the spokesman and vicar of the Most High, himself anointed with His words.” And later: “Lord Robert, a fountain of preaching, a fountain of religious life, a singular sower of the word, an illustrious and outstanding teacher, admirable in word and deed, a man to be exalted and imitated.” These and other things, however, may be read below in Baldric himself.

Peter II, bishop of Poitiers, in a document written at Poitiers in 1106, says: “A certain apostolic man, named Robert of Arbrissel, vigilantly devoted to the word of divine preaching and, by the thunderclap of holy exhortation, recalling many men as well as women from worldly luxury, founded in our diocese a church in honour of Saint Mary the Virgin, in a place called Fontevraud. [Col. 1028A] Aremburgis, wife of Wido son of Osmund, and her daughter Rivaria gave this place to him for the building of the aforesaid church.” In another document the same Peter calls him “a religious man, devoted to the word of holy preaching”; and elsewhere, “a man of great religious devotion and good repute.” Girard, bishop of Angoulême—a very great man, had he not later disgraced himself by supporting the schism of Anacletus—calls him “a man of good memory and great holiness.”

25. Peter Abelard, abbot, calls him “an outstanding herald of Christ.” The records of the abbey of Saint Mary of La Roë call him “a man of great authority and boundless religious devotion.” Fulk, count of Anjou: “a most illustrious man of great religious devotion and uprightness.” The younger Fulk, likewise count [Col. 1028B] of the Angevins: “a most religious man, whose admirable teaching shines throughout the whole Church in its eloquence, through the word of holy preaching and the thunderclap of holy exhortation.” Countess Aremburgis, Fulk’s wife: “a man of great religious devotion, a discerning dispenser of the word of evangelical preaching.” Finally, others call him “a most holy man.”

Andrew begins the Life, which we shall give below, thus: “May the grace of the Holy Spirit be present with me through the interceding merits of him of whom I am about to speak.” Later he calls him “the lamp of hermits, a man praiseworthy in every mouth.” The abbots whom Blessed Robert consulted when the election of the first abbess was under discussion said: “Dearest Father, your counsel ought rather to be followed in this matter, especially since we know for certain that, [Col. 1028C] among the mortals of our age, your counsel is powerful: for God has given you to the world as a counsellor of souls.”

26. If anyone seeks testimonies of more recent writers concerning this same holy man, he has above, § I, no. 2, that of the great cardinal Caesar Baronius. In the epitome of his *Annals*, under the year 1117, Henry Spondanus, bishop of Pamiers in France, calls Blessed Robert “a man of exceptional learning and probity.” Antony Yepes, volume VII of the *Benedictine History*, calls him “a pious and holy man.” Claude Robert, in the *Gallia Christiana*, discussing the abbey of Saint Mary of La Roë, calls him “a man of great authority and boundless religious devotion.” Andrew Saussay and James Rinaldi, previously cited, likewise composed an outstanding encomium of him, calling him simply “Blessed Robert.”

27. Léger, archbishop of Bourges, collected or surpassed most of the praises of others. As it is said in the *Glory of Blessed Robert*, “when he could not retain intact in his diocese, where he had died, the venerable servant of God’s relics, lest the diocese of Bourges be wholly deprived of so great a treasure, he at last obtained at least the heart from Petronilla, the first abbess, who was present; and he himself accompanied the dead man’s body as far as the greater monastery of Fontevraud.” [Col. 1028D] There he honoured him with a funeral oration, published in French by Fr. Ivo Magister. The following passages from it have been rendered in Latin:

“The Lord preserves the bodies of His saints: this is attested by their sacred relics. The body of your Father also bears witness: although it was treated with no spices, it has emitted no foul odour to this day, even though it remained lifeless for many days. This is a most certain proof of his outstanding holiness, which he cultivated only by abstinence from worldly pleasures, fervour of spirit, and an austere manner of life,” etc.

28. “God had provided this age with the most devoted Father and teacher Robert, so that, as long as he lived, he might be a lamp not hidden under a bushel, illuminating the minds of sinners with the rays of the Sun of righteousness after driving away the darkness of wickedness. For who among you does not know that outstanding cultivator of the wilderness, who was indeed to some an aroma of life unto life, but to others a sharp arrow of the mighty? [Col. 1029B] I venture to say that this reverend Father lacked neither Joseph’s patience, Jeremiah’s steadfastness, Phinehas’s zeal, nor Tobit’s charity. He resembled David when he passed through the wilderness and made his way to a kingdom through a thousand perils of life. He shared Daniel’s counsel and prudence, and possessed Samuel’s equity. Following the Lord’s Forerunner, he led the life of an anchorite; he relieved hunger with herbs and thirst only with cold water, and covered his body with haircloth. I say that he shared in Paul’s eloquence,” etc. “He was a foot to the lame, an eye to the blind, consolation to the afflicted, father of orphans, spouse of holy widows, guardian and paranymph of virgins, refuge of the wretched, expeller of every vice, promoter of virtues, reconciler of the discordant,” etc. This last quality is noted as especially remarkable in Blessed Robert: that each person has his own gift from God, who distributes to every individual as He wills.

29. These and other things were said by that archbishop at the funeral of Blessed Robert. His tomb, as Baldric calls it, stood before the high altar, supported by four columns; on the upper stone his image was carved. He wore priestly dress, held a pastoral staff, his hands were covered with gloves, and a ring was placed upon his finger. That tomb was held in such veneration that the nuns once made religious vows before it.

In 1623 a new and far more magnificent altar was erected, consecrated on 8 October by Philip Cospéan, then bishop of Nantes. He enclosed in it relics of the Virgin Mother of God and of Saint John [Col. 1029D] the Evangelist—to whose honour it was especially dedicated—as well as some relics of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Louis the King. Because of the construction of this altar, Blessed Robert’s tomb had to be moved somewhat farther away and placed beneath another new, skilfully wrought mausoleum. At its corners were various sayings from Holy Scripture, inscribed in gold letters upon black marble. His image, in white marble and wearing priestly vestments, lay upon a likewise marble tomb.

When the former tomb was opened, several bones were found whole. They were placed in a leaden casket, together with a considerable quantity of dust into which the remaining limbs had dissolved, as well as dust found in the tomb of Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

[Col. 1030A]

30. The following inscription was added to that new tomb:

“Robert of Arbrissel, once venerable, a man exceedingly devout and aflame with zeal for souls, by the divine eloquence in which he was most powerful, led many mortals of both sexes—who followed him into desert places—to the service of God and contempt for the world. On that occasion he was the first to establish the Order of Fontevraud, and he saw to the construction of various dwellings, especially for the devout female sex. He wished this monastery to be head of them all. In it he placed an abbess over not only virgins and women consecrated to God, but also religious men who follow this way of life—an institution approved by the holy apostolic see from its beginning to the present time and enlarged by various privileges and royal benefactions. He died in the year 1117. To cover his bones and sacred ashes, Louise de Bourbon, superior of this monastery and thus of the whole order, caused this mausoleum, adorned with a new structure, to be completed in the name of the entire order, as for its most excellent parent, in the year 1623.” [Col. 1030B]

§ IV. Blessed Robert’s first companions in the eremitical and apostolic life

31. Of Robert’s encomia assembled in § II, no. 18, one point remains: to show that his holiness was confirmed from heaven by miracles. But first there must be appended a kind of supplement concerning deeds performed by him which both writers of his Life omitted, though they are handed down by ancient authors.

Concerning Blessed Robert’s first companions and helpers when he undertook apostolic labours, William of Newburgh—who testifies that he was born in 1135—writes in book I, chapter 15, of *The Affairs of England*, already cited:

“In the lands beyond the sea, as I have heard from my elders, three memorable men flourished at one time: Robert, surnamed of Arbrissel, Bernard, and Vitalis. These men, not without distinguished learning and fervent in spirit, travelled through castles and villages; and, sowing according to Isaiah upon all waters, they gathered abundant fruits from the conversion of many. By a pious agreement among themselves, it was established that Robert should indeed have charge of the women converted by their common labour to better things, while Bernard and Vitalis should provide more particularly for the men. Robert accordingly built and formed by regular discipline that most famous monastery for women [Col. 1030D] at Fontevraud. Bernard at Tiron, and Vitalis at Savigny, having established monks under a rule, each distinguished his own followers from the others by certain distinctive regulations. And when religious offshoots of servants and handmaids of God sprang up in different provinces from these three roots, some Savignian monks founded our Bellelande.”

This should be understood to mean that, while Bernard and Vitalis established congregations of men, Robert also gathered women, and indeed with special concern, since he subjected men—and even himself—to their spiritual ministry. Hence women, perhaps even those converted by those other two, flocked especially to him.

32. The manner in which friendship was formed among those holy men is related by the contemporary author Geoffrey Grossus in chapter 11 of the *Life of Blessed Bernard Pontivensis*, first abbot of Tiron. For when Bernard administered the monastery of Saint-Savin with the title of prior, after Abbot Gervasius had gone abroad and had already died, “having learned,” as that writer says, “the intention of the monks, who were planning to make him their abbot, he secretly departed from them, intending to seek what he had desired for many years: namely, the pursuit of the anchoritic life and the earning of his livelihood by the labour of his hands.

“Not far from the monastery of Saint-Savin there lived a venerable and religious hermit, Peter by name, of Les Étoiles, who later became the founder of the monastery called Fontaine-Gombaud. Bernard turned aside to him, because he was already known to him and on familiar terms with him, and disclosed the reason for his arrival. Peter received him with great eagerness of spirit; but because he was in the neighbourhood of the monks who were striving to make Bernard their abbot against his will, he could not keep him with himself long, though he greatly wished to do so.

“Bernard, burning both with desire for the poverty and solitude he now longed for and with intense fear that, unless he departed more quickly, he would be compelled—at the urging of his abbot or bishop—to become an abbot and be entangled in the cares of pastoral responsibility, earnestly begged Peter to remove him swiftly and secretly from there and lead him to unknown solitudes in the remotest region. Peter therefore yielded to his petitioner’s prayers, became his guide, and accomplished what he sought.

“Now on the border of the regions of Le Mans and Brittany there were vast wildernesses, which at that time, like another Egypt, flourished with a multitude of hermits dwelling in separate cells—holy men renowned for the excellence of their religious life. Among them the leaders and masters were Robert of Arbrissel, Vitalis of Mortain, and also Ralph of La Fustaye, who later became founders of many great congregations. By Peter, who had previously known them, divine providence took care to add this fourth man to them, so that, when the fourth was joined to the three, there might be a firm fourfold square, destined later to support great and wide-ranging structures.” [Col. 1031D]

33. He continues in chapter 12: “Peter of Les Étoiles, after completing a journey of many days, came to Lord Vitalis, one of those mentioned above, whom we have already said to have been leaders and masters of hermits.” So he writes.

“Ralph—who is here joined with those three holy hermits—was also, like Blessed Robert, a director of nuns. John Baptist Souchet, canon of Chartres, writes in his observations on chapter 11 of the *Life of Blessed Bernard*, p. 178:

“Ralph was first a monk of the ascetical house of Hendion, now called Saint-Jouin-de-Marnes in Poitou; then a cultivator of the wilderness; and at last director and procurator—by which title Robert of Arbrissel is also called in the list of the Le Mans manuscript, in Sirmond’s observations on letter 47, book IV of Geoffrey of Vendôme, where it means ‘founder’—of the nuns of Saint-Sulpice. He died among them on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September [16 August] 1129, and was buried in their church amid a great reputation for holiness.” [Col. 1032A]

34. That dwelling of the holy men in solitude occurred after the Council of Clermont, held in 1095, but before that of Poitiers in 1100. Ivo of Chartres writes of the latter, in letter 211 to Ralph, archbishop of Reims:

“At another time, in the aforesaid court—that is, as he previously said, the court of the lord pope—the envoys of Fulk, count of Anjou, calculated and proved the same consanguinity, when Philip, king of the Franks, was accused of having taken from that count, his kinsman, his wife, whom he was also retaining unlawfully. On account of this accusation and the proof of the crime committed, the king was excommunicated by Pope Urban at the Council of Clermont. And when, after the divorce, the aforesaid king had returned to the company of the aforesaid woman, he was excommunicated at the Council of Poitiers by Cardinals John and Benedict.” [Col. 1032B]

Ivo elsewhere also mentions that council; Baronius recounts its canons under that year in his *Annals*. Blessed Robert of Arbrissel and Blessed Bernard of Tiron attended it, as Geoffrey relates in chapter 23 of Bernard’s Life:

“At the same time two cardinals, John and Benedict, acting as legates of the apostolic see, summoned a council to the city of Poitiers, at which 140 Fathers were present. They struck Philip, king of the Franks, with the punishment of anathema because of the wife of Fulk, count of Anjou, whom he held in adultery.”

35. “When this excommunication became known, William, duke of Aquitaine, who was present, an enemy of all chastity and holiness, fearing that he might suffer a like punishment for like offences, was inflamed with excessive rage and ordered them all to be plundered, scourged, and killed. When his servants began to do this, bishops and abbots fled in every direction and strove to find safe hiding-places in order to preserve their temporal lives.

“But Bernard and Robert of Arbrissel, who were present at the council—most valiant defenders of justice and destroyers of all wickedness and injustice—while the others fled shamefully, remained so unmoved and steadfast that they did not abandon the excommunication they had begun; rather, they judged it most glorious to suffer death or insult for Christ. And although their persecutors did not inflict death upon them, they nevertheless suffered martyrdom, so far as lay within them.” [Col. 1032D]

36. Souchet, citing the Chronicle of Maillezais in Besly, notes the following:

“On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October] a council was held by the two cardinals John and Benedict … To one of them, named John, Saint Hilary appeared and said to him by way of encouragement: ‘John, do not fear; act manfully; tomorrow I shall be with you.’ And he excommunicated King Philip.”

John Bouchet, in part III, chapter 2, of the *Annals of Aquitaine*, relates that when the king learned that the council was to be assembled at Poitiers, he asked William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, his kinsman, not to allow such an injury to be done him in his city. William immediately ordered the legates and other bishops to leave the city at once. One of the legates requested time for deliberation, and during the following night Saint Hilary appeared to him and warned him not to be frightened by the duke’s threats, since he would be with him. When the legate reported this to the duke the next day, the duke allowed him to complete all things as he chose.

The same account is narrated by Baronius from Bouchet, and in the notes to the Council of Poitiers in volume XXVI of the *Councils*, as published at Paris by the Royal Press. The same council is discussed in the fragment of the *History of the Franks* in volume IV of Duchesne, but there is no mention there [Col. 1033B] of Saint Hilary’s appearance. That Duke William mentioned here was the father of the William whom Saint Bernard of Clairvaux recalled from schism to obedience to the lawful pope. We treated the father on 10 February in the Life of Saint William the Hermit, § III, and later the son.

37. At the time of the Council of Poitiers, Blessed Bernard was abbot of the monastery of Saint-Cyprien near Poitiers. Robert had perhaps already left the abbey of La Roë, or certainly left it soon afterward, as Bernard also left his own. Geoffrey says of Bernard in chapter 24 of his Life:

“Burning with love of poverty and solitude, he returned to the secret place of the wilderness from which fraudulent violence had torn him away, and found there the mind he had left behind. Joined with Lord Robert of Arbrissel and Vitalis of Mortain, of whom we have already spoken, he travelled barefoot through the regions of Gaul. In villages, castles, and cities they preached the word of God, drawing people out of the errors of their life. Like strong and most powerful battering-rams, aided by the strength of divine power, they struck and shattered the walls of unbelief and vices. They tore human hearts away from the error of perishable things; they destroyed their evil conversations that corrupt good morals; they scattered the wickedness of evil works; they dispersed the accumulated mass of every iniquity; and, by God’s agency, they planted virtues in their hearts, strengthening by example and building up the virtues they had planted. [Col. 1033D] Although they were not raisers of dead bodies, they did what is greater: they restored to life souls dead in sins, and joined those restored to life with God, the true life. Performing such signs, they travelled at times together and at other times separately through different provinces; nor, through the machinations of the devil, did they lack tribulations.”

38. The same writer says in chapter 42: “While Bernard was building his monastery in Francia, Robert of Arbrissel had built his in Aquitaine, Ralph of La Fustaye in Brittany, and Vitalis of Mortain was constructing his in Normandy. The supreme Judge wished them, though far apart and separated in different regions, to remain so, because each of them built monasteries so numerous and so great that one region could not contain them, and one province could not suffice for the congregations gathered by them.” Thus he writes.

The monastery of the Holy Trinity at Tiron, founded by Blessed Bernard, lies in the diocese of Chartres, beyond the Loire, which is the northern boundary of Aquitaine, as was said above concerning Fontevraud. Savigny lies in the diocese of Avranches, on the furthest edge of Normandy; it was afterward attached to the Cistercian observance by the Venerable Serlo together with twenty-seven others, in 1153, under the authority of Pope Eugenius III. Ralph built the convent of nuns of Saint-Sulpice near Rennes. In his observations on the said forty-second chapter of Geoffrey, Souchet enumerates individually all the monasteries dependent on Savigny, Tiron, and Fontevraud.

§ V. Miracles of Blessed Robert

[Col. 1034B]

39. We now come to miracles. The author of the *Glory of Blessed Robert* rightly says at the very beginning of his little work: “Supreme pontiffs, archbishops, bishops, abbots, historians, and various writers have commended his holiness. The honour and veneration accorded to his sacred relics attest the esteem in which his holiness is held; miracles also bear witness.”

40. Bishop Baldric seems either to have known firsthand, or to have wished to publish, only those miracles performed by Robert in the healing of souls. “Let each person,” he says in the Life, “express what he has experienced; I boldly say that Robert was abundant in miracles, commanding over demons, glorious over earthly princes. For who of our time healed so many sick, cleansed so many lepers, raised so many dead? He who is of the earth speaks earthly things and admires miracles in bodies; but he who is spiritual testifies that the sick, the leprous, and even the dead recover health whenever someone provides for and heals souls that are sick, leprous, and in need of resurrection. Finally—to say it without offence to anyone—through what shepherd has the Lord spoken so much and accomplished so much?” [Col. 1034C]

In agreement with this are the things we cited in the preceding section, no. 37, from Geoffrey concerning Blessed Robert and Blessed Bernard: that they did something greater when “they restored to life souls dead in sins and joined those restored to life with God, the true life,” than if they had completely healed the gravest bodily illnesses and wounds.

41. What more illustrious miracle could be desired than a religious order shaped by the eminent institutions he established and expanded so greatly that, while he was still alive, it numbered three thousand members and thirty monasteries—and, most importantly, after so many centuries flourished with an enduring reputation for holiness, surely not without its founder’s manifest patronage before God?

I recall that about forty-four years ago, when conversation arose with Matthias Hovius, archbishop of Mechelen and primate of our Belgium, concerning the enrolment of Blessed Ignatius, father of our Society, among the sacred lists of saints, someone said that miracles ought to be produced in order to accomplish the matter. That most wise and weighty prelate said that he desired no miracles other than the Society founded by Ignatius itself. He had laboured for so many years to establish a seminary, supported by the revenues of an extensive archbishopric, the favour of the Austrian rulers Albert and Isabella, and the willing assistance of the clergy and every rank; yet Ignatius, relying on no resources of fortune and no favour or recommendation of princes, had in a short time established so great a body of religious persons, seen it secured by excellent laws, extended to the furthest parts of the earth, and bearing most abundant fruit. [Col. 1035A]

The same may certainly be said with justice of the Order of Fontevraud. It could not have grown together in so brief a time through the energy of one man without particular divine assistance; nor could zeal for perfection have remained vigorous in it for so long unless its founder, received into heaven, continually cared for it, stirred holy desires by heavenly aid, and advanced the labours of nuns and monks alike.

42. Yet Robert did not lack even those external miracles which mortals especially tend to admire. In the *Corollary to the Gallican Martyrology*, Andrew Saussay writes of him: “Having been perfected in every holiness, he happily breathed his last at the monastery of Orsan, afterward made glorious by divine signs, by which he still shines.” James Rinaldi, in the previously cited *Lilies of Holy France*, says: “From the monastery of Orsan he departed to heaven to receive crowns due for his struggles and victories, while here he triumphs in miracles.”

It is no wonder that Baldric records no miracles occurring after Blessed Robert’s death, since he compiled Robert’s Life in an excessively concise form after only a short interval had elapsed from his death. Andrew, moreover, pursued almost only those matters which Robert performed near the end of his life. Archbishop Léger himself, as he testifies above, § III, no. 27, regarded as bearing a genuine appearance of miracle the fact that “although his body was treated with no spices, it emitted no foul odour even though it remained lifeless for many days. This,” he says, “is a most certain proof of his outstanding holiness.” [Col. 1035C]

43. Nicquet relates some more recent events in his *History of Fontevraud*. The first, as we said from book I, chapter 36, was this: Blessed Robert’s heart was placed in the church of the monastery at Orsan atop a marble pyramid three feet high. It is still seen there, near the principal altar, on what is called the Gospel side, close to the church wall. Yet it is no longer whole. In 1570, when the duke of Zweibrücken entered France with German troops to assist the heretics, one of his soldiers, wishing to break it, battered it with several blows.

Nor was heavenly vengeance lacking. The sacrilegious man was struck with blindness and, according to some accounts, with stiffness in one arm. But soon, as though light had been transferred into his mind, he recognized why this punishment had been inflicted upon him, detested both his crime and the heresy from which it had arisen, and vowed to maintain there a nine-day vigil in prayer. When these were completed, his power of sight was restored. This is still related by the inhabitants of Orsan, who received the account from their parents, eyewitnesses.

[Col. 1036A]

44. In the same church at Orsan, in 1634, where Blessed Robert’s heart is kept—which the people call the holy heart and visit and venerate with great devotion—masses of the Most Holy Trinity began to be celebrated, so that thanks might be given to God for the outstanding gifts divinely bestowed on that holy man. Then the same church was spontaneously filled with a most sweet fragrance, a certain heavenly and invisible incense.

The nuns of that monastery publicly testified to this; Nicquet, book II, chapter 15, gives their names. So also did Dr. Hugault and others who were permitted to enter the enclosure of the monastery to treat the sick. Louis Perrier, a priest of the same order, testified that he had perceived the same fragrance both at Orsan before that holy heart and at Fontevraud, when he had some relics of Blessed Robert within his cell.

45. At the same monastery of Orsan, Sister Gabrielle d’Assy had both arms paralysed from December 1633 for a full five months. Very many remedies were applied, without result. At last, on Easter Monday, 17 April, it was decided that continuous prayers should be made for forty hours, so that divine goodness might be moved to aid the infirm woman and thereby manifest the glory of the holy founder. All received the sacred Eucharist for this purpose, and Gabrielle’s health was divinely restored. This is confirmed by the testimony of all the nuns and of the aforementioned physician.

46. A foul carcinoma, the size of a walnut, had tormented the left hand of Joan Mousse, a nun of Orsan, for several months. After Blessed Robert’s aid was repeatedly implored and no other medical treatment was employed, on the feast of All Saints in 1634 the disease subsided and wholly disappeared. She herself and the physician testified to this. [Col. 1036C]

47. In 1635 at Coudan, in Bourbonnais, an acute fever had brought Henry Assy almost to the point of death. All the physicians’ skill was in vain. His mother, Marguerite Lassaigny, recalled the miracles said to occur through Blessed Robert’s merits and made a vow to him. At once the fever abated, and the boy’s health returned.

48. I shall conclude this chapter with the following words found in the *Glory of Blessed Robert*, p. 49: “How many people, indeed, have been freed from various illnesses through the invocation of the servant of God, or through some act of devotion performed at his tomb, or by drinking the water of the spring named after Saint Robert, may be seen in the inquiry made in June 1644 at the monastery of Fontevraud by authority of the most illustrious and most reverend lord bishop of Poitiers. And because his canonization is now being pressed before the holy apostolic see, God continues to reveal the holiness of His servant by wondrous signs.” [Col. 1036D]

§ VI. Refutation of the forged letter directed against Blessed Robert under the name of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme

49. Before we present the Life of Blessed Robert published by two contemporary writers, I perceive that one stain must incidentally be wiped away here, which might obscure all the honours already mentioned by us and those to be mentioned in the Life. It was spread by a disgraceful letter appearing as number forty-seven in book IV of the letters of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, under this title:

“Geoffrey, humble servant of the monastery of Vendôme, to his brother much beloved in Christ: preserve the measure of discretion and be content with the bounds established by the Fathers.”

Then, in the text of the letter itself:

“To do nothing beyond what ought to be done is angelic perfection, which our condition cannot possess while we remain here. Therefore, since we do not possess an angel’s perfection, let us by no means possess the devil’s presumption. We have proposed these things, venerable brother, because, as hostile rumour spreads abroad, we have heard that you have done—and still do—such things. If they are true, we admonish your simplicity from the bowels of sincere charity not to defend them by any excuse, but to correct them with all speed.

“For we have heard that concerning the female sex, whose direction you have undertaken, you make yourself solicitous in two ways utterly contrary to one another, so that in each case you wholly exceed the measure of discretion. You permit certain women, it is said, to live with you in excessive familiarity; you often speak private words with them and are not ashamed frequently to lie at night with them and among them. Hence, as you maintain, you seem to yourself worthily to bear the cross of the Lord and Saviour while you endeavour to extinguish the evil-kindled burning of the flesh. If you act thus now, or have ever acted thus, you have devised a new and unheard-of, yet fruitless, kind of martyrdom.” [Col. 1037C]

50. After certain intervening remarks to the same effect, the letter adds:

“You have indeed climbed in the world as though onto a high mountain, and therefore have turned toward yourself the tongues and eyes of men. Therefore, standing on the mountain, take care not to fall; and do not, through a martyrdom wholly unknown to holy martyrs, leave upon the beginning of your religious life a mark of infamy. By no action of yours stir up scandal in the world, which almost wholly follows you. For your condemnation would become more severe through the ruin of very many.

“You often speak privately, as rumour has spread and as we have said before, with certain women; and you torment yourself by lying with them through some novel kind of martyrdom. To them you always show yourself pleasant in speech and cheerful in manner, and offer every kind of kindness without retaining any restraint. But to others, whenever you speak with them, you always appear excessively harsh in speech and excessively severe in correction; you also torment them with hunger, thirst, and nakedness, abandoning all pity,” etc.

Finally, the writer concludes the letter thus: “Farewell, and we humbly pray you to make us participants in your holy prayers.” [Col. 1037D]

1. It has at all times been the devil’s craftiness that, when he saw men distinguished in virtue and learning applying themselves to the salvation of others as well, and incapable of being ensnared by any of his deceits or recalled from their purpose of cultivating piety and inculcating it in others, he should endeavour to brand them with some infamy by casting suspicion upon their teaching [Col. 1038A] or morals. He supposed that, if any opinion of error or even ignorance, of greed, lust, or at least frivolity were raised, they would immediately be despised and avoided, and the salutary counsels they had previously sown would be rejected.

There is no need to establish this with examples, since wicked people even alleged that Christ Himself, eternal Wisdom and author of all holiness, was a drunkard and a blasphemer, and used the works of demons to perform miracles.

### 52.

But especially when someone begins to devote effort to forming women for a holier life, the ministers of the devil in this matter strive to brand him with the disgrace of some impurity. For women are by nature [Col. 1038B] more modest and timid; and so, as soon as they hear anything of this sort, they fear that subtle conversations may gradually inflict a blemish upon their modesty, or at least bring disgrace upon the good repute of their name.

Saint Jerome—that eminent and most chaste teacher—because he expounded the sacred Scriptures to certain Roman matrons and virgins, whose diligence in the pursuit of piety was exceptional, was denounced by many as a man insufficiently modest, especially after these women had renounced worldly luxury and display. He himself testifies to and refutes the jealous accusations of this kind in Letter 99, to Asella, where among other things he writes:

> “For almost certainly three years I lived with them. A great company of virgins frequently surrounded me. As I was able, I often expounded the divine books to many of them. Reading produced assiduity; assiduity, familiarity; [Col. 1038C] familiarity, confidence. Let them say what they ever perceived in me otherwise than befitted a Christian. Did I receive anyone’s money? Did I fail to reject gifts, whether small or great? Did another person’s coin ring in my hand? Was there any suggestive speech, any wanton glance? Nothing else is alleged against me except my sex; and even this is never alleged except when Paula and Melania set out for Jerusalem.”

And a little later:

> “Before I knew the house of Saint Paula, the enthusiasm of the whole City was in harmony toward me; by the judgment of almost everyone I was declared worthy of the highest priesthood. Damasus, of blessed memory, spoke of me; I was called holy, humble, and eloquent. Did I ever enter the house of any more licentious woman? Did silken garments, glittering jewels, painted faces, or the ambition of gold ensnare me? [Col. 1038D] There was no Roman matron able to subdue my mind except one mourning and fasting, foul with dirt, almost blinded by tears, whom the sun often found, through continual nights, beseeching the Lord’s mercy. Her song was the Psalms, her speech the Gospel, her delight continence, her life fasting. No other woman could delight me except she whom I never saw eating. But after I began, as her chastity deserved, to venerate, honor, and receive her—did all virtues immediately desert me? O envy, first to bite at your own! O Satan’s craft, always pursuing what is holy!”

He adds much more to the same effect.

### 53.

But if the virtue of any such initiator into sacred mysteries has been publicly proved so thoroughly that no suspicion of disgrace can fall upon him, wicked persons invent something by which they may at least fasten upon him some charge of rashness or excessive self-confidence.

That well-known member of a most religious order in our annals, being ill-disposed toward our people and unable to bear their integrity, and their prudent manner of associating with every rank and sex, being celebrated in the speech of all the people, spread among the public the report that they restrained the stirrings of lust by means of a certain foreign herb.

More grievous was the calumny cast upon the most holy man Robert of Arbrissel—whether spread abroad in the mouths of men as malicious rumors, or fabricated under the name of Geoffrey, a man of the highest standing, in the letter of which we have spoken. The author of this [Col. 1039B] letter says that he had heard what he writes “as an evil report circulated.” But how could such a report have circulated, when the nuns were so strictly excluded from the sight even of religious persons of the same institute that not even an abbess, deaness, or prioress, if stricken with illness and wishing to confess, could summon a priest to her bed? Rather, it is prescribed in these words in the constitutions, in Nicquet, book III, chapter 12, that, whoever she may be, she is to be “carried to the chapel, confess and receive communion there; and, after she has communicated and the priest has departed, be carried back to her bed.”

How, then, could Robert approach women thus enclosed, or they approach him? Or who could believe that he who wished with such care to provide for the security of their modesty himself associated with them even at night?

### 54.

[Col. 1039C] Moreover, if this report had spread so widely as to reach Geoffrey at Chartres, how did it not reach the neighboring bishop of Poitiers and prevent him from so conspicuously commending Robert to the pope, or even from tolerating him in his own diocese? How did the report not then reach the papal court by some means, where matters reported concerning ecclesiastics—especially those not far away—which deserve censure are seldom unknown?

But the popes would not have pursued Robert with such favor or honored the order with such extensive privileges, had anything of this kind even faintly come to their notice. So many most respectable matrons and virgins would not have attached themselves to this order if they had heard that anything of the sort had happened. So many pious men would not have wished to adhere to it if they felt that Robert’s example was casting them into such temptations.

What of his holy companions Bernard and Vitalis? Would they have entrusted women especially to his instruction, as to a man divinely endowed with a particular aptitude for that work, if they had suspected him of such great imprudence—or rather, shamelessness? Would not the same report have reached them too and drawn them out of their monasteries so that they might resist him to his face? He would indeed have been blameworthy if he had attempted anything of the kind. How could the spirit of piety and fear of God have been kindled and nourished in the souls of women—very many of whom he had drawn out of the mire of sins—unless he kept them as far as possible from every such enticement?

Let the sons of Belial, then, depart—if any, even in jest, have said anything of this kind concerning that most holy man. Nor [Col. 1040A] do I think that anyone so untrained in Christian discipline could suppose that such thoughts could have entered the mind of a pious and wise man.

### 55.

What then of Geoffrey? Why did he rebuke his friend in words of such weight, if he did not believe the charge? Why did he not rather write that he had heard such an accusation but had been unable to believe it?

I do not deny that certain men, endowed with vehement zeal and otherwise learned, sometimes give credence to charges fabricated against pious men even if they have heard them from only one or two persons; or at least, because they fear that they may be true, are more deeply disturbed on hearing them. I could, were I not forbidden by the reverence owing to religious antiquity, bring forward several persons who, on the report even of one witness—false or rashly exaggerated—hurled a violent [Col. 1040B] pen against certain men.

Did this writer too suffer some human weakness, and call the taunt of some insolent person “a report circulating”? He certainly seemed harsher than some.

### 56.

I shall state plainly what I think. That letter was not written by Geoffrey; nor can anyone easily show a time when it could have been written by him, or an occasion supplied by Robert for its writing.

In the time of Urban II, Robert’s eloquence, joined with the highest piety, was so celebrated in the favorable speech of men that this pope summoned him to himself, ordered him to preach at Angers before an almost innumerable multitude, and afterward appointed him an apostolic preacher—or, as Baldric says, “the second seed-word of God after himself.” Therefore that adverse report concerning [Col. 1040C] Robert had not yet reached Geoffrey. Otherwise, given his very close friendship with the pope, he would have warned him not to arm with such authority a man whose public conduct was so dangerous.

And how could that charge then have been conveyed to Geoffrey, and by him to the pope, when no women had yet begun to follow Robert—not even in the immediately following years, when he established and governed the abbey of Rota of regular canons?

### 57.

The Council of Poitiers was held in the time of Paschal II, in the year 1100, as we said above. “And not long afterward,” as our Sirmond notes from the Chronicle of Tours on Geoffrey’s Letter 32, book IV, “the abbey of Fontevraud was built in the diocese of Poitiers.”

[Col. 1040D] At that time, you may say, if the deed was not committed by Robert, it was at least spread abroad and reported to Geoffrey, since the nuns were not yet so strictly enclosed. But Geoffrey had no need then to write to Robert, for he himself was frequently at Fontevraud, even before the nuns were enclosed in the cloister and entirely removed from men’s sight. Geoffrey himself testifies to this in book IV, Letter 32:

> “The reason I was not with you at Easter was the infirmity of my body. For a hump grew upon my back, and I had to be cut. And although, amid the hands and tearful voices of the nuns beloved by God at Fontevraud, while the razor wrote its letters in our flesh, my body—equally exhausted by infirmity and wound—was held in no slight distress, [Col. 1041A] neither illness, nor the cruelty of the cutter, nor the harshness of the salt immediately applied, could make me forget you even for a moment.”

Geoffrey was so intimate at Fontevraud that he wished to have his hump removed there, under the very beginnings of the monastery, as I think, when the nuns are said to have attended him and when he calls them “beloved by God.” Why did he not then also warn Robert, beloved by God, if he had heard anything about him of the kind alleged? Why was it necessary to send so biting a letter, and to preserve it among his papers so that it might become known even to posterity?

In book I, Letter 24, he writes that he came to Fontevraud to speak with the bishop of Poitiers. Then in Letter 26 he says that he “could not safely proceed beyond Fontevraud.” [Col. 1041B] Therefore he was frequently there and familiar with the place, no less with Robert than with the nuns.

### 58.

Nor can anyone suppose that the letter was written after the order had already been founded and shaped by its own laws. For how could the same Geoffrey then have wished to enter into a most holy fellowship with Robert and the nuns, when he ought rather then to have shunned both him and them on account of such great recklessness and the violation, if not of chastity itself, at least of chastity’s fair appearance?

This fellowship is found in the Cartulary of the Greater Monastery of Fontevraud, charter 27, in the following form:

> “We make known to future persons as well as to those present that Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, before and above all abbots, possesses friendship and benefaction with this place called Fontevraud; and when [Col. 1041C] he dies, each year we shall solemnly celebrate his anniversary. As for the brothers of the monastery of Vendôme, concerning whom we possess a list, we shall do as much as for ourselves. The lord abbot himself gave to our monastery in perpetuity, and granted it to be possessed, the share of the toll on salt which he held at Saint-Florent. These things were done in the chapter-house of Fontevraud, in the presence of Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, and Lord Robert our master, in the year 1114, indiction VII.”

### 59.

Is it not now sufficiently clear that neither could such a report have been spread concerning Robert nor could the letter have been written by Geoffrey? Indeed, the letter does not occur even in the monastery of Vendôme, in [Col. 1041D] the manuscript codex of the minor works and letters of Geoffrey, the abbot of that very place. This was attested and subscribed in their own hands by the prior and subprior of the same abbey, at the request of the most excellent and most reverend Joanna Baptista de Bourbon, general abbess of the Greater Monastery and of the entire Order of Fontevraud, as we said above; and the attestation is preserved in the archive of that monastery.

Since this concerns an extraordinary calumny directed against the most holy founder, indeed against the entire order, many wondered why our Father Jacques Sirmond, when he published Geoffrey’s letters and other minor works from two manuscript codices—one from the monastery of Saint Peter de la Couture at Le Mans, the other from the abbey of Vendôme—did not at least note that the letter is absent from the latter. From this, at the least, a doubt might have arisen in the reader that it was not genuinely Geoffrey’s. He does indeed admit that in his edition of Geoffrey’s letters he chiefly followed the Le Mans manuscript, because not all were present in the Vendôme manuscript.

But from this we infer that the person who first compiled the Le Mans manuscript gathered together into one volume, from every quarter, letters which seemed to be Geoffrey’s, including this one that bore his name. From a certain authority I also learned concerning Jacques Sirmond himself—for while he lived, despite our frequent and familiar literary intercourse, it never occurred to me to question him concerning that letter of Geoffrey; but I received this from another sincere and grave man of our company—that he later declared unequivocally that the letter was not Geoffrey’s genuine offspring, after more mature consideration of the matter and after weighing Peter Abelard’s letter, which we shall cite shortly; and that he resolved, if he should again send Geoffrey’s works to press, to remove that letter.

### 60.

Who then was the author of the letter? One might suspect that, because Robert had stood so vigorously for the authority of the Apostolic See at the Council of Poitiers in 1100, someone among the subjects of King Philip, angered with him for that reason, hurled this virulent writing against him while he was living in Aquitaine under Duke William’s rule. Or perhaps some member of the sacred order, driven by the frenzy of envy because, as the letter itself says, the whole world went after Robert, fashioned this calumny.

For certainly in many monasteries too, as Jacques de Vitry complains in the passage cited above, piety had been extinguished and discipline relaxed. Secular priests in Brittany, as may be gathered from Baldric, and in Normandy, as Geoffrey writes in the Life of Blessed Bernard—perhaps elsewhere also—polluted the dignity of their estate with the foulest vices. For this reason Norman priests and “the wives of priests,” as he calls them, conspired to kill Bernard. Someone, therefore, from that class of men may have devised this calumny against Robert, who was too unlike them in his manner of life.

### 61.

But, as Sirmond also thought, Peter Abelard seems to me to indicate its true author in Letter 21, to G., bishop of Paris—namely Rozelin or Roscelin, who was condemned at the Council of Soissons in 1140 and compelled to commit his writings to the flames. Among other things, Abelard says of him in the cited letter:

> “I give thanks to God . . . [lacuna] because I now seem to be numbered among good men, through the hostility of one whose life and teaching are known to all. This man dared TO FORGE AN INSOLENT LETTER against that distinguished herald of Christ, Robert of Arbrissel; and against that magnificent teacher of the Church, Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, he blazed forth in insults so violently that, by command of the king of England, his shameless insolence was disgracefully expelled from England, and he scarcely then escaped with his life. For he wants to have others share in his own disgrace, so that he may console his disgrace by the disgrace of [Col. 1043A] good men; and he hates only the good, because he cannot endure to be good.”

These are Abelard’s words, along with others against the frauds and deceptions of that wicked man. What must especially be considered is that he calls it “a forged letter.” For the slander is not merely composed in some fashion; rather, because it has the form of a letter and is issued under another’s name, it is rightly called “forged,” not simply written.
