And perhaps it was composed neither while Robert was alive nor while Geoffrey himself was alive—[Col. 1044A] Geoffrey died in 1129—but afterward, so that a stain might be affixed to the name of each, redounding to the contempt of the entire order and to the injury of public piety, unless the deception of that criminal man had been promptly exposed and suppressed. Abelard rightly calls it “an insolent letter,” because, while the innocence of the order and the founder’s holiness were celebrated in everyone’s speech, it shamelessly reviled both with a certain obstinate malice.

[Col. 1043]

# Life of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, by Baldric, Bishop of Dol

*(Published from the ancient manuscripts of Fontevraud at La Flèche in 1641 and 1647.)*

## Author’s Prologue

[Col. 1043A]

BALDRIC, by the grace of God priest of Dol, though unworthy, to CHRIST’S handmaid PETRONILLA [Note: [Col. 1043C] Nicquet discusses her at length in book IV of the *History of Fontevraud*, chapter 2, and judges that she had previously been married to someone from the ancient and distinguished family of Chemillé or Camilliac, commonly called de Chemillé.], venerable abbess of the monastery of Fontevraud, and to all the nuns of that monastery under her rule, [Col. 1043B] greeting.

### 1.

Not without [Note: [Col. 1043C] Cosnier’s edition: “not without cause.”] reference to you—indeed, for your instruction, you who are the bride of God—I think the following saying was spoken: “Hear, daughter, and see” (Psalm 44:12), etc. For you have heard, and truly heard, the voice of Him who proclaims: “Go forth from your land and from your kindred” (Genesis 12:1). You went forth from all your households; you fled your paternal home; you abhorred the seductive enticements of the flesh that flattered you; and you came to Fontevraud, where you found and drank from a plentiful fountain—the fountain of preaching, the fountain of religion—namely Lord Robert, in our age the singular seed-word of God [Note: [Col. 1043C] Both editions read thus; elsewhere, *seminiverbium*, “seed-word.”], an illustrious and exceptional teacher, admirable in words and deeds, a man to be exalted and imitated.

Having at one time remained among the sisters [Col. 1043C] and been instructed in holy conduct, you forgot your people and your father’s house; and, with the Holy Spirit going before and Lord Robert cooperating, you were made abbess, although you had previously been devoted to the disturbances of marriage chambers. For the necessity and benefit of Holy Church frequently—and not without reason—obscure human institutions.

Therefore God raised [Note: [Col. 1044C] Another manuscript, as Cosnier formerly informed us: “exalted.”] you to that lofty throne and set you over His people, Pope Paschal approving [Note: [Col. 1044C] By a diploma given on 25 April, indiction XIII, in the year 1106. This pope was created 12 August 1099 and died 22 January 1118.]. Such a [Note: [Col. 1044C] Cosnier’s edition: “especially such a.”] mother was needed by that people—[Col. 1044A] a poor people, a fatherless people. Such a stewardess, I say, was needed to support women who had accepted poverty for God alone.

You, however, will do well if you devote yourself wholly to their care; if you sacrifice yourself to the burden you have undertaken as a beast of burden; [Col. 1044B] if you regard yourself as the lowest of all.

### 2.

[Col. 1044B] The aforesaid Robert has entered upon the way of our fathers and, as is believed, having put off mortality, has obtained from God, crowned with laurels, the robe of immortality. Yet whether in remembering him it is especially fitting to weep or to rejoice can scarcely be decided: humanity compels us to weep for the absence of our dearest one, while confidence bids us rejoice because our Robert has flown to the court of our God, there to intercede for us.

But since we do not yet know which of these we ought especially to do, let us for the present devote ourselves to both, and exercise ourselves in both until we are gradually drawn out of the valley of tears. Let our eye therefore weep and flow with tears, because a good and eloquent teacher and friend [Col. 1044C] of God has departed from us. Let our heart rejoice, because our Robert has gone before us from this muddy exile of the world to the dwelling prepared for us.

Dearest Mother, you commanded that his manner of life, so long as he lived upon earth and so far removed from the common manner of life of human beings, should be described by my insignificance, so that it might be committed to the record of letters and thereby perhaps someday provide in some measure for the benefit of human frailty. For if we find the footsteps of the Fathers written down, we imitate more willingly those whom we trust are intercessors pleading for us.

This work would require a Virgilian or Ciceronian style. Lady Petronilla, you have imposed a great and heavy burden upon my weakness, when both the storm of this wandering world disturbs me greatly and, above all, that of Lesser Brittany, where I dwell among scorpions and am surrounded by a twofold, brutish savagery. [Note: [Col. 1045D] Another reading, according to the same editor: *turbella*, “a little storm.”] Finally, how shall one hold to the polished law of writing when not even a drop from Sallust’s inkwell has ever bedewed him? I ask: with what rash boldness, with what gaping mouth, shall I call Robert a holy and just man when I am weighed down by manifold sin?

What shall I say at last? You gave me certain little sheets which contained almost nothing concerning Lord Robert except [Col. 1045B] that he was said to have sprung from our Bretons.

### 3.

Nevertheless, when I recall that I have heard that God bestows His grace even upon the undeserving, and remember reading that the supreme Creator for a time granted to a brute animal, namely Balaam’s she-ass, the function of human speech, I do not doubt that He who makes the tongues of infants eloquent will inspire in me [Note: [Col. 1045D] Another reading, according to the same editor: “also in me.”] eloquence—not for my merits, but for the merits of Robert, so often to be named. And, if He wills, through my leaden pipe He will pour out for the age to come the clearest water, which will be of use.

Therefore, most holy sisters, assisted by your prayers, to which I especially commend myself, I shall attempt to say a little concerning our master, for whom you continually sigh. Yet I fear [Col. 1045C] that, as a wandering traveler, I may fail upon the road. If in this endeavor I say anything well, I beg you to attribute it to God’s gift. But if otherwise—which I greatly fear—attribute it at last either to our decrepit age, or to a trembling hand, or to my dullness, or to my life long hardened in sins.

Yet remember that all human beings, except One, have lived subject to sins. Farewell.

## Chapter One. Blessed Robert’s birth, studies, archpresbyterate, public teaching of the sciences, and penance

### 4.

Let us give thanks to the Lord our God, who until now has not ceased to visit us like the morning sun rising from on high (Luke 1). Nor is this surprising, since Truth itself foretold it, since Jesus Himself promised it in these words: “Behold, I am with you [Col. 1045D] all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

But if God is with us, how could Emmanuel—how could the maker and [Col. 1046A] ruler of all things—be idle among us? How can there be a day without light, fire without heat? Can there be ice without frost, the sun without brightness? Since God can never and nowhere be idle, He nevertheless worked more visibly before our eyes in our days, when He gave to the world the venerable Robert of Arbrissel: a mirror, a destroyer of vices, a propagator and educator of virtues, a consolation and guide for all persons who are desolate and straying.

For Robert, a ray of the rising sun, an undimmed morning star, a powerful preacher, illuminated the western region of the world and drove away the darkness of ignorance by the power of his speech.

### 5.

I, Baldric, metropolitan of Dol [Note: [Col. 1045D] The bishops of Dol in Armorican Brittany once claimed this title, while the archbishops of Tours opposed them; many authors have written about the right of each party. According to Claude Robert, the bishops of Dol still use a processional cross in their diocese.], [Col. 1046B] though unworthy, have undertaken, in compliance with the wishes of the nuns of Fontevraud, to commit and publish in writing his marvelous conduct among mortals, though my style is unpolished, so that in future ages the fragrance of his examples may be redolent and Christian learning may profit from his teaching.

For the material of any history of deeds will be of greater value than the sequence of reading can commend. Many things remain concerning Robert that ought to be recorded by a more celebrated pen, and my lack of skill greatly harms them; old age also harms them, dulling my intellect, and forgetful old age, its rival. Therefore I undertake this work not supported by the aids of literary learning, but only because I trust in the Lord. May the Holy Spirit therefore assist my obedience, and may the holiness of Lord Robert aid me. [Col. 1046C] Amen.

### 6.

As I am about to speak of the venerable Robert, I call upon the Holy Spirit, the inspirer of truth, to supply what is worthy of this subject. Without His aid, the very loquacity of dialecticians is mute and the very thought of philosophers is dull. Therefore, so that we may trace more deeply the foundation of this history, let us briefly discuss from what country and what parents he sprang, and in what times he flourished, that we may bear witness to the truth in every point. For we shall not seem to stray if we first examine his origin.

### 7.

The blessed Robert, of whom we have resolved to speak, was an heir and son of Christian profession, a native of Lesser Brittany—a province which [Col. 1046D] the priest adorned. He was born in the district of Rennes [Note: [Col. 1045D] This name was discussed above, §2.], a native inhabitant and tenant of the village now called Arbrissel [Note: [Col. 1045D] In observations on chapter 11 of the *Life of Blessed Bernard of Tiron*, Jean-Baptiste Souchet reproaches Cosnier for having deleted certain words here and subsequently cut away much in bad faith. Cosnier seemed [Col. 1046D] to me a thoroughly sincere man, both in letters sent to me and in the *Life of Blessed Robert* itself, to whose margin he added variant readings from other Fontevraud manuscripts, sometimes quite slight, and in the copy sent to us noted in his own hand other readings observed later. Souchet, however, cites no manuscript from which he could prove his case against him. A little earlier he does cite a transcript from a Rota manuscript, which Jean Picard had formerly supplied to him, where *Abrincello* was read instead of *Abrisselo*; yet he himself does not follow this reading. Whether he drew from the same manuscript what he charges against Cosnier, he does not indicate at all. And indeed, if he asserted this, [Col. 1047C] one might ask whether that manuscript should be preferred to several Fontevraud manuscripts, unless he produced the Fontevraud manuscripts themselves, or at least most of them, or the most ancient and best-attested. Yet what he complains was omitted here by Cosnier detracts nothing from Robert’s holiness, but pertains only to his birth.].

His father was named Damaliochus, [Col. 1047A] and his mother Orguendis [Note: [Col. 1047C] Nicquet gives *Orghendis* or *Oruandis*, book I, chapter 3, where he cites these words from the Necrology—or, as he there writes, the Martyrology—of Fontevraud: “Oruandis, mother of our lord Robert, our Father, died on the third day before the Nones of February.” He adds that her brother was Fulcodius or Fulcoius, of whom the Martyrology says: “Fulchodius, brother of our lord Robert, our Father, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.”].

Robert himself began from childhood to grow into mature conduct. For he did not, as is customary, follow the licentiousness of youth; rather, as far as he could, he embraced shining chastity and inwardly loved purity. He seemed to pursue through the world learning that fled from him, since from his childhood years he had been devoted to literary studies which he could not fully attain. Restlessly he traveled through regions and provinces, and he could not but be diligent in literary pursuits.

Since France then flourished more abundantly in the advantages of schools, he left his paternal borders as an exile and fugitive, went to France, and entered the city called Paris [Note: [Col. 1047D] Medieval writers commonly use this form. We usually call it *Parisios*, in the plural, because of the multitude. Yet this was the name of the people, but it attached itself to the metropolis formerly called Lutetia. Thus, as we have often noted elsewhere, Samarobriva—or more correctly Samarobriga—of the Ambiani is now called Amiens; Nemetocenna, the capital of the Atrebates, is now Arras; and so with other cities.]. There he found, as he desired, a suitable discipline of learning, [Col. 1047B] and began to attend assiduously as a student.

He labored wholly in those exercises, yet did not on that account neglect the observance of an approved way of life. Among his fellow students he displayed a majesty of measured severity, and by certain signs clearly indicated what he would become. At that time King Philip [Note: [Col. 1047D] Philip I, king of France, succeeded his father Henry I in 1060 and died in July 1108.] son of King Henry ruled the dominions of the Franks, and Gregory VII [Note: [Col. 1047D] Saint Gregory VII died in 1086, having been made pope in 1076; his feast is kept on 25 May.] held the papacy of the city of Rome. We have said this in order to show plainly in what times Robert grew up and studied.

For he rendered to scholars what belonged to scholars, and did not therefore make himself any less fit for God’s service. Those who knew him already anticipated something from him, for they perceived something great in him.

### 8.

[Col. 1047C] Meanwhile the city of Rennes [Note: [Col. 1047D] This is the city of the Redones or Rhedones, called Rennes in French, situated in the middle of the duchy of Armorican Brittany, according to Claude Robert, on the river Vicenonia, also found under the name Vidiana; now commonly called the Vilaine, according to Papirius Masson.] had been deprived of its bishop [Note: [Col. 1048C] Claude Robert calls him Mainus or Maino, commonly Meen.]. Turning to God and offering prayers beforehand, it chose as bishop a certain Silvester [Note: [Col. 1048C] Albert the Great of Morlaix calls him Silvester de la Guerche and says that he bore arms against Conan, duke of Brittany, later served as his chancellor, was made bishop in 1071, and died in 1095. But this does not sufficiently agree with the *Life of Blessed Robert*. After Silvester’s death, Robert is said to have gone to Angers, to have worn a hair-shirt next to his skin beneath fine garments for two years, then to have withdrawn into the wilderness, mortified himself with rough outer clothing and abstinence, instructed the crowds coming to him, and gathered companions. [Col. 1048D] After this account, no. 14 adds: “It happened in those days that the Roman pontiff Urban II, pressed by the necessity of the times, came into Gaul,” etc. Yet Urban came into Gaul in 1095, indeed in midsummer. It consequently appears that Silvester died some years earlier, if Baldric narrates all events in their order. Claude Robert, indeed, in his catalogue of the abbeys of France, under “Rota,” writes that Urban II approved in 1096 that Robert should be the first abbot of Rota, which he had founded after Reginald, lord of Credon, had contributed resources and possessions for its foundation. This cannot have occurred before his withdrawal to the wilderness, since he spent those two years at Angers.], [Col. 1048A] whom uprightness of character and his own nobility commended. As he was noble in birth, so he was nobler in merits; and though not very learned himself, he eagerly embraced learned men. Spiritual discipline flourished in him, so that divine teaching clearly instilled in him what flesh and blood had not inspired.

He therefore summoned from elsewhere whatever learned persons he could find, a kind of person then exceedingly rare in Brittany. When inquiries were made concerning Robert, his strictness, and his diligence, the answer was given:

> “Robert, lord, of whom we speak is your own native; for he is from Rennes and is quite suited to your institutions. He is most excellently trained in the liberal arts, vigorous in body, and ordered by moral uprightness.”

[Col. 1048B] Having made preparations for travel, the venerable bishop sent to Paris and addressed Robert when he had been summoned:

> “You see, dearest brother, how your mother, the holy Church of Rennes, wavers without governance, especially at this time when I have happened to preside over it almost as a layman. Therefore, I beg you, be our interpreter in ecclesiastical affairs: I shall hear you, and you shall speak in me. Without doubt you will be able to benefit God’s people if, possessing zeal for God, you are willing to serve with us for a little while.”

### 9.

Robert assented to the entreaties of the speaker and was soon diligently occupied with ecclesiastical duties and necessities. In everything he did he kept God before his eyes; in nothing was he idle. He freed himself from the desire for shameful gain, and in every matter lawfully governed himself. He faithfully [Col. 1048C] supported his bishop in all things; and the bishop, though a patron, did not disdain Robert’s support.

Having thus remained four years with the bishop as archpriest [Note: [Col. 1048D] Nicquet further says that he was an official and vicar of the bishop.], he restored peace among those at discord, freed churches [Col. 1049A] from the shameful servitude of laymen, dissolved incestuous unions of priests and laypeople, utterly abhorred simony, and vigorously resisted every vice.

10. After two periods of two years had elapsed, the reverend bishop, afflicted by a severe bodily illness, put off the human frame and, it is believed, departed to the stars. Robert remained alone, an orphan among orphans—alone, I say, because the brethren themselves envied his worthy deeds, and their envy had already produced hatred toward him. He therefore resolved within himself to yield to envy and, in accordance with his Master's saying, to flee from city to city (Matt. 10:23). For he did not wish to be a cause of scandal to anyone, knowing this to be a great and grave sin. He accordingly came to Angers, and there devoted himself to academic studies.

[Note: Col. 1049D. Nicquetus, bk. I, ch. 5, and Albert the Great of Morlaix report that Marbod, archdeacon of Angers, who afterwards became bishop of Rennes, established the schools of Angers on the model of an academy. Marbod was a learned man and wrote several Lives of saints, as we have said elsewhere; he was eventually appointed to the bishopric of Rennes in succession to Silvester.]

Yet he did not on that account grow lukewarm in religion; for after his reading he attended to divine philosophy. He avoided idleness, now giving himself to prayer, now to reading. Resolving, therefore, to rule the enticements of the flesh more severely, he put on a coat of mail next to his flesh. He wore this garment for two years before entering the wilderness. Afterwards he did indeed enter the wilderness and devoted himself wholly to contemplation. During the two years in which he subdued his flesh by this iron garment, he covered himself outwardly with fine clothing, concealing himself from the eyes and favor of men but making himself known only to the sight of God. For throughout his life he despised the trifling attentions of favor-seekers and rejected every flattering speech as though it were poison. At times he used rare and cheap foods, and at times he gave himself to vigils.

## CHAPTER II. The Blessed Robert’s austere life in the wilderness; the conversion of many; the foundation of the abbey of La Roë; and the notable office of an apostolic preacher.

[Col. 1049C]

11. The day came when, renouncing the world and taking with him a certain priest, he hastened to the long-desired wilderness. He withdrew into a forest,

[Note: Col. 1049D. It is called the forest of Craon—in French, *la forêt de Craon*—after the town of Craon in the province of Anjou. A great part of this forest has nevertheless been cut down.]

despising human company and becoming the companion of wild beasts. Who could worthily recount the cruelties with which he wholly afflicted himself there; how many and how great were the crosses by which he sacrificed himself; by what dreadful assaults he wore himself away? Besides such outward observances as wearing a hair-shirt made from pigs’ bristles, shaving his beard without water, scarcely knowing any bedclothes other than the ground, wholly abstaining from wine and rich, fattening foods, and rarely taking the very little sleep to which natural frailty compelled him—there was within him a conflict, a roaring of the mind, a groaning from the innermost places, which one might judge cruel and pitiless, incapable of any final remedy,

[Col. 1050A]

and which many whispered was impossible and excessive for one made of clay in his weakness. For he contended with God in incomparable lamentation and vowed his whole self as a sacrifice. Gentle and modest toward all others, toward himself alone he was hostile, relentless, and harsh.

12. He was cheerful and lively, approachable and discerning, judicious in doubtful matters and ready in answering, to the crowds who came—for many crowds came to see him. There breathed from him, in some manner, the fragrance of divine eloquence; for few equaled him in eloquence. Hence it came about that, on hearing him, many struck their own hearts and renounced their depraved ways of life. Some returned home improved by his preaching; others wished to remain with him

[Col. 1050B]

and serve under him, and begged to cleave to him as steadfast companions. He would voluntarily have fled such crowds and hidden himself alone, had he not feared thereby to incur blame. For he had read: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22:17). He therefore applied himself to distributing the talent entrusted to him, which the Lord, returning from the wedding feast, would require with interest. Thus it seemed to him that he ought to gather many together and give them food, lest they faint on the way; for some of them had come from afar. Those gathered were called Regulars, because they strove to live according to rule after the manner of the primitive Church. Thus there flew together from the world’s allurement that congregation of canons.

[Note: Col. 1050D. Saint Mary of La Roë, or of the Wood, was a house of Canons Regular of the Order of Saint Augustine. Its foundation has already been discussed in the note to the preceding chapter, note 18. Nicquetus writes that it was fifteen leagues from Angers.]

Robert presided over them, teaching them in the honey-producing manner of the most prudent bee.

[Col. 1050C]

They therefore built a common dwelling and diligently embraced the instruction of their teacher.

13. It happened in those days that the Roman pontiff Urban II, compelled by the necessities of the time, came into Gaul and turned aside to Angers. He heard of Robert, for so great a lamp ought not to have been hidden under a bushel. He ordered him to be summoned and earnestly desired conversation with him. He was to celebrate there the solemn dedication of a certain church,

[Note: Col. 1050D. This is the church of Saint Nicholas at Angers, of the Benedictine Order, dedicated by Urban II on 10 February 1096, as Claude Robert and Nicquetus write. Nicquetus, bk. I, ch. 9, enumerates several churches in Gaul dedicated by the same pontiff.]

to which one might have thought the whole expanse of the world had gathered. In that great assembly he commanded Robert to speak:

> And he orders him to employ no unfamiliar speech.

[Col. 1050D]

14. Robert accordingly spoke brilliantly to the people, and his words greatly pleased the lord pope. For he understood that the Holy Spirit had opened Robert’s mouth. Finally, he commanded and enjoined upon him the office of preaching, and, though Robert resisted somewhat, entrusted to him the ministry of this obedience. He appointed him, second only to himself, as a *seminiverbum*—“sower of the word of God”—

[Col. 1051A]

[Note: Col. 1051D. So in both editions. Others read *seminiverbium*.]

and urged him to apply himself to this work everywhere.

15. From that time onward he began eagerly to undertake the mission of the supreme pontiff and to travel through the territories of neighboring bishoprics. He was honored by all, as indeed he deserved to be, for the grace of God plainly went with him. His speech was neither barren nor idle, being commended by the praiseworthy accompaniment both of words and deeds. What he preached he fulfilled in works, lest, while preaching to others and not acting himself, he should immediately be found reprobate. So great a multitude of newcomers attached itself to him that even the number of canons was thought excessive. For the number would soon exceed all number if he added to the canons even a tenth part of those petitioning him.

[Col. 1051B]

Yet he, broad of heart, would have wished to deny no one, had the will and rule of the brethren allowed it. He therefore considered leaving them. But he reflected on how he might accomplish this without causing them distress. They came into the presence of the bishop of Angers,

[Note: Col. 1051D. Geoffrey, concerning whom see Claude Robert and Nicquetus.]

in whose diocese the canons lived; and, after consideration of the matter, at the pope’s command, by the bishop’s advice and with the clergy’s permission, Robert departed freely, so that he might devote himself more freely to preaching and, unencumbered, might advance wherever and among whomever he could.

## CHAPTER III. The Blessed Robert’s preaching; the establishment of the community at Fontevraud and of others; the institution and governance of the order.

[Col. 1051C]

16. Torn from the canons not without shared tears, he began to travel through regions and provinces. At first accompanied by few followers, he scattered the seed of God’s word everywhere through streets and crossroads. Before long many persons of both sexes joined him, because he did not dare reject anyone whom God had inspired. He still had nowhere to lay his head except where necessity compelled him. After leaving the canons, he had not yet wished to choose any place, so that he might proceed freely, without staff and without bag. But seeing the multitude of followers growing, and lest anything be done without deliberation—because women had to live with men

[Note: Col. 1051D. That is, with males, in a French idiom. So shortly below: “he assigned the men to labor”; and in no. 20: “the men were separated from the women.”]

where they might live and conduct themselves without the peril of scandal—

[Col. 1051D]

he determined to search for a wilderness, if one could be found. There was an uncultivated and desolate place, overgrown with thorns and brambles, long called the Fountain of Evraud, not, therefore, as some maintain, after the brigand Ebrald, whom Robert converted there,

[Col. 1052A]

removed from human habitation and about two miles from the cell of Candes, adjoining the diocese of Poitiers.

[Note: Col. 1051D. In this village, now a town, Saint Martin died, as will be said in his Life on 11 November. Nicquetus spells it in French *Candes*; Chevalier calls it *Cande*.]

He chose this little wood or thicket, in which God’s new household and new army might dwell and labor; he received it as a gift from certain proprietors and brought there the mixed recruits of Christendom.

[Note: Col. 1052D. Who these persons were is stated by Peter, bishop of Poitiers, in a charter issued at Poitiers in 1106, in these words: “In our time a certain apostolic man, named Robert, … founded in our diocese a church in honor of Saint Mary the Virgin in the place called Fontevraud. Aremburgis, wife of Guy, son of Osmund, and Rivaria, her daughter, gave him that place to build the aforesaid church, adding land to be cultivated by four oxen in two seasons.” Nicquetus, bk. I, ch. 15, and the Sammarthani, etc., discuss this donation.]

17. For the time being they made there certain little huts, merely sufficient to protect them from the untimely onset of weather. They also built some small oratory, in which God might be invoked and might dwell in the midst of his camp. Those soldiers desired to converse alone with their God and preferred to be refreshed by communion with him. Then they went out to work, so that they might live by the labor of their hands

[Col. 1052B]

and never presume to live in idleness. He nevertheless separated the women from the men and, as it were, confined them within an enclosure, assigning them to prayer; but he assigned the men to labor. He seemed not to do this without discernment, since he entrusted the more delicate and weaker sex to psalmody and contemplation, while applying the stronger to the exercises of the active life. Laymen and clerics went about together; except that the clerics sang psalms and celebrated Masses, while the laymen willingly undertook labor. Silence was enjoined on all at fixed times. They were commanded to answer gently and not to swear, and all were bound together by fraternal love. There was among them no bitterness, no envy, no discord. They walked with bent neck and lowered face; they avoided chattering and knew nothing of idle talk.

[Col. 1052C]

Such was the fellowship of the subjects; such was the rule under which they served. They called their superior only “Master,” for he would not be called either lord or abbot.

18. For a long time he rode no beast of burden, nor tasted wine or savory foods. He always walked barefoot and wore rougher tunics and sackcloth, until, at the advice of priests, when his body had already begun to fail, he put on shoes, mounted a beast, and indulged his frail body somewhat—not for pleasure, but that he might somehow be strengthened for labor. For he took care not to make provision for the flesh in its desires (Rom. 13). He often prolonged fasts, frequently spent the night in prayer, wore down his limbs by long hunger,

[Col. 1052D]

and no hardship made him harsh toward anyone. He utterly uprooted hypocrisy from himself: cheerful and pleasant in countenance, simple and gracious in answering, generous in giving, he allowed little to himself but much to the brothers and

[Col. 1053A]

sisters. In speaking against sinners he seemed vehement; but he consoled those who abandoned sin with fatherly affection. Hence many tax collectors and prostitutes attached themselves to him and obeyed him with all their power. He did not dismiss anyone who had gone astray, but at last cherished each penitent who had been placed in his bosom. His speech could not fail to be effective because, so to speak, he was all things to all: gentle to penitents, stern to the vicious, kind and accommodating to mourners, a rod to the irreverent, a staff to the old and unsteady, groaning in heart, wet-eyed, serene in counsel. I should certainly call him a dwelling-place of Jesus Christ, a temple and instrument of the Holy Spirit, the spokesman and vicar of the Most High.

[Col. 1053B]

19. So great became the throng of those, anointed by his words, who renounced sins, that their number was almost beyond numbering. He wished them to be called by no other name than “the poor of Christ.” Men of every condition flocked together; women came together—poor and noble, widows and virgins, old and young, prostitutes and women who rejected men. The prepared huts no longer held that countless multitude; indeed, Christ’s recruits needed more spacious dwellings. He who fed the children of Israel in the wilderness with his abundant, savory provision supplied every resource for them. In those thickets he also sustained his poor and beggarly little household with food, although they had not yet ploughed, sown, or harvested there. For God inspired all the needy inhabitants dwelling round about

[Col. 1053C]

to send them daily food and prepare for them a daily meal. Nor could this happen without God, who continuously directed the will of the neighboring peasants to send bread. Whatever was present was received with thanksgiving, and God was praised with thanksgiving when anything was lacking. They did not wish to be ungrateful in either condition: they joyfully gave thanks for what was at hand, while awaiting the future with confidence and strengthened by hope. They accepted abundance and endured want without complaint; and in both, God was blessed. Robert went out to seek food, the mother-bee, the most prudent bee, and conversed with everyone. No longer were stews alone sent to God’s household,

[Col. 1053D]

but gifts of every sort of clothing were sent to cover their nakedness, and donations were bestowed to build dwellings. All had one will; all seemed to possess unfailing means. The wealth of the donors appeared to increase, since no want afflicted them as a result of their giving.

[Col. 1054A]

Princes and peoples came to visit God’s new household, emaciated and pale from regular austerity. Nor did they depart fasting, since they first heard there a word of edification and then tasted the bread of charity in fellowship.

## CHAPTER IV. Various monasteries built by the Blessed Robert and others; his piety, miracles, and death.

20. They now pressed on with widening and raising the walls of the oratory; abundant funds were given, necessary supplies offered, and cloisters upon cloisters prepared. Yet not even three or four cloisters sufficed for such great communities of women. The men were separated from the women, and houses upon houses were prepared for them separately in more remote places.

[Col. 1054B]

The prudent Master again separated the women from one another and divided them further into cells and groups. He established both men and women in companies, because the number of each sex was growing with unpretending simplicity. In the larger cloister he housed more than three hundred together; elsewhere he entrusted others in groups of a hundred, sixty, or some other number—more in one place, fewer in another. He likewise assigned the men into distinct companies.

21. He neither wished nor could remain with the workers, because he had to preach to many nations. He therefore appointed one of the sisters, named Hersendis, as assistant and mistress in direction and works. Rejecting the noble rank by which she had been distinguished, she had joined the companies of women;

[Col. 1054C]

indeed, she had been the first convert. Hersendis lived a life of great religious devotion and likewise possessed great judgment. To Hersendis he joined Petronilla, skilled in the management of the household, whom Robert himself afterwards chose as abbess; for Hersendis had already departed to the heavenly realm. Since he knew these two women to be prudent, industrious, and persons of great caution, he set them, as has been said, over the other sisters. But enough of them. Lord Robert was never diverted from preaching or prayer by any small pretext; wholly devoted to strenuous labor, he traveled through neighboring and distant regions. He was received favorably by kings, bishops, and princes, clergy, and people of every kind.

[Col. 1054D]

22. Kings and counts sent lavish gifts into the treasury of the exceedingly poor monastery of Fontevraud.

[Note: Col. 1053D. Nicquetus, bk. I, ch. 22, enumerates many men and women, including princes, who conferred estates and diverse gifts upon the monastery of Fontevraud. A passage in the monastery’s cartulary says: “I, Soficia Rainfredis, daughter of Peter Achard, desiring to receive the religious habit of monks from Lord Robert and the nuns of Fontevraud gathered there under regular discipline, give and grant forever, first myself and then my allodial estate of Polineio.” Nicquetus interprets these words as though she were the first of all the girls to consecrate herself and her property there to God; but their sense seems to me to be that she gives first herself, then her possessions. The same writer rightly observes that people were chiefly prompted by God for two reasons to furnish the necessities of the Fontevraud community with splendid gifts: first, because it gave such abundant assistance to the poor and sick—for God commonly rewards this kind of mercy with abundance of all things; second, because outstanding piety and innocence of character flourished there, so that all desired, as far as possible, to share in the merits and fruit of such exceptional virtue.]

Princes gave, and almost everyone gave, what appeared necessary. Some gave their estates, and each person whatever resources he had chosen.

[Col. 1055A]

Thus in a short time that place grew in houses and oratories, and also in domestic equipment. Moreover, from what was sent they gave abundant alms. They received the poor and did not turn away the infirm; they rejected neither incestuous persons nor concubines, neither lepers nor the disabled. For Robert the Master built both little dwellings and monastic enclosures for lepers and established means by which each might be fed; and, as long as he lived, he himself very humbly visited such persons again and again. He applied himself with all devotion and tears to the celebration of Masses and, so to speak, knowingly admitted nothing irreligious. He alone was lord; he was wholly anxious, though he seemed tranquil amid the crowd. Every conversation of his was moral edification,

[Col. 1055B]

for whatever he said savored of God. Although he needed many stonecutters, masons, and craftsmen of different kinds, he regarded this care as last in importance, for his soul was concerned only with holy religion. Whose pen, do you think, can set Robert forth completely—he whose mind, conscience, and spirit always clung to God? The more I say of Robert, the more astonished I become; for I find even more that remains to be said of him. But since I am altogether unequal to what ought to be said, I cease, overwhelmed as though I had said nothing, and am compelled shamefacedly to cry: “Abundance has made me poor.”

23. Behold, we have discoursed at some length on Robert’s manner of life, worthy of proclamation. Though we may seem to have said something, we have said almost nothing, since we long to express how great was his intimacy with God but cannot do so adequately. For through whom in our days has God worked more abundant miracles? Did not Robert shine clearly as the imitator of him who said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18)? He truly preached the Gospel to the poor, called the poor, and gathered the poor. For if any woman hastened to him from noble rank, one who understands would recognize there Nicodemus and Jesus, Cornelius the centurion and Peter. For the abundance of God’s graces draws all and rejects no one, because he wills all people to be saved

[Col. 1055D]

(1 Tim. 2:4). Let each say what he thinks; I boldly declare Robert abundant in miracles, commanding over demons, glorious above earthly princes. For who in our time cured so many sick, cleansed so many lepers, raised so many dead? He who is of the earth speaks of the earth and marvels at miracles in bodies; but the spiritual person testifies that the sick, lepers, and dead too have recovered whenever anyone tends and heals sick and leprous souls, raising them up. In short—to say it with the consent of all—through whom has the Lord spoken so much and worked so much among pastors?

[Col. 1056A]

24. Our contemporaries—ourselves also, bishops and abbots, clerics and priests—have entered into others’ labors. We have grown fat from the scarcity that those before us endured, and perhaps have made little progress. And, what must be feared, perhaps it has been said in reproach against us: “Their iniquity came forth as from fatness” (Ps. 72:7). This Robert—this Robert, I say—made poor in every way for Christ, exiled from his homeland and his own kindred, surrounded by the crowds to whom he had preached, lest he seem to fail them, built in the solitude of Fontevraud many dwellings for the poor for Christ’s sake, without income from any revenue. There he took care that oratories should be built; he laid the first foundation and the first stone; he gathered servants and handmaids of God to more than two thousand, or nearly three thousand,

[Col. 1056B]

and distributed such great companies of Christians through cells and districts. He prepared the means by which they might be sustained—an undertaking that would have been most difficult for great kings to accomplish in so short a time. Come then: who would not testify that this beggar, this needy man, this poor man, was rich? He was truly rich, since nothing was lacking to him that could suffice for many. Rich, I say, was he who could prepare for God himself, not for himself, so many and such great works as still remain, and who could feed so many crowds in wilderness places. But, to speak more truly, he could not do these things himself; rather, he manifestly merited that they should be done. God was the giver and master; Robert the steward and minister. One poured forth *dapsilōs*—“abundantly”—

[Note: Col. 1055D. That is, generously.]

while the other faithfully distributed the drops.

[Col. 1056C]

They seemed to have between themselves a friendly contest over which could do more: God in supplying, or Robert in distributing. Truly God knew Robert to be a faithful administrator, to whom he had entrusted his household, and he increased the resources. For it is written: “Who then is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has set over his household?” (Matt. 24:45). How indeed could these things happen without God? I confess—and confess truly—that the purposes of those whose works agreed so surely did not conflict. And these too, if you do not know it, are miracles which Blessed Robert performed: to love God, to serve God, for God to answer Lord Robert’s wishes so effectively, and through his hand to provide all things needed by his followers.

[Col. 1056D]

God knew his faith and did not wish to thwart his will. Finally, while he lived, God always exalted his Robert, so that his household might increase daily in his hand and that he might continually bestow the means by which every need should be supplied.

25. Time followed upon time, and Robert never grew cold in the covenant he had made with God: always more fervent in God’s love, always fresh, always more devout. As years passed upon years, Blessed Robert perceived by certain signs that his end was approaching, because, as his limbs failed, he began to be deprived of bodily strength. He determined to go and visit and greet

[Col. 1057A]

the brothers and sisters, and he went. He strengthened all in the Lord and addressed each one with a kindly voice. He commended his passing to his fellow disciples and exhorted them never to grow lukewarm in their good institutions.

26. Having addressed both sexes, and having received Holy Communion, spending himself in a worthy consummation—in such greetings and good exercises—as his illness grew worse, or rather as God called his foster-child, he gave up his spirit at a place called Ursanum,

[Note: Col. 1057A. Rinaldus calls it Ursonium. Nicquetus gives the French name *Orsan*.]

in the hands of his weeping flock,

[Col. 1058A]

and, it is believed, departed to the stars, there to enjoy eternal joys as a perpetual citizen of the heavenly country, or rather, according to the Apostle, as “an heir of God and fellow-heir with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). His little body, moistened with the tears of the rich household of God, especially the handmaids of Christ, was returned to the monastery of Fontevraud and buried in a fitting tomb: while Louis reigned in France,

[Note: Col. 1057A. This is Louis VI, surnamed the Fat, who succeeded his father Philip in 1108 and died on 1 August 1137.]

while Paschal administered the papacy of the city of Rome,

[Note: Col. 1058A. Paschal II has been discussed above. He died on 22 January, in the nineteenth year of his pontificate.]

and while Jesus Christ our Lord reigns through endless ages. Amen.

[Col. 1057]

# THE SECOND LIFE OF THE BLESSED ROBERT OF ARBRISSEL, OR HIS FINAL WAY OF LIFE AND PASSING, by a monk of Fontevraud—believed to be Andrew—his disciple and confessor.

## CHAPTER I. The Blessed Robert’s illness and deliberation concerning the election of an abbess.

[Col. 1057B]

1. The Life of Master Robert having been written in brilliant language by the venerable Baldric, metropolitan of Dol,

[Note: Col. 1057C. Another manuscript: “birth.”]

and his way of life and uprightness of character having also been narrated briefly, it is pleasing

[Note: Col. 1057C. Another manuscript: “it is permitted.”]

to recall in brief for the memory of posterity how he conducted himself near the end of his life and how he passed from this world. Yet I make known to the reader of this work that I shall not record in this treatise everything that ought to be said, but shall rather indicate briefly what is to be said. For if I wished to recount in detail all that the Lord deigned to accomplish through him during the final year of his life, I confess that, oppressed by so great a weight, I should collapse even against my will. But since my little talent possesses scarcely any knowledge for investigating these matters, may the grace of the Holy Spirit be with me through the interceding merits of him of whom I am to speak.

[Col. 1058B]

2. First, however, it must be said why Robert was so called, for he did not receive such a name without divine dispensation. For he was called Robert as though *roboratus*, “strengthened,” or *robore certus*, “made sure by strength.”

[Note: Col. 1057C. This etymology is not satisfactory. The name was formed from the Teutonic, or Sicambrian, language used by the ancient Franks. Concerning it, at the end of Jean Robert’s *Hubertine Questions*, our Arnoldus Bocopius derives it from *Ru*, meaning “rest,” and *bert* or *beart*, meaning “endowed with disposition,” so that it means, as it were, naturally tranquil; or from *Rot* or *Root*, “red,” so that it means red or ruddy; or from *rot*, “troop” or “order,” as though inclined by disposition toward military companionships. Others derive it elsewhere. At any rate, it is not a Latin word.]

And in truth he was strengthened, since the Holy Spirit strengthened him continually to act well. He was also made sure by the strength of faith, and persevered in holy religion to the end. Of him a certain religious man, melodious in verse, said not without merit:

> If you seek one like him, none will be found.  
> What and how great he was, the fruit that bears witness makes known.

3. This Robert, then, after having for many years preached without weariness and distributed God’s words not only among neighboring peoples but also among foreign nations, suddenly began to fail in strength as his bodily weakness and other former illnesses grew worse.

[Col. 1058C]

Finally, at Fontevraud, compelled by the necessity of illness, he lay in his bed and ordered all the brothers living in that place to be summoned to him. When all had quickly assembled,

[Note: Col. 1058C. Another manuscript: “to whom.”]

he said: “Behold, my dearest sons,

[Col. 1059A]

whom I have begotten in the Gospel: afflicted with bodily sickness, I am entering upon the way of all flesh. Therefore deliberate among yourselves while I am still alive whether you wish to remain in your purpose: namely, that for the salvation of your souls you should obey the command of the handmaids of Christ. For you know that whatever I have built anywhere, with God’s help, I have subjected to their authority and dominion. But if you do not wish to remain with them as you have begun, I grant you leave, though with my counsel, to enter another religious order.” On hearing this, almost all said with one voice: “Far be it from us, dearest father, ever to leave them, since, as you yourself testify, we can by no means do better elsewhere! Far be it from us,” they said, “to abandon your counsel! Rather, before God and his saints, we all unanimously and freely promise stability and perseverance to the Church of Fontevraud in your hand.”

[Col. 1059B]

4. Thus the congregation of our brothers and sisters having been brought into agreement, he wished to provide for the welfare of his posterity, taught, I think, by divine inspiration. For after a few days had passed, while he burned daily with fever, he sent for several bishops and abbots and announced through messengers that he wished to seek their counsel.

[Note: Col. 1059D. The passage from here to “I perceive” was absent from Cosnier’s edition; Cosnier himself nevertheless wrote to me that he had found it in another manuscript.]

And because at that time the Church of Poitiers, deprived of its own protector,

[Note: Col. 1059D. Namely Peter, who suffered much at the hands of Duke William and died holy in exile, as William of Malmesbury and, following him, others report.]

was suffering under Prince William, he ordered several leading men of that church to be summoned to his council.

[Col. 1059C]

At length, when a considerable assembly of religious and noble persons had gathered, he disclosed to it the purpose for which he had caused so great a multitude to assemble. “My brothers,” he said, “I perceive that my end is near. Therefore I summoned you so that through your counsel I may beneficially provide for the welfare of our church concerning the election of an abbess.” All replied unanimously and reverently: “Your counsel, dearest Father, ought rather to be followed in this matter, especially since we know for certain that your counsel flourishes among all other mortals of our age. God gave you to the world as a counselor of souls, and with his aid it is very easy for you to provide counsel for the future life of your people.”

[Col. 1059D]

5. Then he said to them: “You know, my dearest friends, that whatever I have built in the world I made for the service of our nuns, and that I have granted them full authority over all my resources; and, what is greater than this, for the salvation of our souls, I have subjected both myself and my disciples to their service. Therefore, with your counsel, I have resolved, while I am still alive, to appoint an abbess for this congregation, lest—God forbid!—after my death someone presume to oppose this determination of mine. And therefore,

[Col. 1060A]

according to the admonition of the Wise Man, I wish to do all things with counsel, so that after acting I may not repent (Ecclus. 32:24). For one who conducts his affairs without the counsel of elders shows himself to be indiscreet. I ask one thing of you: may I appoint as abbess a laywoman who has been converted? So that, when this is done, your authoritative

[Note: Col. 1060D. Another manuscript, as Cosnier observed, reads “your,” perhaps better.]

authority may restrain any detractors who may arise. For I know the dignity of this order; I know that it requires a virgin. Indeed, it is written that one who guards virgins ought to be a virgin. But how can any cloistered virgin fittingly administer our external affairs, when she knows nothing except how to sing psalms? What rational care can she have of earthly matters when she has always been accustomed to practice spiritual things? How, I ask, will she bear the burden of the practical life,

[Col. 1060B]

when she knows only the joys of contemplation? By what reasoning will that tongue answer concerning external matters, which from childhood has been accustomed to speak with the Lord in prayer, singing, and reading? It is also most difficult to compel one who rejoices that she has already washed her feet to put on again the tunic of temporal things which she has cast off. For I have read: ‘A wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one destroys what has been built’ (Prov. 14:1). For this reason I do not wish to entrust this office of superiority to any cloistered virgin, lest I seem—may it never happen!—to destroy what I have built. For if I knowingly entrust this care to one who does not know how to perform it, I may rightly be blamed for what I have built with God’s cooperation. Let there therefore be chosen, if it pleases you, a coarse sackcloth covering, which may cover the tabernacle of the Lord on every side and bravely withstand the storms of external affairs,

[Col. 1060C]

so that scarlet of perfect color may shine red within (Exod. 26:7). Let Mary continually long for heavenly things, and let Martha be chosen who knows how diligently to minister in external matters” (Luke 10).

6. When they heard this, the elders who were present gave their assent and affirmed that all he had said was true. And so that this judgment of Master Robert might be held firm and inviolable for ever, there was present at this council a certain archpriest of Angers, a man of good conduct. He declared that, when he had once been at Rome, he had heard Pope Urban—namely, the one who had enjoined upon our Robert the office of preacher—grant that a certain [Col. 1060D] matron, who had had four husbands, should become abbess for a time and because of the need of a certain church. The venerable man knew well that what the necessity of our human frailty compels, without injury to the faith, divine mercy—maintaining its moderation everywhere—does not punish. When this became known, those councillors rejoiced; and, because the prudent man wished to act prudently, they all spoke in agreement. When the venerable assembly had ended, they confirmed the wise man’s counsel with praise, and went back joyfully, doubly satisfied, to their own homes.

## CHAPTER II. The election of Abbess Petronilla; the ordinances of Blessed Robert

[Col. 1061A]

7. When the seventh month had passed since the aforesaid council had assembled, and the end of October was now approaching, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November [28 October], our fosterling, with the counsel of religious men, fulfilled what he had requested from the aforesaid council. Thus he chose to the dignity of so great an honour Petronilla of Camilliac.

> [Note: Col. 1061D] She is called Chemilliac by others, as we said above on Nicquet’s authority.

She had abandoned her paternal possessions and had been his disciple almost from the beginning of his religious life. Yet he first took the sound counsel of several wise persons, saying:

> “It seems fitting to me that she who shared with me the hardship of pilgrimage and poverty should also bear whatever burden may attend our consolation and prosperity. For although [Col. 1061B] she has been the wife of one man, nevertheless, under compelling necessity, no one seems to me more suited to this pre-eminence. For, more than the others, she knows our resources, and, according to the Apostle, knows both how to abound and how to suffer want [Phil. 4:12]. She knows how to give a timely answer to the wise, and also how suitably to accommodate herself to the unlearned.”

8. Once what the eminent teacher had done became publicly known, not only our brethren, but also secular persons, praised this election.

> [Note: Col. 1061D] Therefore, in the archive of the Order, cited by Nicquet in book I, chapter 28, she is said to have become “Mother by the grace of God and by the election of all”; and likewise: “Petronilla was elected by Master Robert and established as abbess by the common will and request both of the nuns and of the religious brethren.”

Finally, once the election had been made known to Petronilla herself, it would take long to relate how she wished to flee, or by what means she tried to decline her election. Not without reason—for it was indeed something to be feared—she dreaded taking upon herself the immeasurable burden of honour belonging to so great an office. [Col. 1061C] On the one hand, as a wise woman, she feared her own weakness; on the other, she considered the immeasurable magnitude of the office itself. What more need be said? Although she resisted greatly, at last, God consenting, overcome by the prayers of her own people—or rather, constrained by obedience to Master Robert—she consented. There is much besides, worthy of narration, that I could tell about her way of life. But since I confess myself to be her son, though unworthy, I am silent for the present, lest—God forbid!—I should be judged to be anointing her head with the oil of flattery. Thus, after the election of our most beloved mother had been carried out in this manner with the common consent of religious men, each returned home.

[Col. 1061D] 9. Not long afterward, when the oft-mentioned Robert had, by God’s favour, begun to recover somewhat from his illness, he sought confirmation of the election already described through the authority of Gerard, the venerable legate of the people of Angoulême.

> [Note: Col. 1061D] This Gerard was, as we indicated above, an apostolic legate in the time of Paschal II, a distinguished man; but afterward he obstinately supported the party of Anacletus against Innocent II. These events occurred at least one year before the death of Paschal II, namely toward the end of the year 1116.

Gerard not only approved on his own part the action of the wise man, but also—and this was more important—caused a privilege of Paschal, Pope of Rome, concerning the election made by Robert to be obtained by envoys whom he sent. Hence it happened that our Robert gave a general command to the abbess whom he had chosen: no woman from among those brought up in the cloister of Fontevraud was ever to become abbess there.

> [Note: Col. 1062D] Nicquet nevertheless observes that, after Petronilla, only two abbesses who governed the Order had not vowed virginity to God in a monastery from their earliest years. These two were Matilda, whom we mentioned above as betrothed to the son of Henry I, king of England; and Mary, daughter of Theobald the Great, count of Champagne, widow of Odo II, duke of Burgundy, who was the seventh abbess.

For the holy man knew well that many churches had been ruined through the negligence and inexperience of abbesses who had been raised in cloisters. And so that this command might be kept inviolably by his successors, it was committed to the custody of written documents among his other ordinances, which were written down at Fontevraud and are preserved to this day.

[Col. 1062B] 10. For Robert, that lamp of hermits, gave certain commands to his religious community: namely, that both men and women should unanimously preserve the holiness of their religious vocation in speech, conduct, food, and clothing. The man worthy of praise by every mouth knew indeed that religion is vain when it is constantly accompanied by unrestrained speech. He knew also that one boasts in vain of possessing faith unless one follows that same faith with good works; for, as the Apostle James testifies, “Faith without works is dead” [Jas. 2:20]. The kindly man had also read, “It is good not to eat flesh” [Rom. 14:21]. Therefore he wished both himself and his household to abstain from such food for the love of God. Finally, he knew how a coarse garment displays contempt for the world; [Col. 1062C] and for this reason he wished both himself and those subject to him to be clothed in humbler garments. For he used to tell us that garments sufficient for all religious persons were those able to ward off the cold of human frailty, not those able to adorn a body destined one day to die; such adornment is undoubtedly blameworthy and worldly.

Yet this was the rule concerning clothing established by him in our religious order: in accordance with the teaching of Saint Benedict, neither our brothers nor our sisters were to be reproached for the natural colour, coarseness, or width of their clothing [Rule, ch. 55]. But anyone who wishes to know these commands in full should humbly seek them at Fontevraud, where they were written down both out of love for so great a man and because of the greatness of the gift.

## CHAPTER III. Peace restored among those at variance; the works of Blessed Robert; new monasteries built and visited

[Col. 1062D]

11. This Robert of whom we speak had, with God’s help, built several dwellings in different provinces. In them he enclosed communities of nuns, tested in the divine religious life of the cloister of Fontevraud, according to what was suitable to the places; and he assigned some of our brethren to serve them. Moreover, he had this unbending custom: wherever he caused monasteries for his nuns to be built, he always constructed them in honour of Saint Mary ever-virgin. And because Saint John the Evangelist, at Christ’s command, served that same Virgin diligently as a devoted master—until she ceased to live bodily in the world—

> [Note: Col. 1063D] Another manuscript reads “minister.”

—the prudent man decreed that the brothers’ oratories should be dedicated in John’s veneration. I believe this was done not without divine inspiration, so that the brothers might rejoice in having as patron of their oratories [Col. 1063B] the very one whose example of service to the brides of Christ they possessed. Yet I do not say this because I wish to compare our service with John’s delightful attendance; for I firmly believe that this most excellent Virgin, set in heaven beside her Son, is unique and without an equal.

12. Those dwellings in which the memorable man, with the advice of neighbouring bishops, enclosed the Lord’s sheep, he frequently visited in the manner of a good shepherd, so that if at any time, through diabolical persuasion, any seeds of vices should spring up, he might uproot them completely so far as he was able. It happened that a deserted place was granted to him in Gaul, with the permission of Louis, king of the Franks; it is now commonly called Haute-Bruyère.

> [Note: Col. 1063D] This was Louis VI, of that name, as stated before.

> [Note: Col. 1063D] Others call it Alta Brueria, in French Haute-Bruyère. It is eight leagues from Paris. There Bertrada, repudiated by King Philip, ended her life piously. In the bull by which he confirmed the Order in 1119, Callixtus II speaks of this monastery as follows, in Nicquet, chapter 31: “We confirm the enclosure of Aubert, by gift of Louis, king of the Franks; the place Haute-Bruyère, by gift of the aforesaid king and of Bertrea, his stepmother, from whose dower it came.”

He truly disdained to establish communities of his holy religious order within castles or villages, clearly recognizing that such places were harmful to the purpose of holy religion. Once the place had been built, within a few years of the events of which we speak, he sent some of our sisters ahead to it through our Abbess Petronilla, whom he himself had chosen; the place had chiefly been built for them. The venerable man himself followed them there attentively and without delay.

13. One day they came, for hospitality, into the territory of Chartres, to the village of Bonneval, where there was an abbey of monks.

> [Note: Col. 1064D] It is an abbey of the Benedictine Order.

At that time Ivo was governing the bishopric of Chartres.

> [Note: Col. 1064D] The celebrated Ivo of Chartres, renowned for learning and holiness; various works of his survive.

For certain reasons he had fallen out so severely with Bernard, abbot of Bonneval—

> [Note: Col. 1064D] Another manuscript calls him Bernerius, as Cosnier observed; and so Nicquet printed him in no. 31.

—that their disagreement was almost irreconcilable. Many religious persons had repeatedly tried to reconcile them, but could not restore peace between them. When the pious [Col. 1064A] master heard reluctantly of so great a discord, he deeply grieved for those who were at variance and began to consider how he could make peace between them.

He therefore sent his nuns ahead to their appointed place through Angardis, a religious nun who was then prioress of Fontevraud. But he himself, joined by the religious Abbot Bernard—

> [Note: Col. 1064D] This is the Abbot of Tiron, as this same writer relates.

—and his own Abbess Petronilla, hurried to Chartres to reconcile the aforesaid dispute. For the peaceful man was grieved that teachers of the Church should faithlessly submit to the freedom of detestable dissension. And, to tell the truth, when the prudent preacher, led by charity, arrived at Chartres, although he laboured greatly, he not only utterly destroyed that demonic discord, but also restored them to their former friendship—something many had already thought impossible.

14. When peace had been restored among the teachers of the holy Church, and the Lord’s Nativity was approaching, the aforesaid mediator of the dispute went to the place of Haute-Bruyère mentioned shortly before. There he celebrated the Lord’s Nativity with his beloved daughters, whom not long before he had sent to the same place through Angardis.

> [Note: Col. 1064D] Another reading: Augardis. The material which follows, down to no. 26, was absent from Cosnier’s edition, but was later supplied from another manuscript through his efforts.

Constant in fasts, outstanding in prayers, insatiable in reading, spending whole nights in vigils, overflowing in tears, admirable in teaching—by how many means he offered himself to God upon the altar of his heart, and what fruit he gained for the Lord among his household or the crowds gathering to him, remains, I think, unknown to other mortals even now.

15. At length, once the splendid feast of the Lord’s Incarnation had been celebrated in that place with the greatest reverence, and once the community of the Lord’s sheepfold there had been ordered inwardly and outwardly, he was again summoned to Chartres. For the bishop of Chartres whom we mentioned above had now died, and another had been enthroned in his place by the common election of the clergy. But such an uproar prevailed between the clergy and the count of that city that some of the canons, stripped of their property, feared that by the count’s order they would be mutilated limb by limb. Several powerful persons had gathered at Chartres because of this affair. At last Abbot Bernard, worthy of the remembrance of all good people, came also; his praise endures to this day throughout all the churches of Gaul. But entirely in vain: they could no longer calm that dispute; indeed, at the instigation of the enemy of all good, it grew daily. The ruler of that city had already plundered the canons’ houses and shut them up [Col. 1065A] within their cloister. And—something even shameful to say—he had driven from the city that eminent man named Geoffrey, whom the clergy had canonically enthroned in the episcopal chair in place of the dead bishop.

16. But why delay? For the canons themselves, their only hope after God now rested in our Robert. Hence they sent envoys and with every supplication sought his assistance. The canons knew well that God had granted such favour to the man of whom we speak that He who can do all things might deign to accomplish through him what was wholly impossible for others. Though held by a most severe illness, when asked whether he could come to Chartres, he replied that all things were possible for him [Col. 1065B] up to the point of death.

When he arrived, however much our tongue may be silent, the result of what was done plainly shows how truly he was a servant of God. For the Lord had bestowed such grace upon him that not only all religious people revered him, but kings and princes also most willingly obeyed his command. It was fitting that the creature should love the one whom it did not doubt was loved by the Creator, as the evidence of his works showed. Speaking to both parties according to the wisdom given him by God, and with God’s grace at work, he uprooted from the depths that entire diabolical contrivance. For at his urging, the count of the aforesaid city restored to the clergy everything he had taken from them; and, accepting the election of that Geoffrey—

> [Note: Col. 1065D] He was the successor of Ivo. In the *Life of Saint William*, 10 February, book 3, no. 12, he is called “a man of virtue, full of the spirit of counsel and strength.”

—who had been canonically elected to govern the bishopric, he allowed him to return to the city, [Col. 1065C] and, what is likewise pleasant to relate, canonically joined him in their former friendship. I believe that the Lord wished to extinguish this deadly slaughter through his beloved Robert in order that those who did not know might learn how great was the merit our Robert possessed before Him.

It is beyond my ability to investigate what blessings, or how great, the Lord deigned in those days to bestow upon the aforesaid city through His servant. Yet it is pleasant to report that the Simoniac heresy, which had long defiled the basilica of the canons of Chartres, was extinguished in perpetual condemnation by our Robert—with the consent of Bishop Geoffrey, whose life gives forth a most sweet fragrance even in our own age, and with the consent of all the canons of that same community, from greatest to least. [Col. 1065D] And so that this execrable plague might be condemned altogether in that church for ever, they confirmed by oath the vow they made.

## CHAPTER IV. Captives visited by Blessed Robert; robbers softened by kindness; events at Ursan and at the abbey of Déols

17. Once the people of Chartres had been reconciled, the faithful steward of the Lord’s word left the city of Chartres, never to return to it thereafter. Joined by the venerable Bernard, abbot of Tiron, whose company had always been most welcome to him, both arrived together at the castle commonly called Blois.

> [Note: Col. 1065D] Blois, or Blaesae, is a city on the Loire, above Tours. Concerning it, the *Life of Saint Aigulphus, Abbot of Lérins*, 3 September, says: “The castle of Blois is situated on the side of a mountain, beside which lies the shore of the river Loire; as it flows past, the Loire provides that place, beyond the abundance of fish which it supplies there more generously than elsewhere, with a great bounty also of other produce—wine, grain, and the other necessities of human life.” In French it is called Blois.

In this same castle William, the religious count of Nevers, was held in prison because he had supported Louis, king of the Franks, against the count of Chartres in maintaining peace.

> [Note: Col. 1066D–1067D] This was William III, count of Nevers. Near the end of his life he entered the Carthusian Order, indeed in the rank and condition of a lay brother, as they call it; but he died during his novitiate, 20 August 1148. So Nicquet.

This William was beloved by both men because of the merits of his life. Clearly, that count then held honourable rank, since these two pillars of the holy Church came to visit him in prison. He is said to have been so strengthened that he declared: “Who would not rejoice to be imprisoned for a long time, if he could be visited by such men?” I have said this in order to show that our Robert did not give himself to idleness, but at one time visited prisoners according to the Gospel command, and at another recalled those at variance to peace.

Having visited the count dear to him and comforted him beyond what his prison punishment required, these two visitors—never thereafter to see one another in this life—were separated, so to speak, inseparably. They were inseparably separated because those whom charity joins are not divided by the distance between lands. For the bond of perfect charity is indissoluble, since, as Blessed Augustine says: “Charity which can be divided was never true.” Oh, if they could then have known that they would no longer see one another in this mortal flesh! I believe certainly that they would scarcely, or never, have parted from one another while still alive in the flesh, especially if they had known their deaths to be so near.

18. Abbot Bernard then returned to his own place. But our shepherd turned his path toward the province of Bourges, distributing in many ways the talent entrusted to him. The provident man knew that for all those whom someone builds up by his example, he will receive from the Lord a reward of recompense on the Day of Judgment. For as a fruitful bee-garden scatters its swarms in every direction, so our most loving Father distributed sweetly teeming companies of nuns from the cloister of Fontevraud among other places. From this mystical bee-garden of venerable bees, he had formerly dispersed very many of our sisters throughout the district of Bourges; and, having first prepared a wooden cloister, he had settled them in a place called Ursan by the people. Because of his love for them, he was now undoubtedly preparing to visit those parts also, to instruct them in the faith.

19. But if we wish to recount one thing that happened to him on the journey, we shall make plain to our successors [Col. 1067A] how great were his patience and holiness. For, as one of our brothers named Peter—a priest eminent in rank, faithful in word and life, who was with him at that time—told us: while they were making their intended journey, one day they fell among robbers. In accordance with their custom, filled with an evil spirit, they not only took the beasts belonging to his companions, but also—and this was more serious—seized by the reins the mount on which that most gentle man sat, insulted him, and set him down upon the ground. But he, being kind, began gently to rebuke them in a dove-like voice and exhorted them with mild words to refrain from robbery. Surely the merciful man grieved more over their ruin than over the distress caused to himself or his companions.

[Col. 1067B] 20. But his companion Peter, from whose account I learned this, unable calmly to bear what had been done to his master, addressed the robbers in these words:

> “Tell me, wretches, where will you flee, you who were not afraid to harass such a great man? Consider, I beseech you, consider what reverence must be shown to holy men, so that at least your madness may cease to be hostile in this way. For, as the Holy Scriptures say, holy men are temples of God. ‘For the temple of God is holy,’ says the Apostle, ‘and you are that temple’ [1 Cor. 3:17]. Therefore, whenever any holy person is provoked to anger, it is surely evident that God, the inhabitant of that temple, is provoked to vengeance. Let your fury then cease; and let fruitful repentance blot out the evil which you have committed against God’s holy man. Do you not know that this man, [Col. 1067C] whom you have just unjustly thrown down from his horse, is Robert of Arbrissel, whose sweet fragrance fills the whole world?”

When they heard Robert’s name, the band of robbers was immediately struck with fear, fell at the holy man’s feet, and begged earnestly for pardon. Rejoicing in their repentance and graciously granting their request, he calmly forgave everything they had done wrongly against him, raised them from his feet, and kissed them kindly. He not only granted the forgiveness they sought, but also, though they deserved it less because of their sin, made them participants in the whole of his beneficence.

21. O ineffable man, abounding in wondrous mercy! With God’s help, prosperity did not deceive him, nor did adversity overcome him. For since, as it is written, “The teaching of a man is known through patience” [Prov. 19:11], it is plainly clear how great Robert’s patience was, and how excellent his teaching, since in the manner we have described he rewarded even his enemies. Let us consider, if we can, with what ardour of love this man of blessed memory loved his friends, since in accordance with the Lord’s command [Col. 1068A] he voluntarily bestowed such great benefits even on his adversaries. Since Scripture says, “Whatever happens to him will not grieve the righteous” [Prov. 12:21], it is clearly apparent how lofty was this man’s righteousness: neither provoked by injuries nor even for the sake of friends did he depart from the straight course of the way.

Brothers, I may say that in this action the man was comparable to Saint Samuel, who, wishing to repay his enemies, promised to pray for them [1 Sam. 12:23]. Nor did he differ from the one who said, “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” [Ps. 119:7]. What, then, shall we miserable people say before God within his congregation, we who do not even love our friends as we ought?

22. Once the lover of peace had in some manner peacefully left the enemies of peace, he came, not without a preceding dispensation of faith, to the place of Ursan toward which he was travelling. There he remained about fifteen days with his beloved sons and daughters, tirelessly devoted to reading, prayer, preaching, and the other exercises of virtues. For he was awaiting Abbess Petronilla there, who was to come to him from Fontevraud. When she arrived, he decided to go out to places beyond, for the usefulness of preaching. Certain people, greatly hungry for the words of his preaching, had begged him to deign to impart to them the benefit of holy preaching. Assenting to their pious prayers and wishing, with God’s help, to satisfy their desirable hunger, he set out upon the journey already begun. Accompanied by Petronilla and several others, one day he arrived for hospitality at the abbey of Déols.

> [Note: Col. 1067D–1068D] Masson, in his book *On the Rivers of Gaul*, mentions the monastery of Déols, apart from Claudius Robert; he says it is situated on the river Anger or Angerim, called Andria by some, in French the Indre. The village of Déols itself lies in the territory of Bourges and is commonly called Déols, Bourg de Déols, Bourg-Dieu, or Bourg-Dol. It belongs to the Benedictine Order.

The monks of that monastery received him joyfully and honourably offered him the duties of hospitality; with the utmost humility they begged him to deign to refresh their souls with the nourishment of holy preaching.

23. Moved by their prayers, the Lord’s generous sower of the word entered the monks’ chapter-house on the following day with some of his companions. There, delivering at length the final sermon he would make to the people, he taught his hearers—by rebuking, entreating, and reproving them—to turn from evil and do good, with such sweetness, piety, mercy, devotion, prudence, charity, simplicity, and discernment that even those privileged to be present confess themselves unable to relate it. But what wonder if he fulfilled this discourse so excellently, when God had given the world through him so many and such great discourses, almost incomparable, as those allowed to hear them testify? For the Lord had given him such grace in holy preaching that whenever he made a general address [Col. 1069A] to the people, each person received what suited that person. His preaching was not ineffective, but crushed the hearts of his hearers so powerfully that it was plainly understood who was present there. The Holy Spirit was surely present, without whose aid the teacher’s outward discourse labours in vain.
