Of this it is also written: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father” [Matt. 10:20].

When he had ended that sermon, he completely reconciled to himself, in that same place, those monks who had a certain complaint against the Church of Fontevraud; and he also reconciled with them a certain prince of that land named Alard.

## CHAPTER V. The final illness of Blessed Robert, the reception of the viaticum, and holy anointing

[Col. 1069B]

24. Once these things had been done, he instructed Petronilla and Angardis, the administrators of Fontevraud who were with him, to go and visit the brothers and sisters. But he himself, with his chaplain Andrew—

> [Note: Col. 1069D] If Andrew was the author of this Life and was Robert’s companion on this journey, how is it that, concerning the events in the preceding chapter, no. 20, he says that he “learned them from Peter’s narration,” although he himself had witnessed them?

—went on to the people who, as we said above, eagerly desired his preaching and repeatedly begged for it. On the very day on which he left the monastery of Déols—considered to be Friday—he began frequently to dismount from his horse during the journey and to tell his companions that he was becoming very ill. When they said to him, “Dearest Father, return, we beg you, return, lest your illness weigh more heavily upon you,” he answered: “Do not, my sons, do not say such things to me; rather let us go [Col. 1069C] as far as the town called Graçay, so that, when the people to whom I promised my coming hear that I have arrived there, if I cannot undertake the journey I began, they may at least believe that I returned under the compulsion of necessity.”

On arriving at the aforesaid castle, they lodged there.

> [Note: Col. 1070D] It is called Grassay or Graçay in French, a town in the territory of Bourges.

25. But on the following day, Saturday, our teacher was so severely burdened by illness that he could no longer ride at all. When he perceived this, he said to his companions: “My dearest ones, prepare for me a wooden bier and carry me back to the place of Ursan, for I know that I shall die of this illness.” When his host heard this, he said to him: “Master, I beg you, do not do what you say; rather rest here until you see whether you can recover from this sickness.” But he privately said to his companions: “Whatever others may say, pay no attention; quickly do what I have commanded you.”

It is clear that he felt his death approaching; but, lest his community should have trouble on account of his body, he wished to return to Ursan while he was alive. Therefore, once the wooden bier had been prepared as he ordered, they carried him to the castle called Issoudun, and lodged there.

> [Note: Col. 1070D] Issoudun in French, a town in the territory of the same people of Bourges.

The host who received him began in many ways to beg them [Col. 1070A] to permit him to care for their sick man. When this reached Master Robert’s ears, he summoned his companions and said: “My sons, do not agree to our host’s plan; rather, as I have already told you, take me back to Ursan.” And because he had sent Petronilla and Angardis, as stated above, to visit the Lord’s flock in other places, foreseeing that his end was near, he sent a messenger after them, directing them to come quickly to Ursan to visit him.

26. At dawn they left Issoudun and carried the most holy sick man to Ursan, as he himself had ordered. At that time a noble nun named Agnes held the priory of Ursan. She was exceedingly dear to him because, by his counsel, she had abandoned the deceptive riches of the world, which had greatly flattered her, and had chosen poverty for Christ. When she learned how severe her master’s illness was, it is not easy to say how great was her grief. For who could tell how great was the sorrow of the brothers and sisters of that place when they heard of our teacher’s grave illness? They truly feared being deprived of so great and such a shepherd.

As evening approached on the Lord’s Day on which he had been carried to Ursan, sick but *sanus* (‘sound’ or ‘healthy’? uncertain), he began lovingly to repeat the name of Fontevraud: “O Fontevraud, Fontevraud, how greatly I had hoped to lie in you!” When Andrew, his faithful companion, said to him, “Noble master, what are you saying? If you feel that your end is here, at least do what lies within your power: command that your body be carried to Fontevraud after your death,” he replied: “And why should my corpse be carried from here? For it would be taken from you through every *busnachia* [meaning uncertain; perhaps ‘ambush’ or ‘obstruction’].”

27. On the next day, namely Monday, he asked to be given the viaticum of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since he foresaw that he was about to set out on a more distant journey, he requested that most saving viaticum with the humblest devotion; without it every traveller, wandering, goes completely astray. When the Lord’s body was brought to him, he began with inward groans and deep sighs to ask from it gratuitous mercy, to call himself an unprofitable servant, and to accuse himself in all his works. Yet the wise reader knew that God had commanded thus: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants,’” etc. [Luke 17:10]. For he imitated that righteous man who, though perfect, confessed that he feared all his works. He made a twofold lament: he grieved greatly because he had sometimes transgressed the Lord’s commands; on the other hand, he repented because he had not observed all the commandments. And, to summarize his words, [Col. 1071A] he wept and wailed that in every respect he had been an unprofitable servant.

After he had accused himself beyond measure, received penance, presumed nothing from his own merits, and continually entreated mercy, he received the Lord’s body. Let those hear this who dare indiscreetly to receive the Lord’s body to their own condemnation: let them either erase their sins through holy penance while they may, or, if they refuse, at least fear to receive so wondrous a sacrament unworthily. For the Apostle plainly cries: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily,” etc. [1 Cor. 11:29; the supplied citation reads v. 19]. If so great and such a man received the most sacred body of the Lord with such fear, how much more must we sinners approach trembling and weeping; even if we have made much progress, [Col. 1071B] we do not dare to make our own end equal in worth to his.

28. When Monday had passed, because the good man did not doubt that his end was near, he wished, as a most Christian man, to receive in himself all the sacraments of holy Church. Therefore, on Tuesday he devoutly requested to be anointed with blessed oil, believing indeed the words of the Apostle James (5:15), namely that through the operation of this mystery sins are forgiven to human beings. Having been anointed with the saving unguent, he again fortified himself, not without inward groaning, with the body of the Lord. Nor did he fortify himself with Christ’s Eucharist only on those two days, but on every day during which he lay in that illness. But who could tell how, or in what ways, he always strove to accuse himself before the body of the Lord [Col. 1071C]? Those who were worthy to be present testify that they do not know whether he ever accused himself more severely before the body of the Lord. No robber—no robber indeed [Note: Cosnier’s edition reads “shame”; but he later noted that another manuscript has “robber”]—in short, no thief so accused himself. For since it is written, “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17), it is surely clear that he himself was righteous, who, although he had lived a singular life, nevertheless accused himself in so many ways.

## CHAPTER VI. Burial requested by Blessed Robert at Fontevraud

29. At that same time Leodegarius, a man flourishing in life and years, held the archbishopric of the diocese of Bourges. An inseparable affection, unless I am mistaken, united him closely to Master Robert; for, I think, they were joined to one another by so great a love that what one wished the other would scarcely refuse. I could indeed recount many praises of Leodegarius’s virtues; but because he is still sailing uncertainly amid the countless storms of this exile, human ignorance itself compels me, willing or unwilling, to be silent. For not everyone who has begun, but the one who has persevered unto the end, shall be saved. [Note: He died, as the learned Robert writes, 31 March 1120; from this it is clear when this Life was written.]

Accordingly Robert, of happy memory, sent a messenger to him and requested him, with entreaties, to deign to visit him. [Col. 1072A] On hearing of his illness, Leodegarius hastened devoutly to visit him. When he arrived, he ordered that very small town to be carefully guarded by his servants day and night; for he feared to be deprived of so great a patron, and therefore commanded that the little town itself be diligently watched. Not only did the archbishop of Bourges then visit our Robert, but certain princes of that land also came to visit him attentively. Likewise, the people of Orsan fortified their town diligently with guards, saying that they would count themselves blessed if they deserved to be adorned by so great a patron. All who came to visit him received from him, assuredly, the reward of consolation. Although he was infirm in body, he nevertheless endeavoured, as was his custom, to offer salutary exhortations of preaching to the people standing around.

30. Meanwhile the messenger who had been sent after the abbess reached La Puye [Note: French, *La Puye*]. Finding her there, he immediately explained why he had come after her and urged her to return quickly to Orsan. She, together with Angardis, who was with her, terrified by so sad a message, knew no delay in setting out, but departed from La Puye before daybreak. At length they came, miserable and weeping, to Orsan. When they came before the sick man, still alive, Petronilla cried out and said: “Alas, good master! From now on you will do no good thing for us.” But Angardis [Note: Another manuscript: “sent.”], who had come with her, gently rebuked her, saying: “Cease, good woman, to speak such words; rather ask God that he may deign still to grant him health. For he who gave him this illness will, when it pleases him, also grant health.” Some also said that he would not die from that illness; but he himself declared otherwise.

31. It would indeed take long to recount in detail how the wise sick man, in this illness, endeavoured to admonish visitors of both sexes with speech seasoned with salt. But, since I do not wish to weary my reader, I wish to proceed to the things that he did on the third day before his end. Therefore, on Wednesday before his death, he ordered [Note: Another manuscript, as above: “Augardis.”] the venerable Leodegarius, archbishop of Bourges—who, as we have said, had come to visit him—to be summoned to him, and said:

“O dearest Father, you are my archbishop, my primate, and [Col. 1072D] patriarch. You know how I have always loved you until now and how I have obeyed you. You also know that I first came into these regions because of my sweet love for you. For you asked me to give you some of my good women, and I gave them to you. At your command and request I sent them into this province. As you know, I had here neither houses nor any possessions nor lands. For the salvation of your soul and those of your people, you prepared this place for them; inspired by God, you built this dwelling in which they might perform God’s service day and night. They brought here no possessions: neither gold nor silver nor, in short, household goods. You acquired for them lands, food and clothing, and other necessities, both in deed and word. You rejoiced greatly at their arrival, and until now you have honoured them in many ways and guarded them well.

“Behold, therefore, by God’s will I undertake the journey of all flesh, and now the time of my dissolution draws near; for I am no better than our fathers. Therefore, while breath remains in me, while I can speak, I commend my daughters and all that belongs to them to your love, so that you who caused them to come here may guard them mercifully and henceforth take diligent care of them.

32. “Moreover, I wish to tell your friendship the desire of [Col. 1073B] my heart; I wish to disclose my longing to your holiness. Let it appear at the end whether you ever loved me while I lived; let it be manifest whether you ever held me dear, as you said. For you do not fail to know that true love does not consist in words alone, but, as holy Scripture testifies, the proof of love is its manifestation in deeds: ‘Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth’ (1 John 3:18).

“Therefore, dearest Father, I make known to you that I do not wish to lie in Bethlehem, where God deigned to be born of the Virgin; nor in Jerusalem at the Holy Sepulchre. Nor do I wish to be buried in Rome among the holy martyrs, nor in the monastery of Cluny, where beautiful processions are held. Yet I say this not because I despise the most holy places, which, I know, are truly to be loved, commemorated, and venerated because of reverence for the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 1073C]. For all the faithful ought magnificently to venerate holy Bethlehem, which, praised by the prophets, deserved to be adorned by the Lord’s birth. Although God is everywhere, nevertheless all ought with a certain special honour to honour blessed Jerusalem in love, for there the Son of God deigned by his death to redeem the world. Nor should anyone despise happy Rome, which, purpled by the precious blood of so many martyrs, surpasses all the beauty of the world, as sacred Scripture testifies. [Note: Rather, the hymn concerning Saints Peter and Paul.] Finally, what sound-minded person would dare disparage the supreme monastery of Cluny, where each day, by God’s grace, so great a benefit is bestowed?

33. “Finally, I do not wish to be buried in any other place [Col. 1073D] except Fontevraud alone. For you know, my Father, that I established the place of Fontevraud as the head of all other places; there too is the greater part of our congreg[ation?; the text is truncated], and there is also the foundation of our religious life. I do not ask you to bury me in the monastery or in the cloister, but only among my little brothers in the mud of Fontevraud. There too are my priests and clerics; there too are holy virgins, widows, and continent women, persevering day and night in God’s praises; there are my most beloved sick men and women; there are my dearest lepers, male and female; there are the good companions of my pilgrimage; there are those who long endured poverty and labours with me for Christ [Col. 1074A]; there are those who patiently endured cold and heat, miseries and tribulations for the salvation of their souls; who, inspired by God at the call of my preaching, left both themselves and their possessions. Some of them live in body; others died while persevering in obedience. There lies the nun Hersendis, my good helper, by whose counsel and work I built the buildings of Fontevraud. There lie my good sons, by whose prayers I trust that I am aided before God. There sleep my good nuns, by whose merits I believe I am helped before God.

“This, dearest one, is the reason why I reject burial in the most holy places: namely, because I wish to be buried in the mud among my little brothers and sisters. For I know that those living desire me to lie there, so that on the day of the holy resurrection I may be able to go with them, in this same flesh, to God’s judgment.

34. “For if I am buried there, those living will love that place more, and those whom the devil holds captive through disobedience will come seeking mercy. They will hear it said that I lie at Fontevraud; and when they recall that through me God rescued them from the evil world, and that through me he distributed many good things to them, bound by love for me, they will hasten to return to their obedience. For who of my congregation has a heart so hard as not, when he perfectly remembers me, to be softened either by groaning or by sighing? Therefore, when they call to mind how I always [Col. 1074C] loved them, how I instructed them, and how God through me satisfied them with his teaching, some, called by such great benefits through divine inspiration and moved to repentance, will come before my tomb to seek mercy from God.

“And because I perceive that this will happen, I commend to my successors that the benefit of reconciliation be denied to no one seeking this mercy. But if it should please the Author of mercy ever to grant me anything—not through my merits, of which I presume nothing, but by his free loving-kindness alone—I shall endeavour continually to entreat that very fountain of mercy for all my congregation; for there is no life there, and true love is lacking there. I shall love them according to my ability, because in this life I shall not be able [Col. 1074D] not to love them. For I know that no kind of burial harms the dead; I believe without doubt that the Lord can grant help anywhere to whomever he wills. Yet this aforementioned reason is why I ask to lie in these places; this is the cause why I order my corpse to be buried in the cemetery of Fontevraud. Therefore I humbly implore your venerable holiness with prayer: return my body to our nuns, bring it as far as Fontevraud, and there perform with your holy mouth the office of my burial. Now at the end it will appear whether you truly loved me in life. Therefore, if you have been a friend to me from your heart, if I have ever been your friend, grant me, I beseech you, what I have asked.”

35. But he, unwilling that his diocese be deprived of so great a treasure, answered him and said: “Dearest master, as I began long ago, I love you greatly with undivided mind; but what you ask of me is not wholly in my power, but depends in large part on the princes of this land. For you know that this place lies in the territory of a certain lord named Alard, who himself also built it in large part. I do not wish to promise you an outcome which I may afterward be unable to fulfil; but allow me tomorrow to take counsel concerning this matter.”

36. On hearing this, the priest Andrew said to the master: “Let your belovedness know, good master, that Agnes, prioress of this place, can greatly help or harm [Col. 1075B] your request. Therefore entreat her to accomplish your request insofar as lies in her power. For she is native to this land, and Alard, lord of this town, was her husband.” Therefore the wise man summoned her and said: “Lady Agnes, I command you by entreating, and entreat you by commanding, as my lady, daughter, and disciple, to do whatever you can in this matter that I have requested the archbishop to perform.” She replied: “Good master, do you wish me to do that?” He said: “Daughter, I wish it entirely and desire it; and on this condition I command you to kiss my hand.” Kissing his venerable hand, she promised to fulfil the desire he had expressed.

## CHAPTER VII. Blessed Robert’s prayers at death, profession of faith, and public sacramental confession of sins

37. After this, those standing around him began to say: “O good master, you ought to pray to God, since you perceive yourself to be so near to death.” He answered them: “I indeed greatly desire to pray to God; but because of you, who hinder me, I am altogether unable. Withdraw and go away, so that at least from now on I may be able to pray to my God.” When all had gone out, he began humbly to ask God, in his mercy, to deign to preserve to the end the Roman pope and all the doctors [Note: Another manuscript: “of holy.”] of his Church in the purpose of holy religion [Col. 1075D].

Then he began to name his guests individually and to offer prayer to God for each of them. He also prayed for all his benefactors and enemies, and for all faithful persons, living and dead. Finally he began to entreat the Lord for William, count of Poitiers, who at that time, as his merits required, had been wounded by the sword of excommunication: that, if it were in God’s providence, he might in his kindness deign to call him back to the way of truth. It is surely evident how great was the charity with which this man was filled, since he persevered to the end in praying so devoutly for his friends and enemies. It is plainly clear that he loved his enemies as himself, since in prayer he wished them to receive what he desired God to grant to himself [Col. 1076A]. Indeed, it is even more clearly established how wisely he loved his friends, for whom he sweetly offered the gift of prayer to the Lord God. Let us pursue, if we can, with what vigilance he observed the other commandments of the law. Indeed, what is usually more difficult, he repaid good to his enemies. Although he himself, by God’s will, died in peace, I nevertheless believe that he did not lose the palm of martyrdom. And lest what I say perhaps displease anyone in any respect, let him hear holy Scripture affirming and saying: “You shall accomplish martyrdom not in the shedding of blood alone, but in abstaining from sins and in practising God’s commandments.” Hence again it is written: “The whole life of a Christian man is a cross and martyrdom.”

38. After he had poured forth prayers to the Lord for the whole Christian people for a very long time, when almost everyone had withdrawn from him, in the silence of the late night he summoned to himself a certain lay brother Peter, who was constantly with him, and said: “Call the priest Andrew to me.” When Andrew came, he said to him: “Bring me, I beseech you, the wood of the holy cross.” When the holy cross had been brought, he sprang joyfully from his bed with such strength as he could muster; before the cross he bent his knees with great reverence and disclosed to those standing around what he believed concerning God.

Then he affirmed that he believed that almighty God, one in Trinity and three in unity, made heaven and earth themselves, and all things in them, by the command of his will [Col. 1076C]. He also confessed that God placed Lucifer, who rose in the morning, who is the beginning of God’s ways, having the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and beauty, adorned with every precious stone, in paradise. He also declared that he believed how Lucifer, with no one urging him, freely fell through his pride, and how, for his restoration, God wonderfully created man from the mud of the earth in his own image and likeness. [Note: To restore, as it is commonly said, the ruins of the fallen angels, or to fill the spaces of the heavenly city from which they were cast down.] He recalled how death entered the world through the devil’s envy, and how the deceitful enemy expelled man from paradise. He also recalled what great darkness of blindness and what miseries the human race will endure [Col. 1076D] until the end of the world because the first man transgressed the Lord’s command. To these he added how the human race perished in the waters of the Flood because its sins required it, and how God saved eight souls in Noah’s ark. He joined to these how gloriously God freed the children of Israel from Egyptian slavery and how wonderfully—when the murmurers perished in the wilderness—he led believers into the land of promise.

39. Prostrate before the holy cross, he also declared how the Son of God, descending into the womb of the holy Virgin, made a new heaven and earth, as he had promised [Col. 1077A]; and how, for our salvation, with none of our merits preceding but by mercy alone, he willed to be born in Bethlehem, laid in a manger, and wrapped in lowly swaddling-clothes. He also professed that God not only deigned to become man for human beings, but also—what is more wondrous—to be circumcised, baptized, and to fast. With sighs he recalled that the living bread who came down from heaven in order to satisfy us was hungry; that the living fountain, in order to free us from everlasting thirst, was thirsty. Groaning and sighing, he also recalled that he who made all things by his will, having become man for human beings, deigned willingly to endure mockery and spitting, blows and scourges, insults and wounds, and finally the death of the cross for the redemption of humankind [Col. 1077B]. The devout man joined to these the Lord’s resurrection, ascension into heaven, and the coming of the Holy Spirit; likewise he added the judgment to come at the end of the age, in which God will render to each according to his merit.

40. Finally he added how almighty God caused him to be born of a certain very old man and a certain poor little woman, and how afterward he bestowed upon him innumerable good things without preceding merits. After this he gave manifold thanks to almighty God for these and countless other benefits freely bestowed upon the human race. He also returned magnificent thanks to God because, through the merits of others, he had granted him so many and such great benefits.

41. After the Catholic man had fully set forth his belief before the holy cross, in the hearing of those who were there [Col. 1077C–1078A], he then publicly revealed the confession of his sins, accusing himself in an unheard-of fashion. He said:

“Hear my sins, priest; indeed hear them, heaven and earth. The Son of God came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. Behold, I was conceived in iniquities and reared in sins; in innumerable ways I have sinned through my own fault.”

Then, reproving himself before everyone, he confessed that when he was a small child and ate with his mother, he took the more attractive foods; and that when it rained, he wished for dry weather. Conversely, he related in self-accusation that, while he was still a layman, he once fell into the poison of simony at the ordination of a certain bishop of Rennes. [Note: This sin appears to be of the same kind as the two just mentioned: that “as a small child he ate the more attractive foods set before him,” and that “when it rained he wished for dryness”—actions in which one can scarcely detect guilt. Yet it belongs to good minds to recognize guilt even where there is no guilt. Thus Blessed Robert said that he had “once fallen into the poison of simony at the ordination of a certain bishop of Rennes.” In his time there were three bishops of Rennes: Mainus, or Meen; Silvester; and Marbodus. Mainus is said to have been ordained about eleven years before Robert’s birth; Silvester when Robert was perhaps twenty-four years old. But what could Robert then have contributed in order that this man should become bishop, when he still possessed no reputation for learning or other recommendation? Nor does he say that he contributed anything, but that he “fell into the poison of simony,” because perhaps, when he heard or even saw that man being ordained, it came into his mind to strive after distinguished learning so as to attain a similar dignity, considering by what means he might win for himself the favour of prince and clergy. But since, under that same Silvester, he as archpriest strove with such zeal to eradicate simony, as recounted above, it is not credible that when Marbodus was made bishop he could in any way have incurred such guilt. Perhaps he had then left Rennes and moved to Angers.]

He also confessed that God had freely granted him great learning and the grace of preaching [Col. 1078B]. He repented that he had not multiplied as he ought the talent entrusted to him by God. Then he said that he had gathered together a religious community of women who excellently endured the labour of holy religious life for God, but that he alone had received their praise.

42. What place is there here for speech, if I wished to recount one by one how and in what ways he accused himself before the holy cross? After he had accused himself beyond recount, rebuking himself and naming individual sins, he humbly begged God for absolution from all his sins, and afterward prayed that God might deign soon to grant him his end. It is certain indeed that God heard his servant in this prayer, freeing him not long afterward from the bonds of flesh and withdrawing him from the exile of this world.

[Col. 1077]

## CHARTER OF THE ABBEY OF GRANDMONT

(Pavillon, *Life of Robert of Arbrissel*, evidences, p. 544, from an old manuscript.)

[Col. 1077D] Robert of Arbrissel, a man fitted to win souls and to preach the word of God, began in the year of the Lord 1106 to build the monastery called Fontevraud on the borderlands of Anjou, Touraine, and Poitou. Gathering religious women there under a most strict rule, he set Petronilla over them as abbess. After her death Matilda, sister of Geoffrey, count of Anjou, succeeded her in the governance of the same monastery [Col. 1078D], etc.

These three were companions in religious life: Vitalis the hermit, who had been chaplain to the count of Mortain in the diocese of Avranches; Robert of Arbrissel; and Ralph of La Fustaye. Each of them founded a separate monastery.

[Col. 1079]

## RULES OF THE NUNS OF FONTEVRAUD

(Michael Cosnier, *Exordium Fontis Ebraldi*, Fleury, 1641, quarto, p. 201.) These are the regulatory chapters of our master Lord Robert of Arbrissel, given while he lived to Petronilla, the first abbess, to us nuns of the Church of Fontevraud, and to the other cells belonging to the same church, for the preservation of religious observance and discipline.

### Concerning fitting dress, or modesty of body

[Col. 1079A]

I. Cloistered nuns shall keep silence at all times, except those who attend to outside affairs; these, however, shall not speak lightly or in a loud voice, but shall speak necessary words.

II. They shall make no signs except necessary ones.

III. As far as they are able, they shall preserve cloistered decency and gravity within and without.

IV. They shall all go together to church and return together, no one remaining in church for any reason.

### Concerning clothing, or outward adornment

V. They shall never have veils except linen ones.

VI. Their white *gimpae* [wimples] shall never be visible, being covered by veils.

[Col. 1079B]

VII. They shall not grow their hair.

VIII. They shall never have tunics or mantles except of the cheapest cloths of that region, of natural colour and undressed, reaching to the foot and no farther.

IX. The sleeves of tunics shall be two feet in width and shall reach to the knees.

X. They shall never have skins, furs, or bed-coverings except lambskin ones.

XI. They shall make the sleeves of fur garments narrow; they shall reach to the tips of the fingers and be half a foot broad at the fist.

XII. They shall have no fringed garments, either for the body or the bed, except a *belamia*; but, like tunics, cloaks, and everything else, they shall be sewn together from cut pieces.

[Col. 1079C]

XIII. They shall never have surplices except white ones. [Note: Some remove “except.”]

XIV. They shall never have girdles for fastening except woollen ones.

XV. They shall never wear gloves.

XVI. They shall never allow their hair to grow, but three times a year shall shave it with a razor or cut it all over to the scalp with shears.

### Concerning journeys outside the cloister

[Col. 1080A]

XVII. The abbess or prioress, when riding, shall not take with her any of the girls being reared or young cloistered women.

XVIII. No woman shall ride without two religious persons and one layperson; or at the least, one religious person and one layperson.

XIX. No one shall speak while travelling except the abbess or prioress, until they arrive at their lodging.

### Concerning the kitchen

XX. The nuns themselves shall do the cooking.

### Concerning the disposition of books

XXI. None of them shall presume, without the abbess’s permission, to give any church book to another outside the community, or receive other books from outside.

### Concerning admission into the cloister

[Col. 1080B]

XXII. No one—not even the dean or prioress—shall presume to admit anyone to religious life without the presence of the abbess.

### Concerning the enclosure and seclusion of nuns

XXIII. Their pupils and teachers shall always have as guardian one of the senior converted sisters.

XXIV. No nun shall be shown outside to anyone except by order of the abbess. When the abbess gives such an order concerning anyone, the prioress or cellarer shall guard her.

XXV. They shall never kiss one another for the peace; rather, all shall kiss a piece of marble passed to them through the window, administered by the sacristan.

XXVI. They shall not leave the cloister for any work to be done outside.

XXVII. Nuns of other churches shall not enter their convent unless the abbess introduces them, or someone appointed by the abbess does so.

XXVIII. No one may enter the cloister, [Col. 1081A] chapter-house, or remaining workshops without the abbess’s presence.

### Concerning the enclosure of nuns

XXIX. If some rich man or Christian pilgrim wishes, in the abbess’s absence, to see their cloister, the nuns shall hide themselves and all necessities shall be secured. Then the church doors shall be opened, and those men shall be led inside from outside by the senior prioress or cellarer and two or three brothers. The cloister, chapter-house, monastery, and refectory shall then be shown to them.

XXX. The outer door to the altar shall never be opened except by the cellarer; and neither the cellarer nor anyone else shall enter the altar choir alone.

### Concerning the celebration of the office and enclosure

[Col. 1081B]

XXXI. In their churches, vigils shall never be held by laypeople.

XXXII. During the day one converted sister shall always guard their dormitory, and at night two or four: one before nocturns, and another afterward until daylight, the latter with a candle.

XXXIII. When the priest comes to celebrate Mass, the door of the nuns’ choir shall never be opened except solely for communion; and when he has communicated them, the abbess, dean, or cellarer shall always keep watch there.

XXXIV. One of the clerics shall remain with the priest and deacon in order to communicate them.

XXXV. When the morning Mass is finished, water shall be blessed; after blessing it the priest shall leave, and the cellarer and sacristan shall secure the door behind him. The cellarer and sacristan shall ensure that no priests ever enter the choir alone at any hour of day or night.

### Concerning the celebration of the church office

XXXVI. A priest or deacon shall never read the Gospel to them at matins, except “The Book of the Generation” at the Nativity of the Lord and “It came to pass” at the Epiphany of the Lord.

XXXVII. At the Purification of Saint Mary, after the morning Mass, the priest shall bless the tapers and candles and shall depart after they have been blessed.

[Col. 1082A]

XXXVIII. On Palm Sunday, after the morning Mass, branches and flowers shall be blessed, and the Gospel, “When he drew near,” shall be said by the priest. Afterwards they alone, without priests or clerics, shall make the procession through the cloister and adore the cross.

XXXIX. On Good Friday they shall sing “My people” (*Popule meus*) with the priests and clerics, and “Holy God” (*Agios*) without them, so that they never respond to the men.

XL. Sick women shall never be anointed or communicated except in church.

### Concerning ecclesiastical rites

XLI. For the dead, the sisters shall perform the office, while priests say only the collects at the altar. When the office has been performed, the sisters shall go out into the cloister, and the cellarer, with one of the senior sisters, shall stand ready at the door to open it for the priests and brothers. Then the priests and brothers shall carry the body to the tomb, while the sisters remain in the cloister and never go to the burial of a deceased sister.

[Col. 1082B]

XLII. They shall knowingly receive no excommunicated person into their cemetery.

XLIII. The senior prioress shall be received everywhere, both in the churches of Fontevraud and in all the cells of that church; she shall be obeyed and, after the abbess, shall have authority in conducting the affairs of the church.

XLIV. When an abbess has died, [the senior prioress] shall remain in the dignity of her office and shall have full authority to govern the church until another abbess is appointed from among the converted sisters [Col. 1082C], as our master Robert ordained, and this shall be done with prayer and fasting.

### Ordinance of the abbess

The abbess also ordained that tithes in money and silver, and gifts of chickens, mares, calves, and horses which are given to the church, shall come into the hands of the senior prioress, so that from such gifts she may provide additional portions in the refectory during the week, but not on Sundays or feast days.

[Col. 1081]

## PRECEPTS FOR RIGHT LIVING

(Cosnier, cited work, p. 208.) Master Robert gave these precepts for right living, obedience to God and Blessed Mary, and service to the nuns of Fontevraud, to priests, clerics, and laymen who had accepted his teaching and the habit of holy conduct; who of their own free will and gratuitous love had promised to serve the nuns, under the bond of obedience, until death, and with the reverence due to subjection. They were to render this subjection not only to the place of Fontevraud, but also to all cells belonging to that place. To these devoted persons he gave the following precepts.

### Concerning the office

[Col. 1081D]

I. They shall celebrate the canonical office.

### Concerning poverty in food

II. They shall maintain cloistered and common life without private property [Col. 1082D], content with what is provided to them by the nuns.

III. They shall observe regular disciplines in silence.

### Concerning clothing

IV. They shall have neither mantles nor black shirts.

[Col. 1083A]

V. They shall have woollen belts and loincloths.

VI. They shall have knives worth two denarii and sheaths worth one denarius, and no more. [Note: Observe the valuation of the period.]

VII. Three times a year they shall have blood drawn.

VIII. The remnants of the brothers’ food shall be carried to the nuns’ gate and there given to the poor.

IX. The standard of food and beds established by the brothers at Fontevraud, together with the regulations written there, shall be observed everywhere.

### Concerning community of life

X. On every Sunday and feast day, all shall come in their habit to Mass and chapter, and shall not leave except with the prior’s permission.

### Concerning separation from secular affairs

[Col. 1083B]

XI. They shall not act as sureties.

XII. They shall not receive the property of others into their keeping, nor rear any animal on shares.

XIII. They shall not give their land to secular persons for habitation.

XIV. The brothers shall not receive women into their houses to perform work for them.

### Concerning processions

XV. In processions the clerical brothers shall wear neither surplices nor albs, except the priest alone.

XVI. The brothers shall make no processions except [Col. 1083C] in the cloister, apart from on Hosanna Sunday and at funeral offices.

### Concerning the surrender of all possessions

XVII. Grain, wine, fish, money, and all necessities shall come into the hands of the cellarer, and she shall distribute them with the counsel and command of the abbess or prioress.

### Concerning faults and penance

[Col. 1084A]

XVIII. If any brother shouts at another brother in chapter, he shall nevertheless make his apology in silence and patiently receive regular discipline.

XIX. If anyone is caught in a grave sin or theft; or if anyone beats another person, possesses private property, or proves disobedient and rebellious toward the abbess or his prior, he shall be severely beaten and sent to prison.

XX. For lighter faults, regular discipline shall be imposed.

XXI. If any disobedient brother departs and afterward returns repentant, he shall be received into the guesthouse by command of the abbess. After he has completed his penance, he shall seek mercy from the abbess and, through her, be received into the community of brothers [Col. 1084B].

XXII. If any brother, from shame, refuses to confess a crime to his prior, he shall confess it to other priests before he dies in his sin.

### Concerning the office

XXIII. No parish priest shall presume to celebrate the office unless this is because of a lack of a priest-brother.

### Concerning not receiving religious persons
XXIV. That no one may presume to receive anyone into religious life except the abbess.

Or concerning outsiders.

XXV. That no outsider be received into the community of the brethren [Col. 1084C] without the abbess’s permission.

Concerning clothing.

XXVI. That they never have fur garments or coverings except those made of lambskin.

XXVII. That they have capes, tunics, and leggings of one colour, of low cost, and unshorn. Thanks be to God.

What follows has been extracted from certain charters communicated to us by the venerable and learned priest Fr. L. Cailleau, monk of Fontevraud.

[Col. 1083]

Among the ancient statutes given by the most reverend Father Master Robert to Petronilla, the first abbess, and to the nuns of the church of Fontevraud, for the preservation of religious life and discipline.

[Col. 1083D]

[Note: [Col. 1083D] From chapters 1 and 2 of the Regular Chapters, above.] That cloistered nuns maintain silence at all times, except those who attend to external affairs.

[Note: [Col. 1083D] ibid.] That they make no signs except necessary ones. That they never eat meat or blood-meats, not even when ill.

[Note: [Col. 1084D] From chapter 40.] That sick women are never anointed or receive communion except in church.

That Petronilla, elected by Master Robert and established abbess by the common will and devout request both of the nuns and of the religious brethren [Col. 1084D], shall have and exercise authority to govern the church of Fontevraud and all places belonging to that church; that they obey her and honour her as their spiritual mother; and that all the church’s affairs, both spiritual and temporal, remain under her judgment, or under that of those to whom she assigns them, and according to her ordinances.

Moreover, the abbess herself, providing for the future, thus ordained these matters [Note: [Col. 1084D] From chapter 43.]: that the senior prioress be received everywhere, both in the church of Fontevraud and in all the cells of that church; that they obey her; and that, after the abbess, she have authority in conducting the church’s affairs.

[Note: [Col. 1084D] From chapter 44.] That, upon the abbess’s death, she remain in the dignity of her office [Col. 1085A] and have full authority to govern the church until another abbess is appointed.

These subsequent precepts were given to priests, clerics, and laymen who, through her teaching, had received the habit of holy life and who, of their own free will and from gratuitous love, had promised to serve the nuns under the bond of obedience until death; this is the reverence due to their subjection. These devout commands concerning such subjection were given not only for Fontevraud itself but also for all cells belonging to that place.

[Note: [Col. 1085C] Thus chapter 1 of the Precepts for Right Living, above.] That they celebrate the canonical office.

[Note: [Col. 1085C] Thus chapter 2.] That they maintain a cloistered and common life without private property, content with what is bestowed upon them by the nuns [Col. 1085B].

[Note: [Col. 1085C] Thus chapter 7.] That they undergo bloodletting three times a year.

[Note: [Col. 1085C] Thus chapter 8.] That the remnants of the brethren’s food be carried to the nuns’ gate and there given to the poor.

[Note: [Col. 1085C] In accordance with chapters 11, 12, 13, and 14.] That they receive neither parish churches nor their tithes.

[Note: [Col. 1085C] Thus chapter 25.] That they do not lend their possessions to secular persons.

[Note: [Col. 1086C] In accordance with the first and second rules for the nuns.] That no outsider be received into the community of brethren without the abbess’s permission.

These statutes, however, were extracted from another manuscript by the same venerable priest.

[Note: [Col. 1086C] In accordance with the first and second rules for the nuns.] If anything is necessary, let it rather be indicated by a sign [Col. 1085C] than by speech.

[Col. 1086A] [Note: [Col. 1086C] In accordance with chapter 40.] Let those dwelling in the cloister maintain silence throughout all workshops.

[Note: [Col. 1086C] Note that the nuns of Fontevraud were accustomed to receive a certain blessing from the diocesan bishops.] If an abbess, deaness, chamberlain, cellarer, or prioress of any place is laid low by illness and wishes to confess, the priest is in no way to approach her bed; rather, she is to be carried to the chapel, confess and receive communion there, and, once she has communicated and the priest has departed, be carried back to bed.

The sisters must never speak with any man without a guardian sitting between them and hearing what is said, in order to determine whether it is useful.

When the abbess wishes to consecrate her virgins, she must by no means presume to take them to cities or castles for blessing; rather, the bishop in whose diocese they are is to be summoned, and they are to be blessed in their own church in the abbess’s presence [Col. 1086B].

Those to be consecrated shall have their heads shorn and suitably bound with wimples; they shall hold lighted candles in their hands and thus be brought before the bishop, near the altar, at the Gospel. Thus, according to custom, in the presence of the virgins’ parents and other secular persons wishing to attend their consecration, they shall be consecrated by the bishop [Note: [Col. 1086C] Note that the nuns of Fontevraud were accustomed to receive a certain blessing from the diocesan bishops.].

Those who have been consecrated shall receive communion for nine days; until the ninth day they shall remain in contemplation; insofar as they can, they shall keep their nights in vigil; during these days they shall by no means sit in the cloister, but shall remain continually in church in prayer.

The same shall be done concerning converts blessed by a priest [Col. 1086C], but only for three days.

[Col. 1085]

## Diplomas of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel

(Joannes de la Mainferme, *Clypeus Fontebraldensis*, Saumur, vol. I, 1684; II, 1688; III, 1691, octavo; vol. I, pp. 119, 150.)

### I. Charter of Robert of Arbrissel by which he commends to Peter, bishop of Poitiers, all the monasteries, both of men and of nuns, namely those situated in his diocese. (Year 1109.)

[Col. 1085D]

To PETER, by God’s grace venerable bishop of Poitiers, to the venerable canons of the holy mother church of Poitiers, and to their successors: Brother ROBERT OF ARBRISSEL, greeting and due submission.

[Col. 1086D] Beloved brethren, we have founded in your diocese, in a place called Fons Euvrandi, a church of nuns in honour of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, aided by the mercy of her Son and by your own, reverend Father Peter, cooperative diligence. After the Lord, we hand it over and commend it in perpetuity to the patronage of your protection, so that, as an obedient daughter, it may cling to your Church as its dearest mother by a special privilege of love; and so that, when the thorns of hostile attacks have been cut away from it by the sickle of your defence [Col. 1087A], this new planting may bear fruit for the harvest of holy religion. Thus may the many nuns whom our Lord Jesus Christ, through me, though I am an unworthy priest, recalled from luxury and assembled in the aforesaid place for the praise and glory of his name, forget worldly cares and, under the shield of your protection, subdue the flesh, strengthen the spirit, and give themselves wholly, as they have begun, to divine service.

We commit to the same protection all places in your diocese belonging to the church of Fontevraud, both those of men and those of nuns: namely, the community of nuns at Podia between Calviniacum and Englam, the obedience of Jarunda, and that of Gaina; and whatever other places they possess or shall hereafter justly and canonically possess [Col. 1087B]. Beloved brethren, this surrender or commendation of the church of Fontevraud to your protection is made by us with the common counsel of the sisters of that church; and you receive it with the counsel of your most beloved father, the venerable Bishop Peter, and of all of yourselves. In return for so great a benefit of defence, the handmaids of Christ who are or shall be in the church of Fontevraud will pray daily for you while living; and, whenever one of you dies, they will render to God for the soul of the deceased as much service as they render for the soul of a nun who departs this world from their congregation. And, as a memorial of so great a love, the church of Fontevraud shall be perpetually subject to the church of Poitiers in an annual due of twelve denarii [Col. 1087C], payable at the synod of Pentecost. May almighty God preserve your brotherhood in religion, beloved brethren.

Seal of Bishop Peter. Seal of Aimeric, dean. Seal of Geoffrey, cantor. Seal of William, archdeacon. Seal of Hervey, archdeacon. Seal of Rainer, capicer. Seal of William, master of the schools. Seal of all the canons. Seal of Robert of Arbrissel. Seal of Hersendis, nun. Seal of Petronilla. [Col. 1088A] Seal of all the nuns of Fontevraud.

Given at Poitiers in synod, in the year 1109 from the Incarnation of the Lord; indiction II; epact XVII; the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June]; in the second year of Pope Paschal; Peter presiding over the see of Poitiers; Louis king of the Franks; and William duke of Aquitaine. Happily in Christ Jesus. Amen.

### II. Charter of Robert of Arbrissel by which he grants to Lord Gerard of Salis a monastery situated in the district of Cadouin. (Year 1115.)

I, Robert of Arbrissel, grant and irrevocably bestow upon Lord Gerard of Salis [Col. 1088B], venerable master, my companion and dearest among indispensable friends, and upon his sons—or rather, upon his fellow servants, both those now living and those to come—both places situated in the forest of Cadouin: namely, both that of the valley of Seguini, which Gerard himself, together with his fellow soldiers, had acquired, built up, and established as though for himself under my person; and that called Salvitas. Universally, whatever has been granted within the aforesaid wood to me or to another in my stead, I leave to their judgment and desire, so that they may there serve God according to the rule of the Lord’s household.

I decree that this authentic concession, solemnly enacted before the general chapter of the nuns, with the assent and grant of their most faithful Petronilla—indeed, handmaid of the handmaids of God—shall remain unshaken [Col. 1088C]; and I wholly exclude, root out, and utterly forbid every complaint of calumny or controversy arising from this matter.

The aforesaid grant of places was made at Fontevraud on the feast of Saint Benedict, the fifth day before the Ides of July [11 July], in the year 1115 from the Incarnation of the Lord; in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal; indiction VIII; during the vacancy of the church of Poitiers, after Bishop Peter had entered the way of all flesh; with Louis king of the Franks and William duke of Aquitaine.

The following bear witness, as they are thus designated: Fulk, count of Anjou; Pagan of Clairs Vallées; Aimeric, viscount of Thouars; and others.

[Col. 1087]

## Agreement between the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre of Sully and the monastery of Fontevraud. (Year 1114.)

(Pavillon, *Life of Robert d’Arbrissel*, p. 609.)

[Col. 1087D] To their most reverend fathers and lords, RALPH, archbishop of the holy church of Tours, and GIRARD, bishop of Angoulême, who most faithfully and prudently administers in these regions the office of the Apostolic See [Col. 1088D], and to the most reverend and God-beloved Bishop PETER: PETER, abbot of Sully, and his whole humble convent; and ROBERT OF ARBRISSEL, most illustrious and God-loving man, together with his whole humble and devout congregation, offer the reverence of due obedience and the gift of holy prayers.

Since it is manifestly an act of Christian perfection to assent to holy desires and just petitions, falling at the knees of your exalted lordship, we humbly and most devoutly beseech the clemency of your sincerity: may you confirm by the weight of divine authority what you shall see written below concerning the peace, concord, and charity made between us—namely, the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre of Sully and the holy church of Fontevraud—over a certain dispute. Thus may neither community ever again be harassed in any way, by the false inventions of utterly wicked men, through any disturbance from those now living or to come [Col. 1089B].

Among the other possessions which Walter, most Christian prince and founder of the church of the Holy Sepulchre of Sully, gave from his own holdings to that church, free and unencumbered and to be possessed by perpetual right, for the remedy of his soul, he is found also to have granted this: in the charter which he himself procured in person from the archbishop of Tours and had sealed with his own seal, namely, the wood of Bort to be cleared, so that the monks should have one half of it. The same is contained in the aforesaid charter; but because it was obscurely stated, it generated disagreement and discord between us, who ought rather to suffer injury than to dispute or litigate.

For we monks of Sully, on the occasion of the aforesaid words [Col. 1089C], laid claim to everything built or constructed in the wood of Bort—for there is there a place [Col. 1090A] called Fons Evraudus—whether in churches, workshops, or other houses, and indeed to all clearings of the wood which the disciples of Father Robert had turned into arable land. Therefore, when we assembled together—namely, the abbot of Sully with his monks, and the venerable Robert of Arbrissel with certain of his disciples and the handmaids of God at Salicum—in the presence of the most illustrious Prince Walter of Montsoreau, whom we have above called founder of the abbey of Sully, we monks of Sully, honouring as was due the presence of so great a man and teacher and yielding to his holy admonitions, preferred to relinquish something of our own rather than grieve the Holy Spirit in him and in his most glorious congregation.

Accordingly, by the following agreement, pact, and terms, peace concerning the aforesaid dispute was made between us, with the support of the aforesaid Walter of Montsoreau: that we monks of Sully should henceforth lay no claim whatever to anything belonging to Lord Robert and his people, etc. [Col. 1090B]

This charter was made in the year 1114 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October [22 September], in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and Fulk, count of Anjou.

I, Girard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, confirm this agreement by the authority of the Apostolic See; I have caused it to be fortified by my seal and have subscribed it with my own hand.

Seal of Ralph, archbishop of Tours.

Seal of Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

## Appendix to Blessed Robert of Arbrissel

[Col. 1089]

# Privileges of Peter, Bishop of Poitiers, for the Order and Congregation of Fontevraud

### I. Charter confirming the order and congregation of Fontevraud, issued by Peter, bishop of Poitiers. (Year 1106.)

(Cosnier, *Exordium Fontis Ebraldi*, p. 144.)

[Col. 1089D]

I, PETER, bishop of Poitiers, make known to all present and future that in our time a certain apostolic man named Robert of Arbrissel, diligently devoted to the word of divine preaching and to the thunder of holy exhortation, recalled many men and women from secular luxury and founded, in our diocese, a church in honour of Saint Mary the Virgin [Col. 1090D], in a place called Fons Ebraudi. Arimburgis, wife of Guy son of Osmund, and her daughter Rivaria assigned this place to him for the building of the aforesaid church, adding land capable of cultivation by four oxen in two seasons. In that church he gathered many women, whom he established as nuns, so that they might live there according to rule and, renouncing worldly pleasures, serve God alone.

Not long afterwards, I went to Lord Paschal, the pope, and obtained from him that nuns should always be there; and he confirmed this by apostolic authority [Col. 1091A]. I too, following the authority of Pope Paschal and by the office granted to me by God, confirm the same: no person may destroy or alter the rule of the nuns, trouble or disturb the nuns themselves, or take away or diminish anything from the goods they rightfully possess. Rather, let them peacefully possess in perpetuity whatever has rightly been given or is owed to them. Should anyone at any time presume to act against the apostolic privilege and our decree, let him be struck by the perpetual sword of malediction, and let his machination fail and come to nothing.

This was done with the consent of our venerable brethren, the canons of the mother church of Poitiers. So that it might remain firm, we signed it with our own hand and handed it over to others for signing.

[Col. 1091B] Mark of Bishop Peter. Seal of Aimeric, dean. Seal of William, archdeacon. Seal of Hervey, archdeacon. Seal of Peter, archdeacon. Seal of William, master of the schools. Seal of Reginald, subdeacon. Seal of Rainer, capicer. Seal of the canons.

Delivered at Poitiers in chapter, in the year 1106 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction XIV, epact XIV; under Pope Paschal, Philip king of the Franks, Peter bishop of Poitiers, and William duke of Aquitaine.

### II. Charter of Peter, bishop of Poitiers, confirming all the possessions of the monastery of Fontevraud. (Year 1106.)

(Cosnier, *ibid.*, p. 146.)

[Col. 1091C]

I, PETER, by God’s grace bishop of Poitiers, providing for the peace of the holy Church and desiring to establish peace within it and to allay occasions for litigation, grant and confirm that the church of the holy Mother of God at Fons Evraudus—founded in our time and diocese by our brother Robert of Herbressel, a religious man devoted to the word of holy preaching, and fortified by Lord Paschal, the pope, through the authority of his privilege—shall peacefully possess in perpetuity, without the claim of any person or church, the possessions it now holds, which the persons named below gave to it for the salvation of their souls. Namely [Col. 1091D]: the land on which the church itself was founded, given to the aforesaid Robert by Aremburgis and her daughter Adelaide, from the land of Berlai above the spring, as the public road divides it, as far as the second mill; further, as much land as four oxen can cultivate in two seasons; and the land given to the aforesaid church by Hugh son of Gregory, Berlaius of Montreuil, their wives, and their sons, from the land of Guy son of Osmund to the wood of Milo of Tuille, and as far as the enclosure of Saint Martin, as far as the land of Saint Radegund; and the whole wood as far as the elm of Maistre.

Further, all customary dues which Walter of Montsoreau gave to the aforesaid church—whatever the men of this place would owe throughout all the land of Loges [Col. 1092A]—together with the viguerie and the other customary dues which Walter held in that land, he gave them all to the same church for the love of God; likewise, whatever the men of Walter himself might wish to give this church, saving the service owed to his knights. Whoever gives land in the wood of Bort to this place, Walter himself gave that church his *secretaria*, his viguerie, and all his customary dues.

We confirm by our authority these things given to this church, that it may possess them peacefully in perpetuity. If anyone presumes to devise anything against these provisions, let him be struck by the sword of anathema, and let his machination fail and come to nothing. We have acted with the counsel of our venerable canons.

+ Seal of Peter, bishop of Poitiers. [Col. 1092B] Seal of Peter, archdeacon. Seal of William, archdeacon. Seal of Raginaud, subcantor. Seal of William, master of the school. Seal of Rainer, archpriest. Seal of William Aleelmus. Seal of Hilary. Seal of William. Seal of John.

Given at Poitiers, in the chamber, in the year 1106 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction XIV, epact XIV; under Pope Paschal, Peter bishop of Poitiers, Philip king of the Franks, and William duke of Aquitaine.

### III. Charter of the same bishop concerning the gift of Roffiac. (Year 1109.)

(Pavillon, *Life of R. d’Arbrissel*, pref., p. 600.)

[Col. 1092C]

I, PETER, by God’s grace bishop of Poitiers, make known to all future and present persons that, at the admonition of our most beloved brother Robert of Erbressel, a religious man, I have given to my bride, the holy church of Poitiers, the church of Roffiac, situated between Laudun and Montsoreau, and the church of Senentium, situated between Englam and Calviniacum, so that henceforth it may have and possess them in perpetuity, etc. Yet if—which God forbid—any bishop or brethren of our Church, through ignorance of this our decree or in any manner, should wish to give the aforesaid churches to another church or otherwise transfer them, I further command and ordain that they belong to the church which the aforesaid Robert, aided by God’s mercy, founded in honour of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary in the place called Fontevraud [Col. 1092D], etc.

Given at Poitiers in synod, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June], in the year 1109.

### IV. Agreement between the abbot of Saint Paul of Cormery and Lord Robert of Arbrissel. (Year 1109.)

(Pavillon, *ibid.*, p. 600.)

I, PETER, by God’s grace bishop of Poitiers, endeavoured to settle peacefully, and by settling to make peace between, Abbot Guy of Saint Paul of Cormery and his monks, who were somewhat at variance, and Lord Robert of Erbressel and the nuns of Fontevraud [Col. 1093A], etc. Therefore, desiring to put an end to this controversy and to provide for peace on both sides, with the consent of the aforesaid abbot and the chapter of each church, I ordained that henceforth the church of Fontevraud should peacefully hold, have, and possess the entire tithe of all its livestock and two thirds of the tithe of the crops of that land of Gaina, etc.

Given at Poitiers in synod, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June], in the year 1109 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction II.

### V. Distinguished charter of the same bishop concerning the foundation of the community of Tucion. (Year 1112.)

(Cosnier, *Exordium Fontis Ebraldi*, pp. 221–222, from the cartulary of Fontevraud, charter 581.)

[Col. 1093B]

I, PETER, by God’s grace bishop of Poitiers, wish all Catholics to know, and by the characters of this present document proclaim, with what diligent reasoning the place commonly called Tucion was established, with the common consent and counsel of ourselves and the canons of our see, for the honour of God and the observance of holy religion.

For the place of Tucion, formerly desolate in the vast solitude of forests and thickly overgrown with thorns and brambles, had long been uninhabitable; nevertheless, traces of a very ancient church were visible there. When a certain man of great religious devotion and good reputation, Robert of Arbrissel by name, was diligently seeking, with vigilant care, solitary places suitable for divine worship in which he might establish [Col. 1093C] the holy women whom he had gathered to serve the living God, a certain illustrious man called Fulcaudus Frenicardi approached him and earnestly begged him to deign to build a church in the aforesaid place. This place was his own possession and subject to his authority.

Yet Robert did not immediately agree to Fulcaudus’s request. Rather, he declared that he would neither build nor accept this or any other place in our bishopric except with the counsel of ourselves and clerical men. Therefore Fulcaudus, ardently desiring to give the place of Tucion to Lord Robert and to the holy women who, under his discipline, were serving God most devoutly at Fontevraud, came to us [Col. 1093D], begging and entreating us to grant the aforesaid place to the aforementioned man, Lord Robert, and persuade him to build a church there.

After these matters had thus been arranged, the aforesaid Robert yielded to our persuasion and ordered a church and workshops to be built there for the honour of God and the observance of holy religion. But the monks of Nanteuil asserted a claim against Lord Robert concerning the aforesaid place, saying that the old church, traces of which, as stated above, were visible there, had belonged by right to the monastery of Nanteuil. Therefore, after we carefully examined the monks’ grounds in the matter, and since they could show us neither any possession nor investiture in that church, nor had any documentary proofs concerning it, we urged Lord Robert not to desist from what he had begun.

But he, unwilling to accept our counsel, answered us with a fixed resolve that he would do nothing further there until the monks’ claim was peacefully settled [Col. 1094A]. We therefore, together with our clerics and Fulcaudus Frenicardi, went to the monastery of Nanteuil and made an agreement concerning the aforesaid claim with the abbot and monks of that place in their common chapter. For Fulcaudus Frenicardi gave the monks of Nanteuil, for this agreement, four measures of grain from the tithe of Saint Médard of Vertou, to be rendered to them annually.

Accordingly, Walter, abbot of Nanteuil, in the chapter of the church of Nanteuil, in our presence and with the counsel and assent of his monks, entirely released and relinquished that claim; and he granted that the church of the place of Tucion and the place itself, in its entirety, should be peacefully and perpetually possessed by Lord Robert, the aforesaid nuns, and the men supplying the church’s needs [Col. 1094B]. Thus, after these matters had been settled by God’s authority, we gave the place of Tucion, with the old church itself whose traces, as has often been said, were evident there, to God and Saint Mary of Fontevraud, to Lord Robert, and to the often-mentioned nuns, with the counsel of clerical men; and we granted that they should possess it peacefully and without disturbance in perpetuity.

We also granted on equal terms that everything they might lawfully acquire in our bishopric through the gifts of the faithful should remain firm and unimpaired to them forever. We further ordained that anyone presuming to disturb or trouble this our settlement, or rashly attempting to oppose it, after a second or third warning should be bound by the bond of anathema until he had made worthy satisfaction for the wrong committed [Col. 1094C]. So that this agreement and grant might remain firm and unimpaired forever, we took care to commit it to writing, confirmed it by our own subscription, and ordered it fortified with our seal.

Present at this aforesaid agreement and grant were William Radulfus, master of the schools of the church of Poitiers; Peter of Saint-Saturnin, canon of the same church; Ademar, prior of the church of Nanteuil; Peter son of Fulcher; Umbert of Vestaul; Aimeric Candidus; Arnaud; Arrius; and many other monks of Nanteuil; Fulcaudus Frenicardi; Ademar his brother; Aimeric of Pindray; and many others, both clerics and laymen [Col. 1094D].

This agreement and grant were made in the chapter of Nanteuil in the year 1112 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction V, during the reign of Louis king of the Franks.

[Col. 1095]

## Charter of Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, for Fontevraud

(Pavillon, *Life of Robert d’Arbrissel*, p. 609.)

[Col. 1095A] We make known to future and present persons that Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, has fellowship and benefaction in this place called Fontevraud before and above all other abbots; and when he has died, we shall solemnly celebrate his anniversary every year. Concerning the brethren of the monastery of Vendôme for whom we have a written notice, we shall do as much as for ourselves.

The lord abbot himself, with the assent of his chapter, gave and granted to us in perpetuity the share of toll which he held at Old Saint-Florent on our lordly salt [Col. 1096A].

These acts were done in the chapter of Fontevraud, in the presence of Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, and Lord Robert of Arbrissel, our master, with the assent of all the sisters, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction VI.

The grant of this toll was made in the chapter of Vendôme on the sixth day before the Nones of August [31 July].

[Col. 1095]

## Various Pious Donations Made to the Abbey of Fontevraud under the Governance of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel

### I. Grant of Sibilla, abbess of Sainte-Croix, to the abbey of Fontevraud.

(Pavillon, *Life of Robert d’Arbrissel*, p. 593.)

[Col. 1095B]

I, Sibilla, abbess of Sainte-Croix, wish to record in writing, for future as well as present persons, the agreement which we ratified with Lord Robert and the sisters of Fontevraud, by the hand and at the request of Hersendis, who is prioress of that place and a religious woman. Thus, in a small wood of our land, commonly called Born, known to adjoin that place in the parish of Cusey, we grant them one half of all revenues, while the other half shall be retained wholly and entirely by the church of Sainte-Croix, to which it belongs, etc.

This gift and agreement which we made concerning that portion of the wood, whatever way it may be cultivated, out of fear of divine piety and love for Lord Robert, friend of our church, etc. [Col. 1095C]

Given in the chapter of Sainte-Croix, in the year 1104 from the Incarnation.

### II. Charter granting the place of Cadouin to Lord Robert of Arbrissel.

(De la Mainferme, *Clypeus Fontis Ebraldi*, vol. I, p. 149, from the cartulary of the abbey of Cadouin.)

When the venerable Robert of Arbrissel came into the region of Périgueux and entered the chapter of Saint-Front, where he refreshed its canons with holy preaching, those canons asked him [Col. 1096B] to deign to accept one of Saint-Front’s places for the support of the nuns serving almighty God in the church of Fontevraud, and to establish it for the sustenance of the holy women. At length overcome by their entreaties, he accepted one of their lesser places, then already almost deserted; and, in honour of Saint Front and in recognition of this gift of ours, he imposed there a pound of incense to be rendered on Saint Front’s feast.

Therefore I, William, bishop of the church of Périgueux and abbot of the canons of Saint Front, together with those canons, gave to Lord Robert and the nuns of Fontevraud, to possess permanently, this place in the forest of Cadouin called Salvitas and everything we possessed there. We subscribed with our own hands and, to confirm this gift, sealed this little charter [Col. 1096C].

With Helias, precentor of Cassey; Bernard, sacristan of Pairac; Itherius, archdeacon of Solis; and very many others as witnesses.

### III. Charter of the gift of the land of Podia.

(Cosnier, *Exordium Fontis Ebraldi*, p. 216, from the cartulary of Fontevraud, charter 686, fols. 168b and 169.)

We, Petronilla of Montorant, Pagan of Vallibus, Theobald Forescherius, Belotus of Clairs Vallées, and John of Tuscha, give and grant in perpetuity to Lord Robert, a most religious man, and to the most devout congregation of monks of Fontevraud [Col. 1097A], namely the land of Podia, from the Carbonaria road to Robert’s Wood, together with the meadow at the spring of Voigi, with tithes, profits, and all renderings, to be possessed free of customary dues.

Besides that gift, we gave them this additional endowment: namely, the wood for all their needs and those of their people, and all rights of pasture for animals and pannage for their pigs, whenever other pigs were excluded. I, Elias of Tellio, together with my son Boamund, likewise give and grant to them forever whatever we held in the above-written gift of this alms. We also, Geoffrey of Chaluiniac and my sons Bocurtus, Hector, Geoffrey, Pagan, and Longus, brother of the bishop +, likewise give and grant to them whatever we have in the land and in the pannage [Col. 1097B].

These saw and heard these things: Peter, bishop of Poitiers; Master Robert; Longus of the Tower; John Oliverius; Arraud Boschet; Aamerus of Gastina; John Vilanus; Benedict of Bernezaic.

### IV. Gift of Fulk, count of Anjou, of meadows in Gaina.

(Cosnier, *ibid.*, p. 201, from the Fontevraud cartulary, charter 348.)

I, Fulk, count of Anjou, for the salvation of my soul and those of my parents, with the consent of my sons Geoffrey and Fulk, give and grant to God, blessed Mary, and the nuns of Fontevraud, through the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel [Col. 1097C], all the meadows which I have in Gaina. Witnesses to this gift are Hugh Rigard and Walter of Poniac.

Done in the reign of Philip, king of the Franks; William, duke of Aquitaine; and Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

### Charter of the same man for the monastery of Fontevraud.

(J. de la Mainferme, *Clypeus Fontis Ebraldi*, II, 200.)

I, Fulk, count of Anjou, for the salvation of my soul and those of my parents, with the consent of my sons Geoffrey and Fulk, give and grant to God, blessed Mary, and the nuns of Fontevraud, through the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, all the meadows which I have in Gaina. Witnesses to this gift are Hugh [Col. 1097D] Rigard and Walter of Poniac.

Done in the reign of Philip, king of the Franks; William, duke of Aquitaine; and Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

### VI. Gift of the younger Fulk concerning Pont de Saugé.

(*Ibid.*, p. 209.)

It is incumbent upon us to do what that evangelical precept enjoins: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail they may receive you into eternal dwellings.” Therefore I, Fulk the Younger, count of the Angevins, moved by this authority to provide alms for God’s needy handmaids, for the salvation of my soul and the remedy of my parents’ souls, grant to the nuns of Fontevraud, from my resources, namely Pont de Cé and the vicariate of that bridge, theft and blood in their entirety [Col. 1098A]. I therefore give these to them freely and peacefully, with all the revenues which my predecessors held there, and with those which I appear to have by hereditary right in the water or outside the water, together with every benefit or advantage which is already apparent to me or may be improved, so that no one may presume to violate or disturb my gift.

Countess Aremburga, my wife, from whose dower it came, and my little son Geoffrey, consented to this gift of alms; and we invested Lady Petronilla, the abbess, by means of a knife with a black handle. Moreover, I granted them my wood and the bridge’s requirements. These witnesses were present: Lisiard of Sablé, Hubert of Champagne, Florus, the count’s brother, Papabovem of Reillé, William of the Mills, Barbotin of Ramfort, Geoffrey his brother, Archard of Escharbot. Of the canons of Saint-Laud: Ralph of Saint-Hilaire, Geoffrey Caiaphas, Odo of Saint-Florent. In the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; Fulk, count of the Angevins; and Renaud, bishop of the Angevins.

### VII. Gift of the same man of mills and meadows at Compignas

*(Ibid., p. 208.)*

I, Fulk the Younger, count of the Angevins, son of Count Fulk, having come to Fontevraud for prayer, for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, [Col. 1098C] give and grant to be held in perpetuity by God, the blessed Mary, and the nuns of Fontevraud, into the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, the mill and all the meadows that are at Compignas in the wood of Monnesio, and the water of the Vienne which I hold at Saumur, for constructing a weir and mills.

Seeing and present were: my mother Bertrada; Peter, bishop of Poitiers; Rainerius the chief officer; Peter of Château-Erault; Peter of Saint-Saturnin; and, among the knights, Galvanus of Chamilliac, Griseia of Montsoreau, and her son Geoffrey of Doué, Borel of Saumur.

Done in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and under Rainald, bishop of the Angevins.

### VIII. Gift of the same man of twenty *julli* of meadow in Véron

*(Ibid., p. 206.)*

[Col. 1098D]

The reading of the sacred word, in its sweetly modulated voice, invites us to care for our souls, saying: “Watch, because you do not know when the Lord will come.” Animated by love of this sacred exhortation and relying on its authority, I, Fulk, count of the Angevins, son of Count Fulk, desiring with ardent longing that my great sins might be forgiven, came, by God’s help and with great contrition of heart, to Fontevraud for prayer.

Therefore, whatever manner of man I may be, continually and humbly beseeching the Lord God with unceasing zeal, and considering the many and great needs of the nuns of that church, who there serve God in the devotion of humility, [Col. 1099A] I took care to give one small portion for their enrichment, so that before so great a Judge the prayer of me, a sinner, might be deemed worthy of being heard. In Christ’s name I assigned and gave to them forever, with full integrity, through Lord Robert of Arbrissel, a most religious man, whose admirable teaching shines throughout the whole Church in the word of holy preaching, the thunder of holy exhortation, and his eloquence: namely, twenty *julli* of meadow which I appear to hold in the pastures of Véron.

For this gift I confirmed to those aforesaid nuns the alms-gift of my father, namely the wood of Rotard, which my father Fulk had given for his sins and which my brother Geoffrey Martel had granted; likewise [Col. 1099B] the land which lay around the aforesaid wood. This gift was made in the hearing of these men: Queen Bertrada, Hugh of Gilleio, Borel of Saumur, Geoffrey Maumon, the religious men Fulk the master-chaplain and Caradoc.

### IX. Gift of the same man of meadows in Gaina

*(Ibid., p. 208.)*

It is salutary for us to sow works of mercy, so that at harvest-time we may deserve the fruit of our labor, according to that prophetic saying: “They shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.” I, Fulk the Younger, count of the Angevins, for the salvation of my soul and the remedy of my parents’ souls, give to God, Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and the nuns of the church of Fontevraud [Col. 1099C] my meadows in Gaina, which I held at rent from the monks of Carrois, to hold at all times, to possess freely, and grant them in perpetuity, under the testimony of these men: Geoffrey of Clairvaux, his brother Pagan, Hugh Rigaud, Drogo Fétard, Aimery Flocel.

### X. Gift of the same man of the half-shares and meadows of Borenna

*(Ibid., p. 205.)*

From several testimonies of Scripture we learn that we should redeem our sins by alms. Hearing this most salutary admonition of sacred authority, [Col. 1099D] I, Fulk the Younger, count of the Angevins, son of Count Fulk, considered giving something of mercy to God’s poor.
