I give indeed to Almighty God, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, a man of great integrity and most religious character, and to the nuns subject to him at Fontevraud—women recalled from the luxury of the world to the observance of monastic religion in the church of Blessed Mary ever Virgin—all the half-shares of Borenna and all the meadows which Geoffrey Martel the Elder, count of the Angevins, my predecessor, formerly had, held, and possessed. May the divine mercy of Almighty God grant me a period of true repentance and grant my predecessors a place of refreshment.

This grant was made in the presence of: Aba of Briblay, Borel [Col. 1100A] of Saumur, and Ralph of Grez. In the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; Ralph, archbishop of Tours; and Renaud, bishop of the Angevins.

### XI. Gift of the same man of the land of the Franks

*(Ibid., p. 206.)*

I, Fulk the Younger, count of the Angevins, heavily burdened by the weight of my sins, make known to all that, for the salvation of my soul and the remedy of my parents’ souls, I give to God, Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and the women subject in Christ’s name to monastic discipline at the place commonly called Fontevraud, the land of the Franks called Barba Nova, to supply their needs and for their own use: I give it free and peaceful, and grant it to be possessed by perpetual right [Col. 1100B], with the consent of my wife Countess Aremburga, at the city of Tours. (At the count’s invitation Robert had gone to that city.)

Seeing and hearing were Odo, dean of Saint-Martin; Ernulf of Montgomery; Renaud of Salmoncay; and Peter Locha.

### XII. Gift of the same man of the land of Brulio

*(Ibid., p. 203.)*

The Apostle Paul says: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am nothing.” Therefore, by the authority of so great a charity, I, Count Fulk surnamed the Younger, son of Count Fulk, desiring heavenly things rather than earthly and seeing that no one can escape the bitter taste [Col. 1100C] of death when its hour comes, give and grant in perpetuity to God, Lord Robert of Arbrissel, a most distinguished man of great religion and integrity, and the women subject to him in Christ’s name, cultivating a place of holy monastic community, commonly called Fontevraud, who there most devoutly serve God the Lord: for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, my land of Brulio, which appears to lie by the bridge of Chinon, and all the revenues of that land, its meadows and rents, for supplying the needs of the aforesaid holy women. I give and grant it as wholly and completely as it appears to be mine, to hold and possess freely, peacefully, and without any claim; and also all my customary dues [Col. 1100D] which appear to accrue to me from all the holdings [lacuna].

Witnesses to this matter are my brother Philip, Borel of Saumur, Peter of Champ-Caprier, Pagan of Pierre-Font, Geoffrey Lesgans, Effred, knight of Queen Bertrada, Richard, tutor of Philip, brother of the count of the Angevins, Gosbert of Morton, Hersendis the prioress, and Petronilla.

The charter was made in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, with Ralph as archbishop of Tours.

### XIII. Gift of the same man of mills at Chinon

*(Ibid., p. 205.)*

Whoever longs for heavenly things with the whole gaze of his mind ought, according as his means furnish him, to give from his earthly substance to the poor and to provide fitting support for churches. [Col. 1101A] For it is written that charity covers a multitude of sins. Therefore, prompted by the testimony of this divine authority, I, Fulk the Younger, count of the Angevins, son of Count Fulk, for healing from my sins and remission for myself and my parents, give to God, Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and the nuns subject to him in Christ’s name, gathered in the church of Blessed Mary at Fontevraud, two mills at Chinon and the weir on which the mills stand, to be possessed freely and peacefully forever.

Under these witnesses: my mother Queen Bertrada, my brother Philip, Gosbert of Morton, Robert Purel—to whom I commanded that the mills be delivered to Amaury of Montfort. Among the sisters: Arsendis the prioress and Petronilla.

### XIII bis. Settlement instituted by Fulk the Younger, count of the Angevins, between the community of Fontevraud and Ralph, son of Ivo

*(Ibid., p. 212.)*

[Col. 1101B]

So that all posterity may know, I, Count Fulk, son of Count Fulk, have ordered it to be recorded in writing that I wholly resolved the dispute which existed between the community of Fontevraud and Ralph, son of Ivo, together with his son-in-law Geoffrey. The cause of this dispute was as follows. William of Montsoreau and his wife Hersendis bought from Ivo, canon and chief officer of Saint-Martin, all the property which he possessed in the town of Saint-Martin of Candes, and gave it to their son Stephen. As [Col. 1101C] they themselves had possessed it, so their son Stephen peacefully possessed it for many years.

At length, after William’s death, his wife Hersendis took the religious habit at Fontevraud. For her soul, her son Stephen gave the aforesaid property, which both his father and mother had left to him, to God, Blessed Mary, and the nuns serving God there, and caused his elder brother Walter to consent to it. But the aforesaid Ralph and Geoffrey challenged this donation. I, Count Fulk, unwilling that this case should be prolonged any further, made the following settlement with the said challengers: by my hand they relinquished their claim with a knife having a black handle; and with that same knife I gave and granted to God, Blessed Mary, and [Col. 1101D] the nuns of Fontevraud, into the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, the aforesaid property—namely, houses, vineyards, and land—to be possessed in perpetual right, with the challengers themselves present and consenting.

Witnesses to this matter are Robert of Blois, Amaury of Montfort, Borel of Saumur, Aimery of Avoir, Renaud of Salmunciac, and Stephen of Montsoreau. This charter was made in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and Ralph, archbishop of Tours.

### XIV. Confirmation of all gifts by Aremburga, wife of Fulk the Younger

*(Ibid., p. 214.)*

[Col. 1102A]

Let all religious faithful of the holy catholic Church, hearing this present document, have sound understanding of all those things which they have seen me, Aremburga, countess of the Angevins, affirm and grant to the distinguished community of nuns of Fontevraud. Indeed, my venerable husband Fulk, count of the Angevins, son of Count Fulk, from his resources and his own possessions, took generous care, by God’s disposing mercy, to enrich Robert of Arbrissel, a man of great religious devotion and a discerning dispenser of the word of evangelical preaching, for building the church which he was establishing in honor [Col. 1102B] of God and the glorious Virgin Mary at the place commonly called Fontevraud, and for the use of the holy community of nuns in that place.

All the goods charitably given or granted at Fontevraud by my aforesaid lord husband, the count, to the aforesaid Robert and the women subject to him, I have fully confirmed under the protection of my assent, under the testimony of Geoffrey of Ramfort, Renaud, Franbaud, Gireius of Escharbot, Hugh of La Haye, Odo of Doué, Boterius son of Engilbaud, Boterius of Le Mans, Matthew of Montreuil, Beatrice, mistress of the countess of the Angevins, and Rivaria, wife of Hugh of Doué; in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, Fulk, count of the Angevins [Col. 1102C], and Ralph, archbishop of Tours.

### XV. Gift by Fulk Foterel of his house

*(Ibid., p. 216.)*

I, Robert of Arbrissel, ordered to be committed to writing the gift which Fulk Foterel made, for the love of God and of me, of his house and of the household goods belonging to the house, to the Lord God, the church of Saint Mary, and the nuns of Fontevraud. Thus Fulk Foterel gave to God, Saint Mary, and the nuns his house with all its appurtenances, at the request and exhortation of Fulk the Younger, count of the Angevins, his mother Queen Bertrada, and Eremburga, the count’s wife, into [Col. 1102D] my hand.

This was seen and heard by Aimery of La Faye, Arduin of Saint-Médard, Segebrand, Conestabulus, and Carbonel of Saint-Michel.

This was done in Fulk’s own house at the castle of Loudun, while Philip reigned in France, Fulk was count of the Angevins, Peter of blessed memory was bishop of Poitiers, and Renaud of Martigné was bishop of the Angevins.

### XVI. Gift by Berlaius of Montreuil of the land of Bornio

*(COSNIER, Exord. Font. Ebrald., p. 110.)*

I, Berlaius of Montreuil, and Hugh, son of Gregory, give to the church of Fontevraud the land of Bornio, bounded as follows: on one side lies the land [Col. 1103A] of Guy, son of Osmund; on another, the wood of Miles of Tuille; on another side, Berlaius’s own enclosed field; on another, the land of Saint Radegund; and on another side stands the elm of Maistre. I, Berlaius, also grant that church the vineyards situated within the wastelands, and the vineyards which were held of my fief, which the very men who held them gave to the aforesaid church, while the customary due of the wine-seller is retained. We made these gifts with the consent of our wives and sons.

### XVII. Charter of the Fontevraud priory of Orsan

*(PAVILLON, *Vie de Robert d’Arbrissel*, p. 557.)*

We wish it to be made known that the barons of the region of Bourges—namely Ralph of Déols, Geoffrey of Issoudun, John of Lignières, Elias of Orval, and Humbald [Col. 1103B] of Sainte-Sévère—for the redemption of their souls, gave to God, Blessed Mary ever Virgin, and the nuns serving God under regular discipline at the place called Orsan, that neither they nor their dependants should ever take from the nuns’ money or goods any customary dues commonly called passage-toll, market-toll, or sales-dues.

This gift and grant were made in the presence of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, under whose governance that place was held, and into the hand of the venerable Leodegarius, archbishop of Bourges, in whose diocese the aforesaid place lies. And so that this gift and grant might remain firm and inviolate for all time, the aforesaid barons, on the counsel and with the assent of the said archbishop, established that [Col. 1103C] if any of their successors—God forbid!—should presume to violate or in any way disturb this gift, he should be deprived of his own possessions and restrained by a sentence of anathema until he assented to this donation.

After these things had been done, the aforesaid archbishop, Lord Robert, and all the other brothers present there granted to the named barons and their successors, on behalf of Almighty God and Saint Mary ever Virgin, the fraternity of that holy place and participation in all its benefits, etc.

Done in the year of the Lord 1113.

I, Leodegarius, archbishop of Bourges, on the counsel of our clerics and others, absolve and establish as exempt from synods and agreements the church of Maisons, [Col. 1103D] in whose parish the place of Orsan is situated, in the presence of the above-named barons.

### XVIII. The multiple gift of Grimaud of Monts

*(DE LA MAINFERME, *Clypeus Font. Ebrald.*, II, p. 309.)*

I, Grimaud of Monts, and my brothers Pippin, Rainald, Berengar, and Geoffrey, wish it to be known that the claim which we were making concerning the weir [lacuna] at Gaina against the nuns of Fontevraud was brought to a settlement through the hand of Peter, bishop of Poitiers. We had asserted that part of the weir had been made on our land without our consent. Hersendis, prioress of Fontevraud, objected [Col. 1104A] that the church of Fontevraud, as we ourselves had seen, had held it peacefully for seven years and had annually paid us twelve denarii in rent for the weir. Therefore, fearing danger to our souls, we relinquish the claim which we made concerning the weir; and moreover, into the hand of Robert of Arbrissel, we give and grant to God, Blessed Mary, and the nuns of Fontevraud the weir, arable land on either side of it, meadows, and marshland, etc.

Present were Bishop Peter himself, who forgave us his grievance for this settlement, Rainerius the chief officer, Burchard of Dercé, and Garnerius of Gaina.

Done in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; William, duke of Aquitaine; and Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

### XIX. Charter of Adelaide’s gift of the valley of Fontevraud

*(COSNIER, Exord. Font. Ebraldi, p. 110.)*

[Col. 1104B]

I, Adelaide, surnamed Rivaria, daughter of Guy son of Osmund, wish to make known to all that, with the consent of my mother Aremburga, I give to Lord Robert of Arbrissel and to the community of religious women whom he assembled for God the valley of Fontevraud, for building a church in honor of Blessed Mary ever Virgin. The valley so given is bounded as follows: on one side lies the land of Berlaius, and on the other the public road as far as the second mill of the valley itself, etc. We did this by the counsel and consent of the lords of the land, namely Geoffrey Maumon and [Col. 1104C] Gislebert of Loudun, under the hearing and testimony of worthy men, namely Walter of Montsoreau, Aimery of Bernezay, and Ivo of Sessiniac.

### XX. Charter of Adelaide, daughter of Guy, concerning the gift of the valley of Fontevraud

*(Ibid., p. 110.)*

I, Adelaide, surnamed Rivaria, daughter of Guy son of Osmund, wish to make known to all that I give to Lord Robert of Arbrissel and the community of religious women whom he assembled the valley of Fontevraud, for building a church in honor of Blessed Mary ever Virgin. The valley so given is bounded as follows: on one side lies the land of Berlaius, and on the other the public road as far as the second mill of the [Col. 1104D] valley itself. To this church we give land to be cultivated by four oxen in two seasons, and two yokes of land before the guest-house. We did this by the counsel and consent of the lords of the land, namely Geoffrey Maumon and Gislebert of Loudun, under the hearing and testimony of worthy men, namely Walter of Montsoreau, Aimery of Bernezay, Hugh son of Gregory, and Ivetus of Sessiniac.

### XXI. Gift by Peter of Gasnachia of the heath at Belloquercu

*(Ibid., p. 217.)*

Whatever is done out of regard for piety assists its author both here and in the future; for the Apostle says: “Each shall receive the fruit of his labor according as he labors.” [Col. 1105A] Secure, therefore, in the authority of this recompense, I, Peter of Gasnachia, by the counsel and exhortation of my lord Peter, bishop of Poitiers, have resolved to found a church in the place called the heath of Belloquercu and to endow it from my own possessions.

Following the counsel of my bishop, so that the affection of my devotion might have a more devout effect, I give and grant the aforesaid place to God, Blessed Mary, and the nuns of Fontevraud, into the hands of Lord Robert of Arbrissel. By his preaching and by the example of his good life, that church, founded under the habit of holy religious life, serves God alone. To this church founded on the heath of Belloquercu in honor of Blessed Mary ever Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist, I give and grant to be held in perpetuity [Col. 1105B] land, much of it heathland, the tithe of the ovens of Belveherio, the tithe of the mills of Noir-Monastier which my uncle Chalo made, my mother’s enclosed vineyard, the marsh of G., and the hides from the houses of Noir-Monastier—except that, if any hunter among the knights wishes to have [one], he shall pay twelve denarii for a stake and six for a doe.

### XXII. Gift by Leonius of Longiacum of Calidus Furnerius in the diocese of Tours

*(Ibid., p. 218.)*

Lord Leonius, fearing the fires of Gehenna, gave to God and Master Robert, a man of blessed memory, the place called Calidus Furnerius, with its land—as he himself had marked it out with his forester Stephen and Walter Troissel—for constructing a church [Col. 1105C] and establishing a community there. Leonius’s wife Barbota granted the gift in the presence of Lord Robert and his disciples Fulk of Coceio, Ruvallo, Rogius, Daniel, Judicael, Peter, Burchard, and other brethren. Drogo, brother of Leonius, granted this gift before he went to Jerusalem; Guy, Drogo’s son, likewise granted the gift to God and Lord Robert of Arbrissel before the doors of Saint-Martin of Tours, etc.

### XXIII. Gift by Sophia, daughter of Rainfredis and Peter Achard, of Rives and other places in the diocese of Tours

*(Ibid., p. 219.)*

[Col. 1105D] I, Sophia Rainfredis, daughter of Peter Achard, desiring to receive the religious habit of nuns, give and grant forever to Lord Robert and the nuns of Fontevraud gathered there under regular discipline, first myself and my allod of Polineio. I also give them land at Achaicum to be cultivated by two oxen in two sowings, and as much land as they wish for establishing vineyards there. I also grant land sufficient there for constructing gardens, a church, houses, cloisters, and groves. I grant woodland for all their needs, and half of the weir at the place commonly called Riva. Aimery, viscount of Château-Erault, in whose fief it lay, assented, with the consent of Arraud, Achard’s son, his daughter Petronilla, and Walter, Petronilla’s son.

[Col. 1106A] Done in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; William, duke of Aquitaine; and Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

### XXIV. Charter of Rainald of Salmanche concerning the gift of the place of Ralaius (Rolay)

*(Ibid., p. 221.)*

Rainald of Salmanche and his mother Juliana, daughter of Geoffrey son of Meynard, gave into the hand of Master Robert, for the remedy of their sins, as alms, whatever they possessed on this side of the ford of Raalio, except the meadow, to the church of Saint Mary of Fontevraud, to be possessed freely and peacefully forever. Aimery Rufus gave to the aforesaid church the whole fief of Peter of Berria, his deceased brother, for his soul, delivering Peter’s daughter to the community of the nuns [Col. 1106B] of Fontevraud to be veiled with the sacred veil. Of this fief, the aforesaid Rainald [the text is defective] dedicated the chapel of Raalio through Lord Peter, bishop of Poitiers, and afterward had the cemetery blessed by William Alcelmus, bishop of that city. Rainald himself there carried holy water on his shoulders in a cask.

And when, at Le Mans, he lay at the point of death, he transferred into its own possession the clearings which he had given to be broken up for the aforesaid church; and through his squires John and Geoffrey, son of Geoffrey Chenfrit, he instructed his wife Corinda, his son Rainald, and his brother Geoffrey to grant and augment this gift. They gladly did so and gave whatever he possessed from the head of Salis [Col. 1106C] as far as the ditch of La Garda and as far as the watercourse. This was granted by his wife Corinda, their sons Rainald and Ralph, their daughter Juliana before she was betrothed, and their uncle Geoffrey.

Witnesses of the first gift: Lady Hersendis, foundress of the church of Fontevraud; and Lady Petronilla, afterward, by God’s grace and the election of all, made its mother.

### XXV. Gift by Walter of Clichon of the mill of Ponzay

*(Ibid., p. 238.)*

I, Walter of Clichon, and my wife Seria give our daughter Roberga to Almighty God and Lord [Col. 1106D] Robert of Arbrissel, for conversion to the life of nuns; and together with her we grant our mill of Ponzay to the aforesaid Lord Robert, freely and forever, for the maintenance of the nuns. This was granted by Seria’s brothers Walter and Bernoin, and by their sons.

Afterward Gerorius, one of the relatives of the nun Roberga, made a claim against the same gift. When Lady Hersendis, prioress of Fontevraud, heard of this, she came to Loudun, to the court of Lord Gislebert, in which that claim was settled. Witnesses are Gislebert of Loudun; his son Alio; Renaud; Bernoin; and many others of the brothers of Fontevraud: Lisiard, Walter the priest, and Gosbert of Bernezay.

### XXVI. Gift by Fromond of Novestolo

*(DE LA MAINFERME, *Clypeus Fontis Ebraldi*, II, 378.)*

[Col. 1107A]

Since we have in the Gospel the words, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice,” no man ought to detract from a work of mercy. This is what Lord Robert of Arbrissel, formerly the first brother and father of your community, did; and what we likewise did for Lord Fromond of Novestolo concerning Hugh his son, once slain at Guirchia: for Fromond himself, his son, and all his relatives together had forgiven the death of his son to the man who killed him. When all had first been prepared, we buried him in the cemetery.

For this reason Fromond, for the redemption of his son’s soul [Col. 1107B] and for the salvation of himself and his own, gave to your church and to you that half which he held at Bremium, both from the rent of the town and from the tithe of the church, and also from the priesthood which Vitalis the priest then held. Fromond and his sons Iherus and Joffred made this gift and grant in your chapter, with your abbot Robert present and the canons seeing it—namely Guarin the prior and Robert the sacrist. Very many laymen were also present, whose names are these: Rainald, Allobrox, Henry his son, and Suhard of Rota.

### XXVII. Gift by Geoffrey Fulchred of the customary dues of the court of Rest

*(Ibid., p. 249.)*

[Col. 1107C] + I, Geoffrey Fulchred, give and grant to Almighty God, Lord Robert of Arbrissel, the church of Fontevraud, and the nuns serving God there, my customary dues of the court of Rest: namely, the port, its lordship, and the wine-dues, etc. My wife, named Burgundy, from whose dower it came, my brother Aimery, and my sister Joanna consented.

Witnesses are Lovel of Daumeric, Bartholomew of Bessay, Fulco Fessard, Hardouin of Vigné, Pagan of Lucay, Peter Briant, Walter of Montsoreau, Ivo of Sessigné, Hernald of Sessigné, Frogerius of Crevé, and Peter of Menealne. This gift was made in the chapter of the pious and just community [Col. 1107D] of nuns, before God and Saint Mary his mother, in the presence of Lord Robert, their most loving father.

For all men should know that Geoffrey Fulchred, being the giver of this alms, commanded Lord Robert of Arbrissel and the community of nuns subject to him, namely through William of Rest, his steward, to make the aforesaid gift and undoubtedly confirm those present, for the remedy of his soul and those of his parents, in the presence of Lord Peter, bishop of Poitiers, Rainerius the chief officer, and Peter of Saint-Saturnin. Witnesses are William of Rest, Hugh of Salmoniac, John Tiramuscam, Clarenbald of Loudun, Rainald of Loudun, and Norman of Saint-Florent.

Given in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; Fulk, [Col. 1108A] count of the Angevins; and Raynald, bishop of the Angevins.

### XXVIII. Gift by Aimery of La Haye and his brother Effred of a mill

*(Ibid., II, 241.)*

+ We, Aimery of La Haye and my brother Effred, grant to Almighty God, Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and the most religious women subject to him in God’s name at Fontevraud, the mill of Ponzay, to hold peacefully—the mill which Walter of Clichon and his wife Seria had given them forever and without any claim. One of my knights, Walter, who held the aforesaid mill from me, also consented; Count Fulk of the Angevins had strongly urged him to do so.

Seeing and hearing were Fulk, count of the Angevins, Chalo of Furnelles, Geoffrey of Clairvaux, and his brother Pagan, etc.

### XXIX. Gift by Aimo Rosel of the land of Pociac

*(Ibid., p. 242.)*

The Prophet + says: “Blessed is he who understands the needy and poor man; in the evil day the Lord shall deliver him.” Therefore, secure in the authority of so great a recompense, I, Aimo Rosel, give to God and grant to Lord Robert and the community of nuns of Fontevraud, humbly serving God there, my allod of Bociac outside Trincheias, to possess freely and peacefully at all times. [Col. 1108C] I placed the confirmation of this gift into the hand of Lady Philippa, countess of Poitiers, for the benefit of the nuns, under the testimony of these men: William of Miribel and Renaud of Pellent. The sons of Aimo Rosel granted this donation in the presence of Philippa, countess of Poitiers. The witnesses were Burchard of Chaorii, Longus of Gastina, and Pons of Beaujeu.

### XXX. Gift by Aimery of Château-Arraud

*(Ibid., p. 241.)*

I, Aimery, viscount of Château-Arraud, give and grant forever to Lord Robert, for the support of the nuns of Fontevraud, as alms, my *froca* which I hold at the mill of Bosco, with all its integrity [Col. 1108D]. Seeing were Belot of Clairvaux and Renaud of Pellent. After this, within this gift and at Jarunda, Viscount Aimery gave the aforesaid nuns land to be cultivated by four oxen; as above, this was granted by my brother Bosus and John of Tuscha.

### XXXI. Charter of Leogart and Adelaide concerning certain quarries granted to the abbey of Fontevraud

*(Ibid., p. 241.)*

Let all know that I, Leogart, my wife Eremburga, and my daughter Adelaide Rivaria gave to God, Saint Mary, Lord Robert, and the nuns of Fontevraud, together with other gifts, stone for making a church and all its works. [Col. 1109A] Afterwards, seeing the church grow and religious life increase, we increased the gift to include all the quarries, etc.

Witnesses are Gerard of Le Puy and Geoffrey of Brezay. Among the brothers: Andrew the prior and Sainfred of Cleia.

Given in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; Fulk, count of the Angevins; and Ralph, archbishop of Tours.

### XXXII. Gift by Basoin and Papin of Monts of a fief

*(Ibid., p. 243.)*

I, Basoin, son of Aimery of the Castle, and Papin of Monts, together with my brothers, give and grant to God, Blessed Mary, Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and the nuns of Fontevraud [Col. 1109B] the fief which we held at Varens from Aimery Flocel, for the remission of our sins [lacuna].

Witnesses are Aimery Flocel, Peter of Montcator, Aubert of Sazay, his son Peloquin, Aimery of Calcea, and others.

Done in the reign of Philip, king of the Franks; William, duke of Aquitaine; and Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

### XXXIII. Gift by Arveus of Gion of his customary dues

*(Ibid., p. 243.)*

I, Arveus of Gion, for the remission of my sins, remit to Saint Mary of Fontevraud, into the hand of Lord Robert, whatever revenue may come to me from their goods, whether they pass through my land or across my water. Moreover, I offer my protection for all [Col. 1109C] their goods.

Witnesses are Affred of Dunione; Maheld, wife of Arveus himself; Gimo the steward; Hugh of Saint-Véran; Alberic of Burliac; and Lord Aimery, disciple of Lord Robert.

This was done in the reign of King Philip.

### XXXIV. Gift by Fulchred of Saint-Léger for building a lodging-house

*(Ibid., p. 246.)*

I, Fulchred of Saint-Léger, give and grant to God, Blessed Mary, and the nuns of Fontevraud, into the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, for the remission of my soul and those of my parents, [Col. 1109D] Tuscha for building a lodging-house for the brethren, and a meadow, with the consent of my son Geoffrey.

Witnesses are Peter Ottalanus, Cosbert of Bernadaic, Geoffrey of Cleta, and Pagan of Chinon.

Given in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; William, duke of Aquitaine; and Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

### XXXV. The multiple gift of Walter of Montsoreau, contained in three charters

*(Ibid., p. 247.)*
Ego, Gautier of Montsoreau, give to God, to blessed Mary, to Robert of Arbrissel, and to the community of religious women, my right of jurisdiction and all the customary dues throughout all the land which they have or shall have at Fontevraud, and for their men throughout [Col. 1110A] all my territory, especially within my castle, and in every other land wherever I have customary dues, from all merchandise and all passages. I also grant the land of Loges, and give the jurisdiction and all the customary dues which I have there, together with whatever the inhabitants may wish to give, etc. And I do this with the consent of my wife Griseia, under the testimony of these men: Geoffrey Maumon, John his brother, Gautier of Gisons, Gautier of Poëry, Marcuard, and Geoffrey of Linières.

### XXXVI. Another gift by the same man

I, Gautier of Montsoreau, and my son William, give and grant in perpetuity to God, to Saint Mary of Fontevraud, and to the nuns serving God there [Col. 1110B] the fishing-water called by the people Concha. Since it was not held from my own demesne but as a fief, I gave to Foulques Fissard, in exchange, my vicariate of Ruisseau, and to Robert his son my horse. Moreover, we give to those same nuns our fishery at Resté, to possess in perpetuity. Witnesses to this grant are Peter Guirchia, William of Tullejo, Oger of Saint-Martin, and Peter of Jarreia.

These acts were done in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou; Petronilla, first abbess of Fontevraud; and Angarde, prioress.

### XXXVII. Charter granting the valley of Seguin in the forest of Cadouin to Lord Robert of Arbrissel

*(Ibid., p. 149.)*

[Col. 1110C]

I, William of Biront, and my wife Alpaidis, with the consent of our sons William and Bertrand, for the salvation of ourselves and ours, irrevocably grant to God, to Saint Mary of Cadouin, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and to the servants of God, half of one holding in the forest called Cadouin, and the place named the valley of Seguin. We also grant whatever from the aforesaid forest may be necessary for the buildings or use of that place. Moreover, we give the place called Basse-Calderie, etc. Count Aldebert of Périgord granted the same gifts. Likewise, on the same day, with the same witnesses—William, bishop of Périgueux, Gerard of Salis, Mainard of Baignac, etc.—he granted whatever Algerius of Moisidan and Arnald of Mont-Incensé and their wives had given in the valley of Seguin. Afterwards they confirmed these things at Moisidan before Lord Robert of Arbrissel, etc.

### XXXVIII. Gift of Gerard of Puy-Brunel: the Long Meadow

*(Ibid., p. 252.)*

That we may be able to obtain mercy from the Lord, I, Gerard of Puy-Brunel, and my wife Aldeardis, acknowledging that we are burdened with great and grievous sins, give and grant to God, to Saint Mary, to Lord Robert, and to the nuns of Fontevraud, to hold in perpetuity, the Long Meadow [Col. 1111A] and the land adjoining that meadow. Witnesses: Pagan, son of Bernard of Poitiers; Benedict, brother of Aimeric of Évraud; and William, brother of Segebrand of Saumur.

This was done in the time of Louis, king of the Franks; William, duke of Aquitaine; and Peter, bishop of Poitiers.

### XXXIX. Another gift by the same man: the mill of Mortonne

*(Ibid.)*

I, Gerard, admonished by divine prompting, together with my wife Aldeardis and Rainaud Audiardus, my son, give and grant in perpetuity to God, to blessed Mary, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and to the nuns serving at Fontevraud [Col. 1111B] whatever by our own right or that of our family we appeared to possess in the mill of Mortonne, situated within the jurisdiction of Saint-Léger of Loudun. We give them seven arpents of land and three of meadow near that mill, into the hand of Lord Peter, bishop of Poitiers. Signed: Rainerius Capicerius; Gerard; Rainaud; Peter, bishop of Poitiers. Witnesses are Rainerius Capicerius and Peter of Saint-Saturnin.

The charter was drawn up while Louis reigned as king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Anjou, and Peter was bishop of Poitiers.

### XL. Gift of Lambert of Bon-Œil and Stephen of Linières: the Plain Land

*(Ibid., p. 254.)*

[Col. 1111C] We, Lambert of Bon-Œil, Stephen of Linières, and our sons, for the remission of our sins and those of our parents, freely give in perpetuity to Lord Robert, to the church of Fontevraud, and to the nuns serving God there, to hold and possess, the Plain Land which until now we have held from the ford of Croallio. I, Peter of Brissac, from whose fief it was held, with good and willing mind grant the whole of the aforesaid donation in its entirety, on behalf of the Lord God and of myself, to the above-named nuns; and furthermore I give them in perpetuity, as a token [argumentum], the meadows at the ford of Croallio and a site for building a mill. Witnesses to this matter are Richard the physician, Peter of Ville-Coperia, [Col. 1111D] Norman of Chanzelles, Peter son of the mayor of Brissac, Alboin of Senecay, Thomas of Marcay, and William of Luchay.

### XLI. Gift of William and Audebert: the place of Villa Salem

*(Ibid., p. 139.)*

William and Audebert of Trémouilles, who had previously given half of the Mas to the monks of Fontgombault, afterwards gave it to certain hermits—namely Geoffrey Gastinelli and Bertrand—living religiously in the place called Villa Salem. These aforesaid brethren of the church, having heard of the manner of life of the religious women of Fontevraud, determined to give and make over their place and everything acquired in that place to the aforesaid nuns, etc. [Col. 1112A] Blessed Peter, bishop of Poitiers, confirmed this gift as chief and superior lord.

From the archive of the priory of Villa Salem.

Peter, by the grace of God bishop of Poitiers, to all who inspect this little charter, eternal greeting in the Lord. We, the aforesaid bishop, as chief and superior lord, at the supplication and request of the aforesaid knight Audebert, lord of the whole castellany of Trémouilles and its appurtenances, have confirmed for ourselves and our successors every one of the aforesaid things, etc.; and, led by the Spirit of God and by the affection of charity which we bear toward the order of Fontevraud, we also promise, as chief and superior lord, for ourselves and our successors, wholly to warrant and defend every one of the aforesaid things for the religious women [Col. 1112B] against all persons, etc. This was done in the church of Saint Peter of Poitiers.

### XLII. Gift of Audeburgis of Montreuil: land and wood in the valley of Suchart

*(Ibid., p. 73.)*

+ I, Audeburgis of Montreuil, make known to those present and future that, for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, I give to almighty God, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, to the church of Fontevraud, and to the nuns serving God there, the land and wood of the valley of Suchart—indeed, whatever I appeared to possess—together with two women whom I have ordained to serve God in the church of Fontevraud under the habit of nuns. My daughter Mansella and Odo, son of my daughter, granted this gift, etc. Witnesses to this matter are Andrew of Prullé, Archambaud of Montreuil, Renaud of Bray, Michael of Chinon, Bodin of Candes, and many others. Present were Lord Robert of Arbrissel, the brethren Hubert the scribe and Prior Andrew, etc., and the sisters Petronilla the prioress and Countess Agnes.

Done while Louis was king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Maine, and Audebert [Hildebert] was bishop of Le Mans.

### XLIII. Gift of Pagan of Mirebeau: the wood of Rareto

*(Ibid., p. 256.)*

Let each person pray that his crimes may be remitted through the benefits of almsgiving. Therefore I, Pagan of Mirebeau, in order that the iniquities of myself, my wife, and my sons may be forgiven, give and grant to God, to Saint Mary, and to the nuns of Fontevraud, into the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, a certain part of my wood called Rareto, around the valley of Genebrosa . . . And in this wood, namely Rareto, I give to Saint Mary land to be cultivated by two oxen in two seasons; and outside the wood we give as much land again. Moreover, I give one yoke of meadow above the Indre. I made these gifts with the consent of my wife Belutia and my sons John, Geoffrey, and Archambaud, under these witnesses: Garnerius [Col. 1113A] of Villars and Hebo, nephew of Lebo of Saint-Michel.

This charter was drawn up while Philip reigned as king, Ralph was archbishop of Tours, and Fulk was count of Anjou.

### XLIV. Another gift of the same Pagan: the holdings

*(Ibid.)*

I, Pagan of Mirebeau, give and grant to God, to blessed Mary, and to the nuns of Fontevraud, into the hand of Lord Robert, whatever shall be given to them from all my holdings, so freely that no further consent of myself, my wife, or my sons shall be required concerning this. Therefore my wife Belutia and my sons John, Geoffrey, and Archambaud granted this. [Col. 1113B] Witnesses are Garnerius of Villars, Raimbaud of Colombiers, Gautier of Dreia, and Rainaud of Aonia.

Done while Philip was king of the Franks.

### XLV. Gift of Oger: land at Vérone

*(Ibid.)*

Let us distribute alms from our possessions to Christ’s poor, that we may have them as intercessors before the supreme Judge. Accordingly I, Oger, and my wife, have given to God, to Saint Mary, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and to the nuns of Fontevraud that land which we possessed at Vérone. Witnesses are Gosbert of Mortonne and Gosbert of Loches. [Col. 1113C] Hugh of Gisois and his son, at our request, also granted this gift.

Witnesses: Peloquin of Nézi and Gerard of Corleum.

### XLVI. Gift of Marcuard: four jugera of meadow

*(Ibid.)*

God, the rewarder of every good deed, does not leave unrewarded a gift made to the poor. Therefore I, Marcuard Malus Monachus, give to God, to most blessed Mary, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and to the nuns of Fontevraud four jugera of meadow beside the meadows of Geoffrey Malus [Col. 1113D] Monachus at Campané. This gift was granted by Bonus the son and his wife Anneis. Witnesses to this gift are Geoffrey Malus Monachus and Guarin of Laval.

Done while Louis reigned as king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Anjou, and Peter was bishop of Poitiers.

### XLVII. Gift of Garsire of Machecoul: the dues of the Loire and the sea

*(Ibid., p. 250.)*

I wish it to be known that I, Garsire of Machecoul, give to God, to most blessed Mary, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and to the nuns of Fontevraud all my customary dues from the Loire and from the sea, for the proper support [Col. 1114A] of the poor of Fontevraud. He placed the aforesaid gift upon the altar of Saint Benedict, in the church called the chapel of the infirm. Witnesses to this gift are Fulk, count of Anjou, Carbonel of Saint-Michel, and Fulk of Daon.

This gift was made while Louis reigned as king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Anjou, and Peter was bishop of Poitiers.

### XLVIII. Gift of John Girbald: the port of Chalcé

*(Ibid.)*

I, John Girbald, give and grant in perpetuity to God, to blessed Mary, and to the nuns serving God at Fontevraud, for the remedy of my soul [Col. 1114B] and those of my parents, into the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, the port of Chalcé and all the land which I possess beside the riverbank, etc. Hersendis the prioress, out of charity, gave me a colt from the revenues of the aforesaid church. Witnesses are my brother Allo, Oger of Saint-Martin, and Girod, provost of the archbishop of Candé.

> **Note:** [Col. 1113D] That is, of Tours. Here mention is made of the archbishop of Candé; the diocese of Candé is also mentioned in the third letter of Sulpicius Severus to his mother-in-law Bassula: “Martin [Col. 1114D] therefore foresaw his death long beforehand. Meanwhile there arose a reason why he should visit the diocese of Candé.”

And among the brethren of the place: Geoffrey of Cleia and Robert of Valleia.

Done while Louis was king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Anjou, and Ralph was archbishop of Tours.

### XLIX. Multiple gift of Hugh Rigaud

*(Ibid., p. 162.)*

[Col. 1114C] I, Hugh Rigaud, give to God, to Lord Robert, and to the nuns of Fontevraud living there under regular discipline, the mills which are in Briandia and the land which I held there. Not many days afterward, however, my nephew Goslin, Bernerius Chamelladus, and Goslin’s wife challenged the benefit of my almsgiving, namely the land and the mills. By the disposing mercy of God, this dispute was peacefully settled at the castle of Mirebeau; and the challengers themselves granted to Lord Robert and the named nuns, freely and quietly, to possess for all time, whatever by their own right they claimed in the mills and land. Under the testimony of Peter, bishop of Poitiers; Robert of Arbrissel; Aimeric [Col. 1114D] viscount of Château-Évraud; Aimeric of Faia; Rainerius the chaplain; the prior of Saint-Paul of Cormery; and Hersendis the prioress.

### L. Gift of Aimeric of Marilley

*(Ibid., p. 327.)*

I, Aimeric of Marilley, give to God and to Mary, mother of his glory, one of my daughters, to serve him under the regular discipline of nuns. With this my daughter I give to Lord Robert and the nuns of Fontevraud five *julla* of land in [Col. 1115A] the Green Field, and this right which I have in the mill of Comprigneio. Those granting this gift were my wife Oda, Archambaud of Melna my uncle, and my sister Aremburgis. Witnesses are Gautier of Tours, Josbert of Vérezia, Gautier of Loudun, Geoffrey of Cleia, and Garin of Ternay.

### LI. Gift of Frogerius Barba

*(Ibid., p. 332.)*

I, Frogerius Barba, a faithful giver, faithfully make known to all that I grant Lord Robert and the community of nuns of the new foundation at Fontevraud full and perpetual possession of my meadow-mill and the meadows which I had there—namely the land and fief of Arraud and Raimbaud, or rather the fief of Peter Cheopel, and likewise that of the mill of Besdum [Col. 1115B] itself—so that my two daughters may become nuns in the church of Fontevraud to the praise of the divine name, etc. In the hearing of Aimeric, viscount of Château-Arraud, Effred of Borno, and others.

### LII. Gift of Foulques Fessard

*(Ibid.)*

I, Foulques Fessard, vowed one daughter to God, to his glorious mother Mary, and to Lord Robert, to serve God the Lord most devoutly under the regular discipline of nuns. With this daughter of mine I gave the nuns of Fontevraud land [Col. 1115C] at Borno, to be cultivated by four oxen in two sowings, a dwelling-place upon that land, and woodland for all their needs. I also gave them four *julla* of meadow at Vérone. Under the testimony of my brother Hugh, Ernaud of Sessigné, and Odo of Saumur.

### LIII. Gift of Robert Fessard

*(Ibid., p. 333.)*

I, Robert, grant to the nuns, entirely and in full, at Fontevraud, whatever my father Foulques Fessard had given to God, to Saint Mary, and to the nuns of Fontevraud, on my part, into the hand of Master Robert and Prioress Hersendis. [Col. 1115D] Present as witnesses: Gautier Revello, my father Foulques, my mother Mary, and Lady Petronilla.

Given while Louis reigned as king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Anjou, and Rainaud was bishop of Anjou.

### LIV. Multiple gift of Peter Oblinc

*(Ibid., p. 214.)*

Let all know that Peter Oblinc, abandoning the world and wishing to devote himself to the contemplative life, at the exhortations of Robert, servant of God, gave himself to the church of Fontevraud; and as a gift he gave the following part of his inheritance to that church: two quarter-measures of vineyards contained in Bellocampo; and two [Col. 1116A] portions of land contained in the same field; and a portion of land in the parish of Saint Peter of Polignac; and in that same parish seven annual rent-pennies in the currency of Poitiers, etc. Witnesses to this gift were Giraud of Vilamorer, Peter Fulcardus the priest, and Isimbert Escoblat. While Philip was king in France and Léger governed the church of Bourges.

### LV. Very many gifts of very many persons

*(Ibid., p. 261.)*

It is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.”

Therefore I, Reginald of Pellent, give and grant to the nuns of Fontevraud, for [Col. 1116B] the salvation of my soul and those of my parents, through the hand of Lord Robert, land to be cultivated by four oxen in two sowings. In like manner, we two brothers, namely Chalo and Hugh of Vivonne, give and grant them land to be cultivated in perpetuity by four oxen in two seasons. Likewise I, Salomon of Château-Évraud, nephew of Vivian of Marigny, give land for four oxen, with the consent of that same Vivian and of John of Tuscha, my kinsman. Besides these aforesaid gifts, we four—namely Reginald, Chalo, Hugh, and Salomon—together give them meadows sufficient for twelve oxen, and from the woods both greenwood and dry wood, as much as they may need for building their houses or for whatever they may wish to make. Witnesses are Aimeric [Col. 1116C] the viscount, Ralph of Talmont, and Belot of Clairs-Vallons. While Philip reigned as king of the Franks; William was duke of Aquitaine; and Peter was bishop of Poitiers.

### LVI. Gift of Robert of Blot: his customary dues

*(Ibid., p. 260.)*

I, Robert of Blot, for the remedy of my soul, of my wife Hersendis, and of my parents, give and grant to almighty God, to gracious Mary, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and to the nuns of his Fontevraud, all my customary dues which ought to arise from my land, water, and all my possessions. Witnesses are Bouchard of Tavern, Simon [Col. 1116D] of Bernezay, William the physician, the abbess of Beaumont, and Hubert, priest of Chinon.

Given while Louis reigned as king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Anjou, and Ralph was archbishop of Tours.

### LVII. Gift of Ralph Barbotin and other barons: the wood of Agudella

*(Ibid., p. 250.)*

Let all know that Ralph Barbotin and his wife named Emperia, for the salvation of their souls and those of their parents, gave to God, to blessed Mary, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and to the nuns of the church of Fontevraud, whatever they possessed in the wood called Agudella. Likewise the other barons gave the aforesaid nuns whatever they possessed in that same wood: Benedict David, Aimeric of Bilzac, Ranulf Tanat, Rigaud of Berbezis, Reminund of Chaillac, and others. Under the testimony of Gofrann of Pirciac, Ranulf of Milliac, and Peter of Grageria.

### LVIII. Gift of the same person

*(Ibid.)*

By this little charter I wish it to be known that I, Galvan of Chamilliac, for the soul of my father and mother, give to God, to blessed Mary, and to the nuns of the church of Fontevraud a tenth of the milling dues of six mills situated at Chamilliac. The gift of two of these mills was made at Chamilliac [Col. 1117B] under these witnesses: Cotard of Mauritania, Geoffrey of Ver, Peloquin of Beaumont, and William of Anneta. But the gift of the tenth from the other four mills was made into the hand of William Frition, venerable dean of the same castle, with the express intention that, when Master Ulger, venerable bishop of Anjou, has returned joyfully from Rome, this gift be confirmed into his hand. Witnesses are William, dean of Chamilliac; Poppo, dean of Chalonnes; and Geoffrey of Ver. Aalina, Galvan’s daughter, granted this gift in the presence of Petronilla, first abbess of the church of Fontevraud. Afterwards Geoffrey of Argenton and Margaret, Galvan’s daughter, granted this gift. Under these witnesses: Rainaud of Melo and Rainaud of Sainzay.

[Col. 1117C] The charter was drawn up while Louis was king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Anjou, and Ulger was bishop of Anjou.

### LIX. Gift of the lords of Chamilliac

*(Ibid.)*

I wish all to know that I, Peter of Chamilliac, give to God, to blessed Mary, and to the nuns of Fontevraud, through the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, all the wool-dues which I possessed within the castle of Chamilliac and outside the castle. This customary due is improperly called a tithe. My son Galvan consents, that God may have mercy on my soul and on those of my wife and children. [Col. 1117D] Witnesses to this gift are Hubert of Campania, Borel of Saumur, and Aimeric of Averio.

Given while Louis was king of the Franks, Fulk was count of Anjou, and Rainaud was bishop of Anjou.

### LX. Gift of Eblon and Garnerius: land near Fonte-Archer

*(Ibid., p. 246.)*

[Col. 1118A]

Let all know that Garnerius and Eblon, Garnerius’s brother, with the consent of their wives Petronilla and Stephana and of their sons, give to God, to the church of Saint Mary, to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, and to the nuns of Fontevraud as much arable land near Fonte-Archer as twenty oxen can plough, together with meadows and woodland for every building need of the nuns.

### LXI. Gift of Peloquin of Île-Bouchard: his customary dues

*(Ibid., p. 257.)*

[Col. 1118B]

I, Peloquin of Île-Bouchard, for the love of God, give and grant to the nuns of Lord Robert of Arbrissel all my customary dues from every kind of thing, by water and by land, which I appeared to possess, etc. Witnesses are Bernerius of Champigny, Bouchard of Tavern, William the physician, and the abbess of Beaumont.

Know, moreover, that this was done in the porch of Saint Peter of Île-Bouchard, in whose church Robert had shortly before delivered a sermon.

### LXII. Charter of the priory at Ursan, of the Order of Fontevraud

*(Pavillon, *Life of Robert of Arbrissel*, p. 556.)*

[Col. 1118C] Adelard of Château-Meillant gives Lord Robert of Arbrissel the wood called Grosboc, the village of Ursan, and the plain land with its mill and pond, etc. This gift was confirmed into the hand of Léger, archbishop of Bourges.

### LXIII. Charter of the same priory of Ursan

*(Ibid.)*

I, Brother John, abbot of Déols, and the community of brethren entrusted to me by the Lord, out of the charity which we owe, give to the handmaids of God serving God at Fontevraud under the direction of Lord Robert of Arbrissel the claim which we have in the church concerning the dwellings, and the plain land and wood [Col. 1118D] of the place called Ursan.

This was done at Déols in chapter, in the presence of Lord Léger the archbishop, of that same Robert, and of his clerics.

[Col. 1117]

## Léger of Bourges: Oration concerning Blessed Robert of Arbrissel

*(See above in the Prolegomena, col. 1028.)*

## In the year of the Lord 1118: Seher, abbot of Chaumousey

[Col. 1119]

# Two Books on the Beginnings of the Monastery of Chaumousey, of the Order of Saint Augustine in the Diocese of Toul, by Seher, Its First Abbot

Edited by Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 1160, from the papers of the Most Reverend Father Hugh, abbot of Clairefontaine and coadjutor of Étival.

## Preliminary Notice

[Col. 1119]

We owe the history of the monastery of Chaumousey, of the Order of Saint Augustine in the diocese of Toul, to the kindness of the Most Reverend Father Hugh, abbot of Clairefontaine and coadjutor of Étival, of the Premonstratensian Order, a most learned man. To assist our studies and contribute something to the public benefit of letters, he sent it to us copied from an old manuscript. Its author, Seher, the first abbot of that monastery, divided his work into two books. In the first he recounts the beginnings of the monastery of Chaumousey and the disputes which he had with the abbess of Remiremont. In the second he treats of the benefactors of his monastery, setting out their gifts one by one. It is certainly an excellent work of its kind, written by a contemporary author and supported by the most solid foundations: that is, letters and various documents of Henry, king of the Romans, the supreme pontiff, the bishop of Toul, and Seher himself—than which nothing more certain could have been adduced to establish its credibility.

Moreover, from the prolonged dispute with the abbess of Remiremont which he recounts in the first book, it is clearer than daylight that the title “canonesses” was then unheard of at Remiremont. Indeed, this is proved by the terms *monastery*, *congregation*, *sisters*, and *nuns*, which Seher uses: these do not suit canonesses but virgins consecrated to God by monastic vows. I could readily prove, if the matter required it, that the observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict also endured for a long time afterward in the nunnery of Remiremont, and that its practice did not become obsolete there until later times. Thus even Pope Urban VIII, in his bull addressed to Catherine of Lorraine, the most devout abbess, declares that he is unwilling to approve the status of canonesses in the church of Remiremont.

## Preface

[Col. 1119]

[Col. 1119] Seher, indeed the first but a less worthy steward of the house of Chaumousey, to all brothers contemporary with him and those who shall come after him, forever.

[Col. 1121A] With the favor of the Godhead, as I am about to write some record, however slight, concerning the beginning and development of the monastery of Chaumousey, consecrated in honor of the holy Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, over which, by God’s appointment, though unworthy, I preside: before all else I wish to speak of spiritual matters, so that all who are to serve the Lord there may know and strive first to seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and thereafter confidently await, according to the Savior’s word, the addition of temporal things when needs require. Therefore, looking to the benefit and peace of those who come after, I wish, as fully as I can, to convey to the knowledge of our posterity how almighty God, in this place called Chaumousey, not through human foreknowledge but by divine providence [Col. 1121B] and ordering, transplanted the vineyard of a new planting from figurative Egypt and caused it to take root; and how gradually, as it pleased him, from a rough forest he mercifully prepared for those wishing to serve him a house of refuge and rest, enriched with the offerings of the faithful.

For divine governance, foreseeing that a community of people cannot stand without human support, touched the hearts of diverse faithful persons of both sexes. They made devout offerings to God in this church, both from their movable goods and from their estates. In the course of the narrative I wish to record in writing the names of the freehold estates, the names of those who gave them, and what was done with those estates in my time, insofar as the Lord grants. It also seems to me not unhelpful to inform posterity how, by the wondrous aid of almighty God, we escaped certain disputes and disturbances, and—more truly, by his ordering, whose ways are unsearchable—how through those very troubles we rather came to a firmer peace. I hope this will greatly benefit not only those who gave these things, but also the brothers who are to possess them: for those ignorant of the facts will be able to learn them clearly from this page [Col. 1122B] if any further dispute should arise from them, as commonly happens. We shall therefore attempt to set forth, in the order of events, by whose agency this new planting began to spread, and how, by God’s favor, transplanted by him into this place, it reached its growth.

## Book One Begins

[Col. 1121]

### 1. At Château Anthenor a priest gathers disciples; after Anthenor’s death Seher is set over them

[Col. 1121C] Through the inspiration of God, the author of all good things, very many poor in spirit, stirred by the Gospel utterance of the Savior in which he says, “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” began with one devotion to seek the seclusion of a more withdrawn life. There, fleeing the shipwrecks of the world, we might devote ourselves more attentively to God alone and prepare for our souls a rest that would endure without end. As we considered this in our minds, it pleased us for this purpose to go to a certain place named Castellum, where a venerable priest called Anthenor—a man devoted to God and greatly beloved by men—led a religious life. This place lies adjacent to Mount Remiremont and had once been distinguished by the dwelling of the most holy confessors Amatus and Romaric.

Therefore, having cast aside worldly things and, no less, according to the Gospel command, renounced our own wills, we entered with him and under him into fellowship of common life. Although we were still uncertain which of the holy Fathers we should chiefly follow in religious habit, nevertheless, striving for obedience under the direction of one father, each of us, aided by divine grace, endeavored to turn aside from the broad paths of his former manner of life and, through the tears of repentance, to renew according to his strength the image of the Lord which we had effaced in the world. As the number of brothers increased, the father rejoiced greatly in the devotion of his sons; but when he had completed the course of this present life, he was received in peace with the faithful, as we believe. After his death, the brothers, by common counsel, demanded from me—the least of all—that through the charity which had gathered us together I should undertake, in my predecessor’s place, care not only of their possessions but also of themselves. Yet I, whom neither secular learning nor a life sufficiently suited to so great a burden commended, at first hesitated to undertake what was laid upon me; then I likewise feared that, if I refused, I would offend against brotherly love. Trusting therefore in divine mercy, I at last yielded to their request, and, not relying on my own powers, committed myself with them to be ruled and governed by him who calls into being things that are not as though they were.

Meanwhile, very many wishing to serve God with us began to gather, and the place that had previously sufficed for our few number was considered less suitable for receiving the multitude. Among the brothers whom fear of hell and love of eternal reward had gathered to live together, for the restoration of the condition of the primitive Church, there was one heart and one soul in God. It therefore pleased us all, whom the diligent nurse of virtues, the love of poverty, cherished, to order our life under the canonical habit according to the institutions of blessed Augustine, and under regular discipline to await from the Lord, through perfected obedience, the prize of heavenly recompense.

### 2. Lutulf, dean of Saint Leo, founds a monastery; Seher governs it and Castellum, and sends brothers in turn from place to place

[Col. 1123A] At almost the same time a venerable man named Lutulf, then dean of the principal church at Toul, came to visit us. Since he had founded outside the city walls a church in memory of blessed Pope Leo, who had formerly been bishop of that city, he humbly asked us to undertake its care and governance and to appoint there, under our direction, some of our brothers to serve God. For he said that he himself willingly wished to order his life under our direction, and that many others within the city were awaiting a suitable leader in order to take upon themselves the yoke of regular discipline. I and all the brothers kindly received his request. Taking several brothers with me, I went to Toul not long afterward for this purpose. Honorably received by him in that church with my brothers, I stayed there for some days; having arranged them to serve God as the Lord granted, I bade them farewell joyfully and returned to my own place.

I then began to govern both places; and because, with divine grace cooperating, many flocked to each for the purpose of religious life, I endeavored to send in turn from place to place those whom I knew to be energetic in training others in regular discipline. But the narrowness of the place in which we had first begun to gather started to burden me and some of the brothers greatly, especially because certain things contrary to religious life threatened us there, things which we could by no means avoid without either changing the place or harming our purpose. Yet divine providence, which was already providing us another place, did not long delay in consoling its servants who hoped in it concerning this matter.

### 3. Theodoric Offers Them a More Suitable Place to Live

For, as we believe, God so disposed matters that, although this remained wholly unknown to us, a report of it spread abroad and reached a certain noblewoman named Hadelvid. Although she still had a husband and possessions, she nevertheless, out of zeal for a good purpose, especially loved those whom she had learned were walking in the right way. When she heard this, the aforesaid woman began to press her husband, Theodoric, strongly [Col. 1123D], to offer and convey to us, from among his allodial lands, whatever place our brotherhood should find most suitable for dwelling. For she often urged him that, since he had no heirs of the flesh, he should strive with all his might to make God his heir.

At last, with God’s favor, both of them acting together, through a certain venerable cleric named Ascelm—then still living in secular dress, but afterward faithfully serving God with us—they devoutly offered us what we have mentioned above, and unanimously and earnestly begged us to come and inspect the place.

Having taken counsel with wise and spiritual men [Col. 1124A], who understood more deeply that this matter was being accomplished by God, we went down to see what was offered. Going around the allodial estate, we chose to establish our dwelling in a great forest, namely in a place that appeared peaceful and remote from the crowding of people. When the God-devoted man Theodoric saw that we had chosen to settle upon his estate, he gave thanks to God. In the presence of Widric of Spinal and many others, both servile and free, he joyfully offered to our holy Savior God, to us, and to our successors, to possess forever, that portion which pleased us as a place of habitation.

### 4. In the Vast Wilderness He Builds the Monastery of Calmosiac

**The knight Theodoric, with his wife Hadelvid, conveyed the allod of Calmosiac to the holy Savior and His Mother.**—Accordingly, we soon arrived with the brothers and began to transform the uncultivated wilderness into domestic buildings. We built a new oratory for the service of God and dedicated it in honor of Mary, the blessed Mother of God.

Meanwhile the aforesaid noblewoman rejoiced that her wish had been fulfilled, and gave thanks to God because she had found heirs of the soul rather than sons of the flesh. By continual prayers she urged her husband that, just as he had already handed over to us one portion for habitation, so he should endeavor to leave our church heir of the entire allod of Calmosiac. At length he consented to her prayers; and, though we knew nothing of it, both announced to the brothers, with equal resolve and desire, that they wished to convey the whole allod to our church.

[Col. 1124C] At that time I had gone to Metz. Recalled by a message from the brothers, I was present when, before many others, free and servile alike—whose names are subscribed as witnesses to this gift—the distinguished man Theodoric, with his wife Hadelvid, gave the allod of Calmoseis to our holy Savior God and to His Mother Mary, and at the same time to me, unworthy though I was, who among the others exercised the office of shepherd, and to all the brothers then and thereafter serving God in the same place.

He conveyed it freely, wholly, and securely, just as he himself had formerly possessed it: namely, with male and female serfs; with cultivated and uncultivated fields; with meadows and pastures; with woodland, both that which he held independently and that which he shared as a benefice; with a usufructuary; and with all revenues.

[Col. 1124D] Along with these, he also conveyed the *eulogiae*—customary dues or offerings—which Theodoric himself and his predecessor had been accustomed to receive from the church’s portion: namely, a one-year-old pig, twelve denarii, twelve loaves, and three hospitality-provisions in the year. The suitable free men who stood as witnesses, guarantors of good faith, and declarants of this donation were Widric Despinal; Landric and Widric, his nephews; Theodoric of Villa; Adolard of Lusda; Renard; Rener; Albric; and Richard. All this, given to our holy Savior God by the lawful investiture of conveyance, our church held securely and peacefully for as long as the aforesaid God-devoted man Theodoric lived.

### 5. Joscelm, Theodoric’s Brother, Ravages and Attacks the Monastery

After Theodoric had entered upon the way of all flesh and had been honorably buried by us in our cemetery, his brother according to the flesh, Joscelm, attempted to alienate the aforesaid allod from God and violently claim it for himself. By the power permitted to him by Him through whose fatherly chastisement we were trained in discipline—lest, if all temporal things prospered according to our wishes, we might perhaps seek less earnestly the city that is to come and remains—he began to ravage the allod by attacks night and day. By every trouble and plundering he could inflict, he relentlessly disturbed us, seeking to force us to leave.

Finally, to crown his evils, he burned with fire the parish church founded there in honor of Mary, the blessed Mother of God; and by such cruelty [Col. 1125B] he began to incur the hatred of very many.

Compelled by such injuries and disturbances, we approached the court of Duke Theodoric and earnestly requested that, by the judgment of his court, he remove us from the injustice and oppression which Joscelm violently inflicted upon us. Although the duke kindly received our complaint and deeply sympathized with our injuries, he repeatedly summoned Joscelm to the hearing of his court, yet delayed doing justice in the matter for two years.

When we repeatedly renewed our appeal to the duke, while our adversary Joscelm wholly avoided justice, the duke at length fixed a definite day and place and summoned both parties before his court. If Joscelm, though summoned, should refuse to come on that day, the duke would then determine, by the judgment of the princes of the land [Col. 1125C], what he ought to do for us. When we came on the appointed day and waited a long time, Joscelm refused to appear; and it became plain to the aforesaid duke and to all present how unjustly he was persecuting us.

### 6. Duke Theodoric and the Nobles Pronounce Judgment Against Him

The duke therefore assembled his nobles and instructed them to determine by judicial sentence what he ought to do, so that contempt for justice should not go unpunished if Joscelm presumed further to harass us with reckless vexations.

The free men then present judged it equitable that those who had summoned him to the plea should prove this publicly, so that the case might proceed in due order and every ground of complaint might be removed from the adversary. Since the summoners to the pleas were present—Stephen of Villa and Humbert of Domnus Medardus—they stood before all and proved by oath that they had lawfully summoned Joscelm, on the duke’s behalf, to the often-mentioned appointed day.

The free judges then declared it likewise equitable that those who had been present at the donation and lawful investiture during the life of the often-mentioned Theodoric should establish this by lawful testimony. Seven free witnesses immediately rose: Widric of Spinac; Theodoric of Villa and his brother Stephen; Adolard of Lusda; Renard; Rener; and Albric. Before the duke and the whole court they proved by oath [Col. 1126A] that they had been present at the aforesaid donation and that, so far as could better be determined by the wise men who had been present with them at the gift, our church had lawfully received from the aforesaid Theodoric, without any legal challenge, the investiture of the whole allod, in their presence.

Once the aforesaid summons to the pleas and the manifest proof of the donation had been established, and since Joscelm, repeatedly called to the court’s hearing, wholly refused to appear, they then ruled that Duke Theodoric ought to seize the allod for our church and, by the exercise of his authority, restrain our adversary from the claims and injuries which he violently inflicted upon us.

The free and qualified judges of this sentence were Fabio, Albert, Levard, Walter, Waldric, and Theodoric. The distinguished Duke Theodoric likewise consented to the judgment, as did the other servile and free persons in whose presence the judgment was held at Waldimac, on the bank of the river Maldonc. [Col. 1126B] A few days later Duke Theodoric came, seized the aforesaid allod for our church, assembled before the doors of our new oratory the household of that allod, and placed them under our fealty.

### 7. Pibo, Bishop of Toul, Strikes Joscelm with Anathema

But because the time of peace had not yet come, our adversary Joscelm did not even then desist from his injuries. Rather, he persistently sought by every means he could to alienate the aforesaid allod from us [Col. 1126C] and violently usurp it for himself.

Seeing that he wholly despised the judgment of the court, we were again compelled by the cries of our household to flee to the bosom of our mother, the Church of Toul, so that at least under the protection of her wings we might be allowed to keep what seemed to us to have been justly and canonically acquired. At that time the episcopal office there was held by Pibo, bishop of the same church, of pious memory. Kindly receiving our complaint, he repeatedly summoned the aforesaid Joscelm to make satisfaction. When he refused, the pastor, solicitous for the peace of his flock, pronounced a sentence of anathema upon him, so that, at least frightened in this way, he might make satisfaction and at last repent of his begun injustice. At length, by God’s favor, our adversary was terrified by this sentence.

### 8. At Last He Repents and, Having Received Twelve Pounds, Desists from His Evil Purpose

Seeing himself hemmed in on every side by the judgment of the court and ecclesiastical censure, Joscelm came somewhat to himself and began to act more mildly toward us. Since he was very poor, certain friends, both ours and his, mediated between us and him, proposing that he should receive some money from us and thereby finally put an end to every claim.

For this purpose we met on an appointed day at Ranegias. Although this seemed burdensome to us—for, placed as we were in a rough and uncultivated place, even necessities themselves did not yet suffice—we nevertheless promised to give him a sum of money, namely twelve pounds [Col. 1127A], in order to end the contentious dispute.

When he had received from us the undertaking concerning this money, he immediately, in the sight of many present, renounced (*wirpivit*) and confirmed the renunciation (*astipulavit*) of the allod of Calmoseio, together with his wife and sons, who were likewise present, and put an end to every claim.

The free and qualified witnesses present at Ranegias for this settlement and peace were Widric and Rener Despinal; Widric and Sandic of Lismac; Stephen of Villa; Albert; another Albert of Darney; Humbert Lupus; Humbert of Domnus Aper; Widric of Strena and his son; Ulric Drogo; Gerard of Bosani-villa; Widric Pinguis of Damviliac; Widric of Vivery; Robert of Senones and his sons Hotto and Hugh; Theodoric of Salsuries; Maselin and his son [Col. 1127B] Drogo; Anscher and Robald of Domnus Martinus; Hugh of Pisney; Robert of Aldon; Cono and Albert of Darnul; Hugh of Folmariac; Lanfrid of Aleia; his nephew Ascelin; Pagan of Monronis Court; and Hugh and Walter of Columbey. Our adversaries were Joscelm himself, his wife Haduidis, and their sons Thonnor and Theodoric.

Afterward we went with him to Toul and recounted in order to Bishop Pibo how we had at last come to a settlement. Joscelm, just as he had previously done at Ranengias, again renounced the often-mentioned allod in the presence of the bishop and many others, and thus finally deserved absolution. Thereafter, by God’s favor, our church possessed the allod so quietly and peacefully [Col. 1127C] that it experienced no further claim concerning it from anyone.

### 9. They Receive Monastic Discipline and the Formation of Conduct from the Brothers of Saint Rufus

When, therefore, by God’s favor, our affairs were peaceful and both churches to which I gave attention—this one and the other which I mentioned much earlier—gradually grew through the coming together of many persons, it seemed good to me and to our other brothers that we should not live without rules and customs, but should receive an example of life from certain holy Fathers who had preceded us in the same religious profession.

We had learned from the widespread and celebrated report of many that the brothers in the monastery of Saint Rufus [Col. 1127D], situated in the regions of Provence, faithfully served God under canonical profession and, being excellently trained in every monastic discipline, illuminated neighboring churches with examples of religious life. Therefore we sent two of our brothers to them with letters from our often-mentioned bishop, so that we too might order our lives according to their manner and rule of life. They received them honorably, instructed them with every diligence by word and writing, and sent them back to us with joy.

### 10. Seher Is Chosen Abbot; the Brothers of Saint Leo and Calmosiac Are Separated

Then, after we had adopted their customs in the manner of cenobites, since they were religious and exemplary for our life, it seemed good to the divine lord Bishop Pibo and to the other leading men [Col. 1128A] of the Church of Toul that we, who lived a common life in the aforesaid churches within their diocese, should canonically appoint for ourselves, with their counsel, a suitable shepherd.

When the brothers were asked which of their number they especially wished to have ordained as abbot, they unanimously chose me, the least of all, as they had done before, to undertake this burden. Called by the bishop for this purpose, I received the ordination of blessing, . . . and [became abbot] in the place where I had previously ministered to the brothers at their request alone.

But because this place had not yet been visited by the bishop and had not yet received the consecration of dedication, it pleased us all that the brothers of both places should be enrolled under the church of Saint Leo, which had already been consecrated, on the condition [Col. 1128B] that, after the ordination of this place, whoever should thereafter assemble here to serve God would receive his title from this church. It was also decreed by the bishop concerning those brothers who had already assembled that each should thereafter remain in whichever place he freely chose.

So that what had been decided by common counsel concerning the two places might remain binding, the bishop drew up a charter, strengthened it with his own seal, and gave it to each church in the following form.

### 11. Pibo’s Letter on the Ordination of Abbot Seher

> “Pibo, by the grace of God unworthy overseer of the Church of Toul, to all sons of the same church, both future and present: health of both the inner and outer person, and the abundance of divine blessing.
>
> [Col. 1128C] “We wish you to know, most beloved sons in the Lord, that we have promoted Brother Seher, chosen as abbot by the harmonious vote of his brothers; and, ordained at Toul under the title of Saints Leo and Nicholas, we have consecrated him, so far as lay in us, with the grace of the Holy Spirit cooperating. Having received from him a profession according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, we entrusted to him the care of all clerics and laypersons who had gathered under him into one body from the stormy tumult of the world, or who might gather thereafter.
>
> “Finally, lest the ordination of certain brothers of clerical profession, who had chosen the quiet of solitude in the forest of Calmesiac, should be voided according to canonical decrees, we judged it necessary that each should profess under the aforesaid abbot, under the same title of Saints Leo and Nicholas. Yet, at the earnest request of the lord abbot and with the advice of our faithful people intervening, we tempered the tenor of lawful profession by this provisional arrangement: as long as the place of Calmosiac should lack the integrity of an independent title, all should serve the Lord, each in his own order, under the assured title of Saints Leo and Nicholas.
>
> [Col. 1128D] “But if at any time the place of Calmosiac should, by God’s mercy, obtain full liberty so as to be an independent title, no necessity of promised obedience and no authority of the title received should bind the aforesaid brothers to remain forever in the church of Saints Leo and Nicholas. Rather, from the entire body of brothers, the abbot should send to be lawfully enrolled under title in the church of Calmosiac those whom he judged suitable, provided their own will freely consented and this was done by the common counsel of the whole chapter.
>
> “That this may not at any time fall from memory, and lest human importunity attempt anything contrary to it, we issue this present enduring document and confirm it by the impression of our seal and by whatever authority we possess; and we strengthen it by the subscribed testimony of upright and credible men.
>
> [Col. 1129A] “We completed these things in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, in the twenty-third year of our ordination, in the second indiction, the fifth concurrent, on the first feria, on the Kalends of December, in the major church consecrated in honor of blessed Stephen, the first martyr.”

### 12. The First Oratory Is Dedicated in Honor of Blessed Mary; After Choosing Between the Two Places, Each Remains Where He Has Chosen

When these matters had been arranged, after no long interval the same bishop came to visit the church of Calmosiac, over which, by God’s appointment, I preside. At the brothers’ request, he dedicated our first oratory in honor of Mary, the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin. Likewise he consecrated the altar in the upper monastery in honor of blessed Peter the Apostle. As is customary in such cases, he forbade by pontifical authority and sentence of anathema, as far as he could and ought, anyone thereafter to presume to disturb our place with reckless vexations.

After these solemn acts were completed, the venerable bishop took leave of the brothers and returned to his own see. [Col. 1129C] Not long afterward, at our request that he come to our chapter at Saint Leo concerning certain of our affairs, he willingly agreed. When he came on the appointed day, after discussing the matters for which we had chiefly invited him, I rose and humbly began to ask him to remember his arrangement. Before the consecration of this church of Calmosiac he had long ago set down by charter the division of the brothers between our two churches. Now, because by his mercy and the cooperation of grace this church had been consecrated and received its own title, I asked that he personally fulfill that arrangement by seeking the brothers’ wishes concerning it.

Without hesitation he kindly received our petition and began to ask the brothers then present, one by one, which of the two places each preferred, so that, having made profession, he might thereafter remain there. When he had learned the wish of each, he immediately sent Lord Tietmar, abbot of Saint Mansuetus, to ask also the wishes of the brothers who at that time lived in this place.

[Col. 1129D] The aforesaid abbot came and in our chapter asked the wish of each man; he decreed that each should thereafter remain in the place he chose. Thus it came about that, just as each church had its own right in possessions from the beginning, so thereafter each also obtained its own right in brothers.

### 13. The Cenobium of Calmosiac Is Placed Under the Protection of the Apostolic See

When, by God’s appointment, I presided over both churches, with the counsel of our brothers and certain spiritual men I obtained at Rome for the house of Calmosiac, coming from the free regions, a privilege from blessed Peter the Apostle and also from his vicar—a refuge established for us by God.
