Since it is inserted in this little work, the attentive reader may prudently observe what the pope himself solemnly decreed, both for the rooting of this new foundation and for the confirmation of present and future offerings. He may also observe how, by apostolic authority, he distinguished and determined how we and our successors ought to stand in matters concerning Christendom in relation to the see of Toul.

[Col. 1130B] We insert in this work, with the other apostolic letters that we were privileged to receive from the same Pope Paschal in our necessities, the privilege itself, so that whoever believes may find them openly set out in the sequence of events; while whoever doubts may know what was obtained by each rescript. He therefore wrote to the Roman pontiff a letter full of supplication, containing the following:

### 14.

> “To Paschal, supreme pontiff of the holy and apostolic see: Pibo, by God and by His gift bishop of Toul, the unwearied rendering of due obedience.
>
> “Since the desire is great,” etc. See Paschal, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII.

### 15. The Lord Pope’s Reply to This, Which Is Preserved Among Us

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Pibo, bishop of Toul: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Just as [one ought] to prevent evil,” etc. See above.

### 16. Dispute Between the Abbess of Remiremont and the Abbot of Calmosiac; Duke Theodoric Favors the Abbess of Remiremont

When this came to the knowledge of the people of Remiremont—namely, that the bishop of Toul had granted to us the altar of the aforesaid church, in which they possessed a share—they took it badly. They were therefore unanimously roused against us. They caused to be summoned to themselves the cleric who at that time held the vicarage of that church and who had customarily paid the aforesaid *eulogiae* to us and to the aforesaid Theodoric for that church.

[Col. 1130D] They began unjustly to demand from him offerings which he had never given them. When he refused and said that it seemed burdensome to give them what he did not owe, while paying us what he had been accustomed to pay, they added that we had no share in the church at all. They stripped the vicar of the church by every means and immediately gave it to a certain castellan of theirs named Walfrid.

They then went to Toul and presented him before the Church of Toul. Duke Theodoric, especially, who was present and had undertaken the defense of their cause against us, pressed with great force that the altar be handed over to Walfrid. But we brought the vicar with us and, before the leading men of the Church of Toul and our adversaries themselves, complained that the cleric had unjustly been deprived by them of his investiture. We humbly requested that they should not hand over to him the altar, which, from the house of the bishop of Toul, belonged rather under our authority.

[Col. 1131A] The archdeacons replied with counsel that they did not dare undertake anything against our just cause. Seeing, therefore, that they could accomplish nothing, our adversaries alleged that the very land on which our new monastery stood belonged rather to the church of Remiremont. Duke Theodoric himself, who until then had adhered to us familiarly in friendship, forbade us to rely any further on his friendship; speaking harshly and threatening worse things, he departed from us exceedingly angry.

We, however, awaiting the outcome, committed our cause to almighty God, whose gracious aid we had already experienced in our necessities, to be governed and protected by Him. When our adversary Walfrid returned from Toul, he immediately invaded the same church by force. Seizing with an armed band of soldiers whatever he could that belonged to the church’s right, he carried it away for himself.

Because they had unjustly raised a claim concerning the land of our place, which we had already made over at Rome to blessed Peter, we took counsel with our brothers and friends and sent to Rome a brother of my flesh, Arnulf of Spinal. Through him we presented to the Roman pontiff, in whose sole aid after God we trusted in this matter, a letter of supplication and complaint [Col. 1131C] in this form:

### 17. Letter of Seher, Abbot of Calmosiac, to the Supreme Pontiff

> “To the most reverend lord pope, father and shepherd of the first see: Seher, however unworthy abbot of the Church of Calmosiac, and the congregation joined to him, devoted submission.
>
> “Among the many distresses that compel us to flee to the bosom of your protection, the chief is the persecution of the abbess of Remiremont. For she pursues us most fiercely and unjustly, both personally and through whomever she can. Because she either cannot or is ashamed openly and violently to expel us, she contrives by whatever schemes she can that our place may be subjected to hers, so that, by expelling us in this way, she may not be burdened by our proximity.
>
> [Col. 1131D] “And because, lest we burden you, we have not set out the schemes upon which she relies—for they are lengthy—let the series of arguments, if it please you, be sought from Lord Richard and Lord Arnulf, bearer of this charter, because they know it; and let it be diligently examined and concluded before you.
>
> “And because, lord Father, after God you have become our singular refuge, we humbly ask that you be our helper in times of need and extend the hand of aid to us now falling, lest we be utterly crushed. We beg you not to delay longer, for it is now close to being said of us in our regions: ‘Where is their God?’ Let us feel, if it please you, what your protection can accomplish. Let our persecutors feel whether the rod of your discipline extends so far that we, breathing again under the protection of your wings, may learn to hope, and that they, returning to themselves, ashamed and converted, may at last deserve to be saved.”

He received our letters kindly. Since at the same time, by God’s dispensation, the abbess of Remiremont had sent her own envoys, he ordered both parties to be summoned into his presence. After diligently investigating the case on both sides, he deferred it for the time being, to be more carefully considered with his brethren, namely the lord cardinals. After they had taken counsel and given judgment, he summoned the envoys back to him and declared what counsel he had received. Both parties assenting to the judgment, he wrote this to the abbess of Remiremont [Col. 1132B]:

### 18.

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter Gisela, abbess of Remiremont: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “The case which is between you and the canons of Calmosiac,” etc. See among the letters of Paschal II, in the volume cited above, no. 130.

### 19.

Upon receiving the letters of the venerable apostolic see, the aforesaid abbess at first promised that she would carry out what the lord pope enjoined upon her. But after delaying it for a long time, when we finally met in a common conference, she flatly refused to do it.

Seeing, therefore, that they would neither comply with the counsel of the lord pope [Col. 1132C] nor desist from their begun injuries, we were again compelled by necessity to send a second letter to Rome. Seeking the lord pope’s aid in the troubles and violences which we frequently endured from them, we wrote to him as follows:

### 20. Second Letter of Seher, Abbot of Calmosiac, to the Pope

> “To Lord Pope Paschal, most reverend father and shepherd of the first see: Seher, however unworthy abbot of the Church of Calmosiac, and the congregation joined to him, devoted submission.
>
> “Reverend Father, we are sufficiently importunate toward you and frequently trouble you irreverently with our complaints. But one who is pressed by excessive tribulation does not forget to have recourse to him from whom he hopes for aid. Since, therefore, lord, all our peace and tranquility depend upon you [Col. 1132D], a twofold reason gives us boldness to utter that evangelical cry: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’ On one side is the immensity of our tribulation; on the other, your most patient mercy, by which you always willingly receive and carefully investigate the causes of the poor.
>
> “You know, holy Father, that you recently examined on both sides the case which we have with the people of Remiremont concerning the parish church and which had been brought before you. When it had been investigated, you most wisely directed, with the agreement of our envoys and theirs, that it be settled by exchange. Once they had returned to us, they indeed promised at first that they would fulfill this; but, continually postponing it and becoming again entangled in their factious schemes, they have now finally refused in a common conference to do so.
>
> [Col. 1133A] “We should not care greatly about this if they allowed us peacefully to possess our share in the church. But the abbess and all her supporters, as though united by some conspiracy, relying on the riches and honors in which they abound and holding us in contempt, set aside every consideration. They threaten to invade both what is ours and what is theirs, and cunningly prepare either to expel us or to subject us to themselves. And who are we, that we can withstand the force of so great a storm unless we are supported by your most powerful protection?
>
> “Therefore, good shepherd, because we and what belongs to us are under your protection, for God’s sake consider us, that we may have peace; and, if perfect peace is not expedient, at least let us not abandon our little place.”

### 21.

The lord pope, deeply troubled that she had delayed fulfilling what he had commanded, wrote a second time, reinforcing his judgment:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter Gisela, abbess of Remiremont, and her congregation: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Because great peace,” etc. See above, no. 131.

### 21. When the Abbess Delays, Seher Has Recourse to Henry, King of the Romans

When she had again received these letters through our messenger, she did not at first object, as she had before. But after taking counsel with those to whom it seemed burdensome that anything should be commanded them by the Roman pontiff for our peace [Col. 1133C], she found a pretext: that they could not carry it out without the king, to whose jurisdiction their abbey belonged. Thus she again delayed acting.

Unable to resist their injustice and oppression, since they abounded in riches and honors, we sought help from heaven alone and humbly asked merciful God to stand by us as protector in our tribulations. Meanwhile Lord Richard, bishop of Albano, who was at that time exercising a legation in our regions, happened to go to the court of King Henry. His companions on that journey were Lord Reybald, archdeacon of Toul, and Arnulf of Spinal. Kindly remembering us, they reported the matter to the king in due order [Col. 1133D]: how poor brothers gathered in a certain forest to serve God had long endured the claims and oppression of the abbess of Remiremont; how, after her frequent molestations, they had twice sought justice and judgment from the lord pope, to whose jurisdiction their little place belonged; what the lord pope had decreed concerning this; what he had repeatedly ordered that abbess by his letters; and how, finally, under the pretext that she could not do this without the king’s permission, she had so far scorned to fulfill it.

They asked the king, for God’s sake, to extend the aid of his protection to the poor and, as a good son of the Roman Church, to order by royal authority the fulfillment of what the apostolic see had decreed. He was still a good Catholic and had not yet turned away from the Roman Church. He willingly received their request and immediately ordered the abbess by letter to carry the command of the apostolic see into effect, removing every excuse. He wrote to her as follows:

### 22. Letter of Henry, King of the Romans, to the Abbess of Remiremont

> “Henry, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to Gisela, abbess of Remiremont: greeting with his favor.
>
> “Because I am a son and defender of the Roman Church, it is fitting that I obey in all things that universal mother of mine, placed under my protection [Col. 1134B]. To offend my mother in any respect is altogether unfitting, because it is dangerous to souls to depart from her commands.
>
> “Whatever the holy and venerable Roman see decrees through the hand of the supreme pontiff, I shall not cease to labor, so far as I am able and until death, that it may never be annulled but may remain ratified and firm.
>
> “Therefore we command—and moreover strictly command—you not to presume in any way to frustrate what the aforesaid see has decreed concerning the brothers of the place of Calmosiac, nor in any respect to diminish the sacred command. Do not dare to provoke your mother, whose daughter you profess yourself to be, treating her not as a mother but as a stepmother; yourself not as a daughter but as a stepdaughter.
>
> “If you stretch out your hand to violate the commands of my mother, you will incur the hatred of the heavenly King [Col. 1134C] and will not escape the wrath of the earthly king, who has taken up the sword for her defense. For, as I said above, I shall not cease to contend for the defense of the Roman see until death.”

Warned also by the aforesaid men concerning this very matter, he sent the following letter to Duke Theodoric, to whose protection the abbey of Remiremont belonged, saying:

23. Letter of the same [King] to Theodoric, Duke of Lorraine.—“Henry, by the mercy of God king of the Roman realm and defender of the churches established therein, to Theodoric, Duke of the Lorrainers, greeting and his favor.

“It has reached our ears that the supreme pontiff of our mother, the holy Roman Church, has ordered you by letter [Col. 1134D] to act as defender of the place of Chaumousey, so that you should permit no one to harass the brethren serving God there. If you are counted a true Christian, you will obey him; and if you are truly her son, you will in no respect diminish any of the commands of your mother. To the petition of our Father I add my own petition, ordering you to uphold manfully, to the extent of your power, what the inviolable dignity of the Roman See has decreed, and not to allow Christ’s peace to be disturbed in the churches situated in your duchy. For the sword has been entrusted to you for this purpose: not that you should destroy the Church, but that, as a soldier of Christ, you should unceasingly defend her from the assaults of her persecutors. If you do this, you will receive from the heavenly King a crown for having fought the good fight and [Col. 1135A] finished the course well, and you will not lose the favor of the earthly king. Finally, this is my fixed determination in this matter: know that no storm can shake me from defending the aforesaid Church and others against the attacks of the wicked, and, with divine grace assisting me, from destroying their destroyers. Farewell.”

24. Seher again takes refuge in the Apostolic See.—But lest the peace which we had gained by the command of the earthly king should prove less than secure, they, as we believe by God’s disposition, refused to comply even with the king’s letters. By every machination they could devise, they strove either to expel us from the place or to make it completely subject to their own house. Having therefore again suffered many injuries from them, we fled once more to the protection of the Roman pontiff—the one singular refuge left to us after God—and by letter again reported [Col. 1135B] how they despised the fulfillment of his command and burned against us with daily increasing malice, saying:

24. “To Paschal, most blessed Father and, by God, established in the first See as the refuge of the afflicted: Seher, unworthy abbot, with the whole congregation united to him, offers the only things they can offer—obedience and prayer.

“Because of him who is of all …,” etc. See under Paschal, in the volume cited above, col. 436.

The lord pope, grieved by their obstinacy, yet with the wonderful gentleness of a father recalling them to satisfaction, threatened them for the second time, by repeated letters, with the sentence of Saint Peter, writing thus [Col. 1135C] to them:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter Gisla, abbess of Remiremont, and her sisters, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“On behalf of the men of Chaumousey,” etc. See above, no. 173.

25. The king of the Romans addresses the abbess of Remiremont.—After receiving these letters, they nevertheless resisted with hardened hearts and at last absolutely refused to do what was commanded them for our peace and quiet. Afterwards, when the king was at Strasbourg, and we learned that Duke Theodoric and the oft-mentioned abbess were to be there in his presence, we went to his court. Having been made known to the king through certain of our associates, we were kindly received by him; through those same persons we humbly asked him to deign at last, by commanding them in person and by word of mouth, to settle what he had ordered the duke and abbess by letters while absent, and which they had delayed to carry out. The king graciously assented to our petition. When the duke and abbess came into his presence, he was urged on our behalf by some of our friends; he addressed them and kindly exhorted them to follow the counsel of the lord pope, accepting an appropriate exchange. They asked him for a truce until they could discuss the matter with their people; but afterwards, through their retainers attached to the king in the palace, they strove to turn the king away from the undertaking he had begun.

[Col. 1136A] 26. Seher, abbot of Chaumousey, approaches the supreme pontiff.—Seeing, therefore, that they would yield in no way, and having taken counsel with our friends, I myself went to the Roman pontiff, who had summoned a general council at the Italian city of Piacenza. When I arrived there with some of my brethren, I found him not there but in another place called Warda-stall. He received us very graciously. I immediately disclosed to him the reason for my journey, reporting both by the letters which I had brought with me and orally in person what unjust harassment and oppression we suffered from the people of Remiremont. He answered kindly: “Behold,” he said, “you have now reached the harbor.” So that these letters also might not be absent from this little work, I have inserted them below:

[Col. 1136B] 27. “To Paschal, supreme pontiff of the holy Apostolic See: Seher, unworthy abbot of Chaumousey, with his brethren, the devoted offering of due obedience.

“Now, holy Father,” etc. See above, col. 458.

28. The lord pope, no longer enduring the contention of their obstinate malice, did not merely threaten, as in his second and third letters, but directed a sentence of anathema against the abbess herself. If she did not fulfill in deed, before the beginning of the coming Lent, what he had now for the third time ordered for our peace, he excluded her from entrance into the church, writing thus to her:

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1136C] daughter Gisla, abbess of Remiremont, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Concerning the injury done to the religious brethren of Chaumousey,” etc. See above, no. 191.

29. He orders both parties to appear before him at Langres. He admonishes the judges against respect of persons. The pontiff arrives to examine the suit more exactly. Judgment rendered by the supreme pontiff.—Having received these letters from the lord pope, we returned home with his greeting and apostolic blessing and sent them to the abbess by certain of our brethren. At length the oft-mentioned abbess, terrified, God favoring us, by this sentence, sent both her chancellors to the lord pope, urgently begging that she might be given an opportunity to set forth her case more fully in his presence. [Col. 1136D] For she maintained that the matter stood otherwise, and affirmed that, if opportunity were afforded her, she would show that they were not guilty of injustice.

The most discerning shepherd, wishing to remove from them every occasion for objection, ordered both parties to appear at Langres, since he himself was at that time coming into our region, so that the case might there be more carefully examined and settled on both sides in his presence. When the appointed day arrived, the abbess of Remiremont went to Langres, having summoned Duke Theodoric and many others with great force; and she took pains to attach to her side all the members of the palace household whom she could, that they might favor her cause as usual. But I, trusting neither in knowledge, nor in money, [Col. 1137A] nor in any earthly assistance, took only three brethren with me. I urged the rest most earnestly to pray that God might aid us; then I approached the presence of the most merciful Father and anxiously awaited the end to which this long-protracted dispute would at last come, God disposing it through him.

The day came on which the lord pope had appointed to deal with our case. But because he had been bled that same day, he could not at first come in person. Summoning the cardinals to himself, he ordered them to examine the case with great discernment, without respect of persons, and, once examined, to settle it by just judgment. When they came into the consistory and both parties were present, the others attended with an innumerable crowd and the favor of the whole court, while we, with few companions, relied solely upon divine help and beat upon the ears of the heavenly Judge. The lord cardinals began to discuss the question and carefully investigate what each party had to say for its own side.

But while this was being done, the universal shepherd, mindful of his poor people, like another Daniel raised up by the Lord to deliver us, came in person and carefully inquired what was being done in the case. When the question began to be debated concerning the site of our new monastery—for which they had often, though unjustly, brought accusations against us—the people of Remiremont, knowing and certain from the adjoining possession of the donors that the site belonged rather to us, promised in the presence of the lord pope, the lord cardinals, and many other bystanders [Col. 1137C] that they would never again bring a complaint against us concerning that portion of the site. Thereupon the lord pope, according to his custom in such matters, received that portion of the site by staff from the hand of Gisla, abbess of Remiremont, and her sisters, who were then present; and he confirmed it to us and our successors, to be possessed forever in peace and entirety.

Afterwards they asserted that the parish church of Chaumousey belonged to their jurisdiction by ancient possession. We denied this, saying that, by the ancient possession of the predecessors of the free man Theodoric, we had received from him investiture of a portion of the same church and had possessed it for a long time. [Col. 1137D] The most discerning Father, having learned the case of both parties, requested the counsel and judgment of the lord cardinals on this point. Recalling the decree of Pope Gregory VII, who, sitting in a general council, had altogether forbidden laypersons to possess anything in the Church and had likewise forbidden the acceptance from them of anything ecclesiastical, they judged that we ought by canonical law to relinquish the portion which we had received from the hand of a layman after the decree of the aforesaid Gregory VII. For they said that, although he had possessed it unjustly, he could not give it lawfully. We accordingly consented to that judgment and agreed to relinquish the portion of the parish church which we had received from the aforesaid man Theodoric—indeed lawfully, according to the custom of our land.

[Col. 1138A] When this had been done, our adversaries thought that they had acquired our tithes, for which the whole dispute between them and us had long been contested, and that thereafter they would have us in every respect subject to their house. But the ineffable providence of God, whom in our tribulation we prayed might stand by us as a helper, did not long delay in consoling his poor people. The lord pope countered their expectation in this fashion: he immediately ordered that the decree of Gregory the Great be read aloud to me, whereby it is plainly forbidden to demand tithes from those who live the common life. Once it had been read, the lord cardinals immediately judged that we, who lived the common life, should pay tithes neither to them nor to any church whatsoever, [Col. 1138B] and that no one should henceforth presume, contrary to the authority of that approved decree, to demand tithes or first-fruits from us.

30. The pope addresses and admonishes the abbess of Remiremont.—Accordingly, the lord pope summoned the abbess of Remiremont and addressed her with fatherly admonition, saying:

“My daughter, I desire and command that, just as you wish the privilege which your house formerly received from the Roman Church, for its own freedom, to be inviolably observed, so you likewise preserve whole and inviolate what we have granted by the present judgment to these brethren: namely, their privilege, which they too have received in like manner from the Roman Church through our hand. Lest any controversy hereafter arise between you through the persuasion of temporal concerns, I have resolved, as testimony to the dispute long carried on between you and finally settled in my presence, [Col. 1138C] to give you my letters confirmed with my seal, so that firm and enduring affection may remain between you by means of this.”

Having briefly said these things, he ended his speech. Thus that good arbiter finally settled the dispute long carried on between us. Having recorded that settlement in letters, he established by apostolic authority that a charter, written in two places with the same sense and the same text and secured by his seal, should be held by both of us and inviolably kept. The form of this instrument is as follows:

31. “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

“Between the monastery of Remiremont and the canonical church of Chaumousey,” [Col. 1138D] etc. See under Paschal, no. 206.

32. The former friendship between the people of Remiremont and those of Chaumousey is confirmed.—With this dispute thus finally ended, God favoring us, by the hand of the lord pope, we received the apostolic blessing and joyfully returned to the brethren, praising and blessing God, who did not abandon those hoping in him, but according to the multitude of his mercies did not disdain to stand by as a merciful deliverer those who called upon his name in the time of tribulation and distress.

But since no mention had been made in the presence of the lord pope of the altar-gift, over which the dispute had first arisen, the people of Remiremont, after returning from Langres, attempted to alienate that same gift from our church. Taking with them their vicar Walfrid, they went to Toul, approached [Col. 1139A] the bishop, and demanded the altar from him, earnestly asking that he hand it over to their vicar in the customary manner. But by God’s ordering, because we were present, we approached their bishop and the other people of Toul. Showing him our own charter and the apostolic letters which he himself had requested and obtained for confirmation of the same gift, we humbly asked him to preserve for us whole and inviolate what he had once granted to our church. The bishop, judging it rash and exceedingly dangerous to go against his own decision—indeed against the apostolic decision—and to give them again what he had long since confirmed to us with such authority, replied that it would be unlawful for him to do so. Thus the people of Remiremont returned again with their attempt frustrated, obtaining nothing that they had requested.

We, however, grieved that the long dispute between us had been prolonged for so great a time, especially since we had formerly experienced their familiar affection, resolved to call them back to concord by another path. When the abbess of Remiremont came into our neighborhood on certain business of her own, we sought, in a spirit of humility, to approach her. Reminding her of our former affection, we made known that we wished to return to harmony and familiarity with her. She kindly received this request, promising that she would most willingly do whatever our mutual friends advised her for restoring peace. The grace of God, working with us, was also present; what we had begun with good intent he hastened to accomplish far better than we had hoped. [Col. 1139C] For afterwards, seeking fellowship with us, she devoutly visited our place with her household. Having sought and received it, she returned to her own monastery, joined to us in friendship.

After some time had passed, certain good men, mutual friends of ours, mediated between us that the people of Remiremont should grant us, at a rent (*ad trecensum*), what was theirs in the same church, and that we should agree to receive it. Both of us assented to their counsel, and through the hand of Abbess Gisla our church received for possession whatever the abbey of Remiremont had hitherto possessed in the parish church of Chaumousey. Yet, because no person may wholly transfer a possession of one church into the right of another without any acknowledgment, it was likewise mediated and firmly established between us that [Col. 1139D–1140A] on the feast of Saint Romaric we should pay seven solidi for the aforesaid church to the church of Remiremont. Thereafter, God favoring us, with every suspicion removed, firm and familiar friendship has endured between us.

33. The bishop of Toul confirms to Chaumousey several churches received from laypersons.—After these events, we began to consider how, in the presence of the lord pope, we had relinquished by canonical judgment a portion of the oft-mentioned church of Chaumousey because we had received it from the hand of a layman. Therefore, lest either we or our successors should hereafter experience anything similar in such matters, we approached the bishop of Toul and humbly asked him to assign, by the authority of his gift, to be held forever by our church, the churches which we had received non-canonically through the hands of laymen. Since Lord Riquin, primicerius, and Rembald, archdeacon, were present and joined us in this request, the bishop willingly assented. We thereafter received from him by his staff, to possess as we had possessed before: the church of Saint Peter, which Cunegund, widow of Richiscourt, had given us for the soul of her son Theodoric; a fourth part of the church of Igney, which Widric of Valcourt and his wife Adelaide had given us; [Col. 1140C] a fourth part of the church of Villers, which Masclin of Dommartin and his wife Hersendis had given us; half the church of Saint Martin of Dombasle, which Widric of Unicourt had granted us; and a fourth part of the church of Rouvres, which Berta, a widow and afterwards our convert, had given us.

34. Let what has been said suffice as an admonition to our successors, lest, ignorant of synodal decrees by which laypersons are forbidden to possess anything in churches, and therefore unable lawfully to give what they possess unlawfully, they should hereafter presume to receive anything ecclesiastical from them. Rather, whenever laypersons offer such things, let them seek the bishop who shall then be in office, so that what is acquired canonically through the hand of the bishop may be retained in peace. But since, by recounting every event as it occurred, we have extended the narrative to great length, we shall bring this little book to an end after adding only the ordering of our monastery, so that we may set forth what remains in another book.

## BOOK II

[Col. 1139D] 1. The church of Chaumousey is consecrated by Richard, bishop of Albano. Abbots present at the consecration.—Since divine mercy, which mercifully provided for us in all things, had bestowed peace upon us on every side, and scarcely any adversaries now remained, we resolved to consecrate to almighty God the dwelling of our new monastery, [Col. 1140D] though it was not yet entirely completed. But because the oft-mentioned bishop of Toul, weakened by old age, was unable to perform this task, he sent his own letters to Lord Richard, bishop of Albano, whom the lord pope, when returning to the Apostolic See, had left as legate in the regions of Gaul. [Col. 1141A] He alleged the weakness of his body and devoutly begged that Richard, summoned in his stead, would deign to dedicate our monastery in his place.

When the venerable bishop of Albano received the letters from us, he kindly assented to the request. On the appointed day he came to perform what had been requested. Very many religious men, invited by us out of devotion for the dedication, also assembled. Foremost among them were Lord Thiemar, abbot of Saint-Mansuy; Lord Widric, abbot of Saint-Èvre; Lord Lawrence, abbot of Saint-Vitton; and Lord Waschelin, abbot of Saint Peter of Brixey. Of the archdeacons of Toul, Lord Rimbald, archdeacon, was present, as were Hugh of Gondrecourt and Hugh the Younger, son of Reinald. An innumerable multitude of faithful people of both sexes, hearing of the bishop’s arrival, also strove to gather from every direction for the solemnity of the dedication.

While all awaited him, the bishop came forth, and on the day before the Kalends of October, with the greatest rejoicing of all, consecrated the principal altar of that monastery and the entire building round about in honor of the holy Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ. On the following day he dedicated another altar, situated on the right side of the monastery, in honor of Saint Stephen, the first martyr. He likewise marked out the enclosure all around and joined it, now sanctified, to the church. After these rites had duly been completed, lest anyone thereafter presume to violate the sacred place, he pronounced in the presence of all, as is customary in such matters, a sentence of anathema forbidding it.

Therefore, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1107, in the first indiction, with epact VI and concurrent I, on the Kalends of October, this monastery was consecrated by Lord Richard, bishop of Albano and legate of the Roman Church, in honor of the holy Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ. Paschal II was presiding over the Apostolic See; Henry the Younger was reigning in the world; but among us our Lord Jesus Christ was ruling—to whom be praise, honor, power, and thanksgiving, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

2. In the preceding little book, as I stated in its beginning, providing for the benefit and peace of our successors, I committed to writing, so far as the Lord granted, how in this place called Chaumousey, having become heirs through the gift of a certain noble man, Theodoric, to this allod, many brethren gathered from every side to serve God; how, renouncing secular life, we adopted the canonical life according to the Rule of blessed Augustine; and how I more fully set forth in the same book both the harassment which we suffered from Joscelin, brother of the aforesaid man, concerning the same allod, and the dispute long contested between us and the abbess of Remiremont concerning the parish church of Chaumousey. I also explained how, by God’s mercy, we at last ended both disputes, as they occurred in my own time. I, who by God’s authority became the first abbot of this church, ordered these things to be carefully preserved by posterity.

[Col. 1142A] 3. It remains, therefore, for me carefully to make known, as best I know, both to those now living and to those who will come after, how almighty God enriched our church with the offerings of the faithful and gradually brought the offshoot of the new plantation to growth. Many faithful people of both sexes in our province, whose hearts God had touched, began eagerly to seek our fellowship and offered devout gifts to our church for our support, both from their lands and from their movable property.

Foremost among them was Benchelm of Châtigny. Often urged by the requests of his wife Leucardis, he devoutly offered before many persons to our church the allods which he possessed near our place: namely, at Lamerey and at Lihercourt of Hugues. These properties had come to him and Leucardis by hereditary right from noble parents; and he strove to leave them to us rather than to the sons of his flesh. As we received them from them, so thereafter, God favoring us, we possessed them peacefully and without claim.

4. Gifts made to the monastery of Chaumousey.—Another Leucardis, a kinswoman of the Leucardis mentioned above, stirred by the latter’s good example and inflamed by the same desire, began persistently to entreat her husband, Theodoric of Ville, to grant to our church the share which had fallen to her from her inheritance in those same three allods. Since he had no sons of the flesh, he willingly consented. As she requested, he handed over with her to us and to our successors, for perpetual possession, a share of the aforesaid allods.

Both Leucardises were of noble birth. Just as they had received the aforesaid allods freely from their parents, so they granted them to our church to be possessed thereafter wholly and securely: cultivated and uncultivated fields, male and female slaves, meadows and pastures, usufruct, and all revenues, retaining absolutely nothing for themselves or their successors. As we received them free from these women, so thereafter, God favoring us, we possessed them peacefully and without every claim.

But as time passed, we exchanged the allod of Lamerey, which seemed less useful to us because of its remoteness and small size, for three quarter-plots of land adjoining and intermingled with the allod of Huguescourt. These belonged to the sacristy of the church of Remiremont, which we properly call the church’s custodianship. In order that our successors may know how reasonably this exchange was made, I shall explain it briefly.

I myself approached Gisla, who ruled the church of Remiremont in my time. In the presence of Lord Reinbald, archdeacon of Toul, and Widric and Walfrid, chancellors, many nuns, and very many other friends both ours and theirs, I, Abbot Seher, placed in the hand of the aforesaid abbess the allod of Lamerey, free and entire, as our church had possessed it until then. In return I received from her hand the aforesaid land belonging to the sacristy, free and entire—as free and entire as the allod which I gave [Col. 1143A]—owing nothing to any authority: neither *ban* nor court-service nor anything else whatever.

On the same day, in the presence of the same persons, we confirmed another exchange between ourselves on the same terms. There were three other quarter-plots of land adjoining and intermingled with the allod of Huguescourt, belonging to the jurisdiction called Cohereis. Since we possessed certain lands from various of our allods around that same village, we gave the abbess from those lands as much as an appropriate exchange required; and again we received from her hand the three quarter-plots, free and entire, exempt from every *ban*, court obligation, and right. We have recorded the names of our lands which we gave for them in the rustic tongue, so that, should any dispute ever arise concerning this matter, the brethren who are then present may know what we gave and what we received. They are as follows. But let this now suffice concerning these matters; let us proceed to the rest.

5. Berta, a noble lady, gives herself and her possessions to the monastery.—There was also a certain lady of noble birth, named Berta, who possessed many allods in the world. When she was left a widow after the death of her husband, with only one son surviving, she began to burn with the strongest desire to abandon everything and withdraw from the contaminations of the world. Wishing to devote herself and all her possessions to divine service, she began wisely to consider how she might take her son with her and, thus unencumbered, transfer all that she had to some church for possession.

While she pondered this and wavered in a hesitant mind over where to turn, she was at last inspired by divine counsel. Through a brother of ours named Aselin, known to her, she humbly asked that we receive her with her son and possessions into the common fellowship of our life. We kindly received her petition and granted what she requested. Through the same brother, Lord Aselin, she immediately summoned her relatives at Saint-Memmie, a village on the river Verisna, and disclosed that she wished, with their counsel, to give herself and all her possessions to our church. They rejoiced in her good purpose and began to discuss among themselves how this might reasonably be done. Since Brother Aselin and I were present, they immediately handed her and all her possessions over into our hands.

But because gifts made through the hands of free sureties are judged firmer and more certain, after taking counsel together they selected from among themselves free men of mature age: William of Châtigny, Maselin of Dommartin, and Widric of Unicourt. Into their hands the aforesaid noble lady placed all her allods: both those which she possessed from her parents by hereditary right and those which, legally given by a free man named Brochard, she had received by right of marriage through succession from her son. With tearful prayers she urgently begged them to confirm these, without delay, to be possessed by our church.

The following free and qualified witnesses were present at this first gift: Widric of Tilley; Walter, his nephew; Drogo of Bossonville; Maselin of Châtigny; Guy of Ozenvillers; Letold of Rainville; Robald and his son Alberic; Ancher; Drogo and Rofrid of Dommartin; and Boso of Domjulien.

A few days later, when Duke Theodoric had come at our request, the aforesaid Berta also arrived with the named free sureties. In the presence of Duke Theodoric, his son Simon, and many other free men, whose names are subscribed as testimony to this gift, the aforesaid lady, through the hand of the three sureties, gave all her allods—which she possessed from her parents and from her husband by right of dower—to our holy Savior, God, and his blessed mother Mary, and to me, who appeared to hold the governance of this place, and to our brethren now present and those to come who would serve God in this place.

Two were from her own patrimony: the allod which she had at Unicourt, and the share of the allod which she had at Maslin. Four were those she had received from her husband by right of dower, namely: the allod of Rouvres with a fourth part of that church; the allod of Daincourt; the allod of Liffoy; and the share of the allod of Manonville. She delivered all these without any opposition, free, entire, and secure, as she had possessed them until then: male and female slaves, cultivated and uncultivated fields, meadows, pastures, woods, usufruct, and all revenues.

The following free and qualified witnesses were present at this second gift, made upon the altar in our church: first Duke Theodoric and his son Simon; Widric of Épinal and his brother Morand; Paulin of Houldmont and Uldric; Videric and his brother of Grimaud; Rainer of Dalahin; Guy of Norroy; Ulderic son of Rudolph; and Gerard of Donparey. This took place on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, 1098, indiction VI, epact XV, concurrent IV, on the feast of Saint Èvre.

When these matters had thus been done and confirmed, the aforesaid lady, having obtained the fulfillment of her vow, gave herself with her son to our monastery. Casting aside secular dress, she resolved to serve chastely in humility. To her son, because he was a boy of good disposition, we gave the canonical habit. After spending nearly two years in it in simplicity and innocence, he departed from this present life.

[Col. 1144D] Although our church had thus been lawfully invested with the aforesaid inheritance, Walter of Berleiville, a knight of the duke’s household, violently attacked. He seized the allods which she had granted us from her husband’s portion, carried off the principal movable goods, and unjustly stripped our church of its possessions. He said that, because he was nephew of the aforesaid Brochard—that is, the son of his brother—the inheritance belonged rather to himself. Harassed by his frequent annoyances and injuries, we were compelled to approach Duke Theodoric and ask him to investigate Walter’s unjust claim by the judgment of his court and thereby remove him from injuring and oppressing us.

The duke kindly received our complaint and repeatedly summoned Walter to the hearing of his court. But Walter, persisting in his rash undertaking, avoided the duke’s presence for nearly two years.

6. Seeing, then, that he held secular justice in contempt, and wearied by the cries of our household, which he ravaged with continual plundering, we approached the bishop of Toul and earnestly asked him to oppose Walter’s tyranny with the spiritual sword. With a father’s affection, the bishop received the complaint of his sons; after examining Walter’s obstinacy and injury, he summoned him before ecclesiastical justice. When Walter refused to come, the bishop pronounced a sentence of anathema against him.

At last, terrified by that sentence through divine prompting, Walter, while he was at Saint-Dié, sought absolution from the bishop. To deserve what he sought, he promised wholly to cease troubling us and invading the aforesaid allods, until his case should be either proved unjust or approved as just by the judgment of the court which he had previously avoided. This undertaking having been confirmed, he was at last released from the bonds of anathema.

Afterwards, when both parties had been summoned into the duke’s presence at Remiremont, and Walter was asked by the duke and the princes to state before the court why he had interrupted our church’s investiture, he was unable to discover any basis at all for a just complaint against us. Since only the judgment remained, by which he would be compelled through a pronounced sentence lawfully to restore what he had unlawfully seized, good men—faithful friends of ours, concerned for our peace—advised us to give sixty solidi from our poverty to soften his malice, so that he might more willingly carry out what he would otherwise have to do by the judgment of the court and might have no opportunity whatsoever thereafter to revive a complaint against us.

Walter himself, seeing that he could in no way retain what he had unjustly seized, accepted from them the promise of money. Thus, standing in the presence of the duke, the princes, and the entire court, he renounced the allods (*wirpivit*) and confirmed the renunciation; he restored in full the principal goods which had been alienated, and brought the whole claim to an end.

7. With this peace between us thus confirmed, there followed almost seven complete years during which the church possessed those estates of ours without any contention or claim. When these had passed, however, Walter, taking up once more the spirit of malice, again seized the same estates, plundered the chief holdings, [Col. 1145D] and, carried away by still greater madness, ravaged and harassed our household with continual pillaging and seizure of possessions. Fearing neither God nor being ashamed before men—in whose presence, as we mentioned above, he had both received our money and relinquished those estates by a settlement—he ceased not. Therefore we again approached Duke Theodoric concerning this wrong and humbly begged him, mindful of what had been settled in his presence, to restrain the pestilent Walter, by opposing with his authority the renewed audacity of his exercise of power. Walter, after long avoiding the court, at last appeared before the duke at Spinal. Admonished by the duke, he restored to our brethren who were present the chief holdings he had taken away and promised henceforth to desist. [Col. 1146A] Thus we again seized the aforesaid estates by right of our church, and, while he desisted, we enjoyed peace for a short time.

8. Seher goes to Rome and obtains a new privilege.—At about the same time, for certain matters of ours, we approached the see of the blessed apostle Peter. We were graciously received by Paschal, supreme pontiff of the apostolic see. After certain other requests, we begged him to record in a charter, secured by his seal, the aforesaid properties and the other possessions bestowed upon us by the offerings of the faithful, and by apostolic authority to confirm them for the perpetual possession of our church. He graciously consented and, as we had requested, gave us a charter confirmed by his own writing and seal. In it, all who should attempt to invade the aforesaid estates [Col. 1146B] or other possessions, or should presume to disturb our church, are anathematized and separated from the body of Christ. Thus supported by an apostolic privilege and having also received his blessing, we returned joyfully to our brethren. We deposited that charter among our other charters. Whoever wishes to read it more fully may find it preserved in our archive-chest.

9. Walter again troubles the men of Chaumouzey, but at last grants them complete peace.—But before we returned from Rome, Walter, so often mentioned, having enlisted as a companion in his malice a certain kinsman-by-marriage, Henry, again seized those estates for the third time, plundered the chief holdings, and, forgetful of all justice and decency, did not cease to harass us and our property with more savage than usual injuries and depredations of every kind within his power. Seeing, therefore, [Col. 1146C] that peace could not be secured for our affairs without ecclesiastical censure, after appealing to the duke and, supported by the counsel of our bishop-elect, Lord Riquin, we were compelled to write a supplicatory letter to the Roman pontiff and humbly to implore him to strike their deserved repression and reckless audacity with the apostolic sword.

The universal shepherd of the Church did not long delay fulfilling the petition of his sons. Through the same bearer of our letter he wrote to Duke Theodoric and to our bishop-elect Riquin, ordering them to repel our adversaries from oppressing us by secular and ecclesiastical censure, and to exclude the invaders of ecclesiastical property from entry into the church until they had made satisfaction. We had already received letters of Lord Riquin, bishop-elect of Toul, [Col. 1146D] addressed to the deans and priests of the whole bishopric, ordering Walter and his kinsman-by-marriage Henry to be barred from communion with the Church, when suddenly Walter, pierced by divine inspiration, at last came to himself and began to repent. He immediately disclosed to his uncle, Lord Reimbald—who had deeply grieved over his wrongdoing—that he wished to make satisfaction to our church. Reimbald gladly accepted this, strengthened his still wavering spirit with suitable exhortation, and brought him to our church on an appointed day to make satisfaction.

Since many free and suitable witnesses were present, Walter, knowing that he had been excommunicated for his frequent injuries and depredations, first [Col. 1147A] humbly sought and received absolution. Then, having been admitted by us into the church, he laid upon the altar of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ the estates which he had unjustly contested; he restored the entire property to our church, relinquished it (*wirpivit*), confirmed the relinquishment, and put an end to every claim. For the chief holdings which had been alienated, because they were many, he left to our church, for perpetual possession, two *quarteria* of land from his own estate at Auncourt.

These matters having been completed, he humbly asked his uncle that we should grant him, for the term of his life and at a rent, the two smaller estates—the estate at Davencourt and that at Lifoi—so that firm and stable concord might henceforth endure between us. Having taken counsel with our friends and brethren, we agreed to his request. In the presence of many witnesses, [Col. 1147B] he received those two estates from my hand on this condition: that each year, as rent, he should pay our church two solidi on the third day after the Nativity of the Lord; and that at his death, without succession by heirs, he should restore them whole and unimpaired to our church.

The following free and suitable witnesses were present at this settlement and at the peace concluded and confirmed between us: namely Widric of Spinal, his brother Morand, and the younger Widric; Walter, son of Morand; Videric, Widric, and Morand, brothers of Gisniac; Stephen of Ville; Richard of Calvomont; Ramer and Cerlad of Spinal. Of the clergy, there were Lord Rimbald, archdeacon of Toul; Arnulf of Spinal; and many others, free as well as servile, whom we have thought it unnecessary to enumerate. [Col. 1147C]

Accordingly, in order that Walter might prove the sincerity of his affection for us after the injuries he had inflicted, on the appointed day he brought his sisters to us at Castiniac in our presence and had them formally relinquish the same estates which he had unjustly claimed, together with the two aforementioned *quarteria* of land. These he had granted from his hereditary property at Auncourt to our church in compensation for our alienated chief holdings. Not long afterward, his aforesaid kinsman-by-marriage Henry returned from Italy; when he learned that Walter and his wife had put an end to every claim, he hastened to our church to make satisfaction, relinquished the estates, sought absolution, and received it. Thus, by the cooperation of divine grace, true and stable concord was confirmed between us. Let this now suffice concerning the estates of our sister Bertha, for our church possessed without any claim the two properties which she had bestowed upon us from her patrimony. [Col. 1147D]

10. Other gifts made to the monastery.—Near the estate at Wocourt which she had bestowed on us, a certain free man, Albric of Hannulville, possessed some very good lands, among which was a site suitable for constructing a mill upon the River Meuse. Knowing these lands would be useful to us because they adjoined our estate, he came to our house with his wife and sons. In the presence of these free witnesses—Hamon of Neufchâteau, his brother Henry, Albert of Rosaltum, his sons Simon and Albert, and Bencelin of Castiniac—he granted to our church, to possess freely and wholly in perpetuity, those lands just as he held them. Then, having sought and received fellowship with us, he requested and earnestly urged us to construct a mill at the aforesaid site. This we did, and our church has possessed it together with the other lands down to the present day. [Col. 1148A]

11. Another free man, named Widric of Wnocourt, likewise made a gift. He had inherited from his parents one half of the church of Saint Martin held under Lord Basolus. Since he had no heirs, he came in person to our house and granted our church possession of that share which he held as an estate, in the manner of a layman.

12. A certain free man, Robald of [Col. 1148B] Dommartin, had lost by death the many children whom he had formerly had. At last, when the one died in whom all his hope of succession rested, he brought him to our church for burial. Because he was now advanced in age, he began to think more earnestly of the salvation of his soul; and in place of the sons for whom he had diligently acquired many estates in the world, but whose inheritance was small because there was no equal succession to possess it, he resolved that our church should succeed him as heir. In the presence of many free men, he confirmed to it the possession of the estates at Hoscelville and Sannuncourt, granting them as freely, wholly, and securely as he had possessed them up to that time: namely, with male and female servants; cultivated and uncultivated fields; meadows and pastures; woods; a certain vineyard; [Col. 1148C] and all revenues. Our church holds them whole and unimpaired, having experienced no claim upon them.

13. Likewise another free man of Dommartin, an old and aged man named Mascelin, when his son Drogo came to us in order to enter religious life, bestowed upon our church the estate at Mattulcut which he had long before assigned to him as an inheritance. We received it as free, and we hold it free and whole without challenge. The same Mascelin afterward gave us another estate. At the death of a daughter whom he had had by his last wife, he bestowed upon our church one fourth of the estate of Truillares, with one fourth of the church belonging to that [Col. 1148D] estate, which was due to the girl as an inheritance from her mother’s side. He did so with the assent of the mother, Adsone, who survived: a free and noble matron; and in the presence of many persons he confirmed it for perpetual possession.

The girl’s mother herself, Hersendis by name, a woman of great respectability and adorned with good character, fell ill as she was leaving us after her daughter’s burial. She was brought back to us and, as her illness grew worse, died and was buried beside her daughter in our cemetery. Our church now holds that estate also.

Another free man, Amaboicus of Humberticourt, had a son, a cleric named Rembald. When this son fled the world and received the canonical habit among our brethren, the father too, concerned for the salvation of his soul and already advanced in age, renounced worldly possessions. Following his son to our house, he resolved to spend the remainder of his life in poverty. Wishing to bestow something from his own resources upon our house, he came and granted us the estate he possessed at Bugneolis, with the consent of his wife and sons, just as he had received and held it freely and peacefully from free parents. [Col. 1149A]

We accepted it from him, but because it was remote from us, in the course of time, with the consent of Lord Pibo, bishop of that city, we exchanged it with the canons of Saint Gengulf who dwell at Toul. We gave them our free estate and received, through the hand of Lord Riquin, primicerius and then provost of that church, their estate, which they possessed at a distance from our house near Hundinville, together with a small church of Saint Martin. The aforesaid estate belongs to that church’s parish; and, just as we received it freely from them, so we have possessed it peacefully and freely down to the present day. [Col. 1149B]

14. There was also a noble matron, Hervidis of Calvomont, who possessed an estate adjoining our house, called Bulherum. After her husband’s death, wishing to leave something from her possessions to our church for the increase of our house, she bestowed on us one half of that estate, which belonged to her own inheritance, in the presence and with the consent of her sons. She granted that portion free, whole, [Col. 1149C] and secure, just as she retained the other portion for her sons: namely, with cultivated and uncultivated fields, meadows, pastures, woods, usufruct, and every revenue. Our church still holds it peacefully.

15. Widric, a most noble and prudent man of Walecourt, and his wife Adelaide, who were bound to us by familiar affection, devoutly came to our house. Having received fellowship with us, they bestowed upon our church, in the presence of these free witnesses—namely Widric of Spinal and his brother Morand; Widric and Walter, sons of Morand; Ulderic and Widric, brothers of Gisniac; and Hugh and his son Peter of Paracio—one fourth of the estate of Igniac, [Col. 1149D] together with one fourth of the church there. Our church has held it free of every claim down to the present, with fields, meadows, pastures, usufruct, and all revenues.

Leucardis, wife of Theodoric of Ville, whom I mentioned much earlier, always loved, cultivated, and frequented our house above all others. After the death of her husband Theodoric, she married another man, Albert of Metz. Not long afterward she was seized by illness and brought to the point of death. When she saw death approaching, she summoned those attending her and, through their hands, assigned to our church the portion of the estate at Darnul which she still possessed from her patrimony. She had retained it specifically so that at [Col. 1150A] her death she might be able to give us something.

Afflicted with grievous sorrow, lest, if she departed this present life, they should bury her in that town, she begged her household and intimate friends with tears, and moreover adjured them, that they should permit her little body to be buried nowhere except in our cemetery. This was done. Immediately upon her death, they lifted her body and, with the great labor of a very long journey, brought it all the way to us. Receiving it reverently, we honorably consigned it to burial in our cemetery beside our monastery. We also received from those free men the estate which she had assigned to us through their hands; our church possesses it to this day free, peaceful, and unimpaired in every use and revenue. [Col. 1150B]

16. Another free and noble matron, Cunegundis by name, wife of the knight Rofrid of Vivery, burned with no less ardent desire of affection toward us. After her husband’s death, she offered our church, to possess, a portion of an excellent estate which she held at Basonmont from her marriage portion.

There was also another matron, Biliardis, wife of Bencelin of Castiniac. After her husband’s death, for love of the heavenly homeland, she granted all her patrimony to our house: namely, whatever she possessed at Rivirum, Aquosa, Landinville, and Berfredmont. Finally, having arranged all her affairs, she gathered together whatever she was able to have, both money and all movable goods, and came to our church in order to enter religious life, abandoning worldly splendors; there she died.

Suitable witnesses to this gift were Lord Rembald and his nephew Walter, a cleric; Arnulf of Spinal; Stephen of Ville; Gislibert and his son Ulderic of Dommartin; Cono; Theodoric of Darnul and his knight Humbert; Landfrid of Castiniac; Gerard of Longchamp; Albert of Beaumont; and his cleric Wido. [Col. 1150C]

> Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Seher, abbot of the monastery of Chaumouzey, and to his successors to be appointed in perpetuity.
>
> “The pious request of [your] will,” etc.

See Paschal, no. 273.

[Col. 1150D]

17. Grants made at Dornale.—We make known to all the sons of the church of Chaumouzey everything that we possess at Dornale. As Sancfrid was setting out for Jerusalem, he, with his son Ulric and his brother Hugh, granted to the church of Saint Savior everything he possessed at Dornale: cultivated and uncultivated land, meadows and woods, and every use-right and *ban* [seigneurial jurisdiction], just as he had possessed them.

Likewise, Beatrix, our religious woman, gave us, for the soul of her son Hugh, one *quarterium* at Dornale. Likewise, Gerard and his brother Widric bestowed on our church a wood nearby for the salvation of their souls. Likewise, Helfa, Gerard’s mother, bestowed on us a field at Alchaei Meadow. Likewise, Jofrid bestowed on us three *jugera* of land next to the place called Impedesecorum. Likewise, Ascelin and his daughter bestowed upon us, at their death, two *quarteria* at Dornale. Likewise, Sibilla, mother of Villerm, bestowed on us the garden in which our house stood. It should further be known what each *quarterium* owes. [Col. 1151A]

18. At the Nativity of the Lord, whoever holds a *quarterium* with a garden owes five denarii. Whoever holds one without a garden is required by custom to pay the same amount in mid-May, and two denarii at the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. By rule, on the feast of Saint Remigius he owes two denarii, and also at the proper time a *croata*, a *brullium*, and a fork. On the feast of Saint Remigius, he owes two measures of wheat grain and one of oats, according to the measure of the court. At the Nativity of the Lord, every garden without a *quarterium* owes three denarii. At Easter, it owes a hen with five eggs, and a *croata*, a *brullium*, and a fork, like the aforesaid *quarteria*. [Col. 1151B]

19. On the feast of Saint Martin, [each tenant owes] two denarii; must prepare the barn; carry hay and grain to the wall of the barn; make fifteen feet of brushwood fencing for the meadow enclosure in March; and must also perform threshing in the barn, amounting to ten cartloads.

Likewise, a certain widow, Hilburgis by name, there bestowed upon our church at her death one *quarterium* for the remedy of her soul; she was also buried before our church. Afterwards her son Richard gave us one *quarterium* for his daughter, whom we received as a religious woman. At a later time, at his death, the same Richard bestowed upon our church two *quarteria* that were pledged for eighteen solidi. Of these, he gave us one outright, which we also redeemed for twenty solidi. We redeemed the other for twenty-eight solidi on this condition: if his sons should repay us twenty-eight [solidi], they should recover their own property; otherwise, it should remain ours in perpetuity.

While still living, the same Richard also gave us a *quarterium* at Pinsincourt, and another *quarterium* which we hold from the same place in pledge and which we redeemed from the monks of Suricis for sixteen solidi. [Col. 1152A] We also had in that village a house which was not convenient for us. Wanting to exchange it, and having no suitable site, we bought from the same Richard two *jugera* of land for seven solidi, one horse, and one *jugerum* of land.

Likewise, at Basonmont, Albert of Parocia gave us one *quarterium* and a small wood called John’s Terp. Beatrix of Dornale also gave us one *quarterium* at Pincuichort. Another free and noble matron, Cunegundis by name, wife of the knight Rofrid of Vivenerio, burned with no less ardent affection toward us. After her husband’s death, she offered our church, to possess, a portion of an excellent estate that she held at Bononismont from her patrimony.

20. In the year 1222, on 6 March, the church of Chaumouzey paid tribute for freedom at Rome, during the pontificate of Pope Honorius III. [Col. 1152B]

Let it be known to all that Idate of Charmon has given and granted in alms to the church of Chaumouzey all that she had or ought to have at Charmon and in its territory: land, meadows and woods, mills, and eleven meadow-plots; at Cubmont, the bridge or Wamolin, of which Tirion holds one half; one half of the first Villenfane, which Demangeant Brunes holds; the field at Le Franc and the lime-tree which Ployresot of Walmont and Thiria of Roblagonde hold; the land of Follane, which Poyera du Chêne holds; and the land of Balloie, belonging to Lambert of Tenimon and his brother Thirion; and the wood in Foillant, with two *états* of land which Thiria and Tillan of Reblagonde hold.

Idate and Sisnea Sychesal are to have these things; and his men are quit, together with one half of Curtille, provided that Lord Virion has three francs of Toul currency over the whole paternal share. The said Virion is to have sixteen old Toul francs, and from a meadow at the mill of Charmois, of which Idate has one third: from Dame Doumeny, who holds the mill of Charmois, one half comes to Geate and her heirs. [Col. 1152C]

## In the Year of the Lord 1117: John the Deacon, Monk of Saint-Ouen

[Col. 1151]

## Historical and Literary Notice

(*Literary History of France*, X, 262)

Studies were held in great honor at the abbey of Saint-Ouen at Rouen in the eleventh century, and worthy pupils were then formed there. John, deacon and monk of that abbey, was among them, and from the age of twenty began to distinguish himself by works, some of which have come down to us. But nothing does greater honor to the monk John than the choice made of him to hold the pen and perform the functions of secretary at the council held at Reims in 1119 by Pope Calixtus II. [Note: [Col. 1153] *Conc.* vol. X, p. 872; Orderic Vitalis, *Hist.*, bk. XII, p. 863.]

John was not yet twenty when he composed, in prose and verse, the Life of Saint Nicholas. At the age of twenty-five, he made additions in verse and rhymed prose to the Life of Saint Ouen falsely attributed by Henschenius to Fridegode, an English author. Scholars now recognize Thierry, monk of Saint-Ouen, as its true author. If one is to believe what is reported in certain manuscripts, John had a vision in which Saint Ouen ordered him to write his Life, and he obeyed. What is more certain, however, is that he undertook this work at the command of his abbot.

The new Life of Saint Ouen which the monk John undertook to write was based upon an older Life of the holy bishop of Rouen, written by an anonymous author of the eighth century and subsequently put into verse by Thierry, monk of Saint-Ouen, with whom John had lived. John’s work consists of additions made to the previous work, adding several miracles omitted by the monk Thierry. Thus it is properly the same Life of Saint Ouen, but enlarged. M. Baillet seems not to have known this new Life.

It is believed that the monk John may be the author of several discourses or sermons, found, together with many other works, in a very fine manuscript from the abbey of Saint-Ouen at Rouen, called the Black Book by Fr. Pommeraye. In the judgment of Dom Martène, this manuscript is six hundred years old and therefore goes back to the period in which the monk John lived. Dom Martène published four pieces from this manuscript, among those thought to have been written by the monk John, though he neither attributed nor denied them to him. [Note: [Col. 1153] *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, III, p. 1669 ff.]

These pieces are four discourses. The first concerns the translation of Saint Ouen in 918; the second concerns another translation of the same saint, when his body was found for the third time whole, without any corruption, and in the same state in which it had been when Saint Ansbert, his successor, first transferred it to place it east of the altar of Saint Peter; and when, one hundred and sixty-five years after this first translation, Archbishop Riculf raised it during the devastation of the Normans in order to put it in a shrine adorned with gold and precious stones.

The continuators of Bollandus published the two pieces just mentioned from Dom Martène’s edition, which they collated with a manuscript, and they added notes to clarify the text. [Note: [Col. 1153] *Bollandists*, 24 August, pp. 820, 824.] The third discourse bears this title: “Translation of Saint Nicaise, martyr, and of his companions, Saint Quirin, priest, and Scuvicul, deacon.” Finally, the fourth discourse or sermon concerns the feast of the saints whose relics were then preserved in the abbey of Saint-Ouen and have since been burned by the fury of the Calvinists.

If the monk John is the author of the third of these discourses, as Fr. Pommeraye supposes, none of them can be denied him. They are so alike in style and in everything that can characterize an author that one cannot attribute one to him without recognizing him as author of all four. Moreover, the time when they were composed agrees very well with the time in which the monk John lived; he will have composed them for use in the office of the various feasts in question. These discourses are less sermons than historical accounts of what occasioned the translations of Saint Ouen and Saint Nicaise and of the various events that accompanied them.

Ambrose, a religious of the same abbey, who employed his pen to celebrate in prose and verse the illustrious Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr, should not be separated from the monk John. This Life is found in the same manuscript that contains the works of the monk John and is written in the same script, which gives reason to believe that these two authors lived at the same time. Fr. Pommeraye conjectures this. [Note: [Col. 1153] Pommeraye, *History of Saint Ouen*, p. 539.]

[Col. 1153]

## Four Sermons of John the Deacon, Monk of Saint-Ouen

(Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, III, 1669.)

### I. Translation of the body of the most blessed Audoen, Archbishop of Rouen

(From a manuscript of Saint-Ouen at Rouen, approximately 600 years old.)

[Col. 1153A]

1. Although, beloved, we ought to rejoice at the feast of every saint, yet especially whenever the celebration of our most holy and beautiful patron and bishop Audoen occurs, it is altogether fitting that we exult and glorify God with worthy proclamations of praise. He provided his people with such a shepherd and, in all things, such a most merciful intercessor. [Col. 1154A]

Therefore, with yearly devotion we commemorate this day on which his most sacred body, brought back from Gaul, poured forth for our whole people the rejoicing of a new exultation. For when almighty God, on account of sins, permitted the people of Gaul—adopted by faith—to be mercifully chastised by enemies for some course of years, just as he had once permitted his own chosen people Israel to be chastised by the Chaldeans, lest he punish them eternally by strict judgment, the army of the faithless and most cruel people of the Danes, joined together in barbaric fashion for plunder and practicing piracy, occupied the shores of the Ocean with a vast fleet. By plundering and burning, it devastated and consumed all the neighboring places of our habitation.

At last, making an incursion up the broad River Seine, it set fire to the monastery of Jumièges with all its buildings, and then resolved to attack the metropolitan city of Rouen. When the citizens learned this, fearing the rage of the heathen, they determined to carry away the bodies of the saints from there. [Col. 1155B]

2. The body of Saint Audoen transferred to Condat. Normandy granted to Duke Rollo, baptized in 912.—The monks therefore took the body of blessed Audoen and brought it to an estate of their own jurisdiction called Condat. They deposited the relics of the martyr Saint Nicaise, together with his companions, at Wambaix. For many years thereafter—that is, until the time of Rollo—the pledges of the saints rested there.

Rollo, relying on his martial strength and an expedition of armed men, burst into the territories of Gaul like lightning. He overthrew the walls of various cities and fortified places, razed, burned, and plundered many towns and rural districts together with the churches of the saints themselves. He also waged most bitter wars against the princes of the Franks, inflicted numerous massacres upon Christians, and could not be overcome by anyone. At last the propitiation of divine majesty looked upon the prayer of the humble and restrained the fury of the raging heathen. [Col. 1155C]

Accordingly, Charles, king of the Franks, made a treaty of peace with Rollo and promised that he would give him his daughter, named Gisela, in lawful marriage if he received the title of Christianity. He also generously granted him by royal gift the whole province of Normandy, which Rollo himself had subdued by warfare. Thus, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 912, Rollo and his army were baptized in the faith of the Holy Trinity by Franco, bishop of Rouen; and in baptism he was named Robert.

There was joy in the holy Church at the conversion of so great a duke and the salvation of the heathen. There was exultation among the holy angels in heaven and among people of good will on earth. There was universal gladness at the restoration of peace to the kingdom and tranquility to the age. Land, long deprived of cultivators, was inhabited; it was worked with plows and oxen; vines were planted; and France was renewed by the abundance of revived fertility. The new ruler, like Constantine, repenting of former evils, devoted himself wholly to restoring the churches of God which he had destroyed, defending the poor, observing the divine law, and giving the saints their due veneration. [Col. 1156A]

3. The people of Rouen complain of Saint Audoen’s absence.—Meanwhile, the people of Rouen lamented the bodily absence of their most merciful shepherd Audoen and the excessive dryness of the air. They remembered well that remarkable miracle: how this herald of divine teaching and sounding trumpet in the house of God had obtained rain from heaven, like Elijah, for the peoples of Spain, who for seven successive years had been afflicted by continual drought and whom he had sprinkled with the word of salvation and the dew of faith.

The murmuring of the people and the tearful complaint of the bishop of that city, namely Franco, struck his ears and stirred his mind to carry out so great a matter. Without delay, he went to the prince’s palace and humbly and fittingly presented his own petition and that of the whole populace. The newly made Christian asked what dignity and excellence belonged to the man for whose relics the whole people labored so earnestly and longed so intensely to have restored to them. In response, the bishop, instructed by this utterance, eloquently began to set forth in order the life of the holy bishop before the prince and all the nobles of the court: namely, how Audoen had been mature in virtue from the very beginnings of childhood; how he had shone in the advancement of holy virtues; how mighty he had been in the working of miracles; how blessedly he had adorned the ending of this present life by his departure; and how glorious he is in that senate of the heavenly court before Christ, the supreme Emperor. [Col. 1156C]

Having listened most attentively, the prince dissolved into tears and, because of the merits of so great a man, broke out in praise of our Savior, the giver of every grace.

4. Rollo asks King Charles for the saint’s body to be restored to its own seat, and obtains it. It is brought back with great honor.—Then Rollo, also called Robert, sent vigorous envoys from his side to King Charles, imploring him in friendly terms to order that his ancient priest, Audoen, most worthy before God, be returned to him and promptly restored to his own metropolitan seat, so that the terms of their recent pact might be kept inviolate on both sides and not, God forbid, violated by any occasion of dissension.

For the faith and devotion of so Christian a duke, the renowned king gave thanks to the King of kings. He then commanded the guardians of the sacred treasure at the town of Condat to satisfy the duke of the Normans and send back the body of blessed Audoen to its own people. Without delay, the divinely ordained task, also commanded by the king, was hastened to completion. By royal authority, moreover, clerics and monks in the churches through whose places the relics were to be transported were ordered to meet the sacred body in festal fashion, with crosses and books, candles and every varied accompaniment of procession, and to escort it with worthy praises of funeral rites as far as Normandy itself. [Col. 1156D]

All proceeded with eager devotion, decently and in order, blessing in hymns and confessions God, who is glorious in his saints. Everywhere resounded choirs of singers—clerics, monks, and virgins—uttering varied melodies in clear voices and sounding forth hymns.
