Nor, as we believe, were heavenly funeral rites absent, nor the angelic ranks of the host, at the translation of so holy a bishop: while still living, he had often enjoyed the speech of angels, and now he rejoices in their everlasting fellowship in heaven. [Col. 1157A]

5. It stood fixed and immovable on the road.—It is most certainly established that the whole course of that honey-sweet journey shone with miracles, although these have grown obscure through the antiquity of time and through the present neglect and remissness of those who were there. The nobles of the Franks, with an innumerable populace, followed the bier, joyful at his glory, yet exceedingly sorrowful at the loss they could not repair. Gaul lamented, despoiled of a treasure beyond price and of the jewel of all adornment, born from the womb of her own stock [Col. 1157B]. The hearts of his fellow countrymen were struck with overwhelming grief, grieving that he should be torn from the body, for they burned with most ardent love for him.

Thus, while a melodious multitude accompanied the remains of the blessed confessor with hymns, they arrived at the boundary dividing the two provinces. From there the Gallican people returned sorrowfully to their homes, while the maritime people joyfully followed in their pastor’s footsteps. At last, when they reached a place one mile distant from the city, the most holy body stood there as though fixed immovably to the ground, and could be moved by no one. Then, while all were dumbfounded with amazement, some of sounder judgment, warned as though by a sign of divine power, were sent ahead to the city walls; the arrival of the sacred body was announced to the duke and the bishop [Col. 1157C].

Immediately the bishop summoned a multitude of citizens and profitably admonished them to go out, with contrite and humble hearts, barefoot and in utmost devotion, to meet the sacred body. Therefore, when everything pertaining to the worship and splendour of the festal procession had been arranged, the entire ecclesiastical and monastic order, together with a great people, went forth from the city to meet their great pastor, as once the Hebrew people went out to meet our Redeemer. Thus the triumphant army of those clothed in white—who, according to the Apostle, while manfully striving in the arena of faith, engage in an unceasing struggle against the invisible powers of this air—came to meet its illustrious bishop with a great proclamation of praise.

[Col. 1157D] 6. Rollo grants gifts to St Audoenus. He bears St Audoenus’ body upon his own shoulders.—Then the most Christian prince said: “This place, at which, having gone a little way from the city, we have hitherto arrived on foot, I decree shall henceforth be called *Long Pedanum* [‘the Long Footway’]. From here as far as the city walls, I freely grant to blessed Audoenus all the land lying below, that it may stand as a protection for me and my heirs before God. Whatever is known to have belonged of old to the lands and possessions under his jurisdiction, I command to be restored to him. And I establish by my authority that his venerable monastery, with all that pertains to the use of the monks, according to the ancient privileges of kings, shall remain immune and free from every judicial exaction.

“But should anyone [Col. 1158A] attempt to bring any accusation or claim against this venerable place, let him seek me first—me, I say, who under the hand of the Lord am the shield of protection and the staff of defence of this same church.”

When he had thus spoken beforehand and had confirmed these matters by princely authority and decree, he prostrated himself upon the ground before the most holy body and, bathed in tears, prayed, repenting of the evils he had committed against the saints of God and groaning deeply over his past offences. Then he approached closely; and the neck which had formerly been proud and stiff with pagan arrogance, but was now tamed beneath Christ’s yoke, he bowed with wondrous devotion beneath the bier. First of all, bearing on his shoulders treasures now dear to him, he rejoiced to carry him, through whom he did not in the least doubt that he might obtain from God the forgiveness of his crimes.

[Col. 1158B] 7. He is laid in the church of St Peter (918).—The Danes also were present, now transformed from wolves into lambs: no longer, as formerly, yearning after prey with bloodstained jaws, but reverencing with the others the precious relics of the saint, according to the prophet’s saying: “The lion and the ox shall eat straw together” (Isa. 65). For they no longer thirst for human blood with beastly rage; nor, in the manner of pagan diviners, do they search for divination in the entrails of animals. Instead, they embrace from the heart a twofold love; they abominate foolish entertainments and the empty chants of idols, and eagerly seek the intercession of the saints.

Everywhere the crossroads resounded with the sweet voices of alternating singers and with an abundance of varied harmonies. But when they came to the suburbs of the city, that pious and solemn *Hosanna* which the Hebrew children sang in harmonious unison to the Lord as he entered Jerusalem [Col. 1158C] was sung to blessed Audoenus; and all together chanted, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 23). For at his blessed return they did not doubt that they would obtain relief from the wretched affliction of drought. A wasting plague also, breaking out from corrupted air, infected human bodies everywhere and destroyed many by sudden death. Therefore they desired to be delivered by his prayer from this deadly contagion, by him who had snatched many from the gulf of hell.

Thus his most holy body, thronged by an innumerable multitude, was carried back with offices of hymns and praise and with the fragrance of incense into the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and there it was most fittingly placed on the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 918 [1 February 918], where it is honoured to this day with the highest veneration, to the praise of Almighty God and for his everlasting memorial.

8. But when the people had departed to their homes, through the merit of the glorious confessor clouds gathered in the air, and suddenly a mighty downpour of rain broke forth and abundantly drenched the thirsty earth. That celebrated miracle was renewed which befell the Hebrew people at the coming of the outstanding preacher, when, like Elijah, bent over in prayer, he opened the barriers of heaven and the hindrances of the rain-clouds. For he flourished, like Elijah, in the steadfastness of particular zeal and in the grace of virginal integrity. By the roughness of haircloth he subdued his body; with iron he bound his neck, arms, and belly, so that, worn down by a prolonged struggle, he might be crowned with the martyrs [Col. 1159A], as a virgin might sing the new song with virgins, might rejoice with angels, and might reign victorious with Christ.

9. He shines with miracles.—All Neustria, which shortly before had been consumed with sorrow, rejoiced in the abundance of divine generosity and in the presence of blessed Audoenus. The bodies of countless sick persons were brought to his sacred pledges, and were restored to their former health. Festering diseases were cured by his healing, and the country was delivered from an impending calamity by heaven. O wonderful kindness of our Saviour! O surpassing glory of the most holy confessor! At his prayers heaven is opened; by his merits the deadly plague is put to flight. With him present the world breathes again; without him it had groaned, battered by wars.

Therefore it is clear from these signs, and is inferred from the evidence of events [Col. 1159B], that no one ever existed in all Gaul more eminent than Audoenus in the glory of merits or more powerful in the efficacy of miracles. How greatly he pleased God from the very cradle of infancy is proved by the testimony of one miracle among many. For by a wondrous omen God’s providence already foreshadowed what manner of man he would become in the episcopal office.

While Christ’s lamp was still concealed among his father’s household, and his pious mother Aïga was nursing the boy, one day—by divine prompting, as I think—he urged his mother more insistently than usual to prepare a bath for him quickly. She said to him: “I cannot do it so quickly, my son, because there is presently no water from which it can be prepared. There is a spring on the estate of the nuns of Mary, Mother of God, from which we must draw. We must wait until those upon whose ground it flows by God’s will have first drawn water for their own needs” [Col. 1159C].

To this the exceptional boy, endowed with Peter’s faith, replied: “The Lord, who is almighty in all things and abounding in charity, will be with us and will supply an abundance of water to us and to the tenants of our land—he who gave drink to a thirsty people from a dry rock.”

Saying this, he struck a rock in the name of the Holy Trinity with the staff he carried in his hand, and immediately a living spring burst forth. Its stream extended as far as the boundary of his jurisdiction; there, making an opening, it entered beneath the earth. For it clearly showed that the Lord drew new waters from cloven rock for the use of his servant, who was to irrigate the parched hearts of servants with the streams of divine teachings.

[Col. 1159D] Such a beginning of childhood befitted this man, whom God chose as priest for the expiation of many, and who, in the sign of Melchizedek, is daily offered at the altar under the appearance of bread and wine. He too, after the example of Moses—who upon the mountain prayed for the Hebrews fighting against Amalek, with arms stretched upward and displaying the form of the cross—bore the Lord’s cross in his heart and constantly entreated the King of Glory on the higher mountain of virtues for the whole people. Even now, most present before the Father of spirits and most clear-sighted beholder of the divine majesty, he does not cease to be a merciful intercessor in heaven for those to whom he left on earth so precious a pledge of his love.

## II. On the Translation of Blessed Audoenus and the Integrity of His Most Sacred Body

*(From the same manuscript.)*

[Col. 1160A]

1. First translation of St Audoenus’ body by St Ansbert. Its elevation by Archbishop Riculf.—When most blessed Audoenus had happily departed to the Lord after the course of his praiseworthy life, and the splendid lamp of all Gaul had suddenly been taken from mortal eyes, his most holy body was reverently and honourably committed to burial by bishops and abbots, a religious gathering of both orders, nobles also and an innumerable people, in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. It was laid in the place which he himself had prepared, in a sarcophagus fittingly made of Parian marble [Col. 1160B], where it rested for three years and nine months.

As much joy as the blessed confessor brought to the inhabitants of heaven by his arrival, so much sorrow did he leave the dwellers on earth by his departure. Afterwards his holy body was translated by his successor St Ansbert and placed on the eastern side of the altar of St Peter the Apostle, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, amid the great splendour and rejoicing of all. It was found wholly intact, untouched by any corruption, as though it had been buried that very day. The aforesaid bishop made over it a mausoleum of gold, silver, and precious stones, where it rested for 165 years, namely until the time of the Northmen, who, raging in pagan fury, devastated Rouen and burned his monastery on the Ides of May [15 May], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 842, during the reign of Charles, king of the Franks.

Then Archbishop Riculf of Rouen, together with bishops and abbots from the whole realm, raised the most sacred body and placed it, entire and without any diminution, in a bier precious with gold and gems. Thereafter, because of fear of the abominable pagans, it was carried by the monks to Wadiniacum, where it rested for several years, shining with miracles. Afterwards, as the savagery of the pagans intensified and the enemy army increased daily, while the province of almost the entire western region was laid waste by frequent incursions and fire, the aforesaid monks translated the bodies of St Audoenus and of the holy martyrs [Col. 1160D] Nicasius, Quirinus, and Scuviculus to their estate of Condatum. Therefore, after Rollo—or Robert—had, by God’s inspiration, become a Christian, the storm of wars was calmed and the serene time of peace restored; by the mercy of the heavenly Emperor, the limbs of our most holy father were brought back from Gaul and restored with great glory to their own church at Rouen.

2. Two monks plotting to steal St Audoenus’ body are divinely punished.—In the time of Richard I, surnamed the Old, the eminent ruler of the Northmen, who built from the foundations the church of the Blessed Trinity at Fécamp, two monks came from France with the intention and plan that, if God allowed them, they would secretly break open the coffin in the silence of the night, steal the remains of our most holy father [Col. 1161A], and carry them away with them.

Accordingly, after undertaking a three-day fast with vigils and earnest prayer, in the deep stillness of the third night, when the guards of the holy things were overcome by profound sleep, they secretly approached the bier to carry away from it the most precious treasure and inflict upon us an irreparable loss and intolerable grief—indeed, mourning upon the whole people of Normandy. But that true Samaritan, who keeps Israel and never sleeps, and whom Audoenus loves with a special, seraphic love, struck the invaders of the sacred temple with the punishment of blindness and deprived them of the power of all their limbs.

Then, perceiving the sign of divine vengeance, they begged forgiveness for their sacrilegious offence and, prostrate upon the ground, implored the mercy of our Saviour and of the holy bishop for the disability of their limbs [Col. 1161B]. Immediately the merciful Lord, through the merits of his servant, graciously pardoned them: he dispelled the darkness from their eyes, restored their sight, and gave back their limbs’ former strength. At dawn they mounted their horses and fled away, and never again appeared in those parts.

3. Richard is divinely warned of the matter.—On the same night on which these things occurred, Audoenus appeared in a dream to the aforesaid Duke Richard, who was staying at Bayeux and constructing for himself a palace and fortress there. Clothed in episcopal vestments, he admonished him twice to rise quickly, hasten to Rouen, command Abbot Hildebert to give more diligent care and guardianship to his church, and make every effort to rouse the brethren earlier before dawn.

But while he still lingered in the sloth of sleep and delayed rising, the illustrious bishop stood before him a third time, threatening and terrible in countenance. In his hand he held not a pastoral staff, but what seemed like part of the shaft of some broken spear; and in rebuke he said: “You build palaces and fortresses for yourself and your heirs, abound in the world’s riches, and proceed in varied adornment of clothing. Yet your forebears, breaking in from foreign and barbarous nations, plundered and burned the estates and possessions which, with divine grace helping, I had given to those serving God and me. Moreover, my monks stripped away my golden garment when famine compelled them by hunger, and, carrying me with them in their wandering and flight, placed the hardship of many privations before me, because of fear of and the rapacity of cruel pagans” [Col. 1161D].

Adding blows to his words, the blessed confessor continued: “See—see that you clothe me with a fitting tunic; that you cultivate my church and those of the other saints in humble devotion; lest perhaps, God forbid, lifted up by the pattern of pride, you undergo the eternal torments of hell.”

He also repeated the plot of the monks, who had intended secretly by night to take away his remains without the guards’ knowledge. Having said these things, he left the staff behind and disappeared. Then the prince, stunned by so great a vision and struck with fear, immediately recounted to the chief men of his court what he had seen, and showed the staff as proof of the truth.

4. He goes to Rouen and grants many gifts to St Audoenus [Col. 1162A].—Then, when the first dawn drove the stars from the sky, he swiftly mounted his horse and reached Rouen that same day, fasting. As soon as he saw the monastery from afar, he sprang down from his horse and, walking humbly barefoot, carrying in his hand the staff mentioned above and attended by a company of his nobles, approached humbly the altar of the holy bishop. He poured out prayers upon the ground with tears, laid the wood before the bier, and offered many gifts there.

Then, summoning the venerable abbot named above, he related in order the vision which he had seen and inquired concerning the monks about what he had heard from the blessed bishop. He discovered that it had happened exactly as described. Therefore he strictly commanded the aforesaid father that in that church two lamps should always shine, by day and by night: one before the altar of blessed Peter the Apostle, the other before the altar of blessed Audoenus the bishop—the two olive trees and the two lampstands shining before the Lord with eternal brightness [Col. 1162B]. He also appointed sacristans and suitable guardians to keep watch there and carefully guard the precious treasures of the relics and every ornament.

The illustrious prince himself gave St Audoenus an estate named Saint-Martin and a tenth of the estate called Ros. Then, summoning skilled goldsmiths, he gave them a supply of gold and precious stones for gilding and adorning the bier of the holy bishop.

5. St Audoenus’ incorrupt body is placed in a precious shrine.—When this work had finally been completed, he summoned bishops, abbots, and his nobles, and had the limbs of the most holy bishop uncovered, with great fear and reverence, by four religious monks of that same monastery [Col. 1162C]. The whole body was found intact with its head and without any diminution, just as it had been arranged by the venerable Archbishop Riculf.

Then, amid great proclamations of praise, it was wrapped in a very precious pallium and covered with clean linen; and, exactly as it was found, wholly intact, it was laid in a chest together with the iron rings by which, while alive, he had afflicted himself through self-binding for the sweet love of him who redeemed us by his own Passion upon the cross. This chest was placed in a bier adorned with gold and gems. There the most sacred body of blessed Audoenus awaits the day of blessed resurrection, that it may receive from Christ the double robe of incorruption and the everlasting crown of glory [Col. 1162D].

Present at this happy service and worthy spectacle were the illustrious Duke Richard himself, with his wife Albereda and his son Robert, surnamed the Dane, who died and was buried at St Peter’s at Chartres, together with other sons and daughters from the same wife. Also present were Lord Hugh, archbishop of that see; Richard, bishop of Bayeux; Roger, bishop of Lisieux; Gerard, bishop of Évreux; Hildebert, abbot of the same monastery; Mainard, abbot of Saint-Michel-du-Mont; Frotmund, abbot of Saint-Taurin at Évreux; and many other venerable bishops and abbots. An innumerable gathering of monks, clerics, and nobles from the entire realm also assembled, together with a large common people.

The four monks who uncovered the most holy body, as stated above, departed to the Lord in that same year by God’s hidden dispensation. We have therefore set forth these matters briefly, beloved, as we learned them through the truthful report of our elders, so that it may be plainly and without doubt believed that the body of our most holy father Audoenus is kept among us, as we have said, intact and undiminished in every part of its limbs [Col. 1163A].

## III. Translation of Blessed Nicasius the Martyr and His Companions

*(From the same manuscript.)*

1. Dearest friends, it is fitting that the most glorious martyrs—namely Nicasius [Col. 1163B] the bishop, Quirinus the priest, and Scuviculus the deacon—be revered with the more earnest and worthy praises of the Church because they stand higher before God in merits for the glory of their most victorious passion. In the army of our King, indeed, the wounds of a noble death make soldiers more glorious, and sweeter remain the rewards of divine recompense for those drenched in purple blood.

From that triumphant company, blessed Nicasius and his companions, formerly made a spectacle of reproach for preaching the truth, purchased the immortal life of angels at the cost of death; and in a blessed exchange they traded earthly things for heavenly, perishable things for eternal. Therefore, leaving aside the matters which the history recounts from the beginning of their passion, let us say a few things about its end, so that we may proceed more fittingly to those things that concern today’s translation [Col. 1163C].

2. Thus the most unconquered athletes of God, after steadfastness in holy faith and preaching, after an abundance of virtues and signs, were finally beheaded by the sword in confessing the Lord and offered before the sight of God. Then, when the silence of dark night followed, these three men—adorned with a threefold martyrdom for faith in the Holy Trinity—rose from the place of their killing and, carrying their heads in their own hands, crossed while singing to the Lord a ford previously unknown, accompanied by a melodious heavenly multitude singing hymns; and they rested upon the most pleasant bank of that river.

O great and wondrous grace of our Saviour, who marked his mightiest warriors and those harder than diamond in the arena of faith with this glory of privilege: that, though slain by the sword, they might walk in the manner of the living with an unfaltering step, and with equal rejoicing and the melody of angels make the name of God resound [Col. 1163D]! O inextinguishable love of charity, burning with seraphic fires, which, though it drank the chalice of passion patiently, still burns wholly in the praises of the Redeemer!

At last the venerable Pientia, converted to faith in Christ by the saints’ admonitions, honourably buried their bodies. She gave to the saints’ memorial the estate under her ownership which is called Wadiniacum; there, afterwards, a church was built in their honour, in which the bodies of the saints rested for a long time.

3. Translation of St Nicasius and his companions for fear of the Northmen.—After the passing of many years, the fierce people of the Danes, practising piracy in barbarian fashion [Col. 1164A], began to invade the territories of France with a great fleet and to consume by devastation the province of the western region now called Normandy. Thus, for fear of those abominable pagans, the bones of the aforesaid martyrs and of holy Pientia were translated, along with the remains of the most blessed bishop Audoenus, to the settlement of Condatum.

After a short interval, the body of Blessed Quirinus for the most part, together with relics of the blessed Nicasius and Scuviculus, was carried with the highest reverence to the place called Malmundarium, where they are constantly made glorious by miracles. There also stands a noble monastery of monks serving Christ, built in honour of Blessed Quirinus for his perpetual remembrance. The reason for this occurrence, the order in which it was done, and the signs by which the Lord declared their merits on that very journey of translation were not at all effaced by forgetfulness; rather, they were committed to writing with care by those to whom this happened at the time [Col. 1164B]. Yet from these outstanding miracles I think it not inappropriate to recall here briefly some things for the glory of those whose memory we celebrate festively today. For the operation of the divine majesty is one everywhere, and no distinction of places matters, provided only that devout faith is not lacking.

4. They heal one mute, deaf, and crippled.—A little boy named Hilpericus, mute, deaf, and crippled from his very cradle, was carried on his mother’s shoulders to the saints’ memorial. Immediately, the bonds were loosed; he broke forth into new speech, laid aside the deafness of his ears, and received the power of walking [Col. 1164C].

5. Another man, deprived of both lights—that is, blind in both eyes—followed the track of the saints’ relics, guided by a staff and walking with hesitant step, and prayed that they might restore his sight. Without delay, the witnesses of the true light, shining with eternal brightness, poured rays of light into his darkened eyes; and, when the darkness of his eyes had been dispersed, they sent him home seeing clearly and praising the Lord.

6. Another man, all whose limbs were weakened, obtained the grace of his former health while entreating the saints’ mercy. Thus it was openly made understood at what height of honour they excel in the glory of the elect, and with what reverent worship they ought to be honoured on earth, since they can so quickly help human afflictions [Col. 1164D].

7. They raise a blind dead girl.—In the same church of Blessed Quirinus, one day while the solemnities of Mass were being celebrated and the deacon was reciting the Gospel reading, a girl named Clena suddenly fell to the ground by an unexpected mischance and breathed out her spirit. Then all who were present, struck alike with fear and astonishment, carried the dead girl outside and decided to commit her to burial.

But one man of no lukewarm faith persuaded the others not to do this; rather, they should all together earnestly implore the holy martyrs, who there shone with continual miracles. When they had done so and had left the oratory for the hour of refreshment, they returned after a little while and found the girl safe and seated. In a clear voice she also related that she had seen blessed Quirinus, splendid in clerical dress, standing in a pleasant place, and that by divine command he had restored her to the world above [Col. 1165A].

8. The holy relics are carried to Wambais.—Meanwhile the monks of Condatum, as famine pressed upon them, carried the relics of the blessed martyrs Nicasius and Scuviculus, together with the relics of blessed Quirinus, to the eastern part of France called Lorraine, to a place belonging to their house called Wambais. There they rested until the time of Henry, king of the Franks.

At this time a venerable abbot named Henry presided over the monastery of blessed Audoenus at Rouen, under whom a considerable company of monks served Christ, the true King, according to the Rule. Among them was an elder named Genricus, advanced in age and mature in counsel [Col. 1165B], who was sent by this father to the place mentioned above for the monastery’s benefit. When he saw that the most precious remains of Christ’s soldiers, then indeed dissolved according to the condition of nature but destined to be restored in an indissoluble union at the general resurrection and adorned with the glory of immortality, were neglected there and, as was fitting, were not regularly attended by the appropriate ministry of servants, he firmly resolved to translate them to his own monastery, if the will of Almighty God, in whose hand are all things, should permit it.

Accordingly, he quickly returned and informed his abbot of the matter. From him he immediately received a command to return, as well as assistance in carrying out what he had planned.

9. Afterwards they are brought back to Rouen.—But the elder feared that, if the matter became known openly, the inhabitants of the place—among whom the holy martyrs stood in the highest reverence and glory—would hinder him, or that a faction and uproar of the people would completely frustrate his undertaking. Therefore, in the silence of the deep night, he secretly came with his companions to the place where so great a treasure was kept [Col. 1165C]. Having broken open the coffins and reverently taken the bodies of the holy martyrs Nicasius and Scuviculus, together with the relics of St Quirinus, he quickly departed.

It is also reported that, when they attempted to open the bier in which the saints had lain, one nail sprang far away from it and disappeared. Greatly terrified lest the hidden deed might perhaps be discovered by this sign, they invoked the Lord’s aid and left all things properly arranged just as they had found them. Thus the aforesaid hero, laden with the greatest treasures and accompanied by divine grace, set out on his journey; and, having completed the route successfully, arrived at Rouen. He sent a messenger ahead to the abbot and disclosed the reason for his arrival.

When these matters became known, the venerable bishop of that city, named Robert, went out in festal observance to meet the saints’ relics with all the companies of both ecclesiastical and monastic orders, accompanied by great proclamations of praise, as was fitting for conquerors and friends of God who “washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” [Col. 1165D].

10. For there was “glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will,” when the lifeless body of the most holy bishop and unconquered martyr returned to the place which, while once living in the flesh, he had not been able to reach, prevented by his glorious passion [Col. 1166A]. For the triumph of martyrdom came before the office of priesthood, and human praise was preceded by the ministry of angels.

O glory of a bishop, who consecrated the beginning of his episcopate with his own blood and, for the salvation of his flock, offered himself beforehand as a chosen ram for sacrifice! Therefore the most reverend Father Henry, with the community of his monks; Lord Isembert, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Trinity on the neighbouring hill, a German by birth, most learned in the liberal disciplines and most approved in every form of religious life; several other religious men; and the illustrious duke of the Northmen, Robert, son of Richard II, with his nobles and a great multitude of both sexes, received the relics of the blessed martyrs, fragrant with the scent of balsam and incense. With hymns and spiritual songs they honourably laid them in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of St Audoenus, the eminent confessor, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1032, on the day before the Ides of December [12 December] [Col. 1166B]. Through their merits the grace of the Lord and Saviour deigns to grant many benefits to all who ask faithfully—he who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## IV. Sermon for the Feast of the Saints Whose Relics Rest in This Church

*(From the same manuscript.)*

[Col. 1166C]

1. Beloved, divine benefits urge us to honour the glory of the saints with frequent solemnities, benefits which their most excellent merits bestow upon us. For it is fitting that the children of the Church should exalt the precious pledges of their mother with worthy services of praise, and should ceaselessly praise God as wondrous and glorious in his saints. Their souls indeed enjoy everlasting glory in the court of angels, while their bodies, fittingly laid among us, abound in a multitude of miraculous signs.

For the illumination of every region of the whole world, that true Sun of righteousness, whom the Virgin Mary, the star of the sea, joyfully bore under the shadow of the Holy Spirit, scattered in different places lights flashing with the radiance of virtues. Thus, in the western parts of Gaul, great Dionysius shone forth like a most brilliant star rising from Athens, most learned in liberal knowledge and most unconquered in the triumph of martyrdom. In his magnificent company, the most holy bishop Nicasius, with Quirinus the priest and Scuviculus the deacon, were martyred, clothed by Christ in purple garments, enrolled in the orders of the heavenly army, and inscribed in their ranks [Col. 1166D].

2. Our most holy father Audoenus, glorious bishop of this holy metropolitan see and brilliant morning star of all Gaul and the western region, completed the course of his praiseworthy life and laid down his limbs here. For the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal King, he continually mortified them with the hardness of iron and the roughness of metal plates. Therefore, an outstanding confessor, made terrible even by fear of himself and purple with the scarlet of martyrdom, entered crowned with laurels into the palace of the supreme Emperor.

The precious head of his eminent predecessor, most blessed Romanus, is cultivated forever in worthy reverence; the proclamation of an angelic voice announced the rising of his illustrious birth. Furthermore, the relics of the holy Innocents are honoured with the greatest love: Herod’s savagery cut them down with its furious sword as the first-fruits and flowers of martyrs, but Christ, himself an infant, adorned them with unfading garlands in heavenly glory [Col. 1167A].

3. May the arm of blessed Pope Callixtus and of St Arnulf, archbishop and martyr, grant us saving protection against all assaults and obstacles of evils. The purple witnesses of Christ and glorious deacons Laurence and Vincent, in whose intercessions we glory, undertook the contest of faith: one roasted upon an iron gridiron, the other tortured cruelly; triumphing, they entered rejoicing into the throne of the heavenly kingdom. As those nearest to Christ, the supreme Emperor, they received from him crowns of glory proportionately more eminent as they had gladly endured more severe torments from the tyrant for his love.

The portion of the body of the unconquered martyr Sebastian gladdens us. For steadfastness in holy faith, he was bound in the middle of the practice-ground, to terrify Christians, and was entirely pierced by blows of arrows. May the precious relics of the illustrious martyr Tiburtius protect us: he gladly walked upon burning coals in praise of the eternal King. May the glorious martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, Abdon and Sennes, Marcellianus and Marcus, Crispinus and Crispinianus, Hermes and Julianus, Marius, Felix, and Januarius grant us protection amid adversities; their sacred memorials flourish here without ceasing [Col. 1167C].

4. May that great light of the Church and golden vessel of heavenly wisdom, Pope Gregory, who refreshes us with the honeycombs of his good utterances, bring us by his merciful intercession to the heavenly kingdom. May blessed Gildardus, bishop of Rouen, whose arms from the sacred body give forth fragrance among us like incense, provide us through his holy aid with the shield of heavenly defence against every assault of enemies. May St Remigius, archbishop of Rouen, whose eminent limbs we embrace, join us through his intercession to the citizens of heaven.

May the heads of Blessed Faro, bishop of Meaux, and of the most holy Paul, the first hermit, which are honoured here with due devotion, join us through the merits of their works to Christ, the supreme Head [Col. 1167D]. Finally, may the holy father of monks, Leutfridus, to whose sacred bones we cling, protect us through his merits and prayers. May the venerable confessor of Christ, Vulganius, distinguished by the splendour of miracles, govern through the power of his merits the church which he adorns by the remains of his sacred body. May Agnes, blooming rose and lily in the whiteness of virginity and the redness of martyrdom, whose precious head we venerate, bring us into Christ’s wedding feast. May also blessed Scareberga, comely and illustrious virgin, obtain for us the joys of eternal blessedness.

Planted with these eternal flowers, with which the fragrant fields of paradise bloom, this field of the Lord breathes forth the fragrances of virtues like spices [Col. 1168A].

5. Therefore, dearly beloved, it is fitting that in this celebration we should exult with the appropriate offices of praise, in which the memory of all the saints whose relics or bodies are kept in this church is venerated with festal devotion. Among them we magnify our most holy father and bishop Audoenus with a fitting cult of reverence. Adorned with the episcopal mitre and distinguished by apostolic dignity, he shone with the gems of spiritual virtues, as a model of all religion.

For the jasper, green in colour and first in the order of such precious stones, represents in him the vigour of holy faith against the accursed error of heretical perversity. The beautiful sapphire, most like the clear sky, plainly bears the image of this priest [Col. 1168B], who, following Him who is “fairer in form than the children of men,” counted earthly things as worthless and was wholly intent upon heavenly things. The chalcedony—pale and dull in shadow, but bright in the open air, like a lamp—signifies the blessed man, who, lest the lamp should lie hidden beneath a bushel, was set upon the Church’s lampstand and illuminated the western regions with the radiance of the divine word; the pattern of whose virtues spread as far as the Alps.

The emerald, of translucent greenness, washed with wine and oil, pleasing to the eyes, makes flowers, herbs, and the air grow green, and renders images as in a mirror. You, illustrious Father, intoxicated with the wine of joy and anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit, effectively carried out the ordinances of the divine law and shone as an example of every holiness. The sardonyx, three-coloured—indeed black below, white in the middle, vermilion at the top—[Col. 1168C] signifies the blessed man, darkened by humility, white with purity, flourishing in rosy beauty, and pleasing to the supreme Godhead through the sincerity of his faith and religion.

The wholly red sardius, though not so precious, displays the host of martyrs, who, afflicted with diverse torments, obtain eternal crowns of reward through their sufferings and their contempt for temporal life. Audoenus, eagerly aspiring to their dignity, strove in his contest utterly to subdue the enticements and pleasures of the flesh, unceasingly bearing in his members the stigmata of our Redeemer. The chrysolite, golden in colour and somewhat blue, is produced in the fields of the Ethiopians, scorched by fire; it figuratively represents the blessed man, adorned with the gold of heavenly wisdom and, amid the adversities [Col. 1168D] of the world, as though rendered pale in the presence of the sun of righteousness. For, through the grace of his most pure love, every bitterness of tribulation was sweet to him.

6. The beryl, clear and pure as the sun’s ray playing in water, greenish and pale, and warm in the hand, fittingly corresponds to the honour of the blessed bishop. Pale through frugality and intent upon the sweetness of contemplation, he often surpassed the measure of human nature by the keenness of divine contemplation. By the example of his virtue many are kindled to the love of God, despising the fleeting flower of temporal life for the joys of the unfading paradise.

The topaz, heavenly in appearance and resplendent with every colour, befits such a bishop, who from his earliest disposition was endowed with every kind of virtue, full of heavenly grace, ardent with speculative sweetness, and [Col. 1169A] languished in love for his Creator, thirsting to be united with Him in heavenly glory—Him who for our sake willed to be sacrificed upon the cross as an innocent lamb.

The chrysoprase, golden and green, according to the property of its name expresses the sighs of the faithful who contend for the truth of faith and hasten with their whole love toward the palaces of heaven. Finally, blessed Audoenus, sighing in many ways during the prolongation of his sojourn, is exalted among the order of chosen bishops above heaven’s throne. The hyacinth, blue in colour, transparent and pleasing in clear weather but dark and dull in cloudy weather, is suited to the blessed bishop, who rejoices in the advancement of the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, while, as a most compassionate father, he grieves for the afflictions of the wretched. With the former he joins in the exultant dance of eternal rejoicing; to the latter he continually brings the remedy of compassionate consolation.

[Col. 1169B]

7. The amethyst, purple in appearance and blended with violet and rosy colour, signifies the lowly humility of the saints and the virtue of invincible patience beneath this world’s tribulation. Therefore the blessed bishop Audoenus—outstanding in the grace of humility, strong in constancy of patience, exalted by the privilege of virginity—having been admitted to [Col. 1170A] the banquet of the heavenly Lamb, rejoices for ever and, among the choirs of chastity, plays the new song upon harps.

Thus blessed Audoenus, catholic in faith, eloquent in speech, magnificent in action, adorned with the precious gems of virtues, fitted into the structure of the heavenly building, and clothed among Christ’s highest bishops with the robe of joy, is wondrously crowned. Therefore, children, be imitators of this most holy Father, so that with him you may be able to attain the lot of the eternal inheritance. Follow the unity of his faith, and arm yourselves vigorously against the arguments of heretical perversity. Love the purity of chastity, because your shepherd, in order to become a temple of the Creator, continually kept inviolate the laws of modesty by mortifying his flesh. Walk in the path of righteousness and truth, so that, with him going before as your guide, you may be able to enter the gates of the heavenly [Col. 1170B] Jerusalem. May the devout intercession of the saints, whose festive commemoration we celebrate today, likewise be present with us, so that through their meritorious aid we may deserve to be enrolled in the company of the heavenly court, through the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1117: Anselm, Scholasticus and Canon of Laon

[Col. 1169]

## Notice

(Casimir Oudin, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 936)

[Col. 1169C] Anselm, canon of the Church of Laon and later dean, flourished in the year 1100, at the end of the eleventh century. This Anselm of Laon and his brother Ralph were regarded as the two brightest lights of Gaul, according to John of Salisbury, and were celebrated in everyone’s speech and preaching. Hence Guibert, abbot of Nogent, speaks thus of Anselm in his preface to Bartholomew, bishop of Laon:

> God gave so great a head two eyes brighter than the stars: at your right you have Anselm, illustrious for his teaching throughout the Latin world, whose severity in maintaining Scripture and the faith is so sincere that by his instruction he is shown to have made more men Catholic than any erroneous heretic of this age could have made heretics; and on the other side Ralph, etc.

And in Book III of his *Life*: “Master Anselm, the light of all France—indeed, of the whole Latin world—in the liberal disciplines and in tranquil conduct.”

Peter Abelard, however, did not think so highly of Anselm. Coming to him about this time to be instructed in the precepts of theology [Col. 1170C], Abelard expressed his opinion of him thus in the *History of His Misfortunes*:

> I approached this old man, whose reputation had been won more by long practice than by talent or memory. If anyone came to consult him, uncertain, concerning some problem, he went away still more uncertain. He was indeed marvellous in the eyes of those who listened, but of no account in the sight of those who asked questions. His command of words was remarkable, but his meaning contemptible and his reasoning empty. When he kindled a fire, he filled his house with smoke rather than illuminating it with light.

Thus wrote the self-display of Abelard’s intellect, together with contempt for his companions, disparagement and mockery of his teachers—whose glory and reputation he took pride in diminishing and depressing—and opposition to them in every matter that might be disputed in the schools.

In 1112 this Anselm alone opposed, against the canons of Laon, the election of Gaudry as bishop of Laon, on the ground that he was an incapable man. According to a contemporary canon of Laon, Gaudry had no ability in learning, utterly despised learned men, [Col. 1171A] loved soldiers above all others, and was at once insolent and presumptuous. Guibert, abbot of Nogent, an eyewitness, writes thus concerning Gaudry’s election, Book III, chapter 4:

> After the death of Ingelram, when the Church of Laon had been vacant for two years, they at last raised up Gaudry, whom they had heard to be the English king’s chancellor and wealthy in gold and silver. Before that election two archdeacons of the church had been raised to the episcopal chair through rival contentions among the electors—Walter and Ebles—but were expelled by the judgment of the Apostolic See. Then, under the wholly false hope of concord, the aforesaid man was chosen by the clergy, Ingelram having first laboured for this and the others striving toward their own ruin. He was sought at Rouen from the court of the king of England, contrary to the canons. Not unaware of the uncertainty of his election, since he bore the title of no church and had received no sacred order apart from clerical status, he arranged by intrigue to be made a subdeacon immediately and to be received as a canon in the Church of Rouen, [Col. 1171B] although until then he had conducted himself entirely as a soldier. Therefore, when all had assented to his reception, Master Anselm alone—the light of all France, indeed of the Latin world, in the liberal disciplines and tranquil conduct—dissented from his election.

A few months later Gaudry perished. Guibert describes in chapter 8 the savage frenzy of the people in slaughtering their bishop. Having explained with what rage and fury the citizens of Laon attacked him, how he tried to secure safety by flight, and how at last he halted in a lane of the clerical precinct before the house of Geoffrey the chaplain, he adds:

> While he most pitiably begged them for mercy, wishing to assure them on oath that he would never again be their bishop, that he would give them unlimited money, and that he would leave the country; while all the rest, with hardened hearts, attacked him, a man named Bernard, surnamed de Brueriis, raised a double-headed axe and brutally dashed out the sacred head—even though it was the head of a sinner. As he fell [Col. 1171C] among the hands of those holding him, before he struck the ground another man, striking him crosswise beneath the eyes through the middle of the nose, killed him. There, after he had been cast down, they cut his legs to pieces and inflicted many wounds upon him; stripped naked, he was thrown into a corner before his chaplain’s house. My God, who could recount how many taunting words passers-by hurled at the man as he lay there, how many missiles, how many stones crushed his body?

This frenzy and this dreadful death of an unworthy bishop moved even his enemies to pity, and among others Master Anselm of Laon, who carried him to burial through the midst of the raging crowd. The same Guibert also recounts this event in chapter 10, in praise of Anselm of Laon, after giving a lengthy account of the disastrous burning of the church, its ornaments, the palace, and other shrines:

> On the following day, since there was almost no one who passed the bishop’s body as it lay there without casting some reproach, insult, or curse upon it, while no one thought of burial, Master Anselm poured out prayers to the authors of this tragedy [Col. 1171D], that they might at least allow a man who had borne the title and insignia of bishop to be buried. They scarcely consented. Since he had lain naked on the ground in a certain dog-like degradation from the evening hours of Thursday until the third hour of the following day, he was at last ordered by the master to be lifted up and, with a coarse cloth thrown over him, carried to Saint Vincent. Brought to the church, he received at his funeral absolutely none of the rites due—not merely to a bishop, but even to a Christian.

Shortly before, Gerard of Chérisy, prince and castellan of Laon, had been killed in the same church, and the pavement had been sprinkled with his blood. Master Anselm, then dean of the Church of Laon and a man most renowned for learning, is said to have declared in certain private conversations that this shedding of blood could be washed away only by the burning of that same church [Col. 1172A], since so great a crime ought to be expiated not by water but rather by fire. This indeed happened not long afterward. So much concerning the life, humanity, and distinction of Anselm, dean of the Church of Laon.

He wrote many works. Bellarmine, under the year 1077, when he was already flourishing, and Labbe, in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the entry “Anselm of Laon,” discuss them, though not entirely correctly. They attribute to him the *Ordinary Gloss*, concerning which there is no doubt. They likewise attribute a commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew, printed in the old editions of the works of Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury—at Cologne in 1573, by Maternus Cholinus, and in all subsequent editions down to that prepared at Lyons in folio by Theophilus Raynaud in 1630, purged of extraneous commentaries on Sacred Scripture. It appears in volume I and begins, “The book of the generation,” etc. At its very opening it sufficiently indicates that it will treat of Christ’s humanity, etc.

[Col. 1172B] Yet this commentary does not bear the style or character of the early twelfth century, in which Anselm of Laon flourished. Hence some hold that this commentary on Matthew, printed among Anselm’s works, belongs to Peter Babion, an Englishman who flourished in 1360, according to Possevino, volume II of the *Apparatus sacer*, p. 240 in my edition. Anyone may readily ascertain and test this, if he wishes, for an indubitable commentary by Peter Babion, under the author’s own name, is preserved in manuscript in the Royal Library of France, codex 4123. It begins: “Our Lord and Redeemer, for the commendation of evangelical faith, willed that the Gospel should not merely be preached to all,” etc.—the same beginning as the prologue of the said commentary published by Theophilus Raynaud in his edition of Saint Anselm’s works.

Others maintain that this commentary belongs to William of Auvergne, bishop of Paris, about the year 1240. But Anselm of Laon’s genuine commentary on Matthew is in the same Royal Library, codex 3819, beginning: [Col. 1172C] “*Evangelium*, in Greek, is interpreted in Latin as ‘good news,’” etc. Through the ignorance of the copyist it is entitled “Of Master Anselm of Montelaon, archbishop of Rheims”; but it should read “of Montelaon,” or “of Mount Laon,” to speak in Latin, and he was never archbishop of Rheims. [Note: [Col. 1171D] The commentary on Matthew is assigned to Anselm of Laon by the Benedictine authors of the *Literary History of France*. See below, col. 1181. ED.]

Sixteen homilies on certain Gospel passages are also attributed to him. They likewise appear among the works of Saint Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, in the old editions and in the new Paris edition of 1675, published by Louis Billaine through the care and labour of Gabriel Gerberon, a Benedictine monk.

Likewise, a commentary on the *Song of Songs*, in the cited old edition of the works of Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, volume I, fol. 184, beginning: “At the beginning of books the reasons must be stated—how or why this book was composed,” etc.

Finally, there is a commentary on the *Apocalypse* in the same work, volume II, fol. 583, beginning: “God and Lord [Col. 1172D] the Father, foreseeing the persecutions which,” etc. It is also found under the explicit name of Anselm of Laon in the Colbert Library, codex 5117, and anonymously in the Royal Library of France, codex 4513, fol. 52, after a work of Hugh of Miramars, Carthusian of Montreuil. So much concerning his writings.

That most celebrated schoolmaster Anselm, canon and dean of the Church of Laon, died in 1117. He was an outstanding teacher of the many disciples who flocked to him from every side, and was buried at Laon in the church of Saint Vincent outside the city. Lucas d’Achery places him first in the succession of deans in his notes on Guibert, abbot of Nogent. He taught first at Paris and afterward at Laon for more than forty years. Bellarmine therefore places him under the year 1077 in his book [Col. 1173A] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. He publicly professed theology until his death.

Among the distinguished men and teachers who attended his lectures were William of Champeaux, who himself held the rank and office of master and was promoted to the bishopric of Châlons; Peter Abelard; Alberic of Rheims, later archbishop of Bourges; Lothulf of Novara; Geoffrey the Breton, appointed archbishop of Rouen in 1111; Philip, later a canon of the Premonstratensian Order and abbot of Bonne-Espérance in Hainaut; and Ralph and William, who succeeded one another in the see of Canterbury.

Concerning William of Canterbury, Herman the monk, who described the restoration of the burned Church of Laon, writes:

> We therefore took up the bier and relics of our lady and came to Canterbury, where Lord William, well known to us, was then archbishop. For some time before, seeking to hear the lectures of Master Anselm of [Col. 1173B] Laon, he had stayed many days in the bishop’s house and had taught there the sons of Ralph, chancellor of the king of England.

This William was William of Corbeil, a Frenchman surnamed de Chiche. In 1123 Henry I, king of England, granted him the archbishopric of Canterbury. He had been teacher of the sons of Ralph, chancellor of that king and one of the most powerful men in the English realm. John Brompton writes that Ralph, though worn down by illness for twenty years, was nevertheless readier than a young man for every crime at court, oppressing the innocent and plundering many lands for himself.

Anselm, dean of Laon, must carefully be distinguished from two other Anselms of Laon living at the same time. The first of these was surnamed Beessus, one of the treasurers of the Church of Laon. Under the pretext of integrity and piety, after deceiving the canons for a long time, he stole a considerable portion of the gems with which the sacred crosses were adorned on more solemn days, handed them over to goldsmiths, [Col. 1173C] and sold them. The author who describes the restoration of the Church of Laon writes concerning this affair and reports Master Anselm’s judgment as follows:

> Thereupon a general assembly [Col. 1174A] of canons and citizens was convened to consider what ought to be done; and, before all others, Master Anselm—then the lamp of the whole world—was consulted. As one most expert in divine law, he immediately recalled the history of Joshua: namely, how the Lord commanded that a theft committed by a servant, without anyone’s knowledge, should be investigated by lot—first through the tribes, then through families and households, and finally person by person. In imitation of this very subtle inquiry, Master Anselm advised that the perpetrator of so great a crime should be sought by the judgment of water: in every parish of the city, one innocent child should be put into a vessel filled with blessed water; in whatever parish guilt should be discovered, one child from each house of that parish should be put into the water vessel; and in whatever house the offender should be detected, all men and women belonging to it should be compelled to clear themselves by the judgment of water.

The latter Anselm was abbot of Saint Vincent at Laon, chosen from the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons in 1131. After ruling his monastery piously, learnedly, and prudently [Col. 1174B] for about seventeen years, and after, as the Laon writer says, travelling to Rome for the benefit of that abbey, he was eventually found there by the clerics of Tournai, elected bishop, and consecrated bishop by Pope Eugenius, unwilling and resisting though he was, bound by the bond of obedience. Thus, through him, the ancient dignity of the Church of Tournai was restored in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1145.

These details have been given somewhat more fully concerning the learning, virtue, and other endowments of Anselm of Laon, whom all ancient writers relate to have revived sacred learning in Gaul and opened theological schools at the close of the eleventh and beginning of the twelfth century. More could suitably have been said of him as prince of theologians; see Bellarmine and Labbe in the passages cited above, and Antonio Possevino, *Apparatus sacer*, vol. I, p. or fol. 86. We have transcribed the present account, with a few additions or alterations, from Caesar Egassius du Boulay, [Col. 1174C] Book IV of the *History of the University of Paris*: under the year 1101, fol. 9; under 1112, fol. 35; and finally under 1116, fols. 46–47—though in an order better suited to our purpose.

[Col. 1173]

## Second Notice

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine Religious, vol. X, p. 170.)

### I.—Life

[Col. 1173D]

Ansel, or Anselm of Laon, surnamed the Scholasticus, was born at Laon or in its vicinity before the middle of the eleventh century, of poor parents reduced to cultivating the soil, *de pauperibus et rusticanis* (“from poor and rural people”). [Note: [Col. 1173D] Peter the Chanter, *Verbum abbreviatum*, ch. 47, p. 125.] He never lost sight of his origins; the awareness of them inspired throughout his life a fund of modesty which infinitely enhanced the excellent qualities of heart and mind with which he was born. Nothing is known of the first years of his youth.

Dom d’Achery [Note: [Col. 1173D] Notes on Guibert, p. 641, ch. 60.] believes that he was sent to the abbey of Bec to study under Saint Anselm. Supporting this conjecture is the fact that his commentary on Saint Matthew, which is merely a compilation of passages selected from the holy Fathers, appears to have drawn many things chiefly from the works of Anselm of Canterbury, his master: *Ubi multa praecipue ex [Col. 1174D] Anselmo Cantuariensi magistro suo congessit* (“where he gathered many things especially from Anselm of Canterbury, his master”). Yet, wherever Anselm pursued his studies, he pursued them very successfully. In a short time he became qualified to teach at Paris alongside Manegold, a celebrated doctor who later became a regular canon and the first superior of the monastery of Murbach in Alsace, of which he is regarded as founder. This may be the reason why Baronius believed Anselm to have been a native of Paris.

Anselm began to give lectures there about 1076 at the latest, if it is true that he taught at Paris or Laon for more than forty years, that is, until the end of his life. [Note: [Col. 1174D] Pagi, vol. IV, under the year 1117; du Boulay, under 1116, p. 47; Marlot, *Metropolis of Rheims*, vol. II, pp. 285–286.] This was the period of the restoration of letters and theology in that capital. According to the expression of Pope Eugenius III, Anselm revived there the study of letters and Sacred Scripture [Col. 1175A] and restored them to honour: *Eugenius III de eo dixisse fertur per eum revixisse litteralis scientiae decus et intelligentiam Scripturarum* (“Eugenius III is reported to have said of him that through him the splendour of literary learning and the understanding of the Scriptures had revived”). [Note: [Col. 1175D] Marlot, ibid.]

Since he joined to learning a brilliance of mind far above his age, he attracted a great number of disciples, among the first and most illustrious of whom was William of Champeaux. [Note: [Col. 1175D] *Journal des savants*, vol. I, p. 196; Martène, vol. V, *Amplissima Collectio*, p. 877.]

Here we see the earliest origin of the University of Paris. The distinction and success with which Manegold and Anselm gave lectures there led Otto of Freising [Note: [Col. 1175D] Preface to Book V of the *Chronicle*.] to say that learning had passed into Gaul—a testimony highly honourable to these two doctors. Étienne Pasquier [Note: [Col. 1175D] *Recherches*, Book III, ch. 29, p. 263.], who had examined this historical point concerning the first origin of the University with great care, postponed its beginning until the reign of Louis the Younger; but this was because he did not know precisely when Anselm began to be known. Pasquier was not the only one mistaken on this matter. Trithemius, [Col. 1175B] the Magdeburg Centuriators, Baronius, Cave, Jean le Mire, Marlot, and others place Anselm only among twelfth-century authors, although it is certain that he spent the greater part of his life in the eleventh century and became famous there, both through the lectures he gave and the writings he composed.

Yet as his reputation increased and, in his native Laon, to which he was recalled toward the end of the eleventh century, he acquired the reputation of a profound theologian, perhaps the authors just mentioned lost sight of Anselm’s early achievements and attended only to his later and still more brilliant ones. This may have led them to regard him solely as a twelfth-century writer. Nevertheless, Pasquier agrees with Otto of Freising in considering Anselm the earliest master of the Paris school, which was the cradle of the University.

Du Boulay [Note: [Col. 1175D] Under the year 1089.] thinks that Anselm was obliged to leave that school in 1089, but offers no proof. It nevertheless seems likely that Anselm settled at Laon before the beginning of the twelfth century. He was elected chancellor, or scholasticus, of that church, an office which obliged him to direct the schools. To all appearance he was already a canon—this is the title ordinarily given him—and later added another when he was elected dean of the same church.

Once established at Laon, Anselm applied himself particularly to theology and gave lectures in it, while his brother Raoul or Radulf taught humane letters and dialectic. If it is he to whom du Boulay refers under the name Arnould—a name found nowhere else—we do not see on what basis he could represent him as one of the most famous adherents of the nominalist opinion. Anselm’s illustrious colleague was animated by the same spirit, which was always opposed to the vain subtleties of the philosophers of his time. He was never accused [Col. 1175D] of adopting the novelty that caused such great disturbances in the school of Paris.

The two brothers, working together, carefully applied themselves to educating the young men entrusted to them and laboured even more to form their hearts than to cultivate their minds: *Plus moribus quam personis, plus ingenio quam generi, plus Deo detulit quam homini*—“he gave more weight to character than to persons, more to ability than to birth, more to God than to man.” Having only God’s glory in view, Anselm never considered in his pupils, wherever they came from, the advantages that ordinarily strike the eye—birth, wealth, appearance, and so forth. [Col. 1176A] He devoted particular attention to those in whom good conduct and teachableness were joined to the abilities needed for learning. [Note: [Col. 1175D] Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 387.]

His principal care was to inspire them with a love of truth and a profound reverence for revealed truths. His theology was properly no more than a simple and sound exposition of Holy Scripture supported by the authority of the holy Fathers, whom he studied throughout his life. Filled with their principles and trained in their school, [Note: [Col. 1175D] *Anglia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 300.] he sensed the danger of seeking to penetrate too far, and in Holy Scripture he investigated only what it was lawful to seek and discover. Thus, Guibert of Nogent says, Anselm made more good Catholics than any heretic of his time had perverted: *Ut plures veros suis probetur documentis fecisse Catholicos, quam instituisse potuerit erroneus quispiam temporis hujus haereticos*—“he is shown by his instruction to have made more true Catholics than any erroneous person of this age could have made heretics.” [Col. 1176B]

With respect to practical truths, his exhortations were all the more effective because he himself gave an example of every Christian virtue. Those who had been educated in the school of Laon were ordinarily recognizable by their wise and modest bearing. [Note: [Col. 1176D] Mabillon, ibid.] Anselm took great care to repress in those distinguished by birth the inclination toward display and vanity that he observed in them. [Note: [Col. 1176D] Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, Book I, ch. 7.] Idung, believed to have been a monk of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, [Note: [Col. 1176D] Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. II, p. 514.] and a disciple of Anselm, recounts in this connection an instance of the firmness and severity of this great man, which he himself had witnessed. [Note: [Col. 1176D] Book *On Four Questions*.]

Under so accomplished a head, the school of Laon soon became the most famous in Europe. Before long, as once in the Lyceum, gifted minds were seen assembling there from every direction to hear the lectures of the two brothers, Anselm and Raoul. Students came from Italy, Spain, Germany, [Col. 1176C] England, and the furthest regions of the North; even the most celebrated doctors and professors took pride in becoming their disciples.

Helmold relates of Blessed Vicelin, apostle of the Vandals and Bohemians, [Note: [Col. 1176D] Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, *Slavic History*, in the Bollandists, 17 May, ch. 58, pp. 42–43.] that after directing the school of Bremen for several years under Archbishop Frederick, he went to France with his disciple Thietmar to receive the lectures of Anselm and Raoul, who were then, the author says, most renowned for expounding Holy Scripture. They studied under them for three years, avoiding curious and superfluous questions.

William of Champeaux was already quite advanced in age and had taught philosophy at Paris to great applause when he went to Laon to place himself among Anselm’s disciples. [Note: [Col. 1176D] Morin, *On Penance*, ch. 22, no. 8.] It was thought that one knew nothing unless one had attended his school. It became like a seminary from which came a large number of pious and learned ministers of the Church, who carried [Col. 1176D] light into every part of Europe and honourably filled the greatest sees. The holiest and most learned bishops who were distinguished by their learning and piety at the beginning and middle of the twelfth century had studied under Anselm and Raoul.

William of Champeaux, of whom we have just spoken, was elected bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne in 1113 and governed that church with apostolic zeal until 1121. Two other disciples of Anselm, [Col. 1177A] Geoffrey the Breton and Hugh of Amiens, were successively placed on the see of Rouen and filled it with distinction for fifty-three years. Orderic Vitalis [Note: [Col. 1177D] Book II, under year IV.] praises the former’s eloquence and profound erudition. Hugh of Amiens was one of the most illustrious prelates of his time, according to the testimony of the Norman historians and the gentlemen of Sainte-Marthe, who speak of him in praise. [Note: [Col. 1177D] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I.]

We learn from one of Hugh’s letters to Matthew, cardinal-bishop of Albano, [Note: [Col. 1177D] Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. V, p. 897.] to whom he was united both by ties of blood and by religious profession, that, having been born in France at the same time, they were educated together at Laon and pursued their studies there; that they afterward went to Cluny and received the monastic habit; and that the Holy See finally drew them from the cloister in order to place Matthew on the see of Albano and Hugh of Amiens on that of Rouen.

Guy of Étampes, bishop of Le Mans, had been educated [Col. 1177B] from his earliest youth under Anselm’s discipline; Anselm devoted himself especially to his formation: *Guidonem laudabilis Anselmi familiaritas commendavit, gravitas coercuit, instituit fides, formavit doctrina, exemplum eliminavit discipulo quidquid displicet in homine*—“the intimacy of praiseworthy Anselm commended Guy, his gravity restrained him, faith instructed him, learning formed him, and example removed from the disciple whatever displeases in a human being.” Guy profited so greatly from his master’s instruction that he himself taught for several years with acclaim [Note: [Col. 1177D] Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. III.] and was judged worthy to replace in the see of Le Mans the learned Hildebert, who was transferred to Tours in 1125.

Agara or Algara, another disciple of Anselm, was distinguished by eminent piety on the see of Coutances in Normandy: *Religionis nomine vir suo aevo clarissimus*, “a man most renowned in his age for religion,” say the gentlemen of Sainte-Marthe. [Note: [Col. 1177D] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II.]

The celebrated Gilbert de la Porrée, bishop of Poitiers, after studying under the ablest masters, especially Hilary of Poitiers and Bernard of Chartres, went to perfect himself in the school of Laon [Col. 1177C] in the understanding of Scripture. [Note: [Col. 1177D] Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, Book I, chs. 46, 50; *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, vol. III, p. 136.] He brought away from it so grave and serious a manner and such profound learning that he could thereafter converse only with the most capable theologians and those most practised in disputation. Yet he did not profit sufficiently from Anselm’s lessons, nor did he sufficiently perceive the danger of trying to penetrate too far into matters above human understanding; we shall have occasion to speak of this later.

Beyond those disciples of Anselm who were raised to episcopal rank, there were many others who became famous for learning and piety, rendered great services to Church and State, and shone alike in the secular and regular clergy, both in France and abroad. Anselm of Custella and Olric, vidame of Milan, who were successively placed, one after the other, upon that great see [Note: [Col. 1177D] Pandulf, *History of Milan*, in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum*, vol. V, ch. 17, p. 487.], after attending various schools, went to perfect themselves [Col. 1177D] under Anselm and Ralph at Laon, regarding it as the most renowned of all. Blessed Vicelin, bishop of Aldenburg, and Blessed Thietmar, two apostolic men, as commendable for their learning as for their holiness, studied for three years under Anselm and Ralph [Note: [Col. 1178D] Bollandists, 17 May, pp. 41–42.]. William of Corbeil, who from prior of the Regular Canons of St Osyth became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1123, had been Anselm’s disciple, [Col. 1178A] as had Robert of Bethune, bishop of Hereford, renowned for learning and piety [Note: [Col. 1178D] *Bullarium*, vol. II, p. 138; *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, pp. 7 and 110; vol. II, p. 209.]. We should never finish if we undertook to enumerate all the great men who came from the school of Laon—almost as celebrated in its age under Anselm as the school of Alexandria had formerly been under Origen. From this school came Guibauld, or Wibald, abbot of Stavelot and Corvey in Saxony; Hugh Metellus, abbot of St Leo’s at Toul; Francon, one of the most learned abbots of Laubes; Philip Hasveng, abbot of Bonne-Espérance; and others.

The success of Anselm’s school neither puffed up his heart nor made him lose sight of his original condition. It is known that he refused several bishoprics offered to him: *Ad pontificales cathedras pluries vocatus, nullatenus acquievit*—“Though repeatedly called to episcopal chairs, he by no means consented.” The bishopric of Laon was among them [Note: [Col. 1178D] *Chronicle of Laon*, edited by Du Chesne, in notes on Abelard, p. 1163; Anthony Belotte, in the catalogue of deans of Laon, in Guibert, p. 819.], although Guibert of Nogent, who on every occasion does justice to his merit, says nothing of it; nor does the monk—not canon—Herman; nor Otto of Freising. It is to be presumed [Col. 1178B] that Anselm’s humility led him to suppress the first reports that circulated and to stop the solicitations of ecclesiastical and secular authorities, who deemed him worthy of the most eminent offices. He could not even bear that his poor relatives should be elevated out of regard for him. Peter the Chanter relates on this subject a striking fact, most worthy of admiration [Note: [Col. 1178D] *Verbum abbreviatum*, ch. 45, p. 105.]. Stephen of Garlande, successively chancellor of France and grand seneschal, proposed to Anselm that he should ennoble his nephews and secure for them distinguished establishments. Anselm opposed this with all his strength, representing that, having been born poor and destined for agricultural labour, it was more advantageous for them to remain in the state in which God had placed them than to be exposed to becoming swollen with pride.

“God forbid that I should consent to what you propose,” answered this humble and modest man. “Let them remain in their condition; I should rather [Col. 1178C] never have given lessons on Holy Scripture than, by giving them, have contributed to procure honours for them which might make them lose humility.” A fine and rare example of modesty, with very few imitators! Such were Anselm’s sentiments near the end of his days, at a time when he was the object of Europe’s admiration.

Anselm gave great proofs of wisdom and prudence amid the troubled times following the death of Enguerrand of Coucy, bishop of Laon, around 1107. The see of that church, becoming the object of ambition among several claimants, was seized by an ambitious man whom Guibert does not deign to name; but divine vengeance broke forth against this rash man and struck him dead during the very ceremony. Since so terrible an example made no impression upon the canons, they had the cowardice, at the solicitation of the king of England, to elect his referendary, Gaudry, [Col. 1178D] a man of no standing and no merit. Anselm alone opposed his election. *Cum igitur omnes assensum in ejus susceptione dedissent, solus magister Anselmus, vir totius Franciae, imo et Latini orbis lumen in liberalibus disciplinis ac tranquillis moribus, ab ejus electione dissentit*—“When therefore all had given their assent to his reception, Master Anselm alone—a man who was the light of all France, indeed of the Latin world, in the liberal arts and in tranquil conduct—dissented from his election” [Note: [Col. 1178D] Guibert, bk III, *On His Own Life*.].

But the opposition of this good man, and the representations he made to Pope Paschal II, whom he went to see at Dijon, had no effect: the money distributed by the usurper [Col. 1179A] prevailed. Gaudry’s conduct matched his entry into the episcopate, and he eventually became its victim. The people, enraged at the murder of Gerard of Crécy, of which they regarded him as the author, and at his desire to dissolve the commune of the city after having himself sworn to it, massacred him, committed every kind of outrage upon his corpse, and set fire to the treasurer’s house. The fire spread to the church and reduced it to ashes, together with the episcopal palace. The city of Laon was then in the most grievous condition. Nothing was to be seen but slaughter and plunder, according to Guibert of Nogent’s description.

In the midst of this disaster, Anselm—whom God had preserved, in the phrase of the monk Herman [Note: [Col. 1179D] In Guibert of Nogent, p. 528.], like another Jeremiah to console the remnant of his people in this desolation—collected several passages or sayings from Holy Scripture best suited to move them to patience and submission to the ordinances of Providence. Not content with fulfilling these duties of [Col. 1179B] charity toward the people of Laon, Anselm also took care to procure for them a good shepherd. It is thought that he had a large part in the election of Bartholomew of Vire, canon and treasurer of the church of Rheims, and in all the good he accomplished during the first years of his episcopate—that is, so long as he governed himself by the wise counsels of Anselm and his brother Ralph. This is why Guibert of Nogent says [Note: [Col. 1179D] Prologue to *Genesis*.] that God had given this worthy head two eyes brighter than the stars: namely, Anselm and Ralph.

Anselm’s school, which does not seem to have suffered greatly from the disorders just described, became more and more flourishing under Bishop Bartholomew. The same concourse of foreigners continued to attend the lessons of the two brothers. The celebrated Abelard, drawn by Anselm’s great reputation, likewise came to Laon in Bartholomew’s first year—that is, in 1113—to hear him. But Anselm’s gravity, [Col. 1179C] tempered by great gentleness, his reserve and prudence in answering, and the little account he made of scholastic subtleties, disconcerted this young philosopher, whose heart was puffed up by vain learning and a remarkable facility of expression. This caused him to conceive a great contempt for Anselm, of whom he speaks in the most unfavourable manner. According to Abelard, Anselm owed his great reputation merely to long practice in teaching, not to intellect or memory. He was a tree that indeed had fine leaves but bore no fruit [Note: [Col. 1179D] Bulleus, year 1113; Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, bk I, ch. 47; Guibert of Nogent, *On His Own Life*, p. 449; Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. III; Helmold, *History of the Slavs*.].

“I approached,” Abelard adds, “this tree in order to gather fruit from it; but I found it to be barren, like that fig tree of which Scripture speaks, which was cursed by the Saviour of the world.” It is easy to understand that Abelard did not long attend the lessons of a master for whom he had so little esteem. But Anselm’s reputation was too firmly established for so inequitable a judgment [Col. 1179D] to damage it. We could set against Abelard the unanimous testimony in favour of Anselm from all the learned men of that age and those who followed. He was so universally esteemed that men prided themselves on having had him as teacher. Otto of Freising, writing in 1146, regarded Anselm and Manegold as the source of the abundance of learning and light then to be seen in France [Note: [Col. 1179D] Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, letters 5, 6, and 7; Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. II, p. 334.]. Sigebert and his continuator, and in general all writers, seem to vie in giving Anselm the most perfect praise, [Col. 1180A] both in respect of his conduct and all his great qualities, and in respect of his theological learning and understanding of Scripture. Thus Guibert calls him [Note: [Col. 1180D] Bk III, ch. 4.] “the glory and ornament of the Latin land,” and John of Salisbury “the doctor of doctors”—which must be understood of the doctors of Anselm’s own time.

For several years he had undertaken commentaries on most books of the Old and New Testaments.
