He continued this great work diligently until his death on 15 July 1117 [Note: [Col. 1180D] Pagi, under year 1117, no. 28.]. The Venerable Rupert, travelling into France to consult William of Champeaux, passed through Laon and had the sorrow of finding him at the point of death. He mourned the loss of this great man [Note: [Col. 1180D] Rupert, bk I on the Rule of St Benedict.], more famous, he says, than any bishop, though he was not himself a bishop: *Quovis episcopo famosiorem, quamvis ipse non esset episcopus*. Though not a bishop, he had given several bishops to the Church and rendered it great services. Anselm was buried [Col. 1180B] in the abbey of St Vincent, where his epitaph may be seen:

## EPITAPH

> In this tomb sleeps that most celebrated master,  
> Anselm, to whom, through the far-spread regions of the world,  
> sound faith, abundant learning, reverence of conduct,  
> a splendid life, a generous hand, prudent action,  
> pleasing speech, vigorous discipline, gentle correction,  
> wise counsel, and a foreseeing, sober, merciful mind  
> won from every side renown and praise.  
> Yet July’s sky, on the unwelcome Ides, dissolved the gifts  
> which God’s long grace had bestowed.  
> May the grace by which he flourished in life accompany him in death.

This epitaph is ascribed to Philip the Almoner, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, in the collection of his works. He may indeed have composed it, since he must have been present at Anselm’s death and funeral; but there it is wrongly applied to St Anselm of Canterbury: the title is certainly the editor’s. It is also found [Col. 1180C] among Hildebert’s poems under the title *Epitaphium magistri Anselli*—“Epitaph of Master Ansel”—which agrees with the manuscript of St Amand, where Sanderus says he saw it. But besides the fact that it is not Hildebert’s, the editor erred in applying it in his note to Ansel, canon of Paris and cantor of the Holy Sepulchre. Finally, it appears in the *Collection of Selected Epitaphs*, p. 58; in Du Chesne’s notes on Abelard; in the Sainte-Marthe brothers; and elsewhere. Marbod, bishop of Rennes, composed another epitaph in which he extols all Anselm’s fine accomplishments: according to him, Anselm was a skilled grammarian, orator, poet, philosopher, mathematician, and so versed in Scripture that God himself seemed to have inspired him with its understanding.

## § II.—Writings

The study to which Anselm chiefly applied himself was that of Holy Scripture. It was the [Col. 1180D] most usual subject of the lessons he gave [Note: [Col. 1180D] “Here, for almost his whole life, he taught sacred letters at Laon.” Marlot, *Metropolis of Rheims*, vol. II, p. 285.] and of the writings he composed. Several years before his death he had undertaken commentaries on most books of the Old and New Testaments, and he was working at them diligently when death carried him off. Here is the enumeration made by Father Le Long [Note: [Col. 1180D] *Sacred Bibliography*, p. 610.]:

An interlinear Gloss on the whole Old and New Testament, together with the ordinary Gloss; printed at Basle in folio in 1502 and 1508, and elsewhere in 1524, 1528, 1539, 1545, 1588, 1617, and 1634.

[Col. 1181A] A commentary on the Psalter.

A commentary on the Song of Songs.

An explanation of several passages of the Gospels.

A commentary on St Matthew, octavo, Antwerp, 1651.

Commentaries on the Epistles of St Paul and on Revelation, under the name of St Anselm of Canterbury.

Anselm’s interlinear Gloss on Scripture, and the marginal Gloss of Walafrid Strabo, which he revised and considerably enlarged, were regarded in the Church as a useful, indeed necessary, work for properly understanding Holy Scripture [Note: [Col. 1181D] Henry of Ghent; Sixtus of Siena.]. In it Anselm explains the sacred text by short notes, selected with great discernment from the writings of the holy Fathers. Exactness and learning are evident in it. *Multa breviter et quasi punctim, sed docte et accurate attingit*, says Possevino [Note: [Col. 1181D] *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 86.]—“He touches upon many things briefly and almost point by point, yet learnedly and accurately.”

Abbé Le Beuf, speaking of this interlinear Gloss [Note: [Col. 1181D] Dissertation on the *History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 140.], [Col. 1181B] seems to regard its true authorship as undecided. “Some,” he says, “attribute it to Anselm of Laon, others to Gilbert, deacon of Auxerre.” Yet the issue seems decided in Anselm’s favour by the unanimous, or nearly unanimous, testimony of ancient and modern authors who assign the interlinear Gloss to him. I do not know whether one could even find anyone who attributes it clearly to Gilbert, deacon of Auxerre. For if some make Gilbert the author of certain glosses, they mean not Gilbert, deacon of Auxerre, but Gilbert of Poitiers. These errors arise because writers who commented on Scripture after Anselm of Laon made extensive use of his Gloss, which served them as a kind of framework upon which they worked. This may be seen in Gilbert of Poitiers and Peter Lombard [Note: [Col. 1181D] Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, vol. III, ch. 1.] in their explanations of the Psalms and the Catholic Epistles, which were likewise called glosses.

Bernard Gui [Note: [Col. 1181D] In Muratori, *Life of Anastasius*.], speaking of [Col. 1181C] Peter Lombard on the Psalter and the Epistles of St Paul, says that he explained at greater length the Gloss of Anselm, continued by Gilbert. This must be understood not of the deacon of Auxerre of that name, but of Gilbert of Poitiers. Cave further observes that a manuscript of this Gloss of Gilbert of Poitiers on the Psalter is still preserved at Oxford. At the end is read this curious copyist’s note: *Explicit glossatura magistri Porretani super Psalterium, quam ipse recitavit coram suo magistro Anselmo*—“Here ends the glossing of Master Porretan on the Psalter, which he himself delivered before his master Anselm.”

Gilbert of Poitiers and Peter Lombard were not the only ones who used Anselm’s Gloss. Most who laboured upon Scripture did the same. Lipomano used it in his Chain on Genesis, and so forth. The two glosses on Scripture—namely, Anselm’s interlinear Gloss and Walafrid Strabo’s marginal Gloss, enlarged [Col. 1181D] by Anselm himself—have survived to our own day without alteration in several twelfth- and thirteenth-century manuscripts. In 1330 Nicholas of Lyra, in Normandy, published a third gloss under the title *Postillae perpetuae* (“Continuous Postils”). Together with the first two and other works, these form a large collection also found in manuscript in numerous libraries of chapters, monasteries, and old colleges.

It has been observed, in speaking of Walafrid Strabo’s writings [Note: [Col. 1181D] *Literary History*, vol. V, p. 62.], with what eagerness this collection was put to press as soon [Col. 1182A] as printing had been invented, and how many editions appeared in succession down to the Antwerp edition of 1634, rightly considered the finest of all. We shall therefore not list them here. We observe only in passing that this multitude of editions shows the zeal of our forefathers for the study of Holy Scripture. Not only the great number of editions proves this; the multitude of manuscripts proves it as well. Even going back only as far as Anselm, there are scarcely any works, even of the Fathers, whose manuscripts are more common than those of the Glosses of this author and of Nicholas of Lyra.

Anselm did not confine himself to his interlinear Gloss, but also wrote particular commentaries on several books of Holy Scripture: the Song of Songs, St Matthew, St John [Note: [Col. 1181D] “No one except the writer of this notice mentions commentaries on John.” Editor.], and Revelation. Trithemius, Sixtus of Siena, and others [Col. 1182B] add a fifth, on the Psalter. Some of these commentaries were at first attributed to St Anselm of Canterbury, the great reputation of that holy doctor leading people to judge him author of every work bearing the name Anselm. Yet the manuscripts of these commentaries, still kept in some libraries not far from Laon, show unmistakably that Anselm of Laon was their real author. At St Amand the commentary on St Matthew bears this title: *Magistri Anselmi glossae sive lecturae super Matthaeum*—“The glosses, or lectures, of Master Anselm on Matthew” [Note: [Col. 1182D] Sanderus, part I, p. 46.]. The same work occurs in a catalogue of St Vaast manuscripts more than three hundred years old, entered under Anselm’s name alone. A similar manuscript exists at Eynsham monastery [Note: [Col. 1182D] Ibid., p. 94.]. The same attribution appears in manuscripts of the commentary on the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 1182D] Ibid., p. 104.]. This proves that Anselm of Laon [Col. 1182C] and not Anselm of Canterbury is author of these commentaries.

It is true that Sanderus [Note: [Col. 1182D] Part II, p. 17.] cites a manuscript from Liessies in which the commentary on the Song of Songs is assigned to St Anselm of Canterbury: *Anselmi Cantuariensis archiepiscopi in Cantica canticorum expositio mystica et prolixa*—“The mystical and extensive exposition on the Song of Songs by Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.” But Eadmer, who has left us a catalogue of that holy archbishop’s works, makes no mention of this one; and it otherwise seems certain that he wrote no commentary on Holy Scripture [Note: [Col. 1182D] Catalogue of his writings in Eadmer; Theophilus Raynaud, edition of St Anselm’s Works, Lyons, 1630; Miraeus, in the *Mantissa* at the end of the supplement to *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.]. Accordingly, Father Theophilus Raynaud, in publishing the edition of that holy doctor’s works, cleared it of all these commentaries falsely ascribed to him. Besides, if St Anselm’s great reputation did Anselm of Laon an injustice by causing him, as it were, to be stripped of his own works in order to attribute them to that saintly prelate, it may be said that it does him honour in another respect: the productions of Anselm [Col. 1182D] of Laon’s pen were judged worthy of Anselm of Canterbury—that is, of one of the Church’s holiest prelates and greatest doctors.

St Anselm is not the only person to whom the productions of our author have been attributed. The historian of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 1182D] Vol. II, p. 486.] seems to credit Gislebert, canon of Auxerre, with the Gloss on Holy Scripture, saying that “Gilbert, canon of Auxerre, was surnamed the Universal, either because he had glossed all Holy Scripture or because of the extent of his learning. [Col. 1183A] One can no longer,” he adds, “distinguish today what belongs to Gilbert in the general Gloss.” Nevertheless, Abbé Le Beuf acknowledges that “scarcely any certain works of his [Gilbert’s] should be counted except a commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, at the end of which he placed his name and rank, *Antissiodorensis Ecclesiae diaconus*—‘deacon of the Church of Auxerre.’”

The same author, speaking of Anselm, deacon-canon of the church of Auxerre, who was living in 1136 and 1145 and distinguished by a perfect knowledge of Scripture, regards the praise given him in the necrology—where he is called *in divinis Scripturis magister egregius*, “an outstanding master in the divine Scriptures”—as grounds “for attributing to him certain works on Holy Scripture, such as some little glosses on the Psalter which Du Cange assigns to an Ansel, the same name spelled differently.” We readily agree that Ansel is the same name as Anselm, but we are at the same time convinced that the Ansel [Col. 1183B] mentioned by Du Cange, to whom he attributes certain little glosses on the Psalter, is none other than Anselm of Laon, who is often called Ansel in ancient documents.

Simon Fontaine was the first to undertake restoring to our author some works whose credit had been taken from him and transferred to others. In 1549 he published at Paris the commentaries on the Song of Songs and Revelation under Anselm of Laon’s name: *Enarrationes Anselmi Laudunensis in Cantica canticorum et in Apocalypsim*—“Expositions of Anselm of Laon on the Song of Songs and Revelation.” But this edition did not overcome the prejudice. Though restored to their true author, these same commentaries were still confused with the works of St Anselm of Canterbury in the Cologne editions of 1573 and 1612. The commentaries on St Matthew and St John were included with them. A few years later, however, Sanderus judged from the two manuscripts he had seen that the two works [Col. 1183C] published by Simon Fontaine belonged rather to the dean of Laon than to the holy Archbishop of Canterbury. Crovée, Possevino, Bellarmine, Fabricius, and other bibliographers agreed with Sanderus.

Nevertheless, all these authorities, though supported by manuscripts bearing Anselm’s name, did not prevent Father Gerberon from regarding these works as productions of a learned monk of Bourg-Dieu in Berry, named Hervé. This gave occasion to attribute to him at least the commentary on St Matthew, although no manuscript bearing Hervé’s name has so far been found. Moreover, it is otherwise known that he wrote no commentary on St Matthew, for the monks of Bourg-Dieu, in their letter on Hervé’s death [Note: [Col. 1183D] *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 514.], where they give a detailed list of his works, make no mention of a commentary on Matthew, John, or the two books of the Song of Songs and Revelation. They say only that he wrote several expositions [Col. 1183D] on readings from the holy Gospels and on the canticles read in church; this does not indicate formal commentaries on the Gospels: *Fecit plurimas expositiones de lectionibus sanctorum Evangeliorum, canticorum etiam quae in Ecclesia leguntur*—“He made many expositions on the readings from the holy Gospels, and also on the canticles read in the Church.”

The opinion of Theophilus Raynaud [Note: [Col. 1183D] Edition of St Anselm’s Works, Lyons, 1630.], who assigns the commentary on St Matthew to William [Col. 1184A] of Auvergne, bishop of Paris, is still less tenable, since the manuscripts of this commentary just mentioned are unquestionably older than the prelate to whom it is assigned, who did not die until 1248 [Note: [Col. 1183D] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, p. 99.]. But, to remove every doubt concerning this work, we shall give here the title of a manuscript of it, numbered 78, preserved at the monastery of St Evroul in Normandy, which bears at its head the name of Anselm of Laon: *Anselmi Laudunensis philosophi expositio ex diversis auctoribus exquisitim collecta super Evangelium Domini nostri Jesu Christi secundum Matthaeum. Ibi multa praecipue ex Anselmo Cantuariensi magistro suo congessit*—“Exposition by Anselm of Laon, philosopher, carefully compiled from various authors upon the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ according to Matthew. Therein he assembled many things especially from Anselm of Canterbury, his master.”

It is now easy to judge, from all that has been said, that the commentaries on St Matthew, St John, the Song of Songs, and Revelation, and the glosses on Scripture and specifically on the Psalter, belong neither to St Anselm, Archbishop [Col. 1184B] of Canterbury, nor to Anselm and Gilbert, both deacons and canons of Auxerre, nor to Hervé, monk of Bourg-Dieu, nor to any other author to whom some of these commentaries have been attributed. All are productions of Anselm of Laon’s pen. The authority of the manuscripts and the other reasons advanced must prevail over all objections and require us to restore these works to their true author. As for the commentary on the Epistles of St Paul, which Father Le Long ranks among Anselm of Laon’s works and which has been attributed to St Anselm, neither is its author; it was written by Hervé, monk of Bourg-Dieu, as we shall see in its proper place [Note: [Col. 1183D] Sanderus, *Bibliotheca Manuscripta Belgica*, part I, p. 2, manuscript 121.].

Besides Anselm of Laon’s works on Holy Scripture, Sanderus found among the manuscripts in the library of St Amand a writing [Col. 1184C] by the same author under this title: *Flores sententiarum ac quaestionum magistri Anselmi et Radulphi fratris ejus*—“Selections of the opinions and questions of Master Anselm and Ralph, his brother.” It seems to be a body of theology treating the questions debated in the schools of Anselm’s time, and may have served as a model for works of this kind subsequently published by Peter Abelard, Robert of Melun, the Master of the Sentences, and others. This work, the oldest known in this genre, is cited by a German monk in a dialogue between a Cluniac and a Cistercian. In this dialogue, printed through the care of Dom Martène [Note: [Col. 1183D] *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, pp. 1570, 1594; Bernard Pez, introduction to vol. V of the *Anecdota*, p. 12; idem, part II, p. 52.], the Cistercian relies on Anselm’s decision, based on St Augustine’s authority, to prove that one may transfer from one monastery to another in which observance is stricter. Yet, the Cistercian adds, the same master—that is, Anselm of Laon—advises one who wishes to transfer to a stricter monastery to ask his superior’s permission: “Ask permission of your superior; [Col. 1184D] if he is unwilling to grant it, know that he has no charity, and go to that monastery, availing yourself of the freedom God himself has given you.” To Anselm’s words the Cistercian adds that a superior who refuses the requested permission acts not only against charity but also against the commandment [Note: [Col. 1183D] “Master Anselm of Laon, in his *Sentences*, proves by the authority of St Augustine that passage from one monastery to another, stricter one, is lawful, Augustine saying: ‘He who passes from one monastery to another stricter one does not break his vow but fulfils it more abundantly.’ Yet the same master gives this counsel to one desiring to transfer: that he ask permission from his prelate. The words of the counsel are these: ‘Ask permission from your prelate, who, if he is unwilling to give it, know that he does not possess charity; and you, go with God’s permission.’ To these words of the master we add that he acts not only against charity but also against the commandment.”].

This is all that can be said of this work of Anselm in order to give [Col. 1185A] an idea of it, since we do not have in hand the manuscript in which it has been preserved.

Dom D’Achéry inserted among his notes and observations on Guibert of Nogent [Note: [Col. 1185C] pp. 612 ff.] a letter from Anselm to the abbot of St Lawrence at Liège, whose name is indicated only by the letter H. It is doubtless Heribrand [Note: [Col. 1185C] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 989.], who had been the Venerable Rupert’s teacher and succeeded Berengar in 1113. This very important letter appears to have been written on the occasion of some question under discussion in the abbey of St Lawrence. Anselm first warns the abbot to whom he writes to beware lest the question be merely a dispute about words. On this subject he says that reasonable persons seek the true meanings of what is written; that disputing about terms belongs only to children, whose understanding is limited and who grasp only faintly what they hear and are told; and that it is to them that St Paul’s admonition is addressed: [Col. 1185B] “Do not be children in mind and wisdom; but be children in having no malice, and in mind and wisdom be mature men” (1 Cor. 14:20).

He adds that the opinions of all Catholics do indeed contain certain differences, but are not thereby opposed and converge at the same point. In expressions, however, there are contradictions which provoke disputes: the weak are scandalized by them, the strong are exercised by them, the proud are afforded an occasion for disputation, and sensible persons—who show how such contradictions might easily be reconciled—are not heard. Anselm takes as an example of such debated contradictions what Scripture says of God: that he does not will evil, and that he wills all things which occur: *Non vult Dominus malum, item vult omnia quae fiunt*—“The Lord does not will evil; likewise, he wills all that happens.” Our doctor of Laon reconciles these apparent contradictions, [Col. 1185C] and takes occasion to explain in what sense God, according to Scripture’s expression, “has mercy on whom he pleases and hardens whom he wills.”

Speaking in this letter of the mercy God shows to one whom he draws out of the abyss of sin, Anselm indicates the dispositions that the sinner must possess in his heart. “If some sin begins to displease a person,” he says, “and he wishes to abandon it; if he does this for God’s sake, it is good and proceeds from the gift of grace: *Si homini peccatum aliquod incipit displicere, et vult deserere: si propter Deum hoc facit, bonum est, et ex dono gratiae procedit*. But if it is done otherwise, it is not good: *Si aliter fit, bonum non est*. Thus one sometimes abstains from pleasures and does not give oneself over to dissipation in order to preserve one’s money or something similar; this is not done with God in view and does not come from grace. [Col. 1186A] Likewise, if someone gives away his goods, fasts, prays, and so forth: if he does all this for God, it is good; but if he does it from some other motive, it is not good.”

Finally, Anselm advances this great maxim by which one must judge what is good or evil: namely, that in acting, a person loves the end for which he does something, and that what he does should be called good or evil according to that love: *Illud autem pro quo facit, diligit, et secundum dilectionem illam, bonum seu malum debet dici*—“For he loves that for which he acts, and according to that love it ought to be called good or evil.” This is, in almost the same terms, the great principle and rule of Christian actions so solidly established by St Augustine and so often repeated against the Pelagians.

The same letter contains several other important matters concerning the love of God, which Anselm calls the light of the heart and the remedy for our wounds. He compares it to a lamp spreading its rays throughout the house, and describes [Col. 1186B] the various effects produced by this love, which cannot be idle. He speaks there of clerics and monks; of the account they shall give at God’s judgment: first, as rational human beings; secondly, as Christians; thirdly, as persons called by their state to share the inheritance of the saints; and of their misuse of their soul, God’s name, and his grace. He compares knowledge of the Scriptures, in those who do not conform their lives to them, with manna that became corrupt when the Israelites kept it until the following day. We shall have occasion to speak again of Anselm’s letter in the article on Rupert, where we shall examine its subject.

Sanderus [Note: [Col. 1185C] Part II, p. 171] speaks of two other letters which he had seen at Louvain, in the library of Parc; they have not yet been published. Trithemius [Note: [Col. 1186C] *De script. eccles.*] attributes certain letters to him in general terms, but testifies that he has not seen them: “Certain letters.”

At Oxford, among the manuscripts of Magdalen College [Col. 1186C] [Note: [Col. 1186C] *Cat. mss. Angl.*, part II, no. 2197], and at Cambridge, among those of the monastery of Saint Benedict, there is a work under the title: *Anselmus de Antichristo* [Note: [Col. 1186C] Ibid., part III, no. 1411]. If this work differs from our Anselm’s commentary on the Apocalypse, it may perhaps be the treatise of Adso, abbot of Montier-en-Der. The copyist, finding in his exemplar only the initial letter of his name, A., as often happens, may have persuaded himself that it designated Anselm and attributed it to him in his copy.

Du Cange cites a work under this title: *Anselmi Peripatelici Rhetorimachia*, manuscript, Codex Thuanus 589. Is this Anselm the Peripatetic the same man as Anselm of Laon? If he is not, he is wholly unknown to us. If he is, we do not know what could have caused him to be given the name Peripatetic, for we do not see that he distinguished himself through zeal for Aristotle’s philosophy.

## Works of Anselm of Laon

(Under the name of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, among his works published at Cologne in 1573 and 1612, they are at last restored to Anselm the scholastic of Laon.—The interlinear Gloss on both Testaments, a genuine work of Anselm of Laon, written above the words of the sacred text, cannot in any way be edited separately because of the close connection by which it adheres to that text. It is found in editions of the Ordinary Gloss issued at Basel from 1502 onward and elsewhere.)

[Col. 1187]

## Expositions on the Song of Songs (G)*

[Col. 1187A] At the beginnings of books, the reasons ought to be stated why or how the book itself was composed; Jerome calls such reasons a preface. The author of the work of which we intend to speak had three names; corresponding to the number of his names, he composed three books, and distinguished their purpose by the interpretation of those very names.

In the first book, affectionately and sweetly, after the manner of a father piously admonishing his son and, as it were, offering milk, he instructs every believer who is still rather weak and not yet willing wholly to renounce earthly things. In that book, because of this great sweetness, he is called Idida, meaning “Beloved.” There he teaches that the harlot must be avoided, along with associations with evil persons and the other things which ought to be done in accordance with honour and uprightness, while one still remains in the world, as we have said. [Col. 1187B]

His second name is Coëleth, which in Greek is *Ecclesiastes*, and in Latin is called *concionator*, “public preacher.” By a public preacher we mean one who, in a gathering of people—that is, in an assembly—is a public speaker, fearing no one in uttering the truth and flattering no one. This is what he does in his second book. For, so that by certain steps of ascent he might draw toward perfection the one whom his teaching had first mercifully—but lawfully—allowed to make use of these earthly things together with works of mercy, because he believed that a carnal and still weak mind could not grasp heavenly and more perfect things, he now invites that person, as though stronger and capable of receiving higher things, in this second book to despise all earthly things. He shows how fleeting and transitory all temporal things are, saying: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1:2). [Col. 1187C]

This belongs to the contemplative life: namely, despising all worldly things and longing for heavenly ones. But what was permitted in the first book belongs to the active life. Furthermore, he shows, by certain earthly comparisons understood spiritually, for what purpose he has persuaded them to undertake so great a labour in this third book: certainly so that through contempt for earthly things we may attain the glory of eternal things. [Col. 1188A] In this work he is called Solomon, that is, “peaceful.”

This book is called the *Song of Songs*, also in the plural because of the great excellence of its dignity. Solomon first composed parables—that is, the book of Proverbs—in which he simply showed how we should rightly use these worldly things. This belongs to the active life and may be called simply a “song.” Proverbs are precepts concerning human life expressed through certain comparisons. Next he composed Ecclesiastes, in which he proclaimed that all worldly things are to be despised, as when he says, “All things are vanity.” This is a certain step from the active life to the contemplative, and it too may be called simply a song. After these he composed this book, in which, now that the world has been despised, he teaches concerning the love of God. This belongs to the contemplative life; hence it is called the *Song of Songs*: a song more excellent than the preceding two and others like them. [Col. 1188B]

The name of this book in Hebrew is *Sir hasirim*, which among us means “Song of Songs.” Solomon is said, according to these three books which he wrote, to have had thirty names. According to the parables he is called Idida, that is, “Beloved”; for, while instructing the unlearned there, he began to be loved by them. By this name Christ is signified, who is pre-eminently called the Beloved, concerning whom God says: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 17). Ecclesiastes is the name both of the book and of the author, and it means “public preacher,” one who causes diverse persons to agree in one thing. For diverse persons are gathered together in that book so that they may agree with one another in contempt for the world. [Col. 1188C] This is drawn from the comparison of a singer, who arranges the voices of different persons into a single harmony.

Likewise, Christ is signified by this name: he is the true preacher, teaching that transient earthly things are to be despised and heavenly things loved. He is also called Ecclesiastes because he governs the Church excellently and gathers it into one faith. According to this book Solomon is called “peaceful,” by which likewise Christ is signified, for he is the true peacemaker, gathering all persons to his love. [Col. 1189A] In Proverbs the author is called an ethicist, that is, one treating morals; in Ecclesiastes, a natural philosopher, that is, one treating the nature of things; and in the Song, a theologian, discoursing concerning divine things.

The matter of this book consists of the bridegroom and bride, the bridegroom’s friends, also called *paranymphi* (“attendants of the bridegroom”), and the bride’s female companions. The bridegroom is God, since he promises himself to the Church: namely, if she keeps faith with him and does not commit fornication with the devil, he will at last join her to himself in marriage. The Church—that is, those firm in faith—is called the bride, because, perfectly receiving faith, she pledges herself to God and renounces the pomps of Satan. The bridegroom’s friends are holy angels and more perfect persons, such as the apostles, who assist the bridegroom in keeping his beloved, warning and helping the Church not to commit fornication with another but to cling to God alone. [Col. 1189B]

The bride’s companions are those still tender in faith, who do not fully know how to love the Bridegroom but already show themselves capable of imitating the bride, so that, well instructed by her, they too may become a bride. He treats this subject by showing how, in this life, the bridegroom addresses his beloved both in person and through his friends; with how great an affection she receives the bridegroom’s words; how the bride’s companions show themselves ready to imitate the bride and speak to her; and sometimes how they themselves speak also to the Bridegroom.

Solomon, while still possessing the gift of wisdom and enlightened by the Holy Spirit, prophesies how the Church, before Christ’s coming and then in each successive state until the end of the world, will conduct herself toward God. His end and purpose are to compel his hearers to the love of God. [Col. 1189C] This author writes as a comic poet: he says nothing in his own person, but introduces the characters themselves as speaking. And because in no love are words of love found so affectionate as between bridegroom and bride, he makes them speak as though in the language of carnal love.

These are the first words of the Church, now near Christ’s advent and, through excessive love, already desiring his presence; like those who said: “Do you think I shall see it? Do you think I shall endure? Do you think that birth will find me?” And as a carnal bride, to whom the bridegroom had already become exceedingly pleasing through messengers, growing weary of the envoys and longing for his personal presence, might say, “May he himself come, speak with me in person, and kiss me,” so those faithful persons immediately before Christ say here:

## Chapter One

[Col. 1189D] “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, because your breasts are better than wine; fragrant with the best ointments, your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens have loved you.”

God himself, as he was foretold through the patriarchs and prophets—he himself now—“let him kiss me,” that is, let him now delight me with the kiss, that is, the presence, of his mouth, that is, of his Son. The Son is called the mouth of the Father, as he is also called the Word, because through him the Father is revealed to the world.

“Because your breasts are better.” Here the Church, now present with Christ, speaks. As if, turning toward him through excessive affection, she said: Because your breasts, evangelical doctrine, are better than wine. That doctrine is sweet and refreshing nourishment, pleasant as milk. It is better than wine—that is, than the doctrine of philosophers—which does not nourish but intoxicates those who receive it, makes them proud, and finally leads them to destruction. Or by “wine” we may understand the carnal understanding of the Old Testament. [Col. 1190A] We may also understand by “breasts” the twofold love, or the two Testaments understood spiritually, or spiritual graces; the sense will nevertheless be the same as above.

I call the breasts “fragrant,” that is, giving forth a sweet smell and drawing persons to themselves by their fragrance. That doctrine indeed gives forth its scent and draws persons by its good repute and fame; “with the best ointments,” that is, through the best ointments. For in evangelical doctrine there are ointments, that is, spiritual gifts, which are excellent in comparison with bodily ointments, with which lovers—and also diners—used to anoint themselves in order to be more pleasing. These ointments are deservedly called the best, for those whom they anoint they make true kings and priests.

“Oil poured out.” Another reason why she desired him: your name is poured out like oil. While oil remains in a vessel, it neither gives forth fragrance nor heals pains; but poured out, it both emits its fragrance and heals pains. Thus, while God was still kept hidden in the Father’s bosom, his name was little or not at all known. [Col. 1190B] But after he took flesh and visited the world by his presence, he presented himself for all to know; he emitted fragrance—that is, renown and a good reputation—concerning himself; and, poured in through the preaching of those who rightly received him, he healed pains and sins.

“Therefore the young maidens”: because you are so worthy and so sweet, therefore not I alone, but also the young maidens—that is, the lesser and weaker, still tender in faith—have loved you: that is, out of all things they have chosen you alone as the one to be loved. Although they still derive consolation for themselves from temporal things, they nevertheless judge that God must be preferred to those temporal things.

## Voice of the Church

“Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments. The king has brought me into his storehouses. We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts above wine. The upright love you.”

“Draw me after you.” Christ’s contemporaries, seeing, as it were, his ascension and the consequent absence of his consolation already imminent, ask him to draw them after himself—that is, to make them his imitators. He appropriately says “draw,” as though by a certain force. For force seems to be employed when a body born in sins is liberated from sins. [Col. 1190C]

“We shall run in the fragrance.” This is the voice of the bride’s companions. Hearing of the Bridegroom’s goodness and that their superiors wish to become his imitators, they say to the bride, namely to their teachers, now that they have tasted God’s sweetness: “You wish to go after him, and we certainly shall run with you”—that is, we shall labour with you to obtain the joy of the marriage feast—established and grounded in your fragrance, that is, in your preaching and reputation which draw us. This fragrance is “of your ointments,” that is, proceeding from the spiritual gifts through which you act. They rightly say, “We shall run,” for we shall not attain that heavenly prize by acting sluggishly and idly.

“The king has brought me in.” This is the voice of the Church to the lesser persons whom she has trained. Hearing that they desire God, she wishes to invite them to the same thing, as if those greater persons answered: “You say that you will run with me; and it is good that you should run, because those who reach him find supreme refreshment. And he has shown that this is open to me when he says: ‘The king has brought me in,’ that is, he has given me manifest knowledge, ‘into his storehouses,’ that is, into the secrets of the Church, so that I may know what mysteries signify: for example, that the Spirit is given in baptism, that infants are saved by grace alone, and similar matters which are not open to everyone.” [Col. 1191A]

Or by “storehouses” we may understand the fullness of blessedness, that is, eternal life. For in storehouses an abundant supply of goods is customarily stored; and perfect persons have already been brought, in hope, into the blessedness of eternity.

“We shall exult.” This is the voice of the lesser persons, who, having progressed somewhat through faith, now dare to speak to the Bridegroom in these words: “Because you, Lord, have already brought your bride into your secrets, we too shall make ourselves fit to be brought in with her.” This is “we shall exult,” namely in body: that is, we shall act well with exultation. “And we shall rejoice” in soul, because we shall think good thoughts. Or, “we shall rejoice,” namely, if we do good not under compulsion but willingly; and this “in you,” that is, we shall attribute all things to you as the first cause, from whom every good proceeds at its root. And we shall do this “remembering your breasts,” that is, your sweet doctrine, “above wine,” as was said above. [Col. 1191B]

“The upright love you”: we ought rightly to exult in you and love you, because all who are upright do this; therefore, unless we do it, we cannot be upright. The purpose of all the foregoing is clear: whether we desire to imitate the more perfect or the lesser persons, we are invited by their words to the love of God.

## Again, Voice of the Church

“I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon. Do not consider that I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me. The sons of my mother have fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep. Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

“I am black.” The bride speaks to the lesser persons. For, hearing the lesser persons’ promise that they would run with her, and fearing that they might fail in persecution—being those who had not yet tasted anything but the love of God and who regard saints as mad, because saints are held contemptible in the world—she forewarns them not to consider the evils, that is, not to abandon their promise on that account, but to consider what rewards they will receive for persecution. [Col. 1191C]

Thus she says: “You say that you will run with me; but then you must be made black in body, just as I am outwardly black because of my many tribulations.” She states the effect in place of the cause. Outwardly I am indeed black, but inwardly beautiful—that is, adorned with good virtues—I say to you, daughters of Jerusalem: those whom I have begotten to faith and who now also behold peace. These lesser persons are called daughters because they are of the weaker sex and can quickly be deceived and called away from faith; because greater vigilance and care must be given to them than to sons, that is, to stronger persons; and because these persons, once confirmed, beget others.

I say that I am black like the tents of Kedar—that is, like Kedar dwelling in tents. Kedar was, as Genesis 25 and 1 Chronicles 1 say, a son of Ishmael; but he was so wicked that no one received him into a house, and he always lived in tents. Origen says of him: “His hand against all, and the hand of all against him.” I am black like Kedar, beautiful like the skins of Solomon. [Col. 1192A] The skins in which Solomon lived were well stripped of hair, dyed red, and adorned with varied paintings. Thus holy persons are stripped of every superfluity and adorned with many kinds of virtues.

He fittingly compares saints to skins, because as a skin is called the hide of a dead animal, so saints, mortifying themselves, become in a sense mere skins. And he fittingly adds “of Solomon,” because these skins—that is, the saints—are the tabernacle in which the true Peacemaker serves as a soldier.

“Do not consider.” I say that I am black, but do not attend to this so as to abandon what you have begun, because the sun—that is, Christ, who is the true brightness—has discoloured me: namely, I have suffered all these things for his sake, and he will at last be able to reward me.

“The sons of my mother.” She shows through what ministers God thus tested her in persecutions: namely, through the sons of my mother, who first bore me in carnality. She ought to have been a spiritual mother to me and nourished me with the milk of divine understanding. Those who were my brothers fought against me through diverse kinds of persecutions; and, by thus persecuting me, they made me keeper in the vineyards—that is, in the churches of the Gentiles. [Col. 1192B] “My own vineyard,” that is, the vineyard which I ought naturally to have cultivated and guarded, “I did not keep.”

Here we note that state of the Church when the apostles transferred themselves from Judaea to the Gentiles, as the Apostle Paul says in Acts 13: “Because you have rejected us and shown yourselves unworthy of the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.”

“Tell me.” This is the voice of that Church which, leaving Judaea behind, now begins to build among the Gentiles. Here she prays to God, not in her own person but in that of those newly converted; and she asks God to give them knowledge of himself: namely, that they may know in whom God dwells so as to imitate them; and that they may know who are heretics so as not to follow them. Thus she says: “I have been made keeper in the vineyards; and in order that I may be able to keep them and present to you fruit from them, tell me”—that is, tell these new persons, which certainly is to your honour—“where you pasture,” that is, in whose conduct you are refreshed; or, “where you pasture,” that is, whom you feed, either with your body or with the refreshment of the divine word. [Col. 1192C]

“Tell me also where you lie down,” that is, rest: namely, where no offence disturbs you, “at noon,” that is, in the brightness of your majesty or in the fervour of charity; namely, those who are not in evening, so that love has already grown cold in them, nor in morning, so that love is only now tender in them. Tell me, I say, you whom my soul loves—that is, the whole affection of my mind. She adds the reason for this prayer: “lest I begin”—that is, I pray you to tell me, lest these Gentiles, still new in faith, begin to wander and follow bypaths after “the flocks of your companions,” that is, by imitating heretics. They are called Christ’s companions because, in order to deceive more effectively, they preach something true, agreeing with Christ; yet they are different because they insert heresies. If they agreed in all things, they would not be called companions but, as it were, Christ himself. Or they are called companions because they call themselves his companions and friends. He aptly says “flocks,” because they are both numerous and devoid of true reason. [Col. 1193A]

“If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth and go after the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds. I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots. Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove; your neck like necklaces. We shall make for you golden ornaments, patterned with silver.”

## The Church

“While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My beloved is for me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts. My beloved is for me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

“If you do not know yourself.” This is the Bridegroom’s voice. Here he does three things: he threatens; he flatters the bride; and he also sets forth the means by which the Church may obtain self-knowledge.

Connection: Do you seek knowledge of me? To obtain it, it is necessary for you, O beautiful one—beautiful through virtues and through my election—to know yourself: namely, the dignity which I have given you through faith, by giving you my body and blood, and besides these other spiritual gifts. For if you do not know what dignity you possess because you are my bride, go forth from the fellowship of the Church; depart—that is, become far from the Church—so that you may also lose the virtues which you formerly had. [Col. 1193B]

Go, I say, after the tracks—that is, by imitating the deeds—of the flocks, and thus pasture your kids: that is, delight in your foul acts and let them be your food. Do this beside the tents of the shepherds: by imitating those who call themselves shepherds and soldiers serving God in tents, but are not such; they are heretics. Or, remain beside the tents of true shepherds, but not within them. For heretics seek to draw authority for their impurities from the Holy Scriptures, in which holy persons serve as soldiers of God: such as certain people called Nicolaitans, whose heresy is condemned in Revelation 2 [and by the Church therein—the printed reading is uncertain]; and certain heretics mentioned in *Decretum*, Causa 24, Question 3, who preach that women ought to be held in common and say that the Apostle declared all things to be held in common, and other such things.

“My cavalry.” Having set forth threats, he gives flatteries, as though saying: “If you do not know yourself, go forth; but you ought neither to go forth nor to be ignorant of yourself, because I so honoured you as to make you my beloved and free you from Egypt.” This was prefigured in the liberation of the children of Israel from Egypt in Exodus 12. The Gentile world is led out of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of unbelief and the power of Pharaoh, that is, the devil’s yoke—through the Red Sea, because through baptism all enemies, that is, all sins, are submerged. [Col. 1193C]

This is what he says: “I have compared you to my cavalry”—that is, to those in whom I served as a soldier, going among the chariots, or at the time of Pharaoh’s chariots. By the chariots in which the powerful sat are signified the pride or instability of this world.

“Your cheeks are beautiful.” Having set forth threats and flatteries, he shows that she possesses means through which she may retain true knowledge of herself. I said, “If you do not know yourself, go forth”; but you ought not do so, because you have cheeks and a neck by which you can retain true knowledge. Cheeks are that part of human beings which grinds food and sends it into the stomach. Thus, in the Church, those higher persons are called cheeks who grind the Scriptures and make them digestible for the lower persons. And as the cheeks are the sign of modesty, so those persons always preach modesty and chastity. These cheeks are beautiful through many virtues and are like those of a turtledove, because, just as a turtledove never has more than one mate and sings only by mourning, so they have Christ alone as their Bridegroom and very often mourn for their own sins and those of others. [Col. 1194A]

The neck’s office is to allow food, once ground, to descend into the stomach and to hold the body to the head. By it are signified the disciples of those higher persons, as Timothy was to Paul; through them the Scriptures descend to the lower persons, and by their preaching they join the Church to Christ. I say that the neck is “like necklaces.” A necklace admonishes someone where to take refuge and protects the breast of its wearer so that no one may lay hands upon it. So these persons by their teaching both fortify the Church lest the adulterer, the devil, lay hands on it, and warn the lesser persons of the Church where they should take refuge and whom they should follow.

“Golden ornaments.” This is the voice of the bridegroom’s friends. Wishing to help the bridegroom in preserving the Church’s self-knowledge, they say: “The Bridegroom gives you cheeks and a neck, and we shall give you ornaments for the ears.” If those who are cheeks or neck speak these same words, it causes no difficulty. An ornament, *muraenula*, takes its name from the *muraena*, the eel which coils itself into a circle; by *muraenae* we signify rounded and perfect sayings, by which saints adorn the inner ear, that is, the understanding. [Col. 1194B] They are golden, that is, seasoned with divine wisdom and charity; “patterned with silver,” that is, distinguished by excellent eloquence.

Or, they know how to distribute, according to each person’s capacity, both the sayings and the wisdom they possess, by suitable forms of expression—to the wise according to their condition, and likewise to the humble. Silver is a metal that rings more clearly than others, and by it speech is signified. “And we shall do this while the king is at his table,” that is, in the confession of God: namely, while he is bodily absent from the Church.

Or this is connected with what follows: “While the king was at his table.” This is the Church’s voice responding as follows: “The Bridegroom and his friends give me such ornaments; and therefore my beloved will dwell for me—that is, for my honour—between my breasts,” that is, in my inmost love. The reason has been given beforehand, as if she said: “I ought deservedly to love him, because he gave me nard, namely virtues, and this while he was at his table,” that is, in his Passion and Resurrection. Namely, because he suffered and rose again, he gave me virtues, which gave forth their fragrance—that is, the good reputation fitting to him. [Col. 1194C]

Or, “while the king was at his table”: because he chose the tranquility of my mind as the place where he would dwell, therefore my nard gave forth its fragrance. Nard is an ointment made from a lowly herb; the herb itself is likewise called nard. By it humility is signified; and it is of a warm nature, by which charity is signified.

The Beloved, I say, will dwell between my breasts; and he will be for me both great sorrow and great joy. I shall grieve over all the adversities which he suffered, and rejoice over those by which he was not burdened. This is what is meant by “a bundle of myrrh.” By myrrh bitterness is signified, because it is an exceedingly bitter substance; and thus bodies anointed with it remain intact, because worms do not approach on account of its excessive bitterness. By the bundle is signified the multitude of bitter sufferings.

Likewise, my beloved will be to me “a cluster of Cyprus,” that is, great joy. From a cluster we have wine, in which there is gladness. Cyprus is a place in which excellent wine grows. The Church rejoices with the Bridegroom concerning the Resurrection and similar things. [Col. 1195A] I said, “My beloved will dwell between my breasts,” and this “in the vineyards of Engaddi,” that is, in the churches, where there is “the fountain of the kid,” because there foul persons are washed in baptism and become white. Engaddi is interpreted “fountain of the kid,” or “temptation of the eyes.” The Church is set amid the temptation of the eyes in this world, in which all things are offered to us for the testing of our eyes.

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves.”

## Voice of the Church

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely; our little bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress.”

“Behold, you are beautiful.” The Bridegroom’s voice, hearing the bride’s great affection toward him when she said, “My beloved will dwell between my breasts,” answers her:

“Because I remain with you in so great love, behold, you are beautiful.” He says this twice; note that she is beautiful both in body and in soul. “Your eyes are those of doves,” that is, dove-like: namely, seeing simply and lacking gall and envy.

“Your eyes,” that is, your preachers, who provide for you as eyes do for the body, “are those of doves.” This is said intransitively: that is, they will truly be doves, having the seven virtues denoted by the seven natures of the dove. [Col. 1195B] For a dove lives beside streams, so that, when it sees a hawk, it may plunge into the water and escape; it chooses the better grains; it nourishes other birds’ young; it does not tear with its beak; it lacks gall; it nests in hollows of the rock; and it has groaning instead of song.

Thus holy preachers live beside the streams of divine Scripture, by which their hearts are watered, so that by their protection they may escape the devil’s attack. They choose the better grains—that is, better interpretations, not those of heretics. They nourish by their teaching and example the young of others—that is, people formerly alienated from Christ, who had been the devil’s young, that is, his children. They do not tear with their beak—that is, unlike heretics, they do not pervert sound interpretations by tearing them apart. They lack gall—that is, they lack irrational anger. They nest in hollows of the rock: that is, they establish their nest, their refuge or hope, in the wounds of Christ’s death; Christ is the most firm rock. For by a nest refuge and hope are signified: when rain approaches, the dove flees to its nest and has hope in its nest. [Col. 1195C]

It has groaning instead of song: just as others delight in singing, so they delight in tribulation and groaning. The dove also has the nature of recovering lost sight; similarly, the preachers and overseers of the Church, if they have lost a gift of the Holy Spirit through some fault, recover it—as David recovered the spirit of prophecy which he had lost. It also has the nature of flying in flocks. Likewise, preachers, flying in flocks—that is, holding the catholic faith—make for the heights through the steps of good works and virtues. For as many good works as we do, by so many steps we hasten toward God. The dove protects itself with its wings; likewise good preachers strengthen and defend themselves with the teachings of the Fathers.

“Behold, you.” This is the bride’s voice. “You, Bridegroom, call me beautiful; and I ought to be such because you are beautiful, and therefore, unless I were beautiful, I could not be joined to you.” He is called beautiful according to his divinity; comely according to his humanity. The bridegroom is beautiful and the bride beautiful; therefore their coverings are beautiful. [Col. 1196A] By the little bed we understand those in whom God rests: for, though he rests but little in those in whom he rests, the Church is not offended, but rests. Such persons are flowering, that is, possessing the beginnings of good works. By the flower we understand a beginning because the flower precedes the fruit.

“The beams of our houses”: by beams we understand the strong persons who bear the weight of the Church, who are of cedar. The cedar is an incorruptible tree and kills worms by its fragrance. Thus these persons, because they already possess eternity at least in hope, and by their preaching and good reputation, destroy vices in the hearts of others. Ceilings hang from beams and ornament a house; by them are signified those who, depending upon the more perfect, adorn the Church by good instruction and reputation, and who are of cypress. The same applies to the cypress as was said about the cedar. When she says “our houses,” she gives us to understand the Church from among the Gentiles, now somewhat grown.

## Chapter Two

## Voice of Christ

[Col. 1196D] “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.”

## Voice of the Church

“As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat. The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered charity within me. Sustain me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love. His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.”

“**I am a flower.**” The voice of the Bridegroom: he moves the Church to endure suffering and offers himself to her as an example, because he endured much without any necessity of his own. It is as though he said: “I have called you beautiful, and you are so, like a lily [Col. 1197A] among thorns.” For just as thorns, stirred by the wind, tear and pierce a lily, so the daughters—that is, those devoted to the pleasures of the world—agitated by the devil’s prompting, tear the holy Church. Yet you should not flee; rather, be a lily, because I, though I had no need, was a lily: that is, I was a flower of the field and a lily, namely one pierced by many persecutions. I who was a lily in order to be pierced was also a lily, that is, the ornament of the valleys, namely of the humble.

Christ is rightly compared with a flower, because, as a flower grows of itself and is the ornament of the field, so Christ, born without human seed, was the ornament of the Church and of the whole world.

“**Like an apple tree.**” The voice of the Church speaking thus: “My beloved urges me toward suffering, and I am ready to obey him, trusting in his support, who is like an apple tree.” Just as the apple tree attracts travellers [Col. 1197B] by the fragrance of its fruit and its pleasant shade, and then restores them by the refreshment of its fruit more than other trees do, so Christ does so better than anyone: by the fragrance of good works; by shade, that is, protection, which he provides through spiritual gifts; and by fruit, that is, the Eucharist.

She therefore adds: “**Under his shadow I sat**,” that is, I rest under his protection against the heat of the devil; “**and his fruit**,” that is, his body and blood, or the refreshment of the divine word, “**is sweet to my throat**,” that is, to my heart.

Besides these things the king introduced me—he who is able to support and defend me in every tribulation—into the wine-cellar: into a certain gathering of the Gentiles, enclosed by faith and works as a cellar is enclosed. Thus he multiplied the Church. It is called a wine-cellar because the Church offers wine, that is, the love of God, [Col. 1197C] by which those who drink are made drunk so that they forget their parents and their former life.

“**He ordered love within me**”: that is, he disposed love in me according to order, so that first, according to worthiness, I love God with all my strength; then my neighbour, and this in different degrees—first my father, last my enemy—and this for God’s sake. Yet love is established in us in this order: that we first love ourselves and afterwards our neighbour; that is, we should wish the same nature to be saved everywhere which we wish to be saved in ourselves. And because we love our nature, we are led to love the Creator of that nature; and thus the love of God, though judged more worthy, comes later in time. Hence John says: “If anyone does not love the brother whom he sees, how can he love God [Col. 1197D] whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

And because he has done these things for me, “**I languish with love**”: that is, I afflict myself even to the failing of the flesh. And because I so languish, “**strengthen me**,” that is, bring me consolation from beginners and from the perfect. By flowers are meant beginnings; by apples, mature works, namely those of the perfect. For the good works of others are consolations to the saints.

“**His left hand.**” Solomon says in Proverbs 3: “Length of days is in his right hand, and in his left are riches and glory.” Thus here, by the left hand, or the left side, we understand temporal things; by the right hand, eternal things. The bride therefore says: “I languish with his love,” but he will not forsake me, for “**his left hand**,” that is, these temporal things, “**is under my head**,” that is, beneath my mind, because [Col. 1198A] my mind despises them, though it is sustained by them. For it could not keep vigil and perform similar things if the body were not refreshed by them. His left hand, I say, is under my head; and his right hand, that is, eternity, will at last receive me—an eternity which now I possess only by hope. As the left hand is less worthy than the right, so temporal things are less worthy than eternal things.

**CHRIST**

> “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,  
> by the gazelles and the stags of the fields,  
> that you do not rouse or awaken my beloved  
> until she herself wills it.”

**THE CHURCH**

> “The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes,  
> leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.  
> My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag.  
> Behold, he stands behind our wall,  
> looking through the windows, peering [Col. 1198B] through the lattices.  
> And my beloved speaks to me:  
> ‘Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.  
> For now winter has passed;  
> the shadow has gone away and departed.  
> Flowers have appeared in our land;  
> the time of pruning has come.  
> The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land;  
> the fig tree has put forth its early figs;  
> the flowering vines have given their fragrance.  
> Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come—  
> my dove, in the clefts of the rock,  
> in the recesses of the wall.  
> Show me your face;  
> let your voice sound in my ears.  
> For your voice is sweet, and your face beautiful.’”

“**I adjure you.**” The voice of the Bridegroom. Seeing his beloved languish with love for him and now persist wholly in tranquillity of mind and contemplation, he commands the lesser and subordinate members [Col. 1198C] not to remove her from that rest by sins and disobediences. It is as though he said: “Because my beloved languishes with love for me, I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem”—that is, you who are generated in the vision of peace—“by the gazelles and stags of the fields,” that is, if you wish to possess the natures of the gazelle and the stag, which the saints possess.

The nature of the gazelle is to seek high places, to have keen sight—whence it is called *dorcas*, that is, “seeing clearly”—to choose clean food, and, if pierced by an arrow, to know how to heal itself. So the saints seek the heights of virtues, behold the Scriptures clearly and subtly, are refreshed by the clean food of the divine word, and, if wounded by some arrow of the devil, heal themselves through repentance and prayer, running to Christ, who, like a physician, draws the iron from the wounded.

The stag [Col. 1198D] has this nature: it runs swiftly; and when several pass from one place to another, they help one another bear the burdens of their heads. They swallow a serpent and afterwards run back to a living spring; as though having drunk, they expel the poison and are renewed. So the saints run swiftly through this field of the world, tending toward their true fatherland; they bear one another’s burdens by having compassion on one another and supplying what is necessary. If at any time they have received poison, that is, the inspiration of the devil, they run back to Christ, the living spring, through whom they vomit forth the devil’s poison which they have received and are renewed by God.

If you wish to become such, daughters of Jerusalem—that is, you who are still immature—I adjure you not to rouse my beloved: do not remove her from that repose of mind in which [Col. 1199A] she languishes while contemplating God, so that she must labour for you. Nor awaken her: do not, by sinning, interrupt her repose in any way, on account of which, if she perceives it, she will labour, even when she need not labour.

“**The voice of my beloved.**” The voice of the bride. Understanding the Bridegroom’s affection toward her when he said, “Do not awaken her,” she says: “This is the voice of my beloved; that is, he who gives this command loves me. And because he said, ‘until she herself wills it,’ I understand that he wishes me to descend for the sake of some who are to be begotten for God.” In this he gives me his own example and help. The Apostle likewise gives us both example and authority when he says in Philippians 1: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ,” which is far better; “but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake,” namely for a time.

“**Behold, he.**” She sets forth his example, as though saying: “I ought rightly to descend in order to win some for God, because behold, he himself did so.” This is the meaning: He who thus urges me came into human nature, “**leaping upon the mountains**,” that is, setting his feet and dwelling in those who are mountains through the perfection and eminence of their virtues. He also made them leap, as Paul, whom he quickly made from a persecutor into the greatest preacher. He leaps upon the mountains, “**bounding over the hills**,” by which are meant those somewhat lower than mountains. Although God does not leap in them as he does in the apostles and the other mountains, yet he bounds over them; that is, he touches them with his shadow, because he reveals to them a certain knowledge of his mysteries, though not as full as that given to the most perfect.

“**Like a gazelle.**” He can fittingly leap because he is like a gazelle: no one ever possessed the natures of the gazelle as fully as Christ did. “**Like a young stag.**” He is indeed the son of stags, that is, of prophets and patriarchs, who were swift stags. Christ is compared with a young stag because, as the young stag is light, unburdened by the weight of flesh and marked with spots, so Christ was not weighed down by any mass of flesh and was distinguished by every virtue.

“**Behold, he.**” Having shown Christ’s example, she shows that his help is present to her, as though she said: “I ought to labour to gain others as he did, and I shall accomplish it, because he is ready to help me.” This is the meaning: “**He stands**,” ready to bring aid to beginners, “**behind our wall**,” that is, in the flesh of our nature. In others besides Christ this flesh is properly called a wall, because it is a barrier between God and human beings, since [Col. 1199D] flesh is the tinder of sin.

Other translations have “after the building,” because whenever someone begins to build in virtues, Christ stands behind the wall, that is, secretly supplies assistance; “**looking through the windows**,” that is, visiting and consoling them openly through clear Scriptures, such as the Gospels, or through manifest miracles; “**peering through the lattices**,” that is, through narrow and obscure Scriptures, such as prophecies, or through unknown miracles, or the blinding of the Jews, and so forth. A lattice is a narrow opening in a wall.

“**My beloved speaks to me.**” He looks upon me and urges me where I should proclaim him, saying: “Arise,” that is, descend from your contemplation so that you may gain some for me. “Make haste,” because the time is short [Col. 1200A]; “my friend,” that is, you whom I have chosen from all; “my dove,” because of your simplicity; “my beautiful one,” according to your virtues. Thus come, because to gain others is for you to come to me.

“**For now.**” These too are Christ’s words, but the bride represents them to herself as spoken:

“I say: Arise, preach; and your preaching will not be fruitless, because unbelief and persecution have now ceased among the Gentiles. This is the meaning: ‘Winter,’ that is, unbelief, has now ceased among the Gentiles—not that they had yet received the faith, but that they were making themselves receptive. ‘The shadow,’ that is, persecution, namely crushing hail, has now gone away and departed; that is, it has ceased so completely that those who persecuted now follow. ‘Flowers,’ that is, the beginnings of virtues, have appeared in our land, that is, in the Church, which is well cultivated. ‘The time of pruning,’ that is [Col. 1200B] of purification, has come: the time to cut away superfluities through repentance and, if any refuse, to cast them outside the Church through excommunication.

“‘The voice of the turtledove,’ that is, the admonition of the Holy Spirit, has been well received in our land. The turtledove, which seeks high places, properly signifies the Holy Spirit, whose office it is to grant the height of virtues. Likewise the dove, which dwells in valleys, properly signifies the same Spirit, because it is his to grant humility.

“‘The fig tree,’ that is, Judaea, ‘has put forth and released its early figs’: its empty fruits according to the carnal understanding of the law, which never attain ripeness because they do not lead to perfection. Judaea is compared to the fig tree because of its empty works: it produces empty fruits, that is, early figs which never attain maturity. ‘The flowering vines,’ that is, those entering the Church and beginning to work well, ‘have given their fragrance’: they have sent forth a good report about themselves.”

Through all these things—when he says, for example, that persecution has ceased and the like—he indicates the condition of the Church, now well grown among the Gentiles. Therefore, arise, my beautiful friend; labour among others, and so come, “**my dove, in the clefts of the rock**.” The dove indeed nests in a rock, but not in a place shut in; rather, where there are openings, that is, shelters and protections against kites and other annoyances.

By the rock we understand Christ, on account of his firmness. In him are openings, that is, places of refuge, because he rejects no one who comes to him; and these are a protection against heretics and the other attacks of the devil. Or, by the openings may be understood the wounds of the Lord’s own body, which the Church is commanded to proclaim and in which to ground your faith.

The dove also builds “**in the recesses of the wall**.” A wall is called an assemblage of stones, where the stones are so arranged that none falls away; and in it are recesses, that is, certain shelters. By the wall are signified those gathered from diverse nations into the unity of the Church’s faith and so ordered that none falls away or dissents from Catholic teaching. In it are recesses: that is, they themselves are refuges for all who come to them.

The meaning, briefly, is this: Arise, my friend, and be a dove in the clefts of the rock and the recesses of the wall; that is, with simplicity proclaim Christ, who does not exclude those who come but protects them; [Col. 1201A] preach his wounds, and proclaim the lives of the saints as worthy of imitation, in whom those who join their way of life will find refuge.

“**Show me.**” These too are the Bridegroom’s words, but the Church represents them. The Bridegroom said to me, “Arise,” and he also said: “Show me,” that is, in order that you may please me and also be an honour to me, “your face,” that is, your good work; and let “your voice,” that is, your admonition and correction, “sound in my ears,” that is, be pleasing to me. And you will truly please me, because you are sweet and your face beautiful, that is, your works are beautiful—though at one time your voice and works displeased me.

> “Catch for us the little foxes  
> that destroy the vineyards,  
> for our vineyard has blossomed.  
> My beloved is mine, and I am his,  
> who feeds among the lilies, until [Col. 1201B] the day breathes  
> and the shadows decline.  
> Return; be like a gazelle, my beloved,  
> or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel.”

“**Catch.**” Again these are the Bridegroom’s words, but the Church represents them. The Bridegroom asks his friends to assist the Church, namely by removing heretics. It is as though he said to his beloved, “Arise,” and to his friends: “Catch,” that is, surround them and expose their false and useless doctrines; “the foxes,” that is, heretics, who are compared to foxes because of their craftiness; “the little foxes,” that is, those who display themselves as humble and just in order more effectively to deceive. I say, “Catch them,” because “they destroy,” that is, dig holes in and gnaw away the vineyards.

“For our vineyard”: it is necessary that they be caught, because the vineyard—that is, the Church from among the Gentiles, for which I have expended great care—has blossomed; that is, it has already shown certain beginnings of virtues in itself, whose fruit the heretics are preparing to impede.

“**My beloved.**” It is as though she said: “My beloved instructs me in the ways described above, and he is always my helper. I therefore shall obey and cleave to him, insofar as I can, in order that I may gain some for him, who ‘feeds,’ that is, delights and refreshes himself, ‘among the lilies’: in the works of those who are lilies, that is, radiant in virtues, until the day breathes, that is, until the general resurrection, which will be true light and will refresh us with every joy after the labours of this life, and until the shadows decline, that is, until the ignorances of this life pass away. Meanwhile God delights in our good works, which will not exist afterwards.”

“**Return.**” The Church herself, wishing to labour for the correction of other Gentiles, asks God to help her, namely to reveal himself to those whom she seeks to gain. This is the meaning: “Return,” that is, condescend to these people and breathe upon them inwardly, for otherwise our labour will be fruitless. Or: “Return,” because you withdrew from them through the sins of the first parent; return to their knowledge, and dwell in them.

“Return and be like a gazelle or a young stag.” The nature of the gazelle and the young stag is that, though they live upon mountain summits, they nevertheless descend to the hills, so that they may be seen by those below. I mean, like a gazelle “**upon the mountains of Bethel**,” that is, the house of God. For when Christ dwells upon mountains—that is, in those more eminent in virtues—he is asked to descend from [Col. 1202A] them and through them even to the knowledge of those below.

## CHAPTER III

> “Upon my bed I sought by night  
> him whom my soul loves;  
> I sought him and did not find him.  
> I will arise and go about the city;  
> through the lanes and streets I will seek  
> him whom my soul loves.  
> I sought him and did not find him.  
> The watchmen who guard the city found me.  
> ‘Have you seen him whom my soul loves?’  
> Scarcely had I passed beyond them  
> when I found him whom my soul loves;  
> I held him and shall not let him go  
> until I bring him into my mother’s house  
> and into the chamber of her who bore me.”

“**Upon my bed.**” The voice of the lesser members. Where the conversion of the lesser is shown, the effect of the preaching of the greater is made manifest [Col. 1202B], as though the lesser now replied: “You, our mother, pray that God may inspire us, which is necessary for us, because otherwise we cannot come to him. For we cannot find him through our former life of pleasures.” This is what she says: “Upon my bed,” that is, in worldly pleasures in which I rested entirely, “I sought him.” For every mind naturally dreams of and seeks the good.

“I sought him,” she says, but “by night,” that is, through ignorances, namely through these temporal things—as when someone expects sufficiency through riches—“him whom now my soul loves,” that is, the whole affection of my mind; “and I did not find him.” For no one can attain God through these loves. Her twice saying “I sought” indicates the affection of the seeker and the multiplicity of the search.

“**I will arise.**” Since I did not find him upon my bed, I will arise from the bed; namely, I will abandon the desire of the world. “And I will go about,” that is, I will diligently turn to the weak and inquire after the knowledge of God; “the city,” namely my mother Jerusalem, the assembly of saints, which preached to me; “through the lanes,” that is, by inquiring from those who follow stricter precepts. By “streets” we understand those who follow looser precepts, such as married persons, for whom it is lawful to use the world.

“I sought him and did not find him.” She gives the reason why she seeks from these people: because she first sought where he was not and did not find him.

“**The watchmen found me.**” I said, “I will arise”; I arose and sought. And the watchmen found me while I was seeking: that is, the holy pastors who guard the Church of God recognized my desire [Col. 1202D]. When she says that she was found before she found, she indicates for us the watchfulness and diligence which pastors ought to have in the Church: as soon as anyone is moved by compunction, pastors should be ready to admonish that person and lead him to the knowledge of God.

“**Have you seen him.**” The watchmen found me, and I said to them: “Have you seen him?” that is, do you possess knowledge of my beloved? In saying that the seeker spoke first, although she had first been found by the watchmen, she indicates the seeker’s diligence and great affection.

“**Scarcely.**” I sought from them, but I was not content with what they showed me. I went further, seeking him more deeply; and through them, because they taught me how we ought to seek him, I finally found him—that is, I tasted somewhat of his goodness and sweetness. She says “scarcely” because the knowledge of God is attained without great labour. Once God perceives the seeker’s desire, he offers himself and willingly makes himself known.

“I found him,” she says, “and held him,” that is, I clung to him firmly; “and I shall not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house,” that is, into the fulness of the Gentiles, which reared me in carnal desires, “and into the chamber of her who bore me,” that is, until I make some among the Gentiles into a bed for him, in which he may rest without offence. She calls her “mother” with reference to her upbringing; “she who bore me” with reference to her creation. Here the Church is indicated in the state in which the fulness of the Gentiles entered in.

> “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,  
> by the goats and the stags [Col. 1203B] of the fields,  
> that you do not rouse or awaken my beloved  
> until she herself wills it.  
> Who is this who comes up through the wilderness  
> like a slender column of smoke,  
> from the spices of myrrh and frankincense  
> and every powder of the perfumer?  
> Behold Solomon’s bed:  
> sixty mighty men surround it,  
> from among the mightiest of Israel,  
> all holding swords and most skilled in war;  
> each man has his sword upon his thigh  
> because of the terrors of the night.”

“**I adjure you.**” The voice of the Bridegroom. Seeing the affection of this Gentile body which has been brought in and which says, “I shall bring him into my mother’s house,” Christ again commands his subordinates not to disturb her, as he did above concerning this one’s mother.

“**Who is this?**” The voice of the Jews.
