Seeing so full a conversion of the Gentiles, they say in wonder: “Who is this who rises from virtue [Col. 1203C] to virtue, striving to reach God himself through the wilderness?” That is, through the whole Gentile world, which is called a wilderness because it lacks every divine observance—circumcision and the other legal institutions which we possess.

“She rises like a slender rod,” that is, upright and thin, with the body made lean and not fattened; a rod “of smoke,” that is, light, not weighed down by any burden of sins, so that it may freely seek the heights. Of smoke, I say, not smoke that harms the eyes, but that proceeds from spices, namely from every kind of virtue. He specifies these spices in detail when he says “myrrh and frankincense.” By myrrh are signified those devoted to the bitterness of the flesh, such as martyrs. By frankincense, which signifies prayers, we understand those who persist in prayer. Thus the meaning is: some ascend through mortification; others bring forth to God a sweet odour, namely the devotion of prayers.

Nor is ascent made only through these two kinds of virtue, but through “every powder.” By perfume we understand certain virtues; by powder, those virtues reduced to a certain lowliness. Virtues have no value in arrogance; rather, a person ought to account himself lowly, recognizing that he can never suffice for himself.

“**Behold Solomon’s bed.**” The voice of the Gentile Church in reply. The Church from among the Gentiles invites the Jews to love Christ, as the queen of the South (3 Kings 10), coming from afar to hear Solomon’s wisdom, might invite those who were present and familiar with him to the same thing. “You ask what I am, and I tell you that I am Solomon’s bride. You can know this through these tokens of his, all of which you will find in me.”

This is what she says: “Behold Solomon’s bed”: that is, manifestly you have among us a bed—people in whom the true peaceful one rests without offence. Sixty mighty men surround this bed: that is, we have guardians in the Church. By sixty we understand those perfect in the ten commandments. They are called mighty because they are humble and powerful in resisting adversaries. All these are chosen from the mightiest of Israel, that is, from men who see God; and all hold swords, that is, the word of God; and all know well how to strike with that sword: this is what is meant by “most skilled in war.”

This teaches us what pastors ought to be: possessing divine knowledge inwardly, they must also know how to explain it fittingly in preaching, to each person according to that person’s capacity. “Each man’s sword,” that is, the word of God entrusted to each of them, each places “upon his thigh,” that is, upon his flesh; because each demonstrates in himself the mortification of the flesh which he preaches to others, “because of the terrors of the night,” that is, because of the devil’s hidden assaults and suggestions.

> “King Solomon made himself a litter  
> from the woods of Lebanon.  
> Its columns he made of silver,  
> its headrest of gold,  
> its ascent of purple;  
> he paved its midst with love  
> for the daughters of Jerusalem.  
> Go forth and see, daughters of Zion,  
> King Solomon [Col. 1204C] in the diadem  
> with which his mother crowned him  
> on the day of his espousal,  
> on the day of the joy of his heart.”

“**He made himself a litter.**” Here the Church shows certain tokens of Solomon found within herself, through which she might be recognized as the bride of the true Peaceful One; she shows others also. A *ferculum* is a portable chair, so called from *ferre*, “to carry,” in which a judge sits. It is as though she said: “Besides the things mentioned, he made among us certain judges in whom and through whom he might judge. He did not choose them weak or impure, but from the woods of Lebanon.” By woods we note that they are sturdy and not broken by adversities. By Lebanon, which means “whiteness,” is signified that they are clean and radiant in virtues.

“He made its columns”—that is, its supporters, namely more perfect judges on whom others lean—“of silver,” that is, clearly sounding with the highest brilliance of divine speech.

“**Its headrest of gold.**” A headrest is that upon which someone’s head is laid in rest. By it we understand those who contemplate the divinity of God especially; these are golden, that is, radiant with love and wisdom.

“**Its ascent of purple.**” Those ascending by the steps of virtues are said, as it were, not to ascend, because they do nothing good of themselves, but Christ ascends in them, through whom or through whose aid we do every good thing. He made such persons purple, that is, ready for every persecution. And he “paved” this, that is, adorned it with love: namely, so that love might be the ornament of all other virtues, as blessed Paul very beautifully explains (1 Corinthians 13).

By “love in the midst” is meant love in which all may equally share. Or: he paved with love all the other, lower virtues; they are paved because without love they profit nothing, as Saint Paul clearly explains (1 Corinthians 3). Or “in the midst” means that he paved the aforesaid things—the litter and the rest—which are placed in the middle.

The king placed all these ornaments in us for the daughters of Jerusalem: that is, for the encouragement of those who are lesser and still immature, so that they too may hasten toward these dignities and become a litter, an ascent, and all the rest in like manner. Or let us say “for the daughters of Jerusalem” means for the Jews: that, considering our dignity, the Jews may be converted.

“**Go forth.**” Again the voice of the Gentile Church to the Jews. It is as though she said: “By all these ornaments you can recognize me as Christ’s bride; therefore, daughters of Zion—that is, you Jews,” for Zion is put for all Judaea—“go forth,” that is, abandoning carnality, cleave to Christ. And in order that you may be able to go forth, “see,” that is, consider King Solomon, that is, Christ, “in the diadem,” that is, in the victory of the Passion which he obtained through his mother, namely the Synagogue, which fastened him to the cross.

Or otherwise: consider Christ in the diadem, that is, in the Passion in which he obtained the crown of the defeated devil; in this Passion his mother, namely the Synagogue which fastened him to the cross, crowned him. I mean, the mother who crowned him “on the day of his espousal,” that is, of Christ’s espousal, when Christ first became the Church’s bridegroom in the virgin’s womb. Her womb is called the chamber of espousal because there divinity, uniting itself to human nature, from which it had been divided through sin, pledged itself thereafter to the rest of the same nature.

Secondly—and more appropriately to the present purpose—we say that the espousal was made in the Passion for those who grounded their faith in it. O daughters of Zion, recognize the king himself “on the day of the joy of his heart,” that is, in the resurrection and ascension, and consider the other things, all of which will call you back to love for him.

## CHAPTER IV

> “How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful you are!  
> Your eyes are like doves, apart from that which lies hidden within.  
> Your hair is like a flock of goats  
> which have gone up from Mount Gilead.  
> Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep  
> which have come up from the washing;  
> all bearing twins,  
> and none is barren among them.  
> Your lips are like a scarlet thread,  
> and your speech is sweet.  
> Like a fragment of pomegranate  
> are your cheeks, apart from that which lies hidden within.  
> Your neck is like the tower of David,  
> built with battlements;  
> a thousand shields hang from it,  
> all the armour of mighty men.  
> Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle,  
> which feed among the lilies  
> until the day breathes and the shadows decline.”

“**How beautiful you are.**” The voice of the Bridegroom, considering the affection of that Gentile Church, which wished to draw into friendship with itself as many as it could, and therefore commending her.

“**Your eyes**,” that is, your overseers, who attentively behold the Scriptures, “**are like doves**”: they behold simply and shine with every inward simplicity. I say that the eyes are dove-like “apart from that which lies hidden within,” that is, apart from the intention, which is far more beautiful.

“**Your hair**,” that is, those closely joined to the head and slender and delicate, like true poor people, “is like a flock of goats.” A flock, because of multitude; they are called goats because they seek high places and have the other virtues of the goats described above, “which have gone up from the mountain,” that is, from the eminence of virtues, striving toward perfection. The mountain is Gilead, that is, the place where there is a heap of testimony. For the saints do not keep their virtues silent, but bring forth manifold testimony to Christ. Gilead is called “heap of testimony” because Jacob and his uncle Laban built there a heap of stones as a testimony, as it were, of their peace.

“**Your teeth**,” namely those fixed in the cheeks and through which food is crushed, are those saints who break down the Scriptures and render them intelligible to those below. Such persons are like flocks of shorn sheep: flocks, because they are many; shorn, because, as a sheep in shearing puts off its old covering, so they have put off all their oldness. They “have come up from the washing”: the saints indeed rise to virtues from the washing of baptism. And all, in their greater part—eyes, head, and teeth alike—beget children for God from both peoples, namely Jewish and Gentile. “All bear twins,” because each has faith and works.

“**Your lips are like a scarlet thread.**” The office of a thread or band is to bind the hair around the head. Thus the lips—that is, the preachers through whom God speaks—bind the hair to Christ, [Col. 1206C] lest it fall away from the head. They are called scarlet because of the redness of the Lord’s Passion. Or by hair may be understood thoughts, which depend from the mind and adorn it. These thoughts are restrained through the preaching of the divine word and bound around the mind.

“**Your speech**,” that is, your teaching, is sweet and nourishing like milk.

“**Like a fragment of pomegranate.**” The pomegranate is red outwardly, but when broken, white appears within. So your cheeks—that is, those more perfect saints, inwardly like teeth—are outwardly worn down by many persecutions and are despised by the world. Yet, when known inwardly, they are found white with many virtues, apart from that which lies hidden within, namely their intention, which is far more beautiful.

“**Your neck is like the tower of David.**” The neck signifies the saints through whom the Scriptures descend to those below; they also possess the other offices of the neck. They are like a tower, that is, a defence for others fleeing to them, in which the true David dwells and serves. This tower is “built with battlements,” that is, with firm and excellent interpretations, by which they drive away attacking enemies from afar.

The thousand shields remain around the neck: they possess these battlements. Those who go forth to war receive from those who are the neck all the interpretations by which to protect themselves—this is what is meant by the thousand shields. They also receive other interpretations by which they may conquer and draw others to themselves: this is what follows, “all the armour of mighty men.”

“**Your two breasts**,” that is, your preachers, in whom holy teaching is contained from the Gentile and Jewish peoples; or even those peoples themselves, nourished by teaching, “are like two twin fawns of a gazelle”: that is, they possess the virtues of the fawn and the gazelle, and are twins, namely alike and agreeing in the same teaching. Or the two breasts may be taken as the two Testaments, which are now no longer said to disagree with one another. Or this may be said of all the foregoing things.

They “feed,” that is, are refreshed and delight themselves, “among the lilies,” namely in the brightness and sweet fragrance of good works, until the day breathes, namely eternal blessedness, and the shadows decline, that is, until these ignorances pass away.

> “I will go to the mountain of myrrh  
> and to the hills of frankincense.  
> You are altogether beautiful, my friend,  
> and there is no blemish in you.  
> Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon,  
> come; you shall be crowned  
> from the summit of Amana,  
> from the peak of Senir and Hermon,  
> from the dens of lions,  
> from the mountains of leopards.  
> You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride;  
> you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes  
> and with one lock of your neck.  
> How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!  
> Your breasts are more beautiful than wine,  
> and the fragrance of your ointments above all spices.  
> Your lips, bride, drip honeycomb;  
> honey and milk are under your tongue,  
> and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.  
> A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride;  
> a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.  
> Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates  
> with fruits of orchards:  
> cypress with nard,  
> nard and saffron,  
> sweet cane and cinnamon with all the woods of Lebanon,  
> myrrh and aloes with [Col. 1207C] all the finest ointments.  
> A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters  
> which flow impetuously from Lebanon.  
> Arise, north wind, and come, south wind;  
> blow through my garden,  
> and let its spices flow.”

“‘I will go to the mountain of myrrh’: as though the Bridegroom himself were saying, ‘Such are your members; and beyond this I shall make all things better, by bestowing and multiplying grace.’ This is what he says: ‘I will go,’ that is, I shall bestow grace upon the mountain of myrrh and the hills of incense. By the mountain of myrrh we understand the martyrs; by the hills of incense, the confessors, who offer the Lord the sweet fragrance of prayers. And deservedly will I do this for you, because you are wholly beautiful, and no stain—that is, no grievous sin—is in you. And because you are such, come to me from Lebanon, that is, from the good work accomplished in life [Col. 1207D]; come according to the soul, namely, as the soul departs from the body. Come from Lebanon, because the brightness of virtues and good works lead it to God. Come by resuming the body in the general resurrection; and then you shall be crowned, that is, you shall receive the reward of victories.

You shall be crowned in body and soul from the summit of Amana, that is, from the chief men among those in whom the devil keeps watch, that he may tear some to pieces. For *Amana* is interpreted “tooth of watchings.” And you shall be crowned from the peak of Sanir, that is, from the rulers of those who deceive people through certain ignorances and follies. *Sanir* is interpreted “night-bird”; by this we understand ignorance and those who deceive secretly. And with these you shall be crowned from Hermon: that is, you shall convert some who were Hermon [Col. 1208A], that is, anathema, which means separation. You will call back to the Lord such persons as were no longer merely said to be separated, but were separation itself from God.

I say that you shall be crowned from the dens—that is, from those in whom the lion, namely the openly raging devil, lies and rests. And this is the sense: you shall receive a reward both for open persecutions and for those mentioned above; and you shall be crowned from the mountains of leopards, that is, from heretics whom you also convert from enemies. They are called mountains because of their excessive pride; leopards because they are marked by diverse sects and heresies, as a leopard is by various spots.

“‘You have wounded my heart.’ I say, ‘Come; you shall be crowned,’ because I love you greatly; and this is what I mean: you have wounded my heart with your love. He calls her sister because, according to his humanity, she is of the same nature, and through the grace of adoption she is a co-heir of the kingdom [Col. 1208B], as St Paul teaches (Rom. 8; Gal. 4). I say, ‘You have wounded my heart’: the repetition arises from the overwhelming intensity of love. You have wounded me, I say, in one of your eyes: that is, because those eyes which are in you are united in contemplating and seeking me as one; likewise those which are your hairs. You have also wounded my heart because your breasts—that is, your teaching, which is nourishing milk—are beautiful: they sweetly nourish peoples unto God. Your breasts—that is, your very teaching—are more beautiful than wine, that is, than all worldly wisdom, which intoxicates and makes its possessors proud. And the fragrance—that is, the good repute of the spiritual graces which are in you—surpasses all spices, that is, all earthly ointments.

Therefore, Bride, you have wounded my heart, because your lips—that is [Col. 1208C], the holy preachers through whom you speak—are a honeycomb, that is, a vessel containing honey, namely most sweet teaching. They do not deny it to others, but are a dripping honeycomb, because by their word they provide nourishment to others. Beneath your tongue—that is, in the hidden place of your heart; for what is there is said to be beneath the tongue because it is made manifest by the tongue—are honey and milk, nourishing children and adults alike. By milk, which is the food of children, we understand the teaching by which the lesser are instructed. By honey, which children do not wish to taste, nor touch in even a small amount from their mother’s breasts, though adults gladly eat it, we understand the teaching by which the greater are fed.

Or otherwise, honey and milk—that is, these bodily foods—are beneath your tongue, that is, inferior and less worthy [Col. 1208D] than your tongue, namely the spiritual teaching which is in your tongue. And the fragrance of your ointments, that is, the good repute of your works by which you cover shameful parts, is like the fragrance of incense: that is, it is as pleasing to God as the good devotion in the prayers of the saints. For these two things, prayers and good works, please God together in a person; one does not please him without the other.

“‘A garden enclosed.’ Thus, together with the things already mentioned, you have wounded my heart because you are properly a garden: that is, producing diverse kinds of virtues, in which I delight and am fed, just as a garden produces diverse kinds of herbs. I say, a garden enclosed: that is, fortified and fenced with faith and works, so that no entrance into you is ever open to enemies and thieves. You are also a sealed fountain. The Church is called a fountain because all who belong to the Church are washed from it by baptism [Col. 1209A]. Or it is a fountain because the Church itself has within it divine wisdom, from which many waters flow, namely many teachings.

His saying “garden” twice arose from the excessive affection of one who loves; or by this he indicates a garden from the Jews and a garden from the Gentiles. “Your offshoots”: he has called her a garden; now he sets forth what kind of fruit this garden produces, namely pomegranates and similar things. This is what he says: “Your offshoots,” that is, those whom you beget for God, are pomegranates: that is, red and ready for every persecution, together with fruits of apples, that is, with ripe fruits. By these we understand those saints who, although they are not devoted to sufferings, nevertheless perform ripe works, by whose fragrance God is refreshed. Such fruits are to me a paradise, that is, delights; for God delights in such persons [Col. 1209B] as someone delights in paradise.

Again, your offshoots are henna with nard. Henna is a slender shrub which grows to great height and bears grains from which royal ointment is made; and it has nard with it, which is a lowly herb. By henna we understand saints who rise to great heights of virtue and bring forth grains, that is, good works by which God is anointed and delighted; and they are always joined to humility, signified by nard. Again, your offshoots are nard with saffron. Saffron is a herb bearing a golden flower, by which divine wisdom is understood; this ought not to exist in anyone without fear, but with nard, that is, with humility.

Your offshoots are also reed and cinnamon together. Reed is a herb with red bark and is particularly effective in cleansing swellings of the lungs; cinnamon is of a humble colour, namely ash-grey. By reed we understand those who keep the Lord’s Passion in memory, which removes swellings from their hearts; and they make themselves humble and comparable to ashes, presuming nothing of themselves but attributing everything to God’s goodness. I speak of your offshoots: these, with all the trees of Lebanon—that is, together with the persons mentioned above you send forth all the trees, namely all who are strong and robust enough to bear the burden of the Church, who are Lebanon, that is, bright in virtues.

Your offshoots are also myrrh and aloe: that is, those who endure greater and lesser persecutions. Aloe is less bitter than myrrh. Or, by myrrh let us understand martyrial suffering. By aloe [Col. 1209D], bitter to the taste but healing when received inwardly, let us understand the mortification of the flesh by vigils, fasts, and similar practices. Though these seem burdensome and unbearable to perform, they nevertheless heal the soul inwardly. “With all the chief ointments”: that is, all are chief ointments, namely spiritual gifts, which are chief and worthier than all carnal ointments. Or, by chief ointments let us understand charity, which is first among all virtues.

He has shown the fruits; now he explains from where the garden itself receives irrigation. It is as though he said: in the garden there is a fountain, namely baptism or divine wisdom: a fountain, I say, of gardens, irrigating the garden from the Jews and the garden from the Gentiles. It is not a fountain which can quickly be exhausted, but is a well, that is, lofty and deep; for the more divine wisdom is investigated [Col. 1210A], the deeper it is found. Deep are the things signified in baptism. I say, a well of waters from which waters flow. Waters indeed flow from divine wisdom, washing and making souls clean. Waters also flow from baptism, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit received in baptism. I mean waters of life, that is, enlivening souls, which run for the correction of those below from Lebanon, that is, from the greater and perfect persons who are bright in virtues. They flow, I say, not sparingly but abundantly and impetuously.

“‘Arise, north wind.’” It is as though he said: my garden ought to produce such fruits; and, lest its fruit perish, arise, north wind—that is, you devil—and flee. The north wind freezes trees because it is cold, in order to destroy their fruit. So the devil constricts and freezes [Col. 1210B] by removing charity from human hearts, lest they bring forth the fruit of good works for God. I say, arise, north wind; and come, south wind, that is, warm wind, namely the Holy Spirit, conferring the fervour of charity. Breathe through my garden, removing the freezing of unbelief and inspiring love of God; and thus may its spices flow, that is, its fruits, the fragrant offerings of good works.

Or otherwise: because my beloved is such a garden and ought to produce fruits of this sort, therefore arise, you north wind—that is, devil—and stir her; and you, south wind, Holy Spirit, revive her with your mild breeze. And both of you breathe through my garden. For the north wind, stirring the trees, makes them bud, so that the south wind which follows may cause them to bring forth fruit. So persecution, followed by the fervour of charity through the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1210C], causes the Church to bear fruit.

## Chapter V

“‘Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple-trees.’ ‘I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, dearly beloved.’”

“Let my beloved come”: the voice of the Bride herself from the Gentiles. The Church, observing that Christ had thus commended her, calling her a garden and the like, and had also commanded the south wind to breathe through her, prays that he himself may come—that is, by multiplying his grace in her. It is as though she said: “Because I ought to produce such fruit [Col. 1210D], which I can never produce by myself, let him come; that is, let him multiply his grace in me, which is his coming; and thus let him eat, that is, be satisfied with good fruits, namely the works of his own people.” I mean fruits which are fruit, not blossom: let him delight in their ripe and perfect works.

“I have come into my garden”: the Bridegroom’s voice to the Church. “You pray that I may come into the garden, but I have already come; that is, by bestowing and multiplying grace, I have visited my Church.” This is what he says: “I have come into my garden; and from this my garden I have gathered my myrrh,” that is, I have collected and stored in secret places myrrh, namely the holy martyrs whom I have gathered, “with my spices,” that is, my spices, namely my confessors, in whose prayers I delight [Col. 1211A], as someone delights in good fragrances. “I have eaten,” that is, I have readily and delightfully received and stored those who were a honeycomb with honey, that is, thus dripping with most sweet teaching: namely, I have gathered certain preachers.

Or otherwise: I have gathered myrrh and others who were ripe; those who were not yet ripe I led to perfection, so that they might produce fruit for me. This is “I have eaten”: that is, I have brought certain persons into my body, making them my honeycomb. “I have drunk wine”: that is, in like manner I have brought into my body some who were wine, fervent in faith and truth and intoxicating others by teaching, together with my milk—that is, with my simple people, who are nourished with milk, namely the teaching of faith, and do not hold lofty opinions. These I have drunk: that is, I have incorporated them into myself delightfully and without labour. Or “I have drunk” because I have assumed such ripe persons into blessedness.

“Eat”: again the Bridegroom’s voice to his friends. He exhorts them, after unbelief has been removed through him, because some are still lukewarm and sluggish, to labour among them and remove the ignorances of their hearts. Here is indicated the state of the Church in these present times, in which preaching is more faithfully carried out. It is as though he said: “I have eaten some and drunk; and you, my friends, eat and drink,” that is, delight in those who through your preaching have abandoned evil works and ignorances. He speaks of eating in relation to those who must be crushed and won with labour; of drinking in relation to those who readily comply. I say, drink and be intoxicated: that is, through the overwhelming delight of correcting them, like persons drunk, abandon every temporal care and forget all your persecution, so that you may render them pure to God [Col. 1211C].

“‘I sleep, but my heart keeps watch. The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one; for my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night. I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch. I arose to open to my beloved. My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh. I opened the bolt of my door for my beloved, but he had turned aside and passed on.’”

“I sleep”: the voice of the Church. It is as though she said: “You command us [Col. 1211D] to labour and preach for the building up of others; but I sleep,” that is, I have given myself to tranquility of mind, sleeping and ceasing from worldly anxieties. “Yet my heart watches,” that is, my reason, intent only upon God, contemplates heavenly things, just as a good beloved, even while sleeping, dreams of her beloved.

“The voice of my beloved”: I say that I sleep, but I must interrupt my rest, because there is a voice, that is, an admonition of my beloved, knocking—that is, through many signs and sayings of saints urging me to preach—by these words: “Open to me,” that is, by preaching make the hearts of others open to me, namely to my honour, so that I may have my dwelling in them. I said, “Open to me,” and it is necessary, because “my head,” that is, certain prelates in my Church, are full: that is, they possess an abundance of fortified ignorances [Col. 1212A], signified by the dew which falls in the night.

Or “my head” means that I myself am in them, full of dew; and “my locks.” Locks are twisted hairs that cling badly to the head; by them are signified those who, although they belong to the Church, twist themselves away and evade the divine commandments. Thus, in withdrawing from the head, they are full of drops, that is, great errors of the nights, because those errors arise from the darkness of ignorance.

“I have taken off”: the Bridegroom admonishes me thus; but how shall I resume temporal care, so as to provide food and similar things for those under correction, when I have already divested myself of all these matters? This is what she says: “I have taken off my tunic,” that is, I have laid aside all temporal concerns which I carried while girded in a tunic. “I have washed my feet,” that is, by the tears of devout compunction I have cleansed [Col. 1212B] even the daily and slight faults which, like dust, cling to our affections. “How shall I defile them?” Yet preachers must sometimes assume the bearing and actions of an angry person in order to correct certain sins more easily; and in such zeal they seem to defile their consciences. Nevertheless, because by this means they gain some for God, they receive a manifold reward from God.

“My beloved”: I said, “How shall I become entangled in secular cares by preaching to others?” But I must do it, because when the Lord inspires them and shows them ready to receive, how could I refuse my office? This is what she says. “My beloved put,” that is, inspired those beneath me with, “his hand,” that is, his aid and working: namely, how he himself acted, in what things they ought to imitate him, and how he aids those who desire to act according to him. And he did this “through the opening,” that is, by visiting them secretly. “At his touch,” that is, at the inspiration of his Passion and of the other things he did, and of his help, “my inward parts trembled”: that is, one trembled within oneself, grieving for past deeds and desiring instruction in better things.

“I arose”: the Bride’s voice expressing her obedience. It is as though she said: “Those beneath me have now trembled through his inspiration; therefore I arose, ceasing for a time from the rest of contemplation and resuming the labour of preaching, that I might open the hearts of others to a perfect knowledge of God. And immediately my hands,” that is, my works, “dripped with myrrh,” that is, became bitter. For preachers must show in themselves [Col. 1212D] the mortification of the flesh which they proclaim that others must practise. No preacher declares that the flesh, which is the fuel of sin, should be nourished. “My fingers,” that is, certain of my distinct works, “are full of the first myrrh”: that is, they display the greatest mortifications of the flesh, both in preaching and in offering the example of themselves.

“I opened to my beloved,” that is, I prepared the hearts of others for the knowledge of God; and I did this by removing the bolt from the door. By the door we understand ignorances and blindnesses which block hearts, so that they do not advance to good action. We call the bolt the cause by which someone is kept in such ignorance: for example, when someone delights in worldly things and offers the excuse that he supports his widowed mother. “But he had turned aside”: I say that I opened the door, but before I had opened it, he had turned aside, that is, had manifested himself to them. Here he touches upon the goodness of God: once someone begins to wish for him, God himself is ready to help and to render a reward for his gifts. I say that he had turned aside, but “he had passed on,” that is, he had shown himself incomprehensible to them [Col. 1213A].

“‘My soul melted when my beloved spoke. I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me. The watchmen who went about the city found me; they struck and wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my cloak.’”

“My soul”: the voice of those beneath, whom he above called the inward parts; or the voice of the Church correcting, but in the person of the corrected one. Thus she says: “My beloved visited me by putting his hand through the opening and admonished me through his preachers; therefore my soul,” that is, my reason and understanding, “melted,” that is, was enlightened by the heat of the Holy Spirit and separated from the hardness of unbelief, when my beloved spoke—that is, after I heard God’s voice and admonition. I said that he had turned aside and passed on; and because he passed on, I sought him, that is, I laboured to attain his perfect knowledge, “and did not find him.” I called, that is, I sent forth prayers that he might perfectly reveal himself to me; “and he did not answer me,” that is, I did not obtain the fulfilment of my calling.

While I sought thus, the true shepherds, whom he calls watchmen because they apply watchfulness and diligence to guard their flocks and acquire others for God, found me [Col. 1213B]: that is, they perceived my affection. They went around the city: that is, they carefully examined each person in order to correct the ignorances of those who wandered. I say that they found me and struck me: that is, they moved me to compunction through grief and the remembrance of past things. They wounded me with love of God. The keepers of the walls—that is, the greater persons, such as bishops, who guard those who are walls and a defence for others, namely bishops and similar persons whom we above called watchmen—took away my cloak: that is, they removed from me every covering of error [Col. 1213C].

“‘I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love. What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest of women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us? My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.’”

“I adjure you”: the one newly introduced now speaks and urges her companions to help her seek him. This is what she means when she says: “If you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love,” so that, knowing my love and affection, he may fully reveal himself to me.

“What is your beloved?” The voice of one urged to seek. It is as though she said: “You ask me to seek and tell you, but first make known by what signs I may recognize your beloved.” This is what she says: “What is your beloved, according to divinity, more than a beloved? What is your beloved, according to humanity?” I ask what he is like because I hear that he is wonderful; this is why you have thus adjured us.

“My beloved” [Col. 1214A]: the voice of the one who had just urged others to seek and tell her of her beloved. She describes certain things concerning him, so that they may imitate such a one and understand one far loftier. This is what she says: “My beloved is white,” that is, made white by many virtues; “and ruddy” because of the Passion; “chosen from among thousands,” that is, from among all things, because among all things nothing better could be found by which the human race might be redeemed.

“‘His head is finest gold. His locks are like the uplifted branches of palms, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and resting beside full-flowing waters. His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers; his lips are lilies dripping with the first myrrh [Col. 1214B]. His hands are rounded gold, full of hyacinths. His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires. His legs are columns of marble, founded upon golden bases. His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as cedars. His throat is most sweet, and he is wholly desirable. Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem. Where has your beloved gone, O fairest of women? Where has your beloved turned aside, that we may seek him with you?’”

“His head”: he now describes him according to humanity; now he shows him according to the other part, that is, according to divinity. “His head,” that is, the divinity which is the head of the Lord’s human being, “is finest gold”: that is, the excellent and perfect divine wisdom of God by which he made all things.

“His locks,” that is, those joined to the head, subtle and slender, “are like uplifted” branches—that is, always stretching upwards. The branches of the palm that come forth at the summit and always direct themselves aloft are called uplifted, and victors carry them. Thus he fittingly compares the hairs of Christ to them, for they are true victors. Such locks are black [Col. 1214C], that is, despised by the world, “as a raven”: that is, talkative and chattering like a raven.

Or otherwise: they are like ravens because it is the raven’s nature not to feed its young until they are black, that is, like itself. Meanwhile little flies come to their mouths because of a certain stench, and they devour them. So the saints are unwilling to feed anyone with spiritual food whom they do not see made like themselves: that is, renouncing the devil and obedient to the Catholic faith.

“His eyes,” that is, those who penetrate the Scriptures with subtle insight and provide foresight for others, “are like doves beside streams and beside full-flowing waters.” It is the dove’s nature to nest or build beside water, so that it may refresh itself there and see the shadow of a kite or hawk there, enabling it to escape. So the saints remain beside waters, that is, the divine Scriptures, that they may be refreshed from them and there provide for their own safety against the devil’s snares. By streams we understand lesser teachings, such as expositions and sermons of the saints. By full-flowing waters we understand the teaching of the Gospels, in which the complete correction of humankind is contained. He calls the doves “washed with milk” because those faithful persons whom he calls eyes are purified and cleansed by milk, that is, sweet and pleasant teaching, and by the love of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1215A].

“His cheeks,” that is, those higher saints who grind the Scriptures and render them intelligible to those below, “are like beds,” that is, land well cultivated and planted by God himself. I mean beds of spices: that is, from which the most sweet fragrances of prayers and works are offered to God. These beds, that is, these saints, are planted by perfumers: that is, by the holy apostles and prophets, who build them up and plant them by their teaching. They are called perfumers because they grind everything down, reducing it to humility, just as perfumers grind spices into powder.

“His lips,” that is, the preachers through whom he speaks, “are dripping,” that is, proclaiming, “myrrh,” that is, mortifications of the flesh. For no preacher teaches that the flesh should be nourished. He says “the first” because the flesh ought above all to be mortified: the more the flesh is mortified, the stronger the spirit becomes.

“His hands,” that is, workers even in secular occupations—called his hands because God works also in such persons—are “rounded,” that is, smooth and gentle, so that God is not offended in them. They are golden, that is, working by divine wisdom; they are also full of hyacinths, that is, of heaven. For good manual workers are wholly intent upon heavenly things and know how to work by divine wisdom. By hyacinth we signify heaven, which is sky-coloured.

“His belly,” that is, the softer part of the Church, such as married persons who use the world more freely, is ivory: that is, chaste. For the elephant is of a cold nature, and thus by ivory we signify chastity. Ivory is so cold in nature that a cloth laid upon ivory is not burned by a coal [Col. 1215C]. I say, a belly adorned with sapphires: that is, at times intent upon heavenly things. Married persons must at times attend to the concerns of their wives, but at other times also persist in contemplation; the Apostle calls such persons divided (1 Cor. 7). By sapphire, which is sky-coloured, we understand heaven.

“His legs,” that is, those who are near the last times—those who bear him and proclaim him in these final times—are columns: that is, supporters of others, silvery, shining and resounding with the brightness of divine speech, founded upon golden bases, that is, upon the apostles and prophets, who are golden because full of charity and wisdom.

“His appearance is like Lebanon.” It is as though he said: “Why should I enumerate each thing?” His appearance—that is, he himself altogether, head and body—is like Lebanon: bright and fragrant. “Chosen,” that is, Christ himself in his own person, “as a cedar,” because just as the cedar is the noblest of all other trees, so Christ surpasses all human beings; and as it is incorruptible and kills worms with its fragrance, so Christ does this spiritually. “His throat,” that is, his inward word, namely the meaning of his words, is most sweet to all who receive it. What more need be said? He is wholly desirable. Behold, I have described to you what my beloved is like, daughters of Jerusalem, so that you also, knowing him as such, may cling firmly to him; and you ought to believe me about him, because he is my friend, that is, familiar and well known to me [Col. 1216A].

“Where has he gone?” Again, the voice of those urged to seek. Having heard his qualities, they inquire, as it were, for the place and land in which to seek him, just as worldly female friends speak with one another and one urges another to help seek her beloved. Thus they say: “O fairest of women,” that is, among all women, namely philosophers, who are called women because they nourish others in their sects. Fairest, I say, tell me where he has gone: that is, under what place may I find him? This is said with reference to his being incomprehensible according to his own essence. “Where has he turned aside?” is said with reference to those things which can be known about him. It is as though they said: “Tell me who those are in whom God dwells and to whom God grants knowledge of himself.” And why do we ask? Because, behold, we shall seek him with you [Col. 1216B]. Great affection is indicated among those who thus invite one another to seek the knowledge of God.

## Chapter VI

“‘My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, that he may feed in the gardens and gather lilies. I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine; he who feeds among the lilies.’”

“My beloved”: the voice of those inviting others to seek God. Thus they say: “You ask where my beloved has turned aside; behold, I announce to you that he is known in his Church and dwells there.” This is what he says: “He has gone down into his garden,” that is, from the kinship of angels he humbly lowered himself, taking flesh, as far as human knowledge. He went down [Col. 1216C], I say, to the bed: that is, to those who are a bed, namely well-cultivated land, planted according to God’s will. I mean a bed of spices: those who offer to God the sweet fragrance of prayers and works. He went down in order that he might feed and delight in the gardens, that is, in the faithful of his Church, and gather lilies: that is, assume and store in his secret places lilies, namely those bright in virtues. Or he gathers and draws certain persons into his Church and makes them lilies, that is, bright with every virtue.

“I am my beloved’s.” And you should again believe me concerning this, because I obey my beloved as far as I can and am closely familiar with him; therefore my beloved is present to me, offering his help and his knowledge, he who feeds and delights among the lilies [Col. 1216D].

“‘You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps. Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me flee. Your hair is like a flock of goats which have appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of sheep which have come up from the washing. All bear twins, and none among them is barren. As the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks apart from your hidden parts. There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and young women without number. One is my dove, my perfect one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her. The daughters of Zion saw her and called her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her.’”

[Col. 1217A] “You are beautiful”: the Bridegroom’s voice. Christ, hearing the Church’s affection, therefore commends her, saying, “You are beautiful, my beloved,” and so forth. He calls her beautiful because she has so great a desire to know him; sweet because she invites others to the same thing and does not begrudge her Bridegroom other beloveds; lovely because of her works. “As Jerusalem,” that is, as beautiful as heavenly Jerusalem and as lovely as your mother, namely that Church which begot and nourished you. You are terrible to enemies as an army’s battle-line, because I wage war in you and you fight in my service, as fighting is done in camps; and you are ordered by the instruction of the saints.

“Turn away your eyes.” You are so worthy of praise; nevertheless, cease thinking that you now believe, so that you may attain to perfect knowledge of me. This is what he says: “Turn away your eyes,” that is, the understanding which you exercise toward my full knowledge, or those very eyes which gaze more subtly, “for they have made me fly away,” that is, separate from every human knowledge. For the more subtly and profoundly someone investigates God, the loftier and more incomprehensible he knows him to be [Col. 1217B].

Now, because he said, “Turn away your eyes,” lest she complain that she is less worthy than her mother, namely Jerusalem, he commends her as he had earlier commended her mother, saying, “Your hair,” and so forth. I said, “Turn away your eyes”; yet you have eyes and the rest, equally beautiful as that Church which preached you. He did not say that she should turn away her eyes because it is sinful to wish fully to know God; rather, it is sinful to suppose that one can attain this.

“There are sixty queens.” Queens or wives are called all those in the holy Church who beget children for God from love of God alone, not from hope of worldly gain. Concubines, however, are those who preach not from love of God but for the sake of temporal advantage, yet nevertheless beget good children for God. Concubines are cast out from the house of the father of the household, but their children are retained. The young women are those who are begotten. He says this because of these beauties: you have queens and the rest, who are said to be sixty. By sixty, which is made from ten and six, we understand those perfect in the ten commandments of the Law through the six works of mercy. By eighty, which is made from eight and ten, we understand those who, although they somewhat keep and preach the ten commandments, are nevertheless occupied with worldly affairs. Eighty, when understood negatively [Col. 1217D], signifies temporal cares and entanglements, because the course of the age is conducted through four seasons and the world itself is divided by four quarters—east, west, north, and south. Concubines, therefore, are those who proclaim Christ out of love for temporal things.

“One is my dove.” Since he has spoken of so many members of the Church, someone might think that discord, and never unity, is found in the Church. Removing this thought, he says: although I have named so many parts of the Church, she herself is nevertheless one, that is, one in faith; and she is one to her mother, that is, one as her mother is, namely the Church which nourished and educated her with sweet teaching. And she is one to her begetter: that is, as her begetter is, and as those preachers who converted her. “Mother” is understood with respect to instruction; “begetter” with respect to conversion. And because she is such, as has been made clear by all the foregoing, all the other daughters who saw her marvelled at her; and queens and concubines called her most blessed because of her glory to come, and praised her, queens and concubines alike, for her virtues in this present life [Col. 1218A].

“‘Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps?’”

What is this? The voice of the Jews who, seeing so great an advance of the Churches among the Gentiles, begin to be moved to compunction and, in admiration rather than envy, say: “What is this?”—that is, of what kind and how great is she—who goes forth [Col. 1218B] like the dawn; that is, she is spread abroad over the earth like the rising dawn. In her some are like the moon, that is, enlightening those in darkness; some like the sun, that is, enlightening even certain persons already bright; and some in her are terrible to enemies, some are battle-lines of camps, namely, fortified by the rampart of faith and arrayed with many virtues.

> “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to examine whether the vine had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded. I did not know. My soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab. Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may behold you.”

I went down. The voice of the Bridegroom, answering the Jews in this manner: “You ask what she is? She is indeed my beloved and the garden into which I went down.” A garden of nuts, because [Col. 1218C] in the nut there is bitterness on the outside; within, a certain fragile shell; and inside, a sweet kernel. In the same way, the saints outwardly endure many bitter trials in the body, which is a fragile shell; but inwardly there is what is most sweet, namely the soul adorned with many virtues. “I went down,” I say, “to see,” that is, to test and to grant the help of grace to those who are fruits—that is, who offer to God mature works—and who are valleys, that is, humble persons; “and to examine.” God’s examining is the conferring of grace and the testing of believers: whether the vines—that is, those upon whom great cultivation is bestowed—had blossomed, that is, had produced the beginnings of virtues; and whether the pomegranates—that is, those who show themselves ready for every suffering—had budded, that is, had gained some [Col. 1218D] fruit for God.

“I did not know.” The voice of the Jews moved to compunction: “You say that she is your beloved, and you examine her by bestowing spiritual gifts on her. Yet I did not know, because my soul—that is, the knowledge which I possessed in the Law according to the carnal understanding—troubled me; that is, it rendered me disturbed and estranged from the knowledge of God because of the chariots of Aminadab, namely the four Gospels of Christ, which seem to me to destroy the Law that I had formerly received.” Aminadab is interpreted “the Lord’s willing one,” or “for the people”; by him Christ is signified, who willingly offered himself to God, and this for the redemption of the people. By the chariots borne on four wheels we understand the Gospel, borne throughout the whole world by the four Evangelists.

[Col. 1219A] “Return, return.” The voice of the Church from the Gentiles. She recognizes the error of the Jews and urges them to conversion. She says “return” four times because she calls them back from the four parts of the world. She calls her the Shulammite, that is, one taken captive by the devil into Babylon—that is, into the confusion of vices. There was indeed a certain Shulammite taken captive in Babylon. “Return,” I say, “that we may behold you,” that is, that we may behold our own life in you; or that we may marvel at you because of your exceeding goodness.

## CHAPTER VII

> “What will you see in the Shulammite but the dances of camps? How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince! The joining of your thighs is like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan. Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups. Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies. Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a doe. Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus. Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like royal purple bound in channels. How beautiful you are and how lovely, dearest one, in delights! Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters.”

“What will you see?” The voice of Christ, urging the Church of the Gentiles to labour for the conversion of the Jews, because her labour and preaching will not be useless. As if he said: “You ask her to return; you must not cease from doing so, because you will see in the Shulammite—that is, in the Jews, captive to the devil—dances, that is, persons singing and chanting to the Lord: dances, I say, of camps, in which God wages war and which are well fortified.”

“How beautiful!” Again he urges the Church from the Gentiles to preach to the Jews for another reason: namely, because it will be very profitable, and this final Church, in which converted Jews will be found, will yield great fruit for God. Yet it is not said that all Jews will finally be converted, but the greater part. Therefore labour, Church of the Gentiles, for the conversion of the Jews, because those steps of yours—that is, the last believers, who will bear you and your teaching—will be exceedingly beautiful: beautiful [Col. 1219C] in sandals, that is, in mortification of the flesh, because sandals are made from dead animals; or “in sandals,” that is, in the apostles and other saints, by whose examples and authority the last believers will be protected, as feet by sandals. “Daughter of a prince,” that is, of God.

Or this may be the voice of Christ, by apostrophe, addressed to the Jews themselves. “The joining of your thighs,” that is, the uniting of the two peoples, is like necklaces, because they both fortify and admonish others: those who consider their beauty and the spiritual gifts flourishing in them will desire to cleave to them. They fortify subjects against the devil’s snares and teach them chastity. These necklaces are fashioned by the power and operation of the supreme Artisan, that is, God himself.

“Your navel.” In this part of the belly a woman has the seedbed of generation; and by this part, which is in the belly, we understand those who, though among the carnal—for example, married persons—nevertheless have the seedbed of preaching and of begetting children for God. Such persons are a bowl, that is, drinking and making others drunk with love for God. A bowl “rounded,” that is, so fashioned according to God’s will that God’s hand finds in it no offence; a bowl that never lacks cups, because such saints will never lack the teaching by which they may give others to drink. Or such holy preachers are called the navel because, as the navel is in the middle of the belly, so they are in the midst of the people, preaching and reconciling them to God.

“Your belly,” that is, that softer part of the Church, who do not beget others, is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies. He calls it a heap because many such persons are in the Church; wheat because such persons too are sweet and delightful food [Col. 1220B] for God, and are surrounded—that is, well fortified—by lilies, namely virtues. “Your two breasts,” that is, preachers: breasts, namely vessels of milk, that is, of teaching which sweetly nourishes. Such men are fawns because they are light and swift in running, not weighed down by the burden of flesh. He calls them twins because, as twin brothers, though distinct, are nevertheless alike, so these two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, will be alike, because they will both follow and teach the same instruction of the Law. They are “of a doe” because they will possess the virtues of a doe.

“Your neck,” that is, those who in the final Church will perform the office of a neck, will be like a tower because those fleeing to them will find defence; “ivory” because of chastity. “Your eyes,” that is, those holy persons who foresee and subtly contemplate the depth of the Scriptures, [Col. 1220C] are like pools—that is, waters refreshing by the teaching of God’s word all who thirst. “In Heshbon,” which is interpreted “girdle of sorrow,” are those saints who are called eyes and waters; and they are in Heshbon because they are always girded with sorrow for their own sins and those of others. These pools—that is, teachings—are “at the gate,” that is, ready for the refreshment of the daughter of the multitude, namely many children. They are as if at a gate, because they stand ready to refresh with spiritual water all who wish to approach.

“Your nose.” In the nose is the discernment of good and bad smell; by it are signified those who possess discernment of good and evil, so that they distinguish those of good will and instruct them, while rejecting those who are pretenders and deceitful. Such persons are a tower of Lebanon: a tower because they provide fitting protection to those who flee to them; of Lebanon because they are made white by virtues. Or they are a tower because, just as a tower is a strong defence, so the saints are not overcome in their discernment, since they are strong: as they are not deceived in their choice so as to judge good evil or evil good. “Which looks toward Damascus.” Damascus was always opposed to Jerusalem, and their citizens carried one another off. Damascus is interpreted “drinking of blood”; by it are signified bloodthirsty persecutors, who inflict persecution or rejoice in others’ evils. Against them the aforesaid saints look, in order to draw some citizens away from them and bring them into their own body.

“Your head,” that is, your mind, or the higher persons in the Church, are like [Col. 1221A] Carmel, that is, possessing knowledge of circumcision. For by the foreskin cut off—where the seat of lust is, and through which all generation proceeds—they understand that every old generation must be cut off from us: namely, the putting away of every defilement, which will at last be perfected in the common resurrection. Carmel is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision.”

“And the hair of your head,” that is, those who most closely cleave to the head of the Church—namely true poor persons, who cleave most closely to Christ—are also as an adornment of the head itself. Such persons are like royal purple, that is, imitators of the Passion of Christ, who is the true King: purple, I say, bound in channels, that is, their suffering is joined to and dependent upon channels, namely thoughts and hearts, so that when they set themselves forward as imitators of Christ’s Passion, this may not be merely outward but inward also. The channels are those vessels in which purple cloths are dyed; and as purple is dyed better if it clings well to the channel, so these persons are better conformed to Christ’s Passion if, in outward and inward things alike, they show themselves compassionate in suffering.

“How beautiful.” Why speak of each part? You are wholly beautiful according to inward virtues, and lovely according to works, “in delights,” that is, in every spiritual refreshment. “Your stature,” that is, your upright direction, is like that of a palm tree. For as the palm always rises upward, so these believers always strive toward the height of virtues. And “your breasts,” that is, your teachings, are like clusters—that is, like wine; for as wine does, so your teachings make men drunk.

> “I said: I will climb the palm tree and take hold of its fruits. And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your mouth like the fragrance of apples. Your throat like the finest wine, worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew. I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me. Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field and lodge in the villages. Let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the blossoms bring forth fruit, whether the pomegranates have flowered. There I shall give you my breasts. The mandrakes gave their fragrance at our gates. All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you.”

“I said: I will climb.” He gives another reason why the Church of the Gentiles ought to preach to the Jews, as if he said: “You ought to preach because your preaching will be profitable and many will be converted: both because those converted will be such worthy and upright persons as has been said, and because I myself came especially to redeem them. Hence it is said in Matthew 15: ‘I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.’” And this he says: “I said,” that is, I disposed from eternity, “I will climb the palm,” that is, the cross, in which a part was said to have been from that tree; or, “the palm,” because there he won victory over the devil and triumphed over the conquest of the world. “I said: I will climb and take hold of its fruits,” that is, they will beget children for me and bring forth good works.

Now the Bridegroom himself turns to her when he says: “And your breasts,” that is, your teachings, are like clusters—not of ivy, but of the vine: sweet to drink [Col. 1222A] and making drunk those who listen to them diligently. “And your fragrances,” that is, the reputation and devotion of your people, are like the fragrances of apples. For as fruits draw some people by their scent, so these persons also draw and join some to themselves by their reputation. Those final Jews will indeed be very good, as the Apostle shows when he says, Romans 2 [cf. Rom. 11:12]: “And if their diminution is the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?” For although not all will be converted, yet the greater part will be converted.

“Your throat,” that is, your inward words, namely the meaning of your words, is like the finest wine: nourishing and making people drunk, so that they forget their entire former life. “Worthy for my beloved.” The voice of the Church, commending those words, which are so worthy that Christ received them from God the Father, as though she said: “I call your throat like the finest wine, and so fine that it is worthy for my beloved—that is, Christ—to drink: that Christ may drink it, that is, without labour and with delight; worthy for lips—that is, preachers—and teeth—that is, stronger persons who grind the Scriptures—to chew, that is, worthy for lips and teeth to chew, namely to grind and labour to understand.”

“I am my beloved’s,” as if she said: “I am to be believed, because I am always intimately present to him through knowledge of his secrets, and he loves me.” This is what she says: “His turning is toward me,” that is, he directs his love toward me.

“Come, my beloved.” Now the Church, having heard Christ’s exhortation and being ready to preach to the Jews, invites the Bridegroom to be with her in that preaching, granting her help. As if she said: “You commanded me to preach to the Jews, but this will profit nothing without your aid. Therefore, my beloved, come—that is, breathe upon them inwardly—and let us go out, that is, proceed beyond the Gentiles into the field, namely to the preaching of those who bear fruit without great labour; and let us lodge in the villages, that is, in their building up and ordering. Let us rise early,” that is, labour diligently, for the diligent rise early for their work.

By vineyards we understand those in whom labour is required before they render fruit. “Let us see whether the vines,” that is, those cultivated with such labour, “have blossomed,” that is, sent forth beginnings of virtues; “whether the flowers,” that is, those in whom the beginnings of virtues already appear, “bring forth fruit,” namely mature works; and let us see whether “the pomegranates,” that is, future martyrs, have yet blossomed. [Col. 1222D] “I said: Come, my beloved”—come with me to those whom you ought indeed to visit with me—“because there I shall give you,” that is, for your honour, “my breasts,” namely my teaching, by which I shall acquire for you excellent children.

“The mandrakes.” I say that there I shall give you my breasts, which I shall well be able to do because the Jews themselves have already given me a good opinion of their conversion, showing themselves fit to receive faith. Mandrakes are plants resembling human limbs without a head; by them are signified the Jews lacking a head, that is, Christ. By gates we understand faith, because it is the gate and entrance for all to salvation.

“All fruits.” I said that I would give you my breasts; this I shall truly do, because I have kept [Col. 1223A] for you—that is, for your honour—the teachings of the New and Old Testaments, by which I shall make some fruits for you; and these teachings are sweetly fragrant and draw listeners sweetly, like fruit.

## CHAPTER VIII

> “Who will give you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you alone outside and kiss you, and no one may henceforth despise me? I shall take hold of you and lead you into my mother’s house and into the chamber of my mother who bore me. There you will teach me, and I shall give you a cup of spiced wine and new wine from my pomegranates. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.”

“Who will give?” Here the effect of the Church’s preaching is shown: the Jews, hearing Christ announced to them [Col. 1223B] and inflamed by love for him, break forth in these words: “Who will give me”—that is, would that someone would announce to me—“my brother,” namely Christ, born from my flesh and sucking the breasts of his mother, that is, nourished by the teaching of the Synagogue.

Now, out of excessive love, she turns to him himself. “Who will give me,” I say, “that I may find you outside,” that is, that I may know you as a man, concerning whom I erred shamefully, “and kiss you,” that is, delight in your humanity now recognized; “and no one will henceforth think me contemptible,” though I was formerly an object of contempt to all. “I shall take hold of you,” that is, we who were formerly separated from you will now cleave to you firmly. “I shall take hold,” I say, “and lead you into my mother’s house,” that is, I shall cause those who now serve the Synagogue to serve Christ; “and into the chamber of my mother who bore me,” that is, I shall make certain persons from the Synagogue such that God may lie and rest in them without offence.

“There,” that is, while I announce you to the children of the Synagogue, “you will teach me,” because I shall open my mouth and you will fill it, as you promised (Ps. 80). “And I shall give you a cup,” that is, I shall convert many Jews for you, who will be to you a cup, namely a delightful drink and refreshment through their good works and many virtues. God thirsts for such a drink, as he himself said on the cross, “I thirst” (John 19), that is, “I bring the human race into my body.” A cup “of spiced wine,” that is, a cup which is wine, namely men warm with love for God and making others drunk with love for God. This wine is “spiced,” that is, made with many spices, namely the diverse virtues [Col. 1223D] of the saints themselves. And I shall give also a cup, namely new wine—wine hot, fervent, and bubbling—by which are signified holy martyrs burning with love of martyrdom. They are also called pomegranates because they are outwardly red by suffering and inwardly white by virtue.

“His left hand”—and rightly ought I to labour to acquire such persons for him, because he bestows consolation upon me both through temporal things and through hope of eternal things.

> “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not stir up or awaken the beloved until she herself wills. Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved? Under the apple tree I raised you up. There your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated. Set me as a seal [Col. 1224A] upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, because love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell.”

“I adjure you.” The voice of the Bridegroom. Christ, hearing the great affection of the Church of the Jews, commends her as he did those above and commands her subjects not to disturb her.

“Who is this?” The voice of the Church from the Gentiles. Seeing her daughter, the Church from the Jews, attain so great a perfection, she rejoices rather than envies and says in admiration: “Who is this who comes up through the steps of virtues from the wilderness and from her unbelief, in which she was deserted by God; abounding in delights,” that is, rich in many virtues; “leaning upon her beloved,” namely Christ, whom she has as the foundation of all right conduct?

“Under the apple tree.” The voice of Christ to that Church from the Jews now converted, commending his love to them. It was fitting, since this whole book concerns the love of God, that at the end of its treatise it should commend love.

Connection: the Church from the Jews leans upon me, her beloved. Therefore, you Church from the Jews, set me upon your heart—that is, as ruler of your heart and thoughts. Or, in another sense, set me “upon,” that is, as suppressor of all your iniquity. Set me, I say, “as a seal,” so that it may be evident to friends that you keep my secrets, and likewise evident to enemies that you do not belong to their party; or so that the secrets you possess may be closed and unknown to them. Or “as a seal”: set me so that you may retain my image in your heart, namely, dispose yourself to become like me in suffering and in all other things according to your measure. And set [Col. 1224C] me upon your arm, that is, upon your action, so that you may have me as guide in all your works. Set me, I say, “as a seal,” so that by those very works it may be evident to friends that you are intimate with me, and so that enemies may understand that you are removed from their life and conduct and from their fellowship.

The cause why they ought to do this was given before, when it was said, “Under the apple tree”; as if he said: “You ought rightly to set me upon your heart, because I delivered you when you were dead in sins.” This he says: “I raised you up when you lay weak beneath the tree,” that is, beneath sin committed through the evil tree, namely in the sin of the first parent. Or: weak beneath the sin of the cross, which likewise was made from this tree, that is, an apple tree. For it is read in Greek books that from the same [Col. 1224D] tree in which Adam sinned a certain branch was brought to Jerusalem; planted there, it grew into a great tree, from which afterward the Lord’s cross was made, so that life might be restored from that from which death had come. Adam too is said to have been buried in the same place where the Lord’s cross was later fixed. “There,” that is, at that tree, “your mother”—that is, the Synagogue—“was corrupted and violated.” By “corrupted” he notes the punishment of sin, in whatever sense, namely the judgment by which, because of the crucifixion of the Lord, the Jews incurred punishment: the destruction inflicted upon them by Titus and Vespasian. When he says “violated,” he denotes the eternal condemnation incurred through that sin by all who did not repent.

This verse may also be connected differently: the Church says to her beloved, “And you ought rightly to love me, because [Col. 1225A] I delivered you from the sin of the first parent.”

“Because love is strong.” Namely, you ought therefore to set me upon your heart because my love is strong as death. For as death cannot be prevented from coming, so God’s love cannot be prevented by any persecution from accomplishing salvation, as Paul demonstrates (Rom. 8). Or, as death destroys bodily senses, so does God’s love: one well occupied by God’s love no longer draws any carnal pleasure from sight or from the other senses. Or “as death,” that is, the devil himself, who is the cause of all death. For as the devil unfailingly brings damnation to his own, so God’s love brings salvation.

“Jealousy,” that is, the affection of love—namely, the concern and burdensome demands upon the flesh required in doing what love commands—is insatiable like hell. For no one in whom love abounds thinks that what he gives, or the other things love requires, are enough; rather, he always wishes to do more.

> “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames. Many waters could not extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it. If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as though it were nothing.”

“Its lamps.” Again he describes the nature of that love, as if he said: “You ought to hasten toward that love, because its lamps,” that is, the ardours of this love, “are like lamps of fire,” that is, the ardours of the Holy Spirit. This is what he means by “fire”: as fire supplies heat, so the Holy Spirit [Col. 1225C] supplies the heat of love. And because there could be fire which did not shine, he adds “and flames,” that is, the lamps of love are such that they also shine: those who possess this love shine for others, because they enlighten others by word and example. We may also understand by lamps those persons in whom love dwells as fire in a lamp.

“Many waters.” He again displays another property of love so that we too may wish to embrace it, as if he said: “Such is love. Neither threats nor small or great persecutions can extinguish this love.” By water we understand threats and similar small tribulations, because they extinguish human loves; by rivers we understand greater adversities.

“If a man should give.” Again he commends this love in order strongly to invite us to preserve it, saying that it is such that, if anyone gives all his substance—that is, all his possessions—and even himself for love, he will judge that substance contemptible [Col. 1225D] in comparison with what he will obtain.

> “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed? If she is a wall, let us build upon it silver battlements. If she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards.”

“Our sister,” says the Bridegroom. The law of love is so weighty; but our sister—that is, the Church from the Jews, called Christ’s sister because she is of the same flesh and co-heir of the kingdom with Christ—having been newly converted, is [Col. 1226A] still little and tender in faith, and has no breasts, that is, no teaching from herself. Therefore, unless we provide her aid, she cannot bear the law of love.

“What shall we do?” The Bridegroom says to his friends: “Because our sister is still little, we must grant her aid. And what shall we do for her on the day when she is to be addressed?” That is, in this present time, in which she must be instructed and addressed so that after this life she may be found worthy to be united with Christ in marriage. “What shall we do?” I say, this: “If she is a wall,” that is, if there are persons in this Church who are a wall and defence for others, “let us build upon it silver battlements,” that is, teachings by which they may know how to defend themselves and assail others; “silver,” that is, sounding with the composition of eloquence—let us make them wise and eloquent. “If she is a door,” that is, if there are persons in this Church who introduce others, “let us fasten it,” that is, add something which will be for their honour. Let us fasten it, I say, “with boards,” that is, let us join to them persons who are boards, namely subtle persons, richly endowed according to Christ’s will, so that such persons may assist those who are a door. “Cedar boards,” that is, such as are cedar-like: incorruptible and killing worms by their fragrance.

> “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower; from the time that I became before him like one finding peace. There was a vineyard for the Peaceful One in her who has peoples. He gave it to keepers; a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit. My vineyard is before me. Your thousand, Peaceful One, and two hundred for those who keep its fruits.”

“I am a wall.” The voice of the Church of the Jews, setting forth her own perfection, as if she said: “You say, ‘If she is a wall, let us build.’ I do indeed have a wall: there are some within me who are a wall and defence of others; and I have breasts, that is, holy teachers, who are like a tower, unassailable and invincible in their teaching. I say that I have this from the time when I became before you,” that is, in your good pleasure, “like one finding peace,” whereas previously I had discord through sin.

“There was a vineyard.” The Church from the Jews shows that she ought to find peace in Christ, because the Church from the Gentiles, which had received no worship of God, found peace with God. This is what she says: “A vineyard,” that is, the Church from the Gentiles, in whose cultivation the greatest labour was required, “for the Peaceful One,” that is, it found peace with God. “In her,” supply “peace,” “who has peoples,” that is, in which peace are many Gentiles with God. I say that the vineyard was for the Peaceful One, and therefore he gave it to keepers, that is, he appointed in it pastors and teachers, or angelic guardians. This Church is of such dignity that the person who wishes to be a man—that is, to act manfully—brings, distributing fittingly, a thousand silver pieces: that is, he brings and presents to God everything he possesses from the world, for its fruit, namely eternal life, which is the fruit of the Church.

“My vineyard.” The voice of the Bridegroom. “You said that the Church from the Gentiles was at peace with me. Not that Church alone pleases me, but my entire vineyard, that is, the whole Church [Col. 1227A] both from Jews and from Gentiles, is before me,” that is, always exists in my good pleasure. “Your thousand, Peaceful One,” that is, the united offering of all possessions, is before me. But those who guard its fruits, such as holy pastors who take care that holy subjects do not lose the fruits of eternity, receive two hundred silver pieces, that is, a double reward. For two hundred is double one hundred. The guardians of holy Church offer God a double reward because they keep themselves unstained for God and gain others as well; therefore they are recompensed with a double reward.

> “You who dwell in the gardens, friends listen to you; make your voice heard. Flee, my beloved, and be like a doe or a fawn of stags upon the mountains of spices.”
