[Col. 1227B] “You who dwell in the gardens.” Because the Bridegroom had just said to the Church, “My vineyard is before me,” and similar things, lest the Church think herself immediately taken up to the marriage, he warns her that, while she is not yet taken up, she must again labour and work, so that, well prepared, she may be united in marriage. Thus he says: “You, bride, who are not yet led into the bridal chamber, [Col. 1228A] but still dwell in gardens”—for each of the faithful dwells in gardens, that is, in the Church—“make me hear,” that is, make yourself worthy of my hearing. And you have my friends through whom you may convey to me both prayers and works pleasing to me. This is what he says: “Friends listen,” that is, they are ready to present your good works to God. Litanies are indeed made in the Church for this purpose, that through the intercession of the saints we may deserve to find the Lord gracious.

“Flee, my beloved.” Because I must dwell in gardens and cannot yet be joined to you in the bridal chamber as you wish, I endure the absence of your bodily presence. Yet I ask that you condescend to us and show your knowledge not only to the perfect but, through them, also to the lower. This is what he says: “Be like a doe or a fawn of stags,” namely descend into the hills so that you may be seen by the humble. You who dwell upon mountains, that is, upon the higher villages, those eminent in virtues: mountains of spices, that is, from which the fragrance of virtues and good works is offered to God.

[Col. 1227]

# EXPOSITIONS ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1227C]

The Book of the Generation. At the very beginning he sufficiently indicates that he is about to treat of Christ’s humanity, since he begins with a bodily generation. For who shall recount His divine generation? (Isa. VIII.) It should be noted that, in keeping with the subject of the opening, he also gave his book its name, following the custom of the Hebrews, whose books are entitled from their beginnings: thus the first book of Moses is called Genesis because its opening treats of the generation of the world; and Exodus, because at its beginning the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt is discussed. The New Testament fittingly corresponds to the Old: the latter begins with the generation of the first man and the creation of the world, while the former likewise begins with the generation of the second man and the restoration of the world. The former is called Genesis; the latter, the Book of the Generation. The former [Col. 1227D] deals with commandments, but imperfect ones; the latter with ordinances, but perfect ones. The former deals with a priesthood and sacrifices, but figurative ones; the latter with a certain priest—namely, the true one—and also with a perfect sacrifice completing all the rest. The former deals with deliverance from Egypt; the latter with deliverance from hell. The former deals with entry into the land of promise, and the latter with the admission of our captivity into heaven. But this generation is opposed to the former: that one led us to condemnation; this one to restoration. That one expelled us from paradise; this one brought us back.

Let us therefore say, “The Book of the Generation,” that is, “Here is the book,” as it is said, “The vision of Isaiah, son of Amos” (Isa. I), without the pronoun “this.” But whose generation it is, he subsequently adds. It is not the generation of Adam, who destroyed us, but of Jesus—that is, the Saviour. Not of one expelling us from paradise, but of Christ—that is, of one bringing us back to paradise. In ancient times many were given this name, Jesus, but as a figure of this One, such as Jesus son of Nave—that is, Joshua son of Nun (Jesus and Joshua are the same). Nave and Nun are the same. Jesus is Hebrew and is called in Greek σωτήρ, “Saviour,” and in Latin *salvator*, “saviour.” Jesus was His proper name, as the angel announced; Christ, however, is the name of His office. For Christ signifies that He was anointed as king and priest.

Note that it was not enough to say “Jesus” unless he also said “Christ.” For, wishing to show the faithful Jews the generation of Him who had been promised in the Law and the Prophets, he ought to use the name customary among the Jews, namely *Meschiah*. It should be known that *meschiah* among the Hebrews is the same as *christus* among the Greeks and *unctus*, “anointed,” among us. Matthew, therefore, writing in Hebrew, did not say *Christi*, “of Christ,” but *Meschiae*, “of Messiah”; but the Greek translators wrote *Christi*.

There follows another specification: “Son of David.” For he shows that He was born from those fathers from whose seed He had been promised, namely, from the seed of David and Abraham. Therefore He is called especially the Son of David and Abraham, since He had been promised to those two alone: to Abraham, where it was said, “In thy seed shall all nations be blessed” (Gen. XXII); and to David, “Of the fruit of thy womb” (Ps. CXXXI), etc. And in Paralipomenon [Col. 1229A] (which means “Words of the Days”): “And it shall be,” He says, “when thy days are fulfilled”—that is, when thou shalt sleep with thy fathers—“that I will raise up thy seed after thee” (Par. XVII), etc. This is clearly not said of Solomon, who began to reign while his father was alive.

It is asked why David is placed before Abraham. Because, if Abraham had been put first and David afterwards, Abraham would have to be repeated in order to weave the sequence of the genealogy. David also is set first because he sinned in many things, rather than Abraham, who appeared righteous in all things, so that Christ might be proved to have been born from mercy alone, not from human merits. David is also set first because it was more expressly promised to David that Christ would take flesh from his stock. Hence, when unbelieving Jews were asked whose son Jesus was, they answered: David [Col. 1229B] (Matt. XXII).

Note that one of those to whom the promise was made is the first of the patriarchs, while the other is the first of the kings. These are the two pillars before the entrance of the Temple, between which one passed to the doorway, because through those two one comes to Christ by hearing the promise made to them. They are said to be bound by a threefold cord of twelve cubits because the twelve apostles adhere to them, confirming through their preaching the promise made to them.

“Abraham begot Isaac.” It is asked why he begins the genealogy with Abraham. Because Christ was first promised to him. It is also asked why Matthew reckons the genealogy by descending, but Luke by ascending. Matthew proceeds by descending because he intends to show Christ’s humanity, by which God descended to humankind. Thus he narrates by descending, in order to show how Christ came to us by descending from those fathers. Luke, however, by recounting it in ascent, makes known to us the figure of a certain mystery. For after he had treated of Christ’s baptism, in which he had signified many mysteries concerning us, he added the series of Christ’s generation as a sign of a certain instruction for us, beginning from Joseph and reaching as far as God. For when he had said, “It came to pass, when all the people were baptized, and Jesus also being baptized and praying” (Luke III), etc., he added: “And Jesus himself was beginning, being about thirty years old, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who was of Heli, who was of Mathat” [Col. 1229D], etc., and finally, “who was of Adam, who was of God” (ibid.). By this he signified that everyone regenerated in baptism ought, by ascending from virtue to virtue, to advance until he is made a son of God; and therefore he demonstrated Christ to be the Son of God by ascending through the succession of the fathers.

He also wished to show, by the number of fathers—seventy-seven—that full remission of sins is obtained in baptism and that one is thereby made a son of God. For seventy-seven is the number of remission. Hence it is said to Peter: “I say not unto thee, seven times, but unto seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII). As though He said: “Thou shalt forgive every transgression.” Seventy-seven is made up from eleven and seven: for seven times eleven makes that number. [Col. 1230A] Eleven pertains to transgression of the commandments, because ten signifies the ten commandments of the Law. Seven pertains to universality, because the seven days comprise all time. Thus the gifts of the Holy Spirit are called seven, not because there are only seven, but because all gifts are understood through seven gifts. Therefore, in commanding forgiveness “seventy times seven,” He commands, as it were, that all offences be pardoned.

Accordingly, since Matthew intends to show the bodily generation, he gives only natural fathers. But Luke, wishing to suggest that one baptized becomes an adopted son of God, inserts into the genealogy not only natural but adoptive fathers as well, such as Heli and all those included down to David. Note that in each of the fathers three things should be observed: history, morality, and allegory—that is, how each father prefigured Christ. The moral sense is observed in this, that from each father some virtue is built up in us either through the meaning of his name or by his example. Hence forty-two fathers are also reckoned. For just as the children of Israel reached the promised land through forty-two stations, so the faithful come to the Lord through forty-two virtues. What this number signifies will be explained below.

It is asked, since Abraham had several sons, why he mentions only Isaac. And since Isaac begot Jacob and Esau, why he mentions Jacob alone, when he reckons all Judah’s brothers with him in the genealogy. Namely, because Ishmael and Esau did not remain in the worship of the one God, whereas Judah’s brothers are counted among God’s people and were figures of the twelve apostles. Since history leaves no doubt that Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac Jacob, and similarly of the others, let us follow the moral and allegorical senses.

**MORAL SENSE.** Abraham signifies in us the virtue of faith by his example, since it is read of him: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness” (Gen. XV). For he was the first way of believing; when he saw three and worshipped one, he indicated to us the mystery of Trinity and Unity. Isaac follows, and signifies hope, because Isaac means “laughter.” He was the joy of his parents, and also his father’s hope, when Abraham, giving faith to the promise, hoped that he would have a son, or when through him he hoped that he would be multiplied. Hope likewise is our joy, because it makes us hope for eternal goods and rejoice in them.

Therefore Abraham begot Isaac because faith begets hope, according to the Apostle, who says: “Faith is the substance”—that is, the foundation—“of things hoped for” (Heb. XI). For one hopes in vain who does not believe. Jacob is born from these two parents, namely charity, which is born from faith and hope. For what we believe and what we hope, we love. Let us see why Jacob signifies charity. Jacob has two names: first he was called Jacob; afterward, after wrestling with the angel, when he had seen God in the angel, he was called [Col. 1231A] Israel, that is, “the man seeing God.” Then he went to Laban and served him seven years for Rachel; but Leah, who had bleary eyes because she was the elder, was substituted for him. Then he served another seven years and had Rachel. Leah bore many children; Rachel, few. All this signifies charity.

For love has two branches: love of God and love of neighbour. Love of God is prior in nature and dignity; love of neighbour is prior in time. This is shown in the following way. God is the highest good, and good through Himself, not through another; other things are good from the highest good. Therefore God must be loved because He is good through Himself; other things must be loved because they are good through that highest good, not for their own sake, since they are not good through themselves. Therefore, since creatures are good, they must be loved through that highest good insofar as they are from Him.

But the rational creature that cleaves to God, serves God, and loves Him, is to be loved in a twofold manner: both because it is from God, insofar as it is a creature, and because it freely cleaves to and serves God. A neighbour, therefore, because he is good through cleaving to God, is to be loved in two ways: both because he is God’s creature and because he is good. An evil neighbour, however, is to be loved only because he is God’s creature. Feed, therefore, by sustaining it, that substance which God made; but hate the sin, which is neither good through itself nor from the good God. Thus a human being is to be loved insofar as he is from the good, insofar as he is God’s creature.

Jesus son of Sirach seems contrary to this when he says: “Give nothing to the ungodly” (Ecclus. XII). But this is commanded lest someone support him in carrying out his wickedness. Therefore it is forbidden that the ungodly person be maintained, but it is not forbidden that the human being be fed. “Let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. VI).

Other creatures are to be loved less because they are not rational. They are good only because they were made by the Good, but they are not so like the highest Good as rational beings are. And since certain animals, such as wolves and lions, are given to us as punishment because they harm our neighbour, they must be pursued by us for the sake of love of neighbour, to whom we owe more. Yet in doing so we shall not be contrary to God’s disposition, because God so afflicts us through them that, while sparing us, He also allows us to kill them.

Behold, we have that love of neighbour naturally proceeds [Col. 1231D] from love of God, because we love our neighbour for God’s sake, from whom he is. But we ought to love God more, because He alone is good through Himself. Yet in time one reaches the love of God through love of neighbour. For God is not known except through creatures. Therefore the visible goods are loved first, and through them their Creator is loved. But that perfect love will not exist until we see Him face to face. Nevertheless, while in the present we see Him through a mirror and through faith, let us love Him above all things.

Therefore Jacob was first called Jacob and afterward Israel, because in the present a person must first wrestle against vices and labour in love of neighbour, so that afterward he may be called Israel—that is, so that afterward he may love God and, by loving Him, see Him: in the present through faith, in the future in reality. Behold, Jacob signifies charity, as we have said. Charity embraces two lives, the active and the contemplative. The active is signified by Leah; the contemplative by Rachel. Leah means “labouring,” because the active life is in labour; Rachel, “the beginning seen,” because in it the Beginning—that is, God—is seen.

When charity desires to devote itself to contemplation and unite it to itself, Leah is substituted by night, because the neighbour must first be loved, since that love is prior in time and in that life many children are produced. Leah is rightly said to be bleary-eyed because, so long as we are engaged in worldly matters, we cannot see God clearly. Rachel is received afterward because one reaches contemplation of God through love of neighbour, where few children are produced; and she is said to have clear eyes. He served the same number of seven years, while he keeps the seven commandments concerning love of God and neighbour. The seven years also signify the present time, which is measured by seven days. He doubles the number seven according to the perfection of life, if only he can reach that which he desires.

In these three virtues lies the whole perfection of life, and no virtues without these can lead to the homeland. Hence God is called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Exod. III): the God only of those who have these virtues. He is called rather the God of Jacob than of Israel, because in the present people are rather Jacob—that is, supplanters of vices and wrestlers—while in the future they are Israel.

**ALLEGORY.** Having set forth the moral sense of these three fathers [Col. 1232C], let us see what they prefigure in Christ. Abraham bears the figure of Christ in many ways and places, and besides this in his name. For Abraham means “father of many nations,” and Christ is Father of many faithful persons. Therefore, when Abraham departed from his kindred and dwelt in a foreign land, namely in the land of Canaan, to which he crossed at God’s command, he signifies Christ, who, leaving the Jewish people, passed over to the Gentiles through His preachers.

Again, Abraham signifies Christ in having two sons, one by a bondwoman and the other by a free woman (Gal. IV); one according to nature, the other by promise. He bears the person of Christ because Christ begot two peoples: the Jewish people, signified by Ishmael, whom He had by Hagar—that is, by the old Law. Ishmael means “hearing,” because the Jews were hearers of the Law, not doers. Hagar means “alienation,” for the old Law, understood carnally, alienated them from God. The other, namely the Gentile people, is denoted by Isaac, who was born of Sarah—that is, of the New Testament. Isaac means “laughter,” because the conversion of the Gentiles was the joy of angels and of all faithful believers. Sarah means “princess,” because the new Law holds pre-eminence among all laws. The Jewish people was generated according to nature, because it was kept in the worship of the one God through the blandishments of this world; but the Gentile people by promise, because it served God not for temporal things but for the promise of invisible things.

Again, Isaac bore the person of Christ in many places and signified Him by his name. For Christ is our laughter, of whom it is said: “No one shall take your joy from you” (John XVI). Isaac was led by Abraham to be sacrificed, accompanied by two servants. When Abraham reached the mountain on the third day—the mountain upon which God had commanded Isaac to be sacrificed—he said to them: “Wait here with the ass until we return to you” (Gen. XXII). Then Isaac carried the wood, while Abraham carried the sword and fire. Yet Isaac was not sacrificed, but a ram caught by its horns among brambles.

Abraham figures God the Father, who delivered His Son to the Passion. The two servants signify the Jewish people divided into two kingdoms, the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom [Col. 1233B] of Israel. The ass signifies the Jews’ folly. The Jews wait with the ass because they still persist in their folly. The ram, not Isaac, was sacrificed, because Christ’s flesh, caught by the horns of the cross among the brambles of tribulation, suffered, not His divinity, which is signified by Isaac. And this occurred on the third day, that is, in the time of grace. For there are three times: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Isaac carried the wood, and Christ bore the cross. Abraham carried the fire and sword, because the sword of Christ’s death and the fire of persecutions were in God’s hand.

Again, in Isaac, Christ’s person is expressed in his receiving Rebecca. The servant sent to seek Rebecca for Isaac signifies the company of preachers sent to convert the Gentile people. The fountain at which the servant stood signifies the streams of evangelical Scripture. Rebecca draws from it with a pitcher because converted Gentile society receives instruction from Scripture according to the measure of its capacity. Rebecca means “patience,” for the Gentile Church suffered much for God. She first places the pitcher upon her shoulder, then upon her arms, because she first places preaching in her mind and then fulfils it in action.

The ornaments with which the servant adorned Rebecca are the virtues and commandments of teachers. The earrings signify the will to hear God’s words, which must be received with love; for the two commandments of charity are understood through the weight of two shekels. The bracelets, ornaments of the arms, denote good works [Col. 1233D], and they weighed ten shekels because all our work consists in the ten commandments of the Law. Rebecca’s giving drink not only to the man but watering the camels as well signifies that the converted Church of the Gentiles offered the drink of preaching to all, not only to the wise but also to the foolish. Hence Paul says: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the unwise” (Rom. I).

Laban, who invites the servant into the house and calls him “blessed of the Lord,” signifies all carnal persons who proclaim and honour the virtues of holy teachers, yet do not go with them to Isaac—that is, to Christ. The spacious place which Rebecca said she had at home is the natural law possessed by the Church before it came to Christ. Through this law, therefore, access was opened to Christ’s evangelical law. The maidens who followed Rebecca as she went to Isaac signify faithful souls who live simply within the Church but do not attain the bridal chamber of contemplation.

Rebecca found Isaac on the way leading to the well named “of the Living and Seeing One” (Gen. XXIV). That well is the Old Testament, because through Scripture we live and see God. The way leading to the well is Christ’s Passion, through which one comes to understand the ancient Law. For all sacrifices are fulfilled in it. On this way the Gentile people found Christ, because when it came to faith it found Him already having suffered. When Rebecca saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel (ibid.), because the Church, having known Christ, abandoned Gentile life. She covered her face with a veil [Col. 1234B] because, coming to Christ, she was ashamed of her former rite.

Moreover, Isaac’s entering the field when the day was already declining signified that at the final time of this world, as at day’s end, Christ came forth, as though into a field. Hence Christ Himself says in the Gospel: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John XVI), because though He is invisible, He nevertheless showed Himself visible in this world to the Church gathered from the Gentiles.

Again, Isaac signifies Christ because he had two sons, or two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile; and the elder served the younger, because the Jewish people, scattered throughout the world, now serves the Gentiles, not only by bodily servitude but also by the confirmation supplied by their books. Isaac’s desire to eat his son Esau’s venison signifies Christ’s desire to be refreshed by the good works of the Jewish people. But as Esau neglected this and was occupied with outward things, as though with hunting, Rebecca—that is, the mother of grace—substituted the younger son, the Gentile people, and took away the elder’s dignity.

Isaac’s foretelling the future blessing to his son Jacob while his sight was dim, yet not seeing him, signifies that Christ repeatedly foretold through the prophets the calling of the Gentiles, but did not see them, because He did not preach to them in His own person. Jacob’s preparing food for his father not from game but from a domestic animal denotes that the Gentile people offered in itself a holocaust to God, according to the Psalmist: “Upon me, O God, are thy vows, which I will render: praises to thee” [Col. 1234D] (Ps. LV). Esau’s garments, in which Rebecca clothed the younger son, are the adornments of the commandments of the old Law, with which the Gentile Church is adorned through sound interpretation. The hands and neck being covered with kids’ skins denotes that the nations coming to faith confess to God the sins of mind and body. He approached and kissed him when Christ reconciled the Gentiles to Himself; concerning this kiss, the Song says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Cant. I). Afterwards he is blessed when he is multiplied in virtues. Esau’s late return to his father and eventual blessing signifies that the Jewish people will be converted at the end of the age.

Jacob likewise signifies or figures Christ. Jacob’s sleep on the journey signifies Christ’s death or Passion on the cross. The stone placed beneath his head signifies humanity placed beneath divinity. This is the stone that makes both one (Eph. II). The ladder, touching earth and stretching to heaven, on which angels ascended and descended, signifies the preaching of the saints, in which sometimes heavenly things and sometimes earthly things are discussed; sometimes Christ’s humanity and sometimes His divinity. Paul was a chief angel, ascending when he said: “We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. I); descending when he said: “I judged not myself to know anything except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified” (1 Cor. II).

His rising in the morning and setting up the stone as a pillar signifies Christ’s resurrection at dawn. His pouring oil upon it signifies [Col. 1235B] that this resurrection occurred through the operation of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, the oil poured out signified that He is king and priest, for kings and priests were anointed with oil. Hence He is also called Christ—that is, “anointed.” He also signifies Christ in taking two sisters to himself. For the two sisters signify the two Churches, namely of the active and contemplative; for both of these He served seven years, because in the present life He served God in order to acquire both. Seven signifies the present life because all time runs through seven days. Jacob had twelve sons, and Christ begot twelve apostles through faith. Jacob means “supplanter” and signifies Christ, of whom it is said: “Thou hast supplanted beneath me those rising up against me” (Ps. XVII).

Because Christ is especially signified in these fathers, God is in many places called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. In these three is noted every manner of generating the children of God. For God often generates through a good preacher a good son, and through a bad preacher a bad one; this is denoted by Abraham, who had a faithful son by his free wife and begot an unbelieving son by a bondwoman. At other times He generates through a good preacher both a good and a bad son; this is signified in Isaac, who begot one good son and another bad one by the free woman. At other times He generates good persons through both a good and a bad preacher; this is signified in Jacob, who had good sons both by free women and by bondwomen.

“Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.” He names Judah specifically because the Lord descended from him alone. Judah, however, begot Phares, etc.

**HISTORY.** Judah had three sons: Her, Onan, and Shelah. He gave a wife named Tamar to his elder son, Her. But because Her was most wicked and harmful, God killed him without offspring. Tamar was therefore given to his second son, Onan, so that he might raise up seed for his brother. But he, unwilling to raise up seed for his brother, spilled his seed upon the ground. Thus the second son also died. Shelah, however, was still a little child. Judah therefore said to Tamar: “Go and remain a widow in thy house until my son is grown” (Gen. XXXVIII).

Later she took counsel for herself. For she heard that Judah was going to Timnah with his shepherd, Hira, an Adullamite [Col. 1236A], to shear the sheep. She therefore assumed the appearance of a prostitute and, veiling her face, sat at a crossroads, so that by lying with her father-in-law on this occasion she might have some seed from him. Judah came and, not recognizing her, promised her a kid in return for intercourse. When she requested a pledge, however, he gave her a ring, a bracelet, and a staff. After intercourse, he told her to wait there until he sent the kid. He sent it through Hira, but she had departed with the pledge.

Tamar therefore conceived twins, Phares and Zarah. In the birth Zarah wished to come out first and put forth his hand, which the midwife bound with scarlet. Yet Zarah drew back his hand, and Phares was born. When the midwife saw this, she said: “Why has the wall—or nature—been divided through thee?” (Gen. XXXVIII), as though saying: “Why hast thou interrupted nature’s structure?” Therefore she named him Phares, that is, “division.”

Phares begot Esrom. Judah begot Phares and Zarah before entering Egypt; both later crossed into Egypt with their father. In Egypt Phares begot Esrom; Esrom, Aram; Aram, Aminadab; and Aminadab, Naasson. Moses then led them out of Egypt, and Naasson was leader under Moses in the tribe of Judah through the wilderness, where he begot Salmon. After his father’s death, this Salmon was chief in the tribe of Judah. He entered the promised land with Joshua and married Rahab the prostitute, who received the spies.

The children of Israel besieged Jericho and, blowing trumpets, went around its walls for seven days. On the seventh day the walls fell at the seventh trumpet [Col. 1236C]. But Rahab the prostitute, who had put scarlet in the window as the messengers instructed, was saved together with her whole household. Salmon later married her.

Note that the judges began with Joshua and lasted until David. But those reckoned in this line from Salmon to David were merely certain heads in the tribe of Judah, not princes or leaders. For after the tribes were divided in the promised land, each tribe did not have its own rulers, but all had only one chief judge, who was made so according to election, not according to tribe.

In the promised land Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab. Boaz begot Obed by Ruth. Elimelech was a certain poor man of Boaz’s tribe, and his wife was Naomi. With his wife and two sons he went to the land of the Moabites. There his sons took wives from the land of the Gentiles. When the father and his sons had died without offspring, Naomi returned with Ruth the Moabitess, one of her daughters-in-law, to her own land. At her mother-in-law’s urging, Ruth went into Boaz’s field to glean.

On the following day Naomi persuaded her to wash, put on better clothes, observe at night the place where Boaz slept in the field, come, uncover the covering at his feet, and cast herself down there. And so it happened. Boaz, disturbed, asked what she wanted. She said that she wished him to raise up her husband’s seed, because he was her kinsman. But he said that another was a closer kinsman, to whom one had first to go; if that man rejected her [Col. 1237A], he himself would take her. When the other had rejected her, he married her and begot Obed by her.

The evangelist included this Gentile woman in order to show that Christ was born not only from Jews but also from Gentiles, and thus to fulfil the prophecy saying: “Send forth thy lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness” (Isa. XVI)—that is, from the Gentile world, which is hard as rock because full of idolatry, and wilderness because without Law.

Obed begot Jesse. David’s father has two names, for he is more often called Isai. But because the prophet called him not Isai but Jesse, saying, “There shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI), the evangelist used Jesse in order to show that this prophecy was fulfilled in Christ and Mary.

**MORAL SENSE.** Let us again see what virtues these fathers build up in us. Since faith, hope, and charity are the foundations of all virtues, the virtues that follow are, as it were, additions to them. Judah means “confession.” For someone might believe, hope, and love, and yet, through fear, be said to deny before rulers, as Peter did; therefore confession of faith is necessary. Confession is twofold: one confession of faith, the other of sins. Therefore, if after the three virtues mentioned above a person sins, confession not only of faith but also of sins is necessary.

Judah fittingly receives the fourth place because he also holds fourth place among the brothers, and because confession is rightly placed fourth in the allegorical order. Reuben is first, Simeon second, Levi third, Judah fourth. Reuben signifies concupiscence, because it is said of him in the blessings: “Reuben, poured out as water” [Col. 1237C] (Gen. XLIX), because he flowed away in concupiscences. Simeon means “his persistent fury,” and therefore signifies anger. Levi, because priests were chosen from his tribe and the Law was entrusted to priests, signifies reason, which by its law ought to moderate both powers of the soul. But if these three sin, confession of sins ought to follow, cleansing everything.

After Judah come Phares and Zarah. Phares means “division,” Zarah “rising,” and Tamar “bitterness.” Thus confession produces separation from vices and the rising of virtues from Tamar—that is, from the bitterness of penitence. After Phares follows Esrom, which means “arrow.” For after someone has separated himself from vices and worldly things, he ought to become an arrow, so as by preaching to punish vices in others and pierce human hearts with love of God. Aram follows, meaning “chosen” or “lofty,” because after someone has withdrawn from the world and benefits others, it is necessary that he be regarded as exalted and distinguished, chosen by God, and lofty in virtues.

Aminadab follows, that is, “a willing people.” For it is necessary that a person do whatever he does with willing intent and good purpose, not through compulsion or fear. Naasson follows, meaning “augury.” This augury is not worldly but heavenly. Joseph gloried in it when he ordered his servant to say to his brothers as they carried off the cup in the sack: “You have taken my lord’s cup, in which he is accustomed to practise augury” (Gen. XLIV). The cup is divine Scripture [Col. 1238A], in which is the drink of wisdom. In it the wise person practises augury because there he sees future things—that is, heavenly things. Thus he divines divine things who, from good will, is intent on his neighbour’s benefit.

Salmon follows, that is, “perceptive.” After someone studies divine Scripture, he becomes perceptive—that is, able through the taste of reason to distinguish what is good and what evil, what sweet and what bitter. Boaz follows, that is, “strong.” For one instructed in good Scriptures becomes strong to endure every adversity. Note that he is called simply “strong,” in distinction from David, who is called “strong of hand,” which signifies something else. This strong man is the son of Rahab—that is, of the Church.

Obed follows, that is, “service.” Whoever is a strong servant can become fit for service; for no one is fit for God’s service unless strong. This service is generated by Ruth—that is, by readiness. For a servant must be prompt, not sluggish, but running, lest any carnal pleasure detain him. Jesse follows, that is, “incense.” For if we serve, devotion will be in the heart from fear and love; and from the heart’s fire and desire it offers God most sweet incense.

### ALLEGORY

Let us now see how these fathers prefigure Christ. Judah is interpreted “confessing.” And of Christ it is said: “I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Luke 10). According to the historical sense he also bears the person of Christ.

Tamar signifies the ancient people of God, to whom two husbands were given, namely pastors; in these two are indicated two kinds of pastors: those who harm and those unwilling to help. Er signifies those most wicked pastors who not only do not help but even harm the people of God. Hence he is interpreted “skin-clad,” that is, covered with sins, which are signified by the skins of dead animals. Therefore Adam and Eve, after sin, wore garments of skin.

Onan, however, who spilled his seed upon the ground, signifies those pastors who, although able to be of service, are unwilling. Rather, they spill their seed upon the ground—that is, they cling to earthly things and apply to secular concerns the zeal for fruitfulness which they owe to the people of God. Hence Onan is called “their sorrow,” because useless prelates bring great sorrow upon those subject to them.

That Shelah does not take her signifies the interruption of the kingdom which occurred in the time of Herod. For although there were many sons from the tribe of Judah, none of them ruled the people of God. Hence Shelah is called “dismissal,” because at that time the tribe of Judah was set aside and a foreigner entered upon the kingdom.

Then Judah—that is, Christ—came to Timnah, that is, into the world; for Timnah is interpreted “decline,” because the whole world was in decline. He came, I say, to shear the sheep, that is, to remove the burdens of sins, with his companion Hira, that is, with John the Baptist. Hira is interpreted “vision of a brother,” because he saw his brother, that is, Christ, who was of his own tribe. This Hira was an Adullamite, interpreted “having testimony in water,” which fittingly applies to John.

Tamar—that is, the Church—desires to be joined to him; but, having changed her appearance, that is, no longer deriving from the Jews but rather bearing, from the Gentiles, the appearance of a harlot, because she had previously fornicated enough with idols, she was as though unknown to Judah. Hence David says: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17).

She sat at a crossroads, that is, amid the errors of this age. Having therefore been joined to Christ, she receives a ring, that is, faith; a bracelet, the ornament of the arm, namely good works; and a staff, that is, his kingdom. Hence each person is called both king and priest. For Christ promised her a kid, that is, a rebuke for sins when she sinned, which he would send her through his ministers.

Afterwards Hira—that is, John, in whom is signified the whole order of preachers who daily prepare the way for the Lord—comes with the kid, that is, with the rebuke of sins, and seeks the harlot at the crossroads but does not find her. For, after receiving faith, the Church ceased to be a harlot, [Col. 1239B] and rebuke has no place in her.

Tamar is interpreted “bitterness,” because she lives amid the bitter things of this age.

But in the sons there is another mystery in itself, not continued from what precedes. Zerah, who first puts out his hand, signifies the first faithful people—namely Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others—who first displayed the hand of good works. This work was bound and confirmed by scarlet, that is, by the passion of Christ, in which they believed and which they awaited. For they knew that their good works availed them nothing without redemption by Christ’s blood. Hence Zerah is interpreted “rising,” because upon that first people the sun of righteousness first appeared.

But he withdrew his hand, because with their passing away the work of faith ceased; and the Jewish people and the Law intervened. The Law was, as it were, a dividing wall between peoples, because it separated the first faithful people from the last, which existed at Christ’s advent, and, as it were, placed itself between them. Hence Perez is called the Jewish people, that is, “division.” But Christ destroyed that intervening people and the Law, and joined together the divided wall of the two faithful peoples—that is, their building.

It is asked why, while passing over the names of holy women, namely Sarah, Rebekah, and others, the Evangelist noted in Christ’s genealogy notable women—namely Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba. He did this in order to show that Christ was born not only from Jews but also from Gentiles, not only from righteous persons but also from sinners. Therefore the paschal lamb is commanded in the Law to be taken not from a sheepfold where there are only sheep, but from one where there are sheep and goats, because he was to be born from righteous persons and sinners.

To be born from sinners does no harm, because “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18). This is said of one who has not imitated his father’s wickedness. But if he has imitated it, he will also be punished for his father’s iniquity—not by transmission of corruption, but because, remaining with him in imitation of wickedness, he is as it were the same as he and is punished with him. Hence: “I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Exod. 20).

Also, in the blessing which he received from his father Jacob, Judah signified Christ. For Jacob says: “Judah, thy brothers shall praise thee; thy hands shall be upon the inward parts, or necks, of thy enemies; the sons of thy father shall worship thee. Thou hast gone up for prey, my son; resting, thou hast lain down like a lion. [Col. 1240A] Who shall rouse him? The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations, binding his colt to the vine and his she-ass to the vine-stock. He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape. Thy eyes are more beautiful than wine, and thy teeth whiter than milk” (Gen. 49).

All these things pertain to Christ. His brothers praise him: this is the whole multitude of saints. His hands are upon the necks of his enemies because he humbles his adversaries and subjects their necks to his faith. The sons of his Father worship him because all the children of God venerate him as God.

Christ went up for prey when he came to battle against the devil, in order to rescue his own who were in hell; this was fulfilled on the day of the Passion, when he descended to the underworld. “He went up” is well said, because he had first lived humbly in the world, but then revealed his power. He lay down resting when he lay in the tomb; he lay down like a lion because on the third day, like a lion, he was roused by the voice of the Father. And who raised him? No one but the Father.

“The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, until he comes,” and so forth. For all the kings of the Jews were from the tribe of Judah until the time of Herod, who was a foreigner, under whom Christ was born. Christ himself was the expectation of the nations because he redeemed them and converted them to the faith.

He bound the colt to the vine when he joined the Gentile Church in faith to the primitive Church. He calls the apostles, and others called or converted by Christ, the vine; to them Christ says: “I am the true vine, but you are the branches” (John 15). The colt is the Gentile people, which was the offspring of the yoked she-ass, that is, of the Jewish people, which was under the yoke of the Law; for through them the Gentiles were converted to faith.

He bound the she-ass to the vine because through himself, who is the vine, he converted the Jews. He washed his robe in wine when he drenched his flesh with the blood of his Passion. He washed his cloak in the blood of the grape when he washed his Church from sins in his blood. The Church is Christ’s garment, according to the prophet: “With all these thou shalt clothe thyself as with a garment” [Vulgate: “an ornament”] (Isa. 49). She herself is the grape from which wine came forth, because he is the body from which blood proceeded.

His eyes are the preachers who provide for those subject to them in the Church, [Col. 1240D] and they are more beautiful than wine—that is, than the preachers of the Old Law—because evangelical doctrine is clearer than legal tradition. The preachers of the Old Law are called wine because of the severity of its threats, where it was said: “Tooth for tooth, eye for eye” (Deut. 19), and so forth.

The teeth are the interpreters of the New Law, who crush and chew the obscurity of Scripture so that it may be incorporated by the belly, that is, by the weaker members of the Church. They are whiter than milk because they are purer than the teachers of the Old Law, which is called milk and was given to a rudimentary people that they might be nourished.

Perez follows, because Christ is Perez, that is, “division,” because he will separate the sheep at his right hand from the goats at his left; he is also the discerner and illuminator of hearts. He is likewise Hezron, that is, “arrow” [Col. 1241A] or “court,” because like an arrow he penetrates the hearts of his hearers. He is a court in that he signifies the breadth of charity, because he loved his enemies.

Aram signifies Christ, who is interpreted “chosen” or “exalted,” for of him it is said through the prophet: “Behold my chosen servant, whom I have chosen” (Isa. 43); and through another: “The Lord is exalted above all nations” (Ps. 112).

He is also Amminadab, that is, “a willing people,” who says: “I will sacrifice to thee willingly” (Ps. 53). Nahshon also, who is called “divination,” signifies Christ, who knows all things—past, present, and future. Nahshon is also interpreted “serpentine,” because Christ, in the manner of a serpent, avoided every snare. He is likewise Salmon, that is, “perceptive,” because he perceives all things.

He took Rahab, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, which had prostituted herself with idols and which displayed scarlet in the window—that is, through confession made known Christ’s Passion by love. Rahab is interpreted “hunger,” “breadth,” or “impetuosity,” because the Church of the Gentiles hungers and thirsts for righteousness, has been extended throughout the whole world, and by the force of doctrine converted philosophers and kings.

The Jews who went around Jericho for seven days, sounding trumpets, signify the Church’s preachers, who encircle the world while sounding trumpets—that is, while through their preaching they rebuke the preachers of the world, who are signified by Jericho. For Jericho is interpreted “moon,” that is, “decline”; secular things gradually decline, but on the seventh day, that is, at the end of the age, they are utterly destroyed.

Boaz again, who is interpreted “strength,” [Col. 1241C] signifies Christ, of whom it is said: “The Lord shall come in strength” (Isa. 40). He also takes Ruth, that is, the Gentile Church, which is interpreted “seeing,” “hastening,” or “defining,” because the Church sees God, hastens toward the prize, and ceases to persevere in good works. He is likewise Obed, “serving,” because “he came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20). He is Jesse, who is interpreted “sacrifice,” because he was made an offering for us.

David begot Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s.

### HISTORY

The name Bathsheba is passed over in silence so that, by naming Uriah, the Evangelist may recall that very great crime which David committed against him. It is also passed over because the other women, though notable, deserved not only blame [Col. 1241D] but praise as well. But this woman is so blameworthy that she is unworthy of being named; whereas the righteous man is worthy of a name. Nevertheless, in her there is a very great mystery.

For the history says that David, standing upon the roof, saw Bathsheba washing herself; she pleased him, he summoned her, and lay with her. When she had become pregnant, he recalled Uriah from the campaign, so that on this occasion he might enter his house and the child might thus be ascribed to him. Uriah refused to enter, but lay in the vestibule, saying that, while the ark of God was in tents, it was not fitting for him to enter his house. Having received the letter containing his own death, he returned to the campaign and died through Joab’s contrivance, as David had commanded.

Solomon, as though *Salemon*, from *sal*, which is peace, begot Rehoboam; Rehoboam Abijah; [Col. 1242A] Abijah Asa; Asa Jehoshaphat; Jehoshaphat Joram; Joram begot Uzziah.

Observe that Joram did not beget Uzziah according to the history in the Book of Kings. Rather, he begot Ahaziah; Ahaziah begot Joash; Joash Amaziah; and Amaziah Uzziah (4 Kings 11, 14). But because the Evangelist had proposed to set forth forty-two generations from Abraham to Christ in the different states of the times, and because Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, had allied himself with the utterly impious stock of Jezebel, marrying her daughter and being converted to idolatry, therefore his memory is removed as far as the third generation, lest he be placed in the order of the holy birth.

Joram, therefore, having committed fornication, killed his brothers; whence he was afflicted with an intestinal pain so that he expelled his entrails. His son followed him. Ahaziah entered into the ways [Col. 1242B] of the house of Ahaz.

Of this Ahaziah it is read in Chronicles that he was forty-two years old when he began to reign and reigned for one year (2 Chron. 22). This cannot be, because Joram his father was thirty-two years old when he began to reign and reigned for eight years, which together make forty; thus the son would already have been two years older than his father. But the book which says forty-two has been corrupted; and it is more correctly read in the Book of Kings that he was twenty-two years old (4 Kings 8).

Joash, therefore, the son of Ahaziah, consented to worship carved images; and he commanded Zechariah, son of the priest Jehoiada—who had nourished him, made him king, and kept him safe lest Athaliah kill him—to be put to death because he rebuked him for idolatry. Amaziah likewise worshipped the gods of Seir. Therefore these three, although they held the kingdom in some fashion, are excluded from the genealogy, as the Law says: “I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 20).

But it must be understood that this is said of those who follow the sins of their fathers. For a good man born of an evil man is worthy of mercy, and an evil man born of a good man is struck with punishment. The others who are included, although evil, either beget good persons or are begotten by good persons, as Joram was the son of the righteous man Jehoshaphat.

Uzziah, however, was almost entirely upright, except that he himself wished to burn incense. Therefore he was struck with leprosy on his forehead, as though at the place of the veil. It should be noted that under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, Isaiah prophesied concerning Christ.

Observe concerning Hezekiah [Col. 1242D] that, because he had no children, it was said to him: “Set thy house in order, for thou shalt die” (Isa. 38). Therefore he wept, not for a longer life—for he knew that Solomon had pleased God by not asking for more years—but because he feared that God’s promise might not be fulfilled. He knew that he was of David’s line, through which Christ had to come, and he himself had no children. Hence he said: “I shall not see God; I shall not look upon man any longer” (ibid.). Yet, on the other hand, he believed that he who had promised was faithful. But God altered the sentence which he had pronounced for the testing of faith and granted him time for begetting children.

Uzziah begot Jotham; Jotham begot Ahaz; Ahaz begot Hezekiah; Hezekiah begot Manasseh; Manasseh begot Amon; Amon begot Josiah.

### MORAL SENSE

Let us consider what moral meaning these fathers produce in us. After someone is a fit servant and has become a most sweet sacrifice to God, it follows that he should be David, that is, “strong of hand,” who fought bravely against enemies and made the foreign Idumeans tributary. Likewise, he ought to subject carnal people to God by word and example, as Paul did when he converted the Gentiles, who are designated by the Idumeans.

Solomon follows, who is interpreted “peaceful.” For then one becomes peaceful when one serves God and converts others to God. Then all unlawful impulses are calmed within him and, as though already established in eternal tranquillity, he can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

He is rightly placed fifteenth, a number composed of seven and eight: after the seven, which belongs to the legal ordinances because of the Sabbath, the eighth seems to pertain to eternal rest and the future resurrection, signified by the number eight because Christ rose on the eighth day.

Rehoboam follows, that is, “breadth of the people.” Once he has nothing further to see in himself, he ought to embrace others and draw the people of God broadly upward with himself. Abijah follows, that is, “the Lord is father.” Passing beyond these things, he may profess himself a son of God and say: “The Lord is my Father.”

Because he has such a Father who is in heaven, recognizing himself to be in the pilgrimage of this world, he ought to be Asa, that is, “one lifting up,” so that he may ascend from virtue to virtue to the Father, despising this pilgrimage. Then he will be Jehoshaphat, that is, “judging.” For the one who raises himself to God judges others, is judged by no one, and discerns all things lest he be deceived in anything. Thus he becomes Joram, that is, “exalted”—dwelling in heavenly things and looking down upon all things; yet he does not therefore become proud, but attributes his strength to God.

Hence he becomes Uzziah, that is, “the Lord’s strong one,” ascribing the strength of his virtues to God and persevering in his purpose. But because he might persevere in the same state and yet never grow, Jotham follows, that is, “perfect,” because he advances daily to greater things. And the better he advances in virtues, the more he becomes Ahaz, that is, “comprehending.” For the better one performs the Lord’s commandments, the better one comprehends God. Knowledge is increased through action. Hence David says: “They declared the works of God, and [Col. 1243D] understood his deeds” (Ps. 63). They first declared them and then understood them.

Hezekiah follows, that is, “the Lord is strong.” For while he comprehends the Lord, he understands God to be strong: God made and rules all things, conquered the devil, and makes him conquer. Thus, inflamed with love for him, he becomes Manasseh, that is, “forgetful,” because for the love of God he consigns all temporal things to forgetfulness.

He who forgets temporal things, as believers are accustomed to do, becomes Amon, that is, “faithful.” For the person who despises and forgets temporal things defrauds no one of what is his. Josiah follows: for one who despises earthly things and is faithful merits heaven and confidently awaits the salvation of the Lord. Josiah is interpreted “the salvation of the Lord.”

### ALLEGORY

We must see in what way Christ is prefigured in these fathers. David signifies Christ, because David overcame Goliath and Christ likewise overcame the devil. David is called “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance.” He is the one of whom it is said: “The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord, mighty in battle” (Ps. 23); and again: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44).

David also bears the person of Christ in taking Bathsheba. Christ, seated upon the throne of his Father, saw the Church of the Gentiles washing away her sins; she pleased him, and he joined her to himself. She is interpreted “the seventh well,” or “the well of abundance,” because the Church abundantly contains the depth of sevenfold spiritual grace.

Uriah—that is, the devil—is killed, who had formerly been the husband of Gentility. Uriah is interpreted “my light is God,” because the devil, created in the beginning, said that his own light was God’s, since because of it he wished to make himself God.

Or Bathsheba signifies the Law, in which was contained under figures the depth of sevenfold grace. It had been joined to Uriah, that is, to the Jewish people, who gloried in the light of God, that is, in knowledge of the Law. Christ saw from the throne, that is, from heaven, the Law washing itself, that is, laying aside its figures; and it pleased him. Then he summoned the Jewish people and wished to bring it into the house, that is, into the spiritual understanding of the Law. But it refused and said that the ark, that is, the Church, was in tents, that is, under figures. Therefore it said that it would not enter the house, that is, receive another understanding.

It therefore received the letters of its own death, that is, the literal understanding which leads it to death while it refuses to understand the Law spiritually.

Christ is called Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” because “he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2). He is Rehoboam, that is, “the rushing of the people,” who after the Ascension swiftly converted peoples to the faith through the apostles. He is again Abijah, that is, “the Lord is Father,” because he is the one who says: “I shall be to him a father” (2 Kings 7), because as Lord he made all that he willed.

Christ is also Asa, that is, “lifting up,” because he is the one who took away the sins of the world. He is likewise Jehoshaphat, that is, “judging,” because he is the one who shall judge the world. Christ is called Joram, that is, “exalted,” because he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended” (John 3). He is Uzziah, that is, “the Lord’s strong one”; he is the one of whom it is said: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Ps. 117).

He is Jonathan, that is, “our progress,” because he advances daily in his Church. He is Ahaz, that is, “comprehending God,” because “no one knows the Father except the Son” (Matt. 11). Christ is Hezekiah, that is, “the Lord strengthened me.” He is the one who says to the apostles: “It is I; do not be afraid” (John 6).

He is Manasseh, that is, “forgetful,” who says to the converted sinner: “I shall remember none of his iniquities” (Ezek. 18). He is Amon, that is, “faithful” or “nourishing,” of whom it is said: “The Lord is faithful in all his ways” (Ps. 144), who gathers his children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings (Matt. 24). He is Josiah, that is, “the Lord’s incense,” [Col. 1245A] because he is the one who says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight” (Ps. 140).

### HISTORY

Josiah begot Jeconiah. It is read in the Book of Kings that Josiah begot Joahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. Joahaz succeeded his father in the kingdom; when he was taken by the king of Egypt, his brother Jehoiakim was put in his place. But Nebuchadnezzar came up against Jerusalem and took Jehoiakim. He became his servant for three years, then rebelled against him again; and the Lord sent many evils against him through his enemies. At last he died, and his son Jehoiakim—also called Jeconiah—reigned in his stead. He was taken by the king of Babylon, and Zedekiah was installed in his place. In Zedekiah’s time Jerusalem was destroyed, and he himself, after his eyes had been put out, was led with the entire people into Babylon. But in the thirty-seventh year of his exile, Merodach, king of Babylon, spared Jehoiakim and made him eat bread in his presence all the days of his life (4 Kings 25).

It is asked why Jeconiah is called Josiah’s son when Josiah begot Jehoiakim and Jehoiakim begot Jeconiah. For if we say that Josiah begot Jeconiah through Jehoiakim, then, since we count the same Jeconiah twice—at the end of the preceding group of fourteen and at the beginning of the following one—in order that three complete groups of fourteen may be found, there will no longer be forty-two fathers, nor will three distinct groups of fourteen be found.

This is solved in various ways. Jerome [Note: [Col. 1245] St Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew*, book I, chapter 1, verse 12 ff., ed. Migne.] says that both father and son—that is, Jehoiakim and Jehoiakim—are called Jeconiah. Thus we have one at the end of the preceding group of fourteen and the other at the beginning of the following one. When it says, “Josiah begot Jeconiah,” we are to understand Jehoiakim; but when it says, “Jeconiah begot Shealtiel,” we are to take Jeconiah.

It should be known that the name of the earlier Jehoiakim is written with *c* and *m*, that of the later with *ch* and *n*; through scribal fault these were confused for a long time.

Augustine, however, says that the same Jeconiah—that is, Jehoiakim—must be understood, on account of the meaning of a certain mystery. For the migration into Babylon from Jerusalem signifies the migration of the apostles from Judaea to the Gentiles, in which migration Christ became the cornerstone, embracing both peoples. Therefore, when dealing with the migration, he wished to place the same Jeconiah, as it were at the corner of the two groups of fourteen, so that he might embrace both walls and bear the person of Christ embracing both peoples.

It is asked: Why is Josiah said to have begotten his sons “at the migration,” when he did not see the migration? Because the Evangelist, knowing the outcome of the event already past, said that he begot sons not at the time of the migration but “for the migration,” that is, in order that they might migrate. He mentions his brothers so that those whose iniquity was common might share their misery.

Jeconiah begot Shealtiel, and Shealtiel Zerubbabel, [Col. 1246A] and Zerubbabel Abiud. But this appears contrary to the genealogy read in Chronicles. For it is said there: “Jeconiah begot Shealtiel and Pedaiah; and Pedaiah Zerubbabel; and Zerubbabel Meshullam” (1 Chron. 3), and the sons of Shealtiel are not enumerated.

But we know that many things in Chronicles have been corrupted through scribal fault, whence arise many indeterminate genealogical questions, which the Apostle commands us to avoid (1 Tim. 1). Or it may be said that Shealtiel and Pedaiah were one person with two names; or that Shealtiel and Pedaiah were brothers and had sons of the same name, and that the historian followed the genealogy of Zerubbabel son of Pedaiah, not Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel.

From Abiud to Joseph no history is found in Chronicles. Nevertheless, it must be believed that the Apostle received from the Holy Spirit what he says concerning the subsequent generations, just as he did the other things which he says. It is also read that the Hebrews had many other annals, called *Words of Days*, like those among the Romans in which the events of each entire year were recorded. Of these it is said that Herod, the foreign king, burned many in order that the order of the royal line might be confused. Perhaps Joseph had read the names of his ancestors there at that time, or had hidden some of the annals themselves, or had preserved them in some other way by which the Evangelist could know the sequence of this genealogy. Yet this must be believed: the Evangelist was certain of that genealogy, for he arranged it thus.

Jacob begot Joseph. It is asked why Matthew calls Jacob Joseph’s father, whereas Luke calls him and records him as the son of Heli, and Heli the son of Matthat. But it should be known that Matthat, who descended from David through Nathan, had a wife named Esta, by whom he begot Heli. After Matthat’s death, Mathan, who descended from David through Solomon, took the same wife and begot Jacob by her. Thus Heli and Jacob were uterine brothers.

Heli took a wife and died without offspring. Jacob therefore raised up seed for his brother and begot Joseph by that same wife. Thus Joseph is called Heli’s son according to the Law, and Jacob’s son according to nature.

Matthew cannot say, “Joseph begot Christ,” although Joseph is named as his father by adoption; rather, he says “the husband of Mary” and places Joseph and Mary in the same degree. Since, according to Hebrew custom, a genealogy is not ordinarily reckoned through women, he names Joseph, who had married Mary by the law of kinship. Thus, through Joseph, Mary is proved to be of David’s line. This can sufficiently be proved elsewhere, namely from the fact that Mary went with Joseph to Bethlehem to register, because he was of the house and family of David; and the angel gives testimony concerning Christ that he is of David’s line, when he says to Mary: “The Lord God shall give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1).

“Of whom,” he says, not “of whom [plural],” in order to prove that the Messiah was born from the virgin alone and to show that he was born by a manner of generation different from the others—not by the desire of the flesh, [Col. 1247A] but by the Holy Spirit.

### MORAL SENSE

Let us see what moral meaning these fathers produce in us. Jeconiah, that is, “the Lord’s preparation.” After someone has merited the salvation of the Lord, nothing else remains except that he should meet the Lord coming to the wedding feast, prepared with a lamp, or prepared to endure adversities if they should occur.

Shealtiel follows, that is, “God is my petition.” For one who is prepared asks for nothing but God alone. Yet meanwhile he becomes Zerubbabel, that is, “teacher of Babylon.” For a citizen of Jerusalem sometimes becomes the teacher of earthly people—namely, when a holy person becomes prelate over people dwelling in confusion, whom he instructs by word and example.

But now, conversely, wretches that we are, we make a citizen of Babylon into a teacher of Jerusalem. When a righteous prelate has well instructed those subject to him, he causes them to recognize concerning God that “this is my father,” which is the meaning of Abiud; and then that people rises from vices. For Eliakim follows, which is interpreted “the Lord’s resurrection.” Then it is helped to work well, which is the meaning of Azor, and thus becomes righteous. Zadok is interpreted “righteous”; hence *ṣedeq* means “righteousness,” and from it comes Melchizedek, that is, “king of righteousness.”

Just as Christ rose and ascended and sent the Holy Spirit, so the people of God first rise in baptism, are helped by the Holy Spirit to work well in confirmation, and thus become righteous—truly righteous because they love neighbour and God, as we have through the following names. Achim is called “this is my brother,” and Eliud, “my God.” Thus the faithful person says, through love of neighbour: “This is my brother”; and through love of God acknowledges: “My God.”

Eleazar follows, that is, “my God is helper.” For it is compounded from Eliud and Azor: Eliud means “my God,” and Azor “helper” or “helped.” For what purpose he acknowledges God as his helper, Mathan shows; Mathan is called “gift” or “giving.” For through good works he awaits God the giver; and just as he struggled at the beginning and overthrew vices, so also at the end of his life he must struggle continuously. Therefore Jacob follows afterwards, and thus one comes to the fullness and increase of virtues, signified by Joseph. [Col. 1247D] Joseph means “increase.”

But above all virtues the incarnation of Christ is necessary, without which no one can be saved; it is designated by Mary. For Christ’s incarnation was for us a star on the sea and a light in darkness. Through that incarnation Jesus was born, who will lead us into the promised land—he who is called Christ. This is said in order to show that he is the Messiah. He saved us and made us kings and priests.

### ALLEGORY

Let us now come to the allegory. Jeconiah, that is, “the Lord’s preparation,” applies to Christ. For he is the one who says: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14).

Note that the former Jeconiah is called the resurrection of the Lord, while the latter Jeconiah is called the preparation of the Lord. [Col. 1248A] Both apply to Christ, who says: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11). Salathiel, that is, “my petition is God,” applies to him who says: “Holy Father, keep those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, even as we are” (John 17). Zerubbabel, that is, “master of Babylon,” namely of confusion, applies to him who converted the world from the error of idolatry to the life of truth. Abiud, that is, “this is my father,” applies to him of whom the Father says: “He shall call upon me: Thou art my Father” (Ps. 88 [89]). Eliakim, that is, “God raising up,” is he who says: “Everyone who sees the Son and believes in him has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6). Azor, that is, “helped,” is he who says: “Behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the protector of my soul” (Ps. 53 [54]). Zadok, that is, “justified,” [Col. 1248B] is he of whom it is said: “The Lord is righteous and loves righteous deeds” (Ps. 10 [11]). Achim, that is, “this is my brother”—who else but he who wished to become man so that he might have brothers, of whom he himself might say: “I will declare thy name to my brethren” (Heb. 2)? Eliud, that is, “my God,” applies to Christ, who says: “My God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27; Mark 15). Eleazar, that is, “my God is helper,” is he who speaks in the person of humankind: “My God is my helper, and I will hope in him” (Ps. 17 [18]). Mathan, that is, “giving” or “given,” is he who “gave gifts to men” (Eph. 4), and of whom it is said: “Thus God loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3). Joseph, that is, “adding,” applies to Christ, because he added the Gentiles to the Jews.

Therefore all these generations [Col. 1248C] are divided into three sets of fourteen. The first runs from Abraham to David, David being included in it; the second runs from David to the deportation, David not being included in it, but being contained under the deportation; the third runs from the deportation to Christ, in which, if Jeconiah is counted twice, the deportation is included. In the first set of fourteen are signified people before the Law; among them one finds certain people of the natural law, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all down to Solomon. In the second set of fourteen are signified people under the Law, and all those found in it were under the Law. In the third are people of grace, in which Christ is included, who was the giver of grace; [Col. 1248D] in it also took place the liberation from Babylonian captivity, signifying the liberation from the captivity of the devil wrought through Christ.

Thus all those placed in this genealogy through the distinction of different times are said universally to signify Christ’s faithful people, both because of the worthiness of their lives and because of the interpretation of their names. Hence they are all counted by the number fourteen, because all who are justified must fulfill the commandments of the Old Testament, represented by ten, which signifies the Decalogue, and the commandments of the New, represented by four, which signifies the four Gospels. For fourteen is made up of four and ten. Or, in this number the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is signified. [Col. 1249A] For it is itself made up of seven and seven. Its doubling signifies that the grace of the Holy Spirit is necessary for body and soul if they are to be saved. Taken together, they are forty-two, if the two Jeconiahs are understood; in them the totality of the faithful is expressed. For this number is composed of six and seven, since six times seven is forty-two. By six are understood the six works of mercy; by seven is signified eternal rest, because “on the seventh day God rested from all his work which he had done” (Gen. 2). All saints attain eternal rest through works of mercy. Or, by seven is understood the present life, which revolves through seven days.

But if, according to Augustine, only forty are counted, [Col. 1249B] Christ being excluded, all the saints are likewise understood by this number, because it is composed of four and ten. Ten refers to the Decalogue; four to the present life, which is spent through the four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. For all saints ought to keep the commandments of the Law in the present life. Or, as understood above, ten signifies the Old Testament and four the New.

“But the generation of Christ was thus.” It is as though he said: the other generations arise from the desire of the flesh, but Christ’s generation differed from those, being solely from the Holy Spirit. It was thus, as I shall say, established from the beginning of the world in Providence. Or otherwise: such are the divisions into three sets of fourteen. But the generation [Col. 1249C] of Christ, taken as a whole in the mass, was as we have said.

“When his mother Mary had been betrothed.” Matthew here omits many things related by Luke: namely, Christ’s annunciation by Gabriel to Mary; how, after the annunciation, Mary arose and went in haste into the hill country, to a city of Judaea; how she entered the house of Zachariah and greeted Elizabeth; how Mary’s conception was revealed to Elizabeth by the Holy Spirit when the child leaped for joy in her womb; and how Mary remained there for three months and returned to her own house. After that return, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit; and Matthew begins at this point, saying: “When [Col. 1249D] she had been betrothed.”

Betrothal took place some time before continuous cohabitation. Meanwhile the wife was under the protection of her husband, with frequent visits, until the marriage solemnities were celebrated. The question is asked: why did Christ wish to be born of a betrothed virgin? For many reasons: so that the genealogy might be traced through Joseph, and that Mary might be defended from disgrace. Since a woman is of the weaker and more modest sex, he wished that his mother should not protect herself from disgrace. He himself, indeed, was said to have a demon, was called a carpenter’s son and a drinker of wine, and yet willingly endured these and other reproaches. Moreover, he did not wish to give virgins an occasion for excuse on the grounds that the Lord’s mother had been defamed. For another reason also he wished to be born of a betrothed virgin: lest, [Col. 1250A] condemned for fornication, she should be overwhelmed with stones; and also so that she might have someone to provide for her, to take the child and her into Egypt and bring them back, and to be his foster-father.

Finally, there is another principal reason: that the virgin’s childbirth might be concealed from the devil, so that, when he saw her pregnant, he might think that she had been made pregnant by her betrothed, who was permitted even during the time of betrothal. Mary also signifies the Church, which is both virgin and bride. He therefore says:

“When Mary his mother.” Not that she was already a mother, but the Evangelist calls her mother from the standpoint of his own time.

“Had been betrothed to Joseph,” as has already been said.

“Before they came together,” that is, before the solemnities [Col. 1250B] of the marriage were celebrated; or before they came together in common cohabitation; or before they came together for physical union. Yet this is not said because they afterward came together. This manner of speaking is like someone saying, “He died before he repented”; it does not follow that he repented after death.

“She was found.” By Joseph, as a man solicitous concerning his wife. “With child,” that is, pregnant after three months, namely when she had returned from Elizabeth. It occurred by divine will that the virgin did not disclose the angel’s annunciation to her husband. For if the young woman had revealed it to him, he would not easily have believed her; indeed, he might perhaps have suspected some fault. Therefore it was to be concealed from him [Col. 1250C] until that secret should be disclosed to him by an angelic manifestation.

“By the Holy Spirit.” The Evangelist adds this on his own part, so that, when she was said to be with child, every evil suspicion might be removed from the minds of the hearers. It should be noted that Christ was born of Mary in one manner and of the Holy Spirit in another. When it is said that he was born of Mary, this must be understood as being from her substance; thus “of” is material. But when he is said to have been born of the Holy Spirit, the birth is understood as having taken place, as it were, through the power of the Holy Spirit; thus “of” is potential. Compare: “From whom are all things,” that is, from whose power, though all things are not from his substance. Therefore he is said to have been born by the power of the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit cleansed his mother from every sin. [Col. 1250D] He also prepared the place in which the divinity would be incarnate. And just as lustful desire separates seed from the father, so the operation of the Holy Spirit separated from the mother that little flesh in which the Word of God was formed; it gradually grew in the womb like other children, and, when others are given life by a soul, Christ himself was given life by a soul. Although this operation is attributed to the Holy Spirit, it is common to the whole Trinity. But those things which occur by the grace and goodness of God alone are called gifts of the Holy Spirit, who is called God’s goodness, love, and concord, because he proceeds from both persons of God.

“But Joseph.” Since Joseph discovered so wondrous a matter, he was uncertain what to do. Since he knew her to be chaste and did not know whence he could suspect evil of her, it would have been impious to defame her. [Col. 1251A] On the other hand, justice did not require him to join himself to a matter unknown to him, since she was either good or bad. If she was bad, he ought not to associate himself with an evil matter; if she was good, he feared that he was not worthy. Thus he found a middle course: to dismiss her secretly, so that, though dismissed, she would not seem to have been dismissed. He would continue to speak with her and provide for her, yet would not receive her into continual cohabitation.

“When he wished to dismiss her, because he was righteous”: he is called compassionate because he defended her from disgrace. And this is the meaning: because he was righteous, he wished to dismiss her; because he did not wish to expose her publicly, that is, to defame her, he wished to do this secretly. Where we have “expose publicly,” the Greeks have *propalare*, “make public.” Or: because he did not wish to bring her into his house for continuous cohabitation. Thus he reflected for a long time. [Col. 1251B] In this is marked the disposition of a wise person, who wishes to undertake nothing rashly.

While he was considering these things, he merited divine counsel. The angel impressed its image upon his sleeping soul—not that his mind saw a body, but that it seemed to see one. Angelic appearance occurs in two ways: to one awake, by assuming an airy body; to one asleep, by impressing an image upon the imagination. Yet the angel present with Joseph had no body. Such visions were familiar and frequent among the Jews. He is called “an angel of the Lord,” lest he be thought evil. And he said: “Joseph.” By calling him by name, he presents himself as known and familiar to him, and makes him attentive when he says: “Son of David.” In a sense he urges him to recall that he and Mary are of the line [Col. 1251C] of David, to whom the promise was made; therefore he should by no means doubt that the promise could be fulfilled in Mary, when he adds: “Do not fear.” He shows why Joseph had been considering this: namely, because he feared to associate himself with an unknown matter.

“Take Mary thy wife,” into marital union and continual cohabitation. When he calls her his wife, Augustine says that this example splendidly teaches married believers that, even when continence is preserved by mutual consent, they may remain and be called a marriage—not through bodily intercourse, but through a preserved affection of mind. “For that which is born in her,” etc. It is as though he said: Do not fear, because it is not evil. For that which has been born in her is of the Holy Spirit. It is one thing to be born in her, another to be born from her. To be born from her [Col. 1251D] is to come forth into the light; to be born in her is to be conceived.
