“But she shall bear a son.” And lest Joseph should seem to himself no longer necessary to the marriage, since the conception had taken place without his service, the angel shows that, although he was not necessary to conception, he was useful for care: for she would bear a son, and then he would be necessary to mother and son—to the mother, to defend her from disgrace; to the son, to nourish and circumcise him. This circumcision is indicated when he says:

“And thou shalt call his name Jesus.” For it is customary for a name to be given at circumcision. He says, “thou shalt call,” but not “thou shalt impose,” because it was imposed from eternity.

“For he shall save.” He gives the reason for the name: because he shall save, not just anyone, but his own people in faith—not from bodily enemies, as [Col. 1252A] Joshua and David did, but from their sins. This belongs not to human beings, but to God alone.

“But all this was done”: that the virgin should be betrothed, that she should be preserved chaste, that she should be found pregnant, that it should be revealed to Joseph through an angel, and that she should be said to have conceived and to be about to bear. All this, I say, was done “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet Isaiah, saying” (Isa. 7): “Behold, a virgin.” For the prophecy that the virgin would conceive and bear would not have been fulfilled unless she had been betrothed, lest she be stoned; unless she had been found pregnant, so that Joseph might afterward dismiss her secretly and, thus made public, she might not be stoned; and unless the secret had been disclosed by an angel, so that Joseph might take her, lest it should somehow be reported that she had been dismissed because of disgrace and she should then perish by stoning. [Col. 1252B] Therefore, if she had perished before giving birth, the prophecy that says, “She shall bear a son,” would have been nullified. It was necessary that this be fulfilled.

One kind of prophecy proceeds from God’s predestination and must happen in every way, so that it is fulfilled without our free choice; such is the prophecy now under discussion. Another proceeds from God’s foreknowledge, with which our choice is involved: cooperating with grace, we attain reward; or, justly abandoned by it, punishment. Another is not from foreknowledge, but is a kind of threat made in the human manner. Such are: “Thou shalt die, and shalt not live” (Isa. 38), and “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 4). These are not fulfilled according to what the words appear to say, yet are true according to their meaning. Just as, when threatening our servant, we say, “I will kill you,” while understanding, “unless you correct yourself,” [Col. 1252C] so God, speaking in the human manner, says, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,” meaning, unless the Ninevites amend themselves; and, “Thou shalt die, and shalt not live,” unless you weep. It may also be understood otherwise.

“But all this was done, that it might be fulfilled,” etc. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.” Note that he follows Isaiah’s sense rather than his words: instead of “shall conceive,” he says, “shall have in the womb”; and instead of “shall be called,” “people shall call.” The prophet wished to give more particularly this name Emmanuel, which expresses both natures. For it is interpreted, “God with us,” as though to say: God is with us, that is, in our nature. “Which being interpreted”: do not wonder if a Hebrew speaker, speaking with Hebrews, explains Hebrew by Hebrew, since among Latin speakers there are likewise many things explained by other Latin words.

“But Joseph, rising up.” He did not merely do what the angel commanded, but did it in the very manner commanded.

“MORAL SENSE.—BEDE. Whoever is moved by God should delay no longer: let him rise from sleep and do what he is commanded.”

“Until she bore.” It is sufficiently certain that, after Christ was born, after Joseph heard the shepherds, after he saw the Magi, after Simeon and Anna prophesied concerning him, he did not dare touch her. Thus the time is excluded in which there might be greater suspicion, as David says: “Until I place” (Ps. 109 [110]), etc.

“Her firstborn son.” “Her,” that is, from her substance. “Firstborn,” that is, begotten of the Father before all begotten things. In these words the natures [Col. 1253A] of divinity and humanity are indicated. Or he is called firstborn according to customary speech, without reference to a second child, because whatever is born first is called firstborn. Or he is firstborn in relation to all the faithful, according to Paul: “that he might be the firstborn among many brethren,” and this in dignity.

“And he called.” Here Matthew omits many things related by Luke, who shows how and where he was born, namely in Bethlehem, and on what occasion Mary and Joseph went there. For he says: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus” (Luke 2), etc.; and he tells how angels appeared to the shepherds. Matthew, however, makes mention only of the day of circumcision, saying: “And he called his name Jesus,” which Luke recounts more fully.

## CHAPTER II

“Now when he had been born.” Although Matthew omits Christ’s birth, he touches on it briefly in order to relate the arrival of the Magi, noting place, time, and tribe. He notes the place when he says “in Bethlehem”; the tribe, when he says “of Judah”; and the time, when he adds, “in the days of King Herod.” He adds “of Judah” to distinguish it from the Bethlehem in the land of Zebulun. For there are two Bethlehems: one in the land of Zebulun, the other in the tribe of Judah. The latter was formerly Ephrathah and was afterward called Bethlehem as an omen of Christ’s coming. Ephrathah is interpreted “seeing fury” or “mirror,” because Herod afterward exercised his fury [Col. 1253C] against the children and, as though in a mirror, awaited Christ’s coming. But Bethlehem is interpreted “house of bread,” because the bread of angels was born there. It was fitting that he who came forth from the tribe of Judah should be born in Bethlehem of Judah.

The time also accords. For behold, a foreigner had become king of Israel, so that the prophecy might be fulfilled which says: “The sceptre shall not be removed from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49). From the time the children of Israel entered the land of promise, they had judges until Saul, then kings until the Babylonian deportation. But after their return from Babylon, the supreme government was administered by high priests down to Hyrcanus, both high priest and king. When he was harassed by his brother’s envy and finally killed by Herod, the kingdom of Judaea was handed over to Herod by Augustus’s command. [Col. 1253D] Thus the prophecy was fulfilled which says: “When the Holy of Holies comes, your anointing shall cease.”

“Behold, Magi.” These three Magi were not, as is said, sorcerers, but learned astrologers from the land of the Persians and Chaldaeans, where the river Saba is. Hence the region is called Sabaean; beside it lies Arabia, from which these three kings came. For there are two Arabias: one where Sinai is, of which the Apostle says, “Mount Sinai is in Arabia” (Gal. 4); the other in the torrid zone. Hence Lucan:

> “You Arabs, you have come into an unknown world.”

They saw a new star in the sky, signifying that a new king had been born. For the Babylonians and Chaldaeans are skilled in the stars. It is uncertain whether the star arose in the east, or whether they, situated there, saw a star that had arisen near the land of Israel. It could have arisen for them in the east and led them to Jerusalem; but when they came to Jerusalem, as to the capital of the kingdom, and turned aside to Herod, they lost it for a time. When they departed from him:

> “Behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was.”

It could also be that, while they were in the east, the star appeared near Jerusalem; remembering Balaam’s prophecy—Balaam being from Chaldaea—“A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man from Israel” (Num. 24), and stirred by the star’s appearance as its fulfillment, they came to Jerusalem. When they turned aside to Herod, it disappeared until they left him; then the star again went before them and led them as far as Bethlehem. [Col. 1254B] But the actual truth of the matter cannot be determined from the Gospel. For when they say, “We saw his star in the east,” this may mean either, “We, being in the east, saw the star near Jerusalem,” or “We saw his star situated in the east.”

Yet they are believed to have been stirred by divine inspiration, since they believe him to be God whom they seek to worship. Jerome, however, says on Isaiah: “The Magi, taught by demons from the east, or understanding from Balaam’s prophecy that the Son of God had been born—the one who would destroy all the power of their art—came to Bethlehem; and, with the star showing the way, worshiped the child.” They are said to have been taught by demons because they had been instructed through astronomy, which demons taught. For the demons did not know of Christ’s birth.

The Gospel does not report how many kings there were; their number is inferred from the number of gifts. They are believed to have come not alone, but attended by many soldiers, though the Gospel mentions only the kings. The Magi are said to have come from the east because they were truly situated in the actual east; yet everything beyond Jerusalem toward the east is called east in relation to them. The star is believed to have appeared only from the day of the Lord’s birth and, being new, to have ceased after accomplishing its task. Fulgentius says: “When the child was born, he made a new star.” Nor should one wonder that they came to Bethlehem in thirteen days, since they had Arabian horses and dromedaries and were not very distant from Judaea. Haymo nevertheless relates that the star appeared even before Christ’s birth, that they began their journey at once, and that after accomplishing its office the star fell into the well of Bethlehem and sometimes appears there only to virgins. This is considered frivolous.

“GREGORY. Rightly, when the Lord was born, an angel appeared to the shepherds; but it was not an angel, but a star, that led the Magi. For to the Jews, as beings who used reason, a rational creature—that is, an angel—had to preach. But the Gentiles, because they did not know how to use reason, had to be led through signs. For signs were given to unbelievers, not to believers. It was also fitting that Christ should be shown through a star to the Chaldaeans, who knew about stars, and through angels to the Jews, who had heard much of angels in the prophets [Col. 1255A] and had themselves sometimes seen them. Yet both languages were from heaven, both that of the stars and that of the angels, because the language of the prophets had now ceased.”

“Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” Observe how the Jews are refuted by such an inquiry. The Gentile seeks God, declares that he has been born, and asserts that he is king of the Jews. But the Jew scorns to seek the one beside him, as though he did not recognize him when found, and utterly refuses to acknowledge his own king. All this signifies the illumination of the Gentiles and the blindness of the Jews. Hence they did not merit to see the star. When they said, “Where is the king of the Jews?” lest they seem to be asking after Herod, they specify by saying, “who has been born.” Allegorically, in the firstfruits of the Gentiles salvation is signified, and the Gentiles’ coming to Christ. With the star leading—that is, with the illumination of faith, lacking which the Jews will not come to Christ—when they turn aside to the Jews, they lose the star; because when they seek counsel from wicked people and from the devil, they lose true illumination.

“For we saw his star in the east.” They rightly call it his, because although all stars were his, having been created by the same one, this one belonged to Christ in a particular sense because it announced him as newly born. The other stars were made from the beginning of the world to distinguish times and to effect certain things hidden from us. But King Herod, hearing that another king of the Jews than himself had been born, was troubled—on his own account, because he feared the destruction of his kingdom; and because of the anger of the Romans, which he would suffer if he assented. For [Col. 1255C] the Romans had decreed that no one should be called king or god without their consent. He was troubled because of the crowd accompanying the Magi, as though ashamed that a king other than himself was being sought. Hence note that he is here called king, so that, in comparison with the one sought, he may be understood to be an outsider. See that when the King of heaven is born, the king of earth is troubled: for when heavenly exaltation is revealed, earthly height is confounded.

“And all Jerusalem with him,” wishing to favor the one whom it feared. For people are more than justly inclined to favor those cruel rulers whom they endure. Hence Solomon: “An unjust king has all his ministers wicked” (Prov. 29).

“And assembling,” etc. Herod investigates two things: the place and the time. He learns the place from the Jews, who knew it from the prophets; [Col. 1255D] he learns the time from the Magi, who knew it from the star, so that he may search for the child around that place, and, if deceived by the Magi, kill all children of that time and that place. The scribes were very learned, adding their own traditions to the other traditions of Moses. The Magi did not know the place because they had not read the prophets.

“It is written through the prophet Micah: ‘And thou, Bethlehem, land of Judah,’ etc.” (Mic. 5). It should be noted that, in giving scriptural testimony, the writers sometimes quote less, through forgetfulness or envy, and say some things differently; nevertheless, they express the prophet’s meaning and truth. For it is written thus in Hebrew: “And thou, Bethlehem Ephrathah, art small among the thousands of Judah; from thee shall go forth one who shall be ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (ibid.). [Col. 1256A] According to these words, the sense is this: O Bethlehem, formerly called Ephrathah, although you are a small village among the thousands of cities of Judah, nevertheless Christ shall be born from you, and he shall be ruler of Israel. He is not only from David, but his going forth is from the beginning, because from the beginning he was born from the Father, as it is written: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). And lest he seem to have a beginning, it is defined by saying, “from the days of eternity.”

This sense does not differ greatly from the words set down in the Gospel. When it says “land of Judah,” it means as much as Ephrathah. And when it says, “Thou art by no means least among the rulers of Judah,” that is, among the chief cities of Judah, this is understood not of size but of dignity.

“Then Herod, having secretly summoned the Magi.” Such is the diligence of one seeking, so that if he finds the child he may do what he afterward shows himself to desire; but if not, he may be excused before the Romans. He also investigates whether their king will make the Jews sad or glad. Therefore he wished secretly to investigate this matter from the Magi, away from the Jews, because he feared that the Jews might conceal the king promised, as though by a divine oracle, if they perceived that he wished to kill him. [Col. 1256B] He also promised to worship him, lest they recognize his deceit, and so that they might instead report to him concerning the child without suspicion. Therefore, sending them to Bethlehem, he said: “Go, inquire diligently concerning the child.” Having learned the place and the time, he does not wish to be ignorant of the child’s identity. Note that he commanded what they would have done without a command. But when he adds, “And when you have found him, report to me,” the command is exceedingly presumptuous, because he thinks that everyone must obey him. But, to invite them to report, he adds: “That I too may come and worship him.” Here Herod plays the part of hypocrites, who, while they seek God falsely, never deserve to find him.

“And behold, the star.” Once the counsel of the wicked had been left behind, behold, true knowledge returned. A star is any good exhortation leading to Christ, or rather faith, which is the illumination of the mind. “Until it came,” etc. Here it appears that the star was placed in the air, because it was very near the house in which the child was. Otherwise they could not have distinguished that house from another. “And when they saw the star, they rejoiced with joy.” One rejoices with joy who rejoices because of God, who is true joy; just as one lives with life who lives in virtues, and dies with death who is in sins. He adds “great,” because it concerned a great thing, and “exceedingly,” because nothing is greater than it.

“And entering the house.” It occurred by divine guidance that Joseph was not present, lest any occasion of evil suspicion be given to the Gentiles. “And falling down, they worshiped him.” They did not do to Herod what they did to the child, because they believed the Word to be in the flesh. “And opening their treasures.” Although the Arabs follow the custom of their nation in offering gifts, since they abound in gold, frankincense, and various kinds of spices, they nevertheless understand something mystical in the gifts. Gold signifies royal power; frankincense, divinity and priesthood, for frankincense is offered only to God and by a priest. Myrrh signifies mortal humanity. For the bodies of the dead are embalmed with myrrh, because through its extreme bitterness it destroys worms.

[Col. 1257A] “POPE LEO. The question is whether they each offered one gift, or whether each offered all three. But it is more fitting to the mystery to confess that each offered all three. For each believed him king, God, and capable of suffering.”

“MORAL SENSE.—GREGORY. We offer gold to the newborn king if we shine in his sight with the brilliance of heavenly wisdom. We offer frankincense if, through devotion to prayer, we burn the thoughts of the flesh upon the altar of the heart. We offer myrrh if, through abstinence, we mortify the vices of the flesh.”

“MYSTICAL SENSE. The Gentiles come, leaving Herod—that is, the devil, who is interpreted ‘clothed in skins’—or leaving hypocrites, who are truly clothed in skins, that is, clothed in dead skins, namely sins. Hence Adam and Eve are read to have been clothed in garments of skins after sin. [Col. 1257B] They come with the star leading, that is, faith; and they enter the house, that is, the Church, when they become part of the Church; and they find Christ with his mother. The mother of Christ is the preachers, who give birth to him in the minds of their hearers. Joseph was absent, that is, the Jewish people, who because of their perfidy and unbelief have no place in the fellowship of the Church. They are three because the Gentiles come from the three parts of the world: Asia, Europe, and Africa; or because they sprang from Noah’s three sons. They open treasures in the house when they show the faith of the heart through confession of the mouth. A treasure is properly opened in the house, not on the road, lest it perhaps be seized by robbers. By this we are taught not to disclose boastfully the treasure of a good conscience, [Col. 1257C] lest it be stolen from us by spiritual enemies through vain glory; rather, let us offer it to God alone in a secure place, that is, in the secret place of our hearts.

“They offer three gifts,” that is, faith in the Holy Trinity; or, having opened the treasures of the Scriptures, they offer the historical, moral, and allegorical sense; or logic, physics, and ethics, making them serve the Catholic faith. The child does not speak to them, lest the divinity be revealed before the time and so that his true humanity may be acknowledged; hence he is immediately sent into Egypt.

“And having received an answer,” etc. For in their minds they sought what the divine will wished concerning their return to Herod, and therefore they merited divine counsel. It should be known that all saw the same vision [Col. 1257D] in one night.

“By another way.” It is said that the Magi entered the sea and, hiring ships, reached Persia. When these ships had returned, Herod, thinking to overtake them and hearing of their passage, burned in fury the ships that had carried them.

“MORAL SENSE. The faithful are warned that, having found Christ, they should not return to Herod, that is, to the devil; but by another way than the devil’s way—that is, by the way of virtues—they should return to the heavenly homeland.”

“After they had departed.” Here Matthew omits the day of purification, on which all firstborn were offered in the temple, together with a lamb or a pair of turtledoves or pigeons. Although they feared Herod, they nevertheless did not dare transgress the Law by failing to bring the child to the temple. There Simeon received him into his arms and [Col. 1258A] Anna prophesied many things concerning him. When this had been done, they withdrew to Nazareth. Therefore, when the report concerning the child had begun to spread, the angel Gabriel was sent to have the child carried into Egypt.

“Arise and take the child.” It is the custom of Scripture often to call him “the child,” so that we may recognize him of whom it was said: “A child is born to us” (Isa. 9).

“MORAL SENSE. Christ’s flight teaches us that whenever we have something reasonable to do, we should not expose ourselves to danger. Hence it is said: ‘If they persecute you in one city, flee into another’ (Matt. 23 [probably 10:23]). He also fled because it was written: ‘Thou shalt not kill a lamb in its mother’s milk’ (Deut. 14); that is, Christ was not to be killed in infancy. For if Christ had died before his preaching, the purpose of his incarnation’s coming would have been frustrated. Isaiah foretold this flight: ‘Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt, and its idols shall be moved’ (Isa. 19). This happened because, when the Lord entered Egypt, the idols of the temples fell. After he had remained hidden there for seven years, he lived for a longer time in a certain city called Heliopolis, that is, City of the Sun.”

“MYSTICAL SENSE. Joseph figures the preachers who increase the Lord’s people, whence his name is interpreted ‘increase.’ They carried the child and his mother into Egypt when they brought the faith of Christ and of the Church to the Gentiles, leaving Herod, that is, the unbelief of the Jews. They carry them in the night, namely so long as the Jews remain in the night of ignorance. But at last, when Herod has died—[Col. 1258C] that is, when Jewish unbelief has died through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch—the faith of Christ is transferred to the Jews. Herod also represents the persecutors who were in Judaea in the time of the apostles, when Christ, in his members, that is, in his apostles, fled to the Gentiles. Note also that he called Mary “the mother of the child,” not Joseph’s wife, because thereafter Joseph was regarded not as her bridegroom but as her guardian.

Through the prophet Hosea. Then Herod, etc. Once the child had been taken into Egypt, Herod was allowed to rage and go mad, and to realize that he had been deceived by the Magi. It should be known that the slaughter of the children did not take place immediately, but was delayed for a considerable time. For when [Col. 1258D] nothing had been reported back to him, he believed that the Magi had been deceived and had therefore not returned to him; consequently he ceased for so long from seeking the child. But afterwards, when what Simeon and Anna had said about the child became widely known, he perceived that he had been deceived by the Magi, and then pursued them as far as Tarsus in Cilicia. Not finding them, he destroyed the ships by which they had crossed. On his return, however, he deferred the slaughter of the children. For he feared that the child might be hidden by his parents, and therefore thought that, while the parents were unwary, he might more successfully deceive or kill him later. Others, such as Haymo, say that he was accused at Rome and went to Rome, and that, because of these occupations, he delayed the killing of the children for two years, and therefore killed children two years old and under. But it is more probable that after a year and four days [Col. 1259A] Herod vented his cruelty upon the children; perhaps in that year he was hindered by certain affairs. Hence Augustine says: “The number and magnitude of the occupations by which royal concern might be distracted, and for many days either wholly diverted from or impeded in that purpose, cannot be enumerated; nor can the causes by which this might happen be counted.” And because he feared that the child whom the stars served might conceal his appearance somewhat above or below the age, he seems to have killed children from two years old down to children one day old. And lest the child be concealed within the borders of Bethlehem, he killed children not only in Bethlehem but throughout all its borders, so that amid such a multitude he could not escape; and perhaps for this reason he killed them from two years old, so that, as he extended the place by tyranny, he might extend the time also.

These martyrs descended into the underworld [Col. 1259B], because Christ had not yet suffered; consequently, on their feast the voices of joy are also silent—that is, the *Alleluia* and “Glory to God in the highest.” The age of two years was reckoned from Christ’s birth, which could be determined from the time of the star that he had learned from the Magi.

A voice in Ramah. According to the historical sense, this prophecy concerns the slaughter carried out by Nebuchadnezzar. Foreseeing it, the prophet says: “A voice in Ramah” (Jer. 31), as if to say: there will be such slaughter in the tribe of Benjamin that the voice of weeping and wailing will be heard in Ramah, a place twelve miles from Bethlehem; and then Rachel, who was Benjamin’s mother, will weep for her children—that is, for those who belong to her tribe—and they would not be comforted because they were not, that is, because they were dead. He spoke with reference to the likeness of [Col. 1259C] that grief and slaughter described in the book of Judges: a certain Levite came with his wife into the tribe of Benjamin, where certain utterly wicked men seized his wife and, through the excessive persistence of their sexual violation, killed her. Her husband divided her into twelve parts and sent them through the twelve tribes of Israel, displaying Benjamin’s wickedness. Therefore the other tribes rose against Benjamin and destroyed that tribe, except for three hundred men; and then such grief was experienced that the voice of mourners was heard in Ramah.

But although the prophet said this concerning Nebuchadnezzar’s persecution, he nevertheless understood what it signified. For Nebuchadnezzar denotes all persecutors of the Church, who kill the children of Rachel, that is, of the Church. [Col. 1259D] For *Rachel* is interpreted “sheep” or “one seeing the beginning.” The Church, however, is innocent and contemplates God; she is the hundredth sheep which the shepherd carried back upon his shoulders. Thus, in the time of Herod, that prophecy was fulfilled according to its signification. For Herod was the first-fruits of persecutors, and the children the first-fruits of martyrs.

Therefore the Church, through compassion, weeps for the slain martyrs, and that voice is heard in Ramah—that is, in the height, that is, in heaven. For *Ramah* is interpreted “height.” The voice is therefore said to be heard in heaven because God avenges the blood of his martyrs. And although the Church weeps over their temporal death, she nevertheless does not wish to be comforted concerning this, because they are not—that is, because they are dead—if the consolation would be that they should be recalled into the world. Or she does not wish to be comforted [Col. 1260A] so that they may be restored to this age, because her children are not, namely, of this age.

Or otherwise: he calls the persecutors themselves children of the Church, though they are children only by her affection, because she would wish them to be her children. The Church rather weeps for them also and does not wish to be comforted—that is, to have her grief assuaged—so long as she lives, because they are not, that is, because they have utterly perished.

But according to the literal sense it is asked: How did Rachel weep for her children, when the tribe of Judah, which possessed Bethlehem, arose not from Rachel but from her sister Leah? This is easily resolved, because the children were slaughtered not only in Bethlehem but in all its borders. Now the tribe of Benjamin, which arose from Rachel, was close to the tribe of Judah; hence it may be believed that not a few Benjaminites were killed [Col. 1260B]. Or because Rachel was buried near Bethlehem, the prophet wished to designate the people of that place by Rachel.

But after Herod’s death. Herod died a most shameful death, as Josephus reports. In his place his son Archelaus ruled over all Judaea and Galilee; later he was condemned by the Romans, banished into exile at Lyons, and died there. Afterwards the kingdom was divided into four parts, and Galilee was given to Herod, son of Herod and brother of Archelaus, according to Luke, who says: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate governing Judaea, Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests [Col. 1260C] Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John” (Luke 3). Therefore, although Archelaus had reigned when Christ returned from Egypt, by the time of John’s preaching the kingdom had already changed.

And go into the land of Israel. The angel does not specify what place in the land of Israel, so that Joseph, being uncertain, might return again and be made more certain by the angel’s more frequent visitation. It is asked: Why was Joseph not afraid to go into Galilee as he was into Judaea, since Archelaus ruled there also? But that craftsman could more readily remain hidden with the child in Nazareth than in Jerusalem, where the royal capital and Archelaus’s constant presence were found.

For they are dead. He uses the plural, “they are dead,” because the priests and scribes sought to kill him just as much as Herod did [Col. 1260D]. Jesus’ return to the Jews after Herod’s death signifies that, once Jewish unbelief has died, the Jews will at last be converted to Christ at the end of the age. Yet not all of them: there will be few among whom Archelaus—that is, Antichrist—will reign. For *Archelaus* is interpreted “prince of the people.” Christ, however, will withdraw into Nazareth—that is, into holiness, that is, among those in whom the flower of holiness will be found—which is in Galilee, that is, “migration”: where there has been a migration from vices to virtues. *Nazarene* is interpreted “holy”; hence Christians were formerly called Nazarenes. But later at Antioch, in a common council, this name was changed by Peter, and they were called Christians.

In those days. Here Matthew omits the entire [Col. 1261A] period from the return out of Egypt up to John’s preaching; but Luke inserts only that event when, at about the twelfth year, Christ went up to Jerusalem with his parents and remained there alone. Luke says concerning John the Baptist: “The child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was in the wilderness until the day of his manifestation to Israel” (Luke 1). For he lived in the wilderness, clothed in camel-hair sackcloth and eating desert foods, thus subduing the flesh and preparing himself for preaching. But when the suitable time had appeared—namely, about thirty years of age—he began his preaching and prepared the way for the Lord, so that Christ might not bear witness about himself: “There was a man sent from God, that he might bear witness concerning the light” (John 1).

Joseph in Egypt was thirty years old [Col. 1261B] when he received the kingdom of Egypt. David began his kingdom at the same age. Ezekiel began to prophesy at thirty. Christ likewise preached at that age, because kingship, priesthood, and preaching ought to be exercised at a perfect age. John, therefore, is believed to have begun preaching a little before Christ at roughly the same age, as one older in years. Luke marks that time by dates of offices: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar” (Luke 1), etc.; Matthew does not specify it when he says:

## CHAPTER III

In those days John came—that is, he made himself known, having been silent for so long before. He came preaching; he came baptizing, so that in both respects he might prepare the way for the Lord [Col. 1261C], who was both to preach and to baptize. For unless people had become accustomed to being baptized, they would have recoiled from Christ’s baptism. John’s baptism, however, did not confer forgiveness of sins, because Christ’s blood had not yet been shed; but people nevertheless became accustomed to washing.

It is therefore asked: if those washed in John’s baptism died, were they saved? If they possessed faith, they descended into Abraham’s bosom, awaiting redemption in the underworld, as did Abraham and Isaac, who received no forgiveness of sins except in expectation. For all the ancients retained original sin and their own actual sins; yet they were said, as it were, to be forgiven them, because they believed that through the shedding of Christ’s blood these would be remitted to them in the future. Likewise [Col. 1261D], while they performed penance under John, they received no forgiveness of sins except in expectation. Thus the penance of those baptized by John benefited them as much as penance benefited David and all the ancients. They therefore had to be baptized again in Christ’s baptism; hence some are found in the Acts of the Apostles who, having been baptized with John’s baptism, were baptized again by Paul into Christ’s baptism. Therefore, just as John was the forerunner of preaching, so also of baptism. Thus it is said:

“In those days,” that is, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, John came—that is, made himself known—and it adds what kind of person he came as: the Baptist and preacher. For he did both: he baptized and he preached. It adds the place: in the wilderness. He preaches in the wilderness so that [Col. 1262A] by the place he may show where they should rise to perform penance. Whoever wishes to do penance must withdraw to a desert, either in mind or even in location. A person can make a wilderness for himself in his mind if he puts aside the tumult of the world. He therefore preached in the wilderness of Judaea in order to show that Judaea had been made desolate by God and should therefore do penance.

“Preaching and saying.” Preaching is one thing and saying another, because he was saying, “Do penance,” which was to be done presently; and preaching, “For the kingdom of heaven will draw near,” which was future after Christ’s Passion. Christ himself may be called the kingdom of heaven, through whom the saints reign; or it may mean Christ’s Gospel, through which hearers are invited to the kingdom of heaven. Both would draw near, since Christ was not yet preaching.

To repent is one thing; to do penance is another. To repent is to mourn deeds already done and not to commit deeds that must be mourned. To do penance is, after repentance, to make satisfaction by fasting, giving alms, and so forth.

For this is he. Truly he preached in this way, for the prophet had foretold it: “A voice crying,” etc. (Isa. 40). A word is one thing; a voice another. A word is the meaning of the voice. It is sometimes in the heart and sometimes in the mouth. A voice is the vehicle of understanding, conveying meaning to the hearers’ ears and revealing what had previously been hidden in the heart. Hence Christ is called the Word: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). John is the voice: “A voice crying in the wilderness” (Isa. 40). Christ was the Word in the Father’s heart, the formed Word as it were in the mouth; when Christ was born, he had a voice to convey him to the hearer—namely, John. John, therefore, was as it were the voice of the crying Word: for the Word cried in the voice, that is, Christ in John. He cried in the wilderness, as Maximus says, lest an unfamiliar crowd drown out his preaching with its noise or an unbelieving hearer mock him because he did not recognize him as preaching truth. Typologically, however, according to Bede, that wilderness signifies the life of the saints, set apart from the enticements of the world.

Prepare the way of the Lord. That is, receive faith and good works, which are the way to him whom I preach, etc.; and make his paths straight. A way is one thing; a path another. A way is broad and signifies looser precepts. [Col. 1262D] A path is narrow and signifies stricter ones, such as the contemplative life, loving one’s enemy, or doing other good works.

“Straight,” that is, so that these things are done with upright intention, not for earthly but heavenly reward; or, according to Gregory: the way of the Lord is directed to the heart when his word is heard attentively. It is as if he said: Believe my preaching, so that you may be better prepared, whether for the looser or the stricter precepts of the Lord, when he preaches.

John himself showed by example what he preached in word. For he wore the garb of penance, being clothed in camel-hair sackcloth, eating wild foods, and having a leather belt about his loins. He had made coverings from the dried skins of animals about his loins in order to restrain lust. [Col. 1263A] Locusts are small creatures, resembling ours but of another flavor, as though full of honey and sweet to eat, though they have a bitter head; they fly by leaping, like ours. He found wild honey in tree trunks or reeds. For certain reeds are naturally full of honey.

The moral sense lies in John’s clothing: that we should use rough garments to subdue the flesh. In his food: that we should use rough and natural foods, not being overly anxious to seek exotic and distant foods.

Allegory. He was clothed roughly because he did not flatter vices, but reproved sinners with harsh rebuke. He had a leather belt about his loins because he crucified his flesh with its vices and concupiscences. He eats honey because his preaching tasted sweet to the crowds. It was wild because his preaching was bestowed upon wild people. [Col. 1263B] He eats locusts because the locust has a wing and flight, yet quickly falls. Likewise John flew when he was thought to be Christ, but quickly fell when he was asked, “Are you the Christ?” He answered, “No.”

Note that sackcloth was made from the hair of camels and goats. In it were punished the sins understood through the goat because of its stench and through camels because of their crookedness.

Then they went out. The literal sense is clear: those who were nearer and more simple were the first to run to receive the word of salvation. Mystically, it was signified that one who comes to baptism must leave worldly conduct and come to the Jordan, which is interpreted “descent”—that is, to the humility of confession and amendment. They must be Jerusalem and Judaea, that is, those seeing God and their own sins.

But seeing. There were two Jewish sects, namely the Pharisees and Sadducees. The Pharisees invented new traditions, which they preferred to Moses’ precepts, and called themselves more righteous than others. Hence they were called Pharisees, that is, those separated from others. The Sadducees accepted the five books of Moses but rejected the prophets and did not believe in the resurrection. *Sadducees* is interpreted “righteous.” They approached John’s baptism after hearing of the coming wrath and thought they could escape it through baptism alone, without repentance for sins. John thus rebukes them: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. 9). They are called children of vipers because they are children of the Jews, who killed their spiritual parents, that is, the prophets. For it is the nature of vipers to kill their parents. “Who showed you” how to flee from the coming wrath in this manner, that is, without penance? “Therefore do” [Col. 1263D] fruits worthy of penance according to the nature of the offense; and do not trust in Abrahamic descent, believing that you can be saved merely because you are his fleshly children. This is the meaning of: “And do not wish to say,” etc.

For I say. As if to say: you ought not therefore glory in Abrahamic descent, since those who descend carnally from Abraham are not Abraham’s children; rather, those who imitate his faith are. Thus Gentiles also who imitate Abraham’s faith are called his children, as he implies when he says:

[Col. 1264A] God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones. Since he was beside the Jordan, he pointed to the twelve stones there, which prefigured the Gentiles. For Joshua, when he was leading the children of Israel into the promised land, came to the Jordan and by his prayer caused it to divide: the upper part stood still and the lower flowed into the sea. When they had crossed, he commanded that twelve stones be taken from the riverbed onto dry ground and twelve from the dry ground into the river, in remembrance of Israel’s crossing (Josh. 4).

The river signifies the passing flow of this age. The twelve stones signify the Gentiles, who had formerly been in the flow of this age while devoted to idolatry. The other twelve signify the Jews, who were, as it were, outside the flow because they possessed the Law and the worship of God. Joshua therefore signified that the Jews would be submerged, while the Gentiles, coming to faith, would be saved or drawn back from the worldly flow and made children of Abraham. John therefore says: “God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones,” that is, from these figurative stones.

And now the axe, etc. That they may turn more quickly to penance, after exhorting them he threatens them, as if to say: “Therefore produce fruits worthy of penance, because now,” that is, soon, “the axe is laid,” namely Christ. Christ is called an axe because it consists of a handle and iron—that is, humanity, by which it is held, and divinity, by which it cuts. It is laid there because, even if it waits patiently, what it will do is nevertheless sufficiently known. It is laid at the root of the tree, that is, at the end of the Jewish people’s kingdom. The whole present Jewish people is called the tree. The root [Col. 1264C] means those final persons who were taken captive under Titus and Vespasian. Christ destroyed them, because he was the cause of their destruction, as he himself says: “There shall not remain in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19).

Or the tree is each human being, planted in this present life, from which each is uprooted when he dies. The axe does not yet strike, because people are not yet cut off from life or sent into eternal fire; but it is ready because it will strike soon. Or the root may be called the will, from which good and evil proceed, like branches cut off in each person’s death, according to the Psalmist: “His spirit shall go forth and he shall return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145). Or the axe is the judicial sentence, or the Gospel word, which is given to some for life and to others for death.

Therefore every tree, etc. And since the axe is laid at the root of the trees, therefore every tree which does not, etc. It should be noted that trees fit for burning are of several kinds: some are dry, lacking leaves; some have leaves but lack fruit; others have leaves and fruit, but bitter fruit. Hypocrites have leaves, because they put on an appearance of piety but inwardly lack good work. Pagans lack both the fruit of good work and the appearance of religion. Heretics, however, bear the appearance of religion and produce fruit by preaching to others, but it is called deadly or bitter. Thus he says: Every tree, whether dry, or green and fruitless, or green and deadly, [Col. 1265A] all of which lack good fruit, will be cut off from this present life and afterwards cast into eternal fire.

I indeed. Someone might say: Whence do you make such threats, or whence comes your confidence? He replies: such confidence and power do not come from me, but from my Lord: for I baptize only in water, not in the Spirit; the Lord, however, baptizes in the Spirit and in penance. Although John believed that all sins could be blotted out in Christ’s baptism, he nevertheless called people to penance before Christ’s baptism, because he wished to prepare and dispose them so that, their hearts contrite and humbled, they might receive forgiveness of sins through so great a sacrament. Hence blessed Clement and certain other holy men imposed seven days of abstinence, [Col. 1265B] or even more, as preparation upon those who had lived shamefully and, having converted, wished to be baptized. Therefore even now a certain period is established for catechumens before baptism.

But he who, etc. I baptize only in water; but my master, who will come after me—not by being born, but by making himself known through baptism and preaching—is stronger than I. I am strong in calling people to penance; he is stronger in forgiving sins. I am strong in preaching the kingdom of heaven; he is stronger in giving it. I baptize in water; he in the Holy Spirit.

Whose I am not worthy. It is asked, since the other Evangelists say, “whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie,” whereas this Evangelist says that John said, “whose sandals I am not worthy to carry”: which of these words did John say? Augustine says: either he said both at different [Col. 1265C] times, or both in the same utterance, saying: “Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie, nor his sandals to carry.”

The sandal is the whole mystery of the Incarnation, or the whole Gospel. Hence the apostles are said to have had sandals, which have soles beneath but are open above and fastened by straps, because the apostles’ feet are shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace. For the Gospel ought to equip preachers so that they do not cling to earthly things, yet it must be open to those whom they approach. John, therefore, was not worthy to be sent to carry the Gospel through the world—that is, to exercise the office of the apostolate. Yet John was not inferior to the apostles in merits, but only [Col. 1265D] in the office of ministry. For there was no greater mystery than the apostolate; nevertheless, John was not of less dignity than the apostles in heaven. Why, however, he did not choose John also for the apostolate, but as God’s forerunner, we do not know his counsel.

Or he was not worthy to untie the sandal strap—that is, to explain how divinity is joined to humanity in one person, and the bonds of the other sacraments. Or otherwise, “to untie the strap”: it was the custom in the Law that, if a proud man rejected a wife who was rightly his, another man who wished to marry her by the right of kinship should remove the sandal from the man who had rejected her in the middle of the gate; and she herself should spit in his face; and he would be called, to everlasting reproach, “the unsandaled one among the people” (Deut. 25). But Jesus has a bride, that is, the Church; [Col. 1266A] John is the bridegroom’s friend and does not envy him, nor does he wish to usurp his office by being called bridegroom. This is the meaning of “I am not worthy to untie his sandal strap,” that is, to take his bride. As if he said: I am not worthy to be called bridegroom, but only the bridegroom’s friend, because “he who has the bride is the bridegroom.”

He himself will. And because he is stronger than I by his divinity, he will give you what I cannot give, namely forgiveness of sins: for he himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit, forgiving sins in baptism, and afterwards in fire, namely in confirmation. For people receive the Holy Spirit for the strengthening and kindling of good action. Although the same Spirit is conferred in baptism and confirmation [Col. 1266B], different gifts are received there: in baptism the Holy Spirit is given for forgiveness of sins, but in confirmation for the strengthening of good works.

Or these designate two kinds of purification: one in water, where original and actual sins are forgiven through the Spirit; the other when some stain has crept in after baptism, which is cleansed either by the fire of penance, or of some worldly persecution, or finally—if some light stain remains—by purgatorial fire. Hence in the old Law a perpetual fire was set beside the altar, signifying that those once offered to God through faith and regeneration should always have a fire prepared in which they may burn away the rust of sins.

Whose winnowing fan. Having set forth the benefit [Col. 1266C], he adds a threat, so that those whom he cannot move through love he may move through fear. A winnowing fan is an instrument by which grain is shaken in the wind away from chaff; then the grain falls upon the threshing floor, while the chaff is separated by flying away. This fan signifies the discrimination of the Last Judgment, when he will place sheep at the right and goats at the left. In the present Church, signified by the threshing floor, grain and chaff are mingled—that is, the just with the wicked. But at the Last Judgment the Lord will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, that is, the Church, separating the wicked from the good. The fan is said to be in his hand because the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5). And he will gather [Col. 1266D] the wheat, that is, the good, who are not light like chaff but steadfast in a good purpose, into the granary of heavenly glory.

But the chaff—that is, the light-minded—although they were born with the grain from the sacraments of faith, have not been made firm in the Lord’s commandments; he will burn them in infernal fire. Note that unbelievers will not be judged, because they have already been judged. They are neither grain nor chaff: neither good, nor born with the good in faith; rather, they are tares, entirely distinct from the wheat harvest. Of them the Gospel says: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). Consequently, only his wheat and chaff are mentioned here.

Then Jesus came. After the preaching of his forerunner, Christ was at last proclaimed. He who had remained hidden for so long wished to make himself known to humankind [Col. 1267A], and did so first by example rather than word. Therefore he approaches the first sacrament of our redemption, not to receive forgiveness of sins, for he was free from sin, but to invite people to baptism by his example. He was thirty years old when he made himself known, thereby showing that no priest or preacher ought to be appointed unless he is of mature age. Joseph, at thirty, received the kingdom of Egypt. David began his kingdom at that age. Ezekiel was granted to begin prophesying at the same age.

There are several reasons why Christ approached baptism. First, to invite us by example, lest anyone perhaps be ashamed to be baptized by an inferior person or to be unclothed before people, and thus avoid the perfection of all righteousness—that is, [Col. 1267B] baptism. Second, to confirm John’s baptism by his own baptism. Third, to confirm the waters and give them the power of washing away sins, which was lacking in John’s baptism. Fourth, to declare the operation of the Trinity through the descent of the dove, the voice of the Father, his own presence, and the other mysteries of baptism.

Since John was preaching and baptizing in this way:

Then Jesus came. That is, he began gradually to appear, having remained hidden for a long time. From Galilee, namely Nazareth, to the Jordan. *Galilee* is interpreted “migration”; *Jordan*, “descent.” Whoever therefore wishes to be baptized—that is, to migrate from vices to virtues—should humble himself in coming to baptism, as the interpretation of Jordan signifies. To John. The Lord came to a servant [Col. 1267C], the superior to the inferior, so that no one, however powerful, may disdain to be baptized by an inferior or a servant.

But John, etc. Since we have recognized the Lord’s most humble dispensation, let us attend also to the servant’s prudent obedience. He wished to obey, but since he knew Christ to be free from sin, he wished to know why the Lord sought baptism. Thus for a time he prevented him, saying:

I ought to be baptized by you. As if to say: I, earthly, ought to be baptized by you, heavenly; I, mortal, by you, eternal; I, a sinner, by you, righteous. I have need, and you have no need. Why, then, do you come to me?

Jesus answering. John asks what he was seeking. Jesus said to him: “Allow it now” [Col. 1267D]—that is, yield now to my will, and allow me now to be baptized by you. He briefly adds the reason why he wishes to be baptized: “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.” Baptism is the completion of all righteousness. However just, religious, charitable, given to fasting, chaste, and so forth a person may be, if he lacks the grace of baptism, it profits him nothing. Hence Cornelius was sent to Peter. Baptism without virtues sometimes avails by itself, as in a child; but virtues without baptism never avail, since it is said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit,” etc. (John 3).

It is therefore called the completion of righteousness. Since the Lord wished to invite people to it, lest they disdain baptism by an inferior person or being unclothed before people, he wished by example to teach what others ought to do, so that no one after him might be ashamed. This is the meaning of “thus”: namely, while I, the superior, who have no need of baptism, am baptized by you, the inferior. It is fitting for us—namely, for me, the Lord receiving baptism, and for you, the servant baptizing me—to fulfil all righteousness, that is, to teach the completion of all righteousness, which is to invite people to baptism. Then he allowed him. That is, he consented and asked no more, because he understood what he had sought.

And when Jesus had been baptized, immediately he went up from the water. In accordance with the lay of the land, because he was in a valley, Jesus is said to have gone up to Jerusalem. His ascent after baptism signifies that everyone baptized ought to rise from virtue to virtue without delay.

And behold, the heavens were opened, etc. For he wished to show [Col. 1268B] that heaven, previously shut because of sins, was opened to him after baptism through grace. It is asked why he wished the sacrament of forgiveness to occur in water. Namely, that he might extinguish for us the flaming sword—that is, the fire of Gehenna—because water is the element contrary to fire.

And he saw the Spirit of God. It is asked whether there was a real dove, how the Holy Spirit appeared in it, and why the Holy Spirit is said to have descended when he is wholly everywhere. It should be known that God, invisible by nature, shows himself to people through various new forms: to Moses in the form of fire in the bush; to Abraham in angels under human form; and in many other forms which ceased to exist once their services or purposes had been completed. Thus this dove was real, a new creature, through which [Col. 1268C] the Holy Spirit showed that his presence was in Christ. He did not then first begin to be in Christ, for the whole Trinity was fully in him. But because people did not know that the Spirit was present in him, he wished to represent that presence to them through a visible form.

It is further asked whether the Holy Spirit was in that dove and whether he is therefore said to have become incarnate. The Spirit was indeed in the dove, as in other creatures, because we confess that he is wholly everywhere; but not in the manner in which the Son was in the Lord’s human being. For there divinity was united with humanity in one person. The Holy Spirit, however, was not one person with the dove, which afterward ceased to exist when its office had been performed. Likewise the Father’s voice was one of the forms declaring what God wished to be heard. The Father does not have a mouth and breath by which to emit a voice.

The Holy Spirit is said to have descended by means of a form in the way that someone is said to have addressed another through an envoy. He is also said to have descended in another sense, because he humbled himself when he manifested his presence through so humble a form. It should also be noted that the dove settled above Christ’s head so that no one might think that the Father’s voice was addressed to John rather than to the Lord.

This is my Son. Once the dove had been placed above his head, the Father’s voice followed, saying: “This.” It is demonstrative, addressed to human beings, in order to make them more certain by this pointing-out. “My Son,” that is, my Son by substance. [Col. 1269A] “In whom,” with respect to his humanity, “I have been well pleased.” This is said by comparison with a painter, who is pleased with himself when he beholds his own good painting. As though he were saying: Adam was the devil’s son; this one is mine. In Adam I was displeased with myself, because I regretted having made him; in this one never, but in all things I have been well pleased with myself. That one is hateful to me; this one beloved.

It is asked, since the Evangelists report the Father as having proclaimed different words—for Matthew says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have been well pleased”; Mark, “You are my beloved Son; in you I have been well pleased”; and Luke, “In you I have been well pleased”—which of these, then, did the Father say? But, as Augustine says: “If the Evangelists give varying accounts of this voice, it is not greatly surprising, provided only that the substance of the meaning is the same; just as if different messengers were to convey someone’s words, they might take care to state not the same words, but the same meaning.” [Col. 1269B]

All these things are full of mysteries. Christ did not wish to manifest himself for his own sake, but for ours, since in all these things he showed what each person receives in baptism. For this reason the whole Trinity was manifested here: the Father in the voice, the Spirit in the dove, the Son in the man, so that the whole Trinity may be believed to work in each baptized person. Therefore the Holy Spirit preferred to appear in the form of a dove, in order to signify the perfect form of his gift bestowed upon the baptized. For in baptism he grants the guilty innocence and simplicity, as is indicated by the innocent and simple bird that lacks gall. This innocence is granted when forgiveness of sins is bestowed upon human beings. [Col. 1269C] Therefore, in order to signify the nature of the charism, he wished to appear above Christ when baptized in the form of a dove; above the apostles in fire; at the Transfiguration in a shining cloud. For the Spirit grants, as has been said, innocence to the baptized; ardour for preaching and illumination of knowledge to apostles and disciples; and brightness of body—which is the cloud of the soul—to those who will rise again.

The dove also signifies seven virtues among the faithful. For the dove dwells beside streams, so that, on seeing a hawk, it plunges into the waters and thus escapes. It chooses the better grains. It nourishes the young of others. It does not tear with its beak; it lacks gall; it nests in hollows of rocks. It has groaning instead of song. Thus holy preachers dwell beside the streams of divine Scripture, by which [Col. 1269D] their hearts are watered, so that by their protection they may escape the devil’s assault. They choose the better grains, that is, the better teachings—namely, non-heretical teachings—by which they may be fed. They nourish by their teaching and example the young of others, that is, people previously alienated from God, who had been the devil’s young, that is, his imitators. They do not tear with their beak: that is, they do not corrupt sound teachings by tearing them apart in the manner of heretics. They lack gall, that is, irrational anger. They nest in the hollows of the rock: that is, they place their nest in the wounds of Christ’s death, he who is the firm rock. For by the nest refuge and hope are signified. When rain approaches, doves flee to their nest and place the hope of their offspring in it. They have groaning instead of song: that is, [Col. 1270A] as others delight in singing, so they delight in tribulation and groaning.

Therefore it is said, “This is my Son,” because the faithful are made sons of God in baptism. To each person it is said: “This one, who was formerly the devil’s son, is now my son; who was formerly hateful, is now beloved; in whom I was formerly displeased, I am now well pleased.” This great mystery of baptism was prefigured by many figures in ancient times: in Noah’s ark, in the Red Sea, in circumcision, and in many other things; and it is at last fulfilled here.

## CHAPTER IV

Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness. Luke makes clear by which Spirit, saying that Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan, and then adding: “And he was led by the Spirit in the wilderness” [Col. 1270B] (Luke 4). For one must not suppose that an unclean spirit did violence to him who had received the Holy Spirit.

This wilderness lies between Jerusalem and Jericho, where robbers used to dwell. Hence the Lord said: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” (Luke 10). By “man” I mean one bearing the figure of Adam, who was conquered by demons, wounded by sins, and stripped of virtues. This place is called *Damin*, that is, “of bloods,” because of the shedding of blood committed there by robbers. It was fitting, therefore, that Christ should overcome the devil where the devil was said to have overcome man in figure.

Once baptized, Christ immediately goes into the wilderness under the Spirit’s guidance, because every believer after baptism ought to set the world aside and either seek a bodily desert or, free from the turmoil of the age, make a wilderness in the mind and, under the Spirit’s guidance, gird himself for battle against the devil. [Col. 1270C] For the devil then persecutes a person when he sees that he has withdrawn. Hence Christ permitted himself to be tempted after baptism, not before it, in order to teach that temptations are sent upon the baptized. Before baptism the devil, thinking people his own, does not attack them so fiercely.

The children of Israel remained in the wilderness after crossing the sea—that is, after baptism—until they came to the promised land. Nor is anyone worthy to eat manna, that is, the Lord’s body, unless he remains in the wilderness—that is, unless he leaves behind, if not bodily then at least in mind, the turmoil and desires of this age. And [Col. 1270D] because temptations then threaten, they should gird themselves for battle.

Observe, therefore, the order. There are three kinds of temptation: what is called temptation of the eyes, in the pride of life. All other evils proceed from these: anger, envy, contention, hatred, murder, theft, and other kinds. From gluttony come lust, delight in sleeping, and other pleasures. Riches, honours, and similar things belong to the desire of the flesh. Desire is for external things. Pride of life is vain glory over good works.

Naturally, however, the devil first tempts through desire of the flesh, which is nearer to man and as it were natural; afterwards through external things. Desire of the flesh generally begins with gluttony, because a full belly seeks lust and other pleasures. Therefore the faithful person ought [Col. 1271A] first to subdue gluttony, which is the gate and beginning of the other pleasures; and because it first rises up against gluttony, he begins with fasting, which is the bridle of gluttony.

“And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights.” This number was consecrated for fasts first by Moses and afterwards by Elijah, so that it might be confirmed by the Law and the Prophets.

Then by Christ, who is the bearer of the New Testament. Moses fasted forty days, strengthened by angelic converse. Elijah likewise, in the strength of angelic food, went for forty days to Horeb, the mountain of God, while fleeing Jezebel. But Jesus had no outward comfort, neither the service of an angel nor food; rather, he had inwardly that which sustained him, lest he fail through human frailty. They are not said [Col. 1271B] to have hungered; but he afterwards chose to hunger, in order to conceal his power from the devil and give the devil an occasion for temptation.

Christ also hungered mystically because he desired our salvation. The number forty signifies the whole duration of the present life, in which all human beings, gathered from the four parts of the world, ought to be armed with the ten commandments against temptations. Hence it is composed of four and ten. Or the four signifies all illicit movements of the body, which arise from the four humours—that is, the four elements of which flesh consists—against which movements the ten commandments ought to be set. The ten commandments are divided into three and seven: three concern God, seven one’s neighbour, because a human being consists of a soul, which has three powers, and a body, which consists of [Col. 1271C] four elements. For this reason the children of Israel were in the wilderness for forty years.

He mentions the nights so that it may not be believed, as heretics say, that he fasted during the days and ate during the nights. For forty days, while he lived as mortal and needed food, he fasted. For forty days after the resurrection, when he did not need food, he ate with his disciples. In the first forty days, being a man placed in temptation, he taught humanity what a human being ought to do in the contest; and through the other forty he showed beforehand that, so long as they fought and fasted from the vanity of the age, he would be with them and eat in them—that is, delight in them. For the number forty signifies both the present and the future life.

Note that there are two kinds of abstinence: one when we subdue the flesh; the other when, with passions quieted, through excessive contemplation and desire of the future life we forget to eat. Thus one abstinence is of sorrow, the other of joy. [Col. 1271D] The Lord voluntarily chose to hunger in order that an occasion for tempting him might be given to the devil. Christ also hungered so that it might be concealed that he was God; yet this hunger signifies the desire for our salvation that he had. Elijah and Moses, however, do not hunger, in order that they might be examples of divine power.

Christ wished to fast only as much as those two, who were human beings, had fasted; for if he had fasted more than human beings, the tempter would understand that he was above human beings and therefore would not dare to tempt him. If less, the heretic would deny that he was God and assert that he was a mere man, because he would not even have done what he knew mere human beings had done. [Col. 1272A] He fasted forty days and forty nights in order to show that we ought to fast from unlawful things both in the time of prosperity, signified by days, and in the time of adversity, marked by nights.

“And the tempter approached.” Seeing his hunger, the tempter approached, because he did not suppose him to be God, whom he saw to be frail. He had seen the stars; he had seen the magi; he had heard John crying, “This is the Lamb of God.” Perhaps he had heard the Father’s voice from heaven; yet he thought him called an adoptive son, as were the other saints. He had heard the prophets and knew that Christ was to come. Yet although he had seen all these signs, he nevertheless did not believe him to be God; and this was the result of his pride. For he believed that, just as he himself had never wished to suffer weakness but had wished [Col. 1272B] to be exalted above all things, so God would not wish to suffer any weakness. Judging God from his own disposition, he therefore in no way believed him to be God when he saw weakness in Christ; nevertheless he tests him when he says, “If you are the Son of God,” and he tempts him when he says, “Command that these stones become loaves.” For through the sight of bread he wished to stir up gluttony. One who is hungry desires more when food is seen. Through the change he wished to test his power; yet even if he saw a miracle, he would not on that account believe, because he had seen prophets perform greater deeds. Rather, he wished to mock the man through bread.

Quite fittingly he offers stones, being hard and impenitent himself; and because he had heard it written, “He spoke, and they were made,” he flatters him as though on the basis of power, saying, “Only speak, and it will happen, if you are the Son of God.”

“But he answered and said.” [Col. 1272C] He teaches us to set the shield of the Scriptures against temptation. He does not use divine power, although he could have driven him away as God, because he did not wish to reveal the truth of his divine power, so that he who had come uncertain might return uncertain.

“Not by bread alone.” This authority is taken from Deuteronomy. Moses, seeing that a human being is made of a double substance, namely body and soul, and that neither can subsist without support—for the body seeks to be sustained by earthly food, but the soul, which is a spiritual substance, by heavenly bread—said: “A human being does not live by bread alone” (Deut. 8), and so forth. God is the bread of angels, but a human being cannot eat God unless he is made milk; therefore he is shown to the human being through figures, that is, through words and through other manifestations, all of which are called “words.” Therefore he says that a human being lives by every word, that is, by every kind of divine utterance—that is, those in which God is manifested. [Col. 1272D]

It is asked how this answer opposes the aforesaid temptation. The solution is this: it means as if he had said, “Your persuasion is evident, because it is that of a tempter. You are concerned with bodily food, which is shared with beasts, not with the food of the mind, which we share with angels. For if you were acting as a friend, you would first admonish me about the better food, without which no one can truly live: ‘Not by bread alone,’ and so forth.”

“Then he took him.” Observe that Luke places this temptation last, and the temptation from the mountain second, which seems to accord more with the historical sequence. For nature requires that the devil first tempt through desire of the flesh, then through desire for external things, and finally through pride in a good life. But Matthew narrates according to the sequence in which these things happened in Adam and through which Adam was conquered, so that the second Adam may be shown to have conquered in the same order in which man was first conquered.

For Adam is said first to have been tempted through gluttony, when it is said: “And seeing the tree, that it was beautiful to look upon and pleasant for eating” (Gen. 3); [Col. 1273A] afterwards through vain glory, when it is said: “You will be like gods” (ibid.). This was pride: namely, to go beyond oneself and wish to make oneself equal to one’s Lord. Finally, through avarice, when it is said: “Knowing good and evil” (ibid.). For desire for knowledge is as much avarice as desire for money. This sequence then occurred according to what seemed more expedient to the devil. But after nature was corrupted, the other order mentioned above was established by nature: first through desire of the flesh, then through external things, and so on. In Adam, however, there was naturally no order, since he felt no desire.

It is asked how these temptations occurred, since Mark says that he was in the wilderness forty days and was tempted by Satan. Mark seems to mean that all the temptations took place in the wilderness. Some therefore say that these temptations were effected in the mind by the devil, who did not visibly appear. For the devil suggested to him that he should make loaves out of stones, climb upon the pinnacle, cast himself down from it, and worship the devil for the kingdoms of the world. Others say [Col. 1273B] that he appeared visibly to him as a human being—which is truer—and spoke with him. They say that he called Jerusalem “the wilderness,” that is, a place abandoned by God, so that all temptations might be said to have occurred in the wilderness. But this is not necessary, because Mark’s wording does not compel it: he says only that he was tempted by Satan. It is indeed true that Satan tempted him in the wilderness, but Mark does not say that he did so only in the wilderness.

Again, it is asked how he “took him.” Some say that the devil transported him and set him upon the pinnacle; this is not remarkable if he permitted himself to be transported by the devil, he who permitted himself to be lifted upon the cross by the devil’s members. Others say that he led him by the road as far as Jerusalem, which Luke seems to imply, when he says: “And he led him into the holy city, and they went up upon the pinnacle,” like other people. [Col. 1273C] This was the final temptation, after he had returned from the wilderness and come into the city. This one who tempted the Lord is believed to have been the master of demons.

It is the custom of architecture in Palestine that roofs be flat on top rather than pointed. Likewise Solomon’s temple had been made flat on top; and around it were railings enclosing walkways, lest anyone unwarily slip from them. There was also a seat for teachers there, from which they spoke to the people below. The *cancelli* are the surrounding structures from which people look out. Hence those who address the people concerning the commands of a king or emperor are called *cancellarii*, because royal commands are customarily proclaimed from the railings. *Cancelli* are likewise called windows from which one looks out. Therefore he led him upon the pinnacle of the temple when he wished to tempt him with vain glory, because there, in the teachers’ chair, he had deceived many through glory; [Col. 1273D] he therefore thought that he could also lift this man into vain glory when placed in the chair of teaching.

“If you are the Son of God.” Again he tests him when he says, “If you are the Son of God,” and tempts him when he says, “Cast yourself down.” The advice, “Cast yourself down,” was foolish, especially when addressed to the Son of God. He ought rather to have said: “If you are the Son of God, ascend into heaven”; if he did this, he would prove himself truly to be the Son of God. But it is characteristic of the devil to urge someone toward a precipice.

“For it is written that he will command the angels,” and so forth. Christ defends himself by the authority of Scripture, and the devil persuades him to sin by the authority of Scripture. But it should be noted that he perverts Scripture. Scripture says of every good person that the Lord commanded his angels, [Col. 1274A] as ministering spirits, to lift up a good person in their hands—that is, by their help—and so guard him lest he strike his foot, that is, the affection of the mind, against a stone, that is, the old law written on tablets of stone.

Jesus said to him again: “You shall not tempt,” and so forth. It should be noted that these words are not directed against the devil. For he moderated his words so as not to make it known that he was God; rather, they are taken from Moses, who says in Deuteronomy to every person: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. 6). We must not tempt God so long as we have something reasonable that we can do, as Abraham did concerning his wife, whom he called his sister. But once necessity presses, then we ought to call upon God and ask for what is necessary, as the children of Israel did at the Red Sea; and when we ask, we should do so not with temptation but confidently.

The children of Israel asked with temptation when they said: “Can God prepare a table for us in the wilderness?” And if someone has been seized for death, he should place everything in God’s will, unless he sees that his own deliverance would be useful to his enemies, as did the three youths in the fiery furnace. [Col. 1274B] It would be tempting God if he threw himself down when he could descend as other people do.

“Again he took him,” and so forth. To tempt him through avarice, he leads him onto a mountain, because pride is the worm of riches and because ambition always seeks high places. “And he showed him all the kingdoms of the world,” and so forth. Either, simply, it is said that the whole world was seen by him when he rose up to that place; or the devil set forth to him the vanity of worldly pomp, saying: “Such and such are the kingdoms of the world.” Nor is it sinful to hold desirable things in the mind without covetousness, as physicians are accustomed to observe kinds of diseases without labour or harm. He promises all these things by lying, whereas God rather gives them, as to Saul and David and many others. For he himself can give nothing in the world except insofar as God permits.

“If, falling down.” He truly falls who worships him. Behold the devil’s ancient pride: just as in the beginning he wished to make himself like God, so now he wished to arrogate divine worship to himself. Then Jesus said to him: “Go, Satan,” that is, you who oppose salvation by commanding a creature to be worshipped. For *Satan* means “adversary.” [Col. 1274C] Peter, however, is not condemned by the same sentence as Satan, as most people suppose. For Peter is told: “Go behind me, Satan” (Mark 8), that is, “Follow me, you who are opposed to my will.” But here he hears: “Go, Satan,” with no addition, “behind me,” so that it may rather be understood: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for you.”

Here again is an authority from Deuteronomy, where Moses cries to every person: “You shall worship the Lord your God” (Deut. 6). It is as though he said: “I ought not worship you, for Moses prohibited idolatry.” It is asked why, when it says “him alone,” service to a king or another human being is not prohibited. Not at all; for among Hebrews and Greeks a certain special service of God is distinguished, called *latria*. We, however, have no proper name for it, but use a common name; just as they have a certain common term signifying every kind of service, namely *dulia*.

[Col. 1275B] “Then the devil left him.” If we say that the final temptation occurred in the city, it must be read thus: “Then,” that is, after all temptations had been completed, the devil left him, having nothing further to do and being conquered in every respect.
