According to Luke, this departure must be understood as taking place above the pinnacle of the temple. But if we say that Matthew follows the historical order, the devil left him on the mountain.

“And behold, angels,” and so forth. As if from a distance, the angels watched the Lord’s contest, lest it seem that he had needed their aid or had conquered through it. But once the defeated devil withdrew, they came ready to serve him. In this it is shown that in our contest, once the devil has been conquered, angels come to us rejoicing with us.

“But when he had heard,” and so forth. So long as the servant preached, the Lord waited. But once he had been put in chains, [Col. 1275C] he began his public preaching. The other things he had done privately; and if he had spoken, he had not spoken to crowds but, as it were, in secret. The three Evangelists begin with Christ’s public preaching, from the point when John was arrested. But John the Evangelist relates many things omitted by these Evangelists, things done before John was handed over.

For John relates that after Christ’s return from the wilderness, he was near the Jordan, and two disciples of John, Andrew and another, came to him and said: “Master, where are you staying?” and so forth. He also relates concerning Nathanael how the Lord spoke with him. Then he went to Cana of Galilee and performed the miracle of the wine. Afterwards he withdrew to Capernaum, where he lived with his mother and disciples. The Evangelist calls them disciples not because they were disciples at that time, but calls them by the name which they had later, just as if we now said, “The apostle Paul was born at Tarsus”—not because he was then called an apostle. [Col. 1275D]

Then at Passover he went up to Jerusalem, found sellers and buyers in the temple, and drove them out. He also did this on another occasion later, namely around his passion, as Matthew relates. For, as Augustine says, he performed this miracle twice. During that visit Nicodemus spoke with him by night. From there he came into Judaea and baptized, although he himself did not baptize but his disciples did. For John was then baptizing at Aenon near Salim; John had not yet been sent to prison. From these words it is understood that all these things [Col. 1276A] happened before John was arrested.

Then John’s disciples said to him: “Rabbi, he to whom you bore testimony—behold, he is baptizing and making more disciples than you” (John 3). But when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that he was baptizing and making more disciples than John—though Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did—he left Judaea and went again into Galilee. Augustine says here: “Then we understand that John had already been handed over.” Thus the three Evangelists do not treat of Christ’s first coming into Galilee, but begin with this latter one.

It is asked how many years Christ’s preaching and miracles lasted. On this matter different people hold different views. Some, following John, who mentions only three Passovers, say that he preached and performed miracles for two and a half years. Others say three and a half, which has greater truth. The former arrange matters thus: after baptism Christ fasted; afterwards, on returning, he did in the same year the things John the Evangelist relates concerning John’s two disciples and Nathanael, the water he changed into wine, and the stay at Capernaum. [Col. 1276B] These occurred from the time of the Theophany.

Then he went up at Passover, drove the sellers and buyers out of the temple, and spoke with Nicodemus. Then he came into Judaea and remained there until John was handed over, which occurred between Passover and the Kalends of May, because Christ is then said to have begun his preaching; and in certain *computi* the day is marked. On hearing this, he withdrew into Galilee and began his public preaching. About the next Passover John was killed; this can be known from Matthew’s and John’s words. Matthew says that after John’s death, his disciples came and informed Jesus. When Jesus heard this, he withdrew into the wilderness and there performed the miracle of the five loaves and two fish. John says that when he performed this miracle, Passover was near; thus John is understood to have been killed a little before the coming Passover. At the following Passover occurred the Lord’s passion. Thus they show that Christ preached and performed miracles for two and a half years.

But contrary to this opinion is the fact that the miracle at the wedding, on the day on which he was baptized after a complete year had elapsed, is celebrated and preached by the universal Church. This is false if it is said [Col. 1276C] to have happened between the day of the Theophany and Passover after his return from the wilderness, to which he is said to have been led by the Spirit immediately after baptism. For Mark says: “And immediately the Spirit sent him into the wilderness, and he was there forty days” (Mark 1).

Therefore, for this opinion to stand, it must be said that one Passover was omitted by John the Evangelist, and that he says nothing about the first year, which ran from the first day of baptism to the corresponding anniversary, except only what he says about John’s two disciples and Nathanael. Once the year had elapsed, on the same day on which he had been baptized, he performed the miracle at the wedding. Afterwards he remained at Capernaum until Passover. The other matters do not change, and thus from the day of baptism to the passion we have [Col. 1277A] three years, plus as much time as there is from the day of Theophany to the first Passover.

But let us come to the literal sense, as though it said: So long as John preached, the Lord did not wish to undertake public preaching. But when he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee from Judaea. As Luke relates, he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up; he entered the synagogue, stood up to read, and, having received the book, found the place where it was written in Isaiah:

> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to preach release to captives, sight to the blind, to send the broken away in release, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense” (Luke 4).

“And when he had closed the book, he sat down and said: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.’” [Col. 1277B] He said many things there, because of which they led him to a mountain and wished to cast him down; but he himself passed through and went away, and then descended to Capernaum. Hence Matthew now says:

“And having left the town of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in maritime Capernaum, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, that it might be fulfilled,” and so forth.

In this city, as Luke relates, he healed a demoniac in the synagogue and from there began to preach publicly.

Note that there are two Galilees: one called that of the Jews, the other called that of the Gentiles. Galilee was divided from the time of Solomon. For Solomon had the closest friendship with Hiram, king of Syria, because Hiram assisted him with timber for the building of the Lord’s temple. Therefore Solomon gave him twenty cities in Galilee, [Col. 1277C] though Jews remained there under that king’s rule. That part was afterwards called Galilee of the Gentiles, and the remainder Galilee of the Jews. Zebulun is in Galilee of the Jews; Naphtali in Galilee of the Gentiles. Capernaum lay on the boundary of both. It was therefore reasonable that he should begin his preaching there, so as to signify that it was to be offered, as it were, to Gentiles and Jews alike. Yet he did not preach to Gentiles, but only to Jews, except on some occasion. For he himself said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15), and, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles.”

Furthermore, it was fitting that the proclamation of the Redeemer should first be known where Israel’s first captivity under the Assyrians occurred. Capernaum was maritime because it was situated beside the body of water called in one place the Sea of Galilee, in another the Sea of Tiberias, and in another Lake Gennesaret. Yet it is not a sea but a very large collection of fresh waters; nevertheless, it is the custom of that people to call such a body of water a sea. Jerome says on Isaiah: “Here he calls the Sea the Lake of Gennesaret, which is formed by the inflow of the Jordan, [Col. 1277D] on whose shore Capernaum, Tiberias, Thebaida, and Chorazin were situated, in which region the Lord chiefly lived.”

First note that the Evangelist, seeking a mystical rather than a historical sense, omits much from the prophet’s words, because he directs attention only to the words that concern the Lord’s preaching. For the prophecy reads thus: “In the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was relieved; and in the last it was burdened—the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles. The people who walked in darkness saw a great light; upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light arose” (Isa. 9).

The meaning is as follows. In the first period of Christ’s preaching, the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were relieved of the burden of sins, because the first converts came from there; for in these tribes were villages from which our apostolic leaders believed. But in the last period their faith was burdened, since very many Jews remained in error. This is what is meant by “in the last, the way of the sea was burdened,” that is, that same region situated by the sea. [Col. 1278A]

In the Gospel, however, various nominatives are brought back to the same verb thus: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, which is the way of the sea”—that is, the way beside the sea—“and which is beyond the Jordan,” namely the people of Galilee of the Gentiles, “who dwell in darkness, saw a great light,” that is, heard Christ’s preaching and his first miracles. By Zebulun is understood the Judaea of the Jews; by Naphtali, Galilee of the Gentiles. The other Galilee, namely Galilee of the Jews, is the way of the sea, since it lies beside the sea. The other, namely Galilee of the Gentiles, is beyond the Jordan, that is, near the Tyrians. But although he mentions both, he dwells more upon Galilee of the Gentiles when he says, “the people of Galilee of the Gentiles,” which especially pertains to the mystical meaning, as will appear below.

“And light arose for them,” that is, knowledge of truth for those sitting in the region of the shadow of death. He calls eternal death “death,” and sins “shadow,” since they are darkness leading to death. [Col. 1278B] Jerome, however, says: “I think that the difference between death and the shadow of death is this: death belongs to those who have gone to hell with works of death. For ‘the soul that sins, it shall die’ (Ezek. 18). The shadow of death belongs to those who, though they sin, have not yet departed from this life. For they can, if they wish, do penance.”

Therefore they sit in the region of the shadow of death, that is, in the region of Galilee, where the shadow of death, namely sin, first reigned. The phrase concerning Galilee can also be divided in another way, so that we say: “beyond the Jordan of Galilee,” that is, beyond the Jordan insofar as it pertains to Galilee. For Judaea is on the other bank; and then it will be read separately: “the people of the Gentiles,” and so forth.

## ALLEGORY

John is the voice preceding the Word, [Col. 1278C] as are the other prophets. After that prophecy had ceased and been bound, the Word came, fulfilling what voice and prophecy had proclaimed. He withdrew into Galilee, that is, into migration: from figures to truth, from shadow to body. Or into Galilee, that is, into the Church, where there is a migration from vices to virtues.

A migration truly occurred, because he left Nazareth and came to Capernaum. Nazareth is interpreted “flower”; Capernaum, “most beautiful village.” Therefore he left the flower of figures which designated the fruit of the Gospel, just as a flower foretells the coming fruit; and he came into the Church, which is Christ’s most beautiful village through Christ’s virtues and miracles. It is maritime because it is situated beside the sea—that is, beside the fluctuations of this age [Col. 1279A]—and is battered by the storms of tribulations or persecutions.

This Church is situated in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, that is, common to Jews and Gentiles, and constituted from them. Zebulun is called “dwelling of strength,” because the apostles chosen from Judaea were strong. Naphtali is called “breadth,” because the Church of the Gentiles was spread throughout the world. Isaiah signified this when he said: “The land of Zebulun,” that is, of the Jews, “and the land of Naphtali,” that is, of the Gentiles, “which is the way of the sea,” because it is both beside the sea, as has been said, and only a way, because through it one may go to the homeland of life; “and is beyond the Jordan,” that is, beyond baptism, because it has been baptized.

The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali saw a great light, but especially the people of Galilee of the Gentiles: that is, the Gentile people situated in migration, who walk in darkness because of idolatry, saw a great light. The rest is unchanged.

Walking, however. Once Christ’s preaching had begun, it was fitting that he should have helpers whom he might send out to preach. He therefore chose apostles—but lowly, obscure, and unlearned men—in order to show that the Gospel had been received through its own power, not through the nobility or wisdom of men. He therefore did not wish to make Nathanael, who was wise, although most holy, an apostle. The proof in the earliest preachers that Christ’s faith was received through the power of Christ himself lies in this: unlearned men shone with miracles, and men were converted not by the wisdom of speech. Only later were Paul and other learned men added, such as Cyprian and Augustine.

Concerning this calling, the three Evangelists seem to disagree. John says that at the beginning, after the baptism, two disciples of John, one of whom was Andrew, came to Jesus and asked him: “Rabbi, where do you dwell?” He said: “Come and see.” They came, therefore, and stayed with him for one day. Andrew found his brother Simon and said to him: “We have found the Messiah”; and he brought his brother to Jesus. Jesus, looking upon him, said: “You are Simon, son of Johanna; you shall be called Cephas,” that is, Peter. He did not say to him, “You are now called this,” but announced what was to be. On the following day he saw Philip and said to him: “Follow me.” Philip found Nathanael and said to him: “We have found the Messiah, the son of Joseph from Nazareth.” Nathanael, however, wondered that a prophet should arise from Galilee—especially from Nazareth, which was a small village, whereas all the prophets were found in Judea—and said: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” That is, “Can it be believed that anything good comes from Nazareth?” that is, any prophet? And so forth, as follows.

Luke, on the other hand, relates: “Now it came to pass, when the crowds pressed upon him to hear the word of God, that he stood by the Lake of Gennesaret and saw two boats standing there. Entering one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he taught the crowds. When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: ‘Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.’ Simon answered and said: ‘Master, though we have laboured all night, we have caught nothing; yet at your word I will let down the net.’” And they filled both boats with fish. Peter being astonished, Jesus said: “Do not fear; from now on you will be catching men.” And, leaving everything behind and drawing the boats up on land, they followed him. James and John, Simon’s partners, were in the other boat (Luke 5).

Matthew, however, reports that Jesus, walking beside the Sea of Galilee, saw two brothers and called them; and that he did not find James and John together with them, but, proceeding from there, saw two other brothers, whom he also called. But it must be understood that when Andrew came to Jesus and brought his brother, their calling did not then take place. Rather, only Peter was foretold what his future name would be; afterward they returned to their own affairs.

Again, regarding what Luke relates, it must be understood, as Augustine says, that it occurred before this calling, and that they were not then called by the Lord. Rather, Peter alone was foretold that he would catch men; this was not said as though he would never again catch fish. For after the Resurrection we read that they were fishermen, though for food and not for profit. Hence there is room to understand that they returned, according to their custom, to catching fish, although it is said that they left everything; for then they left it only for a time. But this was the final calling, which Matthew relates; and then they left possessions, wives, and fathers. Thus they never afterward returned to their former affairs. And although Luke relates this as though it occurred after the preaching carried out at Capernaum, it did not occur then; rather, he recalls what he had omitted at that point.

Likewise, concerning the calling which Matthew relates, it is unknown, as Augustine says, whether it took place before or after the public preaching. It can be read either way: either that Christ thus began his preaching and had already chosen disciples for this preaching, or that he chose them later.

He who, walking beside the sea—this too has a mystical sense—saw them, etc. Although he had chosen twelve, he relates the calling of only four. Matthew, however, recounts his own calling later, among the miracles. For it was a great miracle that a tax-collector became an apostle, and that these four alone suffice for the mystery.

And he said to them: “Come after me,” etc.—not so much with the feet as by a change of disposition. “And I will make you,” etc.: you who were formerly fishers of fish shall become fishers of men. He fittingly says, “I will make you become”: for otherwise a man labours in vain unless God brings it about that he may accomplish it, yet in such a way that free choice is not destroyed. When such a doubling occurs—“I will make you become,” “I have fought the fight”—it signifies continuance, as though he said: “I shall so act that you will persevere in this deed.”

But they immediately, etc. They possessed little, but they left even that little behind. In this is indicated that what is sought in renunciation is disposition more than possession. “And proceeding from there,” etc. Here is given the example of those who forsake possessions alone for love of Christ; but here is set forth the example of those who put aside for God not only possessions but also fleshly affections. Note that some were casting nets into the sea, while others were mending them [Col. 1281A]. This has figurative value; the literal sense is sufficiently clear.

The allegory is as follows. Jesus walked beside the sea when he came to us through the Incarnation, though according to his divinity he is immovable. He walked beside the sea, and not in the sea, because he was immersed in no carnal pleasure. Walking, he saw spiritual fishermen: he had seen them from eternity, but, as regards us, he was then seen to have seen them spiritually when he called them. He saw them casting nets—that is, occupied with secular concerns—and called them.

Note that he saw them two by two, just as elsewhere we read that he sent them two by two before his face (Luke 10) to preach. Whoever is sent to preach must be united to his neighbour by brotherly love, so that he may be found to preach not for earthly gain but out of love; and therefore he saw two brothers.

Their names also suit the mystery. Simon is interpreted “obedient”; for he who preaches ought to obey the Lord’s commands. Thereafter he ought to be Peter, that is, “firm,” so that he may persevere in his purpose, lest, after preaching, he himself become reprobate (1 Cor. 9). Then he becomes Andrew, that is, “manly,” so that he may preach courageously to others and not be disturbed by fear or by any affection; and, preaching to others, he becomes James, that is, “supplanter of vices.” But when he is perfect in all things, humility will then be necessary, lest he attribute anything to himself rather than to the grace of God alone; and therefore he becomes John, which is interpreted “grace of God.”

These men were mending their nets because they attended to earthly matters and wished to repair the losses of worldly affairs; and they were with their father Zebedee—that is, with the devil. For Zebedee is interpreted “fugitive,” while the devil flees from God. He wished to place only four in the calling because through them he signified all preachers called from the four regions of the world.

“And he went about,” etc. Having joined helpers to himself, he devoted himself to preaching, and teaches that a preacher ought not to be idle, but should go about Galilee—that is, the Church—and teach in the synagogues, that is, in congregations, since preaching ought to be public. A congregation is called a synagogue. Here he openly shows that he did not preach to the Gentiles, since he is said to preach in synagogues, which belong to the Jews; and he preached not temporal things, not fables, but the Gospel [Col. 1281D], which pertains to the kingdom of God.

“Teaching and preaching,” etc. He is called “teaching” with respect to the formation of morals, “preaching” with respect to the recompense of God’s kingdom, which is not yet seen. “And healing,” etc. A *languor* is a long-lasting sickness; an infirmity is any illness, whether momentary or not. Mystically, God healed our *languores*, that is, long-established sins, and our infirmities, that is, recent sins.

The moral sense is that a preacher ought to give not words only, but whatever benefits he is able.

“And his report went throughout all Syria, and they brought to him all who were ill, afflicted with various …” The moral sense is that a preacher ought to have a good testimony from those outside. For if anyone’s life is contemptible, it follows that his preaching too is despised.

[Col. 1282A] Allegorically, his good reputation ought to extend even to the proud of this world, who are signified by Syria, which is said to mean “exaltation.” Once his holiness is known, they will offer and reveal to him both themselves, who are ill, and others occupied by diverse vices. A *languor* is a prolonged illness; a torment is an acute illness, such as toothache, pain in the side, and other diseases that sharply afflict men. He enumerates by categories the demon-possessed and the lunatics. Lunatics are those afflicted by demons around the phases of the moon, so that men may blaspheme God’s creature, believing that they suffer this from the moon.

The allegory is this. The demon-possessed are idolaters. Lunatics are unstable persons, who believe now and then withdraw. Paralytics are sluggish and lax men, who do nothing.

“And great crowds followed him.” This refers to the Church, which is denoted by many names. It is Galilee. It is Decapolis, that is, the region of ten cities, which signifies the Decalogue. It is Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace,” because it constantly contemplates the peace above. It is Judea, that is, “confession.” It is from beyond the Jordan, because all the faithful have received baptism.

## Chapter V

“Now when he saw the crowds.” Luke and Matthew seem to disagree concerning this discourse. For Luke relates that the Lord went out to pray on the mountain, spending the night in prayer. When day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve from them, whom he also named Apostles; and, coming down with them, he stood in a level place [Col. 1282C], with a crowd of disciples and a multitude of people. Raising his eyes toward the disciples, he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Luke 6). Luke sets down many things which Matthew also sets down, omits many, and inserts many others.

Matthew, however, relates that Jesus avoided the crowds and therefore went up the mountain with his disciples; there he addressed them while sitting, not standing, as Luke says. Yet, as Augustine says, the discourse may be understood either as the same one or as another. If it is the same, then it may be said that the Lord, the disciples, and the crowds went up the mountain to a certain broad and level place on its side, which could hold a great multitude. But afterward he went up to the summit of the mountain with the disciples alone and there chose the apostles. After choosing them, he descended to the level place and stood there until the crowds gathered around him; afterward he sat down—something Luke does not mention—and when he had sat, his disciples drew nearer as his intimate companions. Thus he gave the discourse principally both to the disciples and to the crowds.

We shall then say that Matthew mentions the Lord’s ascent to the summit of the mountain, avoiding the crowds, because he wished to choose the disciples. But Matthew passes over how he chose the apostles, how he descended from the summit, and how he afterward stood; he begins from the ascent. Yet it seems better that there were two discourses: one which he gave intimately and privately to the disciples, to whom he wished to hand down the New Testament, which they were also to bear, since not everything is to be said to everyone; and another which he gave in a low place before all, in which he also recapitulated many things which he had said in the other.

It should then be understood that Matthew passed over much which Luke says concerning the ascent of the mountain, namely, that he spent the night in prayer when he chose the apostles. Let us come to the literal sense. Christ, about to send the apostles to preach, delivers the New Testament to them; and because he was about to deliver profound and lofty things, he ascends the mountain, to signify the height of the mysteries. But he teaches the people below, because they did not have lofty understanding. In their ordination the apostles received not only the name of apostleship but also a spirit of greater understanding. Thus, once they had been chosen, he spoke lofty things.

Moses likewise received the Law on the mountain because he understood the entire mystery of the Law. But he taught the people below because it was uncultivated and of lesser capacity. The precepts of the old Law were rudimentary and imperfect with respect to righteousness. The precepts which Christ was about to give would remove the imperfection which those precepts possessed, and in these righteousness was to be brought to completion. Hence he was to say: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes” (Matt. 5), etc.

Connection. The crowds followed him. “Now Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain,” in order to avoid them, because such lofty things were not to be preached before them. In this, therefore, he teaches that the preacher ought to speak according to the capacity of the hearers.

“And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him.” He sat down in order to show himself a teacher. For it belongs to masters and teachers to sit. The disciples draw near so that they may hear more closely what they hasten to fulfil.

“And opening his mouth.” By saying “opening,” he signifies that he was about to say not a few things but many, not lowly matters but profound ones, as though opening a treasure.

Allegory. Christ went up the mountain, that is, into the Church, so that what David had said might be fulfilled: “But I have been established by him as king upon Sion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2), etc. What Sion signifies there, this mountain signifies here. To sit is to humble himself through the humanity assumed. Otherwise he would not teach us unless, by assuming our form, he sat—that is, inclined himself toward us. Seeing this humble sitting, the disciples could approach him, because while he was upon the throne of his majesty, men could not comprehend him. Hence it is said: “He was in the world, and the world did not know him” (John 1).

He who had formerly spoken to us in the prophets spoke in his Son, and now the Son himself opened his own mouth to us. The former Law was given in terror, because smoke, crowds, and a storm were around the mountain. But in the giving of the New Testament none of these things occurred; all was done in tranquillity, to teach that this Law must be fulfilled not through fear but through love. The former Law was written upon stones; this one, upon hearts. Otherwise the New Testament would not differ from the Old. Hence the Apostle says: “He is the mediator of a far better covenant” (Heb. 8). And the Lord says through the prophet: “This is the covenant which I shall establish with the house of Israel after those days: giving my laws into their minds, and I shall inscribe them upon their hearts” (ibid.), etc.

“Blessed,” etc. As Moses gave the Law in ten commandments, which contained all the rest, so Christ bestowed the New Testament in seven. And as Moses later dealt more fully with those commandments, making more than three hundred commands from them, so Christ afterward treats more extensively and in detail of these same matters. There are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer, and these seven are commandments; all correspond to one another.

In the prophet the gifts are reckoned from the higher to the lower: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11), because he was speaking of Christ ascending to the earth. But Christ, following the practice of a good teacher, begins from the lower and tends upward; thus he begins with poverty, that is, the removal of evil, and with fear. For whoever wishes to approach God must first remove evils, renounce the world, and fear God.

Note that there are seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer: three concerning heavenly things, namely the first three; three lower petitions concerning earthly things; and the middle one is, as it were, a boundary, though it adheres more closely to heavenly things. The higher petitions are placed first, then the lower; and nevertheless, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6) is naturally first, just as fear is first among the seven gifts, Scripture saying: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). Those two correspond with poverty, from which he began.

Let us first discuss poverty, and afterward the two connected matters. This poverty is the renunciation of oneself and one’s possessions. For two kinds of things must be renounced: external and internal. External things are nobility, riches, and other possessions. Internal things are intelligence, strength, beauty, speed, and the like. We must therefore renounce these things, so as not to trust in riches, nobility, our intelligence, or other such things, but to place our hope in God alone. We must possess other things as though we did not possess them.

This poverty can exist even amid riches. Hence David says: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61). Yet it is safer not to possess them, whence the Lord says: “Sell all that you have” (Matt. 19), etc., because they can scarcely be possessed without attachment.

The same thing is requested where it is said: “But deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6). For to be delivered from evil is never to be enticed by this wicked world, but to be freed from desire for this world, which draws men to itself by displaying present goods and ridiculing invisible ones. We cannot do all this except through the spirit of fear.

For there are four kinds of fear: two earthly and two divine. One is when we fear people lest they take our possessions away, and therefore sin; or whenever, because of some fear, we sin lest we be thought contemptible or be mocked—for example, when we become followers of a faction. The Lord forbids this when he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10). This is called human fear.

There is another fear called servile fear: when we fear punishment and therefore do not sin, though we do not lose the will to sin. Thus the Jews refrained from evil solely out of dread; they had no love in doing good and did not love God. These two fears contribute nothing to salvation, but are harmful.

There are two others. One is when we fear God because of hell and therefore refrain from evil, yet with love of the good and without a will to sin; thus we begin to love God. The Lord commands this fear when he says: “Rather fear him who has power to cast body and soul into the hell of fire” (ibid.). Of this fear it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). For then we fear God when through fear we love him. We fear punishment alone when we do not love God, though we refrain from evil because of punishment. This third fear belongs to the imperfect, though they are to be saved, even if they do not have perfect charity. For perfect charity casts out this third fear.

Whoever has perfect charity, even if he knew that there were no punishment, would nevertheless serve God solely out of love and fear to offend him. This is like a good wife, who loves her husband so greatly that she fears to offend him, even if she knew that, should she sin, she would not be beaten. Thus, from imperfect charity comes the fear of reverence, not of punishments.

The question is therefore raised: how was the fear which is the beginning of wisdom present in Christ, in whom there was always perfect charity, when Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11)? But just as he wished to tremble, be sorrowful, and fear the pains of the Passion, so too he feared the punishments of hell—not for himself but for us—and yet did so with perfect charity, knowing in his conscience that, even if every punishment were absent, he would nevertheless not offend God.

It should be noted that a beatitude arises from each individual virtue. For he says:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit”—that is, by will, not by compulsion.

“Blessed are the meek.” Meekness springs from poverty. Meek is one who cannot be stirred by any injury or loss. Whoever loves earthly things cannot help being stirred by their loss. But the true poor person, just as he did not love them when possessed, does not grieve over them when lost. This is the virtue praised in Moses. If he struck, he was nevertheless meek, acting from zeal for righteousness and not departing from charity. Of this the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

This is prayed for when one says: “And lead us not into temptation” (Luke 11). It is one thing to be tempted, another to be led into temptation. The faithful person does not reject the former—that is, being tempted—nor does he ask for its removal; but he fears being led into it, that is, succumbing to temptation, and prays that this may not happen. The faithful person is tempted when wrong is done to him or his possessions are taken away. He is led into temptation if he grieves and is distressed by grief. The spirit of piety grants this meekness. For if one is pious, one must also be meek.

But it is asked how the poor person can be saved without these things, when each virtue is said to confer beatitude. It should be noted, however, that it is one thing to possess a virtue, another to exercise a virtue. The poor person thus has meekness in his mind but may not have it in exercise—for perhaps he has been in the desert, where no one injured him—yet he is blessed. For if he has even one virtue in exercise, he nevertheless does not have the contrary of the others. If he had the contrary of another virtue, what is said would apply: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (Jas. 2).

“Blessed are those who mourn.” Although the faithful person has renounced worldly things and does not grieve at injuries, he nevertheless sometimes falls into many things; and so tears are necessary continually to wash him clean, because we always sin and see ourselves to be amid the miseries of this world. We also grieve over the sins of our neighbours.

There are two kinds of compunction: when we groan over the miseries of this world and our own sins, and when we groan from desire for heavenly things. Hence the daughter of Caleb asked her father for an upper watering-place and a lower watering-place (Judg. 1), because the soul asks God for compunction both for sins and for desire for the heavenly homeland. But mourning over the miseries of this life and longing for the heavenly homeland belongs only to one who is poor and meek, who does not love the world but recognizes himself as wretched and therefore longs for heaven.

It is fitting for those who mourn over their own and others’ sins to ask: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6). This virtue, which senses the misery of the world and distinguishes it from the heavenly homeland, descends from the spirit of knowledge. For knowledge concerns earthly things, so that we may know what this earthly dwelling is—how burdensome and how miserable. Our thought of the heavenly homeland serves to make us understand, by comparison, the misery of this life.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” These first three virtues concern earthly things only and may be called, as it were, separation from the wicked world. For in these ways the world is despised: by renouncing earthly things, by not grieving at injury, by wiping away sins with tears, and by thinking of the world’s misery.

Now begin the virtues that concern heavenly things, the first of which is righteousness. Righteousness is rendering to each what belongs to him—that is, to God, oneself, and one’s neighbour. To God we owe his proper worship and love with the whole heart. To ourselves we owe the preservation of God’s creation within us by food and clothing, and the subjection of the flesh to the soul. To our neighbour we owe doing for him what we wish to be done for ourselves, provided that this does not depart from the good.

But this righteousness of ours is not called righteousness, but the desire for righteousness. For perfect righteousness cannot be possessed in the present life, until we dwell in the heavenly homeland, where God will be all in all [Col. 1287A]. Therefore our righteousness is not called righteousness, but desire for true righteousness. So Pythagoras called human wisdom not *sophia*, “wisdom,” but *philosophia*, “love of wisdom.” Since we cannot exercise righteousness perfectly in the present, we at least show desire for it. This desire is signified by hunger and thirst.

Thus “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” means the same as if it were said: Blessed are those who practise righteousness in the present time—a righteousness which is here imperfect, being as it were hunger for true righteousness, but which will be perfect in heaven. And because they hunger, and it does not suffice them merely that they are righteous, they ask: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11). For the bread of the faithful, through which righteousness is given and strengthened in them, is the grace of God, the word of God, a ministering angel, and everything that serves to strengthen righteousness; all this is called the grace of God.

This is the food of righteousness in whose strength Elijah travelled for forty days to the mountain of God, Horeb. Therefore righteousness is said to descend from the Spirit of fortitude, who sustains the righteous person lest he fail on the way. This righteousness cannot be established in the mind unless one renounces the world through the virtues mentioned above.

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy,” etc. Because no one can ascend to lofty things through righteousness alone unless God, by his mercy, makes a way for us beyond what is just, God’s mercy must be obtained, so that it may supply what our righteousness cannot attain [Col. 1287C]. He gives counsel on how it may be obtained when he says: “Be merciful, because your Father is merciful” (Luke 6).

Behold the way by which one reaches the mercy of God: by becoming merciful. Mercy must therefore be added to righteousness, so that we do not merely do what is just for our neighbour, but more than is just. Mercy has two parts: giving and forgiving. Hence it is said: “Give, and it shall be given to you; forgive, and it shall be forgiven to you” (Luke 6). These two virtues are so joined that each ought to be tempered by the other. Justice without mercy is cruelty; mercy without justice is laxity. We ought to correct rebels through justice; we ought to pardon penitents through mercy.

But because some are exercised more in justice than in mercy, and others more in mercy than in justice, the latter are called blessed on account of mercy, the former on account of justice, although the two are not separated. This mercy is requested when we say: “May your will be done in us,” namely, that we may be merciful and forgive others. For this is the will of God; it descends from the spirit of counsel. For this is the counsel given to us: if we wish to obtain God’s mercy, let us show mercy to others.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” etc. Purity of heart is placed sixth because on the sixth day man was made in God’s image. This purity is the image of God, through which, once every disturbance and all the darkness of vices have been removed, we see God clearly. Those are called pure in heart who, having put off every cloud of worldly things, fix the gaze of their minds upon God alone in contemplation.

This image had been darkened in man through sin but has now been re-formed through the grace of God; and now, on the sixth day—that is, in the sixth age—man has again been made in God’s image. This contemplation is the image of God because through it we form an image of God for ourselves and, as it were, see God through the image. It fittingly follows the preceding things, because unless they come first, a pure heart is not created in a person. In this pure heart the Lord reigns, because there he is more fully known and loved. Hence we ask: “May your kingdom come in us,” that is, may you reign in us through purity of heart. This purity of heart descends from the spirit of understanding. For the image of God is nothing other than understanding God.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Once a person has all the virtues mentioned above, nothing remains except that he should have God, who is true peace, as his reward. God possesses such peace that there is no discord whatever among the persons, but perfect concord; nor does he vary in himself, although the things in which he is present vary. He will make his own people like himself, because they will be incorruptible, incapable of suffering, and unchangeable; and they will be so harmonious that they will rejoice in the goods of others as in their own.

This is placed seventh because in the true Sabbath, after the seven ages have passed, that peace of rest will be given which Adam did not yet have, but which, after complete obedience, he would have received when transferred to heaven. This is the peace of which the Apostle says: “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4). This is the peace of which Christ says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave to you” (John 14). There I give it; here I leave it, because that peace cannot be possessed except in the future. Yet certain remnants are given in the present, as may be seen in those who have so subdued the unlawful movements of the body that they suffer no civil war within themselves. Their soul has its rest in this life and could not be disturbed in any way, however much they might be beaten; they remain inwardly at peace and labour to reconcile others.

Hence it is said: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law,” though it is not yet perfect. That perfect peace and the spirit of wisdom do not differ. Understanding is one thing, wisdom another. Understanding is when a matter is investigated and examined. Wisdom is when we no longer investigate but are already wise and delight in the good of wisdom itself. This is also that peace in which we shall not labour to search out God but shall delight in him once known. Then we shall be sons of God because we shall be made like him. This is prayed for when we say: “Hallowed be your name,” that is, may your holy name be given to us, so that we may be called your sons and gods.

[Col. 1289A] There are seven virtues that make people blessed. The eighth, which concerns persecution, is common to all. It is nothing but the testing of the virtues mentioned above. For the true poor person is tested in this furnace; so too are the truly meek, the truly righteous, the truly merciful, and the rest. If they are genuine, they become stronger and purer in the fire. If false, they fail and recoil. The same can be said of each virtue: some suffer and some do not suffer; and at every level those who suffer become better.

The eighth is nothing but the first repeated. Hence it has the same reward as the first. But let us now discuss the rewards. To the poor is promised the kingdom of heaven, because nothing greater can be possessed than that which is the common and general reward. But although the same recompense is repeated in the eighth, it must nevertheless be understood differently. Thus it is understood: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Those who renounce earthly things already possess the kingdom of heaven in hope; and even if some of them are purified for a time in purgatorial fire, they nevertheless do not doubt that they will receive the kingdom of heaven.

But those who suffer persecution possess the kingdom of heaven not merely in hope, but in actuality. For those who die for Christ ascend to heaven immediately. This is read in this way, not because both groups will not receive the kingdom of heaven in actuality, but in order to indicate that as great as the difference is between one who possesses it in hope and one who possesses it in reality, so great is the difference in recompense between one who does not suffer and one who suffers.

[Col. 1289C] It is fitting that the meek should possess the earth, as may be seen from the contrary. The unmeek do not possess themselves, much less their possessions; rather, they are always quarrelling and always divided. But the meek, who have possessed and restrained themselves, will possess the Father’s inheritance in the future. To possess is more than merely to have. We have many things that we lose tomorrow. But the recompense of the meek person is greater than that of the poor person alone.

Note also that the kingdom of heaven is promised to the poor person who has stripped himself of earth, just as to the devil, who stripped himself of heaven, the lower regions were given.

To those who mourn consolation is fittingly promised, so that one who has been sad in the present may rejoice in the future. And just as it is greater to rejoice in a kingdom already possessed than merely to have or possess a kingdom for a time—for we possess many things with sorrow—so the reward of one who grieves is greater than that of the poor and the meek. For whoever has the subsequent virtues also has the preceding ones. But whoever does not have the preceding ones always has the subsequent ones—not, I say, in merit, but in exercise. To those who hunger for righteousness, the satisfaction of righteousness is rightly given; for just as it is greater to be filled in a palace than to be consoled after mourning, so the reward of the righteous is greater than being separated from evil—a separation which, as we have said, is denoted in the three preceding blessings. Mercy is deservedly bestowed on the merciful, so that they receive more than they had merited. Just as in a king’s palace, when someone has been filled by three or four courses, many further dishes are nevertheless added, so certain blessed persons, though a lesser blessedness could suffice, nevertheless receive a hundredfold [Col. 1290A]. And just as one who receives beyond satiety receives more than one who has only enough for satiety, so the glory of the merciful is greater than that of those preceding them.

A fitting reward is given to the pure in heart: having the clear eye of the mind, they may clearly see and understand God. These have a greater recompense than the first, just as one in a king’s court not only dines but also beholds the king’s face. Yet he is supreme who is called the king’s son; that dignity belongs to the peacemakers, though all are blessed. For blessed is one who desires nothing evil and possesses whatever he wishes. The inferior person in heaven would not wish to possess the superior’s glory, since he would be desiring what is unjust; but through charity he will possess all things, since in the superior he will love that exaltation as much as it is in himself.

“You are blessed.” Having briefly set forth the seven general precepts, upon which all things depend, he expounds them more fully. And having spoken generally, “Blessed,” he now turns to the disciples, who were to bring these precepts forth to others, but first had to be trained in them themselves, so that what they preached in word they might show by example. Since they were to suffer evils and be sent as sheep among wolves, they first had to be strengthened in patience and humility, which is the safeguard of virtues; and after sad things have been heard, joyful things are announced for consolation. He therefore begins with the eighth blessing, expounding it more broadly in its parts.

**Connection.** I said that all who suffer will be blessed, and you especially, whose particular lot—and that of vicars—is to suffer. Note the three forms of persecution: of heart, [Col. 1290C] mouth, and hand. Yet the order there is reversed. It should also be known that in another translation, where we have “they have spoken evil,” there stands “they have hated”; but this translator has put the expression of hatred in place of hatred itself, that is, a curse in place of evil-speaking. For it is great hatred when one person curses another in person. “To persecute” signifies every persecution by the hand; and to speak evil is persecution by the mouth. In another translation, moreover, where we have “they have persecuted,” there stands “they have driven out.” And since, if they spoke evil that was true, they would not be blessed, he added, “lying.” And since they could suffer reproaches for an earthly lord or for some other reason, like heretical martyrs, he added, “for my sake.” For it is not punishment that makes a martyr, [Col. 1290D] but the cause. And because this might at first make them sad, he says: “Rejoice” in mind and “exult” in body, because your reward is not merely great, like that of others, but also abundant in the heavens—not only in material things, but also in spiritual things: incorruption, immortality, and impassibility, in which heavens God is.

“For so,” etc. Do not be surprised if my servants suffer, for this is not unusual: the prophets too suffered before them. “So,” that is, the same punishments and for the same cause—that is, for me—who were before you. As though he said: If they suffered, who had no example, then you too ought to suffer and are able to do so, because you have an example.

“You are the salt of the earth.” This is why you ought not fail in tribulation. As though he said: You must endure tribulations steadfastly, because you are the salt of the earth—that is, the strength of earthly people—and therefore your failure would be the failure of others. Note that they are called both salt and the light of the world. For believers need two things: illumination of mind and strength in action. The apostles are light, through whom others are enlightened and cleansed from the darkness of ignorance; and they are called salt, as it were *salus* (“salvation”), by which these same persons are preserved from corruption of mind and body. For just as salt preserves flesh from decay, destroys worms in it, and dries up its watery humors, so the apostles, after enlightening some persons, ought to preserve them in a good purpose, extinguish the worms of vices, and dry up all carnality. Hence in the Psalm: “The Lord is my illumination and salvation” (Ps. 26 [Vulgate]). [Col. 1291B] For if someone knows God but lacks firmness of purpose, it is of no benefit. And elsewhere the prophet says: “I have set you as a light of the nations, that you may be my salvation unto the end of the earth” (Isa. 49).

Salt indeed makes land barren; whatever is salty is barren. Therefore, after cities had been destroyed, conquerors ploughed over their foundations and sowed salt upon them, to signify barrenness and devastation. The apostles are therefore called salt because their preaching is the seasoning of others. No preaching has force unless it is supported by the seasoning of apostolic doctrine. “But if the salt has lost its savor”—that is, if your strength fails in tribulation—“wherewith shall it be salted?” That is: by whom will the weaker people be strengthened? “It is good for nothing” [Col. 1291C]. As though he said: After those who are leaders and examples for others have failed, they are fit for no use except to be cast out from the office of teaching and trodden underfoot by men—that is, despised by carnal people.

Or otherwise: “But if the salt”—that is, those called seasoning—“has lost its savor,” that is, has failed by falling into some error, “wherewith shall it be salted?” As though he said: The apostles are the source of doctrine and have no teachers above them; if therefore they fail, who will salt them—that is, who will instruct them? The same must be said of the pope: after his preaching tastes of heresy, he is good for nothing further except to be cast out from the Church and despised by men. Those supreme shepherds who cannot be deposed by others are properly called salt [Col. 1291D]. Or, if we wish to understand other prelates, the passage is read thus: “By what salt will the earth—that is, its earthly subjects—be salted?” Note that every prelate who departs from the faith must be cast out and accused by men. If he loses savor through wickedness in his life but his preaching is good, he is to be tolerated by men, according to the saying: “Do what they say; but do not do what they do.” But if the pastor’s life corrupts the life of the sheep, Gregory and other saints decreed that he must be expelled.

“You likewise are the light of the world.” Even if the world is at times not enlightened by it, it nevertheless does not remain in it. “A city cannot,” etc. Might someone say: Could they not remain concealed in a corner and be good there? The answer is: No, because you are a city fortifying the Church [Col. 1292A], fighting against the world, “set upon a mountain,” that is, Christ. This is the meaning of “it cannot,” etc.

“Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand,” etc. Another comparison: Christ was a lamp, that is, light in the vessel of humanity. He was not hidden through fear of present things or love of them; nor was he hidden in the figures of the old law, as though he intended those rites always to be observed. Similarly, the apostles did not hide beneath the bushel of fear or temporal hope, or in Jewish rites, but preached the truth before all. The lampstand is the Church; the house is the Church. “And may they glorify your Father,” etc. He removes the aim of human praise: thus they are to glorify God in us, not with the intention that you yourselves may be praised.

[Col. 1292B] “Do not think that I have come to destroy the law or the prophets,” etc. As though the apostles said: Why do you give new precepts? Do you wish to destroy the old law and establish another? The answer: Do not think that I destroy the law, but that I fulfill it. There are three things in the old law: moral precepts; figures in sacrifices; and promises, such as, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isa. 7). The precepts were elementary and imperfect, and some permitted things because of human frailty. Christ fulfilled these by removing their imperfection and destroying the permissions. Thus love of neighbour is commanded in the law, but not perfectly, because hatred of an enemy is permitted. Behold, that tolerated evil is destroyed, and love of every neighbour is commanded. The law permits an eye for an eye and a tooth for [Col. 1292C] a tooth to be taken, tempering human anger at least a little, so that people may not repay more evil than they received. Behold, he utterly destroys anger when he says, “For everyone who is angry with his brother,” etc., and forbids vengeance. He fulfills the figures by doing what they signified; for they would then be dissolved if they remained without the things signified. He also fulfills the promises by doing what they promise.

“Amen I say to you,” etc. They will truly be fulfilled, because I say to you, *amen*, that is, truly, that not one word shall pass from the law—indeed, not even one smallest figure—without accomplishing something in the law. *Iod* is the smallest letter among the Hebrews; yet the Evangelist did not name it by its Hebrew name but by the Greek name, *iota*, because the Lord likewise, when speaking [Col. 1292D] to the disciples, pronounced *iota*, not *iod*. This was not without reason, as will be explained below. Nor shall even one apex pass from the law without accomplishing something. The Hebrews represent different letters by the same shape: by *aleph* they represent both A and E, but distinguish them by certain points placed above or below. The distinctions placed above letters are called apices. He speaks only of these because of their mystical significance. As though he said: No form of a letter, nor any part of its form, shall pass away without having something to accomplish in the law.

“Until heaven and earth pass away.” For not all things were completed at Christ’s coming; some are still being gradually fulfilled. But at the consummation [Col. 1293A] of the age all things will be complete. As though he said: Not the least precept, nor any part of a precept, will be annulled without being fulfilled either in the head or in the members, because things considered least in the law, such as “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass” (Deut. 22), are full of great sacraments. Yet the Pharisees annulled and rendered them void through their traditions.

He used *iota*, not *ioth*, because *iota* among the Greeks is the ninth letter and signifies ten; and by this number the Decalogue is understood. As though he said: Not one *iota*—that is, not one of the ten commandments, through which the other commandments depending upon them are understood—will pass away. Nor will one apex—that is, one thing signified by the figures or promises of the law—pass away. We refer the moral commandments to the *iota*, and the figures and promises to the apex [Col. 1293B]. We have understood “the thing signified” through the apex because it shows the signification of a letter—what A or E is meant to signify. He mentioned upper apices rather than lower distinctions of letters because through the former he conveys the allegorical sense. The allegorical sense is higher, and is signified by the apex, which is a height.

“Until heaven and earth pass away.” These will not pass away materially, but in their form. Corruptible things, such as earth and air, will be changed into a better nature. Heavenly things, however, will be changed because they will be brighter—the sun, moon, and heaven—and no longer movable. Judgment will take place before they are changed. When that has occurred, there will be an end of all ages, and then they will be changed; hence he rightly said, “Until they are changed.”

“Whoever therefore breaks one of these least commandments” (Matt. 5)—what then? After saying that he did not wish to destroy the law and that all things must be fulfilled, he gives judgment concerning breakers and fulfillers. Breakers are those who refuse to do what the moral commandments command, and those who interpret the figures of the law or its promises badly and deny that they contain a thing signified, as do the Jews. There are two kinds of these. Some break them and teach others to break them; others break them but do not teach. Those who break and teach are worse. Again, fulfillers differ: some act but do not teach, benefiting themselves but not others; others act and teach, benefiting both themselves and others, and these are greatest. There is a third class, who ought not to be called fulfillers [Col. 1293D]: those who teach but do not act, benefiting others but not themselves; these are least. Here, however, he gives judgment concerning the worst breakers, who break and teach, and the greatest fulfillers, who act and teach.

**Connection.** Since fulfillment is necessary, therefore whoever breaks, as has been said, one of these commandments—that is, commandments of the law—not only the greatest but even the least, and not only breaks it but teaches thus, that is, teaches others to break it, although he may be called great among his own people, will nevertheless be judged least in the kingdom of heaven. He will be judged there, not because that least person is present where none but great persons are found, but because he will be so judged in the court of heaven, that is, among the saints. Jews who know how to interpret the figures badly, so that they are not understood concerning Christ, [Col. 1294A] are called wise among their own people; but in heaven they are considered foolish and least—that is, worse than those who break but do not teach.

That there are only great persons in heaven was signified by Peter’s catch after the resurrection, when the net was filled with one hundred and fifty-three large fish. All are called large because, in the resurrection, only the great are gathered into the heavenly Church; whereas in the present Church good and bad are gathered together. This was prefigured in the first catch, when the net was filled with large and small fish, good and bad, and the net was torn: for in the present Church good and bad are held without distinction. But whoever does and teaches “will be called great in the kingdom of heaven,” although he is rejected here [Col. 1294B].

“But I say to you.” Having given judgment concerning breakers and fulfillers, he teaches how the commandments of the law must be fulfilled: namely, by supplying what is lacking in the law. The old law punishes only actual sins, not sins of the heart. No one was put to death for adultery of the mind or for murder. In the New Testament he promises punishment not only for actual deeds but also for intentions.

**Connection.** He said that whoever fulfills and teaches will be great in heaven; but this is how you must fulfill. “But I say to you.” By this he makes them attentive. “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees,” etc. He sets forth the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees because [Col. 1294C] they seemed more righteous under the law, since they not only performed Moses’ commandments but also observed new traditions. The scribes were secretaries who expounded the law and wrote new traditions. But the Lord commanded that the apostles’ righteousness should be more abundant than that of the Pharisees, because the Jews followed only Moses’ elementary and imperfect commandments. Christ commanded them to follow those commandments, but in their perfected and consummated form; and he teaches their perfection and fulfillment. But in order that his law may be more burdensome, he adds a penalty: otherwise you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

“You have heard that it was said,” etc. He sets forth the righteousness of the Pharisees and explains his own fulfillment. For while [Col. 1294D] the law forbids killing by the hand, Christ forbids killing by intention, commanding that one not be angry. Let us therefore consider what anger he forbids. First, there is suggestion in a person, either outwardly from the devil or inwardly from the frailty of the flesh. Neither is sin, but both are material for struggle and victory. After suggestion comes *propassio*, that is, a sudden movement. This involves some fault, but is venial without any deliberation about good and evil. Then follows *passio*, when one not only has the movement but also deliberates how to act; this is death in the house. This passion is twofold. One person delights in that thought, finds it good to linger there, and yet would not wish to carry it out even if opportunity were available. Another not only delights in it but also seeks the opportunity, which sometimes fails and does not happen as he wishes; this does not differ from a hidden act [Col. 1295A]. The first passion is called delight; the second consent, although the names are sometimes exchanged. Then follows the act, which is death at the gate. Finally comes habit, which is the death of one four days dead.

Since, then, he forbids anger, he seems contrary to the one who says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4 [Vulgate]). But the one who says “Be angry” speaks of passion, which cannot be taken away and is not criminal; indeed, it is natural. God, however, forbids the anger of passion arising from deliberation, which is criminal and is death. He forbids anger, and also the very will to commit adultery. By these two are understood all movements toward harming one’s brother and all movements toward desiring carnal pleasures. These two movements are called anger and concupiscence, from which all acts arise. It should be known that all movements toward harming one’s brother are reckoned among kinds of homicide—for example, detraction, which is an effect of hatred and anger and is called homicide. Hence the apostle John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3).

He therefore says: “Everyone who is angry,” etc. Some manuscripts add “without cause,” but it is not added in Greek, nor is it necessary. The sense is the same if one considers what it is to be angry with a brother. Whoever is angry with his brother, rather than with his brother’s sin, is angry without cause. For if someone is angry for his brother’s correction, he is angry not against his brother but against the sin. But if someone hates his brother because of an insult to himself, he is improperly angry without cause [Col. 1295C]. He ought not to be angry for that reason. He rightly says “brother,” for every human being is a brother by the first generation, and every believer spiritually by the second, that is, by regeneration. By saying “brother,” he excludes *propassio*, for it is not yet directed against a brother.

“Whoever says to his brother, *Racha*,” etc. *Racha* is an interjection and signifies the feeling of anger. As though he said: Whoever is not merely angry but breaks forth into a cry of indignation earns a greater punishment. But whoever says “fool”—that is, disgraces his brother by an insult, which is more—will receive a worse punishment. Note that judgment, council, and Gehenna all signify infernal punishment. But because the quality of punishment varies according to the quality of fault, the Lord wished to signify these differences by these names. Judgment is less, when a case is being conducted against an accused person and he has an opportunity for defense, than council. For “council” is called that situation in which judges have assembled not to hear the case but to give sentence. And it is more serious to impose punishment already than merely to pronounce sentence. Likewise, punishment will be greater according to the greater gravity of sin; the degrees of punishment alone are signified by those names.

Gehenna is first found in the Gospel, and the term is drawn from history. It was a valley, not very pleasant or delightful, in which the Jews, abandoning the Lord’s temple, used to sacrifice to idols. But Jeremiah, foreseeing Jerusalem’s future destruction by Nebuchadnezzar, foretold that the place [Col. 1296A] where they sacrificed at that time would be filled with dead bodies. This was fulfilled during the captivity. For such a slaughter of the Jews took place that the place, filled with corpses, was turned into a place of the greatest stench. Comparing infernal punishment with that stench, the Lord calls hell the land of Hennon, that is, Gehenna. For *ge* means “land,” and it is called *henna* or *hennon*.

Thus God commands one neither to be angry nor to injure by word. But if one has injured his brother in any way, the Lord teaches both what will happen to him and how he may heal himself. This evil will happen to him which happened to Cain: namely, that the Lord will not look upon him or upon his gifts, just as he did not look upon Cain, who envied and hated his brother. He gives him this remedy: that he be reconciled to his brother [Col. 1296B], and then his gifts will please the Lord. For love of neighbour always comes first in time, and love of God follows. One first loves one’s neighbour, and after that acquires love of God.

**Connection.** He commanded: do not injure your brother either in mind or deed. Therefore, if you have injured him and wish to offer your gift before the altar, etc.—as though he said: If you offer your gift, whether bodily, such as a candle, or spiritual, such as prayer, at an altar, whether material or spiritual, that is, Christ; and if you remember that your brother has something against you, that is, some complaint against you—not that you have something against your brother—then do not offer your gift at that time. Yet do not put off prayer, because David says: “Pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. 49 [Vulgate]); but “leave,” that is, defer offering, there—that is, after you have remembered—before—that is, before you offer at the altar—and go first to be reconciled to your brother. If he is present, humble yourself before him and do what lies within your power. If he is absent, promise and have the good will that, as soon as you find him, you will humble yourself before him; repent well in your heart, and then return to your offering.

“Be well-disposed.” Someone may say: And if he will not forgive me, what shall I do? “Be,” he says, “well-disposed toward him,” that is, be benevolent toward him; be his friend and pray for him. But this must not be delayed: you ought quickly to be reconciled to him, love him, and repent of the injury, “while you are on the way,” that is, in this age with him. If he dies before [Col. 1296D] you are reconciled, it will be more dangerous for you. Yet if you repent, you may then also be saved, though with greater penitence.

“Lest perhaps.” This is why you must be reconciled while you are on the way: lest perhaps the adversary be the cause why you are handed over to the Judge, that is, God, and the Judge to the officer, that is, the reaping angel, etc. Or otherwise: the adversary is the divine word, which opposes the pleasures of our flesh. And so long as the one whom we have injured and the divine word are our adversary, he commands the person who has injured another to be reconciled to the divine word, which commands us to love our adversaries and to be reconciled to them, lest it likewise be the cause why he is handed over to the Judge.

He calls the farthing (*quadrans*) the least sins, because a *quadrans* is a type of coin containing two mites. As though he said: “Until he pays,” that is, pays even the least sins—which will never occur. Or the “last farthing” is called earth, because there are four elements: the lower and worse quarter is earth. Fire signifies charity, air our life, water baptism, and earth every corruption. This is the meaning: “Until he pays the last farthing,” that is, all sins signified through earth [Col. 1297A].

“You have heard,” etc. Up to this point he has dealt with every movement toward harming another; now he treats every movement toward concupiscence, understood through adultery. As though he said: I still show how your righteousness is to exceed the righteousness of the scribes. The law forbids actual fornication; I forbid even adultery of the heart [Col. 1297B]. If someone objects that the law commands, “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife” (Deut. 5), this did not seem to the Jews to have been said except concerning taking away another’s wife: namely, that no one should wish to take another’s wife away; and they did not believe it to be adultery to desire intercourse with another’s wife. Therefore the Lord says:

“But I say to you that everyone who looks upon a woman,” not with bodily sight but in order to lust after her—that is, with the eyes of concupiscence. These are the eyes opened in Adam and Eve. For concupiscence for outward and carnal pleasures had been closed in them; but after human nature was corrupted, concupiscence began to open and flow here and there toward every carnal pleasure. This opening, however, was evil. Here “woman” is understood broadly to include every carnal pleasure [Col. 1297C] and fornication. For a human being ought to be Christ’s bride and cleave to him as the eternal good. If, therefore, someone abandons the eternal good and cleaves to something lower—whether idols, gold, a woman, or another pleasure—he commits fornication against God.

He sets the conclusion of the commandment, adding also concerning action. As though he said in every instance: “Remove from yourself every evil understanding and action” (Prov. 4). By the eye he understands understanding; by the hand, action. By these two alone do human beings sin; but he first deals with the eyes. This eye is taken so broadly that it signifies whatever pertains to understanding. First, an eye means a good teacher, who illuminates understanding by teaching the Scriptures. If he teaches worldly things, he is the left eye; if he teaches heavenly things, the right. Therefore, if even that teacher who is right—that is, one who expounds divine things—causes you to stumble by introducing some heresy, pluck him out from yourself and separate from him even at a distance.

Again, the eye is reason and our exercise in the Scriptures. If, therefore, our study of divine Scripture leads us into some error through the subtlety of our intellect, we ought rather to give up the study of those Scriptures and live simply than perish as learned heretics. Again, our eye is the contemplative life. If that causes us to stumble by driving us into idleness, as it does many monks, let us abandon it and move to the active life, undertaking some labor, so that we may rather be saved in it than perish there while lamenting [Col. 1298A]. And so with the rest: for it is more expedient—that is, more fitting—that one member perish, that is, our friend or other things called our members, which help and sustain us, than that the whole body, that is, both I and my friend, perish.

“And if your right hand,” etc. Likewise, a right hand means someone cooperating with me in good works; a left hand, someone cooperating with me in evil things. If the right hand—that is, a right-hand co-worker—causes you to stumble by urging you to commit some sin, and you can escape in no other way, you ought to leave him, just as many hermits left their companions. Or the hand may similarly signify a good work or the active life, which should be abandoned if it harms us. For if I visited and fed a poor woman, and the devil tempted me in connection with her, I ought immediately to abandon that almsgiving. Or if my abbot sent me to incompatible work and I could not be saved there, I ought to excuse myself. But if he compelled me more frequently and I could not otherwise escape, I ought rather to flee from him [Col. 1298B].

“But it was said,” etc. Again he shows a more abundant righteousness. Moses (Deut. 24), because of the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, permitted—not commanded—the dismissal of wives if they were displeasing because they were quarrelsome, ugly, or for many other reasons, rather than that the men should kill them. For dismissal was a lesser evil than killing, and those who dismissed them sinned and were not saved. Many things are permitted in order to avoid graver evils; and it is as though counsel is given when it is necessary to sin either more lightly or more gravely, so that they may be punished more lightly in hell. Then the man who dismissed her gave a bill of divorce, though what was written in that document is unknown, unless perhaps it included the cause of divorce and the revenues of vineyard and land from which the wife would live.

But I say that a wife is not to be dismissed, except only for the cause of fornication, because everyone who dismisses his wife makes her commit adultery, so far as he is concerned, although she may sometimes not wish to commit adultery. He seems to contradict himself when he says elsewhere, “Whoever does not hate father or mother,” etc., “is not worthy of me” (Matt. 7 [citation as printed]), and elsewhere, “Whoever has not left father or mother or wife for my sake cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). But he does not. The meaning is this: a human being ought to love the highest good, and in comparison with it ought to hate and despise all the miseries [Col. 1298D] of this world, to wish them not to exist, and to hate all worldly conditions, such as being born from a father and having intercourse, even with one’s wife, etc.

But we ought to wish persons to be with us in heaven; and this is what it means to hate father or mother, etc. Yet we ought to endure those conditions, because they have been given to us as punishment and humiliation. But if father or wife draws us into some sin, then we ought to leave them for God’s sake, because we owe them nothing against God. Here, however, he commands that a wife not be dismissed except for the cause of fornication alone. If she has broken the law of marriage, a man may separate her from himself, so as to remove from himself the union which she violated. Yet the sacrament [Col. 1299A] of marriage remains, so that he may not take another wife. It is lawful to retain her if he wishes, according to the Apostle, who commands either abstinence or reconciliation (1 Cor. 7); for either is lawful.

Yet it is found written: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and wicked” (Prov. 18 [citation as printed]). But this is said of one who sins continually, lest he become a partner in her adultery if he knowingly tolerates her. “Fornication” is taken broadly here: if she turns her husband’s heart toward idolatry or another grave offense, so that he could not be saved with her, he should leave her. Thus the cause of the wife’s fornication requires that he dismiss her; likewise the cause of spiritual fornication, lest she herself commit fornication. But if by mutual consent they wish to abstain, they may separate, so that he becomes a monk and she a nun; then it is not a human being but God who separates them. This [Col. 1299B] is not contrary to the saying: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19; Mark 10).
