Likewise, if someone marries a relative of his deceased wife or of himself, he should dismiss her and marry another, because she was not his wife. Similarly, if he unknowingly marries a female slave, after he knows it he should labor to free her or dismiss her, because it was not a marriage but a false substitution. God’s law does not wrong earthly masters by taking away their male or female slaves. If a husband is of a frigid nature, the marriage is not complete; she should leave him and marry another.

“Again you have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely.’” Moses, seeing that he could not abolish swearing, abolished perjury. Again, because people hold in great reverence the things by which they swear, lest they make creatures into gods for themselves, he commanded them to render their oaths to God and not swear by creatures. But the Lord removes them more perfectly from perjury when he forbids swearing altogether. An oath, however, is neither good nor evil in itself, because it is both commanded and forbidden with qualification. Some things are to be sought in themselves and some avoided in themselves, such as fornication. Other things are to be avoided for another reason, such as a cleric’s living with a woman—namely, because of suspicion and temptation. Other things are to be done for another reason, such as swearing because of people’s unbelief, lest neighbours sin by wrongly suspecting us; for it is cruelty to disregard one’s reputation, in which one’s neighbour is killed. An oath belongs to this latter category: it is not evil in itself, since, if it were evil, it would never be commanded; nor is that good which is forbidden. Yet it is commanded because of necessity and forbidden when it is idle, for then it is evil. It is also idle and superfluous, and produces perjury, if it is too frequently employed.

Neither by heaven. Since he had forbidden swearing altogether and without qualification, lest you should think that he had forbidden only swearing by God, and that it was no sin to swear by creatures or to forswear oneself by them, he adds: “Neither by heaven,” that is, by the higher creatures; “nor by earth,” that is, by the lower. Heaven is not called a throne, nor earth a footstool, because God occupies such a position—he who is wholly everywhere—but because he wished to indicate heaven’s dignity: heaven possesses greater beauty than earth [Col. 1300A], and we admire God more in the creation of heaven than of earth. Hence he is said to sit in heaven, and earth is said to be beneath his feet, because it seems lower in worth, like things trampled underfoot. Yet by this God is signified to possess both: the one as more worthy, the other as less worthy.

There are three reasons why we ought not to swear by creatures: first, because they were made good by the supreme Good; second, because God dwells in them, and whoever swears by creatures swears by the indwelling One; third, because they are signs of great sacraments. For heaven signifies the souls of the righteous, in whom God reigns and judges; earth, earthly people, whom he has beneath his feet, that is, under his power; Jerusalem, the Church, which is truly the city of God. Therefore, because of the things signified, the figures are to be revered, lest one who swears by the figures violate the things signified. [Col. 1300B]

“Nor by your head.” The head signifies Christ, as though he said: You ought not therefore to swear by your head, because it is not your work but God’s; and truly it is not yours, because you cannot create even one hair, nor even give it its color. Note that one who lies sins; but one who affirms by God and afterward deceives sins doubly—both by lying and by the falsity of the affirmation made through an oath, which is perjury.

“But let your speech,” etc. “How then shall we speak?” those will say who are accustomed always to swear. The answer is this: if someone says, “Is it so?” answer, “It is,” if you wish to affirm. But if someone says, “Is it not so?” answer, “No,” if you wish to deny. Or let your speech be “Yes, yes,” so that there is affirmation both in word and sign; or “No, no,” lest speech say one thing and signs or deeds another. [Col. 1300C]

“But whatever is more,” etc. He prohibited an idle oath; but if it is necessary, he does not prohibit it, because Paul swore in the Epistles, where he says: “God is my witness” (Rom. 1); and God swore: “By myself I have sworn” (Gen. 22). Therefore he adds: “Whatever is more than this speech,” that is, “Yes, yes; no, no,” “is from evil.” It is as though he said: If you are compelled to swear, it is from evil—that is, from the unbelief of the hearer. He does not say, “It is evil,” but “from evil”: the need to swear proceeds from the suspicion of the person compelling it. For if an innocent person is accused, let him swear, in order to satisfy those who harbor evil suspicions about him; for reputation, in which one’s neighbor is killed, must not be neglected.

“You have heard,” etc. Again he teaches a more abundant [Col. 1300D] righteousness. Moses gave a certain command both for those injured and for rash persons who inflict injury. Lest all should be rash in injuring others, he imposed a penalty to restrain them. Again, because he could not altogether draw the hands of the injured away from vengeance, he at least wished to moderate their anger, lest they avenge themselves beyond the injury, but return equal retaliation for an equal wrong. Those who are injured also tend to avenge an injury more severely than it was; indeed, they may kill a person even for a word.

But Christ teaches a more perfect righteousness: namely, not to resist evil at all—that is, the person doing harm—but to endure the injury and not return it. Yet vengeance is not altogether prohibited. For the Lord punishes the wicked when he says, “Depart from me, you cursed” (Matt. [Col. 1301A] 25), etc.; and he who “gave his cheek to the one striking him” (Lam. 3), and David, who said, “If I have repaid evils to those repaying me,” may these and these things happen to me (Ps. 7), punished many people.

For secular powers are God’s vicars: they condemn the wicked in God’s stead, both for the offenders’ benefit and for the terror of others. Such persons may indeed exact punishment for evil deeds, but from zeal for justice, not delight in punishment, as God does; David punished in this way. One may also avenge one’s own injuries, not as a private person but as a judge. But all other persons are forbidden to take vengeance, for the injured would not do so out of love for justice but from hatred. Hence the Lord says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. 12), either in my own person or through a vicar, who strikes not the human being but sin, so that the person may be corrected.

[Col. 1301B] He sets forth three injuries: bodily harm, the taking away of possessions, and forced service; he commands all of these to be endured. He addresses bodily injury when he says: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek,” etc. Although it is not absurd to understand this literally, the Lord is not recorded to have done this; rather, when struck on the cheek, he answered: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong” (John 18), etc. Nor did the apostles do likewise.

Therefore, by the right cheek is understood an open injury in a worthy matter. By “cheek,” openness; by “right,” a worthy matter is understood. It is as though he said: If anyone reproaches you because you are a Christian or religious, or for some other worthy thing of this sort—an injury open and in a worthy matter—offer him the other also. He does not say “the left,” but “the other right,” [Col. 1301C] with the implied sense: for a good person has nothing left-handed in himself, but all things are right-handed. Hence it is read in the book of Judges (ch. 3) that the left was used for the right in this sense. It is as though he said: Offer him the other also; that is, be willing to suffer even injury in another right-hand action, if occasion requires. For if he reproaches you because you are a Christian, and you are ready to endure this, and for that reason calls you a hypocrite because you are religious.

“And to him,” etc. He deals with the injury of having possessions taken away. He prohibits us from recovering what is ours if it has been taken away, if we cannot do this without contention. But otherwise, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 6), we ought rather to suffer fraud than contend in court with a brother. Therefore the Lord says: “And to him who wishes to contend with you in court,” [Col. 1301D] etc. For if he wishes to contend, we should rather relinquish our possessions.

By the tunic, which is nearer to the flesh, necessities are understood; by the cloak, superfluities. Luke uses a better order when he says: “If anyone takes your cloak, let him also have your tunic” (Luke 6): that is, if anyone takes what is superfluous, let him have even what is necessary, if need be.

“And whoever,” etc. Here is the third injury, concerning forced service. If someone, I do not say harms a believer or takes away his possessions, but compels him to serve him—as often happens in captivity—let him endure it and serve, even beyond what has been commanded. But if he compels him to do something unlawful, namely a sin, he should rather allow himself to be killed. This is understood in this metaphor: “Whoever compels you for a thousand paces”—that is, to some lawful work. A thousand paces are a Sabbath-day’s journey, [Col. 1302A] during which servile works are prohibited; therefore a thousand paces are not servile work but lawful work, as is also signified by the number one thousand, which signifies perfection. It is as though he said: If he compels you to some servile work, that is, a sin which a slave performs, do not do it. But if he compels you for a thousand paces, that is, to something lawful, such as digging in his vineyard, go—that is, carry out what he compels—and not merely a thousand paces, but two thousand.

He gives “a thousand” three times, because he commands service in three ways: in body, soul, and spirit—so that one may work with the whole body, and in spirit, that is, with the will, and in soul, that is, with reason; namely for God, not out of fear, not out of greed, but because one awaits God as rewarder.

Some things are also understood mystically. Thus, if a heretic wishes to violate a right doctrine, [Col. 1302B] set against him another testimony of Scripture, and offer another again until he grows weary. Spiritually, the teacher takes away the tunic when he causes inward things to be confessed—that is, vices of the soul, such as anger, envy, and the like. The one who does not blush to confess outward things as well—that is, vices of the flesh, such as fornication and the rest—adds the cloak.

“And whoever,” etc. Since it is not enough to endure losses unless we also give what is ours, he adds: “Give to the one who asks of you.” He does not say, “Whatever he asks, give,” but “Give.” If he asks for an honorable thing, give either all of it or part, if you cannot give all; and if you can do neither, give goodwill. If he asks for a dishonorable thing, give correction.

“And do not turn away from one wishing to borrow from you,” but willingly lend. Lending is indeed a kind of mercy, but not so that one receives more in return. [Col. 1302C]

“You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’” This was a permission, not a command. “But I say to you: Love,” etc. He sets forth three kinds of enemies: some harm with the hand, others with the tongue, others with the heart; and he commands these to be loved. Those who hate are enemies in heart; those who slander, in speech; those who persecute, in hand.

The prophets seem to oppose this command when they call down evils upon their enemies. But they appear to approve God’s will: they did not utter imprecations, but gave assent to the divine judgment. Again, since he commands prayer for enemies, John seems to say the contrary: “If anyone knows that his brother is sinning not unto death, let him pray, and the Lord will give him life. But there is sin unto death; [Col. 1302D] I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5). Here it is plainly shown that there are certain brothers for whom we are not commanded to pray.

Sin unto death is when, after recognizing the truth, a person nevertheless perversely attacks brotherhood, envies a good person, hates what is good, and is altogether obstinate in evil. This sin is called obstinacy or impenitence. Such a stain is of a kind that the person cannot submit to the humility of repentance and prayer, even though he may sometimes repent, as Judas did when he said, “I have sinned, betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27). Yet he would not humble himself and ask forgiveness, but ran more readily to the noose; and God does not forgive this repentance.

A person of this kind, who has incurred the devilish sin, is already condemned with the devil; and one should no more pray for him than for the devil. But [Col. 1303A] not everyone recognizes him—only spiritual persons, such as John. Therefore no one is commanded not to pray for him except the person who knows; hence we pray indiscriminately for all, because we do not know how to discern.

Other sins are not called unto death, because people can repent of them; and, since they can be healed, the medicine of prayer should not be denied. But one should not pray for impenitence, because it is already in hell—that is, in despair. Here, however, the Lord commands prayer for unbelieving persecutors. John, on the other hand, speaks of brothers; therefore there is no contradiction. Or he does not command prayer for all, just as he himself is not believed to have prayed for all in the Passion, but for those who were not in devilish sin and did not knowingly or through envy attack the truth, but did so through ignorance. Hence [Col. 1303B] he says: “For they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). These are evidently those whom Peter afterward converted, to whom Peter said that they had acted through ignorance, as had certain of their rulers.

“That you may be sons of your Father,” etc. It is as though he said: that you may imitate him who is always your Father, that is, benevolent toward you, even though you are not his children. Thus in the Gospel the man who had lived wastefully said: “Father, I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15). He called him Father, yet denied that he was his son. He then adds how they ought to imitate him: “Who makes his sun rise,” etc. It is as though he said: he freely does good to the good and the evil alike.

Understand the visible sun, not the Sun of righteousness, because that has not risen upon all. Likewise understand material rain, not spiritual doctrine, because [Col. 1303C] that was withheld from certain cities; thus the statement is not universal.

“For if,” etc. Love enemies, not friends only, because if you love only because you are loved, you will have no reward. Nevertheless, if friends are loved not from carnal affection but because of God’s command, who says, “Honor your father” (Exod. 20), etc., then there is a reward. Publicans are so called because they collect public taxes; or they are called from Publius, a Roman leader, who established officials of this sort.

“And if you greet your brothers only,” etc.: that is, if you wish good only to your friends, what more do you do in this—how are you more excellent than the nations, that is, better than they? *Ethnos* means “nation”; hence *ethnicus*, that is, “gentile.”

“Be therefore,” etc. Since that is not sufficient, therefore be ready—not only toward friends, [Col. 1303D] but like your Father, who loves friends and enemies because they are his creatures, and therefore gives them temporal necessities.

## CHAPTER VI

“Take heed that you do not do your righteousness,” etc. Having instructed them in a more perfect righteousness, he treats of the end or purpose: they are not to do these things for that end, namely human favor. He treats of three virtues—almsgiving, fasting, and prayer—removing this end from each of them. He does not prohibit works from being done before people, because above he said, “Let your light shine before people” (Matt. 5); but he prohibits their being done with this intention, that they may be seen—that is, that people may desire to be seen.

“When therefore,” etc. Since you are to perform no righteousness for praise, therefore do not perform even almsgiving for praise. [Col. 1304A] He touches upon the custom of the Jews: when they wished to gather poor people, they sounded a trumpet in public places. This was done especially by hypocrites, who sought praise under the appearance of goodness. It is as though he said: Do not sound a trumpet—that is, do not make your deeds known or seek to become known—with the intention of hypocrites, because they have received the reward of praise. Or some of them have received their reward in hell, that is, the reward suited to them.

“But you,” etc. Someone might say: “I shall do it for both purposes, both for eternal good and for human praise.” He prohibits this, because God does not permit a partner alongside himself. The right hand is love of heavenly goods; the left, love of temporal goods, namely praise and the rest. Therefore these loves must not be joined; nor should the left—that is, the pursuit of human praise—know what the right does, [Col. 1304B] that is, love and regard for heavenly things: “That your almsgiving may be in secret,” that is, in the pure conscience, where a human being does not see but God alone.

“And when you pray,” etc.—those who love to pray standing, as though laboring, in synagogues, that is, at the corners of streets. He marks two kinds of hypocrites: some pray openly in public to be seen, like those who pray in synagogues, where the whole assembly of people is; others, although praying in public, pretend to wish to conceal themselves while still wishing to be seen, like those who pray in streets but at the corners.

“But when you pray, enter,” etc. Literally, it is good to do this; yet it is more fittingly understood of the inner chamber of the secret conscience. In this bedchamber there must not be a quarrelsome wife—that is, carnality—which disturbs and makes the mind wander outside, not allowing it to rest. Therefore it must be tamed and restrained, so that it may not disturb and quarrel. But retreating to the chamber is of no avail unless the door is shut, lest a crowd of phantasms enter. The doors are, as it were, the five bodily senses, and especially earthly fear and love. For through these two doors all phantasms of sins enter, and they must be shut. [Col. 1304C]

“Praying.” Having shown where prayer should be made, he teaches how it should be made, removing the false intention of the Gentiles from our prayers. The Gentiles, who served demons, did not believe their gods to be present in different places—as indeed they were not—and therefore made long prayers with much speaking, confident that by them they could summon their gods back from other places. Moreover, demons cannot understand thoughts unless these are indicated by certain signs. Therefore everything had to be urged upon them in words. The Gentiles also believed that the composition of words could move gods to compassion, as it does people; therefore they made long prayers with much speaking, in confidence.

Christ removes this—not because he prohibits long prayers, since he is recorded to have spent the night in prayer, and, when the Passion was imminent, is said to have prayed at greater length; and the Apostle says, “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5). Rather, he prohibits their being made long with this intention: that people should put their confidence solely in much speaking, and not in their own conscience. Hence he says: “Do not speak much.” By “much” I mean: in the same way, that is, with the same intention as the *ethnici*, that is, Gentiles. [Col. 1304D] “For they think.” He explains their intention: that they will be heard because of much speaking.

“For your Father,” etc. It is as though he said: he is not like their gods, who do not know human wishes unless they hear words. The question therefore arises: why are words uttered in secret prayers? Namely, that we may serve God in deed, voice, and heart; and chiefly for our own sake: that, while praying, we may be stirred by words and not become foolish, and that certain words heard by us may move us to compunction.

“Thus therefore,” etc. He has taught prayer—where and how one should pray. He now teaches what should be prayed for, setting forth briefly the sum of all that ought to be requested from God. And just as above he taught seven virtues by which people are made blessed, upon which all the others depend, so he sets forth the subject matter of petitions, lest people err in their requests or ask anything not included [Col. 1305A] in one of these. He uses few words, full of mysteries, so that the unlearned person may retain and understand the summary, while the wise person may find there profound mysteries in which to exercise himself for a long time. Whatever is requested at length in prayers is all found here briefly.

“Our Father.” There are seven petitions, corresponding to the seven gifts of the Spirit and the seven virtues explained above. Through the petitions one comes to the gifts; through the gifts, to the virtues; through the virtues, to blessedness. These petitions are distinguished according to two lives: one temporal, the other heavenly. One passes through the temporal to the heavenly life if the pilgrim makes good and right use of the temporal, so that he does not cling to this world but is freed [Col. 1305B] from it.

The last three petitions pertain to temporal life, and the first three will be fulfilled in heavenly life. The middle petition, although it concerns heavenly things, is nevertheless fulfilled here, because spiritual bread is requested so that we may enjoy it in the present and be strengthened through it.

But before the petitions, an appeal for favor is prefixed, in the manner of one praying, when he says, “Our Father.” Each faithful person praying is directed not toward his own but toward humanity’s common salvation, so that the charity and unity of the Church may be signified, in which a brother desires his brother’s salvation as earnestly as his own. Therefore he says: “Our Father.” Since one calls him Father, one ought to be a son and not degenerate from so great a Father, who is Father in affection and benevolence. When we call him Father, we signify that we are no longer servants but [Col. 1305C] sons. When he says “our,” he signifies that he belongs to many, not to one alone. He who had one Son by nature wished through his grace to add other sons by adoption. Behold, he is the common Father of us all; by this all are admonished of the same brotherhood and unanimity. Let not a rich man, nobleman, or master flatter himself, for the poor, ignoble, and enslaved person is likewise a son of God. Therefore we are all brothers.

When it is said, “Who are in heaven,” the person who is below seems to pray that he may ascend to his Father, who is in heaven—that is, in immutability, eternity, and impassibility—so that he may become with him immutable and impassible. Having prefaced the appeal for favor, he comes to the petitions. But they are arranged otherwise than they are fulfilled in human beings. For the petitions that will be fulfilled in the future are put first, because they are more worthy; afterward come those that pertain to the present life, because they are less worthy.

Just as Isaiah did, who set forth the worthier gifts of the Holy Spirit first and descended to the lesser ones; and Moses, who placed love of neighbor before love of God, although the latter is later in time. Therefore, in order better to see both their dignity and how one arises from another, let us follow the natural order in which they are fulfilled in us first, and afterward return to this arrangement. [Col. 1306A]

The final petition is: “But deliver us from evil,” though it is first in us. A person who wishes to ascend to heaven, seeing that he cannot otherwise ascend unless he is freed from this world’s evils, cries: “Deliver us from evil,” that is, from original and actual sin and from desire for this world, so that I may be able to cast aside both temporal things and myself, and become poor in spirit. All this is accomplished through the spirit of fear, as has been explained more fully above in the treatise on the virtues.

“And lead us not,” etc. Once all earthly things have been renounced, inward and outward temptations must necessarily press in. Therefore meekness is necessary, so that one may be gentle and humble toward those who harm one, and that no anger or rancor—that is, pride—may move one. This is accomplished through the spirit of piety. One does not pray that temptations may not occur, but that one may not be led into them. That person is led into temptation who yields to temptation and is submerged in it. [Col. 1306B]

“And forgive,” etc. Although one has been freed from evil, although one is not broken by temptations, still one cannot be changed so as not to offend God in many things. A ship passing through the sea takes in water through its cracks; therefore mourning is necessary, by which sins may be washed away: that one may be forgiven and may forgive others, and may grieve for the miseries of this age. All this is accomplished through the spirit of knowledge. Knowledge concerns earthly things; and the spirit of knowledge makes a person mourn, because it makes one know how great present misery is, and, once sins are known, makes one cry: “Forgive us our debts,” that is, the sins for which we ought to mourn.

“As we forgive our debtors.” Debtors are those who owe us money and those who have done us some injury. If they owe money and you are perfect, forgive it. If you are imperfect, you may lawfully demand it if the person has means to repay. But if not, you must forgive it. If someone has done an injury and has [Col. 1306C] humbled himself before you, forgive him. If he is unwilling to humble himself, be ready to pardon and do what lies within your power. What you do, however, profits him nothing unless he asks; but you have freed yourself.

“Give us this day our daily bread,” etc. These three petitions belong to earthly life, because deliverance from evil, temptation, and mourning for sins are present realities, and this is called separation from the world. Now he passes to heavenly things, and first requests that heavenly bread be given to him, by which he may do good works and be strengthened on the way lest he fail.

The bread is indeed requested from heaven, but so that it may be eaten here; therefore this petition is the boundary from temporal to heavenly life, because a heavenly reality is requested to be bent down so as to be possessed in the present. This bread is God, who feeds angels. And just as bread eaten by a mother is changed in the mother into milk [Col. 1307A] so that the child may enjoy it, so God, whom angels enjoy as he is, has been changed for us into milk so that we may be able to enjoy him. For he assumed a visible form in order to teach people, so that at least in this way we might know him.

Therefore we always eat him under some form: in the sacrament of the altar, in the Scriptures, in the word of preaching, and in all the ways by which he is revealed to us. We also enjoy that bread when we feed upon earthly bread, so that, strengthened more vigorously by it, we may serve him. He calls this bread *supersubstantial*, because it is above all substances; Luke calls it daily, because each day we eat it in one of the aforesaid ways. “Today” denotes the present time. Through this bread we hunger and thirst for future righteousness. For present righteousness is imperfect and, as it were, hungry; of this hunger it is said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.” The desire for heavenly righteousness, which is imperfect, and this bread are possessed through the gift of fortitude. [Col. 1307B]

“Let your will be done,” etc. These three remaining petitions cannot be fulfilled perfectly except in heaven. Nourished by that bread, one asks that God’s will may be done on earth as in heaven. There are two wills in God. One is the will of mercy, which does not compel and takes nothing from free choice, by which he wills all people to be saved; this, however, is placed in their free will. The other concerns the effects of things, of which it is said: “He has done all things whatsoever he willed.” No one can resist this will; of it it is said: “Who has resisted his will?” [Col. 1307C] This always accords with providence; the other does not always do so.

For if through mercy he wishes some wicked person to be righteous and bestows his grace upon him, yet that person contradicts by free choice and does not consent to God’s grace, this will of God does not accord with providence; for although he bestows grace through sweetness, he nevertheless knows that the person will not consent. The will concerning effects is of two kinds: one permitting, the other approving. The permitting will is that by which he causes evil whenever he wills. The approving will is that by which he does good whenever he wills. Both are from justice. Therefore people resist the will of mercy and do not resist the will of justice.

In Paul, however, God’s will appears compelling; but it is not, because although Paul was struck, his will was free to resist if he wished. In heaven all God’s wills are present, and no one there resists God’s will. But on earth many oppose God’s will—namely, that which is from mercy. For although he wishes even the wicked to be saved, if they will it, they themselves oppose this will by their deeds. Therefore this person prays that, as God’s will is in all the citizens of heaven, so he may make himself and other earthly people such that they in no way resist God’s will. This is fulfilled perfectly in no one except in heavenly life, though in some measure it is fulfilled in this life in the saints, even if not in works, since no one can live without stain. [Col. 1307D]

“As in heaven and on earth.” This may be interpreted in different ways. We may say: “As in heaven,” that is, in Christ, in whom the deity sits in the Lord’s humanity, and that humanity did not oppose his will; “so on earth,” that is, in the Church, may it be done. Or: “As in heaven,” that is, in angels; “so on earth,” that is, in human beings. Or: “As in heaven,” that is, in the soul of a righteous person; “so on earth,” that is, in the flesh, so that the flesh may in no way oppose the Spirit but may consent with it in the same will. Or: “As in heaven,” that is, in holy men; “so on earth,” that is, in sinners.

This, however, is through the spirit of counsel, which gives us good counsel by which we may attain that mercy, namely by being merciful. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

“Let your kingdom come.” After attaining that mercy, so as not to resist God’s will, he asks for a higher gift: that he may see God clearly, [Col. 1308A] once every cloud of phantasms has been removed. This will not be perfectly fulfilled except in the future. And although these gifts are not given in heaven in an order, they are requested according to an order of dignity, because, although they are not given fully, they have been received by saints on earth in an order.

This petition is sixth, because on the sixth day—that is, in perfection, signified by the number six—man was made in God’s image (Gen. 1); this image was afterward corrupted by sin. Now the person asks to be re-formed perfectly into the same image: that is, into the same understanding, so that he may understand God openly. This image is called God’s kingdom. For to see the highest good is the kingdom of heaven. The restoration of this image is the same as purity of heart. [Col. 1308B] Hence it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. 5), etc. This is possessed to some extent in the present. This petition is fulfilled through the spirit of understanding.

“Hallowed be your name.” This is the seventh petition, beyond which there is none; it fittingly follows the vision of God. For it would avail nothing to see God unless a person delighted in that vision. This rest and delight were prefigured on the seventh day, on which God is said to have rested. Hence it is also said: “God sanctified the Sabbath day” (Gen. 2), because in future rest the faithful will be truly holy. This is the peace of which it is said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5). For when they are like God—impassible, immortal, incorruptible, moved by no disturbance, but living in eternal peace, [Col. 1308C] in which God is—they will then be sons of God and will also be called gods by participation.

This person prays: “May your name be hallowed in us,” so that you may be called Father and we your children, and even gods. It is as though he said: Our holiness will not be ours but yours in us; therefore “may it be hallowed,” that is, may your holiness come to be and appear in us, and may your holy name appear in the dignity of your children. This petition is fulfilled through the spirit of wisdom.

Wisdom and understanding differ, as we can see among ourselves. Understanding within us is the very exercise of investigating the Scriptures. Wisdom, however, is the delight of knowledge itself: because we no longer investigate anything, but, as if we knew everything, delight in what we know. Similarly in heaven, understanding is seeing itself—not that there is any [Col. 1308D] labor in heaven—whereas wisdom is delighting in things known.

Thus the person who is on earth ascends to heaven, and the seven petitions are fulfilled in this order. Now let us read them according to the order in which they are arranged in descent. Since the petitioner had called him Father reigning in heaven, he prefixed the petition nearest to that Father, concerning the peace in which people are made children of God, as though he said:

“Our Father who are in heaven, grant that your name may be hallowed in us,” that is, that we may remain with you in heaven and become your children. But we cannot have that delight unless your kingdom comes—that is, unless you restore in us the image that has been corrupted. Therefore: “Let your kingdom come.” And since that image and purity of heart cannot be restored [Col. 1309A] until we consent to your will: “Let your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” And because we cannot obey God’s will in all things unless we are strengthened by bread: “Give us this day our daily bread.” And because we are unworthy of Christ’s body so long as we are defiled by sins: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”

But so that we may recognize our sins and be able to mourn for them, we must pray that the enemy’s temptations may not subject us to him; therefore it must be said: “And lead us not into temptation.” We cannot resist these temptations unless we renounce earthly things; therefore we must ask: “But deliver us from evil.”

“For if you forgive people their sins,” etc. He had laid down a certain severe condition, namely, “Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors.” To invite us to it, he commends it to us, calling it, as it were, the medicine for our sins: if we are willing to pardon others their sins committed against us, God too will pardon ours. But if not, neither will he pardon ours. Note that he says “people” and does not say “us people,” because those to whom forgiveness must be granted are sinners. [Col. 1309B]

“But when you fast, do not become,” etc. He had said concerning almsgiving and prayer that, if they were performed under the influence of a desire for human favor, etc. In the same way he now gives warning concerning fasting. He does not prohibit the sorrow of repentance, because “God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50), but sorrow through hypocrisy. For if a wolf puts on the skin of a sheep, a sheep ought not for that reason to be deprived of its own skin.

“They disfigure,” that is, they mar their faces through pallor and emaciation.

“For they disfigure their faces,” etc. The expression is taken from exiles: that is, beyond the boundary of other people who are truly repentant, they make their faces pale and thin, but with this intention—that they may appear righteous to people. [Col. 1309C]

“But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,” etc. He has taught what ought not to be done; now he teaches what ought to be done. “Anoint your head.” Banqueters, as Horace says, are accustomed to anoint their faces. It was the custom of Palestinians to anoint the head and wash the face on festival days, in order to express the joy of the days; and they customarily soothe and make the flesh cheerful with oil. Therefore one must not suppose that God commanded those who fast to do what belongs to the luxurious and amorous; he spoke metaphorically.

Therefore those troublesome interpreters are false—vehement in both directions—who wish to understand nothing in the Old Testament literally and nothing in the New allegorically. Here two fasts are noted: one of joy and the other of sorrow. The fast of sorrow is for sins; the fast of joy is when a contemplative person delights so greatly in thinking upon God that he forgets even to eat temporal food. Therefore he commands:

“When you have fasted, wash your face”: that is, your conscience, in which God knows you as fasting for sins. Or anoint your head with the oil of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1309D] that is, your mind, delighting and rejoicing in God. The order there is reversed. Therefore wash your face, anoint your head, so that when you fast you may not appear to fast for human praise. “Who is in secret,” that is, invisible in his eternity. “He sees in secret,” that is, in the conscience.

Do not lay up for yourselves treasures, etc. I have said that you should perform neither almsgiving, nor prayer, nor fasting for the praise of men or for earthly reward. And why should I speak of these individually? I command that you should wish to do nothing for temporal things. This is what is meant by: Do not lay up—that is, gather and make—your treasures on earth, that is, in earthly things, where rust and moth destroy, and thieves break in and steal. He sets out three things according to the three kinds of riches. Metals are destroyed by rust [Col. 1310C], garments by moths. There are other things that fear neither rust nor moth, such as precious stones; therefore he adds a general loss, namely thieves, who can carry off every kind of wealth.

This prohibition may also be understood not only of money, but of all earthly things. Whoever fixes his love upon any earthly thing lays up treasure on earth; and if anyone loves something such as gluttony or lust, or any earthly thing, or does a good deed with an evil intention, that person places treasure on earth, and rust and moth destroy it. Rust darkens, consumes, and is visible; whereas a moth consumes but is not visible. Rust, therefore, signifies visible carnal sins; the moth signifies the invisible spiritual sins of the soul, such as [Col. 1310D] anger and envy; the thieves are demons. Rust and moth consume the treasure of temporal things: from love of gluttony or vain glory there arises the corrosion of lust, drowsiness, and other pleasures, which darken that love of gluttony; and from vain glory there arises the moth of envy, fear, and anxiety, which consume that glory. But if, as we have said, people do good deeds for praise, thieves—that is, demons—take these deeds away. He proves that neither fasting nor almsgiving performed hypocritically profits anything. In heaven, however, none of these things exists.

For where your treasure is, etc. Therefore you ought not to lay up treasure on earth but in heaven, because whatever is of greatest importance to a servant, upon that he fixes his heart—that is, his intention. If the heart is in heaven, it is pure, because heavenly things are pure [Col. 1311A]; but if it wallows on earth, how is it pure? For the nobler thing is sullied when mixed with the lower, as gold is with silver.

The lamp, etc. Above he indicated that no good acts ought to be done with an evil intention, especially in the immediately preceding statement: Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. This is proved as follows. You must do everything with a pure intention, because your eye—that is, good intention—is the lamp, that is, the illumination, of your body: namely, of the whole collection of good actions. If your eye, etc. He explains how the eye is a lamp: if the intention is single—that is, pure, not double, namely partly for temporal things and partly for heavenly things—then the whole body is full of light, that is, the entire action will be good.

This must not, however, be understood to mean that evil actions become good if performed with a good intention [Col. 1311B]. No act evil in itself can be good, even if it is done with a good intention. To commit theft in order to give to the poor would not be good. But some things are indifferent, and through intention can be directed toward good or toward evil: for example, lifting a stone in order to place it in the construction of a temple, or lifting a stone in order to strike someone. And if, while I do good with a good intention, evil nevertheless happens to someone through it, that is not to be imputed to me as sin—for example, if, while I raise a stone for the construction of a church, the stone falls upon someone and kills him. But good deeds, if done with an evil intention, are evil: for example, if I fast for praise. Hence it follows:

But if your eye—that is, your intention—is evil, that is, perverse, then your whole body [Col. 1311C]—that is, your entire action—is evil. If therefore, etc. Since good deeds become evil because of an evil intention, how great will evils be which are evil in themselves and are done with an evil intention? This is what is meant: Therefore, if the light—that is, the intention which ought to be the light of works—that is in you, that is, in your power, is darkness, namely deeds perverse and evil in themselves, done with an evil intention, how great will the darkness be once they are joined to an evil intention?

Or otherwise: intention is called “light” because it is known to the one who intends. But the outcome of a matter, because it is uncertain, is called “darkness.” For one who intends, although knowing what one intends, nevertheless does not know what will result from the act, whether good or evil. Thus, when I give or do something for someone, I do not know whether it will turn out for that person’s good or harm. He therefore says: If the intention with which you act, which is known to you [Col. 1311D], is stained by desire for temporal things, how much more so is the deed itself, whose outcome is uncertain? Even if it turns out well for someone, what you do without a good intention brings you no benefit, because you are judged according to how you acted, not according to what happened to that other person.

You cannot serve two masters, etc. Someone might still say: “If good deeds are evil because of an intention directed to temporal things, I too will do good deeds both for the Church and for temporal things.” To this the Lord says: You cannot serve two masters—namely, contrary masters—as though they were one master. By these two masters God and the devil are understood.

For either he will hate one, etc. He gives the reason concerning the devil: either he will hate the one—that is, the devil, whom a human being naturally hates—and love the other, that is, God; or he will endure the one, that is, the devil [Col. 1312A]. He does not say, “or he will love the devil,” for no one is so wicked as to love the devil; rather, one loves something for whose sake one endures his rule. It is as if someone loved the maidservant of a thoroughly wicked man and, for her sake, endured the rule of that evil master. Nor does he say that one hates God, but that one despises him. No one naturally hates God, but because of one’s own will one despises his commandments.

You cannot, etc. He explains who the two masters are. *Mammon* is the Syriac word for riches. By riches we understand the devil, who presides over riches—not because he can give them except insofar as God permits, but because through them he deceives human beings.

Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious, etc. Since you cannot serve God and Mammon [Col. 1312B], do not be anxious about temporal riches for the sake of food and clothing. There are two kinds of anxiety: one arises from things themselves, the other from human vice. Anxiety arises from the things themselves because we cannot have bread unless we sow, labor, and do similar things. This anxiety he does not prohibit, for the Lord says: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3). Prudence and labor are therefore allowed us.

But there is a superfluous anxiety arising from human vice: when people, despairing of God’s goodness, store more grain and money than is necessary and, abandoning spiritual matters, devote themselves to those things. This is prohibited here when it is said: Do not be anxious for your soul—that is, for your life—namely about your food, by which life is sustained, etc.

[Col. 1312C] Is not the soul more, etc. Truly you ought not to be anxious beyond measure, because he who gave the greater thing, namely life, will give the lesser, namely food. Consider the birds of heaven, etc. This is an argument from the lesser: if God provides for birds, much more does he provide for human beings. Are you not worth more, etc. Here the comparative is used for the positive.

But which of you, etc. Read it in this way in order to see more clearly: “And why are you anxious about clothing?” As regards the body, it is of no account, because the entire body is in my work; thus none of you can add anything to it. This is what is meant: Which of you, etc. If you cannot add anything to your body, but God alone makes the whole of it, then do not be anxious for clothing for the body, because he who made the body will clothe the body—though by means of human prudence—after he acts and gives [Col. 1312D] when he wills, when he does not will, and as much as he wills.

Consider the lilies of the field, etc. Again there is another comparison, namely concerning clothing. The former concerned food; lilies are clothed in their colors. He calls the furnace an oven. The Gentiles have no knowledge of God, do not trust in him, and do not think of future things; if they make provision for such things, it is not surprising.

Seek therefore, etc. You ought not to be anxious about temporal things, but about heavenly things. This is what is meant: seek the kingdom of God as the chief thing, as that end toward which one tends. Seek it, I say, and seek this first: that is, set the kingdom of God before all other things. And seek not the righteousness of the Pharisees, but his—that is, that of the kingdom of God, because no other righteousness leads to the kingdom of God; or, “his,” that is, God’s righteousness, which God gives [Col. 1313A].

He said, “Seek first the kingdom of God,” and does not then add that temporal things are to be sought; rather, he says: They shall be added unto you. For, as he says, your Father knows that you need all these things, and therefore he himself will add them freely. Notice that he says “they shall be added,” that is, laid on in addition, because they are not the principal gift but an addition. He does not, however, prohibit asking for them as necessary things; indeed, he called them necessary when he said, “Your Father knows that you need these things.” But they are not to be sought as primary goods, but as provisions by which people are sustained on the way.

Do not therefore, etc. He had prohibited anxiety about present temporal things; now he prohibits anxiety arising from human vice, not from things themselves. If an abbot, making provision for himself and his monks, gathered grain sufficient for the present year [Col. 1313B], that would be prudence, not vain anxiety. But if he feared or despaired of God’s goodness, and therefore wished to keep it for use in subsequent years, that would be vain anxiety; and this would be to think about tomorrow.

For he calls “the present day” this period which our prudence ought to observe. We do not reap more than once in a year; therefore, with regard to harvests, one year is, as it were, the present time. “Tomorrow” is another year; and so with other matters, according to the nature of the things concerned. That he does not deny us prudence he himself showed, since he had money-bags with which he fed himself and his disciples, and entrusted them to Judas.

For tomorrow, etc. There are two days: Adam’s day and the Lord’s day, of which David says: “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Ps. 117). [Col. 1313C] Adam’s day is full of miseries. After sin, Adam was placed in misery and labor. Hence it was said to Adam: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3). He therefore says: It would be pointless for you to have vain anxiety about the future, because the future time will certainly bring sufficient anxiety and labor of its own. This is what is meant: tomorrow will be anxious for itself, and it will bring its own anxiety with it.

Sufficient for the day, etc. It would be pointless for you to add your anxiety, arising from your own vice, to the anxiety of things; thus the evil—that is, the labor and hardship—of the time sufficiently occupies the day, and there is no need for you to add anything on your part. Job cursed this day of Adam: “Cursed be the day on which I was born” (Job 3); and Jeremiah: “Cursed be the man” [Col. 1313D] (Jer. 11), etc. For the saints wished this misery not to exist; and their cursing means nothing other than wishing it not to exist.

# Chapter VII

Do not judge, etc. He removed anxiety; now he removes also that which follows from anxiety, namely rash judgments. Those who love earthly things readily entertain evil suspicions concerning others’ actions. From this arise envy, detraction, hatred, and rash judgments. For those who love the world, if they see a just man reserving money for his own use, call him greedy, name him a hypocrite, and reject him, because they judge others from their own conscience. The Lord prohibits such rash judgments.

It should be noted that he speaks here of rash judgments only when they are made by equals, not by prelates. For some judgments are permitted in the Church: when the vicar of Christ—that is, a prelate—judges someone in Christ’s stead, but only a person who has confessed or been convicted [Col. 1314A]; otherwise it would be a rash judgment. But if anyone judges his brother, whether convicted or a sinner, it is clearly a manifestly rash judgment. Correction by one brother of another is not taken away, but judgment is. This is what it means to judge: when one neither speaks nor eats with the person, indeed draws others away from association with him.

Continuation. And by this: Do not judge your brother rashly, because perhaps tomorrow he will be good. Or thus: perhaps you are, or will be, worse or alike; and therefore it is not yours to judge, and you shall not be judged. Therefore—that is [Col. 1314B], because of rash judgment—you shall not be condemned in the future; for certainly you shall be judged, that is, condemned, in that judgment, that is, on account of that judgment by which you judged him rashly.

And with what measure, etc. That is, the measure of your punishment will correspond to the measure of your fault. For according as you judge your brother more rashly and gravely, in the same measure the quality of punishment will be measured out to you in hell.

But why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, etc. Here he speaks of correction. He entirely removes judgment from equals, not from prelates. But he permits correction only to the pure. For if an impure person corrects, he does not do so out of love for correction, but from envy or hypocrisy, so as to appear just. If he had love for correction, he would certainly first cleanse the vices in himself [Col. 1314C], and only afterwards those in his brother; and then with gentleness, love, and a pure intention toward justice.

For there is an order in every matter: first, one must see whether sins are present in oneself; then one may cast a stone at another; next, one must not foster another’s sin by flattery; third, one must not be negligent concerning another’s sin by failing to correct him, because otherwise this would be consent. Hence Ambrose: “To consent is not to rebuke when you could do so.”

You must abstain not only from rash judgment but also from unlawful correction. This is what is meant: Why do you see the speck—that is, notice the speck, namely a light sin arising from worldly matters—which obstructs the eye, that is, the mind, of your brother, and do not see—that is, notice—the beam in your own eye, namely adultery in your own conscience? And not only do you notice it [Col. 1314D], but you even speak—that is, correct him—saying: “Allow me,” etc. Here permission to correct is given, but only to the pure.

Do not, etc. I permit correction to everyone as something common, but I do not command—indeed, I forbid—that the deep mysteries of God be given to everyone. Do not give what is holy to dogs—that is, heretics, who bark and tear apart—or to swine, that is, those who live in the mire of vices and despise the word of the Lord. For one ought not discuss the body and blood of the Lord with tearing heretics, nor expound it to swine—that is, prostitutes and drunkards—and to whatever laypersons despise it, or even clerics who treat it with contempt.

That Scripture is called “holy” which is inviolable, unconquerable, and sanctified. Pearls are stones found in shells, which are precious when polished [Col. 1315A]. Likewise, allegories drawn from the shell of figures and well polished are precious. Lest perhaps, etc. By analogy it is said, as though they might cheapen them; and lest the dogs, turned against the one who gives them this holy thing, tear you apart with their barking. I do not mean that holy thing which is inviolable in its own nature, but that they may tear you apart.

Ask, etc. Some may say: “How shall we be able to observe so many and such great things?” Christ replies: Ask God for the ability to act well; seek where the thing you desire is found; and when you have found it, then knock, and it shall be opened to you. Two things are necessary to a human being: action and understanding; and we must act before we understand perfectly. Hence David: “They declared the works of God” (Ps. 63), and afterward they understood. Therefore action is commanded to be sought first.

He adds two things pertaining to understanding: first, that they should seek in what authority the matter they investigate is found; and, once the authority is found, if they do not understand, they should knock and inquire, and God will open it to them [Col. 1315B]. Let them act like an infirm person, who first seeks strength in order to go, then the road by which to go, and finally, when he has reached the place, knocks so that it may be opened.

Or which of you, etc. I said, “to you,” without qualification: everyone who asks, etc. To make you believe this more readily, listen: if earthly fathers give good things to their children, how much more will the heavenly Father do so. He gives two examples, bread and fish; Luke adds a third, an egg.

Bread, which is common food, signifies charity, without which the other virtues avail nothing in us. The fish signifies faith, which arose from the water of baptism and is battered amid the waves of this world, yet lives. The egg, which is the hope of an animal, though not yet an animal, signifies hope [Col. 1315C]. Against charity he sets a stone, that is, the hardness of hatred. Against faith he sets a serpent, that is, the poison of unbelief. Against the egg, that is, hope, he sets a scorpion, that is, despair, which stings from behind like a scorpion. For hope stretches itself toward what lies ahead, while despair looks backward.

Therefore whatever you wish people to do to you, etc. He will give the good Spirit, and from the Spirit once given all virtues proceed. But although he ought to set out all the virtues, he sets out love of neighbor, because it is the fulfilment of the law. Whoever has love of neighbor arrives at love of God; and whoever, again, has love of neighbor has love of self. For a person is commanded to love his neighbor [Col. 1315D] as himself. Yet he cannot love himself in evil, since it is written: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10). Therefore, since he is commanded to love his neighbor with equal love, and does not love himself in evil, neither can he love his neighbor in evil.

Whoever therefore has love of neighbor does no evil, neither to himself, nor to his neighbor, nor even to God. Hence the Apostle: “Love of neighbor works no evil” (Rom. 13). Behold: the prohibitions of evils contained in the law are fulfilled in love of neighbor. From love of God likewise one acts well toward God and toward one’s neighbor. Thus love of God and neighbor is the fulfilment of the law. He therefore invites people, after they have received the Spirit, to this love, as though saying: Since he gives the good Spirit [Col. 1316A], ask for it; and once you have obtained it, devote yourselves to love of neighbor. This is what is meant: Whatever you wish, etc. If you want good done to you, do good to others. If you want to be corrected, correct others also. For this is the law, that is, the fulfilment of the law, and the prophets, that is, the fulfilment of the prophets. By “the law and the prophets” he means the moral teaching of the books of Moses and the prophets.

Enter through the narrow gate, etc. It is as though he says: “The things I command seem hard and narrow to you; yet through this hardship and narrowness you must enter into life—and truly through the narrow gate, not through the broad way. For through the broad way one enters death.” This is what he says. But the gate that leads to life is not only narrow but also confined [Col. 1316B], because it is opened through labors and fasts.

It should be considered that he has fittingly spoken of each way. Many walk the broad way; few find the narrow way. We need not seek the broad way, nor is investigation required: it offers itself spontaneously to one wandering on the road. But not everyone finds the narrow way, and those who find it do not immediately enter by it. For many, having found the way of truth, are captured by worldly pleasures and turn back from the middle of the journey.

Beware of false prophets, etc. Few find it, and many obstacles cause this. He sets out three: heretics, who sow errors under a semblance of religion; another obstacle, namely false brethren, who speak well but live badly and corrupt others through their conduct; and a third [Col. 1316C], namely certain persons from whom people can scarcely protect themselves, who preach in the Lord’s name and perform miracles in the Lord’s name. There are other obstacles, but he mentions these because greater care is needed in dealing with them.

Continuation. Since few find the way and many hinder them, guard yourselves against obstacles; and among other things beware—that is, carefully guard yourselves—against heretics. I do not mean manifest heretics, for that is easy, but those who are prophets, that is, preachers, though false and hidden, because they come in clothing—that is, in fasts, prayers, and other works—of sheep, that is, of the faithful, etc.

By their fruits, etc. If not from all things, you will know them at least from some things. Do men, etc. Thorns and thistles are heretics, who tear and [Col. 1316D] prick the minds of people. The grape is the fervor of love; the fig is the sweetness of good conduct. Just as grapes do not grow from thorns, nor figs from thistles, so heretics neither burn with love nor devote themselves to good works.

So every tree, etc. It is asked how he can say that evil fruit does not proceed from a good tree, when David, who was good, is said to have sinned in adultery and homicide, and similarly in other cases. But here an evil tree means an evil will, and a good tree a good will. Thus a good action never proceeds from an evil will, nor does a good will produce an evil action. Yet, in order that we may better explain the following text, “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down [Col. 1317A] and thrown into the fire,” which cannot properly be read of good will alone, a good tree must be understood as not only a good will, but also a person possessing a good will; and an evil tree as a person possessing an evil will.

Not everyone, etc. He set out one obstacle on the way to life, namely heretics; now he shows another, namely false brethren, who profess God in word but deny him in deeds. This depends upon what precedes as follows: I say that you will know them by their fruits because people are not always known by their words, since not everyone who says to me, etc.

This seems contrary to: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts 2), and: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” But that calling upon, and that saying, must not be understood merely as spoken words, but in a weightier sense, according to the Psalmist: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144). One truly calls upon the Lord who makes oneself a fit servant. Likewise, no one can truly say, “Jesus is my Lord,” unless that person is himself a fit servant of his. But when he says, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven,” “says” is understood as mere verbal utterance [Col. 1317B].

Many will say, etc. He adds the third obstacle, namely other false brethren who preach well and even perform miracles by invocation of the Lord’s name. They too must be guarded against, because in fact casting out demons and performing other miracles is sometimes not due to the merit of the person performing them, but to the invocation of the Lord’s name—for the performer’s condemnation and for the benefit of those who see it—so that, although the invoker is despised, God, who performs such things, may nevertheless be glorified.

That certain false brethren prophesy and perform miracles in the Lord’s name is confirmed by the profession they will make at the Last Judgment, at which they cannot lie. This is what is meant: Many will say to me on that day—that is, on the day of judgment, which need not be specified, since it is sufficiently famous and known—etc. And then I shall confess that I did not know you—that is, I did not approve you—insofar as you were false brethren [Col. 1317C].

Depart from me, you who work iniquity. He does not say, “you who worked,” because, although they now have no opportunity to sin, they would still wish to sin if they were still alive.

Therefore everyone who hears, etc. [Col. 1317D] As the Lord is about to conclude his sermon, he commends it by passing judgment on its observers and despisers.

Continuation. Since those who work iniquity depart from God, do the things that I commanded, because everyone who hears my words and does them shall be likened to a strong man, etc. Primarily, Christ himself is that wise man who built his Church upon the rock, that is, upon himself; and then every kind of temptation assailed it, yet it did not fall. The rain which gradually increases is carnal concupiscence, or a lighter temptation of the devil. The rivers are persecutions by the ungodly. The winds are greater attacks of demons.

As we have said, the person who hears God’s words and does them can be compared to him [Col. 1318A], because that person has built his house—that is, the collection of virtues—upon the rock, that is, Christ, since it cannot be destroyed by any persecution. The remaining points do not change.

And everyone, etc. He sets out the judgment upon those who despise, contrary to the preceding one, saying: Everyone who hears and does not do is like a fool, who built his house—that is, his highest good—upon other sand, that is, upon temporal things, which are unstable and unfruitful. Persecutions take that good away in the present, and in the future there will be a great ruin, when it will be said: “Go, you accursed,” etc.

And it came to pass, etc. This verse can be understood in two ways. If we say that it is the same sermon which Matthew and Luke report, then the wording is evident: when Jesus had finished these [Col. 1318B] words, the crowds, who are not doubted to have been present at that sermon, were astonished. But if two sermons are said to be involved, it should be understood that Jesus first delivered the sermon to his disciples alone on the summit of the mountain; afterward he descended to a level place on the mountainside and there restated the same sermon to the people, though interspersing certain new matters and omitting some things already said. Matthew omits this latter sermon, but nevertheless indicates it in some manner when he says, “When he had finished these words,” as though saying: “When he had uttered these things once to the disciples and had completed them by repeating them in the second sermon”—which completion occurred in the level place—etc.

For he was teaching them as one having authority, etc. The scribes and Pharisees preached only the weak precepts given by Moses to the untrained; but Christ taught perfect commandments, as one having authority to add what he wished and to transform figures into spiritual understanding [Col. 1318C].

# Chapter VIII

When he came down from the mountain, etc. When Christ had finished the sermon, he wished to confirm his preaching by miracles, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16). Matthew also, in confirmation of the sermon, counts among the many signs miracles which had nevertheless occurred before the sermon. Thus Matthew includes among the miracles his own conversion, which is not doubted to have occurred before the sermon, since he himself was ordained an apostle with the other disciples on the mountain [Col. 1318D].

Luke and Matthew disagree concerning the healing of the leper. Matthew narrates it before the entry into Capernaum; Luke, after the entry. But Matthew seems especially to follow the historical order when he says, “And behold.” Luke, unconcerned with order, includes this miracle among the other mighty works. He therefore says: When he had come down from the mountain, that is, from the level place on the mountainside, great crowds followed him. Many followed for different reasons: some, like the Pharisees, in order to entrap him; some from love; some to hear his teaching; some from wonder at his miracles; and some for healing, because they were sick.

And behold, a leper came, [Col. 1319A] approaching both with the steps of good devotion and with bodily steps; he worshipped him—that is, venerated him with humble entreaty—saying, thereby displaying inward devotion and humility of countenance through an outward confession of the mouth: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” Because he calls him Lord, he does not doubt that he is powerful to heal him. But when he adds “if you will,” he seems in some way to doubt his will and mercy. He does not doubt his mercy with regard to the one whom he worshipped, but rather with regard to himself, judging himself unworthy of mercy. Hence Augustine: “Displaying his wound, he asks for the remedy; and the confession itself is full of religion and faith.” “If you will,” he says, “you can cleanse me.” He attributes power to God’s will. Yet he did not doubt the Lord’s compassion as an unbeliever [Col. 1319B], but, conscious of his own defilement, did not presume to claim healing.

He therefore came to him; before asking, he began to worship; before making his request, he showed reverence. He came in faith, worshipped in reverence, and spoke in confession: “Lord,” etc. He truly recognizes the Lord, whose will and power he confesses to follow when he says: “If you will, you can.” And stretching out his hand, he touched him, etc. Though the law forbids touching a leper, he sets aside the law in order to show himself Lord of the law, who made it and can set it aside. For the law’s injunction not to touch a leper was a permission, not a command, granted because of human weakness; and it is a figure, lest anyone share in another’s sins.

He who teaches the perfection of humility and mercy abolishes the permission and teaches perfection: that we should not shrink from frail flesh in a poor person [Col. 1319C]. He touched him also for another reason: namely, to show humility and teach that no one is to be despised because of any bodily injury sent by God. By stretching out his hand he signifies that he has an affection of mercy toward him; by touching him he signifies that he fulfills this affection through action. What he had shown by deeds he then declares more plainly in words when he says: “I will; be cleansed.” By “I will” mercy is indicated, which he had signified by stretching out his hand; by “be cleansed” the act of mercy is indicated, which was afterwards figured by the touch of the leprosy.

And immediately, etc. There is no interval between the divine work and his command, because God’s work is in the command: “He spoke, and they were made.” And Jesus said to him: See that you tell no one, etc. Mark says that he began to preach and spread the news. Why is he commanded to tell no one, when Christ truly knew that the miracle would be made known by him, except to teach that our good deeds ought not to be publicized but rather concealed, so that we abstain not only from the reward of money but also from the reward of popular favor? Therefore he prohibited it not for his own sake but for ours.

For different reasons he sends the leper to the priest: for humility, so that the leper may render honor to the one to whom the law commands the cleansed to bring offerings; so that those who see may believe him, or, if they do not believe, may be without excuse; so that he may not appear to violate the law; and so that the priests may understand that the man was healed above the law not through the legal order but through God’s grace [Col. 1320A]. He commands him to offer sacrifice in order to show that he did not abolish the law but fulfilled it: walking according to the law, he healed above the law those whom the remedies of the law had not healed.

If anyone is troubled by how the Lord appears to approve the Mosaic sacrifice when the Church has not received it, that person should remember that the pure sacrifice of the Holy of Holies, which is Christ’s body, began. For Christ had not yet suffered, and the shadow had to remain until the truth of sacrifice came.

For a testimony to them. It is as though he says: Moses commanded the leper to offer a gift so that it might be a testimony of the leper’s healing to those priests whose duty it was to cast lepers out of the Temple and receive them when healed. It was also a testimony to them that the legal priesthood ought to be revered, since through it lepers and others were healed so wonderfully. Or otherwise: “for a testimony to them,” so that the healing itself and the gifts offered figuratively might testify to another healing and another offering [Col. 1320B].

In typology, his descent from the mountain signifies his incarnation, because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Afterwards great crowds followed him, because after “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), he who had previously been known only in Judaea and whose name had been great among one people became wonderful throughout the whole earth.

The leper signifies the human race; leprosy, sins that defile. The one who comes to Jesus comes in faith, worships in reverence, and speaks in confession: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” He stretches out his hand, that is, his help, when he comes to human beings; he touches the leprosy when he assumes the weakness of our flesh and cleanses us from sins. When he says, “Go, show yourself to the priest,” he indicates the office of the ministers of the Church, through whose ministry people ought to be cleansed and absolved from sins.

When he had entered Capernaum, etc. Luke reports that the centurion did not come to him but sent Jewish elders to him, because, being a Gentile, he lacked confidence that he could obtain the request himself. The elders therefore said: “He has done many good things for our nation and built us a synagogue.” But Matthew says that he came through faith. Thus the centurion approached with the steps of faith and made his request through messengers, saying: “Lord, my servant,” etc. In that time many people asked for various illnesses: one for a son, another for someone else; but no one asked for a servant except this man. It was an increase of blessedness and a crown of glory for him that he so humbly interceded with the Lord for a servant, saying: “Lord,” etc.

He carefully sets out each misery of the servant: he lies bedridden, whose continual state burdens a sick person; he is at home, where I see him continually; he is paralyzed, that is, his limbs are disabled; and he is grievously tormented by the acute suffering of illness—in order to move Christ to compassion.

**Moral application.** Thus people who have male or female servants ought to think of them, pity them, grieve with them, pray for them, and care for their servants [Col. 1321A] or maidservants, just as that blessed centurion did.

And Jesus said to him: “I will come,” etc.

### Moral Application

He was unwilling to come to heal the royal official’s son, lest he seem to have paid honor to wealth. Here, lest he seem to have despised servile status, he immediately consented to go to the centurion’s servant. This promise was fulfilled when he came by his aid, and even began to come bodily.

“And answering,” etc. This answer, as Luke says, was conveyed through messengers. For Luke says: “Jesus was going with them, and when he was now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying: ‘Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof’” (Luke VI), and the rest which follows. In this answer the centurion’s humility is noted: he recognizes himself as unworthy of the visitation of so great a guest and says, “[Col. 1321B] Lord, I am not worthy,” etc. Great faith is also noted when he adds: “But only say the word,” etc.

### Moral Application

For he believed that by a command Christ could do all things, and that his bodily presence was not necessary.

### Moral Application

Likewise, when approaching the sacrament of the Lord’s body, every believer should say in humility: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

Having displayed the centurion’s humility and faith, he also sets forth his prudence. For he answered as though to an objection raised by someone using an *antipophora*: “And how do you know that all things obey Christ’s word?” His answer is: “Because if those subject to me obey me, then all things subject to you obey you.” This is what he means: “For I am a mere man; you are God. I am under a master’s authority; you are the God of all. I have soldiers under me; you have angels [Col. 1321C] or all things. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; you say to this infirmity, ‘Go,’ and it will go. And to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and you say to health, ‘Come,’ and it will come. And to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it. You say to an angel, ‘Heal him,’ and he will heal him.”

“But when Jesus heard it, he marveled and said to those following him.” He did not marvel for his own sake, since he knows all things, but in order to invite us to admiration of the centurion’s faith. “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.” He did not say this concerning all the patriarchs and prophets, but concerning all those of the present time to whom he preached. The centurion’s faith is preferred to theirs because they had been instructed by the warnings of the Law and the Prophets, whereas he believed in Christ with no one teaching him. For even the apostles were not at that time of such great faith.

[Col. 1321D] “But I say.” He shows the meaning of this figure: the centurion represents all the Gentiles. It is as though he said: “That you may believe this man to be of great faith and to bear the figure of the Gentile people who are to be converted, I say to you, I testify, I proclaim, that many will come from east and west”—that is, from every nation beneath the sun as it goes from east to west—“and those who come are like those of whom it was said that ‘the scattered children may be gathered into one.’”

Or: from the east will come those who, immediately enlightened, pass from west to east—that is, those who endured sufferings unto death for the faith. They will indeed come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. They will recline, I say, not as persons powerful in temporal affairs, but as those happily feasting; not lying down carnally, but resting spiritually with the holy fathers who believed in the Son of the Creator.

It follows: “But the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness,” etc. The children of the kingdom signify the Jews, among whom God formerly reigned. “Outer,” not because they are outside God, who contains all things, but as a blind person under the sun is said to be outside the sun because he does not see it, although the sun sees him: thus, placed in punishments, they will not see God, although he is present. Weeping, which comes from the affection of the mind, signifies anguish of mind; grinding of teeth, anguish of body. In the member in which the sinner sinned more, he will be tortured more.

And Jesus said to the centurion: “Go,” etc. He gives to each according to the measure of faith. The centurion believed [Col. 1322A] that Christ could heal by a word even while absent; Christ healed by a word.

Mystically, the centurion signifies the first fruits of the Gentiles. He was accompanied by a hundred soldiers because believing Gentiles, striving by virtues toward heaven, are so accompanied. This is said because the numbers up to ninety-nine are counted on the left, whereas one hundred is on the right; therefore, this number denotes virtues striving toward heaven. These pray for others who still lie as useless slaves of idolatry, disabled and harassed by the devil. To them the Lord says: “I will come through the apostles and heal him from sins.” And the Gentiles say that they are not worthy for him to pass in his own person to idolaters; therefore, he heals them by the words of the apostles’ preaching—and so it came to pass.

“And when he had come,” etc. The miracles that follow [Col. 1322B] were performed before the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, as Luke relates. This may also be seen in the calling of Matthew, which he places among the miracles.
