Matthew wished first to set forth the discourse of the New Testament, and, to establish the authority of so great a teacher, he adds many miracles performed at various times; nevertheless, he arranged them suitably.

When he had descended from the mount, as it were from divinity, he first showed through the leper that the whole human race was healed. He divides it into parts: namely, the Gentile people, signified in the servant; and the synagogue, signified by Peter’s mother-in-law. Since greater grace and a greater miracle occurred in the converted Gentile, he first recounts the servant; or because, at the end of the age, the synagogue will be fully [Col. 1322C] converted when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered. He does not say, “And after he entered Capernaum,” or “Behold,” or “Then,” or anything similar, because historically this is not continuous with what precedes.

Peter’s house was at Bethsaida. But one asks why, in accordance with its signification, the synagogue is called Peter’s mother-in-law. Peter was the teacher of the circumcision and, after Christ’s ascension, converted to Christ the primitive Church of the Jews, which was as Peter’s wife. But the unbelieving synagogue, from which the Jewish Church was carnally born, was its mother; hence it can be called Peter’s mother-in-law. Yet the Lord in the beginning partly converted it to faith—then through the apostles, then through others—but for the most part at the end of the age he will recall it from the death of unbelief through Elijah and Enoch.

[Col. 1323A] “But when evening had come, they brought to him many who had demons,” etc. The setting of the sun signifies the passion and death of him who said, “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” With the sun setting, more demoniacs than before and more sick persons are healed. He who, while living temporally in the flesh, taught few Jews, after trampling down death’s kingdom sent the gifts of faith to all nations throughout the world. To his ministers, as heralds of life and light, the Psalmist says: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting” (Psalm LXVII). He ascended above the setting when he set in his passion; by rising again he displayed his greater glory.

“He himself took our infirmities.” Literally, according to this present passage, he himself took our infirmities—that is, [Col. 1323B] the lighter infirmities of human beings, such as fevers and the like—by healing them, that is, by taking them away; and he bore sicknesses—that is, lasting infirmities—as though carrying them away, that is, removing them. According to the mystical sense, on the cross he took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses, that is, those lasting infirmities, because he endured passion and death for our lesser and greater sins.

“But Jesus, seeing many crowds,” etc. On the day after Peter’s mother-in-law was healed, Jesus went into the desert to avoid the crowds. Later, on another day, when crowds had followed him there, he commanded the disciples to cross the sea. Matthew is silent about the day on which he went into the desert, though the others report it. While they were proceeding on the way to the sea, this scribe happened to wish to follow Christ and [Col. 1323C] to learn something from so good a teacher—about the Scriptures, about performing miracles—not because he wished to become good, but in order to gain something from it or win glory. He desired the same thing that Simon Magus wished to buy from Peter.

Such faith, therefore, is condemned according to the Lord’s judgment, and he is told: “Why do you wish to follow me in order to gain worldly wealth, when I am so poor that I have not even lodging and do not use a house of my own?” Or otherwise: the fox, a deceitful animal, signifies deceit; the birds of heaven, exaltation and pride. It is as though he said: “I do not want you to follow me, because the foxes—that is, deceitfulness—have their den in you, since you wish to follow me deceitfully, feigning a disciple’s service; and the birds of heaven—that is, pride—have their nest in you. But the Son of Man, that is, [Col. 1323D] I, has nowhere in you to lay his head, that is, to rest his divinity.” For the head of Christ is God. There was pride in him because he wished to follow Christ for empty glory.

“But another,” etc. He rejected the one who asked, and called the one who did not ask; but he knew both minds well, he who searches the reins and hearts. For he knew that this man was evil, but that the other, with grace bestowed, would become good. “Lord.” He does not reject discipleship, but after first fulfilling the duty of a father’s funeral he wishes to follow more freely. But Jesus said to him: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead.” We must understand a double death, one of the body and the other of the soul. It is as though he said: [Col. 1324A] “Leave those dead in sins to bury those dead in body.” He does not forbid the burial of a father because it is not a great act of humanity to bury the dead, but because it is a better office to preach the Gospel and to raise those dead in soul. Lesser goods must sometimes be set aside for greater ones.

Otherwise, according to Gregory—though this does not pertain to the present passage—the dead bury the dead when flatterers encourage sinners in their sins. Thus it is said: “The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins and bury them.” For when they praise sin, they virtually deny that it is sin, and so cover the sinner. It should be noted that he announces his father dead; but because Christ is not asked concerning him, he does not raise him. So he does not raise one dead in sins after neither that person nor another prays for him.

[Col. 1324B] “And when Jesus went up,” etc. As he had performed miracles on land, so he wished to perform them on the sea, that he might prove himself Lord of sea and land. Having entered the little boat, therefore, he caused the sea to be disturbed, stirred the winds, and raised the waves. Why did he do this? That he might cast the disciples into fear, so that they would seek his help and he might show his power to those who asked. That storm did not arise of itself, but obeyed the authority of him who brought the winds out of his treasuries. It was great, not slight, in order to show a great, not slight, work.

He slept in body, who does not sleep in divinity, according to the Psalmist, who says: “Behold, he who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm CXX).

[Col. 1324C] “And a storm arose; the disciples came and awoke him, saying: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’” They were so terrified by fear, and almost beside themselves, that they rushed upon him; they did not gently or quietly make their request, but disturbedly woke him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” The disciples were still small and weak, not yet fully strengthened; for the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension, nor the descent of the Paraclete Spirit, had yet confirmed them. Therefore they feared through frailty, and he says to them: “Why are you afraid?” It is as though he said: “Life is with you, and are you anxious about death? If you have known me to be powerful on land, why do you not believe me powerful on sea?” He who believes little is rebuked; he who does not believe is despised. Those weak in faith are reproved; those wholly estranged from faith are classed as pagans and heretics.

[Col. 1324D] “But the people marveled.” By “people” here, others than the disciples seem to be meant—namely, sailors and some others who were on the sea—who merely marvel at the divine power but do not glorify it. Or let us understand the same disciples, who had not yet been strengthened by the Holy Spirit and had not yet attended to the full divine power, saying: “What kind of man is this, that sea and winds obey him?”

Typologically, the sea which the Lord desires to cross with his disciples is understood as the bitter condition of the present age. The little boat which he enters is understood as the wood of the blessed passion; aided by it, the faithful safely reach, having crossed the waves of the world, as it were the stability and dwelling-place of their heavenly homeland’s [Col. 1325A] secure shore. Therefore, when Christ was placed on the cross, a great commotion occurred because the minds of the disciples were shaken by his passion; and the little boat was covered by waves, because the whole force of persecution was directed around Christ’s cross, where he set in death. Hence it was said: “But he slept.” His sleeping is his dying.

The disciples awaken the Lord when, troubled by his death, they seek the resurrection with their strongest prayers, saying: “Lord, save us by rising again, because we perish through the disturbance caused by your death.” But he, rising on the day of resurrection, rebukes them and the hardness of their hearts. This rebuke is read as having occurred after the resurrection in many ways, as in: “He reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen” [Col. 1325B] (Mark XVI); and again when he says: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets spoke! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and thus enter into his glory?” (Luke XXIV). Does he not say in these words: “Why are you fearful, you of little faith?”

Rising, he commanded the winds because he overthrew the pride of the devil. He commanded the sea because he cast down the madness of the Jews. And there was a great calm because the apostles’ minds were calmed when they saw the resurrection. We may also understand the boat as the universal Church, which is troubled amid the waves of this age and by great persecutions. God is then said to sleep when he permits tribulations to happen to his own. But the faithful pray: “Lord, save us, because we are perishing.” Rising to help, he restores peace to the Church.

[Col. 1325C] “And when Jesus had crossed the sea into the country of the Gerasenes.” Gerasa is a city of Arabia beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead, which the tribe of Manasseh possessed, not far from the Lake of Tiberias, into which the swine were cast headlong. It signifies the nation of the Gentiles, which, after the sleep of his passion and the glory of his resurrection, the Savior deigned to visit by sending preachers. Hence Gerasa is appropriately named. For Gerasa, as some read it, means “casting out a settler” or “an approaching stranger,” plainly suggesting that the Gentile people drove the devil, by whom it had been inhabited, from its heart, and that one who was far off became thus near in Christ’s blood.

“Two possessed by demons met him, coming out of the tombs, [Col. 1325D] exceedingly fierce,” etc. Matthew says that there were two demoniacs suffering that legion of demons which was permitted to enter the swine. But Mark and Luke mention one. Understand, therefore, that one of them was a person of greater distinction, whom that region respected and for whose deliverance it took especial pains. Wishing to signify this, the two evangelists judged that only the one should be mentioned, because the report of the event had spread more widely through him. Or, because Mark and Luke wrote for Gentiles and wished to signify the Gentile people, they wrote of only one demoniac. But Matthew, writing for Jews, set down two, in order to signify not only the Gentile but also the Jewish people. For both peoples were devoted to demons: one by worshipping idols, the other by transgressing the commandments of the Law.

[Col. 1326A] Or, what is denoted by one is also denoted by two: namely, the Gentile people, which proceeded from Noah’s two sons, Ham and Japheth. For from Shem came the Jewish people. The literal sense is sufficiently clear.

“And behold, they cried out, saying: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God?’” etc. One asks why they called him Son of God. If they believe him to be the Son of God, why do they cause him to be crucified? If they do not believe him to be so, why do they call him Son of God? But it should be believed that they did not at all know Christ to be God, but merely suspected it because of the greatness of his signs, and spoke such words from suspicion and fear. Therefore, since they suspected him to be God, they feared his presence and believed that he had come to judge them. Later, when they saw him capable of suffering and in need, [Col. 1326B] they gave up believing that he was God.

Hilary, however, says that the demons knew Christ, in these words: “This is not a confession of will, but an extortion of necessity, compelling the unwilling. Like fugitive slaves who, after a long time, see their master and ask for nothing except to be spared beatings, so too the demons, seeing the Lord on earth, were suddenly terrified and believed he had come to judge them. For the presence of the Savior is torment to demons.”

Ambrose also seems to agree with this view when he says: “He became known to them only as much as God willed; and he willed as much as was fitting. Yet he became known not as he is known to the holy angels, who enjoy his eternity according to which he is the Word of God, but as he needed to become known in order to terrify those from whose tyrannical [Col. 1326C] power he was to free those predestined for the kingdom. Therefore he became known to demons not through that which is eternal life, the light by which he enlightens the devout, whose hearts are cleansed by seeing through faith in him, but through certain temporal effects of his power and signs of his most hidden presence, which can be more evident to angelic spirits, even evil ones, than to human weakness.”

But if it is objected that the Apostle says, “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Corinthians II), Bede answers this objection. The Jew did not persuade others to crucify him because he thought him to be Christ or Son of God, but because he did not foresee that he himself would be condemned by Christ’s death. For the Apostle truly says concerning this mystery hidden from ages that “none of the rulers of this age knew it. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (ibid.).

They say, therefore, either understanding him to be Christ or suspecting it: “What is common between us and you, Son of God?” It is understood: “What is common?” It is as though they said: “Those who have something in common within themselves ought to visit one another. But why do you come to us?”

“Have you come to torment us before the time of judgment?” etc. One asks why the demons request to enter the swine. It is, of course, from their wickedness: so that, unable to harm human bodies, they might harm external possessions. They request permission from God because they cannot even harm people’s possessions except by God’s permission. But God permitted them to enter the swine, so that he might correct the people through the loss and, when they saw the miracle of divine power, convert them to faith.

[Col. 1327A] But the wretches refuse to be converted; indeed, they began to ask him to depart from their borders. Yet they did this not from pride, but conscious of their own frailty, they judged themselves unworthy of God’s presence and, because of their sins, thought that the presence of so great a man would burden rather than help them. So too the woman who, because of Elijah whom she had entertained as a guest, believed that God had recalled her sins and that she had therefore lost her son. She said: “What have I to do with you, man of God? Have you entered to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and you might kill my son?” (III Kings XVII).

Mystically, Jesus came into the country of the Gerasenes because he came into the world in which Gerasenes dwell—that is, Jews and Gentiles alike, who formerly were inhabited by the demon, some because of idolatry and others because of transgression of the Law. [Col. 1327B] But when Christ came, they cast out the settler, that is, the devil, and drew near as strangers to the Lord. Then two demoniacs met him through free choice by believing: that is, the two peoples coming from tombs, namely from the deeds of a dead body. For the bodies of unbelievers are certain tombs of the dead, in which souls lie dead in sins.

“Exceedingly fierce,” because they could be restrained from the fury of desire neither by divine nor by human laws. Hence Mark relates that they broke chains and fetters.

[Col. 1327C] “No one could pass by that way.” That way is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). On this way—that is, in the Savior’s true faith—while both peoples were still unbelieving and the devil raged within them, they opposed those who walked rightly, that is, who believed rightly and preached the faith. In Mark, a legion is said to have been in them because the human race was enslaved to many errors and the worship of idols.

The fact that the demons, driven out from the possessed bodies, enter the swine signifies that, expelled from the minds of believers, they pass to other unbelievers living impurely, cast them headlong into the current of the age, and destroy them within it. The fact that the herdsmen fled and reported all that they had seen signifies certain leaders of the ungodly, who, although they flee from the Christian faith or law, nevertheless proclaim Christ’s power by being astonished and marveling at it. The fact that the whole city comes out to meet him signifies that other unbelievers marvel at Christ’s miracles and [Col. 1326C] nevertheless wish him to pass away from their borders—that is, from themselves—lest he have a dwelling in them.

[Col. 1327D]

## Chapter IX

“And having gone up into a little boat, he crossed over and came to his own city,” etc. It may warn us that Matthew relates this paralytic as having been healed in the Lord’s city. But Mark says that it did not occur in his city, which is certainly called Nazareth, but rather in Capernaum. Thus a question remains between Mark and Matthew. It would be more easily resolved if Matthew named Nazareth; but now Galilee itself can be called Christ’s city, because Nazareth was in Galilee, just as the whole kingdom, constituted in so many cities, is called the Roman city. Likewise, although the city concerning which it is written, “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Psalm LXXXVI), is situated among many nations. Therefore, when God’s people dwelling among so many cities are called one house, the house of Israel, who would doubt that the Lord did this in his own city? For since he did it in Capernaum, a city of Galilee, to which he had crossed from the country of the Gerasenes, and since on coming into Galilee he was said to have come into his own city, it was in his city wherever in Galilee he might be—especially since Capernaum was the metropolis, where they brought the paralytic lying on a bed.

[Col. 1328A] Augustine says that it is a lie when something is said otherwise than it is thought in the mind. Hence a lying person is said to have a double heart. Deceit occurs when one thing is done and another is feigned. Justice is a habit of mind rendering to each what is its own: namely, that a person dress according to measure, eat, and provide for himself according to measure. For if he were to kill himself through hunger or through some other labor performed beyond measure, he would be a murderer. Likewise, it is just to love one’s neighbor as much as oneself. Likewise, it is just to love God with the whole affection of the mind and to render oneself to him. Prudence concerns worldly affairs. Fortitude is that we are not broken too much by adversities, nor raised beyond measure by prosperities. Temperance is that each person knows how to restrain himself in all things. Opposed to these four virtues are four other vices.

“But seeing,” etc. The paralytic, burdened by infirmity, was incapable of any discernment; but Christ, seeing the faith of those presenting him, remitted his sins [Col. 1328B] and healed him. How great, therefore, is each person’s own faith before God, when another’s faith had such power? “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.” Intending to heal the man, the Lord first loosed the bonds of sins, in order to show that he had deserved the loosening of his limbs because of faults. Wondrous humility: he calls “son” one whom the priests did not deign to touch; or appropriately “son,” because his sins are forgiven. Since sins were the cause of the infirmity, he removes the cause so that the infirmity may be removed.

[Col. 1328C] There are indeed five kinds of causes for which we are afflicted by bodily troubles in this life. Either the just are burdened by bodily infirmity to increase their merits through patience, as were the blessed fathers Job and Tobias, and innumerable martyrs in both Testaments. Or infirmity comes to preserve virtues already received, lest they perish through pride’s temptation: as the Apostle Paul, to whom, lest the greatness of his revelations exalt him, was given a thorn in his flesh to buffet him. Or it comes that we may understand and correct our sins: as Miriam, Aaron’s sister in the wilderness, was struck with leprosy for words of rashness and pride; and as the paralytic of whom we are speaking, who could be healed of infirmity only after his sins had first been forgiven. Or it comes for the glory of God who saves, either by himself or through his servants: as the man born blind in the Gospel, who neither sinned nor whose parents sinned, but was so afflicted that the works of God might be manifested in him; and as Lazarus, whose sickness was not unto death but for [Col. 1328D] the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified through it. Or it comes as the beginning of their eternal condemnation, which is peculiar to the reprobate: as Antiochus and Herod, both of whom in their time opposed God, and through present affliction showed all people the misery of the punishments they would endure perpetually in Gehenna. [Col. 1329A] To them applies the Prophet’s saying: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jeremiah XVII).

“And behold, certain persons,” etc. When they heard Christ forgive sins, which belongs to God alone, they said that he blasphemed, because they did not believe him to be God. To blaspheme is to detract from something belonging to divine power; this is what Christ seemed to them to be doing when he appropriated an office that belonged to God. Thus it is said more plainly by them in Mark: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Mark II). They spoke truly, because no one but God alone can do this; but they erred in denying that Christ is God.

“And when Jesus saw,” etc. [Col. 1329B] Because they doubted that he was God, he showed himself to be God by an evident sign when he disclosed their thoughts, as though saying to them: “By the power by which I behold your thoughts, I can also forgive sins. Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’?” Both are equally easy for me, because by the same power by which I heal I also forgive sins.

“But that you may know,” etc. He performs a bodily sign in order that the spiritual one may be proved. These words may be Christ’s or the Evangelist’s, as though the Evangelist said: “They doubted that he could forgive sins; but that you may know that the Son of Man has authority, he said to the paralytic,” etc. But if Christ is said to have uttered these words, they are read thus: “You doubt that I can forgive sins, but that you may know that the Son of Man—that is, I—can do so.” Then he said to the paralytic. The deed follows upon that incomplete speech.

[Col. 1329D] This paralytic represents those baptized under another’s faith, whose soul is disabled by sins and lies in the bed of the body, that is, in its pleasures. Those presenting him are the teachers of the Church, who pray for one sick in sins. To him Christ forgives sins and says: “Rise from vices, and take up your bed”—that is, govern the flesh, corrected by the reins of continence, so that the soul may rule the body, which formerly served and was governed by it—“and go into your house,” that is, return to paradise.

“But when the crowds saw it, they feared and glorified God,” because, etc. For when a sinner is converted to faith, the whole Church rejoices.

“And as he passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth,” etc. From this it may be understood that these miracles were performed before the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, since the Evangelist recounts his conversion in their midst. Note that Matthew had two names: he was called Matthew and Levi. Mark and Luke call him Levi, to spare the Evangelist, as it were, from shame, lest by calling him by his customary name they publicly mark him out because of his former life. But Matthew himself, as his own accuser, calls himself by the common name, and in the catalogue of apostles even adds “the tax collector” to his name, so that through this he may offer publicans [Col. 1330A] and sinners confidence of salvation, and that no one reading of his conversion may despair of God’s mercy when he sees an Evangelist made from a tax collector.

It is not surprising that, at the first voice of the commanding Lord, the tax collector left behind earthly gain and joined his company, which he saw was without riches. For he who called externally also taught inwardly and invisibly by his word, pouring into Matthew’s mind the assurance that, if he abandoned treasures on earth, he would have incorruptible treasures in heaven. He gave us a perfect pattern of renunciation, because he left behind not only gain and concern for tax revenues but also disregarded the danger that might arise from the rulers of the age, since he had abandoned the accounts of tax revenues in disorder and without explanation, having an excessive desire to follow the Lord.

[Col. 1330B] But let us return to the literal sense. “He saw a man sitting,” etc.: that is, desiring human gains, “at the tax booth,” that is, in the place where tax payments were collected—where public revenues were brought together. For he was called a *telonarius* [tax collector] from the Greek *telon*, “tax” or “tribute.”

“And it came to pass,” etc. Here Matthew did not state in whose house he reclined, except Mark and Luke, who similarly recount this banquet, saying that he reclined in Levi’s house. Therefore, when he says “in his house,” he identifies the man of whom he had spoken above. It should be noted that he reclined with tax collectors and sinners. The conversion of one tax collector was an example of repentance and pardon for many. Those who reclined with Jesus and his disciples had already ceased to be tax collectors and sinners; nor, if they had resolved to remain and persevere in sins, would they have dared to dine with him who is without sin—nor perhaps would God have dined with them.

[Col. 1330C] “Tax collectors” are those stained by public crimes, or entangled in public business, which can scarcely or never be conducted without sin. And it was a beautiful presage that he who was to become apostle and teacher of the Gentiles, at his very first conversion, drew a flock of sinners after himself to salvation. The work of evangelizing, which he would fulfill as his merit in virtues advanced, he began already from the first rudiments of his faith, so that he who was to make progress by word might already make progress by example. It should also be noted that, according to Luke, Matthew prepared a great banquet for Christ in his house, making a fitting return for heavenly benefits: he offered Christ his temporal goods, from whom he expected everlasting goods.

It follows:

“And the Pharisees, seeing it, said to his disciples: ‘Why does your master eat with tax collectors and sinners?’” The Pharisees are held in a twofold error. They criticize the teacher of truth for receiving sinners, imagining themselves just when they were far from justice; and they accuse as unjust those who, by repenting of sins, were drawing no little nearer to justice. The Pharisees therefore erred, knowing neither other hearts nor their own. But God, who knows the secrets of the heart, further strengthens in faith those whom he had already received as penitent, and invites those whom he still endures as proud [Col. 1330D] and impious to the grace of humility and devotion. For Jesus, hearing and observing their wicked thoughts, said:

“The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill.” Here he touches the scribes and Pharisees who, considering themselves just, avoided association with others. He calls himself the physician who, by a wondrous manner of healing, was wounded for our iniquities in order to heal the wound of our sins. He calls “healthy” those who, wishing to establish their own justice, are not subject to God’s justice. He calls “ill” those who, overcome by consciousness of their own frailty and seeing that they cannot be justified through the Law, submit themselves in repentance to grace.

“But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy [Col. 1331B] and not sacrifice.’” To the Pharisees, swollen with false justice, he gives counsel for correction. They often made sacrifices in the Temple in order to appear just before the people, but did not perform works of mercy, in which true justice is proved. For if they were truly just, they would show compassion to sinners and labor for their salvation as for their own. It is as though he said: “You consider yourselves just; but go to the prophets and learn what true justice is. Learn what the Lord says through the Prophet: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’” Yet God does not despise sacrifice, but sacrifice without mercy.

“For I did not come to call the just, but sinners.” This has a twofold meaning. It is as though he said: “This is why I associate with sinners: to invite them to repentance.”

[Col. 1331C] “For I did not come into the world to call the just”—understand, “to repentance,” as Luke says—“but sinners.” For one who is just, such as Nathanael, to whom Christ bore testimony, or John the Baptist, was not to be invited to repentance. Or otherwise: “I did not come to call false righteous persons,” who gloried in their own justice, such as the Pharisees, who, ignorant of God’s justice and wishing to establish their own, were not subject to God’s justice; “but those who recognize themselves as sinners and bend their necks to God’s grace.” For as long as they are wise and just in their own eyes, they cannot be converted to faith; but after they recognize their sins, those same people—sinners, not righteous—can be called to faith.

[Col. 1331D] **MYSTICAL SENSE.** Matthew signifies the person who hankers after earthly gain and sits at the tax-office, that is, who is diligently occupied in secular affairs. Jesus sees him when He regards him with the eye of mercy and instils in him the will for good conduct; and He says to him—whether through preaching, through the admonition of Scripture, or through inward inspiration—“Follow me,” that is, setting aside the desires of the world, imitate Me. And he, rising from vices, follows Him, the way of truth, and is fittingly called Levi or Matthew. For *Levi* means “taken up,” and *Matthew*, “given.” Thus the penitent is taken up from the mass of the lost and, by God’s grace, is given to the Church. And then the sinner prepares a banquet for God in his own house when he delights God in his breast with the spiritual feast of good works. [Col. 1332A] When his repentance has been observed, other sinners are converted and are refreshed at the same feast.

“Then they came,” etc. The other Evangelists show clearly enough that it was not John’s disciples alone, but also the Pharisees, who raised this question. For when He had answered them concerning the sinners’ banquet and His participation in it, they attack Him concerning eating, asking: “Why do Your disciples, as though free to give themselves to eating, not fast?” To this objection He replies:

“Can the children of the bridegroom fast?” etc. He calls Himself the Bridegroom, since He is the Bridegroom of the Church. He calls the Apostles the children of the Bridegroom, whom He Himself had begotten in faith. John’s disciples needed to fast in order to subdue the flesh, lest it rebel against the spirit. But Christ’s disciples had no need of fasting, because the presence of [Col. 1332B] Christ the Bridegroom gave them strength to restrain the flesh—indeed, greater strength than John’s disciples possessed through fasting. Therefore they were to be nourished gradually, not burdened with the austerity of commandments, until the time when they should be strengthened through the Holy Spirit.

And it should be noted that there are two kinds of fasting: one of sorrow for sins; the other of joy arising from excessive contemplation, when the soul delights in contemplating the eternal good alone and forgets food. They could not have the fast of sorrow, because they ought not to grieve so long as the Bridegroom was with them. They could not have the fast of joy, because they were still carnal, did not yet strive after heavenly things, and were not yet devoted to contemplation [Col. 1332C] of heavenly things—until the Bridegroom had been taken from them in His ascension into heaven, and then, strengthened by the promised Paraclete, they might desire and seek heavenly things. They did observe the fast of sorrow, though not for their own sins, during Christ’s Passion: thus James, the Lord’s brother, vowed not to eat until he saw the Son of Man risen from the dead. They observed the fast of joy after Pentecost, when, that is, they were intent upon heavenly things.

“But no one,” etc. He shows that the fast of joy was not to be imposed on them, because it is an inseparable part of the new life. The new life is to attend to heavenly things and abstain from temporal ones. But the Apostles, being carnal, believed that Christ would rule in an earthly kingdom. Hence John and James, through their mother, asked the Lord [Col. 1332D] that one might sit at His right hand and the other at His left. Thus they did not yet seek heavenly things, though they had set earthly matters aside because the Lord had commanded it; nevertheless, they did not yet know what reward they would receive. Hence Peter too asked the Lord: “We have left all things” (Matt. 19), etc. Therefore they were still an old garment. They were to become a new garment after beholding the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, and after being strengthened by the Holy Spirit; a new patch must not be sewn onto an old garment. For one who puts a new patch on an old garment takes away from the old garment the fullness of the new garment; yet he does not give the human being the fullness of the new life, but takes away, so that he has no share. Thus one who wishes to impose fasting from food seeks to put the new life into a person [Col. 1333A] who is still old. It is as though He said: that new life cannot be given in parts; first the soul’s intention must be lifted up to things above, and then heavy burdens may be imposed. For if anyone seeks to impose upon the old person some weighty burden of that life, the tear becomes worse, because the person thereby becomes worse and sets aside every good thing.

“For it takes away,” etc. Therefore an unshrunk patch, that is, a new one, ought not to be put on an old garment, because it often takes from the garment its fullness, that is, its perfection, and then the tear becomes worse. For a heavy burden imposed upon one still untrained often destroys the good that was formerly in him; and this, we see, happens even in our own times. For when bodily continence is imposed upon clerics and marriage is taken away, what is worse, they roam abroad in fornications.

[Col. 1333B] “Nor new wine.” This is the austerity of the new life, placed into old wineskins—that is, the Apostles, who, although they had set aside everything they possessed, were not yet new but old, that is, carnal. If harsher commands had therefore been handed down to them, they would have burst and spilled the whole teaching. But after receiving the Holy Spirit they will become new, that is, fit to receive the austerity of the new life; then new wine, that is, must, will be secretly entrusted to new wineskins.

**MORAL APPLICATION: Gregory.** A teacher must therefore take care not to lay heavy burdens upon the shoulders of the simple and carnal. Although different comparisons have been given for the same point, wine and garment differ. By wine [Col. 1333C] we are refreshed within; by a garment we are covered without. The garment, therefore, is the good works we perform outwardly, by which we shine before human beings. Wine is the fervour of faith, devotion, and charity, by which we are inwardly renewed in the sight of God through newness of mind.

“While He was speaking these things,” etc. Matthew relates that the ruler of the synagogue told the Lord that his daughter was altogether dead. But the other two Evangelists say that she was near death, though not yet dead, so much so that they say messengers subsequently came announcing that she had died and that the teacher should no longer be troubled. It must therefore be understood that Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, when he came to the Lord, was uncertain whether his daughter still lived or had already died; and consequently he requested both things, saying: “My daughter [Col. 1333D] is at the point of death; come, lay Your hand upon her, that she may be saved”; or, “My daughter is dead, but come, lay Your hand upon her, and she shall live.” Therefore, since Jairus said both things, Matthew, for the sake of brevity and looking to the outcome, says that she was dead, taking only one side of his uncertainty; the others took the other side. The literal sense is sufficiently clear.

“And behold, a woman who suffered from an issue of blood,” etc. While He was on His way to raise the girl, a woman came to Him in the crowd, having suffered an issue of blood for twelve years. As the other Evangelists report, she had spent all her substance on physicians and could be healed by none; she touched the fringe of His garment and was healed (Luke 8). [Col. 1334A] Note that Jairus’s daughter was twelve years old, as Luke reports.

“But Jesus,” etc. Here Matthew omits certain details reported by the other two. They relate that Jesus said: “Who touched me?” When all denied it, Peter and those with him said: “Master, the crowds press and afflict You, and You say, ‘Who touched me?’” And Jesus said: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me.” Seeing that she had not escaped notice, the woman came trembling, fell at His feet, and declared before all the people why she had touched Him and how she had been healed immediately (Luke 8). What Matthew relates happened afterwards.

“But Jesus, turning,” etc. When it says, “and she was made whole from that hour,” from the hour in which Jesus turned toward her, it should be understood as referring to the hour in which she touched the garment, not the hour in which Jesus turned toward her. For when Jesus turned to her, she had already been healed. The other Evangelists plainly show this, and it may be inferred from Jesus’ words when He says: “Your faith has made you whole”; He does not say, “May it make you whole,” but, “It has made you whole.” Let us return to the allegory, for the letter is sufficiently plain.

Thus the ruler of the Synagogue is understood most fittingly as Moses himself. Hence he is aptly called Jairus, that is, “enlightening” or “enlightened,” because he receives words of life in order to give them to us, and thereby enlightens others; and he himself is enlightened by the Holy Spirit, so that he may write and teach life-giving admonitions. For according to Luke’s Gospel, seeing Jesus, [Col. 1334C] he fell at His feet, because, foreseeing in the spirit that the Lord would come in the flesh, he humbly submitted himself to His power. He knew that near the end of the age He would be incarnate as a human being, while not doubting that before all times He was eternal. For if God is the head of Christ, what are His feet more plainly than the assumed humanity by which He touched the earth of our mortality? And for the ruler of the synagogue to fall before Jesus’ feet is for the lawgiver, together with the whole lineage of the Fathers, to recognize the Mediator of God and humankind as surpassing him by a glory of dignity far beyond his own, and to confess with the Apostle that “the weakness of God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1).

The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, therefore, is the Synagogue itself, fashioned solely by legal instruction, as though the only daughter of Moses. In the twelfth [Col. 1334D] year of her age, as she was approaching puberty, she was dying: nobly educated by the prophets, after reaching the age of understanding—after she ought to have borne spiritual offspring to God—she was struck down by the sickness of errors. In desperate disregard, she abandoned the paths of spiritual life; unless Christ raised her up, she would have fallen into a dreadful death. As the Lord goes to heal the girl, He is pressed by the crowd, because, while offering the Jewish people saving admonitions by which to raise their conscience from vices, He was burdened by the harmful custom of carnal peoples.

“And behold, a woman suffering an issue of blood for twelve years.” The woman with the issue of blood, healed by the Lord, is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which, polluted by the great flow of carnal pleasures, [Col. 1335A] had already been separated from the company of the faithful. But when the Word of Christ determined to save Judaea, she seized first, in assured hope, the salvation prepared and promised to others. It should be noted that the ruler’s daughter is twelve years old and that this woman had been bleeding for twelve years: that is, at the very time the girl was born, the woman began to be sick. For at almost one and the same age of this world, the Synagogue began to be born from the patriarchs, while the nation of foreign Gentiles began throughout the world to be defiled by the foulness of idolatry. The issue of blood may also fittingly be understood in two ways: under the pollution of idolatry, and in relation to those things done in the pleasure of flesh and blood. Therefore, so long as the Synagogue flourished, the Church suffered; her decline is the other’s strength. “Through their offence salvation came to the Gentiles.” According to Luke’s Gospel, she had spent [Col. 1335B] all her substance on physicians and could be healed by none. By physicians are meant false theologians or philosophers and teachers of secular laws. But when she learned that the Jewish people had fallen sick and that the true physician from heaven was present, she too began alike to hope for and seek a physician for her sickness.

Why did she approach from behind and touch the fringe of His garment? For she said within herself: “If I touch the fringe of His garment, I shall be whole.” This woman with the issue of blood did not come to the Lord in a house or in a city for the healing of her bloody infirmity. The Church approaches and touches the Lord when, through the truth and power of faith, she draws near to Him. She approaches from behind in accordance with what He Himself says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 2); and elsewhere it is commanded: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” [Col. 1335C] [Deut. 13:4]. For, not seeing the Lord present in the flesh, after the mysteries of His Incarnation had already been accomplished, she came to the grace of faith and knowledge of Him. Thus, having merited salvation from sins through participation in His sacraments, as though by touching His garments, her issue of blood ceased—that is, the first stirring of unclean thought, from which every sin arises. The garment is called the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, with which divinity is clothed. The fringes of the garment are the words dependent upon the Incarnation of Jesus. The Gentile people touches the fringe of Christ’s garment because, though it had not seen Christ in the flesh, it nevertheless received the words concerning His Incarnation.

“But Jesus, turning and seeing her, said,” etc. The Lord does not disdain to look upon those who hope in Him; rather, He judges all who merit salvation worthy of His regard [Col. 1335D] and mercy, saying: “Take courage, daughter.” I call you daughter because “your faith has made you whole.” He did not say, “will make you whole,” but it has already made you whole in that she believed. The Church of the Gentiles, having been converted, comes to raise the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, because, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, Israel will finally be saved at the end of the age. The ruler’s house is Judaea, in which lies dead the Synagogue, daughter of Moses and the Patriarchs.

“And when Jesus came,” etc. The flute-players are corrupt teachers, who teach the Jews nothing but figures: these are a mournful song, that is, a delight leading to mourning and death. The tumultuous crowd are those who resisted and murmured against Christ’s teaching. These depart [Col. 1336A] at the end of the age, when the Synagogue receives faith in Christ and no longer gives assent to their persuasions. Then Christ will take her hand, because through their works He will cleanse and raise her; then her fame will go out through the world, and many will be converted through them.

Note that He says, “The girl is sleeping,” because those who sin in the present life are not yet dead but sleep, since they can still be raised through repentance. Likewise, in the literal sense, the girl sleeps in relation to Christ, because it is as easy for Him to raise the dead as it is for someone else to awaken a sleeper. He takes the girl’s hand and raises her because, unless the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, have first been cleansed, they cannot be raised.

According to the **MORAL APPLICATION**, the three dead persons raised by the Lord signify three kinds of those dead in sin. One sins in thought without bringing it into action; this person is signified by this girl dead in the house and can blot out sins through secret repentance. Hence only a few witnesses are admitted at the raising of the girl, and He sternly commands them to tell no one of it. Another proceeds as far as the actual commission of sin; then he is not merely dead in the house, but is already carried out, as it were, beyond the gate. He is signified by the widow’s son; and because a public fault needs a public remedy, the widow’s son is raised in the sight of the people. Another is already established in habitual sin, and is understood through Lazarus. Among these, moreover, lighter or heavier acts of repentance are indicated according to the nature of the crime. For with an easy word He raises the girl, saying: [Col. 1336C] “Girl, arise.” In raising the young man, however, He uses more words: “I say to you, arise.” But over Lazarus He wept, groaned in spirit, and cried with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth.” Thus it may be observed that some are raised from the death of sins with greater difficulty and others more easily.

**MORAL APPLICATION.** Therefore the girl dead in the house is the soul dead in thought. The flute-players are flatterers who encourage the dead girl. The murmuring crowd is the multitude of pressing thoughts. When the crowd of phantasms has been cast out, He raises the soul, yet with few witnesses: that is, not through public repentance but through private repentance, in the presence of a minister of the Church.

“And as Jesus passed on from there,” etc. Matthew alone relates this episode of the two blind men [Col. 1336D] and the mute demoniac. For the two blind men of whom the others speak are not these, since Matthew himself speaks of those same men later. From this it may be perceived that similar events took place, since the same Evangelist sometimes mentions both. Therefore note that, if you sometimes find individual events of this sort in separate Evangelists and encounter in them a contradiction that cannot be resolved, you should say that this is not the same event as the one reported by another Evangelist, but a different one.

As Jesus departed from the house of the aforesaid ruler, two blind men followed Him, crying and saying: “Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David.” The two blind men are the two peoples, because those who lost the light of eternity in the first parent are rightly called blind. Since there is no changeableness in divinity, and passing itself is to change, this passing of the Lord is plainly in His flesh, not in His divinity. For in His divinity He is always present, because He is present everywhere. Therefore the blind cry out to this incarnate God and say: “Have mercy on us, Son of David,” as if to say: “Through the grace of Your Incarnation restore light to us who are blind.” For He was called Son of David according to the flesh.

“And when He had entered the house, the blind men came to Him; and He said to them: ‘Do you believe that I can do this for you?’ They say to Him: ‘Indeed, Lord.’” Then the Lord, knowing their faith, touched their eyes, and they were opened. **MYSTICALLY**, the house in which the blind men were enlightened is the Church, in which through faith we receive the light of the vision of God that we lost through the sin of the first parent. The Lord’s question to the blind men [Col. 1337B] does not mean that He was ignorant of what or how much they believed. Rather, He asks so that our faith, by praying, may be found more deserving of reward: what He is ready to grant by prevenient grace, we should seek by the will of free choice. And when they had been enlightened, Jesus warned them not to make it known; nevertheless, they spread the report throughout the whole land. Although the Lord knew that, as indeed happened, they would make it known, He gave this command because in His humility He fled the boastfulness of glory. But they could not keep silent about the benefit for the glory of its remembrance.

“But when they had gone out, behold, they brought Him a mute man possessed by a demon. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke.” Those who brought this man are understood most fittingly as the holy preachers, who present the human race—not in one place, but in one faith—to the sight of God, to be healed not only in body but also in soul. For just as both peoples, Jews and Gentiles, were signified in the two blind men, so in the mute and demoniac man the whole human race is signified generally. It was, as it were, mute in confessing the true faith and did not open its mouth in praise of God its Creator; it had a demon while it worshipped false inventions in place of God. But when the Lord came in the flesh, the demon was cast out and the mute man spoke. The crowds marvelled, saying: “Never has such a thing appeared in Israel,” that is, it has never been seen in Israel; *appeared* may be read impersonally. The crowds marvel, but the wicked Pharisees slander, saying that He does this by the prince of demons. In the crowd [Col. 1337D] which confesses and marvels, the faith of the nations is expressed. But since the Pharisees could not deny the power, they slander the works; by their slander they display the unbelief of the Jews even to this day.

“And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues,” etc. It should be noted that He preached the Gospel equally in villages, towns, and cities—that is, among small and great—without distinction of persons, considering not the power of nobles but the salvation of believers. After preaching He healed every infirmity among them, so that the greatness of His works might persuade those whom His word had not persuaded. By *languor* He means a long-lasting infirmity, and by “every infirmity,” lighter illnesses. Up to this point [Col. 1338A] the Evangelist is said to have recorded miracles performed before the Sermon on the Mount, beginning with the healing of Peter’s mother-in-law. He has prudently linked them all together, either by continuity or by similarity; now he returns to other events that occurred after the sermon.

“But seeing the crowds,” etc. He wishes to have assistants in preaching; therefore He sends those whom He had chosen to preach. Why? He first states that He had compassion on people who were harassed by various errors and were lying down—that is, sluggish and making no effort to rise—and who, though they had shepherds, were as though they had none. People are called a harvest because they can be reaped by preachers: if not all, at least some may be separated from the mass and gathering of the lost, like grains shaken free from chaff, [Col. 1338B] and afterwards stored in barns.

“Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest,” etc. It is as though He said: “You see that people are fit for conversion. Pray, therefore, the Lord to send labourers into His harvest.” The Lord must be asked, through His mercy, either by inward inspiration or through His ministers, to send preachers into His Church. For preachers do not come to preach unless they are sent. And He rightly says, “send”: persons wishing to remain at rest are, as it were, compelled to go to preaching when God inspires them or when their superiors send them.

## CHAPTER 10

“And having called together,” etc. When He sends the disciples to preach, He gives them power to perform miracles, so that they may confirm their preaching with the signs that follow it. He lists the twelve Apostles by name, lest pseudo-apostles arrogate to themselves the glory of belonging to the number of the Apostles. The number of the Apostles is not without mystery. Twelve, made up of three and four, signifies that they would preach through the four regions of the world the faith of the Holy Trinity. This number was prefigured by many figures in the Old Testament: by the twelve sons of Jacob; the twelve princes of the children of Israel; the twelve springs found at Elim, a place in the desert; the twelve stones on Aaron’s breastpiece; the twelve loaves of the Presence; the twelve spies sent by Moses; the twelve stones taken from the Jordan, from which an altar was made; [Col. 1338D] the twelve oxen supporting the bronze sea; the twelve stars placed in the crown of a bride; and, in the New Testament, the twelve foundations of Jerusalem seen by John, and the twelve gates.

“Simon, who is called Peter,” etc. This is said to distinguish him from the other Simon, who is called the Cananaean.

**RABANUS:** Although Mark says in this place that He gave Simon the name Peter, it must be understood that Simon was not now given the name Peter for the first time, but long before, when he had been brought to Him by his brother Andrew. Jesus looked upon him and said: “You are Simon, son of Johanna; you shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted “Peter” (John 1). But because Mark, wishing to enumerate the names [Col. 1339A] of the twelve Apostles, had to say “Peter,” he briefly indicated that Simon had not been called this before, but that the Lord had surnamed him so—not then, but when John set down the Lord’s very words. *Peter* means the same in Greek and Latin as *Cephas* does in Syriac; and there can be no doubt that in both languages the name is derived from the Rock of which Paul said: “And that Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

“James, [son] of Zebedee.” This is added to distinguish him from the other James, called [son] of Alphaeus. “And John his brother.” As Mark reports, Christ gave these men the name *Boanerges*, meaning “sons of thunder” (Mark 3). They were fittingly surnamed sons of thunder, for one of them, thundering forth a voice of heavenly things, uttered that theological declaration which no one had known how to make before: “In [Col. 1339B] the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1), etc.

“James [son] of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus.” He gives James the addition “of Alphaeus” to distinguish him from James [son] of Zebedee. He is the one called in the Gospels, and in the Epistle to the Galatians, the Lord’s brother. For Mary, Alphaeus’ wife, was the sister of Mary, the Lord’s mother; John the Evangelist also calls her Mary of Cleophas. Perhaps this was because Alphaeus was also called Cleophas, or because Mary herself, after Alphaeus’ death and after James was born, married Cleophas. That James was fittingly surnamed son of Alphaeus—that is, “the learned one”—is attested by the Apostles themselves, who immediately after the Lord’s Passion ordained him bishop in Jerusalem.

Thaddaeus is the same person whom Luke, both in his Gospel and [Col. 1339C] in the Acts of the Apostles, calls Judas of James. For he was the brother of James, the Lord’s brother, as he himself writes in his Epistle; hence he too was called the Lord’s brother. His fellow citizens, astonished at his mighty works, testified to this, saying: “Is this not the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon?” This same Thaddaeus was called by some Jebeus.

“Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Him.” He gives these also with additions, to distinguish them from Simon Peter and Judas, brother of James. Simon the Cananaean received his surname from Cana, a village of Galilee; Luke the Evangelist gives it with an interpretation: “Simon the Zealot.” For *Cana* means zeal; *Cananaean*, *Zealot*, that is, an emulator. Judas was chosen so that the Lord might have an enemy within His household. For the person who does not fear a member of his own household is perfect. Thus He teaches us to endure evil persons among us, to reject none except one who has been convicted, and to show that apostleship is not merit but ministry, since through this evil man, as through Peter, He performed miracles and sacraments so well.

These names are suited to the significance of preachers. For every preacher ought to be Peter, that is, firm in faith; and Simon, that is, obedient—for *Simon* means “obedient.” He ought also to be Andrew, that is, strong in patience—for *Andrew* means “manly.” He ought also to be James, that is, a supplanter of vices; and John, that is, ascribing everything to God’s grace—for *John* means “grace of God.” Let him also be Philip, who is called “mouth [Col. 1340A] of the lamp.” For every preacher ought to confess with the mouth the knowledge and illumination of the mind, so that he may have in his mouth the lamp that he has in his mind. No less should he be Bartholomew, which means “son of him who suspends the waters,” clearly signifying the Son of God, who raises and suspends the minds of His preachers for the contemplation of heavenly things, so that the more freely he proclaims lofty matters, the more truly he may intoxicate earthly hearts with the drops of his words.

He ought also to be Thomas, which means “twin” or “abyss.” The first interpretation belongs to Thomas’ own person, since he was twin—that is, doubtful—regarding the Resurrection. The second applies to every preacher who knows the depth of God’s mysteries. He ought also to be Matthew, that is, “given” or “taken up”: given by God’s grace, [Col. 1340B] taken up from the mass of the lost. Thaddaeus means “little heart,” as though one who cultivates the heart, because every preacher ought to cultivate the heart, not the body. He ought to be Cananaean, that is, Zealot, an emulator of God. It is also fitting that he should be Judas, that is, a confessor, and Iscariot, that is, mindful of the Lord’s Passion. For *Iscariot* means “memory of death.”

**Rabanus:** Judas Iscariot derived the name that foretold his condemnation either from the town in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar. For *Issachar*, which means “reward,” suggests the price of betrayal. But *Scarioth*, which is interpreted “memory of death,” indicts him as having committed the wickedness of delivering up the Lord not through a sudden persuasion but after long deliberation.

[Col. 1340C] “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles,” etc. The Lord sent His Apostles twice to preach. The first mission was plainly to the Jews, to whom preaching ought first to have been offered, since the promise had been made to them; when they rejected it, the Apostles were to turn to the Gentiles. The second was to the Gentiles, where it was said: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature.” Some things are common to these missions and some special. In this mission the special command is: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles”—that is, do not preach to the Gentiles—nor to the Samaritans, as is here commanded.

The Samaritans were Gentiles settled in the land of Israel by Nebuchadnezzar after the captivity he had effected. Compelled by many dangers, they converted to Judaism, accepting circumcision and the five [Col. 1340D] books of Moses, while rejecting everything else altogether. Hence the Jews had no dealings with the Samaritans. Before being sent, the Apostles are first instructed where to go and what place to avoid.

“But as you go,” etc. After teaching them where to go and what they must avoid, He indicates what they are to preach and what they are to do. Behold what they are to preach: “As you go, preach,” etc. Behold what they are to do: “Heal the sick, raise the dead,” etc. “Freely you have received; freely give.” Since He foresaw that some would turn this gift of the Spirit received by them into a means of trade, like Simon Magus, He wished to forbid such trafficking.

“Do not possess gold or silver,” etc. Since they ought to invite others to contempt of secular things, He commanded them to possess neither gold nor silver nor coins [Col. 1341A] in their belts. For anyone who saw them concealing and possessing coins would suppose that they preached for gain. By gold and silver He means all riches. By money in belts and by a bag He means all provisions for a journey. Provision has two parts: the means by which necessities are bought, or the necessities themselves. By money is understood the provision by which necessities are bought. In a bag, however, cheese, bread, pepper, candles, and similar necessities are usually carried; therefore by it every necessity for the road is understood. Thus by these two all travel provision is forbidden.

He who in this mission forbids the carrying of necessary coins commands His disciples at the Passion: “He who has a bag, let him take it,” that is, carry it. For as long as He was in the world, He was their steward and had a purse to feed them; therefore He did not wish them to be anxious about expenses while they remained under His provision. He sent them out without supplies because He Himself provided the means of their living by inspiring the minds of those who received them. But after He had been removed from their sight, He permitted them to take His place, so that they might have purses, as He Himself had had one, if they wished to live from the goods of their subjects. Paul too did this, although he often earned his living through labour.

“Nor two tunics, nor footwear, nor a staff.” This does not mean that someone in the freezing places of Scythia, with their icy snow, ought to be content with a single tunic. Rather, He commands this so that, wearing one garment, we may not keep another out of fear for the future. Nor are double pairs of footwear to be carried, in the same way. They are also commanded not to carry a staff, so that [Col. 1341C] one who always has the Lord’s help may not seek the support of a walking-stick. Since He had sent the Apostles to preach, as it were naked and unencumbered, and this condition seemed harsh, He moderated the severity of the command by saying:

“The labourer is worthy of his food.” That is, receive from them only as much as is necessary for your food and clothing.

But **mystically**, it is not permissible for teachers of the Church to possess gold, silver, and money in belts: that is, they must not regard wisdom, signified by gold, and eloquence, expressed by silver, as their own, or as received from someone other than God. This is said against private and heretical teachings. Or, understood mystically, they must not possess gold and silver—that is, keep them for themselves—but rather multiply the talent entrusted to them. They ought not to carry a bag, that is, to be weighed down and hindered by the burden of the world; nor should they be double-minded, which is signified by a double garment, so that we may not present ourselves one way to God and another way to the world.

He also forbids them to carry footwear, lest their feet—that is, their affections—be bound with deadly bonds; rather, entering holy ground, they should have senses bare and always removed from evil examples. A person ought not to carry footwear—that is, he ought not to look to examples of foolish deeds, lest he think his own deeds defended, as it were, by the skins of dead animals. For there are many who defend [Col. 1342A] their own depravity by other persons’ depravity: seeing that others have done such things, they think themselves free to do them. Plato likewise says that the two extremities of the body ought not to be covered, and that the head and feet ought not to become accustomed to softness, because when they have this weakness, the other parts are stronger. “Nor a staff.”

**Augustine:** The question is raised how Matthew and Luke record the Lord as telling the disciples not to carry a staff, whereas Mark says that He commanded them to take nothing for the way except a staff only. It should be understood that “staff” is spoken under one meaning as something to be carried according to Mark, and under another as something not to be carried according to Matthew and Luke—just as temptation is understood under one meaning in the statement, “God tempts no one” (Jas. 1), and under another [Col. 1342B] in the statement, “The Lord your God tests you” (Deut. 15), that He may know whether you love Him. The former is temptation to deception; the latter, testing.

Thus it is also said that they were to carry a staff and not to carry a staff. For when, according to Matthew, He said: “Do not possess gold,” and immediately added, “The labourer is worthy of his food,” He therefore commanded that they should not carry even a staff, showing that believers owe necessary support to their ministers. Another Evangelist denotes this same authority by the name of a staff when he says that they should take nothing for the way except a staff only, so that it may be understood that through the authority received from the Lord, which is signified by the name of a staff, even things not carried will not be lacking. It follows:

In whatever city or village you enter, inquire who there is worthy to be your host. The Apostles, entering [Col. 1342C] a city, could not know who or what sort of person each inhabitant was. The people’s reputation, and the judgment of the neighbours, must be followed, lest the dignity of preaching be disgraced by the ill repute of the host. Although they ought to preach to all, one host is chosen—not as conferring a benefit upon one who is to stay with him, but as receiving one. Hence it is said, “who in it is worthy,” so that he may recognize that he receives grace rather than gives it.

“On entering the house, say: Peace to this house,” etc. The peace offered from the preacher’s mouth either rests upon the house, if there is in it a son of peace, or returns to that same preacher. For either there will be someone predestined to life, who follows the heavenly word he hears; or, if there is no one who listens, the preacher himself will nevertheless not be without fruit, [Col. 1342D] since peace returns to him, when the Lord repays him for his labour with the reward of his work.

“And whoever does not receive you,” etc. Here he pronounces judgment upon those who do not receive them. “Shake off.” The sacraments must not be cheapened. For dust is commanded to be shaken off sacramentally, as a testimony against them. Dust upon the feet is a sign of the labour of the journey. Therefore let them shake it off against them, to show that they have undertaken the labour of the journey for them in vain, and that what they undertook in vain is to be turned back upon them and punished. For the shaking off of dust signifies that nothing earthly is to be received from them, even if it is offered, after they refuse to hear spiritual things. The dust on the feet also signifies venial sins which cling to preachers as they pass through the world. Yet these are forgiven because of love for one’s neighbour. [Col. 1343A] This is signified by the washing of feet at the supper, and by the washing performed by holy women, who customarily wash the feet of the saints: for both the Lord forgives, and the love of faithful souls—for whose sake the feet had been defiled—washes them, so that those sins are punished in no respect. But if those sins were undertaken in vain, they are nevertheless not punished in the Apostles, but in those who caused them to labour in vain; and as a sign of this, dust is shaken off against them. Or dust is shaken into their faces so that the preachers may plainly show that they seek nothing earthly from them, since they do not allow even the dust of their land to cling to them.

“Amen, I say to you,” etc. As though he said: They will be so condemnable that they will suffer more grievously in hell [Col. 1343B] than the Sodomites and Gomorrhites, because they heard the Gospel and refused to believe the Gospel. The Sodomites, however, perished without the Gospel.

“Behold, I send you,” etc. Since many adversities threatened them, lest they despair when these came upon them, he therefore foretells the evils to come, because weapons foreseen wound less. As though he said: They will despise you, but you must show every patience. For, “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves,” etc. The Father sent his Son to suffering, yet did not despise his love; so the disciples are sent by the Lord. But because he had first called them sheep, on account of simplicity and patience, he commanded them also to be serpents, on account of prudence. The serpent has its heart near its head; and therefore, preserving its head, it exposes the rest to the assailant, because it does not die unless its head is injured. Our head is faith, which works through love; if this dies, all else dies. Therefore, preserving this, the preacher ought to expose all worldly possessions, and even his body, to the persecutor, and endure their being taken away. The serpent also commonly seeks out narrow crevices, through which, in passing, it strips off its old skin. Likewise, as the preacher passes through the narrow way, let him wholly put off the old man. The sheep differs from the dove in this: the sheep is merely gentle and does not kick when it is killed; the dove, although it has no anger because it lacks gall, nevertheless seems to have anger when it strikes with its beak. Likewise, the preacher ought both to be gentle toward one who kills him and, from love of correction, to show something like anger [Col. 1343D] toward his brother.

“But beware,” etc. He shows who the wolves are—namely, human beings—as though he said: These wolves are rational, and therefore you must be serpents against their cunning, that is, prudent. “For they will hand you over to councils,” etc. It was the custom of the Jews that, if anyone preached things contrary to the law, they convened a council; and, having summoned the one opposed to their law, they first forbade him to preach such things further. If he did not cease because of the prohibition, he was corrected in the synagogue with scourges, as we read of Paul. But if he still would not submit, then he was handed over to governors or kings for condemnation, as James was to Herod. And this is why it is necessary that you be serpents, that is, prudent. For they will hand you over: first to councils, forbidding you [Col. 1344A] to preach in my name; then they will scourge you if you remain uncorrected; finally, you will be led before kings and governors for condemnation, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles, because the torments of the saints will be testimonies to the deserved condemnation of the ungodly. For those who killed their own preachers are rendered without excuse. It should be noted that all these predictions of evils pertain not only to the first mission but also to the second.

“But when they hand you over,” etc. Since the hearts of the weak might be troubled by hearing of so many sufferings, he therefore adds consolation when he says: “But when they hand you over, do not be anxious what you are to say, or how”—that is, with what rhetorical colours and what ornament of language. As though he said: You have come to the contest, but I do the fighting; you utter words, but I am the one who speaks. “But brother will hand over,” etc. Having first offered consolation, he adds graver dangers. For injuries inflicted by relatives cause more grievous pain; and so they are appropriately placed after consolation, that they may wound less severely. These evils are foretold not only to the Apostles but also to all martyrs.

“But whoever perseveres,” etc. The greatest virtue is not to have begun, but to have completed; hence the tail of the victim is commanded to be placed in the sacrifice. The tail is the end of the work in the sacrifice. To place the tail is to bring a good work to its end.

“But when they persecute you in this city,” etc. Since he had invited them to patience, lest they appear not to be permitted to flee, he commanded them to withdraw for a time, [Col. 1344C] lest they die while they can still be of use. Thus Paul fled from Damascus in order to convert many nations to the Lord. Fittingly, after perseverance, he adds the matter of flight; for flight is not contrary to perseverance. “Amen, I say to you,” etc. And perhaps they might say: “The land of the Jews is small; we shall therefore quickly be able to convert it. When it has been converted, to whom shall we go?” He answers this objection: “Amen, I say to you, you will not finish”—that is, you will not bring to completion—the cities of Israel, that is, all the Jews, until the Son of Man comes, that is, rises from the dead. As though he said: Do not suppose that, in this first mission, the Jews will not suffice for your labour; for certainly enough work will remain among them for you until another mission, since I shall send you to the Gentiles. [Col. 1344D] This will be after the resurrection, when they are commanded:

“Go, preach the Gospel to every creature.” He does not say “until the Son of Man comes” because he might then convert them, but because he would then send them to the Gentiles. Or otherwise: You will not fully convert the children of Israel to faith until the Son of Man comes, that is, until the second coming draws near. Then the fullness of the Jews will be converted through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah; and then this saying will be directed not only to the Apostles but to all believers.

MYSTICALLY, we may say: “When they persecute you in one city”—that is, in one book or testimony of the Scriptures—“flee to other cities,” that is, to other volumes of books. For although the persecutor may prevail in dispute, the Saviour’s aid will nevertheless arrive before victory is granted to adversaries. [Col. 1345A]

“The disciple is not above the master,” etc. He sets himself forth as an example of patience, so that what the Lord suffers may not be burdensome for servants to endure. As though he said: Do not be surprised if they persecute you thus; they will treat me, the Lord, likewise. Therefore let it not be shameful to suffer what I suffer, because the disciple is not above the master—that is, my disciple is not of greater merit than I, the master. It is enough, therefore, for my disciple—that is, it ought to suffice him—to be like his master, that is, to imitate him; and he adds in what he is to imitate him. “If they have called the master of the house”—that is, me—“Beelzebub,” that is, prince of demons, how much more you? [Col. 1345B] That is: If they assailed me with insults, though I am God, much more will they assail you, who are mere human beings.

“Nothing is covered,” etc. As though they said: “Since they are full of wickedness and heap insults upon us, while you are religious, it is fitting that we repay them in kind, expose their evils, and proclaim our own good deeds.” To this he answers: Do not repay insults in kind, because if their evils are now covered, the day of judgment will come in which they will be revealed. And do not glory in your good deeds, because they too will then be made manifest. And this is:

“No evil is now covered that shall not be revealed, and no good hidden that shall not be known. What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light,” etc. Do not glory in your good deeds, but make your unconquered preaching known to all. And this is: “What I tell you in darkness,” [Col. 1345C] that is, in figures and obscurities, “speak in the light”—that is, openly; and “what you hear in the ear,” that is, privately, “preach from the housetops,” that is, publicly. For it was customary in Palestine, where roofs are not peaked but flat above, to address the people from the rooftops; and therefore we should understand “preach from the housetops” as “speak publicly.” Or, “What I tell you in darkness,” that is, while you are still in carnal fear, “speak in the light,” that is, in the confidence of truth, when you have been enlightened by the Holy Spirit. And “what you hear in the ear,” that is, receive by hearing alone, preach by carrying it out in deed, standing upon the housetops—that is, upon your bodies, which are the dwellings of souls. And, preaching, “Do not fear those who kill [Col. 1345D] the body; they cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.”

The name Gehenna is not found in the ancient books, but is first used by the Saviour, and not without reason. For the idol Baal is read to have stood at the foot of the mountain near Jerusalem, where Siloam was. This valley was watered and wooded, full of delights, and in it was a grove consecrated to the idol. The people of Israel therefore came to such madness that, abandoning the Temple, they offered sacrifices there and burned their children to demons. The place was called Ge-Hinnom, that is, “the Valley of the Sons of Hinnom.” This is read in Chronicles, in the Book of Kings, and in Isaiah; and the Lord threatened to fill that place with the corpses of the dead, so that it should no longer be called Baal but Polyandrium, that is, “the tomb of the dead.” [Col. 1346A] Future punishments, therefore, and eternal penalties by which sinners are to be tormented, are denoted by the name of this place. It follows:

“Are not two sparrows,” etc. As though he said: You ought not to fear, because if God does not forget the tiniest animals, which seem to wander through the air, neither will he forget you, who were made in God’s image; therefore do not be terrified by those who kill the body.

Perhaps someone asks how the Apostle can say, “Is God concerned about oxen?” (1 Cor. 9), when an ox is surely more valuable than a sparrow. But concern is one thing, knowledge another. Not only do I say that God does not forget you, but not even the number of the hairs of your head.
