And this is: “Even the hairs of your head [Col. 1346B] are all numbered” (Luke 12)—not in the act of calculation, but in the capacity of knowledge. We carefully count what we wish to preserve. As though he said: God’s grace toward human beings is so immense that nothing of ours escapes him. “Do not fear therefore, for you are better” (ibid.), that is, of greater merit and dignity, than all the birds of heaven.

“Everyone therefore who confesses me before men,” etc. He said above, “Do not fear,” because there is nothing to fear; and since there is nothing to fear, therefore confess me boldly. He gives the reason: everyone who confesses me before people, so as not to fear suffering death for my sake, I too will confess before my Father, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive [Col. 1346C] the kingdom.” And because above he had said, “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves. Again, they will hand you over to councils,” etc., lest anyone, frightened by persecutions, should say: “I shall preserve in myself the faith which I owe to God alone; and so long as I know it, even though I may not declare it among people, I shall yet preserve in my heart that faith which I do not dare to profess because of the rage of persecutors,” the Lord answers this weak thought: “But whoever denies me before people,” that is, denies that I was born, suffered, and died, “I also will deny him,” etc. Even pagans cannot deny that God exists; yet unbelievers can deny that he is the Son of God, and that he is the Father. Each person is denied by the Son before the Father when the Son and the Father are revealed to him in the power of divinity. He will be confessed by the Son before the Father who has access to the Father through the Son. It follows:

“Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon earth,” etc. As though he said: Not only do I will that fear of death should not cause you to cease confessing my name, but I also will that, for my sake, you break all attachments to parents and friends, so that neither fear of death nor carnal love may separate you from me. [Col. 1346D]

“For I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.” The whole world, in coming to faith in Christ, has been divided against itself. Every household had both unbelievers and believers, and for this reason a good war was sent, so that an evil peace might be broken. Isaiah sang this prophetically under the figure of Egypt, saying: “Behold, the Lord will ascend [Col. 1347A] upon a swift cloud and enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence; and I will set Egyptians against Egyptians” (Isa. 19)—some, namely, fighting against the faith, others for it. It follows:

“For I have come to separate a man against his father,” etc. As though he said: Through the sword of the divine word I shall divide every carnal attachment. We may understand the devil as the father whose children we once were—not because he created us, but because we imitated him—as the Lord reproached the Jews: “You are of the devil” (John 8). But after we heard the voice exhorting us, “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44), the sword came—the word of God—separating us from one another and showing us another Father, [Col. 1347B] to whom we might say: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” “And a daughter against her mother.” The mother is the Synagogue; the daughter is the primitive Church. “And a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.” The mother-in-law is the Synagogue; the daughter-in-law is the Church from the Gentiles and from Gentile life. The bridegroom of the Church, Christ, is the son of the Synagogue, as the Apostle says: “whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh” (Gal. 4 [cf. Rom. 9:5]). The mother-in-law, therefore—that is, the bridegroom’s mother—is divided against her daughter-in-law, as we said, and against her daughter. The carnal Synagogue does not cease to persecute those who believe, whether from circumcision or from uncircumcision; but they themselves are divided from their mother-in-law and mother, refusing to receive carnal circumcision, as the Acts of the Apostles teach. In this place Luke says: “There will be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three” [Col. 1347C] (Luke 12). How then are there five? See, he adds the names of the persons: father and son, mother and daughter, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law. But the mother of the son is herself the mother-in-law of his wife; and thus she is said to be divided against her own daughter and against her daughter-in-law. It follows:

“And a man’s enemies are those of his household,” etc.—those with whom the soul was bound by habitual association. For no bonds of peace can be preserved among those between whom there is a war of faith. “He who loves father or mother more than me,” etc. Since he had promised before, “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword”—that is, to divide the union of carnal affections, lest anyone should prefer devotion to parents over religion—he adds: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me,” etc. Hence we read in the Song of Songs: “He set love in order within me” [Col. 1347D] (Song 1 [cf. 2:4]). “And he who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10). The cross takes its name from the torment of the body, and it is borne in two ways: either when the body is afflicted through abstinence, or when the mind is affected through compassion for one’s neighbour. We must therefore bear the cross, yet in such a way that we follow not the world but Christ. For there are some who have borne the cross hypocritically but have not followed Christ. It follows: “He who finds his life will lose it,” etc. As though he said: A person truly ought to abandon himself in order to possess me, because whoever does not abandon himself loses himself. Hence it is plainly added: “And he who loses his life for my sake will find it,” etc. [Col. 1348A] I say “loses” in the sense that he undergoes temporal death for my sake. Therefore, lest they be made excessively desolate, he strengthens them.

And note the most beautiful order. He sends them to preach; he teaches them not to fear dangers; he does not set affection above religion; he removes gold and silver; he shakes copper from the belt. O how harsh is the condition of evangelists! Whence then come necessities? He tempers the severity of the commands with the hope of promises, when it is said:

“He who receives you receives me; and he who receives me receives my Father,” etc. To show how great their dignity is, and thus to strengthen them, and so that each believer, in receiving the Apostles, might judge that he had received Christ, he says:

“And he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man,” etc. [Col. 1348B] In these words it should be noted that he does not say, “will receive a reward from the prophet,” or “from the righteous man,” but “will receive the reward of a prophet and of a righteous man.” For what does “will receive a prophet’s reward” mean, except that one who sustains a prophet by his generosity, though he himself does not have prophecy, will nevertheless have before God the reward of a prophet? For perhaps this man is righteous; and the less he possesses in this world, the greater freedom he has to speak for righteousness. When one who possesses something in this world supports such a man—who perhaps does not yet dare freely to speak for righteousness—he makes himself a participant in that righteous man’s righteousness, so that he may receive with him the rewards of righteousness, assisting him by receiving him. For if the prophet is not refreshed, it is certain that the voice itself will be withdrawn. There could have been a hidden response from believers: “Then must we also receive false prophets and Judas the betrayer?” Foreseeing this, the Lord says that not persons but names are to be received, and that the receiver does not lose the reward even if the person received is unworthy. It follows: “And whoever gives a drink of cold water to one of these little ones,” etc. Since someone might say and excuse himself, “Poverty prevents me and my limited means restrain me; I cannot be hospitable,” Jesus healed this wound with an easy command, saying that we should offer a cup of cold water with good will. He says “cold water,” not hot, lest even in hot water the lack of means and the need for firewood be alleged as an excuse.

“And it came to pass,” etc. After the Lord, in sending his disciples to preach, had instructed them with such words, he himself also fulfilled in deeds what he had taught in words, offering the first preaching to the Jews. [Col. 1348D]

## CHAPTER XI

“Now when John had seen,” etc. Concerning this Gospel passage, different authors hold different views. Hilary of Poitiers says that John did not doubt for his own sake, but had regard for his disciples’ ignorance. For one must not believe that he who, even while imprisoned, possessed the grace of the Holy Spirit—and who had said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world,” and again, “I am not worthy to loosen his sandal,” (John 1), and again, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3)—was ignorant. But, seeing his own death [Col. 1349A] near, he wished to join his disciples to Christ before he departed. And because his disciples still doubted that he was the Messiah, although John had borne testimony to him, he sends them to Jesus, asking, as it were under the guise of his own person, for them and not for himself; and he sends two because every word stands on the testimony of two witnesses. He therefore sends his disciples, as though saying to them: “If you doubt whether he to whom I bore witness was the Messiah, go to him and inquire in my name: ‘Are you he who is to come,’ that is, whom the prophets foretold would come, ‘or do we await another?’” Gregory, however, reports that John doubted. For although he did not doubt that Christ had come into the world in his own person, had been baptized, and had preached to others, he did not know whether he was to die [Col. 1349B] and descend to hell for the liberation of his own. Therefore, when John saw his death approaching and knew that he himself was to descend to hell, he wished to know of Christ’s coming to hell, so that he who had been the forerunner of his birth might be the announcer of his descent to hell. John therefore asks through his disciples: “You who came into the world by being born—are you coming to hell by dying, or do we who remain in hell await another?” And Jesus answered and said to them: “Go, report to John what you have heard and seen,” etc. As John, in his own person, had asked as though he doubted for himself, so Christ replies not to the disciples but, as it were, to John’s doubt; and in his answer removes the disciples’ doubt and confirms their hearts by his works and preaching. For the disciples had heard the words of his preaching and seen the miracles of his power. He therefore says: “Go, report to John what you have heard,” with respect to preaching, “and seen,” with respect to miracles. He enumerates the miracles to them:

“The blind see,” etc. “The poor are evangelized,” that is, are converted by the Gospel. For only those who despise earthly things love heavenly things. This is what he says of himself through the Prophet: “He sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor.” “And blessed is he,” etc. Having recounted the miracles, he then removes the doubt, saying: “And blessed is he who is not scandalized in me,” that is, who does not doubt my coming. According to Gregory, however, he answers John, not the disciples: “Blessed is he who is not scandalized in me,” that is, in my death. [Col. 1349D] For John, as stated, doubted concerning his death.

MYSTICALLY, John signifies the old law. For just as John announced Christ, preached forgiveness of sins, and promised the kingdom of heaven, so too the ancient law foretold all these things. But just as John is held in chains lest Christ be announced, so the law is bound by the Jews’ evil interpretation lest it appear to announce Christ. Yet the law sends its disciples to behold Christ’s works, that they may consider fulfilled in him whatever it contains.

“But as they were going away,” etc. Because the crowds had heard John ask this, lest it should seem that he had acted from fickleness—having at one time borne witness that he was Christ and [Col. 1350A] then again doubted—he removes fickleness from him, saying: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see?” As though he said: What do you suppose him to be, whom you so often went out into the wilderness to see? Did you go out to see a reed—that is, a fickle man, bent this way and that by every wind of prosperity or adversity? Again, “What did you go out to see?” Lest they again suppose that he was moved by some desire for vain glory—namely, wishing to make himself Christ or something of that sort—he removes vain glory from him. As though he said: He is not eager for vain glory, for he seeks not crowds of people but the wilderness; not soft clothing but haircloth; not delicate food but locusts. And this is: “Behold, those who wear soft garments,” etc. [Col. 1350B] As though he said: If he sought glory, he would love costly garments and live among eminent men. But yet, what did you go out to see? “A prophet,” etc.

After removing from John the suspicion of fickleness and vain glory, he then dwells on John’s commendation, because, once the authority of the one who preached Christ is confirmed, Christ’s authority is confirmed. He therefore calls him not only a prophet but more than a prophet, because he pointed with his finger to what does not belong to prophets. For it belongs to prophets to foretell future things, not also to point out things foretold. He says this so that they may receive the one to whom John bore testimony.

“For this is he,” etc. He further commends him by the authority of the prophet Malachi, who introduces the Father speaking to the Son. As though he said: He is truly more than a prophet, because he is the forerunner of the coming of the Son [Col. 1350C] of God, of whom the Father says to the Son:

“Behold, I send my angel”—that is, my messenger—“before your face,” that is, before your manifestation, “who will prepare your way before you,” by preaching and baptizing. “Amen, I say to you”—and what need is there to speak individually of his commendation? “Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist.” “Among those born of women,” he says, not of virgins; for women, properly speaking, are those who have been defiled. Thus Christ, who is known to have been born not of a woman but of a virgin, is not thereby denied to be greater. But if Mary is at times called “woman” in the Gospel, it must be understood that the translator used *woman* for *female*, as in: “Woman, behold your son,” and, “What is there between me and you, woman?” [Col. 1350D] From these words we have that none of the ancients was greater than John; yet it is not thereby proved that John was greater than the ancients, since he was only denied to be lesser: for he did not set John above the others, but made all the others equal to John. “But he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” As though he said: He is not lesser than the saints, but he is lesser than the angels. For anyone who is subject to passibility in mortal life is evidently lesser than angels, who are immortal. Hence Christ too is said to have been made a little lower than the angels. And this is: “But he who is least”—that is, the least angel who is in the kingdom of heaven—is greater than he. Or otherwise, the kingdom of heaven is called the present Church. The lesser one in the present Church is Christ—that is, the humbler one—who did not come [Col. 1351A] to be served but to serve, and who humbled himself unto death. Therefore, when he had said that none born of women was greater than him [than John?], lest John thereby appear greater than Christ, he adds:

“But he who,” etc. Or otherwise: Christ, who is lesser than John in the opinion of the Jews, is greater than him—not, however, among human beings, but in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the Church of the saints.

“But from the days,” etc. He still dwells on John’s commendation, recounting wonders that occurred in John’s time and did not occur in the times of other prophets. And this is: “From his days,” that is, from John’s preaching, “until now,” that is, until my preaching, “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence”—that is, seems to suffer violence; [Col. 1351B] and this is spoken by comparison. For if a kingdom were given to strangers and taken from the children of the kingdom, it would seem to be violence. Likewise, the Pharisees and scribes, who appeared righteous in the sight of men, seemed to be children of the kingdom of heaven; but tax collectors and sinners seemed far from the kingdom. He therefore says that the kingdom of heaven suffers violence. For when Jews righteous in the law seemed to be children of this kingdom, they are cast out, while prostitutes and tax collectors, who appear unworthy of so great a kingdom, enter an alien place through confession of sins; born on earth, they possess the seat of heaven by virtue, where they could not enter by nature. And “the violent”—that is, those who forcibly subdue their flesh—seize heaven, although they are strangers. Or [Col. 1351C] it may be understood of the Gentiles: because, when the kingdom of heaven—the glory promised by the prophets to Israel’s fathers—is occupied by believing Gentiles, it suffers violence, or seems to suffer it.

“For all the Prophets,” etc. It was said above that the kingdom of heaven suffers violence when it is seized by sinners who act rightly and is taken from you, O Jews; and not undeservedly, because you reject the light and wish to remain in shadow. Therefore you are utterly without excuse. For “all the Prophets and the Law”—that is, the five books of Moses—“prophesied until John”; that is, the state of the Old Testament endured until John. For with John the new grace begins, and truth replaces the shadows. This is not to be understood as meaning that John is the end of the prophets, but that he whom John’s testimony foretold is [Col. 1351D] intended; nor does it exclude prophets after John, since we read in the Acts of the Apostles that Agabus prophesied, and that the four virgin daughters of Philip did so. Rather, it means that the Law and the Prophets which we read, whatever they prophesied concerning the Lord who was to come, foretold. Therefore, when it is said, “All the Prophets prophesied until John,” Christ’s time is indicated: John shows to have come the one whom they said would come. In this too John is commended; and, that he may appear yet more worthy of commendation, it is added: “He is Elijah who is to come.” This is not because the same soul, as philosophers and heretics suppose, existed both in Elijah and in John, but because they had the same grace of the Holy Spirit, or the same measure of the Spirit. Their ascetic severity of life [Col. 1352A] and rigour of mind were also alike: the one in the wilderness, the other in the wilderness. The one was girded with a leather belt, and the other is reported to have had a similar girdle. The one, because he rebuked King Ahab and Jezebel for impiety, was compelled to flee; the other, because he rebuked the unlawful marriage of Herod and Herodias, was beheaded. Some think John is called Elijah because, just as Elijah, according to Malachi, will be the forerunner at the Saviour’s second coming and announce the coming Judge, so John had done at the first coming; thus each becomes a herald—this one of the first coming, that one of the second. Hence it is fittingly added:

“He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” For if the sense were plain and the meaning clear, what need was there to invite us to understand it, unless he meant to warn us that what the Lord said concerning Elijah ought to be understood not carnally but spiritually? [Col. 1352B]

“But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace,” etc. John is so great, yet you were unwilling to believe either him or me; therefore, to what shall I judge you like? By “generation” he understands both the Jews generally and also himself together with John; otherwise he would not say, “It is like children,” etc., when not only the Jews but John himself and Jesus are compared to children. Children say to their companions at play: “You are not our companions, because when we sang in play, you did not dance; and when we wept in play, you refused to weep with us.” Likewise, there are two conditions among the saints: mourning for sins and joy for our redemption; and both were foretold by the ancient prophets. One says: “Turn to me with all your heart,” etc.; but David invites us to joy when he says: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.” Likewise Christ and John invited us: one to mourning, like John, who fasted and invited people to repentance; the other to joy, like Christ, who, as a sign of eternal refreshment, did not fast with the Apostles but ate, and invited people to rejoice in our redemption. As though he said: I and my followers—the Apostles and prophets—sang in the marketplace, that is, in Jerusalem, where all assembled; that is, we preached the joy of your redemption, [Col. 1352D] and you, who were our equals because you came from the same people and promise, were unwilling to dance—that is, to rejoice in mind and body at your redemption with us. John and the other prophets lamented, that is, invited you to the mourning of repentance, and you refused to mourn with them. Indeed, you called John demoniac because he could fast so much, while you called me a glutton because, as a sign of your joy and eternal refreshment, I eat. But whatever you may say, I, who am the wisdom of the Father, am justified by my children—that is, I am declared to act justly by the Apostles. Or wisdom is justified by her children, that is, by her works: the works which she herself performs and brings forth show that wisdom is just.

Then he began to reproach, etc. He who hitherto had rebuked the Jews generally [Col. 1353A], now began to rebuke by name certain cities to which he had preached especially, yet which were unwilling to be converted, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” Chorazin is a town of Galilee; it is now deserted. Bethsaida is a city of Galilee, the city of Peter, Andrew, and Philip, near the lake of Gennesaret; and not far from these is Capernaum. These cities were given over to idolatry and vices. They are preferred in blame because Tyre and Sidon had despised only the natural law; but these, after transgressing both the natural and the written law, also despised the signs performed among them. One may ask where it is written that the Lord performed signs in Chorazin and Bethsaida; but above we read that he went about all the cities [Col. 1353B] and villages, healing every infirmity. Therefore, among the other towns and villages, we should suppose that the Lord performed signs in these places.

AUGUSTINE. But the question arises why the Lord pronounces a curse upon them when elsewhere he commands us to love our enemies. And the Apostle says: “Do good, and do not curse” (Rom. 12). But this is easily resolved: such words are not spoken as the wish of one who desires evil, but in the spirit of one who foresees. For when the Lord says, “Woe to you,” it means nothing other than that some evil will befall them because of their unbelief. Chorazin is interpreted “my mystery”; and this interpretation of its name is the height of its confusion. For the more it knew the mysteries and works of God, the more it was to be condemned because it did not believe. Bethsaida is interpreted “house of fruits” or “of hunters.” By this interpretation too we can show this city to be blameworthy. He therefore says: “Woe to you, Chorazin, which knew my mysteries and yet refused to believe! Woe to you, Bethsaida, which ought to have borne fruit for me and did not bear fruit! For if the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Sidon and Tyre”—that is, if among the Gentile peoples, afflicted and hunted by diabolic temptations, that is, deceived—“I had performed so many signs, they would long ago have done penance in ashes,” recalling their condition, “and in sackcloth,” that is, mortifying the flesh by fasts. For Tyre is interpreted “narrowness,” and Sidon “hunting.”

For this reason he did not earlier preach to Tyre and Sidon, nor perform signs there—though afterward he did—because at that time there were among them those who were not to be saved and did not deserve to be restored to life. Therefore, by a subtle and hidden judgment, holy preaching is withheld from certain people’s ears because they do not deserve to be raised by grace. Thus today we see fulfilled the Savior’s saying: Chorazin and Bethsaida refused to believe while the Lord was present. But Tyre and Sidon afterward believed when the disciples evangelized; and they showed such faith and devotion that, when Paul was leaving Tyre, all the citizens, with their wives and children, escorted him outside the city. It was a most beautiful sight: so great a multitude of people led their very few, but dearly loved, guests all the way to the ships to bid them farewell. Although God foresaw that these people were capable of conversion, it was not injustice; rather, he was unwilling to call those who were sinners and therefore unworthy, because “he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills”: the one through mercy, the other through justice. [Col. 1354A]

The Lord had ordained that salvation should not be offered to the Gentiles until it had been offered to the Jews and rejected by them. Tyre and Sidon, however, were Gentile cities, which were afterward converted through the apostles. But why God denies grace to persons who would gladly receive it and consent to grace is not for us to know. We dare affirm only this: that he acts justly if he rejects sinners. But why he chooses this man, who will not consent to grace, and neglects that other man, who would consent to grace so well, is known to God alone and to those to whom God wishes to reveal it. Grace is therefore offered to those who will not receive it, so that they may be rendered inexcusable, and so that the preaching first offered to the Jews and rejected by them may at the fitting time [Col. 1354B] pass to the Gentiles.

“Nevertheless, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon.” Although preaching was not given to them and they were not converted to the faith, it will nevertheless be more tolerable for them on the day of judgment than for you. For it is more fitting that those who received preaching and yet did not assent to it should be punished than those who never heard it.

“And you, Capernaum,” etc. Not only Bethsaida and Chorazin will receive woe, but you also, Capernaum, because “will you be exalted unto heaven,” etc.? This has a double meaning. It is as though he said: Because you have risen up in pride against me unto heaven and against my preaching, you shall descend to hell. Or otherwise: Will you, who are to be exalted unto heaven by the praise of believers because my preaching began in you and my miracles were displayed in you, not descend unto hell, since you were unwilling to believe either my preaching or my miracles? “For if in Sidon,” etc. The Sodomites were sinners and therefore unworthy that God’s grace should be offered to them; nevertheless, they were able to assent if it had been offered. Yet the Lord justly condemned them and neither sent preachers to them nor performed such mighty works among them, because the time of preaching and Christ’s coming had not yet arrived. Why he was unwilling to offer grace to those who would have assented, he knows who knows all things.

It should be known that Capernaum is interpreted “most beautiful village.” It shone with the Lord’s miracles, but its own name turned to its opposite when it remained in unbelief.

“At that time,” etc. Because he knew that many would doubt concerning this question, he answered their thoughts, saying: “I confess [Col. 1354D] to you, Father”—that is, I give thanks to you and rejoice in you—“Lord of heaven and earth.” It is as though he said: You can make whomsoever you wish into heavens—that is, you can reveal your hidden counsels to anyone—and can conceal those same counsels from others, so that they are no longer called heaven but earth. “I confess,” I say, “because you have hidden these things from the wise”—namely, why preaching was not to be given to these persons and why it was given to those, and other such matters—“and prudent,” that is, from the Pharisees and also from others who seem wise to themselves in divine matters and prudent, that is, shrewd, in human affairs; “and have revealed them to little ones,” that is, the humble. You have revealed them, I say, in part, even if not wholly. And lest anyone again press the question and ask why this is so, he adds: “So it is, Father, because it was pleasing [Col. 1355A] before you,” that is, in your sight. Yet nothing is pleasing to you without reason: whatever you do, you do either justly or mercifully.

AUGUSTINE. “Confession” is understood in two ways: confession of sins, and confession of praise, which belongs to Christ alone. Scripture calls confession in general whatever is openly declared as it is perceived. And when he said, “You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones,” he said this to show that he condemned pride. But when he adds, “Yes, Father, because thus it was pleasing to you,” he speaks to the Father with the affection of one who lovingly entreats, that the benefit begun in the apostles may be completed. For this is pleasing to him: that the one who departed from him through pride should return in humility. Hence follows: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father,” as though he said: [Col. 1355B] They are revealed to the little ones who do not presume upon themselves because they are revealed through me. And truly they are revealed and can be revealed through me, because all things have been delivered to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, etc.

It is as though he said: Not only has the Father given me those who have access to him through me, but even the making known of my name is from the Father. The Father alone is said to know the Son because the Son’s being known is attributed solely to the Father’s grace. Understand the Son here as incarnate. Conversely, no one knows the Father except the Son; for the incarnation of the Word of God the Father was a making known of the divine majesty. To show a certain intimacy, and as it were a union between head and members—that is, between Christ and believers—he adds: “And he to whom the Son wills to reveal him.” [Col. 1355C] For a certain identity of knowledge between Father and Son, and the Son’s intimacy with the Father, are thereby shown. He did not say, “to whom the Father wills to reveal him,” but “to whom the Son wills to reveal him.” Note that when he says, “except the Son,” he understands the whole Trinity through one person.

“Come,” etc. Since revelation is through me and all things have been delivered to me, therefore come to me, as John exhorted you. For John’s commendation was directed to this, and again his own commendation was directed to this: that all should come to him. This is the meaning: “Come by the steps of faith, you who labor under the law,” that is, under the yoke of the law, which neither you nor your fathers were able to bear, “and are burdened” by the weight of sins; “and I will refresh [Col. 1355D] you.” That is, I shall not only unburden you, but also satisfy you with the refreshment of eternal life.

“Take upon yourselves”—that is, upon your higher part, namely the soul—“my yoke,” that is, the yoke of my commandments; and in taking it, “learn from me,” that is, from my example, “to be gentle,” so that you may not murmur, “and humble,” so that you may endure adversities patiently. And in this way, having rest of mind, you will at last find everlasting rest for your souls. And lest you shrink from bearing my yoke, know that the yoke of faith is sweet and the burden of my commandments light. What is sweeter than his yoke? What lighter than his burden? To become acceptable to God; to abstain from crime; to will what is good; to refuse what is evil; to love all; to hate none; to attain eternal things; [Col. 1356A] not to be captivated by present things; not to wish to inflict upon another what is burdensome to endure oneself—these are light things.

## CHAPTER XII

“At that time.” The events which follow are believed to have occurred after John’s death. For all the following matters seem to form one continuous sequence, after recounting which it later adds: “Herod the tetrarch heard the report of Jesus and said: This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead” (Matt. 14). From this it is inferred that all these things were completed after John’s death. For after John had sent his disciples to Jesus, he is believed to have been beheaded shortly afterward. Thus, when it says, “At that time,” the period seems to be marked off from that point. But let us return to the literal sense.

Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath, and his disciples began [Col. 1356B] to pluck ears of grain and eat. We read later that many were coming and going, and the disciples had no opportunity even to eat; and so, being human, they were hungry. That they rubbed the ears of grain in their hands and relieved their hunger shows the austerity of their life: they sought not prepared dishes but simple food.

But the Pharisees, seeing this, said to him, etc. They judged the apostles concerning the Sabbath, not concerning the plucking of another’s produce, because Moses commanded in the Law: “If you enter your friend’s vineyard or grainfield, eat as much as your soul desires; but you shall not reap with a sickle or carry anything away” (Deut. 23). Therefore they slander them only concerning the Sabbath and not concerning the grain.

MYSTICALLY, the disciples pass through grainfields when holy teachers carefully observe, with the concern of devout solicitude, those whom they seek to instruct by the word of truth. With diligent consideration they weigh how and in what order they ought to draw each person to salvation; and they hunger for the salvation of human beings. To pluck ears is to pull persons away from the earthly intention in which they had fixed the root of their heart. To rub the ears, as the other Evangelists relate, is to strip people—like grains—from the chaff of vices, using the hands of virtues. To eat is to incorporate those made clean into the body of the Church. [Col. 1356C]

But he, etc. The Lord defends his disciples by the necessity of hunger, and likewise shows that David, through necessity, violated the law when he ate on that day the loaves of the presentation, which priests alone ought to eat. Yet David is not reproved. From this it is plainly apparent that Moses never intended, when he commanded that no servile work be done on the Sabbath, that anyone should do no small work whatsoever out of necessity. For that person is properly said to do servile work who commits sin. Thus the apostles act against the letter but not against its meaning. In that deed David prefigured that these figures were at last to be destroyed, just as Samuel prefigured the destruction of the priesthood.

David, fleeing Saul, came to Nob; received by Abimelech the priest, he asked for food. Since the priest had no common loaves, he gave him the consecrated loaves, which no one but priests and Levites might eat. He asked only whether the young men were clean from women; and when David replied, “since yesterday and the day before,” [Col. 1357A] he did not hesitate to give the loaves (1 Sam. 21). He judged it better, as the prophet says, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice,” to deliver people from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God. For a sacrifice pleasing to God is the salvation of human beings. Figuratively, David and his young men receiving consecrated bread shows either that priestly food would pass into common use among the people, or that we must all imitate the priestly life, or that all children of the Church are priests.

“Or,” etc. Having defended the apostles through necessity, he also adduces an example in which the Jews violate the law without necessity—namely, when priests violate the Sabbath by killing and skinning sacrificial victims on that day, and doing similar things. “But I say to you,” etc. They could say that service in the Temple excused them. The reply is: If the Temple’s service excuses them, then Christ’s service ought to excuse those apostles, because he is greater than the Temple. Since they are occupied with Christ’s preaching, they cannot seek food; therefore they pluck ears of grain. Or, if they wished to excuse David and his companions by royal authority, Christ is likewise king and can excuse his own by royal authority. [Col. 1357B]

“But if,” etc. You ought to have spared them not only because of necessity, but also because of mercy. But because you are merciless, you do not know how to spare. This is the meaning: “If you had known,” etc. He adduces the prophetic authority concerning mercy, explained above. “For the Lord is,” etc. There is also another reason why they may violate the law: they are servants of him [Col. 1357C] who is Lord of the Sabbath, and therefore he who made the law can change it according to his will.

“And when he had passed from there,” etc. This would seem to have happened on the same Sabbath, unless Luke said: “And it came to pass on another Sabbath that he entered into the synagogue and taught. And there was a man there” (Luke 6), etc. “And they asked him.” Matthew reports that they asked whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, whereas Mark and Luke report that Christ asked whether it was lawful to do good on the Sabbath. But it should be known that both questions were asked. When they asked whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, Christ replied: “Is it not lawful to do good on the Sabbath?”

“Which of you,” etc. He resolves the proposed question in such a way as to condemn the questioners’ greed. “If you,” he says, “hasten on the Sabbath to rescue a sheep, or any animal, that has fallen into a pit, you do so not for the animal’s sake but to serve your own greed. How much more ought I to free a human being, who is much better than a sheep?” Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. [Col. 1357D]

ALLEGORY. The man who had a withered hand signifies the human race, dried up by the barrenness of good work but healed by the Lord’s mercy. His right hand, which had withered in the first parent when he plucked the fruit of the forbidden tree, was restored to the saving power of good works through the grace of redemption when innocent hands were stretched out upon the tree of the cross. And fittingly the hand was withered in the synagogue, because where the gift of knowledge is greater, there is a graver danger of inexcusable [Col. 1358A] guilt. The withered hand is commanded to be stretched forth in order to be healed, because the weakness of an unfruitful soul is cured in no better way than by the generosity of almsgiving. Hence, when the crowds asked John the Baptist what they should do so as not to be cast into the fire like dry trees, he prescribed only this: “He who has two tunics, let him give to one who has none; and he who has food, let him do likewise” (Luke 3). And Ecclesiasticus says: “My son, let not your hand be stretched out to receive and drawn back when you ought to give” (Ecclus. 4). For in vain does one stretch out his hands to God in prayer for sins when he does not stretch them out to bring help to the needy person who asks.

“And it was restored, sound as the other,” etc. By the left hand evil action is understood, and by the right, good action. Therefore, as evil action formerly flourished in them, so good action began to flourish in the same persons. [Col. 1358B]

But the Pharisees, going out, took counsel against him, etc. Since they could not ensnare him either by words or deeds, they wished to attack him by deceit and plotted his death. They are therefore rightly said to go out, for they were removed from the presence of divine grace.

But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there, and they followed, etc. Jesus withdrew because he spared their madness, lest he make them worse by exposing himself to danger; and the hour of his Passion, whose place was not outside Jerusalem, had not yet come. He came to a place where he found many who followed him out of fear. “And he commanded them,” etc. He cultivates this humility in us, so that when we have done some great thing [Col. 1358C] we may not seek human praise. Spiritually, he withdrew from them when he abandoned them by withholding grace, and he passed to the Gentiles, among whom many followed him by faith and good works; and he healed them by the remission of sins.

“That it might be fulfilled,” etc. By Isaiah’s authority he shows that Christ sought the Jews’ salvation, not their destruction. Therefore, when they insulted him, he did not protest, but endured everything with equanimity until the day of the resurrection. Many things in this authority do not pertain to confirming the matter presently at hand, but the entire passage of Scripture is introduced because of the Father’s grace. The words of the authority are explained as follows. It was said through Isaiah the prophet, speaking in the person of the Father: “Behold my servant, who, taking the form of a servant, was made less than I; whom I chose for the work for which no one else was fit; my beloved in a special sense, in whom my soul was well pleased, because through him I wished to restore the lost human race. Therefore I shall place my Spirit upon him”—namely, the spirit of wisdom, understanding, strength, knowledge, piety, fear, and counsel (Isa. 2). This Spirit is said to have descended upon him in the form of a dove, not upon the Word of God and Only-Begotten who came forth from the Father’s bosom, but upon him of whom it was said: “Behold my servant”; “and he shall announce my judgment to the Gentiles” (Isa. 42). Hence the Psalmist: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son” (Ps. 71). And in the Gospel: “The Father [Col. 1359A] judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

And such a one “will not contend,” because he was offered as he himself willed, when he freely delivered himself into the hands of his persecutors. “Nor will he cry out,” because “as a sheep he was led to slaughter; and as a lamb before its shearer will be silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). “Nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets,” because narrow and confined is the way leading to life, but broad and spacious is the way leading to destruction, and many enter by it (Matt. 7). These are those who do not hear the Savior’s voice, because they are not on the narrow way but the spacious one. Therefore he spoke to those who were outside not in his own voice, but through parables. It follows:

“A bruised reed he will not break.” By the reed he means the Jews, shaken by the wind and as though scattered from one another; he will not at once condemn them, but will patiently bear with them. “And smoking flax he will not quench,” that is, the people gathered from the Gentiles, who, when the warmth of the natural law was extinguished, were enveloped in errors of bitter smoke, harmful to the eyes, and dark gloom. He not only did not quench them and reduce them to ashes, but on the contrary, from a small and nearly dying spark, kindled the greatest flames, so that the whole world burned with the fire of the Lord and Savior, which he came to cast upon the earth. Whoever despises the small spark of faith in little ones quenches this smoking flax—which Christ did not do. For he came to save what had perished. “He will not break,” I say, “nor quench, until he casts out [Col. 1359C] the ruler of this world,” who has already been judged, “unto his victory.” Hence elsewhere: “Now the ruler of this world shall be cast out.” Or: until the hidden judgment of God is made manifest, “and in his name the Gentiles shall hope.” Hence Isaiah: “There shall be a root of Jesse” (Isa. 11), and he who rises to rule the Gentiles—in him shall the Gentiles hope.

Or the wood may signify the Jews, who had within themselves some spark of truth through the Law, but uttered most bitter judgments. Christ, so far as he was concerned, did not make them worse or quench that fire, but wished to increase preaching and correction. That is, he was unwilling to destroy or condemn them, but endured all things until he cast out, unto his victory, the judgment executed upon him; this occurred on the day of the Ascension. After his Ascension he destroyed them through Titus and Vespasian. Or: until he casts out, that is, makes manifest, his own judgment, formerly hidden while he spared them; this he did on the day of their captivity and at the time of other punishments. [Col. 1359D]

Then a man possessed by a demon was brought to him, etc. This demoniac is shown to have been not only mute but also blind, and he was cured of the demon, so that he spoke and saw. What then happened bodily is fulfilled daily in the conversion of believers: after the demon has first been expelled, they behold the light of faith; then mouths formerly silent are opened for the praises of God.

When this was done, all the crowds were amazed and said: “Is this not the son of David?” etc. The crowds were amazed and confessed him to be God, because he performed such signs. [Col. 1360A] But the Pharisees slandered the works of God, saying: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons.” It was not some of the crowd but the Pharisees and scribes who uttered this slander. For the crowds, who seemed less learned, always marvelled at the Lord’s deeds; on the other hand, the others labored either to deny these things or to distort by a perverse interpretation what they could not deny, as though these had been works not of a divine but of an unclean spirit—that is, of Beel, the god of Ekron in that place. Hence they are called Ekronites. For Beel is Baal itself, while *zebub* means “fly.” Thus Beelzebub means “Baal of the flies,” that is, “man of flies” or “one having flies,” on account of the filth of sacrificial blood; from this utterly foul rite or name they called the prince of demons.

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, etc. He answers not their words but their thoughts, so that they might thereby be compelled to believe in his power. Or: this argument was spoken and written more for the edification of believers than for the correction of the Pharisees. This argument, made through discriminating reasoning, leads the adversary’s position to an absurd conclusion. Since they said that he cast out demons by Beelzebub’s power, he brings this assertion to the incongruity that, if he cast them out through demons, then demons would seek the destruction of their own kingdom. The argument is arranged thus: If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, then Satan casts out Satan; and if Satan casts out Satan, then Satan is opposed to Satan and therefore divided against himself. [Col. 1360C]

We have this consequence where he says: “And if Satan casts out Satan, and if Satan is divided against Satan, how shall his kingdom stand?” He puts this in the form of a question: “How shall his kingdom stand?” He proves this final consequence by universal premises, as though he said: Truly, if it is divided against itself, its kingdom will be laid waste; for every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste; and truly every kingdom, because every city; and truly every city, because every house—again, from the lesser. Therefore, since on this account—namely, that Satan casts out Satan—the desolation of his kingdom would follow, Satan would seek the desolation of his own kingdom if one opposed another. Let the Pharisees, then, choose whichever they wish. [Col. 1360D] If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they could find nothing to say against the Lord; but if he can, then they should take much greater care for themselves and withdraw from his kingdom, which, divided against itself, cannot stand.

“And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” Again, another argument. Among the Jews there were exorcists who, by exorcisms devised by Solomon, often expelled demons from possessed bodies. Truly, I cast demons out of people by divine power, because your sons cast them out by the power of God.

If, then, in the case of your sons the expulsion of demons is attributed to God and not to demons, why should the same work in my case not have the same cause, when my works [Col. 1361A] appear only good and I cast out demons at the invocation of God, just as they do? This is the meaning: “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons”—that is, your exorcists—“cast them out?”

Or the apostles may also be called sons. It was certain that they were conscious of no evil art, since they were uneducated and illiterate; nevertheless, the Pharisees saw them daily shining with miracles and casting out demons. Therefore, if his disciples cast out demons through the Holy Spirit, this ought much more to be believed of their master.

“Therefore they themselves,” etc. This may be read concerning either the exorcists or the disciples. Because the exorcists cast out demons through the invocation of God, they will be the cause of the Jews’ condemnation, since the Jews see pure men of lesser merit able to cast out demons by divine power and nevertheless presume to doubt this of the Son of God. They will therefore be judges, not by authority but by being the cause. It is also said of the apostles thus: Because the apostles, performing miracles under my discipleship, are witnesses of my power and condemn your wickedness, they will be your judges, since, seated over the twelve tribes, they will condemn you together with the impious. [Col. 1361B]

“But if,” etc. Behold the other part of the argument, as though he said: Either I cast out demons through the Holy Spirit or through Satan; but if through Satan, the things already stated follow. But if through the Spirit, this is for your benefit: “the kingdom of God has come upon you,” that is, has come into your midst. The diminution of the devil’s kingdom is the increase of the kingdom of God.

“Or how,” etc. Another proof. Truly, I do not cast out demons by Beelzebub, because I am opposed to him. And truly I am opposed to him, because I entered his house—that is, the world—and plundered his goods—that is, human beings in whom he dwelt, whom I withdrew through faith. In order to plunder them from him, I first bound him, that is, deprived him of the power of harming human beings. For how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man, etc.? “He who is not with me is against me,” etc. I am opposed to him because he is opposed to me. This is the meaning: “He who is not with me is against me”; and he is truly opposed to me because I gather and he scatters. He draws people toward many secular goods; I toward the one highest good. He draws them to discord; I to love. [Col. 1361D]

“Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to men, but blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven,” etc. Having shown by reasoning that he does not cast out demons by Beelzebub, he wishes to pronounce judgment upon the Jews who sin against the Holy Spirit—namely, that this sin is unforgivable for them. But let us see what it is to sin against the Holy Spirit.

An angel was created with strength of knowledge and substance, so that he had both profound knowledge and, through the strength of his substance, the capacity to carry things out. Since, then, he abounded in so great a good and saw the divine essence to surpass him greatly, he began, against his conscience and not through any weakness, to envy God and wished to make himself equal to him. Therefore he sinned against God neither through weakness of ignorance nor of substance, but through his own perversity: knowing him nevertheless to be God and his Creator, he nonetheless envied him against his own conscience. God, therefore, a just judge, withdrew his grace and did not wish to visit him, but permitted him to be completely blinded and to fall into the same obstinacy. [Col. 1362A]

But man was created with less intelligence and weaker substance, because he did not possess so great a capacity of understanding or such ability to execute. He could therefore be deceived by another’s persuasion; and when Adam sinned, he thought that God could easily be reconciled to him, and therefore he was unwilling to cause his wife scandal. Since he sinned through weakness of knowledge and substance at another’s persuasion, his fault was remissible, because, when God’s grace visited him, man humbled himself and repented.

Likewise, when others sin through adultery, gluttony, and similar things out of weakness of the flesh, and humble themselves by acknowledging their weakness—even if they have not yet returned—God mercifully visits them, invites them to repentance, and heals them. Again, there are sins of weakness: to sin against the Father or against the Son, or through ignorance or weakness to believe either that God has no Son or that the Son is less than the Father. Since these arise from weakness or ignorance, they are remissible. I do not say that they are always forgiven, because if people do not repent, they die and are thus condemned. But it is possible for them to come to repentance and thus for their sins to be forgiven. [Col. 1362B]

But some recognize the truth and nevertheless, out of envy and perversity of mind, resist the goodness of God against their conscience. Therefore they hate and slander what is good. Such were the Jews: understanding the prophets, seeing the signs of fulfillment, and wishing to find no evil in Christ’s works, they nevertheless slandered Christ out of envy and resisted the goodness of God against their conscience, preferring never to be saved rather than receive Christ and abandon their own law. Such people fall into a diabolic sin, and God abandons them as he abandoned Judas, so that they cannot repent or humble themselves but are held fast in obstinacy. This sin is unforgivable, and it is called sinning against the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is the goodness of God, and whoever thus resists God’s goodness sins against the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1362D]

But it is also customarily explained otherwise. To sin against the Holy Spirit is said to be to remain unrepentant. For the remission of sins is properly attributed to the Holy Spirit. Thus the passage is read:

“He who sins against the Father”—one must supply, “and does not sin against the Spirit,” for he is not unrepentant—“shall be forgiven.” Likewise, he who sins against the Son and does not sin against the Holy Spirit, that is, is not unrepentant, shall again be forgiven. But he who sins against the Holy Spirit, that is, who persists without repentance, shall never be forgiven. For pardon is promised only to the repentant.

In this authority the heresy of Origen is extinguished, who asserts that after the universal judgment, after many ages, all sinners will obtain forgiveness. This is refuted when it is said: “But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in the present age nor in the future” (Matt. 12). [Col. 1363A]

From this authority the existence of purgatorial fire is also confirmed. For Gregory says: “From this it is given to understand that certain faults are forgiven in this age and certain others in the age to come. For when something is denied of one, the consequent meaning is clear: it is granted in the case of some.” Yet this should be believed possible only concerning small and very minor sins, such as habitual idle speech, excessive laughter, or the sin involved in the care of household affairs, which scarcely is conducted without fault even by those who know how faults ought to be avoided. Or it may concern serious sins arising from an error of ignorance, which weigh upon people even after death if they have not been remitted while they yet lived in this life. [Col. 1363B] Nevertheless, it must be known that there no one will obtain purification even from the least sins unless, while still placed in this life, he has merited by good deeds to obtain it there.

“Either make the tree good,” etc. Another proof, as though he said: If you blaspheme me deservedly, show that my works are evil. This is the meaning: “Either make the tree good,” that is, acknowledge that I am good, because you see my fruit to be good.

“Or make the tree evil.” That is, show me to be evil through evil fruit. I say that one must look to the fruit because “the tree is known by its fruit”; that is, a person’s life is judged from works. “Offspring of vipers, how can you be good when you are evil,” etc.? It is as though he said: Truly the tree is known by its fruit, because your wickedness is evident from your words. He calls them offspring of vipers—that is, sons and imitators of the devil—because, though they are evil trees and abound in the fruit of envy, they sin knowingly and knowingly slander good works; this is diabolic. Hence follows:

For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Augustine. That person speaks from the abundance of the heart who does not know the intention from which words are uttered. Wishing to show this more clearly, he adds: “A good person brings forth good things from a good treasure, and an evil person evil things.” The treasure of the heart is the intention of knowledge, from which the inward judge assesses the outcome of an action. Hence it often happens that some perform lesser good works yet receive the reward of greater heavenly grace because of the intention of their heart—namely, because they would have accomplished greater things if they had been able; while others, displaying greater works of virtue, receive lesser rewards from the Lord because of the negligence of a lukewarm heart. This fittingly follows the preceding statement. For just as a good person cannot bring forth evil, nor an evil person good, so Christ cannot do evil works, nor the devil good works. It follows:

“But I say to you that every idle word,” etc. This too fittingly follows the preceding statement, as though he said: If an idle word—which never edifies its hearers—is not without danger to the speaker, who will have to render an account for it on the day of judgment, how much more will you, who slander the works of the Holy Spirit, have to render an account for your slander? [Col. 1364A] An idle word is one uttered without benefit either to speaker or hearer; to establish this he adds:

“For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” The sense still depends on what preceded, where he said: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” For there is no doubt that a person will be condemned by the words he has uttered, if they are evil; since in no way can he be justified by good words unless he has uttered them from the inward good intention of his heart—just as Caiaphas was not justified by prophesying.

Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, etc. After they are wholly unable to disprove his words, they still seek to test him in his works; and, as though the signs they had seen were no signs, they demand signs. Thus those Pharisees and scribes, whose cunning was most wicked, reply and say: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” But another Evangelist explains more fully what they sought. He specifies that they were seeking a sign from heaven. Either, after the manner of Elijah, they desired a sign to come from on high; or, in the likeness of Samuel, that in summer, contrary to the nature of the region, thunder should roar, lightning flash, and rains fall—so that they might slander these things, as though such rains could not fall, and say that they had issued from hidden heavens and arisen from various atmospheric disturbances. For those who slander what they see with their eyes, grasp with their hands, and experience by its benefit—what will they do concerning things that come from heaven? Certainly they will answer that magicians in Egypt also performed many signs from heaven.

[Col. 1364C] Therefore the Lord answered them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet,” etc. He rightly called it adulterous, because it had abandoned its husband and, according to Ezekiel, joined itself to many lovers.

But it should be noted that he had been assailed by a twofold question. Some had slandered him, saying that he cast out demons by Beelzebub; these had already received an answer. Others, testing him, sought a sign from heaven; to these he now answers, saying that he will give them no sign from heaven, because they were unworthy to see one, but rather a sign from the depth of hell: Jonah the prophet swallowed by the sea-monster—that is, Christ delivered from the abyss and the jaws of death. They will receive such a sign; and through it he gave them the sign of the Incarnation, not of majesty; of the Passion, [Col. 1364D] not of glorification. But to his disciples, who were worthy, he gave a sign from heaven: first, when transfigured on the mountain, he showed them figuratively the glory of eternal blessedness; and afterward, when he was truly raised into heaven, he showed it to them. It follows:

“For as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights,” etc. Scripture bears witness that the three-day period itself was not entirely complete. But the first day was counted as whole from its final part; likewise the third day, from its first part. The middle day, that is, the second day, was wholly complete, consisting of twenty-four hours—twelve of daylight and twelve of night. You are to count the part of Friday on which he was buried, together with part of the night, as a night and a day, that is, as a whole day; Saturday with its night and day; and the Lord’s Day night with the dawn of that same day, likewise as a whole day. Thus you have three days and three nights.

This three-day period is found in Scripture to signify the Lord’s single death and single resurrection. For the death of the Lord Jesus was not in his soul, but in his flesh alone. Our death, however, is not only in the flesh but also in the soul: in the soul because of sin, and in the flesh because of sin’s punishment. But he who had no sin in his soul did not die except in the flesh alone, and this because of the likeness of sinful flesh which he derived from Adam. His death was in the flesh, and so was his resurrection. For it was not his soul that rose, but only his flesh; just as his soul did not die, but [Col. 1365B] only his flesh. Yet his single death and resurrection benefited our twofold death and resurrection. Through his death, the death of hell and the death caused by sins were taken away from us. Likewise, through his single resurrection, which was in the flesh alone and not in the soul, both resurrections will be given to us: that of the soul in baptism, and that of the body in the general resurrection.

Therefore, since in the reckoning already given there is one day—namely, the Sabbath—and two nights, that is, the night of the Sabbath and that of the Lord’s Day, Christ’s single death is understood by the day, while the twofold death of human beings is understood by the nights. Thus, as one day is set against two nights, Christ set his single death against our double death, and by dying subdued our double death. But if we count the hours from the hour of his death to the hour when his resurrection was manifested, forty hours are found. For on the first day there are four hours from the ninth hour; on the following day, twelve nighttime and twelve daytime hours; and after the Sabbath, twelve nighttime hours are counted. All these collected together amount to forty. Therefore the Lord fittingly restored forty days of joy in exchange for forty hours of sorrow.

Or a longer interval may be understood in the three days and nights. For the words, “So shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth,” may be read thus: “in the heart of earthly people,” that is, in their power, so that for three days and three nights they might fulfill their desire upon him. [Col. 1365D] From the night in which he was betrayed until the dawn of the resurrection, he was in their power. Thus the first two days are found complete, while on the third only the night is found, as above. And it should carefully be noted that the night until the dawn in which the Lord rose belongs to the third day, because the Lord who commanded light to shine out of darkness, so that through the grace of the New Testament and participation in Christ’s resurrection we might hear, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5), thereby intimates to us in some fashion that the day also takes its beginning from the night. For as the first day, because of humanity’s coming fall, was reckoned from light to night, so these days, because of humanity’s restoration, are reckoned from darkness to light.

Let us return to the literal sense. As that historical Jonah [Col. 1366A] was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man—namely Christ, the true Jonah, that is, “sorrowing,” and bearing our sorrows—was, as has been explained, for three days and three nights in the heart of the earth: namely, in the tomb; or in the heart of the earth, that is, in the hearts of earthly people, already despairing and saying, “We had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24). Thus Christ was in the human heart of some as one lying in a tomb, or in the hearts of earthly people—that is, in their power.

Christ may also be fitted to Jonah in every respect. The sailors are the Jews; the fish is death. The sailors hand Jonah over to the fish, and the Jews hand Christ over to death. On the third day the fish vomited Jonah out at the harbor, and on the third day death restored Christ to the firmness of life. Jonah preached to the Ninevites, and after the resurrection Christ, through the apostles, announced the truth to the Gentiles.

“The men of Nineveh,” etc. Because this generation saw Christ’s works and signs and nevertheless refused to believe, the Ninevites, who are Gentiles, will rise in judgment with this generation—not to judge them by authority, but by comparison. For the Ninevites were converted to repentance without signs, while the Jews would not be converted even through signs. He introduces this comparison when he adds: “Because they repented at the preaching of Jonah.” “And behold,” etc. That is: among the Jews there is one greater than Jonah, namely Christ, God and man, in whose preaching they are unwilling to believe.

“The queen of the south,” etc. We read in Chronicles and in the Book of Kings that the queen of Sheba, overcoming many [Col. 1366C] difficulties and leaving her own realm, came into Judaea to hear Solomon’s wisdom; bringing him many gifts, she received still more from him (3 Kings 10).

Connection. Not only will the Ninevites condemn it by comparison, but also the queen of the south, because from the uttermost ends of the earth she came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, without law and without prophets. But the Jewish people have the Law, have the prophets, see Christ, see his works, and yet refuse to hear his wisdom. Therefore she will likewise condemn them by comparison, because behold, here—that is, among the Jews—is one greater than Solomon, namely Christ.

Mystically, however, the Ninevites and the queen signify the whole Gentile people converted to faith. The Ninevites signify those who cease to sin; the queen, those who do not know how to sin. For repentance abolishes sin; wisdom guards against it. Nor is it said that the queen had not sinned because Scripture says nothing of her sins; rather, it asserts that she devoted herself to wisdom.

“When an unclean spirit,” etc. He had compared the Gentiles to the Ninevites and the queen of the south; now he sets forth to whom the Jews ought to be compared: namely, to a person from whom an unclean spirit went out and to whom, when it later returned, it re-entered with other more wicked spirits after finding him empty, and afflicted him more severely than before. The person to whom the Jewish people are compared is anyone converted to faith, from whom the devil has been cast out through baptism. Having been expelled, the devil goes to other believers; finding no place there, he returns to the one from whom he had gone out, [Col. 1367A] and sees him empty—that is, negligent—and therefore hopes to possess him again. Yet he sees him cleansed of vices by brooms, that is, by doctrines and sacraments, and adorned with false virtues. He nevertheless sees the sevenfold Spirit dwelling there—not that the seven gifts are actively present in that person, but present as a capacity. Therefore, in fear, he seeks seven spirits more wicked than himself: that is, seven vices contrary to the seven virtues which the Spirit gives; and through them he dwells within. They are called more wicked because sins after baptism are more serious than before it.

The Jewish people must be fitted in every detail to such a person. For he says at the end of the parable: “So shall it be also with this most wicked generation.” Before the Law, the devil reigned among the Jewish people while they transgressed the natural law; for the correction of that transgression, this written Law was given through Moses. Then, through fear of the Law, through observance of legal commands, and through the Jews’ confirmation by the greatness of benefits in the ancient sacraments—namely circumcision and sacrifices—and in the worship of the one God, the unclean spirit withdrew from that people, not having as great a power to harm them as before the Law. Yet it should be known that he did not withdraw from all of them; for the Jewish people are discussed here without distinction, and some among them were always exceedingly good.

Therefore the devil, going out, passed over to the Gentiles, among whom he remained until the preaching of the apostles. Whereas they had formerly been moist, flowing in carnal pleasures, [Col. 1367C] they became dry—that is, firm and solid—through the fire of the Holy Spirit. Then, walking through dry places, that is, going around the strong hearts of the Gentiles and finding no rest for himself, he returns to the ancient Jewish people. After Christ’s coming he completely blinded them—for once the Gospel had been given, no one can any longer be saved through the state of the old Law. Finding that house empty, that is, finding the people negligent and not providing well for themselves from the Scriptures, because they refused to understand Christ’s coming; and finding it swept, that is, seemingly cleansed from vices by carnal observances; and adorned with false virtues, like that Pharisee who boasted in the temple—he takes seven spirits more wicked than himself and dwells there. By the seven spirits all vices are understood, for the number seven signifies universality. They are deservedly called more wicked because, after Christ’s coming, the Jews were hurled into more grievous sins: namely blasphemy against Christ, assault upon the truth, and contempt for faith. Thus the last state is worse than the first.

But the literal connection is this: The Ninevites repented, and the queen of the south heard Solomon’s wisdom; but the Jewish people are like a person from whom an unclean spirit went out, and when it had gone out, etc.

“While he was still speaking,” etc. This preaching was in a house, as what follows will make clear. His mother and brothers were standing outside the house, waiting and seeking to speak with him. Bede. The brothers of the Lord are not, as Helvidius held, sons of blessed Mary, ever Virgin; nor, as some suppose, sons of Joseph by another wife. Rather, they should be understood as his relatives. Certainly, when the Lord, asked concerning his mother and brothers, declines to leave the work of the word, he does not reject the dutiful service owed to his mother—for it was earlier commanded, “Honor your father and your mother”—but shows that he owes more to his Father’s ministries than to maternal affections. By example and word alike he commends the same to us when he says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10). He does not contemptuously reject his brothers, but, preferring spiritual work to carnal kinship, teaches that the union of hearts is more religious than that of bodies.

Mystically, the mother and brothers of Jesus are the synagogue, from whose flesh he was born, and the Jewish people. While the Savior teaches within, they come but cannot enter, because they neglect to understand spiritually his words. For the crowd goes in before them, enters his house, and listens to his discourse, as the Evangelist Matthew makes clear; because, while Judaea stood apart, the Gentiles flocked to Christ and drank in the inward mysteries of life with minds more capacious in proportion as they were nearer in faith, as the prophet says: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33).

And someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and brothers,” etc. The Word is within; the light is within. Hence elsewhere: “That those who enter,” he says, “may see the light” (Luke 8). Therefore, if even his parents standing outside are not acknowledged—and perhaps are not acknowledged for our example—how would we be acknowledged if we stood outside? For his own relatives standing outside wish to see the Lord when the Jews, not seeking the spiritual sense in the Law, fixed themselves outside upon the observance of the letter; and, as it were, compel Christ to come out in order to teach carnal things, rather than consenting themselves to enter in order to learn spiritual things.

Stretching out his hand toward the disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers,” etc. That whoever does the will of God is called the Lord’s sister and brother, on account of both sexes gathered to the faith, is not surprising. But it is very remarkable how such a person is also called mother. For he deigned to call faithful disciples brothers, saying: “Go, announce it to my brothers” (Matt. 28). Therefore, if someone can become the Lord’s brother by coming to faith, it must be asked how that person can also be mother. But we should know that one who is Jesus’ brother and sister by believing becomes his mother by preaching. For one gives birth to the Lord, as it were, by instilling him into the hearer’s heart; and becomes his mother if, through that person’s voice, the love of God is generated in the neighbor’s mind.

## CHAPTER XIII

“On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea, and great crowds were gathered to him,” etc. Not only the Lord’s deeds and words, but also the journeys and places in which he performs miracles and preaches, are full of heavenly mysteries. After the discourse delivered in the house, where he was said to have demons through that wicked blasphemy, he went out and taught beside the sea, to show that, leaving Judaea because of the guilt of unbelief, he would pass over to save the Gentiles. For the hearts of the Gentiles, long proud and unbelieving, are deservedly compared to the swollen and bitter waves of the sea; and who does not know that, through faith, Judaea was the Lord’s house? But, leaving the house in which he had endured the blasphemies of the ungodly, he began to teach beside the sea, because, leaving the synagogue because of its unbelief, he came to gather through the apostles the multitude of the Gentile people. Hence it is fittingly stated beforehand that, while he was preaching in the house, his mother and brothers stood outside, as though they were not acknowledged by him; and thus, departing from the house, he passed over to the sea, to lead them there. For after the synagogue fixed itself outside upon observance of the letter and preferred the figures of the Law to the inward mysteries of the Lord’s faith, the Lord bestowed upon the nations throughout the world the mysteries of salvation which it had despised.

[Col. 1369B] “And great crowds were gathered,” etc. The great crowd gathered to the Lord while he teaches signifies the multitude of peoples flocking to Christ through the preaching of the apostles. That he entered the boat and sat upon the sea signifies that Christ would ascend through faith into the minds of the Gentiles and gather the Church in the sea—that is, in the midst of contradicting nations. In that Church he is said to sit, that is, to reign and rule. But the crowd standing on the shore, which was neither in the sea nor in the boat, bears the figure of those receiving God’s word and already separated by faith from the sea—that is, from the reprobate—yet not yet admitted into the Church through the grace of baptism.

“And he spoke many things to them,” etc. We read in the Gospels that Christ spoke in parables sometimes for punishment, because those who heard God’s mysteries were unworthy to know them. Thus we read of those to whom he is now preaching; for in what follows he says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to others in parables” (Luke 8). At other times he spoke in parables for clarity, so that by known things he might raise the minds of the unlearned to unknown things, showing invisible realities through likenesses. Although the Lord expounds this parable in what follows, each point must nevertheless be explained more clearly. The sower, then, is Christ, who went forth from the bosom of the Father and came into the world to sow the word of God; or he went forth to sow when, leaving Judaea, he passed over through the apostles to the Gentiles.

[Col. 1369D] “And another fell beside the way,” etc. When the word of God is received by people not yet on the way of good works, but who by their will already stand, as it were, beside the way, birds also come—that is, demons, called by Luke “birds of heaven,” either because they are spiritual natures or because they dwell in the air. “And they ate it,” that is, they snatched it away from human minds. According to Luke, it was trampled by people, because it was taken away through the perverse persuasion of the ungodly (Luke 8).

“Another fell on rocky ground,” etc. The rock signifies the hardness of an obstinate mind; the earth, the gentleness of an obedient soul; the sun, the heat of persecution. Therefore the word of God falls on rocky ground when it is received into hard [Col. 1370A] minds, temporarily, in which there is little earth, because for a time they are softened toward desire for heavenly life. But when persecution comes, these withdraw in time of temptation.
