They have no root because they have been trained by no pursuit of discipline, softened by no trials of temptations, nor rooted in charity.

“But another fell among thorns,” etc. The thorns are riches, which prick human minds with many anxieties and draw them back from good work through excessive desire. “But another fell on good soil.” Good soil is the faithful conscience of the elect, which gladly receives the entrusted seed of the word and brings it to fruit; and “one yields a hundredfold,” etc. Three orders of the Church are designated here: married persons and the continent, in the active life and the contemplative life. The principal division of the righteous should be this: some are contemplative and some active. The active are subdivided into married persons and continent persons. The thirtyfold and sixtyfold fruits are given to the active, but the hundredfold to the contemplative, because, as Bede relates, the ancients used to count on the left hand up to the number one hundred. The hundredfold number was transferred to the right hand; hence Juvenal:

> …now the right hand counts the years.

Since the left hand signifies temporal goods and the right hand heavenly goods, according to the words, “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2), the number of the left is deservedly assigned to active persons who lawfully use temporal things. But the number of the right is assigned to contemplatives, who devote themselves solely to heavenly things. The hundredfold number, because it is perfect and signifies heavenly things, suits the contemplative. The thirtyfold, however, which is made from three times ten and is the number of fervent age, is assigned to married persons. They are still in the heat of battle, since they cannot wholly restrain the ardor of lust; yet they are in the faith, signified by three, and observe the commandments of the Law, denoted by ten. The sixtyfold suits continent active persons; it is made from six and ten and is the number of mature and cooling age. Six expresses perfection, because the Lord completed all things in six days, and because six is composed from its divisors; [Col. 1370D] while ten, as stated, signifies the Decalogue. It is therefore deservedly assigned to the continent, who have already subdued the flesh, cooled from temptations, and are found more perfect in works of the Law than married persons.

“He who has ears,” etc. Bede. Whenever this exhortation is inserted, whether in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it indicates that what is said is mystical. The ears for hearing are the ears of the heart.

“And the disciples came,” etc. The disciples, understanding that the things said to the people were obscure, wished to suggest to the Lord that he should not speak in parables. The phrase “coming to him” notes that, although they were in the same boat, they were nevertheless at some little distance from him. He answered them: “Because to you it has been given,” etc. He spoke to the crowds in parables to increase their blindness, because although they followed him to hear his words or see his miracles, they were hard of heart and unwilling to be converted to faith. Thus, by a hidden judgment, the Lord cast them into greater blindness and concealed the mysteries of God from the unworthy.

“For to the one who has, it will be given,” etc. As though he said: To you the mysteries of the kingdom of God are to be revealed—that is, the hidden matters of Scripture are to be opened to you—because you love them and give faith to the things spoken to you. This is what he says: “To the one who has”—understand, faith or love of the divine word—an abundant understanding will be given. But from the one who does not have love for the divine word, even the faith by which he ought to be saved, which he seems to have through natural ability or study of Scripture, will be taken away, so that it benefits him nothing. For no one can clearly understand anything who does not have the beginning of wisdom. “Therefore I speak to them in parables.” He gives the apostles the reason why he spoke parabolically to those crowds: because although they saw Christ’s miracles and heard his preaching, they still refused to believe in him. And this is:

“Because seeing miracles,” etc. They do not see with the eye of the heart—that is, they do not understand that I am God; and although hearing my preaching with outward hearing, they do not hear—that is, they do not grasp with inward understanding. He explains this when he adds: “Nor do they understand.” This is confirmed by Isaiah’s authority, who fittingly prophesied concerning them: “Hearing Christ’s preaching with outward hearing, you shall not understand; and seeing his miracles with outward sight, you shall see but not see inwardly” (Isa. 6).

“Their heart has grown fat,” etc. He gives the reason why they do not understand: namely, their heart has grown fat with pride and hardened with envy, and therefore they have heard with heaviness of ear. Those hear heavily who despise what they hear, and therefore what is proclaimed is burdensome to them. “And they have closed their eyes”: as though he said, they were neither willing to hear from another and learn what they did not know, nor did they open the eyes of their heart by their own understanding and inward attention, so as to understand the things they saw. Therefore they closed them, lest at any time they should see with their eyes. He corresponds each thing to each: “and they have heard with heaviness,” lest at any time they should hear with their ears. What it means to see with the eyes and hear with the ears, he later explains when he says: “and understand with their heart.” One hears with the ear who learns from another; one sees with the eye who understands through oneself; and both are comprehended in the understanding of the heart. “And lest they be converted to repentance, and I heal them,” namely through the remission of sins.

It is asked why, when another Evangelist says, “The Lord blinded their eyes” (John 12), this was done: whether so that they might never see, or so that at some time they might see, despise what they hear, grieve over their blindness, and thus, humbled, repent and seek God. But it is doubtful whether the Lord foresaw them to be so blinded that they would never [Col. 1372A] repent thereafter. What Mark says concerning them, “lest at any time they should be converted and their sins forgiven them” (Mark 4), should it be understood thus: that they had deserved by their sins that they could not understand and repent by their own power? Yet even this was done by God’s mercy, so that they might recognize their sins and merit pardon.

“But blessed are your eyes,” etc. As though he said: The eyes of those who see yet refuse to believe are miserable; but your eyes are blessed, and blessed are your ears. Yet this should not be understood merely of outward sight. For the eyes of the scribes and Pharisees are not blessed, though they saw only the Lord’s body; rather, only those are blessed who recognized his mysteries, of whom it is said: “And you revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11).

“For truly I say to you that many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see, and did not,” etc. It is proof that those are blessed who deserved to see and hear in Christ’s presence what none of the earlier persons, however great their merit, deserved to see, though they greatly desired it. Abraham rejoiced to see Christ’s day; he saw it and was glad. Isaiah likewise, Micah, and many other prophets saw the Lord’s glory, and for that reason were also called seers. But they saw from afar, and as though greeting it through a mirror and in an enigma. The apostles, however, having the Lord present with them, eating with him, and learning whatever they wished by asking, had no need at all to be taught through angels or diverse forms of visions.

“But you,” etc. As though he said: Since it was not given to such persons to know the kingdom of God, you to whom the mysteries of heaven are entrusted, understand the parable.

“Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand,” etc. It must be construed thus: Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom—that is, my preaching, which avails for attaining the kingdom of heaven—and does not understand. But how such a person does not understand, he adds parenthetically: “For the evil one comes,” that is, the devil, “and snatches away what was sown in their heart.” Every person who is such is the one sown beside the way. It should be noted that “sown” is understood in different ways. Both the seed is said to be sown and the field to be sown, and both usages occur here. Where he says, “he snatches away what was sown,” it must be understood of the seed. But where he continues, “he was sown beside the way,” it must be understood not of the seed but of the place of the seed—that is, of the person, who is like a field sown and made fruitful by the seed of the divine word. The rest that follows has been explained above.

“He set another parable before them, saying: ‘The kingdom has become like …’” It should be known that then, after explaining the preceding parable to the apostles, he turned again to the crowds, as is noted in what follows. “Jesus spoke all these things in parables to the crowds”: the literal sense is plain. The moral application, however, is as follows. [Col. 1373A] Through this parable we are urged, if we apply diligence, to strive to possess good will, caution, patience, discernment, long-suffering, and justice; all of which are distinctly found in their respective places in the parable. Where he says, “He sowed good seed,” he calls for the good will found in the elect. Where he says, “The enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat and went away,” he wished to intimate that caution must be exercised. When, after hearing that the tares were growing, he did not blaze into anger but patiently said, as it were, “An enemy has done this,” he commended patience to us. Again, when the servants wished to gather them for burning and he said, “No, lest perhaps in gathering you uproot the wheat with them,” he gave us an example of discernment. When he added, “Let both grow until the harvest,” he wished to commend long-suffering. Finally, he commended justice when he said: “At the time of harvest I will say to the reapers: Gather the tares and bind them into bundles to burn.” But the allegory is as follows.

Augustine. “While people were sleeping, the enemy came,” etc. That is, while the rulers of the Church acted negligently, or when the apostles underwent the sleep of death, the enemy came and oversowed those whom the Lord interprets as evil children. But it is rightly asked whether these are heretics or badly living Catholics. Heretics too can be called evil children, because, begotten from the same seed of the Gospel and the name of Christ, they turn through perverse opinions toward false doctrines. But since he says that they were sown among the wheat, they seem to signify those who share one communion.

Nevertheless, since the Lord interpreted the field itself not as the Church but as this world, heretics are rightly understood: not united with the good by membership in one Church or one faith, but mingled with them in this world by association in the Christian name alone. But those who are evil while remaining in the same faith should rather be counted as chaff than as tares, because chaff shares with wheat even the same foundation and a common root. In that net which encloses both good and bad fish, badly living Catholics are not unreasonably understood. For the sea, which more particularly signifies this world, is one thing; the net, which seems to signify communion in one faith or one Church, is another. The difference between heretics and bad Catholics is that heretics believe false things, whereas the latter believe true things but do not live as they believe. But enough of these. It follows:

“But when the blade had grown and produced fruit, then the tares appeared,” etc. For when a person begins to be spiritual, judging all things, then errors can appear to that person and the corrupt doctrines of heretics become evident. When these appeared, the servants said to him:

“Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where, then, are the weeds from?” We must consider whether these are the servants whom he later calls reapers. But who would dare say that the reapers—that is, the angels—did not know who had sown the weeds, and that the weeds first became visible to them when the blade had borne fruit? It is therefore more fitting to understand that the faithful people themselves are signified by the name of servants, whom he also calls good seed. For he does not say, “At harvest time I shall say to you: Gather the weeds first,” but, “I shall say to the reapers.” Hence the duties of servants are understood to be different from those of reapers. For the servants do not possess as great a power of discernment as the latter. This is also why the servants say: “Do you wish, then, that we go and gather them?” To them Truth itself, which patiently bears with all, replies: “No, lest perhaps, while you uproot the weeds, you uproot the wheat with them.” In this he teaches that a human being is not so situated in this life as to be able to know with certainty what each person, whose error he presently sees, will later become, or what contribution that person’s error may make to the growth of the good. He therefore says that such people are not yet to be removed from this life, lest, while they try to kill the wicked, they kill the good—who may perhaps become good—or harm those good people to whom they may perhaps be useful even unwillingly. But this is to be done fittingly then, when at the end there remains no further time either for worldly life or for advancement in virtue through the occasion of another’s error.  

The question is therefore asked: why are certain heretics excommunicated by bishops and separated from the Church, while some are even killed by secular authorities? But the matter here is not excommunication, since it was given for the correction of people, but the common separation from the field—that is, from the world. For bishops ought not to kill, that is, separate from the world, just as Peter and the other apostles, when they were not received in a certain [Col. 1374C] city, asked the Lord whether they should call down fire from heaven and destroy them. And the Lord said: “You do not know what spirit you are of” (Luke 9). And although some, already judged, convicted, and overthrown, are put to death by secular power for the correction of others, nevertheless no universal separation of the wicked is to be made, because few good people would remain, and this is a time of change: those who are evil today will be good tomorrow.  

It may also be asked why he says later, “Bind them into bundles,” rather than into one bundle or one heap of weeds. Perhaps this is said because of the diversity of heretics, who differ not only from the wheat but even from one another. Therefore the binding into bundles will take place at the end, so that each may be punished not indiscriminately but according to the measure [Col. 1374D] of his perversity. But what follows—“Gather the wheat into the barn”—is to be understood thus: after those who followed divisions and schisms have been punished, those who loved the unity of charity are received and kept in the heavenly barn.

“Another parable,” etc. A parable is a comparison drawn from unlike things, that is, a comparative likeness, because in that comparative likeness it displays figures of speech and images of truth. He heaps parables upon parables in order to produce, through the multitude of figures in them, a greater blinding.

“The kingdom of heaven is like,” etc. The present Church is called the kingdom of heaven; it is compared by various figures, not according to its whole self, but according to some part of itself. Here it is likened to a mustard seed in respect of [Col. 1375A] faith, which a man—that is, Christ—sowed in a field, that is, in the hearts of believers. It is the least of all seeds. For our faith appears more worthless than all philosophical teachings. What indeed was judged more foolish by the wise of this world than to believe in one who was killed and buried, to despise visible things, and to long for invisible ones? The other seeds, namely the books of philosophers, seem to excel, because they treat with subtlety of the greatest matters and are adorned with rhetorical composition. Yet, as the Apostle says, “what is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1). Therefore, when it grows in the mind of the one who receives it and is exalted throughout the whole world, it appears greater than all herbs and becomes a tree, so that, etc. Philosophical sciences are indeed herbs, but they do not attain the strength of usefulness for anyone, and therefore they readily wither from their own vanity. The branches of this tree are the many parts of faith, in which the birds of heaven—that is, the souls of the faithful—delight and feed, flying heavenward on the wings of virtues. Hence it is said: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly and be at rest?” (Ps. 54).

“He spoke another parable to them. The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal,” etc. Here the Church, according to one part of itself—that is, according to the ardour of charity—is compared with leaven, which a woman takes and hides in measures of meal. A *satum* is a unit of measure, according to the custom of the province of Palestine, holding one and a half *modii*. The three measures are the three virtues indicated where it is said: [Col. 1375C] “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Deut. 6); or they signify the three classes of people expressed above by the hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit. Or they signify all believers gathered from the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe. Or those descended from Noah’s three sons. The woman is the wisdom of God, who hides in us the leaven, that is, the ardour of charity, and deposits his grace in us, by which our hearts are leavened, that is, set ablaze with love of God.

“All these things he spoke in parables to the crowds,” etc. “That what was spoken through the prophet David might be fulfilled: ‘I shall open my mouth in parables’” (Ps. 77). It is as though he said: “I who formerly spoke through the prophets shall now, in my own person, open my mouth in parables and utter forth”—that is, from the treasury of my secret counsel I shall bring forth in my preaching—“mysteries hidden from the foundation of the world.” The remaining matters that follow, concerning the interpretation of the weeds, have been explained above. Let us therefore pass on to the other parables.

“The kingdom of heaven is like,” etc. He who above spoke parabolically to the crowds for their blinding also speaks to the apostles in parables, not for blinding but for edification, and in order to teach them to speak in parables. Hence Gregory says: “The kingdom of heaven is said to be like earthly things so that, from those things which the mind knows, it may rise to those unknown things which it does not know; thus, by the example of visible things, it may be drawn to invisible things.” [Col. 1376A] In this connection it should be noted that the treasure of the mind is hidden in order to be preserved. For one who does not hide the pursuit of heavenly desire from human praise cannot sufficiently guard it from malicious spirits. In this present life we are as though on a road by which we journey to our homeland. But malicious spirits, like robbers, lie in wait for our journey. Thus, whoever carries a treasure openly on the road desires to be plundered. I say this not so that our neighbours may not see our works, since it is written, “Let them see your good works” (Matt. 5), but so that we may not seek outward praise for what we do; thus the work may be public, while the intention remains hidden. The treasure, therefore, as we have said, is heavenly desire; and the field in which the treasure is hidden is the discipline of heavenly pursuit. Those who renounce pleasures of the flesh and trample earthly desires through the keeping of heavenly discipline certainly purchase this field by selling all they possess.

Or otherwise: this treasure is the word of God, in which are all treasures of wisdom; it is hidden in human flesh. Again: the treasure hidden in the field is the two Testaments of the law in the Church. When someone reaches them in part through understanding, he senses that great things lie hidden there; and he goes, sells all that he has, and buys that field—that is, through contempt for temporal things he obtains leisure for himself.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls,” etc. It is as though he said: The question is whether the plural number has passed into the singular: when the man seeks fine pearls, he finds [Col. 1376C] one precious pearl, which, after selling all he has, he buys. Either this man, seeking good people with whom he may live profitably, finds one above all others without sin—the mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus—or, seeking commandments by serving which he may conduct himself rightly among people, he finds love of neighbour, in which the Apostle says all things are contained. The individual pearls are: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” and the other such commands, which are contained in this saying: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” Or otherwise: the person seeks these understandings and finds him in whom all are contained, namely: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” Again, he says that the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant who seeks fine pearls but finds one precious pearl; on finding it, he sells all things and buys it, because whoever has come, insofar as he can, to know perfectly the sweetness of heavenly life willingly leaves behind the things he loved on earth, and in comparison with it all things become worthless. He abandons what he possesses, scatters what he has amassed, and his mind burns only for heavenly things.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea,” etc. The net is the Church entrusted to fishers, that is, to preachers. It draws fish from the sea—that is, people from the world—and this from every class: free and slave, rich and poor, strong and weak. Hence the Psalmist says: “All flesh shall come to you” (Ps. 64). “When it was full, they drew it out and sat down beside the shore.” As the sea signifies the age, [Col. 1377A] so the shore signifies the end of the age. It will then be full when all the elect are completed in God’s predestination. Those who draw it out and choose are the angels, who will draw out the good through resurrection and choose them by separating them from the wicked; they will place them in vessels, that is, in eternal dwellings, but cast the wicked outside. They are said to sit because sitting belongs to a judge; and in a sense they will judge, as they carry out the whole mystery of judgment, consigning the wicked to punishments and introducing the good into the kingdom.

“Therefore every scribe,” etc. It is as though he said: “Because you understand the mysteries that I reveal to you, I shall make you preachers, and you shall be like me, who am the householder—that is, the Lord Sabaoth, meaning ‘of hosts,’ namely of human beings and angels—who brings from the treasure of my knowledge things new and old,” that is, sayings of the New and Old Testaments. You too will preach in like manner, bringing forth sayings from both Testaments. Or he calls “new and old” the threat of punishment and the promise of heavenly glory, because descent into hell was ancient, while ascent into heaven is new. Thus he preaches the old who threatens the punishment of hell; he announces the new who promises the kingdom of heaven. And this is what he says: “Therefore, because you understand, every learned scribe among you in the kingdom of heaven”—that is, in the present Church—“will be like me, the householder,” etc.

“And it came to pass, when he had finished, that he came into his own country,” that is, Galilee, or more specifically Nazareth. “Whence has this man this wisdom?”—with regard to teaching—[Col. 1377C] “and these mighty works?”—with regard to miracles. “Is not this the carpenter’s son?”

Bede. They taunt him with the reproach of his father’s trade, though he was truly the son of a carpenter, begotten by the supreme maker of all things; and he refines human beings with fire when he baptizes them in the Holy Spirit and fire. He also fashions vessels of different kinds and, by softening with the fire of the Spirit vessels of wrath, changes them into vessels of mercy.

“Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?” The brothers of the Lord are not to be thought, with Helvidius, to be sons of the blessed Mary, nor, with certain others, sons of Joseph by another wife; but rather they are sons of that Mary who is called the mother of James the Less, Joseph, and Jude. Among the Jews, however, relatives are customarily called brothers, not only those related in the degree of brothers and sisters, who are also very commonly called brothers among us, but even an uncle and a sister’s son, as Jacob and Laban are found to be called brothers. But Jesus said: “A prophet is not without honour except in his own country.” That the Lord Jesus is called a prophet in the holy Scriptures is attested by Moses, who, foretelling his future incarnation, said to the children of Israel: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, whom you shall hear as you hear me” (Deut. 18). Not only he, who is the head and Lord of the prophets, but Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets were held in less honour in their own country than in foreign cities, because it is almost [Col. 1378A] natural for fellow citizens always to envy fellow citizens.

“And he did not perform many mighty works there because of their unbelief.” This does not mean that he could not have performed mighty works among those unbelievers, but that, by not performing many, he would condemn his unbelieving fellow citizens more severely.

Bede. It may also be understood otherwise. The Lord is despised in his household and in his own country—that is, among the Jewish people—and therefore he performed few signs there, lest they become utterly without excuse. That he did perform some miracles there is known from Mark, who says: “And he could perform no mighty work there, except that he healed a few sick people by laying his hands upon them” (Mark 6).

## Chapter XIV

“At that time Herod the Tetrarch heard the report of [Col. 1378B] Jesus,” etc. The events that Christ performed after the sermon concerning John, which he gave to the people and which the evangelist narrated earlier, took place after John’s death, in the final year of his preaching. He therefore relates John’s death, which he had passed over, in order to connect the other events that occurred after John’s death. It is clear that John was beheaded near Passover, because immediately after Jesus was informed of John’s death, he crossed the sea and performed the miracle of the five loaves and two fish, which indeed occurred near Passover. For John the Evangelist, relating that miracle, says: “The Passover of the Jews was near” (John 2).

“And he said to his servants,” etc. Matthew and Luke seem to differ in these words. Matthew says that this Herod—the son of the other Herod who killed the children—said that John had risen from the dead. But Luke writes of the matter thus: “Herod the Tetrarch heard all that was being done by him, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead; but by others that Elijah had appeared,” etc. (Luke 9). We must therefore understand either that, after this perplexity, he became convinced in his own mind of what was said by others, when he said: “John, whom I beheaded—this man has risen from the dead” (Mark 6); or these words must be pronounced so as to judge him still uncertain. For if he had said, “Can this be?” or, “Can this perhaps be John the Baptist?” there would have been no need to give any instruction about a pronunciation indicating doubt and hesitation. But because those words are absent, they may be pronounced in either way: either we take him as having spoken as one convinced by others’ words, or as still hesitant, as Luke records.

“And therefore,” etc. In every respect they rightly thought concerning the power of resurrection: namely, that the saints, when they rise from the dead, will be of greater power than they were while still burdened by the weakness of flesh. They also taught that the miracle of resurrection itself is not incredible.

“For Herod feared John, and bound him and put him in prison because of,” etc. Since he had spoken of the belief that John had risen without saying anything about his death, he returns and relates how he died. Ancient history recounts that Philip, son of Herod the Great—under whom the Lord fled into Egypt—and brother of this Herod under whom the Lord suffered, had married Herodias, daughter of King Aretas. Later, however, her father, after certain hostilities had arisen against his son-in-law, took back his daughter and, to grieve her former husband, joined her in marriage to his enemy. The evangelist Luke teaches more fully who this Philip was: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, while Philip his brother was tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis” (Luke 3). Therefore John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, rebuked Herod and Herodias with the same authority with which Elijah had rebuked Ahab and Jezebel: they had contracted an unlawful marriage, and it was not lawful to take the wife of one’s brother while that brother was alive. He preferred to risk danger [Col. 1379B] with the king rather than, through flattery, forget the Lord’s commandments.

“And wishing to kill him, he feared the people, because they regarded him as a prophet,” etc. Here Matthew and Mark seem to differ. Mark reports that Herod heard him gladly: “For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just man.” But it should be understood that he wished one thing and pretended another. For though he wished to kill him, he feared the people. Thus he frequented him, testing whether he might somehow turn him away from rebuking himself.

“But on his birthday,” etc. Herod is not excused because he committed murder unwillingly and reluctantly on account of an oath, for perhaps he swore precisely in order to prepare devices for a future opportunity. Otherwise, if she had asked for the death of his father or mother, would he have done it because of the oath? What he would have rejected in himself, he ought to have scorned in the case of a prophet.

“When she had gone out, she said to her mother,” etc. Herodias, fearing that Herod might someday come to his senses or become reconciled to his brother Philip, and that the unlawful marriage might be dissolved by repudiation, urged her daughter to ask at once, during the very banquet, for John’s head. A fitting reward of blood for the fitting work of dancing.

“And the king was grieved; but because of the oath, and those who reclined with him, he ordered it to be given,” etc.

Bede. It is the custom of Scripture for the historian to recount the opinion of many as it was believed by people at that time. Thus Joseph is called the father of Jesus even by Mary herself; likewise Herod is now said to have been [Col. 1379D] grieved because this was what those reclining at table thought. For this dissembler of his own mind and contriver of murder displayed sadness on his face while holding joy in his mind; he excuses his crime by an oath, so that under the pretext of piety he might be impious. And when it adds, “and because of those reclining with him,” it seeks to make all of them accomplices in his crime, lest bloody dishes be served at a wanton and impure banquet.

John bears the figure of the Law. Herod signifies the Jewish people, who joined to themselves as though a wife the unbelief of the Gentile people, born from the same parent. Because John, as the Law, forbids this unbelief, he is held shut up and is not permitted to give voice. Finally, at Herod’s birthday—that is, at the fulfillment of natural pleasure—the daughter dances: that is, depraved pleasure arising from unbelief exults; and she asks that John’s head be added to her delights—that is, that Christ be removed from the understanding of the Law. It is therefore brought by the daughter to the mother, because through depraved will satisfaction is given to unbelief. When this is done, John’s disciples—that is, the hearers of the Law—bury John’s body: that is, they extinguish within themselves the carnal observances. Thus, coming from the Law to the Gospel, they become attentive hearers of the word of God. Even to this day, however, we see in the head of John the prophet that the Jews have lost Christ, who is the head of Jews and prophets.

Otherwise: John’s beheading indicates the diminution of John’s renown, by which he was believed by the people to be Christ, just as the Lord’s exaltation on the cross signifies the pre-eminence of our faith. Thus John was diminished in head, while the Lord was exalted on the cross, because, as John himself says, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3). Josephus relates that John was brought in chains to the fortress of Machaerus and there beheaded. Ecclesiastical History relates that he was buried in Sebaste, a city of Palestine formerly called Samaria; and that, in the time of Emperor Julian, hostile to Christians who frequented his tomb with devout care, pagans attacked the monument, scattered the bones across the fields, gathered them again and burned them with fire, and scattered them anew over the land. Monks from Jerusalem were present there at that time; mingling with the pagans who were gathering the bones, they collected the greater part of them and carried them to their father Philip at Jerusalem. He sent them to blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and they were preserved there until the time of Theophilus, bishop of the same city. Then, by order of Emperor Theodosius, when the temples of all the nations were destroyed, the temple of Serapis was cleansed of its filth; a basilica was erected there in place of the shrine of Serapis and consecrated in honour of Saint John. Read the eleventh book of *Ecclesiastical History*.

“When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there by boat into a deserted place apart,” etc. On hearing of the death of his Baptist, the Saviour withdrew into a deserted place. This was not, as some say, from fear of death, but in sparing his enemies, lest they add murder to murder; and so that he might give us an example of avoiding the recklessness of those who surrender themselves, since not all who offer themselves to be tortured persevere with the same steadfastness in torments. Hence elsewhere he commands: “When they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10). But after the head of the prophet had been cut off by the Jews and the kings of the Jews, and the prophet lost among them his tongue and voice, Jesus, awaiting the fitting time, withdrew into a deserted place and taught separately, because, having left Judaea, he passed over to the wilderness of the Gentiles.

“And when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the cities,” etc. They did not travel in beasts or vehicles but with the labour of their own feet, to show the ardour of their minds. Mystically, when the Gentiles heard Christ’s preaching, they followed him with the steps of faith; abandoning the old ways of their former manner of life, they went out, as it were, from the cities.

[Col. 1381A] “And going out, he saw a crowd,” etc. That going forth signifies that the crowds had the will to come but not the strength to arrive. Therefore the Saviour goes out to meet them, as though responding to their desires. “And he had compassion on them.” The Lord has compassion when he inspires his grace in believers and calls them through preachers. He heals the sick when he forgives the sins in the souls of those who are ill.

“When evening came, the disciples came to him and said: ‘The place is deserted and the hour has already passed,’” etc. It is evident that when the disciples said such things, they were ignorant of the coming miracle. Mystically, he came from Judaea into the wilderness of the Gentiles, as was said, and this “when evening came,” that is, at the end of the ages. For the time of grace is called the end of the world, because there are three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace; and the period of grace is reckoned the last. Or “when evening came,” that is, after the Lord’s passion had been accomplished, when the sun of righteousness set through death, Christ passed through preachers to the Gentiles.

It should be noted that John inserts certain words here. For he says that Christ said to Philip:

“Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?” (John 5).

It should be understood that the disciples first approached the Lord and asked him to dismiss the crowds, as Matthew relates; then Christ looked upon the crowds and afterwards spoke to Philip, as John records, while the others omit it. But what Philip answers in John—“Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not enough for them” (John 6)—Mark records as an answer from the disciples, intending it to be understood that Philip answered from the mouth of all the other disciples.

Mystically, however, the disciples approach Jesus and say, “The place is deserted,” when the preachers in the primitive Church marvel at the conversion of the Gentiles, almost despairing that they can thereafter convert to the faith those who had remained so long in idolatry and without the Law. Therefore they say, “The place is deserted,” because the Gentile world is without Law and without any knowledge of God; and “the hour has already passed,” because they remained in blindness until the end of the age. “Dismiss the crowds, then; do not proclaim the word of truth to them in vain, so that they may go into the towns”—that is, the fortifications of philosophical opinions, which are as though defended by many arguments—“and buy, at the cost of study and labour, food,” that is, doctrines in whose nourishment they delight. But Jesus said to them: “They have no need to go,” that is, they have no need to seek various foods and abandon me, the heavenly bread, in order to seek unknown breads.

“Give them yourselves something to eat,” etc. He calls the apostles to the breaking of bread, that is, to the opening of the Scriptures. “They answered him,” etc. “We have here only five loaves and two fish.” The five loaves signify the five books of Moses, which are rightly called barley loaves by another Evangelist, because barley is food for beasts. For only coarse and rough commandments were given to the untrained Jews. “The natural man does not receive the things of God.” Yet in barley lies hidden the kernel of the sweetest meaning, which is to be given to perfected believers. By the two fish we understand the prophecies and the Psalms. For the whole Old Testament is completed in these three. Hence after the resurrection the Lord says that everything had to be fulfilled which was written concerning him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms. “He said to them: ‘Bring them here to me.’” It is as though he says mystically: “Know that the meaning of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms is to be referred to me.”

“And he ordered the crowd to recline on the grass,” etc. By ordering the crowd to recline on the grass, he mystically taught that the flesh must be trampled down through the practice of abstinence. “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. 40). But when another Evangelist says that some reclined in groups of fifty and others in groups of a hundred (Mark 6), he intended to signify the diverse gatherings of church members, which nevertheless form one Catholic Church. The rest of Jubilee indeed signifies the mystery of the number fifty; and fifty is doubled to arrive at a hundred. Thus one first rests from evil action, so that afterwards the soul may rest more fully in thought. Some recline by fifties and others by hundreds because some have rest of action from wicked deeds, while others have rest of mind from perverse thoughts.

“Having received the five loaves,” etc. When the crowds were hungry, the Saviour did not create new foods but blessed what the disciples had, because, coming in the flesh, he did not preach things other than those foretold, but showed how pregnant with the mysteries of grace were the writings of the Law and the Prophets. He looks toward heaven in order to teach that the mind’s gaze must be directed there and that the light of knowledge must be sought there. He breaks the bread and distributes it through the disciples to be set before the crowds, because he disclosed the mysteries of prophecy to holy teachers, who preach these things with their whole heart; and, while they ministered, all ate and were satisfied. They ate when they understood; they were satisfied when, according to their capacity, they had complete understanding in these things.

“And they took up twelve baskets full of fragments left over.” What are those fragments except things which the people could not eat? Thus certain more hidden meanings are understood which the multitude [Col. 1382D] cannot grasp. What remains, then, except that those more hidden meanings which the people cannot grasp should be entrusted and committed to those fit for understanding and for teaching others, such as the apostles were? Hence twelve baskets were filled, because the number twelve customarily signifies the sum of every kind of perfection. The whole choir of spiritual teachers is rightly represented by twelve baskets full of fragments, because they are commanded, through meditation, to gather the obscure things of Scripture which crowds cannot understand by themselves, and to preserve for their own use and that of the crowds what they have meditated upon and committed to writing. They are despised outwardly, indeed, but inwardly heaped with saving food to nourish humble hearts. Why are the baskets said to be full of fragments? For it is well known that servile tasks are customarily done with baskets. Christ, who filled baskets with fragments, chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong.

“The number of those who ate was five thousand.” It should be noted that two feedings are read in Matthew: this one, in which five thousand people are said to be refreshed with five loaves, and another in which four thousand are said to be satisfied with seven loaves. For there are two kinds of people in the Church: the active and the contemplative. This feeding seems to belong to the active, the other to the contemplative; hence five thousand people are fittingly said to have been here. They are granted the lawful use of outward things, which are subject to the five senses, provided that they use worldly things well and perfectly; that perfection is signified by five thousand. Therefore, because in the old Law permission is granted to possess worldly goods, those eating are instructed through the five books of Moses, as though through legal commandments. According to this interpretation they are fittingly said to recline on grass, so that riches may be understood by the grass and they may rule over them as things placed beneath themselves while possessing them. But four thousand people were fed with seven loaves because, as though instructed by evangelical commandments, they strive to sell all that they have, give to the poor, and neglect temporal things. The seven loaves signify evangelical teaching because the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is contained in it. There is no mention of grass there because they have entirely renounced worldly things. All this will be discussed more fully there; here it is enough to have shown why there were five thousand.

[Col. 1383C] “Besides women and children.” It is as though he said: the perfected active persons were fed, and with them also other weaker persons. Some are women—that is, soft and given to vices—and others are children—that is, weak in faith and not yet fit for battle; yet all alike hear the words of preaching.

“And immediately he ordered the disciples to get into the boat,” etc. John relates that, after the people saw the miracle of the loaves, they wished to seize Christ and make him king. Therefore Christ commanded the disciples to cross the water, while he himself fled alone to the mountain to pray (John 6). In this he gave us an example that, in the good things we do, we should avoid the recompense of human favour; refusing offered prosperity, we should turn to prayer and fix our hope on high. Not everyone who prays ascends a mountain. For there is prayer that produces sin. But one who prays well, who seeks God in prayer, ascends the mountain as he advances from earthly things to things above. But one who anxiously prays concerning riches or an enemy’s death lies among low things and sends worthless prayers to God. The Lord prays, not in order to entreat for himself, but to obtain things for us.

But the question is asked: how can Matthew report that the disciples crossed to the land of Gennesaret, while Mark, speaking more precisely, says that they crossed to Bethsaida, which is near the lake of Gennesaret, when Luke seems to say that that memorable miracle and heavenly feeding occurred in the regions of Bethsaida? For he says: “Taking them, he withdrew apart into a deserted place which is Bethsaida. When the crowds learned this, they followed him; and he received them” (Luke 9), followed by the rest up to the completion of that history of sacred feeding. But perhaps we should understand, in Luke’s phrase “into a deserted place which is Bethsaida,” not the vicinity of the city itself, but the desert places belonging to it. For Mark clearly says that they were to go ahead of him into Bethsaida, where the boundaries of the city itself are certainly marked. But Luke, who says not “into a deserted place which is Bethsaida” but “which is of Bethsaida,” may rightly, I think, be understood as intending not the city itself but its desert region, that is, a place belonging to its territory. The Evangelist John relates that the crowds ate bread near [Col. 1384B] Tiberias and that, having boarded the boat, the disciples came across the sea to Capernaum. Both are cities in Galilee by the lake of Gennesaret, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias after the city of Tiberias.

“But when evening came,” etc. The disciples’ labour signifies the labour of the Church; the movement of the waves, the movement of persecutions; the sea, the world; the wind, the breath of the devil; and the boat, the Church. Christ is said to be alone—that is, separated from the Church—and he appears also to have abandoned it when he permits it to be in tribulation. The storm is rightly said to occur in the evening, because when the Church is in tribulation, it is as though in night, and the sun of righteousness is said to have hidden himself from her.

In the fourth watch of the night, etc. The military stations [Col. 1384C] and watches divide the intervening hours. Therefore, when he says that the Lord came to them in the fourth watch of the night, he shows that they had been endangered throughout the entire night, and that help was given them at the night’s end. As day approached, the Lord came walking upon the sea, because when human frailty considers the weakness of its own powers, it sees around itself nothing but darkness and the constricting pressures of enemies. But when it raises its mind toward divine protection, it sees, as it were, amid the darkness the rising of daylight. Note that the first watch is *conticinium* [the quiet of night], the second *intempestum* [the dead of night], the third cockcrow, and the fourth daybreak. The Lord came to them, signifying that after much tribulation he visits his Church; he walks upon the sea while he calms the persecutions of the world.

[Col. 1384D] And seeing him, they thought him a phantom, etc. Heretics say that, if a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom. If Christ had a phantom body, why do the disciples fear that he is a phantom? And they cried out in fear. For the Church is often placed in such distress that it cries to the Lord: “Why have you forsaken me? And why do I go mourning while my enemy afflicts me?” (Ps. XLI). But he comforts them, saying: “Take courage, for I am.” For when, at first, a true deliverance is not yet believed by those who fear, this is signified by the phantom, and therefore they cry out. At last it is made known to them that they are truly delivered; that is what is meant by saying, “I am.” In the literal sense, he says “I am” in order to remove despair and the notion [Col. 1385A] of a phantom. He does not add who he is, because they could sufficiently recognize him from his well-known voice; or because he is the one who says, “He who is sent me to you,” and of whom it is said, “I am who I am” (Exod. III).

But Peter answered and said, etc. The sacramental meaning concerning Peter considered in himself is one thing, and the figure another. For the same reality is often expressed through different figures. Here, therefore, Peter bears the same person as did the boat above: namely, the person of the Church in distress. Thus the Church says: “If you are that true deliverer—as indeed you are—command me to come to you.” For the Church always desires to come to the Lord. She adds, “upon the waters,” as though saying: “Make me, after your example, overcome the pressures of the world.” To one desiring to come, he says, “Come,” because he always brings help to everyone who asks.

[Col. 1385B] And descending, etc. Let one who thinks that the Lord’s body was not real because he walked upon the waters answer how Peter walked, whom they cannot deny to have been a true human being. Mystically, the boat, which above signified the Church, represents human assistance, because a ship is a human instrument for crossing to the nations. Peter descends from the boat when the Church, setting aside every human aid and humbling herself, flees to God alone. Through this she is enabled to tread underfoot the tribulations of this world, so as to come to Jesus—that is, to be conformed to him. But seeing the strong wind, he was afraid. Behold, lest Peter should literally become proud, as though equal to the Lord, the Lord sent him a wind to frighten him and make him recognize human frailty. He is permitted to fear and to sink, so that help may be more welcome after fear.

[Col. 1385C] Likewise, he permits the Church to stagger in persecution, so that he may show her her weakness and be invoked by her more earnestly. To him as he cries out, he extends the hand of help and rebukes him in his tribulation, saying: “O you of little faith.”

And when he had entered the boat, etc. Now he returns to the earlier figure, because the whole matter concerning Peter was, as it were, another figure inserted in between. When above he had said, “I am”—that is, when he had comforted his Church—he entered the boat, that is, the Church. For as long as he allowed his Church to be harassed, he seemed to be absent; but when tranquillity was given to the Church, he seemed to have drawn near, and then the wind of tribulation ceased. Those who were in the boat [Col. 1385D] are to be understood either as the sailors or as the apostles. In the same manner, once peace has been restored to her, the Church worships God in thanksgiving.

And when they had crossed over, etc. *Genezar* is interpreted “garden,” and therefore signifies paradise. Rightly, after shipwreck and navigation upon the sea, they arrive at the shore of Gennesaret, because after the persecutions of the world and the course of this present life, the Church will arrive at the delight of paradise. And when they recognized him, etc. BEDE: They recognized him by report, not by sight. Or certainly because of the greatness of the signs he performed among the people, and because his face was known to many. But see how great was the faith of the people of the land of Gennesaret: they are not content merely with the healing of those present, but send to the surrounding towns so that all may run to the physician.

[Col. 1386A] The people of Gennesaret are said to signify the Gentiles. For Gennesaret is, by another interpretation, called something like “producing a breeze.” But paganism produced the mist of manifold errors. Having heard the preaching, they bring all who are ill—that is, those entangled in various sins. And they begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment, etc. The garment signifies Christ’s incarnation, with which divinity was clothed. The fringe signifies the preaching concerning Christ’s incarnation which hangs from it. The Gentiles do not touch the garment, because they did not see the presence of the flesh; but they touch the fringe, because they received the preaching of the incarnation and were saved through faith.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 1386B] Then they approached Jesus, etc. The less learned people of Gennesaret believe; but those who seem wise come for battle, according to that saying: “You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI). “Why do your disciples, etc.?” Wonderful is the folly of the scribes and Pharisees, which supposes that the Son of God is subject to their traditions.

“For they do not wash, etc.” BEDE: The Jews had many washings which were not in the Law. Taking carnally the spiritual words of the prophets—which commanded them concerning the correction of heart and deed, saying, “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I), and “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII)—they observed them as though they concerned washing the body alone. In vain do all Jews wash their hands and observe their baptisms so long as they despise being washed in the font of the Savior.

[Col. 1386C] Therefore, understanding carnally that salvation spoken of by the prophet, they observed that commandment in washing hands and body, and thus decreed that one should eat only after washing one’s hands. But he answered and said to them:

“Why do you also transgress, etc.?” BEDE: The Lord refutes a false accusation with a true answer. Since you despise the commandments of the Lord for the sake of human traditions, why do you judge that my disciples ought to be rebuked because they disregard the commands of the elders, in order to keep God’s ordinances—since, by fulfilling spiritually the prophet’s washing, they remove the stain of deeds and thoughts? For God said.

[Col. 1386D] He shows how they transgress the Lord’s commandment through their tradition. God had commanded in the Law that father and mother be honored. But the Pharisees, serving avarice, so that people might offer gifts in the Temple which would come into their own use, interpreted the honor due to a father as requiring that God be honored with gifts. Thus they said that one’s earthly parents ought to be set aside under the name of piety. And this is what God said:

“Honor your father and mother.” This honor in the Scriptures is understood not so much as the rendering of greetings and services, but as almsgiving and the bestowal of gifts. Hence the Apostle says: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. V). Here “honor” means a gift. And elsewhere: “The elders are to be honored with double honor” [Col. 1387A] (1 Tim. V), as if he said: They are to be given not only services but also gifts. “But whoever curses father or mother,” by withholding from them their due support, “shall surely die.”

But you say to the children of certain parents: “Young men, vow offerings from your goods, however poor you may be. If you cannot both feed your parents and make an offering to God, disregard your parents and vow your possessions to God. And if your father wishes to receive your goods, say that you have vowed them to God.” And this is: “Whoever”—that is, whichever one of you, young men—“shall say,” that is, may be able to say or does say, to a father or mother wishing to take your possessions: “O father, will the gift which has already been dedicated to God by me benefit you?”—said by way of surprise, that is, would it pass into your use? Certainly you ought not take it,

[Col. 1387B] lest you become guilty of sacrilege. Or thus: “The gift which I offer to God will benefit both me and you; and therefore you ought not take my goods for your own use, but allow me to offer them to God.” Or, by ellipsis: “Whoever says to his father, etc.”—understand: “will perform God’s commandment,” or “will fulfill the Law,” or “will be worthy of eternal life.” And so, through these persuasions serving your avarice, that young man will not honor his father or mother. Therefore you have made void the commandment of God because of your traditions. It follows:

“And he shall not honor his father or mother.” As though he said: Yet you persuaded the children to what is most wicked; and because you persuaded them of this, the child afterward did not honor father or mother. Thus you made void God’s commandment concerning the support of parents because of your tradition [Col. 1387C]—that is, serving your own avarice.

“Hypocrites!” That is, most evil pretenders, who feign what they are not, after the manner of a theatrical mask. Isaiah rightly and fittingly prophesied of you in accordance with your conduct, saying: “This people honors me with their lips” (Isa. XXIX), etc. Isaiah indeed foresaw the Jews’ pretense: that they would oppose the Gospel deceitfully. They also honored him with their lips when they said, “Teacher, we know that you are true” (Matt. XXII), etc. Or again, by commending outward purity they honored him; but because they lacked the inward purity which is true, their heart was far away, and such honor is useless to them. Hence it follows: “In vain do they worship me,” because they will not have reward with true teachers, teaching [Col. 1387D] the doctrine and commandments of human beings while despising divine precepts.

And having called the crowds to him, he said to them: “Hear, etc.” “Not what enters the mouth defiles a person.” Neither does food sacrificed to idols, insofar as it is God’s creature; rather, what defiles is that which comes forth from the mouth—that is, speech expressing the impurity and wickedness of a depraved mind. Hence Augustine: “I do not fear the impurity of food, but of desire.”

Then his disciples came to him, etc. The Pharisees’ great religion concerns foods; having heard this saying, they were scandalized—that is, offended. *Scandalum* is Greek; we may call it an obstacle, a downfall, or a stumbling of the foot. Hence it is said: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble” (Matt. [Col. 1388A] XVIII), that is, whoever gives occasion for a fall, etc. But he answered and said:

“Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted.” This planting signifies the teachers of the Law together with their followers, who did not have Christ as their foundation; therefore they are to be uprooted. It follows: “Leave them alone.” As though he said: Allow them, by their own free choice, to go according to the desires of their heart, because they are beyond recall. Hence Paul: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction” (Tit. III). “They are blind,” that is, deprived of the light of God’s commandments through their traditions, “and are guides of the blind,” who not only fail to provide for themselves but also drag others headlong with them, wandering and sending others into error.

But Peter answered [Col. 1388B] and said: “Explain this parable to us.” What had been said plainly Peter thinks was said parabolically, and in plain words seeks a mystical meaning; therefore he is rebuked by the Lord when it is said: “Are you also still without understanding?” From this we observe that a hearer is at fault if he wishes either to understand obscure matters plainly, or plain statements obscurely. Thus he says: “You are without understanding, since you think that what was said is mystical.” It follows: “Do you not understand that everything which enters the mouth, etc.?” He explains more openly what he had said above: “Not that which enters the mouth, etc.”

But when he said that evil thoughts come out of the heart, it should be noted that the principal seat of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart. By this statement, those are also to be refuted who think that thoughts are injected by the devil rather than arising from one’s own will. The devil can be an assistant and instigator of evil thoughts, but not their author, because he does not know inward things except through certain outward habits and gestures.

[Col. 1388C] For example: if he sees you frequently looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that your heart has been wounded by the dart of love.

And Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. Leaving the scribes and Pharisees, he enters the borders of Tyre and Sidon in order to free the Syrophoenician’s daughter from a demon, and through the faith of a Gentile woman to rebuke the unbelief of the scribes. This is signified by the fact that, after leaving the slanderers, he would go after the resurrection to the Gentiles through preachers. Tyre and Sidon are cities of the Gentiles. It follows: “And behold, a Canaanite woman, etc.”

Here Mark seems to disagree with Matthew. Matthew says that the woman cried after the apostles, when they say, “Send her away, for she cries after us.” Thus it appears possible to understand that she followed them on the road, and that all the words recorded in this Gospel were completed on the road. Mark, however, reports that Christ came into the region of Tyre and Sidon, then entered a certain house, and that there the Canaanite woman asked him concerning her daughter, and that the following words were spoken there. Therefore it should be understood that, as Christ entered the region of Tyre and Sidon, the Canaanite woman came out and cried on the road: “Have mercy on me, Lord”; and that [Col. 1389A] he did not answer her on the road, but that Christ and the woman entered the house silently; thereafter the disciples asked for her, “Send her away,” etc. In all other respects they agree.

“Lord, have mercy, etc.” The Canaanite woman’s great faith is noted here. She believes him to be God when she calls him “Lord,” and human when she names him “son of David.” She believes because she has already gone out from the borders of Gentilism—that is, from its errors. She asks for nothing on the basis of merit, but earnestly seeks only God’s mercy when she says, “Have mercy.” She does not say, “Have mercy on my daughter,” but “Have mercy on me,” because a daughter’s pain is her mother’s. But, in order to move him more strongly to compassion, she recounts the whole suffering, saying:

“My daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.” She exposes the wounds to the physician and shows both the character and the magnitude of the disease: its magnitude when she says “grievously tormented”; its character when she adds “by a demon.”

[Col. 1389B] “But he answered her not a word.” There are many reasons why he did not answer: namely, that by delaying and not answering he might show us the woman’s patience and perseverance. For though she was so often despised and even compared with dogs, nevertheless she accepted everything willingly with patience and humility. He again did not answer so that the disciples might ask for her, thereby showing that their prayers, or those of the saints, are necessary for obtaining something. He does not answer lest he seem contrary to his own statement in which he had said, “Into the way of the Gentiles, etc.” He delays healing in order to prefigure that the salvation of the Gentiles was to be delayed until after the resurrection.

For the Canaanite woman signifies [Col. 1389C] the Church of the Gentiles, which, having gone out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon—that is, from the rites of Gentilism—was burdened by the weight of sins and by the devil’s hunting. For Tyre is interpreted “distress,” Sidon “hunting.” She prays for her daughter—that is, for peoples not yet believing and tormented by the devil. He delays hearing the woman, who was a figure of the Gentiles, thereby signifying that the salvation of the Gentiles would be delayed. Likewise, under the person of this woman, the Church’s faith, humility, and patience are designated: faith, by which she believed that her daughter could be saved; patience, by which she persevered in prayer as often as she was rejected; humility, by which she compares herself not to dogs, but to little dogs.

And his disciples came to him, etc. Behold, the divine silence has its effect, because the apostle Matthew says: “But he answered and said, ‘I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.’” First, that I might preach first to the Jews and afterward to the Gentiles. For preaching was first to be offered to the Jews, to whom the promise had been made; afterward, when it had been rejected by them, it was to be transferred to the Gentiles. Therefore he says: “I was not sent, in my own person and principally, except to the sheep,” that is, the Jews. Yet sometimes, as a prefiguration of the conversion of the Gentiles, he healed some of them on a particular occasion.

[Col. 1389D] But she, etc. “It is not good, etc.” The children are the Jews, begotten and nourished under the worship of the one God through the Law. The bread is the Gospel, miracles, and other things belonging to our salvation. It is therefore not fitting that these be taken from the children and given to the Gentiles,

[Col. 1390A] who are dogs, until the Jews reject them. As though he said: “You Gentiles are unworthy for me to preach to you and perform miracles for you.” He says all this in order to test the woman’s faith. But she replies: “Yes, Lord”—that is, it is true. “Lord, it is not good that you should give us bread, for crumbs suffice us.” And this is: “For even the little dogs do not eat bread, but crumbs,” that is, their masters’ leftovers. As though she said: “The Jews are our masters, who sit at the table of the Scriptures. We are not worthy to sit at the table because we are dogs; but as those beneath them, we would at least have some scraps, such as the healing of my daughter.” Mystically, the dogs—that is, the Gentiles—eat crumbs, that is, inward mysteries; the Jews, however, eat crusts, that is, outward figures.

[Col. 1390B] Then Jesus answered and said to her: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you have asked.” The woman’s faith is proclaimed great by the Lord: first she calls the Savior Son of David; then Lord; finally she worships him as God. She therefore deserved to be told: “Let it be done as you wish.” In healing the centurion’s servant and the Canaanite woman’s daughter without coming to their homes, he signifies the Gentiles, whom he did not come to heal by the presence of his body but by his word.

That the daughter is healed at their request should be understood in reference to the Church, which is both mother and daughter to herself. For all together, of whom the Church consists, are called mother; but each individual among them is also called her child. “And her daughter was healed from that hour.” Because of her humble and faithful speech, the demon left her daughter.

[Col. 1390C] Here an example is given for catechizing and baptizing infants: through the faith and confession of their parents in baptism, little children who are not yet able by themselves to understand or to do anything good or evil are freed from the devil.

And when Jesus had passed on from there. Leaving the borders of the Gentiles, he comes into Judaea, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI). Mystically, the sea beside which Jesus came signifies the troubled and swelling waves of this age, in which the wicked delight like fish in the sea. But that sea became Galilee when they began to pass from vices to virtues.

And ascending the mountain, etc. Because he ascends the mountain, he invites his hearers to higher things. For the Lord is on the mountain; the Word is on high. It should be noted that he speaks not standing but sitting, because he humbled himself in order to speak to us. Human beings would not have understood him shining in his majesty. Or he is said to sit upon the mountain because he taught that a seat—that is, rest—is to be sought in heavenly things.

[Col. 1390D] And they came to him, etc. Since he so humbled himself in the world, many were converted to faith in him. Many do not praise God or confess the faith. The blind are those who do not understand or perceive the way of life. The deaf are those who do not obey, although they understand. The lame are those who fulfill the commandments in part and in part do not fulfill them; or those who are strong in carnal understanding but limp in spiritual understanding. Those who cast them at his feet are the teachers of the Church [Col. 1391A] who humble unbelievers beneath the Lord’s feet. Hence Zechariah: “To direct our feet into the way of peace” (Luke I).

But Jesus, having called his disciples, etc. It should be noted that he first removes infirmities and afterward feeds, because sins must first be removed, and then the soul must be nourished and fed with the word of God. He calls the disciples and tells them what he is about to do, in order to teach the teachers of the Church that they ought to share their counsels with those below them. Thus he says to the disciples: “I have compassion on the crowd, etc.” He has compassion as a human being; he wishes to feed as God.

Mystically, the crowd waits for God for three days because, although it is established in faith in the Holy Trinity, it nevertheless desires to be fed with the bread of the word. He has compassion when he sends preachers. Or it is said to endure the Lord for three days because it is already well established in the light of threefold activity: thought, speech, and good action. Yet it desires to be nourished and satisfied by the divine word.

[Col. 1391B] “And they have nothing to eat, etc.” As though he said: “Therefore it is necessary that I feed them with heavenly doctrine, since without my passion they can do nothing and have nothing from which to be strengthened. Therefore I do not wish to send them away fasting from the food of my preaching and exhortation, lest they fail on the road of this pilgrimage.” Or people endure me for three days—that is, in the present life, which consists of three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. The fourth period remains in the future, where there will be day without night. Therefore the Lord is awaited in the present age until the fourth is reached.

[Col. 1391C] They say to him: “Where are we to get so many loaves in the wilderness as to satisfy so great a crowd?” These words show that the disciples are still inexperienced, since they do not remember that five thousand people were satisfied with five loaves.

MYSTICALLY. The preachers stationed in the wilderness of this world, seeing the Church daily expanding more and more, wonder where so many teachings can be found to satisfy so many thousands. “How many loaves do you have?” He asks not from ignorance, but because he is about to answer by teaching. But they answered: “Seven, and a few little fishes.” Mystically, the Lord answers his preachers who fear that the word of preaching will fail. As though he said: “You wonder where so many thousands can be fed, but do not wonder, because the preaching of the Gospel [Col. 1391D] and the examples of blessed men will be fully sufficient to refresh them.”

Seven loaves are rightly set forth in the mystery of the New Testament, in which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is more fully revealed to all believers as both to be believed and, once believed, given. They are not said to be barley loaves like those five by which five thousand people were fed, so that life-giving nourishment might again, as in the Law, be concealed beneath bodily sacraments. For the kernel of barley is covered by a very tough husk.

The few fishes signify the other Scriptures which we possess besides the New Testament for our edification; or the few perfect faithful of the New Testament who, snatched from the waves of this age, refresh us by instructing us with their example so that we may not fail on the way. And he commanded the crowd to recline upon [Col. 1392A] the ground, etc., because through the Scripture of the New Testament we are commanded not only to tread underfoot desires of the flesh, but also to abandon temporal possessions, signified by the ground.

And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks. He gives thanks in order to show that he rejoices together with humanity’s salvation and to form us to give thanks in temporal matters. He broke the loaves when he opened the sacraments of the figures by which the faithful people were to be nourished. He gave them to the disciples, and the disciples to the people, because evangelical doctrine is ministered to the people through preachers. “And they ate” when they heard the divine word and received it in the mind. “And they were satisfied” when they fulfilled in deed what they heard. “And they took up seven full baskets of the fragments that remained,” etc.

[Col. 1392B] The baskets are preachers, because baskets are made of reeds and are usually woven from palm leaves. Reeds generally grow over water; palm is given to victors. The elect are therefore fittingly compared with vessels of reeds, since they place the root of the heart in the fountain of life lest they wither away from good works. They are also compared with palms because they are conquerors of this world. They are remembered as seven because of the sevenfold grace with which they are filled. The fragments signify the subtlety of God’s mysteries, which the people cannot grasp; and therefore they are entrusted to baskets—that is, reserved for teachers of the Church.

“But there were, etc.” Rightly four thousand people were fed, because they were gathered from the four parts of the world; or through the four Gospels [Col. 1392C] by which they were fed. “Besides little children and women, etc.” By the four thousand we understand the perfect, because one thousand is a perfect number. Little children signify those weak in faith. Women signify those soft and given over to flowing vices, who nevertheless receive preaching among the good.

It should be noted that two feedings are read in the Gospel: one pertains to the active life, the other to the contemplative. In the other, five loaves were ministered under the figure of the Old Testament, in which permission for temporal things is given. In this one, seven loaves were set before the people under the figure of the New Testament, in which it is commanded: “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX). Both feedings were celebrated on a mountain because the Scripture of each Testament, rightly understood, commands us to the height of heavenly precepts and rewards.

[Col. 1392D] In the other, they sat upon grass; in this one, upon the ground. Grass signifies flesh and fleshly desires, according to the saying: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. XL). The ground signifies temporal goods. Thus the active are commanded to tread upon grass—that is, desires of the flesh. The contemplative are commanded to abandon and trample upon the ground—that is, earthly possessions. There five thousand are fed, here four thousand, because the active are subject to the five bodily senses while attending to outward goods. The contemplative, however, are stripped of temporal possessions according to what the Gospel commands; and therefore they are four, as though fed by the doctrine of the four [Col. 1393A] Gospels or adorned with the four principal virtues.

And having dismissed the crowd, he entered the boat and came into the region of Magadan, etc. Here he teaches that preachers, after ministering the word of life to the people, ought themselves to be refreshed within the chamber of the heart by the fruits of virtues. Hence they are rightly said to make for the region of Magadan, which is interpreted “fruits” or “messengers.”

## CHAPTER XVI

And Pharisees and Sadducees came to him, seeking a sign from heaven, etc. They asked in order to test him: that, after the manner of Elijah, he might make fire come down from on high; or, like Samuel, make thunder roar in summertime; or that he who had satisfied many with a few loaves might also send [manna?] from heaven after the example of Moses. Otherwise he would not appear to be perfect and sent from God unless he showed signs from heaven—as though they could not also slander even those signs and say that they happened from hidden and varied conditions of the air.

[Col. 1393B] But he answered and said to them, etc. He rebukes them because, though they appeared to be teachers of the Law and prophets, they could not understand Christ’s coming through prophecy; and though they recognized the character of coming weather from preceding signs, they neglected to recognize from its signs a matter so necessary. This is what he means: “You say that tomorrow will be fair, because at evening you see the sky red; and in the morning you say, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is darkly red’”—that is, the sun appears red. Thus you have known how to discern the face of the sky, but you cannot perceive the signs of the times of my coming.

[Col. 1393C] Mystically, evening, in which the sky is red, signifies Christ’s passion, in which he was reddened by his own blood. The fair weather of the following day signifies the joy of the Lord’s resurrection. Hence David: “Weeping will linger in the evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. XXIX). But when he adds, “In the morning indeed you say, ‘Today there will be a storm, because the sky is darkly red,’” he subtly teaches that, after the joy of the Lord’s resurrection signified by morning, tribulations of his faithful followers would follow. By these it could also in some manner be understood and foreseen that the universal judgment would come.

“A wicked and adulterous generation seeks a sign, etc.” It was wicked in its vices; adulterous in departing through unbelief from Christ, who is the true bridegroom, and adhering to the devil as though to an alien husband. A carnal generation seeks a sign from heaven, and, according to its deserts, no sign from heaven is offered it. Those who were heavenly deserved a sign from heaven, such as the apostles, who saw the Transfiguration on the mountain and beheld him ascending into heaven.
