[Col. 1393D] But to those who were going to put him to death, he wished to show the sign of his death. Jonah signifies Christ, who was dove-like in the simplicity of innocence; for Jonah is interpreted “dove.” The sailors signify the Jews, who delivered him to the sea-monster and to death. The storm signifies the blast of unclean spirits. The sea-monster vomited Jonah out on the third day, and death restored Christ to life on the third day.

“And leaving them, he went away,” etc. Note that it is not read, as in other places, “having dismissed the crowds, he went away”; rather, because the error of unbelief possessed the insolent minds of these people, he did not dismiss them but left them. By this he again signifies that he would leave the Jews and pass to the Gentiles.

[Col. 1394A] “And when his disciples had come across the sea, they forgot to take bread.” Someone may ask how they had no bread when, immediately after filling seven baskets, they entered the boat and came into the region of Magadan, where, while sailing, they also hear that they ought to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees. But Scripture says: “They forgot to take them with them.” This is evidence that, in other matters, they took little care for the flesh. Even the bodily necessity of food, naturally present in all, had slipped from their minds because of their attention to the Lord’s company and the sweetness of the true bread who was with them. [Col. 1394B]

He said to them: “Look and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, etc.” The leaven of the Pharisees is to prefer the decrees of human traditions to the divine Law; or also to preach the Law in words and oppose it in deeds, to test the Lord, and to believe neither his teaching nor his works. He commanded them to beware of such leaven. But they were thinking among themselves, saying: “Because we have not taken bread, he does not want us to eat their bread, and perhaps we shall fail while fasting.”

Jesus, knowing this, said to them: “Why do you reason among yourselves, etc.?” As though he said: “Why do you not understand that something mystical is signified by the five loaves and five thousand, by the seven loaves and four thousand, and by the twelve baskets and seven hampers [Col. 1394C]—so that, since spiritual doctrines are signified by the loaves, you may understand that the Pharisees’ perverse traditions are signified by their leaven?”

Then Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, etc. Because he wished to reveal his death to the apostles, he first desired to confirm them in faith, lest, hearing of the weakness of his passion, they should waver. Therefore, intending to confirm them in faith, he first wished to remove from their minds the opinion and error of others. Coming into the region of Caesarea Philippi, he questions the disciples. This is the place where the Jordan rises at the foot of Mount Lebanon, from the two springs Jor and Dan. There Philip, Herod’s brother, also built Caesarea in honor of Tiberius Caesar, imitating his father Herod, who called Caesarea, in honor of Augustus Caesar, the city [Col. 1394D] which had previously been called Straton’s Tower. It follows:

“Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?” He calls himself the Son of Man, and asks concerning himself as Son of Man whom people say he is. Appropriately, those who hold a different opinion about the Lord are called “people.” But concerning the apostles he says:

“But you, whom do you say that I am?”—as though separating them from the number of people. As though he said: “But you, who are not people but sons of God, and therefore gods, whom do you say that I am?”” On account of humility, he calls himself Son of Man rather than Son of God; or because people regarded him as Son of Man, not Son of God.

[Col. 1395A] Others [say] John the Baptist, etc. They could be mistaken about Elijah and about Jeremiah, just as Herod was mistaken about John, saying: “John, whom I beheaded—he has risen from the dead, and mighty works are at work in him” (Mark VI; Luke IX). Peter answered: although all the apostles had the same conviction, Peter nevertheless answered for them all: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” He embraced everything, because he expressed both the nature and the name in which the sum of the virtues resides. He calls God “living” in distinction from false gods. It should be noted that, when the Lord professes the humility of his assumed humanity, he makes known of himself what is lesser; whereas the disciple makes known of him what is greater. The Lord makes known of himself what he became for our sake; the disciple, that he is the one who made us.

Jesus answering [Col. 1395B] said to him, etc. Since you possess so perfect a confession of faith, I—whose speaking is doing—say to you: “O Simon, you are blessed.” I say Simon Bar-Jonah, that is, one who, by such a confession and pious simplicity, ought to be called son of the dove, or son of divine grace, which is said to have descended upon him in the form of a dove. *Bar-Jonah* in Syriac is called in Latin “son of the dove”; and this name was rightly bestowed upon him by the Lord, because the dove is a very simple animal, and Peter himself followed the Lord with prudent and pious simplicity, mindful of that command: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X). He was indeed a son of the Holy Spirit from the time when, enlightened by him, he received the grace of divine knowledge; and because the will and operation of the Holy Trinity are one and the same, [Col. 1395C] rightly, after saying, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,” that is, son of spiritual grace, he immediately added: “for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

The Father sends the Spirit; the Son sends the Spirit; “the Spirit blows where he wills” (John III). For indeed, as we have said, the will and operation of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one; and therefore it is fittingly said that the Father revealed to the son of the dove the mystery of faith which flesh and blood could not reveal to him. “Flesh and blood” are rightly understood as paternal and maternal lineage, or as persons swollen with carnal wisdom and ignorant of dovelike simplicity—such as those who said that Christ was John or Elijah. Or certainly, by “flesh and blood” he properly signifies [Col. 1395D] the Jews: that it was revealed to Peter not through the teaching of the Pharisees but by God’s grace that Christ the man is the Son of God. Hence Paul: “Immediately I did not confer with flesh and blood” (Gal. I), designating the Jews. It follows:

“I say to you that you are Peter,” etc. This should not be understood as though he received this name at that time; rather, he received it when it was said: “You shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted Peter (John I), so that the Lord might later address him by this name, saying: “You are Peter.” He did not say, “You shall be called Peter,” but, “You are already Peter.” Or, when Andrew brought his brother Peter to see the Messiah, when the Lord said to Peter—or when it was said—“You shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted Peter, we may say that this name was then [Col. 1396A] promised to him but is now fulfilled. Therefore then it was said, “You shall be called,” but now, “You are Peter,” because of the strength of your faith and confession: Peter, I say, named from me, the rock.

“And upon this rock,” that is, upon myself, “I will build my Church.” As though he said: You are Peter from me, the rock, yet the dignity of the foundation is reserved to me. But you, to whom, as my lover and confessor, I have given a share in my name, shall arrange clean stones upon me, the foundation, and remove the reprobate; and “the gates of hell”—that is, sins, heretics, enticements, or anything of that kind—shall not prevail against that Church. For whoever has received Christ’s faith in the inward love of the heart will easily overcome whatever assails from without.

[Col. 1396B] “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” etc. He who confessed the King of heaven with such devotion was deservedly granted the keys of the heavenly kingdom, so that it might be evident to all that without faith and confession no one can enter the kingdom of heaven. By “the keys of the kingdom of heaven” he means the judgment and power of discernment itself: the power by which one binds or looses, and the discernment by which one distinguishes worthy persons from unworthy. For, as Gregory says, whoever unworthily looses or binds deprives himself of his own authority. If he possesses the knowledge to discern but has not received the power of binding and loosing, he binds and looses no one. But if he has received the power and yet does not discern rightly, then, if he binds or looses anyone, although in the sight of human beings, nevertheless in the sight of God the person bound without merit or loosed without merit [Col. 1396C] is considered neither bound nor loosed. Therefore what follows must be explained thus: “Whatever you bind”—understand, with these keys, that is, through power and discernment—“on earth, shall be bound also in heaven,” etc.

Notice that he says “on earth.” For human beings have not been given power to bind or loose the dead, but the living. The power to bind or loose the dead is reserved to God alone. Hence it is said: “God, to whom alone it belongs to bestow healing after death.” To bind and to loose is to excommunicate or absolve the living on earth. But whoever should absolve or bind a dead person would do this not on earth but after earth. It should be observed that this authority was not given to Peter alone; rather, just as Peter answered for [Col. 1396D] all, so in Peter he gave this authority to all. Hence after the Passion it was said: “Whose sins you forgive” (John XX), etc. This authority was granted not to the apostles alone, but also to all bishops and priests. Yet he granted it in a special manner as if to Peter alone in order to invite us to unity. For this reason he appointed him prince of the apostles: so that the Church might have, as it were, one principal vicar of Christ, to whom the diverse members of the Church might have recourse if perhaps they disagreed among themselves; for if there were different heads in the Church, the bond of unity would be broken by different schisms.

Then he commanded his disciples to tell no one, etc. It is asked: since in the earlier mission he had commanded them to announce that the kingdom of heaven was drawing near—and that drawing near was through his coming—[Col. 1397A] why does he now forbid them to show that Jesus Christ himself is he? The answer: when he was approaching his Passion, knowing that his Passion would produce scandal in the minds of believers, he wished that henceforth, before the Passion, he should not be preached as Christ, lest those newly converted to faith, seeing him die, should turn back and wander even more grievously from the truth. In the earlier mission, however, he did not forbid it, since people could still be confirmed in faith. Then, once the minds of the apostles had been confirmed in faith, he at last revealed his Passion to them, while strengthening them by foretelling the resurrection.

The text is clear enough. “And taking [him],” etc. Peter’s fervor toward the Lord was excessive; and so, on hearing of the Passion, out of the affection of one who loved him, he took him aside [Col. 1397B] and rebuked him—aside, lest he seem to rebuke his master. Turning, he said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan,” etc. *Satan* means adversary or opponent: “Because,” he says, “you speak things contrary to my will, you ought to be called an adversary.” To the devil it was said: “Go, Satan” (Matt. IV); but to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan.” As though he said: Do not go ahead of me by suggesting what I ought to do. Rather, get behind me—that is, follow me and learn my will.

Many think that Peter was not rebuked, but rather the hostile spirit which suggested this utterance to the apostle. But an apostolic error arising from an affection of piety should never be regarded as an instigation of the devil. “You are a stumbling-block to me,” that is, you offend me by wishing to go before me, “because you do not savor the things that are of God.” For it is [Col. 1397C] my will, and that of the Father whose will I came to do, that I should die for the salvation of human beings; but you, considering only your own will, do not wish the grain of wheat to fall into the earth so that it may bear much fruit.

Then Jesus said to the disciples, etc. After showing the disciples the mystery of his Passion and resurrection, he exhorts them to the example of his Passion, so that through patience they may receive the same reward, saying:

“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross,” etc. As though he said: I shall suffer; and if anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself. Elsewhere, where it is said: “Unless anyone renounces all that he possesses, [Col. 1397D] he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV), we are commanded to deny our possessions; here, however, we are commanded to deny ourselves. We deny ourselves when we avoid what we were through oldness and strive toward that to which we are called through newness. Consider how Paul had denied himself, saying: “Yet I live, now not I” (Gal. II). That most savage persecutor had indeed been extinguished; the pious preacher began to live. For if he himself were still there, he would certainly not be pious. But he who denies that he lives, let him say whence it comes that the holy words proclaim through the teaching of truth: “Christ lives in me” (ibid.). It is as though he openly said: I have indeed been extinguished from myself, since I do not live carnally; yet I am not essentially dead, since I live spiritually in Christ.

Let Truth therefore say [Col. 1398A]—let it say: “If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself,” because unless someone departs from himself, he does not draw near to him who is above himself; nor can he grasp what is beyond himself unless he knows how to put to death what he is. But once someone has denied himself in regard to vices, he must seek virtues in which to grow. For when it has been said, “If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself,” it is immediately added:

“And let him take up his cross and follow me.” The cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the mind is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor. Consider how Paul bore his own cross in both ways, when he said: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate” (I Cor. IX). [Col. 1398B] Here, in the affliction of the body, we have heard of the cross of the flesh; now let us hear of the cross of the mind in compassion for one’s neighbor. For he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. XI). The perfect preacher bore the cross in his body in order to provide an example of abstinence; and because he drew into himself the harms of another’s weakness, he bore the cross in his heart.

“For whoever wishes to save his life shall lose it,” etc. Therefore one ought to deny oneself and bear the cross, because whoever wishes to preserve his life in this world, should a time of martyrdom come, shall lose it—that is, life in the world to come. As though he said: Whoever refuses to lose temporal life for Christ should not doubt that [Col. 1398C] he will lose eternal life. He then adds the converse:

“But whoever loses his life,” that is, destroys temporal life, “for my sake, shall find it” in the future—not, indeed, the same life, but life for life: eternal life for momentary life. All this must be understood of the time of persecution, because what follows pertains to times of peace, when he says:

“For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world,” etc. Here two martyrdoms are indicated: one in the shedding of blood, occurring in time of persecution; the other in the mortification of desires, which continues toward the same end in time of peace. Truly he ought to take up the cross, enduring all evils and losses. For what does it profit a person to have prosperity in the world [Col. 1398D] and to possess and love temporal goods, if through this he suffers loss of soul? It is better to suffer adversities and losses in the world than to suffer punishment in hell. And this is: “For what does it profit,” etc.

“Or what shall he give,” etc. This may be understood in two ways. “What shall a man give in exchange for his soul?” That is: what recompense can he render the Lord for his redeemed and saved soul? Certainly “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy” (Rom. VIII), etc. Or, for a soul lost in hell, what exchange—that is, what redemption—can be given? Certainly, if parents gave all the wealth of the world for the soul of one condemned, they would accomplish nothing, because the Lord will give to each according to what he has deserved, not according to the merits of his parents. And this is: “For the Son of Man,” etc.

[Col. 1399A] According to the former interpretation, the sequence is as follows: no recompense can be paid to Christ for a saved soul, because the glory is so great that the Son will come in glory with the angels. “Amen I say to you,” etc. The loving Master wished to show the joys of the eternal promise to certain of his disciples while they still dwelt on earth, so that both those who saw and all who could hear might endure present adversities more lightly, repeatedly bringing to mind the gift of future recompense which they awaited. He indicates this in these words, as though he said: I said that he would come in the glory of the Father. But do you wish to know how great that glory is? “Amen I say to you, there are some standing here”—that is, Peter, John, and James—“who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom,” that is, appearing [Col. 1399B] in the splendor which he was to possess in the kingdom. This was fulfilled in the Transfiguration, concerning which the Evangelist immediately says:

## CHAPTER XVII

“And after six days,” etc. Matthew and Mark say that this took place after six days; Luke, however, says after eight. We must therefore say that Matthew and Mark counted only the intervening days, not including the first and last; thus they say “after six days,” that is, when six whole days had passed after the day on which these things were said. Luke, however, counts the first and last together with the intervening days. Thus they agree in meaning.

He fittingly showed his glory after six days and on the eighth day, because the resurrection is to come after the six ages of the world, and on the eighth [Col. 1399C] day—that is, when the time of the world, which is conducted through seven days, is ended—he will come in his ineffable glory. He took three with him to signify that only the faithful, instructed in faith in the Holy Trinity, are to be taken up into the splendor of the future resurrection. The names also correspond. Every faithful person ought to be Peter, that is, firm in faith; then James, that is, a supplanter of vices; then John, that is, attributing everything to God’s grace, against the pride of life which usually arises from virtues.

“And he leads them up a mountain,” etc., signifying that those who are to rise again will ascend to glory, that is, to heaven. Or he goes up a mountain in order to teach that all who desire to see this grace should not lie among low [Col. 1399D] pleasures, but should rather be raised to things above, according to: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). He leads them apart in order to signify through this that the righteous are to be separated from the wicked at judgment.

“And he was transfigured”: not by losing the substance of his flesh, but by displaying the glory of the future resurrection. “And his face shone like the sun,” that is, as an example of the future brightness which the righteous will receive when the wicked have been removed. He compared his face to the sun because nothing brighter could be found in the world. “And his garments became white as snow.” Christ’s garments signify the saints, of whom Isaiah says: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with a garment” (Isa. XLIX). The garments are compared to snow because they were bright in virtues and all the heat of vices had been removed from them.

[Col. 1400A] According to Mark (Mark IX), the garments were shining, white as snow, such as no fuller on earth can make white, because no one can live upon earth without the taint of some sin. But what a fuller—that is, a teacher of souls, or some outstanding purifier of his own body—cannot do on earth, the Lord will do in heaven, cleansing the Church, that is, his garment, from every defilement of this flesh and spirit.

“And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” Moses and Elijah—of whom we read that one was taken up into heaven (IV Kings II), while the other died—appearing in majesty with God, as Luke writes (Luke IX), signify the future glory of all saints: namely, those who at the time of judgment will either be found alive in the flesh or, having long ago tasted death, will be raised again, and will reign together with him. As the Apostle says: “The dead who are in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive” (I Thess. IV), etc.

[Col. 1400B] Moses and Elijah, therefore, signify all who shall reign with Christ: Moses, who died, the dead; Elijah, who lives, all those who will be found alive. Alternatively, Moses and Elijah—that is, the lawgiver and the foremost of the prophets—appear and speak with the Lord about his Passion and resurrection, to show that he is the one promised by every oracle of the Law and the Prophets. They appear not in low places but with him on the mountain, because only those who in mind transcend earthly desires behold the majesty of Holy Scripture fulfilled in the Lord. They also spoke with him because they related that the words of the prophets concerning his coming and the salvation of humankind had proved true.

They also signify two regenerations. One is in baptism, where the soul is raised again; the other is in the resurrection, where the flesh will be raised, concerning which it is said: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit” (Matt. XIX), etc. Moses, whose name is interpreted “watery,” signifies the first, baptismal resurrection. Elijah, whose name is interpreted “sun”—for *Elias* is said in Greek to mean “sun”—signifies the second regeneration, in which the righteous shall shine like the sun. Fittingly, therefore, these two such men appeared, signifying the faithful who share in the first regeneration and through it await the second.

Peter answering said to Jesus: “Lord, [Col. 1400D] it is good,” etc. Because lower things become worthless once heavenly sweetness has been tasted, Peter, seeing the majesty of the Lord and the saints, wishes to cling forever to these alone, saying: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” O how great is the happiness of the vision of the Godhead among the choirs of angels, if the transfigured humanity of Christ and the company of two saints, seen only for a moment, delight so greatly!

According to another Evangelist (Mark IX), Peter did not know what he was saying. He had forgotten that the kingdom was promised by the Lord to the saints not somewhere on earth but in heaven; and he seeks tabernacles in heavenly glory, where no blast of adversity need be feared, because almighty God and the Lamb are its temple. Yet in this he knew what he said, “It is good for us to be here,” because truly the sole and perfect good of humankind [Col. 1401A] is to enter into the joy of its Lord and remain there.

FULGENTIUS. If Peter, seeing glorified humanity, is filled with such joy that he never wishes to be separated from this sight, what must be thought of those who shall be worthy to see the divinity?

It should be noted that Peter sins in this also, by placing the Lord and his servants on an equal footing, saying:

“Let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” At the same time it should be observed that he did not deserve the Lord’s answer because he made his request imprudently. But he received the mystery of a certain figurative reality. For he sought a material tabernacle and received the shelter of a cloud, so that he might learn that, in the resurrection of the dead, the saints are to be protected not by the covering of houses but by the glory of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1401B] Hence follows: “While he was still speaking,” etc. “And behold, a voice,” etc. It should be noted that the mystery of the second regeneration fittingly corresponds with that of the first. At Christ’s baptism, the operation of the whole Trinity was manifested: the Son was there incarnate; the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove; and the Father was declared in a voice. Likewise, in the Transfiguration, which was the sacrament of the second regeneration, the whole Trinity appeared: the Father in the voice, the Spirit in the cloud, and the Son in the flesh.

It is asked, however, why the Spirit was manifested there in a dove but here in a cloud. He customarily manifests his gifts through forms. At baptism, innocence is given, signified by the bird of simplicity. But in the resurrection he will give [Col. 1401C] brightness and refreshment from every pleasure and carnal fuel. In the cloud, refreshment is figured; in the radiance of the cloud, the brightness of resurrected bodies.

When he says, “Hear him,” he agrees with Moses’ words, in which Moses bore witness to the Lord’s incarnation, saying: “The Lord will raise up for you from among your brethren a prophet like me; hear him in all things whatsoever he shall speak to you. And every soul that does not hear that prophet shall be cut off from the people” (Deut. XVIII). Therefore, the one whom Moses foretold, when he came in the flesh, must be heard by every soul wishing to be saved—him, now coming in the flesh, God the Father shows to the disciples as one to be heard, and by a heavenly voice marks him as his Son.

“And when the disciples heard [this], they fell,” etc. They are terrified for three reasons: either because they knew that they had erred, or because the shining cloud had covered them, or because they had heard the voice of God the Father. For human frailty cannot bear the sight of greater glory. Therefore, trembling in body and soul, they fall to the earth, because the more exalted things anyone seeks, the more he falls to lower things if he does not know his own measure. “And Jesus came,” etc. Since they lay there and could not rise, he mercifully approaches and touches them, so that by his touch limbs weakened by fear may be strengthened; and he consoles them in word, saying: “Rise; do not be afraid.” “But lifting up their eyes,” etc.

[Col. 1402A] When the Son began to be identified, the servants immediately departed, lest the voice sent out by the Father appear to have been uttered for them. They saw Jesus standing after the cloud had been removed, while Moses and Elijah had vanished, because, once the shadow of the Law and Prophets which had covered the apostles with its veil had departed, the true light of the Gospel is found. Alternatively: “When the voice came concerning the Son, he alone was found” (Luke IX), because when he manifests himself to the elect, God will be all in all. Indeed, he himself with his own will be one Christ in every respect—that is, the head with the body will shine. Because of this unity it is said: “No one has ascended into heaven” (John III), etc. Note that at the Father’s voice Moses returned to his own place, whereas Elijah departed to his own region.

“And as they were coming down,” etc. He does not wish this to be preached among the people, lest it be incredible because of the greatness of the event, and lest the cross which followed such great glory become a scandal to untutored minds.

[Col. 1402B] “And they asked,” etc. The Pharisees’ tradition, according to the prophet Malachi, the last of the Twelve, is that Elijah will come before the Savior’s advent, turn the hearts of fathers to children and of children to fathers, and restore all things to their former state. The apostles thought that the transformation they had seen on the mountain was the final glory, and they say: If you have now come in glory, why does the forerunner not appear? They say this especially because they had seen Elijah depart so quickly. This is the sense: “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” Since we see you already in the kingdom of your glory, where is Elijah, who ought to go before?

But he answered them: “Elijah indeed shall come and restore all things,” as Malachi prophesied, saying: “Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the day of the Lord comes” (Mal. IV), etc. In saying, “Elijah shall come,” he shows that this is not the second advent and thus removes their mistaken opinion. “But I say,” etc. As though he said: I have not merely said that Elijah will come, to prove that this advent is not the second; to confirm the first advent as well, I say that Elijah has already come, but they did not recognize him or love him. That Elijah, namely, who is to come at the Savior’s second advent according to bodily reality, has already come in spirit and power through John, the forerunner of my first advent.

[Col. 1402D] “And they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished,” and finally beheaded him, with the Pharisees consenting. So also the Son of Man will suffer from them. For just as the party of the Pharisees consented to John’s murder, so Herod joined his will to the Lord’s killing, because, after clothing him in a white garment and mocking him, he sent him back to Pilate (Luke XXIII). Note that Christ, who was to suffer death from them, is called Son of Man, because when Christ suffered in the flesh, his divinity remained impassible.

“Then the disciples understood,” etc. They understood, I say, through the indication of his Passion, which he had often foretold to them, [Col. 1403A] and through the indication of the Passion of his forerunner, which they had seen fulfilled.

“And when he came to the crowd,” etc. The places themselves suit the events. On the mountain the Lord prays and is transfigured before the disciples, displaying the hidden things of his majesty. Descending to lower places, he is met by a crowd: he hears, corrects, teaches, and strengthens the afflicted. Above, he reveals the spiritual voice of the Father to the perfect; below, he casts evil spirits out of those whom they tormented. According to the quality of their merits, he ascends to some and descends to others.

Mark calls this man deaf and mute; Matthew calls him lunatic—not because the moon is subject to demons, but because the demon observes the moon’s course and torments people in order to defame the Creator through the creature. In a typological sense, the lunatic is [Col. 1403B] one who changes toward vices at every moment of the hours and does not remain firm in purpose, but waxes and wanes: now he is carried into the fire of lust, by which the hearts of adulterers are inflamed, or into the fire of anger, by which they seem to seek high things; now into the waters of carnal pleasure, which soften and dissolve minds in worldly matters. Of these waters it is said: “Many waters could not quench love” (Song VIII).

“And I brought him,” etc. By this saying he covertly accuses the apostles, since the possibility of healing is sometimes attributed not to the weakness of healers but to the faith of those to be healed, as the Lord says: “Let it be done to you according to your faith” (Matt. IX). “Jesus answering said,” etc. He did not burst into these words as one overcome by weariness and fury—he who is gentle as a lamb—but in the manner of a physician who, seeing a sick person acting contrary to his instructions, says: “How long must I come to your house? How long must I waste the skill of my art upon you, when I command one thing and you do another?” Thus the Lord is angry not with the person but with the vice; and, in order to rebuke unbelief through one person and the Jews, he immediately added: “Bring him to me.”

[Col. 1403C] When he was brought, Jesus rebuked—not the demon, in order to show that the boy had been handed over to an unclean spirit because of his own sin or that of his parents; or, which is better, he rebuked not the boy who suffered violence but the demon that inflicted it. For whoever desires to correct a sinner must certainly drive out the vice by rebuking and hating it, and restore the person through love.

“And it came out of him,” etc. Mark says of this person (Mark IX) that when the spirit saw the Lord, it immediately convulsed him; thrown to the ground, he rolled about; and, when the Lord commanded it to come out, it cried out and came out tearing him apart. For often, when after sins we wish to turn to the Lord, we are attacked more fiercely by the devil, either that he may instill hatred of virtue or avenge the injury of his expulsion. As it is about to leave, it tears apart and frightens onlookers with a raging cry, because, when it is expelled from the heart, the one who previously possessed it quietly often stirs up sharper temptations. “And the boy was healed from that hour,” because no disease prevails where the hand of the Almighty intervenes.

Then the disciples came privately to Jesus and said: “Why could we not cast it out?” He said [Col. 1404A] to them: “Because of your unbelief.” Here it is plainly made understood that when someone praying is not heard, the cause is not an inability in the giver but fault in the petitioner.

“For amen I say to you: if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.” He compares perfect faith to a mustard seed: humble in outward appearance and fervent in the hidden breast; common and of no apparent strength to casual observers, yet, when crushed by pressure, showing what perfection it bears within.

It should also be noted that mustard seed is especially beneficial for cleansing the head. For if you grind and sift it thoroughly, mix it with lukewarm, rich honeyed wine, and gargle with this while fasting, facing the warm sun or in a bath, it cleanses every harmful humor from the head, even if rather thick, and causes the dangers of impending weaknesses to be avoided.

[Col. 1404B] Thus perfect faith, tested in the mortar of temptation, chastened by the sieve of discernment from every surface trace of frivolous thoughts, and sweetened with the honey of perfect love, draws out from the heart—which is the head of the inward person—all the cesspools of vices; it fortifies not only for the present but also against their gathering again in the future. Let us come to the literal sense.

“If you have faith”—I say, faith that exists—“like a grain of mustard seed,” that is, faith comparable to a mustard seed according to its nature; “if you say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ it will move.” This may be understood literally, just as it is read that the blessed Benedict moved by a word a stone obstructing his garden. Or: “You will say to this mountain,” that is, to the devil, “Move away from this possessed body,” and it will pass into another or into the depth of the sea.

“And nothing [will be] impossible,” etc.: that is, no affliction will be incurable.

“This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” While teaching the apostles how a most wicked demon should be expelled, he instructs all for life: that we should know that the more grievous temptations of human beings are to be overcome by fasts and prayers. He also teaches that the wrath of God, when kindled in vengeance for our crimes, can be appeased by this singular remedy.

[Col. 1404D] Fasting in general consists not only in abstinence from food but also from all enticements of the flesh—indeed, from the passions of every vice. Likewise, prayer in general consists not only in words, but also in everything we faithfully and devoutly do in obedience to our Creator, as the Apostle testifies: “Always rejoice; pray without ceasing” (II Thess. III). Therefore this kind of demon—that is, this instability of pleasures—is not cast out except through prayer, not merely of words but also of devotion, and fasting, not merely from food but also from vice.

“While they were staying in Galilee,” etc. The Lord frequently wished to announce his Passion because he knew that they would be greatly troubled by it; but after the message of sorrow he added his resurrection as consolation.

“And when he came to Capernaum,” etc. Judaea was made tributary under Caesar Augustus; hence Joseph and Mary registered at Bethlehem in order to pay taxes. For Luke says: “Joseph went up to Bethlehem to register with Mary, his betrothed” (Luke II). Therefore tribute is demanded of the Lord; and because he was brought up at Nazareth, a town of Galilee subject to the city of Capernaum, tribute was demanded from him there when he came to the larger city. But because of the greatness of his miracles they did not dare ask him directly; rather, they approached the disciples, maliciously investigating whether they paid tribute or not.

[Col. 1405B] “Does not your master pay the didrachma?” etc. And Peter answered: “Yes”—that is, it is true that he does not pay it. When Peter entered the house, he wished to tell the Lord that the Herodians were demanding tribute, but the Lord anticipated him, saying: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their sons or from strangers?” etc. Christ was the Son of the almighty King and descended from David’s stock; therefore, because he was a king’s son, he did not owe tribute. But because he wished to give an example of every humility and not cause people to stumble, he preferred to pay tribute. Yet he did not wish to pay it from common funds, morally teaching that no one should spend what belongs to the community of brothers, but what belongs to his own property.

He therefore sent him to the sea. The foreknowledge of the Lord and Savior and the greatness of Christ’s powers are marvelous: his foreknowledge, because he knew of the stater in the fish’s mouth; the greatness of his power, because the stater may have been created at his word, so that he made by speaking what was to happen.

[Col. 1405C] It was customary for each person to pay a didrachma for himself; a stater, however, is the weight of two didrachmas. Something mystical may nevertheless be understood in this matter. The fish is Christ; the sea, the world; the hook, death. Christ bore the price of our redemption. That the price was found in the fish’s mouth signifies that our redemption was announced to human beings by Christ’s mouth. It is given for Christ and for Peter, but in different ways. Here Peter bears the person of the Church. Christ pays the price for himself because his Passion was for him the price of exaltation, according to: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name,” etc. (Phil. II); and for Peter, that is, for the Church, in order to free it from captivity.

## CHAPTER XVIII
At that hour they came, etc. Because Christ had paid the tribute for Peter alone, the others, offended and supposing that Peter was being preferred, therefore ask: “Who is greater in the kingdom of heaven?” Wishing to crush their pride, he sets before them an example of humility, lest they should wish to be preferred one above another. He therefore placed a child in their midst, so that they might imitate by training and virtue the innocence which a little child possesses by nature. Many say that this little child was Saint Martial of Limoges. Many also believe that this was said of Christ himself, who was a child in malice and not in age, and truly humble, who “came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20). The text is read thus: “Amen, I say to you, unless you are converted,” etc.—from this exaltation and indignation in which you now are—and become as innocent and humble through virtue as little children are through age, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.

“But whoever shall humble himself,” etc. Since entry is otherwise impossible, whoever humbles himself like this little child—who, on seeing a beautiful woman, takes no delight in her, and who does not think one thing and say another—shall enter the kingdom of heaven. And the humbler he is, the greater he will become.

“And whoever shall receive one such little child,” etc. Because the apostles, murmuring among themselves out of ambition, might by their example incite the weak and simple to ambition [Col. 1406B], he therefore commands that the weak be received and threatens punishment to those who cause them scandal. This is the meaning: “Whoever shall receive one such little child in my name,” drawing him gently toward instruction, according to the Apostle, “Receive the weak” (1 Thess. 5), “receives me”; or whoever receives him by hospitality and beneficence receives me.

“But whoever shall scandalize one of these little ones,” either by evil teaching or by a bad example—as you are now doing, corrupting others by the bad example of your ambition—“it is expedient for him that a millstone be hung about his neck and that he be drowned,” etc. Literally it is explained thus: this was a most disgraceful punishment, imposed upon criminals; as though he said: It is expedient—that is, it would be better for him to perish by so shameful a death than to scandalize a brother, because to scandalize a brother is a sin, whereas to die is not a sin.

Or otherwise: secular people are said to be devoted to the wheel of this world, according to the saying, “The wicked walk in a circle” (Ps. 2). By the ass’s millstone, therefore, the revolving course and toil of secular life are expressed; and by the depth of the sea, final damnation is signified. He says, then: It would be better for a contemplative person to turn an ass-mill—that is, to be secular, turning over worldly cares—and thereby be plunged into the depths of hell, than to be a contemplative person scandalizing his brethren; for his punishment in hell would be lighter. Or otherwise: in the Scriptures an ass signifies the Gentile people, which is bound to the mill, that is, to gods of stone, around which they circle with blind eyes in frequent error, and thus are plunged into the depth of hell. As though he said: It would be better for him to be a Gentile, bound to gods of stone and perishing in hell, than to be a believer scandalizing his brethren. For it is better not to know the truth than, after recognizing it, to turn back.

“Woe to the world because of scandals.” Therefore it is expedient for him that an ass’s millstone be hung about him—that is, that he should be a Gentile or secular person—because the world, that is, human beings, will suffer a very great woe from scandals, that is, on account of the scandals which he himself brings upon his brethren.

“For it is necessary,” etc. As though someone were asking: “Will there be scandals in the world?” There certainly will, because they are necessary, so that those who are approved may thereby be made manifest; but [Col. 1407A] nevertheless the one through whom scandals come will not therefore escape punishment. This is the meaning: “Nevertheless, woe to the man through whom scandal comes.”—“But if thy hand,” etc. Above he commanded that believers should not scandalize others; now he teaches how carefully we must guard ourselves against those who scandalize us, saying thus: If anyone is so closely joined to you that he may be called your hand, whose work and help are necessary to you, or your foot, whose movement or administration you need, and yet harms you in some respect concerning the cause of your soul, exclude him from your fellowship rather than perish with him in the fire of Gehenna.

“It is good for thee,” etc. Take care not to cause scandal in faith: you must break off every attachment to friends, because it is better for you to enter into life weak or lame [Col. 1407B], that is, content with one foot—your own course—and deprived of your neighbor’s course, than, having two hands, that is, two fellow-workers, namely yourself and a friend, or two feet, that is, two runners, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna. Understand the same concerning the eye. He calls someone’s provider his eye.

“Take heed.” As though he said: Because so great an evil arises from scandalizing brethren, I say, “Take heed lest you despise one of these little ones.” “For I say to you that their angels,” etc. They are not to be despised, because they are so dear to God that angels are assigned to them for their protection, as he indicates when he says:

“For I say to you that their angels behold the face,” etc. Note that although angels are sent, they nevertheless behold the Father. This happens because God is everywhere [Col. 1407C], and they run beside him. Another reason is given why they must not be despised: because I have loved them so greatly that I came to save them.

“What think you?” etc. By a certain comparison he shows that God came to save all human beings who had perished. He is the shepherd who has one hundred sheep. The hundred sheep are the orders of angels and human beings persevering in their perfection. One went astray when man sinned; and when the number was diminished, it became imperfect. Christ left the ninety-nine on the mountains, that is, in the heavenly places, when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). He found the sheep when he restored man; and there is greater joy in heaven over the sheep found than over the ninety-nine, because [Col. 1407D] his glory and the material for praise were greater in the restoration of human beings than in the creation of angels. For he created human beings wonderfully, but restored them more wonderfully. Nothing was more wonderful than that the Son of God emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and humbling himself unto death (Phil. 2).

Or otherwise: the lost sheep signifies only sinners who are reconciled to God through repentance, whom, according to another evangelist, he carried back upon his shoulders (Luke 15), because by humbling himself he raised such persons up. He called those ninety-nine which he left on the mountains because they signify the proud, as bearing swelling or solitude in their minds, since they want to appear to be alone; and they also lack unity for perfection [Col. 1408A]. For whenever someone is torn away from true unity through pride, desiring to be his own master, he does not follow the One who is God. Therefore, by the meaning of those ninety-nine sheep, those who presume upon themselves set themselves above sinners returning to salvation. And when he finds the sinner, he will rejoice over him—that is, he makes his own rejoice more over him than over the ninety-nine, that is, than over false righteous persons.

But in Luke it is written: “There is greater joy over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no penance” (Luke 15), because, as we experience daily, those who have committed unlawful deeds often permit themselves indulgence in lawful things, do not anxiously aspire to heavenly things, and, because they are secure, remain sluggish in doing good. On the contrary, a sinner [Col. 1408B] often causes greater joy concerning himself than a righteous person who remains standing; just as a commander in battle loves more the soldier who, after fleeing, returns and presses the enemy bravely than the one who never fled and never acted bravely. Yet there are some righteous persons concerning whom there is such joy that no penitent person can be set above them: although conscious of no evil, they nevertheless despise lawful things and humble themselves in all things. How great, then, is the joy when a righteous person humbly laments, if there is joy when an unrighteous person condemns what he has done wrongly.

“Thus it is not the will,” etc. He returns to the point proposed above, where he had said, “Take heed lest you despise,” etc., teaching that this parable was set forth so that they should not despise a little one. When he says, “It is not the will of the Father that one should perish,” note that no one perishes by the will of the Father [Col. 1408C].

“But if thy brother shall sin against thee,” etc. As though he said: Do not despise a little one; rather, if he sins against you by wronging you, labor so earnestly for his salvation that you first rebuke him by yourself, then through others, then through the whole Church, and finally through excommunication—desiring not so much vengeance as brotherly correction. Some wish this to be understood of every sin, not merely of injury; and it is said thus: “If thy brother sin against thee,” that is, publicly—for every public sin is said to be committed against each person, because one who sins publicly corrupts his neighbor—correct him privately, lest you appear to be the betrayer of another’s crime rather than his corrector. But if he is unwilling to be corrected even thus, or says that it is not a sin, take others with you, so that he may be ashamed before many persons [Col. 1408D], or that they may prove it to be a sin. But if he is unwilling to be corrected even so, tell the whole Church, that he may suffer greater shame. After all these things follows excommunication, which ought to be carried out only through the mouth of the Church, that is, through the priest. For when the priest excommunicates, the whole body of the Church acts.

“Amen, I say to you,” etc. And lest some proud person should despise excommunication, saying, “If you despise me, I despise you; if you condemn me, I condemn you,” he therefore confirms the sentence of excommunication, saying: “Whatever you shall bind,” etc. And he gives confirmation not only concerning excommunication, but also concerning every petition made by persons agreeing in the unity of the Church, saying: “Again I say to you [Col. 1409A] that if two of you shall agree upon earth,” whether in receiving a penitent, rejecting a proud person, or concerning another matter which they ask and which is not contrary to the unity of the Church, “it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.” It is not without significance that he says, “who is in heaven.” By this he shows that he is above all things and can therefore fulfill it. Or, he is in the saints; this serves to prove that whatever worthy thing they ask will truly be done for them, because they have within themselves the one from whom they ask.

“For where two are,” etc. As though he said: The sentence of those who agree is valid because God dwells with them.

Then Peter came to him, etc. Above he said that brother should rebuke brother. Now Peter asks: if the rebuked brother repents, how often should he be forgiven? Sevenfold forgiveness seemed quite sufficient to him, and he therefore asks whether he should forgive “up to seven times.” This is understood in two ways, either of an injury or of every sin, according to the twofold exposition above. Thus it may be said: “If my brother sins against me,” injuring me, either by insults or by loss, “shall I forgive him up to seven times?” Or it may be understood, or read, of every sin thus: Peter here bears the person of the Church and says: “If my brother sins against me,” that is, against the Church—namely, if he sins criminally, because one who sins criminally sins against the Church, from which he deserves to be separated for criminal acts—“shall I forgive him up to seven times?” This is expounded thus against those who allow only one penance in the Church.

[Col. 1409C] Jesus said to him: “I do not say to thee, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven,” etc. Jerome explains this number so as to mean four hundred and ninety times, so that one is commanded to forgive a sinner in one day as often as he could not possibly sin in one day. Augustine, however, takes “seventy times seven” to mean seventy-seven times, understanding by this number every transgression. For that number is made up of eleven and seven: seven times eleven are seventy-seven. Eleven signifies transgression because it exceeds ten, by which the Decalogue is understood. Seven signifies universality because it encompasses the whole duration of the world. He therefore commands forgiveness “seventy times seven,” that is, for every transgression. But the following parable seems to indicate that the foregoing should be understood not of every sin, but only of injury.

“Therefore the kingdom of heaven is likened to a king,” etc. By a certain comparison he shows that brethren ought to be forgiven, and what danger follows if forgiveness is not granted. He follows the custom of Syrians, and especially of Palestinians, who attach parables to every discourse, so that what listeners cannot retain as a simple command may be retained through the likeness of an example. The wording is sufficiently clear, but the meaning is terrible when he says: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” For if we do not forgive our brethren small things [Col. 1410A], great things are not forgiven us by God; and even that is demanded of us which we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through penance. Yet it must be carefully observed that we are commanded not to forgive sins indiscriminately, but to forgive one doing penance; and first, indeed, where it is said that the sinner is to be rebuked mercifully, so that there may be someone whom we ought afterward justly to forgive.

In the mystical sense, the one who owed ten thousand talents signifies the Jewish people, because, being guilty of many transgressions of the Law, it owed the fulfillment of the Decalogue. But since it had nothing with which to pay—that is, since by its own strength it could not fulfill the Decalogue—the Lord commanded it to be sold, that is, by a just judgment permitted it to become the servant of evil spirits; and he commanded its wife, children, and all that it possessed to be sold and payment made—that is, he commanded it to pay penalties for desire and works, as though for wife and children.

“But that servant falling down,” etc. Since the wicked man would not willingly do so, as a penitent person compelled, he prayed to him, saying:

“Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all.” That is: Spare me for my sins, and I will pay thee all—that is, through faith and penance I will make satisfaction for the things in which I offended by transgressing thy commandments. But the lord of that servant, moved with pity, released him and forgave him the debt, because the Lord is merciful: that is, he not only released them from the Jewish captivity, in which they were held as though captive, but also promised to grant forgiveness for all sins if they were willing to persevere in what they had begun. Or otherwise: he released him because he freed him from the burden of carnal observances, and forgave him when he pardoned his previous transgressions [Col. 1410C].

“But when that servant went out,” etc. That is, the aforesaid one, freed from captivity or advanced to the liberty of faith, found one of his fellow-servants, namely the Gentile people, which owed him one hundred denarii—that is, it ought to acknowledge the salvation bestowed or to be bestowed upon it through him. Seizing him, he choked him as though he were his debtor; and, saying that the grace of Christ was insufficient for salvation, he demanded carnal observances not merely by persuasion but also by harsher torments. He said: “Pay what thou owest,” that is, observe carnal observances. But the humble one worshipped him, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all: I will fulfill spiritually whatever the Law commands.” But he would not—that is, the carnal man rejected spiritual things [Col. 1410D]—but rather went away, that is, withdrew from spiritual understanding, and put him into prison, that is, into narrow tribulation, until he paid the debt—that is, until he fulfilled the Law carnally, which seemed to him to be what was owed.

But when his fellow-servants, namely the preachers of the Gospel, saw what was being done—the persecution inflicted upon the Christian Church by the Jews—they were grieved, and, in compassion, came and reported everything to their lord, imploring help against the deceit of the persecutors.

“Then he summoned him,” etc. This summons is inward, in the conscience. And he said: “Wicked servant, I forgave thee every debt,” that is, all the transgressions of the Law for which you ought to have paid me penalties, because you asked me in your distress [Col. 1411A]. “Now, having been set free, you have shown no compassion; rather, you persecute my prophets and apostles, presume upon your righteousness with ingratitude, and despise the Gentiles, judging them unworthy of fellowship in Christ.

“Oughtest thou not also to have had mercy, since I had mercy on thee?” “Then his lord, being angry,” etc. In accordance with the judgment, he delivered him to the torturers, who may be understood as the Roman princes Titus and Vespasian, or the infernal ministers to whom the Jews are at last to be delivered. He delivered them, I say, until he should pay the entire debt—that is, until he should understand the Decalogue spiritually, or until he should pay penalties by suffering continually, that is, never ceasing from punishments.

## Chapter XIX

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these discourses” [Col. 1411B], etc. After the evangelist narrated what he did and taught in Galilee, he proceeds to what he did, taught, and suffered in Judaea. This journey signifies that Christ will pass over by faith to the Jews at the end of the age, first beyond the Jordan to the east, and afterward on this side of the Jordan, when he came to Jericho and Jerusalem. For although the whole province of the Jews, in general distinction from other nations, is called Judaea, yet its southern region is specifically called Judaea, in distinction from Samaria, Galilee, Decapolis, and the other regions in the same province.

“And great crowds followed him,” etc. Because at the end of the age, when all Israel shall be saved, many will be converted to faith, and he will heal them from their sins.

[Col. 1411C] “And Pharisees came to him,” etc. The crowds come in order to be taught and healed; the Pharisees, however, in order to attempt to deceive the teacher of truth. The devotion of piety brought the former; the goad of envy brought the latter. They therefore ask whether it is lawful to dismiss a wife for any cause, so that he may be caught in a horned syllogism. For whichever side he chooses, they are prepared to trap him. If he says that she should be dismissed and another taken, the preacher of chastity seems now to teach what is contrary to chastity. But if he answers that she ought not to be dismissed for every cause, he will be held guilty of violating a command and will be said to act against the law of Moses.

But he tempers his answer so as to pass through the snare, because he adduces Holy Scripture as testimony, along with the natural law; and he opposes God’s first decree to the second, which was granted not by God’s will but from the necessity arising from sinners. This is the meaning: “He answering said to them: Have you not read that he who made man from the beginning made them male and female?” He does not say “females,” but “female,” excluding a plurality of marriage partners; and, to confirm the same point further, he says: “For this cause”—that is, because of this one union—“a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife,” not to wives. “And the two shall be one flesh,” not three—that is, in carnal union. Therefore, because carnal union makes one, they are now not two but one flesh, which carnal union produces.

“Therefore what God has joined together,” making one flesh, “let no man separate.” If marriages are lawful [Col. 1412A], then God has joined them; but if they are not lawful, then God has not joined them, and a human being may separate them. A human being cannot separate lawful marriages, though God can. For sometimes persons become continent for God’s sake, so that one becomes a monk and the other a nun.

They say to him: “Why then did Moses,” etc. When God had answered with words of authority, they oppose authority to authority, since they cannot oppose person to person; as though they said: Since God commanded this in the beginning, why then did Moses afterward command marriages to be altered and a bill of divorce to be given as a sign of abandonment? He says to them: “Because Moses, on account of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to dismiss your wives,” etc. Moses did not command the dismissal of wives but permitted it. It was a permission, not a command, and this [Col. 1412B] was because of the hardness of your hearts. Moses saw such hardness of heart in the Jews that, when they hated their wives for some cause, if dismissal were not allowed, they would kill them. He therefore permitted what was lighter so that the graver evil might be avoided. “But from the beginning it was not so”: that is, the natural law did not have it so.

“But I say to you.” A servant, compelled by the weakness of human beings, commands; but I, Lord and Master, say and command you to put off the old man and keep the precepts of the new law. “For I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery.” Fornication alone is a cause of separation. For after a woman joined to her husband and one with him in carnal union has transferred that unity into another flesh and divided that union by fornication [Col. 1412C], she does not indeed lose the bond of marriage, but deserves no longer to be joined carnally with her husband, against whose union she sinned. And because the marriage bond remains, he adds: “And whoever marries her that has been dismissed commits adultery.” He frightens the man who takes her, because the adulteress does not fear disgrace. The same must be understood of the husband; yet reconciliation to the husband after separation is not prohibited.

The disciples say to him: “If the case of a man with his wife is thus”—that is, if he is so bound to her that he cannot dismiss her—“it is not expedient to marry,” that is, it is good to be continent. He said: “Not all receive this saying.” That is, not all keep this saying, that it is good to be continent. He did not say, “Not all can receive,” that is, keep it, for they could indeed do so if they were willing to conquer the weakness of the flesh. But he said, “Not all receive,” that is, not all are continent, except those to whom it is given by divine grace. In these words he shows that unless we receive the help of grace, we have no power of ourselves.

“For there are eunuchs.” Therefore I said, “to whom it is given.” It is good to be continent, but continence is not good for everyone. For there are certain eunuchs who are eunuchs from birth—that is, persons of a frigid nature who feel no desire of lust. Again, there are others who have been made eunuchs by human beings; and abstinence is not a virtue for either of these classes. For they abstain not by will but by compulsion and necessity. And there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven [Col. 1413A]: namely, those who are continent voluntarily so as to acquire the kingdom of heaven; for these alone continence is a virtue.

“He who can receive it, let him receive it.” This is the voice of one urging continence, as though he said: Whoever can receive this saying, that is, whoever can abstain, let him abstain.

“Then there were offered,” etc. While Christ was speaking about the continent, children were brought to him. Although they were not continent by virtue, he wished to show in them, as a figure of the truly continent, what is fulfilled in the truly continent. He laid hands upon them in order to signify that the grace of his help would be conferred upon truly continent and truly humble people, and to show them worthy of his blessing and grace. This is the point into which he now enters: “Then little children were brought to him, that he might lay hands on them and pray.” As though he said: that he might bless them by hand and voice [Col. 1413B]. But the disciples rebuked them—not because they did not want them blessed by the Savior’s hand and voice, but because, still inexperienced and simple, they thought that their Master, like other human beings, was wearied by the importunity of those presenting them.

But Jesus said to them: “Allow the little children to come to me,” etc., signifying by this that the truly humble and continent come to God; and because these children are a figure of the truly continent, he adds:

“Of such is the kingdom of heaven.” He said “of such,” not “of these,” in order to show that age does not reign, but character; and that the reward is promised to those who resemble children in innocence and simplicity, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Do not become children in understanding, but be little children in malice” (1 Cor. 14). Nor was there any reason why they should be removed. For if they were going to be saints, why do they prevent children from coming to their Father? If they are going to be sinners, why is sentence pronounced before guilt?

“And one came to him and said,” etc. This man had perhaps heard from the Lord that only those who wished to become like little children were worthy to enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, wishing to be more certain, he asks to have it explained not by parables but openly, by what merits he might attain eternal life. It should be noted that, according to Jerome, this man was young, rich, and proud. Others say that he asked not with the intention of testing, but seriously, when he said: “Good Master,” etc. “Why dost thou ask me concerning good? One is good, God,” etc. The Lord rebukes him [Col. 1413D] because he considered him a mere human being, not God, and good only from himself. Therefore he reproves him thus: “Why dost thou ask me concerning good?”—understand, “a good master,” that is, by seeking from a good master. That this is the meaning is taught by another evangelist, when he says: “Why dost thou call me good?” (Mark 10). “I am not good in the way you think,” that is, good from myself according to my humanity. For no one is good from himself except the one good God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But where he had said, “Good Master,” he reproves him for a bad question; to the sound question he responds, giving the solution: “If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments.” He does not say “learn,” but “keep,” for he was skilled in the commandments. He says to him—as though he said: Because there are many, he asks, “Which?” Jesus says: “Thou shalt not kill,” etc.

[Col. 1414A] Here two lives are proposed, the active and the contemplative. The active is proposed first; when the young man asserts that he has fulfilled it, he is afterward urged toward the contemplative when he says:

“If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell all that thou hast,” etc. For the perfect person must sell everything, not only part, as Ananias and Sapphira did (Acts 5); and, after selling it, give to the poor. Nor does this suffice for perfection unless, after despising riches, he follows the Savior. For it is easier to despise a purse than one’s will; and many people leave riches but do not follow the Lord.

“And when the young man heard the word, he went away sorrowful,” etc. Note that different conclusions are drawn from the various words of this evangelist concerning the young man. For when he had said above, “All these things I have kept,” Mark subsequently adds: “And Jesus, looking upon him, loved him” (Mark 10). From these words Bede concludes that he did not come with the intention of testing. He says: “This man must not be supposed either to have come with the intention of testing the Lord, as some have thought, or to have lied about his life when he said that he had kept the commandments of the Law. Rather, he simply confessed how he had lived; for if he had been guilty of falsehood or pretense, Jesus, who looked into the secrets of his heart, would by no means be said to have loved him.”

But the words that follow, “he went away sorrowful,” deny that he was good. Therefore Jerome maintains that he came with the intention of testing; and according to this view, that look was not directed to his present state but to what followed, because it should be believed that he was converted afterward [Col. 1414C]. But since it is said of him, “he went away sorrowful,” it should not be believed that he had a good conscience; rather, he lied when he confessed that he had love for his neighbor. For he did not truly love his neighbor if he grieved that he was commanded to give his possessions to his neighbors. Hence, taking the occasion, he says that a rich person can scarcely be saved.

But Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you that a rich person shall with difficulty enter the kingdom of heaven,” etc. HILARY. On the occasion of this avaricious man, he spoke about the avaricious. It should be noted that “rich” here means one who possesses riches with love for them. For many possess them without loving them. He does not say: “It is impossible for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven,” but “It is difficult.” What is impossible cannot happen at all; what is difficult can happen with labor. It can indeed happen, but with the greatest labor and God’s grace assisting: those who possess money, or trust in money, may enter the gate of the kingdom of heaven after casting off the chains of *philargyria*, the love of money.

“And again I say to you: It is easier for a camel,” etc. This camel is Christ, who, voluntarily humbled, bore the burdens of our weakness. The needle is a piercing, through which the narrowness of the Passion is signified. By that Passion, as by a needle, he deigned to mend, that is, restore after the fall, the torn garments of our nature. It is therefore said: “It is easier for a camel to enter through a needle’s eye”—that is, it is easier for Christ to suffer for lovers of worldly things than for lovers of worldly things [Col. 1415A] to be converted to Christ.

Otherwise: It is easier for the Gentile people, deformed by the hump of sins, to enter by the narrow way of life than for a Jew, glorying in many things and unwilling to humble himself to bear Christ’s light burden. Another explanation says that there was at Jerusalem a certain gate called the Needle’s Eye, through which a camel could not pass except after laying down its burden and bending its knees. By this gate are signified rich people, who cannot enter the narrow way which leads to life unless they lay aside riches, at least by not loving them, renounce the filth of sins, and have their hearts contrite through humility.

When the disciples heard these things, they were greatly astonished, saying: “Who then can be saved?” What bearing has this question, since the incomparably greater multitude of the poor could be saved if the rich were lost, unless because they understood that all who love riches, even if they do not have them, are to be counted among the rich? But Jesus, looking upon them, said, etc. Note that by his look he makes them attentive. “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” This must not be understood as meaning that the greedy and proud, signified by the name of that rich man, will enter the kingdom of heaven with their greed and pride; rather, it is possible for God, through his word—as has happened and as we see happening daily—to convert them from the desire for temporal things to the brightness of eternal things, and from destructive pride to most health-giving humility.

Then Peter answered [Col. 1415C]. When Peter heard that it was difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven, he wished to know the merit of those who leave riches, saying: “Behold, we have left all things.” Great confidence! Peter was a fisherman; he had not been rich, but sought food by craft and hand. Yet he speaks confidently, saying: “We have left all things”; and because leaving alone is insufficient, he adds what is perfect: “And we have followed thee,” etc. We have done what you commanded; what then will you give us as a reward, or what reward? He left much who retained nothing for himself. Each person possesses in mind as much as he desires. Therefore, he gives up much who sets aside every desire.

But Jesus said:

“Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me,” etc. [Col. 1415D] He did not say, “You who have left all things.” Socrates and many other philosophers did this, despising riches; rather, he said, “You who have followed me,” which properly belongs to believers.

“In the regeneration,” etc. There are two regenerations, two adoptions, and two resurrections. One regeneration is that of which it is said: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3). The other is that of which he now speaks. The first adoption is that of which the Apostle says: “You have not received the spirit of bondage in fear, but the spirit of adoption as sons” (Rom. 8). The second is that of which the same Apostle says: “We groan, awaiting the adoption as sons, the redemption of our body” (ibid.). What the first and second resurrection are is sufficiently clear.

[Col. 1416A] “In the regeneration,” I say, “when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty”—that is, when he who appeared in the form of a servant shall exercise judicial power—“you also shall sit upon twelve thrones,” etc., that is, judging, because those people refused to believe when you believed. By the twelve thrones is understood the universality of those judging; by the twelve tribes, the universality of those judged, on account of the two parts of seven, by which universality is often signified. These two parts, namely three and four, one multiplied by the other, make twelve. For every believer is completed by this number seven in the inward and outward person: inwardly, by memory, understanding, and will; outwardly, by flesh, moisture, breath, and heat—that is, cold, dry, moist, and hot.

[Col. 1416B] Therefore, whoever is such by divine grace that he loves the one God, who is Trinity, with all his heart, understanding, and will; knows how to govern all the affections of the fourfold body by prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude; and does not cease to proclaim to others that they should similarly believe in the one triune God and be prudent, just, strong, and temperate—such a person is contained in this number seven and twelve. Otherwise, since we read that Matthias was ordained in the place of Judas the traitor (Acts 1), where will the Apostle Paul, who labored more than all, sit in order to judge? Yet he himself says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6).

There is likewise a reason concerning those who are to be judged together in this number twelve [Col. 1416C]. For because it is said, “judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” it does not follow that another tribe, namely Levi, which is the thirteenth, will not be judged by them—unless we understand the saying as stated, or suitably in another way.

And everyone who has left house, etc. The preceding statement does not appear to apply only to the apostles: he says, “everyone,” etc. By brothers, sisters, father, and mother are understood fleshly affections. By fields are signified all temporal riches.

“He shall receive a hundredfold,” etc. [Col. 1416D] On the occasion of this saying, some propound the Jewish fable of a thousand years after the resurrection of the righteous, when all that we have relinquished for God’s sake is to be restored to us with manifold interest, and eternal life bestowed besides. These foolish people do not see that, although the promise may be worthy in other respects, in the matter of wives it would, according to the other evangelists, display a shameful multiplicity of hundreds—especially since God declares both that there will be no marrying in the resurrection, and that the things left for his sake are not to be received in this present time, even with persecutions. Rather, the hundredfold must be understood thus: whoever leaves fleshly things shall receive spiritual things. For the number one hundred belongs to heavenly things, because in calculation one hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right; and as the left pertains to temporal things, so the right pertains to heavenly things. Therefore, since one hundred belongs to the right hand, it fittingly signifies heavenly things. What follows—“and he shall possess eternal life” [Col. 1417A]—is an explanation and specification: or, “he shall receive a hundredfold,” that is, the disposition of possessing nothing.

“But many shall be,” etc. But because not all persevere in the same good purpose and fall back into vices, a terrible pronouncement follows: “Many who are first shall be last.” Look at Judas, changed from an apostle into an apostate, and say: many who are first shall be last. Look at the thief made a confessor upon the cross, rejoicing with Christ in paradise by the grace of faith on the very day on which he was crucified for his sins, and say: the last shall be first. And daily we see many established in the lay condition excel in great merits and rewards of life, while others, fervent from their earliest age in spiritual pursuit, at the end of life languish in idle sluggishness and, through inert foolishness, bring to completion in the flesh what [Col. 1417B] they began in the Spirit.

## CHAPTER XX

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder,” etc. He shows parabolically who are first becoming last and last becoming first. This householder is our Creator, who rules those whom he created and possesses his elect in this world as a master possesses subjects in his house. He has the universal vineyard, namely the Church, which, from righteous Abel to the last elect person who is to be born at the end of the world, has sent forth as many branches as it has produced saints. This Father hires labourers to cultivate his vineyard at the third hour of the morning, the sixth, the ninth, and the eleventh, because from the beginning of this world until its end he has not ceased to send preachers to instruct the people of the faithful.

[Col. 1417C] “Having made an agreement with the labourers for a denarius a day,” etc. The denarius bears the image of the king; it is called a denarius because among the ancients it was reckoned as worth ten coins. Therefore each person approaches the worship of the divine name in order to receive in Christ the image of deity which he had lost in paradise through the serpent’s envy; and the more earnestly he strives to fulfil the Decalogue, the more fully he is refashioned into the image of him who created it.

“And he went out about the third hour,” etc. The first hour was from Adam to Noah; the third, from Noah to Abraham.
