In this third hour he saw others standing in the marketplace, as though for sale, and ceasing from good work; these are the idle persons of whom he speaks, whom he sent into the vineyard. [Col. 1417D] Again he did likewise about the sixth hour, which is from Abraham to Moses; and likewise about the ninth, which is from Moses to the Lord’s coming. But about the eleventh, which is from the Lord’s coming until the end of the world, he himself went out—that is, he appeared in person, having previously made himself known through prophets and angels—and found others standing: namely, the Gentile peoples, languishing in idleness from good work. He says to them: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” For those who, after so long a time of the world had passed, had neglected to labour for their own life, stood idle, as it were, all day. Consider what they answered.

“Because no one,” etc. For no patriarch and no prophet had come to them. What, then, does it mean to say, “No one has hired us,” except that [Col. 1418A] no one showed us the paths of life? We may also distinguish these same different hours in each individual according to the stages of age. Morning is the childhood of our understanding. The third hour is adolescence, because the sun, as it were, is now rising high while the heat of age increases. The sixth is youth, when the fullness of strength is established. The ninth is old age, when the sun—that is, the heat of age—declines. The eleventh is called decrepit or very advanced age. In all these stages some are brought to a good life. But one who neglects to live for God until the final stage of age has stood idle, as it were, until the eleventh hour; hence it is rightly said to such persons: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” etc. At least in your last days come to your senses, and come to the paths of life, now having not much labour left to perform. And this is what he says: [Col. 1418B] “Go also into my vineyard.”

“When evening had come,” that is, when the end of each person—or the end of the world, that is, the last age of the world—had arrived. Of this end John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2); and the Apostle: “Upon us the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10).

“The lord of the vineyard says to his steward,” that is, the Father says to his Son, into whose hands he gave all things: “Call the labourers before the tribunal and render to them their reward according to what each has done, beginning from the last unto the first,” that is, from the time of the last. The time of the last is from Christ’s passion to the end of the age. The first are called all those from the beginning of the world until Christ’s passion. For Christ preached only to the Jews until the passion, according to what [Col. 1418C] he says: “I was not sent” (Matt. 15), etc. But as Christ approached his passion he said: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10). In the passion he also signified the second mission when he said: “But now, let him who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag” (Luke 22). For there were two missions of the apostles. The first was particular, to the Jews, when they were told: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10); in it both purse and bag were forbidden. The second was universal, both to Jews and Gentiles; in it purse and bag were permitted, which he signified in the many words previously cited—namely: “He who has a purse, let him likewise take a bag.” As if to say: Now, that is, in this other mission, whoever has a purse, [Col. 1418D] let him take it, that is, carry it. He declared this mission more plainly after the passion, saying: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). The first period, then, lasted as long as it was not permitted to preach except to Jews alone. But after this obedience had been fulfilled, because the Jews did not wish to be converted by Christ’s preaching, he gave authority to offer the word of God to all people. Therefore he begins to render recompense in the time of the last, when he saved the thief in the passion and brought the ancient fathers out of hell, introducing them into heaven on the day of the Ascension. Thus it was fulfilled that he began both to give first to the last, as to the thief, and, in the time of the last, to pay recompense to all, because until [Col. 1419A] the time of the passion all descended to hell.

“When they had come, therefore,” etc. Eternal life itself will be equally the same for all, and one denarius will be assigned to all. Yet there are many distinctions there, according to the saying: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). Thus, one denarius, and individual denarii.

“But when the first came, they thought,” etc. The question arises: how can they be said to envy and murmur, when in receiving the reward there will be neither envy nor murmuring? But it is customary in the divine page to take many persons together as a collective body, and for certain words to suit certain persons and other words others, rather than the entire collective. Therefore, when the first are said [Col. 1419B] to have murmured and yet to have received their reward, this must be understood of different persons in different respects. The Jews are those who murmured, and who, at the beginning of the Church, set themselves above believers called from the Gentiles, saying that they were God’s people from the beginning, whom God loved and cherished, and who bore the burden and heat in legal ceremonies. They also said that the Gentile people were dogs rather than human beings, judging them unworthy, though they had served idols, to be considered their equals. But the Lord, who came not to call the righteous but humble penitents, and to whom humble confession arising from evil works is more pleasing than proud boasting over good ones, adds: “Friend, I do you no wrong.” This murmuring was among the Jews, who thought in the world that they would receive more in the future. [Col. 1419C] These did not receive the reward; rather, the perfect, who did not murmur, received it. Thus it is to be read in the collective sense: the first—that is, Jews converted in the first period—supposed in some of their members that they would receive more in the future than the Gentiles. But those same first received individual denarii in other persons; thus, while receiving in some persons, they murmured in others. This is the Jews’ complaint against the Lord:

“These last,” that is, the Gentiles, “have worked one hour,” that is, have laboured. “But we Jews have laboured throughout the whole time under the law. And we have borne the burden and heat of the day,” that is, we have long sweated under the burden of the law, or endured the more prolonged temptations of the flesh. [Col. 1419D] To them the Lord answered through those who were more perfect among them: “Friend”—a friend by faith, but not a friend by works—“did you not agree with me for a daily denarius,” that is, eternal life? That is, did you not receive my faith? But because you have begun to envy and murmur, therefore take what is yours, that is, what you have deserved—namely, condemnation—and go, that is, depart from me. “But I wish to give to this last,” that is, the Gentile people, “according to merit, as I give to you according to merit.” Such is my will.

“Or is it not lawful for me to do what I will?” I act according to the goodness of my mercy. “Or is your eye evil,” that is, envious, “because I am good?” Thus the first shall be last and the last first. As if to say: As you see the Jews, [Col. 1420A] who seemed first—that is, greatest—becoming last—that is, most contemptible—through condemnation, and the Gentiles, who were formerly last—that is, liable to condemnation through idolatry—becoming first, that is, exalted through faith, so it shall happen in many other cases. Others say that no one murmured, but that the Lord inserted this in order to show that no one can justly complain concerning his own work.

“For many.” The first shall become last, that is, liable to condemnation. For not all called to faith will be saved. And this is: “For many,” etc.

“And Jesus going up,” etc. Christ, going up to Jerusalem in order to suffer, again prepares them for temptation by making his death known to them, lest they be disturbed when they see him dying. He also announces the resurrection [Col. 1420B] for their consolation. “We are going up,” he says, according to the situation of the place. The wording is straightforward.

“Then there came to him,” etc. The question arises: whence did the sons of Zebedee acquire their idea of a kingdom? From this cause, I think: they had heard that he would rise on the third day. Therefore they thought that after the resurrection he would reign in the world; eager for honour, they desired to hold the first place with him. But since they did not dare to ask this themselves, they ask through their mother.

“Who said to her,” etc. He does not ask as though ignorant of what she wants, but so that, when she had explained it, he might make the irrationality of the request plain. For they asked as irreligious lovers of glory, lacking discernment in useful requests. Notice that the Lord frequently permits his disciples to [Col. 1420C] say, do, or think something wrongly, so that from their fault he may find occasions to teach and expound the rule of godliness.

“She said to him,” etc. The mother of Zebedee’s sons asks through feminine error and maternal affection, not knowing what she asks. Nor is it surprising that she is reproved for ignorance, when Peter is said, at the point where he wished to make three tents, not to have known what he was saying (Mark 9). It should be noted that Matthew writes that the mother asked this for her sons; Mark, wishing to disclose their own desire and intention to readers, is silent about the mother and says rather that they themselves made the request, which he knew had been made through their mother at their urging (Mark 10). Note also that their desire was good indeed, but their request inconsiderate. Therefore, although they ought not to obtain it, the simplicity of their request did not deserve to be put to shame, because it was born of love for the Lord. Accordingly, he blamed neither their will nor their purpose, but reproved only their ignorance, saying:

“You do not know what you ask.” Note that, satisfying both evangelists, the Lord replied not to the mother but to those whose petition it was: they do not know what they ask who seek from the Lord a seat of glory which they do not yet deserve. The height of honour delighted them, but first they ought to have undertaken the path of labour. They desired to reign sublimely with Christ, but first they had to suffer humbly for Christ.

“Can you drink the cup,” etc. As though he said: Since you wish to be exalted with me, can you be humbled with me through [Col. 1421A] suffering? By the name of the cup he signifies the suffering of martyrdom, by which it was fitting that both he himself and they should be brought to completion. The Lord was not ignorant that they could imitate him through his passion; but he said this to them so that, as the Lord questions and they answer, we all may hear that no one can reign with Christ unless he has imitated his passion.

“They say to him: We can.” They answered not so much out of confidence in their own heart as from ignorance of suffering. For war seems desirable to those who do not know it; so too the trial of suffering and death seems light to the inexperienced. For if the Lord could say, “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26), how much more would they not have said, “We can,” [Col. 1421B] had they known what the trial of death was like? For suffering entails great pain, but death entails even greater fear.

“He says to them: You shall indeed drink my cup,” etc. James was beheaded by Herod. John was cast into a vat of boiling oil and exiled to Patmos; in spirit he did not fail of martyrdom. Thus many others drank the Lord’s cup, although the persecutor did not shed their blood. But what follows:

“But to sit is not mine to give to you, but to those for whom it is prepared by my Father,” etc., is to be understood thus: the kingdom of heaven belongs not to one who gives, but to one who receives. For there is no respect of persons with God (Rom. 2); rather, whoever proves himself such that he is worthy of the kingdom of heaven will receive what is prepared not for a person, but for a life [Col. 1421C] of such a kind. If, then, you are such as will obtain the kingdom of heaven, which my Father prepared for those who triumph and conquer, you shall receive it. Or otherwise: “It is not mine to give to you,” that is, to the proud—which you still are—but it is prepared for others. Therefore do not be proud, but become others, that is, humble yourselves, though you already wish to be exalted; then it is prepared for you.

“And when the ten heard,” etc. The ten apostles are indignant not with the woman and do not attribute the boldness of the request to her, but to the sons, who, ignorant of their own measure, had flamed up with excessive ambition or desire. For just as, as John says, those two asked carnally, so these were carnally distressed. For if they had understood and had right discernment, neither would the former have asked such a thing nor the latter been grieved at such a request. Thus these were ambitious, those envious; yet both are set before us.

“But Jesus,” etc. Jesus, the humble and gentle teacher, neither rebukes the two petitioners for excessive ambition nor reproves the remaining ten for indignation and envy. Rather, he gives such an example as teaches that the greater is the one who has become lesser, and that he becomes lord who is the servant of all. In vain, therefore, did the former seek immoderate things or the latter grieve, since one comes to the highest summit not by power but by humility. Whoever, then, as he says, desires to hold the greatest heights of divinity must pursue the lowest places of humility. And whoever wishes to surpass a brother in reigning must first surpass him in serving. He therefore says: [Col. 1422A] “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles,” etc. As though he said: You wish, in the manner of secular people, to surpass one another by precedence in order to gain possession of the kingdom; but it shall not be so, because one reaches exaltation rather through humility. And this is what follows:

“It shall not be so among you; but whoever,” etc. “As the Son of Man,” etc. He sets forth an example, so that if they made light of his words, they might at least blush before his deeds, saying: “As the Son of Man came not to be served,” that is, to rule temporally, “but to serve,” not only by preaching or admonishing through miracles, but by expending for us the life which he received—not for all, but for many, that is, for those who wished to believe.

“And as they went out.” Luke relates that the Lord, as he approached Jericho, gave sight to one blind man. [Col. 1422B] Matthew, however, reports that Christ, as he went out from Jericho, gave sight to two blind men. Mark reports one. In this matter no one should suppose that the evangelists write contradictory accounts. Rather, Luke supplies the healing of one blind man on entering Jericho, which Matthew omitted. As for Mark’s narration that one was healed on entering Jericho, while Matthew says two: this must be understood in that one of them was well known, and Mark mentions him, whereas the other was of no name. Hence Mark gives the former’s own name and his father’s name, saying: “The son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind man, was sitting by the way begging” (Mark 10). But if he was noble, why was he a beggar? Having been cast down from some great prosperity, his was a most notable and famous [Col. 1422C] misery. Therefore Mark wished to mention him alone, because his healing brought to this miracle a fame as conspicuous as his calamity had been. Mystically, Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” and through it is signified the waning of our mortality. Thus, approaching Jericho, he restored light to the blind man, because before the passion, as he was drawing near to death, he converted the Jewish people. The Lord is rightly said to have converted the Jewish people close to death, because they maintain that he preached the Gospel only a few years before the passion. Going out from Jericho, he gave sight to two, because after death and resurrection he caused the Gospel to be preached to Jews and Gentiles. But Mark’s statement that one was healed refers to the salvation [Col. 1422D] of the Gentiles, whose blindness was especially well known. Moreover, since Mark wrote for Gentiles, he appropriately commemorates one, so that the figure might suit the salvation of those whom he was training in the faith. Matthew, however, who wrote the Gospel for Hebrews and whose Gospel was also to come to the knowledge of the Gentiles, rightly says that two were healed, teaching that the grace of faith belongs to each people. The two blind men sat beside the way because both peoples, being blind, sat not on the way but beside it, while already adhering through desire to the Christian faith and longing to be enlightened by God.

“They heard that Jesus was passing by.” That passing signifies the mystery of the Incarnation. For when he was born, suffered, rose again, and ascended, he then, as it were, made a passage. [Col. 1423A] Both peoples heard this mystery through the apostles’ preaching and, having heard, cried out in faith, desiring to be enlightened:

“Lord, Son of David.” They recognize God and man: when they say “Lord,” they recognize God; when they say “Son of David,” they confess him as man.

“But the crowd,” etc. This crowd consists of fleshly desires, which are accustomed to obstruct good inclination; or else, persecutors, who commonly oppose those wishing to come to faith through threats or enticements. But the blind men pressed more earnestly by knocking and praying, until they overcame the uproar of the crowd, saying:

“Lord, have mercy.” “And Jesus stood,” etc. Passing, he hears; standing, he gives sight: because he had mercy through humility when he passed by, and through the eternity of the Word, [Col. 1423B] which is never moved, he restores light.

“And he said to them: What do you wish me to do for you?” He was not ignorant what the blind men wanted; but he wishes them to ask for what he foreknows that we ought to ask and that he will grant. For he urgently exhorts us to prayer, and yet says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matt. 6). He therefore asks in order that it may be requested. They say to him: “Lord, that [our eyes] may be opened,” etc. The blind seek from the Lord not gold but light. They judge it of little worth to seek anything apart from light, because, although blind people might possess anything whatever, without light they could see nothing. Let us therefore imitate them: let us seek from the Lord not false riches, not earthly gifts, not fleeting honours, but light. “But Jesus, having compassion on them, touched their eyes.” Because he enlightened their hearts with his own light, [Col. 1423C] they immediately saw, because they believed and were enlightened; and they followed him, because they prepared themselves for imitation. The person who sees and follows is one who practises the good which he understands.

## CHAPTER XXI

“And when he had drawn near to Jerusalem,” etc. In this figure is represented the calling of the whole Church, as is understood in the exposition of this Gospel. But according to the letter, he who had so often come to Jerusalem without praise now wished to be received with palm branches, boughs, and the voices of children, because in earlier times his hour had not yet come; and therefore, when they wished to seize him, he hid himself from them.

**JOHN CHRYSOSTOM.** [Col. 1423D] But now, as the time of the passion approached, he willingly advanced to the passion, willingly offered himself, and by his honourable reception provoked them to greater envy. For their wickedness demanded this: those who would not be corrected should become worse. The miracle heard concerning Lazarus stirred the crowd to this honourable meeting. Hence John says: “Because he raised Lazarus from the dead, the crowd came to meet him” (John 12). Nor did he come to Jerusalem on this day without reason. For it was the tenth day of the month, as we have from John’s Gospel. He says that six days before Passover he came to Bethany, where a supper was held and Martha served. Lazarus was one of those reclining at table, and then Mary anointed Jesus’ feet. But on the next day he came to Jerusalem, and they received him with palm branches (ibid.). [Col. 1424A] Thus we know that he came to Jerusalem on the fifth day before Passover, which was the tenth day of the month; for Passover was celebrated on the fourteenth day. He wished to enter on the tenth day because this had been prefigured in the Law, where it is commanded: “On the tenth day of this month each shall take a lamb according to families and households” (Exod. 12). And shortly afterward it says: “You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening” (ibid.). Therefore on the tenth day of the first month the lamb to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded to be brought into the house, because the Lord was to enter, on the tenth day of the same month—that is, five days before Passover—the city in which he would suffer.

Now let us return to the mystery. Bethphage is “the bond of priests” [Col. 1424B] on the Mount of Olives, and is interpreted “house of the mouth.” It therefore signifies the first preachers, who were the house of the mouth, to whom Christ came first, because he first converted the apostles and their other fellow disciples. The Mount of Olives also signifies the primitive Church. For the olive produces the nourishment of light, namely oil, which also warms and gladdens the flesh and is used in the sacrament of baptism. Furthermore, it is the tree of peace, all of which is fitting for the Church. For the Church is peaceful and proclaims peace to others; Christ sanctifies it by the anointing of spiritual gifts, enlightens it with the light of knowledge, and makes it rich with the oil of gladness, that is, spiritual grace. Or otherwise: the Mount of Olives signifies the loftiness [Col. 1424C] of the Lord’s love and mercy, which is deservedly compared to oil. For as oil floats above all other liquids, so mercy and love excel all other virtues.

“Then he sent two disciples,” etc. Therefore, when the Lord had converted the primitive Church, he wished to convert others through it, whom he might lead to the heavenly Jerusalem. He therefore sent two disciples, that is, two kinds of preachers: some to the Gentiles, others to the Jews. Some say that these were Peter and Philip, because Peter baptized Cornelius, the first converted Gentile. Philip, however, preached in Samaria, which is interpreted “she-ass.” Thus Philip brought the she-ass, while Peter brought Cornelius as the colt of a she-ass. Or, he sent two in order to remind them that they must be perfect in doctrine and [Col. 1424D] action; or two because of the sacraments of love.

“And he said to them: Go into the village,” etc. That is, go against the world, which is fortified with the many opinions of philosophers. The village signifies the world, which is always opposed to us. The two disciples are the teachers of the Church, who must always loose and preach to the people through prayers, confessions, penance, and fasting. The she-ass signifies the Church, or the Synagogue, bound in the old Law and now loosed in the new Law. The humble and gentle people are signified by the colt, on which he sits and rests; and that people, spreading branches on the way, signifies all faithful people, who place faith in Christ and bear the fruit of good work.

[Col. 1425A] “And immediately you shall find a she-ass tied, and a colt with her,” etc. **JOHN.** The she-ass, which had been under the yoke and tamed, signifies the Synagogue, which had been pressed under the yoke of the Law. The playful and free colt of the she-ass signifies the people of the nations; yet another evangelist says that the colt was tied. For each people was bound with the cords of sins and needed to be loosed. The former sinned by making bad use of the Law it had received; the latter sinned by never receiving it. Therefore all sinned and need the grace of God (Rom. 3). The other evangelists, who wrote for Gentiles, mention only the colt as being brought to the Lord. But Matthew, a Hebrew of Hebrews, wrote the Gospel in the Hebrew tongue and also mentions the she-ass, by a providential arrangement, so that he might mystically teach that [Col. 1425B] those whose salvation the evangelists sought in writing were prefigured as persons to be saved by the Lord. Note that Mark says that the colt of the she-ass was found before a door, at a junction of two ways. The door is Christ; outside him the Gentile people stood bound, not in one way of faith but amid diverse errors.

“And if anyone says anything to you,” etc. That is, if anyone wishes to deny their obedience, say that the Lord has need of them. “Say,” that is, do not cease to preach that the Lord is simply Lord of all things, to whom every creature ought to serve, and that he has need of them so that they may serve him.

The apostles and other teachers are commanded that, if any adversity stands in their way, if anyone prevents sinners [Col. 1425C] from being loosed from the devil’s snare and brought to the Lord through confession, they must not merely continue preaching but steadfastly make known that the Lord needs such persons to build his Church.

However savage the persecutor may be, he cannot obstruct the salvation of those whom the Lord knows to be his own.

“The Lord has need of them,” etc. For it is just that those who serve the creature should serve the Creator. At times God left the Gentiles in the devil’s power for a season in order to test them; he did not despise them eternally so as to destroy them.

“And immediately he will send them.” Namely, to be devoted to the Lord’s service. Or, as it is read, the animal, after it had entered Jerusalem, was sent back to its [Col. 1425D] owner. But the prophetic meaning of the animal remained in the Church. Moreover, Christ had need not of the visible animal but of what was understood by it: not the flesh, but the rational faculty. Therefore the flesh was sent away, while the rational faculty was retained. In saying, “and immediately he will send them,” note that he does not say this of the devil, who previously held them, but of their own free choice assisted by the gift of grace.

“All this was done in order that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled” (Isa. 62), etc. The testimony of prophecy is applied to this event, so that it might appear that the Lord fulfilled all that had been written concerning him, while the Scribes and Pharisees, blinded by envy, refused to understand the things which they themselves read.

[Col. 1426A] “Say to the daughter of Zion.” The daughter of Zion is the Church of the faithful, belonging to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, and whose portion among the people of Israel was then very small. The Lord therefore commanded his preachers: “Say to the daughter of Zion.” According to the letter, this means the Jewish people; mystically, the Church.

“Behold, your king,” etc. **JOHN.** “Behold” is an adverb of showing, as if to say: See not with bodily sight but with spiritual understanding; behold the works of his virtues. And do not say: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19), because this truly is your king, and he comes for you if you believe, against you if you do not believe.

“Meek,” etc. Because the first coming was humble, the second will be terrible; because he sits upon a she-ass and a colt, not in a golden chariot but upon a beast [Col. 1426B] friendly to peace. Mystically, he sits upon each people, humbled under its Lord. But when it says “upon a colt and a she-ass,” this should not be understood literally as though he sat upon both, but as dwelling in the hearts of both peoples signified by those two animals.

“And the disciples went,” etc. Great was Christ’s power, which thus prepared the heart of the owner to give the animal. “And they brought [them] to Jesus and put,” etc. Because, by Christ’s power, teachers called both peoples to faith.

“And they put their garments upon him.” That is, they adorned them with the good examples and sayings of the holy fathers. For the Lord ought not to mount a naked she-ass or a naked colt, because whether one is Gentile or [Col. 1426C] Jew, unless adorned with the sayings and deeds of the saints just mentioned, one cannot have the Lord as one’s rider. The garments of the apostles are divine commandments and spiritual grace, by which the shamefulness of our flesh is covered. The peoples had previously been naked of these, but now, adorned through the apostles, they have Christ as their rider. The lesser crowd could not put garments upon the she-ass but laid them on the way, because the holy martyrs, stripping off the flesh—which is, as it were, the covering of the soul—prepare by their blood a way of example for the simpler people, so that they may not hesitate to go where they see the martyrs preceding them in the battle of martyrdom. Otherwise: the garments are the carnal commandments of the Law, which Christians were to trample upon on the way—that is, in Christ. Observe also that [Col. 1426D] the apostles put garments upon the beast, but the rest of the Jewish crowd puts garments beneath the beast’s feet, because Christians are instructed and adorned by the apostles’ commandments, whereas the commandments of the Law are trampled underfoot—that is, when we reject all fleshly customs and circumcision.

**MORAL APPLICATION.** Our Saviour sits upon the beast and proceeds toward Jerusalem whenever each faithful person, governing his own soul—that is, his own beast—leads it toward the inward vision of peace. Those who spread garments in the way signify those who subdue their bodies through abstinence, in order to prepare for him a path to the mind, or to furnish good examples to those who follow.

“Others were cutting branches from the trees.” They cut branches or boughs who extract good words and sayings [Col. 1427A] from the books of the Fathers, by which the hearts of simple Christians are built up, lest they err on the way of truth. “But the crowds,” etc. Those who went before signify those who lived before Christ’s coming; those who followed signify those who lived after his coming. Yet both agree in the same voice of confession, all crying out and saying:

“Hosanna to the Son of David,” etc. **GREGORY.** Hosanna is a Hebrew word, composed of a corrupted and an intact element. For *hosanna* is said as though *osi anna*. *Osi* is interpreted “save,” “make saving,” or “make safe.” *Anna* is an interjection of entreaty, like our “I beg you.” Hence Jerome translates it thus: “Hosanna,” that is, “Save, I beg you.” This verse is taken from the one hundred and seventeenth Psalm, where it says: [Col. 1427B] “O Lord, make me safe; O Lord, grant prosperity; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”; and so it reads in the translation of the Seventy Interpreters. But in the Hebrew truth it says only: “I beg you, O Lord, save; I beg you.” It follows: “Blessed,” that is, glorious, is he who was incarnate in the name—not his own, as Antichrist is, but in the name of the Lord, that is, of his Father, whom he glorifies. Again they repeat *hosanna*, that is, “Save, I beg you,” and declare where they wish to be saved: namely, “in the highest,” that is, in heavenly things, not earthly ones.

And when he had entered Jerusalem, the city was stirred, etc. It wondered at the crowd, not knowing the truth. And they ask: “Who is this, whom they thus meet with praises?” But the people said: “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.” The common people [Col. 1427C] confess Jesus, that the confession of his name, beginning with the lesser, might reach the greater. And he entered, etc. Because, upon entering the city, he first went to the Temple, he showed us the pattern of religion which we ought to follow: wherever we arrive at a house of prayer, if one is there, we should first enter it; and, commending ourselves to God through prayer, should then approach our business more securely. He also entered for another reason: for Luke relates that, when Jesus drew near, he saw the city, wept, and foretold its destruction (Luke 19); then, entering the Temple, he began to cast out the sellers, in order to show that the cause of the city’s destruction depended especially upon the iniquity of the priests.

And he cast out, etc. The priests had devised how they might [Col. 1427D] make plunder from the people: they would sell, as dearly as possible, the animals and other things to be offered; then have the offerings back again, and sell once more whatever they could not consume. And because perhaps some had no ready money with which to buy, they also appointed their own money-changers to lend money. Since the Law forbade the taking of usury, for that loan they took small gifts—namely apples, grapes, and vegetables—as though Ezekiel had not guarded against this sin when he said: “You shall not take usury or excess” (Ezek. 18). Therefore, when the Lord saw this commerce in the Temple, he was stirred by grief at the robbery, or by zeal of spirit. Hence the Psalmist says: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68); and he cast them out.

[Col. 1428A] He had already cast them out once before, as John alone relates; but the others speak of the final expulsion, when, having made a whip of cords, he cast them all out. It should be noted that he found in the Temple only things being sold or bought which were necessary for the Temple’s ministry. If, then, he would not permit even those things to be sold in the Temple which he wished to be offered there, because of the pursuit of greed or fraud, how greatly would he punish if he found there persons occupied with laughter or idle talk, or enslaved to some other vice? Yet another meaning is to be understood spiritually. For in this figure the Simoniac heresy is condemned. Simon Magus wished to buy from blessed Peter the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the apostle pronounced upon him this sentence of condemnation: “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8). Nor are buyers alone condemnable, but sellers also.

[Col. 1428B] Hence the Lord cast all sellers and buyers from the Temple. For all Simoniacs are excluded from the Temple of God, either by the sentence of men or before the eyes of God.

And he overturned the tables of the money-changers, etc. These tables signify altars. The money-changers are priests, who attend more to money than to divine service. He overturns the altars when he frequently permits them to be overturned by a hidden judgment.

And the seats of those selling doves, etc. Since the Holy Spirit appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove, the charisms of the Holy Spirit are rightly signified by the dove. Who, then, are those now in God’s Temple who sell doves, except those who in the Church receive a price for the laying on of hands, through which laying on of hands the Spirit is bestowed from heaven? Therefore the dove is sold when the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price.

GREGORY. But our Redeemer overturns the seats of those selling doves, because he destroys the priesthood of such traders. It should also be noted that one sort of price comes from the hand, another from the tongue, another from office. A gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favour; a gift from office is service. Whoever grants the gifts of the Holy Spirit to someone because of any of these things receives a price for doves. Therefore the Prophet says: “Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. 33). By saying “every,” he wished to signify the diversity of gifts.

[Col. 1428D] And he said: “It is written” (Isa. 56): “My house shall be called a house of prayer.” As though he said: My house is called an oratory; let no one do in an oratory anything except that for which it was made and from which it receives its name.

“But you have made it a den of robbers.” For those who sat in the Temple to receive gifts would undoubtedly seek to inflict injuries upon certain persons who did not give. Thus the house of prayer had become a den of robbers, because they knew how to stand in the Temple for this purpose: either to strive bodily to persecute those who gave no gifts, or spiritually to kill those who did give them. The Temple and house of God also are the very mind and conscience of believers; when these produce perverse thoughts from injury done to a neighbour, robbers, as it were, dwell in a den.

[Col. 1429A] And blind and lame persons came to him, etc. Having entered the Temple, he healed the infirm, in order that what the children testified in words he himself might confirm by miracles. Mystically: having cast unworthy priests out of the Temple, he daily heals simple sinners who approach him through repentance: first enlightening those blind in understanding, and directing those lame in action into the way of uprightness.

But when the chief priests saw, etc. The scribes, distressed and indignant at his so manifest power and at his praise celebrated by children, sought anxiously whether the rulers could seize him in some statement, saying: “Do you hear what these children are saying?” As though they said: “Do you attribute this praise to yourself?” But Jesus tempers his judgment and answer moderately.

[Col. 1429B] For he did not say: “The children do well, because they bear witness to me,” which the scribes would not have wished to hear. Nor again did he say: “The children are mistaken; spare their age.” Rather, while he himself is silent, he confirms the children’s words by the testimony of David, who says (Ps. 8): “Have you never read: ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise,’” etc.? Witnesses of Christ’s miracles are called infants, not in age but in simplicity of heart, nursing, as it were, on milk—that is, on the sweetness of miracles, which are called milk; whereas bread is perfect doctrine.

And leaving them, as unbelievers and opponents, he went out beyond the city to Bethany, that is, to the house of obedience, already then prefiguring the calling of the Gentiles.

[Col. 1429C] Hence it is said: “A people whom I did not know has served me” (Ps. 17), etc. Note also that Christ, truly poor and flattering no one, found no host in the city, but was received as a guest by Lazarus and his sisters in a small town. But returning to the city in the morning, he was hungry. Note the practice of the diligent worker: he is said to have returned to the city in the morning in order to preach and to gain some persons for God the Father. By the statement that he was hungry, the reality of his flesh is indicated; or it is said that he hungered for the salvation of believers. We may also discern in this morning return to Jerusalem his resurrection itself, when, the darkness of night having been dispersed and the devil condemned, the radiance of the morning resurrection illuminated the whole world.

[Col. 1429D] He was hungry: either showing the reality of human flesh, or hungering for the salvation of believers, burning with desire for Israel’s faith.

And seeing a fig tree, etc. God sometimes preaches by words, sometimes by deeds. For what reason was there for him, being hungry, to seek fruit on a fig tree when it was not its season—for the Jewish Passover was near—and to condemn the tree with a curse, unless he wished by an action to frighten the people whom he instructed by word? The fig tree is the Synagogue, which was not on the road but beside the road: that is, not in the Spirit which leads to Christ, who is the true Way, but in the letter of the Law, which leads outside the true way. And he came to it and found nothing on it but leaves only, etc. He came through the Incarnation. The leaves are the words of the Law and Prophets.

[Col. 1430A] He found words in them, not the fruit of good action. It is therefore condemned, because Judaea, which sounded forth the words of Scripture without works, was worthily punished by vengeance. Yet I say this not because the whole Synagogue was rejected, from which, as is evident, the primitive Church was built; but that portion of the Synagogue deserved condemnation which refused to feed the hungry Christ by good works, and which wished rather to be shaded by the leaves of spiritual words than laden with the fruits of the Spirit.

And the disciples, seeing it, marvelled and said: “How did it wither at once?” etc. Since the Lord was about to endure the scandal of the cross, he wished to prepare the minds of his disciples beforehand by some sign, so that they might see that by the same power by which the fig tree withered he could destroy his enemies, unless he awaited their salvation through patience.

[Col. 1430B] But Jesus answered and said, etc. Certain Gentiles are accustomed to write insults against the Church and reproach our people because they have not had complete faith in God, since they have never been able to move mountains. They must be answered that not everything which has occurred in the Church has been written down, as Scripture itself testifies concerning the deeds of Christ, our God and Lord (John 21). Thus this too could have occurred: a mountain might be removed from the earth and cast into the sea, if necessity required it. We read that, by the prayers of our blessed father Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a man eminent in merits and miracles, a mountain moved back on land only so far as the inhabitants of the city needed.

[Col. 1430C] For when, wishing to build a church in a suitable place, he saw that it was narrower than the undertaking required, because it was hemmed in on one side by a rocky sea-cliff and on the other by a neighbouring mountain, he came by night to the place and, bending his knees, reminded the Lord of his promise, that, according to faith, he should make the mountain retreat farther off. In the morning, when he returned, he found that the mountain had left the church-builders as much space as they required.

Mystically, these miracles are fulfilled in the saints. For the devil is truly a mountain of pride, which is driven from the hearts of unbelievers through the preaching of the saints and cast into the sea; that is, he is permitted to exercise greater madness among those predestined for death. Ambrose, however, says otherwise. Because the Gospel was preached through the apostles, the Lord himself, who is called a mountain, was removed from the Jews in order that he might be cast, as it were, into the sea among the Gentiles through the apostles’ preaching.

[Col. 1430D] “And whatever things,” etc. A distinction among those praying should be noted: whoever has perfect faith, which works through love, can obtain by prayer—or even by command—what he asks.

And when he had come into the Temple, they came to him, etc. Not so much in faith as in body, as appears from their words, by which they tempted him, saying: “By what authority do you do these things? And who gave you this authority?” In various ways they construct the same accusation as above, when they said: “This man casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Luke 11 [the source reads II]). For when they say, “By what authority do you do these things?” they doubt God’s authority and intend it to be understood that what he does is of the devil; and when they add, “Who gave you this authority?” they most clearly deny the Son of God, whom they suppose performs signs not by his own powers but by another’s.

[Col. 1431A] Jesus answered and said, etc. The Lord could have refuted the slander of the tempters with an open answer, but wisely asks a question, so that they may condemn themselves by their own silence, according to the saying: “The Lord broke their teeth in their own mouth” (Ps. 57). For if they had answered that John’s baptism was from heaven, the consequent reply was: “Why then were you not baptized by John?” But if they had said that it was devised by human deception and had nothing divine, they feared a popular uprising. For all the assembled crowds had received John’s baptism and regarded him as a prophet. Thus this most impious contest answered with feigned humility: “We do not know.” It used the word “do not know” in order to lay its own traps.

[Col. 1431B] Jesus therefore said to them: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things,” etc. In answering that they did not know, they lied. Accordingly, following their answer, the Lord too would have had to say, “Neither do I know”; but Truth cannot lie, and therefore he says: “Neither do I tell you.” Thus he shows both that they knew but would not answer, and that he himself knew well; and therefore he did not tell them, because they did not tell what they knew. Justly confounded, therefore, they departed shamefully.

[Col. 1431C] Note that truth is concealed for two reasons: either because the hearers are incapable. Hence it is said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16). Or because they are contemptuous. Hence it is said: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7).

“But what do you think? A certain man,” etc. Having confuted the priests by a cautious reply, he immediately adds a parable by which he both accuses them of impiety and teaches that the kingdom of God is to be transferred to the Gentiles; or, more simply, this parable concerns not Gentiles and Jews, but sinners and righteous persons, as the Lord afterwards said.

“Amen, I say to you that tax collectors and prostitutes,” etc. We must see who this man was. This man is God, who loves with fatherly affection all whom he created.

[Col. 1431D] Although he is Lord by nature, he nevertheless prefers to be loved as Father rather than feared as Lord. Hence, at the beginning of the commandments of the Law, he did not say: “Fear the Lord your God,” but said: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Exod. 20), etc.

Such a father had two sons: the Gentile and the Jew. Approaching the first—that is, the Gentile people—he said: “Son, go today,” that is, at this present time, “work in my vineyard,” that is, do my will. This means: what you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another. But we must see how God spoke this natural law to his sons. He spoke not to their face, as a man does, but in the heart, as God does; not a word sounding in the ears, but understanding in the hearts.

[Col. 1432A] But he answered and said: “I will not,” etc. He said “I will not” indeed in thought. For one who has knowledge of good and evil, leaves the good, and follows evil, appears to answer God who persuades him: “I will not.”

But afterwards, moved by repentance, etc., he went and corrected the defiance of his speech by labour; and this occurred at the coming of the Saviour. Then, approaching the other, he spoke likewise. But he answered that he would go, and yet did not go. For the Jewish people answered the Lord through Moses: “All that he has said, we will do” (Exod. 24), and yet did not do it: namely, it did not cultivate the vineyard. Rather, it killed the Lord of the vineyard outside the vineyard.

“Which of the two did the father’s will?” They said to him: “The first.” Behold how they are condemned by their own judgment. Therefore, lest the meaning of the parable, which seemed especially to concern them, should escape them, the Lord wished—

[Col. 1432B] Jesus said to them: “Amen, I say to you that tax collectors,” etc., such as Matthew, “and prostitutes,” such as Mary, “will go before you into the kingdom of God”: that is, into the Church in the present age, or into the future, namely the heavenly Jerusalem. And he gives the reason why: “For John came,” etc. The literal sense is plain. “Hear another parable.”

“There was a householder,” etc. The chief priests, who had asked the Lord by what authority he did these things and wanted to catch him in a word—him who was the fountain of all wisdom—are now overcome by their own art, and hear in parables what they did not deserve to hear openly. The householder is understood to be God,

[Col. 1432C] who planted the vineyard of which Isaiah says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts” (Isa. 5); and David: “You transplanted a vine from Egypt” (Ps. 79).

“And he put a hedge around it”: that is, he assigned to it the guardianship of angels. “And he dug a winepress in it”: that is, he imposed upon it the legal disciplines, through which they might be compelled to live well. Or the winepresses are those persons—namely martyrs—after whom three psalms (8, 70, 83) are entitled, when it is said, “A psalm for the winepresses”: that is, he placed in it such men as were ready to be tortured for Christ’s name, so that through them some abundance of the Holy Spirit might flow out.

“And he built a tower”: that is, the Temple, of which it is said through Micah: “And you, misty tower, daughter of Zion” (Mic. 4).

[Col. 1432D] “And he leased it to tenants,” whom elsewhere he called workers in the vineyard. “And he went abroad.” This was not a change of place, but a leaving of free choice to work well. For God, by whom all things are filled, from where could he be absent?

“But when the season of fruits came,” etc. He properly says the season of fruits, not of produce. For there was no fruit in the stubborn people; yet to receive that fruit he sent servants, whom they seized and either beat, as Jeremiah; or killed, as Isaiah; or stoned, as Naboth and Zechariah, whom they slaughtered between the Temple and the altar.

Again he sent other servants, etc. That is, he sent companies of prophets through successive generations, especially at the time of the captivity brought about by the Babylonians. Yet through each successive stage of divine mercy shown to them, the heap of Jewish malice grew, and human wickedness contended against God’s mercy.

[Col. 1433A] But last of all he sent to them his son. I say “his son,” not as though bearing a sentence of punishment to the guilty and deserving, but still reserving for them, after so many ages, room for merciful pardon. And when he says, “They will respect my son,” this does not arise from ignorance; rather, he is always said to speak as though uncertain, so that free will may be preserved to man. Note that he sent him to shame them, not to punish them, because for a good and gracious lord, after so many injuries, the sole vengeance of shame was sufficient.

But when the tenants saw the son, they said among themselves:

[Col. 1433B] “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.” The Lord plainly proves that the Jewish rulers crucified the Son of God not through ignorance but through envy. For they understood him to be the one to whom it was said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance and your possession” (Ps. 2). Therefore, as though taking counsel for themselves, they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12); “if we let him go on thus, all will believe in him” (John 11). Therefore Christ’s inheritance is the Church, which he himself possessed when he rose again. The Jewish leaders sought to destroy it, when, faith in him having been extinguished, they tried to persuade the Gentiles to adopt the righteousness which is from the Law.

“And having seized him, they cast him out of the vineyard and killed him.” Mark reverses this order, saying:

[Col. 1433C] “They killed him and cast him out of the vineyard” (Mark 12), like a worthless corpse. In this he notes their obstinacy, because, after the Lord was killed and raised again, they excluded him from their borders and, so far as lay in their power, handed him over for the Gentiles to receive. Note again that he was cast outside the vineyard, because he suffered outside the gate; or because he was first expelled from the hearts of unbelievers and then crucified.

“When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes,” that is, when he comes to judge, “what will he do to those tenants?” The Lord asks not because he does not know what they will answer, but that they may be condemned by their own answer.

They say to him: “He will miserably destroy those miserable men,” etc. Some others, seeing that this was said against them, said, according to Luke (Luke 20), “Certainly not!”—although according to Matthew the Lord had also said:

[Col. 1433D] “He will miserably destroy those miserable men, and lease his vineyard to other tenants, who will render him its fruits in their seasons.” Mystically, a vineyard is leased to each person for cultivation when the mystery of baptism is given, so that he may exercise it through works. One servant and another are sent when the Law, the Psalms, and prophecy are read, by whose warning he may work well. But the servant sent is beaten or cast out when the word is despised, or, what is worse, blasphemed. So far as it concerns himself, he kills the heir who has trampled underfoot the Son of God and insulted the Spirit of grace. When the wicked man is destroyed, the vineyard is given to another: the gift of grace which the proud man lost is received by the humble. That the vineyard will be leased to others he confirms by a prophetic example, saying to them:

[Col. 1434A] “Have you never read in the Scriptures” (Ps. 117): “The stone which the builders rejected,” etc.? This stone signified Christ, whom the Jews, building their own traditions and wishing, as it were, to establish a house of their own from the people subject to them, rejected. As they had formerly been inventors of evil, so now they became most wicked masons, trying to take from their hearers faith in Christ—the faith which, like a chosen stone, ought to have been placed in God’s building, joining in itself two walls, that is, two peoples. For this is the stone of which Isaiah says: “I will lay in the foundations of Zion a chosen, precious cornerstone, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 28).

“Therefore I say to you that it shall be taken away,” etc. As though he said: Behold, from your own admission and also from prophetic authority I conclude against you that the kingdom of God will be taken from you Jews,

[Col. 1434B] so that you will no longer be what you presumed yourselves to be. “And it will be given to a nation,” namely the Gentile people, “producing its fruits.” We have said several times that the kingdom of God signifies the Holy Scriptures, which the Lord took from the Jews and handed over to us that we might produce their fruits; and this is the vineyard which he handed over to tenants and cultivators of the vineyard. Those who do not labour in it, while possessing only the name of the Scriptures, will lose the vineyard’s fruit.

“And whoever falls upon this stone,” etc. It is one thing to offend Christ by evil works, another to deny him. One who sins and yet believes in Christ falls upon the stone and is broken, but is not altogether crushed. For he is preserved for salvation through patience or repentance.

[Col. 1434C] “But upon whomever it falls,” etc. That is, the one whom that stone overwhelms—the one who utterly denies Christ—upon him it will come down from above in judgment with the punishment of destruction; meanwhile it destroys every good thing, because there is no good without faith.

And when the chief priests and Pharisees heard his parables, they understood that he spoke of them. And seeking to seize him, they feared the crowds, etc. Though hard of heart and unbelieving, they nevertheless understood that all the Lord’s judgments were directed against them. They understood that he was the heir and that they were wicked tenants, and they were restrained only by human fear, so that they did not dare kill him until his hour came. Mystically, this happens daily in the Church,

[Col. 1434D] when any person a brother in name alone, who does not love the unity of faith and peace, is ashamed or afraid to attack it because of the good people dwelling with him; yet, like the most foolish bird, the ostrich, the Lord says: “When the time comes, she raises her wings on high” (Job 39), because in persecuting the Church he will rejoice to deliver the Lord, as it were, to crucifixion and public display.

## CHAPTER XXII

And Jesus answered and again spoke to them in parables: “The kingdom has been made like,” etc. When the Lord put forward the parable of the vineyard and said that God’s righteousness was to be taken from the Jews, they were not frightened but were more enraged. They wished to lay hands on him; perceiving this, the Lord did not remain silent. Instead, meeting their wicked thought concerning his death,

[Col. 1435A] he foretells by another parable that the heavier wrath of God would come upon them. For if those who ought to have feared did not fear but were rather enraged, how much less ought Christ to have been silent, he whom it was not fitting to fear. Their own malice makes them bold; his own power makes him bold. The kingdom of heaven, which is likened to a man who is a king, is here the present Church of holy and righteous persons, namely those whom God rules. It is called the kingdom of heaven because, while the hearts of the saints desire nothing on earth and already sigh for things above, the Lord already reigns in them as though in heavenly places. This man, to whom the kingdom of heaven is likened, is God the Father. Although he is called a man, he did not assume human nature, but is called a man parabolically because of the comparison.

[Col. 1435B] “Who made a wedding feast for his son.” God the Father made a wedding for God the Son when he joined to him human nature in the Virgin’s womb, he whom he begot as God before the ages.

GREGORY. But because this union is usually made from two persons, far be it from our minds to believe that the person of God and man is united from two persons. For we say that he exists from two natures and in two natures; but we avoid, as impious, the belief that he is composed from two persons. Therefore it may be stated more openly and safely that in this the Father made a wedding for his Son the King: through the mystery of the Incarnation he joined the holy Church to him. The Virgin’s womb was the bridal chamber of this bridegroom’s wedding,

[Col. 1435C] whence David says: “The Lord goes forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18).

“And he sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding, and they would not come.” When he sent servants, they had already been invited. For the people of Israel had been invited to eternal glory through the Law, or, better, through the admonitions of the patriarchs. Therefore those sent later to call the invited were undoubtedly Moses, David, Nathan, Solomon, and the other prophets, whom those invited refused to believe. Again he sent other servants, namely the apostles. Thus he sent servants twice to invite: through the prophets he foretold the future Incarnation of the Son, and through the apostles he announced its accomplishment. Through them, in the invitation, it is now said:

[Col. 1435D] “Behold, I have prepared my dinner,” etc. The dinner is the doctrine of righteousness and the words of heavenly mysteries concerning the Son of God. It is as though he says: Behold, I have set a table from all the Law and from all the Prophets and Scriptures.

“My oxen and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready”: that is, examples of the fathers of the Old and New Testaments have been set forth. The oxen are the fathers of the Old Testament, who, since they had received permission under the Law to strike their adversaries in hatred of retribution, were like oxen striking their enemies with the horn of bodily strength. But the fattened animals are the fathers of the New Testament, who, receiving the grace of inward richness, are raised to lofty things upon the wing of their contemplation. It is not enough for them to love only friends;

[Col. 1436A] they also burn with love for their enemies. That the oxen and fattened animals are called slaughtered must be understood either because they had been killed or because, through the death of the flesh, they had already been placed in rest. Note that in the first invitation nothing is said of oxen and fattened animals. But in the second, the oxen and fattened animals are mentioned as already slaughtered, because almighty God, when we refuse to hear his words—as they did at the first invitation—adds examples, so that what we believe impossible may more easily become believable through examples. It follows:

“Come to the wedding.” This is a kind of conclusion: since you see that so many and such men have gone before as participants in the wedding and feast, who had faith in the Lord’s Incarnation, come therefore and agree with the others in this faith.

[Col. 1436B] “But they neglected it.” They received such an exhortation as we have described; but, though exhorted, they would not come—indeed, they neglected the proclamation of their salvation.

“And they went away, one to his farm, another to his business.” To go to a farm is to devote oneself excessively to earthly labour. To engage in business is to yearn after earthly things.

“But the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.” They not only rejected the grace of the one calling them, but also persecuted him in his servants. This is the meaning: “But the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, beat them, and afterwards killed them.” Note that the killing of the bridegroom is silent here, but contempt for the wedding is shown through the death of the servants.

[Col. 1436C] Note also that he is silent concerning his own death, of which he had already spoken in another parable, but shows the death of the disciples, whom the Jews, especially the priests, killed after his ascension. For this reason Jerusalem was afterwards destroyed by the Romans, as the literal account continues: “But when the king heard, he was angry.” When he invited them to the wedding and performed works of mercy, he was called only a man. But now, when he comes for vengeance, “man” is unmentioned and he is called king only. It follows: “And sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their cities.” The Roman army is called God’s because “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23). For the Romans would not have come to Jerusalem unless the Lord had stirred them up under the leadership of Vespasian and Titus, who, after killing the Jews, burned the treacherous city.

[Col. 1436D] Mystically, having sent angels, he destroyed the murderers because he killed the persecutors; he burned the city with fire because not only their souls but also the flesh in which they had lived is tormented by hell-fire. Then he said to his servants:

“The wedding indeed is ready,” etc. Because the king sees himself despised as he invites certain people, and does not wish his son’s wedding to be empty, he sends to others; for though labour is spent among some, there is nevertheless sometimes found a place where the word of God may rest. Therefore he says:

“The wedding is ready,” etc. As though he said: Every mystery of the human dispensation—birth, passion, resurrection, ascension—has been accomplished.

[Col. 1437A] “But those who were invited,” that is, the Jews, “were not worthy,” since, wishing to establish their own righteousness, they would not be subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10).

“Go therefore to the exits of the roads,” that is, to the diverse nations of the Gentiles, “and invite whomever you find,” that is, persons of every condition, to Christianity—that is, to the Christian faith signified by the wedding. The roads are understood as errors and the varied doctrines of the Gentiles, but from all of them some come to the wedding, that is, believe in Christ.

“And whomever you find,” etc. Just as there is no distinction in the nature of human creation, so no difference is made in their call to salvation. And his servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, good and bad, etc. The Gentile people to whom his servants went out from Judaea were not indeed on the roads but at the exits of roads:

[Col. 1437B] they were not in doctrines which were roads to Christ, but only at the exits of roads, because by natural law some were near the true law of the divine Scriptures. One who is at the exit of roads is neither wholly removed from the road nor on the road. Note that they are commanded to gather good and bad: those who were in some measure good through the natural law and moral decency, and those who, setting aside natural law, lived wickedly and had previously existed without distinction between good and evil. Or “good and bad” means those predestined to life and those predestined to death, who indiscriminately share the life of the present Church. In another sense, roads signify actions. The exits of roads signify the failure of actions, because those whom no prosperity follows or accompanies in earthly undertakings are often easily converted.

[Col. 1437C] “And the wedding was filled with those reclining at table.” Behold, the very character of the guests now openly shows that by this king’s wedding the present Church is signified, in which the evil associate with the good. For God gives birth to all in the faith in such a way that, because of their sins, he nevertheless does not bring all through renewal to the freedom of spiritual grace. This life, situated between heaven and hell, stands as it were in the middle and receives in common citizens of both regions. The holy Church now receives them indiscriminately, but later separates them at their departure. Hence the dreadful sentence immediately follows:

[Col. 1437D] “But the king entered to see those reclining at table.” The king is Christ himself, who entered to see those reclining, not because there is anything where he is not, but because where he wishes to look, he becomes present; where he does not wish, he appears absent. He entered, then, to see those reclining: the companies of believers resting, as it were, in faith in the Lord. They are rightly called reclining, as though resting—that is, through the very faith which they hold, awaiting eternal rest. “And he saw there a man not clothed,” etc.: that is, not adorned with charity, which is especially called the garment of God. He enters the wedding without a wedding garment who, standing in the holy Church, has faith but lacks charity, which is rightly called the wedding garment. For it was solely through God’s love

[Col. 1438A] that our Creator took flesh in order to join the Church to himself and to dwell in the minds of the elect. Hence he himself says: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world” (John 3). Therefore, because he found the man not adorned with charity, he at once says to him, as though angered: “Friend, how did you enter here, not having a wedding garment?” etc. It is remarkable that he calls him both friend and yet rejects him, as though saying: “Friend and not friend”—friend through faith, not friend through works or charity. Or he calls him friend because he had been invited to the wedding. Note that he accuses him of shamelessness: by lacking that garment, he had defiled the wedding’s purity. But he was silent, because, conscious of evil, he had no argument of excuse.

[Col. 1438B] Yet it must be known that whoever does not possess this wedding garment perfectly ought not, for that reason, despair of pardon and entry into the wedding; for he also gave us hope through the Psalmist, saying: “Your eyes saw my imperfection” (Ps. 138). But since we have said this in consolation of one who possesses it imperfectly and is infirm, let us now turn to the one who does not possess it at all, of whom what follows speaks:

Then the king said to the servants, “Bind him hand and foot,” etc. Then, by the severity of the sentence, the feet and hands of those who now refuse to be bound from evil deeds by amendment of life are bound. Or rather, punishment then binds those whom guilt now binds from good works. For feet which neglect to visit the needy, [Col. 1438C] and hands which give nothing to those in want, are already voluntarily bound from good work. Those who are now willingly bound in vice are then unwillingly bound in punishment. It is fittingly said that he is cast into the outer darkness. By inner darkness we mean blindness of heart; by outer darkness, the eternal night of condemnation.

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” etc. That is, there the teeth may gnash which here rejoiced in gluttony, and the eyes may weep and grieve which here were occupied with unlawful desires; so that each member may be subject to punishment, since here they served in subjection to each individual vice. It follows:

“For many are called, but few are chosen.” Therefore, after the rejection of the one man—in whom, namely, the entire body of the wicked is represented—[Col. 1438D] a general judgment is immediately added when it is said, “Many are called,” etc. As though he said: Understand what I said of one to apply to many. And note that this brief saying encompasses all the parables: in the work of the vineyard, the building of the house, and the wedding feast, it is not the beginning but the end that is sought.

Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel how they might ensnare him in speech, and they send their disciples to him with the Herodians, etc. The scribes, seeking to seize Jesus, feared the people. Therefore, what they could not accomplish by themselves, they attempted to accomplish through others, so that they themselves might seem free from responsibility for his death. Thus they send their disciples, but with Herodians. By disciples I mean persons less known and [Col. 1439A] less suspected, so that they might more easily deceive him secretly, or, if rebuked, might be less ashamed before him. For when an evil plan is discovered, the more inferior the person is, the less shame arises. Yet the disciples of such masters, though younger in age, were equal to them in malice.

“With the Herodians” means with Herod’s soldiers. Under Caesar Augustus, when the registration was made, Judaea became tributary. Herod, son of Antipater, a foreigner and proselyte, was placed over these taxes and appointed king of the Jews under Augustus. There was therefore dissension among the people. Some said that taxes ought to be paid for security and peace, since the Romans fought on behalf of all; the Pharisees, on the contrary, maintained that the people ought not to pay tribute, since they paid tithes and the other things [Col. 1439B] prescribed by the Law, nor ought they to be subject to human laws. The Pharisees therefore send them, if perhaps they might deceive him. Note that the Jews, humbled for their sins, paid tribute, as had been foretold to them in the Law. It follows:

“Teacher, we know that you are truthful, and the way,” etc. These are the disciples’ words to Jesus. They call him Teacher and truthful, so that, as one honored and praised, he may simply disclose to them the mystery of his heart, as though wishing to have them as disciples. Note the fraudulent question, which urges the respondent toward fearing God rather than Caesar and saying that taxes ought not to be paid, so that the Herodians, immediately upon hearing it, may seize him as the instigator of sedition against the Romans [Col. 1439C]. And note that they say, “You care for no one,” as though to say: You do not fear a person in authority, nor do you regard human persons—that is, you declare truth without distinction to both greater and lesser persons.

But Jesus, recognizing their wickedness and deceit, said, “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” etc. Their words are not flattering to him; rather, according to their conscience, he answers harshly to their harshness, speaking to the soul, not the body; not to their words, but to their intentions. The first and greatest virtue of one answering is to know the minds of the questioners and to call them not disciples but temptations. For they were one thing and pretended another.

He therefore says to them: “Show me the coin of the tax.” [Col. 1439D] That is, the denarius, reckoned as ten small coins, which bore Caesar’s image. When they showed him the denarius, Jesus said: “Whose image and inscription are these?” It is clear that he asks not from ignorance, but so as to reply suitably to their words. They say to him, “Caesar’s”—namely, Tiberius Caesar, Augustus’ stepson, under whom the Lord also suffered. Then he says to them: “Render therefore the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God.” Render tribute and money to Caesar; tithes and sacrifices to God.

Or otherwise: Render Caesar’s things to Caesar, and God’s things to God. For as Caesar demands the imprint of his own image, so God desires the soul marked with the light of his countenance. Hence the Psalmist: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV).—And when they heard, they marveled. Those who ought to have believed because of [Col. 1440A] such great wisdom marveled, because they had found no opportunity for testing him.

And leaving him, they went away and carried off unbelief. On that day—that is, the day on which the Pharisees departed—the Sadducees approached, whose name is interpreted “righteous,” though they were not so. It was one day, but many conflicts. Perhaps they kept coming with this design: to overcome by frequency and weariness him whom they could not overcome by reasoning, or to overthrow one who answered them all.

And note that there were two sects among the Jews: one of the Pharisees and the other of the Sadducees. The Pharisees preferred the righteousness of traditions and observances, which they call *Deuteronomium*, that is, “the second law”; hence they are also called “separated” from the people. But the Sadducees did not [Col. 1440B] believe in the resurrection of bodies and thought that the soul perishes with the body. They invented an indecent tale, which might expose to ridicule those who asserted the resurrection of bodies.

And they questioned him, saying: “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If anyone dies,’” etc., up to “Jesus answered.” Note that the seven brothers proposed by the Sadducees are the reprobate in this life, which is conducted through seven days. They are barren of every good thing; when they have miserably died, worldly conduct, like a barren wife without fruit, will finally pass away. It follows: But Jesus answered and said to them: “You err, not knowing,” etc.—namely, the Scriptures which affirm the resurrection, nor the power of God, which can raise bodies.

Therefore, in the resurrection men neither marry nor women are given in marriage, [Col. 1440C] but they will be like the angels of God in heaven, enjoying the vision of God without the stain of corruption. These things he gives in answer to the proposed question concerning the conditions of the resurrection. But concerning the resurrection itself, against their unbelief, he says thus:

“But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God, saying,” etc. Note that he adduces a testimony which seems rather ambiguous or insufficiently relevant to the truth of the resurrection. He does this because they did not accept the Prophets, where there are clear testimonies to the resurrection of human beings, but only the five books of Moses. Note also that here concerning the resurrection, and elsewhere concerning divinity, the Lord is found to have said certain things before those who tested him [Col. 1440D]—not in order to give what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine, but because among those who tested him were some who heard profitably and who ought not to be neglected because of the uncleanness of the others.

And note further that, when he says “the God of Abraham,” he properly proves the immortality of souls and immediately adds, “He is not God of the dead, but of the living,” so that, after proving that souls remain after death, the resurrection also of the bodies which performed good or evil deeds with the souls may consequently be introduced.

And when the crowds heard, they marveled at his teaching, etc. As though he said: Those who came simply, or revered his miracles, follow his teaching; but the Pharisees do not. And this is what follows:

But the Pharisees, hearing that Jesus had silenced [Col. 1441A] the Sadducees, gathered together, and one of them, a doctor of the Law, questioned him, testing him, etc. Having already been refuted in the matter of the denarius, they ought to have been moved by the example not to devise snares again of their own accord. But ill will and envy nourish folly. They gather, therefore, so that they may at least overcome by numbers him whom they cannot overcome by reason. And they say among themselves: Let one speak for all, and let all speak through one. Thus, if he wins, we may all appear to have won; but if he is defeated, he alone may appear confounded.

And note that, just as we read that Herod and Pilate made peace in the killing of the Lord, so now we see the same to have happened with the Pharisees and Sadducees. Previously opposed to one another, they came together with a common purpose to test the Lord. [Col. 1441B] Therefore all say through the mouth of one: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?” etc. He calls him Teacher whose disciple he does not wish to be, desiring not to know but to test.

Jesus said to him: “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc. Note that in answering first he strikes the feigned conscience of the questioner, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” that is, with perfect understanding, so that in confessing the divinity you leave no room for error. “And with all your soul,” that is, with your whole will, so that you will nothing contrary to him. “And with all your mind,” that is, with your whole memory, remembering nothing that might prevent you from thinking rightly concerning him. This is greatest in dignity and first in order.

We call it the first and greatest commandment with respect to the dignity [Col. 1441C] of the commandments, not with respect to their usefulness. The usefulness of the commandments is one, and all commandments are so joined together that one cannot exist without the other. But it is called the first and greatest commandment because before all things we must place it in the innermost heart as the unique foundation of devotion.

It follows: “And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” See that “You shall love the Lord” is both the first and the greatest commandment.
