But “You shall love your neighbor” is indeed great, but is not first; therefore he said, “It is like,” not “It is least.” It is like it because it concerns love, yet it is not equal in dignity. “On these two commandments hang the whole Law,” etc. That is, the entire Decalogue [Col. 1441D] and the admonitions of the Prophets are referred to these two commandments and find their end there.

Note that two tablets of the Law were given, on which were ten precepts, the ten-stringed psaltery. On one tablet were three, which concern God; on the other, seven, which concern one’s neighbor. On the first, the first is: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. You shall have no strange gods” (Exod. XX), because Christ with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one God. The second: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (ibid.). The name of Christ must not be taken in vain, so that we suppose him to be made through whom all things were made; for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. But in the Holy Spirit—that is, in the gift of God—rest is promised to us. Hence the third follows: “Remember the Sabbath day, to sanctify it; you shall do no servile work on it” [Col. 1442A] (ibid.).

On the other tablet: “Honor your father and mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (ibid.). Nor should it trouble you that Matthew says the man by whom the Lord was questioned was presented as testing him. Luke, however, passes this over, and Mark concludes by saying that the Lord said to him, when he answered wisely, “You are not far from the kingdom of God” (Mark XII). For it may be that, although he came with the mind of one testing, he was corrected by the Lord’s answer. Or at least we should not take the testing itself as evil, as that of an enemy wishing to deceive, but rather as cautious, like that of one wishing to test further someone unknown. For it is not without reason that we read: “He who readily believes is weak and diminished in heart” [Col. 1442B] (Ecclus. XIX).

When the Pharisees had gathered, Jesus questioned them, etc. Those who had come to test him, by the occasion of their own refutation, give Christ an occasion to question them. Note that this question of Jesus is of great benefit to us even today for refuting Jews, who confess that, according to them, Christ is to come as a mere human being and a holy man. Christ therefore questions them, saying:

“What do you think concerning Christ? Whose son is he?” I mean, according to the flesh. They say to him, “David’s.” As though they said: This son of David is a mere human being, not also God, the Son of God. He says to them: If he is a mere man, as you say, how does he call him his Lord—not uncertainly, nor from his own will, [Col. 1442C] but in the Holy Spirit? He calls as his Lord one who, according to you, does not exist before him. He calls him Lord, I say, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’”; the Father said to his Son: “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies” (Ps. CIX), etc. If he were merely human, David would not call him his Lord.

And note that they are not rebuked because they call him David’s son, but because they do not believe that he is the Son of God. For he himself is David’s Lord, remaining God before time, and he appeared as David’s son by being born. But the enemies being subjected by the Father to the Son signifies not the Son’s weakness but unity of nature. For the Son also subjects enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father upon [Col. 1442D] earth.

“If therefore David calls him Lord”—which he truly is according to divinity—“how is he his son according to the flesh?” And no one could answer him a word, because they had plainly been refuted in their arguments. Nor did anyone dare question him any further. But they were already openly considering handing him over to the Roman authorities. Note that the poisons of envy may indeed be overcome, but scarcely come to rest.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds, etc. That is, after refuting those who were deceitful, he instructs these who were receptive, nevertheless exhorting them to submit to the former because of the dignity of their priesthood and office, considering not their deeds but their teaching. And [Col. 1443A] note that the wicked were refuted in order that the good might be corrected. The Lord spoke to the crowds, etc.—that is, to the simpler people—and to the disciples—that is, to the more perfect.

“Upon the seat of Moses.” That is, in the teaching office of the doctrine taught by Moses sit the scribes and Pharisees, who rightly instruct conduct but do not act according to what they teach. “Therefore observe and do whatever they tell you”—namely, those things that belong to the chair, not to their life.

Observe by believing in the heart, and do in the deed itself; but do not do according to their works. As though he said: Hold to their teaching, not their life. For they say and do not do; that is, their teaching does not accord with their life.

[Col. 1443B] “For they bind burdens heavy and unbearable,” because they collect traditions from every source which do not lift but burden the conscience, since no one can fulfill them by his own strength. He calls the commandments of the Law unbearable burdens, which God had especially given because of sin, and which the scribes and Pharisees taught when they mingled in their own traditions, urging people to live according to these and not to come to the easy and delightful grace of Christ. Hence above: “Come to me, you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. XI). And Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why do you wish to impose a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither you nor your fathers were able to bear? But through the grace of Christ we believe that we shall be saved” (Acts XV).

Such [Col. 1443C] burdens they laid upon people’s shoulders, as though people were strong enough for this. Those, therefore, who are not righteous in doing wish at least to appear righteous in speaking. It follows:

“But they are unwilling to move them with their finger.” That is: They are unwilling even in the least matters to help, by fulfilling them, those whom they teach. Such also are indiscreet priests, who prescribe every kind of righteousness to the people while themselves keeping not even a small part of it, and who lay a heavy burden upon those coming to repentance—things which they command others but do not do themselves. Then, if they err by imposing a small penance, is it not better to render an account because of mercy than because of credulity?

“But all their works,” etc. He said that such teachers ought to be heard, not imitated. Now he shows the reason [Col. 1443D] why they cannot believe Christ: namely, because they do their works in order to be seen by people. For one who desires earthly glory cannot believe in Christ preaching heavenly things. “For they enlarge their phylacteries.” When God had given the commandments of the Law through Moses, he added at the end: “You shall bind them upon your hand, and they shall be fixed before your eyes” (Deut. VI), as though to say: Let them be in your deeds; let them be in your meditation. But the Pharisees, interpreting this wrongly, wrote the Decalogue on little parchments and bound them upon the forehead, in order to seem religious to the people.

Moses also commanded that fringes be made at the four corners of their cloaks (Num. XV), and that by this there might be a distinction of the Israelite people. But they made large fringes and tied sharp thorns to them, so that in walking or sitting they might [Col. 1444A] sometimes be pricked—that is, as though thus stirred they might be recalled to the duties of God. But understand that these things are to be borne not on the body but in the heart. Therefore, just as bookcases have books, so they too possess knowledge of God.

“But they love the first places at feasts,” etc. As though he said: At feasts they pursue gluttony, namely the reward of their religion; and in public, glory and the dignity of teaching. Note also that he does not forbid their being greeted in the marketplace, nor their sitting or reclining in the first places, when this truly belongs to them by the order of their office; rather, he rebukes those who desire these things, whether they possess them or not. For he rebukes not dignity but the desire for dignity.

“But you are not to be called,” etc. As though he said: The Pharisees and scribes are lovers of this worldly glory; but you, my disciples, who ought to be worthier in conduct [Col. 1444B] and life, must not be called *Rabbi*, that is, must not arrogate to yourselves what you owe to God. For one is your Teacher, who enlightens a person by giving understanding. A human being, however, does not teach by conferring understanding. For you are all brothers. This is the reason why one ought not to set oneself above another.

“And call no one your father,” etc. No other is to be called father or teacher except the Lord Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. He is Father because all things are from him; Teacher because all things are through him, or because through the dispensation of the flesh we have all been reconciled to God. Yet Paul declares himself to be a teacher of the nations in faith and truth. The answer is as follows: [Col. 1444C] It is one thing to be father or teacher by nature, another by indulgence. God is called Father and Teacher by nature; a human being is called father by indulgence, so that honor may be paid to age, not so that he may be considered the author of life. A teacher, moreover, is so called through fellowship with the true Teacher, as his minister, according to the condition or merits of his life, by him from whom he is sent.

“He who is greatest among you,” etc. Here he teaches that there must be no contention for preeminence. For whoever wishes to surpass his brother in ruling must first surpass him in serving. According to the Apostle: “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Rom. XII). The literal meaning is clear.

“But woe to you, scribes,” etc. After warning his disciples about humility and kindly setting forth spiritual [Col. 1444D] teaching to those who received it, he refutes and restrains the swelling of Pharisaic unbelief by repeated imprecation, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees”—that is, you who possess knowledge of the Law and Prophets and even pride yourselves on this, as though separated from others—“hypocrites,” who pretend to be what you are not.

“You who also shut the kingdom of heaven before people,” etc. That is, you conceal Christ’s coming through the pretense of your teaching. Or, you shut it by giving people an evil example. Hence every teacher who builds up hearers by word but gives scandal by example shuts the kingdom of God, so that he neither enters himself nor permits others to enter. Hence it follows:

[Col. 1445A] “For you do not enter into faith, nor do you permit those entering”—that is, those wishing to believe—to enter. Again, woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who devour widows’ houses. That is, in your superstition you aim at nothing except to make plunder from the people subject to you. You, I say, pray with long prayer in order to deceive more effectively. On this account you will receive a greater judgment.

Again, woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who traverse sea and dry land—that is, the whole world—in order to make one proselyte, converting even one person from the Gentiles to your Jewish rites. And when he has been made, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves, because, seeing your vices, he returns to being a Gentile; and for the greater transgression he deserves a greater punishment, so that he is deservedly called a son of Gehenna. For everyone is called the child of him whose [Col. 1445B] works he does.

And note that proselytes from the Gentiles were received in the Synagogue. This is indicated by “one,” because scarcely anyone after Christ assented to their teaching. Their traversing the whole world to make some proselyte signifies that they disparage the Gospel throughout the world. Again, woe to you, blind guides—guides of the blind (Matt. XV)—who say: “Whoever swears by the Temple, it is nothing.” That is, he is not liable if convicted of falsehood. But whoever swears by the gold of the Temple is bound—that is, he must pay what he swore, if he can.

Here the Pharisees are convicted, since they did everything for profit. For they said that the offerings were holier than the Temple or altar, so that people might be readier to offer gifts than to pour out prayers [Col. 1445C] or do acts of justice. In this they pursued not fear of God but their own greed. Therefore the Lord rebukes them for folly and fraud, saying that the Temple is much greater than the gold sanctified by the Temple, and the altar than the offerings sanctified by the altar. The Temple, as John says, and the altar pertain to God’s glory and the spiritual salvation of human beings. The gold in the Temple and the gift upon the altar likewise pertain to God’s glory, but more to human delight or the benefit of priests.

Mystically, however, the Temple and altar are praises and sacrifices of prayers offered to God; the gold and gift are sanctified not by themselves but through it [Col. 1445D] [the Temple and altar]. The literal sense needs no exposition.

Again, woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who tithe mint and dill. That is, for your own advantage you exact tithes of every trivial thing, yet leave uncorrected the weightier matters whose neglect is grave: just judgment in the examination of cases, mercy to be shown to the poor and widows, and faith to be kept with all people. You ought indeed to do the greater things and also not omit the lesser—that is, tithes—but rather to exact and give them, lest alms from the fruits of the earth seem despised. Yet through them immunity is not purchased for those remaining in impiety.

“Blind guides, straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel,” etc. As though he said. AUGUSTINE: [Col. 1446A] In matters of money, where profit is involved, you are careful; but you devour and neglect the great commandments concerning judgment, mercy, and faith. Mystically, by the name of the gnat is signified the seditious man Barabbas, because this animal disturbs by buzzing and delights in blood. By the name of the camel, because of its humility in bearing burdens, the Lord is understood. Therefore the Jews strain out the gnat—that is, they observe the lesser matters—because they released Barabbas, who had not violated the Sabbath; and they swallow the camel—that is, they despise the greater matters—because they killed Christ, who taught the Sabbath spiritually through judgment, mercy, and faith, which they despised.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who cleanse,” etc. In different words but with the same meaning as above, he rebukes the Pharisees for pretense [Col. 1446B] and falsehood: one thing is shown outwardly to people, another is done within. This is not because superstition was meant by their dish—that is, their cup—but because outwardly they show people holiness in dress, speech, phylacteries, fringes, long prayers, and such things, while inwardly they are or would be full of the filth of vices.

The brightness of the cup, indeed, is inward in the righteous person. If it has become filthy, what benefit is there in washing the exterior? Thus the brightness of the inner conscience must be obtained, so that the things of the body may be washed outwardly. Luke says thus (Luke XI): “Fools, did not he who made what is outside also make what is inside?” That is, he who made both natures of the human being willed both to be cleansed. Therefore let no one think that fornication and similar bodily vices [Col. 1446C] alone are serious, while thinking greed, pride, anger, and the other spiritual vices light. The literal sense of the preceding statement is clear.

Again, woe to you who are like whitewashed tombs, etc. By another comparison he repeats the same point. Again, woe to you who build the tombs of the Prophets. That is, for the favor of the crowd you raise memorials to those who were killed and adorn the monuments of righteous persons who were killed, in order to seem righteous. Condemning the crimes of your fathers, you say—if not with your voice, at least in your conduct—“If we had been in the days of our fathers,” etc.

Therefore you bear witness against yourselves that you are the children of those who killed the Prophets. For while you detest your fathers’ deeds, for the appearance [Col. 1446D] indeed of your holiness, you prove that you are the children of murderers; while by persecuting Christ and the apostles you do the same things, you prove most certainly that you are their children not only in flesh but also in imitation. In this it is also clear that you sin knowingly.

AUGUSTINE. By building the Prophets’ monuments, the Jews condemned their fathers’ acts in killing them; but by imitating their fathers’ crimes while persecuting Christ and his own people, they turned the judgment back upon themselves, doing the very things which they condemned in their parents: “And you, fill up the measure of your fathers,” etc. Having proved that they are children of murderers, he sets down, as if in conclusion, what he had been aiming at when he said:

[Col. 1447A] “And you, fill up the measure of your fathers,” etc. That is, complete what was lacking in them. They killed the Prophets; you kill the Lord of the Prophets. Note that he does not command them to do this, but shows what they were going to do. “Serpents, brood of vipers,” etc. As though he said: You murderers born of murderers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna? By building the tombs of the saints, or rather by cleansing your hearts from malice? Will the saints whose monuments you adorn set you free? Certainly not, because the saints are not friends of God’s enemies.

“Therefore, behold, I send,” etc. As though he said: Therefore, that you may fill up in relation not only to me but also to my followers what your fathers lacked, I send to you prophets, who foretell future things; wise persons, who expound the Scriptures or are learned in heart—hence David also says, “and those learned of heart in wisdom”—[Col. 1447B] and scribes, teachers of conduct, who bring forth new and old things from their treasures. Some of them you will kill, as Paul; crucify, as Peter; and some you will scourge in your synagogues, as the apostles in the Acts of the Apostles; and persecute from city to city, from Judaea to the Gentiles.

“So that upon you may come all righteous blood,” etc. He does not mean only those then present, but every generation of the wicked, preceding and future, because all are one city of the devil and one body of the devil. “All righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth,” etc.—that is, all due vengeance for the blood of righteous persons that has been shed. “From the blood of righteous Abel,” whose righteousness was approved by the acceptance of his offering, “to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple [Col. 1447C] and the altar”—your generation, namely, within the Temple and the altar, though the altar stood in the open air. As though he said: whom you killed in the court of the Temple.

JEROME. The question is who this Zechariah is. Some say Zechariah son of Barachiah, the eleventh of the twelve Prophets, whose father’s name agrees; but Scripture does not say where he was killed, especially since in his time the Temple had scarcely been ruined. Others say that he was Zechariah, father of John, relying on apocryphal writings to prove that he was killed because he proclaimed the Savior’s name and coming; but since we have no authority for this, it is rejected as easily [Col. 1447D] as it is established.

Others hold that he is Zechariah, killed by Joash king of Judah between the Temple and the altar, as the history of Kings relates. This is more to be believed. But we must consider that this Zechariah was not the son of Barachiah, but of the priest Jehoiada. Hence Scripture reports: “Joash did not remember the good things which Jehoiada his father had done for him” (2 Chron. XXIV). Since, therefore, we identify him as Zechariah and the place suits the killing, let us ask why he is called son of Barachiah and not of Jehoiada.

*Barachias* in our language means “blessed of the Lord,” and by the name of the priest Jehoiada is signified the righteousness of the Hebrews. In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes, moreover, we find written “son of Jehoiada” instead of “son of Barachiah”; on account of the grace of his merits, the Lord in this passage surnamed him son of Barachiah—that is, “blessed [Col. 1448A] of the Lord.”

But the question still remains why the blood of righteous Abel up to the blood of this Zechariah should be required of their generation, although it killed neither of them. John answers that this is not to be understood as though one generation paid the deserts of all preceding and subsequent generations. For it is not just that one person should be punished for another’s sins; rather, as on the day of vengeance, each generation will be punished for its own sins.

It will appear to have been avenged upon this very generation. For, as we have already said, all the wicked from Cain to the end of the age are one generation. Though they are not all at one time, they are nevertheless all one body of the devil.

[Col. 1448B] And the question still remains why only as far as this man, when many were killed after him before Christ’s birth, and, immediately after Christ was born, children were slain by this generation. But because Abel was a shepherd of sheep and was killed in the field, whereas Zechariah was a priest and was killed in the court of the Temple, he wished by their names to indicate martyrs of both ranks: lay people, namely, and those devoted to service at the altar.

“Amen, I say to you: All these things,” etc. He adds: The evil vengeance for the blood of God’s servants shed upon the earth will come upon the generation reckoned from the first parricide to the final son of perdition; and those alike in guilt will be alike in punishment.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the Prophets”—that is, the heralds of the Lord of the Prophets—[Col. 1448C] “and stone those who are sent to you”: you repel them by hardness of heart, or you stone bodily those sent to you for your salvation. Note that with a father’s affection he laments not stones but people; grieving, he uttered such words as those immediately added when he says: “How often I wished to gather your children,” namely the heirs of the patriarchs, “so that they might be in the unity of faith, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings?” As though he said: With as great an affection as a hen calls and nourishes her chicks, with that great an affection I wished to gather your children into the unity of faith and nourish them with catholic doctrine; yet you were unwilling to cooperate with calling grace.

AUGUSTINE. This kind of animal has such great [Col. 1448D] affection for its young that, affected by their weakness, it becomes weak itself; and, what you will scarcely find in other animals, it protects its young with its wings and fights against the kite. Thus our mother, the Wisdom of God, was in some manner made weak through the assumption of flesh. Hence the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. I). It protects our weakness and resists the devil, lest he snatch us away.

Note that he said, “I wished to gather, and you were unwilling,” as though God’s will were overcome by human will and thus it were untrue that “whatever the Lord willed, he did” (Ps. CXIII). But it must be understood thus: “I wished, and you were unwilling.” As though he said: All whom I gathered, I did so by my ever-effective will, even against your will, because you were always ungrateful.

[Col. 1449A] “Behold”—that is, soon, because you have deserved it—“your house,” namely the Temple or the entire city, “will be left,” that is, stripped of God’s help and left to its own power. Thus it will be deserted when the Romans take away place and nation. They could have known this already foretold in the person of Jeremiah. For he said: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance; my inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest” (Jer. XII). It follows:

For I tell you: from now on you will not see me until you say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” He means: unless you repent; and unless you confess that he of whom the prophets sang is the Son of God, and understand that he who comes is blessed—that is, free from every sin—in order to glorify the name of my Father, you will no longer see me as the author of your salvation. That is, after the Passion you will not see me until, on the day of judgment, you most certainly say and believe, with your consciences bearing witness, that “Blessed is he who comes,” etc.; for then both good and evil alike will confess. Note that, according to the first interpretation, the Jews think that an opportunity for repentance is still granted them. According to the second interpretation, however, it should be noted that when the crowds said to the Lord as he came to Jerusalem, “Blessed is he who comes,” then in the first advent there was already prefigured what will occur at the second advent of his glory: the conscience of all will cry this out.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Jesus went out from the Temple,” etc. The literal sense is clear. Mystically, however, when the Lord departed from the Temple, the structures of the Law and the ordering of its commandments were so destroyed that nothing can be fulfilled by the Jews; rather, when the head has been removed, all the members fight among themselves. It was also divinely provided that, as the grace of the Gospel increased, that Temple together with its ceremonies should be removed, lest anyone weak in faith, while these remained standing, should have an occasion for approaching it. In historical fact, the Temple was destroyed by the Romans in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion.

“But when he was sitting upon the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him,” etc. After he had said these things, it happened that the Lord returned to the Mount of Olives and sat there with four disciples, as Mark relates—namely Peter, James, John, and Andrew [Col. 1449D]—who asked him privately when those things would occur which he had foretold concerning the destruction of Jerusalem. Moreover, they asked what would be the sign of the second advent, and at what time the consummation of the age would take place.

It should be known that this sitting took place opposite the Temple of Jerusalem. For Mark says: “When he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the Temple” (Mark 13). The Evangelists do not determine whether this sitting opposite the Temple, and the disciples’ question concerning the end of the city or of the world, occurred on the same day or the following day; nor is it for us to decide what they left undiscussed.

Mystically, the Mount of Olives signifies the fruitful height of holy Church. Olive groves are effective in driving away the darkness of night by the soothing application of oil, in relieving infirmities, in giving rest to the weary, and in signifying peace. All these things suit the Church spiritually, of which it is said: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51). For she removes the darkness of errors by preaching; the infirmities of sins by the imposition of penance; gives rest to those wearied by tribulations through consolation; and proclaims peace to all. God sits upon this Church, reigning and judging, and this is opposite the Temple of Jerusalem—that is, against the arrogance of the proud. For the Temple signifies pride because it was the cause of the Jews’ pride.

“And Jesus answered them and said,” etc. They had asked about two signs: the destruction of Jerusalem and the second advent. He therefore sets forth signs common to both events, and also some peculiar to each. For when the destruction of Jerusalem or the consummation of the age was imminent, many would say that they were Christ. The first of these was Simon Magus, of whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles that all in Samaria listened to him and said: “This is the power of God which is called great” (Acts 8), because for a long time he had driven them mad by magical arts. Many other heresiarchs also arose in the times of the Apostles, sowing many errors; and some of them asserted that the day of the Lord was at hand. Because of all this, he exhorts not only the Apostles but all the faithful, saying:

“See that no one leads you astray; and when you hear,” etc. I say that you are not to be deceived, because you will hear of wars with respect to enemies, and reports of wars with respect to the expectation and fame of those future conflicts. But see that you are not troubled—that is, do not abandon Judaea in fear—for the end will not yet come: either the end of the age or the destruction of the city. From the time of the Lord’s Passion, wars abounded among the Jewish people until the forty-second year, when the city was destroyed by Titus and Vespasian. Likewise, many wars will occur before the end of the age.

“Nation will rise,” etc. This will happen historically before the end of the age because, as Gregory says, many evils must come beforehand in order to announce the evil without end. Some will come from heaven, others from earth, others from the elements, others from human beings. “Nation will rise against nation.” Behold the disturbance of human beings. “And there will be pestilences and famines.” Behold the disorder of the elements and the barrenness of the earth. “And earthquakes.” Behold evil from the earth. When Luke says, “There will be signs in sun and moon” (Luke 21), behold evil from heaven. Luke also notes evil from the sea when he says, “Through the bewilderment caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves” (ibid.). Because we have sinned in all things, in all things we are afflicted, as it is written: “The whole world will fight for him against the senseless” (Wis. 5).

This can also be understood mystically. For nation will rise against nation—that is, heretics against the faithful—and the kingdom of the devil against the kingdom of Christ; pestilences of error will seize many; there will be a famine of the Word of God; and earthquakes—that is, the separation of earthly-minded people from the true faith.

“All these things will be the beginnings of sorrows,” pertaining to [Col. 1451A] the destruction of the city or to the consummation of the age. “Then they will hand you over to tribulation.” This too will be a great cause of the city’s destruction: after the killing of the Lord, the Jews will persecute the Apostles. But if this is understood of the times of Antichrist, in the Apostles the person of all the faithful is signified.

“And then many will be scandalized,” etc. All these things will occur before the destruction of the city, but more fully in the times of Antichrist. “And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached.” Since the Lord knew that the disciples’ hearts would be grieved at the destruction of their nation, he raises them by this consolation: they were to know that far more companions in eternal joy would be gathered from the whole world, and this before the city’s destruction occurred. Mark implies this when he first says: “And the Gospel must first be preached among all nations” [Col. 1451B] (Mark 13).

Ecclesiastical History also reports that before the devastation of Judaea all the Apostles were dispersed throughout the whole world to preach the Gospel, except the two Jameses: one, namely the son of Zebedee, fell by Herod’s sword; the other remained in Jerusalem after being made bishop, and at last, thrown down by the Jews from the pinnacle of the Temple, ended his life.

He says “in the whole world,” that is, in the four quarters of the world, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth.” “As a testimony to all nations.” For the preaching of the Gospel is a testimony to the nations of the coming of the Son of God and of the redemption of humankind, so that they may be rendered without excuse. “And then the consummation will come.” He does not say immediately; rather, the consummation of the city or of the world will not come earlier.

“When therefore you see the abomination.” He means an idol, and therefore adds “of desolation,” because an idol was set up in the desolated and abandoned Temple. This may be understood of the image of Caesar which Pilate placed in the Temple of the Lord, or of Hadrian’s equestrian statue, which stood for a long time in the place of the Holy of Holies. Or, if the abomination is understood of the end of the age, Antichrist is meant, who will sit in the Temple of the Lord. We read of this abomination in the prophecy of Daniel; therefore he says: “When you see the abomination of desolation, which was prophesied by Daniel” (ch. 9), “standing in the holy place”—that is, in the Temple of the Lord, namely the idol or Antichrist—then let the one who reads Daniel’s prophecy understand [Col. 1451D] that the destruction of the city or the consummation of the age is at hand.

“Then let those who are in Judaea,” etc. If the destruction of the city is meant, this must be understood literally. For when the Roman war was approaching, the Christians who were in Judaea were divinely warned and departed, as Ecclesiastical History relates. They fled across the Jordan into the kingdom of Agrippa, king of the Jews, who is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles. He was always subject to Roman rule, together with that part of the Jews that wished to obey him; and they remained there in the city for the duration of the war. He mentions this flight when he says:

“Then let those Christians who are in Judaea flee to [Col. 1452A] the mountains,” where Agrippa’s kingdom was. He indicates extreme tribulation and terror. Since he urges that flight be made speedily at God’s command, none of those fleeing should come down to take anything from the house or return for a tunic. “But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing,” etc., because for the former a child in the womb, and for the latter a child in their arms, will hinder flight.

“Pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on a Sabbath.” In winter, the harshness of the cold will hinder your flight; on the Sabbath, the commandment of the Law will restrain you. For according to the Law it is not permitted to travel more than a thousand paces on the Sabbath.

But if all these things are understood of the consummation of the age, they must be received mystically. Thus we may say: Then those who are in Judaea—that is, in the confession of the true faith—should flee to the mountains, that is, ascend to the summit of virtues. And the one who is upon the roof—that is, who has overcome the flesh by which the soul is covered—should not descend to the lowest deeds of the former way of life, nor return to the desires of the flesh. And the one who is in the field—that is, who works in the Church as Paul by planting and Apollos by watering—should not return to take his tunic, that is, should not take up again worldly things of which he had stripped himself.

The pregnant are those who labour to acquire riches, whose souls are weighed down with sins. The nursing are those who, having obtained riches, cherish and increase them. A person flees in winter whose faith or charity has grown cold, and who has been removed from God. A person flees on the Sabbath who is sluggish in the divine work through idleness.

“For then there will be great tribulation,” etc. These words properly suit the times [Col. 1452C] of Antichrist, when not only will more frequent and harsher torments than before be inflicted on the faithful, but—what is more grievous—the working of signs will accompany those who inflict the torments. The Apostle bears witness when he says: “Whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in every deception, with lying signs and wonders” (2 Thess. 2). Whose faith will not be shaken when the persecutor of truth is also a worker of powers? Therefore, in provident mercy, he adds:

“And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved.” He calls the days shortened not, as some think, because the moments of time are changed, although we read: “By your ordinance the day endures” (Ps. [Col. 1452D] 118); rather, they are called shortened with respect to the estimation of those who thought they would reign for a long time. Or they are called shortened, that is, short—indeed, exceedingly short—because unless those days had been short and few, all the elect of that time would perish because of the greatness of the miracles and persecutions. For that persecution will last three and a half years.

“Then if anyone says, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’” etc. Before the consummation of the age, many heresies will arise, such as the Donatists, who say that they alone possess Christ, or the Arians and other heretics. Many will arise who say that they are Christ, and they will perform signs—that is, lesser marvels—and wonders—that is, greater marvels—so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error. He does not say this because the divine election is frustrated; rather, those who seemed elect by human judgment will be led into error.

“If therefore they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the desert,’” that is, in the doctrine of Gentile philosophers, who are altogether deserted by God, do not go out from your faith. Or if they say, “Behold, Christ is in the inner chambers,” that is, in the secret sects of heretics, do not believe. For if the devil transforms himself into an angel of light, declaring himself Christ and appearing to certain people—as is related of a monk in the time of blessed Martin—the faithful should not believe.

“For as lightning comes out of the east and appears as far as the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be manifest.” For he will be seen by all people throughout the whole world, according to the Apocalypse: “Every eye will see him” (Rev. 1). And elsewhere: “All flesh will see [Col. 1453B] the salvation of God” (Luke 3). Nor will he appear in secret, for God will come openly and will not keep silence. Hence it follows:

“Wherever the body is, there also the eagles will be gathered”: that is, God’s elect, as the Apostle says, “We shall meet Christ in the air, in the clouds” (1 Thess. 4). The saints are called eagles because, just as eagles gaze upon the sun with eyes undazzled by its rays, so the saints fix their gaze upon the splendour of the true Sun. Christ’s body is called, as it were, a corpse on account of the Passion.

“But immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened,” etc. Nothing prevents this from being understood truly: at that time the sun and moon, with the other stars, will temporarily be deprived of their light, as is known to have occurred to the sun at the time of the Lord’s Passion. For the moon, then being full, lay concealed beneath the hiddenness of the earth. Thus that prophecy of Joel remains incompletely fulfilled to this day. After saying, “The sun will be turned into darkness,” he added, “and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2).

And Isaiah, speaking of the day of judgment, says: “The moon will blush and the sun be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified in the sight of his elders” (Isa. 24). But after the day of judgment has been completed, and the glory of the future life shines forth, when there is a new heaven and a new earth, then what the same prophet says elsewhere will occur: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days” (ibid.).

Although it may be understood historically in this way, it also has a mystical sense, as follows:

“After the tribulation of those days,” that is, after it has begun, not ended, “the sun will be darkened and the moon”—that is, certain greater and lesser prelates in the Church who gave light to others—and those who seemed stars, that is, to shine through the gift of divine grace in the house of God, will fall from heaven, that is, from the Church, having been deprived of their light. “And the powers of heaven,” that is, the angels, will be moved at the future judgment of the people to whose guardianship they were assigned, as blessed Job testifies when he says: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his coming” (Job 26).

“And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” Let us understand this sign to be the cross, so that they may see him whom they pierced; or it is the banner of the faith’s triumphant victory. “And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn”: that is, all earthly-minded people, [Col. 1454A] not the heavenly-minded, whom an evil conscience will torment. “And they will see the Son of Man”—that is, his humanity, not his divinity—“coming in the clouds of heaven,” that is, in his saints. For just as a cloud bore him up when he ascended, so it will bear him when he descends, according to what the angels said: “He will come in the same manner as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1); or, as existing in the clouds of heaven, that is, in his saints.

“With great power,” that is, with great might; “and majesty,” that is, with great brightness and glory. For the first advent was in humility; the second, in power. The first was for benefit; the second, in glory. “And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice,” which will summon all the dead to the resurrection. That voice is compared to a trumpet because, as a trumpet terrifies enemies and encourages its own people, so that voice will terrify the impious and gladden the pious. By that voice he will gather his elect from the four winds of the earth—that is, from the four quarters of the world. And lest anyone should suppose that human beings are not to be gathered from the middle of the world, he specifies more precisely: “from the heights of heaven,” that is, from the middle of the world, “to their ends,” that is, to the limits of the earthly globe. By “the summit of heaven” the middle of the world is understood, because the summit of heaven rests above the middle of the world.

“Now learn from the fig tree,” etc. By the example of the fig tree he shows that the preceding events are signs of the consummation of the age. Note that when he says, “It is near, at the doors,” one must not suppose that the consummation of the world will follow immediately, but that certain preliminary events will show that it is now near, as it were, at the doors. Or let us put it this way: when you see [Col. 1454C] these things occurring—not merely some of them, but all of them already having occurred—then know that it is near, at the doors. That is to say: it is present.

Mystically, the fig tree signifies the people of Israel, which was the condemned fig tree, cursed and dried up for its barrenness. But when on this dry tree a branch of faith and charity appears, and leaves—that is, words of preaching—spring forth, summer is near: the eternal serenity that is awaited, and the desired renewal of those who are reborn. For when at last the faithlessness of the mind has been removed and Israel is saved, there can be no doubt that the day of judgment is near.

“Amen, I tell you, this generation will not pass away,” etc. That is to say: believe the things I have said, for know this with certainty, that this generation—that is, the whole human race—will not pass from mortality to immortality. Or, more particularly, the Jewish nation will not perish until all these things occur—that is, until the day of the Lord, or judgment, comes. You may safely believe these things concerning me, for my words are not transitory, though other things pass away. Therefore he says:

“Heaven and earth will pass away,” etc. How? Because they will be renewed after their former form has been laid aside, while their substance remains, as is read in Ecclesiastes: “The earth stands for ever” (Eccl. 1). But my words will not pass away; rather, they will be fulfilled exactly as spoken, without any change, sooner than heaven and earth will undergo their transformation—the transformation which they themselves announce to us by their alternating changes. For heaven is now covered with darkness, now renewed with brightness; while the earth now loses its appearance through winter dryness, now grows green with springtime splendour.

“But concerning that day.” Lest, after hearing the signs, they might seek that fixed limit, he speaks of the last day and of after how many years or days it will come. Do not be anxious, because no one knows—that is, no human being knows—neither the angels of heaven, except the Father alone, in whom the Son and the Holy Spirit are understood.

In some manuscripts there is added: “nor does the Son himself know.” He knows all things equally with the Father, but does not cause human beings to know, just as the Apostle says that in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2). I mean that he does not cause them to know what would be useless to know. For he wishes us always to be uncertain of the Judge’s coming, so that we may live every day as though we were to be judged the next day.

Such a manner of speaking is found often enough in Holy Scripture. Thus it is said: “The Holy Spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8), that is, causes us to intercede; just as it is said, “The Son does not know,” that is, causes people not to know. Or it may be read thus: if the words “nor the Son” are found in manuscripts, then “no one knows that day,” and afterward the statement is divided: no one, namely neither angels nor the Son nor any righteous human being, except the Father alone. And where the Father knows, the Son and the Holy Spirit are also understood. For by any one name of the persons, the entire divine essence is understood, since the three persons possess the same essence.

“But as in the days of Noah,” etc. He proves that the day is known to no one because it comes unforeseen and sudden to all, and he shows this by a comparison: “As it was [Col. 1455C] in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” That is: as the day of the Flood was unknown and unforeseen by all, so the coming of the Son of Man will arrive unforeseen. Note that by several examples he affirms that the day of his coming will occur suddenly. For the first advent was in humility, the second in majesty. He whom he had shortly before compared to passing lightning, he now compares to the days of Noah, when sudden destruction overtook mortals.

This is the meaning: “As they were in the days of Noah before the Flood, eating and drinking”—that is, given over to gluttony—“marrying and giving in marriage,” that is, persisting in these things, up to the day Noah entered the ark; and, despising God’s judgment, “they did not know,” that is, they refused to know, even though Noah preached, until the Flood came [Col. 1455D] and took them all away. So will be the coming of the Son of Man. But note that where he says “eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage,” he rebukes not food and marriage but their immoderate use.

Mystically, Noah builds the ark when the Lord builds the Church by gathering true believers together as though they were smoothed timbers. He enters it when it has been perfectly completed, when, on the day of judgment, as its eternal inhabitant he illumines it with the presence of his vision. But while the ark is being built, the wicked give themselves to excess. He is not believed now; but those who here insult the saints while they struggle will there, when the saints have been crowned, be punished with eternal damnation.

“Then,” namely on that day of consummation, “there will be two in the field”: that is, two will be found equal in sowing, [Col. 1456A] but not reaping equal fruit. There are two kinds of preachers labouring in the Church as in a field: those who sincerely proclaim Christ, and those who adulterate the word of God. They are mentioned in the Song of Songs, where it is said: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines” (Song 6), etc. Of those two, one will be taken into glory for reward; the other to eternal condemnation.

“Two will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left.” These two are those who love leisure and quiet, signified by the name of a bed. Occupied neither with secular nor ecclesiastical affairs, one is taken up: namely, the one who devotes himself to God, seeking only the things that are God’s. But the one who has pursued the monastic life for human praise or through some occupation of vices will be left by God.

“Two women grinding”: that is, again there are two kinds of people following the world of revolving things. Those will be taken who possess as though not possessing, like Job and those like him; the others will be left, namely those who hoped in the uncertainty of their riches. Both are aptly designated by the feminine gender because, like women in relation to men, they need the governance of others.

The three kinds of human beings may also be signified here by the three names given by the prophet Ezekiel: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14), by which rulers, the continent, and married persons are signified.

“Watch therefore.” Since Christ’s coming will be sudden, watch—that is, be vigilant. This is why the Lord wished his coming to be unknown: that you [Col. 1456C] might watch. I say, watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come, etc., whether at judgment or at the death of each person. Note that he did not say, “We do not know,” but “You do not know.”

“But know this,” etc. He proves by a comparison that they ought to watch. While the master of the house does not know, a thief breaks into the house; so, when the spirit sleeps from guarding itself, unforeseen death comes and breaks into the dwelling-place of our flesh, and drags to punishment the master whom it finds asleep. He would resist the thief if he watched, because by taking precautions through repentance he would meet the secretly approaching Judge. From this preceding comparison the exhortation also follows when it says: “Therefore you also be,” etc.

“Who do you think?” This indicates the difficulty, not the impossibility, of achieving virtue, as when the Psalmist says, “Who is wise and will keep these things?” (Ps. 107): he signifies not no one, but a rare person. “Who do you think is,” I say, “the faithful”—in faithfully dispensing his master’s money—“and prudent”—in discerning each person’s capacity—“whom the Lord has set over his household,” namely the Church, “to give them food in due season” according to each one’s capacity: the food of the divine word or of his own example.

The following words look back to what precedes, as though he said: You must indeed be admonished to be ready, because rare is the person serving the Lord who feeds Christ’s sheep not for gain but for Christ’s love, prudent—that is, providing for his own future. “Whom he has set again,” etc. That is: rare is the person called by God, as Aaron was, rather than thrusting himself forward, and who does not feed himself more than the sheep.

“Blessed is that servant,” etc. As I have said, a faithful and prudent servant is indeed rarely found; yet the one who is found to be such is made blessed by the Lord. This is the meaning: “Blessed is that servant,” who will be glorified with eternal blessedness, whom, when he comes, etc.—that is, who at the Lord’s coming for judgment is found dispensing the provision of the word and watching over those subject to him in the care of the flock.

“Amen, I tell you, he will set him over all his goods,” etc. Not so that he alone possesses them, but so that before others he receives eternal rewards, both for his own life and for guarding the flock.

“But if that evil servant says in his heart, ‘My master delays,’” etc. Just as the entire order of good rulers is taught in the one faithful steward, so in the utterly wicked servant is described the condemnable conduct and eternal damnation of all evil prelates: neglecting the fear of the Lord, they not only devote themselves to excess, but also provoke their subjects by injuries.

Typologically, however, “to strike the servants” can be understood as corrupting by evil example the consciences of the weak, not yet strengthened in hope, faith, and charity. “To drink with the drunken” means becoming drunk with crimes and with the enticements of the world, which make a person mad. Note that among the vices attributed to the evil servant is his thinking that the advent or return of his master was slow. But among the virtues of the good servant it is not stated that he thought the coming swift and prompt; rather, it is stated that, in view of the command of his master who would come at some time, [Col. 1457C] he distributed food to the servants in due season.

It is therefore shown to be best, although we greatly desire, if it were permitted, to know when the Lord will come, patiently to endure not knowing what we are not permitted to know; and whether he is near or far off, to bear it patiently and to love his coming whenever he arrives. It follows:

“The master of that servant will come,” etc., in whom all such evil persons are understood. He will come, I say, when he is not expected, and will separate him from the fellowship of the faithful and assign him a portion with the hypocrites—namely, those who were in the field and those who were grinding, and who nevertheless were left behind. They are called hypocrites because they did one thing and intended another.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 1457D]

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like,” etc. When our Lord was asked by the disciples about the consummation of the age, among the many things he said he also gave this example of the ten virgins, five of whom are said to be admitted and five excluded. This admission and exclusion signifies the future separation of the good from the evil.

But it must be asked: if the name of virginity is honourable, why is it common both to those received and to those excluded? For both these and those practise continence, though they differ in intention. All are virgins who abstain from the indulgences of the world. They are called five because continence from the enticements of the flesh is fivefold; but some abstain with a good intention and zeal for God’s righteousness, and are called prudent. [Col. 1458A] The other five, however, abstain not with zeal for God but rather for human glory. Thus they are deservedly called foolish. With the other five they took their lamps—that is, good works performed in continence—and went out to meet the bridegroom and bride: that is, by doing good works they appeared to agree with the will of the bridegroom, namely God, and of mother Church.

But five of them, as we have said, were foolish, because they acted well without a good intention; and five were prudent, serving the Lord for God, not for the world. “But the five foolish, having taken their lamps,” etc. They took lamps—that is, good works accompanied by certain displays—but did not take oil with them: that is, they did not possess within their consciences the glory of the good work itself. I think David spoke of this oil when he said: “God, your God, has anointed you above your companions” (Ps. 45). For the oil of the mind is the joy possessed inwardly by one who pleases God.

It follows: “But the prudent took oil in their vessels,” etc. That is, they placed the joy of good works in heart and conscience. Hence the Apostle says: “Let a person test himself” (1 Cor. 2), and then he will have glory in himself and not in another. They took oil, namely their own oil, in their vessels together with their lamps—that is, together with the outward display of good works.

“But while the bridegroom delayed”: that is, while Christ postpones the final judgment. For the time between Christ’s first and second advents is by no means short. “They became drowsy,” etc. Because while the Judge delays judgment, elect and reprobate alike are lulled into the sleep of death. For to sleep is to die. But to become drowsy before sleep is, before death, to languish from salvation, since through the weight of sickness one reaches the sleep of death.

Yet since all, both prudent and foolish, are said to have become drowsy, it is remarkable in what sense they became drowsy, if this means languishing from salvation before death. Unless perhaps we say that the prudent languish in some manner through the delay of their reward—if it is permissible to say that they grow slack in a good work. Or rather, let us say that they languish: that is, through longing for the divine bridegroom and consideration of the salvation to be granted, they fail within themselves.

“But at midnight”: that is, when all are secure and no one expects it. Hence it is said: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thess. 5). “A cry was made”: namely, in the voice of the archangel and in the trumpet of God. And when that cry was made, “Behold, in a moment the bridegroom, Christ, comes,” to unite the bride perpetually to himself. The cry, I say, was made; and behold the nature of that cry:

“Go out to meet him.” Run to meet him in the air. Then, having heard the cry, all rose from the sleep of death—all those virgins, both good and evil—and trimmed their lamps: that is, they diligently considered and counted their works, for which they expected reward.

“But the foolish,” etc. That is, those who, deceived by confidence in themselves, were inwardly empty, said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil,” etc. That is, help us through your merits, because our lamps—that is, our works—are going out: they are darkened because they are deprived, as it were, of the light of true testimony. To say this is nothing else than to desire to be aided by the merits of the saints.

“Give us,” etc. Those whose deeds are supported by another’s praise fail when that praise is removed; and habit always seeks what the mind has been accustomed to enjoy. Therefore they want to have before God, who searches hearts, the testimony of people who do not see hearts.

“The prudent answered, ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you,’” etc. We will not give you some of our oil. It is as if they said: each person will render an account for himself. Each scarcely suffices for himself, much less can he aid others by his merits. Then, mocking them, they add: “Perhaps not,” because each person will render an account for himself, and no one is helped before the Lord—who sees secrets—by another’s testimony; and each person scarcely suffices for himself, so that his own conscience may bear him witness.

“Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.” That is: go rather to the flatterers who were accustomed to sell you praise. As though under this mockery they said: now it appears what benefit your flatterers provide you. “But while they went to buy,” etc.: that is, while through recollection they went to their sellers and reflected on how much evil they had done with them.

“The bridegroom came; and those who were ready”—namely, those to whom the witness of conscience bore good testimony before God—“entered with him into the wedding feast,” where the pure soul is united with the everlasting fellowship of God. “And the door was shut”: that is, the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. For once those who are to be imitated for their manner of life in the angelic life have been received, after judgment has taken place, the entrance will afterward be opened by no prayers. [Col. 1459C] For after judgment there is great severity, whereas before it there is the kindness of ineffable mercy.

“Last of all, the others come,” etc. They come last indeed because through late repentance and unfruitful tears they knock while left outside. It is not said that they bought oil; therefore they must be understood as returning, when no joy remains for them from others’ praises, amid anguish and sorrows to the entreaty of God. But what kind of God? One most severe after judgment. It follows:

“Lord, Lord, open to us,” etc. Compelled by the pain of rejection, they repeat the address of dominion, not calling him Father, whose mercy they had despised during their life.

[Col. 1459D]

“But he answered and said: ‘Amen, I tell you, I do not know you.’” That is: I abandon you because I do not recognize you by the merit of your life.

“Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour,” etc. You know not only the day of judgment, when the bridegroom will come; you do not even know the hour of your drowsiness. Note that in a brief conclusion he made clear the purpose toward which the preceding parable tends.

“For as a man going on a journey,” etc. So that we may prepare for ourselves the testimony of a good conscience, and may not remain outside with the foolish virgins; and because Christ desires to find us prepared, he adds another parable on the same subject.

GREGORY. Who is this man who sets out on a journey, if not our Redeemer, who in the flesh which he had assumed went up into heaven? For the proper place of flesh is the earth; yet it is led, as it were, into foreign parts when through Christ it is placed in heaven. This man, then, setting out on a journey, entrusted his goods to his servants, because he granted spiritual gifts to his faithful ones.

“And to one he gave five talents,” etc. That is, knowledge of outward things, acquired or expressed through the five senses. “But to another two,” etc. Namely, understanding and action. “But to another one,” etc. That is, understanding alone.

“To each according to his own ability.” As if he said: He distributed more to one and less to another, not through stinginess or generosity, but according to the capacities of the recipients. “And immediately he departed,” etc. Not by changing place, but by allowing him free power to act and leaving him to his own judgment.

“But he who had received five talents went away.” As if he said: He advanced himself in outward knowledge; and although he could not penetrate mystical matters, he acted in these things by restraining himself from delight in visible things, and gained another five. He did so by admonishing others, by the example of good works, by shaping their conduct, and by restraining them from those same outward things. There are some who, as though endowed with two talents, receive understanding and action; and while they understand subtle matters, they perform remarkable works concerning outward things. And when by understanding and acting they preach to others, they carry away, as it were, a doubled profit from the transaction. Rightly, moreover, are another five or another two said to have come as profit, because, when preaching is bestowed upon both sexes, the talents received are, as it were, doubled. But he who had received one—that is, understanding—and had received it freely, went away and, instead of admonishing with it, hid it in secret; this is indicated when it is said that he “dug in the earth.” Or, going away on his own and not returning to himself, he dug into the earth: that is, he laboured in earthly things and hid his lord’s money—that is, the understanding entrusted to him by the Lord—by applying it to earthly pursuits, not seeking spiritual profit. For there are some who have received the talent of understanding, yet savour only the things of the flesh. Of them it is said through the prophet Jeremiah: “They are wise to do evil, but they have not known how to do good” (Jer. IV).

“But after a long time.” That is, from the Ascension until Christ’s second coming.

“The lord of those servants came and settled accounts with them.” That is, he began to examine the deeds of each person, while conscience accused or excused each one.

“And he who had received five talents came,” as though preparing to render his account, “and offered another five talents”: namely, those whom he had taught to do good works by the example and teaching of his own good action. For as many as he converted from error, so many he offered to the Lord, his conscience bearing witness that through the grace given to him he had benefited not only himself, but had also gained for the Lord those whom he could. Hence it follows:

“Lord, you delivered five talents to me; behold, another five,” etc. “His lord said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant, because over,” etc. Rejoicing in his servant’s progress, he commands him to enter into joy, where he is set over many things because he had proved faithful over few. For all the goods of the present life are few, though they seem many, since they are not without trouble. But eternal goods are many, because they are without the trouble of all corruption. Therefore the Lord rightly calls those goods joy: for one who has attained them so rejoices inwardly in the gift that there is no longer anything outwardly over which to grieve because of corruption.

“And he who had received two came also,” etc. The master of the household speaks kindly to both servants: both to the one who had made ten talents from five and to the one who had made four from two. But the servant who refused to work with his talent, having the most wretched testimony from his own conscience, returns to his lord with words of excuse, saying:

“Lord, I knew that you are a hard man,” etc. Hard on account of his harsh teaching. For the way which leads to life is steep, because the higher the ascent, the more grievous the fall. And it must further be noted that the useless servant calls his lord hard, though he pretends to serve him for gain; and he says that he was afraid to employ the talent for gain, though the one thing he ought to have feared was bringing it back to his lord without gain. For there are many in the Church whose image this servant bears: they fear to undertake a better life, yet they do not fear to lie in the slothful indolence of their time [or: “torpor”]. When they consider themselves sinners, they tremble to take up the path of holiness, yet they do not dread remaining in their iniquities.

Therefore the wicked servant says: “Lord, I knew that you are a hard man,” etc. That is, you have hard and narrow commandments; and in this I recognize your severity, that you reap where you have not sown. The Gentiles are those among whom you have not sown the written Law—indeed, they were without the Law—and yet you reap them: that is, you cut them down with the sickle of judgment and condemn them because they act wickedly, although they lack the seed of the written Law.

“And you gather where you have not scattered.” Because you gather some of the Gentiles where you have not scattered the written Law; that is, from those among whom you have sown no preaching, you wish to gather fruit for yourself into the heavenly granary. For you save some through the natural law, such as Job, to whom the written Law was not proclaimed; and by comparison with those who keep the natural law, you condemn those who neglect the written Law. And therefore I, fearing to undertake the degree of a higher life lest, in seeking another’s salvation, I should endanger myself—I myself went away, by free choice, and hid your talent: that is, I did not preach what I understood through your gift, but hid it in the earth; dwelling in a carnal life, I kept your talent just as I had received it, neither increasing nor diminishing it. Behold, you have what is yours.

“But his lord answered and said to him: Wicked and slothful servant,” etc. Because you slander your lord through pride, and because you neglected to make gain. [Col. 1462A] “You knew that I reap where I do not sow, and gather,” etc., as has been explained above. As if he said: Why did this thought of yours not strike fear into you, when you knew that I would seek my own more diligently? Behold: what you offered as your excuse rather accuses you. For the more you knew me to be severe, the more you ought to have entrusted my money to bankers. And this is the meaning of “You ought therefore,” etc. As if he said: Since I require from those to whom I did not entrust anything, and according to your judgment demand what I did not give them to distribute, how much more must I require from you what I gave you to distribute? The bankers are those able to put divine preaching heard into practice and multiply it by words and deeds. To give money to bankers, therefore, is to impart some knowledge to those who can fulfil it by words and deeds.

“He takes the talent from him,” etc. He shows the twofold punishment which the Lord often assigns to those who neglect the entrusted talent of understanding: one in the present, the other in the future. For in the present the following often happens in the Church:

“Take the talent from him and give it to him who has ten talents,” etc. For the person who has knowledge of the Scriptures but neglects it while engrossed in worldly business loses the knowledge of Scripture, and it is given over to forgetfulness. But the one who has five talents in the present Church—that is, not knowledge of the Scriptures but knowledge of outward things—by multiplying and administering these well, has merited another five through added grace: namely, he receives knowledge of the Scriptures and reaches mystical understanding. Thus the talent taken from the wicked servant is bestowed on the faithful minister.

“For to everyone who has, shall be given, and he shall abound.” As if he said: To everyone who has charity shall be given greater progress in virtues and greater understanding of the Lord’s commandments; and this is the meaning of “and he shall abound.”

“But from him who has not,” namely charity, even what he seems to have from a natural good—such as natural ability and literary learning—is taken away from him. For he either hands it over to forgetfulness; or, if he retains it, that natural good is as though taken away from him while it remains unfruitful. Or otherwise: to everyone who has love for the word of God is given understanding to comprehend it. But he who does not have that love, even though he possesses natural knowledge, falls away from it. For those who are idle, even if naturally acute, lose their natural good and the reward promised them. But because they are diligent and instruct others, what they have less of by nature they acquire through industry.

Or otherwise: those who have faith and good will, even if they have less in their works, will receive from the good Judge what is lacking. But one who does not have faith loses even the other virtues which he possesses naturally; for without faith even virtues are not virtues.

“And cast the useless servant into darkness,” etc. He shows the punishment which the slothful servant will receive in the future. As if he said: Cast the useless and unfruitful servant, who by his own will and negligence has fallen into inner darkness, into outer darkness.

Outer darkness may be understood as bodily punishments. For the body is outward in relation to the soul. Inner darkness, therefore, consists in the evils of the soul, in which, turned away from the light of charity, it delights in sins. Outer darkness consists in the evils of the body, by which we shall be eternally tormented in fire. Again, the distribution of the money is unequal, but the diversity is not to be attributed to the distributor.

For he says that each received according to his own ability; and, as we have said, the master of the household is Christ. The period of the journey is the span of repentance. He to whom he gave five talents is the Jewish people, who possessed the five books of Moses and, according to some, multiplied and fulfilled them through evangelical grace, bringing back as profit the fruit of the Decalogue. But she to whom two talents are entrusted is the Gentile people, to whom two things are given: faith of the heart and confession of the mouth; and these two she again multiplied. But he who received one talent signifies those among the Jewish people who, remaining in the carnal Law, understood carnally and hid the spiritual understanding of the Law in the letter, as a talent in the earth; neither using it themselves nor, through envy, dispensing it for others—namely, the Gentiles—to use; and thinking that this carnal understanding of the Law sufficed for their salvation. Let the reader investigate the rest more subtly according to this interpretation.

“But when the Son of Man shall come,” etc. After the parables, the Lord now proceeds to explain the manner of the future judgment at the end of the world. Note that he set forth beforehand the glory of the triumphant one who was to be crucified, so that the scandal of the cross might be removed by so great a promise. He says therefore: “When the Son of Man shall come”—that is, when he comes at his second advent—“in majesty,” that is, in the power of divinity, to judge, since he came in the humility of a servant to be judged. “And all his angels with him,” because the angels are witnesses of human acts, under whose guardianship people have acted either well or badly.

“Then the king shall sit upon the throne of his majesty.” That is, upon the Church, in which his omnipotence will then appear.

Note that he said “Son of Man.” This is effective against heretics who deny that Christ will come in the assumed form of a servant because the Apostle says: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (II Cor. V). Therefore the Son of Man and the Son of God will come. The Son of Man is other according to humanity, yet not something else: he is one and the same in both natures, the true and proper Son of God.

“And all nations shall be gathered before him,” etc.: those of every age, every condition, and every sex. “And he shall separate them from one another,” though they are now mingled together, “as a shepherd separates sheep from goats”: namely, the good from the evil.

Note that there will be two classes in the judgment: the elect and the reprobate. But among the elect, some will judge, of whom it is said: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). Others will be judged, to whom it is here said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat.” Likewise, among the reprobate there are some outside the Church who will not be judged, and others who will be judged, to whom it is said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat.” It follows: “And he shall place the sheep on his right hand.” That is, he shall establish the good in eternal blessedness. “But the goats,” etc.: namely, he shall establish the wicked in eternal misery. And he rightly says goats, not she-goats, which can bear young. For a male goat is a wanton and foolish animal, offered for sin under the Law, and it signifies sinners.

“Then the king shall say to those on his right,” etc. This saying took place in their consciences.

[Col. 1464B] “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. That is, advanced by the benefit of my Father to obtain the promised glory.

“Possess the kingdom prepared and predestined for you from the foundation of the world,” so that you may reign in it without end and without corruption, as you have deserved.

“For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,” etc. In the literal sense, note the works of mercy and charity. Mystically, however, whoever feeds one hungering and thirsting for righteousness with the bread of the word, or refreshes him with the drink of wisdom, also performs works of charity. Whoever recalls one who has wandered into the house of Mother Church, receives one weak in faith; and whoever aids, through compassion or consolation, one oppressed by some tribulation or by imprisonment for righteousness, fulfils true love. Note that the righteous answer: “Lord, when did we see you hungry?” etc. They do not doubt the Lord’s words, but are astonished at so great an exaltation, at the greatness of his majesty, or because the good they had done seems small. Hence it is said: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come” (Rom. VIII).

“And the king answering shall say to them: Amen I say to you, insofar as you did it to one of these,” etc. By these words he indicates that he did not speak generally of all poor people, but only of those who are poor in spirit: those, namely, who lay aside their own will and do the will of the heavenly Father. “Then he shall say also to those on the left: Depart from me, cursed,” etc. The wicked appeared to be with God while they were mingled with the good in the present age; but at last the ungodly will be removed, lest they see God’s glory, and they will be sent into eternal fire, prepared for the devil and his angels, not for human beings from the foundation of the world, as the kingdom was prepared for the good. “I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat,” etc. He does not say, “You who committed murders,” but, “because you refused to redeem them by alms.” Consider what he deserves who seizes another’s goods, if the one who did not give his own is eternally condemned. Then they too shall answer him: “Lord, when did we [see] you,” etc. They endeavour to excuse themselves, as if they could deceive God, whom they had sought to deceive among men; but they have no excuse, since they refused to turn from evil and do good. Hence he adds: “Insofar as you did not do it to one of the least,” etc. “And these shall go into eternal punishment,” etc. In vain, therefore, does Origen promise release to wicked human beings after many years, and even to the demons themselves.

## CHAPTER XXVI

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples,” etc. He had completed everything concerning the consummation of the age and the day of judgment; or, from the beginning of the Gospel until the Passion, he had completed all things by doing and preaching. But now, after the discourse in which he foretold that he would come in glory, he showed that he would suffer, in order to remind them that the sacrament of the cross is joined to the glory of eternity. He says therefore:

“You know that after two days the Passover will take place,” etc.

We must consider on what day the Lord spoke these words with the apostles on the Mount of Olives, so that we may understand more clearly what he means by “after two days.” From John’s narrative it is gathered that Jesus came to Bethany six days before the Passover, and there a supper was made at which Jesus was present. On the following day he came to Jerusalem, seated upon a she-ass. On the same day, as Matthew relates, he returned to Bethany and remained there. But in the morning, as the same writer relates, he returned to the city; then, being hungry, he found a fig tree and sought fruit on it. This happened on Monday. Mark mentions the fourth day.
