For after recounting how he found and cursed it, and what he had done in the temple, he added: “And when evening had come, he went out of the city”; then he added: “And when they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree dried up. And Peter remembered and said to him: Rabbi, behold, the fig tree which you cursed has withered” (Mark XI). Then, after relating many other things, he shows that the Lord sat on the Mount of Olives and spoke there to the apostles all these things already mentioned concerning the consummation of the age. In that discourse Matthew says: “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these sayings, he said to his disciples:

“You know that after two days the Passover will take place,” etc. Hence it may be understood that he said these things on Tuesday, so that after two days—that is, on Thursday—the Passover was to be celebrated. The day on which the lamb was sacrificed is called Passover; and it is called Pascha not from suffering, as many suppose, but from passing over. For *Pascha* is interpreted in Greek as “passing over,” and in Hebrew is called *phase*. That day is called a passing over because on the night when the lamb was sacrificed in Egypt the children of Israel passed out of Egypt. Or it is called a passing over because the destroying angel then passed over the houses of the Jews when he saw the lamb’s blood on the doorposts; or because the Lord himself, giving assistance, passed over his people. Mystically, that day is called Passover because Christ passed from this world to the Father. Hence John says: “Before the feast day of the Passover, Jesus knew that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII). The seven days following the day of Passover were called Unleavened Bread, because during them the Jews used unleavened bread and observed their greatest solemnity. But the Evangelists commonly use “the day of Unleavened Bread” and “Passover” interchangeably. For Mark says: “Passover and Unleavened Bread were after two days.” Luke says: “The feast day of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover.” Likewise John, speaking of the day on which Christ was crucified, says: “They did not enter the praetorium, lest they should be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover” (John XVIII). They do this because the day of Passover was commanded to be celebrated with unleavened bread, and because we too, as though keeping a perpetual Passover, are commanded always to depart from this world. For after one lamb has been sacrificed at evening, seven days of Unleavened Bread follow in succession: because Christ Jesus, having suffered once for us in the fullness of time in the flesh, commands us throughout the whole course of this age, represented by seven days, to live in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

[Col. 1466B] “And the Son of Man shall be delivered up,” etc. As his Passion drew near, he wished to foretell not only the Passion but also its day, in order to show that all things were open to him and that he willingly chose to undergo death, since he in no way avoided it. Therefore he wished to foretell it in order to strengthen the apostles.

“Then the chief priests gathered together,” etc. He shows the preparation and plotting of the Lord’s Passion. This is the meaning: Then the chief priests, who ought to have prepared themselves for the Passover, instead arm themselves against the true Lamb. They do this by deceit and counsel, fearing that the people might take him away from them. Hence they say:

“Not on the feast day, lest perhaps there be an uproar among the people,” etc., and thus he escape their hands. “But when Jesus was in Bethany,” etc. Having shown the counsel, he wishes to set forth its execution: namely, how Judas made an agreement with the Jews to hand Christ over. But first he states the cause of the betrayal, when he says: “When Jesus was in Bethany.” For Judas kept the money-box and, because he was a thief, retained what was contributed to Jesus. Therefore, when he saw Mary spend a pound of ointment in anointing Jesus, he was grieved because it had not been sold and its price handed over to him, so that he might skim something off from it. Judas, therefore, wished to compensate for the loss caused by the waste of the ointment by the price of his Master’s betrayal. Thus, when he was about to say:

“Then Judas went to the chief priests,” etc., in order to show the cause, he returns to the account of the pouring out of the ointment, which occurred in the house of Simon the leper. Note that the discussion is interrupted. For this pouring out took place six days before Passover, as John relates, on the day when Jesus was received with palm branches. But it is inserted here because it was the cause of the betrayal, as though he were saying: When the chief priests had thus assembled and taken counsel, then one of the Twelve went to the chief priests, etc. And this was not without a cause, but because, when Jesus was in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, etc. This Simon had been a leper but was healed by the Lord; nevertheless he still retained his old name. This woman was Mary Magdalene, Lazarus’s sister, whom Jesus raised from the dead, as John expressly records. She is the same woman, not another, who formerly, as Luke writes, came as a sinner to Jesus, moistened the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance, anointed them with the ointment of devout confession, and because she loved much obtained from the merciful Judge forgiveness for many sins. But now, justified and made familiar with the Lord, she poured holy oil not only over his feet, as John relates, but also over his head, as Matthew and Mark testify.

Alabaster is a kind of white marble marked with various colours, which people customarily hollow out into vessels for ointment because it is said to preserve such substances best from decay. Nard is an aromatic plant; from its leaves and spikes was compounded the ointment brought by Mary, which was more precious than others. Hence Matthew calls it precious ointment, saying: “Having an alabaster vessel of precious spikenard ointment.” But John says: “She took a pound of precious *nardus pistica*” (John XII).

*Pistis* in Greek is called *fides*, “faith,” in Latin, and *pisticum* means “faithful.” That ointment was faithful, that is, genuine and pure, not adulterated. Augustine, however, says: “By *pistici* we should understand some place from which this precious ointment came.” Mystically, Christ is in Bethany, that is, in the house of obedience, and in the house of Simon, that is, of the obedient; for Simon is interpreted “obedient,” because the Lord dwells in the minds of the obedient. Mary’s devotion signifies the faith and piety of the Church, which speaks in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I). When the Church preaches his divinity, she anoints his head; when the humility of his flesh, his feet.

“But when the disciples saw it, they were indignant,” etc. John says that Judas spoke this from greed, because he was a thief. But Matthew and Mark use “disciples” in the plural by synecdoche, the plural for the singular. It may also be understood that the other disciples either thought or said this, or were persuaded when Judas said it; and that Matthew and Mark expressed the will of all in words. But Judas said it because he was a thief; the others, because of concern for the poor.

“But Jesus, knowing, said to them,” etc. “For in pouring this ointment,” etc. As if he wished it to be understood: What you think waste is an office of burial and piety. Nor is it strange if she gives me the fragrance of faith, for whose sake I shall soon pour out my blood. Let us therefore allow her to represent my burial, that she may pour oil upon me for whom I shall pour out my blood. It follows: “Amen I say to you, wherever this Gospel shall be preached,” etc. That is, wherever the Church is spread abroad, throughout the whole world, what she has done shall also be spoken of in memory of her. This addition indicates that, just as Judas, by his opposition, gained the infamy of faithlessness, so this woman gained the glory of devout devotion. But the Lord, praising only what was good, passed over Judas’s infamy in silence.

“Then one went”—namely, when the chief priests had assembled, one of the Twelve went. He went not invited, not compelled, but voluntarily entered into his wicked counsel, wishing to compensate for the loss caused by the pouring out of ointment with the price of his Master. He certainly does not ask a fixed sum in order to make the betrayal profit-making, but, as though selling a worthless slave, leaves it to the buyers to decide what price they would give. But they agreed to give him thirty pieces of silver—the same price for which Joseph was sold by his brothers. It follows:

“And from then on he sought an opportunity to deliver him without crowds,” etc. Many today who abhor Judas’s deed do the same thing. For when they give false testimony for a reward, because they deny truth they sell God, who is truth. When they violate charity, they betray God, who is charity—especially when they do this not from ignorance but after seeking an opportunity to do it.

“Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread,” etc. He calls the first day of Unleavened Bread the fourteenth day of the first month, when, after leaven had been removed, they customarily sacrificed—that is, killed—the lamb at evening. Although Christ was crucified on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth lunar day, yet on this night, when the lamb was sacrificed, he handed over to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated; and, seized and bound by the Jews, he consecrated the beginning of that sacrifice—that is, of his Passion. It follows:

“Where do you wish us to prepare the Passover for you?” etc. Note that they had no fixed house. Hence the building of houses is proved superfluous.

“But Jesus said: Go into the city to a certain man,” etc. [Col. 1468C] But Mark says: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you; follow him. And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house: ‘Where is my dining room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’” (Mark XIV).

“And he will show you a large furnished upper room, and prepare it there,” etc. Thus he made the man known not by name but by signs, in order to show the foreknowledge of his divinity, by which he could foretell or disclose elsewhere to the disciples things that were to happen. Therefore he again chose to identify him by signs rather than by name, because in the signs he wished to signify something mystical. Whoever wishes to celebrate the Lord’s Passover must follow the water-bearer. Water signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said elsewhere: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John VII). Now he said this concerning the Holy Spirit. The water-bearer signifies the preacher, who ought to offer spiritual grace to all. The jar signifies the preacher’s frailty, of which the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV). Therefore whoever wishes to celebrate the Lord’s Passover should follow the preacher, who will lead him to the house of the Church. There the master of the house—that is, the prelate of the Church—will show him where the Lord’s Passover ought to be celebrated.

For he will show him a great upper room. The upper room, being on high, signifies the loftiness of the mystery of God’s sacraments. Therefore whoever wishes to celebrate the Lord’s Passover must celebrate it on high, not below. He celebrates it on high who understands something other than a mere animal in the sign—that is, in the lamb—and does not observe only the figures of the old Law. He celebrates Passover below who accepts only the figures of the Law and understands nothing spiritual beneath them. Therefore the names both of the water-bearer and of the master of the house are omitted, because their significance existed before their names. For as yet there was no honour in the Christian name, whether of prelates or preachers.

“But when evening had come,” etc. Therefore he reclined at table with the disciples in the evening, because in Christ’s Passion, when the true sun hastened toward its setting, eternal refreshment was prepared for all the faithful.

“And while they were eating, he said: Amen I say to you, that,” etc. Out of the greatness of his mercy the Lord wished by many means to call his disciple, the betrayer, back to repentance: by hidden indications, by threats, by the sacrament of unity, and by the example of humility. By hidden indications, in this way: when Judas thought that God was unaware of his conscience, Christ showed it to be known, yet without naming the disciple, lest public rebuke make him more shameless. By touching on the crime, he invites him to repentance. He keeps silent about the name lest Judas become more shameless. He calls him back by threats when he says: “Woe to that man through whom the Son of Man shall be betrayed,” etc.; by the sacrament of unity, when he gives him his body; and by the example of humility, when he washes his feet.

“And they were saddened,” etc. It is certain that the eleven disciples were not conscious of this in themselves, yet they trust the Master more than themselves. Fearing their own frailty, lest a future will to betray might be in them, they ask him to whom all future things lie open, saying: “Surely it is not I, Lord?” etc. “He who dips with me,” etc. While the betrayer persists in evil, Christ rebukes him more openly, yet still does not identify his name directly. While the others are saddened and withdraw their hands, Judas, with the recklessness and shamelessness by which he was to betray, put his hand into the dish with the Master, so that by audacity he might pretend to have a good conscience. Matthew says “in the *paropsis*”; Mark, “in the bowl.” A *paropsis* is a four-sided dish for food, named from equal boards, that is, equal sides. A bowl is an open earthen vessel for putting in liquid; and it may have happened that an earthen vessel was contained within a four-sided vessel upon the table. It follows:

[Col. 1469D] “Indeed the Son of Man goes, as it is written of him. But woe to that man through whom,” etc. Corrected neither the first nor the second time, he does not draw back his foot from betrayal; rather, the Lord’s patience nourishes his shamelessness, and he stores up God’s wrath for himself. Therefore punishment is foretold to him, so that announced torments might correct one whom shame could not overcome. But both today and forever, woe to that person who approaches the Lord’s table in malice, who, stained by some crime of the heart, does not fear to partake of the most holy mysteries while defiled.

“For it would have been good for him,” etc. This must be understood simply and in the ordinary sense. As if he said: It would have been much better not to exist at all than to exist wickedly. Yet it is not thereby said that one who does not exist can be well; it is an ordinary mode of speaking. But the statement, “if that man had not been born,” can be understood in two ways. “If he had been born,” as if he said, “that man”—that is, Judas—“had not existed.” Or: “if that man had not been born,” that is, Christ. This verse may also be explained in another way. “It would have been good for him,” that is, it would have been a lesser evil for Judas; thus a milder evil is called good in comparison with a greater evil. “If that man”—that is, Judas—“had not been born in faith and in the election of the apostles through Christ’s calling.” For unless he had been born through calling, he would not have become an apostate through betrayal. Or, it would have been good for him, that is, a lesser evil, if he had not been born into the world but had died in his mother’s womb like an abortive child.

“But Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” Because the other disciples had questioned him sadly, he too questions him, lest by keeping silent he seem to betray himself as guilty. The others say, “Lord”; but he says, “Rabbi,” as though judging it a lighter thing to betray a Teacher than the Lord, or showing an affectionate manner while betraying him. It follows:

He said to him: “You have said it.” As if to say: “You have betrayed yourself, not I.” And while they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, etc.

When the solemn rites of the old Passover had been completed—rites performed in commemoration of the ancient deliverance of God’s people from Egypt—he passes to the new rite, which he wished the Church to celebrate in remembrance of his own redemption: namely, that in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb he might institute the sacrament of his body and blood, and show himself to be the one to whom the Lord swore: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” [Col. 1470C] (Ps. 109).

Accordingly, he himself breaks the bread which he offers to his disciples, in order to show that the breaking of his body would occur not without his own will and purpose, as he himself said: “I have power to lay down my life” (John 10). Before breaking this bread, he blessed it by the grace of a sure sacrament, because he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, filled with the grace of divine power the human nature which he had assumed and was about to suffer in. Therefore, after supper he gave them his body, because the typical Passover first had to be completed, and then the sacraments of the true and new Passover established in its place. But we, out of reverence for so great a sacrament, are first nourished by the Lord’s sacraments before bodily [Col. 1470D] food.

It follows: “Take,” that is, understand; “and eat,” that is, incorporate it spiritually into yourselves. “This is my body,” which you see under the appearance of bread. He gave such a body as it was by nature: namely, immortal and incapable of suffering, because it was free from sin. It was not necessary for him to die or suffer, except because he so willed it.

And taking the cup, signifying beforehand his passion, he gave thanks amid adversities and for adversities, which he endured not for himself but for us. And he gave it to them, saying: “Drink of this, all of you.” Be representatives and participants in my passion. He shows what each person ought to do under the scourge of his own fault, when he himself so patiently endured the scourges due to another’s fault.

Because bread strengthens the body, and wine intoxicates and draws the mind away from the world toward heaven, [Col. 1471A] Christ chose these two things to be changed into his body and blood, so that believers might understand this from their outward forms. Wine, moreover, produces blood in the flesh. Mystically, the former refers to the body of Christ, the latter to his blood. Hence, because it is necessary both that we remain in Christ and that Christ remain in us, water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s cup. For John testifies that waters are peoples; and it is permitted to no one to offer either water alone or wine alone, just as neither a grain of wheat alone, without water being mixed in and without its preparation into bread, may be offered. Otherwise such an offering would seem to signify that the head should be separated from the members, and that Christ could have suffered death without the admixture of our redemption, or that we could be saved and offered to the Father without his passion. It is necessary, [Col. 1471B] therefore, that we live to him, that he remain in us, and that we remain in him.

But when he says:

“This is the blood of the new covenant,” it is said in contrast with the old covenant, which was consecrated by the blood of calves and goats; although that blood was shed, it nevertheless did not remit sins.

“But I tell you: I will not drink”—that is, I will no longer take delight in the ceremonies of this people, among which the chief sacraments are those of the paschal lamb. For the day of my resurrection will come, when, established in the kingdom of God—that is, exalted in the glory of immortal life—I shall enjoy with you a new joy concerning the salvation of this same people, reborn by spiritual grace.

Likewise, Augustine wishes “old” to be understood here when he speaks of “new.” Since, therefore, he had taken a body from the offspring of Adam, who is called the old man, [Col. 1471C] a body which was delivered to death in the passion, what else does he promise by “new wine” than that we should understand the immortality which he was to give to renewed bodies? When he says, “I will drink with you,” he also promises them the resurrection of their bodies for the putting on of immortality. “With you” should not be understood as referring to the same time, but to the same renewal. And when he says “of this fruit,” he signifies that these same bodies, which now are to die according to oldness, will indeed rise according to heavenly renewal.

But if by the vine, from whose oldness he now drinks the cup of passion, you understand the Jews themselves, he also signifies that this people will come to the body of Christ through newness of life, [Col. 1471D] when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel will be saved.

“And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives,” etc. This is what we read in the Psalm: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord,” etc. (Ps. 21). That hymn may also be understood as the one which, according to John, the Lord sang while giving thanks to the Father, in which he prayed for himself, his disciples, and those who would believe. And fittingly he leads the disciples, nourished by the sacrament of his body and blood and commended to God the Father by the hymn of his pious intercession, to the Mount of Olives, in order to signify typologically that through receiving his sacraments and through the help of his intercession we ought to ascend to the higher gifts of the Holy Spirit’s virtues, by which we are purified in heart.

[Col. 1472A] Then he says to them: “You will all suffer scandal,” etc. He foretells what they will suffer, so that, when they have suffered it, they may not despair of salvation, but may be delivered by doing penance. And rightly he says, “in the night.” For “those who sleep, sleep at night”; so too those who are scandalized are scandalized in the night.

For it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered,” etc. This is written in different words in the prophet Zechariah, and is spoken from the person of the prophet to God: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. 13).

“But after I have risen,” etc. Just as he foretold the place of his passion, so he foretells the place of his resurrection; and he does so also to console their weakness by the promise of his return.

Peter answered and said: [Col. 1472B] “Even if all are scandalized,” etc. What Peter says is not a lie, nor is it rashness, but faith and burning love. For he was so carried away by love for Christ that he did not consider either the weakness of his flesh or the truth of Christ’s words.

Jesus said to him: “Amen, I tell you,” etc. Peter promises out of ardor; Christ, as God, foretells what is to come. Note that he says simply, “before the cock crows, three times.” Mark alone says, “before the cock crows twice.” If Peter’s threefold denial had all begun after the first cockcrow, the three Evangelists who say, “before the cock crows,” would appear to be mistaken. Likewise, if it had all occurred before the first cockcrow, Mark would superfluously say, “before it crows twice.” But because it began before the first, the other three attended not to when [Col. 1472C] he would complete it, but to how great it would be whenever it began. Or the whole denial was completed in Peter’s mind before the first crow; it was begun in words before the first and completed before the second. For so great a fear had seized his mind as to make him deny three times.

Note also that Matthew and Mark place Peter’s denial after Jesus had gone out of the house where he ate the Passover; John and Luke place it before he went out. But we readily understand either that the former recapitulated or that the latter anticipated the account. Unless, rather, the very different words—and not only words, but also sayings—of the Lord which they set beforehand suggest that, stirred by them, Peter uttered his presumption that he would die with him. Thus we are more compelled to understand that he expressed his presumption on different occasions in response to Christ’s speech, [Col. 1472D] and that the Lord answered him three times that he would deny him before the cockcrow. Thus after his resurrection he asked him three times whether he loved him, and commanded him three times concerning feeding the sheep.

Then Jesus came with them to the estate called Gethsemane. Luke says to the Mount of Olives; John, across the torrent Kidron. This is the same place, because Gethsemane, where he prayed, is at the foot of the Mount of Olives, where there is a garden and where a church has also been built. Gethsemane is interpreted “valley of the rich” or “valley of the fat ones”; and note that places and times are full of figures. When it says that he prays on the mountain, it teaches us to have our hearts raised upward in prayer. When it says in the valley, and in this valley of fatness, it teaches that in prayer humility and the richness of eternal love must be labored for. So far as the dispensation of the Lord’s passion itself [Col. 1473A] is concerned, the Lord fittingly prayed as he approached death in the valley of fatness, because through the valley of humility and the richness of charity he underwent death for us.

And he said to the disciples: “Sit,” etc. He had received the disciples’ faith and the steadfastness of their devoted will, but he foresaw that they would be troubled and scattered; therefore, figuratively, he orders them to sit in one place while he goes forward to pray.

It follows: “And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful,” etc. He began to be sorrowful in order to prove the truth of the assumption—that is, of the assumed human being—not through fear of the passion, since he had come for this, but because of the stumbling of the apostles, the rejection of the Jews, and the destruction of Jerusalem. Note that it says “began”: for beginning to be sorrowful is one thing, being sorrowful another.

AUGUSTINE. [Col. 1473B] Christ fears when Peter does not fear. Peter, as a human being, does not know the power of death. God, constituted in a body, displays the frailty of the flesh so that he may exclude the impiety of those who reproach the mystery of the incarnation; for he who assumed a body had to undergo everything that belongs to a body. Hence it follows: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” Note that it is not death, but the time of death, that is feared, until he frees the apostles by his passion. For through the power of the resurrection the faith of believers was afterward to be strengthened.

“Remain here,” etc. HILARY. He does not prohibit them from sleeping, since the time was not yet at hand amid so great a danger; rather, he admonishes them to remain wakeful with him against the sleep of unbelief and the torpor of mind.

“And going a little farther, he fell upon his face,” etc. [Col. 1473C] Having given them the command to remain and keep watch with him, he went a little farther and fell upon his face, in order to show humility of mind by the posture of his body and to teach a like humiliation to those for whom the same passion was imminent.

Therefore he prays when he says: “My Father, if it is possible”—namely, that death may die without my dying, or that the Gentiles may believe without the destruction of the Jews—“then let this cup pass from me,” etc. As if to say: “Then I refuse the passion; otherwise, let your will be done.” He uses the voice of our nature and pleads the cause of human frailty and trembling, so that in the things which must be endured patience may be strengthened and fear removed. For these words must not be believed to have been spoken from fear of his own passion by him who had come to suffer it.

[Col. 1473D] Therefore, laying aside this fear of our weakness, excusable in some manner but not fit to remain, he passes to another disposition and says:

“Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” AUGUSTINE. He calls his own will that which he took temporally from the Virgin; but he calls the will of him who sent him that will which, as eternal, he eternally possesses in common with the Father.

“Let this cup pass from me.” He says this not from fear but from mercy, lest the Jews, who have no excuse of ignorance, kill me. Hence he says, “this”—that is, the Jewish people—not simply “the cup.” Or, “Let the cup pass from me” simply means: let death die without my dying. “Nevertheless,” etc. As if returning to himself, he says: [Col. 1474A] “Not as I will, insofar as I am human, but as you will.” Here he teaches that the will of God is to be preferred to human will. He made himself equal in affection to humanity, because he showed the truth of the body, so that he might say: “Not as I will, but as you will.” He took up my will; he took up my sorrow, who took up my flesh. I confidently name sorrow, who preach the cross of Christ. He was without sin and willingly endured the penalty of sin. Therefore he transfigured his own in himself, who wills nothing other than the Father does, when he says: “Not as I will,” etc. Just as elsewhere he says: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9).

“And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping,” etc. For because of their excessive sorrow, they could not overcome sleep. [Col. 1474B] And he says to Peter: “So, could you not watch with me one hour?” etc. HILARY. He rebukes Peter alone among the others because he had promised more than the others that he would never be scandalized.

“Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation,” etc. Note that he does not say, “lest you be tempted,” but “lest you enter into temptation”: that is, lest you be conquered and overcome by temptation.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” etc. HILARY. He certainly does not say this about himself, for this discourse concerns those who had pledged themselves never to deny him. Their spirit was willing, but their flesh was weak, because they had not yet been clothed with power from on high. Their spirit, therefore, was willing [Col. 1474C] to confess, but their flesh weak to endure.

“Again he went away a second time,” etc. This is to say: “If Nineveh—that is, the Gentile world—cannot be saved unless the gourd withers—that is, the Jewish people, because the tabernacle was formerly theirs—let your will be done, so that it may kill me.”

And he came again, when the denial was already near, and found them sleeping. For their eyes were heavy. The eyes of the apostles were growing weak because the denial was near. And leaving them, he went away again, etc. It should be noted that the Lord prayed three times, so that we too may pray for forgiveness of past sins, protection from present evils, and caution against future dangers; and so that we may direct every prayer to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, just as there is a threefold temptation of desire—concupiscence of the flesh, concupiscence of the eyes, and worldly ambition—so there is a threefold temptation of fear: fear of death, fear of abasement, and fear of suffering. Against all these he teaches us to fortify ourselves in prayer. Hence, on account of the threefold temptation of the passion, the Lord may also be understood to have prayed three times.

Then he came to his disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest,” etc. AUGUSTINE. It is remarkable how he commands them to sleep and rest, when he adds: “Behold, the hour is at hand,” etc., and therefore says: “Rise, let us go.” Those disturbed by this apparent contradiction, when they read it, try to pronounce the words “Sleep now and rest” as if spoken reproachfully rather than commandingly. But it should be known that after these words the Lord kept silent, so that what he had promised might occur; and afterward, according to [Col. 1475A] Mark, he added: “It is enough; you have now rested,” and added:

“Behold, he who betrays me is at hand. Rise, let us go.” Let us offer ourselves freely, so that he may not find us as though fearful and shrinking back, but voluntarily presenting ourselves, so that they may see the confidence of those about to suffer. He had found them fearful; now he invites them so that they may see the confidence and joy of those about to suffer.

HILARY. The reason why, on returning the first time, he rebukes them; the second time, is silent; and the third time, commands them to rest, is this: first, after the resurrection he rebuked them when they were scattered, distrustful, and fearful. Second, after the Paraclete Spirit had been sent, he visited their eyes, heavy for beholding the freedom of the Gospel. For, detained for a while by love of the Law, they were occupied by a kind of sleep of faith. Third, that is, at his return in glory, [Col. 1475B] he will restore them to security and rest.

“While he was still speaking, behold, Judas,” etc. After John the Evangelist says that he entered the garden with the disciples, he does not mention what he did there until the traitor came to seize him with swords and clubs. It is foolish to seek with swords him who freely surrendered himself, and to search for him at night through a traitor, as though he were hiding, when they saw him teaching daily in the temple.

Therefore he says: “But he who betrayed him,” etc. “Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one.” He still has some shame as a disciple, since he did not openly hand him over to the persecutors, but by the sign of a kiss. Note that he thought the signs he had seen Christ perform were done not divinely but magically; and having heard him transfigured on the mountain, he feared that he might now in such a manner [Col. 1475C] escape from their hands, and therefore gave a sign.

And immediately approaching Jesus, he said: “Hail, Rabbi,” etc. O what shameless and wicked boldness: to call him master and join a kiss to him whom he was betraying! Yet the Lord accepted the kiss, not to teach us to dissemble, but lest he seem to flee the betrayal, according to David: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119).

Jesus said to him: “Friend, for what have you come?” The word “friend” is spoken ironically and has the opposite meaning, just as in: “Friend, how did you enter here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. 12). In this manner something is said craftily, whether as accusation or mockery.

And note that Jesus, who was betrayed, was handed over by Judas, against Judas, for us, [Col. 1475D] apart from Judas. Rejoice, Christian: in the transaction of your enemies you have conquered. What Judas sold and the Jew bought, you have acquired.

“And behold, one of those who were with Jesus,” etc. Peter, as John explains, with the same ardor with which he had done the other things, cut off the servant’s ear, knowing how Phinehas received the reward of righteousness and an everlasting priesthood by punishing sacrilegious persons—he who also pierced through the genitals a Jew joined with a Midianite woman (Num. 25). Luke also adds that the Lord healed the servant’s ear (Luke 22). Therefore the Lord never forgets his mercy: he does not allow even his enemy to be wounded. They inflict death upon the righteous one; he heals the wounds of his persecutors.

Mystically, he also teaches [Col. 1476A] that those who contracted a wound of soul by consenting to his death can attain salvation if they bear worthy fruit of repentance. The servant of the chief priest mystically signifies the Jewish people, wrongly enslaved to the chief priests, who in the Lord’s passion lost the right ear—that is, spiritual understanding. Its being content with the left ear, that is, with the bareness of the letter, was made manifest as removed not by Peter’s act but by divine judgment; the right ear is restored by the Lord’s mercy in those who preferred to believe.

Or the severed ear signifies hearing renewed through the removal of oldness, so that it may be in newness of spirit and not in oldness of letter. This hearing, when given to anyone, is given by Christ, and is said to reign with him. Therefore Malchus is fittingly called “king” or “one who will reign.” That he was found to be a servant pertains to the old covenant, which gives birth into [Col. 1476B] slavery; but when healing came, freedom was prefigured.

Note that there are two swords in the Church: one material, the other spiritual. The spiritual sword acts only upon those who are willing, whereas the material sword compels even the unwilling. For more people are compelled into the Church by the sword than by the stole. There are also secular ministers, through whom temporal matters are administered, and spiritual ministers, to whom spiritual matters ought to be entrusted. Therefore the material sword is given to carnal persons, but the spiritual sword to spiritual ministers. But just as it is not fitting for kings to exercise what belongs to the stole, so neither should a bishop exercise what belongs to a king. Since Peter, who bears the figure of spiritual persons, in some way exercised the material sword when he cut off the servant’s ear, he deserved to be rebuked by the Lord. Hence he added:

[Col. 1476C] “Put your sword back into its place,” etc. As if he said: “Let vengeance cease, and let patience be displayed, so that we may teach our people patience, not vengeance.”

“For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword,” etc. A crowd armed with swords had come out against the Lord, and he orders the sword put back, signifying that he would destroy them not with a human sword but with the sword of his mouth. Moreover, if according to his judgment all who use the sword will perish by the sword, then the sword was rightly used for the destruction of those who used it for crime. Or they will perish by that sword which turns in fire before Paradise—that is, the sword of divine vengeance—and by the sword of the Spirit, that is, the word of God.

“Do you think that I cannot,” etc. He means that he does not need the help of twelve apostles, since, if he wishes, he can have [Col. 1476D] twelve legions of angels, in which are seventy-two thousand, represented by the languages of all nations. For among the ancients one legion was reckoned as six thousand men. Six times twelve, or twelve times six, makes seventy-two. The seventy-two thousand angels, because the human race is divided into so many languages, signify the whole human race together with the Roman Empire contending against the wicked Jewish people. These are the angels of God who, forty-two years after the resurrection, together with Titus and Vespasian destroyed those murderers and set fire to their cities.

“How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?” He shows [Col. 1477A] a mind ready to suffer, since in his passion he affirms the words of the prophets.

“As against a robber,” etc. As if to say: It is foolish to seek with swords one who freely surrenders himself, and to search for him at night through a traitor, as though he were hiding, when he taught daily in the temple. But you assemble in darkness because your power is in darkness. All this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter” (Isa. 53), etc. What follows is plain.

Then the disciples, leaving him, fled. Just as Peter, who washed away his denial with tears and utterly extirpated the confession of God, signifies the restoration of those who fall in martyrdom, so the others who fled teach the prudence of fleeing to those less fit [Col. 1477B] to bear adversities, for whom it is safer to hide than to expose themselves to danger.

Likewise, the young man who, according to Mark, left behind his linen cloth and fled naked signifies the work and soul of those who, that they may be safer, cast aside everything they possess in the world. They have learned rather to serve God naked than, by possessing worldly things, to provide material for temptation and for being drawn back from him. This is according to the example of Joseph, who, leaving the garment with the adulteress, preferred to serve God naked rather than clothed with a harlot’s desires.

But those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas, etc. According to John, he was first led to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas. Mark and Luke, however, do not name the high priest. Josephus testifies concerning this Caiaphas that he had bought the high priesthood from the Roman ruler without merit of office. It is not surprising, therefore, if, as he says, [Col. 1477C] an unjust judge judges unjustly. The name Caiaphas also suits the action: “investigator” or “shrewd,” for carrying out his wickedness; or “vomiting from the mouth,” because he was shameless in uttering falsehood and committing murder.

But Peter followed him from a distance, etc. Rightly from a distance, since nearby he was about to deny him. For he could not deny him if he were near Christ; yet in this he is especially admirable, that he did not leave the Lord even though he was afraid. His fear belongs to nature; his following, to devotion; his denial, to being carried away; his repentance, to faith.

Augustine: He signified that the Church would indeed follow—that is, imitate—the passions of Christ, but in a very different way. For the Church suffers for herself, but he suffers for the Church.

“And having entered,” etc. He did this either from love of justice, because he was a disciple, or from human curiosity, wishing to know what the high priest would judge concerning him: whether he would sentence him to death or release him after scourging. Note here the difference between him and the other disciples. They fled; he, though at a distance, still follows Jesus.

“The chief priests,” etc. “At last two false witnesses came,” etc. A false witness is one who does not understand words in the sense in which they are spoken. The Lord had spoken of the temple of his body; but they slander him even in the wording, and, adding or changing a few things, bring what appears to be a just accusation.

Christ had said: “Destroy this temple”; they change this [Col. 1478A] and say: “I will destroy this temple made with hands.” “You,” he says, “destroy it,” not I, because it is unlawful for us to inflict death upon ourselves. Likewise, the Lord had said: “and I will raise it up,” which he said concerning a living temple. They came saying that he had said: “I will build another made with hands,” so that it might seem properly said of the Jewish temple. For to build is one thing, to raise up another.

And rising, the high priest said to him: “Do you answer nothing?” etc. Rash and impatient anger could find no ground for slander. Therefore, by the movement of his body he displays the madness of his mind and provokes him to answer, so that he may find some occasion for accusation. But Jesus did not answer, knowing as God that whatever he answered would be twisted into slander. Yet when finally adjured whether he was the Son [Col. 1478B] of God, he answered the high priest himself, an answer which confirms all his preceding words and deeds and is therefore most necessary.

Jesus said to him: “You have said it.” But Mark says: “I am,” which is the same. We should understand that Jesus said both, namely “I am” and “you have said it”; but it sufficed for one Evangelist to report one and another the other. Note the similar answer before Pilate and Caiaphas, so that they may be condemned by their own statement.

“Nevertheless I tell you: from now on you will see,” etc. As if to say: “You despise me as a human being, but through this you will see me exalted above all the heavens.” The literal sense is plain: coming in the clouds of heaven for judgment, or working wondrously in the saints.

Then the high priest tore his garments, etc. [Col. 1478C] Rage had shaken him from the priestly throne, and frenzy drove him to tear his garments. This occurred as a great mystery, since the Lord’s garment could not be torn even by the soldiers crucifying him. For it signifies that their priesthood, because of the crimes of the high priests, was to be wholly dissolved, whereas the integrity of the Church, which is the garment of its Redeemer, would remain unbroken until the end of the age.

Note that it was the custom of the Jews to tear their garments when they heard something blasphemous. Then, because they thought him a blasphemer, they spat in his face and struck him with fists; others struck his face with the palms of their hands. Here was fulfilled the prophecy which says: “I gave my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away [Col. 1478D] from those who spat upon me” (Isa. 50). But he who was then struck with the fists of the Jews is even now struck by the blasphemies of false Christians. He who was then spat upon with the saliva of unbelievers is now also dishonored and provoked by the insane reproaches of those faithful in name only.

AUGUSTINE. Those who spat in his face signify those who reject the presence of his grace. Those who strike him with fists signify those who prefer their own honors to him. Those who strike his face with their palms signify those who, blinded by unbelief, assert that he did not come, as though banishing and rejecting his presence.

“Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” etc. This is said to him in contempt, because he wished to be regarded by the people as a prophet. And according to Mark, [Col. 1479A] they covered his face, not so that he might not see their crimes, but so that they might conceal from themselves the grace of knowing him, just as there was a veil over Moses’ face which remains to this day. But for us who believe it has been removed. For we, with unveiled face (2 Cor. 3), etc.

But Peter was sitting outside, etc. He did not approach Jesus lest the servants become suspicious.

And one maidservant came to him, saying: “You too were with Jesus the Galilean.” But he denied it, etc. Since he was not yet willing to die, he was afraid of being recognized. Why is it that a maidservant first exposes him, when men might more readily have recognized him, unless so that this sex too might appear to have sinned in the Lord’s death and to have been redeemed through the Lord’s passion? Therefore a woman first reveals—or receives—the mysteries of the resurrection [Col. 1479B] and keeps the commandments, in order to abolish the old error of transgression.

But when he went out, etc. Here Mark supplies what this Evangelist omitted for brevity. “He went out,” he says, “outside before the courtyard, and the cock crowed” (Mark 14); when he returned into the courtyard, the denial occurs. In this second denial he is addressed by two persons: by a maidservant, as Mark and Matthew say, and by another, as Luke says: “And after a little while another said: ‘You too are one of them.’” During this short interval he went out and, having returned, standing by the fire as John says, denied again.

“But when he went out”—that is, as he was going out, or was rising to go out—the maidservant noticed him and said to those who were at the fire; upon returning, Peter swore to them: “I do not know the man,” that is, I am not his disciple, [Col. 1479C] in which he also denied Christ himself.

Note also that the first time he says: “I do not know what you are saying.” The second time he denied it with an oath. The third time he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man. Perseverance in sin increases crimes; and whoever despises small things falls into greater ones.

Note also that the conversations of wicked people are harmful. They compelled the apostle Peter to deny the Lord among unbelievers, or to deny knowing as a man the one whom among his fellow disciples he had confessed as the Son of God.

“And immediately the cock crowed,” etc. Bede: After the third denial, the cockcrow follows. Note the sacraments of events through the stages of times. At midnight [Col. 1479D] he denies; at the cockcrow he repents; after the resurrection, in the light of day, he professed three times that he loved the one whom he had denied three times. For what he had done wrongly in the darkness of forgetfulness he corrected by remembrance of the light now hoped for; and by the presence of that same true light he completely raised himself up and corrected whatever had wavered.

LEO. He was allowed to waver so that, in the prince of the Church, the remedy of repentance might be considered, and so that no one might dare to trust in his own strength, since not even blessed Peter could escape the danger of mutability.

Mystically, a cock is a teacher who rebukes the sleepy, saying: “Awake to righteousness, and do not sin.” Peter’s denial before the first cockcrow signifies those who, shaken by Christ’s death, did not think him to be God before his resurrection. His two denials before the second cockcrow signify those who now err concerning him either according to Godhead or according to manhood, in both substances, and therefore deny the truth. The first cockcrow is the Lord’s resurrection in himself; the second is his resurrection in the body of the Church.

[Col. 1480A] And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, etc. In another Evangelist it is said: “The Lord looked upon Peter” (Luke 22). Jesus, though he was held only in body among the high-priestly council, looked upon the mind of his trembling disciple standing outside, raised it up, and stirred it to tears of repentance. Hence it follows:

“And he went out”—namely, so that he might have a free place for weeping—“and wept bitterly.” Detained in Caiaphas’s courtyard, he could not do penance. Therefore he goes outside, [Col. 1480B] so that, separated from the counsel of the ungodly, he might wash away more freely with tears the stains of his fearful denial.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“And when morning came,” etc. Mark and Matthew continue the narrative of the events concerning the Lord until morning. But afterward they return to relate Peter’s denial; when that is finished, they return again to the morning in order to continue the remaining events from there. Observe the priests’ diligence in evil: they stayed awake all night in order to commit murder.

“And they led him bound and handed him over,” etc. For they had this custom: that one whom they had condemned to death they handed over bound to the judge. Yet it should be noted that they did not bind him for the first time then; rather, [Col. 1480C] as John explains, they bound him immediately after seizing him in the garden and thus brought him first to Annas (John 18).

“Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing,” etc. HILARY. Judas returned the price to the priests, as if it were within his power to change the persecutors’ judgment. Thus, although he changed his will, he did not change the first outcome of his will. For the magnitude of his greed excluded the weight of his impiety.

JEROME. It did him no good to have repented, since he could not correct the crime. But when a brother sins against a brother in such a way that he can correct it, that sin can be forgiven him; whereas, if the deeds remain, repentance is vainly taken up in words. This is [Col. 1480D] what is said concerning Judas himself: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 153), so that he not only could not correct the wickedness of his betrayal, but added the crime of his own homicide to his former crime.

“I have sinned, betraying innocent blood,” etc. How much more, therefore, did those sin who bought him! Yet these utterly wicked men hear that they bought him and still believe themselves free from guilt; they locate the crime in the seller, saying: “What is that to us?” Understand: “What does it concern us?” “You,” etc. As if to say: “You know what you did.” Or: “What does the price we received concern us? You approved and wished for it; do with it whatever you wish.”

And having thrown the silver coins into the temple, he departed, etc. Just as his repentance was fruitless, so his offering in the temple was unacceptable. For he pretended as though he were offering it and as though by such [Col. 1481A] an offering he would be cleansed from that sin. And going away, he hanged himself with a noose. Not immediately, but on the day of the resurrection, once the resurrection had become public knowledge and had everywhere been proclaimed. He chose this kind of death in order to show that by such a death he was hateful to heaven and earth. Note that those who sin unto death incur such ignorance of themselves and blindness of mind that they are neither disturbed by their crimes nor tormented by the sorrow of repentance.

The chief priests, having received the silver coins, said: “It is not lawful to put them into the *corbona* [treasury], because they are the price of blood,” etc. Woe to those who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. For if they do not put the money into the *corbona*, that is, into the treasury among God’s offerings, because it is the price of blood, [Col. 1481B] why then is the blood itself shed? And what profit can they have before God if they bought with its price a field for burying strangers? There is a great mystery in deeds of wickedness. God is the potter, in whose hand it is to make from the same clay a vessel for honour or for dishonour. His field is the world, purchased in its entirety by Christ’s price, so that all strangers who have died with him may be buried there—not Israelites, certainly, but foreigners—who, buried in the price of Christ’s blood, will obtain eternal rest.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: “And they received thirty pieces of silver,” etc. This testimony is not found in Jeremiah, but almost in sense, though not in words, in Zechariah (Zech. 11). Hence some manuscripts do not have “through Jeremiah,” but only “through the prophet.” Yet by God’s hidden counsel it happened that [Col. 1481C] Jeremiah came to Matthew’s mind instead of Zechariah, because all the prophets spoke by the same Spirit, so that each prophet’s words belong to all, and all belong to each. Why, then, should Matthew correct what he had done under the Spirit’s guidance? It was so that we might be warned by this that there is such harmony among the prophets that what is said by one is credited as fitting another. Or again: Jeremiah contains the matter of a field being bought, though not under this designation of a price; Zechariah contains the thirty silver coins, but nothing about the purchase of the field. The evangelist therefore brings both together into one concerning what was fulfilled in the Lord: the thirty silver coins from Zechariah, and [Col. 1481D] the purchased field from Jeremiah. What follows—“whom they valued,” etc.—is found in neither; it is to be understood as spoken in the person of the evangelist, who knew it by revelation from the Lord.

HILARY. Such a prophecy pertains to this matter, which was done concerning the price.

But Jesus stood before the governor; and the governor questioned him, saying: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus says: “You say so,” etc. Since Pilate asked him about no other crime than whether he was King of the Jews, the Jews are convicted of impiety in that they were unable to find even a false accusation to bring against the Saviour. Jesus, however, so moderated his answer that he spoke the truth, yet his words were not open to slander. Observe that he gave some answer to Pilate, who was unwillingly [Col. 1482A] pronouncing sentence; but to the priests and chief priests he refused to answer, judging them unworthy of his speech. And when he did answer, he answered differently from the way in which he had answered Pilate. To the priest asking whether he himself was the Christ, he had said: “You have said it” (Matt. 26), as though answering about what had already been declared. This was because the whole Law had proclaimed the Christ to come, and the priest himself had spoken from the Law of Christ. But to Pilate, ignorant of the Law, asking whether he was the King of the Jews, he says: “You say so,” because the salvation of the Gentiles lies in the faith of a present confession. And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.

HILARY. The one who condemns Jesus is indeed an enemy, but he refers the case back to the Jewish people. He was unwilling to answer him [Col. 1482B] at all, lest, by clearing away the charge, he should be released, and thus the benefit of the cross should be delayed. According to Luke, they had made two accusations: that he forbade tribute to be paid to Caesar, and that he said he was a king. Pilate therefore asks about the kingdom, because he does not know. He does not ask about tribute because he had heard that Jesus answered: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22). Jesus therefore disregards their charge as an obvious lie. Hence Mark says: “Their testimonies were not consistent” (Mark 14).

Then Pilate says to him: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” etc. See how he transfers the case to the Jewish people.

Now at the feast, etc. The governor did not do this [Col. 1482C] under a sanction of imperial law, but by an annual custom of the nation, whose favour he delighted to win by such measures. He had then a certain notorious prisoner—that is, one distinguished by wickedness—called Barabbas. In the Gospel written according to the Hebrews, his name is interpreted “son of their teacher” or “of their father.” He is the Antichrist, whom they prefer to Christ, they to whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8). Pilate, whose name means “the mouth of the hammerer,” signifies the devil, the hammer of all misery, through whom the Lord allows vessels to be tested and whom he finally crushes when he breaks him in ultimate damnation. Observe that it says “Jesus who is called Christ,” whereas Mark says “King of the Jews” (Mark 15), whose kings were called “christs,” that is, anointed ones.

[Col. 1482D] For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy, etc. John explains what this envy was, saying: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him. If we let him go on like this, all will believe in him” (John 12).

But while he was sitting on the judgment-seat, etc. Observe that the tribunal is the seat of judges, the throne of kings, and the chair of teachers.

“For I have suffered many things,” etc. Observe that dreams are often revealed by the Lord to Gentiles; thus, in Pilate and his wife confessing the Lord’s righteousness, there is the testimony of the Gentile people. What the wife of a Gentile man understands in visions, the Jews, awake, refused to believe. And observe that now at last the devil, understanding that through Christ he would lose his spoils, seeks—just as he first brought death in through a woman—to free Christ from the Jews’ hands through a woman, lest through Christ’s death he lose death’s dominion. [Col. 1483A]

The chief priests, etc. Wickedness has gone out from the elders and judges of the people. For when a choice was offered between Jesus and the robber, they ask for the robber instead of Jesus, a murderer instead of the Saviour, the devil’s son instead of the Son of God: that the former may be released and the latter—namely, the Son of God—condemned. Their petition clings to them to this day: they have lost nation, place, and liberty, because they preferred to destroy the giver of liberty rather than lose their nation and place.

Pilate says to them: “What, then, shall I do with Jesus?” They all say: “Let him be crucified.” The governor says to them: “For what evil has he done?”

HILARY. Pilate gave many opportunities for Jesus to be released: first, by comparing the robber with the righteous man; then by asking, “What, then, shall I do [Col. 1483B] with Jesus?” And when they answered, “Crucify him,” he did not immediately comply. Rather, following the prompting of his wife, who had sent word, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man,” he too answered: “For what evil has he done?” By this statement Pilate acquits Jesus. But the more they saw that Pilate wished to release him, the more they cried: “Let him be crucified,” and their voices prevailed, so that what was spoken might be fulfilled: “I expected them to do justice, but they did wickedness; not righteousness, but an outcry” (Isa. 5).

But Pilate, seeing that he accomplished nothing and that rather a tumult was arising, took water and washed his hands before the people, etc. He washed his hands so that, in the washing of hands, the works of the Gentiles might be prefigured mystically, and so that he might in a sense separate us Gentiles from the impiety of the Jews who cried, [Col. 1483C] “Crucify him,” testifying, as it were, and saying: “I indeed wished to free an innocent man; but because a riot is arising, and because through rebellions I am charged with a crime against Caesar...”

“I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man,” etc. The judge, compelled to pronounce sentence against Christ, does not condemn the one presented to him, but reproves those presenting him, declaring righteous the one who is to be crucified. But was God, the judge, deceived? Pilate himself did incur some share of guilt by what he did, because, if he had wished, he could have rescued him well; but compared with them, he was far more innocent.

Then all the people answered and said: “His blood [Col. 1483D] be upon us and upon our children,” etc. This imprecation remains upon the Jews to this day, and Christ’s blood is not removed from them. Hence Isaiah says: “When you stretch out your hands to me, I will not hear; for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1). The Jews left their children an excellent inheritance when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” etc.

Then he released Barabbas to them; but having scourged Jesus, he handed him over to be crucified. The seditious robber, full and author of murders, was released to the Jewish people—that is, the devil, who long ago had been expelled from the homeland of light because of pride and sent into the prison of darkness. Therefore the Jews cannot have peace, because they preferred to choose the prince of seditions. [Col. 1484A] Or: Barabbas bears the type of Antichrist.

But he handed Jesus over to them after scourging him. Jesus is to be understood as scourged by Pilate himself, not by another. Pilate is believed to have done this so that the Jews, satisfied by his punishments and insults, might not press further for his death; and also in order to follow Roman law, which ordered one to be scourged before crucifixion. Mystically this occurred because it was written: “Many are the scourges of the sinner” (Ps. 31), so that, with him scourged, we might be freed from blows, as Scripture says: “The scourge shall not come near your tent” (Ps. 90).

Then the soldiers of the governor, etc. Since he had been called King of the Jews—and this was the charge which the priests had brought against him, that he was claiming authority for himself among the people of Israel—[Col. 1484B]they mock him by stripping him of his former garments and clothing him in purple, which ancient kings wore; instead of a diadem they place a crown of thorns on him; instead of a royal sceptre they give him a reed; and they worship him as king.

But let us understand all these things mystically. Just as Caiaphas said, “It is necessary for one man to die” (John 18), etc., not knowing what he was saying, so these men, whatever they did, did so unknowingly. Though they had another intention, they nevertheless conferred mysteries upon us who have believed. For by the cloak, which Mark calls purple, Christ’s flesh exposed to sufferings is signified. Hence the Prophet says: “Why, then, is your garment red?” etc. (Isa. 63). In the crown of thorns is the taking upon himself of our sins, [Col. 1484C] which are denoted by thorns. Therefore the Lord said to the first-formed man after his fall into sin: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3); that is, your conscience shall produce the pricks and stings of vices.

According to Luke, he is clothed by Herod in a white garment, signifying the innocence and chastity of the assumed humanity and the glory of the immortal kingdom which he received through his passion; or he is clothed in purple, that is, in holy martyrs, and in a white garment in other saints. Because writing is commonly done with a reed, they strike Christ’s head with a reed—those who, contradicting his divinity, try to confirm their error by the authority of Holy Scripture. Alternatively: in the reed is signified the weakness and emptiness of the same Gentile peoples, pressed down and even [Col. 1484D] placed upon his head. For a blow from a reed does no great injury to the head; but a typological meaning is present here: namely, that the weakness of Gentile bodies, first taken into Christ’s hand, should also submit to God the Father, who is his head. They spit in his face who reject the presence of his grace with execrating words and deny that Jesus came in the flesh. And just as those men worshipped falsely and maliciously, so today there are those who believe in him, but by perverse actions despise his words as though they were fables and scorn the promises of the kingdom. He is not mocked in his own garments, but in those which he bore because of our sins.

HILARY. When he is crucified, he receives his own adornment; immediately the elements are disturbed, and creation bears witness to its Creator.

[Col. 1485A] Now as they went out, they found a Cyrenian man, etc. Care must be taken lest there seem to be a contradiction with John’s statement that the Lord himself carried the cross. The other evangelists report that this Simon of Cyrene carried it. But it is to be understood that Jesus first carried the cross himself as he went out toward the named place; Simon was compelled into service on the road to carry it. Thus both occurred: first what John says, then what the other three say. This is a very fitting order in mystery, because Christ suffered for us, leaving an example that we should follow in his footsteps.

Since Simon is said to have been not an Israelite but a Cyrenian, from Cyrene, a city of Libya, he fittingly represents the peoples of the Gentiles, who were once strangers and aliens to the covenants but now, through obedience, [Col. 1485B] are fellow citizens and members of God’s household. Thus Simon is aptly interpreted “obedient.” Cyrene means “heir”; Simon comes “from the country,” that is, from Gentile life. For *villa* is called *pagos* in Greek. Hence the pagans, once alien to the city of God, leave their pagan nets behind and imitate the footprints of the passion. Or, in the Lord are figured those who voluntarily carry the Lord’s cross; in Simon, those who do so unwillingly.

And they came to the place called Golgotha, which in Syriac is interpreted “of the Skull.” There are places outside a city where the heads of condemned persons are cut off; they received the name “Skulls,” that is, “places of the scalped.” Therefore the Lord too was crucified there, so that where there had formerly been the place of the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be raised, and so that, just as for us he became the curse of the cross, [Col. 1485C] scourged and crucified, he might likewise be crucified for the world’s salvation as though guilty among the guilty.

But if anyone wishes to say that the Lord was crucified there so that his blood might drip upon Adam’s tomb, let us ask why the other robbers were also crucified in the same place. It is clear from this that Calvary signifies not the burial-place of the first man, but the place of beheadings, so that where sin abounded, God’s grace might abound all the more (Rom. 5). We read, moreover, in the Book of Joshua that Adam was buried near Hebron.

And they gave him wine mixed with gall; and when he had tasted it, etc. The Jewish people were a foreign vine turned into bitterness. But Mark says “wine mixed with myrrh” (Mark 15); Matthew [Col. 1485D] must be understood to have said “mixed with gall,” using gall to denote bitterness. Myrrh is indeed a very bitter substance, although it is possible that gall and myrrh made the wine exceedingly bitter. But when he says, “and when he had tasted, he would not drink,” this shows that he did indeed taste bitter death for us, but rose on the third day.

AUGUSTINE. Mark’s statement, “he did not receive it” (ibid.), means that he did not receive it in order to drink it; but he tasted it, as Matthew testifies.

After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots. John states this more fully: the soldiers divided them into four portions according to their own number, but cast lots for the seamless tunic (John 19). The fourfold garment signified his [Col. 1486A] Church distributed throughout the four quarters of the world. The tunic, not torn but assigned by lot, signifies the unity of all the Church’s parts, held together by the bond of charity.

The wood of the four-branched cross also seems suited to the interpretation by which the fourfold garment signifies the Church spread through the four regions of the world; by this four-branched cross, the four regions of the world seem to be embraced. But we should also observe carefully that the apostolic saying is suited to this four-branched cross: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. 3). The breadth of the cross, namely where the hands are nailed to the transverse beam, signifies the cheerfulness of the worker. Through the hands we have works; through breadth, [Col. 1486B] the cheerfulness of one who works. For sadness produces narrowness. By the height, to which the head is joined, is understood the expectation of recompense from the lofty justice of God, who will render to each according to his works. The length, by which the entire body is extended, signifies patience itself; hence those who endure are called long-suffering. The depth, fixed in the earth, prefigures the hiddenness of the mystery.

And sitting, they kept watch over him. The diligence of the priests and soldiers benefits us. For through it the power of him who rose appeared greater and more evident.

And they placed over his head the written charge against him: “This is Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.” The superscription clearly shows that not even by killing him could they bring it about that they should not have him as king—the king who [Col. 1486C] will most manifestly render to them according to their works. Hence in the psalm: “But I have been established king by him” (Ps. 2). And he is rightly king, because he is at once king and priest, since he offered to the Father the exceptional sacrificial offering of his own flesh upon the altar of the cross, through which he saved us. Thus “Jesus” is fittingly added. And the word “here” (*hic*), which is added there, may be understood adverbially, as though it said: “Let the king be called here,” that is, in this place, crucified in this manner and dead in this manner, he is himself king, himself Jesus, himself Saviour and Redeemer. Yet it may also be read pronominally.

Then two robbers were crucified with him, etc. The robbers crucified with the Lord, one on either side, signify those who undertake either the contest of Christ’s martyrdom or any [Col. 1486D] precepts of stricter continence. But those who seek or perform this solely for eternal and heavenly glory are certainly marked by the merit and faith of the robber on the right. Those, however, who renounce the world either for the sake of human praise or from any less worthy motive rightly imitate the mind and deeds of the blaspheming robber on the left. Of such persons the Apostle says: “If I deliver my body,” etc. (1 Cor. 13).

But those passing by blasphemed, etc. Those who pass beyond the way blaspheme: they refuse to fix their steps upon the true path of the Scriptures, and they shake their heads to signify that they are mobile toward evil with their whole mind and affection. And they say:

“Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days!” etc. The foolish [Col. 1487A] people shout in derision the very same thing which the false witnesses had alleged when they crucified him; in this their instability of mind, signified by the shaking of the head, is further demonstrated. “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” If he had then yielded to the mockers and come down from the cross, he would not have shown us the virtue of patience. But he waited a little, endured reproaches, bore mockery; and he who would not come down from the cross rose from the tomb. For it was greater to rise from the tomb than to descend from the cross; greater to destroy death by rising than to preserve life by descending.

Likewise the chief priests said: “He saved others,” etc.

HILARY. Even unwillingly they confess what is true and are condemned by their own statement. He who saved others could certainly save himself if he wished; but he did not wish to do the lesser thing, in order to do the [Col. 1487B] greater. It follows: “If he is King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we shall believe him,” etc. What a deceitful promise! He did the greater thing by rising from the tomb, and yet they did not believe. But demons inspired this demand in them, wishing him to come down, for they had immediately felt the power of the cross and their own strength broken. Therefore the Lord remains, in order utterly to destroy the devil and take his spoils from him.

The robbers who were crucified with him did the same, etc.

AUGUSTINE. How could those crucified with him revile him, when, according to Luke’s testimony, only one of them reviled him and the other restrained the reviler? The plural is used for the singular for brevity’s sake, as in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “They stopped the mouths of lions,” although this is understood of Daniel alone; “they were sawn asunder” (Heb. II), of [Col. 1487C] Isaiah alone. But according to Luke’s testimony, one said: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us”; while the other rebuked him and prayed to the Lord with faithful supplication: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23).

We see this occurring in the Church to this day, when both true and false Christians are struck by worldly afflictions. Those who have tasted the mysteries of the Lord’s passion with a pretended mind desire the Lord to free them for the joys of this present life. But those who, with simple intention, glory with the Apostle in the Lord’s cross wish rather to be delivered from present hardships in such a way that they may also commend their spirit into the hand of their Creator and desire with him to be sharers in the heavenly kingdom. Therefore the one who prayed to the Lord with doubtful faith [Col. 1487D] was wholly despised and deemed worthy of no answer. But the Lord deigned to receive with merciful hearing the prayer of the one who sought from him eternal salvation.

HILARY. The two robbers may also signify the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles. At first both peoples blasphemed the Lord when Jews and Gentiles alike consented to the Lord’s death. But afterward one, terrified by the greatness of the signs, repented and to this day rebukes the Jews who blaspheme.

Now from the sixth hour darkness came, etc. Those who have written against the Gospel suppose that Christ’s disciple, through ignorance, called this an eclipse of the sun, which ordinarily occurs at fixed and appointed times; [Col. 1488A] for a solar eclipse can occur only at the new moon. But no one doubts that at Passover the moon was full. And lest it seem that the moon’s shadow, or the shadow of its disk cast against the sun, had produced merely brief and dusky darkness, a period of three hours is specified, so that every excuse of those who offer objections might be removed. This occurred in fulfilment of the prophecy: “The sun shall set at noon, and the light shall be darkened in the day” (Amos 8). And elsewhere: “The sun set while it was still noon.” It also seems to me that the sun withdrew its rays lest it should see its Lord hanging on the cross, or lest the impious blasphemers should enjoy its light.

Observe that he says “the sixth hour”: that is, he was crucified when the sun was departing from the centre of the world. But the mysteries of his resurrection [Col. 1488B] were celebrated at dawn, when the sun was already rising. By the state of time he signified what he accomplished by the effect of his work: he died for our sins and rose for our justification. He suffered at the sixth hour because Adam became a sinner at about that hour. Hence it is written that he heard the voice of God walking in Paradise in the breeze after noon (Gen. 3): after noon, because the light of faith was already declining; in the breeze, because the warmth of charity was cooling; and he was heard walking because he was departing from the man who had already sinned.

Therefore reason—indeed, the order of divine mercy—required that at the very point of time when he had then shut the gate of Paradise upon Adam in transgression, he should now open it to the repentant robber; and that at the hour when the first Adam, by sinning, brought death into the world, the second Adam should [Col. 1488C] destroy death by dying. But Mark says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, while John says that Pilate sat on the tribunal at about the sixth hour, in the place called Lithostrotos. This shows more clearly that the Jews, though they excuse themselves, crucified the Lord with their tongues more than the soldiers did with their hands: for the Jews cried at the third hour that he should be crucified. When he was actually crucified, it was about the sixth hour.

And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying: “Eli,” etc. Human nature had been so abandoned because of sin; but because the Son of God became [Col. 1488D] our advocate and pleader, he laments the misery of those whose nature he assumed. In this he showed how much those who sin ought to weep, when he who never sinned wept so. Observe that when the day had declined toward evening and the sun’s heat had cooled, he completed his passion, showing that he dies for our sins, through which we have fallen from divine light and love into this night. He rose in the morning, teaching that he will bring those raised in soul into the light of eternal blessedness.

But some of those standing there, etc.

HILARY. Not all, but some—whom I suppose were Roman soldiers—not understanding the character of Hebrew speech. But if you understand some Jews, that too is fitting: they act according to their usual custom, slandering the Lord as weak because he calls for Elijah’s help, regarding him as [Col. 1489A] inferior to Elijah.
