And immediately one of them, etc. John explains why vinegar was given to him: “Jesus, knowing that all things were now completed, so that this might be fulfilled, ‘In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink’” (Ps. 68), said: “I thirst” (John 19). The Jews were vinegar, degenerate from the wine of prophets and patriarchs, filled as though from a full vessel with the wickedness of this world, having hearts like a sponge—hollow, as it were, and fraudulent with twisting hiding-places. A sponge is said to be an empty and cavernous plant. The hyssop placed around it is a lowly herb but one that cleanses the chest; it signifies Christ’s humility. They surround the sponge with hyssop because they surrounded Christ’s humility [Col. 1489B] and thought that they had entrapped him. The reed signifies Scripture, which was fulfilled by this act. Thus they put the sponge on the reed: that is, they join the outcome of the event to the prophecy that preceded it.

But Jesus, crying with a loud voice, gave up the spirit. Luke states this plainly: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and, he says, “having said this, he expired” (Luke 23). John says that, when he had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, gave up the spirit (John 19). Between “It is finished” and “bowing his head, he gave up the spirit,” that loud cry was uttered—a detail John passed over but the other three recorded.

HILARY. It is an indication of divine power to give up the spirit, just as he himself says: “No one can take my soul from me; but I lay it down, and I shall take it again” [Col. 1489C] (John 10).

And behold, the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom. Josephus reports that the angelic powers once set over the Temple cried out: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” According to the anagogical sense, the veil of the Temple is torn so that the ark of the covenant and all the mysteries of the Law that had been concealed may appear and pass to the people of the nations. The veil called the outer veil was torn, because now we see in part; but when that which is perfect comes, the inner veil will be torn apart, so that we shall see all things now hidden from us.

Observe that it is said to have been torn in two parts. Formerly it had been said: [Col. 1489D] “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75); and in the Gospel: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10). After his passion he says: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. 28), Jews and Gentiles alike. It is also in two parts, namely, into the New and Old Testaments.

“From top to bottom.” This may be said to mean from the beginning of the world, when man was created, to the consummation of the age. And the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split: all things declare their Creator crucified. The earth moves because it cannot endure to bear the Lord hanging upon it. Mystically, the hearts of earthly people are changed for the better by Christ’s passion; the rocks are split because Jewish [Col. 1490A] hardness was to be softened in part. Or the rocks were split in order to reveal the hardness of the Jews, who were not pierced or softened when Christ suffered, though even stones seemed in some manner to be pierced. Or the rocks are the hearts of Gentiles, or the prophecies of the prophets, called rocks from Christ the rock, so that whatever had been closed to them within the hard covering of the Law might, when split open, lie revealed to the Gentiles.

It follows: the tombs were opened, as a sign, of course, of the future resurrection. And many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep rose; yet not before the Lord rose, so that the Lord himself might be the firstborn from the dead. “And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city, Jerusalem.” That is, the earthly Jerusalem, called holy because of the worship of the one God; or the heavenly Jerusalem. For those who rose when the Lord rose are, according to Bede’s [Col. 1490B] testimony, also to be believed to have ascended with him when he ascended. Nor is any credence to be granted to the rashness of those who say that afterward they returned to ashes.

But when it says, “They appeared to many,” it shows that this was not the general resurrection, which would have appeared to all if it were general; rather, it was a special resurrection for many, so that those worthy to see might see.

But the centurion and those with him, etc. How blind are the Jews, who do not believe even amid so many miracles, while they see the centurion believe! In the centurion is signified the faith of the Church, which, with the veil of heavenly mysteries opened by the Lord’s death, confesses Jesus to be the Son of God while the Synagogue is silent. Observe that the centurion [Col. 1490C] confesses him to be truly the Son of God before the cross, in the very scandal of the passion; but Arius proclaimed in the Church that he was a creature.

Now there were many women there at a distance, who had followed the Lord from Galilee, etc. It was a Jewish custom, and not considered blameworthy, for women to provide food and clothing for their teachers from their own resources. Yet because this could cause scandal among the nations, the Apostle recalls that he did not do so, saying: “Have we not the authority to lead about women who are sisters?” (1 Cor. 9). But let us see what women Christ had as companions: namely Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons; and Mary, the sister of his mother, namely the mother of James and Joseph, [Col. 1490D] his maternal aunt; and others whom we read of in the other evangelists.

But how is the same Mary Magdalene said by Matthew and Luke to have stood at a distance, yet according to John to have been beside the cross? It was because they were at such a distance that they could be called both near—since they were present before his eyes—and far, compared with the crowd standing close by. We may also say that those who were with Mary, the Lord’s mother, began to leave after he had entrusted her to the disciple, in order to escape the press of the crowd and see from a distance what was taking place.

When evening had come, a certain rich man came from Arimathea, etc.

JEROME. Arimathea is the city itself of Ramatha of Elkanah and Samuel, [Col. 1491A] in the Tauric region, near Ospolis. Observe that this Joseph was indeed of great dignity in the world, but of greater dignity before God. Such a man was fittingly required to bury the Lord’s body: one worthy of such a ministry by the righteousness of his merits, and able to render this service by the nobility of worldly power. For if he had been any poor or unknown person, he would not have dared approach the governor to request the body.

Observe that in rendering this final service to Jesus’ body, he cared less about the Jews, although he had previously been accustomed to avoid their hostility by hearing the Lord as a hidden disciple of Christ.

Then Pilate ordered the body to be given to him, etc. Here it is noted how great Joseph’s worldly rank was.

And Joseph, having received the body, etc. See how great his merit was before the Lord. Observe that, in the Lord’s simple burial, [Col. 1491B] the ambition of the rich is condemned, who cannot lack riches even in their tombs. For there was neither gold, nor jewel, nor silk, but clean and pure linen. Hence also the Church customarily celebrates the sacrifice of the altar not upon silk or dyed cloth, but upon earthly linen. We read that this was decreed by blessed Pope Sylvester in the pontifical acts. Mystically, however, the person who receives Jesus with a pure mind wraps him in a clean shroud.

It follows: “And he placed it in his own new tomb,” etc. It was new so that, if he were laid in a tomb where another had been placed, someone else might perhaps be imagined to have risen. It was hewn in rock so that, if it had been built of many stones, people might say that, after the foundations of the tomb were dug out, he had been stolen away.

[Col. 1491C] BEDE. There were people who saw the tomb itself with bodily eyes. It was a round chamber cut from the underlying rock, of such a height that a man standing inside could scarcely reach the roof with an outstretched hand. It had an entrance from the east, against which the great stone was rolled. On the northern side of this chamber was the sepulchre itself—that is, the place of the Lord’s body—made from the same rock, seven feet long and three palms in measure, rising above the rest of the floor. This place was open throughout not from above but from the southern side, through which they brought in the body. The colour of this tomb and burial-place is said to have been a mixture of reddish and [Col. 1491D] white.

And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb, etc. They rolled a great stone there so that the entrance of the sepulchre could not be opened without the assistance of many persons. But Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

BEDE. When Jesus’ acquaintances had returned home after the body was laid down, the women alone watched the burial service of him whom they loved more ardently, awaiting what Jesus had promised; and therefore they were the first to see the resurrection.

Mystically, the holy women do the same thing on the day of the *parasceve*, that is, Preparation: when humble souls, the more conscious they are of their greater frailty, the more fervently they burn with Christ’s love, clinging to the traces of his Passion in this world, in which future rest must be prepared, they diligently perform their service; and, if perhaps they are able to imitate it with devout curiosity, they consider in what order that same Passion was accomplished. “But on the next day, which is after the *parasceve*.” *Parasceve* means “preparation.” By this name is called the sixth day of the Sabbath, on which they prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath, as was also said concerning the manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather double” (Exod. V), because on the sixth day man was made, and on the seventh day God rested from all his work. Therefore Jesus dies for man on the sixth day. Hence he also said: “It is finished.” And on the sixth day the work for the redemption of the world was completed, and on the Sabbath he rested in the tomb. Thus we too must suffer for the Lord in this sixth age; in the seventh, which is that of the dead, we must rest in the hiddenness of the Pasch, until the eighth day of resurrection comes. [Col. 1492A–B]

In Genesis likewise the seventh day is not said to have an evening, because in that age [or: hidden state] the rest of souls is not consumed by any sorrow, but the joy of the future resurrection is increased. They also say concerning that day which followed the Sabbath that it was the Preparation of the Jewish Passover, since the unleavened bread had already begun from that same time. Yet the true Passover, which was enacted in the Lord’s Passion, began to be prepared as the *parasceve* not of the Jews but of Christians. They say that the *parasceve* is reckoned from the ninth hour of the night, in which the Lord was being prepared by the Jews for death. For *parasceve*, as we have said, means “preparation.” Therefore, from that hour of the night in which he was in the house of Annas and Caiaphas until his crucifixion—at the sixth hour of the *parasceve* according to John, and at the third hour of the day according to Mark—we rightly understand the *parasceve* of our Passover, that is, the preparation for Christ’s death, to have begun. [Col. 1492B–C]

But when we carefully calculate the years from the creation of the world down to the Lord’s Passion, we find that in the very year in which the Lord was crucified, according to lunar years, the eighth day before the Ides of March was the New Moon, that is, the beginning of the new moon, and, according to the Hebrews, the beginning of that year; and that on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, at the very vernal equinox, on Friday, the fourteenth day of the moon, the Passover of the Hebrews occurred later, so that on that day the Lamb of God might hang on the cross for the salvation of humankind, on which day the lamb was commanded to be killed for the deliverance of the people; and that by his very death he might seem to divide light from darkness, that is, believers from unbelievers, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “This one is set for the fall and rising again of many” (Luke II). And: “He delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son.” [Col. 1492C–D]

The Evangelist also agrees with this interpretation when he says that the Jews did not enter Pilate’s praetorium, lest they should be defiled, but so that they might eat the Passover. And if anyone asks, “Why then did the Lord not celebrate the Passover at that time?” let him know that he was not under the Law; and he wished first to hand over to his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood, and afterward to offer that very body upon the altar of the cross. This is the true *parasceve*, not of the Jews but of Christians, because “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V). For the Jews’ *parasceve* had been on the preceding day. According to this calculation, we also find that at that time, namely on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, the Son of God rose from the dead—the same time, namely the tenth day before the Kalends of April, at which we find the first-created Adam to have been formed from the clay of the earth. It follows:

“The chief priests assembled and said to Pilate: ‘Sir, we remember,’” etc. The crime of death was not enough for them, unless after his death they also tore apart his reputation. Note that he says, “after three days”: the whole is taken from a part. The part of the sixth day on which he was crucified, together with its night, is counted as one day; the Sabbath is whole; and the third day, beginning with its first part, namely the night, is whole with its day. Thus there are three days. And it should be noted that they call him a deceiver: they attributed to the Lord what they themselves were. It follows: “And the last error will be worse than the former.” Unknowingly they speak the truth; for contempt of repentance is worse than the error of ignorance. [Col. 1493A–B]

Pilate said to them: “You have a guard,” etc. As though he said: “Let it suffice you that I consented to the killing of an innocent man; let the error remain with you.”

“But they went away and secured the tomb.” HILARY. It had not been enough for the chief priests to crucify the Lord, unless they guarded the tomb, obtained a cohort, sealed the stone, and, as far as lay in their power, opposed a hand to him as he rose. But this was done so that their diligence might benefit our faith. For the more carefully they guard it, the more clearly the power of the Risen One is shown. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“But late on the Sabbath,” etc. JEROME. The fact that different times are described for these women in the Gospels is not a sign of falsehood, but the service of diligent visitation: they repeatedly go away and return, and do not allow themselves to remain far from the Lord’s tomb. After the Lord’s burial, for as long as it was lawful to work, that is, until sunset, they prepared spices; and because, owing to the pressure of time, they could not complete the task, after the Sabbath had passed—that is, when the sun had set, and permission to work had returned—they bought aromatics. And because night came on before them, they could not go to the tomb, and so they came in the morning. “Very early on the first day of the week”: in this he does not disagree with Luke and John. Matthew, however, denotes the night from its first part, that is, from evening, whose end was the time when they came to the tomb. He names it thus because, after the Sabbath had passed, it was then lawful to do what they wished. Thus, late on the Sabbath—that is, during the night of the Sabbath day—they began indeed to come in the evening, that is, to prepare the spices; but they arrived when morning was bright. Matthew states this more obscurely for brevity’s sake; the others more explicitly. It follows: [Col. 1493C–D]

“Which was dawning toward the first day of the week,” etc. The order of time is that evening darkens into night rather than dawns into day; but mystically he says “dawning” because of the glory of the impending resurrection. Until this point the day was said to precede the night. Now the order is changed, and the night in which he rose is joined to the day on which he showed himself. And fittingly the night formerly followed the day, because humanity had fallen from light into darkness. But now day follows night, because through the resurrection we are brought back from sins to life. [Col. 1494A]

“Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb,” etc. The two women, of one name and of the same devotion and love, signify the two peoples who, with equal devotion, embrace Christ’s Passion and resurrection.

“And behold, there was a great earthquake,” etc. That an earthquake occurs at the resurrection as at the Passion signifies that hearts formerly earthly, cast down from heavenly hope, are to be moved to repentance through faith in the Passion and resurrection.

“For an angel of the Lord,” etc. The angel performed the service owed by his ministry to the Lord, because he came and rolled away the stone, not to open the door for the Lord as he departed, but to furnish people an indication that his departure had already taken place. [Col. 1494A–B]

This rolling away of the stone, indeed, mystically suggests to us the opening of Christ’s mysteries, which had been concealed by the covering of the letter of the Law. For the Law was written on stone; once its covering was removed, the glory of the Lord’s resurrection was shown.

“And he sat upon it.” It should be noted that the angel, witness of the Lord’s resurrection, appeared seated, whereas those who announced to the world the joy of his birth are recorded to have stood beside the shepherds. For standing belongs to one who fights, sitting to one who reigns. Rightly, then, the angel who proclaimed Christ’s coming into the world appeared standing, so that by standing he might signify that the one whose coming he announced had come to overthrow the prince of this world. But the herald of his resurrection is remembered as having sat, so that by sitting he might also signify that, the author of death having been cast down, this same one had ascended the throne of an everlasting kingdom. Hence he himself, shortly afterward appearing to the disciples, said: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” Note also that he sat upon the stone that closed the door of the tomb, to teach that Christ by his own power had both overcome and overthrown the bars of hell. [Col. 1494B–C]

“His appearance was like lightning, and his garments white as snow,” etc. In his bearing and countenance he signified that the one whose resurrection glory he announced would be both terrible in condemning the reprobate and gentle in consoling the elect. For in lightning is the terror of fear; in snow, the gentleness of brightness. And it should be noted that Mark says: “The women, entering the tomb, saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe” (Mark XVI). This may cause difficulty unless we understand either that Matthew passed over in silence the angel whom they saw when they entered, or that Mark speaks of the one whom they saw outside upon the stone—so that they saw two angels and heard the same things separately from the two—or else that by “entering the tomb” we must understand their entering some walled enclosure, by which it is credible the place was then protected, namely some space before the rock in which the place of burial had been cut out; thus they saw, on the right in that same space, the one whom Matthew says sat upon the stone. [Col. 1494D]

“But for fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men,” etc. The angel himself also appeared with the severity of divine judgment, so that he might strike the impious guards of Christ’s tomb with terror and cast them down upon the ground like the dead, while refreshing the most devout women who visited that same tomb with kindly consolation and strengthening them not to fear, saying:

“Do not be afraid,” etc. As though he said: “Let those fear who do not love the coming of the citizens of heaven, who, burdened by carnal desires, despise and despair of reaching their fellowship. But why are you terrified, who see angels as your fellow citizens?” [Col. 1495A]

“For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified: he is not here,” etc. At that time many could be called by this name, though not substantially but only by appellation. Therefore it is made clear of which Jesus he speaks when he says “crucified,” and afterward adds: “He is not here,” etc. As though he said: “He is absent through the presence of his flesh, though through the presence of his majesty he is absent nowhere.”

“He has risen, as he said.” As though he said: “Because he said he would rise, he has risen. For it is impossible that what he said should not happen.” It follows:

“Come and see the place.” As though he said: “If you do not believe words, believe the empty tomb.”

“And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen: behold, he will go before you into Galilee,” etc. That through the angel he foretold to the disciples that they would see him in Galilee mystically declares both the truth of his resurrection and the advancement of our spiritual life. For Galilee is interpreted “migration.” Therefore he promises that the glory of his resurrection will be seen by those who migrate from corruption to incorruption, from death to life. And note that the angel urges them to go quickly and tell the disciples. The joy of so great a victory was not to be concealed, but rather immediately disclosed to those who loved in like manner; and this also mystically admonishes us to do the same. [Col. 1495B–C]

“And the women departed quickly from the tomb with fear and joy,” etc. One asks how Mark can say: “But they went out and fled from the tomb. For trembling and amazement had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone” (Mark XVI). Yet we may understand that they did not dare to say anything to the angels—that is, to answer what they had heard from them—or certainly to the guards lying there. Moreover, the joy mentioned by Matthew does not conflict with the fear narrated by Mark. We must understand that both were present in their minds. Thus a double emotion of fear and joy held the women’s minds: the one because of the greatness of the miracle; the other because of desire for the Risen One.

“Behold, Jesus met them, saying: ‘Hail.’” BEDA. As they were thus running in mind to announce the matter to the disciples, Jesus met them and greeted them, mystically showing all who begin the path of virtues that he meets them by helping them, so that they may be able to attain eternal salvation. And it should be noted that Christ first met and greeted these women so that we may understand the first curse upon woman to have been removed. [Col. 1495D–1496A]

“But they came and held his feet,” etc. It was said above that he rose and went out while the tomb was closed. Yet now we read that the women held his feet. For he rose and went out while the entrance of the tomb was closed, in order to teach that his body had now become immortal. But here his feet are held, in order to prove that it was true flesh. And because they were afraid at such a sight, fear is first driven away when they are told, “Do not be afraid,” so that with tranquil minds they may hear what is said afterward. But what was said above—“they held his feet”—should be noted. For those women hold his feet who adore him risen again. But she who did not yet know that the Son of God had risen hears, rightly:

“Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. Go, tell my brothers,” etc. O marvelous kindness of God! Before his Passion he had been accustomed to call them servants; now after his resurrection he calls them his brothers, so that he might prove or show that in rising again he had resumed the condition of the same humanity which he had previously possessed; or that he might raise them up to earn the crown of that same immortality, in which he now excelled. This appears when he says: “Let them go into Galilee.” When he says: “Go, tell my brothers,” note that the guilt of the human race is cut off at the point from which it proceeded. [Col. 1496A–B]

GREGORY. For because woman in paradise offered death to man, from the tomb woman announces life to men; and she who had repeated the death-dealing words of the serpent now relates the words of the Life-giver.

As though he said to the human race, not in words but by the facts themselves: “From the hand by which the cup of death was brought upon you, receive now the cup of life and salvation.” And it should be noted that he says: “Let them go into Galilee, and there they will see him.” He was not seen by the disciples only there, nor was he seen there first. For Luke and John say quite plainly that on the day of resurrection itself the Lord was seen in Jerusalem: first by Mary Magdalene, when she was told, “Do not touch me”; then by that same Mary and the other Mary, as they were running to announce the news to the disciples, when they also held his feet. On that same day he was also seen by two disciples on the road. He was seen also by Peter, although the Evangelist does not state when this occurred. He was also seen by the disciples when those who had recognized him in the breaking of bread returned and were speaking, when he stood in their midst and said: “Peace be with you!” Yet Mark and Matthew say especially that the angel, or the Lord himself, said he would be seen in Galilee. [Col. 1496C–D]

Mystically, Galilee means “migration.” He will therefore go before them into Galilee; that is, the grace of God will migrate from the Jews to the Gentiles. “He will go before you,” I say, preparing the way in their hearts; “and there you will see him,” that is, his members, and you will find a living body. Or Galilee means “revelation”: not in the form of a servant, but in that form in which he is equal to the Father, he has gone before us to that place where we shall be like him, and there we shall see him as he is. And this is the blessed revelation, or migration from this world into eternity. [Col. 1497A]

“When they had gone, behold, some of the guards came into the city and reported to the chief priests the things that had occurred,” etc. Such miracles occurred around the tomb that the soldiers themselves saw them—the soldiers who had come as guards so that they might become witnesses, if they wished to report the truth. But that avarice which had captivated Christ’s companion, namely Judas, also captivated the guards of the tomb. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave the soldiers a great sum of money taken from the Temple, just as they had previously given thirty pieces of silver, etc. Therefore all those who misuse the revenues of the Temple and what is offered for the uses of the Church for other purposes by which they fulfill their own will are like the scribes and priests who purchase a lie with the Savior’s blood. [Col. 1497A–B]

AUGUSTINE. O foolish madness! You produce sleeping witnesses. Truly you yourself have fallen asleep—no longer a priest but a parricide—who have failed by scrutinizing such things. For if they were asleep, how could they see? If they saw nothing, how are they witnesses? You have failed in the very carrying out of your counsels.

But having accepted the money and been reassured that they would incur no loss or danger, they did as they had been instructed. And that report—the error of a purchased lie—still persists among the Jews to this very day, because even now they do not believe in the Savior. [Col. 1497B]

“But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them; and when they saw him, they worshiped him,” etc. It is not without mystery that after the resurrection the Lord appeared to the disciples in Galilee, or that he appeared upon a mountain: to signify that the body which he had assumed by birth from the common earth of the human race, he had now, by rising again, lifted above all earthly things; and to admonish believers that, if they desire there to see the height of his resurrection, they should here strive to pass from low pleasures to heavenly desires. But what does it mean that Jesus goes before them into Galilee to be seen by them, and they follow and, seeing him, worship him? It means that Christ rose from the dead as the firstfruits of those who sleep. [Col. 1497C]

Those who belong to Christ follow, and each in his own order migrates from death to life; and there, seeing him, they worship him, contemplating him in the hope of divinity. The interpretation of Galilee as “revelation” accords with that vision. For then, with the Lord’s face unveiled, we shall behold his glory. It follows:

“But some doubted,” etc. At first, those who had learned that this was he worshiped with faces lowered to the ground; nevertheless, some uncertainty was in their minds, because they thought that they saw not the body in which he had suffered raised again, but only the spirit which he had handed over when the Passion ended. Therefore the just Master immediately strengthens them in faith and calls them to the grace of faith, showing to what greatness of glory the humanity assumed for humankind, and given over to death for humankind, had attained. Hence he adds: [Col. 1497D–1498A]

“All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth,” etc. It is clear that he speaks this not of his divinity coeternal with the Father, but of his assumed humanity, in which he was first made lower than the angels, and in rising from the dead was set above all creatures. Note that the angelic powers, even before Christ rose from the dead, recognized themselves as rightly subject to the man whom they saw had been specially assumed by their Creator. But other people on earth, blind, despised to understand his power even in his miracles. Therefore, wishing his power to become known on earth as in heaven, he said:

“All power has been given to me,” etc. He also sent teachers to preach throughout the whole world the Gospel of his power, saying: “Go therefore, teach all nations,” etc. As though he said: “Since that which had hitherto been doubtful to people for certain reasons has now come into the light, go therefore and teach.” And note the fitting order. First the hearer must be taught; then instructed in the sacraments of faith; then trained to keep the commandments. According to Hilary, the body cannot receive the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received the truth of faith; nor, as Bede says, can one yet be cleansed by baptism unless afterward one persists in good works. He says therefore: “Teach”—that is, first instruct your hearers in faith, catechize and strengthen them in the knowledge of truth—and afterward baptize, because unless one is born again, etc. [Col. 1498A–C]

“Baptize,” I say, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” that is, in confession of the Trinity. And because faith or baptism is of little or no value without works, he adds: “Teach them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.” Lest we think the things he commanded to be trivial or few, he said “all.” And he next declares what reward for devout conduct, what pledge of future blessedness, even in the present, awaits believers, saying:

“Behold, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age.” From this it is understood that until the end of the age there will not be lacking in the world those worthy of divine indwelling and habitation. Nor should it be doubted that, after the conflicts of this age, those remain with Christ in the kingdom who, while struggling in the age, deserved to have Christ dwell as a guest in the lodging of their heart. [Col. 1498C–D]

“The first day of the week.” At dawn, as all agree, they came to the tomb, and what Matthew alone says concerning the earthquake, the stone rolled away, and the terrified guards had already occurred.

“Mary Magdalene came.” She was more fervent than the others. Therefore John mentions her, leaving the others unmentioned, in all that concerned her. Seeing the stone removed, before examining more carefully, she believed that the body had been taken away; she ran and reported it to Peter and John. They too ran to the tomb and, not finding the body, believed what Mary had said—that the body had been taken away—and departed.

“But Mary stood outside weeping.” In the garden, where they had already gone out. Then they saw the angel sitting upon the rolled-away stone, of whom Matthew and Mark speak.

He said to them: “Do not be afraid; I know that you seek Jesus,” etc. Mark [John?] did not pass over similar words. At these words, while Mary wept, she bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels, one sitting at the head and the other at the feet, clothed in white; and they said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said: “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John XX). Here the angels must be understood to have risen so that they were also seen standing, as Luke says, who also reports them as having said:

“Why do you seek the living among the dead?” etc. [Col. 1499A–B]

After this Mary turned backward and saw Jesus standing, as John says, and she did not know that it was Jesus (ibid.), thinking that he was the gardener; there, when he called her by name, she recognized him, and to her it was said: “Do not touch me.” Then she went out of the tomb, that is, from the place hollowed out before the stone, and with her the other women, whom, as Mark says, fear had seized, and they said nothing to anyone. Then, according to Matthew: “Behold, Jesus met them, saying—” [text breaks off]. [Col. 1499B]

[Col. 1500A]

“—‘Hail.’ And they came and held his feet.” Thus we gather that they had the angels’ conversation twice when they came to the tomb; and that they had God’s own conversation once when Mary thought him the gardener, and now again when he met them, so that this very sudden appearance might strengthen them. Mary Magdalene therefore came reporting to the disciples, and also the other women who had been with her, whom Luke mentions. There were indeed more appearances, as Paul indicates when he says: “He was seen by James; then he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once” (I Cor. XV). But we read ten in the Gospels, five on the very day of the resurrection. First he appeared to Mary Magdalene as she wept at the tomb. Afterward he appeared to that same Mary and the other Mary as they were returning to report to the apostles. Third, to Simon. Fourth, to Cleophas and his companion. Fifth, to those who had returned and were relating how they had recognized him in the breaking of bread: he appeared with the doors shut, where Thomas was absent. Sixth, after eight days, when Thomas was with them. Seventh, to those fishing at the Sea of Tiberias. Eighth, on the mountain of Galilee, which was far from Jerusalem. Ninth, to the eleven as they reclined, on the day when he ascended. Tenth, they saw him no longer standing on earth but lifted into the air and seeking the heavens, while the angels said: “Thus he will come, as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I). [Col. 1500A–B]

[Col. 1499]

## EXPLANATIONS OF THE APOCALYPSE (G)\*

God and Lord the Father, foreseeing the tribulations which the holy Church would suffer after it had been founded by the apostles, arranged with the Son and the Holy Spirit to reveal those tribulations and their rewards. For missiles that are foreseen wound less. Thus God revealed it to Christ according to his humanity; Christ revealed it to John; and John in turn to the Church. And deservedly Christ revealed to John, who excelled all others in the privilege of chastity, and whose name is interpreted “the grace of God,” because he ascribed to divine grace all the good things he did, and because he endured every enormous torment with equanimity of mind. But since it is clear that this revelation was made by a vision, we must see what kind of vision it was. Vision is of one kind bodily, of another spiritual, of another intellectual. [Col. 1499C–D]

Bodily vision is that by which we see heaven, earth, and other bodies. Spiritual vision is when something else is set forth in what is seen. Such was the case with Moses, who saw the burning bush not consumed by fire (Exod. III), which signified something else. Intellectual vision, however, occurs when, with the Holy Spirit inwardly prompting, someone conceives something mystical, as Saint John did in this book. For he did not really see these things, but, through the inward prompting of divine inspiration, he formed in his intellect fitting signs that signified the passions. Let us now see what its subject matter is. Its subject matter consists of seven signs signifying tribulations. Its purpose is to invite us to patience, so that through patience we may come to contemplation, through contemplation to revelation, and thence to blessedness. In this we have the final cause of this work. Since in divinity the question is not of philosophy but of life, let us see to what life it belongs. One kind of life is theoretical, that is, contemplative; another is practical, that is, active. Yet it is clear that it is referred to contemplation. [Col. 1500C]

And it should be noted why it invites us to patience rather than to other virtues. The answer is that, as faith is the foundation of all virtues, so patience is in some way their support. It should also be noted that a certain part of this book is taken as a prologue, namely as far as “I, John, your brother.” In that part it invites us to hear, to read, and to keep; because if we do this, we shall attain blessedness. Thus at the beginning it commends its work. This book should be read because it is an Apocalypse, that is, a revelation, and not that of just anyone but of Jesus Christ; or thus: This book should be read because blessed is the one who reads and the one who hears the words of the prophecy of this Apocalypse, that is, revelation of Jesus Christ. [Col. 1500D]

The reason that prompted blessed John to write was that, while he was held in exile by Domitian, many evils had grown up in the churches over which he presided. For their correction he is admonished through an angel in a vision, whether while asleep or spiritually rapt. By the fact that John, deprived of every human word and help, is divinely visited, we are taught that the more we withdraw from this earthly tumult, the more fit we are judged to be for divine visitation. The subject matter of this book is the Church, concerning which all the visions are made. What is introduced concerning Antichrist and demons is done to establish the Church. Now, however, he treats the subject matter by showing the condition of the Church in its present and future state: in its present state, that the Church must suffer many persecutions here, and, conversely, must receive many dignities in the present or future, such as remission of sins, illumination of souls, and other such things; and in the future, must obtain life and unending joy. Its final cause is to encourage those subject to him, to whom he chiefly writes, and then all others, to endure tribulations with patience, not despairing of recompense. Approach to the text.

## CHAPTER ONE

“The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave to him to make known openly to his servants the things which must shortly come to pass; and he signified it, sending through his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever things he saw. Blessed is he who reads and he who hears the words of this prophecy and keeps those things which are written in it. For the time is near.”

“The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ.” As though he admonished them thus: “Attend to this vision, because this vision was revealed to Jesus Christ; and this is the Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God, namely the Father, gave him to make openly known to his servants”—that is, that he might make it known openly to his humble servants, not to proud Jews or philosophers—“namely those things which must come to pass,” that is, tribulations in the Church and rewards. “Shortly”: lest anyone say, “Who will be able to endure for so long?” he says “shortly,” namely, the labors will pass and the rewards will be given. And by saying that these things must happen, he encourages them by showing them to be inevitable. “And he signified it.” The order is this: God showed it to Christ; Christ to John; John to the seven churches. And he rightly says, “he signified it,” because he showed it to him through certain figures, like seals. God wishes his Scriptures to be closed, lest there be a place of access for enemies; that his own people may be exercised; and that what is discovered by them may be held more precious. And this is the meaning of: “And he signified it, sending through his angel”—sometimes speaking in Christ’s person, as when he says in this first chapter, “I am Alpha and Omega”; sometimes in his own person, as when he forbids himself to be worshiped, as is said below in chapter XIX—“to his servant John.” [Col. 1501B–D]

Although John had not yet composed the Gospel, in his preaching he had nevertheless given much testimony to the Son of God, to the Word of God—that is, to his divinity—when he said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I). The Son is called the Word because, as understanding is made known through a word, so God is made known to us from the works he has made through his wisdom. And he bore witness to Jesus Christ according to his human nature, to which these designations belong, “whatever things he saw,” whether with bodily or spiritual eye.

“Blessed is he who reads.” When he ought to say, “John to the seven churches,” after showing that the vision had been shown to him by Christ, he puts this beforehand in order to make them attentive to the vision, as though he said: “Because this vision is of such a character, blessed is he who reads”—namely the clergy—“and he who hears the words”—namely the laity—“of the prophecy,” that is, of this vision, “and keeps those things which are in it,” fulfilling faith by works, avoiding the things threatened and desiring the things promised. “For the time is near”: and you can keep them, because these labors will soon end. This is the meaning of: “For the time is near.” [Col. 1502A]

“John to the seven churches which are in Asia: grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come; and from the seven spirits who are before his throne; and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and ruler of the kings of the earth; who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father. To him be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.” [Col. 1502A–B]

John. Christ to John; John himself, however, speaks to the seven Churches—literally, or let us understand by the seven all the Churches, since all things were made in seven days. “Which are in Asia”: that is, all Churches are in exaltation; for Asia is interpreted “exaltation.” What he prefaced before the greeting was, as it were, a prologue. In this greeting, however, he says nothing of the person of the Father, because there was no error concerning it; but he speaks of the person of the Son and of the Holy Spirit against the heresies of certain people.

“Grace be given to you,” namely, by which your sins may be forgiven and virtues infused; or, “grace,” that is, may God’s favor be with you [Col. 1502C] in all that you do; “and peace,” that is, rest from every vice, or the peace by which you may always agree with God and the holy angels through good will and holy action; “from him,” that is, from the Son, “who is,” that is, who truly exists—against those who said that he began in time—“and who is to come” in judgment. Here the error of Ebion, Arius, and many other heretics is refuted, who said that Christ took his beginning as a mere man from Mary; “and from the seven spirits,” that is, from the Holy Spirit. Or he says “seven spirits” so that we may understand the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; or, by seven let us understand all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, “who are before his throne,” so that the righteous, in whom God sits as judge, may be enlightened. The throne is the judicial [Col. 1502D] seat; “and from Jesus Christ.” He repeats concerning the Son because he was going to say much about him.

“Who is the witness,” not denying that he is the Son of God even when death threatened; and he states what sort of witness he is: “faithful, firstborn of the dead,” born first to a life in which he will not die again; or the worthiest of all the dead; or of those dead to the world, because he himself was free from sin, as is said in 1 Peter 2; “and ruler of the kings of the earth,” literally, because whether earthly kings wish it or not, they can do only as much as he permits; or because he is the head and ruler of all who govern their own land well.

“Who loved us,” whom you ought to hear and venerate, because he loved us with the greatest love: “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life” (John 15), etc.; “and washed us from our original sins, and also actual sins, in his blood” [Col. 1503A]—not in animal blood, as under the old law, as Saint Paul sets forth at length throughout Hebrews 9, and Saint Peter; “and made us a kingdom,” by giving us faith in the heavenly kingdom, “and priests to God and his Father,” as Saint Peter very beautifully explains in 1 Peter 2. He is called God according to creation; likewise Father, because he provides for all.

A king is one who governs and restrains unlawful impulses; a priest, one who worthily offers his prayers and sacrifices himself to God through good will and right action, thus dedicating himself wholly to God. Here Saint John is not speaking of priesthood as an order. “To him be glory”: because he is such, therefore may he be regarded as glorious among us; “and dominion for ages of ages,” and may we be subject to his rule through the ages succeeding these ages, not merely for an hour. [Col. 1503B] “Amen.” Amen is an affirmative adverb among the Hebrews, as though he cried aloud: “It is true that glory is due to him.”

“Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him. Yes, amen. I am α and ω, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.”

“Behold, he comes with the clouds,” and we ought rightly to glorify him, because he now comes as the rewarder of the good and punisher of the wicked. Let the clouds be understood literally. For the Judge will come with a cloud, as he ascended, as is said in Acts 1; this cloud will be refreshment and comfort to the good, blindness to the wicked. This was signified in the [Col. 1503C] cloud by which the children of Israel were led out of Egypt (Exod. 13). Or, by “clouds” let the righteous be understood, because they both flash with miracles, thunder with threats, and water the hearts of the faithful with the teaching of God’s word.

“And every eye shall see him”: literally, including the eyes of those who pierced him. “And they shall mourn over themselves,” because of their own misery, “and over him,” that is, so that the calamity of the damned may be increased most greatly by his infinite glory and that of the blessed. “All the tribes of the earth,” that is, those devoted to earthliness. “Yes, amen”: a confirmation of praise and honor.

“I am α and ω.” Having prefaced the greeting, before beginning the narration of the vision, in order to make them attentive for understanding what follows, he says that these are not his own words but that the Lord God says them, so that this may be proof: truly [Col. 1503D] the Lord is to come, because the Lord God himself says: “I am indeed he who was, who is, and who is to come.” This is what he says: “I am α and ω”; and its explanation follows when he says, “the beginning and the end.” God is called the beginning because he was before all things and all things proceeded from him: “All things were made through him” (John 1). He is called the end because there will be nothing after him, and because, once he is attained, nothing desirable remains. This is: “I am α and ω, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who was, who is, and who is to come.”

“I, John, your brother and partner in tribulation and kingdom and patience in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ. I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard [Col. 1504A] behind me a great voice, like a trumpet, saying: What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven Churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”

“I, John”: the greeting having ended, before he narrates, he explains how and when he saw; and there he commends the vision from four things: the person of the seer, the place, the cause, and the time. Thus he says, “I, John”: a commendation from the person. As though he said: Attend to what I, an apostle of so great a name, saw—your brother in unity of faith and partner in tribulation; and because tribulation without patience is useless, he therefore adds “and patience,” and finally “kingdom.” These matters are fully treated in Romans 5 and James 1, all of them being set beforehand in Jesus; for the Lord, having suffered tribulation patiently, [Col. 1504B] possesses the kingdom.

“I was on an island,” literally; and this is a commendation from the place. For a solitary place is suitable for heavenly secrets to be revealed to the faithful. “Which is called Patmos.” Patmos is interpreted “a strait.” “Because of the word of God”: a commendation through the cause, “and the testimony of Jesus Christ,” namely, because I bore witness to the divinity and humanity of the Savior. “I was in the Spirit,” that is, I saw spiritually, “on the Lord’s day”: a commendation from the time.

For the character of events is customarily indicated by time: Abraham saw angels at midday (Gen. 18), that is, in the fervor of faith; Adam saw the angel in the person indeed of God after midday (Gen. 3), namely after the fall; Lot saw the destruction of Sodom in the evening (Gen. 19), because it was soon to occur; Solomon received wisdom at night (3 Kings [Col. 1504C] 3), because he did not preserve it well. The Lord’s day signifies that true rest which he who rose on the Lord’s day now possesses and promises to the saints; therefore on that same day we cease from work. The same rest was signified in the old law by the Sabbath (Exod. 20); but, once the reality was fulfilled, the figure ceased.

In this rest the apostle was already wholly present, at least in hope; therefore the revelation, which was made at that time, deserves attention. “And I heard,” that is, I understood, “a great voice,” that is, an admonition concerning great matters. “Behind me”: he says “behind him” because, when he himself had already been drawn away from present things and in contemplation attended only to things before him, he is admonished to look to the correction of others. Or he hears behind him because he understood that the same thing had been admonished by the Law and the Prophets. [Col. 1504D] “Like a trumpet,” because he is stirred up for battle. “What you see, write in a book,” that is, store it in memory, or literally; “and send it to the seven Churches.” By seven we may understand all Churches, or literally these seven alone.

“And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me. And when I turned, I saw seven golden lampstands; and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like the Son of man, clothed in a long robe and girded at the breasts with a golden belt. His head and hair were white as white wool and as snow; his eyes like a flame of fire; his feet like bronze, as if glowing in a furnace; and his voice like the sound of many waters. He held seven stars in his right hand; from his mouth came a two-edged [Col. 1505A] sword; and his face shone like the sun in its strength.”

“And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me,” that is, I recollected the matters set forth below, so that I might understand the admonition. It should be noted that this entire book is divided into seven visions; therefore this first one concerns the correction of the Church. “And I turned,” and because I had thus turned, “I saw seven golden lampstands,” that is, the seven Churches named above, or indeed all Churches. We signify the Churches by lampstands because, just as lampstands bear light and provide it to others, so the Church bears the true light, which is Christ, to others and displays his brightness to others by preaching. “Golden,” because the Church is founded in brightness and wisdom.

“And in the midst,” that is, ready [Col. 1505B] to aid all, that is, to be shared by all, “of the seven golden lampstands,” that is, the Churches, “one like the Son of man”: Christ. He calls him not “the Son” but “like the Son,” because he himself was free from sin and was already immortal and incapable of suffering. “Clothed in a long robe.” The long robe was a priestly, ankle-length garment under the old law; by it is signified Christ’s flesh, which was a garment because divinity was hidden in it; priestly, because in it he offered himself to God; ankle-length, because it remains until the end of the age. “Girded at the breasts with a golden belt”: with the girdle of charity and true love.

Daniel saw the same angel, namely in the person of Christ, girded at the loins in the Old Testament (Dan. 10), because there carnal works are restrained. Here he constricts the breasts, because under the Gospel even thoughts are judged; from this we are signified that we ought to restrain our thoughts. [Col. 1505C] “His head and hair”: he describes what he saw in a figure. By the head is understood Christ’s own person; by the hair, those closely attached to him, who are white and thoroughly cleansed of sins. “White as white wool,” that is, a garment driving away cold, that is, vices; “and as snow.” Snow is the whitest among all created things; to it is compared the brightness of immortality.

“And his eyes like a flame of fire.” His eyes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the spiritual persons in the Church, or the divine commandments, which enlighten all who receive them and make them burn with the fire of love. “And his feet like bronze, as if glowing in a furnace”: the feet, that is, the faithful [Col. 1505D] who are to come in the last times. He saw them like refined bronze, because as bronze is changed by refining into the color of gold, so those faithful people, through excessive tribulation in the time of Antichrist, will be transformed for the better. Another translation has “bronze of Lebanon.” From this it is noted that Antichrist is to come in the same region in which the Lord dwelt.

“And his voice like the sound of many waters,” that is, his admonition contains the force of many teachings, which teachings wash like water; or it is like a voice received by many peoples, who are compared to water because of their fluctuation; or it is a voice giving many graces. “And he held seven stars in his right hand.” By the stars he understands bishops, who ought to enlighten others by word and example. Although some of them [Col. 1506A] did not then shine, nevertheless he calls them such according to what they had been instituted by John to be, and also because they were in the right hand, that is, in the more honorable part. “And from his mouth,” that is, from the holy Fathers through whom God speaks, “came a sword,” that is, the word of God, “two-edged,” that is, cutting on both sides: in the Old Testament carnal works, and in the New also desires. “And his face shone like the sun in its strength,” that is, those who strove to be like him shone and enlightened others, just as the sun at midday is obscured by no cloud; or like Christ himself.

“And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead; and he placed his right hand upon me, saying: Do not fear. I am the first and the last, and the living one; I was dead, and behold, I live for ages [Col. 1506B] of ages; and I have the keys of death and hell. Write therefore what you have seen, what is, and what must happen after these things. The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven Churches.”

“And when I saw him,” that is, because I recognized him both in his own person and in his members, “I fell,” that is, I humbled myself before his feet, so that I might now be prepared to suffer as much as his feet are to suffer, “as though dead”: though dead to the world, yet truly living. Therefore “he placed his right hand,” that is, his help or strengthening hope, “upon me,” that is, beyond the powers of humanity, “saying,” that is, admonishing me through the Scriptures: “Do not fear to suffer tribulation for me, [Col. 1506C] because I, who had no need of it, was dead for you.” This is indicated where he says: “I am the first and the last.” Since he who had no need chose to suffer for us and now lives without end, we ought to be greatly encouraged to suffer for him, we who are in need, so that we may at last live eternally with him. This is: “I am the first and the last, and the living one”—true life according to divinity—“and I was dead, and behold I live”—according to the body—“for ages of ages; and I have the keys of death.”

Because someone might say, “Who will be able to endure for so long?”, he says: “I will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10). This is: “And I have the keys of death and hell,” that is, of the devil and his members. He is called death because he is the cause of all death; his servants are called hell because [Col. 1506D] it is the place in which he dwells. But neither the devil nor his servants can harm anyone except as much as God permits them.

“Write therefore what you have seen,” whether with spiritual or bodily eye, as Paul did; “and what is,” namely present tribulations and present help; “and what must happen after these things,” namely all the tribulations which the saints will suffer in the last times. By their example the present Church ought especially to be encouraged to fulfill these lighter things. “The mystery of the seven stars”: supply, “write.” A mystery is where one thing is said and another understood. That the angel explains the mysteries of certain figures indicates that allegory must be sought in all; nevertheless, he does not explain them all, lest there be an entrance for thieves into Holy Scripture.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1507A]

“To the angel of the Church at Ephesus write: These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven lampstands. I know your works, your labor and patience, and that you cannot endure the wicked; you tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them liars. You have patience, and you have endured for my name’s sake and have not failed. But I have against you that you have abandoned your first charity. Remember therefore from where you have fallen, repent, and do your first works. Otherwise I will come to you quickly and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent. But this you have: you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. Let whoever has ears hear what the Spirit says to the Churches. To the one who conquers [Col. 1507B] I will give to eat from the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God.”

“To the angel of the Church at Ephesus write.” He writes to the bishop, from whose hand he requires the sins of those subject to him; nor does he presume that subjects are to be judged without his admonition. In this Church of Ephesus there were some who pleased God well; according to this aspect Ephesus is interpreted “will.” In the same Church were others who had great need of divine counsel; according to this aspect Ephesus is interpreted “counsel.”

Before writing of the Church’s works, he says beforehand something of the one commanding, by which he shows that he is fit to command such things. When he says that he holds the seven stars, etc., he signifies that those who sinned should not despair, but may be reconciled by repentance, [Col. 1507C] because God has not yet cast them out of his hand; but he shows the good that they should labor patiently, trusting in the crown. “These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand,” as though he said: Though you have sinned, I have not yet cast you away. “Who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands,” as though distributing the gifts of the Holy Spirit; or “walks,” namely, because he is not pleased to remain at rest in any of them.

“I know,” that is, I approve, “your works.” He speaks first of the good part, so that by their example the rest may be corrected: “your labor and patience, and that you cannot endure the wicked,” that is, according to your human condition, without the abundant help of mercy you can no longer endure their wickedness; or, you cannot endure the wicked without correcting them or expelling them from the Church. “And you tested them,” [Col. 1507D] that is, you proved their teaching—those who say they are apostles, and are not, that is, sent by God, so that they may deceive more easily—and such are pseudo-apostles. “And you found them liars,” that is, preaching falsehood and living wickedly; “and you have patience” against the evils which these bring about through tyrants. For what they could not accomplish by persuasive deception, they sought to achieve by force. “And you have not failed.” Here he indicates that they suffered things so great as might compel someone to fail.

“But I have against you,” concerning the other part, “that you have abandoned your first charity,” which is the principal virtue. “Remember therefore”: and because I have this against you, therefore remember from where you have fallen, that is, from the excellent rank of the faithful; “and repent,” that is, render worthy fruits of repentance (Luke 3); “and do your first works,” [Col. 1508A] namely works of charity. “Otherwise,” if you do not do this, “I will come to you” to your harm, “and remove your lampstand from its place”—namely, I shall cast them out from all ecclesiastical institutions—unless you repent.

“But this good thing you have.” Though I have the foregoing against you, nevertheless do not despair, because these things please me in you: “you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate,” and therefore you rightly hate them. Nicholas was one of the seven deacons. Because he returned to his wife after having repudiated her, he preached that all women should be held in common; he preached the eating of things sacrificed to idols. This heresy is condemned by the Church in the chapter *Quidam autem haeret.*, 24, chapter 3. Nicholas is interpreted “foolish people”: such are the heretics or pagans of this time, who both judge the use of women to be common [Col. 1508B] and eat things sacrificed to idols.

“Whoever has [ears]”: that is, what I say to one, I say to all. “Ears”: divine understanding. “Let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.” As though he said: These are not the words of John or of an angel, but of the divine substance itself. “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life.” And why should he hear? Because it is given “to the one who conquers.” He does not say to one who acts only at some time, but to one who perseveres (Matt. 10 and 24): “Whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved.” “Which is in the paradise of my God,” that is, in the garden of delights, namely the Church.

Christ is called the tree of life because he performs in his Church what the tree of life did in paradise. The function of that tree was to preserve those enjoying its fruit from death and old age; Christ accomplishes the same in his Church. For he preserves his faithful both from true death and from every failing. [Col. 1508C] Adam, by eating from the forbidden tree, lost what the tree of life bestowed on him and gained, through experience, knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 3). Previously, placed in delights, he did not know what good or evil was; at last he knew both, having experienced both.

“To the angel of the Church at Smyrna write: These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives. I know your tribulation and poverty—yet you are rich—and that you are blasphemed by those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan. Fear none of the things you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested; and you will have tribulation for ten days. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. Whoever has ears, let him hear [Col. 1508D] what the Spirit says to the Churches. The one who conquers will not be harmed by the second death.”

“To the angel of the Church at Smyrna write.” The bishop is signified by the angel because he too ought to be a messenger of God’s word. Smyrna is interpreted “song,” because this whole Church pleased God. As in the other cases, he first shows the one commanding to be fit to command such things; and he describes Christ as one able to console those who suffer tribulation in his name: “These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives.” Therefore you too should not fail, because you too will live with me eternally.

“I know your tribulation and poverty,” literally. “Yet you are rich” in hope of reward; and this is a kind of comfort. “And you are blasphemed by them”: tribulation is increased if one is troubled by a familiar enemy. “Who say they are Jews,” that is, confessing that they are, “and are not.” For if they were children of Abraham, they would do Abraham’s works, as Christ reproaches them [Col. 1509A] in John 8. “But they are a synagogue,” that is, a congregation, “of Satan,” that is, of the adversary. *Synagogue* means a gathering, which seems to belong to irrational creatures, as though it were a herd; but *Church* means a convocation, which is plainly said of rational beings.

“Nevertheless, fear none of the things you are about to suffer,” even if they are more grievous than what has gone before. “Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison.” And truly you will suffer, for behold the devil is about to cast some of you into prison. He uses prison for every tribulation: “that you may be tested,” that is, proved. “And you will have tribulation”—and for how long? Throughout the whole time of your life; this is “for ten days,” or seven, [Col. 1509B] that is, all the days in which the commandments of the law are to be observed, namely throughout the whole time of the present life. The life of the righteous is therefore signified by ten, because it is subject to the ten commandments of the law. Secular life is suitably signified by seven because it passes through seven days.

“Be faithful unto death”: whatever they may inflict, you must always be faithful; “and I will give you the crown of life,” namely the excellence of blessedness. “Whoever has ears”: that is, what God promises or threatens to one, he likewise promises or threatens to those similar to him. “The one who conquers will not be harmed by the second death.” There are two lives of the soul and two deaths, and likewise of the body. The first life of the soul is constancy in virtues; the second life is being granted eternal life. The first death of the soul is lying in sins; the second is being punished eternally. The first life of the body is union [Col. 1509C] with the soul; the second is resurrection to life. The first death of the body is separation from the soul; the second is condemnation at judgment.

“To the angel of the Church at Pergamum write: These things says he who has the two-edged sword: I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; yet you hold fast my name and have not denied my faith. Even in those days Antipas, my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells. But I have a few things against you: you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to eat and commit fornication; so you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Likewise repent; otherwise, I will come to you quickly and fight against them with the sword of my mouth. Whoever has [Col. 1509D] ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches. To the one who conquers I will give hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, and upon the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.”

“To the angel of the Church at Pergamum write.” Pergamum is interpreted “division of horns.” Horns are set forth where battle is signified; thus in this Church a certain evil party was attacking the good. “These things says he who has the two-edged sword.” When he says that the one commanding possesses the sword, that is, the sword cutting by the New and Old Testaments, he shows himself fit to separate evil persons from good and good persons from evil; and he intimates that they likewise must separate good from evil, so that they may follow good and flee evil.

“I know.” He speaks to the good. “Where you dwell,” namely in the midst of a perverse nation. “Where Satan’s throne [Col. 1510A] is,” among those in whom the adversary already sits and rests. “And you hold my name” against assailants, “and have not denied my faith,” even in such tribulation as might compel someone to deny it. “And in those days”: in that time, among the rest, this man Antipas shone most brightly in my sight. Or, “in those days,” that is, in that time of tribulation which illumines the faithful. “Where Satan dwells”: and therefore they killed him.

“But I have [against you].” Though the things stated above please me in you, “you have there”—namely, you do not expel from the Church—those who hold the teaching of Balaam, “who taught Balak.” He touches on the old history of how Balaam taught Balak, king of Midian, to destroy the children of Israel by causing them to sin in God’s sight: namely, to entice them through beautiful women to fornication and idolatry (Num. [Col. 1510B] 28). These sins, however, are reproved in some belonging to this Church.

This also pertains allegorically to the present Church. Balaam is interpreted “vain people”; Balak, “one who crushes.” Heretics are called a vain people, who teach earthly rulers, who are crushers, how to deceive Israel, that is, men who see God. Or demons are called a vain people, who teach the human body to crush and confuse within itself certain virtues. “So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans,” as [others hold] the teaching of Balaam. “Likewise repent”: therefore, as concerning those, so also concerning these. “Otherwise,” that is, if in any of these things you do less than is required, “I will come to you quickly,” namely, to kill you in soul and body, “and fight against them with the sword of my mouth,” namely with the word of God, saying: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. [Col. 1510C] 25).

“To the one who conquers I will give hidden manna,” that is, Christ, who was signified in the former manna, who is the true food refreshing without failing, as is said in John 6. *Manna* is also said to derive from *manhu*, that is, “what is this?” When the Lord had promised food to the children of Israel, and in the morning they found such a thing, they said in wonder, *manhu*, that is, “What is this?” (Exod. 16). “And I will give him a white stone.” A *calculus* is a solid, shining stone, by which the divine word is signified: shining in respect of truth, solid because it cannot be broken. Or by the stone is signified the human body, solid against vices and shining with a multitude of virtues. Other translations have “carbuncle” [Col. 1510D] or “coal,” but the same thing is always signified. “And on the stone a new name written,” that is, the Son of God, “which no one knows except the one who receives [it]”: no one has known that name fully according to its own property except one in whom the divine word dwells—that is, one who receives the stone.

“To the angel of the Church at Thyatira write: These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire and feet like bronze: I know your works, charity, faith, ministry, and patience, and that your latter works are more numerous than the former. But I have against you that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication and eat things sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she is unwilling to repent [Col. 1511A] of her fornication. Behold, I cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her shall be in great tribulation, unless they repent of their works; and I will kill her children with death. All the Churches shall know that I am he who searches the reins and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works. But to you I say, the rest who are in Thyatira: whoever do not hold this teaching and have not known the depths of Satan, as they say, I will not lay upon you another burden. Yet hold fast what you have until I come. And to the one who conquers and keeps my works to the end, I will give authority over the nations; he shall rule them with an iron rod, and they shall be broken like a potter’s vessel, as I also received from my Father; and I will give him the morning star. Whoever has ears, let him hear [Col. 1511B] what the Spirit says to the Churches.”

“To the angel of the Church at Thyatira write.” He writes to the bishop of this Church as to the others, whether saying all things about his subjects or also some things concerning their own persons. Thyatira is interpreted “inflamed,” because in it some are inflamed—namely, the wicked. “These things says the Son of God.” He states this first to show the one commanding to be fit to command, who has eyes like flame; whose eyes are like flame.

“I know your works”: I approve your chastity and the other good works insofar as they concern yourself, and the foundation of works, namely charity, and the foundation of charity, namely faith. Faith comes first: one believes, then loves the things believed, and after this performs good works. Thus he says, “charity and faith,” “and ministry” [Col. 1511C] toward true neighbors. As though [he said]: toward true Christians, you did not withhold what you could; “and your patience,” because you also endured enemies patiently; “and your latter works”: I know that both charity and your other good works are continually increasing.

“But I have [against you].” The foregoing things please me, but this displeases me: “you permit the woman Jezebel,” by not expelling or excommunicating her. Jezebel is interpreted “flowing,” “flow of blood,” or “dunghill,” because of excessive uncleanness; and she was the wife of Ahab (3 Kings 16), or perhaps also the wife of this bishop. Or, if this was not her name, she must nevertheless be called so because of her uncleanness. For in our own time all who are devoted to uncleannesses, preach fornication, and the eating of things sacrificed to idols may be called Jezebels.

“A prophetess,” one seeing divine secrets: why do you permit her to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication, either with women or in whatever manner with a demon? [Col. 1511D] “Behold”—and because she is unwilling—“behold, I cast her onto a bed,” that is, into security in sinning. Another translation has, “I cast her into mourning,” that is, into everlasting sorrow. The same thing is signified to us by mourning. “And those who commit adultery with her,” that is, those who carry out what she teaches. This he says of her contemporaries. “And her children,” that is, her followers, namely those who even now imitate her, “I will kill with death,” by perpetual damnation. “And all the Churches shall know”: although some still have too low an estimate of me because I do not immediately punish the wicked, at last they shall clearly know when I grant to each according to his own [Col. 1512A] merits.

“Searching,” knowing and carefully discerning, “the reins,” carnal works, “and hearts,” thoughts and desires. Thus he threatens the wicked. “But to you I say, the rest,” that is, those far different from the persons named above, “who are in Thyatira,” that is, who are truly inflamed: to you indeed I say, “I will not lay upon you another burden,” that is, anything from the ordinances of the old law, “as they say.” For some said that a person could not be saved by the new law alone without circumcision and other such things. Now there is a change of person. As though he said: All those are Thyatira who do not have this teaching, that is, who have not known by approving it “the depth of Satan,” that is, pride. Although those people say that something else ought to be used by you, nevertheless hold fast what you have [Col. 1512B] until I come to reward.

“And to the one who conquers,” so as not to yield to them, and moreover “who keeps my works to the end of life, I will give authority”—also in this age, because they can excommunicate those living as pagans and condemn them eternally—“and he shall rule them with an iron rod,” that is, with inflexible justice. “And they shall be broken like a potter’s vessel”: some so that they perish, some so that they may become a better vessel. “As I also received from my Father,” according to humanity; “and I will give him the morning star,” and at last I will give him myself. The morning star signifies Christ, because that star both illuminates the night and precedes the day; so Christ both illuminates the world and preceded the day of the general resurrection. Or the first resurrection is called the morning star.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 1512C]

“To the angel of the Church at Sardis write: These things says he who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. I know your works: you have a name that you live, yet you are dead. Be watchful, and strengthen the remaining things that were about to die. For I have not found your works complete before my God. Remember therefore how you received and heard; keep it, and repent. If, then, you do not watch, I will come upon you like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come upon you. But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments; they shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy. The one who conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments, and I will not blot his name [Col. 1512D] out of the book of life; and I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.”
