And to the angel of the Church in Sardis write: Sardis is interpreted “the beginning of beauty.” Yet there were in this Church some who wished to appear good, but were not. “These things says he who has the seven spirits of God and the stars.” He shows that the one giving the command is competent, as though he said to the good: “Work, because I can repay you”; to the evil: “Be converted, because otherwise you will perish.” “I know your works,” that is, they cannot be hidden from me. “I know that you have a name,” that is, that in your works you love human praise, “and you are dead” in sins; for whoever offends in one point is guilty of all. “Be watchful,” and therefore be diligent and solicitous concerning salvation, “and strengthen the rest.” Here it is implied that one found guilty of any grave sin loses, as regards salvation, all good deeds, when it says, “which were about to die”; but when that sin is corrected, all alike avail unto life. “Watch,” I say, “for I do not find your works complete.” The works are not complete because they are without charity, or because they are done for praise, or because they are joined to some grave sin before God. Though they are complete in the sight of men, they are not so before God; and because they are not complete, strive that they may be complete. And this is: “Therefore keep in mind how you have received,” that is, by what reasoning you began to act, “and heard” from the holy Fathers. For they say: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (Jas. 2); “If I do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13); and similar things. And only one who watches is pleasing to me. “If therefore you do not watch, I shall come like a thief,” namely, to kill and despoil you. The condemned person is despoiled when he is not aided by virtues; “and you will not know at what hour I shall come to you.” “But you have a few names.” He says “names” because, just as by names we know the properties of things, so the Lord knows all deeds and properties as if by names. “In Sardis”: those who truly are Sardis, because they already begin to be beautiful. “Who have not defiled” themselves with the stain of grave sin, or have washed away their deeds by tears; “their garments,” namely immortality and innocence, with which they are clothed in baptism. “And they shall walk with me in white,” from virtue to virtue with me, that is, as I too did—clothed in white garments, namely innocence and immortality. “He who conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments”; and not only those who remained good, but likewise one who was at some time evil, if he conquers. “And I shall not blot his name from the book of life.” The book of life is called divine foreknowledge, in which, according to God’s divinity, nothing is entered or erased; but this is said according to each person’s present condition: if someone stands in good, he is said to be entered in the book of life; if he turns to evil, he is said to be erased from the book of life. “And I shall confess,” etc., saying: “Come, blessed ones,” or rewarding according to God’s good pleasure. “And before the angels of God,” so that the angels may rejoice in their fellowship.

And to the angel of the Church in Philadelphia write: “These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens: I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door which no one [Col. 1513D] can shut, because you have little strength, and have kept my word, and have not denied my name. Behold, I shall give you some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie. Behold, I shall make them come and worship at your feet; and they shall know that I have loved you, because you have kept the word of my patience, and I shall keep you from the hour of temptation which is to come upon the whole world, to test all who dwell on earth. I shall come quickly. Hold fast what you have, that no one may take your crown. He who conquers, I shall make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go out no more; and I shall write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from heaven from my God, and my new name. [Col. 1514A] He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.”

And to the angel of the Church in Philadelphia write. Philadelphia is interpreted “brotherly love.” For brotherly love was present in this Church. As in the others, he shows the one giving the command to be competent to command such things. For since he admonishes them to labor for the conversion of their brethren, and promises that he will grant them a reward for this, he first sets forth the highest reward, because he is true; hence they can know that he will give to those who confess him as he promises. And he indicates that he can give, where he says: “He who has the key of David,” etc. “These things says the holy one.” Having first supplied proof that he is true, because he has become holy and true in his promises. “Who has the key of David.” He shows that he who has power can fulfil his promises—the power which we signify by a key—namely, according to the flesh taken from David; or the power of opening David and the other prophets. If he opens either hearts or the Scriptures, no one shuts; if he shuts, no one can open. “I know,” that is, I approve, “your works; and therefore, behold, I have set before you an open door”: either hearts formerly closed, or the enclosed meanings of the Scriptures. “Because you have little,” that is, humble, “strength,” and “have kept my word,” that is, my preaching. “And you have not denied my name,” even in distress; and because you are such, “behold, I shall give you some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews.” They lost this name by denying Christ the Son of God, when they said, “We do not know you”; “but they lie.” Here they are shown to be convicted by certain analogies, and “I shall make them come to faith and worship,” that is, reverence the teachers, as Joseph’s brothers did. “At your feet,” that is, ready to imitate your works, or the least faithful persons. “And they shall know that I have loved you.” While they are outside the Church, they do not know that God loves either them or his faithful, since he permits them to be afflicted; when brought back to faith, they proclaim the same. “Because you have kept the word of my patience,” that is, those things related concerning my patience, so that they too may love their enemies after my example. As in the visions which follow, he often marks something concerning the tribulation to come in the last times in the sixth [vision]; so here, in the sixth angel, certain Jews in that tribulation will, through Elijah’s preaching, understand the Law spiritually and be saved. “Because you have kept [my word], I also shall keep you from the hour of temptation,” so that it may not harm you; “and I shall come”—as though he said: “But who will be able to endure for so long? Do not lose heart and succumb; I shall swiftly come to your aid.” And this is what he says: “I shall come to you quickly.” “Hold fast what you have.” Meanwhile hold what you have, “that no one may take your crown,” that is, that no one may be brought into the place assigned to you, as the Gentiles were brought into the place promised to the Jews. “He who conquers, I shall make him a pillar,” that is, a support of others. “And he shall go out no more,” that is, he shall no longer depart from the Lord. The younger son who squandered his substance with prostitutes, after he was received by his father, did not wish to return to his former life (Luke 15); he signifies the Gentile people, formerly separated from God, who, through the death of the fatted calf—that is, Christ’s Passion—have been reconciled to God and shall go out no more. “And I shall write upon [Col. 1515A] him,” so that in him it may be manifest and an example to others, “the name of my God,” because he shall be called God; “and the name of the city of my God,” that is, he shall be called the vision of peace. And this city, the new Jerusalem, in which nothing of oldness remains but there is the true vision of peace, shall be well fortified by virtues. “Which comes down from heaven,” from the fellowship of heavenly beings; “from my God,” God sending virtues; “and my name,” that is, Son of God. For “Christian” means anointed by grace. “New,” which he does not have from Adam. “He who has ears”: what I say to one, I say to all.

And to the angel of the Church in Laodicea write: “These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation: I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I shall begin [Col. 1515B] to vomit you out of my mouth. Because you say, ‘I am rich and have become wealthy, and need nothing,’ and do not know that you are wretched and pitiable, and poor and blind and naked, I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire, that you may become rich; and that you may be clothed in white garments, and that the shame of your nakedness may not appear; and anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see. Those whom I love I rebuke and chastise. Be zealous therefore and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me. He who conquers, I shall grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne. He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.”

And to the angel of the Church in Laodicea write. Laodicea is interpreted “vomiting.” For there were some in this Church who were lukewarm. Lukewarm people are those who observe certain rules, abstaining from evil, and judge these to be sufficient; hence they become sluggish and are unwilling to labor in any good work. Since he was about to say the remarkable thing that the lukewarm—whom men believed good—were to be excommunicated and cast out from his mouth, he first declares himself truthful, so that he may seem worthy of belief in these matters as well. “Amen,” that is, truth: for through him all the Father’s promises are fulfilled. “The faithful witness,” because he made known to us what he heard from the Father; or witness of our works before God, and true in all his words. “Who is the beginning of God’s creation,” whether of the first creation or of creation unto righteousness; from him, if they wish to come to their senses, he can justify them. “I know your works.” They are not hidden from me, because you are neither cold nor hot. The cold person is one who acts openly and shamefully, or indeed does not receive [the faith]. “Nor hot.” The hot person is one who burns with love. “Would that you were cold or hot!” Not because it is good to be cold, but because such persons come more quickly to good, since they put no confidence in themselves. “But because you are lukewarm,” that is, having received faith, you grow dull and idle in working, “I shall begin, through excommunication, to vomit you out of my mouth,” that is, to remove you from the fellowship of the faithful through my preachers, who are called the mouth because God speaks through them. “Because you say, ‘I am rich,’” cleansed in baptism, or rich in knowledge, “and have become wealthy” through certain works, and therefore seem sufficient, “and need nothing,” and therefore think no virtue any longer necessary [Col. 1516A] for yourself; “and you do not know that you are wretched,” that is, insufficient for salvation through what you possess, “and pitiable,” because you yourself do not know your misery; “and poor” in good works; “and blind,” because you do not see that you are insufficient; “and naked” of the garment, indeed, of modesty and innocence. But I do not deny mercy; this is what is meant: “I advise you to buy from me the fruit of repentance, gold refined by fire,” that is, charity which may set you aflame—or myself. “That you may become rich” in works of virtue, “and may be clothed in white garments,” that is, innocence. “And that the shame of your nakedness may not appear.” It is better to blush before a few than eventually before all. “And anoint your eyes with eye-salve”: with the divine command, or the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or whatever illuminates reason; and so that you may be able to do this: “Be zealous” for your other brothers [Col. 1516B] who are afflicted. And lest they should say that God does not love those whom he allows to suffer, he gives the reason beforehand when he says: “Those whom I love I rebuke,” that is, I make them know their sins, “and chastise,” thus making them chaste; and because I love such persons, “be zealous therefore and repent.” And you ought to repent, because I have not utterly rejected you: behold, I still wait for you to open your heart. And this is: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock,” that is, I rebuke. “If anyone hears my voice” by understanding it, “and opens the door to me” by acting rightly, “I shall enter in to him” in the secret place of his heart, “and dine with him,” that is, delight in his faith and works; “and he with me” shall rejoice in my consolation. “He who conquers, I shall grant him to sit with me,” that is, to judge with me, “on my throne, as I also conquered”; for both his victory and his sitting are the cause of the victory [Col. 1516C] of others. “And I sat with my Father on his throne.” The throne is the judicial seat. “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.”

## Chapter IV

## Second Vision

“After these things I saw, and behold, an open door in heaven. And the first voice which I heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, said: ‘Come up here, and I shall show you what must happen after these things.’ Immediately I was in the Spirit; and behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one sitting upon the throne. And he who sat was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius; and there was a rainbow around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald. And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones twenty-four elders sitting, clothed round about [Col. 1516D] in white garments, and on their heads golden crowns. And from the throne proceed lightnings and voices and thunders; and seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God. And before the throne was something like a glassy sea, like crystal. And in the midst of the throne, and around the throne, were four living creatures full of eyes before and behind.”

“After these things.” In this second vision the restoration of the human race is treated, by showing the Lamb receiving the book from the hand of the one sitting on the throne and opening the seals of that book. The deeds of the Lamb can rightly admonish us not to hesitate to suffer for him. Since he wished to encourage his own to endure tribulation, he fittingly first set forth the correction of the Church, because punishment is then most beneficial when it does not punish sins. “After [Col. 1517A] these things I saw”: as to the sequence of visions, not at another time, but on the same Lord’s Day. “And behold, an open door in heaven”: namely, the closure of the Scriptures, which is the way to life; or the obscurity of heavenly mysteries; or in those who are heaven. “And behold, the first voice”: the first admonition, or the Old Testament. “Which I heard, like a trumpet,” namely one exhorting to battle; “speaking with me,” not dissenting from my reason; “saying, ‘Come up here’”: enlarge your soul so that it may be able to see this, “and I shall show you what must happen after these things,” in the last times. “Immediately I was in the Spirit”: having cast aside attention to earthly things, I was seeing spiritually. “And behold, a throne was set in heaven.” Angels and other greater saints are also called thrones: they sit over those subject to them; and one higher still sits upon the throne. “And he who sat,” that is, God the Father, formerly unknown to us, is now known through the incarnation of the Son and is, as it were, seen as a stone. “He was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius.” Jasper is green in color and watery; sardius is red. By the watery color is signified for us the judgment already carried out through the water of the Flood, as is found in Genesis 7; by the red color, that which is to come through fire. Or, by the watery color is signified the water of baptism; by the red, the gifts of the Holy Spirit received in baptism, through which sins are burned away and we are kindled toward love. Yet, although such, he was not dreadful, because the rainbow—that is, the peace or propitiation of God—was around the throne, as though fortifying and protecting them. “Like an emerald.” Emerald is a stone having green and red color; so also the rainbow, by which are indicated the things we have mentioned. “And around the throne,” as though appendages and conscience to the judgment, “twenty-four seats”: teachers in the Church, both in the New and in the Old Testament. We understand teachers through the number twenty-four because this number consists of twelve and twelve; and this number in turn consists of three and four. Holy preachers proclaim the name of the holy Trinity through the four regions of the world. “And upon the thrones,” that is, upon the aforesaid seats, “twenty-four elders.” This number is not understood according to persons, but according to office; for by the twenty-four are here understood all preachers of both the old and the new law. “Sitting, clothed round about in white garments,” [Col. 1517D] which they received in baptism; “and on their heads,” that is, in their minds, “golden crowns,” victories through charity or wisdom. “And from the throne,” namely from the seat of God, as from the apostles and such persons, “proceed lightnings,” that is, miracles; “voices,” admonitions; “and thunders,” threats. “And seven lamps before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God.” These gifts are before the throne, that is, they kindle and illuminate all the righteous unto love, in whom God sits judging. “And before the throne, as an image, something like a glassy sea, like crystal,” signifies baptism, bright through the sincerity of faith. It is called like crystal because, just as crystal hardens from water into stone, so baptism makes those who are soft and fluid firm and unconquerable. “And in the midst of the throne,” as though supporting it, “and around it,” as though on watch, “four living creatures.” The living creatures are called the Evangelists and the other holy preachers, who, being gentle and well-spirited, give spirit to others. They are not called four according to persons, but according to the office of fourfold preaching, because they proclaim the natures of these four living creatures, which, although they ought to be in every person, are properly said of Christ. Christ is called a lion because he is strong and without fear; and because, just as a lion is born seemingly dead and on the third day is roused to life by the voice of its father, so Christ rose to life on the third day. He is called a calf because he was sacrificed; a man, because of his true human nature; an eagle, according to his divinity and ascension. “Full of eyes before and behind.” [Col. 1518B] It says “full of eyes before and behind” either because they remembered past sins and made provision for themselves in the future, or because they possessed knowledge both of things past and of things future.

“And the first living creature was like a lion, and the second living creature like a calf, and the third living creature had a face like a man, and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle. And the four living creatures, each of them, had six wings, and around and within they were full of eyes. And they had no rest, day and night, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.’ And when those living creatures gave glory and honor and blessing to him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages, the twenty-four elders fell down before him [Col. 1518C] who sits upon the throne and worshipped him who lives for ages of ages, amen, casting their crowns before the throne, saying: ‘You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power, because you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.’”

“And the first living creature was like a lion,” etc., “and the fourth living creature like a flying eagle.” John is compared with the eagle because at the beginning he treats of divinity; and likewise the others take their names from what they set forth in their Gospels. Yet each one expounds the aforesaid natures. Ezekiel set this vision in another order (Ezek. 1), for he first put the man, then the calf, then the lion, and then the eagle; but because he saw things which were future, he set them in the order in which they were to come: first the man, then the rest. [Col. 1518D] John, seeing them fulfilled, placed the lion first, as the foundation of all our faith. For our faith is especially united in the Lord’s resurrection, and the four living creatures were well equipped to preach this according to the four aforesaid natures of Christ. “Each of them,” not according to persons but each order, “had six wings.” The six wings are the six works of mercy: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, and visiting the sick and the imprisoned. They are called wings because by these we are lifted on high. Or the six wings are knowledge of all things made in six days; for through these visible things we are led to know invisible things. Or let the first wing be the natural law, which was in Abraham [Col. 1519A] and the other first Fathers; the second wing, the Law of Moses; the third, prophecy; the fourth, the Gospel; the fifth, the instructions of the apostles; the sixth, those of Augustine and others who ordered the vestments, etc., in the Church. “Around,” that they might shine to others by a good example; “and within,” as regards themselves, “they are full of eyes,” namely divine commandments. “And they had no rest”: they did not cease, “day and night,” in prosperity or adversity, or continually, saying: “Holy, holy, holy,” three times because of the Trinity of persons; “Lord,” once because of unity in divinity. “Lord God Almighty, who was,” without beginning, “and is,” without change, “and is to come” to judgment. “And when those living creatures gave glory,” that is, when the holy preachers preached God as glorious, as shown by the resurrection; “and honor,” as worthy of veneration because of his works, or through his ascension; “and blessing,” of heavenly reward, or above all angels. “To him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages, the twenty-four elders fell down before him who sits upon the throne”: that is, all judges, of both the new and old law, humbled themselves before him. Nor does it matter if they are now called judges and now living creatures. “And they worshipped him who lives for ages of ages,” expecting from him in word and deed what they did not possess of themselves, “casting their crowns before the throne,” attributing to him their victories over vices or tribulations; saying: “You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive”—to whom we render—“glory and honor and power, because you created all things, and by,” that is, according to, “your will they existed and were created”: not suddenly, but you held all things in your eternal disposition.

## Chapter V

“And I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice: ‘Who is worthy to receive the book and to loose its seals?’ And no one in heaven, or on earth, or under the earth, was able to open the book or to look upon it. And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to see it. And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep. Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and to loose its seven seals.’ And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and [Col. 1519D] seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth. And he came and received the book from the right hand of him who sat upon the throne. And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb, each having harps and golden bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying: ‘You are worthy, Lord God, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us to God by your blood, from every tribe and tongue and people and nation; and you have made us a kingdom and priests to our God, and we shall reign upon the earth.’”

“And I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without.” He takes the book to be the divine disposition concerning the restoration of the human race, which he sees in the right hand, that is, in the Son of God. The whole restoration of the human race is attributed to the person of the Son, through whom it was accomplished. The book is “written,” that is, manifested within through the New Testament and without through the Old, which is the enclosure of the New. Or “without” may be understood as the New Testament, which is outwardly manifest; and “within” as the Old, which is obscure. “Sealed,” that is, closed, “with seven seals,” that is, with every obscurity, or with the sevenfold Spirit through whom faith works. “And I saw a strong angel”: any one of the first Fathers, who is called an angel because sent from God, strong, proclaiming with a loud voice, inquiring, announcing to others, and, from excessive longing, lamenting that it was delayed so long. “Who is worthy to receive,” that is, to fulfil, “the book,” etc.? Where he shows that those first Fathers desired Christ so fervently when they grasped him only by the slightest consideration, he implies that we, who now possess the reality itself, ought to love more fervently and not shrink from suffering for him. John says, “And no one in heaven,” such as an angel, “nor on earth,” nor “under the earth,” such as souls stripped of the body, “could open,” that is, fulfil, “the book, nor look upon it,” that is, understand it perfectly. Hence Isaiah 53: “Who shall declare his generation?” Here he takes on the person of the other earlier Fathers: “And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open,” that is, fulfil, “the book, nor to see it,” that is, to understand it fully. “And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep.’” Any prophet who, by announcing Christ’s advent, consoles [Col. 1520C] the rest. “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David,” proceeding from David, or David’s foundation, “has conquered the devil, to open,” that is, fulfil, “the book, and to loose its seven seals.” He shows how he saw the object desired; now he proceeds to show that he saw it fulfilled. And just as the elder had foretold, “I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne,” as the support of all, “and of the four living creatures, a Lamb,” Christ, who was the true victim, “standing,” as though laboring and aiding the saints in their struggles, “as though slain”; for though dead, he lives by the power of God. “Having seven horns and seven eyes.” The horns and eyes are the Holy Spirit, who gives kingship and exaltation, signified by the horns, and illumination, signified by the eyes. Or the horns are the more eminent saints, clinging most closely to the head and surpassing the flesh. And he came to our knowledge through the assumption of flesh; and, having become man, he received the book from the right hand of him who sat upon the throne—from the Word united to him. “And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures,” namely all holy preachers, “and the twenty-four elders,” all judges, “fell before the Lamb,” presuming nothing of themselves but thinking humbly before the Lamb, that is, imitating him. Hence follows: “Each having harps.” The harp signifies mortification of the flesh; and in the harp there are wood and strings. By the wood, the cross of Christ; by the strings, the flesh of the saints. “And bowls.” Bowls are broad vessels, by which are signified hearts enlarged even to love of enemies; they are called “golden” because of charity [Col. 1521A] and wisdom, “full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints.” For just as someone delights in a pleasant odor, so God delights in the prayers of the saints. “And they sang a new song” with exultation: the New Testament, which the Church professes in deed when it is baptized into his death, saying: “You are worthy, Lord God, you alone free from sin; for unless you were free from sin, you would not have redeemed us. By your blood”: not from one order alone, but “from every tribe.” A tribe is so called from the three orders—namely, laborers, soldiers, and sacrificers—which orders include seventy-two languages; each language contains many peoples, and peoples, nations. A nation is so called when some people leave their people and inhabit a new [Col. 1521B] place. By this he indicates those redeemed from every diversity; and this is what he says: “and tongue,” etc. “And you have made us a kingdom to our God,” reigning spiritually; “and priests,” offering ourselves and praying for them; “and we shall reign upon the earth,” either well-cultivated earth, or over earthly persons by excommunicating them.

“And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing.’ And every creature which is in heaven and upon the earth and under the earth, and the sea and the things which are in it, I heard all saying to him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb: ‘Blessing and honor [Col. 1521C] and glory and power for ages of ages.’ And the four living creatures said, ‘Amen.’ And the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces and worshipped.”

“And I saw”: I remained in the spiritual vision, “and heard” not only the living creatures and elders who bore witness to Christ, but also the angels who with all zeal and affection aid and guard the Church. Rejoicing at the restored fellowship, they bear witness concerning the Lord’s incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension, since they ministered to him in all these matters and testify that he himself will come as judge. Or the angels may be called those subject to the living creatures and elders, namely those who lead an angelic life, who surround and adorn their preachers [Col. 1521D] and judges, assenting to and confirming their testimony. He gives a finite number because their number is finite to God, though infinite to us. “Around the throne,” as defenders; “and their number.” He gives a great number because the greater the multitude, the greater the attestation and the greater the exultation. “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power,” freedom from sin, “and divinity,” because he was God although he appeared dead, “and wisdom,” knowledge and discernment of all things, “and strength,” because he conquered the devil by persevering in obedience, “and honor” in the resurrection, “and glory,” impassibility and immortality, “and blessing,” exaltation. And he expounds this: “and every creature,” as though saying: “That at the name of Jesus every knee may bend” (Phil. 2): [Col. 1522A] those in heaven, heavenly beings; those upon the earth, earthly beings; those under the earth, infernal beings; “and the sea,” literally, or the world, “and the things which are in it.” By all these things which he attributes to Christ, he refutes many heresies, each of which took away from Christ some one of these things. Then I heard all together—the living creatures, elders, and angels—confirming the testimony and saying to him who sits upon the throne, God the Father, and to the Lamb according to the flesh: “Blessing,” exaltation; “and honor,” impassibility; “and glory,” in the resurrection; “and power,” because he is almighty, “for ages of ages,” that is, not for an hour but forever. “The four living creatures said, ‘Amen.’” He speaks again of them because the office of preachers is to confirm testimonies. “And the twenty-four elders,” not being proud of the judgment entrusted to [Col. 1522B] them, “fell upon their faces”: they humbled themselves before him in their conscience, namely seeing where they would fall. For one who falls in another direction does not fall well, because he does not see where he falls. “And they worshipped,” reverencing God with the whole intention of the mind.

## Chapter VI

“And I saw that the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals. And I heard one of the four living creatures saying with a voice like thunder: ‘Come and see.’ And behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he went forth conquering, that he might conquer.”

After showing through the Lamb that the restoration of the human race had been accomplished, he also wishes to announce to the Church the tribulations to come, and, against them, help; and finally crowns for victory: so that the Church, [Col. 1522C] trusting in so great a support and rejoicing in the promise, may endure tribulation altogether patiently and gladly. “And I saw that the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals”: every obscurity, so that the faithful may understand the holy Scriptures. “And I heard one of the four living creatures saying,” not personally, but because all holy preachers are one: “Come,” advance in faith and deed, “and see,” understand that truth has been fulfilled. And as John is admonished, so he must admonish others; likewise, others must invite to the same those whom they can. “And behold, a white horse,” that is, the Church made white in baptism, which continually bears Christ; “and he who sat upon it,” Christ, “had a bow.” The bow signifies the divine Scriptures, by which God both protects his own and harms enemies. In the bow there are two things, wood and string. By the wood, which is useless by itself, is signified the Old Testament; by the sinew, which tensions and makes the wood effective, is signified the New Testament, through which the old Law has force. “And a crown was given to him.” Christ is crowned in his own through many victories, or he himself according to his humanity. “And he went forth,” borne by holy preachers, “conquering in Judaea, that he might conquer among the Gentiles.” Seeing that the Church was established to fill the place from which he himself had fallen, the devil strives with all his power to hinder and pervert it.

“And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying: ‘Come and see.’ And another red horse went forth; and to him who sat upon it was given [Col. 1523A] to take peace from the earth, so that they should kill one another; and a great sword was given to him.”

“And when he had opened the second seal,” in the order of seeing, or also in time, “I heard the second living creature,” according to the order, saying: “Come and see,” from virtue to virtue, that you may understand. “And another horse went forth,” fulfilling in thought what it does, far different from the first because utterly evil; “red,” bloodthirsty, namely an open persecutor. “And he who sat upon it,” that is, the devil, still higher than the horse itself, “was given,” that is, permitted by God, “to take peace from the earth,” to remove every quiet from those devoted to earthly things, “so that they should kill one another,” with the material sword or with that of persuasion. “And a great sword was given him,” namely, the power to harm not only lesser persons but greater ones also, as Peter and those like him; or “great,” because it extends throughout the whole earth. Here is marked the persecution carried out by heretics: because after the devil makes no progress through open persecutors, he sends in heretics, who, in order to persuade more easily of their falsehoods, mingle truths among them; and because this persecution deceives more quickly than even open tribulation, he immediately sets against it a certain aid.

And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: “Come and see.” And behold, a black horse; and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand. And I heard, as it were, a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying: “A two-pound measure of wheat for one denarius, and [Col. 1523C] three two-pound measures of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and the oil.”

And when he had opened the third seal, as the others, behold a black horse, obscuring its vices by certain works. And he who sat upon it—that is, because what his followers accomplish through him is attributed to him—had a balance, because they say that they possess true discernment in the Scriptures, and therefore that their opinions outweigh others, in his hand, because they fulfill in deed what they preach. Behold the aid: namely, they are forbidden to harm their own; and this is, “And I heard, as it were, a voice,” of the angel standing in the midst of the four living creatures, saying: “Do not harm my faithful ones, because a two-pound measure—that is, the Church made up of two peoples—costs me one denarius, [Col. 1523D] that is, one price, namely my blood.” A two-pound measure is said to be a measure holding two sextarii. The wheat are the more perfect, who have been ground by tribulation and baked by fire: a sweet food for God, that is, without any chaff. The barley are those who are not so perfect, in whom, although they are much ground, there is nevertheless some chaff. “And three two-pound measures of barley for a denarius,” that is, for the single price of blood; “and wine,” those who intoxicate others. The wine are those who, fervent within themselves, intoxicate others unto spiritual love. The oil are those who, united to the Holy Spirit and full of prayers, persevere in contemplation.

And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying: “Come and see.” And behold, a pale horse; and he who sat upon it was named Death, and Hell followed him. And there was given to him [Col. 1524A] power over the four parts of the earth, to kill by sword, famine, and death, and by the beasts of the earth.

“And behold.” Here is indicated persecution by false brethren. For when the devil does not succeed through open tribulations or manifest heresies, he sends false brethren, who under the appearance of religion bring forth the poison that harms. But these have no effect except through those previously mentioned. The pale horse, as though afflicting itself from religious devotion; and he who sat upon it, the devil, was named Death, because he is the cause of all our death; or because he kills some in body, others in soul. “Hell,” that is, those insatiable for earthly things, or those assigned to hell. And power was given over the four parts of the world, that is, over all evil people in every region of the earth: “to kill by sword,” through open murderers; [Col. 1524B] “by famine,” of the divine word, namely through heretics; “and by death,” through evil persuasion; “and by the beasts of the earth,” through tribulations and murderers, or literally.

And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held; and they cried with a loud voice, saying: “How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” And white robes were given to each of them, and it was said to them that they should rest yet a little while, until their fellow servants and their brethren, who are to be killed as they were, should be completed.

The tribulations having been shown, lest these persons fail, he shows them an excellent consolation: namely, the crown and glory that those will receive who do not refuse to be troubled in patience. [Col. 1524C] And when he had opened the fifth seal, “I saw beneath the altar,” beneath Christ. Christ is understood as the altar, upon whom we offer to God. For through him as mediator we can please God, beneath whom are all the souls of the faithful, because both the less worthy and the more worthy are under his protection; or “beneath,” that is, in concealment, because no one perceives in this life how they are there. “The souls of those slain,” either by open martyrdom or by some affliction, “for the word of God,” because they fulfilled God’s commandments in themselves, “and for the testimony,” because they bore witness to others. “And they cried with a loud voice,” in a tempered desire: “How long, Lord, holy,” possessing all holiness, “and true” in promises, “will you not avenge our blood,” by making [Col. 1524D] a distinction between evil and good, so that our fellowship may be completed, “and avenge,” by inflicting punishments, “upon those who dwell” in love upon the earth, in earthly things? Holy souls indeed desire that the number of their brethren should be completed, and the just sentence—that the wicked should be punished—pleases them. And individual white robes were given to them, that is, the blessedness of the soul alone, not yet of the body; and it was said—that is, it was inspired in them by God—that they should wait patiently. And this is, “that they should rest yet a little while, until their fellow servants should be completed.” He exhorts them to this waiting in two ways: namely, by the grace of God, in saying “their fellow servants”; and likewise through brotherly love for those whom they desire, in saying “and their brethren.”

[Col. 1525A] And I saw, when he had opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as a sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became as blood; and the stars of heaven fell upon the earth, as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a wind. And heaven withdrew like a scroll being rolled up; and every mountain and island was moved from its place. And all the kings of the earth, princes, commanders, rich, mighty, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and in the rocks of the mountains. And they say to the mountains and rocks: “Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb; for the great day of their wrath will come, and who will be able to stand?”

And I saw, when he had opened the sixth seal. As in the other sixths, so in this sixth seal he indicates the persecution that is to occur in the time of Antichrist, [Col. 1525B] and what end it will have: namely, the coming judgment. These things may be read literally or allegorically. “And there was a great earthquake”: earthly people are greatly disturbed by Antichrist’s persecution. “And the sun became black”: Christ, the true sun, now bright, will in the time of Antichrist be dark—that is, shining forth in no miracles. Or the sun may be said to be those greater persons in the holy Church who enlighten the rest: they will be black, that is, bound in their preaching and making no progress; “as a sackcloth,” that is, though outwardly black, nevertheless retaining their brightness within; “of hair,” that is, held to be guilty and sinful in others’ estimation. “And the moon,” that is, the whole Church, which waxes and wanes, “became as blood,” namely bloodstained and crushed. “And the stars [Col. 1525C] of heaven,” namely the lesser ones, yet bright and enlightening the Church, “fell upon the earth”: they were called away to earthly things, “as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a wind.” An unripe fig is empty fruit and falls quickly. By this comparison it is understood that those whom God permits to fall from the Church are not firmly bound by true love. For those who love God can by no temptation be torn away from his love. “And heaven withdrew like a scroll being rolled up”: that is, holy preachers will cease preaching to the ungodly. “And every mountain,” that is, everyone eminent in virtues; or, if mountain is taken in an evil sense, every mountain, that is, those exalted in pride; “and islands,” that is, those troubled by secular affairs, withdraw from faith and good [Col. 1525D] works. Or islands are those who either will be moved from their former condition by persecutions, or will be separated from the ungodly in faith and deed.

“And the kings of the earth.” Behold, he sets forth the end, namely what happens at the judgment: persons of every condition will wish literally to hide themselves at the Judge’s coming. Or “kings” are those resisting the flesh; “princes and commanders,” greater and lesser persons; “the rich,” rich in good works; “the mighty,” strong against temptations; and “every slave,” that is, every married person, “and free,” free from marriage, hid themselves, seeking assistance in “caves,” that is, in shadowing and protection, and in “rocks,” the solidity of mountains—that is, of angels, who are mountains through the eminence of their virtues. Or, if we speak of those utterly lost, they hid themselves, that is, they will flee for the aid of the demons whom they served. And they will say [Col. 1526A] to the mountains and rocks: “Fall upon us,” either literally or according to the foregoing allegories, “from the face of him who sits,” from his knowledge, “and from the wrath of the Lamb.” And this is now necessary, “for the great day of their wrath has come; and who will be able to stand,” unless aided by your assistance?

## CHAPTER VII

After this I saw four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, so that no wind might blow upon the earth, nor upon the sea, nor upon any tree. And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God. And he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it had been given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: “Do not harm the earth, the sea, or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God upon their foreheads.” And I heard the number [Col. 1526B] of those sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed, from every tribe of the children of Israel. From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Gad, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Asher, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Naphtali, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Manasseh, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Simeon, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Levi, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Issachar, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Zebulun, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Benjamin, twelve thousand sealed.

Having described so great a war against the Church, lest his own should fail, he strengthens them through a certain aid of his: namely, although the devil is prepared everywhere to harm the faithful, he is forbidden by the Lord ever to impede his own. [Col. 1526C] “After this,” according to the sequence of visions, “I saw four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth,” that is, devils, who are called angels only by reason of the dignity of their creation; or because they are sent to punish the wicked and test the good. He calls them four because they are to harm in the four parts of the world, “holding the four winds of the earth.” By winds he understands preachers, because, as wind shakes the clouds, waters the earth, causes it to bear fruit, and makes the face of the earth cheerful, so preaching does to human minds. These are called four, like those mentioned above, “so that no wind might blow upon the earth.” By earth he understands those dwelling on earth or devoted to earthly things; by sea, those dwelling on islands or tossed by diverse vices. By the tree, which has now [Col. 1526D] grown somewhat from the earth, he understands one who has received faith, or is already prepared to bear fruit. Behold the aid against the aforementioned angels: Christ forbids them to harm his own. “And I saw an angel,” that is, Christ, “another,” that is, different from those mentioned above, ascending into the world “from the rising of the sun,” that is, enlightening like the sun; “having the seal of the living God,” that is, the cross, by which he would mark his own, or immunity from sin, from which God becomes manifest. “And he cried with a loud voice to the four angels,” when in his Passion he cast down demons from their power with great authority, “to whom it had been given to harm the earth and the sea,” saying. He is silent concerning the tree, because it itself has grown from the earth. “Until we seal the servants of our God”: until I distinguish them inwardly and outwardly by the sign of the cross upon their foreheads. [Col. 1527A] The sign upon the forehead, which is manifest openly, signifies confession by the mouth, which ought not to be silent even in tribulation; the sign upon the breast signifies confession of the heart. “And I heard”—that is, I understood—the number of those sealed: all those to be sealed who are signified by these, one hundred and forty-five thousand. He gives a finite number of the sealed because it is finite to God, though infinite to us. He gives this number because by its parts it signifies preachers of the Holy Trinity. For it consists of twelve multiplied by itself. By twelve, which consists of three and four, we understand those sealed by faith in the Holy Trinity throughout the four parts of the world; by a thousand we signify perfection. “From every tribe,” that is, from all nations, of the children of Israel, who are men seeing God.

[Col. 1527B] “From the tribe of Judah,” that is, confession. This suffices for those who do not have time to act. Judah, who was the fourth among Jacob’s sons, is here put first; hence we are given to understand that this enumeration is not historical but spiritual. He passes over Dan, the sixth son, because Antichrist will be born from his progeny; from this it is implied that Antichrist is to be excluded from every number of the saints. “From the tribe of Reuben,” that is, seeing sons, as are those who do some work. “From the tribe of Gad,” that is, girded, namely against every temptation. “From the tribe of Asher,” that is, blessed, namely not intent upon worldly matters. “From the tribe of Naphtali,” that is, breadth: namely those who from charity distribute what is theirs to others. “From the tribe of Manasseh,” that is, forgetting; by whom is signified the Gentile people, who, having forgotten [Col. 1527C] idols, served God. He is fittingly introduced in sixth place because Christ was born in the sixth age. “From the tribe of Simeon,” sorrow, or remembrance of past sins, which is the chief safeguard for preserving virtues. “From the tribe of Levi,” that is, added; by whom are signified those who are not content with what has been prescribed but undertake many good things on their own initiative. “From the tribe of Issachar,” that is, reward: namely those who now despise earthly habitation and wholly attend to recompense, like him who says, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). “From the tribe of Zebulun,” that is, dwelling-place of strength: namely those not refusing labor, but sometimes descending from contemplation to action for their brethren’s necessity. “From the tribe of Joseph,” that is, increase: namely those multiplying the Church in the number of saints. [Col. 1527D] “From the tribe of Benjamin,” that is, son of the right hand: these are those who attribute everything to God’s mercy, nothing to themselves.

After this I saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands. And they cried with a loud voice, saying: “Salvation to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” And all the angels stood around the throne, the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell before the throne upon their faces and worshipped God, saying: “Amen. Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and [Col. 1528A] strength be to our God for ages of ages. Amen.”

“After this.” What he now says is, as it were, an exposition of the foregoing: namely, what above he spoke of under the finite number of the sealed, here he calls an innumerable multitude; what there he expressed through twelve tribes, here through the universality of nations. It is as though he said: “As was foretold, so I saw it fulfilled.” “After this I saw a great multitude, which no one could number”: although its number is known to God, it is uncertain to human beings; “from all nations,” even the most barbarous; “and tribes” within each nation; “and peoples, and tongues”—there are diverse languages within the same people—that is, from every diversity of languages; “standing before the throne,” that is, ready to obey God the Judge, or also their prelates; “and in the sight [Col. 1528B] of the Lamb,” Christ, so that they may both behold and be beheld; and these “were clothed in white robes,” in innocence and immortality, “and palms were in their hands,” that is, victories proceeding from works. “And they cried”: both now, and especially in the future, they will cry. By all these things the Church ought especially to be encouraged, “with a loud voice,” that is, with great affection, saying: “Salvation to our God”—namely, whatever goods we have, whether forgiveness of sins, good action, or eternal glory, nothing comes from ourselves, but all comes radically from God and is consummated by him, as is said in 1 Corinthians 12, Galatians 3, and Philippians 2. Nevertheless, we are God’s fellow workers, as St. Paul concludes in 1 Corinthians 3—“and to the Lamb,” Christ the Son of God.

“And all the angels stood.” He introduces the angels as rejoicing in the fellowship of the saints and confirming their testimony. “And they fell”: they humbled [Col. 1528C] themselves before him, “before the throne,” that they might behold and be beheld, “upon their faces,” that is, into their consciences, rationally seeing what they do; “and they worshipped God, saying: Amen.” “Amen”: namely, whatever you attribute to him is true. Or let us connect “Amen” with what follows: “Amen,” that is, true in all promises. “The Lord is faithful in all his words” (Ps. 144). “And blessing,” exaltation, because he is above every creature; or our exaltation in virtues. “And glory,” impassibility; or our glory in good works. “And wisdom,” because he knows all things, or because he makes us knowing. “And thanksgiving,” that is, we ought to render him thanks for all the goods we have. “Honor,” that is, veneration, which every good person offers to him; [Col. 1528D] “and power,” the power to hinder enemies, which he also gives to his own; “and strength,” the vigor of virtue, which he has from himself and does not need to seek elsewhere. By these things ascribed to God, diverse heresies are crushed. “For ages of ages”: and this is not temporary, but eternal.

And one of the elders answered, saying to me: “Who are these clothed in white robes, and whence have they come?” And I said to him: “My lord, you know.” And he said to me: “These are those who have come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple. And he who sits upon the throne dwells over them. They shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more; neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat; for the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, shall rule them and [Col. 1529A] lead them to the springs of the waters of life. And God shall wipe every tear from their eyes.”

After blessed John had recognized that multitude in such dignity, he seeks to know by what path it could have reached these things, so that he might teach others to aim at the same. “And one of the elders answered,” that is, satisfied my desire, as though I had asked. All are one, in that they teach the same thing. “Who are they?” How worthy they are. “My lord, you know,” that is, teach me, who do not know. “These are those who have come,” and who are yet to come, “and have washed their robes” by good action—their innocence, or their bodies. “Therefore they are before the throne of God”: namely, they please God the Judge; “in his temple,” either in the present Church, or, stripped of the body, they are his temple and dwelling-place. Thus they enjoy the true bread, and this is what he says: [Col. 1529B] “And he who sits upon the throne,” who gave knowledge to the angels, “dwells over them”: he will give the same knowledge also to them. “They shall neither hunger nor thirst any more,” being given to drink from the fountain of life; “neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat,” neither greater nor lesser tribulation; “for the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, shall rule them,” leading them from virtue to virtue. “And he shall lead them to the springs of the waters of life,” and through this shall at last lead them to the springs of the waters of life—that is, to unfailing refreshment. “And God shall wipe every tear from their eyes”: now absolutely no pain can remain in them.

## CHAPTER VIII

And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.

[Col. 1529C] THIRD VISION

And I saw seven angels standing before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood before the altar, having a golden censer. And much incense was given to him, that he might offer it from the prayers of the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne of God. And the smoke of the incense from the prayers of the saints ascended from the angel’s hand before God. And the angel took the golden censer, filled it with the fire of the altar, and cast it upon the earth. And there were thunders, voices, lightnings, and a great earthquake. And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound the trumpet.

And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven: peace, because throughout the world [Col. 1529D] there will be peace after Antichrist’s death for about half an hour; that is, that rest will not last long, because judgment will come quickly.

“And I saw.” In this third vision he treats of the office of preaching imposed upon seven angels. By their preaching, seven persecutions and deadly plagues of the reprobate will be shown to occur. Nor does he here depart from his purpose; rather, he greatly exhorts and invites those in the Church patiently to bear tribulations. Otherwise they will be outside the Church and struck down. He presents this vision in likeness of that figure in which the children of Israel, sounding trumpets, overthrew the walls of Jericho (Joshua 6). “And I saw seven angels,” all angels, or those imbued with the sevenfold Spirit, “standing,” ready to obey God; or not ceasing to aid the devout, “before [Col. 1530A] God,” because the condemnation of the wicked does not displease God. “And seven trumpets were given to them,” that is, the office of preaching. “And another angel,” far more worthy, namely Christ, “came” through the humanity united to him. “And stood,” that is, was prepared, after the likeness of a priest, to offer our prayers to God “before the altar.” Christ himself is called the altar, upon whom we offer to God: for whatever we do would profit nothing unless he mediated—that is, unless it were done in the power of his Passion. This altar, so far removed from our knowledge, is signified by the golden altar in the Holy of Holies, “having a golden censer,” that is, a vessel of fire, by which is signified the body of Christ or of the apostles, who are vessels of the Holy Spirit. “And much incense was given to him,” that is, prayers offered to God by many saints, [Col. 1530B] “that he might offer from the prayers of all the saints,” that is, that he might present to God the Father the prayers of the saints, “upon the golden altar,” that is, upon himself, because he is the foundation of every good; or upon the divinity, which is above the humanity, “which is before the throne of God,” that is, in the good pleasure of him seated upon the throne. Here he indicates that what pleases the altar also pleases him who is seated. “And the smoke ascended,” that is, compunction produced from prayer, “from the hand of the angel,” by Christ’s working. “And the angel,” Christ, “took the censer,” those whom he had earlier held ready so that he might accomplish something through them. “And he filled it with the fire of the altar,” that is, with the Holy Spirit, with whom he himself was full, “and cast it upon the earth,” to bear fruit. And from them there arose thunders, that is, threats; voices, admonitions; lightnings, miracles; and an earthquake: earthly persons [Col. 1530C] were thereby moved, some to good and some to evil. “And the seven angels,” all preachers, “prepared themselves to sound the trumpet,” that is, they prepared within themselves by works what they wished to preach to others; or they considered what suited each person, giving deeper things to Solomon.

And the first angel sounded the trumpet. And there was hail and fire mingled with blood, and it was cast upon the earth. And a third part of the earth was burned up, and a third part of the trees was burned. And every green plant was burned up.

“And the first angel sounded the trumpet,” first in the order of narration; or because this was the first blinding, namely in Judea while the apostles preached. He sounded the trumpet; he thundered forth with mighty preaching. “And there was hail,” grievous to some, sweet to others, “and fire”: the irascible were angered against the preaching; “mingled with blood.” These two were the cause of their destruction, “and it was cast upon the earth”: all this was cast upon Judea, the earth well cultivated by Law and prophets. “And a third part of the earth” was burned. The two parts, namely the more perfect and the less perfect, were saved; the third—that is, all the reprobate—perished. It “was burned,” that is, blinded by God and condemned by his ministers. [Col. 1530D] “And a third part of the trees was burned.” Trees are those who have grown from the earth, namely those higher in the Law, whose reprobate portion was condemned. “And every green plant” means all those wholly devoted to worldly delights.

And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea. And a third part of the sea became blood, and a third part of the creatures having souls in the sea died, and a third part of the ships perished.

“And the second angel sounded the trumpet,” in the order of narration, or also in fact. For when the Jews had been rejected, the apostles turned to the Gentiles, of whom likewise a third part was condemned. “Like a great mountain,” that is, the devil because of his pride; “burning with fire,” that is, raging with envy to do harm. “And it was cast into the sea,” among the Gentiles. The devil is said to have been cast among the Gentiles, although he was already in them, because, when he previously possessed all the Gentiles securely, he slept and rested in them, no longer compelling them to sin. But after he had lost two parts among them, he raged against the remainder, desiring to keep them. [Col. 1531B] “And a third part of the sea became blood,” sinners; “and a third part of the creatures died,” that is, of the philosophers, who possess greater discernment among the Gentiles. The Gentiles are called the sea because they are tossed by the greatest vices. “And a third part of the ships perished,” that is, of the rulers among the Gentiles.

And the third angel sounded the trumpet, and a great star, burning like a torch, fell from heaven; and it fell upon a third part of the rivers and upon the springs of waters. And the name of the star is called Wormwood. And a third part of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the waters because they had become bitter.

“And the third angel sounded the trumpet,” in the order of narration; or because, after the devil could not blind the Jews and Gentiles, he sowed heresies and thus perverted some. “And a great star fell”: it appeared that he had fallen from heaven literally, or from the Church—the star, that is, the devil, who is called a star by reason of his creation, “burning” with envy, “like a torch.” A torch burns and is consumed; so the devil, always burning with envy, will at last be consumed—that is, when he has no power but is tormented with the others. “And it fell upon a third part of the rivers”: namely, he sowed a third sense into the Scriptures, [Col. 1531C] “and upon the springs of waters.” Springs are said to be that from which rivers flow, and by this the Gospel is signified to us, which is the spring and summary of our whole faith. From it flow rivers, that is, expositions, in all of which there are two senses of the faithful: historical and allegorical. The third is introduced when heresies are brought in. “And the name of the star was Wormwood,” bitterness.

And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, and a third part of the sun, a third part of the moon, and a third part of the stars were struck, so that a third part of them was darkened and a third part of the day did not shine, and likewise a third part of the night. And I saw and heard the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice: “Woe, woe, woe to those dwelling upon the earth, because of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet.”

“And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet,” fourth in the order of narration, or also in fact. Since the devil could not blind all the Jews or Gentiles, and had also sown heresies, he finally undertook to attack the children of the Church and drew some away from it, both from the greater and lesser. And a third part—namely all the reprobate—[Col. 1532A] of the sun, the greater teachers, was struck by the removal of grace; and a third part of the moon, the lesser yet well-shining persons; and a third part of the stars, that is, the simpler, though still enlightening, persons. Thus a third part of them was darkened: that is, they will lose right knowledge and good action. And a third part of the day did not shine, that is, those who had been illuminated by the greater persons; and similarly of the night, those enlightened by the moon and stars, namely the lesser persons. He has related these four condemnations without any forewarning, as things past and occurring daily. For the remaining three, which are to follow, he gives a forewarning, because those three are future in the last times. “And I saw”: I remained in the vision. “And I heard [Col. 1532B] the voice of one eagle.” All holy preachers are called eagles because they fly high on the wings of virtues and gaze penetratingly upon the matter. “Flying through the midst of heaven,” that is, of the Church, which conceals divine mysteries within itself; “saying with a loud voice,” because it must be preached throughout the whole world, or because it announces a great thing: “Woe, woe, woe,” three times, “because of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet,” taking this as its subject.

## CHAPTER IX

And the fifth angel sounded the trumpet. And I saw a star descend from heaven to earth. And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to it. And it opened the pit of the abyss, and smoke ascended from the pit like the smoke of a great furnace; and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit. And from the smoke locusts came forth upon the earth. And power was given to them, such as [Col. 1532C] the scorpions of the earth have. And they were commanded not to harm the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of the living God upon their foreheads. And it was said to them not to kill them, but to torment them for five months; and their torment was the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it; they will desire to die, and death will flee from them. And the likenesses of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle; and upon their heads were, as it were, crowns like gold; and their faces were like human faces. And they had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like lions’ teeth; and they had iron breastplates. And the sound of their wings was like the sound of many chariots of horses rushing into [Col. 1532D] battle; and they had tails like scorpions, and stings were in their tails. Their power was to harm people for five months. And they had over them as king the angel of the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon, in Greek Apollyon, and in Latin he has the name Exterminator.

And the fifth [angel], both in sequence and in the narration. This is the condemnation of those whom the devil sends forth to prepare the ways before the face of Antichrist. “And I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth”: literally, one striving that no one should fill his place. “And there was given to him the key,” that is, authority was granted him by God, “of the pit of the abyss.” Dark and deep sinners are called abysses; the deeper among them are pits. “And he opened the pit of the abyss”: he caused the heresies concealed in their hearts to be brought forth. [Col. 1533A] “And smoke ascended from the pit,” that is, their evil, blinding doctrine, “like the smoke of a great furnace,” that is, like the doctrine of Antichrist, which is a furnace testing the good and reducing the wood—that is, the wicked—to ashes. Or literally: “the sun was darkened,” namely certain persons who enlighten others, “and the air by the smoke of the pit,” that is, certain enlightened persons. “And locusts came out of the smoke upon the earth,” that is, the forerunners of Antichrist.

It is the nature of the locust to arise from smoke. Such disciples are aptly compared to locusts, because, just as locusts cannot fly yet strain and leap, but immediately fail and fall to the ground; and cannot walk upon the ground, while gnawing green things—so those heresiarchs can neither fly aloft through profound knowledge nor walk steadily through good works. [Col. 1533B] Rather, they leap through pride, fall back into worse things, and are destroyers of the good. “And power was given to it,” granted by God, “such as the scorpions of the earth have power.”

They are aptly compared to a scorpion because, just as it stings secretly with its tail while appearing gentle in front, so heretics deceive through temporal things, persuading people that these are the highest goods and sufficient for life, although they are the lowest and most worthless things. Or they are compared to the scorpion because, just as a scorpion stings and its victim does not feel it at once, but the poison gradually spreads and burns, so those deceived by heretics do not at first perceive it, but are finally destroyed. “And it was commanded them”: behold the aid which God gives the saints against these men—namely, he forbids them to injure any of his own: “that they should not hurt in soul the grass of the earth,” that is, those still carnal and untrained in faith, and therefore easily [Col. 1533C] deceived; “nor any green thing,” that is, those already advanced; “nor any tree,” those prepared now to bear fruit—except only those who “do not have the sign of the living God in truth upon their foreheads,” that is, in open confession.

“And it was given them”: God permitted them to torment bodies, but not to injure souls. This is indeed what heretics do: after they fail in persuasion, they seek by force to harm others. And here, concerning the good, it is said, “that they should not kill them” by spiritual death, “but that they should be tormented five months,” that is, according to their bodies, which employ the five senses. Another text has “six months,” on account of the six ages by which this life is distinguished. “And their torment [was] as the torment of a scorpion”: namely, when they could not themselves do harm, they accused them before rulers. Thus “in those days men shall seek [Col. 1533D] death,” fearing a fall, “and shall not find it,” in order that they may be rendered more proved; “and death shall flee from them,” because care for the flock will bind them to their labor.

Above he said that these harm like scorpions; now, in describing them, he wishes to show what sort of persons they are who can harm in this way. “And the likenesses of the locusts”—imaginary locusts—were “like horses prepared for battle,” because they are swift in ranging about, fierce in attack, and do not take heed whom they rush upon, whether fellow citizens or not. “And upon their heads,” that is, upon their teachers—or in their minds, where they are proud both in themselves and before others—were “as it were crowns,” victories over those whom they have cast down, “like gold”: not through true wisdom, but through worldly wisdom. “And their faces [were] as the faces of men.” Literally: [Col. 1534A] outwardly they will display themselves as humane and pious, but inwardly their wickedness will be concealed.

“And they had hair like women’s hair”: hair signifies effeminate morals, hanging loose and flowing, indeed ready for the deception of others; or hair signifies lesser persons, who through deceits adhere to these men. “Their teeth,” that is, they themselves as those who tear apart, “were as lions’,” because they both rend and emit stench—that is, foul words and perverted opinions. “And they had breastplates like iron breastplates,” that is, hardness of heart which the arrow of truth cannot pierce; or breastplates signify doctrines of falsehood which admit no doctrine of truth. “And the sound of their wings,” that is, the tumult of opinions which they create after reason fails them, was “like the sound of chariots of many horses running to battle.” [Col. 1534B] Literally; or, just as different horses run by different roads toward the same battle, so these men advance by different heresies to attack the Church.

“And they had tails like scorpions.” By tails he understands earthly rulers, to whom heretics have recourse after they profit neither by reasoning nor by tumult. Rulers are called tails because, just as a scorpion strikes with its tail, so heretics strike through rulers after they make no progress by persuasion. Or tails are deceitful opinions: with them they flatter openly but sting secretly. “And stings,” that is, sin by which they incite others to sin, “were in their tails.” “Their power [was] to harm men,” and even the good in their bodies, “five months.”

Having shown what they are among themselves, he also shows through whom they can do these things: “and they had over them a king, the angel [Col. 1534C] of the abyss,” that is, the devil, who rules all who are in the depth of vices. His name in Hebrew is *Abaddon*, as though to say, “From him, all the Church, guard yourselves.” Therefore he names him in every language—Greek, Hebrew, and Latin—languages in which the Gospel was written: in Greek, *Apollyon*; in Latin, “Destroyer.” The same thing is signified in the other languages by an equivalent expression.

“One woe has passed. Behold, two woes still come.” After this, the sixth angel sounded the trumpet: “and I heard one voice from the four horns of the golden altar, which is before the eyes of the Lord, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: Release the four angels bound at the great river Euphrates. And the four angels were released, [Col. 1534D] who had been prepared for the hour and day and month and year, to kill a third part of men. And the number of the army of horsemen was twenty thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number. And thus I saw the horses in the vision, and those sitting upon them having fiery, hyacinthine, and sulphurous breastplates; and the horses’ heads were like lions’ heads, and from their mouths proceed fire, sulphur, and smoke. By these three plagues a third part of men was killed: by the fire, smoke, and sulphur proceeding from their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails. For their tails are like serpents, having heads, and with these they harm. And the rest of men, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands, so that they might not [Col. 1535A] worship demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders, nor of their sorceries, nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts.”

“One woe has passed”: one condemnation has been narrated. “After this the sixth angel sounded the trumpet,” in the order both of the narrative and of time. For this is the condemnation of the wicked in the time of Antichrist. “And I heard one voice from the four horns of the golden altar.” The altar is called Christ; the horns are preachers who uphold Christ and are prepared to die for him, just as blood was placed upon the horns of the altar. Or the altar is the Church offering itself in sacrifice, in which the horns are defenders of others. These holy preachers are called four because of the four things [Col. 1535B] that they proclaim concerning Christ; or the four horns are the four Gospels, which teach how to uncover the deceits of Antichrist. “Which is before the eyes of the Lord”: whatever is offered upon it, God holds acceptable. “Saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet”: heralds of past times forewarn future persons of what is to come.

“Release the four angels”: preach that they have been released, so that the elect may beware; or release the wicked through excommunication, and thus they shall be loosed and shall reign in those “who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” Two opposing cities are represented, Jerusalem and Babylon. Babylon, which means “confusion,” is called the dwelling-place of the devil; the other, of God. Near Babylon is literally the river Euphrates, by which worldly rulers are signified, overflowing and surging. The devil is said to be bound in them while he works through them secretly; he is loosed in them when he works openly. [Col. 1535C] Or they may be called loosed because, restrained by Christ’s Passion, they could not formerly do as much as they then will be able to do.

“And the four angels were released,” and what had been commanded was fulfilled: “who had been prepared for the hour and day and month and year.” By “hour” we understand half a year; by “day,” a year; by “month,” a year; and by “year,” likewise a year. Thus we have three and a half years, namely the time of Antichrist’s persecution.
