Or by “hour” let us note that they continually sought to harm, since they did not cease even for an hour; and by the remainder, that they did this for a long time: “to kill a third part of men,” that is, the reprobate.

“And the number of the army of horsemen”: once the devil has been released, many are hurled headlong—“twenty thousand times ten thousand.” Ten thousand are the saints, made perfect by the ten commandments of the law; a double number is set against them because the wicked are more numerous. [Col. 1535D] “I heard their number.” As if to say: I rightly give their number, because I heard it—that is, I understood them to be far more numerous than the good.

“And thus I saw horses in the vision.” As I understood that they rode to the destruction of others, so I understood that they did this through the devil, whom they bear as horses bear their masters. Or the devil may be understood as the horse, and the wicked as the riders who rest upon him. “And those who sat upon them had fiery, hyacinthine, and sulphurous breastplates,” that is, they fortified themselves with opinions from which follows eternal punishment, where there are smoke, fire, and stench; here the effect is put for the cause. [Col. 1536A] For such a breastplate results in eternal punishment. Or the breastplate is eternal punishment itself, which never releases those whom it receives.

“And their heads”: he describes the horses themselves, so as to show them fit to do harm. By heads he means the chief persons among the devil’s ministers. They “were as lions’ heads,” because they rend and stink, as was said above in the plague of locusts. Here he aptly assigns them a lion’s face after having said that they had a human face, because heretics show some semblance of humility; but the ministers of Antichrist compel men by every torment to confess what they teach. “And from their mouths,” that is, from their preaching, because it is itself the cause of punishment, “proceed fire, smoke, and sulphur.” He signified the same thing above through hyacinth, a stone of smoky color.

These three distinct punishments are indeed also inflicted [Col. 1536B] in hell according to the different sins committed in this world. There fire is given to those who here had excessive heat of desires. There smoke afflicts those who in this world are blinded by the ignorance of pride; stench arises from the filth of evil deeds. “By these plagues a third part of men was killed, by the fire, smoke, and sulphur proceeding from their mouths.” “The power of the horses is in their mouths.” He rightly said that these punishments proceed from the horses’ mouths, because their harmful power lies in evil preaching; “and in their tails,” that is, in secret deceits.

“For their tails also”: I rightly said that their power is in their tails, for they are like serpents too; they flatter with their face and secretly pour out poison. “Having heads, and with these they harm”: these tails have heads, namely certain leaders through whom they bite. “And the rest of men who were not killed by these plagues.” Of those who were in the Church, all the reprobate died; and the rest, namely those who were never of the Church, likewise died in their sins, whether pagans or Jews. [Col. 1536C] “Neither did they repent of the works of their hands.” He shows that these too are dead: “that they might not worship demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone.” He shows the various kinds of idols, so that their folly may be denoted in each; this applies properly to the Gentiles, “which can neither see nor hear.” By this he plainly shows that they ought not to be worshipped and rebukes the stupidity of those who worship such things. “And they did not repent of their murders.” We may likewise understand these matters of the Jews. [Col. 1536D] “Nor of their sorceries, nor of their fornication”: by these parts let us understand the remaining vices.

## CHAPTER X

“And I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud; and a rainbow was upon his head, and his face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire. And he had in his hand a little open book; and he placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth. And he cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roars. And when he had cried, the seven thunders uttered their voices. And when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write; and I heard a voice from heaven saying: Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write it.”

[Col. 1537A] Having described the persecution that shall occur in the Church in the time of Antichrist, he sets against it the aid impending for them, namely Christ. For the faithful, considering such things, shall be refreshed by Christ’s consolation. “And I saw another,” opposed to those previously mentioned, “mighty,” whom the enemy cannot resist, “coming down,” humbling himself even to our knowledge, “from heaven,” from the knowledge of angels. “Clothed with a cloud,” concealed in flesh, which is refreshment to some and blinding to others. “And a rainbow was upon his head,” that is, peace in respect of his own person, according to the saying, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5).

“And his face was like the sun”: whoever possesses true knowledge of him shines and gives light. “And his feet,” those who bear him, “were like a pillar,” [Col. 1537B] that is, firm in faith and supporting others; “of fire,” because they are kindled by the Holy Spirit. “And he had in his hand an open book,” that is, he had fulfilled all the Scriptures by his work; or he had already openly accomplished for all through himself the restoration of humankind. “And he placed his right foot,” the stronger preachers, “upon the sea,” that is, upon those more unstable in sins; “and his left,” that is, the less steadfast, “upon the earth,” upon those who were somewhat sluggish, though not wholly so. “And he cried with a loud voice”: through these feet he spoke great things, “as when a lion roars.”

The lion’s voice displays its strength and instills terror. Or, just as no beast dares cross the lion’s circuit but remains in the forest upon hearing its roar, so every faithful person enclosed by faith and the gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1537C] remains in the Church, hearing what God threatens against those who depart. “And when he had cried”: because these men sent by him preached, “the seven thunders uttered their voices,” that is, all their successors preached, inspiring terror in others; their voices were suited to their respective times. “And when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write, and I heard”: the saints understood a divine voice of admonition from heaven, directing them not to cast pearls before swine, as is said in Matthew 7. “Seal,” namely with seals, so that it may be open to friends and hidden from enemies. Here he implies that what the seven thunders said ought not to be kept silent from the faithful; “and do not write it,” that is, do not reveal it to unbelievers, in whom it produces nothing beneficial.

Here, by his own person being forbidden to write, he signifies to us that preaching will cease in the time of Antichrist. For saints wishing, in imitation of their predecessors, to preach publicly will understand it to be fruitless, and that in that time the word of God should rather be trampled underfoot. [Col. 1537D] For in that time there will be a destruction contrary to Christ’s edification: for just as Christ is the head of preaching and of all goodness, so Antichrist will be the head of all wickedness and of the extinction of God’s word.

“And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth raised his hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven and the things in it, and earth and the things on it, and sea and the things in it, that there shall be time no longer. But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins [Col. 1538A] to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be completed, as he declared by his servants the prophets.”

Against that immense tribulation which shall come in the time of Antichrist, and against the failure of preaching—which is the highest refreshment in a time of persecution—he sets before them the consolation promised by Christ to his own: that for them there will be time no longer, that is, they will be free from all changeability. To make them secure, he first sets forth, as it were, the proof of his own example: he has been taken up into heaven and is now immortal; and he swears to them this stability by him who lives for ever and ever.

“And the angel,” that is, Christ, “whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth, raised,” that is, exalted, “his hand,” that is, his human nature, by which he acted, “to heaven, [Col. 1538B] and swore,” firmly established, that as Christ rose again, so we too shall rise again, “by him who lives for ever and ever,” namely by himself. God’s swearing by him who lives for ever and ever means nothing else than that, just as he truly lives, so what he promises is certain. “Who created heaven and the things in it.” Now he shows that he has power to raise us, since he made all things from nothing: “and earth and the things on it, and sea and the things in it.”

When he says that all these things were created by God, he destroys the heresies of certain persons who asserted that some things were created by a demon. “That there shall be time no longer.” For the good there shall be no changeability, because they will be impassible and immortal; for the wicked, eternal changeability according to their various punishments. “But in the days of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be completed,” namely the reward of the saints, a secret which “eye has not seen,” and so forth, “as he declared by his servants the prophets.” For the prophets foretold the Lord’s first and second advents.

“And I heard a voice from heaven again speaking with me and saying: Go and take the open book from the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth. And I went to the angel, saying to him that he should give me the book. And he said to me: Take it and devour it; and it shall make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it shall be sweet as honey. And I took the book from the hand of the angel and devoured it; and it was sweet as honey in my mouth. And when I had devoured it, my belly was made bitter. And he said to me: You must prophesy again to peoples, nations, [Col. 1538D] tongues, and many kings.”

“And I heard a voice from heaven,” a divine admonition, “again,” that is, treating the same matters, speaking with me and saying: “Go”: advance in the power of God and make yourself worthy by God’s grace. “Take the book from the hand of the angel”: thus understand the Scripture fulfilled by God through the assumed flesh of him who stands upon sea and land, ready to help those who approach him. “And I went to the angel”: as one obeying, I enlarged my mind. Here he plainly teaches what one ought to do. “Saying to him,” by deed and prayer, “that he should give me the book,” that is, that he should open to me the sense of the Scriptures. “And he said to me”: when he sees someone prepared, he freely offers what is good.

“Take and devour it,” that is, examine it diligently through action and [Col. 1539A] inquiry; “and it shall make your belly bitter,” because it is hard for the flesh to fulfil God’s commandments. By the belly, which is soft and frail, he means the flesh. “But in your mouth it shall be sweet as honey,” that is, in preaching and contemplation. “And I took the book from the hand of the angel,” through Christ’s work and grace, “and devoured it; and it was sweet as honey in my mouth. And when I had devoured it, my belly was made bitter”: for it is burdensome to our flesh to fast and do the other things that are commanded. “And he said to me,” that is, he exhorted me to preach, revealing to me that I should escape that captivity: “You must prophesy again to peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings.” By enjoining preaching, he gave me the Scriptures as an aid.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 1539B] “And there was given to me a reed like a rod, saying: Rise and measure the temple of God, and his altar, and those worshipping in it. But cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles. And they shall trample the holy city for forty-two months. And I will give [power] to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth. These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing in the presence of the Lord of the earth. And if anyone wishes to harm them, fire shall come out of their mouths and devour their enemies. And if anyone wishes to injure them, so must he be killed. These have power to shut heaven, so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy; and they have power over waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every plague as often as [Col. 1539C] they wish. And when they have finished their testimony, the beast which shall ascend from the abyss shall make war against them, and shall overcome them and kill them. And their bodies shall lie in the streets of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified. And persons from peoples, tribes, tongues, and nations shall see their bodies for three and a half days, and shall not permit their bodies to be placed in tombs. And the inhabitants of the earth shall rejoice and exult over them and send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who dwelt upon the earth.”

“And there was given to me a reed,” that is, Scripture—for the ancients wrote with a reed—“like a rod,” like a sceptre, because it appoints kings, saying and exhorting: “Rise,” go forth; do not be sluggish in preaching. “Measure”: preach to each person according to that person’s capacity, so that you may thus make them the temple of God, just as one wishing to establish a temple measures as he lays out foundation, length, breadth, and so forth. “The temple of God and his altar,” that is, Christ. For to the lesser persons the Incarnation and similar matters ought to be preached; to the greater, the unity of the Trinity and such things. “And those worshipping in it”: establish how they ought to worship in him.

“But the court which is outside the temple,” that is, false Christians who pretend to be the Church while denying it by their deeds, “cast out.” The preceding reason for their being cast out is that they are outside, namely that they do not act as the Church. Thus he says, “The court which is outside the temple, cast out,” by excommunicating them; [Col. 1540A] show that they are outside, “and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles,” that is, entirely withdraw preaching, because they are conformed to the Gentiles. “And they shall trample the holy city”: these persons shall persecute the Church gathered for righteous living, “for forty-two months,” namely throughout the whole period of Antichrist’s preaching. By this he seems to imply that every persecution of the holy Church, at whatever time, is from Antichrist, as is that which shall occur in his own time.

In order to strengthen those presently living, lest they cease preaching on account of persecution, which is still light, he says that in the time of that most savage persecution Elijah and Enoch will preach. Thus he says: “And I will give the word of God to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy one thousand two hundred [Col. 1540B] and sixty days”: they shall preach for three and a half years; and then Antichrist, beginning to reign, shall openly kill them. “Clothed in sackcloth,” that is, in penitential clothing—not because they need repentance, but because they fulfil in their own works what they teach others.

“These are the two olive trees.” The olive is a tree full of sap, and they are full of the Holy Spirit; “and the two shining lampstands,” because they supply light to others, “standing before the Lord of the earth,” in the good pleasure of God. Now he shows how God gives his own invincible power to condemn the impious: “and if anyone wishes to harm them,” by leading them away from truth, “fire shall come from their mouths,” that is, a spiritual judgment, “and shall devour,” that is, condemn, “their enemies.” “And if anyone wishes to injure them bodily, so must he be killed”: thus, by spiritual judgment. “And these have power [Col. 1540C] to shut heaven,” that is, the Scriptures, which conceal the mysteries of God, “so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy,” because they will not preach except at a suitable time.

This was prefigured when Elijah literally caused rain to cease for three and a half years (3 Kings 17). “And they have power over waters,” that is, their doctrines, which water the minds of believers, “to turn them,” as regards those who perversely understand them, “into blood,” into sin, just as Moses is recorded to have done in Egypt (Exod. 7); “and to strike the earth,” earthly persons, “with every plague,” as the Egyptians were struck, as is evident in the book of Exodus, “as often as they wish.” “And when they have finished,” that is, completed, “their testimony,” namely their preaching, “the beast,” Antichrist, “which shall ascend to kingship from the exceedingly dark abyss, shall make war against them,” literally, or by disputations, “and shall overcome them and kill them” bodily.

“And their bodies shall lie in the streets,” that others may thereby be frightened from imitating them, “of the great city [Col. 1540D] Jerusalem,” once great in virtues, now in wickedness, “which is spiritually called Sodom,” that is, mute, because preaching will not then occur in it, “and Egypt,” that is, dark, because it will then lack knowledge of God, “where their Lord was crucified.” “And persons from tribes, tongues, and nations shall see their bodies for three and a half days.” Some will see them with their eyes, others by report alone, because throughout the entire time of that most wicked impostor and heresiarch Antichrist it will be proclaimed: “See that you are not like those who lie thus unburied.” “And they shall not permit their bodies to be placed in [Col. 1541A] tombs. And the inhabitants of the earth,” namely the wicked, “shall rejoice over them and exult and send gifts to one another”: this is a sign of joy, because “these two prophets tormented” those dwelling on earth, that is, by crushing their wickedness.

“And after three and a half days the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon those who saw them. And they heard a great voice from heaven saying to them: Come up here. And they ascended to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies saw them. And in that hour there was a great earthquake; and a tenth part of the city fell, and seven thousand names of men were killed in the earthquake; and the rest were sent into fear and gave glory [Col. 1541B] to the God of heaven.”

Having shown the tribulation of those by whose example he invited this man to preach, and, if necessary, to suffer, he also shows their crowns, so as similarly to assure this man concerning the reward. “And after three and a half days the spirit of life,” the soul giving eternal life—not now a soul merely serving the senses—“from God entered into them”: that is, I saw that it would enter them. “And they stood,” now impassible and immortal, “upon their feet,” that is, firm and needing nothing upon which to lean, as they had before when living in old age. “And great fear fell upon those who saw them,” like an oppressive weight: that is, upon those who saw them glorified. “And they heard a great voice,” one of great efficacy, “from heaven,” from Christ or an archangel, saying to them and fulfilling it in the very act, [Col. 1541C] “Come up here,” to the fellowship of the saints. “And they ascended to heaven in a cloud,” which was refreshment to them and terror to their enemies. “And their enemies saw them.”

“And in that hour,” the time of their glorification, “there was a great earthquake”: earthly persons shall be moved; or the Church shall be shaken at their killing. “And a tenth part of the city,” that is, the wicked—though they were established to restore the tenth order from humankind—“fell” into punishments, or fell away from the Church. “And seven thousand names of men were killed in the earthquake,” by eternal death, or because afterward they did not come to their senses: namely, those whom God foreknew as wicked by their individual distinctions, as though by names—seven thousand, all perfect in wickedness. “And the rest,” namely the good, [Col. 1541D] who did not fall into punishments, “were sent into fear,” that is, they fear the fall, or are in reverence of God, “and gave glory to the God of heaven,” attributing nothing to themselves.

“The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe shall come quickly. And the seventh angel sounded the trumpet, and great voices arose in heaven, saying: The kingdom of this world has become [the kingdom] of our God and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ever and ever. Amen. And the twenty-four elders, who sit before God upon their thrones, fell upon their faces and worshipped God, saying: We give you thanks, Lord God Almighty, who are and who were, because you have taken your great power and have reigned. And the nations were angry, and your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and to render reward to your servants the prophets, and to the saints, and to those fearing your name, [Col. 1542A] small and great, and to destroy those who corrupted the earth.”

“The second woe has passed”: the second condemnation has been stated. “And behold, the third woe shall come quickly,” in the narrative, or also in time. “And the seventh angel sounded the trumpet,” in the order of both the narrative and time. Since this angel announces judgment, it is not called a woe except in respect to the portion of the wicked. “And great voices arose in heaven saying,” that is, praises to God for the salvation of the just and the condemnation of the wicked. “The kingdom of this world has become [the kingdom] of our God”: he who was formerly despised and rejected by the world now obtains for himself a kingdom, crowning the good and punishing the wicked; “and of Christ his Son. And he shall reign”: he shall possess that kingdom for ever and ever. The saints and the condemned shall not return [Col. 1542B] to inhabit the world again, as certain heretics wish.

“And the twenty-four elders,” namely not only lesser but also greater persons, “shall glorify God, who sit before God,” that is, considering what pleases God, and who “sit,” that is, judge even now upon their thrones among those subject to them. “They fell upon their faces,” that is, humbled themselves in true conscience, “and worshipped God, saying: We give you thanks, Lord God Almighty, because you saved us and condemned the impious. You who are and who were, who have taken your great power,” by rising again, giving the Holy Spirit to your own, and gathering the Church, “and have reigned,” by defending your own from the devil and also breaking his power. “And the nations were angry” because of your kingdom, “and your wrath came,” and now at last your wrath appears in [Col. 1542C] them.

“And the time of the dead came”: the proper time of both good and wicked people “to be judged,” so that the good may be separated from the wicked; “and the time came to render reward to your servants, the prophets,” those who foresee for themselves and others; “and to the saints,” at least established in faith; “and to those fearing your name”—here he comprehends all the faithful—“small and great; and to destroy them”: the time came for those “who corrupted the earth,” namely themselves by evil action and others by teaching or example, to be placed outside the bounds of the true homeland.

## FOURTH VISION

“And the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple. And there were lightnings, voices, an earthquake, and great hail.”

[Col. 1542D] This fourth vision concerns the battle of the Church and the devil, and shows by what helps the devil is conquered by the Church. Therefore the faithful ought especially to be encouraged not to depart from the Church. Before treating this fourth vision, he prefaces something from the second, namely the revelation of mysteries, and from the third, namely the office of preaching fulfilled through the seven angels. For this vision depends upon those, since from the restoration of humankind and the condemnation of the wicked the Church which fights here is brought forth.

“And the temple of God in heaven was opened”: the mysteries of the Church, which were figured by the tabernacle, were disclosed. “And the ark of his covenant was seen,” that is, Christ, “in his temple,” in whom the treasures of wisdom are hidden (Col. 2), and in whom are the Old and New Testaments, just as the ark contained the tablets, [Col. 1543A] manna, and the other things. Or: it was fulfilled in his temple, in the Church which is in heaven through good life. “And there were”: behold, from the third vision, “lightnings,” miracles, as was previously said of the angels; “and voices,” admonitions; “and an earthquake”: some were moved toward good, others were not; “and great hail,” because preaching that punishes and crushes was seen as intolerable.

## CHAPTER XII

“And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars. And being with child, she cries out in travail and is tormented to give birth.”

And a great sign appeared: from these things I saw a certain figure coming forth, signifying something great, in heaven, because what appeared was a heavenly reality. A woman [Col. 1543B]—behold, a sign—because she signifies the Church, clothed with the sun, Christ, who both overshadows and illumines her; and the moon, the world, because it wanes and grows, was beneath her feet, because she is supported by the world in necessities. The woman signifies the Church: for as a woman gives birth and nurses, so the Church brings human beings to the light and to faith, and nourishes them with every divine word. And upon her head was a crown of twelve stars, that is, in Christ the victory over the world acquired through the twelve apostles. Or, upon her head—that is, at the Church’s beginning—was the same crown; and she had something in her womb, that is, something lies hidden in the memory as in a womb: she had the word of God, and cried out in preaching, travailing, laboring to bring some persons forth into the light; and she is tormented by enemies or by herself, because she cannot give birth to Christ in those whom she would wish. Or, because she afflicts herself so that she may herself fulfill in deed what she preaches to others, in order to give birth.

And another sign was seen in heaven. And behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns; and upon its heads were seven diadems; and its tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them upon the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had given birth, it might devour her son. And she gave birth to a male child who shall rule all nations with an iron rod; and her son was caught up to God and to his throne. And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, so that there they may feed her for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.

And against this woman another sign was seen in heaven. And behold, a dragon, that is, the devil, who is called a dragon because of his strength, great because of his great [Col. 1543D] power. He therefore says that the dragon was seen in heaven, in order to show him near at hand to attack the Church: for if he had said that he was in hell, there would seem to be no reason why he could fight with the Church, which he had seen in heaven. Red, because of slaughter; having seven heads, all the rulers through whom he works; and ten horns, that is, ten kingdoms. Historically, ten kings will adhere to Antichrist, to whom the rest will answer. Through these ten are understood all evil persons adhering to the devil. Or the ten horns are called riches, by which powerful persons attack the Decalogue. And upon its heads were seven diadems: every victory over the wicked. And its tail is the deceptions by which vices are concealed, as shameful parts are by a tail [Col. 1544A]; it drew all the reprobate into unbelief. And this is what he says: a third part of the stars of heaven, namely, those who once illumined the Church; and it cast them to earth, into delight in earthly things.

Having described the woman separately and the dragon separately, he shows their conflict. The dragon, the devil, trusting in such power, stood ready before the woman to injure and attack the Church, which was about to give birth, which labored in childbirth; and therefore the dragon thought that she would yield to him more quickly, so that, when she had given birth, he might devour her son. Therefore he stood there, so that, when the woman had brought someone forth into the light of faith, this dragon might devour him into sin. And she gave birth to a son, namely Christ, male because of strength. The Church gives birth to Christ because it introduces him into the individual minds of believers; or because Christ [Col. 1544B] according to the flesh came from those who were the Church. He shall rule all nations with an iron rod, with inflexible justice. And behold: here he sets forth the ground on which the Church has hope to begin the struggle. Because her son was caught up to the right hand of God, trusting in so great a help she begins to fight; secure of her own resurrection, she prevails. And this is what is meant: her son was caught up—his flesh contrary to the nature of flesh—to God, to equality with God, and to his throne, so that he may judge with the Father. And the woman, the Church, by her Son’s help fled from glory into the wilderness, so that in mind she might abandon the pride of this world. Why there? Because there she has a place prepared by God. And this is what he says: where she has a place prepared by God—that is, because God prepared such a place for her. It is a certain consolation: so that there he may feed her with the teaching of preaching for [Col. 1544C] one thousand two hundred and sixty days, three years and a half; that is, by the preaching which the Lord continually carried out for so long a time the Church is fed.

And a great battle took place in heaven. Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail; nor was their place found any longer in heaven. And that great dragon was cast down, the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world; he was cast down to earth, and his angels were sent with him. And I heard a great voice in heaven saying: Now have come salvation and strength and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ, because the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night. And they conquered him [Col. 1544D] by reason of the blood of the Lamb and by reason of the word of their testimony; and they did not love their lives even unto death. Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them.

And it came to pass—behold another help—a great battle in heaven. Michael and his angels fought with the dragon. Michael indeed fights by inspiring believers with the means by which they may overcome the devil’s frequent temptations, or by bringing bodily assistance, either personally or through any lesser angel, because all are subject to him. And the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail to cast the Church into sin; nor was their place any longer found in heaven, namely, they could no longer overcome that woman through temptations. Here the matter is the hidden war, namely, through [Col. 1545A] suggestions. And that great dragon was cast down from the good by the help of the Son and of the angels. A serpent because of cunning; ancient because of the first seduction; who is called the devil—as if he said: “All of you beware of him, because this one is called the devil,” that is, flowing away from the good, namely toward evils; and Satan, the adversary, who deceives the whole world insofar as concerns the reprobate. Cast down to earth, having fallen away from the faithful, he attacks the rest more fiercely; and his angels were sent with him.

Behold, he sets forth a certain exultation in heaven over this victory of the Church. And this is what is meant: “I heard a great voice in heaven saying,” whether from angels or from holy souls: “Now,” from the time of Christ, “have come salvation,” the remission of sins in baptism, “and strength,” strengthening for action in confirmation; “and the kingdom” [Col. 1545B], because he rules his own from virtue unto virtue, “of our God, and the authority of his Christ,” because he worked all these things through Christ, “because the accuser of our brothers has been cast down,” that is, the devil, who, by leading people into sin, makes them liable to accusation; “who accused them”—namely, it is his office to accuse, from which office he himself will never cease—“before the presence,” because nothing is hidden from him. By this he strongly warns us to beware: “before the presence of our God day and night,” continually. “And they conquered him,” by not yielding to his suggestions, “by reason of the blood of the Lamb,” namely by imitating Christ’s passion, “and by reason of the word of their testimony,” because they do not keep silent about the divine word where there is occasion, and about the faith which Christ testified; “and they did not love their lives unto death,” namely their animal impulses: that is, they did not satisfy [Col. 1545C] the flesh, so that their souls might thereby perish. “Therefore rejoice, O heavens,” angels or holy apostles, “and you who dwell in them,” among them, namely the lesser ones.

Woe to earth and sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has little time. And after the dragon saw that he had been cast down to earth, he persecuted the woman who had given birth to the male child. And two wings of the great eagle were given to the woman, so that she might fly into the wilderness to her place, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, away from the face of the serpent. And the serpent sent water from its mouth after the woman, like a river, so that it might cause her to be carried away by the river. And the earth helped the woman; the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river which the dragon had sent from its mouth [Col. 1545D]. And the dragon was angry with the woman and went away to make war with the rest of her offspring, those who keep God’s commandments and have the testimony of Jesus. And he stood upon the sand of the sea.

“Woe to earth and sea, because the devil has come down to you”: and because the devil has been cast down from the good, woe to you in whom he now dwells, because he will now adhere so closely that he cannot be separated. Having great wrath, because he sees many withdrawn from him and restored to their proper place. Knowing that he has little time, he rages all the more. And after the dragon saw that he had been cast down to earth: when the devil sees that he cannot succeed through hidden fraud, he persecutes the woman, openly setting himself to attack her, she who gave birth to the male child, from whom she has help in open battle. And two wings were given to the woman [Col. 1546A]: God gave the two wings—the two Testaments, or the twofold love, or the two lives, active and contemplative—of the great eagle, because they fly on high, namely as far as God himself, and have penetrating vision in the Scriptures, so that she might fly into the wilderness, to her place, namely, the place given her by God, where she is nourished with the sustenance of the doctrine of truth preached by God, for a time and times and half a time, namely for three years and a half, away from the face, from the presence, of the serpent, that is, of cunning deception.

And the serpent sent from its mouth, from the inspiration of preaching, after the woman, in order to overtake her; but it could not even reach her—water, tribulation, like a river, especially overflowing and surging—so that it might make her be drawn away by the river, into sin. And the earth helped the woman: namely, Christ gave the Church strength to endure [Col. 1546B] adversities; or the saints helped by prayer. The earth signifies Christ because of stability, who swallowed every tribulation, because he made himself fit to receive whatever might be inflicted upon him; because, receiving unjust death, he condemned death, and likewise all the other tribulations which he endured unjustly. And this is what follows: “And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river which the dragon sent from its mouth.” And the dragon was angry with the woman because, although he cannot overcome her, he nevertheless does not cease to envy her and seek a point of attack. And he went away to make war, now abandoning the stronger, with the rest, namely the weaker, of her offspring, who keep God’s commandments, such as those who fulfill them in deed, and have the testimony of Jesus, namely, whom they confess openly before others. And he stood upon the sand of the sea: [Col. 1546C] he did not stand upon the remnant, because he does not attach all of them to himself, but upon the sand, namely the unfruitful, who are not bound by the bond of faith. He stood, that is, he remained securely, among those in whom his footprints appear.

## Chapter XIII

And I saw a beast rising from the sea, having seven heads and ten horns; and upon its horns ten diadems, and upon its heads a name of blasphemy.

And I saw from the sea, from the world, a beast, the gathering of all who live beastially, rising by exalting itself through others, having seven heads, rulers in their entirety, and ten horns, namely kingdoms and powers through which they attack the ten commandments of the Law. And [Col. 1546D] by those ten kingdoms which will in fact adhere to Antichrist are signified all things in which there is an attack upon the Law. And upon its horns were ten diadems, because there is no commandment which is not broken by rulers and concerning which they themselves are not crowned. And upon its heads, in its rulers, was a name of blasphemy, because they say that Christ was not God and the like; or because they call this one their god, this one their household. Therefore he represents it to us so that we may see it as capable both of holding the sand fast in its unbelief and of drawing others to itself.

And the beast which I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like those of a bear, and its mouth like the mouth of a lion. And the dragon gave it its power and great authority. And I saw one of its heads as though slain unto death, and its deadly wound [Col. 1547A] was healed; and the whole earth marveled after the beast. And they worshiped the beast, saying: “Who is like the beast, and who can fight with it?” And a mouth speaking great things and blasphemy was given to it, and authority was given to it to act for forty-two months. And it opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his tabernacle and those who dwell in heaven. And it was given to it to make war with the saints and to overcome them; and authority was given to it over every tribe and people and language and nation. And all who dwell on earth worshiped it, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world. If anyone has an ear, let him hear. Whoever leads into captivity goes into captivity. Whoever kills with the sword, must be killed with the sword. [Col. 1547B] Here is the patience and faith of the saints.

And the beast which I saw was like a leopard, because, as a leopard is a spotted animal, so these are stained by diverse heresies; or also because they are assembled from diverse peoples. And its feet were like those of a bear: runners who, by proclaiming the beast, carry it abroad; they are fierce and rashly trample down, like a bear. And its mouth—those greater in speech—was like a lion’s mouth, because they rend the holy Scriptures and emit foul opinions. And the dragon gave it its power, to work miracles, and great authority to deceive many. And I saw one of its heads, namely Antichrist, the chief head, as though slain unto death: that blasphemous rogue will indeed pretend to die and to rise again on the third day, and its deadly wound was healed by a feigned resurrection. And [Col. 1547C] the whole earth marveled after the beast, imitating the beast; and they worshiped the beast through its chief head, namely through Antichrist, saying: “Who is like the beast? And who can fight with it?”—that is, resist its will? And a mouth speaking great things was given to it, for its own magnification, and blasphemy, in saying that it is the Son of God; and authority was given it to do such things for forty-two months. And it opened its mouth in blasphemies: it burst into such confidence that what it had formerly dared to blaspheme secretly, it now dares publicly to blaspheme against God, denying that Christ is God; to blaspheme his name, that is, his entire institution through which he appears praiseworthy; and his tabernacle, that is, those in whom he served as a soldier, calling [Col. 1547D] them degenerate and ragged, while displaying its own kings; and those who dwell in heaven, even the heavenly spirits. And it was given to it, by God’s permission, to make war with the saints and overcome them bodily; and authority was given to it over every tribe and people and language and nation. And those who dwell on earth, namely the reprobate, worshiped it, the beast, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world in his own people, as in Abel; or because this had been ordained from the beginning of the world.

“If anyone has an ear, let him hear.” This is a warning not to imitate this beast, although we see that it has such power, because in the end the beast and all its followers will be condemned. “Whoever leads into captivity,” namely by seducing us away from faith, as Antichrist does, “goes into captivity,” into condemnation. “Whoever kills with the sword,” material or persuasive, as Antichrist and his followers do, “must be killed with the sword,” by the word of God. [Col. 1548A] Here, because these persons will perish, we must have faith and patience against them, lest we perish with them: patience against tribulations and faith against evil persuaders—of the saints.

And I saw another beast rising from the earth, and it had two horns like those of the Lamb, and it spoke like a dragon. And it exercised all the authority of the first beast in its presence. And it caused the earth and those who dwell upon it to worship the first beast, whose deadly wound was healed. And it performed great signs, so that it even caused fire to come down from heaven to earth before people; and it deceived those who dwell on earth because of the signs which were given [Col. 1548B] to it to perform in the presence of the beast, telling those who dwell upon earth to make an image of the beast which has the wound of the sword. And it lived; and it was given to it to give spirit to the image of the beast, so that the image might speak. And it will cause all who have not worshiped the image of the beast to be killed. And it will cause all—small and great, rich and poor, free and slave—to have its mark on their right hand or on their foreheads, and that no one may buy or sell unless he has the mark of the beast, or its name, or the number of its name. Here is wisdom. Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the beast. It is the number of a human being, and its number is six hundred and sixty-six.

Having described the tribulation which will occur through Antichrist and his greater followers, he adds another which will occur through his [Col. 1548C] apostles, whom he will scatter throughout the whole world. And this is what he says: “And I saw another beast,” lesser than the former, “rising” to the height of pride, “from the earth,” through those devoted to earthly things; “and it had two horns like those of the Lamb,” because they will pretend to possess innocence, true doctrine, and miracles such as Christ had; or they will arrogate the two Testaments to themselves. “And it spoke like a dragon,” namely, they will speak seductively, as the devil does in Antichrist. “And it exercised all the authority of the former beast,” that is, every manner of deceiving and harming which Antichrist possessed, “in its presence,” in order to please Antichrist. “And it caused the earth and those who dwell upon it”—that is, the earthly and those who persist in love of the earth; or the earth according to the body, those dwelling in it according to [Col. 1548D] their souls—“to worship the first beast,” Antichrist, “whose deadly wound was healed.” For this will be the foundation of their preaching, just as Christ’s resurrection was the foundation for the apostles. “And it performed great signs,” to confirm its preaching, “so that it even caused fire to descend from heaven to earth before people”: for as the apostles received the Holy Spirit in the form of fire, so these will make their evil spirit descend in the form of fire, and in this they will seem to surpass the apostles, because they will do this openly as well. “And it deceived those who dwell upon earth because of the signs which were given to it to perform in the presence of the beast,” to Antichrist’s praise, because their signs were done by invocation of his name, “telling those who dwell upon earth to make an image of the beast,” namely, to make [Col. 1549A] themselves conformable to Antichrist by imitating his works, “which has the wound of the sword and lived.” Behold, again he sets forth the foundation of their preaching. “And it was given to it”—permitted by God for the testing of his own, for those who do not yield to it will be perfect—“to give an evil spirit to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might speak,” that is, so that in them it might have the effect of the Holy Spirit, namely, speak in diverse languages. “And the lesser beast will cause, through worldly rulers, all who have not worshiped the image of the beast,” the imitators of Antichrist, “to be killed” bodily. And it will cause, by preaching the goodness of its faith, all small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to have its mark on their right hand, namely a sign, because by their works they showed that they served it.

That is to say: these pseudo-apostles [Col. 1549B] will say that this their lord rejects no person of any condition; while others will say: “The one who came before, who was called Christ, had only the poor with him.” “Or upon their foreheads,” namely, they will openly confess him to be God. “And that no one may buy or sell,” literally, or in relation to the word of God. For one who preaches gives the price, namely the word of God, and receives a reward; and the people who receive the word either sell themselves. “Unless he has the mark of the beast,” that is, unless he says that he is conformed to it; “or its name,” that is, unless he is called an adherent of Antichrist, namely confessing that he is God; “or the number of its name.” Those receive the number of its name who expect recompense from him; the text indicates that this must be done according to the numerical value of the letters of the name.

“Here is wisdom.” This is a warning, because [Col. 1549C] there will be much deception in this matter. “Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the beast”: by calculating, he will understand also from the numerical value of the name that it is not a rewarder. “For it is the number of a human being, and its number is six hundred and sixty-six.” Although his followers will preach through this number that he is God, the wise person will perceive that this number is not God’s, but belongs to a mere human being. Because this book was written in Greek, the number concerning which he speaks here must be sought according to Greek numerals. For among the Greeks all letters signify a number. Its name is ANTEMON, which is fitting for it insofar as it is called Christ’s adversary, from the letters of that name. A is counted as one, N as fifty, T as three hundred, E as five, M as forty, O as seventy, S [Col. 1549D] as two hundred. There are many other names, but from each is gathered the same sum, namely six hundred and sixty-six.

Six, which is the first perfect number, signifies those less perfect persons who are married and keep the Lord’s commandments according to their capacity. Sixty, which is made from six and ten, signifies those moderately perfect. One hundred signifies the most perfect, who preserve integrity of mind and body. These yield fruit, some sixfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold; and Antichrist’s disciples will preach that no one can be saved unless he offers Antichrist some of these fruits.

## Chapter XIV

And I saw, and behold, the Lamb stood upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand having [Col. 1550A] his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the sound of many waters and like the sound of great thunder; and the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing upon their harps. And they sang as it were a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders; and no one could sing the song except those one hundred and forty-four thousand who were redeemed from the earth. These are those who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. These follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These were redeemed from among all as first fruits to God and to the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouth; they are without blemish before God’s throne.

Having shown the most savage persecution which the Church will suffer from Antichrist and his apostles, for its consolation [Col. 1550B] he sets forth Christ as helper and his household. And this is what is meant: “And I saw”—I remained in the vision—“and behold,” clearly, “the Lamb,” Christ who appeared sacrificed for us, “stood,” in order to help, “upon Mount Zion,” that is, upon the Church, lofty in the eminence of virtues and contemplating God; “and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand,” namely those gathered from the four parts of the world in faith in the Holy Trinity, “having his name,” because they are called Christians, “and the name of his Father,” either because they are called God’s or because they do not keep silent that he is God, “written upon their foreheads,” by open confession in word and deed.

“And I heard a voice,” desire or exhortation, “from heaven,” namely from those who were with him, “like the sound of many waters,” that is, of many peoples, because they had been gathered from many peoples; [Col. 1550C] “and like the sound of great thunder,” because it is a terror to all enemies. “And the voice which I heard was like that of harpists,” persons who have mortified the flesh, “playing on their harps,” namely afflicting their own flesh, so that by doing it in themselves they might fulfill what they preached to others. “And they sang as it were a new song,” namely, with great exultation they proclaimed the restoration completed through the Lamb; or they sang a new song, rejoicing in integrity of soul and body—an exultation which never grows old in them, but always flourishes and is new—“before the throne,” so as to please God who sits upon it, or before those in whom God judges; “and before the four living creatures,” that is, in the presence of holy preachers, so that their song might please them also; and before [Col. 1550D] the elders, the judges.

“And no one could sing the song,” render perfect exultation to God, “except those one hundred and forty-four thousand,” except those whole in soul and body, “who were redeemed from the earth” by the Lamb’s blood. Therefore, you who are of the earth, do not despair. Here blessed John’s authority is taken concerning the glory of the innocent. “These are those who have not been defiled with women,” literally, or by any worldly softness. “For they are virgins. These follow the Lamb,” that is, imitate Christ, “wherever he goes,” in body and in soul. “These were redeemed from among all as first fruits,” the better part, “to God and to the Lamb; and no lie was found in their mouth,” even if there had once been some; “without blemish,” namely without the stain of deed or word, even if there had once been some, “before the throne of God the judge,” so that they may please God himself.

[Col. 1551A] And I saw another angel flying through the midst of heaven, having the eternal Gospel, so that he might proclaim the Gospel to those who sit upon the earth, and over every nation and tribe and language and people, saying with a great voice: “Fear the Lord and give him honor, because the hour of his judgment has come. And worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and all things which are in them, and the springs of waters.”

Having described the attack made by the two beasts, and having set forth the help of the Lamb and shown the dignity of his household, he adds an exhortation that we should come to this household. And this is what is meant: “And I saw another angel,” that is, preachers, who are other than Christ, “flying,” withdrawing themselves from earthly things, “through the midst of heaven,” through the Church and also through the middle of the Church, so that they may be understood equally by all; or “through the midst,” through common things, namely catholic things, not making sects of their own; “having the eternal Gospel,” the good message, namely preaching which promises eternal things and rewards those who fulfill them accordingly, so that he might proclaim the Gospel—that is, having it for the purpose of proclaiming it—“to those sitting upon the earth,” that is, those abiding in contempt of the world; “and over every nation and tribe and language and people,” as if he said: so that he might proclaim the Gospel to every diversity of humankind; “saying with a great voice,” with powerful persuasive proclamation: “Fear the Lord,” with chaste fear, namely because of his own goodness; “and give him honor,” offer him every sort of veneration in work and word, glorifying him, “because the hour of his judgment has come.” Do not fail, because you will not suffer for a long time [Col. 1551C]; “and worship him, and ask from him what you cannot do by yourselves: he who made heaven and earth, and he himself can make you such, because he made all things from nothing, and the sea, and all things which are in them, and the springs of waters.”

And another angel followed, saying: “Fallen, fallen is that great city Babylon, which made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication.”

And another angel, because he announces something else, followed, saying: “Fallen, fallen.” He says “fallen” twice because he announces a twofold fall, of body and soul; or by the doubling we understand complete ruin. But he could not repeat it so many times: Babylon, a city of confusion fortified with evil vices, that great city because of pride, “which made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication.” Babylon indeed makes those living as Gentiles drink, by leading some from every nation away from the true path, of the wine of fornication—of many evils which are wine to them, namely a sweet and intoxicating drink. This fornication is the cause of God’s wrath, because divine vengeance follows it. Or it is called the wrath of God because God permitted them thus to commit fornication.

And the third angel followed them, saying with a great voice: “If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives its mark upon his forehead or upon his hand, he too will drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is mixed with unmixed wine in the cup of his wrath; and he will be tormented with fire and sulphur in the presence of the holy angels and before the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torments will ascend for ever and ever. They have no rest day or night, those who worshiped the beast and its image and [Col. 1552A] anyone who received the mark of its name. Here is the patience of the saints, who keep God’s commandments and the faith of Jesus.”

And the third angel makes another announcement, because this angel threatens and frightens us lest we follow the beast: “If anyone worships the beast,” Antichrist, “and its image,” so as to make himself conformable to its followers, “and receives its mark,” the sign of its faith, “upon his forehead,” so as openly to confess it, “or upon his hand,” so as to imitate it in deed, “he too will drink,” like Babylon, “of the wine of the wrath of God,” the punishment which God in anger gives to drink. By wine we signify punishment because it intoxicates; or it is called wine because it is rendered in contrast to the delight understood in wine: “which is mixed with unmixed wine in the cup of [Col. 1552B] his wrath.” One drinks of wine, not of correction but rather of damnation; and this is what he says, “mixed with unmixed wine,” namely with dregs, that is, eternal damnation. By the Lord’s cup we understand vengeance, because it is given by measure. In this cup is unmixed wine and dregs. The unmixed wine is corrective vengeance; the dregs are condemning vengeance. “And he will be tormented with fire and sulphur,” with stench, “in the presence of the holy angels,” so that they may be the more greatly ashamed; “and before the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torments will ascend for ever and ever,” that is, darkness. He mentions the condemnation of the wicked not in order to describe damnation, but so that by it he may deter us from conformity with them; and thus, if he says something anywhere about these matters, it should not be called superfluous, because it is said for another purpose. “And they have no rest day and [Col. 1552C] night.” Nor is it surprising if Antichrist and those who saw him in person are thus punished, because both his predecessors and his servants, who worship the beast and its image, will be subject to the same punishment; and anyone who receives the mark of its name. Here, namely in view of eternal punishment, is the patience of the saints, who keep God’s commandments by fulfilling the twofold love in deed, and the faith of Jesus; and who, even if they have no opportunity to act, at least confess God.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: “Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labors. For their works follow them.” And I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and upon the cloud one sitting like the Son [Col. 1552D] of Man, having upon his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle.

And I heard a voice from heaven. Again, an outstanding consolation; as though the faithful were to say: “The wicked will be condemned in this way; but what shall happen to us, who follow Christ?” Every blessedness. And this is what is meant: saying to me, “Write,” store it in firm memory and communicate it inwardly to others: “Blessed are the dead,” dead to the world, “who die in the Lord,” who are dissolved in true confession of the Lord: they are blessed. “From henceforth,” says the Spirit. And this, as though he said: these are not my words, but the Spirit says this, “that from henceforth,” from the time of the resurrection, “they may rest from their labors,” which they have suffered until now. “For their works follow them,” that is, the reward of their works follows them. While they were in the world, their works seemed lost because [Col. 1553A] they were always afflicted, but now they will find them flourishing.

After the promise and fulfillment of blessedness, for the greater strengthening of his own, he also sees the condemnation of the wicked, for the strongest discouragement. “And I saw, and behold, a white cloud”: either the flesh in which the Lord was hidden, or the saints who overshadow him, or a literal cloud; “and upon the cloud one sitting,” namely Christ, “like the Son of Man,” because he is now impassible and immortal, having, in the manner of a conqueror, “upon his head,” according to his own person or according to his divinity, “a crown,” victory over the devil, “golden,” because of wisdom, “and in his hand,” in his power, “a sharp sickle,” the judgment by which the good are separated from the evil.

And another angel came out from the temple, crying with a [Col. 1553B] great voice to him who sat upon the cloud: “Send forth your sickle and reap, because the hour has come to reap, since the harvest of the earth has dried up.” And he who sat upon the cloud sent his sickle upon the earth, and reaped the earth.

And another angel came out, appeared openly, from the temple, having previously lain hidden among the wicked, crying with a great voice, showing by great longing that he desired the separation of the wicked from the good, so that their company might be made complete, to him who sat upon the cloud, Christ: “Send forth your sickle,” exercise judgment, “and reap,” gather your own, “because the hour has come to reap,” it is the fitting time because the number of your own is now complete, “since the harvest of the earth has dried up,” because the wickedness of the evil has reached completion. And he who sat upon the cloud sent his sickle upon the earth, that is, he exercised judgment as was his [Col. 1553C] due, and reaped the earth: he separated the good from the evil.

And another angel came out from the temple which is in heaven, himself also having a sharp sickle.

Having shown God’s power to judge, he likewise shows that the saints will judge by the Lord’s command, through which great consolation is given to the saints, so that they may persevere in faith and in good works. And another angel, saints having another office, came out—his character became visible—from the temple, from the hidden place which is in heaven, himself also having, like Christ, a sharp sickle.

And another angel came forth from the altar, who had power over the fire; and he cried with a loud voice to him who had the sharp sickle, saying: “Send forth your sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe.” [Col. 1553D] And the angel sent his sickle into the earth and gathered the vine of the earth. And he cast it into the great winepress of the wrath of God; and the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood came forth from the winepress up to the horses’ bridles for one thousand six hundred stadia.

And another angel, namely Christ, came forth from the altar: he appeared plainly, coming from the altar—that is, from the more secret place—being then recognized by all as consubstantial with God. He had power, being well able to preach and to inflict punishment over the fire, that is, over eternal punishment. And he cried with a loud voice, with great authority, to him who had the sharp sickle, saying: “Send forth your sickle and gather the clusters: separate those ripe in wickedness, the clusters of the vine of the earth.” A grape is called *grapa*; the grains of grapes are clusters. “For its grapes are ripe,” because their wickedness [Col. 1554A] is complete. By the harvest of the earth—that is, by the grapes of the vine of the earth—is meant the condemnation of the wicked; but it is signified in different ways, because by the vine we understand those who work evil with greater zeal, just as greater care is bestowed upon a vine in order that it may bear fruit. And, at such a command, the angel sent forth his sickle and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great winepress of God’s wrath, that is, into hell, where many will suffer God’s wrath. And the winepress was trodden—that is, they were punished, being placed in hell—outside the city, because that punishment will not be purgatorial. And blood came forth from the winepress, namely eternal punishment for sin, not wine to be placed in God’s storehouse, up to the horses’ bridles—that is, up to their rulers who are to be punished, namely the devils—for one thousand six hundred stadia. A stadium is said to be the distance Hercules ran [Col. 1554B] in one breath; and the Greeks measured by the stadium the open places in which they played. By this it signifies all those to be condemned who are devoted to games and to the riches of this age; or the less perfect, by the six; the more perfect, by the hundred; or the most perfect, by the thousand.

## Chapter XV

## Fifth Vision

And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wonderful: seven angels having the seven last plagues, because in them the wrath of God is consummated. And I saw something like a sea of glass mingled with fire, and those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing upon the sea of glass, having harps of God and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song [Col. 1554C] of the Lamb, saying: “Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the ages. Who will not fear you, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy; because all nations shall come and worship before you, because your judgments have been made manifest.”

In the visions set forth above, he has pursued the condition of the Church from the order of its restoration up to the judgment. In the three which follow he dwells upon the last times, because little and obscurely had been said of these matters in the other Scriptures. The subject of this fifth vision is the seven angels having seven bowls, from the pouring out of which come seven plagues—that is, destructions of the wicked who will exist in the time of Antichrist. This destruction [Col. 1554D] especially exhorts those now living to endurance. “And I saw another sign,” namely a certain figure signifying something else, “in heaven,” because those signified were heavenly; “great,” because great events follow from it; and “wonderful,” because it is remarkable that one human being can condemn others: “seven angels,” all preachers, “having” plagues imposed by God upon them to pour out upon the wicked, “the seven last plagues,” that is, the complete blinding of the wicked in the time of Antichrist, “because in them the wrath of God is consummated.” They will truly have plagues, because God will exercise his wrath upon the wicked through them; and they are truly last, because God will inflict no others upon the wicked. “And I saw something like a sea of glass,” that is, baptism, because there purity of faith is required, “mingled with fire,” because there the gifts of the Holy Spirit are possessed; “and those” [Col. 1555A] “who had conquered the beast,” Antichrist, avoiding conformity to him, “and its image,” and “the number of its name”: they were not deceived by the number; “standing upon the sea of glass,” resting upon the baptism which they received; “having harps of God,” mortifying the flesh. It says “of God” because God first did this, or because he ordained that it should be done thus; “and singing,” joyfully fulfilling, “the song of Moses, the servant of God,” the Old Testament, which is understood to be one and the same with the New, “and the song of the Lamb,” the New Testament, “saying,” while admonishing others: “Great,” in the first creation, “and wonderful,” in the re-creation, “are your works, Lord God almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the ages.” The ways are God’s ordinances through which he comes to us and we go to him. They are true, and deservedly just, because they render [Col. 1555B] to each according to merit. They are true because they lead where they promise. “Who will not fear you, O Lord?” And from this, who will not serve you in love, and also glorify your name by work and preaching, because you alone are merciful and truly to be feared, since you justify freely? “For all nations shall come,” and they will truly glorify you, because some from every nation will come to you by receiving faith; “and worship,” in spirit and truth, “before you,” in what pleases you, “because your judgments have been made manifest.” Having shown the dignity and power of those who must inflict the plagues, he wishes to show why the wicked seem deserving to endure plagues. First he shows that, although the mysteries of the Church are revealed to them, [Col. 1555C] they, blinded by their evil merits, cannot enter.

And after these things I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened. And the seven angels came out of the temple, having the seven plagues, clothed in clean, white stone, and girded around their breasts with golden belts. And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls, full of the wrath of God who lives for ages of ages. And the temple was filled with smoke from the majesty of God and from his power. And no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels should be completed.

And after these things he saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony was opened: that is, the mysteries of the Church were openly revealed. It is a tabernacle because God [Col. 1555D] dwells in it and serves as a soldier in it for a time; it is testimony in heaven because it contains within itself the New and Old Testaments. And they came out; and because these things were so open, the angels—the preachers—came out: that is, they openly rebuke those who work evil, “having the seven plagues from the temple,” the members who are the Church having been confirmed, “clothed in stone,” that is, in steadfastness, “clean” from vices, “white” because of virtues, “and girded about their breasts,” that is, restraining even their thoughts, “with golden belts,” with the belt of charity. “And one”—all are one, one because all preach the same thing—“of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls, full of the wrath of God who lives for ages of ages”: that is, he made them capacious vessels for God through wisdom and charity, full of God’s wrath for the destruction of the ungodly. “And the temple was filled” [Col. 1556A] with smoke: although the mysteries of the Church were open to the good, they were nevertheless obscure to the wicked, through smoke, that is, obscurity, from God’s majesty, from his presence, and from his power; because “what he shuts, no one opens” (Rev. 3). And no one among the reprobate could enter the temple—that is, enter the Church, namely become part of the Church—until the seven plagues of the seven angels should be completed, until every kind of condemnation is complete. He does not determine this in such a way as to mean that they will then be received; rather, it is certain that they will not enter afterward.

## Chapter XVI

And I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels: “Go, and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God upon the earth.” And the first angel went and poured out his bowl upon the earth. And a fierce and most grievous sore came upon the people who had the mark of the beast [Col. 1556B] and worshipped its image.

“And I heard,” that is, I understood, “a voice,” divine inspiration or some admonition, “from heaven, saying to the seven angels: ‘Go,’” proceed in obedience; now is the time for the condemnation of the wicked; “‘pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God upon the earth,’” upon those devoted to earthly things. Since these angels already preach and the mysteries they preach are open, yet some refuse to enter, the angels have a fitting reason to strike them; and they are admonished to do so by the divine voice. “And the first angel went and poured out his bowl upon the earth; and a fierce sore came about,” a harmful condemnation, “and most grievous,” incurable, “upon all who had the mark of the beast and worshipped its image.” It seems that the same thing was said under the sixth angel, yet it is different. For there it was shown what evils the saints would suffer in the time of Antichrist; and whatever was introduced concerning the condemnation of the wicked was for the consolation of the righteous. Here, however, the condemnation of the ungodly is shown particularly. Thus, if the same words are put here that were put there, they are not superfluous, because they are introduced for different purposes. Likewise, it seems that under the sixth angel the same thing was said as when the trumpet sounded; but there he chiefly shows the persecution which the wicked will inflict upon the saints. If anything was said beyond this concerning the condemnation of the ungodly, it was incidental. Therefore, if some of the same things are said here, where the condemnation of the wicked alone is considered, it is not superfluous. There is also another difference: there was no distinction among the condemned, whereas here the individual angels inflict plagues upon different classes [Col. 1556D] of the wicked.

And the second angel poured out his bowl upon the sea, and it became blood like that of a dead man; and every living soul died in the sea.

And the second angel, in his office, poured out his bowl upon the sea, upon those who crush the saints; and blood came about, namely condemnation for the blood which they shed, “like that of a dead man,” because they will not escape that condemnation. When a living man sheds blood, he himself cannot escape it. And every living soul died in the sea: that is, everyone consenting with them will be condemned—those who seem to live because they do not persecute openly.

And the third angel poured out his bowl upon the rivers and upon the springs of waters, and they became blood. [Col. 1557A] And I heard the angel of the waters saying: “You are just, O Lord, who are and who were, the Holy One, who have judged these things; because they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink: for they are worthy.” And I heard another angel saying: “Yes, Lord God almighty, true and just are your judgments.”

And the third angel poured out his bowl upon the rivers, upon perverse teachers, both greater and lesser—and this is what he says by “upon the springs of waters”—and they became blood, because these too shed blood, either spiritually or bodily. “And I heard the angel of the waters saying”: that is, I understood that the preachers themselves ascribe this vengeance not to themselves but to the Lord, and affirm that it is done justly. By waters we understand good teachings: “You are just, O Lord, who are and [Col. 1557B] who were.” He does not add “who are to come,” because from the imminence of his coming he sees him as already coming. “Who have judged these things,” namely, who have assigned such condemnation to the wicked. “Because they have shed the blood of saints,” the lesser persons, “and prophets,” the greater persons, “and you have given them blood to drink,” namely eternal punishment. He says “to drink” because, in exchange for the delight they had in the saints’ torments, they will receive these things. “For they are worthy.” You are just in judging, because they were worthy. And because testimony is to be accepted when several confirm it, he introduces others confirming the testimony of the former. “And I heard another angel,” the disciples of the former, “saying: ‘Yes, Lord God almighty,’” that is, whatever you have said concerning him is true; he gives testimony from himself: “True and just are your judgments,” [Col. 1557C] because they fulfill what they promise, namely they assign to each one his deserts, so that if anyone has shed blood, he may drink in return the punishment of blood.

And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun; and it was given to him to afflict people with heat and fire. And people were scorched with great heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has power over these plagues; and they did not repent so as to give him glory.

And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, upon Antichrist, who calls himself the light of the world. And it was given—that is, permitted by God—to him, Antichrist, to afflict people with heat, a lesser tribulation, and with fire, a greater tribulation. And people were scorched with great heat, failing because of tribulations; and they blasphemed the name of God. Thus those who confess [Col. 1557D] Antichrist to be God blaspheme, as do they in other ways, the God who has power over these plagues. Although they blaspheme, he nevertheless has power, because he gives to whom he wills and takes away from whom he wills. “And they did not repent”: they did not come to their senses, so as to give him glory; even if they grieved inwardly as compelled persons, yet they did not openly proclaim God by word or deed.

And the fifth angel poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast. And his kingdom became darkened, and they gnawed their tongues for pain; and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores, and they did not repent of their works.

And the fifth angel poured out his bowl upon [Col. 1558A] the throne of the beast, that is, upon the familiar associates of Antichrist. And his kingdom—that is, those who most gloried in their intimacy with him—became darkened, or rather blinded. “And they gnawed their tongues,” that is, they will refresh themselves with their evil works, or some with the words of others. The phrase is spoken by comparison with a dying person who, because of excessive pain and inward sickness, eats his own tongue; “for pain,” because of envy and the other vices which they nourished within. “And they blasphemed God,” saying that he was great, because of their pains, on account of the plagues inflicted, or on account of inward vices, and because of their sores, which they themselves made for themselves by gnawing their tongues. “And they did not repent of their works.”

And the sixth angel poured out his bowl into [Col. 1558B] that great river Euphrates, and its water dried up, in order that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. And I saw three unclean spirits come forth like frogs from the mouth of the dragon, from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet. For they are spirits of demons working signs; and they go out to gather the kings of the whole earth for battle on the great day of God almighty. “Behold, I come like a thief. Blessed is he who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame.” And he shall gather them into the place called in Hebrew Hermagedon.
