And the sixth angel poured out his bowl into the river, into the world, that great Euphrates; and he dried up its water, because he will preach that the world and all its abundance, or substance, [Col. 1558C] is to be burned, in order that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. For, when the world is ended, there will be a resurrection of faithful dead persons, who will come from the rising of the sun—that is, from Christ, who will then begin to shine, that is, to make himself manifest to all. Another translation has: “for King Christ.” “And I saw [spirits] from the mouth of the dragon,” from the devil’s inspiration; “and from the mouth of the beast,” from the words of Antichrist; “and from the mouth of the false prophet,” from the word of Antichrist’s apostles. He sets three down for the generation of the unclean spirits, in order to indicate that the persuasion of each of them suffices for the ruin of wretches: “three unclean spirits came forth,” namely demons, whom these aforesaid persons generate. They are called unclean because they persuade people to uncleanness. “Like frogs”: for just as frogs live in mud and, being noisy, deprive others of quiet, so these too are truly unclean. [Col. 1558D] “For they are spirits of demons working signs,” miracles; “and they go out to gather the kings of the whole earth,” to bring them into one will, “for battle,” against the faithful, “on the great day of God almighty,” but to their own harm, because they will soon be led to the day of judgment. I mean the God who says: “Behold, I come.” Or thus: he will truly come, because he himself testifies: “like a thief.” He calls himself a thief because he will kill the negligent and sleeping, and despoil them of all good things. Therefore, “Blessed is he who watches,” who diligently concerns himself with the salvation of his soul, “and keeps his garments,” innocence and immortality, which he received in baptism, lest he walk—or rise again—naked, stripped of virtues, and the saints see his shame, namely his sins. For the sins of every individual will be revealed as though [Col. 1559A] they themselves were before them in the very acts. “And he shall gather them.” Above it said that they go out to gather; and behold, it now gives the result, because they will accomplish what they seek. This is it: “He shall gather them into the place,” according to his own will, “which is called in Hebrew Hermagedon.” Hermagedon is interpreted “mountain of thieves,” by which Antichrist is signified: he is the head of all who wish to steal faith from the saints, and the utterly wicked take refuge with him; and thus all who adhere to him are gathered in him.

And the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came forth from the temple, from the throne, saying: “It is done.” And there were flashes of lightning, voices, and thunders; and there was a great earthquake, such as had never been since human beings were upon the earth—such [Col. 1559B] an earthquake, so great. And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. And great Babylon came into remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath. And every island fled, and mountains were not found. And great hail, like a talent, descended from heaven upon people; and they blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, because it became exceedingly great.

And the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, that is, upon the aerial powers, namely the devil, to whom that place has been assigned. For if they had the earth as their place, we could not endure their corruptions. And a loud voice came forth—that is, one plainly announcing great things—from the temple, from the Church, from the throne, saying: but [Col. 1559C] the Church receives these things from God: “It is done,” that is, all things are consummated and the end is at hand. And there came, from these same seven angels, lightning, miracles, voices, admonitions, thunders, threats, and a great earthquake, because the earthly will be stirred against the good—such as had never been since human beings were upon the earth, such an earthquake so great, from the time of Abel. Having shown upon whom the angel pours out his bowls, according to the division of those condemned, he adds what finally comes about from that pouring out: namely that, although the condemned resist, as though they had gained strength from the very pouring out, nevertheless they are submerged in hell. “And the great city was divided into three parts”: Babylon was condemned because of the three condemnations mentioned above. He says “into three parts” [Col. 1559D] because of the Jews, the Gentiles, and false Christians. Here Babylon means the greater persons; and the other “cities of the nations fell,” the other assemblies of those living in Gentile fashion. In this condemnation I understand that they are punished for individual sins. This is it: “And great Babylon came into remembrance before God,” namely God remembered each sin, which he had previously seemed to disregard when he did not punish, “to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath,” God’s. It came to this, that God should give them the cup—that is, punishment measured out—of wine, in opposition to the delights they had enjoyed. I mean punishment proceeding from an angry and indignant God. Indignation is spoken of when a punishment both more severe and enduring is inflicted. “And every island fled, and mountains were not found,” and so forth. There was not found [Col. 1560A] any of the saints among them. By mountains we understand those more eminent in virtues, such as the apostles; by islands, those who have suffered the buffeting of the world. Or let us say literally that then neither mountain nor island will exist, for the world will be burned. “And great hail,” namely eternal punishment which will crush, weighty and apportioned by measure, “like a talent.” A great talent is one hundred and twenty pounds; a medium one, seventy-two; a lesser, fifty. He speaks here of the medium talent, because sinners from the seventy-two languages will not escape this vengeance. “It descended from heaven upon people, and they blasphemed God because of the plague of hail.” For, placed in hell and knowing that they are justly punished, they will nevertheless grieve over the Lord’s power and hold him in the highest hatred, because [Col. 1560B] it became exceedingly great.

## Chapter XVII

And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: “Come; I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot, who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication, and those who inhabit the earth became drunk with the wine of her prostitution.” And he carried me away in spirit into a wilderness.

And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: just as John here bears the person of the speaker in relation to the angel, so we ought to bear it in relation to John. After he has shown the plagues which the angels will inflict in the time [Col. 1560C] of Antichrist, and the condemnation which the ungodly will suffer from them, he is admonished to show the causes of that condemnation. Thus he warns us what we must now avoid, because the same devil who will then capture openly deceives daily in secret and hurls people toward the same end. “Come,” advance in understanding; “I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot,” the cause of the condemnation of those who, having abandoned God, have fornicated with the demon. This harlot is called Babylon because she both entices and deceives, as Antichrist and others do in their own time. “Who sits upon many waters,” that is, rules over many peoples, whom she draws to herself through lust. Thus the Lord says to Job: “His strength,” that is, the devil’s, “is in his loins, and his force in the navel of his belly” (Job 40). For he deceives men, whose seed-bed [Col. 1560D] is in the loins; and he deceives women in the navel, whose seed is in the navel. Therefore the prophet says to Jerusalem as to a harlot: “At the time of your birth,” that is, at this very time, “your navel was not cut” (Ezek. 16), that is, you did not restrain lust. “With whom the kings of the earth committed fornication,” namely the powerful; “and those who inhabit the earth became drunk,” because, like a drunken man, they will for a time be blinded so as neither to love nor fear God—those who inhabit the earth, that is, who are intent upon earthly glory—“with the wine of her prostitution,” namely with the delight of open fornication. “He carried me away in spirit into a wilderness,” namely in order that I might see the reprobate, who are deserted by God.

And I saw a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast, full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads [Col. 1561A] and ten horns. And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand, full of abominations and the uncleanness of her fornication; and on her forehead was written: “Mystery: Babylon the great, mother of fornications and abominations of the earth.”

“And I saw a woman,” namely Babylon, because such people are effeminate and deceived like Eve, “sitting upon a beast.” They have the devil as their foundation, through whom they act; “scarlet,” that is, bloody, because he has shed the blood of the saints, or makes people understand God’s words wrongly; “full of names of blasphemy,” because they say that the evils they do displease God not. “Having seven heads”: the five senses, by consenting through which we are deceived, and by which alone childish life is governed; the sixth head, error, as in those who can use reason; the seventh head, Antichrist. By these seven the devil leads people into sin. “And ten horns,” ten kingdoms which will exist in the time of Antichrist, through which other things are understood. Such was the beast. “And the woman was clothed in purple,” namely in royal apparel, whereby her power is signified; “and scarlet,” because they kill those unwilling to consent to them; “adorned with gold,” because they will seem illuminated by divine wisdom, or even worldly wisdom, which is the most precious thing among worldly things; “and precious stone”: by the precious stone he understands the charity which they pretend to possess, just as the carbuncle is the most precious among stones; “and pearls”: by pearls he understands the other virtues [Col. 1561C] which they pretend to possess. “Having a golden cup in her hand,” that is, the divine Scriptures, from which the faithful drink unto salvation, which they hold in their hand in perverse interpretations, or because they pretend to act well; “full of abominations and the uncleanness of her fornication,” because according to their interpretations they teach many uncleannesses and fornication with the demon, by which they are separated from the good, because their end is evil. “And on her forehead was written: ‘Mystery,’” that is, they have openly a sign which is a mystery to the unlearned but open knowledge to the wise. It is also a certain consolation to the faithful, lest they be deceived by her, in whom they plainly see such things: “‘Babylon the great,’” confusion, “‘mother of fornications,’” setting themselves forth as an example of sinning, by whom the earthly are driven away from the salvation of the faithful, “‘and abominations of the earth.’”

And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of Jesus’ martyrs. And when I saw her, I wondered with great amazement. And the angel said to me: “Why do you wonder? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast which bears her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The beast which you saw was, and is not, and will ascend from the abyss, and will go into destruction; and those who inhabit the earth—whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world—will wonder, seeing the beast which was and is not.”

“And I saw.” Having stated the cause of condemnation, he also states the condemnation itself, as though he said: I saw her sinning; I also saw her condemned for sin. This is it: “I saw the woman [Col. 1562A] drunk with the blood of the saints.” He calls her drunk because vengeance is taken for the shedding of blood, so that through excessive pains she no longer knows where she is; “and with the blood,” and so forth, “of the greater persons,” namely those who do not fear to testify that Christ is God. “And when I saw her,” and so forth. Here he bears the person of those who, seeing the wicked exalted in the world, wonder when they hear what punishments are promised to them, and ask why God allows them to be exalted when they are to be punished thus. But they are taught to understand that this exaltation is given for greater blindness. And the angel said to me: “Why do you wonder? Do not wonder, but understand what it is. I will tell you the mystery,” and so forth: that is, why the wicked are punished, and the devil who makes them sin—a matter not plain except to the learned. “Which has seven heads and ten horns.” “The beast,” and so forth, means the devil, who makes people beastlike. “It was”: it reigned before Christ’s coming. “And is not”: when Christ was born, its power perished. “And will ascend,” and so forth, because in the time of Antichrist it will receive power and have a place among the wicked, “from the abyss,” from the depths of vices; “and will go into destruction,” because, when Antichrist is dead, it will no longer have a place. “And those who inhabit the earth will wonder”: the wicked will grieve when they see their power, which was so great, thus annihilated—those “whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world,” who are not foreknown unto salvation in God’s eternal foreknowledge—seeing the beast which was and is not, which had power before Christ’s time, whose power Christ’s death destroyed.

[Col. 1562C] “And here is the meaning which has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. Five have fallen; one is; and another has not yet come. And when he comes, he must remain a short time. And the beast which was and is not is itself an eighth, and is of the seven, and goes into destruction. And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom; but they will receive authority as kings for one hour, after the beast. These have one purpose, and will give their strength and authority to the beast. These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings; and those with him are called, chosen, and faithful.”

[Col. 1562D] “And here is the meaning,” namely that the wise person’s faculty of understanding must be exercised in considering eternal punishment, in order to show that power ought to be despised, since eternal punishment and condemnation arise from it. “Which has wisdom.” “The seven heads are seven mountains,” and so forth, because by these seven the devil raises people into pride; “and they are seven kings.” These are the same as the mountains, and are called kings because of secular power. “Five have fallen”: the assent of the five senses has passed away with childhood; “and one,” error, remains with us even in mature age; “and another has not yet come,” Antichrist, who will compel people most forcefully to sin. If Adam had remained in obedience, he would not have used the bodily senses for any pleasure more in one respect than in all the rest. But through his sin the senses have been so corrupted that it is now [Col. 1563A] natural to seek things pleasant to the touch, savory things, things that sound sweet, and things beautiful to sight. These are the five kings through whom the devil rules people in childhood, because he himself was the cause of their corruption. These are the five husbands of the Samaritan woman, of whom John speaks. In youth, error deceives or succeeds them. For once a person has discernment, if he sins, it is no longer attributed to the senses but to error; concerning which the Lord says: “And now he whom you have is not your husband” (John 4). We also have these five kings in the five kings whom Abraham conquered, spoken of in Genesis 14. “And when he comes, he must,” and so forth: this is a certain consolation, as though he said, “Do not be dismayed.” “And the beast which was and is not is itself,” and so forth, “of the seven,” because the devil sins in the same way and will likewise be punished. “It is an eighth,” because it will surpass all in [Col. 1563B] wickedness and punishment. “And it goes into destruction.” “And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings,” in the time of Antichrist, as Daniel says (ch. 7): there will be ten kingdoms principally adhering to Antichrist. Their kings are signified by the horns because of their pride and aggression. They “have not yet received a kingdom”; although they have not yet received a kingdom, indications of them nevertheless precede in many people. “But they will receive authority as kings,” because they are not truly kings but tyrants, “for one hour.” And because the time is short, resist; never yield to him. “After the beast,” not later in time, but as its followers and inferiors. “These have one purpose,” namely denying Christ and consenting in every evil; “and will give their strength,” which they possess from their own powers, “and their authority,” because it comes from subjects, “to the beast,” [Col. 1563C] because they attribute all things to Antichrist. “These will fight with the Lamb,” by word and deed, in order to seduce his faithful; “and the Lamb will overcome them,” by granting steadfastness to his own and finally blinding the others. For he is “Lord of lords,” using even the wicked for the benefit and purification of his own, and “King of kings,” and therefore he will also overcome the kings of the earth, because he has a precious household. This is: “and those with him,” called through preachers, chosen from eternity, and faithful in keeping the faith and carrying out works.

And he said to me: “The waters which you saw, where the harlot sits, are peoples, nations, and tongues. And the ten horns which you saw upon the beast: these will hate the harlot and make her desolate and naked, and they will devour her flesh and burn her with fire. For God gave it into their hearts to do what pleased him, to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are consummated. And the woman whom you saw is the great city which has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

And he said to me: “The waters,” and so forth, are Babylon, or Antichrist, who already reigns by mystery: peoples, that is, those flowing about in vices, nations gathered from every race of humankind, and tongues. “And the ten horns,” and so forth: therefore do not conform yourselves to her, because those who now adhere to her will finally grieve and hate the beast, grieving and knowing that they were deceived by her. “And they will make her desolate,” because the consolation which they now provide her will finally cease; “and naked,” because her dominion, which had grown through them, will no longer [Col. 1564A] have a place. “And they will devour her flesh,” that is, they will suffer torments in return for the delights which they enjoyed from her. “And they will burn her with fire,” because they themselves will be the cause why the devil is punished, since they were deceived through him. “For God”—as though one were to say, “If they know such an end, why do they follow him?”—has blinded them because of their evil merits. This is it: “For God gave it into their hearts,” and so forth, that they should do what pleased him, namely the devil; “to give their kingdom to the beast”: they do what pleases that beast, because they allow themselves to be the devil’s kingdom, “until the words [of God] are consummated,” namely until the things promised concerning the reward of the wicked and the good are fulfilled, until the good are separated from the wicked. “And the woman whom you saw,” and so forth, means a great multitude of powerful persons fortified in every perverse obstinacy, which has [Col. 1564B] dominion, and so forth, because it dominates and compels through great pride.

## Chapter XVIII

## Sixth Vision

And after these things I saw another angel descending from heaven, having great authority; and the earth was illuminated by his glory. And he cried out with a strong voice, saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and it has become a dwelling-place of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean bird; because all nations have drunk of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth have become rich through the abundance of her luxuries.”

[Col. 1564C] In this sixth vision the final punishments that the ungodly will suffer in hell for their individual sins are treated; and first he shows this concerning Babylon, and in her he shows different ranks; afterwards concerning Antichrist and the false prophets, and then concerning the devil himself. The vision is plainly distinguished from those passages in which the condemnation of the wicked is shown, since here not condemnation but the punishments which follow condemnation are shown. Therefore, if anything concerning the condemnation of the wicked is displayed, it is not superfluous, because it is introduced for another purpose. Since he is about to execute these punishments, he shows Christ as powerful to do this, and also Christ himself announcing it, so that faith may be greater.

“And after these things I saw another angel,” Christ, “coming down from heaven,” humbling himself from the knowledge of angels to the knowledge of human beings, [Col. 1564D] or from equality with the Father to the assumption of flesh, “having great authority,” both according to divinity and according to humanity. Hence it is said (Matt. 28): “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” What one so powerful says, he can accomplish. “And the earth was illuminated,” that is, the Church, with the shadows of ignorance driven away, “by his glory,” by glorious preaching; “and he cried,” announced, “with a loud voice,” because he brought to effect what he said, saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon.” The repetition marks a twofold fall, namely of body and soul, or an endless fall; “great,” because it embraces many. He first states the cause of its ruin: “and it has become,” etc. A demon is an assemblage of demons. “And a prison of every,” etc., because by obeying the devil in depraved actions it keeps him within itself; “of every unclean bird,” etc. Here [Col. 1565A] the devil is compared to a bird, because he causes a person to exalt himself and take pride in his uncleanness. “For all nations have drunk of the wrath of her fornication,” that is, of the fornication for which God is angry; “and the kings of the earth,” namely the powerful of this age; “and the merchants of the earth,” etc., literally, or all are called merchants who sell their souls for worldly things. “From the power of her luxuries,” from the effect of sinful delights. Hence it is said: “Every rich man is either wicked or heir to a wicked man”; they have become rich.

“And I heard another voice from heaven saying: Come out of her, my people, lest you share in her sins and receive of her plagues; for her sins have reached unto heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities. Render to her as she [Col. 1565B] rendered to you, and repay her double according to her works; in the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment and mourning give her; for she says in her heart: I sit as a queen, and am not a widow, and I shall not see mourning. Therefore in one day her plagues shall come: death, mourning, and famine; and she shall be burned with fire, for mighty is God who has judged her. And the kings of the earth, who committed fornication with her and lived in luxury, shall weep and mourn over her when they see the smoke of her burning; standing afar off for fear of her torments, saying: Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that mighty city, for in one hour your judgment has come.”

“And I heard.” He sets forth an admonition: if we now [Col. 1565C] come out from them, we shall not finally be condemned with them. “Another voice,” Christ’s inspiration or preaching, “from heaven, saying: Come out,” etc.: do not perform their works; “and do not share,” etc., nor give assent. Those give assent who praise and flatter, and one who ought to correct but does not. “And receive not of her plagues”: then you will not be participants in her punishments. She will receive these plagues because “her sins have reached,” etc., that is, to contempt of God through impenitence.

Sins are then said to reach heaven when they attain that sinfulness in sinning beyond which they would never pass by sinning: namely, contempt of God. Hence the same eternal punishment is repaid to one who sinned for three years [Col. 1565D] and to one who sinned for a hundred years, because each reached that point beyond which he would never pass by sinning. “And the Lord has remembered,” etc., even lesser sins, which he seemed to have forgotten while he allowed them to prosper.

“Render to her.” He also exhorts the saints to exercise divine vengeance upon them: “as she rendered to you,” namely, as they inflicted punishments upon you, although purgatorial ones, so render punishments to them—but eternal ones. “And repay double,” that is, to soul and body; render double punishments, twice as grievous as those which they inflicted upon you, “according to her works”: not equal punishments for all, but to each according to merits. “In the cup in which,” etc.: namely, as they inflicted torments upon you, so do you upon them. Sometimes it is repaid also in the same kind.

“As much as she glorified herself and,” etc. They will be punished not only for what they did to others, [Col. 1566A] but also for the glory and pleasure which they enjoyed among themselves; or, to show how much is to be repaid to each, namely according as each sinned—some more, some less. Torment pertains to the body; mourning, to the soul. “For she says in her heart.” He shows how she glorified herself. “I sit,” as though secure; “a queen,” in rank and power; “and am not a widow”: I do not lack servants; or, because she has consolation in temporal things. “And I shall not see mourning”: she does not fear the loss of her power. “Therefore in one day,” at the hour of judgment, “her plagues shall come.” He previously set forth the causes of condemnation; now he sets forth the causes themselves and the punishments: “Death,” separation from true life; “and mourning,” contrary to the joys which she had here; “and famine,” from true refreshment. “For mighty is the Lord,” whom no one can resist, [Col. 1566B] or who is at last unyielding to every entreaty.

He spoke generally concerning Babylon’s condemnation; now he distinguishes it by the various ranks of the condemned. “And they shall weep,” they shall grieve in mind, “and mourn over her,” etc.: they will display the grief of their hearts, because they will grieve both over the suffering they endure and over their own misery and the condemnation of their subjects. “The kings of the earth”—even good kings, or those who at one time committed fornication with her—will grieve that they were ever like her, “when they see the smoke of her burning,” when they see the signs of her punishment. “Standing afar off,” in will. What follows is plain.

“And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her, because no one shall buy their merchandise any more: merchandise of gold and silver and precious stone and pearl and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet, and every [Col. 1566C] citron-wood, and every vessel of ivory, and every vessel of precious stone and bronze and iron and marble, and cinnamon and amomum and spices and ointment and incense and wine and oil and fine flour and wheat and cattle and sheep and horses and carriages and slaves and human souls. And the fruits desired by your soul have departed from you; and all rich and splendid things have perished from you, and they shall no longer find them. The merchants of these things, who grew rich from her, shall stand afar off for fear of her torments, weeping and mourning, and saying: Woe, woe, that great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious stone and pearls, for in one hour such great riches have been laid waste. [Col. 1566D] And every helmsman, and all who sail upon the lake, and sailors, and those who work upon the sea, stood afar off; and seeing the place of her burning they cried out, saying: What city is like this great city? And they cast dust upon their heads and cried out, weeping and mourning, and saying: Woe, woe, that great city, by whose prices all who had ships upon the sea became rich, for in one hour she has been made desolate.”

Another rank of the condemned consists of those who are in Babylon. “And the merchants of the earth,” literally, or all who sell their souls for earthly things, “shall weep over her and mourn,” that is, they shall have continual sorrow, because they will grieve that the things in which they hoped to attain happiness have perished, “because no one shall buy their merchandise any more.” Namely these: “merchandise of gold,” etc. “And silk,” made among the Seres; “and every citron-wood”: no one will buy it; “and bronzes,” such as basins; “and spices,” namely merchandise; “and human souls.” Only the body is sold, as when a Christian is sold to a Christian; but then it is as though the soul were sold, as when, among pagans, he cannot save his soul.

“And the fruits desired by your soul have departed from you.” Here Babylon indicates that human beings are condemned even for the smallest things if they take delight in these small things, etc. “And every helmsman,” such as heads of households; “and everyone who sails upon the lake,” such as those who set before themselves some fixed object—for example, marks of gold or something of that kind; “and sailors,” such as the servants of helmsmen; “and those who work upon the sea”—to include all Babylonians, he says, “those who [Col. 1567A] work upon the sea,” that is, those who hope and delight in the world—“stood afar off,” in will, lest they be burned, “and cried out, saying: What city is like this city?” in misery. “And they cast dust upon their heads,” which is a sign of repentance, although late; or “dust,” that is, they set the desire for earthly things above their head, that is, above the soul. “By her prices,” literally, or by her sins.

“Rejoice over her, O heaven, and holy apostles and prophets, because God has judged your judgment upon her. And one mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: With this violence shall that great city Babylon be cast down, and shall no longer be found. And the sound of harpists and musicians and flute-players and trumpeters shall no longer be heard in you. [Col. 1567C] And no craftsman of any craft shall any longer be found in you, and the sound of a mill shall no longer be heard in you, and the light of a lamp shall no longer shine in you. And the voice of bridegroom and bride shall no longer be heard in you, because your merchants were princes of the earth; because by your sorceries all nations perished, and in her was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who have been slain upon the earth.”

Having set forth the condemnation of the ungodly, he sets forth rejoicing and exhorts the saints to rejoice in the divine judgment. This is the meaning: “Rejoice over her, O heaven,” that is, O angels; “God has judged your judgment upon her,” judging the things which she sinned against us. After he has shown the condemnation of the separate ranks, the manner is shown to him: namely, what had been prefigured to him, he sees fulfilled.

“And one mighty angel took up.” God raises up the world in its powers in order to sink it more heavily: “one mighty angel,” Christ; “a stone,” those having hearts of stone; “like a great millstone,” ever rolling through these worldly things, because it grinds others; “and cast it” into hell. “With this violence shall Babylon be cast down,” as you see in this figure; or, the more they are exalted, the more grievously they will fall. “And shall no longer be found,” as certain heretics suppose. “And the sound of harpists”: he enumerates also those things which will perish, of which he had not spoken. “And the voice of bridegroom and bride,” the joy of weddings; “because your merchants were princes of the earth,” that is, by giving their souls for earthly things, they had exercised excessive power—which I now no longer wish to endure.

Now, as it were, he speaks to Babylon herself concerning her fall, grieving for her misery; now [Col. 1568A] he turns to the hearers, in order to exhort the faithful: “because by your sorceries,” literally, or by poisonous persuasions, “all nations perished”—some from every nation. “And of all who have been slain”: for if a wicked person kills a wicked person, the wickedness of the slain does not excuse the killer.

## Chapter XIX

“After these things I heard as it were a great voice of many trumpets saying: Alleluia. Praise and glory and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just: he has judged the great harlot, who corrupted the earth by her prostitution, and has avenged the blood of his servants at her hands. And again they said: Alleluia. And her smoke rises for ages of ages. And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down. [Col. 1568B] And they worshipped God seated upon the throne, saying: Amen, Alleluia. And a voice came forth from the throne, saying: Give praise to our God, all his servants, and you who fear him, small and great.”

He saw the condemnation of Babylon fulfilled; now he hears the rejoicing of the saints over this condemnation, as they had been exhorted when he said, “Rejoice, O heaven.” “After these things I heard as it were a voice,” the rejoicing, “great, of many trumpets in heaven,” of the saints, who are trumpets, that is, resounding with preaching, saying: “Alleluia.” Alleluia is not a word of any language, but an angelic word; it has no proper interpretation in any language, and signifies the Trinity: by *alle*, the Father; by *lu*, the Son; by *ia*, the Holy Spirit. Nor does it signify the divine substance simply, but that substance with praise, [Col. 1568C] and with praise that is inexpressible. “Praise,” because he is praiseworthy through the resurrection; “and glory,” through the ascension and immortality. “And power belongs to our God,” because he conquered the devil; and therefore these belong to him, for he accomplishes what he promises. Thus “his judgments are true and just,” according to the merits of each, “he who judged the harlot who corrupted the earth,” one corrupting another, “by her prostitution, and avenged the blood of his servants,” demanding it, “at her hands.” “And again they said, Alleluia”: by this repetition we understand infinite praise. “And her smoke,” etc., “for ages of ages.” He avenged the blood not temporally but eternally.

He sets forth the rejoicing of the greater ones over the aforesaid condemnation; and these confirm the testimony of those preceding and bear testimony on their own behalf. “And the elders fell down,” the judges, “twenty-four,” “and the four living creatures,” the teachers. “And they worshipped God seated upon the throne, saying”—a confirmation of what went before—namely, it is true that God is thus glorious: “Alleluia.” Where they say *Alleluia*, he gives praise of his own accord. “And a voice,” an admonition, “came forth from the throne,” from the secret place, or from those in whom the Judge sits, “saying,” for all to hear. Having set forth condemnation and the saints’ rejoicing because of it, he gives an admonition that we may escape conformity with such people. “Give praise to our God”: do good works, all his saints, and you who fear him with chaste fear, “small and great,” according to age; or those who cannot accomplish greater things, such as “Sell all” (Matt. 19), while according to Christ those who can accomplish these things are great.

[Col. 1569A] “And I heard as it were the voice of a great trumpet, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of great thunders, saying: Alleluia, for the Lord our God Almighty has reigned. Let us rejoice and exult and give glory to him, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself; and it was given to her to clothe herself in bright white fine linen. For fine linen is the justifications of the saints. And he said to me: Write: Blessed are those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he said to me: These words of God are true. And I fell before his feet to worship him. And he said to me: See that you do not do it; I am your fellow servant and that of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus. Worship God. For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.”

Having shown the joy which the saints have over condemnation, [Col. 1569B] he adds another which they have over the fulfillment of their fellowship and the coming of God’s kingdom. “And I heard as it were a voice,” the rejoicing of the aforesaid saints, “of a great trumpet,” those who resounded like a trumpet by preaching, “and as the voice of many waters,” because they have been gathered from many peoples; “and as the voice of great thunders”: for the saints’ rejoicing will terrify the ungodly—saying, “Alleluia, for the Lord our God Almighty has reigned,” as though the kingdom had formerly belonged to the ungodly. “Let us rejoice,” according to the blessedness of the soul, “and exult,” from the glorification of the body, “and give glory to him,” namely, let us acknowledge that we have all things from him, “because the marriage of the Lamb has come,” because the Church has been joined to Christ. “And his wife has prepared herself”: it was fitting that she should be joined to him, because the Church herself [Col. 1569C] made herself fit to be received. “And it was given to her,” meanwhile, “to clothe herself in fine linen”: in her present condition the Lord gave his Church the justifications with which she might clothe herself and show herself prepared for God; “bright.” “For fine linen is the justifications of the saints.”

“And he said to me: Blessed.” He invites those present to the aforesaid marriage: “Blessed are those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb,” called perfectly, so as actually to arrive. “These are the words of God”; and to make a greater exhortation, he says that these words are God’s, and because they are God’s, they are true. “And I fell before his feet,” because I understood him to be greater than myself; ready to obey, I humbled myself before him—and you too ought to humble yourselves before your teachers—“to worship him,” that is, to venerate him as greater. And he said: [Col. 1569D] “See that you do not do it.” Before Christ’s incarnation, the angel did not forbid himself to be worshipped, because he saw every human being as inferior to himself. But after Christ’s ascension, because he saw a human being exalted above all angels, he feared to be worshipped by a human being. “I am your fellow servant, and that of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus”: I, you, and your other brothers have one God. “Worship God.” “For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy,” because all the prophets bear witness to Jesus, and not from themselves, but the Holy Spirit does so through them.

“And I saw heaven opened. And behold, a white horse, and he who sat upon it was called Faithful and True, and in justice he judges and makes war. His eyes were like a flame of fire, and upon his head were many diadems; he had a name written which no one knows except himself. [Col. 1570A] And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called the Word of God. And the armies which are in heaven followed him on white horses, clothed in white and clean fine linen; and from his mouth proceeded a sharp sword, that with it he might strike the nations; and he shall rule them with an iron rod; and he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty; and he has written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.”

Having shown Babylon’s condemnation and the exaltation of the saints, he adds the condemnation of Antichrist and the false prophets, where he says, “And the beast was seized” (below); he first gives the cause of their condemnation when he says that they will fight against Christ. Since it might seem incredible that Antichrist and his followers, who will be so powerful, could thus be condemned, he first sets forth the power of the condemning one, [Col. 1570B] both according to divinity and according to humanity, a power which no one can resist. From his dignity he also invites us to imitate him.

“And I saw heaven opened”: the mysteries of the Church were revealed to me, and that a human being can ascend to heaven and know God. It is as though he said: I saw those called to the marriage feast; I saw that they could come, because we have both a good helper and good guides. “And behold, a horse”: that is, a horse appeared—the flesh of Christ bearing the Word of God—“white,” because without sin. “And he who sat upon it,” the Divinity, “was called Faithful,” because he fulfills promises; “and True,” because he lies in nothing, as is said in Titus 1 and Hebrews 6. He also makes others true; “and in justice he judges,” because he renders to each according to works, as is said in Romans 2; “and makes war” in his own members against the devil.

“His eyes were like a flame of fire”: the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the divine commandments, or charity, which burns up vices, enlightens its possessor, and kindles love of God. “And upon his head,” according to divinity, “were many diadems,” because through it both he himself and his own are crowned. “Having a name written which no one knows,” that is, fully understands, except himself and the one to whom he has revealed it. “And he was clothed in a garment,” flesh, “sprinkled,” in the Passion, “with blood”; or the Church, which is slain in its martyrs. “And his name is called the Word of God,” through whom the Father announced himself to the world and through whom he made all things (John 1).

“And the armies which are in heaven,” the faithful who fight against the devil and are in the Church, “followed him,” [Col. 1570D] that is, imitated him, “on white horses,” that is, in bodies whitened by many virtues; “clothed in fine linen,” that is, justice, “white,” according to virtues, “clean,” from criminal stain. “And from his mouth,” that is, from his preaching, “proceeds a sword,” that is, the divine sentence, sharp on both sides because it strikes both body and soul; or through the New and Old Testaments; or both peoples, Gentile and Jewish. “That with it he might strike all nations,” some unto life, some unto death. “And he shall rule them”: the good from virtue to virtue, the evil from vice to worse, “with an iron rod,” unbending justice. “And he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty”: that is, rising again, he destroyed death, which an angry God inflicted upon the first human being when he sinned; or the winepress is tribulation, which God, angry and wrathful, [Col. 1571A] inflicts, from which tribulation wine comes forth, that is, certain saints are drawn out. The phrase “fury of wrath” denotes continuance. “And he has upon his garment,” that is, in his flesh, “and upon his thigh”: by this he indicates that Christ was of true human descent. “Written,” such that it could not be erased therefrom, or written in the hearts of the faithful, who are the garment: “King of kings,” of saints, “and Lord of lords,” of all who rule over subjects.

“And I saw one angel standing in the sun, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying to all the birds which fly through the midst of heaven: Come, gather together for the supper of the great God, that you may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of tribunes, and the flesh of the mighty, and the flesh of horses and of those seated upon them, and the flesh of all, free and slave, small and great.”

[Col. 1571B] Having shown the dignity of Christ, through which he will be able to overcome the devil, he adds an admonition to those present that they should adhere to one such as this. “And I saw an angel,” the preachers, “standing in the sun,” openly, so that he might be heard by all; “and he cried with a loud voice,” that is, with an admonition which ought to be heard, “saying to all the birds,” that is, to the faithful, who are both swift and winged with virtues, “which fly through the midst of heaven,” that is, through the catholic faith, making no sect of their own: “Come,” by doing good works; “gather together,” from the diverse regions of heaven, or in the one faith, adding nothing of their own. For unity pleases God. “For the supper of the great God.” By supper he understands Christ himself, who is the true supper, refreshing and never failing; or the fellowship of the saints. And appropriately it is supper, not a midday meal, because no labor follows such refreshment, [Col. 1571C] but everlasting rest. “That you may eat the flesh of kings,” that is, delight in the torment of greater and lesser wicked persons; “and the flesh of the mighty,” in bodily strength; “of horses,” subjects; “and of those seated upon them,” prelates; etc.

“And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to make war with him who sat upon the horse and with his army. And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophet who performed signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the beast, who worshipped its image. These two were cast alive into the lake of fire burning with sulphur, and the rest were killed by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth, and all the birds were satisfied with their flesh.”

[Col. 1571D] “And I saw the beast,” Antichrist, who is the principal head of the beast, “and the kings of the earth,” the false apostles, “and their armies gathered,” that is, all who serve him, “to make war with him,” against Christ and his own, through blasphemies, tribulations, and miracles, “who sat upon the horse,” etc. It is as though he said: You ought to be very solicitous to come to this supper, because the devil is ready to harm you; yet by God’s help you will be able to conquer him. “And the beast was seized”; and therefore the beast was punished eternally, and with it “the false prophet who performed signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the beast,” those who believe in him, “and who worshipped its image.” “These two were cast alive”: namely, Antichrist and his [Col. 1572A] chief followers will feel greater punishments than others, just as those who are burned alive feel punishment, whereas one burned after death feels nothing; “into a lake,” because of darkness, “of fire burning with sulphur.” “And the rest,” namely their followers, “were killed”: they will indeed be punished with a lesser penalty, “by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth.” “And all the birds were satisfied”: the saints will delight in their punishment.

## Chapter XX

“And I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years; and cast him into the abyss, and shut and sealed it over him, so that he might deceive the nations no longer until [Col. 1572B] the thousand years should be completed. After this he must be released for a short time.”

Having stated the condemnation of Babylon, Antichrist, and his false apostles, he adds the condemnation of the devil himself, determines the time of condemnation—namely, shortly after the seduction—and likewise sets forth the cause of condemnation: namely, because when released he will rage without restraint. He also foreshows the power of the one who condemns him: since Christ could bind him in his humble coming, and even while dead, he is now glorified in impassibility and immortality and can utterly destroy him.

“And I saw an angel descending from heaven,” Christ humbling himself in the flesh, “having the key of the abyss,” that is, authority over all depths of wickedness, because they can do only as much as God permits, [Col. 1572C] “and a great chain,” the irresistible power by which Satan will be bound, “in his hand,” namely in his operation through Passion and resurrection. “And he seized the dragon, the serpent,” he held him unawares, namely because he showed him to have sinned when he judged as a sinner a human being free from every sin; “ancient,” because he has harmed from the beginning of the world. “Who is the devil and Satan”: he gives, as it were, an interpretation of the name.

“And he bound him,” deprived him of his former power, “for a thousand years,” from the time of Christ to the time of Antichrist. He says a thousand because that number is perfect; and here the Apostle uses a determinate number for an indeterminate one, because, as Christ said to his disciples (Acts 1): “It is not yours to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power.” “And he cast him into the abyss,” because, expelled from the faithful, he rules over all the wicked. It should be known that the devil was bound in Abraham and other faithful persons just as in those now present; but in the former the hope of the future Christ bound him, while in the latter Christ himself did so. “And he shut [Col. 1572D] him up,” because he does not know whether he can retain those whom he now has, or acquire those whom he does not have. “And he sealed it over him,” that is, he overcame him by the sign of the cross and drove him back from the minds of the faithful, so that he might no longer deceive the nations as freely as before, until the time of Antichrist, “until the thousand years should be completed.” I said, “until they should be completed,” because afterwards he will be released in the manner stated; that is: “After this he must be released for a short time,” because God has so ordained, that then he may again deceive freely—but do not fear, for it is for a short time.

“And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given to them; and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the Word of God, and those who worshipped neither the beast nor its image, nor received its mark on their foreheads or hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. The rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power; but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him for a thousand years. But when the thousand years have been completed, Satan shall be released from his prison and shall go out and deceive [Col. 1573B] the nations which are upon the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and shall gather them for war; their number is like the sand of the sea. And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city; and fire came down from heaven and devoured them; and the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, where the beast and the false prophets shall be tormented day and night for ages of ages.”

“And I saw thrones”: with the devil bound, I saw the faithful released, and lesser persons ready to obey prelates, and prelates judging among their subjects. This is said of the state of the present life. “Judgment was given to them” by God. “And I saw,” during the time of this binding, “the souls of those beheaded,” the faithful in glory, never descending to hell as [Col. 1573C] Abraham and the prophets descended, though righteous, “for the testimony of Jesus,” according to humanity, “and for the Word of God,” according to divinity; “and those who worshipped neither”—and also other faithful persons who were not beheaded—“the beast,” Antichrist, “nor its image,” his false apostles, “nor received its mark,” his sign, “on their foreheads,” in open confession, “or on their hands,” in action. “And they lived and reigned with Christ”: they will also be able to perform miracles. “For a thousand years.” Nor do I say that this will occur only after the general resurrection, but also during the time of the binding.

“And the rest of the dead did not live,” that is, those dead in soul will be punished immediately after bodily dissolution. He introduces this because some would have it that no one is punished throughout the whole period of Satan’s binding, until the thousand years are completed. [Col. 1573D] But then it is plain that they do not live.

“This is the resurrection”: namely, that the faithful in their lifetime are delivered from sins, and that their souls immediately after bodily dissolution enjoy eternal glory; “the first,” because the resurrection of soul and body follows. “Blessed,” because he will attain blessedness; “and holy,” confirmed, because that blessedness will not fail: “the one who has a share in the first resurrection,” because not all can possess the same blessedness and perfection. “Over these the second death has no power,” and he is truly blessed because the condemnation of soul and body together will not be in him. “But they shall be priests of God and of Christ,” offering themselves and continual praises to God in the Trinity, and to Christ according to his [Col. 1574A] humanity; “and they shall reign with him for a thousand years,” not only after the general resurrection.

“But Satan shall be released”: he will receive power “from his prison,” from the hearts of the reprobate, in which he is now bound; “and shall go out,” openly, to the “four corners of the earth,” in the four regions of the world. “Gog and Magog,” literally, are peoples shut up in the mountainous regions toward the north; once released and first deceived, they will deceive others. Or allegorically, all wicked people are understood by them. Gog means “covered,” by which all who harm secretly are understood. Magog means “uncovered,” by which all who harm openly are understood. “And he shall gather them for war, whose number is like the sand of the sea,” barren and innumerable. “And they went up,” exalting themselves, “over the breadth [Col. 1574B] of the earth,” throughout the whole world, “and surrounded the camp of the saints”: invading the saints, they will not be able to enter those in whom God makes war; “and the beloved city,” fortified by virtues and therefore beloved by God.

Having stated the cause, he sets forth the condemnation: after that seduction, the devil and his ministers will be condemned by God. This is the meaning: “and fire came down from heaven,” etc., “where the beast and the false prophets shall be tormented.” Because he assigns the same place of punishments to the devil and his followers, he especially frightens us from becoming his followers. “Day and night,” continually; or by day, through the glory of the saints, and by night, through their own misery. “For ages of ages”: that is, eternally.

“And I saw a great white throne, and one seated upon it, from whose presence earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great [Col. 1574C] and small, standing before the throne; and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is that of life; and the dead were judged from the things written in the books, according to their works. And the sea gave up the dead who were in it; and death and hell gave up the dead who were in them. And each was judged according to his works; and hell and death were cast into the lake of fire: this is the second death. And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.”

Having distinguished the devil from his followers, he adds the destruction of the world. For the world will be destroyed because it is corrupted by evils—namely earth, air, and water. Yet their substance will not perish, but their form will be changed as far as the sphere of the moon. The ether will remain; nevertheless, all things which now move there for the service of human beings will be fixed. [Col. 1574D] And I saw the throne: the Church, great in its multitude; white by its virtues, or because of impassibility and immortality; and Him seated upon it, Christ, from whose sight—that is, presence—earth fled from this appearance, and heaven, that is, the air; and no place was found for them according to their former condition.

And I saw the dead, the wicked, great and small, both greater and lesser, standing bodily. Though he had often spoken of the glorification of the saints and the punishments of the ungodly, he had not openly mentioned their bodies, whether they would be received together with their bodies; this he now plainly does. Before the throne, because the saints will openly behold the merits of each individual; and the books—that is, the consciences of each individual—[Col. 1575A] were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life: those who have imitated it will have life; others will be condemned. And the dead—that is, the wicked—were judged from those things written in the books, namely their works, because one will receive a greater punishment, another a lesser.

And the sea gave up its dead who were in it, their bodies however scattered they might have been. Some maintained that only those bodies would be revived which were found living or intact; against this he shows that all bodies, however scattered in it, are equally revived. And death—that is, the devil—and hell, that place, gave up the dead who were in them, the souls of the dead. This is against those who said that new souls would then be created. And hell, that is, all the insatiable or those deep in vices, and death—the devil—[Col. 1575B] were cast into the lake of fire: this is the second death. There is a certain warning here: Beware of the first death, from which comes the second; and whoever was not found in the book of life, predestined unto life.

## CHAPTER XXI

## SEVENTH VISION

“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and the sea is no more. And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a great voice from the throne saying: Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he shall dwell with them; and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them as their God. And God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints. And death shall be no more, [Col. 1575C] nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain any longer, because the former things have passed away.”

In this seventh vision he treats of the renewal of the elements and the glorification of the saints, showing the merits by which the saints are to be so glorified. And I saw heaven, that is, the renewed air. For the first heaven and the first earth passed away: their former state is changed. And the sea is no more, neither in motion nor in its former qualities; yet it is not certain whether water is purified by the fire by which air and earth will be purified, or by some material purification of its own.

And the city—the Church—holy, established in every peace; Jerusalem, now seeing Christ fully, who is true peace; new because of the resurrection of the bodies; coming down, that is, humbling herself, because [Col. 1575D] she understands that whatever good she possesses she has received from merits and from God’s grace; prepared by God as a bride adorned for her husband. For just as a bridegroom sends gifts before the wedding so that she may adorn herself from them and finally please him at the wedding, so Christ pours faith and the theological virtues into the Church in baptism.

Having said that he saw the renewal of the elements and the glorification of the saints, since this was unknown and might seem incredible, he therefore adds the authority of the saints who told him these things, and also that of God. And I heard a voice, an admonition, great because it concerns great secrets of God, speaking from the throne, from those in whom God sits: “Behold”—it is manifest—“the tabernacle of God is with human beings,” that is, the humanity in which God served as a soldier [militavit] is in the [Col. 1576A] same glory with the human beings who have imitated him; “and he shall dwell with them,” that is, just as that glory will be eternal for Christ, so also for his own. “And they shall be his people,” offending in nothing—which cannot be while they are in this flesh—“and God himself,” even according to his divinity, “shall be with them as their God,” as it were uniquely, because he will never be separated from their presence.

Having set forth glory, he removes all sadness: “And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes,” every sorrow whatsoever, both from the eyes of the mind and from those of the flesh; “and death shall be no more.” He shows that there will be no tears because there will be no cause of tears: neither death, the dissolution of soul and body, nor separation from Christ; nor mourning, continuous pain; nor crying, some great disturbance taking away peace; [Col. 1576B] nor pain, any small movement. That is, there is now no place for these things, since there is no sin, from which all these proceed. Having set forth the authority of the saints, he sets forth that of God himself.

“And he who sat upon the throne said: Behold, I make all things new. And he said: Write, because these words are most trustworthy and true. And he said to me: It is done. I am α and ω, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give, freely, from the spring of the water of life. He who conquers shall possess these things, and I shall be God to him, and he shall be a son to me. But the fearful and unbelieving and accursed, and murderers, and fornicators, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars—their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.”

[Col. 1576C] And he who sat upon the throne said: “Behold, I make all things new,” both the elements and the glory of the saints. And he said: “Write”—a certain admonition—as though saying: Whatever has been shown me concerning this renewal is for the benefit of those now present, so that they too may hasten to attain that glorification; “because these words are most trustworthy,” fit to receive belief, “and true,” because they will be fulfilled.

And he said to me: “It is done.” Lest he should ask what would happen after that renewal, he is told that nothing remains to be done, but that then all things are consummated. “I am α and ω”: he shows that he can bring about this renewal because he created all things, and in him all things shall be consummated. “And to the thirsty,” that is, to one desiring me, “I will give from the spring,” namely myself, who am the source of all blessedness, “of living [Col. 1576D] water,” because it makes one live, “freely,” through grace alone. “He who conquers,” that is, who remains thirsty, or who overcomes temptations, “shall possess,” shall firmly obtain, “these things”: God and the blessed renewal. “And I shall be God to him,” eternal satisfaction, “and he shall be a son to me,” as above, a holy people in whom the Lord has been well pleased.

“But the fearful,” that is, those who, having received faith, fear to profess it, or fear to receive it; “and unbelievers,” who, like infidels, doubt the resurrection; “and accursed,” excommunicated persons; and murderers, and fornicators, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, to whom lying is habitual: “their portion,” that is, each one shall share these punishments according to his merits. Having described the glory which the saints will possess, [Col. 1577A] he says by what merit and with what help they will obtain these things.

“And one of the seven angels having bowls full of the seven last plagues came. And he spoke with me, saying: Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb. And he carried me away in the Spirit onto a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down from heaven, having the glory of God. Its light was like a precious stone, like a jasper stone, like crystal. And it had a great and high wall, having twelve gates, and at the gates twelve corners. And names were written, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel. On the east three gates, and on the north three gates, and on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had [Col. 1577B] twelve foundations, and upon them the twelve names of the apostles and of the Lamb.”

And one of the seven angels came, one of the holy preachers, etc. “Come”: enlarge your understanding; “I will show you the bride,” now made the Lamb’s wife. And he carried me away in the Spirit, that is, spiritually raised me up so that I might know Christ and the Church founded upon him, onto a mountain, because she is the defense of her own; great because she fills the entire world; and high because she is unconquerable, etc. “Having the glory of God,” that is, open knowledge of God.

He shows why the Church has glory. For “its light,” that is, the Church itself, shining according to its measure, showed itself like Christ, who was a precious stone because firm [Col. 1577C] in purpose and shining with the splendor of every virtue. This is what he says: “Its light was like a precious stone, like a jasper stone.” Jasper is hard and green; so the Church flourishes in faith and is firm in it. “Like crystal,” concealing nothing, because there is pure confession there.

“And it had a great and high wall,” that is, Christ the defender, who is great according to the resurrection and high according to the ascension; or defenders of others, who are great by overcoming heretics, high and unconquerable. “Having twelve gates,” the prophets, by whose example others are introduced into faith; and “at the gates twelve corners”: by the corners we understand the apostles, who persevered in faith and in the footsteps of the prophets. “And names written,” because all believers are founded, and as it were inscribed, in the prophets; [Col. 1577D] or because all believers stand in the love of the earlier fathers, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel, that is, of all believers, according to the interpretations already stated.

“On the east three gates, on the north three gates.” The Jews are called the east, from whom the Sun of righteousness arose, and among them are three gates because to them faith in the city was first announced. The north signifies cold peoples, who believed after the Jews; the south, burning persons, such as holy martyrs; the west signifies those in whom faith and charity grow cold, or those who will believe in the last times through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch. The number of twelve gates, set under the number three through the four parts of the world, belongs to the ministry of the apostles, through whom faith in the Trinity is spread through the fourfold world. [Col. 1578A]

“And the wall,” that is, whatever defenders of the Church are founded upon the prophets, in whom faith came first, “having twelve foundations,” that is, the prophets, upon whose faith the apostles were founded: for from them faith passed on to the apostles, and they also had belief from the prophets, who had said the same things. Or let us understand the foundations as the apostles, upon whom rests all the fortification of the Church. This he adds: “and upon them the twelve names of the apostles”—this explains which foundations he means—and upon them is the name of the Lamb, because they always preached him. It is as if he said: See the city so fortified and adorned, yet not all equal, but each perfect according to his measure.

“And he who spoke with me had a measuring rod, [Col. 1578B] a golden reed, that he might measure the city and its gates and wall. And the city is laid out as a square. Its length is as great as its breadth. And he measured the city with the golden reed: twelve thousand stadia. Its length and breadth and height are equal. And he measured its wall: one hundred and forty-four cubits, the measure of a human being, which is that of an angel.”

And he who spoke with me—the angel in the person of Christ—had a measure, namely a measured distribution of graces; a reed, this measure indeed, that is, divine Scripture; golden, composed by God’s wisdom, in order to measure the city—that is, to give all understanding of the Scriptures according to measure—and its gates, those who introduce others [Col. 1578C] into faith, and its wall, the defenders of others.

“And the city is laid out as a square,” because it has four equal sides: faith, hope, charity, and action. These are called equal because as much as one believes, so much one hopes; as much as one hopes, so much one loves; as much as one loves, so much one acts. Or let us call the square the four principal virtues, none of which should exceed another in a human being: prudence, that is, discernment of good from evil, followed by temperance, namely that one avoids the evil recognized; after these, fortitude, that one may endure adversities and manfully accomplish what ought to be done; then justice, that one may render to all according to their merits.

He explains the squareness: length, that is, long-suffering which is in faith, is as great as breadth, [Col. 1578D] namely charity, because as much as one believes, so much one loves. “And he measured the city: twelve thousand stadia,” that is, those perfect persons from the four parts of the world, united in faith in the Trinity. Streets in which competitors run are customarily measured by stadia; by this he indicates that these citizens must run and strive for the prize (1 Cor. 9). Its length is long-suffering, its breadth an expansion according to charity, and its height is equal in the things it hopes for; for as much as one believes and loves, so much one hopes.

“And he measured the wall,” the defenders, “at one hundred and forty-four cubits.” The cubit, in which the hand is found, signifies action. “The measure of a human being, which is that of an angel,” shows that the angel had human form, so as plainly to indicate that he who was signified was the true Angel, the Son of God, and a true [Col. 1579A] human being. He had said that this city had walls, gates, and foundations, themselves unequal among one another; here he explains what the wall itself is like in material, and thus says:

“And its wall was built of jasper; but the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone: the first foundation, jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, chalcedony; the fourth, emerald; the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sard; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, topaz; the tenth, chrysoprase; the eleventh, hyacinth; the twelfth, amethyst.”

“And its wall was built,” namely its chief defenders, “of stone,” that is, as stones because of [Col. 1579B] firmness, “of jasper,” because flourishing in faith. “But the city itself,” that is, that whole Church, both the walls and those protected by them, is gold because of wisdom, pure from every defilement, “like clear glass.” By this he indicates the purity of faith: whatever one says with the mouth, one believes in the heart. “The foundations of the wall of the city,” the prophets or apostles, “adorned with every precious stone,” are adorned in themselves with every kind of virtue.

“The first foundation, jasper,” because the first foundation of all virtues is faith.

Jasper, green in color, signifies the unfading freshness of faith. Sapphire, like the serene sky, which when struck by the rays of the sun emits a burning brilliance, signifies the loftiness of the saints’ hope, whose citizenship is in heaven; renewed by the pure sun, they seek eternal things more ardently and teach others to seek them. [Col. 1579C]

Chalcedony shines like the pale fire of a lamp, and shines in the open air, not in a house; it signifies the flame of inward charity, which does good in secret, but when commanded to benefit others immediately reveals what brilliance it possesses within. It resists engravers; glowing from the stroke of the sun or the rubbing of fingers, it draws chaff to itself—that is, the saints can be overcome by no one, and draw the more fragile to themselves.

The emerald, exceedingly green, is found above the herbs and foliage of Scythia; that is, it signifies a strong confession of the same faith amid adversities denoted by cold. Since this faith became so greatly known to the world through the Gospel, it is called the fourth, on account of the four Gospels.

Sardonyx signifies humility among virtues: black [Col. 1579D] below, white in the middle, red above; that is, the saints are red in suffering, inwardly white, yet despised in their own eyes through humility. Since humility descends from the weakness of the body, which is governed by the five senses, it is fifth. Sard, blood-colored, signifies the glory of martyrdom; it is sixth because Christ was crucified in the sixth hour.

Chrysolite shines like gold and emits burning sparks; that is, spiritual preaching amid miracles. By gold is signified heavenly wisdom; by sparks, exhortation or also miracles. Since this is done through the Holy Spirit, it is placed seventh.

Beryl is the perfect action of preachers. For as water struck by the sun shines, so it is polished only into a seven-angled form, because brilliance is sharpened by striking the angles. Water signifies the human mind; the brilliance of the sun, divine wisdom, by which it shines more fully. But neither divine nor human wisdom is perfect unless it is completed by works; perfection of works is understood by seven, because the work of the world was made in this number. It burns the hand of its holder, because whoever is joined to a saint is set aflame by that saint’s conduct. [Col. 1580A]

Topaz: the rarer it is, the more precious; two-colored, shining most brightly with gold and ethereal brilliance when touched by the splendor of the sun; surpassing the brightness of all gems; uniquely drawing those who look upon it to gaze upon it. If you polish it, you make it dim; if you leave it to nature, it is brighter. Nothing is dearer to kings among their treasures. It signifies the contemplative life, which holy kings prefer to all riches of works [Col. 1580B] and gems of virtues, and toward which they direct their minds especially; and this all the more insofar as they are more frequently illuminated by divine grace. Its golden color comes from inward brightness, its ethereal color from the sweetness of contemplation, which, by rubbing, often becomes worthless. For scarcely can anyone at once be distressed by pains and behold the joys of heaven with a tranquil mind.

And as active life is in eight, so contemplative life is in nine, which is the life of angels, whose orders are nine; or because it is one degree distant from ten, namely death. Chrysoprase, a mixture of green and gold, and according to some also purple with golden drops, is born in India. It signifies those who earn the freshness of the eternal homeland through charity, and display to others the purple of martyrdom. Since they follow the Lord’s example, they are in India, that is, [Col. 1580C] near the rising of the sun; and because they await reigning with Christ, they are in the number ten, and the Decalogue will be fulfilled through love of God, which was the ninth. Therefore in chrysoprase the work and reward of martyrdom are indicated.

Hyacinth changes with the air: in clear weather it is transparent; in cloudy weather it withers. It indicates teachers raised to high things but condescending on account of the weak. Amethyst is purple, with a blended color of violet and rose, gently casting out certain flames: its purple beauty signifies the attire of the heavenly kingdom; the violet, the modesty of the saints; the rose, precious death. They are those who amid adversities are highest in mind, and who pour out the flame of charity not only among themselves but even toward persecutors. Therefore amethyst signifies the perpetual remembrance in the mind of the humble of the heavenly [Col. 1580D] kingdom.

## HYMN. (G)

Citizens of the heavenly homeland,  
sing in harmony to the King of kings,  
who is the heavenly maker  
of the celestial city,  
in whose building  
such a foundation is found.

Jasper, of green color,  
brings forth the freshness of faith,  
which in all the perfect  
never withers utterly,  
by whose strong protection  
the devil is resisted.

Sapphire has an appearance  
[Col. 1581A] like the heavenly throne;  
it signifies the heart of the simple,  
who seek assured hope,  
whose life and conduct  
delight the Most High.

Chalcedony has  
the image of pale fire;  
it is refined in public,  
gives brightness in cloudiness,  
and bears the virtue of believers  
who serve in secret.

The exceedingly green emerald  
gives an olive-colored light:  
it is most whole faith,  
open to every good,  
[Col. 1581B] which nowhere knows how to fail  
in the work of devotion.

The steadfast three-colored sardonyx  
is borne by the inward human being,  
whom humility makes black,  
in whom chastity grows white,  
and to crown uprightness  
martyrdom too makes red.

Sard is scarlet,  
whose blood-red color  
also shows martyrdom  
of those who contend lawfully.  
It is sixth in the catalogue;  
it clings to the mystery of the cross.

Golden chrysolite  
[Col. 1581C] sparkles like a furnace;  
it displays the character of human beings  
who are perfectly wise,  
who shine with the sacred ray  
of sevenfold grace.

Beryl is watery,  
like the sun in clear water;  
it figures the desires of people  
of penetrating intelligence,  
who more gladly choose  
the leisure of beautiful repose.

The rarer topaz is,  
the more precious it is;  
it glows with golden brilliance  
and ethereal appearance,  
[Col. 1581D] and shows the customary task  
of the contemplative life.

Chrysoprase is purple,  
golden-colored, and flaming;  
its brightness in darkness  
shoots flames into the eyes.  
This is perfect charity,  
which no savagery overthrows.

Hyacinth is purple,  
green in its middle,  
whose beautiful appearance  
changes as does the weather;  
it signifies the angelic life,  
endowed with discernment.

[Col. 1582A] The excellent amethyst,  
violet in color  
and marked with purple spots,  
displays the heart of the humble  
who die together with Christ.

“And the twelve gates are twelve pearls, each gate severally consisting of one pearl. And the streets of the city are pure gold, like transparent glass.
