And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it, for now the glory of God will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb. And the nations shall walk in its light, and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honor into it; and its gates shall not be shut by day. [Col. 1582B] For there shall be no night there. And they shall bring into it the glory and honor of the nations; and nothing defiled, or doing abomination and falsehood, shall enter it, except those written in the book of life of the Lamb.”

“And the twelve gates are twelve pearls, each severally”: that is, all those who introduce others in the four parts of the world, founded in faith in the holy Trinity, introduce twelve—that is, all from the four parts of the world—to faith in the Trinity; they are pearls, that is, bright and solid. “And each gate consisted of one pearl”: that is, each one of those who introduce others is shining and firm in virtues.

“And the streets of the city,” that is, those permitted to use broader precepts, such as married persons, are gold, full of wisdom and charity, pure from criminal stain, “like transparent [Col. 1582C] glass,” concealing no stains in themselves; or because evildoers can recognize their own wickedness in their works as in a mirror.

“And I saw no temple in it”: there is only here a place of prayer and offering, which have no place there. “For the Lord God Almighty is its temple”: complete rest. “And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it,” literally, or of greater and lesser preachers, whom those on earth need here for illumination. For the glory of God the Father, and its lamp, is the Lamb. A lamp is a vessel containing light; so the humanity of Christ contains divinity, by which all who are willing are illuminated.

“And the nations shall walk in its light.” He shows the light of that coming city to be great and marvelous, for even in its present state it illuminates human beings [Col. 1582D] and leads them to that eternal city through vision and through certain rays of the knowledge of that eternal blessedness. “And the kings of the earth,” those who rightly govern themselves and others, “shall bring their glory,” after the likeness of victors who carry spoils into their cities: so these shall bring their glory in those won for God; they shall bring it into that city, that is, they shall do so to its praise, not their own; “and honor,” purity of conscience, into it, for the sake of possessing it.

“And its gates shall not be shut by day”: he speaks of the future, for here the gates are shut by preaching lest evildoers rage and trample God’s word. “For there shall be no night there.” He shows why they need not be shut there: because there is no ignorance, no darkness, and therefore no place for thieves, but there will be complete serenity there. [Col. 1583A] “And they shall bring”: the kings themselves shall present to God glory, that is, glorified nations, and honor, nations honorable according to the purity of their own consciences. “And nothing shall enter it”: although there is no night there and no closed gate, not everyone will nevertheless enter; no defiled person, no one consenting to uncleanness; nor one doing an abomination, some criminal deed, nor falsehood, one delighting in devising lies—except those written in the book of life of the Lamb.

What more need be said? No one will enter except one foreknown in God’s eternal dispensation, or except imitators of Christ’s life, he who is set before us as a book to imitate.

## CHAPTER XXII

“And he showed me a river of living water, shining like crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and [Col. 1583B] of the Lamb, in the midst of its street; and on each side of the river, the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit in each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations; and there shall be no curse any longer. And the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it; and his servants shall serve him, and shall see his face, and his name shall be on their foreheads; and night shall be no more. And they shall need neither lamplight nor sunlight, because the Lord God illuminates them, and they shall reign for ages of ages.”

After showing the city’s position, dignity, walls, and foundations, he describes the refreshment which God gives the city both in the present and especially in the future. For here he gives refreshment in some measure through baptism and the sacrament of his body and blood; yet this is little in comparison with that future blessedness, where Christ will be all in all.

The question is raised concerning baptism: why is it performed with water rather than with some other element? The answer is that water has the nature of extinguishing, and in baptism the heat of sins is extinguished. “He showed me a river,” abundance, “of living water,” refreshment which gives life to all its inhabitants; shining, namely Christ, who will be complete refreshment; “like crystal,” because there is there purity alone and nothing discordant; “proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb,” from the greater persons in whom God sits, for through their instruction the lesser receive that blessedness; “in the midst of its street,” in the communities of those who follow a broader way of life. [Col. 1583C]

“[Col. 1583D] “On each side of the river,” both in this present life and in the future, is “the tree of life bearing twelve fruits”: Christ, who gives refreshment and gives those who prepare others for the same refreshment. They are called twelve because they make fruitful for God the four parts of the world in the same faith of the Trinity; “yielding its fruit each month,” throughout all ages or continually.

On this side of the river, that is, in this life, we have the tree of life, namely the body and blood of Christ by which we are refreshed; beyond the river we shall have Jesus Christ present and unfailing refreshment. Or by “this side of the river” let us understand the time before baptism: for those earlier saints, such as Moses and others, had Christ as their refreshment, though through instruments other than those now used. [Col. 1584A] By “beyond the river” let us understand the time after baptism, by which we signify the righteous in the New Testament. Moses prefigured this when he led the children of Israel as far as the Jordan River, and Joshua son of Nun when he led them from the river into the land of promise.

“And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations”: Christ’s commandments, which cover and adorn the fruit, and, if fulfilled, confer healings. These are scattered through the twelve fruits, namely the prophets and apostles and their successors. “And there shall be no curse any longer,” that is, no withdrawal of grace. “And the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it,” that is, God and the Lamb shall rest in them without any offense. “And his servants shall serve him”: they shall praise him forever; “and shall see his face,” not in an enigma as now, but God and Christ as they are, as is said in 1 Corinthians 13. “And [Col. 1584B] his name shall be on their foreheads,” because they shall openly be called God’s and the Lamb’s, just as they openly confessed him here.

“And night shall be no more,” no ignorance; “and they shall need neither lamplight,” that is, the teaching of the old law, or lesser preachers who illuminate the night, “nor sunlight,” the teaching of the new law, or greater preachers. As he commended the vision at the beginning, so he does at its conclusion.

“And he said to me: These words are most trustworthy and true, and the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants what must shortly take place. And behold, I come quickly. Blessed is he who keeps the words of this book.”

And he said to me, that is, the angel who said the other things: “These words,” whatever has been shown in words and figures [Col. 1584C], “are true,” because they will be fulfilled; “most trustworthy,” fit to receive belief. And you ought rightly to believe, because the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets, he who has in his power the gifts of the Holy Spirit through whom the prophets spoke, sent [the angel], and so forth. Although God in the Trinity gives gifts of mercy, they are nevertheless attributed to the person of the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit signifies kindness, and all these gifts proceed from God’s kindness. He “sent his angel to show”: and as the angel showed me, so I show you, his servants, not philosophers or the proud of the world, “what must shortly take place,” because these things cannot fail to be fulfilled as they have been foreknown. “And behold, I come quickly”; and truly shortly, because he himself says so. He also says: “Blessed is he who keeps,” fulfills in work, “the words of this book.” [Col. 1584D]

“And I, John, who heard and saw these things. And after I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who showed me these things. And he said to me: See that you do not do this: I am your fellow-servant and of your brothers the prophets, and of those who keep the words of this book. Worship God. And he said to me: Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let him who harms, harm still; and let him who is in filth become filthy still; and let the righteous do righteousness still, and let the holy become holy still. Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each according to his works. I am α and ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have power over [Col. 1585A] the tree of life and may enter by the gates into the holy city. Outside are dogs, and sorcerers, and the shameless, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and makes falsehood.”

“And I, John”: again a commendation of the book from his own person, as though he said: I, who am not accustomed to announce anything false to you, heard the voices and saw these things, the figures. “And after I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship,” as though forgetting the earlier prohibition. He wishes again to honor the angel as greater; from this he intimates to us that, just as he honored the angel, so we ought to hold him in veneration, yet not worship him as God. We should understand that by keeping the book angels are reconciled to us.

“Before the feet of the angel,” as though to show myself wholly contemptible in comparison with him, namely for this reason, because he showed me these [Col. 1585B] things. “See,” etc.—[I am] fellow-servant of the greater prophets and of the lesser ones. “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book,” nor shut up the sayings of this book, as was commanded concerning the words of the seven thunders; rather, command them to all. These words ought indeed not to be shut up, so that by this some brothers may be gained, because the time is near.

And because someone might object that these things should not be preached because wicked people would become worse, he replies, as it were, to the objection: it is just that the wicked person become worse; that is, “let him who harms others harm” more, and “let him who is in filth become filthy still,” become more filthy in himself. “And let the righteous do righteousness still”: let the righteous person become more righteous toward another; “and let the holy become holy still”: let him be holier in himself. And truly the time is near, because “behold, I come quickly,” and [I will render] according to works, more to one, less to another. [Col. 1585C]

And I can rightly do this because “I am α and ω,” first before all creatures and last, because no creature comes after him; “the beginning,” because all things proceeded from him; “and the end,” because all things shall be consummated in him. And because he had said, “Let him who harms harm, let him who is filthy become filthy,” lest the wicked person say that repentance would therefore profit him nothing, he says that even such persons will be blessed if by repentance they wipe away their sins. This is what is meant: “Blessed are those who wash their robes”—I say that they wash them so that they may be refreshed by the tree of life; that is, “that they may have power over the tree of life and enter by the gates,” through the introduction of the saints, “into the holy city.” “Outside are dogs,” those contradicting and barking at truth, and those unclean in themselves shall be outside the city. This is what is meant by “everyone who loves falsehood,” by hearing it, “and makes it,” by inventing it. [Col. 1585D]

“I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify to you these things in the churches. I am the root and offspring of David, the bright and morning star. And the bridegroom and bride say: Come. And let him who hears say: Come. Let him who thirsts come; let him who wishes receive the water of life freely.”

[Col. 1586A] He commends the book by the dignity of the angel and by his own person, now on Christ’s authority, as though saying: “Know, all of you, that these words proceed from me: ‘I, Jesus, sent,’” and so forth. And I ought rightly to be believed, because I am David’s support and begotten from him; that is, “the root,” his support, “and offspring of David,” generated from him according to the flesh; “the bright star,” that is, bringing light to the world and announcing the day like Lucifer, that is, the general resurrection through my own resurrection; and “morning,” accomplished in the morning.

After other commendations, he sets forth commendations from the bridegroom, or the Spirit, that is, from the Trinity and the faithful. “And the bridegroom and the bride,” the faithful, say: “Come,” to knowledge of the book; and “he who hears,” that is, understands, “let him say: ‘Come’”; namely, let the greater [Col. 1586B] say to others that they should come. “And let him who thirsts come”; yet not everyone shall enter, but only he who desires and fulfils in deed what he desires. “And let him who wishes receive the water of life freely”: an effective will is sufficient.

“I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone shall add to these things, God shall add upon him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his share from the tree of life and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book. He who bears testimony to these things says: ‘Indeed, Amen. I come quickly. Amen.’ Come, Lord Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

“I testify”: after he has commended the book through [Col. 1586C] many authorities, because he knew that certain heretics in Asia had the custom of removing from the books of the saints whatever ran contrary to their heresies, and of inserting their own heresies so as to confirm their errors from the saints, he excommunicates all who either add to this book or subtract from it; and this is the meaning of “I testify,” and so forth.

He says, as though saying: “I excommunicate—and Jesus excommunicates—who bears testimony to these things,” namely Jesus; “Yes, Amen,” that is, all that has been said is true, and therefore, if anyone alters it, let him be excommunicated. “I come quickly. Amen; and preserve yourselves from altering the words, because I come quickly to avenge those who alter them,” says the Lord. These are the Apostle’s words, and he confirms that Christ will come quickly. “Come, Lord Jesus,” says [Col. 1586D] the Apostle to the Lord out of the excessive affection of one desiring that he come to reward.

“The grace,” and so forth. “Amen,” that is, without failure; for *amen* means “without,” and *defectio*, “failure.” “I,” that is, a father in preeminence, yet a brother in the rebirth of one mother, the Church. Blessed in all things be God. Amen, that is, truth. Let all assent. Amen.

[Col. 1587]

## Letter of Anselm of Laon to H., Abbot of St. Lawrence at Liège

*(Works of Guibert of Nogent, ed. d’Achery, p. 642.)*

[Col. 1587A] To the venerable Abbot H. of Saint Lawrence, Anselm, humble son of the Church of Laon, greeting.

[Note: [Col. 1587D] Heribrand. See the notice on Anselm above, col. 1183.]

It must be considered, Lord, lest the question being so treated among you consist not in doctrine but in battles of words. To examine the sound meanings of men belongs to men; to quarrel over words belongs to boys, who understand only faintly what they say or hear. The Apostle rebukes them: “Do not become children in understanding” (1 Cor. 14:20). Yet he commands: “Be children in malice” (ibid.). Not attending to this, some—especially puffed up by the name of knowledge and ignorant of the Fathers’ meaning—are sick, as the Apostle says, “with questions and battles of words.” The judgments of all Catholics are indeed diverse but not opposed; they converge in one harmony. Yet in words there sound certain apparent contrarieties [Col. 1587B] and disputes, in which little ones are scandalized, the vigorous are exercised, the proud contend, and the approved stand forth, showing readily to others who are sick that the discordant things are harmonious.

Among this kind of word-fighting, these propositions are set forth in Scripture: “The Lord does not will evil.” Again: “He wills all things that occur,” among which are evils also; nor does anything occur against his will, while he is unwilling and compelled. He does not will evil, indeed—that is, he does not love it, regard it as pleasing, or approve it—but hates, forbids, and condemns it.

It is further established that God made the rational creature with free will, that it might be able to merit. But free will itself cannot by itself either be directed toward what is greater or persist in the good in which it was made; it can, however, of itself, if left to itself, fall. [Col. 1587C] Therefore divine grace is at hand for it, ready to help but not to compel—for that would remove the freedom which God had given. If, therefore, free will, being forewarned, listens and consents, it is directed by grace; if it refuses, it is abandoned, and, left to itself, falls.

Who, moreover, would deny that God wills both to direct the one consenting to him and to abandon the one renouncing him? For since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:11), just as he wills what belongs to mercy, so no less does he will what belongs to justice. Therefore, through mercy, he wills to help the consenting person; through justice, he also wills to abandon the refusing person. This abandonment is called in Scripture handing over to a reprobate mind, hardening, and casting down. For God is not the author or inciter [Col. 1587D] of evil; but when, as we have said, he justly abandons, the rational creature is handed over to a reprobate mind, hardened, and cast down. Let no one therefore deny that the merciful and just God both wills to show mercy and wills to harden, as the Apostle says: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills [Col. 1588A] he hardens” (Rom. 9:18). And Augustine [Note: [Col. 1588D] *On Free Will and Grace*, ch. 21.] says on that verse, “God gave them over to dishonourable passions” (Rom. 1:26): “It is manifest that God works in human minds, inclining their wills wherever he wills, whether toward good according to his mercy or toward evil according to his judgment—sometimes manifest, sometimes hidden, but always just.” The divine page is full of expressions of this sort, which no hasty person should take perversely, but should attend to carefully and wisely.

Avarice is properly called the service of idols. For the avaricious person ascribes to money what is owed and fitting to God; and this occurs in three ways. The avaricious person desires to have money, to increase what he has, and not to lose it. So the worshipper of God desires to possess charity, [Col. 1588B] which is God, to increase it both in himself and in his neighbors, and not to lose it. Therefore that vice is spiritually called idolatrous worship, because in the manner stated it offers to money what is owed to God, making money, by worshipping it thus, into its god. For whatever each person loves above all else, placing there his heart and desire, he establishes as his highest good and worships as though it were God.

Love of earthly things is poison; love of higher things is oil. Of itself the soul inclines and descends toward earthly things; toward higher things it is raised and ascends not through itself but through God. But when it is anointed with the higher oil, torn away from earthly things, it desires and loves eternal things. Between the barrenness of poison and the richness of oil there is a certain [Col. 1588C] middle state and a certain step: namely, that the soul should will not to will lower things and should will to will higher things. In these two are grace with free choice; and these two steps are equal and equal in merit, though distinct and ordered. Love of higher things is from God alone; love of lower things is from man.

If God rescues and draws a human being from the pit of sin, this is wonderful mercy; but if he abandons him, it is supreme equity and justice. For he first points out the pit and teaches the danger, forbidding him to approach. But the human being, despising all these things, falls willingly; therefore God justly abandons him there. When the sinner is scourged by God, God visits him in order that he may be rescued: this is mercy. But if he prospers, he becomes more defiled and entangled: this is justice.

[Col. 1588D] If a certain sin begins to displease a person and he wishes to abandon it, if he does this for God’s sake, it is good and proceeds from the gift of grace. If it happens otherwise, it is not good; for instance, sometimes lust is restrained in order that money may not be spent, or for some similar reason. This is not [Col. 1589A] for God’s sake, nor from the gift of grace. Likewise, if anyone gives what is his, fasts, prays, and so forth: it is good and a gift of grace if done for God’s sake; if otherwise, it is not good. What one does it for, one loves; and according to that love it ought to be called good or evil.

In sensuality a human being is like brute animals, which are not condemned for sensuality, to which they obey and consent. A human being, however, is condemned for it because he possesses reason; and yet he becomes like senseless beasts. So too the evil angel, because of the excellence of his nature, was condemned more severely and irrecoverably; the human being, because he was weaker, was restored.

The human soul, preserving the likeness of the Trinity, consists in a threefold nature. For it has being, life, and governance of the body; it also has reason, desire, [Col. 1589B] and anger. This is the natural Trinity. Upon reason faith is founded, and faith is its light; and as reason naturally precedes—for we discern before we desire—so faith, which is the first light of the soul, precedes the other virtues. Upon desire is hope, which is its light; upon anger, charity, governing and enlightening it. As anger naturally burns, so charity spiritually glows. To these three correspond understanding, will, and memory, and the three previously stated: being, life, and governing the body.

There are three things that overthrow and expel the spiritual Trinity: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. These three are opposed to faith, hope, and charity; and when a person consents to them, he falls away from the virtues, each being opposed to its counterpart. [Col. 1589C] But there are three things which call back and cause return to remembrance of the spiritual Trinity: fear of death, fear of judgment, and hope of eternal things. There are three things that bring it to completion [perhaps “confirm it”]: justice, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

The love of God is the light of hearts and the medicine of wounds; it loosens the bonds of sins. It works in angels and works in human beings; for this love is not idle. It is like a lamp in the middle of a house, by whose rays the individual things in the house are discerned—stones, wood, and so on. So the spiritual person judges all things. This love works in different persons and in many ways. In those still in the world, it causes them to clothe the naked, feed the needy, and visit the sick. Those in the cloister do not perform this work; they have [Col. 1589D] hands fixed and feet bound beneath the yoke of obedience. In them the love of God works fasting, prayer, voluntary submission, concern for virtues, and advancement in them. In angels it works so that they cleave to God without ceasing, delight in him, and love him. The same will operate in the righteous after this life, for charity never fails.

It is like a ladder having two sides, love of God and of neighbor, and intermediate rungs by which one ascends to the summit, until increase and perfection are added, which will be in the future. The Apostle enumerates the rungs when he says, “Charity is kind,” and so forth; and these, I think, are fifteen rungs. Whoever climbs the ladder supports himself with one foot upon earth and places the other on high. By earth are signified earthly supports, which are necessary even for those ascending, for use and sustenance, not for pleasure. The other foot is the advancement [Col. 1590A] of virtues, tending toward the summit.

Charity is also a city set in a square: for it loves God, loves itself, loves a friend, and loves an enemy. It likewise has joined and adhering to it the four principal virtues, which form the square of the city: humility, prudence, fortitude, and temperance. Humility is the fruitful mother and nurse of virtues. It is twofold. The first kind is that a person should abase himself, despise what is from himself, and be subject to others. This is the beginning and mother of virtues. Even after one has advanced and possesses an abundance of virtues, humility is necessary, lest one be proud of what one has, but should humble oneself lest one fall. This is shown in the Song of Degrees.

Fortitude likewise is twofold. By it we resist vices in the present; in the future we shall cleave strongly to God. According to the latter effect it will endure; according to the former it will cease. The same may be said of the other two.

[Col. 1590B] The clerics’ crown, which is round, signifies perfection. In a circle there is neither beginning nor end, because the eternal things which are their inheritance lack beginning and end. They have no portion on earth, as Levi did not; rather, they receive tithes from the brethren, which again look toward perfection. But when they seek to have a portion on earth, they act contrary to their profession and lose their inheritance; they persist neither in the lot of the brethren nor in the lot of Levi, though they ought to stand between God and human beings.

Clerics were chosen to preach and to teach [Col. 1590C] those subject to them, whereas monks were chosen to pray, because clerics could not continually devote themselves to prayer because of the distractions of office and affairs. Yet in a case of necessity, at the bishop’s command, monks often undertake the office of preaching and teaching.

The virtues are called weapons of light: weapons because they cut down their opposites; of light because, when darkness is driven away, they bring light to the mind. Continence precedes lust, humility pride, and so in the other cases. With the nails of virtues the nails of vices are driven out; with the nails of justice the righteous person is fastened to the cross of penitence. The nails of justice are the recollections of sins and each act of contrition of the heart. The first and greatest nail, which prepares the way for the others, is fear of the Lord. When this precedes and prepares the way, the others can be driven in, and never otherwise.

[Col. 1590D] We shall render an account of three things: of being human beings, namely rational beings, lest we have received our soul in vain; of being Christians, lest we have taken up the Lord’s name in vain; and of being called to some part of the lot of the saints, whereby we are called clerics or monks, namely lest we receive God’s grace in vain.

Those who read and understand the divine page but do not live according to it know how to build the house of God and to teach others about it, but do not themselves wish to enter. While through study and great avidity they store that knowledge in memory, they gather manna, as it were; but it putrefies, because they have a weak and feeble stomach, and the nourishment of that food is not distributed through the members [Col. 1591A] of the soul, nor can it be digested. The manna putrefied as though because of a certain unbelief in those who stored more than was necessary. Likewise these people gather more than they need, who are unwilling to live and be formed spiritually; they do not distribute it into life and conduct, but gather it for glory and profit. Though it putrefies, they do not feel the rot and the worms’ stings, because they are occupied with vain and useless things, the flowers of the world that hold their minds captive. But when these have passed, they will feel the punctures and stings of the worms proceeding from the aforesaid corruption.

Drunkenness, wholly enfeebling, first destroys memory, disperses perception, neglects the mind, confuses understanding, arouses lust, entangles the tongue, impedes speech, corrupts the blood, dulls sight, disturbs the veins, weakens the sinews, stops the ears, disorders the inward parts, overturns perception, moistens the brain, debilitates the limbs, breaks sleep, and hinders the monthly courses. [Col. 1591B] Drunkenness is the mother of shameful deeds, the material of faults, the root of crimes, the origin of vices, a whirlwind of captivity, the overthrow of perception, a storm of the tongue, a tempest of the body, the shipwreck of chastity, a disgraceful illness, easily persuaded toward evil, deformity of conduct, dishonor of life, the infamy of respectability, and corruption of the soul. Wine is not rejected in its use, but is condemned in its excess.

Sobriety is wholly beautiful and wholly useful. First, [Col. 1591C] it preserves memory; sharpens perception; makes the mind pure; directs the countenance; preserves modesty intact; mitigates vice; restores the face; refines the ears; relieves the brain; frees the tongue; unfolds speech; strengthens the blood; heals the veins; tightens the sinews; despises lust; enjoys sleep; renews the body; prolongs old age. Without these, every person becomes contemptible.

A stadium contains one hundred and twenty-five paces; eight stadia make one mile; one and a half miles make one league; three miles make two leagues.

AUGUSTINE [Note: [Col. 1591C] *Sermon 3 on the Times*, near the end.]:

> “The prophet Isaiah more plainly designates holy Mary when he says: ‘A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root’ (Isa. 2:1). That this rod produced nuts was an image of the Lord’s body. For the nut has in its body a threefold union of substance: husk, shell, and kernel. In the husk the flesh is compared; in the shell, the bones; in the kernel, the inner soul. In the husk of the nut is signified the Savior’s flesh, which had in itself the harshness or bitterness of the Passion. In the inner kernel is declared the sweetness of divinity, which provides nourishment and supplies the service of light. He who inserted the wood of the cross into the shell did not separate [Col. 1592B] what was outside from what was inside, but united by the interposition of the wood the earthly and heavenly things of the Mediator, as the Apostle says: ‘For through the blood of his cross he made peace with things in heaven and things on earth’ (Col. 1:20).”

“For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:20). There is a burden that carries the one carrying it and makes him light; that is, the Gospel is a light burden, and Christ’s yoke is sweet to those converted to Christ. One who previously could not bear the commandments of the Law subsequently finds light the commandments of the Gospel through cooperating grace. One who at first could not fulfil “You shall not kill” subsequently finds it light to lay down his life for his brothers; and likewise in the rest.

Thus, when a heavy burden is laid upon a beast of burden and it draws back as though it were uncarryable, a moving four-horse chariot is brought up—that is, [Col. 1592C] the Gospel coursing through the whole world—and the burden which at first it shunned as though heavy, it afterwards draws double without effort. So a little bird, featherless and without wings, cannot carry itself; when burdened with feathers and wings, it flies away without effort. So also hard bread, which cannot pass by itself, becomes able to be swallowed in the throat by the addition of milk or another liquid.

## In the Year of the Lord 1118: Leo of Marsi, Cardinal Bishop of Ostia

[Col. 1591]

## Leo’s Chronicle of Monte Cassino and Minor Works

*(See below, under the year 1138, in Patrology, vol. CLXXIII, in Peter the Deacon, continuator of the Chronicle of Monte Cassino.)*

## In the Year of the Lord 1118: Richard, Cardinal Archbishop of Narbonne

[Col. 1593]

## Historical Notice

*(Gallia Christiana, new edition, vol. VI, col. 44.)*

[Col. 1593A] Richard, born of his father, a namesake viscount of Amilian in Rouergue and Gévaudan, who died before January 1051, and of his mother Rixende, daughter of Berengar I, viscount of Narbonne, had as brothers Berengar, Hugh, Raymond, Roger, and Bernard. He first professed as a monk in the monastery of St. Victor at Marseilles. Then, while still very young, he was made cardinal by Pope Alexander II. Later, in 1070, after the death of his brother Bernard, he was appointed in his absence by election of the monks as abbot of that same monastery, with the approval of Pope Gregory VII, to whom he was especially dear because of his outstanding qualities. On this matter see letter 21 of this pontiff, book V, and letters 16 and 17, book VII, vol. X of the Councils.

Already sent earlier by the same pope as legate to Spain, in the year [Col. 1593B] 1076 he assembled a council of bishops at Burgos. There, complying with the wish of Constance, wife of Alfonso, king of Castile, he abolished the ancient custom of the Goths in conducting divine matters and established sacred ceremonies in the Roman manner of prayer, according to Juan Mariana, *History*, book IX, ch. 11. When another legate had been substituted in Richard’s place, he himself was entrusted in 1080 with the reform of the abbeys of Montmajour and Lagrasse.

Later he offended Pope Victor III, Gregory’s successor, because he supported the party either of Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, hostile to that pope through envy and ambition, or even of Guibert of Ravenna, who called himself Pope Clement III, by following the schism, as Ciaconius writes. For this reason he was punished by Pope Victor with excommunication in the synod [Col. 1593C] of Benevento. But when this pope died within a few months, he returned to the favor of the Holy See, and thereafter adhered steadfastly to the legitimate Roman pontiffs. We read, however, that Urban II, at the request of Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, took the legation from him; perhaps it was nevertheless restored to him. For, as appears in vol. II of the new *History of Occitania*, p. 344, he was legate in Spain when, after Bertrand’s deposition, Richard was chosen as archbishop by the common counsel and petition of all the clergy and people [Col. 1594A] on 5 November 1106. Pope Paschal confirmed this election shortly before he came into France at the end of that year [Note: [Col. 1594C] Vol. X of the Councils, col. 669.]. In the following year, by a bull issued at Brioude in the district of Vivarais, on 13 July 1107, the eighth year of his pontificate, the pope confirmed for Richard’s benefit the privileges of the Church of Narbonne.

Perhaps someone may say that Richard mounted the see of Narbonne earlier, since he subscribed the acts of the dedication of the church of Blessed Mary in the town of Bertrand, in the territory of Petralata [Note: [Col. 1594C] Appendix to Marca’s *History of Spain*, col. 1223.], performed on the third day before the Ides of November in 1100 by Bernard, bishop of Girona, in whose diocese it was located, and by other bishops. But Richard’s subscription was made long after the dedication, as a sign of confirmation, [Col. 1594B] as we have observed more than once commonly occurred. The same must be said of a charter granting to the monastery of Blessed Mary of Quadraginta a donation by William Bernard of St. Nazaire, on the Ides of April in 1098. In the cartulary of Cruzy we read that Richard, archbishop of Narbonne and legate of the Apostolic See, subscribed it with Arnald of Lévédo, bishop of Béziers.

At the very beginning of his rule Richard suffered a most serious opposition from Aimeric, viscount of Narbonne, and Matilda, his mother, who, when Richard’s predecessor had been removed, had seized the property of the Church of Narbonne. Therefore he launched excommunication against them, as may properly be inferred from the complaint [Col. 1594C] which he brought in 1107 before Pope Paschal II against Peter, abbot of St. Pons, and Raymond, abbot of Alet, who kept company with the excommunicated [Note: [Col. 1594C] Vol. X of the Councils, col. 670.]. Nevertheless, some time later a settlement was reached between Aimeric and the archbishop, to whom the viscount rendered homage.

In a hearing held on the last day of March 1110, the brothers Bernard and Remigius of Canet relinquished, in accordance with the judgment of Amelius, bishop of Toulouse, and Raymond, bishop of Carcassonne, the village of Canet, which they had hitherto unjustly possessed. About this time Richard made an agreement with [Col. 1595A] Olivier of Termes concerning the castle of La Redorte, unlawfully alienated from his church; and he settled certain rights with Bernard, viscount of Béziers, receiving from him an oath of fidelity. See these two undated charters in our appendix.

A bitter dispute, now breaking into war, between Bernard Aton, viscount of Béziers, and Raymond Berengar, count of Barcelona, was amicably checked by Richard, kinsman of both, and several lords on either side, who brought them to a mutual agreement. On this matter we read two documents: one issued in July 1112—or on 8 July, as appears in book II, ch. 89, of the Sammarthani’s *Counts of Barcelona*—and, equivalently, on the sixth day before the Ides of July [Note: [Col. 1595D] Vol. I of Martène’s *Anecdota*, col. 334.], in the royal charter treasury [Col. 1595B] at Carcassonne; the other, if indeed it is different, dated the fifth day before the Ides of June in the aforesaid royal charter treasury, and the sixth day before the Ides of June in the proofs to vol. II of the new *History of Occitania*, p. 382, and in the cartulary of the castle of Foix from the Colbert Library, and in Catel, *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, p. 1115.

In the same year, on Friday, 25 October, Archbishop Richard and Viscount Aimeric, moved by compassion for the sad lot of shipwrecked Christians, decreed with the counsel and assent of the barons that no one henceforth should claim anything for himself from their goods, but that everything should be restored to them—or to their heirs, should the shipwrecked persons have died. Finally, on 26 November of that year, in the presence of clergy and laity, they established peace between themselves [Note: [Col. 1595D] Proofs, vol. II, *History of Occitania*, cols. 384 and 504.]. This did not last long, because Aimeric refused [Col. 1595C] recognition of the goods which he held from the Church of Narbonne.

In 1113 Bernard, surnamed Gerald, with his wife Guillelma, offers to Lord God and the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor, through the hands of Lord Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, his son Gerald to be made a regular canon, together with all, he says, “our tithes and ecclesiastical possessions,” to be held in the canonry by perpetual right. This charter was made on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, during the reign of King Louis [Note: [Col. 1595D] Vol. III of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 472.].

Richard was present in 1115, on the day before the Nones of October, at the dedication of the church of St. Mary of Cassan in the diocese of Béziers, together with Aton, archbishop of Arles, and the bishops Arnald of Béziers, Walter of Maguelonne, Bernard [Col. 1595D] of Agde, Arnald of Carcassonne, John of Nîmes, and Raymond of Barbastro. In the same year he gave to the canons of Narbonne the churches of St. Mary of Peyrouse, St. Michael of Dulancho, and St. Stephen, according to the chapter cartulary, where he is also mentioned in 1113, 1114, and 1117. In that year he granted to the monastery of Psalmodi the church of St. Saturninus of Anicianum, of Nîmes.

He seems in the same year to have held a council at Narbonne, at which the arbiters Ato of Arles, Arnald of Béziers, and Arnald of Carcassonne, bishops, settled the complaint between Archbishop Richard [Col. 1596A] and Hugh, abbot of St. Paul. About the same time the controversy between Richard and Viscount Aimeric flared up again. Aimeric had rendered homage to Richard for what he possessed from the Church of Narbonne; but because he disputed certain matters with Richard and would not submit them to the judgment of arbitrators, Richard excommunicated him. For this reason the archbishop was captured by the viscount and committed to prison, and was compelled to yield to the viscount and be reconciled with him. This reconciliation was indeed very short-lived, as may be inferred from Richard’s complaint, in which he lamented to posterity the new injuries inflicted upon him by the viscount.

In the following year he met Gelasius, Paschal’s successor, at Alès with other bishops. In his presence, in that same year, the eleventh indiction and first year of the pontificate, he subscribed a charter of Guy, bishop of Lescar, granting the church of St. Faith of Morlaàs to Pons, abbot of Cluny. He was present in 1119, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, at the Council of Toulouse [Note: [Col. 1596D] Vol. X of the Councils, col. 860.], presided over by Pope Callixtus II. He subscribed both the decree in favor of Raymond, abbot of Alet, against Berengar of Lagrasse concerning the abbey of St. Polycarp, and another in favor of the monks of Aniane against the monks of Caunes.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, Raymond Berengar yielded to him the church of Ouvillan, which he unjustly possessed. In January of that year he was witness to a confirmation made by Aton, archbishop of Arles, according to the records of St. Victor at Marseilles. He is also found in 1120 in a charter of Bernard of Mont-Serein, and [Col. 1596C] in one of William Raymond relinquishing certain tithes to him. In that same year, Richard, being at St. Thibéry with Aton of Arles, Arnald of Béziers, Bernard of Agde, Arnald of Carcassonne, and other bishops, settled a dispute arising between Arnald, abbot of St. Thibéry, and the spouses Eleazar of Castries and Engelrada.

Finally, in 1121 he received Bernard Aton’s homage for the castle of Auriac. Having held office for fourteen years, three months, and ten days, he died in that year on the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day before the Kalends of March; for the necrologies vary, perhaps through scribal error. The first necrology of Mount-Olive gives the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March and calls him a monk of that place, perhaps because the place belonged to the congregation of St. Victor at Marseilles. [Col. 1596D] The other necrology of the same place gives the sixteenth day before the Kalends, agreeing with the Chronicle of Narbonne. Finally, the day of his death is marked as the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March in the necrology of the Canonry and in an excerpt from the necrology of St. Justus.

As to the year of his death, 1121 is clearly recorded in the Necrology of Narbonne and in the excerpt from the Chronicle of St. Victor of Marseilles, vol. I of the new Library of Labbe, p. 340. Yet in 1123, according to our Martène, Viscount Bernard Aton and his son Roger relinquished to Richard the homage which they used to exact at Capestang [Note: [Col. 1596D] Proofs, vol. II, *History of Occitania*, col. 369.]. [Col. 1597A] But the recent historian of Occitan affairs more correctly assigns this to about 1107.

Baluze likewise teaches that in the cartulary of the Church of Narbonne there survives an old instrument dated the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September in 1125, in the time of this archbishop and Udalguerius, bishop of Elne. Nevertheless, the same Baluze says, it is established that Udalguerius had not yet then occupied the see of Elne and that Richard was not alive at that time. Another charter is cited from 1127—not 1117, as was mistakenly introduced in the appendix—namely, the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, lunar day XIV, feria VII, epact XVII, in which Elysiar and his wife Engeliarda mention an arbitration agreement made by themselves and Arnald, abbot of St. Thibéry, with Richard, archbishop of Narbonne; Aton, archbishop of Arles; Arnald of Béziers; Bernard, bishop of Agde; and Arnald, bishop of Carcassonne. But this arbitration agreement and hearing had taken place long before, namely in 1120, as we related above. Moreover, Bernard had already ceased to be bishop of Agde, and Arnald of Béziers had transferred to the Church of Narbonne, as must now be said.

[Col. 1597]

## Account of the Harassments Which Archbishop Richard Suffered from Aimeric, Viscount of Narbonne

*(Gallia Christiana, new edition, vol. VI, documents, col. 28.)*
[Col. 1597B] Let it be known to all men, present and future, faithful of the Catholic Church, that, when Lord Dalmatius, archbishop of Narbonne, of blessed memory, died, the Church was deprived of its shepherd, and its dignities came into the hands of Aimeric the Prior, who then held the viscountcy of Narbonne, and of his wife Mahald; so far as they were able to subject them to themselves—although, according to the evil custom of the land, they did not belong to them but to the count.

After an interval of some time, Bishop B. of Nîmes was transferred to the archbishopric of Narbonne by the Roman pope, the clergy and people, and the bishops of the province. But because the aforesaid Aimeric opposed him, he was never able peacefully to possess either the see or its dignities. When he went to Jerusalem, moreover, the aforesaid archbishop was deposed by judgment of the Roman See. Meanwhile his aforesaid wife and son held the dignities of the Church, and by wrongful possession converted wholly to their own uses and lordship whatever they could.

Not long afterward, when the Church had been stripped of both property and dignities, I, R., cardinal-priest of the Roman Church and abbot of Marseilles, a man devoted to the goods of that Church and ignorant of the frauds and malice of the land, was at last promoted to the government of that Church by the apostolic lord of that time, Paschal II, with the common counsel and petition of all the clergy and people. After this was done, Aimeric, son of the other Aimeric just mentioned, who had succeeded his father in the viscountcy after his death at Jerusalem, came, according to the custom of his predecessors, with certain barons of the land, in the presence of a general synod of the province of Narbonne. He performed homage to me with his own hands, as he ought to have done, and received through my hand the fiefs which he held from the Church. I granted them to him as Guifred, my predecessor, who had governed the Church before Lord Dalmatius, had granted them to his great-grandfather Berengar.

[Col. 1597C] [Col. 1597D] [Col. 1598B] After this, before he made the oath which he ought to have made to me, I asked him, as my faithful friend and man, to tell me what fiefs he held from the Church and what other dignities of the Church had been held by his father and mother—who was present—and by themselves and their bailiffs. For I did not know them at all, but trusted him, who ought to have been faithful to the Church, his lady, to tell me the truth, as one who, by holding and possessing nearly all things for a long time, could know them. Because of their report, with lies intervening, we came into dispute: he said that certain customs of the city between himself and me were otherwise than they in fact were, customs which his predecessors and mine had augmented; while he maintained that certain others, newly added by his mother, belonged wholly to his own right.

Finally, since his party could not refute my charters and testimony, by which the Church obtained half in all the past, present, and future customs, and since his fiefs had been diminished in the churches and in half the tithes which he had relinquished, mutual friends spoke, urging an agreement between him and me: that I should enlarge his fief, and that he should wholly and peaceably leave to the Church all the other matters then in dispute between us, insofar as they belonged to it by right. Unable to resist their counsel, I added to his fief a third part of half the *botaticum* [a levy or due], while retaining all other things concerning which, as stated above, we disputed, each by half as they had been, he relinquishing the Church’s right, as is written in the cartulary.

Thereafter certain malicious men came on his behalf, saying that they wished by no means for a further dispute to arise between us, by which we might be provoked to anger. Pretending that he wished always to be peaceful and faithful to the Church and to me, they added that among the other customs was one which my predecessors had never possessed or claimed, although those predecessors had established it and mine had held it in their own time for a long period without complaint: namely, half the tolls, commonly called *comparas*. They wished this to be determined expressly, lest perhaps afterward we might become angry with one another about it.

[Col. 1599A] I replied to them, as was true, that I knew nothing whatever about it; but that, if he greatly wished it, I would place the matter upon his soul and faith, since he was the Church’s man and mine and ought to bear me fidelity and tell the truth. Yet if at any time I should be able to discover by charters or witnesses that my predecessors had claimed or possessed them, I would undoubtedly claim and wish to possess them. Thus, retaining them for himself by this malice and deceit, he swore to me fidelity for life and limb, and [to preserve] all the dignities of the Church which he possessed or ought to possess, as my predecessors had possessed them.

After these things had been done, I later examined the Church’s charters and found that Guifred, my predecessor, had claimed the aforesaid tolls, held pleas concerning them, and recovered them. When I had discovered this, I approached the aforesaid Aimeric, not once or twice but very often, in person and through friends of mine and his. I admonished him by the fidelity which he had sworn to me and by the homage which he had performed, not to inflict so great an injury upon the Church by taking its dignity from me. If he believed himself to have any right in those tolls, he should come with me before the presence of worthy and impartial men of the land, who desired peace and agreement between him and me, and should do for me what they judged.

[Col. 1599B] [Col. 1599C] The aforesaid Aimeric not only refused to hear and do this, but, angered, extended his hands to other customs and dignities of the Church. Whatever he could convert to his own uses, he began shamelessly to take from me; he committed many evils and threatened worse, declaring that there was no one in the territory of Narbonne who would dare defend either my cause or that of the Church by word or deed. He also alleged that I had given him as a fief those tolls which I was claiming—that is, the *comparas* [perhaps *comparatas*]—although that grant had been made through such deception as you have heard above, and had been retained upon such a condition.

On hearing this, I again began to admonish him through his private friends, the neighboring barons of the land, bishops, abbots, viscounts, knights, and finally through all whom I could. I adjured him by the oath which he had made and by the not inconsiderable benefices of the Church which he held, to cease from such malice, infamy, and faithlessness, and either to leave his dignity peaceably to the Church or to come to judgment. But when I saw that I could make no progress, unable to endure the importunity of the evils inflicted upon me, and having subjected that same Aimeric and all his land to excommunication, I withdrew, compelled by fear of death, to other regions, intending somehow to survive.

Yet I could not withdraw so far that I was not captured, imprisoned, and dishonored in various ways by his friends before he was ever willing to come to a just settlement.

[Col. 1599D] [Col. 1600A] Finally, neither the acknowledgment nor the attestation of my right by all the barons of the land availed me, so that I might reach an end with him concerning the other causes, until, unwilling, grieving, and compelled, I unjustly renounced the aforesaid tolls. The laws say that a renunciation made by one who has been despoiled is void unless he has first been effectively restored to possession; and the Church had been fraudulently and violently despoiled of this dignity, nor had it ever been restored to possession. Thus, though I adjured him by the fidelity he had sworn to me not to have the Church’s dignities granted to himself against my will and taken from the Church, I could not obtain what I ought.

Once this had been done, he promised again that he would be faithful to me and would firmly keep all the agreements which he had made with me. But it wearied him to keep this promise for long. For after only a little time had passed, breaking the agreement which we had made, he took away the toll of Vermiculi, which in the first settlement he had left to me—when, in other matters as written above, he had deceived me. I had thereafter possessed it, together with the judicial rights over those persons which, through the authority of ancient charters and witnesses, I had recovered in the settlement. He had relinquished this to me, except under the condition of only two offences, as is contained in the written agreement of the Church and himself. He seized a man of the Church and compelled him, against my objection, to make redemption for what he had wrongly done in connection with the Church’s dignity and within the Church’s jurisdiction. And because he dared to come at my summons, he made him clear himself by oath, imposing a sextary of barley as compensation, lest a greater affront be inflicted upon him.

[Col. 1600B] [Col. 1600C] Finally, I then claimed from him the tolls which, as you have heard, he had fraudulently and violently taken from me, as well as the gate and half the October revenue from the third part of the salt. These two matters I never in any way renounced, but retained under claim in the settlement, as written above. Thus he dealt with me—he who had sworn fidelity to the Church and to me, performed homage, and by oath promised that he would preserve all the Church’s dignity wholly and faithfully.

I write these things to you who shall come after me into my place for the service of God and the Church, so that you may know how badly, unjustly, and violently the aforesaid Aimeric oppressed the Church and me, his lord; how, through his taking, the Church lost its right; and I pray and beseech you that what has been lost from the Church’s dignity through my negligence or weakness, because I was unable to bear the evils inflicted upon me, may be recovered by your courage and firmness.

[Col. 1600D] The Church has this right against Aimeric and his successors, as you have heard. If anyone should oppose you, you can without doubt establish and defend, for certain and true reasons, the things which are written here [perhaps “the written things here”], as shall be justly adjudged to you. For God knows that we declare these things from truth and the pure intention of our heart; and, so that you may believe in truth, with every ambiguity of falsehood removed, we commend them to you with firm faith.

[Col. 1601A] Concerning all these matters we can name many witnesses for you: Aton, archbishop of Arles; John, bishop of Nîmes; Bernard Rainard and Adhemar, archdeacons of Narbonne; Hugh, abbot of Saint-Paul; Peter de Saltu, sacristan of Girona; Miron of Caputstagno; his brother Gauceran; Berengar Guillelmi; Raymond Guifredi; and many others, clerics as well as laymen, who, seeing and hearing all these things, know them most fully and certainly. Peter wrote, at the dictation of Raymond, who saw and heard these things.

[Col. 1601]

# LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF RICHARD, CARDINAL AND ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE

## I. Letter of Cardinal R. to King S.

[Note: [Col. 1601D] This letter is by Cardinal Richard, who afterward became abbot of Saint-Victor at Marseilles. He was made cardinal by Alexander II and was sent as legate to Spain by Gregory VII and Urban II. It was written to Sancho V, king of Navarre, whom certain persons accuse of cruelty and injustice.]

Cardinal R. to King S.—He confirms the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the people of Pamplona and forbids the king to have any communion with them.

(D. Martene, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 497, from the archives of Saint-Victor.)

[Col. 1601B]

R., cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, to the venerable King S., greetings . . . . . .

From our lord the pope, in the churches of your kingdom, we were faithfully seeking with much labor the honor and glory of that holy and universal Church, setting aside other matters . . . . . . Yet, not deceived by the winding evasions of your men, we recognize from one side that in your actions you seek more the favor of men than the fear of God and the salvation of souls. For we believed that by your counsel you were demanding salvation for the people committed to you. Since this is not so with you, if out of charity toward you we promised to do anything for any particular person, we now unquestionably renounce it; but we shall strive, if we can, to give counsel otherwise.

[Col. 1601C] We again and again confirm, by the same apostolic authority, the sentence of excommunication which we imposed by apostolic authority in the council of bishops and abbots upon the bishopric of Pamplona and the men of that bishop, wherever they may be, even if they are fighting in an expedition against enemies. We command you henceforth to have no communion with the excommunicated people of Pamplona until the feast of Saint John—and this not merely in ecclesiastical office—by the authority of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and our own, until they have an elected bishop in that Church confirmed by apostolic authority.

[Col. 1601D] We impose this interdict in such a manner that, from the feast of Saint John onward, the dead are by no means to be buried; no one is knowingly to have Christian communion with the living; and no divine office is to be performed in the churches, except the baptism of children if danger of death or illness threatens them.

We do this because we see that they have conspired for the destruction of the Church with other princes of your kingdom, whom we do not yet name expressly. They shall experience, to their perpetual infamy and confusion, the sword of Saint Peter and the power of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1602A] [Col. 1602B] Do not put confidence in victory, you who have abandoned justice; for it is written: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.” You might place confidence in Him if you sought the growth of God’s kingdom more than your own glory. For you seek what is yours, not what belongs to Jesus Christ. And because you have made void the commandment of God and the apostolic precept through the seduction and . . . . . . of perishing human souls, may God require their blood from your hand. Therefore, as we depart from the city, we shake off the dust of our feet as a testimony against you.

## II. Agreement between Archbishop Richard and Bernard, Viscount of Béziers, his kinsman

(About 1110) [*Gallia Christiana*, VI, instruments, col. 31.]

[Col. 1602C]

Let it be known to all men that there was discord between Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, and Bernard, viscount of Béziers. The viscount refused to receive his fief through the archbishop unless the latter gave him Caputstagno. The archbishop, however, said that he ought not to give it to him. After many pleas they came to an agreement, and the archbishop granted him his fief without the gift of Caputstagno. The viscount agreed that he would not fail in his service and fidelity because Caputstagno was not given to him; he performed homage and swore fidelity and the requisite oaths.

[Col. 1602D] Since he was a kinsman and an old friend, the archbishop gave him, from his own money, more than the other archbishops had given his grandfather and other predecessors. In the hearing of Amelius of Toulouse and Raymond, bishop of Carcassonne; Adhemar, archdeacon of Narbonne; William Poncii; Poncius Deusde; and Raymond Udalardi, it was agreed between them that this which the archbishop had done out of friendship should not be claimed by custom against his Church and the archbishop’s successors. Rather, the viscount or his successors should always perform homage and all the stipulated obligations to the archbishop for the fief and for such money as Gaufred had given to Peter Raymond, his grandfather.

[Col. 1603A]

## III. Charter of the agreement made between Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, and Olivarius de Termino

In the name of the Lord. This is the record of the agreement made between Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, and Olivarius de Termino. It was made after the death of Guifred, archbishop of Narbonne, when Peter Berengar, bishop of Rodez, had violently invaded the Church of Narbonne and, contrary to God and the rights of the canons, had occupied it simoniacally for many days. Among other acts, he pledged to Berengar, son of Peter de Petrapertusa, and alienated from the Church the castle of Villarrubea with the dignity belonging to it.

[Col. 1603B] On account of this pledge a dispute arose between the aforesaid Berengar and Peter, son of Olivarius de Termino. It did not cease until that same Berengar, giving his daughter in marriage to the aforesaid Peter, gave him as dowry a part of the aforesaid dignity which he had unjustly received from so great a destroyer of the Church. When Dalmatius, archbishop of blessed memory, heard this, he pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon both of them and kept them under it until Berengar, son of Peter, acknowledging his fault, wholly relinquished the part of that dignity which he had retained for himself. Peter, son of Olivarius, persisted in wickedness until his death.

[Col. 1603C] When Dalmatius the bishop and Peter, son of Olivarius, had departed this life, Richard was promoted to the archbishopric of Narbonne. Hearing how great an injury the Church of Narbonne suffered from Olivarius, son of the aforesaid Peter, he admonished him for a long time. When he saw that he could make no progress, he hurled the dart of excommunication against him. Compelled by the excommunication, and with all the worthy men of the land declaring that the dignity had been unjustly taken from the Church of Narbonne, Olivarius at last, after many disputes, came to an acknowledgment. Having received 1,100 Melgueil solidi from the aforesaid archbishop, he relinquished and quitclaimed whatever he, his mother, and his brothers claimed in the Church of Narbonne concerning that dignity on account of this injustice.

[Col. 1603D] The aforesaid archbishop and his successors were henceforth to possess and hold it fully, as Guifred the archbishop had ever possessed and held it most advantageously and freely, etc.

## IV. Donation made by Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, to Bertrand, abbot of Psalmody

This is the charter of donation which Lord Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, made, with the counsel of his clergy, concerning the church of Anitian. A gift to God and to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose venerable memorial is kept in the monastery of Psalmody, and to Bertrand, most reverend abbot of that place, with his monks, who unanimously requested it and pressed their request strongly and persistently.

[Col. 1604A] Therefore, in the name of almighty God, I, Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, with the counsel of the clergy of the see of the Church of Saints Justus and Pastor, to whose jurisdiction it belongs, give and grant the church of Saint Saturninus of Anitian, with its tithes, first fruits, offerings, lands, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated holdings, and all its appurtenances, to the Lord God and Saint Peter, to the monastery of Psalmody, and to the venerable Abbot Bertrand and the monks of that place, present and future. They are to possess it by perpetual right, without anyone’s opposition, saving the right which I and the clergy of the aforesaid see reserve there for ourselves and our successors: namely, a fourth part of the tithes belonging to the archbishop; the synod; ordinations; lodging-rights; and a third part of that portion which our parishioners, when dying, ought to distribute for their souls according to the decrees of the canons.

[Col. 1604B] We also reserve that the chaplain who has the care of souls shall enter and leave the church with our counsel; and that the same chaplain and church shall be subject to us in ordination, obedience, and justice. But all other things, except the aforesaid matters, as stated above, I, the aforementioned archbishop, and the clergy of Saints Justus and Pastor have fully given and granted with the aforesaid church, without any deceit, etc.

This charter of donation was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1117, on Thursday, the eighth day before the Kalends of March [22 February], [Col. 1604C] in the reign of King Louis, with the approval and confirmation of Richard, bishop of Narbonne, and the clergy of that see, and of Abbot Bertrand and the monks of Psalmody.

## V. Charter of Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, and Aimeric, viscount of the same city, concerning the law of shipwreck

[CATEL, *History of Languedoc*, II, 383.]

It is evident to all men how great are the calamities and dangers endured by those who entrust themselves to the waves of the stormy sea. Sometimes they fall into sudden captivity, encounter death, lose their property, and miserably pass a life full of pains and hardships while ranging over the broad sea. Yet they cannot rest, because they know no other occupation by which to live. After many such perils, when they reach the shore, they rejoice that they have somehow escaped. Often, driven by the violence of the winds, their ships broken apart, they flee the storms with whatever they are able to rescue.

[Col. 1604D] Concerning such shipwrecked persons, a most wicked custom has become established in our regions: whenever such misfortune befalls them, the authorities and inhabitants of the land plunder their goods; if they rescue anything, they take it; and they apply to their own advantage the property which these persons acquired with so many hardships, surpassing by their injustice the cruelty of the elements.

Seeing this evil, Richard, archbishop of Narbonne, Aimeric, viscount of the same city, and the other barons of the land, inspired by the counsel and grace of almighty God and considering how great an evil and greed it was, have given, relinquished, and quitclaimed, without fraud, to the most merciful God and to all his faithful, that neither they nor their agents, nor anyone with their consent, shall ever hereafter seize anything from such shipwrecks in any manner.

[Col. 1605A] Rather, wrecked ships and money, whatever its kind, shall be restored to the control of those to whom they are known to belong by right. And if those who suffered the shipwreck have perished in it, everything found shall be restored without anyone’s opposition to their heirs and relatives when they come, from wherever they may be; and they shall have the power to do with it whatever they wish.

As written above, the aforesaid men approved and promised this to the Lord God. Above all, the aforesaid Archbishop Richard confirmed it under excommunication, binding by the bond of anathema, through the authority of almighty God, anyone who, led by malignant greed, should wish to violate this decree, of whatever rank or order he might be, until he comes to repentance through worthy satisfaction.

[Col. 1605B] If, however—which may it not happen—the archbishop or viscount, personally or through his agents, should presume to destroy this our ordinance, I, Richard aforesaid, excommunicate and anathematize him. But one who has received his share—that is, a half—from the side of the transgressor of the contrary party is not to be held under excommunication until the violator makes amends; if he retains it after amends have been made, he shall be subject to excommunication.

[Col. 1606A] But if the shipwreck belongs to Saracens, it shall be divided equally between the archbishop and the viscount, whatever it may be. Thus we aforesaid approve and confirm this, and command our successors to observe it forever for the remission of sins. If merchants, intending theft, evade the tolls and suffer shipwreck, they shall make good the tolls fraudulently avoided and recover all the rest.

[Col. 1606B] This relinquishment was made on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October], Friday, the first lunar day, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1112, in the reign of King Louis, with Aton and William, monks; William Raymond of Redorta; Berengar Stephen; Peter Bernard of Narbonne; and many others as witnesses.

Richard, archbishop, confirms.

Aimeric, viscount, confirms.
